P0002.crumb: The Sponsored Products default bid prices…
P0002.title: The Sponsored Products default bid prices every search the same
P0002.alt: Blue ceramic vase, amber bottle, linen pouch, black mug, wrapped soap and herb jar on a wooden shelf with blank brass labels
P0002.ttag: The Sponsored Products default bid prices every search the same | Kwontified
P0002.desc: One default bid prices every search in an ad group the same, though searches differ in what a click is worth. Set bids per keyword from conversion value.
P0002.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 2, 2018.
P0002.body:
The default bid in a Sponsored Products ad group looks like the cautious choice: one number, set once, applied everywhere. It is usually the most expensive setting in the account. It charges every search the same price even though searches differ widely in what a click is worth. The result is overpaying for searches that rarely sell and losing the ones that do. Brands should set bids keyword by keyword, from what each term’s clicks are worth.

The Sponsored Products default bid sets one price for searches of unequal value

Sponsored Products charge only when a shopper clicks, and the click lands on the product’s own detail page, Practical Ecommerce explained in October 2016. An ad runs only on listings that hold the Buy Box, so the traffic reaches the advertiser’s own offer.

The keywords that trigger those clicks are not equal. Not all search queries are worth the same to a seller, even when the same keyword triggers them, the same publication noted in November 2016. A phrase-match keyword such as “merino sweater” also catches shoppers who typed a competitor’s brand, and those shoppers buy less often.

Automatic campaigns widen the spread. With automatic targeting, the campaign bids on the searches Amazon judges relevant to the product, according to Amazon’s Seller Central notes as quoted in the November article. Those searches come in at one price, set by the ad group.

Why one bid overpays where clicks are worth least

Here is the counterintuitive part. A bid that is too high everywhere would at least be honest about its cost. A single bid that is right on average is worse, because averages hide where the money actually goes.

The mechanism is simple. A click is worth what it is likely to earn. That is the product’s price, times the share of the price a brand can spend on advertising, times the chance the click becomes a sale. Searches differ most in that last number, so they differ in value too.

Take a hypothetical $40 product with a target advertising cost of sale of 25%, so the brand can spend $10 to win one sale. On an exact search for the product, 15% of clicks convert, so a click is worth $1.50. On a loose search that mentions a rival brand, 3% convert, so a click is worth $0.30.

Now set one default bid of $0.75 for both. On the loose search, the brand bids two and a half times what a click is worth, and it wins those clicks easily, because few competitors want them at that price. On the exact search, it bids half of what a click is worth, and it loses the top placements to rivals who bid closer to $1.50.

So spend flows toward the searches that are cheapest to win and least likely to sell. The account reports a respectable average, while the strong searches go underfunded and the weak ones absorb the budget. Each $0.75 click on the loose search returns $0.30 of value, and the brand pays more to reach fewer buyers than a per-keyword bid would.

The same arithmetic explains why raising the default bid rarely fixes performance. A higher bid wins more of the strong searches and also buys more of the weak ones, so the waste grows with the gains.

There is a fair caution. A brand with little search data cannot yet price each keyword, and an automatic campaign with a modest default bid is a reasonable way to collect that data. The cost comes from leaving it there. Advertising is also how a brand sees Amazon’s search data at all, as the October article noted, so the first weeks of a campaign buy information as much as sales.

How to bid each keyword on Sponsored Products

Run automatic campaigns to learn which searches sell, not to carry the account. Download the search term report, find the searches that convert, and move them into manual campaigns where each keyword carries its own bid.

Price each keyword from its own conversion rate. Multiply the product’s price by the advertising share of price, then by the keyword’s conversion rate, and set the bid at or below that figure.

Separate the weak searches instead of paying full price for them. The November article’s fix was to pull underperforming queries, such as competitor-brand searches, into their own ad group with a lower bid, and to block them in the original group with negative keywords.

Review bids on a schedule. Conversion rates shift with price changes, reviews and the season, so a bid that was right in January can be wrong by spring.

Watch the daily budget alongside the bids. When an ad group’s budget runs out by early afternoon, its strongest keywords stop showing for the rest of the day, so the weak searches that spent the money crowd out the strong ones twice. Cut spend on weak searches before raising the budget.

Treat the default bid as a placeholder. It belongs on keywords too new to have data, and it should be replaced once each keyword has enough clicks to price.

What to do

  1. Download the search term report for every automatic campaign and list the searches that produced sales.
  2. Calculate a value per click for each converting search and move it into a manual campaign with that bid.
  3. Move underperforming searches into a separate ad group with a lower bid, add them as negatives in the original group, and review all keyword bids monthly.

We manage Sponsored Products bidding keyword by keyword for brands on Amazon. If one default bid is still running most of your spend, talk to our team.

P0003.title: Amazon Brand Registry decides who controls a brand’s listings
P0003.alt: A brass key ring with a lion-engraved fob on a wooden table, with a glass cabinet of ceramics and leather goods behind.
P0003.ttag: Amazon Brand Registry decides who controls a brand’s listings | Kwontified
P0003.desc: On Amazon, control of a product page follows registration, not ownership. Why brands lose listings to resellers, and how the new Brand Registry helps.
P0003.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 4, 2018.
P0003.body:
A brand manager searches Amazon for the company’s best-selling product and finds a page she did not write: an old photo, a misspelled title, a description promising a feature the product dropped long ago. Nobody at the company changed it. That is the point. On Amazon, a product page belongs to the catalog, not to the brand, and the right to edit it follows Brand Registry enrollment, not ownership. The new Brand Registry gives that control back, but only to brands that hold a registered trademark and enroll.

Amazon Brand Registry, not ownership, decides who edits a listing

The surprise for most brands is that owning the product does not mean owning the page. On Amazon, each product has one detail page, and every seller of that product sells from it.

Control of the content on that page is assigned through Brand Registry. A seller who neither owns the brand nor holds its registration cannot change a product’s bullet points, description or images; only the registered brand owner can, one longtime seller wrote in Practical Ecommerce in February 2017. The rule cuts both ways. A brand that never registered has no more say over its own page than any reseller does.

Here is how it usually takes hold. A distributor lists the product to clear some inventory and writes the page in an afternoon, with the photo it has on hand. Shoppers buy, reviews accumulate, and the page climbs in search because it sells. Other resellers join the same page rather than start their own, since the reviews and the ranking already live there. By the time the brand’s team looks, the page has years of history attached to someone else’s words, and rewriting it means asking Amazon for authority the brand never claimed.

That is how the stale photo and the wrong description arrive. A distributor, a liquidator or an early reseller often created the page years before the brand thought about Amazon. Their version stays until someone with the authority to change it does so.

Why the old system left brands exposed

The structure underneath is a shared page with no clear owner, and for years Amazon’s rules made the owner easy to claim.

Before 2017, a seller could register a brand on Amazon with little proof. It had only to show that it held the brand’s domain name and that the brand’s name appeared on the packaging and the product, Practical Ecommerce reported in June 2017. That bar did little to separate a brand from anyone with its boxes in hand.

The same article describes what followed. Sellers could source counterfeit or look-alike goods and sell them from a brand’s own listing, and shoppers sometimes received the copies instead of the originals, discovering it only when they tried a warranty claim. The damage landed on the brand’s name, through reviews written about products it never made.

Brands responded the way institutions often do: they treated Amazon as a channel someone else managed. Wholesale accounts sold there, distributors sold there, and the brand’s own team looked after its website and its retailers. The page drifted because no one inside the company was responsible for it.

There is a structural reason the problem stayed hidden. A brand’s dashboards measure its own sales. A page that a reseller wrote, selling the brand’s genuine product, reports nothing to the brand at all. The loss shows up only as conversion that never happens and a reputation shaped by someone else’s photos.

What the new Amazon Brand Registry changes

Amazon rebuilt the program in 2017, and the new rules move control back toward the brand, for brands willing to meet them.

The new Brand Registry is open only to sellers that hold a registered trademark for their brand, according to the June 2017 article. Registering a trademark with the United States Patent and Trademark Office typically takes six to ten months, the same article notes, so a brand that starts now will not be enrolled for most of 2018.

Enrollment also changes how infringement is handled. Amazon said counterfeit claims from enrolled brands would be dealt with within four hours, without the test purchase brands once needed before filing, and it added a search tool that finds suspected violations by image, text and keyword.

There is a fair caution. Registration settles who may edit a page; it does not remove genuine resellers. A distributor selling authentic stock can still win the sale from the same page, and the fight over who wins it is decided by price, seller ratings and inventory, not by the brand’s registration.

The deeper change is organizational. Once a brand enrolls, the page has an owner again, and the brand must decide who inside the company holds that job. Enrollment without an owner just moves the neglect from Amazon’s rules to the brand’s own org chart. The owner’s job is ordinary but constant: check the top pages each week, approve every change to titles and images, and answer for the page the way the store team answers for a shelf.

What to do

  1. Search Amazon for your top 20 products today and record who created each page and what it says.
  2. Confirm the status of your US trademark registration, and file now for any brand name sold on Amazon without one.
  3. Name one person who owns your Amazon listings, and enroll in the new Brand Registry as soon as the trademark allows.

We help brands take back their Amazon listings, from Brand Registry enrollment to rewriting the pages resellers left behind. If your product pages say things your team never wrote, talk to our team.

P0005.crumb: Headline Search Ads earn their cost on…
P0005.title: Headline Search Ads earn their cost on searches without a brand
P0005.alt: A quiet European street of cream-colored buildings with shopfronts under pale awnings and a cobbled sidewalk.
P0005.ttag: Headline Search Ads earn their cost on searches without a brand | Kwontified
P0005.desc: The banner atop Amazon search pays for itself where shoppers have not chosen a brand. On a brand’s own name, it often buys clicks the brand already had.
P0005.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 9, 2018.
P0005.body:
The banner across the top of an Amazon search page is the most visible ad a brand can buy, and the first instinct is to run it on the brand’s own name. Headline Search Ads earn their cost elsewhere: on category searches, where the shopper has not chosen a brand and the banner can change the choice.

On searches for the brand’s own name, they often pay for clicks the brand’s products would have won for free, because the shopper arrived already decided. Brands should spend on category searches first and defend their own name only where a rival is bidding on it.

How Headline Search Ads work, and who can now buy them

Headline Search Ads sit at the top of the search results page and combine a headline the advertiser writes, a brand logo and three product images, eSellerHub explained in August 2017. They target keywords and charge only when a shopper clicks, like Sponsored Products.

The buyer list grew last summer. Amazon opened the format to third-party sellers in Seller Central in August, provided they were enrolled in its Brand Registry, according to the same report. Until then, the ads ran through Amazon Marketing Services for vendors.

That change matters for the auction. The same report expected bids to rise as sellers competed with vendors for the same keywords. More buyers for the same space at the top of the page means the price of being wrong about where to run it goes up.

Why the banner pays where shoppers have not chosen a brand

Here is the counterintuitive part. The searches that look safest for a banner, the brand’s own name, are the ones where it adds the least. An ad is worth the sales it causes, not the sales that follow it.

The mechanism is incrementality. A banner changes behavior only when the shopper’s choice is still open. On a search for “running socks,” no brand has been chosen, and the banner can put a brand in front of a shopper who would otherwise have bought someone else’s. On a search for the brand’s own name, the shopper has already chosen, and the brand’s products usually fill the first results anyway.

Take a hypothetical brand that sells socks. On searches for its own name, its products already sit at the top of the results and win most of the sales. It runs a banner at $1.00 a click and records 100 clicks and 20 sales a day. If 15 of those 20 shoppers would have bought from the organic results below, the banner caused 5 sales. Its true cost per added sale is $20, not the $5 the report implies.

Now run the same banner on “running socks.” The brand’s products appear on page two, and few shoppers scroll that far. The banner records 100 clicks and 12 sales, and nearly all of them are sales the brand would not have had. The cost per added sale is close to $8.33.

Most campaigns mix both kinds of search under one budget, so the report cannot separate them. Splitting branded and category keywords into separate campaigns is the first step, because a blended number hides exactly the difference that decides where the money should go.

The report shows the opposite ranking. The branded campaign posts the better advertising cost of sale because it collects credit for sales that were coming anyway. Budget follows the report, so it flows to the searches where the banner matters least.

There is a fair caution. A brand’s own name is not always safe. Now that more sellers can buy the banner, a rival can buy the top of the page on your name, and the shopper who searched for you sees someone else first. Defending the name is worth paying for when a competitor is actually there, and a quick look at the results page shows whether one is.

There is a second caution. Category searches are expensive because everyone wants them, and a brand whose product pages convert poorly will pay to send shoppers to a page that loses the sale. The banner rewards brands whose pages already sell.

When to run Headline Search Ads, and on what

Start with category searches where the brand ranks below the first few results. That is where the banner can change the choice, and where organic results cannot carry the sale.

Measure added sales, not reported sales. Before running a banner on your own name, note how many sales the brand’s organic results produce on that search without it, and judge the banner by what it adds.

Defend your name where rivals appear. Search your brand name weekly; if a competitor’s banner shows up, run yours there, and stop when they leave.

Send clicks where they convert. A banner that sends shoppers to a page of the brand’s best sellers, or to the three products in the ad, should point at the pages with the best reviews and images.

Keep the headline specific. A promise about the product earns the click from a shopper still choosing; a slogan about the brand rarely does.

What to do

  1. List your top 20 category searches and note where your products rank without ads.
  2. Run Headline Search Ads first on the category searches where you rank below the top results.
  3. Run a banner on your own brand name only where a competitor’s ad appears, and review that choice each month.

We plan Headline Search Ads around the searches where a banner changes the sale. If your banner budget mostly runs on your own name, talk to our team.

P0007.crumb: Vendor Central or Seller Central is an…
P0007.title: Vendor Central or Seller Central is an org chart decision
P0007.alt: Two twine-tied wrapped parcels on a wooden table, linked by strings to a peg board of blank cards on a sage wall.
P0007.ttag: Vendor Central or Seller Central is an org chart decision | Kwontified
P0007.desc: Choosing Vendor Central or Seller Central decides which team runs Amazon inside a brand. Most brands choose the channel and forget to staff it.
P0007.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 11, 2018.
P0007.body:
Brands usually frame the choice between Vendor Central and Seller Central as a question of margin and control. It is also a question of who will run Amazon inside the company, and that part rarely gets decided on purpose. Selling to Amazon is a wholesale account that belongs to the sales team. Selling on Amazon is a retail business that needs operators. Brands should decide who will do the work before they decide the channel.

Vendor Central or Seller Central: two different jobs

The two options describe different relationships, and each one assigns the work to a different part of the company.

In Vendor Central, Amazon is a customer. It buys the brand’s goods at a wholesale price, sets the selling price and sells them under its own name. The brand’s job looks like any other wholesale account: negotiate terms, fill purchase orders, manage the relationship. That work sits naturally with a sales or key-account team.

In Seller Central, the brand is the retailer. It sets the price, holds the inventory, answers the customer and pays Amazon a fee for each sale. That work looks like running a store, and it needs people who think like merchants: someone watching prices daily, someone forecasting stock, someone reading reviews.

The choice is often described as a trade-off between volume and control. Follow the value, though, and it is a trade-off between two kinds of labor.

Where the value goes in each model

Each model moves value and effort to a different place, and that movement is what the org chart has to absorb.

In the wholesale model, the value is negotiated once a year, and it tends to drift toward Amazon after the first. One brand described this in a Web Retailer comment thread in February 2017: its first-year terms were good, and then Amazon asked for new fees and wanted to move payment from 60 to 90 days, with no new incentives offered. The person who holds that line is a negotiator, and the brand needs one assigned to Amazon all year, not only at renewal.

James Thomson of Buy Box Experts replied in the same thread. He had seen many brands succeed with Vendor Central in the short term, then lose control or margin as their Amazon sales grew, and in his experience those problems were easier to manage through Seller Central. That is a statement about structure as much as channels. A wholesale relationship works while the account is small enough for a sales team to handle alongside everything else.

In the retail model, the value is earned daily, through price, stock and the product page. A brand selling on Seller Central keeps the retail margin, but only if someone runs the store. The fight for the sale on a shared product page depends on price, seller ratings and inventory, as one longtime seller described in Practical Ecommerce in February 2017. None of those runs itself.

Staff the channel before you choose it

The common failure is a brand that chooses a channel and leaves Amazon with whichever team was closest.

A brand selling through Vendor Central often hands Amazon to the sales team, which treats it like a large retail account. The product pages, the reviews and the search results go unwatched, because no one in sales was hired to read them. Prices fall when Amazon matches a cheaper seller elsewhere, and the first sign is a call from an angry retailer.

A brand selling through Seller Central often hands Amazon to the ecommerce marketer who already runs the website. That person knows advertising and content but not replenishment, and the products run out of stock in the busiest week of the year.

Neither choice removes the other kinds of work. Thomson made a related point in April 2017: Amazon is an open marketplace, so the 1P or 3P choice does not stop other sellers from listing the brand’s products. Whichever channel a brand picks, someone still has to watch the page.

Consider a hypothetical apparel brand that moves from Vendor Central to Seller Central to win back control of its prices. The decision is made in a pricing meeting, and the account stays with the sales director who ran the wholesale relationship. Within a season the brand controls its prices but has no one forecasting stock, answering customers or running ads. The channel changed; the job description did not, and nobody noticed until the busiest weeks. The margin it moved for leaks out through stockouts and slow replies.

The fix is to decide in a different order. Name the owner first. Decide which person will be accountable for Amazon results, and what else that person is responsible for.

List the work each model requires. For Vendor Central: terms, purchase orders, the product page and pricing outside Amazon. For Seller Central: pricing, inventory, customer service, advertising and the product page.

Match the team to the list, or hire for the gap. A brand that cannot staff a retail operation should not choose one for its margin, and a brand that chooses wholesale still needs someone reading the page.

What to do

  1. Write down who owns Amazon results inside your company today, by name.
  2. List the work your current Amazon model requires, and mark each task with the person who does it.
  3. Before changing between Vendor Central and Seller Central, staff the tasks the new model adds.

We help brands decide between Vendor Central and Seller Central and build the team to run either. If Amazon sits with whichever team was nearest, talk to our team.

P0009.crumb: Automatic campaigns are research, not an…
P0009.title: Automatic campaigns are research, not an Amazon ad strategy
P0009.alt: Small sample vials on a metal tray and an open notebook with a magnifying glass on a sunny windowsill overlooking a garden.
P0009.ttag: Automatic campaigns are research, not an Amazon ad strategy | Kwontified
P0009.desc: Amazon automatic campaigns find searches a brand never thought of. Left in charge of the budget, they bid one price on all of them. Harvest, then negate.
P0009.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 16, 2018.
P0009.body:
Amazon automatic campaigns are the easiest Sponsored Products campaigns to launch, and for many brands they quietly become the whole account. That is the mistake. An automatic campaign is a research tool: it finds searches by reading the listing, then bids one price on everything it finds. Brands should cap its budget, move every search that sells into a manual campaign, and block those searches in the automatic campaign so the two stop competing.

How Amazon automatic campaigns choose searches

The appeal is real. An automatic campaign needs no keyword list, because Amazon decides which searches to show the ad on, using the product’s own information. Amazon’s notes describe automatic targeting as bidding on the top relevant searches for the product, Practical Ecommerce reported in November 2016.

That makes it a fast way to learn. Within a few weeks, the search term report shows the actual words shoppers typed before clicking, and the same Practical Ecommerce coverage counted that data among the best reasons to advertise at all. Many of those searches are ones the brand would never have written down: misspellings, use cases, competitor names.

The competition for those searches is growing. Sponsored Products took about 82% of Amazon ad budgets and grew about 52% from the second to the third quarter of 2017, Merkle’s Mark Ballard estimated, MediaPost reported in October 2017. A campaign that spends without direction is spending in a crowded auction.

Why the automatic campaign becomes expensive when left in charge

Here is the counterintuitive part. The feature that makes automatic campaigns good at research makes them poor at spending.

An automatic campaign bids one price on every search it matches. Discovery needs breadth, so that is fine for finding searches. Once a search has proved it sells, though, it deserves its own price, and the automatic campaign cannot give it one. The search that converts well is underbid and loses impressions; the search that rarely converts is overbid and keeps spending.

Take a hypothetical brand whose automatic campaign spends $1,500 a month at a $0.80 bid. The search term report shows 30 searches that each produced at least three sales, and dozens more that spent money and sold nothing. The 30 winners are worth more than $0.80 a click; the rest are worth far less. One bid prices them all the same.

The arithmetic makes the gap concrete. Suppose the product sells for $25 and the brand can spend 30% of the sale price, $7.50, to win an order.

A search that converts 12% of clicks into sales can afford up to $0.90 a click. A search that converts 2% can afford about $0.15. At $0.80, the automatic campaign underbids the first by a little and overbids the second by more than five times. The losses on the weak searches are paid for by the strong ones, and the campaign’s average looks merely acceptable.

Leaving those winners inside the automatic campaign has a second cost. If the brand also adds them to a manual campaign without blocking them in the automatic one, both campaigns can bid on the same search, and the brand’s report splits the results between them. Neither campaign’s numbers then describe what the search is really worth.

The harvest loop that turns research into strategy

The fix is a routine, run every two weeks.

Read the automatic campaign’s search term report and mark every search with enough sales to judge, using a threshold the brand sets in advance.

Move each marked search into a manual campaign as an exact-match keyword, with a bid priced from that search’s own conversion rate and the brand’s margin.

Add the same search to the automatic campaign as a negative exact keyword. The automatic campaign stops buying it, and the manual campaign owns it.

Add searches that have spent without selling as negatives too, after enough clicks to be fair to them. A fair test is usually the number of clicks at which the search, converting at the product’s normal rate, should have produced a sale twice over. Blocking a search after a handful of clicks throws away research the brand has already paid for.

Set the manual bids from the same arithmetic as the example above, then revisit them monthly. A search’s conversion rate shifts with season, price and competition, and the bid should follow it.

Cap the automatic campaign’s budget as a share of total spend. Its job is to keep exploring, so it should always run, but it should not grow simply because it is easy.

Expect the first harvest to be the largest. A campaign that has run unattended for months has collected a long list of proven searches and a longer list of wasted ones, and clearing both at once usually changes the account’s results within a few weeks. Later harvests are smaller and quicker, because the loop keeps the automatic campaign working on genuinely new searches.

Over time, the account changes shape. Most of the spend moves to manual campaigns with prices set search by search, and the automatic campaign becomes a small, steady source of new searches to test.

What to do

  1. Download your automatic campaigns’ search term reports for the last 60 days.
  2. Move every search with at least three sales into an exact-match manual campaign, and block it in the automatic campaign.
  3. Set a ceiling for automatic campaign spend as a share of your Amazon budget, and run the harvest every two weeks.

We run this loop for brands across Amazon Marketing Services. If your automatic campaigns are most of your Amazon spend, talk to our team.

P0010.title: NRF 2018 signaled that stores are becoming warehouses
P0010.alt: A small-business stockroom with wooden shelves of towels and ceramics in front of stacked shipping boxes on a navy wall.
P0010.ttag: NRF 2018 signaled that stores are becoming warehouses | Kwontified
P0010.desc: NRF 2018 was optimistic about stores for a reason brands should note: retailers are turning stores into warehouses, and shoppers now choose online first.
P0010.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 18, 2018.
P0010.body:
I spent this week at NRF 2018, the National Retail Federation’s Big Show in New York, and the mood was better than the headlines of the past year would suggest. The reason for the optimism matters more than the mood itself. Retailers are turning their stores into warehouses for online orders. That means the shopper’s choice of brand increasingly happens before the store is involved, on search pages and social feeds. Brands should plan to win that choice there, and treat store stock as part of their online business.

What NRF 2018 was optimistic about

The opening note was confidence. Walmart’s chief executive, Doug McMillon, spoke with NRF’s Matthew Shay on January 14. Asked about the death of retail, he borrowed Mark Twain’s line that reports of his death had been greatly exaggerated, IBM’s coverage of the session reported. Walmart still views retailing as a people business, Coresight Research noted the next day.

NRF had set the theme in advance. The retail industry is going through a transformation, and every speaker would address it, NRF’s Cristina Ceresoli said before the show, Mass Market Retailers reported in December.

The optimism rests on a strong holiday. Target’s comparable sales rose 3.4% in November and December, beating its own forecast, the company said on January 9. Department stores joined in: Kohl’s reported a 6.9% rise in holiday comparable sales and J.C. Penney 3.4%, the Star Tribune reported on January 10.

A good season changes the conversation in a room full of retailers. A year of store closings had made survival the question; a strong December made strategy the question again. That is the context for what follows, because the strategies on display were not about bringing shoppers back to the aisles.

How the store became a warehouse

The more telling evidence came from what retailers did in the weeks around the show, not from the stage.

Target’s stores fulfilled 70% of its digital orders in November and December, the same January 9 release said. That is a store working as a warehouse: the shopper chose the product online, and the store packed it.

Walmart moved in the same direction two days later. On January 11 it said it would close 63 Sam’s Club stores and turn about ten of them into e-commerce distribution sites, AP reported. A building that used to wait for shoppers will now ship to them.

Here is how this took hold. Online growth first looked like a threat to stores, so retailers defended the store as a destination. Then they noticed that the store was already close to the customer, and that a building full of stock near every suburb is a delivery network. The store’s value moved from the aisle, where brands compete for the shopper’s eye, to the stockroom, where they compete for space on a shipment.

Instagram’s presence pointed the other way. Instagram is increasingly a platform through which businesses connect with consumers, Coresight noted from the first day. If the store is becoming the place an order is filled, the feed is becoming one of the places a brand is first seen.

What the warehouse store means for brands

The shift moves the brand’s decisive moment earlier. A shopper who orders online for store pickup has already chosen the brand on a screen, usually by search. The shelf no longer has a chance to change her mind.

It changes what the retailer’s own website is for, too. When a shopper buys online and collects in a store, the product page on Walmart.com or Target.com does the selling that the shelf used to do. The images, the title, the reviews and the rank in that retailer’s search results now decide whether the brand gets the order. Many brands that manage Amazon closely have never looked at how their products appear on the websites of the stores that carry them.

It also changes what store stock means. When stores fill online orders, a product missing from the local store can mean a lost online sale too. Store availability becomes part of the brand’s online business, and someone has to watch it that way.

There is a fair objection: the store experience still matters, and many shoppers still browse in person. That is true, and nothing at NRF suggested stores are going away. The point is narrower. The growth retailers celebrated this week came from stores doing a new job, and brands planning for 2018 should plan for that job.

Planning for it is mostly a matter of attention. Review your Target.com and Walmart.com product pages as carefully as your Amazon pages. Track local stock as an online number. Treat Instagram as a first impression rather than an afterthought. A brand that does those three things is ready for the retailer that showed up in New York this week.

The brand still planning around the aisle will find the decision has already been made by the time the shopper reaches it, on a screen, in a search box, before she ever drives to the store to collect the order.

What to do

  1. List the retailers that fill online orders from stores, and ask each for store-level stock data on your products.
  2. Review how your products appear in search on Amazon, Walmart.com and Target.com, where shoppers now choose before they pick up.
  3. Decide who owns your brand’s presence on Instagram as a place shoppers first see your products.

We help brands plan for retailers whose stores now fill online orders. If your store and online teams plan separately, talk to our team.

P0012.title: Amazon’s 2018 fee changes cut the advertising ceiling first
P0012.alt: A tall stack of gold coins propping up the corner of a heavy wooden table in a sunlit blue room.
P0012.ttag: Amazon’s 2018 fee changes cut the advertising ceiling first | Kwontified
P0012.desc: Amazon’s 2018 fee increases lower the most a brand can spend on ads for each sale by the same amount. Model it product by product before February 22.
P0012.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 23, 2018.
P0012.body:
Most brands will read Amazon’s 2018 fee changes as a margin problem and plan a price review. The first place the change bites is quieter: the advertising account. Every dollar added to fees comes out of the money available to win each sale, so the most a brand can spend on advertising per order falls by exactly the fee increase. Bids set for the old fees start losing money on February 22 and April 15. Brands should recalculate the advertising ceiling for every product and reset bids before each date.

What the Amazon fee changes 2018 actually change

There are two sets of changes, on two dates.

Fulfillment by Amazon fees rise on February 22. Amazon said in December that the new fulfillment fees will apply year-round, with no separate October-to-December rate, and that dimensional weight will be calculated by dividing a unit’s volume by 139 rather than 166, EcommerceBytes reported on December 19.

Referral fees change by category. In a notice dated January 18, Amazon said the Clothing & Accessories referral fee rises from 15% to 17% from April 15, and that Shoes, Handbags & Sunglasses items priced above $75 will pay 18%, according to the notice sellers posted. Eligible jewelry pays less from February 22: 20% on the first $250 and 5% above that.

For an apparel brand using FBA, both changes apply, one after the other.

Why the fee increase lands on the advertising budget

The counterintuitive part is that the price is not the first number to move. The advertising ceiling is.

A brand selling on Amazon has a fixed amount of money per sale after product cost and fees. Call it contribution. Advertising has to come out of that contribution, and the most a brand can spend to win an order without losing money is the contribution itself. Any target advertising cost of sale is a share of it.

Take a hypothetical $40 dress that costs $14 to make. Today it pays a 15% referral fee, $6.00, and suppose its FBA fee is $4.00. That leaves $16.00 of contribution, so the brand can spend up to $16.00 in advertising to win a sale and still break even, a 40% advertising cost of sale.

On April 15 the referral fee becomes 17%, or $6.80. Suppose the February change also adds $0.30 to its FBA fee. Contribution falls to $14.90. The break-even advertising cost of sale falls from 40% to about 37%.

The price has not changed, and neither have the bids. A campaign that was running at 39% advertising cost of sale, just inside break-even, now loses money on every sale it wins. Nothing in the advertising report will say so, because the report does not know about fees.

The effect is largest where it is least visible. Products with thin contribution lose the most room in percentage terms, and those are usually the products advertising most heavily to hold their rank.

The same arithmetic runs the other way for jewelry. A hypothetical $600 necklace paying a flat 20% referral fee today pays $120. From February 22 it pays 20% of the first $250 and 5% of the remaining $350, or $67.50. Contribution rises by $52.50 per sale, and so does the most the brand can spend to win it. A jewelry brand that leaves its bids where they were is underinvesting in its best-margin products for a year, the length of the reduction.

Not every product is affected the same way. Products sold through Vendor Central pay no referral fee, because Amazon buys them wholesale, so these changes leave their advertising math alone. Products the brand ships itself avoid the FBA changes but not the referral changes. The model has to follow each product’s actual route to the customer, which is one more reason to build it product by product rather than with a single account-wide adjustment.

How to model the change before it reaches the margin

Rebuild the per-product math with the new fees. For every product, write down price, product cost, referral fee and FBA fee under the old and the new rules, and calculate contribution for each.

Check the dimensional weight. The new divisor makes a box’s dimensional weight larger, so products with bulky packaging relative to their weight may move into a higher FBA tier. Measure the packaging rather than assuming the 2017 tier.

Set a new advertising ceiling. Convert each product’s new contribution into a break-even advertising cost of sale, then set a target below it that leaves the profit the brand wants.

Reset bids on the right dates. Lower bids for affected products to the new targets before February 22 for FBA changes, and before April 15 for apparel and handbag referral changes.

Then decide on price separately. Raising prices may restore the margin, but it also changes conversion. Make that decision with the new numbers in hand, not as a reflex.

Finally, write the new ceilings down where the people setting bids can see them. A model that lives in a finance spreadsheet does nothing if the advertising team is still bidding against the old targets. The ceiling should sit next to each product in the same place the team reviews campaigns, and it should change again whenever Amazon’s fees do.

What to do

  1. Calculate contribution for every Amazon product under the old fees and the new ones.
  2. Convert each into a break-even advertising cost of sale and a new target.
  3. Reset bids before February 22 and again before April 15, then review prices.

We model fee changes into advertising targets for brands on Amazon. If your bids were set for the 2017 fees, talk to our team.

P0014.crumb: Staying off Amazon does not keep a brand…
P0014.title: Staying off Amazon does not keep a brand off Amazon
P0014.alt: A ceramic vase in a shop window, with an open parcel holding a matching vase on the cobbled doorstep beside a bicycle.
P0014.ttag: Staying off Amazon does not keep a brand off Amazon | Kwontified
P0014.desc: Brands that refuse Amazon over counterfeits rarely leave it. Their products stay, sold by others, and the brand gives up its say over the page shoppers read.
P0014.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 25, 2018.
P0014.body:
When a brand refuses to sell on Amazon because of counterfeits, it usually imagines its products disappearing from the site. They rarely do. Resellers keep listing genuine stock, and counterfeiters keep listing copies. What the brand removes is itself: its say over the page shoppers read. In 2018, brands should weigh that cost honestly against the counterfeit risk, rather than treating absence as protection.

Why brands choose staying off Amazon over counterfeits

The fear is reasonable, and the most public example shows why.

Birkenstock said in July 2016 that it would stop selling to Amazon in the US from January 1, 2017, and would no longer authorize third parties to sell its shoes there. The marketplace was filled with counterfeits and unauthorized sellers, the company said, RetailWire reported. Shoppers share the worry: roughly one in five said counterfeits were their main concern about shopping on Amazon, in a 2016 survey of 2,000 consumers reported by CNBC.

Leaving felt like a principled stand, and for a brand with strong stores and loyal customers, it looked affordable. Birkenstock extended the decision to Amazon’s European sites in December 2017, World Footwear reported.

What the brand leaves behind when it leaves

Here is the human detail that the decision tends to miss. The shopper who types the brand’s name into Amazon after the brand has left does not see an empty page. She sees whatever the remaining sellers have listed, at whatever price they chose, with whatever photos they had.

Birkenstock’s own account a few months later showed the bind. A spokeswoman told the Boston Globe in April 2017 that the company had seen improvements on the marketplace in addressing unauthorized sellers and counterfeit goods, but that it still did not sell directly to Amazon, the Globe reported. The problem was easing, and the brand was still on the outside of the page that carried its name.

That is the structural cost. A brand that is not present has no product page it controls, no reviews it answers, no advertising on its own name and, until it registers, little standing to remove the copies. Leaving does not hand the shopper back to the brand’s own stores. It hands her to whoever is still selling.

The consequences compound quietly. Prices drift with whichever reseller is cheapest that week, and that price becomes the one shoppers remember. Reviews collect on listings the brand cannot answer, including reviews of copies that read as reviews of the real product. Searches for the brand’s name return its competitors’ ads, because no one is bidding to hold the top of the page. None of this appears in the brand’s own sales reports, which is why the cost of absence is so easy to underestimate.

Brand Registry and Nike changed the choice in 2017

The counterfeit problem did not vanish in 2017, but the terms of the choice moved.

Amazon rebuilt its Brand Registry for brands with registered trademarks, promising to handle counterfeit claims from enrolled brands within four hours and adding a search tool to find copies by image and text, Practical Ecommerce reported in June 2017.

The most watched holdout moved the other way. Nike, which had refused to sell directly to Amazon for fear of undermining its brand, agreed in June 2017 to supply some products directly in exchange for Amazon policing counterfeits and third-party sales, according to a Wall Street Journal report. Amazon began telling third-party sellers they had until July 13 to stop selling certain Nike products, the report said.

Nike’s choice was not a verdict that the counterfeit problem was solved. It was a judgment that the brand would have more control inside the store than outside it. For a brand of Nike’s size, the counterfeits were going to be on Amazon either way; the open question was whether Nike would have a hand in removing them.

There is a fair objection: a direct relationship with Amazon brings its own costs, from pricing pressure to new fees, and some brands are right to decline. The argument here is narrower. Whatever the brand decides about selling, it should not assume that staying off removes it. The decision is between representing the brand on Amazon and letting others do it.

There is also a middle path for brands that will not sell directly. James Thomson of Buy Box Experts described one in an April 2017 Web Retailer comment thread. The brand creates a material difference that other sellers cannot reproduce, such as a manufacturer warranty valid only when the product is bought from the brand’s authorized seller, and says so on the listing.

Sellers offering the product without that warranty are then selling something materially different under the brand’s trademark. That gives the brand grounds to have their listings removed. It takes legal work and discipline, and the brand has to honor the warranty it promises. But it keeps the brand present on the page without handing its whole range to Amazon, and it turns the counterfeit fight from an occasional complaint into a standing policy.

What to do

  1. Search Amazon for your brand name and count the sellers, listings and suspected copies that appear today.
  2. Register your trademark and enroll in Brand Registry, whether or not you plan to sell on Amazon yourself.
  3. Decide, with that picture in hand, whether to sell directly, authorize a small set of resellers, or stay off and police the listings.

We help brands decide how to show up on Amazon when counterfeits are part of the picture. If your brand is on Amazon without your consent, talk to our team.

P0015.title: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q4 2017: Sponsored Products sold best
P0015.alt: Wooden blocks rising in height beside a twine-tied kraft parcel and dried flowers on a windowsill against a mustard wall.
P0015.ttag: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q4 2017: Sponsored Products sold best | Kwontified
P0015.desc: Public Q4 2017 data shows Amazon ad spend rising fast, Headline Search Ads growing fastest and Sponsored Products earning the most sales per click.
P0015.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 30, 2018.
P0015.body:
The public Amazon ad benchmarks for the fourth quarter of 2017 show spend rising fast, with Headline Search Ads growing fastest of all. The more useful number is quieter. Sponsored Products still produced the most sales per click, by a wide margin over every other format. Brands should read the growth as holiday seasonality and set their 2018 budgets from the format comparison.

Amazon ad benchmarks Q4 2017: what the public data shows

The source is the Q4 2017 Digital Marketing Report from the agency Merkle, released on January 25, 2018, which draws on its clients’ spending. This post uses only that public data, not Kwontified client results.

Spending jumped. Investment in Sponsored Products rose 64% from the third quarter to the fourth, and investment in Headline Search Ads rose 75%, Merkle said when it released the report.

Sponsored Products kept most of the budget. The format took 85% of Amazon ad spend in the fourth quarter, according to the report itself, and drove the highest sales per click of any Amazon format. Headline Search Ads produced 12% lower sales per click than Sponsored Products, and Product Display Ads 72% lower, the report said. Product Display Ads spending fell from the third quarter.

The fourth quarter continued a trend. Sponsored Products took about 82% of Amazon ad budgets in the third quarter and grew about 52% from the second, Merkle’s Mark Ballard estimated, MediaPost reported in October.

Why the growth rate is the wrong benchmark

Here is the counterintuitive part. The headline numbers, 64% and 75%, are the least useful figures in the report for planning.

Quarter-over-quarter growth from the third quarter to the fourth mostly measures the holiday. Shoppers search more in November and December, advertisers raise budgets to meet them, and spending rises for every format. A brand that compares its own fourth-quarter growth to these figures learns little about whether its money was well spent.

The faster growth of Headline Search Ads has a specific cause, too. Amazon opened the format to third-party sellers enrolled in Brand Registry in August 2017, eSellerHub reported at the time. Part of the 75% is new advertisers entering the auction, not existing ones finding the format more productive. More bidders for the same space at the top of the page usually means higher prices, not better returns.

The sales-per-click comparison is different. It measures what a click is worth in each format, holiday or not, and the gaps are large. A click on a Product Display Ad produced barely a quarter of the sales of a Sponsored Products click.

Sales per click is simple to calculate and rarely looked at. Divide the sales attributed to a format by the clicks it received. Because it ignores the price of the click, it isolates what the shopper did after clicking, which is the part of performance a brand’s product pages and targeting control. Cost per click then tells you what you paid for that behavior.

Take a hypothetical brand that spent $10,000 in the fourth quarter, $8,000 on Sponsored Products and $2,000 on Product Display Ads, at $1.00 a click in both. If Sponsored Products clicks produced $5.00 of sales each, they returned $40,000. If Product Display clicks produced 72% less, $1.40 each, they returned $2,800.

The account’s blended result, $42,800 in sales on $10,000, is an advertising cost of sale of about 23%, which looks healthy. Split by format, Sponsored Products ran at 20% and Product Display Ads at about 71%, a rate few products’ margins can carry. The blend hides the loss inside the display spend, and the brand keeps funding it because the total looks fine.

How to use the Q4 2017 numbers in 2018 planning

Start budgets from the format comparison, not from what competitors appear to be spending. Sponsored Products earned the most per click and should carry most of the budget, which is where Merkle’s clients already put it.

Treat Headline Search Ads as a targeted tool. A format that earns 12% less per click can still be worth buying where it changes the shopper’s choice, on category searches where a brand ranks below the top results. Buying it broadly because it grew fastest is following the crowd into a more expensive auction.

Be cautious with Product Display Ads, the format with the widest gap. Spending on the format fell from the third quarter, and the gap in sales per click explains why. Keep it for specific jobs, such as appearing on competitors’ product pages, and measure it on its own.

Compare your own results by format, not in total. A brand’s blended advertising cost of sale hides the same gaps the report shows. Split results by format and by branded versus category searches before deciding where the next dollar goes.

Keep the limits of the data in mind. These are averages across many advertisers and categories, and a brand’s own numbers will differ by category, price and the strength of its product pages. Merkle’s figures describe its own clients, who are mostly large advertisers, and normalized sales per click compares formats rather than giving a target a brand should hit.

What to do

  1. Split your fourth-quarter Amazon results by ad format and calculate sales per click for each.
  2. Keep most of your 2018 budget in Sponsored Products, and buy Headline Search Ads on category searches where you rank low.
  3. Review Product Display Ads separately, and stop any placement that cannot show its own sales.

We set Amazon budgets from format-level results rather than headline growth. If your plan for 2018 started from last quarter’s spend, talk to our team.

P0016.title: Walmart Marketplace in 2018 is still early enough to shape
P0016.alt: A freshly poured concrete slab at the base of a cream wall, with two plastering trowels resting on the soil beside it.
P0016.ttag: Walmart Marketplace in 2018 is still early enough to shape | Kwontified
P0016.desc: Walmart’s online catalog tripled in a year as its marketplace grew faster than its own sales. For brands, 2018 is a chance to shape the shelf before it fills.
P0016.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 1, 2018.
P0016.body:
The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands in 2018 can be summed up in one sentence: the shelf is still being built. Walmart’s online catalog more than tripled in a year, and the marketplace is growing faster than Walmart’s own online sales. That makes 2018 a rare window. Brands that list and build their pages now help decide how their products appear. Brands that wait will inherit pages that resellers wrote, as many did on Amazon.

Walmart Marketplace 2018: the catalog is growing faster than the store

Walmart’s online business is growing quickly, and the marketplace is growing faster still.

Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 50% in the quarter that ended in October, and its gross merchandise volume, which counts the value of everything sold on its sites including marketplace sales, rose 54%, The Motley Fool reported on November 16. When the total grows faster than Walmart’s own sales, the difference is coming from other sellers.

The assortment shows the same thing. Walmart more than tripled the number of items available online, to more than 70 million from 20 million a year earlier, the Associated Press reported. Walmart’s own buyers did not add 50 million products in a year. Marketplace sellers did most of that work.

Walmart is not building on one site alone. Moody’s lead retail analyst credited Walmart’s online performance in part to its substantial investments, including its purchase of Jet.com, according to the same AP report. For brands, that means two Walmart-owned storefronts with their own shoppers, and a decision about whether to appear on both, through whom and at what price. The pattern of Walmart’s spending, from Jet.com to new distribution sites, points in one direction even where its plans are not public: toward selling online.

The growth is also spreading to the physical business. In January, Walmart said it would turn about ten closing Sam’s Club stores into e-commerce distribution sites, AP reported.

How Amazon’s catalog took hold, and why Walmart’s is at an earlier stage

The useful comparison is with Amazon a decade or more ago, when its marketplace was also filling a catalog quickly.

Here is how that took hold. Sellers listed products, often before the brands themselves arrived, and wrote the product pages with whatever photos and descriptions they had. Reviews and sales history attached to those pages. By the time many brands paid attention, the pages had years of history, and changing them meant asking for authority the brand had never claimed.

Walmart’s marketplace is at an earlier point on the same path. The catalog is growing quickly, and many of its pages are new. A brand that sets up its own listings now writes the first version of the page shoppers will read, rather than correcting someone else’s later.

There is a structural reason the window will not stay open. A marketplace that is adding tens of millions of items a year attracts more sellers each quarter, because every new product is a new opportunity to resell someone else’s goods. The early arrivals on any marketplace tend to be resellers and liquidators rather than brands, since they move fastest. Each month a brand waits, more of its products acquire pages written by someone with less interest in how the brand looks.

The pressure is lower, too. Walmart is a far smaller place to sell online than Amazon today, which means fewer sellers competing for the same products and less crowding in search. That is a disadvantage for volume and an advantage for a brand learning how the platform works.

There is a fair objection: the volume is small, and a brand’s Amazon business needs every hour it can get. That is a reasonable caution for 2018 sales targets. It is a poor reason to ignore the platform, because the cost of arriving late is paid in control, not just in sales, and control is hardest to recover.

What brands should do on Walmart.com in 2018

Find your products first, including the ones you never chose to sell online. Search Walmart.com for every product you sell and note who lists each one, what the page says and whether the price matches your policy.

Decide how you will sell there. Some brands will supply Walmart directly, some will sell through the marketplace and some will work through a reseller they trust. The choice matters less than making it deliberately, because each route decides who controls the page.

Write the pages. Titles, images and descriptions should be as complete as on Amazon. On a catalog this new, a good page has less competition for attention than it will in a year or two.

Watch the price you see on Walmart.com, not only the price you set. Walmart and its marketplace sellers can price differently from Amazon, and shoppers increasingly compare the two sites before buying. A brand whose Walmart price drifts below its Amazon price may find Amazon matching it, which turns a small marketplace into a large pricing problem.

Learn the operations. Walmart’s requirements for shipping, returns and seller performance are its own, and a brand that learns them on a small business will be ready if Walmart becomes a large one.

What to do

  1. Search Walmart.com for all your products and record who sells each one.
  2. Choose, product by product, whether to supply Walmart directly, sell on the marketplace or authorize a reseller.
  3. Rewrite the pages you control to the same standard as your Amazon pages before the 2018 holiday.

We help brands set up and run their business on Walmart.com. If you have not yet looked at how your products appear there, talk to our team.

P0018.title: Amazon advertising revenue grew three times faster than its store
P0018.alt: A tall stack of coins beside three twine-tied kraft parcels on a wooden desk with pencils and a fern against a terracotta wall.
P0018.ttag: Amazon advertising revenue grew three times faster than its store | Kwontified
P0018.desc: Amazon’s ‘other’ revenue, mostly advertising, grew 62% in Q4 2017 as store sales grew 20%. For brands, the cost of being found is rising faster than sales.
P0018.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 6, 2018.
P0018.body:
Amazon reported its fourth-quarter 2017 results on February 1, and the number brands should read most closely was not sales or profit. It was the “other” revenue line, which Amazon uses to report advertising. It grew 62%, while sales in Amazon’s online stores grew about 20%.

When advertising grows three times faster than the sales it sits on, the cost of being found rises faster than the sales it buys. Brands should track advertising as a share of their total Amazon sales, not only advertising cost of sale, and plan for it to rise in 2018.

What the other line says about Amazon advertising revenue

Amazon does not report advertising on its own. It includes it in a line called “other,” alongside smaller items.

That line rose 62% to $1.74 billion in the fourth quarter, Reuters reported. Sales in Amazon’s online stores grew about 20% from the year before, according to New York Times reporting summarized by ETCentric. Total net sales, lifted by the Whole Foods acquisition, rose 38% to $60.5 billion, The Motley Fool reported.

Amazon’s chief financial officer, Brian Olsavsky, called advertising a key contributor to the company’s growth and said it was particularly strong in North America, according to the earnings call transcript.

The agency data points the same way. Merkle’s report released January 25 showed advertisers’ Sponsored Products spending up 64% from the third quarter to the fourth, the company said.

Why faster ad growth raises every brand’s cost of being found

Here is the counterintuitive part. Brands tend to read rising ad revenue as a sign that advertising works, so they should buy more. The same number is also a measure of what they are paying.

Amazon’s advertising revenue is, almost by definition, what advertisers spent. When it grows faster than the sales happening in Amazon’s stores, advertisers as a group are spending a larger share of each dollar of sales to be seen. Some of that is new advertisers joining, and some is existing advertisers bidding more for the same searches. Either way, the price of a place in search is rising faster than the volume of sales that place can win.

For a single brand, that shows up as a slow squeeze. Take a hypothetical brand that sold $1 million on Amazon in 2017 and spent $100,000 on advertising, 10% of its sales. Suppose its sales grow 20% in 2018, in line with Amazon’s stores, but holding its position in search costs 40% more because more competitors are bidding. It sells $1.2 million and spends $140,000.

Advertising rises from 10% of sales to almost 12%, and the brand’s margin shrinks even though every campaign report says the ads are working.

That is why advertising cost of sale alone can mislead. It measures each campaign against the sales the campaign claims. It does not show whether advertising is taking a larger share of the brand’s whole Amazon business, which is the number that decides profit.

There is a fair caution about the data. The “other” line includes more than advertising, and Amazon does not say how much of the $1.74 billion is ads. The direction is still clear: Amazon’s own finance chief named advertising as a key contributor, and the agency data shows advertisers spending faster. A brand does not need the exact figure to see which way its costs are moving.

The squeeze is not inevitable. A brand whose product pages convert better than its competitors’ pays less per sale for the same clicks. A brand that ranks well in organic search needs less advertising to be found. Those are the levers that let a brand grow faster than its ad bill. They take longer to pay off than a bid change, which is why most brands underinvest in them, and why the brands that do invest find their advertising getting cheaper relative to their competitors’ over the year.

How brands should plan Amazon advertising in 2018

Measure advertising as a share of total Amazon sales, every month. Divide total ad spend by total Amazon sales, including sales that no ad claims. Watch the trend rather than the level.

Set a ceiling for that share. Decide in advance how much of total Amazon sales the brand can afford to spend on advertising and still meet its margin, using each product’s contribution after Amazon’s fees.

Separate defense from growth, because they answer different questions. Spending to keep a product’s existing rank is a cost of doing business; spending to win new searches is an investment. Budget them separately, so the rising cost of defense does not crowd out growth unnoticed.

Invest in what lowers the cost of being found. Better images, titles and reviews raise conversion, and higher conversion lowers the cost of every sale an ad wins and improves organic rank over time. In a market where the price of attention is rising, those improvements compound.

Read Amazon’s next results the same way, starting with the first quarter of 2018. Each quarter, compare the growth of the “other” line with the growth of Amazon’s online store sales. As long as the first grows faster, assume the cost of being found is still rising.

What to do

  1. Calculate your 2017 Amazon advertising as a share of total Amazon sales, month by month.
  2. Set a 2018 ceiling for that share from each product’s margin after fees.
  3. Split your ad budget into defense and growth, and fund one project that raises conversion before the end of March 2018.

We plan Amazon advertising against total sales, not only campaign reports. If your ad spend is rising faster than your Amazon sales, talk to our team.

P0019.crumb: Zalando’s Partner Program lets brands run…
P0019.title: Zalando’s Partner Program lets brands run their own shelf
P0019.alt: Wooden shelves of mugs, bowls, jars and soaps on a pale blue display wall inside a warm, orange-toned home goods shop.
P0019.ttag: Zalando’s Partner Program lets brands run their own shelf | Kwontified
P0019.desc: Zalando grew 23% in 2017 and is opening its platform to brands that sell their own stock. For brands in Europe, the choice is how much of the shelf to run.
P0019.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 8, 2018.
P0019.body:
For most fashion brands, Zalando has been a wholesale customer: a buyer who places orders, sets prices and decides what to carry. That is changing. Zalando grew about 23% in 2017, and through its Partner Program it now lets brands list and ship their own stock alongside what it buys. For brands selling in Europe in 2018, the question is no longer only whether Zalando will order. It is how much of their Zalando shelf they want to run themselves.

Zalando Partner Program: from buyer to platform

Zalando is large and still growing quickly. Its revenue grew by about 23% in 2017, to between 4.48 billion and 4.50 billion euros, according to preliminary figures the company released on January 17. Fourth-quarter revenue rose between 21% and 23%. Full results are due on March 1.

The structural change is how it gets its assortment. Zalando is moving beyond its traditional model of retailing inventory it owns, Coresight Research noted in July 2017: its Partner Program allows brands and retailers to list and dispatch their own inventory on the site.

Large brands have joined, which matters because it signals the program is a channel brands use for their main lines, not only for clearance. Nike, Lacoste, Pepe Jeans and Esprit joined the Partner Program in the first half of 2017, Fibre2Fashion reported.

How a retailer becomes a shelf the brand runs

Here is how this kind of shift takes hold. A retailer grows by buying more of what sells. At some point the assortment it wants is larger than the inventory it can afford to own, and the cheapest way to add range is to let suppliers sell directly. The retailer earns a fee instead of a margin, the supplier keeps control of its stock and price, and the shopper sees a larger selection without knowing who owns each item.

Amazon followed this path years ago, and the result for brands was a choice between selling to Amazon and selling on it. Zalando is now offering European brands the same choice, in a market where fashion is the whole business rather than one category among many.

The choice changes the brand’s job. When Zalando buys, a brand’s work is a wholesale relationship: negotiate the order, ship it, wait to see what sells. When a brand sells through the Partner Program, the work looks more like running a store: deciding which styles to list, keeping stock available, setting prices and watching how products appear.

There is a reputational side the shopper never sees. On a platform that mixes stock it owns with stock brands sell directly, the shopper usually cannot tell who is behind each item. A late parcel or a missing size on a brand’s own listing reads as a failure of the brand, and of Zalando, in the same moment. The brand that takes on the shelf takes on its customer experience too.

There is also a data side. A brand that sells only through a buyer’s order learns what sold at the end of a season, in aggregate. A brand selling its own stock sees which styles, sizes and colors sell in which countries as it happens. For a fashion business that plans collections months ahead, that is information worth having even if the margin were the same.

That is more work, and it brings more control. A brand selling its own stock can carry styles Zalando did not buy, keep sizes in stock that a buyer’s order missed and see how its products sell day by day rather than season by season.

What brands should decide about Zalando in 2018

Start with what Zalando already buys. List the styles Zalando orders today and compare them with the brand’s full range. The gap between the two is the assortment a Partner Program listing could add.

Decide who runs the shelf. Selling directly needs someone watching stock, prices and product pages every day, across several countries and languages. Brands that cannot staff that work should not take it on for the margin alone, a lesson many learned on Amazon.

Keep prices consistent. A brand selling both to Zalando and through its own Partner Program listings, alongside its own website and other European retailers, needs a pricing policy that holds across them. Inconsistent prices invite comparison and erode the brand’s position with wholesale partners.

Plan the logistics. Shipping across Europe from the brand’s own warehouse is a different operation from shipping a wholesale order to one distribution center. Count the cost of returns, which are common in online fashion, before setting prices.

There is a fair objection: a wholesale order is simpler, carries less risk and keeps Zalando’s buyers invested in the brand. For many brands that will remain the right core of the relationship. The Partner Program is a way to extend it, not necessarily to replace it.

The deeper point is that Europe’s largest online fashion platform is becoming a place where brands manage their own presence. Brands that learn to run that shelf in 2018 will be better placed as more of European fashion shopping moves online.

What to do

  1. Compare the styles Zalando buys from you with your full range, and list the gaps.
  2. Name the person who would run a Partner Program listing, and what else they own.
  3. Write a European pricing policy that covers Zalando, your own site and your other retailers before you list.

We help brands decide how to sell on Zalando and run the operation across Europe. If Zalando is still only a wholesale account for you, talk to our team.

P0020.crumb: Mercado Libre is buying its growth with…
P0020.title: Mercado Libre is buying its growth with free shipping
P0020.alt: A yellow pickup truck piled high with roped cardboard boxes on a cobbled street lined with colorful colonial buildings.
P0020.ttag: Mercado Libre is buying its growth with free shipping | Kwontified
P0020.desc: Mercado Libre’s sales accelerated in 2017 as it paid for free shipping. For brands entering Latin America in 2018, shipping eligibility decides who wins.
P0020.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 13, 2018.
P0020.body:
Mercado Libre, Latin America’s largest online marketplace, had its fastest growth in more than five years in 2017, and it paid for that growth itself. The company spent heavily on free shipping, and its gross margin fell from 63% to 47% in a year. Items shipped through its own logistics service grew faster than items sold. For brands entering Latin America in 2018, the lesson is that shipping eligibility now decides who wins the sale, so it should be treated as the price of competing rather than an option.

Mercado Libre free shipping: what the numbers show

Mercado Libre reported its third-quarter 2017 results on November 2, and the numbers show a marketplace accelerating.

Gross merchandise volume passed $3 billion in a quarter for the first time, reaching about $3.08 billion, up 50.7% in US dollars from a year earlier, the company said. Items sold rose 55.8% to 74.2 million, which the company described as its fastest unit growth in more than five years. Live listings passed 100 million for the first time, reaching 106 million.

Shipping grew fastest. Items shipped through Mercado Envíos, its logistics service, rose 80.4% to 41.7 million, driven mostly by investment in free shipping, its loyalty program and customer acquisition, the company said.

The bill for that growth shows up in the margin. Gross margin fell to 47.4% from 63.1% a year earlier, and the company attributed most of the decline to the cost of providing free shipping.

The competition is large, too. That volume came from about 4.6 million unique sellers, Marketplace Pulse reported. Amazon’s marketplace in Brazil is new but growing quickly, from about 1,400 sellers on October 17 to more than 3,000 by November 6, the same report said.

Why a subsidy changes which sellers win

Here is the counterintuitive part. Free shipping looks like a gift to shoppers. For sellers, it is a change in the rules of competition.

When a marketplace pays to make shipping free, shoppers learn to expect it. Listings that qualify for free shipping convert better than listings that do not, because the shopper sees a lower total price and a familiar delivery promise. A marketplace that has just spent 16 points of margin on that promise has every reason to show qualifying listings first, since those are the sales its investment was meant to produce.

The effect on a seller outside the program is a slow disadvantage. Its product may be cheaper before shipping and more expensive after. It may rank lower in search, convert worse when it does appear and collect fewer reviews as a result. None of that shows up as a fee. It shows up as sales that went to the seller next door.

Mobile shopping sharpens the effect. Mobile’s share of Mercado Libre’s merchandise volume rose to 47% from 36% in a year, Marketplace Pulse noted. On a phone screen, shoppers see fewer listings at once and lean harder on simple signals such as a free-shipping badge, so the gap between qualifying and non-qualifying offers widens as more shopping moves to mobile.

The numbers support the direction. Items shipped through Mercado Envíos grew about 80% while items sold grew about 56%, which means a rising share of everything sold on the marketplace now moves through its own shipping service. A brand that does not plan around that service is planning for a shrinking part of the market.

There is a fair caution. Mercado Libre cannot cut its margin like this forever, and the terms of its shipping program may change as it looks for profit. A brand should build its prices so they still work if the subsidy shrinks. The safest plan treats today’s free shipping as a temporary advantage to win early reviews, not as a permanent cost the marketplace will always carry.

How brands should enter Mercado Libre in 2018

Start with the shipping program, not the listing. Before choosing which products to list, confirm which can qualify for Mercado Envíos and free shipping in each country, and what that requires of the brand’s logistics.

Price the delivered product. Shoppers compare the total they pay. Build each price from the product cost, Mercado Libre’s fees and the brand’s share of shipping, and compare that total with the leading offers in the category.

Choose countries in order. Mercado Libre operates across several Latin American countries, and each has its own currency, logistics and shoppers. Brazil is the largest; Mexico grew fastest in shipped items in the third quarter, with items shipped up 285%, the company said. Enter one market well rather than several thinly.

Watch Amazon in Brazil. A second large marketplace changes the bargaining position of brands and sellers. Its arrival is a reason to build a direct presence on Mercado Libre now, while the leading marketplace is still investing heavily to keep sellers and shoppers.

Treat listings as a long-term asset. With more than 100 million live listings, a new product starts at the bottom. Reviews, sales history and complete product pages are what move it up, and shipping eligibility is what gets the first sales.

What to do

  1. List the products you would sell in Latin America and check each for Mercado Envíos and free shipping eligibility.
  2. Build delivered prices for one country and compare them with the top three offers in each category.
  3. Launch in one country with a small range, and expand only after its products are collecting reviews.

We help brands plan and run their entry into Mercado Libre. If you are considering Latin America in 2018, talk to our team.
