P0022.crumb: Instagram shopping is free to join, but…
P0022.title: Instagram shopping is free to join, but reach will not stay free
P0022.alt: A smartphone with a glowing pink screen leaning against a pink wall beside an old brass coin box on a wooden ledge.
P0022.ttag: Instagram shopping is free to join, but reach will not stay free | Kwontified
P0022.desc: Instagram opened shoppable posts to more US brands in 2017 and plans to charge for reaching new shoppers. For brands, 2018 is the cheap year to learn it.
P0022.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 15, 2018.
P0022.body:
Instagram shopping for brands in 2018 looks like an open door. Tagging products in posts costs nothing, the audience is enormous and businesses are arriving by the million. The door will not stay this cheap. Instagram has said it plans to earn money from shopping by charging businesses to show their shoppable posts to people who do not already follow them. Brands should use 2018, while organic reach still carries those posts, to build their catalog, their imagery and their audience there.

Instagram shopping in early 2018: what exists and who can use it

Shoppable posts let a business tag products in a photo, so a shopper can tap to see the price and a description and click through to the product page on the brand’s own site.

The feature is still new and limited. Instagram began testing shoppable tags in November 2016 with 20 US retail brands, including Kate Spade, JackThreads and Warby Parker, and in October 2017 opened the feature to US merchants using the BigCommerce platform, TechCrunch reported. Merchants using it get data on how many people viewed product information or clicked through, the report said.

The audience is large. Instagram has 800 million monthly active users and two million advertisers, double the number in March 2017, according to the same report. Business use is growing quickly: Instagram had more than 25 million business profiles by late 2017, up from 15 million in July, Statista noted, and 200 million users visited a business profile every day.

How the free shelf turns into a paid one

The plan for making money is the important part. Instead of taking a cut of each purchase, Instagram plans to let business accounts pay to show their shoppable photos in the feeds of users who do not already follow them, TechCrunch reported.

Here is how this path usually takes hold. A platform gives businesses free tools and lets their posts reach followers organically. Businesses invest in building those followings because the reach is free. As more businesses post, each one’s share of attention shrinks, and the platform offers a paid way to reach more people. The tools stay free; the reach becomes the product.

The businesses that built strong followings early keep an advantage, because their organic posts still reach people while newcomers start by paying.

Facebook’s pages followed this course, and Instagram is owned by Facebook. A brand that watched organic reach on Facebook shrink as more businesses posted has seen the second half of the story already.

The shopper’s path matters too. A shoppable post does not complete the sale on Instagram; it sends the shopper to the brand’s own product page. That makes the brand’s site part of the Instagram experience. A slow mobile page, a missing size or a checkout that asks for too much will lose a shopper who arrived ready to buy, and the brand will have paid, in time now and in money later, to bring her there. Before investing in posts, it is worth checking what happens after the tap on a phone.

Two numbers suggest the crowding has begun. Business profiles grew from 15 million to more than 25 million in about five months. Advertisers doubled in about six months. More businesses competing for the same feeds means each organic post reaches a smaller share of followers.

That does not make Instagram shopping a bad investment. It makes the timing important. A brand that builds its catalog, learns what imagery sells and grows a following while organic reach still works will spend less later, because its paid posts will start from a stronger base.

What brands should build on Instagram in 2018

Get the catalog ready. Shoppable tags depend on a clean product catalog connected to the brand’s online store. If your site runs on a supported platform, set it up; if not, prepare the catalog data so you can connect when Instagram opens more widely.

Learn which images sell. Instagram is a place for discovery, and the photos that earn attention there are rarely the white-background product shots that sell on a marketplace. Test lifestyle images, product details and customer photos, and measure which ones lead people to product pages.

Treat followers as an asset with a shelf life. The audience a brand builds while reach is free is the base its paid reach will start from. Grow it deliberately, with content worth following, rather than with contests that bring followers who never buy.

Connect Instagram to the rest of the business. A shopper who discovers a product on Instagram may buy it on the brand’s site, on Amazon or in a store. Watch searches for your brand on Amazon and your own site around Instagram activity, so you can see the effect the click-through numbers alone will miss.

There is a fair objection: shoppable posts are still limited to a narrow set of brands and platforms in the US, and the sales they drive today are small. That is a reason to keep the investment modest, not a reason to wait. The cost of learning will only rise.

What to do

  1. Check whether your online store can connect to Instagram shopping, and prepare your product catalog if it cannot yet.
  2. Run a three-month test of different product images and track which lead to product page visits.
  3. Set a target for engaged followers on Instagram by the end of 2018, and plan content to earn them.

We help brands build their shopping presence on Instagram alongside their marketplace business. If Instagram is still only a brand channel for you, talk to our team.

P0024.title: Amazon Marketing Services only reaches shoppers already searching
P0024.alt: A brass magnifying glass hangs on a rope above footprints in the aisle of an old bookshop lined with shelves.
P0024.ttag: Amazon Marketing Services only reaches shoppers already searching | Kwontified
P0024.desc: Almost all Amazon Marketing Services spending buys search ads, which capture demand that already exists. For brands, that sets a ceiling on growth from AMS.
P0024.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 20, 2018.
P0024.body:
The state of Amazon Marketing Services for brands in 2018 can be summed up in a single number: about 85% of AMS spending goes to Sponsored Products, which appear when a shopper searches. Search ads are the most efficient advertising on Amazon, and they have a built-in limit. They can only sell to shoppers who are already searching. Brands should treat AMS as the way to win existing demand at the lowest cost, and plan separately for creating new demand, because spending more on search past that limit buys the same shoppers at higher prices.

Amazon Marketing Services in 2018 is a search business

AMS offers three formats: Sponsored Products, which appear in search results and on product pages; Headline Search Ads, the banner across the top of search results; and Product Display Ads, which appear on product pages.

The money goes overwhelmingly to search. Sponsored Products took 85% of Amazon ad spend in the fourth quarter of 2017 and drove the highest sales per click of any Amazon format, according to Merkle’s Q4 2017 Digital Marketing Report, released on January 25. Investment in Sponsored Products rose 64% from the third quarter to the fourth, and in Headline Search Ads 75%.

The format that is least tied to a search moved the other way. Product Display Ads grew more than 100% from the second quarter to the third, Merkle’s Mark Ballard said, MediaPost reported in October, but spending on them fell from the third quarter to the fourth, according to the Q4 report.

The pattern is clear. Brands are concentrating their Amazon budgets on the moment a shopper types a search. That concentration makes sense for efficiency, and it also means most brands’ Amazon growth now depends on how many shoppers arrive already looking for what they sell.

Why search advertising has a ceiling

Here is the counterintuitive part. The efficiency of search ads and their limit come from the same place.

A search ad works because the shopper has already said what she wants. That is why it converts well and why it earns the most sales per click. It is also why its volume is fixed by something the advertiser does not control: the number of people who search for that category or that brand in a given week.

Up to a point, more spending wins more of those searches. Higher bids buy better positions; broader keywords reach more variations. Past that point, the brand is already showing up for most of the relevant searches, and extra money mostly raises the price it pays for the same shoppers. The cost per sale rises while the number of sales barely moves.

Take a hypothetical brand whose category gets 100,000 searches a month on Amazon. Its ads win clicks on enough of them to make 2,000 sales at $8 of advertising each, $16,000 in total.

Doubling the budget to $32,000 does not double the searches. If it buys 500 more sales by bidding higher on the same terms, those extra sales cost $32 each, four times the average. The report shows a total cost per sale of $12.80, which looks acceptable, and hides the fact that the last $16,000 bought sales at a price the brand would never accept on its own.

The point where the ceiling appears differs by category and brand, but every search budget has one. Most brands find it by accident, when a larger budget produces a disappointing month. The better way is to find it on purpose: raise the budget in steps, measure what each step adds and stop where the extra sales start costing more than the brand is willing to pay for them.

How brands should use AMS in 2018

Use AMS to win existing demand as cheaply as possible. Harvest the searches that sell, price each one from its own conversion rate, block the ones that do not and defend the brand’s own name where competitors bid on it. That is the work search ads do best.

Measure the marginal sale, not the average. When raising an AMS budget, compare the extra sales with the extra spending. If the last dollars are buying sales at several times the average cost, the account has reached its ceiling.

Plan demand creation separately. The shoppers who do not yet search for a category or a brand are reached through other channels: display advertising on and off Amazon, the brand’s own marketing, social media and retail partners. Their effect shows up later as more searches, which search ads can then capture. Judge them on that effect, not on the sales they claim directly.

Treat rising searches as the real growth signal. When searches for the brand’s name and its categories on Amazon rise, the brand is creating demand, and AMS can convert it. When they are flat, more AMS spending mostly raises prices.

There is a fair caution. For most brands in 2018, AMS is still where the next efficient dollar goes, because few have reached their ceiling. The point is to know where it is before spending through it.

What to do

  1. Calculate the extra sales and extra spend from your last AMS budget increase, and the cost per extra sale.
  2. Track searches for your brand name and top categories on Amazon each month as a measure of demand.
  3. Set a separate budget for demand creation, judged on growth in those searches rather than on direct sales.

We plan AMS budgets around the ceiling search advertising imposes. If a bigger Amazon budget has stopped producing proportionally more sales, talk to our team.

P0025.crumb: Amazon Vendor Central’s real price comes…
P0025.title: Amazon Vendor Central’s real price comes after the purchase order
P0025.alt: A cream envelope on a wooden table with a trail of coins and small paper slips leading toward a potted succulent.
P0025.ttag: Amazon Vendor Central’s real price comes after the purchase order | Kwontified
P0025.desc: Amazon vendors negotiate a wholesale price, then lose part of it to co-op, allowances, chargebacks and payment terms. The real price is what remains.
P0025.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 22, 2018.
P0025.body:
Ask a brand that sells through Amazon Vendor Central what Amazon pays for its products, and the answer is usually the wholesale price on the purchase order. That number is only the beginning. Co-op payments, allowances, chargebacks and payment terms each take part of it back, and they are usually handled by different people and recorded in different places. Few brands ever see the real price whole. In 2018, vendors should total every deduction by product before their next negotiation with Amazon.

How Amazon Vendor Central prices a product twice

The first price is the one everyone sees. Amazon issues a purchase order at an agreed wholesale cost, the brand ships and an invoice is raised.

The second price is assembled afterward. A vendor agreement typically includes co-op, a percentage Amazon keeps from each invoice for marketing; allowances for freight or damaged goods; and chargebacks, fees for shipments that break Amazon’s rules on labeling, packaging or timing. Payment terms add a cost of their own: the longer Amazon takes to pay, the more working capital the brand ties up.

None of these is unusual for a large retailer, and none is hidden from the brand that looks. What is unusual is how quietly they move. One vendor described the pattern in a Web Retailer comment thread in February 2017: good terms in the first year, then requests for new fees and a move from 60-day to 90-day payment, with no new incentives in return.

James Thomson of Buy Box Experts, replying in the same thread, said that in his experience brands often succeed with Vendor Central in the short term but lose control or margin as their Amazon sales grow. The deductions are one of the reasons the margin moves.

The question in the room: who sees the whole price?

Here is the question most brands have not asked, and it is a question about structure rather than arithmetic.

The wholesale price is negotiated by the sales team. Co-op and allowances may be agreed in the same negotiation but booked by finance as marketing or as a reduction in revenue. Chargebacks arrive weeks later as deductions from payments, and they land with whoever handles accounts receivable or operations. The cost of slow payment never appears as a line at all.

Take a hypothetical product with a $10.00 wholesale price. Co-op and allowances take $1.00. Chargebacks, spread across the year’s shipments, take another $0.30 per unit. Waiting 90 days for payment, at an 8% annual cost of capital, costs about $0.20.

Amazon’s real price is about $8.50, fifteen percent below the number on the purchase order. On a product with a thin margin, that gap can be the whole profit, and nobody inside the brand sees it unless someone deliberately adds the pieces together.

Each person sees a piece. The sales lead sees a healthy wholesale price. Finance sees a co-op line that looks like a marketing cost. Operations sees chargebacks as a compliance problem. No one is responsible for adding them up product by product, so no one can say what Amazon actually pays for any one item.

That matters most at the negotiating table. Amazon arrives knowing what it takes from each vendor. A brand that arrives knowing only its wholesale price is negotiating one number while the other side negotiates five.

It also matters for the larger decision. A product that looks profitable on the purchase order may lose money after deductions, and a brand weighing Vendor Central against selling through Seller Central cannot compare them honestly without the real price.

There is a fair objection: much of this is the normal cost of selling to any large retailer, and Vendor Central brings real benefits in volume, simplicity and Amazon’s own retail strength. All true. The argument is not that Vendor Central is a bad deal. It is that a brand cannot know whether it is a good deal without the full price.

What vendors should do before the next negotiation

Gather every deduction in one place. Pull co-op, allowances and chargebacks for the past twelve months from Vendor Central reports and the payment remittances, and match them to products where possible.

Calculate the real price per product. Start with the wholesale cost, subtract each deduction, and add the cost of the payment terms at the brand’s cost of capital. The result is what Amazon actually pays.

Sort chargebacks into avoidable and disputed. Many come from fixable operational problems, such as labels, shipment timing and paperwork. Fix the avoidable ones at the source and dispute the ones that are wrong, because both raise the real price without a negotiation.

Name one owner. The real price needs someone who sees all of it, usually in finance or in the team that owns Amazon, with the authority to change how the brand negotiates. That person should be in the room for the next negotiation.

Compare the alternative honestly. With the real price in hand, a brand can compare Vendor Central with selling the same products through Seller Central, and decide product by product rather than by habit.

What to do

  1. Pull twelve months of co-op, allowances and chargebacks from Vendor Central and match them to products.
  2. Calculate the real price Amazon pays for your top 20 products after every deduction and the cost of payment terms.
  3. Assign one person to own the full Vendor Central price and bring the analysis to your next negotiation.

We help vendors calculate what Amazon really pays and prepare for negotiation. If you know your wholesale price but not your real one, talk to our team.

P0026.title: Test the Amazon Advertising Platform against a holdout group
P0026.alt: Two raised garden beds, one with young seedlings and one lush with vegetables, in a cottage garden full of flowers.
P0026.ttag: Test the Amazon Advertising Platform against a holdout group | Kwontified
P0026.desc: The Amazon Advertising Platform reaches shoppers before and after they search, and its reports credit it with sales that would have happened anyway. Test it.
P0026.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 27, 2018.
P0026.body:
The state of the Amazon Advertising Platform for brands in 2018 is simple to describe and hard to judge. AAP is the one way to reach Amazon’s shopper audiences beyond Amazon’s own sites, before and after they search, which makes it the natural partner to search ads. The difficulty is measurement. AAP’s reports credit it with sales that would often have happened anyway, because it is shown to people already likely to buy. Brands should start AAP with a holdout test and judge it on what it adds, not on what it claims.

Amazon Advertising Platform: what it is and who uses it

Amazon sells advertising in three ways, and the names cause confusion. Amazon Media Group is the in-house team that sells managed display and video campaigns. Amazon Marketing Services is the self-serve search advertising suite. The Amazon Advertising Platform, AAP, is Amazon’s programmatic buying platform, Digiday explained in December 2017.

AAP’s distinctive feature is reach. It is the only way advertisers can reach Amazon’s audience segments off Amazon’s own properties, the same report said. Advertisers can work with an Amazon team or buy through a self-serve platform Amazon introduced in 2014. Both brands that sell on Amazon and brands that do not use it.

Interest from large advertisers is rising quickly. The large agency groups WPP, Publicis and Omnicom were looking to spend more than $800 million combined on Amazon advertising in 2018, Digiday reported, citing the Wall Street Journal.

Why AAP’s reports overstate what it adds

Here is the counterintuitive part. The audiences that make AAP attractive are the same reason its reports flatter it.

Search ads appear after a shopper says what she wants. AAP chooses whom to show an ad to based on what Amazon knows about their shopping, such as the products and categories they have viewed. The most valuable audience, people who looked at a brand’s product page and did not buy, is also the audience most likely to come back and buy without any ad at all.

When one of those shoppers buys after seeing an AAP ad, the report credits the ad. It cannot tell whether the ad changed her mind or simply arrived before a purchase she was already going to make. The more precisely the audience is chosen, the larger that share of credited sales is likely to be.

Take a hypothetical campaign shown to 200,000 shoppers who viewed a brand’s products in the past month. Over the next two weeks, 4,000 of them buy, and the report credits AAP with all 4,000 sales. Now suppose a similar group of 200,000 shoppers who saw no ads produced 3,400 purchases in the same period. The campaign’s real contribution is 600 sales, not 4,000. If the campaign cost $9,000, the cost per added sale was $15, not the $2.25 the report implies.

That does not make AAP poor value. A $15 added sale may be excellent for a brand with good margins, and campaigns aimed at shoppers who have never seen the brand may add far more than this example. The point is that the report alone cannot say which is true.

There is a second effect worth measuring. Advertising that reaches shoppers before they search should show up later as more searches for the brand and its products on Amazon, which search ads can then convert. A brand that judges AAP only on the sales it claims directly will miss that part.

The link between the two runs deeper than searches. In Amazon Marketing Services, ad rankings are largely determined by product popularity and sales rather than by advertiser optimization alone, Edelman’s Todd Silverstein told Digiday. If that is right, demand AAP creates for a product does not only produce new searches. The extra sales also strengthen the product’s position in search, which makes its search ads cheaper to run. That benefit never appears in an AAP report, and it is one more reason to measure the brand’s whole Amazon business rather than each campaign alone.

How brands should start with AAP in 2018

Begin with a holdout, before the first dollar is spent. Split the audience you plan to reach into two similar groups, show ads to one and not the other, and compare purchases. Amazon’s team or an agency running AAP can set this up; insist on it before scaling.

Separate retargeting from prospecting. Ads shown to people who already viewed the product are closest to the sale and most likely to be over-credited. Ads shown to new audiences are further from the sale and more likely to add genuinely new demand. Measure them apart, because their reports mean different things.

Watch searches as well as sales. Track searches for the brand name and its main products on Amazon during and after prospecting campaigns. A rise there is evidence AAP is creating demand that search ads will capture.

Budget it as an experiment first, separate from the search budget it will later support. Start with a defined test budget and a clear question, such as how many added sales each thousand dollars produces, and decide whether to scale only when the answer is in.

What to do

  1. Choose one product line and one audience for a first AAP test, with a holdout group that sees no ads.
  2. Measure added sales against the holdout, and searches for your brand on Amazon, for four weeks.
  3. Scale only the audiences whose cost per added sale fits your margin.

We plan and measure AAP campaigns against holdout groups, not just platform reports. If you are considering Amazon’s programmatic advertising, talk to our team.

P0028.crumb: Unauthorized Amazon sellers start with a…
P0028.title: Unauthorized Amazon sellers start with a brand’s own distribution
P0028.alt: A warehouse aisle of pallet racks stacked with wrapped boxes, leading to an open roller door onto a sunny yard.
P0028.ttag: Unauthorized Amazon sellers start with a brand’s own distribution | Kwontified
P0028.desc: Most unauthorized Amazon sellers get their stock from a brand’s own wholesale, liquidation and supplier channels. The fix starts with how the brand distributes.
P0028.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 1, 2018.
P0028.body:
Most brands treat unauthorized Amazon sellers as outsiders who appeared from nowhere. Usually they did not. The stock those sellers list tends to come from the brand’s own channels: a wholesale customer selling on its overflow, a liquidation of last season’s excess, sometimes the factory that makes the product. In 2018, brands should treat unauthorized sellers as a question of distribution design. Map where product leaves the brand’s control and close those exits before chasing sellers one listing at a time.

Where unauthorized Amazon sellers get their stock

The sources are not mysterious, even when the sellers are. Genuine product has to come from somewhere, and the first sale in that chain is usually one the brand made or approved. Distributors and retailers are a common route. Amazon’s customer base is large enough that some distributors and retailers break their distribution agreements to become gray-market sellers, often under business names that hide who they are, Buy Box Experts wrote in March 2017. The same article noted that Amazon rarely gets involved in distribution disputes between brands and resellers, which leaves the brand to solve the problem itself.

The effect reaches the brand’s other channels. Product diverted from stores to online is usually sold at lower prices, Buy Box Experts noted, which undermines the brand’s efforts to keep online and store prices aligned. A store buyer who sees the brand’s products undercut online has every reason to ask for better terms, or to order less next season.

How the leak takes hold

Here is how a brand usually arrives at the problem. Each decision makes sense on its own.

The brand sells to an off-price chain to clear a slow style. The chain sells most of it in stores and passes the rest to a reseller, who lists it on Amazon below the brand’s normal price.

The brand runs a year-end liquidation to free warehouse space. The buyer pays a fraction of wholesale and has every reason to sell online, where the margin on cheap stock is best.

The brand signs a distributor in a new region with an agreement that says nothing about online marketplaces. The distributor’s customers discover that Amazon pays faster than their own shops.

The brand’s factory produces a few thousand units beyond the order, or keeps seconds that were meant to be destroyed. Some of them appear online months later.

None of these decisions was made with Amazon in mind, and that is the point. The brand’s distribution was designed for a world of stores, where excess stock could move quietly through outlets and regional sellers. Amazon makes every one of those exits visible, searchable and priced next to the brand’s own products.

That visibility has a direct cost on Amazon itself. When several sellers offer the same product, the cheapest offer often wins the Buy Box, the button most shoppers use to buy. A reseller holding liquidation stock bought at a fraction of wholesale can price below anything the brand’s own channels can match, so the brand’s authorized offer, or its wholesale customer’s, sits behind a cheaper one. The brand loses the sale and its control of the price signal at the same time, often for good.

Brands usually respond by pursuing the sellers: test purchases, warning letters, complaints to Amazon. That work has its place, especially against counterfeits. But against genuine product sold by someone the brand cannot identify, it tends to go in circles. Remove one seller and another appears, supplied from the same source.

The honest test is whether the brand knows where the stock came from. If it does not, it is treating the symptom.

There is a fair objection: some leakage is unavoidable, and liquidation and off-price channels are legitimate tools for managing inventory. Both are true. The goal is not to stop using them. It is to use them knowing that product sold through them may reach Amazon, and to price, contract and track accordingly.

How brands should redesign distribution in 2018

Map every exit. List each route by which product leaves the brand’s direct control: wholesale customers, distributors, off-price buyers, liquidators, factories and returns processors. For each, ask whether that product could end up on Amazon.

Write marketplaces into contracts. Distribution and wholesale agreements should say clearly whether, where and by whom the brand’s products may be sold online, and what happens when that is breached. Existing agreements written before Amazon mattered often say nothing.

Trace the stock. Serial numbers, lot codes or channel-specific packaging let a test purchase reveal which channel a product came through. Without tracing, the brand is guessing at its own supply chain.

Rethink excess inventory. Liquidation is a common source of cheap stock online. Selling excess through the brand’s own controlled channels, including its own Amazon listing, may return more than a liquidator pays and keeps prices intact.

Consider selling on Amazon directly. A brand that runs its own Amazon presence controls its product pages and gives shoppers an authorized option, which makes unauthorized offers easier to spot and harder to sustain.

What to do

  1. List every channel through which your product leaves your control, and mark those that could reach Amazon.
  2. Review your distribution and wholesale agreements for clauses on online marketplaces, and update those that are silent.
  3. Add lot or channel codes to your next production run so test purchases can identify the source.

We help brands trace where unauthorized stock comes from and redesign distribution to close the exits. If you are chasing the same sellers every month, talk to our team.

P0030.crumb: Negative keywords: when to block an…
P0030.title: Negative keywords: when to block an Amazon search, by the numbers
P0030.alt: Brass mesh sieve sifting grains and small stones onto a wooden table beside a brass tally counter.
P0030.ttag: Negative keywords: when to block an Amazon search, by the numbers | Kwontified
P0030.desc: Negative keywords are Amazon advertising’s cheapest efficiency gain when added by rule: block irrelevant searches at once, weak ones after enough clicks.
P0030.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 6, 2018.
P0030.body:
Negative keywords are the cheapest efficiency gain in Amazon Marketing Services. They cost nothing to add and stop spending on searches that cannot return a sale. The catch is timing. Block too late and the money is gone; block too early and a search that would have sold is cut off after a few unlucky clicks. The rule that works is simple: block irrelevant searches as soon as they appear, and block relevant but unprofitable searches only after they have had two to three times the clicks a sale should take.

Negative keywords Amazon advertisers need, and why

Most Amazon ads reach shoppers through keywords that match many different searches. Not every search has the same value, even when the same keyword triggers the ad, Practical Ecommerce noted in a guide to Sponsored Products in November 2016. A broad keyword for a brand’s sweater might match a shopper ready to buy it and a shopper looking for a competitor’s brand.

A negative keyword tells Amazon not to show the ad for a particular search. It is the only tool that removes spending outright rather than reducing it. Lowering a bid makes a bad search cheaper; blocking it makes it free, and the budget it was using goes back to searches that sell.

The stakes are rising. Sponsored Products took 85% of Amazon ad spend in the fourth quarter of 2017, and investment in them rose 64% from the third quarter, according to Merkle’s Q4 2017 Digital Marketing Report. More money flowing through broad keywords means more money flowing to the searches that never sell.

Why a search with no sales may still be worth keeping

Here is the counterintuitive part. Zero sales is not proof that a search does not work.

Start with what a sale can cost. Take a hypothetical product that can afford $10 of advertising per sale. If its clicks cost $0.80 each, a search breaks even when it converts at 8%, one sale for every 12.5 clicks.

Now suppose a relevant search has had 13 clicks and no sales. It has spent $10.40, more than a sale is worth, and the temptation is to block it. But if that search truly converts at 8%, the chance of seeing no sales in 13 clicks is about 34%. One time in three, a search that is exactly break-even looks like a failure at this point.

Wait for 30 clicks, and the picture changes. The chance that a search converting at 8% produces no sales in 30 clicks is about 8%. At that point, zero sales is strong evidence the search really converts below break-even, and blocking it is the right call. That is where the rule comes from: two to three times the clicks a sale should take.

The cost of waiting is the price of the evidence. In this example, the extra 17 clicks cost $13.60. Blocking every search after 13 unlucky clicks would cost more, because about one in three of the searches blocked would have paid for themselves.

Irrelevant searches are different. A search for a competitor’s brand, a product the brand does not make or an accessory for a different device does not need evidence. The shopper cannot be satisfied by the product, so every click is wasted. Those should be blocked the first time they appear in a search term report.

How to run negative keywords in 2018

Review the search term report weekly. Sort searches by spending and look first at those with clicks and no sales, since they are where the money leaks fastest.

Sort them into two groups. Searches the product cannot satisfy go straight to negatives. Searches the product could satisfy go on a watch list until they reach the click threshold.

Calculate the threshold for each product. Divide the most the product can afford per sale by its typical cost per click to get the clicks a sale should take, then multiply by two or three. Use three for products with high margins, where a false block costs more.

Use the narrowest match that solves the problem. Block the exact search where possible. Block a broader phrase only when every search containing it is irrelevant, such as a competitor’s name.

Use negatives to keep campaigns from competing. When an automatic or broad campaign finds a search that sells, the usual step is to give that search its own exact-match campaign with a bid set from its own results. Add the same search as a negative in the original campaign at the same time. Otherwise both campaigns bid on the same shopper, the brand competes with itself, and the report splits the search’s results across two places so neither shows the full picture.

Keep a shared list of irrelevant terms. Competitor names, products the brand does not make and wrong-device accessories tend to recur across products. Add them to every relevant campaign when it is built rather than waiting for each one to rediscover them at the brand’s expense.

Recheck blocked searches occasionally. A search that failed months ago may convert after a price change, new reviews or a better product page.

What to do

  1. Pull your last 60 days of search terms and list those with clicks and no sales.
  2. Block the irrelevant ones today, and calculate the click threshold for the rest.
  3. Block relevant searches only once they pass two to three times the clicks a sale should take.

We run negative keyword programs by rule, not by instinct. If your Amazon search term report has not been reviewed in weeks, talk to our team.

P0031.crumb: Amazon apparel in 2018 is a store, not an…
P0031.title: Amazon apparel in 2018 is a store, not an overflow channel
P0031.alt: Sunlit boutique with neutral-toned clothes on a wooden rail, folded knits on shelves and a rustic display table.
P0031.ttag: Amazon apparel in 2018 is a store, not an overflow channel | Kwontified
P0031.desc: Amazon apparel changed in 2017: forecast to pass Macy’s, it signed Nike, grew its own labels and raised clothing fees. Brands need a plan for its store.
P0031.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 8, 2018.
P0031.body:
For years, many clothing brands treated Amazon as a place where overflow ended up: last season’s styles, odd sizes, stock their retail partners passed on. That view no longer fits. In 2017, Amazon apparel came to look like a department store, with Amazon buying major brands directly, growing its own labels and raising what it charges sellers in clothing. Apparel brands should plan their Amazon range in 2018 the way they would plan a department store assortment: deciding which products belong there and on what terms.

Amazon apparel in 2017: scale, house labels and a big brand

Start with scale. The investment bank Cowen predicted that Amazon’s US apparel sales would pass those of Macy’s in 2017, reaching more than $28 billion, CNBC reported in April 2017.

Amazon is also building its own labels. Sales of its private-label fashion brands grew 26% in the fourth quarter of 2016 from a year earlier, according to Slice Intelligence data in the same report. They were still small: Macy’s Alfani label sold nearly ten times as much online over the same period. Dresses accounted for more than 40% of Amazon’s private-label apparel sales, Slice found.

The largest brand in the category changed its approach. Nike had long refused to sell directly to Amazon, fearing damage to its brand, but agreed in 2017 to supply some products in exchange for Amazon policing counterfeits and unauthorized third-party sales, the Wall Street Journal reported, via Fox Business.

And selling clothing costs more. From April 15, 2018, the referral fee for Clothing & Accessories rises from 15% to 17% of the sale price, with a $1.00 minimum, according to Amazon’s notice to sellers dated January 18. Higher Fulfillment by Amazon fees took effect on February 22.

How the overflow channel became a store

Here is how the shift took hold. For a long time, the clothing on Amazon came mostly from resellers and smaller sellers, and the large brands stayed out. Shoppers learned to buy basics there and fashion elsewhere.

As the audience grew, three things happened at once. Amazon began to court major brands directly, offering protection from unauthorized sellers in return for supply, as the Nike agreement shows. It launched its own labels in the categories where shoppers already bought. And it adjusted its fees in ways that change who can profit as an independent seller.

The result is a store with three kinds of shelf. One holds the brands Amazon buys from directly. One holds Amazon’s own labels, priced to compete. One holds everyone else, selling through the marketplace and paying higher fees for the privilege.

The private-label data shows where the house labels aim. A category such as dresses, where many shoppers search by style, color and price rather than by brand name, is easier for a new label to enter than one where shoppers ask for a brand by name. Brands whose products are bought that way face the most direct competition from Amazon’s labels.

There is a fair objection: Amazon’s own labels are still small next to an established department store label, and many apparel brands do most of their business elsewhere. That is true today. The point is that the store is being organized now, and the brands present when it takes shape will have more say in where they stand.

How apparel brands should plan Amazon in 2018

Choose the range deliberately, as a buyer would. Decide which part of the collection belongs on Amazon: core styles that sell year-round and are bought by brand, rather than whatever is left at season’s end.

Complete the size and color grid. Clothing shoppers abandon a product when their size is missing. A full grid of sizes and colors in stock matters more on Amazon than another new style.

Recalculate prices with the new fees. Add the higher referral fee and the February fulfillment changes to every product’s costs, and set prices that still leave a margin. For a $20 item, the referral fee alone rises from $3.00 to $3.40.

Protect the products shoppers ask for by name. Where shoppers search for the brand, make sure the brand’s own offer, or an authorized one, is the one they find. Where they search by style or price, expect competition from Amazon’s labels and invest in images and reviews.

Decide how to supply the store. An apparel brand can sell its range to Amazon as a vendor, sell it through the marketplace itself, or split the two. Selling to Amazon hands over pricing and depends on Amazon’s buyers choosing the right sizes. Selling through the marketplace keeps control of price and stock but means paying the higher clothing fees and running the operation.

Many apparel brands will be better served by one approach for core products and another for the rest. The choice should be made product by product, with the full cost of each route in view, rather than by habit.

Plan for returns. Fit-driven returns are part of selling clothing online. Clear size charts and accurate descriptions reduce them, which protects both margin and the product’s standing.

What to do

  1. List the products in your current collection that shoppers buy by your brand name, and make them the core of your Amazon range.
  2. Recalculate the margin on each Amazon product with the April 15 referral fee and the February fulfillment fees.
  3. Fill the gaps in sizes and colors for those core products before adding new styles.

We help apparel brands plan their Amazon range and pricing. If Amazon is still where your overflow ends up, talk to our team.

P0032.crumb: Set Amazon ACoS targets from margin, not…
P0032.title: Set Amazon ACoS targets from margin, not from a benchmark
P0032.alt: Brass balance scale weighing a twine-tied parcel against a pan of coins, beside a clipboard on a wooden table.
P0032.ttag: Set Amazon ACoS targets from margin, not from a benchmark | Kwontified
P0032.desc: A benchmark ACoS means opposite things for products with different margins. Set each Amazon ACoS target from the product’s own margin and its goal.
P0032.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 13, 2018.
P0032.body:
Advertising cost of sale, or ACoS, is the share of a product’s price spent on advertising to sell it. Brands often pick a target from a benchmark, an industry average or a number someone used at the last company. That target means nothing until it is set next to the product’s margin. One ACoS can be wildly profitable for one product and a guaranteed loss for another. The rule for 2018: calculate a break-even ACoS for each product, then set targets below it for profit or above it, deliberately and with a budget, for growth.

What an Amazon ACoS target has to cover

A sale on Amazon has costs before any advertising. There is the cost of the product. There is Amazon’s referral fee, a percentage of the price that is 15% in many categories; from April 15, it rises to 17% for Clothing & Accessories, according to Amazon’s notice to sellers dated January 18. For products sold through Fulfillment by Amazon, there is the fulfillment fee, which rose for many products on February 22, EcommerceBytes reported when the changes were announced.

What is left after those costs is the most the brand can spend to make the sale and still not lose money on it. Divided by the price, that is the break-even ACoS. Spend less and the sale makes money; spend more and it loses money.

The stakes are rising with spending. Investment in Sponsored Products rose 64% from the third quarter of 2017 to the fourth, according to Merkle’s Q4 2017 Digital Marketing Report. The more money flows through one target, the more a wrong target costs.

Why the same target means opposite things

Here is the counterintuitive part. Two products with the same price and the same ACoS can have opposite results, because ACoS is measured against price while profit is measured against margin.

Take two hypothetical products, each priced at $30 and each paying a 15% referral fee of $4.50. Product A costs $9.00 to make and $4.00 to fulfill, leaving $12.50 before advertising. Its break-even ACoS is about 41.7%. Product B costs $15.00 to make and $5.50 to fulfill, leaving $5.00. Its break-even ACoS is about 16.7%.

Now apply a 25% benchmark to both. Product A spends $7.50 per advertised sale and keeps $5.00, a healthy profit, while the brand is holding back spending that could have won more sales at a profit. Product B also spends $7.50 per advertised sale, but it only had $5.00 to spend, so it loses $2.50 on every one.

The benchmark did not just miss. It pushed the brand in opposite wrong directions on two products at the same time. And because a report that blends both products may show a combined ACoS near the benchmark, the brand may never notice.

Price changes move the line too. Suppose Product A goes on promotion at 10% off, to $27. Its referral fee falls to $4.05, but its costs do not, so it has $9.95 left before advertising and a break-even ACoS of about 36.9%. A brand that keeps bidding to the old target during a promotion spends more per sale exactly when each sale earns less.

Vendors face a version of the same problem. When Amazon buys the product and sets the price, ACoS is measured against Amazon’s retail price, but the brand’s margin is the wholesale price minus its own costs and Amazon’s deductions. A vendor’s break-even ACoS is that margin divided by the retail price, and it is often lower than the brand assumes.

That is why ACoS benchmarks mislead. An average across many brands blends products with margins as different as A and B. It cannot tell any one product what it can afford, because what a product can afford depends on costs no benchmark sees.

How to set ACoS targets by product

Calculate break-even for each product. Subtract the product cost, the referral fee and the fulfillment fee from the price, and divide what remains by the price. Recalculate whenever a fee, cost or price changes, including this spring’s fee changes.

Decide the goal product by product. A mature product with steady demand should usually run below break-even, keeping a profit on each advertised sale. A new product building reviews and sales history may run above break-even for a set period, as an investment.

Budget the investment explicitly. When a product runs above break-even, record how much it is losing per advertised sale, for how long and why. Growth spending without a limit becomes a permanent loss, and it is easy to miss because the product’s sales look healthy while its advertising quietly costs more than it returns.

Account for sales advertising does not track directly. A shopper who first finds a product through an ad may later buy it without one, and a product that sells more tends to rank better in search. Those effects can justify a target somewhat closer to break-even, but they should be estimated, not assumed.

Report ACoS next to break-even. A target on its own invites comparison with benchmarks. A target shown beside each product’s break-even shows whether the product is making or losing money on advertising.

What to do

  1. Calculate break-even ACoS for each of your top 20 Amazon products with the current fees.
  2. Assign each product a goal, profit or growth, and set its target relative to its own break-even.
  3. Replace any single account-wide ACoS target with product-level targets in your next bid review.

We set Amazon advertising targets from each product’s margin. If your account still runs on one benchmark ACoS, talk to our team.

P0034.crumb: Amazon reviews are a shared reputation…
P0034.title: Amazon reviews are a shared reputation built by the first five
P0034.alt: Plain kraft shipping box on a worn wooden table with five gold stars lined up in front against a sage wall.
P0034.ttag: Amazon reviews are a shared reputation built by the first five | Kwontified
P0034.desc: The first few Amazon reviews do most of the work, they are harder to earn since 2016, and every seller on a listing shares them. Plan reviews deliberately.
P0034.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 15, 2018.
P0034.body:
Shoppers on Amazon read reviews before they read almost anything else a brand writes. Reviews behave less like customer feedback than like a reputation: built quickly by the first handful, held in common by every seller of the product and easily damaged by one careless order. Amazon has also made those first reviews harder to earn since it banned incentivized reviews in October 2016. Brands should plan the first reviews into every launch and protect the shared reputation by controlling who sells their products and how orders are fulfilled.

What the research says about Amazon reviews and buying

The first reviews carry most of the weight. The purchase likelihood for a product with five reviews is 270% greater than for a product with none, according to a June 2017 study by Northwestern University’s Spiegel Research Center, conducted with the reviews company PowerReviews. The effect was larger for more expensive products, the study found.

Who writes the review matters too. Reviews from verified buyers averaged 4.34 stars, compared with 3.89 for anonymous reviewers, according to a summary of the same study.

Amazon has tightened the rules. In October 2016, it banned reviews from shoppers who received free or discounted products in exchange for writing them, and it has been deleting older incentivized reviews, Retail Dive reported. Amazon has since launched a program of its own to gather reviews for products that have fewer than five, Digital Commerce 360 noted in 2017.

How a reputation takes hold on a product page

Here is how a product’s reputation usually forms, and why it is fragile.

A new product starts with nothing. Shoppers who find it see no reviews and mostly move on, so it sells slowly. The few who buy are a mix: some delighted, some indifferent, a few unhappy. Because there are so few reviews, each one carries great weight. One early complaint about sizing or packaging can sit at the top of the page for months.

As reviews accumulate, the reputation settles. The average star rating stops moving much, and shoppers read it as a fact about the product. That is why the first handful matters so much. They set a reputation that is slow to change.

Price changes the stakes. Because reviews carry more weight for expensive products, as the Spiegel study found, a higher-priced launch suffers more from an empty or thin review section. A brand launching a premium product should expect slower early sales until the first reviews arrive and plan its advertising and stock to carry the product through that period.

The reputation is shared. On Amazon, every seller offering the same product sells it through the same product page, under the same reviews. A brand’s product sold by a reseller who ships slowly, sends damaged stock or sells an older version will collect complaints about the product, not the seller. The brand inherits them.

That is the structural point most brands miss. They manage their own service carefully and then leave their reputation in the hands of whoever else is selling the product. A single reseller with poor fulfillment can do more damage to the star rating than any number of the brand’s own good orders can repair.

Shoppers’ habits sharpen the effect. Many read the most recent reviews and the most critical ones first, looking for the reason not to buy. A cluster of complaints about the same problem, even if old, tells the shopper what to fear.

There is a fair objection: reviews mostly reflect the product, and a good product will earn good reviews in time. In the long run, that is broadly true. But “in time” can mean months of slow sales, and a poor start can sink a product that would have succeeded with a better one.

How brands should manage reviews in 2018

Plan the first reviews into every launch. Use the methods Amazon allows, such as its own early-review program for eligible products or its Vine program for vendors, and time advertising so the product reaches enough real buyers to earn its first five reviews quickly.

Avoid shortcuts. Since the October 2016 ban, offering products in exchange for reviews outside Amazon’s own programs puts the brand’s account at risk, and deleted reviews can leave a product with fewer than it had. Earning the first reviews legitimately is slower, but it builds a reputation that will not be taken away.

Read reviews as product feedback. Recurring complaints about sizing, durability or packaging are information about the product. Fix the cause, and update the product page so shoppers’ expectations match what they receive.

Control who sells the product. Since every seller shares the reviews, unauthorized sellers with poor fulfillment are a direct threat to the brand’s reputation. Tightening distribution protects the star rating as much as the price.

Watch the variations. Grouping too many different products under one page blends their reviews, so a weak variant drags down a strong one. Group only products that shoppers would judge the same way, such as sizes or colors of one design, and keep different designs on their own pages.

What to do

  1. Count the reviews on each of your top products, and plan how new products will reach five quickly through Amazon’s own programs.
  2. Read the most recent critical reviews on your top ten products and list the problems that recur.
  3. Check which sellers offer your products, and investigate any whose orders appear in complaints.

P0037.title: Google Shopping Actions turns retailers into sellers in one cart
P0037.alt: Wicker basket filled with twine-tied wrapped gifts on a sunlit wooden step against a terracotta wall.
P0037.ttag: Google Shopping Actions turns retailers into sellers in one cart | Kwontified
P0037.desc: Google’s Shopping Actions charges retailers per sale and puts them in one cart, so a brand’s products compete on price across retailers. Plan for it.
P0037.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 20, 2018.
P0037.body:
Google launched Shopping Actions on March 19, a program that lets shoppers buy from several retailers through Google Search and the Google Assistant with one shared cart. Retailers pay Google for each sale rather than each click. That detail matters most for brands. A platform paid per sale has every reason to favor the offers most likely to sell, so a brand’s retail partners now compete as sellers of the same products, side by side, in Google’s cart. Price consistency and product data across retailers matter more than they did before March 19.

What Google Shopping Actions does

The program offers a shareable list, a universal cart and instant checkout with saved payment details across Google.com and the Assistant, Reuters reported. Early partners include Target, Walmart, Home Depot, Costco and Ulta Beauty, and they will pay Google for each product purchase made through Search, Google Express and the Assistant, according to the same report.

The listings appear in the sponsored Shopping unit on Google’s results and on Google Shopping, while Google said organic rankings will not change, Voicebot reported.

Google points to early results. Target’s Google Express baskets have grown by nearly 20% over the last six months, and Ulta Beauty’s average order value on Google Express has risen 35% since 2016, according to Google’s announcement.

Why paying per sale changes who wins

Here is the counterintuitive part. Paying per sale sounds like a better deal for retailers than paying per click, and in one sense it is: no sale, no charge. But it also changes what Google is selling.

Under a per-click model, a platform earns money whenever a shopper clicks, whether or not she buys. Under a per-sale model, it earns only when she buys. A platform paid that way has every reason to show the offer most likely to turn into a sale. For a given product, that usually means the lowest price, the item in stock and the fastest delivery.

Google has not published how it ranks offers within Shopping Actions, and it would be wrong to claim to know. But the incentive points in a clear direction, and it is the same one that shapes a marketplace’s buy button: when several sellers offer the same product, the one with the best combination of price and service tends to win the sale.

Now apply that to a brand. Its products may be sold by several of the participating retailers at once. On their own websites, those retailers never appear side by side. In a shared Google cart, they can. A shopper searching for the brand’s product may see the same item from three retailers and pick the cheapest, and Google, paid only when she buys, has no reason to discourage that.

The cost per sale also changes what retailers choose to list. A retailer paying Google on every sale will put forward the products where that fee still leaves a margin. A brand’s best sellers are likely to make the cut; its slower or lower-margin products may not, which means the brand’s range on Google is decided by its retailers’ arithmetic rather than its own.

So Shopping Actions does two things to a brand’s retail relationships. It makes price differences between retailers visible, and it rewards the retailer that undercuts. Brands that tolerate uneven pricing across retailers will see it amplified in front of shoppers.

There is one more effect, for brands that also sell on marketplaces. The program is open to all US retailers, according to Reuters, as reported by BizTech Magazine. Amazon is not part of it. For a brand that sells directly on its own website as well as through Amazon, that creates a choice: Shopping Actions is a way to reach Google’s shoppers with a checkout that does not send them to Amazon.

That choice has costs. The brand would pay Google on each sale, run its own fulfillment to Google’s delivery standards and compete in the same cart as its own retail partners. For brands whose direct sales are small, the program is more likely to matter through their retailers than through their own site.

How brands should prepare in 2018

Check price consistency across retailers. List each top product’s price at each retailer likely to join Shopping Actions. Where prices differ widely, expect the cheapest retailer to win more of the Google sales and the others to complain.

Treat product data as shared. Shopping Actions uses retailers’ product feeds. The names, images and descriptions a brand supplies to each retailer will shape how its products look on Google, so make them complete and consistent.

Ask partners what they will list, and why. Retailers decide which products to put into the program. A brand should know which of its products each partner is listing, and push for its best sellers to be included.

Watch the channel closely. Search Google Shopping for top products each month and record which retailers appear and at what prices. That is the clearest signal of how the new cart is treating the brand.

What to do

  1. List the price of your top 20 products at each large retail partner and flag differences of more than a few percent.
  2. Review the product data you send each partner for completeness and consistency.
  3. Ask each partner whether it is joining Shopping Actions and which of your products it will list.

We help brands manage price and product data across retailers and marketplaces. If your partners are about to sell your products side by side on Google, talk to our team.

P0039.crumb: Instagram shopping tags turn a brand’s…
P0039.title: Instagram shopping tags turn a brand’s posts into a shelf
P0039.alt: Smartphone in camera mode propped on a wooden shelf among handmade ceramic cups, bowls and vases.
P0039.ttag: Instagram shopping tags turn a brand’s posts into a shelf | Kwontified
P0039.desc: On Amazon shoppers search; on Instagram products find them. Tagged products turn a brand’s posts into a shelf, which changes what brands photograph and measure.
P0039.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 22, 2018.
P0039.body:
On Amazon, shoppers search. On Instagram, products find them. That difference is why shopping on Instagram, which expanded to eight more countries on March 20, matters more than a new button. A product tag joins the moment a shopper discovers something while browsing to the product page itself, so every post a brand publishes becomes a shelf. Brands should plan their Instagram content as merchandising in 2018, photographing products the way shoppers discover them and measuring posts by the shopping they start.

What changed with shopping on Instagram

Instagram opened shoppable posts to businesses in the UK, France, Italy, Germany, Australia, Brazil, Canada and Spain on March 20, Marketing Land reported. Businesses can tag up to 5 products in an image or 20 in a carousel, and shoppers see prices and product details in the feed and through a Shop tab on the business profile, Marketing Dive reported.

The audience is already shopping-minded. About half of Instagram’s daily active users in the US follow a shopping business, and more than 200 million accounts visit a business profile every day, according to the company, as reported by Marketing Land.

Before tags, the path from a post to a purchase was clumsy. A brand that wanted to send shoppers to its site from Instagram could mostly do so only through the link in its profile, FashionNetwork noted. Early users report results: beauty brand Tyme saw traffic grow 44% after tagging its products, Retail Dive reported, citing Instagram.

How discovery shopping takes hold

Here is the behavior underneath. A shopper on Amazon arrives with a question: she types what she wants and compares the answers. A shopper on Instagram arrives with no question at all. She is scrolling through accounts she chose to follow, and a product catches her eye in a photo of someone wearing it, using it or living with it.

Until now, that moment of interest was easy to lose. To act on it, the shopper had to leave the post, find the brand’s profile, tap a link and search the brand’s site for the product she saw. Many did not bother, and the interest faded before the shopper ever reached a page where she could buy.

A tag removes those steps. The shopper taps the product in the photo, sees the price and goes to the page. The moment of discovery and the product page are now one tap apart.

That changes what a brand’s posts are. They used to be advertising for the brand in general. Now each post is also a display of specific products for sale, closer to a shop window than to a magazine ad. The photograph is doing the job a product listing does on Amazon, but in the context where the shopper first sees the product.

It also changes which images work. On a marketplace, a clean product shot on a white background helps a shopper who already knows what she wants. On Instagram, the shopper is not yet looking. The image that works is the one that shows the product in use, in a setting the shopper wants to be part of.

Discovery on Instagram does not always end on Instagram. A shopper who sees a product in a post may tap the tag and buy from the brand’s site. She may also leave the app and search for the product on Amazon, where she already has an account and fast delivery. That is not a failure of the post. It is a reason to make sure the product carries the same name on Instagram, on the brand’s site and on Amazon, so the shopper finds the right item wherever she goes to buy it.

It also suggests a way to read the results. A brand that posts a product heavily on Instagram should watch searches for that product’s name on Amazon over the following days. If they rise, the post is creating demand that another channel is collecting, and the tag count alone will understate what the post did.

There is a fair objection: Instagram’s shoppers browse more than they buy, and a tap on a tag is a long way from a sale. That is true. But a tap tells a brand which products and which images spark interest, information a search-driven marketplace rarely provides.

How brands should use product tags in 2018

Plan posts as merchandising. Decide which products each post should sell, not only what it should say about the brand, and tag them.

Photograph products the way shoppers discover them. Invest in images of products in use and in context, alongside the clean shots marketplaces need.

Keep the catalog accurate. Tags depend on a connected product catalog, so prices, names and availability must match what shoppers find on the product page.

Measure by the shopping a post starts. Track taps on tags and visits to product pages for each post, and compare them across products, images and formats.

Use the new markets. Brands selling in the eight newly eligible countries can now tag products for local shoppers; set up each market’s catalog with local prices before posting.

What to do

  1. Review your last 20 Instagram posts and note which products each one could have tagged.
  2. Commission product-in-use images for your top products, alongside your existing marketplace photography.
  3. Start tagging products in every relevant post and report tag taps and product-page visits monthly.

We help brands plan Instagram content as a shopping channel alongside their marketplaces. If your posts show products shoppers cannot buy, talk to our team.

P0040.crumb: The Amazon Buy Box is a rule set: a gate…
P0040.title: The Amazon Buy Box is a rule set: a gate, then a race
P0040.alt: Open wooden gate beside a block wall leading onto a curving red running track in morning sun.
P0040.ttag: The Amazon Buy Box is a rule set: a gate, then a race | Kwontified
P0040.desc: The Amazon Buy Box works in two stages: an eligibility gate, then a contest on price and fulfillment. Brands should fix the gate before they cut prices.
P0040.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 27, 2018.
P0040.body:
The Buy Box, the button through which most Amazon purchases are made, is often described as a black box, but it behaves more like a rule set with two stages. First, Amazon decides which offers may compete at all, based on stock, condition and seller performance. Then it weighs landed price and fulfillment among the offers that passed. Brands that lose the Buy Box usually respond by cutting price. The rule for 2018 is to fix the gate first, because a lower price cannot win for an offer that fails it.

How the Amazon Buy Box works

The stakes are large. The Buy Box accounts for about 82% of sales on Amazon, according to a 2017 guide from the repricing company xsellco.

Amazon does not award the box to one seller permanently. It rotates it among eligible sellers, switching between them depending on price, performance metrics and other factors, the same guide explains. To be eligible, a seller needs a history of sales on Amazon, must be selling the item new, must have stock available and must maintain high performance metrics.

Price is measured as landed price, the total the shopper pays including shipping. The lowest price does not guarantee the box, especially if the seller’s performance metrics are poor, xsellco notes.

There is a second reason the box matters for brands that advertise. Sponsored Products ads appear only for offers that hold the Buy Box, Practical Ecommerce noted in 2016. A brand that loses the box does not just lose sales to another seller. Its ads stop serving too.

Why cutting price is usually the wrong first move

Here is the counterintuitive part. When a brand loses the Buy Box, the obvious response is to lower the price. That works only if the brand is already through the gate.

Think of the two stages separately. In the first stage, an offer either qualifies or it does not. An offer that is out of stock, or whose seller performance has slipped, is not competing on price at all. Cutting its price changes nothing, except the margin on the sales it eventually makes.

In the second stage, price matters, but alongside fulfillment. An offer fulfilled through Fulfillment by Amazon brings Amazon’s own delivery promise with it, so it can compete against a slightly cheaper offer that ships more slowly. Two offers with the same fulfillment compete mostly on landed price.

Take a hypothetical brand that sells its own product through FBA at $25.00, with a reseller offering the same product at $24.50, merchant-fulfilled with $4.00 shipping. The reseller’s landed price is $28.50, so the brand’s offer is cheaper to the shopper despite the higher item price. If the brand loses the box anyway, price is not the problem. The likely causes are in the first stage: a stockout, a lapse in performance, or a new reseller with Prime-eligible stock.

Now suppose the reseller switches to FBA at $24.50. Fulfillment is equal, landed prices differ by 50 cents, and the box will rotate largely on price. Only now does a price decision make sense, and the brand should weigh whether winning more of the rotation is worth 50 cents on every sale.

The advertising link raises the stakes of getting this right. Every hour the brand’s offer is out of the box is an hour its Sponsored Products ads are not serving. A stockout costs the sales the ads would have made as well as the organic ones.

Vendors face the same rule from the other side. When Amazon buys a brand’s product and sells it as the retailer, Amazon’s own offer competes for the box like any other. If Amazon runs out of stock because a purchase order was late or too small, a reseller’s offer can take the box, and the vendor’s Sponsored Products ads stop serving even though the vendor did nothing wrong in the advertising account.

For vendors, keeping Amazon in stock is part of keeping the ads running, and purchase order gaps deserve the same daily attention as bids.

How brands should manage the Buy Box in 2018

Check the gate daily, before anything else. Track stock levels, performance metrics and whether each top product holds the box. Losing it because of a stockout is the most common and most avoidable cause.

Compare landed prices, not list prices, because shipping often decides the comparison. When a competing offer appears, add its shipping to its price before deciding whether to respond.

Match fulfillment before matching price. If a competing offer has Prime-eligible fulfillment and yours does not, fixing fulfillment may win back more of the rotation than a price cut would.

Tie advertising to the box, product by product. Pause or reduce bids on products that have lost the box, and restore them when it is regained, so the budget goes to offers that can serve.

Control who can compete. Fewer unauthorized sellers mean fewer offers in the rotation, which is a distribution question, not a pricing one, and the most durable way to keep the box.

What to do

  1. List your top 20 products and record, for each, whether you hold the Buy Box and why not if you do not.
  2. For each product you are losing, check stock and performance first, then compare landed prices and fulfillment.
  3. Set a rule that reduces advertising on any product while it is out of the Buy Box.

We monitor Buy Box status alongside advertising so neither runs blind. If you lose the box and reach for a price cut first, talk to our team.

P0042.crumb: The Amazon product page does every job a…
P0042.title: The Amazon product page does every job a store used to split
P0042.alt: Navy leather handbag on a rustic shop counter with a brass mirror, leather goods display, cash register and box.
P0042.ttag: The Amazon product page does every job a store used to split | Kwontified
P0042.desc: A store splits selling across packaging, signs, staff and brochures. On Amazon the product page does all of it, on a phone, with content others can edit.
P0042.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 29, 2018.
P0042.body:
In a store, selling a product is a team effort. The packaging catches the eye, the shelf sign states the price and the main benefit, a salesperson answers questions and a brochure explains the details. On Amazon, the product detail page has to do all of those jobs at once, increasingly on a phone, with content other sellers can shape. Brands should treat each top product page as their most important piece of merchandising in 2018, assigning each part of the page its store job and securing control of it.

How the Amazon product detail page took over the store’s jobs

Think of the parts of the page as the parts of a store.

The main image is the packaging. In a search result, it is often the only thing a shopper sees before deciding whether to look closer, the way packaging competes on a crowded shelf.

The other images are the display. In a store, a shopper picks a product up, turns it over and holds it against herself. On Amazon, the gallery has to stand in for that: the product from every side, in use, next to something familiar for scale.

The title is the shelf sign. It tells the shopper what the product is and, ideally, the one reason to choose it.

The bullet points are the salesperson. They answer the questions a shopper would ask in a store: what it does, what it fits, what it is made of, how big it is.

The description is the brochure. For brands, it has become much richer. Amazon now offers Enhanced Brand Content to sellers in its Brand Registry, letting them build a richer product description from images, text and the brand’s story, Practical Ecommerce explained in July 2017.

The reviews are word of mouth, and they carry great weight. A product with five reviews is 270% more likely to be bought than one with none, according to a June 2017 study by Northwestern University’s Spiegel Research Center.

Why the page is harder to run than a shelf

Here is how the page became harder to manage than the store it replaced.

In a store, each job belongs to someone. The packaging team designs the box, merchandising writes the shelf sign, the retailer trains its staff. On Amazon, the same jobs land on one page, and often on no one in particular. The image comes from a photographer, the title from whoever set up the listing, the bullets from a product manager years ago.

The screen keeps getting smaller. Customer orders through the Amazon app more than doubled on Prime Day 2017 compared with the year before, Amazon said. On a phone, a shopper sees the main image, part of the title and the price before anything else. The jobs at the top of the page carry more of the load.

And the page is shared. On Amazon, a product has one page no matter how many sellers offer it, and its content can be shaped by more than one of them. That is why Amazon’s Brand Registry matters: it is the program that gives brand owners more control over the content on their product pages. Amazon launched a new version of it in 2017, and brands enrolled before April 30, 2017 had to re-enroll to keep its benefits, Amazon said in November.

The result is that many brands have pages built by accident. A strong product with a weak main image is a good product in a forgettable box. A page whose bullets do not answer the obvious question is a store without a salesperson.

There is a fair objection: great pages cannot save a weak product, and shoppers on Amazon rely heavily on price and reviews. True. But between two products with similar prices and ratings, the page that does its jobs well wins the sale, and the brand controls the page in a way it does not control price competition or reviews.

How brands should run product pages in 2018

Assign each part of the page a job. Review the main image as packaging, the title as a shelf sign, the bullets as a salesperson and the description as a brochure, and judge each against its job.

Design for the phone first. Check every top page on a phone, the way a growing share of shoppers now see it, and fix what is cut off. Make sure the main image and the first words of the title do the most important work.

Answer the questions shoppers ask. Read the questions and reviews on each product and make sure the bullets answer the common ones before a shopper has to ask.

Use the brand tools. Enroll in the current Brand Registry, re-enrolling if the brand joined before April 30, 2017, and use Enhanced Brand Content on top products.

Name an owner. Give one person responsibility for the content of each top product page, with a schedule for review. Pages drift: a competitor’s new product changes what shoppers ask, a packaging change makes the main image out of date, a new size never makes it into the bullets. Someone has to notice.

What to do

  1. Open your top ten product pages on a phone and note what a shopper sees before scrolling.
  2. Rewrite the bullets on each to answer the three questions shoppers ask most in reviews and questions.
  3. Confirm your brand is enrolled in the current Brand Registry and add Enhanced Brand Content to your top products.

We help brands plan and maintain their most important product pages. If your pages were built by whoever set up the listing, talk to our team.
