P0044.title: FBA or merchant-fulfilled: compare the cost per sale, not per box
P0044.alt: Brass balance scale weighing a twine-wrapped parcel against coins in a packing room with kraft paper rolls.
P0044.ttag: FBA or merchant-fulfilled: compare the cost per sale, not per box | Kwontified
P0044.desc: Fulfillment by Amazon often costs more per box but less per sale, because the Prime badge lifts conversion and Buy Box share. Model both before choosing.
P0044.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 3, 2018.
P0044.body:
Brands choosing between Fulfillment by Amazon and shipping orders themselves usually compare one number: what it costs to get a unit to a customer. That comparison misses half the decision. FBA changes revenue as well as cost, because its Prime badge affects how often a brand’s offer wins the Buy Box and how often a shopper who clicks goes on to buy. A method that costs more per box can cost less per sale. The rule for 2018 is to model fulfillment product by product on the full cost of a sale, including advertising.

What FBA or merchant-fulfilled actually changes

The cost side moved in February 2018. Amazon’s new FBA fees took effect on February 22, applied year-round rather than with a separate holiday rate, and dimensional weight is now calculated by dividing a unit’s volume by 139 rather than 166, EcommerceBytes reported when Amazon announced the changes. Light, bulky products pay more as a result.

The revenue side is less visible but often larger. Fulfillment method is one of the main factors Amazon weighs in awarding the Buy Box, alongside landed price and seller performance, according to a 2017 guide from xsellco. An offer fulfilled by Amazon carries Prime eligibility, and Prime shoppers can filter for it.

That link reaches advertising too. Sponsored Products ads serve only for offers that hold the Buy Box, Practical Ecommerce noted in 2016, so the fulfillment choice also decides how often a brand’s ads can run.

Why the cheaper box can be the more expensive sale

Here is the counterintuitive part, worked through with a hypothetical product priced at $30.

Suppose FBA costs the brand $4.50 per unit, including storage, while shipping the order itself costs $6.00 for packing and postage. On cost per box, merchant fulfillment looks $1.50 worse. Many brands would stop there.

Now add advertising. Suppose the product’s clicks cost $0.75 each. With the Prime badge, 12% of shoppers who click go on to buy; without it, 9% do. At 12%, each sale takes about 8.3 clicks, or $6.25 of advertising. At 9%, it takes about 11.1 clicks, or $8.33.

The full cost of an advertised sale through FBA is $4.50 plus $6.25, or $10.75. Through merchant fulfillment, it is $6.00 plus $8.33, or $14.33. The fulfillment difference of $1.50 has become a difference of $3.58 per sale.

The numbers can also run the other way. Suppose instead that the brand ships its own orders for $3.50, cheaper than FBA, and its products sell slowly enough that FBA storage fees climb. A slow-moving product that sits in Amazon’s warehouses for months can cost far more to store than to ship from the brand’s own warehouse. For that product, merchant fulfillment may be the better choice even after the conversion effect.

The point is that the right answer depends on the product. Fast sellers with good conversion gains usually favor FBA. Slow sellers, oversized products and those whose shoppers do not care about Prime often favor shipping in-house. A single policy for the whole range is almost always wrong for some of it.

There are also middle paths. Amazon offers a program that lets qualifying sellers keep the Prime badge while shipping orders themselves, in exchange for meeting strict delivery standards. For a brand with a capable warehouse, that can capture much of the conversion benefit without FBA’s storage costs, though the delivery promises leave little room for error.

A brand can also run both methods on the same product. Keeping a merchant-fulfilled offer active alongside FBA stock acts as insurance. If FBA inventory runs out, the brand’s own offer keeps the product available while new stock is in transit. Without it, the Buy Box, and the ads that depend on it, can pass to another seller for days.

There is a fair objection: brands rarely know their conversion rate with and without Prime for the same product. That is true, and it is why the decision should start with a test on a few products rather than an assumption about all of them.

Choose fulfillment product by product in 2018

Calculate the cost per box both ways. Use the FBA fees that took effect on February 22, 2018, and the brand’s real costs for packing and postage, including labor.

Add the conversion effect. Where possible, compare the conversion rate of the same product with and without Prime eligibility, or of similar products. Where the data does not exist, test.

Include advertising. Multiply the cost per click by the clicks a sale takes under each method, and add it to the fulfillment cost.

Watch the speed of sale. Products that sell slowly carry storage costs in FBA that grow with time. Set a rule for how long stock may sit before moving it or switching methods.

Split the range. Use FBA for products where it wins on the full cost of a sale and ship the rest in-house. Revisit the split each quarter, because fees, click costs and sales speed all change, and a product that belonged in FBA in the spring may not belong there by the holidays.

What to do

  1. For your top 20 products, calculate the cost per box under FBA and under merchant fulfillment with the February 2018 fees.
  2. Add advertising cost per sale under each method using your own click costs and conversion rates.
  3. Choose fulfillment product by product, and test the method on three products where the answer is unclear.

We model fulfillment and advertising together so the cheaper choice is the cheaper sale. If you chose your fulfillment method once for every product, talk to our team.

P0045.title: Amazon beauty in 2018: prestige brands trade supply for control
P0045.alt: Vintage glass perfume bottle and brass key under a glass cloche on a wooden table by a pink wall.
P0045.ttag: Amazon beauty in 2018: prestige brands trade supply for control | Kwontified
P0045.desc: Luxury beauty was Amazon’s fastest-growing category in 2017. Prestige brands are entering on new terms: selling to Amazon in return for control of their pages.
P0045.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 5, 2018.
P0045.body:
For years, prestige beauty brands kept their distance from Amazon. Their products appeared there anyway, sold by resellers at prices and with presentation the brands did not choose. That is changing quickly. Luxury beauty was Amazon’s fastest-growing category in 2017, and much of the growth came from brands entering directly on new terms: supplying Amazon in exchange for control over who sells their products. For beauty brands in 2018, the question is no longer whether to be on Amazon but on what terms.

What changed in Amazon beauty in 2017

The growth was concentrated at the top. Luxury beauty was the fastest-growing category on Amazon in 2017, up 47% to an estimated $400 million, according to One Click Retail’s annual review, the Motley Fool reported in January.

Cosmetics grew at both ends. Estimated US sales of mass cosmetics on Amazon grew 45% in 2017 to $110 million, and luxury cosmetics grew 51% to $35 million, One Click Retail reported in February. The top sellers in both segments lost market share as more brands entered.

The entrants came on new terms. Much of the growth in luxury cosmetics came from brands entering Amazon as first-party sellers, rather than from brands already there growing, Chain Drug Review reported, citing One Click Retail. Some brands, such as Calvin Klein and Bliss, sell selected products in Amazon’s Luxury Beauty category in return for having their brands gated, which bars third parties from selling them, Glossy reported.

How a category prestige brands avoided became one they enter

Here is how the shift took hold.

Prestige beauty depended on control. Brands chose where their products were sold, how they were displayed and what they cost, because the store experience and the price were part of the product. Amazon offered none of that control, so many brands stayed away.

Staying away did not keep their products off Amazon. Resellers bought stock through distributors and other channels and listed it themselves. The brand’s products were on Amazon, but on someone else’s terms: inconsistent prices, uncertain freshness and pages the brand never approved.

Amazon offered a trade. By supplying Amazon directly and accepting a selective presence in its luxury store, a brand could get its products gated, so that resellers could no longer list them. The brand gave up some independence and got back control of how it appeared.

The trade has a cost on the other side. A brand that sells to Amazon as a first-party vendor hands Amazon the retail price. For a prestige brand whose department store and specialty partners expect consistent pricing, that is a real concern: Amazon may price below what other retailers charge, and those partners will notice. The brands that make the trade work tend to agree carefully which products go to Amazon, keeping signature items or exclusives for other channels.

Each brand that accepted made the category more credible for the next. That is why the growth data looks the way it does. New entrants drove much of the luxury growth, and the brands already there lost share as the shelf filled.

Shopper behavior is changing the content too. Beauty shoppers on Amazon search for ingredients, especially those with functional benefits, One Click Retail’s chief executive Spencer Millerberg said, GCI Magazine reported. A page built around a brand’s story but silent on ingredients can miss the search that matters.

There is a fair objection: for some prestige brands, the store experience and selective distribution are the brand, and no amount of control on Amazon replaces them. That may be right for a few. For most, the question is whether their products will be on Amazon on their own terms or someone else’s.

What beauty brands should decide in 2018

Find out who sells your products on Amazon today. Search for every product and record the sellers, prices, page quality and the age of the reviews. That is the starting point for any decision.

Decide on terms, not just presence, before the first conversation with Amazon. If you enter, decide which products, through which program, and what control you need in return, including gating where Amazon offers it.

Build pages for ingredient searches. Name the key ingredients and what they do in titles and bullet points, so shoppers searching by ingredient find the product. Use the same ingredient names shoppers use, not only the brand’s own vocabulary, and check the search terms in your advertising reports to see which ones actually bring buyers.

Protect freshness and authenticity. Beauty products age, and gray-market stock often comes through long chains of distributors, so it can arrive close to expiry or poorly stored. A shopper who receives a dried-out product does not blame the reseller. She blames the brand, in a review that every future shopper reads. Control of who sells is also control of what arrives.

Move before the shelf fills. The data shows brands already on Amazon losing share as new brands arrive. Waiting means entering against more established competitors, with more reviews and longer sales histories than a newcomer can quickly match.

What to do

  1. Search Amazon for your top 20 products and list every seller, price and page problem you find.
  2. Decide which products you would offer Amazon directly, and what control you would ask for in return.
  3. Rewrite the titles and bullets of your top products to name key ingredients and their benefits.

We help beauty brands decide how to enter Amazon and run the business once they do. If your products are already on Amazon on someone else’s terms, talk to our team.

P0046.crumb: Amazon long-term storage fees: slow stock…
P0046.title: Amazon long-term storage fees: slow stock now costs every month
P0046.alt: Sunlit stockroom shelf with open cardboard boxes and a small pile of coins on bare wooden boards.
P0046.ttag: Amazon long-term storage fees: slow stock now costs every month | Kwontified
P0046.desc: From September, Amazon assesses long-term storage every month, with a 50-cent monthly minimum on year-old units. Small, cheap products are hit hardest.
P0046.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 10, 2018.
P0046.body:
Amazon is changing how it charges for inventory that sits too long in its warehouses. Long-term storage fees, now assessed twice a year, will be assessed every month from September 15. From August 15, units stored for a year or more will pay at least 50 cents each per month. The effect is that slow inventory stops being a twice-yearly cleanup and becomes a monthly cost, so brands should send in only what sells within months.

Small, inexpensive products are hit hardest, because the new minimum can exceed what they earn. Brands should plan how much stock to send in by how fast each product sells, and decide what to remove before the deadlines arrive.

What is changing in Amazon long-term storage fees

Amazon announced the changes on March 1, EcommerceBytes reported. Monthly inventory storage fees rise by 5 cents per cubic foot for standard and oversize items from April 1. From September 15, long-term storage fees will be assessed monthly rather than twice a year. From August 15, a minimum long-term storage fee of 50 cents per unit per month will apply to units stored for 365 days or more, and Amazon will charge whichever is greater, the minimum or the regular long-term fee.

The new monthly rates are $3.45 per cubic foot for items stored six months to a year and $6.90 per cubic foot for items stored a year or longer, SellerEngine explained on April 5. Until the change, Amazon assesses long-term fees twice a year, in February and August.

Amazon also announced storage limits, with an overage fee of $10 per cubic foot for inventory above a seller’s limit, EcommerceBytes reported.

Why the minimum hits small products hardest

Here is the counterintuitive part. Storage fees are usually thought of as a problem for bulky products, because they are charged by volume. The new minimum reverses that for old stock.

Take a hypothetical small product, such as a lipstick or a phone case, that takes up 0.02 cubic feet. After a year in storage, the volume-based fee would be 0.02 times $6.90, or about 14 cents a month. The minimum is 50 cents, so Amazon will charge 50 cents. Over a further year, that is $6.00 per unit.

The jump at the one-year mark is the cliff to watch. Between six months and a year, the same unit pays 0.02 times $3.45, or about 7 cents a month. On the day it crosses 365 days, the charge rises to 50 cents, about seven times as much. A product that was cheap to hold in its first year becomes expensive overnight in its second.

Now suppose the product sells for $12 and leaves the brand $3 after its costs and Amazon’s other fees. A unit that sits for a second year costs twice its margin in storage before it sells. A large product paying $6.90 per cubic foot on several cubic feet is expensive to store, but the minimum adds nothing to it. The small product, which was cheap to store by volume, is the one the minimum turns into a loss.

The monthly assessment changes the timing too. Under twice-yearly assessment, a brand could clear old stock before the February or August date and avoid the fee. Under monthly assessment, every unit that crosses the six-month or one-year mark starts paying that month. There is no cleanup date to work toward, only a steady cost on anything slow.

There is a fair objection: most of a brand’s stock should sell long before it reaches six months. True for the best sellers. The problem is the tail: slow sizes and colors, last season’s styles, products whose demand dropped after the stock arrived. Those are the units the new rules are designed to price.

How brands should plan FBA inventory in 2018

Calculate days of cover for every product. Divide units in Amazon’s warehouses by average daily sales. Any product with more than 180 days of cover will start paying long-term fees on part of its stock.

Send in what sells within months. Ship smaller quantities more often rather than a season’s supply at once, especially for slow products. The cost of an extra shipment is usually lower than the cost of stock that waits.

Find the small, slow products first, because they hide well in reports. Sort products by size and speed of sale. Small, inexpensive products with long cover are where the 50-cent minimum will do the most damage after August 15.

Decide on removals before the deadlines. Compare what a unit is likely to earn when it eventually sells with what it will cost to keep storing. Where storage will exceed the margin, remove the stock, sell it through another channel or price it to move. Removed stock is not lost: it can return to the brand’s own warehouse and be sent back in smaller quantities when demand returns, such as before the holidays.

Keep fulfillment flexible, product by product. For products that sell slowly, shipping orders from the brand’s own warehouse may cost less in total than holding them in Amazon’s.

What to do

  1. Pull your FBA inventory and sales reports and calculate days of cover for every product.
  2. List products with more than 180 days of cover, and flag those small enough for the 50-cent minimum to apply.
  3. Decide for each flagged product whether to remove, reprice or move it before August 15.

We plan FBA inventory around sales speed and storage cost together. If your Amazon warehouses hold a season’s supply of slow products, talk to our team.

P0048.crumb: Amazon footwear in 2018: fit decides what…
P0048.title: Amazon footwear in 2018: fit decides what sells
P0048.alt: Brown leather brogues on a brass foot-measuring device beside an open shoebox with tissue paper.
P0048.ttag: Amazon footwear in 2018: fit decides what sells | Kwontified
P0048.desc: Amazon’s shoe sales reached an estimated $3.7 billion in 2017, and its top seller was a sandal. Fit uncertainty decides what sells, and brands can reduce it.
P0048.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 12, 2018.
P0048.body:
Shoes are bought on fit, and online shoppers cannot try them on. That simple fact explains much of what is happening in Amazon footwear. Amazon’s shoe sales reached an estimated $3.7 billion in 2017, and the best-selling shoe of the year was a women’s sandal, close to one-size-fits-all. The products that win on Amazon are those whose fit a shopper can predict. For footwear brands in 2018, the job is to make fit knowable: full size runs, clear sizing information and consistent fit across styles, priced with the new fee threshold in mind.

What Amazon footwear looked like in 2017

The category is large and growing. Amazon’s shoe sales reached an estimated $3.7 billion in 2017, according to One Click Retail’s review of apparel and shoes on Amazon, Chain Store Age reported. Athletic shoes remained the largest category, but comfort and juniors’ shoes grew much faster. The top shoe of the year was a women’s sandal.

The growth outpaced the market. Amazon’s shoe sales rose 35% in 2016, while US shoe sales overall grew about 5%, and Amazon’s shoe sales were up 18% in the first half of 2017, Retail Dive reported, citing One Click Retail. Comfort and outdoor brands such as Keen and Crocs were among the top sellers in their categories.

Amazon invested in the category. It launched a private-label line of shoes and handbags called The Fix on July 25, 2017, after introducing Prime Wardrobe, which lets Prime members try clothing and shoes before buying, in June, PYMNTS reported. Nike also agreed in 2017 to sell some products directly to Amazon.

How fit uncertainty shapes the category

Here is how the pattern took hold.

A shopper in a shoe store tries on a pair, walks a few steps and decides. Online, she has to guess. If she guesses wrong, she returns the shoes, and the sale is lost along with the cost of two shipments. Online shoe shoppers learned to reduce that risk in two ways: by buying shoes whose fit they could predict, and by buying brands whose sizing they already knew.

The 2017 data reflects both. A sandal that fits most feet in a given size carries little fit risk, so it sells well online. Comfort brands with a reputation for consistent sizing let a shopper reorder with confidence. Athletic shoes from brands whose sizes shoppers already know have the same advantage.

Children’s shoes fit the pattern in a different way. Children outgrow shoes quickly, and a parent who knows a style fits will often reorder the same shoe in the next size up. The fit question has already been answered by the previous pair, which makes the reorder one of the lowest-risk purchases in the category and helps explain why juniors’ shoes grew so quickly on Amazon.

Amazon’s own moves aim at the same uncertainty. Prime Wardrobe removes the cost of guessing wrong by letting shoppers try before they pay. Private labels let Amazon control sizing across a range and learn from its own returns data.

For a brand, the lesson is that marketing alone does not sell shoes on Amazon. A beautiful product page cannot overcome a shopper’s doubt about whether the shoe will fit. What overcomes it is information and consistency: a full run of sizes in stock, clear guidance on how the shoe fits compared with other shoes, and reviews that mention fit.

Fees add a pricing question this spring. From April 15, 2018, Amazon’s referral fee for shoes, handbags and sunglasses priced above $75 rises to 18%, while items up to $75 stay at 15%, according to Amazon’s notice to sellers dated January 18. A hypothetical shoe priced at $79 would pay about $14.22 in referral fees, while one priced at $75 would pay $11.25. Brands with styles just above the line should check whether the price still makes sense.

There is a fair objection: some footwear brands sell on the experience of the store, the fitting and the service, and Amazon cannot offer it. True. But shoppers are buying shoes on Amazon in growing numbers whether or not those brands are there, and the brands present will be the ones they learn to trust on fit.

How footwear brands should sell on Amazon in 2018

Keep full size runs in stock. A missing size is a lost sale and a shopper who may not come back. Plan stock by size, not just by style.

Make fit knowable. State how each shoe fits, such as true to size, narrow or roomy, and how it compares with the brand’s other styles. Use the same sizing language on every product page.

Keep lasts consistent. Shoppers who know one of a brand’s styles will buy another with confidence if it fits the same way. Inconsistent sizing across styles produces returns and reviews that warn others off.

Watch reviews for fit complaints. When several reviews say a style runs small, update the page and adjust future production if needed.

Check prices near $75. Review every style priced just above the threshold and decide whether to stay above it or move below it.

What to do

  1. Check the size availability of your top 20 styles on Amazon and fill the gaps.
  2. Add a clear, consistent fit statement to every footwear product page.
  3. List styles priced between $75 and $85 and recalculate their margins with the 18% referral fee.

We help footwear brands plan size-level inventory and pages that answer the fit question. If returns and fit complaints are holding back your shoes on Amazon, talk to our team.

P0050.title: Sponsored Products match types price certainty, not just reach
P0050.alt: Fishing nets with floats hanging on a weathered blue boathouse wall on a dock beside moored wooden boats.
P0050.ttag: Sponsored Products match types price certainty, not just reach | Kwontified
P0050.desc: Broad, phrase and exact match on Amazon differ in how sure a bid can be about the search it buys. Price each match type from what its clicks are worth.
P0050.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 17, 2018.
P0050.body:
Type “merino sweater” into a manual Sponsored Products campaign and Amazon asks one more question: broad, phrase or exact. Most teams answer it the way they answer a form field, pick broad for reach, and move on. That choice is a pricing decision. The match type sets how wide a spread of shopper searches one bid will buy, and a wider spread at the same bid means paying the same price for clicks that are worth very different amounts.

So the same keyword entered three times, once in each match type, is really three products. Each deserves its own bid.

How Sponsored Products match types widen the net

The three types sit on one scale. Exact match buys the search the advertiser typed, or something very close to it. Phrase match buys any search that contains the phrase, with words before or after it. Broad match buys searches that contain all the words of the keyword in any order, with others mixed in, as Perpetua’s guide to Sponsored Products basics lays out.

Each step outward adds searches the advertiser did not write. Some of them are better than the keyword itself. Many are worse. A phrase-match keyword such as “merino sweater” also catches shoppers who typed a competitor’s brand name around it, and those shoppers buy less often, Practical Ecommerce pointed out in its guide to Sponsored Products.

The trade runs both ways: broad match finds searches nobody on the team thought to bid on, which is valuable. It also mixes them, at one price, with searches the team would never have chosen.

Why one bid across match types overpays

The mistake is not using broad match. The mistake is giving broad match the same bid as exact.

A click is worth what it is likely to earn: the product’s price, times the share of that price the brand can spend on advertising, times the chance the click becomes a sale. Match type changes the last number, because it changes which searches arrive.

Take a $60 sweater with a target advertising cost of sale of 25%, so the brand can spend $15 to win one sale. Say exact-match clicks on “merino sweater” convert at 12%, phrase at 6% and broad at 3%. A click is then worth $1.80 on exact, $0.90 on phrase and $0.45 on broad.

Now put one bid of $1.00 on all three. On exact, the brand bids little more than half of what the click is worth and loses top placements to rivals who bid closer to $1.80. On broad, it bids more than twice what the click is worth, and wins easily, because few competitors want those mixed searches at that price. Spend drifts toward the match type that is cheapest to win and least likely to sell.

The ordering in that example is the usual one, not a law. Sometimes a broad search converts better than the exact keyword, because shoppers who add a word such as “women’s” or a size know exactly what they want. That is why the bids should come from each match type’s own results, not from a rule that exact always beats broad.

Broad match is research that charges as it goes

Broad match is a research tool with a meter running. Its job is to surface searches worth owning, and the search term report is where those searches show up.

Read that report weekly. A search that converts well under broad or phrase match has earned an exact-match keyword of its own, with a bid priced from its own conversion rate. Once it has one, add it as a negative keyword in the broad and phrase groups, so the cheaper, less certain bid stops competing for the same shopper. Without that step, the brand bids against itself and the broad group keeps buying a search the exact group should own.

A search that spends without selling is the other half of the harvest. It goes into the negative list in the group that found it. The broad group then gets narrower and better each week, without losing its ability to find something new.

The approach also changes what a manager should read in the reports. A broad group with a high cost per sale is not necessarily failing; it may be paying to find the next exact keyword. A broad group whose best searches never graduate is failing, however good its average looks.

Teams with a small catalog sometimes object that this is too much structure for a handful of products, and for a brand spending a few hundred dollars a month they have a point. Three ad groups per keyword can wait until there is enough traffic to read. The principle does not wait: even one ad group should carry a lower bid on broad keywords than on exact ones.

Rules for setting match-type bids

  • Bid exact highest, phrase lower, broad lowest, and set each from its own value per click rather than from one number for the keyword.
  • Treat the gap between bids as a test. If broad clicks start converting close to exact ones, narrow the gap; if they convert at a fraction, widen it.
  • Graduate any search that converts in broad or phrase into its own exact keyword, and block it in the group that found it.
  • Judge broad groups on how many good searches they find, not only on their cost per sale.

Match types are where an Amazon advertising budget either learns or leaks, and pricing them separately is the first thing we set up in the Sponsored Products accounts we run for brands.

P0051.crumb: Mother’s Day on Amazon rewards listings…
P0051.title: Mother’s Day on Amazon rewards listings written for the giver
P0051.alt: Pastel spring bouquet in a ceramic vase beside a twine-tied parcel, blank card and fountain pen on a wooden table.
P0051.ttag: Mother’s Day on Amazon rewards listings written for the giver | Kwontified
P0051.desc: On a marketplace, a Mother’s Day gift is chosen by someone who will never use it. The listings that win answer the giver’s questions, not the user’s.
P0051.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 19, 2018.
P0051.body:
In a department store in early May, the gift table near the entrance does most of the selling. Someone in visual merchandising has already decided what a son in a hurry should buy: a candle in a box with a ribbon printed on it, a scarf folded so the label shows, a card stand within arm’s reach. On Amazon there is no table. There is a search box, and a shopper typing “gifts for mom” at eleven at night, scrolling past listings written for someone else entirely.

That someone else is the user. Most product pages are written for the person who will wear the scarf or burn the candle. A Mother’s Day gift is chosen by a person who will never use it, and the listings that sell in the next three weeks will be the ones that answer the giver’s questions.

The gift buyer is not the product’s customer

Mother’s Day is large enough to change how a category behaves for a month. Shoppers planned to spend a record $23.6 billion on the holiday in 2017, an average of $186.39 each, according to the National Retail Federation’s 2017 survey of 7,406 consumers.

Look at where that money went and the gift buyer’s habits show through. Jewelry took $5 billion, flowers $2.6 billion, clothing $2.1 billion, consumer electronics $2 billion and personal services such as a spa day $1.9 billion, in NRF’s figures. Those are categories where the buyer cannot try the product on the person who will use it, so the buyer leans on signals: a recognizable brand, a clear photograph of the box, reviews that mention the reaction rather than the fit.

A daughter buying a moisturizer for her mother does not know her mother’s skin type with any confidence. She knows the price she wants to pay, the date it has to arrive and whether it will look like a present when it is opened. Most beauty listings answer the first question only, and only for the user: texture, ingredients, skin concerns.

What the search results page leaves out

The physical gift table works because it does three jobs a search page does not do by default. It narrows the choice to a handful of safe options, it shows the product already presented as a gift, and it removes the worry about timing, because the gift leaves the store in the shopper’s hand.

On a marketplace, each of those jobs falls to the listing. The main image is usually the bare product on white, which is right for the user and wrong for the giver, who wants to see what will be unwrapped. The title is built around search terms the user types, such as size, shade and formulation, while the giver types the relationship and the occasion. The delivery promise sits further down the page, in a box the brand does not write, and in the final week before the holiday that box decides more sales than the copy does.

The pattern holds well beyond beauty. The categories that carry the holiday share a feature: the buyer’s confidence matters more than the product’s specification. A $40 scarf with a clear photo of its gift box and a line about returns can outsell a $40 scarf with better wool and no such reassurance, because the giver is buying the absence of risk.

Follow the value: who captures the gifting week

Mother’s Day falls on May 13 in 2018. On a marketplace, much of the value of that date goes to whoever controls the last mile of certainty.

Amazon controls most of it. Its delivery promise, its gift options at checkout and its returns policy are what a nervous giver relies on, and a brand selling through Fulfillment by Amazon inherits that promise for as long as its stock holds out. A brand that ships its own orders has to make the same promise itself and keep it in the busiest week of its spring.

Retail buyers know the season matters, and in stores the brand negotiates the gift table months ahead. On a marketplace there is nothing to negotiate. The brand’s share of the week depends on inventory placed in time, a listing that speaks to the giver and enough stock to survive a spike that ends abruptly on a Sunday. That puts the work squarely inside the brand: the e-commerce team owns the listing, supply chain owns the inventory, and the brand team owns the gift story. At many brands, those three groups plan Mother’s Day on different calendars.

Gift demand is not shrinking: the holiday’s spending set a record in 2017. What remains unclear is how much of that gift demand starts with a brand’s name and how much starts with the relationship typed into a search box. Brands can find out from their own search term reports before May 13.

Questions for the planning meeting this week

  • Does our main image for each gift-friendly product show what the recipient will open, or only the product on white?
  • Which search terms brought shoppers to us in the three weeks before last Mother’s Day, and how many named a relationship rather than a product?
  • When does our last inbound shipment need to reach Amazon’s warehouses for stock to sell through to May 13, and who owns that date?
  • Who decides what happens to the gift copy and the gift image on May 14?

The brands that do well on Mother’s Day treat the listing as a gift table they are allowed to arrange themselves. Running those listings, and the inventory under them, through the gifting weeks is part of the channel management we do for brands.

P0052.title: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q1 2018: spend nearly doubled across AMS
P0052.alt: Two vases of fresh flowers, ranunculus and lilies, on a sunlit wooden table by a window.
P0052.ttag: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q1 2018: spend nearly doubled across AMS | Kwontified
P0052.desc: Amazon Sponsored Products spend rose 96% a year in Q1 2018 while Google search grew 20%. What the public benchmark says about the price of a click.
P0052.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 24, 2018.
P0052.body:
Advertisers in Merkle’s client base spent 96% more on Amazon Sponsored Products in the first quarter of 2018 than a year earlier, according to the agency’s Q1 2018 Digital Marketing Report. Their Google paid search budgets grew about 20% over the same period. One of those numbers describes a mature auction. The other describes an auction absorbing new money faster than it is adding shoppers, and that is the one brands should plan around, because more money chasing the same searches pushes up the price of every click.

Amazon ad benchmarks for the first quarter

The public benchmark for the quarter comes from Merkle’s report, released on April 19. Its Amazon figures cover Amazon Marketing Services, the self-serve program that runs Sponsored Products and Headline Search Ads.

Measure, Q1 2018FigureWhat it tells a brand
Sponsored Products spend, year over year+96%Budgets in Amazon’s main ad format nearly doubled
Headline Search Ads spend, year over year+90%The banner format grew almost as fast
Sponsored Products share of AMS spend86%Most money still goes to product-level ads
Headline Search Ads share of AMS spend10%A small slice, with room to grow
Google paid search spend, year over year+20%The comparison: a maturing auction

Two caveats come first. These are one agency’s clients. That sample skews toward larger advertisers who were already on Amazon a year earlier. And the release reports spend, not cost per click, conversion or return on ad spend, so the table describes how much money arrived, not what each dollar bought. Any figure for those three that a brand sees quoted for the quarter should be checked against its source and date before it goes into a plan.

Why spend growth this fast shows up in the price of a click

Sponsored Products are sold by auction, one search at a time. The number of shopper searches on Amazon grows, but nowhere near as fast as the budgets chasing them. Now bring nearly twice the money to a set of searches that grew by much less. The extra money has to go somewhere. Most of it goes into higher bids.

Take a brand that held a top placement on its main category search in early 2017 by bidding $0.80 a click. A year later, two rivals with doubled budgets want the same placement and raise their bids to $1.10 and $1.20. The brand’s clicks did not change in quality. Its conversion rate is the same. To keep the same placement it now has to bid above $1.20, which means paying at least 50% more for an identical shopper.

That is the bias to watch in a benchmark season: reading spend growth as a sign that Amazon ads are working better. Some of the growth reflects real results, since advertisers keep adding money to channels that sell. But the same number also measures competition, and competition shows up as cost. A brand whose spend rose 96% while its sales rose 40% did not get a better channel; it bought a more expensive one.

Headline Search Ads are the format to watch

The 90% growth in Headline Search Ads spend matters more than its 10% share suggests. Each search carries only one Headline Search Ad, across the top of the results, so there is far less inventory than in Sponsored Products, which run in many slots on the page and on product detail pages. A format with a single slot per search and budgets growing at nearly the same rate as the larger format is where prices are most likely to climb fastest.

Merkle’s report also showed spend on Google Shopping ads, the product-image ads in Google results, accelerating to 40% growth in the quarter from 32% in the fourth quarter of 2017. Brands are shifting product-level budgets toward formats that look like a shelf, on both platforms at once. That is a second source of pressure, because the same planning meeting now weighs a Google Shopping budget against an Amazon one. For a brand selling on Amazon and running Google Shopping on its own site, the two auctions now compete for the same planning dollars.

What to check in your own Q1 numbers

A public benchmark is useful only as a frame for a brand’s own account. The questions worth asking this week:

  1. Cost per click by search, Q1 2018 against Q1 2017. If the top ten searches by spend are each 30% to 60% more expensive, the auction is repricing them, and bids set a year ago are now losing placements.
  2. Spend growth against sales growth. If advertising spend grew faster than attributed sales, the account is paying more per sale. Find the searches where that happened before raising budgets for the summer.
  3. Headline Search Ads cost per click on brand terms. A brand’s own name is the cheapest search to defend until a competitor starts bidding on it. A sudden rise there says someone new is in the auction, and it is usually cheaper to answer early than after the rival has built a history of clicks.
  4. Maximum affordable cost per sale for each product. Set it from margin, not from the benchmark. A product that could afford $8 per sale in early 2017 can still afford $8 if its margin has not changed. The market’s spending does not change that number. It only changes how often the brand can win at it.

The quarter’s real lesson is that the price of an Amazon click is set by other advertisers’ budgets, and those budgets nearly doubled. Reading cost per sale by search, against what each product can afford, is the core of how we manage Amazon advertising for brands.

P0054.crumb: Amazon search is a search engine that…
P0054.title: Amazon search is a search engine that brands manage like a store
P0054.alt: Sunlit wooden shelves of amber skincare bottles and boxes on a blue wall, with a brass magnifying glass on top.
P0054.ttag: Amazon search is a search engine that brands manage like a store | Kwontified
P0054.desc: Nearly half of US online shoppers start product searches on Amazon, yet most brands still run it from the sales team. Why the org chart lags the shopper.
P0054.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 26, 2018.
P0054.body:
Ask a brand’s marketing team who owns search and they will name the person who manages Google: the agency, the keyword budget, the monthly report on organic rankings. Ask who owns the search box on Amazon and the answer usually comes from a different floor. It is the sales team, or an e-commerce manager who reports to sales, and the conversation turns to purchase orders and promotions.

Shoppers do not make that distinction. For a large share of them, Amazon search is where looking for a product begins, and brands that manage it as a store account are leaving their most important search engine to the team that thinks least about search.

Where shoppers start looking

About 49% of US online shoppers went to Amazon first when searching for a product in 2017, according to a Survata survey reported by Bloomberg in December. Google and other search engines were the first stop for 36%, up from 28% a year earlier. Individual retailers’ own websites came first for only 15%.

The share starting on Amazon actually slipped from 55% in 2016, and Survata’s chief executive put Google’s gain down partly to its better experience on phones. That matters, because it shows the contest is still open. It does not change the larger picture: roughly half of product searches begin on a marketplace, and the retailers that carry most brands’ wholesale business are the starting point for very few.

The reasons are easy to see from the shopper’s side. A search on Amazon returns the product, the price, the delivery date and the reviews in one view, and the shopper can buy without leaving the page. A search on Google returns places to go and look. For someone who already knows roughly what they want, the marketplace skips a step.

In a store, those two jobs were separate. The directory by the entrance told a shopper which aisle to walk to, and the shelf in that aisle did the selling, arranged in a planogram the brand negotiated with the retailer’s buyer once or twice a year. On Amazon the search results page is the directory and the shelf at the same time, rearranged every time someone types, by an algorithm that reads the words in a listing and the sales it has made. The brand no longer negotiates its position in the aisle. It earns it, search by search, through copy, price, reviews and advertising, and it can lose it overnight.

How the search box ended up with the sales team

Brands did not choose this arrangement; it accumulated. Amazon entered most companies as a customer, a retail account that placed orders, so it was handed to the people who manage retail accounts. Search, meanwhile, grew up inside marketing as a media discipline, with its own agencies and its own budget line. Each team was organized for a channel as it looked a decade ago.

The result is a split that shows up in ordinary ways. The marketing team knows which words shoppers use to describe the category, because it buys them on Google every day. The Amazon team writes product titles and bullet points from the specification sheet, because that is what the account requires. Nobody in the room connects the two, so the words a brand has paid to learn on Google never make it into the listing where half its shoppers actually begin.

The same split governs the advertising. Sponsored Products ads are search ads in every respect that matters: keywords, bids, match types, a results page. At many brands they are still run as a trade expense attached to the retail relationship, judged on sales in the account rather than on what they teach the brand about demand.

Why the question is getting more urgent

The search engines are not standing still. Google launched Shopping Actions on March 19, 2018, letting shoppers buy from retailers such as Target and Walmart through a single Google cart in Search and on the Google Assistant, according to Google’s announcement. It is a direct attempt to make Google behave more like a marketplace, and it means a brand’s product data, supplied to its retail partners, now travels into Google’s results too.

So the shopper’s starting point is contested from both directions. Amazon is the most common first stop, Google is trying to win searches back, and retailers’ own sites are losing ground to both. For a brand, all three are search problems: the right words, the right product information and the right price must show up wherever the search begins. That work is the same discipline, whichever logo sits above the search box.

The evidence leans toward search becoming the organizing idea for e-commerce teams, not the account. What remains unsettled is whether brands will merge their Google and Amazon search work under one owner or keep them in separate departments that happen to buy the same keywords.

Questions to put to the team

  • Which ten words do shoppers use most to find our category on Google, and do they appear in our top Amazon product titles?
  • Who reads the Amazon search term report, and does anyone in marketing ever see it?
  • If roughly half our shoppers start their search on Amazon, does our search budget and headcount reflect that?
  • When we brief our retail partners on product data for Google Shopping Actions, is anyone checking that it matches what we show on Amazon?

Treating Amazon as the search engine it has become, with the listing and the ads run as one search discipline, is a large part of the channel management we do for brands.

P0056.title: Amazon other revenue, Q1 2018: 139% includes new accounting
P0056.alt: Open blank ledger and a cloth-bound book on a worn wooden table beside small stacks of coins.
P0056.ttag: Amazon other revenue, Q1 2018: 139% includes new accounting | Kwontified
P0056.desc: Amazon’s other revenue rose 139% in Q1 2018, but $560 million came from new accounting rules. Like for like, it still grew about four times faster than retail.
P0056.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 1, 2018.
P0056.body:
Amazon’s “other” revenue, the line where it reports its advertising business, rose 139% to $2.03 billion in the first quarter of 2018, according to the company’s results on April 26. That headline will be repeated in a lot of brand planning decks in May. It overstates the growth. About $560 million of the line came from a change in accounting rules, not from new advertisers, and the honest figure is closer to 70%. That is still the fastest-growing business Amazon reports, and it still means the price of reaching an Amazon shopper is rising much faster than the number of shoppers.

What Amazon’s other revenue line contains

Amazon does not report advertising as a separate line. It sits inside “other,” alongside a few smaller items such as co-branded credit card agreements. On the April 26 earnings call, chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said advertising makes up the majority of that line, according to the call transcript.

The same call explained the jump. From January 1, Amazon adopted a new revenue recognition standard. Under it, certain advertising services that used to be recorded as a reduction in the cost of sales are now recorded as revenue. Dave Fildes, Amazon’s director of investor relations, said the change added $560 million to other revenue in the quarter, mostly in North America. Amazon’s quarterly filing with the SEC describes the same reclassification.

That kind of money was already flowing to Amazon. It was reported in a different place. Vendor programs where brands pay Amazon for placement are the likely candidates, though Amazon did not itemize them.

The reclassification is worth reading as a signal, not only as a footnote. Money that used to be booked as a discount on what Amazon paid its suppliers is now booked as revenue from selling them visibility. Amazon is, in its own accounts, treating more of what brands pay it as advertising. A vendor negotiating its annual terms should expect the same framing across the table: support that once came as allowances will increasingly be offered back as ad programs, measured and priced like media.

The change also distorts more than one quarter. Unless Amazon restates earlier periods, each quarter of 2018 will compare a line that includes these services with a prior-year line that did not, so reported growth in other revenue will look inflated until the change laps in early 2019. Anyone tracking Amazon’s ad business quarter by quarter through 2018 should keep a like-for-like column beside the reported one.

Backing out the accounting change

The arithmetic is short. Growth of 139% on $2.03 billion means the first quarter of 2017 had about $850 million in the same line. Remove the $560 million that moved in from elsewhere, and like-for-like other revenue is about $1.47 billion, up roughly 70% from the year before.

Q1 2018Figure
Other revenue, as reported$2.03 billion
Reported growth139%
Moved in by the accounting change$560 million
Other revenue, like for likeabout $1.47 billion
Like-for-like growthroughly 70%
Online stores revenue$26.9 billion
Online stores growth18%

Online stores, Amazon’s own retail sales, grew 18% to $26.9 billion, the Motley Fool reported, or about 13% excluding currency moves, according to the call. So even on the conservative reading, the line that holds advertising grew about four times faster than the store it advertises in.

A caution on the 70%. Not all of “other” is advertising, and Amazon did not say how much of the $560 million was advertising either. The like-for-like figure is the best public estimate available, and it should be treated as a range, perhaps 65% to 75%, rather than a precise number.

Why the gap matters to a brand

Amazon’s advertising revenue is, from a brand’s side, the cost of being seen on Amazon. When that cost grows four times faster than the store’s sales, the share of each sale that goes to buying visibility is rising.

Take a brand whose Amazon sales grew in line with the store, 18%, and whose advertising spend grew in line with Amazon’s like-for-like ad revenue, 70%. If ads were 10% of its Amazon sales a year ago, they are now about 14.4% of sales. Nothing about the product changed. The brand is simply paying more of its revenue to stay in place, and that 4.4-point rise comes straight out of margin.

Not every brand will see that pattern. Some of Amazon’s ad growth comes from new advertisers and new formats rather than higher prices for the same placements. But the direction is consistent with what agencies saw in the auction: Merkle’s clients spent 96% more on Sponsored Products in the quarter than a year earlier, according to its Q1 2018 Digital Marketing Report.

Numbers to check before the next budget review

  1. Advertising as a share of Amazon sales, by quarter, for the last five quarters. Total advertising cost of sales, or TACoS, is the cleaner measure than ACoS for this, because it compares ad spend with all sales, not only the ones the ads claim.
  2. Like-for-like growth in your own ad spend, separating new products and new formats from the same campaigns year over year.
  3. The quote in the deck. When someone cites Amazon’s 139%, ask whether it includes the accounting change. For planning, use the like-for-like range, and say so on the slide, so the next person who copies the number copies the right one.

The 139% will make a good headline. The 70% is the one to plan with, and tracking total advertising cost of sales by quarter is the first number we put in front of brands whose Amazon advertising we manage.

P0058.crumb: Product Display Ads on rival pages pay…
P0058.title: Product Display Ads on rival pages pay only for better offers
P0058.alt: Mug on a plain cardboard box next to a ribboned gift box holding a ceramic pour-over dripper set on a sunlit shelf.
P0058.ttag: Product Display Ads on rival pages pay only for better offers | Kwontified
P0058.desc: An ad on a competitor’s Amazon page reaches a shopper who has already chosen. Product Display Ads pay only when your offer wins the side-by-side comparison.
P0058.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 8, 2018.
P0058.body:
Every brand team that discovers Product Display Ads has the same first idea: put our product on the competitor’s page. The ad format, sold to vendors through Amazon Marketing Services, lets an advertiser choose the product detail pages where its ad appears, and a rival’s best seller is the obvious target. Sometimes it is the best money in the account. Often it is the worst. The difference has little to do with the bid and almost everything to do with whether the advertiser’s offer wins when a shopper puts the two side by side.

Product Display Ads reach a shopper who has already chosen

A shopper on a product detail page is further along than a shopper on a search results page. They have searched, compared a row of options and clicked one. On a competitor’s page, the shopper has, for the moment, chosen the competitor. An ad there is asking them to change their mind.

That is a harder job than winning a search, and the arithmetic shows it. Take a $35 product with a target advertising cost of sale of 25%, so the brand can spend $8.75 per sale. On its category search, its clicks convert at 10%, so a click is worth about $0.88. On a competitor’s page, shoppers who click away have to be persuaded twice, first to leave and then to buy. If those clicks convert at 4%, a click is worth $0.35.

The bid has to follow. A brand that brings its search bid to a competitor’s page pays more than twice what those clicks are worth, and the account reports a poor return that gets blamed on the format.

When targeting a competitor’s page pays

The 4% in that example is not fixed. It depends on what the shopper sees when the two products sit next to each other, and the brand controls much of that.

Product Display Ads pay on a rival’s page when the advertiser’s offer wins one of the comparisons a shopper makes in a few seconds:

ComparisonWins the clickLoses the click
PriceClearly lower for the same pack sizeHigher, or the same
Rating and reviewsA higher star rating with a comparable countFewer, newer or lower
Fit to the needA larger size, a bundle, a variant the rival lacksThe same product with a different logo
AvailabilityIn stock with fast deliveryLonger delivery or low stock

Where the advertiser wins one of those clearly, conversion on a competitor’s page can approach the brand’s search conversion, and the ad is cheap reach to a shopper already in the market. Where it wins none, the ad buys curiosity: a shopper who clicks, compares, and returns to the product they had already chosen.

There is a second use that matters as much. A brand’s own product pages are also targets, for the brand and for its rivals. A competitor showing its ad on your best seller’s page is betting that your offer loses the comparison. Running your own Product Display Ads there, promoting a related product or a larger size, keeps that space in the family and costs little, because few shoppers on your page need persuading.

What the spend data can and cannot tell you

The format is growing quickly. Among Merkle’s clients, Product Display Ads spend grew more than 100% from the second to the third quarter of 2017, MediaPost reported. That is fast growth on a small base. In the first quarter of 2018, Sponsored Products and Headline Search Ads together took 96% of Amazon Marketing Services spend in Merkle’s Q1 2018 report, which leaves Product Display Ads a small slice.

A small share is not a verdict. It mostly reflects that Product Display Ads are a vendor format with fewer advertisers using them. What the share cannot say is whether the money that is spent there earns its keep, and that depends on the comparison table above, page by page.

The test is straightforward. Split Product Display Ads campaigns into three groups: the brand’s own pages, competitor pages where the brand’s offer clearly wins on price or rating, and competitor pages where it does not. Run each for four weeks with bids set from its own conversion rate. The last group usually tells the brand where to stop spending.

Read the results by page, not by campaign. A campaign average can hide one competitor page that converts as well as search behind five that convert at a fraction of it. The pages worth keeping tend to share a reason: the rival is out of stock often, sells a smaller size at a similar price, or carries a weaker rating. When that reason disappears, so does the return, which is why the target list needs an owner who checks the rival pages themselves, not only the report. A page that earned its place in March can be a waste by June because the competitor fixed the thing that made it vulnerable.

Rules for competitor-page targeting

  • Bid on a competitor’s page from that page’s own conversion rate, never from the search bid.
  • Target only rivals your offer beats on price, rating, size or availability, and drop a page when that changes.
  • Defend your own best-selling pages with your own related products before a rival takes the space.
  • Review the target list monthly, because a competitor’s price cut or a run of good reviews can turn a winning page into a losing one overnight.

Conquesting a competitor’s page is a pricing judgment more than a creative one, and checking that comparison before setting each bid is part of how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

P0061.crumb: Walmart’s Flipkart deal is a bet on…
P0061.title: Walmart’s Flipkart deal is a bet on marketplaces outside the US
P0061.alt: Blue twine-tied parcel and a desk globe on a wooden pier with a loaded container ship in the harbor behind.
P0061.ttag: Walmart’s Flipkart deal is a bet on marketplaces outside the US | Kwontified
P0061.desc: Walmart paid about $16 billion for 77% of Flipkart rather than build in India. The deal shows where the largest US retailer thinks marketplace growth now lies.
P0061.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 10, 2018.
P0061.body:
For most of its history Walmart grew by building. It chose the land, poured the concrete and opened the store, and it did that thousands of times.

On May 9 it did something different. It agreed to pay about $16 billion for a stake of approximately 77% in Flipkart Group, India’s largest e-commerce company, according to Walmart’s announcement. The Walmart Flipkart deal is the clearest statement yet from the largest US retailer about where it thinks marketplace growth lies. The answer is abroad, in markets where e-commerce is still taking shape, and in platforms already built rather than ones it would have to start.

Walmart’s Flipkart deal buys a marketplace already in motion

The scale is unusual for Walmart. Coverage called it the largest deal in the company’s history, Talk Business & Politics reported. The price values Flipkart at $20.8 billion, TechCrunch reported, for a business with gross merchandise value of $7.5 billion in its latest fiscal year.

That is a price for the future, not the present, and Walmart said so. On the call with analysts, chief executive Doug McMillon described India’s 1.3 billion people and growing middle class and said Walmart expects e-commerce there to grow at four times the rate of overall retail, according to the call transcript.

Read the deal as a retailer reading its own limits. Walmart has been building its US marketplace for years and has grown it quickly, more than tripling the items on Walmart.com to over 70 million in a year, the Associated Press reported in November 2017. Even so, its US e-commerce growth slowed to 23% in the holiday quarter, the AP reported in February. In India, Walmart judged that building from scratch would take too long. It bought the shoppers, the sellers and the habits instead.

Follow the value: what Walmart is really buying

A marketplace’s value is not its warehouse or its website. It is the network: the shoppers who come because the selection is wide, and the sellers who come because the shoppers are there. That network takes years to form and is hard to copy once it has. Whoever owns it collects a commission on trade it did not have to stock.

That is what $16 billion buys. Walmart’s stores in the US took decades to build their position; Flipkart’s network formed in roughly a decade online. A buyer who believes the network will keep growing at four times the rate of retail is paying for a position that would cost more, and take longer, to reach any other way.

That has a consequence brands should not miss. An owner that has paid a premium for a network will protect the network first: the breadth of selection that keeps shoppers coming and the seller base that supplies it. Individual brands matter to that network as sources of selection and demand, but no single brand is essential to it.

On a marketplace bought at this price, a brand earns its place the way any seller does, through availability, price and the quality of its listings. A brand that waits to be invited in by its distributors will find the network has grown around it, and that its products are already there, sold by someone else. The lesson is the same one many brands are learning on Amazon, now applied at the scale of a country.

For brands, the more important point is what this says about Walmart as an institution. A retailer that measured itself by stores has now made its largest bet on a marketplace it does not run day to day. Its own marketplace at home will be watched against that standard. The questions Walmart’s leaders ask about Flipkart, how many sellers, how much selection, how fast it grows, are the questions they will increasingly ask about Walmart.com.

Where the next marketplace growth is

The deal fits a pattern. The US marketplace battle is maturing: Amazon is large, Walmart is growing, and the cost of reaching a shopper on either rises every quarter. The faster growth is in markets where shoppers are coming online for the first time and where the dominant marketplace is still being decided.

India is one. Latin America, where Mercado Libre leads, is another, and Europe’s fashion platforms show the same pattern in a single category. Walmart’s move says the largest retailers now see these markets as where their next decade of growth will come from, and that they are willing to buy their way in.

It is too early to say how the bet will turn out. The deal still needs approval from India’s regulators, and Walmart and Amazon will now compete for the same shoppers and sellers in another large market. What the evidence does show is direction. A brand that thinks of marketplaces as a US question, answered by its Amazon and Walmart accounts, is planning for the market that is growing more slowly.

Questions for the leadership team

  • Which of our international markets have a dominant marketplace, and are we on it as the brand or only through distributors?
  • If a large retailer is willing to pay $16 billion for a position in India, what would it cost us to build a position there later rather than now?
  • Who in the company owns our international marketplace plan, and does it sit with the international team or the e-commerce team?
  • What will we watch at Walmart.com between now and mid-2019 as the company applies what it learns from running Flipkart?

Deciding which international marketplace to enter first, and with which local partners, is the work we do with brands and partners on international marketplaces.

P0064.crumb: Zalando returns make the shopper’s home…
P0064.title: Zalando returns make the shopper’s home the fitting room
P0064.alt: Open orange delivery box with unpacked clothes draped over a wooden chair in a bright hallway beside a tall mirror.
P0064.ttag: Zalando returns make the shopper’s home the fitting room | Kwontified
P0064.desc: On Zalando, a return is part of how fashion shoppers buy, not a failure of the sale. Brands joining the Partner Program inherit that habit and its cost.
P0064.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 17, 2018.
P0064.body:
In a department store in Berlin or Milan, the fitting room does quiet work for the retailer. A shopper takes three sizes of the same jacket behind the curtain, keeps one and leaves two on the hook, and nobody counts the two as lost sales.

On Zalando, the fitting room is the shopper’s bedroom. The shopper orders the three sizes, keeps one and sends two back, and on a spreadsheet the two look like returns. They are the same behavior. Zalando built its business on accepting that, and brands that sell through it need to plan for returns as part of the purchase, not as a failure of it.

Returns are how Zalando’s shoppers buy

Zalando has never pretended returns are rare. Its management said in 2013 that a return rate of around half was normal for the business, as Twinkle magazine reported at the time. A retailer that says that publicly is telling shoppers something: order freely, and send back what does not fit.

That promise helped Zalando grow into one of Europe’s largest fashion platforms. Zalando expected revenue of between EUR 4,478 million and EUR 4,500 million for 2017, up roughly 23% on the year, it said in its trading update on January 17, 2018. Growth on that scale in apparel and shoes, where fit is uncertain, depends on shoppers feeling no risk in ordering.

The behavior is a rational response to the shelf. A shopper looking at a jacket on a screen cannot feel the fabric or see how the shoulders sit. Sizes vary between brands, and sometimes between styles from the same brand. Ordering two sizes is the shopper’s way of doing what the fitting room used to do, and a generous returns policy is what makes that habit cheap for the shopper.

Who carries the cost when the platform opens to brands

For most of its history, Zalando bought stock, sold it and handled the returns itself. The cost of the bedroom fitting room sat inside its own business.

That is changing. Through its Partner Program, Zalando lets brands and retailers list and ship their own inventory on the platform, Coresight Research noted in 2017. Nike, Lacoste, Pepe Jeans and Esprit joined in the first half of 2017, according to Fibre2Fashion, and management said on its fourth-quarter 2017 call that the program doubled in size over the year.

Follow the value and the shift is clear. When Zalando owns the stock, it carries the returns. When a partner brand owns and ships the stock, the returned parcel comes back to the brand’s side, and the brand bears the cost of inspecting it, restocking it or writing it off. Zalando keeps the shopper relationship and the commission. The cost of the shopper’s habit moves to the brand’s side of the ledger.

Zalando has offered an answer that also brings the work back inside its walls. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions, launched in June 2017, takes over customer-facing logistics, including returns, for Partner Program brands, FashionUnited reported. For a brand, that solves the operational problem. It does not change the economics: someone still pays for every jacket that travels twice.

What returns change in a brand’s plan

Brands coming from wholesale tend to see Zalando through the lens of a department store account. They plan sell-through and margin, and treat returns as a line that finance will deal with later. On a platform built around the bedroom fitting room, that is the wrong order. A brand’s return rate on Zalando is shaped by decisions it makes before the first order ships. Consistent sizing matters, and so do product pages that show fit, with photographs and size notes that tell a shopper how a garment runs.

Take a jacket priced at EUR 120 that sells through Zalando’s Partner Program. If half of the units shipped come back, the brand needs to ship two jackets to keep one sale, and each returned jacket carries handling and shipping costs and a chance it cannot be resold at full price. A brand that brings that rate down to four in ten does not just save on logistics. It sells the same number of jackets with less stock tied up in transit, and more of its inventory is available to sell rather than sitting in a returns queue.

The same logic reaches into the brand’s own organization. In a wholesale business, the design team hands over a size range and the sales team sells it to buyers who take the risk of fit. On a platform where the brand owns the stock, fit becomes a cost the brand pays directly, every time a parcel comes back. That makes the size chart, the fit notes on the product page and the consistency of grading across styles commercial decisions, and they belong in the same planning meeting as price and margin. A brand that leaves them to the product team alone will find out what they cost from the returns report.

The evidence leans toward returns becoming a measure brands compete on, not a fixed cost of fashion online. What is not yet clear is how much of the cost Zalando will keep pushing toward its partners as the program grows, and how much it will absorb to keep shoppers ordering freely.

Questions to ask before joining the Partner Program

  • What return rate should we expect by category, and how does our sizing compare with the brands next to us on the page?
  • Will we handle returns ourselves or through Zalando’s fulfillment service, and what does each cost per returned unit?
  • Do our product pages tell a shopper how the garment fits, or only what it is?
  • Who in the company owns the return rate, and is it in the plan before launch?

Planning a European marketplace launch around the return rate rather than despite it is how we approach the international marketplaces we run with partner brands.

P0065.title: A customer list under GDPR is worth only what its consent proves
P0065.alt: Open wooden box filled with old index cards and wax-sealed envelopes on a table by a window.
P0065.ttag: A customer list under GDPR is worth only what its consent proves | Kwontified
P0065.desc: From May 25, 2018, a brand’s customer list counts for European marketing only where it can prove consent. How to value the list by its records, not its size.
P0065.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 22, 2018.
P0065.body:
Ask a brand how valuable its customer list is and the answer is usually a size: 400,000 addresses, a million subscribers. From Friday, May 25, 2018, that number stops meaning much for customers in Europe. On that date the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation takes effect across the European Economic Area, including the UK. Fines reach up to 4% of global turnover or EUR 20 million, whichever is greater, according to a briefing by law firm HFW. Under the new rules, the value of a customer list sits in the records a brand can prove, not in the addresses it holds.

This post explains how the rules change the economics of a list. It is not legal advice: what a brand may do with its own list depends on how each record was collected, and that is a question for counsel.

What changes for a customer list under GDPR on May 25

Marketing to a list does not become illegal. Lists remain usable after May 25 where consent was validly obtained, a McGuireWoods note for retailers pointed out on May 10. What changes is the burden. The business must be able to show how and when each person agreed, and what they agreed to.

That turns a list into two lists. One holds records with a clear, documented opt-in: the date, the form, the wording the person saw. The other holds everything else: addresses from old promotions, a pre-ticked box at checkout, a list bought from a partner years ago. The first list keeps working. The second is a liability that grows with every email sent to it.

The obvious repair, emailing everyone to ask for fresh consent, is a question to put to counsel before anyone presses send, because the request itself is an email to people who may never have agreed to receive one. Brands that have not already re-permissioned their lists have very little time left to do it carefully.

Valuing the list by its records

The useful arithmetic starts with records, not addresses. Take a brand with 400,000 addresses, of which 120,000 have a documented opt-in. Say each email campaign earns $0.05 in sales per address that receives it, and the brand sends four campaigns a month. Before May 25, the list looked like it was worth $80,000 a month in campaign sales.

After May 25, the part the brand can safely mail is 120,000 records, worth $24,000 a month on the same assumptions. The other 280,000 addresses still cost money to store and secure, still carry fine exposure, and earn nothing for European marketing until each one is brought under a documented basis.

That gap is uncomfortable, and some brands will be tempted to keep mailing the whole list and hope. The trade-off is lopsided. The extra $56,000 a month in that example is real money, but it is small next to a fine scaled to global turnover, and smaller still next to the cost of a complaint that brings a regulator into the brand’s data practices.

Some brands have made a cleaner choice. The UK pub chain JD Wetherspoon told customers in June 2017 that it would stop sending email newsletters and delete its email database, MediaPost reported. The company said the emails could be seen as intrusive, and commentators read it as an early answer to GDPR. Deleting the list is the extreme case, but it makes the logic visible: an address without provable consent is closer to a cost than an asset.

What the list is worth next to the marketplace

The rules also change a comparison many brands make without writing it down. On Amazon, the customer relationship belongs to the marketplace: the brand sees orders and search terms but not the shopper’s email address. The usual case for a brand’s own site has been that it builds a list the brand owns, which pays off for years in repeat sales without paying for each visit again.

GDPR does not remove that advantage. It prices it more honestly. A brand that counts 400,000 addresses as an owned asset, and justifies its direct site’s costs on that basis, may find the defensible asset is less than a third of that size for European customers. The direct channel’s value has to be recalculated on mailable records, and the marketplace’s lack of a list looks less costly by comparison.

The reverse is also true. A brand that built its list with clean, documented opt-ins now holds something its competitors may have lost overnight. In a market where many lists will shrink, a list that survives intact becomes a real advantage, and it is worth knowing exactly how large it is.

The last week before May 25

For a brand with European customers, the remaining days are for sorting, not for building.

  1. Split the list by provenance. Tag every record with its source, the date of consent and the wording shown. Records that cannot be traced go into a separate segment.
  2. Stop mailing the untraced segment to European addresses until counsel has reviewed it. Do not email it to ask for consent without that review.
  3. Fix the forms. Every sign-up form, checkout box and loyalty enrollment should capture the date, the source and the exact consent wording from now on.
  4. Report the list by records. Replace “list size” in the marketing dashboard with “mailable records with documented consent,” and track it monthly.

The list that survives May 25 will be smaller and more valuable per record. Measuring that list honestly, and the sales it actually drives, is part of the measurement work we do for brands.
