P0067.crumb: Mercado Libre is one door into Latin…
P0067.title: Mercado Libre is one door into Latin America’s separate markets
P0067.alt: Open yellow doors reveal a sunny tiled courtyard with potted plants, blue, green and red doors, and a cat on a bench.
P0067.ttag: Mercado Libre is one door into Latin America’s separate markets | Kwontified
P0067.desc: Mercado Libre bundles shoppers, shipping and payments across a region that shares little else. What its Q1 2018 results tell a C-suite about entering.
P0067.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 24, 2018.
P0067.body:
When a board discusses Latin America, the conversation tends to break into countries within a few minutes. Brazil needs a local entity and its own tax advice. Mexico has different distributors. Argentina’s currency changes the math every quarter. By the end of the meeting the region looks like a dozen small projects, each too expensive to start.

Mercado Libre offers a different picture: one platform that brings the shoppers, the delivery and the payment together, across markets that share little else. For a leadership team weighing Latin America, that makes it the most practical door in. It is also a company spending heavily ahead of profit, and brands that walk through the door should expect the room to change.

What Mercado Libre bundles that the region does not

The scale is real and growing. Mercado Libre sold 80.1 million items in the first quarter of 2018, up 50.6% from a year earlier, and gross merchandise volume reached $3,126.4 million, up 34.0% in US dollars, according to its first-quarter results. It had about 4.6 million unique third-party sellers late in 2017, Marketplace Pulse reported.

The more important number for a C-suite is delivery. Items shipped through Mercado Envíos, the company’s logistics service, reached 52.5 million in the quarter, up 92.4%, driven by free shipping, its MercadoPuntos loyalty program and customer acquisition, the company said. In a region where reliable delivery is one of the hardest things for a brand to arrange on its own, the marketplace has made itself the delivery network.

Payment works the same way. Mercado Pago, the company’s payments business, lets shoppers pay inside the platform in markets where card use and trust in online payment vary widely. A brand selling on Mercado Libre does not need to solve shipping and payment separately in each country. The platform has already done it, at least in part.

That is the bundle a board should weigh: shoppers, delivery and payment in one relationship. Entering country by country through wholesale means building or buying each of those three separately, and doing it again in the next market.

Follow the value: who pays for the bundle

The bundle is not free, and the first-quarter results show who has been paying for it. After adopting a new accounting standard, Mercado Libre now reports its revenue net of what it spends on free shipping. That subsidy was $112.5 million in the quarter, according to the release. The company recorded an operating loss of $29.4 million and a net loss of $12.9 million, the Motley Fool reported, which also pointed to a sharp increase in rates charged by Brazil’s national postal service, Correios.

Read as an institution, Mercado Libre is doing what a platform does when it wants to own a market: spending to make the shopper’s experience good enough that buying anywhere else feels harder. Brazil shows the result. Gross billing there rose to $276.3 million in the first quarter from $159.8 million a year earlier, according to the release.

For brands, the lesson is about timing. A platform that is subsidizing shipping to grow is a generous host. The same platform, once it turns its attention to margins, will look for that money somewhere, and sellers are the obvious place: fees, shipping charges, advertising. Brands that enter now get the generous terms, and should plan for them not to last.

Platform or country by country: the decision in the room

There is a competitor to watch as well. Amazon’s Brazilian marketplace grew from about 1,400 sellers in mid-October 2017 to more than 3,000 in early November, Marketplace Pulse reported in the same article. It is far smaller than Mercado Libre’s seller base, but a brand that enters Latin America through one platform now may be choosing between two in a few years.

The decision in front of most leadership teams is not whether Latin America matters. It is whether to enter through a single regional platform or to build a presence country by country. The evidence so far leans toward the platform for most brands, because it collapses three hard problems into one relationship. What remains uncertain is how much that relationship will cost once Mercado Libre stops paying for the shopper’s shipping.

The country-by-country route still has its place. A brand with an established distributor in Mexico, or a store business in Brazil, already holds part of the bundle and may want to keep the customer relationship for itself. Even then, the marketplace is where much of the region’s online demand is gathering, and a brand absent from it leaves that demand to whoever lists its products there.

A board that enters through Mercado Libre should do so with its eyes open. The platform will own the customer relationship, the delivery promise and the payment, which is exactly why it is easy to start. It also means the brand’s terms will be set by an institution whose priorities will move from growth to profit at a time of its choosing.

Questions for the leadership team

  • Which Latin American market matters most to us, and how much of its online demand already runs through Mercado Libre?
  • If we sell through Mercado Libre, which of shipping, payment and customer service do we hand to the platform, and which do we keep?
  • What would our margin look like if the platform’s shipping subsidies shrank and we paid the full cost of delivery?
  • Who in the company owns Latin America: the international team, the e-commerce team, or a distributor?

Deciding how to enter Latin America, and whether a single regional platform is the right door, is part of the international marketplace work we do with partners.

P0070.title: Instagram storefronts rent the shopper’s attention, not the sale
P0070.alt: A phone on a lilac stand and an old key with a blank tag sit on a weathered wooden table outside an empty storefront.
P0070.ttag: Instagram storefronts rent the shopper’s attention, not the sale | Kwontified
P0070.desc: Instagram lets brands turn posts into a storefront, and the sale still happens on the brand’s own site. What a brand gives up is control of who sees the shelf.
P0070.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. Instagram Shop
P0070.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 31, 2018.
P0070.body:
A brand that opens a shop on a busy high street pays for two things at once: the floor where the sale happens and the window that people walk past. Instagram has split those two apart. Since late 2017, a brand can tag products in its posts and gather them in a Shop tab on its profile, while the purchase itself still happens on the brand’s own website. The sale stays home. What the brand rents from Instagram is the window, and the platform decides how many people walk past it.

That is the trade an Instagram storefront asks for, and it is a better deal than it first appears, as long as the brand remembers who owns the street.

How the Instagram storefront took shape

Instagram built the feature quickly. It opened shoppable posts to US merchants on BigCommerce’s platform in October 2017 after a test with 20 brands, TechCrunch reported. It said at the time that it planned to make money from shopping by charging businesses to show posts to people who do not follow them. In March 2018 it extended shopping to businesses in eight more countries, including the UK, Germany, France and Brazil, Marketing Land reported.

Instagram has made the format generous. A business can tag up to 5 products in a single image or up to 20 in a carousel, and shoppers see prices and details in the feed and in a Shop tab on the profile, Marketing Dive reported. Before shopping, the only way to send traffic from organic posts to a website was the single link in a brand’s bio, FashionNetwork noted.

The audience is the reason brands are interested. About half of Instagram’s daily active users in the US follow a shopping business account, and more than 200 million accounts visit a business profile every day, according to the company, as reported by Marketing Land. One beauty brand, Tyme, tagged products and saw its traffic grow 44%, Retail Dive reported, citing Instagram.

What the brand keeps, and what it gives up

Follow the value and the structure of the deal is unusual for a platform. On a marketplace, the platform owns the checkout, the customer record and the delivery promise. On Instagram in 2018, the tagged product leads to the brand’s own product page. The brand keeps the transaction, the customer’s details and the margin, without paying a commission on the sale.

What it gives up is the shelf’s visibility. A store window is seen by whoever walks down the street. A post on Instagram is seen by whoever the platform chooses to show it to, and the brand has no lease on that decision. The number of business profiles shows why that matters: there were more than 25 million by late 2017, up from 15 million in July, according to Statista’s chart of Instagram’s figures. Every one of them is competing for the same feed.

Inside a brand, this trade lands in an awkward place. The social team owns the posts and the follower count. The e-commerce team owns the product pages and the sales. The catalog that makes tagging possible usually belongs to whoever manages product data. A storefront that depends on all three tends to be owned by none of them, and its results show up in three different reports.

The physical comparison is useful here. A brand that rents a window on a busy street negotiates the lease, knows the footfall and decides what goes in the window each season. On Instagram the brand decides what goes in the window, but the footfall is set by a feed it cannot see into, and the lease can be rewritten without a conversation. The work that makes the window pay, the photography, the product tags, the catalog behind them, is still the brand’s cost. That is why the storefront needs one owner who can see the reach, the clicks and the sales in the same place, and who can say whether the window is earning its keep.

Where the trade is heading

Instagram said from the start that it intended to charge for reach beyond a brand’s followers. That is the natural direction for a platform that has given away the storefront: once brands have built their windows on its street, the platform can price the foot traffic. The likely direction is organic reach for shopping posts becoming harder to earn as more businesses tag products, with paid distribution filling the gap.

None of that makes the storefront a bad deal. A brand that keeps the sale and the customer on its own site, and treats Instagram as the window rather than the store, gives up less than it would on a marketplace. The risk is in forgetting which part is rented. A brand that builds its discovery entirely on Instagram’s feed has handed its window display to someone who can dim the lights at any time, or charge for keeping them on.

Questions before the storefront becomes a budget line

  • How much of our site traffic from Instagram comes from tagged posts, and how much would we lose if organic reach fell by half?
  • Who owns the product catalog that feeds our tags, and is it accurate in every market where we sell?
  • Does our social team see the sales that tagged posts produce, and does our e-commerce team see the reach?
  • What would we pay to reach people who do not follow us, and how would we know whether it was worth it?

Running Instagram shopping as a sales channel, with the catalog, the posts and the product pages managed together, is part of the social commerce work we do for brands.

P0072.crumb: The Amazon pricing algorithm follows your…
P0072.title: The Amazon pricing algorithm follows your lowest price anywhere
P0072.alt: Three corked bottles of amber liquid on wooden plinths in arched windows of a teal shopfront, the middle one with a blank tag.
P0072.ttag: The Amazon pricing algorithm follows your lowest price anywhere | Kwontified
P0072.desc: A weekend discount on your own site can reset your Amazon price for months. Amazon’s pricing machinery reads every visible price as a reference.
P0072.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 5, 2018.
P0072.body:
A beauty brand runs 25% off on its own website for a holiday weekend. On Tuesday the website goes back to full price. Three weeks later, its best-selling serum is still selling on Amazon at the weekend price, and nobody at the brand touched the Amazon listing. Nothing broke. The weekend discount was read by software that follows prices, and that software has no reason to stop following.

The Amazon pricing algorithm is better understood as a system of followers than as one decision. Amazon’s own retail prices, resellers’ repricing tools and the Buy Box each take some other visible price as their input. Whatever price a brand shows anywhere becomes one of those inputs, so brands should treat every discount, on every channel, as a possible new Amazon price.

Why brands think the Amazon price is theirs to set

The belief is reasonable. A seller types a price into Seller Central and the listing shows it. A vendor agrees a cost with Amazon and sees a retail price close to the list price it suggested. In both cases the price looks like a decision someone made.

What has changed is how many other decision-makers sit on the same page, and how fast they move. Amazon made more than 2.5 million price changes a day in November 2013, according to Profitero’s tracking, while Walmart made 54,633 changes in the whole month, RetailWire reported. No person reviews prices at that rate. Software does, and software needs a reference to react to.

Amazon has also shown it will change a price the seller did not change. In November 2017, the Wall Street Journal found Amazon cutting prices on some third-party items at its own expense, by less than 10%, to be more competitive with other sites, while paying sellers their full price, Engadget reported. Sellers with price agreements could opt out. The reference, in other words, was the market outside Amazon.

How the price-following loop works

Picture a room full of thermostats wired to each other instead of to the air. Each one sets itself a degree below the coldest reading it can see. Open one window for a weekend and the whole room drops, and closing the window does not bring it back, because every thermostat is now reading the others.

Amazon prices behave the same way when they are set by rules such as “match the lowest offer” or “beat it by a cent.” Take a $40 serum that a brand sells to authorized resellers at $20 wholesale. Each reseller runs a repricer with a floor of $28. The brand’s weekend sale puts the serum at $30 on its own site. One reseller’s tool, or one person watching the web, moves to $29.99 to stay credible. The other repricers follow that offer, not the brand’s website, and within hours the listing sits near the $28 floor.

On Tuesday the brand returns to $40. The Amazon offers stay where they are. Each repricer is matching the other repricers, and none of them is programmed to be the first to raise its price and lose the sale. The resellers’ margin has fallen from $20 a unit to about $8 before Amazon’s fees, and the brand’s own full-price site now looks expensive next to its Amazon listing.

The Buy Box adds weight to the low end. It rewards a combination of price and fulfillment, and the comparison is not always a like-for-like price. In a September 2016 study of 250 frequently bought products, ProPublica found that Amazon’s own offers, or offers fulfilled by Amazon, won the Buy Box about 75% of the time ahead of cheaper offers, partly because shipping was left out of their price. Buying every Buy Box item would have cost nearly 20% more. Whatever the exact formula, the offer that wins is the one the other tools will chase next.

Oddly, the discount does its most lasting damage after it ends. During the sale, every channel is cheap and shoppers expect it. Afterward, the brand’s own channels return to full price while the marketplace keeps the sale price, so the brand ends up competing against its own promotion.

What brands can and cannot control

A brand cannot set the prices other sellers charge, and should get legal advice before trying to. It can control which prices exist for the software to read. That makes the brand’s lowest visible price, on any channel, an Amazon pricing decision whether or not anyone planned it as one.

Some parts of the rulebook depend on geography. Amazon stopped enforcing price parity on its European marketplaces from August 31, 2013, after pressure from Germany’s and the UK’s competition authorities, and the UK regulator noted that the policy would not change outside the EU, Inside Global Tech reported. Brands selling in the US should read their own seller agreement and Amazon’s current pricing policies before assuming how a lower price elsewhere will be treated.

What would change this view is evidence that a listing’s Amazon price recovers on its own after a brand’s promotion ends. The test is cheap. Record the Amazon price of your top products every day for two weeks after your next site-wide sale, and compare it with the two weeks before.

Rules for the next promotion

  • Price the promotion as if it will appear on Amazon. If the margin at the sale price is unacceptable on Amazon, the sale price is too low.
  • Prefer offers that are hard for software to read, such as a gift with purchase or a bundle with its own product code, over a cut to the headline price of a best seller.
  • Know your resellers’ floors. A repricer floor near your wholesale price tells you where the listing will settle after any discount.
  • Track the Amazon price daily for two weeks after every sale, and treat a price that has not recovered as a channel problem, not a reporting quirk.

The rule of thumb: your Amazon price is the lowest price you show anywhere, plus however long it takes software to notice. Pricing control across channels is part of the channel management work we do with brands, and the Amazon side of a promotion plan is usually where it starts.

P0073.crumb: Prime Day 2018 planning starts after the…
P0073.title: Prime Day 2018 planning starts after the deal deadline has passed
P0073.alt: A brass hourglass on a wooden desk with wrapped parcels, a wax-sealed envelope, notebooks, a succulent and an ink pen.
P0073.ttag: Prime Day 2018 planning starts after the deal deadline has passed | Kwontified
P0073.desc: The Prime Day 2018 deal list closed in May, before most brands had a plan. What is still open six weeks out, and who in the company owns it.
P0073.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 7, 2018.
P0073.body:
Picture the first Prime Day meeting of the year taking place in June, when someone in finance asks what the event will add to the July forecast. If that is how your brand starts, one of the biggest decisions is already made. For third-party sellers, Lightning Deal submissions for Prime Day 2018 closed on May 18, ChannelX noted in May. Whoever had Seller Central open that week chose the brand’s deals, or chose none.

So Prime Day 2018 planning, six weeks out, is less about the deal and more about everything around it: stock, advertising money and who is watching on the day. Those three decisions usually sit with three different teams on three different calendars, and the event punishes any gap between them.

Prime Day 2018 planning: what is settled and what is still open

Amazon has not announced the date. Last year’s event ran 30 hours, and Amazon said sales grew more than 60% over the same period in 2016, making it the biggest day in the company’s history, according to its announcement. Until Amazon confirms the date, planning for mid-July is the reasonable working assumption.

The size of the stakes is not in doubt. Coresight Research’s June 4 preview put Prime Day 2018 at about $3.4 billion worldwide, against an estimated $2.4 billion for 2017, in its forecast. Those are outside estimates, since Amazon does not publish event sales, but they describe an event that now rivals the holiday peak.

Working back from mid-July, the calendar for a brand looks roughly like this:

WhenDecisionUsual owner
Mid-May (passed)Which products carry Lightning Deals, at what discountWhoever runs Seller Central or Vendor Central
Now to late JuneHow much stock to send to Amazon’s warehouses, and of which sizes and colorsOperations or supply planning
Late JuneAdvertising budget for the event week, and the rules for raising itMarketing or the agency
Early JulyPrice and coupon changes on products without a dealE-commerce, often with finance
Event dayWho watches stock, budgets and the Buy Box hour by hourFrequently no one in particular

Why the decisions split across teams

The split is a product of how most brands came to Amazon. The marketplace arrived as an operations task: get the products listed, keep them in stock. Deals were added later by whoever held the login. Advertising arrived later still, and was handed to marketing because it looked like media.

Prime Day exposes that history because all three levers move at once. A deal that sells through by noon wastes the advertising behind it for the rest of the day. An advertising budget sized for an ordinary Tuesday runs out early. After last year’s event, Bobsled Marketing’s specialists found that campaigns could exhaust their budgets quickly, and that only about one client in three saw cost per click rise more than 50% against July 1–10, in its review of its accounts.

The price of traffic, in other words, moved less than many expected. The volume did not, and it ran through budgets set by people who were not in the inventory meeting. The same gap appears on the stock side. A supply planner sizing the June shipment works from last July’s sales, which already include last year’s deal; nobody tells her whether this year’s deal is deeper, on a different product, or absent.

Amazon reads the day differently from brands, and that explains why the pressure keeps growing. Amazon said more new members joined Prime on last year’s Prime Day than on any single day in its history. In April it raised the annual Prime fee to $119 from $99, with existing members renewing at the new price from June 16, CNBC reported. An event that recruits members just as the fee rises is worth a great deal to Amazon, and brands’ discounts are part of what pays for it.

The question for the room this week

The useful meeting in early June asks one question: who owns Prime Day from now until the event ends? Not who owns the deal, which is done, or the budget, which marketing will defend. One person, with authority to move stock, money and prices together.

Without that owner, the familiar failure plays out. Take a brand spending $5,000 a day on Sponsored Products. On Prime Day traffic, that budget can be gone by early afternoon, just as the brand’s deal product is selling out and the rest of its range is getting the visits the deal attracted. Nobody made a bad decision. Three teams made sensible ones that did not meet.

The better model already exists inside most companies. A store opening gets one name on it, across merchandising, stock and marketing, and nobody finds that strange. Prime Day deserves the same treatment.

Before the date is announced

  • Name the owner this week, with authority over stock, ad budget and price for the event.
  • Check the deal list you already have. Confirm which products were accepted, at what price, and whether the stock behind them is enough for a deal that sells out.
  • Set the budget rule now: how much the event-day advertising budget can rise, and who approves it on the day.
  • Plan the non-deal products, which can draw traffic from shoppers who arrive for a deal and keep browsing.

Next year’s deal deadline will arrive in spring again. The question for leadership is whether it falls on the desk of someone who knows the July plan. When it helps, a channel management partner can hold that seat; it is a conversation we have with brands every spring.

P0076.crumb: Heritage brands on Amazon gain control…
P0076.title: Heritage brands on Amazon gain control only by showing up
P0076.alt: A vintage brown leather suitcase on a pale wooden shelf beside ceramic vases, linen baskets and dried flowers against a pink wall.
P0076.ttag: Heritage brands on Amazon gain control only by showing up | Kwontified
P0076.desc: Birkenstock walked away from Amazon and Nike walked in, a year apart. For heritage brands, the price of control on Amazon is being a supplier it wants.
P0076.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 14, 2018.
P0076.body:
Two letters, a year apart, set out the choice every heritage brand now faces. In July 2016, Birkenstock’s US chief executive told thousands of retail partners that the company would stop supplying Amazon from January 1, 2017. It would also stop authorizing third-party sellers there, because policing counterfeits and unauthorized selling “has proven impossible.” In June 2017, Nike, which had not been selling directly to Amazon, agreed to supply some of its products to Amazon. One brand chose distance to protect its name; the other chose presence for the same reason.

The second choice is the one that buys control. Heritage brands on Amazon gain a say over counterfeits, pricing and their own product pages only by becoming a supplier Amazon wants to keep. Staying away surrenders the bargaining chip and leaves the shelf to others.

Why heritage brands said no

The resistance made sense from inside these companies. A heritage brand is built on controlled distribution: selected stores, trained staff, prices that hold. Its wholesale team spent decades deciding who may carry the line. Amazon, where anyone with stock can list against the same product page, looked like the opposite of all that.

Birkenstock’s reasoning was explicit. According to the July 2016 letter, the only way to keep fakes off the site would have been to sell directly to Amazon, and Birkenstock chose to leave instead, Retail Dive reported. A year later its chief executive was still describing the problem in the strongest terms, accusing Amazon of “modern day piracy,” the Bangor Daily News reported.

Read as an institution, Amazon’s position was just as consistent. Amazon is built to offer selection and to keep the shopper on its site. An offer to buy the whole catalog is what a retailer says when it wants to be the seller of record and to control the page. Each side was protecting what it measures.

Leaving Amazon does not take the brand off the shelf

The difficulty is that leaving does not remove the shelf. Shoppers keep searching for the brand on Amazon. In Mary Meeker’s Internet Trends report on May 30, a Survata survey of US consumers found 49% of product searches started on Amazon, MarTech Today reported. And the supply of sellers keeps growing: more than half of the units sold on Amazon in 2017 came from third-party sellers, Jeff Bezos wrote in April, as Quartz reported.

So a heritage brand that withdraws does not disappear from Amazon. Its products still arrive through diverted wholesale stock and resellers, its page is still written by someone, and the shopper still finds a price. What the brand gives up is its standing to ask Amazon for anything. A former supplier that refuses to sell has little to offer in return for enforcement.

The point is not that Amazon would be a gentle partner. It is that a brand with something Amazon wants can ask for something in return, and a brand that has walked away has already spent that chance.

What Nike’s deal shows about control

Nike’s move a year later reads as a test of that idea. Under the arrangement reported in June 2017, Nike would supply some products directly to Amazon, and in return Amazon would police counterfeit and unauthorized third-party sales of the brand, according to a Fox Business report citing a person familiar with the matter. Nike’s chief executive later confirmed the pilot, NBC News reported.

Follow the value and the logic is clear. Amazon wanted Nike’s selection; Nike wanted the page cleaned up. Supply was the currency. A brand that already refuses to sell has nothing left to spend. The bargain also changes the brand’s own organization. A supplier relationship comes with an Amazon buyer, a forecast, a person accountable for the page and a reason to read Amazon’s data every week. A refusal creates none of those, which is why a brand that stays away can end up knowing least about how it looks there.

It is too early to say how well the enforcement has worked, and any brand watching should ask for evidence rather than assume it. The structure of the bargain is still instructive. Control on Amazon has become something a brand negotiates for, with product, rather than something it keeps by staying out. For smaller heritage brands without Nike’s weight, the same logic applies at a smaller scale. The rebuilt Brand Registry, open since 2017 only to brands with a registered trademark, gives enrolled brands authority over their pages, Practical Ecommerce explained.

Questions for the leadership team

The decision rarely gets framed this way inside a heritage brand. It usually arrives as a wholesale question (“should we let Amazon carry us?”) when it is really a question about control of a shelf the brand is already on.

  • Who is selling our products on Amazon right now, and where did they get the stock? The answer shows whether staying away is protecting anything.
  • What would we ask Amazon for if we were a supplier it wanted? Enforcement, page control and pricing discipline each have a price in product.
  • Who inside the company owns the Amazon page? A listing nobody owns drifts, whoever supplies it.
  • What is the smallest version of presence we could test (a few hero products, a registered brand, our own content) before deciding on the full range?

Heritage brands spent decades choosing which doors their products went through. On Amazon, the door is already open; the remaining choice is whether the brand stands in it. Helping brands set terms on that shelf is the channel management work we do.

P0078.crumb: Walmart search ranking feeds on clicks…
P0078.title: Walmart search ranking feeds on clicks, so the first weeks decide
P0078.alt: A young seedling in a blue ceramic pot beside a brass watering can on a wooden windowsill.
P0078.ttag: Walmart search ranking feeds on clicks, so the first weeks decide | Kwontified
P0078.desc: Walmart’s search engine learns from what shoppers click, so a new marketplace listing’s first weeks of price, content and stock shape where it ranks for months.
P0078.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 19, 2018.
P0078.body:
A brand lists 40 products on Walmart Marketplace in the same week. A month later, five of them take most of the sales and the rest sit on page three for their own product names. The tempting explanation is that the five are simply better products. Often the more useful explanation is timing: the five happened to earn clicks first, and Walmart’s search learned from those clicks.

Walmart search ranking compounds. Walmart has not published a list of ranking factors, but it has said its search engine learns from what shoppers do, and a listing that collects clicks and sales early is shown more and collects more. That makes the first weeks of a listing, and anything that hides or weakens it during them, more expensive than they look.

What Walmart has said about how its search works

The clearest public description dates from 2012, when Walmart launched Polaris, a search engine for Walmart.com built by its @WalmartLabs unit, TechCrunch reported. The engine was designed to infer what a shopper means rather than match words literally, and what shoppers click on, add to cart and buy helps train it, TechCrunch noted. Walmart said shoppers completing a purchase after a search rose by 10 to 15% after the change, Computerworld reported.

The site keeps moving in the same direction. In April 2018 Walmart announced a redesigned Walmart.com, with a homepage that is largely personalized, including a section of top-selling items in the customer’s location, according to Walmart. A store that shows each shopper what sells nearby is a store that rewards whatever is already selling.

Treat the details with care. A 2012 description of a search engine is not a 2018 rulebook, and Walmart has had six years to change it. The principle it describes, learning from shopper behavior, is the part worth planning around.

How the click loop compounds

Take two similar listings in the same category. Listing A lands on page one for its main search and gets 2,000 views in its first month; at a 3% conversion rate it sells 60 units. Listing B lands on page three, gets 200 views and, converting at the same 3%, sells 6.

Nothing about the products differs. But a search engine that learns from clicks and sales now has ten times as much evidence that A satisfies shoppers. Next month A is likely to be shown more, and B less.

Improve B’s content so that it converts at 4%, and on 200 views it sells 8 units. A, with no improvement at all, keeps selling around 60. The better page loses to the earlier one.

The bias this sets up is easy to fall into. A brand reading the month-one report sees five winners and thirty-five laggards and concludes it has a product problem. It cuts the laggards’ stock or stops working on their pages, which confirms the ranking. The report measured exposure as much as appeal.

What hides a listing during the weeks that count

Anything that removes a listing from search, or makes shoppers skip it, starves the loop when it is most sensitive.

Price is the hardest stop. Walmart unpublishes marketplace items whose price looks uncompetitive against other sellers, and a listing can stay down for 24 to 48 hours even after the price is fixed, Zentail explained in May 2017. An unpublished listing earns no clicks at all, and its competitors earn them instead.

Shipping is the quieter one. Walmart’s free two-day shipping on orders over $35, launched in January 2017, did not include marketplace items, according to Walmart. A marketplace listing next to a Walmart-sold item with a two-day promise has to win the click with price, images and reviews.

Stockouts and thin pages complete the list. A listing that runs out cannot convert, and one with a single image and a manufacturer’s one-line description gives shoppers little reason to choose it. Neither problem is fatal on its own. In the first weeks, each one hands engagement to someone else.

What would change this view

If Walmart’s ranking were driven mainly by text relevance, improving content on a laggard would move it quickly, regardless of its sales history. Brands can test this. Pick five listings stuck on page two or three, improve their titles, images and descriptions, keep their prices competitive and their stock full, and compare their search position and sales over six weeks with five untouched listings of similar rank.

Record the search position by hand, or with a tracking tool, once a week for each listing’s main search term, because sales reports alone cannot separate a listing that shoppers rejected from one they never saw. If the improved listings climb and the untouched ones do not, content is doing the work and the loop is weaker than this post assumes. If both groups stay put while the early winners hold their places, history is doing the work, and the first weeks of the next launch deserve most of the attention.

Rules for a Walmart launch

  1. Launch fewer products, fully. Ten listings with competitive landed prices, complete content and deep stock will teach the search engine more than forty half-ready ones.
  2. Check unpublished status daily for the first month, and fix price problems the same day.
  3. Judge laggards on conversion, not rank. A listing that converts well on few views has an exposure problem, not a product problem.
  4. Hold stock on the early winners. A stockout in month two gives away the rank month one earned.

The rule of thumb: on Walmart, rank is a lagging indicator of the clicks a listing earned while nobody was watching. Planning those first weeks is part of how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

P0079.crumb: Amazon home and kitchen in 2018 sells the…
P0079.title: Amazon home and kitchen in 2018 sells the sofa without the showroom
P0079.alt: A plastic-wrapped white sofa in a sunny living room with a bookshelf, fiddle-leaf fig and round coffee table, seen past a terracotta wall.
P0079.ttag: Amazon home and kitchen in 2018 sells the sofa without the showroom | Kwontified
P0079.desc: Amazon’s furniture sales reached an estimated $4 billion in 2017. In home and kitchen, the products that win are the ones whose page does the showroom’s job.
P0079.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 21, 2018.
P0079.body:
A furniture showroom sells a sofa with three things a website does not have: a cushion to sit on, a fabric swatch to take home and a salesperson who can say the frame is kiln-dried hardwood. For years that was the reason the category stayed in stores. The numbers now say otherwise. Amazon did about $4 billion in US furniture sales in 2017, up 51% from the year before, according to One Click Retail’s research, CFN reported.

So the change in Amazon home and kitchen in 2018 is less about kitchen gadgets, which already sold well online, and more about the big, considered purchases that used to need a showroom. The products winning those searches are the ones whose page, box and returns policy do the showroom’s work.

Amazon home and kitchen moved from gadgets to big purchases

Kitchen appliances sold well online early, and for an obvious reason: shoppers knew what they were buying. On Prime Day 2016, members bought more than 215,000 Instant Pot pressure cookers in the US, The Next Web reported, and the Instant Pot was again the best-selling item in the US on Prime Day 2017, The Motley Fool reported. A multi-cooker has a model number, a capacity and thousands of reviews. Nobody needs to touch it first.

Furniture is different, and its growth is the story of 2017. One Click estimated that mattresses and box springs, Amazon’s largest furniture category, grew 82% to more than $1.1 billion, and that Amazon has more than tripled its annual furniture sales since 2015, Furniture Today reported. These are outside estimates. They include marketplace sales, Amazon did not comment on them and One Click declined to detail its method, so treat the precise figures with care. The direction is not in doubt.

The mattress is the telling product. It is the purchase shoppers were once most reluctant to make without lying down in a store, and it became Amazon’s biggest furniture category anyway. The product changed to fit the channel: compressed, rolled into a box that a parcel carrier can lift, often sold with a home trial meant to replace the ten minutes on a showroom bed.

The page has to do the showroom’s work

Inside a traditional furniture brand, the showroom is where the selling skill lives. Merchandisers build vignettes, staff learn the vocabulary of frames and fills, and the fabric library sits by the door. None of that travels to a product page unless someone deliberately rebuilds it there.

Picture a $900 sofa listed with two images: a cut-out on white and a close-up of the arm. The shopper cannot tell whether it fits the room, whether the cushions are firm or soft, or how it arrives. She scrolls on to a rival listing with seven images, a photo in a styled room, a dimensions diagram, a fabric close-up and a picture of the box. The second page is doing what the salesperson used to do, and it wins the sale without being a better sofa.

The same logic runs through the box itself. A sofa that ships in pieces needs assembly instructions that a shopper can follow alone, and a box size that carriers will take. Returns matter even more. A showroom absorbed the risk of a wrong choice before the sale; online, the returns policy absorbs it after. Brands that treat returns as a cost to minimize, rather than as the substitute for the showroom visit, make the shopper carry a risk the store used to carry.

Amazon is now a furniture brand too

The category also has a new competitor on the shelf. In November 2017, Amazon launched its first private-label furniture lines: Rivet, a mid-century modern range, and Stone & Beam, a higher-priced transitional range, TechCrunch reported.

Read as an institution, the move is consistent with what Amazon does in any category that grows fast: it learns what sells, then sells it itself. For furniture brands, that means the search results for “mid-century sofa” now include a seller that also owns the store. It does not mean the category is closed. It does mean that a generic product with a thin page is competing with the retailer on the retailer’s terms, and the brands with a distinctive design, a clear story and complete content have the better position.

What to ask before the next season’s range goes online

It is too early to say how large furniture on Amazon will get, and the estimates will keep being argued over. The evidence so far leans one way: considered purchases are moving online when the product and the page are built for it.

  • Which of our products would a shopper buy without seeing it first? Those belong online now; the rest need a better page, a better box or a different product.
  • Who owns the product page the way someone owns the showroom floor? If the answer is the e-commerce coordinator, the brand’s best selling skills are not reaching a fast-growing channel.
  • Does our returns policy replace the showroom visit, or punish the shopper for not having made one?
  • Where do we sit against Rivet and Stone & Beam in design, price and content, and what would a shopper see as the reason to choose us?

The furniture showroom took decades to teach shoppers what a good sofa looks like, and most of that knowledge still lives with the people who work there: the merchandiser who knows which fabric photographs badly, the salesperson who knows the question every couple asks about cushion depth. Getting it onto the page means interviewing them, not just the product team. On Amazon, the brands that win will be the ones that teach it again in seven images and a box. Rebuilding that selling skill on the product page is part of the channel management work we do with home brands.

P0085.crumb: Pricing power on marketplaces belongs to…
P0085.title: Pricing power on marketplaces belongs to whoever holds the stock
P0085.alt: An old key with a blank tag rests on a wooden pallet overlooking a warehouse full of boxed stock on shelves and pallets.
P0085.ttag: Pricing power on marketplaces belongs to whoever holds the stock | Kwontified
P0085.desc: A brand’s price list was built for stores. On marketplaces, price is set by whoever owns the stock and by the platform’s rules, not by the price committee.
P0085.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 28, 2018.
P0085.body:
The traditional way to set a price happens in a room. Finance, sales and the brand team agree a list price for the season, publish a minimum advertised price policy and send it to retail partners. Then someone searches Amazon and finds the season’s new jacket at three different prices, none of them the one agreed in the room.

That gap is not a policy failure. It reflects where pricing power sits on marketplaces: with whoever owns the inventory, and with the platform’s own rules about what a price should be. A brand that wants a say over its marketplace price has to decide who holds its stock. The price list cannot do that job.

Three parties set the price the brand thought it owned

Resellers are the most familiar of the three. A distributor or retailer that bought the jacket owns it and can price it as it likes; a brand’s minimum advertised price policy governs what is advertised, not what an owner may charge. On Amazon, where the price on the listing is the advertisement, that line blurs, and a brand’s enforcement depends on who it can identify and what it can withhold from them.

Then there is the marketplace itself, acting as a retailer. A brand that sells to Amazon as a vendor hands over the stock, and with it the price.

Amazon’s systems reprice constantly: they made more than 2.5 million price changes a day in November 2013, RetailWire reported on Profitero’s count. In November 2017 Amazon went a step further and began cutting prices on some third-party sellers’ items at its own expense, by less than 10%, while paying the sellers in full, Engadget reported on a Wall Street Journal finding. Retail Dive noted that such discounts could put sellers at odds with price-parity agreements they hold with other retailers, such as Walmart, in its coverage.

Finally, the platform’s rulebook. Walmart unpublishes marketplace items whose price looks uncompetitive against other sellers, Zentail explained in May 2017. That sets a ceiling no price committee voted on.

Take a $60 jacket, and a reseller with spare stock that lists it at $54. Amazon, selling units it bought from the brand, undercuts at $51. The brand’s own site holds at $60, and now looks 15% too expensive to anyone who checks.

Each party acted reasonably for itself. Nobody in the original room was asked. The reseller needed to clear stock before the next delivery; Amazon’s systems saw a lower price on the same page and responded; the brand’s own e-commerce team held the line. It now watches conversion fall on a site where the jacket has become, relative to the rest of the web, the most expensive it has ever been, without its price changing at all.

Why the price list stopped working

The price list was built for stores. A department store buyer agreed to a price, a promotion calendar and a markdown schedule, and the brand could see its products on the shelf. The structure assumed a small number of known retailers, each with a reason to keep the relationship.

Marketplaces replaced that structure with an open shelf. Anyone holding stock can sell, each seller answers to its own margin, and the platform answers to its shoppers. Read as an institution, Amazon is consistent about this. When Birkenstock weighed its options in 2016, the only way to keep fakes off the site, according to its US chief executive, was to sell directly to Amazon, Retail Dive reported. Control comes through ownership of the stock, and selling direct would have made Amazon the owner.

Follow the value and the logic is plain. The platform captures the shopper’s trust in its low prices; the resellers capture volume; the brand keeps the cost of a price that drifts down on every channel. Nike’s 2017 arrangement to supply Amazon directly was framed in the trade press as a move to take back control of pricing and distribution. That headline captures the shift: control is now negotiated through supply.

Where pricing power now comes from

The structural change is that pricing power has moved from the price list to the distribution map. A brand that knows who holds its stock on each marketplace, and has decided who should, has a lever. A brand that sells into a wholesale network and hopes the price holds has a policy document.

That does not mean every brand should sell direct on every marketplace. Selling to Amazon as a vendor gives up price in exchange for scale; selling as a seller keeps the price but adds the work of running the channel; allowing a few authorized resellers keeps the work away but shares the price. Each is a legitimate choice. The mistake is not choosing, and leaving the price to whoever ends up holding the stock.

It is too early to say how far platforms will go in setting prices themselves. The evidence so far leans toward more of it, not less: Amazon’s November 2017 discounting was a retailer reaching into its sellers’ prices to stay competitive with other sites.

Questions for the price committee

  • Who holds our stock on each marketplace right now, and did we choose them?
  • Which of our resellers buy from us directly, and which get stock through someone else?
  • Where is our minimum advertised price policy actually enforceable, and where is it a request?
  • If Amazon or Walmart priced our best seller 10% below our list next week, who inside the company would find out first, and who could act?

The price committee still matters. It now has to sit with the people who manage distribution. Mapping who sells a brand’s products, and deciding who should, is the channel management work we do with brands.

P0087.title: After Wayfair, marketplace sales tax follows the order count
P0087.alt: A brass tally counter beside a stack of twine-tied kraft paper parcels and a wax seal stamp on a rustic wooden table.
P0087.ttag: After Wayfair, marketplace sales tax follows the order count | Kwontified
P0087.desc: After Wayfair, a state can tax a marketplace seller by order count, and below a $500 average order the 200-transaction test arrives well before the dollars.
P0087.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 3, 2018.
P0087.body:
On June 21, 2018, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in South Dakota v. Wayfair that a state may require an out-of-state seller to collect its sales tax, overruling the 1992 Quill decision that made physical presence the test, the Washington Times reported. Most of the commentary since has been about Wayfair and Amazon. The sellers with the most to work out are the brands selling through Amazon’s marketplace, because the law the Court upheld counts orders, and marketplace sellers have a lot of small ones.

The South Dakota law reaches sellers that deliver more than $100,000 of goods into the state in a year or make 200 or more separate sales there, according to a Faegre Baker Daniels summary of the decision. Divide one number by the other and you get the figure that matters: $500. A brand whose average order is below $500 crosses the transaction test before the revenue test, in every state that copies the law.

Why marketplace sales tax after Wayfair looked like someone else’s problem

The comfortable view had good grounds. Amazon collects sales tax on its own retail sales, but it generally does not collect for merchandise sold by third-party sellers, who account for about half of its sales, Reuters reported in its coverage of the ruling. Before the ruling, Amazon collected for marketplace sellers in only a few states, including Washington and Pennsylvania, Retail Dive reported ahead of the April argument.

So a brand selling as a third-party seller could reason that its exposure was limited to states where it had a warehouse, an office or an employee. For a brand using Fulfillment by Amazon, that list was already longer than most finance teams realized, because Amazon places inventory where it chooses. But it was still a list defined by where the stock sat.

Wayfair changes the question from where the inventory is to where the buyers are.

The order count is the threshold that binds

A marketplace brand rarely has large orders. Take a skincare brand doing $1.5 million a year through Amazon at an average order of $30. That is 50,000 orders. If a state accounts for 1% of them, the brand ships 500 orders there, worth $15,000.

On revenue, the brand is far below South Dakota’s $100,000 line. On transactions, it is two and a half times over the 200-order line. If that state adopts the same test, the brand owes it a registration and a filing calendar on the strength of $15,000 of sales.

Run the same arithmetic across states and the pattern holds. Any state that takes even 0.4% of this brand’s orders (200 of 50,000) brings it over the line. Most of the populous states will clear that easily. The dollar threshold, the one executives remember from the headlines, is not the one that applies to them.

The cost lands in compliance, not in the tax itself. Sales tax is collected from the shopper, so the direct charge to the brand is small if it collects correctly. What costs money is registering, filing and reconciling in many states, and the risk of being asked for tax that was never collected. The Online Merchants Guild told Retail Dive that a major worry for its members was back taxes.

The Court left room on that point. The South Dakota case went back to the state courts for further review, so the law the Court described is a model, not yet a bill for anyone. Which states copy it, with which thresholds and from which date, is still open on July 3, 2018.

What the ruling does to price on a shared listing

There is a second effect, and it shows up on the product page. When a brand sells on a listing where Amazon also sells as a retailer, Amazon has been charging sales tax at checkout and many third-party offers have not. Once more states require collection from remote sellers, that gap narrows, and the offers compete on the pre-tax price alone.

For brands that relied on tax-free third-party offers to win the Buy Box against resellers or against Amazon’s own retail offer, that is a quiet loss of advantage. For brands that sell only through Vendor Central, it changes nothing, because Amazon is already the seller of record.

The longer-run question is who collects. A tax consultant for the Retail Industry Leaders Association told Retail Dive he considered it a virtual certainty that most sales tax states would expand their definition of a retailer to include marketplaces if Quill fell. If that happens, the marketplace would collect on third-party sales, and the seller’s filing burden would shrink in those states. That is a forecast, not a law, and a brand should plan for both outcomes.

A short tax check for marketplace sellers

None of this is tax advice, and the state rules are not written yet. These are the numbers a brand should have before the first state acts:

  1. Orders by state, last 12 months. Pull the shipment report from Seller Central and count orders, not dollars, per state. Flag every state above 200.
  2. Average order value. If it is under $500, assume the transaction test applies first, and plan around order counts.
  3. Where the inventory sits. List every state where Fulfillment by Amazon has held your stock; those are physical-presence questions under the old rule.
  4. Your selling model, listing by listing. Note which listings sell through Vendor Central, where Amazon collects, and which through Seller Central, where you may have to.

Take the list to a sales tax adviser before the end of the quarter. A brand that hands its Amazon operation to us gets that state-by-state order report as part of how we run the channel day to day, so the tax conversation starts from real counts.

P0088.crumb: A generic Amazon brand store sells like a…
P0088.title: A generic Amazon brand store sells like a search page
P0088.alt: Empty wooden shelving units line the walls of a bare concrete storeroom lit by a single high window.
P0088.ttag: A generic Amazon brand store sells like a search page | Kwontified
P0088.desc: Most Amazon brand stores are a banner and a grid of best sellers, so shoppers compare them on price and stars the way they compare a search page.
P0088.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 5, 2018.
P0088.body:
Walk through the cosmetics floor of a department store and every brand has built its own small room. The counters, the lighting, the order of the shelves and the person behind the counter all belong to the brand, and a shopper can tell where one ends and the next begins with her eyes half closed. Now open three Amazon brand stores in the same category, one after another. Each has a wide banner, a row of best sellers and a grid of product tiles with prices and star ratings. Swap the logos and few shoppers would notice.

That sameness has a cost. A store built as a grid of products asks the shopper to do what she does on a search results page: compare prices and stars. The Amazon brand store is worth building only when it does the job a product page cannot, which is to show the range and the reason to choose this brand, and most stores miss it because nobody owns them once they launch.

What Amazon built, and why the stores converge

Amazon describes a Store as a free, customizable, multipage shopping experience that showcases the brand and a curated product selection, built from customizable templates with a brand-specific Amazon URL and multimedia features, in its November 2017 announcement that brought its ad programs to Amazon.ca.

The templates are the important part. The builder gives every brand the same set of templates and the same tiles, and the fastest way to fill them is with the products the brand already sells most. A team building a store in an afternoon will reach for the best-seller grid first, because it is accurate and it is done. So stores converge, the way the product pages of a category converge on the same white-background hero image: each sensible decision on its own produces a shelf where nobody stands out.

The department store never let that happen, because the fixtures cost money. A brand that paid for a counter, a shelf plan and staff had a budget line, and a budget line has an owner who answers for it at the next review. A free store has no budget line. Work with no line of its own tends to get done once, at launch, and then sits.

Who the store is really for

The traffic tells you what the store is for. A shopper rarely wanders into a brand store on her own; she arrives from the brand name on a product page, from outside Amazon, or from an ad. Headline Search Ads, the banner at the top of search results, can send shoppers to a brand’s Store, Amazon said when it described the program.

That makes the store, for most brands, a landing page for their own advertising, and it changes the cost of a generic one.

Say a brand pays $1.00 a click to send shoppers from a Headline Search Ad for “vitamin C serum” into its store. If the shopper lands on the same grid of products she just left, with the same prices and the same stars, the brand has paid a dollar to show her a smaller search page. If she lands on a page that sorts the range by skin concern, explains which serum suits which routine and shows the set that pairs with it, the dollar bought something the search page could not give her.

Follow the value and the logic of Amazon’s design becomes clear. Amazon gives the store away because a better-built store converts more of the shopper’s attention into sales on Amazon, and the ad that sends her there earns Amazon a click either way. The brand captures the extra value only if it does the work of making the store different. Amazon has every reason to provide the tools and no reason to do that work for anyone.

A store organized around the shopper’s question

A store reads as the brand’s own when it is organized around the questions a shopper brings rather than around the catalog. A running shoe brand sorts by the kind of running, not by model number. A skincare brand sorts by concern, then by step in the routine. An apparel brand shows a full outfit and the sizes it comes in, which no single product page can do.

It also means using the parts of the builder that cost effort. Video and slideshows are there because a product page shows one item at a time, and a store can show how items relate: the refill next to the bottle, the case next to the phone, the full kit next to its pieces.

None of this requires a design agency. It requires someone to decide, at regular intervals, what the store should say this season and to check whether shoppers who arrive there buy more than shoppers who land on a product page. That is a job description, and a free tool does not come with one.

Questions for the team before the next season

  • Who last changed our Amazon Store, and when? If the answer is the launch date, that is the problem.
  • How much of the traffic to our store comes from our own ads, and what do those shoppers see when they arrive?
  • If we removed our logo, could a shopper tell our store from our closest competitor’s?
  • Does our store answer a question our product pages cannot, and which question is it?

A store with an owner, a seasonal plan and a measure of what it adds is the kind of Amazon shelf we run for brands day to day. The first step is a hard look at the store as it stands.

P0089.crumb: The Zalando Partner Program commission is…
P0089.title: The Zalando Partner Program commission is the smaller cost
P0089.alt: Worn cardboard boxes, a bag of coins and stacks of folded sweaters and poly mailers piled on a wooden table by a yellow wall.
P0089.ttag: The Zalando Partner Program commission is the smaller cost | Kwontified
P0089.desc: Brands negotiating the Zalando Partner Program commission argue over the smaller cost; with about half of orders returned, logistics decides the margin.
P0089.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 10, 2018.
P0089.body:
A brand weighing the Zalando Partner Program usually starts with one number: the commission. It is the figure in the contract, the one finance asks about and the one that gets negotiated. It is also the smaller of the two costs that decide whether the channel makes money. On a platform where shoppers send back about half of what they order, the brand pays to ship and handle every parcel but earns only on the items that stay, so the return rate moves the margin more than the commission does.

Why the Zalando Partner Program commission gets all the attention

The Partner Program lets brands list and dispatch their own inventory on Zalando instead of selling only through Zalando’s buyers, Coresight Research noted in June 2017. It is growing fast: Zalando’s management said on its fourth-quarter 2017 call that the program had doubled in size in 2017, according to the call transcript.

Zalando does not publish a standard commission. The rate sits in each partner’s contract, which is one reason it dominates the conversation: it is the cost a brand can see and argue about before launch. Wholesale habits reinforce it. A brand used to selling to Zalando’s buyers thinks in terms of the margin it gives up on each unit, and the commission looks like the direct replacement for that discount.

What wholesale never showed the brand was the return, because the cost of a return sat on the retailer’s books. When Zalando bought the stock, a dress sent back by a shopper in Hamburg was Zalando’s problem. When the brand sells through the Partner Program, the parcel comes back to whoever shipped it.

The arithmetic of a kept item

Returns are not an exception on Zalando; they are part of the model. The company’s management said as early as 2013 that a return rate of around half was normal for its business, Twinkle magazine reported.

So the useful unit is not the item shipped but the item kept. If half of shipments come back, a brand ships two items to sell one. Every cost charged per parcel is paid twice for each sale, and the handling cost of the return is paid once.

Take a €60 dress. Say the contract sets a 20% commission on items kept, so €12 a sale. Say the outbound parcel costs the brand €5 and receiving, checking and restocking a return costs €4. Here is the cost per kept item at three return rates, before the cost of the dress itself:

Return rateItems shipped per item keptCommissionOutbound shippingReturn handlingTotalShare of €60 price
50%2.0€12.00€10.00€4.00€26.0043%
40%1.7€12.00€8.33€2.67€23.0038%
30%1.4€12.00€7.14€1.71€20.8635%

At a 50% return rate, logistics costs €14 per kept item against €12 of commission. The return rate has overtaken the commission as the larger cost.

The table also gives the exchange rate between the two. Lowering returns from 50% to 40% saves €3.00 per kept item. Negotiating the commission down by five points, from 20% to 15%, also saves €3.00. On these numbers, ten points of return rate are worth five points of commission, and the brand controls the first far more than the second.

What moves the return rate, and what does not

Some returns come with the category. A shopper who orders two sizes of the same shoe intends to send one back, and no product page will change that. Others are the brand’s to reduce, and they are worth finding in the data style by style. Size charts that match the cut, photos that show the true color, and descriptions of fit (“runs small”, “relaxed through the hip”) all lower the share of parcels that come back.

The second lever is who carries the parcel. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions, launched in June 2017, takes over customer-facing logistics for Partner Program brands, from stock arriving at the warehouse to the returns, FashionUnited reported. For a brand shipping into several countries from one warehouse, Zalando’s per-parcel costs may be lower than its own, which shrinks the €5 and €4 in the table. That is a contract question with a price attached, and it should be compared item kept by item kept, not parcel by parcel.

Price changes the picture too. Parcel costs are fixed per parcel, not per euro, so the same €14 of logistics is 23% of a €60 dress and 12% of a €120 coat. Commission scales with price; shipping and returns do not. That makes low-priced, often-returned items the weakest candidates for selling direct, and premium lines the strongest, even before anyone negotiates a rate.

The trade-off runs the other way for slow sellers. A style that sells once a month and comes back half the time carries all of the logistics cost and little of the revenue. Leaving it with Zalando’s wholesale buyers, or off the platform, can be the better margin.

Rules for the Zalando business case

  • Model every Partner Program style on cost per item kept, using the return rate for its category, not the commission alone.
  • Use ten points of return rate as worth roughly five points of commission at a €60 price, and recompute the ratio for your own prices and parcel costs.
  • Ask Zalando for the Zalando Fulfillment Solutions rate card before launch, and compare it with your own shipping and returns cost per kept item.
  • Fix fit information on the twenty styles with the highest return rates before negotiating the commission.

Brands planning a European launch can test their numbers with us; we launch and operate Zalando alongside other international marketplaces, and the return model is where that work starts.

P0091.crumb: Gifting on marketplaces starts with the…
P0091.title: Gifting on marketplaces starts with the person, not the product
P0091.alt: Ribbon-tied gift boxes, floral gardening gloves, a trowel, a blue-patterned teacup and old books on a wooden shelf by a navy wall.
P0091.ttag: Gifting on marketplaces starts with the person, not the product | Kwontified
P0091.desc: Gift shoppers on marketplaces start from the person they are buying for, and most product pages are written only for the person who will use the product.
P0091.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 12, 2018.
P0091.body:
Take a shopper looking for her father’s birthday present. She types “gifts for dad who runs” into Amazon’s search bar. She does not know his shoe size, his preferred brand or whether he already owns a heart rate monitor. Every product page she opens answers questions she cannot ask: cushioning, drop, battery life, compatibility. After twenty minutes she buys a gift card.

That scene is the whole problem of gifting on marketplaces. The person buying is not the person who will use the product, and the product page is written for the user. Gift shoppers start from the recipient, a price and a fear of getting it wrong. Brands that write only for the user hand that demand to gift cards and to the competitors who answer the giver’s questions.

Gifting on marketplaces is a large share of the year

The calendar of gifts runs well beyond December. Americans planned to spend $23.1 billion on Mother’s Day in 2018, and 31% of shoppers planned to buy on e-commerce sites, according to the National Retail Federation’s survey. Father’s Day spending was projected at $15.3 billion, with clothing the most common gift at 43% of shoppers and gift cards close behind at 42%, the same survey series found.

The holidays repeat the pattern at a larger scale. Gift cards were the most requested holiday gift for the eleventh year in a row in 2017, asked for by 61% of those surveyed, ahead of clothing and accessories at 55%, NRF reported.

Read those numbers from the giver’s side. Gift cards are popular because they move the risk of choosing from the giver to the recipient. A shopper who cannot tell which product is right will pay to avoid deciding. Every gift card bought on a marketplace is a gift that could have been a brand’s product, if the brand’s page had made the decision easy. The categories that top the gift lists, clothing above all, are also the ones where the fear of a wrong size or a wrong style is sharpest, which helps explain why the gift card sits so close to them on every list.

The product page was built for someone else

The way brands write for marketplaces has a history. Product detail pages grew out of catalog copy and the spec sheet. They list features in the order an engineer or a merchandiser thinks of them, and reviews accumulate from people who used the product. Both serve a shopper who is buying for herself and knows what she needs.

The giver brings different questions. She wants to know whether he will like it if he already owns one, and what happens if it does not fit. She needs it to arrive by Sunday. She wonders whether it will look like a gift when it arrives or like a replacement part in a brown box. None of those questions appears in a feature list, and a brand reviewing its pages for conversion will not see the gap, because gift orders and self-purchases land in the same sales report.

There is a structural reason the gap persists. Brand teams write marketplace content around the product, organized by SKU and owned by whoever manages the catalog. Gifting belongs to the seasonal marketing calendar, owned by a different team and usually aimed at the brand’s own website and its stores. So the marketplace pages, where nearly a third of Mother’s Day shoppers planned to buy, are the ones least likely to carry the gift message.

What a page written for the giver looks like

The physical store solved this decades ago with the gift table near the entrance. It held a few curated items at clear price points, already boxed, with a salesperson nearby to suggest what a father or a sister might like. A marketplace has no gift table, but a brand can build most of its function into the listings it controls.

It starts with language. Titles and bullets that name the recipient and the occasion (“a gift set for new runners”) match the way givers search. Gift sets and bundles remove a choice the giver is afraid of making: one item, one price, nothing to size. Sizing guidance written for someone who does not know the recipient’s measurements (“if unsure, choose the larger size”) lowers the fear of a wrong fit. Images that show the packaging, not only the product, answer the question of whether it will look like a gift.

Delivery is part of the gift. A giver shopping on Wednesday for a Sunday occasion is buying a delivery date as much as a product, which is one more reason Prime-eligible stock matters most in the weeks before a gifting day.

Reviews deserve a look too. A brand cannot write its own reviews, but it can notice which reviews mention a gift and make sure the questions those reviewers raise, about packaging, about sizing for someone else, are answered in the listing itself.

None of this replaces the self-purchase page. It adds a second reader to the same listing, and the brands that write for both will take a share of the demand that now ends in a gift card.

The season to prepare is the next one

Mother’s Day and Father’s Day have passed, and the holiday gifting season is the next large test. The work that matters (gift sets built and listed, sizing copy rewritten, packaging photographed, stock positioned for fast delivery) takes months, not weeks, because new bundles need inventory and listings before shoppers start searching.

The question I would put to a brand’s leadership team in July 2018 is simple: which of our top twenty marketplace listings would help a shopper who has never used our product choose it for someone she loves? If the answer is none, the holiday plan has a gap that no advertising budget will close, and we work with brands to rebuild those listings for the giver as well as the user.

P0095.title: Back-to-school 2018 is shopped from a list, not from a brand
P0095.alt: A clipboard with blank grid paper, pencils, an eraser and a notebook beside a blue and tan canvas backpack against a light blue wall.
P0095.ttag: Back-to-school 2018 is shopped from a list, not from a brand | Kwontified
P0095.desc: Back-to-school 2018 is shopped from a school’s supply list, so marketplace brands win by matching the list’s words and the parent’s budget, not by brand pull.
P0095.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 19, 2018.
P0095.body:
Every July a sheet of paper decides a large share of a category’s sales. A teacher writes “two wide-ruled composition notebooks, 24 count crayons, one pack of glue sticks,” the school posts it, and a parent carries it, folded or photographed, into a store or onto a phone. Nobody on that list asked a brand for anything. That is the first thing to understand about back-to-school 2018: the demand is written by schools and children, and the shelf, physical or digital, only fills the order.

The season is large and steady. Spending on K-12 and college combined is projected at $82.8 billion in 2018, close to last year’s $83.6 billion, the National Retail Federation said on July 12. Families with children in K-12 plan to spend $684.79 each, and clothing is the largest single category at $236.90. A season that size does not need a brand to create demand. It needs a brand to be the one picked when the list is filled.

How parents actually shop back-to-school 2018

The list makes the shopper literal. A parent searching for a back-to-school item types what the list says, often down to the count and the ruling, and accepts any product that matches it at a fair price. Brand matters most where the child has a say (shoes, backpacks, clothes) and least where the teacher does.

Deloitte’s survey, released on July 11, shows where that order gets filled. Parents expect to spend about $510 per household on back-to-school in 2018, or nearly $28 billion in total. Mass merchants are the most-planned destination, named by 83% of respondents, ahead of dollar stores at 38%, online-only retailers at 36% and off-price stores at 32%. Parents plan to spend $292 in stores against $115 online.

That split is easy to misread as a verdict on online. It is better read as a picture of two different jobs. The trip to the mass merchant handles the list in one cart, because nobody wants to price-check glue sticks item by item. Online handles the things that need research or are hard to find in the aisle: the specific calculator a math teacher named, the backpack a child picked from a video, the refill pack that ran out in October. Marketplace brands compete for the second job far more than the first.

Who writes the demand, and who captures it

Follow the money through a back-to-school purchase and the brand sits near the end of the chain. The school sets the specification, the child sets the taste, the parent sets the budget and the retailer sets the price comparison. A brand’s ad budget arrives after all four have spoken.

On a marketplace, that order shows up in search. A parent searching the list’s exact phrase sees a results page sorted by relevance and sales history, with sponsored listings at the top. Whoever’s product title repeats the list’s words, shows the count in the main image and carries a price per unit that holds up next to the mass merchant wins the click. A brand name in the title does little for a parent who was told to buy “wide-ruled,” not a brand.

Apparel and footwear work differently, and they are where the money concentrates. The $236.90 clothing figure is a child’s choice filtered through a parent’s budget. Here a brand’s name does carry weight, but the purchase still turns on fit, returns and delivery before school starts, the same questions that decide footwear on a marketplace the rest of the year.

The calendar is the parent’s, not the retailer’s

Timing is the part most brands plan from their own side. The NRF found that 77% of back-to-school shoppers plan to start at least three weeks before school begins. School start dates differ by district and state, so the season does not peak on one date; it rolls across the country through August, with each region’s peak arriving a few weeks before its first day.

That has a plain consequence for a brand selling on Amazon or Walmart.com. Stock and ad budgets set against a single national peak will be too early for some regions and too late for others, and the search terms for list items will build for weeks before sales peak. Deloitte’s survey found that parents expect to spend most of the season’s money in stores, so the online sale often comes from the item the store did not have, at the moment the parent discovered it was missing.

The season also carries a second wave. Lists are completed, notebooks fill, and a child outgrows shoes in October. The September and October searches for refills and replacements look small next to August, and they are the ones a brand can win with less competition from the big-box trip.

Questions for the back-to-school review

Before the season peaks, put these to the team:

  • Do our titles and main images use the words on a typical supply list for our category, including counts and specifications, or the words our brand team prefers?
  • Is our price per unit competitive against the multipack a parent would find at a mass merchant on the same trip?
  • Which of our products does a child choose, and do those listings show fit, colors and delivery dates as clearly as the store shelf does?
  • Will our stock and our budget still be in place in September, when the second wave arrives and most competitors have gone quiet?

The brands that do well in back-to-school 2018 will be the ones that read the list before they read their own plan. That is the kind of seasonal planning we build into channel management for brands on Amazon and Walmart.
