P0096.crumb: Prime Day 2018 results beat the forecast…
P0096.title: Prime Day 2018 results beat the forecast because 2017 moved
P0096.alt: A vintage brass caliper measures a twine-tied kraft paper parcel on a sunlit wooden table.
P0096.ttag: Prime Day 2018 results beat the forecast because 2017 moved | Kwontified
P0096.desc: Prime Day 2018 results beat the $3.4 billion forecast on outside estimates, but the estimates disagree on 2017, and a brand’s own lift needs a baseline test.
P0096.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 24, 2018.
P0096.body:
Six weeks before Prime Day, Coresight Research forecast that the event would bring in about $3.4 billion worldwide. A day after it ended, Wedbush Securities estimated $4.2 billion. On the face of it the forecast missed by $800 million, almost a quarter of its own number. Look at the growth rates behind the two figures and most of that gap disappears: the firms agree on how much Prime Day grew and disagree on how big it was in 2017.

That matters beyond the scoreboard. The Prime Day 2018 results Amazon published are counts and comparisons, not dollars, so every revenue figure is an estimate built on another estimate. For a brand, the number worth grading is its own, and that grade needs a baseline the event reports do not provide.

What Amazon said, and what it did not

Amazon’s recap on July 18 said Prime members bought more than 100 million products over the 36 hours, and that sales beat Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Prime Day 2017 when each is compared over a 36-hour period, according to its announcement. Small and medium-sized businesses selling on Amazon passed $1 billion in sales during the event. Amazon gave no total for revenue.

The comparison window flatters the event, and that is by design. Black Friday is a single day in a season that runs for weeks; Prime Day is a 36-hour peak with nothing around it. Comparing 36-hour blocks says Prime Day is the most concentrated buying Amazon has seen. It does not say how much of that buying would have happened anyway, or how much of it was pulled out of the weeks on either side of the event, which is where a brand’s own reports have to do the work.

Grading the forecast on growth, not dollars

2017 base2018 figureImplied growth
Coresight forecast (June 4)$2.4 billion$3.4 billion42%
Wedbush estimate (July 19)about $3.2 billion$4.2 billion33%

Wedbush analyst Michael Pachter put sales at $4.2 billion, up 33% on a year earlier, the Columbian reported. Working back from those two numbers puts Wedbush’s 2017 base near $3.2 billion. Coresight’s 2017 base was $2.4 billion, in its preview. The $800 million gap in 2018 is almost exactly the gap in their views of 2017.

So on growth, the forecast was not too low. If anything it was the more optimistic of the two: 42% against 33%. The honest grade is that nobody outside Amazon knows the dollar size of Prime Day to within a quarter, and any plan built on a precise outside number is built on a guess. The event clearly grew; Feedvisor’s clients saw sales in the first 12 hours rise 89% on 2017, Bloomberg reported, though that sample is one software firm’s customers rather than the market.

Added sales and borrowed sales

The question the totals cannot answer is the one that decides whether a brand’s Prime Day paid. Some of the event’s sales are new: shoppers who would not have bought that month at all. Some are borrowed: shoppers who held off for a week before the event, or bought in July what they would have bought in August. Both look identical on Prime Day itself.

Take a brand that normally sells $10,000 a day on Amazon. Over the 36 hours it sells $60,000. In the seven days before the event, sales slipped to $9,000 a day as shoppers waited for deals; in the seven days after, they ran at $8,000 a day. The normal baseline for 36 hours is $15,000, so the event looks like $45,000 of extra sales. Subtract the $7,000 lost in the week before and the $14,000 lost in the week after, and the real lift is $24,000, a little over half of what the event-day report shows.

Deal pricing makes the gap bigger. Those borrowed sales were often bought at the deal price, so the brand gave a discount on sales it would have made at full price. If the deal was 30% off, the borrowed sales cost the brand margin as well as timing.

The same arithmetic applies to the ad budget. Sponsored Products spend on Prime Day bought clicks from shoppers who were already in a buying mood, and a share of those shoppers would have found the brand’s deal through the deals page or organic search. Return on ad spend during the event therefore overstates what the ads added. The only clean way to know is a holdout: leave a matched set of products, or a matched set of keywords, without extra ad spend during the event, and compare their lift with the rest.

Outside evidence points the same way. Adobe found large US retailers with over $1 billion in annual revenue saw online sales 54% above an average Tuesday on Prime Day, while retailers with under $5 million saw an 18% decline, TechCrunch reported on July 18. Demand moved toward the date and toward the biggest stores. Some of it came from somewhere.

Rules for reading your own Prime Day

  • Measure lift against a baseline from at least two weeks before and after the event, not against a normal day.
  • Report sales during the event and net lift after the dip; only net lift belongs in next year’s budget.
  • Price the borrowed sales: the post-event dip times the deal discount is margin given away.
  • Treat any outside dollar estimate of Prime Day as uncertain by a quarter either way, and plan on growth rates.

Two weeks of post-event data will be in by early August, which is the right time to grade a brand’s own Prime Day and the starting point for the baselines we build before every tentpole event.

P0098.title: Prime Day 2018 deals were committed before anyone knew the date
P0098.alt: An open blank spiral notebook and a kraft string-tie envelope on a worn wooden desk by a window.
P0098.ttag: Prime Day 2018 deals were committed before anyone knew the date | Kwontified
P0098.desc: Brands locked in Prime Day 2018 deals in May, Amazon named the date in July and Target answered four days out. Retailers now own the promotional calendar.
P0098.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 26, 2018.
P0098.body:
In most brands, the promotional calendar is a document someone owns. It lists the year’s price events, the margin each one may cost and the stock it needs, and it is argued over in a planning meeting long before the season.

Prime Day 2018 ran on a different order of events. Sellers had to submit their Lightning Deals by May 18. Amazon announced the date on July 3, 13 days before the event. Target announced its answer on July 13, four days before it ran. The brands that took part committed their price and their inventory first and learned the date second.

That sequence is the real lesson of Prime Day 2018, more than any sales total. The retailer now holds the information that sets the calendar, and the brand plans around a date it does not know.

The order of decisions on Prime Day 2018

Look at who knew what, and when. A brand that wanted a Lightning Deal on Prime Day had to choose its products, its discount and its quantities by May 18, ChannelX reported at the time. Two months later, Amazon told the public that the event would start at noon Pacific on July 16 and run for 36 hours across 17 countries, with deals in Whole Foods Market stores as well, 9to5Mac reported on July 3.

Then the rest of retail moved. Target announced on July 13 a one-day sale on Target.com for July 17, open to all shoppers with no membership required, according to its announcement. A brand sold at both retailers found out four days ahead that it would be on promotion at two of its largest customers in the same 36 hours, on terms one of them set months earlier and the other set that week.

Inside the brand, those decisions sit with different people. The Amazon deal was most likely approved by an e-commerce manager in the spring. The Target promotion, if the brand funded one, came through the sales team that manages Target. Finance saw both as margin, after the fact. Nobody in that chain held the whole picture, because the picture did not exist until four days before the event.

Who gains when the retailer holds the date

Follow the value and the answer is plain. A retailer that holds the date can plan traffic, staffing and its own inventory around it, then ask brands to fund the discounts. Amazon said Prime members bought more than 100 million products over the 36 hours, and that small and medium-sized businesses selling on Amazon passed $1 billion in sales, in its July 18 recap. Target said its July 17 sale was its biggest online day of the year so far, in both traffic and sales, CNBC reported.

The gains did not spread evenly. Adobe found that US retailers with more than $1 billion in annual revenue saw online sales 54% above an average Tuesday on Prime Day, while retailers under $5 million saw an 18% decline, TechCrunch reported. The large retailers had the traffic and the planning capacity to react to Amazon’s date. Small ones lost shoppers to the event.

Brands sit in a similar position to those small retailers. The ones with the most to lose are those whose promotional plan is fixed a year ahead and cannot react: the deal is already promised, the stock already shipped and the price already printed on a retailer’s circular. The ones that do well can move price and budget within days.

A calendar the brand no longer writes

The shift is easy to miss because it looks like more of the same. Brands have always run promotions on dates retailers chose: Black Friday, back-to-school, the circular. What changed in 2018 is how late the date arrives and how quickly rivals respond. A summer peak now has its own deal deadline, its own counter-events and its own winners, and its date is announced with less notice than most brands need to move a truckload of stock.

Shoppers have adjusted faster than brands. When Amazon’s site returned errors in the first minutes of the event on July 16, the company said some customers were having difficulty shopping and that it was working to resolve the issue quickly, Fortune reported, and the event still set Amazon’s sales record by its own 36-hour comparison. People came back because the date, not the website, had become the appointment. A shopper who plans her July around a retailer’s event is a shopper whose purchase timing the retailer now controls, and the brand inherits that timing whether it planned for it or not.

It is too early to say whether retailers will give more notice as the event matures. The evidence so far leans the other way: every party learns more by waiting, and only the brand has to commit early.

Questions for the post-Prime Day review

  • Who in our company approved the Prime Day deals, who approved any competing retailer promotion, and did they ever meet?
  • Which of our deals were set before the date was known, and would we have chosen the same discount and quantity if we had known Target’s plan?
  • How quickly can we change a price, a budget or an allocation once a retailer names a date: in four days, or in four weeks?
  • Did the event add customers, or did it move sales we would have made in August at full price?

A brand that can answer the third question with “four days” is in a position to plan Prime Day 2019 rather than wait for it, which is the planning we run for brands across Amazon and Target.

P0099.title: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q2 2018: Sponsored Products spend up 165%
P0099.alt: A tall stack of silver coins beside a shorter stack of copper coins on a sunlit wooden windowsill.
P0099.ttag: Amazon ad benchmarks, Q2 2018: Sponsored Products spend up 165% | Kwontified
P0099.desc: Public Amazon ad benchmarks for Q2 2018 show Sponsored Products spend up 165% at Merkle, faster than Amazon ad sales grew. Read your growth as price first.
P0099.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 31, 2018.
P0099.body:
Advertisers working with Merkle spent 165% more on Amazon Sponsored Products in the second quarter of 2018 than a year earlier. In the first quarter the same figure was 96%. The growth rate rose by more than two-thirds in three months, at a time when spending on Google search ads was slowing. The quick reading is that brands found a better channel and poured money in. The more useful reading for anyone running an account is that a jump this large, in a marketplace with a fixed number of searches, is mostly a jump in price.

Amazon ad benchmarks for Q2 2018 outran search everywhere else

Measure, Q2 2018FigureSource
Sponsored Products spend, year over year+165%Merkle
Headline Search Ads spend, year over year+162%Merkle
Sponsored Products share of Amazon search ad spend88% (86% in Q1)Merkle
Amazon’s share of digital ad spend, Marin clients active on Amazonover 20%Marin Software
Sponsored Products share of Amazon spend, Marin clients79%Marin Software
Global average search CPC, Marin clients$0.85, up from $0.80Marin Software

Merkle’s figures come from its Q2 2018 Digital Marketing Report, released on July 19, and coverage of it in MediaPost. Merkle also found that clicks on Sponsored Products and Headline Search Ads converted at more than three times the rate of Google Shopping clicks, Search Engine Land reported. Marin’s numbers are from its Q2 2018 benchmark report, published on July 18.

Neither report publishes an Amazon cost per click or a return on ad spend. Benchmarks for those two numbers are still private, and any figure quoted for “average Amazon ROAS” should be treated as one agency’s client mix, not the market.

Why the spend number looks like good news

Higher spend usually follows results. If Amazon clicks convert at three times the rate of Google Shopping clicks, moving budget to Amazon is a rational choice, and Merkle’s conversion finding gives brands a reason to keep doing it. The bias at work is a familiar one: we read growth in spend as growth in opportunity, because in most channels it has been.

That reading breaks on a marketplace. The number of people searching Amazon for “running shoes” in a given week does not grow 165% because advertisers want it to. Sponsored Products appear on search results and product pages, and both are limited by how many shoppers show up. When advertisers’ budgets rise faster than the shopper traffic underneath them, the auction converts the extra money into higher prices per click.

How spend growth splits into price and volume

Spend is clicks times cost per click, so spend growth is click growth combined with CPC growth. The two reports cannot be split this way from the outside, but Amazon’s own results give a reference point. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which is mostly advertising, came to $2.19 billion in Q2 2018 against $945 million a year earlier; after adjusting for an accounting change, it grew roughly 64%, the Motley Fool estimated on July 30. Amazon’s ad business as a whole grew far more slowly than Merkle’s clients’ spending.

That gap says the clients in these benchmarks are growing faster than the average Amazon advertiser, which is plausible for agency clients, and that some of their growth comes at the expense of other advertisers’ share of the same auctions.

Take a brand whose Sponsored Products spend rose from $20,000 to $40,000 a quarter, doubling. If its clicks rose 40%, its average CPC rose about 43%, from $1.00 to $1.43. If its conversion rate held at 10% and its average order is $30, its cost per sale went from $10 to $14.30, and its return on ad spend fell from 3.0 to 2.1. The account grew. Each sale got 43% more expensive.

What the benchmarks leave out

Both reports describe agency and software clients, and those are not the average Amazon advertiser. They tend to be larger brands that adopted Amazon advertising early and are adding budget, keywords and products each quarter. A sample like that will show faster growth than the market, and it will include accounts that only started advertising in the past year, whose spend grows from a small base.

The mix inside the number moves too. Sponsored Products now runs on product detail pages as well as search results, so some of the growth is new placements rather than higher prices on the same ones. That is one honest reason spend can outgrow search traffic. It does not change the arithmetic for a brand bidding on the same keywords it bid on in Q2 2017, where extra competitors mean a higher price for the same click.

What would change this reading is a public CPC series for Amazon. If one showed flat prices alongside 165% spend growth, the growth would be reach, and the advice below would soften. Until then, price is the safer assumption for planning the second half of 2018.

What to check against these benchmarks

  • Split your Q2 2018 spend growth into click growth and CPC growth before comparing it with 165%.
  • Compare Sponsored Products’ share of your Amazon search spend with Merkle’s 88%.
  • Track cost per sale by quarter alongside spend; spend growth shows what others paid, not what they got.
  • Hold the bid ceiling to margin. A rising auction is a reason to recheck it, not to match the market.

Q3 brings back-to-school and the start of holiday planning, when the same auctions get busier. A brand that knows how much of its growth was price is in a position to set Q4 bids from margin rather than from momentum, which is the work we do on Amazon advertising accounts.

P0100.crumb: Pet food on Amazon is won at the second…
P0100.title: Pet food on Amazon is won at the second order
P0100.alt: A plain kraft paper sack and an empty ceramic pet bowl on a doormat before a weathered red door framed by ivy and potted plants.
P0100.ttag: Pet food on Amazon is won at the second order | Kwontified
P0100.desc: Amazon launched its own dog food for Prime members in May. In pet, whoever holds the reorder holds the customer, and brands should plan for the second bag.
P0100.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 2, 2018.
P0100.body:
A 30-pound bag of dry dog food is the least pleasant thing most households carry out of a store, which is why so few of them want to keep carrying it. In May, Amazon began selling a dog food of its own, Wag, in chicken, beef and lentil, and salmon recipes at $12.99 for five pounds and $44.99 for thirty, available to Prime members. A retailer that already sells every major brand chose to put its own bag of kibble in front of its members. Why?

Because in pet food the sale that matters is not the first one. A household that finds a food its dog will eat tends to buy it again and again, and on Amazon that repeat purchase can happen without a single new search. Pet food on Amazon is won at the second order, and Wag tells you Amazon has noticed where the customer is held.

Pet food on Amazon has become a reorder list

The category is large and dominated by food. Americans spent a record $69.51 billion on their pets in 2017, and food was the biggest line at $29.07 billion, according to the American Pet Products Association’s annual figures, released in March. The association expects $72.13 billion in 2018.

A growing share of that food never sees a store shelf. Amazon drew 55% of shoppers who bought pet products online in Packaged Facts’ latest outlook, ahead of Chewy at 26%, PetSmart at 19%, Petco at 17% and Walmart and Sam’s Club together at 14%.

Think about what replaces the aisle. In a pet store, the brand fights for attention every visit: the end cap, the new bag design, the store associate’s recommendation, the competitor’s coupon on the shelf edge. On Amazon, the first purchase looks like that fight, with a search page full of bags. The second purchase often looks like nothing at all. It is a line in the order history, a “buy again” button, or a scheduled delivery the shopper set up once and stopped thinking about.

Amazon built that last option into a program. Subscribe & Save gives shoppers 5% off a scheduled delivery and 15% off when five or more subscriptions arrive together, Tinuiti explained in its guide to the program. For a household buying dog food, litter and treats every month, five items is not hard to reach.

What PetSmart paid for, and what Amazon wants

The clearest price anyone has put on the pet reorder was paid in April 2017, when PetSmart agreed to buy Chewy for a reported $3.35 billion, the largest e-commerce acquisition on record. A national store chain paid that sum for an online pet retailer, in a category where the asset is the household that comes back for the next bag.

Read Wag through the same lens. Amazon does not need a dog food brand to sell dog food; it already sells the leading ones. What a house brand gives Amazon is a product it can recommend to the household at the moment that household is choosing which bag to make its default. Tying Wag to Prime adds a second reason to stay. The membership pays for the shipping on the heavy bag, and the heavy bag gives the member another reason to renew.

None of this means Wag will take the category. Pet owners are cautious about changing food, and a dog’s stomach is a stern product reviewer. The evidence so far leans toward a narrower conclusion: the retailer, the specialist and the store chain have all decided the reorder is the asset worth paying for. A pet brand that treats Amazon as a place to clear volume is competing for the least valuable sale in the category.

The second bag changes what the first one is worth

Take a $45 bag that a household reorders every six weeks, about eight bags a year. Say the brand spends $15 in advertising to win that household’s first order. Judged on the first bag, the brand spent a third of the sale on advertising. Judged on the first year, if the household stays, the same $15 is about 4% of $360 in sales.

That arithmetic explains why pet brands should accept a higher cost for the first order than the first order alone can justify, and why they cannot afford to lose the customer after it. A household that switches at the second order costs the brand the whole year.

It also moves the work. The product page has to answer the questions a cautious owner asks before changing food: ingredients, feeding guidance by weight, the transition from the old food. The bag has to arrive intact, because a split bag of kibble on the doorstep becomes a review that every later shopper reads. The brand has to stay in stock, because a scheduled delivery that cannot be filled is an open invitation to choose something else.

Questions to put to the pet team

  1. Of the households that bought from us on Amazon in 2018, how many placed a second order, and how many set up a scheduled delivery?
  2. What does our product page tell an owner who is nervous about switching food, and where does it send them if their dog will not eat it?
  3. If the account went out of stock for two weeks, how many scheduled deliveries would fail?
  4. Which of our products would a shopper choose to make a default, and are those the ones we advertise?

The pet aisle on Amazon looks like a search page. The business underneath is a list of households and the dates their next bag is due, and running the channel day to day is how a brand keeps its place on that list.

P0102.title: Amazon’s Q2 2018 ‘other’ revenue says ads now outgrow sales
P0102.alt: A tall stack of gold coins beside three small twine-tied kraft parcels with tags on a wooden windowsill.
P0102.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2018 ‘other’ revenue says ads now outgrow sales | Kwontified
P0102.desc: Amazon’s ‘other’ revenue line, mostly advertising, grew far faster than its sales in Q2 2018, even after an accounting change. What that gap costs brands.
P0102.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 7, 2018.
P0102.body:
On July 26, Amazon reported a line that grew 132% in a year. “Other” revenue, which Amazon says consists mainly of advertising, came to $2.19 billion in the second quarter against $945 million a year earlier, Campaign Asia reported. Headlines called the ad business booming. Part of that growth is an accounting change. The part that is left still says something every brand advertising on Amazon should hear: the ad line is growing faster than the store it sits in, and the difference comes out of advertisers’ margins.

Amazon’s Q2 2018 other revenue mostly measures advertising

Amazon does not report advertising as its own line. It reports a bucket called “other,” which it describes as primarily advertising sales plus some smaller services, and analysts treat that bucket as the closest public measure of Amazon’s ad business.

The 132% figure compares two different things. The Q2 2018 number is reported gross, while the Q2 2017 number was reported net, after a change in how Amazon books certain advertising services, Campaign Asia noted. Read naively, the line more than doubled. Adjusted for the change, the Motley Fool estimated growth at roughly 64%.

So the honest headline is smaller. It is still large. Amazon’s total net sales rose 39% to $52.9 billion in the quarter, according to its release, and net income reached $2.5 billion against $197 million a year earlier. On the conservative reading, advertising grew more than one and a half times as fast as the company.

Why an ad line can outgrow the store it sits in

That gap looks odd at first. Advertising on Amazon sells products that are bought on Amazon. If shoppers buy 39% more, why would advertisers spend 64% more?

The answer sits on the search results page. A search for “stainless water bottle” shows a limited number of sponsored placements, and every advertiser that wants one is bidding for the same few spots. The price of a click is set by what rival bidders are willing to pay. When more brands decide that Amazon is where their customers shop, the number of bidders rises faster than the number of placements, and the price of each click climbs even if the number of shoppers searching grows only modestly.

Amazon’s ad revenue is clicks times price. Store sales are shoppers times what they buy. The two can grow at different speeds for years, because one depends on how many brands are competing and the other depends on how much shoppers spend. In Q2 2018 the first grew faster.

Brian Olsavsky, Amazon’s chief financial officer, told analysts that advertising was starting to have an effect on gross profit, the Motley Fool reported. That is the institutional half of the story. A business that discovers a high-margin line growing faster than its core has every reason to make room for more of it.

Take a brand selling $100,000 a month on Amazon with $10,000 a month in advertising, a TACoS of 10%. TACoS, total advertising cost of sale, is ad spend divided by all of the brand’s Amazon sales, not only the sales the ads claim.

Say the brand’s sales grow 20% in a year, to $120,000, while the price of the clicks it buys rises 30%. Holding the same share of clicks now costs $13,000, and TACoS rises to almost 11%. If click prices rise 40% instead, the same share of clicks costs $14,000 and TACoS reaches nearly 12%. Nothing went wrong in the account. The auction simply got more crowded, and the brand paid for the crowd out of its margin.

What the line can and cannot tell a brand

The “other” line is Amazon’s revenue, not your cost per click. It mixes Sponsored Products, Headline Search Ads and the display business run through Amazon Media Group and the Amazon Advertising Platform, plus non-advertising services. A brand in an uncontested category can see flat click prices in a quarter when the line grows sharply, and a brand in a crowded one can see prices climb faster than the average.

What it does tell you is the direction of the auction across the whole marketplace. When Amazon’s advertising revenue outgrows its sales, the average sale on Amazon carries more advertising cost than it did a year earlier. That is a fact about the market, and it shows up in individual accounts as a slow rise in TACoS that no bid change seems to fix.

It also tells you where Amazon’s attention is going. A retailer that books more profit on each ad dollar than on each product it ships will tend to make ads more visible, more varied and easier to buy. Brands should expect more ad formats and more sponsored placements, not fewer.

What would change the reading: a quarter in which the adjusted ad line grows no faster than retail sales, or accounts in your category where click prices hold flat while sales rise. Either would suggest the auction has room. Neither describes Q2 2018.

A rule for reading the next quarter

Track one number every quarter: your advertising spend as a share of all your Amazon sales. If it rises while your click-through and conversion rates hold steady, the auction is getting more expensive, and the fix is a margin decision about which searches are still worth buying, not a bid adjustment. If it rises while those rates fall, the problem is in your listings, and spending more will only buy the problem faster.

Then compare it with the gap between Amazon’s adjusted ad growth and its sales growth when the next quarterly results arrive. If your share is rising faster than that gap, your category is getting crowded faster than the marketplace, and the searches at the edge of profitability are the first to cut. We read this number with brands every quarter when we run their Amazon advertising.

P0104.title: Marketplace team structure puts brand media on a sales scorecard
P0104.alt: A clipboard holding a blank grid chart with one gold star sticker, beside a pen, folder and plant on a wooden desk.
P0104.ttag: Marketplace team structure puts brand media on a sales scorecard | Kwontified
P0104.desc: Amazon advertising is turning into one of a brand’s larger media budgets, yet many marketplace teams still report into sales and answer to quarterly orders.
P0104.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 9, 2018.
P0104.body:
Look at the slide that shows who runs Amazon at a consumer brand. You will usually find the marketplace team in one of two boxes: under the head of sales, next to the key account managers for Walmart and Target, or under e-commerce, which itself reports to sales. Its targets are shipped revenue and margin for the quarter. Meanwhile the team spends a growing share of its budget on advertising that shapes how shoppers first meet the brand. That is a media decision judged on a sales scorecard, and the mismatch explains a good deal of what goes wrong.

The question for leadership is whether the box the marketplace team sits in lets it make the decisions the channel now requires. In 2018, at many brands, it does not.

How marketplace team structure took its shape

The reporting line made sense when it was drawn. For most established brands, Amazon arrived as a customer: a buyer at Vendor Central issued purchase orders, and someone had to manage the account the way someone managed every other retailer. That someone sat in sales. Advertising, when it existed on Amazon at all, was a line in the account plan, funded alongside promotions and co-op, and it was small enough that nobody questioned where it lived.

That is no longer the scale of things. Amazon’s “other” revenue, the line that consists mainly of advertising, reached $2.19 billion in the second quarter of 2018, Campaign Asia reported after the July 26 results. Earlier in the year, coverage of the first quarter was already describing Amazon’s ads as a multibillion-dollar business. Brands are not funding that from experimental budgets any more. Eric Heller, who runs the Amazon-focused agency Marketplace Ignition, told Business Insider that marketers are increasingly shifting brand marketing dollars to Amazon.

So the money has started to move from the brand side of the house. The people deciding how to spend it, at many companies, have not.

What a sales scorecard does to media decisions

Picture the marketplace lead’s quarter. The number that matters is shipped revenue against plan, with a margin floor. Advertising that converts this week helps that number. Advertising that introduces the brand to a shopper who will buy next month, or a year later, does not show up in time.

Given that scoreboard, the sensible choices are predictable.

Spend concentrates on searches for the brand’s own name, where shoppers are already decided and the reported return looks excellent. Display and video, which build awareness and are bought on a cost per thousand impressions, look like waste. When the quarter is short, the advertising budget becomes the promotional lever, turned up to hit a number and down to protect margin. None of this is bad management. It is good management against the wrong measure.

Say the team is $200,000 short of its quarterly target with four weeks left. The fastest lever is to move $20,000 of display budget into searches for the brand’s own name, where the reported return is highest. The quarter closes closer to plan. What nobody records is the shoppers who would have met the brand through that display and bought in the following quarter, so the next quarter starts with a smaller audience and the same target.

The brand team, meanwhile, often sees none of it. Its media plan covers television, social and search engines, bought through an agency and measured on reach and awareness. Amazon appears in that plan, if at all, as a retailer the sales team handles. The result is two budgets aimed at the same shopper with no shared view of who she is or what she has already seen.

Follow the value and the cost of the split becomes clear. Amazon gains from both teams: the sales team buys the searches that close, the agency may buy display through Amazon’s media group. The brand gains less than it pays for, because neither team can see the whole path from first impression to the order and the reorder.

Where the structure is heading

The fix is not to move the whole marketplace team into marketing. Sales owns things that genuinely belong to sales: the vendor relationship, terms, purchase orders, chargebacks, inventory. Those are account management, and a brand that hands them to a media team will regret it at the next negotiation.

What needs to move is the decision about advertising and content, or at least the scorecard it is judged on. Some brands are starting to split the role: an account owner in sales for the retailer relationship, and a channel or media owner, measured on new customers and share of category searches as well as revenue, who sits closer to the brand. Others keep one team but give it two targets and a budget that does not get raided when the quarter is short. The evidence so far leans toward either arrangement working better than a single sales target, though it is too early to say which will become standard.

The deeper shift is that the retailer has become a media company, and the brand’s org chart has not caught up with the retailer’s. Until it does, a growing share of the brand’s media budget will be spent by people who are paid to close the current quarter.

The question worth asking at the next planning meeting is short: who here is accountable for the shoppers Amazon introduces to us, and what are they measured on? If the answer is a sales target, that is where to start, and running the channel day to day so the brand team can own that question is work we do with brands.

P0105.crumb: Q4 Amazon ad budget: phase it by the cost…
P0105.title: Q4 Amazon ad budget: phase it by the cost per sale, not the month
P0105.alt: Coin stacks rising in height from left to right beside twine-tied linen parcels and dry leaves on a rustic wooden table.
P0105.ttag: Q4 Amazon ad budget: phase it by the cost per sale, not the month | Kwontified
P0105.desc: Most Q4 plans split the Amazon ad budget by month. The better split follows the cost of each extra sale, which falls on peak days even as clicks get dearer.
P0105.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 14, 2018.
P0105.body:
Most Q4 plans for Amazon advertising start with a spreadsheet that splits the quarter’s budget the way last year’s sales split: a slice for October, a larger slice for November, the largest for December. It looks prudent. It usually leaves the account short on the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday and long in the quiet weeks of October. The better way to phase a Q4 Amazon ad budget is by what the next sale costs on each day, and that cost often falls on the peak days, even though every click costs more.

The Q4 2018 calendar, and what the 2017 peak looked like

The 2018 calendar is the place to begin: Thanksgiving falls on November 22, Black Friday on November 23 and Cyber Monday on November 26. The same stretch in 2017 set the pace for the whole season, and it is the best public guide to how concentrated the 2018 peak will be.

Day or period (2017)What happenedSource
Black FridayUS online sales of $5.03 billion, up 16.9%Adobe Analytics
Cyber MondayUS online sales of $6.59 billion, up 16.8%Adobe Analytics
Thanksgiving to Cyber MondayClose to 140 million items ordered from Amazon’s small business and entrepreneur sellersAmazon
November 1 to December 24US online sales up 18.1%, against 4.9% for all retailMastercard SpendingPulse

The figures come from Adobe’s Cyber Monday release, Amazon’s season summary and Mastercard SpendingPulse. The point of the table is concentration. A handful of days carry a share of the quarter’s demand that no monthly split captures.

Two 2018 rules sharpen the calendar for some brands. In Toys & Games, only eligible sellers may sell from October 17, 2018 to January 5, 2019, under rules summarized by SellerEngine. And from September 15, Amazon assesses long-term storage fees monthly rather than twice a year, EcommerceBytes reported, so stock sent in early for the holidays and left unsold costs more each month it sits.

Why the monthly split feels right, and where it fails

The monthly split is anchored on the most available number in the room: last year’s sales by month. Spending in proportion to sales sounds like spending in proportion to opportunity. It ignores that an ad budget buys clicks, and the price and the yield of a click both change with the calendar.

The number that matters is cost per sale: cost per click divided by the share of clicks that convert. Both halves move in Q4. Click prices rise because more advertisers bid on the same searches. Conversion rises because shoppers arrive ready to buy and deals make the decision easier. The question for each day is which half rises faster.

Take a $30 product. In mid-October, a click costs $0.80 and 10% of clicks convert, so a sale costs $8.00. On Cyber Monday, competition pushes the click to $1.40, but 20% of clicks convert, so a sale costs $7.00. In the second week of December, the click still costs $1.20 while conversion falls back to 12%, and a sale costs $10.00.

On those numbers, the most expensive clicks of the quarter buy the cheapest sales, and the quiet weeks on either side are where the budget earns least. A monthly split that runs out of money by Cyber Monday afternoon has spent its budget on the worst days and saved none for the best.

The peak days have a ceiling of their own. Within a single day, each extra dollar buys a weaker position or a looser search than the dollar before it, so cost per sale climbs as spend rises. Peak days deserve more budget, not unlimited budget. The rule is to keep adding money to a day while its next sale still costs less than the next sale on any other day.

What the 2017 account data can tell you, and what it cannot

Pull daily data for October through December 2017: spend, clicks, orders and sales for each campaign. Calculate cost per sale by day. Then look for the shape. If the pattern above holds, cost per sale dips around the peak days, but the size of that dip varies by category, price point and how many deals a brand ran.

Last year’s data has two weaknesses. Budgets that ran out early censor the peak days, so the account never saw what more money would have bought on Black Friday afternoon. And a brand that ran a deal in 2017 and will not in 2018 cannot assume the 2017 conversion rates.

What would change the plan: if the 2017 cost per sale on peak days was higher than in October, your category may be one where competition outruns conversion, and the budget belongs earlier in the season. Check before assuming the pattern. It takes an afternoon.

Budget triggers for the 2018 peak

  1. Raise daily budgets on the campaigns with the best cost per sale at least 48 hours before Thanksgiving, so changes are live before the event starts.
  2. Set an hourly check from November 22 to November 26 and add budget to any campaign that will run out before midnight while its cost per sale is below its October level.
  3. Cut spend in the second and third weeks of December first if the quarter’s budget runs tight, because that is where cost per sale tends to rise.
  4. Match the inventory plan to the ad plan: a campaign that wins the peak but sells out by Saturday wastes the Monday it was funded for.

This is the phasing we build with brands before every Q4 when we run their Amazon advertising, and it starts with last year’s daily data, not its monthly totals.

P0106.crumb: Price transparency makes a brand’s lowest…
P0106.title: Price transparency makes a brand’s lowest price its real price
P0106.alt: A speckled ceramic vase of eucalyptus and dried grass beside three blank tags in brass holders on a dark wooden shop table.
P0106.ttag: Price transparency makes a brand’s lowest price its real price | Kwontified
P0106.desc: Shoppers who compare across retailers in seconds see one price for a brand: the lowest. Why price architecture is now a brand decision, not an account one.
P0106.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 16, 2018.
P0106.body:
Stand in a department store and watch a shopper pick up a moisturizer, turn it over, then take out her phone. Within a few seconds she has the same jar on Amazon, the price on the retailer’s own site and, often, a cheaper listing from a seller she has never heard of. The store’s shelf tag was one price among several. Price transparency has turned the brand’s lowest visible price, wherever it appears, into the only price that shopper believes, and many brands still set price one account at a time.

The structure behind that habit was built for a world where shoppers saw one shelf at a time. That world is gone, and the brands that adjust are treating price architecture as a brand decision, owned above the account teams.

Price transparency starts with where shoppers look

The comparison happens constantly. In a BloomReach survey of 2,000 US shoppers, about 55% began their product searches on Amazon, CNBC reported, and only 16% started on a retailer’s own site. About 90% said they would check Amazon even after finding a product somewhere else, Retail Dive noted.

So the Amazon listing has become the reference price for products that are not even bought there. A shopper standing in a store, or browsing a brand’s own site, is often checking that number before deciding. Whatever it shows is what the brand appears to cost.

Amazon works hard to make sure that number is low. In late 2017 it began cutting the prices of some third-party sellers’ items at its own expense, to stay competitive with other websites, while still paying sellers their full price, according to a Wall Street Journal report summarized by Engadget. A retailer that will absorb part of the discount to match a rival elsewhere has made price comparison its business model.

Why brands still set price account by account

Inside a brand, price usually lives in several places at once. The list price sits with finance. Promotional prices are negotiated retailer by retailer by the account teams, each measured on its own customer’s sales. Online sellers, authorized or not, set their own prices from whatever cost they paid. Nobody is assigned to the question every shopper is asking: what does this product cost, anywhere, right now?

The shorthand many sales teams use for this is “channel conflict,” which frames it as a fight between retailers. From the shopper’s side it is something simpler. A 25% promotion run by one retailer to clear stock shows up on the phone of a shopper in another retailer’s aisle the same afternoon. The second retailer’s price now looks high, the second retailer asks the brand for support, and the brand funds a matching discount it never planned. The brand’s real price was set by its most aggressive account.

Some brands have decided that this is a brand problem, not an account problem. When Nike agreed to sell a limited range directly to Amazon in 2017, part of the arrangement was tighter policing of fakes. Some third-party sales of Nike products were also halted, The Drum reported, which the publication framed as an effort to take back control of pricing and distribution. Few brands have Nike’s bargaining power. The decision behind it, to manage where and how a product appears as one question, is available to any brand.

Price architecture is the brand’s answer

The practical response is price architecture: deciding, at the brand level, which products carry the brand’s price promise and which are built for channels where comparison is fiercest.

The products a shopper searches by name, the hero items, need one price story across every channel, held with the same discipline a brand applies to its logo. Promotions on them should be planned across retailers, so that a discount in one place is a decision rather than an accident.

Say a brand’s best-known face cream sells at $48 everywhere. If one retailer runs it at $36 for a weekend, every shopper who checks a phone that weekend learns the cream is worth $36, and the other retailers learn it too. A matched promotion across all of them, planned months ahead, costs margin too, but it is margin the brand chose to spend, and no retailer is surprised by it.

Other products can be designed for comparison. A two-pack sold only online, a larger size for a warehouse club, a gift set for the holidays: each gives an account team something to promote without moving the price of the item shoppers check first. Pack and size differences are how a brand gives each channel room to compete without each channel undercutting the others.

The harder part is organizational. Someone has to own the view across all channels, with the authority to say no to a promotion that would reset the brand’s visible price. At many brands, that person does not yet exist. The account teams will reasonably object that a central owner slows them down in negotiations, and the trade is real. The alternative, though, is that the brand’s price is set by whichever account moves first.

What to ask before the holiday plan locks

A brand heading into Q4 2018 can test where it stands with one exercise. Search its ten best-selling products on Amazon, Walmart.com, Target.com and its own site on the same day, and record the lowest price for each. Then ask the account teams which of those prices they chose, which a retailer chose, and which a seller nobody knows chose.

If the answers are mostly the last two, the brand does not have a price; it has a range that shoppers resolve in the retailer’s favor. Bringing those decisions into one place, and running the marketplace side day to day so the lowest price is a choice, is work we do with brands before every holiday season.

P0108.title: Amazon Advertising Platform beats search where habit drives sales
P0108.alt: Terracotta mug of coffee, glass carafe and plain kraft coffee pouch on a rustic wooden shelf by a window.
P0108.ttag: Amazon Advertising Platform beats search where habit drives sales | Kwontified
P0108.desc: Search ads look cheaper than Amazon Advertising Platform display on every report. On the cost of a sale the ad actually caused, the ranking often flips.
P0108.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 21, 2018.
P0108.body:
Put a Sponsored Products campaign next to an Amazon Advertising Platform campaign in the same quarterly review and search wins every time. Its return on ad spend is often several times higher, its cost per sale lower, its sales easy to trace. The display line looks like an awareness tax. Yet the comparison is rigged by what each report counts. Measured on the cost of a sale the ad actually caused, display on the Amazon Advertising Platform beats search wherever search is mostly collecting sales from shoppers who were going to buy anyway.

What the Amazon Advertising Platform buys, and why search looks better

The two products buy different things. Amazon Marketing Services sells search ads through a self-service console, priced per click. The Amazon Advertising Platform, or AAP, is Amazon’s programmatic demand-side platform. It buys display and video impressions, usually priced per thousand, and it is the way to reach Amazon’s audience segments on sites and apps beyond Amazon’s own, as Digiday explained in December 2017. Amazon Media Group sells display and video to brands and agencies as a managed service, according to a Marketing Dive summary of the three units in early August.

Advertisers have voted with their budgets. Sponsored Products took 85% of Amazon ad spend among Merkle’s clients in the fourth quarter of 2017, the agency reported in its quarterly digital marketing report.

That preference is reasonable on the evidence most brands see. A search ad appears at the moment a shopper types what she wants, and the report credits the ad with the sale that follows. A display ad appears while she is reading about something else, and the sale it prompts may come days later through another route. Search reports look better because search sits next to the purchase.

The comparison that strips out habit

The trouble is that sitting next to the purchase is not the same as causing it. Some of the shoppers who click a search ad were on their way to the product anyway, especially on searches for the brand’s own name. The ad is a greeter paid to say hello to customers who are already at the till.

So the honest unit of comparison is cost per incremental sale: what each format pays for a sale that would not have happened without it.

Take a $40 product. On a branded search, a click costs $1.50 and 12% of clicks convert, so each attributed sale costs $12.50. Say a holdout test shows that 70% of those buyers would have bought anyway. Only 30% of the sales are incremental, so each incremental sale costs about $41.70. On a broader category search, the same $12.50 attributed cost might be 80% incremental, which brings the incremental cost down to about $15.60.

Now an AAP campaign aimed at shoppers who viewed the category in the last 30 days but never bought the brand. Say it pays a $6 CPM, and a holdout shows it adds one incremental purchase for every 2,000 impressions. That is $12 of media for each incremental sale. The report will show a much weaker attributed ROAS than either search campaign, because the sales it caused trickle in through other routes and some fall outside the attribution window. On the number that matters, it beats both.

The rule that falls out of the arithmetic: display wins wherever the incremental cost of search is higher than the incremental cost of display. That happens most on branded and near-branded searches, where habit does most of the work, and least on category searches, where search is reaching undecided shoppers.

What the data can and cannot settle

Neither side of this comparison can be read from an ad console. Attributed ROAS tells you which ads stood nearest the purchase. Incrementality requires a holdout: a group of shoppers or a region that does not see the ads, compared with one that does, over the same weeks.

Both formats have real costs the arithmetic leaves out. AAP asks for more work than a search campaign: audiences to define, display creative to build and, in its managed form, a sales conversation with Amazon. That overhead puts it out of reach for many small brands, and its audiences are only as good as the definitions behind them.

Search, for its part, does defensive work a holdout may undervalue: on a branded search, the slot a brand does not buy can go to a competitor. The numbers lean toward display for brands whose search spend is mostly branded and whose growth depends on new buyers, and toward search for brands still building demand in a category where shoppers search by need rather than by name.

Amazon is reported to be consolidating its three ad businesses into one, according to the same Marketing Dive summary of Digiday’s reporting. If that brings search and display into one buying view, the comparison will get easier to run. It will not run itself.

Tests before the Q4 budget is set

  1. Split search reporting into branded and non-branded campaigns, and estimate the incremental share of each with a two-week holdout on the branded side.
  2. Run one AAP campaign aimed at category shoppers who have not bought the brand, with a matched holdout group, for at least four weeks.
  3. Compare the three on cost per incremental sale, and move budget from whichever is highest.
  4. Rerun the branded holdout before the holiday peak, because the mix of habit buyers and new buyers on a search can shift with the season.

We plan Amazon display alongside search on exactly this basis when we run DSP and Sponsored Ads together, and a first holdout is the quickest way to settle the argument.

P0110.crumb: E-commerce packaging is designed for a…
P0110.title: E-commerce packaging is designed for a shelf the box never sees
P0110.alt: Open cardboard shipping box holding a gift box wrapped in leafy botanical paper on a wooden table.
P0110.ttag: E-commerce packaging is designed for a shelf the box never sees | Kwontified
P0110.desc: Much consumer packaging is still briefed for a store shelf. Online, the same pack travels unseen, is billed by its size and is judged on a doorstep.
P0110.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 23, 2018.
P0110.body:
Walk any store aisle and you can read the packaging brief that produced each product. The box is a little larger than the bottle inside, so it claims more of the shelf. The front is loud, because it has a moment to stop a shopper walking past at a steady pace. The clear plastic window lets the product be seen without being touched, and the hard clamshell keeps it from walking out of the store. Every one of those choices was right for a shelf.

Online, most of them work against the brand: e-commerce packaging is still briefed for a store, while the pack is now billed by its size, judged on a doorstep and seen first as a thumbnail.

E-commerce packaging inherits a brief written for the aisle

The reason is who writes the brief. At many consumer brands, packaging belongs to the brand or marketing team, working with design agencies and a retail sales team that knows what each store buyer will accept. The criteria are shelf impact, planogram fit and theft protection. The e-commerce team, if it is consulted at all, inherits the result.

That made sense when almost every unit reached the shopper through a store. It makes less sense as a growing share travels through a warehouse, a carrier and a mailbox. Nobody walks past a corrugated shipping carton at a steady pace. The shopper never sees the pack until after paying, and by then its job is different: arrive intact, open without a fight, and not leave a pile of plastic on the kitchen floor.

Online, the pack is billed by its size

The first cost of a shelf-shaped pack shows up in fulfillment fees. Amazon bills some items on dimensional weight, a figure calculated from the package’s size rather than its actual weight. From February 22, 2018, Amazon changed the divisor it uses for that calculation in Fulfillment by Amazon to 139 from 166, EcommerceBytes reported, which raises the billable weight of every bulky, light item.

Take a box that measures 18 by 14 by 8 inches, about 2,016 cubic inches. Divided by 166, it bills as roughly 12.1 pounds. Divided by 139, it bills as roughly 14.5 pounds, whatever is inside. A box made a little larger to dominate a shelf now costs more every time it ships, and the extra inch of air was bought for a shelf it will never stand on.

Shipping costs fall on the brand, not the shopper. In the National Retail Federation’s winter 2018 consumer survey, 68% of consumers expected free shipping on orders under $50. When delivery is expected to be free, the cost of a bulky pack lands on the seller’s margin rather than the shopper’s receipt.

The doorstep is the new moment of truth

The second cost is harder to see. The shopper meets an online pack for the first time at home, after a trip through sorting machines and delivery vans. A clamshell that looked secure in a store becomes something to cut open with scissors. A glass bottle in a thin retail carton, fine on a shelf, arrives cracked.

Shoppers have been telling retailers how much the arrival matters. In Walker Sands’ 2018 Future of Retail survey, 54% of US consumers said free returns or exchanges would make them more likely to shop online, up from 43% a year earlier. A return is the most expensive way to learn that a pack did not survive the trip: the brand pays for the outbound shipping, the return and often a unit it cannot resell. On a marketplace, the review that comes with it stays on the product page for every later shopper to read.

The image is the new shelf facing

The third change is where the pack does its selling. Online, the shopper sees the package first as a small image in a search result, often on a phone. The loud front that worked at six feet becomes a blur at the size of a fingernail. Fine print, metallic finishes and clear windows that show the product inside rarely survive the reduction.

The brief for the selling surface has moved from the box to the hero image. The box needs to support it with a front that reads at thumbnail size, a product name and size that are legible without zooming, and a shape that photographs cleanly from the front.

What a separate brief looks like

The answer at many brands will not be two completely different packs for every product, at least not soon. The cost of a second set of tooling and inventory is real, and retail buyers still have planograms to fill. What the evidence leans toward is a second brief: written by the e-commerce team, owned jointly with the brand team, and applied first to the products that sell most online.

That brief judges a pack on four things the shelf brief never asked about:

  1. Its cost to ship at billed weight, which can be well above its actual weight.
  2. Whether it survives a drop from a conveyor and opens without tools.
  3. Whether the front reads at thumbnail size on a phone.
  4. What the shopper sees on the doorstep, and what they do with the pack next.

A simple test for any brand is to order its own top five products from its own Amazon listing, to an ordinary home address, and open them at the kitchen table with the brand team watching. The packaging that arrives tells you whose brief it was written for, and helping brands get the online pack and the listing that sells it written for the shopper who buys online is part of running the channel day to day.

P0111.title: Amazon Brand Registry makes listing protection a weekly routine
P0111.alt: Open ledger with a brass magnifying glass, a small padlock and blank paper tags on a wooden table.
P0111.ttag: Amazon Brand Registry makes listing protection a weekly routine | Kwontified
P0111.desc: Brands enroll in Amazon Brand Registry expecting the problem sellers to vanish. What enrollment really changes is the cost of each enforcement action.
P0111.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 28, 2018.
P0111.body:
A brand finishes its trademark filing, waits most of a year, enrolls in Amazon Brand Registry and expects the problem sellers to disappear. A month later the same look-alike listing is still there, and someone asks what the enrollment was for. The answer is less dramatic than the launch materials suggested. Brand Registry does not remove anyone by itself. It changes the cost of each enforcement action, from a test purchase and a long wait to a report handled within hours, and that changes how often enforcement is worth doing.

What Amazon Brand Registry changed in 2017

Amazon rebuilt the program in 2017. The new Brand Registry is open only to brands with a registered trademark, a process that typically takes six to ten months, Practical Ecommerce reported in June 2017. Under the old program, registering needed little more than a domain name and the brand’s name on the packaging. Amazon told brands enrolled before April 30, 2017 that they would need to enroll again under the new rules, according to its Brand Registry announcement of November 2017.

Three changes matter for enforcement. Counterfeit claims from enrolled brands are handled within four hours. Brands no longer need to make a test purchase before filing a claim. And enrolled brands get a search tool that finds suspected violations by image, text and keyword, according to the same Practical Ecommerce report.

Enrollment also controls the page. A seller that is not the registered brand owner cannot change a product’s bullet points, description or images, Practical Ecommerce noted in February 2017. It also opens tools that need a verified owner. Headline Search Ads became available to third-party sellers in 2017 only for brands in Brand Registry, eSellerHub reported, and Enhanced Brand Content is limited to brand-registered sellers.

Why the cost of each report decides the outcome

The puzzle is why brands with the same protection get such different results. The difference is frequency, and frequency follows cost.

Think of a parking meter that is checked once a month. The fine may be large, but drivers who overstay are rarely caught, so overstaying pays. Check it every hour and the same fine changes behavior. Enforcement on Amazon works the same way: what matters is how long a bad listing earns before someone acts.

Under the old process, acting was expensive. A brand that suspected a counterfeit had to buy the product, wait for it to arrive, inspect it and then file, with days or weeks passing before anything changed. Many brands rationed that effort to their worst cases. Under the new process, a report with no test purchase, handled within four hours, costs an analyst minutes. That makes it rational to look every week.

Take a $30 product selling $2,000 a day on Amazon.

Say a seller offering look-alike stock wins 40% of the sales on that page. That is $800 a day the brand does not earn, plus whatever the look-alike does to the reviews.

Found and resolved in two days, the episode costs $1,600. Found at a monthly review and resolved two weeks later, the same listing earns for six weeks and costs $33,600. The protection is identical in both cases. The schedule is not.

The same logic applies before enrollment. A brand that has not yet filed for a trademark cannot enroll, and at six to ten months for registration, a filing made in August 2018 will not produce an enrolled brand until 2019. Every month of delay is another month in which the brand’s reports go through the slower, older routes, so the trademark filing is the first enforcement decision, not a legal formality.

What enrollment does not do

Brand Registry decides who controls the page and how quickly a brand’s claims are heard. It does not stop genuine resellers. A distributor selling authentic stock bought from the brand’s own channel is not infringing, and it can keep selling from the same page, competing on price and fulfillment.

The data side is also thinner than many brands hope. A weekly routine is only as good as the record it leaves behind. A brand should not count on Amazon to hand it a scorecard. To know how many claims succeeded across its catalog, how quickly look-alike listings reappear or what share of its traffic they took, it needs its own log: date found, date reported, date resolved, and the sales on the page in between.

That log answers the question executives ask a month after enrollment. If resolution times are falling and repeat offenders are fewer, the routine is working. If the same sellers return under new names within weeks, the brand has a distribution problem, and Brand Registry is treating the symptom. The fix for that sits in the brand’s own contracts with distributors and wholesale customers, where the stock is leaking from, and no amount of weekly reporting will close it.

A routine worth running

  1. Search the catalog weekly with the image and keyword tool, starting with the 20 products that bring in most of the revenue.
  2. Log every report with the dates found, reported and resolved, and the daily sales of the page affected.
  3. Check each month that every top listing’s title, bullets and images match the brand’s approved version.
  4. Trace repeat offenders back to the distributor or retailer that supplied them before filing the next report.

A brand that runs this routine every week gets more from the same enrollment than one that checks when someone complains, and running it as part of managing the channel day to day is work we do with brands on Amazon.

P0112.title: Amazon’s Choice badge: Amazon recommends what it can deliver
P0112.alt: Brown paper parcel tied with twine and a gold rosette ribbon sitting on a van step in a sunny lane.
P0112.ttag: Amazon’s Choice badge: Amazon recommends what it can deliver | Kwontified
P0112.desc: The Amazon’s Choice badge reads to shoppers like a store clerk’s tip. It also shows what Amazon rewards, and on Alexa it can be the only product offered.
P0112.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 30, 2018.
P0112.body:
In a hardware store, a shopper standing in front of forty kinds of picture hook does something brands spend fortunes trying to prevent: she asks the person in the apron which one to buy. Whatever the clerk points to goes in the basket. On Amazon, the Amazon’s Choice badge has quietly taken that clerk’s job. A small dark label on one listing in a search result tells the shopper which product the store itself would pick. The question for brands is what the badge rewards, and the answer is mostly the operating record of the listing rather than anything a brand team would recognize as marketing.

The Amazon’s Choice badge works like a clerk’s recommendation

A recommendation from the store carries a kind of authority a brand’s own claims cannot. The shopper does not have to weigh the brand’s adjectives against a rival’s. Someone neutral has done the weighing.

That authority is strongest where the shopper has the least to go on. On a screen full of near-identical phone chargers, garden hoses or batteries, a badge that says the store has chosen one ends the search. Shoppers who already know which brand they want can ignore it; shoppers who searched by need rather than by name are the ones it moves.

Amazon describes the program modestly. An Amazon spokeswoman said the badge is simply a recommendation, and that customers can always ask for a specific brand or product, according to a Wall Street Journal report republished in March. The same report said the selection weighs factors such as ratings, price and shipping speed.

On Alexa, the badge can be the whole shelf

The badge matters on a screen. On a voice assistant, it can be the entire store.

Bain & Company tested voice shopping on Amazon’s Alexa. For first-time purchases where the shopper did not name a brand, Alexa’s first recommendation was an Amazon’s Choice product more than half the time, according to the same Wall Street Journal report. There is no search page to scroll and no second row of products. The shopper hears one suggestion and says yes or no.

Analysts have drawn the obvious conclusion about who holds the power in that exchange. Voice-based ordering gives virtually all of the power to retailers, Bernstein argued in an analysis of Amazon’s effect on food retail, FoodNavigator-USA reported. In a store, a brand can buy an end cap or a better shelf position. In a voice order, the retailer’s recommendation is the only position there is.

Voice shopping is still a small share of how people buy. The point is the direction. Every interface that narrows the shopper’s choice to one recommendation, whether a badge on a phone or a single answer from a speaker, hands more of the decision to whoever does the recommending.

What the badge rewards, and who inside a brand owns it

Follow the criteria and the badge looks less like a marketing prize and more like a report card on operations. High ratings come from a product that works and a listing that sets honest expectations. A competitive price comes from the brand’s pricing decisions across every channel. Fast shipping comes from inventory placed where Amazon can ship it quickly, and from never running out.

That list explains a pattern worth noticing. The badge can land on products from sellers that a brand’s marketing team has never heard of, because those sellers are excellent at the boring parts: keeping stock, pricing sharply and answering every bad review. Amazon is recommending what it can deliver reliably, which is a reasonable thing for a retailer to want and a demanding standard for a brand to meet.

It also explains why the badge is hard to manage from the brand side. Brands cannot apply for it, and Amazon has not published the formula. The things that earn it are owned by different people: reviews and product quality by the product team, price by sales and finance, stock by supply chain. Nobody’s job description includes “be Amazon’s Choice.”

Picture one way the badge is lost. Supply chain lets the best-selling charger run out for two weeks while a shipment clears customs. Sales agrees a deeper promotion with another retailer, and a reseller undercuts the Amazon price to match. Each decision is sensible inside its own department. Together they hand the recommendation, and every shopper who would have followed it, to a rival.

The value at stake flows in a particular direction. Amazon gains a recommendation engine that steers shoppers toward listings that are cheap to fulfil and unlikely to disappoint. The brand that earns the badge gains the shoppers who did not know which brand they wanted. The brand that loses it pays to advertise to those same shoppers, often on the same search where a rival carries the badge for free.

The badge is a weekly report card worth reading

One measure is simple to collect: for the ten searches that matter most in your category, which listing carries the badge each week, and whose is it? When the answer changes, look at what changed underneath: a stock-out, a price move, a run of poor reviews. The badge is a lagging indicator of operating discipline, and its movements tend to point to a specific failure.

The question for the leadership team is who would notice if the badge moved to a competitor tomorrow, and who would be responsible for winning it back. If the honest answer is nobody, that is the gap. Running the listing well every day, in stock, priced deliberately and reviewed honestly, is how a brand earns the store’s recommendation, and it is the part of the channel we run for brands.

P0114.crumb: Enhanced Brand Content needs a control…
P0114.title: Enhanced Brand Content needs a control group to prove it converts
P0114.alt: A young and a mature Chinese money plant in terracotta pots side by side on a wooden windowsill.
P0114.ttag: Enhanced Brand Content needs a control group to prove it converts | Kwontified
P0114.desc: A before-and-after look at Enhanced Brand Content mixes its lift with season, price and ads. A matched control group shows what the page itself added.
P0114.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. All channels
P0114.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 4, 2018.
P0114.body:
A brand spends a month building Enhanced Brand Content for its top product: comparison charts, lifestyle images, a cleaner story below the fold. Four weeks later the conversion rate is up, and the team credits the page. Some of that credit is real. Much of it usually belongs to the calendar, the price and the ad budget, which moved in the same four weeks. The only way to separate the page’s lift from everything else is to compare the products that got the new content with comparable products that did not.

What Enhanced Brand Content is expected to do

Enhanced Brand Content is the module layout Amazon gives brand-registered sellers for the description area of a detail page; vendors get the equivalent through A+ pages. The promise is simple. Shoppers who scroll past the bullets see richer images and clearer comparisons, and more of them buy.

Amazon has put a range on that promise. An Amazon study from 2015 found that adding A+ content raised conversion rates by 3% to 10%, Salsify noted in June 2018. The same post made a second point that matters more for measurement: Amazon does not report how an individual A+ page performs.

So the range is a population average, and each brand has to work out its own number. Most do it the obvious way. They read the unit session percentage, Amazon’s conversion figure for orders per session, in the Seller Central business reports, compare the weeks before launch with the weeks after, and call the difference the lift.

Why the before-and-after number overstates the page

The comparison treats the launch as the only thing that changed in those weeks, and in August it rarely is. Prices move, ad budgets move and the season moves, often all at once.

Take a product with 2,000 sessions a week converting at 10%, or 200 units. The brand publishes its new content in early August, and four weeks later the product converts at 11.5%. That reads as a 15% lift, well above Amazon’s own range.

Now look at 20 comparable products in the same category that did not get new content. Over the same weeks their conversion rose from 9% to 10%, because back-to-school traffic was arriving with more intent to buy.

The category moved 1.0 point without any new page. The product with Enhanced Brand Content moved 1.5 points. The page’s share is the difference, 0.5 points, a lift of about 5% on the starting rate. That sits inside the range Amazon published and a long way below the number the team was ready to report.

This method is called a difference-in-differences: measure the change in the products you treated, measure the change in comparable products you did not, and credit the treatment only with the gap. It removes whatever hit both groups at once, such as the season, a sitewide sale or a shift in Amazon’s search traffic.

It cannot remove what hit only one group. If the brand also cut the price on the featured product, raised its Sponsored Products bids or picked up a burst of reviews in the same month, the gap includes those too. A clean test holds price and ad spend steady on both groups for its length.

How much noise hides a 3% lift

There is a second reason a single product cannot prove the case: the lift Amazon describes is small next to ordinary weekly variation.

At 2,000 sessions a week and a 10% conversion rate, random variation alone moves the weekly rate by roughly 0.7 points in either direction. A 3% lift takes that product from 10% to 10.3%, a change of 0.3 points. In any one week, the page’s effect is smaller than the noise.

Pooling more sessions fixes this, though slowly. Four weeks at that traffic is 8,000 sessions, which roughly halves the noise, and adding more treated products helps more. That is why the test works best across a group of products rather than on a single hero, and why it needs four to six weeks rather than two.

None of this argues against Enhanced Brand Content. Even a 3% lift on a product with steady traffic adds up over a season, and a well-built page keeps working after the design team has moved on. The point is narrower. A brand that claims a 15% lift from one launch will plan the next quarter’s content budget on a number the page did not earn.

A content test you can run this quarter

Decide on the split before anyone builds a module. Choose two matched groups of products with similar traffic, price points and review counts, and publish Enhanced Brand Content on one group only. Hold back the other for four to six weeks.

Keep prices and Sponsored Products bids unchanged on both groups for the length of the test, and note any coupon or Lightning Deal that runs in either one, since a promotion on one side breaks the comparison.

When the weeks are up, compare the change in unit session percentage for the treated group with the change for the held-back group, and report only the difference as the content’s lift. If the gap is smaller than the week-to-week swing in either group, extend the test or add products before deciding anything.

Then roll the content out to the control group. A held-back product is a short-term cost of knowing what the page is worth, and a brand that knows the figure can decide how much to spend on the next 20 pages. Setting up that kind of baseline before a change goes live is the part of content measurement we build with brands on Amazon.
