P0116.crumb: Amazon toys in 2018: the Toys R Us aisle…
P0116.title: Amazon toys in 2018: the Toys R Us aisle moves into search
P0116.alt: Row of painted wooden toy animals and toy trains lined up on a wooden shelf outside a shuttered shop.
P0116.ttag: Amazon toys in 2018: the Toys R Us aisle moves into search | Kwontified
P0116.desc: With Toys R Us gone, the 2018 holiday toy aisle splits between bigger Walmart and Target shelves and Amazon search. Toy brands need a plan for each.
P0116.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 6, 2018.
P0116.body:
For decades the toy superstore did something no other retailer bothered to do: it let a child walk the whole category. Board games, ride-ons, dolls and building sets sat in aisles long enough to get lost in, and the shopping list was often written on the spot. By June 29 that store was gone; Toys R Us closed its remaining US locations that week. This holiday season is the first in which brands must sell toys without that aisle, and the browsing it supported is not moving to one replacement. It is splitting between general-store shelves and Amazon’s search results, which reward a toy a shopper already knows by name.

Where the Toys R Us sales are going

Analysts have spent the year arguing over who inherits the business. As the closures began in January, Jefferies estimated that Amazon could take as much as 40% of the sales lost at shuttered stores and Walmart about 30%, Fortune reported. By March, with liquidation under way, the worry had grown: 10% to 15% of Toys R Us’s own sales volume could disappear rather than move anywhere, CNBC reported on a toy industry bracing for the loss of its biggest specialist.

The general merchants have now shown their hands. Walmart plans to expand its toy assortment by 30% in stores and 40% online this holiday, CNN reported on August 30. Target said this week it will add more than 2,500 new and exclusive toys, nearly double last year’s count, according to the Motley Fool.

Those numbers describe more shelf, but a different kind of shelf. At Walmart and Target the toy department sits between groceries and housewares, and it is planned around the items the buyer expects to sell in volume. A deep assortment of small brands, which the specialist could afford because people came to browse, is harder to justify in a general store where most visitors came for something else.

Toys on Amazon are found by name

Amazon inherits the other half of the toy aisle’s job: finding a specific thing. A parent who knows the name of the toy on a child’s list types it in, and the search results do the rest. That works well for a toy with a television campaign behind it, and much less well for the board game a family would have noticed on an endcap and picked up on impulse.

The difference changes what a toy brand needs from its listing. In a store, the box sells itself to a child at eye level. On Amazon, the product page sells to an adult reading on a phone, often comparing age ranges, piece counts and battery requirements across three similar toys. A brand whose page still carries the distributor’s single photo is competing for that adult’s attention with a stock image and a thin description.

Amazon is guarding its toy store for the holidays

Amazon reads the toy season as a risk to its own reputation, and its rules show it. For the 2018 holidays, only sellers that meet its criteria may sell in the Toys & Games store from October 17 through January 5, SellerEngine summarized in early August. A seller needed its first Amazon sale before August 18 and at least 25 orders shipped between August 1 and October 1, and Amazon said it would send eligibility notices by October 17.

Read as an institution, Amazon is choosing customer trust over seller supply. The rule shuts out pop-up sellers who appear in November with doubtful stock, the same sellers whose late shipments and counterfeit toys would land on Amazon’s reviews rather than their own. Orders fulfilled by Amazon from accounts in good standing were exempt, EcommerceBytes noted, which tells brands where Amazon wants holiday toy inventory to sit: in its own warehouses.

For a toy brand, the rule has a side effect that is easy to miss. If the brand relies on a new reseller, or plans to open its own seller account in the autumn, that account will not qualify to sell merchant-fulfilled toys this season. The brand’s listing will still be live, but the holiday sales may go to whichever established sellers hold its stock.

What the empty aisle means for a toy brand

Toys R Us took the browsing aisle with it, and neither of its successors fully replaces it. The general stores offer more space for proven sellers. Amazon offers search for toys parents already know and holds its holiday toy store to sellers it trusts. The value of being discovered by accident, which small and mid-sized toy brands relied on, has no obvious new home in 2018. It may return as retailers learn what the specialist’s shoppers want, but a brand cannot plan this holiday around that hope.

That leaves toy brands with an inventory and ownership question more than a creative one, and it is worth asking before October:

  1. Which of our sellers on Amazon meet the holiday Toys & Games criteria, and who will hold the Buy Box on our top listings if they do not?
  2. How much of our holiday stock should sit in Amazon’s warehouses, given that orders fulfilled by Amazon are exempt from the restriction?
  3. Which items did Walmart and Target pick up for their expanded assortments, and are they planned for stores, online or both?
  4. Does each top product page answer what a parent checks first, such as age range, piece count and what is in the box, without the help of a box on a shelf?

The brands that answer those questions now will spend the season selling rather than chasing listings, which is the part of a holiday plan where day-to-day channel management matters most.

P0117.crumb: FBA storage limits reward profit per…
P0117.title: FBA storage limits reward profit per cubic foot, not unit volume
P0117.alt: Stack of coins on a small linen block beside an old wooden crate topped with a coin and paper.
P0117.ttag: FBA storage limits reward profit per cubic foot, not unit volume | Kwontified
P0117.desc: When Amazon caps FBA storage, cubic feet become the scarce resource. Rank what you ship for Q4 by weekly profit per cubic foot, not by units or margin.
P0117.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 11, 2018.
P0117.body:
Every September, brands selling through Fulfillment by Amazon build a Q4 shipping plan from the sales forecast: the items expected to sell most get the most units. In 2018 that plan runs into a ceiling. Amazon now sets FBA storage limits for some sellers, and once space is capped, the forecast is the wrong place to start. The scarce resource is cubic feet, so the right ranking is weekly profit per cubic foot of space an item occupies. That ranking often puts a small, low-margin item ahead of the bulky hero product the team most wants to protect.

How FBA storage limits work in 2018

Amazon announced on March 1 that, starting July 1, it would evaluate storage limits every quarter for professional sellers, EcommerceBytes reported. The deciding number is the Inventory Performance Index, a score Amazon calculates from how efficiently a seller’s stock moves. A seller whose score is below 350 six weeks before a quarter begins is told it may face limits for that quarter.

The same announcement raised monthly storage fees by $0.05 per cubic foot from April 1 and introduced a storage overage fee. Inventory above a seller’s limit is charged $10 per cubic foot a month, Feedvisor explained, on top of the normal storage charges.

For Q4, the warning date fell in late August. A brand that received limits now has a fixed number of cubic feet for the holiday quarter, and the only open question is what goes into them.

Why the forecast is the wrong ranking

A sales forecast ranks items by units, and a margin report ranks them by profit per unit. Both feel like sensible ways to protect the holiday. Neither accounts for the thing Amazon is now rationing.

Take a brand with three products and a limit of 20,000 cubic feet:

ProductProfit per unitSizeWeekly salesWeekly profitSpace for eight weeks of coverWeekly profit per cubic foot
A$120.5 cu ft50$600400 units, 200 cu ft$3.00
B$302 cu ft20$600160 units, 320 cu ft$1.88
C$50.1 cu ft100$500800 units, 80 cu ft$6.25

Product B has the best margin per unit and ties for the most weekly profit, so it usually gets first claim on the shipping plan. Per cubic foot it is the worst use of the space. Product C, the item nobody brags about, earns more than three times as much from each cubic foot it occupies.

Scale that up across a catalog and the pattern holds. When space is unlimited, the order of shipments barely matters. When it is capped, every bulky unit sitting in an Amazon warehouse displaces several small units that would have sold in the same week.

Cover is the second lever

Space depends on how many weeks of stock you hold, not only on the product’s size. Cut Product B to four weeks of cover and it needs 80 units and 160 cubic feet, which lifts its weekly profit per cubic foot to $3.75. Same product, same margin, a better use of the limit, paid for with more frequent replenishment.

That is the trade-off a capped seller has to price. Shorter cover on bulky items saves space but raises the risk of running out during the busiest weeks, when inbound shipments slow down. Longer cover on small, fast items costs little space and protects the sales that pay best per cubic foot. The overage fee sets the penalty for getting it wrong: 1,000 cubic feet over the limit costs $10,000 for the month, before any storage fees.

A third option for a bulky item is to fulfill it from the brand’s own warehouse for the quarter. That moves the space problem rather than solving it, and it changes the delivery promise shoppers see on the listing, so it suits items whose buyers will wait a little longer. It also frees FBA space for the small, fast items that need Amazon’s speed most.

The ranking should reach the advertising plan too. A Sponsored Products budget built for the full forecast will keep buying clicks for an item that the limit has left with two weeks of stock. Ads on an item that sells out early pay for traffic that lands on an unavailable page, so cut the bids for any product held to short cover before the peak weeks start.

The arithmetic has limits of its own. A product that drives a customer’s first purchase from the brand, or that anchors advertising for the rest of the line, may deserve space beyond its own profit per cubic foot. Make that exception on purpose and write down what it costs, rather than letting the forecast make it by default.

Before the next inbound shipment

  1. Put the cubic feet per unit next to every product in the Q4 plan, and calculate weekly profit per cubic foot at the cover you intend to hold.
  2. Fill the limit from the top of that ranking, then cut cover on bulky items before cutting any item entirely.
  3. Ship any product deliberately held below its ranking with a note of the profit it gives up, so the choice is visible at the holiday post-mortem.
  4. Clear slow and stranded units before October, since every cubic foot they hold is space the fast items cannot use.

The Inventory Performance Index is evaluated again before the next quarter, so the same discipline that fits Q4 into its limit is the one that raises the score for Q1. Building that space-based plan alongside the advertising budget is part of how we run Amazon inventory and channel operations for brands.

P0119.crumb: Amazon customer questions show what your…
P0119.title: Amazon customer questions show what your product page left out
P0119.alt: Corkboard covered in blank pinned cards above a wooden desk with a plain shipping box, pens and twine.
P0119.ttag: Amazon customer questions show what your product page left out | Kwontified
P0119.desc: The questions shoppers post on an Amazon product page are the brief your listing never got. Most brands leave the answers to strangers and never read them.
P0119.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 13, 2018.
P0119.body:
Scroll down almost any busy Amazon product page and, a little below the bullet points, you reach a box of strangers talking. “Does this fit a queen mattress?” “Is the color closer to navy or black?” “Can you put the lid in the dishwasher?” Under each question sits an answer, usually from someone who bought the product, sometimes confident, sometimes a guess. These Amazon customer questions are the most honest brief a product page ever gets: each one marks a fact the listing failed to give. Most brands never read them, and they leave the answers to whoever happens to reply.

The sales associate moved to the bottom of the page

In a store, the questions went to a person. A shopper picked up the box, could not find the answer on the side panel, and asked the associate standing nearby, who either knew or went to check. The brand trained that associate, or at least supplied the retailer with the facts to train them.

On Amazon the question still gets asked, but the associate has been replaced by the crowd. A shopper types it into the product page, and Amazon routes it to people who might know: the seller, the brand and, in many cases, past buyers, whom Amazon invites by email to answer. The first reasonable-sounding reply then sits on the page for every later shopper to read.

That arrangement works better than it sounds. Past buyers have used the product in their own homes, and they often answer the practical questions (does it fit, does it smell, does it last) more convincingly than any copywriter could. Researchers at the University of California, San Diego took the format seriously enough to build a system that answers shoppers’ product questions automatically from reviews, trained on questions already answered on Amazon pages, in a paper presented in 2016. The questions, in other words, are a known and recurring part of how people shop on Amazon, not a quirk of a few listings.

The trouble is that the crowd answers for the brand without being accountable to it. A buyer who misremembers the dimensions, confuses this year’s version with last year’s, or answers “I don’t know” in good faith still adds a line to the page. The brand’s name sits at the top of that page, and the shopper reading the answer has no way to tell a careful owner from a careless one.

Why nobody owns the questions

The reason so many brands ignore this part of the page is organizational, not technical. Look at who touches a product page inside a typical brand. The product team supplies the specifications. A marketing or ecommerce manager, sometimes an agency, writes the title and bullets, usually once, at launch. Customer service handles complaints that arrive by email or phone. Reviews, at least, get watched, because a falling star rating shows up in someone’s report.

The question box falls between all of them. It is not copy, so the content team does not own it. It is not a complaint, so customer service does not see it. It is not a rating, so it never reaches a dashboard. Questions arrive one at a time, months apart, on dozens of products, and nobody’s weekly routine includes reading them.

So the answers default to whoever replies first. For a brand that sells through resellers, that might include a seller who knows the product less well than the brand does, writing in a voice the brand would never approve. For a brand with no seller presence at all, it is entirely the crowd.

Read the questions as research

The questions do more than fill a gap on one page; they show, in the shopper’s own words, what the brand’s marketing assumed people already knew. If six people have asked whether a jacket runs small, the size chart is not doing its job. If the most common question on a blender is whether the jar is glass or plastic, the material belongs in the title or the first bullet, not in a specification table nobody opens. A question that keeps coming back is a sentence missing from the listing.

That makes the question box one of the cheapest sources of shopper research a brand has. It is unprompted, specific to the product and written at the moment of decision, which is more than most surveys can claim. It costs nothing to read, and the answer to each question can be fixed twice: once in a reply, and once by moving the fact into the listing so the next shopper never has to ask.

There is a structural shift underneath this. On Amazon the product page is no longer a brochure a brand writes and leaves alone; it is a running conversation between the brand, its resellers and its customers, and the brand is only one voice in it unless it chooses to take part. The brands that do will gradually write better pages, because their shoppers are telling them what to write.

Questions for the team that owns your listings

  1. Who in the company reads the customer questions on our top products, and how often?
  2. Which questions have been asked more than once, and does the answer now appear in the title, bullets or images?
  3. Are any of the current answers wrong, and has the brand posted a correct one under its own name?
  4. When the product changes, who checks that older answers about the previous version do not mislead new shoppers?

Treating the question box as part of the page, with an owner and a routine, is a small change in how a brand runs its listings, and it is the kind of ongoing upkeep we fold into day-to-day Amazon channel management.

P0121.title: Amazon Advertising’s rebrand changes the bundle, not the auction
P0121.alt: Paper-wrapped gift tied with a linen ribbon beside crumpled mustard tissue paper on a wooden table.
P0121.ttag: Amazon Advertising’s rebrand changes the bundle, not the auction | Kwontified
P0121.desc: Amazon Advertising puts search, display and media under one name. The auctions are unchanged; the risk is a blended report that hides weak spend.
P0121.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 18, 2018.
P0121.body:
Two weeks after Amazon folded its ad businesses into Amazon Advertising, advertisers are asking what the rebrand will do to their results. The honest answer is nothing, at least not directly. Every auction, bid and budget works as it did before September 5. What changes is the way Amazon sells advertising: three businesses now speak under one name, and a single name makes it easier to sell search, display and media as one plan. The risk for a brand is a blended report, where strong search results quietly cover for weaker spend elsewhere.

What Amazon Advertising actually changed

Amazon announced on September 5 that it was retiring three names: Amazon Media Group, which sold display and media packages; Amazon Marketing Services, which ran the self-service search ads; and the Amazon Advertising Platform, its programmatic buying tool. Amazon’s announcement put all three under Amazon Advertising, renamed Headline Search Ads as Sponsored Brands and renamed the platform the Amazon DSP.

The products did not change. The rebrand does not alter how the ads work or how Amazon’s teams are organized, AdExchanger reported, and the same console still runs cost-per-click campaigns for Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands. Buyers read it the same way. The move is “more to streamline their naming conventions versus actually changing how advertisers buy ads,” Merkle’s Todd Bowman told Business Insider.

So a Sponsored Brands campaign that converted at a given rate in August will convert at the same rate in September, other things equal. Nothing in the auction has a reason to move.

The Sponsored Brands name is the most useful part of the change for anyone reading reports. Headline Search Ads always sat in the same keyword auction as Sponsored Products, bought by the click and placed above the results; the old name made it sound like a separate display product. Grouping the two as sponsored search formats describes how they are actually bought, and it makes the line between search and display, the line that matters for budgeting, easier to draw.

Why a single brand still matters

A name is how a business is sold, and Amazon’s ad business has become large enough to sell hard. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, mostly advertising, reached $2.19 billion in the second quarter of 2018, up from $945 million a year earlier, the Motley Fool noted. When Digiday first reported the consolidation in early August, the plan described was one advertising business serving both vendors and sellers, Marketing Dive summarized.

One brand selling search, display and video invites one plan, and one plan invites one number. That number is usually a blended return on ad spend (ROAS): total attributed sales divided by total spend. It feels like the natural way to judge a combined budget. It is also the number most likely to mislead, because it averages products that earn very different returns and are measured in different ways.

How a blended ROAS hides the weak dollar

Take a brand spending $50,000 a month on Amazon. Of that, $30,000 goes to Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands at a reported ROAS of 5, or $150,000 in attributed sales. The other $20,000 goes to the Amazon DSP at a ROAS of 1.5, or $30,000. The blended figure is $180,000 on $50,000, a ROAS of 3.6.

Now a bundled proposal suggests moving $10,000 from search into display, and the deck shows that the total still clears a healthy blended return. Suppose the last $10,000 of search spend earns a ROAS of 3, lower than the search average, as the last dollars in any campaign usually do. Moving it out of search gives up $30,000 of attributed sales. Placing it in display at 1.5 adds $15,000. Attributed sales fall to $165,000 and the blended ROAS falls to 3.3, a result that still looks respectable and hides a $15,000 loss in attributed sales every month.

The bias at work is anchoring on the average. A blended ROAS describes where the whole budget landed. Budget decisions are made at the margin, one dollar at a time, and the average says nothing about what the next dollar earns in either product.

None of this means display spend is wasted. Attributed sales understate what upper-funnel ads do for shoppers who buy later, and overstate what search ads do for shoppers who were already searching for the brand. Those are arguments for measuring each product on its own terms, with a holdout where possible, not for averaging them together.

Rules for the new single brand

Keep budgets separate by product even when one Amazon team presents them together, so search, Sponsored Brands and the Amazon DSP each carry their own spend and return line.

Judge every shift at the margin: before moving money between products, estimate what the last dollar earns where it is and what the next dollar earns where it would go.

Ask for line-item pricing on any bundled proposal, including the cost of DSP inventory and any service fee, so the bundle can be compared with buying each part alone.

Watch what Amazon does with reporting next. If the single brand is followed by reports that compare search and DSP results on the same attribution rules, the blended number becomes easier to check; until then, treat any combined figure as two figures added together.

Treat the new names as a reporting change, not a performance event; if a campaign’s results move in September, look for the cause in bids, prices or stock, not in the rebrand. Keeping search and display measured on separate, honest lines is how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

P0122.title: Amazon counterfeits reach a brand’s reviews before its lawyers
P0122.alt: Two worn cardboard boxes beside a scatter of brass star badges and patches on a woven mat on a table.
P0122.ttag: Amazon counterfeits reach a brand’s reviews before its lawyers | Kwontified
P0122.desc: Counterfeit sales show up first as one-star reviews on a brand’s own page. Brands that leave enforcement to legal see the damage last and act latest.
P0122.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 20, 2018.
P0122.body:
When the Government Accountability Office went shopping in 2017, it bought 47 popular items from third-party sellers on five large websites, Amazon among them, and sent them to the brands to check. Twenty were counterfeit, according to the report made public in February 2018. Every one of the 13 Urban Decay cosmetics was fake. Every one of the 15 pairs of Nike Air Jordans was real.

A sample that small proves nothing about either company, but it frames the question worth asking about Amazon counterfeits in 2018. Why do some brands treat fakes as a central business risk while others leave them to the legal team, and which brands pay for that choice?

Where a counterfeit actually does its damage

Most brands file counterfeits under intellectual property. The legal department sends takedown requests when someone notices a problem, and the cost appears, if anywhere, as outside counsel’s fees.

The shopper sees something else. A counterfeit sold on Amazon is usually sold from the brand’s own product page, because a shared catalog lets any seller offer the same item. When the fake arrives, the shopper does not write to the brand’s lawyers. She writes a review, on the page the brand depends on, saying the product smelled wrong, fell apart or did not match the photo. The review stays with the listing whoever sold the item, and every later shopper reads it.

Shoppers already arrive wary. About one in five consumers said counterfeits were their main concern when shopping on Amazon, in a survey of 2,000 shoppers for BloomReach, CNBC reported in 2016. A review that confirms that fear lands on fertile ground.

Follow the value and the asymmetry is plain. The counterfeiter takes the margin on the sale. The brand keeps the review, the return and the lost conversion on every honest unit that follows. None of that cost appears in the legal budget, which is why the department that owns the problem rarely sees its size.

Returns carry the same signal and are read even less. A shopper who receives a fake may send it back as defective or not as described, and complaints about the product reach the brand through customer service with no note of which seller shipped it. A brand that reads those complaints only as a quality report will go looking for a manufacturing fault that does not exist.

Why so many brands look away

The brands that ignore counterfeits are rarely careless. They are organized in a way that hides the problem.

At many companies the Amazon business sits with sales or ecommerce, while trademarks sit with legal and reviews with no one in particular. Each team sees one piece. The ecommerce manager sees a dip in conversion and blames price. Legal sees nothing until a complaint arrives by email. The product team hears about quality and checks the factory, which made nothing wrong.

Some brands also hold back on purpose, worried that admitting fakes exist will draw attention to them, or that enforcement will start a dispute with resellers they need. Those worries are understandable, and they treat silence as neutral when it is not. The fakes keep selling either way; the only open question is whether anyone is collecting the evidence.

The brands that act have usually done one thing differently: they put the product page, not the trademark, at the center of the problem. Nike, which refused for years to sell directly to Amazon, agreed in 2017 to supply some products in exchange for Amazon policing counterfeit and unauthorized third-party sales of its goods, as reported at the time. Whatever one thinks of that bargain, it treated counterfeits as a term of the commercial relationship rather than a matter for lawyers after the fact.

The tools exist, and they need an owner

Amazon has given brands more to work with. The rebuilt Brand Registry, open to brands with a registered trademark, promises to handle counterfeit claims within four hours and offers a search tool that finds suspect listings by image and keyword, Practical Ecommerce explained when it launched. Those are real powers, and they arrived only in 2017. They also do nothing on their own. A claim must be filed by someone, a search must be run by someone, and the person doing it must know which sellers are authorized and which are not.

That is where the institutional reading matters. Amazon’s marketplace is built to welcome sellers quickly, and it relies on rights owners to say when a seller has crossed a line. A brand that never says so has, in effect, told Amazon it has no objection. The shift under way in 2018 is that brand protection is becoming operational work, done weekly by the people who manage the listings, rather than legal work done when a lawyer finds time.

What to ask before the holiday peak

  1. Who reads the one- and two-star reviews on our top 20 products each week, and do they flag the words shoppers use for fakes, such as “smelled different” or “not genuine”?
  2. Which sellers on our listings are authorized, and is that list written down where the person filing Brand Registry claims can see it?
  3. When did we last buy our own product from an unfamiliar seller to check it?
  4. Do our conversion reports separate weeks with new sellers on the listing from weeks without, so a counterfeit’s effect can be seen?

The brands that answer those questions treat their product page as the place counterfeits do their harm, which is also where the ongoing work of running an Amazon channel begins.

P0125.title: Department stores are turning into Amazon’s service counter
P0125.alt: Rows of taped cardboard shipping boxes stacked behind a long wood and brass counter against a mustard wall.
P0125.ttag: Department stores are turning into Amazon’s service counter | Kwontified
P0125.desc: Amazon is taking the department store’s role as the place to choose apparel, while stores take on returns and pickup. Brands should plan for both.
P0125.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 27, 2018.
P0125.body:
In a growing number of Kohl’s stores, a shopper can walk in with an Amazon purchase she does not want, hand it over at a counter and leave without buying anything. Kohl’s began taking Amazon returns at 82 stores in Chicago and Los Angeles about a year ago and added 21 stores in southeastern Wisconsin in July, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported in August.

It is a small program, and it answers the question this post asks better than any sales chart. Department stores and marketplaces are not simply replacing each other. They are splitting the department store’s old job in two: Amazon is taking the choosing, and the store is keeping the handling.

Who is winning the choosing

For most of the last century, the department store’s value was assortment. A shopper went to Macy’s or Kohl’s because the store had already chosen, from hundreds of brands, the clothes worth considering, and laid them out by floor and department. Brands paid for that curation through wholesale terms and markdown allowances, and accepted the department store buyer as the gatekeeper to the shopper.

That job is moving online, and mostly to one place. Morgan Stanley put Amazon’s share of US apparel sales at 7.9% in 2017, just behind Walmart at 8.6%, and expected Amazon to lead in 2018, ExchangeWire reported in April. This month Wells Fargo estimated that Amazon’s apparel and footwear sales could pass $30 billion in 2018, CNBC reported. On Amazon the curation is done by search results and reviews, not by a buyer, which is why it scales to more brands than any department store floor could hold.

The traditional stores are holding on, not collapsing. Macy’s reported second-quarter net sales down 1.1% to $5.572 billion, with its digital business growing by double digits, according to its earnings release. Kohl’s reported a 3.1% rise in comparable sales and digital growth in the mid-teens, CNBC reported. Neither looks like a business being replaced outright. Both look like businesses whose growth now comes through a screen.

Stores are keeping the handling

The Kohl’s numbers hide the more interesting shift. Its stores fulfilled close to 40% of its digital units in the quarter, Digital Commerce 360 reported. The store is becoming a warehouse and a pickup point for the company’s own website, and, through the Amazon program, a returns desk for its largest competitor.

Kohl’s management was candid about the trade-off. The Amazon returns bring people into stores, the chief financial officer said, but they also add store payroll and reverse logistics costs, and the chief executive declined to quantify the results, the Journal Sentinel reported. That is an institution deciding that foot traffic is worth paying for, even when the traffic arrives carrying someone else’s box.

Read as institutions, the two sides want different things. Amazon wants the shopper’s choice and the data that comes with it, and is happy to rent physical space for the parts of retail it does not want to own, such as returns. The department store wants the shopper in the building, because its leases, staff and credit card programs are built around visits. Each is giving the other what it values least.

The general merchants show the same pattern from the other side. Target’s comparable digital sales rose 41% in its second quarter, according to its earnings release, at a retailer that still does most of its business in stores. Growth at the large store chains is coming through their websites, and their buildings are being asked to support that growth rather than replace it. The department store is not alone in turning its floor space into infrastructure; it is simply the format whose original purpose, curating a wide range of brands, is most exposed to a search box that curates for free.

What the split means for a brand’s wholesale plan

For brands that grew up selling through department stores, the split changes what the wholesale account is for. A few years ago the buyer at a department store chose a brand’s assortment and the store sold it. Now the same account increasingly behaves like two businesses: a website with its own search results and product pages, and a set of buildings that fulfill orders and process returns, including returns from other retailers.

That has practical consequences. A brand’s department store product pages now need the same attention as its Amazon listing, because that is where more of the store’s growth is coming from. Store inventory matters to online sales, since a store shipping 40% of digital units is drawing on the same stock a walk-in shopper sees. And the brand’s own Amazon business is now the larger assortment decision, made by shoppers in a search box rather than by a buyer in a showroom.

Questions for the next wholesale review

  1. What share of our sales at each department store account now comes through its website, and who on our team manages those product pages?
  2. Does our allocation to each account reflect that its stores fill online orders, or are we still shipping as if every unit sells off a shelf?
  3. Is our Amazon assortment planned with the same care as the line we present to department store buyers?
  4. Which account would we choose if we had to keep only the one where shoppers actually choose our products?

The brands that answer those questions will stop asking who is replacing whom and start planning for both halves of the job, which is the kind of cross-retailer planning we do when we run Amazon alongside a brand’s other channels.

P0127.title: Sponsored Brands headline tests usually stop too early
P0127.alt: Brass hourglass with sand running beside two empty wooden picture frames on a rustic shelf.
P0127.ttag: Sponsored Brands headline tests usually stop too early | Kwontified
P0127.desc: A Sponsored Brands headline test needs far more impressions than most brands give it; size the test before you write the second headline or scale the first.
P0127.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 2, 2018.
P0127.body:
Two headlines, two weeks each, and one of them posts a click-through rate a fifth higher than the other. The brand keeps the winner, rolls it across every campaign and moves on. In most accounts that winner was picked by a coin. The gap between two reasonable headlines is usually smaller than the random swing in a few weeks of impressions, so the test measured luck and the brand scaled it.

The ad is the same one most brands knew until last month as Headline Search Ads. Amazon renamed it Sponsored Brands in September 2018, when it folded its ad products under the Amazon Advertising name. The creative did not change: a headline of up to 50 characters, a logo and up to three products, sitting above the search results on the keywords you choose, as Feedvisor’s walkthrough lays it out. Fifty characters is not much copy, and the temptation is to treat every word as a lever worth testing.

Why a Sponsored Brands headline test feels conclusive

The instinct is sound. The headline is the only sentence a shopper reads before deciding whether to click, and a better one should earn more clicks for the same bid. A brand that tests at all is ahead of one that writes a headline once and forgets it.

The trouble is how fast the result appears to arrive. A click-through rate is a percentage, and percentages look settled after a few thousand impressions. The dashboard shows two decimal places whether the sample was ten thousand impressions or ten million. Nobody sees the error bar, because the console does not draw one.

Most of us also read a recent, vivid number as more reliable than it is. A headline that “won” by a visible margin feels like evidence. It is a story told by a small sample.

Chance alone moves a click-through rate by half

Clicks on a banner arrive at random, even when the true rate is fixed. Take a headline whose real click-through rate is 0.45%, shown 20,000 times. You expect 90 clicks. Chance alone will regularly hand you anything from about 71 to 109, which reads on the dashboard as a click-through rate between 0.36% and 0.55%. Run the same headline in two different fortnights and it can “beat itself” by half.

Now put two genuinely different headlines side by side. Say one truly earns 0.40% and the other 0.50%, a one-in-four improvement that most copywriters would be delighted with. To tell them apart with the usual statistical standard (95% confidence, and an 80% chance of catching a real difference of that size), you need roughly 70,000 impressions on each headline.

That is where most tests fall short. If your keyword set delivers 3,000 impressions a day, each headline needs about 23 days to reach the mark, and the test runs for well over a month. Two weeks apiece gets you 42,000 impressions per headline. That is enough to produce a confident-looking chart, and not enough to trust it.

It gets harder once you care about sales instead of clicks. A headline promising a discount can lift clicks and still send shoppers who do not buy. Comparing conversion rates of 10% and 12% takes about 3,800 clicks per headline. At 70,000 impressions you will have collected something like 315 clicks on each. At a $1.20 cost per click, a test sized to read conversion properly costs about $9,120 in clicks before it tells you anything.

Comparing two headlines on a few weeks of data is like judging two restaurants by one Friday night each. You learn something, but mostly about that Friday.

Season makes the sequential test worse

Many brands test one headline after the other because it is simpler to set up. In October that choice adds a second problem. Search traffic usually builds through the fourth quarter on its own, so the headline that runs in the second fortnight inherits a busier, more purchase-minded audience. It wins for reasons that have nothing to do with its words.

Running both headlines at once, in campaigns with the same keywords, the same bids and the same budget, removes most of that drift. It does not remove noise, and it does not guarantee an even split of impressions, so check the impression counts before you compare rates. If one headline received twice the exposure of the other, its numbers are more reliable and less comparable.

What a headline test can tell you before the holidays

A test that cannot reach its sample size is still useful if you change what it asks. Small wording swaps (“New” against “Introducing”) produce small differences that only large samples can see. Big differences in the claim itself (price against ingredient, a gift angle against a product benefit) produce gaps large enough to show up in a smaller test. If your keywords cannot deliver about 70,000 impressions per headline in a month, test claims, not words.

Write the stopping rule down before the first impression. Decide how many impressions each headline gets and which metric decides it: click-through rate if the products and landing page are identical, conversion rate or sales per impression if they are not. Then do not peek and stop early because one line is ahead. Stopping when a result looks good is the most reliable way to crown a lucky headline.

The rule of thumb for the fourth quarter of 2018: before you write the second headline, divide the impressions you need by the impressions your keywords deliver per day. If the answer is longer than the season, test a bolder claim or skip the test and spend the effort on the keywords. Sizing tests like this is part of how we run Sponsored Brands for the brands we manage.

P0128.title: Direct-to-consumer brands on Amazon negotiate terms, not entry
P0128.alt: Open notebook in a leather folio, a fountain pen and a small blue gift box on a wooden table by a window.
P0128.ttag: Direct-to-consumer brands on Amazon negotiate terms, not entry | Kwontified
P0128.desc: Two famous holdouts gave opposite answers to the same Amazon offer. For direct-to-consumer brands, the open question is now the terms of selling there.
P0128.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 4, 2018.
P0128.body:
In July 2016, Birkenstock’s US chief executive wrote to the company’s retail partners that the sandals would no longer be supplied to Amazon in the US from January 1, 2017. The letter explained why. Amazon had made it clear, he wrote, that the only way to a marketplace clean of counterfeits and unauthorized sellers was to sell the complete product line to Amazon directly, CNBC reported. Birkenstock refused the offer.

A year later Nike heard the same offer and took a version of it. On its June 2017 earnings call, chief executive Mark Parker confirmed “a new pilot with Amazon with a limited Nike product assortment,” Engadget reported, when Nike products had reached Amazon only through outside sellers, Fortune noted. In return, Amazon would police fakes more tightly, and from July 13 third-party sellers could no longer list certain Nike items, The Drum reported. Amazon offers holdout brands control of their listings in exchange for direct supply, and as more product searches start on Amazon, refusing that offer costs more.

Two brands, one bargain. The direct-to-consumer brands still holding out face the same offer, and their real decision is no longer whether to sell there but on what terms.

Why direct-to-consumer brands on Amazon feel like a contradiction

The holdout position is not stubbornness. A direct-to-consumer brand is built around owning the relationship with its buyer: the email address, the reorder reminder, the second purchase that pays back the cost of the first. Its investors value it on that relationship. An order placed on Amazon arrives inside Amazon’s account, and the second purchase happens wherever Amazon’s search results send the shopper next.

So inside these companies, Amazon sits in a strange place on the org chart. Growth reports to a team measured on customer lifetime value and site conversion. Nobody’s bonus rewards a sale the brand cannot see. Refusing Amazon is, for many of them, simply what the incentive structure says to do.

The shopper did not sign the same plan

The brand’s plan assumes the shopper starts at the brand. Fewer do. Roughly 54% of product searches began on Amazon in the second quarter of 2018, up from 46% in 2015, according to Jumpshot’s analysis of shopping behavior across 500 ecommerce sites and marketplaces. A shopper who hears about a mattress, a razor or a pair of sneakers from a friend increasingly types the name into Amazon first.

What that shopper finds depends on the brand’s choice. If the brand is absent, the results page is not empty. It holds resellers with the brand’s products, imitators with the brand’s look, and competitors who bid on the brand’s name. Birkenstock’s letter was about exactly this: counterfeits and unauthorized sellers that the company could not clean up from outside.

Amazon reads the situation as an institution would. It wants the selection, and it has spent years building doors for exactly these brands. Amazon Launchpad, announced in July 2015, recruits young product companies through more than 25 venture firms, accelerators and crowdfunding platforms, and offers to handle their inventory, fulfillment and customer service. A retailer that builds a program like that is telling you what it values: the brands it does not yet carry.

Follow the value and the bargain looks different from each side. Amazon gains the brand’s catalog and the shoppers who search for it. The brand gains control of a page shoppers are already reading, and gives up some pricing and data in exchange. What a holdout keeps by staying away is the customer relationship with the shoppers who come to its site. What it loses is the conversation with the larger group who start somewhere else.

From whether to which terms

Nike’s pilot shows what the decision becomes once a brand stops treating it as a yes or no. Nike’s chief executive described a pilot with a limited product assortment, sold directly with conditions attached on third-party sellers. That is a negotiation over scope, not a surrender.

For a direct-to-consumer brand, the terms worth arguing over are concrete. The first is range: which products go to Amazon and which stay exclusive to the brand’s own site, where the reorder program and the bundles live. The second is the selling model, whether the brand sells to Amazon as a vendor or sells on the marketplace itself and keeps its hand on price. The third is enforcement, meaning who may resell the products and what the brand will do about the ones who should not. The last is the page itself, and which person on the team writes it and answers for it.

I expect more of the remaining holdouts to fold during 2019, and the evidence leans that way: searches keep moving to Amazon, and Amazon keeps sweetening the offer to the brands it wants. It is too early to say whether the brands that join late get worse terms than the ones that join early. The ones that join on purpose, with a limited range and a named owner, will at least know what they traded.

Questions to put to the leadership team

  1. When a shopper types our brand name into Amazon, what do they find, and who put it there?
  2. What would we be willing to sell on Amazon without weakening the reason to buy from our own site?
  3. If we joined, would we sell to Amazon or sell ourselves, and which choice keeps the pricing control we care about?
  4. Who in the company would own the Amazon page, and what number would they be measured on?

The last question is the one most holdouts have never had to answer, because the answer has been “nobody.” Running that channel day to day, on the brand’s own terms, is work we take on for brands that want those shoppers back.

P0131.crumb: Cyber Week 2018 planning is decided six…
P0131.title: Cyber Week 2018 planning is decided six weeks out, by three teams
P0131.alt: Wooden table by an autumn window spread with open binders of layout sketches, a mug and wrapped parcels nearby.
P0131.ttag: Cyber Week 2018 planning is decided six weeks out, by three teams | Kwontified
P0131.desc: The Cyber Week 2018 decisions that matter, deal depth, inventory and ad budget, close in mid-October with three teams that rarely meet. Who should decide.
P0131.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 11, 2018.
P0131.body:
Thanksgiving falls on November 22 in 2018, which puts Black Friday on November 23 and Cyber Monday on November 26. Count back six weeks from Thanksgiving and you land on this week. Most brands will spend the next month talking about Cyber Week as if it were still ahead of them. In practice it is being decided now, in three separate rooms: finance setting how deep the discounts can go, supply chain deciding how much stock reaches Amazon in time, and the marketplace team guessing at a budget. The brands that do well tend to be the ones where one person makes those three calls together.

The stakes are clear enough. Adobe Analytics counted $6.59 billion in US online sales on Cyber Monday 2017, up 16.8%, and $5.03 billion on Black Friday, according to its 2017 holiday results. For the season now starting, Deloitte expects online sales to grow 17% to 22% against 5% to 5.6% for retail overall, Retail Dive reported in September. The online share of the holiday keeps growing, and so does the cost of arriving unprepared.

Who actually decides Cyber Week 2018 planning

Ask a brand who owns its Cyber Week plan and the answer is usually the e-commerce or marketplace lead. Look at what the plan is made of and the picture changes.

Deal depth is a margin decision, so finance signs it. A 30%-off Lightning Deal on a hero product is a promise about gross margin in the most important quarter of the year, and in most companies nobody below the CFO’s team can make that promise.

Inventory is an operations decision. How many units go to Amazon’s warehouses, and when, is set by a planner balancing Amazon against wholesale accounts and the brand’s own site, often weeks before anyone has agreed which products will be promoted.

The advertising budget is a marketing decision, but frequently a marketing decision made last, from whatever is left once the deals and the stock are settled. That order is backwards. Clicks get expensive during big events: in its review of Prime Day 2017, Bobsled Marketing found that about one client in three saw cost per click rise more than 50% against the first ten days of July, as its review reported. A deal that is discounted and stocked but not advertised is a deal the shopper has to find on their own.

Each of these teams is working to its own calendar, and each calendar makes sense from inside that team. Finance closes its quarter forecast, operations books its inbound shipments, marketing waits for the deals to be final. None of them is wrong. The problem is that the three calendars only meet on the day itself.

The event sets the calendar, and the calendar closes early

Retailers plan the holiday further ahead than most of their suppliers do. Target said in September that it plans to hire about 120,000 seasonal workers, up 20% on its 2017 hiring, including 7,500 people to pack online orders in its warehouses, Reuters reported. A retailer staffing its warehouses in September is telling its suppliers when the season really starts.

Amazon’s own deadlines say the same. For Prime Day on July 16, Lightning Deal submissions for third-party sellers closed on May 18, ChannelX reported, roughly eight weeks before the event. Toy sellers face a harder line in 2018. From October 17, 2018 to January 5, 2019, only sellers who met Amazon’s holiday eligibility rules may sell new items in Toys & Games, with orders fulfilled by Amazon from accounts in good standing exempt, SellerEngine reported in August. Rules like these reward brands that made their Amazon plans in the summer.

Working backward from November 22

A brand that wants to compete on the week can still plan it if it treats the next six weeks as one schedule rather than three.

This week and next. Pick the products. Not the whole range: the handful with the stock depth, the reviews and the margin to carry a deal. Finance signs the deal depth for those products now, in writing, so the discount is not renegotiated after the deal is submitted.

Late October. Inventory for those products should be on its way to Amazon’s warehouses. Stock that arrives the week of Thanksgiving may not be available to sell when the traffic comes, and a promoted product that goes out of stock on Black Friday spends the rest of the week sending shoppers to a competitor.

Early November. Set the advertising budget for the promoted products and the days around them, with room for prices well above October’s. Decide in advance what happens when a campaign’s budget runs out by mid-afternoon on Cyber Monday: who is allowed to add more, and up to what limit.

Thanksgiving week. Watch stock and spend by the hour, not the day, and keep the person who can approve changes reachable. Most of the expensive mistakes of the week, a deal running without stock or a budget exhausted before the evening rush, are visible within an hour of starting and fixable only by someone with authority.

Questions to put to the team this week

  1. Which three products are we prepared to discount, stock and advertise together, and has finance signed the discount?
  2. When will that stock arrive at Amazon, and who checks it has been received?
  3. Who can raise the ad budget on Cyber Monday afternoon without calling a meeting?
  4. Which single person owns all of the above until November 27?

If the answer to the last question is three people, the plan will run on three calendars. Bringing the deal, stock and budget decisions into one plan is the kind of channel work we take on for brands during the holiday, and October is when it has to start.

P0134.title: Instagram influencer sales often finish in an Amazon search
P0134.alt: Smartphone mounted in a ring light on a mini tripod beside a sealed cardboard box against a pink wall.
P0134.ttag: Instagram influencer sales often finish in an Amazon search | Kwontified
P0134.desc: An influencer post on Instagram starts the purchase, but many shoppers finish it in an Amazon search, where another team owns the result. How to connect them.
P0134.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 18, 2018.
P0134.body:
A creator holds a serum up to the camera in her Stories, talks about it for fifteen seconds, and moves on. Since September 17, she can put a shopping sticker on that frame, because Instagram opened shopping in Stories to every business approved for shopping, Instagram announced. Some viewers will tap it.

Many will remember the name, close the app and type it into Amazon later that evening. The post started the purchase; a search somewhere else finished it. Instagram influencer sales are real, but many of them land in a report the influencer team never reads.

That is the structural problem behind most arguments about whether influencer marketing works. The team that pays for the post measures one half of the purchase. The team that runs the marketplace measures the other half. Neither sees the whole.

Where Instagram influencer sales actually happen

Instagram has become a serious place to discover products. About half of its US daily users follow a shopping business, and more than 200 million people visit a business profile every day, Marketing Land reported when Instagram took shoppable posts to eight more countries in March. A tagged post can name up to five products in an image and 20 in a carousel, Marketing Dive noted.

But Instagram does not take the payment. A tag leads to a product page and then out to the brand’s own website, and the brand must connect a catalog through Facebook’s Business Manager, Shopify or BigCommerce to tag at all, as Candid’s guide to the requirements explains. The shopper who taps is sent to a checkout they may never have used, on a site where they have no saved address.

Meanwhile, the default starting point for product search has moved. Roughly 54% of product searches began on Amazon in the second quarter of 2018, Jumpshot found. A shopper with a Prime account, a saved card and two-day delivery has every reason to see a product on Instagram and buy it on Amazon. The tap was never the only path. For many shoppers it is not even the easiest one.

Two teams, two halves of one purchase

Inside a brand, these two paths usually belong to different people. The influencer program sits with brand marketing or social, and it reports what Instagram can count: reach, engagement, sticker taps, clicks to the website, sales on the website. The marketplace team reports Amazon sales and Amazon advertising. Its numbers rise and fall for reasons it is rarely told about, including a creator’s post on a Tuesday afternoon.

The consequences show up in budget meetings. The influencer program looks expensive, because the sales it caused on Amazon are credited to Amazon’s organic search or, worse, to the Amazon ads that sat on top of the brand’s name that evening. The Amazon team looks efficient for the same reason. Each team is reporting honestly, and the company is still misreading what its money did.

The way creators are briefed tends to lock the split in. A brief that asks a creator to drive clicks to the brand’s website, and judges the partnership on those clicks, rewards the path fewer shoppers take. A creator whose audience goes straight to Amazon will look weak in that report, and the brand may drop the partner who was doing the most good. Nobody in that decision is careless. They are each reading the only number their system gives them.

There is a further twist. If the product page on Amazon does not look like the product in the post (a different hero image, a different name, a missing shade), the shopper who searched for it may not recognize it, and buys the nearest look-alike instead. The demand the creator built goes to whoever ranks first.

Instagram wants to close the loop, eventually

Instagram’s direction is easy to read. It has moved from tags in posts to tags in Stories to a Shopping channel in Explore, now in testing. It told advertisers in 2017 that it planned to let businesses pay to show shoppable posts to people who do not follow them, TechCrunch reported. A platform building each of these steps is trying to keep more of the purchase inside its own walls.

It is too early to say whether shoppers will follow. For now, the evidence leans toward discovery on Instagram and purchase wherever checkout is easiest, which for many shoppers means Amazon. Brands should plan for that split rather than wait for it to resolve.

Put both halves of the purchase in one report

The most useful thing a brand can do is put the two halves of the purchase in the same report. Take the date of each significant creator post, then look at the product’s Amazon sales for the seven days after it against the seven days before. It is crude, and other things move sales, but a consistent lift after posts tells you where the influencer program’s sales are landing.

Ask creators which retailer their audience actually buys from, and brief them accordingly. Some audiences are loyal to a brand’s own site; many are loyal to their Prime account. Knowing which is which changes what a good post looks like.

Make the Amazon page match the post. The name, the hero image and the shade or variant the creator used should be what a shopper sees when they type that name into Amazon.

Then ask the question few brands put to both teams at once: when a creator’s post works, which team’s numbers go up, and does the other team ever find out? Getting that answer is part of how we run Instagram Shop and the marketplace side together for brands, because the shopper does not treat them as separate.

P0137.crumb: Retailer relationships on Amazon now run…
P0137.title: Retailer relationships on Amazon now run on exclusives
P0137.alt: Brass stanchions with a burgundy velvet rope in front of shelves of amber bottles, pottery and books.
P0137.ttag: Retailer relationships on Amazon now run on exclusives | Kwontified
P0137.desc: Brands that sell on Amazon fear their store buyers’ reaction. The retailers are busy building their own online businesses and want exclusives, not loyalty.
P0137.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 25, 2018.
P0137.body:
The meeting a brand dreads goes like this: the buyer from its largest store account slides a printout across the table, an Amazon listing of the brand’s best seller at a lower price than the store’s shelf. For years that printout was a threat, and brands answered it with a promise to keep their distance from Amazon. In 2018 the promise is worth less than either side pretends. The retailers are building their own online businesses as fast as they can, and what they now need from a brand is a reason to be the only place for something.

Retailer relationships on Amazon used to mean staying away

The old bargain made sense. A store buyer controlled shelf space, and shelf space was the brand’s route to shoppers. Selling on Amazon looked like supplying a competitor that would undercut the store, so brands that valued their wholesale accounts kept Amazon at arm’s length or pretended not to notice the resellers.

Birkenstock put the bargain in writing. In July 2016 its US chief executive told the company’s retail partners that it would stop supplying Amazon in the US from January 1, 2017, citing counterfeits and unauthorized sellers, CNBC reported. The letter was addressed to retailers, and it reassured them as much as it criticized Amazon.

The trouble is that staying away rarely kept a brand’s products off Amazon. In slides from late 2017, CPC Strategy ranked the most common sources of unauthorized product on Amazon, and the first was the brand itself, through its own wholesale customers, ahead of liquidation sales and the brand’s suppliers, according to its presentation. The store relationship the brand was protecting was often the leak.

The retailers stopped playing the same game

Look at what the large retailers did in 2018 and the old bargain looks out of date.

Target’s comparable digital sales grew 41% in its second quarter, inside total comparable growth of 6.5%, the company reported in August. On October 23 it said it would offer free two-day shipping with no minimum order from November 1 to December 22.

At Kohl’s, stores fulfilled close to 40% of digital units in the second quarter, Digital Commerce 360 reported, and the company handles Amazon returns at about 80 of its stores, Fortune reported. A department store taking back Amazon’s parcels is not a retailer at war with Amazon. It is one deciding which part of the shopper’s trip it can own.

What these retailers increasingly compete on is having something no one else has. Target said in September it would carry more than 2,500 new and exclusive toys this holiday, nearly double the year before, Motley Fool reported. Walmart is widening its toy range 30% in stores and 40% online, CNN reported. When every shopper can compare prices on a phone in the aisle, an identical product at an identical price gives the store no reason to exist. An exclusive does.

Amazon, meanwhile, is coming the other way. Its Amazon 4-star store, which opened in SoHo on September 27, stocks only products rated four stars and up, TechCrunch reported. The line between the online store and the physical one is blurring from both sides.

What the buyer is really asking for

Read the store buyer as an institution and the printout means something different. The buyer is measured on margin and sell-through in a category. An Amazon price below the shelf price threatens both. But the buyer’s company is also asking for traffic it does not have to share, and the buyer knows that a brand cannot police every reseller on Amazon.

So the conversation that works in 2018 is not “we will stay off Amazon.” It is a division of the range, agreed before the printout appears rather than after. Some products, sizes, bundles or colors belong to the store as exclusives. The core range sells everywhere, at prices the brand actually enforces through its distribution terms. The brand runs its own Amazon presence for the core range, so the page, the price and the reviews are under its control rather than a reseller’s.

Nike’s pilot with Amazon, confirmed in June 2017, offered a template: a limited assortment sold directly, Engadget reported. Nike also won concessions from Amazon to police counterfeits more strictly and restrict unsanctioned sales, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Fortune. A limited, deliberate presence is easier to explain to a store buyer than an uncontrolled one built by resellers.

The harder work is internal. At many brands the people who manage the big retail accounts and the person who watches Amazon report to different leaders, plan on different calendars and are paid on different numbers. The account team is rewarded for keeping the buyer happy this season; the Amazon lead is rewarded for growth on a channel the buyer resents. Until the two plan the range together, every new product launch reopens the same argument, and the store buyer’s printout keeps arriving as a surprise.

Questions for the leadership team before the next line review

  1. Which of our wholesale accounts are, directly or through their own liquidations, the source of our products on Amazon?
  2. What could we offer each major retailer as its own: a size, a bundle, a color, a first-to-market window?
  3. If a buyer brings an Amazon printout, can we say who the seller is and what we are doing about the price?
  4. Who owns the Amazon channel and the key retail accounts, and do they plan the range together?

The brands that keep both relationships healthy will be the ones that stop treating them as a choice. Planning the range across stores and Amazon together is part of the channel work we do for brands that sell in both places.

P0138.crumb: FBA weeks of cover should count forward…
P0138.title: FBA weeks of cover should count forward sales, not past ones
P0138.alt: Yellow arrows painted on the concrete floor of a sunlit, mostly empty warehouse with pallets and racking.
P0138.ttag: FBA weeks of cover should count forward sales, not past ones | Kwontified
P0138.desc: Weeks of cover built on last month’s sales looks safe in late October and runs out in December. How to compute FBA cover from forward demand instead.
P0138.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 30, 2018.
P0138.body:
On the last day of October, the inventory report says you are safe: 2,000 units at Amazon, selling about 200 a week through September, which makes 10 weeks of cover. Ten weeks from now is early January. Nobody reorders. The same stock runs out in the first week of December, two and a half weeks before Christmas, because the number in the report was computed from the wrong weeks. Weeks of cover is a division, and FBA weeks of cover is only as good as the sales rate you divide by.

The fix is not a better spreadsheet. It is choosing the right denominator: the sales you expect next, not the sales you just had.

Why trailing sales feel like the safe number

Most inventory reports compute cover from recent history, and for most of the year that is reasonable. Sales in one September week look a lot like sales in the next. Using what actually happened feels more honest than using a forecast, which is a guess with a confident font.

That instinct is a bias, and a useful one to name: we trust the recent and the measured over the expected, even when we know the expected is coming. Every brand selling online knows the holiday will be bigger than September. Deloitte expects e-commerce sales to grow 17% to 22% between November and January, Retail Dive reported. The report still divides by September.

The trailing report behaves like a fuel gauge that reports your remaining range from yesterday’s speed. On a flat road it is close enough. Before a long climb it tells you that you will make it when you will not.

FBA weeks of cover, computed forward

Take the same product. Suppose the brand’s own history says November and December weeks sell about 1.8 times a September week. That multiplier has to come from the brand’s own sales, not from a benchmark, because categories differ enormously.

The simplest way to build it is to divide last year’s average weekly sales in November and December by last year’s average in September, product by product, then adjust for how much faster or slower the product is growing in 2018. A product that launched in the spring has no holiday history of its own; borrow the multiplier from the closest product that does, and say so in the plan, so nobody mistakes the borrowed number for a measured one. At 1.8 times, the forward rate is 360 units a week, and 2,000 units cover 5.6 weeks, not 10. Counting from October 30, that runs out around December 7.

Lead time turns that into a deadline. Say stock takes three weeks from the brand’s warehouse to being available for sale at Amazon in the holiday, and the brand wants two weeks of safety stock on top. The reorder point is five weeks of forward demand, or 1,800 units. The brand is already close to it. To land before December 7 with three weeks in transit, the replenishment has to ship by about November 16, and the trailing report will not raise that flag until it is too late.

The same arithmetic runs the other way after the holiday, and it is just as expensive. Say January sales fall to 150 a week and the brand is holding 1,000 units. On a trailing December rate the report says two or three weeks of cover; on the forward January rate it is nearly seven. A brand reading the trailing number reorders into a slowdown.

Why overstock now costs more than it did

When stock runs short, the brand loses sales it had already paid to attract. When it runs long, the cost used to arrive only twice a year, when Amazon assessed long-term storage. That changed in 2018. Amazon raised monthly storage fees from April 1 and moved long-term storage fees to a monthly assessment from September 15, EcommerceBytes reported when the changes were announced. The new monthly long-term charge is $3.45 per cubic foot for stock held six to 12 months and $6.90 for stock held longer, SellerEngine reported.

So the error that used to be cheap, sending too much after the holiday, now shows up on every monthly bill. A forward forecast matters as much in January as in November.

There is an advertising cost too. A product that sells out in early December disappears from the shopper’s view just as traffic peaks, the advertising that built its autumn demand stops paying back, and the sales momentum it built over the autumn may have to be rebuilt in January. The inventory plan and the ad plan are the same plan seen from two desks.

What the forecast can and cannot do

A forward rate is a guess, and it will be wrong. The point is to be wrong in a known direction by a known amount, and to update it weekly. Compare each week’s actual sales with the forecast. If actuals run more than about a fifth above or below for two weeks in a row, change the multiplier, not just the order.

Forecasts also hide product differences. A best seller with a deal on Cyber Monday and a slow-moving accessory need different multipliers. Do the arithmetic for the products that carry most of the holiday revenue first, then the rest.

Reorder from forward demand before mid-November

Rebuild your cover report with a forward rate in the denominator: next month’s expected weekly sales, from your own holiday history. Then set each product’s reorder point as weeks of lead time plus weeks of safety stock, times that forward rate, and ship anything already below it now. Building forward forecasts of this kind is part of how we plan inventory and advertising together for the brands we work with, because a sold-out product also wastes the advertising that built its demand.

P0139.crumb: Amazon category management now answers to…
P0139.title: Amazon category management now answers to an algorithm
P0139.alt: White robotic arm picking a labeled bottle from a wooden shelf of amber and cream bottles in a sunny shop.
P0139.ttag: Amazon category management now answers to an algorithm | Kwontified
P0139.desc: Amazon’s retail team hands forecasting, ordering and price talks to software, so vendors win by managing the data its buyer reads, item by item.
P0139.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 1, 2018.
P0139.body:
In a store, category management still happens across a table. Once or twice a year the brand’s sales team sits down with the retailer’s buyer for a line review. It brings a deck about the category: where it is growing, which items earn the shelf, which should go, and why the brand deserves the space. The buyer pushes back, the two sides trade terms, and next season’s plan comes out of the room. On Amazon Vendor Central, the chair on the other side of that table is emptying.

Amazon has been moving the buyer’s core decisions into software. Under a project its retail team calls Hands off the Wheel, algorithms now forecast demand, order inventory and negotiate prices with vendors, and employees who want to override the software have to justify it, Bloomberg reported in June. Amazon category management, in other words, increasingly answers to an algorithm. A vendor that still prepares for Amazon the way it prepares for a line review is pitching to the wrong reader.

How Amazon’s buyer became a forecast

The shift did not happen overnight. At first the software’s suggestions could be overruled freely. As its forecasts proved reliable, the burden of proof flipped, and the people who once made the call began to audit it.

That history matters because it explains what the vendor manager’s job has become. A vendor manager at Amazon still exists and still answers email, but the purchase order that lands each week is shaped by a model reading sales history, availability, cost and price. The relationship has not gone away. It has moved from the meeting into the data.

There is a second reason the retail team behaves the way it does, and it sits in Amazon’s own accounts. Bloomberg put the marketplace’s profit margin at about 10%, against about 5% for Amazon’s first-party retail business. A retail organization measured against a marketplace that earns twice its margin has every reason to automate, to cut items that do not pay, and to push marginal products toward sellers who carry their own costs.

What the merchant is actually weighing

Brands tend to think about Amazon one item at a time: this product’s sales, this product’s price, this product’s reviews. A merchant thinks about the category and asks a harder question of each item: what job does it do for the store, and does it pay for its place?

Take a $9 multipack that Amazon buys from the vendor at $5.50. If it costs Amazon about $3.75 to pick, pack and ship one order, the item loses $0.25 every time it sells alone. A merchant looking at that line would want it bundled, priced up or sold only alongside larger baskets.

Now take the same product as a three-pack at $24, bought at $15, with about $5 of fulfillment. The bigger pack earns Amazon $4 a unit and solves the same shopper need. No algorithm is sentimental about the first item.

A brand that thinks like the merchant arrives with that analysis already done. It knows which items in its range bring shoppers to the category, which ones earn the margin, and which ones only work as part of a larger order. It shapes the assortment it offers to Amazon accordingly, instead of listing everything it makes and waiting to see which purchase orders stop.

The same logic applies to availability. A model that orders inventory reads stock-outs and late deliveries as signals about the vendor. Every short shipment or slow confirmation teaches the forecast to trust the vendor less. In a store, a strong relationship with the buyer could cushion a bad quarter. With software placing the orders, the vendor’s operating record is the relationship.

Managing the data the buyer reads

The practical consequence is that category management on Amazon becomes an operating discipline rather than an annual presentation, and most of the weight falls on three areas.

Start with the assortment itself. Review the range the way a merchant would: traffic items, margin items and items that only make sense in a bundle or a larger pack. Retire or restructure the items that cannot pay for their own shipping before Amazon’s systems do it for you.

Then look at what feeds the forecast. Cost, case pack, lead times, fill rates and content all feed the software that decides what to order. When a vendor’s data is late or wrong, the forecast learns from the error. Clean, consistent data is how a vendor argues its case now.

Price across retailers belongs in the same plan. A retailer selling the same item as its competitors watches their prices, and a vendor whose products are priced lower elsewhere is handing the algorithm a reason to squeeze cost or cut orders. Pricing discipline across channels is part of the category plan, not a separate conversation.

Amazon’s business is large enough that these choices compound. Net sales rose 29% to $56.6 billion in the third quarter of 2018, the company reported on October 25. Every week, that volume runs through models that reward vendors whose items pay their way and whose operations are predictable.

The question for the leadership team

The useful question for a CEO is who inside the brand owns Amazon’s view of the category. In many organizations the answer is a key-account manager whose skills were built for line reviews, supported by an operations team that sees the purchase orders and a marketing team that sees the product pages. Each holds a piece of what the algorithm reads, and nobody holds the whole.

The brands that do best with a software buyer will be the ones that put assortment, data quality, availability and pricing under one owner who thinks like Amazon’s merchant does. That is the role we play when we run Amazon as a channel for a brand, and it starts with the question every merchant asks first: which of these items deserve the shelf?
