P0143.crumb: Amazon product titles should read like a…
P0143.title: Amazon product titles should read like a package front
P0143.alt: Cream product box printed with an olive branch on a weathered table beside ceramic cups and dried grasses.
P0143.ttag: Amazon product titles should read like a package front | Kwontified
P0143.desc: An Amazon product title has 200 characters and a phone shows far fewer. Brands that write it like a package front win the shopper’s first glance.
P0143.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 8, 2018.
P0143.body:
Put two pairs of socks side by side on a store shelf and the package does the talking. The brand sits at the top, the product name below it, and one or two claims (cushioned, merino, six pairs) are printed large enough to read from the aisle. Somebody at the brand fought over every word on that panel, and a designer made sure it could be read in three seconds.

Now search for the same socks on Amazon. The title under each photo is often a run of keywords: socks, women, crew, hiking, running, athletic, winter, gift for her. That gap says a lot about who owns the words. At many brands, the package front belongs to the brand team, while Amazon product titles belong to whoever loads the listing, and they get written for the search algorithm instead of the shopper. The brands that treat the title as the front panel of the package will win the first glance, which is increasingly the only one they get.

What Amazon product titles are allowed to carry

Amazon gives the title a fixed amount of room. It told sellers in 2015 that titles must stay within 200 characters, including spaces, and that listings created after July 15, 2015 with longer titles would be suppressed from search, EcommerceBytes reported. The marketplace treats the title as the product’s name, not as advertising space.

Two hundred characters is generous on a desktop screen. It is not generous where a growing share of shoppers now read it. Customers shopping on the Amazon App rose nearly 70% over the 2017 holiday season, Amazon said in its year-end recap, as the Motley Fool reported. Orders placed through the app on Cyber Monday 2017 rose more than 50% from a year earlier, according to TechCrunch. Open the app, search your own category and look at the results: the opening words of each title survive, and the rest disappears behind an ellipsis.

So the real title, the one a phone shopper sees in search, is the first handful of words. The full 200 characters still matter on the product page and for search matching. But the decision to tap happens on the short version.

Why titles turn into keyword lists

The keyword list is not the work of careless people. It comes from how the job is divided.

The title is usually written by the person who builds the listing: an e-commerce coordinator, an agency, sometimes the operations team that uploads files to Vendor Central or Seller Central. That person is measured on whether the product shows up in search, so every new search term goes into the title. Over time the title fills with the words of whoever last asked for a change. The SEO consultant adds “hiking socks.” Sales adds “gift for her” before December. Nobody takes anything out.

The brand team, meanwhile, approved the packaging and moved on. In many organizations it never sees the Amazon title at all, because Amazon content sits in a spreadsheet owned by another department. The result is a product with a carefully written package front in stores and an unsigned list of nouns online, for the same item, sold to the same shopper.

Here is what that looks like for a fictional sock brand. The keyword version, at 180 characters:

Brightmoor Socks Women Crew Socks Cushioned Merino Wool Socks Hiking Socks Running Socks Athletic Socks Boot Socks Warm Winter Socks Gift for Her Moisture Wicking 6 Pairs Size 9-11

And the package-front version, at 73 characters:

Brightmoor Women’s Cushioned Crew Socks, Merino Blend, 6 Pairs, Size 9-11

On a phone, the first version spends its opening words on “socks” twice before it reaches the product’s main claim. The second tells her the brand, the product, its main benefit and the count in the space a phone will show. The search terms that were cut (“hiking,” “boot,” “gift”) still have homes: in the bullet points, the description and the back-end search terms, where they can help matching without crowding the name.

Writing the title the way a package is written

A package front follows an order that shoppers already know: brand, product, the claim that sets it apart, then the facts needed to choose (size, count, color). The same order works on Amazon because it answers a shopper’s questions in the order she asks them: whether this is the brand she knows, whether it is the thing she wants and whether it is the right size.

The brand’s voice lives in the choice of the one claim. “Cushioned” or “merino” or “flat toe seam” is a positioning decision, the same one the brand made when it chose what to print largest on the box. It belongs to the brand team, and it should match across the package, the product page and the ads that point to it.

Consistency across a range matters as much as any single title. When every product in a line follows the same pattern, a shopper scanning a search page can compare them at a glance, the way she compares packages lined up on a shelf. When each title was written by a different person at a different time, the line looks like five unrelated products.

There is a fair worry that a shorter title will lose search traffic. It can, if the cut words are simply deleted. Moved into the fields built for them, they keep doing their job, and the title can get back to its own.

The question to put to the team

Ask who signed off on your top ten Amazon titles, and when. If the answer is nobody on the brand team, or a date from several product cycles ago, the most-read words about your products are being written without the people who decide how the brand speaks. Putting the title under the same approval as the package front is a small change in process. On a phone, it decides what a shopper reads first, and keeping that decision with the brand is part of how we run Amazon listings for the brands we work with.

P0146.crumb: Holiday shipping cutoffs decide your last…
P0146.title: Holiday shipping cutoffs decide your last profitable sale date
P0146.alt: Twine-tied parcel with a pine sprig on a snowy loading dock under a lamp as a delivery truck drives off at dusk.
P0146.ttag: Holiday shipping cutoffs decide your last profitable sale date | Kwontified
P0146.desc: The 2018 carrier cutoffs set the last day a holiday sale ships cheaply. After it, each order costs margin, so brands should agree that date in advance.
P0146.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 15, 2018.
P0146.body:
At many brands, somewhere around December 18, a familiar conversation starts in the operations channel. Orders are still coming in, the warehouse is asking which shipping method to use, and someone points out that ground shipping will no longer arrive by Christmas. Nobody has decided whether the brand will pay to upgrade every order, stop promising delivery or keep advertising as if nothing has changed. The decision gets made in a hurry, order by order, and it tends to be the expensive one.

The date that matters is not December 25, or even the last day a carrier will accept a package. It is the last day a holiday sale can ship by the cheapest method that still arrives in time. Call it the last profitable sale date. For brands that ship their own orders, through their own sites or as seller-fulfilled offers on marketplaces, the 2018 holiday shipping cutoffs set it. The teams involved should agree on it in mid-November rather than discover it in the third week of December.

The 2018 holiday shipping cutoffs, working backward

The carriers have published their calendars. The US Postal Service announced its 2018 holiday deadlines on October 18. For delivery by December 25, Retail Ground should be sent by December 14, First-Class Mail and Priority Mail by December 20, and Priority Mail Express by December 22, according to EasyPost’s summary of the carrier schedules. UPS does not publish an official holiday cutoff for its Ground service, the same summary notes, so brands using it need to work from their own transit times by zone.

Read backward from Christmas, those dates describe a staircase. Each step down costs more per order:

  • Up to the ground cutoff, the cheapest service still arrives, and holiday sales carry their normal margin.
  • Between the ground cutoff and December 20, only faster, pricier services make it.
  • December 21 and 22, only express services, at the highest price, arrive in time.
  • After that, a sale cannot arrive by the holiday at all, and any message implying it can will come back as a complaint or a return.

The ground step is the one that sets the last profitable sale date, and for a brand’s own warehouse it falls earlier than the carrier’s deadline. Take ground transit of five business days to the farthest zone, plus one day to pick and pack: the last profitable order lands several days before the carrier’s published date.

Large retailers have made the later steps look normal to shoppers. Amazon said on November 5 that every US customer would get free shipping with no minimum on orders arriving in time for Christmas, in its announcement; non-Prime shoppers normally need to spend $25. Target is offering free two-day shipping with no minimum through December 22, CNBC reported. Shoppers trained by those offers expect late orders to arrive free. A brand shipping its own orders pays for that expectation itself.

Where the margin goes after the cutoff

Take a $30 item that contributes $12 per order before shipping. Shipped ground at $7, the order still earns $5. Upgrade it to a two-day service at $18 and the order loses $6, while an overnight service at $35 loses $23. The sale looks identical in the e-commerce dashboard. In the profit and loss statement, it has turned from a contribution into a cost.

This is why the date belongs in the plan. Once it passes, the brand has three honest options for each product. It can keep selling and pay for faster shipping on purpose, because the customer is worth more than one order. It can stop promising holiday delivery and say so clearly on the page. Or it can send shoppers to a channel that can still deliver, such as a retailer or marketplace that holds the stock closer to them. What it should not do is keep running the same advertising and the same delivery promise as in early December, letting each order decide the policy.

Returns arrive at the other end of the season, and late, rushed orders add to them. UPS expected returns to peak at 1.4 million packages on January 3, 2018, EcommerceBytes reported at the end of 2017. A holiday plan that ends on December 25 has not counted the bill.

Why nobody owns the date

The reason this decision is made in a hurry is structural. Three teams each hold one piece of it, and they work from different calendars.

Supply chain knows the carrier cutoffs and transit times, and plans from the warehouse outward. Finance knows the margin on each product and will close the quarter on December 31, which makes it alert to cost but not to dates. E-commerce runs the promotions, the advertising and the delivery promise on the product page, and plans from the promotional calendar, where the biggest days are still ahead. Each team’s plan is reasonable. None of them includes the date when the economics of a holiday order change.

So the date falls between them. The warehouse finds out first, because it is the one asking which service to use.

The decisions to settle this week

  • Agree the last profitable sale date for each shipping method and region, using the 2018 carrier cutoffs and your own transit times.
  • Decide, product by product, what happens after it: pay for faster shipping, stop promising holiday delivery, or redirect shoppers to a channel that can still deliver.
  • Schedule the advertising and on-page delivery messages to change on that date, rather than leaving them to run until someone notices.
  • Ask finance to price the expedited-shipping budget in advance, so the cost of the choice is known before December 18.

The question for the leadership team is short: who owns this date? If the answer is the warehouse, it will be decided one order at a time. That cross-functional calendar is a small piece of the holiday work we do when we run marketplace and e-commerce channels for brands, and it matters most in the third week of December.

P0148.crumb: Since the incentive ban, Amazon reviews…
P0148.title: Since the incentive ban, Amazon reviews are bought with sales
P0148.alt: Paper and canvas gift bags with gold star tags lined up on a rustic bench against a terracotta wall.
P0148.ttag: Since the incentive ban, Amazon reviews are bought with sales | Kwontified
P0148.desc: Amazon’s 2016 ban on incentivized reviews tied review counts to sales volume. The real price of a launch’s first five reviews is the sales it takes.
P0148.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 20, 2018.
P0148.body:
A new product on Amazon with no reviews converts poorly, so it sells slowly, so it collects reviews slowly. Every brand launching in 2018 knows the loop. Before October 2016, many sellers broke it by giving product away in exchange for disclosed reviews. That door is closed, and what replaced it is less obvious: since the ban, a product’s first Amazon reviews are bought with sales, at a price set by how many buyers bother to write one.

That price is easy to underestimate, and it is the number that should decide how a launch is funded.

What the incentive ban changed

On October 3, 2016, Amazon changed its community guidelines to prohibit incentivized reviews, meaning reviews written in exchange for a free or discounted product, unless they come through its own Vine program, TechCrunch reported. Until then, reviewers could post such reviews as long as they disclosed the deal. The change followed a ReviewMeta analysis of more than 7 million reviews that found products with incentivized reviews carried higher average ratings.

The ban made sense from Amazon’s side. A review system that sellers could fill with discounted product was a review system shoppers could not trust. But it removed the cheapest lever a launch had, and the stakes of the first few reviews did not change. A product with five reviews is 270% more likely to be bought than one with none, according to a June 2017 study by Northwestern University’s Spiegel Research Center.

Reviews now accumulate at the rate of sales

Without incentives, the number of reviews a product collects is its sales multiplied by the share of buyers who write one. Brands control the first number. They barely influence the second.

Say one buyer in 100 leaves a review. Five reviews then take about 500 sales. A product selling 10 units a day reaches them in about 50 days; one selling 25 a day, in about 20. The launch is slow in exactly the period when slowness costs most, because the product converts worst before it has reviews.

Advertising is how most brands speed that up, which makes ad spend the hidden price of reviews. Say each launch sale bought through advertising costs $8 in ad spend. Five hundred of them cost $4,000, or $800 for each of the five reviews they produce. If one buyer in 50 reviews instead, the sales needed fall to 250, the spend to $2,000 and the cost per review to $400. The review rate, which nobody reports, moves the cost of a launch more than most bid changes do.

This is why launch plans written before the ban now run late. When a few dozen discounted units could produce a page of reviews within weeks, a launch calendar could assume the reviews would simply be there by the time advertising scaled. Today the reviews arrive only behind the sales, so a plan that waits for reviews before spending on ads waits a long time, and a plan that spends without counting reviews cannot say when the product will start converting on its own.

Amazon also sells a shortcut. Its Early Reviewer Program asks buyers of an enrolled product to write a review in exchange for a $1 to $3 Amazon gift card, whatever rating they give. It collects up to five reviews per product, according to a seller guide from June 2017. One seller told Digital Commerce 360 he paid $60 per product; Amazon declined to comment on the price. If the program delivers all five reviews, that is $12 a review.

Where each channel earns its place

The comparison is not as lopsided as $12 against $800 makes it look. The program only raises the share of existing buyers who review; it still needs sales to work on, and it does not promise five reviews. Advertising, meanwhile, buys sales that count for their own sake, not only for the reviews that follow.

So the useful comparison is per review, channel by channel, with the sales the channel brings counted separately. On that basis the program is close to free for any product a brand intends to advertise anyway. Vine works differently again, because Amazon sends product to reviewers it selects itself; its cost is the units given away. And advertising should be judged twice: once on its cost per sale, once on how quickly it moves a new product past the point where reviews start to carry conversion.

Brands sometimes treat the launch ad budget as a fixed sum spread over a month. The arithmetic argues for the opposite shape: spend heavily early, when each sale also buys the reviews that make later sales cheaper, then ease off once the product has its first reviews and converts on its own.

There are real limits to this. The review rate varies by category and price, and a brand that has never measured it is guessing. The first number to pull is the ratio of reviews to units sold on your last three launches. That ratio tells you what a review costs you, and it will change your mind about the launch budget faster than any benchmark.

A rule for every launch

Before a product goes live, write down three numbers: your expected review rate, the sales needed to reach five reviews, and what those sales will cost in advertising. Enroll the product in the Early Reviewer Program if it qualifies, then fund the first weeks of advertising to reach five reviews by a date, not to hit a monthly ACoS target. That is how we plan launch advertising for the brands whose Amazon Sponsored Products we run, and it starts from what a review costs.

P0149.crumb: Amazon product images have to answer what…
P0149.title: Amazon product images have to answer what the store used to
P0149.alt: Ceramic bottle on a turntable lit by softbox studio lights in a small product photography setup.
P0149.ttag: Amazon product images have to answer what the store used to | Kwontified
P0149.desc: In a store, shoppers lift, turn and read a product before buying. On Amazon the image set has to answer those same questions, and six photos can do it.
P0149.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 21, 2018.
P0149.body:
Watch someone choose a frying pan in a store. They lift it to feel the weight, turn it over to look at the base, run a thumb along the handle, read the side of the box for the oven-safe temperature, and set it next to the smaller size to compare. It takes about a minute, and every one of those moves answers a question the shopper would not think to write down.

On Amazon, none of that is possible. The images are the only way a shopper can lift, turn, compare and read, so the image set has to do the store’s work. Many brands still fill it with whatever photography already exists, which is usually campaign imagery built to make people want the product, not to help them choose it. Amazon product images work when they are planned around the questions a shopper asks in the aisle, and six well-chosen photos answer most of them.

What shoppers say they need from Amazon product images

Shoppers are clear about this when asked. In a survey of 1,512 US online shoppers that Splashlight ran from June 22 to July 1, 2017, 47% named high-quality product images as the most influential factor when considering a brand’s product, Agility PR reported. Some 50.5% wanted at least three to five photos, such as front, back and side views, before buying, and another 26.5% wanted six or more.

The screen makes the job harder. Customers shopping on the Amazon App rose nearly 70% over the 2017 holiday, Amazon said, as the Motley Fool reported. On a phone, the image set is the page: the shopper swipes through the photos before reading a single bullet point, if they read the bullets at all.

Why the image set gets the leftovers

The gap between what shoppers need and what brands provide comes from where photography lives inside a brand. Photo shoots are planned and paid for by the brand or creative team, around a season’s campaign, a catalog or a retailer’s lookbook. The brief is about mood and desire. Amazon images, if they are discussed at all, are an item on the shot list after the hero shots are done, or an afterthought solved by cropping campaign images into squares.

Follow the value and the problem becomes plain. The campaign photography is judged by the brand team on how the brand looks. The Amazon listing is judged by the e-commerce team on conversion. The images are produced by the first team and used by the second, and neither owns the question of whether a shopper can choose the right product from them. Meanwhile, the page they sit on may be a brand’s busiest storefront.

Amazon’s own rules shape the first slot and leave the rest open. The main image, the one shown in search, must show the product alone on a plain white background under Amazon’s image requirements. The other slots are the brand’s to use, and they are where most of the store’s work can be done.

Six photos that do the store’s job

Each image should answer one question a shopper would otherwise answer with their hands or eyes in the aisle.

  1. The main image: is this the thing I searched for? The product alone, on white, filling the frame, shot so it reads at thumbnail size on a phone. This is the shelf facing.
  2. Scale: how big is it really? The product in a hand, on a counter or next to a familiar object, or with dimensions marked. It replaces picking it up.
  3. In use: what will it be like to own? The product doing its job, in a real setting, with the result visible. It replaces the demonstration and the display.
  4. Detail: is it well made? A close view of the material, finish, closure or mechanism that justifies the price. It replaces the thumb on the handle.
  5. What is in the box, or which version: am I choosing the right one? The contents laid out, or the variants side by side. It replaces comparing two boxes on the shelf.
  6. The facts: will it fit my need? A clean graphic of the specifications a shopper checks, such as the size chart, ingredients or care instructions. It replaces reading the side of the box.

The order matters as much as the content. On a phone, many shoppers will not swipe past the first few images, so the questions that decide the purchase go first. For apparel and footwear, fit and scale move forward; for beauty, the facts slide often belongs second, because many beauty shoppers check ingredients early.

Not every product needs all six, and some categories need more. The principle is to plan the set from the shopper’s questions rather than from the photography that already exists.

Who should own the image set

The practical change is small. Give the Amazon image set a brief of its own, written by whoever owns the listing and approved by the brand team, and put it on the shot list before the campaign images rather than after. Then review it the way a merchandiser reviews a shelf: on a phone, in search results, next to the competing products a shopper will see first.

The question for a CEO is simple: when your team last planned a photo shoot, did anyone bring the Amazon listing to the meeting? If not, the most-viewed pictures of your products were planned as an afterthought. Building the image set around the shopper’s questions is part of how we run Amazon listings for the brands we work with, because on a phone the photos are the store.

P0150.title: Amazon campaign structure: group by margin, then by theme
P0150.alt: Wooden trays with compartments sorting colorful painted wooden blocks by color on a rustic table.
P0150.ttag: Amazon campaign structure: group by margin, then by theme | Kwontified
P0150.desc: One bid prices every product in a Sponsored Products ad group alike. Group products by what a sale is worth, then organize campaigns by search theme.
P0150.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 27, 2018.
P0150.body:
Ask two Amazon advertisers how to build a campaign and you will hear two confident answers. One says put a single product in each ad group, so every bid is precise. The other says build one campaign per theme, with every relevant product inside it, so the account stays manageable. Both are partly right, because they are answering different questions. Amazon campaign structure has two levels, and each level should be organized around the thing it controls.

The ad group controls the bid. The campaign controls the budget. So group products into ad groups by what a sale is worth, and group ad groups into campaigns by the kind of search they serve.

Why the one-campaign-per-theme habit seemed right

Theme campaigns grew out of a reasonable instinct. A brand selling a range of cookware thinks in categories: frying pans, saucepans, sets. Putting every frying pan into one “frying pan” campaign, with one ad group and one keyword list, mirrors how the brand plans, keeps the number of campaigns small and lets the best seller in the group collect most of the traffic.

For a range of near-identical products, that works. The trouble starts when the products in one ad group are not worth the same per click, which is common in any range that runs from an entry price to a premium one.

One bid, products of unequal value

In a Sponsored Products ad group, the products share the keywords and the default bid that applies to them. When a search matches a keyword, the bid is the same whichever product’s ad ends up showing.

Take a $20 frying pan that can afford $5 of advertising per sale and a $60 pan that can afford $15. Both convert one click in ten. A click is worth $0.50 to the first and $1.50 to the second. Put them in one ad group with a $1.00 bid on “nonstick frying pan” and the bid is wrong for both. It pays twice what a click is worth for the cheap pan and bids a third too little for the premium one. Each sale of the $20 pan costs about $10 in clicks, double its limit, while the $60 pan loses the auctions it could afford to win.

The same problem shows up in the reports. Keyword results for an ad group come back as one line across all its products. A team looking at “nonstick frying pan” sees a blended cost per sale and cannot tell that one product is losing money on it while the other is underfunded. Not every search is worth the same even when one keyword triggers it, Practical Ecommerce noted in 2016. Not every product behind that keyword is worth the same either.

There is a second cost that rarely shows up in a review. Amazon, not the brand, decides which product’s ad appears for a given search, and that choice knows nothing about the brand’s margin, so the traffic can drift toward whichever product converts a little better, even when it earns far less per sale. A team that set up the ad group months ago may never notice that most of its clicks now go to the entry-price item.

That is the case for narrow ad groups. One product per ad group, or a few products with nearly the same price and margin, lets each bid be set from that product’s own value per click.

Why the campaign should still follow a theme

Taken to its extreme, one product per ad group, each in its own campaign, creates a different problem. Budget is set at the campaign level, and a brand with two hundred campaigns has two hundred small budgets to manage, most of them too small to absorb a busy day.

The better split is by search intent. Searches that contain the brand’s own name behave differently from category searches and from searches for a competitor. In Merkle’s Q3 2018 report, brand keywords accounted for 42% of Sponsored Products sales and 61% of Sponsored Brands sales. Branded searches tend to convert well and cost little; category searches bring new shoppers at a higher price. Put both in one campaign and the cheap, high-converting branded traffic makes the whole campaign look efficient while the category spend underneath it is never judged on its own.

Campaigns organized by theme (brand, category, competitor, and perhaps one per product line) let each budget follow one kind of shopper. Inside each, the ad groups are cut by product value.

What the structure costs, and when to simplify

Narrow ad groups and themed campaigns mean more objects to build, more bids to review and thinner data per ad group, which makes each bid noisier when traffic is low. For a brand with ten products and a modest budget, a simpler structure that is reviewed every week will beat an elaborate one that nobody maintains.

The lean, in our view, still favors splitting by value. A blended bid is wrong on every click, while a noisy bid is only wrong some of the time and improves as data comes in. Where data is thin, combine products that share a price and margin rather than products that share a category.

The rule to apply on Monday

Two products can share an ad group if the most each can afford per sale is within about 20% of the other’s. If not, split them. Then sort the ad groups into campaigns by search intent, starting with a clean separation of branded and non-branded searches. That is the structure we start from when we take over Amazon Sponsored Products for a brand, because every later decision about bids and budgets depends on it.

P0153.title: Online returns: marketing makes the promise, operations pays
P0153.alt: A green paper shopping bag on a wooden counter in front of a stockroom stacked with shipping boxes.
P0153.ttag: Online returns: marketing makes the promise, operations pays | Kwontified
P0153.desc: Shoppers judge a brand by how it handles returns, and the policy is written in marketing while the bill lands in operations. Price it before January.
P0153.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 29, 2018.
P0153.body:
The return policy on a brand’s website was probably written in a marketing meeting. Someone compared it with a competitor’s, someone else argued that “free returns” would lift conversion, and the line went onto the checkout page. The cost of keeping that promise shows up months later in a different department, as warehouse labor, carrier invoices and markdowns on items that came back worn or without a box. The people who wrote the promise rarely see the bill.

That gap matters more each holiday, because online returns are where shoppers decide whether to buy from a brand again. They want returns to be easy and clear, and they will reward the brands that make them so. Giving them that is worth doing, but only if someone owns both the promise and its price.

What shoppers want from online returns

The clearest recent evidence comes from Narvar, which released a survey of nearly 1,300 US online shoppers on November 14. Some 96% said they would shop again with a retailer based on an easy returns experience, according to Narvar’s release. More than two-thirds said fees for return shipping or restocking deterred them.

The more interesting finding is about information rather than money. Some 59% of shoppers wanted notifications about the status of their refund, and half wanted updates on the return package itself. Narvar pointed to Amazon as the example: its return process takes more steps than some, but shoppers put up with that because Amazon tells them clearly where the return and the refund stand, MediaPost reported.

Shoppers have also become more willing to send things back. In Narvar’s 2018 survey, 31% said they had kept an unwanted item to avoid the hassle of returning it, down from 53% the year before. More of the items customers do not want are coming back to the brand.

Retailers have noticed the shift. Kohl’s began accepting Amazon returns, free and without a box, at 82 stores in Los Angeles and Chicago in October 2017, Fox Business reported, a test that brings Amazon’s customers through its own doors. When a department store wants another company’s returns, the returns desk has become a place where customer relationships are won.

Follow the cost of a return

The cost side is less visible. US retailers lost more than $351 billion in sales to merchandise returns in 2017, and return fraud and abuse cost them $17.6 billion to $22.8 billion, according to an Appriss Retail report from December 2017. At brand level, the number is made of small charges that land in several places.

Take a $60 jacket bought online. The return label costs the brand $8. Receiving, inspecting and restocking it costs another $4. If 15% of returned jackets cannot be sold again at full price, the expected loss on resale is about $9 per return.

Each return therefore costs roughly $21. If one jacket in five comes back, that is $4.20 on every jacket sold, a figure that sits in shipping, warehouse and inventory lines rather than next to the marketing decision that created it.

That split is the structural problem.

Marketing owns the policy and is measured on conversion. Operations owns the warehouse and is measured on cost per unit handled. Finance sees the markdowns at the end of the quarter. Each sees one piece. Nobody sees the return as a single transaction with a price, so the policy is never priced at all.

Where the season puts the bill

The timing makes the gap worse. Holiday orders placed in late November and December come back in early January, after the holiday sales have been celebrated. UPS expected returns to peak at 1.4 million packages on January 3, 2018, EcommerceBytes reported in late 2017. The return wave arrives when the holiday plan has already been judged a success.

Marketplaces add another layer. On Amazon, the return experience is largely Amazon’s, and shoppers judge the brand partly on a process the brand does not run. The brand’s own site is the one place it controls the promise completely, which makes it the place where getting it right, and getting it priced, matters most.

What a priced return policy looks like

Pricing the return does not mean making it harder. Narvar’s findings point the other way: much of what shoppers value is information, and information is cheap. An email when the return is received and another when the refund is issued cost almost nothing and answer the questions that otherwise turn into calls to customer service.

Pricing does let a brand be generous on purpose. It can keep returns at no charge on full-price items, where the repeat purchase is worth the $21, and charge for returns on final clearance, where it is not. It can steer shoppers to a drop-off point that costs less than a prepaid label. It can fix the products that come back most often, because a size chart that prevents one return in five can be worth more than a policy change. Each of those choices needs the same input: a number for what a return costs, by product, next to a number for what an easy return earns.

The question for the leadership team

The useful question for a CEO is who owns the return. One owner should hold the policy, the communication and the cost together, with a monthly number for what each return costs and what easy returns are worth in repeat purchases. Shoppers in Narvar’s survey said clearly what earns their next order: easy returns and honest updates. A brand that knows the price of giving them can decide how generous to be, rather than finding out in January. Putting returns under one view is part of how we run e-commerce and marketplace channels for brands, because the returns desk is now part of the storefront.

P0155.title: Cyber Week 2018 results beat forecast; December grades them
P0155.alt: Kraft-paper wrapped gifts with ribbons and greenery beside a brass caliper, under a pinecone wreath.
P0155.ttag: Cyber Week 2018 results beat forecast; December grades them | Kwontified
P0155.desc: Cyber Week 2018 beat Adobe’s forecast on every day it named. Whether the weekend added sales or borrowed them is a question only December can answer.
P0155.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 4, 2018.
P0155.body:
Adobe’s last forecast before the day had US shoppers spending $7.8 billion online on Cyber Monday. They spent about $7.9 billion, up 19.7% on 2017, the largest online shopping day the US has recorded, Adobe said.

Thanksgiving Day did better still against its forecast. Every headline since has said the same thing: the forecast was too low. That is true for the days it covered. It does not yet tell anyone whether the weekend added sales or moved them.

Cyber Week 2018 results against the forecast

Adobe published its holiday forecast on November 1, raised two of the daily numbers as the weekend approached, and reported results through Cyber Monday. Here is how the two line up:

PeriodAdobe’s last forecast before the dayResult
Thanksgiving Day$3.5 billion$3.7 billion, up 28%
Cyber Monday$7.8 billion$7.9 billion, up 19.7%
Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday$23.4 billion$24.2 billion
November 1–26no separate forecast$58.5 billion, up 19.9%
November 1–December 31$124.1 billion, up 14.8%not yet known

The five days came in about 3% above forecast, which is a good miss as forecasts go. Thanksgiving Day beat its number by about 6%. Amazon, which does not publish daily sales, said Cyber Monday was the single biggest shopping day in its history by products ordered, and that customers ordered more than 180 million items between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday.

The tempting conclusion is that demand ran hot and the forecasters were timid. Before taking that to a 2019 plan, look at the last row.

A weekend can beat its forecast by borrowing

Adobe forecast 14.8% growth for the whole season. The first 26 days of November grew 19.9%. Those two numbers can both be right only if the rest of the season grows more slowly than the start.

The arithmetic is short. A $124.1 billion season up 14.8% implies a 2017 season of about $108.1 billion. November 1–26 at $58.5 billion, up 19.9%, implies about $48.8 billion for the same days in 2017. Take the second from the first and the 2017 remainder, November 27 through December 31, was about $59.3 billion. To land on the forecast, 2018’s remainder needs $65.6 billion: growth of about 10.6%.

So there are two readings of the same weekend. If December grows at the season’s forecast rate of 14.8%, the year finishes near $126.6 billion and the forecast was simply low. If December grows near 10.6%, the season lands where Adobe said it would, and the strong November was spending that moved earlier on the calendar.

There was evidence of movement before the weekend began. Adobe measured $2.39 billion of online spending on November 21, the day before Thanksgiving, up 31.8% on a year earlier, a faster rise than Black Friday’s. Retailers started their deals early and shoppers followed them. Money spent on the 21st for a gift that would otherwise have been bought on December 10 shows up as a beat in November and a shortfall in December.

The pull is to grade the forecast on the days that have results, because those are the days with headlines. That is recency doing the grading. A forecast for a season is a claim about the season, and most of December has not happened yet.

What your own Cyber Week numbers can and cannot show

The same trap sits inside every brand’s Cyber Week report, at a smaller scale.

Say your brand sells $50,000 a week on Amazon through October. Cyber Week brings in $140,000, a lift of $90,000 over the usual week. Now look either side of it. In the two weeks before, shoppers who had seen the deals coming held off, and sales ran at $40,000 a week. In the two weeks after, the shoppers who bought early are done, and sales run at $42,000 a week.

The four weeks around the event came in $36,000 under the usual pace.

The net added sales across those five weeks are $54,000, not $90,000. Forty percent of the event’s headline lift was borrowed from its neighbors. The event still paid, but its return on ad spend, its deal cost and its case for next year’s budget should be built on $54,000.

A report that covers only the event week cannot see any of this. Neither can a ROAS figure, since a sale pulled forward by a deal and an ad still counts as an attributed sale. What would settle it is a window wide enough to contain the borrowing and a baseline that is not itself distorted by the event:

  • Measure Cyber Week inside a window of at least five weeks, from early November to mid-December, against the same weeks of 2017, adjusted for your growth rate through October.
  • Use the weeks before deals were announced as the baseline, since the week before the event is already depressed.
  • Hold judgment on the event’s return until mid-December, when the after-weeks are in.

The grade to give Cyber Week 2018

On the evidence through December 3, the Cyber Week 2018 forecasts were low for the days they covered, by about 3% for the five days and more on Thanksgiving Day itself. Whether they were low for the season depends on a December that has not happened. If the remaining weeks grow by more than about 10.6%, the event added demand. If they grow by less, some of November’s beat was borrowed.

The rule for your own report is the same one: never grade an event on the event week. Grade it on the window that contains everyone who changed their timing because of it, and write the baseline down before the event starts. That baseline is the first thing we set up when we measure a tentpole event for a brand.

P0156.crumb: Cyber Week 2018 showed retailers now own…
P0156.title: Cyber Week 2018 showed retailers now own the holiday calendar
P0156.alt: Wrapped holiday gifts, ornaments and holly on a wooden table below a framed pin-board calendar on a teal wall.
P0156.ttag: Cyber Week 2018 showed retailers now own the holiday calendar | Kwontified
P0156.desc: Fewer people shopped the 2018 Thanksgiving weekend and they spent more online. The retailers who started first set the calendar every brand followed.
P0156.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 6, 2018.
P0156.body:
On the Friday after Thanksgiving, ShopperTrak counted 1.7% fewer visits to American stores than a year earlier. On the same day, Adobe measured $6.22 billion of online sales, up 23.6%. Read side by side, the two figures look like a story about channels, stores losing and screens winning. The more useful story for a brand is about the calendar. Black Friday was no longer a day in 2018, and the companies that decided when it began were the retailers, each choosing a start date that suited itself.

Cyber Week 2018 stretched across ten days or more

Amazon opened its Black Friday Deals Week on November 16, a full week before Black Friday, and ran its deals store through November 25. Walmart announced its Black Friday plans on November 8 and opened its online sale at 10 p.m. Eastern on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, two hours earlier than in previous years. By the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, when Adobe measured $2.39 billion of online spending, up 31.8% on a year earlier, much of the holiday’s buying was already under way.

The shoppers followed. The National Retail Federation counted more than 165 million Americans shopping in stores or online over the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, fewer than the 174 million it counted in 2017. Yet the number who shopped both in stores and online rose to 89 million, up nearly 40%. Fewer people went looking, and the ones who did moved easily between the store and the phone in their hand. Adobe reported that buy online, pick up in store orders over the weekend rose 50%.

Put those numbers in a planning meeting and the old map stops working. A holiday plan built as a column for Black Friday and a column for Cyber Monday, with a promotion assigned to each and a sales target beside it, assumes a shopper who buys by the day. Shoppers did not buy that way in 2018. Take one who saw an Amazon deal on the 16th, compared it on Target’s site on the 20th and picked the gift up at a Walmart store on the weekend: she shows up in three retailers’ reports and in none of the brand’s plan columns.

Who gains from starting first

Retailers did not stretch the event by accident. Each had a reason to go early, and the reasons explain why the calendar will not shrink back.

A gift is bought once. The retailer that reaches a shopper first with a convincing price takes the gift off her list, and every rival that waits for the traditional weekend competes for what is left. For Amazon, which has no doorbusters to stage, an early start also moves the contest onto its own ground: a website open around the clock, where the deals rotate through the day and the competition is one search away. For retailers with stores, the answer was to open online deals early too and to use the store as a pickup counter, which is what the 50% rise in pickup orders suggests they did.

The value from that early start goes to the retailer that owns the shopper’s first visit. It does not go to the brand, which supplies the same product to every one of them. A brand that funds a deep discount on Amazon in the first week and a different one at Target in the second has paid twice to help two retailers compete for one customer.

That is the uncomfortable part for a brand team. On the old calendar, the retailer chose the date and the brand chose whether to take part. On the new one, the retailer still chooses the date, but the date now moves each year, differs by retailer and arrives earlier. A brand that plans its promotions around the weekend is planning around the one fixed point that has stopped mattering most.

What the stores were really for

The store traffic figures deserve a second look. A 1.7% fall in Black Friday visits sounds like decline, and some of the coverage read it that way. Thanksgiving Day and Black Friday together fell only about 1%, and 89 million people used both a store and a screen over the weekend.

The stores did not empty over the weekend; they changed jobs. A store that hands over an order placed online is doing the work of a warehouse with a parking lot, and the brand’s product sitting on that shelf is now also inventory for someone’s website. For a brand, that turns a store allocation into a digital decision. If a retailer’s pickup business is growing at this pace, the stock a brand ships to its stores in November is also the stock it is selling online, and an out-of-stock on the shelf becomes an out-of-stock on the screen.

One weekend of preliminary data, measured by firms with their own panels and methods, cannot settle a structural argument, and the season’s full results are weeks away. Even so, the evidence leans one way: the event is longer, the shopper moves between channels freely, and the retailers are competing on who starts first.

Questions to put to your team before the 2019 plan

The useful post-mortem for Cyber Week 2018 is less about how much was sold and more about who decided when. Four questions are worth an hour of a leadership meeting:

  1. When did our first holiday offer go live at each retailer, and who chose that date, our team or theirs?
  2. Did we fund the same discount at two retailers in the same week, so that we paid to compete with ourselves?
  3. Is our 2019 holiday plan organized by day, or by the weeks each retailer actually ran its event?
  4. Which store allocations were also serving online pickup orders, and did anyone on the e-commerce team see those numbers?

A brand whose answers are mostly “the retailer” and “we don’t know” is learning its holiday calendar from its customers’ inboxes. Running that calendar across Amazon, Walmart and Target as one plan is a large part of how we run marketplace channels for brands, and the 2019 version starts being decided well before next November.

P0157.title: The 2019 Amazon advertising plan starts from margin, not ACoS
P0157.alt: A brass balance scale weighing coins against a small wrapped parcel beside an open grid notebook and plants.
P0157.ttag: The 2019 Amazon advertising plan starts from margin, not ACoS | Kwontified
P0157.desc: A 2019 plan that copies 2018’s ACoS target is budgeting against a margin tariffs and ad competition have already moved. Rebuild the target first.
P0157.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 11, 2018.
P0157.body:
Open a 2019 Amazon advertising plan in December 2018 and last year’s numbers are already in it. Sales get a growth rate. Advertising gets a budget. The advertising cost of sale (ACoS), the share of each sale’s price spent on the ads that produced it, keeps its 2018 target, because the target worked.

That last cell is the one to question. An ACoS target is a margin calculation, and the margin under it moved in 2018.

Why copying the ACoS target looks safe

Carrying the target forward has a real logic. It held up through a year of trading. The team knows how to manage to it, and changing it reopens an argument with finance. A target that produced profitable growth in 2018 seems like the least risky assumption in the plan.

The trouble is what the number stands for. A target ACoS is the answer to one question: how much of a sale’s price is left after the product, the freight and the retailer’s fees, and how much of that the brand is willing to spend to win the sale. Change any input to that question and the answer changes, whether or not anyone updates the cell.

The three inputs that moved in 2018

InputWhat the 2018 plan assumedWhat changed by December 2018
Landed costStable product and freight costA 10% tariff on about $200 billion of Chinese imports took effect September 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on January 1; on December 1 the US agreed to delay that increase for 90 days
Ad competitionRoughly stable cost per clickMerkle measured Sponsored Products spend up 62% and Sponsored Brands spend up 86% year over year in the third quarter
Sales taxNot a factor for most online salesThe Supreme Court ruled on June 21 that states can require sellers without a physical presence to collect sales tax

The tariff is the input with a date on it. The Section 301 list finalized on September 18 put a 10% duty on goods across thousands of tariff lines, with the rate set to reach 25% at the start of 2019. The truce agreed in Buenos Aires on December 1 pushed the increase out to March 1 while talks run. A plan that assumes the 10% rate holds all year is betting on how those talks end.

Ad competition is the input that compounds. Merkle’s third-quarter report showed advertisers raising Sponsored Products spend by 62% in a year. Amazon’s own “other” revenue line, which is mostly advertising, reached about $2.5 billion in the quarter, up 122%, though an accounting change flatters part of that growth. More money bidding into the same searches tends to push up the price of a click, and a brand that holds its bids still loses placements to the brands that raised theirs.

Sales tax mostly changes the shopper’s price rather than the brand’s margin, and in the states that now make the marketplace collect it on sellers’ behalf, it stays out of the seller’s own math. It still belongs in the plan, because a price that rises at checkout can lower conversion, and conversion is what turns a click into a sale.

How a frozen ACoS target loses its margin

Take a $40 product that costs $16 to land in a US warehouse, $12 of it the factory price. Amazon’s fees for referral and fulfillment come to $11 a unit. That leaves $13 before advertising. In 2018 the brand set a 25% ACoS target, $10 of ad spend per sale, and kept $3.

Now run the 2019 inputs. If the tariff on that factory price goes from 10% to 25%, landed cost rises by $1.80, and the margin before advertising falls to $11.20. If clicks cost 10% more and convert at the same rate, the ad cost of each sale goes from $10 to $11. The brand that keeps bidding to hold its placements spends $11 a sale, an ACoS of 27.5%, and keeps $0.20 a unit.

The ACoS barely moved, and the business underneath it went from profitable to break-even. Nothing in the advertising report flags it: 27.5% against a 25% target reads as a small miss, because ACoS is measured against price, and the price did not move.

The break-even ACoS is the margin before advertising divided by price: $13 on $40 was 32.5% in 2018, and $11.20 on $40 is 28% under a 25% tariff. The distance between the target and the break-even line is the brand’s real cushion, and in this example it fell from 7.5 points to 3.

Write the 2019 target as a formula

There are two honest ways to respond, and they pull in opposite directions. A brand can hold its target and accept fewer placements as clicks get dearer, which protects margin and gives up share on the searches where rivals bid harder. Or it can hold its placements and accept a thinner margin per sale, betting that the volume and the reviews it buys pay off later. The numbers above lean toward the first for products already near break-even, and toward the second only where a product’s repeat purchase or new-customer value is known, not hoped for.

Either way, the target belongs in the plan as a formula:

  • Recompute margin before advertising for each top product with the landed cost at both 10% and 25% tariff rates, since the March 1 outcome is unknown.
  • Set the ACoS target as a share of that margin, with the break-even line written next to it.
  • Check the cushion each quarter against actual cost per click, and move the target when an input moves, without waiting for the next annual plan.

The rule for 2019: an ACoS target is only as current as the cost sheet it came from. Rebuilding that sheet before the budget is set is how we start every Amazon advertising plan we run.

P0159.title: In 2018, online marketplaces replaced the buyer with the seller
P0159.alt: A sunlit wooden desk and leather chair beside a market stall filled with woven textiles, pottery and fruit.
P0159.ttag: In 2018, online marketplaces replaced the buyer with the seller | Kwontified
P0159.desc: In 2018 the businesses deciding what sits on a brand’s Amazon shelf were mostly independent sellers, not retail buyers. Brand org charts still assume a buyer.
P0159.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 13, 2018.
P0159.body:
A brand’s year with a big retailer used to turn on a meeting: the line review, where the sales team sat across a table from the buyer and argued for shelf space, a price and an order. That meeting still happens at Walmart and Target. On Amazon, the shelf most shoppers see is no longer filled by anyone sitting across a table. In April, Amazon told shareholders that in 2017, for the first time, independent sellers supplied more than half the units sold on its site.

That was the structural story of online marketplaces in 2018: the seller replaced the buyer as the person who decides what a brand’s shelf looks like, and brands built around wholesale are still organized to talk to a buyer.

How online marketplaces in 2018 moved the shelf to the seller

The buyer was a useful invention. For most of the last century, a retailer’s buyer decided which products a store carried, at what cost and in what quantity, and a brand’s sales organization was built to persuade that one person. Key account managers, trade budgets, annual line reviews and joint business plans all assume a single counterpart with authority over the shelf.

A marketplace has no such person.

When Jeff Bezos wrote in his April letter that third-party sellers now supplied more than half of Amazon’s units, he was describing a store where most of the stocking decisions are made by businesses Amazon does not employ. Amazon said its customers ordered more than a billion items from small and medium-sized businesses during the 2017 holiday alone, Fortune reported a year ago. Some of those sellers are brands selling their own products. Others are resellers selling someone else’s, choosing which of a brand’s products to list, how to price them and how much stock to send.

This is why the Amazon shelf so often surprises the brand that makes the products on it. Nobody approved the assortment. It emerged from dozens of independent decisions, each made by a seller looking at its own margin.

The other retailers chose the same shape

What made 2018 feel like a shift rather than an Amazon quirk was how many other companies moved toward the marketplace model in the same twelve months.

In March, Google launched Shopping Actions, a program that lets retailers including Target, Walmart, Costco and Ulta Beauty sell through Google Search and the Google Assistant with a single cart, paying Google only when a sale happens. Google does not hold the inventory; it hosts other merchants’ offers. In August, Walmart completed its purchase of a 77% stake in Flipkart, India’s largest online store, for about $16 billion. The largest acquisition in Walmart’s history, larger than its 1999 purchase of Asda, was a marketplace rather than a chain of stores.

And in June, the Supreme Court’s decision in South Dakota v. Wayfair opened the door for states to require online sellers without a physical presence to collect sales tax. Some states, including Minnesota and Washington, had already written rules that put that duty on the marketplace itself, collecting on behalf of the sellers on its platform. Policy is starting to treat the marketplace as the responsible party for transactions it does not own, which is one more sign that this is now the expected way to run a store online.

What a brand’s org chart still assumes

Inside a brand built around wholesale, the structure lags. Sales teams tend to be organized by account: a Walmart team, a Target team, an Amazon team. The Amazon team commonly sits in sales and is measured, like the others, on shipments to the retailer. That works for the part of Amazon that buys from the brand as a vendor. It does not reach the half of the shelf that sellers control.

That half needs different work. Someone has to watch which sellers list the brand’s products and at what prices. Someone has to decide which resellers the brand wants and which it does not, keep the product pages accurate, and enroll the brand in Amazon’s Brand Registry so it can control what those pages say. The stakes reach past Amazon: a reseller’s price cut there becomes the number every other retailer’s buyer sees when she checks the web before the next line review. None of that is account management. It is closer to running a channel: a store the brand does not own, stocked partly by people it does not employ, where the brand’s job is to set the rules it can set and police the rest.

Walmart and Target still run their stores on buyers and line reviews, so the old model has years left in it. The direction across 2018 still pointed one way. The biggest new bets of the year, from Walmart’s Flipkart purchase to Google’s cart, went to platforms that host other people’s inventory.

Questions for the 2019 org chart

Before the next planning cycle, three questions sort a brand that has adjusted from one that has not:

  1. Who in the company can name the five largest third-party sellers of our products on Amazon, and the prices they charged last week?
  2. Is our Amazon lead measured on shipments to Amazon, or on what shoppers buy from every seller on our pages?
  3. If a new marketplace asked to carry our products tomorrow, which team would decide, and on what criteria?

A brand that cannot answer the first question is letting sellers write its shelf by default. Building the team, rules and reporting to run that shelf is what we do as a marketplace channel manager, and 2019 is a good year to start, while the seller-run shelf is still new enough to shape.

P0161.crumb: A Sponsored Products daily budget spent…
P0161.title: A Sponsored Products daily budget spent by noon skips the evening
P0161.alt: An empty glass jar beside a brass clock, lamp, notebook and pen on a wooden desk against a teal wall.
P0161.ttag: A Sponsored Products daily budget spent by noon skips the evening | Kwontified
P0161.desc: A Sponsored Products campaign that spends its daily budget by noon reports a steady ACoS while missing the late hours that carried a fifth of Cyber Monday.
P0161.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 18, 2018.
P0161.body:
A Sponsored Products campaign with a $100 daily budget spends its $100 every day, posts the same ACoS week after week, and looks like the most dependable line in the account. Look at when the money goes and a different picture appears: by noon, the budget is gone. The campaign has not been buying a day of shoppers. It has been buying a morning, and the report has no way to tell you what the afternoon and evening would have sold.

Why a fully spent budget looks like success

A campaign that spends its whole budget feels like a campaign with more demand than money. The natural reading is that it is working, and the natural fix, when someone asks for more sales, is a bigger budget. A budget review that checks spend against budget and ACoS, the advertising cost of sale, passes a campaign like this on both counts.

The trouble is that both numbers describe only the hours the campaign was live. A daily budget is a cap: once the campaign has spent it, the campaign stops buying clicks for the rest of the day. Every search after that moment goes to someone else, and none of those lost searches shows up anywhere in the report. A campaign that ran out at noon and one that ran until midnight can post the same spend and the same ACoS.

It is the arithmetic of a shop that closes at noon every day and judges its business by the morning till. The till is accurate. It simply never sees the evening crowd.

The hours after noon can carry much of the buying

The hours a noon cutoff skips are not quiet ones. On Cyber Monday, Adobe estimated that the three hours from 10 p.m. to 1 a.m. Eastern brought in about $1.7 billion of US online sales, on a day that totaled about $7.9 billion. More than a fifth of the day’s spending landed in three late hours, all of them after the workday had ended on both coasts.

Cyber Monday is extreme, and an ordinary Tuesday will be flatter. Still, a campaign whose budget is gone by lunchtime is absent for whatever share of the day’s buying happens later, and the biggest shopping day of the year shows how large that share can be. It is also absent when it would have mattered most during the last shipping days before Christmas, because a shopper ordering on the evening of December 18 for delivery in time is no less valuable than one who orders at 9 a.m.

How the cap picks the wrong hours

Take a campaign for a $30 product with a $100 daily budget and bids that average $1 a click. In the morning, its clicks convert at 10%. After noon, they convert at 12%.

At $1 a click, the campaign buys 100 morning clicks and runs dry at noon. It makes 10 sales, $300 in revenue, at an ACoS of 33.3%.

Now cut the bids so clicks average $0.80. The campaign wins fewer of the top placements, so clicks arrive more slowly, and the same $100 stretches across the day: 50 clicks before noon and 75 after. The morning clicks produce 5 sales. The later clicks, at 12%, produce 9. That is 14 sales and $420 in revenue for the same $100, an ACoS of 23.8%.

Bids at $1.00Bids at $0.80
Clicks before noon10050
Clicks after noon075
Sales1014
Revenue$300$420
ACoS33.3%23.8%

The lower bid wins because the budget, not the bid, was setting the hours. At $1, the campaign paid top prices for the hours with the weaker conversion rate and then sat out the stronger ones. The higher bid did not buy better shoppers. It only spent the money faster.

The trade has a limit. Lower bids lose placements, and a click from lower on the page may convert at a lower rate than the scenario assumes. If the bid falls so far that the campaign stops winning visible positions at all, the evening hours it now reaches are worth little. The numbers above lean toward a moderate cut, enough to keep the campaign live all day, and no further.

A bigger budget is the other answer, and sometimes the right one. If the after-noon hours convert well and the product’s margin supports the ACoS, raising the budget buys the evening without giving up the morning placements. But a bigger budget at the same bids also buys more of the morning’s weaker clicks first. Test the cheaper fix before paying for the dearer one.

The test is easy to run. Lower bids on half of the campaigns that run out early, leave the other half alone for two weeks, and compare sales per dollar of spend between the two groups. Judge on sales, not ACoS alone, since the campaigns that stay live longer will also reach searches the old ones never saw.

Rules for a campaign that runs out early

  • Find the hour each campaign runs out of budget, every week, not just whether it spent its budget. A campaign that hits its cap before mid-afternoon is buying a partial day.
  • Before raising the budget, lower bids on the campaign’s broadest keywords by 10% to 20% and watch whether it stays live into the evening at the same or better ACoS.
  • In the last shipping days of the year, check budgets daily. The evening shopper in mid-December may be a gift buyer with a deadline.

The rule of thumb: when a campaign spends its full budget, ask what time it ran out before you ask for more money. That question is the first one we ask when we manage Sponsored Products budgets for a brand.

P0162.crumb: Small brands on Amazon win specific…
P0162.title: Small brands on Amazon win specific searches, not broad ones
P0162.alt: A small brass padlock with its key beside a large rusted iron padlock on a slate stone ledge.
P0162.ttag: Small brands on Amazon win specific searches, not broad ones | Kwontified
P0162.desc: Marketplaces let a small brand skip the buyer and the slotting fee, but favor it only on specific searches. On broad ones, scale and the platform win.
P0162.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 20, 2018.
P0162.body:
Walk the shampoo aisle of a big-box store and the shelf tells you who won the negotiation: a few national brands at eye level, the retailer’s own label beside them, and a narrow strip for anything new. A small brand gets onto that shelf by persuading a buyer, paying for the space and shipping enough stock to fill it. On a marketplace, none of that applies. The shelf is a search results page that rearranges itself for every query, and small brands on Amazon can appear on it the day they list. Whether they stay there depends on a question the aisle never asked: how specific was the search?

Marketplaces opened the door to small brands on Amazon and beyond

The scale of the opening is real. Amazon said that more than 300,000 small and medium-sized US businesses started selling on its marketplace in 2017, and that more than 140,000 small and medium-sized businesses passed $100,000 in annual sales. For a company that size, the old route to a national shelf ran through a buyer, a slotting negotiation and an opening order large enough to fill the stores. The marketplace route needs a listing.

Etsy’s marketplace is built around makers and vintage sellers, offering things no buyer would stock in volume. The long tail, in other words, is not a theory any more. It is how several large marketplaces fill their catalogs.

Where the marketplace actually favors the niche

The search box is what makes the niche work. Type “shampoo” and a marketplace has to choose among thousands of products for a shopper it knows little about. Type “sulfate-free shampoo for curly hair, fragrance-free” and the shopper has done most of the choosing herself. Amazon does not publish how it ranks results. Relevance to the words typed is the obvious first test, and on that second search a small brand built for exactly that need can pass it better than a national brand built for everyone.

Try it in your own category. Search Amazon for the most specific version of the problem your product solves, then for the broad category word, and compare the two first pages. On the specific search, the products are chosen by fit. On the broad one, expect the page to favor what a large brand is good at: years of reviews, deep stock, and an advertising budget big enough to buy the top of the page.

That is the honest answer to whether marketplaces favor small brands. They favor the niche on niche searches. On the category’s main search terms, the advantages of scale return, and the small brand is back in the narrow strip of the aisle, only this time the strip is page three.

The marketplace has its own interests in the tail

A marketplace values the long tail because selection brings shoppers, and shoppers who find unusual things come back. It also has every reason to earn more from the tail once it is there.

Etsy showed how that works in 2018. In June it raised its transaction fee on each sale from 3.5% to 5%, applied for the first time to shipping charges too, effective July 16, and said the money would help fund more marketing to bring buyers to the site. For a seller of a $30 item with $3 shipping, the fee went from $1.05 to $1.65. The niche sellers got more traffic in exchange for a bigger cut, whether or not they wanted the trade, and some said publicly that they did not. A marketplace that depends on the tail can still decide what the tail pays.

Amazon’s version is quieter. Sponsored Products sell placements on search pages, specific searches included, so a small brand that wins a niche search organically may find a rival buying the slot above it. And Amazon now sells its own brands, with names like Mama Bear, Solimo and Wag, in everyday categories such as baby care, household staples and pet food. A store brand on a physical shelf competes for the eye-level spot. On a marketplace, the platform’s own brand competes for the search.

None of this closes the door the marketplace opened. The 300,000 new sellers of 2017 got a route to customers that did not exist a decade earlier, and for a company that size the alternative was waiting for a buyer’s yes. What the fees and the store brands do mean is that the door leads into a building with a landlord, and the landlord’s interests and the small brand’s interests overlap only some of the time.

What a small brand should do with this

A small brand gives itself the best chance in the tail by treating search terms the way a store brand treats shelf positions: as specific places to win and defend. A few questions are worth putting to the team before the 2019 plan:

  1. Which ten specific searches does our product answer better than anything else on the page, and do we appear on the first page for each of them now?
  2. How much of our advertising goes to broad category terms where we are outspent, and how much to the specific searches where we are the natural answer?
  3. If the marketplace launched its own version of our product, which of our searches would it reach first?
  4. What would our margin look like if our marketplace’s fees rose the way Etsy’s did in 2018?

A small brand that can answer the first question has a strategy. One that cannot is hoping the category’s biggest search will someday notice it. Mapping those specific searches and building a catalog and ad plan around them is a core part of running a marketplace channel.

P0163.crumb: Amazon search term report winners are…
P0163.title: Amazon search term report winners are often lucky; bid for it
P0163.alt: Two worn wooden dice resting on an old leather-bound book in a beam of sunlight against a navy wall.
P0163.ttag: Amazon search term report winners are often lucky; bid for it | Kwontified
P0163.desc: The best rows in an Amazon search term report usually convert worse once promoted. Price each new keyword on its clicks blended with the campaign average.
P0163.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 24, 2018.
P0163.body:
Anyone who runs automatic Sponsored Products campaigns knows the ritual. Download the search term report, sort by conversion rate, and pull the stars into a manual campaign with their own exact-match keywords and higher bids.

Then watch many of them disappoint. A phrase that converted at 33% in the report can settle near 12% once it has its own keyword. Nothing broke. The report’s best rows were chosen partly because they got lucky, and luck does not come along when a search is promoted.

What the Amazon search term report is for

The report is the closest thing a brand has to a transcript of its shoppers. Advertising on Amazon comes with the search terms people typed before they clicked, which one longtime seller argued was reason enough to run Sponsored Products at all. The terms show which words shoppers use for a product, which rivals they compare it with and which needs they bring.

The report also feeds the keyword plan. The standard practice, laid out in Practical Ecommerce’s guide to the program, is to give searches their own ad groups and bids and to block the weak ones with negative keywords. We covered when to block a search in March. This post is about the other half: how much to bid on the searches you promote.

Why the best rows fall back

A report with 400 search terms is 400 small experiments run at once. Many terms have only a few clicks. With samples that small, some ordinary searches will post extraordinary rates by chance, and the sort order puts exactly those at the top.

Take a product whose searches convert at 8% on average. A term with three clicks needs only one sale to show 33%. Across hundreds of terms with three clicks each, plenty will catch that one sale, and most of them are ordinary 8% searches having a good week. Pick the top of the list and you have selected for luck as much as for quality. Once those terms get their own keywords and more clicks, their rates drift back toward what they really are, which for most of them is much closer to 8% than to 33%.

It is the same reason a rookie hitting .500 after ten at-bats is not a .500 hitter. Nobody doubts he is good. The ten at-bats just cannot tell you how good.

The bias that makes this costly is the pull of the vivid number. A 33% conversion rate is easy to remember and easy to defend in a meeting, and it sits in the same column as a 20% rate earned over 120 clicks. The report gives both rows the same line.

How to price a promoted search term

The fix is to blend each term’s own record with the campaign’s average, weighting the term by how many clicks it has earned. A simple version treats the campaign average as if it were worth 20 clicks of evidence:

Blended conversion rate = (term’s sales + 20 × campaign average) ÷ (term’s clicks + 20)

Then price the bid from the blended rate: product price times target ACoS times conversion rate. Take a $40 product with a 25% ACoS target, so $10 of ad spend per sale, and a campaign average of 8%.

Search term recordRaw conversion rateBlended rateBid from raw rateBid from blended rate
1 sale from 3 clicks33.3%11.3%$3.33$1.13
6 sales from 30 clicks20.0%15.2%$2.00$1.52
24 sales from 120 clicks20.0%18.3%$2.00$1.83

The two 20% terms look identical in the report. The blend tells them apart: the one with 120 clicks has earned nearly its full rate, and the one with 30 clicks gets a more cautious bid until it proves itself. The three-click term still gets promoted, since it may be a real find, but at a bid that will not lose money if it turns out to be an ordinary search.

The weight of 20 is a judgment, not a law. A product whose search terms vary widely in quality can use a smaller weight so strong terms pull away from the average faster; a product with steady conversion across terms can use a larger one. What matters is that the weight is chosen before anyone looks at the winners.

The blend also tells you what would change your mind. A promoted term that keeps converting well above the average for another 50 or 100 clicks pulls its blended rate up on its own, and its bid follows. A term that was lucky drifts down as clicks arrive, at a cost capped by the cautious bid it started with.

Building the keyword plan from the report

The blend changes how the plan is built, not only the bids:

  • Promote terms in batches each month, priced on blended rates, and recompute the blend as clicks arrive. A promoted term that keeps converting earns its way to a higher bid.
  • Keep brand-name searches in their own campaign. Merkle’s third-quarter tracking found brand keywords accounted for 42% of Sponsored Products sales among its advertisers, and mixing them into the average would let one kind of search set the baseline for every other.
  • Read the promoted terms for language, not just numbers. A phrase shoppers use repeatedly belongs in the product title and bullets, where it helps every visit, paid or not.
  • Add each promoted term as a negative in the automatic campaign, so the two campaigns do not bid against each other for the same shopper.

The rule for the new year: never bid on a conversion rate the term has not earned. Blend it with the average, let clicks move it, and the report’s winners will cost what they are worth. That pricing is part of how we build Sponsored Products keyword plans for brands.
