P0165.title: European marketplaces reward brands that plan country by country
P0165.alt: Four orange-wrapped gift boxes in a row on a wooden table, each tied with a different ribbon or twine.
P0165.ttag: European marketplaces reward brands that plan country by country | Kwontified
P0165.desc: US brands often plan Europe as one Amazon account. Zalando’s growth and Allegro’s $3.25 billion sale show the shelf is national, and the plan should be too.
P0165.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 27, 2018.
P0165.body:
Ask a US brand where it sells in Europe and the answer often arrives as a single word: Amazon. On the planning slide, the continent becomes one row, managed from one account, with one forecast. The shoppers do not see it that way. A woman in Warsaw, a man in Berlin and a family in Lyon each shop in their own language, on sites their friends use, with their own ideas about how a parcel should arrive and how a return should work. European marketplaces are a set of national shelves, and the brands that do well there plan country by country.

Amazon is strong in Europe, in specific places

Amazon’s reach in Europe is real, and it is concentrated. In early 2018, Coresight Research, working from Amazon’s own reports, put Germany at just under 10% of Amazon’s net sales and the UK at about 6%, against roughly two-thirds for the US. Those are large businesses by any standard. They are also two countries.

That concentration is the first thing a brand’s European plan should reflect. A brand that sells well on Amazon.de has learned how to sell to German shoppers on Amazon. It has not learned how to reach a Polish shopper, and it may find that the marketplace Polish shoppers use first is not Amazon at all.

The national champions are not small

The clearest evidence that Europe’s shelves are national came from investors. In October 2016, Naspers agreed to sell Allegro, the Polish online marketplace often described as the country’s answer to eBay, to funds advised by Cinven, Permira and Mid Europa for about $3.25 billion. Allegro had more than 20 million registered users. Buyers do not pay that much for a regional curiosity. They pay it for a business that owns the habits of a country’s shoppers.

That is the value a national champion holds, and it is worth following. The champion owns the first search. It owns the payment methods local shoppers trust, the delivery points they expect and the language they read without thinking. A brand selling there is renting access to all of that, and the champion’s terms reflect what it owns.

Zalando is the other European model, and it shows how a marketplace can cross borders by specializing rather than by generalizing. It built a fashion platform country by country, and by the end of 2017 it reported €4.49 billion in revenue, up 23.4%, with 23.1 million active customers across its European markets. In fashion, the parts that do not travel are sizes, returns and the language of a product page, and a platform that crosses many borders has to handle each country’s version of them.

Zalando’s Partner Program lets brands sell their own stock on that shelf, which is why it belongs in a brand’s plan alongside Amazon rather than as an afterthought behind it.

Why brands still plan Europe as one market

The single row on the planning slide has a structure behind it. A US brand often reaches Europe through the team that already runs Amazon in the US, because that team knows the tools. The tools are Amazon’s. So the European plan inherits Amazon’s map of Europe, which is organized around the countries where Amazon is strongest.

Then there is the cost of doing it properly. Each country needs listings in its own language, sizing that matches local conventions in apparel and footwear, customer service that answers in the shopper’s language, and a decision about which marketplace leads. That is real work, and a brand’s international budget is often sized for one more channel, not for five more countries. The single row is cheaper to manage, and it is easy to mistake for a strategy.

The likely result is a brand that performs well in Germany and the UK, sees little elsewhere, and concludes that the rest of Europe has no demand for its products. The demand may well exist. It may simply live on a different shelf.

The decision a leadership team is actually making

In practice the European question reaches a leadership team as a choice between two kinds of growth. One is wider: take the Amazon business that works in Germany and the UK and list it on Amazon’s other European sites, where the tools and the team are already familiar. The other is deeper: pick one more country, find out which shelf its shoppers actually use, and build a local presence there, whether that shelf is Amazon, a specialist such as Zalando or a national champion.

Wider is faster and looks cheaper. Deeper is slower and costs more per country, but it is the only route to the shoppers who do not start on Amazon. A brand does not have to choose one forever. It does have to know which one each country in its plan is getting, and why.

The questions for a 2019 European plan

The useful conversation for a leadership team is not “should we expand in Europe?” but “which countries, on which shelves, in what order?” Four questions sort it out:

  1. In each country we sell to now, which marketplace do shoppers in our category open first, and are we on it?
  2. For our next country, is the leading shelf Amazon, a national champion, or a specialist such as Zalando, and what does each charge us to reach the same shopper?
  3. Do our listings, sizes and returns policy read as local to a shopper in that country, or as translated?
  4. Who on our team owns each country, rather than owning “Europe”?

A brand that can answer these has a plan. One that cannot is managing a row on a slide. Launching and running marketplaces such as Zalando, country by country and alongside local partners, is the work of our international marketplace practice, and we are glad to compare notes with partners who serve the same brands there.

P0167.title: Sponsored Products product targeting starts on your own pages
P0167.alt: Two corked amber bottles flanking a brass arrow ornament on a rustic wooden shelf against a terracotta wall.
P0167.ttag: Sponsored Products product targeting starts on your own pages | Kwontified
P0167.desc: Sponsored Products product targeting lets any brand buy space on your detail page, so the first targets to fund are often your own ASINs, not a rival’s.
P0167.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 2, 2019.
P0167.body:
A shopper who reaches your product page has already done the hard part. She searched, compared, clicked and is reading your bullets. Until late 2018, the ads she saw underneath were mostly bought through keywords or in display packages. Then Amazon added product targeting to Sponsored Products campaigns, letting advertisers aim a cost-per-click ad at a specific product or a whole category, ChannelX reported in November.

The obvious use is offense: put your product on a rival’s page. The more valuable use, for most brands, is defense. Sponsored Products product targeting turns every detail page into a small auction, including yours, and the shoppers on your page are the ones closest to buying.

Why attacking a rival’s page feels like the right first move

The case for offense is easy to make. A rival’s best seller gets steady traffic, and its shoppers have already shown they want the category. Bidding on that page reaches buyers at the bottom of the funnel without guessing at keywords.

That logic is sound as far as it goes.

It misses how a page-level auction converts. An ad on a detail page sells only when the shopper prefers the advertised offer to the one she is already reading. If your product costs the same, has fewer reviews and a lower star rating, the click is cheap and the sale rarely comes. Product Display Ads, Amazon’s older page-targeted format, worked the same way: a rival’s page paid off only for an advertiser with a better offer. Product targeting inside Sponsored Products makes the same auction easier to enter, not easier to win.

What a detail page is worth when someone else is bidding on it

Think of your best-selling page as a shelf you already own, with an empty slot under the product where someone else can rent a facing. Before product targeting, reaching that slot took a separate display product. Now any advertiser with a Sponsored Products account can bid for it by the click.

Take a product page with 20,000 visits a month that converts at 15%, so 3,000 orders. Suppose rival ads placed there pull away 2% of those visitors who would otherwise have bought from you: 400 visitors, or about 60 orders at your 15% conversion rate. At a $25 average order, that is $1,500 a month of sales leaving through the ad slot.

Now price the defense. If you place your own complementary or premium products in that slot at $0.50 a click and win 1,000 clicks a month, you spend $500. Those clicks come from shoppers already in your brand, so they convert well, and every slot you hold is a slot a rival does not. For many best sellers, the defensive budget costs less than the leak it stops.

Setting the bid follows the same logic as any Sponsored Products bid. The most you can pay for a click is the conversion rate on that page times the most you can pay for a sale. If a target page converts your ad’s clicks at 8% and your margin allows $8 of ad cost per sale, your ceiling is $0.64 a click. Defensive placements on your own pages usually convert better than that, because the shopper already chose your brand, so their ceiling is higher and their bids can be too.

The arithmetic flips for weak pages. A product with few visits and middling reviews is not worth defending; its shoppers are already leaving through search results. Defense pays on pages where traffic is high and the brand’s offer is strong.

Categories are a research tool, not a strategy

Product targeting also lets advertisers target whole categories and subcategories. That behaves like a broad match for pages: the ad can appear on thousands of detail pages, most of which the advertiser has never looked at. It is useful for finding which rival pages convert for you, in the same way automatic campaigns find which searches convert.

Treat category targets as a two-week experiment. Run them with a modest bid, pull the report of which products the ads appeared against, and move the pages that produced sales into their own ASIN targets with bids set from their conversion rates. Leave the category target running only at a low bid, as a scout that keeps finding new pages as rivals launch products and old ones fade.

What the data can tell you is narrow. The search term report for product targets shows the product the ad appeared on and whether it sold. It does not show how many of your own page’s visitors left through someone else’s ad. That loss has to be estimated by watching your page’s conversion rate when rivals start bidding on it, which is why the defensive case is easy to miss.

Rules for the first quarter of product targeting

  • Start with your own top 10 detail pages by traffic, and place your own related products on them before bidding on any rival page.
  • Bid on a rival’s page only where your offer beats theirs on at least one thing the shopper can see: price, rating or review count.
  • Run category targets for two weeks as research, then promote the converting pages to ASIN targets with their own bids.
  • Watch the conversion rate of your best pages month by month. A fall with no change in price, stock or reviews is the signature of someone else’s ad.

Product targeting is new enough that most brands are still deciding what it is for, which makes early 2019 a good time to set up the defensive layer we build into the Amazon advertising accounts we run.

P0168.title: Amazon brand protection starts with deciding who may sell
P0168.alt: Red velvet rope on brass stanchions beside a blank clipboard stand at the entrance of a sunlit market hall.
P0168.ttag: Amazon brand protection starts with deciding who may sell | Kwontified
P0168.desc: Apple cleared unauthorized sellers off Amazon with a commercial deal, not a lawsuit. Brands should run Amazon brand protection from the sales plan.
P0168.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 3, 2019.
P0168.body:
From tomorrow, an independent seller with a box of new iPhones has nowhere to list them on Amazon. Apple’s deal with Amazon, confirmed in November, limits sales of Apple products on the marketplace to Apple-authorized resellers, and listings from everyone else are due to come down after January 4, Resource Recycling reported. Sellers who want to stay were told to apply to Apple for authorization.

What is striking is where the result came from. Apple did not win control of its Amazon shelf through a court order or a stack of takedown notices. It won it at the negotiating table, in exchange for letting Amazon sell its products directly. For most brands, that is the lesson worth taking into 2019: Amazon brand protection is decided by who gets your product and on what terms, which makes it a job for the people who run distribution, with legal as the backstop.

What Apple traded for a cleaner shelf

The terms, as reported, are commercial ones. Amazon will sell a wider range of Apple devices, including the latest models, and only Apple-authorized resellers will be able to sell them on the marketplace, TechCrunch reported on November 9, citing the original CNET report. The arrangement covers the US, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Japan and India. “We look forward to expanding our assortment of Apple and Beats products globally,” an Amazon spokesperson said.

Follow the value and the logic is plain. Amazon gets to sell Apple’s current devices itself, a range it previously left to marketplace sellers or did not carry at all. Apple gets a short, known list of sellers on every Apple listing, and with it control over price, condition and presentation. The independent resellers, who had been filling a gap Apple left open, absorb the cost.

Few brands carry Apple’s bargaining power, and no one should expect Amazon to strike the same deal for a mid-sized skincare or footwear line. The shape of the deal still applies. Apple solved a marketplace problem by changing the inputs: who is allowed to sell, and what Amazon itself carries. Those are decisions every brand already makes, usually in a sales meeting, often without anyone thinking about Amazon at all.

Counterfeits are where open distribution shows up

The case for treating this as a legal matter is easy to understand, because the most visible damage looks like fraud. When the Government Accountability Office bought 47 items from third-party sellers on five popular e-commerce sites, including Amazon, it found that 20 were counterfeit, a report published in February 2018. Fakes call for trademark law, and trademark law lives with counsel.

Amazon’s own tools reinforce that framing. The relaunched Brand Registry gives trademark owners text and image search to find listings that use their marks, and builds predictive protections from the infringements a brand reports, according to a client alert from the time. Registration also gives the brand owner more control over the content on its product pages, as Practical Ecommerce explained. Every one of those tools starts from a registered trademark and ends in a report, which is why the work so often lands on the desk of whoever handles trademarks.

The trouble is that a takedown only deals with the listing in front of you. Counterfeits are one part of the problem. The larger part, for many established brands, is genuine product sold by sellers the brand never chose: stock bought from a distributor, a liquidator or a retailer’s clearance, listed on Amazon below the brand’s own price. No trademark claim removes a genuine product sold legitimately, so the legal route stalls exactly where the commercial damage is greatest.

Every one of those sellers got its inventory from somewhere. That is why the fix sits upstream, in the decisions the sales team owns: which distributors receive product, what their agreements say about online resale, how much stock goes to off-price channels and when, and whether the brand sells to Amazon directly so that a reliable offer holds the listing.

The decision in the room for 2019

Inside most brands, those levers are split across teams that rarely meet. Sales sets distributor terms and chases volume targets. Finance approves the year-end clearance that moves aging stock. The e-commerce team sees the result on a product page, often weeks later. Counsel is asked to clean it up. Nobody owns the whole chain, so each team optimizes its own piece and the marketplace inherits the gaps.

The leadership question for 2019 is less about whether to enroll in Brand Registry (any brand with a registered trademark should) and more about who owns the shelf. A brand that hands Amazon brand protection to its commercial lead, with a mandate that covers distributor agreements, allocations and the Amazon relationship itself, can cut off unauthorized supply before it becomes a listing. A brand that leaves it with legal will keep filing reports against a stream it cannot see the source of.

Apple will not be the last brand to use distribution as a lever. The evidence so far leans toward marketplaces rewarding brands that can show them a clean, reliable supply, because a clean shelf is better for the retailer’s customers too.

Questions to put to the team in January

  1. How many sellers offered our top 20 products on Amazon in December, and how many of them do we recognize as authorized?
  2. For each unrecognized seller, which distributor, retailer or clearance buyer is the likely source of their stock?
  3. What do our distributor and wholesale agreements say about online marketplace resale, and who enforces it?
  4. Who in the company is accountable for the Amazon listing as a whole, from supply to content to price?

Owning that chain day to day, so that brand teams can focus on the brand, is the kind of channel management work we take on for brands on Amazon.

P0172.crumb: Shoppers trust the Amazon Prime badge…
P0172.title: Shoppers trust the Amazon Prime badge because Amazon keeps the promise
P0172.alt: A cardboard parcel and a brass alarm clock on a stone doorstep outside a blue house at dusk.
P0172.ttag: Shoppers trust the Amazon Prime badge because Amazon keeps the promise | Kwontified
P0172.desc: Shoppers arrive on Amazon loyal to a brand and buy whichever offer carries the Prime badge, because the badge is Amazon’s promise, not the brand’s.
P0172.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 10, 2019.
P0172.body:
Most online shoppers know what they want before they start. In an NPR/Marist poll last June, 73% of online shoppers said they set out looking for a particular brand. The same poll found that 44% go to Amazon first when they buy online, against 33% who start with a search engine, according to the poll’s summary. So picture the shopper who already knows the serum she wants, types its name into Amazon, and finds three offers for it. She buys the one with the Prime badge.

She came for the brand and chose by the badge. That is less of a contradiction than it looks. She trusts the brand to make the product and trusts Amazon to get it to her, take it back and sort out any problem. The Amazon Prime badge is a bundle of operational promises, and the shopper trusts it more than the brand because Amazon, not the brand, stands behind every one of them.

The shopper splits her trust in two

The scale of that habit is large. Amazon said in April 2018 that it had passed 100 million paid Prime members worldwide, TechCrunch reported, the first time it had disclosed the figure. In the Marist poll, 44% of Americans said they use Prime, either through their own membership or a shared one, and among online shoppers the share was 64%.

Trust in the retailer goes beyond delivery. Two-thirds of online shoppers, 67%, told Marist they had a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in Amazon to protect their personal information, while 52% had little or no confidence in most online retailers to do the same.

Put those together and the shape is clear. Shoppers bring brand preference to Amazon and leave the transaction, and much of the research, to the retailer. On a brand’s own website, a shopper has to read the shipping terms, guess at the returns process and decide whether to hand over a card number. On Amazon, the badge answers those questions before she asks them.

What the badge actually guarantees

The badge is trusted because it is enforced. For years, products carried Prime only if they sat in Amazon’s warehouses under Fulfillment by Amazon. Sellers who ship their own orders can now earn the badge through Seller Fulfilled Prime, and the terms show what Amazon is protecting. A seller must ship more than 99% of orders on time, keep cancellations under 1%, use Amazon’s supported carriers, accept Amazon’s returns policy and let Amazon handle all customer service enquiries, ChannelX set out in February 2018. Entry requires a trial of 50 Prime orders delivered 100% on time, or 100 orders at 99%.

Read that list as an institution’s priorities. Amazon allows a third party to carry its badge only if the shopper cannot tell the difference: same speed, same returns, same voice on the phone. The badge works because Amazon will take it away from anyone who breaks the promise.

Where the decision sits inside the brand

Inside most brands, Prime eligibility is not discussed as a brand question at all. Whether a product goes into FBA, ships from the brand’s own warehouse or is left to resellers is usually settled by operations and finance, on fulfillment fees and storage costs. Customer service sits in another department again. Each choice is sensible on its own terms, and together they decide whether the shopper who searched for the brand by name sees it with the one symbol she trusts.

Picture the review where this gets decided. The operations lead shows that shipping a bulky gift set from the brand’s own warehouse costs less per unit than FBA, and the decision is made on that slide. Nobody in the room asks what happens to the shopper who searches the brand’s name in December and sees the gift set without the badge, next to a reseller’s offer with it. The saving is real and easy to count. The lost preference never appears in a report, because a sale that goes to the reseller still shows up somewhere as units of the brand’s product sold.

When a brand’s own offer lacks the badge and a reseller’s offer has it, the brand has handed its most loyal shopper to someone else at the last step. When the brand’s top product is out of stock at Amazon’s warehouses for a week, the badge disappears and so does much of the preference the brand spent years building. Fulfillment has become part of the brand, and the people who run it are now, in effect, brand managers.

The larger shift for 2019 is that retailers are turning operational reliability into a brand of its own, one that shoppers rank alongside, and sometimes above, the names on the products. The evidence so far leans toward that trust growing as delivery gets faster.

Questions for the planning meeting

  1. Which of our 20 best-selling products on Amazon carried the Prime badge on our own offer every day in December, and which did not?
  2. Who decides whether a product is fulfilled by Amazon, by us or by resellers, and is brand preference part of that decision?
  3. When the badge drops off a top product because of a stock-out, who finds out, and how quickly?
  4. Do our own website’s delivery and returns terms give a shopper the same confidence the badge does, and if not, what would it cost to match them?

Keeping the badge on the right products every day is part of the day-to-day channel management we run for brands on Amazon.

P0174.title: Amazon advertising portfolios cap the budget, not who spends it
P0174.alt: A glass jar of coins with striped paper straws through its lid, beside a small plant on a wooden console.
P0174.ttag: Amazon advertising portfolios cap the budget, not who spends it | Kwontified
P0174.desc: Amazon’s new portfolio budget caps stop total spend but do not pace it, so the fastest-spending campaign decides where a product line’s ad money goes.
P0174.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 15, 2019.
P0174.body:
Amazon began rolling out portfolios for Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands in December, and on paper they give advertisers what finance teams have wanted for years: one budget for a group of campaigns, with an optional end date, CPC Strategy explained on December 12. Amazon formally introduced the feature on December 18, describing portfolios as a way to organize campaigns to mirror how a business is structured, according to its announcement. Set a quarterly ad budget for a product line, put its campaigns in a portfolio, and spending stops at the number.

That is true, and it is the trap. A portfolio cap stops total spend. It does not decide which campaign gets the money. The portfolio budget “does not pace advertising spend over any period of time,” in CPC Strategy’s summary, so one campaign can use up the whole budget, and when the cap is reached every campaign in the portfolio pauses, including those that had not spent their own budgets. The campaign that spends fastest decides where Amazon advertising portfolios send your money.

Why a portfolio looks like a P&L

The appeal of a single cap is real. Most brands set Amazon advertising budgets the way they set any other: a number per product line per quarter, agreed with finance. Before portfolios, that number lived in a spreadsheet, and someone had to add up dozens of daily campaign budgets and watch them by hand. A single cap per line, with an end date, maps the console onto the plan.

It also works as a safety rail. If a bid change or a seasonal spike sends spend up, the cap holds. For a finance lead who has seen an account overspend in December, that alone is worth the setup time.

A cap without pacing rewards the fastest spender

The problem is what happens inside the cap. Campaigns do not spend at the same speed. A broad automatic campaign, a generic keyword campaign or a high-traffic category target can win thousands of impressions an hour. An exact-match campaign on your brand’s own product names sees far fewer searches. Put them in one portfolio and the broad campaign reaches the money first.

Take a skincare line with $200,000 of expected Amazon sales from January 15 to March 31 and a 30% margin before advertising. Finance agrees to spend 12% of sales on ads, a total ACoS (ad spend divided by all Amazon sales, organic included) that leaves 18% of sales as profit. That is a $24,000 portfolio cap.

Two campaigns share it. A branded exact-match campaign returns $6 in attributed sales for every $1 spent. A broad discovery campaign returns $2. At a return of $2, each $1 of ad spend buys $2 of sales carrying $0.60 of margin, so the discovery campaign loses $0.40 of margin for every dollar it spends, before counting any repeat purchase it may earn later.

Now let them run. The discovery campaign wins more auctions and spends three times as fast. By the first of March it has spent $18,000 and the branded campaign $6,000. The cap is hit, both pause, and for all of March the line has no advertising at all, including on the searches that paid best. The portfolio did exactly what it promised: it held spending at $24,000. It also let the least profitable campaign take three quarters of the money.

The trade-off is not imaginary. Discovery campaigns find new customers and new search terms, and a brand that only funds branded campaigns will see its account shrink to the shoppers it already has. The question is whether discovery should compete with the campaigns that protect your margin for the same dollars. On these numbers, it should not.

Run each portfolio like a line in the P&L

A P&L line has an owner, a budget and a return it is expected to make. Build portfolios the same way.

Group campaigns that should compete for the same money, and split those that should not. In the skincare example, two portfolios fix the problem: a core portfolio of branded and proven exact-match campaigns with a $15,000 cap, and a test portfolio of discovery and category campaigns with $9,000. The test portfolio can still run out early, but now it stops itself rather than its neighbors.

Set each cap from margin, not habit. The cap for a line is the sales you expect times the total ACoS you can afford, and the total ACoS you can afford is the margin before advertising minus the profit you want to keep. When the forecast or the margin changes, the cap changes.

Keep daily campaign budgets doing the pacing. The cap is a ceiling for the period, and CPC Strategy noted Amazon’s advice to set campaign budgets high with the target at portfolio level. That is the right default for a core portfolio. For a test portfolio, a modest daily budget on each campaign is what stops one of them from taking the period’s money in a week.

Check spend against the calendar every week. The figure that matters is the share of the cap spent against the share of the period gone. Halfway through the quarter with 75% of the cap spent is a warning; cut bids on the fastest spender before the cap does it for you.

What the reports will and will not show

Portfolio reporting adds up spend and attributed sales for the group. It will tell you that a portfolio hit its cap; it will not tell you which campaign crowded out which. For that, compare each campaign’s daily spend over the period with its return, and look for the pattern in the example: the low-return campaign front-loaded, the high-return one starved.

The deeper limit is the same as for any Amazon ad report. Attributed sales are sales that followed a click, not sales the ad caused, so the $6 branded return overstates what those campaigns add. That argues for keeping branded spend modest. It does not rescue a discovery campaign that loses margin on every attributed sale.

The rule to apply this week: no portfolio should contain campaigns whose returns differ by more than double, unless you have set daily budgets that stop the fast one from taking the slow one’s money. Setting those caps from margin, line by line, is the kind of budget work we do on Amazon advertising accounts.

P0170.crumb: Amazon dynamic bidding up and down…
P0170.title: Amazon dynamic bidding up and down overpays on your own brand’s searches
P0170.alt: A glass jar overflowing with coins, with more coins spilled across a wooden windowsill shelf.
P0170.ttag: Amazon dynamic bidding up and down overpays on your own brand’s searches | Kwontified
P0170.desc: Amazon’s up-and-down bidding raises bids where a sale is most likely, which on branded searches means paying more for shoppers who were already buying.
P0170.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 16, 2019.
P0170.body:
Amazon gave Sponsored Products advertisers three bidding strategies on January 9: fixed bids, and two dynamic options that adjust bids in real time based on how likely a click is to convert, according to Amazon’s announcement. “Dynamic bids, down only” lowers your bid when a sale looks unlikely. “Dynamic bids, up and down” also raises it when a sale looks likely, by as much as 100%, Marketing Land reported. The same release lets advertisers add bid adjustments of zero to 900% for top-of-search and product page placements.

The obvious move is to switch the best campaigns to up and down. More money behind the clicks most likely to sell sounds like exactly what a bid should do. On many accounts it will be right for discovery terms and wrong for the account’s most important ones. Amazon dynamic bidding raises bids where Amazon predicts a purchase, and the searches where a purchase is most predictable are often the ones where the shopper would have bought from you without the ad.

Why paying more for likely buyers sounds right

The case for up and down rests on sound arithmetic. A click is worth the product’s price, times the share of price you can spend on advertising, times the chance the click turns into a sale. If Amazon knows that one shopper is twice as likely to buy as the average, that click is worth twice as much, and a bid that doubles for it keeps your advertising cost of sale (ACoS) where you set it.

Take a $30 product with a 25% ACoS target, so you can spend $7.50 to win a sale. The campaign converts 10% of clicks on average, so you bid $0.75. When Amazon predicts a 20% chance of purchase, up and down can lift that bid toward $1.50. A $1.50 click that converts at 20% costs $7.50 per sale. Same ACoS, more sales. Down only, meanwhile, trims the bid on clicks Amazon rates at 4% to something closer to $0.30 and saves the money you would have wasted.

On paper, the two strategies differ only in how much of that logic Amazon applies. Up and down applies all of it.

Where the prediction and the payoff split

The flaw is in what “likely to convert” measures. Amazon’s model predicts whether a shopper will buy your product after clicking your ad. It does not predict whether the shopper would have bought it anyway. Those are different questions, and on some searches they have nearly the same answer.

The clearest case is your own brand name. A shopper who types your brand and product into Amazon converts at a high rate, and Amazon’s model knows it, so up and down raises your bid on precisely those searches. But your organic listing usually sits a few pixels below the ad. Many of those shoppers would have scrolled and bought.

Go back to the $30 product. On a branded search, say the ad converts at 20% and up and down bids $1.50. If half of those buyers would have found your organic listing without the ad, the ad caused a sale on only 10% of clicks. The console still reports $7.50 per sale. The cost of each sale the ad actually added is $1.50 divided by 0.10, or $15, which is 50% of the price. You doubled your real ACoS while the report held steady.

Searches where you already rank first organically behave the same way, in milder form. The stronger your organic position, the more of the predicted conversion was yours already, and the more an upward bid pays for sales you owned.

On generic searches where your product sits on page three, the logic reverses. Shoppers searching “vitamin c serum” are not on their way to your listing; if the ad does not win, a competitor’s product does. There, a predicted 20% conversion is mostly sales the ad creates, and paying more for it is the right trade. Up and down earns its keep exactly where your organic shelf is weak.

Placement adjustments deserve the same caution. A 900% ceiling is a range, not a recommendation. Top-of-search placements on your own brand’s searches are where the overlap between paid and organic is greatest, so a large adjustment there buys mostly visibility you already had.

How to read your own results

The console will not settle this for you. Sponsored Products reporting credits the ad with every sale that follows a click, whether or not the shopper would have bought anyway. A falling ACoS after you switch strategies tells you the clicks got cheaper or converted better; it does not tell you whether they added sales.

The test that does is a comparison of total sales. Split comparable products, or comparable weeks, between the two strategies and watch total units for each product, ad-attributed and organic together. If up and down lifts attributed sales but total sales barely move, the extra spend bought credit, not customers. Give the test at least two weeks on each side; one week of January data is mostly noise.

What would change my mind is a test where up and down on branded terms raises total sales by more than the extra spend. That can happen when competitors bid aggressively on your brand name and the ad is defending a sale you would otherwise lose. Watch who else appears on your branded results before assuming the sale was yours.

A starting rule for each campaign

Set branded campaigns, and any search where you already rank on the first page organically, to down only. Use up and down on generic and competitor terms where your organic rank is weak, with a placement adjustment no higher than your margin can carry. Keep fixed bids for the campaigns you are actively testing, so Amazon’s adjustments do not blur the result.

Separating branded from generic campaigns is the first thing to check, because a single campaign that mixes them cannot be set correctly either way. That separation, and the bid tests that follow it, are a large part of the Sponsored Products work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0175.title: NRF 2019 showed stores becoming warehouses and media channels
P0175.alt: Stacked shipping boxes in the aisle of a bright bookshop with wooden shelves of books, ceramics and plants.
P0175.ttag: NRF 2019 showed stores becoming warehouses and media channels | Kwontified
P0175.desc: At NRF 2019, Target and Kroger described the store as a fulfillment hub and a data asset. Both change what retailers will ask brands for this year.
P0175.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 17, 2019.
P0175.body:
The most telling line at NRF 2019 was not about technology at all. Target’s chief executive, Brian Cornell, told the show that three of every four Target digital orders are fulfilled by a store, and called stores “our single biggest competitive advantage,” Digiday reported. On the show’s final day, Kroger released its chairman Rodney McMullen’s five predictions for the future of retail. The fifth read: “Retail will disrupt the ad industry,” according to Kroger’s release.

Put those two statements side by side and the signal from Retail’s Big Show is clearer than anything on the exhibition floor. The largest store chains have stopped defending the store as a place to shop and started treating it as two businesses: a fulfillment network for online orders, and a source of shopper data they can sell to brands as advertising. Both change what those retailers will ask of brands in 2019.

The store as a warehouse

Target had the numbers to back its chief executive’s line. In November and December, its comparable sales rose 5.7% and its digital sales grew 29%, and store pickup and drive-up orders rose about 60%, accounting for roughly a quarter of digital sales, the Associated Press reported from the company’s holiday update. In its statement, Cornell credited “placing our stores at the center of every way we serve our guests.”

The holiday also showed what happens to retailers without that model. Macy’s cut its full-year forecast on January 10 after a weak finish to the season, Bloomberg reported, the day after Target reported its holiday sales.

Read Target as an institution and the incentive is plain. A store that ships and hands over online orders turns its rent, staff and stockroom into a delivery network a pure online seller would have to build. Every order that leaves from a store instead of a distribution center lets the store earn twice from the same rent and staff.

For brands, the consequence is practical and easy to miss. If three of four digital orders at Target come from a store, then a brand’s online availability at Target depends on its store-level stock. A product that is on Target.com but thin on the shelf in a given market is, for that shopper, out of stock online too. The store allocation plan, once a sales and supply chain matter, is now part of the digital plan.

The store as a media channel

Kroger’s prediction was the sharper statement of intent. Advertisers spend about $100 billion a year, the release noted, and Kroger argues that retailers can make that spending work better by using what they know about customers’ behavior. Its vehicle is Kroger Precision Marketing, powered by its data unit 84.51°, which the company says can reach more than 60 million customers.

Follow the value. A grocer earns thin margins on the cereal it sells. The same grocer knows which households bought which cereal, how often and with what else, and that knowledge is worth a great deal to the company that makes the cereal. Selling advertising against it turns a by-product of running stores into a high-margin business, and it gives the retailer a second reason to want a brand’s money.

Kroger is not alone. Walmart has sold advertising through Walmart Exchange since 2014, Digiday reported in 2017, and Amazon’s own advertising-heavy “other” revenue grew 122% to $2.5 billion in the third quarter of 2018, as the Motley Fool noted. What NRF added is that a traditional grocer’s chief executive now says it out loud, from the main stage of the industry’s largest show, as one of five things that define retail’s future.

What it means for the year

The two signals meet in the same place: the brand’s account team at each retailer. A brand selling to Target and Kroger in 2019 should expect conversations that used to happen separately to arrive together. The retailer wants inventory placed where it can fulfill online orders, and it wants a share of the marketing budget spent on its own media.

Inside most brands, those requests land with different people. Store allocation and trade terms sit with sales and supply chain; media budgets sit with marketing. The retailers are organizing around the store as one asset with two revenue streams, and brands that keep the two conversations apart will negotiate each one without seeing the whole deal.

Picture how that reaches a mid-sized beauty brand. The retailer’s buyer asks for deeper store inventory on twenty items so that pickup orders can be filled locally, which ties up more working capital in stores. A month later the retailer’s media team proposes a campaign on its own site and channels. The first request goes to sales, the second to the brand manager, and nobody adds up what the retailer is asking for in total, or what the brand gets back.

It is too early to say how large retailer media will become outside Amazon, and Kroger’s release is a prediction, not a result. The evidence from New York leans toward the direction being settled, with the pace still open.

Questions to take back from New York

  1. For each of our top retailers, what share of their online orders do stores fulfill, and do our store allocations reflect it?
  2. Which retailers offered us their own advertising in 2018, and who in our company answered?
  3. When a retailer asks for media spend alongside trade terms, who has the authority to weigh one against the other?
  4. Are we measuring retailer media on sales it added, or on sales it was near?

Keeping store availability, online listings and retailer advertising in one plan is the kind of Walmart and Target channel work we take on for brands.

P0179.crumb: Retail media splits each retailer into a…
P0179.title: Retail media splits each retailer into a merchant and a publisher
P0179.alt: A stationery shop with a wooden table of notebooks and an antique letterpress machine against a teal wall.
P0179.ttag: Retail media splits each retailer into a merchant and a publisher | Kwontified
P0179.desc: Retailers now sell brands attention through separate media units with their own targets, so every retail account has a merchant and a publisher behind it.
P0179.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 24, 2019.
P0179.body:
A brand’s account manager at a large grocer used to have one counterpart: the category buyer. In 2019 there are two. The buyer still decides what goes on the shelf and at what cost. Down the hall, or in a separate company the retailer owns, a media team wants to talk about the brand’s marketing budget. Kroger’s chairman, Rodney McMullen, put the intent plainly at NRF last week. His fifth prediction for the future of retail: “Retail will disrupt the ad industry,” according to Kroger’s release.

Retail media, the business of selling advertising against a retailer’s shoppers and data, has quietly split each large retailer into two institutions with different goals. The merchant wants your best cost and your best products. The publisher wants your media budget. Brands that treat them as one relationship will misread both.

How the second desk was built

The publisher side did not appear overnight. Kroger’s data unit, 84.51°, was formed in 2015 when Kroger bought out dunnhumbyUSA, its marketing partnership with Tesco, and in October 2017 it launched Kroger Precision Marketing to sell brands campaigns built on purchase data from 60 million households across 2,800 stores, Daily Research News reported. The offer covers ads on Kroger.com and co-branded digital media across the open web, with measurement that connects exposure to household-level sales.

Walmart has sold advertising through Walmart Exchange since 2014, including banners, search ads and sponsored products on Walmart.com, and it buys ad inventory on outside platforms such as YouTube and CBS Interactive to resell to advertisers, Digiday reported in 2017. Target presented its own media business, Target Media Network, to the industry in December 2017. Amazon’s advertising, reported inside its “other” revenue line, reached $2.5 billion in the third quarter of 2018, up 122%, as the Motley Fool reported.

Notice the structure these share. The media business has its own name, its own sales team and, in Kroger’s case, its own company. It sells inventory the merchant never controlled, such as off-site display on the open web. And it is judged on what it sells, which is advertising.

Two desks, two scorecards

Read each desk by what it is rewarded for. The category buyer is measured on the category’s sales and margin. That buyer wants the brand’s products in stock, priced to sell and supported by promotions that move units. A dollar of brand money matters to the buyer insofar as it lowers cost or lifts the category.

The media team is measured on advertising revenue. It wants the brand’s marketing budget, and it can sell the same placement to a competitor. Its strongest card is measurement: Kroger’s offer promises to link ads to actual purchases, and Walmart pitches the combination of online behavior and in-store sales data, something a television network or a social platform cannot offer.

Those incentives overlap, but they are not the same. A buyer might trade a brand’s promotional money for better shelf space; the media team would rather the same money arrive as a campaign. The publisher also reports the results of the media it sold, using data only it can see. Kroger and 84.51° said their pilots showed better marketing efficiency than other strategies, and that claim came, necessarily, from the companies themselves.

Take a snack brand planning a spring launch at a grocer. The buyer asks for an introductory allowance and a temporary price reduction to earn the new items a place on the shelf. The media team proposes a campaign aimed at households that bought the category in the past six months, on the grocer’s site and across the web, with a sales report at the end. Both requests are reasonable, and both draw on the same launch budget. The report that judges the campaign will come from the company that asked for the money, with no outside view of whether the shoppers it counts would have found the new items on the shelf anyway.

The decision the leadership team faces

For a brand, the question in the room is no longer whether to work with retailer media. It is which budget pays for it and who decides. If the money comes from trade spending, the sales team will want it to buy shelf and promotion outcomes. If it comes from the marketing budget, the brand team will want reach and new customers, and will compare it with every other media buy.

The answer most brands are drifting into, letting each request land wherever it arrives, gives the retailer the stronger hand. The buyer and the media team know what each other is asking for. The brand’s sales lead and its media lead often do not.

There is real value on the publisher’s side of the table. A retailer that can show which households bought after seeing an ad offers something brands have wanted for decades. The evidence so far leans toward retailer media becoming a standing line in brand budgets. What remains open is whether brands will buy it on the retailer’s measurement alone, or insist on checking it.

Questions to settle before the next joint business plan

  1. Which of our retail partners now has a separate media team, and who on our side is its counterpart?
  2. When retailer media is proposed, does the money come from trade, from marketing, or from neither by default?
  3. What would we need to see, beyond the retailer’s own report, to believe a campaign added sales?
  4. Does our account plan with each retailer show trade and media requests side by side?

Bringing those two conversations into one plan for each retailer is part of the Walmart and Target channel work we do with brands.

P0180.title: Amazon’s 2019 fee changes move every product’s advertising ceiling
P0180.alt: A giant column of stacked coins propping up a wooden roof beam in an empty green attic room.
P0180.ttag: Amazon’s 2019 fee changes move every product’s advertising ceiling | Kwontified
P0180.desc: Amazon’s February 19 fee changes shift margin product by product, and every point of margin they move changes how much you can afford to bid.
P0180.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 29, 2019.
P0180.body:
Three weeks from today, on February 19, Amazon’s 2019 fee changes take effect. Referral fees fall on low-priced beauty, health, baby and grocery items, the minimum referral fee drops from $1.00 to $0.30 in most categories, and Fulfillment by Amazon fees rise for most products over 10 ounces, ChannelX reported from Amazon’s December 19 notice. Storage changes start on February 15.

Most brands will see the new fees for the first time on a settlement report in March. By then the advertising has already been bought at February’s prices. The cost of a fee change is not only the fee: every cent of fee that moves also moves the most you can afford to pay for a sale through advertising, because both come out of the same unit margin.

What changes on February 15 and 19

The referral fee for Beauty, Health & Personal Care and Baby (excluding baby apparel) falls from 15% to 8% on items with a total sales price of $10 or less, and Grocery & Gourmet pays 8% on items at $15 or less. Furniture pays 10% instead of 15% on the part of the price above $200, and Jewelry pays 5% instead of 20% on the part above $250, according to Jungle Scout’s summary of the notice. The minimum fee falls to $0.30 across 30 categories, and from $2.00 to $0.30 for jewelry and watches.

Fulfillment fees do not change for small and large standard-size items with a shipping weight of 10 ounces or less; other size tiers see increases, and dangerous goods with aerosols or lithium-ion batteries get their own fees. Amazon said it expects more than 40% of FBA units shipped to see no change or a decrease.

Storage moves in the other direction. From February 15, long-term storage fees no longer apply to units stored 181 to 365 days, and the minimum long-term fee on units held more than a year falls from $0.50 to $0.15.

Why the fee and the bid are the same decision

Start with the number every ad manager should have for each product: the break-even advertising cost of sale (ACoS). It is the share of the price left after product cost and Amazon’s fees. Spend more than that on advertising per sale, and the sale loses money.

Take a $9 facial cleanser that costs $3.00 to make, with a fulfillment fee of $2.50. Today its referral fee is 15%, or $1.35, which leaves $2.15, so its break-even ACoS is about 24%. From February 19 the referral fee is 8%, or $0.72, which leaves $2.78. The break-even ACoS rises to about 31%. Nothing about the product or the shopper changed, and the brand can now bid about 30% more per sale and still break even.

The minimum fee works the same way at the bottom of the catalog. A $4 accessory in a 15% category paid the $1.00 minimum, a quarter of its price. From February 19 it pays 15%, or $0.60. The 40 cents go straight to margin, and a product that could not carry any advertising may now carry some.

Fulfillment increases run the arithmetic backward. On a $25 product, every 10 cents of extra FBA fee takes 0.4 points off its break-even ACoS. That is small for one product and large across a catalog of products just over 10 ounces, which is where the increases begin.

The model has a limit worth stating. It assumes price and conversion rate stay where they are. If competitors in the same low-price beauty categories use their lower fees to cut prices, the extra margin may go to the shopper rather than to your ads. Treat the new ceiling as the most you could spend, and watch competing prices on your top search terms for the first two weeks after February 19 before bidding all the way to it.

The pull here is to treat the fee schedule as finance’s problem and the bids as marketing’s, and to update each when its own report arrives. That ordering guarantees about a month of bidding to the wrong ceiling, in both directions: overspending on products whose fees went up, and leaving sales on the table for products whose fees went down.

A timeline back from February 19

Now to February 1

Pull every active product’s price, product cost, size tier and current fees. Recalculate referral and FBA fees on the February 19 schedule from Amazon’s fee pages, not from estimates.

February 1 to 8

Recompute break-even ACoS for each product, then the target ACoS after the profit you want to keep. List the products whose ceiling moves by more than two points either way.

February 8 to 15

Prepare bid changes for those products, raise targets on beauty, health, baby and grocery items under the price thresholds, and lower them on products over 10 ounces whose fulfillment cost rises. Review long-term storage: with the 181-to-365-day fee gone, slower sellers are cheaper to hold, which changes how hard you need to advertise them to clear stock.

February 19

Apply the new targets on the day the fees change, and check the first week of settlements against the model.

One pricing question deserves its own line. Items priced just above $10 in the beauty, health and baby categories pay 15% on the whole price, and those at $10 or below pay 8%. A product at $10.49 pays about $1.57; at $9.99 it pays about $0.80. The 50-cent price cut costs less than the fee it saves.

The rule

Recompute break-even ACoS whenever a fee changes, and change bids on the date the fee changes, not on the date the invoice arrives. Building that fee model into every product’s bid targets is part of the Amazon advertising work we do for brands.

P0177.title: Sponsored Products benchmark, Q4 2018: spend growth slowed to 15%
P0177.alt: A wooden spinning top tilted mid-spin on a sunlit table against a soft green wall.
P0177.ttag: Sponsored Products benchmark, Q4 2018: spend growth slowed to 15% | Kwontified
P0177.desc: Public Q4 2018 data shows Sponsored Products spend growth slowing to 15% from 62% in Q3, and says nothing about CPC or ROAS. Here is how to benchmark your own.
P0177.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 30, 2019.
P0177.body:
Advertisers in Merkle’s client base increased their Sponsored Products spending by 15% in the fourth quarter of 2018 from a year earlier, down from 62% growth in the third quarter, according to Merkle’s Q4 report released on January 29. Sponsored Brands spending rose 26%, down from 86%. Read quickly, that looks like advertisers pulling back from Amazon in its biggest quarter.

It is mostly arithmetic. Q4 2017 was itself a huge quarter, so growth measured against it was always going to shrink. And the public data says almost nothing about the numbers brands actually manage: no public benchmark released by the end of January gives Amazon cost per click, conversion rate or return on ad spend for the quarter. The useful Sponsored Products benchmark for Q4 2018 is your own spend and sales growth, set against the market’s.

The public numbers for Q4 2018

MeasureQ4 2018ComparisonSource
Sponsored Products spend growth, year over year+15%+62% in Q3 2018Merkle
Sponsored Brands spend growth, year over year+26%+86% in Q3 2018Merkle
Share of Amazon orders generated by ads, Thanksgiving weekend25.1%16.3% in 2017Quartile sample
US online retail sales growth, Nov 1 to Dec 24+19.1%+5.1% for all retailMastercard SpendingPulse
Paid search cost per click, year over year (all search engines)-13%+2% from Q3Kenshoo
Amazon CPC, conversion rate, ROASnot published

The Q3 comparisons come from Merkle’s Q3 report as summarized by ChannelX in October. The Thanksgiving figure is from Quartile’s study of more than a million orders across 108 brands, Marketing Dive reported. Holiday sales growth is from Mastercard SpendingPulse. The search figures are from Kenshoo’s Q4 report, released January 24, and describe search engines, not Amazon.

Why 15% is not a retreat

Year-over-year growth from a fixed set of advertisers depends as much on the prior year as on the current one. Merkle reported that Sponsored Products investment in Q4 2017 rose 64% from Q3 2017, Digital Commerce 360 noted a year ago. A quarter that large becomes the base for the following year’s comparison.

Take an advertiser who spent $100,000 on Sponsored Products in Q3 2017 and $164,000 in Q4 2017, the 64% seasonal jump. Say spending in Q3 2018 grew 62% to $162,000, and Q4 2018 came in at $189,000. That is a 17% rise from Q3 to Q4 2018 and 15% from a year earlier. Same advertiser, still spending more, still leaning into the holiday; the headline growth rate fell by three quarters because the 2017 holiday had already done so much of the work.

The pull to read a falling growth rate as a falling market is strong, because the most recent number feels like the trend. Guard against it. The order data points the other way: in Quartile’s Thanksgiving sample, ads drove a quarter of orders, up from about a sixth a year earlier. Shoppers did more of their holiday buying through ads, not less. That is demand moving into paid placements, and a slowing spend growth rate read on its own would hide it.

What the public data cannot tell you

None of these reports answers the question a budget owner asks in January: did each advertising dollar earn more or less than in 2017?

Spend growth is not efficiency. If a brand’s Sponsored Products spend rose 15% and its attributed sales rose 15%, its return held steady; if spend rose 15% because clicks cost more, the same money bought fewer shoppers. Merkle’s spend figures cannot separate the two, and no public source available by the end of January published Amazon click prices or return on ad spend for the quarter.

One Merkle figure does bear on efficiency, and it is a warning. In Q3, brand keywords, searches containing the advertiser’s own name, produced 42% of Sponsored Products sales and 61% of Sponsored Brands sales. Shoppers searching a brand’s name were already looking for it, so a large share of attributed sales came from demand the ads did not create. A brand whose holiday return on ad spend looked strong should check how much of it came from its own name before treating the number as a benchmark worth repeating.

The search benchmarks are a poor substitute. Kenshoo found search cost per click down 13% from a year earlier, with spending up 14% and clicks up 31%, but those figures describe search engines. Amazon’s auction has different bidders and a different holiday calendar.

How to benchmark your own Q4

Three comparisons do most of the work, and you have the data for all of them.

  1. Spend growth against 15%. If your Sponsored Products spend grew much faster than Merkle’s advertisers, you were buying share of the holiday. Check that your sales grew to match.
  2. Sales growth against 19.1%. US online sales grew 19.1% over the holiday. If your Amazon sales grew less, you lost ground to the market even if your own numbers look good.
  3. Total ACoS, Q4 2018 against Q4 2017: total ad spend divided by total Amazon sales, attributed and organic together. If it rose, each dollar of sales cost more advertising to win, whatever the console’s return on ad spend says.

The rule for setting Q1 budgets: if your total ACoS rose by more than a fifth from Q4 2017 to Q4 2018, find which campaigns grew spend faster than sales before adding a dollar in 2019.

Building that baseline, so that the Q4 2019 benchmark starts from your own numbers rather than a client panel, is the kind of measurement work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0181.title: Walmart Marketplace wants fewer sellers who behave like Walmart
P0181.alt: Rows of wooden market stalls with baskets of vegetables and jarred goods in a sunlit hall with blue walls.
P0181.ttag: Walmart Marketplace wants fewer sellers who behave like Walmart | Kwontified
P0181.desc: Walmart is choosing marketplace sellers the way a store chooses suppliers. Brands that apply as if Walmart.com were Amazon will pitch the wrong strengths.
P0181.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 31, 2019.
P0181.body:
In the spring of 2018, while Walmart.com was growing quickly, Walmart slowed the pace at which it let new Walmart Marketplace sellers onto its site. Bloomberg reported in April that the company was becoming more selective about its web sellers after a growth spurt, at a point when Walmart.com had about 18,000 third-party sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse figures cited in a RetailWire discussion of the report.

That choice says more about what Walmart wants from marketplace sellers than any rulebook. Amazon built its marketplace on the idea that more sellers mean more selection and lower prices. Walmart is building a marketplace the way a store chain builds a supplier list: fewer partners, chosen to fill gaps and to protect what shoppers expect when they see the Walmart name. Brands that approach Walmart Marketplace as a listing exercise will pitch the wrong strengths.

A store company running a marketplace

Read Walmart as an institution and the selectivity follows. Its brand promise rests on everyday low prices and the trust of families who shop it every week. When Marc Lore, who runs Walmart’s US e-commerce business, introduced the redesigned Walmart.com in April, the language was about that trust: “Every single day, busy families trust us to make shopping faster and easier for them,” he wrote in Walmart’s announcement. The redesign added local, personalized elements, specialty shopping experiences starting with home and then fashion, and better ways for brands to tell their stories.

A marketplace seller on that site is, to a shopper, Walmart. A late shipment, a confusing return or a price far above what the shopper saw in the store damages the retailer’s name, not the seller’s. A store company that has spent decades managing suppliers to protect that name will naturally manage marketplace sellers the same way.

The returns question shows the instinct. In a memo reported in October, Walmart told merchants that new functionality would make it “easier, faster and more efficient for you to manage returns on our platform,” and the company may let shoppers return marketplace items to its roughly 4,700 stores, the Motley Fool reported. The aim is plain: a marketplace order should feel like a Walmart order from checkout to return.

Why sellers are lining up anyway

Selectivity has not cooled interest. In Feedvisor’s survey of merchants, 25% sold on Walmart or Jet.com in 2018, up from 17% the year before, and 36% of Amazon sellers said they were considering Walmart’s marketplace, up from 29%, according to the same Motley Fool report. The reason is growth. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 43% in the quarter to October 31, Walmart reported in November.

That combination, rising demand from sellers and a retailer choosing among them, changes the balance of the conversation. Amazon’s marketplace was built to be open. On Walmart, a brand is asking to be let in, and Walmart is weighing what the brand adds against what it might cost the Walmart name.

What that means for a brand’s pitch

Inside many brands, Walmart Marketplace is handled by the e-commerce team as a second Amazon: the same catalog, the same content, a different upload. That framing misses what Walmart is selecting for. The strongest case a brand can make looks more like a supplier presentation than a seller application.

The first test is assortment. Walmart has room for products its stores and its own buyers do not carry, and the brand that can show which of its items fill gaps on Walmart.com, by category and price point, is offering Walmart something it wants.

Then price discipline. Walmart’s promise is low prices, and a brand whose products appear on Walmart.com at prices well above the same items elsewhere undermines it. A brand that can show it controls its pricing across channels, including resellers, removes a risk Walmart would otherwise carry.

Then reliability. Shipping times, stock levels and the returns experience are where a marketplace seller can hurt Walmart’s name fastest. A brand that already ships on time for Amazon’s Prime program, or runs a dependable direct-to-consumer operation, should lead with that record.

Last, decide who carries the pitch. Many brands already sell to Walmart’s stores through a sales team that knows its buyers, its scorecards and what it expects of suppliers. That team understands what Walmart rewards better than an e-commerce group used to Amazon’s self-service model, and bringing it into the marketplace application is often the fastest way to make the brand’s case in Walmart’s own terms.

Picture two applications from apparel brands of similar size. One uploads its full catalog and asks to be approved. The other submits the 150 items Walmart.com does not carry in its category, a pricing policy that applies to every channel, and its on-time shipping rate from the last holiday. Everything Walmart has said about its marketplace points to the second kind of partner, and the first brand will wonder why the answer takes so long.

Questions before the application goes in

  1. Which of our products are not on Walmart.com now, from Walmart or anyone else, and why would a Walmart shopper want them?
  2. Are our prices consistent across Amazon, Walmart, our own site and our resellers, and who enforces it?
  3. What is our record on shipping, stock and returns for our own and Amazon orders, and can we show it?
  4. Who inside our company owns the Walmart relationship: the e-commerce team, or the sales team that already sells to Walmart’s stores?

Walmart’s selectivity is likely to persist as long as its e-commerce business is growing and sellers are lining up. The evidence so far leans toward a marketplace that rewards brands which behave like good suppliers. Preparing that case, and running the account once Walmart says yes, is the Walmart Marketplace work we do for brands.

P0183.crumb: Amazon other revenue, Q4 2018: the ad…
P0183.title: Amazon other revenue, Q4 2018: the ad pool outgrew advertisers
P0183.alt: A large glass bowl filled with coins beside three small cups on a weathered wooden table by a teal wall.
P0183.ttag: Amazon other revenue, Q4 2018: the ad pool outgrew advertisers | Kwontified
P0183.desc: Amazon’s ad line nearly doubled in Q4 2018 while established advertisers raised Sponsored Products spend 15%. New bidders explain the gap for brands.
P0183.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 5, 2019.
P0183.body:
Two numbers from Amazon’s holiday quarter do not fit together. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which the company has said is mostly advertising, rose 95% to $3.39 billion in the fourth quarter of 2018, the Motley Fool reported. Over the same quarter, the advertisers Merkle manages raised their Sponsored Products spend by only 15% from a year earlier, according to Merkle’s Q4 2018 report.

Both can be true, and the reason matters more than either figure. Established brands did not double their budgets. Amazon’s ad pool grew because more sellers joined the auction and Amazon opened more places to show ads. For a brand that held its budget steady, that means the same money bought a smaller share of the searches its customers run.

What Amazon other revenue in Q4 2018 does and does not say

Start with what the line is. Amazon does not report advertising on its own. It reports a line called “other,” and on the first-quarter call in 2018 its finance chief said advertising was the majority of it (call transcript). So the line is a proxy, a good one, with known noise in it.

The largest piece of noise is accounting. Amazon adopted a new revenue standard at the start of 2018, and in the first quarter alone it added $560 million to “other,” mostly in North America, according to the same call. Every 2018 quarter is therefore compared with a 2017 quarter kept under the old rules, which flatters the year-over-year rate. On the fourth-quarter call, an analyst still asked about backing out “the advertising accounting change” to read the underlying trend (call transcript).

The cleaner read is inside 2018, where every quarter sits under the same rules. “Other” ran $2.0 billion in the first quarter, $2.2 billion in the second, $2.5 billion in the third and $3.4 billion in the fourth, for $10.1 billion across the year, GeekWire tallied. That is a 70% rise from the first quarter to the fourth within a single year. Some of it is seasonal. Not much of it can be accounting.

Why a 15% budget increase can lose ground

The instinct is to read Merkle’s 15% as a slowdown and Amazon’s line as hype. Each measures something different. Merkle tracks a panel of advertisers that were already spending, so its growth rate tells you what an established brand did. Amazon’s line counts every advertiser, including the ones that started bidding in 2018.

That difference is the whole story. Sponsored Products is an auction, and each search results page has a fixed number of ad slots. When a new seller starts bidding on “insulated water bottle,” the slots do not multiply; the bidders compete for the same ones, and the price of a click is set by the bids around yours. Amazon has also widened the inventory: it added Sponsored Brands placements last fall, MarTech reported, which adds slots but also adds more ways for new entrants to appear above you.

Say a brand spent $100,000 on Amazon ads in the 2017 holiday quarter and $115,000 in 2018, in line with Merkle’s panel. If total ad spending in its category doubled, the brand’s share of that spending fell from whatever it was to a little over half of it. Its spend went up; its presence went down.

A second way to see the same shift is to compare the ad line with the selling it sits on top of. Online stores, Amazon’s own retail sales, were $39.82 billion in the quarter, and third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from marketplace sellers, were $13.38 billion, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Against those two lines, “other” was about 6.4 cents per dollar in the fourth quarter of 2018.

A year earlier, $1.74 billion against $35.38 billion and $10.52 billion came to about 3.8 cents. The accounting change inflates the jump, and Amazon does not say by how much. The direction still tells you that advertising now takes a larger slice of the money that moves through Amazon’s store.

What the console can and cannot show you

A brand’s own Sponsored Products reports show spend, clicks, cost per click and attributed sales. They do not show the bidders you are now competing with, or what share of a search’s ad impressions you won. That makes a lost share of voice easy to misread as a weaker product or a seasonal dip.

The data that does help is already in the account. Impressions per keyword, held against your own bids, show whether you are being seen less on the searches that matter. If impressions on your top ten non-branded keywords fell while your bids and budgets held, someone else is buying the slots. If impressions held and cost per click rose, you are paying more to keep the same position. Those are different problems with different answers.

Amazon’s own outlook adds one caution. It guided first-quarter 2019 net sales to $56 billion to $60 billion, growth of 10% to 18%, the Motley Fool noted. Retail growth at that pace leaves the ad pool to keep outgrowing the sales underneath it, which is the condition that pushes the price of a click up.

Budget for a share of search, not last year’s spend plus a raise

Set the 2019 Amazon ad budget from the share of your category’s searches you want to hold, not from last year’s spend plus a percentage. Check impressions on your ten most valuable non-branded searches every month; when they fall with bids unchanged, you are being outbid, and the decision is whether those searches are worth the new price.

A 15% raise held the line in 2017. In a category where the bidders doubled, it buys retreat. If you would like a second pair of eyes on where your share went, our retail media team reads these reports every week.
