P0184.title: Walmart Marketplace in 2019 fills its aisles with specialists
P0184.alt: Three market stalls with blue scalloped awnings selling tea, cheese and pottery inside a glass-roofed hall.
P0184.ttag: Walmart Marketplace in 2019 fills its aisles with specialists | Kwontified
P0184.desc: Walmart is handing whole categories of Walmart.com to specialist operators. For brands, the question in 2019 is who runs the aisle you sell in.
P0184.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 7, 2019.
P0184.body:
A shopper looking for an NFL jersey on Walmart.com in February 2019 lands in a shop run by Fanatics, the company behind NFLShop.com and MLBShop.com. Walmart announced the long-term partnership on January 29, timed to the Super Bowl, and the shop brings in Nike, New Era and Mitchell & Ness, brands Walmart had not carried before, the Motley Fool noted.

It would be easy to read that as one more partnership. Next to the others it forms a pattern: Walmart is building Walmart.com category by category, inviting specialist operators to run the aisles where it lacks credibility, rather than opening the gate to every seller.

For a brand weighing Walmart Marketplace in 2019, the first question is no longer whether to apply. It is who runs the aisle you would be selling in.

Walmart Marketplace in 2019 is a set of rented aisles

The Fanatics shop is the newest of several. In October, Walmart and Advance Auto Parts announced an automotive specialty store on Walmart.com, planned for the first half of 2019 and rolled out in phases. It is to carry Advance’s parts and product information alongside Walmart’s tire, lube and battery services at about 2,500 Auto Care Centers, Ratchet+Wrench reported. Before that came the redesigned Walmart.com, which Walmart said in April 2018 would include a fashion destination with a Lord & Taylor flagship (Walmart’s announcement).

Sports licensing, auto parts and department-store fashion have one thing in common. In each, a shopper’s trust sits with a specialist, not with the store. Nobody walks into a Walmart expecting the full range of a team’s licensed gear or the right brake pads for a 2009 sedan. Walmart’s answer online is to bring in the company the shopper already trusts and give it a shop with Walmart’s checkout underneath.

Meanwhile the open marketplace has grown more slowly than the headlines suggest. Walmart had about 18,000 third-party sellers in April 2018, by Marketplace Pulse’s count, RetailWire reported, and it was becoming more selective about who it let in. Amazon grows its marketplace by open registration. Walmart adds sellers selectively and adds partners by press release.

Why a merchant builds a marketplace this way

The behavior makes sense once you remember who runs Walmart’s categories. Walmart is a merchant organization: category leaders are measured on assortment, price and the customer’s trust in both. When Eric O’Toole, the general manager for sports and fitness e-commerce, explained the Fanatics deal, he described Walmart.com as offering more than 75 million items and adding harder-to-find specialty goods, Retail Insight Network reported. That is a merchant talking about gaps on a shelf, not a platform manager talking about seller counts.

Follow the value and the trade is clear. Walmart keeps the customer, the checkout and the traffic; the specialist brings the catalog, the content and the expertise Walmart would take years to build. The operator gets Walmart’s audience at a time when that audience is moving online: Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 43% in its third quarter, the company reported in November.

The brands that lose a little in this trade are the ones that assumed Walmart.com would work like Amazon, where any brand that registers can build its own page and compete for the same search. On Walmart.com, a category with a specialist operator is a category where the operator decides which brands to carry and how to present them.

That changes the work inside a brand. The team that negotiates with a specialist like Fanatics is usually the wholesale or licensing team, which thinks in sell-in, margin and allocation. The team that would run a marketplace account thinks in search rank, reviews and content. When Walmart rents an aisle to an operator, the brand’s presence on Walmart.com is decided in the first room, while the second room is still drafting a plan to apply.

The shift brands should plan for

The evidence so far leans toward more of these shops, not fewer. Walmart has used them for three very different categories in under a year, and each one gives it range without the cost of building expertise. It is too early to say how well they convert, and Walmart has not said.

Sellers are coming anyway. In Feedvisor’s survey of merchants, 25% said they also sold on Walmart or Jet.com in 2018, up from a combined 17% the year before, the Motley Fool reported. Many of those sellers carry other companies’ brands, which means a brand can appear on Walmart.com without having decided to be there.

So a brand now has three doors into Walmart.com: as a supplier selling to Walmart’s buyers, as a marketplace seller of its own goods, or through a specialist’s shop. They lead to different pages, different prices and different owners of the shopper’s first impression. In the planning meetings where Walmart comes up, the conversation is often still about whether to “do Walmart,” as if there were one Walmart to do.

Questions for the team before you apply

  • In our categories, does Walmart.com have a specialist operator now, or is it likely to get one, and is our brand in that operator’s assortment?
  • Which of our products already appear on Walmart.com through resellers, and who wrote those pages?
  • Do our wholesale terms say anything about how distributors may sell on Walmart’s marketplace?
  • If Walmart’s buyer, a specialist and our own seller account all wanted the same listing, which would we choose, and who on our team decides?

The brands that answer those questions first will choose their door. The rest will find out which one they came through by searching for themselves on Walmart.com. Working out that map, aisle by aisle, is how we start every Walmart Marketplace plan.

P0185.title: Zalando’s Partner Program hands brands the markdown risk
P0185.alt: A white clothing rack of neutral shirts with blank red tags beside an orange-wrapped parcel against a mustard wall.
P0185.ttag: Zalando’s Partner Program hands brands the markdown risk | Kwontified
P0185.desc: Zalando’s partner sales grew over 60% in the quarter a heatwave pushed it to a loss. On the Partner Program, the next bad season lands on the brand.
P0185.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 12, 2019.
P0185.body:
Zalando had the summer every fashion retailer fears. Record heat in 2018 delayed the start of the autumn season, which cut into the weeks when full-price autumn stock usually sells and pushed discounts above the previous year’s level, the company said in September. The company swung to an adjusted operating loss of €39 million for the third quarter, against a small profit a year earlier, Retail Gazette reported.

In the same quarter, Zalando’s Partner Program, where brands sell their own stock on Zalando and pay a commission, grew more than 60%, according to Zalando. Those two facts belong together. Every brand that moves from wholesale to the Partner Program takes over the risk that cost Zalando its third quarter. The next late autumn will show up in the brand’s results, not Zalando’s.

Why the Zalando Partner Program looks like the better deal

The case for the Partner Program is real, and it explains the growth. Under wholesale, a brand sells its collection to Zalando at a wholesale price and loses control of what happens next: which items are shown, at what price and when they are discounted. Under the Partner Program, the brand keeps its stock, sets its own prices and pays Zalando a commission on what sells, while shoppers see one store. Brands including Nike, Lacoste, Pepe Jeans and Esprit joined in the first half of 2017, Fibre2Fashion reported.

Zalando has made the move easier. Its Zalando Fulfillment Solutions service, launched in June 2017, takes over customer-facing logistics for partner brands, including returns (FashionUnited).

From Zalando’s side the logic is just as clear. Every style that moves to the Partner Program is a style Zalando no longer has to buy months before it knows what the weather will do. After a quarter in which discounting turned a profit into a loss, a retailer has every reason to prefer selling space to buying stock, and to make that choice attractive to brands.

The change also shows up in Zalando’s reporting. In the third quarter, gross merchandise volume grew 16.6% while revenue grew 11.7% to about €1.2 billion. The gap is the Partner Program: Zalando counts the full value of partner sales in merchandise volume but books only its commission as revenue.

The same coat under two contracts

The difference between the two models is who owns the coat when the weather turns. Take a brand with 1,000 winter coats that retail at €200 on Zalando.

Under wholesale, say Zalando buys them at €90 each. The brand books €90,000 when the order ships. If autumn starts late, Zalando holds the coats and takes the discount.

Under the Partner Program, say the commission is 20%, so a full-price sale returns €160 to the brand and a sale at 40% off returns €96. Now run two seasons.

SeasonSold at full priceSold at 40% offUnsold, back on the brand’s booksBrand receives
Normal autumn70025050€136,000
Late autumn400300300€92,800

In the normal season the Partner Program pays about 1.5 times the wholesale order. In the late season it pays only slightly more than wholesale, and the brand also owns 300 coats that wholesale would have left with Zalando. The average looks generous. The spread between the two rows, €43,200 on a single style, is the risk Zalando used to carry and the brand now does.

Returns widen it further. A returned coat comes back to the partner’s stock, not Zalando’s, and in fashion e-commerce returns are routine: Zalando’s management said back in 2013 that a return rate of around half was normal (Twinkle). Each return is another chance for a unit to miss its full-price window.

What the averages hide, and the number that decides

The case for the Partner Program is usually made on margin per unit, and on that basis it wins. The figure that settles the decision is the sell-through rate a brand can count on in a bad season, because that is the season in which the risk arrives.

Timing matters as much as the total. Under wholesale, the brand is paid on the order, on its usual terms. Under the Partner Program, cash arrives coat by coat as shoppers buy and keep them, and the unsold stock sits in a warehouse the brand pays for. A late autumn delays the cash as well as cutting it, which matters most to a brand financing next season’s production.

A brand can estimate its bad-season sell-through from its own history. Look at the share of each autumn collection that sold at full price in the weakest season of the last three, across all channels where the brand controls price. If that share is low, the brand is better off letting a retailer hold the stock for its most weather-exposed styles, and putting the evergreen lines, where a late season costs little, on the Partner Program.

Zalando itself expected fourth-quarter revenue to grow 20% to 25% once the cold arrived. A retailer with a balance sheet that size can wait out a warm October. Many brands cannot, and the contract they choose decides who has to.

A rule for choosing the model

Run the Partner Program numbers on your worst autumn, not your average one. If the brand still earns more than the wholesale order after markdowns, returns and the stock left over, move the style to the Partner Program. If it does not, keep that style on wholesale and let Zalando own the weather.

Splitting a collection between the two models style by style is the work we do when we launch brands on Zalando.

P0187.crumb: Mercado Libre for brands in 2019: growth…
P0187.title: Mercado Libre for brands in 2019: growth the dollar hides
P0187.alt: A hammered brass disc leaning on a wooden bench with yellow goldenrod rising behind it against a sage wall.
P0187.ttag: Mercado Libre for brands in 2019: growth the dollar hides | Kwontified
P0187.desc: Mercado Libre’s sales volume fell 2.6% in dollars last quarter and grew 27.9% in local currency. Brands that read it in dollars misjudge the region.
P0187.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 14, 2019.
P0187.body:
In a brand’s quarterly business review, Latin America usually gets one slide near the end, in dollars. Read that way, Mercado Libre’s third quarter of 2018 looked like a stall: gross merchandise volume of almost $3 billion, down 2.6% from a year earlier. Read in local currency, the same quarter grew 27.9%, and shoppers bought 83.5 million items, up 12.5%, Mercado Libre reported on November 1.

The gap between those two numbers is a currency effect, and it shapes decisions. A brand that reads Mercado Libre in dollars sees a flat channel and leaves it to a distributor. A brand that reads it the way its shoppers live it sees a marketplace whose customers are buying more each quarter, and a company spending heavily to change what they expect from online shopping. For brands, the case for Mercado Libre in 2019 rests on that second reading.

Mercado Libre for brands looks smaller from headquarters

The habit has an obvious origin. Most US and European brands manage Latin America from a regional desk, through importers and distributors, and judge it by sell-in converted at the reporting rate. In the third quarter of 2018, that conversion turned 27.9% growth into a decline on the slide.

The arithmetic is simple enough to run on any brand’s numbers. Take a brand whose sales on Mercado Libre Mexico rose from 10 million pesos to 12 million in a year, a 20% gain. If the peso bought 10% fewer dollars at the end of the year than at the start, the dollar slide shows growth of only about 8%. The shoppers bought a fifth more; the review meeting hears that the channel barely moved.

The shopper in São Paulo or Guadalajara does not experience the exchange rate that way. She experiences more products, delivered faster, often with no shipping charge. Items shipped through Mercado Envíos, the company’s logistics service, reached 54.3 million in the quarter, up 30.2%, which the company attributed mainly to its expanded free shipping program.

What Mercado Libre is paying for

Read Mercado Libre as an institution and its priorities are plain. It is willing to give up margin to make free, fast delivery normal. Its gross margin fell to 47.8% from 57.7% a year earlier, mostly because of higher free shipping subsidies, and it posted an operating loss of $11.0 million against a gain the year before, according to the same report. That is a company choosing to train its customers, at its own expense, to expect an Amazon-like experience before Amazon gets there.

Amazon is trying to close the gap. Its Brazilian marketplace grew from about 1,400 sellers in October 2017 to more than 3,000 by early November, Marketplace Pulse counted, when Mercado Libre already had 4.6 million unique third-party sellers. The scale gap is wide, and Mercado Libre’s spending on shipping is how it intends to keep it.

For brands, the subsidy changes the shelf. When free shipping becomes the norm, a listing that charges for delivery, or that ships slowly from a distributor’s warehouse, looks worse next to one that does not. The brand’s product may be identical. The page the shopper sees is not. A shopper who has learned to expect delivery without a fee reads the delivery promise as closely as the product description, and a listing that cannot match it loses the comparison before price comes into it.

Who on the team owns this decision

This is where the reporting habit becomes an organizational problem. The leadership team debating Latin America for 2019 usually has two options on the table: keep selling through the regional distributor, or invest in a direct presence on Mercado Libre. The dollar slide makes the first option look prudent.

The local-currency view argues the other way. If shoppers are buying more and the marketplace is subsidizing delivery to win them, then whoever controls the brand’s listings, stock and shipping on Mercado Libre controls how the brand competes there. A distributor optimizing its own margin may not use Mercado Envíos, may not keep stock where the free-shipping program needs it and may not price the way the marketplace rewards. The brand will not see any of that in a sell-in report.

Caution still has a place in the plan. Mercado Libre’s own margins show how expensive this race is, and a company losing money on shipping can change its rules quickly when costs move. Currency risk is real for the brand too: revenue earned in pesos and reais will convert to fewer dollars if those currencies keep falling. The evidence so far leans toward a marketplace that is gaining shoppers and will keep investing to hold them, but a brand going direct should plan for fee and shipping terms to change within the year.

Questions to put to the team

  • What did our Latin America business do in local currency in 2018, and how does that compare with the dollar figure we reported?
  • Who writes our product pages on Mercado Libre now, and do our listings qualify for the shipping subsidy?
  • If a distributor sells for us, can we see its sales, prices and stock on the marketplace each month?
  • What would it take to run our top 20 products on Mercado Libre ourselves for six months, and how would we judge the result in local currency?

The brands that answer those questions in local currency, and keep reading the region that way, will see a growing market where the dollar slide shows a flat one. Running that test, country by country, is how we launch brands on Mercado Libre.

P0189.crumb: Instagram shopping in 2019 hands the sale…
P0189.title: Instagram shopping in 2019 hands the sale back to your website
P0189.alt: A weathered wooden bench with a phone on its seat beside a stone path leading to an ivy-covered cottage door.
P0189.ttag: Instagram shopping in 2019 hands the sale back to your website | Kwontified
P0189.desc: Instagram shopping tags cost nothing, but the sale still closes on your own mobile site. In 2019 your checkout limits what a shopping post can earn.
P0189.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 19, 2019.
P0189.body:
Brands that start tagging products on Instagram tend to tag everything, because the tag costs nothing. A few months later the sales report has barely moved, and the conclusion in the room is that Instagram shoppers browse but do not buy. The tag is rarely the problem. An Instagram shopping post is the first step of a four-step funnel, each step multiplies the one before it, and the last step, the purchase, happens on the brand’s own mobile website, where Instagram has no say over how well it works.

Instagram shopping is a free tag on a paid funnel

The free part is real. When Instagram opened shoppable posts to more US brands in March 2017, no money changed hands between brands and Instagram, MarTech reported, which made it a free alternative to Instagram’s direct-response ads. A shopper taps the post to see product details and a price, then taps through to the brand’s site to buy, inside Instagram’s in-app browser.

The audience is large. In September 2018 Instagram said more than 90 million accounts tapped the shopping tags in posts every month, and it rolled Shopping in Stories out to businesses approved for shopping worldwide, along with a shopping channel in the Explore tab, MarTech reported. The flow was unchanged: tap the shopping bag, see the product, follow the link to the brand’s website.

So the tag is free, the attention is real, and the sale is the brand’s job. That split explains most of the disappointing reports.

Each step of the funnel multiplies the one before it

Instagram’s own test gives the first two steps. Across the 20 brands that tested shoppable posts from November 2016, only 4% of people shown a shoppable photo tapped to reveal product information, and on average 19% of those who tapped went on to the brand’s site, according to the same March 2017 report.

Now run a post through it. Take a tagged post seen by 10,000 people. At 4%, 400 tap the tag. At 19%, 76 reach your product page. If your mobile site converts 2% of those visitors, that is 1.5 orders. At a $60 average order, the post earned about $91.

Three things follow from the multiplication. Adding tags to more posts scales the 10,000, which is the step Instagram’s feed controls, not you. A better caption or photo moves the 4%. But the cheapest step to fix is usually the last one, because it sits on your own site. Lift mobile conversion from 2% to 3% and the same post earns half as much again, with no change on Instagram at all.

That last step is also harder than it looks from a desk. The shopper arrives in Instagram’s in-app browser, on a phone, and is often not signed in to your site, so the saved address and card that make a returning customer’s checkout quick may not be there. Every extra field is asked of someone who was scrolling a feed a moment earlier. A checkout that converts well for email traffic can convert noticeably worse here, and the only way to know is to measure it separately.

The pull toward tagging is understandable. Tags are visible, countable work, and a weekly report of “products tagged” looks like progress. The checkout is owned by another team, often the one that runs the website, and its numbers rarely appear in a social media review. That is how a brand ends up tagging hundreds of products and never asking what happens after the click.

Instagram counts the taps; your website counts the orders

The measurement problem follows the same split. During the 2016–2017 test, brands had to ask Instagram for basic numbers such as taps to view product information and clicks through to their site, and Instagram did not say how many sales the feature drove. Its September 2018 announcement again gave taps, not purchases.

That leaves the brand to join two reports. Instagram can tell you how many people tapped and clicked. Only your site’s analytics can tell you how many of those visits became orders, and only if the visits are labeled. Add campaign parameters to the product links in the catalog that feeds your shopping tags, so the analytics can separate Instagram shopping traffic from everything else.

Reach is the other cost the free tag hides. A shopping post reaches the people the feed shows it to, and growing that number usually means paying for it. Facebook’s fourth-quarter 2018 results showed what that price is doing: ad impressions rose 34% while the average price per ad fell 2%, with growth led by Instagram feed and Stories ads, Marketing Land reported on January 30. Cheaper Stories ads make it more affordable to buy the top of this funnel. They do nothing for the bottom.

Mark Zuckerberg named Instagram shopping as the area he was most excited about for 2019 on the earnings call. It would not be surprising if Instagram tried to keep more of the purchase inside the app. Until it does, the brand’s checkout remains part of every Instagram shopping post’s math.

Before the next shopping post

  • Calculate sales per 1,000 views for your last ten shopping posts: taps, click-throughs and orders, joined through your site analytics.
  • Open your product pages inside Instagram’s in-app browser on a phone and complete a purchase. Count the screens and the fields.
  • Compare mobile conversion for Instagram visits with your site average. If Instagram traffic converts at half the rate, fix the page before adding tags.
  • Spend on reach only for posts whose sales per 1,000 views already clear your target.

Judge Instagram shopping by orders per thousand views, and fix the last step before you scale the first. That last step is where we start when we run Instagram Shopping for a brand, and it is the first thing we would check in your funnel.

P0190.crumb: Walmart advertising in 2019 is a nearly…
P0190.title: Walmart advertising in 2019 is a nearly empty shelf, for now
P0190.alt: A blue metal shelving unit holding glass jars and bottles above stacked cardboard boxes in a sunlit room.
P0190.ttag: Walmart advertising in 2019 is a nearly empty shelf, for now | Kwontified
P0190.desc: Walmart sells ads on a sliver of its searches and has run them through an agency. Taking them in-house shows it wants the budgets brands spend on Amazon.
P0190.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 21, 2019.
P0190.body:
“We have a tiny ad business,” Doug McMillon told investors in October. “It could be bigger.” Chief executives rarely call any part of their company tiny in front of shareholders, and when they do, it is usually because they intend to change it. This week Walmart showed how: it is taking the sale of advertising on its websites back from the agency that ran it and building its own team. For brands, the lesson is less about a new ad product than about a retailer deciding that the attention of its shoppers is something it should sell itself.

The admission came via Bloomberg’s reporting on February 11, and the move was reported by Ad Age on February 19. Read together, they describe a company that has left a valuable shelf mostly empty and has just decided to stock it.

Walmart advertising has been run from outside the building

Until now, the people selling ads on Walmart.com did not work for Walmart. WPP’s Triad handled the retailer’s website ad sales and the analytics behind them, and Walmart is now moving that work to its own Walmart Media Group, with the transition expected to last through May and hundreds of employees to be added, Marketing Dive reported, citing Ad Age. Triad will reportedly enforce noncompete clauses, so many of the people brands dealt with will not follow the work to Walmart.

An outsourced sales desk tells you how an institution ranks a business. Walmart’s merchants own the shelf, its buyers own the supplier relationship, and advertising sat with a vendor, outside the reporting lines that decide what matters at Bentonville.

The results show on the page. Amazon is estimated to monetize 16% of the searches on its site, against 1% for Walmart, according to a Gartner L2 estimate cited by Ad Age. At 1%, a shopper searching Walmart.com for a household staple will usually see rows ranked by Walmart, with no brand paying to be there. That is an empty shelf, and in retail an empty shelf rarely stays empty for long once someone is paid to fill it.

Walmart has sold this attention before

None of this is new territory for Walmart. About 20 years ago it ran an in-store TV network that reached 180 million monthly viewers by 2004 before digital media overtook it, according to the Bloomberg report. The audience never went away. About 300 million shoppers visit Walmart stores each month, Forrester Research estimates, and the stores now sit beside an online business whose US e-commerce sales grew 43% in the fourth quarter, Walmart reported on February 19.

What is different this time is who Walmart is hiring and what it can offer. It has brought in executives from NBCUniversal and CBS to build the business, Bloomberg reported, which is how a company staffs a media sales operation, not a merchandising one.

It also holds something no agency could sell on its behalf: the link between an ad and a purchase, online and in the store. Advertisers say that link is what they want from retailers. A Coca-Cola North America executive told Bloomberg that targeting with third-party data got the company “close to the pin, but not close enough,” while a grocer’s own data showed whether ads led to sales.

Follow the value and the motive is plain. Every dollar a brand spends on Walmart advertising through an agency shares its margin with the agency, and every sale it drives is measured by someone other than Walmart. Bringing the desk inside puts the margin, the data and the conversation with the supplier in one place.

The budget question arrives inside the brand

Walmart’s move lands on an organizational seam inside most suppliers. At many brands, the Walmart relationship belongs to the sales team that negotiates with the buyer, while Amazon advertising sits with an e-commerce or media team that has its own budget. When Walmart starts selling ads in earnest, it will ask that sales team for media money, and the e-commerce team that knows how to spend it may not be in the room.

The marketplace adds bidders as well. Walmart’s fourth-quarter release pointed to new Marketplace features, including free two-day shipping on millions of new items, and every third-party seller that joins Walmart.com is another potential buyer of the same search slots a brand will want once they carry a price.

Some caution is warranted. The transition runs into May and changes staff, tools and contracts at the same time, which leaves room for gaps in service. Walmart’s ad business is still tiny by its own chief executive’s account. The evidence leans toward a shelf that fills quickly once Walmart Media Group is staffed, because Walmart has the audience, the purchase data and now the incentive. Prices on a shelf that is mostly empty tend to be low; they rarely stay that way once the retailer’s own sales team is working it.

Before the transition finishes in May

  • Who at our company owns Walmart advertising: the team that sells to the Walmart buyer, or the team that runs Amazon ads?
  • Which of our Walmart.com searches show no ads now, and what would we pay to hold the top of those pages?
  • Who is our contact during the move from Triad to Walmart Media Group, and what happens to campaigns booked through May?
  • What would we need to see in Walmart’s purchase data before moving any Amazon budget?

The brands that answer the first question now will meet Walmart’s new sales team with a plan instead of a request for funds. Running Walmart’s marketplace and its advertising together is the work we do for brands on Walmart, and the ownership question is usually where it starts.

P0191.title: Vendor Central in 2019: Amazon’s margin decides your terms
P0191.alt: An antique brass platform scale beside a weathered wooden crate in an old warehouse.
P0191.ttag: Vendor Central in 2019: Amazon’s margin decides your terms | Kwontified
P0191.desc: On Vendor Central your margin is fixed at the wholesale price and Amazon’s floats. When Amazon’s drops below zero, it is your terms that change next.
P0191.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 26, 2019.
P0191.body:
Amazon told Coca-Cola it was losing money on small shipments of Smartwater, such as the $6.99 six-pack, the Wall Street Journal reported in December. The default automatic reorder became a 24-pack at $37.20, the price per bottle rose from $1.17 to $1.55, and Coca-Cola will ship those orders to customers itself, according to the report. Nothing was wrong with demand for the six-pack. The problem was Amazon’s margin on it.

That is the part of Vendor Central most vendors never model. On Vendor Central, a vendor’s margin is fixed by the wholesale price it negotiates, while Amazon’s floats with the retail price it sets and the cost of getting the box to a customer. When Amazon’s margin sinks toward zero, the vendor’s terms are what change next.

Vendor Central fixes your margin and floats Amazon’s

The arrangement looks simple from the vendor’s side. Amazon Retail buys the product at a wholesale cost, pays for it on terms, and resells it at a price Amazon chooses. Once the purchase order is accepted, the vendor’s margin on that unit is settled.

Amazon’s is not. Its margin on each unit is the retail price, less what it paid the vendor, less the cost of storing, picking and shipping the item. Two of those three numbers move after the order is placed. The retail price moves because Amazon sets it to compete with every other offer for the same product, including resellers, and the shipping cost moves with weight, size and how many units go in each box.

That asymmetry explains a pattern vendors find baffling. An item can sell well, earn the vendor its expected margin on every unit, and still be the item Amazon most wants to change.

Why a cheap, heavy item turns red for Amazon

Internally, Amazon calls these products “CRaP,” for “can’t realize a profit.” They are typically priced under $15, heavy or bulky, and sold directly by Amazon, the Journal reported, and Amazon has been eliminating or repackaging them, in some cases halting sales of certain package sizes.

The arithmetic shows why the price threshold matters. Take a $14 multipack of snacks that Amazon buys from the vendor at $8.40. Say storing, picking and shipping it costs Amazon $4.50 a unit. Amazon keeps $1.10 on each sale. Now a reseller lists the same multipack for $12.50 and Amazon meets that price. The vendor still collects $8.40, and Amazon now loses $0.40 on every unit it ships. At 10,000 units a month, a best-seller becomes a $4,000 monthly loss for the retailer, and the vendor sees nothing in its own reports.

A $60 item with the same shipping cost tells a different story, because a fall of a dollar or two in its retail price leaves plenty of margin to absorb it. Weight works the other way: a heavier box costs more to ship whatever its price, so it needs a higher price to stay in the black. That is why the pressure lands on low-priced, heavy goods, and why it arrives as a conversation about packs, costs or fulfillment, not about sales.

Amazon has three ways to close the gap, and each moves cost toward the vendor. It can change the pack so each shipment carries more revenue, as with Smartwater. It can ask the vendor for a lower cost or more support: wholesale vendors already pay a percentage of sales into Amazon’s co-op fee, which funds marketing, Digiday reported in December. Or it can hand the shipping back, as Coca-Cola is now doing.

Why Vendor Central felt like the safe choice

Vendors chose 1P for good reasons. Amazon buys the stock, pays the invoice and handles the customer, and the first year of terms can be generous. One vendor described exactly that sequence in a 2017 comment on Web Retailer: good first-year terms, then new fees, then payment terms stretched from 60 to 90 days. James Thomson of Buy Box Experts wrote in the same thread that brands often succeed on Vendor Central in the short term and lose control or margin as their sales grow. Both observations fit the mechanism. Terms tighten when an item’s volume makes Amazon’s margin on it worth fixing.

Amazon’s direction points the same way. Recode first reported, and Digiday followed in December, that people who work with brands expected a system called One Vendor that would merge Vendor Central and Seller Central and give Amazon more control over how brands appear; Amazon told Digiday it has no program by that name. Whatever it is called, a retailer that already sees more than half its business come from third-party sellers has an easy alternative for any item that loses it money.

Test your top items through Amazon’s eyes

The useful habit is to run Amazon’s margin calculation on your own catalog before Amazon’s team does.

  • For your 50 best-selling items, estimate Amazon’s margin: the current retail price, less your cost, less a fulfillment estimate based on the item’s weight and size.
  • Flag every item where Amazon’s margin is under a dollar or under 10% of the retail price; a pack change, a cost request or direct fulfillment is most likely there.
  • Check what is pulling the retail price down. If a reseller is undercutting, the fix may be in your distribution, not in your Amazon terms.
  • Price the alternative now: what each flagged item would earn you on Seller Central with a fee per sale and your own price.

The rule of thumb is simple: the thinner Amazon’s margin on an item, the sooner your terms on it will change. Running that calculation and the Seller Central comparison side by side is part of how we manage Vendor Central for brands, and it is the first thing we would run on your catalog.

P0194.crumb: Amazon DSP in 2019 has no natural owner…
P0194.title: Amazon DSP in 2019 has no natural owner inside most brands
P0194.alt: A home office with a navy wall, desk chair, computer monitor and stacks of file folders on a wooden desk.
P0194.ttag: Amazon DSP in 2019 has no natural owner inside most brands | Kwontified
P0194.desc: Amazon DSP falls between the media agency’s budget and the trade team’s, and the team that pays for it decides what it is used for, often the wrong thing.
P0194.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 28, 2019.
P0194.body:
In a consumer brand’s annual plan, Amazon often appears twice. The media agency presents a display and video plan that may include Amazon inventory, judged on reach and cost per thousand. Later, the e-commerce or sales team presents its Amazon plan, judged on sales and return on ad spend. Amazon DSP, the company’s programmatic display business, can sit on either slide, and the slide it lands on decides what the brand uses it for. That makes ownership, more than targeting or creative, the first decision a brand has to get right with Amazon DSP in 2019.

Amazon DSP sits between two budgets

The product itself is easy to describe. Amazon renamed the Amazon Advertising Platform as Amazon DSP in September 2018, when it folded its ad businesses under the Amazon Advertising name, Amazon announced. The platform buys display and video ads programmatically and is the way to reach Amazon’s audience segments off Amazon’s own sites, either through Amazon’s managed service or self-serve, Digiday explained in December 2017.

The difficulty is where the money comes from. Consumer goods companies usually buy Google ads through their media agencies, but they buy shopper marketing, the spending that runs from shelf displays to store promotions, directly from retailers, Digiday reported in November. Those are two different budgets, two different teams and two different sets of measures. Amazon DSP is display media bought from a retailer, so it belongs to both and neither.

Moving money between those lines is harder than it sounds. “Rigid financial and accounting structures” make it hard for brands to shift budget, particularly out of shopper and trade marketing, Tod Harrick of Wunderman’s Marketplace Ignition told Digiday. The size of that pool explains why Amazon wants it: consumer goods companies spend around $100 billion a year on shopper marketing, according to Cadent Consulting figures in the same report. Even a small share of that pool, moved online, would make Amazon DSP one of the larger media lines in many consumer brands’ plans.

The team that pays decides what Amazon DSP is for

Follow the budget and the behavior follows. When the e-commerce or trade team funds Amazon DSP, it judges the spend the way it judges Sponsored Products, by the sales Amazon attributes to it. Under that measure, the audiences that look best are the shoppers who already viewed the product or bought it before, because they were the closest to buying anyway. The DSP drifts toward following people who were already at the shelf.

When the media agency funds it, the measure changes to reach and cost per thousand, and Amazon DSP competes with every other display buy on price. Under that measure, Amazon’s audience data is a targeting feature the agency may or may not use, and the purchase reports that come with the DSP can go unread.

Neither arrangement makes much use of what is distinctive about the product: the chance to reach shoppers who are browsing a category on Amazon but have not yet searched for the brand. That is upper-funnel work with a sales signal attached, and most brand org charts have no box for it. It ends up as an afterthought on two slides instead of a decision on one.

Amazon is building a media business around this gap

Amazon is not waiting for brands to settle the question. Its “other” revenue, mostly advertising, rose 95% to $3.39 billion in the fourth quarter of 2018, according to its results. Amazon took 5.5% of US digital ad dollars, according to eMarketer figures cited by Bloomberg in February. And it has pursued shopper marketing budgets more aggressively than Google, Merkle’s Liz Rutgersson told Digiday.

Brands are moving too, unevenly. iCrossing said its clients raised their 2018 Amazon ad spend by between 9% and 295% over 2017, which is less a trend line than a sign of how differently brands are treating the channel. Some CPG clients are seeing 50% to 60% annual growth on Amazon against about 2% in traditional grocery, VMLY&R’s Dan Pereira told Digiday. Where sales grow that fast, budgets tend to follow, and the question of which budget becomes harder to ignore.

The evidence leans toward Amazon DSP becoming a larger line in consumer brands’ plans over the next few years, because Amazon is investing to sell it and brands are following their sales. It is too early to say which team will end up holding it. A useful sign of progress inside a company is when the agency and the e-commerce team report Amazon DSP results in the same meeting, against the same definition of a new customer.

The same seam will open at other retailers. Walmart is moving the sale of its website ads in-house to Walmart Media Group, Ad Age reported on February 19, and any retailer that sells display against its own shopper data will raise the same question of which team pays. A brand that settles ownership of Amazon DSP now will have an answer ready when it does.

Four questions for the next planning cycle

  • Which budget paid for Amazon DSP last year, and does that team’s main measure match what we want the DSP to do?
  • What share of our DSP spend went to shoppers who had already viewed or bought our products?
  • Who in the company reads the purchase reports that come with Amazon DSP, and what decision did they change?
  • If we gave one team the whole Amazon budget, search and display together, which team would it be, and what would it need from the other?

The brands that answer the first question deliberately will spend Amazon DSP on the shoppers they cannot otherwise reach. Planning Amazon DSP alongside Sponsored Products, with one owner and one set of measures, is the work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0197.crumb: Amazon brand tools in 2019 all open with…
P0197.title: Amazon brand tools in 2019 all open with one trademark
P0197.alt: A brass wax seal stamp beside a ring of antique skeleton keys on a worn wooden table against a teal wall.
P0197.ttag: Amazon brand tools in 2019 all open with one trademark | Kwontified
P0197.desc: Project Zero, Brand Analytics, Stores and Sponsored Brands share one entry rule on Amazon, and a trademark takes months, so the filing date sets your plan.
P0197.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 5, 2019.
P0197.body:
Last Thursday, Amazon gave a small group of brands a button that deletes counterfeit listings without asking Amazon first. Project Zero is invitation-only, and the entry rule is short: a government-registered trademark and enrollment in Brand Registry, TechCrunch reported. That is the same rule that stands in front of almost every brand tool Amazon has built in the last three years.

So the state of Amazon’s brand tools in 2019 is easy to summarize and expensive to ignore. The tools keep getting more powerful, and they all open with one key. A brand holding a registered trademark gets each new tool on the day it ships. A brand without one waits for its trademark office, and that wait is measured in months.

Amazon brand tools in 2019, and the one gate in front of them

Lay the tools side by side and the pattern is hard to miss.

ToolWhat it doesEntry ruleSince
Brand RegistryLets the rights owner control the product page and report infringementRegistered trademarkRebuilt 2017
Enhanced Brand ContentReplaces the plain description with images and formatted textBrand Registry2016
StoresA free, multipage brand store on AmazonBrand Registry2017
Sponsored BrandsSearch ads with the brand’s logo and headlineBrand Registry, for sellersOpened to sellers August 2017
Brand AnalyticsSearch and purchase data for the brand’s categoryBrand RegistrySeller Central, February 2019
Project ZeroSelf-service counterfeit removal, optional serializationRegistered trademark plus Brand Registry; invitation onlyFebruary 28, 2019

The sources line up. The rebuilt Brand Registry accepts only brands with a registered trademark, and only the registered owner can change bullets, descriptions and images on its pages (Practical Ecommerce; Practical Ecommerce). Enhanced Brand Content reached Brand Registered sellers in 2016 (CPC Strategy). Stores arrived in 2017 for registered brands (CPC Strategy). Headline Search Ads opened to third-party sellers with Brand Registry in August 2017 (eSellerHub) and became Sponsored Brands when Amazon retired its old ad names on September 5, 2018 (Amazon Advertising).

Why the gate matters more each year

The table hides the mechanism, which is that the credential is cheap and the waiting is expensive. A trademark costs little to file. It typically takes six to ten months to register, Practical Ecommerce noted when the new Brand Registry opened.

The value of holding the key grows with every tool behind the gate. In 2017 the key bought control of the page and a faster hearing: Brand Registry participants had counterfeit claims handled within four hours, with no test buy, Practical Ecommerce reported. By 2018 it also bought a Store and a second ad format. In 2019 it buys data and enforcement.

Brand Analytics is the clearest case. Until February, Amazon’s search-term data was a vendor product, with pricing starting at $30k, and now it sits in Seller Central for brand owners enrolled in Brand Registry, ChannelX reported. Information that a vendor paid for in 2018 is open to a registered seller in 2019. For an unregistered brand, it is out of reach at any price.

Project Zero works the same way. Enrollment is free, and serialization, the optional unit-level code that lets Amazon check each item, costs between $0.01 and $0.05 per unit depending on volume, according to TechCrunch. The price is low. The gate is the trademark, and then the invitation.

The arithmetic of delay is simple, and it is worth doing before Q4 planning starts. Say a brand wants a Store and Sponsored Brands running by October 1, 2019. At six to ten months for registration, the filing had to go in between December 2018 and April 2019. A brand that files in May starts the holiday season with the plain product page and Sponsored Products only, and the trademark arrives in time for the January returns.

What registration does not buy

Registration has a cost on the other side, and it is real. It gives the brand control of its pages, and it also makes the brand answerable for them. Amazon said it would monitor how accurately Project Zero brands use the removal tool (TechCrunch), so a brand that enrolls is signing up for a weekly job, with someone accountable for every listing it deletes.

Registration also does not stop anyone from selling the product. Amazon is an open marketplace, and choosing Vendor Central or Seller Central does not change who may list a brand’s goods, as James Thomson put it. The tools decide who controls the page, the data and the ads. They do not decide who holds the inventory.

Vendors should read the table too. A brand selling to Amazon wholesale reached many of these tools through Vendor Central and paid for the data, and it now watches registered sellers get the same search data in Seller Central. That narrows one of the reasons brands gave for staying 1P, and it is worth a line in any 1P-or-3P review this spring.

Still, the numbers lean one way. The cost of registering is a filing fee and a few hours of someone’s time each week. The cost of not registering is every tool in the table, plus whatever Amazon ships next with the same entry rule, and each new tool has so far shipped with that rule.

File first, then budget the tools

Put the trademark filing date at the top of the Amazon plan, and count six to ten months forward before any tool in the table goes into a budget. Then check one thing this week: whose name is on the Brand Registry account. If it is a distributor’s, an agency’s or a former employee’s, the key to every tool above is in someone else’s pocket. Getting it back is dull work, and it comes before anything else in the Amazon channel we run for brands.

P0199.title: Amazon apparel in 2019: shoppers moved before brands did
P0199.alt: A vintage delivery van loaded with wrapped parcels on a cobbled street beside a rack of linen clothes in a shop doorway.
P0199.ttag: Amazon apparel in 2019: shoppers moved before brands did | Kwontified
P0199.desc: Amazon became America’s most-shopped apparel retailer in Coresight’s 2019 survey, taking shoppers from Walmart and Target while brands plan around them.
P0199.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 7, 2019.
P0199.body:
Picture the spring restock of a family’s basics: socks, leggings, a pack of undershirts, a pair of sneakers for a child who outgrew the last ones. In 2017 that list went to Walmart or Target. In early 2019 a growing share of it goes into the Amazon app, and Coresight Research has now put a ranking on the move. In its annual US apparel survey, Amazon became the most-shopped retailer for apparel in the US, up from second place a year earlier, Coresight reported on March 4.

The shopper has already moved. Most apparel companies are still organized around the stores she left, with account teams, sell-in calendars and markdown money built for Walmart’s and Target’s buyers. That gap, more than any feature Amazon launched, is what changed in the category.

What changed in Amazon apparel in 2019

The survey is specific about where Amazon’s apparel shoppers came from. Walmart is the retailer they most often said they had moved some or all of their apparel spending away from, followed closely by Target. Roughly three-quarters of Prime members said they had bought apparel on Amazon in the past year.

The direction was visible in 2018, and the 2019 survey confirms the turn. Morgan Stanley put Amazon second only to Walmart in US apparel after a 1.5-point share gain in 2017, and expected Amazon to take the lead in 2018, CNBC reported. By September, Wells Fargo was estimating that Amazon’s apparel and footwear sales could pass $30 billion in 2018, according to CNBC.

Both were estimates, made from the outside. Coresight’s survey measures something different and, for a brand, more useful: habit. “Most-shopped” counts how many people bought there, which says nothing about dollars, but it does say where the restock list now starts.

Who sets the terms on the new shelf

Follow the value and the shift looks less like a new channel and more like a new landlord. In a department store or a big-box apparel aisle, the brand negotiates with a buyer: placement, margin, markdown support. On Amazon, much of that negotiation has been replaced by a published fee schedule and a search box.

The fee schedule moved against apparel in 2018. Amazon raised the referral fee for Clothing & Accessories from 15% to 17% from April 15, with a $1.00 minimum per item, so a $20 shirt now pays $3.40 instead of $3.00, according to the notice sellers posted. Few categories pay more. A retailer raises the price of a shelf when it believes the shoppers will come anyway, and the 2019 survey suggests Amazon read its apparel customers correctly.

The search box has a house brand in it, too. Apparel and footwear account for almost 5,000 of Amazon’s 6,825 private-label products, close to three-quarters of the range, according to Coresight’s 2018 analysis. No other category gets that much of Amazon’s own merchandising effort. In apparel, more than anywhere else on the site, Amazon is both the landlord and a tenant competing for the same shoppers.

So the value in the category is splitting three ways. Amazon collects the higher fee and sells its own labels. The shopper gets convenience and Prime shipping on the basics list. The brand keeps whatever it can defend with a strong product page, a clean set of sizes and a reason to choose it over the house label one row down.

The account map most apparel brands still use

Inside many apparel companies, the org chart still reads like a list of store buyers. There is a team for each big wholesale account, a calendar of market weeks, and a planning process that starts with what each buyer committed to take. Amazon often sits inside that map as one more account, or with whoever already runs the website.

That structure made sense when the buyer decided what the shopper saw. It fits poorly when the shopper has moved her restock list to a site where no buyer stands between her and the search results. The team that owns Walmart and Target can lose volume it has no way to win back through those accounts, and the team that could win it is often the smallest one in the building.

None of this means wholesale is finished, and the brands that built their businesses on it are right to protect it. Walmart and Target still sell enormous volumes of apparel, and the survey measures where people shopped, not where the most money went. It does mean that the spring planning meeting, where the year’s assortment and allocations get set, should now start with the store where the shopper begins, and for a growing share of basics that store is Amazon.

Questions for the spring planning meeting

  1. Which of our products are on the family restock list, and do we control their Amazon pages, sizes and images, or does a reseller?
  2. Have we recalculated margins on Amazon at the 17% referral fee, and which items fall below our floor?
  3. Where does an Amazon house label compete with our bestsellers, and what on our page tells a shopper why ours is worth more?
  4. Who in the company owns the Amazon apparel number, and does that person sit in the room when the wholesale accounts are planned?

The last question is the one that decides the others. The apparel brands that answer it this spring, with a named owner and a seat at the planning table, will be the ones setting terms on the shelf their shoppers now use first. Giving that owner a team that runs the channel day to day is the Amazon work we do for apparel brands.

P0200.crumb: Amazon vendor cuts: price your Seller…
P0200.title: Amazon vendor cuts: price your Seller Central fallback now
P0200.alt: High wooden shelves stocked with bagged goods above a rope cargo net in a sunlit pink-walled storeroom.
P0200.ttag: Amazon vendor cuts: price your Seller Central fallback now | Kwontified
P0200.desc: Amazon stopped ordering from thousands of small vendors last week. A brand moving to Seller Central keeps more of the price, and takes on everything Amazon did.
P0200.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 12, 2019.
P0200.body:
On Monday, March 4, thousands of smaller Vendor Central suppliers did not receive the purchase order they normally get from Amazon each week. By Tuesday, many had been told the change was permanent and that they would do better selling on Amazon’s marketplace, Digiday reported. By Saturday, some accounts were being restored, with Amazon encouraging those vendors to enroll in Brand Registry and hinting that fighting counterfeits was one reason for the purge, Bloomberg reported.

A week of mixed messages makes one point clear. A vendor that loses its purchase order does not lose its shoppers; they are still searching for the product. It loses the company that carried its inventory, set its price and paid for its traffic. The fallback is Seller Central, and the time to price it is before the order stops.

Why Amazon would stop buying from suppliers that sell

The cuts look irrational at first. These vendors had products shoppers bought, and Amazon was making money reselling them.

Look at it from Amazon’s side of the ledger and the logic is tidier. When Amazon buys wholesale, it pays for the inventory, stores it, ships it and carries the risk that it does not sell. When the same product is sold on the marketplace, the supplier carries all of that, and Amazon earns fees on each sale. Amazon is determined to raise profits in its core e-commerce business, Bloomberg reported on March 7. Moving suppliers to the marketplace offloads the cost of purchasing, storing and shipping, and the push comes with an automated self-service system that needs no Amazon manager.

The vendors chosen fit that logic. Digiday described them as businesses selling $10 million or less a year on Amazon, without an assigned vendor manager. Those are the accounts where Amazon’s buying team spends time on relatively small sales.

Amazon vendor cuts and the Seller Central arithmetic

What changes for the brand is who pays for each piece of the sale. Take a product that sells for $40 on Amazon, costs the brand $10 to make and has been sold to Amazon at $20.

As a vendor (1P)As a seller (3P), FBA
Who sets the shelf priceAmazonThe brand
Brand’s revenue per unit$20 wholesale$40 retail
Referral fee, 15%Paid by no one$6.00
Fulfillment feeAmazon’s cost$5.00 in this example
Brand’s cash per unit before ads$20.00 less allowances$29.00
Who carries unsold stockAmazonThe brand
Who pays to be foundMostly AmazonThe brand

The 15% is Amazon’s referral fee in many categories (the Motley Fool’s fee table). The $5.00 fulfillment fee is an assumption for a small, light product; the real figure depends on size and weight and should come from Amazon’s current fee table.

On paper the seller column wins by $9 a unit. That gap is real, and it is also the price of the jobs Amazon used to do. Inventory now sits on the brand’s balance sheet until it sells. Price is now the brand’s decision, made against every reseller on the page. Traffic is the brand’s cost: say the product needs $4.00 of Sponsored Products spend per unit to hold its position, and the $9 gap is down to $5 before returns and storage.

So the move to Seller Central is a trade of margin for work and risk. Returns add to the bill as well: on 1P, a returned unit is mostly Amazon’s problem; on 3P, it comes back to the brand’s inventory or its write-offs, and in categories with high return rates that alone can eat a dollar or two of the gap. For many brands it is a good trade. It is a bad one for a brand that makes the move in a hurry, without the staff, the cash for inventory or the account set up.

What the console will not tell you during the switch

A vendor moving to Seller Central loses its history in one sense. Sales rank and reviews stay with the product page, but the brand’s advertising data, its pricing history as a seller and its in-stock record start from zero. The first weeks will look worse than the steady state. That is the switch, not the business.

Watch two numbers in those weeks. First, whether the brand holds the Buy Box on its own listings at its chosen price, since resellers who bought earlier stock may undercut it. Second, the share of sales arriving through ads versus organic search, because a falling organic share means the listing is losing ground, and the ad spend is covering for it.

Give the switch a quarter before judging it. A product that took years to build its position as a vendor will not show its seller economics in a fortnight, and a brand that pulls back after three weeks of weak numbers can hand the page to the resellers it was trying to displace.

Brand Registry matters here more than usual. It is what lets the brand control the content of its pages when other sellers are listing the same products, and it is the step Amazon pointed restored vendors toward.

The fallback, priced in advance

The rule is one line: price the Seller Central version of your top ten products in March 2019, at the real referral and fulfillment fees and a realistic advertising cost, whether or not your purchase orders arrive on schedule.

Then do the parts that take the longest. Open or reactivate the Seller Central account, finish Brand Registry enrollment, and decide which products you would move first if orders stopped tomorrow. A brand with those three done can switch in weeks. A brand without them spends the first month on paperwork while resellers fill the page, and setting that groundwork in place is part of the Amazon channel work we do for brands.

P0202.title: Target Plus makes the merchant relationship the only way in
P0202.alt: A red paneled door with a brass lock plate and an old key in the keyhole, set in a cream plaster wall.
P0202.ttag: Target Plus makes the merchant relationship the only way in | Kwontified
P0202.desc: Target Plus has no application form. Its invitations go to brands Target’s merchants already trust, and every seller borrows Target’s promises to guests.
P0202.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 14, 2019.
P0202.body:
Amazon and Walmart both publish a form for would-be marketplace sellers. Target Plus has none. When Target opened Target.com to third-party sellers on February 25, it said each partner is “carefully selected and invited into the program,” according to Target’s announcement, and TechCrunch noted that there is no application process at all. So the question every brand team will ask, how do we apply, has a short answer: you don’t.

You get invited, by people at Target who already know your products and trust you to carry Target’s promises to its guests. That makes the merchant relationship the only way into Target Plus, and it asks something of brands that an open marketplace never does.

Target Plus is a merchant’s shelf, opened to a few

Look at the first sellers and the program reads like a merchandising plan rather than a marketplace launch. The partners named at launch include SVSports, Mizuno, Kaplan Early Learning Company, Serenity Health & Home Décor and Music123, adding running shoes, outdoor décor and patio accessories, STEM learning toys, musical instruments and baseball gear to home, toys, electronics and sporting goods. Those are gaps in an aisle, filled by people whose job is managing aisles. Engadget reported that the first partners were brands Target had approached, Mizuno and Kaplan among them.

Target calls Target Plus “an initiative in its earliest stages.” It also accepts what that choice costs: TechCrunch reported that Target expects the curated model to keep quality high at the price of a smaller assortment. The contrast with the open marketplaces is stark. Third-party sellers accounted for 52% of the products Amazon sold in the fourth quarter of 2018, CNBC reported, and Walmart.com already had about 18,000 third-party sellers in April 2018, by Marketplace Pulse’s count as reported by RetailWire. Target is building a marketplace that is small on purpose.

The shopper is not meant to notice the seam. Target Plus items sit inside Target.com’s regular categories and turn up in ordinary browsing and search, with no separate Target Plus section to filter by, TechCrunch reported. Open the running shoe category and a partner’s listing shares the page with products Target bought and stocked itself. For a guest, it is all Target. That design explains almost everything else about the program, including who gets let in.

Every seller borrows Target’s promises to its guests

The reason for the gate sits in the shopper’s fine print. A guest who buys a Target Plus item gets the benefits of a Target purchase: 5% off with a REDcard, free shipping and easy in-store returns, Rick Gomez, Target’s chief marketing and digital officer, said in the announcement. Yet the partner, not Target, sells and ships the order. Until this launch, TechCrunch noted, some third-party items on Target.com shipped from vendors but were bought from Target.

So a Target Plus seller’s late parcel or wrong size becomes a Target guest’s complaint, and possibly a return at a Target service desk. Those stores already do most of the digital work. Target’s comparable digital sales grew 31% in the fourth quarter of 2018 and 36% for the year, and stores fulfilled nearly three quarters of fourth-quarter digital sales, the company reported on March 5. With about 1,850 US stores doing that work, Target has little reason to let strangers into the system.

The rest of the business points the same way. Owned and exclusive brands account for roughly one-third of its sales, according to its annual report for fiscal 2018. An institution whose identity is a curated shelf will treat a marketplace as one more part of the merchant’s job. Read that way, the invitation is a buying decision, and it will be made by people who think like buyers.

The invitation lands between two teams at the brand

Here the burden shifts to the brand. If your Target account sits with a wholesale sales team and your marketplaces sit with e-commerce, Target Plus lands squarely between them. The wholesale team holds the relationship that produces an invitation. The e-commerce team would run the listings, the shipping and the customer service. Finance has to decide whether direct sales on Target.com help or compete with the purchase orders Target already places. None of those teams can say yes alone, and a call from Target is a poor moment to start that conversation.

There is a quieter question of presentation too. Because Target Plus listings sit beside Target’s own products with no label to set them apart, the brand’s product titles, images and descriptions will be judged against the standard of the aisle around them. A listing written in haste for an open marketplace may read fine on Amazon and look out of place on a page Target’s merchants curate. The merchant who issued the invitation will see it.

It is too early to say how far Target will widen the circle. The evidence so far leans toward slow growth through invitations, with brands Target’s merchants already know getting the first calls. A brand that wants one should prepare before the phone rings rather than after.

Questions to settle before Target calls

  1. Who at our company owns the Target relationship, and does that person know Target Plus exists?
  2. Can we ship every Target Plus order to the standard Target promises its guests, from our own warehouse or a partner’s?
  3. Which of our products fill a gap in Target’s assortment, and which would compete with what Target already buys from us?
  4. Who answers when a Target guest returns one of our marketplace orders at a store counter?

Target Plus looks set to stay small for a while, and the brands invited early will be the ones whose wholesale and e-commerce teams already act as one; that is the kind of channel we run alongside Amazon and Walmart, and we are glad to compare notes on Target Plus readiness.

P0204.crumb: The Brand Analytics search terms report…
P0204.title: The Brand Analytics search terms report measures share, not size
P0204.alt: A peach and berry pie with one slice served on a plate with a fork on a sunlit wooden table.
P0204.ttag: The Brand Analytics search terms report measures share, not size | Kwontified
P0204.desc: Amazon’s Brand Analytics search terms report shows rank and share, not search volume. Read it for how concentrated a search is and who converts best.
P0204.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 19, 2019.
P0204.body:
Until February, a brand that wanted to see what Amazon shoppers search for, and which products they click afterward, needed vendor access and a budget: Brand Analytics was open only to vendors, with pricing starting at $30k, ChannelX reported when Amazon released it in Seller Central for brand owners enrolled in Brand Registry. Now the Amazon search terms report sits under the Reports tab for free, and the first question most teams ask of it is how big each search is. The report cannot answer that.

Every number in it is a share or a rank. The Brand Analytics search terms report tells you how a search divides its clicks and purchases among the top products, and how popular the search is relative to others. Read that way it is good market research. Read as a demand forecast, it misleads.

What the Brand Analytics search terms report counts

The report lists popular search terms for a period, each with a search frequency rank, and the three products shoppers clicked most after searching that term, according to ChannelX’s walkthrough. For each of those three products it shows two numbers. Click share is the product’s clicks after that search divided by all product clicks after that search. Conversion share is the same calculation with purchases. The two are calculated independently, so a product’s conversion share can be higher than its click share.

You can look at it from either side: search a term to see which products win its clicks, or search one of your products to see which terms send it clicks. Data is generally available within 72 hours after a period closes.

What it does not show is a count. There is no number of searches, clicks or purchases anywhere in the definitions, only ranks and fractions of totals the report never states.

Rank is an order, and shares are fractions of an unknown total

The pull toward reading volume into the report is strong, and it comes from the first column. A search frequency rank of 500 looks like a size, and it is tempting to sort by it and treat a term ranked 500 as twice as big as one ranked 1,000. Nothing in the definition supports that. Rank only says which of two terms was searched more often in the period. The gap between neighboring ranks can be large at the top of the list and tiny further down, and the report does not say which.

Shares have the same limit. A 40% click share on a search with heavy traffic and a 40% click share on a search almost nobody types look identical in the export. The report describes how a search divides its shoppers, never how many shoppers there are.

That is a narrower question, and a useful one. Take a search for “merino crew sock” with these top three products:

ProductClick shareConversion share
A40%30%
B15%25%
C10%12%
Top three combined65%67%

Two readings fall out of the table without any volume at all. First, the search is concentrated: three products take 65% of clicks and 67% of purchases, so a new entrant is fighting for roughly a third of the shoppers. A search where the top three take 25% would be open ground. Second, product B converts well above its clicks, 25% of purchases from 15% of clicks, while product A converts below its clicks. Shoppers look at A first and buy B more often than its visibility would predict. Whatever B does on its detail page (price, reviews, images) is worth studying before anyone raises a bid.

What the report leaves out, and how to fill the gap

If your product is not among the top three for a term, the report shows nothing about your share of it. That absence is information too: on the searches you care about most, it tells you whether you are in the conversation at all.

Movement over time is the other thing worth reading. Because each period is reported separately, the same term can be compared across periods. A rival whose conversion share climbs while its click share holds steady has probably improved something on its page, and the report shows it without waiting for your own sales to move.

For volume, use the data you already own. Sponsored Products reports list the actual search terms shoppers typed before clicking an ad, Practical Ecommerce explained in 2016, and the same reports show how many clicks and orders each of those searches produced for your ads. Those numbers are counts, limited to your own ads. Put the two reports side by side and you have the size of your slice from the ad report and the shape of the market from Brand Analytics, which is closer to a market picture than either gives alone.

How to read a priority search in five minutes

  1. Add the top three click shares and the top three conversion shares. Above about 60% the search is concentrated; treat entry as a share-taking fight, not a land grab.
  2. Subtract click share from conversion share for each product. A gap of five points or more in either direction says the detail page, not the ad, is doing the work.
  3. Check whether your own product appears for the term, and if it does not, find the terms where it does by searching your product instead.
  4. Pull clicks and orders for the same term from your Sponsored Products search term report before you set a budget against it.

The 60% and five-point thresholds are rules of thumb for sorting, not laws; adjust them once you have read a few dozen of your own searches. Reading these shares against ad data is part of how we plan Amazon advertising for brands, and we are glad to walk through your search terms report with you.

P0206.crumb: Project Zero gives brands power over…
P0206.title: Project Zero gives brands power over fakes, not over resellers
P0206.alt: A green gift box tied with twine and a brass crest beside open cardboard shipping boxes on a wooden table.
P0206.ttag: Project Zero gives brands power over fakes, not over resellers | Kwontified
P0206.desc: Project Zero lets invited brands delete counterfeit Amazon listings themselves. The power is real, but it covers fakes only, and it needs an owner inside.
P0206.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 21, 2019.
P0206.body:
Before Project Zero, one of the strongest moves a brand could make against counterfeits on Amazon was to leave. Birkenstock stopped selling on Amazon in the US, and Swatch walked away from a 2017 deal after Amazon declined to offer the proactive protections it wanted, TechCrunch recalled when Amazon launched Project Zero on February 28. Project Zero offers brands a different kind of power, one they exercise by staying: invited brands can now delete counterfeit listings themselves.

It is a real shift, and a narrower one than many brand teams will assume. The delete button covers fakes, not the resellers a brand would rather see gone, and it lands on whichever team inside the company is ready to hold it.

Project Zero hands over three tools, and one of them sits in the factory

Amazon describes three parts. Automated protections scan the more than 5 billion product listing updates Amazon processes each day, using logos, trademarks and other data the brand supplies, according to the company’s announcement. A self-service tool lets the brand remove a counterfeit listing directly, without reporting it and waiting for Amazon to investigate. And optional product serialization puts a unique code on every unit during manufacturing, so Amazon can check each one before it ships to a customer.

The last tool changes where brand power lives. A serialized product carries its own proof of authenticity, which means the decision to use it belongs to operations and the contract manufacturer as much as to the brand team. It costs $0.01 to $0.05 per unit depending on volume, TechCrunch reported. Enrollment itself is free, but it requires a government-registered trademark enrolled in Brand Registry, and for now it is open by invitation only, with a sign-up list for brands that want to be considered.

The serialization arithmetic is small next to the organizational work. Take a brand that ships 200,000 units a year through Amazon: at $0.05 a unit, codes cost $10,000 a year, and at $0.01 they cost $2,000. The harder part is getting a code printed on every unit at every factory, on every production run, and keeping the records that match them.

The four brands that tested the tools were Vera Bradley, Thunderworks, Kenu and Chom Chom Roller. During testing, Amazon said, its automated protections stopped on average 100 times more suspected counterfeits than it removed in response to brand reports. That figure is likely to fill the sign-up list quickly.

The delete button covers counterfeits and nothing else

Brand teams may hear “remove listings yourself” and think of the resellers they have spent years trying to dislodge. Project Zero does not reach them. A genuine product bought through a distributor and resold on Amazon is not a counterfeit, however unwelcome the seller. Removing that listing would be the kind of inaccurate report Amazon has warned about. “Brands must maintain a high bar for accuracy in order to maintain their Project Zero privileges,” its FAQ says, and Amazon monitors how brands use the tool.

So the power is over fakes. Control over who sells a brand’s genuine goods still comes from the older levers: what distributors are allowed to do in their contracts, where the inventory goes, and whether the brand sells on Amazon itself. Brand Registry adds one more, since only the registered brand owner can change a listing’s bullets, description and images. Project Zero sits alongside those levers. It does not replace them.

That distinction matters because a brand team that treats the delete button as a distribution tool will eventually misuse it, and the privilege can be withdrawn. A brand that loses Project Zero over a dispute with a reseller loses its fastest defense against the counterfeiters too.

The power lands on whoever inside the brand is ready

Counterfeits touch three functions at a consumer brand, and they seldom report to the same person. Legal holds the trademark registrations. E-commerce watches the listings and hears from shoppers who received something wrong. Operations manages the factories where serialization codes would be printed. Project Zero needs all three, and it needs someone to answer to Amazon for every removal.

The brands best placed to use it will be those that have already put those pieces in one place. Its rules reward a brand that keeps its trademark records current, knows what its genuine packaging looks like across every production run, and can tell within a day whether a listing is a fake or a legitimate reseller. That is a working process with an owner, more than a legal file.

Amazon is pulling in the same direction elsewhere. When it restored purchase orders to smaller vendors after its March cuts, it said that only vendors enrolled in Brand Registry would get automatic purchase-order fulfillment, and gave them 60 days to enroll, Modern Retail reported on March 12. Brand Registry is turning into the credential that decides what a brand can do on Amazon, and Project Zero is the most powerful privilege attached to it so far.

The shift, then, is in what brand power on Amazon means. It used to be measured by whether a brand could afford to walk away. Increasingly it will be measured by whether a brand has the trademark, the data and the internal owner to use what Amazon hands it, and to use it accurately. Before asking for an invitation, a leadership team should be able to name the person who will hold the delete button and the reseller policy that tells that person when not to press it.

If neither exists yet, building them is the kind of channel work we take on with brands on Amazon, and we are glad to talk through a Project Zero readiness plan.
