P0207.crumb: Amazon Stores insights credit sales the…
P0207.title: Amazon Stores insights credit sales the Store may not have made
P0207.alt: Stacked paper-wrapped parcels on a hand truck outside a brick shopfront with a fabric star in the window.
P0207.ttag: Amazon Stores insights credit sales the Store may not have made | Kwontified
P0207.desc: Amazon Stores insights count sales within 14 days of a visit, across the brand, so a Store looks strongest where shoppers already meant to buy. Tag traffic.
P0207.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 26, 2019.
P0207.body:
Open the insights dashboard for an Amazon Store and the sales column tends to make the Store look like a success. That number is generous by design. Stores insights count sales and units from Store visitors within 14 days of their last visit, and they include “halo” sales of the brand’s other products that were not on the page the shopper viewed, Tinuiti explained after Amazon’s January update to the dashboard.

So the Store gets credit for purchases that shoppers who already wanted the brand would have made anyway. A Store that earns its keep is one that brings in traffic the brand would not otherwise have had, and the dashboard only shows that if you split the traffic yourself.

Why the Store’s sales column looks so strong

Amazon Stores have been free to registered brands since they launched in 2017, multi-page and built from templates. The dashboard invites a simple reading: visitors, page views, and sales. The figures are reasonable on their own terms. They are also tilted toward the Store in three ways.

Start with the window, which stays open for 14 days after the last visit. That is plenty of time for a shopper to come back through a search, a Sponsored Products ad or a reorder, and still count as Store sales.

The credit is also wider than the page the shopper saw. Direct sales cover products on the page the shopper viewed; halo sales cover the brand’s other products, credited to the last page viewed. A visitor who looks at socks on the Store and buys a jacket nine days later counts.

And the audience arrives already sorted toward the brand. Someone who taps a brand’s logo in an ad after searching for the brand by name is already shopping that brand, and was likely to buy before arriving.

None of this is a flaw in the dashboard. It answers a narrow question, what Store visitors bought from the brand, and teams read it as a wider one, what the Store caused.

The attribution arithmetic, worked through

Think of a greeter at the door of a department store who is credited with every purchase a customer makes in the building over the next two weeks. The greeter’s numbers will look excellent, mostly because the people who walk through the door came to shop.

Take a Store that receives 2,000 visits in a month from Sponsored Brands ads on branded searches. Say 6% of those visitors buy one of the brand’s products within 14 days at an average order of $40. The dashboard reports 120 orders and $4,800 in sales.

Now suppose 4% of the same shoppers would have bought the brand anyway, since they had typed its name into the search bar. That is 80 of the 120 orders. The Store’s real contribution is the other 40 orders, about $1,600, a third of what the sales column shows. The 6% and 4% here are illustrations; the point is that the gap between them, not the total, measures the Store.

The same logic explains why Stores fed by branded search look better than Stores fed by anything else. The more a traffic source is made up of people already loyal to the brand, the larger the share of reported sales that would have happened without the Store.

A Store earns traffic only through sources you can separate

Stores insights split visits into four sources: Sponsored Brands ads (the former Headline Search Ads), Amazon organic traffic, tagged sources, and other. Tags are the useful one. A brand can create a source tag for any link it sends to the Store, from an email, a social post or a search ad on another site, and see that traffic on its own line. The January update raised the number of tags broken out from the top 30 to the top 100 and allowed all qualifying tags to be exported.

That makes a practical rule possible. Traffic from outside Amazon, carried by a tagged link, is the clearest case of the Store adding something: those shoppers were not on Amazon until the brand sent them. Organic Store traffic sits in the middle. Sponsored Brands traffic on the brand’s own name is the weakest evidence of all, because those shoppers were already there.

Two more details change how the dashboard should be read. Sales are reported by visit date, not purchase date, so a busy week’s results keep filling in for 14 days afterward and should not be read early. And sales data only runs back to December 25, 2017, so year-on-year comparisons for older Stores are limited. The same update added sales per visitor, orders per visit and units per order, which are useful for comparing pages within a Store even though they cannot say what the Store itself caused.

How to judge a Store from here

Treat the Store’s sales column as a ceiling, not a result. The number that matters is how much of that traffic came from tagged sources and non-branded Sponsored Brands campaigns, because those are the shoppers the Store had to win. If most visits come from ads on the brand’s own name, the Store is a pleasant landing page for people who were going to buy anyway, and budget spent pushing more of them there buys little.

The rule for a Monday review: tag every link you send to the Store, read results only after 14 days have passed, and report the share of visits from sources other than branded ads next to the sales figure. A Store that grows that share is earning traffic. Setting up that kind of baseline before a Store redesign is part of the measurement work we do, and we are glad to help you read your Stores insights.

P0209.crumb: Moving from Amazon vendor to seller turns…
P0209.title: Moving from Amazon vendor to seller turns a customer into a store
P0209.alt: An open wooden crate cabinet displaying honey jars, ceramics, baskets, linens and dried flowers in warm window light.
P0209.ttag: Moving from Amazon vendor to seller turns a customer into a store | Kwontified
P0209.desc: A brand that moves from Amazon vendor to seller stops serving a customer and starts running a store: price, stock and data come home, and so does the work.
P0209.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 28, 2019.
P0209.body:
For a brand that sells to Amazon as a vendor, the week starts with a purchase order. Amazon’s systems decide what to buy, the brand confirms and ships, and the order becomes the number the account team reports. On Monday, March 4, thousands of smaller vendors opened Vendor Central and found no order at all, Modern Retail reported, and some were told to sell on the marketplace instead. Most had their orders back within the week. The question the scare raised has not gone away: what does a brand actually take on when it moves from Amazon vendor to seller?

Control, mostly, and the work that comes with it. A vendor serves a customer called Amazon. A seller runs a store on Amazon’s property. The two sound similar on a slide, and they need different teams.

The weekly purchase order hides who is in charge

The vendor relationship is built around one ritual. Amazon forecasts, Amazon orders, Amazon sets the price shoppers see, and the brand’s job is to fill the order on time and negotiate the terms. That is a familiar shape for any company that sells wholesale to retailers. It lets a sales team run Amazon the way it runs any large account.

It also means the brand learns about its own Amazon business at one remove. When Amazon decided to stop ordering, the vendors affected had no lever to pull. One small brand owner told Modern Retail his orders were canceled after he had placed his own purchase orders based on Amazon’s 2019 projections; vendors had expected a 14- or 30-day warning before changes of that size, the follow-up report said. The order is a convenience until it stops; then it shows who was making the decisions all along.

What comes back to the brand as a seller

On the marketplace, pricing and fulfillment are the main differences, and sellers set their own prices, Modern Retail noted in its first report. That control widened in March, when Amazon dropped the rule that barred US third-party sellers from offering lower prices on other websites, TechCrunch reported. It is not total: Modern Retail also reported that Amazon had begun setting a maximum retail price for products.

Decisions about stock come back to the brand as well. A seller decides how much inventory to send and when, and can use Fulfillment by Amazon to keep the Prime badge, instead of waiting for a weekly order to tell it how much Amazon wants. The brand page comes with it. Once the brand is enrolled in Brand Registry, only the registered owner can change a listing’s bullets, description and images.

The data moves too, and it may be the largest change of all. Brand Analytics, which shows the top search terms and the products shoppers click after each one, was open only to vendors, with pricing starting at $30k, until Amazon released it in Seller Central in February for brand owners in Brand Registry, ChannelX reported.

Every one of those controls arrives with a job attached. Setting a price means watching competitors and the Buy Box. Sending stock means forecasting it and paying for storage. Owning the page means writing and maintaining it. John Ghiorso, chief executive of the agency Orca Pacific, told Modern Retail that Seller Central and Vendor Central “in most respects, actually mirror each other.” The screens may. The work behind them does not.

The team and the scorecard have to change with it

Here the real friction sits inside the brand. If the Amazon account has been run by a sales team measured on orders shipped to Amazon, that scorecard stops making sense on the marketplace, where nothing ships until a shopper buys. A seller business is judged on sell-through after referral fees, fulfillment fees and advertising, which is a retailer’s measure, and it needs someone who thinks like a merchant: about the price on the page, the stock in the warehouse and the search results around the product.

Amazon’s own direction is not hard to read. Modern Retail reported that Amazon wants its retail business to be as hands-off as possible and is trying to maximize volume on a marketplace that is growing faster than its retail arm. Third-party sellers already accounted for 52% of the products Amazon sold in the fourth quarter of 2018, CNBC reported. Whatever happens to any single vendor account, the weight of Amazon’s business is moving toward stores that brands run themselves.

Even the vendors who kept their orders were handed a seller’s condition. When Amazon restored purchasing, it said only vendors enrolled in Brand Registry would keep automatic purchase-order fulfillment, gave them 60 days to enroll, and pointed vendors that do not own a brand toward Seller Central, Modern Retail reported on March 12. Brand ownership, the credential that gives a seller control of its page, is becoming the price of remaining a vendor as well.

That is why the move is better treated as an organizational decision than a paperwork one. The brands that make it smoothly will be the ones that decide, before Amazon decides for them, who owns the Amazon P&L as a retailer would own it. The question for a leadership team now is simple to ask and harder to answer: if the purchase orders stopped next Monday, who in the company would set the price, send the stock and answer for the result by Friday?

If that question has no clear owner yet, running the channel as a store is the work we take on with brands on Amazon, and we are glad to talk through a vendor-to-seller plan.

P0211.crumb: Amazon DSP audiences are ranked by ROAS…
P0211.title: Amazon DSP audiences are ranked by ROAS in the wrong order
P0211.alt: Three trophy cups on a white winners podium set on grass against a deep blue wall.
P0211.ttag: Amazon DSP audiences are ranked by ROAS in the wrong order | Kwontified
P0211.desc: Amazon DSP remarketing tops every ROAS report because its shoppers were already close to buying. Rank in-market and lifestyle audiences by added sales.
P0211.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 2, 2019.
P0211.body:
Open almost any Amazon DSP report and the audiences line up the same way. Remarketing sits on top with a return on ad spend (ROAS) several times the others, in-market audiences come second and lifestyle audiences trail. The tempting move is to keep feeding the top line. That order mostly measures how likely each group was to buy before it saw an ad, so it says little about which audience the money changed.

The fix is to rank Amazon DSP audiences by the sales each one adds, which usually means testing for it, and to accept that the answer may put lifestyle above remarketing.

What the three Amazon DSP audiences actually select

Amazon DSP is the programmatic display and video platform Amazon called the Amazon Advertising Platform until it folded its ad brands into Amazon Advertising in September 2018. Its draw has always been the audiences: it is the way to buy Amazon’s shopper segments on sites and apps beyond Amazon’s own, Digiday explained when it was still AAP.

The segments are defined by how recently and how often someone shopped. In Amazon’s own pitch to agencies, published by Digiday, lifestyle audiences draw on up to the past year of habitual searching, browsing and buying, such as shoppers who browsed or bought health and fitness products in the past 12 months. In-market audiences are people who recently browsed a product in a given category. Remarketing and the brand’s own matched customer lists sit in separate groups.

Read those definitions as a ladder of purchase intent. A remarketing audience has already looked at your product page. An in-market audience is shopping your category this month. A lifestyle audience fits the profile of a buyer but may not be shopping at all. Each step down the ladder makes the group larger and less likely to buy this week, with or without an ad.

Why the ROAS ranking follows the ladder

DSP reports credit a sale to the campaign when a shopper who saw or clicked the ad buys within the attribution window. That rule has no idea whether the shopper would have bought anyway. So the audience with the highest baseline purchase rate collects the most credit, almost by definition.

Take a $40 product and three DSP lines, each spending $10,000 to reach 100,000 shoppers. Suppose that, unknown to the report, most of the remarketing buyers were coming back regardless.

AudienceAttributed salesWould have bought anywayAdded by the adReported ROASCost per added sale
Remarketing3,0002,65035012.0$28.57
In-market1,2009003004.8$33.33
Lifestyle6002004002.4$25.00

The report shows remarketing returning $120,000 on $10,000, in-market $48,000 and lifestyle $24,000. A planner who reads only that column moves money up the table. Count only the sales the ads caused and the order changes: lifestyle adds $16,000 of sales for its $10,000, remarketing $14,000 and in-market $12,000. On this incremental ROAS, the bottom line becomes the top one.

The shift comes from the baseline. In this scenario 88% of remarketing’s attributed buyers were already on their way back, 75% of in-market buyers were shopping the category anyway, and only 33% of lifestyle buyers would have bought without the push. Remarketing does real work. It just gets paid for a great deal of work it did not do.

None of these numbers is a benchmark, and the reorder is not guaranteed. A brand with a long consideration cycle, such as a $300 stroller, may find remarketing adds far more than in this table, because many viewers really do drift off without a reminder. A brand whose product is a weekly staple may find lifestyle buyers hard to move at any price. The point is narrower: the reported ranking cannot tell these cases apart, because it rewards the baseline in every case.

The trade-off between certainty and reach

There is a sound argument for remarketing, and it is not ROAS. Its buyers are close, so the money rarely goes to strangers, and the line is easy to defend in a budget meeting. Lifestyle money is the opposite: most of it lands on shoppers who will not buy this month, and the payoff, if any, is slower and harder to see.

The numbers lean the other way once a brand needs growth rather than defense. A remarketing pool is capped by the traffic the brand already earns, so the second $10,000 lands on the same people again and adds less than the first. A lifestyle pool is large, and the new buyers it brings in feed next quarter’s remarketing pool. That makes the bottom of the ladder the place where the next quarter’s sales are made, even when it looks weakest in this quarter’s report.

Testing each audience for the sales it adds

The test is a holdout per audience. Split each audience at random, keep about 10% from seeing any DSP ads for four weeks, and compare the purchase rate of the exposed group with the held-out group. The gap, multiplied by the size of the exposed group, is the number of sales the line added. Divide spend by that number to get the cost per added sale.

Run it on all three lines at once if the budget allows, because the comparison is the point. If remarketing still wins on cost per added sale, fund it with a clear conscience. If it loses, the case for shifting money down the ladder rests on your own data, not on a scenario in a blog post.

The working rule is short. Rank Amazon DSP audiences by cost per added sale, never by reported ROAS, and treat any line whose reported ROAS is far above the rest as the first one to test. If you would rather have someone design those holdouts with you, our team plans and runs Amazon DSP alongside Sponsored Ads.

P0212.crumb: Handbags on Amazon in 2019 are priced…
P0212.title: Handbags on Amazon in 2019 are priced around a $75 fee line
P0212.alt: A row of leather handbags in assorted colors on a wooden shelf, divided by a brass rod, against a blue wall.
P0212.ttag: Handbags on Amazon in 2019 are priced around a $75 fee line | Kwontified
P0212.desc: Amazon’s fee schedule now sorts handbags into tiers at $75, and brands that set prices from a wholesale grid are landing on the wrong side of it.
P0212.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 4, 2019.
P0212.body:
On a department-store floor, a handbag’s price is set by the room it sits in. Contemporary bags hang near the escalator, bridge brands one aisle in, designer pieces behind glass. Nobody prices a bag at $79 because of the store’s commission schedule. On Amazon, a growing number of handbag brands effectively do, because since April 2018 the fee Amazon charges on a bag changes sharply at $75.

That line, more than any trend in silhouettes or colors, is what changed for handbags on Amazon over the past year. The brands doing well in 2019 price around it on purpose. The ones that carried their wholesale price grid over unchanged are giving away margin at exactly the price points where accessories sell best.

Amazon’s apparel shoppers now outnumber Walmart’s

The stakes rose this year. Amazon overtook Walmart as the retailer the most Americans shop for apparel, moving up from second place a year earlier, according to Coresight Research’s annual survey of US apparel shoppers published in March 2019. Accessories ride along with that traffic: a shopper looking for a work tote today is often the same one who bought jeans there last month.

So the category is no longer a test channel run by an e-commerce coordinator with a spreadsheet of leftover SKUs. For many accessory brands it is becoming the largest single door, and the decisions that used to be made in a buyer’s office now happen inside a fee table.

How the handbags fee schedule merchandises the category

The rule is plain. From April 15, 2018, items in Shoes, Handbags & Sunglasses priced above $75 pay an 18% referral fee on the sale, while items at $75 or less stay at 15%, according to the notice Amazon sent sellers in January 2018. Because the higher rate applies to the whole price, not just the part above $75, the step is steep.

Take a crossbody bag. At $74, it pays $11.10 and the brand keeps $62.90. Raise the price to $79 and the fee becomes $14.22, so the brand keeps $64.78. The shopper pays $5 more and the brand sees $1.88 of it. The bag only pulls clearly ahead again much higher up: at $95, the fee is $17.10 and the brand keeps $77.90.

Follow the value and the pattern is clear. Between $75 and roughly $80, Amazon captures most of any price increase. That makes the band just above $75 the worst place on the shelf for a brand’s own margin. It is also where many contemporary handbag lines sit, because their wholesale grids were built around department-store markups and retail prices like $78 or $79.

The bottom of the category moved the other way. Amazon cut the minimum referral fee per item from $1.00 to $0.30 in most categories from February 19, 2019, Business Insider reported when Amazon announced the change in December. A $4 accessory in a 15% category now pays $0.60 instead of the old $1.00 floor. Small leather goods, key charms and bag straps that used to be bundled to clear the minimum can now stand on their own listings.

Why a brand name still carries the accessory shelf

There is a second change, quieter and arguably more encouraging for established brands. Amazon’s own labels have not taken over women’s fashion the way many feared. Apparel made up 88% of Amazon’s private-label brands but about 1% of their sales, and 82% of its women’s clothing labels sold fewer than 100 units a month, Bloomberg reported on a Jungle Scout study in October 2018. Nine of the ten weakest performers were women’s or girls’ clothing labels.

That study covered clothing, not handbags, so it is a signal rather than proof. Still, it fits what any shopper sees in a bag search: the listings that sell carry names people already know or reviews in the hundreds, and the anonymous ones compete on price alone. A handbag is a purchase people make partly for what the name says to others, and a search results page does not remove that.

What it does remove is the room that told the shopper which tier a bag belonged to. On Amazon, a $68 bridge-brand tote and a $28 unbranded one can sit next to each other in the same row. The brand has to carry its own positioning through photography, product titles that name the leather and the hardware, and a price that looks deliberate rather than inherited.

Questions for the handbag team before the summer line

The fee line turns a merchandising choice into a finance choice, which is why it tends to fall between teams. The people who set wholesale prices rarely look at Amazon’s fee table, and the people who run the Amazon account rarely have the authority to change a retail price. A few questions bring the two together:

  1. Which of our handbags are priced between $75 and $85 on Amazon, and what would we keep if each moved to $74.99 or up past $90?
  2. Are any small leather goods bundled only because the old $1.00 minimum made them uneconomic alone?
  3. Does our Amazon price ladder match the story our department-store floor tells, or does it blur bridge and entry lines in one search row?
  4. Who owns the decision when the fee table and the wholesale grid disagree?

I expect more accessory brands to build a separate Amazon price architecture this year, with fewer SKUs between $75 and $85 and more single-item listings below $20. The signal will be visible in search results by the holiday: price points clustering just under the line, and almost none just above it. If the fourth question has no clear answer at your company, that is the kind of gap we close when we run the channel day to day for accessory brands.

P0213.crumb: Without a frequency cap, Amazon DSP buys…
P0213.title: Without a frequency cap, Amazon DSP buys its costliest sales last
P0213.alt: Water from a brass faucet overflowing a glass tumbler onto a wooden counter edge.
P0213.ttag: Without a frequency cap, Amazon DSP buys its costliest sales last | Kwontified
P0213.desc: An average cost per sale on an Amazon DSP line hides what the fifth and tenth impressions cost. A frequency cap set from marginal cost stops the waste.
P0213.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 9, 2019.
P0213.body:
A DSP line can post a healthy cost per sale and still waste most of its budget. The number on the report is an average across every impression the line bought, and impressions are not equal. The first one a shopper sees does most of the work; the eighth, shown to the same person the same week, mostly adds cost.

That is why the frequency cap is the most consequential setting on an Amazon DSP line. A frequency cap is a limit on how many times one person can see a line’s ads in a set period. Set it from the marginal cost of each extra impression, and the line stops paying full price for exposures that barely move anyone.

Why the average cost per sale looks reassuring

Programmatic reports are built on averages, and averages are comforting. A line that spent $5,000 and reports a cost per sale under the brand’s limit looks like a line that worked. The mind anchors on that single figure, and it is hard to argue with a number that is already inside the target.

The trouble is that the average blends cheap sales with expensive ones. Advertisers have known for a long time that the early impressions carry the load. A study of CPM campaigns from 38 advertisers in the second half of 2003 found the first impression converted at about 2.5 times the campaign average, MediaPost reported on the Atlas DMT research. The first five impressions drove most of the actions.

The same study found the best cap varied from campaign to campaign, which is the honest part: there is no universal number. A later Search Engine Land analysis of a single display campaign found its return held above target up to eight impressions and then fell well below as conversions tapered.

Amazon DSP, the platform Amazon called the Amazon Advertising Platform until September 2018, sells the same kind of impression on the same kind of price, so the same curve applies to it.

How a falling curve and a flat price work together

The price of an impression does not fall when its effect does. At a fixed CPM, the tenth impression to one shopper costs exactly what the first did. So the cost of each added sale climbs with every repeat.

Take an Amazon DSP line reaching 100,000 shoppers at a $5 CPM, or half a cent an impression, for a $40 product the brand can spend $10 to sell. Suppose each impression adds a little less purchase probability than the one before:

Impression to the same shopperAdded chance of a purchaseCost per added sale
1st0.20%$2.50
2nd0.15%$3.33
3rd0.10%$5.00
4th0.06%$8.33
5th0.03%$16.67
6th and later0.01% each$50.00

Run the line uncapped and let it average ten impressions per shopper. It buys 1,000,000 impressions for $5,000 and adds 590 sales, or $8.47 per added sale, comfortably under $10. Cap it at four and it buys 400,000 impressions for $2,000 and adds 510 sales, $3.92 each.

The comparison is the useful part. The last $3,000 of the uncapped line bought 80 added sales at $37.50 each. In other words, 60% of the budget bought 14% of the added sales, and the report’s average never showed it.

Frequency on a DSP is also lumpier than an average of ten suggests. Some shoppers see two impressions and some see 20, because the platform keeps finding the people who browse the most. The heavy end of that distribution is where the $50 impressions pile up, and it is also where the shopper is most likely to start ignoring the ad altogether.

What the data can and cannot settle

These curves are a scenario, not a measurement, and the shape varies with the product and the audience. A considered purchase may keep earning through a sixth or seventh impression; a cheap repeat item may be done after two. Small audiences make it worse: a remarketing pool of a few thousand shoppers fills up quickly, so a generous budget turns straight into frequency.

The report often holds most of what you need. Where a line’s report shows reach as well as impressions, dividing one by the other gives average frequency. When that average climbs week over week while reach stays flat, the line is buying repeats, not new shoppers.

To find the cap itself, split a line into two or three copies with different caps, say two, four and eight a week, for the same audience and budget. Then compare the added sales per dollar across them, ideally against a held-out group that sees nothing. The cap where the next band’s cost per added sale crosses what you can afford to pay for a sale is the cap to keep.

Price the next impression, not the average one

A cap changes how the line spends, and that change is informative. If a capped line cannot spend its budget, the audience is smaller than the budget assumed. That is not a delivery problem to fix by lifting the cap. It is the platform telling you the extra money had only repeat impressions left to buy. Widen the audience, add a second segment, or move the money, and let the underspend stand as evidence.

Never run an Amazon DSP line without a frequency cap, and never set the cap from habit. When an extra impression per week costs more per added sale than the product can pay, lower the cap and move the money to new shoppers. If you would rather set those caps with someone who runs them every week, our team plans and runs Amazon DSP alongside Sponsored Ads.

P0215.crumb: Amazon beauty in 2019 fills the shelves…
P0215.title: Amazon beauty in 2019 fills the shelves that stores left empty
P0215.alt: An open cardboard box of skincare jars and bottles beside an empty wooden bookshelf against a teal wall.
P0215.ttag: Amazon beauty in 2019 fills the shelves that stores left empty | Kwontified
P0215.desc: Amazon beauty is growing fastest at the two ends of the aisle that Ulta and the drugstore serve least: everyday refills and independent brands.
P0215.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 11, 2019.
P0215.body:
Walk the cosmetics aisle of a drugstore and the brands at eye level are the ones you would expect: Maybelline, L’Oréal, COVERGIRL. Amazon’s version of that aisle looks similar at the top and strange just below it. In the mass cosmetics ranking for 2018 through early December, Maybelline led with 11% of sales and L’Oréal followed with 9%, but the fourth-largest brand was Wunderbrow, a brow gel, with 5%, ahead of COVERGIRL at 3%, according to Edge by Ascential’s estimates. A brand built around one product outsold a drugstore staple.

That ranking is a useful map of what changed in Amazon beauty over the past year. The category is growing fastest at the two ends of the aisle that physical stores serve least: the everyday refill a shopper does not want to drive for, and the independent brand that has no chain store to sit in. Amazon’s own rules now pull toward both ends at once, and the brands doing well have worked out which end they belong to.

Where Amazon beauty is growing

Start with the refill end. Makeup removers nearly tripled on Amazon in 2018, to more than $17 million in estimated sales through early December, making them one of the three largest mass cosmetics subcategories alongside eyes and lips, in the same Edge by Ascential data. Mass cosmetics as a whole reached an estimated $140 million, up 20%. Few shoppers browse for a makeup remover; they run out of it, and Amazon is where running out now gets solved.

The other end looks very different. In the first quarter of 2018, Luxury Beauty sales on Amazon grew 57% to about $200 million, while total beauty grew 30% to $900 million, One Click Retail, the firm now called Edge by Ascential, estimated. Professional salon and spa products grew 93%. The firm’s vice president of sales and marketing described growth moving “away from mass market consumables in favor of higher-end beauty products.”

Those two findings can sound contradictory. They are describing the same shopper doing two different jobs: replacing what she already uses, and finding something a store did not offer her.

Amazon is recruiting the brands its rivals do not carry

Read Amazon as an institution and its recent beauty moves line up with that split.

In June 2018, Amazon was preparing an Indie Beauty Shop, a storefront for independent brands. The entry rules were telling. A brand had to be at least 50% independently owned and could not be sold at Ulta, Target or Walmart, an Amazon business development lead told Glossy. Amazon was not asking for the brands everyone already stocks. It was asking for the brands that its biggest competitors had passed over or not yet found, and offering them a shelf.

The fee table points the other way. From February 19, 2019, Amazon cut the referral fee on Beauty and Health & Personal Care items priced at $10 or less from 15% to 8%, ChannelX reported when sellers were told in December. Items above $10 still pay 15%. On a $9 cleansing wipe, the fee falls from $1.35 to $0.72 a unit. That is a direct subsidy to exactly the kind of low-priced refill that used to be hard to sell profitably online, where the fee and the shipping could swallow the margin.

Put the two together and Amazon’s intent is plain enough. It wants the purchases that a shopper makes most often and the brands she cannot buy anywhere else. Both make Amazon the first place she checks. The prestige middle, the department-store and specialty-store brands that already have a strong home elsewhere, is the part these two moves do least for, and Luxury Beauty, at about $200 million a quarter, is still a fraction of the $900 million total.

What this changes for beauty brands

The practical consequence is that “selling beauty on Amazon” is no longer one strategy. A brand has to decide which end of the aisle it is selling to, because the two ends reward different things.

At the refill end, the product page competes on price, pack size and availability, and the shopper often searches by brand name because she knows what she wants. A mass brand with a hero product under $10 now keeps more of each sale, which makes it worth checking whether a product priced just above that line would sell more units just below it. The risk is running out: a shopper who finds the regular product out of stock will try a substitute, and the substitute may become the new refill.

At the discovery end, the work looks more like a launch. An independent brand without a chain door needs reviews, imagery and content that do the job a store tester would do, and it needs them before it spends on advertising. The Indie Beauty Shop gives such a brand a place on Amazon’s shelf; it does not explain the product to a shopper who has never heard of it. Wunderbrow’s rank shows that a single-product brand can outsell a household name when the page answers the shopper’s question.

Brands in the middle, with a prestige price and a specialty-store presence, face the hardest choice, and it is mostly about distribution politics rather than Amazon’s tools. A brand that already sells through Ulta or Target will not qualify for the indie storefront, and its first decision is whether an authorized Amazon presence helps or harms the relationships it already has.

The question I would bring to a beauty brand’s planning meeting this spring is simple: for each of your top ten products on Amazon, is the shopper refilling or discovering? The answer decides whether the next dollar goes to pricing and stock or to content and reviews, and it is usually different for products the same team manages side by side. If that sorting has not been done, it is the kind of channel work we take on for beauty brands on Amazon, so the brand team can focus on the products themselves.

P0217.crumb: FBA Small and Light pays when the fee…
P0217.title: FBA Small and Light pays when the fee saving beats lost sales
P0217.alt: A small twine-tied kraft paper parcel on a brass pedestal stand beside a white feather on a wooden table.
P0217.ttag: FBA Small and Light pays when the fee saving beats lost sales | Kwontified
P0217.desc: FBA Small and Light saves a fixed amount per unit. Whether it pays depends on your margin and on how many sales a slower or narrower offer costs you.
P0217.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 16, 2019.
P0217.body:
Every seller of a $7 lip balm or a $9 phone cable has done the same sum. The standard Fulfillment by Amazon fee for a small item has been $2.41 since February 2018, and when Amazon raised other FBA fees on February 19, it left that fee unchanged for items under 10 ounces and left Small and Light rates where they were. On a $7 product, that one charge is a third of the price before the referral fee is counted.

FBA Small and Light exists for exactly that product, and it charges less per unit. The program does not pay by default. It pays when the cents it saves are worth more than the sales the enrolled offer gives up, and that comparison comes down to a single ratio that most sellers never write down.

Why enrolling every eligible product looks right

The case for enrolling everything is simple and mostly correct. A fulfillment fee is a fixed cost per unit, and fixed costs fall hardest on cheap products. A flat discount on postage barely matters on a parcel worth $200; on a letter worth $5 it can be the whole profit. Small and Light was built on that logic. When Amazon launched it in June 2015, it offered free shipping on items under 8 ounces, delivered in three to eight business days instead of the two days Prime members expected, Yahoo reported. A year later it raised the weight limit to one pound and the package size to 16 by 9 by 4 inches, SellerEngine noted.

So the instinct is to check eligibility, see a lower fee, and enroll. The trouble is that the fee is only one side of the ledger. The program has limits on weight, size and price, and its offers have historically come with different delivery terms from standard FBA. Anything that makes the enrolled offer a little less attractive to a shopper reduces units sold, and lost units cost margin on every unit you no longer sell, not just a few cents.

How a fixed saving trades against a proportional loss

The arithmetic fits on one line. Call the saving per unit S and your margin per unit after fulfillment on standard FBA M. Enrolled, each unit earns M + S. If enrollment costs you a share d of your sales, you come out ahead only when (M + S) × (1 − d) is larger than M. Rearranged, the most sales you can afford to lose is S divided by (M + S).

Take three products, and say the program saves 70 cents a unit on each. Check the current rate card in Seller Central for your own figure, because the saving is the whole case.

ProductPriceMargin per unit on standard FBAMargin enrolledMost sales you can lose and still gain
Lip balm$7$1.30$2.0035%
Phone cable$12$3.30$4.0017.5%
Hair clips$14$6.30$7.0010%

The lip balm can lose a third of its sales and still earn more in the program, because the saving adds more than half again to a thin margin. The hair clips break even at a 10% loss. If a slower or narrower offer costs them 15% of their units, enrolling them lowers profit even though every unit sold is cheaper to ship.

The same ratio explains why the program tends to suit the cheapest items in a catalog and disappoint on the rest. The saving does not grow with price; the margin does. As the margin rises, S divided by (M + S) shrinks, and the program has less room to absorb any loss in sales.

Two smaller costs sit alongside the ratio. A product priced near the program’s ceiling cannot take a price increase without leaving the program, so enrollment quietly caps your pricing. And sellers who run the same product in both programs have had to manage two separate inbound processes, according to the same SellerEngine guidance, which means two stock positions to watch for one item.

What the data can tell you before you commit

The only unknown in the ratio is d, the share of sales you lose, and it is knowable. Most sellers never measure it because they enroll a product and compare its next month with its last month, which mixes the program’s effect with seasonality, price changes and competitors.

A cleaner test enrolls half of a group of similar low-priced products and leaves the other half on standard FBA for four to six weeks, then compares the change in units for each group over the same weeks. If the enrolled group’s units fall by less than the break-even share, the program is paying for that type of product. If they fall by more, it is not, however attractive the fee looks.

The test can mislead in one direction. A product with few competitors and loyal repeat buyers may show almost no loss, because its shoppers would have waited for it anyway. That is a real result, but it does not carry over to a product sitting in a crowded search results page next to faster offers.

A rule for enrolling a product

Before enrolling a product in FBA Small and Light, divide the per-unit saving by the margin you would earn with it. If that share is larger than the sales you expect to lose, enroll; if it is close, test first; and if the product earns more than a few dollars a unit, assume the program will not pay until a test says otherwise. Running that check across a catalog is part of how we manage FBA costs for brands on Amazon, product by product rather than program by program.

P0218.crumb: Instagram Checkout turns the social team…
P0218.title: Instagram Checkout turns the social team into a sales team
P0218.alt: An ornate antique brass cash register beside a vintage film camera, old books and mugs on a wooden desk.
P0218.ttag: Instagram Checkout turns the social team into a sales team | Kwontified
P0218.desc: Instagram Checkout moves the sale into the app, along with returns, fees and stock. Brands should decide which team owns Instagram as a sales channel.
P0218.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 18, 2019.
P0218.body:
At most brands, the Instagram account is run from the marketing floor: a social manager, a content calendar and a weekly report on reach and engagement. That team is rarely the one that handles returns. Since March 19, at the roughly 20 brands in Instagram’s Checkout beta, someone will have to. A shopper who buys inside the app now manages the order in a new Orders section, where she can cancel, start a return or contact the merchant, and Instagram tells her when it ships, TechCrunch reported. The merchant gets her contact details and address, and pays a selling fee Instagram has not disclosed.

That list of jobs is the real news in Instagram Checkout. The feature moves Instagram out of the marketing budget and into the sales channel, and it brings pricing, stock, service, returns and fees along with it. The brands that do well with it will be the ones that move ownership of Instagram to match.

Instagram was built into brands as a marketing channel

The way brands organize around Instagram made sense for the product Instagram used to be. When it began testing shoppable tags in November 2016 with 20 US retailers, including Kate Spade and Warby Parker, a tap showed a product’s name and price and then sent the shopper to the brand’s own site to buy, TechCrunch reported. Instagram did not charge the first partners for it.

For two and a half years, that was the deal. Instagram produced interest and the brand’s website closed the sale, so Instagram sat with the people who produce interest. The audience for that interest grew quickly: 90 million Instagram users tapped product tags in September 2018 and 130 million in March 2019, Fortune reported. Every sale those taps produced closed somewhere the e-commerce team already ran.

What moves when the register moves into the app

Checkout changes where the transaction happens, and every job attached to the transaction follows it.

Price is the first. A product tagged in a post now sells at the price shown in Instagram, which someone must keep in line with the brand’s site, its Amazon listing and its wholesale partners’ promotions. Stock is the second. An order placed in the app draws on inventory, and a post that sells out by lunch is a customer service problem by dinner. Then come the “contact the merchant” messages and the returns, which reach whoever is on the other end of the brand’s Instagram account unless someone decides otherwise. Finally there is the fee, a cost of sale that has to sit in somebody’s margin.

None of those jobs belong naturally to a social media team. They belong to the people who run a brand’s website or its Amazon business, who sit in a different department, report to a different executive and are measured on different numbers.

Instagram has also tied the two sides together. It said that interactions with Checkout will be used as a ranking signal for content, and that it will tell merchants which sales it generated, according to the same TechCrunch report. A post that converts well may travel further. So the social team’s own measure, reach, now depends partly on work it does not control: a price that holds, a size that is in stock, a return that is handled quickly.

Marketing leaders will argue that the social team knows the audience best and should keep the account, and they are partly right. The content, the voice and the timing of posts still belong with the people who make them. What changes is that the account now needs an operator as well as an editor. Brands that split the roles cleanly, with the social team choosing what to post and an e-commerce lead owning everything after the tap, avoid the slow version of this problem, in which a sold-out product keeps appearing in posts because nobody on the content calendar knew it had sold out.

Read Instagram as a retailer now

Instagram’s own description of its goal is plain. “Our intention was to build a complete shopping experience for people,” Vishal Shah, its head of product, told Fortune. A company that wants to complete the shopping experience is acting less like a media channel and more like a store, and stores have rules, fees and expectations of the brands they stock.

The launch list hints at where it expects to start. Among the brands TechCrunch named in the beta were Nike, Adidas, Zara, H&M, Uniqlo, Burberry, Dior and Prada, alongside nine beauty and cosmetics brands from MAC and NARS to Kylie Cosmetics and Huda Beauty. These are categories where the post already does the work of the shop window, and where shoppers arrive at Instagram ready to buy.

It is too early to say how many brands will be admitted, or what the fee will be. The direction is clear enough. For brands in fashion and beauty, the Instagram account is becoming a storefront, and the org chart at most of those brands still treats it as a billboard.

Questions to settle before asking for a Checkout seat

  • Who sets the price shown in Instagram, and who checks that it matches your site and Amazon each week?
  • Which stock does an Instagram order draw on, and who sees it before a tagged product sells out?
  • Who answers when a shopper taps “contact the merchant,” and how quickly?
  • Whose budget pays the selling fee, and whose sales target gets credit for the order?

A brand that can answer all four is ready to treat Instagram as a channel, and running it alongside Amazon and the brand’s own site is part of how we operate Instagram Shop for brands.

P0221.title: Mother’s Day 2019 rewards listings that settle the buyer’s guess
P0221.alt: A navy windowed gift box with oil, soap, sage and a bead keychain beside a vase of spring flowers.
P0221.ttag: Mother’s Day 2019 rewards listings that settle the buyer’s guess | Kwontified
P0221.desc: Mother’s Day gifts are chosen by people guessing what someone else wants. On marketplaces, the listings that settle that guess win the sale.
P0221.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 25, 2019.
P0221.body:
Last spring, 52% of family members said they thought mothers wanted flowers for Mother’s Day. Only 38% of mothers said they did, according to an Ebates survey reported by Retail TouchPoints. That gap describes the whole occasion. A Mother’s Day gift is chosen by someone who will not use it, guessing at the taste of someone who often wants something else.

On marketplaces, where the buyer is alone with a search box and a page of results, that guess decides the sale. With Mother’s Day 2019 falling on Sunday, May 12, the brands that do well will be the ones whose listings settle the giver’s question, not just the user’s.

Mother’s Day 2019 shoppers are buying in a category they do not use

The occasion is large and partly online. The National Retail Federation expects a record $25 billion of Mother’s Day spending this year, up from $23.1 billion in 2018, with 84% of adults celebrating and an average of $196 a person, against $180 last year, Chain Store Age reported on April 24. The 2018 survey, in the same Retail TouchPoints report as the Ebates figures, showed where the money went: 31% of shoppers planned to buy online, close behind the 35% who planned to shop at department stores.

Look at what they bought in 2018 and the guessing shows. Jewelry took $4.6 billion, flowers $2.6 billion and clothing $2.1 billion. Each is a category where taste is personal and a wrong choice is obvious. And 45% of shoppers planned to buy gift cards, worth $2.5 billion.

The gift card is the giver’s way out. It is what a buyer chooses when no product convinces them that it is the right one, and it means a brand’s real competitor on Mother’s Day is often not another brand at all. It is the decision to stop guessing.

Experiences pull the same way. A special outing such as brunch was planned by 55% of shoppers and was worth $4.4 billion, and 29% of mothers told the NRF they wanted a “gift of experience.” When a buyer cannot judge a product, a morning she will enjoy is the safer bet. A brand selling something in a box on a marketplace is competing with brunch as well as with the gift card, and both win by removing the risk of choosing wrong.

Product pages are written for the person who uses the product

Most product detail pages on Amazon and Walmart.com are written for the user. They list ingredients, materials, dimensions and care instructions, and they show reviews from people who bought the product for themselves. That suits most of the year, when the shopper and the user are the same person.

On Mother’s Day, the shopper is often a son who has never bought a serum, or a husband who does not know his wife’s ring size. He reads the same page and finds answers to questions he did not ask. What he needs to know is different: whether this is something she would want, whether it will look like a gift when it arrives, and what happens if he got it wrong.

The reason pages stay this way sits inside the brand. The team that writes product content usually works to a launch calendar and a category brief built around the core customer. The seasonal calendar belongs to a different group, often the promotions or marketing team, who plan the Mother’s Day push as a discount on the hero product. A deeper price cut does nothing for a buyer who is unsure the product is right in the first place. The gift buyer falls between the two teams, and nobody rewrites the page for him.

What a listing can do before May 12

The fixes are modest and mostly in the content, which makes them fast enough for the next two weeks.

A listing can say who the product suits. A main image or a line in the title that shows the product as a gift, with the box it arrives in, tells the giver he is in the right place. A bullet that describes who tends to like the product, in plain terms, does more for him than a list of active ingredients.

A listing can lower the cost of a wrong guess. Return and exchange terms are already set by the marketplace, but many pages never mention them where a nervous buyer would look. A gift set or a sampler that lets the recipient choose takes some of the guess away, and it competes directly with the gift card on the giver’s terms.

A listing can borrow the user’s voice. Reviews that mention buying the product as a gift, or receiving it as one, answer the giver’s question better than a five-star review about texture. Brands cannot write those reviews, but they can make sure their best customer questions and answers address gifting, and the Q&A section is theirs to work with.

Delivery still matters. Ebates found that 26% of shoppers admit they periodically forget the holiday, and late buyers default to whatever arrives in time. Stock that is in place early keeps a brand in that late-buyer search, but a page that settles the guess is what turns a late search into an order rather than a gift card.

Questions for the planning meeting

  • If someone who has never bought from your category landed on your best-selling page tonight, what on it tells him the recipient would want it?
  • Which of your products could be offered as a set or sampler that lets the recipient choose?
  • Who on your team owns gift-occasion content, as distinct from the Mother’s Day discount?

Brands that answer those questions before May 12 will have a better read on gifting before the next holiday arrives, and adapting product pages for the occasion is part of the channel work we do for brands on Amazon and Walmart.

P0223.crumb: Amazon other revenue grew 34% in Q1 2019…
P0223.title: Amazon other revenue grew 34% in Q1 2019, its first clean read
P0223.alt: A glass of water beside a tall stack of coins on a sunlit wooden table.
P0223.ttag: Amazon other revenue grew 34% in Q1 2019, its first clean read | Kwontified
P0223.desc: Amazon’s other revenue, mostly advertising, slowed from 95% growth to 34% in Q1 2019. Most of that drop is an accounting base effect, not a slump.
P0223.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 30, 2019.
P0223.body:
On April 25, Amazon reported that its “other” revenue, the line that mostly holds its advertising business, grew 34% in the first quarter of 2019 to $2.7 billion, or 36% excluding currency, in its results release. Three months earlier the same line had grown 95%. The same day, Modern Retail wrote that the line had grown about 100% a year for four quarters and suggested “the early gold rush could be coming to an end.”

That reading is understandable and mostly wrong. Most of the drop from 95% to 34% comes from an accounting change in early 2018 that inflated every growth rate that year. The first quarter of 2019 is the first quarter in which both sides of the comparison are counted the same way, and on that clean basis Amazon’s advertising is still growing about three times faster than its online store sales.

Why Amazon other revenue looked like it collapsed

Big swings in a growth rate pull attention, and the most recent swing pulls hardest. After a year of figures near 100%, a 34% quarter looks like a business hitting a wall, and it fits a story already in the air about advertisers cooling on Amazon.

The figures behind the story are real. Merkle’s first-quarter report, published on April 23, showed Sponsored Products spend among its clients up 19% from a year earlier and Sponsored Brands up 77%, ChannelX reported. That is healthy growth, but nowhere near 100%. So the slowdown looks confirmed from two directions.

The problem is the 2018 growth rates, not the 2019 one.

How the accounting change inflated 2018

In the first quarter of 2018, Amazon adopted a new revenue recognition standard. On its earnings call that April, it said the change added about $560 million to other revenue in that quarter alone, according to the call transcript. The change put revenue into the other line that the old rules had recorded differently.

That creates a base effect. Through 2018, each quarter was counted under the new rules and compared with the same quarter of 2017, counted under the old ones. It is like a store that adds a new department in January and reports the department’s sales as same-store growth for the rest of the year. The growth is real revenue, but part of it is a change in what is being counted.

The other line reached about $2.0 billion in the first quarter of 2018, $2.2 billion in the second, $2.5 billion in the third and $3.4 billion in the fourth, GeekWire reported. The first quarter of 2019, at $2.7 billion, is compared with that $2.0 billion, which already included the change. Both sides are now counted the same way.

Amazon disclosed the size of the change only for the first quarter of 2018, so any adjustment to the later quarters needs an assumption. Take the fourth quarter. It grew 95% to $3.39 billion, which puts the fourth quarter of 2017 near $1.74 billion. If the accounting change added about the same $560 million in the fourth quarter as it did in the first, underlying growth would have been about 63%, not 95%. Against that figure, 34% is a slowdown, but a far smaller one than the headline suggests.

Q4 2018Q1 2019
Reported growth in other revenue95%34%
Growth if the change added $560 million to Q4 2018about 63%34% (both periods on the new basis)

The 63% is an estimate built on one disclosed number. The direction it points does not depend on the exact figure: every 2018 growth rate in this line was flattered by the change.

What the clean number says about Amazon advertising

Read on a like-for-like basis, the first quarter tells a consistent story about where Amazon’s money comes from. Online store sales grew 10% to $29.5 billion. Third-party seller services grew 20% to $11.1 billion. Other revenue grew 34%. Advertising is growing more than three times as fast as Amazon’s own retail sales.

That ratio is the number brands should watch. In the first quarter of 2018, other revenue was about 3.9% of Amazon’s $51.0 billion in net sales. In the first quarter of 2019 it was about 4.5% of $59.7 billion. Each dollar a shopper spends on Amazon now carries more advertising revenue with it, which is another way of saying more brands are paying to reach the same shopper.

For a brand, that shows up as auction pressure. When ad revenue grows faster than the sales the ads sit beside, the cost of being seen on a search results page rises unless the brand’s own sales grow as fast. The Merkle data is consistent with that: Sponsored Brands spend among its clients grew 77% from a small base as more advertisers moved into the format.

Two things would change this reading. If Amazon discloses that the accounting change added much less than $560 million in later quarters, more of 2018’s growth was real and the slowdown is steeper than the table shows. And if the other line’s share of net sales stops rising for two or three quarters, the gold-rush story would start to fit the numbers.

A rule for reading the other line

Never compare a growth rate across an accounting change until both periods are on the same basis. For Amazon’s other revenue, that means treating 2018’s growth rates as inflated and the first quarter of 2019 as the first clean read. Then watch the share of net sales the line represents, quarter by quarter; if it keeps rising, plan for higher costs per click on the searches that matter to you, and budget for them in the same way we build retail media budgets for the brands we run.

P0224.crumb: Target Plus lends its store promises to…
P0224.title: Target Plus lends its store promises to only a few sellers
P0224.alt: Brown paper parcels tied with twine sit by a shop doorway behind a red velvet rope on brass stanchions.
P0224.ttag: Target Plus lends its store promises to only a few sellers | Kwontified
P0224.desc: Target Plus hands a seller Target’s own promises, from REDcard savings to in-store returns. That is why the invitation list is short and what it rewards.
P0224.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 2, 2019.
P0224.body:
Buy a pair of Mizuno running shoes from a third-party seller on Target.com this spring and something unusual happens if they do not fit. You can take them back to a Target store, the way you would return a Target T-shirt. Pay with a REDcard and you also get 5% off. Target described those perks when it announced Target+ on February 25: a curated assortment from outside sellers, with free shipping and easy in-store returns.

That detail explains the rest of the program. Target Plus does not give a seller a storefront. It lends the seller Target’s own promises, and a retailer that lends its promises has to choose carefully who carries them. For brands, the question is not how to get onto Target Plus. It is whether the brand already behaves like one Target would vouch for.

Target Plus is a marketplace built like a shelf

Target has said little about the program, and what it has said is cautious. Sellers cannot apply; Target reaches out to brands by invitation, and the company called the effort “in its earliest stages,” Retail Dive reported the day after the launch. The early partners CNBC named were Mizuno, the educational toy maker Kaplan and Casio, which makes keyboards. Sporting goods, early learning and musical instruments are aisles where a guest might trust Target’s store less than a specialist, and where the specialist can fill in range Target’s buyers do not stock.

Set that beside the two marketplaces brands usually compare it with. Amazon’s third-party sellers accounted for 58% of its physical gross merchandise sales in 2018, Jeff Bezos wrote in his annual letter to shareholders in April. Walmart had about 18,000 sellers on Walmart.com in April 2018, by Marketplace Pulse’s count, RetailWire reported, and grows by applications. Target launched with a short list it picked itself.

A merchant protects the edit

The choice makes sense once you look at what Target sells. Approximately one-third of Target’s 2018 sales came from its owned and exclusive brands, the company said in its annual report filed in March, with Cat & Jack among them. A guest who walks into Target is trusting the store’s edit: someone has already decided which throw pillows deserve the endcap and which stay in the stockroom. That edit is the brand, and the owned labels exist to protect it.

Amazon earns its trust differently. It promises the widest selection and lets ratings, reviews and the Buy Box sort the sellers. A bad seller there is a review problem. A bad seller on Target Plus is a Target problem, because the shopper returns the goods at a Target service desk and remembers whose name was on the bag.

Follow the value and the arrangement is clear. Target keeps the guest, the REDcard relationship and the store visit that a return creates; the seller gets Target’s traffic and Target’s promises. Target pays for that trade with its reputation, so it rations it. The same logic shapes its merchandising teams. A buyer who owns a category’s sales and the guest’s trust in that category will not hand a slot to a seller who might ship late, or one who undercuts an owned brand on the next shelf over.

That tells a brand what the program is likely to reward, even before Target publishes any criteria. A clear reason to exist next to Target’s owned brands, rather than a cheaper copy of one. Fulfillment that a store team would not have to apologize for. Product pages and imagery that look as if they belong on Target.com. And a category where Target’s own range is thin, which is what the first partners have in common.

The slow marketplace may be the point

It is too early to say how large Target Plus will become. Target has not published seller counts or sales, and an invitation-only program grows only as fast as Target’s merchants want it to. The evidence so far leans toward slow growth by design: a retailer whose identity is curation would rather add a few dozen sellers it trusts than thousands it has never met. Each new seller is another company whose late package or broken toy ends up at a Target guest service desk, and Target’s merchants, not an algorithm, will answer for it.

That pace changes how a brand should plan. On Amazon, a brand can register on Monday and compete for the same search by Friday. On Target Plus, the brand’s relationship with Target’s merchants comes first, and the marketplace is one of the places that relationship can lead. For a brand already selling to Target as a vendor, that conversation may sit with the wholesale team rather than the e-commerce team, which is where Target Plus can fall between two desks.

Questions for your team before Target calls

  1. If a Target merchant looked at our Amazon detail pages and reviews this week, would they see a brand they could put Target’s return policy behind?
  2. Which of our categories are thin in Target’s own assortment, and where do we compete head-on with an owned brand?
  3. Who owns the Target relationship inside our company, and does that person know Target Plus exists?
  4. Could our fulfillment meet a standard set by a store’s guest service desk rather than a marketplace’s minimum?

A brand that can answer those four will be ready whenever the invitation arrives, and in better shape on Amazon and Walmart.com in the meantime. Getting the pages, the reviews and the fulfillment into that shape across retailers is the work behind our Target and Walmart marketplace practice.

P0226.crumb: One-day Prime moves FBA costs from the…
P0226.title: One-day Prime moves FBA costs from the fee table to inventory
P0226.alt: A vintage stopwatch sits on a wooden shelf in a stockroom lined with cardboard boxes and crates.
P0226.ttag: One-day Prime moves FBA costs from the fee table to inventory | Kwontified
P0226.desc: Amazon is spending $800 million on one-day Prime without raising FBA fees. Sellers will still pay for the speed, mostly in inventory they hold in the network.
P0226.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 7, 2019.
P0226.body:
Amazon will spend about $800 million in the second quarter to move Prime from two-day to one-day shipping, CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the April 25 earnings call, starting in North America, Retail TouchPoints reported. For a seller the obvious question is when the FBA fee goes up. It may not need to, at least not soon. The cost of one-day delivery is more likely to reach Fulfillment by Amazon sellers through their inventory than through the fee table, because speed is bought with stock sitting close to the shopper.

Why sellers look at FBA fees first

The fee table is where Amazon’s costs have always reached sellers, so it is the natural place to look. Amazon changed fulfillment and referral fees on February 19 and storage fees on February 15, it told sellers in December. A seller who has watched fees adjust every year reasonably expects an $800 million quarter to show up there next.

Two details point the other way. Amazon has not attached one-day Prime to any new seller fee, and Olsavsky gave no date for when one-day becomes the standard for all members, only “steady progress quickly and through the year,” according to CNN’s report of the call. And in February Amazon dropped long-term storage fees for units held 181 to 365 days, ChannelX noted. A company about to ask sellers for more inventory makes holding inventory cheaper first.

Amazon also needs those sellers on board. Third-party sellers made up 58% of physical gross merchandise sales in 2018, Jeff Bezos wrote in April. One-day Prime cannot be the standard unless most of that 58% is in buildings near the customer.

How one-day delivery raises the inventory a seller holds

Two-day delivery lets Amazon ship from a building a long way from the shopper. One-day delivery mostly does not, so the same SKU has to sit in more buildings, closer to more shoppers.

Splitting stock across buildings raises the total a seller must hold. Each building faces its own swings in demand, and each needs its own buffer against selling out. When all the stock sat in a few places, a slow week in one region and a busy week in another cancelled out inside the same pile. Spread across many places, they no longer cancel, so the buffers add up.

Take a $30 SKU that costs $10 to land and earns $8 after fees and advertising. It sells about 70 units a week, 3,600 a year. Under two-day delivery the seller keeps six weeks of cover in the network: 420 units. To stay in stock in enough buildings for one-day, say the seller needs nine weeks: 630 units.

The extra 210 units tie up $2,100 of stock. At a carrying cost of 20% a year (capital, storage and the risk of the stock ageing), that is $420 a year. To break even, one-day eligibility has to sell 53 more units a year, about 1.5% more volume.

That is a low bar, and it is why the trade usually favors sending the stock. The risk sits elsewhere. Those 630 units are a bet on the forecast, and a SKU that slows down now has nine weeks of stock in Amazon’s buildings instead of six, where it ages toward storage fees and removal decisions.

What it does to Seller Fulfilled Prime and the FBA choice

Sellers who ship their own orders feel the change first. A merchant that can deliver in two days can be certified to ship Prime orders itself; under a one-day standard, more sellers will have to ship through Amazon unless they can match the speed, Modern Retail argued the day after the call. Most brands cannot run one-day delivery nationally from one warehouse.

Analysts read the same arithmetic from Amazon’s side. Morgan Stanley’s Brian Nowak suggested one-day Prime may be Amazon’s “Trojan Horse” for building its third-party logistics network, Buy Box Experts reported. Whatever the motive, the effect for a seller is the same: the Prime badge gets harder to earn outside FBA, and FBA rewards the sellers who can keep more stock in more places without letting it age.

Nobody outside Amazon knows yet how much one-day eligibility lifts conversion, and Amazon has not said which SKUs will qualify first. A seller can still check the break-even before deciding, and then measure the lift instead of assuming it.

The cleanest reading comes from the Business Reports in Seller Central. Unit Session Percentage, the share of detail page sessions that end in an order, is the number one-day delivery should move. Track it weekly for the SKUs that gain the one-day promise and for a comparable set that has not yet, so the seasonal swing in May and June does not get credited to shipping speed.

If both groups rise together, the lift came from the season. If only the one-day group rises, the difference is the number to put into the break-even. Sessions matter too: a faster promise can help a listing’s ranking as well as its conversion, but that effect is slower and harder to separate, so treat it as upside rather than plan on it.

The rule for one-day Prime

Divide the extra carrying cost by the unit margin, then by annual units. If the lift you need is below 2%, send the stock and watch sell-through by week. If it is above 5%, the SKU is a candidate to stay on two-day delivery until the data says otherwise. Between those, run the test on your best sellers first, where the forecast is most reliable. Planning that inventory across FBA and your own warehouse is part of how we run Amazon channels for brands.

P0228.title: Instagram Checkout moves the impulse aisle into the feed
P0228.alt: Small glass jars of colorful sweets in a wire caddy beside a smartphone on a rustic wooden table.
P0228.ttag: Instagram Checkout moves the impulse aisle into the feed | Kwontified
P0228.desc: Instagram Checkout lets shoppers buy a tagged product without leaving the app. That turns the feed into a checkout lane, which sells a different product mix.
P0228.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 9, 2019.
P0228.body:
Every supermarket stocks the same things by the register: gum, batteries, lip balm, a magazine. Nobody drives to the store for them. They sell because the shopper is already holding a wallet and the decision takes a few seconds. On March 19, Instagram moved that lane into the feed. Instagram Checkout lets shoppers buy tagged products from 23 brands, Nike, Burberry and H&M among them, without leaving the app, in one tap once their payment details are saved, Fortune reported.

The button matters less than what it does to the purchase. Social commerce on Instagram has been a discovery business: the shopper sees a product, taps the tag, leaves for a website and often never finishes. Checkout removes the trip, and with it the pause in which an impulse cools. Brands now have an impulse channel, and it sells different products, at different prices, to a different frame of mind than the search-led channel they run on Amazon.

Instagram Checkout shortens the distance from discovery to purchase

The demand was already there. Instagram said 130 million people were tapping product tags on shopping posts each month by March, up from 90 million in September, according to the same Fortune report. In Curalate’s survey of 1,000 US consumers, 76% said they had bought something after seeing it on a brand’s social media, and 49% said an easy payment system would make them more likely to buy, Philadelphia Magazine reported in November 2017.

That intent had to survive several screens. Until March, buying from a tagged post meant tapping through to the retailer’s website in a browser outside the app, where the shopper met a login screen, a shipping form and a card number she had not memorized. Each step is a chance to reconsider. A shopper who types “running shoes” into Amazon has already decided to buy something, so she will tolerate a form. A shopper scrolling past a friend’s beach photo has decided nothing, and every extra screen is a reason to keep scrolling.

Checkout collapses those screens into one. In store terms, Instagram has taken the register out of the back of the shop and put it next to the display.

What sells in a checkout lane

The register has rules, and the feed will learn them quickly. Products that sell at the till are cheap enough that a bad choice costs little, simple enough to judge at a glance, and need no comparison with the shelf behind them. On Instagram that looks like a lipstick shown on a face, a graphic tee, a phone case, a bottle of nail polish in this season’s color. A $180 serum with a long ingredient story, or a mattress, will still send most shoppers to reviews and search, and a button in the feed will not change that.

This creates an awkward mismatch inside brands. The products a brand features on Instagram tend to be chosen for how they look in the grid: the launch, the campaign piece, the item the creative team photographed. The products most likely to sell from a tap are often the cheaper, simpler items that rarely make the campaign. A brand that tags only its hero products in Checkout may conclude the feature does not work, when the assortment was built for a different shelf.

The first buyers will also be closer to the brand than a search shopper is. In Avionos’s survey of 1,409 consumers, about 55% had bought something through a social channel, yet 60% had never bought a product promoted by an influencer or celebrity, Retail Dive reported. Social selling works best where trust already exists. Early Checkout sales will lean on people who follow the brand and see its own posts, which makes the post itself the shelf and the caption the shelf talker.

Who owns the lane

The harder question is organizational, and it is one leadership teams will face within the year if Instagram opens the beta as planned. At most brands, Instagram belongs to brand marketing, which is measured on reach and engagement. The e-commerce team runs Amazon and the website and is measured on sales and margin. Checkout puts a sales line inside the brand team’s channel.

Someone now has to decide which products are tagged, at what price, and whether the stock behind them comes from the website’s inventory or a separate allocation. Instagram charges brands a fee on each transaction and has not said how much, so the margin on a Checkout sale is still unknown. Leave those calls with the team that picks photos for the grid and the lane will be stocked for looks. Hand them to the e-commerce team without the creative voice and the posts will read like a product feed, which is the one thing Instagram users scroll past fastest.

The lane is also about to get longer. On April 30, Instagram said it would start testing product tags in creators’ posts, limited to brands in the Checkout beta, TechCrunch reported. Once creators can sell, the question of who sets the price and who pays the commission arrives in the influencer contract as well as the media plan.

The brands that get value early will treat Checkout as a new store format rather than a new button: pick the products that would sell at a register, show them in posts built to be bought from, and give one person the sales number and the authority to change the assortment every few weeks. Choosing that assortment and running the shop behind it is part of the Instagram work we do for brands, and we are glad to walk your team through a first Checkout assortment.
