P0229.crumb: Amazon removal orders cost less than the…
P0229.title: Amazon removal orders cost less than the slow tail of FBA stock
P0229.alt: A hand truck stacked with worn cardboard boxes stands in a warehouse aisle between tall wooden shelves.
P0229.ttag: Amazon removal orders cost less than the slow tail of FBA stock | Kwontified
P0229.desc: Aged FBA units cost about ten times more a month to hold once they pass 365 days. Work out where your slow tail stops paying and remove it before October.
P0229.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 14, 2019.
P0229.body:
Most sellers treat an Amazon removal order as an admission of defeat. The stock was bought, shipped and received, and paying Amazon to send it back, or to destroy it, feels like paying twice for a mistake. So the units stay. For the slow tail of an aged SKU that is usually the more expensive choice, because FBA charges for holding a unit every month and raises that charge at dates anyone can read off a calendar, while a removal is charged once.

The fee schedule makes the steps unusually sharp in 2019. Since February 15, Amazon no longer charges a long-term storage fee on units held 181 to 365 days, and the minimum fee on units held longer fell from $0.50 to $0.15 a unit, ChannelX reported. Units past 365 days still pay $6.90 per cubic foot, assessed monthly on the 15th since September 2018, on top of monthly storage of $0.69 per cubic foot from January to September and $2.40 from October to December for standard-size items, SellerEngine reported when the schedule was announced.

What an aged unit costs to hold on FBA

Take a standard-size unit of 0.1 cubic feet, roughly a boxed candle. Here is what one unit costs a month to hold, by age and season, at those rates.

Monthly cost per unit (0.1 cu ft)January–SeptemberOctober–December
Under 365 days old$0.07$0.24
365 days or older$0.76$0.93

The jump at 365 days is the one that matters. A unit that cost seven cents a month in the spring costs about ten times as much once it ages past a year, and more again from October 1. Under the old schedule, the first long-term charge arrived at six months. Under the 2019 rules the six-month charge is gone, which makes it easy to forget that the one-year charge is now the whole problem.

Where the slow tail stops paying

Say that candle sells for $24 and leaves $6 of margin after referral and fulfillment fees. You hold 600 units, all received in the spring of 2018, and the SKU sells 20 a month. At that pace the last unit sells two and a half years from now.

Each month an aged unit waits costs about $0.76, more in the fourth quarter. Divide the $6 of margin by $0.76 and you get roughly eight months. A unit that will sell within about eight months still earns something after its storage bill. A unit that will sit longer than that has already spent its margin on rent before it sells. With 20 sales a month, that is the first 160 units or so. The other 440 are the tail, and each of them is worth less in the building than out of it, whatever happens to it next.

Removal changes only one line of that arithmetic. Say removal costs $0.50 a unit for this item (check the current rate for its size tier in Seller Central before you run the numbers). That is less than one month of aged storage. Paying it once to move the tail to your own warehouse, a discount channel or a donation is cheaper than paying $0.76 or more every month until the last unit sells. Disposal is priced separately and makes sense only for stock with no value outside Amazon.

Why sellers hold on anyway

The pull to keep the units has a name: the money already spent on them. The landed cost, the inbound freight and the label time are gone whatever you decide, but they make removal feel like a loss being recorded. Holding feels like keeping an option open. On a SKU selling 20 a month, the option costs more each month than it is worth.

A second pull is optimism about velocity. The forecast that bought 600 units assumed a faster sell-through, and the plan to hold is usually a plan to be right about it after all. If a price cut or a deal could move the tail faster, run it first, and run the same arithmetic on the new velocity. If the tail still runs past eight months, remove it.

Aged stock also has a cost that does not show on the storage invoice. Since July 2018, FBA storage limits have been tied to the Inventory Performance Index, with an overage fee of $10 per cubic foot above the limit, according to the same SellerEngine report. Slow, aged units weigh on that index at the moment you need room for the fourth quarter.

The timeline back from October

Work back from the two dates that raise the bill: each unit’s 365-day mark, assessed on the 15th of the month, and October 1, when standard-size storage rises from $0.69 to $2.40 per cubic foot.

  1. In May, pull the inventory age report and list every SKU with units that will pass 365 days before the end of the year, with its current monthly sales.
  2. In June, work out for each one how many months its stock will take to sell, and divide margin by the aged monthly cost to find where the tail begins. Try a price cut or a deal on the SKUs closest to the line.
  3. In July and August, place removal orders for the tail on any SKU whose units cross 365 days before October, so the units leave before the next assessment on the 15th.
  4. In September, remove the remaining tail before October 1, and use the space the removals release for fourth-quarter inbound.

A removal order is a pricing decision about the last units of a SKU, made with numbers you already have. Working out that tail SKU by SKU is part of the marketplace operations work we do for brands on FBA, and we are glad to run it on your aged inventory before October.

P0230.crumb: Department store brands on Amazon have no…
P0230.title: Department store brands on Amazon have no concession counter
P0230.alt: An empty glass display case roped off with burgundy velvet ropes and brass posts in a vacant store.
P0230.ttag: Department store brands on Amazon have no concession counter | Kwontified
P0230.desc: Brands built on department store counters are back on Amazon, often run like a wholesale account. Amazon rewards the brand that runs it like its own shop.
P0230.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 16, 2019.
P0230.body:
Walk through a large department store and the floor tells you which brands have power. The strongest ones have a shop within the shop: their own fixtures, their own lighting, staff who know the line, and an assortment the brand chose. Everyone else gets a rack. For years, brands built for that floor kept their distance from Amazon. In the spring of 2019 they are arriving in numbers, and most of them are walking onto a floor with no concession counter at all.

The movement is plain in the trade coverage. Chico’s plans to close at least 250 of its namesake stores, and has grown its Amazon shop to about 2,300 styles, nearly six times its count at launch in May 2018, Reuters reported on April 9. Lands’ End started selling flannel shirts and down coats on Amazon in February 2018, partly to make up for sales lost at Sears. Aldo moved its roughly ten-year Amazon relationship to a wholesale model in 2019, and Nike, Under Armour and Levi Strauss all distribute through Amazon. The department store brand has come back to Amazon. The question is whether it brought the right habits.

How department store brands on Amazon learned the wrong lesson

The habits come from the floor plan. A department store relationship runs through a buyer: the brand sells in a season’s assortment at wholesale, negotiates space and markdown support, and measures itself on what the store ordered. The store does the rest, from shelving to the sales associate who answers the shopper’s question. That model made sense when the store controlled the shopper’s path through the building. It is how a generation of sales teams learned to think about a retail partner.

When those brands first came to Amazon, many simply added it to that list of accounts. Amazon placed purchase orders, so it looked like a buyer. The account went to the wholesale team, the measure was sell-in, and the product pages were whatever the catalog feed produced. But Amazon has no shop within the shop, no associate and no floor manager placing the brand near the entrance. Every brand gets the same rack, a product detail page in a search result, and the brands that win are the ones that act as their own concession staff.

What Amazon wants from these brands

Read Amazon as an institution and its interest in these particular brands is easy to see. It wants to be taken seriously in fashion. The same Reuters report notes that Amazon has sponsored fashion weeks, runs photo studios in several cities and offers Prime Wardrobe in the US, Britain and Japan, and that a Coresight survey found it had overtaken Walmart as the most-shopped clothing retailer in the US. Established brands give a fashion business credibility that private label cannot buy on its own.

That gives the brands more bargaining power than they tend to use. Aldo, for one, said its wholesale arrangement gives it data on the basket makeup of customers who buy its products, which can shape how it designs collections. A brand that negotiates for the data, and for control over how its pages look, is treating Amazon as a partner it can shape. A brand that only accepts purchase orders is treating it as another rack.

The pressure runs both ways. Amazon had 109 of its own clothing, shoe and jewelry brands at the start of 2019, more than five times as many as two years earlier, according to TJI Research figures cited by Reuters, and Lands’ End’s swimwear already competes with Amazon’s Coastal Blue label. Amazon says private label is about 1% of its retail sales. A brand that shows up without content, inventory discipline or a point of view leaves the shelf open to whoever does.

The department store has become Amazon’s front desk

The clearest sign of how far the floor has shifted came on April 23. Kohl’s said it would accept Amazon returns, unpackaged and unlabeled, at all of its more than 1,150 stores from July, expanding a pilot that began in 2017 and runs in about 100 stores, CNBC reported. A department store chain is now offering its floor space to the online retailer its brands are moving toward, in the hope that the shoppers who come in with a return will stay to buy.

For a brand that grew up on department store counters, that is a striking reversal. The store that once decided where its products sat is now a returns desk for Amazon, and the shelf that matters is a page the brand can write itself if it chooses to. The concession counter still exists. It has moved onto the page.

Questions for the next Amazon review

  1. Who runs our Amazon business: the team that sells in to wholesale accounts, or a team measured on sell-through, conversion and page quality?
  2. If Amazon is a wholesale partner, what did we ask for besides a purchase order, and do we receive any customer or basket data?
  3. Which of our products already have a credible Amazon private label alternative, and what on our pages makes the case for paying more?
  4. Would we accept, at our best department store account, the product pages we show on Amazon now?

A brand that answers the first question with “the wholesale team” has probably answered the other three as well. Running Amazon day to day as the brand’s own shop, with the pages, assortment and inventory a concession team would once have managed, is the channel work we do for brands, and we are glad to compare notes on how your Amazon account is run.

P0232.crumb: Seller Fulfilled Prime costs what your…
P0232.title: Seller Fulfilled Prime costs what your farthest customer costs
P0232.alt: A white delivery van drives down a narrow country lane through green fields toward a distant farmhouse.
P0232.ttag: Seller Fulfilled Prime costs what your farthest customer costs | Kwontified
P0232.desc: Seller Fulfilled Prime standards look like the hard part. The real cost is set by geography: the share of Prime orders ground shipping cannot reach in time.
P0232.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 21, 2019.
P0232.body:
Ask a seller what makes Seller Fulfilled Prime hard and the answer is usually the scorecard. Amazon’s thresholds are strict: since July 31, 2018, Prime orders shipped by the seller must go out on time at least 99% of the time, cancellations must stay at or below 0.5%, and at least 98% of Prime labels must be bought through Amazon’s Buy Shipping service, Amazon told sellers on its Seller Central forums. Those numbers decide whether a seller keeps the badge. They rarely decide whether the badge pays. That is set by a map: how much of the country a seller’s warehouse can reach by ground inside the Prime promise.

Seller Fulfilled Prime, or SFP, lets a seller ship Prime orders from its own warehouse instead of sending stock to Amazon’s fulfillment centers. The appeal is real. A brand keeps its inventory, its packaging and its warehouse costs, and still shows the Prime badge that Prime members look for. The catch is that Amazon’s promise is national and a seller’s warehouse is not.

Why the Seller Fulfilled Prime scorecard looks like the main cost

The scorecard gets attention because it is visible and unforgiving. A 99% on-time rate means a warehouse has to be staffed for its busiest day, not its average one. A 0.5% cancellation ceiling means inventory counts have to be right in real time. ChannelX described the autumn 2018 version of these rules as a tightening, and for a small operation they are: one bad week of carrier pickups can cost the badge.

But a warehouse that meets the scorecard can still lose money on every Prime order. The scorecard measures whether you kept the promise. It says nothing about what the promise cost to keep. A seller can post a perfect week and still find, at the end of the month, that its carrier invoice grew faster than its Prime sales. That gap is where SFP decisions should start.

Where the cost of the Prime promise comes from

Ground shipping from one warehouse reaches nearby states in a day or two and the far side of the country in four or five. Every Prime order outside the two-day ground footprint has to be upgraded to an air service to arrive in time. So the blended shipping cost of SFP depends on one number: the share of Prime orders that fall outside that footprint.

Take a brand shipping 2,000 Prime orders a month from a single warehouse in the Midwest. Say 60% of those orders sit inside two-day ground range at $6 a package, and the other 40% need two-day air at $11.

SetupShare by groundGround costShare by airAir costBlended cost per order
One warehouse, two-day promise60%$640%$11$8.00
Two warehouses, two-day promise90%$610%$11$6.50
One warehouse, one-day promise25%$675%$18$15.00

Start with the first row. Prime costs this brand $2 more per order than ground shipping everywhere would, and all of the extra comes from the far 40% of customers. The scorecard did not move that number. The map did.

The second row shows the structural fix: a second warehouse on the other coast, which pulls most orders back inside ground range and cuts the premium to 50 cents. A second warehouse has its own price, in rent, staff and inventory split across two buildings, so it pays only above a certain order volume. The third row is the one sellers should be modeling now.

What one-day Prime does to the map

Amazon said on April 25, with its first-quarter results, that it expects to spend about $800 million in the second quarter moving Prime toward one-day delivery, AP reported. If the promise shortens to one day, the ground footprint around a single warehouse shrinks to the nearest few states. In the third row, three in four orders need overnight service, and the blended cost of $15 a package wipes out the margin on many products.

Modern Retail made the same point when the plan was announced: sellers who can deliver in two days can now qualify as Prime shippers without using Amazon’s fulfillment, but under a one-day standard more of them will have to ship through Amazon unless they can match it, it reported. Amazon has not said whether or when the SFP standard itself will change. The direction is still clear enough to plan for.

The trade-off then becomes a choice between three costs. A seller can keep one warehouse and pay for air on most Prime orders, open more warehouses and pay for split inventory, or move Prime volume into FBA and pay Amazon’s fees and storage. Which wins depends on the product’s margin and size. For a $45 item with $15 of margin before shipping, the $8 two-day blend leaves $7, while a $15 one-day blend leaves nothing, and FBA is likely the cheaper way to keep the badge on that item.

The SFP check before the next peak

  1. Export three months of Prime orders, assign each to a delivery zone from your warehouse, and calculate the share outside two-day ground. That share sets your Prime premium.
  2. Price the same orders under a one-day promise, using your real Buy Shipping rates for overnight service.
  3. Compare the result with FBA fees and storage on the same SKUs, and with the cost of a second warehouse.
  4. Keep SFP on the SKUs where the premium stays below the conversion lift you measure from the badge, and move the rest.

The scorecard keeps the badge, and the map decides whether it is worth keeping. Modeling that map is part of the marketplace operations work we do for brands on Amazon, and we are glad to run the zone math on your Prime orders.

P0234.crumb: Amazon private label presses hardest on…
P0234.title: Amazon private label presses hardest on products bought by spec
P0234.alt: Two kraft boxes holding coiled black hoses sit on a wooden shelf; one is plain, one has illustrated packaging.
P0234.ttag: Amazon private label presses hardest on products bought by spec | Kwontified
P0234.desc: Amazon’s own brands are about 1% of its retail sales, yet they sit in a few aisles where shoppers buy by spec. That is where national brands feel the pressure.
P0234.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 23, 2019.
P0234.body:
In a supermarket, the store brand usually sits right next to the national brand it copies, often in a similar color, at a lower price. Nobody pretends it is an accident. The store brand is there to set a floor: a shopper who does not care about the name can pay less, and a shopper who does care can see exactly what the name costs. Amazon has been building the same arrangement, quietly, and in 2019 it is worth asking which of a brand’s products sit next to that floor.

The scale is easy to overstate. Amazon says private label is about 1% of its retail sales, Reuters reported in April. The concentration is easy to miss. Coresight Research counted 74 Amazon private labels and 6,825 products in June 2018, and almost 5,000 of those products, about three-quarters, were clothing and footwear; 66 of the 74 labels sold apparel, and home and kitchen came second with 852 products, Coresight reported. A small business spread across a few aisles is a big presence in those aisles.

Where Amazon private label sits

Look at the aisles Amazon chose and a pattern appears. Amazon Basic Care, a line of about 60 over-the-counter medicines made by Perrigo, launched in August 2017, Business Insider reported. Solimo covers household staples, Mama Bear covers baby products and Wag covers pet products, PYMNTS noted in its Prime Day 2018 coverage.

Rivet and Stone & Beam arrived in furniture in November 2017, TechCrunch reported. In apparel, Coastal Blue swimwear competes with Lands’ End and The Fix shoes compete with Aldo, according to the April Reuters report, which counted 109 Amazon clothing, shoe and jewelry brands at the start of 2019 using TJI Research figures.

What most of these aisles share is that shoppers buy by specification. An ibuprofen tablet is defined by its dose, a diaper by its size, a basic tee by its fabric and fit. The shopper reads the specs, glances at the stars, and chooses on price. Those are the aisles where a store brand has always done well in physical retail, and they are where most of Amazon’s own labels sit.

How a store brand changes the aisle

A store brand changes category behavior less by taking share than by changing the question a shopper asks. Before it arrives, the shopper compares national brands with each other. Afterward, every national brand on the page is also being compared with a cheaper product carrying the retailer’s own name, and the retailer’s promise behind it. The national brand has to answer a new question: what does the shopper get for the difference?

Say a brand sells a three-pack of basic cotton tees at $28 and an Amazon label sells a similar pack at $20. The brand’s page now has to show what the extra $8 buys: a heavier fabric, a longer cut, a fit that holds after washing.

For a brand that differentiates on formula, design or fit, the answer is usually ready, and the store brand can even help by making the premium visible. For a brand selling a product that is, honestly, the same as the basic version, there is no good answer. That product was competing on habit, on distribution, or on the absence of a cheaper alternative, and on Amazon none of those hold for long.

There is also the matter of what the retailer can see. Retailers selling on Amazon worry that Amazon could use the sales data it collects to build out its own labels, and the European Commission has opened a preliminary investigation into whether Amazon uses competitors’ sensitive data, the Reuters report noted. Amazon owns the shelf, the search results, the advertising and the label next to yours. Whatever the investigation concludes, a brand planning its Amazon assortment should assume that a product with strong sales in a spec-driven aisle is visible to someone deciding where the next private label goes.

Who should be asking the question

Inside most brands, the private label question lands in the wrong room. The Amazon team sees it as a listing problem and asks for more advertising to defend the page. Finance sees a price problem and asks for a margin plan. The product team, which could actually change the answer, rarely hears about it at all, because Amazon is treated as a channel rather than as a retailer with its own merchandising strategy.

The decision a leadership team actually faces is which products deserve a defense and which should be redesigned, repositioned or quietly let go on Amazon. That is a category management decision of the kind brands already make with every large retailer that runs a store brand, and it belongs with the people who make it there.

Questions for the next category review

  1. Which of our Amazon products are bought by specification, and how does each compare on price, rating and specs with the closest Amazon-owned alternative?
  2. For each one, what does the shopper get for the difference, and does our detail page say so in the first image and the first bullet?
  3. Where we cannot answer the second question, should we change the product, move the price, or step back from the aisle?
  4. Who on our team watches for new Amazon private labels in our categories, and how quickly does that reach the product team?

A brand that can answer these for its top twenty products on Amazon has turned the private label from a threat into a benchmark. Running that review alongside the day-to-day Amazon channel is part of the work we do for brands, and we are glad to compare notes on your categories.

P0235.crumb: Vendor Central to Seller Central pays…
P0235.title: Vendor Central to Seller Central pays only if your price holds
P0235.alt: A blank paper tag held by a brass bulldog clip on a worn wooden table against a blue wall.
P0235.ttag: Vendor Central to Seller Central pays only if your price holds | Kwontified
P0235.desc: A brand moving from Vendor Central to Seller Central keeps more of each sale and absorbs 85% of every price cut. The switch pays only while the price holds.
P0235.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 28, 2019.
P0235.body:
Every comparison of Vendor Central and Seller Central starts with the same table, and the table always flatters the move. Sell a $40 product to Amazon at a $20 wholesale price and the brand’s revenue is $20. Sell it yourself on the marketplace and you keep $40, less a 15% referral fee and a fulfillment fee. The gap looks like found money, and in a good month it is. What the table leaves out is the line that decides the switch: what happens to each model when the retail price falls.

On 1P, a lower shelf price looks like Amazon’s problem, because the brand’s wholesale price does not move. On 3P, the brand feels most of every cut directly. That asymmetry, more than the fee schedule, is what a brand is buying or selling when it switches.

Why the move from Vendor Central to Seller Central looks like a clear win

The case for switching is strong, and 2019 has made it more urgent. In March, Amazon stopped sending purchase orders to thousands of smaller vendors and told many of them to sell on the marketplace instead, Modern Retail reported. Back in 2017, Buy Box Experts’ James Thomson argued that brands often do well on Vendor Central at first but lose either control or margin as their sales grow, and that the business is easier to manage through Seller Central, in a comment to Web Retailer.

Our March analysis of the vendor cuts priced the standard case: a $40 product, $20 wholesale, a 15% referral fee, a $5 fulfillment fee and about $4 of advertising per unit. The seller keeps around $25 a unit before returns and storage. The vendor keeps $20 less its allowances. Wholesale vendors also pay a percentage of sales into Amazon’s co-op for marketing, Digiday reported in December. Call it 8% in this example, or $1.60, and the vendor’s $20 becomes $18.40.

How a falling price lands on each model

Now let the retail price fall. On Seller Central, Amazon’s referral fee is a percentage, so it shrinks with the price, but the fulfillment fee and the ad cost do not. Every dollar off the price takes 85 cents off the seller’s margin. The vendor’s number stays flat because Amazon, not the brand, owns the shelf price.

Retail priceSeller cash per unit (3P)Vendor cash per unit (1P)
$40$25.00$18.40
$36$21.60$18.40
$32.24$18.40$18.40
$30$16.50$18.40

The break-even sits at about $32.24. Above it, Seller Central pays more. Below it, the vendor’s fixed wholesale price wins. In this example the brand can let its price slip almost 20% before the switch stops paying.

The vendor column looks immune to price. It is not. When Amazon’s own selling price falls on a 1P product, Amazon’s margin absorbs the cut, and Amazon has been building tools to respond when that margin disappears. Amazon has been telling more vendors that it will not let them pay to promote products it cannot sell at a profit, items it calls CRaP, for “can’t realize a profit,” often priced under $25, CNBC reported on March 20. In December, Amazon asked some brands, including Coca-Cola, to ship heavy, low-value items themselves, Engadget reported from a Wall Street Journal story.

So the vendor’s exposure to price is real, just indirect. It shows up as an ad campaign that stops serving, a product that drops out of Amazon’s orders, or a request to change the terms. The seller’s exposure is direct and immediate, and it comes with the one thing the vendor never had: the right to set the price.

What decides whether the price holds

That right is only worth something if the brand can use it, and what decides it is not in the fee table.

Other sellers on the same page come first. If resellers bought the product cheaply from distributors, they can list it below the brand’s price on the same detail page, and the brand either matches them or loses the sale. Distribution agreements and minimum advertised price policies are the brand’s tools here, and Brand Registry is what lets it control the page itself. A brand that cannot name every distributor selling to Amazon resellers does not yet know its own price floor.

Amazon’s leftover stock matters for the first months. A vendor that switches may still have units in Amazon’s warehouses that Amazon bought at wholesale. Amazon will sell those at its own price until they run out, and that price may sit below the brand’s.

Then there is the brand’s own discipline. A seller that cuts its price to rescue a slow month moves itself down the table, and at 85 cents on the dollar it does not take many cuts to reach the break-even.

The switch test

Before moving a product from Vendor Central to Seller Central, write down three numbers: today’s retail price, the break-even price at which the seller column equals the vendor column after allowances and co-op, and the lowest price the product has sold at on Amazon in the past year. If that low price sits above the break-even, the switch pays even in a bad month. If it sits below, the brand is betting on price control it has not yet shown it has, and the first job is to fix distribution and resellers, not the account type.

Start with the top ten products by sales, since they carry most of the margin at stake.

Running that comparison product by product is part of the Amazon channel work we do for brands, and we are glad to build the break-even for your catalog.

P0236.crumb: First page of Amazon search is the shelf…
P0236.title: First page of Amazon search is the shelf; page two is storage
P0236.alt: A tidy shelf of ceramics, linens and baskets beside an open door revealing a cramped room stacked with boxes.
P0236.ttag: First page of Amazon search is the shelf; page two is storage | Kwontified
P0236.desc: Two-thirds of Amazon product clicks land on the first page of results. Brands that manage ranking and ads as separate jobs are splitting one shelf in two.
P0236.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 30, 2019.
P0236.body:
Walk down a grocery aisle and watch where hands go. They reach for the shelves between the waist and the eyes, and only the determined shopper crouches for the bottom row. Merchants have built entire negotiations around that habit: eye-level space costs more because it sells more. Amazon has the same habit in a harsher form. Its shoppers barely leave the first page of search results, which means that page is not the top of the shelf. It is the shelf.

The numbers make the point plainly. In Jumpshot’s analysis of Amazon traffic in the second quarter of 2018, 65% of all product clicks came from the first page of results and 36% came from the first two rows alone, Retail Dive reported. Nearly 90% of Amazon product views started in Amazon’s own search, not in advertising elsewhere, merchandising pages or comparison sites. For a brand, the search results page is the store, and its first screen is most of the store.

How shoppers use the first page of Amazon search

The click pattern is not a simple ladder. In the same Jumpshot data, the fourth position drew 7% of clicks, more than the second at 5.7% or the third at 5.2%. Shoppers are not reading a ranked list from the top down; they are scanning a screen of products and picking from what they can see without scrolling much. Position one helps, but being on the visible screen matters more than the exact slot.

That changes what a brand should measure. A weekly report that tracks “rank for our hero keyword” captures a number that is easy to move and hard to interpret. Moving from fifth to third may change little. Moving from the first page to the second removes the product from the place where about two-thirds of clicks happen.

Shoppers also take their time. Jumpshot found that 20% of Amazon product searches led to a purchase within five days, against 35% for Google product searches, and that the average time from search to purchase was 25.9 days on Amazon. A gap that long suggests many shoppers search more than once before they buy. A product that appears on page one only in the week of a promotion is visible for one of those searches and missing from the rest.

Who owns the shelf

The harder part is inside the brand. The first page holds two kinds of placement: organic results, earned through sales history, reviews and relevance, and sponsored placements, bought in an auction. At many brands those are run by different people. Content, catalog or an SEO specialist work on organic rank. A media team or agency buys Sponsored Products against a cost-per-sale target. Each reports its own numbers, and nobody reports the one number that matters: how much of page one the brand occupies, by either route, for the searches that sell its category.

Say a sock brand ranks eighth organically for “running socks” and also buys the top sponsored slot on that search. The media team reports a healthy cost per sale. The content team reports a page-one rank. Neither report says how many of the visible positions the brand holds in total, or that a rival with a better image and more reviews holds three of them.

A merchant would find that division odd. No one at a grocery brand manages the shelf placement it negotiated separately from the end-cap display it paid for; both are space in the same aisle, judged by the same sales.

Amazon is renting out more of the shelf

Follow the value and the reason for urgency becomes clear. Jumpshot’s chief executive told Retail Dive that Amazon was using more sponsored placements to earn revenue from product search. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, mostly advertising, rose 34% to $2.7 billion in the first quarter of 2019, VentureBeat reported. Each sponsored slot on page one is a slot that is no longer available organically. As the paid share of the shelf grows, a brand relying on organic rank alone is competing for a shrinking number of free positions, while a brand relying on ads alone is paying to stand where its organic listing might have stood anyway.

The evidence leans toward one conclusion: the first page should be managed as a single piece of shelf space. Where the brand ranks well organically for a search, ads on that search may add less than they appear to. Where it ranks on page two, ads may be the only way onto the shelf at all, and the spending should be judged against the cost of earning that place organically over time. None of this makes ads a poor buy. It makes them part of the shelf plan rather than a separate budget with its own scorecard.

Questions for the team that manages Amazon search

  1. For our twenty most valuable searches, how many of the first-page positions do we hold, organic and sponsored combined, and how has that changed since January?
  2. Which of those searches show us on page one only because we pay, and which would we hold without ads?
  3. Who on our team owns the combined number, and do the people running content and the people running ads see the same report?
  4. When a product slips to page two, who is told, and how quickly?

A brand that can answer the first question every month has turned a pile of rankings into a picture of its shelf. Managing organic and sponsored placement together for the searches that matter is part of the Amazon advertising work we do for brands, and we are glad to map your page-one share with you.

P0238.title: Amazon Attribution recovers sales your other ad reports miss
P0238.alt: A drawn-back curtain reveals twine-tied paper parcels in a crate beside a desk with a magnifying glass and books.
P0238.ttag: Amazon Attribution recovers sales your other ad reports miss | Kwontified
P0238.desc: Traffic a brand sends to Amazon from Facebook or Google shows up as non-converting in those consoles. Amazon Attribution counts it, but only the clicks.
P0238.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 4, 2019.
P0238.body:
Every brand that sells on Amazon and advertises on Facebook has seen the same report: a campaign with healthy click-through rates and a return on ad spend that says it is losing money. The usual response is to cut it. Often the campaign is fine and the report is blind, because many of the shoppers it reached bought on Amazon, where the Facebook pixel cannot follow them. Amazon Attribution, a measurement tool Amazon has offered in beta since at least last October, exists to count those sales. A brand should put it on any off-Amazon channel before deciding that channel does not work.

Why the Facebook report looks right

The ad console is the obvious place to judge an ad. It counts the clicks it bought and the purchases its pixel saw, and the arithmetic is simple. For a brand that sells only on its own site, the count is close to complete.

For a brand that also sells on Amazon, it is not. A shopper who clicks an ad, lands on the brand’s site and then buys the same product on Amazon becomes invisible to the brand’s attribution systems, MightyHive explained when it described the beta. The shopper is recorded as a non-converter, and the paid media gets no credit for the sale.

Nobody set out to undercount. The pixel reports what it can see, and a purchase on Amazon is outside its view.

How Amazon Attribution recovers the missing sales

Take a $30 serum sold on the brand’s site and on Amazon. The brand spends $10,000 a month on Facebook at $0.50 a click, which buys 20,000 clicks to its own site. Of those visitors, 2.5% buy there: 500 orders, $15,000 in sales, a return on ad spend of 1.5. On a product with a thin margin, 1.5 looks like a loss.

Now say another 3% of the same visitors leave, search for the serum on Amazon (where they have a saved card and Prime shipping) and buy it there. That is 600 more orders and $18,000 more in sales. The campaign actually sold $33,000, a return of 3.3. Facebook reports 1.5 because it saw only the first $15,000.

Sending the click straight to the Amazon detail page makes the report worse, not better. The pixel then sees no purchases at all, and the campaign shows a return of zero while Amazon’s sales quietly rise.

Amazon Attribution closes that gap from the other side. The brand creates a tag for each campaign, ad set or creative and adds it to the link that sends shoppers to Amazon. Amazon then reports what those tagged visitors did on Amazon: detail page views, the purchase rate and sales, according to MightyHive’s summary of the beta’s metrics. Each campaign’s link can carry its own tag, so the brand can compare channels on the same Amazon outcomes.

That turns the serum campaign into two readable numbers: the $15,000 on the brand’s site from the Facebook console, and the Amazon sales from the tag. Neither report alone describes the campaign.

The tags also settle an argument most brand teams have every quarter: where the ad should send people. Run the same creative to the brand’s site and, with a tag, to the Amazon detail page, at equal budgets for the same weeks. Add each version’s site sales and tagged Amazon sales, divide by spend, and the better destination is the one with the higher combined return. Before the tags, that test could only be scored on one side.

What the tags can and cannot tell you

The tag counts sales that followed a tagged click. That is a better count than zero, and it is still a count of clicks.

It misses the shopper who saw the ad, did not click, and searched Amazon later. It also credits the click with sales that would have happened anyway: a loyal customer who clicks a retargeting ad on the way to a reorder shows up as a tagged purchase. Those two errors push in opposite directions, and nobody can say from the tag report alone which one is larger for a given campaign.

The temptation is to treat the new number as the answer. A team that has just learned its Facebook campaign “really” earned 3.3 will want to defend the budget with it, the same way it once cut budgets on the 1.5. Both readings anchor on whichever report arrived last. The tag fixes a counting error. It does not show that the ads caused the sales they now get credit for.

Two checks keep the tag honest. First, compare tagged sales with the brand’s total Amazon sales for the same products over the same weeks. If tagged sales rise and total sales do not, the tags are relabeling sales the brand was already making. Second, when a channel’s budget is large enough to matter, hold some of it back: pause the campaign in a set of regions or for a few weeks and see whether Amazon sales for those products fall. That test answers the question the tags cannot.

A rule for traffic sent to Amazon

Before cutting any off-Amazon campaign that sends shoppers to Amazon, run it with Attribution tags for four weeks and add the tagged Amazon sales to the platform’s own count. If the combined return clears your target, keep the campaign and plan a holdout to confirm it. If it still falls short with the Amazon sales included, cut it with a clear conscience.

Ask your Amazon account team or agency whether your account can join the beta before the next budget review. Setting up those tags and the holdout behind them is part of how we measure what brands’ advertising adds on Amazon.

P0239.crumb: Prime Day 2019 planning now starts with…
P0239.title: Prime Day 2019 planning now starts with where the stock sits
P0239.alt: Three model warehouses on a desk show stock rising from a few boxes to completely full.
P0239.ttag: Prime Day 2019 planning now starts with where the stock sits | Kwontified
P0239.desc: Prime Day 2019 deal slots closed in May. The decision still open six weeks out is whether stock sits where one-day Prime can reach it, and who owns it.
P0239.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 6, 2019.
P0239.body:
In most brand offices this week, the Prime Day meeting opens with a deal list: which products, how deep, which days. Much of that list was settled weeks ago. Amazon’s deadline to apply for Lightning Deals passed on May 10, Feedvisor noted, and Amazon has still not said when the event will run. So what is left to decide six weeks out?

For Prime Day 2019, the answer is the stock: how much of it sits in Amazon’s buildings, and in which ones, by early July. Amazon’s move to one-day Prime has made inventory placement the planning decision that matters most, and at many brands the people who make it are not in the Prime Day meeting.

Prime Day 2019 planning inherits the scale of 2018

The event a team is planning for has a known shape even without a date. Prime Day 2018 ran 36 hours across 17 countries, offered more than one million deals and sold more than 100 million products, Amazon said afterward. Feedvisor expects mid-July again, and a leaked press release reported on June 5 points to July 15, though Amazon has not confirmed it.

Shoppers arrive with their minds half made up. In survey figures Feedvisor cited, 48% of Prime members said they planned to buy during the event, against 31% of consumers overall, and 83% of members named free two-day shipping as the top benefit of Prime. For those shoppers the delivery promise is part of the deal, as much as the discount.

One-day Prime moves the deadline into the warehouse

That promise is getting shorter. Amazon said in April it would spend about $800 million in the second quarter moving Prime from two-day to one-day shipping, Retail TouchPoints reported. One-day delivery depends on stock sitting near the shopper before the order is placed, which means more units, in more buildings, earlier.

Amazon has started paying for exactly that. On May 22 it offered US sellers who use Fulfillment by Amazon up to 75% off their fees for holding stock at Amazon’s suggested levels on eligible products, so those products can ship with one-day delivery, ChannelX reported. Follow the money and the message is plain. A retailer that discounts its own fees to pull inventory forward is telling sellers what it will reward on its busiest days: offers it can deliver tomorrow. Sellers who ship orders themselves face a higher bar as well; under a one-day standard, more of them will have to ship through Amazon unless they can match it, Modern Retail observed in April.

So a Prime Day deal on a product that arrives in two days now sits beside rivals that can promise the same Prime member delivery tomorrow. The discount can be identical and the offer still weaker. The deal list cannot close that gap on its own; only the stock plan can.

The stock decision belongs to a team that plans by the month

Look at who owns each half of the plan. The deal list usually belongs to the e-commerce or marketing team, which lives on Amazon’s calendar of deadlines and events. The stock belongs to demand planning, which works from a monthly forecast built on sell-through history and signed off with finance. In June those two calendars rarely line up. By the time the e-commerce team knows which deals won slots and how deep they run, the planning cycle that decides what ships in late June has often closed.

None of this is carelessness. Demand planners are judged on forecast accuracy and on not leaving excess stock in a warehouse, and a forecast that doubles a product’s July on the strength of an event that lasted a day and a half in 2018 is exactly the number their reviews punish. The caution that serves a planner well in an ordinary month is the same caution that leaves a Prime Day deal short.

The outcome is a familiar mismatch: a deal approved in May for a product whose July stock was set in April, at a level built for an ordinary July. One-day Prime makes that gap more expensive. A product that runs short in some regions can lose its fastest delivery promise there well before it sells out everywhere, and the deal then runs on a weaker offer in exactly the hours it was meant to win.

Vendors face a version of the same problem with less control, because their stock arrives only when Amazon orders it. Bloomberg reported on May 28 that Amazon had not renegotiated annual terms with many smaller vendors this spring and planned to buy less from those selling under $10 million a year, a report Amazon called wrong, PYMNTS noted. Whatever the truth of it, a vendor counting on a large July purchase order should know by now whether one is coming.

Questions for this week’s Prime Day meeting

  • Who in this room can change what is in Amazon’s buildings by early July, and if no one can, who should be invited?
  • Which products on the deal list are at Amazon’s suggested stock levels now, and which are not?
  • If a deal product runs short in its first hours, what happens to its ads and its delivery promise?
  • For vendor products, which July purchase orders have arrived, and what is the seller-account fallback for the ones that have not?

The deal list will get most of the airtime. Whether the stock already sits in the right buildings decides if those deals reach shoppers with the delivery promise they now expect, which is why we put the stock plan beside the deal plan when we run Prime Day for the brands whose Amazon channel we manage.

P0240.crumb: Amazon vendor terms are traded against…
P0240.title: Amazon vendor terms are traded against one number, item margin
P0240.alt: An antique brass balance scale weighs a single gold coin against a tall twine-tied bundle of old papers.
P0240.ttag: Amazon vendor terms are traded against one number, item margin | Kwontified
P0240.desc: Amazon vendor terms negotiation looks like a list of separate asks. Each one buys Amazon profit per item, so price every ask by what it costs you.
P0240.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 11, 2019.
P0240.body:
Every spring a vendor manager sends the list. A point more co-op. A damage allowance. Longer payment terms. A change to the case pack. Most brands answer it line by line, with marketing defending co-op, finance defending the payment terms and operations arguing about the boxes. That is the wrong way to read the list. In an Amazon vendor terms negotiation, every line buys Amazon the same thing, its profit on each item it sells, and the useful question is which route to that number costs the brand least.

Since at least March, that number has decided more than the size of the deal. Amazon has been suspending advertising on vendor products that lose it money, telling vendors a product “no longer qualifies for advertising” because its sales result in a loss to Amazon, CNBC reported. The fix it offers is to lower the item’s cost to Amazon.

Why Amazon vendor terms get negotiated line by line

The line-by-line habit has a reason. The terms look like separate contracts, and inside a brand they belong to different people: co-op sits in a marketing budget, payment terms in a treasury forecast, allowances in operations. Each owner defends a budget line, and each concession feels like a loss on that line alone.

The 2019 list is also longer and slower. Annual vendor negotiations remain a challenge, Cleveland Research wrote in April, with Amazon asking for more vendor funding, packaging changes, logistics savings and new price-pack architecture, and talks starting later because each vendor manager now handles more brands. Some vendors are not getting a negotiation at all: Bloomberg reported in May that Amazon had not renegotiated annual terms with many smaller vendors this spring, a report Amazon disputed, PYMNTS noted.

How each ask reaches the same margin

Amazon’s item margin is simple in outline: the retail price, less what Amazon paid the vendor, less what it costs Amazon to store, pick and ship the unit, plus whatever the vendor funds back. Every term on the list moves one of those parts.

Take an item Amazon sells at $30 and buys at $18. Say it costs Amazon $7 to handle and ship each unit. Amazon keeps $5 before any vendor funding. Now price four common asks, per unit, on both sides of the table.

AskWorth to Amazon per unitCost to the vendor per unit
4% more co-op on cost$0.72$0.72
2% damage allowance$0.36$0.36
Payment terms from 60 to 90 daysabout $0.09 (at 6% a year)about $0.15 (at 10% a year)
Smaller box that cuts shipping cost by $1.00$1.00$0.25

The funding asks are transfers: a dollar to Amazon is a dollar from the vendor. The payment-terms ask is worse than a transfer, because the vendor’s cost of carrying 30 more days of receivables is usually higher than Amazon’s. The packaging change is the only one that creates money. It is worth $1.00 to Amazon’s margin and costs the vendor $0.25, so it buys Amazon almost as much as the co-op and damage allowance together ($1.08) for less than a quarter of their cost to the vendor.

That asymmetry is the whole negotiation. Amazon’s retail team is chasing item profitability, as the advertising suspensions show, and the list arrives in whatever form is easiest to request. A vendor that offers the cheaper route to the same margin can often hold the costly lines.

The CRaP list (“Can’t Realize a Profit,” Amazon’s internal label for items that lose money after shipping) shows the stakes at the bottom of the range. Amazon pushed vendors of heavy, low-priced goods to change how products ship, asking Coca-Cola among others to ship its own products, Engadget reported on the Wall Street Journal’s account. In the table’s terms, those items started below zero, and no amount of co-op fixes a box that costs more to ship than the item earns.

What the vendor cannot see, and how to estimate it

The weak point in this arithmetic is the $7. Amazon does not tell vendors what it costs to handle their items. Its own fee table for sellers who use its warehouses gives a usable proxy, because those fees are set by size tier and weight, as the 2018 fee changes showed, the same things that drive Amazon’s cost for a vendor’s unit. Use the fee for the item’s size tier as the handling estimate, and treat the result as a range, not a figure to quote back to the vendor manager.

The estimate does not need to be precise to be useful. It needs to rank items. A $30 item with a $7 handling cost has room for a co-op point. A $9 item in a large box may already be under the line, and for that item the negotiation is about the box, or about whether it belongs in Vendor Central at all.

The trade-off cuts both ways. Packaging changes cost money up front, take months to reach the shelf and can complicate retail packaging elsewhere. When the item already clears Amazon’s margin comfortably, a point of co-op can be the cheaper concession. The numbers lean toward logistics offers only where Amazon’s handling cost is large relative to the price, which in most catalogs means the bulky, low-priced end.

Before the next review

  1. Estimate Amazon’s margin per unit for your top 20 items: retail price, less your cost price, less the size-tier handling proxy.
  2. Price every ask on the list twice, in dollars per unit to Amazon and to you, and sort by the gap.
  3. Bring one logistics or packaging offer for the items closest to zero, before Amazon asks for funding to cover them.
  4. Recheck which of those items still carry advertising, since an item Amazon loses money on can lose its ads first.

The rule fits in one line: never give a dollar of funding where a cheaper change buys Amazon the same margin. Building that item-by-item view before the vendor manager’s list arrives is part of how we run Vendor Central accounts for the brands we work with.

P0242.crumb: Zalando gives premium brands control and…
P0242.title: Zalando gives premium brands control and asks them to run a store
P0242.alt: A small shop interior with an open door, key in the lock, wooden shelves, a hanging apron and a brass cash register.
P0242.ttag: Zalando gives premium brands control and asks them to run a store | Kwontified
P0242.desc: Zalando’s Partner Program gives premium brands the price and presentation control they want, then asks them to meet a retailer’s service standard every day.
P0242.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 13, 2019.
P0242.body:
In a premium label’s wholesale meeting, the conversation about Zalando usually goes one way. The retailer marked last season’s coats down too early, the brand’s pictures sat next to a cheaper rival, and the team wants its price and its image back. Zalando has an answer ready. Its Partner Program lets the brand sell its own stock on Zalando’s site, set its own price and decide how it appears. What it asks in return is less discussed in that meeting, and it is the harder part: the brand has to run a store, every day, to a retailer’s service standard.

That trade is the real decision for premium labels on Zalando in 2019. Control is what Zalando pays with. Operation is what it buys.

What Zalando offers premium brands through its Partner Program

Zalando has been explicit about the offer. “The brands are put in the driving seat. They keep control over the assortment, prices and brand representation,” Carsten Keller, who runs its partner business, told Reuters in December 2017. Partner brands then accounted for nearly 10% of the value of goods sold on the site, against a long-term goal of 20% to 30%.

For a premium label, that is the most attractive sentence a retailer can say. Price and presentation are what premium houses protect most closely, and wholesale is where they most often lose them. On Zalando’s site the brand decides the price on the morning a markdown would otherwise happen, and the brand decides the photographs.

The reach is real. Zalando counted 27.2 million active customers in the first quarter of 2019, up 14.1%, it reported in May. And it has told investors where the partners fit: the goal is to become “the starting point of fashion,” with 20 billion euros of gross merchandise volume by 2023 or 2024, and a sharper focus on the number of partner products on the site, FashionUnited reported in March.

What Zalando asks in return

Read Zalando as an institution and the asks follow from its goal. A platform that wants to be the first place a shopper looks for fashion needs every item on it to behave the same way: delivered free, returnable for 100 days, shown properly. It cannot let a partner’s coat be the one item with a slower delivery or a stingier return window.

So the standard comes with the control. When Zalando opened its Partner Program in Norway in September 2018, it said partners are chosen for product quality, assortment relevance and the ability to meet customer expectations of free delivery and a 100-day return period, and must meet its standards for logistics, delivery and product presentation, according to its announcement. Partner brands ship orders to customers themselves; Zalando handles payment, returns and customer service.

That division of labor is where premium labels feel it. The brand now holds stock that must ship to a customer in another country fast enough to keep Zalando’s delivery promise, and it carries the cost of a return policy written for Zalando’s customers rather than its own boutiques. Zalando offers help: about 30% of Partner Program orders in the first quarter of 2019 went through Zalando Fulfillment Solutions, its warehousing service for partners, the company said. The other 70% were shipped by the brands or their logistics providers.

The team that does not exist yet

Inside a premium house, the Zalando opportunity lands on a structure built for wholesale. The sales director owns accounts and sell-in. Merchandising plans two or four collections a year and allocates them to buyers. Finance books revenue when the wholesale order ships. None of those roles sets a price on a Tuesday morning, watches which sizes are about to run out on a single site, or answers for a return rate.

That gap explains a pattern worth watching in the meeting room. Brands sign up for control and then manage the account the way they manage a wholesale door: a quarterly review, a stock allocation, a promotion calendar agreed in advance. The control goes unused, and the service standard becomes a cost line nobody owns. The brand ends up with a retailer’s obligations and a wholesaler’s habits.

The labels that get the most from the program tend to treat it as a store that happens to sit on someone else’s site. They give it a person who owns daily pricing and availability, a stock pool that can ship to Zalando’s markets in time, and a returns process that can grade and resell a returned jacket quickly. The control is then worth something, because someone is using it.

Questions to put to the team before signing

  • If we sell on Zalando as a partner, who sets our prices there each week, and who has authority to hold a price when the wholesale accounts are discounting?
  • Can our current stock and logistics deliver at no charge to the shopper and accept returns for 100 days in each market we would open, and what does a return cost us end to end?
  • Should we use Zalando’s fulfillment service for some markets, and what would we give up in visibility of stock if we did?
  • Which collections belong on the partner model, where we carry the stock, and which still belong with Zalando as a wholesale buyer?

Zalando is making a clear offer to premium labels: the brand keeps the decisions it has always wanted to keep, and takes on the operation it has always left to retailers. Whether that is a good trade depends less on the commission than on whether the brand has, or builds, the team to run it, which is the work we do when we launch and operate Zalando for brands alongside their wholesale business.

P0245.title: Amazon health and household in 2019 shares its shelf with Amazon
P0245.alt: Plain white product boxes line up beside boxes with colorful floral and abstract patterns on a wooden shelf.
P0245.ttag: Amazon health and household in 2019 shares its shelf with Amazon | Kwontified
P0245.desc: In Amazon health and household, the retailer is now the store brand, the profit gatekeeper and the delivery promise at once. Brands have to plan for all three.
P0245.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 20, 2019.
P0245.body:
Walk down a drugstore’s pain-relief aisle and the arrangement is familiar. The national brand sits at eye level, and right beside it, in a box of nearly the same color, is the store’s own version with a “compare to” label and a lower price. Shoppers have accepted that arrangement for decades. It is the retailer reminding the brand, politely, who owns the shelf.

On Amazon, health and household has been rearranged along the same lines in 2019, with two additions a drugstore never had. Amazon now sells its own brands in the category, decides which of the brand’s products it can afford to sell and promote, and sets the delivery promise every product is measured against. Brands in the category are planning for a neutral marketplace. They are selling inside a retailer with three roles.

Amazon health and household now has a store brand

Amazon’s private labels arrived slowly and then all at once. It had about 40 private label brands in 2017 and about 80 by mid-2018, and its top in-house brands were Mama Bear, Basic Care, Presto, Solimo and Wag, One Click Retail’s analysis showed, PYMNTS reported in June 2018. Read the list as a category map. Basic Care sells over-the-counter medicines, Presto sells household cleaning and paper goods, Solimo covers everyday basics and Mama Bear covers baby care. Four of the five leading names are health, household or baby brands.

That is the drugstore store brand, rebuilt for search. The difference is placement. A drugstore’s store brand sits next to the national brand on one shelf. Amazon’s sits wherever the search results and the product page allow, including on the brand’s own page.

The retailer decides what it can afford to sell

The second role is newer. Late in 2018, Amazon began pushing harder against products it cannot sell at a profit once shipping is counted, which it calls CRaP, for “Can’t Realize a Profit.” Heavy, low-priced goods such as bottled water were the obvious targets, and Amazon asked some brands, Coca-Cola among them, to ship products themselves, Engadget reported on the Wall Street Journal’s account.

By March, the push had reached advertising. Amazon was suspending ads for vendor products it loses money on, telling vendors a product “no longer qualifies for advertising,” and the affected items were often under $25, CNBC reported, with a $5 water bottle as its example. Health and household is full of exactly those products: large, heavy, inexpensive and bought again and again.

So the category team at a household brand now faces a gate that did not exist in its planning templates. A product can sell well on Amazon and still be shut out of advertising, or pushed toward a different route to the shopper, because of what it costs Amazon to move. The screen works product by product, and a vendor that wants an item back in advertising has to lower its cost to Amazon, the CNBC report said, which turns a pricing negotiation into a test the product either passes or fails.

The delivery promise sets the bar

The third role is the one shoppers notice. Amazon said on June 3 that more than 10 million items now carry free one-day delivery for Prime members, TechCrunch reported. In a category bought on replenishment, where the shopper knows the product and mostly wants it soon, speed is close to the whole decision. A product without the one-day badge is asking that shopper to wait.

Independent sellers fill much of that shelf too. Third-party sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, Jeff Bezos wrote in his April letter to shareholders, CNBC reported. A brand’s product may be sold by the brand, by Amazon, or by resellers, each with a different delivery speed, and the fastest offer usually gets the sale.

Why category plans still assume a neutral shelf

Many health and household brands learned category management with grocery and drug chains, where the retailer’s roles were clear and separate: it bought the product, it ran the store brand in its own lane, and the brand paid for space and promotion through trade terms. That model taught brands to negotiate for shelf position and promotional slots, and to judge a retailer by sell-through.

Amazon combines those roles in one system and runs them on its own data. The store brand, the profitability screen and the delivery promise all draw on the same information about what shoppers buy and what each unit costs to ship. A brand that plans for Amazon as if it were a drug chain with a website will negotiate for the things a drug chain sells and miss the decisions Amazon is making about its products automatically. The questions below are a way to find out which of those decisions are already being made for the brand’s products, and by whom.

Questions for the category team

  • Which of our top products face an Amazon-owned brand on the same search, and how does our page answer a shopper comparing the two?
  • Which of our products are heavy, low-priced or slow enough to be at risk of losing advertising, and what pack or price change would move them clear of it?
  • Who sells our products on Amazon now, and which offer, ours, Amazon’s or a reseller’s, carries one-day delivery?
  • When did our Amazon plan last change because of something Amazon decided, rather than something we negotiated?

The drugstore shelf taught brands to watch the store brand. On Amazon in 2019 they have to watch the store brand, the shipping cost and the delivery clock at the same time, which is the day-to-day work we take on when we run the Amazon channel for health and household brands.

P0249.crumb: Mercado Libre earns buyer trust by owning…
P0249.title: Mercado Libre earns buyer trust by owning the payment and the parcel
P0249.alt: A yellow leather wallet tied with twine rests on a paper parcel on a market table beside terracotta pots.
P0249.ttag: Mercado Libre earns buyer trust by owning the payment and the parcel | Kwontified
P0249.desc: Mercado Libre has taken payment and delivery into its own hands, even at the cost of slower buyer growth. For brands, the platform now sets the terms of trust.
P0249.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 27, 2019.
P0249.body:
Buying from a stranger online asks a shopper to believe three things at once: that the payment is safe, that the parcel will arrive, and that someone will put it right if it does not. On a marketplace, the stranger is usually a seller the shopper has never heard of. In much of Latin America, where many shoppers are new to buying online, those three doubts decide whether a sale happens at all.

Mercado Libre’s answer has been to stop asking shoppers to trust sellers and ask them to trust Mercado Libre instead. Over 2018 and into 2019 it has taken the payment and the delivery into its own hands, and it has accepted slower buyer growth and thinner margins to do it. For a brand, that changes what selling on Mercado Libre means. The platform supplies the trust, and the platform sets its terms.

Mercado Libre buyer trust starts with the payment

The clearest signal came in the fourth quarter of 2018. Mercado Libre made payment through Mercado Pago, its own payments business, mandatory in Chile and Colombia, and said that decision, along with pricing changes and the removal of low-priced items, slowed growth in unique buyers to 7.5%, its results showed. A marketplace chose fewer new buyers in exchange for every payment passing through its own system.

Read that as an institution’s priorities. A platform that holds the money can stand between buyer and seller: it can withhold payment from a seller who does not deliver and refund a buyer who was let down. A platform that lets buyers and sellers settle among themselves cannot. Mercado Libre decided the first kind of platform was worth some growth.

The payments business has grown well beyond the marketplace. Mercado Pago processed $5.6 billion in the first quarter of 2019, up 35.1% in dollars, and more than $2.5 billion of it came from payments outside the marketplace, up 118.8%, the company reported in May. Outside investors read the same signal. In March, PayPal agreed to buy about $750 million of Mercado Libre shares, and the two companies agreed to work toward a commercial agreement, Mercado Libre’s filing shows.

The parcel is the second promise

Delivery is the other half of the trust, and Mercado Libre has been paying for it. Mercado Envios, its shipping network, carried 62.1 million items in the fourth quarter of 2018, up 28.5%, growth the company put down mainly to its free shipping program. Those shipping subsidies, $108.1 million netted from revenue in the quarter, helped pull gross margin down to 47.8% from 56.8% a year earlier, the same results show. By the first quarter of 2019, Mercado Envios was shipping 62.9 million items a quarter.

Follow the value and the logic is plain. Free, managed shipping costs Mercado Libre margin today. In return it owns the shopper’s experience of the parcel: when it arrives, how it is tracked, who answers when it does not. A shopper who has had three parcels arrive on time through Mercado Envios trusts the next listing a little more, whoever the seller is.

The trade-off shows up in the headline numbers. Gross merchandise volume was $3.1 billion in the first quarter, down 1.7% in dollars and up 26.6% on a currency-neutral basis, while net revenue rose 47.6% to $473.8 million, according to the May results. The company is growing its services faster than the goods sold through them. Its money and attention are going into the payment and the parcel.

What it means for a brand

For a brand used to wholesale in Latin America, this is a different kind of retailer. A department store’s buyer takes the stock and the risk, and the brand’s reputation rests on its own name and the store’s. On Mercado Libre, the shopper’s confidence rests mostly on the platform’s payment and delivery promises, and the brand sits inside them.

That is a gift and a constraint. A brand entering Mexico or Brazil does not have to persuade shoppers that it will deliver; Mercado Libre has done that work, at its own expense. In exchange, the brand plays by rules the platform sets and can change: which payment methods are accepted, which shipping options carry the free-delivery promise, what a seller must do to keep its standing. The removal of low-priced items in late 2018 is a reminder that the platform will reshape its catalog when its own economics call for it.

Inside many brands, Latin American marketplaces still sit with an importer or a regional distributor, judged on sell-in. That structure was built for the department store model. It is poorly suited to a platform where the brand’s results depend on meeting the platform’s payment and shipping standards week to week, and where the useful data, what shoppers searched, what they returned, which listings converted, sits with whoever operates the account.

Questions for the team

  • Who operates our Mercado Libre listings now, and do we see their sales, returns and customer questions, or only their orders from us?
  • Are our products shipping through Mercado Envios with the platform’s no-cost delivery promise where it applies, and if not, what is that costing us in conversion?
  • If Mercado Libre changed its payment or shipping rules in one of our markets tomorrow, who on our team would know, and who would decide what to do?

Mercado Libre has spent heavily to become the party Latin American shoppers trust. Brands that treat it as a distributor will borrow that trust without understanding its terms, which is why we work with brands to launch and operate Mercado Libre directly alongside their regional partners.

P0251.title: Walmart Marketplace item setup starts with the UPC, not the copy
P0251.alt: Close-up of a cardboard box with a barcode label sitting on a blue-painted wooden shelf.
P0251.ttag: Walmart Marketplace item setup starts with the UPC, not the copy | Kwontified
P0251.desc: On Walmart Marketplace the item page belongs to the product ID. Get the UPC, pack and variant setup right before writing copy, or the copy never shows.
P0251.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 2, 2019.
P0251.body:
When Marketplace Pulse counted Walmart’s marketplace in September 2017, its sellers listed about 26 million products, many of them duplicates, and only 24.5 million items could be confirmed on Walmart.com against the 67 million SKUs Walmart had reported. Those numbers do not line up because a seller on Walmart does not create a page. It attaches an offer to a catalog organized by product identifier, and the page that results is shared by everyone selling that identifier.

That is the first fact of Walmart Marketplace item setup, and it reorders the work. The copy a brand writes is not the asset that lasts. The identifier is. A brand that gets the UPC, the pack structure and the variant group right keeps a page its content can live on; a brand that starts from the title and images can find that work merged into someone else’s listing, or unpublished.

How Walmart Marketplace item setup ties content to a product ID

Any product on Walmart’s marketplace can be listed by multiple sellers, as on Amazon, Marketplace Pulse noted when the marketplace passed 15,000 sellers. By April 2018 there were about 18,000, RetailWire reported. Each of them submits the same fields: product name, key features, description and images. When several sell one identifier, shoppers see one item page, so only one version of each field can appear.

Suppliers feed the same catalog from the other side. From April 1, 2017, Walmart required suppliers to add online descriptions, images and product features, through its supplier tools or one of 10 approved content companies, and to have items complete online six weeks before launch, Talk Business reported. In October 2018 Walmart cut that list of content providers from 25 to 12 connected content partners after surveying 650 suppliers on cost and return, the same publication reported.

Put those together and the logic of the shared page is clear. Walmart wants one clean page per product, fed by whichever source it trusts, and the seller who typed a title does not decide whether that title is the one shoppers read.

The setup rules that decide where an item lands

Walmart’s 2019 QuickStart guide to item setup content policies reads less like style advice than a list of ways an item gets removed (the guide). Every listing needs at least two images. The primary image is a frontal view on a seamless white background (255/255/255 RGB) with no added text, logos or watermarks. Product names may not carry promotions, shipping promises, “best selling” claims or references to other marketplaces, and breaking the copy rules can lead to warnings, unpublished listings or suspension.

The structural rules matter more, because they decide which page an item lands on:

  • A multi-pack takes the Product ID for the whole pack, not the ID of the single unit inside it.
  • A variation group holds up to 100 variants on one attribute, or 500 across two (the guide’s example is pants in 25 sizes and 20 colors).
  • Bundles a seller assembles from other makers’ products are not supported; a group needs its own Product ID.

Each rule protects the one-identifier, one-page logic. A six-pack uploaded under the single unit’s UPC does not create a six-pack listing. It lands on the single unit’s page, with a six-pack price next to a one-unit description, and the shopper sees an item that looks overpriced.

Performance closes the loop in some categories. Baby and grocery items must expand Walmart’s existing selection and follow its pricing rules, and the guide says items with a cancellation rate above 2% and a return rate above 5% are unpublished, with performance reviewed every 7, 15 and 30 days.

What an unpublished item costs

Take a $25 item selling 30 units a day on Walmart.com. A setup error unpublishes it, and the fix takes a week of feed corrections and support cases. That week costs 210 units, or $5,250 in sales, before the item starts rebuilding whatever search position it held. The team may well have spent two days polishing that item’s description the month before. The description was worth something only while the page stayed up.

The shared page has its own arithmetic. Say four sellers carry the item and the brand’s listing is one of them. If the page displays a reseller’s title and images, the brand’s copywriting reaches no shopper, however good it is. Content work earns a return only once the identifier is clean and the brand’s version is the one on screen.

That is why the setup order matters more than the setup effort. A team that writes first and fixes identifiers later pays for its content twice.

A setup order that keeps the content on the page

Start with identifiers. For every SKU, confirm the GTIN or UPC matches the unit actually being sold, give every pack size its own identifier, and keep each variant group inside the 100 and 500 limits before anything is uploaded.

Then check what already exists. Search Walmart.com for each identifier before setup. If a page is already live, the brand is adding an offer to a page someone else built, and the question becomes how to get the brand’s content displayed there, not how to write it.

Use the supplier route where the brand has one. A brand that also sells to Walmart as a supplier can load content through Walmart’s supplier tools or a connected content partner, the channel Walmart has spent two years building. A marketplace-only brand should keep a complete content file for every identifier, so it can resubmit quickly when a page shows the wrong version.

Write the copy last, to Walmart’s rules rather than Amazon’s habits: plain product names, a white-background frontal image, at least two images, and no claims the guide bans.

The rule we use: if a SKU’s identifier is wrong, no amount of copy will fix its page, so clean the UPC before anyone writes a word. Getting catalogs to hold on Walmart.com is much of the day-to-day work when we run Walmart Marketplace for a brand.
