P0252.title: Amazon channel profitability is split across four budgets
P0252.alt: Yellow, green, red and blue envelopes fanned out on a sunlit wooden table.
P0252.ttag: Amazon channel profitability is split across four budgets | Kwontified
P0252.desc: Amazon’s costs land in four budgets owned by four teams, so finance rarely sees one P&L for the channel. Here is what a CFO needs on a single page.
P0252.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 3, 2019.
P0252.body:
Amazon’s retail staff have a name for products they cannot sell at a profit: CRaP, for “can’t realize a profit.” In March 2019 Amazon began telling more vendors it would no longer let them pay to promote those items, which are often priced under $25, CNBC reported. The retailer knows, product by product, which of a brand’s items earn it money. The obvious question is whether the brand’s own finance team knows the same thing.

At most brands it does not, and the reason is structural rather than careless. Amazon channel profitability is hard to see because its costs land in four budgets owned by four teams, and finance usually sees them only after they have been netted, deducted or spent. In 2019 Amazon is changing those terms quickly, and a channel that no single person can read is the one that gets surprised.

Why finance sees Amazon in pieces

A brand selling to Amazon as a vendor sees an invoice, a payment and a list of deductions. A brand selling on the marketplace sees a payout that has already had referral and fulfillment fees taken out of it. Advertising arrives as a separate bill, usually charged to marketing. Inventory sitting in Amazon’s warehouses belongs to supply chain, and its storage fees show up wherever that team books them.

Each of those lines is reasonable on its own. The trouble is that no one line tells the CFO whether the next unit sold on Amazon makes money. The e-commerce lead presents sales, marketing presents return on ad spend, supply chain presents weeks of cover, and finance presents the cash that actually arrived. At many brands those four numbers are rarely put side by side, so the channel’s margin is a figure everyone assumes someone else has worked out.

The terms underneath keep moving. Amazon cut the minimum referral fee in most categories from $1.00 to $0.30 per item from February 19, 2019, Business Insider reported, and its storage fee changes took effect on February 15. Each change lands in a different budget, so a brand can absorb a fee cut, a storage change and a rise in ad costs in the same quarter without anyone seeing the net effect.

Amazon already reads the channel as one P&L

The contrast with the retailer is the part leadership teams tend to miss. The CRaP rule was one sign of an Amazon managing its retail business item by item. In the same month thousands of smaller vendors stopped receiving weekly purchase orders and were pointed to the marketplace, Digiday reported. Amazon was pushing to raise the profit of its core retail business, and moving suppliers to the marketplace shifts the cost of buying, storing and shipping their goods onto them, Bloomberg reported.

Read as an institution, Amazon is doing what any disciplined retailer does: it measures item-level margin and acts on it. The brand across the table is often measuring revenue in one room and costs in three others. When one side of a negotiation has the item P&L and the other has a revenue target, the outcome is easy to predict.

Switching to the marketplace changes what finance sees

The shift to selling on the marketplace makes the problem sharper. Independent sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, Jeff Bezos wrote in his April 2019 letter to shareholders, as CNBC reported. More brands are moving in that direction, by choice or not.

Consider what the move does to the numbers finance actually reports. Sold to Amazon at a wholesale price of $12, a $24 product books $12 of revenue, less whatever allowances and deductions the vendor terms carry. Sold on the marketplace at $24, it books $24 of revenue, from which the brand pays a 15% referral fee of $3.60, a fulfillment fee of around $4.00 and perhaps $3.00 of advertising per unit sold. What reaches the brand is $13.40 before the cost of the product. Revenue has doubled; the money kept has risen by $1.40 plus whatever the vendor terms used to deduct, and much of what used to be Amazon’s margin is now the brand’s own cost, paid out of three budgets.

A finance team that tracks the channel by revenue will see a triumph. One that tracks it by contribution margin will see a channel that earns about the same, carries more of the work and depends more on the advertising budget, a line Amazon is working hard to grow. Amazon’s “other” revenue, mostly advertising, rose 34% to $2.7 billion in the first quarter of 2019, VentureBeat reported.

Questions for the next finance review

The fix is organizational before it is analytical: one channel P&L that the e-commerce lead and the CFO both sign, with every cost line on it whichever budget pays the bill. These are the questions I would put to the team first:

  • What does each of our top 20 Amazon products earn after referral and fulfillment fees, storage, advertising and returns?
  • Which budget pays for Amazon advertising, and who sees it on the same page as the sales it drives?
  • If our purchase orders stopped next Monday, what would the same products earn on the marketplace, and which would we stop selling?
  • Which of our products would Amazon itself call unprofitable, and do we already know why?

A brand that can answer the last question before Amazon does is the one setting its own terms. Putting the channel on one page, so finance and e-commerce argue from the same numbers, is part of how we run the Amazon channel for brands.

P0253.crumb: Your average Amazon CPC can rise when no…
P0253.title: Your average Amazon CPC can rise when no single click got dearer
P0253.alt: Two glass jars on a rustic shelf, one filled with copper coins and the other with silver coins.
P0253.ttag: Your average Amazon CPC can rise when no single click got dearer | Kwontified
P0253.desc: An average Amazon CPC mixes market prices with your own keyword and placement choices. Split the two before blaming the auction for a 2019 cost rise.
P0253.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 9, 2019.
P0253.body:
Most Amazon advertisers can point to the number that worries them in 2019: the average cost per click in the console, up sharply on a year ago. The easy explanation is that the auction got crowded, and part of that is true. Spending on Sponsored Products among Merkle’s clients rose 19% year over year in the first quarter of 2019, and Sponsored Brands spending rose 77%, ChannelX reported from Merkle’s quarterly report. More money chasing the same searches pushes prices up.

But an average CPC is a blended number, and blends move when the mix moves. A team that shifted budget from cheap branded keywords to expensive generic ones, or raised its bids for the top of search, will see its average Amazon CPC rise even if every individual price held still. Before a brand blames the auction, it should split the rise into the part the market caused and the part its own decisions caused. Usually the second part is larger than anyone expected.

Why the auction gets the blame for higher Amazon CPC

The market story is easy to believe because the evidence for it is everywhere. Amazon’s “other” revenue, which is mostly advertising, rose 34% to $2.7 billion in the first quarter of 2019, VentureBeat reported. Merkle’s Sponsored Products spend growth had been 15% in the fourth quarter of 2018, according to ChannelX’s summary of that report. When advertisers add money faster than shoppers add searches, prices rise.

There is also a pull toward the explanation that puts the cause outside the room. A CPC that rose because “Amazon got expensive” is nobody’s decision. A CPC that rose because the team moved budget into generic terms is someone’s, and it invites the question of whether that move paid off. Most reviews accept the first story because it is comfortable, and the comfortable story is the one that needs checking.

How the mix moves the average

Think of a grocery bill. If it rose 25% in a year, prices may have gone up, or the household may simply have started buying more steak. You only know which by pricing last year’s basket at this year’s prices.

The same test works on an Amazon account. Take a brand with two kinds of keywords. Branded terms are cheap and convert well; Merkle found brand keywords drew about a quarter of Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands clicks but about half of sales in the first quarter of 2019. Generic terms are pricier.

Q1 2018 clicksQ1 2018 CPCQ1 2019 clicksQ1 2019 CPC
Branded keywords6,000$0.406,000$0.42
Generic keywords4,000$1.208,000$1.26
Account average10,000$0.7214,000$0.90

The console says CPC rose 25%, from $0.72 to $0.90. Now price the 2018 basket at 2019 prices: 6,000 clicks at $0.42 and 4,000 at $1.26 come to $7,560, or $0.756 a click. That is the market’s share of the rise, about 5%. The rest, roughly 19% on top, came from the brand’s own decision to double its generic clicks.

Neither part is good or bad on its own. Doubling generic reach may have been the right call; generic searches are where a brand finds shoppers who did not already know it. The point is that the 25% headline describes a strategy choice as if it were inflation.

Placement bids are the second lever you pull yourself

Mix has a second dimension: where the ad shows. Early in 2019 Amazon replaced Bid+, which allowed a 50% bid increase for the top of search results, with placement adjustments that let advertisers raise bids by up to 900% for the top of search and for product detail pages, Feedvisor reported. In Merkle’s first-quarter data, 33% of Sponsored Products clicks came from the top of search and 41% from product detail pages, so these are the placements that carry the account.

Say a keyword has a $1.00 bid and the team adds a 50% top-of-search adjustment. Its effective bid there becomes $1.50. If rivals were already pushing the top slot toward $1.35, the brand now wins clicks it used to lose, and the keyword’s CPC rises by around a third with no change in the market at all. The console will report it as the same keyword getting more expensive.

What the data can and cannot tell you

A fixed-basket comparison isolates price from mix, but it still cannot say whether the extra spend was worth it. That needs the sales side: what the generic clicks and the top-of-search clicks returned per dollar compared with the clicks they replaced. Attribution makes this harder, because branded clicks collect credit for shoppers who were already coming.

What would change my mind about a given account is simple: if like-for-like CPCs on unchanged keywords and placements rose as fast as the average, the auction really is the story. Then the response is bid discipline, not a strategy review.

Seasonality is the other trap. CPCs climb into the fourth quarter and ease in January, so comparing March with December mixes calendar effects into the answer. Comparing the same quarter in both years removes most of that, which is why the test below uses year-over-year quarters rather than consecutive ones.

The CPC review, in four steps

  1. Export search term and placement reports for the same quarter in both years.
  2. Keep only keyword and placement pairs that ran in both periods, and price last year’s clicks at this year’s CPCs.
  3. Compare that fixed-basket change with the console’s average change; the gap is your mix.
  4. For the mix you chose, check return on ad spend by keyword group before cutting anything.

Our rule of thumb: never quote an average Amazon CPC increase in a budget meeting without the fixed-basket number next to it. Splitting the two is the first thing we do when we review an Amazon advertising account.

P0255.title: Amazon product content loses budget fights to the ads it helps
P0255.alt: A sunlit desk against a pink wall with a blank monitor, framed photo of a vase, old books, mug and succulent.
P0255.ttag: Amazon product content loses budget fights to the ads it helps | Kwontified
P0255.desc: Product content raises conversion, but the gain shows up in the ad report and the cost in a creative budget. That is why brands keep underfunding it.
P0255.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 11, 2019.
P0255.body:
When Amazon studied the effect of richer product pages in 2015, it found that adding A+ content raised conversion rates by 3% to 10%, Salsify noted in a June 2018 guide to the format (Salsify). In the same guide, Salsify pointed out that Amazon gives brands no data on how an individual A+ page performs. Put those two facts together and you have most of the story of why brands underinvest in content.

In May I argued on our Substack that the product detail page is the shelf nobody at the brand runs. Ownership is only half of it; the other half is the ledger. A leadership team that will argue for weeks over a 5% cut in click costs leaves a lift of that size unfunded because of where the money sits. Amazon product content is paid for once, from a creative budget, while its return shows up later as better advertising results credited to someone else. Nobody’s scorecard improves when the page does, so the page loses the budget fight.

Where the cost of Amazon product content lands

Inside most brands, product photography, copy and A+ or Enhanced Brand Content pages are commissioned as projects. Someone briefs an agency or the in-house studio, a set of images and modules is delivered, and the line is closed. The work is treated like packaging design: done well once, then left alone until the next relaunch.

The formats themselves are not new. Enhanced Brand Content, the seller-side version of A+ pages, has been open to brands enrolled in Brand Registry since 2016 (Tinuiti). What most brands lack is a reason to revisit those pages once they are live, because nothing in the annual budget cycle asks anyone to.

Advertising is budgeted the opposite way. It is a monthly line with a dashboard, a target and a person whose bonus moves with it. Merkle’s clients increased Sponsored Products spending 19% year over year in the first quarter of 2019, ChannelX reported, and Amazon’s “other” revenue, mostly advertising, rose 34% to $2.7 billion, VentureBeat reported. Media budgets keep growing because they can show what each dollar did.

Content cannot, at least not in the platform’s own reports. A brand can see what its ads cost and what they sold. It cannot see, anywhere in Amazon’s tools, what its new image stack or comparison chart added. That absence shapes behavior more than any belief about content’s value.

The gain shows up in someone else’s report

Follow one product through a month and the accounting problem becomes concrete. Take an item selling at $30 that buys 20,000 Sponsored Products clicks a month at $0.80, or $16,000. At a 10% conversion rate those clicks produce 2,000 orders, $60,000 of attributed sales and a return on ad spend of 3.75.

Now the brand rebuilds the page and conversion rises to 10.5%, a 5% relative lift, in the middle of Amazon’s own range. The same $16,000 of clicks now produces 2,100 orders and $63,000. Return on ad spend climbs to about 3.94, and organic shoppers who reach the page without an ad convert better too.

Where does the $3,000 a month appear? In the advertising report, as an improvement the media team will reasonably present as its own. The content work that caused it was a one-time cost, already closed in last quarter’s creative budget. At the next planning meeting, the media lead has a rising ROAS to defend and the creative lead has an invoice. It is not hard to guess which budget grows.

Walmart has been circling the same problem from the retailer’s side. It required suppliers to add online descriptions, images and product features from April 2017, Talk Business reported. In 2018 it surveyed 650 suppliers about what content providers cost and returned, finding wide disparities, before narrowing its approved providers from 25 to 12 (Talk Business). Kellogg’s e-commerce lead told the same publication that item page content can “make or break a shopper’s experience.” Retailers can see the effect across their whole catalog. Most brands, looking product by product through ad reports, cannot.

What changes when content is budgeted like media

The fix is less about persuading anyone that content matters than about moving it into the same system as the advertising it supports. A few brands already do this, and the pattern is simple to describe: content becomes a recurring line with an owner, a refresh calendar and a measured target, sitting in the same review as the media plan.

Measurement does not need to wait for Amazon to provide page-level data. Comparing conversion on the products whose pages changed with a matched set whose pages did not, over the same weeks, separates the content effect from the season and the ad budget. It is rougher than an ad report and far better than nothing. Give it four to six weeks on each side, because a lift of a few percent hides easily inside normal weekly noise.

These are the questions I would put to a CEO who wants to know whether the brand is underfunding content:

  • When did our top 20 Amazon products last get new images or A+ pages, and who decided the timing?
  • Which budget line pays for product content, and does it appear in the same review as Amazon advertising?
  • If conversion on a hero product rose half a point next month, whose report would show it?
  • What would we cut from media to fund one full content refresh, and what would we expect back?

The brands that answer the third question honestly tend to find the first one embarrassing. Keeping product pages on a schedule, measured against the media they support, is part of how we run Amazon for the brands we work with.

P0257.title: Walmart two-day delivery pays sellers only where ground reaches
P0257.alt: A blue van parked where a paved road meets a winding gravel track through green hills and forest.
P0257.ttag: Walmart two-day delivery pays sellers only where ground reaches | Kwontified
P0257.desc: A two-day badge on Walmart lifts conversion only if it costs less than it earns. For most sellers that means promising it where ground shipping already arrives.
P0257.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 16, 2019.
P0257.body:
Walmart taught its shoppers to expect speed before it asked its marketplace sellers to provide it. In January 2017 it launched free two-day shipping on more than two million items with a $35 minimum and no membership, and left marketplace items out of the offer, Walmart announced. In May 2019 it added free next-day delivery on about 220,000 items in its first cities, the Associated Press reported. A seller’s listing now sits beside Walmart’s own fast offers, and a slower delivery date is visible to every shopper comparing them.

So the question sellers ask about Walmart two-day delivery is usually framed as “should we get the badge?” The better question is how much conversion the badge has to buy back. In May, Seller Fulfilled Prime costs what your farthest customer costs looked at the cost side of a speed promise on Amazon. On Walmart the deciding number sits on the other side of the ledger: the lift in orders needed to cover the upgrade, on a page where Walmart’s own items already show a fast date. A two-day promise raises conversion, and it also raises shipping cost on every order that ground service cannot reach in two days. It pays where ground already arrives in time and rarely where the seller has to buy air shipping to keep it.

What the two-day badge does on a Walmart page

Walmart’s own fast-shipping offers set the reference point. Its two-day program covered its own inventory with a $35 threshold, and NextDay ships from the fulfillment center nearest the shopper so that orders arrive in as few boxes as possible, according to the AP’s account of Marc Lore’s explanation. A marketplace offer showing a delivery date three or four days later looks slower than the retailer’s own items on the same search page, whatever its price.

Walmart opened the badge to its marketplace in October 2018. It said it would work with “hundreds of our high-performing marketplace sellers” to make millions of their eligible items available for free two-day shipping, with no membership fee and on orders over $35 in the contiguous United States, Walmart announced. The announcement did not publish the eligibility rules or the on-time standard a seller must hold, so those terms are worth confirming with Walmart before switching the promise on. What follows does not depend on them; it depends on arithmetic every seller can run.

Performance rules also raise the cost of a missed promise. Walmart’s 2019 item setup guide says that in baby and grocery, items with a cancellation rate above 2% and a return rate above 5% are unpublished, with performance reviewed every 7, 15 and 30 days (Walmart). A promise the warehouse cannot keep shows up first as late orders and cancellations, and those are exactly the numbers Walmart watches.

The break-even lift for Walmart two-day delivery

The decision comes down to one comparison: the conversion lift the badge earns against the extra shipping it costs.

Take a $30 item that leaves the seller $8.00 of contribution per order after product cost, fees and standard ground shipping. Say the seller ships from one warehouse, and ground reaches half its orders in two days. To promise two days everywhere, it must upgrade the other half to a faster service, at an extra $3.00 an order. Spread across all orders, that is $1.50 each, and contribution falls to $6.50.

Without badgeBadge everywhereBadge where ground reaches
Extra shipping per order$0.00$1.50$0.00
Contribution per order$8.00$6.50$8.00
Orders needed to match 100 orders today100123100

At $6.50 an order, the seller needs 123 orders to earn what 100 earn today, a conversion lift of about 23% just to break even. A badge can lift conversion, but that is a high bar for a delivery date, and the seller pays the upgrade on every order whether the badge won it or not.

The right-hand column is the point of the exercise. If the promise is shown only where ground already arrives in two days, the extra shipping cost is zero and any lift is profit. The seller gives up the badge in distant regions and keeps it where it is free.

Where the trade-off leans the other way

There are cases where the full promise pays. A higher-priced item has more contribution to absorb the upgrade: at $30 of contribution, the same $1.50 needs only about a 5% lift. Light, small products cost less to upgrade than bulky ones. And a seller that adds a second warehouse on the other side of the country can turn most of its “air” orders into ground orders, which changes the table entirely, at the cost of splitting inventory across two buildings. Timing matters as well: in the weeks before a holiday, when shoppers care most about arrival dates, the same badge may earn more lift than it does in March, so the break-even test is worth rerunning each quarter.

Those cases share a feature: the seller has measured contribution per order and the real upgrade cost before turning the badge on. Most of the losses come from treating the badge as a marketing decision when it is a shipping decision.

Running the numbers before switching it on

  1. Map the last 90 days of Walmart orders by ground transit time from each warehouse, and find the share that already arrives in two days.
  2. Price the upgrade for the rest with your carrier, per order and by weight band.
  3. Compute break-even lift per item: extra shipping per order divided by the contribution left after it.
  4. Turn the promise on first for items and areas where the upgrade cost is zero, and measure conversion against the period before.
  5. Watch late shipments and cancellations weekly; a missed promise costs more than the badge earned.

Our rule of thumb: if the break-even lift is above 10%, keep the badge to the regions ground already reaches. Working out where speed pays, item by item, is part of how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

P0259.title: Back-to-school 2019 now opens on Prime Day, weeks before school
P0259.alt: A canvas backpack, straw hat and striped towel rest on a sunlit wooden bench against a blue wall.
P0259.ttag: Back-to-school 2019 now opens on Prime Day, weeks before school | Kwontified
P0259.desc: Retailers now treat the Prime Day week as the start of online back-to-school. Brands still plan the season around August, and the gap costs them July.
P0259.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 18, 2019.
P0259.body:
In a survey RetailMeNot published ahead of Prime Day 2019, 84% of retailers said the week surrounding Prime Day was the most important time for their online back-to-school sales, and parents said they had budgeted about $162 for Prime Day itself, Retail Dive reported. That week fell on July 15 and 16. In most of the country, school does not start for another month.

So when does back-to-school 2019 begin? For retailers, it began this week. For many brands, it still begins in August, when the school-supply aisle fills and the trade calendar says it should. That gap between the retailer’s season and the brand’s plan is where July sales go missing.

Parents shop the season earlier than the plan assumes

The season was already drifting earlier. In the National Retail Federation’s 2018 survey, released in July of that year, 77% of families with school-age children planned to start shopping at least three weeks before school began, and K-12 families expected to spend $684.79 each, according to the release. Clothing was the largest category, at $236.90 per shopper. The total was not growing: NRF expected K-12 and college spending combined to reach $82.8 billion in 2018, slightly below $83.6 billion the year before. In a season that is flat overall, retailers compete on when the money is spent and who gets it first, which is exactly what a July event is designed to win.

Where they shop matters as much as when. Deloitte’s 2018 survey found 83% of back-to-school shoppers planned to buy at mass merchants and 36% at online-only retailers, and estimated the average household would spend $115 online against $292 in stores, in its July 2018 release. The store still carries most of the money. The online share is the part that moves first, and it moves to whichever retailer gives parents a reason to start.

In 2019 the retailers gave them several. Amazon ran Prime Day for 48 hours on July 15 and 16. Target scheduled Deal Days on the same two days, with early-access deals of up to 50% off some kitchen items before them, and eBay ran three weeks of deals from July 1, CBS News reported. Walmart ran its own online sale from July 14 to 17, Techlicious reported. A parent with a supply list and a backpack to replace now has four retailers asking for the order in the middle of July.

The retailers’ calendar now sets the season

Back-to-school was built around the school calendar. Districts set start dates, stores reset their aisles a few weeks before, and brands planned shipments, promotions and media to land in that window. Target’s own one-day sale in July 2018, which it called “one of our biggest days of the year for online sales,” WTKR reported, shows how quickly the retailers learned that a summer event could pull demand forward.

Read the retailers as institutions and the incentive is plain. Prime Day exists to sell memberships and fill a quiet month; once it worked, every competitor needed a July answer, and back-to-school is the summer’s biggest planned purchase. So the retailers’ event calendar, rather than the school calendar, now decides when the online season starts.

Brands feel this as a series of small mismatches. The back-to-school promotion is approved for August. The inventory arrives at the warehouse in late July. The advertising plan ramps after the Fourth of July holiday but peaks with the store reset. Each decision is reasonable on the old calendar, and each leaves the brand underweight in the week its retailers say matters most.

What the season asks of marketplace brands

The structural change is simple to state: on marketplaces, back-to-school now has two peaks, a July event peak driven by retailers and an August peak driven by school dates, and brands need a plan for each. The July peak rewards different things. Deals and stock must be in place before the event rather than ahead of the store reset. Product pages must say what parents are actually shopping for: grade level, list items, sizes. And the advertising budget has to carry through a week that used to be quiet.

The product page is the piece brands most often leave on the old calendar. A backpack listing written in spring for a general shopper does not tell a parent in July whether it fits a binder, survives a year of fifth grade or matches the colors on the school’s list. Those answers decide a July purchase made from a phone with the list in the other hand, and they cost little to add before the event.

The evidence on how much of the season July now captures is still thin, and it will vary by category. Supplies and basics shift earliest; apparel and shoes, where fit and the child’s preference matter, may hold out for August. I would watch two things in the weeks after Prime Day: whether back-to-school searches on Amazon peak in July or August in your category, and whether your August sales fall where July sales rose.

These are the questions I would bring to the next planning meeting:

  • When did our back-to-school promotion start on Amazon, Target and Walmart, and who chose that date?
  • How much stock did we have in place for July 15, compared with August 1?
  • Did our ad budget for the season start before or after the retailers’ events?
  • In our category, did July sales add to the season or simply arrive earlier?

The last question decides next year’s calendar. Planning marketplace seasons around the retailers’ calendar rather than the trade calendar is part of how we run the channel for the brands we work with.

P0262.crumb: Prime Day 2019’s rivals competed on what…
P0262.title: Prime Day 2019’s rivals competed on what Amazon could not offer
P0262.alt: Three neighboring shopfronts on a stone street show a café table, a fitting room and a leather workbench.
P0262.ttag: Prime Day 2019’s rivals competed on what Amazon could not offer | Kwontified
P0262.desc: Target, Walmart and eBay ran events on Prime Day 2019 built on what Amazon lacks: no fee, stores, partner funding. Brands now face four July events, not one.
P0262.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 25, 2019.
P0262.body:
Target announced its July sale on June 26, the day after Amazon set the dates for Prime Day 2019, and chose exactly the same two days. It did not try to out-discount Amazon. It said shoppers would need no membership, could pick orders up in a store the same day, and would get 5% off with a Target card, CNBC reported. eBay offered a “crash sale” in case Amazon’s site went down again. Walmart ran an online sale from July 14 to 17 and a week of Google device deals alongside it.

Look at those choices together and a pattern appears. Each rival built its Prime Day 2019 answer on something Amazon could not match, rather than on Amazon’s own terms. That is what the event revealed, and for brands it means July is no longer one promotion. It is four, each with its own ask.

Each rival sold what Amazon does not have

Target sold access without a fee. Prime Day requires a membership that costs $119 a year; Target Deal Days required nothing, a point Target made the center of its pitch, WTKR reported. Its early-access deals of up to 50% off some kitchen items, and same-day pickup and delivery, leaned on the stores Amazon lacks, CBS News reported.

eBay sold insurance and duration. Its three weeks of deals began on July 1, with the crash sale timed for July 15, playing on the outage at the start of Prime Day 2018. A three-week event also meant eBay’s prices were in front of shoppers long after Amazon’s ended.

Walmart sold a partner’s products under its own banner. Its “Google Week” from July 8 to July 16 featured the Google Home Mini at $25, according to the same CBS report, an answer to Amazon’s habit of discounting its own Alexa devices, built around another manufacturer’s products.

None of these are copies of Prime Day. They are the institutional strengths of each rival, scheduled against Amazon’s date.

The results were shared, unevenly

Retailers with at least $1 billion in annual revenue saw sales 68% above a normal day across the two days, Adobe Analytics found, Practical Ecommerce reported. Adobe also found that retailers with strong email programs lifted revenue 52% over the two days, against 23% for those without. Amazon, for its part, said Prime members bought more than 175 million items and that the event’s sales beat its 2018 Black Friday and Cyber Monday combined.

Membership cut both ways. Searches for canceling Amazon Prime were 18 times higher on the Monday of the event than the day before, Captify found, according to the same Practical Ecommerce report, a sign that some shoppers joined for the deals and planned to leave. Target’s no-fee pitch was aimed squarely at them.

The spread between 52% and 23% is the detail worth dwelling on. The retailers that gained most were the ones that could reach their own customers directly and tell them the event was on. Prime Day has become a moment when shoppers expect deals everywhere, and the rivals that benefited were the ones with a direct line to their shoppers on the day.

So the event that Amazon built to sell memberships now lifts a whole tier of large retailers. Moody’s analyst Charlie O’Shea said before the event that the longer Prime Day would make “an already acutely-competitive retail environment even tougher” and expected Walmart and Target to respond, Retail Dive reported. They did, and on their own terms.

Four events mean four negotiations

For a brand, the shift shows up in the inbox before it shows up in the results. Follow the value through each rival’s event and the brand is asked for something different by each one: a deal price and stock for Amazon, a matching price and perhaps store inventory for Target, support for a Walmart theme week, and a price on eBay that its resellers will set whether the brand likes it or not.

The questions brands tend to ask after Prime Day are about Amazon alone: what sold, what the ads cost, whether the deal paid. The more useful review looks across all four. A deal price on Amazon becomes the reference price shoppers carry to Target’s site the same afternoon. A Walmart theme week built around one manufacturer sets an expectation for the next. And a three-week eBay event keeps discounts visible well into August. The brand’s own channels are a fifth venue: if Adobe’s email finding holds for retailers, it likely holds for brands too, and the ones that told their own customers where to buy during the event kept more of the attention it created.

The evidence on how much each rival’s event added, rather than moved, is not public, and it will differ by category. The direction is clearer. Each of Amazon’s largest US rivals now has a July event, and each is built around what it can offer that Amazon cannot.

Questions for the post-Prime Day review

  • Which retailers asked us for a July price or support, and did we decide each request on its own or as one plan?
  • Did our Amazon deal price appear, or get matched, on Target, Walmart or eBay within the same week?
  • Did our own email and social channels tell customers where to find us during the event?
  • Which retailer’s July event should we fund in 2020, and what do we expect it to add?

The answer to the last question shapes the next July more than any Prime Day bid. Planning the season across every retailer’s event, rather than Amazon’s alone, is part of how we run the channel for brands.

P0263.title: Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark, Q2 2019: top of search paid off
P0263.alt: A gold-wrapped parcel sits atop rustic shelves of ceramic pots and folded linens beside a leaning wooden ladder.
P0263.ttag: Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark, Q2 2019: top of search paid off | Kwontified
P0263.desc: Top of search took 45% of Sponsored Products spend in Q2 2019 and returned over half the sales. The dearest click in the account was the cheapest sale.
P0263.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 30, 2019.
P0263.body:
The most expensive seat in an Amazon search result is the row of Sponsored Products ads across the top of the first page. In the second quarter of 2019 it served just 3% of the format’s impressions among Merkle’s advertisers and took 45% of their Sponsored Products spend, Merkle’s quarterly report showed. Accounts that see that number tend to cap the placement.

The same report credited top of search with more than half of all sales attributed to Sponsored Products. Put the two figures together and the dearest click in the account was the cheapest sale. The second-quarter benchmark is mostly a lesson in reading cost per click against what each click brings back.

What the Q2 2019 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark shows

Merkle’s advertisers got more for their money than a year earlier. Sponsored Products clicks rose 58% while spend rose 12%, and attributed sales rose 102%. Divide those growth rates and three ratios fall out.

Sponsored Products, Merkle advertisersQ2 2019 vs Q2 2018What it implies
Spend+12%
Clicks+58%Average cost per click down about 29%
Attributed sales+102%Sales per click up about 28%; ROAS up about 80%

The placement split shows where the money sat. Product detail pages carried 82% of Sponsored Products impressions but 40% of clicks. Top of search carried 3% of impressions, 35% of clicks and 45% of spend.

Q2 2019Share of clicksShare of spendShare of attributed salesCost per click vs account averageSales per click vs account average
Top of search35%45%more than 50%about 1.3xmore than 1.4x
Every other placement65%55%less than 50%about 0.85xless than 0.77x

The first quarter looked similar. Merkle’s Q1 2019 report put top of search at 33% of Sponsored Products clicks and detail pages at 41%, with spend up 19% year over year, ChannelX reported. So spend growth slowed from the first quarter to the second while clicks drifted toward the top of the page.

Why advertisers bid top of search down

The instinct to cap it is reasonable. A cost-per-click report ranks top of search as the worst line in the account, and advertisers long had only one blunt lever for it. The old Bid+ setting raised bids by at most 50%, and only for top of search. In February 2019 Amazon replaced it with an option to adjust bids by placement, up to 900% for top of search and for product detail pages, Feedvisor explained. The same change let advertisers view performance by three placement groups: top of search, rest of search and product pages.

A placement that charges more per click looks like the place to save. That holds only if its clicks are worth the same as everyone else’s, and the benchmark says they are not. The auction prices top of search higher because many advertisers want it. It did not price it high enough to cancel out how well those clicks sell.

The arithmetic of a dearer click

Take an account that spends $10,000 a quarter on Sponsored Products at a ROAS of 4.0, so $40,000 in attributed sales. Split it the way Merkle’s advertisers split theirs in the second quarter.

Top of search takes $4,500 of the spend and brings in more than $20,000 of the sales, a ROAS above 4.4. Every other placement takes $5,500 and brings in less than $20,000, a ROAS below 3.6. Each top-of-search click costs about 1.5 times a click elsewhere, and each one brings in at least 1.8 times the sales.

Now cut the top-of-search adjustment to save money. Each dollar moved out of top of search buys clicks that earn less than $3.60 instead of more than $4.40. The cost-per-click line improves and the account sells less for the same budget.

What the benchmark cannot tell you

Two things limit the read. The first is the sample: these are Merkle’s advertisers, not the whole auction, and their categories and price points may not match yours.

The second matters more. Brand keywords made up 43% of Sponsored Products sales in the same report. A shopper who types your brand name is already close to buying, and the ad that shows above your organic listing collects that sale. The report does not say how much of top of search’s lead comes from branded searches, and a placement that wins mostly on your own name has not proved it finds new customers.

Merkle also compared Sponsored Products with Google Shopping and found conversion rates 240% higher on Amazon, while warning that the comparison is hard because not every advertiser runs both. Treat any single average from a mixed sample with the same care.

Your own account settles it. Separate branded and non-branded campaigns, then compare cost per sale by placement inside the non-branded ones only. If top of search still sells for less there, the benchmark applies to you.

Bid triggers for the third quarter

  • Judge each placement on cost per sale, never on cost per click. A placement that costs 50% more per click and sells twice as often is the cheaper one.
  • Raise the top-of-search adjustment only where non-branded top of search beat the rest of search on ROAS by 20% or more over four weeks. Move in steps of 25 percentage points, so each change shows in a week of data.
  • Give detail-page placements a separate look. They carried 82% of impressions and 40% of clicks in the benchmark, so a small change in their bids moves a lot of traffic.
  • Read the third-quarter report with Prime Day in it. The event ran July 15 and 16, 2019, so expect a different placement mix next quarter.

Bidding each placement on what its clicks sell is how we set Sponsored Products bids for the brands we run.

P0264.crumb: Amazon grocery in 2019 is arranged by the…
P0264.title: Amazon grocery in 2019 is arranged by the cost of the box
P0264.alt: Three cardboard boxes of produce, jars and paper parcels on a wooden table beside an antique brass scale.
P0264.ttag: Amazon grocery in 2019 is arranged by the cost of the box | Kwontified
P0264.desc: Amazon grocery sorts products by what each order costs to deliver, so pack sizes built for a supermarket shelf often lose money in Amazon’s delivered box.
P0264.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 1, 2019.
P0264.body:
A supermarket sells bottled water by the pallet near the front door, where it is cheap to restock and easy to carry to the car. Amazon tried selling it the other way. A six-pack of Coca-Cola’s Smartwater cost $6.99 at the tap of a Dash button, and every one of those orders lost money once shipping was paid. Amazon first raised the minimum to a 24-pack at $37.20, and then asked Coca-Cola to ship the water itself, the Wall Street Journal reported in December 2018.

That story is the clearest guide to Amazon grocery going into the second half of 2019. Amazon does not arrange the category by aisle. It arranges it by what a delivered box costs, and a brand whose pack sizes were designed for a supermarket shelf is often offering Amazon the one product it least wants to carry.

What shoppers actually buy in Amazon grocery

Amazon’s grocery shopper is easy to picture once you look at the bestsellers. Consumables (grocery, health and personal care, and pet products) passed $10 billion in sales on Amazon in 2018, and grocery accounted for about $3 billion of it, according to Edge by Ascential’s year-end review. Coffee and cold drinks each sold about $600 million. Single-serve pods made up more than 80% of the coffee.

That is a stock-up shopper, not a weekly-shop shopper. The top three grocery items on Amazon in the second quarter of 2018 were a 72-count box of coffee pods, a 12-pack of meal-replacement shakes and a 100-count box of pods, One Click Retail found. Nobody buys a 72-count box of pods on impulse. They buy it because they ran out, and because the box is big enough that the delivery makes sense to everyone involved.

The growth is also cooling. Edge by Ascential put Amazon’s 2018 grocery growth rate about 25% below its pace the year before. A shopper who already reorders pods and snacks on Amazon is not the hard part; the harder part is the shopper who still buys produce, dairy and bread in a store, and Amazon has been trying to reach that shopper through a different door.

The structure behind it: a grocery P&L that is really a shipping P&L

Amazon’s own vocabulary says how it judges the category. Internally, the heavy, cheap items that lose money after delivery are called CRaP, for “can’t realize a profit.” The label measures an item by the order it travels in, which is a different test from the one a supermarket buyer applies to a facing on a shelf.

Several of Amazon’s grocery mechanics follow from that test. Prime Pantry makes the shopper fill a box before it ships, so the delivery cost is spread over enough items to pay for itself. The Smartwater minimum went from six bottles to 24. Each is a way of turning a low-value item into a box worth sending.

The shipping promise is getting faster, which makes the test stricter. Free one-day delivery reached more than ten million items for Prime members by the end of June, Amazon said in its second-quarter results, and the cost of the shift came in slightly above the roughly $800 million the company had planned for the quarter, GeekWire reported. A $7 pack that was marginal on two-day shipping gets harder to justify on one-day.

Follow the value and the incentive is plain. When a heavy item cannot pay its way, Amazon has three options: make the shopper buy more of it, make the brand ship it, or stop selling it. Every one of those moves pushes cost or work back toward the brand. None of them requires a conversation with the brand’s category manager first.

Fresh food went through a different door

For fresh food, Amazon’s biggest moves in 2019 have been in a store rather than a box. Whole Foods began its third round of price cuts on April 3, with an average saving of 20% on the reduced items and a focus on produce, and doubled the number of weekly deals for Prime members, CNBC reported.

Amazon is also planning a separate grocery chain, apart from Whole Foods, with stores of about 35,000 square feet and the first expected in Los Angeles, possibly by the end of 2019, the Wall Street Journal reported in March. The stores themselves are not growing fast. Physical-store sales were $4.33 billion in the second quarter, flat on the $4.31 billion of a year earlier.

So the Amazon grocery shelf a brand faces in 2019 is really three shelves with different economics. Amazon.com rewards the multipack and the subscription. Prime Pantry rewards the item that fits in a mixed box. Whole Foods, and whatever the new chain becomes, takes the fresh and the chilled. It is too early to say how the new stores will treat national brands; the reporting so far says little about what they will stock. The evidence leans toward an online business that wants fewer, larger orders and a store business that carries what a box cannot.

Questions for the next category review

The useful conversation inside a food or beverage brand is about pack architecture, and it rarely happens, because pack sizes belong to supply chain while Amazon belongs to sales. Four questions bring the two into the same room:

  1. Which of our Amazon items would still make money for Amazon if the shopper ordered only that item, one-day, at the current price?
  2. If Amazon asked us to ship our heaviest items ourselves next quarter, could we, and what would it cost us per order?
  3. Who decides the pack size we sell on Amazon, and does that person see Amazon’s sales data?
  4. Is each fresh or chilled item an Amazon.com conversation or a Whole Foods conversation, and who at our company owns each?

A brand that answers the first question honestly may find items it should resize before Amazon resizes them for it. Sorting a catalog that way, item by item, is part of how we run the Amazon grocery channel for food and beverage brands.

P0266.title: Amazon’s Q2 2019 other revenue slowed only on paper
P0266.alt: A stack of brass coins beside a blank sheet of paper and a pencil on a worn wooden table.
P0266.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2019 other revenue slowed only on paper | Kwontified
P0266.desc: Amazon’s ad-heavy other revenue grew 37% in Q2 2019. The slowdown from 2018 is an accounting base effect; ads still outgrew Amazon’s retail sales.
P0266.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 6, 2019.
P0266.body:
Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which is mostly advertising, grew 129% in the second quarter of 2018 and 37% in the second quarter of 2019. The coverage wrote the obvious headline: Amazon’s ad business was still expanding, but its growth slowed for the second quarter in a row.

Most of that slowdown happened in an accounting office, as Amazon other revenue grew 34% in Q1 2019, its first clean read set out in April. The second quarter answers a different question: what an auction growing about twice as fast as Amazon’s retail business does to a brand whose ad budget grows only with its own sales. A flat ratio of ad spend to sales buys a smaller share of that auction every quarter, and that gap is what a brand’s budget should be built on.

What Amazon reported for Q2 2019

Amazon does not report advertising on its own. It reports a line called “other,” which advertising dominates. Here are the second-quarter figures from Amazon’s July 25 results, in millions of dollars:

LineQ2 2018Q2 2019Reported growth
Online stores$27,165$31,05314%
Third-party seller services$9,702$11,96223%
Other (mostly advertising)$2,194$3,00237%
Total net sales$52.9 billion$63.4 billion20%

The same release shows the growth rate of “other,” excluding currency moves, quarter by quarter: 132%, 129%, 123% and 97% through 2018, then 36% in the first quarter of 2019 and 37% in the second.

Why the 2018 growth rates looked so high

In brief, because 2018 had a second engine. Amazon adopted a new revenue accounting standard at the start of 2018, and on its first-quarter call that year the company said the change added about $560 million to “other” revenue in that quarter alone. Every 2018 quarter compared revenue booked under the new rules with 2017 revenue booked under the old ones. A base effect like that lifts every comparison for four quarters, then disappears all at once, which is why the drop to 36% in the first quarter of 2019 looked like news. The second quarter, at 37%, is the steadier like-for-like pace.

The number that matters is ad revenue per dollar of retail

A growth rate on its own does not tell a brand much. What a brand pays for is a share of an auction, and the auction gets more expensive when advertising grows faster than the sales it competes for.

So compare “other” with Amazon’s retail revenue: what it books from its own online store sales plus the fees it collects from third-party sellers. In the second quarter of 2018, “other” was about 6.0 cents for every dollar of that retail revenue. In the first quarter of 2019 it was 6.7 cents. In the second quarter of 2019 it was 7.0 cents. Retail revenue grew 17% year over year; “other” grew 37%.

Now take a brand that sells $500,000 a quarter on Amazon and spends 7% of those sales on advertising, a total ACoS (ad spend divided by all Amazon sales, organic included) of 7%, or $35,000. Its sales grow 17%, in line with Amazon’s retail revenue, and it holds total ACoS at 7%. Its ad budget rises to $40,950. That feels like a 17% increase in advertising, and it is.

But the money in the auction grew 37%. The brand’s share of total ad spending is now 1.17 divided by 1.37 of what it was, about 85%. Holding total ACoS flat while the auction grows this fast means buying roughly 15% less of the auction than a year earlier. In a keyword auction that shows up as lost top-of-search placements and fewer impressions on the terms that matter, often before it shows up in sales.

Amazon is still investing to make the auction bigger. Marketing spending rose almost 50% year over year in the quarter, and Amazon told analysts it was invested in the long-term success of Sizmek, the ad server it bought during the quarter, AdExchanger reported. The company guided third-quarter net sales to $66.0 billion to $70.0 billion.

What the line can and cannot tell you

“Other” is a proxy, and it has two weaknesses. It includes revenue that is not advertising, so the ratio overstates ad intensity by an unknown amount. And third-party seller services are fees, not the value of what sellers sold, so the denominator understates the retail sales that ads compete for. Neither weakness changes the direction. Both the numerator and the denominator are defined the same way in both years, and the ratio rose by a full cent in a year.

It also says nothing about a single category. Ad intensity in coffee pods is not the same as in serums. The useful test is in the brand’s own data: the cost per click on its ten largest non-branded keywords in the latest quarter against the same quarter a year ago. If those prices rose faster than the brand’s sales, the brand is living inside the 37%, whatever its total ACoS says.

What would change the picture is a quarter in which “other” grows no faster than retail revenue. In each of the five quarters in Amazon’s latest release, “other” grew faster than both online stores and seller services. The second quarter of 2019 was no exception, with “other” up 37% against 14% for online stores and 23% for seller services.

A rule for the 2019 plans

Set the Amazon ad budget against the growth of the auction, not the growth of the brand. If category click prices are rising faster than your sales, a flat total ACoS is a decision to shrink, and it should be taken on purpose. Measuring that gap keyword by keyword is the starting point when we plan Amazon advertising budgets with brands.

P0267.crumb: Delivery promises now decide what goes in…
P0267.title: Delivery promises now decide what goes in the basket
P0267.alt: A wicker basket of bread, apples, herbs and lavender next to a brass carriage clock on a wooden table.
P0267.ttag: Delivery promises now decide what goes in the basket | Kwontified
P0267.desc: Amazon’s one-day Prime and Walmart’s NextDay set different rules for the basket, and those rules now change which products shoppers buy online.
P0267.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 8, 2019.
P0267.body:
Two retailers made the same promise in the spring of 2019 and wrote very different fine print. In April, Amazon said it was evolving free two-day Prime shipping into a free one-day program; when it expanded the program in June, there was no minimum order. In May, Walmart launched free NextDay delivery on up to 220,000 frequently purchased items, with no membership but a condition: every item in the cart has to be NextDay-eligible, and the cart has to pass $35.

Read the fine print side by side and a pattern appears. A delivery promise is also a set of rules about the basket, and the rules change what people buy. Brands planning for faster shipping have mostly treated it as a logistics question. It is turning into a merchandising one.

Two promises, two kinds of basket

Amazon’s version is built for the single urgent item. Free one-day delivery reached more than ten million items for Prime members by the end of June, Amazon said with its second-quarter results. With no minimum, a Prime member who runs out of phone chargers on a Tuesday evening can have one by Wednesday without adding anything else. That is the role a corner shop plays in a neighborhood: a small, expensive-to-serve order, placed because waiting is worse.

Walmart’s version is built for the replenishment basket. The NextDay assortment leans on diapers, household needs, toys and electronics, and the all-eligible rule means a shopper who wants next-day speed has to build a $35 order from the same pool, TechCrunch reported. Marc Lore, who runs Walmart’s U.S. e-commerce business, explained the logic: the items ship from the fulfillment center closest to the shopper, in one box or as few boxes as possible, which he said costs Walmart less than a multi-box order shipped from several buildings. That is the weekly-shop aisle of a supercenter, delivered.

Neither design is an accident. Amazon is spending to make the single item free and fast, and the shift cost slightly more than the roughly $800 million it had planned for the second quarter, GeekWire reported. Walmart is making speed pay for itself by asking for a bigger basket. Each retailer’s promise reflects what it can afford and what it wants its shopper to become.

The Walmart rule will not stay regional for long. NextDay started in Phoenix and Las Vegas, and Walmart plans to reach 75% of the U.S. population, including 40 of the 50 largest metro areas, by the end of 2019. By the holidays, a large share of online shoppers will be choosing between two different ideas of what a fast basket looks like.

What shoppers do when speed changes

Speed matters to shoppers, though usually less than price. In a survey of nearly 1,300 shoppers by the fulfillment software company Temando, 26% said they had abandoned a cart because shipping was too slow, against 54% who had abandoned one over high shipping costs, Retail Dive reported in 2017. But 47% said they would buy from a competitor if a premium delivery option was not available.

That last figure explains why both retailers moved. Once a shopper knows a product can arrive tomorrow at no charge, a two-day badge on a rival’s listing reads as a cost, even though nothing about the product has changed. The shopper does not compare delivery speeds the way an analyst would. She notices which option asks her to wait.

For a brand, the consequence lands on the product page. Two listings for similar sunscreens can sit next to each other on Amazon, one carrying a one-day promise and one not, and the difference has nothing to do with the formula, the photography or the price. It comes from where the units happen to be stored.

The decision behind the badge sits in supply chain

That is the part of the change most brand teams have not absorbed. Whether a product shows one-day delivery depends on whether there is stock in a building close enough to the shopper, and that is set by the inventory plan: how many units a brand sends to Amazon, how they are split, and how quickly they are replenished. On Walmart, it depends on whether the item is in the NextDay assortment at the nearest fulfillment center at all. A unit sitting in the wrong building is invisible to the shopper who needed it tomorrow.

Inside most brands, those decisions sit with supply chain and finance, who are rewarded for keeping inventory low and turns high. The people who want the badge, in e-commerce and marketing, rarely own the stock that earns it. The result is a familiar argument in a new form: the e-commerce team asks for more units in more places, and the planning team asks what the extra weeks of cover will cost.

Both are right, which is why the argument needs a shared number rather than a winner. Amazon has said little about how one-day changes conversion for an individual product, and the honest position is that the evidence for any single brand will come from its own data. What a brand can see is whether its fastest-moving items carry the one-day promise, and whether the items that lost it also lost sales.

The question to put on the next planning agenda

Faster shipping changes the basket in a way a media plan cannot. On Amazon, it rewards the product someone needs by tomorrow; on Walmart, it rewards the product that belongs in a $35 replenishment order. A brand selling both should know which of its products fit which basket, and stock them accordingly.

The question for the next quarterly plan is simple to ask and hard to answer: which of our ten best-selling online products carry the fastest delivery promise on each retailer now, and who in the room is responsible when one of them does not? Getting e-commerce and supply chain to answer it together is a large part of how we run marketplace channels for brands.

P0268.crumb: A Q4 2019 budget should follow the value…
P0268.title: A Q4 2019 budget should follow the value of a click
P0268.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a gold coin against a twine-tied parcel, with autumn leaves on the table.
P0268.ttag: A Q4 2019 budget should follow the value of a click | Kwontified
P0268.desc: Q4 2019 has six fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas. Phase Amazon ad budgets by what a click is worth in each week, not by the calendar.
P0268.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 13, 2019.
P0268.body:
Thanksgiving falls on November 28 in 2019, the latest date it can. A year earlier it fell on November 22. That leaves 27 days between Thanksgiving and Christmas instead of 33, and Cyber Monday lands on December 2.

Most Q4 advertising plans start from the calendar: a share of the budget for October, a bigger share for November, the peak for Cyber Week, the rest for December. The calendar is the wrong unit. What should set the spend in each week is the gap between what a click is worth and what it costs, and those two numbers move on different schedules. In a short season the gap opens late and closes early.

The Q4 2019 budget in one table

Take a $60 product on Amazon with a target advertising cost of sale of 20%, so the brand can spend $12 to win one sale. A click is worth $12 times the chance it converts. That value and the price of a click might move through the quarter like this:

Period (2019)Conversion rateValue of a clickCost per clickHeadroom per click
October 1–318%$0.96$0.75$0.21
November 1–279%$1.08$0.90$0.18
Cyber Week, Nov 28–Dec 215%$1.80$1.20$0.60
December 3 to shipping cutoff11%$1.32$1.15$0.17
After the shipping cutoff5%$0.60$1.00–$0.40

The figures are a worked example, not a forecast for any category. The shape is what matters. Headroom is thin in October and November, widest in Cyber Week and negative once shoppers can no longer get a gift in time. A budget that follows the headroom spends heavily in five days and pulls back hard in the last week before Christmas.

Why the calendar plan feels right

Calendar plans are not careless. They match how sales arrive: the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday 2018 brought in $24.2 billion of US online sales, up 23% on the year before, out of $126 billion for the whole November–December season, Adobe Analytics reported. Those five days were about 8% of the season’s days and about 19% of its sales. Cyber Monday alone was $7.9 billion.

So putting more money where the sales are seems obvious. The trouble is that every competitor reads the same report. The extra money arrives in the same week, the auction gets more crowded, and the price of a click rises. The calendar tells you when demand peaks. It cannot tell you whether your clicks are worth more than they cost when you get there.

Conversion rate and click price move on different schedules

A click’s value is set by the shopper; its price is set by the other bidders. In early November, shoppers are browsing and comparing, so conversion rates are modest, while advertisers who plan by the calendar have already raised bids for the season. That is how headroom can narrow before Cyber Week rather than widening. During Cyber Week, shoppers arrive ready to buy, and conversion rises faster than the click price. After the last shipping day for Christmas, intent collapses but bids lag, because automated rules and daily budgets set for December keep spending.

Each side of that trade-off has a real case. Spending early builds reviews, sales rank and new customers who may return in the peak, and a brand that goes dark in October can find its organic rank weaker at Thanksgiving. Spending late chases the highest-converting days at the highest prices. The numbers lean toward the peak, as long as the brand has measured its own conversion rate by week. Early spend earns its place only when it is buying something the peak needs, such as reviews on a new product.

The short season sharpens both ends. Six fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas means the profitable window after Cyber Week is shorter, and the post-cutoff loss arrives sooner. Amazon’s one-day promise, now on more than ten million items for Prime members according to its second-quarter results, may push the last useful ordering day later for eligible products. Plan the December cut item by item once Amazon publishes its holiday cutoff dates.

What the data can tell you before October

The table needs three inputs a brand can pull from its own reports now: conversion rate by week for October through December 2018, average cost per click for the same weeks, and the date its sales fell away in late December. Those give the shape of 2018’s headroom. The 2019 calendar then shifts the Cyber Week columns six days later.

What the 2018 data cannot tell you is how many more competitors will bid in 2019. Amazon’s ad-heavy “other” revenue grew 37% in the second quarter, faster than its retail business, so the cost-per-click column should be assumed higher than 2018’s for the same week. A brand that copies 2018’s click prices into the plan is likely to run out of budget early in December.

Budget triggers for the quarter

Hold a share of the quarter’s budget in reserve and release it on evidence rather than dates:

  1. Release reserve in Cyber Week only for keywords whose conversion rate in the first 24 hours is at least one and a half times their November average.
  2. Cut bids on any keyword where cost per click passes its value per click for three consecutive days, in any period.
  3. Set a date, a day or two after Amazon’s last shipping day for each product, when daily budgets drop to a maintenance level, and put it in the plan now so no automated rule overrides it.
  4. Keep October spend tied to a goal, such as reviews on a product launched for the season, and stop it when the goal is met.

Building this headroom table from a brand’s own 2018 data, keyword by keyword, is where we start when we plan holiday advertising on Amazon.

P0270.crumb: Amazon agency or in-house: the real…
P0270.title: Amazon agency or in-house: the real question is who joins it up
P0270.alt: Paper cups linked together with twine like string telephones on a sunlit wooden table.
P0270.ttag: Amazon agency or in-house: the real question is who joins it up | Kwontified
P0270.desc: Choosing an agency, a consultant or an in-house team for Amazon matters less than deciding who owns the joins between operations, ads and content.
P0270.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 15, 2019.
P0270.body:
On Amazon’s second-quarter earnings call in July, the company’s chief financial officer said something unusual for an executive of a business that prides itself on serving customers. Brian Olsavsky conceded that Amazon’s internal organization, with separate teams across seller services, vendor services, advertising and other parts of the business, can get “out of hand” for customers, AdExchanger reported. “We need good coordination across our teams,” he said.

The customers he meant include the brands that sell on Amazon, and most of them have built their own Amazon effort in the same shape: one group for operations, another for advertising, a third for content. When those brands debate whether an agency, a consultant or an in-house team should run the channel, they are usually choosing who gets one of the pieces. The better question is who owns the joins between them.

A channel that arrives in pieces

Look at what running Amazon involves for a brand in 2019. Someone has to keep inventory flowing and listings accurate. Someone has to run Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands, set bids and read the search term reports. Someone has to write the product pages, shoot the images and answer the questions shoppers post. Each piece has its own console, its own reports and, inside Amazon, often its own team. Even the advertising was sold under three names (Amazon Marketing Services, Amazon Media Group and the Amazon Advertising Platform) until September 2018, when Amazon folded them into Amazon Advertising.

Brands rarely planned this. Many of them sold to Amazon wholesale through Vendor Central, where Amazon handled most of the operations and the brand’s job was negotiation. That arrangement wobbled in March, when Amazon stopped placing purchase orders with a large number of vendors, then reversed course for most of them and said that only brands enrolled in Brand Registry would get automatic purchase orders, with 60 days to enroll, Modern Retail reported. Vendors that did not own their brands were pointed to Seller Central. A brand that moves to Seller Central inherits the operations Amazon used to do for it, on top of the advertising it was already buying.

So the pieces multiply, and the people who handle them sit in different places. The advertising often went to an agency first, because media buying is what agencies already did. Operations problems, such as a suspended listing or a stranded shipment, often went to a consultant brought in to fix them. The profit and loss stayed with someone in-house. Each of the three sees a different slice of the same shelf.

Why each model sees only part of the shelf

Each option has a real strength, and each has a blind spot that comes from where it sits.

An agency brings scale in execution: people who manage bids across many accounts every day and see changes in the auction before a single brand would. Its blind spot is usually the rest of the shelf. An agency paid on media can make a campaign efficient while the product it advertises runs out of stock, because inventory is not in its brief.

A consultant brings judgment for a defined problem: an account-health crisis, a Vendor-to-Seller transition, a pricing policy. The blind spot is time. The engagement ends, and the daily decisions that keep the fix in place go back to whoever was making them before.

An in-house team owns the profit and loss and knows the brand’s constraints, from the factory’s lead times to the finance team’s margin floor. Its blind spot is depth and pace. Amazon changes its tools often, and a team of two at a mid-sized brand is rarely current on all of them while also running the weekly business review.

None of these blind spots is a failing of the people involved. They follow from the brief each one is given.

What Walmart’s decision shows about which pieces to keep

Retailers face the same choice from the other side, and their answers are instructive. In February, Walmart moved its website ad sales and the related analytics work in-house to Walmart Media Group, away from the agency that had run it, Marketing Dive reported, with the transition running through May. The piece it took back sits closest to its shopper data and its advertiser relationships, and the coverage tied the move to that data and to competing with Amazon, which had already brought its own media sales in-house.

Brands can make the same cut. Some pieces belong to the brand whatever model it chooses: the decision about price, the commitment of inventory, the brand’s own sales and search data, and the final word on what the product page says. Other pieces are execution that can be rented well, such as daily bid management or building listings at volume. The model follows from the split. A brand that keeps the decisions and the data can use an agency or a consultant for execution without losing the joins. A brand that hands over the decisions along with the work will find, sooner or later, that nobody owns the whole.

Before the next pitch meeting

Two questions help more than any request for proposal:

  • Who, by name, is accountable for Amazon profit, including stock, price, advertising and content, and do they see all four reports every week?
  • Which decisions will we never hand to an outside partner, and does every partner’s contract say so?

The answers matter more than the logo on the proposal. A brand that can answer both can choose any of the three models and make it work. Running the channel day to day, with the brand keeping the decisions, is how we manage Amazon for brands that want one owner of the whole.

P0272.desc: Enhanced Brand Content costs nothing, but it pays only through conversion rate, which also sets what every paid click is worth. Test it with matched pairs.
P0272.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. All channels
P0272.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 20, 2019.
P0272.body:
Brand owners selling through Seller Central have had their own version of the vendor A+ page since 2016, under the name Enhanced Brand Content. The two tools use very similar templates, so this piece calls both A+ Content: a brand selling through both Vendor Central and Seller Central is managing one kind of page under two names.

The name matters less than the question the page invites. A+ Content does nothing for a listing on its own. It is worth exactly the change it makes to conversion rate, and because conversion rate multiplies the value of every click, paid or organic, a small lift is worth more than it looks. It is also easy to mismeasure.

What the A+ Content pages can do for sellers

The sellers’ version replaces the plain-text product description with images and formatted text, built from a set of modules, Tinuiti’s guide to Enhanced Brand Content explains. Its version, dated August 2018, lays out the limits: the first two modules are fixed for a brand logo and a short description, the remaining five can be arranged freely, there is no HTML and no self-service video, and each product gets up to 250KB of images and text. Amazon reviews submissions within seven days, and most within two.

Eligibility runs through Brand Registry: a seller can add the content only to products in its approved brand catalog. Tinuiti also noted that the tool was in a promotional free period, so a seller pays nothing to use it and, if a fee arrived later, content already published would stay up.

The seller pages were built to look like the vendor ones. A strategist quoted in the same guide described the seller templates as very similar to vendor A+ templates, and called vendor A+ Content effective for improving conversion rate. That is the claim to test, and it is a claim about conversion, not about how polished the page looks.

Free is the important word. A tool that costs nothing gets judged loosely, and it is easy either to fill every slot or never get round to it. Both habits skip the arithmetic.

Why a conversion lift is worth more than it looks

Take a $30 product with 1,000 page sessions a week and a 10% conversion rate: 100 units, $3,000 a week. Suppose A+ Content lifts conversion by 8%, from 10% to 10.8%. That is 108 units, or $240 a week more on the same traffic, about $12,480 over a year.

That is the obvious gain, and it is the smaller one. Conversion rate also sets what a click is worth. If the brand will spend 25% of the price to win a sale, a click on that product is worth $30 times 25% times the conversion rate: $0.75 at 10%, $0.81 at 10.8%. The brand can bid 8% more on every keyword and keep the same advertising cost of sale, which wins more placements, which brings more sessions to a page that now converts better.

The lift may reach organic traffic as well, if the extra sales improve the product’s position in search over time. That effect is slow, and nobody outside Amazon can put a number on it for a given product.

What the 8% figure can and cannot tell you

The 8% in the example is not a benchmark. It comes from the one case study in Tinuiti’s guide, in which the Polaris Optics product with Enhanced Brand Content outperformed the rest of the brand’s catalog by 8% over a 25-day before-and-after comparison. One brand, one product, under a month.

A before-and-after test is also the easiest way to fool yourself. Publish A+ Content in late October and conversion will rise in November whatever the page says, because November shoppers arrive ready to buy. Publish it the week a competitor runs out of stock and the lift belongs to the competitor. The comparison credits the content with everything else that changed.

A matched test avoids most of that. Take pairs of similar products (same category, similar price, similar traffic) and publish A+ Content on one product in each pair. Compare the change in conversion rate between the two groups over the same four to six weeks. Seasonality, competitor moves and ad changes then hit both groups alike, and the difference that remains belongs to the content.

Products with steady traffic can show a lift within that window; a product with a few dozen sessions a week needs longer before the difference means anything. A brand with too few products for pairs can alternate: publish, measure two weeks, then compare with a similar product that stayed plain.

What would change the conclusion is a lift smaller than the noise. If conversion on the test products moves no more than it does week to week on the controls, the content is not doing its job, and the fix is usually the content: images that answer the questions shoppers post, comparison charts against the brand’s own range, sizes and materials stated plainly.

A rule for the A+ Content queue

Publish A+ Content first on the products where a conversion lift is worth the most: the ones with the most sessions and the biggest advertising budgets. Amazon allows up to 20 pending submissions at a time, so a brand with a large catalog should queue products by value, not by catalog order. Run them as a matched test, and once the lift is measured, raise bids on those products by the same percentage. A content change that lifts conversion is also a bid change, and a brand that does not adjust its bids leaves part of the gain unspent. Pairing content tests with bids is part of how we run Amazon advertising for brands.
