P0273.crumb: Boards ask how big the Amazon channel is.…
P0273.title: Boards ask how big the Amazon channel is. Ask who controls it
P0273.alt: A wooden ship's wheel and coiled ropes on a sailing boat deck, with open sea behind.
P0273.ttag: Boards ask how big the Amazon channel is. Ask who controls it | Kwontified
P0273.desc: A board’s Amazon slide usually shows growth. The questions that matter in 2019 are about control: of price, of supply, of ads and of the profit left over.
P0273.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 22, 2019.
P0273.body:
In many board packs, the Amazon channel occupies one slide. It shows a revenue line, a growth rate and perhaps a share of total sales, set beside the department stores and the brand’s own website. The format is inherited from wholesale reporting, where each retailer was a customer and the question that mattered was how much it bought.

That format answers the wrong question for 2019. Amazon is a customer, a landlord, a media owner and a rule-maker for the same brand at the same time, and in the first half of the year it changed the rules several times without asking anyone. A board that sees only the size of the Amazon channel cannot see how much of it the brand actually controls.

How the one-slide view took hold

The single revenue line made sense when Amazon behaved like other retailers. A vendor sold to Amazon at an agreed cost, Amazon set the retail price, and the board’s job was to watch the customer’s growth and the terms of trade. Advertising, if any, sat in the marketing budget alongside every other retailer’s co-op.

That picture has been shifting for years. Independent third-party sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, up from 3% in 1999, Jeff Bezos wrote in his April letter to shareholders. Many brands now sell on Amazon both ways, as a vendor and as a seller, and each route has different economics. A single revenue line blends them.

What Amazon decided for brands in 2019

The decisions that mattered most in 2019 were made by Amazon, often by email.

In March, Amazon stopped placing purchase orders with a large number of vendors, then reversed course for most and said only brands enrolled in Brand Registry would get automatic purchase orders, with 60 days to enroll, Modern Retail reported. The same month, Amazon began emailing vendors that certain products no longer qualified for advertising because they lost Amazon money once storage, packing and shipping were counted, CNBC reported. To regain eligibility, the vendor had to lower the product’s cost to Amazon.

Some changes loosened control rather than tightening it. Amazon stopped barring US third-party sellers from offering lower prices on other websites, TechCrunch reported in March, after Senator Richard Blumenthal had urged an antitrust investigation of the clause. Separately, in its annual report, Amazon told investors for the first time that it may be unable to prevent sellers from offering counterfeit goods, CNBC noticed.

Each of these touches a different part of the business. The purchase-order change is a supply question. The advertising rule is a margin question. The price-parity change is a pricing question across every channel the brand sells through, and the counterfeit warning is a brand-risk question. None of them shows up on a revenue slide until the quarter after it happens.

Read together, the moves describe an institution tidying its own profit and loss: fewer unprofitable vendors, no advertising behind items that lose money, more of the catalog carried by sellers who hold their own inventory. Bloomberg’s reporting on the vendor cuts described that aim directly, a push to raise core e-commerce profit by letting the marketplace absorb the cost of buying, storing and shipping, as the Seattle Times carried it. A board should read Amazon’s rules as the policies of an institution with its own targets.

The brand pays Amazon in more than one place

The other change a board should see is where the money goes. Amazon’s “other” revenue, which is mostly advertising, grew 37% to $3.0 billion in the second quarter, Amazon reported in July, faster than its online stores. For a brand, that line is a cost, and it rarely sits next to the Amazon revenue it supports. Advertising is usually charged to marketing, fees and storage to operations or cost of goods, and the vendor’s margin concessions to sales. The board sees Amazon revenue in one place and Amazon’s charges spread across three.

That is how a channel can grow on the slide while its contribution shrinks. Take a brand whose quarterly Amazon revenue rose from $800,000 to $1 million, up 25%. If its Amazon advertising rose from $40,000 to $110,000 over the same period, the extra $70,000 consumed more than a third of the $200,000 of new revenue before a single fee or concession is counted. On the slide, only the 25% appears.

Nobody hides anything. The reporting was built for a customer who only bought, and Amazon now also sells the brand its shelf space, its delivery and its audience.

Five questions for the next board meeting

A board does not need more Amazon slides. It needs a different set of questions, and the management team needs a week to answer them well:

  1. What did the Amazon channel contribute after advertising, fees, storage and margin concessions, and how has that moved over four quarters?
  2. If Amazon stopped ordering from us for a month, as it did with many vendors in March, what would happen to inventory and cash?
  3. Who sets our price on Amazon now: us, Amazon, or a third-party seller we do not know?
  4. Which of our products could lose advertising eligibility under Amazon’s profitability rules, and what would it cost to keep them eligible?
  5. Who in the company owns the Amazon relationship end to end, and does that person attend this meeting?

A management team that cannot answer the first question within a week has found its first project, and the fifth question tends to answer the other four. Running the channel so that one report covers all of it is part of how we manage Amazon for brands.

P0274.title: Zalando Fulfillment Solutions pays for steady sellers only
P0274.alt: A long conveyor line of taped orange boxes running through a warehouse lined with stocked shelving.
P0274.ttag: Zalando Fulfillment Solutions pays for steady sellers only | Kwontified
P0274.desc: Zalando’s fulfillment service saves partner brands parcel costs and splits their stock in two. That second pool costs most on small, unpredictable styles.
P0274.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 27, 2019.
P0274.body:
When UBS interviewed some of the brands that hold the most stock on Zalando, their complaint about its fulfillment service was not the fee. It was the split. “Split inventory means less flexibility in stock allocation,” the report found, and the brands said they were reluctant to send more volume to Zalando’s warehouses, ChannelX reported in May. Zalando answered that 30% of Partner Program items already went through the service.

Both sides are right, about different products. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions saves a brand money on every parcel, and it also gives the brand a second pile of stock that can only sell on Zalando. A second pile needs its own safety buffer, and that buffer costs the most, relative to sales, on the styles that sell slowly and unpredictably. The service pays on steady sellers. On the long tail it usually costs more than it saves.

How Zalando Fulfillment Solutions works for Partner Program brands

The Partner Program lets a brand sell its own stock on Zalando at its own prices. Out of the box, the brand ships each order itself. Zalando launched Zalando Fulfillment Solutions (ZFS) in June 2017 to take over customer-facing logistics for partner brands, including returns, FashionUnited reported at the launch. The brand keeps ownership of the stock but moves it into Zalando’s warehouses, and it pays a storage and delivery fee per order.

The service has grown quickly. About 30% of Partner Program orders in the first quarter of 2019 went through ZFS, Zalando said in May. Responding to the UBS report, Zalando said most of that growth came from adding smaller brands and from taking existing brands into new countries, and that it expected bigger partners to join.

Why the parcel saving looks decisive

The case for ZFS is easy to see on an order-by-order basis. A brand shipping its own Zalando orders pays for picking, packing, a parcel and a return. Zalando already runs that operation for its own stock, and a ZFS order can travel in the same box as the shopper’s other Zalando items. Brands on ZFS can also offer express delivery, the ChannelX report noted.

For a small brand with no warehouse of its own in a market, that comparison usually ends the discussion, and Zalando’s growth among small brands reflects it. A large brand with its own logistics contracts sees a smaller saving per order, which is what the UBS interviewees said.

What the order-by-order view leaves out is the stock.

The second pile of stock

A brand that ships its own Zalando orders keeps one pool of stock for every channel: its own webshop and Zalando can draw from the same shelves. A brand on ZFS has two pools. The units in Zalando’s warehouse can only sell on Zalando, and pulling them back costs money; “if you want it back they will charge you again,” one seller told UBS.

Each pool has to cover its own busy weeks. A bank with one queue feeding five tellers keeps customers moving better than five separate queues, because a slow teller in one line does not strand the people behind it. Stock works the same way. In one pool, a strong week on the webshop and a quiet week on Zalando offset each other. In two pools, they do not, so the brand has to hold more stock in total to avoid running out in either.

Take a dress that sells 50 units a week on Zalando and 50 on the brand’s own site, where sales in each channel swing by about 20 units either way and the swings are unrelated. One shared pool needs a buffer for the combined swing, which is about 28 units because the two swings partly cancel. Two separate pools need 20 each, 40 in total. Splitting the stock adds about 40% to the buffer.

Now look at that buffer against sales. On a dress selling 100 units a week, 12 extra units is about 12% of a week’s sales. Take a slower style that sells 5 units a week in each channel, swinging by 4 either way. The pooled buffer is about 6 units, the split buffer 8, and the extra 2 units are about a fifth of a week’s sales. The penalty grows as volume falls, because a small, lumpy channel needs a buffer close to its whole demand.

Which styles belong in Zalando’s warehouse

The rule that falls out of the arithmetic is simple. Send ZFS the styles with high, steady weekly sales on Zalando, where the parcel saving recurs every day and the extra buffer is small next to volume. Keep new styles, short-season pieces and long-tail sizes in the shared pool and ship those Zalando orders yourself, because their buffer cost is high and their stock is the hardest to rebalance once a season turns.

Zalando’s own direction makes the decision more pressing. It reported 28.3 million active customers in the second quarter of 2019, up 15.2%, and said it would start building a new warehouse in the Netherlands in summer 2019, according to its results. In its response to UBS, Zalando also said it was considering multi-channel solutions. Until a brand’s other channels can draw on the stock it places with Zalando, every unit sent there is committed to one channel.

Run a pooling test on each Zalando style

  1. List your Zalando styles by average weekly units and by how much those units swing week to week.
  2. For each style, compare the yearly parcel saving from ZFS with the cost of carrying the extra buffer, plus the fee to pull stock back if the style stalls.
  3. Move the styles where the saving clearly wins, review the split every season, and keep a style at home whenever you cannot say what it will sell next month.

Splitting a range between Zalando’s warehouses and the brand’s own stock, style by style, is part of how we run Zalando for brands.

P0276.crumb: For a new brand, the first five Amazon…
P0276.title: For a new brand, the first five Amazon reviews replace the buyer
P0276.alt: Five brass stars lined up on a cream gift box on a wooden shelf against a pale blue wall.
P0276.ttag: For a new brand, the first five Amazon reviews replace the buyer | Kwontified
P0276.desc: In a store, a buyer’s yes tells shoppers a new brand is worth a look. On Amazon the first five reviews do that job, and launch plans rarely budget for them.
P0276.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 29, 2019.
P0276.body:
Put two facial moisturizers in the same row of an Amazon search result: one with thousands of reviews and, a few places along, a newcomer with three. The newcomer may have the better formula, a cleaner label and a lower price. Shoppers glance at the number under the stars first, and three reads as a risk. In a store, a new brand arrives with a quiet endorsement already attached: a buyer chose to give it shelf space. On Amazon nobody vouches for it until strangers do, and the first handful of Amazon reviews does the job the buyer used to do.

Most launch plans have not caught up with that. They budget for traffic, for photography and for the first purchase order, and treat reviews as something that arrives later. The brands that get from zero to credible fastest plan the first five reviews as a stage of the launch, ahead of the advertising that depends on them.

Shoppers read the count before the claim

The early reviews carry most of the weight. In research first published in 2017, the Spiegel Research Center at Northwestern University found that the purchase likelihood for a product with five reviews was 270% greater than for a product with none, according to its study. The benefit of further reviews began to diminish rapidly after the first five. Price raised the stakes: displaying reviews lifted conversion 190% on lower-priced products and 380% on higher-priced ones.

The same research cuts against chasing perfection. Purchase likelihood typically peaked for ratings between 4.0 and 4.7 and fell as ratings approached 5.0, and badges marking verified buyers improved the odds of purchase by 15%. Shoppers are reading reviews as evidence from people like them, and a flawless page looks less like evidence.

For a new brand, that means the gap between three reviews and a dozen matters more than the gap between a dozen and a thousand. It also means that the advertising a brand buys in its first weeks lands on a page that converts at a fraction of its eventual rate.

Amazon closed the shortcuts and kept the gate

Until late 2016, many brands filled that gap the easy way. They gave products away or sold them at deep discounts in exchange for reviews. On October 3, 2016, Amazon banned incentivized reviews tied to free or discounted products, except those that come through its own Vine program, where Amazon rather than the seller chooses the reviewers, TechCrunch reported. The trigger was evidence that those reviews were inflated: in a ReviewMeta study of more than 7 million reviews, incentivized reviews averaged 4.74 stars against 4.36 for the rest.

Read Amazon as an institution and the rule makes sense. Amazon hosts sellers it has never met, and the review section is what lets a shopper buy from one of them with confidence. Every inflated review spends that confidence. So Amazon allows a new product a push only through channels it controls.

The Early Reviewer Program is one. A brand-registered seller can enroll a product with fewer than five reviews and a price of at least $15, and pays $60 per SKU, Feedvisor explained. Amazon then asks buyers to review it and rewards them with a $1 to $3 voucher whatever rating they give, for one year or until five reviews come in. The program’s own ceiling of five reviews says where Amazon thinks the launch problem ends.

Regulators now patrol the edge as well. In February 2019 the Federal Trade Commission brought its first case challenging fake paid reviews on an independent retail website, against the seller of a weight-loss supplement on Amazon who paid a site to post five-star reviews, the FTC said. The owner had told the site’s operator the product needed an average of 4.3 stars to generate sales. The settlement carried a $12.8 million judgment, suspended after a $50,000 payment.

The launch plan was written for a store

The first reviews also carry information the brand needs. They are the earliest unprompted account of how the product arrives, how the packaging survives the trip and whether the claim on the label matches the experience. A store buyer might have passed that feedback along at a quarterly review. On Amazon it is posted in public, in the first weeks, for the next shopper to read.

Inside many brands, a launch is still organized around the moment of sell-in. Marketing owns the launch budget and spends it on awareness. Sales owns the retailer relationship. Customer service owns reviews, if anyone does, and meets them only after shoppers have written them. Nobody’s plan includes the weeks between the listing going live and the page earning enough reviews to convert the traffic marketing is paying for.

That structure made sense when the retailer’s buyer supplied the endorsement. On Amazon it leaves a gap, and brands fill it in the most expensive way: by buying clicks for a page that is not ready to convert them, then judging the launch on those numbers. The evidence leans toward a different sequence, in which the first weeks after launch are spent earning the first reviews through Amazon’s own programs and the product’s first real buyers, and advertising scales once the page can hold its own.

Questions for the next launch meeting

  • Who on the team owns the first five reviews of each new product, and what is their plan and their date?
  • Are the new products enrolled in the programs Amazon allows, and does the launch budget include those fees?
  • Does the advertising plan start before or after the page has reviews to show, and what conversion rate is the budget built on?
  • When the first reviews arrive, who reads them for product and packaging problems before the brand spends to bring in more shoppers?

A launch that plans for its first reviews before its first ads is how we bring new products onto Amazon for the brands we work with.

P0279.crumb: Tariff landed cost on Amazon takes more…
P0279.title: Tariff landed cost on Amazon takes more price than the duty
P0279.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a small wooden shipping crate against a pile of coins.
P0279.ttag: Tariff landed cost on Amazon takes more price than the duty | Kwontified
P0279.desc: A $3.00 tariff on a jacket sold on Amazon needs about $4.11 of extra price to recover, because referral fees and ad budgets take a share of every dollar added.
P0279.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 3, 2019.
P0279.body:
A 15% duty landed on about $112 billion of Chinese imports on Sunday, September 1. It reaches the goods most of our readers sell: 87% of textiles and clothing imported from China and 52% of shoes are now taxed, the Associated Press reported. The instinct in most pricing meetings this week will be to add the duty to the price and move on. On Amazon that leaves money on the table every time, because several of a seller’s costs are charged as a share of the selling price, and they take a cut of the increase too.

So the tariff landed cost and the price rise needed to cover it are two different numbers. The gap between them is where fourth-quarter margin goes missing.

Who actually pays a tariff on landed cost

Start with who carries it. The duty is charged on the import value of the goods, at 15% ad valorem under the USTR notice published August 30, and the importer pays it at the border. Counting on the factory to absorb it is a weak plan. Economists at the New York Fed studied the 2018 rounds and found complete pass-through into the prices of imports. Chinese exporters did not cut their prices, so US buyers paid the full tax on top, Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein wrote in May.

A supplier may still share some of the cost for a brand that brings it volume. Plan for the case where it does not.

The price rise has to cover the fees it creates

Take a jacket sold through Fulfillment by Amazon at $80. It has a $20 import value and a landed cost of $24 before the new duty. Amazon’s referral fee for Clothing & Accessories is 17% of the price, a rate in force since April 15, 2018. Say the fulfillment fee is $6.00 a unit and the brand budgets advertising at 10% of sales.

Per jacketBefore the tariffPrice held at $80Price raised by the duty, $83Price raised to $84.11
Referral fee (17%)$13.60$13.60$14.11$14.30
Advertising (10% of sales)$8.00$8.00$8.30$8.41
Fulfillment fee$6.00$6.00$6.00$6.00
Landed cost$24.00$27.00$27.00$27.00
Contribution$28.40$25.40$27.59$28.40

The 15% duty adds $3.00. Raise the price by $3.00 and the brand keeps only $2.19 of it, because 27 cents of every added dollar goes to the referral fee and the ad budget. To keep $28.40 a unit, the price has to rise by the duty divided by what is left of each dollar: $3.00 ÷ 0.73, or about $4.11.

That is the gross-up, and it is why the counterintuitive answer holds. A seller that charges fees as a share of price takes a share of every increase, so a brand recovering a cost through price must ask for more than the cost.

Holding the margin percentage, the way many finance teams set targets, asks for even more. The jacket earned 35.5% of its price before the tariff. Keeping 35.5% after it takes a price of $88.00, an $8.00 rise for a $3.00 duty. Few apparel brands can push a price that far in one step, which is a good reason to set the target in dollars per unit for this round.

What volume can the new price afford to lose

A higher price sells fewer jackets, so the gross-up is only half the decision. The other half is a break-even.

Hold the price at $80 and each sale earns $25.40. Raise it to $84.11 and each sale earns $28.40. The higher price wins as long as it loses fewer than about 10.6% of units, since $25.40 is 89.4% of $28.40. A 5% price rise that costs a tenth of the volume leaves the brand where holding the price would have.

Nobody knows the volume response in advance. A brand can estimate it from its own history: past price changes on the same item, or on a similar one, and what happened to units over the following four weeks. Amazon search adds a twist. Fewer sales can mean a lower organic rank, which costs more units than the price alone would, so a brand with a thin review count should be more cautious than one whose listing leads its category.

The timing of the margin hit

The tariff applies to goods entering the country from September 1. Jackets already in a warehouse carry the old cost, so the margin falls only when taxed stock starts selling, often weeks later for a brand holding eight or ten weeks of cover.

That lag argues for repricing on a date tied to inventory, not to the headline. Track which purchase orders cleared customs after September 1, estimate when they become the stock Amazon ships, and move the price then. Moving earlier gives away volume on units that cost the old price; moving later sells taxed units at a price that no longer covers them.

Two scheduled changes make the calendar tighter. Goods on the list that USTR moved to December 15, including certain footwear and clothing, face 15% then. And the duty on Chinese goods already taxed at 25% is set to rise to 30% on October 1, CNBC reported.

Set the new price from dollars, volume and stock dates

Price each affected SKU from the dollar contribution you want to keep, grossed up by the share of price that fees and advertising take. Check the result against the volume break-even, using your own price history, and set the change for the week taxed stock reaches the shelf.

Then reset the ad targets. An advertising budget set as a share of sales grows with the higher price, so a brand that also cuts spend to save margin should lower the percentage deliberately rather than let a stale target decide. That review of ad targets against new landed costs is part of the Q4 planning we run for brands on Amazon.

P0280.crumb: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2019…
P0280.title: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2019 squeezes the middle brands
P0280.alt: Three cardboard boxes on a wooden table, from battered and crushed to intact, against a sage green wall.
P0280.ttag: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2019 squeezes the middle brands | Kwontified
P0280.desc: Amazon’s sports and outdoors shelf is splitting into famous brands it may badge and its own cheaper labels. The brands in between need a reason to be picked.
P0280.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 5, 2019.
P0280.body:
Search Amazon for “running shorts” in the middle of August and a New Balance pair might come back with a small badge reading “Top Brand.” Speedo had one on “swimming goggles.” Under Armour and Fruit of the Loom had them on “t-shirt,” Marketplace Pulse found when it spotted the test on August 16. Amazon confirmed it was trying the label on fashion items and said it is based on brands that are popular with customers, and that brands do not pay for it, Fortune reported.

It is a small test, and it shows where sports and outdoors on Amazon has been heading for two years. The famous athletic names have come onto the shelf on their own terms, Amazon has built cheaper labels to sit beside them, and the brands in between, good products without a household name, now compete with both at once.

How sports and outdoors on Amazon changed shape

Walk into a sporting goods store and the floor is arranged by activity. Running shoes cover one wall, swimming has its own rack, camping sits near the back with the tents pitched. Within each section the big brands get their own fixtures, and a specialist brand with a strong product gets a spot because a buyer chose it. The store does the sorting before the shopper arrives.

Amazon’s search page has no walls. A shopper types an activity, and the page sorts brands by reviews, price, delivery promise and whatever badges Amazon decides to show. Before this August test, as Marketplace Pulse put it, products there were “created equal, only differentiated by the number of reviews.” A new brand with a few thousand good reviews could sit beside a household name.

The big athletic brands spent years outside that system. Nike sold on Amazon only through third-party sellers until June 2017, when it confirmed a pilot to sell a limited assortment directly. Chief executive Mark Parker said the aim was to elevate “the way the brand is presented,” and the Wall Street Journal reported that Nike won commitments from Amazon to police fakes and unauthorized sales in return, Fortune noted. The reason for coming in was control: of price, of presentation, of who is allowed to sell the shoes.

That is the first tier of the 2019 shelf. Brands with name recognition, selling direct, increasingly protected from resellers, and now in some searches carrying a badge that tells the shopper which name to trust.

Amazon’s own labels fill the price below

The second tier arrived at the same time. In late 2017, Amazon confirmed three activewear labels of its own: Goodsport, aimed at budget performance brands; Peak Velocity, a premium men’s line that could challenge Nike or Under Armour; and Rebel Canyon, an athleisure line, TechCrunch reported. By mid-2018, Coresight counted 74 Amazon private labels and 6,825 products, almost three-quarters of them in clothing and footwear, in its analysis.

A private label does not need to win the search to matter. It sets a reference price on the same page. When a shopper sees a plain performance tee from Amazon’s label beside a branded one, the branded tee has to explain the difference, and Amazon has started placing its own versions in more places to make that comparison happen. In late August, The Washington Post found a “similar item to consider” box just above the add-to-cart button that promoted cheaper Amazon-brand versions of everyday products, Fox News reported.

Put the two tiers together and the middle gets uncomfortable. A mid-priced brand of hiking socks or yoga pants does not have the fame to earn a badge, and it is priced above an Amazon label that looks similar in a thumbnail. In a specialty store a buyer’s choice would have carried it. On a search page it has to carry itself.

The specialty store is still growing online

None of this means the store is losing the category. Dick’s Sporting Goods grew its online sales 21% in the second quarter, to about 12% of total sales, and same-store sales rose 3.2%, the company reported on August 22. Shoppers who want a buyer’s edit of the category still go to the retailer that provides one, and more of them now do it online.

That matters for the mid-tier brand, because it has a choice the famous names and Amazon’s labels do not face in the same way. It can win on Amazon by earning the signals the page rewards, or it can lean on the specialty retailer’s curation and treat Amazon as a place to protect its listing from resellers. Most brands in the middle are trying to do both without deciding which comes first.

The decision usually sits in the wrong meeting

At many sports and outdoor brands that grew up in wholesale, Amazon still sits with the sales team, measured on sell-in, while the product pages, images and reviews are nobody’s full-time job. That arrangement made sense when Amazon was one more account. It makes less sense on a shelf where the page itself does the selling.

The questions worth putting to the team this autumn are concrete. Start with the brand’s top 20 search terms and count how many show an Amazon label or a badged competitor on the first page. Then check whether the products that appear for those terms are sold direct or through resellers the brand does not control. Last, for each hero product, ask what the page says that a cheaper lookalike cannot: a fabric, a fit test, a warranty, the sport-specific detail a specialist store clerk would point out. A page that cannot answer that last question is asking the shopper to pay for a name the shopper may not know.

The brands that answer those questions with their pages will hold their place when the next badge or box appears. Running that work across pages, pricing and resellers is what our channel management team does for brands on Amazon.

P0283.crumb: Regional brands on Amazon get a national…
P0283.title: Regional brands on Amazon get a national shelf, not a following
P0283.alt: A single jar of dark jam alone on a long rustic wooden shelf against a terracotta plaster wall.
P0283.ttag: Regional brands on Amazon get a national shelf, not a following | Kwontified
P0283.desc: Amazon lets a regional brand reach all 50 states without slotting fees, but shoppers outside its home market do not search for it. Plan for two audiences.
P0283.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 12, 2019.
P0283.body:
For decades, a regional food brand that wanted to go national had to pay its way onto the shelf. In 2003 the Federal Trade Commission studied slotting fees in grocery and found that introducing a new product nationally could cost from a little under $1 million to more than $2 million in those fees alone, Supermarket News reported. That was before a single unit sold. Today the same brand can list on Amazon on Monday and be one search away from a shopper in any of the 50 states by Friday.

The shelf, in other words, has become national for anyone who wants it. What has not followed is the shopper. A regional brand on Amazon has two very different audiences: the people at home who already know it and search for it by name, and everyone else, who has never heard of it and will only find it if it wins a category search. Most regional brands run their Amazon business as if those were one audience.

Regional brands on Amazon arrive with an audience in one place

Amazon has made the national shelf an explicit pitch. When it opened Amazon Storefronts in September 2018, it gathered nearly 20,000 American small and medium-sized businesses from all 50 states into one store reached from its homepage, CNBC reported, and ran its first national TV advertisement to promote it. In May, Amazon said third-party sales in its stores had passed $160 billion in 2018, more than half of all units sold. It added that the number of small and medium-sized businesses with more than $1 million in sales had grown 20%, according to its 2019 SMB Impact Report announcement.

Picture what that looks like for a hot sauce made in Louisiana or a coffee roasted in the Pacific Northwest. In its home region it has a following built over decades: grocery placement, local press, the bottle on the table at a favorite restaurant. Those shoppers type the brand’s name into Amazon when they move away or cannot find it in the store. Their orders arrive early, convert well and earn reviews.

Outside the region, the brand is a stranger on a page full of strangers. A shopper in Ohio searching “hot sauce” sees whatever ranks: national names, Amazon’s best sellers, sponsored listings. Shoppers there do click on what is in front of them. Jumpshot’s data showed that 65% of Amazon product clicks come from the first page of results, Retail Dive reported in 2018. A regional brand that is not on that first page for the category term is, to that shopper, not on the shelf at all.

Why the early numbers mislead

This is where many regional brands misread their first year. The early sales look national, because orders arrive from everywhere: transplants, gift buyers, travelers who tried it on vacation. The team concludes that the brand travels, raises its Amazon forecast and starts talking to national retailers.

Look closer and the orders usually cluster. Take a brand whose Amazon sales are 70% branded searches, people typing its name. Most of those shoppers already knew it, so most of that 70% is the home market shopping in a new place, not new demand from new markets. The 30% that came from category searches is the real test of whether the brand can win where nobody knows it, and that is the number to grow.

The same split shows up in the advertising. Ads on the brand’s own name are cheap and look wonderful because the shopper was coming anyway. Ads on “hot sauce” or “whole bean coffee” compete against national budgets and look expensive. A team judging the two together will keep funding the branded ads and starve the category ones, which is the opposite of what a national expansion needs.

The organization was built for a different shelf

Regional brands are usually organized around regional retail. There is a sales lead who knows the grocery buyers, perhaps a broker, perhaps a direct-store-delivery route, and a pricing structure set by what those retailers will accept. Amazon tends to land with whoever has time: a marketing coordinator, the founder, or an outside seller who offered to handle it.

That arrangement creates two quiet conflicts. The first is with the home-market retailers. If the brand’s local fans start buying on Amazon at a lower price or with free shipping, the grocery buyer sees weaker sales on the shelf, and nobody in the meeting connects it to the Amazon listing. The second is with the national ambition. Winning category searches in markets where the brand is unknown takes content, reviews and steady ad spend, and that work rarely has an owner when Amazon sits with whoever had time.

None of this means the regional brand should hold back. The national shelf is real, and it costs a fraction of what slotting once did. It means treating the two audiences as two businesses with different questions.

Questions for the next planning meeting

  • What share of our Amazon sales comes from searches for our own name, and how much of that comes from our home states?
  • For the three category terms that matter most, are we on the first page, and what would it cost to get there?
  • What happened to sales at our largest home-market retailer in the months after the Amazon listing went live, and was the Amazon price below theirs?
  • Who owns the national category work, by name, and what budget do they have that is separate from the branded ads?

The brands that answer those questions separately will know whether they have a national brand or a regional one with a national address. Sorting the two, and running the category work that turns one into the other, is what we do for brands growing through Amazon.

P0285.crumb: Mercado Libre Product Ads should be bid…
P0285.title: Mercado Libre Product Ads should be bid from margin, not price
P0285.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a piece of sourdough against coins, beside a cut loaf on a board.
P0285.ttag: Mercado Libre Product Ads should be bid from margin, not price | Kwontified
P0285.desc: Mercado Libre Product Ads sell search position by the click. Today’s low prices reflect few bidders; set the maximum bid from what a click is worth to you.
P0285.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 17, 2019.
P0285.body:
Mercado Libre sold 88.7 million items to 20.4 million unique buyers in the second quarter of 2019, and the value of goods sold on its marketplace grew 33% in local-currency terms, its results showed. A brand arriving from Amazon soon meets the ad product that sits on top of that traffic. Its annual report describes advertisers buying “improved search standing and/or specific categories, on a cost-per-click basis” (MercadoLibre 10-K for 2018).

The usual first move is to bid what the clicks seem to cost. That anchors the budget on the wrong number. In a cost-per-click auction, what a brand pays depends on how many others are bidding for the same search, and on Mercado Libre that competition is still forming. The number to plan around is what a click is worth to the brand, worked out in pesos or reais, with today’s prices read as a measure of how crowded the auction is.

Why the price of Mercado Libre Product Ads looks like the answer

Brands that run Amazon Sponsored Products have learned to read the cost per click as a market price. On a mature auction that is roughly right: many advertisers bid on the same keywords, the price settles near what the clicks are worth to the more efficient bidders, and a new entrant has to match it.

Mercado Libre’s sellers came to advertising later. The company opened its Product Ads programming interfaces to outside developers in 2017, describing Product Ads as ads whose cost per click the advertiser sets. It said its advertising division had grown revenue 40% in the first quarter of that year, TI Inside reported. Many categories are likely to have fewer advertisers than the same search would draw on Amazon. A low cost per click on Mercado Libre may therefore say little about value and a lot about the number of people bidding.

A click’s value comes from the brand’s own numbers

The value of a click is the margin a brand is willing to spend to win a sale, multiplied by the share of clicks that become sales. Work it in the currency the shopper pays.

Take a pair of headphones priced at R$200 on Mercado Livre in Brazil. Say the brand is willing to spend 15% of the price on advertising to win a sale, R$30, and that 3% of the shoppers who click buy.

Per clickValue
Advertising budget per sale (15% of R$200)R$30.00
Conversion rate3%
Maximum the click is worth (R$30 × 3%)R$0.90

R$0.90 is the ceiling. Bid above it and every sale costs more than the brand decided to spend. Now say the brand bids R$0.90 and the auction charges it R$0.35 a click on average. Each sale costs R$11.67 in ads (R$0.35 ÷ 3%), well under the R$30 budget. The account looks highly efficient.

That efficiency is borrowed from the absence of rivals. If a competitor with a similar product and a similar budget enters the same search, the price the brand pays will move toward the ceiling, R$0.90, and the cost per sale toward R$30. Nothing about the brand’s product or listing will have changed. A plan built on R$0.35 will look broken by the next quarter. A plan built on R$0.90 will still hold.

What the data on Mercado Libre Product Ads can tell you

Mercado Libre’s annual report describes what advertisers buy, not how the auction sets the price a winner pays. Brands can still learn a lot from their own reports.

The gap between the maximum bid and the average price actually charged is the first signal. If the auction charges well below the bid, the price is being set by something other than the bid, most plausibly the bids of fewer or weaker rivals. If the charged price sits at the bid, either the auction charges what you bid or the competition is already at your ceiling. Raising the bid in small steps on one product for two weeks will show which, because a price that follows the bid up is a price set by the bid.

The trend in that gap is the second signal. Track it weekly for the top ten search terms. A gap that narrows month after month is competition arriving, and it tells the brand when its cost per sale will rise before the monthly results do.

Currency adds a third check. Mercado Libre’s 33% growth in local currency was only 8.4% in dollars over the same quarter, the same results showed. A brand that sets its ceiling in dollars and converts each month will find its bid ceiling drifting with the exchange rate rather than with what the click is worth to a shopper paying in reais. Set the ceiling in the local currency, from the local price and local conversion rate.

The conversion rate deserves the most care, because it moves the ceiling one for one. A product with 200 clicks a month and six sales has a measured rate of 3%, but one more or one fewer sale moves it by half a point. Use at least two months of clicks before trusting the number, and recompute the ceiling whenever the listing, price or shipping offer changes, since each of those can move conversion.

Set the ceiling before the rivals arrive

Set the maximum bid on Mercado Libre Product Ads at the advertising budget per sale times the conversion rate, in local currency, for each product. Treat any price charged below that as temporary and do not raise sales targets on it. Watch the gap between bid and charged price as the earliest sign of new competition, and keep the margin model ready for the day the gap closes. Building that model for each product is part of how we launch and run Mercado Libre for brands.

P0286.crumb: Amazon bundles work when they finish a…
P0286.title: Amazon bundles work when they finish a job, not clear a shelf
P0286.alt: Twine-tied paintbrushes beside a dripping can of mint green paint and a roller tray on a wooden table.
P0286.ttag: Amazon bundles work when they finish a job, not clear a shelf | Kwontified
P0286.desc: Shoppers pay for Amazon bundles that complete a task and discount add-ons they never wanted. Each kit is a new product to run, so build few and build them well.
P0286.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 19, 2019.
P0286.body:
Every holiday season the endcap at the front of a drugstore fills with gift sets: a shampoo and conditioner tied with ribbon, a razor with three cartridges and a travel case. Someone in merchandising chose each set, the store gave it prime space, and the shopper could pick it up and see exactly what was inside. On Amazon the same kit lives on a search page beside the individual products it contains, and the shopper does the arithmetic.

That comparison decides whether Amazon bundles sell. Shoppers will pay for a bundle that completes a task they came to do, and they tend to mark down items that feel bolted on. Amazon’s rules, meanwhile, make every kit a new product with its own listing, its own reviews and its own inventory. The brands that do well with bundles build a few around a shopper’s job and run each like a hero product. The ones that struggle build many around stock they want to move.

What shoppers value in Amazon bundles

Two pieces of consumer research explain most of what happens on the page. Researchers at the University of Heidelberg found that shoppers judging options one at a time tend to prefer a single product to a bundle. When they see the bundle beside the same product without the add-on, though, they notice the extra item and choose the bundle more often, the researchers reported in the Journal of Consumer Research in 2015. Their example was a coffee maker sold with a milk frother.

Amazon’s search page is, by accident, the side-by-side comparison that study describes. A kit often appears in the same results as its own components, so a shopper can see whether the frother is worth the difference. A bundle that adds something the shopper needed for the task wins that comparison. A bundle that adds something nobody asked for loses it in plain view.

The second finding is less comfortable. Ayelet Fishbach and Franklin Shaddy at the University of Chicago found that people offer to pay less for items added to a bundle than for the same items sold separately. They also want more compensation when an item is taken away from a bundle, the university said in 2017. “For bundles, consumers both pay less, yet demand more,” Fishbach said.

Put those together and the shopper’s view of a kit is clear enough. The bundle is judged as a whole, the extras are discounted, and anything that goes wrong with one piece sours the entire purchase. A starter kit with a broken applicator is a failed kit, not a good kit missing one part.

What Amazon allows, and what it costs to run

Amazon treats a bundle as its own product. A June 2019 guide from fulfillment company eFulfillment Service summarized the rules. A bundle needs its own ASIN and its contents cannot change, generic products are not allowed in bundles, “three of a kind are not a bundle” (that is a multipack), warranties cannot be mixed, and the referral fee follows the bundle’s category (eFulfillment Service). Walmart’s marketplace is stricter still; its 2019 item setup guide for sellers does not support seller-created bundles at all (Walmart Marketplace).

Each of those rules turns a merchandising idea into an operating commitment. A new ASIN starts with no reviews and no sales history, so the kit has to earn its place in search from zero while its components keep the reviews they already have. Fixed contents mean that when one component is discontinued or out of stock, the kit stops too. A change to the kit’s contents means a new listing, and the reviews start over again. A kit that sells well for a season and then needs a new formula or a new size gives up everything it earned on the page.

There are real savings on the other side of the ledger. The same eFulfillment guide described a company whose fulfillment cost fell from $3.20 to $2.10 an order once it pre-assembled its most common multi-item order into a kit, at $0.20 a kit plus a $20 setup fee. A kit that matches how people already buy can pay for itself in the warehouse.

Where bundles go wrong inside the brand

At many brands, bundles start in the e-commerce team as a way to lift order value or move slow inventory, and the rest of the business hears about them late. Supply chain learns that it now has to assemble kits. Finance sees a new item with a margin nobody modeled. The product team sees its slowest item packaged with its best one and wonders why the best one’s sales dipped.

The shopper research explains why the slow-stock bundle disappoints. Packing a weak seller with a strong one asks the shopper to pay for an add-on, which they discount, beside the strong product sold alone, which they can compare directly. The kit loses the comparison and the slow item stays slow.

Questions to ask before the next kit goes live

  • What job does this bundle finish for the shopper, in one sentence they would recognize?
  • Would a shopper who sees it beside its main component think the extra item is worth the difference?
  • Who owns the kit’s inventory, and what happens to the listing when one component runs out?
  • How many bundles do we have live, and how many have earned more reviews than their best component?

A brand that can answer those well usually needs fewer bundles than it has, and the ones it keeps tend to be the kits shoppers would have assembled for themselves if the page had let them. Sorting which kits to keep and running them as products in their own right is part of how we manage Amazon catalogs for brands.

P0287.crumb: Mercado Libre cross-border pricing is a…
P0287.title: Mercado Libre cross-border pricing is a bet on the currency
P0287.alt: A hanging brass balance holding silver coins on one pan and gold coins on the other, beside yellow craspedia.
P0287.ttag: Mercado Libre cross-border pricing is a bet on the currency | Kwontified
P0287.desc: A brand selling into Brazil or Argentina from the US must decide who carries the currency: its margin in dollars or its shoppers’ prices. Set a band and a rule.
P0287.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 24, 2019.
P0287.body:
On Monday, August 12, Argentina’s peso closed 15.27% weaker at 53.5 to the dollar, after trading as low as 65 during the day, as markets reacted to the government’s defeat in the presidential primaries, Al Jazeera reported. Three weeks later the government told companies they needed central bank permission to buy dollars, and individuals needed permission to buy more than $10,000 a month, RNZ reported.

For a brand selling from the US into those markets on Mercado Libre, that was a pricing month, whether or not anyone changed a price. Cross-border pricing on Mercado Libre always puts the currency risk somewhere. Hold the local price and the brand’s dollar margin absorbs the move. Hold the dollar price and the shopper sees the price jump. There is no setting that avoids the choice, so the brand should make it on purpose, market by market.

Why a steady local price feels safe

The instinct for most brands is to set a price in reais or pesos that looks right on the page and leave it alone. Shoppers compare prices in their own currency, competitors’ listings sit beside yours in the same currency, and a price that moves every week looks unreliable.

Mercado Libre’s own numbers show what that steadiness costs in dollars. In the second quarter of 2019 the value of goods sold on its platform grew 33% in local-currency terms and only 8.4% in dollars, its results showed. That gap was a currency effect across the whole marketplace. A brand holding local prices steady through the same period would have seen the same kind of gap between the growth it saw in its Mercado Libre reports and the growth its finance team saw in dollars.

The cross-border pricing mechanism in one table

Brazil shows how quickly the arithmetic changes. The real had a bad August: on August 16 it fell 2% to below 4.05 per dollar, its weakest since May, and the central bank announced its first outright dollar sales in more than a decade, MercoPress reported. A move of that size goes straight into the contribution of every product priced in reais.

Take a kitchen gadget a US brand sells on Mercado Livre in Brazil. At an exchange rate of 3.80 reais per dollar, the brand prices it at R$399, or $105. It costs $55 landed in Brazil, all paid in dollars, plus selling fees charged as a share of the price, say 15%. Now the dollar rises 9.7% to 4.17 reais.

Before, 3.80Hold the price in reaisHold the price in dollars
Price in reaisR$399R$399R$438
Price in dollars$105.00$95.68$105.04
Fees at 15%$15.75$14.35$15.76
Landed cost$55.00$55.00$55.00
Contribution per unit$34.25$26.33$34.28

Holding the price in reais keeps every shopper and every search position, and cuts contribution per unit by 23%. Holding the price in dollars keeps the margin and asks Brazilian shoppers to pay 9.8% more for the same product, overnight, beside competitors who may not have moved.

The two columns are the ends of a range. Neither is right in general. Which one is better depends on how many sales a 9.8% price rise would cost, and that varies by product. Contribution at the old price falls 23%, so the higher price wins as long as it keeps more than about 77% of unit sales ($26.33 is 77% of $34.28). A product with loyal repeat buyers may keep most of its sales through a rise like that; a product competing with near-identical listings from local sellers can lose far more.

When the currency moves this fast

Argentina is the harder case, and the August move shows why. A drop like 15% in a day does not leave time for a weekly pricing review, and capital controls add a second risk: the brand’s money collected in pesos may be slower or costlier to convert. A brand selling into Argentina in pesos is carrying both the price risk and a conversion risk until the money is home.

That changes the rule by market. In a market whose currency moves a few percent a month, a band works: hold the local price while the exchange rate stays within, say, 5% of the rate the price was set at, and reprice when it leaves the band. In a market where the currency can move 15% in a day, the band has to be narrower and the review daily, or the brand should keep its exposure small enough that a bad week is affordable.

Reporting needs the same discipline. A Mercado Libre dashboard in local currency can show growth through a devaluation while a finance report in dollars shows a decline for the same weeks. Both are correct. Report contribution per unit in dollars beside sales in local currency for each country, so the team that sets prices sees the margin it is spending and the team that books results sees why the volume held up.

Set the band before the next move

For each country, write down three numbers: the exchange rate the current price assumes, the band around it, and the contribution per unit at each edge of the band. When the rate crosses an edge, reprice to the middle of the band rather than chasing the day’s rate.

Check unit sales two weeks after each repricing to learn how much volume that market gives up for a given rise, and narrow or widen the band with what you learn. The brands that do this decide in advance who carries the currency. The rest find out after the quarter closes. Building those bands for each Mercado Libre country is part of how we launch and run Latin American marketplaces for brands.

P0289.title: Amazon influencer storefronts move the sale to Amazon’s shelf
P0289.alt: A ring light holding a smartphone aimed at a styled shelf of skincare bottles, flowers and a candle.
P0289.ttag: Amazon influencer storefronts move the sale to Amazon’s shelf | Kwontified
P0289.desc: The same creator can send a follower to your Instagram checkout or to an Amazon storefront. Who pays the creator decides whose shelf the shopper lands on.
P0289.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 26, 2019.
P0289.body:
A beauty creator posts a morning routine on Instagram. Her followers want the serum, and there are two common ways for them to get it. They can follow the link she was given to the brand’s own site. Or they can follow the link in her bio to a personal page on Amazon, at amazon.com/shop followed by her name, where the serum sits beside the other products she likes. The first route usually exists because the brand paid her. The second exists because Amazon pays her a fee on every purchase she drives, whoever made the product.

Both routes reach the same shopper. They end on different shelves, with different owners, and that difference matters more than which platform has the bigger audience. Amazon influencer storefronts turn a creator’s recommendation into an Amazon sale, priced and compared on Amazon’s page, while the brand’s own Instagram deals try to keep the sale at home. Most brands manage the two from different teams and never notice they are competing with themselves.

How Amazon influencer storefronts work

Amazon launched its Influencer Program in 2017. Each approved creator gets a storefront at a personal web address on Amazon and earns a fee on the purchases it drives, with the amount depending on the product category, AdExchanger reported on September 16. YouTube, Twitter, Facebook and Instagram accounts qualify, and Amazon looks for creators who have shown they can drive traffic rather than simply the most popular ones. The storefront also solves a practical problem on Instagram: it gives creators a single link to send people to from places where clickable links are not possible, such as Stories.

The same report described Amazon working on a tool to let creators and brands pull images and video from Instagram, YouTube and brand websites into those storefronts. One agency executive put the direction plainly: “Amazon is teaching influencers on other platforms to point back to Amazon.”

Instagram has been building the other route. At its developer conference in April, it said creators would be able to tag products in their posts so that followers can buy them, starting with brands in its Checkout beta, TechCrunch reported. Checkout itself, launched in March, lets a shopper pay without leaving the app.

Two routes, two shelves

Picture the shopper’s next few seconds on each route. On Instagram, she lands on the brand’s product, sees the brand’s price and its photography, and buys from the brand. Nothing else competes for her attention at that moment.

On the Amazon storefront, she lands on a shelf the creator assembled, inside a store that will show her ratings, delivery dates and, very often, other serums. The creator’s endorsement got her to Amazon. Amazon’s page decides what she buys there. If the brand’s listing is weak, out of stock or more expensive than a similar product a scroll away, the recommendation can turn into a sale for someone else.

The money moves differently too. On the Instagram route, the brand pays the creator a fee it negotiated and gets a post it approved. On the Amazon route, the brand pays the creator nothing directly; Amazon pays her a share of the sale. That sounds cheaper, and in a narrow sense it is, but the brand has no say in what sits beside its product on the storefront, and the sale shows up in the Amazon channel’s numbers rather than marketing’s.

Shoppers do not all respond to creators the same way, either. In a 2018 survey of 1,409 consumers by Avionos, about 55% said they had bought something through social channels, but 60% said they had never bought a product promoted by an influencer, Retail Dive reported. The audience that does act on a creator’s word is valuable precisely because it is a minority, and a brand should know which shelf that minority ends up on.

The structure behind the blind spot

At many brands, influencer deals sit with PR or the social team, measured on reach and engagement, and Amazon sits with e-commerce, measured on sales. The social team signs a creator for three Instagram posts. Nobody checks whether the same creator has an Amazon storefront listing the brand’s product, or a competitor’s, earning a commission on whichever sells. The Amazon team sees a spike in sessions and credits its ads.

Neither team is doing anything wrong by its own measures. The problem is that the shopper treats the creator as one voice, and the brand treats her as two line items in two budgets.

The gap shows up in the planning calendar. A brand books a creator for a launch, sends her to the brand’s site, and builds the Amazon listing a month later on a separate schedule. Her followers, some of whom shop on Amazon by habit, search for the product there in the meantime and find a reseller, an old version or nothing at all. The money spent on her posts produced the demand; the Amazon page that should have met it was not ready.

Questions for the next influencer brief

  • Does this creator run an Amazon storefront, and which of our products, and our competitors’, are on it?
  • When she posts about us, where do we want her followers to buy, and does the link we give her match that?
  • If the answer is Amazon, is our listing ready for that traffic: in stock, competitively priced, with reviews and images that hold up beside the alternatives on her page?
  • Who reports the sales that creators drive on Amazon, and do the social and Amazon teams see the same number?

A brand that can answer those has turned two routes into one plan. Connecting creator programs on Instagram with the Amazon listings they send people to is part of how we run social commerce for brands.

P0291.crumb: Instagram Checkout fees pay off only on…
P0291.title: Instagram Checkout fees pay off only on sales your site loses
P0291.alt: A black cash register and a smartphone with a glowing purple screen on a wooden shop counter.
P0291.ttag: Instagram Checkout fees pay off only on sales your site loses | Kwontified
P0291.desc: Instagram’s Checkout fee is charged on every in-app order, including ones your website would have closed anyway, so incremental orders set the break-even.
P0291.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 1, 2019.
P0291.body:
When Instagram launched Checkout in March 2019, it told brands it would charge sellers a fee and then declined to say how much. “We aren’t sharing the specific number right now,” a spokesperson told TechCrunch, adding that the fee would not change the price shoppers pay. Six months on, most brands weighing Checkout are comparing a fee they cannot see with the payment processing they already pay on their own site. That comparison misses the cost that matters. The fee lands on every order placed inside Instagram, including the ones your website would have closed anyway.

So the useful question about Instagram Checkout fees is narrower than “is the rate fair?” It is how many extra orders Checkout has to create before the fee on all of them is covered.

What Instagram Checkout fees replace

Start with what Checkout changes. Before March, a product tag on Instagram showed a name and price and sent the shopper to the brand’s website to buy. With Checkout, the shopper pays inside the app, with payments run through PayPal, and the brand receives the order with the shopper’s name, contact details and shipping address but not their payment details, according to TechCrunch. Shoppers can choose to share their email for marketing. The launch group was a closed beta of more than 20 brands, among them Nike, Zara, H&M and Warby Parker.

The appeal is obvious. Every step between a tap and a paid order loses people, and the handoff from the app to a mobile website is a large step: a new page load, a login or a form, and a card number typed on a phone. Instagram said about 130 million people tap product tags in shopping posts each month, Fortune reported. Removing the handoff should convert more of them.

That is why the obvious comparison feels right. Your site already pays a processor on every order, so Checkout looks like swapping one payment cost for another, plus a few more sales. If the fee is close to what you pay now, the decision seems easy.

The fee is charged on the orders you already had

The swap is not one for one. Instagram charges its fee on every Checkout order.

Your site’s processing cost goes away only on the orders that move from the site to the app. If a shopper would have bought on your site anyway, you now pay Instagram’s fee instead of your processor’s, and the difference comes out of margin with no new sale attached. The fee is paid on the whole base. Only the increment pays for it.

Take a $60 order with $24 of contribution before payment costs. Say your own processor charges 2.9% plus 30 cents, or $2.04 on that order, leaving $21.96. Instagram’s rate is unknown, so run two cases. At a 5% fee, the fee is $3.00 and the order leaves $21.00. At 10%, the fee is $6.00 and the order leaves $18.00.

Now say Instagram sends your site 100 orders a month today. Switch those shoppers to Checkout and you pay the higher cost on all 100: an extra $0.96 each at 5%, or $96 a month, and an extra $3.96 each at 10%, or $396. New orders have to cover that. At $21.00 of contribution each, the 5% case needs about five extra orders a month, a 5% lift. At $18.00 each, the 10% case needs 22 extra orders, a 22% lift.

Selling fee (assumed)Fee on a $60 orderContribution leftExtra cost on 100 existing ordersExtra orders needed
5%$3.00$21.00$96about 5 (5%)
10%$6.00$18.00$39622 (22%)

The required lift is roughly the fee minus your current processing cost, divided by what an order still earns after the fee. That is why a few points of fee move the break-even so far. The 5-point difference between the two cases quadruples the extra cost and more than quadruples the orders needed to cover it.

The same arithmetic shows which brands should move first. A brand with thin margins needs a larger lift for the same fee, because each new order carries less money to cover it. A brand whose Instagram buyers are mostly first-time visitors, who abandon the mobile handoff often, has more orders to gain.

What the Checkout report can and can’t tell you

Instagram has said it will tell merchants which sales it generated. That report will count every Checkout order, and the number will look larger than the site orders it replaced, because some shoppers who used to buy on your site will now buy in the app. A rising Checkout total is consistent with a 30% lift and with no lift at all.

The test that settles it is a split. Put Checkout tags on half of a comparable set of products and leave the other half linking to your site, then compare orders per thousand tag taps for each half over the same weeks. If Checkout’s half beats the site’s half by more than the break-even lift for your margin and your assumed fee, keep it. If the gap is smaller, you are paying Instagram to process orders you already had.

Two costs do not show up in that test. Checkout buyers reach you without an email unless they opt in, so the repeat business your site captures through its own list is harder to earn. And the fee rate you plan around is a guess until Instagram publishes it.

The rule for Monday: before turning on Checkout, write down your contribution per order and your current processing cost, compute the lift needed at a 5% and a 10% fee, and run the split long enough to see whether Checkout clears it. Building that test for Instagram Shop is part of how we run social commerce for brands, and we are glad to set one up with your team.

P0292.crumb: Seller Fulfilled Prime in Q4 bets the…
P0292.title: Seller Fulfilled Prime in Q4 bets the badge on your own dock
P0292.alt: Pallets piled high with parcels and holiday-wrapped gifts on the loading dock of a small brick depot.
P0292.ttag: Seller Fulfilled Prime in Q4 bets the badge on your own dock | Kwontified
P0292.desc: Choosing FBA or Seller Fulfilled Prime before Q4 decides where a holiday failure would happen, and most brands make that call on parcel rates alone.
P0292.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 3, 2019.
P0292.body:
Every autumn, somewhere in a brand’s operations team, a shipping manager lays two carrier rate cards side by side and works out the parcel budget for the holidays. For 2019 the cards look kind. On August 16 UPS said it would add no peak surcharge to residential deliveries for the 2019 season, after charging $0.28 a package on ground and $0.99 on air in 2018, Supply Chain Dive reported. The meeting ends with a cost per parcel and a sense that the hard part is done.

It is not, at least for brands selling on Amazon. The real holiday decision is whether Prime orders ship from Amazon’s warehouses through Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA) or from the brand’s own building under Seller Fulfilled Prime, and that choice is less about rates than about where a December failure would land. Seller Fulfilled Prime in Q4 puts the Prime badge on the performance of your own dock and carrier. FBA puts it on stock you had to send to Amazon weeks earlier. Most brands make the call in the room with the rate cards, and the people who live with the result are not in it.

Two routes, two ways to fail

The carrier picture really did shift in 2019. FedEx said on August 7 that it would not renew its US ground delivery contract with Amazon when it expired at the end of August, two months after its Express unit declined to keep flying Amazon packages, Al Jazeera reported. Amazon accounted for about 1.3% of FedEx’s sales the previous year. Amazon, meanwhile, has been building its own delivery network and pushing Prime toward one-day delivery, which reached more than ten million items by July, its second-quarter results said.

For a brand using FBA, that is mostly Amazon’s problem. Amazon picks the carrier, makes the delivery promise and keeps the badge on the listing. The risk sits earlier and upstream. Inventory has to be in Amazon’s buildings before the rush, and once it is there the brand cannot move it to another channel quickly if Amazon sales disappoint or another retailer reorders. An FBA brand that underestimates November cannot fix it by shipping faster from its own warehouse in December; it can only send more stock into Amazon’s queue and wait.

For a brand on Seller Fulfilled Prime, the risk sits on its own dock. Since July 31, 2018, sellers in the program have had to ship at least 99% of orders on time and keep cancellations at or below 0.5%. They must also buy shipping through Amazon for at least 98% of Prime orders, according to Amazon’s notice to sellers. Those are eligibility requirements, and the holidays are when they are hardest to meet.

A short-staffed shift, a carrier pickup that does not come, a printer jam on the Monday after Thanksgiving: each turns into late shipments at the moment the badge is worth most. As Prime moves toward one day, Modern Retail noted in April, more sellers will have to ship through Amazon unless they can match the new speed themselves (Modern Retail).

The season itself is shorter. Thanksgiving falls on November 28, the latest date it can, leaving six fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas than in 2018. The same holiday volume squeezed into fewer days asks more of every dock, Amazon’s included.

The decision sits with the wrong budget

Brands rarely make this choice as a choice. Fulfillment is usually decided in operations or supply chain and judged by cost per order, while the Prime badge and its sales belong to the e-commerce team. At many brands, the shipping manager who signs the carrier contract is not measured on Amazon revenue, and the Amazon lead who loses the badge in December had no say in September.

That split produces a predictable failure. Say a brand moves Prime orders to its own warehouse because the per-order math beats FBA’s fees, then finds in the second week of December that a few hundred late orders have put the badge at risk. The savings were real and showed up in operations’ budget. The loss shows up in someone else’s.

Amazon, read as an institution, is clear about what it wants: speed it controls. It committed about $800 million in a single quarter to move Prime to one day and is building delivery capacity of its own. Seller Fulfilled Prime survives in that plan only for sellers who can meet Amazon’s promise as reliably as Amazon does. That is a high bar for a brand whose own building was designed for wholesale cartons rather than single parcels.

None of this makes FBA the safe answer. A brand with volatile demand, many sizes or wholesale accounts competing for the same units can be hurt more by stock trapped in Amazon’s network than by a few late parcels. The point is that the two routes fail differently, and the choice should be made by someone who owns both failures.

Questions for the room before Q4

  1. If our own dock missed its on-time rate for one week in December, which Amazon listings would lose Prime, and what would that week cost in sales?
  2. If November sales run 30% above plan, how many days would it take to get more stock into Amazon’s warehouses, and is that inside the season?
  3. Who owns this decision, and is the same person measured on both the fulfillment cost and the Amazon revenue?
  4. Which products should sit in FBA for the holidays even if they ship from our own building the rest of the year?

The brands that get through December cleanly tend to make this a joint decision of operations and e-commerce in September, product by product. Running the Amazon channel day to day, including that fulfillment call, is work we do for brands, and we are glad to walk through your Q4 split.

P0293.crumb: Lifetime value on Amazon is rented back…
P0293.title: Lifetime value on Amazon is rented back through the ad auction
P0293.alt: An antique brass turnstile in the doorway of a small shop with wooden shelves of bottles and linens.
P0293.ttag: Lifetime value on Amazon is rented back through the ad auction | Kwontified
P0293.desc: A repeat Amazon customer is worth what each reorder earns after the ad you may need to win it back, which is why brands misjudge lifetime value on Amazon.
P0293.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 8, 2019.
P0293.body:
Ask a direct-to-consumer team what a customer is worth and you will get a number, usually to the cent, built from reorder rates and email performance. Ask the Amazon team at the same brand and you will often get a shrug. Amazon’s terms are blunt on the point: sellers may not contact buyers for marketing or promotional purposes, as Seller Labs noted in a December 2018 survey of sellers. No email, no customer file, so no lifetime value. Or so the reasoning goes.

The customer is still there, and still worth something. What changes on a marketplace is the route back. A shopper who buys your moisturizer a second time usually returns to Amazon’s search box, not to your inbox, and on that results page you may have to buy the click again. So lifetime value on Amazon is margin times reorders, less the ad cost of winning each reorder. Most brands either ignore the first part or forget the second.

Why lifetime value on Amazon looks unknowable

The shrug has a basis. Amazon shares little about who bought. Its closest tool is the new-to-brand metric, with data from November 2018, which marks an ad-attributed purchase as new when the shopper has not bought the brand on Amazon in the previous 12 months, Marketing Dive reported in January. It covers Sponsored Brands and display ads bought through Amazon DSP, not Sponsored Products, and it describes one purchase rather than a customer’s history.

That makes the familiar formula hard to fill in. A DTC model tracks a cohort from its first order and counts what each customer spends over two or three years. On Amazon there is no cohort to follow. So teams fall back on what they can see: the cost of the first sale. Every Amazon order then looks like a one-off, and every ad is judged on the order it closed.

That is an anchoring problem. The number on the screen becomes the whole value of the customer, because it is the only number on the screen.

Each reorder passes back through the auction

A repeat buyer on Amazon tends to come back by searching. Many type the brand name, and on that page the brand’s own listing competes with sponsored placements, including rivals bidding on its name. Brand searches are a large share of the ad business already: in Merkle’s third-quarter 2018 report, brand keywords produced 42% of Sponsored Products sales among its advertisers, ChannelX reported. Some of those sales are repeat customers whose second order the brand paid for.

Take a $30 face moisturizer that leaves $12 of contribution after Amazon’s fees and product cost. Say a satisfied buyer reorders three times in the 12 months after the first order. If every reorder came back free, the customer would be worth the first order plus $36.

Now add the toll. Say four in ten of those reorders arrive through a sponsored click on your brand search, at a cost per order of $3, a 10% advertising cost of sale. Each reorder then earns $12 minus 40% of $3, or $10.80, and the three reorders are worth $32.40. That is a 10% haircut, and it is the price of keeping the shelf when the customer returns.

Share of reorders through a paid brand clickAd cost per paid reorderNet value of three reorders
0%$3.00$36.00
40%$3.00$32.40
80%$3.00$28.80

The haircut is not the main risk. Losing the reorder is. If a competitor’s ad takes the top of the brand search and a third of returning shoppers switch, the same customer is worth two reorders, not three. The ad cost is the fee for keeping the customer, and in this example it is cheap next to the margin it protects.

That reframes the first sale. If a customer is worth $12 on the first order plus about $32 over the following 12 months, a brand can afford to pay more than $12 to win the first order, as long as the reorders really come.

What new-to-brand data can and can’t tell you

New-to-brand shares are the best public window into repeat behavior on Amazon, and they are easy to misread. A high share means many buyers are new, which is good for growth and says nothing about whether they come back. Marketing Dive’s report cited a pet brand that found 86% of its Amazon sales since November 1 came from new-to-brand customers, a number inflated because the brand had started selling on Amazon within the previous year. In a mature brand, a falling new-to-brand share can mean either that acquisition is weakening or that repeat buying is rising.

The test that separates them is a holdout on the toll. Pick a set of products with steady brand-search sales, pause the ads on your brand terms for two weeks, and watch total sales from those searches, organic and paid together. If sales hold, your reorders were coming back anyway and the toll was optional. If they fall, the ad was buying retention, and its cost belongs in your lifetime value math rather than in the acquisition budget.

The rule for Monday: estimate an Amazon customer’s value as contribution per order times expected reorders, minus the ad cost of each reorder you must win back. Then set what you will pay for a first order against that figure, not against the first order alone. Building that estimate and the holdout behind it is part of the measurement work we do for brands on Amazon, and we are glad to run the numbers with you.
