P0295.title: Vendor Central relationships fail where the buyer became a system
P0295.alt: A weathered vintage vending machine on a wooden platform in a blue-grey room beside a tall window.
P0295.ttag: Vendor Central relationships fail where the buyer became a system | Kwontified
P0295.desc: Brands run Amazon vendor accounts like a buyer relationship while Amazon runs most vendors through systems, and Vendor Central relationships break at that seam.
P0295.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 10, 2019.
P0295.body:
On Monday, March 4, 2019, thousands of smaller Amazon vendors opened Vendor Central and found no weekly purchase order. Those who asked were first told it was a technical glitch. By Tuesday many were told the change was permanent and that they would do better selling on the marketplace, Modern Retail reported. Most of the affected brands sold $10 million or less a year on Amazon and had no assigned vendor manager.

The detail that stays with me is the last one. These brands did not lose a relationship that week. They found out they had not had one for some time. Vendor Central relationships tend to break at exactly this seam: the brand runs its Amazon account the way it runs a department store account, around a buyer, while Amazon runs most of its vendors through systems. When the system changes, there is nobody to call.

Brands staff Amazon like a wholesale account

Look at who owns Amazon inside a typical vendor brand. Often it is a key-account manager from the wholesale sales team, someone whose craft is the buyer relationship: the annual line review, the negotiation over terms, the dinner at the trade show, the phone call when a shipment goes wrong. That model works with a department store, where a named buyer owns the category and has the authority to fix things.

The habit carries over to Amazon because, for the largest vendors, it still partly works. They have a vendor manager, an annual negotiation and someone to escalate to. Smaller vendors assume they have the same thing in miniature.

Many of them do not, and the signs were visible before March. A vendor who placed purchase orders with his own suppliers based on Amazon’s 2019 projections had those orders canceled, and vendors said they had expected 14 or 30 days’ notice of a change, Modern Retail reported that week. Notice is what a buyer gives. A forecast that stops does not.

Amazon runs most vendors through systems

Read Amazon as an institution and the design is plain. Bloomberg described the vendor purge as part of a push to raise e-commerce profits, moving suppliers toward a self-service system with no Amazon manager in the loop, as carried by the Seattle Times. Most vendors had their orders restored within days, but only brands enrolled in Brand Registry kept automatic purchase-order fulfillment, with 60 days to enroll, Modern Retail reported on March 12.

The same pattern runs through the rest of 2019. Annual vendor negotiations started later and moved more slowly because each vendor manager now covers more brands, and Amazon asked for more vendor funding and logistics savings, Cleveland Research noted in April. In May, Bloomberg reported that Amazon had not renegotiated annual terms with many smaller vendors that spring, which Amazon disputed, PYMNTS reported. And when Amazon decides a product loses it money, the vendor learns from an email saying the product “no longer qualifies for advertising,” CNBC reported in March.

None of this is hostility. A retailer buying from as many suppliers as Amazon does cannot staff a buyer for each one, and Amazon has long leaned on software where other retailers use people. What it means for the brand is that the counterpart on the other side of the account is, for most vendors, a set of rules: order forecasts, cost thresholds, compliance requirements and the emails that report them.

Where the relationship breaks

The break comes from managing the wrong counterpart. A brand that still thinks in buyer terms waits for a conversation that does not come, escalates through channels built for the largest suppliers, and treats each automated change as a slight rather than a signal. Meanwhile the signals that matter go unread: purchase orders shrinking week by week, products dropping out of advertising eligibility, chargebacks piling up in a report nobody owns.

Inside the brand, the structure makes this worse. The key-account manager is measured on shipments to Amazon, so orders feel like the relationship, and a good quarter of shipments can hide a listing that is quietly losing its place in search.

Finance sees the deductions. Operations sees the compliance problems. Marketing sees the ad eligibility emails, if anyone forwards them. No one sees the whole account the way Amazon’s systems do, and so no one notices it drifting until a purchase order fails to arrive. By then the decision was made weeks earlier, by a rule the brand could have read.

The shift leaders should plan for is that a vendor account, for all but the largest brands, has become an operating interface rather than a relationship. It rewards the brand that reads its data every week and changes cost, packaging or assortment in response, and it punishes the brand that waits for a call. The evidence through 2019 leans that way, and it is likely to lean further as Amazon moves more of the work into Seller Central’s self-service tools.

Questions to put to the team that owns Amazon

  1. Do we have a named Amazon vendor manager now, and when did we last hear from one?
  2. Who reads our weekly purchase-order trend, deductions and ad-eligibility notices together, and what changed in the last quarter?
  3. Is the person who owns Amazon measured on shipments to Amazon or on what sells through to shoppers?
  4. If our purchase orders stopped on a Monday, what would we do by Friday?

A brand that can answer the last question has stopped waiting for a buyer. Running the Amazon account as the system it is, week to week, is the channel management work we do for brands, and we are glad to look at your vendor account with you.

P0297.title: Marketplace price parity now binds through retailers’ discounts
P0297.alt: Two red teapots with blank tags displayed in the windows of a weathered grey shopfront on a cobbled street.
P0297.ttag: Marketplace price parity now binds through retailers’ discounts | Kwontified
P0297.desc: Amazon dropped its price parity clause, but retailer-funded discounts now set a brand’s lowest public price, and every marketplace price check follows it.
P0297.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 15, 2019.
P0297.body:
On October 14, Bloomberg reported that Walmart had started cutting the prices of some products on its third-party marketplace and paying sellers the difference out of its own pocket. Under the program, called Competitive Price Adjustment, the seller still receives its listed price, Walmart chooses the sellers and items, and sellers cannot ask to be included, Fortune reported. It sounds like free money. For a brand that also sells on Amazon, it may be the most expensive discount it never gave.

Marketplace price parity used to be a contract term. In 2019 it became something else: a set of price checks that read whatever price a shopper can see, including prices a retailer lowered with its own money. The rules that bind a brand’s price now run through other retailers’ discounts.

Marketplace price parity left the contract in March

Until March 2019, Amazon’s agreement barred US third-party sellers from offering lower prices on other sites. Amazon dropped that requirement that month, TechCrunch reported, six years after it stopped requiring parity from European sellers following investigations by British and German competition authorities. Amazon confirmed the change but declined to elaborate, Modern Retail reported.

Many brands read that as the end of parity. It was the end of the clause. A month earlier, Amazon had told sellers they “need to be price competitive,” defining the problem as an item price plus shipping above what other retailers charge, with offers at risk of losing the Buy Box, Digiday reported in February. The check compares prices. It does not ask who set them.

Retailers now cut your price with their own money

That gap matters more now that the retailers themselves move prices. Walmart’s Competitive Price Adjustment lowers the shopper’s price on a marketplace listing while paying the seller in full. Amazon has run similar programs for longer. Its Discount Provided by Amazon, introduced about two years ago, lets Amazon cut a third-party product’s price for a limited time and pay the seller the difference. Sellers in its Sold by Amazon program let Amazon lower prices at will in exchange for a guaranteed payout, according to the same Fortune report.

Each program is generous on its own terms. Together they create a chain. The retailer cuts the price on its site, the lower price becomes public, and the other marketplace’s price check finds it and reads it as your price.

Take a $50 serum listed at $50 on both Amazon and Walmart. Say Walmart’s program cuts the Walmart price to $44 for a week and pays you the $6 on each of the 30 units you sell there, $180 in all. Amazon’s check now sees the same item at $44 elsewhere. If your Amazon offer loses the Buy Box, and you normally sell 200 units a week on Amazon, two choices remain:

ResponseWeekly Amazon unitsCost to you that week
Hold $50 and lose the Buy BoxFewer; say half, 100$5,000 of Amazon sales
Match at $44 to keep the Buy Box200$1,200 of margin ($6 x 200)

Walmart spent $180 to make the Walmart price lower. The brand pays at least $1,200 to stay competitive on Amazon. The subsidy was paid by one retailer and charged to the brand by another.

The logic of each retailer is sound. Walmart, Marketplace Pulse’s Juozas Kaziukenas told Bloomberg, gives up some revenue “but it buys them sales.” Amazon, for its part, wants its shoppers to see the lowest price available. Neither is targeting the brand. The cost arises in the space between them, which no single retailer owns.

Vendors feel the chain from the other side. When Amazon buys a product wholesale, its retail team sets the shelf price, so a match to a Walmart cut comes out of Amazon’s margin on that item first. That margin does not stay Amazon’s problem. In March, Amazon began telling more vendors that products it sells at a loss would no longer qualify for advertising, CNBC reported, and the remedy offered was a lower cost to Amazon.

The same chain runs through wholesale. Fortune noted that a temporary Walmart cut can frustrate shoppers when the price returns to normal and can bring complaints to manufacturers from buyers who paid more elsewhere. A department store that matches online prices sees the cut too.

What the price checks can and can’t tell you

You will not get notice. Walmart picks the items, and sellers cannot opt in, so a brand learns of an adjustment when its price changes on the page or when the other marketplace reacts. The only defense is to watch your lowest public price for each important product every day, across every site that sells it, and to know which retailer set it.

That data also answers the strategic question. If one retailer’s subsidies keep setting your lowest price, you are effectively letting that retailer price you everywhere. Some brands will accept that, because the volume is worth it. Others will narrow which products they sell through that marketplace, or use their own pricing policies with resellers; those are commercial and legal choices to review with counsel, not reactions to make in a week.

The rule for Monday: treat your price as the lowest price any retailer shows for your product, whoever paid for it. For your top 20 products, find that number every day, and decide in advance which retailer’s price you will match and which you will let go. Running Walmart and Amazon pricing as one map is part of how we manage marketplaces for brands, and we are glad to map yours with you.

P0298.title: Cyber Week 2019 crosses into December, and monthly plans break
P0298.alt: An autumn leaf wreath and a frosted evergreen wreath with a red bow side by side on a wooden front door.
P0298.ttag: Cyber Week 2019 crosses into December, and monthly plans break | Kwontified
P0298.desc: A late Thanksgiving pushes Cyber Monday 2019 into December, so plans, budgets and targets built by calendar month will misread the season unless changed now.
P0298.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 17, 2019.
P0298.body:
Open almost any brand’s holiday plan and you will find it laid out by month: a November column, a December column, targets and budgets in each. In 2018 that worked well enough, because Thanksgiving fell on November 22 and the whole run from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, November 26, sat inside November. In 2019 Thanksgiving falls on November 28, the latest date it can, and Cyber Monday lands on December 2.

The season is six days shorter between Thanksgiving and Christmas, but the more expensive change is quieter. Cyber Week 2019 straddles the line between two months that most plans treat as separate worlds. Demand is not expected to shrink much. It is expected to move, and a plan built in calendar months will misread where it went. The decisions due six weeks out, around October 18, are mostly about redrawing those lines.

What the forecasts expect, and what they assume

The forecasters still see growth. The National Retail Federation expects November and December sales to rise 3.8% to 4.2%, with online and other non-store sales up 11% to 14%, DC Velocity reported on October 3. Deloitte forecast online holiday sales up 14% to 18%, Consulting.us reported in September, and noted that its 2019 numbers assume steady growth through the season.

That assumption deserves attention, because Deloitte’s 2018 call ran well ahead of the result: it forecast online growth of 17% to 22%, and the season delivered 11.2%, which it put down to a weaker than expected December. The five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday 2018 brought in $24.2 billion online, about a fifth of the season’s $126 billion, according to Adobe’s 2018 figures reported by Marketing Land. In 2019 that same block of spending starts six days later and ends in December.

Working back from December 2

Six weeks out, mid-October: deal depth

Decide which products carry the deepest discounts and on which days. With fewer shopping days after Thanksgiving, more of the season’s discounting will cluster in one week, and deals that had 33 days from Thanksgiving to Christmas in 2018 have 27 in 2019. Choose fewer, deeper deals on the products that already sell, rather than spreading thin offers across the catalog.

Four weeks out: inventory

Holiday stock needs to be where it will sell before the rush, in a retailer’s warehouse or Amazon’s network. A plan that sends stock against November’s sales target alone will undersupply the first days of December, when Cyber Monday now falls.

Two weeks out, mid-November: budget by day

If advertising budgets are set in monthly buckets, Cyber Monday’s spend now comes out of December’s budget, which was sized for a different job. Move the event to its own budget line that runs from Thanksgiving through December 2.

The last shipping days: delivery promises

The short season also raises the value of the days after Cyber Monday. Amazon offered free one-day delivery to Prime members on more than ten million items by July, its second-quarter results said, and a shopper who trusts next-day arrival can leave gifts later. Keep stock and budget for the middle of December rather than spending it all by December 2, and know which of your products carry the fastest delivery badges.

The month line is the real problem

Inside most brands, the calendar month is more than a planning convenience. It is how targets are set, how teams are paid and how leadership reads results. That is where the late Thanksgiving does its damage.

Consider what each team will see. The e-commerce lead measured on November revenue will see Cyber Monday’s sales, which in 2018 counted toward November, land in December, and November will look weaker against 2018 even if the event goes well.

Finance, comparing November with November, will see a miss and may ask for spending cuts in the week that matters most. The team that owns December will see an early bump and may conclude the month is running ahead, just as the post-Cyber Monday lull arrives. None of those readings is about shoppers. All of them come from the column headings, and each can trigger a decision, a frozen budget or a rushed markdown, in the one fortnight when a wrong call costs the most.

The fix is plain and rarely made in advance: define the event by its days, not its month. Report Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday 2019 against Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday 2018, compare the full November-December season as one period, and tell the people whose bonuses depend on November that the comparison has changed before the numbers arrive. A brand that does this in October avoids a December argument about a shortfall that never happened.

None of this requires knowing how the season will turn out. Forecasts have missed before. It requires only agreeing in advance how the results will be read, so that the plan responds to what shoppers do rather than to where a date fell.

Questions to settle this week

  1. Which of our holiday targets, budgets and bonuses are set by calendar month, and who needs to know that Cyber Monday 2019 falls in December?
  2. Have we agreed to compare the 2019 event, Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, with the same five days in 2018 rather than November with November?
  3. Is our advertising budget for December 2 coming out of a December line sized for something else?
  4. If the season runs closer to Deloitte’s 2018 miss than to its 2019 forecast, what would we cut first, and who decides?

Running the holiday plan for a brand’s Amazon and Walmart channels, day by day rather than month by month, is work we do with brands every fourth quarter, and we are glad to walk through your Cyber Week 2019 calendar.

P0302.title: Marketplace channel conflict starts with what your buyers can see
P0302.alt: An open laptop showing a mountain lake beside a succulent in the window of a stone shopfront on a quiet street.
P0302.ttag: Marketplace channel conflict starts with what your buyers can see | Kwontified
P0302.desc: When a brand lists on Amazon, its wholesale buyers read the move through the prices, products and priority they can see, and channel conflict follows.
P0302.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 24, 2019.
P0302.body:
On June 21, 2017, word spread that Nike had agreed to sell some products directly to Amazon. Shares of Foot Locker fell 5% and Finish Line 4% that day, the Wall Street Journal’s newswire reported. Nike was the largest vendor to both chains, accounting for 68% and 71% of the merchandise they bought the year before. Nobody at either retailer had to say a word. The market said it for them.

Most brands that move onto a marketplace are not Nike, and their wholesale partners are not public companies. But the reaction follows the same path.

Marketplace channel conflict rarely starts with the announcement. It starts with what a wholesale buyer can see afterward: the price on Amazon, the products listed there, and how much of the brand’s attention the new channel seems to get. Brands that plan for those three signals keep the conflict small. Brands that plan only the announcement usually meet the buyer’s reaction later, in a line review.

What a wholesale buyer hears

The first signal is price, because it is the one a buyer can check from a phone. A department store or specialty chain buys at wholesale, prices for its own margin, and plans markdowns months ahead. When the same item appears on Amazon below its price, the buyer hears a request to cut margin or lose the sale. The pressure no longer comes only from the brand’s own choices. In October, Walmart began cutting prices on some marketplace listings with its own money, and Fortune noted that such temporary cuts can bring complaints to manufacturers from buyers who paid more elsewhere (Fortune).

The second signal is product. A buyer who sees the full line on a marketplace, including the styles the store fought for, hears that exclusivity is over. Nike’s arrangement was described from the start as covering only some products, and the same report noted that Nike makes different tiers of product for different retailers. For a buyer, that detail matters more than any statement.

The third signal is priority. Buyers notice where a brand spends its effort: which channel gets the new colors first, whose stockouts get fixed first, which team gets the budget. In October 2017 Nike told investors it would concentrate on 40 retail partners, naming Amazon among the newer ones alongside Foot Locker and Nordstrom. It added that “undifferentiated, mediocre retail” would not survive, and every account outside the 40 heard its place in the queue (Fox Business).

The conflict is built into both org charts

Follow the value and the reaction makes sense. A wholesale buyer is measured on the margin and sell-through of a category. A marketplace listing can take sales from that category and set a public price below the buyer’s, while the brand collects the marketplace’s sales data. From the buyer’s chair, the brand has opened a competing store across the street, and the brand can see the store’s traffic while the buyer cannot.

That last point is newer than it looks. Since February 2019, sellers enrolled in Brand Registry can see Amazon’s Brand Analytics, which shows the search terms shoppers use and the products they click, a report that had been available only to vendors, ChannelX reported. A brand on the marketplace now walks into a line review knowing more about how shoppers search for its category than the buyer across the table does, and buyers know it.

Inside the brand, the incentives point the other way. The e-commerce team is rewarded for marketplace growth, the wholesale team for sell-in to accounts, and the two often report to different leaders. Neither is told to protect the other’s price. That is how a marketplace promotion run for a quarterly target becomes a markdown argument with a key account two months later.

The ground is shifting under the old fight

The conflict is real, but its shape is changing, because wholesale accounts are making their own arrangements with marketplaces. Kohl’s said in April that it would accept eligible Amazon returns, without a box or label, at more than 1,150 stores from July 2019, CNBC reported. Aldo moved its roughly ten-year Amazon relationship to a wholesale arrangement in 2019, and Lands’ End began selling on Amazon in 2018 partly to offset losses at Sears, according to a Reuters report in April.

That changes the conversation a brand can have with its buyers. When the retailer itself works with Amazon, a brand’s listing is less a betrayal than a negotiation over terms: which products, at what price floor, with what support for the store. The evidence through 2019 leans toward that kind of negotiated coexistence rather than a choice between channels, and the brands that arrive at the line review with a plan for price, product and priority are the ones setting the terms.

Questions to settle before the next line review

  1. For our top wholesale accounts, which of our products can their buyers find on a marketplace, and at what price compared with theirs?
  2. Do we offer different products or pack sizes to marketplaces and to stores, and does every buyer know which is which?
  3. Who inside the brand decides marketplace promotions, and do they see the wholesale price calendar before they act?
  4. If a retailer cuts our price on its marketplace with its own money, who calls our key accounts, and what do they say?

Planning that conversation before a marketplace launch is part of running the channel well, and helping brands run Amazon and Walmart alongside their wholesale business is work we do; we are glad to map your channel signals with you.

P0303.crumb: Amazon coupons vs price cuts: only one…
P0303.title: Amazon coupons vs price cuts: only one resets your deal baseline
P0303.alt: Blank paper tags with string, a torn card and brass scissors on a rustic table beside a spool of twine.
P0303.ttag: Amazon coupons vs price cuts: only one resets your deal baseline | Kwontified
P0303.desc: Amazon’s ranking rewards units, not the discount that sold them, so choosing a coupon or a price cut turns on who gets the discount and on your deal price.
P0303.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 29, 2019.
P0303.body:
Every October someone on an Amazon team asks which discount the algorithm likes better, a coupon or a lower price. It is a reasonable question with a misleading premise. Amazon does not publish how it ranks search results. When the Wall Street Journal reported in September that the company had changed its ranking to favor more profitable listings, Amazon said it had “not changed the criteria we use to rank search results to include profitability,” SiliconANGLE reported. What sellers can observe is that units sold move rank, whatever sold them.

So the algorithm is mostly indifferent between the two. The difference between Amazon coupons and price cuts lies elsewhere: who receives the discount, and what it does to the price that your holiday deals will have to beat.

Why the algorithm question misleads

The belief that coupons carry a special ranking boost is easy to understand. A coupon is visible. Prime shoppers see a green coupon button just below the price on the product page, Jungle Scout described in March, and its author argued that coupons lift sales and with them best sellers rank. That is the point: rank moved because sales moved. The author also noted that the coupon results could not be tested statistically, and nothing in them separates the coupon’s effect from the discount’s.

If rank follows units, the question becomes which discount buys units more cheaply, and which leaves you better placed for the next event.

A coupon discounts only the shoppers who ask for it

A price cut is unconditional. Everyone who buys gets it, including the shoppers who would have paid full price. A coupon is conditional: a shopper has to clip it, and only clipped coupons cost you anything. Amazon charges a fee each time a coupon is redeemed; Jungle Scout’s example used $0.60.

Take a $40 item that leaves $16 of contribution and sells 100 units in a typical week. Say a $4 price cut lifts sales 25%, and a $4 coupon lifts them 15%, with 40% of buyers clipping it. Ignore any change in Amazon’s fees for simplicity.

UnitsDiscounted unitsCost per discounted unitContribution
No discount1000—$1,600
$4 price cut125125$4.00$1,500
$4 coupon11546$4.60$1,628

The price cut sells more units and earns less, because it gives $4 to every buyer. The coupon sells fewer but pays the discount and fee only on 46 of 115 sales. In this scenario it is the only option that beats doing nothing. Change the assumptions, a much higher clip rate or a much weaker coupon lift, and the answer can flip, which is the point of running the numbers rather than asking which tool the algorithm prefers.

The table leaves out one effect that favors the cut. Amazon’s referral fee is a share of the price, 15% in many categories, so a $4 cut also saves about $0.60 a unit in fees (the Motley Fool’s fee table). That lifts the price cut to about $1,575 in this example, closer, but still below doing nothing.

A price cut also travels. The listed price is the number other retailers and Amazon’s own checks compare: Amazon has told sellers they “need to be price competitive,” judged on item price plus shipping against other retailers, Digiday reported in February. A coupon clipped on an Amazon product page does not change the price a rival’s shopper sees.

A price cut resets the baseline your deals must beat

The second difference matters more in late October. Amazon’s deals measure your discount against your own price history. For Prime Exclusive Discounts around Prime Day 2019, the deal price had to be at least 20% off the seller’s price and lower than the lowest price in the previous 30 days, Feedvisor reported in June.

That rule turns an October price cut into a November problem. Cut the $40 item to $36 four weeks before Black Friday and the lowest recent price is now $36. A holiday deal has to clear that new floor, not $40, so the discount you can show shrinks or the deal price has to go lower still. The cut you made to lift October sales is charged again in the deal you run at the peak.

A coupon leaves the listed price where it was. Whether Amazon’s deal checks count a clipped coupon toward the lowest recent price is not spelled out in the published terms summarized above, so check the reference price Amazon’s deal tool shows for the product before you submit. In general, though, the listed price is what the rules measure, and a coupon does not move it.

What the data can and can’t tell you

Your coupon report will show clips and redemptions, and your sales will show the lift. Neither tells you how many coupon users would have bought anyway. A clean read comes from timing: run the coupon on a set of comparable products for two weeks and leave a matched set without one, then compare units and contribution, not just redemptions. If the coupon group’s contribution beats the matched group’s by less than the coupon’s cost, the coupon bought sales you already had, and a smaller coupon or none is the better choice.

The rule for the next six weeks: if a product is going into a holiday deal, do not cut its listed price in the 30 days before the deal. Use a coupon if it needs a lift, and only where the coupon still earns more than no discount at your real clip rate. Planning promotions around Amazon’s deal rules, not just its ranking, is part of how we run Amazon advertising and promotions for brands.

P0304.crumb: Wholesale to marketplace: a brand trades…
P0304.title: Wholesale to marketplace: a brand trades seasons for days
P0304.alt: A row of cardboard shipping boxes and padded mailers lined up against a gray brick wall on a wooden floor.
P0304.ttag: Wholesale to marketplace: a brand trades seasons for days | Kwontified
P0304.desc: A brand moving from wholesale to marketplace selling swaps a seasonal clock for a daily one, and most of the change is in who may decide what, and how fast.
P0304.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 31, 2019.
P0304.body:
A wholesale brand’s year is built around a handful of dates. Market week, when buyers walk the showroom and write orders. The line review, when a key account decides how much shelf the brand gets next season. The ship window, when the goods leave the warehouse.

Between those dates the work is preparation, and the people who matter are the ones who can move an order. A brand that has run that way for decades is not slow. It is tuned to a clock that ticks a few times a season.

A marketplace runs on a different clock. Prices on Amazon move by the hour, search rank shifts with yesterday’s sales, and a run of weak reviews can change a product’s week. So the culture change from wholesale to marketplace is mostly a change of clock, and the hardest part is not learning new tools. It is moving the right to decide, on price, content and spend, to people who see the daily data, and trusting them with it.

Two clocks, one company

How the old clock took hold is no mystery. For brands that grew through department stores and specialty chains, wholesale was the business. Even at Nike, nearly three-quarters of sales, $22.6 billion, came from wholesale partners in the year ended May 2016, the Wall Street Journal’s newswire reported. Approvals, calendars and pay plans were built around that money, and they worked.

The marketplace clock is faster than most brand teams expect. Researchers at Northeastern University tracked sellers of 1,641 best-selling Amazon products for four months and identified more than 500 using algorithmic pricing, some changing prices tens or even hundreds of times a day, their 2016 study found. Those sellers won the Buy Box more often. A brand whose price change needs a sign-off from the head of sales and finance is answering software with a memo.

Large brands have started to rebuild for speed, and the size of the rebuild shows how deep the old clock runs. In June 2017 Nike said it would halve its product creation cycle, cut its number of styles by 25% and concentrate on 12 key cities. Its brand president said the plan would “deliver innovation, at speed, through more direct connections,” Fortune reported.

That October it told investors it aimed to raise digital from 15% of revenue to 30% within five years, Fox Business reported. A reorganization on that scale is what a change of clock looks like at a company that size.

Where the old clock hides

Most brands moving onto marketplaces do not reorganize. They add an e-commerce team and keep everything else, and the old clock survives inside the approval chain. Watch where a marketplace decision waits.

A price change waits for the person who sets wholesale price lists, because a public price touches every account. A new main image waits for the brand team’s seasonal photo approval. An advertising budget increase waits for the monthly forecast meeting.

A stockout waits for the next production run planned against wholesale orders. Each of those approvals made sense when the decision happened four times a year. Applied to a channel that changes daily, they mean the marketplace team spends its time asking permission while the listing loses ground.

The people in those chairs are not the problem. They are protecting things that matter: price integrity with accounts, brand standards, margin. The structure asks them to protect those things by approving each move, when the marketplace needs them to protect those things by setting limits in advance.

Guardrails replace one-at-a-time approvals

That is the shift brands should plan for. The wholesale habit is to approve decisions one at a time. The marketplace habit is to set boundaries once and let the team move inside them. That means a price floor and ceiling per product, agreed with the people who manage wholesale accounts, and an image library pre-approved by brand. It means an advertising budget band tied to a target cost of sale, and inventory set aside for the marketplace rather than whatever wholesale leaves behind.

Inside those lines, the marketplace team acts the same day. Outside them, the old approvals still apply.

The evidence through 2019 leans toward brands that make this trade early, because the channel rewards speed and the speed has to come from somewhere. It is too early to say which organizational model will win: a separate team, a merged team or an outside operator.

Every version that works shares one feature. Decisions that need to happen daily are made daily, by people who can see the data, and the people who used to approve them spend their time setting and revisiting the limits instead. That is a different job for a head of sales or a brand director, and it deserves to be described to them as a promotion of their judgment, not a loss of control.

Questions for the leadership team

  1. For each of price, main image, ad budget and marketplace inventory, who must approve a change now, and how long does it take?
  2. Which of those could we turn into a pre-agreed range, so the marketplace team can act the same day?
  3. Who sets the price floor that protects our wholesale accounts, and has the marketplace team seen it?
  4. Does anyone on the marketplace team have authority to act without a meeting, and do they know it?

Running the marketplace channel on its own clock, inside limits a brand sets, is the channel management work we do for brands moving from wholesale, and we are glad to walk through your approval chain with you.

P0307.crumb: Amazon AdCon 2019 was a recruiting drive…
P0307.title: Amazon AdCon 2019 was a recruiting drive for your auctions
P0307.alt: Rows of empty wooden folding chairs face a podium with a microphone in a sunlit hall with yellow walls.
P0307.ttag: Amazon AdCon 2019 was a recruiting drive for your auctions | Kwontified
P0307.desc: Amazon’s first brand ad conference trained hundreds of new bidders. For brands already advertising, that means more rivals in every Q4 auction.
P0307.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 5, 2019.
P0307.body:
Amazon held its first big advertising conference for brands in Seattle at the start of October, and almost nobody outside the room saw it. AdCon 2019 was invite-only and closed to the press, and about 400 people attended, CNBC reported the following week. There was no product launch to recap. The breakout sessions taught attendees how to reach new customers and use Amazon’s sponsored ads, with best practices for hardlines, softlines and consumables.

For a brand that already advertises on Amazon, the news from Amazon AdCon 2019 is the guest list. Every company that left Seattle with a better campaign is another bidder on searches you already buy. In an auction, more bidders raise the price of a click even for an advertiser who changed nothing, and the timing puts those new bidders in your fourth-quarter searches.

What Amazon AdCon 2019 told brands, and who heard it

The format says a lot. Paul Kotas, who runs Amazon Advertising, and Colleen Aubrey, its vice president of performance advertising, took questions from the floor. Case studies came from Tuft & Needle, the mattress brand, and I and Love and You, a pet food company. Sellics and Teikametrics, two firms that sell bidding software to Amazon advertisers, sponsored it.

The audience says more. Franz Jordan, chief executive of Sellics, told CNBC that attendees were mostly small and medium-sized companies, because large brands typically have their own Amazon representatives. Amazon’s smaller event a year earlier, Rev2018, was aimed at agencies; AdCon was built to court brands directly, AdExchanger noted.

So Amazon spent two days teaching hundreds of self-service advertisers to bid with more confidence. That is a sensible thing for Amazon to do, and the money shows why. Amazon’s “other” revenue, which is mostly advertising, reached $3.6 billion in the third quarter, up from $2.5 billion a year earlier, Amazon reported on October 24. Excluding currency effects the line grew 45%, after 36% and 37% in the first two quarters, and chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said advertising itself grew faster than that, CNBC reported. He called it “increasingly popular with vendors, sellers and third-party advertisers.”

Compare that with what large advertisers already in the auction are spending. Merkle’s clients raised Sponsored Products spend 19% year over year in the first quarter, ChannelX reported. The samples and quarters differ, so treat this as directional, but one reading of the gap is that a good share of Amazon’s growth comes from advertisers outside the big agency books: the companies AdCon invited.

Why a fuller room makes your click dearer

Amazon’s ad revenue is the sum of every winning bid. It can grow because the same advertisers spend more, because prices rise, or because new advertisers arrive. The third source is the one that changes your costs without any decision on your part.

Take a generic search such as “orthopedic dog bed” with four advertisers bidding $1.40, $1.10, $0.90 and $0.70 a click. In an auction that charges the winner roughly what it takes to beat the next bid, the top advertiser pays a little over $1.10.

Now two newcomers arrive, fresh from a session on reaching new customers, bidding $1.25 and $1.00. The top advertiser keeps its placement and now pays a little over $1.25, about 14% more for the same shopper. The brand bidding $1.10 drops a position. Neither of them touched a setting.

That is why recruiting advertisers is rational for Amazon even when the recruits spend modestly. A newcomer’s own budget is small; its effect on what everyone above it pays is not. Each extra bidder near the top of a search lifts the clearing price for the whole column of ads above it.

The effect is largest where newcomers cluster. Small and medium-sized brands tend to bid on generic category searches, where they hope to be discovered, and on rivals’ names. They rarely bid on yours.

What your Q4 reports will and will not show

Your cost per click will rise in November and December regardless, because the holiday brings bigger budgets from everyone. The report will not tell you how much of the rise is the season and how much is new competition. Two comparisons get you closer.

First, split cost per click by search type. Branded searches, where few newcomers bid, show something close to the seasonal effect alone. If generic category searches are rising much faster than branded ones, the extra is competition.

Second, read the search term report for the products appearing next to yours. New brands showing up on your top generic searches week after week are the auction filling up, and their arrival dates tell you when your prices moved.

What the data cannot show is whether paying more is still worth it. That depends on your own conversion rate, not on the market.

Bid rules for a fuller auction

  1. Set each product’s maximum bid from what a click is worth to you: price, times the share of price you can spend on advertising, times the conversion rate of that search.
  2. When a generic search climbs past that ceiling, step back from the top placement rather than chasing it. A newcomer bidding above its own value will not do so for long.
  3. Hold firm on branded searches, where you convert best and newcomers rarely compete.
  4. Review generic bids weekly through December, because the number of bidders can change faster than your monthly report.

A bigger auction is good for Amazon and neutral for a brand that bids from its own numbers. Keeping bids anchored to the value of each click, search by search, is how we run Amazon advertising for brands through Q4.

P0308.alt: An open cardboard box holding a speckled ceramic mug beside wrapping paper and blue ribbon on a wooden table.

P0308.desc: After December the person deciding whether your product stays is the recipient, a customer you never marketed to. Plan January returns for that person.
P0308.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 7, 2019.
P0308.body:
On the first working days of January, a particular customer stands at the returns counter or the post office. She holds a sweater in a size someone guessed, a gift receipt with no price on it, and no attachment to the brand on the label. Somebody else did the choosing. She is doing the judging.

That customer is the one most holiday plans leave out. From November to Christmas a brand markets to the giver, and the giver decides. After December the decision passes to a recipient the brand never courted, and many of the January returns that look like product failures in the reports are really a mismatch between one person’s guess and another person’s taste. Gift returns need their own plan, written for the recipient.

The January returns counter serves a different customer

The volume is large and arrives in two waves. UPS expects consumers to ship more than a million return packages a day in December, a pace that continues into early January, it said this week. The first spike comes in the week of December 16, at 1.6 million packages a day, as early shoppers send back what they bought for others and for themselves. The biggest day is January 2, which UPS calls National Returns Day, at 1.9 million packages, 26% more than last year’s peak.

The second wave is the gift wave, and its customers behave differently from the first. In a WalletHub survey early this January, 34% of Americans said they would return gifts received over the holidays, Fortune reported. Among them, 68% planned to return clothing. Nearly half said they would not want store credit and would rather have cash.

That last finding is the recipient talking. A giver who chose your brand accepted your price and your promise. A recipient wants the value back in the most flexible form available, because the product was never her decision.

What the gift receipt hides inside the brand

The gift receipt is a polite piece of paper. It hides the price from the recipient. It also hides something from the brand: once the return is processed, most reports cannot tell a gift that missed from a purchase that disappointed.

Inside a brand, that distinction is easy to lose. Returns land with operations as a cost per unit and with finance as a reserve against revenue. The product team sees a return rate and a column of reason codes, and in January the codes say “didn’t like it” or “wrong size.” Those are honest answers from a recipient who never saw the size chart. If the team reads them as a quality signal, they lead to the wrong fix: a reworked product, when the real gap sat on the product page the giver used to guess.

The stakes are higher than one refund. In the same UPS study, 73% of shoppers said the returns experience affects whether they will buy from a retailer again, and 68% said it shapes their overall view of the retailer. For a gift, the person forming that view is a new customer meeting the brand for the first time, at the moment it disappointed her.

Where the return happens now decides who meets the customer

The counter itself is moving. Kohl’s began taking Amazon returns in all of its more than 1,150 stores in July, CNBC reported when the plan was announced in April, without a box or a label. A sweater bought on Amazon this December may well go back at a Kohl’s service desk in January.

Retailers want that trip to the counter because it sells more: 82% of shoppers who collect online orders in store said they would likely pick up other items while there, Adobe found in its holiday survey. A returns desk works the same way, for whoever owns the store.

So the brand may not be in the room for its own return. On a marketplace, the retailer’s policy, the retailer’s counter and the retailer’s credit decide how the recipient feels when she hands the product back. The brand’s only lever is everything that happens before: the information the giver saw, and what the recipient can do instead of returning.

Some will say this is simply the cost of the season, and that no brand can write a product page for two people at once. The evidence leans the other way for categories where fit and taste decide the return. Clothing tops the list of returned gifts. It is also where a page can tell an unsure giver what to choose: which size to pick between two, what the color looks like in daylight, what to buy if the recipient’s style is unknown.

Questions for the January returns review

Before the holiday reports come in, put these to the team that owns returns and the team that owns the product page:

  1. Can we separate gift returns from ordinary returns in January, by gift receipt, gift wrap or order notes, so the product team reads them on their own?
  2. Does each top holiday product page answer the giver’s guess (size between two, fit, color, a safe default) as clearly as it answers the buyer’s?
  3. When a recipient returns our product, what does she get, from whom, and is there an exchange path that keeps her with the brand?
  4. On which retailers’ counters will our returns land this January, and what does each one’s policy say to our customer?

The brands that learn the most from January will be the ones that treat the recipient as a customer from the start, which is the kind of cross-team question we take on when we run a brand’s marketplace channel through the holidays.

P0312.title: Shoppers buy sustainability claims they can check on the page
P0312.alt: A brass magnifying glass leans against a small kraft paper box next to a green maple leaf on a wooden table.
P0312.ttag: Shoppers buy sustainability claims they can check on the page | Kwontified
P0312.desc: Sustainability-marketed products took half of US packaged-goods growth, but on a product page only the claims a shopper can verify carry weight.
P0312.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 14, 2019.
P0312.body:
Search Amazon for laundry detergent or paper towels and read the first row of results. Several titles say “natural,” “eco-friendly” or “plant-based,” often more than one of them in the same line. In a store, a shopper could turn the bottle over, look for a seal she recognizes and compare the ingredient panel with the one next to it. On a product page she gets a phrase in a title and a bullet point, set beside a dozen rivals using the same words.

Shoppers do pay for sustainability, and the evidence for that is now strong. What the product page changes is which sustainability claims they can act on. A claim the shopper can check (a named certification, a measurable ingredient or packaging fact, a third-party seal in the image) carries weight. A claim she cannot check becomes part of the noise of the shelf. Brands that treat sustainability claims as copy, rather than as evidence, are spending the advantage.

Sustainability claims already move real money

Shoppers say it matters to them. In Nielsen’s global survey, 81% of respondents said it was extremely or very important that companies implement programs to improve the environment. And 73% said they would definitely or probably change their consumption habits to reduce their impact, Nielsen reported in October 2018.

What people say in surveys is cheap; what they buy is not, and here the buying matches the saying. Products marketed for their sustainable attributes accounted for 50.1% of US packaged-goods growth from 2013 to 2018. They made up 16.6% of dollar sales in 2018, up from 14.3% in 2013, according to research by NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business and IRI published in March. Those products grew 5.6 times faster than conventionally marketed ones, and outpaced their category in more than 90% of the 36 categories studied.

So the question for a brand is no longer whether sustainability sells. It is whether the version on its product page is the version that sells.

Why vague claims fail on a product page

Regulators worked out years ago what shoppers hear in a vague environmental claim. The Federal Trade Commission revised its Green Guides in 2012. Its consumer research found that unqualified claims such as “environmentally friendly” or “eco-friendly” suggest a product has “specific and far-reaching environmental benefits,” and that very few products have all the attributes shoppers read into those words, the FTC said. The Guides also treat certifications and seals as endorsements and warn against seals that do not make clear what they certify.

On a shelf, a vague claim at least sits on a package the shopper can inspect. On a search results page, it sits in a title next to identical claims from competitors, and the shopper has nothing to separate them. The words stop working as a reason to choose. The claims that survive are the ones that answer the follow-up question a careful shopper would ask: certified by whom, made from what, how much less plastic.

Inside many brands, the people who could answer that question are not the people writing the page. The sustainability team prepares claims for the annual report and the packaging, where legal review is routine. The e-commerce team writes titles and bullets to a search deadline, often from a brief that says “eco” without saying what it can prove. The proof exists in the company; it just never reaches the page.

Amazon is building its own rules for what counts

Read Amazon as an institution and its direction is clear: it prefers environmental claims it can measure, and it is starting to charge for the ones it cannot.

Its Frustration-Free Packaging program certifies product packaging against Amazon’s own standard. For large items, Amazon now charges sellers $1.99 per order shipped in packaging that has not been certified, after offering a $1 credit for early certification; the rules were set to begin in August and moved to September 3, Fortune reported. Amazon says the program, which dates to 2010, has avoided 244,000 tons of packing material.

Follow the value in that rule. Amazon captures the shipping savings and the credit for less waste, and it decides the standard. A brand’s own packaging claim matters less on Amazon than Amazon’s certification of the same box. It would be consistent with this direction for retailers to give certified attributes more prominence on the page over time, though it is too early to say how far Amazon will take it; the evidence so far is limited to packaging.

Questions for the team that owns the page

Before the next round of listing updates, put these to the people who write your product pages and the people who own your sustainability claims:

  1. For each sustainability claim on our top product pages, what document proves it, and could a shopper see that proof on the page, in an image, a certification name or a number?
  2. Which claims use words the FTC has flagged as too broad, such as “eco-friendly,” without a qualifier?
  3. Are our large items certified under Amazon’s packaging program, and if not, what does the $1.99 charge cost us across a year’s orders, compared with the cost of redesigning the box?
  4. Who signs off sustainability wording on the product page, and is it the same person who signs it off on the box?

A claim a shopper can check, on a page she cannot touch, is worth more on a marketplace than one she has to take on trust, and building product pages around that difference is part of how we run a brand’s marketplace channel.

P0315.crumb: Brand loyalty on Amazon lives in the 22%…
P0315.title: Brand loyalty on Amazon lives in the 22% of searches naming you
P0315.alt: A pear and almond crumble pie with one slice served on a plate beside a ceramic pitcher on a rustic table.
P0315.ttag: Brand loyalty on Amazon lives in the 22% of searches naming you | Kwontified
P0315.desc: Most Amazon searches name a need rather than a brand, so loyalty shows up only when shoppers type your name. Brands must win the other searches too.
P0315.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 21, 2019.
P0315.body:
A shopper who has bought the same whitening toothpaste for ten years runs low on a Sunday night. In the drugstore she would walk to the oral-care aisle and reach for the familiar box without reading anything else. On Amazon she types “whitening toothpaste,” because that is what she needs, and the screen shows her forty choices. Her loyalty did not change. The shelf did.

Brand loyalty on Amazon is real, but it only shows up when a shopper types the brand’s name, and that happens in a small minority of searches. Everywhere else, even a loyal customer is choosing again from a full shelf, with prices, reviews and sponsored placements from rivals in view. Brands that judge their Amazon position by branded sales are measuring the easy part.

The search box asks for a need, not a name

Marketplace Pulse looked at Amazon’s 100,000 most popular search terms, which it estimates make up 64% of all search volume, and found that 78% of them did not include a brand. Shoppers search for “laptop,” “mattress” and “aa batteries”; “Duracell aa batteries” appears less often, Marketplace Pulse reported in July. Running shoes are an exception: “nike shoes men” is searched more than “running shoes men,” because the category’s buyers already know the names.

That sits awkwardly beside what shoppers say about themselves. In an NPR and Marist poll in June 2018, 73% of online shoppers said they set out to look for a particular brand, and 44% said Amazon was their first stop, according to the survey findings. Both can be true. A shopper can have a brand in mind and still type the need, trusting the results to show it. Whether they do is the brand’s problem, not hers.

A store helps loyalty in ways nobody notices until they are gone. The planogram puts the same box in the same place every visit, at the same height, beside the same neighbors. Habit does the rest, and the shopper’s hand finds the brand before her eyes compare anything.

A search results page offers no fixed address. The order moves with sales, price, stock and advertising, and the familiar product can sit first one week and eighth the next. The shopper is loyal to a picture in her head; the page is showing her something else.

Naming the brand does not end the contest

Even a branded search is not a closed door. Marketplace Pulse found an ASICS shoe among the first results for “Nike running shoes,” and a search for “Casper mattress” showed Casper first and then about fifty other mattresses. Rivals can buy their way onto a brand’s own search with sponsored ads, Marketplace Pulse noted, and similar products fill the rest of the page.

Nike’s decision to end its direct sales pilot with Amazon shows how little control a famous name brings. A search for “nike shoes men” returns more than 10,000 products, of which Amazon itself sells 335, and more than 4,000 third-party sellers list Nike products, Marketplace Pulse reported on November 13. The loyalty belongs to Nike. The shelf belongs to whoever is selling that day.

Branded searches are still the most valuable searches a brand owns, and they deserve protecting even while the generic searches get more attention. In Merkle’s first-quarter data, brand keywords drew about a quarter of Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands clicks but about half of their sales, ChannelX reported. A shopper who types the name is already halfway to the cart, which is exactly why rivals bid on it.

Who owns the searches that do not name you

Inside many brands, the two kinds of search fall between two teams. The brand team owns awareness and loyalty, and measures them with surveys and tracking studies that never see a search box. The Amazon team owns sales, and its reports are dominated by branded search because that is where conversion is highest. The generic searches, where loyal customers are re-choosing every month, are nobody’s scorecard.

That gap matters more each year. Marketplace Pulse credits generic searching with turning AmazonBasics batteries into best sellers; the private labels grow on exactly the searches where brands assume their loyalty will carry them. There is one place where a loyal shopper can skip the search box: a subscription or a reorder, where the product arrives without a fresh comparison. That is valuable precisely because it removes the shelf from the decision, though as Jordan Taylor’s post on Subscribe and Save this week shows, it comes at a price the brand pays on every order.

The evidence leans toward a simple conclusion: on Amazon, loyalty has to be re-won on the unbranded shelf, with reviews, content and placement, or it slowly leaks to whatever sits beside the brand on the page.

Questions for the next Amazon review

Put these to the brand and e-commerce leads together:

  1. What share of our Amazon sales comes from searches that name us, and what share from searches that do not, and how has that split moved since last holiday season?
  2. On the five generic searches our customers are most likely to use, where do we appear without paying, and who appears above us?
  3. Who is bidding on our brand name, and what are we paying to keep our own shoppers?
  4. Which team’s scorecard includes our position on generic searches, and if none, whose should?

The brands that keep their customers on Amazon will be the ones that treat every unbranded search as a chance to be chosen again, which is the cross-team work we take on when we run a brand’s Amazon channel.

P0317.crumb: Zalando’s profits show Europe is many…
P0317.title: Zalando’s profits show Europe is many home markets, not one
P0317.alt: Orange parcels wait on the doorsteps of colorful painted doors along a cobblestone street.
P0317.ttag: Zalando’s profits show Europe is many home markets, not one | Kwontified
P0317.desc: Zalando makes money in Germany, Austria and Switzerland and loses it elsewhere. Brands should plan European marketplaces as separate home markets.
P0317.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 27, 2019.
P0317.body:
In many brands’ international plans there is a slide with a map of Europe shaded in one color and a single launch date. The marketplace is live in a dozen countries, so the brand will be too. Zalando’s own accounts tell a different story. Zalando, which calls itself Europe’s leading online fashion platform, does not report one European business. It reports two, and they behave like different companies.

In the third quarter, Zalando’s fashion store earned adjusted EBIT of €40.1 million in Germany, Austria and Switzerland and lost €30.7 million in the rest of Europe. The platform is the same, the brands are largely the same, and the results are opposite. For brands, that is the clearest evidence available that Europe is a set of home markets, each built and paid for one at a time, and that a European marketplace plan has to be written country by country.

Zalando Europe reports two businesses

The numbers come from Zalando’s third-quarter results on October 31. Fashion store revenue in the region it calls DACH rose 22.9% to €666.7 million, and in the rest of Europe it rose 30.8% to €731.1 million. The newer markets are now the larger revenue base and the faster-growing one. They are also where the losses sit, while DACH swung from a €7.8 million loss a year earlier to a profit.

The pattern is steady. In the first quarter, DACH made €26.3 million of adjusted EBIT while the rest of Europe lost €18.0 million, Zalando reported in May. The platform makes its money where it has been longest and invests it, at a loss, everywhere else.

Follow the value and it becomes clear why. In a home market, the customer base, the delivery network, the brand recognition and the payment set-up are already paid for. In a newer market, each of those has to be bought again. Zalando named Spain, the Nordics and the Czech Republic as especially strong in the third quarter, and said the Czech business has grown quickly since it launched a year ago; it plans to open its off-price Zalando Lounge there in the fourth quarter. Each of those is a separate investment decision, made one country at a time.

What makes each country its own market

The differences are not abstract. They show up at checkout, in the delivery promise and in the loyalty program.

Payment is the plainest example. In the Netherlands, iDEAL, the bank-transfer system run by Dutch banks, accounts for 59% of online payments, while credit cards, the second choice, account for 10%, according to iDEAL’s own figures. A checkout built around cards, as many American brands’ sites are, misses most Dutch shoppers. Other markets have their own preferences, and a marketplace has to support each one locally.

Loyalty programs roll out the same way. Zalando Plus, its premium membership, was available to all customers in Germany by May, with a pilot live in Switzerland and France and Italy to follow within twelve months. Zalando did not launch Plus “in Europe.” It launched it in its home market and is extending it one country at a time.

Service promises are set locally too. When Zalando opened its Partner Program in Norway in 2018, it chose partners for their ability to meet customers’ expectations of free delivery and a 100-day return period, Zalando said. Those expectations are built country by country, and a brand selling into a market has to meet them there, whatever it offers elsewhere.

Returns follow from the promise. Zalando’s management said as early as 2013 that a return rate of around half was normal for its business, Twinkle reported. A brand that plans its first season in a new country on its home market’s return rate will overstate both its sales and its margin until the parcels come back.

Why brands still plan Europe as one market

Inside many brands, Europe is one line in the plan because it is one person’s job. A head of Europe or an international director owns the region, with one budget, one inventory pool and one target. That structure made sense for wholesale, where a distributor in each country absorbed the local work. On a marketplace there is no distributor in between, and the local work lands on the brand.

The marketplace’s own reporting can reinforce the habit. A partner dashboard that rolls every country into one sales figure makes a strong home market look like a strong European business, and hides the countries that cost more to serve than they bring in.

So the brand switches on a dozen countries at once, finds that two of them sell and the rest disappoint, and concludes that Europe is hard. The more accurate conclusion is that it opened ten new home markets with one market’s investment.

Questions for the European plan

Before the 2020 plan is signed off, put these to whoever owns Europe:

  1. Which country is our home market on each marketplace, where we already have customers, stock and recognition, and what is our profit there on its own?
  2. For each other country, what would it cost to build what we have at home: local payment, delivery and returns that meet expectations, content in the language, and enough stock?
  3. Which one or two countries will we build properly next, rather than switching on ten?
  4. Do our reports show profit by country, or only for Europe as a whole?

The marketplaces themselves invest one country at a time, and so should the brands that sell on them, which is how we approach launching and running Zalando and other European marketplaces with brands and their partners.

P0320.title: Amazon variation listings share one rating; merge only true twins
P0320.alt: Two matching stoneware vases of dried wildflowers on a wooden mantel by a sunlit window and a yellow wall.
P0320.ttag: Amazon variation listings share one rating; merge only true twins | Kwontified
P0320.desc: An Amazon variation family shares one review pool and one star rating. Merge children shoppers would swap; split any child that could earn a different score.
P0320.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 3, 2019.
P0320.body:
A brand adds a new color of its best-selling jacket to Amazon as a standalone listing, and the page opens at zero reviews next to a sibling with hundreds. Move the new color under the same parent and it shows the full count and the full star rating on day one. That is why catalog teams merge almost everything they can. The catch is that Amazon variation listings share one review pool, so a merge is a bet that every child deserves the same score. Merge the children a shopper would happily swap for one another; split anything that could earn a different rating.

Why merging Amazon variation listings looks like free reviews

The appeal is real. Amazon lets sellers group true variations, such as colors or sizes, on one product page, and its guidelines draw the line in one sentence: “Do not list different products together,” as BuzzFeed News reported when it examined how listings reuse reviews. Reviews follow the family, so a new child borrows the credibility its siblings earned.

Some sellers push that to fraud, which shows how much the borrowed reviews are worth. BuzzFeed found a cheese knife listing carrying 3,421 reviews, 640 of them written about a rolling pin. Britain’s consumer group Which? found headphones with 40 meaningless color variations, and a smartwatch first listed in January 2019 showing 938 reviews dating back to 2011. Amazon told Which? that “any attempt to manipulate customer reviews is strictly prohibited.”

A brand adding a genuine new color to its own parent is doing nothing of the kind. But it is using the same lever, and the lever works in both directions.

The pooled rating is an average, and averages travel

A shared review pool means one rating for the whole family. Every child displays it, whichever child the reviews were written about.

Take a running shoe with 500 reviews averaging 4.6 stars. The brand launches a wide-fit version on a new last that runs short, and it collects 100 reviews averaging 3.4 stars. As a separate listing, the wide fit shows 3.4 and the original keeps its 4.6. Merged under one parent, the family holds 600 reviews worth 2,640 stars in total, and every child, including the original that never changed, now shows 4.4.

SetupOriginal shoe showsWide fit shows
Separate listings4.6 (500 reviews)3.4 (100 reviews)
One parent4.4 (600 reviews)4.4 (600 reviews)

The merge helped the weak child and taxed the strong one. Whether that trade is worth making depends on which child sells more. If the original carries most of the volume, a fifth of a star off its rating is a cost charged on most of the revenue, to rescue a child that should have been fixed or kept apart.

The damage is also slow to see. Reviews arrive a few at a time, so the family rating drifts down over months rather than dropping on launch day, and nobody connects the drift to the merge that caused it. A catalog report that shows the parent at 4.4 stars gives no hint that one child is pulling the others down. Pull the reviews apart by child, which most brands can do by reading which size or style each reviewer bought, before deciding the merge worked.

The size of the review pool matters too. A family of 5,000 reviews barely moves when 100 weak ones arrive; at 4.6 stars, 100 reviews at 3.4 take the family to about 4.58. A young family of 150 reviews is far more exposed, because the same 100 weak reviews would make up two-fifths of the pool. Young products are where merging is most tempting, and where it costs the most when the guess is wrong.

Run it the other way and the merge is a bargain. A new colorway of the same shoe, built on the same last in the same factory, will probably earn the same reviews as its siblings. Merging it costs nothing and saves it months at zero. The arithmetic only turns against you when the children are different enough to be reviewed differently.

Merge what shoppers swap; split what they judge

A practical test follows from the arithmetic. Ask whether a review written about one child would be true of the others.

Sizes and colors of the same construction usually pass. A shopper decides to buy the product, then picks a size and a color, and the review describes the product. Merge those.

Different formulations, materials, fits, functions or quality tiers usually fail. A fragrance-free version of a moisturizer, a leather upper instead of mesh, a multipack priced as a value buy: shoppers judge each on its own terms, and a review of one is weak evidence about another. Keep those on separate listings, even if it means starting a child at zero.

There is also a line the arithmetic does not draw. The FTC told BuzzFeed that “it’s deceptive to misrepresent that reviews for one product apply to a different product.” Grouping a different product under a parent to borrow its reviews is the practice Amazon prohibits and regulators describe as deceptive, whatever the rating math says.

Questions before you merge a child

  1. Would a review of this child be an accurate review of its siblings? If you hesitate, split.
  2. Does the child share the same construction, formula and supplier as the parent’s best seller?
  3. What happens to the family rating if the new child lands a full star below the rest? Run it with your real review counts.
  4. Which child carries most of the revenue, and how much rating can it afford to lend?

Variation structure looks like catalog housekeeping, and it is really a decision about whose reputation each product borrows. Getting it right is part of the day-to-day catalog work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0322.crumb: A founder’s first Amazon listing is a…
P0322.title: A founder’s first Amazon listing is a self-portrait, not a shelf
P0322.alt: A glazed stoneware mug between an open sketchbook of mug drawings, paintbrushes, and a potted fern on a wooden table.
P0322.ttag: A founder’s first Amazon listing is a self-portrait, not a shelf | Kwontified
P0322.desc: Founders write their first Amazon listing as a story about themselves. Shoppers read it as one option on a shared shelf, and the gap shows in sales.
P0322.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 5, 2019.
P0322.body:
The first Amazon listing at a young brand is usually written late at night by the person whose name is on the incorporation papers. The title carries the origin story, the first image is the lifestyle photo commissioned for the website, and the bullets read like the founder talking. Nobody else is allowed to touch it.

That attachment is understandable, and it is also why so many first listings underperform. The founder writes a self-portrait. The shopper, scrolling a results page on a phone, is looking at a shelf, and the brands that grow on Amazon are the ones whose founders notice the difference early enough to hand the top of the page to someone else.

Why the first Amazon listing feels like the brand itself

For a founder, the product page is often the first place the brand meets strangers at any scale. Amazon has courted exactly this kind of company. When it launched Launchpad in July 2015, it offered startups custom product pages and a marketing package to bring new products to its customers. The pitch was a storefront built around the startup’s story.

The marketplace those founders join keeps growing. Independent third-party sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, up from 3% in 1999, Jeff Bezos wrote in his April 2019 letter to shareholders, as CNBC reported. Many of those sellers are small companies where one person still approves every word.

So the attachment has real roots. The founder chose the materials, argued with the factory and paid for the photography, and reviews land as verdicts on those choices. A two-star review about packaging reads, to the person who designed the box, like a review of their judgment, and the instinct is to answer it the way one answers a personal criticism, in public, under the product.

Founders are also wary of the platforms they sell on, with reason. The founder of Shhhowercap told Modern Retail in March that the brand treats Instagram as a second landing page and does not want to be too reliant on a platform that can change the rules. Holding the Amazon page close is the same instinct, applied to a bigger platform with stricter rules.

The detail page belongs to a shared catalog

What the founder experiences as a brand page, Amazon treats as a catalog record. The detail page is shared by every seller who offers that product, and with Brand Registry only the registered brand owner can change the bullets, description and images, Practical Ecommerce explained. The founder has editorial control. The page, though, sits inside a structure built for comparison: the same title format as its neighbors, the same image slots, the star rating under the name, and a row of rival products below the fold.

Shoppers read it that way. They arrive from a search, see the first image beside a dozen others, and scan for whatever separates one option from the next: size, count, material, what is in the box. A title that opens with the brand’s mission pushes those facts past the point where a phone screen cuts the text off. A lifestyle photo in the first slot looks beautiful on the founder’s laptop and like a mood board in a grid of products shot on white.

The company’s own structure makes this hard to fix. In a founder-led brand, the listing often has an owner but no editor. Changes wait for the founder’s sign-off, which waits for the founder’s calendar. The person who reads the search terms report, often a junior hire or an outside agency, can see that shoppers search by what the product does, yet has no authority to move that phrase into the title. Replies to reviews come straight from the founder, sometimes defensive, where every shopper deciding whether to buy can read them.

None of this is a failure of taste. The founder’s instinct for the brand is usually the company’s best asset. It is simply the wrong instrument for a page whose job is to win a comparison in a few seconds.

Handing the page over without losing the brand

The brands that make the transition tend to split the page in two. The founder keeps what only the founder can know: the materials, the reason the product exists, the claims the company will stand behind. Someone else decides how those facts are arranged for a shopper scrolling a results page, and that person is judged on conversion rate rather than on whether the founder likes the copy.

The story does not disappear; it moves down the page. A+ Content and the brand’s Store are where narrative earns its place, after the shopper has already decided the product might fit. The title, the first image and the first two bullets go to the facts that win the click.

Reviews get a routine instead of a mood. Someone reads them weekly, sorts them into product problems, listing problems and shipping problems, and sends the product problems to the founder as information rather than as insults. The founder still sees every complaint about the product, in a form the company can act on, and the public replies come from a calmer voice.

Questions for a founder-led brand

  1. Who can change the title of your best-selling listing this week without asking the founder?
  2. Does the first image look like the website, or like the results page it actually appears on?
  3. When did someone last read the search terms report and the reviews in the same meeting, and was the founder in the room?
  4. Which parts of the page are the founder’s to protect, and which are an operator’s to test?

A founder’s voice is worth keeping on Amazon. It just belongs further down the page than the founder first puts it, and taking over the top of that page is part of the day-to-day channel management we do for brands, so the founder can stay on the product.
