P0325.crumb: Cyber Week 2019 belonged to retailers who…
P0325.title: Cyber Week 2019 belonged to retailers who own the calendar
P0325.alt: Kraft-wrapped gifts tied with twine sit on a wooden desk below a fabric wall calendar marked with colored pins.
P0325.ttag: Cyber Week 2019 belonged to retailers who own the calendar | Kwontified
P0325.desc: Cyber Week 2019 set records, but the lasting change is who ran it: retailers set the dates, the deals and the pickup counter, and brands planned around them.
P0325.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 12, 2019.
P0325.body:
On November 18, ten days before Thanksgiving, Amazon told shoppers that its Black Friday deals week would start on November 22. For any brand still planning its deals around a day called Black Friday, the date on the calendar had stopped meaning much. The event started when the retailer said it did.

That small scene is the real story of Cyber Week 2019, more than the records. Cyber Monday reached $9.4 billion online, up 19.7%, Adobe Analytics said, as CNBC reported. Behind the scoreboard, the week showed who now runs the season: the retailers who set the dates, run the deal pages and own the counter where the order is picked up. Brands showed up as guests.

Cyber Week 2019 ran on the retailer’s calendar

The short season made the pattern easy to see. With Thanksgiving on November 28, there were six fewer peak shopping days than in 2018, and Adobe predicted in October that “the compressed shopping cycle will see retailers launching offers far earlier than ever before,” according to its forecast. They did. Amazon’s deals week ran for a full week before Black Friday, and the deals that mattered most to shoppers lived on retailer pages, under retailer banners, in an order the retailer chose.

The money followed the biggest hosts. On Cyber Monday, retailers with more than $1 billion in annual revenue saw online sales rise 540% over an average day, while those with less than $50 million saw a 337% rise, Adobe told CNBC. The gap says less about the smaller retailers’ products than about traffic: on the busiest day of the year, shoppers went to the stores they already trusted to have the deal.

For a brand, that changes the nature of the event. A brand does not have a Cyber Week so much as it takes part in Amazon’s, Walmart’s and Target’s. Its deal depth is negotiated with a buyer or entered into a retailer’s deal tool; its placement depends on the retailer’s merchandising; its results arrive in the retailer’s reports, on the retailer’s timetable.

The pickup counter is now part of the store’s marketing

The second thing the week revealed is how much of online retail now ends at a store. About 40% of online shoppers had chosen to buy online and pick up in store by Thanksgiving, Adobe said, CNBC reported. On Cyber Monday, pickup orders rose 43%, and retailers offering pickup converted better than those that did not, Practical Ecommerce reported from Adobe’s data.

The shoppers themselves moved between channels without much ceremony. Of the 189.6 million people who shopped from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, 142.2 million shopped online, 124 million in stores and 75.7 million did both, the National Retail Federation’s survey found.

Read Target as an institution and the strategy is plain. In its third quarter, Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt delivered 80% of Target’s digital sales growth, the company reported on November 20. A retailer that wins online through its parking lots has every reason to reward brands whose products are in stock in those stores, and little reason to care whether the sale is booked as digital or physical.

That creates an awkward fact inside many brands. The team that plans Amazon and Walmart.com promotions often sits apart from the team that manages store inventory with the same retailers. During Cyber Week, a shopper’s pickup order drew on the store shelf the wholesale team was planning, through a promotion the e-commerce team had funded.

Brands behaved like guests

Put the two lessons together and the brands’ role in Cyber Week 2019 comes into focus. Brands funded much of the discounting, through deal fees, promotional allowances and lower prices, and planned their stock to the retailers’ dates. In return they got access to the traffic. That is a reasonable trade, and for most brands the only one available, but it is the trade of a guest rather than a host.

Amazon’s own account of the week makes the point from the other side. Independent sellers, mostly small and medium-sized businesses, sold more items on Cyber Monday than in any other 24-hour period in the company’s history, Amazon said on December 3. The record belonged to the sellers; the stage, the dates and the checkout belonged to Amazon. Even the most successful guests were selling inside a house someone else had built.

Hosts set the agenda. Amazon decided the week started on November 22. Target decided its stores were its fulfillment network. The brands in the best position were the ones that planned for those decisions early: inventory placed where pickup orders would draw on it, deals agreed before the retailer’s deadline, budgets ready for a week that began before the date on the calendar.

None of this means brands should stop taking part. It means the planning should start from the retailer’s calendar and the retailer’s fulfillment model rather than from the brand’s own idea of when the holiday begins.

Questions to ask before planning 2020

  1. Whose calendar did your Cyber Week plan follow, and when did you learn each retailer’s dates?
  2. Did the people who plan store inventory and the people who plan online promotions with each retailer meet before the week, or only after it?
  3. How much of your Cyber Week revenue came through pickup or ship-from-store orders, and does any report in the company show it?
  4. Which retailer events in 2020 are worth hosting your own promotion around, and which are you simply attending?

The 2020 season will again belong to whoever sets the dates, which is why the work starts with each retailer’s calendar and the team that owns it, the kind of channel planning we run with brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0328.title: The 2020 plan should copy 2019’s events, not its dates
P0328.alt: An open planner with colorful dot stickers on a wooden desk beside a succulent, ink bottle, and linen notebook with pen.
P0328.ttag: The 2020 plan should copy 2019’s events, not its dates | Kwontified
P0328.desc: Most 2020 plans start from 2019’s sales by date. The holidays move, so a plan built on dates books false growth in one month and false losses in the next.
P0328.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 17, 2019.
P0328.body:
Most 2020 plans being finished this month start the same way: take 2019’s sales by month or by week, apply a growth rate, and hand each team its number. It is the obvious method and, for any brand with seasonal sales, the single assumption most worth changing. The holidays do not sit still. Easter moves nine days earlier in 2020, Thanksgiving two days earlier, and Prime Day has no date at all yet. A plan built on 2019’s dates will report growth and decline in months where demand did not change.

The 2019 season showed how much a moving date matters. Thanksgiving fell on November 28, the latest it can, which left 22 days between Cyber Monday and Christmas, six fewer than in 2018, Adobe noted in its holiday forecast. Every report that compared December 2019 with December 2018 by date was comparing two different seasons.

Why a 2020 plan built on dates seems safe

The date-based plan has real virtues. The finance team’s calendar runs on months, the board reads months, and last year’s monthly actuals are the most trusted numbers in the building. Rolling them forward with a growth rate is fast, easy to explain and easy to audit.

It also tends to work in a year when the big events stay put. Christmas is always December 25, and for a brand whose sales cluster around fixed dates, last year’s December is a fair guide to next year’s. The trouble is that most of the events that move a brand’s sales are not fixed.

The 2020 calendar moves almost every event

Event20192020Shift
EasterApril 21April 129 days earlier
Mother’s DayMay 12May 102 days earlier
Father’s DayJune 16June 215 days later
Prime DayJuly 15–16Not announcedUnknown
ThanksgivingNovember 28November 262 days earlier
Days from Cyber Monday to Christmas22242 more

Two more quirks sit inside those dates. February 2020 has 29 days, so a February-to-February comparison gives 2020 one extra selling day, about 3.6% more time to sell. And Christmas Day moves from a Wednesday in 2019 to a Friday in 2020, which changes when the last shipping cutoffs fall.

Prime Day is the hardest line to plan. Amazon set the 2019 event for July 15 and 16, its first 48-hour Prime Day, Retail Dive reported on June 25, only three weeks ahead. A 2020 plan that books Prime Day sales into the third week of July is making a guess that will not be confirmed until the summer.

How a moved holiday books growth that is not there

Take a brand that sells Easter baskets. In the 14 days before Easter it sells 2,000 a day; on every other day, 300. Demand in 2020 is exactly the same as in 2019. Only the date moves.

In 2019, with Easter on April 21, the whole 14-day rush fell inside April: 28,000 baskets, plus 16 ordinary days at 300, for 32,800. In 2020, with Easter on April 12, the rush runs from March 29 to April 11. April keeps 11 rush days, or 22,000 baskets, plus 19 ordinary days, for 27,700. March picks up the other three rush days.

The monthly report will say April fell 16% and March jumped. Nothing happened to demand. A team judged on April will be asked to explain a decline it did not cause, and a team judged on March will collect credit it did not earn. Ad budgets set by month make it worse: if the plan funds April at 2019’s level, the money arrives after the first three days of the rush.

Smaller shifts do the same thing on a smaller scale. A two-day move in Thanksgiving pulls Black Friday into November 27 and Cyber Monday into November 30, so November 2020 holds the whole Cyber Week that November 2019 split with December.

The pull of the date-based plan is a kind of anchoring. Last year’s monthly actuals are vivid, trusted and already in the spreadsheet, so they become the reference point even when the reason behind them has moved. Admitting that a month’s number belonged to a holiday, not to the month, means rebuilding the baseline, and few planning teams have the week to do it in December.

Build the 2020 baseline on the event clock

Rebuild 2019 around its events before applying any growth rate. Label each day by its distance from the nearest event that matters to the brand (fourteen days before Easter, two days after Cyber Monday) and roll that event-relative curve onto the 2020 calendar. Then sum it into months for finance.

Keep weekdays lined up where no event is near. Comparing each day with the same weekday 52 weeks earlier, 364 days back, keeps Saturdays against Saturdays, which matters for brands whose sales swing through the week. Matching by date never did that, and the leap day widens the gap from March onward: a date-matched March 3 compares a Tuesday with a Sunday, while the 364-day match still compares Tuesday with Tuesday.

Give Prime Day a placeholder window and a rule, not a date. Plan the stock and budget for a July event, with a trigger to move both once Amazon announces the date.

Grade results the same way. In 2020, compare each event with the same event in 2019, and each month only after the event effects are removed. A month that looks weak on the calendar may be strong on the event clock.

Building that event-relative baseline is the first step of the forecasts we prepare with brands each December, because every number that follows inherits its mistakes.

P0329.title: Marketplaces in 2019 charged brands for the aisle and the truck
P0329.alt: A blue delivery truck parked outside an open loading door, framed by stockroom shelves of boxes, baskets, and crates.
P0329.ttag: Marketplaces in 2019 charged brands for the aisle and the truck | Kwontified
P0329.desc: In 2019 marketplaces earned more from selling visibility and delivery speed than from the sale itself, and brands’ budgets have not caught up with that shift.
P0329.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 19, 2019.
P0329.body:
Put a brand’s Amazon statement from December 2019 next to one from three years earlier and the biggest change is not the commission. It is everything around it: the advertising line, the fulfillment fees, the cost of keeping stock close enough to make a one-day promise. The sale itself still pays the marketplace a referral fee. The money marketplaces chased hardest in 2019 came from selling two other things, the aisle and the truck.

That is the structural story of marketplaces in 2019. The big retailers turned into media companies and delivery networks at once, and brands paid both tolls from budgets that rarely meet.

Marketplaces in 2019 sold the aisle

Amazon’s “other” revenue, which is mostly advertising, reached $3.59 billion in the third quarter, up from $2.50 billion a year earlier, CNBC reported. Chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said advertising itself grew faster than the 45% constant-currency growth of that line, according to the Motley Fool’s account of the call.

The others moved in the same direction. In February, Walmart began bringing the sale of advertising on its website in-house to Walmart Media Group, taking it back from WPP’s Triad, Marketing Dive reported. In January, Kroger’s chief executive listed “Retail will disrupt the ad industry” among his predictions for the future of retail, Kroger said. And in September, Amazon folded its Product Display Ads into a new self-service product, Sponsored Display, that reaches shoppers on and off Amazon, as one agency reported on launch day.

Read those as institutions rather than as product launches and the logic is plain. A retailer’s search results page is the last shelf a shopper sees before buying, and the retailer already owns it. Every new ad format is a way of selling more of that shelf, or of following the shopper off it.

They also sold the truck

The second toll was speed. In April, Amazon said it would move Prime from two-day to one-day shipping. It spent just over $800 million on the change in the second quarter and included close to $1.5 billion in its fourth-quarter guidance, Olsavsky said on the October call. In May, Walmart launched free NextDay delivery on about 220,000 items with a $35 minimum and no membership, CBS News reported.

Speed is paid for in inventory placement and fulfillment, and brands meet it there: in the fee to have Amazon pick and ship, in the pressure to keep stock in the right warehouses, in the carrier the marketplace will allow. The point was made bluntly in December. On the night of December 15, Amazon told sellers that ship their own Prime orders that they could no longer use FedEx Ground for them through the holidays, citing slipping performance, Bloomberg reported. The delivery promise belongs to the marketplace, and the marketplace decides which trucks may keep it.

What the shift means inside a brand

Follow the value and the picture is clear. Marketplaces still take their commission, but the growth is in the two tolls around it. Independent sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, up from 3% in 1999, Jeff Bezos wrote in April, CNBC reported. Those sellers, and the brands among them, are the ones buying the aisle and the truck.

Inside many brands, the two tolls are paid by different people. Advertising sits with marketing or the e-commerce team and is judged on return on ad spend. Fulfillment and inventory sit with operations or supply chain and are judged on cost per unit. Neither team sees the other’s bill, though both are paying for the same thing: the chance to be seen and chosen on a marketplace’s results page.

Picture the two bills on one page. Say a $30 serum sells on Amazon, and the brand spends $4 in advertising for every unit sold and $5 to have it picked, packed and shipped. Marketing reports a healthy return on the $4; operations reports a reasonable fulfillment cost on the $5. Nobody’s report shows that the two tolls together take $9 of every $30, before the commission and before the product is made, or that both rose in the same year.

That split was manageable when the tolls were small. It is harder to defend when a one-day badge changes how often an ad’s click turns into a sale, and when a carrier rule can take the badge away in the middle of December. The ad team’s return depends on the operations team’s stock placement, and the operations team’s cost depends on how hard the ad team pushes.

It is too early to say how high either toll will go in 2020. The evidence of 2019 leans one way: marketplaces will keep adding ad formats and faster delivery, because both earn the marketplace money beyond the commission and both make the marketplace harder to leave.

Questions that put both tolls in one meeting

  1. Who in the company sees the total cost of selling on each marketplace (commission, advertising and fulfillment together), and how often?
  2. When the ad team plans a push, does the operations team know which products and warehouses it will draw on?
  3. Which products earn enough to pay both tolls, and which only look profitable because the tolls sit in other budgets?
  4. If a marketplace changed its delivery rules next month, who would be told first, and who would need to act?

Seeing all three costs of a marketplace in one place is where our channel management work with brands starts, because the commission is no longer the only toll on the bill.

P0330.crumb: Keyword harvesting on Amazon needs more…
P0330.title: Keyword harvesting on Amazon needs more clicks than it gets
P0330.alt: A fishing net with a few silver fish spread on a wooden pier in a harbor lined with wooden fishing boats.
P0330.ttag: Keyword harvesting on Amazon needs more clicks than it gets | Kwontified
P0330.desc: Most keyword harvesting acts on a handful of clicks, where a search term’s conversion rate is mostly noise. Set click thresholds before you move or block terms.
P0330.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 24, 2019.
P0330.body:
Every week, someone on an Amazon team opens the search term report for the automatic campaigns, sorts by orders, and moves the winners into manual campaigns. Terms with clicks and no orders go into the negative list. The routine is sound. The trouble is the size of the evidence. A search term with ten clicks and one order looks like a 10% converter, and a term with ten clicks and none looks like a dud, but at ten clicks neither number means much.

Keyword harvesting on Amazon is a statistics problem dressed up as housekeeping. The rule that fixes it is simple: decide how many clicks a term needs before you act on it, and hold to that number in both directions.

Why keyword harvesting on Amazon works in the first place

The case for harvesting is real. Sponsored Products advertisers can see the actual search terms shoppers typed before they clicked, Practical Ecommerce noted in 2016, which makes an automatic campaign a cheap way to discover how shoppers describe a product. Not every query is worth the same, even when one keyword triggers it. The fix the same publication described was to move queries into their own ad groups with their own bids and block them in the original group with negative keywords.

That structure gives each proven search term a bid of its own and stops the automatic campaign from buying the same click at a different price. It is the right destination. The error is in how quickly terms are sent there.

Ten clicks cannot tell a good term from a bad one

Conversion on a search term behaves like a coin that comes up heads one time in ten, or one time in twenty. A handful of flips cannot tell you which coin you are holding.

Take a $25 product with a target advertising cost of sale of 30%, so the brand can spend $7.50 to win a sale. At a $0.75 cost per click, a search term breaks even if 10% of its clicks convert.

ClicksOrdersObserved ratePlausible true rate (95% interval)
10110%0.3% to 44.5%
50510%3.3% to 21.8%
2002010%6.2% to 15.0%

All three rows show the same 10%. Only the last one tells you the term is near break-even. At ten clicks, the same result is consistent with a term that almost never sells and one that sells to nearly half the people who click.

The negative side is worse, because it is irreversible in practice. A term that truly converts at 10% will still show zero orders in its first ten clicks about 35% of the time. Negate every term with ten clicks and no order, and roughly one good term in three goes onto the block list, where nobody looks at it again.

The two mistakes do not cost the same. Promoting a weak term into a manual campaign wastes some clicks until the next review catches it. Negating a strong term removes it from the campaign that found it, and nobody is likely to test it again.

What the report can and cannot settle

The search term report counts clicks and orders, and for the strongest terms it eventually has plenty of both. For the long tail it never will. Many terms collect a few clicks a month, and no amount of patience turns them into a sample. For those, the honest answer is that the report cannot tell, and the decision should be made on groups (all the terms that mention a competitor’s brand, all the terms with a size in them) rather than term by term.

Seasonality muddies the read further. A term harvested from December’s numbers was judged on holiday shoppers, who convert differently from the shoppers who will type it in February. Read a term over at least a few weeks of ordinary trading before trusting its rate.

Bids add a second layer of noise. A manual bid priced from a term’s observed rate inherits that rate’s error: price the 10-click term at its observed 10% and the bid is right only by luck. A safer habit is to price a newly harvested term from the low end of its plausible range, then raise the bid as clicks accumulate and the range narrows. The term loses a little traffic in its first weeks and avoids the larger cost of paying full price for a rate it never had.

Harvesting thresholds to set before the next review

Promote on orders, not on rate. A term with three orders has shown it can sell. Give it an exact-match keyword in a manual campaign, priced from the low end of its plausible conversion rate, and add it as a negative exact in the automatic campaign so the two do not buy the same click at different prices.

Negate on a click count tied to break-even. A useful rule of thumb from statistics is that zero events in n tries puts the plausible rate below about 3 divided by n. With a 10% break-even rate, that means about 30 clicks with no order before a term is very likely below break-even; a term converting at 10% shows zero orders in 30 clicks only about 4% of the time.

Leave the middle alone. Terms with some clicks and no clear verdict stay in the automatic campaign, at that campaign’s bid, until they cross one of the two lines.

Write the thresholds down. A threshold that is set in advance survives a bad week; one chosen while staring at the report bends toward whatever the last few clicks said.

Harvesting is where much of an Amazon account’s structure comes from, and the thresholds decide whether that structure is built on evidence or on noise. Setting them is part of the Sponsored Products management we do for brands.

P0332.crumb: Walmart’s online shopper wants a basket…
P0332.title: Walmart’s online shopper wants a basket; Amazon’s wants an item
P0332.alt: A shopping cart piled with groceries and an empty wire basket beside an orange wall in warm sunlight.
P0332.ttag: Walmart’s online shopper wants a basket; Amazon’s wants an item | Kwontified
P0332.desc: Walmart.com’s shoppers look like Amazon’s on a survey, but they arrive for a different job: a household basket built around a store trip, not a single search.
P0332.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 26, 2019.
P0332.body:
At many brands, the Walmart.com listing is a copy of the Amazon listing, made by the same team in the same afternoon, with the same title, the same images and the same pack sizes. The reasoning sounds fine: an online shopper is an online shopper, and the work has already been done once. The Walmart shopper and the Amazon shopper may even look alike on a survey. They are still not on the same errand.

On Amazon, the typical visit is a search for one thing, repeated often. On Walmart.com, more and more of the visits are about a basket, built around groceries and a trip to the store’s pickup point. A listing written for the first job sells poorly to the second.

On paper, the Walmart shopper and the Amazon shopper look alike

The surprising finding in the research is how similar they are. A University of Arkansas study of 547 US shoppers, run in December 2017, found that people who shop Walmart.com resemble Amazon’s online customers more than they resemble Walmart’s own in-store shoppers, the university reported in May 2018. The brand team that copies its Amazon listing to Walmart.com is not wrong about who the shopper is.

The same study shows where the two part ways. Walmart shoppers who use home delivery were younger than Amazon’s shoppers and more likely to have young children at home. And the habit was different: 32% of respondents had Amazon deliver several times a month, against 10% for Walmart. Amazon is where people go back to, again and again, for the next thing they need. Walmart.com, for most of its shoppers, was still an occasional stop.

The basket is built around the store

What has changed since that survey is the reason people visit Walmart.com. The company’s growth online in 2019 ran through groceries and its stores. In the third quarter of its fiscal year, Walmart’s e-commerce sales rose 41%, with online grocery a meaningful contributor, and it offered grocery pickup at more than 3,000 locations and delivery at more than 1,400, the Motley Fool reported on November 14. Its free NextDay delivery, launched in May, had reached more than 75% of the US population.

Picture how that shopper uses the site. She opens the app on a Sunday evening to order the week’s milk, cereal and diapers for a Monday pickup. The laundry detergent and the children’s toothpaste go into the same cart because they are on the same list, and the store is already packing the order. The search is part of a list, the comparison is with the price she paid last week, and the cart matters more than any one product page.

The Amazon shopper’s visit is shaped differently. A search for one item, a scan of the results page, a decision based on reviews and the delivery date, then out. Amazon has spent 2019 reinforcing exactly that habit with one-day Prime delivery on more than ten million items, as it said in July.

Read the two retailers as institutions and the difference is intended. Walmart’s advantage is the store down the road and the weekly shop; its online business is built to bring that shop into the app. Amazon’s advantage is selection and speed for the single item; its site is built to make the next search effortless.

What the copy-paste listing misses

A listing copied from Amazon is written to win a single search against a page of rivals. On Walmart.com, the product often has to earn a place on a list.

Pack size matters more. A shopper filling a weekly basket thinks in household quantities and in what fits a family budget this week. That can make a mid-size pack or a multipack the natural choice, where an Amazon shopper might buy the single unit again in a fortnight.

The title has a different job too. A shopper working down a list is looking for the thing she wrote down, so the product name, the size and the count need to be readable at a glance in a cart or a search result on a phone. A title stuffed with the search phrases that win on Amazon can make a familiar product harder to recognize in that list, which is the opposite of what the weekly shopper needs.

Price is read against the store. A Walmart shopper who also buys in the store knows the shelf price, and a Walmart.com price that sits well above it reads as a mistake rather than as a premium.

Availability for pickup becomes part of the product. An item that ships separately, from a marketplace seller’s warehouse, arrives on its own schedule rather than with the Monday pickup order, which makes it a harder item to add to the list however good its page looks.

None of this means the Amazon listing is wrong. It means it was written for a different errand, and the team that often owns both channels rarely has time to ask which errand each retailer serves.

Questions to ask before 2020’s Walmart plan

  1. Which of your products do shoppers buy on Walmart.com as part of a grocery or household basket, and which as a one-off search?
  2. Are your Walmart.com pack sizes and prices set for the weekly shop, or copied from Amazon?
  3. Can your best sellers be picked up in a store, or do they arrive separately from the rest of the order?
  4. Who on your team has actually built a Walmart pickup order, and what did they notice?

The shopper may be the same person on a Tuesday and a Sunday; the errand is not. Planning Walmart.com around its own errand is part of the Walmart marketplace work we run with brands.

P0333.crumb: Total ACoS shows if Amazon ads grew sales…
P0333.title: Total ACoS shows if Amazon ads grew sales or just claimed them
P0333.alt: Two stacks of kraft paper parcels tied with twine, one stack with blank tags, on a worn wooden table.
P0333.ttag: Total ACoS shows if Amazon ads grew sales or just claimed them | Kwontified
P0333.desc: ACoS divides ad spend by the sales Amazon credits to ads, so it can improve while total sales stand still. Total ACoS, and its change, shows what the ads added.
P0333.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 31, 2019.
P0333.body:
A brand doubles its Amazon ad budget in the fourth quarter. The advertising cost of sale barely moves, the ad-attributed sales climb, and the year-end review calls it a success. Then someone looks at total sales on Amazon and finds they grew far less than the ad report suggests. Both reports are correct. They are measuring different things.

ACoS, the advertising cost of sale, divides ad spend by the sales Amazon credits to the ads. Total ACoS divides the same spend by all of the brand’s sales on Amazon, from ads and from organic search alike. The first tells you how the ads performed by their own accounting. The second, and especially how it changes when spend changes, tells you what the ads did to the business.

Why ACoS seemed like the right number

ACoS earned its place. It is in every campaign report, it ties spend to sales at the keyword level, and it gives bid managers a target they can act on daily. A brand that knows its margin can set a break-even ACoS and manage every keyword against it.

The trouble is in the denominator. An attributed sale is a sale that followed an ad click within Amazon’s attribution window. It is not necessarily a sale the ad caused. Many attributed sales come from shoppers who were already looking for the brand.

Brand searches make up a large share of them. In Merkle’s third-quarter 2018 report, searches for the advertiser’s own brand accounted for 61% of Sponsored Brands sales and 42% of Sponsored Products sales, ChannelX reported. A shopper who types a brand’s name and clicks its ad at the top of the page would often have found the organic listing a few pixels lower.

The error runs the other way too, which is why ACoS deserves a fair hearing. Ads can lift sales the report never credits to them. Extra sales from ads can help a product rise in organic search, and a shopper who first met the brand through an ad may come back weeks later, after the attribution window has closed. ACoS misses that halo just as it misses the relabeled sales. Total ACoS catches both, because its denominator is everything the brand sold. That is its real advantage: it does not depend on Amazon’s rules for deciding which sale belongs to which click.

Which metric to use depends on the decision in front of you. ACoS is the right tool for setting a keyword’s bid. Total ACoS, and its change, is the right tool for setting the budget.

When ads take credit instead of adding sales

The share of orders that pass through an ad has been rising. Over Thanksgiving weekend 2018, ads generated 25.1% of the Amazon orders for the 108 brands Quartile tracked, up from 16.3% a year earlier, Marketing Dive reported. Some of that is new demand the ads found. Some is demand that used to arrive organically and now arrives through a paid click.

Take a brand selling $100,000 a month on Amazon, $20,000 of it attributed to ads on $5,000 of spend. ACoS is 25%; total ACoS is 5%.

BeforeAfter doubling spendChange
Ad spend$5,000$10,000+$5,000
Ad-attributed sales$20,000$35,000+$15,000
ACoS25%28.6%Slightly worse
Total sales$100,000$108,000+$8,000
Total ACoS5.0%9.3%Nearly doubled

The ad report shows $15,000 of new attributed sales for $5,000 of spend, a respectable 33% ACoS on the increase. The total shows the business grew by $8,000. The other $7,000 of attributed sales were orders the brand would have taken organically; the ads now carry the label. On the extra $5,000, the brand bought $8,000 of sales, a marginal total ACoS of 62.5%. At most margins that is a loss.

What total ACoS can and cannot tell you

Total ACoS has weaknesses of its own. Total sales move for many reasons besides ads: price changes, stockouts, reviews, seasonality, a competitor running out of stock. A rising total ACoS in a quiet month might mean the ads are wasted, or that organic sales dipped for reasons unrelated to them. Read alone, it can mislead as badly as ACoS.

Two habits make it useful. Watch its trend over several months rather than one, and compare it with the trend in organic sales. If spend rises, total ACoS rises with it and total sales stay flat, the ads are mostly relabeling sales. If total ACoS stays steady while spend and total sales both grow, the ads are adding.

The cleaner answer is a test. Pause or cut spend on one group of products, or on branded keywords alone, for two to four weeks while keeping a comparable group running, and compare total sales across the two. The difference is the closest a brand can get to the sales the ads actually caused, and it is worth running before a budget increase, not after.

Set the 2020 ad budget on total sales

  1. Report total ACoS beside ACoS in every monthly review, by brand and by major product line.
  2. Judge every budget increase by the change in total sales divided by the change in spend, and set a ceiling for that marginal figure from the product’s margin.
  3. Run a holdout on branded keywords at least once a year to measure how much of their attributed sales would arrive anyway.
  4. Treat a falling ACoS with flat total sales as a warning, not a win.

Reading both numbers side by side is part of how we manage Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands for brands, because the ad report alone will always give the ads the benefit of the doubt.

P0334.crumb: The 2010s moved the start of shopping to…
P0334.title: The 2010s moved the start of shopping to Amazon product search
P0334.alt: A tablet with a blurred glowing screen stands beside an open, string-tied paper journal on a sunlit wooden table.
P0334.ttag: The 2010s moved the start of shopping to Amazon product search | Kwontified
P0334.desc: Over the 2010s shoppers moved the first step of buying into Amazon product search. Most brands are still organized around the store they left.
P0334.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 2, 2020.
P0334.body:
Walk through a department store in December 2019 and the decade’s change is hard to see: the same counters, the same holiday displays, a few new signs pointing to in-store pickup. The change shows up in the receipts. Between November 1 and December 24, total sales at department stores fell 1.8%, even as online sales across US retail grew 18.8%, Mastercard SpendingPulse reported on December 26. The shopper of the 2010s kept visiting stores. What she moved was the first step of shopping, and by the end of the decade that step usually happened in a marketplace search box.

That is the lesson worth carrying into the 2020s. Brands spent the decade adding marketplaces as one more account to manage. Shoppers spent it turning Amazon product search into the place where most purchases begin, and where a brand is one result among many.

Amazon product search became the first aisle

In 2016, about 55% of US shoppers said they began their online product searches on Amazon, CNBC reported on a BloomReach survey. By early 2019 the share was 66%, and 74% of shoppers said they go to Amazon when they are ready to buy a specific product, according to a Feedvisor consumer survey. Search engines and retailers’ own sites, which organized online shopping when the decade began, now often come second.

The shift changed what shoppers expect to find when they arrive. A shopper who types “running shoes for flat feet” into Amazon expects the options, the prices, the reviews and the delivery dates on one screen. A department store organized the same decision by floor, by brand and by the salesperson who knew the stock. The results page organizes it by relevance, ratings and the Prime badge, and it rearranges itself every day without asking the brand.

The first screen of that page carries most of the weight. About 65% of Amazon product clicks came from the first page of search results in Jumpshot’s 2018 data, Retail Dive reported. For most shoppers, a brand that sits on page two of its category search is missing from the only shelf they ever see, however well it is stocked in stores.

Shoppers learned to trust the marketplace and look past the seller

The decade’s second habit was quieter. Shoppers learned to buy from sellers they had never heard of, because the marketplace stood behind the order. Independent third-party sellers accounted for 58% of physical gross merchandise sales on Amazon in 2018, up from 3% in 1999, Jeff Bezos wrote in his April 2019 letter to shareholders. Over the 2019 holiday those sellers’ worldwide unit sales grew by double digits and passed a billion items, Amazon said.

To the shopper, most of that growth is invisible. The listing looks the same whoever ships it, and the promises that matter, the delivery date and the returns policy, are Amazon’s. Brands that spent the decade protecting their name on a store shelf found that on the marketplace the shopper reads the badge first and the label second.

The decade closed with that promise getting faster. The number of items delivered with Prime Free One-Day and Same-Day Delivery nearly quadrupled over the 2019 holiday compared with the year before, and 60% more customers shipped holiday orders to an Amazon pickup point, according to Amazon’s December 26 announcement.

Brands are still organized around the 2010 store

Inside many brands, the org chart still describes the start of the decade. Retail account teams own the relationships with buyers. The brand team owns the story. The marketplace sits with a small e-commerce team, or with a distributor, and reports through sales.

That arrangement made sense when a store’s buyer decided what shoppers saw. It fits poorly when the first thing a shopper sees is a page of search results the brand does not arrange and a competitor can buy its way onto.

The structure produces familiar symptoms. Product copy is written for a line sheet rather than a results page. A slipping star rating is handled as a customer service ticket. The marketplace delivery promise is planned by a logistics team that never sees the conversion rate. Each team is doing its job, and the shopper’s first aisle has no owner. Even the sales report can hide the problem: when a distributor sells on the brand’s behalf, the marketplace shows up as one more wholesale order, with none of the searches, ratings or lost sales behind it.

Stores still matter. Total holiday retail sales grew 3.4% in Mastercard’s count, and Target and Walmart spent the decade turning their stores into pickup counters for online orders. But the decision about what to buy now starts on a screen, and on one marketplace more than any other.

A 2020 plan starts with the first aisle

The decade’s lesson is easier to state than to act on. Four questions test whether a plan reflects how a brand’s shoppers now behave:

  1. Who owns the first page of Amazon product search for our category, and does that person sit in the room where the annual plan is set?
  2. If a shopper compared our listing with the three beside it, which one would she trust, and why?
  3. Which of our products would lose their place in search if our delivery promise slipped by a day or two?
  4. What would we change if we treated the marketplace as our largest store rather than one more account?

A leadership team that answers them in January plans for the shopper it actually has. If that first aisle has no owner on your team yet, we can run it with you.

P0337.crumb: Sponsored Display views audiences pay off…
P0337.title: Sponsored Display views audiences pay off on slow purchases
P0337.alt: A brass hourglass with a blank paper tag rests on a velvet armchair beside a sunlit window and terracotta wall.
P0337.ttag: Sponsored Display views audiences pay off on slow purchases | Kwontified
P0337.desc: Sponsored Display views targets anyone who looked in the past 30 days. That window fits a stroller’s purchase cycle and wastes money on a phone case.
P0337.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 7, 2020.
P0337.body:
Every brand that tries Sponsored Display views asks the same question first: why does the same campaign look brilliant for one product and useless for another? The audience is built the same way for both. Amazon finds shoppers who viewed the advertised product, or similar ones, in the past 30 days without buying it, and follows them with an ad.

The difference is what happened to those shoppers after they left. For a product people buy in a day, most of the audience has already bought something else. For a product people deliberate over for weeks, most of it is still shopping.

That one variable, how long your product takes to buy, decides whether a views campaign earns its clicks.

How Sponsored Display views works in the beta

Amazon released Sponsored Display as a self-service beta in September 2019, open to vendors, agencies and professional sellers enrolled in Brand Registry in the US, Feedvisor reported in October. The views strategy reaches shoppers who viewed your advertised products or similar products within the last 30 days and did not buy, and it shows them ads on third-party websites and apps, off Amazon.

The creative is generated automatically: product image, price, badge, star rating and a “Shop Now” button that leads back to the detail page. The beta’s other strategies, interests, products and categories, place ads on Amazon’s own pages, including detail pages and search results. Views is the one that follows shoppers off Amazon, which is why it attracts the retargeting budget.

You pay by the click, not the impression. Amazon picks which of the campaign’s products to feature, choosing the one most likely to convert. What you control is the products you put in the campaign, the bid and the budget. You do not control the lookback window. It is 30 days for everyone.

Why the 30-day views audience looked like a sure thing

Retargeting has earned its reputation. A shopper who has already looked at your product has told you more than any interest category can, and on Amazon the signal is unusually clean: a detail page view is a shopper considering a specific purchase. It is reasonable to assume that a reminder, delivered while she reads the news, brings some of those shoppers back.

The trouble is the word “some,” and how fast it shrinks. A detail page view is a snapshot of intent on one day. The 30-day audience treats that snapshot as if it held for a month.

The purchase cycle sets the value of a views click

Think of a salesperson who follows a customer down the street to offer a coupon, after she has already bought the same thing next door. The pitch is fine. The timing is wrong. A views audience is full of shoppers like her whenever the product is one people decide on quickly.

Take two products, each with 1,000 shoppers in its views audience. The first is a $20 phone case, bought by most shoppers within a day or two of starting to look. By the time the ad reaches them, say 900 of the 1,000 have bought a case somewhere, and a click from this audience converts 2% of the time. The second is a $250 car seat that parents research for weeks. Say 600 of its 1,000 are still deciding, and a click converts 8% of the time.

Price the click and the gap becomes plain. A click is worth the product’s price, times the share of the price you can spend on advertising, times the conversion rate. With a 25% advertising share on the case, a views click is worth $20 × 25% × 2%, or $0.10. With a 15% share on the car seat, it is worth $250 × 15% × 8%, or $3.00. Put both products in one campaign with a $0.60 bid and you pay six times what the case clicks are worth while bidding a fifth of what the car seat clicks are worth.

The numbers are a scenario, but the shape holds for any catalog. Long purchase cycles keep the views audience alive for the whole 30 days. Short ones leave it full of shoppers who are done.

What the campaign report can and cannot show

The Sponsored Display report will tell you which campaigns produced orders after a click. It will not tell you how many of those shoppers would have come back on their own, and retargeting audiences are the ones most likely to return unprompted. Treat a views campaign’s ROAS as an upper bound, and compare it across products rather than against your Sponsored Products ROAS.

A four-week test settles the question for your own catalog. Run separate views campaigns for a fast-turning product and a considered one, with bids set from each product’s own value per click, and hold the budgets equal for four weeks. If the considered product converts at several times the rate of the quick one, the purchase cycle is doing the work and the catalog should be split that way permanently.

Bid rules for Sponsored Display views

  • Put products with long purchase cycles in views campaigns first: higher prices, gifts that need research, anything with a comparison table on its detail page.
  • Keep impulse and replenishment products out of views until you have tested them, and expect them to fail.
  • Set each campaign’s bid from price × advertising share × the campaign’s own conversion rate, and never share one bid across products with different cycles.
  • Recheck the split each quarter, because a product’s purchase cycle shortens when it goes on sale.

The 30-day lookback is a fixed setting, so the only lever is which products you trust it with. That choice is part of the Sponsored Ads work we run for brands on Amazon.

P0339.crumb: Valentine’s Day gifts on Amazon now reach…
P0339.title: Valentine’s Day gifts on Amazon now reach far beyond the partner
P0339.alt: Red-wrapped gifts with blank tags and a vase of red tulips on a wooden table against a pink wall.
P0339.ttag: Valentine’s Day gifts on Amazon now reach far beyond the partner | Kwontified
P0339.desc: Almost two-fifths of a Valentine’s budget now goes to family, friends, classmates and pets. That shopping starts in January and runs on different listings.
P0339.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 9, 2020.
P0339.body:
Ask a brand team to describe its Valentine’s Day shopper and you will usually hear about one person: a partner, late, standing in the card aisle or scrolling for jewelry on February 13. That shopper exists, and he spends heavily. But he is no longer the whole holiday. In the National Retail Federation’s 2019 survey, the average celebrant planned to spend $161.96, and only $93.24 of it was for a significant other, Talk Business reported. The rest went to family, friends, classmates, coworkers and pets.

That second budget, almost two-fifths of the total, behaves differently. It is planned, bought in multiples and bought early. On a marketplace, it starts in January, weeks before most brands put up their Valentine’s Day gifts on Amazon.

Valentine’s Day gifts on Amazon have two buyers

The NRF numbers describe two shopping trips. The first is the familiar one. Men planned to spend $229.54 on average and women $97.77, and the big categories were jewelry at $3.9 billion, an evening out at $3.4 billion, clothing at $2.1 billion and flowers at $1.9 billion. Total spending was expected to reach a record $20.7 billion, even though the share of Americans celebrating fell to 51% from 55% a year earlier.

Count shoppers instead of dollars and the picture tilts. Candy was the most widely bought Valentine’s gift, planned by 52% of celebrants, followed by cards at 44%, flowers at 35% and an evening out at 34%. Jewelry, the largest category by spending, was planned by 18%. The holiday’s dollars sit in a few expensive gifts; its shoppers sit in the small ones, and small gifts are the ones people buy for several recipients at once.

The second trip is smaller per gift and larger in count. The average celebrant planned $29.87 for other family members, $9.78 for friends, $8.63 for children’s classmates, $7.78 for coworkers and $6.94 for pets. Add those up and $63.00 of the $161.96, about 39%, goes to someone other than a partner. Spending on other family members alone rose $4.58 from the year before, and total pet spending reached $886 million.

Picture the person behind that second trip. It is often a parent with a class list of 24 names, a deadline set by the school and a budget for each child measured in single dollars. It is a manager buying something small for a team of eight. These shoppers do not wander a store on February 13. They search, compare multipacks and order once, early enough to sort and sign everything.

The calendar inside the brand runs late

Most brands plan Valentine’s Day the way the first shopper buys: late and in one burst. The seasonal content goes live in February, the ad budget peaks in the final week, and the products featured are the ones that photograph well for a partner. The structure behind that is easy to see. Valentine’s Day sits in the trade calendar between the holiday recap and spring resets, so it gets whatever attention is left over in the last weeks of January. The merchandising brief is written by the team that sells the romantic hero product.

The marketplace calendar runs differently. A shopper buying 24 classroom cards or a box of treats for the office starts looking soon after the holiday decorations come down, because the order has to arrive, be sorted and be handed out. In 2020, Valentine’s Day falls on a Friday, so classroom exchanges and office gifts land in the school and work week, and the planning shopper will want everything delivered by the weekend before.

The result is a gap in January. The early buyer searches for a multipack, a teacher-friendly treat or a coworker gift under $10, and finds listings written for a candlelit dinner, or listings that never mention the occasion at all.

What the earlier window asks of a listing

The planning shopper reads a listing for different facts. She needs the count in the pack, the size of each piece, whether it is individually wrapped, and whether it arrives in time. A partner gift listing leads with feeling. A classroom or office listing leads with quantity and logistics.

That changes what a brand puts in front of each buyer. A chocolate brand might keep its heart-shaped box as the hero for the late shopper, while building a 24-count, individually wrapped pack, titled and photographed for classroom use, for the January one. A pet brand can market a Valentine’s treat to owners who are already planning $6.94 for the dog. Neither requires a new product line. Both require someone to decide that Valentine’s Day has two seasons.

Jewelry is the reminder that the late shopper still matters. Over the 2019 holiday, online jewelry sales grew 8.8% while total jewelry sales grew 1.8%, Mastercard SpendingPulse reported. Expensive gifts are moving online too, and the partner shopper will still be searching on February 12. The point is that he is the second wave, not the only one.

Questions for the Valentine’s plan this week

  1. Which of our products would a parent, a teacher or a manager buy in multiples, and does the listing say how many come in the pack?
  2. When does our Valentine’s content go live, and does anything reach the shopper who starts in January?
  3. Who writes the seasonal brief, and do they see the search terms early buyers use?
  4. If Valentine’s Day ran in two waves, which products would lead each one?

A brand that answers those in the second week of January still has time to catch both shoppers. Running the marketplace calendar alongside the trade calendar is part of how we manage seasonal plans for brands.

P0341.crumb: NRF 2020 showed store staff now working…
P0341.title: NRF 2020 showed store staff now working for the online order
P0341.alt: Stacks of cardboard boxes and twine-tied paper parcels on a wooden table against a pale blue wall by a window.
P0341.ttag: NRF 2020 showed store staff now working for the online order | Kwontified
P0341.desc: At NRF 2020 Walmart and Sam’s Club described moving their people to the floor and the pickup counter. For brands, the aisle display now reaches fewer buyers.
P0341.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 16, 2020.
P0341.body:
The most telling number from the opening day of NRF 2020 was not about technology. Walmart U.S. chief executive John Furner told the audience that one Walmart store now had more than 60 people working in grocery click-and-collect, a job that did not exist five years earlier, Supermarket News reported on January 13. Sixty people is the staff of a small supermarket. In that one store, they work for shoppers who never walk the aisles.

That is what Retail’s Big Show signaled about the year ahead. Retailers are reorganizing their people around the online order, and brands that still put most of their in-store money into what a shopper sees in the aisle are paying to reach a shrinking share of buyers.

At NRF 2020, the talk was about people

A year earlier, the show’s message was about buildings. At NRF 2019, Target chief executive Brian Cornell said three of every four Target digital orders were fulfilled by a store and called stores the company’s biggest competitive advantage, Digiday reported. In 2020 the conversation moved from the building to the people in it.

The big stage at the Javits Center usually belongs to technology. Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella duly urged retailers to build what he called “tech intensity,” citing figures that 30% of e-commerce sales come from recommendations and 80% of shoppers expect personalized offers. But the sessions that stuck were about who does the work.

Furner described how Sam’s Club, starting in early 2017, moved its highest-paid associates out of back-office roles and onto the sales floor, with raises of up to $8 an hour for team leaders. He also warned retailers against assuming they had solved anything, since what customers expect keeps moving. Christopher Baldwin of BJ’s Wholesale Club, the outgoing NRF chairman, opened the show with survey findings. In them, 83% of consumers considered convenience more important than five years earlier, and 80% of online shoppers believed retail innovation had improved their shopping.

Put those together and the direction is plain. The labor inside the store is being pointed at the shopper’s convenience, and a growing part of that convenience is an order placed on a phone and collected at the curb.

Target’s holiday results put a number on it

The day after the show closed, Target gave the clearest measure of the shift. Comparable sales for November and December grew 1.4%, below plan, while comparable digital sales grew 19%, Target reported on January 15. Its same-day services, Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt, grew more than 50% and accounted for about three-quarters of its digital growth.

Read that as an institution would. Target’s growth is coming through orders that its own stores fill, picked by its own staff from its own shelves, for shoppers who decide what to buy before they arrive, if they arrive at all. The store is still central; it is the shopper’s walk through it that is disappearing.

What changes for brands when the shopper skips the aisle

Brands have long bought their way into the store visit. Endcaps, displays, shelf position and in-store promotions all work on a shopper who walks past them. A pickup shopper never does. Her shelf is a search box and a list in the retailer’s app, and the person who walks the aisle on her behalf is an associate with a handheld scanner, choosing a substitute when the item is out of stock.

That moves several decisions out of the aisle and into places most brand teams do not watch closely. Which products appear first when the shopper searches the retailer’s app. Whether the product’s name and image on the retailer’s site match the package the picker is holding. What happens when the item is missing and the system offers a substitute. Each of those is now part of the shelf, and each is managed by a different team at the retailer than the buyer the brand meets every quarter.

Nadella’s recommendation figure belongs here too. If recommendations drive anything like 30% of online sales, the retailer’s own app decides a large part of which products a pickup shopper even considers, based on data the brand does not see. The brand’s influence on that list comes from what it can control: accurate product data, ratings and, increasingly, the search ads that retailers sell on their own sites.

Inside many brands, the structure has not caught up.

The retail sales team owns the buyer relationship and the in-store plan. The e-commerce team owns Amazon. The retailer’s own website and app sit between them, often funded from whichever budget has money left in the quarter. The NRF stage made it clear that retailers see the online order and the store as one operation. Brands that still split them in two will find that nobody owns the shopper who orders from Target’s app and picks up at the curb.

Questions to bring back from NRF 2020

  1. What share of our sales at Walmart and Target now comes through pickup and delivery orders, and who on our team watches it?
  2. When a shopper searches the retailer’s app for our category, where do we appear, and who decides?
  3. How often is our product substituted when it is out of stock for a pickup order, and with what?
  4. Is our in-store marketing budget still sized for a shopper who walks the aisle?

The answers will tell a brand whether its retail plan for 2020 follows the store’s people or the store’s floor plan. Running Walmart and Target as one shelf, online and in the aisle, is part of the channel work we do for brands.

P0344.title: Amazon 2020 fee changes favor pricier items over cheap ones
P0344.alt: A small rainbow toy horse, a tall stack of blank brass coins, and a stoneware jar on a wooden table.
P0344.ttag: Amazon 2020 fee changes favor pricier items over cheap ones | Kwontified
P0344.desc: Amazon’s February 18 fees cut percentage charges on pricier items and raise fixed charges on every unit. Model them by price before they hit margin.
P0344.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 21, 2020.
P0344.body:
When Amazon announces new fees, most brands ask one question: how much more will we pay? For the changes that take effect on February 18, the honest answer is “it depends on the price tag,” and that is the more useful finding.

Amazon told sellers on December 23 that fulfillment fees will rise by about 3% while select referral fees fall, according to its notice. Referral fees are a percentage of the price. Fulfillment and storage fees are fixed amounts per unit. Cut the first and raise the second, and expensive products gain while cheap ones lose.

So the right way to model Amazon 2020 fee changes is not one average across the catalog. It is a list sorted by price.

What Amazon 2020 fee changes actually move

The details, as Feedvisor summarized them on December 23, run in both directions.

ChangeBeforeFrom February 18
Shoes, handbags, sunglasses: referral on the part of the price above $7518%15%
Outdoor furniture: referral on the part above $20015%10%
Personal care appliances at $10 or less15%8%
Activewear referral15%17%
Standard-size storage, January to Septemberbase rateplus $0.06 per cubic foot
FBA label service$0.20 per unit$0.30 per unit

Fulfillment fees rise for small standard, large standard and medium oversize items. Clothing loses its $0.40 per-unit surcharge, but its standard-size fees go up. Fees apply by the date a unit leaves the fulfillment center, so stock already in Amazon’s network pays the new rate on anything that ships after February 18.

Why a single average misleads

Amazon’s own framing, about 3% on fulfillment, invites an average. Finance teams like a single number, and a 3% rise on one cost line sounds small enough to absorb. That is anchoring at work: the first figure in the announcement becomes the figure in the budget, and the shape of the change disappears.

The shape matters because the two kinds of fee behave differently as price changes. A 15% referral fee on a $12 item is $1.80; on a $95 item it is $14.25. A fulfillment fee is roughly the same dollar amount on both if they are the same size. So a cut in percentage fees is worth most on expensive items, and a rise in fixed fees hurts most where the price is low and the margin is thin.

Three products, three different years

Take three products, each with its own fees and margins, chosen to show the range.

A $12 skincare item with a $3.20 fulfillment fee and $2.00 left after fees and product cost. A 3% rise in fulfillment adds about $0.10 a unit. That is 5% of the item’s margin gone, and the share of the price the brand can spend on advertising and still break even falls from 16.7% to 15.8%.

A pair of $95 shoes with a $5.00 fulfillment fee and $30.00 left after fees and cost. The referral fee used to be 15% of the first $75 and 18% of the remaining $20, or $14.85. From February 18 it is 15% of $95, or $14.25, a saving of $0.60. Take off about $0.15 for the higher fulfillment fee and the shoe keeps about $0.45 more per pair. Its break-even advertising share rises from 31.6% to just over 32%.

A pair of $40 leggings sold as activewear. The referral fee rises from 15% to 17%, from $6.00 to $6.80, before any change in its fulfillment fee. That is $0.80 a unit from one line.

The skincare item and the leggings lose ground, the shoes gain it, and an average fee increase across the three would describe none of them. Storage widens the gap further for slow sellers. A product taking half a cubic foot that sits for six months between January and September pays about $0.18 more in storage under the new rate, a cost that lands entirely on items that do not turn.

Model it before February 18

Rebuild the margin table by price, not by category average. For each product, recompute the referral fee with the new rates, add the higher fulfillment fee for its size tier, and add storage at the new rate for the months it typically sits in the network.

Then move the advertising ceiling with it. The break-even advertising cost of sale is the margin left after fees and cost, divided by the price. Where that ceiling falls, lower the target before February 18 rather than after a month of bids set to last year’s margin. Where it rises, as on footwear above $75, there is room to bid a little harder.

Look hard at the cheapest items. When a fixed fee is a large share of the price, the fixes are structural: a larger pack, a bundle with a related product, or a price increase. A smaller ad budget on a product that barely clears its fees only slows the loss. Where none of those fixes is possible, the honest answer may be to stop advertising the item and let it sell on organic demand alone.

Check the category assignments. The activewear move from 15% to 17% applies to products Amazon classifies as activewear, and the $75 line on shoes and bags now rewards prices just above it. A product priced at $74 pays the full 15% either way; one at $79 now saves on the last $4.

Fee changes are announced once a year and absorbed for twelve months, which is why the hour spent sorting the catalog by price pays back. Building that margin table, and the bid targets that follow from it, is part of the Sponsored Ads work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0346.crumb: Target Plus extends the aisles where…
P0346.title: Target Plus extends the aisles where Target’s stores struggle
P0346.alt: Red shelves stocked with folded textiles, jars, and boxes line an aisle leading into a warehouse of palletized cartons.
P0346.ttag: Target Plus extends the aisles where Target’s stores struggle | Kwontified
P0346.desc: Target’s invitation-only marketplace grew slowly in 2019 and sits in the categories its stores sold weakest this holiday. The invitation is a merchant’s tool.
P0346.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 23, 2020.
P0346.body:
Eleven months after it opened, Target’s marketplace is still small enough to list on a page. Target launched Target Plus in February 2019 with 30 brands, and six months later Marketplace Pulse counted 55, selling about 115,000 products, against nearly 40 million on Walmart’s marketplace, Modern Retail reported in August. By the standards of Amazon or Walmart, that is a marketplace barely trying.

It is trying at something else. Target built a marketplace by invitation because it runs Target Plus the way it runs a store department: as a merchant’s tool for filling particular aisles, in the categories its stores find hardest to carry. Read that way, the slow growth is the design working.

Target Plus was built by merchants

Target described the program, when it launched on February 25, 2019, as a curated assortment from partners “carefully selected and invited,” and as an initiative “in its earliest stages,” according to its announcement. There was no application form. The first sellers were brands Target approached, among them Mizuno in athletic apparel and Kaplan Early Learning in toys, and the stated aim was to widen the online range in home, toys, electronics and sporting goods.

That is how a merchant thinks. A Target buyer’s job is to decide what earns a place in a limited space. Target has long favored its own judgment over open shelves: about one-third of its 2018 sales came from owned and exclusive brands, the company said in its annual report. A marketplace that anyone can join would hand that judgment to an algorithm. An invitation keeps it with the buyer.

The categories Target Plus fills are the ones its stores found hard this holiday

Target’s holiday results, released on January 15, show why those particular aisles matter. Comparable sales for November and December grew 1.4%, below plan, and the weakness was concentrated in electronics, toys and parts of home, which together make up about a third of Target’s holiday sales, the company said. Electronics fell more than 6%, toys were roughly flat and home fell about 1%.

Set that beside the Target Plus brief. Home, toys and electronics were three of the four categories the marketplace was built to extend. These are the departments where a big-box store struggles most to carry everything shoppers want: the range is wide, the products are bulky or fast-changing, and the long tail of brands never earns floor space. A marketplace lets a buyer say yes to the tail without stocking it.

The same results show what Target protects. Same-day services, Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt, grew more than 50% and drove about three-quarters of digital growth. Those services run on inventory in Target’s own stores. A third-party item shipped from a seller’s warehouse cannot be picked up at the curb that afternoon. Publicis’s Jason Goldberg made the same point in August. Most marketplace vendors, he told Modern Retail, “can’t offer anything like a one-day delivery service.”

Every marketplace item is an item outside Target’s fastest promise, which is a reason to keep the list short and the sellers known. Target does lend those sellers part of its promise: guests can return third-party items at Target stores, Retail Dive reported when the program opened. A retailer that takes back a stranger’s product at its own service desk has every reason to choose its strangers carefully.

What the invitation tells a brand

Walmart offers the contrast. It opened its marketplace to thousands of sellers first, about 18,000 by April 2018 by Marketplace Pulse’s count, and only then grew more selective about whom it admitted, as RetailWire reported. Target skipped the first step, and in doing so chose a smaller marketplace with fewer surprises over a larger one it would have to police.

Follow the value and the arrangement becomes clear. Target keeps the guest, the data on what guests search for and buy, and the store-based promise that drives its growth. The invited brand gets a place on Target.com in categories where the store cannot give it one, under Target’s rules. Nobody is shut out by accident; the door opens only where Target’s merchants want more range.

For brands, that changes the pitch. A brand hoping for a Target Plus invitation is not applying to a marketplace. It is being considered by a buyer for a gap in an assortment. The questions that matter are the buyer’s: does this fill something our stores cannot carry, will it hold Target’s standards for content and service, and does it compete with an owned brand we would rather sell?

It also changes how to read Target’s next moves. If the program begins to grow quickly, with hundreds of new sellers or new categories far from the original four, that would signal a shift from a merchant’s tool to a traffic business. Until then, the evidence leans toward a marketplace that grows exactly as fast as Target’s buyers find gaps they want filled.

Questions for a brand that wants a Target Plus invitation

  1. Which of our products sit in a category Target’s stores struggle to range, and could we show the buyer the gap with search or sales data?
  2. Who at our company already talks to Target’s merchants, and do they know the marketplace exists?
  3. Does any product compete with a Target owned brand, and how would we answer that objection?
  4. Could we meet Target’s delivery and service standards from our own warehouse, starting next month?

A brand with good answers is pitching a buyer, not filling in a form. Working Target and Walmart as merchant relationships, online and in store, is part of the channel work we do for brands.

P0348.crumb: Amazon Stores serve shoppers who have…
P0348.title: Amazon Stores serve shoppers who have already chosen the brand
P0348.alt: Cobblestone street of limestone buildings with a lamppost and an open boutique door under a dark awning.
P0348.ttag: Amazon Stores serve shoppers who have already chosen the brand | Kwontified
P0348.desc: Most visitors to an Amazon Store have already picked the brand and want help choosing within it. Stores built like a lookbook leave them to fend for themselves.
P0348.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 30, 2020.
P0348.body:
Watch what happens when a shopper reaches a brand’s Amazon Store. She did not wander in. She typed the brand’s name into the search box, clicked the brand’s logo under a product title, or tapped a Sponsored Brands ad with the brand’s name on it.

By the time the Store loads, the big decision is behind her. She has chosen the brand. What she wants now is help choosing within it: which of the twelve moisturizers, which size, which one is new.

That is the job most Amazon Stores fail to do. They are built as display windows, beautiful and static, for a visitor who has already been sold on the brand and now needs something closer to a good sales assistant.

Who arrives at Amazon Stores

The shopper who arrives looking for a brand is common. In a June 2018 NPR and Marist poll, 73% of online shoppers said they set out looking for a particular brand, according to the poll’s findings. Amazon is where many of those searches happen. In Feedvisor’s 2019 survey, 74% of consumers said they go to Amazon when they are ready to buy a specific product, and every respondent said they at least sometimes visit Amazon to search for brands, Marketing Dive reported in March 2019.

The same survey carried a quieter finding. Only 41% strongly agreed that they were satisfied with the number of brands they know on Amazon. Shoppers come looking for brands they recognize and often find the brand experience thin.

The Store is the one place on Amazon where a brand can fix that. Amazon introduced Stores in 2017 as free, multipage brand destinations built from templates, open to brands registered with Amazon, Tinuiti explained at the time. Since then the Store has also become a landing page for Sponsored Brands ads, and its insights report splits visits by where they came from: Sponsored Brands, Amazon’s own pages, tagged outside links and other sources, Tinuiti noted in January 2019.

The shop-in-shop most brands forget to staff

The nearest physical comparison is a shop-in-shop in a department store. A shopper who walks into a brand’s counter has already crossed the floor to get there. The good counters are arranged for that person: the bestsellers within reach, the new season up front, a clear way to compare one cream with another, and someone who can say which one suits her. The poor ones are a wall of product with a poster above it.

Many Amazon Stores are the poster. They open on a full-width brand image and a mission statement, followed by every product in a grid sorted the way the catalog file was sorted. The shopper who arrived wanting to know which moisturizer is for dry skin has to open each detail page to find out. Some leave for the search results, where a rival’s listing answers the question in its title.

The cause sits in how Stores get built. A Store is usually a launch project: the brand or creative team designs it when the brand registers on Amazon, often alongside the first product pages, and then moves on. Nobody owns it after that. The e-commerce team manages listings and ads, the brand team guards the look, and the Store, which belongs to both, is updated by neither. A Store built for a launch in 2018 can still be showing that season’s hero products in 2020.

What a Store visitor expects to find

Read the Store from the visitor’s side, and the brief writes itself. She expects to see what the brand is known for first, because that is often what she came for. She expects the range organized the way she shops, by need, skin type, size or occasion, rather than by internal product line names. She expects to find what is new without hunting. And she expects the page to reflect the season she is shopping in, the way a counter does.

The traffic sources in the insights report say which of these jobs each page has. A page that receives most of its visits from Sponsored Brands should be built for the ad that sends them. A shopper who taps an ad for a vitamin C serum and lands on the Store’s homepage has to find the serum again, while one who lands on a page about brightening serums finds the comparison she came for. A page fed mostly by brand searches should serve the loyal customer, with reorders and new arrivals near the top.

The season matters as much as the source. A Store that changes its first page for Valentine’s Day, back to school and the holiday tells a returning shopper the brand is paying attention, the way a counter that changes its display does. One that never changes tells her the opposite.

None of this requires a bigger budget. It requires someone to own the Store as a selling space, to look at its insights report every month, and to treat each page as a shelf with a job.

Questions to ask before the next Store update

  1. Who owns our Amazon Store, and when did they last change it?
  2. If a loyal customer landed on our Store wanting help choosing between two products, how many clicks would it take to find the difference?
  3. Is our Store organized by how shoppers describe their needs, or by how our catalog names products?
  4. Do our Sponsored Brands ads land on a Store page that continues the ad’s promise, or on a generic homepage?

The answers usually show that the Store is the most visible shelf a brand controls on Amazon and the least attended. Keeping it staffed, season by season, is part of the channel work we do for brands on Amazon.
