P0350.title: Amazon Q4 2019 other revenue outgrew units sold nearly two to one
P0350.alt: A tall stack of coins beside twine-tied kraft paper parcels on a rustic wooden table against a teal wall.
P0350.ttag: Amazon Q4 2019 other revenue outgrew units sold nearly two to one | Kwontified
P0350.desc: Amazon’s ad-heavy other revenue grew 41% in Q4 2019 while paid units grew 22%, so the ad money behind each unit sold rose about 16% in a year.
P0350.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 4, 2020.
P0350.body:
Amazon’s 2019 holiday quarter sold units faster than the one before it: worldwide paid units grew 22%, excluding Whole Foods Market, against 14% a year earlier, Amazon reported on January 30. Its “other” revenue, which Amazon says is mostly advertising, grew 41% to $4.78 billion. The ads grew nearly twice as fast as the units they help sell.

That gap is the number in the Q4 2019 release a brand should carry into its 2020 budget. It means the advertising money behind each unit sold on Amazon rose by about a sixth in a year. A brand that kept its own ad spend per unit flat through 2019 bought a smaller share of the shelf than it did in 2018, and nothing in its own reports would have said so.

Why Amazon Q4 2019 other revenue looked like a slowdown

Read quarter by quarter, the line seems to be cooling. Excluding currency, other revenue grew 97% in the fourth quarter of 2018, then 36% in the first quarter of 2019, 37% in the second, 45% in the third and 41% in the fourth.

The 2018 figures are the wrong anchor. Amazon moved certain advertising from cost of sales into revenue on January 1, 2018, and the company said on its first-quarter 2018 call that the new accounting standard added about $560 million to the line in that quarter alone. Growth rates close to doubling were partly a change in where the money was recorded. Anyone who anchored on them saw 2019 as a fall from a peak that was never a real growth rate.

On a clean base, 2019 shows acceleration: from 36% in the first quarter to 45% in the third, then 41% in the holiday quarter on the largest base the line has carried, $3.39 billion a year earlier. Amazon does not break advertising out, but AdExchanger reported that advertising grew about 40%, in line with the line as a whole.

Ad revenue per unit is the price brands pay

Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands are sold by auction. They are paid per click. Brands pay for clicks because clicks become units. So the ratio between the two growth rates says something about price: when ad revenue grows faster than the units sold, the average ad money attached to each unit rises.

The arithmetic is short. Other revenue grew by a factor of 1.41 and paid units by 1.22, and 1.41 divided by 1.22 is about 1.16. Each unit sold on Amazon in the quarter carried about 16% more other revenue than a unit a year earlier.

More bidders explain most of it. Third-party sellers accounted for 53% of paid units, up from 52%, and third-party seller services revenue grew 30%. On the call, chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said brands were building multi-page storefronts and curated product feeds, and that advertising lets them “tell customers who they are,” as AdExchanger reported. Each of those brands is one more bidder on the same searches.

Take a brand that sold 50,000 units on Amazon in Q4 2018 and spent $100,000 on Sponsored Products, or $2.00 a unit. In Q4 2019 it grows units 22%, to 61,000, and holds $2.00 a unit, so it spends $122,000. Its budget grew 22%. The pool it competes in grew 41%. Its share of all the ad money on Amazon fell to 1.22 divided by 1.41 of what it was, about 13% smaller, while its own dashboard showed a steady cost per unit and growing sales.

That steady cost per unit is what makes the loss hard to see. Most brands judge a year by comparing it with their own prior year, and on that test the brand above did well: more units, the same efficiency, a budget that grew with sales. The comparison that matters is with the other bidders, and none of them shows up in a brand’s own reports. The auction has no memory of your 2018 budget. It cares what the next brand is willing to pay for the same click today, and in the holiday quarter of 2019 that brand was willing to pay more.

What the other line can and can’t tell you

The ratio is a direction, not your bill. Other revenue also includes services that are not advertising, and Amazon’s footnote says only that it “primarily” covers advertising. Some of the ad money may come from display and video buyers whose products Amazon does not sell, so the 16% is not the change in what sellers and vendors paid per unit.

What would change my mind is a brand’s own data. If your ad spend per unit rose about as fast as the market’s and your share of units held, you kept pace. If it rose much faster and units did not follow, the extra spend bought clicks you would have had anyway, and a holdout test on your branded terms is the cheapest way to find out.

A flat budget per unit is a shrinking budget in 2020

  1. Compute ad spend per total unit sold, for Q4 2019 against Q4 2018. It is TACoS (total advertising cost of sale, ad spend over all sales) measured in units rather than dollars, and it removes price changes from the comparison.
  2. If yours rose much less than 16%, assume you lost placement on your highest-volume searches and check your placement report for top-of-search share before blaming the creative.
  3. Plan 2020 spend per unit to rise with the market where the units are incremental. Amazon guided first-quarter 2020 net sales growth of 16% to 22%, so a flat budget per unit is a shrinking one.

A cost per unit that rises with the auction is fine; one that rises without new units is a bid problem, and it is the check we build into the Amazon ad budgets we plan with brands.

P0351.title: Walmart Marketplace in 2020 sits outside your store buyer’s aisle
P0351.alt: A single cardboard box sits at the corner of a blue-walled store back corridor beside stocked aisles.
P0351.ttag: Walmart Marketplace in 2020 sits outside your store buyer’s aisle | Kwontified
P0351.desc: Walmart runs store and online merchandising as separate teams, and its marketplace answers to the online side. Brands need a plan for each counterpart.
P0351.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 6, 2020.
P0351.body:
Every spring, a brand’s Walmart account team flies to Bentonville for the line review. They bring the sell-through numbers, the new items and the promotional calendar, and they leave knowing which products will be on which shelves across Walmart’s US stores. Then someone back at headquarters searches for the brand on Walmart.com and finds a listing nobody in that meeting discussed: a reseller’s price, a two-year-old image, a pack size the brand stopped making.

That gap is not carelessness on Walmart’s part. It is how Walmart is organized going into 2020. The store buyer and the people who shape Walmart.com work in different merchandising teams, and the marketplace that fills most of Walmart.com reports to the online side. A brand that treats its store buyer as its whole Walmart relationship is managing the smaller half of the website.

How Walmart split its merchants

In July 2019, Walmart combined the supply chain and finance teams of its US stores and its e-commerce business, but kept merchandising separate. Ashley Buchanan became chief merchandising officer for US e-commerce, reporting to Marc Lore, and was to work with Steve Bratspies, chief merchandising officer for Walmart U.S., Talk Business & Politics reported from Doug McMillon’s memo. Jeff Shotts, who leads the US marketplace business, also reports to Lore.

Read those titles as an org chart for a brand’s own Walmart business. The store merchant decides what goes on a physical shelf with a fixed number of facings. The e-commerce merchant decides what Walmart itself sells online. The marketplace team decides how outside sellers fill everything else. Each has a different scorecard, and none of them was hired to look after one brand’s whole presence.

The marketplace is the largest of the three by count. Walmart says it sells about 75 million unique items online, most of them from third-party sellers, Bloomberg reported in Fortune in October 2019. For many brands, that means more of their Walmart.com listings are shaped by sellers the brand never approved than by the buyer the brand flies to see.

What Walmart wants from its marketplace

To see where this is heading, follow what Walmart is paying for. In the same report, Bloomberg described a program called Competitive Price Adjustment: on selected items from selected sellers, Walmart lowers the price the shopper pays and covers the difference itself, so the seller still receives its listed price. Sellers cannot ask to join. Walmart is spending its own margin to make marketplace prices look like Walmart prices.

It is moving on delivery too. In September 2019, Marc Lore said Walmart was testing a fee-based service called Fulfilled by Walmart to store and ship products for marketplace sellers, Bloomberg reported (via Transport Topics), with no details on fees or timing. Walmart’s own next-day promise, launched in May 2019, covers about 220,000 frequently bought items shipped from the fulfillment center closest to the customer, which is to say inventory Walmart controls.

The online business those programs serve is growing fast. Walmart U.S. e-commerce sales rose 41% in the quarter to October 31, Walmart reported in November. A price subsidy and a warehouse offer both point the same way: Walmart wants the marketplace to behave like Walmart, with Walmart’s prices and Walmart’s speed, and it is willing to pay for the parts that matter most to shoppers.

Two counterparts, one price

None of this means the store relationship matters less. For most brands in Walmart’s stores, the line review still sets most of the volume. It means the website now runs on a second set of decisions that the store relationship does not reach, and Walmart’s July memo said further organizational changes could follow. Whether merchandising stays split is an open question; the money Walmart is spending on marketplace prices and fulfillment suggests it wants the two halves to look like one store to the shopper, whatever the org chart says.

Brands feel the split first in price. A store price agreed in the line review and a marketplace price set by a reseller, then lowered by Walmart’s own adjustment, can sit side by side in the same search results. The shopper sees one Walmart and one brand. Inside the brand, the store account team and the e-commerce team often see different reports and answer to different targets.

Advertising adds a fourth desk. In February 2019, Walmart began moving its website ad sales and analytics in-house to Walmart Media Group, taking them over from an outside agency, Marketing Dive reported from Ad Age. A brand that buys Sponsored Products on Walmart.com is now dealing with a Walmart team whose goal is ad revenue, sitting beside merchants whose goals are sales and margin. Each conversation is reasonable on its own terms; the brand is the only party that has to add them up.

The brands that handle this well tend to give one person the whole of Walmart.com, not just the items their buyer carries, and to treat the marketplace team as a second account with its own plan rather than a website problem.

Questions to put to your team before the next line review

  1. Of our products on Walmart.com, which are sold by Walmart, which by us and which by resellers we did not choose?
  2. Who in our company owns the Walmart.com listing for an item our store buyer does not carry?
  3. If Walmart lowers a reseller’s price on our product, who on our side would notice first, and what would they do?
  4. Do our store account team and our e-commerce team review one Walmart price list, or two?

If the answer to the second question is “nobody,” that is the place to start, and running Walmart’s marketplace alongside the store business is the work we do with brands on Walmart.

P0352.title: Zalando Partner Program pays best on items Zalando would buy
P0352.alt: Neutral linen shirts with orange tags hang on a pipe rack in a sunlit green boutique with potted plants.
P0352.ttag: Zalando Partner Program pays best on items Zalando would buy | Kwontified
P0352.desc: On Zalando, the Partner Program earns a brand most on its surest sellers, the same items Zalando’s buyers most want to own. Split your range by sell-through.
P0352.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 11, 2020.
P0352.body:
Zalando keeps telling investors that its gross merchandise volume will grow faster than its revenue. “We will continue to see GMV growing faster than revenues, fully in-line with our long-term strategy,” finance chief David Schröder said when Zalando reported its second quarter of 2019. For a company that sells clothes, that sounds like a warning. It is a description of the business model Zalando wants for 2020.

The gap comes from the Zalando Partner Program. When Zalando buys a brand’s goods wholesale and resells them, the whole retail price counts as revenue. When the brand sells through the Partner Program, holding its own stock and setting its own prices, Zalando books only its commission and fees, while the full sale still counts in GMV. Each item a brand moves from wholesale to partner grows the first number and shrinks the second.

The question for a brand in 2020 is which items to move, and the answer runs against intuition: the commission model pays a brand most on its surest sellers, which are the items Zalando’s own buyers most want to keep.

Why Zalando wants the platform

Zalando’s stated aim is to become “the starting point for fashion” in Europe, and its 2019 strategy put more weight on the number of partner products, FashionUnited reported in March 2019. Assortment is what a starting point sells, and partners bring assortment without Zalando paying for the stock.

The platform has customers to offer. Zalando had 29.5 million active customers at the end of September 2019, up 17.5%, and GMV grew 24.6% in the third quarter, the company reported on October 31. It is also pulling in stock it will never own: more than 1,300 physical stores were connected to the platform by August 2019.

Partners keep control of their range. “The brands are put in the driving seat. They keep control over the assortment, prices and brand representation,” Carsten Keller, managing director of Zalando’s partner solutions, said in December 2017. Control comes with the stock, and with the risk that it does not sell.

Wholesale and partner trade places at a sell-through rate

Take a €100 jacket sold on Zalando. Say Zalando buys it wholesale at €45 and carries the risk from there. Through the Partner Program, say the brand keeps €80 of each full-price sale after a 20% commission, spends €12 a unit on fulfillment and returns, and clears what does not sell at half price, keeping €28 after the same costs. Those rates are an illustration; the real commission depends on the category and the brand’s agreement with Zalando.

Per unit the brand sends to Zalando, the partner route earns €28 plus €40 multiplied by the full-price sell-through rate. At 42.5% sell-through the two routes earn the same €45. At 85%, the partner route earns €62, and wholesale still earns €45. At 30%, partner earns €40 and the brand would have done better selling wholesale.

Now look at the same jacket from Zalando’s side. Bought at €45, an 85% sell-through item earns Zalando a large retail margin on almost every unit. Through the Partner Program, the same item earns Zalando a commission of €20 per full-price sale. A weak seller is the reverse: as a wholesale buy it ties up Zalando’s cash and ends in markdown, and as a partner item the brand carries that markdown.

So the incentives of the two sides cross. Zalando’s buyers earn most by owning the strong sellers and inviting partners to carry the uncertain ones. A brand earns most by keeping its strong sellers on the Partner Program and placing its uncertain lines wholesale. Neither side is being unreasonable; each is pricing the same risk from opposite ends.

What the arithmetic leaves out

Sell-through is a forecast, and it is easy to overrate your own. A line that sold 85% at full price last autumn sold in a different season, and the brand that moves it to partner on that number takes the risk that it was the weather. Returns matter as much as commission: Zalando’s management said as far back as 2013 that a return rate of around half was normal, and every return is a cost the partner pays twice, once to ship and once to receive and resell.

Fulfillment is the cost line most likely to change. About 30% of Partner Program orders went through Zalando Fulfillment Solutions in the first quarter of 2019, Zalando reported, so for many partners the €12 in the illustration is a Zalando fee rather than a cost in their own warehouse. That makes the break-even partly Zalando’s to set, and worth recomputing whenever the fee schedule changes.

The break-even also depends on cash. Wholesale is paid on the order; partner revenue arrives only as units sell. A brand short of working capital may rationally choose wholesale on items where partner earns more.

The split to bring to your Zalando meeting

  1. Rank every line you sell on Zalando by full-price sell-through over the last two seasons, using your own data, not Zalando’s buying history.
  2. Compute your break-even sell-through with your real commission, fulfillment and return costs. In the illustration above it is 42.5%.
  3. Offer Zalando’s buyers the lines near or below break-even as wholesale, keep the lines well above it on the Partner Program, and expect the buyer to ask for the reverse.
  4. Recheck the split each season, because the line that clears break-even in spring may not in autumn.

The brands that do well on Zalando in 2020 will be the ones that decide the split themselves, item by item, and it is the work we do when we run Zalando alongside a brand’s other marketplaces.

P0354.crumb: Target Plus shoppers assume Target picked…
P0354.title: Target Plus shoppers assume Target picked your product
P0354.alt: A speckled ceramic vase on a red wooden box in a softly lit plaster alcove beside shelves of pottery.
P0354.ttag: Target Plus shoppers assume Target picked your product | Kwontified
P0354.desc: Target.com puts Target Plus items on the same shelf as Target’s own, under the same promises, so partners should build every listing like a Target buy.
P0354.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 13, 2020.
P0354.body:
Every product on a Target store shelf has been through a buyer. Someone at headquarters chose it, agreed its cost with the vendor and gave it a place in the planogram, and the guest who picks it up never thinks about any of that. The red bullseye on the shelf tag does the thinking for them.

Online, that guest cannot tell which products went through the same process. A Target Plus item sits in Target.com’s regular categories, carries Target’s promises and cannot be filtered out by seller. To the guest, Target picked it. That is the most useful thing a brand can know about Target Plus in 2020. Every partner listing is judged as if a Target merchant had bought it, so it has to be built to that standard rather than to the standard of a marketplace listing.

Target Plus items sit on Target’s own shelf

Target designed it that way. When it opened Target Plus in February 2019, partners were carefully selected and invited, and guests buying from them still get 5% off with a REDcard, free shipping and easy returns in Target stores. Partner items appear in the regular categories with no separate Target Plus search, TechCrunch reported, and partners sell and ship the orders themselves.

Six months in, guests still could not filter search results by third-party seller, Modern Retail found. Nor was the blend new. Before Target Plus, some of the items on Target.com were already shipped by vendors while Target owned the sale, TechCrunch noted. The guest has been looking at a mixed shelf for some time without being asked to notice.

So the Target Plus shelf is not a separate aisle with a different sign over it. It is the same shelf, and the guest gives every product on it the same benefit of the doubt.

A bigger list, and an uneven shelf

The list of partners is growing. Target Plus opened with 30 brands, and by August Marketplace Pulse counted 55 selling about 115,000 products, Modern Retail reported. By December it had nearly 100 sellers offering about 250,000 products, according to the Star Tribune. The number of products on offer roughly doubled in the last four months of 2019.

It is still a small marketplace next to Amazon’s or Walmart’s, and Marketplace Pulse’s Juozas Kaziukėnas described its sellers as an eclectic mix of smaller brands. The more interesting finding in the August count was about the pages themselves. Brands had little room to customize their storefronts, and what they did with it varied: Mizuno’s page was rich with images, while other partners’ were basic product listings.

That variation is the part of Target Plus a guest can see. In a store, a Target visual merchandiser sets the shelf and a planogram keeps one brand’s facings from looking unlike the next. Online, each partner builds its own product pages and sends its own images and copy. A basic listing beside a Target-bought item with full imagery does not look like a different seller to the guest. It looks like Target cutting corners, and Target is the one that pays for that impression in the next visit.

Why Target guards the shelf

Follow what Target is lending to each partner and the curation makes sense. The REDcard discount is Target’s offer, made to Target’s cardholders. The free shipping promise and the service desk that takes returns are Target’s operations. When a guest is disappointed by a Target Plus item, the guest’s complaint, and often the return itself, lands with Target, not with a seller the guest never knew was there.

Target keeps the guest, the search data and the brand promise; the partner gets a place on Target.com under Target’s rules. A retailer that has spent decades teaching guests to trust what is on its shelves has every reason to choose partners whose pages will not undo that work, and to grow the list only as fast as it can find them. Doubling the product count in four months suggests Target is finding more of them, though it is too early to say whether the bar will hold as the list gets longer.

The listing is a merchandising job

For a brand, that turns Target Plus from an operations project into a merchandising one. The tests that decide whether it works are the ones a Target buyer would apply to any item. The main image has to be as clear as the ones next to it. The copy has to answer what a guest would ask in the aisle, and the sizes and colors have to be complete. A partner that cannot meet both is asking Target to lend its name to a page it would not have approved.

Many brands already have someone who knows Target’s standard well: the account team that sells into Target’s stores and has sat through the item reviews. In many organizations that person never sees the marketplace listings, which are built by whoever runs the brand’s other marketplaces, often from the same image library used for Amazon. The result can be one brand appearing twice on Target.com, polished where Target bought it and plain where the brand sells it directly.

If Target already buys some of your products, the simplest test takes ten minutes. Pull up one of those items and one you sell through Target Plus, side by side on a phone, and ask whether a guest could tell which is which. If they could, the Target Plus page is the one to fix before asking Target for more room on its shelf, and building those pages to Target’s standard is part of how we run Target Plus for brands.

P0356.crumb: Mercado Libre fees in Brazil turn on a…
P0356.title: Mercado Libre fees in Brazil turn on a single R$120 line
P0356.alt: A brass balance scale with both pans piled with small yellow twine-tied parcels against a blue wall.
P0356.ttag: Mercado Libre fees in Brazil turn on a single R$120 line | Kwontified
P0356.desc: On Mercado Livre, orders under R$120 pay a R$5 fee per unit and pricier new items must ship free. Brands should price packs around that line, not across it.
P0356.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 18, 2020.
P0356.body:
Ask a brand what Mercado Libre charges and the usual answer is a percentage: 11% on a Classic listing, 16% on a Premium one. That answer is right, and in Brazil it leaves out the part of the fee table that does the most damage to a price plan.

Since July 2, 2018, Mercado Livre (the Brazilian site) has added a fixed R$5 per unit to orders below R$120, on both listing types, Tecnoblog reported when the change was announced. Above R$120, the R$5 disappears, but a new product must be offered with free shipping, and the seller pays for it through Mercado Envios. The cost of selling on Mercado Libre’s largest market is therefore a step, not a smooth line, and the price a brand should avoid is the one just above R$120.

Why the percentage looks like the whole fee

The percentage is the number brands quote. For many products it is most of the cost. The R$5 came later and arrived as an add-on, framed by the company as a response to higher Correios postage. A brand reviewing its Mercado Libre margin sees commission as one line, fixed fees as another and shipping as a third. It is easy to report only the first.

Mercado Libre has been tightening the other two lines on purpose. In the first quarter of 2019 its free-shipping costs in Brazil fell almost 40%, to $56.2 million. Stelleo Tolda, its executive vice president for Latin America, said the company had revised its policy of giving free shipping “indiscriminately,” Tecnoblog reported in May 2019. The same article tied the company’s return to profit to the fixed fee and the leaner shipping policy.

Shipping is also where the volume runs. In the third quarter of 2019, Mercado Libre sold 98.0 million items and shipped 81.2 million through Mercado Envios, up 47.5%, and it netted $69.9 million of shipping subsidies out of its revenue, according to its quarterly results. Roughly five in six items sold went through its own logistics. For most brands, the shipping charge is not an edge case. It is part of the price.

A pack just above R$120 can cost more to sell than one below it

Take a skincare brand listing on a Classic ad at 11%, and say Mercado Envios bills it R$20 to ship a typical box at its reputation level. The single item sells for R$40. The brand is deciding between a three-pack at R$115, the same pack at R$125 and a larger set at R$150.

Listing priceCommission (11%)Fixed feeSeller-paid shippingTotal cost to sellShare of price
R$40R$4.40R$5.00noneR$9.4023.5%
R$115R$12.65R$5.00noneR$17.6515.3%
R$125R$13.75noneR$20.00R$33.7527.0%
R$150R$16.50noneR$20.00R$36.5024.3%

The single item pays almost a quarter of its price to sell. A R$5 fee is heavy on a R$40 product. Bundling it into a pack below the line spreads that R$5 across three units and cuts the cost to 15.3%. Crossing the line to R$125 swaps a R$5 fee for a R$20 shipping bill, and the cost to sell jumps to 27%.

The jump has a width.

At R$119 the brand keeps R$100.91 after commission and fee. Above R$120, it keeps 89% of the price minus R$20, which only gets back to R$100.91 at about R$136. Every price between R$120 and roughly R$136 nets the brand less than R$119 would have. With a R$15 shipping bill the dead zone narrows to about R$130; with R$25 it stretches past R$141. The width depends on the brand’s own shipping rate, which is why the calculation has to be run per brand.

What a fee report will and won’t show you

A Mercado Libre settlement report shows what was charged. It does not show what the brand could have kept at a different price, and that comparison is the one that matters here. A pack priced at R$125 looks healthy on commission alone (11%, as advertised) while its total cost to sell in the scenario above is 27%.

The scenario also leaves out what the step does to demand. A free-shipping badge above R$120 may convert better than a R$115 pack with a delivery charge, and in some categories that lift will be worth the R$15 gap. The way to know is to test it: list the pack at R$115 and at a price above R$136 for comparable periods, and compare units and net revenue per order rather than conversion alone. If the badge does not lift units by more than the extra cost, the lower price wins.

Two caveats belong next to the table. The rules here are Mercado Livre’s in Brazil; other Mercado Libre countries publish their own fee schedules. And the line itself is a policy, not a law of nature: Mercado Libre drew it in 2018 to absorb higher postage costs, and it can redraw it.

Pricing rules for Brazil

A brand entering Mercado Livre in 2020 can set its first assortment from three numbers: the commission rate for its listing type, the R$5 fixed fee, and its own Mercado Envios rate for its typical box. From those, find the price at which a pack above R$120 earns as much as a pack just below it, and keep every list price out of the gap between the two.

Then build packs to land below R$120 or clearly above the gap, not in it. A brand whose single items sit around R$40 has more room than it thinks: the three-pack at R$115 is the cheapest product on the page to sell. Recheck the threshold every quarter, because the most expensive mistake in the table is a price that was right when the brand set it.

Running that check before the first listings go live is part of how we launch brands on Mercado Libre.

P0357.crumb: Roundel sells what Target knows about its…
P0357.title: Roundel sells what Target knows about its shoppers, not its shelf
P0357.alt: A worn red drawer pulled open from a wooden card catalog cabinet, packed with aged index cards.
P0357.ttag: Roundel sells what Target knows about its shoppers, not its shelf | Kwontified
P0357.desc: Target built Roundel from its marketing team to sell what it knows about identified shoppers, in stores and online. Plan it as media, not trade spend.
P0357.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 20, 2020.
P0357.body:
Since October, a Target guest can join Target Circle at the register by giving a phone number. It takes a few seconds, earns 1% back on the trip, and turns an anonymous store purchase into one Target can tie to a person. Multiply that across Target’s stores and you have the asset Roundel, Target’s advertising business, is really selling.

Most brands still meet Roundel as an ad slot on Target.com, priced and discussed somewhere near their Target buyer. That undersells it and puts it in the wrong part of the company. Roundel was built by Target’s marketing department to sell what Target knows about its guests, online and in the aisle. A brand should judge it the way it judges any media that claims to reach a known audience: by what it can prove about sales.

Roundel grew out of Target’s own media buying

Target’s media business began in 2016 as Target Media Network. It was led by Kristi Argyilan, Target’s senior vice president of marketing since 2014, and on May 2, 2019, at its first NewFronts presentation, it took the name Roundel, another word for a bullseye, Tubefilter reported. Argyilan described it as Target “not only being on the buy side of media, but being on the sell side of media,” in an Adweek interview.

That origin explains the shape of the business. A retailer that buys a great deal of media knows what advertisers want to buy: audiences, reach and proof. Roundel works with brands that are not sold at Target at all, in categories from financial services and automotive to travel, and it named Disney, Dyson, Mastercard and Unilever among its clients. Target said its media business helps sell products from about 1,000 brands in its stores and that it engages 25 million guests digitally each week.

The new name did a job of its own. A business called Target Media Network sounded like the ad space on Target’s website. A business called Roundel, with its own logo, sounds like a media company that happens to own the best data on Target’s shoppers, which is closer to what Target wants advertisers to believe.

What Target knows that a website does not

Argyilan’s pitch rests on identity. “Our first-party data allows us to base our audiences off of real people,” she told Digiday, and Roundel can trace in-store behavior as well as clicks. Its ads run on Target.com, in stores, on a curated list of publisher sites, on TV and elsewhere, and brands get reporting on engagement, impressions and sales.

The store half of that sentence is what separates Roundel from an online-only ad business. Target Circle widens it. The loyalty program ran in test markets from April 2018 and signed up more than 2 million guests before Target took it national in early October 2019, Talk Business & Politics reported. Guests can enroll online or with a phone number in a store. Each enrollment is another shopper whose aisle purchases carry a name.

Read Target as an institution and the incentive is plain. Target’s business runs through its stores, which fulfilled nearly three-quarters of its digital sales in the 2018 holiday quarter, Target reported. A media business that can see store purchases has something to sell that a pure website cannot. It is too early to say how much of Circle’s data will reach Roundel’s audiences, and a Target employee told Digiday the company does not share customer data with outside vendors. The direction of the investment, though, points one way: more of Target’s shoppers identified, more of their trips measurable.

Where Roundel sits in a brand’s plan

Media buyers have not caught up, at least not yet. In a Digiday survey of media buyers published at the rebrand, 90% said they bought ads on Amazon, 23% on Walmart and 16% on Target. Some of that gap is scale: Amazon’s ad business is far larger, and Target has not published the size of its own. Some of it is where Target sits inside a brand.

At many brands, Target is owned by the account team that sells to the stores. Its money with Target is trade money (promotions, displays, allowances) negotiated with the buyer and judged against shipments. Roundel’s offer belongs in a different budget.

It sells audiences that reach beyond Target.com and reports sales that happen in the aisle, which is a media plan’s job. When the account team holds the relationship, Roundel tends to get bought as an add-on to a promotion. When the media team holds it, Roundel tends to get compared with Amazon’s ads on numbers that leave out the store, and loses.

Neither team is wrong about its own scorecard. The difficulty is that Roundel’s best evidence, a store sale traced to a known guest who saw an ad, lands between the two. A brand that wants to know whether Roundel works has to put someone in charge of reading that evidence, and give them a budget that is measured on Target’s sales in every channel.

The question for the next planning cycle

Before the next Target review, a brand’s leadership can ask one thing: when we spend with Roundel, who decides, and do they see the in-store sales report? If the answer is the account team and no, Roundel is being bought as a promotion. If it is the media team and no, it is being judged as a website. Either way the brand is paying for the part of Roundel that Target built it to sell and not looking at the result. Setting up that reading, alongside the Target business itself, is part of how we run Roundel for brands.

P0358.crumb: Instagram shopping ads should be judged…
P0358.title: Instagram shopping ads should be judged per order, not per click
P0358.alt: A brass tally counter and a smartphone beside a twine-tied stack of kraft envelopes on a wooden sill.
P0358.ttag: Instagram shopping ads should be judged per order, not per click | Kwontified
P0358.desc: Instagram shopping ads put a product page between the ad and your site, so site clicks look dear while orders can be cheaper. Compare them on cost per order.
P0358.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 25, 2020.
P0358.body:
Put an Instagram shopping ad next to an ordinary link ad in the same report and the shopping ad can lose on the first number anyone checks: it sends fewer people to the brand’s site for the money. That number is measuring the wrong thing. A shopping ad does part of the site’s job inside Instagram, and the clicks it does send are the ones that survived it.

The reason is one extra page. When a shopper taps a tagged product in a shopping post, Instagram opens a product page of its own, with the price and details, before anyone reaches the brand’s site. The shoppers who balk at the price or the color leave there, where the brand’s analytics never see them. So the right comparison between a shopping ad and a link ad is cost per order, and the wrong one is cost per click.

Instagram shopping in 2020 still ends on your site

The scale is no longer in question. Instagram brought in about $20 billion of advertising revenue in 2019, more than a quarter of Facebook’s total, Bloomberg reported from unnamed sources, as Marketing Dive summarized. Facebook does not break the figure out itself. More than 130 million accounts tap to reveal the tags on shopping posts every month, according to Instagram as reported in September 2019.

That same September, Instagram began letting a few selected businesses run their existing shopping posts as ads in feed. A shopper who taps one goes to a product description page within Instagram and then completes the purchase on the business’s mobile site. Instagram said it planned to test checkout inside these ads later.

Checkout itself is still narrow. Instagram opened it in March 2019 as a closed beta with about 20 brands, Tubefilter reported, and in January Sheryl Sandberg said Checkout needed full integrations and would take time to broaden, MarTech Today reported. For most brands in early 2020, an Instagram shopping sale is a two-page funnel: Instagram’s product page, then the brand’s own mobile site, opened in Instagram’s in-app browser.

One extra page changes what a click is worth

A link ad sends everyone who is curious straight to the site. The site then does all the filtering, and every shopper who leaves on seeing the price counts as a visit that did not convert. A shopping ad moves that first round of filtering inside Instagram. Fewer people reach the site, and the ones who do have already seen the price and the product.

Take a brand spending $1,000 on each ad type to reach 100,000 people, at a $10 cost per thousand impressions. Say the link ad earns a 1% click-through rate and the site converts 1.5% of those visitors. Say the shopping ad gets 2.5% of viewers to tap through to Instagram’s product page, 16% of them continue to the site, and those better-informed visitors convert at 5%.

Link adShopping ad
Spend$1,000$1,000
Visits to the brand’s site1,000400
Cost per site visit$1.00$2.50
Site conversion rate1.5%5%
Orders1520
Cost per order$66.67$50.00

On cost per site visit, the shopping ad looks two and a half times as expensive. On cost per order, it is 25% cheaper. Neither ad changed the shopper; the shopping ad only moved the point where the uninterested ones leave to a place the site cannot see.

What the report can and cannot show

Cost per click became the habit for a good reason. For link ads it is a fair proxy: every click lands on the same kind of page, so a cheaper click usually means a cheaper order, and teams that compare dozens of ads a week need one quick number. The proxy breaks the moment one ad type does some of its selling before the click.

The trap works in both directions. A team that judges ads on cost per click will cut the shopping ad. A team that looks only at the site’s analytics will see conversion jump on Instagram traffic and may credit a site redesign that had nothing to do with it.

The scenario’s rates are illustrative, and the mechanism only pays if the filter works. If shoppers who reach the site from a shopping ad do not convert meaningfully better than link-ad visitors, the extra page is just friction, and the link ad wins. Which way it goes depends on the product. A product whose price or look decides the sale benefits most from being seen on Instagram’s product page first. A product that needs a long explanation may lose shoppers on a page the brand does not control.

The test that settles it is plain. Run both ad types for the same products, to the same audience, with equal budgets for two weeks, and measure orders on the site with the same attribution window for each. Compare cost per order, and check the conversion rate of each ad’s site visitors to see whether the filter is doing the work.

Report shopping ads on orders, and fix the mobile checkout

Report Instagram shopping ads on cost per order, and never put their cost per site visit in the same column as a link ad’s. The click from a shopping ad has already been through a product page, and it is worth more than a click that has not.

And since the sale still finishes on the brand’s mobile site, inside an in-app browser where the shopper may not be signed in to the brand’s site, the mobile checkout is part of the ad. Every field a shopper has to fill in there is paid for in the cost per order. Running that comparison alongside the shop itself is part of how we operate Instagram Shop for brands.

P0360.crumb: Vendor Central in 2020 negotiates for the…
P0360.title: Vendor Central in 2020 negotiates for the slower half of Amazon
P0360.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet on a pallet jack beside a roller conveyor carrying boxes in a bright warehouse.
P0360.ttag: Vendor Central in 2020 negotiates for the slower half of Amazon | Kwontified
P0360.desc: Amazon’s own store grew 15% last quarter while seller services grew 30%. Vendor negotiations should start from where a brand’s Amazon units are really sold.
P0360.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 27, 2020.
P0360.body:
For a brand that sells to Amazon as a vendor, the start of the year brings Amazon’s annual proposal. It usually asks for more: more marketing funding, more allowances, sometimes new pack sizes or packaging that costs less to ship. In 2019 Amazon asked vendors for more funding, packaging innovations, logistics savings and price-pack changes, and the talks started later and ran slower because each vendor manager was handling more brands, Cleveland Research noted. Inside the brand, the negotiation gets a team, a deadline and a place on the CEO’s calendar.

It deserves the attention. But the negotiation is about a narrower part of Amazon than it was a few years ago. The figures Amazon published for the 2019 holiday quarter show its own store growing at half the pace of the marketplace beside it. A brand that treats Vendor Central terms as its Amazon strategy in 2020 is negotiating hard over the slower half of the business and leaving the faster half to whoever happens to sell there.

Amazon’s own store is the slower half

In the fourth quarter of 2019, Amazon’s online stores, the line that holds the products Amazon buys and sells itself, grew 15% to $45.7 billion. Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon earns from the marketplace, grew 30% to $17.4 billion, and third-party sellers accounted for 53% of the paid units Amazon shipped, up from 52%, Amazon reported.

Those lines are not a perfect split between vendors and sellers. Online stores also include digital media, and seller services are fees rather than the value of goods sold. The direction is still plain. More of what shoppers buy on Amazon each year comes from sellers, and Amazon’s own buying grows more slowly.

The shift has been visible on the ground for a year. By the time Amazon had paused orders from thousands of smaller vendors in March 2019, and Bloomberg had reported its plans to buy more from large brands, the marketplace was already handling more than half of goods sold, Retail Dive noted. In a Feedvisor survey cited in the same piece, more than 81% of wholesale brands said they wanted to move to the marketplace.

Amazon’s buyer is choosing items, not brands

Read Amazon’s retail team as an institution and its behavior makes sense. It is spending its own money on inventory, and it wants that money in the items that earn it a margin. In March 2019 Amazon began telling vendors that some products no longer qualified for advertising because their sales resulted in a loss to Amazon, and that they could regain eligibility by lowering their cost to Amazon, CNBC reported.

In May, Bloomberg reported that Amazon planned to buy more from major brands and let orders from smaller suppliers dry up, a report Amazon called wrong, PYMNTS noted. Whether or not that plan exists in the form Bloomberg described, the incentive behind it is easy to see. A retailer judging each item by the margin it earns will keep buying the items that earn it and stop buying the ones that do not, one item at a time.

Put those together and the shape of Vendor Central in 2020 comes into view. Amazon still buys, and buys heavily, from brands whose items move in volume at a margin it likes. For everything else, the marketplace is the default, and the question is only who sells there: the brand, an authorized reseller or a seller the brand has never met.

That is the hidden cost of an account-level negotiation. The vendor terms apply to the items Amazon chooses to buy. The items it does not buy, or stops buying, still sell on the same detail pages, often through third-party sellers whose prices and stock levels the brand does not set. The negotiation can go well and the brand’s position on Amazon can still get worse.

Inside the brand, the scorecard counts shipments

The team that runs the vendor negotiation at many brands sits in sales, and it is usually measured on what it ships to Amazon. That is a fair measure of a wholesale account. It says little about the brand’s total business on Amazon, because it leaves out every unit a third-party seller sold on the brand’s pages.

When the faster-growing half of Amazon sits outside the scorecard, nobody is paid to notice it. A reseller can take the Buy Box on an item Amazon stopped reordering, and the vendor team will see a dip in purchase orders rather than a competitor on the page. Moving the whole account to Seller Central is not the only answer either. Wholesale stock already at Amazon has to sell through before a brand’s own marketplace offer can take its place, Retail Dive noted, and for some items Amazon’s own buying may still serve the brand better than a marketplace offer would.

What changes is the starting point for the conversation. A brand that walks into this year’s negotiation knowing which of its items Amazon buys, which it sells itself and which third-party sellers carry has something to trade. A brand that knows only its shipments is negotiating over half the shelf without seeing the other half.

So the leadership team has one question to ask before the terms are signed, simple to ask and hard to answer. Of every unit of our products sold on Amazon in 2019, how many did Amazon sell, how many did we sell, and how many did someone else sell? Getting that number, and running the vendor and marketplace sides as one Amazon business, is the work we do with brands on Amazon.

P0362.crumb: Amazon DSP in 2020 is worth its shopping…
P0362.title: Amazon DSP in 2020 is worth its shopping data, not its screens
P0362.alt: A wicker basket of bread, tomatoes, carrots and greens on a wooden table before a wall-mounted TV.
P0362.ttag: Amazon DSP in 2020 is worth its shopping data, not its screens | Kwontified
P0362.desc: Amazon now lets rival platforms sell some of its screens but keeps its shopping data inside Amazon DSP. Price every DSP line on the audience, not the placement.
P0362.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 3, 2020.
P0362.body:
In July 2019 Amazon opened a door it had kept shut. Connected-TV apps that sell ads through Amazon Publisher Services could now strike private marketplace deals with buyers on Dataxu and The Trade Desk, two rival demand-side platforms, Marketing Dive reported. What Amazon did not open matters more. Those platforms get neither the Fire TV and IMDb TV inventory Amazon sells itself nor any data on what people browsed or bought on Amazon.

That split tells a brand what it is paying for in Amazon DSP in 2020. The screens are becoming available elsewhere. The shopping data is not. So the right way to price a DSP line is by the audience it reaches, and any line whose audience adds nothing is a placement bought at a data premium.

Amazon DSP in 2020, in five facts

Amazon DSP is the self-serve and managed platform for buying display and video ads programmatically, on and off Amazon’s own sites, using Amazon’s audience segments. Amazon gave it that name in September 2018, when the Amazon Advertising Platform was folded into Amazon Advertising.

What changedWhenWhy it matters for a DSP line
“Other” revenue, mostly advertising, reached $4.782 billion, up 41%Q4 2019More advertisers bid for the same shoppers
New-to-brand metrics added for DSP display and videoJanuary 2019DSP can be judged on new customers, not just sales
Amazon bought Sizmek’s ad server and dynamic creative toolMay 2019Amazon now serves and measures more of the ad itself
Fire TV had 34 million active usersMay 2019Video reach on Amazon’s own screens
Rival platforms can buy some connected-TV apps, without Amazon’s shopping dataJuly 2019The placement is no longer the scarce part

The revenue line is from Amazon’s fourth-quarter results, where “other” covers sales of advertising services; the year-earlier quarter was $3.388 billion. The Sizmek deal covered the ad server and the dynamic creative optimization tool, CNBC reported. The new-to-brand definition counts a purchase as new when the shopper has not bought the brand on Amazon in the prior 12 months, Marketing Dive explained.

Why the placement looked like the product

For most of DSP’s short life, brands bought it as access. Amazon’s pitch decks sold reach into Amazon’s own pages and apps. The audience segments came along with it: lifestyle audiences built from up to a year of habitual search, browsing and purchase behavior, and in-market audiences of shoppers who had recently browsed a category, as Digiday reported. If the only way to show a video ad to a Fire TV viewer was through Amazon, the placement and the data were one purchase, and nobody had to price them apart.

That was reasonable while it lasted. The July change separates them. An advertiser can now reach some of the same connected-TV viewers through another platform, at that platform’s price, without Amazon’s purchase history attached. Whatever Amazon DSP charges above that is the price of the data.

Price the audience, then check what it adds

An impression’s cost is set by the placement and the auction. Its value is set by who sees it. Those two numbers move separately, and a DSP report that shows only cost per thousand impressions (CPM) and attributed sales blends them together.

Take a brand selling a $40 product with $10 it can spend to win a sale. It runs two DSP video lines of 1,000,000 impressions each. Line A buys an Amazon in-market audience at a $12 CPM, costs $12,000 and produces 600 purchases from new-to-brand shoppers. Line B buys broad connected-TV reach with no Amazon audience at an $8 CPM, costs $8,000 and produces 200 such purchases.

Line A costs $20 per new-to-brand purchase; line B costs $40. The cheaper placement is the more expensive customer.

Now reverse the result. If line A had produced 300 new-to-brand purchases, its cost per new customer would be $40, the same as the line with no data. The brand would be paying a 50% higher CPM for an audience that found nobody new. That line should move to the cheaper placement or stop.

The trade-off runs both ways. Audience data narrows reach, so a brand launching a product nobody has searched for yet may need the broad line first, because the in-market audience does not exist until someone creates demand. The numbers lean toward the audience line only once a category has shoppers to find.

What the report can and cannot settle

New-to-brand purchases are a better yardstick than total attributed sales, because remarketing audiences full of past buyers inflate the second and barely move the first. They still measure attribution, not cause. A shopper counted as new may have bought anyway after seeing a friend’s purchase or a store shelf.

The test that settles it is a holdout: keep a share of each audience out of the line for a few weeks and compare purchase rates. If the exposed group does not buy more than the held-out group, the audience premium is paying for sales that were coming regardless.

Four DSP checks before the next tentpole

  1. Write the CPM of every DSP line next to the CPM you would pay for the same placement without Amazon’s audience. The gap is your data premium.
  2. Report each line on cost per new-to-brand purchase, not attributed return on ad spend.
  3. Cut or move any line whose cost per new customer matches a line with no Amazon audience.
  4. Hold out part of the largest audience before the next tentpole and measure the difference in purchase rates.

Amazon is betting that its shopping data is the one thing other platforms cannot sell, and the July decision shows it intends to keep it that way; we plan and run Amazon DSP alongside Sponsored Ads on exactly that basis.

P0363.crumb: Walmart Media Group opened its search…
P0363.title: Walmart Media Group opened its search shelf before its store data
P0363.alt: Blue wooden shelving holding an old clasped book, a brass magnifying glass, ceramic vases and woven baskets.
P0363.ttag: Walmart Media Group opened its search shelf before its store data | Kwontified
P0363.desc: Walmart Media Group now sells walmart.com search ads self-serve, but its store data is still locked away. Brands should decide who owns that shelf now.
P0363.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 5, 2020.
P0363.body:
On January 3, any brand with a login could buy a sponsored product ad on walmart.com without calling a Walmart sales representative. Walmart Media Group opened a self-serve portal for search and sponsored product ads, plus an API that lets four software partners (Teikametrics, Flywheel Digital, Kenshoo and Pacvue) buy the same inventory, AdExchanger reported. Until then, these ads were sold only as a managed service.

The same report listed what the portal does not offer: Walmart’s retail and audience data for targeting, much attribution of online searches to store sales, or detailed reporting. So the first thing Walmart has opened is the search results page, which works like a shelf. The thing that would make Walmart unlike Amazon, what roughly 160 million weekly shoppers buy in its stores and online, is still behind the counter. For brands, the practical conclusion is to treat Walmart Media Group as shelf space today and decide, before the data arrives, which team inside the company owns it.

How Walmart’s ad business took shape in a year

Walmart has run advertising for a long time; it has not run it as a business of its own. Doug McMillon told investors in October 2018, “We have a tiny ad business,” and said it could be bigger, Bloomberg reported. Until early 2019, website ad sales ran through Triad, a WPP-owned firm. In February 2019 Walmart said it would bring those sales and the analytics in-house to Walmart Media Group, Marketing Dive reported. A Gartner L2 estimate cited at the time put the gap plainly: Amazon earned ad money on 16% of searches, Walmart on 1%.

The order of the moves since then reads like a merchant’s checklist more than a media company’s. First the sales team came home. In April 2019 Walmart bought Polymorph Labs, whose technology includes an ad server and a self-serve interface, TechCrunch reported. Then, in January, the shelf opened to self-serve buyers. The data, the part an advertiser cannot get anywhere else, is still on the list.

That sequence tells you what Walmart wants. A merchant fills the shelf before selling end caps. Walmart is making sure brands can rent the top of its search results with as little friction as possible, while it works out how much of its store knowledge to sell, and to whom.

The store comparison is useful because it shows what has changed for brands. In a Walmart store, the merchant decides which products sit at eye level, and a brand earns that spot through the line review, the cost of goods and the promotion calendar. On walmart.com, the first rows of a search for a product type now go partly to whoever bids for them. The line review still decides whether a product is carried. The auction now decides whether a shopper sees it first.

Who holds the portal login

In February, Walmart Marketplace in 2020 sits outside your store buyer’s aisle looked at the split on Walmart’s side, between its store and online merchants. Self-serve search ads open a second split, on the brand’s side, and it is about who spends the money. Inside many consumer brands, Walmart belongs to the sales team that negotiates with the Walmart buyer, often from an office near Bentonville, while Amazon advertising sits with an e-commerce or media team. Self-serve search ads cut across that line. The person with the portal login can now spend money on walmart.com without the buyer’s involvement and without the sales team’s trade budget.

Early results suggest the money that flows through the portal behaves like Amazon search money. About 85% of the orders Teikametrics drove through Walmart sponsored ads came from non-branded search queries, Teikametrics told AdExchanger. Those are shoppers who had not yet chosen a brand, which is exactly the moment a store’s merchant cares about most.

That puts two teams in charge of one shelf. The sales team owns the planogram and the promotions in stores, and often the funding for them. The e-commerce team can now buy the top of the digital aisle from its own budget. Neither sees the other’s numbers by default, and Walmart’s reporting, which shows little more than device type and search frequency, will not join them up.

It matters because Walmart.com is where the retailer’s growth sits. Walmart U.S. e-commerce sales rose 35% in the holiday quarter and 37% for the year, against comparable-store growth of 1.9%, Walmart reported on February 18. A brand whose Walmart plan is run from the store side is planning the slow half of the business.

What changes when the store data arrives

The evidence leans toward Walmart selling its store data eventually; the AdExchanger piece calls attribution to store sales “early days,” which is not a refusal. When it does, the walmart.com search shelf will stop being a cheaper copy of Amazon’s and become the one place a brand can see whether an online ad moved a product off a store shelf. That is the asset the sales team understands best and the e-commerce team can buy.

It is too early to say how Walmart will price that data or who will be allowed to use it. It is not too early to decide who in your company answers for the search shelf, because whoever holds the login on the day the data arrives will hold the budget that follows it.

Questions for the next Walmart planning meeting

  • Who holds the Walmart Media Group login, and does the sales team know what it spent last month?
  • Are Walmart search ads funded from trade spend, from media, or from whatever was left over?
  • Which non-branded searches on walmart.com should our products win, and are we bidding on them or only on our brand name?
  • When Walmart offers store-sales attribution, which team will read it, and will it change how we fund in-store promotions?

The brands that answer the first question this spring will be ready for the last one, which is why we run Walmart Marketplace and its advertising with both teams in the room.

P0364.crumb: Falling Amazon CPCs are a bargain only if…
P0364.title: Falling Amazon CPCs are a bargain only if conversion held
P0364.alt: A blank tag rests on a stack of coins beside a glass funnel on a wooden shelf against a navy wall.
P0364.ttag: Falling Amazon CPCs are a bargain only if conversion held | Kwontified
P0364.desc: A cheaper click is good news only if it still converts. When Amazon CPCs fall, reset each bid from what the click is worth, not from what it now costs.
P0364.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 10, 2020.
P0364.body:
For most of 2019 the average Sponsored Products click got cheaper. In Merkle’s second-quarter report, advertisers’ Sponsored Products spend rose 12% from a year earlier while clicks rose 58%, Marketing Dive reported, which puts the average cost per click (CPC) about 29% lower. Then the fourth quarter reversed it: CPC rose 15% on clicks up 42%, in a summary of Merkle’s Q4 2019 report.

Clicks get dearer into the holidays and cheaper after them, and that seasonal swing is where bids go wrong. Falling Amazon CPCs do not change what should set the bid, which is the value of a click: the product’s price, times the share of it the brand can spend on ads, times the conversion rate. A cheaper click is a bargain only if conversion fell less than the price did, and after the holidays it often falls more.

Account teams have two reflexes for the cheap phase, and both miss this. Some cut bids to “match” the lower prices. Others treat the fall as found money and raise budgets. Each reads the CPC as though it measured something about the click, when it is only a price, set by how hard rivals are bidding this week.

A click is worth price times allowance times conversion

The value of a click to a brand has three parts: the product’s price, the share of that price the brand can spend on advertising, and the conversion rate, the share of clicks that end in an order. Multiply them and you have the most a click can cost before the ad loses money.

Take a $25 product where the brand can spend 30% of the price, $7.50, to win an order. In December, its main keyword converts 15% of clicks, so a click is worth $1.125. The brand bids $1.10 and pays an average of $0.95.

By February the same keyword’s CPC has fallen to $0.70, a drop of about 26%. It looks like relief. But January and February shoppers convert less on this product, and the keyword now converts 10% of clicks. A click is worth $0.75. The price fell by about a quarter; the value fell by a third.

DecemberFebruary
Average CPC$0.95$0.70
Conversion rate15%10%
Value of a click$1.125$0.75
Bid left unchanged$1.10$1.10
Margin on the average click$0.175$0.05

The margin per click has almost disappeared, and the $1.10 bid is now well above what a click is worth. On any search where a rival pushes the price close to the bid, the brand pays more than the click returns. The cheaper auction made the account worse.

Now change one assumption. If the keyword still converts 15% in February, the click is still worth $1.125 and the $0.70 price leaves $0.425 of margin on every click. That is real headroom, and the right move is to keep the bid where value puts it and let the budget buy more clicks.

Why the falling price feels like the signal

The CPC is the number in the dashboard that moves first and moves most. Conversion rates need weeks of clicks to read, so the price change arrives before the value change and anchors the decision. A team that cuts bids to follow CPC down is pricing its offer from the market, not from its own margin. A team that spends the savings is assuming the clicks are the same clicks.

Bid adjustments add a multiplier to the same error. Since February 2019, Amazon has let advertisers raise bids by placement, up to 900% for top of search and product pages, Feedvisor explained. A 50% top-of-search adjustment set in December, when that placement converted best, carries a $1.10 bid to $1.65. If top-of-search conversion drops with everything else after the holidays, the adjustment is now multiplying a bid that was already too high.

Reading the auction after the holidays

The CPC tells you how hard competitors are bidding. It cannot tell you whether your own shoppers are still buying, and a seasonal drop in both can look like a bargain on the price line alone.

Three things decide whether a cheaper click is headroom. The first is conversion over the last four weeks compared with the four weeks before. The second is the share of spend on brand searches, which convert steadily and can hide weakness elsewhere. The third is whether any product went out of stock or lost the Buy Box, which drags conversion without touching CPC.

Conversion is also the noisier of the two numbers. Say a keyword had 100 clicks in February and 10 orders. One order more or less moves its conversion rate by a full percentage point, and its click value by a tenth. A CPC averaged over the same 100 clicks barely moves.

So read conversion over enough clicks to trust it, and for small keywords pool them by product: the product’s conversion rate across all its keywords is a better estimate than any one keyword’s month. A bid change on thin data is a guess presented as arithmetic.

The rule is short. Set each bid at or below the value of a click, recalculated from recent conversion, and let the CPC set only the margin.

The post-holiday bid check

  1. Recompute click value for your 20 largest keywords from the last four weeks of conversion, and lower any bid above it.
  2. Remove or reduce placement adjustments set during the holidays until each placement’s own conversion supports them.
  3. Where conversion held and CPC fell, keep the bid and raise the budget, so the cheaper clicks become more orders.
  4. Repeat the check weekly until conversion rates settle, then monthly.

Pricing every keyword from what its click is worth is how we run Sponsored Products bidding, in falling auctions and rising ones.

P0366.crumb: Apparel on Amazon in 2020: brands can…
P0366.title: Apparel on Amazon in 2020: brands can leave, products stay
P0366.alt: Earth-toned shirts on a wooden rail with many empty hangers above a table of folded clothes in a mustard room.
P0366.ttag: Apparel on Amazon in 2020: brands can leave, products stay | Kwontified
P0366.desc: Nike’s exit showed apparel brands can stop selling to Amazon but cannot take their products off it. The 2020 choice is who stands behind the listing.
P0366.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 12, 2020.
P0366.body:
On November 13, Nike said it would “complete our current pilot with Amazon Retail,” ending two years of selling to Amazon as a wholesaler, Fortune reported. Nike’s sneakers and clothing did not disappear from Amazon. Independent sellers still list them, and Amazon was reported to be recruiting more of those sellers so the products stay widely available.

That is the clearest lesson apparel on Amazon offers going into 2020. A brand can choose whether to sell to Amazon. It cannot choose whether its products appear there. The only real decision is who stands behind the listing: the brand, a set of resellers it does not control, or Amazon itself. Brands that treat Amazon as a door they can close are planning for a store that no longer works that way.

Apparel on Amazon grew without waiting for brands

Shoppers settled the question before most brands did. In Coresight Research’s annual survey of US apparel shoppers, published in March 2019, Amazon overtook Walmart as the retailer Americans most often bought clothing from, after placing second the year before (Coresight). Around three-quarters of Prime members had bought apparel on Amazon in the past year, the survey found.

Amazon spent 2019 adding the things a fashion retailer needs and a warehouse does not. In May it announced The Drop, limited collections designed with influencers, each on sale for 30 hours and made on demand, FashionUnited reported. In August it began testing a “Top Brand” badge in some searches, mostly in clothing and shoes, Marketplace Pulse found; an Amazon spokeswoman told Bloomberg the badge reflected brands popular with customers and that brands do not pay for it (Fortune).

Both moves point the same way. Amazon wants fashion shoppers to see brands, trends and newness, not only a grid of similar shirts sorted by review count. Those features work best for brands that show up with a complete, well-kept catalog.

Why apparel brands keep their distance

The instinct to stay off Amazon comes from how apparel distribution was built. A clothing brand protects its image by choosing its doors: which department stores, which specialty shops, which outlets, and at what point in the season markdowns begin. The wholesale account manager’s job is to keep the brand in the right doors and out of the wrong ones. Amazon looked like the wrong door, crowded with resellers, discounted stock and, in the worst cases, fakes.

Nike’s pilot showed why the instinct is understandable and why it does not work. Before the pilot, the only Nike products on Amazon were gray-market goods and counterfeits sold by others, and during it Nike reportedly struggled to control listings, as removed sellers came back under new names. Ending the wholesale relationship did not fix that. It only removed Nike from the conversation.

The tools for a brand that stays have also changed. In February 2019 Amazon launched Project Zero, which lets brands enrolled in Brand Registry remove counterfeit listings themselves instead of reporting them and waiting, and later add a serial code to each unit, TechCrunch reported. Those powers belong to the brand that registers and manages its catalog. A brand that walks away leaves them unused, and leaves its page to whoever is still selling.

The structure that produces the instinct is still in place at many brands. The wholesale team owns the accounts and the calendar. Amazon, if anyone owns it, sits with a small e-commerce team, or with nobody. So the reseller listing a brand’s jackets on Amazon is often better informed about the brand’s Amazon shoppers than anyone at the brand.

Follow the value on the apparel page

Ask who captures what when a brand stays away. The reseller keeps the margin between the price it paid, often in liquidation or from an overstocked account, and the price it sets on Amazon. Amazon keeps its referral fee, which rose for Clothing & Accessories from 15% to 17% of the sale price in April 2018, according to the fee notice sellers posted. The shopper gets a product page written by whoever got there first.

The brand gets the reviews. Every complaint about sizing, color or a seam that split after two washes attaches to the brand’s name, whether the item was this season’s stock or a three-year-old return. On a category page where products are otherwise hard to tell apart, those reviews are a large part of what the next shopper sees. A shopper choosing between two pairs of nearly identical navy chinos reads the stars and the fit comments long before she reads the fabric content, and a reseller has no reason to fix the size chart that caused them.

A brand that runs its own listings captures something different: the product content, the size chart, the images that match what ships, and the search data that shows which styles shoppers look for. It is also better placed for the features Amazon is building for fashion, which favor a brand that is present and organized.

Questions for the 2020 apparel plan

  • Who in the company owns our products’ Amazon listings, and who wrote what shoppers are reading on them?
  • Which of our styles are on Amazon through resellers, and where did that stock come from?
  • What do our Amazon reviews say about fit and quality, and does the merchandising team read them?
  • If we stopped selling to Amazon tomorrow, what would change for the shopper searching our name, and what would change for us?

Nike has the size and the direct business to accept the trade it made. Most apparel brands do not, and for them the 2020 question is how to take charge of the page; that is the work we do in running Amazon as a channel for apparel and footwear brands.

P0368.crumb: Brand Analytics market basket ranks the…
P0368.title: Brand Analytics market basket ranks the popular, not the paired
P0368.alt: Wire baskets holding a sourdough loaf and a ceramic teapot with cups on a sunlit table by a terracotta wall.
P0368.ttag: Brand Analytics market basket ranks the popular, not the paired | Kwontified
P0368.desc: Amazon’s market basket report ranks what is often bought with your product, which favors popular items. Check the base rate before you bundle.
P0368.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 17, 2020.
P0368.body:
Open the Market Basket Analysis report in Amazon Brand Analytics for a skincare serum, and the product most often bought with it may be a phone charging cable. Nobody at the brand thinks the serum and the cable belong together. The report is not wrong, though. It is answering a narrower question than the one most brands ask of it.

The Brand Analytics market basket report shows the three products most often purchased in the same order as each of your products, with a combination percentage for each. It ranks by how often a pairing happens, not by how much more often than chance. Products that turn up in lots of Amazon orders rise to the top for that reason alone. The pairing worth building a bundle or an ad around is the one that appears with your product far more often than it appears anywhere else, and the report leaves that comparison to you.

What the market basket report counts

Brand Analytics is open only to brand owners, not resellers, Practical Ecommerce noted in January, and Amazon brought it to Seller Central for Brand Registry brands in February 2019, ChannelX reported. The market basket report shows the top three products bought at the same time as your brand’s products, Jumpfly explained last August. The combination percentage is the share of times each of those products was purchased with yours, measured against all the products bought with your item in the period. The report can be run daily, weekly, monthly or quarterly, and filtered to show your own brand’s products, other brands’ products or both.

The report is, in other words, a frequency table. Its top row is the most common companion of your product. Whether that companion has anything to do with your product is a separate question.

Run both views. Your own-brand companions tell you what to bundle or cross-sell on your detail pages. Other brands’ companions tell you whose detail pages your shoppers are already buying from, which is where product-targeted ads have a reason to appear.

Why the most frequent pairing misleads

A shopper’s basket holds whatever she needed that day. Products that many people need on many days, such as batteries, cables, paper towels and best-selling snacks, sit in a large share of all orders. They will appear next to your product often simply because they appear next to everything.

The pull of the top row is strong because it looks like an answer. A brand manager asked for bundle ideas reads the first companion, sees a high percentage and has a recommendation by lunchtime. The percentage is real. What it lacks is a comparison, and without one a popular product and a true companion look the same.

Take a $28 serum sold in 2,000 orders in a quarter. A charging cable appears in 160 of those orders, a combination of 8%. A refill pad made for this type of serum appears in 60 orders, 3%. The report puts the cable first.

Now add the base rate: how often each companion appears in comparable orders that do not include your serum. Say the cable is in 6% of beauty orders across the category, and the refill pad in 0.2%. Divide each pairing rate by its base rate and you get lift, the number of times more likely a shopper is to buy the companion when your product is in the basket.

CompanionBought with the serumBase rateLift
Charging cable8%6%about 1.3
Refill pad3%0.2%15

A lift near one means no relationship at all. The cable is there by coincidence of popularity. The refill pad is fifteen times more likely in a serum basket than elsewhere, which is what a real pairing looks like, even though it ranks second or third, or misses the top three in a busy quarter.

What the report can and cannot tell you

The base rate is not in the report, and Amazon does not publish category basket rates. A brand can approximate it from its own catalog. Run the report for every product you sell. A companion that shows up next to all of them, at similar percentages, is behaving like a base rate. A companion that shows up next to one product and none of the others is likely a true pair.

The report also cannot tell you direction or cause. A shopper who buys a serum and a refill pad may have come for either. And three slots per product is a short list: a strong pairing with a modest volume can be crowded out by popular items, which is why quarterly runs, with more orders behind them, can show different companions than weekly ones.

What would change the conclusion is a test. If a pairing is real, a bundle or an ad aimed at the companion’s shoppers should lift sales of your product beyond what the same budget earns elsewhere. If it is popularity, it will not.

Using pairings without paying for coincidence

  1. Run the report quarterly for every product, and drop any companion that appears beside most of your catalog.
  2. Rank the remaining pairs by lift against your own catalog, not by combination percentage.
  3. Use the strongest pairs in Sponsored Products product targeting on the companion’s detail pages, and in bundles or A+ Content cross-sells.
  4. Hold the test for four weeks and compare sales of your product against the weeks before; keep only the pairs that move it.
  5. Re-run after Prime Day and the holidays, when popular items crowd every basket.

Treating the market basket report as a list of candidates rather than an answer is how we use Brand Analytics in planning Amazon advertising, and it keeps budgets off pairings that only look close.
