P0370.crumb: Shoppers read Amazon product reviews to…
P0370.title: Shoppers read Amazon product reviews to learn how a product fails
P0370.alt: A magnifying glass reveals a crack in a beige teapot handle beside an intact white teapot on wood.
P0370.ttag: Shoppers read Amazon product reviews to learn how a product fails | Kwontified
P0370.desc: Most shoppers check reviews, and most look for the bad ones first. They want to know how a product fails and whether that failure matters to them.
P0370.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 19, 2020.
P0370.body:
Choose between two pairs of headphones on Amazon on your phone and notice the order you read in. A glance at the stars and the count, then a thumb straight down past the five-star praise to the one-, two- and three-star reviews, read slowly, looking for a pattern: the left ear cuts out, the band cracks after a month, the case is smaller than it looks.

That habit tells you what Amazon product reviews are for. Shoppers do not mainly read them to be reassured that a product is good; the star average does that in a second. They read them to find out how the product goes wrong, and whether that particular failure would bother them. A brand that treats its reviews as a score to defend is managing the wrong thing. The useful part of a review page is the list of failure modes, and shoppers are reading it more carefully than most brand teams do.

Who reads Amazon product reviews

Nearly everyone, and the youngest shoppers most habitually. In a Pew Research Center survey published in December 2016, 82% of US adults said they read online ratings or reviews at least sometimes before buying something for the first time, and 40% said they always or almost always do (Pew Research Center). The habit falls with age: 53% of adults aged 18 to 29 always or almost always read reviews, against 23% of those 65 and older.

PowerReviews put the share even higher in its 2018 survey of more than 1,000 US consumers: 97% consult reviews before buying, and most read between one and ten of them, Agility PR reported. So the reader is not a niche. She is the default customer, and on a phone she has time for perhaps a handful of reviews. Which handful she chooses is the interesting part.

What shoppers look for first

The same PowerReviews survey found that 85% of shoppers look specifically for negative reviews before they buy. That is not pessimism. A shopper comparing two similar products already assumes both mostly work; the stars told her so. What she cannot see from the average is the shape of the complaints. Two blenders with the same 4.3-star rating can fail in completely different ways, one with a lid that leaks and one with a motor that struggles with ice, and only one of those matters to someone who makes smoothies every morning.

Shoppers also distrust a score that looks too clean. The Spiegel Research Center at Northwestern University found that purchase likelihood typically peaks for products rated between 4.0 and 4.7 stars and declines as ratings approach a perfect 5.0, which shoppers read as too good to be true (Spiegel Research Center). The critical reviews are part of what makes the positive ones believable.

Readers are skeptical in general, too. In the Pew survey, 48% of review readers said it is often hard to tell whether reviews are truthful and unbiased. A shopper who half-suspects the praise has a reason to trust the complaints more: nobody is paid to write that the zipper broke.

Why brands read reviews differently

Inside most brands, reviews arrive as two numbers in a dashboard: the average rating and the count. Those are the numbers that get reported upward, so those are the numbers people work to move. The usual responses follow from that. Ask happy customers for more reviews. Reply politely to the angry ones. Escalate anything under three stars to customer service.

None of that is wrong, but it treats the review page as a reputation score, owned by whoever handles customer care. The shopper is treating it as product documentation, written by people who have used the product longer than the brand’s photographer has. The gap shows up in a familiar place: a detail page whose bullets describe the product as designed, sitting above reviews that describe the product as used.

The people best placed to close that gap are usually not in the review conversation at all. Product developers decide whether the lid gets redesigned. Merchandisers decide whether the size chart changes. Copywriters decide whether the listing says, plainly, that the case fits a phone up to a certain size. In many companies, none of them sees the two-star reviews unless someone forwards them.

Reading the critics as a product brief

The shift for brands is to read low-star reviews the way shoppers do, as a list of failure modes, and to decide which ones to fix in the product and which to address on the page. Some complaints are real defects. Others are mismatched expectations, and those can often be resolved with a clearer image, a measurement in the title, or a bullet that says who the product is not for. A shopper who reads “runs small, order a size up” in the listing itself is less likely to need a review to learn it.

That also changes what a good review page looks like. It does not need to be spotless; the research above suggests a spotless page can hurt. It needs complaints that are about things a given shopper can accept, and a listing that already answers the rest.

Questions for the next product review

  • Who in the company reads the one- to three-star reviews on our top ten products each month, and what changed because of them?
  • Which failure modes appear in more than a handful of reviews, and are they product defects or expectation gaps?
  • Does each detail page answer, in its images or bullets, the question its critics keep raising?
  • Do product development and merchandising see review themes, or only customer care?

A brand that reads its critics as a product brief can usually fix the page in days and the product over a season. Making the listing answer the reviews is part of running the Amazon channel for a brand, and it is often the quickest improvement available.

P0371.crumb: With FBA inbound capped, Amazon ads buy…
P0371.title: With FBA inbound capped, Amazon ads buy timing, not extra sales
P0371.alt: An hourglass sits on an empty pallet by a half-open loading dock door, with boxed pallets behind.
P0371.ttag: With FBA inbound capped, Amazon ads buy timing, not extra sales | Kwontified
P0371.desc: When FBA cannot restock a product, its ads stop adding sales and only sell the same units sooner. Re-plan ad budgets around the stockout date.
P0371.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 24, 2020.
P0371.body:
On March 17, Amazon told sellers its US and European fulfillment centers were “temporarily prioritizing household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products,” with the change expected to last until April 5, CNBC reported. Inventory already inside Amazon keeps shipping. New shipments of everything else wait.

For a brand selling outside the priority list, that turns each FBA product into a fixed pile of units. And a fixed pile changes what advertising does. In a normal month, an ad that wins a sale adds a sale. Under the FBA inbound limits, a product whose stock would sell out before restock even without ads gains no units from advertising; the ad only decides how soon. Ad spend on capped stock stops buying sales and starts buying timing, and in most cases the timing it buys is an earlier stockout.

What the FBA inbound limits change, in one product

Take a $30 product outside the priority categories with 1,200 units in FBA on March 17. With its ads running, it sells 60 units a day; without them, 40. The brand spends $5 in advertising for each of the 20 extra daily units.

With ads on, the stock lasts 20 days and runs out around April 6. With ads off, it lasts 30 days and runs out around April 16. Either way, the brand sells 1,200 units from that pile. The ads add none. They cost $100 a day for 20 days, $2,000 in all, to sell the same units ten days sooner.

Ads onAds off
Units sold per day6040
Days of stock2030
Units sold before stockout1,2001,200
Ad cost$2,000$0

The date matters as much as the money. Amazon’s restriction was expected to end on April 5, but a shipment created after it lifts still has to travel to a warehouse and be received alongside everyone else’s backlog. A product that runs out on April 6 is likely to sit empty for longer than one that runs out on April 16, and an empty listing loses more than the sales of those days. The ten extra days of stock are ten more days of a live listing, with ads that can be switched back on as soon as a restock date is in sight.

Why the usual ad logic fails here

The habit is to judge a campaign by its return on ad spend: sales attributed to the ad divided by its cost. That ratio assumes the sale would not have happened otherwise. When supply is fixed, the assumption fails. The shopper who buys today because of an ad displaces a shopper who would have bought the same unit next week. The attributed sale is real; the extra sale is not.

Cutting ads has a cost too. Advertising does more than move units. It keeps a product visible against rivals who are still in stock, and some of the shoppers it wins are new to the brand and will come back. A brand with a long-life product and a strong review position may decide some visibility is worth paying for. The numbers still lean hard toward cutting, because an out-of-stock product loses its voice entirely: Sponsored Products ads run only on listings that hold the Buy Box, Practical Ecommerce explained, so the stockout ends the ads anyway, at the worst moment.

Delivery promises add another reason to slow down. Some non-essential items now show delivery dates a month out, and Amazon has said some of its delivery promises are “longer than usual,” Fortune reported on March 23. A long promise lowers conversion, which raises the cost of every ad-driven sale on exactly the products that cannot restock.

Where the ad money should go instead

The budget does not have to disappear. It can move to where it still creates sales.

Products in the priority categories can still be replenished, so ads on them still add units. The same is true of any product the brand can sell through Fulfilled by Merchant, shipping orders from its own warehouse; the CNBC report noted that option remains open. A merchant-fulfilled offer is limited by the brand’s own stock and shipping, not Amazon’s receiving queue, and where Amazon’s promise for an FBA item has stretched, a brand shipping in a few days may be able to show a shorter one.

Vendors selling to Amazon on Vendor Central face the same arithmetic one step removed. The notice applies to vendors’ shipments too, according to the CNBC report. The stock Amazon holds of a vendor’s non-priority products is just as fixed, and ads the vendor runs against it draw down units nobody can replace until the restriction lifts.

The arithmetic is the same in each case. Ads add sales only where another unit can be delivered after this one sells.

Five checks for products that cannot restock

  1. For every FBA product outside the priority list, divide units on hand by daily sales without ads. That is its runway.
  2. Compare each runway with the earliest realistic restock date, allowing for the April 5 expiry plus transit and receiving.
  3. Where the runway falls short, pause or cut ads and promotions until it does not. Where it runs well past the restock date, keep enough spend to defend visibility.
  4. Move the freed budget to priority-category products and to merchant-fulfilled offers that can ship from your own warehouse.
  5. Check prices before raising any; Amazon has been removing listings it judges to be price gouging, and an increase on an in-demand product can look like one.

Budgets that follow the stockout date rather than last month’s return on ad spend are the approach we take to Amazon advertising whenever supply, not demand, is the limit.

P0373.crumb: Beauty brands on Amazon: holding out…
P0373.title: Beauty brands on Amazon: holding out leaves resellers in charge
P0373.alt: Market stall of amber bottles and jars with blank tags, wooden spoons, dried flowers and baskets.
P0373.ttag: Beauty brands on Amazon: holding out leaves resellers in charge | Kwontified
P0373.desc: Salon and prestige beauty brands that stay off Amazon still appear there, sold by resellers at cut prices. The authorized-seller question starts at home.
P0373.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 26, 2020.
P0373.body:
Eufora International, a salon hair-care brand with more than 1,000 salon partners in North America, built an in-house team of ten people to track inventory that goes missing from salons and reappears on Amazon, Glossy reported in April 2019. When Amazon invited the brand to enroll in Brand Registry, its tool for brands fighting fakes and resellers, the chief executive declined. “I’m holding out,” she said.

Many salon and prestige beauty brands share that instinct, and it is easy to respect. It also rarely works. A beauty brand can decline to sell on Amazon, but its products arrive there anyway, through resellers supplied from somewhere in the brand’s own channel and priced however they like. For beauty brands on Amazon, the authorized-seller question is really two questions the brand controls: who in its own distribution is letting stock leak, and whether the brand wants a seat on the page where that stock is sold.

Where the unauthorized stock comes from

Salon brands sell a promise to their partners: professional products, sold only through professionals. The salon gets a reason for clients to buy in the chair, and the brand gets a premium position. That arrangement creates a gap between what a salon is allowed to sell and what it can sell, and diverted stock lives in that gap. A salon with too much inventory, a distributor with a quarter-end target, or a liquidator holding last season’s packaging all have a reason to find a buyer, and resellers on Amazon are buyers.

The Glossy piece captured what follows on the page. One beauty chief executive, speaking anonymously, said products on third-party marketplaces fail to move because resellers keep offering slashed prices. Virtue Labs’ founder put the problem more simply: “it is hard to control who sells your product and where they sell it.”

Her products had been on Amazon through a reseller since June 2018 before the brand had any presence of its own.

Price is where the damage shows. On a product page shared by several sellers, the lowest price, along with seller ratings and stock, largely decides who gets the order, as one longtime seller described in 2017. A reseller who bought diverted stock cheaply can sit below the salon’s shelf price indefinitely, and every shopper who checks Amazon before buying in the chair learns that the salon price is negotiable.

That is the hidden structure. The brand experiences the unauthorized seller as an Amazon problem. The units the seller holds came out of the brand’s own network, often through partners the brand chose, under contracts the brand wrote.

What a seat on Amazon changes

The brands that have stopped holding out have done so for control, not for volume. Virtue Labs planned to launch with Amazon as a first-party vendor in its Luxury Beauty store. Its founder’s reason: “we know Luxury Beauty can help the reseller problem.” Ziip, which sells a $495 skin-care device, joined the marketplace in late 2018 to control its own pricing, inventory and communications, according to the same report.

Prestige shoppers were already there. Amazon’s Luxury Beauty sales rose 57% to about $200 million in the first quarter of 2018, while professional salon and spa products rose 93%, One Click Retail data showed, as Global Cosmetics News reported. Those shoppers were buying salon brands whether or not the brands had chosen to be there.

Amazon has also shown that it will restrict who can sell when a brand negotiates. Under its November 2018 agreement with Apple, only Apple-authorized resellers may sell Apple products on Amazon’s marketplace in several countries, TechCrunch reported. Few beauty brands have Apple’s bargaining power. The example still matters, because it shows authorization on Amazon is something a brand negotiates from inside, not something it can impose from outside.

And the tools for removing fakes reward brands that register. Project Zero, launched in February 2019, lets brands in Brand Registry remove counterfeit listings themselves, TechCrunch reported. Those tools address fakes, not genuine diverted stock; a reseller selling real product bought from a salon is not a counterfeiter. That is why the contract side matters as much as the Amazon side.

Protecting the salon and owning the page are one decision

For a salon or prestige beauty brand, the debate in the leadership meeting usually sounds like a choice between protecting the salon channel and chasing Amazon’s shoppers. The evidence suggests that framing is wrong. The salon channel is already feeding Amazon. The real choice is between a page run by resellers at their prices and a page run by the brand, with diverted stock still to be traced and stopped through the channel.

A brand can take the second path without abandoning its salons. It can register its trademark and own the content on its pages, price at or above salon levels, and tighten distribution terms so that leaks are traceable and enforceable. Virtue Labs’ plan to price higher on Amazon to protect its salon and Sephora pricing is one model for arriving on Amazon without undercutting its partners.

Questions for the next channel review

  • Which of our products are on Amazon, who is selling them and at what price?
  • Do our salon and distributor agreements say where products may be resold, and do we ever enforce that?
  • Can we trace diverted units back to a partner, through lot codes or serialized packaging?
  • If we took over our Amazon pages, what price would protect our salon partners rather than undercut them?

A brand that answers those questions usually finds the authorized-seller problem was partly its own, and fixing both halves is the work we do in running Amazon for beauty brands alongside their salon and retail partners.

P0374.crumb: Amazon Posts is worth what its clicks…
P0374.title: Amazon Posts is worth what its clicks would cost you in ads
P0374.alt: A corkboard with blank pinned notes beside a glass jar of coins on a wooden desk by a teal wall.
P0374.ttag: Amazon Posts is worth what its clicks would cost you in ads | Kwontified
P0374.desc: Amazon Posts is free, but its value is the ad spend its clicks replace, discounted for weaker intent. Price Posts against your CPC before you staff it.
P0374.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 31, 2020.
P0374.body:
Amazon Posts arrived in beta last autumn as something unusual on Amazon: free. Brands publish images and captions to a feed, each post links to a product detail page, and there is no charge to take part, Digital Operative noted in October. Posts can appear on the brand’s own detail pages, on detail pages of related brands, and in feeds organized by category, in Amazon’s mobile shopping app.

Free invites two opposite mistakes: ignoring Amazon Posts because it never shows up in the ad budget, or handing it to a social media manager because free reach sounds like a gift. Both skip the calculation. Posts costs nothing to place, so its value is the paid clicks it replaces, discounted because people scrolling a feed convert less than people searching, minus the cost of making the posts.

For most brands that number is positive but modest. That argues for running Posts on content the brand already has, and against building a production line for it.

What Amazon Posts gives you, and what it reports

Posts works like a brand’s social feed transplanted onto Amazon. Each post carries category tags, so shoppers browsing a category can scroll into it, and engagement is reported as views, clicks and click-through rate, according to the Digital Operative write-up. At launch the program was free for US vendors with a Store, Pattern reported in October 2019, describing it as a new mobile feature with placements on brand pages, related brands’ pages and category feeds.

Notice what the metrics leave out. Neither description mentions sales. A Posts click lands on a detail page, and whatever happens next is not credited to the post in its own reporting. That is the first thing to test: the program shows activity, and the brand has to infer value.

Views deserve the most skepticism. A shopper scrolling a feed on a phone can pass dozens of posts in a minute, and each one she passes may count. A large view count therefore says more about how many feeds the post was placed in than about how many shoppers noticed it. Clicks are the first number with any intent behind them, which is why the valuation below starts there.

Price a free click like a paid one

The cleanest way to value a free click is to ask what the same click would have cost through Sponsored Products, then adjust for how likely it is to buy.

Take a brand whose Sponsored Products clicks cost $1.00 on average and convert at 10%. Its posts earn 60,000 views a month at a 0.4% click-through rate, which is 240 clicks. A shopper scrolling a feed is browsing, not searching for a product, so assume those clicks convert at half the rate of search clicks, 5%. Then 240 Posts clicks are worth about as much as 120 paid clicks, or $120 a month in ad spend the brand would otherwise need to buy the same orders.

Now the cost side. If a team member spends four hours a month making new posts at an internal cost of $50 an hour, that is $200, and Posts loses money. If the team reuses photography and captions already made for Instagram and spends one hour scheduling them, the cost is $50 and Posts returns more than twice its cost.

New contentReused content
Ad value of 240 clicks$120$120
Monthly production cost$200$50
Net value−$80$70

The point of the arithmetic is not the specific numbers, which every brand must replace with its own click costs, conversion rates and labor rates. It is that Posts has no media cost and a real production cost, so the production cost decides whether it pays.

Where the placement adds something ads do not

One feature changes the calculation in the brand’s favor. Posts can appear on related brands’ detail pages, which in practice means competitors’ pages, and the brand does not pay for the slot. A shopper looking at a rival’s product who taps a post lands on the brand’s page. The same visit bought through product-targeted ads would cost a click on a competitor’s page, often among the dearer clicks in an account, so the replacement value of these particular clicks can be higher than the average CPC suggests.

The reporting described so far, though, does not break views out by placement. Treat the competitor-page upside as possible, not counted.

Testing what the feed is worth

Because Posts reports no sales, the honest test is indirect. Start posting on a set of products and leave a comparable set without posts for six weeks. Compare detail-page sessions and units ordered on the two sets in the brand’s own sales reports, before and after. If the posted products gain sessions and the others do not, the feed is adding visits. If they move together, the clicks were coming anyway.

What would change my mind about Posts being a low-cost channel rather than a growth channel is evidence that its clicks convert like search clicks. If the test shows that, raise the assumed conversion rate and the value of each post roughly doubles.

Running Amazon Posts at the right cost

  1. Reuse existing social photography and captions; budget production time, not new shoots.
  2. Price Posts clicks at your Sponsored Products CPC times the conversion discount you measure, starting at half.
  3. Run a six-week posted-versus-unposted test on comparable products and read sessions and units, not views.
  4. Stop new production if the net value stays below zero after the test.

Putting a price on unpaid traffic is the same discipline we apply to every placement in Amazon advertising, paid or not.

P0375.crumb: Health and household on Amazon became a…
P0375.title: Health and household on Amazon became a rationed aisle in March
P0375.alt: A single paper towel roll on an otherwise empty, sunlit store shelf beside a dark blue wall.
P0375.ttag: Health and household on Amazon became a rationed aisle in March | Kwontified
P0375.desc: In March 2020 Amazon began deciding which health and household products get warehouse space, at what price and how fast they arrive. Brands must plan for it.
P0375.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 2, 2020.
P0375.body:
In the week ended March 7, US sales of hand sanitizer were up 470% from a year earlier, aerosol disinfectants 385%, thermometers 172% and first aid kits 112%, according to Nielsen figures reported by NPR. Toilet paper, the item that filled the photographs of empty shelves, was up a comparatively modest 60%. A week later the lines outside warehouse clubs were the news, and the same shoppers were placing the same orders on Amazon from their kitchens.

Health and household on Amazon has always been a category of habits: the same detergent every month, the same vitamins on Subscribe & Save, the brand chosen once and then reordered without thought. March turned it into something else. By the end of the month Amazon was deciding which products in the aisle got warehouse space, what prices sellers were allowed to charge and how long a delivery would take. For brands in the category, the question for the rest of 2020 is less whether shoppers want the product than how Amazon chooses to allocate it.

The shopper bought the job, not the brand

Look at the Nielsen list again and notice how many of the fastest risers are things a household buys once every few years. Nobody has a habitual thermometer brand. Few people could name the maker of the first aid kit in their hall cupboard. When a shopper buys something she has not bought since 2015, she arrives with no loyalty to defend. She types what the product does (“digital thermometer”, “disinfecting wipes”) and chooses from what the page shows her.

That is a different shopper from the one most health and household brands built their Amazon business around. The replenishment shopper rewards the brand that earned the first purchase. The stockpiling shopper rewards whichever product is on the page, in stock and arriving soon. In March, the second shopper outnumbered the first in the categories that mattered most.

Amazon took three decisions out of the brand’s hands

Warehouse space went to Amazon before anything else. On March 17 Amazon said it was “temporarily prioritizing household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products,” CNBC reported. It stopped accepting new inbound shipments outside six categories: baby; health and household; beauty and personal care; grocery; industrial and scientific; and pet supplies, TechCrunch reported. The limit was set to run until April 5.

A brand inside health and household kept its supply line. A brand one category over did not.

Price followed, and it is the decision brands feel least able to influence. Amazon had begun blocking and removing listings for masks and hand sanitizer sold at inflated prices by early March, Marketplace reported. By March 23 it had removed more than half a million offers and suspended more than 3,900 US selling accounts for “violating our fair pricing policies,” using what it called “dynamic, automated systems,” Fox Business reported. Those systems judge the offer, not the intent behind it, and in health and household many offers belong to resellers rather than to the brand.

Amazon also took over the delivery date. From March 22 some items showed delivery estimates of 30 days, even for Prime members, in the US, Canada, the UK and other European marketplaces, Marketplace Pulse found. Amazon said some of its delivery promises were “longer than usual.” The priority went to the essentials, which means the delivery date on a health and household page now depends on which side of Amazon’s list the product sits.

Read as an institution, Amazon behaved in March exactly as it always says it will. It protected the customer’s trust in the moment: the right product, at a price nobody will screenshot in anger, arriving as soon as the network allows. Everything else, including a seller’s margin and a brand’s launch calendar, came second. Health and household was the category where that promise was under the most strain, so it is the category where Amazon’s hand is now heaviest.

What the rationed aisle rewards

Follow the value and the winners are plain. A brand that sells to Amazon or through FBA in a priority category, priced where it was in February, holds the scarcest thing in the store: a product Amazon wants to show. A brand whose listing is carried mostly by resellers is exposed twice, because a reseller’s price jump can take the offer down and the brand has no say in how fast it comes back.

The harder part is what comes after. Households that bought a year of wipes in March will not buy wipes in May, and the shoppers who tried an unfamiliar thermometer or vitamin brand have now met it. The evidence so far leans toward a category with more first-time buyers and fuller cupboards: a sales line that falls back while the customer list grows. Brands that read only the sales line will cut budget just as their newest customers are deciding whether to reorder.

Questions for the April category review

  1. Which of our products sit inside Amazon’s priority categories, and which sit one category over?
  2. Who sells our products on Amazon right now, and at what prices did those offers sit during the last week of March?
  3. How many of March’s buyers were new to the brand, and what will bring them back once their stockpile runs down?
  4. If Amazon’s rationing lasts into the summer, which products do we want in its warehouses first?

Those are operating questions more than marketing ones. They are answered best by one person who runs the whole channel, which is the part of the work we take on for brands that sell health and household products on Amazon.

P0377.title: Out-of-stock Amazon ads hand their keywords to the next product
P0377.alt: A single corked amber bottle spotlit on a rustic wooden shelf, with apothecary jars on shelves around it.
P0377.ttag: Out-of-stock Amazon ads hand their keywords to the next product | Kwontified
P0377.desc: When a best seller runs out on Amazon, its Sponsored Products keywords keep bidding for whatever is left in the ad group, at the best seller’s price.
P0377.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 7, 2020.
P0377.body:
Say your best seller runs out of stock at Amazon in the last week of March, and its Sponsored Products campaign keeps spending its full daily budget while the sales it reports fall by two thirds. Nothing in the console looks broken. With FBA restocking limited this spring, that puzzle is going to show up in a lot of accounts.

The answer sits in how an ad group is built. When a product stops being eligible to advertise, it leaves the auction, but its keywords and bids do not. They keep bidding for every other product in the same ad group, at prices that were set for the product that left. Out-of-stock Amazon ads do not simply stop; they hand the job to the next product in line.

Why out-of-stock Amazon ads look harmless

The common belief is reasonable. Amazon will not serve a Sponsored Products ad for an item nobody can buy. Ads for products not winning the Buy Box are removed, Seller Labs explained in its guide to the program, and a seller with no stock cannot hold the Buy Box. Without inventory, as Portent put it, you cannot advertise.

So brands assume an empty shelf costs nothing in advertising. The ad goes quiet, the spend stops, and the account waits for the next shipment.

This spring the wait is long. On March 17 Amazon stopped creating new FBA inbound shipments for products outside six categories (baby, health and household, beauty and personal care, grocery, industrial and scientific, and pet supplies), TechCrunch reported. The limit was set to run until April 5 and could be extended. A brand selling sneakers, candles or kitchen tools through FBA cannot replace what sells, so stockouts are arriving product by product and staying.

What happens inside the ad group

An ad group holds products that share keywords and a default bid; Seller Labs describes manual ad groups as SKUs that share similar keywords with the same maximum default bid. The keywords are not attached to one product. They belong to the group, and Amazon serves whichever eligible product in the group fits the search.

Most brands build those groups around a hero. The hero earns the clicks, the reviews and the conversion rate, and the bids get raised until the hero’s numbers look right. The siblings ride along: other colors, other sizes, the older model, the accessory.

When the hero runs out, the group keeps working. Every keyword still bids at the price the hero justified, and the impressions now go to the siblings.

Take an ad group with a $50 hero that converts 12% of its clicks and a $50 sibling that converts 4%. The brand can spend $12.50 to win a sale, so the keyword “running shoes for women” was bid at $1.20, a little under the hero’s value of $1.50 per click ($12.50 times 12%).

Hero in stockHero out of stock
Product shownHeroSibling
Bid on the keyword$1.20$1.20
Conversion rate12%4%
Value of a click$1.50$0.50
Ad cost per sale$10.00$30.00

The same $1.20 click now costs $30 per sale against a $12.50 allowance. The account spends the same budget and buys a third of the sales. Nobody changed a setting.

The broader market makes it worse. Cost per click rose across nearly every category in March, with one agency client seeing a 20% rise in four days, and conversion rates for non-essential items fell by as much as 30%, Modern Retail reported on March 23. A sibling that converted 4% in February may convert less now, at a higher price per click.

There is a logic to Amazon’s side of this. The auction is doing exactly what it was asked: the brand bid $1.20 on a keyword for a group of products, and Amazon found an eligible product in that group to show. The bid describes what the brand will pay for the search. It never said which product the brand meant.

What the reports show and what they hide

The campaign report will show the damage only at the campaign level: spend steady, sales down, ACoS up. It will not say why, because the advertised product report has to be read product by product to see that the hero’s impressions went to zero on the same day the sibling’s tripled.

Two readings are possible, and they call for different fixes. If the sibling’s impressions rose when the hero stocked out, the group is reassigning the hero’s keywords, and the fix is structural. If impressions fell across the group, demand fell, and the fix is the bid.

Turning everything off is the wrong reflex. Agencies quoted in the same Modern Retail piece warned that pulling Amazon ads entirely can hurt a brand’s rankings and its future performance. The goal is to stop paying hero prices for sibling clicks, while keeping the products that do have stock visible.

How to set up Amazon ads for a stockout

Separate the hero. A best seller that carries most of a group’s sales belongs in its own ad group, so its keywords serve only it. When it runs out, those keywords go quiet with it, which is what the brand assumed was happening all along.

Price siblings on their own numbers. If a sibling deserves the hero’s keywords, give it those keywords in its own group at a bid built from its own conversion rate. In the example, that is $0.50 a click or less, not $1.20.

Read stock before you read ACoS. Check FBA inventory for every advertised product each morning while inbound shipments are restricted, and pause the hero’s ad group a few days before its last units sell, since Amazon cannot restock non-essential products until the limit lifts.

Keep one product per keyword where the money is. A shared bid is a promise to pay the same price for any product in the group, and a stockout is when that promise comes due. We run Amazon advertising with inventory in the same view for exactly this reason.

P0379.crumb: Mother’s Day 2020 gifts must travel, and…
P0379.title: Mother’s Day 2020 gifts must travel, and marketplaces sort them
P0379.alt: Open rear doors of a delivery van loaded with cardboard parcels around a kraft-wrapped spring flower bouquet.
P0379.ttag: Mother’s Day 2020 gifts must travel, and marketplaces sort them | Kwontified
P0379.desc: With brunch cancelled and families apart, Mother’s Day 2020 gifts move to marketplaces, where warehouse rules decide what arrives by May 10.
P0379.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 9, 2020.
P0379.body:
The fastest-growing Mother’s Day gift of the last few years was not a thing. In 2018, 55% of people celebrating planned a special outing, worth $4.4 billion, against $2.6 billion on flowers. And 29% of mothers said they would rather have an experience than an object, according to the National Retail Federation’s survey reported by Retail TouchPoints. Brunch, a spa afternoon, the drive over with the grandchildren: that was where the holiday was heading.

Mother’s Day 2020 falls on Sunday, May 10, and almost none of that is available. About 90% of Americans were living under stay-at-home or shelter-in-place orders by April 3, PBS NewsHour reported. The outing is cancelled, and for many families so is the visit. The money and the feeling behind them will look for somewhere to go, and much of it will go into a box shipped to a mother’s front door. On marketplaces in 2020, that box has to clear two hurdles most gift plans never considered: getting into a warehouse and getting out on time.

Mother’s Day 2020 turns the holiday into a delivery

The holiday was already large and growing. The NRF expected a record $25 billion of Mother’s Day spending in 2019, with 84% of adults celebrating and an average of $196 each, NACS reported at the time. In 2018, 31% of shoppers planned to buy online, close to the 35% who planned to visit a department store.

Those shares described a holiday that happened in person. Gift cards, planned by 45% of shoppers in 2018, were the one popular present with no delivery problem at all. In 2020 they are the quiet competitor for every product brand, because a gift that cannot be late looks safer to a giver who is worried about the post.

A daughter in Chicago and a mother in Phoenix used to split the difference: flowers delivered, a call, a visit when the fares were low. In 2020 the gift is the whole gesture. That changes what shoppers will value. They will look first for something certain to arrive before the Sunday, then for something that feels personal once it is unwrapped by a person who cannot see the giver’s face.

Think of the shopper on April 25 scrolling for a present. She is not comparing the scent notes of two candles. She is reading delivery dates.

The warehouse rule sorts the gift aisle

Delivery dates on Amazon this spring are set by a rule written for a different purpose. On March 17 Amazon stopped accepting new shipments into its warehouses outside six categories: baby; health and household; beauty and personal care; grocery; industrial and scientific; and pet supplies, TechCrunch reported. The limit was set to run until April 5.

Lay that list over the Mother’s Day aisle and the sorting is plain. A skincare set or a bath gift basket can be restocked. Jewelry, a robe, a photo frame or a candle sits outside the list, and can sell only what was already in Amazon’s warehouses or what the brand ships itself. Some non-essential items could take a month or longer to arrive, with April 21 dates showing on some products by late March, Fortune reported, citing Recode.

Nobody at Amazon designed this as a Mother’s Day policy. But a beauty brand and a jewelry brand that ran the same promotions in 2019 now face different shelves in the same week. One can refill its best-selling gift set before May. The other has to decide whether the units it has should go to Mother’s Day at all.

What gifting on marketplaces rewards this year

Read the behavior and the institution together, and a few kinds of brand look well placed.

Stock already in the right place beats a better product. A gift that sits in an Amazon warehouse with a Prime delivery date in the first week of May will win against a better gift with a vague one, because the shopper’s question is “will it get there”. Brands should check this week which of their gift products are actually in stock, and in which network, before they spend a dollar promoting them.

Brands that can ship on their own hold a second route. A brand with its own warehouse or a logistics partner, selling through merchant fulfillment on Amazon or through Walmart’s marketplace and its own site, controls its delivery dates while the FBA queue does not. That flexibility is worth more this May than any discount.

The parcel also has to arrive as a gift. When the giver is not in the room, the parcel carries the whole message: the packaging, a note, the way the product looks when it is lifted out of the box. Listings that show what the recipient will see, and that say plainly whether the item can be gift-wrapped or sent with a message, answer the questions this year’s shopper is asking. Everyday packaging that reads as a shipment of household goods does not.

The question for the Mother’s Day meeting

Most brands’ Mother’s Day plans were written in January around a promotion calendar: which products to discount, which ad campaigns to run, which hero image to change. The meeting worth having this week starts from a different place. It asks, product by product, whether the gift can reach a customer’s mother by May 10 through any channel, and only then how to promote it.

That meeting usually needs the e-commerce, supply chain and creative teams in one room, which is the work of running a channel day to day and the part we take on for brands planning gifting on Amazon and Walmart.

P0380.crumb: Amazon Live is free, but its free viewers…
P0380.title: Amazon Live is free, but its free viewers are your own shoppers
P0380.alt: A ring light and phone on a tripod filming handmade mugs on a table, with kraft bags on wooden chairs.
P0380.ttag: Amazon Live is free, but its free viewers are your own shoppers | Kwontified
P0380.desc: An Amazon Live stream costs nothing to broadcast, but the free placement mostly shows it to shoppers already on your product page. Count the new viewers.
P0380.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 14, 2020.
P0380.body:
Amazon charges a brand nothing to broadcast a live video onto its own product page. With most of the country at home this spring and store demonstrations on hold, that sounds like the cheapest new channel in retail. Yet brands that have tried it often struggle to say what a stream earned.

The reason is where the viewers come from. A stream’s free placement sits on the pages of the products it features, so most of the people who see it were already on those pages. The broadcast does not bring them; it meets them. Amazon Live pays only if it makes those shoppers buy more often than the page would have on its own, or if the brand pays to reach people who were not coming.

Why Amazon Live looks like free reach

The case for streaming is easy to make. Amazon launched Amazon Live in February 2019 as its answer to QVC, with hosts demonstrating products and a carousel beneath the video where viewers can buy, TechCrunch reported. The Amazon Live Creator app, released on February 7, 2019, lets US professional sellers registered in Brand Registry stream from an iPhone or a professional camera. Brands could already stream to their product pages, their Store and Amazon.com/live before the app arrived.

The early testimonial was striking. Watch Ya’ Mouth, a card game maker, tested the app early. It said live streaming increased daily visits to its product detail page five times and “significantly grew our sales.” No media cost, a phone, and five times the traffic: it is easy to see why the pitch spread.

The free placement mostly shows the stream to your own shoppers

A live stream has three possible sources of viewers. Shoppers already on a featured product’s detail page see it there. Shoppers browsing the Amazon Live section of the site and app see it if Amazon places it there. And shoppers anywhere else see it only if the brand pays to boost it, which TechCrunch described as a way to pay to reach more shoppers.

Only the first is guaranteed, and it is the brand’s own traffic. The second is real reach, but Amazon decides it. The Amazon Live section runs several streams at once and lets viewers watch recent recordings or see upcoming shows, Marketing Dive noted; which streams it features is Amazon’s call, not the brand’s. A shop assistant demonstrating a blender to people who have already walked into the shop can raise the share who buy. She cannot raise the number who walked in.

Take a $30 product whose detail page gets 800 visits a day and converts 12% of them. Spread evenly, about 33 of those visits fall in a one-hour stream.

During the live hour
Page visits33
Visitors who watch (say 30%)10
Conversion without the stream12%
Conversion for watchers (say 18%)18%
Extra sales0.6
Extra revenueabout $18

Even with a generous lift from 12% to 18%, the live hour on the page adds less than one sale. If the stream took three people an hour each to plan and present, the free broadcast cost more in time than it brought in. The numbers change if recordings keep playing on the page after the live hour, or if a large share of viewers arrive from somewhere else. That is where the five-fold traffic claim needs a careful read: visits that arrive through Amazon’s own placements or through paid boosting are new reach, and visits that were on the page anyway are not.

What the stream analytics show and what they leave out

The Creator app comes with analytics. Launch coverage listed total views, unmuted views and the budget spent on boosting among them. Those are attention measures. None of them says how many viewers would have been on the product page without the stream, and none of them is a sale.

That gap is the whole measurement problem, and it is the one a brand can close with its own reports.

Business Reports in Seller Central show sessions and conversion for each product by day. Compare the days a product was featured in a stream against matched days when it was not: same weekday, similar price, no other promotion. If sessions rose, the stream found new viewers. If sessions held and conversion rose, it persuaded existing ones. If neither moved, the views were the brand’s own shoppers watching a video instead of reading the page.

Boosting deserves the same treatment as any other ad. Divide what the boost cost by the extra sessions it produced, and compare that with what a Sponsored Products click on the same product costs. If a boosted viewer costs more than a click and converts no better, the click is the better buy.

Before the next Amazon Live stream

  1. Write down where you expect viewers to come from: the page, the Amazon Live section, or a boost. If the answer is mostly the page, the stream has to earn its keep through conversion.
  2. Feature products with real page traffic and a reason to be demonstrated, such as a gadget, a texture or a size question, where a live answer can change the decision.
  3. Run streams on alternate weeks for a month and compare sessions and conversion by product against the weeks without them.
  4. Price the boost per extra session, not per view, and hold it to the cost of a click.

Streams that pass those tests are worth the hours. The rest are a video of your own shoppers, which is the kind of question we answer when we run Amazon advertising and measure what each format adds.

P0382.crumb: Grocery on Amazon in 2020 has more…
P0382.title: Grocery on Amazon in 2020 has more shoppers than delivery slots
P0382.alt: Rows of paper grocery bags filled with bread and produce lined up along a brick alley wall by bicycles.
P0382.ttag: Grocery on Amazon in 2020 has more shoppers than delivery slots | Kwontified
P0382.desc: Online grocery use more than doubled in March 2020, but Amazon closed Pantry and waitlisted new Fresh customers. The new habit is forming at other stores.
P0382.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 16, 2020.
P0382.body:
In the last week of March, 31% of US households, about 39.5 million, said they had used an online grocery delivery or pickup service in the past month. In August 2019 the figure was 13%, Brick Meets Click found in its survey of 1,601 adults. That is roughly 23 million more households than seven months earlier, a shift that took about as long as planning a seasonal promotion.

Amazon, the company most people would name first when asked who sells things online, spent the same weeks turning grocery shoppers away. Grocery on Amazon in 2020 is really two businesses, and the pandemic pulled them apart. The boxed, shelf-stable aisle on Amazon.com kept shipping. The weekly shop, the service that would have turned those new households into Amazon grocery customers, stopped taking new ones.

What happened to grocery on Amazon this spring

The weekly-shop services closed one door at a time. Prime Pantry, which sends a box of everyday groceries and household goods, closed to new orders on March 19; a notice on the site said it was “temporarily closed” while Amazon restocked, CNBC reported.

On April 12 Amazon said new Amazon Fresh and Whole Foods Market delivery customers would be added to a wait list, with Amazon “increasing capacity each week” and inviting new customers in as it did, 6abc reported. It is building a feature that gives delivery customers a virtual “place in line” and hands out delivery windows first come, first served. Some Whole Foods stores have shortened their hours so staff can concentrate on online orders, and grocery pickup has grown from about 80 Whole Foods stores to more than 150.

The waitlist tells you what Amazon chose to protect. Faced with more demand than vans, it served the customers it already had and asked everyone else to queue, rather than spreading scarce delivery windows across all comers. For an institution that measures itself by repeat customers, that is a consistent choice. It also means the newcomers of March and April met Amazon grocery as a closed door.

Meanwhile the shelf-stable aisle never closed. When Amazon limited what its warehouses would receive on March 17, grocery was one of six categories it kept accepting, alongside baby, health and household, beauty and personal care, industrial and scientific, and pet supplies, TechCrunch reported. A case of canned beans or a multipack of crackers sold through Amazon.com could still be restocked, even while the same shopper could not book a Fresh delivery for her milk.

Why Amazon’s grocery capacity was small

The split is not an accident of the crisis. It reflects how Amazon built grocery. For most of the last decade the Grocery & Gourmet aisle on Amazon.com has worked like the rest of the site: packaged products, shipped in a box, often in multipacks that make the shipping pay. The weekly shop of fresh food, chilled goods and a full basket ran through separate, smaller services, each with its own vans, stores or warehouses.

Compare that with the grocers whose stores are the warehouse. Walmart had more than 2,700 grocery pickup locations by August 2019, it said with its second-quarter results. Instacart, which shops from existing supermarkets, said on March 23 it would hire 300,000 more shoppers over three months, roughly doubling its workforce, after order volume rose 150% from a year earlier, Supermarket News reported. Amazon’s 150 Whole Foods pickup stores are a fraction of either network.

In the planning meetings of most food brands, “Amazon” has meant the Amazon.com aisle and its account team, while “grocery” has meant the supermarket buyers. The weekly-shop services fell between the two, too small to earn their own plan. That gap made sense when Fresh and Pantry served a modest slice of households. It matters more now that tens of millions of households are deciding where they will do their online shopping.

Where the new habit is forming

A household’s first online grocery order is a decision about routine. Once a family has its list saved, its pickup time chosen and its substitution preferences set with one grocer, the second order is easier there than anywhere else. The evidence so far leans toward the March and April newcomers forming that routine with whoever had a delivery window or a pickup slot when they needed one. In most of the country in those weeks, that was more often a supermarket, a Walmart or an Instacart shopper than Amazon Fresh.

None of that shrinks the Amazon.com grocery aisle. If anything, households that cannot get a Fresh slot will order more boxed staples there. But it does mean that the online weekly shop, the part of grocery that could have grown fastest on Amazon in 2020, is being won elsewhere while Amazon’s own services hold a line of waiting customers.

Questions for the grocery team this week

  1. Which of our products sell on the Amazon.com aisle, which on Fresh and Whole Foods, and does anyone own the second list?
  2. Are our shelf-stable products packed and priced for shipping in a box, and are they in stock in Amazon’s warehouses while grocery stays on Amazon’s priority list?
  3. Which grocers and services are signing up the new online households in our markets, and is our digital shelf there as good as it is on Amazon?
  4. When Amazon starts inviting waitlisted customers in, will our products be the ones they see first?

Answering them takes someone who looks across every online shelf a brand sits on, which is the day-to-day channel work we do for food and household brands selling grocery on Amazon and Walmart.

P0384.crumb: Amazon Vine buys a new product an honest…
P0384.title: Amazon Vine buys a new product an honest verdict, not a good one
P0384.alt: Open cardboard box holding a ceramic mug beside a blank card and brass magnifying glass on a wooden desk.
P0384.ttag: Amazon Vine buys a new product an honest verdict, not a good one | Kwontified
P0384.desc: Amazon Vine lets brands seed early reviews within the rules, but Amazon picks the reviewers and the stars. Enroll only products ready to be judged.
P0384.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 21, 2020.
P0384.body:
Before October 2016, a brand could ship free products to strangers in exchange for an “honest” review, provided the reviewer disclosed it. ReviewMeta studied more than 7 million reviews and found that products reviewed that way averaged 4.74 stars against 4.36 for the rest, enough to move a product from the 54th to the 94th percentile, TechCrunch reported. Incentivized reviewers were 12 times less likely to give one star. On October 3, 2016, Amazon banned the practice in every category except books, with one exception: its own Vine program.

That exception is now open to brands that sell through Seller Central, and it is the only sanctioned way to put free product in front of reviewers. But the reason Vine survived the ban is the reason it behaves differently from what it replaced. Amazon chooses the reviewers, and the brand never touches the rating. Amazon Vine buys a new product an early verdict. Whether the verdict is good depends on the product.

Why Amazon Vine looks like the old review program

The appeal is easy to see. A product with no reviews starts every search at a disadvantage. The Spiegel Research Center at Northwestern found that a product with five reviews is 270% more likely to be bought than one with none, and that the effect is larger for higher-priced products, according to its study of online reviews.

Vine supplies those first reviews. To enroll, a seller must be in Brand Registry, the product must be fulfilled by FBA, in new condition and already live, and its listing must have fewer than 30 reviews, Feedvisor explained in January. Amazon gives the enrolled units free to Vine members, who can start requesting them 24 hours after enrollment. Once the product reaches 30 reviews, the enrollment ends and unclaimed units can no longer be requested.

So far it sounds like the pre-2016 playbook with Amazon’s blessing: give product away, collect reviews, climb the search results.

Amazon holds the one lever that mattered

The old programs worked because the seller chose the reviewer. A reviewer who wanted the next free product had every reason to be kind, and the ReviewMeta numbers show it. Vine removes that lever.

Amazon invites Vine members based on the helpfulness and quality of their past reviews; customers cannot apply. Sellers have no contact with Vine reviewers and cannot influence who receives their products, TechCrunch reported in 2016. Contacting a Vine reviewer about a review, even a negative one, breaks the program’s terms.

Amazon was explicit about its side of the bargain. “We do not incentivize positive star ratings, attempt to influence the content of reviews,” Chee Chew, Amazon’s vice president of customer experience, said when the ban took effect. He added that Amazon limits the total number of Vine reviews it displays for each product.

The comparison that fits is a restaurant inviting critics it cannot choose. The invitation guarantees a review, early and from someone who knows the cuisine. It does not guarantee a kind one. A dish that is not ready gets written up anyway.

The brand keeps two decisions: which product to enroll, and how many units to give. Everything after that belongs to Amazon and the reviewers.

What the units cost, and when they pay

Take a new $40 product that costs the brand $13 a unit to make and send into FBA. Enrolling 20 units costs $260 in product. Say those units produce 15 reviews averaging between four and 4.7 stars. The product moves from no reviews to the rating band where Spiegel found purchase likelihood peaks, and the $260 is likely the cheapest conversion gain the product will ever buy.

If the same 15 reviews average three stars, the $260 has bought something worse than nothing. A three-star average sits beside the product in every search result for months, and a product that might have been fixed quietly after a few dozen private complaints now carries a public verdict. Vine did exactly what it promised. The product was not ready.

That is why Vine rewards confidence, not marketing. The units are the fee, and the product’s quality decides the return.

This spring adds a second cost. Vine requires FBA, and since March 17 Amazon has accepted new FBA inventory only in priority categories, TechCrunch reported. On April 13 Amazon said it would let more products in, but “limited by quantity,” Engadget reported. For a non-essential product launching now, every Vine unit is a unit that cannot be sold from a capped allowance.

Rules for using Amazon Vine within the rules

  1. Enroll only products that have already passed a small test with real buyers, such as early sales on your own site or a first batch with a low return rate. Vine amplifies a verdict; it does not improve one.
  2. Size the enrollment to the decision you need. Once enough honest reviews have arrived to show the product’s rating, more units mostly add cost, and enrollment ends at 30 reviews in any case.
  3. Fix the listing before the units ship. Reviewers judge the product against the page, so a size chart or ingredient list that is wrong will show up in the stars.
  4. Count Vine units against your FBA allowance while Amazon caps inbound quantities, and launch first in the products where a review moves the most money.

None of this needs a workaround, and that is the point of Vine. It is the rule-abiding way to start a product’s reviews, and it works best for brands willing to be judged early, which is the kind of launch plan we build when we run Amazon for brands.

P0386.crumb: The Walmart online shopper now starts…
P0386.title: The Walmart online shopper now starts with a grocery list
P0386.alt: Blue wire basket with reusable bags and a bowl of fresh fruit below a blank list clipped to a teal kitchen wall.
P0386.ttag: The Walmart online shopper now starts with a grocery list | Kwontified
P0386.desc: Over the past year the Walmart online shopper became, above all, a grocery shopper. In April 2020 that path runs through pickup and the grocery app.
P0386.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 23, 2020.
P0386.body:
On April 5, the most downloaded shopping app in the United States was not Amazon’s. It was Walmart Grocery, with average daily downloads up 460% from January and 20% more downloads than Amazon’s app, according to App Annie data reported by TechCrunch. A Walmart spokesperson put it simply: “pickup and delivery are more important now than ever.”

That chart describes a shopper who has been taking shape at Walmart for a year, and the pandemic only sped her up. The Walmart online shopper does not usually begin with a product search the way an Amazon shopper does. She begins with the weekly grocery list, picks a pickup time at her local store, and adds the other things she needs to the same basket. For brands, that changes where the online shelf really sits.

A year of Walmart growth came through the grocery basket

Read Walmart’s own reports from the past four quarters and the pattern is consistent. In May 2019 Walmart reported US e-commerce sales up 37% for the quarter, with online grocery named first among the drivers, alongside Home and Fashion on Walmart.com, its earnings release said. In August it reported another 37% rise, again with strong online grocery growth, more than 2,700 grocery pickup locations and NextDay delivery reaching about 75% of the US population, according to the release.

The growth held through the holidays. US e-commerce sales rose 41% in the quarter to October, Walmart said in November. They rose 35% in the quarter to January, for 37% over the fiscal year, Walmart said in February, while guiding to about 30% growth for the year ahead, its fourth-quarter release showed. The same release noted softness in a few general merchandise categories in US stores.

None of this means Walmart.com sells only food. NextDay, launched in May 2019, offered about 220,000 frequently bought items from the fulfillment center nearest the customer, AP reported. But the item Walmart talked about first, quarter after quarter, was the grocery order, collected in a car park.

The store became the warehouse

That shopper exists because Walmart rebuilt its stores around her, and then its organization. In July 2019 Walmart combined the supply chain and finance teams of its US stores and its US e-commerce business, while keeping merchandising separate, Talk Business & Politics reported from a memo by chief executive Doug McMillon. Moving inventory and money as one business is what a retailer does when the store shelf and the online order draw on the same stock.

The shift in shoppers is wider than Walmart. In the last week of March, 31% of US households said they had used online grocery delivery or pickup in the past month, against 13% in August 2019, Brick Meets Click found. Walmart, with a pickup point in thousands of car parks, was the obvious place for many of them to start.

The people are part of the build. At NRF in January, Walmart US chief executive John Furner described one store with more than 60 people working in grocery click-and-collect, a job that did not exist five years earlier, Supermarket News reported.

Follow the value and it becomes clear what Walmart is protecting. Amazon’s online shopper begins on a search results page that Amazon controls end to end. Walmart’s online shopper begins with a list of things she buys every week, at prices she already knows from the aisle, from a store a few miles away. The grocery basket is the habit Walmart owns and Amazon does not, and every general merchandise item added to that basket rides on it.

In April that advantage became visible. Walmart has been hiring around 5,000 people a day since March toward a target of 150,000, TechCrunch reported. Its grocery app topped the shopping charts while Amazon was putting new grocery delivery customers on a waitlist.

What the basket shopper means for brands

The practical difference is where a brand’s online sale is decided. On Amazon, it is decided in search, product by product, and a brand can buy its way into the results. In a Walmart grocery basket, much of it is decided by what the shopper already buys, what the local store has in stock, and what appears when she reorders. A product that is not stocked in her store may never reach her pickup basket, however good its Walmart.com listing.

That puts the store team back at the center of the online plan. The buyer relationship, the store assortment and in-store availability are now online questions too, because the basket draws on them. Brands that treat Walmart.com as a second Amazon, run by the same team with the same playbook, plan for a search shopper that is only part of Walmart’s online business.

It is too early to say how much of April’s surge will stay once stores are fully open again. The evidence of the past year leans toward a durable habit. Walmart’s online growth was built on grocery before the pandemic, and households who have now set up their pickup routine have little reason to drop it.

Questions for the Walmart team

  1. Which of our products are bought in the Walmart grocery basket, and which only through Walmart.com search?
  2. Are our products in stock in the stores that serve pickup orders, and who checks?
  3. Does our Walmart online plan sit with the team that manages the buyer, the team that runs Amazon, or nobody?
  4. When a shopper reorders her usual basket, what would make our product the one she adds?

Answering them means running Walmart’s stores and website as one channel, which is the work we do for brands that sell through Walmart and its marketplace.

P0387.crumb: The Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmark averages…
P0387.title: The Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmark averages two different markets
P0387.alt: Divided plate with a slice of raspberry chocolate cake on one side and buttered bread on the other, on a rustic table.
P0387.ttag: The Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmark averages two different markets | Kwontified
P0387.desc: Public Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmarks show Sponsored Products spend up 24% and CPCs up 9%, but the quarter mixes a normal market and a disrupted one.
P0387.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 28, 2020.
P0387.body:
The first public read on Amazon advertising in the first quarter of 2020 arrived on April 27, when ChannelX summarized Tinuiti’s Amazon Ads Benchmark Report for the quarter. Here are its headline numbers, measured year over year across Tinuiti’s clients.

Year over yearQ1 2020Q4 2019
Sponsored Products spend+24%+30%
Sponsored Products sales+19%not stated
Sponsored Products clicks+14%not stated
Sponsored Products CPC+9%+12%
Sponsored Brands spend+47%+27%
Sponsored Brands sales+57%not stated

Read as a quarter, the story is calm: growth slowed, click prices rose a little less than before, and Sponsored Brands took a bigger share. That calm is mostly an artifact of averaging. The quarter contained two markets, roughly ten ordinary weeks and three disrupted ones after the middle of March, and a quarterly number blends them into a market that never existed. Brands comparing their own accounts to this Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmark should split the quarter before they compare.

What the Q1 2020 Amazon ad benchmark says on its face

Start with the arithmetic the table allows. Spend growth of 24% is almost exactly clicks up 14% times CPC up 9% (1.14 × 1.09 is about 1.24), so the money went where the report says: somewhat more clicks at somewhat higher prices.

Sales grew less than spend, 19% against 24%. Divide one by the other (1.19 ÷ 1.24) and return on ad spend for the average client fell by about 4% year over year. Sales per click rose about 4% (1.19 ÷ 1.14), so shoppers who clicked bought a little more, but not enough to cover the dearer clicks.

Sponsored Brands is the other headline. Spend growth jumped from 27% to 47%, and attributed sales grew 57%, faster than spend. Tinuiti’s CPC growth of 9% was the first slowdown in three quarters. On the quarter’s averages, then, Amazon advertising became slightly less efficient and more concentrated in branded formats.

Amazon DSP moved the other way on price. Spend rose 4% from the fourth quarter while the cost per thousand impressions fell 26%, and DSP spend held roughly steady through March as CPMs fell from February, the same report found.

Why the quarterly average misleads this time

Every quarterly benchmark is an average, and averages are reasonable when the weeks inside them look alike. In the first quarter of 2020 they did not. The same report shows the break. Between March 11 and March 21, 87% of Sponsored Products conversions happened within 24 hours of the ad click, against 84% from January 1 to March 10, as shoppers bought faster. In the last week of the quarter, ad impressions were down more than 30% year over year, mostly from search placements below the top of the page, though clicks barely moved because those placements had very low click-through rates.

Outside the report, the March weeks looked nothing like January. Agencies told Modern Retail on March 23 that CPCs had risen in nearly every category, one client by 20% in four days, while conversion on non-essential items fell by as much as 30%. On March 17 Amazon stopped accepting new FBA inventory outside six priority categories, TechCrunch reported, so many advertised products were selling down stock they could not replace.

Put a ten-week market and a three-week market into one number and the result describes neither. A brand selling cleaning supplies and a brand selling luggage can both sit near the 24% average for different reasons: one because March spend exploded, the other because it collapsed. The pull to anchor on a headline figure is strong, especially when it is the only public number available. For January to March 2020 it should be resisted.

April adds a further break. Among more than 150 long-running advertisers, Sponsored Products sales on April 15, as government stimulus payments reached bank accounts, were 41% above the average for the first two weeks of the month, and April 16 was 33% above it, Tinuiti found. Whatever Q2 looks like, it will not look like the second half of March either.

How to read your own account against it

The useful comparison is by period, using the break the report itself points to. Pull your Sponsored Products results for January 1 to March 10 and compare them with the same weeks of 2019. That is the closest thing to a normal-market benchmark, and the place to judge whether your bids and structure were sound.

Then pull March 11 to March 31 separately, by product rather than by campaign, and sort the products into three groups: in a priority category with stock, outside it with stock, and out of stock. The averages above mean little for the third group and something different for each of the first two.

Finally, set aside the stimulus days in mid-April when you read Q2 so far. A spike that came from cash arriving in bank accounts is not evidence that a bid change worked.

Benchmark checks for this quarter

  1. Compare January 1 to March 10 against the same weeks of 2019, not the whole quarter.
  2. Read March by product group: priority category in stock, other category in stock, out of stock.
  3. Check whether your ROAS moved with price (CPC) or with shoppers (sales per click); in the benchmark, CPC rose 9% and sales per click about 4%.
  4. Mark April 15 and 16 in your Q2 reporting before anyone credits them to a campaign.

A benchmark is a reference point, not a target, and in a quarter like this one it helps only after the account has been split the same way. Setting those baselines is the kind of measurement work we do on Amazon accounts.

P0388.crumb: Zalando fit and returns decide the sale…
P0388.title: Zalando fit and returns decide the sale long after the order
P0388.alt: Linen shirt on a wooden hanger draped with a tape measure, beside a shipping box and a brass hourglass.
P0388.ttag: Zalando fit and returns decide the sale long after the order | Kwontified
P0388.desc: On Zalando about half of what sells comes back, so a sale counts only when the shopper keeps the size. Brands arriving this spring must plan for fit first.
P0388.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 30, 2020.
P0388.body:
In Zalando’s fitting rooms, models try on as many as 120 pairs of shoes a day, measuring heel, ankle and toe, and three models’ judgments are averaged because fit is subjective. They flag about 30% of stock as too big or too small, Reuters reported in December 2018. “We immediately know there is a fitting problem,” said Stacia Carr, the engineering director who runs the work.

Nobody pays people to try on shoes all day unless something expensive depends on it. At Zalando, about half of the products sold are sent back, the same Reuters report found, so what depends on it is the sale itself. The order is only the start. The sale is made, or unmade, when the parcel is opened and the shopper decides whether it fits. For the brands moving onto Zalando this spring as European stores close, that makes size and fit information the core of every listing, not an afterthought.

How Zalando’s shopper buys

The behavior has deep roots. Germany’s long tradition of catalogue shopping with free returns made customers comfortable sending things back, Reuters noted, and Zalando built its business on the same promise. Brands that join its Partner Program are chosen partly on whether they can meet shoppers’ expectations of free delivery and a 100-day return period, Zalando said when it opened the program in Norway in 2018. Zalando’s management called a return rate of around half normal as early as 2013, Twinkle reported.

So the European shopper on Zalando shops the way she would in a fitting room.

She orders the dress in two sizes, keeps one and sends the other back. She orders boots she is unsure about because sending them back costs her nothing. Dresses, the top-selling category, have the highest return rate. To her, a return is not a complaint. It is part of how she chooses.

The hidden structure behind half the parcels

Once returns are part of buying, fit becomes the business. Every item that comes back has to be shipped, checked, repackaged and sold again, often at a lower price later in the season. Problems processing returns contributed to Zalando’s third-quarter loss in 2018, Reuters reported, and co-chief executive Rubin Ritter named size recommendations as one way to improve profitability on smaller orders.

That is why Zalando treats fit as an engineering problem. It combines what shoppers keep and return with the fitting models’ verdicts, and it learns things a brand’s own sales report never shows. “We know the Nordics like things more loose and oversized,” Carr said. When size-related returns soared for one denim brand after a design change, Zalando flagged it and the brand changed the design back. Carr also pointed at a cause that sits inside the brand: when production is rushed, “the corners that get cut sometimes impact the fit of the garment.”

Follow the value and the picture is clear. On the Partner Program a brand sells its own stock, so a returned dress that ends up marked down is the brand’s loss, while the knowledge of why products come back sits with Zalando. A brand that does not ask for that knowledge is paying for returns it could have prevented.

Why it matters more this spring

The spring of 2020 is sending a new wave of brands and shoppers onto the platform. Zalando said on April 16 that demand fell after social distancing began across Europe, with gross merchandise volume down 8% year over year in the three weeks after March 9. It grew again in the two weeks after March 30, FashionUnited reported. Active customers reached 32 million at the end of March, up 17%.

Partners sold more than a million items over the Easter weekend, more than double a year earlier, and shops in its Connected Retail program, which lets physical stores sell through Zalando, sold around 35,000 items.

Zalando is courting those stores directly. It waived its commission for all new and existing Connected Retail stores from April 1 to May 31, FashionNetwork reported. “For the fashion industry, the time to go online is now,” Ritter said.

Many of the brands and shops arriving this spring sold mostly in stores, where the fitting room did the work of matching body and size before the till. On Zalando the shopper’s sofa is the fitting room, and someone pays for the parcel’s trip both ways. A store that lists its range quickly, with the size chart from its supplier and photographs that show nothing about cut, will meet Zalando’s return rate head on.

The evidence so far leans toward fit as the factor that separates profitable Zalando brands from merely busy ones. It is too early to say how many of this spring’s new shoppers will stay online when stores reopen. But every one of them is learning how the brand’s sizes run, and that lesson is hard to unlearn.

Questions for a brand selling on Zalando

  1. What is our return rate on Zalando by product and size, and how does it compare with what Zalando sees across the category?
  2. Have we asked Zalando what its fit data says about our products, and who on our team would act on it?
  3. Do our listings tell a shopper how each item fits, in words and pictures, or only which sizes exist?
  4. When a product’s returns rise, does anyone check whether production changed?

Brands that answer those questions before they scale tend to keep more of what they sell, and that is the part of launching and running Zalando we take on for fashion brands entering Europe.
