P0390.crumb: Amazon Q1 2020 other revenue grew 44% and…
P0390.title: Amazon Q1 2020 other revenue grew 44% and barely saw March
P0390.alt: Tall stack of gold coins beside a white jar of yellow daffodils on a wooden table by a window.
P0390.ttag: Amazon Q1 2020 other revenue grew 44% and barely saw March | Kwontified
P0390.desc: Amazon’s ad line grew 44% in Q1 2020, but one bad week moves a quarterly rate by a thirteenth. Read April in your own CPC and conversion data instead.
P0390.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 5, 2020.
P0390.body:
Amazon’s “other” revenue, the line that holds its advertising business, rose 44% to $3.91 billion in the first quarter of 2020, the company reported on April 30. Over the same weeks, the typical Amazon advertiser cut its daily spend in the last week of March to half of what it spent in January, according to Merkle data cited by Digiday.

Both numbers are true. The puzzle is how an ad business can grow faster than it did in the fourth quarter while its customers halve their budgets.

The answer is arithmetic rather than spin. A quarterly growth rate is an average of 13 weeks, and a collapse confined to the last two of them barely moves it. The 44% tells you where Amazon’s auction was heading in January and February. It says very little about the auction you are bidding in this week.

Why the Amazon Q1 2020 other revenue figure looks like an all-clear

It is natural to read the number as a stress test passed. Amazon does not report advertising on its own line, so other revenue is the best public proxy. From January to March it outgrew everything around it: online stores rose 24% to $36.7 billion and third-party seller services 30% to $14.5 billion, Marketing Dive reported. Chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said ad growth was in line with the fourth quarter, when it ran at about 40%, according to AdExchanger. Other revenue grew 41% in the fourth quarter of 2019, so on its face nothing slowed.

Olsavsky also gave the reason to expect resilience. “A large portion of our advertising relates to Amazon sales, not things like travel and auto off-site,” he said on the call. Search ads sit next to shoppers who are already buying, and shoppers were buying.

That reading leans on recency in reverse. After weeks of bad news, a strong headline number feels like the latest information. It is not. It is the oldest information in the release, averaged over a period that began before anyone outside a few industries had changed a budget.

One bad week is a thirteenth of a quarter

Tinuiti, which analyzed $400 million of US ad spend, found that Sponsored Products spend had been growing 25% or more for much of the quarter before slowing to 6% in the final week of March, Digiday reported.

Run that through a quarter. Twelve weeks at 25% growth and one week at 6%, on an equal weekly base, average out at about 23.5%. The final week grew at a quarter of the earlier rate, and the quarterly figure fell by a point and a half. Make it two bad weeks and the average still looks like a strong quarter. A quarterly rate can only register a shock in proportion to its share of the 13 weeks.

Amazon’s own commentary fits that pattern. Olsavsky said the company saw “some pullback from advertisers and some downward pressure on price” in March. It was “probably offset a bit by the continued strong traffic we have to the site,” he added. Prices fell, budgets shrank, and traffic rose, all in the last stretch of the quarter. The 44% averages those weeks with the calmer ones before them.

The release itself points to where the weight now sits. Amazon guided second-quarter net sales to between $75.0 billion and $81.0 billion and expects about $4 billion of COVID-19 costs in that quarter. The second quarter is the first that will be all crisis, from its first week to its last.

What the other revenue line can and cannot tell a brand

It can tell you the direction of the auction over a year. Advertising growing faster than the retail it sits beside means more advertisers are competing for each sale on the site, and that pressure does not reverse because of one quarter.

It cannot tell you this week’s price, and it cannot separate a price effect from a volume effect. Amazon’s traffic rose while its click prices fell, and a single revenue figure nets the two together. If the second-quarter line holds near 40% with prices still down, the growth is coming from volume, which is a different auction to bid in than one where every click costs more. That is the figure that would change the reading, and it will not exist for months.

For this week’s price, the account is the better instrument, and it is moving fast. Daniel Tejada of the agency Straight Up Growth saw cost per click fall by as much as 30% in April, according to Digiday, while Tinuiti measured conversion rates averaging 10% lower over the last two weeks of March.

Those two changes partly cancel. Say a $30 product spends $1,000 a day on Sponsored Products at a $1.00 cost per click and converts 10% of clicks. Each sale costs $10.00 in ads. Cut the click price to $0.70 and the conversion rate to 9%, and each sale costs about $7.78. Cheaper, but not 30% cheaper, and only for a product that is in stock and promising a delivery date shoppers will accept.

Reading April without waiting for July

The second-quarter results will not arrive for another three months, long after the decisions they describe. Until then, the useful numbers are weekly and your own.

  1. Track cost per click and conversion rate by week, not by month, for your top 20 keywords, and compute cost per sale from the two.
  2. Compare each week with the same keywords in early February, before demand and supply both moved.
  3. Where clicks are cheaper and the product can ship, raise budgets in steps and watch whether cost per sale holds.
  4. Treat any quarterly figure, Amazon’s or your own, as an average whose last weeks count for one thirteenth each.

Reading the weekly auction rather than the quarterly headline is how we run Amazon advertising while the market is still moving week to week.

P0391.title: Panic brand switching sticks where shoppers reorder by habit
P0391.alt: Row of glass pantry jars filled with oats, flour and lentils on a painted wooden shelf.
P0391.ttag: Panic brand switching sticks where shoppers reorder by habit | Kwontified
P0391.desc: Two-thirds of US shoppers tried a new brand this spring, mostly because theirs was gone. The ones they keep are the ones their order history now remembers.
P0391.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 7, 2020.
P0391.body:
Take a household that has bought the same paper towels for years. In the third week of March, the usual brand is out of stock online and the store shelf is bare. The order goes through with whatever is available: a two-pack from a brand nobody in the house has heard of, or the retailer’s own label. In April, when it is time to buy again, the order history shows the substitute, one tap from the cart. The old brand is back in stock somewhere, but the shopper has to go looking for it.

That small scene is happening across most of the grocery and household aisle, and it decides which panic purchases become habits. Shoppers will keep many of the brands they tried this spring. Whether they keep any given one depends less on how they felt about it than on where the next purchase happens, and online, the next purchase starts from the last one.

Brand switching was forced, and it was wide

The trial itself is not in doubt. In an AlixPartners survey reported on April 20, 65% of US consumers said they had tried new brands during the pandemic, and 79% of them said they did so because their usual choice was out of stock, according to NACS Daily. Trial ran higher for unfamiliar store brands, at roughly 15% to 25% of shoppers, than for other national brands, at roughly 10% to 20%.

The sales data shows the same tilt. In the first quarter, store brand dollar sales rose 14.6% against 11.5% for national brands, and unit sales 12.8% against 9.2%, in Nielsen figures released by the Private Label Manufacturers Association, Grocery Dive reported. The constraint was supply, not demand. “Our private brand sales are through the roof, but the biggest challenge has been staying in stock,” Thrive Market’s Jeremiah McElwee told the publication.

What shoppers say about keeping their discoveries is softer. AlixPartners’ Randy Burt said consumers suggest they will stay with the brands they tried “at a pretty high rate.” The categories where store brands look most likely to stick are confectionery, nut butters, pasta, snacks and staples such as dairy and bread. Those are the purchases a household makes most often and thinks about least.

Where the purchase happens decides what gets kept

That category list is the clue. A frequent, low-attention purchase is rarely a fresh decision. It is a routine, and a routine runs on whatever is easiest to repeat.

In a store, the routine is a walk to the same spot on the shelf, and a brand that comes back into stock reclaims its place by being there. Online, the routine is stored. An order history, a subscription or a saved grocery list holds the last item bought and offers it again. The substitute that arrived in March is now the default, and the original brand, however loved, has to be found through search and chosen again, against a product the shopper has already received, used and not complained about.

More of the routine has just moved online. Target’s comparable digital sales were up more than 275% in April to date, while its stores fell by the mid-teens, the company said in a business update. Instacart said in March that orders had grown more than 150% from a year earlier. Every one of those new online households now has an order history, and much of it was written during a shortage.

The value in that shift flows to whoever filled the gap. A retailer’s own label captures the margin and the reorder. A smaller brand that happened to have stock in March gets something it could never have bought with advertising: a place in the household’s routine, earned in a week when the leader could not ship.

The comeback happens in a place brand teams rarely look

Most brand organizations track loyalty through store scan data and share reports built on it. Those numbers will show the leader returning as its stock recovers, and they may look reassuring. What they will not show is the online reorder share: of the households that bought the brand online before March, how many have bought it again since, and how many reordered the substitute instead. At many brands, nobody owns that number, because the online team reports sales and the brand team reports share, and the reorder sits between the two.

It is too early to say how much of the switching will last. Shoppers say they will keep a good part of it; shoppers also say many things in surveys. The evidence leans toward the reorder being the deciding moment, because it is the first time a shopper chooses between the old brand and the new one with both in stock.

Questions for the restock plan

The useful questions are about the reorder, and they belong in the plan for the day each product comes back into stock.

  • Of last year’s repeat online buyers, how many have bought from us since March, and how many have bought the substitute?
  • When our hero product returns, what does a shopper who bought the substitute see when they search our category, and is our product at the top of that page?
  • Which of our products did shoppers buy on subscription before March, and did those subscriptions survive the stockout or quietly move to another brand?
  • Who in the company owns online reorder share, and is it in anyone’s targets?

The first week back in stock is the cheapest moment to win a household back, because the substitute has not yet become a habit twice. Winning it back is mostly channel work, the listings, search placement and subscription offers that sit around the reorder, and it is the part of running Amazon and Walmart day to day that matters most this summer.

P0392.crumb: With FBA restock limits lifted, IPI…
P0392.title: With FBA restock limits lifted, IPI decides next quarter’s space
P0392.alt: Industrial metal and wood shelving with a brass gauge, cardboard boxes, rope and crates against a mint green wall.
P0392.ttag: With FBA restock limits lifted, IPI decides next quarter’s space | Kwontified
P0392.desc: Amazon lifted its FBA quantity limits on May 9. Sending every slow seller now lowers IPI and can shrink next quarter’s storage space for everything.
P0392.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 12, 2020.
P0392.body:
For most of April, Amazon rationed its warehouses. “Products will be limited by quantity,” the company said on April 13 as it let non-essential goods back into FBA, Engadget reported, and capped items carried a “Limited restock” tag, according to the notice Amazon sent European sellers, quoted by ChannelX. Then the ration ended. “Since May 9, 2020, we have removed quantity limits on products you can send to our fulfillment centers,” Amazon told sellers in a Seller Central news post.

After two months of empty listings, the instinct is to send everything in the warehouse while the door is open. For fast sellers that is right. For slow sellers it is the most expensive decision in the restock plan, because the units you send in the second quarter of 2020 feed the score that decides how much space you get in the third. The FBA restock limits were a cap on this spring. The Inventory Performance Index is the limit that remains, and it works on the next quarter.

Why sending everything feels like the safe call

The case for sending everything is not foolish. Nobody knows whether the limits will return. Amazon stopped most non-essential inbound shipments on March 17, with April 5 as the expected end, CNBC reported, and April 5 came and went. A seller who sent too little in March had no way to fix it. Sending the whole warehouse now looks like insurance against the next freeze.

Delivery promises argue the same way. An item sitting in FBA keeps its Prime badge, and a product shipped from a seller’s own warehouse during a capacity crunch may show a slower date. Units inside the network are worth more than units outside it.

Both points are real. They are also only half the ledger, because inventory in FBA is not just stock. It is an input to a score, and the score is graded on how fast the stock leaves, not on how much of it arrived. A seller who empties the warehouse into FBA is optimizing for the first week after the shipment lands and paying for it in the twelfth, when the slow units are still there.

How this quarter’s shipments set next quarter’s limit

Amazon’s Inventory Performance Index grades a seller’s FBA inventory on four things: sell-through rate, in-stock rate, the share of inventory Amazon counts as excess and the share that is stranded. That is how Marin Software explained it when storage limits based on the score began in July 2018. Below the threshold, a seller gets a storage limit, set separately for standard-size, oversize and apparel items, that lasts through the following quarter. In 2018 storage above the limit cost $10 per cubic foot per month.

The threshold has since risen. “Effective January 1, 2020, we are changing the IPI threshold for storage limits to 400 (previously 350),” Amazon told US sellers in October 2019. It added that “storage limits will continue to be evaluated on a quarterly cycle,” according to a reprint of the notice. The score in the week of December 23, 2019 decided the limits for the first quarter of 2020.

Put those together and the loop is plain. A unit that sells slowly raises excess inventory and lowers sell-through. Both pull the score down. If the score falls below 400 when Amazon next evaluates it, the whole account gets a cubic-foot limit, shared across every product, for the quarter after. The slow seller you shipped in April competes for space with your best seller in July.

The arithmetic of one shipment decision

Take two products with the same $6 profit per unit and 1,200 units of each waiting in the brand’s own warehouse. One sells 300 units a week; the other sells 40.

Fast sellerSlow seller
Weekly sales30040
Units waiting to ship1,2001,200
Weeks of cover if you send them all430
Sensible shipment1,200160–240

For the fast seller, the whole stock is four weeks of cover. Send it; it will sell through before it ages, and it helps the score. For the slow seller, the same 1,200 units are 30 weeks of cover, most of which will sit for months. Each unit still earns its $6 eventually, but in the meantime the pile counts against sell-through and excess inventory. Sending four to six weeks of cover, 160 to 240 units, keeps the product in stock without loading the score.

The trade-off is real in both directions. Ship too little of the slow seller and it may stock out if limits return, which costs sales and in-stock rate. Ship too much and it costs space next quarter for everything else. The numbers lean toward weeks of cover, because a stockout on a product selling 40 a week costs far less than a storage limit on a product selling 300.

Whether Amazon will count the weeks of forced stockouts in March and April against in-stock rate is not something the company has said. That uncertainty is a reason to protect the parts of the score you control: excess and stranded inventory, which move with every shipment you create, and sell-through, which moves with what you choose not to send.

Rules for the restock plan

  1. Set every shipment in weeks of cover, not by what is sitting in your warehouse: four to eight weeks for products that sell steadily, fewer for slow or seasonal ones.
  2. Send everything only for products whose total stock is less than your target cover.
  3. Check your IPI score weekly and keep a margin above 400 going into the end of each quarter, when Amazon evaluates it.
  4. Clear stranded and aged units now, while there is time before the next evaluation, so the products you most need to restock are not crowded out.

Treating warehouse space as a budget to allocate rather than a ticket to use is how we run FBA inventory for brands on Amazon while capacity stays tight.

P0394.title: First-time online grocery shoppers meet your brand as a thumbnail
P0394.alt: Grid of instant photo prints on a wooden table, with a teacup photo raised in the center.
P0394.ttag: First-time online grocery shoppers meet your brand as a thumbnail | Kwontified
P0394.desc: Millions of households ordered groceries online for the first time this spring. They found brands in a search box, not an aisle the brand paid to shape.
P0394.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 14, 2020.
P0394.body:
Take a shopper in her sixties placing her first grocery order online, on a grocer’s site she has used for years only to check the weekly circular. She knows exactly what she wants, because she has bought the same 30 items in the same order around the same store for a decade. On the screen there is no store. There is a search box. She types “chicken broth” and gets a grid of small pictures, a few with prices crossed out, one marked “sponsored,” and the carton she has bought for years somewhere in the third row with a title that reads like a warehouse code.

This spring, millions of households went through some version of that. The first online grocery order is where a lifetime of in-store habit meets a search page, and the brands that will keep these new shoppers are the ones that look like themselves in that grid. Most grocery brands spent years and a large share of their trade budgets shaping the aisle. Almost none of that money shaped the search page their newest online customers now shop from.

How many online grocery shoppers are new

The numbers moved faster than anyone planned for. In late March, 31% of US households, about 39.5 million, had used an online grocery delivery or pickup service in the past month, against 13% in August 2019, according to Brick Meets Click’s March survey. About 26% of those shoppers were using online grocery for the first time, and among shoppers 60 and older the share was 39%.

April went further. Online grocery sales reached $5.3 billion, up 37% from March’s $4.0 billion, across 62.5 million orders averaging $85, the firm’s April survey found, Grocery Dive reported. The publication noted that first-time users faced long waits for delivery slots and trouble finding products.

That last phrase is the one brand teams should underline.

A new shopper who cannot find the product she wants does not leave the store empty-handed. She takes what the grid offers. In an AlixPartners survey reported in April, 65% of US consumers said they had tried new brands during the pandemic, and 79% of them said they did so because their usual choice was out of stock. Some of those choices were made on an empty shelf. Others were likely made on a search page where the usual choice was in stock and simply hard to recognize.

The aisle was negotiated; the search page was left to a feed

Grocery brands know how to win an aisle. The store shelf is shaped by a negotiation between the brand’s sales team and the retailer’s category buyer, and it is paid for: shelf placement, end caps, the weekly circular, the display at the front of the store. A brand’s position at eye level is the product of years of those conversations.

The grocer’s website sits outside most of them. At many brands, the people who negotiate the shelf have never looked at how their products appear on the retailer’s site. The title and images shown there come from a product data feed that someone set up once and nobody has checked since. The shopper sees a small image of the front of the pack, cropped or out of date, and a title written for a database. Meanwhile, the store brand next to it, whose content the retailer controls directly, often looks cleaner.

For a shopper who has bought by sight for years, recognition is the whole decision. In the store she finds the carton by its color and shape from ten feet away. On the screen, the carton is a thumbnail the width of a fingertip, and if the image does not look like the box in her memory, she scrolls past it.

The first basket becomes the next one

What happens in the first order does not stay in the first order. In the April survey, half of households said they were likely to use the same provider next time. Among households that had not ordered online in the prior month, 26% said they were very or extremely likely to do so within three months. The newcomers are still arriving, and the ones who stay will start each order from the last one.

That makes the first basket unusually valuable and the grocer’s search page unusually important. It is the shelf where a household that has never shopped the category online will pick a broth, a cereal and a detergent for the first time, and the picks it makes there will be offered back to it every week after.

It is too early to say how many of these households will keep ordering online once stores feel safe again. The evidence so far leans toward a meaningful share staying, since the share of households likely to return to the same provider rose from March to April. Either way, the households that are new to online grocery this spring are forming their online habits now, with whatever the search page showed them.

What to ask before the next order is placed

  • Has anyone on the brand team placed an order for our top products on each of our five largest grocers’ sites since the middle of March, as a new customer would, and what did they see?
  • Do our product titles and images on those sites match the pack a longtime shopper would recognize, and who owns fixing them when they do not?
  • When a shopper searches the generic term for our category, not our brand name, where do we appear, and who outranks us?
  • Is any part of our trade budget, which buys the aisle, being spent on the retailer’s site, where this spring’s new shoppers are deciding?

The search page is a shelf like any other, and it rewards the same care; it is the part of running a brand’s online channels that grocery brands can fix in weeks rather than a line review cycle.

P0396.title: Multi-channel fulfillment cuts safety stock by pooling demand
P0396.alt: Three wooden chutes carrying wrapped parcels down from a table onto a wooden pallet in a sunlit room.
P0396.ttag: Multi-channel fulfillment cuts safety stock by pooling demand | Kwontified
P0396.desc: Amazon MCF is usually judged on its per-order fee. Its bigger effect is pooling: one stock for two channels needs less safety stock than two stocks do.
P0396.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 19, 2020.
P0396.body:
On April 1, Amazon cut the fees for Multi-Channel Fulfillment, the service that ships orders from a brand’s other channels out of its FBA inventory. Two-day rates fell by up to 30% depending on size tier, and a T-shirt in the 11-ounce shipping tier now costs $5.79 to send by standard shipping, according to the announcement reprinted by My Amazon Guy. Most brands that look at MCF stop there and compare that fee with what their own warehouse or third-party logistics provider charges.

That comparison misses the larger number. Multi-channel fulfillment changes how much inventory a brand needs, not just what each order costs to ship. One pool of stock serving Amazon and a brand’s own site needs less safety stock than two pools serving each separately, because the two channels’ daily swings partly cancel. That saving is often worth more than the fee difference. The catch, which this spring made vivid, is that a single pool also fails all at once.

Why the per-order fee looks like the whole decision

The fee is the number on the page, and it is easy to compare. A brand shipping its own site’s orders from a third-party warehouse knows its pick, pack and postage cost per order. Put it next to the MCF rate card and the answer seems to fall out: cheaper per order wins.

That logic is right for the cost of moving a box. It treats the inventory behind the box as fixed. It is not. A brand with two warehouses has to hold a buffer in each against a bad week. A brand with one has to hold a buffer once.

How pooling shrinks the buffer

Safety stock exists to cover the gap between expected and actual demand during the time it takes to restock. The size of that gap depends on how much daily sales swing, and swings in two independent channels do not add up one for one. A slow day on Amazon and a busy day on the brand’s site offset each other. Statistically, the spread of combined demand grows with the square root of the summed variances, not with the sum of the spreads.

Take a brand selling 50 units a day on Amazon, with a day-to-day standard deviation of 15, and 20 a day on its own site, with a standard deviation of 8. Restocking takes 14 days, and the brand holds two standard deviations of buffer.

Two separate stocksOne pooled stock
Daily variation covered15 + 8 = 23√(15² + 8²) = 17
Safety stock (2 × variation × √14)about 172 unitsabout 127 units

The pooled stock needs about 45 fewer units of buffer for the same protection, about a quarter less. For a brand with dozens of products, that is cash released and storage freed, on top of whatever the fee comparison says. Say the brand’s warehouse charges $7.00 to pick, pack and ship a T-shirt. MCF at $5.79 already wins on the box. The pooling saving makes it win on the balance sheet too.

The arithmetic assumes the channels’ swings are independent. When both move together (a holiday, a viral post that sends shoppers to both), the saving shrinks. It never turns negative, and wherever a brand’s site and its Amazon listings draw shoppers on different days and for different reasons, it stays real.

Checking which case you are in takes one spreadsheet. Pull daily unit sales by channel for a product over a recent stretch of normal trading, compute each channel’s standard deviation, then compute the standard deviation of the combined daily total. If the combined figure is well below the sum of the two, pooling is doing real work for that product. If it is close to the sum, the channels move together and the case for MCF rests on the fee alone. Do it for the products that carry most of the inventory value; the long tail rarely changes the answer.

What March showed about a single pool

The other side of the trade-off arrived in March. From March 17, Amazon’s fulfillment centers prioritized household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products, and new inbound shipments of everything else stopped, CNBC reported. A brand that had pooled its site and Amazon stock in FBA could not replenish the pool for either channel. A brand with a separate warehouse could keep shipping its own site’s orders and could move that stock to Amazon as merchant-fulfilled offers.

Capacity is coming back. Amazon removed its quantity limits on inbound shipments from May 9, it told sellers, but one- and two-day Prime delivery had not been fully restored as of May 13, CNBC reported. The spring showed that the pool is only as reliable as Amazon’s willingness to give it room.

The trade-off resolves to a split rather than a choice. Pool the steady products in FBA and let MCF ship them to every channel, because that is where the safety-stock saving is largest. Keep a smaller separate stock of the top sellers outside Amazon, sized to cover the brand’s own site through a few weeks of interruption.

Rules for using MCF

  1. Compare MCF and your own fulfillment on total cost: the per-order fee plus the carrying cost of the safety stock each setup needs.
  2. Pool products whose channel demands move independently; the saving is smallest where every channel peaks on the same days.
  3. Keep two to four weeks of your best sellers outside FBA, so one warehouse decision cannot stop every channel at once.
  4. Recalculate safety stock after any change in lead time, since the buffer grows with its square root.

Deciding where each product’s stock should sit is part of how we run Amazon and other channels together for brands, weighing the fee and the buffer together.

P0399.crumb: Facebook Shops gives the social team a…
P0399.title: Facebook Shops gives the social team a store to run
P0399.alt: Phone on a tripod filming a table of handmade ceramics and linens in a plant-filled living room.
P0399.ttag: Facebook Shops gives the social team a store to run | Kwontified
P0399.desc: Facebook Shops puts a full store on a brand’s Instagram profile, the account its social team runs. The work of a store belongs to people who rarely touch it.
P0399.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 21, 2020.
P0399.body:
Ask who at a consumer brand runs its Instagram account and the answer is rarely the person who runs its online store. Instagram usually belongs to brand marketing or a social team: the content calendar, the creators, the comments, the weekly report on reach and engagement. The online store belongs to e-commerce: the catalog, prices, stock, shipping and the customer service queue.

On May 19, Facebook put a store on the social team’s side of that line. Facebook Shops lets a business build one storefront that shoppers reach from its Facebook Page and its Instagram profile, as well as from stories and ads, Facebook said.

The question it raises inside a brand is not whether to open one, since it is free. It is who will run it. The brands that answer that before they open will run a good store. The rest will find out what went wrong from a customer’s direct message.

Facebook Shops is a store, not a post

Social commerce on Instagram used to be a lighter thing. Shopping tags in posts sent shoppers to the brand’s own site, and in-app checkout began only in March 2019, as a closed beta with about 20 brands, Tubefilter reported. In January 2020, Sheryl Sandberg was telling investors that Checkout needed full integrations and would take time to broaden, MarTech Today reported. The social team could treat shopping as a feature of its content.

Shops is a different object. A business chooses products from its catalog, styles the storefront with a cover image and its own colors, and lets shoppers either click through to its site or, in the US, check out inside the app, according to Facebook. Shoppers can message the business through WhatsApp, Messenger or Instagram Direct to ask questions, get support and track deliveries. Sellers that use Checkout pay 5% on sales of $8 or more and $0.40 below that, with selling fees waived through the end of June, the Motley Fool reported.

Every one of those features is a store function. A catalog has to be accurate. Prices have to match the brand’s other channels. Stock has to be current, or the Shop sells what the warehouse does not have. And “where is my order” now arrives in the same inbox as “love this color.”

The work of a store sits in another department

At many brands, the catalog connected to Facebook was built for advertising, often by a performance agency, and nobody in e-commerce checks it. Its titles were written to fit ad units and its prices may lag the website. That catalog now stocks the Shop. The first sign of trouble may be a shopper on Instagram asking why the price in the Shop differs from the price on the site.

Customer service is the larger gap. Order questions in Direct and Messenger will land with whoever answers the brand’s social messages, which at many brands is a community manager working from a content brief, not a service agent with access to order records. Facebook has made the message thread part of the store. The brand’s org chart has not caught up.

Reporting has the same split. From Shops, businesses receive aggregated, anonymized information such as traffic, and personal details only when the shopper agrees to share them, while Facebook will use activity in Shops for its own ad targeting, according to the Motley Fool’s account. An e-commerce team used to reconciling every order against its own customer records will get less from a Shop than from its website. A social team used to reporting reach will be asked, perhaps for the first time, to report revenue. Neither team’s dashboard was built for this channel, and someone has to decide which one changes.

Facebook’s own incentives make the store more important, not less. Facebook’s vice president of ads, Dan Levy, said the company will charge small fees on purchases but expects its larger return from driving more advertising, TechCrunch reported. A Shop is designed to be advertised. The brand’s paid social budget, usually planned by the same marketing team, will increasingly send shoppers to a store that team does not operate.

A sales channel arrives through the marketing door

This is the larger shift. For a decade, a brand’s social presence was a media channel: it built awareness and sent traffic elsewhere. Shops, and the Instagram Shop tab Facebook says is coming to the US this summer, turn the same profile into a point of sale. Retailers made the opposite move years ago when Amazon and Walmart started selling advertising; now a media company is adding the checkout.

It is too early to say how many shoppers will buy inside Instagram rather than click through to a brand’s site. The evidence leans toward Facebook pushing hard, since Shops costs nothing to open and its ads business benefits from every sale it can see. Brands do not need to predict the volume to make the organizational decision now.

The questions for the leadership team

  • Who owns the Shop’s results: the social team that controls the profile, or the e-commerce team that controls the catalog and the stock?
  • Which catalog feeds it, who maintains that catalog now, and does its pricing match every other channel?
  • When a shopper asks about an order in Direct or Messenger, who answers, and can they see the order?
  • Will sales through the Shop count toward the social team’s targets, e-commerce’s or both, and how will that change what each team spends?

A Shop needs the same catalog, pricing and order care as any marketplace listing, the operating work behind how we manage Instagram Shop and other social commerce channels for brands.

P0400.crumb: Amazon price gouging rules compare you…
P0400.title: Amazon price gouging rules compare you with your recent prices
P0400.alt: Three blank tags of different sizes hanging on twine from a wooden shelf against a teal wall.
P0400.ttag: Amazon price gouging rules compare you with your recent prices | Kwontified
P0400.desc: Amazon’s fair pricing rule measures a price against recent prices on and off Amazon, so ending a discount can look like a spike. Move prices in steps.
P0400.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 26, 2020.
P0400.body:
In March, Amazon said it had removed well over half a million offers for coronavirus-related price gouging and suspended more than 3,900 US selling accounts, using “dynamic, automated systems in place that locate and remove unfairly priced items,” the company wrote. Most brands read that and relaxed. They were not marking up hand sanitizer.

Some of them got the alert anyway. The reason is in how the rule is written. Amazon’s fair pricing policy does not set a maximum price. It compares a price with “recent prices offered on or off Amazon.” A relative test cannot tell a gouger from a brand ending its own discount, and it lets a seller who was always expensive pass untouched. For normal pricing, the number that matters is not what a product is worth but what it sold for lately.

Why “we don’t gouge” feels like enough

The policy reads as aimed at bad actors, and mostly it is. Its list of practices that harm customer trust includes misleading reference prices, multi-packs that cost more per unit than singles and excessive shipping fees. It also includes “setting a price on a product or service that is significantly higher than recent prices offered on or off Amazon,” according to the policy text quoted by BQool in March. The penalties scale: Amazon may remove the Buy Box, remove the offer, or suspend or end selling privileges.

A brand that has never tried to profit from a shortage sees nothing there that applies to it. The words “gouging” and “emergency” frame the policy as a question of intent. The enforcement, at the scale Amazon described, cannot read intent. It reads prices.

How a relative test treats an ordinary price move

Take a product that sells at $24. In April, with sales soft, the brand runs it at $18 for six weeks to keep the listing moving. In late May the promotion ends and the price goes back to $24.

To a person, that is a return to normal. To a test that compares today’s price with recent prices, it can look like a 33% jump. If “recent” means the last few weeks, the six weeks at $18 are the history that counts, and the years at $24 are not. Meanwhile a competitor that has priced the same product at $30 all spring raises no flag at all, because its price has not moved.

The same logic catches other ordinary changes: a brand passing on a cost increase, a seller whose shipping costs rose, a product whose price was cut on the brand’s own website while Amazon stayed put. In each case the comparison is with a recent number, and the recent number may be the brand’s own discount. “On or off Amazon” means the brand’s site and other retailers are part of the history too.

Amazon has not published what counts as “significantly higher” or how long “recent” is. That silence is the hard part. “Nobody knows what the recipe is that could flag your listing,” an agency founder told Modern Retail in April.

The exposure is measurable before anything is flagged. For each product, compare the price you plan to charge with the lowest price it has carried in recent weeks, on Amazon and on your own site. Any planned price well above that low point is a move an automated check could read as a spike, whatever the reason behind it.

The trade-off moves upstream, into promotion planning. A deep, long discount now carries a second cost on top of the margin it gives away: the deeper and longer it runs, the larger the apparent jump when it ends. A shorter, shallower promotion leaves less of a gap to close. The cost is highest for products like masks and hand sanitizer, which Amazon said a dedicated team is watching.

What the false alarms cost

The cost is not theoretical. One beverage brand described to Modern Retail repeated automated “high pricing error” alerts. They continued even after it cut a price by one cent and checked its prices elsewhere, and its weekly revenue fell from about $50,000 to about $31,000 in the week the alert arrived. In a closed seller group, more than 220 sellers answered yes to a poll asking whether their accounts or products had been deactivated over a price gouging false positive. Appeals that normally drew a response in 72 hours were taking more than two weeks.

Amazon’s position is consistent and, for a marketplace this large, understandable. “There is no place for price gouging on Amazon,” a spokesperson told the publication. An automated test that errs toward removal protects shoppers during a shortage. It also means the burden of avoiding a false alarm sits with the seller, and that a brand’s pricing calendar has become a compliance document as much as a commercial one.

Rules for raising a price on Amazon now

  1. Step prices back up after a promotion instead of jumping. Going from $18 to $24 through $20 and $22 over three weeks keeps each move small relative to the last.
  2. Change prices on your own site and on Amazon together, since the comparison runs on and off Amazon.
  3. Keep a record of the reason for any increase (a cost change, the end of a promotion) to support an appeal if an alert arrives.
  4. Check shipping fees and multi-pack prices against single units; both are named in the policy.

Until Amazon publishes its thresholds, a price plan that moves in small, explained steps is the safest one, and it is how we run pricing on Amazon for brands while the automated checks stay tight.

P0402.crumb: Store closures put a brand’s clearance in…
P0402.title: Store closures put a brand’s clearance in someone else’s hands
P0402.alt: Old wooden handcart piled with empty cardboard boxes in front of closed metal shutters on a brick street.
P0402.ttag: Store closures put a brand’s clearance in someone else’s hands | Kwontified
P0402.desc: When a department store liquidates, the brand’s stock is no longer the brand’s. Without a marketplace plan, others decide where and at what price it sells.
P0402.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 28, 2020.
P0402.body:
Take a closing sale at a department store this summer: the banners in the windows, the racks pushed together, a brand’s spring dresses hanging under a sign that says 60% off and everything must go. Nobody from the brand chose that price. The dresses were bought months ago at wholesale, and from the day the retailer filed for bankruptcy they have belonged to its estate, to be turned into cash by whoever runs the sale.

That scene will be common. J.C. Penney filed for bankruptcy on May 15 and plans to close nearly 30% of its stores. Stage Stores has warned it may liquidate its roughly 700 department stores if it cannot find a buyer, and Neiman Marcus and J.Crew have also filed, CNBC reported on May 21.

For brands that sell through those stores, the question is no longer only what they will be paid. It is where their products will be sold next, at what price and by whom. Brands with a marketplace plan will have some say in the answer. Brands without one will have none.

Store closures turn wholesale stock into someone else’s clearance

In wholesale, ownership passes when the order ships. The brand’s influence over what happens next runs through the relationship: markdown money, return agreements, a buyer who wants next season’s line. Bankruptcy strips most of that away. The estate’s job is to raise cash, and closing sales are how retailers do it.

The odds that a filing ends in liquidation are not small. In 2019, 16 of 25 retailers that went bankrupt liquidated, and 11 of 23 did in 2018, according to Debtwire figures in the same CNBC report. Fifteen retailers had filed in 2020 by May 21, and five had announced plans to shut down.

The timing makes it worse. Sales at clothing and accessories stores fell 78.8% from March to April, according to Commerce Department figures released on May 15, so the stores now closing are full of spring merchandise that never sold. What the closing sales do not clear, closeout buyers will. Some of that stock will be resold online by third-party sellers who bought it cheaply.

The brand’s usual clearance route is crowded

Brands have always had a way to clear excess on their own terms: a negotiated deal with an off-price chain, a sample sale, an outlet. Those routes are now crowded with the brands’ own excess. Off-price is likely the quickest way to clear inventory, but it means “feeding the beast that is beating you already,” Kantar Consulting’s Tiffany Hogan told Modern Retail in April, and retailers such as Gap have asked suppliers to stop fall production.

So the brand’s own surplus and its bankrupt accounts’ surplus will compete for the same discount shoppers, and the brand controls only the first. Follow the value and the liquidator and the reseller capture the margin on the second, while the brand absorbs the cost to its price and its image.

Inside the brand, the warning signs and the remedy usually sit in different rooms. At many wholesale-led brands, the sales team and the credit department watch an account’s health, because they carry the receivable. The marketplace team, if there is one, watches Amazon. Nobody’s job connects the two, so the news that a major account is liquidating reaches finance as a bad-debt problem and never reaches the person who could claim the listings before the closeout stock arrives. The meeting that decides how much to write off is rarely the meeting that decides what to do about the product itself.

Online, the reseller owns the listing the brand never claimed

This is where the absence of a marketplace plan becomes expensive. Beauty brands have lived with a version of it for years. “It is hard to control who sells your product and where they sell it,” a beauty founder told Glossy in 2019, describing salon stock that found its way to Amazon resellers.

On Amazon, sellers of the same product share one detail page, and the order goes largely to the offer with the lowest price, good seller ratings and stock, Practical Ecommerce explained in 2017. A reseller with closeout stock bought at a fraction of wholesale can win that page easily. If the brand has never claimed its listings, the reseller may also be the one who wrote the title, chose the images and set the price that every shopper sees.

Brand Registry does not stop the resale of genuine products. Since Amazon’s Project Zero in February 2019, though, brands in the program can remove counterfeit listings directly, TechCrunch reported. A brand that sells on Amazon itself can also compete for the order with its own stock, at its own price, on the same page. A brand that has done none of this will discover, months from now, that its spring line is on Amazon at closeout prices under a listing it did not write.

Questions for this month’s leadership meeting

  • Which of our wholesale accounts are in bankruptcy or at risk, and how many units of our product sit in their stores and warehouses?
  • Have we claimed and registered every product listing on Amazon and Walmart.com, so that whoever sells our product sells it under our content?
  • If closeout stock appears on Amazon below our price, who will see it first, and what will we do that week?
  • Is our own excess better sold now, through channels we control, than later against our liquidated stock?

The brands that come through the summer with their pricing intact will be the ones that treated marketplaces as their own shelf before someone else did, which is the day-to-day channel work we do for brands on Amazon and Walmart.

P0404.title: Stopped Amazon vendor purchase orders empty the shelf weeks later
P0404.alt: Long row of empty store shelves with only a small cluster of canned goods left on the bottom shelf.
P0404.ttag: Stopped Amazon vendor purchase orders empty the shelf weeks later | Kwontified
P0404.desc: A paused Amazon purchase order does no damage on the day it stops. The cost arrives weeks later, when Amazon’s stock runs out and someone else takes the page.
P0404.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 2, 2020.
P0404.body:
On March 17, Amazon told its vendors that it had “temporarily paused ordering” for products that were not household staples, medical supplies or other high-demand items. Lower-priority suppliers should expect “reduced purchase orders” through April 5, Publishers Weekly reported from the letter. Within days, more than 60% of vendors with a non-essential assortment saw a dramatic drop in orders, a Cleveland Research survey of 68 suppliers found.

Most of those vendors saw no change on their product pages that week. That is the trap. When Amazon vendor purchase orders stop, nothing visible breaks until Amazon’s own stock runs out, and by then the pause may already be over. The damage arrives on a delay set by inventory, and it lasts longer than the pause that caused it.

Why a paused order looks harmless at first

A vendor’s sales on Amazon are Amazon’s sales of stock it already owns. The purchase order refills that stock; it does not make the sale. So when orders stop, shoppers keep buying from the units sitting in Amazon’s warehouses, the sales report keeps printing, and the vendor’s own scorecard shows only a shortfall in shipments.

The March pause also came with longer shipping windows. Amazon extended the windows on some existing orders and asked suppliers to “ship your products toward the end of the extended window,” according to the letter. Orders already placed still arrived, just later. For a week or two, a vendor could reasonably conclude that the pause was an inconvenience.

The out-of-stock arrives one stock cycle later

The cost is set by two numbers: how many weeks of sales Amazon holds when orders stop, and how long it takes the vendor to deliver once orders restart.

Take a vendor whose product sells 200 units a week on Amazon, with Amazon holding 800 units on March 17. That is four weeks of cover. Orders pause that day, and suppose they restart on April 14, four weeks later, with a two-week lead time from order to Amazon’s receiving dock.

DateWhat happensUnits at Amazon
March 17Orders pause800
April 14Stock runs out; orders restart the same day0
April 14 to April 28Product out of stock while the new order ships0
April 28New stock receivedRefilling

A four-week pause produces a two-week stockout that starts on the day ordering resumes. With three weeks of cover instead of four, the outage starts on April 7 and lasts three weeks. The pause length matters less than the gap between cover and pause, plus the lead time added at the end.

That end is also less certain than it looks. Amazon said on April 13 that it would “allow more products into our fulfillment centers” that week, but that “products will be limited by quantity,” Engadget reported. A restart that comes back as a smaller order refills fewer weeks of cover, and the next gap comes sooner.

What fills the page while Amazon is out

The detail page does not close when Amazon’s stock hits zero. It stays live, and any third-party seller with stock can win the Buy Box, the box that holds the Add to Cart button. During the March limits, sellers who shipped their own orders were unaffected, CNBC reported, and only inbound shipments to Amazon’s warehouses were restricted. So the sellers most likely to hold the page during a vendor’s outage are resellers shipping from their own shelves, at prices the brand does not set.

The ads stop at the same moment. Sponsored Products ads run only on listings that hold the Buy Box, Practical Ecommerce noted, and a product Amazon cannot ship does not hold it. A vendor’s campaigns can go dark during exactly the weeks a reseller is selling on its page.

None of this is new to 2020. In March 2019 thousands of smaller vendors received no weekly purchase order and were told to sell on the marketplace, before Amazon described it as a “temporary pause” days later, Modern Retail reported. Then too, wholesale stock already at Amazon had to sell through before a brand’s own marketplace offer could take over, Retail Dive noted. The 2020 pause had a different cause and the same arithmetic.

Plan from weeks of cover, not from the order date

The useful number is not whether Amazon is ordering this week. It is how many weeks Amazon can keep selling without another order, read item by item from Vendor Central’s inventory and sales reports and divided one into the other. Items under three or four weeks of cover are the ones a pause turns into an outage.

For those items, the defense has to exist before the gap opens. A brand that already holds a Seller Central account, with the listing under its Brand Registry, can put up its own offer, shipped from its own warehouse, in the week Amazon’s stock runs out. A brand that opens the account after the outage starts spends the outage setting it up.

The restart needs a date of its own. When orders resume, the outage still has a lead time to run, so the brand that ships the first new order fastest closes the gap first. Agreeing in advance which items get priority in the warehouse, and pre-packing them, takes days off a gap that is otherwise fixed.

Amazon will pause, cut or slow its orders again, for reasons a vendor will not control. What a vendor controls is whether it knows its weeks of cover on the day the letter arrives. Running the vendor and seller accounts as one Amazon business, so the second can carry the first through a gap, is the work we do with brands on Amazon.

P0405.crumb: Curbside pickup hands the local order to…
P0405.title: Curbside pickup hands the local order to the store shelf
P0405.alt: Six paper grocery bags filled with bread, fruit and greens lined up on a weathered wooden bench outdoors.
P0405.ttag: Curbside pickup hands the local order to the store shelf | Kwontified
P0405.desc: Curbside pickup orders are picked from the store’s own shelf, so the brands that win them are the ones the store buyer chose at the line review.
P0405.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 4, 2020.
P0405.body:
At a Target in May, the online order for a bottle of sunscreen starts in the store. An associate with a handheld walks the aisle, takes the bottle off the shelf a shopper might have reached for in February, bags it with the rest of the order and carries it out to a numbered parking space. The shopper never sees the aisle. The product they receive is whichever brand was on that shelf, in stock, that morning.

Curbside pickup has made that walk one of the busiest routes in American retail, and it changes who wins the local online order. A pickup order can only be filled with what the store carries. So the brands that gain from the shift are the ones the store buyer chose at the last line review, and a marketplace seller with a sharper listing and a lower price competes only for the orders that ship.

The online order now runs through the store

The numbers from the spring quarter are hard to overstate. Target said on May 20 that its comparable digital sales grew 141% in the first quarter and that its same-day services, Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt, grew 278%. Stores fulfilled nearly 80% of the company’s digital sales, according to its earnings release.

Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 74% in its quarter to April 30, led by pickup and delivery, which Doug McMillon said “are attracting greater numbers of new customers,” Supermarket News reported. Across retailers, buy-online, pick-up-in-store orders rose 208% year over year in April, Adobe’s Digital Economy Index found. In late March, 31% of US households had used online grocery pickup or delivery in the past month, against 13% the previous August, Brick Meets Click reported.

Even the fastest new services draw on store stock. Walmart’s two-hour Express Delivery, launched on April 30, offers more than 160,000 items and was set to run from nearly 2,000 stores within weeks, the company said.

The store buyer decides what the curbside shopper can get

Read the retailer as an institution and the shift makes sense. A store is the cheapest place to fill a local order: the stock is already there, already paid for, and a short drive from the customer. Every pickup order filled from a shelf is one the retailer did not have to ship from a warehouse. The retailer has every reason to steer shoppers toward it, and the shoppers, wary of crowded aisles, have every reason to go along.

What gets filled, though, is set by the store’s assortment, and the store’s assortment is set by the merchant who runs the category and the plan agreed at the line review. That meeting used to decide which brands a walking shopper could find. It now also decides which brands a phone shopper can get by four o’clock. On a pickup order, there is no third-party seller and no buy box to win. The shelf is the offer.

The marketplace sits on the other side of that line. Walmart’s marketplace is where most of its online assortment lives, about 75 million unique items, most of them from third-party sellers, according to Bloomberg’s reporting last October. Those items ship from a seller’s warehouse or, since February, from Walmart’s new fulfillment service, which stores sellers’ goods for a fee and tags them for two-day shipping, Modern Retail reported. That is a strong offer for the long tail. It is a different race from the one being run in the parking lot.

Inside the brand, two teams now sell the same online order

At many brands, the store account and the e-commerce team sit in different parts of the building. The account team owns the buyer relationship, the line review and the planogram. The e-commerce team owns listings, content and ads on Walmart.com, Target.com and Amazon, and judges its year by online sales.

Curbside pickup puts that division under strain. The retailer reports a pickup order as a digital sale, so it lands in the e-commerce team’s numbers. But the e-commerce team did nothing to win it beyond keeping the product page clean. The account team won it, months earlier, when it kept the item on the shelf. A brand that cut items at the line review to protect store productivity may find it also cut them from the fastest-growing slice of its online business, and nobody on the e-commerce team was in the room.

A brand that sells on Walmart’s marketplace without store distribution sees the reverse. Shoppers who used to browse its listing pick up a rival from the store instead, because the rival is ready in two hours and the marketplace item arrives in two days. The listing did not get worse. The shopper’s definition of convenient changed.

It is too early to know how much of this lasts once stores feel safe again. Some shoppers will drift back to the aisle. But a household that has used pickup for three months has a saved cart and a routine, and retailers that have just learned how cheaply they can fill a local order will keep pushing it.

Questions for the next line review

The useful work is mostly conversation between two teams that rarely share a meeting.

  • Which of our items are in stock for pickup at the stores near our biggest online markets, and which are online-only or marketplace-only?
  • When the buyer proposes cutting an item from the store plan, what share of that item’s online sales came through pickup?
  • Who owns the online in-stock rate at store level, the account team or the e-commerce team, and does either of them see it weekly?
  • For marketplace-only items, is two-day shipping through the retailer’s fulfillment program worth the fee now that the store down the road delivers in two hours?

The brands that do well this summer will treat the line review as an online meeting as much as a store one. Running the Walmart and Target marketplace side while the account team runs the shelf, so that the two plans meet before the buyer does, is part of the work we do on both retailers.

P0406.crumb: The Amazon DSP minimum turns a…
P0406.title: The Amazon DSP minimum turns a retargeting test into prospecting
P0406.alt: Antique balance scale with an iron weight beside a straw archery target on a wooden table against a blue wall.
P0406.ttag: The Amazon DSP minimum turns a retargeting test into prospecting | Kwontified
P0406.desc: A mid-size brand’s retargeting pool cannot absorb the Amazon DSP minimum, so most of that money buys strangers. Plan and judge it as prospecting from day one.
P0406.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 9, 2020.
P0406.body:
Ask a mid-size Amazon seller why they want to try Amazon DSP and the answer is nearly always retargeting: show ads to the shoppers who looked at the product and left. Then the quote arrives. Buying directly from Amazon typically requires a minimum spend of about $35,000, the figure an eStoreFactory guide put on it in May 2019 and the one agencies still quote.

The minimum looks like a hurdle to clear before the test can start. It is really a decision about what the test will be. A mid-size brand’s retargeting audience is too small to absorb $35,000 at any sensible frequency, so most of the money has to go to shoppers who have never seen the brand. A brand that buys DSP at the minimum is buying prospecting, whatever the plan says.

Why retargeting is the natural first buy

Wanting retargeting first is reasonable. Amazon DSP, renamed from the Amazon Advertising Platform in September 2018, sells display and video ads on and off Amazon against Amazon’s own shopping data. It is open to sellers and vendors, and even to brands that do not sell on Amazon at all. Retargeting shoppers who viewed a detail page is the most direct use of that data, and in most accounts it reports the best return on ad spend, because those shoppers were already close to buying.

Amazon’s audiences come in wider rings as well. In-market audiences hold shoppers who searched, browsed or bought in a category in the past 30 days, and lifestyle audiences hold habitual buyers of a category over the past year, eStoreFactory’s guide explained. Those rings are where the minimum ends up.

How a frequency cap moves the budget out of retargeting

Take a brand whose detail pages draw 60,000 shoppers a month who look and do not buy. It commits the $35,000 over one month at a $7 cost per thousand impressions, which buys 5 million impressions.

Retargeting poolRest of the budget
Audience60,000 recent viewersIn-market and lifestyle shoppers
Frequency cap10 impressions per person a monthSet by the plan
Impressions600,0004,400,000
Spend at $7 CPM$4,200$30,800
Share of the $35,00012%88%

Spread across the retargeting pool alone, 5 million impressions would mean about 83 ads per viewer in a month. No brand wants that, and a reasonable frequency cap stops it. With a cap of 10, the pool absorbs $4,200. The other $30,800 has to find people outside it.

Where it goes next is the real planning choice. In-market shoppers, active in the category in the past 30 days, sit closest to a purchase and should take the first dollars of the overflow. Lifestyle audiences are larger and colder, and they are where the remainder lands if the in-market ring is small too.

Pool size moves the split quickly. Double the pool and retargeting takes a quarter of the minimum; halve it and the share drops to about 6%. Only a brand with several hundred thousand monthly viewers can spend the minimum mostly on retargeting, and a brand that size is no longer the one asking.

Judge the money by what it bought

Once most of the budget is prospecting, the retargeting yardstick misleads. A prospecting impression reaches someone who was not about to buy, so its return on ad spend in the first weeks will look poor next to retargeting and next to Sponsored Products. That is what prospecting looks like on a short attribution window, not proof that it failed.

The better measure is the one Amazon built for it. Amazon’s new-to-brand metrics count a purchase as new when the shopper has not bought the brand on Amazon in the previous 12 months, Marketing Dive reported when Amazon introduced them for DSP and Sponsored Brands. Divide the prospecting spend by new-to-brand orders and compare that cost with what a new customer is worth over a year of repeat purchases. For a refill product, that number can justify a buy that looks weak on short-window ROAS. For a once-a-decade purchase, it may not.

Retargeting itself no longer needs the DSP minimum. Sponsored Display, released in beta in September 2019, lets brand-registered sellers and vendors reach shoppers who viewed their products in the past 30 days, on Amazon and on third-party sites and apps, self-service and priced per click, Feedvisor reported. A mid-size brand can run its retargeting there at whatever budget the pool supports.

The test before the commitment

Four numbers decide whether the minimum makes sense, and a brand can get all of them before signing.

  1. Monthly detail-page viewers who did not buy, from the brand’s own traffic reports. Multiply by a frequency cap of about 10 and by the quoted CPM to see what retargeting can absorb.
  2. The share of the minimum left over. That is the prospecting budget, whether or not anyone calls it that.
  3. The value of a new customer over 12 months, from repeat-purchase rates on the brand’s own orders.
  4. Whether the minimum can be spread over a longer flight. Over two or three months, the same commitment buys a smaller monthly prospecting budget and lets retargeting take a larger share.

If the prospecting share cannot pay back on new-customer value, the right first step is Sponsored Display retargeting, and DSP waits until the brand has a prospecting budget it would have spent anyway. If it can, the brand should write the plan as prospecting with a retargeting line, set its targets in new-to-brand cost, and check the result at 30 and 90 days rather than at the first report. Planning Amazon DSP alongside Sponsored Ads, so each dollar is judged by the job it was bought to do, is work we do with brands at exactly this size.

P0408.title: Pandemic demand worth planning around kept growing in May
P0408.alt: Row of terracotta pots on a sunny windowsill holding seedlings that grow taller from left to right.
P0408.ttag: Pandemic demand worth planning around kept growing in May | Kwontified
P0408.desc: Stockpiling faded by late May while online grocery kept adding households. The shifts that grew after the panic are the ones a brand’s plan should keep.
P0408.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 11, 2020.
P0408.body:
In the week that ended May 23, US sales of bath tissue were 10.5% above the same week a year earlier, according to Nielsen figures published by The Shelby Report. Over the 12 weeks to the same date they were up 56.5%. The aisle that became the symbol of the spring was nearly back to normal while the season’s averages still showed a boom.

That gap is the most useful tool a planning team has right now. Most of the pandemic demand in a brand’s spring numbers is the average of a spike and a recovery, and it will mislead anyone who plans from it. The better test is simpler: which changes were still growing in May, after the panic had passed? Those are the ones to build next year’s plan around. The rest is stock that moved from a store shelf to a hall closet.

Three kinds of spring demand, and how each one behaves

Walk through a brand’s spring sales and the spikes tend to fall into three groups, each with its own shape.

Stockpiling is a household buying in March what it would have bought by June. It looks huge for a few weeks and then pays itself back as pantries are used up. Toilet paper is the clean example, and the Census Bureau’s April figures show the same pattern across a whole channel. Grocery store sales rose 27% in March as consumers stocked up, the Motley Fool reported, and then fell 13.2% in April, according to the AP’s report on the Census figures.

At-home behavior is different: households cooking, baking, cleaning and caring for themselves at home because they cannot do those things elsewhere. In the same Nielsen week, flour was still up 63.6%, pasta 24.9% and frozen foods 28.3%. That demand is real, and it does not pay itself back the way stockpiling does. But it is tied to a circumstance. It will last as long as offices, restaurants and gyms stay shut, and fade as they reopen, at a pace no brand controls.

A channel shift means the same household buying the same things in a new place, and it is the one that kept growing. In April, total retail sales fell a record 16.4% while nonstore retailers grew 8.4%. In May, after the worst of the stockpiling was over, online grocery sales rose more than 24% from April to $6.6 billion, and the share of households ordering groceries online reached 33%, up from 31%, Brick Meets Click reported.

Orders per active household rose about 10% in the same survey. People were not just trying it once. They were coming back.

Why the averages hide the difference

Inside most brands, the planning cycle runs on totals by product and by quarter, and the spring quarter’s totals blend all three kinds of demand into one number. A household cleaner might show a 40% quarter that is mostly stockpiling, a baking brand a 40% quarter that is mostly at-home behavior, and both will see a chunk of that volume move online. The forecast that comes out of the next planning meeting usually treats the three as one, either carrying the bump forward or writing it off.

The teams who see the pieces separately sit in different places. Demand planning sees weekly shipments, and it will notice first that the spike has turned into a payback. The e-commerce team sees the online share, and it will notice that the online number did not fall back with everything else. Finance sees the quarter. If those three never compare notes, the plan inherits the quarter.

What looks permanent, and what is still open

The evidence leans one way, though not all the way. Stockpiling is the safest call: it reverses, and the brands that over-ordered for a second wave of it in May are carrying the stock now. At-home behavior is a genuine open question. It depends on a reopening path that changes from state to state and week to week, so it belongs in a plan as scenarios, not as a single number.

The channel shift is the strongest candidate for permanence, because it changes something sticky: the place a household shops. A family that has set up a grocery app, saved a cart and learned which day the pickup slots open has built a routine, and routines are cheaper to keep than to break. Even here, some shoppers will drift back to stores once the aisles feel safe. But the households that kept ordering online in May, after the urgency was gone, are telling a brand something no March figure could.

For a brand, that means the product page, the in-stock rate on Walmart, Target and Amazon and the search terms a shopper types into a grocery app are now part of the core business rather than an extra channel. A brand that plans its 2021 volumes from the spring average will get the size wrong. A brand that plans its 2021 channels from the May trend will get the shape right.

Questions for the next planning meeting

  • For each top product, how much of the spring increase was stockpiling, how much at-home use and how much channel shift, and who in the room can show the split?
  • Which products were still growing in the last two weeks of May, and in which channel?
  • If restaurants and offices reopen faster than expected, which of our at-home gains go with them?
  • What share of our sales now comes through online grocery and marketplace orders, and is that team staffed and funded for the share it has, or the share it had in January?

The brands that come out of 2020 well will be the ones that kept the channel shift and let the spike go. Running the marketplace and online grocery side of that shift day to day is the channel work we do with brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0411.title: Shopify sellers will bring their discounts to the Walmart Buy Box
P0411.alt: Blank string tags laid in a row on an old conveyor belt beside a blue plastic crate in a bright, empty warehouse.
P0411.ttag: Shopify sellers will bring their discounts to the Walmart Buy Box | Kwontified
P0411.desc: Walmart’s price parity rule caps a seller’s Walmart price at its lowest price elsewhere, so new Shopify sellers bring their own-store discounts to the Buy Box.
P0411.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 16, 2020.
P0411.body:
On June 15, Walmart opened its marketplace to merchants who run their stores on Shopify, and Walmart Marketplace vice president Jeff Clementz said he expects to add 1,200 of them in 2020, Talk Business & Politics reported. For a brand whose products sit on Walmart.com, the obvious question is how many of those sellers will list on its items. The more useful question is what price they will bring.

The answer comes from a rule most brands have never read. Walmart’s seller agreement requires a seller’s prices, shipping included, to be at least as favorable to Walmart.com shoppers as on any other online channel. So a Shopify store that runs a 15% sale on its own site has to offer Walmart shoppers that price or better. Each new seller imports its lowest price from everywhere else onto the shared Walmart item page, and the Walmart Buy Box, the offer shown with the Add to Cart button, moves toward it.

Why more sellers looked like a volume question

The first reading of the Shopify deal is about reach. Shopify merchants can connect their stores to a Walmart seller account, keep listings synced and manage orders and inventory from Shopify, and they pay Walmart a referral fee only when an item sells, Shopify’s announcement said. More than 120 million Americans visit Walmart.com each month, by Shopify’s count. For a direct-to-consumer brand, that is a cheap route to a large audience.

For a brand already selling on Walmart, the same deal reads differently. Walmart.com shows one item page per product, with every seller’s offer behind it and one offer featured. New sellers do not create new pages for a brand’s products. They join the existing ones.

How the parity rule sets the featured price

Walmart’s agreement says a seller’s prices, including shipping and handling, must be at least as favorable to Walmart.com shoppers as the best terms it offers on any other online channel, Digiday reported in 2018. Walmart enforces it: one seller who added a $6.95 delivery charge had all his items disabled for failing price parity.

The rule turns each seller’s lowest price anywhere into a ceiling on its Walmart price. Take a $40 item that the brand sells on Walmart.com at $40 with free shipping. A Shopify retailer that carries the item runs a 15% sale on its own site, which brings its lowest online price to $34. Once that retailer lists on Walmart, its Walmart offer cannot be above $34.

Offer on the same Walmart item pageLowest price elsewhereWalmart price ceiling
Brand, free shipping$40 on its own site$40
Shopify retailer, 15% sale at home$34$34
Shopify retailer, clearance at home$30$30

Walmart does not publish how it chooses the featured offer, and price is not the only input. Delivery speed counts too: sellers in Walmart’s new fulfillment service get two-day tags that Walmart says can lift their search ranking, Modern Retail reported. But a $6 gap on a $40 item is hard for speed alone to close. With enough sellers on an item, the featured price drifts toward the deepest discount any of them runs on any channel.

Walmart has its own reasons to like that outcome. It already pays to lower the shopper’s price on selected marketplace items while the seller still receives its listed price, under a program it calls Competitive Price Adjustment, Bloomberg reported last October. A rule that pushes sellers’ own discounts onto Walmart.com delivers the same low price without Walmart paying for it.

What the brand’s numbers will and will not show

The first sign will look like a demand problem. A brand that loses the featured offer on its top items sees its own Walmart sales fall while the item keeps selling, because the sales are going to the seller in the box. Weekly sales reports cannot tell the two apart. Only the item page can.

The rule binds the brand as well. Parity runs one way: a seller’s Walmart price may be lower than elsewhere, never higher. A brand can cut its Walmart price to win the box back without touching its own site, but every promotion it runs on its own site now has to be matched on Walmart. And every reseller’s next sale resets the bar the brand is defending.

Scale tempers all of this. Walmart vets sellers before approving them, Digiday reported in 2018, and 1,200 new sellers is small next to the more than one million businesses on Shopify. On most items, few or none of them will appear in 2020. On a brand’s best-known items, the ones resellers stock first, some will.

Four checks before the new sellers arrive

  1. List the 20 items that carry most of the brand’s Walmart sales and record the seller and price in the featured offer each week.
  2. Find out where those items are discounted online right now, including retailer welcome codes and clearance, because that is the lowest price parity will carry onto Walmart.
  3. Review the brand’s minimum advertised price policy and which Shopify retailers are authorized to sell online, before they connect to Walmart rather than after.
  4. Decide in advance the lowest price at which the brand will defend the Buy Box on each item, and remember that any sale on the brand’s own site must be matched on Walmart.

The brands that handle this well will treat the Walmart item page as a price they manage across every channel, not a listing they set once. Running Walmart Marketplace with that view, alongside a brand’s own store and Amazon, is part of the work we do on Walmart.
