P0412.crumb: Home and kitchen on Amazon favored brands…
P0412.title: Home and kitchen on Amazon favored brands that ship themselves
P0412.alt: Handmade ceramic bowls being wrapped in kraft paper beside an open shipping box, twine, scissors and tape.
P0412.ttag: Home and kitchen on Amazon favored brands that ship themselves | Kwontified
P0412.desc: Demand for bread makers and cookware surged just as Amazon stopped restocking home goods, so the spring’s winners were the sellers who held their own stock.
P0412.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 18, 2020.
P0412.body:
In the five weeks from March 15 to April 18, US sales of bread makers more than quadrupled and electric pasta makers sold more than five times as much as a year earlier, the NPD Group reported. Waffle irons, griddles and rice cookers all grew by double digits. A country told to stay home went shopping for its kitchen.

On March 17, two days after that surge began, Amazon stopped accepting new shipments into its warehouses for almost everything outside six categories, and home and kitchen was not among them. Demand for the category rose in the same weeks that Amazon’s shelf for it stopped being refilled. That collision decided who won home and kitchen on Amazon this spring. It was not the brand with the best listing or the biggest ad budget. It was whoever held the stock and could ship it.

The surge was real, and it was about cooking

The NPD numbers describe a change in how people were living. “Consumers are turning to cooking appliances to help them make the most of their current living situation,” said Joe Derochowski, NPD’s home industry advisor. Families who had eaten lunch at offices and schools were now making three meals a day at home, and the kitchen was where the extra hours went.

Wayfair, which sells almost nothing but home goods, saw the same thing from the other side. Its gross revenue in the second quarter to early May was growing at roughly 90% a year. Chief executive Niraj Shah said needs for “essential products like cookware and kitchen appliances, home office products” accelerated first, on the company’s May 5 earnings call.

Amazon’s shelf for the category stopped refilling

Read Amazon as an institution in March and its choice is easy to follow. Its warehouses were overwhelmed, and it gave the space to baby products, health and household, beauty and personal care, grocery, industrial and scientific, and pet supplies, TechCrunch reported. A stand mixer was not an essential in that triage, however many households wanted one.

So the home and kitchen aisle on Amazon split in two. Brands relying on Fulfillment by Amazon sold through whatever stock was already in the warehouses and then watched their pages show long delivery dates or none at all. Some items showed 30-day delivery estimates from March 22, even for Prime members, Marketplace Pulse noted. Sellers who shipped orders from their own warehouses were not covered by the restriction at all, CNBC reported, and they kept selling at normal speed.

When Amazon reopened its doors in mid-April, it did so with limits. It would allow more products into its fulfillment centers but “products will be limited by quantity,” the company said, as Engadget reported. A brand whose bread maker had sold out in March could send some back in, not all.

Wayfair’s model showed the other path

Wayfair’s call made the contrast plain. About 70% of its volume ships from suppliers’ own warehouses, Shah said, and only about 30% from Wayfair’s buildings. A model in which the brand holds the stock and the retailer takes the order kept working when a central warehouse model hit its limits, because the stock was spread across its suppliers instead of queued at one receiving dock.

Home and kitchen brands should take that contrast seriously, because it runs against how most of them had set up Amazon. Over the past few years, Fulfillment by Amazon became the default for good reasons: Prime eligibility, faster delivery, less work. Inside many brands, merchant fulfillment became the thing they did for oversized items or slow sellers, often handled by a small team with a 3PL contract nobody revisited. When the March restriction came, the brands with a live merchant-fulfilled offer could switch their hero products over within days. The rest found their warehouse team had never shipped to an Amazon customer.

The category also carries a habit problem, and it outlasts the shortage. A household that bought its first stand mixer this spring will be buying attachments, bowls and bakeware for years, and it will start those searches on whatever listing served it first. A brand that was out of stock in April may have handed that first purchase, and the reorders behind it, to a seller who simply had the box.

What the category should keep from 2020

It is not yet clear how much of the cooking boom will outlast the stay-at-home orders; some of it is a phase, and bread makers have filled cupboards before. The fulfillment lesson does not depend on that answer. Amazon has shown it will ration its warehouse space by category in a crisis, and home and kitchen sits low in that order.

The practical response is redundancy. Keep an active merchant-fulfilled offer, even a small one, on the products that matter most, so that the switch is a setting rather than a project. The offer can sit behind the Fulfillment by Amazon one in normal weeks and take over only when Amazon’s stock runs out. Know which 3PL or in-house warehouse would carry Amazon orders, and test it with live orders before the next peak rather than during it. And watch delivery dates on the brand’s own pages as closely as the ad dashboards, because in this category the delivery date decided a great many sales this spring.

Questions worth putting to the team in June: if Amazon closed its warehouses to our category again next week, how many of our top 20 products could we ship ourselves by Friday, and who would pack them? Building that second route, and running it alongside Fulfillment by Amazon, is part of the channel work we do with home brands on Amazon and Walmart.

P0413.crumb: Off-Amazon audiences in DSP are scored…
P0413.title: Off-Amazon audiences in DSP are scored only at Amazon’s checkout
P0413.alt: Dim shop aisle with stocked wooden shelves leading to a spotlit antique brass cash register on a counter.
P0413.ttag: Off-Amazon audiences in DSP are scored only at Amazon’s checkout | Kwontified
P0413.desc: Amazon DSP’s off-Amazon ads are credited only with Amazon purchases, which undercounts sales elsewhere and overcounts buyers who were coming anyway.
P0413.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 23, 2020.
P0413.body:
Amazon DSP can show an ad to an Amazon shopper while that shopper reads a news site, plays a game on a phone or watches a streaming app. That reach is the point of the product, and it has been since Digiday described the Amazon Advertising Platform in 2017 as the way to reach Amazon’s audience segments off Amazon’s own sites. The audience comes from Amazon. The impression happens somewhere else.

The report that judges those impressions still looks at one place: Amazon’s checkout. For a brand that sells only on Amazon, that is close enough. For a brand that also sells at Target, Walmart or on its own site, off-Amazon audiences are graded by a till that sees only part of their effect. The same report also credits them with buyers who were coming anyway. Those two errors pull in opposite directions. Which one is bigger decides whether off-Amazon DSP is underpriced or overpriced for a given brand.

Why the Amazon report felt like enough

Amazon’s case for its DSP rests on data no one else can use. When Amazon opened Fire TV inventory to outside DSPs in 2019, those platforms got no Amazon browsing or purchase data to target with, Marketing Dive reported. The audience segments stay inside Amazon’s own tool.

The measurement follows the same logic. Amazon can see who saw an ad and who later bought on Amazon, and its new-to-brand metric goes further, counting a buyer as new when they have not bought the brand on Amazon in the previous 12 months, Marketing Dive noted. It is a closed loop between impression and purchase that a newspaper’s ad server cannot match. Amazon has even built a tool, Amazon Attribution, to measure how ads outside Amazon drive Amazon sales, and it was free in its 2018 trial, Digiday reported. Every piece of that loop ends at the same checkout.

How one checkout misprices the impression

Take a brand that sells 60% of its units on Amazon and 40% through Target and its own site. It spends $20,000 on an off-Amazon DSP campaign, and Amazon’s report credits it with $50,000 in Amazon sales, a return on ad spend of 2.5.

Two corrections apply, and they push the number in opposite directions.

Amazon cannot see sales made elsewhere. A shopper who sees the ad on a news site may buy the product at Target that weekend. If the campaign’s influence spreads across channels roughly in line with where the brand sells, the $50,000 on Amazon is about 60% of the effect, and the whole effect is about $83,000.

Amazon also counts sales that would have happened anyway. Many people in an Amazon audience were already shopping the category, and some were already on their way to the brand. Suppose a holdout, a group of the same audience that is deliberately not shown the ads, shows that only half of the credited Amazon sales would not have happened without the campaign.

Way of countingSales creditedReturn on $20,000
Amazon report as delivered$50,0002.5
Plus sales at other channelsabout $83,0004.2
Incremental on Amazon only$25,0001.25
Incremental across all channelsabout $42,0002.1

The delivered 2.5 lands between the honest answers. For this brand, the campaign earns about 2.1 across channels, worse than the report says but far better than the incremental Amazon-only figure of 1.25. Change the mix and the answer moves. A brand that sells 90% on Amazon gains little from counting other channels, so the overcount dominates. A brand that sells a third of its units on Amazon gains a great deal from counting other channels and may be underinvesting.

What the report can and cannot settle

The Amazon report is good at one thing: comparing off-Amazon line items against one another on the same basis. If two audiences or two publishers are both graded at Amazon’s checkout, the ranking between them is informative even if neither absolute number is right.

It cannot tell a brand whether to spend the money at all. That needs two pieces of evidence the report does not contain. One is a holdout: a share of the target audience kept out of the campaign, with purchases compared between the two groups. The other is the brand’s own sales outside Amazon, measured over the same weeks and, where possible, in the regions or audiences the campaign reached. Without both, a brand is choosing between two wrong numbers.

What would change this view is evidence that off-Amazon impressions do almost nothing outside Amazon. For an Amazon-exclusive product that is true by definition. For a product on three shelves, it is a claim to test, not to assume.

Before the next off-Amazon flight

  1. Write down the brand’s channel mix for the advertised products: the share of units sold on Amazon against everywhere else.
  2. Hold out part of the audience, even 10%, and compare purchases on Amazon between those who saw the ads and those who did not.
  3. Pull the brand’s own and other retailers’ sales for the same weeks, so the effect outside Amazon has a number, however rough.
  4. Grade off-Amazon line items against each other with Amazon’s report, and grade the campaign as a whole with the holdout and the channel mix.

A brand that does those four things will know whether its off-Amazon audiences are its best buy or a polite way of paying for customers it already had. Planning Amazon DSP so that each line is judged by the job it was bought for is part of the DSP work we do with brands.

P0415.crumb: Trusted brands gained when the aisle…
P0415.title: Trusted brands gained when the aisle shrank to best-known items
P0415.alt: Long sunlit wooden shelving unit with a few ceramic bowls, a basket and a glass bottle against a blue wall.
P0415.ttag: Trusted brands gained when the aisle shrank to best-known items | Kwontified
P0415.desc: When shelves emptied, makers and retailers cut to their core items. Trusted brands and store labels gained, and the long tail between them lost its place.
P0415.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 25, 2020.
P0415.body:
Campbell’s US soup sales rose 35% in the quarter to late April, and the company said its products reached millions of households that had not bought them in the previous year. Soup’s household penetration was up nearly 10 percentage points on a year earlier, chief executive Mark Clouse said on June 3, and “many of the households are younger,” FoodNavigator reported. A brand that many younger shoppers had walked past for years was suddenly in their pantries.

The easy explanation is psychological: in a frightening spring, people reached for names they knew. That is part of it. The larger part is structural. When demand outran supply, manufacturers and retailers cut the aisle down to the items they could make and move fastest, and those were mostly the best-known products of the biggest brands. Trusted brands gained share partly because, for a few months, the shelf held little else.

Shoppers did lean toward familiar names

The behavior is real. “In times of uncertainty, consumers turn to brands that they trust. They want to experiment less,” Kraft Heinz chief executive Miguel Patricio said on April 30, adding that the company’s “leading iconic brands are growing household penetration in almost every market,” FoodNavigator reported. Clouse said Campbell’s repeat rates among the new households were the most encouraging part of the quarter.

Picture the moment from the shopper’s side. A parent ordering groceries online for the first time, with a child at the kitchen table and a delivery slot about to expire, is not reading reviews of an unfamiliar tomato soup. The red-and-white can is a decision that takes no time.

The aisle itself narrowed to core items

What made that decision easy was also what was available. Facing demand they could not meet, the largest manufacturers cut their lines to the products that move fastest. Coca-Cola said it was “ruthlessly prioritizing to deliver on core SKUs,” and Mondelēz said it met demand “by focusing on the most important SKUs.” Procter & Gamble’s Jon Moeller said the crisis could result in “a cutting of the long tail of inefficient SKUs and brands in our categories,” Food Dive reported. Kraft Heinz said it was reducing the number of items it produced to get more out of its lines.

Read that from the retailer’s side and the logic holds. A store or a grocery app with a stretched supply chain wants the items that sell in volume and arrive reliably, and the big manufacturers were promising exactly those. The products that fell out were the slow sellers: the sixth flavor, the new launch, the small brand with one production line. The aisle that came back was narrower and more familiar.

The squeeze fell on the middle, not on store brands

Trusted brands were not the only winners. Store brands grew faster than national brands in the first quarter, with dollar sales up 14.6% against 11.5%, in Nielsen figures released by the Private Label Manufacturers Association, Grocery Dive reported. Retailers control their own labels’ supply and shelf space, so they kept them stocked.

Put the two together and the shape of the spring is clear. The aisle shrank toward its two ends: the leading brands that manufacturers protected, and the store brands that retailers protected. The squeeze fell on everything in between, the challenger brands and long-tail items that nobody in the supply chain was prioritizing. Online, the effect was sharper. A search results page shows what is in stock, and when the middle of the aisle sold out, the first page belonged to whoever still had inventory.

The middle was also exposed in a way the leaders were not. A challenger brand usually grows by doing things the spring made hard: launching a new flavor, buying a feature or a promotion, winning a few more stores at the next reset. Those levers depend on a retailer with time and shelf to spare, and in March and April retailers had neither. The leader’s growth plan, by contrast, was simply to ship more of what it already sold. One plan survived a supply crisis and the other was put on hold.

What the middle of the aisle should do now

It is not yet clear how much of the leaders’ gain will hold. Repeat rates look good for now, and Campbell says so, but younger households that bought soup in April also have more choices in June as lines reopen. The evidence leans toward the leaders keeping some of their new buyers and toward the long tail having to win back distribution it lost by default rather than by preference.

For a challenger brand, the questions are about the places the aisle shrank:

  • Which of our items did retailers or our own operations drop during the spring?
  • Is anyone on the team asking for those items back before the next shelf reset?
  • On Amazon, Walmart and Target, where does our product now appear in the search results for our main category terms, compared with February?
  • Which of the leader’s new households are shoppers we used to reach, and what would it take to put our product in front of them again: a sample, a smaller pack, a sponsored placement on the category search?
  • If supply tightens again in the autumn, which two or three of our products would we protect, and have we told our retail partners?

The leaders earned some of their spring gains and were handed the rest by a narrower aisle. The middle of the aisle has to earn its place back deliberately, item by item and search term by search term, which is the channel work we do with brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0416.title: Walmart Sponsored Products bid floors decide which items go first
P0416.alt: Small pile of gold coins on a wooden floor in front of a blue cabinet holding stoneware jars and baskets.
P0416.ttag: Walmart Sponsored Products bid floors decide which items go first | Kwontified
P0416.desc: Walmart’s $0.30 manual bid floor and first-price auction set a minimum conversion rate for each item. Start with the items that clear it, not the cheapest.
P0416.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 30, 2020.
P0416.body:
Walmart Media Group opened its search ads to self-service in January, letting advertisers buy Sponsored Products through a portal and API partners instead of only through Walmart’s managed service, AdExchanger reported. Six months later, many brands that run Amazon ads every day still have not launched a Walmart campaign, and the usual question is which products to start with.

The answer is set less by strategy than by two rules in the auction. A manual campaign cannot bid below $0.30 a click, and Walmart runs a first-price auction, so the advertiser pays what it bids. Together those rules give every item a minimum conversion rate below which advertising it loses money. The first campaigns should go to the items that clear that floor and already rank on the search page, which is a shorter list than most brands expect.

The rules that shape a first Walmart campaign

The mechanics were laid out in a February guide in Search Engine Journal. Automatic campaigns let Walmart choose where an item’s ads appear, with a minimum bid of $0.20. Manual campaigns target keywords chosen by the advertiser, in broad, phrase or exact match, with a minimum bid of $0.30. Campaign setup asks for at least $100 a day and $1,000 in total.

Two further rules matter more than they look. Ads in the search results grid appear only for items that already rank organically for the term within the first 128 products, about three pages, and only when the advertised item holds the buy box. And negative keywords were not available, so a broad keyword cannot be trimmed of the searches it should not match.

The auction itself is first-price: the advertiser pays its bid, not a price set by the next bidder down. Bid multipliers exist, but only on automatic campaigns.

How a $0.30 floor becomes a conversion-rate floor

Start with what a click is worth. Take a $30 item where the brand is willing to spend 25% of the price on advertising, or $7.50 a sale. If 5% of clicks become orders, a click is worth $0.375. In a first-price auction, the brand pays what it bids, so bidding the full $0.375 leaves no margin for error; a sensible bid sits somewhat below it.

A first-price auction also changes how bids should move. When the price paid is the bid itself, every cent added to win more auctions is paid on every click already being won. A brand that raises a $0.35 bid to $0.45 to gain a few more clicks pays the extra dime on all of them, so increases should be small and judged on the extra orders they bring.

The floor turns that arithmetic around. Divide the $0.30 minimum by the $7.50 the brand can spend per sale and the answer is 4%. Below a 4% conversion rate, every manual click on this item costs more than it is worth, however well the campaign is built.

Item priceAd budget per sale at 25%Conversion rate needed at $0.30
$12$3.0010%
$30$7.504%
$60$15.002%

A $12 item needs one click in ten to convert before a manual campaign breaks even at the minimum bid. Few products do that on a search page. A $60 item needs one in fifty. The floor is the same for every item, so it bites hardest on the cheapest ones, and the lowest-priced part of a catalog may simply not belong in manual campaigns yet.

The organic-rank rule narrows the list further. An item that does not appear in the first 128 organic results for a term cannot buy its way into the grid for that term. Advertising on Walmart amplifies relevance an item already has; it does not create it.

What the first month can and cannot show

The first month is mostly a data purchase. Automatic campaigns, at the lower $0.20 floor and with Walmart choosing the placements, will show which searches and pages produce orders for each item. That is the information a manual campaign needs, and it is cheaper to buy there.

Without negative keywords, broad match on manual campaigns will spend on searches the brand would have excluded on another platform. Exact and phrase match keep that leakage small until the automatic campaign has shown which terms convert.

What the reports cannot yet show is the effect on Walmart’s stores. AdExchanger reported in January that retail and audience data for targeting, and reliable online-to-store attribution, were not yet available in the self-serve tool. A brand that sells mostly in Walmart stores should treat early online results as a partial count.

The first campaigns to run

  1. An automatic campaign containing every item that holds the buy box and sells for enough to clear the floor, bid modestly above $0.20, to collect search terms for a month.
  2. A manual exact-match campaign on the brand’s own name and the two or three category terms where each item already ranks in the first 128 results, with bids set from each item’s value per click and kept below it.
  3. A short list, kept outside advertising for now, of items whose price and conversion rate put them under the $0.30 floor; revisit it when prices, pack sizes or conversion change.
  4. A weekly check of which items hold the buy box, since an item that loses it stops serving.

Brands that start this way will spend less in the first month than the setup screen suggests and learn more from it. Running Walmart Media Group campaigns alongside a brand’s Amazon advertising, with each item judged on its own value per click, is part of the work we do on Walmart.

P0417.crumb: Amazon customer service starts with the…
P0417.title: Amazon customer service starts with the delivery date you promise
P0417.alt: Twine-tied parcel and a brass alarm clock on a wooden porch step beside a potted jade plant.
P0417.ttag: Amazon customer service starts with the delivery date you promise | Kwontified
P0417.desc: When Amazon deliveries slip, the shopper’s complaint goes wherever Amazon routes it, rarely to the brand’s service desk. The date you promise is your service.
P0417.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 2, 2020.
P0417.body:
In the third week of March, a shopper with an ordinary Amazon order could watch the delivery date move a month into the future. From March 22, some items showed 30-day delivery estimates even with Prime, Marketplace Pulse found, and Amazon acknowledged that some of its delivery promises were longer than usual. Many of those shoppers wanted to know where their order was. Most of them never reached the brand.

That is the part of the spring most brand teams missed. The customer service desk a brand has built, with its phone line, its email inbox and its scripts, sees almost none of the questions a late Amazon order produces. Amazon customer service works differently. Amazon decides where the question goes, and for most brands the only service they can still shape is the delivery date they show before the order is placed and the message they send before the shopper writes in.

Where Amazon sends the shopper whose order is late

Walk into a department store with a complaint and you find a counter, a person in the brand’s uniform and a policy printed on a card. On Amazon the counter belongs to whoever ships the box. For products held in Amazon’s warehouses, Amazon has handled the post-order conversation since it launched Fulfillment by Amazon in 2006, managing returns and refunds itself. The shopper asking about a late FBA order talks to Amazon, and the brand learns about it, if at all, from a return report or a product review.

Orders a brand ships itself come through Buyer-Seller Messaging, and Amazon has long expected those messages answered within 24 hours, weekends included. Sellers who answered 90% or more of messages within that window drew nearly 24% less negative feedback, Amazon told UK sellers when it introduced the standard in 2012. The queue sits inside Seller Central, which at many brands is a login held by the e-commerce or channel team rather than by anyone with “customer” in their title.

So the shopper’s question splits in two. If Amazon shipped it, Amazon answers. If the brand shipped it, a channel manager answers, usually between other jobs. Neither path runs through the team the brand pays to care about customers.

The spring showed who owns the marketplace customer

The pandemic made the split visible because Amazon, briefly, carried the cost of late orders for its sellers. It said in March that it would take into account any COVID-related disruption as it related to late shipping and cancellations, and that a seller who told the buyer about a problem through Buyer-Seller Messaging would have the event treated as unforeseen. It then paused account protection for late shipment rate, cancellation rate and order defect rate, a pause first set to end May 15 and then extended by two weeks.

That grace period has ended. From June 1, Amazon restarted tracking and enforcing those standards, though it said it would disregard defects logged before that date. Whatever a brand’s team did with late orders in April cost it nothing on its scorecard. The same behavior in July counts.

Follow the value and the arrangement makes sense from Amazon’s side. Amazon owns the shopper’s account, the order history, the refund button and the review form. It lends the brand a message queue and a set of metrics, and it keeps the relationship. When a delivery slips, Amazon protects the shopper first, because the shopper is the asset it intends to keep. The brand’s standing depends on a scorecard it can read but cannot appeal to a person who knows its products.

Inside the brand, the structure tends to look like this. At many companies the customer service team was built for the brand’s own website and reports to whoever runs direct-to-consumer, while marketplace orders sit with the e-commerce team. Delivery complaints on Amazon often skip both and land in product reviews, under the product’s star rating, where the next shopper reads them. A one-star review about a late parcel is a customer service ticket the brand never received, filed permanently on its shelf.

Service on a marketplace happens before the order

If the counter belongs to Amazon, the brand’s influence moves upstream. The delivery date shown on the product page is a promise the brand helps set, through its fulfillment choice, the handling time it configures and the stock it keeps in the right place. A conservative date that holds does more for the shopper than a fast date that slips and an apology that follows. The same goes for messages. Amazon’s own guidance in March was to write to the buyer before cancelling, and the seller who explains a delay first faces a calmer shopper than the one who answers a complaint.

This is a change in who does the work, more than a change in tools. The person setting handling times and shipping templates in Seller Central is doing customer service, whether or not the org chart says so. The person reading product reviews each morning is reading the complaints inbox. At most brands neither person is measured on what customers experience; they are measured on sales.

It is too early to say how strictly Amazon will enforce its standards over a summer when carriers are still stretched, and seller-fulfilled orders carry the most risk. The evidence from the spring leans one way: Amazon relaxes rules when the delay is its own, and restores them when the system can bear it.

Questions for the team before the next delay

  • Who in the company reads every product review written in the last 30 days, and what do they do with the ones about delivery?
  • Which of our seller-fulfilled products show a delivery date we missed more than once this spring, and who can change the handling time?
  • Who answers Buyer-Seller Messaging on weekends, and is anyone measured on how fast?
  • If a supplier delay hits next month, who writes to the shoppers with open orders, and from which account?

A brand that can answer all four has a customer service function on Amazon; a brand that cannot is relying on Amazon’s. It is the kind of gap we close when we run a brand’s Amazon channel day to day.

P0419.title: Walmart Marketplace approval screens the seller, then the product
P0419.alt: Cardboard parcel on a rustic wooden bench by open iron gates in a blue-walled stone corridor.
P0419.ttag: Walmart Marketplace approval screens the seller, then the product | Kwontified
P0419.desc: Walmart’s Shopify deal opens an app, not the gate. Approval still turns on whether Walmart expects you to ship like Walmart and sell what it lacks.
P0419.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 7, 2020.
P0419.body:
On June 15, Walmart said it expects to add 1,200 Shopify sellers to its marketplace in 2020. Shopify is used by more than a million businesses, Walmart noted in the same announcement. Divide one by the other and the deal makes room for about one Shopify business in 830, or 0.12%. Many brands read the news as Walmart opening its doors. The arithmetic says Walmart installed a faster door and kept the guard.

That guard is the part worth understanding. Walmart Marketplace approval is not a paperwork check on your products. It is Walmart’s main tool for controlling seller behavior, used before the first order instead of after the hundredth, and it rewards applications that answer two questions: will this seller ship like Walmart, and does it sell something Walmart does not?

Why an app looked like an open door

The mechanics did get easier. A Shopify merchant now installs the Walmart Marketplace app from Shopify’s App Store and checks eligibility there, and approved sellers can add an unlimited number of products, with images and inventory changed in Shopify flowing to Walmart.com automatically, TechCrunch reported. The prize is large: Walmart Marketplace draws 120 million monthly visitors, and Walmart’s US e-commerce sales grew 74% in its latest quarter, with marketplace growth outpacing the rest.

Integration cost used to be a real barrier for small brands, so removing it feels like removing the barrier. It isn’t. The cost of connecting a catalog was never what kept most sellers off Walmart.com.

Walmart enforces at the door, Amazon after the sale

Amazon and Walmart run two different control systems. Amazon lets almost anyone list and then manages sellers through metrics: late shipments, cancellations and defects are measured order by order, and accounts that miss the standards lose the right to sell. Walmart does more of its filtering up front. It became noticeably more selective with web sellers in 2018 after a growth spurt, when its marketplace had about 18,000 third-party sellers, according to Bloomberg’s reporting and Marketplace Pulse’s count. The Shopify announcement carries the same instinct in a single line: “we are going to be smart as we grow.”

The behavior looks conservative, even self-defeating, for a retailer racing to catch Amazon. It makes sense once you see what each system costs. Screening after the sale is cheap for the platform and expensive for the shopper who received the late order. Screening before the sale is expensive for the platform, because it turns away sellers who would have been fine. It also protects the one thing Walmart is still building online: shoppers’ belief that an order from Walmart.com arrives like an order from Walmart. A retailer with millions of shoppers still testing its website has more to lose from one bad seller than from a hundred missing ones.

So the approval rules are a forecast. Walmart cannot yet measure your performance on its site, so it predicts it from what it can see.

The approval rules, read as predictions

Walmart’s stated focus is US-based small and medium businesses “whose assortment complements ours” and that have a track record of exceeding customer expectations. The working requirements for Shopify sellers are more concrete. They include a US base and US tax ID, UPC or GTIN codes for each product, products Walmart.com permits, and Walmart’s service requirements, Feedvisor reported, adding that Walmart’s vetting is generally stricter and longer than Amazon’s.

Each rule predicts something. A US entity and tax ID predict that Walmart can hold the seller accountable. Product codes predict that the item can be matched to Walmart’s catalog rather than creating a duplicate page. The track record predicts on-time delivery. And “complements ours” predicts that the seller adds to Walmart’s assortment instead of competing with its own first-party stock for the same shopper.

That last rule is the one brands misjudge. Take a brand with 60 products, 20 of which Walmart already sells itself. An application that leads with those 20 asks Walmart to let a second seller onto pages it already serves. An application that leads with the other 40 offers Walmart items its shoppers cannot buy there today. The catalog is identical; the forecast Walmart draws from it is not.

Fulfillment is the other half of the forecast. Walmart Fulfillment Services, which Walmart formally unveiled in late February, is open to any marketplace seller for products under its size and weight limits, and its products carry a two-day tag that Walmart says can lift search ranking, Modern Retail reported. The same report put the scale of the prize in proportion: Tinuiti said its best Walmart sellers earn about 20% of their Amazon sales there.

How to apply when approval is the performance review

Treat the application as the only performance review you will get before launch. Lead with the products Walmart does not carry, and leave the overlapping ones for after approval, once you have a record on the site. Have product codes and a US tax entity in place before you install the app, because a missing code is the cheapest rejection to avoid.

Then show the service record Walmart cannot yet measure. On-time shipment and cancellation figures from your own site or from Amazon are the nearest evidence of how you will treat a Walmart shopper, and a brand that already ships within two days answers Walmart’s question before it is asked.

The rule of thumb: if your application would read the same to Walmart without the Shopify app, the app was never your problem. Assortment and service decide Walmart Marketplace approval, and both can be prepared before you apply, which is the groundwork we do when we launch brands on Walmart Marketplace.

P0421.crumb: When wholesale orders stop, the brand…
P0421.title: When wholesale orders stop, the brand owns the inventory risk
P0421.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes and crates in a terracotta-walled storeroom behind a padlocked wooden door.
P0421.ttag: When wholesale orders stop, the brand owns the inventory risk | Kwontified
P0421.desc: A department store that stops ordering is not sulking; it is full. The stock it did not buy is now the brand’s to place, and marketplaces are where it will go.
P0421.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 9, 2020.
P0421.body:
Macy’s reported on July 1 that its first-quarter sales fell to $3.0 billion from $5.5 billion a year earlier, a drop of about 45%. Its inventory at May 2 was $4.9 billion, only about 10% lower than a year before, according to the release. Put those two numbers side by side and the department store was holding about 1.6 dollars of stock for every dollar of quarterly sales, against roughly 1.0 a year earlier.

That ratio explains a silence many brand sales teams have been reading as a relationship problem. The wholesale account that stopped ordering this spring is not cooling on the brand. It is full. And when a retailer is full, the risk it used to carry for the brand, the risk of owning stock that does not sell, moves back to the brand’s own warehouse.

Wholesale orders were a way of selling risk

On a department store floor, the brand’s name is on the fixture, but the retailer owns what hangs on it. That is the bargain wholesale has always offered: the brand accepts a lower price per unit, and in exchange the buyer takes the units, the markdowns and the leftovers. The buyer’s open-to-buy, the budget for new purchases each season, became the brand’s real forecast. At many brands the wholesale team plans production around what the big accounts commit to, and everything else follows.

This spring the bargain came undone from both ends. Retailers that could not sell could not pay on the old schedule. Macy’s extended its vendor payment terms to 120 days and Kohl’s pushed some payments out as far as six months, while credit insurers stopped writing cover for Macy’s, the Motley Fool reported in April. J.C. Penney, with 850 stores, filed for Chapter 11 on May 15, after Neiman Marcus, J.Crew and Stage Stores.

Even the strongest brands felt it. Nike said on June 25 that its shipments to wholesale customers fell nearly 50% in the quarter to May 31, and that its own inventory rose 31% to $7.4 billion, mainly because of store closures and lower wholesale shipments. Nike’s digital sales rose 75% in the same quarter. The stock the stores did not take did not vanish; it moved onto Nike’s balance sheet and, in part, onto Nike’s own website.

Who decides where the unbought stock goes

Take a brand that ships a department store $2 million a season and learns in May that the fall order is cancelled, with 40% of it already cut and sewn. The brand now owns $800,000 of product that was designed for someone else’s floor, priced for someone else’s markdown calendar and labeled for someone else’s stockroom. Somebody inside the brand has to decide what happens to it.

At most brands that decision lands with finance or with the wholesale team itself, the people who know the account and the size of the hole. It rarely lands with the e-commerce team, even though e-commerce runs the only channels that grew this spring. So the stock goes where wholesale stock has always gone when an account says no: to off-price buyers and liquidators, in bulk, at a fraction of cost.

Follow that stock a few weeks further and it often turns up on Amazon, sold by resellers who bought it cheaply and price it below the brand’s own listing. The brand that sold its cancelled fall order to a liquidator in June may find itself competing with that order on its own product page in September. The decision that looked like clearing a warehouse was really a decision about who sells the brand online, and at what price.

The alternative is not glamorous. It means treating the brand’s own marketplace accounts as the first outlet for stock wholesale did not take: listing it, pricing it with the brand’s long-term position in mind, and paying for the fulfillment and advertising to move it at a controlled pace. That costs more per unit than a bulk sale. It keeps the price, the product page and the customer in the brand’s hands.

The account that comes back will order differently

Department stores have reopened their doors, and their buyers will be back. The evidence leans toward them returning with smaller orders, later commitments and longer payment terms, because the spring taught them how much risk they were carrying. A buyer who has learned to hold less will expect the brand to hold more, and to replenish faster when something sells.

That turns the wholesale relationship into something closer to a marketplace relationship, where the brand owns the stock until a shopper buys it. Brands that already run their own Amazon and Walmart accounts have the muscles for that model. Brands that have relied on the buyer’s order as their forecast will need to build them.

Questions for the next planning meeting

  • How much of this season’s production was committed against orders that have since been cancelled or cut, and who owns the decision about where it goes?
  • What did we sell to off-price and liquidation buyers this spring, and do we know which of those products now appear on Amazon under other sellers?
  • If our largest account orders 30% less for holiday, which channel absorbs the difference, and does that team know yet?
  • Who in the company is measured on the value of stock that never reached a retailer?

The account that stopped ordering has already made its decision. The brand’s decision is whether its own marketplace channels are ready to carry the stock, which is the work we take on when we run a brand’s marketplace channels day to day.

P0423.title: Walmart Fulfillment Services turns two-day into a stock decision
P0423.alt: Gold wristwatch with leather strap on blue warehouse shelving stocked with cardboard boxes by a window.
P0423.ttag: Walmart Fulfillment Services turns two-day into a stock decision | Kwontified
P0423.desc: Walmart Fulfillment Services prices the two-day promise per unit, not per mile. The catch is stock that must wait in Walmart’s building before anyone orders.
P0423.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 14, 2020.
P0423.body:
Until 2020, a marketplace seller that wanted Walmart’s two-day tag had one way to earn it: ship fast from its own warehouse. Walmart opened free two-day shipping to marketplace items in October 2018, starting with hundreds of its high-performing sellers, and the seller paid the postage. On February 25 Walmart added a second route. Walmart Fulfillment Services stores, picks, packs and ships a seller’s items, handles returns and customer service, and offers two-day shipping with no membership fee, Retail TouchPoints reported at the launch.

Both routes buy the same tag, paid in different currencies. Seller-fulfilled two-day is paid in postage, and the bill grows with the distance between the warehouse and the shopper. Walmart Fulfillment Services is paid in a per-unit fee and in stock that has to sit in Walmart’s buildings before anyone orders it. One cost arrives with each order; the other is committed weeks ahead. The choice is an inventory decision as much as a shipping one.

What Walmart has said about Walmart Fulfillment Services

The public terms are short. Any marketplace seller can apply, items above certain size and weight limits are excluded, and sellers pay a storage fee and a fulfillment fee, Modern Retail reported three days after the launch. Walmart did not say what those fees are. Products in the program carry the two-day tag, which Walmart says can lift their search ranking. The soft launch that preceded it covered footwear, apparel, home décor, sporting goods, automotive and electronics, and Walmart plans to add NextDay delivery later.

The tag is about to matter more. Walmart’s June 15 partnership with Shopify opens the marketplace, with its 120 million monthly visitors, to a much larger pool of sellers, TechCrunch reported. More listings competing for the same searches raise the value of anything that lifts rank, and the fastest delivery date on the page is one of the few levers a seller controls.

The most a fulfillment fee can be worth

Because Walmart has not published the fees, the useful number is the one a seller can calculate now: its own cost of a two-day order everywhere. That is the ceiling a quote from Walmart has to beat.

Take a one-pound, $40 item shipped from a single warehouse. Picking and packing cost $2.50 an order. A ground label costs $8.00, and ground reaches 60% of orders in two days. The other 40% need an express label that costs $14.00 more, which adds $5.60 to the average order.

Per orderShip it yourself, two-day everywhereShip it yourself, ground onlyWalmart Fulfillment Services
Pick and pack$2.50$2.50in the fee
Outbound shipping$13.60$8.00in the fee
Freight to Walmart’s buildingnonenone$0.60
Cost per order$16.10$10.50quoted fee + $0.60

Read the table from the right. A quoted fee below $15.50 a unit makes Walmart’s network cheaper than buying the same promise yourself. A fee below $9.90 makes it cheaper than shipping ground with no two-day tag at all, and at that point the seller gets the faster date and saves money on every order. For an item whose orders already sit mostly within ground reach of its warehouse, the ceiling falls toward the ground-only column, which is the case argued in Walmart two-day delivery pays sellers only where ground reaches.

The stock that can only sell on Walmart

The per-order view flatters the network, because it counts orders and ignores units. Say the item sells 600 units a month on Walmart. To keep the tag, Walmart’s building needs stock before the orders arrive. If inbound takes two weeks and the seller wants four weeks on the shelf, about 900 units sit there.

That is six weeks of Walmart demand that cannot fill an Amazon order or a sale on the brand’s own site. At a $15 landed cost, it is $13,500 of inventory, and the storage fee applies for every week it waits. Stock in the seller’s own warehouse serves every channel from one pool, so a slow week on one marketplace is absorbed by the others.

March showed what it means to hold stock in someone else’s network. On March 17, Amazon began prioritizing household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products at its fulfillment centers, delaying inbound shipments of other third-party inventory, and said the change was expected to last until April 5, CNBC reported. Sellers who shipped their own orders kept selling. Walmart has published no comparable rule for its program, and nothing suggests it plans one. The point is narrower: units in another company’s network follow that network’s priorities when capacity runs short.

Which items belong in Walmart’s building

The numbers lean toward the network for small, light items that sell steadily, from sellers with one warehouse far from much of the country. Those sellers carry the highest cost for a two-day promise, so the ceiling sits well above most plausible fees, and steady demand keeps six weeks of cover from becoming dead stock. They lean the other way for slow or seasonal items, where six weeks of Walmart demand is a large share of the stock on hand, and for bulky products that fall outside the size limits anyway.

A workable rule has two tests. Send an item to Walmart Fulfillment Services when the quoted fee plus inbound freight sits below your own cost of a two-day order everywhere. Then check that six weeks of its Walmart sales is stock you would hold anyway. If it fails either test, keep shipping it yourself and show the tag where ground already gets there. Working through that split item by item is part of how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

P0424.title: Back-to-school 2020 will be late, online and bought with no list
P0424.alt: Olive canvas backpack beside an open laptop and mug on a wooden table near a sunny window with herbs.
P0424.ttag: Back-to-school 2020 will be late, online and bought with no list | Kwontified
P0424.desc: Most families planning back-to-school 2020 still lack a supply list and plan to shop online. Brands should expect a late, long season decided on search pages.
P0424.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 16, 2020.
P0424.body:
Every back-to-school season has been organized by a sheet of paper. The teacher’s supply list arrives, a parent folds it into a pocket, and the store trip follows: the folder aisle, the backpack wall, the shoe department. In early July 2020, only 10% of families still shopping had received a list, and 54% said they did not yet know what they needed, according to the NRF and Prosper Insights survey of 7,481 consumers taken July 1 to 8.

Back-to-school 2020 has lost both the list and the trip. That changes when families buy, where they buy and what they ask before they buy. For brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target, the season will arrive late, last longer than usual and be settled on search pages rather than in aisles, by the listings that answer the questions a supply list used to answer.

The list and the store trip both went missing

The money is not the problem. NRF projects total back-to-school and college spending at a record $101.6 billion, up from $80.7 billion in 2019 and above $100 billion for the first time. K-12 families expect to spend $789.49 each, against $696.70 in 2019. Families are preparing to equip a room at home as well as a backpack.

Where they will spend it has moved. Fifty-five percent plan to do most of their back-to-school shopping online, up from 49%. Planned visits to department stores fell to 37% from 53%, to discount stores to 36% from 50%, and to clothing stores to 30% from 45%. NRF’s chief executive, Matthew Shay, called it “an unprecedented year with great uncertainty.”

The uncertainty is concrete. On July 13, Los Angeles Unified, with about 700,000 students, and San Diego Unified, with more than 100,000, said they would start the year online only, on August 18 and August 31. A family in Los Angeles that was waiting for a list now knows it is shopping for a kitchen-table classroom. A family in a district that has not decided is still waiting.

Why the season will run late and long

At many brands, back-to-school was planned in the spring around retailer floor sets and July promotions, and the selling window was a few concentrated weeks before the first bell. That calendar assumed schools would announce their plans in June and stores would be open. Neither holds in 2020.

District by district, decisions are landing through July and into August, and each one releases a wave of demand on its own schedule. A brand will not see one back-to-school peak in 2020. It will see dozens of small ones, starting whenever a district announces and continuing after school begins, as families discover what remote or hybrid learning actually requires. Some of the spending NRF projects will not happen until September.

The mix inside the cart is shifting too. The survey shows K-12 clothing spending per family slightly down, at $234.48 against $239.82, while total spending per family rose about 13%. Clothing is now about 30% of the K-12 budget, against 34% in 2019.

The rest is going to the things a home classroom needs. For apparel and footwear brands, back-to-school is still a season. It is no longer the season’s center.

What the search page has to do instead of the list

Picture the shelf this replaces. In a store, the back-to-school aisle does the merchandising for you: the folders sit next to the binders, the signage tells parents what grade needs what, and the list in the parent’s pocket narrows the choice. On a marketplace, a parent types “kids headphones for school” or “desk for small space” and gets a grid of thumbnails with no aisle and no list.

The listings that win in that grid are the ones that do the list’s job. They say which ages a product suits, whether it works for video classes, what size space it needs, and when it will arrive. Think of a backpack page that shows the laptop sleeve, or a sneaker page that says whether a young child can put the shoe on alone. A headphone page that names the volume limit does the same work. Those details are what a teacher’s list or a store associate used to supply, and on a marketplace nobody else will supply them.

This is often where the organization gets in the way. The team that writes back-to-school creative for retailer circulars and social campaigns is frequently not the team that edits marketplace listings, and the July campaign was built for a store trip that families are skipping. The result is a season where the circular says “back to school” and the Amazon listing still reads like it did in March, written for a shopper who already knew what she wanted. Fixing that is less about new creative than about moving the same answers onto the page where the decision now happens.

Questions to put to the team this week

  • Which of our products answer a home-learning need, and do their marketplace listings say so in the title, images and bullets?
  • If demand arrives district by district through September, is our inventory planned for a single August peak or for a longer, lumpier season?
  • Who owns back-to-school content for Amazon, Walmart and Target, and is that person in the room where the campaign was planned?
  • What will we know by the first week of August that we do not know now, and who will change the plan when we do?

The season is still there, and NRF’s numbers say it may be the largest on record. It will simply be bought in a different place, on a different schedule, and the brands ready for that will be the ones whose marketplace listings and inventory are run as one plan.

P0428.crumb: Footwear on Amazon now has to answer the…
P0428.title: Footwear on Amazon now has to answer the fitting-room question
P0428.alt: Brown leather shoe on a brass foot-measuring device beside an open shoebox and oval mirror on a wooden table.
P0428.ttag: Footwear on Amazon now has to answer the fitting-room question | Kwontified
P0428.desc: With shoe stores shut for weeks, footwear on Amazon must do the fitting the store once did. Brands that answer size and fit on the page keep the sale.
P0428.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 23, 2020.
P0428.body:
Buying shoes in a store has always involved a small ritual. A salesperson measures the foot on a metal sizing device, brings out two sizes, and watches the customer walk to the mirror and back. In the spring of 2020 that ritual stopped. Foot Locker said its first-quarter sales fell 43.4% and its comparable-store sales 42.8%, with just over 1,400 of its 3,113 stores reopened by late May, according to its results. Nike’s own stores were mostly closed for about eight weeks.

The shoppers did not stop needing shoes. They went online, where nobody measures anything. That is the change in footwear on Amazon in 2020: the product page has to answer the question the fitting used to answer, and the brands that control their own listings are the ones in a position to answer it.

Where the shoe shopper went

The move online was fast and large. Nike’s digital sales rose 75% in its fiscal fourth quarter, which ended in May, and reached about 30% of its revenue, while its shipments to wholesale customers fell nearly 50%, Nike said in June. The store network that used to absorb most footwear sales was already thinner before the pandemic: Payless announced in February 2019 that it would close its remaining 2,100 US stores.

Nike’s move is the clearest illustration of the category’s choice. It ended its pilot selling to Amazon as a wholesaler in November 2019, and its products remained available on Amazon through independent sellers, as they had been before the pilot, along with gray-market and counterfeit goods. Nike can afford to send its shoppers to its own app. Most footwear brands cannot, and their shoppers searching Amazon for “women’s walking shoes” or “kids’ sneakers wide” find whatever listings exist.

The page does the fitting now

Think about what the salesperson actually did. She translated the brand’s sizing into the customer’s foot: this style runs narrow, go up half a size; this one has a deep toe box; this boot fits like the brand’s running shoe. None of that is on a box. It lived in the store’s staff and in the customer’s habit of trying both pairs on.

On Amazon, that knowledge has to sit on the product page or nowhere. A size chart, a line that says how the style fits against the brand’s other styles, an image of the sole and the toe box, an answer to the question that keeps showing up in the reviews. When those details are missing, shoppers do what people did before fitting rooms existed: they order two sizes and send one back, or they order one, guess wrong and leave a review about the fit.

Take a $90 shoe where one in five orders comes back because of fit. If a listing that states the fit plainly brings that down to one in eight, every 100 orders produce 12.5 returns instead of 20, or 7.5 fewer boxes to receive, inspect and resell. The arithmetic is simple. The organizational question is who writes the fit line.

The review section shows the cost of leaving it unwritten. A shoe page is one of the few places on Amazon where shoppers routinely write about the product’s dimensions rather than its quality, and those reviews stay on the page long after the stock that caused them has sold. A style that runs small collects a trail of comments telling buyers to order a size up, and the next shopper reads them before the brand’s own description, if there is one.

At many footwear brands, nobody writes it, at least not for Amazon. The wholesale team owns the calendar and the key accounts. The Amazon listing was often built by a reseller, with the reseller’s photographs and whatever size information came with the stock. The brand’s fit knowledge sits with its product developers and its store partners’ staff, and it rarely travels to the one page where, in 2020, a large share of the category is being decided.

What changed in the economics this year

Amazon made the premium end of the category cheaper to sell in 2020. From February 18, the referral fee on shoes priced above $75 fell from 18% to 15%, Amazon told sellers in December. For a brand whose core styles sit above $75, the case for running its own listing improved before the pandemic began.

The shelf itself has also been changing. Amazon tested a “Top Brand” badge in select searches, mostly in clothing and shoes, Marketplace Pulse noted in August 2019. A category where Amazon experiments with labeling brands is one where the brand’s own presence on the page counts for more, and where a reseller’s listing speaks for the brand whether or not the brand agreed.

None of this means every footwear brand should rush onto Amazon. It means the cost of being absent rose. A brand that is not on the page in 2020 is still there, through resellers, and its fit story is being told by whoever bought its stock.

Questions for the footwear team

  • Who in the company knows how each of our styles fits, and has that knowledge ever been written onto an Amazon listing?
  • What do the last 50 reviews on our top five Amazon listings say about size, and who sold those units?
  • Which of our styles sell above $75, and what did the February fee change do to their Amazon margin?
  • If our largest wholesale partners order less for fall, which listings will carry the stock that is left?

Footwear will go back into stores when shoppers feel safe trying shoes on. Some of the habits formed this spring will stay online. The brands that make their Amazon pages do the fitting will be the ones those shoppers return to, and that is the kind of listing work we take on when we run a brand’s Amazon channel.

P0430.crumb: Live shopping sells what a host can…
P0430.title: Live shopping sells what a host can touch, test and vouch for
P0430.alt: Open jar of cream on a linen cloth beside a steaming mug of tea, with a ring light against a teal wall.
P0430.ttag: Live shopping sells what a host can touch, test and vouch for | Kwontified
P0430.desc: China’s live shopping boom sells what a trusted host can handle on camera at an impulse price. Western platforms now have the tools; most brands lack the host.
P0430.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 30, 2020.
P0430.body:
Picture a woman at a desk under ring lights, holding a bottle of perfume up to the camera while a counter in the corner of the screen ticks down. In China this is not a novelty. Viya, a host with 17.5 million subscribers on Alibaba’s Taobao, sold 15,000 bottles of Kim Kardashian’s perfume within minutes, Marketplace reported in April. Taobao’s livestream channels generated about 200 billion yuan, roughly $28 billion, in 2019.

Western platforms spent the last year building the same stage. What they have not built is the person standing on it. Live shopping sells a particular kind of product, presented by a particular kind of host, and the brands that will make it work outside China are the ones that start from those two choices rather than from the tool.

How big live shopping is, and how small it still is

The Chinese numbers are large and easy to misread. The 200 billion yuan came from more than 60,000 shows that drew 400 million viewers in 2019, and Taobao said livestream sales had been doubling every year for three years. Yet the same figure was only about 3% of Taobao’s 5.7 trillion yuan in merchandise sales. Live shopping is a fast-growing aisle in China, not the whole store.

The pandemic widened it. In February, the number of livestream sessions on Taobao doubled as stores closed. Brands that had sold only through their own shops, from the premium Chinese label Gebang to Coach, moved staff in front of cameras, according to the same Marketplace report.

In the US, the pieces have been arriving one at a time.

Amazon launched Amazon Live in early 2019, with hosts demonstrating products above a carousel of items to buy and an app that lets brand-registered sellers stream from a phone. In May, Facebook said it was testing live shopping product tags alongside its new Shops. And on July 16, Instagram began rolling out its redesigned Shop in Explore, with checkout inside the app, TechCrunch reported. The plumbing for buying from a stream is now in place on the platforms Western shoppers already use. What none of these launches supplies is an audience that already trusts the person holding the product.

What the streams actually sell

The Chinese experience is specific about what works. Clothing is a core category, and items under 500 yuan, about $70, sell best. Hosts try clothes on and turn to show the fit, answer viewers’ questions about texture and delivery as they come in, and run flash discounts that last a few minutes. Above all, they vouch for authenticity on a platform long criticized for fakes; one shopper told Marketplace she had stopped buying from overseas sites because the hosts guarantee what they sell.

Read those details as a filter and three conditions fall out. The product has to be something whose value shows when it is handled: a fabric that drapes, a lipstick shade on real skin, a pan that does not stick. It has to sit under the price at which a viewer buys on impulse, because a stream rewards decisions made in minutes. And it needs someone the viewer trusts, because the stream asks for money before the shopper has touched anything.

Think of the cosmetics counter in a department store. The brand pays for the counter, but the sale is made by the person behind it, who knows the regulars, tries the shade on the customer’s wrist and says honestly when something will not suit her. A livestream rebuilds that counter for an audience of thousands. Most Western brands that have tried streams so far built the counter and forgot the person: a product demonstration run by the brand team, polite and accurate and watched by very few.

Follow the value to the host

In China, the value created by a stream flows in large part to the host. Viya earned over $4 million in commissions in 2018, by Taobao’s estimate, according to Marketplace. That is the market telling brands where the scarce asset sits. A platform can provide the stream, the checkout and the traffic. Only a person can provide the trust that makes a viewer buy a perfume she cannot smell.

That creates an awkward question inside Western brands. The people who manage creators and influencers usually sit in the social or brand team, measured on reach and engagement. The people who manage Amazon and marketplace sales sit in e-commerce, measured on revenue. A live shopping stream is both at once, and at many brands nobody owns it. The likely result is a few streams run by whoever has time, judged by view counts, and quietly dropped.

The evidence so far leans toward live shopping in the West growing first in beauty and apparel, through creators who already have an audience that trusts them, before it spreads to brand-run channels. It is too early to say how large it will become; even in China, it is a few percent of the market.

Questions to settle before the first stream

  • Which of our products only make sense once someone handles them, and do any sit under an impulse price?
  • Who would our customers trust to hold those products on camera, and do we already work with that person in another channel?
  • Which team will own live shopping, and will it be measured on sales or on views?
  • What will we count as a successful first month, before we see the numbers?

The platforms have built the stage. Choosing the products and the people for it is the work, and it is the kind of social commerce planning we do when we run Instagram Shop for brands.

P0432.title: Amazon Q2 2020 other revenue rose 41% while click prices fell 41%
P0432.alt: A tall stack and a short stack of brass coins on a worn wooden table against a pink wall.
P0432.ttag: Amazon Q2 2020 other revenue rose 41% while click prices fell 41% | Kwontified
P0432.desc: Amazon’s ad-heavy other revenue grew 41% in Q2 2020 while a typical Sponsored Products advertiser spent 22% more. The gap is new bidders, and Q4 prices them in.
P0432.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 4, 2020.
P0432.body:
Amazon’s “other” revenue, the line that mostly holds its advertising sales, grew 41% to $4.22 billion in the second quarter, the company reported on July 30. The same week, Merkle published its quarterly benchmark. Among the advertisers it tracks, Sponsored Products spend rose only 22% from a year earlier: clicks more than doubled while the average cost per click fell 41%, according to a summary of the report.

Both numbers can be true at once. Amazon’s total is the spend of every advertiser added together, and in the second quarter that total grew from two directions: each advertiser bought more cheap clicks, and more advertisers and ad formats joined the auction. For a brand reading its own results against Amazon’s headline, the second part is the one that matters, because those extra bidders will still be there when Prime Day lands in the fourth quarter.

Why Amazon’s Q2 2020 other revenue looks like your benchmark

It is natural to treat the earnings line as the market’s growth rate. Amazon does not report advertising on its own. The footnote to the release says “other” primarily includes sales of advertising services, and Amazon’s chief financial officer, Brian Olsavsky, told analysts on the call that “advertising is growing, so that’s a good source of profitability.” If the whole market grew 41% and your account grew much less, the conclusion seems obvious: you lost share.

That reading was close enough in a normal year. Through 2019 and into early 2020, the other line grew at a steady clip, 41% in the fourth quarter of 2019 and 44% in the first quarter of 2020, when Olsavsky said growth was in line with the prior quarter, AdExchanger reported. When the auction’s prices and population change slowly, the total and the typical advertiser move together.

The second quarter of 2020 changed both at once.

The gap between 41% and 22% is new bidders and new formats

Start with what Merkle’s panel saw. Clicks up 107% and cost per click down 41% multiply to spend up about 22% (2.07 × 0.59 = 1.22). Shoppers flooded Amazon, the supply of ad placements grew with the traffic, and many advertisers had pulled back in late March. In the last week of March, the typical Amazon advertiser in Merkle’s data spent half as much per day as in January, Digiday reported in May. More placements chasing fewer dollars is what a falling click price looks like.

Now compare that with the total. If the typical advertiser’s spend rose 22% and Amazon’s ad-heavy line rose 41%, then 1.41 ÷ 1.22 leaves about 16% of growth that the average panel advertiser’s own spending does not explain. Three things can fill that gap, and the public numbers point at each:

Source of growthWhat the public record shows
More advertisers in the auctionThird-party seller services grew 52%, and Olsavsky said third-party units were more than half of unit volume, “helped by improved quarter-over-quarter growth in active sellers”
Formats outside Sponsored ProductsMerkle’s panel increased Sponsored Brands spend 58% while its click price fell 19%
Non-advertising items in “other”The footnote lists “other service offerings” alongside advertising; Amazon does not split them

The last row is a reminder of how much is unknown. Amazon publishes one line, Merkle samples its own clients, and neither covers Amazon DSP or video in detail. Treat the 16% as a direction, not a measurement. The direction is still clear: the second quarter’s growth came from more participants and more volume, while the price of each click went down.

What a crowded, cheap auction means for Q4

A brand that compares its spend growth with 41% will conclude it is underinvesting. A brand that compares it with 22% will learn whether it kept pace with similar advertisers. The second comparison is the useful one, because it holds the population constant.

The harder question is what happens next. Amazon said Prime Day will move into the fourth quarter of 2020, everywhere except India. Olsavsky also said Amazon cut its own marketing by about a third in the quarter “mainly because we’re trying to manage demand” and expects a higher level in the third. Each of those pushes the same way: more demand for the same placements later in the year, bid by a larger field than last year’s.

Take a keyword that cost $1.00 a click in the fourth quarter of 2019 and $0.59 this spring, the panel’s average drop. A Q4 budget built from the spring price expects 1.7 times the clicks the money will actually buy if prices return to last year’s level, and the gap widens if the new bidders stay. The spring price was a product of an emptied auction. It is the wrong anchor for a quarter that now holds both Prime Day and Cyber Week.

Brands that can afford to move early face a genuine choice. Cheap clicks in August and September build sales history and reviews at a lower cost per order, and that history helps organic rank going into the holiday. The case for spending now is strong where conversion has held; where it has not, a cheap click is still a poor buy.

Bid triggers for the rest of 2020

  1. Benchmark your spend growth against an advertiser panel such as Merkle’s 22%, not against Amazon’s 41%, and read the gap as share only after that adjustment.
  2. Build Q4 click-price assumptions from Q4 2019 actuals, then add a margin for a larger field; never from Q2 2020.
  3. Track your weekly cost per click on your top 20 keywords from now on. The first sustained rise is the sign the new bidders are competing for your terms.
  4. Spend into cheap clicks only where conversion rate is at or above last year’s; elsewhere, hold budget for the fourth quarter.

Amazon’s earnings line is a sum, and sums hide who is doing the adding. Reading it as a price signal is how budgets go wrong in the quarter that matters most; we plan Amazon ad budgets from click-price and conversion data rather than headlines.
