P0433.crumb: Target’s same-day boom passed Target Plus…
P0433.title: Target’s same-day boom passed Target Plus partners by
P0433.alt: Open red loading bay filled with brown paper bags, with a red-wrapped parcel on the sidewalk outside.
P0433.ttag: Target’s same-day boom passed Target Plus partners by | Kwontified
P0433.desc: Target’s online surge ran through its stores, and Target Plus items ship from partners’ warehouses. The curated marketplace kept trust and missed the trunk.
P0433.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 6, 2020.
P0433.body:
Stand in a Target parking lot on a weekday afternoon this spring and you would have seen the company’s year in miniature. Cars nose into the orange Drive Up spaces, a team member wheels out a cart, and the bags go into the trunk without the shopper stepping inside. Same-day services, Target’s name for Order Pickup, Drive Up and Shipt delivery, grew 278% in the first quarter, and stores fulfilled nearly 80% of Target’s digital sales, the company reported on May 20.

Nothing in those bags came from Target Plus, the invitation-only marketplace Target opened in February 2019. Its partners sell and ship from their own warehouses, so their products cannot be picked off a store shelf and handed through a car window. That one operational fact explains why the curated marketplace stayed small through the busiest online months Target has ever had, and what it is actually for.

A marketplace built to look like Target’s own shelf

Target designed its marketplace as an extension of the store’s taste, not as a second store. Partners were “carefully selected and invited,” Target said at launch, and shoppers got the same promises as on Target’s own items, including free shipping and in-store returns. Partner products appear inside the regular categories, with no separate marketplace section, TechCrunch noted when it opened.

It grew slowly by design. Target Plus started with 30 merchants and 60,000 products and reached 109 merchants and 165,000 products after a year, Marketplace Pulse counted in February. Walmart’s marketplace listed nearly 40 million products by the summer of 2019, Modern Retail reported. Most Target Plus merchants did not offer two-day or faster shipping, and Target’s own stores already fulfilled more than two-thirds of its estimated $6 billion in 2019 online sales, by Marketplace Pulse’s estimate.

So the structure was in place before the crisis. Target’s online business was a store business with a website on top. Its marketplace was a mail-order business that borrowed the store’s name.

What the crisis rewarded, and who held it

When shoppers moved online in March, the value went to whatever could reach them fastest and most safely. At Target that meant the store. Digital comparable sales rose 141% in the first quarter, accelerating from 33% in February to 282% in April, and Drive Up and Order Pickup carried much of it.

The partner shipping from a warehouse two states away was in a different race. On Target.com its product sat in the same category grid as Target’s own, under the same promise of free shipping, but it could not join the services shoppers were choosing that spring. A shopper who wanted a desk lamp in the trunk tonight bought the one Target stocked.

There was a benefit on the other side of the ledger, and it is easy to miss. Open marketplaces spent the spring policing their own sellers. Amazon said in March that it had removed well over half a million offers for coronavirus-related price gouging and suspended more than 3,900 US selling accounts, in a post on its site. A marketplace of a hundred-odd invited partners has no such crowd to police. The invitation that kept Target Plus small also kept its shelf trustworthy at the moment trust was scarce.

That is the trade Target made, and the crisis made it visible. Target captured the spring’s growth through its stores and its own inventory. The marketplace protected what Target sells most, its reputation as a store you do not have to second-guess, and it did so by staying a curated corner rather than a volume engine.

What a Target Plus invitation is worth now

For a brand weighing an invitation, the spring is a useful corrective. Target Plus is not a back door into the store-fulfilled growth that drove Target’s year. Products shipped by a partner sit outside Drive Up and Order Pickup, and they will stay outside as long as the partner’s warehouse, not the store’s backroom, holds the stock.

What the invitation does buy is a place on Target’s shelf in Target’s voice. Shoppers find partner items in the same grid, judge them by Target’s standards and can return them to a store. A brand that sells there is borrowing Target’s credibility with a guest who assumes Target chose the product. That is worth having for a brand building awareness with Target’s shoppers, and it is worth very little to a brand that needs volume in the second half of 2020.

Partners can narrow the gap, though not close it. The ones that come closest to what a Target shopper now expects from the store itself ship in two days from their own warehouses. They keep stock deep enough that a listing never goes dark, and they treat Target’s in-store return promise as their own cost of doing business. Everyone else is selling from the back of a catalog with Target’s name on the cover.

The evidence so far leans toward Target keeping it that way. Nothing in its first-quarter report mentioned the marketplace, and every number it highlighted ran through a store.

Questions for the team weighing Target Plus

  • Which of our products would a Target shopper want the same day, and are those better placed with Target’s buyers as wholesale items than as marketplace listings?
  • Can we ship in two days or less from our own warehouse, given that most Target Plus partners could not as of February?
  • Are we pricing for volume or for presence? Target Plus rewards presence; build the forecast that way.
  • Who on our team owns the conversation with Target’s buyer, and does the marketplace listing help that conversation or compete with it?

The brands that read the invitation as a standard to meet will get the most from it. If Target and Walmart are both on your plan for the fall, that is the kind of channel decision we work through with brands.

P0436.title: Zalando partners recovered first where brands controlled stock
P0436.alt: Wooden shelves stacked with orange paper-wrapped parcels with tags, seen past an open door with a key in the lock.
P0436.ttag: Zalando partners recovered first where brands controlled stock | Kwontified
P0436.desc: Zalando’s partner sales doubled in the spring of 2020. The brands that recovered first already controlled what Zalando’s shoppers saw, and when.
P0436.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 13, 2020.
P0436.body:
Over the Easter weekend in April, with most of Europe’s shoe shops shuttered, some of them were still shipping orders. Stores in Zalando’s Connected Retail program sold around 35,000 items through the platform that weekend, and Zalando’s partners as a whole sold more than a million, up more than 100% on the year, Zalando said in its first-quarter update. A few weeks earlier its gross merchandise volume had been falling 8% a year.

The Zalando partners who recovered first had one thing in common, and it was not their category or their size. Their stock was already visible to Zalando’s shoppers, and their own teams decided what to show. Brands that reached Zalando only through its buyers waited for someone else to decide.

Lockdown sorted Zalando partners by who held the stock

Zalando runs two businesses on one storefront. In its wholesale business, Zalando’s buyers order a brand’s products and sell them as Zalando’s own.

In the Partner Program, the brand lists its own stock and pays Zalando a commission; brands “keep control over the assortment, prices and brand representation,” as Zalando’s head of partner solutions put it in 2017. Partners were chosen partly on whether they could meet Zalando’s free delivery and 100-day return expectations, the company said when it opened the program in Norway. Connected Retail extends the same idea to physical stores, which list what is on their shelves and ship it to Zalando customers.

When demand collapsed in March, those two models faced the same shopper with different reflexes. GMV fell 8% in the three weeks after March 9 and was growing again in the two weeks after March 30. A partner could follow that turn the day it happened, adding sizes, moving stock from a closed store’s shelf to the platform, pushing the categories that suddenly sold. Zalando also waived its commission for every Connected Retail store from April 1 to May 31, FashionNetwork reported, which made a closed shop’s inventory cheap to put online.

A brand that sold only wholesale could not move that fast. Its products were on Zalando because a buyer had ordered them months before, for a spring that never arrived, and whatever the buyer chose to reorder was the brand’s entire Zalando presence.

A quarter that rewarded the brands already plugged in

The second quarter made the pattern hard to miss. Zalando’s GMV grew 33%, and partner program GMV more than doubled, results published on August 11 showed. Around 180 new partners joined between April and June, more than 1,800 stores in five markets were selling through Connected Retail by July, and more than three million new customers shopped on the platform, Zalando said in July. The items shipped through Zalando Fulfillment Solutions, its warehouse service for partners, grew 180%.

That last figure is the quiet one. A partner whose stock already sat in Zalando’s own warehouses could sell it with Zalando’s delivery promise attached, without reopening its own distribution center under distancing rules. For a brand weighing the program in 2019, the fulfillment service looked like a cost line. In April it looked like a way to stay open.

“Many of our partners have intensified their business on our platform in the last months,” said David Schröder, Zalando’s chief financial officer.

The demand itself moved too. Zalando pointed to higher demand for sports, beauty and kids’ items, a mix that also brought its average return rate down. Those are the categories that fit a life lived at home, and they rewarded the partners who could put more of them in front of shoppers in April rather than wait for an autumn order.

Who decides what Zalando’s shoppers see

Read through the numbers and the real dividing line is organizational, not commercial. In a wholesale relationship, the person who decides what a brand shows on Zalando works for Zalando. In the Partner Program, that person works for the brand, often on the e-commerce team, and can act the same afternoon. The spring of 2020 paid for speed, and speed belonged to whoever held the decision.

That does not make wholesale the wrong choice. A buyer’s order moves inventory risk off the brand’s books, and in a spring when nobody knew what would sell, that was worth something.

But the brands that kept both models running, wholesale for the core range and partner listings for everything else, had a second door when the first one narrowed. Zalando has described its own platform transition as accelerating since 2019. The evidence so far leans toward it wanting more of its growth to come through that second door, and toward the brands that learned to use it this spring keeping their head start when shops reopen.

Questions for the team that owns Zalando

  • When demand turned in late March, who at our company could have changed what Zalando’s shoppers saw, and how long would it have taken?
  • Which of our products sit in Zalando’s wholesale assortment, and which could we list ourselves as a partner if the buyer passes on them?
  • Is our stock for Zalando held where a partner listing can reach it, in our own warehouse or in Zalando Fulfillment Solutions?
  • Does our e-commerce team have the authority to move inventory between wholesale and partner channels, or does that decision sit with the account manager?

The brands that recovered first did not have better products. They had shorter lines between a change in demand and a change on the shelf. If Zalando is part of your plan for the autumn, that is the kind of question we work through with brands expanding in Europe.

P0438.crumb: Q4 2020 ad budgets should follow the last…
P0438.title: Q4 2020 ad budgets should follow the last dollar, not 2019
P0438.alt: A row of upright brass coins on a dark wooden table, with one coin set apart in a pool of sunlight.
P0438.ttag: Q4 2020 ad budgets should follow the last dollar, not 2019 | Kwontified
P0438.desc: Q4 2020 has more peaks than 2019, and one has no date yet. Fund each day until its last dollar earns your target return, and keep a reserve.
P0438.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 18, 2020.
P0438.body:
Most fourth-quarter ad plans start from last year’s spreadsheet: the same weeks, the same peaks, the same share of the quarter’s money parked in Cyber Week. That spreadsheet is about to be wrong in three places. Amazon said on July 30 that it plans to hold Prime Day in the fourth quarter of 2020 rather than the third, as Marketing Dive reported, without naming a date. Target will start its biggest holiday deals in October and, like Walmart, close its stores on Thanksgiving Day, Supermarket News reported.

A Q4 2020 ad budget therefore has to cover more peaks than 2019 had, and one of them cannot be put on the calendar yet. The answer is not a better calendar. It is to stop splitting money by date at all and fund each day until its last dollar stops paying.

Why last year’s split felt safe

Copying last year’s shape is not lazy. It encodes real history: Cyber Monday 2019 was the biggest online shopping day in US history at $9.4 billion, up 19.7%, Adobe’s figures showed. Retailers reinforce the habit. Ahead of Prime Day 2019, Amazon asked some brands to raise their ad spend by as much as 100%, Practical Ecommerce noted in its recap. The pull is anchoring: last year’s numbers are the only numbers on the table, so they become the plan.

The trouble is that a calendar split answers the wrong question. It asks how much of the year’s demand lands on a day. The budget question is how much one more dollar buys on that day, and the two answers can be far apart even on the busiest day of the year.

The last dollar decides the Q4 2020 ad budget

Ad spend inside a single day runs into diminishing returns. The first dollars buy the best clicks: your strongest keywords, where your listing converts and your bids win easily. Each extra dollar reaches further, into weaker searches or higher bids for the same ones, and returns less. A peak day lifts the whole curve, because more shoppers are searching, but it does not remove the bend.

Take a brand that needs every marginal dollar of ad spend to return at least $2 in sales. Here is what each extra $1,000 buys on an ordinary Q4 day and on a peak day with roughly three times the demand.

Spend trancheOrdinary day salesReturn on that $1,000Peak day salesReturn on that $1,000
First $1,000$4,0004.0$8,0008.0
Second $1,000$2,0002.0$5,0005.0
Third $1,000$1,0001.0$3,0003.0
Fourth $1,000——$1,5001.5

Fund each day until the next tranche falls below 2.0. The ordinary day gets $2,000 and reports an average ROAS of 3.0 on $6,000 of sales. The peak day gets $3,000 and reports 5.3 on $16,000.

Two errors follow from looking at averages instead. A team that sees 5.3 on the peak day, and assumes three times the demand deserves three times the money, will spend far past the point of return. Even the fourth $1,000 adds only $1,500 of sales, while the day’s average still reads a handsome 4.4 on $17,500. And a team that caps the peak at the ordinary day’s $2,000 leaves $3,000 of sales on the table for the third $1,000. Three times the demand earned 1.5 times the budget, not three.

What a moving Prime Day does to the plan

The same rule handles the date Amazon has not announced. Instead of guessing, hold back part of the quarter’s budget, say 20%, unassigned until the date is public. When it is, the reserve goes to the days whose next tranche returns most, which will include the Prime Day window and the days just before it, and the rest of the quarter does not have to be torn up.

Prices will move too. Merkle’s second-quarter benchmark showed Sponsored Products clicks up 107% and cost per click down 41%, as summarized by Karooya. A tranche table built on spring prices will overstate what each $1,000 buys once more advertisers crowd the fourth-quarter auctions, so rebuild it from September data, not May’s.

The retailers’ own calendars bend the curve as well. Target’s October deals and the closed stores on Thanksgiving spread holiday demand across more days. That flattens the single Cyber Week spike and lifts the ordinary days around it, which in tranche terms means more days in October and November will have a second $1,000 worth buying.

What the data cannot tell you is the shape of your own curve. Average ROAS hides it completely. The only way to see the bend is to change spend and watch what changes. Raise budgets on a matched set of campaigns by 20% for a week in September, hold the rest steady, and compare the extra sales with the extra spend. That ratio is the number your Q4 plan should be built on.

Budget triggers for the quarter

  • Fund each campaign until its marginal return, not its average, meets your target; recheck weekly from Labor Day.
  • Keep a reserve unassigned until Amazon dates Prime Day, then spend it where the next tranche returns most.
  • Raise daily caps ahead of every peak so campaigns do not run dry by afternoon on the days with the steepest curve.
  • Treat Target’s October deals as their own peak for Roundel and Target.com spend, not as noise around Amazon’s.

The Q4 2020 plan that survives will be the one that never committed its money to a date. That is the Q4 budgeting work we do with brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target, starting from what their own last dollar earns.

P0439.crumb: Latin America’s e-commerce leap will last…
P0439.title: Latin America’s e-commerce leap will last where buying is routine
P0439.alt: Yellow insulated delivery bag hanging beside a blue door on a colorful cobblestone street lined with flowers.
P0439.ttag: Latin America’s e-commerce leap will last where buying is routine | Kwontified
P0439.desc: Mercado Libre sold twice as many items this spring. The habits that last will be the repeat basket and the digital wallet, not the one-off splurge.
P0439.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 20, 2020.
P0439.body:
Take a household in São Paulo or Mexico City that had never bought groceries online. In April it ordered detergent and rice on Mercado Libre because the store felt risky. By June it was ordering them again, from the same app, often paid from a digital wallet that now held money it had never kept anywhere but cash. Multiply that household by millions and you have Mercado Libre’s second quarter: items sold up 101.4%, and gross merchandise volume up 101.5% on a currency-neutral basis to $5.0 billion, the company reported on August 10.

The question every brand selling in Latin America is now debating is how much of that stays when stores reopen. The answer depends less on the size of the leap than on what kind of buying it was. Latin America’s e-commerce growth will hold where buying became a routine, a repeat basket attached to money already sitting in an account, and fade where it was a one-off.

What the new Latin America e-commerce buyer actually did

The headline numbers hide the more useful ones. New buyers on Mercado Libre grew 75% year on year, a record, and the average buyer purchased 5.7 items in the quarter against 4.3 a year earlier, chief financial officer Pedro Arnt said on the earnings call. New registrations reached 16.9 million, against 12.4 million in the same quarter of 2019, and mobile accounted for 69.4% of the volume.

The categories tell you which purchases were routines. Consumer packaged goods reached a mid- to high-single-digit share of the business in Mercado Libre’s strongest markets faster than the company expected, and Arnt said shoppers who buy household goods “are more engaged across other categories,” while calling the data early. Electronics, the classic one-off, only started recovering in May and June.

That pattern matters because a pantry order is not a decision a shopper makes once. It is a decision a shopper stops making. The first order is a trial; the third is a habit, and habits are what survive a reopened store.

A brand can run the same split on its own Mercado Libre sales. The useful number is not how many new buyers arrived this spring but how many of them have ordered a second time, and which products brought them back. A brand whose new buyers came for one gift item has a smaller lasting gain than one whose new buyers came back for refills, even if the spring’s sales looked the same.

The wallet is the hidden structure

The second routine is financial, and it is easy to miss from outside the region. Mercado Pago, the company’s payments arm, reached 52 million payers, up 64%, and Arnt credited government aid for a rise in users receiving account balances. “As people prefer to stay away from cash, we have seen an increased demand of devices,” said Osvaldo Giménez, who runs Mercado Pago; it sold about one million of its payment devices in the quarter.

Money that already sits in a digital wallet changes who wins the next purchase. The friction that used to stop an online order in much of Latin America, a missing credit card or a trip to pay cash at a corner store, disappears when the balance is already on the phone. The shopper does not need to decide to shop online again. The money is already there, one tap from the cart, and the next purchase starts from a balance rather than from a decision.

Delivery reinforces the same loop. Orders arriving in under 48 hours rose by 10 percentage points year on year, Arnt said. A shopper who gets the detergent in two days has fewer reasons to go back to the aisle.

What fades, and what Mercado Libre itself expects

Not everything will hold. Arnt drew the line himself: the adoption of digital buying is a trend he called “sustainable,” while the quarter’s lower marketing spend was “less so,” and the company plans to spend again. Discretionary first purchases made during lockdown, the gadget or the gym mat, carry no routine behind them, and they are the likeliest to slip back to stores and markets.

The evidence so far leans toward durability. Mercado Libre said it entered July “in a stronger fashion” than the start of the quarter across most markets, and its chief executive, Marcos Galperin, called the period a “tremendous fast forward in digital adoption” across the region. It is too early to say how far the curve settles once stores are fully open; a single quarter of data cannot show that, and brands should treat any forecast as a range.

Questions for the team that owns Latin America

Inside many brands, Latin America still sits with a distributor or a regional sales team whose job is getting product onto store shelves. That is the question in the room this summer: who owns the online shelf where millions of households just formed a habit?

  • Which of our products are bought on repeat, and are they listed and in stock on Mercado Libre in each of our markets?
  • Who decides our assortment and pricing there now: our team, a distributor or a reseller?
  • Can a shopper paying from a Mercado Pago balance buy our products as easily as a competitor’s?
  • What would we need to see by the end of the year to treat online as the main route in the region rather than an extra one?

The brands that answer those questions by the end of September will be in the routine before it sets. If Latin America is on your plan, that is the kind of market work we do with brands on Mercado Libre.

P0440.title: Zalando Partner Program growth moves stock risk onto brands
P0440.alt: Platform trolley piled high with orange paper-wrapped parcels in a warehouse with shelving and boxes.
P0440.ttag: Zalando Partner Program growth moves stock risk onto brands | Kwontified
P0440.desc: Zalando’s GMV keeps outgrowing its revenue because partners, not Zalando, own more of the stock. More listings put more markdown risk on brands.
P0440.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 25, 2020.
P0440.body:
Zalando’s gross merchandise volume grew 25.1% in the first half of 2020, to €4.72 billion. Its revenue grew 19.6%, to €3.56 billion, results published on August 11 showed. A retailer whose sales grow faster than its revenue looks like a retailer with a problem, usually discounting or returns eating the top line. Zalando has been telling investors to expect exactly that gap, and it is not a sign of weakness.

“We will continue to see GMV growing faster than revenues, fully in-line with our long-term strategy,” chief financial officer David Schröder said in August 2019. The gap is the Zalando Partner Program at work, and it measures something every brand selling there should price: who owns the stock.

Why Zalando’s revenue looks like it is falling behind

The gap widened in 2020. In 2019, GMV grew 23.6% to €8.2 billion and revenue 20.3% to €6.5 billion, Zalando reported in February, a difference of 3.3 points. In the first half of 2020 the difference was 5.5 points. Revenue was about 79% of GMV in 2019 and about 75% in the first half of 2020. The two measures treat VAT and returns differently, so that ratio is not a take rate, but its direction is the signal.

Over the same period the Partner Program, where brands and retailers sell their own stock on Zalando, accounted for 15% of fashion store GMV at the end of 2019, and its GMV more than doubled in the second quarter of 2020. Around 180 new partners joined between April and June, Zalando said in July.

The same pair of sneakers, booked two ways

Take an €80 sneaker and 100 pairs, of which 70 sell at full price and 30 do not.

Sold wholesale, Zalando buys all 100 from the brand at, say, €36 a pair, 45% of the retail price. The brand books €3,600 and is done. Zalando books the 70 full-price sales, €5,600, as revenue, and the 30 leftover pairs are its problem: it marks them down, holds them or writes them off.

Sold through the Partner Program at a 20% commission, the 70 sales still produce €5,600 of GMV. Zalando books €16 a pair, €1,120 in all, plus whatever it charges for fulfillment. The brand keeps €64 a pair before its own fulfillment and returns costs, and it owns the 30 pairs that did not sell.

Same shoes, same shoppers, same GMV. Zalando’s revenue on the partner version is a fraction of the wholesale version, and its inventory risk is zero. That is why the revenue line lags: every euro of GMV that moves from the wholesale model to the partner model shows up as GMV but only partly as revenue. It is also why Zalando wants it. A business that earns a commission on stock it does not own can grow its assortment without growing its warehouse bill, and it is paid on what sells.

The brand’s side of the trade is not worse, only different. On the 70 pairs it earns more per pair than the wholesale price. On the 30 it carries what Zalando used to carry. Whether that is a good deal depends on how well the brand forecasts its own sell-through, which is exactly the risk Zalando’s buyers used to price into their orders.

Run the same 100 pairs with a worse season. If only 50 sell, the partner brand collects €3,200, less than the €3,600 the wholesale order would have paid, and it holds 50 pairs instead of none. If 90 sell, it collects €5,760 and holds ten. Wholesale pays €3,600 in every one of those seasons. The partner model hands the brand the whole spread between a bad season and a good one, and Zalando’s revenue line no longer moves with it.

What more partner listings change for brands

None of what follows is announced policy, but each falls out of the arithmetic.

The buyer conversation changes. A retailer paid a commission on stock it does not hold has less reason to buy the uncertain items: new styles, wider size runs, colors that might not sell. Expect more of them to be offered back as partner listings, while Zalando’s own buying concentrates on proven sellers.

Fulfillment becomes the second business. Around 40% of partner items shipped through Zalando Fulfillment Solutions in the fourth quarter of 2019, and the items shipped through it grew 180% in the second quarter of 2020. A partner that uses it pays Zalando a fee on top of the commission; one that does not carries its own logistics.

Control moves with the stock. Partners “keep control over the assortment, prices and brand representation,” as Zalando’s partner chief put it in 2017. That control is real, and it comes bundled with the leftover pairs.

Rules for splitting a range between wholesale and partner

  • Put the items you can forecast well into the Partner Program; you keep more per sale and the risk you carry is one you can price.
  • Offer Zalando the items with the widest forecast range as wholesale, where its buyer, not your balance sheet, absorbs the miss.
  • Price your all-in partner cost per euro of GMV, commission plus fulfillment plus returns handling, before every season’s buy, not once at sign-up.
  • Watch the gap between Zalando’s GMV and revenue growth each quarter. While it widens, assume your buyer’s open-to-buy is growing more slowly than Zalando’s headline growth.

Zalando’s shift is a reasonable bet for Zalando. Whether it is a good one for a brand depends on which pairs it ends up holding. That split is the kind of marketplace decision we model with brands expanding in Europe.

P0442.crumb: Blanket Amazon ad spend cuts in March…
P0442.title: Blanket Amazon ad spend cuts in March gave rivals cheaper clicks
P0442.alt: One open produce stall full of vegetables and baskets in a row of shuttered market stalls on a cobbled street.
P0442.ttag: Blanket Amazon ad spend cuts in March gave rivals cheaper clicks | Kwontified
P0442.desc: In March many brands switched off Amazon ads by budget line. Advertisers that stayed bought clicks for far less, and the cut was made far from the shelf.
P0442.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 27, 2020.
P0442.body:
Most brands will remember a version of the same call in the third week of March. Finance asks every department for a list of spending that can stop by Friday. Television is booked, payroll is people, and the agency retainer has a notice period. The Amazon ads can be switched off in an afternoon, so they go first.

Across the industry, that call happened often. In an IAB survey of nearly 400 brand and agency decision-makers reported on March 27, 24% of brands had paused all advertising for the first and second quarters and another 46% were adjusting it. The Amazon ad spend cuts that cost brands most were not the deepest ones. They were the blanket ones, decided on a budget line by people who could not see the shelf.

How March’s Amazon ad spend cuts were decided

The scale showed up quickly in Amazon’s own auctions. By the last week of March, the typical Amazon advertiser in Merkle’s panel was spending half as much per day as in January, Digiday reported. In the IAB survey, 45% of marketers said they were cutting performance budgets, the kind most retail media sits in, and 74% expected a downturn worse than 2008 and 2009.

Some of those cuts were sensible, and the sensible ones looked different. Amazon itself pulled back its Google Shopping and text ads from March 11, Bloomberg reported, days before its warehouses began prioritizing staples and medical supplies. Conversion on non-essential items fell by as much as 30% that month, Modern Retail reported. A team that paused ads on products it could not restock, or on items shoppers had stopped buying, was cutting waste.

The blanket cut is a different animal. It switches off the hero product with twelve weeks of stock along with the accessory that is about to run out. It is made by whoever holds the budget, which at many brands is finance or a brand marketing lead, not the e-commerce team that watches stock and conversion every morning. The budget line was easy to see. The shelf was not.

It is worth being fair to the people who made those calls. Two-thirds of the buyers in the IAB survey had not yet decided what to do about the second half of the year, and nobody in March could say how long stores would stay shut. Preserving cash was a reasonable instinct. The trouble is that Amazon advertising looks like discretionary marketing on a profit and loss statement, while on the site it behaves more like shelf space: when it stops, the product moves down the page at the moment shoppers are looking.

What the brands that kept spending bought

The auction did not stand still while those brands were away. Cost per click fell by as much as 30% in April, Digiday’s sources found. By the second quarter, Sponsored Products advertisers in Merkle’s panel were spending 22% more than a year earlier and getting 107% more clicks, because cost per click had dropped 41%, according to a summary of Merkle’s report.

Read that from the side of a brand that went dark. The shoppers searching in its category did not disappear. They found whoever was still advertising, and those advertisers were paying less per click than a year earlier. Some of those shoppers will have tried a rival’s product for the first time.

Agencies warned in March that pulling all ads would hurt rankings and future performance. Nobody has yet published a clean measure of how much, and brands should be skeptical of anyone who claims a precise figure. The direction is not in doubt.

The harder cost is the one that does not show up in any report. A brand that paused everything in March had no data from April, the month its category’s buying habits were being rewritten. When it came back, it was bidding on a market it had not watched, with keyword lists and bids built for a February that no longer existed. The brands that kept even a small amount running on their core searches came out of April knowing what had changed.

The decision that should move

The lesson is not that brands should never cut. It is about who holds the switch. In March, at many brands, the authority to stop Amazon advertising sat with the person furthest from the information that should have driven the decision. The e-commerce lead could see which products had stock, which were converting and which searches were getting cheaper. The person approving the cut could see a line on a spreadsheet.

The evidence so far leans toward the gap mattering more than the size of the cut. Take two brands that each cut 40%: the one that cut product by product keeps its best positions, and the one that cut across the board gives them away. The second half of 2020 will bring more shocks, and the same meeting will happen again.

Questions to settle before the next cut

  • Who at our company can pause Amazon advertising, and do they see stock and conversion by product when they decide?
  • If finance asks for a number by Friday, do we have a ranked list of campaigns to cut first, by weeks of cover and conversion, ready to hand over?
  • Which of our products went dark in March, and what share of their category searches do they win now compared with February?
  • What would we keep running even in a cash squeeze, because losing it would cost more to win back?

Brands that settle these questions now will make the next cut with a scalpel. That is the kind of planning we do with brands on Amazon before the call comes, not after.

P0444.crumb: Mercado Libre logistics now sort sellers…
P0444.title: Mercado Libre logistics now sort sellers by who carries the box
P0444.alt: A yellow van and a white van parked by a warehouse loading dock with cardboard boxes and wooden crates between them.
P0444.ttag: Mercado Libre logistics now sort sellers by who carries the box | Kwontified
P0444.desc: When Correios workers struck in August, Mercado Livre told shoppers to buy listings marked as delivering normally. The carrier now decides who gets the sale.
P0444.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 1, 2020.
P0444.body:
On August 19, the day after Brazil’s postal workers walked out, Mercado Livre gave its shoppers some unusual advice: buy the offers marked “Entregando Normalmente,” delivering normally. The strike, the company said, would affect only products delivered through Correios, and it was telling sellers and buyers about possible changes to delivery times. Mercado Livre itself works with more than 70 logistics partners in Brazil and expected to keep its own deadlines.

Read that advice as a seller and it is a ranking rule in plain language. In a crisis, Mercado Libre protects its delivery promise by sending buyers to the listings it can still deliver. Mercado Libre logistics have become a way of allocating demand, and a brand’s shipping setup decides which side of that line its products land on.

How Mercado Libre logistics moved away from the post office

The marketplace did not build this in August. It has been pulling volume into its own network for two years. Since July 2018, new products priced above R$120 on Mercado Livre must offer free shipping, paid by the seller through Mercado Envios, Tecnoblog reported at the time, and the company blamed higher Correios postage for the change.

The network behind Mercado Envios then grew fast. In April, Stelleo Tolda, who runs operations in Brazil, said nine distribution centers, all opened in 2019, now carried more than half of Mercado Livre’s deliveries, against a time when Correios handled more than 70%. Correios kept the smaller cities and small businesses, where faster delivery did not pay. Tolda also said the company’s own delivery operation was running at maximum capacity under quarantine, and that buyers could now filter for products delivered by Mercado Livre.

The second-quarter numbers show how much more the platform now handles. Mercado Libre shipped 157.5 million items through Mercado Envios in the quarter, up 124.2%, while items sold rose 101.4% to 178.5 million, the company reported on August 10, adding that Envios ran “without any significant disruptions.”

QuarterItems soldShipped through Mercado EnviosShare
Q2 201988.7 million70.2 million79%
Q3 201998.0 million81.2 million83%
Q2 2020178.5 million157.5 million88%

Mercado Envios still uses Correios for part of that volume, so the share is not the same as Mercado Libre’s own trucks. It is the share of orders where the platform, not the seller, chooses the carrier.

Why steering buyers is the rational move

A shopper who waits two extra weeks for a parcel blames the marketplace, not the post office. Mercado Libre’s promise is the delivery date on the listing, and its gross margin was already tighter, 48.6% in the second quarter against 50.0% a year earlier. When one carrier fails, it has two options: absorb the late orders and the complaints, or move the next orders toward capacity it controls. It did the second, with a label and a filter rather than a fee.

The filter matters more than the label. A buyer who ticks “delivered by Mercado Livre” never sees the listings outside the network, however good their price or reviews. That shopper is not comparing a fast offer with a slow one. The slow offer simply drops out of the results. Nothing in the seller’s own reports shows this happening: the listing’s sessions fall, the conversion rate looks normal, and the cause sits in a setting on the buyer’s side of the screen.

Small online stores that sell outside the marketplaces cannot steer anyone. About 86% of Brazilian online merchants use Correios as their main way to ship, according to a Loja Integrada survey of almost 2,000 stores. Loja Integrada’s chief executive advised them to add about seven days to their delivery promises during the strike. That is the gap a marketplace seller can close or fall into.

Strikes end. The steering habit does not, because every delivery failure outside the network teaches Mercado Libre and its buyers the same lesson, and the holiday season is still ahead.

The arithmetic of carrier exposure

Take a beauty brand selling 2,000 units a month on Mercado Livre. Say 1,400 of them ship through Mercado Envios from a distribution center, and 600 go out on the brand’s own Correios labels to smaller cities or as items priced under R$120 where it never switched. Before August, those 600 looked like a cost decision: Correios was cheaper for them.

During the strike, those same 600 units are the ones whose delivery dates slip by a week or more, and the ones on listings Mercado Livre is no longer pointing buyers to. If a third of them do not sell because shoppers picked an offer marked as delivering normally, the brand loses 200 units a month, 10% of its volume, from a decision its finance team filed under shipping.

The trade-off cuts the other way too. Moving everything into Mercado Libre’s network means accepting its rates, its intake rules and, in 2020, its capacity limits; a network running at maximum capacity cannot take every seller at once. Brands that left part of their volume outside kept some control over cost. In a quarter with a strike, the numbers lean toward the network.

A rule for brands selling on Mercado Libre

Count the share of your monthly units that leave on a carrier Mercado Libre does not control, and treat that number as exposure, not as a shipping line. Above roughly a fifth of volume, the next Correios disruption is a demand problem for your listings, not just a delay for your customers.

Then ask which of those units could move into Mercado Envios before the holiday peak, while there is still room. That conversation, run per listing and per region, is part of how we operate brands on Mercado Libre.

P0446.crumb: Prime Day 2020 planning can’t wait for…
P0446.title: Prime Day 2020 planning can’t wait for Amazon to name a date
P0446.alt: Kraft-paper parcels tied with twine beside an open box with a straw hat, lavender and scissors on a wooden table.
P0446.ttag: Prime Day 2020 planning can’t wait for Amazon to name a date | Kwontified
P0446.desc: Amazon has moved Prime Day 2020 into the fourth quarter without naming a date. Brands that wait for it will make three planning decisions too late.
P0446.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 3, 2020.
P0446.body:
Every brand that sells on Amazon has a Prime Day plan that starts with a date. In 2019 it was July 15 and 16, the first 48-hour Prime Day, announced three weeks ahead, and every other line in the plan (deal submissions, the last inbound shipment, the ad budget) was counted backward from it. In 2020 the first line is blank.

Amazon said on July 21 that it would hold Prime Day later than usual. On its earnings call nine days later, its finance chief said the company planned to host Prime Day in the fourth quarter rather than the third, with India the one exception. That is all brands have. The risk is that each team waits for a date before making its own decision, and the decisions that should have been made six weeks out get made in two. Prime Day 2020 planning has to start from an assumed date, not an announced one.

Prime Day 2020 planning runs through three teams with their own clocks

A Prime Day plan looks like one document, but it is really three decisions owned by three groups. The e-commerce team chooses which products go on deal and how deep. Supply chain decides how many units to send into Amazon’s warehouses and when. Finance signs off on the extra advertising and the margin given up on discounts. In a normal year the date stitches the three together, because each group can see exactly when its piece is due.

Take the date away and each group has a reasonable excuse to hold back. Supply chain does not want to ship deal inventory that might sit for weeks and then collide with holiday stock. Finance does not want to approve a budget for a week it cannot place on the calendar. The e-commerce team cannot promise deal depth without the inventory and the money. Nobody is being careless. The structure simply has no owner for a decision that depends on a date no one has.

The usual fix, a planning meeting with all three in the room, tends to end with an action item to revisit once Amazon announces. That feels prudent. It is also how a brand ends up sending its deal inventory in the same late rush as every other brand that waited.

The fourth quarter changes what Prime Day competes with

In July, Prime Day had the calendar to itself. In the fourth quarter it sits a few weeks from Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and it will draw on the same deal budget, the same warehouse space and the same shopper wallets. Amazon has long measured the event against those days: in 2019 it said Prime Day sales surpassed the previous Black Friday and Cyber Monday combined, with members buying more than 175 million items.

Amazon is also adding weight to the event. At its Accelerate seller conference on September 1 it said it would spend an extra $100 million promoting small businesses during Prime Day and the holiday season, with details to come closer to Prime Day. Third-party sellers, it noted, passed $2 billion in global sales during Prime Day 2019, according to the company. A brand that treats this year’s Prime Day as a separate July-style event, with its own budget and its own inventory, is likely to fund two peaks out of one quarter’s money and space.

The better frame is one long holiday season that opens with Prime Day. Deal depth for Prime Day should be set alongside Black Friday deal depth, because a shopper who sees 30% off in the first event will remember it in the second. Inventory sent in for Prime Day is the first wave of holiday stock, not a separate shipment.

Planning backward from the earliest plausible date

The fourth quarter starts on October 1, so that is the earliest date a brand has to be ready for. Working backward from it gives a calendar that holds whatever Amazon announces.

Take a brand with a hero product that sells 1,000 units a week on Amazon in an ordinary week, and say its own history shows Prime Day weeks running at three times normal. If the event lands in the first week of October, the brand needs those 3,000 units, plus its normal cover for the weeks around it, checked in at Amazon’s warehouses by late September. If it lands in November instead, the same units are simply the early part of the holiday build. The units are not wasted either way, which is why the inventory decision can be made now even though the date cannot.

Deal choices work the same way. A brand can pick its Prime Day products and discount levels from its holiday plan today, then shift the dates on the deals once Amazon names them. Budget is the one decision that genuinely depends on timing, and it can be approved as a single fourth-quarter amount with a share held for whichever week Prime Day takes.

Questions to put to the team this week

  • Who in the company owns the Prime Day plan when the date is unknown, and can that person make the inventory call without waiting for Amazon?
  • Is our Prime Day deal depth set in the same meeting as our Black Friday and Cyber Monday deal depth?
  • If Prime Day were announced for early October tomorrow, what would we not have in Amazon’s warehouses in time?
  • Has finance approved one fourth-quarter Amazon budget, or two separate events?

The brands that answer those questions now will spend the announcement week adjusting dates. The rest will spend it arguing about who should have moved first, which is exactly the meeting we try to save the teams we run Amazon for.

P0447.crumb: Instagram checkout fees cost less than 5%…
P0447.title: Instagram checkout fees cost less than 5% against your own site
P0447.alt: Smartphone lying on a worn wooden table next to a stack of copper and brass coins against a mint wall.
P0447.ttag: Instagram checkout fees cost less than 5% against your own site | Kwontified
P0447.desc: Facebook’s 5% checkout fee already covers payment processing, so against your own site it costs about half a dollar an order. Conversion decides the rest.
P0447.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 8, 2020.
P0447.body:
On August 25, Facebook opened checkout on Instagram to all eligible US businesses and creators and said it would waive selling fees through the end of the year. The waiver makes the question easy to postpone. It should not be, because the fee comes back on January 1, and the brands that are deciding now whether to keep shoppers inside the app are judging it against the wrong number.

The fee is 5%. The cost of using it, compared with sending the shopper to your own website, is much smaller, because the 5% already includes something you pay on your own site anyway. Instagram checkout fees are best read as the gap between Facebook’s rate and your payment processor’s, and that gap is recovered or not by conversion.

A 5% fee reads like a marketplace commission

Brands meet the fee as a headline: 5% per shipment, or a flat $0.40 on shipments of $8 or less, deducted automatically from the payout, ChannelX reported in July. Set beside a website that charges the brand nothing to complete an order, 5% looks like a toll on every sale. Finance teams used to Amazon’s referral fees see another marketplace commission and price it that way.

The comparison is understandable and incomplete. The same article notes that the selling fee includes taxes and the cost of payment processing. A brand’s own checkout is not free; every card payment on the website goes through a processor that takes a percentage and often a fixed amount per transaction.

The arithmetic of Instagram checkout fees

Take a $40 order. Inside Instagram, the fee is $2.00. On your own site, say your processor charges 2.9% plus 30 cents, or $1.46. The extra cost of keeping the shopper in the app is $0.54 an order, a little over one point of the order value, not five.

Now add the reason brands consider in-app checkout at all. A shopper who taps a product in Instagram and has to load a mobile website, create an account or type in a card is a shopper who can give up. Facebook’s own pitch for checkout is that people can buy without leaving the app. If that removes enough abandoned carts, it pays for the $0.54.

The lift it needs is small. Say 1,000 shoppers tap through to a product, your contribution margin before payment costs is $16 on a $40 order, and your website converts 2% of them.

Contribution per order$14.54$14.00
Total contribution$290.8014.00 × orders

Instagram checkout breaks even at about 20.8 orders, a conversion rate of roughly 2.08% against 2%. A relative lift of about 4% covers the fee. If in-app checkout converts even modestly better than a mobile site, it pays.

Low-priced items change the sum. A $6 item pays the flat $0.40, almost 7% of the price, while a processor charging 30 cents a transaction already takes a large bite of a $6 sale too. The cheaper the item, the closer the two costs sit and the more the decision rests on conversion alone.

What the fee does not show

The table leaves out the cost brands argue about most: who owns the customer. When Facebook Shops launched in May, Facebook said businesses would get aggregated, anonymized information such as traffic, with personal information shared only with the user’s permission, and that it would use shopping activity to target ads.

That is the real trade-off. An order completed on your own site comes with an email address you can market to again for the price of a send. An order completed inside Instagram may not. For a brand whose customers reorder (skincare, supplements, coffee), the value of that second order can be larger than the fee gap on the first. For a brand selling one-off gifts, it is close to nothing.

So the decision splits by product, not by brand. Products bought once, on impulse, at prices where the processing gap is small belong in the app. Products whose economics depend on the second and third order belong on the site, where the customer record stays with the brand.

Reading the test without fooling yourself

The waiver months are the cheapest time to measure, and the easiest time to measure badly, usually in one of two ways.

Shoppers who reach the two checkouts are not the same people. Those who tap a product tag in a post are often further along than people who click an ad to your site, so a straight comparison of the two conversion rates flatters the app. Compare the same products, promoted the same way, in the same weeks, with only the checkout path changed.

A free checkout also flatters itself. During the waiver the app costs nothing, so almost any lift looks profitable, and a team that reports the test that way will have a hard conversation in February. Run the numbers as if the 5% were already in place, because from January it will be. And keep the test running long enough to see returns and cancellations, which land on the brand whichever checkout took the order.

A rule for the January decision

Before the waiver ends, run in-app checkout and the website side by side on the same products and compare conversion. If in-app checkout lifts conversion by more than the fee gap divided by your contribution margin (about 4% relative in the example above), keep it on for products that are rarely repurchased. For products that live on repeat orders, keep the checkout on your site unless the lift is several times that.

That test, set up per product and read in money rather than clicks, is part of how we run Instagram Shop for brands.

P0450.title: Beauty on Amazon in 2020 rewarded products that need no tester
P0450.alt: Unlabeled glass bottles and jars, including a dropper and cream jar, lined up on a rustic shelf against a mustard wall.
P0450.ttag: Beauty on Amazon in 2020 rewarded products that need no tester | Kwontified
P0450.desc: When beauty counters closed and testers became display-only, the products that held up online were the ones a shopper could choose without trying them first.
P0450.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 10, 2020.
P0450.body:
When Ulta began reopening stores on May 11, the most telling change was on the shelf, not the door. “Product testers are not available for use in-store,” the retailer said, and open product was now for display only. Sephora followed with the same rule when its first stores reopened later that month. For a category that has always sold by letting people try before they buy, that one sign took away the most persuasive tool on the floor.

The shopper still bought beauty in 2020, but she bought different beauty, and more of it online. The products that held up were the ones she could choose without touching them first. That explains most of what changed in beauty on Amazon in 2020, and what a brand’s product page now has to do.

What beauty on Amazon lost when the counter closed

Prestige beauty was built around the counter. A shopper picks up a lipstick, swatches it on the back of her hand, asks the person behind the counter about a foundation shade and leaves with a sample of a serum. The brand’s real merchandising happened there, in person, and the Amazon listing was often treated as a place where existing fans reordered what they already knew.

The second quarter showed how much depended on that ritual. US prestige beauty sales fell 36% to $2.8 billion, and makeup fell 52% to $869 million, NPD data reported by WWD showed. Skin care, the largest category, fell a more modest 18% to $1.1 billion, and hair care only 10%. Online sales grew more than 90% across the quarter. Ulta’s own numbers tell the same story from the retailer’s side: its e-commerce sales rose more than 200% in the quarter to August 1, while transactions fell 36.2% and comparable sales fell 26.7%, the company reported on August 27.

Amazon was the obvious alternative when stores shut. Beauty and personal care counted as essential, so it could still ship through Amazon’s warehouses in March, and the category’s Amazon sales rose 70% against the start of that month, one agency founder told Glossy.

The products a shopper could choose unseen

Look inside NPD’s quarter and the winners share a trait. Nail care rose 29%, hair treatments 30%, body and facial devices 16% and body exfoliators 15%. Even inside makeup, eye makeup grew 6%, led by false lashes, brow products, eyeliner and mascara, the things a shopper knows how to judge from a photo and a review. NPD’s Larissa Jensen noted that clinical skin care was the top type of skin care brand in the quarter, after natural skin care led in 2019.

None of those products needs a tester. A nail kit, a hair mask or a mascara is judged on what it does, which a product page can describe and a review can confirm. A foundation is judged on whether it matches, which is exactly what a shopper cannot see through a screen. Clinical skin care sells on claims and ingredients, which read as well on a phone as on a counter card.

That is the hidden structure behind the year’s beauty numbers. The categories that fell hardest were the ones whose selling model depended on a person and a tester. The ones that held up were the ones whose selling model already lived in words, pictures and reviews, which is what an Amazon product page is made of.

The product page now has the counter’s job

The shift that matters for brands is that Amazon stopped being only a reorder channel for beauty in 2020. New shoppers found products there who had never stood at the brand’s counter, because the counter was closed or because the tester was behind a sign. Those shoppers rely on the page to answer the questions a beauty adviser used to answer.

For products that need a tester, that is a hard brief, and a brand should be honest about it. A foundation range with 40 shades needs shade descriptions a shopper can map to her own skin, photographs on several skin tones, and reviews organized so that people with her coloring can find each other. For products that need no tester, the brief is easier, and it is worth taking full advantage of. The page should lead with what the product does and how fast, in the terms the shopper would use, with the clinical claim up front if there is one.

It is too early to say how much of this outlasts the pandemic. Jensen expected a slow recovery for stores and warned of challenges into the holidays, and some shoppers will go back to the counter the moment they can. But the shopper who bought a serum or a mascara on Amazon without testing it, and was happy with it, has learned that she can. The evidence leans toward a lasting share of first purchases moving to the page.

Questions to put to the team before the holidays

  • Which of our products can a shopper choose without touching them, and do our Amazon pages lead with what those products do?
  • For the products that do need a tester, what on our page stands in for the counter: shade guidance, photos on real skin, reviews a shopper can filter?
  • Are we still treating Amazon as the place existing customers reorder, or as the place new customers meet us first?
  • Who on the team owns the Amazon page copy, and did they sit in the room when the product was launched in stores?

Sorting a range by how much it depends on the tester, and rebuilding the pages that depend on it most, is part of how we run Amazon for beauty brands.

P0452.crumb: Retail media budget cuts should start…
P0452.title: Retail media budget cuts should start with your best-ROAS ads
P0452.alt: Potted geraniums in terracotta pots beside old garden shears on a wooden bench against a peeling blue wall.
P0452.ttag: Retail media budget cuts should start with your best-ROAS ads | Kwontified
P0452.desc: When a retail media budget has to shrink, cutting the lowest-ROAS ads first removes the spend creating sales and keeps the spend that was only counting them.
P0452.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 15, 2020.
P0452.body:
In the last week of March, the typical Amazon advertiser was spending half as much a day as in January, Merkle data reported by Digiday showed. Amazon itself cut its marketing by about a third in the second quarter, its finance chief said on the July 30 earnings call. Plenty of brands are now planning the fourth quarter with a smaller retail media budget than they hoped, and most will decide what to cut the same way: sort the campaigns by ROAS and trim from the bottom.

That order is close to backward. ROAS measures how many sales an ad was near, not how many it caused. Cutting the lowest-ROAS ads first removes the spend that was creating sales and protects the spend that was mostly counting sales that would have happened anyway.

Why the ROAS ranking feels safe

Return on ad spend is the number every console reports, and it ranks campaigns cleanly. Branded search, the ads that show when someone types your brand name, almost always sits at the top. Ads on generic category searches sit in the middle. Ads on competitors’ brand names, or on new shoppers who have never heard of you, sit at the bottom. Cutting from the bottom protects the account’s average ROAS, which is the figure the finance team will see in the next report.

The ranking is right about one thing. Branded ads really are attached to a lot of sales. The mistake is in what that attachment means. A shopper who searches your brand name has already chosen you; the ad that appears catches a sale that, in many cases, your organic listing one slot lower would have caught for free.

Think of a shop that pays the doorman a commission on every customer who walks through the door. On the commission report the doorman is the best salesperson in the building. That is a fact about where he stands, not about how many people he persuaded to come in.

The retail media budget, sorted by what it causes

The number that matters in a cut is incremental ROAS: the sales an ad caused that would not have happened without it, per dollar. It is ROAS multiplied by the share of attributed sales that are truly incremental.

Take a brand spending $10,000 a week on Amazon search ads, and say it has a rough read on incrementality from past holdout tests.

CampaignWeekly spendROASShare incrementalIncremental ROAS
Branded search$3,0008.015%1.2
Category search$5,0004.060%2.4
Competitor and conquest$2,0002.580%2.0

Now cut the budget by $3,000. Trimming from the bottom of the ROAS ranking removes the $2,000 of conquest and $1,000 of category search. The account’s reported ROAS rises from 4.9 to 5.7, and it loses $6,400 a week of sales the ads were actually creating. Cutting the branded campaign instead makes the report look worse, with ROAS falling to 3.6, but loses only $3,600 of incremental sales. The second cut keeps $2,800 a week more in real sales, and every dashboard in the company will say it was the mistake.

Most brands do not have holdout results on file, and the shares in the table are the part a reader should distrust. Without a test, a rough proxy is available in every search term report: the share of attributed sales that came from searches containing your own brand name. Treat that share as mostly non-incremental until a test says otherwise, and treat sales from generic searches where your product does not rank organically as mostly incremental. The estimate will be crude. It will still rank the campaigns more honestly than ROAS does, because it at least asks the right question.

The pull toward the first cut is understandable. It is the one that protects the number people are judged on, and in a downturn nobody wants to present a falling ROAS. The cost shows up later, in sales that quietly fail to arrive.

Where the downturn changes the arithmetic

Two features of 2020 make the incremental order more valuable than usual. Clicks got cheaper: Sponsored Products cost per click was 41% lower in the second quarter than a year earlier while clicks more than doubled, according to Merkle’s report as summarized by Karooya. Cheaper clicks raise the incremental return on category and conquest search, where the brand is buying attention it would not otherwise get.

Branded search carries a real risk too. If you leave your own brand term, a competitor’s ad can take the top slot, and some of those shoppers will buy the rival product. That is why the incremental share for branded search is not zero, and why the right move is a test rather than a switch-off. The same logic holds on Walmart and on Roundel, Target’s ad business, wherever a search ad can appear on a shopper’s search for your brand name.

A rule for the next cut

Before the fourth-quarter budget is final, pause branded search on Amazon for two weeks on a sample of your products. Measure what happens to total sales of those products, not to ad-attributed sales. If total sales barely move, branded search is the first line to cut and category search on in-stock products is the last. If they fall sharply, your brand term is contested and the defense is worth paying for.

Either way, rank the retail media budget by incremental ROAS before anyone takes a red pen to it. Setting up that holdout before the holiday season is part of the measurement work we do for brands.

P0453.title: Walmart+ leaves marketplace sellers outside its membership perks
P0453.alt: Kraft-paper parcel on a stone doorstep beside brass stanchions and a velvet rope before an ivy-covered blue door.
P0453.ttag: Walmart+ leaves marketplace sellers outside its membership perks | Kwontified
P0453.desc: Walmart+ is built around the store: a fuel pump, a checkout lane and a store-picked basket. Marketplace sellers get the traffic but none of the member perks.
P0453.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 17, 2020.
P0453.body:
Read the list of what a Walmart+ member got on September 15 and notice where each benefit happens. Free same-day delivery on orders of $35 or more, picked from a Walmart store’s shelves. Up to 5 cents off a gallon at nearly 2,000 Walmart and Murphy fuel stations. Scan & Go, so a member can pay with the app and skip the checkout line, TechCrunch reported when Walmart announced the program. Every perk lives in a parking lot or an aisle.

None of them touches Walmart’s marketplace. A seller on Walmart.com ships from its own warehouse or from Walmart’s fulfillment service, not from a store shelf, so its items cannot join a same-day basket, and Walmart added no shipping benefit for Walmart.com orders at launch. The membership tells you what Walmart values most, and the answer for Walmart+ marketplace sellers is that they are welcome in the building but not in the club.

A membership built from what Walmart owns

Walmart did not design Walmart+ from scratch. It replaced Delivery Unlimited, the $98-a-year grocery delivery subscription Walmart had already been running, and its members moved over automatically. The new perks extend that idea to the rest of the store visit: the drive in, the fill-up, the trip down the aisles.

That is a rational choice for a retailer whose advantage is 4,700-plus stores, of which about 2,700 offer delivery. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales grew 97% in the quarter to July 31, Walmart reported. A membership that rewards members for coming back to the store, physically or through the app, protects the part of the business no online rival can copy.

Janey Whiteside, Walmart’s chief customer officer, called the program “the ultimate life hack” for customers, Talk Business & Politics reported. Her framing is about saving the shopper time and money on errands, not about range. Nothing in the launch materials invites the shopper to discover new products or sellers; the program is designed to make an existing routine cheaper and faster, and the routine it has in mind is the weekly Walmart run.

Where the marketplace sits in that design

Walmart’s marketplace has grown quickly. It added 10,000 sellers in 2019 to reach more than 32,000 by November, Modern Retail reported in June, and in June Walmart opened the door to Shopify merchants, expecting about 1,200 to join in 2020. In February it began offering its own fulfillment service to sellers, and items stored there carry a two-day tag that Walmart says can help their search ranking, according to Modern Retail.

So the marketplace has been moving closer to Walmart’s own operations all year. Walmart+ is the first big program since then that leaves it out entirely. Marketplace sellers already had free two-day shipping on many items, with no membership required, since Walmart opened it to marketplace items in October 2018. Walmart+ adds nothing on top of that for them.

Follow the value and the picture is clear enough. The membership fee and the member’s loyalty go to Walmart’s stores. The marketplace seller gets something indirect: more members opening the Walmart app more often, and more searches that might surface its listings.

What changes on the marketplace seller’s shelf

The indirect benefit comes with a cost that is easy to miss. A member searching the Walmart app for a hair dryer or a set of kitchen towels sees store items, which she can have that afternoon at no delivery fee, next to marketplace items that arrive in two days or more. Each extra visit by a member is a visit in which the store’s assortment carries a perk the marketplace item cannot match.

For categories Walmart stores carry heavily (household basics, grocery, everyday beauty) that comparison will sharpen. For categories the stores carry thinly, where the marketplace exists to extend the range, it matters much less. The marketplace’s value to Walmart was always the long tail: the specialty items, sizes and colors a store cannot stock. Walmart+ makes that role more obvious, not less.

Inside many brands, Walmart+ also shifts weight between two teams that rarely sit together. The store business, the items Walmart buys and stocks, usually belongs to the sales or wholesale team that manages the Walmart buyer. The marketplace usually belongs to the e-commerce team, which treats Walmart.com as another online channel alongside Amazon. Walmart+ makes the first team’s work more valuable online: an item on a Walmart store shelf is now an item a member can order for same-day delivery without a fee. A brand that plans its Walmart.com presence without asking the wholesale team which items are in which stores is planning half of its Walmart online business blind.

It is too early to say whether Walmart will extend a member benefit to items it does not stock. Watch for any member perk that applies to shipped orders rather than store orders, because that would be the first sign the marketplace is inside the club.

Questions for a brand selling on Walmart’s marketplace

  • Which of our marketplace items compete directly with items Walmart stores carry, and how do we win those searches without a same-day badge?
  • Is our marketplace range built around the long tail that stores do not stock, or around the same basics members can now get the same day?
  • Are our best items in Walmart’s fulfillment service, so they at least carry the two-day tag next to store items?
  • Who on our team will notice first if Walmart adds a member benefit for shipped orders?

Sorting a Walmart marketplace range by how much it overlaps with the store, and placing it accordingly, is part of how we run Walmart for brands.

P0457.crumb: Work-from-home products now sell to the…
P0457.title: Work-from-home products now sell to the employee, not the office
P0457.alt: Opened cardboard box with packing paper beside a desk, lamp and gray office chair in a teal home office.
P0457.ttag: Work-from-home products now sell to the employee, not the office | Kwontified
P0457.desc: Monitors, webcams and office chairs used to be bought by a purchasing desk. In 2020 the buyer became the employee at home, and the shelf changed with her.
P0457.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 24, 2020.
P0457.body:
In an ordinary year, the person who chooses a monitor, a webcam or an office chair rarely uses it. A facilities manager or an IT buyer picks a model from an approved list, orders it by the dozen, and it arrives on a desk on the fourth floor. In the first two weeks of March 2020, computer monitor sales in the US doubled to 80,000 units, NPD data reported by CNBC showed, and many of those monitors were not chosen by a facilities manager. They were chosen by the person who would sit in front of one at the kitchen table.

That is the change in the category that matters more than the size of the spike. The buyer of work-from-home products changed from a procurement desk to the employee shopping on a marketplace, and with her came a different shelf, different questions and a different idea of what makes a product good. Brands whose listings and teams were built for contract and office-supply channels are now selling to a household shopper comparing looks, size and reviews, and the shift looks durable enough to reorganize around.

The spike, product by product

The early numbers came from technology. Monitor sales doubled in early March, and sales of laptops, mice and keyboards all rose, NPD reported. Webcams went further: on Walmart.com, webcam sales rose 1,864% in March and April against the same months of 2019, and office chair sales rose 234%, according to 1010data figures reported by Retail Dive in August. Regular whiteboards nearly tripled.

Those are the products of an office, bought one at a time and shipped to a house. The categories that grew were not the ones a household normally shops for in spring; they were the contents of a cubicle, rebuilt piece by piece in spare bedrooms and on dining tables. A webcam used to be a line item on an IT order. In the spring of 2020 it was a search on a phone, a shortlist of three listings and a choice made by reading reviews.

Who the listing was written for

Many of the brands that make this equipment built their business on the old buyer. Their products reached offices through contract dealers, office-supply catalogs and corporate accounts, and their product content was written for that sale: model numbers, compatibility tables, ergonomic certifications, case-pack quantities. Those details still matter, but they answer a purchasing manager’s questions.

The employee asks different ones: whether the chair fits in the corner of a bedroom, whether the webcam makes her look washed out on a video call, whether the desk will look out of place in the living room once the workday is over.

On a marketplace, she is comparing a commercial-grade chair with a home-furniture chair that looks better in a photo and has thousands of reviews from people in the same situation. The listing that wins is the one that answers her questions, not the one with the best specification table.

Inside a brand, this often sits awkwardly. The contract or B2B sales team owns the product and its relationships with dealers. The consumer or e-commerce team, if there is one, inherited the marketplace listings, frequently built from the same spec sheets. Nobody’s plan for 2020 assumed that a large share of the volume would arrive one unit at a time through Amazon or Walmart.com, so nobody was asked to rewrite the page. The result is a listing that is accurate and complete, and still loses to a competitor whose main image shows the chair in a sunny room with a plant beside it.

The home office looks like it will outlast 2020

It would be easy to treat the home office as a spike that fades when offices reopen. The evidence so far leans the other way. On July 27, Google told employees its voluntary work-from-home option would run through June 30, 2021, CNBC reported, the first major company to extend that far. When large employers plan for a year at home, their employees stop improvising at the kitchen table and start furnishing a room.

That shifts the buying from emergency purchases to considered ones. The first wave was whatever webcam was in stock. The second wave, the one under way in the fall of 2020, is the better chair, the second monitor, the desk that fits the room and the lamp that fixes the light on video calls. Those are purchases where content, reviews and brand matter more, and where a brand that understands the household buyer can win share from one that still writes for procurement.

It is too early to say how much of the office returns to the office in 2021. But even a partial return leaves a great many people who now own a home workspace and will replace, upgrade and add to it on their own account.

Questions for the team this quarter

  • Who in our company owns the marketplace listings for products that used to be sold through contract or office channels, and were they asked to change anything in 2020?
  • Do our product pages answer the household buyer’s questions (size in a small room, look on camera, assembly at home), or only the purchasing manager’s?
  • Which of our products are being compared, side by side, with home-furniture or consumer-electronics brands we have never considered competitors?
  • If a third of our volume now comes one unit at a time, does our packaging, assembly and returns process work for one person at home?

Rebuilding listings for a buyer the brand was not designed to serve, and deciding which team owns them, is part of how we run Amazon and Walmart for brands.
