P0459.crumb: Amazon repeat purchase data lets sellers…
P0459.title: Amazon repeat purchase data lets sellers price a new customer
P0459.alt: Two twine-tied kraft-paper parcels, one worn and one new, balanced on an antique brass pan scale.
P0459.ttag: Amazon repeat purchase data lets sellers price a new customer | Kwontified
P0459.desc: Amazon Accelerate gave sellers repeat-purchase data. Its real use is setting how much a new customer is worth, and so how high to bid going into Prime Day.
P0459.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 29, 2020.
P0459.body:
Ask a seller how high it can bid for a click on Amazon and the answer usually comes from one order: the margin on the product, times the share the brand will spend on advertising, times the conversion rate. That rule treats every customer as worth exactly one sale. For a brand whose customers reorder (coffee, supplements, skin care, pet food), it is wrong in a predictable direction.

The most useful thing Amazon announced at its Accelerate seller conference on September 1 is the tool that lets sellers fix that number. Repeat Purchase Behavior gives sellers data on how customers come back to their brands, Amazon said. With it, a brand can estimate what an Amazon repeat purchase is worth and set its bids for new customers on the whole relationship rather than the first order.

What Accelerate actually changed

Most of Accelerate was guidance and encouragement: more than 60 sessions for sellers, Amazon’s program said, and an $18 billion figure for Amazon’s 2020 investment in independent businesses. Read for what is new and usable, two tools stand out. Brand Follow lets sellers reach shoppers who have shown interest in their brand, through features such as personalized posts on the homepage. Repeat Purchase Behavior shows how often customers come back.

The first is a channel; its value depends on how many followers a brand builds and how many of them Amazon shows each post to. The second is a measurement, and measurements change decisions immediately. A brand does not need a large follower list to use repeat-purchase data this week.

Judge Brand Follow by what it demonstrably does, not by the launch language. Amazon has described it as an investment in customer relationship management, but it has not said how many of a brand’s followers will see each post, or how often. Until a brand can measure that, a follower is worth nothing in the bid arithmetic below. It may become valuable; the value has to show up in the brand’s own numbers first. The repeat-purchase figures, by contrast, describe orders that already happened, which is why they can be used today.

The arithmetic of a customer, not an order

Take a $30 product with a $9 contribution margin per order after Amazon’s fees and before advertising. On the one-order rule, a brand converting 10% of its clicks can pay up to $0.90 a click and break even on a new customer.

Now say Repeat Purchase Behavior shows that a quarter of the product’s customers bought it again in the period, and the brand’s own order history says those repeat buyers reorder one and a half more times over a year. Each new customer then brings 0.375 extra orders on average, and is worth $9 times 1.375, or about $12.38 in margin.

One-order ruleWith repeat value
Margin per new customer$9.00$12.38
Break-even cost per click at 10% conversion$0.90$1.24

The break-even bid rises by 37.5%. The brand that knows its repeat value can outbid one that does not, for the same click, and still make money over the year.

The gain is not the same for every product. A one-time purchase, such as a phone case or a gift set, has little repeat value, and its ceiling barely moves. A consumable with a monthly cycle can justify a much higher one. That is why the calculation belongs at the product level. A brand-wide average flatters the gift items and starves the refills.

The ceiling only applies to new customers. A shopper who already buys the brand brings no additional repeat value when the brand pays for a second click to win her back, which is why branded search and remarketing should keep the one-order ceiling.

What the data can and can’t tell you

Repeat-purchase data from a single window measures customers who came back in that window. It does not tell you how many would have come back without the brand’s ads, and some of those repeat orders will have been bought again through branded search, at a second advertising cost. Count only the repeat orders that would arrive without fresh spend, and the value is lower than the raw figure suggests.

It also blends old and new customers. A brand’s longtime buyers reorder more than first-timers, so a repeat rate drawn from the whole customer base overstates what a new customer will do. Where the data allows, look at the repeat behavior of customers acquired in a recent month, not of everyone.

Why it matters now: Prime Day on October 13 and 14

Amazon set Prime Day for October 13 and 14 on September 28, Retail Dive reported. Prime Day brings in shoppers who are new to many brands, which makes it the week when the gap between the one-order rule and the repeat-value rule costs the most. A brand bidding at $0.90 for new customers will lose those auctions to one bidding at $1.24 that has done the arithmetic.

Small sellers have a second reason to act early, and it shortens the timetable. From September 28 to October 12, Prime members who spend $10 with select small businesses get a $10 Prime Day credit, according to Pulse 2.0, so the two weeks before the event are also a window for acquiring customers.

Set the new-customer bid ceiling this week

Pull the repeat-purchase figures for your top products, discount them for repeat orders your ads would have paid for again, and multiply your first-order margin by one plus the remaining repeat orders. Use that number, not the first-order margin, as the bid ceiling for non-branded search aimed at new customers going into Prime Day, and keep the old ceiling for branded and remarketing campaigns.

Setting those ceilings product by product, before the event rather than during it, is part of how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

P0460.title: Holiday 2020 shipping capacity, not Black Friday, sets the plan
P0460.alt: A cream vintage van loaded with cardboard boxes parked on a leafy autumn lane beside stone cottages.
P0460.ttag: Holiday 2020 shipping capacity, not Black Friday, sets the plan | Kwontified
P0460.desc: Carriers priced holiday 2020 against February volumes. Brands that plan back from the last promised delivery, not forward from Black Friday, keep margin.
P0460.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 1, 2020.
P0460.body:
Most holiday plans begin with a date everyone already knows. Black Friday falls on November 27 in 2020, Cyber Monday on November 30, and the work runs forward from there: the promotion grid, the ad budget, the inbound shipments that have to land before the rush. In 2020 the date that governs the plan is printed on a parcel carrier’s rate sheet. UPS will charge high-volume shippers extra on residential packages for eight weeks from November 15, priced against how much each one shipped in February, FreightWaves reported.

That one detail changes the direction of planning. When delivery is the scarce resource, the useful starting point is the last day a brand can promise a gift will arrive at a price it can afford, and the calendar runs backward from that day. Brands that keep planning forward from Black Friday will find their busiest week is also their most expensive one to ship.

Holiday 2020 shipping capacity is the constraint, not demand

Deloitte expects holiday online sales to grow 25% to 35% this season, to between $182 billion and $196 billion, against growth of 14.7% to $145 billion in 2019. Total holiday retail sales will rise only 1% to 1.5%, CNBC reported on September 15. Same shoppers, roughly the same money, but far more of it arriving in a cardboard box. Coresight’s Deborah Weinswig put the problem plainly in the same report: “We are already capacity constrained.”

The carriers have priced the squeeze. UPS’s surcharges apply to shippers sending more than 25,000 parcels a week: $1 per ground residential package for volume above 110% of the February average, $2 between 200% and 300%, and $3 above that, with air packages costing more at each step. In the 2019 peak, UPS charged no residential surcharge on ordinary parcels. FedEx added its first peak fees since 2016, running from November 2 to January 17, and the Postal Service introduced peak package surcharges for the first time, Bloomberg reported in August.

Follow where that money comes from and the incentive is clear. A surcharge measured against February volume rewards whoever ships evenly and punishes whoever ships in one spike. Kohl’s has already said higher shipping costs hurt its second-quarter margins and that it plans to encourage earlier holiday shopping, push in-store pickup and bundle orders.

The retailers have already moved the season

Look at what the large retailers announced over the summer and the pattern is hard to miss. Walmart and Target will both close their stores on Thanksgiving, and Target says its holiday deals start in October, online and in stores, Supermarket News reported. Amazon set Prime Day for October 13 and 14, with early deals running from September 28, and its consumer chief Jeff Wilke called the event “the perfect opportunity for Prime members to get their holiday shopping done early” in the announcement.

None of these retailers is short of shoppers. They are short of trucks, sorting hours and store capacity, so they are spreading demand across ten weeks instead of five days. A brand whose promotions, ad spend and inventory still peak in the week after Thanksgiving is planning for the season the retailers have just walked away from.

Inside most brands, the friction is that no one person owns all three dates. Marketing owns the promotion calendar, operations owns the carrier contract and the warehouse, and finance discovers the surcharge in January. A backward plan only works if those three teams build it in the same room.

Working backward from December 24

Start from the gift that has to arrive by Christmas Eve, then walk back through each handoff, writing down your own date at every step.

The last promised delivery date. Carriers publish their holiday shipping deadlines each autumn; until they do, use last year’s and assume they will tighten. On marketplaces, the retailer’s own delivery promise decides when a listing quietly stops showing arrival before Christmas.

The last ship date. For orders you fulfill yourself, this is the deadline minus your pick, pack and handoff time in a December week, not an average week.

The last inbound date. For stock that ships from a marketplace’s warehouse, it has to be received and available, not merely in transit, before the demand arrives. Use last year’s actual receiving times for December, then add a margin.

The purchase order and production dates. Count back again from the inbound date, and this is usually where the plan fails: holiday stock that is still on the water in late October may already be too late for a season that starts on October 13.

The shipping bill rewards the same discipline. Take a brand that averaged 30,000 parcels a week in February and plans 75,000 a week in December. That is 250% of its February volume, so each ground residential package carries a $2 surcharge, or $150,000 a week. Pull enough demand into October to bring December down to 54,000 a week, or 180% of February, and the surcharge drops to $1 a package, $54,000 a week.

Questions for the planning meeting this week

  1. What is the last date we can promise Christmas delivery, by channel, and who owns that date?
  2. How much of our holiday inventory will be received and sellable before Prime Day on October 13?
  3. What would it cost to move a quarter of our December promotions into October and early November, and what would we save in shipping and surcharges?
  4. Which of our marketplace listings will lose their delivery promise first, and what do we promote once they do?

The brands that keep their margin this season will treat the delivery date as the plan, not as a constraint discovered in December. That is the calendar work we do with brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0462.title: An Amazon incrementality holdout test needs weeks, not days
P0462.alt: Wooden raised garden beds full of leafy greens and wildflowers along a gravel path by a stone wall.
P0462.ttag: An Amazon incrementality holdout test needs weeks, not days | Kwontified
P0462.desc: Daily Amazon sales swing more than ads move them, so a one-week holdout proves nothing. Size the test to the noise before you switch anything off.
P0462.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 6, 2020.
P0462.body:
A brand switches off Sponsored Products on a best seller for a week, watches sales dip 4%, and concludes the ads were worth 4% of sales. Another brand runs the same test and sees sales rise. Both tests were too small to say anything. Daily Amazon sales swing by more than most ads move them, so a short holdout measures the noise. The fix is to decide, before switching anything off, how many product-weeks the test needs to see a lift of the size you care about.

Why an Amazon incrementality holdout test is the right instinct

Incrementality is the share of sales that would not have happened without the ad. The holdout, where the ads stop for one group and keep running for a comparable one, is the cleanest way to measure it, because attribution reports cannot separate a sale the ad caused from a sale it merely touched.

The best-known public test shows why. In March 2012, eBay stopped bidding on brand keywords such as “ebay shoes” on Yahoo and Microsoft’s search engine. Almost all (99.5%) of the lost paid clicks came back through the free search result. That finding comes from the field experiment Tom Blake, Chris Nosko and Steven Tadelis published in May 2014. eBay then stopped all non-brand bidding for 60 days in a random sample of 30% of its US traffic, split by Nielsen market area: 68 test markets against matched controls. The whole program of paid search added only 0.66% to sales.

Brands that read that study usually take away the conclusion, that ads get credit for sales that would have happened anyway. The part worth copying is the design. eBay switched off a large, random slice of its business for two months.

The noise in daily sales is bigger than the lift

Measuring a 5% ad effect against daily sales is like weighing a letter on a bathroom scale. The scale works. Its wobble is just larger than the letter.

Randall Lewis and Justin Rao found the same thing at much larger scale. They ran 25 large field experiments with US retailers and brokerages, covering about $2.8 million of digital ad spend. The median confidence interval on return on investment was more than 100 percentage points wide, and informative tests could need more than 10 million person-weeks, they reported in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2015. Their point was not that ads fail. It was that sales are so volatile relative to ad spend that small tests cannot tell.

Take a product that sells 100 units a day, with a typical day landing 20 units above or below that average. Say the ads really add 5%, or five units a day. To see five units through that daily swing with ordinary confidence, you have to compare enough days with ads against enough without that the error in the difference falls below about half the effect. The standard error of the difference between two averages of n days each is 20 × √2 ÷ √n. Setting that to 2.5 units gives n of about 128 days per group.

If the ads add 10%, the same arithmetic gives about 32 days per group. A one-week holdout can detect only an effect of roughly 20% or more, which few Sponsored Products campaigns on an established product produce. The shortcut: days needed per group is about 8 × (daily swing ÷ lift)².

On Amazon, the test has to be built from products and weeks

eBay could split its test by market area because its search engines could target ads by region. Sponsored Products target keywords and products, not places, so an Amazon brand cannot hold out Ohio. That leaves two units of randomization, and each has a cost.

Products. Pair similar ASINs by price and sales history, then switch ads off for one product in each pair, chosen at random. Ten pairs give ten observations a day instead of one, so the 128 product-days needed at a 5% lift take about 13 days, and the test should still run two full weeks so every weekday appears in both groups. The gain is smaller when products move together on the same busy and quiet days, and shoppers who switch between paired products shrink the measured difference.

Weeks. Alternate ads on and off for the same product, a week at a time, for eight to twelve weeks, which yields 28 to 42 days per group: enough for a 10% lift, not for 5%. This handles products with no good twin, but lost ad sales can lower a product’s organic rank, so an “off” week can depress the “on” week that follows. Use whole weeks, not days, and drop the first day after each switch.

Either way, the test has to avoid the calendar. A holdout that spans Prime Day, which Amazon has set for October 13 and 14, measures the event, not the ads.

The test plan, before anything is switched off

  1. Write down the smallest lift that would change the budget. If losing 10% of a product’s sales would not change what you spend, design the test for 10%, not 3%.
  2. Pull the last 90 days of daily units for each product in the test and measure the typical daily swing, then run the arithmetic above for your own numbers.
  3. Choose products or weeks as the unit, assign them at random, and agree the analysis before the test starts, so the result cannot be reread after the fact.
  4. Run it in January or another stretch with no event, price change or stockout, never across Prime Day or Cyber Week.

The rule of thumb: if the swing in daily sales is four times the lift you hope to find, one product needs about four months per group, so add products until the calendar fits. A holdout sized to its noise is worth running; setting one up properly is the measurement work we do before any budget decision rests on it.

P0463.title: Holiday gifting in 2020 makes the shipping box the gift wrap
P0463.alt: A cardboard box tied with a sage green satin bow on a rustic wooden table against a green wall.
P0463.ttag: Holiday gifting in 2020 makes the shipping box the gift wrap | Kwontified
P0463.desc: When the gift travels without the giver, the product page, the delivery date and the box do the work the giver used to do. Brands should plan for it.
P0463.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 8, 2020.
P0463.body:
The usual holiday handover is a wrapped box carried through the front door, opened in the same room as the person who chose it, with a word about why. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s holiday guidance, issued in late September, puts most of that scene in the higher-risk column. Its lowest-risk Thanksgiving is dinner with the people you live with, a “virtual dinner” with everyone else and shopping online rather than in stores on Black Friday, UPI reported.

So the gift will travel without the giver. Shoppers said as much months ago: in Criteo’s May survey of US consumers, 88% planned to keep buying gifts online and sending them to the people they were for, the company reported in July. When the giver is not in the room, three jobs the giver used to do fall to the brand: choosing with confidence, arriving on time and making the opening feel like a gift.

Remote holiday gifting moves the choice onto the product page

A gift bought in a store is chosen with the product in hand. A gift bought for someone in another state is chosen on a phone, often for a person whose size, kitchen or skin type the buyer can only guess.

That changes what the listing has to answer. A self-purchase page answers “will this suit me?”, and the shopper knows their own size and their own sink. A gift page has to answer “will this suit them?”, which is a harder question asked by someone with less information. Gift buyers tend to settle the doubt by trading down to safer choices: the bestseller, the neutral color, the one-size item, the gift card.

Brands can make the bolder choice feel safe. A size guide that compares fit with familiar brands helps, and so does a photo that shows the product at its real scale. A plain line on who it suits and who it does not, and an exchange policy the recipient can use without the buyer, do the reassuring a sales associate used to do across the counter.

The delivery date is now part of the gift

Deloitte expects holiday online sales to grow 25% to 35% in the 2020 season. That would take them to as much as $196 billion, CNBC reported, and with families told to stay apart, more of those orders will be gifts heading to an address the buyer does not live at. A gift that arrives on December 28 is not late in the way a self-purchase is late. It is a broken promise made by the giver, to someone they could not visit.

Gift buyers will read delivery dates more carefully than any other shopper in December 2020, and they will reward the brand whose promise holds. That puts the warehouse and the marketplace listing in the same conversation as the merchandising plan. Inventory that sits in a marketplace’s own warehouses keeps its fast delivery badge; inventory shipped from a brand’s own warehouse in the last week of the season may not.

Retailers have read the same signal. Amazon is holding Prime Day on October 13 and 14, and Jeff Wilke, its consumer chief, called it “the perfect opportunity for Prime members to get their holiday shopping done early” in the announcement. An October gift that ships to a sister in another city is exactly the purchase that sentence is courting.

The box is the wrapping, and someone has to own it

When the parcel goes straight to the recipient, the first physical thing they touch is the shipper box, and the first paper they read is whatever is inside it. In many brand organizations, the packaging budget belongs to the brand team, the shipper box to operations and the marketplace gift options to whoever runs the listing, so nobody is looking at the unboxing as a single moment.

Marketplaces narrow the choice further. An order filled from a marketplace’s own warehouse usually arrives in the marketplace’s box, so the product’s own packaging is the only wrapping the brand controls. That makes the retail carton, the insert and the first line printed inside the lid more important in 2020 than in any season when the giver did the wrapping. A carton designed to win attention on a shelf, with its price sticker and its claims shouting at a shopper, reads differently on a kitchen table in front of someone who did not choose it.

A gift that arrives in a plain mailer with a packing slip showing the price is a self-purchase that got lost. A gift that arrives with a message from the buyer, no price and packaging that reads as a present is a gift. The difference is mostly settings and supplies: gift messaging switched on, gift receipts available, a sleeve or insert designed for the recipient rather than the buyer.

None of this is costly next to the holiday ad budget, and all of it has to be decided before the first October orders ship. The giver cannot fix it on the day, because the giver will be on a video call.

Questions to put to the team before Prime Day

  1. If a customer sends our best-selling product as a gift, what will the recipient see first when the box is opened, and who decided that?
  2. Does each of our top listings answer “will this suit them?” as clearly as “will this suit me?”
  3. Which of our products lose their fast delivery promise first in December, and what do we promote to gift buyers once they do?
  4. Can a recipient exchange a gift without involving the person who bought it?

Gifting from a distance is a test of how well the product page, the warehouse and the package work as one, which is the joined-up channel work we do with brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0464.crumb: Contribution margin by ASIN, not one ACoS…
P0464.title: Contribution margin by ASIN, not one ACoS target, sets ad budgets
P0464.alt: Brass vintage scales holding dried herbs, an amber bottle, a soap bar, crystals and a herb bundle on a wooden shelf.
P0464.ttag: Contribution margin by ASIN, not one ACoS target, sets ad budgets | Kwontified
P0464.desc: A single ACoS target averages thin-margin and thick-margin products together. Price each ASIN’s ads from its own contribution margin instead.
P0464.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 13, 2020.
P0464.body:
Most Amazon ad accounts run on one number. Someone in finance agrees that advertising may cost 25% of the sales it brings in, the agency sets every campaign to that advertising cost of sale (ACoS), and the monthly report shows the account landing close to target. The account can be on target and still lose money on a third of the products it advertises. A single ACoS target is an average of break-even points that differ by product, and it overspends where margins are thin while holding back the products that could carry far more advertising. Setting the ceiling from contribution margin by ASIN fixes both.

Why one ACoS target looks reasonable

The single target is not lazy. It is easy to explain to a CFO, easy to audit and roughly right for a catalog whose products earn similar margins. When most of a brand’s sales come from a handful of similar items, one number is close enough.

It also matches how the money is reported. Amazon bills advertising by campaign, the brand’s P&L shows advertising as one line, and the blended figure that ties them together is the account’s ACoS, or its total ACoS (TACoS): ad spend divided by all sales, paid and unpaid.

The trouble starts when the catalog is mixed, which most are by the fourth quarter: a hero product, a few bundles, some low-priced add-ons, a clearance line.

Contribution margin by ASIN gives each product its own ceiling

Contribution margin is what a unit leaves behind after every cost that rises with each sale: the cost of goods, Amazon’s referral fee, the fulfillment fee, storage and returns. It comes before overhead and before advertising. For a product sold through Fulfillment by Amazon, two of those costs are set by Amazon’s fee schedule. The referral fee is 15% of the price in most categories, and Amazon raised fulfillment fees by about 3% from February 18, 2020, according to its notice to US sellers and Feedvisor’s summary of the changes.

The contribution margin, as a share of price, is also the break-even ACoS. If a product keeps $7 of a $20 sale, ads can spend up to $7 per ad-driven sale, or 35% ACoS, before that sale loses money.

Take three products from one catalog, all sold through FBA.

Hero productBundleAdd-on
Price$20.00$45.00$12.00
Cost of goods$6.00$15.00$4.50
Referral fee (15%)$3.00$6.75$1.80
Fulfillment fee$3.50$5.50$3.20
Storage and returns$0.50$1.25$0.30
Contribution$7.00$16.50$2.20
Break-even ACoS35%37%18%

Now apply a 25% target across all three. The add-on spends $3.00 in ads to win a $12.00 sale that leaves $2.20, so every ad-driven sale loses $0.80. The bundle spends $11.25 to win a sale that leaves $16.50, keeping $5.25 per sale while the target keeps its bids below the level where it would win more of them.

The blended report hides both mistakes. If the bundle and the hero product sell well, the account shows a healthy 25% and a profit, and the add-on’s losses disappear into the average. The target is right on the average product and wrong on almost every real one.

Low-priced products are where this bites hardest, because Amazon’s fulfillment fee is a fixed amount per unit while the referral fee is a percentage. On a $12 item the fulfillment fee alone takes more than a quarter of the price, which leaves little room for anything else.

What the break-even number does not tell you

Break-even ACoS assumes every ad-attributed sale was caused by the ad. Some of those buyers would have found the product anyway, especially on searches for the brand’s own name, so the true ceiling is lower than the table shows. A product that clears break-even only on branded searches may not be profitable to advertise at all.

The arithmetic also leaves out what a sale is worth later. A product that customers reorder every month can justify spending past break-even on the first order, but only if the brand can show the reorder rate from its own data. Without that evidence, treat the first-order contribution as the ceiling.

Fees move too. The fulfillment fee depends on size and weight tiers, and storage costs rise in the fourth quarter, so a margin calculated in the spring can be wrong by December.

What changes when each product has its own target

The budget moves. In the example, the bundle can bid up to a 37% ceiling and win placements it was losing, while the add-on’s bids come down until its ads stop losing money, or the campaign is paused. The account’s blended ACoS may rise. Its profit should rise with it, which is the trade a CFO should prefer once it is shown product by product.

The weak product does not have to disappear from advertising. An add-on that cannot pay for its own clicks can still appear in a Sponsored Brands ad next to the hero product, or be sold inside a bundle that carries the margin. The question changes from “how do we hit 25%?” to “which products earn the right to buy their own traffic?”

Three numbers to put on every advertised ASIN

  1. Contribution per unit after cost of goods, referral fee, fulfillment fee, storage and returns, checked against the current fee schedule.
  2. Break-even ACoS, which is that contribution divided by the price, and a working target set below it to leave room for sales the ads did not cause.
  3. The share of the product’s ad spend that goes to branded searches, since that is where the break-even figure overstates what the ads earn.

The rule of thumb: any ASIN whose contribution is under 20% of price should not share an ACoS target with the rest of the catalog. Building those per-product targets into the bids is part of the Sponsored Products work we do for brands on Amazon.

P0466.crumb: Cyber Week 2020 is now a November season…
P0466.title: Cyber Week 2020 is now a November season, and the plan is due now
P0466.alt: Kraft paper parcels tied with twine and dried flowers on a long wooden table with autumn leaves and a mug of tea.
P0466.ttag: Cyber Week 2020 is now a November season, and the plan is due now | Kwontified
P0466.desc: Walmart and Target have spread Black Friday across November. After an October Prime Day, the deal, stock and budget calls for Cyber Week are due this week.
P0466.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 15, 2020.
P0466.body:
Prime Day ended at midnight. The deal team is tired, the dashboards are still filling in, and the natural instinct is to take a breath before thinking about Black Friday. Walmart did not take that breath. On October 14, while Prime Day was still running, it said its Black Friday would be three events, starting online on November 4, November 11 and November 25, with more of the best deals held for online shoppers, the Associated Press reported.

That turns Cyber Week 2020 into a season that opens in under three weeks. The decisions that used to be made in early November are due now: how deep to discount, how much stock to send in and how much ad budget to hold back. They should be made from what Prime Day just sold, not from last year’s Cyber Week.

Cyber Week 2020 starts from a different calendar

Every large retailer has moved. Target said its Deal Days on October 13 and 14 would open its holiday season and that Black Friday pricing would run throughout November, with an extended price match, Retail Dive reported. Walmart and Target will both keep stores closed on Thanksgiving Day. Walmart will cap store occupancy at 20% during its in-store events, and its chief merchandising officer, Scott McCall, put the bet plainly: “If the deal is right, customers are willing to shop earlier.”

The shopper is expected to follow. ShopperTrak forecasts that the 10 busiest days will carry 34.2% of holiday store traffic, against 46.5% in 2019, according to the same AP report. Online, Deloitte expects holiday e-commerce to grow 25% to 35%, CNBC reported in September.

For a sense of what is being spread out: in 2019, US shoppers spent $4.2 billion online on Thanksgiving, $7.4 billion on Black Friday and a record $9.4 billion on Cyber Monday, according to Adobe Analytics figures reported by CNBC. Brands should not assume those days disappear. They should assume the same money arrives over more days, in more pieces, with more of it online.

The three decisions due this week

Inside most brands, the Prime Day post-mortem and the Black Friday plan are run by the same few people, a week apart. In 2020 they have to be the same meeting.

Deal depth: decide whether November repeats October

The awkward question in the room is whether the Prime Day price comes back. If it does, the brand has trained shoppers that October’s price is the real one, and anyone who bought at full price in between has a reason to feel cheated. If it does not, the brand competes in November against retailers advertising Black Friday pricing for a month.

Target’s month-long Black Friday pricing makes the choice sharper, because a brand’s November price at one retailer will be visible beside its Prime Day price at another. Settle one floor price per hero product for the whole of November, and decide which products, if any, get a deeper Cyber Monday price.

Inventory: read Prime Day sell-through before reordering

Prime Day used up stock that would otherwise have sold in November. The first job is to compare what each product actually sold on October 13 and 14 with the plan, then recalculate weeks of cover through the end of December at the new November pace.

Products that sold through faster than planned need inbound shipments booked this week, because warehouse receiving slows as volume builds and the season now starts on November 4. Products that sold slowly are candidates for the deeper November deal, which is better than carrying them into January.

Ad budget: spread it, but keep a reserve for the peaks

A Cyber Week budget built for five days will run out by mid-November if the season is four weeks long. Divide the November budget into the retailer event windows and weight it toward the days the retailers are promoting hardest. Keep a reserve for Black Friday through Cyber Monday, which will still be the busiest stretch even if it is a smaller share of the total. Search prices will rise on those days whether or not your brand joins in, so the reserve is what keeps your products visible when the auction is at its most crowded.

Budgets also need to follow stock. A product that runs low in mid-November should step down its spend before it goes out of stock, so the reserve can move to products that can still ship.

What Prime Day can and cannot tell you yet

The public results will come out in pieces over the coming weeks, starting with Amazon’s own announcement and ending with its third-quarter earnings. Neither will tell a brand how its own products did, and neither will say how much of Prime Day was demand pulled forward from November.

Your own data can begin to. Compare the two weeks after Prime Day with the two weeks before it, product by product. A product whose sales stay depressed after the event borrowed from its own future, and its November plan should be smaller than the October plan implied.

Questions for the planning meeting this week

  1. Which of our hero products will carry a November price, and is it the same as, above or below the Prime Day price?
  2. Which products sold through faster than planned on Prime Day, and have their inbound shipments been booked?
  3. How is the November ad budget split across Walmart’s three event windows, Target’s month of Black Friday pricing and Amazon’s own Cyber Week?
  4. Who decides when a product’s ads step down because stock is running low?

November 2020 rewards the brands that treat it as one long season run by one team, which is how we run holiday planning across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0471.title: Shoppers forgave 2020’s late deliveries, but only on loan
P0471.alt: A brown paper parcel tied with string and a blank postcard rests on a stone step before a sage green door.
P0471.ttag: Shoppers forgave 2020’s late deliveries, but only on loan | Kwontified
P0471.desc: Shoppers forgave late deliveries in 2020 when they were warned before paying. Most say that patience is temporary, and holiday deadlines will test it.
P0471.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 22, 2020.
P0471.body:
In late March, some products on Amazon started showing delivery estimates a month out. From March 22, shoppers looking at items outside Amazon’s priority categories could see arrival dates around 30 days away, Marketplace Pulse reported. For a company that had trained its customers to expect a package in two days, that was a remarkable thing to print on a product page. Shoppers mostly shrugged and kept buying.

They did not forgive everyone equally. The brands and retailers that came through the year with their customers intact were the ones that told shoppers about the delay before they paid. The ones that kept promising dates they could not meet are now carrying the cost in returns, reviews and lost repeat orders. And the patience that saved the first group was always temporary. Most shoppers say so themselves, and the holiday season is when the loan comes due.

Shoppers forgave late deliveries they were warned about

The forgiveness was real and measurable. In an April survey of more than 1,000 US consumers by Convey, a delivery software company, 94% said they would give retailers more time to deliver, and 60% would accept three or four extra days, MarTech Series reported. In the same survey, 70% said they were less likely to shop with a retailer again if they were not told about a delay in advance. And 75% were more likely to buy when an estimated delivery date appeared on the product page or in the cart.

Six months later the pattern held. In ShipStation’s survey of more than 1,400 North American online shoppers, 79% said they accepted slower shipping under current circumstances, and 93% said they would keep shopping with a retailer that acknowledged a poor delivery experience, Logistics Management reported on October 15. But 89% expected brands to raise possible delays before checkout.

Put those numbers together and the rule shoppers applied is clear enough. A late package was forgiven when it was expected. A late package that broke a promise was not.

The promise is set by one team and kept by another

Inside most brands, the delivery promise a shopper sees is not a single decision. On a marketplace, it comes from the platform’s own logistics and the seller’s handling-time settings. On the brand’s own site, it is a line of copy on the product page and a shipping option at checkout, often written once and rarely revisited. The warehouse that has to keep the promise sits in a different part of the organization, and nobody is paid to notice when the two drift apart.

In a normal year the drift is small, because the warehouse meets the promise most of the time. In 2020 it became a gap. Amazon solved its version publicly by changing the date on the page. Many smaller brands left a three-to-five-day promise on their own sites through weeks when orders were taking twice that, and the first notice their customers received was an apology email after the date had passed.

The marketplaces read this better than most brands, because they own the customer relationship and are judged on it. Amazon chose to show a longer date rather than keep selling against a promise it could not meet, which protected the trust it depends on at the cost of some sales. For a brand selling through a marketplace, the lesson cuts both ways. Orders fulfilled from the marketplace’s warehouses carry the platform’s own, now more honest, dates. Orders a brand ships itself carry whatever handling time the brand entered months ago, and a late shipment there counts against the brand, not the platform.

That gap is what the shoppers in these surveys were punishing. They were not angry that a warehouse was short of staff in April. They were angry that the brand knew and did not say.

The holiday season ends the grace period

The same ShipStation survey carries a warning. Of the shoppers who accepted slower shipping, 60% said their lowered expectations were temporary, and the delivery window shoppers now expect has stretched to eight days, up from five in 2019. Shoppers have widened their tolerance, but they have also started counting.

The holiday season puts a hard deadline on that count. A gift that arrives on December 28 is not eight days late in the way an April order was; it is simply wrong. Retailers and analysts have already signaled that capacity will be tight. Walmart has spread Black Friday across three online events beginning November 4 to thin out the peak, the Associated Press reported, and Coresight’s Deborah Weinswig told CNBC in September that the industry was “already capacity constrained.”

Shoppers who gave a brand the benefit of the doubt in spring will give it once more in December only if the brand earns it the same way. That means a realistic date in front of them before they pay, and an early, plain message when that date has moved.

Questions for the team before November

  1. Who owns the delivery date shown on our product pages and in our cart, and when was it last checked against what the warehouse actually achieved?
  2. What is our last order date for Christmas delivery by channel, and is it already visible to shoppers?
  3. If a shipment slips, how many hours pass before the customer hears from us rather than from the carrier?
  4. Do our marketplace handling-time settings reflect December staffing, or July’s?

The brands that keep their customers through this holiday will be the ones whose promise and warehouse speak to each other, which is the channel operations work we do with brands on Amazon and Walmart.

P0472.crumb: Prime Day 2020 beat its forecast by 5%…
P0472.title: Prime Day 2020 beat its forecast by 5%; December will grade it
P0472.alt: A wooden clipboard with a blank page and gold star beside a citrus wreath on a navy wall, with a mug and glasses.
P0472.ttag: Prime Day 2020 beat its forecast by 5%; December will grade it | Kwontified
P0472.desc: Estimates put Prime Day 2020 about 5% above eMarketer’s forecast. How much was pulled from November will not be known until the holidays are over.
P0472.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 27, 2020.
P0472.body:
Two weeks after the event, the scorecard for Prime Day 2020 looks tidy. eMarketer had forecast $9.91 billion in worldwide sales. Digital Commerce 360’s first estimate after the event came to $10.40 billion. On those numbers the result beat the best-known forecast by about 5%. It is the wrong number to grade, because it covers two days, and Prime Day 2020 was never a two-day event.

The Prime Day 2020 forecast against the estimates

MeasureBefore the eventAfter the event
eMarketer, worldwide$9.91 billion, up 43% on its 2019 estimate of $6.93 billion—
Digital Commerce 360, worldwide$9.7 billion$10.40 billion, up 45.2% on its 2019 estimate of $7.16 billion
Amazon, third-party sellers—more than $3.5 billion, up nearly 60%

The forecasts come from TechCrunch’s report on eMarketer and from Marketplace Pulse, which cited both firms on October 13. The post-event estimate comes from 24/7 Wall St., and the seller figure from Amazon’s own release on October 15.

Only the last row was reported by Amazon. The other two are outside estimates, and they start from different 2019 baselines. Compared on their own baselines, eMarketer expected 43% growth and Digital Commerce 360 estimated 45.2%, so the “beat” is closer to two points of growth than to 5% of sales. The seller figure, $3.5 billion, is about a third of the estimated total.

Why the two-day total is the number everyone grades

The two-day total is what Amazon promotes, what analysts forecast and what the press reports, so it becomes the scoreboard by default. It also matches how most brands report the event internally: sales on October 13 and 14 against a normal day, multiplied by two.

That habit has a bias built into it. A spike is easy to see and easy to credit, and the quiet days around it are not. The days before an event are depressed by shoppers who wait for the deal, and the days after are depressed by shoppers who already bought. Neither shows up in a two-day total.

In 2020 the surrounding window was unusually long. Amazon’s early deals began on September 28, and its spend-$10-get-$10 small-business promotion drove more than $900 million in sales in the two weeks before the event, Amazon said. And because Prime Day moved into the fourth quarter, the buying it borrowed comes from late October and also from Black Friday and the gift season that follows. A summer Prime Day borrowed from August; this one borrowed from Christmas.

Why the forecasters were close

Both firms expected growth above 40%. Both landed near the result. That says something about how predictable the event has become. eMarketer’s principal analyst, Andrew Lipsman, told TechCrunch that sellers had “developed a playbook for their promotions and advertising strategy.” Brands now know the dates weeks ahead, plan deals around them and buy ads into them, so the spike is partly scheduled by the people measuring it.

That predictability is also why the two-day figure says little about what Amazon wanted from the event. Marketplace Pulse argued on October 13 that the point of Prime Day is to remind people to open the Amazon app. An event designed to bring shoppers back for the season should be judged on the season, and so should a brand’s participation in it.

None of this makes the forecasts wrong. A forecast of a two-day total that lands within a few percent is a good forecast. The trouble starts when a brand takes the same two-day frame and uses it to decide next year’s deal budget.

My own September forecast belongs on the same scorecard, with a caveat. Its three cases for a brand’s two-day Prime Day against 2019 were worked examples for an illustrative brand, and the portfolio data that would turn them into a forecast is still outstanding, so the market estimates above cannot grade them. What that post did state from public data was a direction: a bigger everyday baseline after a year of growth in online shopping, and a smaller lift, because a fourth-quarter event borrows from Black Friday. A two-day total cannot confirm either half. Both show up only in the weeks around the event, which is where the grade has to come from.

Added sales and borrowed sales

Take a brand that normally sells $10,000 a day on Amazon. On each Prime Day it sells $50,000, so the two-day report shows $80,000 of lift. In the seven days before the event, shoppers who are waiting hold sales to $8,000 a day, $14,000 below normal. In the 14 days after, shoppers who stocked up hold sales to $9,000 a day, another $14,000 below normal.

Net, the event added $52,000, not $80,000. More than a third of the headline lift was borrowed from the weeks on either side.

For gift categories in 2020 there is a second layer that a three-week window cannot catch. A shopper who bought a December present on October 13 has moved a sale from the holiday season into October. That sale will show up as a weaker November, not as a weaker week after Prime Day.

How to grade your own Prime Day 2020

The two-day number answers the question “how big was the spike?” A budget depends on a different question: how much did October 1 through December 31 grow because the event happened? Brands can only answer that from their own data, and only in January.

Until then, three checks keep the grade honest:

  1. Measure the event over a window, not two days: from the start of the early deals on September 28 to at least two weeks after October 14, against the same products’ daily run rate in early September.
  2. Track gift-heavy products separately. If their November falls short of plan while everyday products hold up, the shortfall is Prime Day borrowing from the holidays, not weak demand.
  3. Compare the full fourth quarter with your own pre-event forecast for it, not with Q4 2019, which had no Prime Day in it.

The rule of thumb: credit an event only with the sales that are still there when the window closes. For Prime Day 2020 the window closes on December 31, and building that end-of-quarter read is the measurement work we do for brands before the next event’s budget is set.

P0474.crumb: October Prime Day rewarded brands that…
P0474.title: October Prime Day rewarded brands that could decide in two weeks
P0474.alt: A brass hourglass surrounded by dry brown autumn leaves on a weathered wooden table against an ochre wall.
P0474.ttag: October Prime Day rewarded brands that could decide in two weeks | Kwontified
P0474.desc: Amazon gave 15 days’ notice and rivals answered within a day. The holiday calendar now moves by announcement, and slow approval chains lose.
P0474.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 29, 2020.
P0474.body:
On Monday, September 28, Amazon announced that Prime Day would run on October 13 and 14, with early deals starting that same morning, in its announcement. Brands had known since July that the event would come “later than usual,” and since Amazon’s July 30 earnings call that it would fall in the fourth quarter. They had 15 days’ notice of the date itself.

The event is over, and the scoreboard has been published. The more useful lesson is what the October Prime Day showed about how the holiday calendar is now set. It moves by announcement, at a few days’ or weeks’ notice, and the brands that did well were the ones whose people could say yes to a price, a deal and a shipment inside that window.

The October Prime Day set the calendar by announcement

Look at how quickly the rest of the industry moved. Target announced its Deal Days for the same October 13 and 14 the next day, along with Black Friday pricing for all of November and, for the first time, a price-match guarantee running from November 1 to December 24, Target said.

Walmart’s Big Save event was set for October 11 to 15, the Motley Fool reported on September 30. On October 14, while Prime Day was still running, Walmart announced that its Black Friday would be three online events starting November 4, the Associated Press reported.

Three retailers rewrote the shape of the season in 16 days. None of it was on the calendar most brands were working from in August.

Inside a typical brand, the holiday plan is a slow document. Deal depths are approved by finance, inventory commitments by supply chain, and retailer events by account teams who each manage one retailer’s calendar. In most years that pace works, because Black Friday does not move and Prime Day sits in July. In October 2020, a plan that needed three approvals and two weeks of lead time was already late on the day the date was announced.

The sellers who control their own price moved fastest

Amazon’s own results hint at who could move. Third-party sellers, mostly small and medium-sized businesses, sold more than $3.5 billion during the event, nearly 60% more than in 2019, and their growth outpaced Amazon’s own retail business, Amazon said on October 15.

There are several reasons that could be true, and Amazon’s own promotion of small businesses is one of them. But it also fits the structure of the two businesses. A third-party seller sets its own price, decides its own deal and sends its own stock to Amazon’s warehouses. A vendor selling to Amazon wholesale needs Amazon’s buyers to order the stock and agree the deal funding. When the calendar compresses to two weeks, the party holding all three decisions can act; the party that has to negotiate each one waits.

The evidence leans that way without proving it. Brands should read it as a signal, not as a verdict on the vendor model. eMarketer’s Andrew Lipsman made a related point before the event: sellers had “developed a playbook for their promotions and advertising strategy,” he told TechCrunch. A playbook is a set of decisions made before anyone knows the date.

The holiday season will keep arriving at short notice

The rest of 2020 will run the same way. Walmart’s first Black Friday event begins online on November 4. Target’s November deals begin on November 1. Amazon will announce its own Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on its own schedule. Each announcement will give brands days, not months, to decide whether to join, how deep to go and whether the stock is there.

Retailers have good reasons to keep it that way. A retailer that announces late keeps its options open on warehouse space, staffing and the competitive picture, and a retailer that answers a rival within a day denies that rival a clear field. Short notice is not an accident of 2020; it is what each retailer’s own interests produce when the others are moving too. Brands should expect it to outlast the pandemic, because the incentive behind it does not depend on the pandemic.

For a brand, the cost of short notice falls on the slowest link. A deal that is approved but has no stock behind it, or stock that arrives without an approved deal, is worth very little in a two-day event. The brands that came through October well tended to be the ones where one person could see both.

That calendar rewards a different kind of organization. The question in the room is no longer “what is our Black Friday plan?” It is “who can approve a deal on Thursday that runs next Wednesday, and within what limits?”

Questions for the next leadership meeting

  1. Which decisions for a retailer event (price floor, deal depth, ad budget, inventory release) can the channel team make without a meeting, and which still need finance?
  2. Do we have a pre-approved playbook for a two-week-notice event at each of our retailers, or will we build it again for Walmart’s November 4 start?
  3. Where we sell to a retailer wholesale, what would it take to control our own price and stock for event weeks, and is that worth exploring for 2021?
  4. Which of our account teams learned about Walmart’s three Black Friday events from the news rather than from their retailer contact?

The October Prime Day was the first holiday event set by announcement, and it will not be the last. Building the standing decisions that let a brand answer within days is the kind of channel management we do for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

P0477.crumb: Amazon ad growth in Q3 2020 says cheap…
P0477.title: Amazon ad growth in Q3 2020 says cheap clicks are over
P0477.alt: An empty wire storage cage stands by a blue wall in a shop with wooden shelves of bottles, pottery and boxes.
P0477.ttag: Amazon ad growth in Q3 2020 says cheap clicks are over | Kwontified
P0477.desc: Amazon’s ad line grew 51% in a quarter without Prime Day, and the growth came back through click prices. Spring bids are now losing auctions they used to win.
P0477.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 3, 2020.
P0477.body:
Amazon’s “other” revenue, the line that mostly holds advertising, was $5.4 billion in the third quarter, up 51%, the company reported on October 29. A year earlier the same quarter held Prime Day, which ran July 15 and 16 in 2019. This year Prime Day moved to October 13 and 14, into the fourth quarter. So Amazon ad growth sped up from the second quarter’s 41% without the biggest promotional event the third quarter usually carries.

That acceleration matters more to brands than the headline. The growth did not come from a flood of new clicks at bargain prices, as it did in the spring. It came back through price. Advertisers returned to the auction, the same search slots had more bidders, and the cost of a click recovered. A bid that won easily in April loses now.

Amazon ad growth in Q3 2020 came through the auction, not the event

Amazon’s own conference pointed the other way. AdCon 2020, its second annual advertiser event, ran online on September 30 and October 1. Amazon’s recap told advertisers to experiment, called streaming TV ads affordable and measurable next to linear TV, and paired Sponsored Brands video and Streaming TV ads with free tools such as Posts, Stores and Follow. The one figure it offered was a 22% increase in new-to-brand customers for campaigns run since March 1, against the previous six months.

That is a pitch for budget beyond search. But the money that showed up in the quarter was mostly search money. Merkle’s third-quarter Digital Marketing Report put Sponsored Products spend up 50% year over year, from 22% in the second quarter. Sponsored Brands spend rose 74%.

The click price came back

Ad spend is clicks times the price of a click, and in 2020 the two moved very differently. In the second quarter, Merkle counted Sponsored Products clicks up 107% while the average cost per click (CPC) was 41% lower than a year before, according to its Q2 report. Many advertisers had paused in March and April, shoppers were searching more than ever, and the few bidders left bought traffic cheaply.

By the third quarter, the Sponsored Products CPC was down only a little more than 8%, and the Sponsored Brands CPC was up 16%. If spend rose 50% while the price fell 8%, clicks rose about 63% (1.50 divided by 0.92 is about 1.63). Volume growth roughly halved and price did most of the recovering. That is a different market from the one most brands planned their holiday budgets against in the summer, when every report said clicks were cheap.

The logic is plain once you see the auction as a fixed shelf. Each search shows only so many sponsored slots. When advertisers came back over the summer, the number of slots did not grow with them, so the same placements cleared at higher prices. Amazon’s paid units grew 46% in the quarter and third-party seller services revenue grew 55%, which means more sellers with more products to promote, nearly all of them bidding on the same search results.

That is also why Amazon wants the streaming TV conversation. Search inventory is bounded by how often shoppers search. Video and streaming placements are not, so they are where Amazon can sell more advertising without simply raising the price of the search shelf.

What the numbers can and can’t tell you

Three cautions keep this reading honest. “Other” revenue also includes services that are not advertising, and Amazon does not break advertising out, so the 51% is a close proxy for ad growth, not a measure of it. Merkle’s figures describe its own clients’ accounts, a large sample but not all of Amazon. And Amazon’s 22% new-to-brand figure is its own aggregate over months when shoppers moved online for reasons no ad caused.

What would change this view: a fourth quarter in which CPCs fall again despite Prime Day and Cyber Week, which would mean the summer recovery was seasonal rather than a refilled auction. Your own search term report will show it before any public benchmark does: pull the average CPC by week for your top keywords since January and look at where the line turned. In most accounts the turn will sit somewhere between May and July, when paused budgets came back on, and the weeks since will look nothing like April.

Re-pricing bids for the holiday

Take a $40 product that can spend 25% of its price to win a sale, so $10, on a keyword that converts 10% of clicks. Each click is worth $1.00. In 2019 that keyword cost about $1.00. In the spring of 2020 it cleared near $0.59, and a brand that cut its bid to $0.70 still won top placement. At about $0.92 in the third quarter, the same $0.70 bid now loses the placement it held, and the account reports falling impressions as if demand had dropped.

So the work before the holiday is mechanical:

  • Re-price every bid set between March and June from the product’s conversion value, not from the CPC it paid in the spring.
  • Compare impression share and top-of-search share for September against June on your twenty largest keywords; a fall with steady bids means rivals came back.
  • Fund Sponsored Brands separately, since its CPC has already passed last year’s level.
  • Treat any streaming TV or video test as its own budget line with a holdout, so search budgets are not drained to fund it.

The auction that rewarded patience in April now rewards whoever priced their clicks correctly, and re-pricing Amazon Sponsored Ads against conversion value is work we do every week.

P0478.crumb: Retail media kept its budget in 2020…
P0478.title: Retail media kept its budget in 2020 because it shows the sale
P0478.alt: A glass display case holds a twine-tied paper parcel with a blank tag and a few coins, set against a pink wall.
P0478.ttag: Retail media kept its budget in 2020 because it shows the sale | Kwontified
P0478.desc: Retail media grew through 2020 while other ad budgets shrank, because it could show the sale next to the ad. That proof has a blind spot worth seeing.
P0478.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 5, 2020.
P0478.body:
In June, eMarketer forecast that Google’s US advertising revenue would fall 5.3% in 2020, its first decline since the firm began estimating it in 2008, while Amazon’s would rise 23.5%, Press Gazette reported. The whole US digital market was expected to grow 1.7%. Four months later Amazon reported its advertising line up 51%. The largest ad business in the country was forecast to shrink, and the retailer selling ads next to its own shelf was speeding up.

Some of that gap is mix: eMarketer said Google’s fall came mainly from travel advertisers, who had nothing to sell. But the larger reason sits inside brands. When every budget line had to justify itself in the spring of 2020, retail media was the one that could answer the question with a sale. That proof kept it funded. It also has a blind spot that most leadership teams have not yet looked at.

Retail media in a crisis: the line that could answer the question

Think about how a spring budget review went in 2020. Each line was asked what it bought. Television and social could offer reach, frequency and brand lift studies. The Amazon or Walmart line could offer a report showing ads, clicks and the orders that followed, in the same system, often by product and by day. In a meeting about cash, the second kind of answer wins.

The cuts still came, and fast. In the IAB’s buy-side tracking, the share of buyers who had paused advertising rose from 24% in the week of March 18 to 37% in the week of April 15. Merkle found that in the last week of March the typical Amazon advertiser was spending half as much per day as in January. Retail media was not spared the shock, but it had a faster way back: once stock returned, the people running it could show finance exactly which campaigns paid, and switch those on first.

By the second quarter Amazon’s ad line was up 41%, and by the third quarter, 51%. Merkle’s clients raised Sponsored Products spend 50% in the third quarter. Money came back to the one place where it could see its own return, and it came back first to the products that were in stock, priced well and already ranking, because those were the campaigns with the cleanest reports.

The closed loop belongs to the retailer

The closed loop (an ad and the sale it led to, recorded in the same system) is the retailer’s asset before it is the brand’s. Amazon sees the search, the click, the purchase and every later purchase. The brand sees a report built from that data, with the rules of attribution set by the seller of the ads. When budgets tighten, that arrangement favors the retailer twice: it gets the spend, and it writes the scorecard the spend is judged on.

A retail media report counts sales only in that retailer’s store. It does not see the shopper who saw the ad on Amazon and bought at Target, and it cannot say which of the reported sales would have happened anyway. Amazon’s own pitch at AdCon, its advertiser conference this fall, a 22% increase in new-to-brand customers for campaigns run since March 1 compared with the previous six months, is a good example. The months it measures are the months shoppers moved online for reasons no ad caused. The figure is true and says little about what the ads added.

None of this made retail media a bad bet during the pandemic. It made it an easy one to defend, which is a different thing.

Where the budget now sits

The shift that matters for 2021 is organizational. At many brands, retail media sits in the e-commerce or sales budget rather than with brand media, and the crisis hardened that placement: the money that survived was money a sales leader could tie to orders. That makes it feel less like advertising and more like a cost of selling on the platform, closer to a fee than a campaign.

There is a real case for that view, and e-commerce leaders make it well. On a crowded search page, where four or five sponsored products can sit above the first organic result on a phone screen, an unadvertised product is often an invisible one, and the e-commerce team is right to protect it. The risk is that a line treated as a cost of selling stops being asked the question every media line should answer: what did this add? Brands that let the retailer’s report be the only judge will keep funding the campaigns that report best, and those are usually the ones capturing shoppers who were already coming.

The evidence so far leans toward retail media keeping the share it won in 2020, because the habit of proof it built in a crisis is hard to give up. What is still open is who inside a brand gets to set its rules.

Four questions that decide who owns retail media in 2021

  • Which budget does retail media sit in now, and who would have to agree to move a dollar out of it?
  • For the campaigns finance protected in the spring, do we know how many of those sales would have happened without the ads?
  • Does anyone outside the e-commerce team see the retail media report before the budget is set?
  • When the retailer changes its attribution rules, who on our side notices?

The brands that answer the second question with a test rather than a report will spend the next crisis better, and building that test, a holdout before the next tentpole, is the measurement work we do with brands.

P0482.crumb: Instagram Shop is the window display that…
P0482.title: Instagram Shop is the window display that lockdown took away
P0482.alt: A tablet on a stand shows a colorful shop window beside wooden shutters on a narrow cobbled old-town street.
P0482.ttag: Instagram Shop is the window display that lockdown took away | Kwontified
P0482.desc: Lockdown closed the shop windows where shoppers found things they were not looking for. Instagram Shop now does that job, and few brands staff it.
P0482.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 12, 2020.
P0482.body:
On any shopping street, the window is where a store sells to people who did not come to buy. Someone walks past on the way to lunch, sees a coat on a mannequin, and goes in. Visual merchandising teams change those windows every few weeks for exactly that shopper. In April, US clothing store sales fell 78.8% from a year earlier. Most of those windows went dark, and the people who used to walk past them were at home, scrolling.

Instagram has spent 2020 building a replacement for that walk. Product tags, the Shop in Explore, checkout and shopping inside video are all ways of putting an item in front of someone who was not searching for it. More than 130 million accounts tap to reveal product tags every month, Instagram told WWD in October. That is the window, rebuilt as a feed. What most brands have not rebuilt is the job of dressing it.

Search finds what you want; the window finds what you did not know you wanted

Amazon and Walmart are built for shoppers who already know what they want. They type “running shoes,” the search results do the rest, and the ad auction decides who sits at the top. That model thrived in 2020. But it does little for the shopper who did not have a running shoe in mind, and that shopper used to be a large part of how apparel, beauty and accessories brands grew. She found them in a window, on a table near the entrance, on someone else at a party.

With stores closed or capped, and with ShopperTrak expecting the ten busiest holiday days to carry 34.2% of store traffic this season against 46.5% in 2019, according to the Associated Press, that kind of unplanned discovery has fewer places to happen. The feed is one of them.

Instagram Shop rebuilt the walk past the window

Instagram’s year reads like a store fit-out. In May, Facebook introduced Shops, a single storefront for a brand across Facebook and Instagram.

In July, a redesigned Shop in Explore began rolling out in the US, TechCrunch reported, with collections curated by Instagram’s @shop account, category filters and suggestions. Reels, launched on August 5, gave short video its own space in Explore.

Checkout on Instagram opened to all US businesses in August, and IGTV shopping launched worldwide on October 7. Instagram has said a shopping tab will join the main navigation and that it will test shopping in Reels before the end of the year, WWD reported.

Each step moves a product closer to the place people browse without intent. A product tag in a creator’s post is a mannequin in a window. A collection in the Shop tab is the table near the door.

Nobody owns the window

Here the structure inside the brand matters more than the platform.

In many companies, the Instagram account belongs to the social or brand team, measured on reach, followers and engagement. The product catalog that feeds Shop belongs to e-commerce, measured on sales. A product tag sits exactly between them: it is a piece of content that is also a shelf position. Visual merchandising used to own the window and answered to the stores. That role rarely exists for the feed.

The result shows up in the details any shopper can see. Open a brand’s Instagram profile and tap through the last dozen posts. Many tag nothing, or tag the same two hero products for months, or tag items that are out of stock or still at full price when the brand’s own site is running a sale. Those are not social media mistakes. They are merchandising decisions that nobody was asked to make.

The brands getting this right treat the tagged assortment like a window plan. They choose which products earn a place in the feed each month and rotate them with the season. They match tagged prices to what the shopper will find at checkout. And they read taps and saves the way a store read how many people stopped at the glass.

It is too early to say how much of this browsing will turn into purchases inside Instagram rather than on a brand’s own site or on Amazon. The evidence so far leans toward discovery staying on social and buying going wherever checkout is easiest. Either way, the brand that is seen in the window gets the first chance at the sale.

There is a practical reason to start before the holidays rather than after. Gift shopping is the most window-driven buying of the year: people shop for someone else, often in categories they do not know, and they want to be shown ideas. A gift guide used to be a store table near the entrance and a printed catalog. In 2020 it is a saved collection on Instagram, a creator’s post with six tagged products, or a brand’s own Shop arranged by price. The brands that set those up in November will be the ones in front of a December shopper who has no list and no store to wander through.

Questions for the team that runs the feed

  • Who decides which products are tagged for December, and what are they measured on?
  • When did someone last check that every tagged product is in stock and priced the same as on our site?
  • Does the holiday feed plan match the holiday promotion calendar, product by product?
  • What would we change if we read taps on product tags the way a store reads footfall at the window?

For brands that want the feed run as a shop window rather than a content calendar, our social commerce team works across Instagram Shop and the marketplaces it sends shoppers to.

P0484.title: A demand forecasting baseline for 2021 should skip 2020
P0484.alt: Three journals in green cloth, taupe with a ribbon, and tan leather lie on a wooden desk with a mug and succulent.
P0484.ttag: A demand forecasting baseline for 2021 should skip 2020 | Kwontified
P0484.desc: A year-over-year forecast for 2021 will copy 2020’s panic weeks and moved events into next year. Take the shape from 2019 and the level from recent weeks.
P0484.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 17, 2020.
P0484.body:
Sometime in the next month, most brands will build their 2021 demand plan the way they always do: take this year’s sales by week, apply a growth rate, adjust for known events. In a normal year that works well enough. For 2021 it is a trap. The weeks it starts from include the hand sanitizer week that ran 470% above 2019, the April trough when shoppers had stocked up and Amazon was rationing warehouse space, and a Prime Day that moved from July to October. A year-over-year baseline copies all of that into 2021.

The fix is not a cleverer growth rate. It is to stop asking 2020 for the two things it cannot tell you: what a normal year looks like, and what a normal week looks like.

What a demand forecasting baseline is made of

Strip any weekly forecast down and it has two parts. The level is how much the product sells in an ordinary week right now. The seasonal index is the shape of the year: how much more or less a given week sells than an ordinary one. December might carry an index of 1.6, a quiet February week 0.8. Events, such as Prime Day or a big promotion, sit on top as lifts.

A year-over-year forecast takes both parts from the prior year at once. It treats the prior year’s week 12 as the right shape for week 12 and that year’s average as the right level, then scales the lot by a growth rate. That is efficient when the prior year was ordinary. It also means every accident of the base year becomes a plan for the next one. Most planning spreadsheets work this way because it needs one input per week and anyone can audit it, which is exactly why it fails quietly: the error sits inside the base, where nobody checks.

Why a 2020 base breaks both parts

The shape is broken because 2020’s weeks were driven by events with no reason to repeat. Nielsen’s data showed bath tissue sales up 212.7% in the week ending March 14 and only 10.5% by the week ending May 23. Prime Day moved into the fourth quarter. Stockouts and Amazon’s spring limits on what it would accept into its warehouses cut sales in weeks where demand was fine.

The level is moving too, in the other direction from what a spring-weighted average suggests. Online sales were 16.1% of US retail in the second quarter, up from 11.4% in the fourth quarter of 2019, the Census Bureau reported, and e-commerce was up 44.5% on a year earlier. Amazon’s paid units grew 46% in the third quarter against 22% a year before. For many products the ordinary week of autumn 2020 is simply bigger than the ordinary week of 2019.

Take a product that sold a steady 1,000 units a week in March 2019, a week with an index of 1.0. In the week of March 16, 2020 it sold 2,600 in a burst of stocking up, then 700 a week in April. By September and October it had settled at 1,400 a week.

A year-over-year forecast for March 2021 starts from 2,600 and adds 10% growth: 2,860 units. Buying to that plan fills a warehouse with stock for a panic that is not coming back. Take the shape from 2019 instead (March index 1.0) and the level from the autumn (1,400), and the forecast is 1,400 units, close to half. December gets the same treatment: the 2019 December index of 1.6 times the 1,400 level is 2,240 a week.

What the data can and can’t tell you

The two-year method makes two bets. It bets that 2019’s seasonal shape still describes how people buy, and that the autumn level is the new normal rather than another phase of the shock. Neither is certain. A category that moved online for good, such as household staples, may have a new shape as well as a new level, with flatter peaks because buying is now routine.

So check the method on your own data before you trust it. Back-cast it: build a forecast for September and October 2020 using 2019’s shape and the level from July and August, and compare it with what actually sold. If the error is small, the 2019 shape still holds for that product. If it misses by more than 25% in either direction, the product’s shape has changed and needs a shorter, more local history.

Events need the same discipline. Prime Day’s 2021 date is unknown, so the baseline should carry no Prime Day at all, with the lift added as a separate line once Amazon announces it. The same goes for the retailers’ November events, which in 2020 started at Target on November 1 and at Walmart on November 4; whether they start that early again is a decision the retailers have not made yet.

One more test is worth running at the level of the whole range. Add up the rebuilt baseline across every product and compare the total with the 2021 sales target finance is about to set. If the target needs the baseline to grow faster than the autumn of 2020 did, the gap is a plan for new products, new retailers or more advertising, and it should be named as one rather than hidden inside the forecast.

The rebuild, in four steps

  • Seasonal shape from 2019 (or the average of 2018 and 2019), never from 2020.
  • Level from the latest eight to twelve clean weeks, divided by the 2019 index for those weeks, with stockout weeks removed.
  • Events as separate lifts on top of the baseline, dated only once the retailer dates them.
  • Re-estimate the level every month in the first half of 2021, since it is still moving.

A plan built this way will look too low to anyone holding a 2020 sales report, and that argument is worth having in December rather than in a warehouse in April. Building that baseline product by product is the forecasting work we do with brands before a plan is locked.
