P0485.title: Walmart Marketplace growth puts more sellers on your item pages
P0485.alt: A stoneware vase sits on a worn blue shelf with blank paper tags hanging from hooks beside sunlit linen curtains.
P0485.ttag: Walmart Marketplace growth puts more sellers on your item pages | Kwontified
P0485.desc: Walmart says its marketplace is the fastest-growing part of its online business. For brands, that means more sellers offering their products on Walmart.com.
P0485.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 19, 2020.
P0485.body:
On Tuesday, Walmart told investors that its US online sales grew 79% in the third quarter and that the fastest growth came from its marketplace, the independent sellers who list products on Walmart.com. Marketplace sales, the finance chief said, grew in triple digits. Most brand leaders will read that as news about Walmart’s race with Amazon. It is closer to news about their own products, because a growing share of the people selling those products on Walmart.com were never sold to by the brand.

For a brand that sells to Walmart’s stores through a buyer, the arrangement has felt settled for decades. The buyer chooses the items, the brand ships to the distribution centers, and the shelf is negotiated once or twice a year. The marketplace sits outside that conversation, and in 2020 it became the part of Walmart that is growing fastest.

Why Walmart Marketplace keeps adding sellers

Follow the value and Walmart’s reasons are plain. A marketplace sale earns Walmart a commission on a product it never bought, never stored in a store and never has to mark down. On the same call, Walmart tied its progress on e-commerce margins to marketplace sales growing faster than the rest. A retailer that has spent years losing money online has found the part of the business that helps fix it, and it will keep feeding it.

The seller count shows how fast. Walmart had a little over 32,000 marketplace sellers in November 2019. By July 2020, Marketplace Pulse counted more than 50,000, double the number a year before, Retail Dive reported, and more than 5,000 had joined in the weeks after Walmart opened its marketplace to Shopify merchants in June. Walmart’s own target for the Shopify channel had been about 1,200 merchants for the whole year.

The catalog moved the other way at the same time. Listings fell from more than 50 million at the start of 2020 to about 36 million, mostly because large sellers pulled whole catalogs of books and home goods. Walmart is not simply piling on items. It is adding sellers, and those sellers increasingly compete on the items Walmart already lists.

What more sellers look like from the brand’s side

Walmart.com shows one item page per product, with the offers from different sellers attached to it. When a new seller lists a product that is already there, it joins that page rather than creating a new one. So a brand’s popular items, the ones with reviews and search rank, are exactly where new sellers want to be.

Take a $30 blender that a brand sells to Walmart’s stores at wholesale. On Walmart.com, the same item page might now carry an offer from Walmart itself, one from a reseller at $27 who bought the blender at a discount elsewhere, and one at $34 from a seller with slow shipping. The shopper sees one page and one featured price. The brand set none of them, and its buyer at Walmart does not manage any of them.

In the store, a brand’s presentation is protected by planograms, buyer relationships and its own merchandising teams. On Walmart.com, the page’s photos, description and price can be shaped by whoever is selling, and the brand’s influence depends on whether someone inside the company is watching. At many brands, nobody is. The store team owns Walmart, the e-commerce team owns Amazon, and Walmart.com falls between them.

The timing makes this more than an organizational detail. Walmart moved much of its Black Friday online, with deal events starting on Walmart.com on November 4, November 11 and November 25, the Associated Press reported in October. The holiday traffic that used to walk past an endcap now lands on item pages, and on many of those pages the brand is one voice among several sellers. A reseller with a lower price and a thin description can hold the featured offer through the busiest weeks of the year without anyone at the brand noticing until the January sell-through report.

The shift: Walmart becomes two retailers for every brand

The evidence leans toward this continuing well past the pandemic. Walmart’s US e-commerce grew 97% in the second quarter and 79% in the third, and its leaders have now said in public that the marketplace is both the fastest-growing piece and good for margins. That combination tells you where the next investment goes.

For brands, the practical result is that Walmart is now two retailers. One is the store business, run through a buyer, measured on sell-through and shelf. The other is a marketplace, run by rules and algorithms, where the brand competes with its own resellers for the featured offer on its own product page. Most organizations are built for the first and are only beginning to notice the second.

There is a real choice in how to respond, and both sides have merit. A brand can join the marketplace itself, list the items the store buyer does not carry, and compete for the featured offer on its own pages. That brings control of content and price, and it also brings the work of fulfillment, customer service and a second relationship with Walmart that the buyer may not welcome. Or a brand can stay out and police its pages through its distribution, limiting who can buy its products to resell. Many will end up doing some of both. The mistake is doing neither.

Questions to put to the team before December

  • Who at our company looks at our top 20 items on Walmart.com every week, and what would they do if a reseller held the featured offer?
  • Do we know how many sellers are offering our products on Walmart.com, and where they are buying them?
  • Should we sell on Walmart’s marketplace ourselves, for the items the store buyer does not carry?

Running Walmart.com as its own channel, alongside the store business rather than inside it, is the Walmart work we do with brands.

P0486.crumb: Q4 deal planning: the second peak needs a…
P0486.title: Q4 deal planning: the second peak needs a shallower discount
P0486.alt: Two sliced sponge cakes on wooden cake stands with plates, a cut slice and fruit on a rustic table by a window.
P0486.ttag: Q4 deal planning: the second peak needs a shallower discount | Kwontified
P0486.desc: Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November sell to the same shoppers. The second deal buys fewer extra units, so on most products it should be shallower.
P0486.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 24, 2020.
P0486.body:
Amazon’s Black Friday Deals Week opened on Friday, November 20 and runs through Black Friday, November 27, five weeks after a Prime Day held on October 13 and 14. For most brands that means the same hero products are being discounted twice in one quarter, to many of the same shoppers. The usual instinct is to repeat whatever depth worked in October. On most products that is the wrong call, because the second deal buys far fewer extra sales for the same giveaway.

Q4 deal planning in 2020 has to start from a simple point: every discount does two things. It wins buyers who would not have bought at full price, and it hands the same discount to buyers who would have. The first is the point of the deal; the second is its cost. In October the first effect was large. By late November, a good share of the shoppers a deal would have won have already bought.

Why repeating Prime Day’s depth feels right

The case for repeating the deal is not foolish. Prime Day 2020 worked: Amazon said its third-party sellers sold more than $3.5 billion over the two days, nearly 60% more than in 2019. A brand that ran 20% off and saw its best two days of the year has a tested number in hand. Black Friday is the bigger shopping moment. And retailers are pushing depth everywhere, with Walmart running Black Friday events online from November 4 and Target changing its “Black Friday Now” deals every week of November.

All of that is true. What it leaves out is who is left to buy. Adobe’s pre-season survey found a record 33% of consumers planning to finish their holiday shopping by Black Friday, and it forecast $56 billion of online sales in the first 22 days of November alone. Many of the shoppers a Black Friday deal is meant to win have already been won, at Prime Day or in the November events.

The arithmetic of the second deal

Take a $50 product that earns a $20 margin at full price.

At Prime Day, it would have sold 300 units over the two days without a deal. At 20% off, a $10 discount, it sold 1,000. Profit with the deal was $10,000 (1,000 units at $10); without it, $6,000 (300 at $20). The deal added $4,000, because 700 extra buyers more than paid for the discount given to the 300 who would have bought anyway.

At Black Friday the baseline is higher, say 400 units over the same span, and the pool of persuadable shoppers is smaller.

The same 20% deal sells 800. Profit is $8,000 either way: 800 at $10 with the deal, 400 at $20 without. The deal adds 400 units and nothing else. A 10% deal, $5 off, sells 600 units at a $15 margin, $9,000, and beats both. It wins only 200 extra buyers, but it gives away half as much to the 400 who were coming anyway.

Same product, same price, five weeks apart, and the best depth halved. The units each deal brings in are a pleasant number to report. Profit after the giveaway is the one that pays the bills.

What the deal report will not tell you

All of this turns on the baseline, the units a product would have sold without the deal, and no retailer report shows it. A deal dashboard reports units sold during the deal. It cannot say how many of them were coming anyway, or how many were borrowed from the weeks after.

Estimate it before the deal runs, not after. A workable method is the average daily sales of the two weeks before and the two weeks after the event, excluding other promotions, with stockout days removed. For Prime Day 2020 that comparison is now available: the weeks after October 14 show whether the deal added sales or only moved them. If a product’s late-October sales sagged below its September run rate, part of the Prime Day spike was borrowed, and the true lift was smaller than the dashboard said. That product’s Black Friday deal should be shallower still.

The cost can reach back to earlier buyers

A deeper late deal can also cost money on sales already made. Target’s price adjustment policy lets shoppers who bought a “Black Friday Now” item from November 1 claim the difference if Target lowers the price again before December 24. Who funds those adjustments depends on the promotional terms a brand agreed with Target, and many teams have not checked. If the brand pays, a deeper Black Friday price on an item that ran earlier in November is also a refund on every earlier sale.

Rules for the second peak

  • Work out each product’s break-even multiple: margin divided by margin after the discount. A $10 discount on a $20 margin pays only if it more than doubles units over the baseline. Check October’s multiple against that line, and expect Black Friday’s to be lower.
  • Run the deepest Black Friday discounts on products that skipped Prime Day, where the pool of persuadable shoppers is still full.
  • Check every retailer’s price adjustment and price-match terms, and who funds them, before setting a deeper price than an earlier event.
  • Keep advertising and deal depth in the same decision. A shallower deal with steady ads often beats a deep deal that needs no ads, because the ad spend reaches new shoppers while the discount mostly reaches old ones.

The trade-off is real: a shallower deal will post fewer units, and someone will ask why Black Friday looked smaller than Prime Day. The answer is in the margin column, and building that answer product by product is part of how we plan retail media and promotions together.

P0487.title: Marketplace data shows demand weeks before purchase orders do
P0487.alt: A brass rooster weathervane on a chimney above old clay roof tiles, with countryside under a blue sky.
P0487.ttag: Marketplace data shows demand weeks before purchase orders do | Kwontified
P0487.desc: Wholesale orders show what buyers decided. The marketplace team sees what shoppers did, often weeks earlier. In 2020 that gap decided who had stock.
P0487.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 25, 2020.
P0487.body:
In the first half of March, two parts of many consumer brands were looking at the same shoppers and seeing opposite things. The marketplace team, watching Amazon every day, saw searches and sales for anything to do with cleaning, health and staying home climb by the hour; Nielsen later put hand sanitizer sales up 470% in the week ending March 7. The wholesale team, watching purchase orders, saw something else entirely.

On March 17 Amazon told vendors it had temporarily paused ordering of products that were not household staples, medical supplies or other high-demand goods. A Cleveland Research survey the next day found that more than 60% of vendors selling non-essential products had seen a dramatic drop in orders.

Both teams were right about what they saw. Only one of them was looking at demand, and it was the one holding marketplace data. The marketplace team saw what shoppers did; the order book showed what a retailer decided. In many brands, it is the order book that runs the planning meeting.

Purchase orders measure a buyer’s decision, not a shopper’s

The purchase order has been the heartbeat of consumer brands for generations, and for good reason: it is firm, it is dated, it turns into revenue. Planning teams forecast from it because it is the number that pays.

But an order is a retailer’s decision about its own inventory, shaped by its warehouse space, its cash, its forecasts and, in March, its priorities. When Amazon paused orders for non-essentials, it said nothing about whether shoppers wanted those products. When grocery-store sales jumped 27% in March as households stocked up, the orders that followed told brands how much the retailers wanted to rebuild their shelves, not how much shoppers would keep buying once the cupboards were full. Orders arrive later than demand and carry the retailer’s own guesses on top of it.

The marketplace team already has the shopper’s signal

A brand that sells directly on Amazon or Walmart.com sees something no wholesale account shows: each shopper’s order, the day it happens. Since February 2019, brand owners registered with Amazon’s Brand Registry have also had Brand Analytics, whose search terms report shows how customers find their products and their competitors’ and ranks each term by search frequency, ChannelX reported at launch. Add conversion rates, reviews and stockout days, and the marketplace team holds a running record of what shoppers want, by product and by week.

That record is getting larger. Independent sellers, which includes brands selling under their own names, made up 54% of the units Amazon shipped in the third quarter. For a brand that sells this way, every one of those units is a shopper’s order it can see the day it happens.

Why the signal stops at the e-commerce team

Look at who sits in the monthly sales and operations planning meeting at a typical mid-sized brand. Demand planning brings a forecast built from customer orders by account. Sales brings the big accounts. Finance brings the plan. The marketplace team, if it is there at all, brings one line: e-commerce sales against target.

That single line is where the signal gets lost. A total tells the room whether the channel hit its number. It does not tell them that searches for a product’s category doubled in three weeks, that a competitor went out of stock and the brand’s conversion rate jumped, or that reviews started mentioning a use nobody planned for. Those are demand signals, and they arrive at the team least connected to the factory.

This is not a failure of the people involved. It is a reporting line. E-commerce teams were often set up as a sales channel, measured on revenue and advertising return, and placed beside the wholesale accounts rather than inside planning. The structure made sense when online was a small slice. It makes less sense when the online slice is where the company first sees what its customers are doing.

In 2021 the order book should confirm, not lead

The evidence so far leans toward the shift being lasting: shoppers who learned to buy staples, beauty and apparel online in 2020 are unlikely to all go back, and the retailers’ own investments point the same way. If so, the brands that plan best in 2021 will be the ones that treat marketplace data as the early read on demand and the purchase order as the confirmation, rather than the other way round.

That does not mean letting one Amazon week rewrite the production plan. Marketplace data is noisy, and a spike driven by a competitor’s stockout or a single ad push is not a trend. It means the marketplace team brings evidence, not just a total, and the planning meeting has a way to weigh it.

In practice that can be modest. A one-page read each month: the five search terms that moved most, the products whose conversion rate changed by more than a set threshold, the stockouts and their causes, and anything new in the reviews. Ten minutes of the meeting, before the order forecast is discussed, so the room hears what shoppers did before it hears what buyers decided.

Questions for the next planning meeting

  • Does the marketplace team attend sales and operations planning, and does it bring signals or only a sales total?
  • Which three search terms for our category moved most in the last eight weeks, and did anyone outside e-commerce see them?
  • When shopper demand and retailer orders disagree, whose number wins, and why?
  • Who in the company would have noticed first if demand for our best seller doubled next month?

Running the marketplace channel so its data reaches the people who plan the business is the channel management work we do with brands.

P0490.crumb: Amazon search ranking after a stockout is…
P0490.title: Amazon search ranking after a stockout is won back from a rival
P0490.alt: A wooden chessboard with a few pieces in play on a rustic table beside a book, glasses and a pencil cup.
P0490.ttag: Amazon search ranking after a stockout is won back from a rival | Kwontified
P0490.desc: A stockout does not just pause your Amazon search rank. It hands your sales history to the product that sold in your place, and that is what you must outsell.
P0490.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 1, 2020.
P0490.body:
The restock lands on a Tuesday, the listing goes live again, and the product that sat third for its main search term a month ago now sits on page two. The units are back. The rank is not. Every brand that ran out of something during Cyber Week will see some version of this in December, and the usual reading is that Amazon is punishing the stockout.

It is a different problem, and a slower one. Amazon search rank is earned relative to the other products competing for the same search, and while your product was gone, one of them took your sales. Amazon search ranking after a stockout comes back only when you outsell that rival again, which means the recovery clock depends on its new sales history as much as on your restock date.

Why the stockout looks like a penalty

The belief has a reasonable basis. Amazon’s own Seller Central guidance names the factors behind search placement: degree of text match, price, availability, selection and sales history, as Search Engine Journal quoted it in its explainer. Availability is on that list, so a product with no stock should fall, and it does.

What brands notice is that the fall outlasts the stockout. A product out for two weeks can take longer than two weeks to climb back, and that lag feels like a fine for having been absent. Research from Profitero, published by The Grocer in November, found that a product out of stock for two days or more took an average of 9–10 days to recover its search placement on Amazon.co.uk and Tesco.com. Ten days to recover from two days away looks like punishment.

Rank is measured against the products that sold in your place

The lag has a plainer cause. The same Search Engine Journal piece makes the point that sales velocity on Amazon is relative to the competition for the same search term, and that conversion drives it. Rank is a comparison. Your product does not hold a score; it holds a position against the products a shopper could have bought instead.

During a stockout the shoppers do not disappear. They search, find your listing unavailable or missing, and buy the next product down. That product’s sales rise, and with them its standing for your keyword. When you return, the comparison has changed on both sides: your recent sales are at zero, and your rival’s are higher than they have ever been.

Take a set of bamboo sheets that sold 140 units a week on its main keyword, against 100 for the product ranked just below it. The sheets go out of stock for two weeks over Cyber Week, and the rival picks up half the lost demand, selling 170 a week. Say the ranking weighs the last four weeks of sales (Amazon publishes no window; four weeks keeps the arithmetic simple).

Weeks since the restockYour last four weeksRival’s last four weeks
0 (restock day)280540
1280540
2280540
3420470
4560400

The table assumes demand splits back the way it was the day you return: you sell 140 a week again and the rival falls back to 100. Even then, you trail for three full weeks and pass the rival only in week four, when the stockout weeks finally drop out of its record. In practice the split does not snap back. The rival now ranks above you, so it gets more of the clicks, and you return with fewer than 140 sales a week. Week four becomes week five or six.

The rival did nothing wrong, and neither did Amazon. A ranking system that rewards what shoppers bought in the last few weeks will hand your position to whoever served your customers while you could not. The penalty people feel is simply the record of those sales.

A 9–10 day average hides a wide spread

Profitero’s 9–10 days is a useful benchmark, and it is an average across products. The arithmetic says the spread around it should be wide. A product whose shoppers had no close substitute loses little to any one rival and recovers quickly. A product in a crowded search, where one competitor absorbed most of the demand, faces a rival with a strong new record and recovers slowly. The length of the stockout matters, but so does how concentrated your lost sales became.

Two numbers tell you which case you are in. Check the Brand Analytics search terms report for your main keywords and see which product gained click share while you were out. Then compare that product’s best sellers rank before and during your stockout. A rival that jumped tells you where your sales went and how big a lead you have to close.

Pulling ads while out of stock adds to the hole. Agencies warned in Modern Retail during the March stockouts, when Amazon had limited FBA inbound shipments to essentials, that stopping Amazon ads entirely could hurt rankings and future performance. Ads cannot serve an unavailable product, but they can keep its sibling sizes and colors selling, and they can be ready on restock day.

Buying the rank back

The useful response is to treat the first weeks after a restock as a separate campaign with its own budget, priced against the sales history you need to rebuild rather than the ACoS target you use in a normal month.

In the sheets example, closing the gap two weeks sooner is worth two extra weeks at the top position, and the sales that come with it. That makes it reasonable to accept a higher ACoS on the main keywords for the first two or three weeks, as long as the extra spend is smaller than the margin on the sales the earlier recovery brings back. Set that ceiling before the restock, not after a week of disappointing reports.

Sequence matters too. Turn Sponsored Products back on for the restocked product on the day inventory is live, and bid on the keywords where the rival gained most. Keep any deal or coupon modest, so the price you train the market to expect is not one you cannot hold in January.

The rule of thumb: a stockout’s cost is the lost sales plus the weeks it takes to outsell the product that took them. Budget for both, and judge the recovery spend against that second number. It is the kind of restock plan we build into Amazon advertising whenever inventory and ads sit with the same team.

P0492.crumb: Price gouging on Amazon put brand names…
P0492.title: Price gouging on Amazon put brand names on prices they never set
P0492.alt: A corked stoneware bottle with a large blank tag beside potted dried flowers on a linen-covered table by a pink wall.
P0492.ttag: Price gouging on Amazon put brand names on prices they never set | Kwontified
P0492.desc: In 2020’s price-gouging scare, shoppers read the brand on the bottle before the seller in small type, so brands carried the trust cost of prices set by others.
P0492.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 3, 2020.
P0492.body:
Search for disinfecting wipes on Amazon last March and the first thing on the page was a name you knew, in large type: the brand on the canister. The price sat just below it, often well above what the supermarket charged before the shortage. The business that set that price appeared further down, in small type next to “Sold by.” Most shoppers never read that line. So when prices jumped in the spring, who did they think was charging them?

The page answers for them. On a marketplace the brand owns the listing but not the offer, and in 2020 the gap between the two became a trust problem. Price gouging on Amazon was the work of some sellers, but it was read through the brand names on the products, and brands that had no say over who sold their goods paid for prices they never set.

What shoppers saw in the spring

The extremes were real. Some third-party sellers raised prices on masks, sanitizer and other essentials by as much as 1,000%, and 33 state attorneys general pressed Amazon to act, Modern Retail recounted in November. Amazon said it had removed more than 500,000 offers and suspended 6,000 selling accounts for violating its pricing policies since the pandemic began, Bloomberg reported in June.

What a shopper took from those weeks was less a list of bad sellers than a feeling about the products. A canister of wipes belongs, in the shopper’s mind, to the brand that made it. The price on the page is read as the brand’s price, and the shortage behind it is read as the brand’s shortage. Few shoppers in a hurry stop to separate the company that made the canister from the company that listed it.

This mattered more in 2020 than it would have a year earlier, because trust itself moved up the list of reasons people buy. In Edelman’s brand trust survey, fielded in late May and early June across 11 countries, trust ranked as the second most important factor in buying a new brand, at 53%, behind only price and affordability, O’Dwyer’s reported. A year earlier it had ranked fifth. Some 40% of respondents said they had stopped using a brand that did not act appropriately during the pandemic.

The aisle emptied of the careful sellers first

The less obvious part of the story is who stayed on the shelf. Amazon’s enforcement arrived as automated warnings through March and April that threatened removal but did not say what price Amazon considered fair, according to the Bloomberg report. State rules added to the confusion: some set a threshold such as 10% above normal prices, others used words like “unconscionable,” and a marketplace seller sets one national price without knowing where the buyer lives.

Faced with that, many legitimate merchants simply stopped selling the products most likely to trigger a warning. One seller with six years on Amazon removed about 100 items, including hand sanitizer and toilet paper, though most had not gone up in price that year. Reinstating a suspended account can take weeks or months, so pulling the product looked safer than risking the business. Bloomberg’s reporting concluded that the crackdown made shortages of sanitizer and wipes worse, though no one can say by how much.

Read Amazon as an institution and its choice makes sense. It answers to shoppers and regulators, it runs millions of offers, and an algorithm that errs toward removal protects the store’s reputation even when it catches honest sellers. A listing held at the same price for months was sometimes flagged, a consultant told Modern Retail. The cost of those errors fell on sellers, and through them on brands: the merchants most careful about their accounts left the aisle first, and the offers that remained came from whoever was willing to take the risk.

So the brand’s shelf space was filled, during the weeks shoppers were paying closest attention, by the sellers least worried about losing it.

Who sets the price your shoppers see

The brands that came through with their trust intact tended to share one trait: they knew who was selling their products and at what price. A brand that sells to Amazon as a vendor, or sells as the main third-party seller itself, sets or negotiates the offer that most shoppers see. A brand that leaves its products to a loose group of resellers has handed that decision to people whose priorities in a shortage are not its own.

The value at stake is the customer relationship, and it moves to whoever controls the offer. Amazon kept the shopper; it removed the offers and protected its store. The reseller kept the margin while it lasted. The brand kept its name on the page and, with it, the shopper’s memory of what that page charged.

None of this is over. Amazon called on Congress in May to pass a federal price-gouging law, saying the patchwork of state rules is a challenge for retailers, and its pricing algorithms are usually busiest in the holiday season. A second wave of panic buying this winter would test the same structure again.

Questions to put to the team before the next shortage

  • Who sold our 20 best-selling products on Amazon in March and April, and at what prices relative to our list price?
  • Which products did we, or our authorized sellers, pull from the shelf to avoid a warning, and who filled the gap?
  • If demand spikes again this winter, which of our offers do we control directly, and which depend on a reseller’s judgment?
  • Does anyone in the company own the price a shopper sees on a marketplace, or only the price we charge our customers?

The last question is usually the one with no clear owner, and it is the one shoppers answered for brands in 2020. Deciding who sells your products, and on what terms, is part of running the Amazon channel day to day rather than a legal clean-up after the fact.

P0493.crumb: Cyber Week 2020 grew 21%, and the rest of…
P0493.title: Cyber Week 2020 grew 21%, and the rest of November grew faster
P0493.alt: A row of wrapped gifts growing in size, tied with twine and fabric, along a wooden table by a teal wall.
P0493.ttag: Cyber Week 2020 grew 21%, and the rest of November grew faster | Kwontified
P0493.desc: Cyber Week 2020 landed at the bottom of the forecasts while November as a whole grew about 31%. The gap is demand that moved, which changes how to grade it.
P0493.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 8, 2020.
P0493.body:
Every forecast for the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday came in high. Adobe had expected $10 billion of US online sales on Black Friday and $12.7 billion on Cyber Monday. The days delivered $9.0 billion and $10.8 billion, and Digital Commerce 360 put growth over the five days at 20.6%, “slower than expected.” Read on its own, Cyber Week 2020 missed.

Read against the month, it did not. From November 1 through Cyber Monday, Adobe counted $106.5 billion of online spending, about 31% more than the same stretch in 2019. The days outside the peak grew faster than the peak itself. Most of what the five days lacked had already been sold earlier in November, and that changes how brands should grade their own event.

Cyber Week 2020 against the forecasts

MeasureForecast before the eventResult
Black Friday (Adobe)$10 billion, up 39%$9.0 billion, up 21.6%
Cyber Monday (Adobe)$12.7 billion, up 35%$10.8 billion, up 15.1%
Thanksgiving to Cyber MondayMy November 10 forecast: +20% conservative, +35% standard, +47% reach$34.4 billion, up about 21%
November 1 to Cyber Monday—$106.5 billion, against $81.5 billion in 2019
Season, November 1 to December 31 (Adobe)$189 billion, up 33%Forecast cut to $184 billion, up 30%

The day-level figures come from Adobe Analytics as reported by CNBC on December 1 and from Adobe’s October forecast. The month-to-date total is from Fox Business, the 2019 comparison from CNBC’s 2019 report, and the five-day growth rate from Digital Commerce 360.

My own forecast belongs on the scorecard. It set the market’s five days at three cases and argued that a brand’s peak would grow less than the headline because early events had already sold part of it. The market landed almost exactly on the conservative case. The advice to commit ad spend to that case and hold the rest in reserve held up; the advice to stock to the standard case left inventory above what the five days needed, which December can still sell.

Where the missing peak sales went

Take the November 1 to Cyber Monday totals and remove the five peak days from each year. In 2019 that leaves about $53.0 billion across 27 days. In 2020 it leaves about $72.1 billion across 25 days, up roughly 36% with two fewer days in the window. The peak grew 21%. The weeks before it grew faster.

That is what a redistributed event looks like in the data. Retailers spent November telling shoppers not to wait. Amazon’s Holiday Dash deals began on October 15, the day after Prime Day, Amazon said. Walmart ran three Black Friday events, starting online on November 4. CNBC’s December 1 report noted that shoppers began gift buying earlier than ever and retailers spread deals out to avoid crowded stores.

Had the five days grown at the 36% rate of the rest of the month, they would have brought in about $38.8 billion instead of $34.4 billion. That $4.4 billion gap is a rough ceiling on what the peak lost to earlier days. Adobe’s season forecast tells the same story from the other side: it fell only from 33% growth to 30%. The holiday is still growing at about the rate Adobe expected. Its biggest days are not.

Why the five-day number still gets the attention

Precise numbers feel like answers, and the five-day total is the most precise number of the season. It arrives the morning after Cyber Monday, it has a forecast to beat, and it maps neatly onto the way brands have always planned the event: a deal calendar, an ad budget and an inventory build aimed at five days. Grading those five days in isolation is the natural pull. It is also how a brand that sold well all November convinces itself that Cyber Week failed.

The opposite error is just as easy. A brand whose five days beat plan may simply have run fewer early promotions, so its shoppers waited. Without the weeks on either side, the two cases look the same.

None of this says the peak was soft for everyone. Amazon said independent sellers sold more than $4.8 billion worldwide from Black Friday through Cyber Monday, up more than 60%, far faster than Adobe’s 21% for US online sales. That figure covers only third-party sellers and a worldwide market, so it does not compare directly, but it is a reminder that a market average hides a wide range of results.

How to grade your own Cyber Week 2020

Use the same arithmetic on your own numbers, and keep the question narrow: how much did the season grow because of the event, not how big was the spike.

  1. Total your sales from October 13, the start of Prime Day, through December 31, and compare them with your pre-season forecast for the same window. That is the number the deal budget should be judged against, and it will not be final until January.
  2. Split November into the five peak days and the rest. If the rest grew faster than the peak, your shoppers moved; if both grew slowly, demand was weak.
  3. Compare products that ran early deals with products that did not. A gap between the two groups at the peak is the clearest read you will get on how much your own promotions borrowed from the five days.
  4. Check ad efficiency the same way. Cost per sale on the five days against the early-November weeks shows whether the peak clicks were worth their price in 2020.

The rule of thumb: credit an event with the sales still there when the season closes, and measure the season from the first deal to the last delivery. Building that window before the next tentpole is the measurement work we do with brands when the budget for it is still open.

P0495.title: Cyber Week 2020 exposed holiday budgets still built for five days
P0495.alt: Five small glass jars filled with coins on a reclaimed wood shelf against a teal wall near snowy windows.
P0495.ttag: Cyber Week 2020 exposed holiday budgets still built for five days | Kwontified
P0495.desc: The 2020 holiday ran from Prime Day in October to Christmas, but most brands’ deal funding, stock and approvals were still organized around one weekend.
P0495.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 10, 2020.
P0495.body:
Open most brands’ 2020 operating plans and the holiday is a single line: a promotional budget, an inventory build and an advertising plan, all pointed at the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday. The plans were written in the autumn of 2019, when that was a reasonable description of the season. By the time Thanksgiving arrived in 2020, the retailers had been running the holiday for six weeks.

That gap is what Cyber Week 2020 revealed. The market did not disappoint; it spread out. What struggled to keep up was the internal calendar many brands use to approve deals, release inventory and fund advertising, which still assumed one peak weekend. The lesson concerns the planning cycle more than the shopper.

The holiday arrived on four calendars

Each large retailer set its own start. Amazon’s Holiday Dash deals began on October 15, the day after Prime Day, Amazon said on December 1. Target ran “Black Friday Now” deals every week from November 1, it announced in October. Walmart’s first Black Friday event opened online on November 4, the Associated Press reported. Adobe stopped calling the period Cyber Week at all and forecast “Cyber Months”.

Shoppers followed the calendars. Adobe counted $106.5 billion of US online spending from November 1 through Cyber Monday, Fox Business reported, about 31% more than the same stretch of 2019, while the five peak days grew by about 21%.

The weekend itself drew fewer people: the National Retail Federation counted 186.4 million shoppers over Thanksgiving weekend, down from 189.6 million a year earlier, Talk Business & Politics reported. And Adobe trimmed its forecast for the whole season only modestly, from 33% growth to 30%. The holiday held up. Its center of gravity moved.

Why the brand’s calendar did not move with it

A brand’s holiday is not one decision but a chain of them, and each link belongs to a different team. Finance sets the promotional budget in the annual plan, usually as a figure for November and December. Sales or e-commerce negotiates which retailer events the brand joins. Supply chain commits the inventory build weeks in advance. The advertising budget is often a separate line again, owned by marketing or an agency.

The store calendar trained everyone in that sequence. A holiday endcap is planned months ahead, set by a merchandising crew in the week before the event and left in place until it sells through, so the decisions behind it can be made slowly and in order. A marketplace deal works on a different clock. It is a price and an allocation of units that a retailer schedules into a specific week, alongside thousands of other brands’ deals, and once the week passes the slot is gone. Brands spent 2020 running the second kind of event with the approval process built for the first.

When the season was one weekend, those links could move in sequence and still meet at Thanksgiving. In 2020 the first decision was due in early October, when a brand had to decide whether to fund an Amazon deal for a week that its plan still called the fourth quarter’s quiet start. The Walmart and Target events followed every week through November, each needing a funded price and stock in the right place. A brand whose approvals run on a monthly finance cycle could not answer four retailers on four schedules. In many cases the answer defaulted to whatever was already approved, which was the Black Friday plan.

The cost of that default showed up in two places. Brands that held their deal funding for Black Friday spent it into the slowest-growing days of the season. Brands that joined the early events without moving inventory found their best sellers short by Thanksgiving, and the market numbers say Thanksgiving no longer carried the season anyway. Neither outcome was a failure of the people involved. It was a calendar built for a season that no longer exists.

The retailer’s calendar is now the one that matters

It is worth reading the retailers as institutions here. Retailers spread their deals partly to keep crowds out of stores, as CNBC noted after Cyber Monday, and Amazon’s season simply continued from an October Prime Day. Some of those reasons belong to the pandemic and will fade. The incentive underneath will not. A retailer that sells more over eight weeks than over five days, with less strain on its stores and carriers, has little reason to go back.

It is too early to say how much of the 2020 pattern survives into 2021, and the date of the next Prime Day will shape it. The evidence so far leans toward a season that starts with the first major retailer event and runs to the last shipping day, with several retailers setting their own peaks inside it. A brand’s internal calendar should be built to that shape.

Questions for the 2021 holiday plan

  • On what date was our 2020 holiday deal funding approved, and how much of it was spent before Thanksgiving?
  • Who in the company can commit a funded price to a retailer event on two weeks’ notice, and does that person also control the inventory to support it?
  • Is our holiday inventory plan set by week and by retailer, or still as a single build for the peak?
  • What will our 2021 plan call “the holiday,” and which retailer’s calendar did we use to decide?

The first question usually reveals the answer to the rest. Bringing deal funding, stock and advertising onto one weekly calendar per retailer is part of running the marketplace channel day to day, and it is easiest to change while the 2021 plan is still a draft.

P0497.title: 2021 Amazon ROAS targets built on 2020 will cut the wrong ads
P0497.alt: A cut flowering branch and red-handled pruning shears on a weathered bench beside a potted pink-flowered shrub.
P0497.ttag: 2021 Amazon ROAS targets built on 2020 will cut the wrong ads | Kwontified
P0497.desc: ROAS is a ratio of conversion rate to click price, and 2020 moved both for reasons that had nothing to do with your ads. Plan 2021 bids from click value.
P0497.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 15, 2020.
P0497.body:
The 2021 planning deck is being built this month, and most Amazon advertising sections in it will open with one number: the ROAS the account achieved in 2020. It will look good. For many accounts it will be the best year on record, and the natural move is to carry it forward as next year’s target and cut whatever falls short.

That target will be wrong, and in a predictable direction. Return on ad spend is not a property of an ad. It is a ratio of two things the advertiser does not fully control, the conversion rate and the price of a click, and 2020 pushed both in the advertiser’s favor for reasons that had little to do with the ads. Amazon ROAS targets for 2021 should be rebuilt from those two inputs, keyword by keyword, rather than inherited as a single number.

Cheap clicks and eager shoppers inflated 2020’s ROAS

ROAS on Sponsored Products is sales divided by spend. Break it down and it becomes product price, times the share of clicks that convert, divided by the cost per click. The price usually holds steady through a year. The other two did not.

Click prices fell sharply in the spring. In the last week of March the typical Amazon advertiser was spending half as much per day as in January, Merkle data showed, as Digiday reported. Over the second quarter, Sponsored Products clicks rose 107% from a year earlier while the average cost per click fell 41%, according to Merkle’s quarterly report summarized by Karooya. Fewer advertisers bidding meant cheaper clicks, whatever the ads themselves were doing.

Conversion moved too, for reasons on the shopper’s side. Online demand jumped: US e-commerce sales were 44.5% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier, and 36.7% higher in the third, the Census Bureau reported in November. Shoppers arriving on Amazon with a need and fewer alternatives convert at a higher rate on any given click.

Then the auction refilled. By the third quarter the Sponsored Products cost per click was only about 8% below 2019, and Sponsored Brands clicks cost 16% more, Merkle’s next report showed, per Karooya. The cheap spring was a passing condition.

The arithmetic of an inherited target

Take a $40 product on a keyword where, in 2019, a click cost $1.00 and 10% of clicks converted. Every dollar of spend bought one click, and every ten clicks bought one $40 sale, so ROAS was 4.0.

PeriodCost per clickConversion rateROAS
2019$1.0010%4.0
Spring 2020$0.5912%8.1
Q3 2020$0.9211%4.8
2021, if both return to 2019$1.0010%4.0

The click prices follow Merkle’s averages (41% and 8% below 2019). The conversion rates are assumptions for this scenario, chosen to show a modest lift that fades.

Average the year and the keyword reports something near 6. Set that as the 2021 target and, the moment click prices and conversion settle back to 2019 levels, the keyword shows 4.0 and fails. Nothing about the ad, the listing or the keyword has changed. The team cuts it anyway, along with every other keyword whose 2020 numbers were flattered by the same two forces, and the cuts fall hardest on the high-volume generic terms that were cheapest in the spring.

The opposite mistake is available too. A team that sees ROAS falling in early 2021 may read it as the ads getting worse and raise bids to chase volume, when the decline is the market returning. Both errors come from treating ROAS as a measure of the ad rather than as a ratio of two market prices.

Where 2020 still tells you something

Throwing 2020 away would cost something. The year produced the largest sample of clicks most accounts have ever had, and some of what it showed is durable: which keywords convert at all, which products sell without a deal, which search terms were never worth bidding on. Discarding that because the averages are distorted would waste the best data the account owns.

The way through is to keep the ranking and drop the level. Use 2020 to rank keywords against each other, since the spring’s cheap clicks and eager shoppers lifted most terms together. Then set the level of each bid from current inputs: the latest four to six weeks of conversion rate, the product’s price, and the share of that price the brand can spend on advertising.

A 2021 bid plan that survives the comparison

Express each target as the most a click is worth, not as a ROAS. In the example, a brand that can spend 25% of a $40 price on advertising can afford $10 per sale. At a 10% conversion rate that is $1.00 a click; at 12% it is $1.20. The bid moves with conversion, and nobody has to explain to finance why ROAS fell when the bid was right all along.

Report ROAS alongside cost per click and conversion rate, every month, so that a falling ratio can be traced to the input that moved. If cost per click rose and conversion held, the auction got busier. If conversion fell at a steady click price, look at the listing, the stock position or the price.

Budget for the auction you expect, not the one you had. With the third quarter already near 2019 click prices and Sponsored Brands above them, a 2021 plan that assumes spring 2020 prices will run out of budget by mid-year.

The rule of thumb: a ROAS target is only as good as the click price and conversion rate it assumes, so write those two numbers down next to it. Setting next year’s bids from click value rather than last year’s ratio is how we plan Amazon advertising for brands going into January.

P0498.title: Marketplaces in 2020 became the default retail model worldwide
P0498.alt: A cobbled old-town street lined with awning-covered market stalls selling produce, textiles and pottery.
P0498.ttag: Marketplaces in 2020 became the default retail model worldwide | Kwontified
P0498.desc: In 2020 Amazon, Walmart, Zalando, Mercado Libre and even Google and Facebook grew by letting others sell. Brands still decide marketplace by marketplace.
P0498.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 17, 2020.
P0498.body:
A decade ago, getting a product onto a big retailer’s shelf meant persuading a buyer. The buyer chose the assortment, placed the order and decided, in effect, who would sell the brand to that retailer’s customers. Amazon’s marketplace was the exception to that rule, a store where anyone who met the terms could list. By the end of 2020, it had become the rule.

Across the US, Europe and Latin America, the retailers that grew fastest in 2020 did it largely by letting other businesses sell to their shoppers. The marketplace became the default way large retailers add selection, and that changes a question brands used to settle one buyer at a time: who sells our products, and where. In 2020 that question was increasingly answered by sellers enrolling themselves.

The same move on three continents

Amazon is the furthest along. Third-party sellers accounted for 54% of the units it sold in the third quarter, and its revenue from seller services rose 55% to $20.4 billion, Amazon reported in October.

Walmart spent 2020 widening its door. In June it made Shopify its first commerce platform partner, letting Shopify’s US merchants apply to sell on Walmart.com, and the company expected to add 1,200 of them in 2020, Talk Business & Politics reported.

In Europe, Zalando’s Partner Program, in which brands sell their own stock on Zalando’s site, more than doubled its sales volume in the second quarter, and about 180 new partners joined between April and June, Zalando said in July. At the end of 2019 the program had been 15% of Zalando’s fashion store volume, according to its annual results.

In Latin America, Mercado Libre’s gross merchandise volume reached $5.9 billion in the third quarter, up 62.1% in dollars and 117.1% on a currency-neutral basis, its results showed in November.

And the companies that were never retailers joined in. In April Google made it free for merchants to list in its Shopping tab. In May Facebook launched Shops, a free storefront across Facebook and Instagram. Each lowered the cost for any seller to put a product in front of shoppers.

How the buyer’s decision moved to the seller

It helps to remember how the old arrangement worked. Under wholesale, a brand’s distribution policy was enforced at the buyer’s desk: if the brand did not sell to a retailer, the retailer did not carry the product. Brands that wanted to control their image or their pricing could do it by choosing accounts.

A marketplace removes that checkpoint. A product can appear on Walmart.com, Zalando or Mercado Libre because a distributor, a reseller or a former wholesale customer chose to list it, with or without the brand’s involvement. The retailer’s own interest is selection and price, and in 2020 more sellers meant both. The brand’s interest is consistency: one price position, one set of images and claims, and a supply chain it can plan.

The difference is visible on the page. Walk through a department store and the brand’s distribution choices are on display: the products are there because a buyer ordered them, at the price the retailer set, beside the fixtures the brand helped pay for.

Open the same product on a marketplace and the page is assembled differently. The title and images may come from whichever seller created the listing first, the price from whichever offer is winning that hour. The seller who ships the order may be a business the brand has never dealt with. The shelf still carries the brand’s name, but the brand no longer decides who stands behind it.

The structure inside most brands

Most brands’ marketplace decisions are still spread across the organization in the way their wholesale business grew up. The Amazon account sits with a US e-commerce team. Walmart.com may sit with the Walmart store account team. Zalando may be run by a European distributor, Mercado Libre by a Latin American one. Each team makes sensible choices for its own retailer, and nobody owns the policy that ties them together: which sellers are authorized where, what price floor applies, who owns the content on each listing.

That arrangement worked when each marketplace was a side door. In 2020 those doors became the main entrances on three continents at once. A brand without a single answer to “who may sell us, where, and on what terms” now has that answer written for it, retailer by retailer, by whoever lists first.

It is too early to know which of 2020’s marketplace programs will matter most to a given brand. Zalando’s model, in which the brand holds the stock, differs sharply from Amazon’s mix of first-party and third-party selling, and Mercado Libre’s growth is measured in currencies that moved hard against the dollar. The evidence leans toward the direction being the same everywhere, even if the pace is not.

Four distribution decisions for the 2021 plan

  • Name one owner for marketplace distribution policy across regions, even if day-to-day operation stays with local teams or distributors.
  • List every marketplace where the brand’s products appeared in 2020, who sold them and at what price, including the ones the brand never chose.
  • Decide which marketplaces the brand will sell on itself, which it will leave to authorized partners, and which it will actively keep resellers off.
  • Agree one content standard, the images, claims and size or ingredient information, that every authorized seller must use.

The first item is the one most brands skip, and it is where the rest start. Bringing those decisions into one place across retailers is part of running the marketplace channel day to day, whether a brand sells on Amazon, Walmart, Zalando or Mercado Libre.

P0499.crumb: Subscribe and Save in a demand surge pays…
P0499.title: Subscribe and Save in a demand surge pays back after it ends
P0499.alt: Wooden crate of glass jars filled with chickpeas beside shelves of jarred grains, lentils and beans.
P0499.ttag: Subscribe and Save in a demand surge pays back after it ends | Kwontified
P0499.desc: When every unit sells anyway, the Subscribe and Save discount looks like wasted margin. It is the price of the customers still ordering after the surge.
P0499.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 22, 2020.
P0499.body:
In March, Amazon told shoppers that some household staples were out of stock and that “delivery promises are longer than usual,” CNBC reported. For brands selling those staples, a different line on the P&L started to look odd. Every unit was selling at full price within days of arriving, yet a share of those units still went out at a Subscribe and Save discount. Why give away margin on a product that would have sold anyway?

Because the discount was never buying that unit. Subscribe and Save pays for a customer who keeps ordering, and in a surge the value of that customer moves out of the current quarter and into the next one. Cutting the discount saves a little margin now. Losing the subscribers costs their future orders, and in 2020 the real choice for most brands was whether scarce stock would last long enough to reach the subscribers.

Why the discount looks like waste

The program’s terms make the cost easy to see. Sellers have funded a discount of 5% per subscription, rising to as much as 15% when a shopper has five or more subscriptions delivered in a month, deducted from the seller’s revenue, ChannelX explained in 2019. In the UK and Germany, Amazon moved in June to enroll eligible items automatically at a 0% base, with sellers choosing to fund 5% or 10% and Amazon funding further discounts on larger deliveries, ChannelX reported. Whatever the level, the discount comes off every subscription unit.

In a normal month that discount is a bet. It costs margin on orders that would have happened anyway, and earns it back on the extra orders a subscription produces. When demand runs ahead of supply, the bet appears to lose on every unit, because no unit needed help to sell. A finance team looking at a sold-out quarter will reasonably ask why the brand is still discounting.

What the subscriber is worth after the surge

The answer depends on what happens to the subscriber when the surge ends. A one-time buyer in a shortage bought whatever was in stock; when supply returns, the shopper goes back to their usual brand or to the cheapest option. A subscriber has set up a recurring order for your product. They are the part of the surge’s demand most likely to still be there in the spring. Their orders are also the easiest to forecast. Few other customers tell you when they will buy next.

Take a $25 household product with $8 of contribution margin per unit and a 10% subscription discount, so a subscription unit earns $5.50 against $8 for a full-price sale. Each subscription unit gives up $2.50. That is the full cost of the program in a shortage. The question is what it buys, and how long the purchase lasts.

Now suppose the brand has stock for 80% of demand through a three-month surge, and must decide whether subscription orders or one-time orders absorb the shortfall. On Amazon the brand cannot earmark units for subscribers, but it can choose whether to keep pulling in one-time buyers with ads, coupons and deals while stock is short. Say a subscriber orders every two months and, if served, stays for another year, six more orders after the surge.

ChoiceMargin given up in the surgeMargin at risk after the surge
Hold stock for subscribers (pause demand generation)$2.50 per subscription unit, against full-price sales not madeNone from subscribers
Sell to whoever arrives firstNoneSix orders at $5.50 = $33 per subscriber who cancels after missed deliveries

The trade-off favors the subscriber unless nearly all of them would stay even after missed deliveries. On these numbers, protecting a subscriber costs $2.50 per order for one or two surge deliveries, about $5 at most, to keep $33 of future margin. A brand would need to believe that fewer than one in six neglected subscribers will cancel before selling to whoever arrives first makes sense.

There is a second cost to running out. Amazon has tied Subscribe and Save eligibility to in-stock performance, at an in-stock rate of 85% or more, according to Tinuiti’s guide to the program. A product that stocks out repeatedly risks losing access to the program altogether, along with every subscriber on it.

Raising price is the costlier way to protect margin

The other instinct in a surge is to raise the list price. Subscribe and Save applies its discount to the price on the day the order is placed, Tinuiti’s guide notes, so a higher list price reaches subscribers too, the customers least likely to comparison-shop. It also carries a policy risk in 2020: Amazon removed more than 500,000 offers for pricing violations during the pandemic, and some state rules treat increases of 10% above typical prices as gouging, Bloomberg reported in June. The margin gained per unit is small next to the subscribers and the listing put at risk.

Running Subscribe and Save through a surge

  • Plan inbound from the subscription forecast first. Amazon’s Subscribe and Save forecasting report shows eight weeks of subscription demand, ChannelX noted, which tells you the minimum stock that must be on hand before any promotion runs.
  • Stop recruiting new subscribers you cannot serve. Pause advertising and coupons aimed at first-time buyers on constrained products, since each new subscription is a promise of future stock.
  • Keep the discount steady. Cutting it during a surge saves a few dollars per unit and signals to subscribers that the deal has changed.
  • Measure the program on retention after the surge, not on margin during it: the share of March subscribers still active in the autumn is the number that shows whether the discount paid.

The rule of thumb: in a shortage, a subscription unit is worth its discount plus every order the subscriber places after supply returns, so protect it first unless you have evidence your subscribers would stay anyway. Planning stock and advertising around that number is part of how we run Amazon accounts for brands in replenishable categories.

P0501.title: E-commerce taught traditional brands every order pays its own way
P0501.alt: Brass balance scale weighing a kraft-paper parcel against a pan of coins on a wooden table.
P0501.ttag: E-commerce taught traditional brands every order pays its own way | Kwontified
P0501.desc: In the store, a cheap item rides home in a full cart. Online it needs its own box, and 2020 showed traditional brands which products could carry that cost.
P0501.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 24, 2020.
P0501.body:
In a supermarket, a bag of chips goes home in a cart with forty other things, and nobody asks whether that one bag paid for the trip. Online, the same bag needs to be picked, packed, boxed and driven to a door on its own. When PepsiCo opened Snacks.com in May, it offered more than 100 Frito-Lay products with free shipping on orders of $15 or more. Its sister site, PantryShop.com, sold Quaker, Gatorade and Tropicana as kits priced at $29.95 and $49.95, PepsiCo said. Why a minimum, and why kits?

Because online the order, not the item, has to make money. That is the lesson the forced test of 2020 taught traditional brands. The store had quietly carried their low-priced products inside a larger basket. When shoppers moved online, the brands that did well were the ones that redesigned what they sold for an order that stands alone, instead of listing their store assortment and hoping.

Everyone moved online at once

The scale of the shift was not in doubt. The online share of US retail reached 16.1% in the second quarter, up from 11.8% in the first, Census Bureau figures show.

Unilever’s online business grew 76% in the third quarter, the company reported in October, while its food service sales fell by more than 20%. Those two numbers sat side by side in one company’s results: the same portfolio losing restaurant volume and gaining online orders within a single quarter, with very different pack and delivery needs on each side. Nike’s digital sales rose 82% in the quarter to August, offsetting lower wholesale revenue, it said in September.

Some of the strain showed exactly where cheap items meet online orders. On March 19, Amazon temporarily closed Prime Pantry, its service for boxes of low-priced household goods, to new orders because of high order volumes, CNBC reported. The service built to make small, inexpensive items worth shipping was among the first to buckle under the rush.

PepsiCo’s sites were a response to the same pressure from the brand side. They went from concept to launch in less than 30 days, the company said. What is telling is not the speed but the design: the company did not simply put its supermarket assortment online. It set a basket threshold on one site and sold bundles on the other.

The pack was designed for the shelf

The reason sits in how traditional brands decide what to sell. Pack sizes, price points and multipacks are usually set by category and brand teams who plan for a shelf: what fits the planogram, what hits a price point a shopper will pick up without thinking, what a retailer’s buyer will take. The e-commerce team typically inherits that assortment. It lists what the store sells, at the sizes the store sells it, because that is what the supply chain makes.

On the shelf, a $4 item is a perfectly good product. In an online order on its own, it is a problem.

Say picking, packing and delivering a single small order costs a brand or its retailer $3. On a $4 item, almost nothing is left for the product, the retailer or the advertising that found the shopper. On a $30 kit, the same $3 is a tenth of the order. The product did not change. The unit that has to carry the cost did. And because the cost lands per order rather than per item, the fix is rarely a price increase on the single item; it is a different thing to sell.

Most brands’ org charts do not have a seat where that decision gets made. The people who own pack architecture think in shelves. The people who own e-commerce were, until 2020, running a channel that was a few percent of sales and could live with the store’s packs. In 2020 the channel stopped being small, and the mismatch moved from a footnote to a margin line.

What the brands that adapted did differently

The adjustments were mostly in the assortment.

Kits and bundles that turn several low-priced items into one order. Multipacks sized for a monthly order rather than a weekly trip. Minimum order values, like Snacks.com’s $15, that make the shopper build the basket the store used to build for them. Subscriptions that make the next order predictable.

None of it is new to brands born online. For traditional brands, 2020 was the year it became urgent.

It is too early to say how much of the year’s online shift will stay once stores are fully open again, and the Census numbers already show some of it easing, with the online share at 14.3% in the third quarter. But the brands that redesigned their online assortment in 2020 did not do it for a single year. A kit that makes money online keeps making money online whether the channel is 14% of retail or 16%.

Questions for the 2021 assortment review

  • Which of our products cannot pay for their own delivery at current online prices, and who decided they should be listed anyway?
  • Do we have a pack, kit or multipack built for an online order, or only the sizes the store shelf needs?
  • Who in the company owns pack architecture for e-commerce, and do they sit with the category team or the e-commerce team?
  • If our online share stays at 2020 levels, which store sizes should we stop listing online altogether?

The first question is the one that tends to change the plan. Building an online assortment that pays its own way is part of running the marketplace channel for brands whose products were designed for the shelf.

P0502.crumb: The marketplace ad tax rises with every…
P0502.title: The marketplace ad tax rises with every seller a retailer adds
P0502.alt: A long row of red and white barrier arms extending over a rural road beside a pink concrete wall.
P0502.ttag: The marketplace ad tax rises with every seller a retailer adds | Kwontified
P0502.desc: Advertising has become a fee that marketplace sellers pay on top of commission, and it grows with the number of sellers competing for a fixed set of placements.
P0502.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 29, 2020.
P0502.body:
The commission on a marketplace sale is printed in a fee table. For most products on Amazon it is 15%, a rate that has barely moved in two decades. The other cost of selling there is printed nowhere. Amazon keeps an average of 30% of each third-party sale once fulfillment, advertising and other charges are counted, up from 19% five years earlier, the Institute for Local Self-Reliance estimated in its July report on Amazon’s seller fees. Advertising is the part of that growth with no published rate.

Call it the ad tax: the share of marketplace sales a brand has to spend on advertising to keep the position it had. It is not set by the retailer. It is set by how many sellers are bidding for the same few placements, and every retailer building a marketplace in 2020 is working to raise that number. That is why the marketplace ad tax rises over time even when nothing about a brand’s own ads has changed.

Why advertising looks like a choice

Most brands treat advertising as discretionary. Commission and fulfillment fees are fixed costs of being on the marketplace; advertising is a marketing decision, budgeted separately and cut when margins tighten. The reports encourage the split. ACoS, advertising cost as a share of the sales the ads are credited with, describes the ads alone, as if the rest of the business ran without them. Finance sees commission as a cost of goods and advertising as an expense, and the two rarely appear on the same page of the plan.

That view made sense when sponsored placements were a small extra on a page dominated by organic results. It makes less sense when the first results a shopper sees are paid, and when the products that stop paying drop out of view. The fee is optional in the way that a toll road is optional: you can take the side roads, but the traffic is on the highway.

Placements are fixed; sellers are not

A marketplace grows by adding sellers and selection. Amazon’s third-party sellers accounted for 54% of the units it sold in the third quarter, Amazon reported in October. Walmart opened its marketplace to Shopify merchants in June and expected to add 1,200 of them in 2020, Talk Business & Politics reported. Each new seller is also a potential bidder.

The number of places worth bidding for does not grow at the same rate. A search results page has a handful of sponsored slots near the top, and shoppers click on the first page far more than the rest: 65% of Amazon product clicks came from page one in Jumpshot’s 2018 data, Retail Dive reported. When more sellers want the same slots, the auction raises the price of each. The advertiser’s choice is to pay it or to sell from lower down.

The retailer’s revenue shows the effect. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which it says consists mainly of advertising services, rose 51% to $5.4 billion in the third quarter, against 37% growth in net sales to $96.1 billion. That line went from about 5.1% of Amazon’s net sales a year earlier to 5.6%. The money came from brands and sellers bidding harder for space on the same pages.

The arithmetic for one brand

Take a brand selling $100,000 a month on a marketplace, spending $8,000 on ads, so total advertising cost of sale (TACoS), ad spend as a share of all sales, is 8%. Its commission is 15% and fulfillment costs another 15%.

Year 1Year 2: more sellers in the auction
Sales$100,000$100,000
Commission (15%)$15,000$15,000
Fulfillment (15%)$15,000$15,000
Ads to hold the same position$8,000 (8%)$10,000 (10%)
Left for product cost and profit$62,000$60,000

Nothing in the fee table changed. The brand’s ads did not get worse. The auction got busier, and the cost of holding the same position rose by a quarter. Over a year that is $24,000 of margin moved to the retailer, the same as a two-point commission increase that nobody announced.

This is the logic of a marketplace built on an ad auction. The retailer does not need to raise fees to raise its take. It needs to recruit sellers, and the sellers raise the price of visibility for each other.

Budgeting the ad tax like a fee

The practical change is to stop treating marketplace advertising as a separate marketing line and to plan it the way commission is planned: as a percentage of sales, per retailer, in the product’s margin.

  • Track TACoS by retailer each month alongside commission and fulfillment, and watch the trend rather than the level. A rising TACoS with steady conversion is the tax rising.
  • Price new products with the ad tax included. A product that only works at zero advertising will not work on a marketplace whose first page is paid.
  • Compare retailers on the full take, not the commission. Walmart Media Group, which opened self-serve search ads only in January, and Target’s Roundel are earlier in their auctions than Amazon, so their ad tax is likely lower for now and likely to rise as sellers arrive.
  • Use the growing seller count as a forecast input. When a retailer announces a seller program, budget a higher ad share for the following year on that retailer.

The rule of thumb: on any marketplace that adds sellers faster than it adds placements, expect the share of sales you spend on ads to rise, and put that rise in next year’s price and margin plan. Planning advertising as a cost of the channel, retailer by retailer, is how we budget retail media for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.
