P0503.title: Marketplace inventory in 2020 sat behind a gate brands don’t hold
P0503.alt: Chain-link gate locked with a padlock and chain in front of a warehouse aisle of shelved cardboard boxes.
P0503.ttag: Marketplace inventory in 2020 sat behind a gate brands don’t hold | Kwontified
P0503.desc: In 2020 brands learned that stock in their own warehouse is not stock on the marketplace shelf. The link between them now runs on someone else’s rules.
P0503.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 31, 2020.
P0503.body:
In late March, plenty of brands had the same picture on two screens. In the warehouse management system, pallets of finished goods sat ready to ship. On Amazon, the same products were marked unavailable. The stock existed. The link between the warehouse and the shelf had closed: on March 17, Amazon stopped creating new inbound shipments to its fulfillment centers for products outside a short list of essential categories, TechCrunch reported.

That picture is the year’s lesson about marketplace inventory. Brands spent 2020 worrying about having too much stock or too little. The risk that hurt many of them was having it in the wrong place, on the wrong side of a gate run by someone else. The marketplace warehouse has become a link in the supply chain that the brand stocks but does not operate, and most planning processes still treat it as a customer.

Amazon and the carriers closed gates at both ends of 2020

The March limit was the most visible gate, but not the only one. On April 13 Amazon said it would allow more products into its fulfillment centers, but that they would be “limited by quantity,” Engadget reported. In Europe, eligible products carried a “Limited restock” tag on the restock page, and Amazon said it was not accepting requests for higher limits, ChannelX reported at the end of April. The quantity limits came off on May 9, according to Amazon’s Seller Central news post.

The gates reappeared at the other end of the year in a different form. On Cyber Monday, UPS told drivers to stop collecting packages from six large retailers, including Gap, Nike and Macy’s, The Wall Street Journal reported, according to Retail TouchPoints. UPS said it would pick up from customers above their allocated volume once it had capacity. In spring the gate was the marketplace’s receiving dock; in December it was the carrier’s truck.

Each gate was reasonable from the side of the company running it. Amazon had to keep space for the goods shoppers needed most; UPS had to keep its network running through what Retail TouchPoints called unprecedented shipping volumes. Neither was designed around any one brand’s plan, and neither had to be.

How the marketplace became a warehouse

It helps to remember how this link took hold. Fulfillment by Amazon is sold to sellers as a convenience: send your inventory to Amazon, let it pick and ship, and earn the Prime badge. For many brands selling on Amazon it has become the usual way to operate, and in February Walmart launched its own version, Walmart Fulfillment Services, to store and ship for marketplace sellers for a fee, Modern Retail reported. Amazon alone opened 100 new operations buildings in North America in the third quarter, it said in October.

More of a brand’s inventory now sits in buildings it does not run.

Inside most brands, though, the planning still reflects the older arrangement. Sales and operations planning counts inventory as one pool, usually in the brand’s own distribution centers, and treats each marketplace as a customer that places orders. Replenishing FBA is often a separate job, owned by the e-commerce team, done in the marketplace’s tools on the marketplace’s schedule. The plan sees the units. It does not see the gate.

That gap is why March felt like a stockout to some brands and a warehouse full of inventory to others, at the same moment. Both were true. The plan had no line for “on hand but not admissible.”

The cost of that blind spot is easy to picture in the planning meeting. Supply chain reports healthy weeks of cover. The e-commerce team reports lost sales on its best products. Finance sees both numbers and cannot reconcile them, because they describe the same units from two sides of a gate that neither team controls. Until someone owns the movement of stock between nodes, that meeting repeats every time a marketplace changes its intake rules.

Planning inventory by node, not by pool

The shift for 2021 is to plan inventory by where it can actually sell. Units in the brand’s warehouse, units in Amazon’s network, units in Walmart’s and units with a 3PL that can ship seller-fulfilled orders are different assets, with different gates, costs and lead times. A brand that sells through all of them needs to know, for its top products, how much sits in each and how fast it can move between them.

It is too early to say whether 2020’s gates were a one-time event. Amazon lifted the spring limits within two months, and carrier caps are a familiar feature of peak season. The evidence still leans toward more gates, not fewer: the marketplaces are building more of their own fulfillment, and each new network comes with its own intake rules. The brands that came through 2020 best tended to have a second path to the shopper, whether shipping orders from their own warehouse, a second marketplace or a retailer’s store network, so that one closed gate did not close the business.

Questions for the 2021 inventory plan

  • How many units of our top products sat in our own warehouse in March and April while the same products were unavailable on Amazon?
  • Does our sales and operations plan show inventory by node (own warehouse, Amazon, Walmart, 3PL) or as one number?
  • If Amazon limited our inbound shipments for six weeks, which products could we ship to shoppers ourselves, and how fast?
  • Who owns the decision to move stock between nodes, the supply chain team or the e-commerce team?

The last question is often the one without an answer, and it decides how fast a brand can react when the next gate closes. Planning inventory across marketplace warehouses as part of running the channel day to day is work we do with brands that sell through more than one network.

A0002.crumb: CPG brands move budgets to retail media…
A0002.title: CPG brands move budgets to retail media networks they can measure
A0002.alt: Oak shelves of blank kraft-labeled bottles, jars and paper packs on a green wall, with a brass balance scale in front
A0002.ttag: CPG brands move budgets to retail media networks they can measure | Kwontified
A0002.desc: Retail media dashboards report a sale by Monday, so CPG trade money is moving there, but the sale they report is not always one the ads caused.
A0002.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 5, 2021.
A0002.body:
Ask a CPG finance team what its 2020 trade promotion returned and the answer shows up weeks later as an estimate. Ask what a retail media campaign returned and the retailer’s dashboard has a figure by Monday. Money follows the faster count, which explains most of the trade and shopper budget now drifting into retail media networks.

That count measures sales the ads touched. What the ads added is a smaller number, and in 2021 the distance between the two is what brands moving money need to manage.

How much is moving into retail media networks

Merkle surveyed 100 marketers at major US brands in August 2020. Of the CPG marketers, 85% planned to buy more ads from retail media networks and 52% planned to do it within a year, Digiday reported. The same piece named Walmart and Kroger next to Amazon among the retailers advertisers increasingly treat as media owners.

Much of that money already existed. Merkle’s media lead told Digiday that some of it is shopper or trade money that would have gone to other retailers, now moving to one with the right audience and reporting, and some is e-commerce money shifting into retail media. It is a transfer between budget lines.

The destination is big enough to absorb it. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which is mostly advertising, grew 51% to $5.4 billion in the third quarter of 2020, according to VentureBeat’s report on the results.

Closed-loop reporting counts every sale an ad touched

A retail media network sells ads on the retailer’s own site and apps, then matches them against that retailer’s own order records. The closed loop is the product. A trade promotion gets judged after the fact from scan data, with plenty of room to argue about cause. A sponsored product ad gets judged by a report that ties the click to the order.

Anyone who has defended a trade budget knows why that feels like progress. The post-event analysis tends to land after the next promotion is already booked, and every number in it can be argued with. A report that names the ad, the shopper’s order and the date is faster and harder to dispute, so it wins the budget meeting. Speed and precision are real advantages. They describe how well the sale was counted, though, and say nothing yet about why it happened.

The match itself is accurate as far as it goes. It answers a narrower question than most finance teams assume. Picture a doorman credited with every guest who walks through the door: some came in because he held it open, and many were coming anyway. Closed-loop attribution records, truthfully, that a shopper saw or clicked an ad and then bought. Whether the ad was the reason stays open.

Take a brand that moves $100,000 out of trade and into sponsored product ads. The retailer reports $400,000 in attributed sales, a return on ad spend (ROAS) of 4.0. Say half of those buyers had typed the brand’s name into the search bar and would have bought without the ad.

Same campaignAttributed viewIncremental view
Ad spend$100,000$100,000
Sales credited$400,000$200,000
ROAS4.02.0

Only the right-hand column describes what the money did.

Where attributed and incremental sales drift apart

Incrementality is the share of sales that would not have happened without the ad. The gap between attributed and incremental is widest where ads reach people who were already buying: campaigns on your own brand name, audiences built from past purchasers, placements on your own product pages. It is narrowest on category searches, where the shopper has not chosen a brand yet.

That pattern gives you a base rate before any test runs. If most of a retail media budget sits on branded terms and repeat buyers, expect the attributed figure to overstate the added one by a wide margin.

A holdout settles it. Pause ads in one region or for one period, keep everything else the same, and watch sales. If they hold up, the dashboard was mostly crediting demand the brand already had. If they fall by roughly what the dashboard claimed, the ads earned their credit. Either answer is worth more than another month of reports.

The design matters less than the discipline around it. Pick a region or a run of weeks that normally behaves like the rest of the business. Write down in advance what drop in sales would count as the ads working, and leave the test alone long enough to cover a few normal purchase cycles for the category. A test that gets cut short the first time sales wobble only proves that someone was nervous.

None of this makes the shift irrational. Finance is right to prefer a dollar it can count, and category search on a retailer’s site reaches shoppers at the moment they choose between products, which few channels can say. The risk is narrower: a dollar counted generously can look better than a trade dollar that did more work and was never measured. The report misses sales the ad drove somewhere else, and it includes sales the ad did not cause.

Before the next trade dollar moves

Split retail media results into branded and non-branded spend, and into new and repeat customers where the retailer reports them, before you set any of it beside trade. Agree with finance on what each budget pool has to prove and over what window.

Then run one holdout per quarter on your largest retail media campaign and set budgets on the incremental return it shows. A brand that knows both errors in the dashboard can show finance why the moved trade dollars are doing more work, and not simply getting easier to count. That baseline and holdout setup is work we do for brands moving trade money into retail media.

A0003.title: Brands undervalue Instagram shopping by measuring it as marketing
A0003.alt: Antique wooden cash register with a smartphone leaning on it, kraft-wrapped parcels and dried flowers against a pink wall
A0003.ttag: Brands undervalue Instagram shopping by measuring it as marketing | Kwontified
A0003.desc: Instagram gave shopping a tab on its home screen in November 2020, yet most brands still grade the account on likes, two desks from the sales target.
A0003.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 7, 2021.
A0003.body:
At most brands the Instagram account belongs to the social team, and its monthly report counts followers, reach and engagement rate. The sales targets live with e-commerce, two desks over. So when a CEO asks what Instagram shopping returns, nobody owns the answer, and the figure that eventually surfaces is low because the channel is graded as a marketing expense while a growing share of its job is selling.

Instagram’s own home screen, rebuilt on November 12, 2020, makes that arrangement hard to carry into 2021.

The Instagram shopping numbers sit on the last slide

Sit in on a typical social review and the order of the deck tells you how the company thinks about the channel. Posts published come first, then engagement rate, then follower growth, and somewhere near the end, if they appear at all, product tags and Shop visits. The e-commerce review a week later reports revenue by channel, and Instagram rarely earns its own line. The sales it starts tend to finish somewhere else: on the brand’s site, or on a marketplace where the shopper searched for the product a day later.

Someone sees a serum in a creator’s post, opens Amazon the next evening and buys it there, and the product tag never learns about it. It works like a shop window dressed with real care by the visual merchandising team while the till sits in a different building. Teams build what they are scored on. A post that sells the product often earns fewer likes than one that entertains, so fewer of them get made, and no one ever has to decide to underinvest in selling on Instagram. The scorecard makes that call every month.

Instagram is not going to resolve the argument for anyone. When it launched the new home screen, it declined to give CNN any figures on shopping, CNN Business reported. A brand that wants to know the return has to build the measurement itself.

The budget line decides what counts as a return

Underneath the reporting problem sits a budgeting one: which pot of money Instagram lives in. Inside brand marketing, its costs are content production, creator fees and the social team’s time, and its benefit is described as awareness. Measured that way, a sale is a pleasant surprise and a missing sale is nobody’s failure.

Move the same activity into a commerce view and the arithmetic shifts. Say a brand spends $20,000 a month on Instagram content and creators, and product tags lead to $15,000 in tracked sales on its site. The marketing review files the channel as a cost center that recovers 75% of its spend.

A commerce review adds two lines to that sum. The first is the shoppers who discovered the product on Instagram and bought it on Amazon or in a store, where no tag could follow them. The second is the share of the content budget the brand would have spent on imagery anyway, for its own site and its retail partners. Count both and the channel rarely looks worse than the marketing review claimed.

Follow the sale to its end and you can see who keeps the value. When a purchase starts on Instagram and finishes on a marketplace, the marketplace records the order and keeps the customer data. The brand that paid for the content gets credit only if it has built a way to see the path. Leave Instagram inside the marketing budget and you are, in effect, funding demand that another channel reports as its own.

Planning season hardens the pattern. The social team asks for money to grow reach. E-commerce asks for money to buy search ads on marketplaces. Each request is judged on its own team’s numbers, and neither describes the connection between them, which is that Instagram creates the interest and the marketplace ad captures it. A leadership team that funds the two separately keeps paying for the capture while questioning the creation.

Instagram is rebuilding the app around the purchase

On November 12, 2020, Instagram redesigned its home screen for the first time in years and put a Shop tab in the main navigation. In his announcement, Instagram head Adam Mosseri wrote that the tab offers personalized recommendations, editors’ picks from the @shop channel and shoppable videos. He also said the company had seen a large amount of shopping move online during the pandemic, with young people looking to creators for advice on what to buy.

Where the tab went says more than the announcement. CNN reported that Shop took the spot where the activity button used to sit, and that people can search for specific products and buy directly on the platform. The other new position went to Reels, Instagram’s short video format. Think of it as the end caps in a store: a retailer gives its most-trafficked shelf space to what it most wants to sell, and Instagram just handed two of its best positions to video and shopping.

How much buying will happen inside the app, rather than starting there and finishing elsewhere, is too early to call. The evidence so far leans toward Instagram wanting more of the purchase to happen in-app. If more of a brand’s tagged sales start completing inside Instagram through 2021, the account stops being a cost of awareness and becomes a store with its own customers, and a store needs someone accountable for its sales.

So the question for the next planning meeting is a blunt one: if Instagram becomes a place where people buy, which budget should pay for it, and who should be judged on the result?

Two changes make the answer visible. Give one person a sales target for Instagram shopping, separate from the social team’s engagement goals, and report it next to the other sales channels. Then track the path beyond the tag, using links, codes or post-purchase surveys to count shoppers who found a product on Instagram and bought it elsewhere. We run Instagram Shop next to brands’ marketplace channels, including the measurement that connects the two.

A0004.title: Amazon’s delayed 2021 fee increase still needs a model now
A0004.alt: Twine-tied kraft parcel on a vintage brass postal scale beside a brass hourglass on a wooden table
A0004.ttag: Amazon’s delayed 2021 fee increase still needs a model now | Kwontified
A0004.desc: Amazon pushed its 2021 FBA fee increase to June 1, and whatever it adds per unit will come straight off the ACoS each of your products can afford.
A0004.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 12, 2021.
A0004.body:
In a normal January, Amazon sellers lose a week rebuilding their margin sheets around a new fee schedule. This January there is nothing to plug in. On December 22, 2020, Amazon postponed its annual fulfillment fee adjustment to June 1, 2021 and promised details in the spring.

It reads like a reprieve, but it behaves like a deadline with the size left blank. Fees sit inside every product’s break-even ACoS, so when the increase lands it will lower the advertising cost each product can afford. The time to set ad targets against a range of fee scenarios is now, five months ahead.

What Amazon said about the 2021 fee increase

In a letter to sellers, Jeff Wilke, the outgoing head of Amazon’s consumer business, wrote that other logistics providers had already announced fee increases for 2021. Amazon would postpone its own annual fulfillment fee adjustments and absorb the costs until June 1, 2021, then share more details in the spring. He added that Amazon had absorbed over $5 billion of costs in 2020 that other companies passed along through surcharges and fee changes.

Bloomberg’s report filled in the pattern. Amazon usually announces fee changes in December to take effect early in the new year, and in each of the last four years that has meant higher costs for many US sellers using its fulfillment services. Early in 2020, fees to ship the most common small items rose 2.9% to 6.1%, and monthly storage rent for most of the year rose 8.7%. The pause covers sellers in the US, Europe and Japan. UPS and FedEx have each announced a 4.9% general rate increase for 2021.

Two readings follow from the letter. The adjustment is postponed, so expect it on or after June 1. And nobody outside Amazon knows its size, which means any plan made today has to be a plan for a range.

How a fee change moves break-even ACoS

Advertising cost of sale (ACoS) is ad spend divided by the sales the ads are credited with. Most Amazon accounts run to an ACoS target, and the target should come from margin. Break-even ACoS is what is left of the price after product cost and Amazon’s fees, divided by the price. Spend above it and every attributed sale loses money before overhead.

Take a $25.00 product with a $7.00 product cost, a 15% referral fee and, say, a $5.00 fulfillment fee. Then raise the fulfillment fee by 5%, inside the range of the 2020 increases for small items.

Per unitTodayFulfillment fee up 5%
Price$25.00$25.00
Product cost$7.00$7.00
Referral fee$3.75$3.75
Fulfillment fee$5.00$5.25
Margin$9.25$9.00
Break-even ACoS37%36%

One point of ACoS sounds trivial. On a campaign already running at 36%, it is the entire profit.

Notice which line moved. The referral fee stays put because it is a percentage of price, so it only changes when the price does. The fulfillment fee is a flat charge per unit, set by the product’s size and weight, and that is why the same increase in cents bites a cheap product far harder than an expensive one.

Across a catalog the damage is uneven. Products with low prices and high fulfillment fees lose more ceiling than expensive, light products, because the fee is a larger share of the price. That sets up the real choice: hold ACoS targets where they are and accept thinner margins from June, or lower them and give up volume on the products with the least headroom. The numbers lean toward lowering targets selectively, on the products where the fee is the biggest share of price, rather than across the whole account.

Working back from June 1

The size of the change is unknown, so the useful tool is a scenario table. Five months sounds like plenty. It is enough only if the slow fixes start early, because price changes, packaging changes that move a product into a smaller fee tier, and supplier negotiations each take months. A brand that waits for the published schedule gets a few weeks to respond to a change it could have prepared for since December.

  1. In January, run every top-selling product through three cases: no change to fulfillment fees, a 3% increase and a 6% increase. The 6% case sits at the top of the 2020 range for small items; treat it as a planning assumption. Record each case’s break-even ACoS next to the ACoS the product’s campaigns actually ran at over the last 90 days.
  2. Next, sort the catalog. Products comfortably under break-even in every case need nothing. Products that cross only in the high case go on a watch list for the spring announcement.
  3. Before June 1, deal with the products already near break-even at current fees, which will slide from small profit to loss as soon as the change takes effect. Open the pricing, packaging, targeting and supplier conversations for those now, so the decisions are ready when the schedule arrives.
  4. When Amazon publishes the schedule, swap the real figure into the table. Most of the decisions should already be made.

The table also changes the meeting with finance. A single forecast invites an argument about whether the number is right. Three cases with stated assumptions invite a better question: which decisions hold up in all three, and which depend on the size of the change? Most of January’s useful work sits in the first group, and it starts from the same margin-after-fees math we use to set ACoS targets that will survive the June fee change.

A0007.crumb: Mercado Libre’s growth asks brands to…
A0007.title: Mercado Libre’s growth asks brands to rethink Latin America
A0007.alt: Yellow delivery motorbike with a large cargo box parked on a cobblestone street lined with colorful colonial houses
A0007.ttag: Mercado Libre’s growth asks brands to rethink Latin America | Kwontified
A0007.desc: Mercado Libre now ships and takes payment at a scale few distributors match, which turns Latin America into a question of who owns the customer.
A0007.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 14, 2021.
A0007.body:
At many US and European brands, Latin America gets one slot in the annual review, presented by the export desk as a single line of wholesale revenue. Distributors and licensees run the region the rest of the year. That arrangement made sense when getting goods across borders and getting paid were the hard part of selling there. Mercado Libre now does both at a scale few distributors can match, which hands leadership a decision it has been able to avoid: whether the brand or its distributor should own the region’s customer.

What Mercado Libre runs besides the marketplace

Mercado Libre calls itself Latin America’s largest online commerce platform, and its third quarter of 2020 shows how far past a marketplace it has moved. The company reported 76.1 million unique active users, up 92.2% from a year earlier, in its quarterly results. Gross merchandise volume, the value of goods sold on the marketplace, reached $5.9 billion, and mobile accounted for 70.0% of it.

For a brand deciding how to enter, the operating lines matter more than the headline. Mercado Envios, the company’s shipping service, shipped 187.6 million items in the quarter, up 131.1%. Mercado Pago, its payments arm, processed $14.5 billion in total payment volume. Listing on Mercado Libre plugs a brand into the region’s delivery and payment systems along with its demand, and those are the two jobs distributors were originally hired to do.

Further into the release sits a small definitional note: the company counts ad sales inside its commerce revenue. It is easy to skim past. It is also the clearest hint of where the business is heading, toward a marketplace that sells media to the brands on its shelves, as Amazon has done in the United States.

What the distributor sees and the brand does not

The distributor model has a logic older than any marketplace. Moving goods across borders, clearing customs, collecting payment in local currencies and offering shoppers installments were all hard for a foreign brand to manage alone, and a good distributor solved them. In exchange it held the inventory, set the prices and kept the relationship with retailers and shoppers.

That last part rarely makes it into the annual review. When a distributor runs a brand’s Mercado Libre listings, the distributor sees the search terms, the reviews, the returns and the questions shoppers ask before they buy. The brand sees a purchase order. In a physical store a brand manager can at least walk the aisle and check how the product is faced. On a marketplace run by someone else, the shelf is invisible from headquarters unless somebody goes looking.

The export team has little reason to look. It is measured on wholesale revenue and on how little management time the region needs, and a distributor delivers both. Nobody on that team is scored on the brand’s search ranking in São Paulo or the reviews it earns in Mexico City, so those questions never reach the agenda.

The size of the marketplace adds a second pressure. Mercado Libre reported 303.9 million live listings in the quarter, up 22.3%. At that scale a brand’s products are often listed by several sellers at once: the distributor, its sub-distributors, and resellers who bought stock somewhere else. Each writes its own titles, picks its own images and sets its own price.

A brand that does not manage its presence on Mercado Libre still has one. In practice it has several, written by companies whose interest is the sale in front of them rather than the brand’s reputation over time.

Payments tighten the loop. Mercado Pago’s mobile wallet reached 13.7 million unique payers in the quarter, more than double a year earlier. As more shoppers keep their money and credit with the company that runs the marketplace, the store, the checkout and the wallet become one relationship, and a brand standing outside it sees a little less each year.

Currency is the argument worth having

When the subject finally reaches the boardroom, the objection is usually risk, and the filing shows why. Mercado Libre’s gross merchandise volume grew 62.1% in US dollars and 117.1% on an FX-neutral basis, which holds exchange rates at 2019 levels. The distance between those two numbers is the currency loss a dollar-reporting company absorbs. The same release recorded a $30.4 million foreign exchange loss linked to Argentina’s multiple exchange rates.

That gap is the real decision. Selling directly through the marketplace means the brand takes on currency exposure the distributor used to carry, and gets margin, data and control of how the brand is presented in return. The distributor model gives those up for predictability in dollars. Either position can be defended. What is hard to defend is drifting into one by default because the export team has always handled the region.

The evidence so far leans toward more brands moving at least their largest market closer to direct control as Mercado Libre’s logistics and payments mature, though it is too early to say how quickly. Logistics is the last argument a distributor can make that a brand cannot answer on its own, so watch how far Mercado Envios extends, country by country, through 2021.

Questions for the next Latin America review

  1. Who currently runs our listings on Mercado Libre, in each country, and who receives the reviews, questions and search data those listings generate?
  2. Which other sellers list our products there, and whose titles, images and prices does a shopper see first?
  3. What does the distributor’s margin cost us against selling through the marketplace, once fees, shipping, payment terms and a stated currency assumption are included?
  4. If Latin America became a direct channel in our largest market, which team would own it, and how would we judge it?

If the answers point toward selling directly, we launch and operate brands on Mercado Libre and the other international marketplaces, market by market.

A0009.crumb: A Target Plus invitation goes to brands…
A0009.title: A Target Plus invitation goes to brands that fill a gap
A0009.alt: Red wooden wall shelf holding white ceramic pitchers, bowls and mugs above a table with a blue vase.
A0009.ttag: A Target Plus invitation goes to brands that fill a gap | Kwontified
A0009.desc: Brands that sell well on Amazon assume a Target Plus invitation rewards size, but Target’s own words say it rewards filling a hole in its assortment.
A0009.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 19, 2021.
A0009.body:
Brands that do well on Amazon tend to treat a Target Plus invitation as a reward for scale: grow big enough and Target will call. Target’s own account of how it picks sellers says something else. It chooses categories that complement its assortment and that guests already search for on Target.com, so the invitation goes to the brand that fills a gap.

The brands that get one usually show Target that gap before they ask.

Target Plus invitations are scarce by design

Target launched its marketplace in 2019 and kept it small on purpose. By December 2019 it had signed nearly 100 sellers offering more than 250,000 products on Target.com, the Star Tribune reported. That is tiny next to Amazon and Walmart, and Target meant it to be.

Brian Cornell, Target’s CEO, said in the fall of 2019 that Target was not opening the marketplace to thousands of new vendors with millions of new items, because guests need to trust Target and the reliability of what it sells. Rick Gomez, Target’s chief marketing and digital officer, described the vetting as the most thorough in the industry and said Target keeps monitoring sellers after they join.

The caution makes sense once you see what a seller borrows. RedCard holders still get free shipping and 5% off marketplace items, and shoppers can return those items in stores, according to the same report. Every Target Plus seller trades on Target’s reputation at the register and the returns desk, so Target lets very few of them do it.

Why the biggest brand is not the obvious pick

Gomez told the Star Tribune that Target picked categories that complement its own assortment of more than a million items online, and that customers had been searching for on Target.com. The early sellers fit that description: Mizuno in athletic gear, an online arm of Guitar Center, and Kaplan Early Learning in educational toys. Sporting goods, musical instruments and toys are categories where specialist national retailers had struggled or closed, which left searches on Target.com with little to answer them.

A mall landlord works the same way. It does not lease to whichever tenant posts the biggest sales elsewhere; it reads the directory, finds what shoppers come in asking for and cannot find, and leases to the tenant who fills that hole. A strong tenant in a category the mall already covers is competing for an existing lease.

The commission math shows why Target thinks like the landlord. Host sites typically take 5% to 15% of a marketplace sale, the Star Tribune noted, while the seller holds the inventory and ships the order. On a $40 item that is $2 to $6 for Target.

Fees that size do not justify the risk of a bad seller trading on Target’s name. Keeping a shopper who came to Target.com for something specific, and who would otherwise leave for another site, does. The invitation is an assortment and loyalty decision that happens to be priced as a commission.

So size alone rarely earns one. A large beauty brand selling the kind of product Target already carries adds little to the assortment. A smaller brand in a category where Target.com searches come back thin adds something Target cannot easily supply itself. Target is effectively buying coverage of searches it currently loses, and coverage is measured by the gaps a seller closes rather than by what that seller sells elsewhere.

Target’s digital growth makes the gaps bigger

The gaps matter more because Target’s digital business has grown so fast. In the third quarter of 2020, digital comparable sales grew 155%, and same-day services such as Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt grew 217%, according to Target’s results. More than 95% of third-quarter sales were fulfilled by its stores.

Read the two numbers together. Target’s growth runs through its stores, and its stores stock Target’s own assortment. Every Target.com search for something the stores do not carry is demand Target turns away, and more traffic means more of those searches. That raises the value of a seller who can answer them.

Say a category gets 50,000 searches a month on Target.com, and Target carries a dozen items in it, most of them out of stock online. Two brands want in.

Brand ABrand B
Products40, well reviewed400
Target’s own range in the categoryA dozen items, mostly out of stock onlineAlready stocked in depth
What the brand adds for TargetAnswers searches Target currently losesCompetes with Target’s own shelves

Brand B is ten times larger, and Brand A is the easier invitation to justify.

The conclusion would change if Target’s policy did. Gomez said Target would keep building Target Plus in a thoughtful, disciplined way. If Target began opening the marketplace widely, scale and price would start to matter more and gaps less. For now the evidence points the other way.

Build the case before you ask

Start on Target.com. Search the core terms in your category and record which ones return thin, off-brand or out-of-stock results; that list is your case for an invitation. Split your catalog into products Target already sells in depth and products it does not, and lead with the second group.

Then bring proof you can meet the service standard of a store that takes returns at the register: shipping times, stock levels and customer service records from your other marketplaces. The rule of thumb is to pitch the searches you answer, and leave the size of your catalog for later in the conversation. Mapping those searches is the first step when we build a Target Plus case for brands alongside running their Walmart and Target marketplaces.

A0017.crumb: The Zalando Partner Program needs a new…
A0017.title: The Zalando Partner Program needs a new owner inside brands
A0017.alt: An antique brass key tied with an orange ribbon on a worn wooden table among stoneware bowls.
A0017.ttag: The Zalando Partner Program needs a new owner inside brands | Kwontified
A0017.desc: Most brands still meet Zalando twice a year at a buying appointment, while Zalando’s growth now comes from partners who list, price and stock their own range.
A0017.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 21, 2021.
A0017.body:
In many brands’ planning calendars, Zalando shows up twice a year as a buying appointment. The wholesale team walks the buyers through the collection, an order gets placed, and the account is judged on sell-through. That rhythm suits a retailer. Zalando’s growth now comes from a different relationship, one in which brands sell directly on its platform, set their own prices and hold their own stock, and that model needs an owner who runs Zalando as a channel. In most brands, that person does not sit on the wholesale team.

How the Zalando Partner Program ended up in the wholesale calendar

The habit has an obvious origin. Brands that first met Zalando as a buyer of their collections ran the relationship through the people who sell to department stores, and order books, margin agreements and seasonal markdowns were the language of the account. The wholesale director spoke it best. Zalando’s own leadership now talks about something else: when the company reported its third quarter, chief financial officer David Schröder listed “driving our platform transition” among its priorities.

The Partner Program changed the terms of the relationship and left the org chart alone. A brand in the program lists its own products on Zalando, decides how deep its range goes and owns the inventory. Its results depend on things a buying appointment never touches, such as the quality of its product content, how quickly stock updates reach the site, and its prices against its own wholesale partners on the same pages. A team built to negotiate an order is rarely staffed to watch those every day.

The two models can collide on a single screen. A brand can sell some styles to Zalando wholesale while listing others itself through the program, and a shopper scrolling a category sees both. It is much like a department store floor that puts a brand’s own concession two aisles from a rail of the same label that the store bought in. If the prices drift apart, or one listing carries better images than the other, the brand ends up competing with itself. Nobody in the wholesale meeting is asked to check, so the problem tends to surface only when a margin conversation turns tense.

Where Zalando’s growth is coming from

Zalando’s third-quarter results make the direction plain. Gross merchandise volume grew 29.9% to 2.5 billion euros, while revenue grew 21.6% to 1.8 billion euros. Zalando credited the growth to demand shifting online during the pandemic and to the strong performance of the Partner Program and Zalando Lounge, its off-price business.

The gap between those two growth rates is what a platform’s results look like. As partners supply more of the volume, Zalando earns a fee on each partner sale instead of the whole price, so volume outpaces revenue. It is a trade Zalando has chosen: less revenue per sale, in return for a wider range than it could ever buy and hold itself, with partners carrying the inventory risk.

Its plans for physical stores lean the same way. Connected Retail, which lets shops sell their own stock through Zalando, had about 2,000 active stores, and Zalando said it aims to triple the number of connected stores in 2021. It extended the program to Denmark, Finland and Norway on November 1, 2020, and named Austria, Switzerland, France, Italy and Belgium as the next five countries for 2021. To carry those partners through the second lockdowns, it waived Connected Retail commissions until the end of the first quarter of 2021.

The audience is what makes the effort worth it. Zalando reported 35.6 million active customers at the end of September 2020, up 20.7% from a year earlier, and 87.2% of site visits came from mobile devices.

A platform asks brands for a different kind of partnership

Look at what Zalando now rewards and the message to brands is clear enough. A retailer wants a good order on good terms. A platform wants a partner who keeps a wide range in stock, updates it quickly and competes on the site every day, and the incentives Zalando now offers, from commission waivers to fulfillment services, favor that second kind of partner.

That puts a question to the leadership team that the wholesale calendar never raised. If the brand’s own listings on Zalando grow, who owns them? The wholesale team holds the relationship but is measured on orders. The e-commerce team has the skills but often files Europe’s marketplaces under later. Whoever takes it on decides whether Zalando becomes a managed channel or stays a buying appointment with a marketplace attached, and they need a scorecard that fits the model: availability, content quality and price consistency, alongside sales.

Moving has a real cost. The Partner Program shifts inventory risk to the brand and asks for daily attention that a wholesale order never did, and some brands will reasonably prefer the simplicity of an order. The evidence so far leans toward growth on Zalando requiring the platform model, because that is where Zalando is putting its traffic and its investment. Its full-year 2020 results should show how much of the volume partners now supply.

The first steps are modest. Work out how much of the Zalando business is wholesale and how much runs through the Partner Program, and who owns each part. Put your own content, prices and stock on Zalando next to what your wholesale partners show on the same site. Then ask the leadership team plainly which team should run Zalando day to day if it becomes the brand’s largest European channel, and on what numbers it should be judged. We run Zalando for brands as a managed channel, including the move away from a wholesale-only account.

A0011.crumb: An Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q4…
A0011.title: An Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q4 2020 splits Prime Day
A0011.alt: A walnut quick bread loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board beside a knife near a window.
A0011.ttag: An Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q4 2020 splits Prime Day | Kwontified
A0011.desc: Prime Day landed in October 2020, so any Q4 Amazon ad benchmark blends two auction peaks. Split the quarter before you judge your CPC or ROAS.
A0011.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 26, 2021.
A0011.body:
Every January someone puts the fourth-quarter Amazon results next to a benchmark and asks whether the team overpaid for clicks. In January 2021 that comparison is unusually easy to get wrong. Prime Day moved from July into October 2020, so the fourth quarter held both Amazon’s largest member event and the holiday season, two peaks with very different auction prices and conversion rates. Split the quarter into periods first, then compare each one on its own terms.

The Q4 2020 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark, period by period

The quarter falls into five periods: October 1 to 12, Prime Day, October 15 to November 26, Black Friday to Cyber Monday, and November 30 to December 31. No public benchmark reports all five. Pacvue draws on data from thousands of Amazon advertisers, and it published separate reports on Prime Day 2020, on the Black Friday to Cyber Monday weekend and on the fourth quarter as a whole. Read together, they show each stretch of the quarter running on its own prices.

PeriodWhat Pacvue’s data showed
Prime Day, October 13 to 14Sponsored Products daily average spend up 311% week over week on the first day and 265% on the second; Sponsored Brands CPC up 23% year over year
Black Friday to Cyber MondaySponsored Products CPC up 23.31% week over week on Black Friday and 39.06% on Cyber Monday; Sponsored Products ACoS 36.01% higher year over year on Black Friday and 48.66% higher on Cyber Monday
November and December, by categoryToys and games CPCs 46% above October in November and 176% above it in December; home and kitchen CPCs down 14.5% in December
Full quarterSponsored Products conversion rate up 10%, to an all-time high; Sponsored Brands ROAS down 6% quarter over quarter and 11% year over year

Return on ad spend (ROAS) is attributed sales divided by ad spend, using Amazon’s standard attribution for Sponsored Products. ACoS, the advertising cost of sales, is the same ratio turned over: ad spend divided by attributed sales.

Tinuiti’s Q4 2020 benchmark report, drawn from more than $2 billion in ad spend under management, adds a 91% increase in Sponsored Brands spend, driven largely by Sponsored Brands video. The event rows compare a day with the week or the year before it. The category row measures each month against October, and the quarterly row measures the quarter against the one before or the year before. So the rows cannot be stacked into one average. That is the point: each period ran its own auction.

The benchmark comes in pieces because of the calendar. Prime Day 2020 ran on October 13 and 14, which placed it in the fourth quarter rather than the third, as VentureBeat noted in its report on Amazon’s third-quarter results. In most years a Q4 benchmark describes the run-up to the holidays. This one also contains a two-day event many brands planned months ahead, with deals, extra budget and higher bids, followed a few weeks later by the Black Friday to Cyber Monday peak and its own bidding pressure.

Event weeks and ordinary weeks do not average cleanly

During a deal event, conversion rates tend to rise because shoppers arrive ready to buy. Cost per click (CPC), the price of each click in the auction, rises too, because more advertisers bid harder at once. In the weeks after, CPC can stay high while conversion falls back. Average the quarter and both movements vanish.

A quarterly figure is a weighted average of its periods, and the weights come from each brand’s own activity: its clicks for CPC, its spend for ROAS. Two brands with identical performance in every period can post different quarterly numbers simply because they spent in different weeks.

Say CPC was $1.50 during Prime Day and $1.00 for the rest of the quarter, for every brand. Brand A bought 40% of its fourth-quarter clicks in those two days, and Brand B bought 10%. Brand A’s quarterly average CPC comes out at $1.20 and Brand B’s at $1.05. Brand B looks like the sharper bidder, yet both paid exactly the market price in every period.

ROAS follows the same arithmetic, weighted by spend instead of clicks. A brand that spent heavily during Prime Day, when shoppers converted readily, can post a strong quarterly ROAS that says more about its calendar than its campaigns. A brand that held its money for December can look weaker for the same reason.

The same thing happens between a brand that pulled budget forward into October and one that saved it for late November. They can post similar quarterly numbers for very different reasons, and neither number says which of them bid well.

The pull to read the quarter as a verdict

A quarterly number feels like a grade for the team. Mostly it records when the budget was spent. Recency makes the error worse: December is freshest in everyone’s memory, so a weak December tends to color the judgment of a quarter that was strong in October. The correction is mechanical, which helps: the advertising console reports any date range you ask for, so splitting the quarter costs a few report downloads rather than an argument.

A market-wide figure has limits too. It describes the market without saying how wide the range across brands is, and categories differ. The toys and home and kitchen figures show it. In one category December clicks cost far more than October’s, while in the other December CPCs fell.

A brand in a crowded category such as beauty should expect CPCs above the market figure, and a brand in a narrow category should expect them below it. The benchmark shows where the market sat. Your own category, period by period, shows whether you paid too much.

Reading your own Q4 against the table

Cut your Q4 2020 Sponsored Ads results into the same five periods before you compare anything. A CPC above the benchmark during Prime Day says something about bidding during the event. A CPC above it in early December says something about the holiday auction. A gap in the quarterly figure, on its own, says almost nothing. Record what share of the quarter’s spend fell in each period, so the quarterly average can be read as a mix.

Then set 2021 targets by period. Amazon has not said when Prime Day 2021 will run. If it returns to the summer, the fourth quarter of 2021 will look different from the fourth quarter of 2020, and a year-over-year comparison of quarterly averages will mislead in the opposite direction, so revisit the targets once the date is announced. The working rule is simple: never benchmark a quarter you could have split. Period-level reporting is how we read Amazon ad results for brands, so budget decisions follow the auction rather than the calendar quarter.

A0013.crumb: NRF 2021 put product availability at the…
A0013.title: NRF 2021 put product availability at the center of brand loyalty
A0013.alt: Wooden shop shelves stocked with clay pots, woven baskets, glass jars and folded linens against a mustard wall.
A0013.ttag: NRF 2021 put product availability at the center of brand loyalty | Kwontified
A0013.desc: At NRF 2021, retailers described anxious shoppers who switched brands when shelves went empty, which puts availability squarely on the brand team’s agenda.
A0013.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 28, 2021.
A0013.body:
Most brands keep loyalty and availability in different rooms. Marketing owns the first, supply chain owns the second, and the two leaders rarely sit in the same review. The first week of NRF 2021, held online in January, suggested the customer no longer respects that separation. Speakers described shoppers who are anxious about money, who switched brands in large numbers during the pandemic, and who now search first for whoever has the product in stock.

Availability has moved to the center of brand loyalty, and the brand team needs a seat wherever it gets decided.

What NRF 2021 heard about brand switching

The National Retail Federation ran its 2021 show as a virtual event, NRF 2021: Retail’s Big Show, Chapter One, over six days from January 12 to 22. Coresight Research’s report on the first day collected the numbers that stood out.

Salesforce reported that one-third of consumers had switched brands since the start of the pandemic, and that 80% of those consumers planned to keep buying the brands they switched to. If those shoppers do what they say, the brands they left have lost more than a few months of sales, because the switch has settled into a habit.

Walmart’s chief customer officer, Janey Whiteside, described a customer under strain. In a session with Deloitte’s chief global economist, Ira Kalish, she said that in a November survey about 50% of Walmart customers were worried about the economy and 40% did not expect a quick recovery. Walmart has leaned on its everyday low price message in response.

The switch started at an empty shelf

The same day of sessions offered a strong clue to why so many shoppers changed brands at once. Carrie Tharp of Google Cloud said that US searches for “who has” plus “in stock” grew 8,000% year over year, and that global searches for “curbside pickup” grew 3,000%, both for March to May 2020.

Those searches belong to a shopper who has stopped asking for a particular brand and started asking who can deliver something now. When the preferred product was missing, the shopper took what was there, and a share of them stayed. The brand that lost the sale did not lose it in an advertising auction. It lost it on a shelf, physical or digital, with nothing on it.

In a store, an empty peg hook at least keeps the brand’s shelf tag in view, a reminder of what should be there. Online the empty shelf has a different shape. The shopper lands on a product page marked unavailable, and the same page offers similar items from other brands that are ready to ship. The competitor needs no better product and no better campaign at that moment, only stock while the shopper is still looking.

Retailers are building around this shopper. Whiteside said more than four times as many Walmart customers had used delivery and pickup since the outbreak, according to Coresight’s report. Walmart added 40% more pickup time slots and began using stores as fulfillment centers. The retailer is organizing around the question its customer keeps asking: who has it, and how fast?

Who keeps the customer when the product runs out

Follow the value in a switch. When a shopper moves from an out-of-stock brand to an available one, the retailer keeps the sale either way. The brand that was in stock gains a customer, and the brand that was out of stock loses one, possibly for good if the Salesforce figures hold. The retailer is indifferent between the two brands. The brands are not.

That changes what availability means inside a brand. In most organizations it is an operations metric, reviewed as a fill rate or an in-stock percentage and discussed when it goes wrong. The report usually lands with the people who place purchase orders, a floor away from the people who pay to win customers. NRF 2021 framed it as something closer to a marketing outcome: the moment a customer is kept or handed to a competitor. A brand that tracks share of voice weekly and in-stock rates monthly is watching the wrong number most closely.

Put rough numbers on it. Take a brand whose average repeat customer buys four times a year at $30 an order. If a stockout sends 1,000 of those customers to a competitor and a third of them never return, the brand has given up $40,000 a year in repeat sales, before counting what it will spend on advertising to win anyone back. A supply chain review records the stockout as a few lost weeks. The brand’s own customer file records a smaller business.

How many of the switches will hold once supply returns to normal is too early to say. The evidence so far leans toward a large share sticking, because the new brand was good enough and the shopper had a reason to stop looking. Through 2021, the telling comparison is between brands that win their share back when stock returns and brands that have to buy it back with promotions and advertising.

Two numbers for the next business review

  1. In-stock rates on your largest marketplaces and retailers, by product, in the same weekly report as sales and advertising.
  2. For every product that ran out of stock in 2020, whether sales recovered when stock came back or a competitor kept the customers.

Then put a direct question to the leadership team: who owns availability as a customer outcome, beyond the supply chain metric, and does that person have a voice in marketing plans? We run marketplace channels day to day for brands, including the stock, content and advertising that decide whether a shopper finds the product.

A0016.crumb: Walmart Marketplace sets your price floor…
A0016.title: Walmart Marketplace sets your price floor everywhere you sell
A0016.alt: A wooden spirit level balanced on three stoneware jars on a shelf against a deep blue wall.
A0016.ttag: Walmart Marketplace sets your price floor everywhere you sell | Kwontified
A0016.desc: Walmart Marketplace pulls a listing when the same product is cheaper anywhere else, so one weekend sale on your own site can cost you the Walmart shelf.
A0016.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 2, 2021.
A0016.body:
Say a brand sells a product for $25 on Walmart, on Amazon and on its own site, then runs a 20% weekend promotion on its own site that takes the price to $20. On Walmart Marketplace, that weekend sale can cost the brand its listing. Walmart removes products that sell for less elsewhere, including on the brand’s own website, which makes your lowest price anywhere your effective price on Walmart.

So any brand weighing Walmart Marketplace in 2021 needs a pricing plan that covers every channel before it launches.

Walmart Marketplace grew fast in 2020 and is still thin

The growth is not in doubt. Walmart finished 2020 with close to 70,000 marketplace sellers, more than double its total from 2019, according to Marketplace Pulse figures reported by Modern Retail. A partnership with Shopify, announced in June 2020, made it easier for Shopify merchants to list on Walmart.com, and Walmart’s overall e-commerce sales grew 79% in its third quarter, the same report noted.

Next to Amazon, which has about 2.4 million active sellers, roughly 70,000 is still a small field. Fewer sellers means less competition for each search, which is part of why early movers on Walmart often do well. It also means each offer gets judged on a short list of factors, and Walmart has been plain about which ones count most: price, then speed.

The rule: no lower price anywhere else

Walmart’s identity is everyday low prices, and it extends that promise to its marketplace. If a product listed on Walmart.com sells for less anywhere else, even on the seller’s own website, Walmart removes the product, Modern Retail reported. That is a more aggressive stance than Amazon takes.

It works like a price-match guarantee that the store enforces on its suppliers instead of honoring at the register. The shopper never has to ask. The seller who undercuts Walmart somewhere else simply disappears from the shelf.

Walmart has a clear reason to hold that line. Its brand rests on the promise that a shopper will not find the same item cheaper elsewhere, and a marketplace with tens of thousands of outside sellers could break that promise quickly if sellers priced freely. The rule protects Walmart’s reputation with shoppers and shifts the cost of protecting it onto the seller.

Speed is the second factor. Walmart launched Walmart Fulfillment Services (WFS) in February 2020 as its answer to Fulfillment by Amazon. Products shipped through WFS receive Walmart’s fast-shipping tags, such as TwoDay, and appear much more likely to win the buy box, the featured offer on a product page, according to the same report. Only about 430 sellers were using WFS, so most of the marketplace still competes without that advantage.

The fees are simple by comparison: a referral fee of between 6% and 20% depending on the product, and no monthly fee. On Walmart, the real cost of selling sits less in the fees than in the pricing discipline.

The two factors stack in a set order. A seller whose price matches the market can still lose the featured offer to a competitor with a faster delivery promise. A seller with fast fulfillment whose Walmart price is higher than its price elsewhere on the web may not be listed at all. Fix price consistency first and add speed second, because speed only counts once the listing survives.

How a promotion costs you the listing

Go back to the $25 product. The weekend the brand’s own site drops to $20, the Walmart listing sits above the brand’s lowest public price, and the brand risks losing it during the same weekend its marketing team is driving traffic. The promotion is often planned by whoever owns the brand’s site, while someone else watches the Walmart account, so the first sign of trouble can be a Monday sales report with the Walmart line at zero for the weekend.

Resellers and retailers who discount the product create the same exposure. A brand does not control every price on the web, but Walmart’s rule makes no distinction between a price the brand set and one someone else set. That puts price monitoring and reseller policy inside the Walmart launch plan from the start.

Brand protection adds a second risk. Walmart had not yet introduced controls similar to Amazon’s Brand Registry for taking down counterfeits, according to the same report. A brand entering Walmart should watch for unauthorized sellers on its own products from the first week, because a low-priced reseller can trigger the pricing rule against the brand’s own listing.

The constraint has a price of its own. Brands that protect their Walmart listings this way give up some freedom to run promotions on their own sites. For a brand whose own site is small, that costs little. For a brand built on frequent promotions to its email list, it can cost a lot, and the decision about whether Walmart is worth the constraint belongs before the listing goes live.

Price the whole map before launch

List every place your products are sold, including your own site and resellers, with the lowest regular and promotional price in each. Set a pricing policy that keeps Walmart at or below that floor, and decide in advance which promotions will run only on Walmart or not at all. Then price out Walmart Fulfillment Services for your top products, since the faster shipping tags improve your chance of winning the featured offer.

The rule of thumb fits on a sticky note: your Walmart price is the lowest price a shopper can find for your product anywhere. We run Walmart Marketplace for brands from launch through pricing, fulfillment and advertising.

A0010.crumb: Walmart Connect asks brands to merge…
A0010.title: Walmart Connect asks brands to merge budgets that sit apart
A0010.alt: Two tilted glass jars pouring coins into a third jar on a wooden table.
A0010.ttag: Walmart Connect asks brands to merge budgets that sit apart | Kwontified
A0010.desc: Walmart Connect now sells ads on its site, in its stores and across the web, yet most brands split those budgets across three teams that rarely meet.
A0010.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 4, 2021.
A0010.body:
At most brands that sell through Walmart, three teams spend money to reach the same shopper. Sales funds promotions through the Walmart relationship. Shopper marketing buys in-store activations. Media buys digital advertising, much of it on other sites. On January 28, 2021, Walmart renamed its ad business Walmart Connect and described a single offer covering its website, its stores and the wider internet.

In effect, Walmart is asking brands to plan three budgets as one. Few brands are organized to do that, and the first decision is who owns the relationship.

Walmart Connect is selling one plan across three places

The announcement was specific. Walmart said its media business, until then called Walmart Media Group, would focus on three areas, with the aim of becoming one of the ten largest advertising platforms in the United States.

On its own properties, including Walmart.com, the Walmart app and its pickup and delivery service, Walmart Connect sells search and display ads. Walmart said this part of the business nearly doubled its revenue and more than doubled its number of advertisers in its last fiscal year. In stores, advertisers can now buy placements on TV walls and self-checkout screens, nearly 170,000 digital screens across more than 4,500 stores. Off Walmart’s properties, a partnership with The Trade Desk will launch a demand-side platform (DSP), the software advertisers use to buy ads across many websites, in time for the 2021 holiday season.

Walmart’s data ties the three together. The company described Walmart Connect as a closed-loop business, meaning it can connect an ad to a purchase in its own records whether the shopper buys online or in a store, and it says it reaches 150 million customers a week.

The three placements usually belong to three teams

Walk the halls of a typical consumer brand and each of those placements has a different home. Search ads on Walmart.com tend to sit with the e-commerce team, which manages the brand’s Walmart listings and reports on online sales. In-store screens look like shopper marketing, a budget often tied to the brand’s annual plan with Walmart’s merchants and negotiated alongside trade promotion. Ads bought through a DSP across the wider web belong to the media team or its agency, which plans reach and frequency across every channel, Walmart being one of many.

Each of those teams also has its own Walmart contact, so the conversations run in parallel, on different calendars, and the budgets rarely meet. It is a little like three departments buying space on the same shelf through three different doors.

Each team has its own goals and its own measures. E-commerce is judged on Walmart.com sales. Shopper marketing is judged on store sell-through and the health of the Walmart relationship. Media is judged on reach and cost, and often on sales across all retailers. Walmart Connect’s pitch is that one measure, sales recorded in Walmart’s own data, can judge all three.

The pitch is attractive, and it carries a risk. Walmart’s figures will count sales at Walmart. They will not show whether an ad bought on Walmart’s DSP also lifted sales at Target or on Amazon, or whether it simply moved a shopper who would have bought anyway. A brand that lets Walmart’s reports decide all three budgets is letting one retailer grade its own work.

Who in the brand should own the Walmart relationship?

For most brands that sell at Walmart, some Walmart Connect spending is already happening under other names. The live question in the leadership meeting is who decides how much, and on what evidence.

Each of the three honest answers carries a cost. The e-commerce team knows Walmart’s digital shelf best but rarely controls trade or media money. The sales team owns the Walmart relationship and the largest budgets, but is measured on orders rather than advertising returns. The media team understands reach and incrementality, but may treat Walmart as one placement among dozens. Whoever takes the lead will need the other two in the room.

In practice the deciding factor tends to be where the money already sits. Trade budgets at large consumer brands are often far bigger than digital media budgets at any single retailer, so the sales team has the most to move. A leader who hands Walmart Connect to e-commerce without access to trade money has handed over responsibility without the means to act on it. A leader who hands it to sales should ask for advertising measures alongside order volume.

Walmart’s broader strategy makes the decision more pressing. It said Walmart+ would build loyal customers and shopper data, and its marketplace counted close to 70,000 sellers as 2020 ended, according to Marketplace Pulse data reported by Modern Retail. Every one of those sellers is a potential advertiser, and more advertisers means more competition for the same placements. Brands that settle internal ownership early will negotiate from a clearer position.

How Walmart sells the DSP when it launches will show which budget it is really after. Priced and reported as a Walmart product, it will land with the trade and e-commerce teams. Sold as media, it will go to agencies.

Before then, a brand can add up what it already spends with Walmart across trade promotion, in-store activation and Walmart.com advertising, team by team, and name one owner with defined roles for the other two. It should also agree, before buying anything new, how it will judge Walmart Connect beyond Walmart’s own reports, including a holdout test for any off-site spend. We plan and run retail media across Amazon, Walmart and Target, including how a Walmart budget fits the rest of the plan.

A0018.title: Amazon advertising revenue outran its sales in Q4 2020
A0018.alt: A tall stack of coins beside twine-tied kraft paper parcels on a wooden table.
A0018.ttag: Amazon advertising revenue outran its sales in Q4 2020 | Kwontified
A0018.desc: Amazon’s ad-heavy revenue line grew 66% in Q4 2020 while units grew only 47%, so brands paid more advertising for every sale, and ROAS hid it.
A0018.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 9, 2021.
A0018.body:
Amazon had a record holiday quarter, so why do so many brands’ fourth-quarter reports show advertising eating a larger share of every sale? Amazon’s own results answer it. The revenue line that is mostly advertising grew 66% in the quarter, while the units Amazon sold grew 47%. Advertisers spent faster than shoppers bought, and the advertising cost of each sale went up.

For 2021, that means setting targets on advertising cost per sale, with return on ad spend as a second check.

Amazon advertising revenue grew faster than the units it sold

The figures come from Amazon’s fourth-quarter release. Amazon does not report advertising on its own. It reports a line called “other,” which it says primarily includes sales of advertising services. That line reached $7.95 billion in the fourth quarter of 2020, up from $4.78 billion a year earlier, a 66% increase. Worldwide paid units, the number of items Amazon and its sellers sold, grew 47%.

Divide one growth factor by the other and you get a rough measure of advertising revenue per unit sold: 1.66 divided by 1.47 is about 1.13. For every unit sold, Amazon collected about 13% more, mostly in advertising, than a year earlier.

The third quarter shows how quickly that gap opened.

Quarter“Other” revenueGrowthPaid unit growthChange per unit
Q3 2020$3.59 billion to $5.40 billion51%46%about 3%
Q4 2020$4.78 billion to $7.95 billion66%47%about 13%

In one quarter, the distance between advertising growth and sales growth went from roughly 3% to roughly 13%.

More bidders than lots

Amazon’s sponsored ads are sold by auction. When more advertisers bid for the same searches, the price of each click rises, even if the number of shoppers searching rises too. The ratio is what counts: if advertiser budgets grow faster than shopper demand, each sale takes more advertising to win.

Picture an auction room where the number of bidders doubles but the number of lots on offer rises only by half. Final prices climb, and nobody has to agree to pay more. The room does it for them.

The fourth quarter of 2020 added more bidders than usual. Prime Day moved into October, inside the quarter, and many brands planned extra budgets around it. The holiday season followed with budgets of its own. Brands that had moved money from stores and other channels into Amazon during the year were now bidding in the same auctions. Shopper demand grew strongly, and advertiser demand grew faster.

Two caveats keep the estimate honest. The “other” line includes services besides advertising, so the 13% indicates direction rather than a precise price index. And part of the line can come from advertisers that do not sell products on Amazon, such as entertainment or automotive brands buying video and display ads, which lifts the figure without competing for a consumer brand’s searches. That makes 13% an upper estimate for search ads specifically. Even a fraction of it changes a brand’s margin over a year, and the direction matches the rising ad costs many brands saw in their own accounts.

What a higher cost per sale does to the plan

The damage hides in the measure brands watch most. Return on ad spend (ROAS) divides attributed sales by ad spend. It can hold steady while the advertising cost of the business rises, because it says nothing about the sales that happened without ads. In a quarter like this one it can even improve, since attributed sales swell when more shoppers are buying anyway and the ads collect credit for demand the season created.

Take a brand that sold $1 million on Amazon in the fourth quarter of 2019, with $100,000 of advertising, a 10% advertising cost of sales. In the fourth quarter of 2020 it sold $1.4 million. If advertising cost per sale rose 13%, its ad spend would be roughly $158,000, or about 11.3% of sales. The brand grew, and each dollar of revenue carried more advertising than before, which comes straight out of margin.

The choice from here has two sides. A brand can hold its advertising cost of sales flat by bidding less, and lose some placements to competitors willing to pay more. Or it can keep its share of the auction and accept a higher cost per sale. Both are defensible. Making the choice by accident, because ROAS looked fine, is not.

The same release gives a reason to expect the pressure to last. Third-party seller services revenue reached $27.3 billion, up 57%, and sellers’ share of paid units reached 55%, the highest in the table. More sellers chasing the same shoppers means more bidders in 2021.

The conclusion would change if advertiser demand slowed while shopper demand held, for instance if brands cut budgets sharply once stores reopen. The first quarter of 2021, for which Amazon expects net sales of $100 billion to $106 billion, will show whether the gap narrows.

A test to run before setting 2021 targets

Work out your total advertising cost of sales, ad spend divided by all Amazon sales, for each quarter of 2020, and lay it next to your ROAS trend. Run it by product family if you can, because the gap is rarely even across a catalog. If ROAS held while the cost of sales climbed, the auction got more expensive and the ROAS chart hid it.

Set 2021 targets on advertising cost per unit or per order alongside ROAS, and decide in advance which products justify paying more to keep their placements. Planning on the full cost of sales is how we budget Amazon advertising for brands.
