A0020.crumb: Target Plus sits outside the engine of…
A0020.title: Target Plus sits outside the engine of Target’s growth
A0020.alt: A red shopping cart standing alone in front of warehouse loading docks beside a parked blue trailer.
A0020.ttag: Target Plus sits outside the engine of Target’s growth | Kwontified
A0020.desc: Target’s holiday digital growth ran through store pickup and same-day delivery, and Target Plus items, shipped from sellers’ own warehouses, ride neither.
A0020.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 11, 2021.
A0020.body:
Picture the Saturday Drive Up order: groceries, cleaning supplies, a few household items, all picked from the shelves of a store a few miles away and loaded into the trunk at the curb. That basket is where Target’s holiday growth came from, and a Target Plus product can’t get into it. Marketplace items ship from the seller’s own warehouse instead.

Many brands hear that Target’s digital sales doubled over the holidays and reach for Target Plus as their way in. They should see the marketplace for what it is: a separate, slower channel, to be weighed honestly against a vendor relationship with Target’s stores.

Target’s growth runs through its stores, apart from Target Plus

The holiday numbers are clear about where the growth came from. Target reported that comparable sales grew 17.2% over November and December, with comparable digital sales up 102%. Its same-day services grew 193% together, counting Order Pick Up, Drive Up and Shipt. Drive Up alone grew more than 500%, and sales fulfilled through Shipt grew more than 300%. About 95% of Target’s sales in the period were fulfilled by its stores.

A service growing that fast tends to become a routine, and routines decide which products get bought without a second search.

Those figures describe an institution that has built its digital business on top of its 1,900 stores. A shopper orders on the app, a store team picks the order from the shelves and hands it over at the curb, often the same day. The stores are the warehouses, and their shelves define what can be delivered that quickly.

Brian Cornell, Target’s chief executive, said in the same release that strong sales had continued into the new year and that Target’s 2021 plans focus on building on the guest engagement and market share it gained in 2020. Nothing in that plan suggests the store-based model is about to change.

Target Plus items take a different route to the shopper

Target Plus works another way. A marketplace seller lists its products on Target.com, holds its own inventory and ships orders from its own warehouse or fulfillment partner. By December 2019, the Star Tribune found nearly 100 sellers offering more than 250,000 products. Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the research firm Marketplace Pulse, pointed out to the paper that most of Target’s online growth came from same-day delivery and store pickup, which did not include marketplace items.

That gives Target Plus real advantages and one structural limit. The advantages are the ones Target designed: marketplace items appear on a site with heavy traffic, Target’s card holders keep their 5% discount and free shipping on marketplace orders, and returns can go back to a store. The limit is speed. A Target Plus product cannot ride the service that grew fastest over the holidays, because it isn’t on the shelf of a store near the shopper.

In some categories that hardly matters. A shopper buying a specialized item Target doesn’t stock in stores expects it to come by mail. For everyday products, where the habit is to add things to a pickup order, the gap is wide.

Take the Saturday basket again. A dish soap on Target’s shelves joins that order with one tap. The same soap sold only through Target Plus arrives separately, days later, in its own box. Most shoppers choose the brand already in the basket, and a product that can’t join it competes for a different, slower moment in the shopper’s week.

The real choice is between the shelf and the site

Seen this way, the brand’s question gets wider: which relationship with Target serves its products best?

A vendor relationship with Target’s stores puts the product on the shelf, and the shelf brings it into Drive Up, Order Pick Up and Shipt automatically. It also brings the obligations of a store vendor. Target buys the inventory, sets the shelf price and controls the assortment, and the brand works inside Target’s planning calendar.

Supplying the stores also means meeting Target’s requirements for shipping to its distribution centers, a different operational muscle from sending single orders to a shopper’s door. Target Plus offers the opposite trade: the brand keeps control of price and inventory and can list a wider range, but ships every order itself and sits outside Target’s fastest-growing service.

Neither route wins in general. A brand with a narrow range of everyday products, strong store sales elsewhere and the capacity to supply Target’s distribution centers may be better served chasing a place on the shelf. A brand with a wide or specialized catalog, or one that wants to test demand before asking for shelf space, may find Target Plus the better first step. Some brands will end up doing both, with everyday lines on the shelf and the long tail of the catalog on Target Plus, which works only if someone keeps the two price lists consistent.

The calculation would shift if Target began bringing marketplace items into its same-day services, or into stores for pickup, and that is worth watching through 2021. Until then, Target Plus is best planned as a mail-order channel attached to a store-based retailer.

The useful exercise is to sort the catalog into products shoppers buy on a regular pickup or delivery run and products they order once and wait for. Then weigh the store route for the first group and Target Plus for the second, operational load included. Put that sorted list in front of the leadership team before an invitation or a buyer meeting forces the decision. Choosing which route into Target fits a catalog is part of how we manage Target Plus and Walmart for brands.

A0022.crumb: Mercado Libre for brands is a…
A0022.title: Mercado Libre for brands is a local-currency business first
A0022.alt: A wooden tray of coins on a striped cloth at an outdoor market stall with clay pots, baskets and corn.
A0022.ttag: Mercado Libre for brands is a local-currency business first | Kwontified
A0022.desc: Mercado Libre’s sales volume grew 117.1% in local terms and 62.1% in dollars in one quarter, so brands judging the channel in dollars are misreading it.
A0022.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 16, 2021.
A0022.body:
The channel team’s dashboard says Mercado Libre sales are growing well. The finance team’s dollar report says something more modest. Both are right, and Mercado Libre’s own results show how far apart they can drift: its sales volume grew 117.1% in the third quarter of 2020 at constant exchange rates and 62.1% in dollars. Currency translation cut the reported growth roughly in half.

A brand that judges Mercado Libre in dollars is misreading the channel. Set the targets in local currency, and treat currency as a separate question with its own owner.

Mercado Libre for brands: two growth rates from one quarter

The figures come from Mercado Libre’s third-quarter release. Gross merchandise volume, the value of everything sold on the marketplace, reached $5.9 billion. In dollars that was 62.1% more than a year earlier. At the previous year’s exchange rates, growth was 117.1%.

Nothing about the business differs between those two numbers. The same shoppers bought the same items in the same quarter. The whole gap comes from converting local sales into dollars: over the period, the currencies of Mercado Libre’s main markets fell against the dollar, so each local sale was worth fewer dollars once translated.

The operating figures, which do not depend on currency at all, show the demand underneath. Mercado Libre’s logistics service shipped 187.6 million items, 131.1% more than a year earlier, and the marketplace had 76.1 million unique active users, up 92.2%. Those are the numbers a brand’s operations will actually feel, in warehouses, delivery times and customer questions.

Why the dollar figure misleads the channel team

A brand selling in Brazil earns reais. Its costs on the ground, from fulfillment to advertising, are charged in reais. Its competitors price in reais, and its shoppers compare prices in reais. Every decision that determines whether the brand wins on the marketplace is made in local currency, and only the final report turns the result into dollars.

Judging that business in dollars is like measuring a growing child with a ruler that shrinks a little each year. The child is growing. The ruler makes it look slower, and the shrinking has nothing to do with the child.

Take a brand that doubles its sales in Brazil while the real falls 25% against the dollar.

Local currencyIn dollars
Sales, first year1 million reaisfull value
Sales, second year2 million reaisworth three quarters as much per real
Reported growth100%50%

A manager judged on the dollar line looks like half as good an operator as one judged on the local line, for exactly the same work. The error runs the other way too. When a local currency strengthens, dollar results flatter the channel and can hide a stall. Neither direction says anything about whether the listings, prices and advertising are working.

Advertising budgets set in dollars drift on their own

Advertising shows the problem most clearly. Bids in Mercado Libre’s auctions are placed in local currency, against competitors bidding in the same currency. A brand that sets its monthly advertising budget in dollars and converts it at the start of each month will see the local budget shrink when the currency weakens and grow when it strengthens. Its share of the auction then rises and falls for reasons unrelated to how well its ads perform. Through a stretch of falling currency, the same dollar budget buys less of the auction each month while competitors budgeting locally hold steady.

The team running the account sees results move, digs through its keywords and bids, and finds nothing wrong, because the cause was the conversion on the first of the month. A budget set in local currency removes that noise and leaves the currency decision with finance, where it belongs.

Currency is a real cost, so give it its own line

None of this makes the dollar figure unimportant. A brand that earns reais and reports in dollars carries the currency risk, and that risk is real money. Mercado Libre itself recorded a $30.4 million foreign exchange loss in the quarter, linked to exchange rates in Argentina, according to the same release.

The point is to separate two questions the dollar figure blends together. One is operational: is the brand gaining customers and share on Mercado Libre? That gets answered in local currency, against local competitors.

The other is financial: how much of the local performance survives conversion, and should the brand hedge, reprice or hold cash locally? That belongs to finance, reviewed in the same meeting on its own line. The channel team can act on the first question every week. It can do nothing about the second.

Pricing is where the two questions collide. A brand can raise local prices to protect its dollar margin when a currency falls, and risk losing share to local competitors who face no such pressure. Or it can hold prices, keep its customers and accept a lower dollar result. Both are reasonable. Making the choice deliberately takes both numbers side by side, and a decision made in advance about how large a currency move would change the answer.

A report that keeps the questions apart looks something like this:

LineMeasured inWho answers for it
Sales, advertising cost and margin by countryLocal currencyThe channel team
Currency effect on those resultsDollars, shown separatelyFinance
Pricing response to a large currency moveBoth, side by sideLeadership, by a policy agreed in advance

The rule of thumb: if a number can move without a single shopper doing anything differently, it should not be the number the channel team is judged on. Reporting every result in local currency next to dollars is how we run Mercado Libre accounts for brands across Latin America.

A0023.crumb: Roundel is built like a media partner, so…
A0023.title: Roundel is built like a media partner, so buy it like one
A0023.alt: A red endcap shelf stocked with pastel product boxes in a bright, empty retail store aisle.
A0023.ttag: Roundel is built like a media partner, so buy it like one | Kwontified
A0023.desc: Target built Roundel as an in-house media company that designs campaigns with brands, so planning it like a self-serve auction misses what it is.
A0023.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 18, 2021.
A0023.body:
Ask a brand’s advertising team how it buys on Amazon and you hear about keywords, bids and daily budgets. Ask how it buys from Target and the answer sounds more like a meeting with an agency: an annual plan, a proposal, a campaign built together over several rounds. That difference in vocabulary is not a quirk of the team. Target built Roundel, its advertising business, as an in-house media company that creates campaigns with brands, and it sells that way.

So brands should plan Roundel as a negotiated partnership, owned by a named leader and judged on measures agreed before the money is spent.

How Roundel took shape as a media company inside a retailer

The history explains the shape. Target has run an in-house media business since 2016, creating digital advertising for major brands, not all of which sell at Target, the Star Tribune reported. In May 2019, Target renamed the business Roundel, from Target Media Network, and said it intended to become a more aggressive player in the field.

The description at the time was a media company’s description. Roundel worked with about 1,000 clients, including companies in financial services, automotive and travel, and helped them build personalized campaigns for Target.com and about 150 other sites and platforms, among them Pinterest and Instagram. Its president, Kristi Argyilan, described the brand as a blend of “math” and “magic”: Target’s data and analytics combined with the design sense the retailer is known for. Target said the business had grown by double digits and was a source of profitable growth, but declined to give revenue figures.

That origin still shapes how brands meet Roundel. A business that began by building campaigns for clients tends to sell through relationships and proposals. Its strengths, the quality of the creative work and what Target knows about its shoppers, are delivered through people rather than through a bidding console.

Target’s 2020 makes the data worth more

What gives Roundel its value is Target’s knowledge of its shoppers, and that knowledge grew sharply in 2020. Target reported that comparable digital sales grew 102% over November and December, and that its same-day pickup and delivery services grew 193%. Each of those orders ties a shopper’s identity to what they bought, whether the item left a store shelf or a delivery van.

For a brand, that means Target can increasingly connect its advertising to purchases, in stores and online. It also means Target holds the measurement. When Roundel reports on a campaign, it is reporting sales recorded in Target’s systems, using Target’s methods.

Walmart offers a useful contrast. On January 28, 2021, it renamed its own media business Walmart Connect and published specific figures: revenue from ads on its site and app came close to doubling over its last fiscal year, and the count of advertisers more than doubled. Walmart also said it aims to rank among the ten largest US ad platforms. Target has been quieter about Roundel’s scale, which leaves brands with less outside evidence to plan against when they set annual budgets.

What a partnership asks of the brand

A partnership can produce better work than an auction, because a team that knows Target’s shoppers designs the campaign. It also asks things of the brand that an auction never does.

Someone has to own it. A self-serve auction can be run by an analyst on the e-commerce team. A partnership with a retailer’s media company needs a leader who can negotiate a plan, judge a proposal and hold Target to its commitments. In many brands the person closest to that role is the sales lead for the Target account, whose main job is the relationship with Target’s merchants, and mixing the two conversations can blur both.

The money often comes from the same place, which makes the separation harder still. When a Roundel plan is funded out of the brand’s trade budget with Target, it can start to feel like part of the cost of keeping shelf space rather than an investment expected to return sales. Say a brand agrees a $500,000 Roundel plan as part of its annual Target negotiation. If nobody sets a target for what that money should return, the plan gets renewed in 2022 on the strength of the relationship, whatever it produced. The same $500,000 spent through an auction would be questioned every week.

The measures also need agreeing in advance. When Target designs the campaign and also reports the result, the brand needs its own view of success. That means a baseline of sales before the campaign, a comparison of similar periods, and where possible a test with shoppers or stores that did not see the ads.

If Roundel adds self-serve buying of the kind Amazon offers, part of the budget will move to the teams that run auctions elsewhere, and the partnership will narrow to the larger campaigns. That would be worth noticing through 2021. It would not remove the need for an owner.

Questions before the next Roundel plan

  1. Who in the company owns the Roundel relationship, and is that conversation kept apart from the annual negotiation with Target’s merchants?
  2. Is the plan funded from trade or from media, and does the answer change how hard anyone looks at its return?
  3. Have we agreed in writing how results will be measured, including a baseline and, where possible, a holdout?
  4. Is Roundel judged against the same return we expect from Amazon and Walmart, and if not, why not?

Answering those is part of how we plan and measure Roundel alongside Amazon and Walmart Connect for the brands we work with.

A0024.crumb: Instagram shopping will look weaker in…
A0024.title: Instagram shopping will look weaker in reports than in sales
A0024.alt: A canvas tote bag filled with bread, greens, bananas and books beside a smartphone on a wooden table.
A0024.ttag: Instagram shopping will look weaker in reports than in sales | Kwontified
A0024.desc: Facebook expects Apple’s iOS 14 changes to weaken ad measurement from late Q1 2021, so Instagram shopping results may drop in reports before sales do.
A0024.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 23, 2021.
A0024.body:
Some time this spring, a brand’s Instagram dashboard is likely to show purchases falling while the warehouse ships about as many orders as before. On January 27, Facebook told investors that Apple’s iOS 14 changes would bring “more significant ad targeting headwinds,” starting late in the first quarter. When a platform loses some of the data it uses to connect ads to purchases, the sales still happen. Fewer of them get counted.

So reported Instagram shopping results may fall before real sales do. Brands that set an independent baseline now will be able to tell the two apart, and brands that rely on Facebook’s reports alone will be tempted to cut spending that is still working.

Instagram shopping spread into every corner of the app

The timing matters because Instagram spent 2020 building shopping into nearly everything. On November 12, 2020, it put a Shop tab on the home screen, replacing the button users had long used to check their notifications, CNN Business reported. Asked how much shopping happens in the app, Instagram gave the network no figures.

On December 10, Instagram added shopping to Reels, its short-video format, so viewers could tap “View Products” to buy, save or learn more about items in a video, TechCrunch reported. With that launch, users could shop from videos in Feed, Stories, Live, IGTV and Reels. TechCrunch noted that Instagram makes money when customers check out inside the app using Facebook Pay, on top of running ads.

Facebook’s results show why the push made sense. Advertising revenue grew 31% to $27.2 billion in the fourth quarter of 2020, Facebook reported. Its finance chief said the business had benefited from the shift toward online commerce and toward buying products rather than services, and warned that a slowdown in either trend could become a headwind.

A scoreboard that stops counting some goals

When a shopper taps an Instagram ad and buys on a brand’s website, Facebook learns about the purchase through tracking that follows the shopper from the app to the site. Apple’s iOS 14 changes ask iPhone users whether apps may track them across other companies’ apps and websites. A shopper who declines can still see the ad and still buy. Some of those purchases simply stop being connected back to the ad.

Think of a scoreboard that stops counting some of the goals. The team plays exactly as well as before, and the score it reports goes down. A coach who manages by the scoreboard alone would bench players who are still scoring.

Take a brand whose Instagram ads drive 1,000 purchases a month on its website, all of them recorded. If a third of those buyers can no longer be tracked after the change, Facebook’s reports show about 667 purchases. Reported return on ad spend falls by a third. Actual sales are unchanged.

The pull to resist is treating the reported figure as the truth because it is the only number on the screen. It is a measurement, and the way it is measured is about to change. That is easy to say in February and hard to remember in a March review, when the chart is pointing down and someone wants a decision.

Why the drop will not land evenly

The change applies to iPhone users, so a brand whose customers mostly use iPhones will see a bigger fall in reported results than a brand whose customers mostly use other phones. Two brands with identical sales trends could see very different changes in their Facebook reports and draw opposite conclusions about the same channel. Comparing your reported results with a competitor’s, or with an industry benchmark, gets less reliable for the same reason, because every brand’s mix of phones differs.

Timing adds a second distortion. Facebook expects the impact to begin late in the first quarter, which overlaps with the usual slowdown after the holidays. A brand that sees reported results fall in March will be tempted to call it seasonality or ad fatigue, when part of it is a change in counting.

In-app checkout keeps the sale in view, at a price

The same mechanism explains why Instagram is pushing checkout inside its app. A purchase completed on Instagram happens where Instagram can see it, whatever the shopper chose about cross-app tracking. Checkout keeps the sale on the scoreboard.

For brands, that sets up a real choice. Selling through Instagram checkout keeps results measurable and removes a step for the shopper. The catch is that the transaction happens on Instagram’s platform, which earns money from it, and the brand gives up the visit to its own site, where it can collect an email address and sell a second item. Sending shoppers to the brand’s site keeps the customer relationship, and more of those sales will go uncounted.

A brand with a strong email program and high repeat purchase rates has more to gain from bringing shoppers to its own site. A brand selling single, impulse items may prefer the shorter path. The mistake would be letting the change in measurement make that decision by default.

Before the counting changes

Record weekly sales from every channel, alongside Instagram-reported purchases, for the weeks before the iOS 14 changes take effect. That record is the baseline everything after it gets compared with. From then on, judge Instagram spending on total sales trends and on controlled tests, such as pausing ads in one region for a period, with Facebook’s reported results as one input among several. And decide product by product which items should use Instagram checkout and which should send shoppers to your own site, based on what the customer relationship is worth.

The rule to carry into the spring: when the report and the warehouse disagree, believe the warehouse until a test says otherwise. Measuring social commerce against total sales is how we run Instagram and TikTok selling for brands.

A0026.crumb: Vendor Central is Amazon’s choice now…
A0026.title: Vendor Central is Amazon’s choice now, not the brand’s
A0026.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet of cardboard boxes at an open roll-up door on a warehouse loading dock.
A0026.ttag: Vendor Central is Amazon’s choice now, not the brand’s | Kwontified
A0026.desc: In March 2019, tens of thousands of Amazon vendors found no weekly purchase order waiting, which is why Vendor Central now deserves a yearly review.
A0026.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 25, 2021.
A0026.body:
One week in March 2019, tens of thousands of Amazon vendors opened Vendor Central and found no weekly purchase order waiting. Many of them had shipped cases to Amazon for years, the way they shipped to any large retailer. Some were told Amazon had decided their business would do better as a third-party seller.

That week is worth remembering in every brand’s annual planning. Amazon’s own figures show its growth coming from third-party sellers, and Amazon has shown it will decide which brands stay vendors. Vendor Central is a status Amazon can change, and brands should review it each year as a choice rather than carry it forward as a fixed relationship.

Amazon Vendor Central took hold when Amazon was mainly a retailer

The habit has a clear origin. For brands that started on Amazon years ago, Amazon first appeared as a buyer. It bought inventory at wholesale prices, set its own retail prices and handled the customer. The relationship sat with the sales team, next to the department store and mass accounts, and it was measured in that team’s language: order volume, margin, payment terms. For a long time the arrangement made sense, and for many brands it still does.

Inside Amazon, the balance has shifted. In the fourth quarter of 2020, third-party sellers accounted for 55% of the units sold on Amazon, up from 53% a year earlier, according to Amazon’s results. Third-party seller services revenue grew 57% in the quarter, faster than the 46% growth in Amazon’s online stores, the line that holds most of its own retail sales. The marketplace, where brands sell directly, is growing faster than the store where Amazon buys and resells.

Amazon has shown it will make the choice

The bigger change is in who decides. When the purchase orders stopped in March 2019, agency executives told Modern Retail that many of the affected vendors did about $10 million or less in annual sales on Amazon and had no assigned vendor manager. In the same period, according to the report, Amazon told some larger vendors that any business they ran at the same time as third-party sellers would be removed, and ended a program for vendors who shipped orders directly to customers.

An agency chief executive told the publication that the days of a brand choosing for itself whether to be first party, third party or both were over. Amazon’s spokesperson said the company regularly reviews its selling partner relationships, and said there was no program called “One Vendor,” the name the press had given to the idea of merging the two systems.

Taken together, the message from Amazon as an institution is consistent. It wants as much of its retail business as possible to run without hands-on management, and it decides which brands justify the attention a vendor relationship requires. A brand’s Vendor Central status rests on how Amazon judges the account’s revenue, catalog and profitability, measures the brand does not fully control. It is a little like a wholesale account the buyer can close on its own terms, which is not how most brands’ sales teams think about their largest customer.

The question this leaves on the leadership agenda

None of this means vendors should rush to Seller Central. Vendor Central still offers real advantages: Amazon carries the inventory, handles pricing and gives the brand a single large customer. For a brand with complex wholesale relationships, letting Amazon set retail prices can head off conflict with other retailers. Selling as a third-party seller means holding inventory, setting prices, running advertising and managing the account every day, and that takes people and systems many vendors do not have.

The question in the room is narrower and harder: has the brand chosen Vendor Central, or simply stayed there? Many brands became vendors when Amazon was mainly a retailer and have renewed the arrangement each year without asking whether it still fits how Amazon now works.

A brand that has never modeled its Amazon business as a third-party seller, with its own pricing, fulfillment costs and advertising, cannot say which arrangement serves it better. And if Amazon one day stops sending purchase orders, that brand will be making the decision in weeks rather than months.

A rough comparison shows why the modeling matters. Take a product that Amazon buys at $20 and sells for $30.

Per unitAs a vendorAs a third-party seller
Retail price$30, set by Amazon$30, set by the brand
Referral fee—$4.50 (15%)
Fulfillment fee—$5
Brand receives before advertising and storage$20about $20.50

On those assumptions the two models look much the same on paper. The real differences sit in who controls the price, who holds the inventory and who pays for advertising, and those vary from brand to brand. Only the brand’s own numbers, product by product, can say which model wins.

The direction of travel is visible in the third-party share of Amazon’s units. Each quarter it rises, Amazon’s own retail team becomes a smaller part of the company, and the list of brands it chooses to buy from directly is likely to narrow with it.

The practical response is modest. Model the third-party version of the business, with real prices, fees and advertising, and set it next to the current vendor terms. Identify which of Amazon’s likely measures, such as revenue, catalog size and profitability, put the vendor status at risk. Then put a date in the calendar each year when leadership decides, deliberately, which side of Amazon the brand wants to be on, and ask when that decision was last made on purpose. We manage Amazon for brands as vendors, as sellers and through the move between the two.

A0028.crumb: Amazon DSP pays off when search ads run…
A0028.title: Amazon DSP pays off when search ads run out of shoppers
A0028.alt: An open door in a green-walled room looking out onto a quiet village road with stone cottages and hills.
A0028.ttag: Amazon DSP pays off when search ads run out of shoppers | Kwontified
A0028.desc: Sponsored ads only reach shoppers who are already searching, so Amazon DSP earns budget once the next search dollar returns less than a tested DSP dollar.
A0028.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 2, 2021.
A0028.body:
Put an Amazon DSP report next to a sponsored ads report and DSP almost always looks worse. The return per dollar is lower, the path from ad to order is longer, and the sales it claims are harder to believe. Brands that started on sponsored ads, the ads in Amazon’s search results, read that comparison and conclude DSP is the weaker channel.

The comparison is accurate and the conclusion is wrong. Sponsored ads can only reach shoppers who are already searching, so each extra dollar buys a weaker search than the last. Amazon DSP, which buys display and video ads on and off Amazon, earns its place at the point where the next search dollar returns less than a tested DSP dollar.

Amazon DSP adoption grew in 2020, and so did the budgets

More brands crossed that point in 2020. In a survey of more than 1,000 US brands fielded from December 16, 2020 to January 2, 2021, 26% more brands said they were using Amazon DSP than a year earlier, Feedvisor reported. The survey described DSP as a way to reach shoppers on and off Amazon, both higher and lower in the path to purchase.

Budgets rose alongside it. In the same survey, 59% of brands said they spend more than $60,000 a month on Amazon advertising, up from 38% a year earlier. Amazon’s own figures tell the same story for the whole market: its “other” revenue, mostly advertising, grew 66% during the fourth quarter of 2020, to $7.95 billion, according to Amazon’s results.

One survey figure needs a careful read. Over half of brands, 51%, said they see a return of seven times or more on Amazon advertising. That is self-reported, from a survey run by a company that sells advertising optimization, and it describes Amazon advertising as a whole. It says almost nothing about where the next dollar should go.

Fishing the same pond harder

Sponsored ads are bought against searches, and on any given day only so many shoppers search for a brand’s category. The first dollars buy the most valuable of those searches: the brand’s own name and the terms most tightly tied to its products. Each additional dollar has to buy something worse, such as broader terms, higher positions at higher prices, or searches where the shopper is less likely to pick the brand.

It is like fishing the same pond harder. The first hour brings in the easy catch, and every extra hour brings in less, because the pond holds only so many fish. In 2020 the pond also got crowded. Other brands bid for the same searches, the auction sets prices from those bids, and when several brands raise budgets at once, as Amazon’s 66% advertising growth in the fourth quarter suggests many did, each pays more for the same shoppers. At some point the better move is to fish somewhere else, even if the new spot looks less promising at first.

Amazon DSP is that other spot. It reaches shoppers who are not searching right now: people who viewed a product last week, people who buy in related categories, people browsing other sites. Its reported return per dollar is usually lower than the best sponsored ads, because those shoppers are further from buying. It also draws on a pool that search ads cannot touch at all. That makes the two channels complements more than rivals, and it is why the useful comparison between them sits at the margin, where the next dollar goes, and not in the averages either report shows.

Comparing the last dollar with the next one

Take a brand spending $50,000 a month on sponsored ads and earning $6 in sales for every dollar. It adds another $20,000, and the extra spending earns only $2 per dollar, because it is buying weaker searches.

SpendSales per dollarSales
First block of sponsored ads$50,000$6$300,000
Added sponsored ads$20,000$2$40,000
All sponsored ads$70,000$4.86$340,000

The blended $4.86 still looks healthy, and it hides how poorly the last $20,000 is doing. Now say a $20,000 test on Amazon DSP, measured against a group of shoppers who did not see the ads, shows $3 of additional sales per dollar. On those numbers the last $20,000 belongs in DSP. The DSP figure is lower than the brand’s best sponsored ads and higher than its worst ones, and the worst ones are where the budget decision actually gets made.

The case against moving the money is real too. DSP is harder to measure. Its reports count sales from shoppers who saw an ad but never clicked, and many of them might have bought anyway. A brand that shifts budget to DSP on the strength of its own dashboard, with no test, may be swapping a small, measurable return for an inflated one. The numbers lean toward DSP only when the brand can show what it adds.

The test before the move

Split sponsored ads results into first dollars and last dollars, by campaign or keyword group, and find the return on the most recent increase in spending. Before moving any of it, run a DSP test with a group of shoppers who do not see the ads, and compare the additional sales per dollar with that last block of search spending. Then repeat the comparison every quarter, because the point where search runs out of shoppers moves with the seasons, with competitors and with your own product range.

The rule of thumb: never judge a channel by its average when the decision is about its margin. Testing where each dollar earns most, across sponsored ads and DSP, is how we plan Amazon DSP for brands.

A0029.crumb: Amazon Marketing Cloud brings the brand’s…
A0029.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud brings the brand’s data into Amazon’s room
A0029.alt: An open wooden index card box with brass latches on a long oak table in a bright white room.
A0029.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud brings the brand’s data into Amazon’s room | Kwontified
A0029.desc: Brands have long asked Amazon to send them more ad data. Amazon Marketing Cloud answers the other way: bring your data into a room that Amazon controls.
A0029.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 4, 2021.
A0029.body:
For years, the request from brand analysts to Amazon has sounded the same in every quarterly review: send us more of the advertising data, at a finer grain, so our own team can study it. On January 4, 2021, Amazon gave its answer, and it runs the other way. Amazon Marketing Cloud invites brands to bring their own data into an environment Amazon designs and controls, analyze it there next to Amazon’s advertising signals, and leave with aggregated answers.

That is a real gain for brands, and it also shows exactly where Amazon draws the line on who keeps the records. Leaders should plan for the arrangement as it is, and invest in the people who can ask it good questions.

What Amazon launched with Amazon Marketing Cloud

Amazon introduced the service in a blog post as a measurement and analytics solution in beta for eligible advertisers. It described a secure, privacy-safe, dedicated cloud-based environment where advertisers can analyze multiple pseudonymized signals and generate aggregated reports. Advertisers, the post said, can only access aggregated, anonymous outputs.

The beta soon widened to more brands, buying agencies and technology vendors across North America, Europe and parts of Asia, Adweek reported. Adweek described the aim as helping marketers measure how their ads perform across channels, from awareness through to sales, by uploading their own first-party data to a data clean room that anonymizes customer information.

According to Amazon’s post, beta advertisers were using it to study the reach and frequency of their campaigns, which combinations of channels delivered results, and the total impact of their media.

Follow the value: answers for the brand, records for Amazon

The design says what Amazon values. Its advertising signals, the record of which shopper saw which ad and what they later bought, are among its most valuable assets. Amazon’s “other” revenue, mostly advertising, brought in $7.95 billion in the last three months of 2020, up 66%, according to its quarterly results. A retailer earning that much from what it knows about shoppers has every reason to keep the knowledge inside its own walls.

Think of a library reading room where you can study the archive as long as you like but cannot take the files home. The brand brings its data in, runs its analysis and leaves with totals and patterns, not lists of shoppers. Amazon keeps the records, and the brand gets better answers than it had before.

The arrangement asks something of the brand in return. To get the most from the service, a brand brings its own customer data into an environment it does not run. Even with that data pseudonymized and only aggregated results coming out, the decision to upload belongs with the brand’s legal and privacy teams as well as its marketers. Brands that treat Amazon Marketing Cloud as a reporting upgrade, and not as a data-sharing decision, risk making that choice by default.

For many brands it is a fair trade, and a sensible one given the direction of privacy rules. On January 27, Facebook warned that Apple’s iOS 14 privacy changes would make its ad targeting harder. Analysis that keeps individual records in one place is likely to become the normal way large platforms share what they know. Brands should expect more retailers to offer the same kind of room, and expect to keep negotiating over what is allowed to leave it.

The person who asks the questions

The harder change is inside the brand. A report that arrives as a spreadsheet can be read by anyone with access to the shared drive. A clean room only answers the questions someone thinks to ask, set up by people who understand both the brand’s data and Amazon’s.

In many brands those skills live in different parts of the building. The analysts who know the customer data sit in the direct-to-consumer or insights team. The people who know Amazon advertising sit in e-commerce, or at an agency. Amazon Marketing Cloud is most valuable when the two groups work on the same question, such as whether shoppers who saw a brand’s video ads on Amazon later bought more on the brand’s own site.

The evidence so far leans toward a capability gap more than a technology gap. The service exists, in beta. The scarce resource is likely to be the person, often hard to hire, who can frame a business question, translate it into an analysis Amazon’s environment will run, and explain the answer to whoever owns the budget.

Agencies and technology vendors were part of the expanded beta too, and for many brands the first access will come through a partner. That is efficient, and it raises the same question in a new form. If the agency writes the questions and holds the answers, the brand learns only what its agency chooses to look at.

Whether Amazon adds ready-made analyses that teams without specialists can run will decide how fast this spreads; without them, the advantage stays with the brands that build the skills.

Before applying for the beta, a brand can do two useful things. It can find out whether it, its agency or its technology partner is eligible, and who would actually run the work. And it can write down a handful of questions about its Amazon advertising that its current reports cannot answer, then decide which team owns them and give that team access to both the brand’s customer data and its Amazon data. Helping brands measure Amazon advertising with tools like Amazon Marketing Cloud is part of our measurement work across sponsored ads and Amazon DSP.

A0030.crumb: Walmart Connect earns Walmart more per…
A0030.title: Walmart Connect earns Walmart more per dollar than its shelves
A0030.alt: A corked glass jar of coins and amber bottles on rustic shop shelving below a blank glowing display screen.
A0030.ttag: Walmart Connect earns Walmart more per dollar than its shelves | Kwontified
A0030.desc: Walmart earns about five cents of operating profit per dollar of US sales and far more per ad dollar, which is why Walmart Connect will shape supplier talks.
A0030.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 9, 2021.
A0030.body:
Walmart’s suppliers keep hearing about advertising, in buyer meetings, in joint business plans, in the margins of conversations that used to be about cases and cost prices. Some of them wonder why the world’s largest store chain cares so much about ads. The answer is in its margins. Walmart earned about five cents of operating profit on each dollar of US sales in its latest fiscal year, and advertising sold on websites and screens it already runs earns far more per dollar.

That gap gives Walmart a strong reason to grow what suppliers spend on Walmart Connect. Brands should set those budgets on the sales the ads add, and settle that before ad commitments show up in the annual negotiation.

Walmart Connect sits inside Walmart’s new profit plan

Walmart said as much in its fourth-quarter release. The company described a strategy to deepen customer relationships and diversify its business model “by growing related businesses with accretive margins,” naming marketplace, advertising, financial services and data monetization. Accretive here means these businesses earn higher margins than the company’s average, so each dollar of their growth lifts overall profitability.

The same release shows why that matters. Walmart US recorded operating income of $19.1 billion on net sales of $370.0 billion in the fiscal year ended January 31, 2021, a margin of about 5.2%. US e-commerce sales grew 79% over the year, and Walmart said it expects to invest nearly $14 billion in the coming year, much of it in supply chain capacity and automation.

Walmart Connect is the advertising part of that plan. When Walmart renamed its media business on January 28, it said that over its last fiscal year its on-site ad revenue had nearly doubled and its number of advertisers had more than doubled, according to its announcement.

A landlord who earns more from billboards than from rent

A dollar of product sales at Walmart carries the cost of buying the product, moving it, stocking it and paying the people who sell it. What is left is a few cents. A dollar of advertising sold on Walmart’s website, its app or its in-store screens carries far fewer added costs, because the pages, the screens and the shoppers are already there.

Think of a landlord who owns a busy building. The rent from the shops inside covers the cost of running the place and leaves a modest profit. Then the landlord puts billboards on the roof. They cost little to add and are seen by everyone who visits the shops, and before long the landlord cares a great deal about keeping them full.

Walmart does not disclose the profit margin on its advertising, so the arithmetic needs an assumption. Say, for illustration only, that half of each advertising dollar is operating profit. At a 5.2% retail margin, Walmart would need about $9.60 of additional US sales to earn the same profit as one dollar of advertising. Put the other way round, every dollar a supplier moves into Walmart Connect is worth as much to Walmart’s profit line as nearly ten dollars of extra product moving through its stores and website. Even if the true ad margin were much lower than half, the gap would stay wide.

Why Walmart’s choices make sense once you see the margins

Seen this way, choices that look odd become logical. A retailer that expects more of its profit growth to come from advertising can afford to keep shelf prices low and accept thin product margins, because the traffic those low prices bring is what makes the advertising valuable. It also has every reason to ask its suppliers to advertise, and to link that request to the wider relationship.

That is where brands need care. When advertising and trade terms share one meeting, the ad budget can drift into being the price of holding shelf space rather than an investment that is expected to return sales. The brand ends up funding Walmart’s profit plan without knowing what it gets back.

None of this makes Walmart’s advertising a bad buy. Walmart sees what its shoppers buy in stores and online, and its ads sit close to the moment of purchase. For many brands those ads will earn a good return.

The interests behind the two sides of the transaction still differ. Walmart profits from every dollar spent, whatever it returns to the brand, and the brand profits only from the dollars that add sales it would not otherwise have made. Keeping those two interests apart is the brand’s job.

Brand leaders are clearly planning to spend more. Of the more than 1,000 US brands Feedvisor surveyed, 71% said they advertise on Walmart and 87% said they plan to increase their Walmart ad spending in 2021, Feedvisor reported. Whether that money gets judged on results or on the relationship is still open.

Before the annual negotiation starts

The answer depends on decisions made before the negotiation, not during it. A brand that walks in with its own view of what Walmart advertising returns can agree to spend more where the evidence supports it and push back where it does not. A brand that walks in without one will tend to accept the figure Walmart proposes, because it has nothing to set against it.

So set the 2021 Walmart Connect budget from the sales it adds, measured with a test where possible, ahead of the first planning meeting. Keep advertising commitments on a separate line from trade terms, so each can be judged on its own results. And make the measurement part of the deal: if Walmart wants a bigger commitment, ask for the sales data by store or region that would show what the money did.

The rule of thumb is short. Whatever share of the plan is advertising, it gets measured like advertising, whichever meeting it was agreed in. Judging each channel on the sales it adds is how we run Walmart Connect alongside Amazon and Target advertising.

A0032.crumb: Apparel on Amazon got easier when Amazon…
A0032.title: Apparel on Amazon got easier when Amazon gave brands control
A0032.alt: An open wooden wardrobe with a brass key in the lock, showing jackets and shirts on wooden hangers.
A0032.ttag: Apparel on Amazon got easier when Amazon gave brands control | Kwontified
A0032.desc: Clothing store sales fell 26.4% in 2020, and Amazon’s Luxury Stores handed brands control of price and selection. The apparel case against Amazon needs a rerun.
A0032.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 11, 2021.
A0032.body:
In many apparel companies, the Amazon question has a fixed place on the agenda. It comes up once a year. Someone from e-commerce makes the case, someone from wholesale reminds the room what it would do to department store pricing, and the item is closed for another twelve months. The reasons have been consistent for a long time. Amazon would cheapen the brand, undercut its partners and take away control of how its clothes were shown.

Two things changed in 2020 that should reopen the item. Shoppers moved their clothing purchases online at speed, and Amazon showed it is willing to give fashion brands the controls they had asked for, including over price. The question for apparel leaders is no longer whether to be on Amazon. It is what terms they need.

The old reasons to stay off Amazon met a new customer

The reluctance was rooted in how Amazon has worked. Its habit has been to absorb each new category into a single, uniform Amazon experience, Modern Retail observed, and its earlier attempts to court luxury brands had met resistance. For a fashion brand, uniform meant the same page design as a phone charger, little say over presentation and none over price. Picture a designer collection hung on the same metal racks as the store’s own basics, under the same strip lighting, with the price tag set by someone else. Staying away was a rational choice.

The pandemic removed much of the alternative. Sales at US clothing stores fell 26.4% in 2020, while sales at nonstore retailers, the category that includes online shopping, rose 22.1%, according to Census Bureau figures reported by Commercial Observer. Department store sales fell by close to 20%.

Those numbers describe a change in where people shopped as well as how much they bought. A brand that relied on department stores and its own shops lost access to many of its customers for much of the year. Its own website could win some of them back. Many shoppers, though, began the search for clothes where they began the search for everything else.

That habit is unlikely to reverse fully when stores reopen. A shopper who has bought socks, gym clothes and a winter coat online for a year has learned where to look first, and the brands that were visible there have had a year to earn repeat purchases. Brands that sat out 2020 off Amazon did more than miss a year of sales. They let competitors build familiarity with customers who may never go back to the department store.

Amazon changed its own rules for apparel

The more telling change came from Amazon itself. On September 15, 2020, it launched Luxury Stores, an invitation-only section of its app for US Prime members. The first brand was Oscar de la Renta, selling ready-to-wear, handbags, jewelry and accessories, according to The Retail Bulletin’s report of the launch. Participating brands would run a “store within a store” and make their own decisions on inventory, selection and pricing.

That last point is the one that matters. Amazon built its retail business on controlling the customer experience, price included. Handing brands control of price and selection is a concession, and Amazon made it because it wants the category. One Amazon strategy consultant told Modern Retail that luxury fashion is “the last big category for Amazon.”

Read as a statement of what Amazon values, the launch is plain enough. Amazon will change its standard terms to win categories it cannot otherwise reach. Luxury Stores began small, with a single brand, and it is too early to say how widely its controls will spread. The willingness to offer them is now on the record.

What this means for apparel brands that are not luxury houses

Most apparel brands will never be invited into Luxury Stores, and the lesson still applies to them. If Amazon will negotiate control of price and presentation with the brands it most wants, the terms on which any brand sells there are more open to discussion than many apparel leaders assume.

There is a practical point too. A brand that stays off Amazon does not keep its products off Amazon. Resellers who buy the goods elsewhere can list them, set their own prices and write their own descriptions, so the brand that refuses to sell there often ends up with exactly the loss of control it was trying to avoid. The real choice is about who decides how the brand appears.

So the question in the room changes shape. Instead of whether Amazon fits the brand, leadership should ask which terms would make Amazon fit: control of price, of how products are shown, of which items are sold.

Some apparel leaders will still decide Amazon is wrong for their brand, and for some that will be the right call. A brand built on scarcity, or on a handful of carefully chosen retail partners, may lose more than it gains. The point is that the decision should rest on current facts with the terms on the table, rather than being inherited from a time when Amazon offered no terms at all. If Amazon extends store-within-a-store controls beyond luxury to premium and mainstream fashion, the old reasons for staying away will weaken further.

Before the item comes back to the agenda

  1. Search Amazon for the brand now and list who is selling its products, at what prices and with what descriptions.
  2. Write down the conditions the brand would need to sell on Amazon on its own terms, such as pricing control, presentation standards or a limited assortment.
  3. Find out when the Amazon decision was last reviewed, and whether its reasons still hold after 2020.
  4. Decide who in the company would own the channel if the answer changed, before anyone has to improvise it.

Working out those terms, for Amazon and the other marketplaces, is part of how we manage marketplaces for apparel, footwear and accessories brands.

A0034.crumb: Walmart Marketplace grows only as fast as…
A0034.title: Walmart Marketplace grows only as fast as its deliveries
A0034.alt: A blue delivery van driving a winding highway through golden hills and mountains at sunset.
A0034.ttag: Walmart Marketplace grows only as fast as its deliveries | Kwontified
A0034.desc: Walmart Marketplace more than doubled its sellers in 2020, yet only 430 of them used Walmart’s own fulfillment. Delivery speed decides who captures the growth.
A0034.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 16, 2021.
A0034.body:
Close to 70,000 sellers were on Walmart Marketplace by the end of 2020, more than double the year before. Only 430 of them used Walmart’s own fulfillment system. Those two numbers sit uneasily together, because every marketplace runs on the same promise: more sellers bring more selection, which brings more shoppers, which brings more sellers. That loop only accelerates if each part can carry the extra load.

At Walmart the part under strain is delivery. Shoppers there expect quick, reliable shipping, and very few marketplace sellers were set up to provide it. Sellers who can promise fast delivery will capture most of the marketplace’s growth.

Walmart Marketplace doubled, but its parts moved at different speeds

The seller count comes from Marketplace Pulse, reported by Modern Retail. For comparison, Amazon has about 2.4 million active sellers, so Walmart’s marketplace is still far smaller and growing quickly from a lower base.

The same report shows where the strain sits. Only 430 sellers were using Walmart’s fulfillment system, according to Marketplace Pulse, while 94% of Amazon sellers use Amazon’s fulfillment service at least some of the time. Walmart also vets each seller and product, which keeps quality up and slows how quickly new sellers become active.

That vetting is a deliberate brake. Walmart could grow its seller count faster by opening the doors wider, as other marketplaces have. It has chosen to protect the experience its shoppers associate with the Walmart name and accept slower growth in exchange. For sellers the choice is informative, because it tells them what Walmart will reward once they are inside: reliability as much as range.

Walmart’s own plans point the same way. In its fourth-quarter results, the company named marketplace among the higher-margin businesses it intends to grow, and reported that US e-commerce sales rose 79% in the fiscal year to January 31. Walmart wants the marketplace to grow. Its problem is making the delivery side keep up with the number of sellers it admits, at a time when its own store-based pickup and delivery has raised what shoppers expect from every order.

A chain that catches on one stiff link

A marketplace flywheel has several links. Sellers list products, shoppers find them, orders get delivered, and satisfied shoppers come back. Adding sellers adds selection, but if those sellers ship slowly, the shoppers who try them have a worse experience and buy less often, and the extra selection never turns into extra loyalty.

Think of a bicycle chain with one stiff link. You can pedal harder, but the chain catches on that link every turn and the bike goes no faster. At Walmart, the stiff link is delivery speed from third-party sellers.

Walmart’s shoppers make that link especially important. Many of them already rely on Walmart for quick pickup and delivery from stores, which sets the standard they bring to every order. A marketplace item that arrives in a week sits poorly next to groceries delivered the same day.

The effect compounds through advertising. As more sellers join, more of them compete for the same searches, and the cost of appearing at the top of results tends to rise. A seller with slow delivery pays the same price for the click as a seller with fast delivery but converts fewer of those shoppers into buyers. Each advertising dollar works harder for the faster seller, which lets it bid more and win more of the traffic. Delivery speed ends up shaping how much each seller can afford to spend to be seen, on top of whether a shopper buys.

Faster delivery costs money, and often pays

For a brand on Walmart Marketplace, that sets up a plain choice. Faster delivery costs money, whether the seller pays Walmart to fulfill orders or upgrades its own warehouse and carriers. Slower delivery is cheaper and puts the brand on the wrong side of the link Walmart is working hardest to strengthen.

Take a brand selling 1,000 units a month on Walmart with five-day delivery and earning $10 of profit on each. Faster delivery costs an extra $2 a unit.

Units a monthProfit per unitMonthly profit
Five-day delivery today1,000$10$10,000
Faster delivery, sales up 30%1,300$8$10,400
Faster delivery, sales up 10%1,100$8$8,800

At a 30% lift the upgrade pays. At a 10% lift it loses money. Everything turns on how much faster delivery raises sales for that particular product, which is worth testing rather than assuming.

The numbers lean toward speed for products shoppers buy often or need quickly, and less so for slow, considered purchases. They also lean toward speed over time. As Walmart grows the marketplace, it has every reason to reward the sellers who make its delivery promise easier to keep, through search placement, badges and programs, and sellers who wait may find the bar has risen around them.

Test speed on the best sellers first

Measure current delivery times on Walmart Marketplace by product and compare them with what Walmart promises on its own items. Then test faster delivery on the best sellers, through Walmart’s fulfillment service or your own network, and measure the change in sales against the added cost. A brand that cannot yet afford faster delivery across the whole range should start with the few products that sell most, where the gain is easiest to measure and the cost easiest to recover. The rest of 2021’s Walmart growth should be planned around delivery capacity as well as listings, so new products do not drag the average down.

The rule of thumb: on Walmart, a new listing is only as good as the delivery promise behind it. Fulfillment choices sit alongside listings and advertising in how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

A0035.title: Instagram checkout moves the customer from the brand to the app
A0035.alt: A kraft paper shopping bag, smartphone and espresso cup on a wooden cafe table by an open door.
A0035.ttag: Instagram checkout moves the customer from the brand to the app | Kwontified
A0035.desc: In-app checkout shortens the path to purchase, but Instagram sends the order emails and keeps the contact, so brands should decide what they are handing over.
A0035.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 18, 2021.
A0035.body:
A shopper watching a creator’s Story taps a jacket, picks a size and pays with a card Instagram already holds. A minute later the order confirmation lands in her inbox, and it comes from Instagram. The brand that made the jacket has a sale and very little else: no email address of its own, no browsing history, no easy way to sell her the matching trousers next month.

For years the path ran differently. A shopper discovered a product somewhere, then came to the brand’s own website to buy, and the brand gained a customer along with the order. In-app checkout collapses that path into one place Instagram controls. It helps conversion, and it moves the customer relationship from the brand to the platform, so leaders should decide deliberately which products and customers they are willing to hand over.

How Instagram checkout spread across the app

Instagram launched Checkout in March 2019 with 26 brands, including Nike, Adidas, Outdoor Voices, Oscar de la Renta and Zara, and widened it slowly, Glossy reported. By February 2020, Facebook’s chief operating officer said hundreds of US businesses were testing it.

The places to buy have multiplied since. In December 2020, Instagram added shopping to Reels, so shoppers could buy from videos across Feed, Stories, Live, IGTV and Reels. TechCrunch reported the launch on December 10 and noted that Instagram makes money when customers complete purchases inside the app with Facebook Pay.

Brands understood the cost from the start. When Checkout was first announced, a direct-to-consumer executive told Modern Retail that the downsides included losing customer behavior data Instagram would not share, and losing the chance for shoppers to browse the brand’s other products. Two years on, the trade-off is the same. What has changed is how many corners of Instagram now offer it.

Follow the value: who keeps the customer

The structure of the arrangement shows where the value goes. When a customer buys through Checkout, communication about the order goes out by email from Instagram, not the brand, according to Glossy’s reporting. A marketer quoted in the same piece described the real contest as one over customer data: unless the shopper opts in to share an email address, the brand has no way to market to that customer directly.

It resembles a concession counter inside a department store where the store keeps the receipt and the mailing list. The brand stocked the counter and made the sale. The store knows who bought.

Instagram also charges for the sale. A Facebook spokesperson told Glossy that Instagram was testing a selling fee of 5%, which it said helps fund the programs that make Checkout possible and offset transaction costs. One direct-to-consumer marketer told the publication the fee felt too high, and that brand declined to join.

Instagram uses its position to reward participation, too. Glossy found that Instagram’s own shopping team promoted Checkout-enabled brands on the Shop tab, and that when a shopper viewed a product from a brand without Checkout, the “similar items” shown beneath it came from brands that did use it. The platform is steering demand toward the brands that keep the customer inside the app.

Read together, the design is consistent. Instagram gains the transaction fee, the customer contact and a stronger story for advertisers. The brand gains a faster sale, and often a sale it would not otherwise have made, which is real value of a narrower kind than a customer it can come back to. Facebook said on January 27 that the shift toward online commerce had helped its business in 2020, and in-app checkout is one way it can keep more of that shift for itself.

What the brand’s model depends on

None of this makes Checkout a bad choice. For an impulse product, a first purchase or a launch aimed at new customers, the shorter path may be worth more than the relationship given up. A customer who would never have visited the brand’s site is still a customer.

The real question is what the brand’s model depends on. A brand that earns its profit from repeat purchases, subscriptions or a broad range bought over time needs the customer’s contact and history, and handing those over on every sale gives away the part of the customer that pays back. A brand selling single, well-known items may care much less.

Take a skincare brand whose average first order is $40, where a customer it can email goes on to buy three more times over the following year. That customer is worth $160 in sales. If the same first purchase happens through Checkout and the shopper keeps her email private, the brand books $40, pays the selling fee, and may never hear from her again unless it pays Instagram to reach her. It has not lost one sale. It has turned a repeat customer into a series of paid introductions.

Much depends on what happens with the email question. If shoppers increasingly share their details with brands at checkout, the trade gets easier to accept. If they do not, the relationship will keep collecting inside the app.

The sorting a leadership team needs is simple to describe and harder to agree on. Split the range into products that win on the first purchase and products that win on the repeat, and consider Checkout for the first group. Track how many Checkout customers share their email address, and treat a low rate as a cost of the channel. And write down, before the next social commerce decision, which customers the brand cannot afford to hand to a platform. Deciding where in-app selling fits is part of how we run social commerce for brands on Instagram and TikTok.

A0036.title: Zalando’s selectiveness is what brands are paying for
A0036.alt: A velvet rope on brass posts in front of a boutique with linen dresses on a copper rack and ceramics.
A0036.ttag: Zalando’s selectiveness is what brands are paying for | Kwontified
A0036.desc: Zalando reached 38.7 million active customers in 2020 while choosing who sells and how. That selectiveness is what brands pay for and must keep earning.
A0036.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 23, 2021.
A0036.body:
Brands on Zalando sometimes ask a fair question: why pay its fees when they already run their own websites in the same countries? The answer lies in what Zalando chooses not to do. Unlike an open marketplace, it decides which brands sell and how their products are presented, and it still buys much of its range itself. That selectiveness has built a base of 38.7 million active customers who trust what they find there.

It is why brands accept Zalando’s terms, and why they should treat their place on it as a position to earn and protect.

Zalando in 2020, in its own numbers

The figures come from Zalando’s full-year results and new targets and the strategy presentation that accompanied them.

Measure2020 or latest
Gross merchandise volume€10.7 billion, up 30.4%
Revenue growth23.1%
Active customers38.7 million, up 25%
Partner Program share of Fashion Store volume, fourth quarter24%
Partner Program items shipped by Zalando’s fulfillment service, fourth quarter51%
Marketing services revenue as a share of gross merchandise volume, fourth quarter1.5%
Orders placed through the app57%
Physical stores connected through Connected Retail, year endmore than 2,400

Zalando now aims for more than €30 billion of gross merchandise volume by 2025. Over the long term it wants partners, brands selling their own stock, to make up half of Fashion Store volume, with about three quarters of their items shipped through Zalando.

The app figure deserves a second look. Shoppers who open a fashion app on their phone are returning to a place they trust, and they are not searching the open web for the lowest price. That habit is the asset brands are buying access to. It also explains why Zalando can sell marketing services at all: a brand pays for prominence inside an app its shoppers open on purpose, which is a different thing from paying to be noticed on the open web.

A department store with a waiting list for concessions

A marketplace usually becomes more valuable as more sellers join, because more selection attracts more shoppers. Zalando adds a second force that pulls the other way. Its shoppers come partly because the range is chosen. They trust that what they find is genuine, current and delivered well, and every brand admitted on poor terms, or allowed to ship slowly, draws down that trust.

Think of a department store that rents space to brands. If it accepts anyone who pays, it fills up quickly, shoppers stop trusting its taste, and the space becomes less valuable to every brand inside. If it keeps a waiting list and holds tenants to standards, each space is worth more and brands pay more for it. The restriction is what creates the value.

That is why Zalando’s choices make sense even where they look like limits on its own growth. Keeping a wholesale business alongside the Partner Program lets it shape the range directly. Pushing partners toward its own fulfillment keeps delivery consistent. Selling marketing services lets brands pay for prominence without Zalando lowering its standards to fill the site.

Each of those choices costs Zalando something in the short term. Wholesale ties up its own money in stock. Running fulfillment for partners takes warehouses and people. Holding brands to standards means turning some away.

An open marketplace would grow its seller count faster and carry less risk. Zalando takes the slower, costlier path because the trust it protects is what lets it charge brands for access at all, and that pricing power is worth more over time than the extra listings.

Brands pay for trust, and keep paying for it

For a brand, the logic has two consequences. The first is about what the fees buy. They pay for access to shoppers who trust the setting, which is more than a listing. A brand that sets Zalando’s commission against the cost of its own website is comparing the wrong things. The fair comparison is with the cost of reaching those same shoppers, in those same countries, any other way, which for most brands means paid media.

The second is that the position is conditional. A platform that values curation will reward the partners who strengthen it and push down those who weaken it, through search placement, campaign slots and the terms offered at the next review. Delivery speed, returns handling, content quality and price consistency should all matter more as the Partner Program grows, because each one feeds the trust that makes the platform valuable. A brand that treats the Partner Program as a place to clear stock slowly is spending down an asset it does not own.

The risk runs the other way too. As Zalando works toward partners making up half of Fashion Store volume, it will admit many more brands. If it opens faster than it can hold its standards, the curation that gives the Partner Program its value could thin. Whether standards for partners tighten or loosen as their number rises is the thing to keep an eye on through 2021.

How to judge a place on Zalando

Price the fees against the cost of reaching the same shoppers through paid media in each country. Review delivery times, returns handling and product content against the platform’s own standards, and close the gaps before they cost placement. Then decide whether to move Partner Program stock into Zalando’s fulfillment service, weighing its fees against the delivery consistency the platform rewards.

The rule of thumb: on a curated platform, the brand’s own standards are part of the price of admission, paid every week. Launching and running brands on Zalando, from content to fulfillment choices, is part of how we manage international marketplaces.
