A0038.crumb: DTC brands are turning to Amazon as paid…
A0038.title: DTC brands are turning to Amazon as paid social costs rise
A0038.alt: Stacked shipping boxes and twine on a workbench in a sunny garage, with a vintage van parked outside.
A0038.ttag: DTC brands are turning to Amazon as paid social costs rise | Kwontified
A0038.desc: Many DTC brands were founded on selling only through their own sites. Rising paid social costs pushed them onto Amazon, which needs planning as a real channel.
A0038.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 25, 2021.
A0038.body:
Plenty of direct-to-consumer brands wrote it into their founding pitch: we sell only through our own website. A growing number have quietly broken that promise, and the reason is that the formula behind it stopped working. Finding customers through paid social media got more expensive, and Apple’s privacy changes are about to make it harder to measure as well.

Amazon offers what those brands now lack, which is shoppers who are already searching. That makes it a fix for the acquisition problem, and leaders should build it as a planned channel with its own owner instead of treating it as a rescue.

How the website-only formula for DTC brands took hold

The direct-to-consumer model rested on two pillars. The first was the brand’s own website, where it controlled the price, the story and the customer data. The second was cheap customer acquisition through Facebook and Instagram, which let young brands reach large audiences without a retail partner.

The second pillar weakened first, for a simple reason. As more brands bid for the same audiences on the same platforms, the price of reaching them went up. By the end of 2019, many direct-to-consumer brands had spent the year trying to reduce their reliance on Facebook advertising as the cost of acquiring customers there rose, in some cases doubling or tripling, Modern Retail reported.

Investors had started asking the same question earlier that year. At a Digiday conference in March 2019, one venture investor said a startup that planned to sell only direct was no longer interesting, and that brands should be ready to explain their plans for Amazon and wholesale, according to Modern Retail.

The pandemic and privacy changes moved the decision forward

The pandemic turned the question into a decision. Direct-to-consumer brands are moving advertising money to Amazon, Digiday reported, much of it money that would have gone to in-person events and shopper marketing. The prebiotic soda brand Poppi said its Amazon ad spending was up more than 500% since March 2020. The supplement brand Olly said it invests a significant share of its Amazon spending in search ads and Amazon DSP, and that it is doubling its marketing budget.

The wider picture matches. Of more than 1,000 US brands in the survey, 78% said they currently sell on Amazon, up from 55% a year earlier, Feedvisor reported.

The pressure on paid social is about to grow. Facebook told investors on January 27 that Apple’s iOS 14 changes would make ad targeting headwinds more significant in 2021. For a brand that finds most of its customers through Facebook and Instagram, that means higher costs and less certainty about what the spending buys.

Amazon fixes acquisition, and only acquisition

The hidden structure here is the cost of finding a customer. On paid social, a brand pays to interrupt people who were not looking for its product, like a sampling team stopping shoppers in a mall corridor. On Amazon, a brand pays to stand where people are already looking, like a well-placed end cap in the aisle they walked down on purpose. When interruption gets expensive, demand that already exists becomes more valuable, and Amazon holds more of it than any other single place in US e-commerce.

Say a brand paid $30 to acquire a customer through Instagram ads in 2019, and that figure has climbed to $50. If the same brand can win a first-time buyer on Amazon for $25 of advertising, Amazon looks like a bargain. The Amazon customer, though, comes with Amazon’s fees on every order and without an email address the brand controls, so the honest comparison has to include what each customer is worth after the first sale.

The trouble is that Amazon shores up one pillar and weakens the other. Selling there means giving up some control of price and presentation, sharing the customer relationship with Amazon, and paying fees the brand’s own website does not carry. A brand that moves to Amazon purely to rescue its acquisition costs can find that its margins and its customer data have taken the hit instead.

Who owns Amazon in a company built around a website

Ownership is where these moves usually go wrong. In many direct-to-consumer companies the organization chart was drawn around the website: the growth team runs paid social, the site team runs conversion, the customer team runs email. Amazon fits none of those seats. Bolted on in an emergency, it tends to be run by whoever has spare time, judged on sales alone, and starved of the planning a channel needs.

So the question for a leadership team is whether Amazon is a temporary fix or part of how the brand intends to grow. If it is the second, it needs a named owner, a profit target alongside the sales target, and a clear view of how it relates to the brand’s own website, especially on price. The brand’s own paid social acquisition cost after the iOS 14 changes take effect will show how urgent that is; if it rises, as Facebook’s warning suggests it may, the case for a planned Amazon channel only gets stronger.

Two comparisons are worth running before the next budget cycle:

  1. The cost to acquire a customer on paid social against the advertising cost per new customer on Amazon, over the same period and for the same product.
  2. What each of those customers is worth over a year, once Amazon’s fees and the lost email address are counted.

If the second comparison still favors Amazon, staff and budget it like the channel it has become. Building Amazon as a planned channel for direct-to-consumer brands, from pricing and content to advertising, is work we do.

A0039.crumb: Live shopping in China works because…
A0039.title: Live shopping in China works because buying stays in the stream
A0039.alt: A smartphone on a ring light filming an antique brass cash register and ceramic bowls on a wooden table.
A0039.ttag: Live shopping in China works because buying stays in the stream | Kwontified
A0039.desc: Taobao Live sold more than RMB400 billion of goods in 2020. The lesson for Instagram live shopping is the purchase path, not the hosts or the hype.
A0039.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 30, 2021.
A0039.body:
When brand teams see China’s live shopping numbers, the usual conclusion is that the format needs bigger personalities or deeper discounts. The more useful lesson is plainer. On Alibaba’s Taobao Live, the example everyone cites, viewers watch inside the same shopping app they already use to buy, and they pay in that app without going anywhere.

Live shopping converts when the path from watching to paying is short. A brand testing live shopping on Instagram should judge the tool first by how many steps sit between the two.

Live shopping in China reached a scale brands cannot ignore

The scale is real. Taobao Live, Alibaba’s livestreaming service, generated more than RMB400 billion of gross merchandise volume in the twelve months to December 31, 2020, according to Alibaba’s December quarter results. Alibaba described it as a branding, marketing and distribution tool that lets shoppers interact directly with brands, merchants and influencers during livestreams.

Alibaba also treats the service as infrastructure. The same results noted that its own units, such as Juhuasuan, Ele.me and Fliggy, increasingly use Taobao Live to reach and engage shoppers. When a company runs a selling format through its own businesses, the format is part of how it trades.

It was growing fast before the pandemic, too. In December 2019, the value of goods sold through Taobao Live and the number of monthly users watching it both more than doubled from a year earlier, according to Alibaba’s results for that quarter.

In the United States the tools are arriving. Since December 10, Instagram has let shoppers buy from Live broadcasts as well as from Feed, Stories, IGTV and Reels, TechCrunch reported. How much of China’s result a brand should expect from that is the real question.

A market stall whose till is at the end of the street

A live stream earns attention in short bursts. A host shows a product, a viewer is interested for a moment, and the stream moves on. Every step between that moment and a completed payment loses some viewers: a tap to open the product, a page that loads, a login, an address form, a card number.

Picture a market stall where the seller is persuasive and the crowd is large, but the till sits at the end of the street. Some of the people who wanted to buy will walk there. Many will not, because by the time they arrive the moment has passed. Put the till on the stall and the same crowd buys far more.

Taobao Live puts the till on the stall. It runs on Taobao, Alibaba’s marketplace, so the viewer is already inside a shopping app where they buy regularly, and the step from interest to purchase is short.

There is a second difference. Someone who opens Taobao has come to buy. Someone who opens Instagram has usually come to see what friends are up to, and shopping is something they drift into. That does not make live shopping impossible on a social app. It means the stream has to work harder to turn attention into intent, and every bit of friction after that point costs more.

Say 10,000 people watch a brand’s live stream and 5% of them tap a product.

ViewersTap a productComplete the purchaseSales
Checkout inside the stream10,00050060%300
Sent to the brand’s website10,00050020%100

The host, the product and the audience are identical. Only the path changed, and it cut sales to a third.

Judge the tool by what it does, not by China’s numbers

On those grounds, a brand should judge a live shopping tool by what it actually does, and leave the size of China’s market out of the decision. Three things settle most of it: whether a viewer can buy without leaving the stream, whether their payment and address details are already stored, and whether the brand receives the customer’s details afterwards.

Instagram’s answers are improving but uneven. Where a brand uses Instagram’s in-app checkout, a viewer can buy without leaving, though order communication then comes from Instagram rather than the brand, as Glossy reported. Where checkout is not available, the product tag sends the viewer out to the brand’s website, and the stream behaves more like a video advertisement with a link.

Neither setup is wrong for every brand or product. They are different tools, though, and should be planned and measured differently. A brand that expects Chinese conversion rates from a stream that sends viewers away to buy will be disappointed, and may conclude that live shopping does not work for its customers when what failed was the path.

Measuring the path before blaming the format

The measurement follows the same logic. Count how many viewers tap a product, how many reach the payment step and how many finish, and compare those rates with the same products bought on the brand’s own website. If most of the loss happens after viewers leave the stream, the fix is the purchase path, and changing the host or deepening the discount will not touch it. Track the same numbers across several streams before drawing conclusions, since a single show can swing on the product, the hour and the host.

The first test is best run on products that suit an impulse purchase and need little explanation, where a short path matters most. Run it with in-stream checkout where possible, and check whether the extra completed orders cover the selling fee.

The rule of thumb: count the taps between “I want that” and “paid”, and expect to lose viewers at every one. Live shopping tests sit within the social commerce work we run for brands on Instagram and TikTok.

A0040.crumb: Footwear on Amazon after Nike: the shoes…
A0040.title: Footwear on Amazon after Nike: the shoes stayed behind
A0040.alt: Pairs of canvas sneakers in assorted colors lined up on a wooden shelf against a pale blue wall.
A0040.ttag: Footwear on Amazon after Nike: the shoes stayed behind | Kwontified
A0040.desc: Nike stopped selling to Amazon in 2019, yet its shoes stayed on Amazon through resellers. Footwear leaders should ask whether they can afford the same choice.
A0040.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 1, 2021.
A0040.body:
Search Amazon for Nike running shoes in the spring of 2021 and you will still find them, listed by sellers Nike does not supply. That is odd, on the face of it, because Nike stopped selling to Amazon in November 2019. Many footwear executives read that exit as permission to keep their own distance from Amazon.

The lesson is narrower than that. Nike could leave because it has the demand to pull customers into its own channels, and its shoes stayed on Amazon anyway, through other sellers. Footwear leaders should decide whether they can afford Nike’s choice, and if they cannot, manage their presence on Amazon instead of abandoning it.

Footwear on Amazon: what Nike’s exit did and did not change

Nike ended a pilot in which it sold directly to Amazon as a wholesaler, a program that began in 2017, Bloomberg reported, in coverage carried by Fortune. Nike said the decision was part of its focus on “more direct, personal relationships” with consumers. It had joined Amazon’s brand registry in 2017 hoping for more control over how its products were sold, more data on its customers and more power to remove fakes. According to the same report, third-party sellers whose listings were removed often reappeared under different names.

Leaving did not take Nike off Amazon. A consultant quoted by Bloomberg put it plainly: just because Nike walks away from Amazon does not mean its products do. Amazon had been recruiting third-party sellers so that Nike products would stay available, Engadget reported at the time. Shoppers searching for Nike on Amazon still find Nike. What changed is who sells it, at what price and with what descriptions.

Think of it as a shoe wall in a busy store that the brand has stopped stocking. The wall does not go empty. Someone else fills it, with whatever stock they can get, priced however they like.

Nike can afford the choice

Nike’s direct business shows why the trade worked for Nike. In the quarter to February 28, 2021, sales through Nike Direct, its own stores and digital channels, reached $4.0 billion, up 20%, and Nike Brand digital sales grew 59%, Nike reported. Nike has also been narrowing its wholesale partners, Modern Retail noted, and Foot Locker had begun piloting a program in which Nike ships orders directly to Foot Locker’s customers.

That is a company with enough demand to bring shoppers to its own front door. When someone wants a particular Nike shoe, they will often go to Nike to get it. Nike can give up Amazon’s traffic because it does not need Amazon to be found.

Most footwear brands sit in a different position. For a brand without that pull, Amazon is where a large share of shoppers begin their search for shoes, and leaving does not move those shoppers to the brand’s website. It hands the brand’s listings, and the impression shoppers form of it, to whoever is reselling its products.

Take a mid-sized footwear brand that sells a running shoe for $110 on its own site and through department stores. After it leaves Amazon, three resellers list the same shoe: one at $89 with stock bought from a clearance channel, one at $129 with a thin description, one with photos of last season’s colors. A shopper comparing them sees a confusing range of prices and pictures, and the department store buyer sees the $89 listing too. The brand chose none of those prices and lives with all of them.

The question for a footwear leadership team

The question in the room, then, is whether the brand has Nike’s pull, more than whether Amazon is good for it. A useful test is how many shoppers search for the brand by name and what share of them buy on the brand’s own site. A brand whose name drives large, loyal search volume to its own channels has real options. A brand whose shoppers mostly arrive through category searches does not, and will lose more by stepping away than it gains.

Footwear adds a practical point. Fit drives returns, and returns cost money on every channel. Zalando, which sells shoes alongside clothing across Europe, started its size advice program with shoes before expanding it to other categories, its head of sizing told FashionUnited in 2019. A brand that manages its own Amazon listings can control size charts, fit notes and product photos. A brand that leaves them to resellers cannot.

For brands that stay, the work is to manage the presence the way Nike tried to: control the listings, price consistently with other channels, enforce against counterfeits and decide which products belong there. Managed presence is a set of decisions made on purpose, covering which styles to offer, at what price relative to the brand’s own site and its wholesale partners, with what imagery and fit guidance, and with how much advertising support. Brands that make those decisions themselves keep Amazon consistent with the rest of their distribution. Brands that do not leave the decisions to others.

The evidence so far leans toward managed presence for most footwear brands. How Nike’s wholesale partners fare as it narrows distribution will say more: if they lose share, the case for going direct strengthens, and if shoppers simply follow Nike’s products to resellers, the case for staying does.

Before the next distribution review, a leadership team can measure how much of its brand search reaches its own website against the demand for its products on Amazon. It can also list who sells its shoes there, at what prices and with what size and fit information. Then it can ask the plain question: are we choosing Nike’s model, or managing our Amazon presence, and have we staffed and budgeted for whichever we chose? We manage Amazon and other marketplaces for footwear, apparel and accessories brands, including how they control listings and price.

A0042.crumb: Zalando size and fit advice turns returns…
A0042.title: Zalando size and fit advice turns returns into an advantage
A0042.alt: A charcoal tweed blazer with a tape measure on a wall hook beside an open shipping box on a wooden table.
A0042.ttag: Zalando size and fit advice turns returns into an advantage | Kwontified
A0042.desc: A third of Zalando’s returns come down to size. Its size advice learns from return data no single brand can match, so brands should feed it and learn from it.
A0042.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 6, 2021.
A0042.body:
About one third of all returns at Zalando happen because an item was the wrong size. Every fashion brand knows the cost of that number, and most try to cut it with better size charts on their own websites. Zalando’s answer works at a different scale: size advice that learns from every purchase and every return across its customers, flags items that run large or small, and recommends a size to each shopper.

Advice like that gets better with volume, which turns a platform’s return data into an advantage no single brand’s website can match. Brands selling on Zalando should treat it as a tool to feed and learn from, with accurate measurements going in and the feedback used to fix products that fit badly.

What Zalando built for size and fit

The clearest public account came from Zalando’s head of sizing in an October 2019 interview with FashionUnited. She said one third of all returns across Zalando’s 17 markets were due to size, and that Zalando offered size advice on about 80% of its range.

The advice comes in two forms. A size flag tells shoppers whether an item runs larger or smaller than standard. A personal recommendation suggests a size based on what Zalando knows about the product and about the shopper’s purchases, returns and stated size and brand preferences.

The product knowledge does not come only from brands. Zalando said measurements supplied by manufacturers were not always reliable, so it used a team of about 30 fit models to try items on and check whether they ran true to size. It started with shoes, then added jeans, women’s dresses and men’s shirts, the categories with the most size-related returns, and later shorts and jackets. It also said it shares with partners which size recommendations it gives shoppers.

A tailor who has measured millions of customers

Every return tells Zalando something: this shopper, who kept a medium from one brand, sent back a medium from another. Multiply that across millions of shoppers and thousands of brands, and the platform learns how each brand’s sizes compare with every other brand’s, and how each shopper’s preferences translate across labels.

Think of a tailor who has measured millions of customers and remembers how every cut fitted each of them. A new customer walks in, and the tailor can say with some confidence which size will fit, because people like them have tried it before. A brand’s own website is a tailor who has only measured its own customers in its own clothes. It knows its sizes well, and it cannot tell a shopper how its medium compares with someone else’s.

That is why size advice is an advantage of scale. The more purchases and returns flow through a platform, the better its advice, the fewer returns its shoppers make, and the more confident they become about trying unfamiliar brands. Zalando’s head of sizing made the same point: if shoppers trust the advice, they will feel confident discovering new brands and looks.

A brand cannot easily build the same loop on its own site. It sees its own customers buying its own products, so it learns how its sizes fit the people who already buy from it. It never sees the shopper who bought a competitor’s jeans in a 30 and kept them, which is exactly the information that would help that shopper pick the right size from a brand they have never tried. The platform sees both purchases, and the gap widens as the platform grows.

What the advice is worth, and what it exposes

For brands, this cuts two ways. On one side is lower returns and more willingness among shoppers to try the brand. Returns are expensive, and a size-related return also costs a sale that might have been kept.

Take a brand that sells 10,000 items a month on Zalando, with 40% coming back and a third of those because of size. That is about 1,330 size-related returns a month. If better size advice prevents a tenth of them, the brand avoids around 130 returns a month, each with its own handling cost and many with a lost sale attached. Over a year that is a meaningful line in the margin, earned without changing a single product.

On the other side is dependence and exposure. Zalando also runs its own private labels, and its head of sizing said the private label team uses the sizing data to improve its products and compares returns with size specifications. The platform advising shoppers on a brand’s fit is also, in some categories, a competitor learning from the same data. The comparison data sits with the platform, and the brand cannot see it anywhere else.

Size advice also exposes inconsistency. If a brand’s mediums vary from one season or factory to the next, the flags will show it to shoppers before the brand has fixed it.

The numbers still lean clearly toward cooperation. The returns saved are real money, the advice will exist whether a brand engages with it or not, and the feedback is information a brand would struggle to collect on its own. The brands that benefit most will be the ones that send accurate measurements, watch which of their items get flagged, and read those flags as quality reports.

Feeding the advice and reading the flags

Send Zalando measured size specifications for every item, checked against finished products and not just samples. Ask for the size feedback it holds on your items, and review which products are flagged as running large or small. Then fix consistency problems at the source, by factory and season, so the same size fits the same way every time.

The rule of thumb: a size flag on Zalando is a quality report the platform writes for you, and the brands that act on it fastest will see it least. Sizing data and returns analysis are part of how we operate brands on Zalando and other international marketplaces.

A0043.crumb: Handbags on Amazon need trust, so Amazon…
A0043.title: Handbags on Amazon need trust, so Amazon is fighting fakes
A0043.alt: A glossy new leather bag and a worn, scuffed leather bag on a wooden table with a brass magnifying glass.
A0043.ttag: Handbags on Amazon need trust, so Amazon is fighting fakes | Kwontified
A0043.desc: Amazon is suing counterfeiters alongside luxury houses because authenticity decides whether handbags sell there. Brands should use the tools and own the job.
A0043.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 8, 2021.
A0043.body:
A shopper buys a crossbody bag on Amazon, and a month later the strap hardware is the wrong color and the lining is peeling. She leaves one star, and the review sits under the brand’s name, on the brand’s product page, for every future shopper to read. The brand never made that bag. A counterfeiter sold it through the same listing and has long since moved on.

That scene is why many accessories brands doubted Amazon could ever promise authenticity, and why Amazon has spent the past year answering the doubt directly: suing counterfeiters alongside luxury houses and widening the tools brands can use to remove fakes. It is investing in trust because the category will not grow on Amazon without it. Accessories brands should use those tools, and keep ownership of brand protection inside the company.

What Amazon has built for handbags and accessories

Amazon launched its Counterfeit Crimes Unit in June 2020, a global team that pursues counterfeiters through the courts and with law enforcement. On February 11, 2021, Amazon and the Italian house Salvatore Ferragamo filed two joint lawsuits against people and companies accused of counterfeiting Ferragamo products, Amazon announced. The same announcement listed earlier joint suits with Valentino, the cosmetics brand KF Beauty and others.

Amazon said it invested more than $500 million in 2019 to protect customers and brands from fraud and abuse, including counterfeits. A vice president for customer trust said the unit was “working closely with luxury and cosmetics brands,” among others.

The tools have widened as well. Project Zero, which lets enrolled brands remove listings they identify as counterfeit and uses automated scanning to block suspected fakes, had more than 10,000 brands enrolled by August 2020, Amazon said when it expanded the program to 17 countries. Salvatore Ferragamo was among the brands it named.

Follow the value: why Amazon is paying for trust

Read as the behavior of a retailer, these moves are an investment in a category Amazon wants. Handbags and accessories carry high prices and strong brand loyalty. They are exactly the products that make a store more valuable to shoppers who spend more, and exactly the products whose makers have kept their distance.

Amazon has worked both ends of that gap. In September 2020 it launched Luxury Stores, letting invited brands control inventory, selection and pricing inside its app. Taking counterfeiters to court alongside a house like Ferragamo is the other half of the offer: control over how the brand appears, plus help defending it.

The value does not flow only one way. Amazon gains brands it could not attract before, and the trust of shoppers who buy expensive goods. Brands gain an enforcement partner with reach no single company has. The tools work best, though, for brands that enroll, register their trademarks, share their product data and in some cases add Amazon’s codes to their products, and each step ties the brand’s protection more closely to Amazon’s systems.

The cost of skipping those steps is easy to underestimate, because of where the damage lands. Take a brand whose best-selling crossbody bag has 200 reviews averaging 4.6 stars, and a counterfeiter who sells 50 fakes through the same listing over two months. If a third of those buyers leave one-star reviews, the average falls to about 4.3. A shopper comparing it with a competitor’s bag at 4.6 now sees a weaker product, though the brand changed nothing.

In a department store, a fake on the shelf would at least sit under someone else’s sign. On a shared listing it sits under yours.

One figure deserves a careful reading. Amazon says 99.9% of products viewed on its site have not received a valid counterfeit complaint. That measures complaints, which is a narrower thing than counterfeits. It depends on shoppers and brands noticing and reporting fakes, and in accessories a fake can be hard to spot from a photo.

Who owns brand protection

The real question for leadership is who owns brand protection, because counterfeits do not stay on one channel. Ferragamo said its own monitoring removed 3 million illicit profiles from social media platforms in 2020, according to the same announcement. A brand that relies on Amazon’s tools for Amazon and on nothing elsewhere will watch the fakes move to the channels it is not watching.

The reverse holds too. A brand with strong monitoring on social media and its own website, but no presence in Amazon’s programs, leaves the largest US marketplace to be policed by others, and by shoppers who only discover the problem after they have bought.

The evidence leans toward enrolling in Amazon’s protection programs, since they give brands powers that are hard to get any other way. Those programs belong inside a brand protection effort the company runs itself, with its own monitoring, its own legal response and its own view of where fakes are appearing. Whether more luxury leather-goods houses join Amazon’s joint lawsuits or its Luxury Stores over 2021 will show how fast the category’s old objection is fading.

In practice that means enrolling in Brand Registry and Project Zero if the brand has not, and deciding whether product codes are worth adding for the most-copied items. It means naming one owner for brand protection across every channel, with a monitoring and legal budget that does not depend on any single platform. And it means checking the Amazon listings for the authenticity signals a shopper can actually see: consistent photography, official brand content and a clear statement of who sells the product. Brand protection is part of how we manage Amazon for accessories, apparel and footwear brands.

A0044.crumb: Walmart competes with Amazon for the…
A0044.title: Walmart competes with Amazon for the weekly trip, not the website
A0044.alt: Paper grocery bag with baguettes, tomatoes and leafy greens beside a blue basket of eggs and milk on a wooden counter.
A0044.ttag: Walmart competes with Amazon for the weekly trip, not the website | Kwontified
A0044.desc: Amazon’s online lead looks decisive by size. Walmart competes on frequency instead, the weekly grocery trip tied to a $98 membership, so plan for both.
A0044.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 13, 2021.
A0044.body:
Put Walmart’s online sales next to Amazon’s and Walmart looks out of reach, which is why many brands treat it as a distant second channel and staff it accordingly. That comparison measures the wrong thing. Walmart’s strength is how often its customers come back: the weekly grocery trip, now tied to a $98-a-year membership that delivers from its stores.

Whoever owns the most frequent purchase has the best shot at the next one. Brands should judge Walmart by how often its shoppers return, more than by its share of online sales.

Walmart vs Amazon: what the numbers show

Walmart’s online business grew quickly in its last fiscal year. US e-commerce sales rose 79% in the year to January 31, 2021, and 69% in the fourth quarter, according to Walmart’s results. Walmart US comparable sales grew 8.6% in that quarter, well ahead of the low single-digit growth it guided for the year ahead.

The online growth reads like a website story, and much of it actually runs through stores. Walmart fills many online orders from its stores for pickup and local delivery, which is how it turns the store network into an online advantage rather than a cost.

The quarter also showed how its customers shopped. In the fourth quarter, Walmart US transactions fell 10.9% while the average ticket rose 21.9%, fewer and larger trips as households consolidated shopping during the pandemic, HFN reported. Walmart said nearly 230 million customers and members visit its stores and websites each week, across about 10,800 stores worldwide. Fewer, larger trips raise the stakes of each one: when a household makes one big run instead of three small ones, a product that misses that basket waits a week for the next chance.

Walmart also gave those weekly shoppers a reason to stay. It launched Walmart+ on September 15, 2020, at $98 a year or $12.95 a month, with unlimited free delivery from stores, groceries included, plus fuel discounts and a Scan & Go feature for paying in stores, TechCrunch reported. Amazon Prime cost $119 a year at the time, Business Insider noted.

The membership’s design matters as much as its price. Fuel discounts bring members to Walmart’s forecourts, and Scan & Go brings them into the app inside the store. Each benefit gives a shopper another reason to open Walmart’s app during a trip they were making anyway, and each opening is a chance to buy something else.

Judging by size instead of frequency

The mistake is a familiar one: competitors get judged by whichever number is easiest to compare. Online sales are reported, easy to rank and large enough to look decisive. Purchase frequency is harder to see, and it is what builds habits. A ranking by size tells you who sells the most online. It says nothing about whose app the shopper will open next Tuesday.

The industry’s own habits reinforce it. Rankings of online retailers, market share charts and investor coverage all lead with online sales, because that is the number companies report and analysts can compare. Few public figures describe how often shoppers come back, so brands that plan from the reported numbers inherit the bias without noticing.

Grocery is the most frequent purchase most households make. A shopper who buys groceries from Walmart every week opens the Walmart app every week, and each visit is a chance to add a phone charger, a set of towels or a bottle of shampoo to the order. A membership that removes the delivery fee makes that addition free to the shopper, and therefore more likely.

Think of the coffee shop on your commute. You pass it every morning, so when it starts selling sandwiches you try one, not because the sandwich beats the deli across town but because you are already standing there. Amazon is the bigger store. Walmart is the one many families pass every week.

None of this means Walmart will overtake Amazon online any time soon. Amazon’s selection, delivery network and Prime base remain far larger. A brand looking only at online share will still underweight a channel whose customers come back more often, for reasons that have nothing to do with the brand’s own category.

Where a brand’s products sit relative to the weekly trip

The implication depends on where a brand’s products sit relative to that trip. Products bought alongside groceries, such as household essentials, personal care, pet supplies and kitchen items, gain most from Walmart’s frequency, because they are the natural additions to a weekly order. Products bought on their own, after research, gain less.

Take a shampoo brand that sells the same volume on Amazon and Walmart today. A Walmart+ member who buys groceries weekly adds the shampoo every six weeks, while the Amazon shopper buys it when the bottle runs out. The Walmart purchase is already scheduled into a trip the shopper makes anyway, and over a year that habit is worth more than the two channels’ current sales suggest.

That means looking at Walmart through frequency: which products fit the weekly basket, and whether they are available for store pickup and delivery rather than only shipped from a warehouse. It means checking how they show up in the searches shoppers make while building a grocery order. And it means tracking repeat purchase rates by channel, so Walmart gets judged on how often its shoppers come back for the brand’s products.

The rule of thumb: rank a channel by how often its shoppers pass your shelf, before you rank it by size. Planning each channel around how its shoppers buy is how we run Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect alongside Amazon.

A0046.title: Mother’s Day 2021 rewards brands shoppers can find by recipient
A0046.alt: Three wrapped gifts with twine and kraft tags beside a ceramic jug of pastel tulips on a rustic wooden table.
A0046.ttag: Mother’s Day 2021 rewards brands shoppers can find by recipient | Kwontified
A0046.desc: Mother’s Day spending hit a record $26.7 billion in 2020, and a third of shoppers look first for gift suggestions. Brands win by being findable by recipient.
A0046.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 15, 2021.
A0046.body:
Someone buying a gift for their mother rarely starts with a product. They start with the person: something for Mom, under a certain price, that will arrive in time. A good department store knows this, which is why the gift table sits by the entrance, mixing candles, scarves and photo frames by occasion while the candle aisle stays at the back sorted by scent.

Marketplaces are built like the aisle. Search results, category pages and most brands’ listings and advertising are organized around products, and that mismatch decides who wins Mother’s Day. Brands that make themselves findable for gifting searches, and deliver before the day, capture the shopper who has not yet decided what to buy. Brands that rely on product listings alone are invisible to her.

How Mother’s Day 2021 got this valuable

The occasion has grown steadily more valuable. US consumers planned to spend a record $26.7 billion on Mother’s Day in 2020, up from about $25 billion the year before, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey, as reported by Talk Business & Politics. Average planned spending reached a record $204.74 and had risen 18.6% over the previous five years.

The pandemic changed how that money was spent. NRF found that 66% of respondents planned to celebrate virtually in 2020, which meant more gifts sent and fewer handed over in person. More shoppers planned to buy electronics, books and housewares than a year earlier, by 24%, 22% and 21% respectively. Greeting cards and flowers remained the most common purchases, with more than 70% of men and women planning to buy them, and subscription boxes were gaining ground.

One finding matters most for brands selling online. A third of respondents said they look first to retailers that offer gift suggestions and coupons. A large share of shoppers, in other words, arrive undecided and want help choosing. They have no product loyalty yet, which makes them the most open customers a brand will meet all year.

Why product listings miss the gift shopper

The way a marketplace is built is the hidden structure here. Results and advertising are organized by what a product is: a candle, a bag, a pair of earrings. A shopper who types “gifts for mom” is asking a different question, and what she sees depends on which products are described, tagged and advertised in a way that answers it.

Take a candle brand whose best-selling scent sits on the first page of results for “soy candle” all year. In late April, shoppers start typing “gifts for mom under $40”. The brand’s listing never mentions gifts, mothers or a gift box, and its advertising bids only on candle terms. A competitor with a similar candle, a title that mentions a gift set and a bid on the occasion search takes the sale, though the two products are almost identical.

Most brands write their listings for the shopper who already knows what she wants. Titles name the product and its features, and advertising bids on product terms. Neither reaches the shopper starting with a person and a budget. She is served by gift guides, occasion searches and seasonal pages, and the brands that show up there are the ones that planned to.

Building for product searches is a sensible habit most of the year, since most shoppers do know what they want and product searches convert well. Gifting occasions break the pattern for a few weeks, and brands that keep their normal setup miss the change.

The calendar from here to May 9

Mother’s Day falls on May 9 in 2021, which leaves little room, and timing is half the game. When most gifts are sent rather than handed over, the delivery date becomes part of the product. A shopper choosing between two similar gifts picks the one that promises to arrive before the day. A brand that runs low on stock in the final week, or whose items show slow delivery, loses sales it had already earned in the search results.

Working back from the day, the sequence looks like this:

  1. Now: search the main marketplaces for gift phrases in the category, such as gifts for mom under a set price, and note which brands appear and why.
  2. Through late April: add gifting language to the titles, descriptions and images of the most giftable products, and start bidding on occasion searches alongside product terms.
  3. Before the final week: check stock and delivery promises on those products, so every listing can still promise arrival before May 9.
  4. After the day: measure the share of sales that came from occasion searches and gift pages against ordinary product searches.

Presentation matters along the way. A gift shopper is buying for someone else’s reaction, so gift sets, gift wrap or a gift message option, and images that show the product as a present instead of a refill, all help her picture the moment of giving. These are small changes. They tend to get made only by brands that treat the occasion as its own season with its own plan, rather than a few busy weeks.

The question to put to the team

The question for leaders is simple to ask and harder to answer: if a shopper searched for a Mother’s Day gift in your category this afternoon, would she find you? The answer depends on decisions made weeks before the day. The measurement afterwards matters as much, because brands that track how much came from gifting searches will plan the next occasion differently, and brands that do not will keep treating the season as a bump in normal demand. Planning content, advertising and stock around seasonal events is how we manage seasonal marketplace demand for brands.

A0048.crumb: Amazon Best Seller rank rewards the…
A0048.title: Amazon Best Seller rank rewards the brands already winning
A0048.alt: Gold trophy cup on the top step of a white wooden podium set on grass before a navy wall.
A0048.ttag: Amazon Best Seller rank rewards the brands already winning | Kwontified
A0048.desc: Amazon’s Best Sellers rank updates hourly from recent and past sales, so sales buy visibility that buys more sales. Fund momentum where it compounds.
A0048.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 20, 2021.
A0048.body:
A brand launches ten new products on Amazon with the same budget behind each. Three months later, two of them sell steadily and eight have barely moved, and the launch review concludes that the eight were weaker products. Often they were not. They simply never sold enough, early enough, to climb.

On Amazon, sales buy visibility and visibility buys more sales. Amazon says its Best Sellers rank is updated hourly to reflect recent and historical sales, and shoppers who decide quickly lean on the signals that rank produces. Products that start selling keep selling, and products that stall find it hard to restart. That runs against the instinct to spread budget evenly across a range: brands should concentrate spending on the products that can hold momentum, and accept paying more than a sale is worth at first when the visibility it earns pays back later.

What Amazon Best Seller rank measures

Amazon has said little about how the rank works, and what it has said is consistent. The Best Sellers calculation is based on Amazon sales and updated hourly to reflect recent and historical sales of every item sold on Amazon, as Helium 10 quoted it. Seller Central’s own help pages make the same point: rank is relative to other products in the category and takes both recent and historical sales into account.

Two details matter. Recent sales count, so a product can climb quickly. Historical sales count too, so a product that has sold well for a long time keeps an advantage a newcomer has to overcome.

The way shoppers buy makes the rank more powerful still. Customers complete 28% of purchases on Amazon in three minutes or less, and half in less than 15 minutes, Jeff Bezos wrote in his letter to shareholders. Shoppers who decide that fast do not read every listing. They choose among the products they see first and trust most, which are the products with sales, reviews and badges behind them.

A snowball rolling downhill

In most physical stores, a buyer sets a product’s position on the shelf and sales follow position. On Amazon, past performance largely sets position, and sales follow position. Each sale improves the product’s standing, which makes the next sale more likely.

Think of a snowball rolling downhill. A small one picks up a little snow and grows slowly, while a large one picks up more with each turn and grows faster. Two snowballs that start a few inches apart can end up very different by the bottom of the hill, though the slope and the snow were the same for both.

That has a consequence that surprises many brand teams. The first sales of a product are worth more than their margin, because each one adds to the rank, reviews and visibility that produce later sales. Advertising that looks unprofitable on a single sale can be profitable over the life of the product, provided the momentum holds.

The reverse holds just as firmly. A product that goes out of stock, or loses its advertising support, stops adding to its sales history while competitors keep adding to theirs. When it comes back, it starts further down the hill.

Reviews compound the same way. A product that sells more collects more reviews, and a product with more reviews converts more of the shoppers who see it. Rank and reviews feed each other, so a lead in one tends to become a lead in both, and a competitor entering the category later has to overcome both at once. That is why late entrants so often need deep discounts or heavy advertising just to be seen.

Concentrating the launch budget

The logic points to concentration. Take a brand with $20,000 a month to support ten new products.

ApproachProducts supportedMonthly spend each
Spread evenlyten$2,000
Concentratedthree, chosen on reviews and marginabout $6,700

Spread evenly, each product gets $2,000, which may be too little to lift any of them into the range where shoppers see them. Concentrated on the three with the strongest reviews and margins, each gets about $6,700, enough to build rank the brand can then defend with less spend. The other seven follow once the first three are established.

When to stop pushing a product

Concentration needs a stop rule, because not every product can hold momentum. A product with weak reviews, poor images or a price far above its rivals will convert badly however much traffic it gets, and buying sales for it only delays the verdict. The test is whether conversion holds as spend rises, measured week by week and not judged on one good or bad day. If conversion holds, the product is building momentum. If it falls as traffic grows, the brand is paying to push a product shoppers do not want.

Stock is the other condition. Momentum built on advertising is lost the moment the product runs out, so inventory belongs in the advertising plan, not in a separate decision made by a different team on a different calendar. Rank lost to an outage is slow to recover.

So rank the new and growing products by reviews, conversion rate and margin, and put launch spend behind the top few. Judge launch advertising over the product’s first months, not by the return on each sale, with the stop rule written down before the money goes out. And keep established winners in stock and supported, because they are the snowballs already near the bottom of the hill.

The rule of thumb: on Amazon, a launch dollar is worth most on the product most likely to keep selling without it. Launch plans that concentrate spend where it compounds are part of how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

A0049.crumb: Retail media redefines brand building as…
A0049.title: Retail media redefines brand building as new customers counted
A0049.alt: Brass tally counter beside a kraft paper parcel tied with twine on a worn wooden ledge against a sage wall.
A0049.ttag: Retail media redefines brand building as new customers counted | Kwontified
A0049.desc: Retail media measures brand building in new-to-brand orders, which makes it accountable but can miss the memory brands build before shoppers buy.
A0049.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 22, 2021.
A0049.body:
Ask a brand team in 2021 what its awareness budget achieved. More and more often the answer comes as a number from a retailer: so many new-to-brand customers, shoppers who bought the brand for the first time in a year after seeing an ad. Brand building used to happen far from the shelf, on television and billboards, wherever a brand could plant itself in a shopper’s memory. Retailers now sell it next to the shelf and measure it in their own sales data.

That makes brand spending more accountable than it has ever been. It also risks undervaluing the memory a brand builds before shoppers are ready to buy, so leaders should decide which brand goals belong in retail media and which need other measures.

How new-to-brand became the measure of retail media brand building

Amazon set the terms early. In January 2019 it introduced new-to-brand metrics for display, video and Sponsored Brands campaigns, measuring whether an ad-attributed purchase came from a shopper buying the brand for the first time in the prior year, Amazon announced. The metrics were not available for Sponsored Products, Marketing Dive noted, which placed them squarely as a measure for the formats closest to brand advertising.

The money followed. Amazon’s “other” revenue line, which it says is mostly advertising, grew 66% to $7.95 billion for the fourth quarter of 2020, according to Amazon’s results. Walmart renamed its ad business in January, calling it Walmart Connect, and described plans that reach well beyond its search results, including nearly 170,000 digital screens across more than 4,500 stores and a demand-side platform for buying ads across the web, Walmart announced.

Brands are using these tools for awareness as well as for sales, and they do it because the retailer can show them a result in its own data. The supplement brand Olly said it puts a significant share of its Amazon spending into search and Amazon DSP as it tries to drive a lot of awareness in a short time, Digiday reported.

What new-to-brand counts, and what it misses

The definition is the hidden structure. When a retailer measures brand building, it measures what it can see: a shopper who saw an ad and then bought the brand for the first time in a year. That is a real and valuable outcome. It ties brand spending to customers, and it hands the brand team a number it can defend in a budget meeting.

The definition also leaves things out. A shopper who saw the ad, remembered the brand and bought it months later in a store or from another retailer does not appear. Neither does the shopper who has not bought yet but now considers the brand. And a lapsed customer who returns after thirteen months counts as new, though the brand did not win them for the first time.

None of this makes the metric wrong. It makes it partial. Retailers can only measure what happens in their own stores and sites, and a brand’s customers rarely shop in just one place. Even the largest retailer sees a slice of a brand’s total sales, so its report describes how brand advertising works inside that slice.

Grading a brand campaign that way is a little like judging a billboard by the till receipts of one shop on the street. The shop’s count is accurate, and most of the people who saw the billboard bought somewhere else or not yet.

A brand that judges all of its brand building by new-to-brand orders will drift toward whatever produces them quickly, and away from the slower work of becoming a name shoppers think of before they search.

Say a brand splits a $1 million brand budget between a retail media awareness campaign and a streaming video campaign. The retail media report shows 4,000 new-to-brand customers. The video campaign shows nothing in the retailer’s report, because its effect appears in searches and store sales weeks later. At the next budget review, money moves to the campaign with a number attached. The brand has not learned which one worked better. It has rewarded the one that was easier to count.

Which brand goals belong at the shelf

The question for a leadership team is which brand goals the company is willing to measure at a retailer’s shelf.

Fits retail media measurement wellFits it poorly
Introducing a product to shoppers already in the categoryBuilding a name over years
Winning first purchases from a competitor’s buyersEntering a category shoppers do not yet search for
Launching in a new retailerReaching people who rarely shop where the retailer can see them

Ownership matters too, because the owner’s targets decide how the money is judged. If retail media brand spending sits with the sales team, it will be judged on sales. If it sits with the brand team, it should carry brand measures as well, such as branded search volume and periodic awareness surveys, next to the retailer’s report.

The share of the brand budget that moves into retail media each year is worth watching against branded search. If that share rises while branded search volume stays flat, the brand is buying customers it already had a chance to win, more than building demand that did not exist.

The fullest check is a test that holds back a brand campaign in some regions once a year and compares total sales across every channel, which is the one view no single retailer’s report can provide. Planning retail media alongside the wider brand budget is how we run brands’ retail media across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0051.title: Q1 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: split out the stimulus
A0051.alt: Pile of brass coins split by a gold divider on a wooden desk with old books and a mug by a window.
A0051.ttag: Q1 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: split out the stimulus | Kwontified
A0051.desc: Q1 2021 Amazon ad results mix a quiet January with a March lifted by $1,400 stimulus payments. Split the quarter before you compare CPC, conversion or ROAS.
A0051.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 27, 2021.
A0051.body:
Every April, first-quarter Amazon results get compared with a benchmark and with the quarter before, and most brands conclude that performance fell. In 2021 that comparison needs more care than usual. The quarter held a quiet January and February, then a late March lifted by a third round of federal stimulus payments that began processing on March 12.

A quarterly average blends those two kinds of demand, and setting it against the holiday quarter, or against March 2020, stacks more distortion on top. A useful Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q1 2021 splits the quarter first and compares each period on its own terms.

March 12 divides the quarter

The stimulus timing is documented. The first batch of about 90 million payments from the American Rescue Plan, worth more than $242 billion, began processing on March 12, with an official payment date of March 17, the IRS said. More batches followed in the second half of the month, so the money arrived in waves. A brand reading daily data may see the lift build over several weeks instead of jumping on a single day.

The effect on spending was large. US retail sales rose 9.8% in March from February as consumers received $1,400 payments, the Commerce Department reported, according to CNBC. Sales were 27.7% above March 2020.

For an advertiser, the last three weeks of the quarter therefore behaved differently from the first ten. More shoppers arrived with money to spend, and that tends to lift conversion; more advertisers competed for them, and that tends to lift CPC, the cost per click, which is the price of each click in the auction.

The Q1 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark, by period

Two public benchmarks cover the quarter. Tinuiti’s Q1 2021 Amazon Ads Benchmark Report measured the quarter as a whole against a year earlier, AdExchanger reported. Tinuiti works from more than $2 billion in digital spend under management.

Sponsored ads measureQ1 2021, year over yearQ4 2020, for reference
Sponsored Products spendup 28%n/a
Sponsored Products clicksup 20%n/a
Sponsored Products CPCup 7%up 1%
Sales attributed to Sponsored Productsup 28%n/a
Sponsored Brands spendup 86%n/a

Return on ad spend (ROAS) means attributed sales divided by ad spend, and it uses Amazon’s standard Sponsored Products attribution model. With attributed sales and spend both up 28%, Sponsored Products ROAS for the quarter was flat on the year, even though each click cost 7% more.

A March-against-February view comes from Skai’s March 2021 spend snapshot, which compares March with February across its retail media advertisers. In March, 67% of retail media accounts spent at least 10% more than in February, against 19% that spent at least 10% less. Click prices were stable to slightly higher: 43% of accounts paid at least 10% more per click, and 19% paid at least 10% less. Tinuiti saw the same turn in one category, with apparel ad impressions up 54% year over year in March after a 13% drop in February.

Neither source separates January 1 to March 11 from March 12 to 31. They report a whole quarter and calendar months, not the stimulus weeks. The split at March 12 has to come from each brand’s own console data.

Anchoring on the quarter before

The most recent quarter is the number everyone remembers, so it becomes the reference for the next one. For most brands, the quarter before Q1 is the holiday season, the strongest stretch of the year. Measured against it, almost any first quarter looks like a decline, and teams spend April explaining a drop that is mostly the calendar.

The year-ago comparison has its own problem in 2021. March 2020 was the month the pandemic changed how Americans shopped, so a comparison with it mixes this year’s stimulus with last year’s disruption. The 27.7% gain in March retail sales says more about how unusual March 2020 was than about how strong March 2021 was.

The quarterly average adds a third distortion. Any quarterly figure averages its periods, weighted by each brand’s own activity. A brand that held budget back until late March, when the payments arrived, will show different quarterly numbers from one that spent evenly, even if both paid the market price every week.

Say CPC was $1.10 from March 12 onward and $0.90 earlier in the quarter, for every brand.

Share of clicks in stimulus weeksQuarterly average CPC
Brand A40%$0.98
Brand B15%$0.93

Brand B looks more efficient, and both paid exactly the going rate in every period.

The split also separates two causes the quarterly number hides. If conversion rose in late March faster than CPC, shoppers were arriving readier to buy and the brand gained from the demand. If CPC rose faster than conversion, the auction captured most of the gain and the brand paid more for the same shoppers. Both can happen in the same quarter, and only the period split shows which one dominated for a given brand.

Category still matters, especially this quarter

A market-wide figure describes the market as a whole, and categories differ. In a crowded category such as beauty, a brand should expect CPCs above the market figure; in a narrow category, below it. Categories that stimulus spending favored, such as clothing and sporting goods, may also show a sharper late-March change than categories people buy regardless of household income.

The same logic applies product by product inside a brand: a discretionary or gift-like item may have moved more in late March than a staple that sells the same way every week. Where the market sat is what the benchmark shows; whether you paid too much is what your own category shows, period by period.

So split the Q1 2021 Sponsored Ads results at March 12 before comparing them with anything. Compare January to early March with the quiet weeks of the holiday quarter, not with its peak, and treat the year-ago March as an outlier. Then plan the second quarter knowing the stimulus effect may fade while Prime Day, which Amazon has not yet dated, may add a new peak.

The working rule: when the calendar has a seam in it, cut along the seam before you read the numbers. Reporting by period, so that budgets track the auction rather than the calendar quarter, is how we read Amazon ad results for brands.

A0054.crumb: Legacy brands on marketplaces need a new…
A0054.title: Legacy brands on marketplaces need a new operating model
A0054.alt: Ornate antique brass cash register beside a modern tablet on a wooden shop counter with shelves of crockery behind.
A0054.ttag: Legacy brands on marketplaces need a new operating model | Kwontified
A0054.desc: Legacy brands were built to sell to retail buyers. Marketplaces reward whoever controls listing, price and stock daily, which calls for a new operating model.
A0054.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 29, 2021.
A0054.body:
The spring line review at a heritage brand runs the way it has for decades. The buyer walks the collection, the wholesale team takes notes on depth and price points, and somewhere in the conversation someone mentions that a reseller has been selling last season’s best-selling jacket on Amazon at a deep discount for months. Nobody in the room owns that listing. Nobody saw it until now.

Legacy brands were organized to sell to retail buyers: a few line reviews a year, orders placed months ahead, and a retailer who decided how the product appeared on the shelf. Marketplaces pay a different kind of company. On Amazon and its peers, the value goes to whoever controls the listing, the price and the stock, every day, so a brand that adds marketplaces to its wholesale organization as one more account hands that control to others. The fix is to rebuild the operating model around daily sell-through.

How the ground moved under legacy brands on marketplaces

The shift is no longer a forecast. US e-commerce sales reached $791.7 billion in 2020, up 32.4%, and rose to 14.0% of total retail sales from 11.0% a year earlier, according to Census Bureau figures reported by CNBC.

Much of that runs through marketplaces where the brand is not the only seller. More than 1.9 million small and medium-sized businesses sell in Amazon’s store and make up close to 60% of its retail sales, Jeff Bezos wrote in his final letter to shareholders. Some of those businesses resell other companies’ brands, bought from wholesalers, distributors or clearance channels.

Categories once anchored in department stores have moved too. Wells Fargo analysts estimated in March that Amazon’s US apparel and footwear sales grew about 15% in 2020 to more than $41 billion, ahead of Walmart, CNBC reported.

Follow the value: listing, price and stock

The way value moves on a marketplace explains why the old model struggles. In wholesale, a brand earns its money when a retailer places an order, and what happens afterwards, how the product is shown, priced and restocked, is largely the retailer’s job.

On a marketplace the order is only the start. The listing decides whether shoppers find the product and believe it. The price, compared in a second with every other seller’s, decides who wins the sale. The stock decides whether the product stays visible at all. Whoever controls those three things captures the value, whether that is the brand, a reseller or the marketplace itself.

A legacy brand that treats the marketplace as one more account tends to control none of them. Its listings are written by whoever created the page first. Its price is set by resellers buying from its wholesale partners or from clearance channels. Its stock depends on orders placed by a retailer or a reseller, not by the brand.

That makes the reinvention an organizational question before it is a marketing one. A wholesale organization is built around sales teams, seasonal calendars and account plans. A marketplace business needs people who manage content, pricing, inventory and advertising every day, working from data that updates hourly. Those jobs rarely fit inside a wholesale team’s targets or rhythms.

The tension goes deeper than workload. A wholesale sales team is paid to sell more to its accounts, including the retailers and distributors whose stock ends up with marketplace resellers. A marketplace team is paid to control how the brand appears to shoppers. Put both under the same targets and the wholesale goal usually wins, because it is larger and familiar, while the marketplace problems it creates surface somewhere the wholesale team is not measured.

Take a heritage outerwear brand that sells $2 million a year to department stores, some of which resell it on Amazon. A reseller lists the best-selling jacket at $40 below the brand’s own price late in the season, and the wholesale team hears about it at the spring line review, months later. A brand running its own marketplace operation would have seen the listing within days and adjusted its own offer, its supply to that reseller, or both.

The rebuild covers ownership, pricing and supply

Part of the rebuildWhat it meansWhat it costs
OwnershipOne leader for marketplace sell-through, with authority over listings, pricing and inventory, separate from wholesale targetsA new leader and team
Pricing policyA single view of where prices are set and enforced across wholesale, the brand’s own site and marketplacesTelling some wholesale accounts no, or tightening who may resell online
SupplyStock positioned for fast delivery and replenished continuously, planned for the marketplace directlyCarrying inventory the brand used to leave to its retailers

Without the pricing policy, the channel with the lowest price sets the price for all of them. Without its own supply plan, the brand’s visibility depends on another company’s purchase orders. Brands that try to avoid these costs by keeping marketplaces inside the wholesale organization usually pay them anyway, in lost control of how they appear to shoppers.

The evidence so far leans toward the brands that make these changes deliberately. The clearest test is who owns the brand’s top listings on Amazon a year from now: if the brand does, it has rebuilt, and if resellers still do, it has only added a channel.

A good first step is simple. Search the main marketplaces for the brand’s top 20 products and record who sells each one, at what price and with which content. Then put that list in front of the leadership team with one question: who here is responsible for fixing it? Building marketplace operations across Amazon, Walmart, Target and international marketplaces is work we do with legacy brands.

A0056.crumb: Apple’s change makes the retail media…
A0056.title: Apple’s change makes the retail media closed loop worth more
A0056.alt: Coiled rope and a smartphone lying on weathered wooden decking against a navy blue wall.
A0056.ttag: Apple’s change makes the retail media closed loop worth more | Kwontified
A0056.desc: Apple’s tracking prompt weakens social ad measurement but not retail media, which sees the sale itself. Budgets will move toward it, and prices with them.
A0056.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 4, 2021.
A0056.body:
Since April 26, iPhone users updating to iOS 14.5 have started seeing a new prompt: allow this app to track your activity across other companies’ apps and websites? Apple’s App Tracking Transparency weakens the measurement social platforms rely on. It leaves retail media’s closed loop untouched, because a retailer does not need to follow a shopper across apps to know what she bought. It sees the sale in its own store.

That makes the closed loop worth more, budgets will shift toward it, and its prices will rise. Brands should take the measurement advantage, and weigh it against those rising costs and against attribution that gives retail media more credit than it has earned.

Why Apple’s change spares the retail media closed loop

App Tracking Transparency requires apps to ask permission before tracking users across other companies’ apps and websites, the PA news agency reported when iOS 14.5 became available. Social platforms depend on that tracking to connect an ad seen in their app with a purchase on a brand’s website.

Retail media works differently. When a shopper sees a sponsored product on Amazon or Walmart and buys it there, the ad and the sale happen in the same place. Walmart made that the center of its pitch when it launched Walmart Connect, describing its ability to connect ads to purchases in its stores and online, Walmart announced.

Two of the largest ad businesses reported their first-quarter results last week. Facebook said its advertising revenue grew 46%, driven by a 30% rise in the average price per ad and a 12% rise in ads delivered, according to its results. It expects growth to come mainly from price for the rest of 2021. Facebook said the iOS changes would begin to affect ad targeting in the second quarter, CNBC reported. Amazon said its “other” revenue line, mostly advertising, grew 77% to $6.9 billion, GeekWire reported.

The one shop on the street whose till still works

Imagine a street of shops where every till has stopped recording some of its sales, except one. Every shop is still selling, and only one can prove it. A buyer deciding where to spend will lean toward the shop that can show results, even if the others are doing just as well.

Retail media is now the shop with the working till. A brand planning its next quarter will see weaker reported results from social campaigns, partly because fewer sales get counted, and steady reported results from retail media. Budgets follow the numbers that can be defended, especially in a year when finance teams are asking marketing to prove every dollar.

The supply side does not stretch to match. There are only so many sponsored slots on a search results page, and when more money chases the same slots in an auction, the price of each click rises.

Facebook’s results show the same pressure from the other side. Its growth now comes far more from the price of each ad than from the number of ads it shows, which is what happens when demand for attention grows faster than the supply of it. If some of that demand moves to retail media, the same pressure will show up in its auctions, and brands that move late may find the move costs more than they planned.

Measured results cost more, and claim more

For brands, the closed loop is a real advantage. Measured results let a brand manage spend with more confidence, and retail media reaches shoppers at the moment they are deciding. The advantage still comes with two costs.

The first is price. Take a brand paying $1.00 a click on Amazon, converting 10% of clicks at a $30 average order.

Cost per clickConversionAverage orderSales per ad dollar
Today$1.0010%$30$3.00
After more budget enters the auction$1.2010%$30$2.50

Nothing about the brand’s ads changed. The auction got more crowded.

The second cost is attribution. Retail media’s closed loop sees the sale, and it also tends to claim sales that would have happened anyway, from shoppers who were already searching for the brand. A report that counts every purchase after an ad is a narrower thing than a measure of what the ad caused. When social measurement weakens, that generosity stands out more, not less. A brand setting a social report that undercounts against a retail media report that overcounts will move money for the wrong reason, even if the move turns out to be right.

The balance still favors retail media for brands whose shoppers buy where the retailer can see them. It favors it less for brands whose growth depends on reaching people who are not yet searching. Cost per click on Amazon and Walmart through the second quarter will show which way the extra money is going: if it rises faster than conversion, the budget is feeding the auction more than the brand.

Before shifting the budget

Track cost per click and conversion rate on each retail media network monthly, so it is clear whether rising spend is buying more sales or only higher prices. Before moving money out of social campaigns, run a holdout test to see what they still contribute after the iOS change. And split retail media reports into branded and category searches, judged on different targets, because branded searches are where attribution is most generous.

The rule of thumb: when one channel becomes the only one that can prove itself, pay for the proof, not for the crowd. Running retail media across Amazon, Walmart and Target alongside social and search budgets is how we help brands decide how far to shift after iOS 14.5.
