A0057.crumb: Chinese sellers on Amazon: when your…
A0057.title: Chinese sellers on Amazon: when your factory becomes your rival
A0057.alt: Two glazed stoneware teapots beside an open shipping box of paper and pottery tools on a workshop table.
A0057.ttag: Chinese sellers on Amazon: when your factory becomes your rival | Kwontified
A0057.desc: Three quarters of new Amazon sellers in January 2021 were based in China, many selling factory direct. Brands should compete on what a factory cannot copy.
A0057.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 6, 2021.
A0057.body:
Search Amazon for the stainless steel bottle a kitchenware brand has sold for years, and a near-identical bottle sits one listing away: same shape, same capacity, a name nobody has heard of, a lower price. It may well have come off the same production line. For decades a brand’s factory was a supplier that made the product while the brand sold it. Amazon has changed that arrangement, because the factories that once made goods for brands and retailers can now sell directly to shoppers, under their own names, on the same results page as the brands they supply.

Three quarters of the new sellers on Amazon’s largest marketplaces in January 2021 were based in China. Brands competing on Amazon should assume their supplier can become their rival, and compete on what a factory cannot easily copy: trust, content, service and a reason to choose the brand.

How factory-direct selling took hold among Chinese sellers on Amazon

The numbers are striking. China-based sellers made up 75% of new sellers across Amazon’s four core marketplaces, the US, UK, Germany and Japan, in January 2021, up from 47% a year earlier and 41% in 2019, Marketplace Pulse reported. In the US alone, China’s share of new sellers rose from 28% in 2019 to 63% in 2021. Earlier estimates, the same report noted, put China-based sellers’ share of Amazon’s gross merchandise volume at 30% to 40%.

It did not happen by accident. Marketplace Pulse quoted an internal Amazon email from 2015, released by the House Judiciary Committee, in which the head of Amazon’s marketplace described Chinese factories that had made goods for big retailers for 20 years. They now realized they could build brands of their own and sell directly to the world, he wrote, with Amazon as “that vehicle.”

The logistics made it work. Most of these sellers ship containers to Amazon’s warehouses instead of single parcels to shoppers, so their products arrive in two days with Prime, the report noted. To a shopper, a factory brand looks like any other listing.

Amazon removed the wall between factory and shopper

The old model had a clear division of labor. The factory knew how to make the product, and the brand knew how to sell it. The brand’s value lay in design, marketing and distribution, all of which depended on access to retailers that a factory could not get alone.

Amazon took that wall down. A factory no longer needs a department store buyer to reach shoppers; it needs a listing, a warehouse slot and some advertising. It often has advantages a brand cannot match, too: lower costs, because it pays no supplier’s margin, and the ability to change a product quickly, because it controls the line.

That puts many brands in an uncomfortable spot. The factory that makes a brand’s best-selling item may sell a near-identical product under another name, at a lower price, one listing away. The brand’s design may be protected; its basic product often is not.

Take the bottle again. Say the brand sells it for $28, and the factory charges the brand $7 to make it. The factory lists a similar bottle on Amazon for $18 under its own name. Shoppers comparing the two see the same shape, the same capacity and a $10 difference, and the brand has to justify that difference with something the listing can show.

The factory’s advantages are real and narrow. It knows how to make the product cheaply and change it quickly. It usually knows far less about the shopper: why she buys, what worries her, what would make her pay more. Those are the things a brand learned over years of selling through retailers, and they are what a listing now has to carry, since the retailer’s shelf, staff and reputation are no longer doing that work. Brands that treated their own marketing as a cost of distribution are finding it is the product’s main defense.

What the brand offers that its factory cannot copy

The question in the room is what the brand offers that its factory cannot copy. Price is rarely the answer, because the factory starts with a cost advantage. The answers that hold up are the ones a factory finds hard to build. A name shoppers trust is one, along with detailed and credible product content and reviews earned over time. Responsive service and guarantees are others, and so is a range that solves a problem rather than a single commodity item.

Leaders should look at supply relationships at the same time. Contracts can limit how a factory uses a brand’s designs, molds and specifications, and brands can protect their listings through Amazon’s brand programs. None of that stops a factory from selling its own products, but it narrows how closely those products can follow the brand’s. The strongest responses do both: tighter supply agreements, and listings rebuilt so a shopper comparing two similar products can see in seconds why one costs more.

The share of top sellers in a brand’s own category that are factory brands is the number worth tracking. If it is rising, the category is drifting toward commodity pricing, and the brand needs a stronger reason to be chosen than it had before.

Three pieces of homework follow. Search the top categories on Amazon and list which competing sellers are manufacturers selling under their own brands, and at what prices. Read the supplier contracts for what they say about designs, molds and selling similar products on marketplaces. And put money into the parts of the listing a factory cannot easily copy, then measure whether they hold a price premium. Competing against direct-from-factory sellers is part of how we help brands win on Amazon and other marketplaces.

A0058.crumb: Amazon ad growth in Q1 shows more sellers…
A0058.title: Amazon ad growth in Q1 shows more sellers bidding per shopper
A0058.alt: Empty wire shopping basket surrounded by rows of wooden paddle-shaped markers on blocks on a wooden table.
A0058.ttag: Amazon ad growth in Q1 shows more sellers bidding per shopper | Kwontified
A0058.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 77% in Q1 2021, far faster than its 44% sales growth. The gap is more sellers bidding for each shopper, and Prime Day will widen it.
A0058.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 11, 2021.
A0058.body:
Amazon’s advertising line grew 77% in the first quarter of 2021. Its total sales grew 44%. Read quickly, that looks like proof that Amazon ads are working better than ever, and plenty of sales decks will use it that way. The numbers support something narrower. Advertising took a larger share of every dollar shoppers spent on Amazon, and sellers took a larger share of the units sold.

That is the pattern of more sellers bidding for each shopper, more than of more shoppers arriving. Brands should plan for higher advertising cost per sale, especially around a June Prime Day, and judge Amazon ads by profit per order instead of by Amazon’s growth.

Amazon ad growth in Q1 2021, set against sales

Q1 2020Q1 2021Growth
“Other” revenue, mostly advertising$3.9 billion$6.9 billion77%
Net sales$75.5 billion$108.5 billion44%
Advertising as a share of net salesabout 5.2%about 6.4%

The figures come from GeekWire’s report on Amazon’s results. Revenue from third-party seller services grew 64% to $23.7 billion. Sellers also took a larger share of what shoppers bought: third-party sellers accounted for 55% of paid units, up from 52% a year earlier, Amazon said on its earnings call. And advertising growth is accelerating, since the same line grew 66% in the fourth quarter of 2020, as Amazon’s results for that quarter show.

Does faster ad growth mean ads work better?

That is the claim worth checking. If better results for advertisers were the main driver, ad revenue would grow roughly in step with the sales those ads produce. It did not. Advertising went from about 5.2% of Amazon’s net sales to about 6.4% in a year. Put differently, for every dollar shoppers spent on Amazon, sellers and brands spent roughly 23% more on advertising than they had a year before.

That is what an auction does when bidders arrive faster than lots. The number of shoppers searching for a product sets the number of ad slots worth bidding on, and the number of sellers wanting those shoppers sets the price. When sellers multiply faster than shoppers, each slot costs more, and advertising takes a larger slice of each sale.

Several forces push the same way at once. More sellers are joining Amazon, many from overseas: China-based sellers made up 75% of all new sellers joining Amazon’s four core marketplaces in January, Marketplace Pulse reported, and most of them advertise to be seen. Brands that once treated Amazon as a side channel are giving it a larger share of their plans as online sales grow. And Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released on April 26, may push more money toward retail media, where results stay measurable.

Facebook’s quarter points in the same direction. Its advertising growth came mainly from the average price per ad, which saw a 30% rise, according to its results. Attention is getting more expensive across platforms.

Two cautions belong with the calculation. Amazon describes the “other” line as mostly advertising, so the share of sales is an approximation. And a single quarter can be distorted by timing. The gap between ad growth and sales growth has now persisted for two quarters running, though, which is harder to explain away.

A June Prime Day concentrates the pressure

Prime Day will bring that pressure to a point, with less warning than usual. Amazon said it would hold the two-day event in the second quarter, and its chief financial officer told reporters it would fall in June, GeekWire reported. That puts the year’s most competitive auction weeks earlier than brands are used to, on top of a quarter in which ad intensity is already climbing.

Take a product that sells for $40, earns $14 of gross profit and costs $6 of advertising per order today. If costs per click rise by a fifth and conversion holds:

TodayClicks a fifth dearer
Advertising per order$6$7.20
Profit per advertised order$8$6.80

The brand sells as many units, and each one earns 15% less.

Prime Day also compresses the time for learning. A brand that discovers in the first hours that its bids are too low has little time to fix them before the event ends, and a brand that discovers they are too high has already paid. Setting the profit floor per order before the event is the way to bid by rule instead of by reaction.

The effect will be uneven. Categories that many new sellers have entered will see prices rise fastest, while categories with few sellers and loyal shoppers will feel less. A brand’s own cost per click, compared category by category with a year earlier, is a better guide than Amazon’s total.

Stopping advertising is not the answer, because the shoppers are on Amazon. Judging campaigns by profit per order after advertising is. A product that converts one shopper in five can carry a higher click price than one that converts one in twenty, and in a crowded auction that difference decides which products are worth advertising at all.

Budgeting for a dearer auction

Work out advertising cost per order and profit per order after advertising for the main products, and track both monthly. Set Prime Day budgets on the profit the brand can accept per order, and use return on ad spend as a secondary check. And move spending toward the products and searches with the highest conversion, where rising click prices do the least damage.

The rule of thumb: when the auction gets crowded, the product with the best conversion rate is the one that can afford to stay in it. Planning budgets on profit per order is how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

A0061.crumb: Prime Day in June squeezes the 2021…
A0061.title: Prime Day in June squeezes the 2021 planning year for brands
A0061.alt: Gift wrapped in botanical paper with lavender and chamomile between wooden bookends on a shelf with a succulent.
A0061.ttag: Prime Day in June squeezes the 2021 planning year for brands | Kwontified
A0061.desc: Amazon moved Prime Day from October 2020 to June 2021, leaving eight months between events and only weeks to prepare. Brands must plan the year around it.
A0061.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 13, 2021.
A0061.body:
Somewhere in most brands’ planning files sits a calendar built around a summer or autumn Prime Day, with stock ordered to match and an advertising budget phased to peak around it. On April 29, that calendar went out of date. Prime Day would take place in the second quarter, Amazon said on its first-quarter earnings call, and the company’s finance chief told reporters it would fall in June.

That leaves about eight months between two of Amazon’s biggest events and only weeks to prepare for the next. A June Prime Day is more than a date change. It pulls inventory, advertising budget and promotions earlier in the year and changes what is left for the autumn, so brands should decide the split across the whole year now.

What Amazon has said about Prime Day in June

On the call, Amazon told listeners it would hold the two-day event during the second quarter and share dates later in the quarter, according to the transcript. Chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said it would be in June, GeekWire reported.

For comparison, Prime Day 2020 ran on October 13 and 14, after the pandemic pushed it out of the summer, VentureBeat noted. In 2019 the event ran for 48 hours on July 15 and 16, and Amazon announced those dates on June 24, about three weeks ahead, TechCrunch reported.

Other retailers follow the date. In 2019, Target scheduled its own two-day Deal Days sale for the same July 15 and 16, ConsumerAffairs reported, and an early Prime Day is likely to pull competing events earlier too.

The dates make the squeeze concrete. Eight months separate the 2020 event from the 2021 one. In 2019, brands got about three weeks’ notice of the exact days. Nothing suggests 2021 will be more generous.

The question in the room: how to split the year

The question for a leadership team is how much of the year’s inventory, budget and promotion to commit to June. In a normal year, a July Prime Day sat comfortably between spring and the holiday season, and brands could plan it as one summer peak and then rebuild stock and budget for the autumn. Moving it up by a month or more is a little like a wedding brought forward with the invitations already printed: everything still happens, and every supplier is suddenly on a different clock.

What movesWhy June changes itThe decision it forces
InventoryStock must be in Amazon’s warehouses before the event, and products ordered from overseas factories now may not arrive in timeBuild deals around what is already in stock or already on the water
BudgetMoney spent in June comes from a year’s budget many brands set around a later eventDecide how much to reserve for the holiday season before June spending starts
CalendarFather’s Day falls on June 20 in 2021, and back-to-school shopping begins in JulyDecide how the event will be judged, since it may pull sales forward from both

Each row is a decision someone in the company owns, whether or not they know it yet.

The inventory point makes the product choice the first decision instead of the last. A brand with deep stock in a few items and thin stock in others should build its plan around the deep ones, even if they are not the products it would have chosen to promote. A deal on a product that sells out on the first morning wastes the advertising behind it and can leave the listing out of stock for weeks, just when the event’s momentum would have been most valuable.

What the budget split looks like

Take a brand with $600,000 of Amazon advertising budget for the rest of 2021 that expected to spend $150,000 around a summer Prime Day. If it spends the same $150,000 in June and also raises spend in the weeks before to build momentum, it may have committed $200,000 by the end of June. That leaves $400,000 for July to December, holiday season included, unless the brand finds more.

Holding back from Prime Day is not the answer. Amazon has more than 200 million Prime members worldwide, Jeff Bezos wrote in his shareholder letter, and the event is built to bring them to the site at once. Brands that sit out lose visibility to those that do not, and some of that visibility, in rank and reviews, carries on after the event ends.

The answer is to make the split on purpose: which products get deals in June, which are saved for the autumn, and how much budget is reserved for the holidays before the June spending begins. Leaders should also agree how the event will be judged. Prime Day sales will look strong. The better measure is total sales across June and July against the same weeks of 2020, which shows whether the event added sales or simply moved them.

When Amazon announces the dates, brands will have weeks, not months, to finalize deals and advertising. The ones that have already decided the split will spend that time executing. The rest will spend it debating, and their deals will go live after the first shoppers have already arrived and checked out.

So check now which products have enough stock in Amazon’s warehouses, or confirmed inbound shipments, to carry a June event, and plan deals only for those. Divide the rest of the year’s Amazon budget into June, the summer and the holiday season before any Prime Day money is spent. Planning Prime Day and the holiday season as one year is part of how we run Amazon advertising and promotions for brands.

A0063.crumb: Amazon’s algorithms are the store manager…
A0063.title: Amazon’s algorithms are the store manager brands never meet
A0063.alt: White robotic arm on a wooden stand picking a jar from shelves of amber bottles and boxes in a shop.
A0063.ttag: Amazon’s algorithms are the store manager brands never meet | Kwontified
A0063.desc: On Amazon, models decide which offer wins, where products rank and what ads cost. Brands cannot persuade that store manager, only change what it sees.
A0063.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 18, 2021.
A0063.body:
In a physical store, a manager decides which products get the best shelf, which supplier’s version goes on the end of the aisle and what gets restocked first. Brands spend years building relationships with the buyers and managers who make those calls. On Amazon, models make the same decisions: which offer gets the sale, which products get shelf space and what visibility costs. That manager cannot be pitched, taken to lunch or persuaded.

The models read data and nothing else. Brands should stop trying to influence the decision and manage the inputs the models read: price, delivery promise, stock, content and conversion history.

Amazon algorithms decide who gets the sale

The clearest example is the Buy Box, the button that adds an offer to the cart when several sellers list the same product. The House antitrust subcommittee estimated that roughly 80% of Amazon sales go through the Buy Box, with an even higher share on mobile, CNBC reported. At a July 2020 hearing, Jeff Bezos acknowledged that the Buy Box algorithm indirectly favors offers that can ship with Prime, the same report noted.

Visibility in search and on category lists follows similar logic. Amazon’s Best Sellers rank is based on sales and updated hourly, reflecting recent and historical sales, in the description Helium 10 quoted.

Advertising works the same way. Since early 2019, Sponsored Products campaigns can let Amazon raise a bid by up to 100% at the top of search when it predicts a click is likely to convert, and lower it when it predicts the opposite, Viral Launch explained. The system is deciding, auction by auction, how valuable each shopper is to each advertiser.

A store manager who reads only the till and the stockroom

Brands are used to thinking that a better product, a better story or a better relationship wins the shelf. On Amazon none of those count directly. They count only through the data they produce.

Picture a store manager who never speaks to suppliers and never reads their brochures. He looks at two things: the till, which tells him what sold and at what price, and the stockroom, which tells him what he can deliver tomorrow. Every morning he rearranges the shelves from those two records. A supplier who wants a better spot has one route, which is to change what the till and the stockroom show.

That is the position brands are in. A product with a strong story and slow delivery loses the Buy Box to a weaker offer that ships with Prime. A product of excellent quality with thin reviews converts less, so the advertising system bids less for it and the rank system shows it less. A brand that runs out of stock disappears from the till, and the manager fills the shelf with something else.

The decisions also compound. A competitive price and fast delivery win the Buy Box; the Buy Box produces sales; sales lift rank and give the ad system better conversion data; better data makes advertising cheaper per sale. A small gap at the start becomes a large one by the end.

And the manager works fast. A department store buyer might review a supplier’s position once a season. Amazon’s rank updates hourly, and its ad system adjusts bids auction by auction. A brand that fixes a stock problem or a price gap sees the effect within days, and a brand that lets one slip sees that within days too.

Take two sellers offering the same product at $25. One ships through Fulfillment by Amazon and qualifies for Prime; the other ships from its own warehouse in four to five days. If the Prime offer wins the Buy Box nine times out of ten, it takes roughly nine of every ten sales the listing makes, though the price, the product and the reviews are identical.

The inputs a brand can manage

The inputs a brand controls are fewer than it might like, and they are concrete.

InputWhat the models read
PriceHow the offer compares with others on the same listing and with similar products
Delivery promiseWhere the stock sits, and whether it qualifies for Prime
StockWhether the product can sell at all; an out-of-stock product feeds the models nothing
ContentImages, titles and descriptions, through their effect on conversion
Conversion historyThe result of all the others, and what the ad and rank systems learn from

None of this removes the need for good products or strong brands. It changes where their value shows up. A brand’s quality reaches Amazon’s models through reviews, return rates and repeat purchases, and its story reaches them through content that turns browsers into buyers. A brand that invests in those and neglects stock and delivery will find the manager never notices. A brand that runs its operations tightly gives its product and story the best chance of being seen.

In practice that means checking who holds the Buy Box on the top 20 listings each week and fixing price, stock or delivery wherever another seller wins it. It means planning inventory so the best sellers never drop out of Prime eligibility, above all ahead of a June Prime Day. And it means treating conversion rate by product as a core operating number, because it is the input Amazon’s rank and ad systems learn from most directly.

The rule of thumb: if you would not show it to the till or the stockroom, it is not part of your Amazon strategy. Weekly reporting on the inputs Amazon’s systems read is part of how we run channel management and advertising on Amazon.

A0064.crumb: Amazon’s review crackdown shows who owns…
A0064.title: Amazon’s review crackdown shows who owns a brand’s reputation
A0064.alt: Brass star-shaped badges pinned to a weathered wooden board on a shelf, with two more badges lying in front.
A0064.ttag: Amazon’s review crackdown shows who owns a brand’s reputation | Kwontified
A0064.desc: Amazon’s removal of Aukey and Mpow shows reviews are among a brand’s most valuable assets, and that Amazon decides if they count. Earn them, never buy them.
A0064.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 20, 2021.
A0064.body:
Around May 10, shoppers searching Amazon for Aukey chargers or Mpow earbuds found most of the listings gone. Two well-known electronics accessory brands had largely disappeared from the store over a few days, shortly after a report on a leaked fake-review database.

For every other brand watching, the lesson was blunt. Reviews have become one of the most valuable assets a brand holds on Amazon, because they drive conversion and rank, and that value makes them a target for manipulation. Amazon, and increasingly regulators, decide whether a brand’s reviews count. Brands should treat reviews as an asset they earn and protect, never one they can manufacture.

What the Amazon review crackdown has looked like so far

The removals came days after the review site SafetyDetectives reported finding an exposed database linked to a scheme in which sellers gave shoppers free products in exchange for positive reviews, Android Authority reported. Amazon would not confirm or deny whether either company was involved, Droid Life reported.

The rule itself is old. On October 3, 2016, Amazon changed its community guidelines to prohibit incentivized reviews, meaning reviews written in exchange for free or discounted products, except through its own Vine program, according to a summary by the law firm Hunton.

Regulators have taken an interest as well. In October 2019, the Federal Trade Commission settled with the skincare brand Sunday Riley over fake reviews its founder and employees had posted on Sephora’s website, Hunton noted. The vote was 3 to 2, with two commissioners dissenting because the settlement carried no payment or admission of wrongdoing.

The dissent matters as much as the decision. When two of five commissioners argue publicly that a penalty was too light, the next case is likely to be judged more harshly. A brand that treats fake reviews as a platform rule it might get away with breaking is also taking a legal risk, one that grows as regulators look harder at online commerce.

Follow the value: why reviews attract manipulation

A review does three jobs at once. It persuades the shopper who reads it. It lifts the listing’s conversion rate, which feeds Amazon’s ranking and advertising systems. And it builds on itself, because more reviews help a product sell more, and selling more brings in more reviews.

Shoppers lean on reviews heavily because they decide quickly. In a letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos wrote that, on Amazon, customers complete 28% of purchases in three minutes or less. In three minutes, a star rating and a review count do much of the persuading that a sales associate once did on the shop floor.

That value attracts people who want it without earning it. A seller who can buy fifty five-star reviews can, for a while, borrow the reputation a competitor spent a year building. The value of reviews depends on shoppers trusting them, though, and if fakes spread, every review on the platform is worth less, honest ones included. That gives Amazon a reason to enforce its rules even against large sellers: it is protecting the asset that makes its store work.

So a review’s value is never fully the brand’s. It exists on Amazon’s terms.

Amazon can remove reviews it judges suspicious, and it can remove a seller entirely, which is the bigger risk. A brand caught manipulating reviews can lose the inflated rating along with every listing, every review it earned honestly and the sales history Amazon’s systems used to rank it. Years of work can disappear in a weekend. A small, temporary gain set against a large and lasting loss is the clearest argument for staying inside the rules.

What this means for honest brands

Take two brands selling similar headphones at the same price.

ReviewsAverage ratingHow they got there
Brand one2,0004.5Earned over two years
Brand two3,0004.7Many of them bought

For a while, the second brand wins more sales. Its listing looks stronger at a glance, ranks higher because it converts better, and earns more organic reviews on top of the bought ones, so the gap widens before anyone outside notices how it was built. When Amazon removes its listings, the first brand inherits shoppers who now have fewer choices, and its slower, earned reputation turns out to be the safer asset.

The honest path is slower, and it compounds. Brands can request reviews through Amazon’s own tools, enroll eligible new products in Vine, and improve the things that produce good reviews in the first place: accurate product descriptions, packaging that arrives intact and responsive service when something goes wrong. They can also make reviews easier to earn. A short insert explaining how to use the product, a follow-up message through Amazon’s tools when an order arrives and quick replacements when something breaks all raise the odds that a satisfied customer says so.

How far enforcement reaches will shape what comes next. If Amazon removes more large sellers in the coming months, categories crowded with manipulated ratings will open up for brands whose reviews are real. Those brands will not need to do anything new to benefit. They will simply still be standing when the listings around them are not.

The practical homework is short. Audit every program that touches the brand’s reviews, agencies and outside services included, and stop any that reward shoppers for reviews outside Amazon’s rules. Track the causes of negative reviews by product, such as damage, sizing and misleading descriptions, and fix them at the source. Review programs that stay within Amazon’s rules are part of how we manage Amazon channels for brands.

A0065.crumb: Amazon bid automation can starve your…
A0065.title: Amazon bid automation can starve your most profitable products
A0065.alt: Garden sprinkler spraying water near a potted tomato plant in the corner of a sage green wooden fence.
A0065.ttag: Amazon bid automation can starve your most profitable products | Kwontified
A0065.desc: Amazon’s bid automation favors products with the most conversion history, which can starve newer, higher-margin ones. Structure campaigns so it cannot.
A0065.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 25, 2021.
A0065.body:
Two weeks after launch, the campaign report looks good. Return on ad spend is healthy, budget is fully spent, and the best-selling product inside the campaign is doing what it always does. What the report does not show is that the newer product in the same campaign, the one with the better margin and the one the brand launched to grow, has barely been shown to anyone.

Amazon’s bid automation is built to spend money where a sale looks most likely, which sounds like exactly what a brand wants. A system that predicts from history will favor the products with the most history, though, and those are not always the products a brand most needs to grow. Brands should structure campaigns by the role each product plays, so the automation optimizes within choices the brand has already made.

What Amazon bid automation optimizes for

Since early 2019, Sponsored Products advertisers have been able to choose dynamic bidding strategies. Amazon can raise a bid by up to 100% in top-of-search placements, and by up to 50% in other placements, with “dynamic bids – up and down,” when its prediction is that a click is likely to convert. When it predicts the opposite, it lowers the bid, Viral Launch explained.

The prediction depends on data. A product that has sold thousands of units through ads gives the system a clear picture of which searches and placements convert. A product launched a few weeks ago gives it almost nothing. The system is not choosing to favor one product over another. It is acting on the evidence it has, and one product has far more of it.

Rank works the same way outside advertising. In Amazon’s description, its Best Sellers rank reflects recent and historical sales, as Helium 10 quoted it. Products with a sales history are easier for every part of the system to place.

The history bias in a shared campaign

Any system that learns from results rewards what it has already seen work. Call it the history bias.

Think of a teacher who calls only on students who raised their hands before. The students who answered last week get asked again, answer again and grow more confident. The quiet student who might have the best answer never gets the chance, and the teacher’s records show the same few students always know the answer. The records are accurate. They are also incomplete.

In a campaign, the effect shows up in how budget gets spent. Products that share a campaign share its daily budget. The product the system predicts best wins more auctions, spends more of the budget and produces more sales, which sharpens its predictions further. The others get fewer impressions, produce less data and stay hard to predict.

Take a brand that puts three products in one campaign with a $300 daily budget.

ProductRoleMargin after costsShare of spend after two weeks
AEstablished best-seller20%about 80%
BNewer item the brand wants to grow45%a small share
CSeasonal item—a small share

The campaign looks efficient. Most of the money, though, is going behind the lowest-margin product, and B has had too little exposure for the system to learn whether it can sell.

Nothing went wrong in the automation. It optimized for the outcome it can measure, attributed sales per dollar, with the data it had. The brand’s own goals, margin and growth of a new line, were never part of the instruction.

The bias is easy to miss because the evidence for it is invisible. A report shows what the system did, never what it declined to try. The brand sees strong results for A and modest ones for B and concludes A is the better product. It may be. Or B may never have been shown to enough shoppers to find out, and the only way to tell is to give B enough budget, on its own, for a fair test.

Structure campaigns by product role

Automation itself is not the problem. It is good at choosing among similar options, and Amazon’s systems see far more auctions than any person could manage by hand. It is poor at weighing goals it has not been given. So the strategic choices come first, and the system optimizes inside them.

In practice that means separating products by role. Established best-sellers belong in campaigns judged on efficiency. New products belong in their own campaigns, with their own budgets and a target that allows for learning, so they cannot be crowded out. High-margin products deserve budgets set on profit as well as on return on ad spend.

It also means reading reports differently. A campaign’s average return can look healthy while one product inside it is never given a chance, so look at spend and sales by product within each campaign as well as at the campaign total. If the single largest product’s share of a campaign’s spend climbs above two thirds, and that product is not the one the brand most wants to grow, the structure is doing the brand’s planning for it.

Start by reviewing spend by product inside every Sponsored Products campaign and flagging the ones where a single product takes most of the budget. Move new and high-margin products into campaigns of their own, and judge each campaign on its products’ goal, whether that is efficiency, learning or profit, instead of one return target for the whole account.

The rule of thumb: let the algorithm choose the bid, never the strategy. Structuring campaigns around each product’s role and margin is how we run Amazon advertising accounts for brands.

A0067.crumb: The future of shopping is a tech fight…
A0067.title: The future of shopping is a tech fight run on brands’ data
A0067.alt: Two small white robotic arms reaching into an open drawer of index cards in a wooden card catalog cabinet.
A0067.ttag: The future of shopping is a tech fight run on brands’ data | Kwontified
A0067.desc: Google, Facebook and TikTok now compete with Amazon for where shopping starts. Every one needs brands’ product data, so a clean feed is now core infrastructure.
A0067.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 27, 2021.
A0067.body:
In many brands, the product feed lives on someone’s to-do list as a chore: a file sent to Google Shopping, updated when somebody remembers, owned by whoever last touched it. For most of the last decade that was a reasonable way to treat it, because the fight over the future of shopping looked like Amazon against everyone else, and the feed mattered only for one kind of ad.

Over the past year, Google, Facebook and TikTok have each moved to compete with Amazon for where shopping starts, whether that is a search engine, a social feed, a video app or a marketplace. Every one of those moves runs on product data supplied by brands and their commerce platforms. Brands should treat their catalog and feed as core infrastructure, and avoid depending on any single front door.

How the fight over the future of shopping took hold

WhenWhoWhat
May 19, 2020FacebookLaunched Facebook Shops, a single store across Facebook and Instagram, working with Shopify and other platforms
October 27, 2020TikTokAnnounced a partnership with Shopify to bring social commerce features to its app
May 18, 2021GoogleExpanded its Shopify partnership so Shopify’s 1.7 million merchants can appear across Search, Shopping, YouTube and Images

When Mark Zuckerberg announced Facebook Shops, he was plain about the model: “Our business model here is ads,” Reuters reported. TikTok’s Shopify deal followed in the autumn, TechCrunch reported.

Google made the most recent move at its I/O conference, announcing that Shopify merchants could feature their products across its services in a few clicks. It described a “Shopping Graph” connecting people with more than 24 billion listings from millions of merchants. It also said that since it eliminated commission fees and made listings free, its product catalog had grown 70% and the number of merchants on its platform 80%.

Amazon, meanwhile, keeps growing the business all of these companies want a piece of. Its advertising line grew 77% to $6.9 billion in the first quarter of 2021, GeekWire reported.

Why every front door needs the same data

Each company describes its move differently: free listings, shops, social commerce, a shopping graph. Underneath, they are all doing the same thing. They want shoppers to begin the search for a product in their service instead of on Amazon, and they want to sell advertising against that moment.

None of them can do it without product data: titles, images, prices, availability and descriptions, kept current. Google calls the result a graph; Facebook and TikTok receive it through Shopify and similar platforms. Shopify sits behind all three announcements, which means a brand on Shopify can reach several of these storefronts through one system, while a brand on a custom-built site may have to connect each one separately. The data that powers a brand’s own website is now the data that decides whether it shows up in a Google search, an Instagram shop or a TikTok video. It is like one stock list sent to every shop window on a long street: get it right once and every window looks right, get it wrong and every window repeats the mistake.

That changes the value of a dull piece of work. A feed with missing sizes, stale prices or poor images carries the same weakness everywhere the brand’s products appear. Fixing it once, at the source, improves every one of those storefronts together.

It also changes the balance of risk in favor of brands willing to do the unglamorous work. A brand that depends on one front door, Amazon or any other, is exposed to that company’s rules, fees and changes. A brand with clean, complete product data can appear across several of them with little extra effort and move its spending to whichever works best.

Who owns the catalog

Take two brands selling similar outdoor jackets. One keeps a complete catalog on its Shopify store, with every color, size, price and image current, so when Google’s new process opens up its products can appear across Google with little work. The other keeps its best product information in spreadsheets sent to retailers, and its own site lists half the range. It will spend months catching up while the first brand is already being found.

So the question for leaders is who owns the product catalog. In many brands nobody does, cleanly: e-commerce manages the website, sales manages the retailer spreadsheets, and marketing manages the ad feeds. Each version drifts from the others, and shoppers notice when a price on Google does not match the one on the brand’s site.

The fight has a cost for brands, too. Each new front door brings its own advertising product, its own reporting and its own claims about results, so more choice means more places to spend and more measurement to reconcile. Brands that add every new channel at once will spread budgets thin and learn little. Those that test one or two at a time, with clear goals, will learn which front doors their customers actually use.

The first moves are organizational. Name one owner for the catalog and feed, accountable for accuracy across the brand’s site, the marketplaces and the new Google, Facebook and TikTok storefronts. Have that owner audit the feed for missing attributes, stale prices and weak images on the top products and fix them once at the source, then track sales and cost by front door each month as these channels compete for shoppers. Running channels across Amazon, Walmart, Target and social and search storefronts from a single product catalog is how we work with brands.

A0069.crumb: A Prime Day 2021 forecast needs a range…
A0069.title: A Prime Day 2021 forecast needs a range, not 2020’s number
A0069.alt: Three white vases of pink roses, lavender and wildflowers on a wooden windowsill against a pink wall.
A0069.ttag: A Prime Day 2021 forecast needs a range, not 2020’s number | Kwontified
A0069.desc: Prime Day 2020 ran in October and 2019 in July, so June has no clean comparison. Forecast 2021 as a range built from both years, not last year plus growth.
A0069.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 1, 2021.
A0069.body:
Nobody outside Amazon knows how big Prime Day 2020 was. Amazon disclosed one figure: third-party sellers sold more than $3.5 billion during the event, nearly 60% more than in 2019. Everything else is an estimate, and the estimates sit billions of dollars apart.

That disputed number is the base most Prime Day 2021 forecasts will grow from, and on its own it is the wrong base. The October 2020 event ran in a pandemic and at the start of holiday shopping. The June event will have neither, and a brand’s own 2020 result carries the same distortions. The forecast worth building is a range drawn from both 2019 and 2020, then adjusted for June’s demand, ad costs and stock.

The Prime Day 2021 forecast starts from a disputed base

Prime Day 2020 figureAmountSource
Third-party seller sales, disclosed after the eventmore than $3.5 billionAmazon, via CNBC
Total sales, JPMorgan forecast before the eventabout $7.5 billionCNBC
Total sales, eMarketer forecast before the eventclose to $10 billionCNBC
Implied total sales worldwide, estimated after the eventaround $6 billionCoresight Research

Amazon did not disclose total sales, CNBC reported. Coresight worked from the same third-party disclosure and still landed far below the most bullish forecast. If serious analysts disagree by billions about a finished event, a brand should be modest about predicting the next one from it.

The event’s date has moved as well. On April 29, Amazon said the two-day event would take place in the second quarter, and its finance chief told reporters it would be in June, GeekWire reported. The 2019 event ran in July and the 2020 event in October. The thing a forecaster normally leans on, a recent event held at the same point in the year, does not exist.

Why last year plus growth looks right, and where it breaks

The default plan takes last Prime Day and adds growth. It looks sensible because Amazon keeps adding shoppers: it has more than 200 million Prime members, according to the shareholder letter Jeff Bezos wrote.

The timing is what undoes it. October put Prime Day in front of shoppers who were stuck at home and starting their holiday buying. June offers neither, and spending is cooling after the stimulus surge: retail sales were flat in April after a 10.7% jump in March, the AP reported. The auction also costs more. Amazon’s mostly-advertising revenue grew 77% in the first quarter, GeekWire reported, while its net sales grew 44%, according to MarketBeat, so the same Prime Day sales may cost more to win.

Think of forecasting a summer football match from last winter’s fixture. The teams are the same, but the pitch, the weather and half the players have changed. The winter score tells you something about the teams. It tells you much less about the summer score.

Category decides which way the error runs. A brand selling gifts, toys or electronics probably saw part of its October 2020 result come from shoppers buying early for the holidays, and that demand will not appear in June. A brand selling everyday essentials, outdoor gear or summer products may find June suits it better than October did. One national event can be a step up for one category and a step down for another, which is why no industry estimate tells a single brand much.

So the claim that Prime Day 2021 will beat 2020 is uncertain for everyone and wrong for some, above all brands whose 2020 event was lifted by early holiday shopping.

Build the range from both years

Take a brand that sold $200,000 on Prime Day 2019 and $320,000 on Prime Day 2020. The 2020 figure includes holiday demand and pandemic shopping that a June event will not have. The 2019 figure predates two years of growth.

The low case starts from 2019 and adds the brand’s underlying growth since then; at 20%, that gives $240,000. The high case starts from 2020 and assumes most of its demand repeats, with a little growth on top: $330,000. The planning point sits between them at $285,000.

Then adjust for what the brand controls. Short stock on the top products cuts the high case, and stock is the hardest of these to fix late, since a purchase order placed after the forecast is set may not arrive before the event. An ad budget tighter than in 2020, while click prices are higher, cuts both ends. More products with strong reviews than a year ago raises the low case.

Write the range down before the event and share it with whoever will judge the result. A range set afterwards is an explanation, and it convinces nobody.

The range then does work a single number cannot. It sets how much stock to hold, how much budget to commit and what result counts as good. A brand that planned on $330,000 and lands at $260,000 will call the event a disappointment. A brand that planned on $240,000 to $330,000 sees a result inside its range, and a sounder base for the next forecast.

The forecast sheet to finish before June

  • Prime Day 2019 and 2020 sales for the brand, each with a note on what was unusual about it: the month, stock-outs, the deals that ran.
  • A low, middle and high case, with inventory and budget set against the middle and a plan for each end.
  • Each adjustment for stock, ad budget and reviews, written next to the number it moved.
  • The result the team will call a success, agreed now rather than after the event.

A range built from a brand’s own event history is how we forecast and run Prime Day on Amazon.

A0071.crumb: How to change agencies without losing…
A0071.title: How to change agencies without losing Amazon momentum or budget
A0071.alt: Silver relay baton lying on a red running track near white lane lines on a sunny day.
A0071.ttag: How to change agencies without losing Amazon momentum or budget | Kwontified
A0071.desc: Amazon keeps only 90 days of campaign change history. Brands changing agencies should own the accounts, plan the handover and avoid switching before Prime Day.
A0071.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 3, 2021.
A0071.body:
A brand that gives notice to its Amazon agency starts a clock that is easy to miss. Amazon’s change history shows only the past 90 days of edits to Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands campaigns, Amazon has noted. The search term report, the record of what shoppers actually typed before they clicked, can be pulled only for a limited window. If nobody downloads that history before the old agency leaves, it is gone.

That is the cost of an agency change most brands underestimate. Momentum on Amazon is held in campaign history, settings and the data Amazon’s systems have learned from, and a careless handover throws it away. Brands can change agencies without losing it, but only if they own their accounts and data, treat the handover as a project and keep the switch away from the eve of a major event.

What a brand loses when it changes agencies carelessly

Brands change agencies for good reasons: results have stalled, the team has turned over, or the brand needs skills its current partner lacks. The trouble is that Amazon’s systems reward continuity. The Best Sellers rank reflects both recent and historical sales, in Amazon’s wording cited by Helium 10, so a gap in advertising that cuts sales also cuts rank. Dynamic bidding adjusts bids by how likely a click is to convert, Viral Launch explained, and that prediction is built on the campaign’s own history. A campaign rebuilt from scratch starts with none, and bids less precisely until it has some.

The stakes are larger than they were. In its survey of about 1,000 brands, Feedvisor found 59% spending more than $60,000 a month on Amazon advertising, a share that was up from 38% in the previous year, according to its 2021 report.

At that level of spend, a rough handover is easy to price. Take a brand spending $80,000 a month on Amazon advertising and earning $4 in attributed sales per dollar. Its new agency pauses the old campaigns and launches a new structure. For three weeks the new campaigns learn: costs per click run high, conversion runs low, and the return falls to $2.50. On the $60,000 spent over those weeks, that is about $90,000 of sales the brand would otherwise have had.

Start from what the brand owns

An agency search pulls attention toward the candidates: their case studies, their fees, the team they will assign. The question that decides how the switch goes sits closer to home. When the current agency leaves, what does the brand actually own? In too many cases the honest answer is less than leadership assumed.

Some agencies run advertising in accounts they created and control. Some keep the only copy of past reports, the keyword research, the negative keyword lists and the notes on what was tested and why. Some hold the logins. When the relationship ends, the brand may discover that the account it paid to build is not one it can simply hand to someone else.

The fix starts long before any change. The brand should own its Seller Central or Vendor Central account and its advertising account, with its own people as administrators and agencies working as invited users. The brand should download and store reports on a regular schedule, rather than leaving the only copies with the agency. And the contract should say what the agency hands over when it leaves: campaign structures, keyword lists, test results and any tools or rules it set up.

Goodwill is usually thin by the time a relationship ends. An outgoing agency has little reason to spend its last weeks documenting its work for a competitor. That is why the obligations belong in the contract from the start, and why the brand’s own copies should be kept as the work happens rather than requested at the exit.

An overlap between agencies keeps the campaigns earning

A planned handover avoids most of that $90,000. The old campaigns keep running while the new agency studies them. The new agency changes structure in stages, starting with the parts that are clearly broken and keeping what works. For a short period both agencies overlap, with written rules about who can change what, so nothing is edited twice or not at all. The brand, as the account owner, writes those rules and holds the administrator access while both teams are in the account.

Timing matters as much as method. Amazon announced on June 2 that Prime Day 2021 will run on June 21 and 22, according to its press release. A brand that changes agencies in the next two weeks will be relearning its campaigns during the most competitive auctions of the summer. Unless the current arrangement is truly broken, it is usually better to finish the event with the existing team and switch afterwards.

The new agency’s first months also need a fair yardstick, agreed in advance. Results in the first few weeks mostly reflect the handover, not the new team’s skill. A fair review compares performance after about 90 days with the same period a year earlier, and asks whether the problems that prompted the change are being fixed.

Questions for leadership before signing a new agency

  • Whose name is on our seller, vendor and advertising accounts, and are our own people the administrators?
  • When did we last download and store our own copy of the campaign and search term reports?
  • What does our current contract require the agency to hand over when it leaves?
  • Does the switch date fall in the weeks before Prime Day or the holiday season?

Staged handovers that keep the old campaigns earning while the new structure learns are how we take over Amazon accounts from other agencies.

A0072.crumb: Mercado Libre or Amazon in Latin America…
A0072.title: Mercado Libre or Amazon in Latin America depends on the country
A0072.alt: Blank wooden signpost with arrows pointing opposite ways on a cobblestone street beside a plaza fountain.
A0072.ttag: Mercado Libre or Amazon in Latin America depends on the country | Kwontified
A0072.desc: Mercado Libre earns most of its revenue in Brazil and Argentina, while Amazon leads in Mexico. Brands entering Latin America should choose by country.
A0072.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 8, 2021.
A0072.body:
In 2011, Mercado Libre held 21.2% of Mexico’s e-commerce market. By the end of 2019 its share was 11.4%, and Amazon, which first overtook it in 2017, held 13.4%, according to Euromonitor figures reported by El CEO. Over the same years, Mercado Libre built a business that now earns more than half its revenue in Brazil.

So which marketplace leads Latin America? Neither, for a brand’s purposes, because the answer changes at each border. Brands that sell on Amazon in the United States often assume Amazon is the natural first step into the region. In some countries it is a reasonable one; in others it is the wrong door. The lead marketplace should be chosen country by country, accepting a trade-off between Mercado Libre’s reach and Amazon’s familiar tools.

Mercado Libre or Amazon: what the country numbers show

Mercado Libre’s scale is not in question. In the first quarter of 2021, its gross merchandise volume reached $6.1 billion, up 114% from a year earlier on a currency-neutral basis, and it had 69.8 million unique active users, the company reported. On its earnings call, it said 74% of its volume was delivered in under 48 hours, according to a transcript of the call.

That revenue is concentrated in three countries. Brazil produced $768.7 million in the quarter, 55.8% of the total, Argentina $297.2 million and Mexico $230.5 million, the quarter’s results show. Mexico, the smallest of the three, is also the one where Amazon held the larger share at the end of 2019.

Each marketplace won its countries with logistics and payments

A marketplace’s value to a brand depends on how many shoppers in a given country start their product search there. That varies by country because each marketplace built its position at a different time, with different logistics, payment systems and local habits.

Think of choosing road maps for a drive across a continent. A single continental map shows the highways and misses the streets that matter in each city. A traveler who needs to find a shop in São Paulo and another in Mexico City needs a map for each.

Mercado Libre built those local advantages itself: its own payments service, Mercado Pago, and its own delivery network, Mercado Envios. In the first quarter, Mercado Pago processed $14.7 billion of payments and Mercado Envios shipped 208.1 million items, the company reported. In Brazil, its largest market, it doubled items sold and nearly doubled gross merchandise volume from a year earlier, executives said on the call, according to a transcript.

Mexico moved the other way over the past decade. Mercado Libre’s share fell from 21.2% in 2011 to 11.4% in 2019 as Amazon and other retailers, including Walmart and Coppel, built online businesses, El CEO’s report showed. Mercado Libre has answered with investment of its own.

The right first channel follows from those country-level positions, not from a brand’s experience in the US. A brand that copies its US channel plan across the region will be strong where Amazon is strong and weak where it is not, and it may not see which is which until the first quarter of sales comes in.

Reach on Mercado Libre, familiarity on Amazon

Choosing Mercado Libre where it leads brings reach. It also brings work that US-focused teams may not be ready for: Portuguese and Spanish listings, local pricing and installment payments, a different advertising system and a different set of rules.

The advertising gap is easy to underrate. A team that has spent years reading Amazon’s reports has to relearn what a good result looks like on a new system, and its first months of data there will be thin. That cost lands on the same people who are building the listings, at the same time.

Choosing Amazon brings familiarity. Teams already know its tools, reports and advertising. In Brazil and Argentina, though, that familiarity may buy a smaller share of shoppers than the same effort would win on Mercado Libre.

Payment habits add another layer. Many shoppers in the region pay in installments or through local wallets, and a marketplace that handles those payments itself, as Mercado Libre does through Mercado Pago, removes friction a brand would otherwise have to solve. Currency is a third. Prices set in local currency, and margins measured in it, behave very differently from US prices, especially in Argentina.

Take a US beauty brand with the budget to launch in one country in 2021. In Mexico, it could launch on Amazon with the team and processes it already has, in a market where Amazon holds a leading share. In Brazil, it would need to build new capabilities for Mercado Libre, but it would reach a larger market, the one where Mercado Libre earns most of its revenue.

A brand with a small team and a short runway may reasonably take the faster, familiar launch. For a brand planning more than a year out, the numbers lean the other way. Mexico itself is part of the reason: Mercado Libre’s revenue there grew 143% in the first quarter in US dollars, faster than in Brazil, the company reported. If that pace holds, Amazon’s lead in Mexico may not last, and brands that picked Amazon there for its share will want a second channel sooner than they planned.

Pick each country’s first marketplace by where its shoppers already start, budget for local language, pricing, payments and logistics from the first listing rather than adapting US pages, and revisit the choice once a year while positions in the region keep shifting. Launching and running Mercado Libre and Amazon side by side is work we do for brands entering Latin America.

A0074.crumb: A fractured org chart holds back the…
A0074.title: A fractured org chart holds back the Amazon business
A0074.alt: Partly assembled countryside jigsaw puzzle with scattered wooden pieces on a sunlit wooden table.
A0074.ttag: A fractured org chart holds back the Amazon business | Kwontified
A0074.desc: Amazon turns a brand’s ads, stock, price and content into one result. Brands that split those decisions across four teams lose value at every handoff.
A0074.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 10, 2021.
A0074.body:
Ask a brand who runs its Amazon business and the answer often comes in four parts. Marketing runs the advertising, supply chain manages the stock, sales owns the relationship with Amazon’s buyers and e-commerce writes the listings. Each team works to its own goals and its own calendar, and each does its job well by its own measures.

Amazon does not see four jobs. Its systems turn advertising, stock, price and content into a single result, whether a shopper finds the product and buys it, and value leaks at every handoff between the teams that control those inputs. Brands should run Amazon as one business, with shared targets, a weekly review across functions and one person accountable, rather than as four teams that each touch it.

What Amazon’s systems read in a fractured org chart

Start with what decides the sale. The House antitrust subcommittee has estimated that roughly 80% of all Amazon sales run through the Buy Box, and Jeff Bezos acknowledged in 2020 that the algorithm favors, indirectly, offers that can ship with Prime, CNBC reported. Stock position and delivery speed, decisions that sit with supply chain, help decide who wins the order.

Advertising runs on the same inputs. With dynamic bidding switched on, Amazon moves bids up or down with its estimate of whether a click will turn into a sale, as Viral Launch explained, and that estimate depends on price, reviews, content and availability. An ad for a product that is out of stock or overpriced does not convert, whatever the bid.

So one Amazon sale passes through every team’s work. Supply chain decided whether the product was in Amazon’s warehouse. Sales or e-commerce set the price. E-commerce wrote the listing that persuaded the shopper, and marketing paid for the click that brought her there. If any one of those fails, the other three teams’ work is wasted on that order.

The leak shows up in someone else’s report

The leaks happen where one team’s decision changes another team’s results and neither notices in time.

Take a brand whose marketing team plans a large advertising push for Prime Day, set for June 21 and 22 in the press release Amazon issued on June 2. Its supply chain team, working to a target for lower inventory costs, has reduced shipments to Amazon’s warehouses for June. Neither team is wrong by its own measures. On the first morning of Prime Day the best-selling product sells out, the ads keep running to a listing that cannot convert, and the product loses rank it took months to build.

The same thing happens in quieter weeks. A sales team agrees a promotion with Amazon’s buyers without telling marketing, so the advertising runs at full bids while the discount already wins the sale. An e-commerce team rewrites a listing in the middle of a campaign, and the advertising team watches conversion move without knowing why. Finance cuts the advertising budget to protect margin in the same month supply chain has built extra stock.

Each of those costs is easy to miss because it lands in another team’s numbers. Marketing sees a lower return on ad spend. Supply chain sees higher storage fees. Sales sees a cooler relationship with Amazon. Nobody’s report shows the whole, so nobody is paid to fix it.

The problem grows with the business. When Amazon is a small channel, one or two people often handle all of it, and the handoffs are conversations across a desk. As it becomes one of the brand’s largest accounts, each function takes its piece, and those conversations turn into emails, tickets and monthly meetings. The channel becomes more important at the moment it becomes harder to run. Amazon’s pace sharpens the mismatch: rank, bids and the Buy Box respond within hours, while a monthly meeting responds within weeks.

One business on paper and in practice

A reorganization is rarely the first answer. Most brands cannot move every Amazon-related role into one team, and many should not, because the same people also serve wholesale accounts, the brand’s own website and other retailers. What they can do is run Amazon as one business on paper and in the weekly rhythm.

That starts with shared targets: one set of numbers for the Amazon business, such as sales, profit after advertising and in-stock rate, that every contributing team is judged on. A supply chain lead whose scorecard includes the in-stock rate on Amazon thinks differently about a June shipment cut.

It continues with a weekly review that brings the four functions together for an hour to look at the same data and agree the decisions for the coming week. Brands that start that review before Prime Day on June 21 will have one cycle of it behind them when the stakes are highest. And it needs one person accountable for the result, with the authority to settle conflicts between teams before they reach the shopper.

There is a simple way to tell whether it is working: how often is a problem on Amazon discovered by the team that did not cause it? When marketing regularly learns about stockouts from its own reports, or supply chain hears about a promotion from a sudden spike in orders, the brand is still running Amazon as four businesses.

The return on fixing it can be large because it needs little new spending. The brand already pays for the advertising, the stock, the content and the people. Running them together makes each of them worth more, which is why weekly reviews that put advertising, stock and content on one page are central to how we run Amazon channels alongside a brand’s own teams.

A0076.crumb: Instagram checkout fees make it a sales…
A0076.title: Instagram checkout fees make it a sales channel to price like one
A0076.alt: Smartphone with a glowing pink screen on a wooden stand beside an antique brass balance scale holding coins.
A0076.ttag: Instagram checkout fees make it a sales channel to price like one | Kwontified
A0076.desc: Facebook’s waiver of Instagram checkout fees runs through June 2021. Once a 5% fee applies, Instagram should be priced like a marketplace, order by order.
A0076.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 15, 2021.
A0076.body:
For a year, selling through checkout on Instagram has cost brands nothing beyond their advertising. Facebook said it would waive its selling fees for businesses using checkout on Shops through June 2021, and the fee waiting on the other side is 5% of each shipment.

That small number changes what Instagram is. A channel that takes a commission on each order and also charges for the traffic that produces it is a marketplace, whatever its owner calls it. Brands should price Instagram order by order, against Amazon and their own website, instead of treating it as a line in the marketing budget.

What Instagram checkout fees will cost

When Facebook opened checkout more widely in August 2020, it said it was waiving selling fees for businesses through the end of the year, according to its announcement. The checkout fee had been set at 5% per shipment, covering the transaction and buyer protection, Glossy reported. Facebook later extended the waiver for businesses selling with checkout on Shops through June 2021, Social Media Today reported.

Next to Amazon, 5% looks cheap. Amazon’s commission fees average around 15%, Wordtracker noted. Instagram carries a cost that Amazon’s referral fee does not capture, though: many Instagram shoppers arrive because a brand paid to put a post in front of them.

A pop-up shop that starts charging rent

A new fee sounds like a burden. It also makes Instagram easier to manage, because it forces a question brands have been able to skip: does an Instagram order make money?

Think of a pop-up shop in a busy building that the landlord lets brands use for free. Brands put up displays, hand out samples and make a few sales. Nobody works out whether the shop pays for itself, because it costs nothing. The day the landlord starts charging rent, every brand has to decide whether its sales there justify the space.

That is Instagram’s position as the waiver runs out. Until now, brands have mostly judged it by engagement, followers and the sales its ads report. Those measures suit a marketing channel. A sales channel is judged by what is left from each order after the cost of making the sale, which is the test brands already apply to Amazon and to their own websites. Instagram escaped it only because selling there was free.

The fee also moves the decision to a different desk and a different clock. A marketing budget is usually set once a year. A channel’s cost per order can be checked every week, product by product, by whoever owns the channel’s profit.

Price each order, channel by channel

Take a brand selling a $60 product through three channels.

ChannelChannel fee on a $60 orderAdvertising to win the orderFee plus advertising
Instagram checkout$3 (5% fee)about $15$18
Amazon$9 (15% referral fee)about $8$17, plus fulfillment
Brand’s own siteabout $2 (payment processing)about $20$22

No channel wins on every product. Amazon’s fee is the highest, but shoppers there arrive searching, so less advertising is needed to win the order. The brand’s own site has almost no fee and the highest acquisition cost, because the brand pays to bring every visitor. Instagram sits in between, and that ranking is fragile.

The advertising column is an assumption, and it moves more than the fees do. A product that needs far more than the $15 of ads assumed here quickly becomes the costliest of the three to sell on Instagram. The only fair comparison puts each on the same basis: revenue per order, minus channel fees, fulfillment and the advertising needed to win it.

The answer also changes by product. Instagram suits things people buy on impulse after seeing them: visual, giftable and modestly priced. Amazon suits products people search for by name or need. A brand’s own site suits loyal customers and larger orders. Priced order by order, most catalogs split, with some products earning their place in Instagram checkout and others better sent to the brand’s site or left to Amazon.

There is a choice inside Instagram, too. Brands can let shoppers buy through checkout, or send them from a product tag to their own website. Checkout is smoother for the shopper and will carry the fee. The website route avoids the fee but adds a step where some shoppers will drop off, and the brand keeps more of the customer relationship. The fee is what makes that choice worth making deliberately.

Checkout data is the number Instagram can still see

Measurement adds a second reason to treat the channel with more discipline in 2021. After Apple’s App Tracking Transparency prompt arrived, early data from Flurry suggested only about 4% of US iPhone users were letting apps track them, 9to5Mac reported. Instagram’s own reports will see fewer of the sales its ads cause on a brand’s website. Orders placed through checkout inside Instagram happen where Instagram can see them, which makes checkout data among the more reliable numbers a brand will get from the platform.

So report the two apart. Checkout orders and the website sales that Instagram ads drive have different costs and different measurement, and blending them hides both.

Facebook decides at the end of June whether the waiver ends. If it does, the fee shows up on July orders; if it is extended again, the fee is still coming, and the extra weeks are time to build the comparison. Either way, every brand selling on Instagram should know one number per product before July: the profit left from a checkout order after the 5% fee and the ads that won it. Tracking profit by channel and order, Instagram included, is how we run Instagram Shop alongside Amazon and other marketplaces.

A0077.crumb: Target Plus lends brands a halo that…
A0077.title: Target Plus lends brands a halo that Amazon’s open shelf cannot
A0077.alt: Ornate gilded empty frame on a white plinth framing a pale blue ceramic vase, beside a terracotta wall.
A0077.ttag: Target Plus lends brands a halo that Amazon’s open shelf cannot | Kwontified
A0077.desc: Target Plus has fewer than 300 sellers against Amazon’s millions. Its scarcity lends brands a halo of Target’s curation, which matters more than its volume.
A0077.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 17, 2021.
A0077.body:
Every product on a Target shelf got there because someone at Target said yes. A buyer chose it, a planner gave it space, and the store put its name above the aisle. Search the same category on Amazon and the shelf is whoever listed: the brand, its resellers, close copies and sellers nobody has heard of, ranked by what sells.

Target Plus, Target’s invite-only online marketplace, carries the first kind of shelf onto the web. It has stayed tiny by design, with fewer than 300 sellers against Amazon’s millions, and that scarcity is easy to read as a weakness. It is also where the value sits: a brand on Target Plus borrows the trust Target has built through curation, its own brands and its stores. Brands should judge Target Plus by that halo and the customers it reaches rather than by volume, and protect it with disciplined pricing, assortment and service.

How Target built the Target Plus brand halo

Target’s marketplace has grown slowly on purpose. Two years after launch it had fewer than 300 sellers, even though traffic to Target’s website grew more than 50% in 2020, according to Marketplace Pulse figures. Amazon had about 2.3 million third-party sellers, the House antitrust subcommittee found, according to a summary of its report.

The trust comes from what Target sells around those few sellers. Its own brands grew a record 36% in the first quarter of 2021, Drug Store News reported. Comparable sales rose 22.9%, and Target gained more than $1 billion in market share in the quarter, the company reported.

Those owned brands, and the store behind them, are why shoppers trust what Target puts in front of them. Target has spent years designing products under its own labels, choosing national brands for its aisles and deciding what not to carry. Shoppers have learned to treat the result as an edit rather than a catalog.

Target has said plainly that the marketplace will work the same way. Chief executive Brian Cornell has said Target will keep curating very carefully to complement its store and online assortment, Marketplace Pulse reported. So Target adds sellers slowly and turns many away, and each invitation signals more because there are so few. A shopper who finds an unfamiliar brand on Target.com assumes, reasonably, that Target chose it.

Who holds the trust, and who can take it back

The halo works in two directions. Outward, it signals quality: a brand that sells on Target.com can say so to retail buyers, to investors and to shoppers who have never heard of it. Inward, it shapes the customer the brand meets, a Target shopper looking for a considered purchase rather than a bargain hunter scanning dozens of near-identical listings.

Amazon’s shelf rewards something else. A brand’s listing may sit beside cheaper copies, unauthorized resellers and products of uncertain origin, because Amazon’s systems reward the offers that sell, whoever makes them. That openness gives Amazon its scale, and it is why many brands still need Amazon. It also means Amazon cannot lend any single brand the endorsement of having been chosen.

Take a premium home-goods brand selling $2 million a year on Amazon that could perhaps sell $250,000 on Target Plus. On sales alone, Target Plus is the small line. If its presence there helps the brand win a meeting with a department store buyer, reassures an investor, or reaches shoppers who would not have trusted an unknown brand on Amazon, its value is larger than that line shows. None of those benefits appears in the marketplace report, which is why a team that judges every channel on monthly sales will undervalue this one. Leadership should decide up front what the invitation is for, and judge Target Plus on that.

The trust, though, stays Target’s. The brand borrows it, and Target decides who keeps the invitation. Target’s shoppers expect the experience to match the store, so the disciplines that protect a brand in Target’s aisles apply online too.

Pricing comes first. A product that costs noticeably less on Amazon than on Target.com tells both Target and its shoppers that the brand does not hold its value. Assortment comes next: Target invites brands that complement its range, so the products a brand lists should fit what Target’s shoppers come for. Service matters because Target Plus sellers ship their own orders, and a late or damaged delivery reflects on Target as well as on the brand. A brand that treats Target Plus as one more feed to switch on, rather than a relationship to keep, risks the invitation that made the halo possible.

The halo also depends on Target staying selective. If Target opens its marketplace widely, the halo fades for everyone on it; while it stays small, an invitation is worth more than its sales. That decision belongs to Target, not the brand, which is one more reason to treat the halo as borrowed.

Before Target’s Deal Days

Target will run Deal Days from June 20 to 22, alongside Amazon’s Prime Day, Retail TouchPoints reported. It is a clear test of how a brand behaves on Target’s shelf while Amazon’s is running hot.

  • Check that prices on Target.com match those on Amazon for the same products before the event, and stay matched through it.
  • Build Deal Days offers for Target’s shoppers instead of copying whatever discount runs on Amazon that week, and hold Target Plus orders to the delivery standard Target’s stores set.

Keeping pricing and assortment consistent between the two is how we manage Target Plus and Amazon together for brands.
