A0078.title: Zalando’s fashion ecosystem rewards brands that buy in stages
A0078.alt: Folded white T-shirt, cream knit sweater and camel coat with a rust scarf laid on a wooden stair.
A0078.ttag: Zalando’s fashion ecosystem rewards brands that buy in stages | Kwontified
A0078.desc: Zalando now offers selling, fulfillment, marketing and store connections. Each is convenient; together they concentrate risk. Buy them one at a time.
A0078.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 22, 2021.
A0078.body:
Zalando wants half of its Fashion Store sales to come from brands selling directly on its platform. In the fourth quarter of 2020 that share was 24%, up from 10% in 2018. Why would a fashion retailer want so much of its own store to be run by other people’s brands?

Because the landlord sells more than space. Around its Partner Program, Zalando is building a service to store and ship brands’ goods, an advertising business and a way to connect physical shops to its website. Each service is convenient, and each one makes leaving the others more expensive. A brand that takes the whole set concentrates its European online business on one platform without ever deciding to. Brands should judge each Zalando service on its own returns, add them one at a time and keep a way out of each.

How the Zalando fashion ecosystem fits together

Zalando’s growth gives these services weight. Gross merchandise volume (GMV), the value of goods sold on the platform, rose 55.6% to €3.2 billion in the first quarter of 2021, and active customers reached 41.8 million, the company reported. It raised its full-year outlook to GMV growth of 31% to 36%.

The services are growing faster than the store around them. At its capital markets day in early 2021, Zalando set out the numbers behind each one, according to its presentation. The Partner Program, through which brands sell directly to Zalando’s customers, was the 24% of Fashion Store GMV. Its fulfillment service shipped 51% of Partner Program items, and its marketing services earned revenue equal to 1.5% of GMV.

The targets go further: a 40% Partner Program share of Fashion Store GMV by 2023 or 2024 and 50% in the long term, about 75% of partner items shipped through Zalando’s fulfillment service, and marketing revenue of 3% to 4% of GMV. Its Connected Retail program had linked more than 3,400 physical stores to the platform by the end of February 2021, Zalando said.

Why each step feels free

The pull here is convenience. When one partner offers several services that work smoothly together, each extra service looks like a small, sensible step, and the decision is always framed as one service at a time. Nobody decides to depend on the platform. The dependence accumulates.

Think of a shopping center whose landlord, having rented you a shop, offers to run your stockroom, staff your tills and buy your advertising on the center’s screens. Each offer saves effort. After a few years the landlord knows your sales better than you do, holds your stock and controls how shoppers find you. Moving to another center would mean rebuilding everything at once.

On Zalando the sequence is easy to picture. A brand joins the Partner Program to reach Zalando’s customers directly. It moves stock into Zalando’s fulfillment network because shipping across Europe is cheaper and faster that way. It buys Zalando’s advertising because it reaches those customers best. It connects its stores because Zalando supplies the tools.

The cost of leaving is what changes underneath. With one service, leaving means finding another way to sell. With four, it means finding another warehouse, another ad channel and another store system in the same quarter, while the sales that fund the move are still running through Zalando. Each service raises the price of exiting all the others, so the switching cost grows faster than the list of services.

Buy in stages, with an exit for each

Take a footwear brand that sells across Europe through wholesale, its own website and Zalando. It joins the Partner Program in Germany and France and measures margin after commission against its wholesale business in those two countries. It tests Zalando’s fulfillment in one country before committing its full European stock. It buys Zalando’s advertising with a fixed share of its partner sales and checks whether results hold when spend is paused. It connects two flagship stores rather than all of them.

Each decision has its own test and its own exit. If the fulfillment trial raises costs or slows restocking elsewhere, the brand stops without unwinding the rest. If advertising returns weaken, the budget moves to other channels. The brand still gets most of what Zalando offers and keeps the ability to change its mind as results come in.

That matters because Zalando’s interests and a brand’s overlap a great deal without matching. Zalando wants more of a brand’s sales, stock and advertising on its platform; a brand wants the best return across all its channels, including the wholesale accounts and own website that sit alongside Zalando. A brand whose stock, advertising and stores all run through Zalando has little room to push back when fees or terms change. A brand that sells on Zalando but ships through its own network, or buys Zalando’s advertising alongside other channels, can compare offers and move volume.

The services may be identical in both cases. The difference is the brand’s position the next time terms are set, and on a fast-growing platform that happens often.

Zalando’s progress toward its 40% target will raise the stakes. More brands selling directly means more competition for the same customers, and the price of reaching them through advertising and fulfillment is likely to rise with it.

Before adding any Zalando service, write down two things: the result that would justify it and the steps it would take to leave. When the second list grows faster than the first, the brand is buying the bundle. Judging each service on its own returns, next to a brand’s other European channels, is how we manage Zalando for brands.

A0082.alt: A brass magnifying glass rests on rustic wooden pantry shelves lined with jars, kraft bags and plain boxes.
A0082.ttag: Health and household on Amazon moved from scarcity to scrutiny | Kwontified
A0082.desc: In 2020, health and household on Amazon was a race for stock. In 2021 it is a test of documentation and trust, and brands that prove quality keep shoppers.
A0082.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 24, 2021.
A0082.body:
In March 2020, health and household was one of the few aisles on Amazon still taking deliveries. On March 17, 2020, Amazon said it would temporarily accept only household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products into its warehouses, with health and household among six prioritized categories, Retail TouchPoints reported. Shoppers were self-isolating, staples were running out, and a product that was simply in stock could sell almost regardless of whose name was on it.

A year later the aisle is governed by something else. Amazon has tightened its documentation rules for dietary supplements, and the shoppers who stocked up in 2020 are now choosing which brands to buy again. The brands that win health and household on Amazon in 2021 will compete on compliance, trust and repeat purchase, rather than counting on availability to carry them.

How health and household on Amazon changed in 2020

In the spring of 2020, availability decided almost everything. A product in stock and eligible for Prime sold. Sellers in the category could restock when sellers in other categories could not, and some brands grew fast simply by being present on a shelf their rivals could not reach. That growth was real, but it said more about a brand’s supply chain than about what shoppers thought of the product.

Scrutiny arrived early, too. A week before the warehouse change, on March 10, Amazon blocked some personal care products offered at prices well above market levels, Coresight Research noted. The category’s importance to shoppers made it a focus of Amazon’s enforcement as well as its logistics, and that attention has not gone away.

Then the shelf filled back up. Amazon began letting more products back into its warehouses in April 2020, Retail Dive reported. Sellers that had been shut out returned, and categories that felt uncrowded during the shortages grew crowded again. A brand that grew because rivals could not restock now meets those rivals on equal terms, with more sellers bidding for the same searches.

In 2021, documentation decides who can sell

The scarcity has eased and the scrutiny has grown. Beginning in February 2021, Amazon required dietary supplements sold in its store to be certified by an independent third-party lab, according to the testing firm Labdoor. Sellers with existing supplement listings had to submit the required documentation and have their listings approved by May 31, 2021, the law firm Harris Beach noted.

That moves the contest to a different part of the building. In 2020 the decisive work happened in the warehouse and the logistics team. In 2021 it happens in quality assurance and regulatory files: a brand with clean manufacturing records and lab results keeps selling, and a brand that cannot produce them may lose a listing however well it was selling.

Shoppers have changed as well. Many who bought in a hurry in 2020 are buying again, more deliberately. On Prime Day this week, the top-selling products Amazon named included Crest Whitestrips alongside robot vacuums and coffee makers, CNN reported. Health and personal-care staples are still among the things shoppers return for. Now they are choosing between brands instead of taking whatever is on the shelf.

What a brand has once stock is no longer scarce

Leadership teams in the category are facing a blunt question: what is our advantage when being in stock is no longer rare? For many brands that grew in 2020, the honest answer is that availability did much of the work. Three things now separate brands.

Compliance is the most concrete. Where Amazon is raising its documentation requirements, the ability to prove quality quickly is an edge, and losing a listing over missing paperwork is an avoidable failure. It belongs to whoever owns quality records, a team that may never have thought of itself as part of the Amazon business.

Trust is slower to build: accurate labels, honest product descriptions and reviews earned over time. Shoppers buying something they will take or put on their bodies care who made it, and in a category Amazon is policing more closely, a record of accurate claims protects the listing as well as the sale.

Repeat purchase is where the money is. Many health and household products are bought again and again, and the brand a shopper picks on the second order, when every option is in stock, is the brand that keeps the customer. Over a year, the second and third orders are worth far more than the first, and a shopper who settles into a routine reorder may never compare brands in the category again.

Take two vitamin brands that both sold well on Amazon in 2020. One kept its lab documentation current and submitted it before the May 31 deadline. The other did not, and its listings were suppressed for several weeks while it caught up. In 2020 both grew. In 2021 the first brand collects the repeat shoppers the second lost during its absence, and some of them will not come back.

Supplements may be only the start. If Amazon extends similar documentation rules to other health and personal-care products, compliance becomes a condition of competing across the whole category, not only in one corner of it.

The practical work does not need to wait for that. Keep lab results and manufacturing records current instead of gathering them when a deadline arrives, and check every label and description for accuracy. Track repeat purchase by product, and back the items shoppers reorder with subscribe-and-save offers where they fit. Listing documentation sits inside the same day-to-day work when we manage Amazon channels for health and household brands.

A0083.crumb: Prime Day 2021 results landed in the…
A0083.title: Prime Day 2021 results landed in the lower half of the range
A0083.alt: Five feathered arrows stuck in a round straw archery target on a wooden stand in a sunny meadow.
A0083.ttag: Prime Day 2021 results landed in the lower half of the range | Kwontified
A0083.desc: Prime Day 2021 grew about 7% on 2020, with smaller orders and faster marketplace growth, which puts it in the lower half of a sensible pre-event range.
A0083.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 29, 2021.
A0083.body:
Amazon called Prime Day 2021 the biggest two-day period ever for its third-party sellers. It did not say how big the event was. Outside estimates put total growth on 2020 at about 7%, with smaller orders and marketplace sellers growing faster than Amazon itself.

On June 1, we argued that Prime Day 2021 should be forecast as a range, because neither the October 2020 event nor the July 2019 event was a clean comparison. The result sits in the lower half of a sensible range. That makes this the moment for each brand to compare its own result with the range it set, find the assumptions that pushed it low and carry them into the holiday plan.

What the Prime Day 2021 results show

MeasurePrime Day 2021ComparisonSource
Amazon Prime Day sales worldwide, estimated$11.19 billionup 7.6% from $10.39 billion in October 2020Digital Commerce 360
Marketplace sales growth, estimated12.0%Amazon’s own retail sales: 5.3%Digital Commerce 360, via Home Page News
Marketplace share of the event, estimatedabout 36%—Digital Commerce 360, via Home Page News
US online spending, all retailersmore than $11 billionup 6.1% from the October eventAdobe, via GeekWire
Average Prime Day order$44.75$54.64 in 2020, $58.91 in 2019Numerator, via Home Page News
Orders of $20 or less, first 32 hours44%—License Global

Amazon itself said members bought more than 250 million items, GeekWire reported, and that third-party sales grew faster than its own retail business. Numerator’s figures come from a panel of US households.

The split between marketplace and retail growth matters for how a brand sells. Amazon pushed shoppers toward small businesses before the event: they spent more than $1.9 billion with small businesses during its “Spend $10, Get $10” promotion, according to Amazon. A brand selling through Vendor Central, where Amazon is the retailer, competed in the slower-growing half of the event. A brand selling as a third party competed in the faster half, against more sellers than before. A brand selling both ways can check the split in its own numbers: did its third-party sales outgrow its vendor sales over the two days?

Testing the June forecast against the result

The claim most plans assumed was that Prime Day 2021 would be bigger than Prime Day 2020. At the level of the whole event it was, narrowly. Growth between 6.1% and 7.6% is modest for an event whose third-party sales grew nearly 60% in 2020, according to Amazon’s own figures reported by CNBC. And with a smaller average order, more of the gain came from the number of orders than from their size.

Think of checking a weather forecast after the fact. A forecast of 65 to 78 degrees that turns out to be 68 was right, and it tells you something a forecast of 72 cannot: the day came in cooler than the middle, so you can ask why.

Here the reasons are visible. The October 2020 comparison included early holiday shopping that a June event could not repeat. Consumer spending had cooled since the stimulus checks: after jumping 10.7% in March, US retail sales held flat in April, according to the AP. Walmart and Target ran competing events on the same days.

Smaller orders suggest many shoppers were buying everyday items at a discount rather than making larger purchases. None of these looks surprising in hindsight, which is the reason to write them down before the next event instead of after it.

Reviewing a brand’s own event

In the June 1 example, a brand forecast Prime Day sales of $240,000 to $330,000, with $285,000 as the planning point. Say it sold $262,000. That is inside the range, so the forecast did its job. It is also below the middle, and the review should explain the gap assumption by assumption rather than settling for “a soft event.”

Start by splitting the result into its two parts: the number of orders and the average order value. Compare each with what the plan assumed. If orders met plan and order value fell, the gap is a basket problem. If order value held and orders fell short, the causes sit in traffic, advertising and stock.

The value of a range is that a disappointing number turns into a list of causes the brand can act on. Ranking those causes also tells the brand where to spend its holiday preparation. The stakes will be larger then, and the window to fix things shorter.

Four places the gap usually hides

  • Order size. If the brand’s average order fell, as Numerator found across Amazon, shoppers may have bought single units instead of bundles or picked lower-priced items. The holiday plan then needs bundles and multi-buy offers.
  • Advertising cost. If click costs rose, the same budget bought fewer visits. The holiday budget should be set on cost per click as it is now, not as it was in October 2020.
  • Stock. If a top product sold out on the first day, the second day’s sales were capped. Inventory planning for the holidays should start earlier than it did for June.
  • Competing events. Some shoppers may have bought the brand’s products at Walmart or Target that week. If they did, the next event plan should cover all three retailers.

Whether the pattern repeats is the next test. If smaller orders and faster marketplace growth show up again in the holiday season, they are a trend to plan around rather than a quirk of one June event. Set the holiday range now, while the reasons for this one are fresh. Turning each post-event gap into the next forecast’s inputs is how we review Prime Day and holiday events for brands.

A0084.title: Prime Day 2021 lessons: everyone now competes for traffic
A0084.alt: Stone village shopfronts with awnings, wooden shutters and potted flowers line a sunny cobblestone street.
A0084.ttag: Prime Day 2021 lessons: everyone now competes for traffic | Kwontified
A0084.desc: At Prime Day 2021, rival retailers, Amazon and brands all chased the traffic Amazon created while discounts stayed modest. Plan the next event for traffic.
A0084.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 1, 2021.
A0084.body:
A shopper who went looking for Prime Day deals in June found sales everywhere. Walmart scheduled its Deals for Days event for June 20 to 23 and Target its Deal Days for June 20 to 22, Retail TouchPoints reported. Kohl’s, Old Navy and Bed Bath & Beyond were among the others running sales on the same days, according to Retail TouchPoints’ running list. Amazon’s event had become the whole industry’s event.

That picture holds the main Prime Day 2021 lesson. The event is usually described as a sale, but its value sat in the traffic Amazon created, and every party in the market acted to capture a share of it. Rival retailers ran competing sales, Amazon paid to steer shoppers toward its marketplace sellers, and brands bought advertising to be seen, while discounts stayed fairly modest. Brands should plan the next event as a contest for attention, priced through advertising and placement, rather than as a question of how deep to discount.

Prime Day 2021 lessons start with who showed up

Rival retailers had the easiest job. Amazon built the expectation of a deal-hunting week, and Walmart and Target only had to schedule their own events beside it. A shopper comparing a Prime Day price with Target or Walmart might buy there instead, especially as Target required no membership for its event. Running a competing sale lets a retailer catch traffic it did not pay to create.

Amazon spent to shape where its own traffic went. It said it would put more than $100 million into supporting small businesses for the rest of 2021, including a $10 Prime Day credit for members who spent $10 with select small sellers, according to its press release. That promotion steered more than $1.9 billion of shopper spending to small businesses, according to Amazon. The credit pushed shoppers toward the marketplace, where Amazon earns commissions and advertising revenue, and it strengthened a group of sellers Amazon relies on.

Discounts were not the story. Adobe said US online spending over the two days passed $11 billion despite relatively muted discounts across most categories, Tech Xplore reported.

Follow the traffic, and the value follows it

Once the traffic is the prize, each party’s behavior makes sense.

Amazon created the traffic in the first place. Millions of shoppers arrived expecting deals, and that attention was valuable before any single sale was made, because it gave every seller in the store, and every retailer nearby, a crowd to sell to. The retailers who scheduled beside Amazon took a share at little cost. Amazon kept the rest and steered part of it with its own money.

Brands, inside Amazon’s store, paid for position. Among millions of deals, the main way to be seen was advertising and promotion. The cost of attention, more than the size of the discount, decided which brands shoppers noticed. Search ads and deal placements sell the same scarce thing in an event week: a spot near the top of a page crowded with offers, which every brand in the category wants at once.

Shoppers, meanwhile, bought small. In the first 32 hours, 44% of orders were for $20 or less, License Global reported, which fits shoppers picking up everyday items rather than holding out for deep discounts on large purchases. A crowd buying quickly and cheaply rewards the brands it finds first.

Plan the next event around being found

Take two brands planning the same event. One starts with the discount: 30% off its best-sellers and its usual advertising budget. The other keeps discounts at 15% and puts the margin it saved into advertising, Sponsored Brands placements and coordinated offers at Walmart and Target the same week. The second brand trades some discount for visibility, and is more likely to be found by shoppers who arrive in large numbers but buy fast.

A deep discount still has its place, for instance on a new product that needs a burst of sales to build reviews. But the 2021 event suggests visibility is the scarcer resource. Shoppers were buying; the open question for any brand was whether they found it at all.

That changes how the event should be judged. A discount-led event is measured by units sold and margin given up. A traffic-led event is measured by how many new shoppers found the brand, how much of the category’s search it captured and how many of those shoppers return afterwards. Amazon’s advertising reports already count purchases from shoppers new to the brand, a closer measure of reach than total sales in a week when many people bought staples they would have bought anyway.

It changes the budget, too. If traffic is the prize, most of the event’s cost lives in advertising and placement and should be planned that way, alongside the discount rather than after it. And if Walmart and Target are capturing shoppers that week, a brand’s offers and stock there matter as much as its presence on Amazon.

The holiday season will show whether the pattern holds. If retailers again stack their events on the same days and discounts stay modest, the Prime Day lesson carries into the most important quarter of the year.

Two questions for the holiday plan

  • How much of the event budget goes to being seen, and how much to the discount, and was that split decided on purpose or inherited from last year’s plan?
  • Where will the brand’s shoppers be that week, and does the brand have stock, offers and advertising at Walmart and Target as well as on Amazon?

Splitting an event’s budget between discount and visibility by what each event rewards is how we plan event weeks across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0087.crumb: Amazon is the third force in digital…
A0087.title: Amazon is the third force in digital advertising, at the shelf
A0087.alt: Vintage stage spotlights shine on a navy velvet curtain beside wooden shelves of bottles and folded towels.
A0087.ttag: Amazon is the third force in digital advertising, at the shelf | Kwontified
A0087.desc: Amazon now takes about a tenth of US digital ad spending, behind Google and Facebook. Its strength is the shelf, so brands must balance it against reach.
A0087.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 6, 2021.
A0087.body:
For years, US digital advertising was described as a two-company market. In 2020, Amazon’s US advertising revenue grew 52.5% to $15.73 billion, taking more than 10% of the US digital ad market for the first time, according to eMarketer estimates reported by The Drum. Google held 28.9% and Facebook 25.2%. In 2019, Amazon’s share had been 7.8%, The Motley Fool noted.

Amazon got there by selling ads at the point of purchase, with the sale attached. That makes it the most measurable place to spend just as measurement elsewhere weakens, and budgets follow measurement. Amazon’s strength is the shelf rather than reach, though, so brands should grow their Amazon spending in steps while protecting the advertising that creates demand before shoppers ever search there.

How Amazon became the third force in digital advertising

The growth has continued into 2021. Amazon’s “other” revenue, which is mostly advertising, grew 77% in the first quarter, to $6.9 billion, GeekWire reported.

Brands are a large part of that growth, and their budgets there are getting bigger. Feedvisor’s survey of about 1,000 brands put the share spending over $60,000 a month on Amazon ads at 59%, against 38% the year before, its report shows.

A shop that counts sales at its own till

Think of a shop that sells advertising space on its own shelves and can tell each advertiser how many units the ad helped sell, because the till is in the same building. No billboard owner or magazine can offer that, and few advertisers would turn it down once offered.

Amazon is that shop. It knows what shoppers searched for, what they clicked and what they bought, and it reports all three to advertisers.

Google knows what people search for and Facebook knows what holds their attention, but both have to infer purchases through tracking that is getting harder. After Apple’s tracking prompt arrived, early data from Flurry showed only about 4% of US iPhone users letting apps track them, 9to5Mac reported. Google said in June that it would push back its plan to remove third-party cookies from Chrome to late 2023, the AP reported, but the direction has not changed.

As other channels lose sight of the sale, the one that can still see it looks better, even at a higher price. A marketing team defending its budget will move money toward the reports it can defend. Amazon has more of that kind of proof than almost anyone else selling advertising.

Amazon’s proof is strongest where demand already exists

The same proof has a blind spot. Amazon advertising mostly reaches shoppers who are already looking for something to buy. It is very good at turning intent into a sale and at winning a shopper away from a rival product on the same page. It is weaker at creating intent in the first place, introducing a brand to someone who was not looking for it.

Take a brand that moves $200,000 a year from social and video advertising to Amazon, because Amazon’s reports show four dollars of sales per dollar spent while the social reports, after Apple’s change, show less than two. For a few months total sales hold, and the move looks smart. Over the following quarter, fewer new shoppers search for the brand by name, because the advertising that introduced them has stopped. Amazon’s reports still look efficient. They are now measuring a shrinking pool of interest.

The shift itself can be right; the mistake is making it all at once, on reports that measure different things. Amazon deserves more budget when it is winning sales the brand would otherwise lose, and less when it is mainly taking credit for demand created elsewhere.

Where the money comes from matters too. For some brands, Amazon budgets first grew out of trade and retail spending, the money once paid to retailers for promotions and placement, before they began drawing on search and social. Taking from trade spending is a close substitute, because both pay for visibility at the point of sale. Taking from social and video replaces a different job, and that is where the caution belongs.

Amazon offers part of the answer itself. Its demand-side platform, Amazon DSP, sells display and video advertising that reaches shoppers on and off its store, and it can be judged by how many new customers it brings in rather than by last-click sales. A brand that uses Amazon only for search ads is buying the shelf. A brand that also uses its broader tools is buying some of the reach.

Let branded search tell you when to stop

The cleanest check on the shift is the volume of searches for the brand’s own name on Amazon. If branded searches hold or grow as budget moves to Amazon, the brand’s demand is intact and the move is paying. If they fall, the brand is spending more to harvest less. Registered brand owners can follow this in Amazon’s Brand Analytics, which ranks search terms by how often shoppers use them, so the check costs nothing but the habit of looking every month.

So move budget in steps. After each step, check whether total sales rose, not only the sales Amazon’s reports credit, and whether branded searches held. Keep a protected budget for advertising that introduces new shoppers to the brand, judged on reach and new customers rather than on attributed sales.

Move money to Amazon until branded search stops growing, then stop and look at what is feeding it. Moving budget between channels by what each one adds, rather than by what each one reports, is how we run Amazon advertising alongside a brand’s wider media plan.

A0088.crumb: Port congestion will decide who has stock…
A0088.title: Port congestion will decide who has stock for the 2021 holiday
A0088.alt: Red gantry cranes tower over stacked shipping containers at a port quay beside a weathered green ship hull.
A0088.ttag: Port congestion will decide who has stock for the 2021 holiday | Kwontified
A0088.desc: Record imports and container rates up 346% in a year mean some shelves will run short this holiday. On Amazon, sales flow to whoever is in stock.
A0088.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 8, 2021.
A0088.body:
In a store, an out-of-stock product leaves a gap on the shelf. The shopper may wait, ask an associate or come back next week, and the brand’s spot is still there when the stock arrives. Online, the gap fills itself. A shopper searching for a product sees whatever is available and buys it, and on Amazon the rank that sale would have earned goes to the competitor too.

That difference is why the 2021 holiday is already being decided in shipping containers. Imports are running at record levels, the ports are congested, and moving a container from Asia to the US costs several times what it did a year ago. Brands should decide now which products to protect, ship earlier than usual and spread stock across channels, rather than wait to see where the shortages fall.

Port congestion started with record demand

Imports at the nation’s largest retail container ports had their busiest April on record, and May was projected at 2.32 million twenty-foot containers, up 51.1% from a year earlier, the National Retail Federation reported. The first half of 2021 was forecast at 12.8 million containers, up 35.3%.

Capacity has not kept up. “Supply chains are finding it difficult to keep up with demand as shipping capacity struggles,” Ben Hackett, whose firm produces the NRF’s port tracker, said in June, gCaptain reported.

Freight prices rose with the demand. Drewry’s World Container Index reached $8,399 per 40-foot container on July 1, 346% higher than a year earlier, with the Shanghai to Los Angeles route at $9,165, Furniture Today reported.

Amazon’s own warehouses add a second gate. In April, Amazon replaced its limits on individual products with limits by storage type, Helium 10 reported. From July 1, sellers needed an Inventory Performance Index score of 500 to avoid storage limits, up from 450, ChannelX reported. Even goods that clear the ports may not all fit into Amazon’s network at once.

On Amazon, the sale goes to whoever has stock

The online version of an empty shelf is not neutral. Roughly 80% of Amazon sales pass through the Buy Box by the House antitrust subcommittee’s estimate, and Jeff Bezos has conceded that the Buy Box algorithm leans indirectly toward Prime-eligible offers, as CNBC reported. A brand that runs out loses the sale and the ranking that sale would have supported. A competitor that is in stock gains both.

So this holiday’s winners are unlikely to be the brands with the best products in the abstract. They will be the brands whose products are actually available in the weeks that matter, in the channels where shoppers look. That outcome is being set now by whoever books the freight, often before the marketing team’s holiday plan is finished, which turns a logistics booking into a marketing decision.

Working back from December

Take a home-goods brand with 40 products and enough freight budget, at today’s rates, to bring in its usual holiday volume for about 30 of them. It can spread the shortfall evenly and risk running low on everything. Or it can protect its top 15 products fully, order the next 15 at reduced volume and accept that the last 10 may sell out.

The second plan is uncomfortable and usually better. On Amazon, a best-seller that stays in stock keeps its rank and its share of the category’s search traffic. A best-seller that runs out in early December may lose both for weeks, and the shoppers it loses may not come back. The products further down the list lose less when they run out, because fewer shoppers were looking for them in the first place.

The calendar moves too. Shipments that would normally leave in September may need to leave in July or August to arrive in time, given the congestion at the ports and the limits on what Amazon will accept at once. That means committing to holiday orders earlier, with less information about demand, than most brands are used to, and it puts the decision in front of finance and operations before the holiday plan has been signed off.

Cost shifts the plan as well. A container that cost a fraction as much a year ago now adds real money to the landed cost of every unit inside it, and low-priced, bulky products feel it most. Recalculate margins on the holiday range at today’s freight rates, then decide which products can absorb the cost, which need a price increase and which should be ordered in smaller quantities.

Advertising has to follow the stock. A brand that keeps advertising a product about to sell out is paying to send shoppers to a page that will soon show the product as currently unavailable. That spend is wasted twice: it buys no sale, and it teaches Amazon’s systems that the listing does not convert. Holiday ad plans should be tied to inventory forecasts week by week, so spend moves toward products with stock to sell and away from those that will run short.

Channel spread is the last protection. Stock held in a brand’s own warehouse or with a third-party logistics provider can serve its own website, Walmart and Target, and refill Amazon as space opens. A brand with all of its holiday stock pointed at one channel has no room to move when that channel’s limits tighten, and in 2021 Amazon raised its storage bar again on July 1.

Deciding product by product and channel by channel where holiday stock should go, before the ports decide for you, is how we plan holiday inventory across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0089.crumb: FBA storage limits reward the brands that…
A0089.title: FBA storage limits reward the brands that send less stock now
A0089.alt: Metal warehouse shelving holds neat cardboard boxes against a slate-blue wall in a bright, empty warehouse.
A0089.ttag: FBA storage limits reward the brands that send less stock now | Kwontified
A0089.desc: Amazon now limits FBA stock by storage type and IPI score. To fit more holiday inventory in Q4, brands should clear slow stock and ship smaller amounts now.
A0089.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 13, 2021.
A0089.body:
Every brand selling through Fulfillment by Amazon wants as much holiday stock in Amazon’s warehouses as it can get. Amazon’s current rules make that harder to get by asking. Storage limits are now set by storage type, based on past and forecast sales and on a score that rewards efficient inventory.

The way to fit more holiday stock in the fourth quarter therefore runs against instinct. Clear slow-moving inventory and ship smaller, more frequent loads now. Both raise the score, and the score raises the limits that apply when the space matters most.

How FBA storage limits work in 2021

Amazon changed the rules in the spring. Effective April 22, 2021, FBA products were no longer limited one product at a time; restock limits were set at the storage-type level instead, based on past and forecast sales, Helium 10 explained.

Amazon’s Inventory Performance Index, or IPI, decides who faces storage limits at all. From July 1, the IPI threshold for storage limits rose to 500, from 450, ChannelX reported. Sellers whose score falls below the threshold at Amazon’s quarterly checks face limits on how much they can store in the following quarter.

That timing is the part brands miss. A score measured in the late summer shapes the limits that apply in the final quarter of the year, which is when most brands need space most. The decisions that set holiday capacity are being made in July and August, through what a brand ships and clears now.

A credit limit for warehouse space

Think of how a credit card issuer sets a limit. It does not raise the limit because the cardholder asks for more. It raises it for cardholders who use the credit they already have well: who pay on time and do not sit at the top of their limit month after month. Borrowing more to prove you need more is the surest way to keep the limit where it is.

Amazon’s IPI works in a similar way. It reflects how efficiently a seller manages inventory: how much of it sells, how much sits unsold, how well listings are kept in stock and whether stranded inventory is fixed. Slow-moving stock drags the score down. Units that sit for months tell Amazon that more space would be wasted. Amazon’s logic is easy to follow: its warehouse space is shared by every seller, and a unit that sits unsold for months occupies room another seller’s best-seller could have used.

So the instinct to ship as much as possible as early as possible can backfire. A brand that sends a full container of everything in July may fill its limits with products that will not sell until December. Those slow units depress its IPI, and its limits come out lower just when it needs to restock best-sellers in November.

How to make room for the holiday

Take a brand with an IPI of 470, below the new threshold of 500, carrying six months of supply on a third of its products. Its holiday plan needs more space than its current limits allow.

It clears the slow stock first, through promotions, removal orders or a move to its own warehouse. That one step does two jobs: it removes the units dragging the score down, and it frees room under the current limits for the products that actually sell.

It fixes stranded listings so that every unit in Amazon’s network can sell. Then it sends its best-sellers in smaller shipments every two to three weeks, sized to recent sales, instead of one large shipment in July. Over the following weeks sell-through improves, the IPI climbs above 500, and the brand goes into the fourth-quarter check with a score that lifts its limits instead of capping them.

The brand ends up with less stock in Amazon’s warehouses in July and more room when it matters. The rest of its holiday stock waits outside Amazon, at its own site or with an outside logistics partner, where it can serve other channels until Amazon has room for it.

Freight costs raise the stakes. A 40-foot container on Drewry’s World Container Index cost $8,399 on July 1, up 346% on a year before, according to Furniture Today. Goods that expensive to land should not sit in the wrong building, shut out of Amazon by limits a better score would have lifted.

New products need particular care. A launch planned for the holiday takes up storage from the day its stock arrives, before it has sold enough to justify the room. Brands launching in the fourth quarter should send a small first shipment, prove the product sells and scale up as space allows, rather than committing a large share of their limits to an untested item.

Forecasting matters more under this system, not less. Because limits follow past and forecast sales, a brand that predicts holiday demand by product and ships to that forecast in steps will use its space far better than one that sends whatever its factory produced. Checking restock limits by storage type every week, against the coming month’s expected sales, is worth the time.

Watch the score, not the shipment size

The number to track through August and September is the IPI, week by week. A rising score means the plan is working. A falling one means slow stock is still crowding out the space best-sellers will need in November, and the next shipment should be smaller, not larger.

The rule is simple to state and uncomfortable to follow: send less now to be allowed more later. Tracking IPI and storage limits weekly against an inbound plan is how we manage FBA inventory for brands heading into Q4.

A0091.crumb: Grocery on Amazon in 2021 is a habit…
A0091.title: Grocery on Amazon in 2021 is a habit business with a new rival
A0091.alt: A canvas tote and a kraft paper bag of groceries left on a stone doorstep beside a blue front door.
A0091.ttag: Grocery on Amazon in 2021 is a habit business with a new rival | Kwontified
A0091.desc: Online grocery cooled in 2021 while Amazon opened Fresh stores and launched Aplenty. Grocery brands should win the repeat order and watch Amazon’s own label.
A0091.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 15, 2021.
A0091.body:
Somewhere in a kitchen cupboard is a bag of coffee that arrives every month because a shopper set up a regular Amazon order in 2020 and never changed it. Nobody searched for that coffee before the latest delivery, and nobody compared it with anything. It simply came, and the brand that made it was paid again.

That order is the center of grocery on Amazon in 2021. The surge that sent shoppers online for food in 2020 has cooled, and what remains is a replenishment business: the shoppers who stayed, buying the same things again. At the same time Amazon has opened more of its own Fresh grocery stores and launched a private-label food brand, Aplenty. Grocery brands should put their effort into winning and keeping the repeat order, and they have to win it against Amazon’s own label as well as other brands.

What changed for grocery on Amazon

The surge has eased. US online grocery sales were $7 billion in May 2021, down nearly 16% from $8.3 billion in May 2020, according to Brick Meets Click and Mercatus, S&P Global Market Intelligence reported. Relaxed restrictions, vaccinations and a return to restaurants all played a part.

The base is still far larger than before the pandemic. Amazon’s online grocery sales tripled in the second quarter of 2020, the same report noted. In a Coresight Research survey in April 2021, 31.4% of respondents said they had bought groceries online from Amazon in the previous 12 months, according to Coresight.

Amazon has kept investing in grocery all the same. It opened four more Amazon Fresh grocery stores in the US in 2021, bringing the brand to 15 locations including three in London. It also launched Aplenty, a private-label line of snacks, condiments and canned goods sold online and in its Fresh stores, FoodNavigator-USA reported.

Who a grocery brand is competing with now

In 2020 the competition was mostly about availability: shoppers bought whatever was in stock. In 2021 three rivals matter more, and none of them is the brand on the next shelf.

The shopper’s own routine is the strongest. Grocery is bought again and again, and a shopper who set up a regular order for a brand of coffee or snack bars in 2020 may keep buying it without ever searching again. For the brand inside that routine, this is the best position in the category. For a brand outside it, the routine is a wall, because breaking into a habit is harder than catching a new shopper who is still looking.

The reopened store is the next. As restrictions eased, many shoppers went back to buying groceries in person. The online orders that remain are the ones shoppers found most convenient: heavy, bulky or regularly replenished items, and products that are hard to find locally. A grocery brand’s Amazon range should be built around those, not around a copy of its supermarket range.

Amazon itself is the newest. Aplenty sits in the same categories as many branded snacks, condiments and pantry staples, and Amazon controls the search results it appears in. A private label does not need to win every shopper to matter. It only needs to take the price-conscious ones from the brands closest to it.

Two snack brands after the surge

Take two snack brands that both grew fast on Amazon in 2020. The first keeps spending most of its budget on search ads for broad category terms, chasing new shoppers. The second shifts budget toward the customers it already has: Subscribe & Save offers, multipacks sized for regular orders and advertising on its own brand name to defend it.

When online grocery cools in 2021, the first brand’s sales fall with the category. The second holds most of its base, because its customers were already in a routine and it kept that routine easy to repeat.

Pricing and pack size need the same attention. When Aplenty or another private label sits beside a branded product at a lower price, the brand needs a reason to be chosen. That might be a pack size that suits regular ordering, a clear difference in ingredients or quality, or reviews that show shoppers prefer it. Matching the private label’s price is rarely the best answer for a branded product, because it gives away margin without giving the shopper a reason.

Reviews carry extra weight here. A shopper choosing between a familiar brand and a cheaper private label often looks at the star rating first. A brand with a long record of strong reviews starts with an advantage a new private-label product takes time to build, and it should protect that record by fixing product and packaging complaints quickly.

Advertising on the brand’s own name matters more than it used to. When a shopper searches for a brand they already buy, other products, including private labels, can appear above or beside it. A modest Sponsored Brands or Sponsored Products budget on the brand’s own name keeps the repeat customer from being redirected at the last step.

Amazon’s Fresh stores matter less to most brands for now, but they are worth watching: they give Amazon another view of what grocery shoppers buy, and they sell Aplenty alongside branded products. The nearer concern is online. If Aplenty or another Amazon label adds products close to yours, the contest for your price-conscious shoppers is about to get harder, and the brands with the strongest routines will feel it least.

Plans built around the repeat order, from subscriptions to defending branded search, are how we manage grocery and food brands on Amazon.

A0093.crumb: Rising Amazon CPCs: how much is the…
A0093.title: Rising Amazon CPCs: how much is the market and how much is you
A0093.alt: An antique brass gauge with a blank dial beside a small standing mirror against a terracotta wall.
A0093.ttag: Rising Amazon CPCs: how much is the market and how much is you | Kwontified
A0093.desc: Amazon CPCs rose about a third in a year. Before blaming the market, split your own increase into auction inflation, keyword mix and your bids.
A0093.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 20, 2021.
A0093.body:
Amazon cost per click (CPC) has risen by roughly a third in a year, and most brands have felt it in their budgets. The usual explanation is that the market went up. That is partly true, and it is also the explanation that asks least of the team giving it.

A brand’s own CPC increase usually mixes three causes: inflation in the auction, a shift in which keywords and placements the brand buys, and the brand’s own bid changes. Each calls for a different response. Brands should separate them, by measuring CPC on the same clicks in both periods, before deciding whether to accept higher costs, change their mix or cut bids.

How much rising Amazon CPCs reflect the market

The market has moved sharply. Advertising on Amazon cost $1.20 per click on average, up 29% from the start of 2021 and 51.9% from June 2020, according to Marketplace Pulse data reported by MediaPost. The same analysis estimated that the average advertising cost of a sale had risen from $6 to $7 in 2020 to $9 to $10.

Agency data points the same way. Pacvue’s Q2 2021 report found that Sponsored Products CPCs rose 36% year over year, while ad spend on Sponsored Products grew 38% and on Sponsored Brands 82%.

Some of that is a comparison with a weak period. Advertisers pulled back in the spring of 2020, so year-over-year figures for the second quarter start from a low base. Marketplace Pulse’s 29% rise within 2021 alone has no such excuse.

Testing the claim that the market did it

“Our CPCs rose because the market did” is the sentence most teams reach for first. It deserves a test, because the answer decides what to do next.

Think of a household grocery bill that rose 30%. Part of that may be prices: the same basket simply costs more. Part may be the basket, because the household started buying more expensive things. Part may be habit, because it stopped looking for the best prices. A household that blames prices for the whole increase will never notice the parts it controls.

A brand’s CPC breaks down the same way. Market inflation is the same keyword, in the same placement, costing more because more advertisers are bidding for it; a brand cannot control that, only respond to it. Mix is the brand buying different clicks than before. It may have added broad, competitive keywords, moved spend toward top-of-search placements, launched Sponsored Brands campaigns with higher CPCs or entered a more crowded category, and each of those raises the average CPC without any change in the market.

Bids are the brand’s own hand on the auction. Automated bidding rules, bid increases made for Prime Day that were never reversed and placement multipliers all push CPC up from the brand’s side. Each was a reasonable decision when it was made, and together they can look exactly like inflation in a monthly report.

How to split a CPC increase

Take a brand whose average Sponsored Products CPC rose from $0.90 in the first quarter to $1.25 in the second, a 39% increase. The team assumes it is the market. To test that, it takes the keywords it bought in both quarters, in the same match types and placements, and compares their CPC.

Clicks measuredFirst-quarter CPCSecond-quarter CPCChange
All Sponsored Products clicks$0.90$1.25up 39%
Same keywords, match types and placements$0.90$1.08up 20%
Broad category keywords added in the second quarter—$1.70new

The matched set rose 20%. That is the market’s share. The rest came from the brand’s own choices: the new broad keywords at $1.70, plus a top-of-search placement multiplier raised for Prime Day and never lowered. Together those account for the remaining increase.

Each part now has its own response. The market’s 20% is a cost of doing business, best answered by improving conversion through better listings, reviews and pricing, because a higher conversion rate offsets a higher CPC. The broad keywords are a decision to review: keep them if they bring new customers at an acceptable cost, cut them if not. The forgotten multiplier is simply an error to fix.

The arithmetic of profitability shows why conversion belongs in the answer. Advertising cost of sale equals CPC divided by the product of conversion rate and average order value. A 20% higher CPC with unchanged conversion raises the cost of each sale by 20%. A brand that also improves conversion by 10% absorbs about half of that increase. Listings, reviews and pricing are the parts of the formula a brand controls directly, and they keep working when the auction does not cool.

Category matters too. Market-wide averages hide wide differences, and a category that drew many new sellers during the pandemic has probably seen a sharper rise than a steadier one. A brand comparing its CPC with a market-wide average may be comparing itself with the wrong market; its own category’s matched-keyword trend is the fairer test.

Measure the same clicks before you blame the market

The quickest diagnostic is the gap between matched-keyword CPC and overall CPC. When the overall figure rises much faster than the matched one, the increase is coming from the brand’s own mix and bids, not the auction. Bid rules and placement multipliers changed for Prime Day or any other event are the first place to look, because they are the cheapest part of the increase to reverse.

Before accepting a higher CPC as the market’s doing, measure it on the clicks you bought in both periods. Reporting each CPC change by its cause, so budget decisions follow what actually moved, is how we manage rising Amazon ad costs for brands.

A0094.title: Back-to-school 2021 starts earlier, so plans must too
A0094.alt: A sunny wooden desk with notebooks, pens, colored pencils, a backpack and a vintage desk fan.
A0094.ttag: Back-to-school 2021 starts earlier, so plans must too | Kwontified
A0094.desc: Shoppers plan to spend most of their 2021 back-to-school budgets by the end of July. Brands need stock and advertising in place weeks earlier than usual.
A0094.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 22, 2021.
A0094.body:
In a normal year, the parent with a school supply list in hand shows up in August. In 2021 that parent is buying in July, after a year of empty shelves and shipping delays, because waiting feels like a risk. Back-to-school 2021 is set to be a record season, and much of it is arriving before the date most brands planned around.

That moves the value of the season forward. Brands with stock already landed and advertising already running in July will capture it. Brands still working to a traditional August peak risk arriving after much of the money has been spent.

What the back-to-school 2021 surveys show

Two of the main surveys agree on size. Deloitte expects back-to-school spending on K-12 students to reach $32.5 billion, about $612 per student, the highest in recent years, according to its release. The National Retail Federation forecast a record $37.1 billion, up from $33.9 billion in 2020, with families planning to spend $848.90 each, $59 more than in 2020, Home Page News reported.

The timing is the bigger change. Deloitte found that 50% of shoppers are concerned about stockouts, especially for technology, and that 59% of back-to-school spending will happen by the end of July, compared with 45% in 2020. Online stays important too: Deloitte expects K-12 families to spend $12.5 billion online this season, up from $10.4 billion in 2020.

The season belongs to whoever is ready in July

Shoppers are spending early because they expect shortages. Many would rather buy in July than risk not finding what they need in August, and that spending goes to whichever brand has the product available and visible when they arrive. In July, that is the brand whose stock has already landed and whose advertising is already running. A brand whose stock arrives in mid-August, as it might in a normal year, meets a smaller share of the season’s shoppers.

Advertising costs follow the crowd. As more brands try to reach back-to-school shoppers in the same few weeks, each click costs more. A brand that starts early buys attention before the peak; a brand that starts late competes for the remaining shoppers at higher prices.

Shipping makes being early harder. On July 1, Drewry’s index priced the average 40-foot box at $8,399, which Furniture Today noted was 346% above the same point in 2020. With ports congested as well, stock planned for late July may land later. The brands best placed for an early season are the ones that ordered and shipped for it in the spring.

A plan built for August misses the season

Take a backpack brand that usually expects most of its back-to-school sales between August 1 and Labor Day, with stock reaching Amazon’s warehouses in late July and advertising starting on August 1. In 2021, with 59% of spending expected by the end of July, that plan misses most of the season. A competitor that moved its stock and its advertising start to early July is in front of shoppers while they are buying.

For brands still adjusting, the most useful change is to start advertising now on whatever stock is available rather than waiting for a planned launch date. Budget should sit behind products that are actually in stock, because advertising a product that is running out sends shoppers to a page they cannot buy from. And the season should be stretched at both ends: early buyers may come back for items they missed, and late buyers will still arrive in August. Stock that will not land until late August is better aimed at those late buyers, and at the season after, than pushed hard against a peak that has already passed.

Product matters as much as timing. Deloitte’s finding that stockout worries are strongest for technology suggests where early buying will be heaviest. Brands selling laptops, tablets, headphones and accessories should expect the most compressed season. Brands selling clothing, footwear and basic supplies may see a more traditional August pattern, though still earlier than usual. A brand selling both should plan the two groups on separate calendars.

Listings deserve a check before the traffic arrives. Back-to-school shoppers search by grade, age and school list, so titles and keywords that mention them help a product appear in the searches that matter in July and August.

Amazon, Walmart and Target all run back-to-school promotions, and a brand that coordinates offers across the three retailers reaches shoppers wherever they choose to buy. With shoppers worried about stockouts, being in stock at more than one retailer is an advantage in itself.

Reading the season while it is still running

Measurement needs a different frame this year. A brand that compares July 2021 with July 2020 will see a large increase and may conclude the season is going well. The better comparison is the whole season, July through early September, against the same weeks of 2020, because strong July sales may simply be August sales arriving early. Comparing each week with the same week a year earlier, rather than with the week before, shows whether the season is growing or simply moving.

The next two weeks will show which it is. If July sales are running well ahead of July 2020 while expectations for the whole season are unchanged, the peak has moved forward, and August stock and budgets should be smaller than they would otherwise have been. Freeing that money now leaves room to follow the late buyers instead of overspending on an August that has already partly happened.

Timing stock and advertising to when shoppers actually buy is how we plan seasonal campaigns across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0095.title: Q2 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: Prime Day bought volume
A0095.alt: A shopping cart overflowing with kraft-wrapped parcels parked against a blue wall on a cobbled street.
A0095.ttag: Q2 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: Prime Day bought volume | Kwontified
A0095.desc: Q2 2021 Amazon ad results combine Prime Day in June with ten weeks of rising CPCs. Split the quarter to see what Prime Day bought and what it cost.
A0095.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 27, 2021.
A0095.body:
A brand’s second-quarter Amazon advertising report shows one return on ad spend (ROAS) for April through June 2021. That single number covers two different businesses. For about ten weeks, costs rose steadily as more brands competed for the same shoppers. Then Prime Day, moved to June 21 and 22, brought a burst of traffic and a burst of spending in the last ten days of the quarter.

A quarterly average blends the two and explains neither. A useful Q2 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark separates the Prime Day weeks from the rest of the quarter, so a brand can see what Prime Day bought in volume and, separately, what the underlying rise in costs did to efficiency.

The Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q2 2021 spans two periods

Costs rose across the quarter. Pacvue’s Q2 2021 report put the year-over-year rise in Sponsored Products cost per click (CPC) at 36%. When it announced the findings, Pacvue said Sponsored Products ROAS was down 10% from a year earlier even though spend was up 38%, according to the release. More money bought less return per dollar.

Prime Day added its own pattern on top. Many advertisers raised budgets and bids around the event. By Digital Commerce 360’s estimate, Amazon took $11.19 billion worldwide over the two days, 7.6% more than at the October 2020 event, its analysis found.

The year-ago comparison is unusual on both counts. In the second quarter of 2020, many advertisers pulled back as the pandemic began, so year-over-year figures start from a low base. And Prime Day 2020 fell in October, so the 2020 second quarter had no event in it at all.

Prime Day 2021 against the weeks before it

The event itself has a public benchmark. Skai published day-by-day Prime Day results for its retail media advertisers, each day set against their daily average from June 1 to 20.

Skai retail media advertisersPrime Day, first dayPrime Day, second day
Ad spend, vs June 1 to 20 daily average3.7x3.6x
CPC, vs June 1 to 20 daily average1.4x1.5x
Sales revenue, vs June 1 to 20 daily average4.8x3.6x
CPC, vs the same day of Prime Day 20201.1x1.2x

ROAS here is attributed sales divided by ad spend, and Sponsored Products results use Amazon’s standard attribution model. Dividing the sales multiple by the spend multiple shows what happened to the return on each dollar. On the first day it was about 1.3 times the June level (4.8 divided by 3.7). On the second it was level with June (3.6 divided by 3.6). Clicks cost more on both days, yet the extra spend bought sales at least in proportion.

For the first quarter, the reference point, Tinuiti measured Sponsored Products CPC 7% above a year earlier, AdExchanger reported. No public source splits the second quarter into April 1 to June 13, June 14 to 22 and June 23 to 30. A brand has to cut those periods from its own console data.

What a quarterly ROAS hides

Prime Day is a trade. Brands spend more, often at higher CPCs and with deeper discounts, to win a larger volume of sales in a short window. Whether the extra volume was worth the lower efficiency is the question the quarter should answer, and a quarterly figure cannot, because it mixes the event with ten weeks of ordinary trading.

The averaging cuts both ways. A brand whose ROAS fell for the quarter may have run Prime Day well and simply paid more for clicks in April and May. Another may have held its quarterly ROAS steady only because it barely took part in Prime Day and missed the volume.

Take a brand that spent $100,000 from April 1 to June 13 at a ROAS of 4.0, and $30,000 in the Prime Day period at a ROAS of 3.0. Its quarterly ROAS is about 3.8. In the Prime Day period it earned $90,000 in attributed sales, three times its spend, some of it from shoppers new to the brand. Whether that was a good trade depends on margin and on how many of those new customers buy again, and the quarterly ROAS shows neither.

The weeks before the event tell a separate story. If CPC rose steadily from April to mid-June while conversion held, the brand was paying more for the same shoppers. That is the underlying cost trend, and it carries on after Prime Day ends. It needs its own response, usually better listings and pricing to lift conversion, not to be buried inside an event average.

Event spending also lands unevenly across ad types. Many brands push Sponsored Brands and Sponsored Display harder around Prime Day to reach shoppers browsing deals, so blended quarterly figures can shift simply because the mix of ad types changed for two weeks. The period split is worth repeating by ad type.

The days after the event matter too. Some brands see a dip as shoppers who bought during Prime Day pause; others see a lift as shoppers come back for products they found during it. The June 23 to 30 period shows which pattern applied to a given brand.

Any benchmark also needs one caution. An industry figure averages across many brands, and categories differ. Brands in categories Prime Day emphasizes, such as electronics and household goods, should expect a sharper event-week swing than brands in categories shoppers buy on a steady schedule. In Skai’s data, computers and electronics advertisers spent 7.9x their June daily average on the first day and 9.1x on the second.

Judge the event and the trend separately

Split Q2 2021 into the weeks before Prime Day, the event itself and the days after before comparing it with any benchmark, including the public figures above. Judge Prime Day on incremental volume, new customers and margin. Judge the rest of the quarter on the trend in CPC and conversion, and plan the holiday quarter on the assumption that the April-to-June cost trend continues and that a Prime Day-style trade of efficiency for volume will be needed again.

Reporting each period on its own terms, so event decisions and ongoing costs are judged separately, is how we read Amazon advertising results for brands.

A0097.title: Walmart marketplace sellers depend on grocery shoppers
A0097.alt: A blue wire basket of bread, leafy greens, tomatoes, apples and a twine-tied parcel on a wooden table.
A0097.ttag: Walmart marketplace sellers depend on grocery shoppers | Kwontified
A0097.desc: Walmart’s grocery trips bring the traffic its marketplace sellers sell to. Sellers should pick products that fit that trip and advertise where shoppers search.
A0097.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 29, 2021.
A0097.body:
A shopper opens the Walmart app on a Sunday evening to order the week’s groceries: milk, bread, dish soap, dog food. Halfway down the list she remembers the cracked phone case and adds one of those too. She did not come to Walmart to shop for a phone case. She came for groceries, and the phone case was one search away.

That is how Walmart’s marketplace finds many of its customers, and it is why it is misread as a smaller copy of Amazon’s. Shoppers come to Walmart most often for food and household essentials, in stores and increasingly online, and the marketplace sells to the people that habit brings in. Marketplace sellers do best with products that fit alongside that trip, priced and advertised for the household shopper, rather than with a copy of their Amazon approach.

Walmart marketplace grocery traffic starts in the store

Walmart started with an advantage no online-only retailer has: it is where most American households already buy groceries. Asked in April 2021 where they had bought groceries over the previous 12 months, 65.1% of shoppers in Coresight Research’s survey named Walmart’s stores, Coresight found.

The pandemic moved that habit online. Walmart built pickup and delivery capacity from its stores, and shoppers used it. In the first quarter of its 2022 fiscal year, Walmart US e-commerce sales grew 37%, contributing about 3.6 percentage points to comparable sales growth, and Walmart gained grocery market share, the company reported. E-commerce sales have more than doubled over two years, Walmart said in the same release.

Shoppers also consolidated their trips. Walmart’s average ticket in the US rose 9.5% in the quarter while transactions fell 3.2%, as people made fewer, larger visits, according to the earnings release.

How the marketplace rides on that traffic

Walmart has said its other businesses grow from that core. On its first-quarter call, chief executive Doug McMillon said marketplace gross merchandise value, fulfillment services and advertising income through Walmart Connect were all strong. He added that Walmart would keep adding brands and assortment to its general merchandise business through marketplace expansion, according to a transcript of the call.

The logic follows from the Sunday-evening order. A shopper who opens the app every week for groceries is already there when she needs a storage bin or a pet bed. The grocery visit creates the traffic, and the marketplace and Walmart Connect turn some of it into general merchandise sales and advertising revenue.

That makes Walmart’s traffic different from Amazon’s. Amazon shoppers often arrive searching for a specific product. Many Walmart shoppers arrive to restock the household and add other items along the way. The products that do well in that setting tend to be ones a household needs regularly or can decide on quickly.

Two catalogs on the same app

Take two sellers listing on Walmart Marketplace. One lists its full Amazon range unchanged, including niche hobby products shoppers research for weeks. The other leads with products that fit the household trip: cleaning tools, storage, kitchen basics and pet supplies, priced competitively and described in plain terms. The second seller’s products show up in the searches Walmart’s grocery shoppers actually make, and convert when those shoppers decide quickly. Much of the first seller’s catalog sits unseen, waiting for a shopper who came to Walmart with a hobby in mind rather than a grocery list.

Price weighs more in this setting, because Walmart’s shoppers come for value and compare quickly. Walmart can remove a marketplace listing if the same item is cheaper elsewhere, including on the seller’s own website, Modern Retail reported, so a seller’s Walmart price is set by its pricing everywhere else too.

Advertising should follow the household shopper. Walmart Connect sponsored products appear in Walmart’s search results, and a seller targeting the everyday terms these shoppers use, rather than the niche terms that work on Amazon, reaches more of the traffic grocery brings in.

Fulfillment speed belongs in the same picture. A shopper used to same-day grocery pickup expects general merchandise to arrive quickly as well, and slow shipping makes a marketplace listing look weak beside Walmart’s own fast-moving range. Walmart Fulfillment Services or a reliable logistics partner closes much of that gap.

Listings need the same care as on Amazon, written for Walmart’s shopper. Clear images, plain product names and short descriptions that answer the obvious questions help someone deciding between chores, not researching for hours. Some sellers copy their listings straight from Amazon, with long keyword-heavy titles that read poorly in Walmart’s app. Rewriting them for a faster, simpler decision is a small change that can lift conversion, and it costs far less than buying more traffic.

Timing within the week matters as well. If a seller’s shoppers are mostly grocery shoppers, their visits will follow grocery patterns, with heavier traffic around the days households restock. Walmart Connect budgets and promotions can be weighted toward those days once a seller’s own data shows the pattern.

None of this means niche products cannot sell on Walmart. It means the marketplace’s largest flow of shoppers is shaped by the grocery habit, and sellers who design their range and advertising for that flow will see more of it. Walmart is still building on the habit through its Walmart+ membership and its pickup and delivery services, and each step that makes the weekly order easier brings more shoppers into the app, one search away from a marketplace product.

Building a Walmart range and its advertising around the shopper the grocery trip brings in is how we manage Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect for brands.

A0099.title: Amazon’s Q2 2021 results: slower sales make clicks more expensive
A0099.alt: A brass hourglass beside a pile of old coins and dry leaves on a worn wooden table.
A0099.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2021 results: slower sales make clicks more expensive | Kwontified
A0099.desc: Amazon’s online store sales grew 13% in Q2 2021 while advertising grew 87%. Slower shopper growth with more advertisers means costlier clicks into the holiday.
A0099.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 3, 2021.
A0099.body:
Amazon’s second-quarter results disappointed Wall Street, and Amazon guided to slower growth for the third quarter. It would be natural to expect advertising on Amazon to get cheaper as shopping cools. The numbers point the other way.

In the quarter, Amazon’s advertising-heavy revenue line grew 87% while its online store sales grew 13%. Slower shopper growth is raising the price of each click, because the number of brands bidding keeps rising faster than the number of shoppers they bid for. Brands should plan the holiday on a higher cost per sale and protect margin through conversion and budget discipline.

What Amazon’s Q2 2021 results show

MeasureQ2 2021Growth on Q2 2020
Net sales$113.1 billion27%
Online store sales$53.1 billion13%, against 37% to 49% during the pandemic
“Other” revenue, mostly advertising$7.9 billion87%
Q3 2021 net sales guidance$106 billion to $112 billion10% to 16%

Net sales came in below analysts’ expectations, GeekWire reported. Amazon’s chief financial officer put the slowdown down to the comparison with the 2020 pandemic surge and to customers getting out more and doing other things besides shopping, the same report noted.

Why slower shopping makes advertising cost more

Think of front-row seats at a show. The number of seats is fixed. If more people want them each season, the price rises. If the audience stops growing but the number of people bidding for the front row keeps climbing, the price rises faster still.

Amazon’s sponsored placements work the same way. There are only so many ad positions on each search page and only so many shoppers searching. In 2020 shoppers flooded in, and new advertisers followed. In 2021 shopper growth has slowed, but the advertisers have not left. Many brands that moved online during the pandemic are still there, still bidding, and new ones keep joining them.

Cost data from the same months agree. Marketplace Pulse put Amazon’s average cost per click at $1.20, a 29% increase since the start of 2021, MediaPost reported. In the second quarter, Sponsored Products clicks cost 36% more than a year earlier by Pacvue’s count in its Q2 2021 report, and its announcement of the findings put return on ad spend down 10%.

A rough way to see the shift is to set Amazon’s “other” revenue against its online store sales. In the second quarter of 2021 it equaled about 15% of online store sales. A year earlier, working back from the growth rates Amazon reported, it was about 9%.

The comparison is imperfect: “other” revenue includes more than advertising, and much advertising supports third-party sales Amazon reports separately. The direction is still clear. Advertising is taking a larger share of each dollar spent in Amazon’s store.

For an individual brand, that shift shows up as advertising taking a bigger slice of each sale. The same budget buys fewer clicks, each click converts no more often than it did, and the cost of every attributed sale creeps up month by month, often without any single change large enough to prompt a review.

Advertisers keep bidding, and the holiday will cost more per sale

Why keep bidding when returns fall? Amazon is still where the shoppers are, even in a slower quarter, and its reports show the sale directly, which counts for more as tracking elsewhere weakens. A brand that stops advertising also hands visibility to rivals who do not. Each reason is sensible for one brand. Together they keep the auction full in a quarter when shoppers are spending more time elsewhere.

The bidding does have a limit. When enough advertisers find that a sale costs more than the product earns, some cut back and prices ease in those categories. That point arrives sooner where margins are thin and later where they are high, which is why cost increases are rarely even across the store.

Take a brand whose holiday plan assumes the same cost per sale as in 2020, $8, and budgets $400,000 to drive 50,000 sales. If cost per sale rises 25% to $10 in 2021, the same budget drives 40,000 sales and the brand misses its target by a fifth. It can spend more to close the gap or accept fewer sales. Either way, the assumption was wrong. Inventory belongs in the same calculation: a budget that will buy 40,000 sales should not sit beside stock ordered for 50,000, and a budget raised to chase the original target is wasted if the stock it advertises runs out first.

A brand facing that holiday has three levers to pull. Planning comes first: build the budget on a higher cost per sale from the start, so budgets and inventory match what the money will actually buy. Conversion is the second lever: better listings, stronger reviews and competitive pricing raise the share of clicks that become sales, which offsets a higher price for each click. Discipline is the last: cut keywords and placements whose cost per sale has risen above what the product’s margin can support, and review bids weekly against a ceiling set by margin rather than letting automated bids follow the market up without one.

Amazon’s third-quarter results in late October will show whether the gap is still widening. If online store sales stay slow while “other” revenue keeps growing quickly, the pressure that raised costs in 2021 will carry straight into the holiday.

Budget the holiday on what a sale costs now, not on what it cost in 2020. Building holiday budgets around current click prices is how we plan and run Amazon advertising for brands.
