A0100.crumb: Retail media metrics beyond ROAS: four…
A0100.title: Retail media metrics beyond ROAS: four signs of health
A0100.alt: Four vintage brass gauges mounted on a plate on a dusty pink wall beside a window with a potted plant.
A0100.ttag: Retail media metrics beyond ROAS: four signs of health | Kwontified
A0100.desc: ROAS is falling across Amazon as costs rise, but it cannot say whether a program is healthy. Four measures give leaders a fuller view of what spend builds.
A0100.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 5, 2021.
A0100.body:
The quarterly review reaches the retail media slide, and the number on it has gone down. Return on ad spend (ROAS) fell again. Someone asks whether the program is still working, and nobody in the room can answer, because the one number on the slide cannot.

ROAS is falling across Amazon as the cost of each click rises, so a decline on its own says little. A healthy program shows up across four measures read together: efficiency, growth in the total business, reach to new customers and the strength of the brand’s organic demand. A program can look efficient on ROAS while the business beneath it weakens, and it can look less efficient while it builds something lasting.

Why retail media metrics need to go beyond ROAS in 2021

ROAS is under pressure across the market. By Marketplace Pulse’s count, the average click on Amazon cost $1.20, 29% more than at the start of 2021, and the ad spend behind each sale had climbed to $9 to $10, against $6 to $7 in 2020, MediaPost reported. Pacvue said second-quarter Sponsored Products ROAS was 10% lower than a year earlier, in its announcement.

When the whole market’s ROAS is falling, a brand’s own decline may say little about how well its program is run. The question worth asking is what the spending is building.

Four questions instead of one

“Is it working?” is really four questions, and each has its own measure.

Efficiency still matters. ROAS answers it, and a program that spends far more per sale than the product’s margin allows is a problem however much it grows. The fair test is ROAS against margin and against the market’s direction, not against last year’s ratio. A falling ROAS that still clears margin is a cost to manage, not a failure.

Growth in the whole business is the next test. Total advertising cost of sale, often called TACoS, divides ad spend by all sales, advertised and organic. If ad spend rises and total sales rise with it, the program is helping the business grow. If ad spend rises while total sales stay flat, the advertising may simply be buying sales the brand would have made anyway.

Reach to new customers comes after that. For some ad types Amazon reports “new-to-brand” purchases, from shoppers who had not bought from the brand in the previous year, as it explained when it introduced the metric. A program whose sales come almost entirely from existing customers is defending the base. That has value, but it is not expansion.

Organic demand is the slowest signal and the most telling. Searches for the brand’s own name, and its organic rank on important category terms, show whether shoppers seek the brand out without being paid for. A program that buys more and more of the brand’s own searches while organic visibility falls is filling a hole rather than building a position. Organic demand moves over months rather than weeks, which makes it easy to leave out of a monthly report and worth keeping in one.

Two programs with the same ROAS

Take two brands that each report a ROAS of 4.0 for the quarter. The first spends mostly on its own brand name. Its TACoS has risen, total sales are flat, few of its ad-driven buyers are new and its organic rank on category terms has slipped. Its ROAS looks strong because it is paying to capture shoppers who were already looking for it.

The second spends mostly on category terms and product targeting. Its ROAS is the same, but total sales grew 20%, a third of its ad-driven buyers were new to the brand and its organic rank improved as sales rose. Its program is building the business. On ROAS alone the two are identical; on the other three measures, one is healthy and one is not.

The four measures also explain a decline. If ROAS falls while TACoS holds, new-to-brand share rises and organic rank improves, the brand is paying more for growth in a costlier market, which may be the right trade. If ROAS falls while every other measure weakens too, something in the program needs fixing.

Each measure points to a different fix. Weak efficiency calls for bid and keyword discipline. Flat total sales call for a look at how much spend sits on the brand’s own searches. A low new-to-brand share calls for more category and competitor targeting. Falling organic demand calls for work beyond advertising, on listings, reviews and the brand’s presence off Amazon.

Most brands already have the data they need. Amazon’s advertising reports provide ROAS and, for some ad types, new-to-brand figures. Total sales come from the seller or vendor reports. Branded search and organic rank can be tracked monthly in Amazon’s own tools or common third-party software.

What changes is the conversation. A monthly review built on four measures, with a short note on each, gives leadership a far clearer picture than a single ratio. It also makes trade-offs visible: a quarter that gave up some efficiency to win new customers looks very different from one that lost both. Targets should follow the same shape, with goals for growth and reach as well as efficiency, so the program is rewarded for building the business.

The holiday season will test the habit. Seasonal ROAS often improves as shoppers convert more readily, which can hide exactly the weaknesses the other three measures would show.

Reporting to leadership on the measures that show what the spending builds is how we run retail media programs for brands.

A0101.crumb: Q4 2021 budget phasing: the holiday is a…
A0101.title: Q4 2021 budget phasing: the holiday is a season, not a weekend
A0101.alt: Wrapped gifts with ribbons and twine on a wooden table, transitioning from autumn leaves to pine boughs.
A0101.ttag: Q4 2021 budget phasing: the holiday is a season, not a weekend | Kwontified
A0101.desc: Cyber Week’s share of holiday online spending fell in 2020 as the season spread out. Phase Q4 2021 budgets from October onward, not around a single weekend.
A0101.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 10, 2021.
A0101.body:
Ask a brand where its holiday advertising budget goes and the answer usually starts with Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Those are still the biggest single days for online sales, and they deserve a full plan. In 2020, though, the week from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday took a smaller share of US holiday online spending than it did in 2019, because the season spread out around it.

Budgets that cluster on Cyber Week are built around the biggest days rather than the biggest periods. Q4 2021 budget phasing should run from October through December, in proportion to where a brand’s demand actually falls.

What Q4 2021 budget phasing has to account for

The 2020 data show the shift. US online spending in November and December 2020 reached a record $188.2 billion, up 32.2%, according to Adobe Analytics. The week from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday accounted for 18% of the season, down from 20% in 2019, CNBC reported.

The peak days still matter. Cyber Monday 2020 reached $10.8 billion and Black Friday $9 billion. But the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday grew 21%, slower than the season as a whole, and 50 days of the season topped $2 billion in online sales, up from 29 in 2019, according to Adobe figures reported by FashionNetwork.

Retailers pulled the season earlier as well. In 2020, Walmart and Target rolled out holiday deals in mid-October to compete with Amazon’s Prime Day, PYMNTS reported.

Why budgets gather around the peak

The biggest day of the year is the easiest number to remember and the most dramatic to plan for, so budgets collect around it. Teams build a Cyber Week plan in detail and treat the rest of the quarter as a holding pattern. Last year’s reports reinforce the habit, because the peak days show the largest sales totals, and a large total is easy to mistake for a large return.

The arithmetic argues against that. If Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday is about 18% of holiday online spending, the other 82% happens on other days. A plan that puts 40% of the holiday budget into that week spends more than twice the week’s share of demand on it, and underspends everywhere else. On a $500,000 holiday budget, that is $200,000 aimed at a week carrying about 18% of the season’s demand.

Cost points the same way. The peak days are when the most advertisers compete, so clicks are most expensive then. By June 2021 an average Amazon click already cost $1.20, 29% above January’s level on Marketplace Pulse data, according to MediaPost. Concentrating budget into the most expensive week compounds the cost.

How to phase the fourth quarter

Take a brand with $500,000 for advertising from October through December. Rather than putting most of it into Cyber Week, it phases spend to match where its own sales and the market’s demand fell in 2020.

PeriodShareBudgetRole
Octoberabout 15%$75,000Build visibility, test new keywords and gather reviews before competition peaks
November 1 to the day before Thanksgivingabout 25%$125,000Early deals and gift research, while clicks are cheaper than at the peak
Thanksgiving through Cyber Mondayabout 25%$125,000The peak, funded fully but in proportion
December through Christmasabout 35%$175,000Late shoppers, gift cards and last-minute orders, shifting to products that can still arrive in time

Compared with a peak-heavy plan, this moves money out of the most expensive week and into the weeks on either side of it, where the same dollar buys more clicks. The exact split should come from the brand’s own 2020 sales by week, not from a template. A brand whose sales peaked sharply in Cyber Week might weight that week more heavily. A brand selling gifts that shoppers research for weeks might weight November more.

Inventory has to follow the same phasing. A brand that spends evenly across the season but runs out of stock in early December wastes its December budget. With shipping slow and Amazon’s storage limits tight in 2021, stock plans and budget plans should be built together and reviewed weekly from October onward.

Early spending needs a fair test. Advertising in October and early November often shows a weaker return in the reports than Cyber Week spending. Shoppers who click early may buy weeks later, outside the attribution window, or come back on a peak day when the last click goes to a different ad. That is a measurement gap, not a performance gap. Judge early-season spend on the new customers it brings in, the reviews and ranking it builds and the brand searches that follow, not only on the sales attributed within days of the click.

Starting early also lowers the cost of the peak. A product that has gained sales history, reviews and organic ranking by mid-November needs less paid support at the point when every click costs the most.

The plan should leave room to move. If early November demand runs ahead of expectations, budget can shift forward; if it lags, more can be held for the peak. Phasing sets the starting point, and weekly reviews adjust it. When the first major holiday deals appear in October will show how far to move: if Amazon, Walmart and Target start earlier than in 2020, demand will shift earlier too, and the budget should follow it.

Fund Cyber Week fully, but in proportion to its share of demand, and give October, early November and December their own jobs. Phasing holiday spend to where demand actually falls is how we plan Q4 advertising across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0103.crumb: A Target Plus P&L: strong unit margins…
A0103.title: A Target Plus P&L: strong unit margins, heavy fixed costs
A0103.alt: An antique brass balance scale weighing a small red twine-tied gift against an iron weight on a wooden table.
A0103.ttag: A Target Plus P&L: strong unit margins, heavy fixed costs | Kwontified
A0103.desc: A Target Plus sale can carry a healthy unit margin, but low volume means fixed costs decide profitability. Build the P&L order by order, then add the overhead.
A0103.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 12, 2021.
A0103.body:
The invitation to Target Plus usually lands with a short list of terms, and the commission line is the one leadership reads first. It looks modest next to Amazon’s fees, so the conclusion comes quickly: this channel will make money. Per order, that is often right. Across a month, the answer depends on how many orders arrive to carry the work of running the channel.

A Target Plus order often carries a healthy margin per unit, because the commission is moderate and there are no warehouse fees. But the seller pays to ship every order, and the marketplace’s volume is small, so fixed costs decide whether it pays. Brands should build the P&L from a single order up, then test it against realistic volume.

The Target Plus P&L starts with what Target takes

Target’s terms are simple next to Amazon’s. Host sites typically take a commission of 5% to 15% on a marketplace sale, the Star Tribune noted. The seller keeps the inventory and does the shipping. On marketplace items, Target’s card holders retain their 5% discount and free shipping, and returns can be made in Target stores, the same report noted.

The channel is also small. In early 2021 Target Plus counted fewer than 300 sellers by Marketplace Pulse’s figures, as Kaspien noted when it joined. That keeps competition low on each listing, and it also reflects how much traffic and attention the marketplace gets compared with Target’s own range.

Where the money goes on one order

Take a shopper who buys a $40 throw pillow from a home brand on Target Plus. The figures are a worked example, not Target’s actual rates for any category.

LineAmount
Sale price$40
Target’s commission, at 15%$6.00
Shipping from the brand’s warehouse$7.50
Packing materials and labor$1.50
Product cost$12.00
Returns allowance (8% of orders at $10 each)$0.80
Left per order$12.20

That is about 30% of the sale. Against many Amazon orders, where fulfillment and storage fees sit beside the referral fee, it is a healthy margin per unit. The returns line is the easiest to leave out, and on a marketplace where shoppers can hand items back at a Target store, it deserves a real rate from the brand’s own history rather than a guess.

The value does not stop there, though. Some of it goes to costs that do not move with each order. Connecting the brand’s inventory and order systems to Target’s platform takes setup and ongoing maintenance. Customer questions have to be answered within Target’s standards. Listings need images and copy that meet Target’s requirements, and someone has to watch prices, stock and service metrics every day.

Suppose those costs come to $8,000 a month, between staff time, software and service. At 300 orders a month, the brand earns $3,660 in contribution and loses $4,340. At 700 orders, it earns $8,540 and roughly breaks even. At 1,500 orders, it earns $18,300 and makes a real profit.

Break-even sits where contribution covers the overhead: $8,000 divided by $12.20 is about 656 orders a month. That is the number to hold the volume forecast against before anything else is committed. The margin per order is the same in all three cases; volume decides the result, and volume on Target Plus is the hardest number in the plan to forecast.

Volume decides whether Target Plus pays

Three things follow for a brand weighing the invitation.

The P&L needs two layers. The order layer, with commission, shipping, packing, product cost and returns, says whether each sale makes money. The channel layer, with integration, service, content and management, says how many orders it takes to cover the overhead. Many brands build only the first and are surprised by the second.

Advertising, once added, sits in the order layer. If a brand spends $2 in Roundel advertising for each order it wins, the $12.20 in the example falls to $10.20, and the volume needed to cover fixed costs rises with it, to about 784 orders a month on the same $8,000. Advertising can lift volume enough to justify itself, but it should be judged against that higher break-even point.

Fixed costs should start light. Integration tools that connect several marketplaces at once spread the setup across channels. A focused range of products that fit Target’s shoppers, rather than the full catalog, keeps content and service work manageable while volume is proven.

And volume should be tested before anyone invests further. A brand can launch a small range, measure orders over a few months, and only then decide whether to expand, add Roundel advertising or hire dedicated staff. Target’s curation means few direct competitors on each listing, but it also means no steady flood of traffic of the kind larger marketplaces provide.

One more line belongs in the decision, even though it is hard to price. A presence on Target.com can carry value beyond its own orders: credibility with shoppers, and a relationship with Target that may matter for future store distribution. That deserves weight, but judged on its own, not used to cover a channel that loses money order by order.

The first full quarter of orders gives the answer. If volume is climbing toward the level that covers fixed costs, the channel can grow. If it stays flat well below that level, Target Plus is a relationship to keep small, not a business to build.

Building the P&L order by order and channel by channel, before the overhead is committed, is how we manage Target Plus for invited brands.

A0105.title: Amazon’s fee structure punishes low prices, so redesign the offer
A0105.alt: A brass hanging balance with one small tied pouch on one pan and bundled fabric sachets on the other.
A0105.ttag: Amazon’s fee structure punishes low prices, so redesign the offer | Kwontified
A0105.desc: Amazon’s fees are largely charged per unit and per click, so they eat low-priced products first. Brands should redesign packs, prices and ranges around them.
A0105.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 17, 2021.
A0105.body:
Brands usually think of Amazon’s fees as a percentage of sales. Part of them is: the referral fee is charged on the sale price. The rest works differently. Fulfillment fees depend on a product’s size and weight, not its price, and the cost of winning a sale through advertising depends on the auction, not the product.

That difference decides which products make money on Amazon. Because so much of what Amazon charges is set per unit or per click, its fees take a far larger share of a low-priced sale than a high-priced one. As those fees rise, brands should redesign the offer, through pack sizes, price points and which products go to Amazon at all, rather than absorb each increase product by product.

How the Amazon fee structure has grown

The share Amazon takes has risen for years. The Institute for Local Self-Reliance estimated that Amazon’s cut of third-party sellers’ revenue, from referral, fulfillment and advertising fees together, rose from 19% in 2014 to 30% in 2019, close to a third of every sale, in its report on Amazon’s fees.

The latest fulfillment change took effect on June 1, 2021, after Amazon postponed it from the start of the year. Fulfillment fees rose about 2% to 3% on average, and Amazon stopped adding packaging weight allowances when calculating shipping weight, SellerEngine reported.

Advertising has grown faster still. On Marketplace Pulse’s data, the ad spend needed to win an average sale rose from $6 to $7 in 2020 to $9 to $10 by June 2021, MediaPost reported.

A toll that charges every car the same

The structure matters more than the level. Think of a toll road that charges every car the same amount, whether it carries one passenger or six. For a full car, the toll per passenger is small. For a car with one person, it is large.

Amazon’s per-unit fees work the same way. A product that sells for $12 and one that sells for $36 may cost almost the same to pick, pack and ship if they are similar in size, so the fulfillment fee is a much larger share of the cheaper sale. Advertising behaves the same way: if it costs $9 in clicks to win a sale, that is three-quarters of a $12 product’s price and a quarter of a $36 product’s.

Take a brand that sells a $12 jar of spice blend. The referral fee at 15% is $1.80, the fulfillment fee is $3.50 and the product costs $3.00 to make, which leaves $3.70 before advertising. If the brand needs $4 of advertising to win each sale, it loses money on every order.

The same brand sells a three-jar set for $32. The referral fee is $4.80, fulfillment for the heavier box is $5.20 and the product costs $9.00, which leaves $13.00 before advertising. With the same $4 of advertising per sale, it keeps $9.00. The fees and advertising barely changed per order. The price they were spread across did.

Another way to see it is the advertising ceiling. The single jar can carry at most $3.70 of advertising per sale before it loses money; the set can carry $13.00. That ceiling, more than the fee itself, decides how hard each product can be advertised when click prices rise.

Low prices buy reach and give up margin

Low-priced single units reach more shoppers. They are easy to try, they appear in more searches and they win more first purchases. But each sale may lose money once per-unit fees and advertising are counted. Larger packs and higher price points earn more per order and suit fewer shoppers. Most brands can find a better balance by redesigning the offer around the fee structure, and three moves do most of the work.

Pack sizes can be set for Amazon specifically. Multipacks, bundles and larger sizes raise the price each fee is spread across. A brand can keep its single unit in stores, where shelf economics differ, and lead with a multipack on Amazon.

The low-priced single unit can stay where it earns its place: as an entry product for new customers, with a clear path to a larger pack or a subscription on the second order. Its job is acquisition, and it should be judged that way rather than on its own margin.

Some products do not belong on Amazon’s fulfillment network at all. A product too light in price and too heavy in size may make more money through the brand’s own site, shipped by the seller on Amazon, or left off the channel.

Pricing deserves the same scrutiny. A brand that holds an artificially low price on Amazon to match its own store or another retailer may be choosing exactly the price point where Amazon’s fee structure works against it. Raising a single unit’s price modestly, or moving the promotion budget to a multipack, can change the economics more than any bid adjustment.

None of this argues for leaving Amazon. For most brands it remains the largest online channel, and its fees buy real reach, fulfillment and trust. The work is in designing what you sell there to fit how Amazon charges.

The test for each product is fees and advertising together as a share of its price. Calculate it for every product on Amazon, and any product where that share is rising toward its gross margin needs a new pack size or price point before the next fee change, not after it. Designing ranges and pack sizes around Amazon’s fee structure is how we help brands manage their Amazon channels.

A0106.crumb: Zalando private label: kept small so…
A0106.title: Zalando private label: kept small so brands trust the platform
A0106.alt: A clothing rack of neutral-toned shirts with a row of orange hang tags in a bright boutique.
A0106.ttag: Zalando private label: kept small so brands trust the platform | Kwontified
A0106.desc: Zalando narrowed its own labels to essentials in 2019 and is growing its Partner Program fast. Brands can treat it as a platform, while watching basics.
A0106.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 19, 2021.
A0106.body:
Every marketplace that also sells its own products has the same conversation with the brands it wants to attract. The brand asks, in some form, whether the platform will use what it learns about the brand’s sales to make a competing product. On Amazon, the honest answer is that it might. Zalando decided in 2019 to give a different answer.

It shrank its own labels to everyday essentials, so that brands would trust it as a platform rather than see it as a rival. That choice now underpins a Partner Program growing faster than the rest of the business. Brands can commit to Zalando with less fear of private-label competition than they face on Amazon, while watching the essentials categories where Zalando’s own labels remain.

How Zalando settled on a small private label range

Zalando’s own labels began as a gap-filler. Its private label business, zLabels, was founded in 2010 to fill “blank spots” in the assortment that partner brands did not cover, co-chief executive David Schneider said in 2019, Retail Sector reported.

In March 2019, Zalando changed course. It said it would close zLabels as a separate business from April 1. Its private labels and partner brands would sit “under one roof,” and from the spring and summer 2020 season its own apparel labels would focus on everyday essentials, alongside a focused footwear and accessories range, FashionUnited reported. Its eleven private label brands, including Anna Field, Even & Odd, Pier One and Zign, would be kept for the time being and reviewed.

“Since we are committed to our platform strategy, and as we continuously onboard new brands and verticals, we decided to refine our assortment including our own labels,” Schneider said at the time, according to the same report.

The platform has grown since. In Zalando’s Partner Program, brands sell directly to Zalando’s customers. The program’s share of Fashion Store sales volume more than doubled, from 10% in 2018 to 24% in the fourth quarter of 2020, and Zalando is aiming for about half, its investor presentation shows. Partner Program sales volume grew more than 100% in the first half of 2021, while total sales volume grew 40% in the second quarter to €3.8 billion, Zalando reported.

Why a small private label range helps the platform

A marketplace’s own labels create a conflict of interest brands can see. The platform sees every brand’s sales, search terms and prices. If it also sells competing products, brands worry that data will be used against them, in what the platform chooses to make and how prominently it shows its own range.

Zalando’s choice reduces that worry. By keeping its own labels to basics, it competes least in the categories where brands invest most in design, marketing and identity. A premium sneaker brand or a fashion label considering the Partner Program can reasonably expect Zalando to grow by selling its products, not by copying them.

That trust has commercial value. Brands that trust a platform put more stock on it, share more data with it and use more of its services, such as fulfillment and marketing. Zalando’s model depends on exactly that: commissions on partner sales and fees for services, which grow as brands commit more.

The choice also cost Zalando something. Own labels typically carry better margins than products bought from brands, and a retailer that shrinks them gives up some of that margin. Zalando judged that commissions and service fees from a growing Partner Program would be worth more over time. Its recent growth suggests the bet is working, though it will take several more years of results to say for certain.

Amazon offers the contrast. It keeps building its own brands across many categories, including a grocery label, Aplenty, launched in 2021. Brands selling on Amazon have to plan for a private-label competitor in their search results. On Zalando, that risk is narrower. Amazon can still be the right choice; the difference is how much a brand should hold back when it commits there.

Where Zalando’s own labels still compete

Take a mid-priced footwear brand choosing between expanding on Amazon in Europe and joining Zalando’s Partner Program. On Amazon it would compete with other brands and possibly with Amazon’s own footwear labels. On Zalando it would compete with other brands, but Zalando’s own labels are focused on essentials. If its range is fashion-led rather than basic, the brand can commit stock to Zalando with less risk of the platform becoming a rival.

The decision should still rest on more than private-label risk. Zalando’s selectiveness, its strength in particular countries and its fulfillment and marketing services all matter, and the economics of each channel should be compared directly. Private-label exposure is one input, but for fashion-led brands it often tips a close call.

The essentials categories are different. A brand selling plain T-shirts, basic socks or simple everyday footwear will meet Zalando’s own labels on the same pages. That does not rule Zalando out, but it calls for the caution a brand would use on Amazon: a clear point of difference, pricing that holds up beside a cheaper own label and a close watch on visibility.

Zalando said in 2019 that its eleven own brands would be reviewed later. That review is the one to follow. If the labels expand beyond essentials, the trust that has helped the platform grow could weaken, and brands that committed on the strength of a narrow private-label range should revisit how much stock and spend they place there.

Weighing Zalando’s Partner Program against Amazon and other European marketplaces, private-label risk included, is part of how we manage Zalando for brands.

A0108.crumb: Three retail media metrics that show…
A0108.title: Three retail media metrics that show which strategy is winning
A0108.alt: Three round brass-rimmed blank dials stand in a row on a wooden table against a navy wall.
A0108.ttag: Three retail media metrics that show which strategy is winning | Kwontified
A0108.desc: The highest ROAS rarely marks the best retail media strategy. Marginal return, profit after ads and share of category search show which approach is winning.
A0108.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 24, 2021.
A0108.body:
Put two retail media strategies for the same brand side by side. Strategy A spends $50,000 at a return on ad spend (ROAS) of 6.0. Strategy B spends $150,000 at a ROAS of 4.0. A review that compares them on ROAS picks Strategy A, and with a 40% gross margin, Strategy A is the one that makes less money.

The ratio misleads because it is an average, and averages reward caution: the first dollars a brand spends are always its most efficient, so spending less almost always lifts ROAS. The return on the last dollar spent, profit after advertising and share of the category’s searches separate strategies far better, and they are the measures to use when choosing between approaches or between agencies.

Average ROAS is the least reliable of the retail media metrics in 2021

Comparing strategies on ROAS has become harder as click prices climb. Pacvue found that the Sponsored Products CPCs rose 36% year over year in the second quarter, and the company reported that ROAS fell 10%. Marketplace Pulse put the average advertising cost of a sale at $9 to $10 by June, up from $6 to $7 in 2020, in data covered by MediaPost.

In a market like that, a strategy can protect its ROAS simply by spending less and staying on the cheapest, most certain clicks, usually searches for the brand’s own name. Its ratio holds up in the monthly deck. Whether the business is better off is a separate question, and the ratio cannot answer it.

A higher ROAS can sit on top of a smaller profit

Take a brand whose products carry a 40% gross margin, running each strategy for one of two comparable quarters.

Strategy AStrategy B
Ad spend$50,000$150,000
ROAS6.04.0
Attributed sales$300,000$600,000
Gross profit at 40%$120,000$240,000
Profit after advertising$70,000$90,000

Strategy A wins on the ratio. Strategy B banks $20,000 more. Nothing in the bottom row is visible from the ROAS row, because ROAS describes the whole budget at once and says nothing about whether the extra spending in Strategy B earned more than it cost.

That missing question is where most strategy comparisons go wrong. A brand that cuts its budget back toward Strategy A will watch its ROAS rise and its profit fall in the same quarter, and the report it reads first will tell it the cut worked.

The reason sits in how a budget gets spent. The first dollars go to the searches most likely to convert: the brand’s own name, its best sellers, shoppers already close to buying. Each additional dollar reaches a shopper a little less certain to buy, so the return on each new slice falls while the average stays high.

The last dollar, the profit line and share of search show who is winning

Return on the last dollar asks what the final slice of the budget returned, instead of what the whole budget returned. In the example, Strategy B’s extra $100,000 over Strategy A produced $300,000 in extra sales, a return of 3.0. With a 40% margin, a sale breaks even at a ROAS of 2.5, so that extra spending made money. Had the extra $100,000 returned only 2.0, it would have lost money while the overall ROAS still looked healthy. Brands can estimate the marginal return by raising or lowering budgets in steps and measuring the change in sales.

Profit after advertising is gross profit on advertised sales minus ad spend, counted in dollars rather than as a ratio. It is the number the business keeps, and it answers the question ROAS cannot: is spending more worth it? Where the data allows, use total sales rather than attributed sales alone, so that advertising which also lifts organic sales gets credit for it.

Share of category search is the measure of position. It tracks how often the brand appears for the important non-branded searches in its category, in paid and organic slots, compared with competitors. A strategy can be profitable for a quarter while giving up ground on the searches that will matter a year later. Another can look expensive while it wins the visibility that future organic sales depend on.

When the measures disagree, the trade becomes visible

The three will not always agree, and the disagreements are the useful part. Strong profit after advertising with a falling share of search means a strategy is harvesting a position it is not renewing. A rising share of search with negative profit after advertising means a strategy is buying ground the business may not be able to afford. Which of those is acceptable depends on the brand’s goals for the year, but at least the choice is on the table rather than hidden inside a ratio.

None of this requires new tools. A budget step test can run on any campaign: change spend for a few weeks and compare results with a similar period. Profit after advertising needs product margins, which finance already has. Share of search can be tracked from search-term reports and periodic checks of the category’s top results.

What changes is the incentive. A team that reports ROAS alone gets pushed toward caution, because caution protects the ratio. A team that reports the last dollar, the profit line and share of search gets pushed toward the spending that grows the business and away from the spending that does not.

The practical test is short. Work out each product’s break-even ROAS from its margin, and hold every extra dollar of spend to that line rather than to the account average. When the average still looks healthy but the last dollar is returning less than break-even, the budget has grown past what the market will pay back, and comparing strategies on those three numbers is how we run retail media for brands.

A0110.crumb: Shopping inside TikTok: what the Shopify…
A0110.title: Shopping inside TikTok: what the Shopify test means for brands
A0110.alt: A smartphone in a ring light faces a small cardboard model storefront on a wooden desk.
A0110.ttag: Shopping inside TikTok: what the Shopify test means for brands | Kwontified
A0110.desc: TikTok’s Shopify pilot adds a shopping tab and product links. It suits brands whose products already spread on TikTok and who can make content to match.
A0110.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 26, 2021.
A0110.body:
Some products travel on TikTok because they are easy to show in a few seconds: a visible before and after, a satisfying demonstration, an unexpected use. Until now, a viewer who wanted one of them had to leave the app and go looking. The Shopify pilot announced on August 24 starts to close that gap, by putting a shopping tab on brand profiles and letting brands tag products in their videos.

That makes TikTok shopping a real channel decision, though not an equal one across brands. It favors brands whose products already spread on the app and whose content, checkout and stock can keep pace with that attention. Readiness, rather than the novelty of the feature, should decide when a brand joins.

What TikTok shopping looks like in the Shopify pilot

The mechanics are simple. Shopify merchants with a TikTok For Business account can sync their product catalogs to a shopping tab on their TikTok profile, a kind of mini-storefront, and add product links to organic posts, according to Shopify. The pilot is open to merchants in the US and UK, with Canada to follow.

The purchase itself still happens on the brand’s own website. TikTok plans to test the features with hundreds of Shopify merchants before a wider launch. Bloomberg had reported earlier in the year that TikTok was preparing a broader push into e-commerce, including product links, a commission program and livestreamed shopping, TechCrunch noted.

Merchants were already moving in this direction: Shopify said installs across its social commerce channels rose 76% from February 2020 to February 2021. For TikTok, the pilot signals an intent to turn the product discovery that already happens on its app into a shopping channel.

The brands that fit are the ones TikTok already talks about

For most marketing leaders, the decision will be framed as whether to join. A more useful framing starts with the product and whether it already moves on the app. If people are already posting about your products, or about products like yours, the pilot gives that attention somewhere to land. If they are not, a shopping tab will not create interest on its own.

Content is the next test, and it asks a brand to work in a way its campaign calendar may not allow. TikTok rewards videos that feel native to the app: quick, personal, often filmed on a phone and frequently made with creators rather than an agency. A brand whose creative calendar is built around a few glossy campaigns a year may struggle to post often enough, and in the right voice, to make a shopping tab worth visiting. A storefront on a profile only earns visits when a steady stream of videos keeps pointing people to it.

Then there is the page the shopper lands on. Someone arriving from a short video on a phone has little patience. The product page needs to answer the obvious questions at a glance, load fast and keep checkout short. A brand whose site is slow on mobile will lose most of the people the pilot sends it.

Brands with traction on the app but weak content or checkout have the most to gain from preparing now, because the demand is already there and only the brand’s readiness is missing. Brands with no traction can reasonably watch and wait.

Preparing even while you wait

Take two skincare brands with similar products, both selling through Shopify and Amazon, both with customers posting results. One joins the pilot, works with a handful of creators on product-tagged videos and fixes its mobile product pages. The other decides to wait.

When TikTok widens its shopping features, the first brand already knows which products, creators and video styles work. The second starts from nothing. The products were never the difference between them; the months of practice with creators, formats and page speed were.

Waiting does not have to mean standing still. A brand can start posting on TikTok to learn what its audience responds to, identify the creators who already talk about its category and improve its mobile product pages, which pays off whatever channel the traffic comes from.

Stock deserves a plan of its own. Attention on TikTok can arrive suddenly, and a product that catches on can sell out in days. A brand joining the pilot should know how quickly it can restock its likeliest candidates and should avoid tagging products it cannot replenish. A wave of new shoppers sent to an out-of-stock page wastes the moment and the creator’s goodwill.

Ownership is harder to see. TikTok sits awkwardly between social media, e-commerce and brand marketing, and the pilot touches all three. The social team may own the account and the e-commerce team the storefront, leaving nobody responsible for the moment a video sells through. Deciding who owns the pilot, who approves creator content and who watches the sales and stock it affects should happen before the first tagged video goes live.

Brands that sell mainly through Amazon should pay attention too. Some shoppers who discover a product on TikTok go on to search for it on Amazon, so a TikTok presence can raise Amazon sales for a brand that never uses the shopping tab. That spillover is a reason to read TikTok activity and Amazon branded search side by side.

How fast TikTok widens the pilot will settle the timing. If it moves beyond Shopify, or brings checkout inside the app, the case for preparing becomes a case for acting, and leadership has to ask whether anyone inside the company owns the moment between a video and a sale. Answering it alongside the marketplace plan is how we run social commerce for brands.

A0111.title: Run Amazon on seven performance dimensions, not just the ads
A0111.alt: Vintage brass measuring tools, including a compass, scale, hourglass, caliper, gauge and level, on a wooden table.
A0111.ttag: Run Amazon on seven performance dimensions, not just the ads | Kwontified
A0111.desc: Most Amazon reviews focus on ads because that data is easiest to see. Seven dimensions, from traffic to account health, show where results are won or lost.
A0111.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 31, 2021.
A0111.body:
Take a brand whose monthly Amazon review shows return on ad spend (ROAS) falling from 4.0 to 3.2. The team spends the meeting cutting bids, but the problem was never in the ads. A reseller had been undercutting the brand on its best-selling product, and its Buy Box share had fallen from 95% to 70%. Roughly a quarter of its ad clicks were landing on a page where its own offer was not the one shoppers saw.

Amazon results are decided across seven dimensions: traffic, conversion, price and the Buy Box, availability, advertising, content and reviews, and account health. Any one of them can cap the rest. Most Amazon reviews still spend their time on advertising, because that is where the data is clearest. A better review starts with whichever dimension is furthest from target, which is often not the one with the best data.

The seven Amazon performance dimensions, and where each is under pressure

Traffic is how many shoppers reach the brand’s product pages, from search, advertising and outside sources. Conversion is the share of those visits that become orders, and it depends on price, images, copy, reviews and the delivery promise. Content and reviews cover the quality of listings, images and A+ content, along with the rating and the number of reviews. These three move together: better content lifts conversion, and higher conversion makes every visit worth more.

Price and the Buy Box decide whether the brand’s own offer is the one a shopper buys. Roughly 80% of all Amazon sales pass through the Buy Box, the House antitrust subcommittee estimated, CNBC reported, so losing it to another seller loses most of the sale.

Availability is whether products are in stock and eligible for Prime, and it has become harder to manage in 2021. Amazon now sets storage limits by storage type and applies an Inventory Performance Index threshold of 500 from July 1, ChannelX reported.

Advertising covers spend, efficiency and share of category search. Its costs have climbed sharply: the average click cost $1.20 by June, up 29% from the start of the year, according to Marketplace Pulse data cited by MediaPost.

Account health covers policy compliance, customer service metrics and product safety, and the stakes there are rising. From September 1, Amazon will pay customers directly for property damage and injury claims under $1,000 involving products sold on its site. It may also step in on larger claims when a seller is unresponsive or rejects a claim, CNN reported.

Why reviews keep looking under the streetlight

There is an old story about a man searching for his keys under a streetlight. Asked whether he dropped them there, he says no, he dropped them in the dark, but the light is better here.

Amazon reviews drift the same way, and for an understandable reason. Advertising is where the light is. The console shows spend, clicks, sales and ROAS by day and by keyword, so the meeting gravitates there, and the team can always find a bid to change. Activity feels like control.

Meanwhile the dimension limiting results may sit in the dark. It might be a top product out of stock for nine days in the previous month, a Buy Box lost to a reseller on weekends, or a rating that slipped from 4.4 to 4.1 after a packaging change.

None of those shows up cleanly in an advertising report. They show up as weaker ad results, which is why the team in the opening example cut bids. Cutting bids treated the symptom. Fixing the reseller problem would have treated the cause. Advertising is also the dimension a brand can change fastest, which makes it the natural place to act even when it is the wrong place to look.

A one-page scorecard puts all seven in the light

The scorecard does not need to be complicated. Each dimension gets one or two measures, a target and a simple status, and some of them bring other teams into the room.

DimensionMeasures to trackWho joins the review
TrafficSessions on top products, and their trend
ConversionOrder rate on those sessions
Price and Buy BoxBuy Box share on top products; price gaps against other sellersSales and finance
AvailabilityIn-stock rate on top products; IPI scoreSupply chain
AdvertisingProfit after advertising; share of category search
Content and reviewsAverage rating and review count on top products; listing completeness
Account healthOpen policy issues; customer service metrics; safety or compliance flagsRegulatory or legal

Keep the scorecard to top products at first. For most brands a small share of products produces most of the sales, and problems there matter most. Once it is routine for the top products, it can widen.

Review it weekly, starting with whichever dimension is furthest from target. In most months one or two dimensions are constraining the rest, and fixing them does more than any amount of tuning elsewhere. The right column matters as much as the measures: a review that covers all seven brings supply chain, finance and compliance into the conversation before a problem in one area shows up as a decline in another.

Advertising keeps its place on the scorecard. It often amplifies the other dimensions, but its results depend on every other dimension being in order. An advertising team asked to fix a problem that sits in availability or price will spend money without solving anything, and the weekly review is where that gets caught or missed.

So the test is the order of the agenda. If your weekly Amazon review opens with advertising every week, whatever changed, it is looking where the light is; open it instead with the dimension furthest from target, which is how we run Amazon channels for brands.

A0112.crumb: Pet on Amazon 2021: the second order…
A0112.title: Pet on Amazon 2021: the second order matters more than the first
A0112.alt: Two kraft paper delivery bags beside a pale yellow cottage door framed by ivy and potted plants.
A0112.ttag: Pet on Amazon 2021: the second order matters more than the first | Kwontified
A0112.desc: Pet spending passed $100 billion in 2020 and more of it moved online. On Amazon, the value of a pet brand lies in the repeat order, so plan for the second sale.
A0112.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 2, 2021.
A0112.body:
Every few weeks, someone in a pet household notices the food bag is getting light and reorders the same brand without a second thought. That habit is the prize in pet on Amazon. A first sale often barely covers what it cost to win; the repeat orders behind it are where a pet brand earns its money.

So pet brands should plan their Amazon business around keeping customers, through Subscribe and Save, dependable availability and strong reviews. What they spend to win a new household should be judged against the orders that household is likely to place over the following years.

Pet on Amazon in 2021: a bigger category, more of it online

The category grew sharply through the pandemic. US pet industry sales reached a record $103.6 billion in 2020, up 6.7% from $97.1 billion in 2019, according to the American Pet Products Association, as Supermarket News reported. Food and treats accounted for $42 billion, up 9.7%, and the association projected 5.8% growth for 2021.

More of that spending moved online. In the same report, 47% of pet owners said they had increased how often they bought pet products online, the Private Label Manufacturers Association noted.

The leading online pet specialist shows what that habit is worth across a whole business. Chewy’s second-quarter net sales rose 26.8% to $2.16 billion, with 20.1 million active customers, up 21%, and net sales per active customer of $404 over the prior four quarters, according to its results. Those are the numbers of a company built on people buying the same things again. For a brand selling through Amazon rather than through its own pet store, the same pattern is available, but only to brands that plan for it.

What one household is worth after the first bag

Take a dog owner who searches Amazon for grain-free dog food and buys a $50 bag from a brand they have not tried before. The brand spent $15 in advertising to win that order. On the first sale alone, after product cost, fees and advertising, it may barely break even, or lose money.

Now follow that owner forward. If the dog likes the food, the household buys the same bag about every six weeks, roughly eight times a year. Over two years, that first click becomes about sixteen orders and $800 in sales. With Subscribe and Save set up, most of those orders arrive without another advertising click at all.

The value, then, sits in the orders that follow the first $50, and in how few of them need to be paid for again. A brand that judges its advertising on the first order will underspend on new customers. A brand that judges it on repeat value can afford to compete for them.

The same arithmetic changes how the advertising team should read its own reports. Seen against one $50 bag, $15 looks steep. Seen against $800 over two years, it is a small part of what the household will spend. The question that matters is how many of the households the ads win actually stay, and that answer lives in reorder data rather than in the ad console.

That value is fragile, and it depends on operations more than on media. Stock comes first. A pet owner whose usual food is unavailable will buy something else, and the rival brand gets its chance to become the habit. In pet, a stockout can cost the whole relationship along with the sale.

Reviews come close behind. Pet owners read them carefully, especially for food, where concerns about ingredients and health are common, and a slip in rating can stop new customers before they start. And the subscription has to work. Subscribe and Save gives the customer a discount and the brand a predictable repeat order. A brand that does not offer it, or lets subscribed products run out, gives up the most valuable part of the relationship.

Planning the Amazon business around the customers who come back

Retention belongs at the start of the plan rather than the end. Advertising should be judged on the expected value of a new customer instead of the first order: a cost per new customer that looks expensive against a $50 sale may be cheap against two years of orders. The discipline is in estimating that repeat value honestly from the brand’s own data rather than guessing at it.

Inventory deserves more attention in pet than in most categories. Bulky, heavy products are expensive to store, and Amazon’s storage limits make extra stock harder to hold. Replenishment plans should protect subscribed and repeat customers first, because those are the sales a stockout puts most at risk.

The product mix carries roles as well. Consumables such as food, treats and litter drive the repeat orders; durable items such as beds, crates and toys are bought less often. A brand that sells both can use the durables to win new households and the consumables to keep them, and should judge each line on the job it does.

Chewy also sets the expectations many pet owners bring to Amazon: fast delivery, easy repeat ordering and good service. Amazon competes on the same terms, so a brand’s listings, subscription offers and customer service there have to meet that standard.

The number that tells a pet brand whether all this is working is the repeat purchase rate. If a high share of new customers order again within two months, acquisition spending is building a durable business. If few do, the problem probably lies in the product fit, the price or availability rather than the advertising, and planning the Amazon channel around that second order is how we manage pet brands on Amazon.

A0114.title: Diversifying beyond Amazon with Instagram: own the customer
A0114.alt: A wrapped parcel on the step of a dark blue front door, with a glowing phone on a wooden bench beside it.
A0114.ttag: Diversifying beyond Amazon with Instagram: own the customer | Kwontified
A0114.desc: Brands diversifying beyond Amazon often judge Instagram on its sales. Its value as a hedge is the customer relationship and demand it builds outside Amazon.
A0114.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 7, 2021.
A0114.body:
In May, Amazon removed the listings of accessory makers Aukey and Mpow. On June 16 it confirmed it had removed RavPower’s products as well, Android Authority reported, and RavPower’s parent company, Sunvalley, disclosed in June that three of its brands had been suspended, ABS-CBN reported. Those removals followed alleged review abuse, but the arithmetic they expose applies to every brand: when one channel holds most of the sales, one decision by that channel can remove them overnight.

Brands that want a hedge often turn to Instagram and then judge it on the sales it closes. On that measure it usually disappoints, because its checkout sales are small next to Amazon’s. The hedge lies elsewhere. Instagram can build an audience and customer records that sit outside Amazon’s control, and it should be judged on those, with checkout revenue counted as a bonus.

Diversifying beyond Amazon got more urgent in 2021

Staying concentrated is also getting more expensive. Amazon’s cut of third-party sellers’ revenue rose from 19% in 2014 to 30% in 2019, the Institute for Local Self-Reliance estimated in its report on Amazon’s fees, and advertising costs have climbed sharply since.

Instagram, meanwhile, has become a real shopping surface. Facebook said in June that its Shops on Facebook and Instagram had more than 300 million monthly visitors and over 1.2 million monthly active Shops, and that it would begin testing visual search on Instagram, Exchange4media reported.

Amazon rents you shoppers; Instagram can give you customers

On Amazon, a brand rents access to shoppers. Amazon owns the customer relationship: it controls the data, the communication and, in the end, whether the brand can sell there at all. A brand with a million Amazon customers cannot email one of them.

Instagram works differently. Followers can be reached directly with every post. Customers who buy through the brand’s own site, linked from Instagram, become the brand’s customers, with their contact details and purchase history. Even shoppers who buy through Instagram checkout sit closer to the brand than an Amazon buyer does.

That relationship is what reduces dependence. If Amazon suspended a brand tomorrow, its Amazon sales would stop. Its Instagram audience, email list and site customers would still be there, and could be pointed to its own site or another retailer.

Take two brands that each sell $5 million a year on Amazon and use Instagram in different ways.

Brand oneBrand two
Amazon sales a year$5 million$5 million
Instagram checkout sales$200,000$100,000
Email list built through Instagram80,000 customers
Own-site sales a year$1 million

Judged on checkout, brand one is winning. Now suppose Amazon became unavailable to both for three months. Brand one would have almost nothing to fall back on. Brand two would keep a meaningful business running, because the customers it gathered on Instagram can still hear from it and buy from it.

It is easy to see why teams reach for checkout revenue anyway. It is the one Instagram number that looks like an Amazon number: sales, in dollars, in a report finance already reads. Set side by side, the comparison usually flatters Amazon, and the Instagram budget becomes the first thing cut in a slow month.

The trouble is that the two numbers measure different assets. Amazon sales measure demand Amazon lets the brand serve. A customer record measures demand the brand can reach again on its own terms, through email, its own site or another retailer, which is what a hedge is supposed to provide.

Instagram also tends to feed Amazon itself. Some shoppers who find a brand there later search for it on Amazon, so a strong Instagram presence can raise Amazon sales even when Instagram’s own sales look small. That makes the channels complementary, and it is one more reason checkout revenue understates what the channel does.

Judge Instagram on the customers it moves outside Amazon

The owned audience has to be built on purpose. Instagram can grow followers, email subscribers and site customers, especially with offers that reward people for joining the brand’s own list, and those numbers deserve a monthly line in the report.

Where buyers end up matters as much. Instagram checkout is convenient, but it carries a selling fee, set at 5% per shipment when Facebook introduced it. Sending buyers to the brand’s own site, where the brand owns the customer record, may be worth more over time even when it converts slightly less well.

The scorecard follows from that: audience growth, customers acquired into owned channels, and the share of total sales that would survive a disruption on Amazon. Checkout revenue belongs on it as one line, not the headline.

Content is the cost of entry. An owned audience on Instagram depends on posting regularly, working with creators and giving followers a reason to join the list. That work is closer to insurance than to a campaign, and budgeting it as a long-term investment in resilience, rather than expecting it to pay back within a quarter, keeps it from being cut at the first slow month.

None of this argues for pulling back from Amazon. It remains the largest channel by far for most brands. Diversifying is about making sure the business would survive if that channel faltered, and about knowing, in numbers, how much of it would.

The number that tells you whether it is working is the share of revenue from customers you can reach directly. If it rises, dependence on Amazon is falling, whatever Instagram’s checkout figures say, and growing that share alongside the marketplace business is how we build channels beyond Amazon for brands.

A0117.crumb: Retail media needs both the spreadsheet…
A0117.title: Retail media needs both the spreadsheet and the strategist
A0117.alt: An open blank notebook and pencil beside a wooden chessboard on a rustic table in warm window light.
A0117.ttag: Retail media needs both the spreadsheet and the strategist | Kwontified
A0117.desc: Automation now handles much of Amazon’s bidding, but it optimizes toward goals someone else sets. Retail media needs analysts and strategists working as one.
A0117.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 9, 2021.
A0117.body:
Take the weekly retail media review at a brand that has automated most of its bidding. The meeting moves fast. Bids adjusted themselves overnight, rules paused the keywords that wasted money, software shifted budget between campaigns, and the dashboard shows the account on target. Almost nobody in the room asks whether the target is still the right one.

That question has become the important one. Automated systems optimize toward whatever goals and constraints they are given, and the choice of those goals now shapes results more than any individual bid. Retail media strategy needs the analytical discipline to run the machinery well and the judgment to point it somewhere useful, with the two working together rather than one after the other.

Retail media strategy moved from setting bids to setting goals

The change came in steps. In January 2019, Amazon introduced new bidding options for Sponsored Products, including dynamic bidding, which adjusts bids in real time based on how likely a click is to lead to a sale, and bid adjustments by placement, Amazon said. From then on, Amazon itself was making bid decisions at the moment of each auction, and third-party tools followed with rules and algorithms of their own.

The gains were real. Bids that once took hours of manual review now update continuously, and well-built rules catch wasted spend faster than any person could. But the shift also changed how some brands thought about the job. Retail media started to look like a technical task: find a good tool and a good analyst, and let them run it.

The stakes of running it well have kept rising. Pacvue reported Sponsored Products CPCs rose 36% year over year during the second quarter of 2021, in its quarterly CPC report. When every click costs more, a mistake in the machinery costs more too.

What the spreadsheet cannot decide

The analytical side, the spreadsheet in shorthand, does essential work. It sets up campaigns cleanly, keeps keywords and negative keywords organized, checks that automated bids behave as intended, finds waste and measures results accurately. A program without that discipline leaks money, however good its strategy.

But automation and analysis answer the question “how do we hit this target efficiently?” They do not answer “what target should we be hitting?”

That second question involves judgments no algorithm makes on its own. Which products to push in a given quarter and which to protect. Whether to accept a lower return to win customers in a growing category, or hold efficiency while a competitor overspends. How advertising should change when a best-seller is about to run short, or when a new product needs reviews before it can convert. How Amazon advertising fits with what the brand is doing on Walmart, on its own site and in stores.

Left without answers, automated systems default to whatever is easiest to measure, usually a return on ad spend target. They will hit it faithfully, by spending on the brand’s own name and its best-sellers, while the opportunities that need judgment go untouched. A return target is the easiest goal to write down and the easiest to defend in a review, which is why it becomes the default. It says nothing about stock, launches or competitors, because those facts live in other teams’ systems and other teams’ meetings.

Take a brand whose software is set to hold a return on ad spend of 5.0, and does, quarter after quarter. A strategist looking at the category sees that a new product line is gaining share in searches where the brand barely appears, and that the brand’s main product will be short of stock for six weeks in November. The right move is to lower the target for the new line, shift budget away from the constrained product before the shortage and accept a lower blended return for a quarter. The software would never make that decision on its own. Once told to, it would carry it out perfectly.

Putting the strategist inside the weekly rhythm

Most brands organize this work in sequence: a strategist sets goals once a quarter, and analysts run the machinery in between. That gap is where value leaks, because stock, competitors and categories change weekly while the goals stay frozen.

Closing it starts with the agenda. Stock positions, competitor moves, new products and goals by product belong on the weekly review next to bids and spend, so the strategic questions get asked at the same cadence as the tactical ones.

It also depends on what each side understands about the other. Analysts who know the strategy well enough can flag when the machinery is optimizing toward the wrong thing; the best of them notice when hitting the target no longer serves the business. Strategists who understand the machinery can turn their decisions into settings instead of leaving them on slides.

Agencies and in-house teams face the same test. A team that reports only the numbers its software produces, however good they look, is supplying the spreadsheet. A team that can explain why the targets sit where they do, and when they should move, is supplying the strategy as well. A brand choosing a partner should ask for both and ask to see examples of each.

A leadership team needs to know how long its automated systems have run on the same goals while its products, stock and category moved underneath them. If the answer is months, the spreadsheet is running without the strategist, and keeping the two in one weekly conversation is how we manage retail media for brands.

A0118.title: Walmart’s private brands decide where marketplace sellers can win
A0118.alt: Blue store shelving stocked with plain boxes, glass jars and canisters in a bright, sparse retail space.
A0118.ttag: Walmart’s private brands decide where marketplace sellers can win | Kwontified
A0118.desc: Walmart’s private brands hold the low-price end of many categories. Marketplace sellers win by offering what Walmart’s own range does not, not by undercutting.
A0118.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 14, 2021.
A0118.body:
Search Walmart.com for paper towels, basic kitchen tools or pantry staples and a Great Value or other Walmart brand option will usually sit at the value end of the page. Every marketplace seller in that category is priced against it, whether the seller planned for it or not.

That makes Walmart’s private brands the floor of the price range in many everyday categories, set by the company that also runs the search page. A seller can fight on that floor or build above and beside it. The numbers lean heavily toward the second choice: the strongest Walmart marketplace businesses sit in the gaps Walmart’s own range leaves.

How large Walmart private brands are, and how fast the marketplace is growing

Walmart does not report its private brand sales regularly. In February 2020, chief executive Doug McMillon said 18 of its private brands each brought in more than $1 billion in sales, and that the largest, Great Value, did more than $27 billion, Modern Retail reported. The same report noted that Walmart has been working with celebrity partners and building internal teams to make some private lines more fashionable, including a crafts brand launched in May 2021.

The marketplace around those brands is expanding at the same time. In its second-quarter results, Walmart said it had added thousands of new marketplace sellers, that US e-commerce sales grew 6% and 103% on a two-year basis, and that US advertising sales nearly doubled, according to its release.

Walmart also polices price on its marketplace. It can remove a listing if an identical item is cheaper at other retailers, including on the seller’s own site, Modern Retail reported.

Undercutting a retailer’s own brand rarely pays

A seller that chooses to compete on price is up against a retailer that controls the shelf, the search results and its own margins, and that operates at a scale no seller can match. Winning that contest usually means giving up margin, and Walmart can respond whenever it chooses, for example by promoting its own item.

The other route is to sell something Walmart’s range does not: a premium version, a specialized product, a recognized brand, a bundle or size Walmart does not carry, or a category where its private brands are thin. There the seller is not fighting the price floor at all. It is filling a space above or beside it.

Both routes have a case. Price competition can move volume quickly in a category with heavy search traffic, and a differentiated product may face a smaller pool of shoppers. But the economics separate quickly once Walmart’s own brand is on the page.

Take two sellers entering Walmart’s marketplace in kitchen storage. One sells plain plastic food containers at $12 a set, close to a Walmart private brand set at $10. It wins some sales by cutting its price to $10, which leaves almost no margin, and loses them whenever Walmart promotes its own set. The other sells glass containers with bamboo lids at $34, a product Walmart’s own brands do not offer. It faces fewer direct competitors on the page, holds its price and builds reviews that compound.

Both sell on the same marketplace to the same shoppers. Only the second has a business that does not depend on Walmart’s pricing decisions.

The difference is margin. At $10, the plastic set earns almost nothing per order. At $34, the glass set has room to pay for advertising, reviews and the occasional return. That is why the numbers lean so clearly one way.

Building a Walmart business in the gaps

The work starts before any listing goes live, with a map of where Walmart’s own brands appear. Searching the terms a brand’s products compete on, and noting which Walmart brands show up, at what prices and how prominently, sorts categories quickly. Those crowded with private brands at low prices are hard places to build. Those where Walmart’s range is absent or thin are easier.

The launch assortment should follow the map. A brand with both basic and premium lines may do better leading with the premium line on Walmart’s marketplace, even if the basic line sells best on Amazon, because the premium line sits furthest from the floor.

Price parity shapes the decision too. Because a seller cannot hold a higher price on Walmart than elsewhere for the same item, a product that has to match the lowest price on the page drags its price down everywhere. Products positioned clearly above the private brand range are less exposed to that pressure.

Advertising should follow the same logic. Walmart’s growing advertising business lets sellers buy visibility on search pages, but bidding on generic terms where a Walmart brand already sits at the top at a lower price often buys clicks that do not convert. Sellers usually get more from terms that describe what makes their product different, where shoppers are already looking past the basic option.

Walmart’s growth still helps sellers who choose well. More marketplace sellers and a fast-growing ad business mean more competition for attention, but also more shoppers coming to Walmart.com to search beyond groceries, and the sellers who benefit most will offer something those shoppers cannot find in Walmart’s range.

The risk to track is where Walmart takes its private brands next. The push into more fashionable lines suggests the gaps may narrow in some categories. If a category can only be won by matching a Walmart brand’s price, it is the wrong category for a seller, and building the assortment around where Walmart leaves room is how we manage Walmart Marketplace for brands.

A0119.crumb: Zalando Marketing Services: buy the data…
A0119.title: Zalando Marketing Services: buy the data to answer a question
A0119.alt: A brass magnifying glass resting on an index card atop an open wooden card catalog drawer.
A0119.ttag: Zalando Marketing Services: buy the data to answer a question | Kwontified
A0119.desc: Zalando sells consumer insights and marketing through Zalando Marketing Services. Brands should buy it to answer specific questions, not as a general add-on.
A0119.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 16, 2021.
A0119.body:
The proposal often looks modest on paper: a package of consumer insights, a campaign on Zalando, a line in the European marketing budget. The debate it starts in a leadership meeting is often framed as whether Zalando’s data is worth the money. That framing is the mistake. Through Zalando Marketing Services, Zalando sells what tens of millions of European fashion shoppers search for and buy, and the data can show a brand things its own sales reports cannot. Its value depends entirely on the decision it is bought to settle.

The better question for the room is what the brand would do differently with the answer. A brand that starts there buys Zalando’s insights and media to close a specific choice, and treats a general, standing subscription with suspicion, because a report without a decision behind it rarely changes a plan.

What Zalando Marketing Services sells

Zalando has described its data ambitions for some time. In early 2020, it said it was building Europe’s leading fashion data platform, offering detailed customer and competitive insights and data-driven marketing to brands, according to its investor presentation.

Zalando’s marketing business is growing quickly: Zalando Marketing Services revenue reached 1.5% of Zalando’s sales volume in the fourth quarter of 2020, up from 0.7% in 2018, and Zalando’s long-term target is 3% to 4%, according to a later investor presentation. Zalando reported 44.5 million active customers in its first-half 2021 results, in its media presentation.

The offer has two halves. One is insight: analysis of Zalando’s customer data showing a brand how it performs, who buys it and how it compares with peers. The other is media: advertising and campaigns on Zalando and beyond, targeted using that data. Read as a retailer’s choice, it is Zalando turning the view it has of every brand on its platform into something those brands pay for.

What Zalando can see that the brand cannot

A brand selling on Zalando knows its own sales, returns and stock. Zalando knows which other brands those same customers buy, what they searched for before buying, which sizes and styles they returned, and how the brand’s customers differ from the category as a whole. That wider view can be valuable, but only when it bears on a real choice.

Targeting is the clearest case. A brand trying to reach a new group, younger shoppers or a different price tier, can use Zalando’s data to see who already buys similar brands and how they shop, and use its media to reach them directly.

A brand that is losing ground is another case. When its sales on Zalando are flat while its category grows, insight into which competitors its customers are switching to, and why, can point to the problem faster than guesswork.

Expansion is the third kind of decision the data serves well. Zalando had around 45 million active customers in 23 European countries as of August 2021, according to its investor factbook. A brand weighing a new market can learn how its category and similar brands perform there before committing stock.

The media side needs the same discipline. Advertising on Zalando reaches shoppers who are already browsing fashion, which can make it efficient, but it should be measured against what the brand would have sold without it. A campaign shown mostly to customers who already buy the brand may look strong in Zalando’s reports while adding little. Asking for results split between new and existing customers, and comparing periods with and without the campaign, keeps the spending honest.

A request with no decision attached, such as a general wish to “understand our customer better,” tends to produce an interesting report that changes nothing.

Two brands, the same budget, different answers

Take two outdoor clothing brands that each spend €50,000 with Zalando Marketing Services in a season. One buys a general insight package and a broad awareness campaign. It receives a detailed report on its customers and a lift in visibility, but nothing in its plans changes, and it cannot tell whether the campaign paid back.

The other starts with a decision: whether to push its premium jacket line in the Nordic countries. It buys insight on how premium outerwear performs there and who buys it, then a targeted campaign to those shoppers, with sales by country measured before and after. It learns that the opportunity is real in two countries and weak in a third, and adjusts its stock accordingly. Both spent the same. Only one of them bought an answer.

Timing decides much of the value. Insight bought before a decision can shape it; insight bought afterwards mostly explains what already happened. A brand planning its Zalando season should schedule any data work early enough for the findings to change stock orders, campaign plans and pricing.

The data’s limits matter as well. It describes Zalando’s customers, not the whole market, and it reflects Zalando’s own view of performance. It is strongest for decisions about selling on Zalando and in markets where Zalando is large, and it should be checked against other sources for anything beyond that.

How Zalando packages the offer as the business moves toward its 3% to 4% target will shape how easy this discipline is. More self-service tools would make it simpler to buy a specific answer, and the options worth choosing are the ones that tie spending to measurable results. Until then, leadership’s task is to ask which decision this season the data would change. Deciding which of Zalando’s services earn their cost is how we advise brands that sell through Zalando.
