A0121.title: Amazon traffic means nothing without conversion
A0121.alt: An empty old shop with a vintage cash register on a wooden counter and dusty footprints leading to an open door.
A0121.ttag: Amazon traffic means nothing without conversion | Kwontified
A0121.desc: With Amazon clicks at $1.20, each point of conversion is worth more than extra traffic. Fix the listing before buying visits that cost more than they earn.
A0121.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 21, 2021.
A0121.body:
Divide two Marketplace Pulse figures and a useful number falls out. An average Amazon ad click cost $1.20 by June, and the average advertising cost of a sale was $9 to $10, which means roughly one advertised click in eight became an order. That ratio, the conversion rate, sets the price of every sale a brand buys.

When brands want more sales on Amazon, they usually reach for traffic: higher bids, bigger budgets, new keywords. Traffic is only half of the calculation. With clicks this expensive, how many visits become orders matters as much as how many visits a brand pays for, and a brand should fix conversion before it scales traffic.

Amazon traffic and conversion both got pricier in 2021

The click itself climbed fast. That $1.20 average was 29% above the level at the start of the year, and the $9 to $10 cost of a sale compared with $6 to $7 in 2020, on Marketplace Pulse data cited by MediaPost. Pacvue measured the second-quarter rise in Sponsored Products CPCs at 36% against a year earlier, in its CPC report.

Those rises land on every brand, but they do not land equally. A brand’s cost per sale depends on what it pays per click and on how well its listings turn those clicks into orders, and only the second half is under its control.

Cost per sale is the click price divided by conversion

The formula is short: cost per sale equals cost per click divided by conversion rate. Hold the click at $1.20 and watch what conversion does.

Ad clicks that become ordersAd cost per sale at $1.20 a click
One in ten$12
One in eight$9.60
One in fifteen$18

The click price is identical in every row. The only thing that changes is how well the listing turns a visit into an order.

Take a brand selling a $40 product with a margin, before advertising, of $14. Its listing converts 8% of ad clicks, so at $1.20 a click each advertised sale costs $15. The brand loses $1 on every advertised order.

The team wants growth, so it doubles the budget. Traffic doubles, sales double and so do the losses, because every extra sale still costs the same $15. More traffic bought more of the same problem.

Suppose instead the brand spends a month on the listing. It adds better images, rewrites the title and bullets around what shoppers search for, answers common questions and works on its reviews. Conversion rises to 12%. At the same $1.20 a click, each advertised sale now costs $10, leaving $4 of margin per order. Now doubling the budget doubles the profit.

The belief that more traffic means more sales is not wrong, which is why it survives. It just leaves out the price. More traffic means more sales at a cost that conversion sets, and at a weak conversion rate it means more loss.

The same arithmetic explains why rising click prices hurt some brands far more than others. A 29% rise in the price of a click raises the cost of a sale by 29% for every brand. But a brand converting at 15% starts from a much lower cost per sale than one converting at 7%, and it has more room to absorb the increase before its margin runs out.

What moves conversion, and the order to fix it in

Conversion on Amazon depends on a short list of things a brand controls. Price comes first: a product priced above comparable options, or one whose Buy Box goes to another seller, converts poorly however much traffic it gets. Then the page itself. Shoppers decide quickly, and the main image, the title and the first lines of the bullets carry most of the weight. The rating and the number of reviews strongly affect whether a shopper buys, especially against competitors with more of both.

Availability and delivery count too. Products that are out of stock, or show a slow delivery date, lose sales even when shoppers want them. And traffic quality matters: clicks from searches that do not match the product convert poorly, so cutting irrelevant keywords raises conversion by removing visitors who were never likely to buy.

Measuring conversion takes reports a brand already has. Amazon’s advertising reports show orders per click for each campaign and keyword, and Seller Central’s business reports show the share of sessions that became orders for each product. Comparing the two shows whether a problem sits in the advertising, such as the wrong keywords, or in the listing, which converts poorly whatever the source of the visit.

The order of work follows from that: measure conversion by product and by keyword, fix the listings and keywords with the weakest rates, and only then raise budgets on products whose conversion makes each sale profitable. Conversion also helps organic results, because Amazon tends to reward listings that turn visits into sales, so a better-converting listing often gains organic visibility and leans less on paid traffic over time.

The holiday calendar makes the order of work more urgent. Clicks are usually most expensive in the weeks around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, when competition for shoppers peaks. A brand that improves conversion in September and October enters that period with a lower cost per sale on every click it buys, while a brand that waits will pay peak prices for traffic its listings cannot convert.

Before raising any product’s budget, divide its cost per click by its conversion rate and set the answer against its margin. If conversion is falling while budgets rise, the brand is buying traffic its listings cannot use, and planning conversion and traffic together is how we manage Amazon for brands.

A0123.crumb: Mercado Pago and Mercado Ads belong in…
A0123.title: Mercado Pago and Mercado Ads belong in every Mercado Libre plan
A0123.alt: A card payment terminal beside a yellow leather coin purse on a sunlit wooden market counter.
A0123.ttag: Mercado Pago and Mercado Ads belong in every Mercado Libre plan | Kwontified
A0123.desc: On Mercado Libre, payments and advertising shape whether a sale happens. Brands should plan for Mercado Pago and Mercado Ads, not just the listing.
A0123.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 23, 2021.
A0123.body:
When a brand prepares to launch on Mercado Libre, the plan often looks like an Amazon plan with a different flag on it: list the products, price them well, manage stock. That plan covers the smallest part of what Mercado Libre is. The company is a payments and advertising business as much as a marketplace, and in markets where many shoppers rely on installments and digital wallets, those two arms decide much of who wins the sale.

Mercado Pago shapes whether a purchase happens at all. Mercado Ads shapes whether the product is found in the first place. A brand’s Mercado Libre plan should include both from the first day, because the listing alone controls neither moment.

How big Mercado Pago and Mercado Ads have become

Mercado Libre’s second-quarter 2021 results show how much of the business runs through payments. Total payment volume through Mercado Pago passed $17.5 billion, up 72% year over year on a currency-neutral basis, according to its results. Of that, $10.3 billion came from payments outside the marketplace, up 93.5%. The marketplace’s own gross merchandise volume was $7.0 billion, up 46%.

That balance matters to a brand. Mercado Pago is used for far more than marketplace purchases, so many shoppers already know and trust it before they reach a listing. A brand selling on Mercado Libre is selling inside a payments system its customers use every day, an advantage few other marketplaces offer.

The company lends as well. Its credit portfolio, Mercado Credito, was over $800 million, almost five times its size a year earlier, according to the same release, and unique active users reached 75.9 million.

Advertising has its own name too. Mercado Libre relaunched its advertising platform as Mercado Ads in September 2020, with Product Ads that turn a seller’s listings into advertisements, Advertising Week reported. At the relaunch, the head of Mercado Ads for the Southern Cone said buyers spend about 50 minutes browsing the platform on average before making a purchase, Forbes Argentina reported.

Where the value sits in a single blender sale

Take a shopper in Brazil who wants a blender. They search Mercado Libre and browse for a while, comparing options across several pages. A brand that appears near the top of that search through Product Ads has a much better chance of being considered than one buried on the fourth page. Mercado Ads decides whether the brand enters the decision at all.

The shopper settles on a blender priced at R$300 and does not want to pay it all at once, so they look for an installment option, which Mercado Pago provides. A listing that offers interest-free installments looks more affordable than one that does not, even at the same price. Mercado Pago shapes whether the sale happens, and with whom.

They pay with a Mercado Pago wallet they also use for other payments, so the purchase is quick and familiar, and a Mercado Credito customer might even finance it there. At each step, a part of Mercado Libre other than the listing decided the outcome. A brand that planned only the listing would have missed the two moments that mattered most: being seen, and being affordable at the point of payment.

Seen that way, much of the value in the sale is captured by the arms the brand did not plan for. Mercado Libre earns from the advertising that put the product on the first page and from the payment rails that made it affordable, and it holds the shopper’s wallet relationship long after the blender ships. A brand that wants a share of that value has to plan for those arms on purpose.

Building payments and visibility into the Mercado Libre plan

Installments belong in the pricing from the start. On Mercado Libre, interest-free installments come with the Premium listing type, which also gives listings more exposure, according to Mercado Libre’s own seller guidance. Premium listings carry their own fee schedule, so a brand should compare them with the Classic listing for each category, decide which products justify the cost and build it into margins before launch. For higher-priced products, installments can be the difference between a sale and no sale.

Mercado Ads needs a budget from the start for the same reason. Where shoppers browse at length, first-page visibility matters, and new listings without reviews or sales history will struggle to appear organically. Product Ads help them win the early sales that build ranking.

The two also work as a pair. A Product Ad that brings a shopper to a listing without installments may waste the click if the shopper leaves to find a payment option they prefer, while a listing with installments but no visibility may never be seen. The products a brand advertises most heavily are often the ones that most need affordable payment options.

That argues for reviewing the whole system together rather than the listing alone. Results on Mercado Libre depend on advertising efficiency, the installment mix and conversion at once, and reviewing them separately hides how they interact: a cheaper price with no installments may convert worse than a slightly higher price with them.

The mix should also be set country by country. Payment habits, installment norms and Mercado Libre’s position differ across Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and its other markets.

The growth of Mercado Pago’s payments outside the marketplace is worth tracking for that reason. The more shoppers use it for everyday payments, the more familiar it becomes at checkout, and the stronger the case for building installments into every product’s price. Planning payments and advertising alongside the listings is how we run Mercado Libre for brands.

A0124.title: Ecommerce unit economics: profitable on paper, short of cash
A0124.alt: An open, empty metal cash box beside a twine-tied stack of old papers on a wooden table.
A0124.ttag: Ecommerce unit economics: profitable on paper, short of cash | Kwontified
A0124.desc: A product can earn a healthy margin per unit and still drain cash. With freight and lead times stretched in 2021, model when cash moves, not just margin.
A0124.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 28, 2021.
A0124.body:
Take a brand that sells a $40 product on Amazon and earns $8 a unit after product cost, freight, fees and advertising, a 20% margin. It sells 5,000 units a month and plans to double that for the holiday. Every unit in the plan is profitable. The plan may still be unaffordable, because a profitable unit still has to be paid for months before anyone buys it.

Margin per unit measures whether each sale earns more than it costs. It says nothing about when cash leaves the business and when it comes back. In 2021, longer lead times, record freight costs and advertising paid ahead of sales have stretched that gap, so ecommerce unit economics need a second column: the cash a product ties up before it pays.

Why ecommerce unit economics look better than the bank balance

The costs of getting a product to a shopper have risen and moved earlier. Drewry’s World Container Index rose to $10,083.84 per 40-foot container on September 9, 2021, Hellenic Shipping News reported. Two weeks earlier, the index stood 351% higher than a year before, the same publication reported. Brands pay that freight weeks or months before the goods sell.

Stock has to arrive earlier too. With ports congested and Amazon limiting how much inventory sellers can send by storage type, Helium 10 reported, brands are ordering further ahead and holding more stock in their own warehouses or in transit.

Advertising is paid as it runs. The average advertising cost of a sale on Amazon reached $9 to $10 by June, which was up from $6 to $7 in 2020, according to Marketplace Pulse data carried by MediaPost. That money leaves the business before the marketplace pays out the sale.

A positive margin feels like permission to grow

The mistake is natural. A product with a healthy margin looks safe to scale, because the number most reports show at the top of every product page is the margin, and it is positive. The more often a team sees that number, the more it starts to read as an answer to a different question: can we afford to grow this?

Margin cannot answer that question, because the cash a business needs depends on the length of its cycle.

A brand pays its manufacturer, often with a deposit months before production and the balance before shipping. It pays freight and duties, then storage, then advertising as the product sells. Only after the sale, and after the marketplace’s payout schedule, does the money come back. The longer that cycle, the more cash is tied up at any moment.

Returns stretch the cycle further. A refunded order can reverse the revenue weeks after the brand paid to make, ship, store and advertise the product. And growth widens the gap: a brand that plans to double its sales must buy twice the inventory, months before the extra sales arrive. Every unit in that plan can be profitable while the business runs out of cash funding it, which is why the bank balance and the margin report so often tell different stories in a growth year.

The cash a doubling plan needs

Go back to the $40 product. The brand pays for inventory four months before it sells, on average, once production, shipping and storage are counted. To sell 5,000 units a month, it has roughly four months of stock paid for at any time: 20,000 units at a landed cost of $18 each, or $360,000 tied up.

Doubling to 10,000 units a month for the holiday means buying the extra inventory four months ahead: another 20,000 units and another $360,000, before the first extra sale. Monthly profit of $40,000 does not cover that, even across four months. On paper the plan earns more. In practice the brand needs financing or a smaller plan, and it needs to know which before it places the purchase order, not after the deposit has cleared.

The arithmetic holds for a smaller brand with smaller numbers. It gets worse when the plan relies on stock arriving on time. If the extra inventory lands three weeks late because of port delays, the cash is already spent and the sales window has partly closed, leaving stock to carry into January.

Sizing growth by peak cash, not by margin

A monthly cash model belongs next to every margin calculation. For each top product, it maps when deposits, balances, freight, storage and advertising are paid, and when the marketplace pays out. The peak cash need, not the margin, decides what growth the business can fund. Building it takes a spreadsheet and the right inputs, not a new system.

Shortening the cycle frees cash without any new sales. Smaller deposits or longer payment terms with manufacturers, stock sent to marketplaces closer to when it will sell, and slow-moving inventory cleared out all reduce the money tied up.

Scaling in steps limits the damage when the model is wrong. Growing a product by 25% at a time, and confirming that sales and cash behave as modeled before the next step, is safer than committing to a doubling months in advance.

Finance and channel teams have to build this model together. Channel teams know the sales plan, the advertising budget and the payout schedule; finance knows the supplier terms, the freight bills and the bank balance. A model built by one of them misses half the timing.

The number to compare each month is cash tied up in inventory and in transit against monthly profit. If the first is rising faster than the second, growth is consuming cash faster than it produces it, and modeling margin and cash together is how we plan marketplace growth for brands.

A0125.title: Five ecommerce business models now compete for the same shopper
A0125.alt: A row of colorful painted shopfronts with plants, books and pottery in the windows along a cobblestone street.
A0125.ttag: Five ecommerce business models now compete for the same shopper | Kwontified
A0125.desc: Retail, marketplaces, DTC, curated platforms and social commerce now compete for one shopper. Brands should give each model a distinct job, not pick one.
A0125.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 30, 2021.
A0125.body:
A shopper looking for a moisturizer online in 2021 might find it on Instagram, check the price on Amazon, read reviews on a retailer’s site and buy wherever delivery is fastest. In that one purchase, five business models are competing: a retailer selling the product as its own, a seller on an open marketplace, the brand’s own website, a curated partner platform and a social app. Each offers the brand a different mix of reach, control and margin.

Those models grew up for different reasons, and treating them as interchangeable, or picking one and ignoring the rest, wastes what each does well. The better plan gives each model a distinct job, sets targets for that job and keeps the models from competing with one another for the same sale.

How the five ecommerce business models grew up

First-party retail is the oldest model online, and it mirrors the store. A retailer buys the brand’s products and sells them as its own; Amazon’s vendor business, Walmart.com and Target.com work this way. The brand gives up control of price and assortment in exchange for a single buyer and the retailer’s reach.

Open marketplaces came next. Amazon opened its store to third-party sellers years ago, and the model has since overtaken its own retail in volume. Third-party sellers accounted for 56% of Amazon’s paid units in the second quarter of 2021, up from 53% a year earlier, Supermarket News reported. Walmart’s marketplace is growing too, with thousands of new sellers added in its latest quarter, according to Walmart’s results. Here the brand controls its price and offer but competes on an open shelf.

Direct-to-consumer sites spread as tools such as Shopify made them easy to build. The brand owns the customer relationship and the data, but has to find its own traffic.

Curated partner platforms sit between retail and marketplace. Some retailers have opened their sites to selected brands rather than everyone. Zalando’s Partner Program, in which brands sell directly to Zalando’s customers, reached 24% of its Fashion Store sales volume in late 2020, according to Zalando’s investor presentation. Target Plus, which is invitation-only, had fewer than 300 sellers in early 2021, according to Marketplace Pulse figures cited by Kaspien. The brand gets a trusted storefront with less open competition, in exchange for meeting the platform’s standards.

Social commerce is the newest, and it puts shopping inside the apps where people already spend time. Facebook’s Shops drew more than 300 million monthly visitors across 1.2 million monthly active Shops, the company said in June, Exchange4media reported. On August 24, TikTok began piloting a shopping tab for Shopify merchants, Shopify said. The brand reaches shoppers at the moment of discovery, often before they were looking.

The models compete because the shopper moves between them

The five models are not separate markets. They pull at the same shopper, often within a single purchase, and each wants the sale on terms that reward the brand differently.

The balance between them keeps shifting. Marketplaces have overtaken first-party retail in Amazon’s unit volume, and Zalando’s partner business expanded by more than 100% in the first half of 2021, Zalando reported, far faster than the platform as a whole. Social commerce is small next to both but growing from a standing start. A channel plan written before the pandemic reshaped how people shop will not fit the years ahead, and the role of each model deserves a fresh look at least once a year.

The competition also shows up inside the brand. Prices must hold across models, because retailers and marketplaces enforce parity. Inventory has to be shared. Advertising in one model often creates demand that another captures. When each model has its own team and its own sales target, the brand ends up competing with itself, and the team whose channel captured the sale gets credit for demand another team paid to create.

Giving each model a job it can be judged on

Take a skincare brand that sells through all five models. Rather than asking each to maximize its own sales, it gives each a job.

Its vendor relationship with a large retailer provides reach and volume on its best-known products. Its marketplace presence covers the long tail of its range and lets it control price and content. Its own website holds the full catalog, gathers customer data and runs its subscription program. A curated platform introduces it to a fashion-conscious audience in Europe. Social commerce drives discovery of new products, measured partly by the search and sales it creates elsewhere.

Each model is then judged on its job. The website is measured on customers acquired and retained, not just sales. Social commerce is measured on discovery, not just checkout revenue. The marketplace is measured on profitable sales and share of search. A model whose job is discovery should not be cut because it closes few sales itself.

The targets change the conversation in the planning meeting: instead of five teams arguing over who gets credit for a sale, the brand asks whether each model did the work it was given.

Few brands need all five; many will use two or three. Whatever the number, each model in the plan should have a clear role chosen for what that model does best, with price, inventory and advertising rules that apply across all of them.

The question for a leadership team is where its new customers come from and where they buy again. If those are different models, the models are working together. If one is quietly taking sales from another without adding customers, its role needs rethinking, and giving each channel a clear role is how we plan channel mixes for brands.

A0127.title: Walmart’s seller scorecard decides who wins the marketplace
A0127.alt: A clipboard with a blank scorecard and a brass star tag beside an empty blue wire shopping basket.
A0127.ttag: Walmart’s seller scorecard decides who wins the marketplace | Kwontified
A0127.desc: Walmart’s seller scorecard looks like a compliance check. It is really how Walmart picks its best sellers, and brands should manage it as a growth plan.
A0127.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 5, 2021.
A0127.body:
When Walmart launched its Pro Seller badge in October 2020, only 350 of its 60,000 marketplace sellers qualified, Marketplace Pulse reported. The rest of its sellers, whatever their standing against Walmart’s minimums, went without the reward. That gap says what the scorecard is really for.

Most brands treat Walmart’s seller performance metrics as a compliance hurdle: stay above the line and avoid trouble. Walmart uses the same measures of delivery, cancellations, returns and listing quality to decide which sellers it puts forward, and as the marketplace fills with competitors those rewards carry more weight. The scorecard works better as a growth plan than as a pass-fail test.

What the Walmart seller scorecard rewards

The badge appears in search results, on product pages and in the cart, and its criteria show what Walmart values, Feedvisor reported.

Pro Seller criterion at launchThreshold
On-time deliveryAt least 95% over 90 days
Seller-related cancellations1% or less
ReturnsFree online or in-store returns across the entire catalog
Listing qualityAt least 60% of trending items scoring 50% or more

The listing quality score combines content and discoverability, the competitiveness of the offer, and ratings and reviews.

Competition for shoppers’ attention keeps rising. Walmart said in its second-quarter 2021 results that it had added thousands of new sellers to its marketplace, according to its release. Each new seller that clears the minimum makes clearing it worth a little less, because a standard most sellers meet cannot set any of them apart. The badge thresholds sit above that crowd, which is where the scorecard starts to separate one seller from another.

Why passing the scorecard is not the same as winning it

The defensive reading of a scorecard is natural, and it is rational for a seller with limited time. Check the metrics, confirm they clear the minimum, move on to the work that seems to grow sales. The minimum, though, is not where the rewards sit.

Every Pro Seller criterion describes something a shopper notices: whether the order arrives when promised, whether it is canceled, whether returns are easy, whether the listing answers the shopper’s questions. Walmart is building a marketplace where those things decide which sellers it puts in front of shoppers, and the badge is its first visible signal of that. From Walmart’s side the logic is simple. Every late or canceled marketplace order is a disappointed Walmart customer, so the retailer has every reason to steer shoppers toward the sellers who disappoint them least.

The badge did not affect search ranking at launch, Feedvisor noted. It still shapes the shopper’s choice. Two sellers offering the same item at similar prices look different when one carries a badge promising consistent on-time delivery and free returns. The scorecard also affects conversion directly, because a listing with weak content and few reviews converts worse wherever it appears.

Take two brands selling similar kitchen products on Walmart’s marketplace, both above the minimum standards. The first treats the metrics as a compliance check. Its on-time delivery is 92%, its cancellations are 1.8%, and most of its listings score below 50% for quality because they have thin descriptions and few reviews. It is never at risk of suspension, but it never qualifies for the badge, and its conversion trails the category.

The second manages the same metrics as a plan. It adds delivery buffers to its shipping templates until on-time delivery reaches 97%, fixes the stock syncing behind most cancellations, offers free returns and rewrites its top listings with full attributes and better images. Within a few months it qualifies for the badge, and its conversion rises on the same traffic.

Both brands passed Walmart’s test. Only the second turned the scorecard into an advantage, and the cost was mostly effort rather than money. Better shipping templates, synced inventory and stronger listings are things a brand controls, and they help on every channel. A brand that does the work for Walmart’s scorecard usually finds its Amazon and direct-to-consumer operations improve at the same time.

Managing the scorecard toward the badge

The badge criteria make a better target than the line that triggers a warning: at least 95% on-time delivery, cancellations under 1% and strong listing quality on the items that sell most.

Hitting them means fixing causes rather than chasing numbers. Late deliveries usually come from shipping promises the operation cannot keep, so handling times and carrier choices need to be realistic. Cancellations usually come from stock that is out of sync across channels, so inventory systems should be connected before the range grows. Both fixes keep paying after the badge is won, because the same late shipments and canceled orders would cost reviews and repeat customers anywhere the brand sells.

Reviews deserve their own plan, because they feed the listing quality score and the shopper’s decision at once, and new listings start with none. Programs that encourage verified buyers to leave reviews, used within Walmart’s rules, help new items reach a credible rating sooner.

Listing quality is often the cheapest part to improve, and the quickest to show up in conversion. Content, offer competitiveness and reviews are measured alongside delivery, and rewriting the top 20 listings can move the score faster than any operational change.

The scorecard also hints at where Walmart is heading. A marketplace that measures sellers on shopper experience will tend to give more visibility to those who score well, and the brands already near the top will be best placed when it does. The test each refresh cycle is distance from the badge, not distance from the minimum, and managing the scorecard that way is how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

A0128.title: Target Plus fulfillment works without Target’s stores
A0128.alt: A battered, taped red box alone on a roller conveyor in an empty industrial warehouse.
A0128.ttag: Target Plus fulfillment works without Target’s stores | Kwontified
A0128.desc: Target’s stores fulfill nearly all its sales, but Target Plus sellers ship their own orders. Brands should choose their Target model with that gap in mind.
A0128.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 7, 2021.
A0128.body:
Open Target.com on a weekday afternoon and much of what you see can be collected the same day: Drive Up, Order Pickup, delivery from a store a few miles away. Target’s stores have become its fulfillment network, and more than 95% of its sales now leave through them. A Target Plus seller’s products sit on the same pages but outside that network, held in the seller’s own warehouse and shipped by parcel.

So when a leadership team asks whether Target Plus will let it ride on Target’s stores, the answer for the order itself is no. That gap should shape which Target model a brand chooses, and Target Plus sellers should compete on delivery speed, content and assortment rather than expecting the stores to work for them.

How Target Plus fulfillment differs from Target’s own

Target’s second-quarter 2021 results put the store network at the center of the business. More than 95% of second-quarter sales were fulfilled by stores, Target reported. Comparable digital sales grew 10%, led by same-day services (Order Pickup, Drive Up and Shipt), which grew nearly 55% on top of more than 270% the year before, according to the same release. Target serves shoppers through more than 1,900 stores.

Target Plus works differently. On Target’s marketplace, inventory stays with the seller, who also ships the order, and shoppers can bring marketplace items back to Target stores, the Star Tribune reported. The marketplace is small and invitation-only: Marketplace Pulse counted fewer than 300 sellers on it in early 2021, figures Kaspien cited when it joined.

What a brand gives up by shipping from its own warehouse

For the order, a Target Plus item ships from the seller’s warehouse, on the seller’s carrier, at the seller’s speed. None of the reach of 1,900 locations applies to it. For a brand used to Amazon, where a marketplace seller can hand its stock to Amazon’s own fulfillment network, that is the biggest adjustment Target Plus asks for.

That matters because the stores are where Target’s growth is. Many shoppers have grown used to picking up an order the same day or having it delivered from a local store. On Target.com they now see two kinds of item side by side: those Target fulfills from its stores, and marketplace items that arrive by parcel in several days. The second kind has to work harder to win the sale.

Speed is not the only difference. Store-fulfilled items benefit from Target’s own inventory planning and from shoppers’ trust in Target as the seller. A marketplace item depends on the seller’s stock, carrier and customer service, and any weakness in those shows up directly in reviews on Target.com.

The stores do help Target Plus sellers in one place: returns. A shopper can bring a marketplace item back to a Target store, which makes buying from an unfamiliar brand feel less risky.

Choosing a Target model with the stores in mind

A brand that wants to be on Target has two routes, and the store network separates them. If Target buys the brand’s products, they enter Target’s own assortment, can be stocked in stores and can be fulfilled through its same-day services; the brand gives up control of pricing and placement, and Target decides what to carry. If the brand is invited to Target Plus, it keeps control of its listings and pricing and can offer a wider range, but it ships every order itself and competes with store-fulfilled items for attention.

Neither route is better in general. Selling to Target suits products that win on availability and price in an aisle, where the brand is comfortable letting Target set both. Target Plus suits a brand that wants its full range on Target.com, its own content and its own price, and is prepared to run the fulfillment that comes with them. Many brands will find that some products belong on one route and some on the other, and the store network is the cleanest way to sort them.

Take a home goods brand selling a $45 throw blanket on Target Plus, shipped from its warehouse with delivery in four to six days. A comparable blanket in Target’s own range is available for same-day pickup at the shopper’s local store. Even at a similar price, a shopper in a hurry will often choose the one they can collect today.

The brand cannot match same-day pickup, but it can narrow the gap. Faster shipping on its best-sellers and stock held in a warehouse closer to its largest markets both shorten the promise. A richer listing, with better images, more detail and stronger reviews, gives a shopper a reason to wait. And products Target’s own range does not carry face no store-fulfilled alternative at all, which makes them the natural lead for a Target Plus assortment.

Content carries more weight here than on a marketplace where every item ships by parcel. A listing with thin images and few reviews loses twice on Target.com, to the faster store-fulfilled item and to the better-presented one, so where speed cannot match the stores, the listing has to do more of the work.

Store returns need planning too. Because shoppers can bring marketplace items back to a Target store, a brand should ask Target how those returns are handled and refunded, and build the expected cost into its margins before it prices the channel.

Whether Target ever opens its store-based fulfillment to marketplace sellers is the development to follow. Until it does, Target Plus is a parcel business inside a store-fulfilled retailer, and the question for the room is which of the brand’s products can win on those terms. Choosing the right Target model product by product is how we approach Target Plus for brands.

A0130.crumb: Zalando returns are partly a brand…
A0130.title: Zalando returns are partly a brand problem, and partly fixable
A0130.alt: A folded sage green shirt in an open mailer box beside a tin sewing kit on a wooden table.
A0130.ttag: Zalando returns are partly a brand problem, and partly fixable | Kwontified
A0130.desc: About half of what Zalando sells comes back, and a third of returns are about size. Brands that improve their size data and content can cut that share.
A0130.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 12, 2021.
A0130.body:
About half of what Zalando sells is sent back. Many brands treat that as a fixed cost of online fashion, something to price in and forget. The number deserves a closer look, because about one third of returns come down to size and fit, and size and fit depend partly on information the brand supplies. A brand cannot take Zalando’s return rate to zero, but it controls more of its own share than the headline suggests.

Why Zalando returns run so high

The rate is high by design. Zalando’s customers can order several items, try them at home and send back what they do not want. The Zalando manager responsible for reducing returns put the rate at around 50% of all items sold, in an interview with NPR, at a time when Zalando carried some 2,000 brands, each with its own variations on sizing.

Size is the biggest single cause, and it is the one most open to change. About one third of all returns happen because clothes are too small or too large, Zalando told FashionUnited.

Zalando has been working on the problem. It uses algorithmic size advice, analyzes the reasons customers give for returns and employs fitting models to test items before they go on sale. It said it had reduced size and fit-related returns by about 4% over the previous couple of years, NPR reported. It has also used size recommendations as part of an effort to make smaller orders more profitable, Reuters reported.

Shoppers’ habits explain some returns, and size data explains more

The common view is that returns on Zalando are driven by shoppers’ habits, so brands cannot do much about them. It is easy to see why the view sticks. Shoppers who order two sizes of the same item intend to return one, and no product page will stop that entirely. Some returns are changes of mind, and free returns are part of the deal Zalando offers its customers, which brands selling there accept.

The rest of the view does not hold. If a third of returns are about size and fit, the information shoppers use to choose a size matters. That information comes from the brand: its size charts, its measurements, its descriptions of fit and the consistency of its sizing from one product to the next. Zalando’s own size advice depends on that data too, alongside what it learns from customers’ purchases and returns.

Reuters reported a telling case: a denim brand saw size-related returns rise after it changed a design, and changed it back once Zalando flagged the issue, according to a syndicated version of the report. The brand’s own product decision moved the return rate, and its own decision moved it back. Brands cannot eliminate returns on Zalando. They do control a meaningful part of them.

What a fifth fewer size returns is worth

Take a brand that sells 10,000 items a season on Zalando. The inputs below are the published averages, applied to one brand. The reduction is an assumption, and a modest one.

StepItems
Items sold in a season10,000
Returned, at about 50%5,000
Size-related, at about one third1,670
Avoided if better size data cuts those by a fifth330

That saving looks small against 10,000 items sold. It compounds, though. The same size data serves every later season, and each new style built on the same size block starts with fewer returns than it otherwise would.

Each avoided return saves the cost of handling, any item that cannot be resold at full price, and the sale the brand would otherwise have lost. It also keeps a customer who received something that fit. A shopper who gets the right size the first time is more likely to keep the item, review it well and buy from the brand again, and those reviews and repeat purchases help the brand on Zalando over time.

Where returns prevention starts

The size data comes first. Size charts on Zalando should be accurate and complete, measurements should match the products as made, and sizing should be consistent across styles. Inconsistent sizing within a brand is one of the hardest problems for any size advice to correct, because the advice learns from patterns the brand keeps breaking.

Fit belongs in the description as well as the size. Copy that says how an item fits, whether it runs small or large, how the fabric stretches and what size the model is wearing helps shoppers choose correctly the first time. Images that show the fit from several angles, on models of different builds where possible, do the same job.

The returns data then points to the outliers. Reviewing return reasons by product shows patterns a brand would not otherwise see: a style returned for being too small, a color that looks different on screen. A product with an unusually high return rate is often fixable through content, sizing or, as the denim case shows, the product itself.

Working with Zalando rather than around it speeds all of this up. Its size advice learns from purchases and returns across the platform, so it can spot a style that runs small faster than a single brand can. Brands that respond quickly when Zalando flags a sizing problem, and share accurate measurements up front, give that advice better data. The work is shared. Zalando supplies the signals, and the brand supplies the fixes.

The place to start is the return rate by product and reason, compared with the category on Zalando. Products well above the category average are where prevention pays first, and building that work into the Zalando plan is how we manage Zalando for brands.

A0132.crumb: Cyber Week 2021 planning needs one owner…
A0132.title: Cyber Week 2021 planning needs one owner and an earlier calendar
A0132.alt: An antique brass key on a wooden table among wrapped parcels, pine cones, a mug and a leather journal.
A0132.ttag: Cyber Week 2021 planning needs one owner and an earlier calendar | Kwontified
A0132.desc: With holiday deals starting in early October, Cyber Week 2021 runs the planning calendar. Brands need one owner who decides which deals to run and when.
A0132.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 14, 2021.
A0132.body:
Cyber Week 2021 has already started. Amazon launched “Black Friday-worthy” deals on October 4, and Target ran its Deal Days and began its holiday price match a week later. The decisions brands used to make in November, which products to discount, how deeply and with how much stock, now set the whole fourth-quarter calendar.

Those decisions touch ecommerce, finance, supply chain and marketing, and at many brands each of them holds a piece. A brand gets through the season better when one owner has the authority to make the calls, working back from the event dates rather than forward from the next meeting.

How Cyber Week 2021 planning moved into October

The holiday season keeps starting earlier. Amazon began offering what it called “Black Friday-worthy” deals with discounts across every category on October 4, Fortune reported. Black Friday-style deals first reached into October in 2019, the same report noted.

Target moved too. Its second Deal Days event was set for October 10 to 12, and its holiday price match guarantee runs from October 10 to December 24, Chain Store Age reported. Walmart had not announced its holiday sales plans at that point, the same report said.

Black Friday falls on November 26, 2021 and Cyber Monday on November 29. For many shoppers, and for the retailers competing for them, the season now runs from early October to Christmas.

The planning meeting where nobody owns the decision

Take a mid-sized home goods brand in mid-October. The ecommerce lead calls a meeting to plan Cyber Week, arriving with a list of products to put on deal. The finance lead asks what discount each will carry and whether the margin survives. The supply chain lead points out that two of the products are on a container still at sea, and a third sold through faster than forecast in September. The marketing lead wants to know which products will feature in the email campaign, which has to be built this week.

Everyone holds a piece of the decision, and no one owns it, so the meeting ends with a follow-up meeting. By the time the group agrees, one retailer’s deal submission window has closed. The email has gone out featuring a product that will be out of stock. The discount on another has been set without anyone checking what Amazon’s early deals have done to competitors’ prices.

Nobody in that room made a bad decision. The structure did the damage. Each function was judged on its own number, so each argued for its own constraint, and the only person who could have traded them off against one another did not exist.

The pattern is easy to recognize once the scorecards are laid side by side. Finance is measured on margin, supply chain on in-stock rates and inventory cost, marketing on campaign results, ecommerce on revenue. A holiday deal moves all four numbers at once, which is why it gets pulled four ways, and why an earlier start to the season makes the pull worse rather than better.

Giving the decision an owner and a calendar

The owner is usually the person accountable for channel revenue. Ecommerce, finance, supply chain and marketing should all advise, but one person should decide which products go on deal, at what discount and with what stock, and be able to make the call within a day.

The calendar comes from the dates. The events set every deadline before them: when deals must be submitted to each retailer, when stock must arrive at the warehouse, when campaigns must be built and when advertising budgets must be approved. Writing those deadlines on one calendar, by channel, shows the owner when each decision is due. With deals now starting in October, some of those deadlines have already passed.

Rules agreed before the meeting make the owner’s decisions faster and easier to explain. Many arguments in the room are really about rules that could have been settled earlier. The common ones are the minimum margin a deal must hold, the stock cover a product needs before it can be discounted, and how the brand will respond if a competitor cuts its price.

One strategic choice belongs to the owner early on: whether to compete in the October deals at all, or hold the deepest discounts for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Early deals can capture shoppers who want to buy before shipping delays and stockouts, but they also risk training shoppers to wait for the next price drop. The answer differs by product, and it is easier to make once, early, than repeatedly under pressure.

Advertising needs the same owner. Deal visibility on marketplaces depends heavily on advertising, and click prices rise as the event approaches. The person deciding which products go on deal should also decide where the ad budget goes, so the brand is not paying peak prices to promote a product with no deal, or running a deep discount that nobody sees.

The review after the event belongs to the same person: which deals sold through, which held margin, which products ran out early and what the brand would decide differently. That review is far more useful when one person was accountable for the decisions it assesses, and it becomes the first page of the plan for the next event.

By early November, leadership needs to know how much of the planned Cyber Week volume has already sold. If shoppers are buying earlier, stock and budget should move earlier too, and building that calendar around a single owner is how we plan holiday events for brands.

A0135.title: Q3 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: conversion up, ROAS down
A0135.alt: A weathered wooden seesaw tilted in a sandy, empty playground with a swing set behind it.
A0135.ttag: Q3 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark: conversion up, ROAS down | Kwontified
A0135.desc: Q3 2021 Amazon ad results look weak next to a Prime Day quarter. Year over year, shoppers converted better, but returns slipped as clicks cost more.
A0135.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 19, 2021.
A0135.body:
An Amazon advertising review of the third quarter of 2021 has a trap built into it. The third quarter of 2021 is the first full quarter since Prime Day moved to June, so set beside a second quarter that contained the event, almost every Q3 number looks weak. That comparison misleads. Set beside the same quarter a year earlier, the picture is more useful: shoppers converted better, but return on ad spend (ROAS) still slipped because clicks cost more.

The fair Q3 2021 Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark is year over year, and it points to bid and keyword work rather than budget cuts.

The Amazon Sponsored Ads benchmark for Q3 2021 across the industry

Pacvue’s Q3 2021 report found that Sponsored Products ad spend rose 41.8% year over year, and that average daily spend and cost per click (CPC) were relatively flat compared with the second quarter. Sponsored Products conversion rate rose 16.1% year over year, while Sponsored Brands conversion fell 3.9%. ROAS fell 6.1% for Sponsored Products and 12.8% for Sponsored Brands, year over year.

Neither the third quarter of 2020 nor that of 2021 included Prime Day, which fell in October in 2020 and in June in 2021. That makes the year-over-year comparison a like-for-like one, at least as far as the biggest event on Amazon’s calendar is concerned.

Pacvue’s second and third quarters, side by side

Pacvue’s Q2 2021 report and the release that announced it supply the reference point. Set beside the third-quarter figures, they show which way costs and returns moved once Prime Day had passed.

Sponsored Products, per PacvueQ2 2021Q3 2021
Ad spend, year over yearup 38%up 41.8%
CPCup 36% year over yearflat quarter over quarter
Conversion rate, year over yearn/aup 16.1%
ROAS, year over yeardown 10%down 6.1%

ROAS divides attributed sales by ad spend, with Amazon’s standard Sponsored Products attribution applied. CPC jumped 36% on the year in the second quarter and then held flat into the third. Over the same stretch, the year-over-year fall in Sponsored Products ROAS narrowed from 10% to 6.1%. Retail media as a whole changed little at the end of the quarter: Skai’s September snapshot found spending flat on August, with the average cost of a click up 3%.

Why the last quarter always looks like the right comparison

The pull is toward recency. Teams look at the most recent quarter, which in 2021 contained Prime Day, and conclude that performance has fallen off. Prime Day concentrates traffic, deal-driven conversion and attributed sales into a few days, so a quarter that contains it flatters almost every metric, and the quarter that follows looks worse even if nothing about the brand’s advertising has changed.

It is an easy mistake because quarterly reviews are built around the latest results. A team reviewing Q3 in early October has Q2 fresh in mind, including the Prime Day spike it celebrated in July. Against that memory, a normal quarter feels like a decline, and the instinct is to cut spending or change strategy when neither is warranted.

Take a brand whose Sponsored Products ROAS was 5.0 in Q2 2021, including Prime Day, and 4.0 in Q3 2021. Against Q2, that looks like a 20% collapse. Its Q3 2020 ROAS was 4.2, though, so the year-over-year decline is about 5%, in line with the market. The first reading invites alarm and budget cuts. The second calls for targeted work on bids and keywords, starting with the terms where cost per click has risen most and conversion has not kept pace.

The year-over-year view also explains the decline. Conversion on Sponsored Products rose, which suggests listings, prices and availability were doing their job. ROAS still fell, because costs per click had risen faster over the year than conversion did. The ads kept working after Prime Day; each click simply cost more than it did a year earlier.

The arithmetic behind that is short. ROAS is conversion rate times order value, divided by cost per click. If conversion rises and ROAS still falls, then unless order values dropped, the cost of each click must have risen faster than conversion improved. That is a price problem in the auction rather than a problem with the listing, and it calls for a pricing response: bids set term by term against what each click now returns.

Reading Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands separately

The two ad types moved differently. Sponsored Products conversion rose while Sponsored Brands conversion fell, and Sponsored Brands ROAS fell about twice as far, according to Pacvue’s figures. Sponsored Brands ads appear higher on the page and often target broader, earlier-stage searches, so they are more exposed when competition for top placements rises. That makes Sponsored Brands the first place to look when a blended ROAS slips.

A brand running both should review them as separate lines. A falling blended ROAS can hide a healthy Sponsored Products program alongside a Sponsored Brands program that needs new targeting, new creative or a smaller budget.

The fourth quarter will test all of this. Holiday traffic raises conversion, but competition raises CPCs further, and a brand that enters November with bids and keywords tuned to Q3’s costs will spend more efficiently than one that reacts once the season has started. Fourth-quarter targets belong next to Q4 2020 results, adjusted for the rise in CPC, rather than next to Q3.

Many advertising dashboards default to comparing a period with the one just before it. Switching that default to the same period a year earlier, at least for quarterly reviews, strips out much of the noise event timing creates. The same habit protects the review of the first quarter, which always follows the holidays, and benchmarking each quarter that way is how we benchmark Amazon advertising for brands.

A0136.crumb: Walmart’s rural advantage is its store…
A0136.title: Walmart’s rural advantage is its store network, not its website
A0136.alt: A brick village shop with a blue awning beside a quiet country road under a cloudy summer sky.
A0136.ttag: Walmart’s rural advantage is its store network, not its website | Kwontified
A0136.desc: Walmart’s edge with rural shoppers comes from stores close to almost everyone. Brands should plan for shoppers who buy online and collect locally.
A0136.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 21, 2021.
A0136.body:
In many rural counties, the nearest Walmart can be the nearest place to buy almost anything, and since the pandemic it has also become the nearest place to collect an online order. That is where Walmart’s edge with rural and small-town shoppers comes from. Its website matters less than the store a short drive away, which now doubles as the engine of its online business.

Brands that want to reach those shoppers through Walmart should plan around store-based pickup and delivery, and around Walmart’s own assortment, rather than treating Walmart.com as a parcel marketplace like any other.

Where the Walmart rural advantage comes from

Walmart’s stores sit close to almost every American, including in small towns many retailers do not reach. “With 90% of Americans living within 10 miles of a Walmart, a closer store isn’t always the answer,” Walmart’s senior vice president of customer product, Tom Ward, wrote, Drug Store News reported. The point of the remark was that Walmart is already close enough to most shoppers that its next gains come from using those stores better.

The pandemic turned that proximity into an online advantage. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales grew 6% in its second quarter of 2021 and 103% over two years, and the company said it gained market share in grocery, according to its results. Grocery is where stores matter most: 65.1% of US shoppers surveyed by Coresight Research had bought groceries in Walmart stores in the previous 12 months, Coresight reported.

In rural areas, where parcel delivery takes longer and costs more, a store a few miles away that offers pickup or same-day delivery is a powerful advantage. A shopper who would wait several days for a parcel can collect an order the same afternoon.

Why the shelf down the road beats the warehouse two states away

The store network shapes what sells on Walmart.com, and how. Items in Walmart’s own assortment, stocked in its stores, can be collected or delivered from a nearby store. Marketplace items are not on those shelves. They ship from wherever the seller holds stock, either its own warehouse or, for sellers using Walmart Fulfillment Services, Walmart’s fulfillment centers, which can earn the item Walmart’s two-day delivery tag, Modern Retail reported. For a rural shopper comparing two products, the one available from the local store today often wins.

Distance raises the stakes for a marketplace seller. In a city, a parcel that arrives in two days competes reasonably well with a store across town. In a rural county, the nearest alternative to the local Walmart may be a long drive away, and a parcel may take longer to arrive than the same parcel sent to a city address. The local store becomes the default for anything needed soon.

That matters most in categories bought frequently and urgently: groceries, household goods, health and beauty, pet supplies, baby care. It matters less for products shoppers are willing to wait for, such as furniture or specialty items not stocked in stores.

Take a pet food brand that sells on Walmart.com through the marketplace, shipping from a warehouse in another state. A rural shopper whose dog has run out of food finds a comparable brand in Walmart’s own range, available for pickup at the store eight miles away, and collects it that afternoon. The marketplace brand did nothing wrong. It simply could not compete with a product that was already in the shopper’s town. No amount of advertising or listing work changes the distance between that warehouse and that kitchen.

Read as an institution, Walmart is doing what its footprint lets it do. The stores were built to sell to people nearby, and the online business now turns that same footprint into delivery speed that a parcel network struggles to match in thinly populated places.

Planning a Walmart business for shoppers who collect locally

For frequently bought, urgent categories, being stocked in Walmart’s stores as a supplier often matters more than any marketplace listing, because it puts the product inside the pickup and delivery system rural shoppers rely on. The first decision for a brand is which of its products belong there.

Marketplace sellers win where the store range is thin. Products Walmart does not stock, sizes and bundles it does not carry, and premium versions of everyday items all give a seller room to compete, and fast, reliable shipping through Walmart Fulfillment Services narrows the gap with store-based items.

Listings should be written for the shopper Walmart serves best. Many rural shoppers use Walmart for a wide range of needs and value practical information: what the product does, how long it lasts, how much it holds. Listings that answer those questions plainly convert better than ones written for urban impulse buyers.

Seasonality widens the gap. Rural shoppers buy more in the holiday season like everyone else, but they may face longer parcel delivery times as carriers’ networks fill up. Products available for pickup at the local store are insulated from those delays, which makes the store-versus-parcel difference larger in November and December than in the rest of the year.

Advertising is the other lever a brand controls on Walmart.com, and it is growing fast. Walmart’s US advertising sales nearly doubled in the same quarter, its results showed, and as more brands advertise on Walmart.com, the ones that understand who its shoppers are, and how they buy, will spend more efficiently.

How far Walmart extends store-based fulfillment to marketplace sellers will decide how long this gap lasts. Until it does, rural shoppers will keep favoring what is already on the shelf nearby, and planning a Walmart business around that store network is how we manage Walmart for brands.

A0138.title: Amazon Accelerate 2021 pays brands to send customers to Amazon
A0138.alt: A white van on a winding country lane past a blank wooden signpost among green hedgerows.
A0138.ttag: Amazon Accelerate 2021 pays brands to send customers to Amazon | Kwontified
A0138.desc: Amazon’s Accelerate 2021 tools give brands more data and new ways to reach shoppers, but they also pay brands to send their own demand to Amazon. Weigh both.
A0138.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 26, 2021.
A0138.body:
A brand spending $10,000 a month on social ads for a $40 product has a routing decision to make. Before October 2021, the question of where to send those clicks, its own website or its Amazon listing, was a judgment about conversion and customer data. Since Amazon Accelerate 2021, it is also a question of who pays whom. Amazon will now pay the brand for sending the shopper to Amazon.

That payment, the new Brand Referral Bonus, sits alongside several genuinely useful tools. Together they make Amazon the cheaper place to grow and the brand’s own site the place where it keeps the customer. Brands should decide deliberately which traffic goes where, instead of letting the incentive make the choice for them.

What Amazon announced at Amazon Accelerate 2021

At the conference on October 20, 2021, Amazon said more than 100,000 brands had started selling in its US store so far in 2021. It said sales by brands grew almost 60% in the 12 months ending June 30, according to its announcement. It introduced four tools for brands enrolled in Brand Registry.

The Brand Referral Bonus pays brands, on average, 10% of the purchase price when they send shoppers to Amazon from their own websites or other non-Amazon marketing. It covers the promoted product and any of the brand’s other products the shopper buys over the following two weeks. Amazon Customer Engagement, still in beta, is an email tool for telling shoppers about new products. A+ Story Cards are visual modules that tell the brand’s story on the product page. Customer Review Resolution lets a brand offer help and a courtesy refund to a customer who leaves a negative review.

Amazon also announced Product Opportunity Explorer, which shows what shoppers search for, click on and buy, in a separate announcement. It is in beta through the end of 2021 and will be free for all sellers in 2022.

Cheaper growth on Amazon, or a customer the brand owns

Most of these tools are straightforwardly useful. Better research data, richer product pages and a way to resolve unhappy reviews help any brand selling on Amazon. The Brand Referral Bonus is different, because it changes the economics of where a brand sends its own demand.

A brand that advertises on social media, search engines or email has always had a choice. Sending shoppers to its own site means paying the full cost of conversion but keeping the customer’s data and the chance to sell to them directly again. Sending them to Amazon usually converts better, because shoppers trust Amazon’s checkout and delivery, but Amazon keeps the relationship.

The same $10,000 of social ads, sent each way, produces two different businesses.

Brand’s own siteAmazon
Orders400550
Sales$16,000$22,000
Referral bonusnoneabout $2,200
Customer emails kept400none

Notice what the table leaves out. Amazon’s referral fee comes off the Amazon sales, and so does the cost of making the extra units. The emails on the left have a value the table cannot show at all, because it depends on what the brand sells to those customers next month and the month after.

On a single month’s numbers, Amazon wins easily. Even after Amazon’s referral fee on each sale, the bonus and the higher conversion leave the brand with more revenue for the same advertising spend.

The monthly view misses costs on both sides. Sending shoppers to Amazon also trains them to buy the brand there, which deepens its dependence on Amazon’s fees, rules and search results. Sending them to the brand’s own site builds an asset the brand controls, but that asset only pays off if the brand actually markets to those customers again.

Over a longer horizon, the numbers lean according to what the brand’s own customers are worth. A brand whose customers buy again and again, and respond to its emails, gives up more by sending them to Amazon than a brand selling one-off purchases.

Splitting traffic by what each customer is worth

The comparison starts with the customer rather than the sale. Before sending paid traffic to Amazon for the bonus, a brand should estimate what a customer acquired on its own site is worth over a year, including repeat purchases and email sales. That figure then sits against the extra sales and bonus Amazon offers.

That estimate usually points to a split by purpose. Launches of new products and broad awareness campaigns fit Amazon, where conversion and the bonus are strongest. Loyalty, subscription and replenishment campaigns fit the brand’s own site, where the customer relationship is worth most. The right balance differs by product line, and it will move as Amazon’s tools develop, so the split deserves a fresh look as results come in.

The bonus also has to be measured to be collected. It depends on attribution tags, so every off-Amazon campaign that points to Amazon needs a tag, and someone has to check that the bonus is credited. A campaign that looked marginal before may now pay for itself. An untagged campaign earns the brand nothing extra, however many shoppers it sends.

The new tools inside Amazon soften the cost of sending customers there. Customer Engagement and Brand Follow give brands limited ways to reach their Amazon customers again, though neither yet substitutes for owning the relationship.

How Amazon develops Customer Engagement after its beta will decide how much of that cost remains. Until then, a brand whose repeat customers are worth more than the bonus should keep its loyalty traffic at home, and deciding that split product by product is how we manage Amazon and owned channels for brands.

A0142.crumb: Mercado Libre co-op marketing should buy…
A0142.title: Mercado Libre co-op marketing should buy data, not discounts
A0142.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a tied stack of index cards against a pan of coins, beside a lemon.
A0142.ttag: Mercado Libre co-op marketing should buy data, not discounts | Kwontified
A0142.desc: Co-op marketing with Mercado Libre can build a brand’s presence across Latin America. It pays when brands negotiate for placement, data and measurement.
A0142.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 28, 2021.
A0142.body:
The request often arrives a few weeks before a big sales event: would the brand like to co-fund a promotion with Mercado Libre? The brand puts money toward a discount or a featured slot, the marketplace promotes it, and sales jump for a few days. Then the event ends, and the brand is left with thinner margins on a batch of orders and very little it can use again.

Co-op marketing on a marketplace with nearly 76 million active users can build a brand’s presence across Latin America. It pays only when the brand gets placement, shopper data and clear measurement in return. Brands should negotiate co-op as a media and data investment, not as a discount they quietly fund.

What Mercado Libre co-op marketing involves

Co-op on a marketplace usually takes two forms. One is promotional: the brand helps fund a discount or a featured placement during a sales event, and the marketplace promotes it. The other is brand-building: the brand and the marketplace create a campaign together, using the marketplace’s audience and media.

Mercado Libre has built tools for both. Its September 2020 relaunch of Mercado Ads brought Product Ads, which turn listings into advertisements, a Brand Lab that builds larger campaigns for leading brands with the creative agency MediaMonks, and insights and data to guide advertisers’ decisions, Advertising Week reported.

The audience is large and engaged. Mercado Libre had 75.9 million unique active users in the second quarter of 2021, and its marketplace sold $7.0 billion of goods, according to its results. At the Mercado Ads relaunch, its head for the Southern Cone put average browsing before a purchase at about 50 minutes, Forbes Argentina reported. The same executive noted that special dates such as Cyber Monday are taking a growing share of activity, and that Mercado Libre has become a privileged place for brands seeking new buyers during them.

Who keeps the value from a co-op campaign

The useful question about a co-op proposal is less whether it is worth the money than who ends up holding what it produces.

In the weak version, most of the value stays with the marketplace. The brand funds a price cut during an event, the marketplace features it, and sales spike. Mercado Libre gets a stronger event, more traffic and the shopper data from every order. The brand gets lower margins on orders some shoppers would have placed anyway, and learns little about the rest.

In the strong version, the brand’s money buys something it keeps. It pays for visibility it could not otherwise get, in front of shoppers it wants to reach, with data that shows who responded and whether they came back.

Take two kitchenware brands that each commit the equivalent of US$20,000 to co-op campaigns with Mercado Libre during a Cyber Monday event in Mexico. One funds a 20% discount on its best-seller, featured on the event page. Orders triple for three days, then fall back. It cannot tell how many buyers were new, and its margin on those orders was thin.

The other negotiates a mix: a smaller discount, a branded placement on relevant search pages, and a report showing how many buyers were new to the brand and how many bought again within 60 days. It sells fewer units during the event but adds more new customers, and it learns which products those customers bought next. Both spent the same. Only the second bought something it can use again.

Negotiating co-op as media and data

Placement belongs in the deal alongside price. A discount alone competes on price with everyone else in the event; visibility in search results, on category pages or in brand placements is what makes the brand stand out while shoppers browse.

Data belongs in it too, agreed before the campaign: new versus returning buyers, the searches that led to purchases and repeat purchases after the event. That reporting is often worth more than the event’s sales.

Measurement should be set before the first order. Whether success means new customers, share of category sales or repeat purchase, and how it will be compared with a period without the campaign, needs agreeing up front. Co-op judged only on event-day sales will always look better than it is.

Co-op also has to be planned with the brand’s own Mercado Ads spending. A co-op placement during an event and the brand’s Product Ads on the same searches can compete for the same shopper, raising costs without adding reach. Agreeing with Mercado Libre which placements each budget pays for keeps the brand from paying twice for one visit.

Stock matters as well. A campaign that sends thousands of new shoppers to a product that runs out of stock on day one wastes most of its effect and can leave them with a poor first impression of the brand. Inventory for the event period should be confirmed before the brand commits, especially when shipping into Latin America takes weeks and a sell-out cannot be fixed mid-event.

The plan should differ by country. Mercado Libre’s position, its events and shoppers’ habits vary between Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and its other markets, and a brand new to a country gains more from co-op’s reach than one already well established there.

How far Mercado Ads extends its reporting for brands will shape how much co-op can deliver. The more data it shares about who buys and who returns, the stronger the case for treating co-op as media, and negotiating it that way is part of how we run Mercado Libre for brands.

A0144.crumb: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2021 changes for…
A0144.title: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2021 changes for advertisers
A0144.alt: An open cardboard box glowing with warm light from inside on a wooden desk against a navy wall.
A0144.ttag: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2021 changes for advertisers | Kwontified
A0144.desc: The headline at unBoxed 2021 was ads on Twitch, but the real change is measurement. Brands should set Brand Metrics baselines before 2022 budgets.
A0144.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 2, 2021.
A0144.body:
The announcement most people will remember from Amazon Ads unBoxed 2021 is Sponsored Display inside Twitch livestreams. It is a real new placement. It is also the least important part of the week for most brands, because a new place to show ads helps only if the brand can tell whether the ads work there. The change that matters is measurement.

Brand Metrics and Brand Lift let brands judge upper-funnel advertising on awareness and consideration, not only on last-click return. That gives Sponsored Display, video and DSP campaigns a fairer hearing, and it makes the next few weeks the moment to record a baseline, before 2022 budgets are set.

What Amazon Ads announced at unBoxed 2021

On October 26, 2021, the first day of the virtual conference, Amazon Ads announced eight advertising and measurement solutions, according to its announcement. Four stand out for brands selling on Amazon.

Brand Metrics, in beta, counts how many shoppers are in the awareness and consideration stages for a brand. It measures all shopping engagement with the brand on Amazon, not just engagement attributed to ads, Amazon Ads said. It is available in the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Spain.

Amazon Brand Lift lets Amazon DSP advertisers run studies on brand campaigns using a panel of opted-in Amazon shoppers, and Amazon is expanding Amazon Marketing Cloud to all of its DSP customers, Modern Retail reported. Sponsored Display ads, which already ran on Twitch’s browse and directory pages, will now also appear inside livestreams.

Judging the announcements by what they let a brand do

Read on launch language alone, unBoxed was about inventory: new places, like Twitch, to reach shoppers. That reading is partly right. The Twitch expansion gives Sponsored Display reach beyond Amazon’s own store, to viewers who are not shopping when they see the ad. For brands whose customers overlap with Twitch’s audience, such as gaming, electronics and snacks, it is a genuine new option.

What a product demonstrably changes is a better test than how it is announced, and on that test the measurement tools matter more. Upper-funnel advertising on Amazon has always had a weak point. Sponsored Display, video and DSP campaigns usually look poor on return on ad spend (ROAS), because the sales they influence often happen later, after a search, and get credited to whichever ad the shopper clicked last.

That habit of attribution pushes budgets one way. Every quarter, brands compare ROAS across campaigns, see that Sponsored Products returns more per dollar and move money there. Over time they stop building the awareness that feeds the searches their Sponsored Products ads depend on. Nobody decided to starve the upper funnel. The report decided for them, one quarter at a time, because it could only see the last click.

Take a brand that puts $20,000 a month on Sponsored Products at a ROAS of 4.0, and $8,000 on Sponsored Display and DSP at a ROAS of 1.5. On ROAS alone, the second line looks like the obvious cut. If the brand makes it, and branded searches for its products fall over the following months, its Sponsored Products results will fall too, and the cause will not appear in either campaign’s report. The cut would look like savings for a quarter and like a sales problem after that.

Brand Metrics and Brand Lift address that blind spot. A brand can now see how many shoppers are considering it, whether that number moves when upper-funnel spending changes, and, with Brand Lift, whether a DSP campaign changed awareness among the shoppers who saw it.

Amazon Marketing Cloud adds a third layer. For brands running DSP, it allows custom analysis of how shoppers moved between ad types before buying, which can show whether display exposure tends to come before branded searches and purchases. It takes analytical skill to use well, but its expansion to all DSP customers puts that analysis within reach of many more brands.

Using the new measurement in 2022 planning

Recording a baseline is the first job. Brands should check whether they are eligible for Brand Metrics and note current awareness and consideration figures before changing any upper-funnel budget. A baseline taken before the holiday season, when advertising spikes, will be more useful than one taken during it, and keeping the figures beside monthly ad spend lets later changes be read against what the brand was doing at the time.

Upper-funnel campaigns then need two measures instead of one. ROAS stays for what it measures well. A brand measure sits beside it: movement in consideration from Brand Metrics, or a Brand Lift result for a DSP campaign. A campaign with modest ROAS that grows consideration may be worth more than its attributed sales suggest.

The link to search closes the loop. Branded search volume and Sponsored Products results on branded terms belong on the same chart as upper-funnel spending. If they move together, the brand has evidence that awareness spending is feeding the searches it pays to win.

These tools are early, and the reading should be cautious. Brand Metrics is in beta, so its figures are best treated as directional until there are several months of history, and no single study should carry too much weight. Directional evidence is still better than judging every campaign on the same last-click measure.

How Amazon Ads connects these brand measures to its bidding and reporting in 2022 will decide how far they change day-to-day management. For now, recording the baseline before budgets are set is the step that cannot be taken later, and measuring across the funnel that way is how we measure Amazon advertising for brands.
