A0145.title: Walmart store fulfillment turns store stock into online stock
A0145.alt: A cart piled with taped cardboard parcels in a stockroom aisle lined with shelves of kitchenware.
A0145.ttag: Walmart store fulfillment turns store stock into online stock | Kwontified
A0145.desc: Walmart fulfills many online orders from its stores, so store stock is online stock. Brands should plan inventory, content and promotions around that.
A0145.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 4, 2021.
A0145.body:
At some brands, the Walmart store business and the Walmart.com business still sit with different teams. One watches shelf sales and store replenishment; the other watches the product page and online orders. Where that split exists, it tends to follow the targets: the store team is judged on what ships to Walmart and sells off the shelf, the online team on Walmart.com sales. Walmart no longer separates the two that way. It fills a growing share of online orders, especially grocery pickup and delivery, from its stores, and some of those stores now contain small automated warehouses.

For a brand in Walmart’s store assortment, that means store inventory is online inventory. Replenishment, product content and promotions belong in one plan, because one shelf now serves both kinds of shopper.

How Walmart store fulfillment works

The store network is the starting point. Tom Ward, Walmart’s senior vice president of customer product, has pointed out that 90% of Americans live within 10 miles of a Walmart, Drug Store News reported, which puts a store within easy reach of most online shoppers.

In January 2021, Walmart said it would turn dozens of its stores into local fulfillment centers, with some becoming small automated warehouses inside the existing store or in an extension, CNBC reported. A system called Alphabot, tested at a store in Salem, New Hampshire since 2019, picks orders within minutes and has them ready within an hour. Walmart had already raised its pickup and delivery slot capacity by 40% during the pandemic, CNBC reported, and some of the new centers will also supply orders collected at nearby stores.

Online sales have kept growing on that foundation. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales grew 6% in the second quarter of 2021 and 103% over two years, according to its release.

One detergent order, picked from a store shelf

Take a shopper who opens the Walmart app on a Tuesday morning and orders groceries and household goods for pickup that afternoon, including a bottle of a brand’s laundry detergent. The app shows what the local store has in stock. If the detergent is out of stock there, it either does not appear as available or is flagged for substitution.

The order is picked in the store, partly by staff walking the aisles and, in stores with an automated center, partly by machines retrieving frequently ordered items. If the store’s shelf count is wrong, or the last bottle sold an hour earlier, the order is substituted with another brand or the item is dropped. The shopper collects the order at 4 p.m.

At every step, the store’s inventory decided whether the brand made the sale. The detergent may be plentiful in a distribution center, but if the local store is short, the online order is lost, and the shopper may try the substitute and keep buying it.

The product page mattered as much as the shelf. The shopper chose the detergent from a product page in the app, and that page, with its images, description and reviews, did the work a shelf display does in the aisle.

Planning store stock as online stock

Store availability becomes an online metric. For products sold through Walmart’s stores, store-level in-stock rates now determine online sales as well as shelf sales, so the store-level data deserves the same attention as the online dashboard. The fastest-moving items, especially those ordered often for pickup, are where replenishment work with Walmart pays first.

Content for store-assortment products needs to catch up. Many brands treat the Walmart.com product page as secondary for items they sell mainly in stores. When those items are ordered online for pickup or delivery, the product page is where the choice happens, and its images, titles and descriptions should be as good as those for products sold mainly online.

Promotions need one calendar across stores and online. Walmart now often runs events online first and in stores later. Its Black Friday Deals for Days events begin online on November 3 and November 10 and reach stores two days later, with early online access for Walmart+ members, according to Walmart’s announcement. Stock has to reach the stores in time for online demand that arrives before the in-store event.

Forecasting has to change with it. Store orders have traditionally been forecast from shelf sales while online demand was planned separately. When the same shelf serves both, a store’s demand includes pickup and delivery orders that may spike around online promotions, Walmart+ member events and holidays, and brands that share online demand signals with their Walmart replenishment plans will see fewer gaps.

Marketplace sellers sit outside all of this. Products sold only through Walmart’s marketplace are not on store shelves, and they ship from the seller’s own warehouse or from Walmart’s fulfillment centers. For them, the store network is a competitor rather than a channel, since a store-stocked alternative available for pickup the same day can win the sale. A brand that sells both ways should know which of its products sit in which system.

Substitution is the quiet cost. When a store-fulfilled order cannot include the item ordered, the substitute introduces the shopper to a competing product, so a brand that is often out of stock in stores is handing trial to its competitors through Walmart’s own online orders.

Each new automated center makes store-fulfilled orders faster and more accurate, and raises the cost of being out of stock in that store. The question for a brand’s leadership is whether one person owns the shelf for both kinds of shopper. Planning store and online as one Walmart business is how we manage Walmart for brands.

A0149.crumb: A Target Plus operations checklist for…
A0149.title: A Target Plus operations checklist for the holiday season
A0149.alt: A clipboard checklist with some boxes ticked beside a stack of red, twine-tied gift parcels.
A0149.ttag: A Target Plus operations checklist for the holiday season | Kwontified
A0149.desc: Target Plus sellers ship their own orders into a store-fulfilled retailer. A holiday checklist covers stock, shipping, pricing, returns and service.
A0149.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 11, 2021.
A0149.body:
It is the Saturday after Thanksgiving, and a home goods seller on Target Plus is watching orders run at four times a normal day. Its warehouse team, two people short because of illness, finishes packing at 9 p.m. A batch of orders misses the carrier’s last pickup and ships on Monday, a day after the promised date.

On Tuesday a shopper who ordered towels as a gift writes to ask where the order is. The inbox has 140 unread messages, and the reply goes out on Thursday. By then the shopper has cancelled, and on Friday leaves a one-star review mentioning the delay. Nothing in that week involved a bad product or a bad price: it was a staffing gap, a carrier cutoff and an inbox nobody owned on a weekend. For a Target Plus seller, which ships its own orders inside a store-fulfilled retailer, the holiday season tests operations more than marketing.

A short operations checklist, reviewed weekly through December, prevents most of those failures. Running it takes a fixed slot in the weekly calendar and one owner who looks at all of it, rather than five teams who each look at a part.

Why the Target Plus operations checklist matters more than usual

Target’s growth runs through its stores. Stores fulfilled more than 95% of Target’s second-quarter 2021 sales, Target reported. Target Plus sits outside that system: each seller keeps its own inventory and ships its own orders, and shoppers can bring marketplace purchases back to a Target store, according to the Star Tribune. Fewer than 300 sellers were on the invitation-only marketplace in early 2021, by Marketplace Pulse’s count, as cited by Kaspien.

That small size cuts both ways. A Target Plus seller faces less open competition than on a large marketplace, but its failures are visible. Its products sit beside Target’s own store-fulfilled range, and a late parcel or an unanswered question looks worse next to an order the shopper could have collected the same day. A curated marketplace notices performance problems of exactly the kind the Saturday seller had.

This season adds pressure. Target’s holiday price match guarantee covers October 10 to December 24, Chain Store Age reported, and holiday deals started earlier than ever, so the busy period is longer as well as more intense.

The weekly holiday checklist

Five areas cover most of the risk. One person should review all of them every week from now until the end of December.

Stock for the top 20 products should be checked against forecast demand through December, including demand pulled forward by early deals. Each product needs a reorder point, and the seller should decide in advance which products to stop advertising if stock runs low.

Shipping promises have to match peak volume rather than an average day. Handling times and delivery promises on listings should reflect what the warehouse and carriers can do in the busiest week, with carrier pickup times, holiday cutoffs and weekend staffing for the days after Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday confirmed. When in doubt, a slightly slower promise that is kept beats a fast one that is broken.

Price-match exposure runs all season, because prices on Target.com are compared with other retailers until December 24. Target Plus prices should be checked against the brand’s own website and other marketplaces, with promotions planned so a discount elsewhere does not open a gap nobody intended.

Store returns of marketplace items need an owner on the seller’s side. The seller should ask Target how store returns of its products are processed and refunded, build the expected holiday return rate into margins and name who handles the returns that come back.

The customer service inbox needs a named owner on every day of the holiday period, weekends included. A response target measured in hours, and short prepared answers for the predictable questions about delivery dates, gift receipts, returns and order changes, keep a busy weekend from turning into a week of complaints.

How the five areas fail together

The areas are linked, which is why one person should look at them together. A stock shortage becomes a shipping failure if a listing stays live after the warehouse runs out, and a shipping failure becomes a customer service problem within days. When each area belongs to a separate team, nobody sees the chain until the review arrives. The one-star review in the Saturday example was the last link in a chain that started with a staffing gap on the Saturday before, and every link was visible to someone who was not looking at the others.

The week after Christmas deserves planning too. Gift returns arrive in late December and January, many of them at Target stores, and gift recipients ask questions the original buyer never would. A seller staffed only for the selling peak can be caught out by the returns peak that follows.

The specific performance standards in a seller’s Target Plus partner agreement and seller portal are the right yardstick, measured weekly. They matter all year, but the holidays are when sellers most often fall behind them.

The checklist also builds a record that outlasts the season. Weekly notes on what went wrong make a stronger case for stock, staffing and carrier decisions in 2022, and a clear account if Target asks about performance. The figures to watch first are late shipments and response times in the week after Cyber Monday. If they hold, the operation is ready for the rest of the season, and holding that line is how we run Target Plus operations for brands.

A0151.crumb: How Buy Box changes quietly drain profit…
A0151.title: How Buy Box changes quietly drain profit on Amazon
A0151.alt: A brass tap dripping water into a blue mug full of coins on a worn wooden counter.
A0151.ttag: How Buy Box changes quietly drain profit on Amazon | Kwontified
A0151.desc: When a brand loses the Amazon Buy Box, sales and ad results fall, and teams often blame advertising. Track Buy Box share weekly to find the real cause.
A0151.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 16, 2021.
A0151.body:
A brand sells a $30 product with a $9 margin and holds the Amazon Buy Box 95% of the time. Then a reseller starts offering the same product at $28.50, and over three weeks the brand’s Buy Box share falls to 60%. Nobody on the brand’s team sees that number move. What they see is conversion dropping in the advertising report, so they raise bids and add $3,000 a month in spend. Sales do not recover, because about 40% of the shoppers the ads attract now buy from the reseller.

That sequence is easy to fall into, because Buy Box losses rarely announce themselves. They surface first as weaker ad results, and the natural response, spending more, makes them worse. Buy Box share deserves its own weekly line in the report, checked before anyone touches an advertising budget.

How Amazon Buy Box changes happen

The Buy Box is the panel on an Amazon product page with the Add to Cart and Buy Now buttons. When several sellers offer the same product, Amazon’s algorithm chooses which offer is featured there, and most shoppers buy that offer without looking at the others.

The criteria matter enough that regulators are examining them. On November 10, 2020, the European Commission opened an investigation into the criteria Amazon uses to select the Buy Box winner and to let sellers offer products to Prime members. It is examining whether those criteria favor Amazon’s own retail business or sellers using its logistics and delivery services, CNBC reported. Reaching Amazon’s more than 112 million Prime members, and winning the Buy Box, both matter to sellers, CNBC noted.

For a brand, the practical point is that the Buy Box can move for reasons outside its advertising: a reseller’s lower price, slower fulfillment, a performance metric that slips, or a change in how Amazon weighs those factors. When no offer meets Amazon’s standards, the Buy Box can disappear altogether, leaving shoppers to pick from a list of sellers.

Why the advertising report gets the blame

The pull here is misattribution. When sales fall, the first report most teams open is the advertising report, because it is reviewed most often and shows clear numbers. If the Buy Box has moved, that report shows the symptoms: lower conversion, lower return on ad spend (ROAS) and a higher cost per sale. It does not show the cause.

So the response targets the symptom. Bids go up, keywords are added, budgets grow. If the cause was the Buy Box, each of those steps makes things worse. The ads keep sending shoppers to a listing where another seller wins the sale, or where the Buy Box has been suppressed and many shoppers leave without buying.

In the example, the second cost arrives when the team finally opens the Buy Box report. Matching the reseller’s price takes $1.50 off every unit and cuts the margin by a sixth. What looked like an advertising problem was a pricing and distribution problem all along, and the extra ad spend bought sales for a competitor.

The arithmetic of the leak is plain. At a 60% Buy Box share, roughly 40% of the clicks the brand pays for end in someone else’s sale. Raising bids buys more of those clicks, not better ones. Every added dollar of spend carries the same leak, so the cost of each sale the brand actually keeps rises with every increase in budget.

Diagnosing the Buy Box before touching the budget

Buy Box share belongs in the weekly report for every important product, next to sales and advertising results. When conversion falls, it is the first thing to check. A drop points to price, fulfillment or seller performance rather than to the ads. The check takes minutes. Skipping it can cost weeks of spend aimed at the wrong problem.

The cause decides the fix. If a reseller is winning on price, the question is where its stock comes from and whether the brand’s distribution agreements are being followed. If the brand’s own offer has slipped on fulfillment speed or performance metrics, the fix is operational. If the Buy Box has been suppressed, the brand should compare its Amazon price with prices elsewhere online.

Advertising on a product that has lost the Buy Box should pause until it is back, because spending to send shoppers to a listing the brand is not winning pays for someone else’s sale.

Vendors selling to Amazon meet a version of the same problem. When Amazon is the retailer its own offer usually holds the Buy Box, but a third-party seller offering the product for less can win it. Sales that would have gone through Amazon’s retail offer go to the reseller instead, Amazon’s own sales of the product fall, and over time that can show up in smaller purchase orders that the vendor never connects to the Buy Box.

Cross-channel pricing needs the same care. A promotion on a brand’s own website, or a retailer’s clearance sale, can make the Amazon price look high by comparison, so promotions are best planned with the Buy Box in mind rather than discovered afterward in the ad reports.

The holiday season raises every one of these stakes. Prices move quickly in November and December, resellers stock up on popular products and fulfillment slows under peak volume, all at the moment advertising budgets are highest. An unexplained conversion drop on a product whose advertising has not changed is the earliest sign, and checking the Buy Box before the bids is how we run Amazon for brands.

A0152.title: Walmart’s in-store returns change the economics of selling online
A0152.alt: Paper mailer bag with bubble wrap beside a blue wire basket of folded towels on a sunlit windowsill shelf.
A0152.ttag: Walmart’s in-store returns change the economics of selling online | Kwontified
A0152.desc: Walmart made returns fast and free using its stores and FedEx. That raises shopper expectations, and marketplace sellers pay to meet them online.
A0152.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 18, 2021.
A0152.body:
A shopper who returns a Walmart.com order can drop it at a store on the way to buy groceries, or schedule a free FedEx pickup from home, and see the refund as soon as the next day. Walmart can offer that experience at a lower cost than most sellers, because its stores do much of the work. A marketplace seller on Walmart.com pays more to match it, and shoppers do not distinguish between the two when they decide whom to trust.

Walmart has turned returns into a service standard that its own network makes cheap and its marketplace sellers have to pay for. Those sellers should treat returns as a planned cost of the channel, budgeted and actively reduced, rather than as noise in the monthly margin.

How Walmart in-store returns and free pickup set the expectation

Walmart has long taken returns at its stores. In December 2020 it extended the convenience to shoppers who never visit one. It launched Carrier Pickup by FedEx, a free service that lets customers schedule a pickup of returns for items sold and shipped by Walmart.com, and said it would continue beyond the holidays, according to Walmart.

Refunds sped up at the same time. Refunds for online returns are credited as soon as the next day, and in-store returns the same day, EcommerceBytes reported. Shoppers can also start a return in the Walmart app to make the in-store step quicker.

The stores underpin all of it. By a Walmart executive’s count, 90% of Americans live within 10 miles of one of its stores, Drug Store News reported, so most shoppers can return an item on an ordinary errand. A store that receives an unopened return may also be able to put it back on its own shelf rather than ship it to a returns center.

Who pays for the expectation

Returns are one of the largest hidden costs of selling online. A returned item costs a shipping label, handling, inspection and often a markdown if it cannot be resold as new. For Walmart’s own products, the store network trims several of those: the shopper carries the item back, the store inspects it, and some of it goes back on the shelf.

Marketplace sellers do not have that network. When a shopper returns a marketplace item, the seller usually pays for the return shipping and handles the item at its own warehouse. Some sellers use Walmart Fulfillment Services, which can simplify the handling, but even then the item travels back through a fulfillment center rather than onto a nearby shelf.

The expectation, though, is shared. A shopper who has returned a Walmart-sold item at a store, with an instant refund, will expect a marketplace seller to make returns just as easy. Walmart’s own standards push the same way: free returns across the catalog were among the criteria for its Pro Seller badge when it launched in October 2020, Feedvisor reported. Walmart sets the standard, and the seller absorbs the cost of meeting it.

That is the hidden structure of the arrangement. The retailer’s investment in stores and carrier partnerships becomes a promise to every shopper on the site, and the parts of that promise its own network does not cover land on the sellers who share the page.

Take a seller moving 2,000 units a month of a $35 kitchen item on Walmart’s marketplace, with 6% returned. Each return costs $8 in shipping and handling, and a third cannot be resold at full price, losing a further $15 each. That comes to about $960 a month in return shipping and handling and $600 in markdowns, roughly 2.2% of sales. During the holiday season, with gift returns arriving in January, both the rate and the cost rise.

Planning returns as a cost of the Walmart channel

The first step is to put returns into the margin. An expected return rate and a cost per return belong in the economics of every product sold on Walmart’s marketplace, with both raised for December and January.

Cutting avoidable returns is the second lever. Many come from products that did not match the shopper’s expectations, and clear dimensions, accurate images and honest descriptions of what is and is not included cut them before they happen. Return reasons reviewed monthly point to the listings that need fixing first. Comparing return rates across channels helps too: a product returned far more often on Walmart than on Amazon or the brand’s own site usually has something specific wrong with its Walmart listing, such as missing details or an outdated image.

Processing should be cheap by design, because some returns will come back whatever the listing says. Packaging that lets unopened returns be resold, a simple inspection routine and an advance decision on which returns will be resold, refurbished or liquidated all reduce what each return costs.

Returns also shape a seller’s standing on Walmart.com. High return rates show up in reviews that mention a poor fit or a disappointing finish, and in the listing quality Walmart measures, so a product with a high rate is often losing sales as well as refunds. Fixing its listing pays twice.

Gift returns make the timing urgent. Items bought in November and December come back in late December and January, often from recipients who never placed the order, and a seller that plans staffing and storage for that wave will refund shoppers before frustration turns into a poor review.

Whether Walmart extends store returns to more marketplace items will decide how long this imbalance lasts. Until it does, building returns into the plan for each product is how we run Walmart Marketplace accounts for brands.

A0153.crumb: Paid and organic growth on Amazon need…
A0153.title: Paid and organic growth on Amazon need each other
A0153.alt: Blue and natural twisted rope toy on a weathered wooden bench beside a ceramic cup and twine spool.
A0153.ttag: Paid and organic growth on Amazon need each other | Kwontified
A0153.desc: Amazon ad costs keep rising, and paid growth alone gets more expensive. Brands should balance ad spend with the listings, reviews and stock behind it.
A0153.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 23, 2021.
A0153.body:
If a click costs the same and conversion rises from 8% to 12%, the advertising cost of each sale falls by a third. Nothing about the bid or the budget has to change. Cost per sale is the click price divided by conversion, so the listing sets the price of every sale the ads buy. That one piece of arithmetic is the strongest argument against treating Amazon advertising and the listing behind it as separate jobs.

Paid traffic on Amazon is getting more expensive per sale. A brand that relies on advertising alone pays more each year for the same growth, while a brand that invests only in organic visibility grows too slowly to be found. Paid and organic growth work as linked engines, advertising to start momentum and listings, reviews and stock to keep it, and they should be budgeted and measured together.

Why paid and organic growth on Amazon depend on each other

Sponsored Products ad spend was up 41.8% on the year in the third quarter of 2021, while return on ad spend (ROAS) fell 6.1%, in Pacvue’s figures. More brands are bidding for the same shoppers, and each sale bought through advertising costs more than it did a year earlier.

Amazon is also handing brands more tools that build organic performance. At Accelerate on October 20, it said brands using Manage Your Experiments to test their product pages had increased sales by up to 25%. It also said brands had added A+ Content to more than a million product pages in 2021, according to its announcement. Amazon Vine, which helps brands gather early reviews on new products, costs as little as $200 per enrolled product, Amazon said.

The two kinds of growth feed each other. Advertising brings shoppers to a product page. Whether they buy depends on the page itself: its images, its reviews, its price and whether it is in stock. And many sellers observe that products with strong, steady sales tend to rank better in organic search over time, which brings more shoppers without paying for each one.

Buying growth versus building it

Every brand faces the same choice about the next dollar. Advertising produces sales quickly and measurably. The listing, reviews and stock work more slowly and are harder to credit. Advertising wins most budget meetings because its results show up within days.

Both sides have a real case. Advertising on a weak listing is expensive, because a page that converts poorly turns each paid click into fewer sales. Organic investment alone has the opposite problem: a new product with an excellent page will still sell slowly if shoppers never find it.

Take two brands launching similar products, each with $10,000 a month to spend.

Brand oneBrand two
Advertising a month$10,000$7,500
Listing, Vine and image testingnone$2,500
Ad conversion8%12%
ROAS2.03.0

Brand one runs its ads to a listing with four images and no reviews. When it cuts spending after three months, sales fall back, because the product has gathered few reviews and little organic ranking. Brand two reaches its higher conversion after two months, a growing share of its sales comes from organic search, and when it cuts spending its sales hold up better.

Both spent the same. The second bought less traffic but got more from each click, and built visibility that kept working after the spending stopped. In a year when clicks keep getting more expensive, conversion is one of the few levers a brand controls completely, which is why the numbers lean toward building alongside buying.

Running both engines together

The page comes before the budget. Before spending rises on a product, its images, title, A+ Content, reviews and stock deserve a check, because every gain in conversion lowers the cost of each sale bought through advertising.

Launch advertising needs a planned exit, written down before the launch starts. As reviews accumulate and organic sales grow, spending can shift from buying every sale to defending key search terms and reaching new shoppers.

Paid and organic sales belong in one report, because ROAS on its own cannot see the organic sales that advertising helps to build. Total sales, organic sales and advertising cost as a share of total sales say more than ROAS alone, and a falling advertising share with total sales holding is the sign the two engines are working together.

The usual obstacle is organizational. In many brands one team runs advertising and is measured on ROAS, while another manages listings and content with no advertising target at all, and each optimizes its own part. Shared goals for total sales and advertising cost as a share of sales make the trade-offs visible and let the budget go where it does the most good.

For products already on sale, a workable order is to take the weakest page among the top advertised products, fix it, then raise its budget, and repeat down the list. Each step is small. Taken together, they can move the cost of an advertising program as much as a round of bid changes, and they keep paying after the bids are changed again.

The holiday season is a useful test. Products with strong pages and steady reviews convert the extra traffic holiday advertising brings, while weak pages waste it at the year’s highest click prices. If advertising cost as a share of total sales keeps rising while total sales stay flat, the brand is buying growth it is not keeping, and running both engines from one plan is how we grow brands on Amazon.

A0154.crumb: Mercado Libre’s push into grocery opens a…
A0154.title: Mercado Libre’s push into grocery opens a door for CPG brands
A0154.alt: Wooden crate of pantry goods and a mustard canvas tote on a doorstep beside a teal door on a cobbled street.
A0154.ttag: Mercado Libre’s push into grocery opens a door for CPG brands | Kwontified
A0154.desc: Mercado Libre is building a supermarket business, and its grocery shoppers buy more often. CPG brands should test it with a focused, well-stocked range.
A0154.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 24, 2021.
A0154.body:
Ask a Latin American consumer goods company where its sales come from and the answer has usually been supermarkets and wholesale. Mercado Libre, where it appears in the plan at all, has been the channel for electronics, auto parts and home goods. That view made sense when the marketplace was mainly a place to buy phones and spare parts. It makes less sense now that the marketplace is building a supermarket business of its own.

Mercado Libre is adding its own inventory, grocery partners and a growing fulfillment network, and it reports that its supermarket buyers purchase more often and stay longer. CPG brands that still treat it as a general-merchandise channel should test it now, with a focused range, dependable stock and early advertising.

What the Mercado Libre grocery push involves

The company has been building the category for months. On its second-quarter earnings call, it said buyer demand in consumer packaged goods and its supermarket experience had surpassed expectations, and that it was accelerating fulfillment operations for the category, according to a transcript of the call. It added that first-party inventory, products it buys and sells itself, would complement partners’ assortment.

The third-quarter call went further. Mercado Libre said its marketplace is increasingly filled with well-known brands in beauty, consumer electronics and consumer packaged goods, from marketplace sellers and its own first-party assortment, according to a transcript. In São Paulo it began working with Mambo, a local food retailer, to offer fresh products, and it is setting up similar partnerships in Buenos Aires and Mexico City. It also said supermarket buyers show higher purchase frequency and better retention than other buyers.

Read as an institution, Mercado Libre’s move makes sense. A shopper who buys detergent every month opens the app every month, and every visit is a chance to sell something else, through the marketplace, Mercado Pago or Mercado Ads. Grocery matters to the company less as a category than as a habit it wants to own.

The scale behind this is large. Mercado Libre sold almost 260 million items in the third quarter, up more than 26% from a year earlier, and its gross merchandise volume reached a record of more than $7.3 billion, the company said on the same call.

The decision on the CPG leadership team’s desk

For a CPG leadership team, the question is usually framed as whether a marketplace can sell detergent, coffee and shampoo profitably. Mercado Libre’s own statements suggest it can, at least for some products. Grocery shoppers who come back often are valuable to a marketplace, and Mercado Libre is investing to serve them with more fulfillment centers, same-day delivery from them and partnerships for fresh food.

The sharper question is which products suit the channel. Low-priced, heavy items are expensive to ship one at a time. Products bought in bulk, in multipacks or at a higher price per unit, such as personal care, baby products, pet food and specialty foods, fit the economics better.

Take a premium coffee brand that sells a 250-gram bag in supermarkets at the equivalent of US$8. On Mercado Libre it offers a pack of four bags, with a grinder-friendly description and subscription-style messaging. The larger basket covers shipping and fees, and buyers who like the coffee come back each month. A brand of basic table salt, by contrast, cannot make a single bag work online, however good the listing.

Mercado Libre’s first-party business adds a decision about the model. A brand can sell to Mercado Libre as a supplier, sell directly as a marketplace seller through an official store, or both. The trade-offs will be familiar from Amazon: selling to the marketplace gives up control of price in exchange for simpler operations, while selling directly keeps control but puts stock, pricing and customer service on the brand. Choosing the model country by country before launch beats drifting into both.

Pricing across channels needs care too. Supermarket partners and distributors will notice if a brand’s products are much cheaper on Mercado Libre than on their shelves, and a range built around multipacks and online-only bundles makes direct comparison harder while keeping existing customer relationships intact.

Running a CPG test on Mercado Libre

A focused range is the place to start: products whose price per order covers shipping and fees, multipacks where they make sense, and one country before several.

Stock belongs in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network. Repeat buyers expect fast, reliable delivery, and fulfillment and same-day services are where Mercado Libre is concentrating its investment. A product that runs out loses exactly the repeat customers that make grocery valuable.

The test should be judged on repeat purchase rather than first sales. The value of grocery to Mercado Libre, and to a brand, comes from shoppers who come back, so the share of buyers who reorder within 60 or 90 days is the number that shows whether the channel will work.

Early advertising establishes the brand before the category fills up. As more CPG brands arrive, search results for everyday products will crowd, and brands that build visibility, reviews and repeat buyers now will be harder to displace. Mercado Ads, relaunched in September 2020, offers product ads and larger brand campaigns, Advertising Week reported.

Whether the grocery partnerships in Buenos Aires and Mexico City launch as Mercado Libre has said will show how fast the window is closing. The question for a CPG leadership team is which line of next year’s plan Mercado Libre belongs on, and answering it with a test is how we manage Mercado Libre for consumer brands.

A0157.crumb: Is Target Plus cannibalizing your direct…
A0157.title: Is Target Plus cannibalizing your direct sales?
A0157.alt: Twine-tied brown paper parcel on a stone doorstep in front of a weathered wooden door on a city street.
A0157.ttag: Is Target Plus cannibalizing your direct sales? | Kwontified
A0157.desc: Brands worry that Target Plus takes sales from their own site. Some overlap is real, but it can be measured through new customers, site trends and price.
A0157.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 30, 2021.
A0157.body:
A Target Plus launch often starts small. A brand launches a slice of its range, sales arrive, and someone in the next planning meeting asks the obvious question: how much of that would we have sold on our own site anyway? The fear is reasonable. The usual answer, taken on instinct, is wrong in the other direction.

Some overlap is real. But many of the shoppers on Target.com are Target’s shoppers first, and they rarely visit a brand’s own website, so the worry tends to overstate the effect. Overlap can be measured directly, through new-customer share, the own-site trend and price alignment, and it should be measured before anyone trims the Target Plus range on an assumption.

Where Target Plus cannibalization would come from

Target Plus is Target’s curated, invitation-only marketplace, where brands sell on Target.com beside Target’s own range while holding their own stock and shipping their own orders, the Star Tribune reported. It is small: Kaspien, announcing its own approval to sell there, cited Marketplace Pulse figures of fewer than 300 sellers in early 2021.

Target.com, by contrast, has a large audience of its own. Target’s comparable digital sales grew 10% in its second quarter of 2021, on top of strong growth a year earlier, and more than 95% of its sales were fulfilled by its stores, Target reported.

The mechanism behind the fear is simple. A shopper who would have bought from the brand’s website buys the same product on Target.com instead. The brand still makes the sale, but it pays marketplace fees and loses the customer’s data, and with it any later direct sale to that shopper.

Why the fear usually overstates the effect

Part of the fear is justified. Some shoppers know the brand, compare prices across sites and buy wherever is cheapest or most convenient. If the products are cheaper on Target.com, or Target offers faster delivery or easier returns, some loyal customers will switch.

The rest usually does not hold. Many shoppers on Target.com are there because they shop at Target, not because they went looking for a particular brand. They are browsing a category, filling a basket or adding something to a store pickup order. Many have never visited the brand’s website and would not have bought from it.

Take a skincare brand that launches 40 products on Target Plus and sells $50,000 a month there after three months. Its own site, which had been growing 2% a month, keeps growing at roughly the same rate, and its own new-customer rate is unchanged. A survey of Target Plus buyers finds that 70% had never bought from the brand before. Most of the $50,000 is new business. Even if part of the remaining 30% would have bought on the brand’s site, the brand gained far more than it gave up.

The survey also caps the possible damage. In the worst case, where every returning customer would otherwise have bought on the brand’s own site, overlap is limited to that minority of buyers. The new customers are pure addition, and the brand’s own-site trend confirms whether even the minority actually moved.

The opposite pattern would tell a different story. If the brand’s own sales had flattened at the moment Target Plus sales began, and most Target Plus buyers were existing customers, the fear would be confirmed, and the range or the pricing would need rethinking.

Measuring overlap instead of assuming it

New-customer share is the first number. Post-purchase surveys, packaging inserts with a code and other first-party signals show how many Target Plus buyers already knew the brand. A high share of new customers means Target Plus is extending reach rather than cannibalizing it.

The own-site trend is the second. Growth on the brand’s site in the months before and after the Target Plus launch, adjusted for seasonality and the brand’s own marketing, shows whether anything broke. A clear break that coincides with the launch is a warning sign. A steady trend is not. Where it is practical, staggering launches, adding some product lines to Target Plus before others, turns the comparison into a test: each line’s own-site sales can be read against lines that have not launched yet.

Price alignment is the lever that matters most. The fastest way to move existing customers to a marketplace is to make the marketplace cheaper. Consistent prices across channels, with exclusive bundles or sizes on Target Plus where the brand wants a difference, keep loyal customers where they are.

Search data adds a cross-check. If searches for the brand’s name on search engines and on its own site hold steady after launch, shoppers are still seeking the brand out directly. A drop in branded traffic to the brand’s site alongside rising Target Plus sales would suggest some existing customers have moved.

The holiday season muddies the reading. Every channel rises in November and December, and gift buyers behave differently from regular customers. A brand that launched on Target Plus in 2021 should compare with the same weeks of the previous year on its own site rather than with the months just before launch.

A Target Plus customer may also be worth more than the first order. A shopper who discovers the brand on Target.com may later visit its own site or buy it at another retailer, which is hard to measure precisely but argues against judging Target Plus on each order’s margin alone. As long as the new-customer share stays high, Target Plus is building reach, and measuring that alongside the brand’s own channels is how we run Target Plus for brands.

A0158.crumb: How Zalando localized across Europe, and…
A0158.title: How Zalando localized across Europe, and what brands should copy
A0158.alt: Row of six orange-wrapped gift boxes tied with different colored ribbons and twine on a wooden table.
A0158.ttag: How Zalando localized across Europe, and what brands should copy | Kwontified
A0158.desc: Zalando entered six European markets in 2021 with local assortments, payments and marketing. Brands selling there should localize just as deliberately.
A0158.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 2, 2021.
A0158.body:
A brand that sells on Zalando in Germany can open in Estonia through the Partner Program with little more than a settings change: switch on the market, let the catalog flow across, translate the descriptions automatically. Zalando did not enter Estonia that way, and the difference explains why its own launches in 2021 went so well.

Zalando entered six Central and Eastern European markets in 2021 and built each launch around local conditions: assortment, payment, delivery and marketing, not just language. It opened its Partner Program in the same markets, so brands can sell there directly. A brand that does should treat each country as its own launch, with its own range, prices and content, rather than as a translated copy of Germany.

What Zalando localization looked like in its 2021 launches

Zalando launched in Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia in early June 2021, and in Croatia, Estonia and Latvia in late July, according to its second-quarter results. At the same time it extended the Partner Program, which lets brands sell directly on the platform, to all six markets.

Each launch was built around local conditions. Customers in the new markets get free delivery and free returns for up to 30 days, and Zalando said it would follow the launches with social-first marketing campaigns run with local influencers and partners, according to its launch announcement. It describes the offer in the new markets as locally tailored assortments with local payment methods, FashionNetwork reported.

The early results for Zalando itself are strong. On its third-quarter call it said it was serving up to 1.5% of the population in the new markets as customers just 12 weeks after launch. Its app was the most downloaded fashion app in all six, according to a transcript of the call. Across the business, active customers reached 46.3 million in the third quarter, up from 35.6 million a year earlier, according to its results presentation. Zalando plans to launch in Hungary and Romania in 2022.

Why one European range sells badly in six markets

Selling across Europe through one platform can look like selling to one market. Shoppers in Zagreb, Tallinn and Bratislava differ in what they wear, what they pay, how they pay and which sizes sell. A store that simply translates its German range carries products that do not suit the climate, prices that do not suit local incomes and sizes that do not match local demand.

The habit has a structural cause. It is easy for a brand to run Zalando from one team, often the one that built the German business, with one range plan and one price list for the whole platform, because the platform presents itself as one storefront. The platform’s own launches show the alternative: delivery and returns treated as part of the local offer, payment methods chosen for local shoppers, and marketing run through local voices rather than one European campaign.

Take an outerwear brand that sells 300 styles on Zalando in Germany and opens in the Baltic markets through the Partner Program with the same 300 styles at the same euro prices. Lightweight rain jackets that sell well in Hamburg barely move in Tallinn in November, while heavier coats sell out in the first week. Its product descriptions, machine-translated from German, describe fits and fabrics in terms that read awkwardly in Estonian. None of these problems shows up in the German results the team watches most closely.

A localized launch would have looked different: a range weighted toward heavier outerwear, deeper stock in the sizes that sell locally, prices set against local competitors and descriptions written or checked by native speakers.

Launching a brand in a new Zalando market

A brand’s range is the first thing to localize. Local climate, seasonality and competitors should decide which styles go into each market and how deep, rather than listing everything. Size curves deserve particular care, because the mix that sells in one country can differ from the next. Stock spread evenly across sizes runs out in some and sits unsold in others, and early sales data from each new market should reset the curve quickly.

Prices should be set market by market. A single euro price ignores differences in income and competition, so it pays to check what comparable products sell for locally and adjust where the brand’s positioning allows.

Content needs native speakers in every market, not just the large ones. Titles, descriptions and size guidance written or reviewed by people who speak the language convert better, and machine translation is a starting point rather than a finished listing. Poor content raises returns as well as lowering conversion, which matters more where returns are free for 30 days.

The choice of model matters in each market too. Selling wholesale to Zalando leaves assortment and pricing largely with Zalando’s buyers. Selling through the Partner Program puts those decisions, and the work of localizing, with the brand. In new markets, where Zalando’s own buyers are still learning local demand, a brand that knows its customers can often do better through the Partner Program, provided it invests in the local range and content.

Launch timing can work in a brand’s favor as well. A brand that is ready when Zalando opens a market benefits from the attention the launch brings: more than 1% of the population in the new markets joined during one four-day sales event, Zalando’s results presentation showed. The next openings, Hungary and Romania, are the ones to prepare for now, and planning a range, price list and content for each of them separately is how we launch brands in new Zalando markets.

A0160.title: Cyber Week 2021 results, measured against the forecast
A0160.alt: Stack of botanical-print wrapped gifts with twine and sprigs, a brass caliper leaning against them on a wooden table.
A0160.ttag: Cyber Week 2021 results, measured against the forecast | Kwontified
A0160.desc: Cyber Week 2021 came in below forecast, but November as a whole grew. Judge results against the season and your planning ranges, not the peak days.
A0160.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 7, 2021.
A0160.body:
Cyber Monday 2021 brought in $10.7 billion in US online sales, down 1.4% from 2020 and below every forecast made in October. Over the same stretch, shoppers had spent $109.8 billion online since November 1, nearly 12% more than a year earlier. One of those numbers is a peak shrinking. The other is a season growing. Both are true, and reading only the first leads to the wrong lessons.

The result confirms that demand moved earlier rather than disappeared. Before changing budgets or plans for 2022, brands should judge Cyber Week against the season and their own planning ranges, not against the size of last year’s biggest days.

Cyber Week 2021 results against the October forecast

In October, Adobe forecast that Cyber Monday would bring $11.3 billion in US online sales, Black Friday $9.5 billion and Thanksgiving $5.4 billion, with $36 billion across Cyber Week, according to its forecast.

The results came in lower. Cyber Week as a whole reached $33.9 billion, also down 1.4%, alongside the Cyber Monday figure, Fox Business reported. Black Friday came in at $8.9 billion, down 1.3%, and Thanksgiving flat at $5.1 billion. Adobe had narrowed its Cyber Monday range to $10.2 billion to $11.3 billion before the day, and the result landed inside it.

The season looked very different from its peak. The November spending figures came from NBC Bay Area’s report, and discounts were weaker too: electronics were discounted 12%, against 27% a year earlier, CNN Business reported.

Amazon called its Black Friday through Cyber Monday record-breaking but gave no sales figures, according to its announcement. In 2020 it had said independent sellers passed $4.8 billion in sales over the same days, Reuters reported.

Stores won back part of their traffic. Black Friday store visits rose 47.5% from 2020 but stayed 28% below 2019, CNBC reported, as some shoppers returned to stores for the event.

Run the two headline numbers together. If online spending since November 1 grew nearly 12% while Cyber Week fell 1.4%, the days outside the peak must have grown faster than the season as a whole. That is where the missing Cyber Week demand went.

Taken together, the figures describe a season that started in October, spread across November and reached a smaller peak than forecasters expected, which is the shape early deals were likely to produce.

How far each day fell short of Adobe’s forecast

Set side by side, Adobe’s October forecasts and the reported results show the same pattern on every day of the event.

DayOctober forecast (Adobe)Result
Thanksgiving$5.4 billion$5.1 billion, flat on 2020
Black Friday$9.5 billion$8.9 billion, down 1.3%
Cyber Monday$11.3 billion$10.7 billion, down 1.4%
Cyber Week$36 billion$33.9 billion, down 1.4%

Every result came in below its October forecast: by a few hundred million dollars on each of the three days, and by $2.1 billion across the week. That is the pattern to expect if part of the peak’s demand had already been spent in October and early November, as the season figures above suggest.

Why the peak gets judged instead of the season

The peak gets the attention first. Cyber Week has been the headline number for years, so teams compare 2021’s peak with 2020’s, and when the peak shrinks the comparison reads as decline.

The data says otherwise. A season growing about 12% online while its biggest days slipped is a season that moved. Shoppers bought earlier, in response to deals that started in October, and paid more because discounts were smaller. The same pattern explains the forecast miss. Forecasters started from Cyber Week’s history of steady growth and adjusted for the early start, but the shift toward October was larger than they expected, and some of the demand they placed in Cyber Week had already been spent.

Take a brand whose Cyber Week sales fell 8% from 2020 while its November sales rose 15%. Two teams can read those numbers in opposite ways. A team looking only at the event concludes its deals failed and cuts the December advertising budget. A team looking at the season sees that customers bought earlier and that the early-November deals worked, and keeps the December plan.

Advertising reviews carry the same risk. Return on ad spend during Cyber Week may look worse than in 2020 if conversion was spread across more days and costs per click stayed high throughout November. Judged over the whole month, the same spending may have performed well, so November as a whole deserves a review before anyone decides the Cyber Week campaigns underperformed.

Forecasts deserve the same reading. A forecast that predicted a smaller peak and a longer season was right, even if the brand’s own Cyber Week number fell short of its target. For 2022, the lesson is to set targets for the season and for each retailer event, rather than raising the Cyber Week target by a fixed percentage every year.

The weaker discounts carry a second lesson. Shoppers bought despite smaller discounts, which suggests that availability and timing mattered more in 2021 than depth of discount, and that brands with stock when others ran out may have won sales without cutting price. Availability itself was a competitive advantage, with out-of-stock messages running far above pre-pandemic levels going into the season.

December is the next test. If shoppers bought earlier, some pre-Christmas demand may have been pulled forward too, while shortages push other purchases later. Daily sales against the December plan, with budget moved toward products still in stock and still selling, will show which way it goes. A brand that reads its results this way also starts its 2022 planning from the right baseline, and reading results against the whole season is how we measure holiday performance for brands.

A0162.title: Cyber Week 2021 lessons: how retailers and brands behaved
A0162.alt: Three wood-framed shop windows with red, blue and gold holiday gift displays on a snowy city sidewalk.
A0162.ttag: Cyber Week 2021 lessons: how retailers and brands behaved | Kwontified
A0162.desc: Cyber Week 2021 showed retailers using deals to build memberships and brands discounting less. Plan 2022 around how they behave, not past peaks.
A0162.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 9, 2021.
A0162.body:
When a kitchenware brand’s Cyber Monday came in below 2020, its CEO asked what had gone wrong. The head of ecommerce had a short answer: nothing. November as a whole was up, margin had held, and the scarcest product had sold out at full price. The peak was smaller because the brand, and the retailers it sold through, had chosen to spread it.

That exchange is a scenario, but it captures what Cyber Week 2021 actually tested. Retailers spread their deals, used them to reward members and published fewer numbers. Brands discounted less and leaned on having stock. Those behaviors, more than the size of past peaks, are what a 2022 holiday plan should be built around.

Cyber Week 2021 lessons start with the numbers

Measured by the peak alone, the season looked flat. Fox Business put Cyber Monday online sales at $10.7 billion and the full Cyber Week at $33.9 billion, each down 1.4% on 2020, in its report. Counting from November 1, US online spending for the season reached $109.8 billion, up nearly 12% on the same stretch of 2020, NBC Bay Area reported, while discounts on electronics averaged 12%, against 27% in 2020, CNN Business reported.

Retailers shaped that pattern through their calendars and their stores. Amazon began its holiday deals on October 4, Fortune reported. Walmart ran three Black Friday events in November, with early access for paying Walmart+ members, according to its announcement. Walmart, Target and Best Buy kept their stores closed on Thanksgiving, CNBC reported.

Amazon, which in 2020 had said its independent sellers passed $4.8 billion in sales from Black Friday through Cyber Monday, called 2021 record-breaking but gave no sales figure, according to its announcement.

How one brand’s season looked from the planning room

Take that kitchenware brand back to September. The head of ecommerce sat down with the finance lead to plan the season. Freight costs had more than doubled, two of the best-sellers were stuck at a port, finance wanted to hold margin and the retail partners wanted deals early.

Between them, they settled on three choices for the season. They offered shallower discounts than in 2020, on fewer products. They put their best deal into Walmart’s first event, because it came with member early access and a slot in Walmart’s marketing. And they held the scarcest product back from any deal, selling it at full price for as long as stock lasted.

October tested those choices almost at once. Amazon’s early deals moved competitors’ prices, and the sales team asked whether to match. The brand matched on two products where its ranking mattered most and held firm on the rest, accepting some lost sales in exchange for margin. In the week before Thanksgiving, part of the advertising budget moved from Cyber Monday to the days around Walmart’s member events, because those days were converting better than the plan had assumed.

When the season closed, the results matched the answer the head of ecommerce later gave the CEO: a smaller Cyber Monday, a stronger November and a best-seller that never needed a discount.

Where the value went, and what to plan for in 2022

Membership is where retailers are taking the value. Walmart+ early access and Prime member offers turn holiday deals into a reason to join, and a member is a shopper the retailer keeps all year. A brand’s deals are helping to build that asset, so the brand should ask what it gets in return: what visibility comes with each member event, and how the deal reaches the retailer’s most frequent buyers. Planning deals for each retailer’s member events, rather than putting everything into one weekend, puts the brand in front of those shoppers early.

For a leadership team, the question is whether the deals funded in 2021 bought anything that lasts beyond the event itself.

Information is the other thing retailers are keeping. Amazon’s decision not to publish a sales figure means a brand cannot rely on retailers to explain the season. It needs its own measures: sales by week across the season and by retailer, set against its own plan. Those numbers also strengthen the brand’s hand in conversations with retailers, because they show what each event actually delivered. A brand that sells through several retailers is the only party that sees all of its own channels together, which makes that view worth building before the next season starts.

Brands kept something back too. They discounted less and won on availability. In a season of shortages, stock was worth more than a deeper discount, and shoppers who could not find a product at one retailer bought what was available at another, often at full price. Inventory planning belongs inside holiday strategy, including an early decision on which products are too scarce to discount.

Store decisions moved demand as well. With Walmart, Target and Best Buy closed on Thanksgiving, more of that day’s shopping went online, and more of the in-store rush moved to Black Friday and the weekend. A brand with products in stores and online needs stock and promotions planned for each calendar separately. The split also changes when advertising should run, since a shopper who bought online on Thanksgiving is no longer looking on Friday.

Spreading deals across more events carries its own cost: more submissions, more stock planning and more chances to make a mistake. A long season needs one owner and one calendar as much as a short one does.

None of this retires the big days. Cyber Monday was still the largest online shopping day of the year. It is now one peak among several, and what a leadership team has to settle is whether next year’s plan follows the retailers’ calendars or last year’s. Planning the season around how retailers now run it is how we plan holiday seasons for brands.

A0163.title: The 2022 ecommerce plan: four assumptions to change from 2021
A0163.alt: Four brass pocket compasses beside a worn leather-wrapped journal on a rustic wooden table near a window.
A0163.ttag: The 2022 ecommerce plan: four assumptions to change from 2021 | Kwontified
A0163.desc: Four planning assumptions broke in 2021: the peak, ad costs, stock and measurement. A 2022 plan copied from 2021 carries every one of them forward.
A0163.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 14, 2021.
A0163.body:
A 2022 budget that copies 2021’s and adds 10% looks like the cautious choice. It is already approved in spirit, easy to defend and familiar to everyone who has to sign it. It is also the plan most likely to fail, because 2021 broke four assumptions that most marketplace plans relied on, and a copied plan carries every one of them into a year that will not behave like 2020.

The four are easy to list: that the season peaks on a few days, that advertising costs rise slowly, that stock arrives when ordered, and that return on ad spend measures what advertising does. None of them held up.

Four 2021 results that break the 2022 ecommerce plan

The peak shrank while the season grew. Cyber Monday online sales in the US slipped 1.4% to $10.7 billion, and Cyber Week as a whole fell 1.4% to $33.9 billion, according to Fox Business. Online spending counted from November 1 still rose nearly 12% on 2020, NBC Bay Area reported.

Advertising got more expensive per sale. Sponsored Products spend climbed 41.8% in the third quarter compared with a year before, while return on that spend dropped 6.1%, Pacvue’s quarterly CPC report showed.

Stock ran short going into the holidays, with out-of-stock messages online up 172% from January 2020, according to Adobe.

Measurement began to move as well. In October, Amazon Ads introduced Brand Metrics, which measures shoppers in the awareness and consideration stages across all engagement with a brand on Amazon, not just ad-attributed sales, Amazon Ads said.

Assumption in a 2021 planWhat 2021 showedWhat the 2022 plan sets instead
The season peaks on a few daysCyber Week down 1.4%, season up nearly 12%Season targets split by retailer event, member events included
Costs per click rise a few percent a yearThird-quarter spend up 41.8%, return on ad spend down 6.1%Budgets from 2021’s actual costs by quarter, with room for further increases
Inventory arrives when orderedOut-of-stock messages up 172% from January 2020Buffers for best-sellers, earlier holiday orders, a rule for pausing ads on low stock
ROAS measures what advertising doesBrand Metrics introduced to measure awareness and considerationA brand measure alongside ROAS

Why the familiar plan carries the most risk

The trouble is that plans compound. A budget built on 2021’s peak sets 2022’s peak expectations, those expectations set the stock order, and the stock order sets the advertising calendar. One outdated assumption at the top runs through every decision below it, so a small error in the premise becomes a large error in spending and inventory. That is why raising the numbers does not fix the plan: it scales the error along with everything else.

Each broken assumption fails in its own way. A plan that sets its biggest targets for Cyber Week and Prime Day, and treats the rest of the year as filler, will over-invest in the days that shrank and under-invest in the weeks that grew. A plan that assumes costs per click rise a few percent a year will run out of budget early, usually in the fourth quarter, when competition is highest and stopping hurts most. A plan that assumes inventory arrives when ordered will be wrong again if supply chains stay tight. It will also keep paying for clicks on products that cannot ship.

The measurement assumption fails more slowly than the rest. A plan that judges every campaign on ROAS will keep cutting the upper-funnel spending that feeds future searches. Over a year or two, branded searches decline, and the campaigns that looked most efficient start to weaken without an obvious cause. Adding a brand measure, such as Brand Metrics where available, gives the plan a way to see that decline before it shows up in sales.

What the same budget does when it is rebuilt

Take a brand whose 2021 Amazon plan spent $600,000 on advertising, 40% of it in November and December, with a ROAS target on every campaign. Rolled forward with a 10% increase, the plan becomes $660,000, and 40% of that, $264,000, still lands in the weeks where demand thinned, while the months where demand grew keep the same small share they had before.

Rebuilt, the same $660,000 is spread across retailer events through the year, with a reserve for stock problems and a separate budget for brand-building campaigns judged on consideration rather than ROAS. The total does not change. What changes is which assumptions the money is betting on.

The rebuild starts from 2021’s actual results, by week and by retailer. It does not start from 2021’s plan. Wherever results and plan differed, the useful question is which assumption failed.

Retailers belong in the rebuild too. Walmart added thousands of new marketplace sellers in its second quarter, according to its earnings release. Amazon now pays brands a bonus, on average 10% of the purchase price, for sending outside traffic to their listings, Amazon announced. A plan that treats Amazon as the whole marketplace business, or that sends all paid traffic to the brand’s own site, misses both.

Ranges and written assumptions make the plan testable

Targets work better as ranges, set by event. Season-long ranges, broken down by retailer event, give teams room to move budget toward what is working rather than chasing a single number.

Ranges also change the conversation with finance. A single target invites a single question: did we hit it? A range, with the assumptions behind it, invites a better one: which assumption moved, by how much, and what should we do about it?

That only works if the assumptions about peaks, costs, stock and measurement are written down before the year starts. The first-quarter results then become a test. If costs, stock and demand behave as the plan assumed, the plan holds; if not, the written assumptions show exactly which line to change. A plan with unstated assumptions cannot be tested against results at all.

A plan is only as reliable as the assumptions it states. Writing those four down and checking them against each quarter’s results is how we build annual marketplace plans for brands.

A0164.title: The year in marketplaces, 2021: the structural shifts
A0164.alt: Snowy construction site with tower cranes and new warehouse buildings in front of a city skyline at dusk.
A0164.ttag: The year in marketplaces, 2021: the structural shifts | Kwontified
A0164.desc: In 2021, marketplaces earned more from ads, logistics and membership than from listings. Plan for platforms that sell services, not shelf space.
A0164.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 16, 2021.
A0164.body:
Ask where a brand’s marketplace money went in 2021 and the answer looks different from a few years ago. Less of it paid for the listing. More of it paid for the advertising that got the listing seen, the fulfillment that got the product delivered quickly, and the member events that brought shoppers in on a particular day.

The biggest change in marketplaces in 2021 was not who sold the most. It was where the value went. More and more of it moved from the listing itself to the services around it: advertising, fulfillment, membership and expansion into new markets and categories. Brands should plan for marketplaces that sell services and attention rather than shelf space, and budget for those services as core costs of each channel.

How services reshaped marketplaces 2021

Advertising took the most visible share. In the first quarter, the line Amazon labels “other” revenue, mostly advertising, rose 77% to $6.9 billion, GeekWire reported. Walmart said its U.S. advertising sales nearly doubled in its second quarter, according to its results. Brands paid more for each result as well: in the third quarter, Pacvue’s figures had Sponsored Products ad spend up 41.8% on the year and return on ad spend down 6.1%, in its CPC report.

Fulfillment grew alongside it. Zalando opened fulfillment centers in Madrid and Rotterdam in 2021 and announced a fourth German site, according to the company, followed by two more in Poland, announced on December 14. Walmart turned stores into local fulfillment centers, CNBC reported.

Membership shaped the holiday calendar. For the first time, paying Walmart+ members got early access to Walmart’s Black Friday events, according to its announcement, and Amazon’s holiday season opened with deals on October 4.

The platforms also kept moving into new markets and categories. Zalando launched in six new European countries, according to its second-quarter results. Mercado Libre built a supermarket business, saying its grocery buyers purchase more often and stay longer, according to a transcript of its third-quarter call.

Some value even flowed back toward brands. Brands that send outside traffic to their Amazon listings now earn a bonus averaging 10% of the purchase price, according to Amazon’s announcement. The platform is paying for something it now values more than a listing: new shoppers.

Not every marketplace moved at the same pace. Target Plus stayed small and curated, with fewer than 300 sellers early in the year, a Marketplace Pulse count that Kaspien cited when it joined. Its value to brands lies in access to Target’s shoppers rather than in a wide range of seller services.

What a single sale carries now

For a brand, the shift shows up in the profit and loss account. A product that once needed a listing and a referral fee now needs advertising to be found, a fulfillment arrangement to deliver fast, deals timed to member events, and a plan for each new market the platform opens.

Take a brand selling a $40 product on a marketplace. In 2019, that sale carried a referral fee and shipping, with little spent on advertising. In 2021, the same sale carries the fee, a fulfillment charge, and an advertising cost that has risen with every year of competition. The shelf price may be exactly where it was, yet the slice of it that goes to the marketplace and its services has grown.

The information brands receive changed too. Marketplaces shared more data through their advertising tools, such as Amazon’s Brand Metrics, while sharing less about their own results: Amazon gave no sales figure for its 2021 Black Friday weekend, according to its announcement. Brands increasingly learn about a marketplace through the services they buy from it.

That is not necessarily bad. The services are often worth it: fulfillment makes products eligible for fast delivery, advertising reaches shoppers who would never have found the product, and member events bring concentrated demand. But they need to be planned and measured, not discovered at the end of the quarter.

Planning a channel that sells services

The accounting has to catch up with the channel. When advertising, fulfillment and promotional costs sit in their own lines for each marketplace, the true cost of selling on each channel becomes visible, and so does the channel that only looks profitable because its services are buried elsewhere.

Each service then deserves its own measure of return. Advertising is best judged on incremental sales and brand growth, fulfillment on the conversion and delivery speed it buys, and member events on the new customers they bring. A service that costs more but returns more is a good trade; one that only costs more is a negotiation waiting to happen.

Expansion deserves a decision rather than a default. When a platform opens a new market or category, a brand can choose whether to join early and build the range, pricing and content for it, rather than letting the listing simply appear.

Smaller brands feel the shift most. A large brand can spread advertising and fulfillment costs across many products and channels. A smaller one may find that the services it needs to compete on a marketplace take a share of each sale that leaves little margin, and should choose its channels and products with that in mind.

The shift also changes negotiation. When so much of a marketplace’s value comes from services, brands have more to discuss than a fee: placement, data, measurement and access to member events can all be part of the conversation.

For leadership, the useful question going into 2022 is which of these services each channel really requires, and what each one returns. How marketplaces price advertising formats, fulfillment fees and membership benefits will say more about each platform’s direction than any change to its commission rates. Budgeting each channel around the services it now sells is how we manage marketplaces for brands.
