A0166.crumb: Why absolute price means little in the…
A0166.title: Why absolute price means little in the Amazon Buy Box
A0166.alt: Two red apples on an antique brass balance scale, one with a blank paper tag, on a wooden table.
A0166.ttag: Why absolute price means little in the Amazon Buy Box | Kwontified
A0166.desc: The lowest sticker price does not reliably win the Amazon Buy Box. Fulfillment, delivery and seller record weigh as much, so compete on the whole offer.
A0166.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 21, 2021.
A0166.body:
An offer at $31.49 with free delivery is cheaper for the shopper than a rival’s $28.99 offer with $4.99 shipping. Yet a brand watching only sticker prices will see itself undercut, cut its price below $28.99 to match, and give up $2.50 a unit on an offer that was already the cheaper one.

That mistake rests on a belief worth checking: that the lowest price wins the Amazon Buy Box. It does not, reliably. The featured offer is chosen on the whole offer, which means the price including delivery, how the order is fulfilled, how fast it arrives and how well the seller performs. Brands that cut price to win it often give away margin without winning. They should compete on the whole offer, and compare prices against what a shopper actually pays from each rival.

Where the Amazon Buy Box price fits in the decision

When several sellers offer the same product, Amazon features one offer in the Buy Box, the panel on a product page where the Add to Cart button sits, with Buy Now beside it. Most shoppers buy that offer without comparing the others.

Price matters, but it is not assessed alone. The featured offer reflects the total price a shopper pays, including delivery, alongside how the order will be fulfilled and delivered, and the seller’s record. Amazon describes those factors in general terms rather than as a published formula.

They matter enough that regulators are examining them. The European Commission’s investigation, opened in November 2020, covers how Amazon picks the Buy Box winner and how it decides which sellers can offer products to Prime members. The question is whether those rules favor Amazon’s own retail business or sellers who use its logistics and delivery services, CNBC reported. An investigation into whether logistics choices tip the outcome would make little sense if the lowest price simply won.

Italy went further in December 2021. On December 9, its competition authority fined Amazon €1.13 billion. The authority found that Amazon tied benefits such as the Prime label and access to events like Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Prime Day to the use of its own fulfillment service, Silicon Republic reported. Amazon said it strongly disagreed and would appeal, adding that the service is optional and not used by most third-party sellers.

The lowest price wins only when the gap is large

Part of the belief holds up. Price is a large factor, and a seller whose price is far above the others will rarely be featured. A wide enough price gap can outweigh every other advantage.

Among offers at similar prices, though, the deciding factors are often fulfillment and performance. An offer that ships fast through Amazon’s own network, from a seller with a clean record, can beat a slightly cheaper offer that ships slowly from a seller with late shipments or cancellations.

The sticker price is also the wrong number to compare, as the opening offers show. What the shopper pays is the price plus delivery, and that is the number the featured offer reflects.

Put numbers on the cost of getting this wrong. Take a brand that moves 3,000 units a month of a $32 product, with a margin of $10. Seeing a reseller at $29.99, it drops to $29.49 and still loses the Buy Box half the time, because the reseller’s offer ships through Amazon’s network while the brand ships from its own warehouse with a three-day handling time. The cut is $32 minus $29.49, or $2.51 a unit. Across 3,000 units, that is about $7,500 a month, and the problem it was meant to solve remains.

Had the brand fixed its fulfillment instead, by shortening handling time or moving its best-sellers into Amazon’s network, it might have won the Buy Box back at its original price.

So the belief fails the test. Price is one input, and often not the one that decides.

Compete on the whole offer, with a floor under price

Competitor monitoring should start from landed prices. Tracking the total each shopper pays, including delivery, and the delivery speed each offer promises shows whether a price change is needed at all, and by how much.

Fulfillment and performance come before any price cut. Handling times, delivery promises, late shipments and cancellations are all worth checking, and for best-sellers, fast fulfillment through Amazon’s network may win more often than a lower price would.

Every product also needs a price floor: the lowest price at which it still earns an acceptable margin, decided in advance and not crossed to win the Buy Box. If a rival consistently undercuts that floor, the issue is distribution and pricing agreements, not the rival’s price.

Brands that sell to Amazon as vendors face a version of the same question. When Amazon’s own retail offer competes with third-party sellers, the brand does not set Amazon’s price. It can still influence the factors around it: keeping Amazon in stock, holding consistent prices with other retailers, and limiting the unauthorized resellers whose offers create price pressure in the first place.

Distribution is often the root cause. When a brand repeatedly loses the Buy Box to resellers offering its own products, the first question is where their stock comes from. Tightening distribution agreements and monitoring authorized sellers can do more for Buy Box share than any price change.

Repricing tools need limits. Automated tools that simply undercut the lowest visible price can set off a race to the bottom between sellers of the same product, with every round cutting margin and none changing who wins. Repricing rules should account for fulfillment and landed price, and stop at the floor.

Buy Box share by product, tracked alongside price changes, settles the question for each listing: if share does not rise when price falls, price was not the problem. Pricing to the landed total and fixing the offer around it is how we protect Buy Box share for brands.

A0168.crumb: Zalando returns are a competitive moat…
A0168.title: Zalando returns are a competitive moat, not just a cost
A0168.alt: Orange wrapped parcel on a wooden drawbridge leading across a moat to a medieval stone castle.
A0168.ttag: Zalando returns are a competitive moat, not just a cost | Kwontified
A0168.desc: Zalando’s free returns look like a cost, but they are a barrier rivals struggle to copy. Brands selling there should use its returns data, not fight it.
A0168.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 23, 2021.
A0168.body:
When a brand’s leadership team reviews its Zalando business, the returns line is the one that prompts the hardest question. Isn’t free, easy returning a weakness, an expensive habit that a profitable retailer would eventually drop? It is a fair thing to ask of a policy that sends so much stock back through the system.

The answer runs the other way. Zalando’s free returns look like its biggest cost, but they also work as a competitive moat. The logistics, data and scale needed to make free returns pay are hard for rivals to copy, and the policy makes customers order more often. Brands selling on Zalando should treat returns as part of the price of access to its customers, and use Zalando’s returns data to cut avoidable returns rather than resist the policy.

How Zalando returns work, and what they cost

Zalando built its business on bringing the fitting room home. In the new markets it launched in 2021, shoppers get delivery at no charge and can send items back free within 30 days of buying, according to the company.

Returns are a large part of the business. In 2019, around half of the items Zalando sold were sent back, NPR reported, and about a third of returns are related to size, according to FashionUnited. Zalando even reports its average basket size after returns, €57.5 over the twelve months to the third quarter of 2021, in its results presentation.

Why rivals cannot simply copy free returns

Start with what the policy does to demand. Customers who can return easily order more readily, and Zalando’s customers are ordering more often: average orders per active customer reached 5.1 over the twelve months to the third quarter, up from 4.8 a year earlier, according to the same presentation.

The harder part of the question is why competitors do not simply copy the policy, and the answer is that free returns are only affordable with the systems behind them. A returned item must travel back, be inspected and be made available to sell again quickly, or its value falls. That takes a dense logistics network close to customers, and Zalando is still building one. Its 2021 openings included fulfillment centers in Madrid and Rotterdam, with a fourth German site under construction, Zalando said, and it announced two more in Poland on December 14, according to its announcement.

The systems also include data. Zalando uses what it learns from returns to give customers size advice and to tell brands when a product fits differently from what customers expect, NPR reported. Every return adds to that knowledge, which makes the next order a little more likely to fit.

The moat grows as Zalando expands. Each new market adds customers to spread the cost across, and each new fulfillment center shortens the distance a returned item travels. A competitor entering the same markets later faces an awkward choice: match the returns policy at a higher cost per return, or offer a weaker policy and lose customers who have come to expect it.

A smaller retailer can offer free returns, but it pays more per return, learns less from each one, and cannot spread the cost across tens of millions of customers. Zalando had 46.3 million active customers in the third quarter, and that scale is the barrier a rival would have to cross.

What a brand on Zalando can actually control

For brands, the policy is part of the price of reaching those customers. Free returns are what shoppers expect on Zalando, and a brand cannot opt out of them by complaining about return rates. What it can do is reduce the returns it causes.

Take a brand selling 10,000 items a month through Zalando’s Partner Program, with half coming back. If a third of those returns are size-related, that is about 1,670 items a month. A size guide corrected using Zalando’s returns feedback, and product images that show fit more clearly, could cut those returns noticeably, and each avoided return saves shipping, handling and the markdown on items that can no longer be sold as new.

Brands selling through the Partner Program feel this most directly, because they carry more of the cost of handling their own returns. For them, returns data is one of the most valuable things Zalando offers. A monthly review of return reasons by product, followed by fixes to the listings, size guides and images behind the most frequent and costly ones, is where that value turns into margin.

That data needs careful reading. A return reason chosen from a drop-down list is a rough signal, and some shoppers order several sizes intending to keep one. The useful pattern is the one that repeats across many orders, not a single comment. Where it shows a product consistently runs small or large, the size guidance should change, and sometimes the product itself.

Returns also belong in the channel’s economics from the start. An expected return rate built into the margin for each product sold on Zalando turns returns into a known cost of access to Zalando’s customers rather than a surprise at the end of the quarter.

December gives all of this extra urgency. Gift purchases made in December come back in January, and brands that plan for that wave will process returns faster and get products back on sale while demand lasts.

Back in that leadership review, the more useful question is whether the brand’s own avoidable returns are falling, and whether Zalando’s average basket after returns holds steady as it grows into new markets in 2022. Reading Zalando’s returns data to cut the returns a brand causes is how we run Zalando channels for brands.

A0169.title: Walmart’s international marketplaces at the end of 2021
A0169.alt: Blue twine-tied gift box beside a white embossed relief globe on a wooden surface.
A0169.ttag: Walmart’s international marketplaces at the end of 2021 | Kwontified
A0169.desc: Walmart is narrowing its international business to a few markets and growing ecommerce there. For US sellers, Canada is the practical next step.
A0169.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 28, 2021.
A0169.body:
Walmart International’s third-quarter net sales fell 20.1% to $23.6 billion, and Walmart’s executives still described the quarter as a strong one. Both statements hold, because $9.4 billion of the decline came from divestitures. Strip those out, and what is left is a smaller business in which Flipkart, China and Mexico delivered strong growth in ecommerce, according to Walmart’s results.

Walmart has narrowed its international business to a handful of markets, and it is growing ecommerce quickly in them. Its Canadian marketplace is now large enough to matter, but it still lacks the seller services available in the U.S. For U.S. sellers, Walmart Canada is a measured next step: a test of proven products in a market they can serve reliably, rather than something to ignore or to rush into before the U.S. business is strong.

How Walmart international marketplaces fit the strategy

On the earnings call, Walmart’s executives said the international business had performed strongly, with China, Mexico and India leading. They added that advertising income was led by the U.S., Flipkart and Mexico, and that the company was starting to ramp in Canada and Chile, according to a transcript of the call.

A smaller set of markets means more investment in each. Advertising growing in Flipkart and Mexico shows Walmart building the same model abroad that it is building at home: marketplace, fulfillment and advertising together.

Canada is the market most U.S. sellers can reach. Walmart.ca opened its marketplace in 2017 with 27 curated sellers, and said sellers on the U.S. marketplace could quickly launch on the Canadian one, Retail Dive reported. By September 2021, it had almost 5,000 sellers and about 30 million items, and its grocery marketplace orders were running at six times 2020 levels, Walmart Canada’s head of marketplace told Retail Insider. He also said fulfillment services for sellers were on the roadmap but not yet in place.

Beyond Canada, the picture is less open to U.S. sellers. Flipkart in India is a separate marketplace with its own seller requirements, and Walmart’s growth in Mexico and China is driven largely by local businesses. They matter for understanding Walmart’s direction, but they are not simple extensions of a U.S. Walmart business.

Reach now, or depth first

For a U.S. seller doing well on Walmart.com, Canada sets reach against capability, and the two pull in opposite directions.

Going now buys reach and timing. Walmart Canada has around 400 stores and a growing online audience, and a marketplace of 5,000 sellers is far less crowded than the U.S. one. Sellers who establish reviews and rankings early tend to hold an advantage as competition arrives.

Waiting buys capability and protects cost. Without a Walmart fulfillment service in Canada, sellers must deliver orders themselves, across the border or from Canadian stock, while meeting delivery promises and handling returns. Customs, duties, French-language content for Quebec and Canadian pricing all add work. A seller whose U.S. business still has gaps in stock, content or advertising may get more from fixing those first.

Two sellers starting from the same place show how the choice plays out. Each makes $120,000 a month on Walmart.com.

Seller that lists everythingSeller that tests a few products
Range in CanadaFull range of 200 products25 best-selling, higher-priced products
StockShips from its U.S. warehouseSmall stock in a Canadian third-party warehouse
Content and priceU.S. listings carried overFrench content, priced against Canadian competitors
Delivery promiseFive to seven daysSet from Canadian stock
After three months$6,000 a month, little profitSlower growth, good reviews, margin held

For the first seller, cross-border shipping costs eat the margin on low-priced items and slow deliveries bring poor reviews. After three months, Canadian sales of $6,000 a month come to 5% of what the business earns on Walmart.com, and that 5% carries little profit. The second seller’s sales grow more slowly at first, but its reviews are good and its margin holds, which gives it a base to expand from.

Customer service is a further cost that sellers often underestimate. Canadian shoppers expect answers in their own time zone, and in French in Quebec, and returns across the border are slower and more expensive than domestic ones. A seller that plans for those costs before launching avoids the poor reviews that slow service brings.

A Canadian test sized to what the seller can deliver

The products that go first should be the ones already proven on Walmart.com: consistent sellers with strong reviews and a healthy margin. A Canadian launch is a poor place to discover whether a product works.

Fulfillment has to be settled before anything is listed. Shipping cross-border and holding Canadian stock each have a cost per order once duties are included, and the delivery promise should come from that cost and from what the seller can actually keep.

Localization is part of the price of entry. That means pricing against Canadian competitors in Canadian dollars, writing French content where it matters, and adjusting the range to Canadian demand rather than listing everything.

Advertising should follow the same discipline. A modest budget on the products being tested, focused on the searches that convert for them in the U.S., can expand where Canadian results justify it. Early reviews matter more than early sales volume in a new market.

The test also needs its own scorecard. Canadian sales, margin, delivery performance and reviews belong in separate lines, so that the decision to expand further rests on Canada’s results rather than on the strength of the U.S. business.

A Walmart Canada fulfillment service for marketplace sellers would change the arithmetic: it would lower the cost of serving Canadian customers, improve delivery promises and tilt the balance toward expanding sooner and more broadly. Until then, the size of the test should match what the seller can deliver, and sizing a Canadian launch that way is how we expand Walmart businesses for brands.

A0170.crumb: Zalando’s logistics network is built for…
A0170.title: Zalando’s logistics network is built for speed across Europe
A0170.alt: Rust-red delivery van driving along a winding dual carriageway through green rolling countryside at golden hour.
A0170.ttag: Zalando’s logistics network is built for speed across Europe | Kwontified
A0170.desc: Zalando is adding fulfillment centers across Europe to serve customers faster. Brands should place stock where its network can deliver quickly.
A0170.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 30, 2021.
A0170.body:
Picture a shopper in Riga who, on a Monday evening in March 2022, orders a pair of boots and a jacket from Zalando, both sold by brands through the Partner Program. The boots sit in one of Zalando’s Polish fulfillment centers, are handed to a carrier on Tuesday and reach Riga on Thursday. The jacket is held in its brand’s own warehouse in Italy, ships on Wednesday and arrives in a separate parcel the following Monday, a week after the order. By then the weekend it was meant for has passed, so it goes back. Nothing was wrong with the jacket; it was simply stored in the wrong place.

The order is imagined, but the logistics network it travels through is real, and Zalando is making it denser across Europe. It is adding fulfillment centers in Germany, Poland, Spain and the Netherlands, and fast, local delivery and easy returns are central to its offer to customers and to its growth plan. Brands selling on Zalando should plan where their stock sits within that network, and how quickly it can reach each market, rather than treating Zalando’s logistics as fixed background.

How the Zalando logistics network grew in 2021

Fulfillment centers in Madrid and Rotterdam went live during 2021. On November 4, Zalando announced it would start building a fourth own-operated site in Germany, in Giessen, according to the company. The 130,000 square meter warehouse will join Zalando’s German sites in Erfurt, Mönchengladbach and Lahr, begin operating in 2023, and serve customers in Germany and neighboring countries.

On December 14, it announced two more fulfillment centers in Poland, in Bydgoszcz and the neighboring village of Białe Błota, creating more than 4,000 jobs in total, according to its announcement. The Białe Błota site, already under construction, will cover more than 100,000 square meters and is scheduled to open in March 2022. Zalando chose the area for its proximity to Polish customers and other nearby markets. The new sites add to Zalando’s existing Polish locations near Szczecin, in Olsztynek and near Łódź, Property Forum reported.

Zalando describes Giessen as a state-of-the-art site, and says it is expanding the network to support its 2025 growth target and to serve customers with fast, convenient delivery. Each new site shortens the distance between stock and a group of customers, for outbound orders and for returns alike, and gives Zalando more capacity for the peaks that come with each new market and each major sales event.

The network serves a customer base that is growing quickly. Active customers numbered 46.3 million at the end of the third quarter, against 35.6 million twelve months before, and Zalando entered six new markets during 2021, according to its results presentation.

Where a brand’s stock should sit in that network

Multiply the Riga order across thousands of orders, and the location of stock becomes one of the largest factors in a brand’s results on Zalando. It decides how fast the brand delivers, how often orders arrive together, how many items come back, and how its products rank as a result. In the Riga order, it decided whether the shopper kept one item or both of them.

The starting point is a map of delivery speed by market. For each market where a brand sells, it is worth checking how quickly its products arrive, whether they are stored in Zalando’s network or shipped from the brand’s own warehouse. Slow markets usually point to stock in the wrong place.

From there, the best-sellers in each region can move closer to demand. For those products, storing stock in Zalando’s fulfillment network may cut delivery times. As Zalando adds centers in Poland, the new Polish sites may suit products selling across Central and Eastern Europe, the region where it has added the most markets.

Returns follow the same geography. Returns that travel back to a site close to the customer are processed and resold faster, so stock positioned well for outbound delivery is usually positioned well for returns too. The jacket in the Riga order paid twice for being far away: a slow trip out, and then a return trip on top.

The calculation differs for each brand. A brand that already has its own warehouses across Europe may deliver quickly without using Zalando’s network. One shipping from a single central site will usually be slower to the edges of Zalando’s footprint, such as the Baltic states or the Balkans, and has more to gain from moving stock.

Spreading stock has real trade-offs as well. Storing stock in more places spreads inventory thinner, and a brand that splits a small range across too many sites may run out in one while holding surplus in another. Concentrating best-sellers where demand is highest, and keeping slower items centralized, avoids most of that risk.

It is also worth asking Zalando which sites can hold a brand’s products. Not every category or product type may be suited to every center, and the answer affects how much of a range can sit close to customers.

The timing of each opening matters as well. New sites open in stages, and a brand planning for the 2022 season should check which locations will be live, and with what capacity, before committing stock to them.

For a leadership team, the question each opening raises is simple to state: which of our markets just got closer to our stock, and which did not? As the Polish sites and the Giessen center come into operation, the fastest route to a group of customers changes with them, and keeping each product where Zalando’s network reaches its buyers fastest is how we plan Zalando stock for brands.

A0172.crumb: Reading ROAS when prices rise: why the…
A0172.title: Reading ROAS when prices rise: why the ratio flatters
A0172.alt: Brass magnifying glass enlarging a small stack of plain gold coins on a wooden table.
A0172.ttag: Reading ROAS when prices rise: why the ratio flatters | Kwontified
A0172.desc: A higher price lifts ROAS even when the ads sell fewer units. In 2022, read the ratio next to units per ad dollar, cost per order and margin.
A0172.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 4, 2022.
A0172.body:
Take an apparel brand that changes nothing in its Sponsored Products account except the price on its product page. A year later its ROAS has gone from 4.0 to 4.14, and it sold 100 fewer units for the same spend. The ads did not improve. Return on ad spend divides ad-attributed revenue by ad cost, so a higher price lifts the ratio on its own, and in 2022 that is a real risk for any team that grades advertising on ROAS alone. Units per ad dollar, cost per order and margin belong beside it, with targets reset whenever a brand moves its own prices.

ROAS when prices rise is pulled two ways at once

Online prices are climbing for the first time in years. November online prices were 3.5% above a year earlier, the biggest increase since Adobe began tracking them in 2014 and the 18th month in a row of rises, according to Adobe’s Digital Price Index. The increases were uneven. Apparel prices rose 17.3%, while electronics fell 0.4% and toys fell 2.9%, WWD reported.

Advertising costs moved faster than prices did. The average cost per click on Amazon reached $1.33 by the end of 2021, up 43% from $0.93 at the start of the year, while the average conversion rate held at 12% to 13%, according to Marketplace Pulse’s year in review. Average advertising cost of sale (ACoS, ad spend as a share of ad-attributed sales) rose from 25% at the start of 2021 to over 30%.

Those two forces push ROAS in opposite directions. Dearer clicks drag it down. Higher prices push it up. A brand that sees a steady or improving ROAS in 2022 cannot tell, from the ratio alone, which force is winning.

The arithmetic behind a flattering ratio

Go back to the apparel brand. It spends $10,000 a month on Sponsored Products and sells 1,000 units at $40, which gives $40,000 in ad-attributed sales and a ROAS of 4.0. Over the following year its own costs rise, and it raises the price 15% to $46. Clicks cost more as well, so the same budget buys fewer of them, and it sells 900 units.

BeforeAfter
Monthly ad spend$10,000$10,000
Price$40$46
Units sold1,000900
Ad-attributed sales$40,000$41,400
ROAS4.04.14
Cost per order$10.00$11.11

On the dashboard, advertising looks slightly better. Underneath, the brand bought 100 fewer orders with the same money, and each one cost $11.11 to win instead of $10.00. If its product costs rose as fast as its price, the margin on each unit did not grow either, so the advertising produced less profit than the year before. The price moved the ratio. The ads did not.

The same logic runs in reverse where prices fall. A brand selling toys or electronics can watch its ROAS weaken while its campaigns sell more units for each dollar than they did. A team that judges on the ratio alone might cut the campaign doing the best work in the account.

What the ratio still tells you, and what it hides

ROAS feels like a quality score for advertising because it puts sales over spend, the same shape as a return on investment. It remains a quick, comparable read of how much revenue each advertising dollar is linked to, and for many day-to-day bidding calls it is still the right number. What it cannot do in a year of moving prices is separate the ad’s contribution from the price tag’s.

Units can do that job. Units sold per ad dollar and cost per order are not inflated by a price increase, so reporting them next to ROAS for every campaign shows whether advertising reached more buyers or the same buyers simply paid more.

Targets need the same correction. If a product’s price rose 10%, a ROAS target set before the increase is about 10% too easy to hit. Reset the target when the price changes, or write it in units or cost per order instead.

Margin is the final check. A healthy ROAS can sit on top of a shrinking profit when product and fulfillment costs are climbing too. Every product has a break-even advertising cost of sale at its current margin, and each campaign should be compared with that line rather than with the 2021 ratio.

Where the distortion does the most damage

Category sets how suspicious to be. Apparel, where prices rose sharply, deserves the hardest look at any ratio that improved. In categories with flat or falling prices the danger runs the other way: cutting campaigns whose ratios fell for reasons outside advertising.

Promotions complicate the picture further. A deep discount during a sales event lowers the price, and the ROAS with it, even in a week that brings in more buyers than any other. Reading event results on units and new customers as well as on the ratio keeps the best week of the year from looking like the worst.

Comparisons across retailers carry the same trap. If a brand raised prices on one marketplace and held them on another, a gap in ROAS between the two may reflect pricing rather than the quality of each platform’s advertising. Year-over-year reviews are exposed too: a 2022 report that sets ROAS against 2021 without noting price changes will mislead anyone who reads it, and budgets built on that comparison will go to the wrong places.

The quickest test sits in the report itself. Compare revenue growth with unit growth for each campaign. When revenue grows faster than units, price is doing part of the work and ROAS is flattering the ads, so the ratio alone should not move a budget. Putting units and margin beside ROAS for every Amazon, Walmart and Target campaign is how we keep price changes from passing as ad gains for brands.

A0173.crumb: Walmart Connect’s first full year: what…
A0173.title: Walmart Connect’s first full year: what brands learned
A0173.alt: Young sapling in a terracotta pot beside an empty blue shopping basket on sunny wooden steps.
A0173.ttag: Walmart Connect’s first full year: what brands learned | Kwontified
A0173.desc: Walmart Connect spent 2021 adding a DSP and store screens to search ads. What brands pay for is purchase data that links ads to sales in stores.
A0173.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 6, 2022.
A0173.body:
Stand at the self-checkout in a Walmart supercenter and there is a screen at eye level, and another on the TV wall a few aisles back. Both are now part of what Walmart sells to brands as media. In its first full year under a new name, Walmart Connect grew quickly and added a demand-side platform and in-store screens to its search ads. What ties the pieces together, and what brands are really paying for, is Walmart’s purchase data, which links an ad seen online to a sale made in a store as well as online.

Walmart Connect grew on every front in 2021

Walmart renamed its media business Walmart Connect on January 28, 2021, aiming to become one of the top 10 advertising platforms in the U.S. within five years, Retail TouchPoints reported. It said the business would use nearly 170,000 digital screens across more than 4,500 stores, expand search and display across its digital properties, and build an off-site platform with The Trade Desk.

Each part of that plan moved during the year. Walmart Connect’s advertising sales grew 95% year over year in the second quarter, and the number of active advertisers rose more than 170%, according to Retail Dive. On August 25, Walmart announced Walmart DSP, built with The Trade Desk, for select suppliers by the end of October, according to its announcement. On its third-quarter call, Walmart said advertising income was led by the U.S., Flipkart and Mexico, according to the call transcript.

The marketplace underneath grew as well. Walmart’s marketplace nearly doubled in twelve months to about 130,000 sellers, Marketplace Pulse reported, and every new seller is a potential advertiser.

Where a brand’s Walmart advertising dollar actually goes

Trace a dollar of Walmart advertising and it ends up in one of three places, each buying something different.

Search is the familiar one. Sponsored Products put a brand’s items in front of shoppers searching on Walmart.com and in the app, at the moment they are choosing between products. For most brands it is where Walmart advertising starts, and where it should.

Reach beyond Walmart’s own sites is the newer purchase. Walmart DSP lets advertisers buy display, video, audio and connected TV through The Trade Desk, targeted with Walmart’s past-purchase and predictive audience segments. It also lets them cap how often the same person sees an ad across Walmart DSP and The Trade Desk, according to Walmart Connect.

The store is the third destination. Screens on TV walls and at self-checkout put brand messages in front of shoppers in more than 4,500 locations, with timing and location chosen by the advertiser.

What the three share is the data, and that is where the value sits. Walmart can connect an ad seen online with a purchase made in a store because it sees both ends of the trip. A general ad network cannot close that loop, so the closed loop is what a brand should be paying Walmart for.

Take a snack brand that runs an off-site video campaign through Walmart DSP, aimed at shoppers who bought a competing brand in the past six months. Online sales rise modestly. Walmart’s measurement then shows that most of the new buyers purchased in stores, during their weekly grocery trip.

Judged on online sales alone, the campaign looks weak. Judged on all Walmart sales, it ranks among the brand’s best. A team reading only the online dashboard would have cut the campaign that found those new buyers, since they checked out in the aisle rather than on the app.

Planning Walmart advertising for 2022 around the data

The base of any 2022 Walmart plan is search that works. Well-structured, well-bid Sponsored Products come before anything else, and product pages and stock need to be ready before off-site spend sends shoppers to them. Search also teaches a brand which shoppers matter: the terms that convert on Walmart, and the products shoppers compare, are the raw material for later audience campaigns.

Off-site and in-store media earn a test where Walmart’s data adds something a brand could not buy elsewhere. That means audiences defined by Walmart’s own purchase records, such as competitors’ buyers or lapsed customers, rather than broad audiences any network could reach.

Measurement has to cover the whole store. Brands should ask for reporting that includes in-store purchases and judge campaigns on total sales and new buyers, not only on online return on ad spend. For brands whose products sell mostly in stores, online-only reporting can understate the value of Walmart advertising by a wide margin.

The harder part is inside the brand. At many brands, Walmart advertising sits with the ecommerce team, while store promotions and trade spending sit with the sales team that manages the Walmart buyer. Closed-loop measurement only helps if both teams see it. When the two budgets come into one conversation, a brand can decide whether a store promotion deserves off-site video support, and judge the pair on the sales they produced together.

Expectations need calibrating too. Walmart’s advertising business is growing from a smaller base than Amazon’s, and its tools are newer. Some campaigns will need more support, more testing and more patience than teams used to Amazon expect.

How far Walmart extends self-serve access and measurement through 2022 will show how much ground it can claim with brand teams. The more of its closed-loop data it puts in advertisers’ hands, the more of a brand’s budget it can justify. Building that plan from Sponsored Products up to Walmart DSP, with store sales in the scorecard, is how we run Walmart Connect for brands.

A0174.title: Amazon’s 2022 fee changes: model them before they hit margins
A0174.alt: Twine-tied brown paper parcel on a vintage brass postal scale beside a dish of coins on a wooden table.
A0174.ttag: Amazon’s 2022 fee changes: model them before they hit margins | Kwontified
A0174.desc: Amazon’s average FBA fee rise of 5.2% hides a wide spread by size and weight. Model each product before January 18, then absorb, reprice or redesign.
A0174.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 11, 2022.
A0174.body:
An average increase of 5.2% sounds like something a brand can absorb across the board and forget. It is an average, though, and Amazon’s 2022 fee changes, which take effect on January 18, spread very unevenly once dimensional-weight pricing and higher storage fees are added in. Some products will barely notice. Others, light items in big boxes above all, will lose a real slice of margin. That spread is the reason to model the new fees product by product now and decide, for each one, whether to absorb the cost, raise the price or change the packaging and stock, before the change shows up in February’s margins.

What the Amazon 2022 fee changes include

Amazon announced the changes on November 16, 2021, EcommerceBytes reported. They bring dimensional-weight pricing to large standard-size products other than apparel, higher monthly storage fees outside the October to December peak, higher removal and disposal fees and higher FBA Prep Service fees. Amazon said it would also reduce some fees, including the returns processing fee.

Fulfillment fees rise by an average of 5.2%, depending on size and weight. The off-peak monthly storage fee for standard-size items goes from $0.75 to $0.83 per cubic foot for January through September, Benzinga reported.

Amazon tied the increases to its costs. It said it had more than doubled its U.S. fulfillment capacity since the start of the pandemic, spent over $15 billion to keep employees safe and hired more than 628,000 people, according to EcommerceBytes. It also said fees for its fulfillment service remained about 30% lower on average than alternatives, Benzinga reported. This round follows smaller increases in June 2021, which Amazon described as about 2% to 3% on average.

Why one average fee rise lands so differently

Dimensional-weight pricing is the reason. Under it, a product is charged on the space its box takes up as well as on what it weighs. A dense item in a snug box is barely touched. A light item in a large box can jump into a higher fee band, and the jump can be far bigger than the headline average suggests.

Take two products a brand sells through Amazon’s fulfillment service. One is a compact, heavy kitchen tool priced at $25, whose fee rises by a few cents. The other is a light but bulky pillow priced at $35 in a large box, which is now priced by dimensional weight and whose fee rises by more than a dollar. Both sit inside the same 5.2% average. Only one of them needs a decision.

Advertising widens the gap. Average cost per click on Amazon rose 43% during 2021, according to Marketplace Pulse. A product whose fees and advertising costs both climbed may have lost more margin than either change alone suggests.

Absorb, reprice or redesign: what each choice costs

Absorbing the increase keeps the price where it is and accepts a thinner margin. It protects sales volume and search ranking, and it suits products with healthy margins or fierce price competition. For the kitchen tool, a few cents is a cost worth carrying, and the brand absorbs it. The bill arrives as lower profit.

Raising the price passes the increase on to shoppers, who are already seeing higher prices everywhere: online prices were up 3.5% in November from a year earlier, according to Adobe. The cost is conversion, and in some cases the Buy Box if competitors hold their prices.

Changing the product’s footprint attacks the fee itself. Smaller packaging, lower stock levels or a different fulfillment method can reduce fees directly, and for a product newly priced on dimensional weight, a smaller box may cut the fee more than any price change could. The pillow is that case. Raising its price risks the Buy Box to a cheaper rival, so the brand redesigns the packaging to compress the pillow and brings the box back into a lower fee band. The cost is time and, sometimes, a packaging project.

Weighed side by side, the numbers lean one way for each product. Where a price increase only offsets a few cents, absorbing is cheaper than the conversion risk. Where dimensional weight caused the jump, the footprint fix goes after the cause, while a higher price only passes it to the shopper.

How to model the fee changes before January 18

The work starts with a full recalculation. For every active product, use the new fee tables, current dimensions and weights, and expected storage volumes to estimate the new cost per unit. Then sort products by the change in contribution margin per unit, after fees and advertising, and spend attention where the increase is largest relative to price. For each product with a material change, record the choice and the reason, so it can be reviewed when sales data come in.

Storage deserves its own pass. Higher off-peak storage fees raise the cost of carrying slow-moving stock for most of the year. Brands that bought deep inventory to protect against supply-chain delays should review which products justify that depth now that holding it costs more.

Timing shapes any price change. Raising prices on many products at once, as competitors do the same, can work; raising them alone, a week before rivals, can cost the Buy Box. Watching competitors’ prices in the days after January 18 helps decide how far to pass the increase on.

The recorded dimensions are worth checking as well. Dimensional-weight pricing depends on the measurements Amazon holds for each product, and if those are wrong, the product may sit in a higher fee band than it should. A correction there can be worth more than any repricing.

February statements will show who did the modeling. A product whose actual fee lands well above its modeled fee points to a wrong dimension or a missed band change, and that gap is the first thing to chase. Modeling fees, dimensions and price together for every listing is how we protect Amazon margins for brands as fees change.

A0176.crumb: Target Plus in 2022: who is getting…
A0176.title: Target Plus in 2022: who is getting invited, and why
A0176.alt: Red envelope with a wax leaf seal on a wooden shelf beside a ceramic cup, dried stems in a vase and old books.
A0176.ttag: Target Plus in 2022: who is getting invited, and why | Kwontified
A0176.desc: Target Plus has about 440 sellers because Target curates it to fill gaps in its own range. The brands invited in 2022 bring a gap, a fit and proof.
A0176.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 13, 2022.
A0176.body:
A search for wireless headphones on Target.com returned 675 products, and more than half of them were sold by Target itself. That short, Target-heavy page is the clearest picture of what Target Plus is for: a small, curated marketplace of about 440 sellers that Target uses to complement its own range, rather than to maximize selection. It also explains who gets a Target Plus invitation in 2022. The brands most likely to join fill a gap in Target’s assortment, fit its brand and can show reliable operations, and they build that case before they ask.

How a Target Plus invitation works

Target launched Target Plus in 2019 as an invitation-only marketplace. Sellers hold their own inventory and ship their own orders, while shoppers can return items to Target stores, the Star Tribune reported.

It has stayed small on purpose. Nearly three years after launch, Target Plus had about 440 sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse; Walmart’s marketplace had about 130,000. Target’s chief executive, Brian Cornell, has said the approach is unchanged: Target will curate very carefully and complement its store and online assortment, Marketplace Pulse noted. The headphone search, from the same report, is that policy made visible.

Target does not publish its invitation criteria. What it does publish is its intent, and the marketplace it has built over nearly three years is consistent with it. Read together, they say a good deal about the brands Target is looking for.

What Target appears to look for in a marketplace seller

The brands that are invited tend to share a few qualities, and the most important is that they fill a gap. Target uses the marketplace to complement its own range. A brand offering something Target’s buyers already stock, at a similar price, adds little. A brand that extends a category Target carries thinly, or offers sizes, colors or variants Target does not, gives the marketplace a reason to exist.

Fit with Target’s brand comes next. Target has built a reputation for design and quality at accessible prices. Products that sit comfortably beside Target’s own brands and national brands, in look, quality and price, are easier to place than products that would feel out of place on the site.

Reliable operations complete the case. Target Plus sellers ship their own orders inside a retailer that fulfills most of its sales from stores, and Target’s shoppers expect the same reliability from a marketplace order as from the store. Strong reviews, consistent delivery and low cancellation rates on other marketplaces are evidence that a brand can meet that standard.

Take two home brands that approach Target. One sells throw pillows much like those in Target’s own ranges, at similar prices, with average reviews. The other sells a well-reviewed line of extra-large and outdoor cushions in sizes Target’s own ranges do not cover, ships reliably from a U.S. warehouse, and has a clear, consistent look. The second has the far stronger case, and its size has little to do with it. It gives Target something Target does not already have.

Building the case before asking for an invitation

Preparation starts on Target.com itself. Study the category: note what Target’s own brands and existing sellers already offer, and identify the products, sizes or price points that are missing. The pitch should begin with that gap, stated in Target’s terms. The same exercise tells a brand whether to ask at all: if Target’s own ranges and current sellers already cover what it makes, at its price, the better move may be to change the products it leads with before it approaches Target.

Evidence of operations belongs beside it. Ratings, on-time shipping, cancellation rates and customer service response times from other marketplaces and the brand’s own site show that it can handle its own fulfillment, which on Target Plus is part of the product. A one-page summary of the gap, the products, the price points and the operational record persuades more than a long deck does.

A brand also needs to be ready for Target’s way of selling. That means pricing consistently with its other channels, supporting store returns of its products, and handling peak-season volume. A brand that has thought through those details is easier to say yes to.

Relationships shape the odds as well. Brands that already sell to Target as vendors, or whose products are known to Target’s buyers, start with an advantage, because the merchandising team already understands what they offer. Brands without that history should make the case in Target’s own language: which category, which gap, which guest.

Some categories are harder than others. Where Target’s own brands are strongest, the bar for a marketplace seller is highest, because the gap is smallest. Categories where shoppers expect wide choice, such as specialty home goods, hobby supplies or niche personal care, may offer more room.

What the invitation means once it arrives

A small, curated marketplace makes each invited brand more visible, and it also means sales start modestly. Target Plus works best treated as a channel that builds over time and a way to reach Target’s shoppers, rather than a source of Amazon-like volume in the first months.

The standard that earned the invitation is the one that keeps it. In a marketplace of a few hundred sellers, one that ships late or cancels orders stands out quickly.

The pace at which Target adds sellers during 2022 will show how scarce invitations remain. If it keeps adding them slowly, as it has since launch, the case a brand brings will matter even more. Building that case, from the gap analysis to the operating record, is how we prepare brands for Target Plus and run the channel once they are in.

A0178.title: How Amazon’s ranking algorithm rewards the prepared brand
A0178.alt: Open case of well-used hand tools beside a stack of brown paper parcels on a worn workbench.
A0178.ttag: How Amazon’s ranking algorithm rewards the prepared brand | Kwontified
A0178.desc: Amazon’s ranking follows sales a listing earns, so ads can start momentum but cannot hold rank for a page that does not convert. Prepare first.
A0178.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 18, 2022.
A0178.body:
In April and May 2021, Amazon suspended nearly 300 seller accounts, including large brands such as Mpow and Aukey, for taking part in fake review schemes. Their combined yearly sales exceeded $1 billion, and some of the suspended products had been best-sellers for years, Marketplace Pulse reported. Rank built over years went with the accounts. The lesson is about the mechanism underneath: Amazon’s search ranking follows the sales a listing earns when shoppers see it, so rank cannot be bought or gamed for long. The brands that hold it are the prepared ones, in stock, converting, reviewed and priced to compete.

What the Amazon ranking algorithm responds to

Amazon does not publish its ranking formula. Sellers generally understand that it weighs how relevant a product is to a search and how well the product sells when shoppers see it, along with factors such as availability and price.

What Amazon has made public is how it treats attempts to manipulate the result. The 2021 suspensions were one answer. The other came in writing: effective November 26, 2021, Amazon updated its Seller Code of Conduct to prohibit price fixing and search rank manipulation, BQool reported.

The stakes are high because Amazon is where many shoppers start. Marketplace Pulse described Amazon as the default search engine for many shoppers, the place they go to find a product they saw somewhere else. Losing organic position there means losing the shopper who already decided what to buy.

Why buying rank looks like it works

The belief that rank can be bought has a real basis. Advertising does bring shoppers to a product, and the sales those shoppers make count. Many sellers observe that a product’s organic position tends to improve after a period of strong, steady sales, whatever drove them. A launch supported by advertising can climb faster than one left to find its own way.

The flaw sits one step later. Advertising delivers the visit, but the listing has to turn the visit into a sale, and only the sale feeds the ranking. If shoppers arrive and do not buy, because of weak images, poor reviews, an uncompetitive price or a missing size, the sales that would lift the product never come. The brand pays for traffic and keeps little of it.

Outright manipulation fails more completely than that. Fake reviews, coordinated purchases and similar schemes may lift a product briefly, but they risk suspension, as the brands removed in 2021 found, and the updated code of conduct now names search rank manipulation as a breach.

Two launches with the same budget

Two brands launch similar water bottles, each with $15,000 to spend.

Brand ABrand B
Launch budget$15,000$15,000
Advertising$15,000$11,000
Preparationnone$4,000
Listing at launchthree images, no reviewsbetter images, clearer title, new-product review program
Stockruns out in week fiveenough for twelve weeks
When ads are reducedranking falls backranking holds

Brand A spends everything on advertising. Sales come while the ads run, but conversion is low, and the product runs out of stock in week five. When advertising stops, its ranking slides back to where it started.

Brand B moves $4,000 of the same budget into preparation: better images, a clearer title, enrollment in Amazon’s review program for new products, and enough stock for twelve weeks. Its conversion is higher, it never runs out, and reviews accumulate. When it pulls advertising back, the ranking holds, because the sales feeding it no longer depend on paid visits.

The budgets were identical. What differed was how many of the visits each brand paid for turned into sales.

Preparing a listing the ranking can reward

Availability comes first, since a product that goes out of stock loses sales, and with them the momentum that supports its position. Inventory plans need lead times built in, especially after a year when goods took far longer to arrive.

Conversion work has to be finished before the traffic arrives: images, titles, bullet points, A+ Content and price should all be strong, because every improvement in conversion makes each paid and organic visit worth more. Reviews have to be earned through Amazon’s own programs and good customer experience, and any tactic that looks like manipulation is worth avoiding however common it seems among competitors.

Advertising still has a job. It helps new products get found, defends important searches and brings in shoppers who would not otherwise see the product. Its role is to start and support momentum, not to stand in for the fundamentals.

Traffic from outside Amazon can add to that momentum. Since October 2021, Amazon has paid brands a bonus averaging 10% of the purchase price for sales driven by traffic they send from outside Amazon, according to its announcement. A brand with an email list, a social following or press coverage can use it to add sales, and the ranking support that comes with them, while earning a credit against its fees.

Patience belongs in the plan as well. Ranking built on genuine sales and reviews takes weeks to establish, and it is also harder to lose. Launches should be planned over a quarter, not a fortnight, and judged on where the product stands at the end of that period. Tracking position for the most important searches, week by week, shows whether organic visibility is building or fading.

The test comes when advertising is reduced. If organic sales hold, the brand earned its rank; if they fall away, the rank was rented, and the next dollar belongs in the listing rather than the bid. Planning stock, product pages and advertising together is how we build Amazon rankings that last for brands.

A0179.alt: Tablet and wicker shopping basket on a white plinth in a glass-walled lobby overlooking falling snow.
A0179.ttag: What NRF 2022 signaled about the retail year ahead | Kwontified
A0179.desc: NRF 2022 met after record holiday sales led by stores, with supply chains on their own stage. Retailers are investing in stores, stock and formats at once.
A0179.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 21, 2022.
A0179.body:
The National Retail Federation’s Big Show filled New York’s Javits Center from January 16 to 18 with more than 700 exhibiting companies, according to NRF, in a smaller form than usual and in person despite the omicron wave. The people walking its aisles had just come through a record holiday season, one carried by stores as much as by online sales. What they spent the show discussing was supply chains, stores and new formats, all at once.

For brands, that combination is the message of NRF 2022: retailers are putting money into stores, inventory and experiments together, and a 2022 plan that assumes growth will come online alone is planning for a different year.

The holiday numbers NRF 2022 opened on

Holiday sales grew 14.1% to a record $886.7 billion, NRF said, far above its own forecast of 8.5% to 10.5% and the average of 4.4% over the previous five years, according to its announcement. Online and other non-store sales rose 11.3% to $218.9 billion. Clothing stores grew 33.1% and sporting goods stores 20.9%.

Those figures set the mood in the room, and they deserve a careful reading. Non-store sales grew more slowly than total holiday sales. Online is still growing, but in 2021 it did not outpace the stores, and the fastest growth of the season came from clothing stores. A brand that put almost all of its 2021 growth effort into online channels has a reason to check whether that balance still fits its customers.

Some of the record also reflects prices. Online prices in November were up 3.5% against a year earlier, according to Adobe, so part of the total is higher prices rather than more goods sold. NRF’s chief executive pointed to strong wages and record savings as well as demand behind a 14.1% increase on top of a strong 2020, according to NRF’s release, and NRF itself said retailers should be prepared for challenges in the coming months. A plan for 2022 should allow for slower growth than 2021.

What the sessions put first

Supply chains had their own stage, with sessions every day, License Global reported. The topic was too pressing to share space. Retailers are not assuming the disruptions of 2021 are over. They are investing in visibility and automation, and they will expect suppliers to plan with them rather than around them. For a brand, the forecast it shares and the delivery date it promises become part of what it sells to a retailer.

Stores were back in the plan, and the show itself made the point. The holiday numbers had clothing stores growing fastest of all, and the Big Show returned to an in-person format, with speakers including Nordstrom’s president, Pete Nordstrom, License Global noted. For brands that sell through retailers, store availability and in-store presence matter again alongside online sales.

New formats were being tried in the corners. The show’s Innovation Lab featured more than 60 retail technology companies, many focused on sustainability and recommerce, according to NRF, and Coresight Research’s coverage of the second day was titled around the retail metaverse. These are experiments. They still show where retailers are spending attention, and where they may soon ask brands to join them.

Take a mid-sized apparel brand that sells online and through two national retailers. In 2021 it shifted stock toward its own site and Amazon, where demand was strongest. In 2022 its retail partners are investing in stores, asking for earlier commitments to secure inventory, and testing livestream shopping. If it keeps its 2021 allocation, it will be short in stores just as they recover, and absent from the new formats its partners are trying.

The mistake in that plan would not be the 2021 decision, which followed demand where it was strongest. It would be carrying that decision into a year whose conditions have changed, without asking whether the reasons behind it still hold. The retailers at NRF 2022 were planning for stores, stock and experiments together, and a supplier’s allocation is easiest to defend when it matches that plan.

Planning stock and partnerships for the year NRF described

Stock allocation is where the plan becomes real. If stores keep recovering, retailers will want inventory there, so a brand needs to decide early how much of each product goes to stores, to retailers’ websites and to marketplaces, and review the split each quarter. The decision works best written down. A short rule, such as protecting a minimum level of store stock for the products retailers promote, keeps the fastest-selling channel from taking everything by default.

Planning with a retailer’s supply chain means sharing forecasts earlier, committing to orders sooner where lead times demand it, and expecting retailers to ask more of suppliers on visibility and timing. Suppliers that can show reliable delivery dates and accurate stock positions are easier for retailers to plan around, and more likely to win space when it is scarce.

New formats call for a lighter touch. When a retailer invites a brand into livestream shopping or a new digital format, a small test is cheap and builds the relationship. A brand does not need a metaverse strategy, but its team should know what its partners are trying.

The size of the show carried its own message. A smaller, more cautious NRF mirrors an industry that is optimistic about demand and uncertain about conditions, and brands can plan with the same mix of ambition and caution. Retailers’ first-quarter results will say whether the picture holds: if store sales stay firm and inventory rises, NRF had the year right. Planning stock across stores, retailers’ sites and marketplaces from one view is how we help brands run the year NRF described.

A0182.crumb: Why October now wins November: holiday…
A0182.title: Why October now wins November: holiday planning for 2022
A0182.alt: Pumpkins and kraft-paper gifts decorated with autumn leaves on a weathered wooden bench against a terracotta wall.
A0182.ttag: Why October now wins November: holiday planning for 2022 | Kwontified
A0182.desc: Cyber Week shrank in 2021 while the season grew, because spending moved into October. Brands that build stock, reviews and rank by then win November.
A0182.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 27, 2022.
A0182.body:
Cyber Week online sales fell 1.4% in 2021 from the year before, Fox Business reported. The season around it did not shrink. Shoppers spent $204.5 billion online from November 1 to December 31, up 8.6% from 2020, according to Adobe, so the money was still there. It had simply spread out and moved earlier, and that changes where a season is won.

The stock, ranking and reviews a brand builds in October now decide how much it can sell in November and December. For 2022, October holiday planning means treating October as the first peak: holiday stock in place by the end of September, and advertising ramped from the first retailer event rather than from Thanksgiving.

What the 2021 season showed about October holiday planning

The busy days multiplied in 2021. There were 38 days on which online spending passed $3 billion, compared with 25 in 2020, Multichannel Merchant reported. The biggest days lost ground while the ordinary ones grew.

Retailers pulled the season forward themselves. Amazon’s holiday deals began on October 4, Fortune reported, and Target held its Deal Days from October 10 to 12, Chain Store Age reported. Shoppers who bought in those weeks had finished before a plan built around Thanksgiving had even started.

Shortages added pressure across the whole season. Shoppers saw more than 6 billion out-of-stock messages online over the season, up 10% from 2020, TechRadar reported, citing Adobe.

Two brands, one season

Take two brands that both sell small kitchen appliances on Amazon and Walmart.

One planned the season as it always had. Its holiday stock arrived in early November, its advertising budget leaned toward Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and its new air fryer launched on November 15. In October, while competitors ran early deals, it had little to offer.

By the time its stock landed, the shoppers who bought early had already chosen, and its new product went into the busiest week of the year with few reviews and little ranking. Its Cyber Monday was busy. Its season was flat.

The other moved its calendar forward. Its holiday stock was in Amazon and Walmart fulfillment centers by late September.

It ran modest deals during Amazon’s early holiday promotion and Target’s Deal Days, and it launched its air fryer on October 1 with enough advertising to bring early buyers. By mid-November the product had several hundred reviews and a strong position in search, and when Black Friday came it converted the extra traffic at full stride. Its Cyber Monday looked much like its rival’s. Its October and early November were far stronger.

What separated them was everything built before the peak: stock in place, reviews accumulated and ranking earned while competition was lighter.

Paying to hold stock from September is the real 2022 decision

For a brand’s leadership, the debate that follows is concrete. Moving holiday stock to the end of September means holding it longer, and storage costs more in 2022. Waiting means arriving after the early buyers have chosen. The choice is between a storage bill a finance team can see and lost October sales that no storage report shows, and it has to be made product by product. For the best holiday sellers, early stock usually earns its storage cost.

Not every product needs the same answer. Gift items, seasonal products and anything with a holiday spike gain the most from an October start. Everyday replenishment products, which sell steadily all year, need less change, though they still face higher click prices if competitors start advertising earlier.

Timing the stock means working back from the end of September. Freight is still slow, fulfillment centers are busiest from October, and lead times stretched to 80 days in 2021, so stock that ships on the old calendar lands in November, just as competition peaks.

New products need the same head start. A product launched in early October can collect reviews and earn ranking by Black Friday; one launched in mid-November cannot. Advertising budgets should ramp from Amazon’s early deals and Target’s October Deal Days rather than from Thanksgiving week. Click prices peak in December, so momentum built earlier, at lower cost, is worth more.

Moving the calendar means moving the people

Retail partners set the earliest deadlines. Retailers that start their events in October need deal submissions, content and stock confirmations in August and September. Brands that treat those deadlines as part of the holiday plan, rather than as early paperwork, secure better placement in the events that now open the season.

Teams follow the same calendar. A brand whose warehouse, customer service and advertising teams staff up for the week of Thanksgiving will be short-handed in October. Moving the peak means moving the people who serve it, including temporary staff and agency support. A customer service team hired for late November will meet October’s early buyers short-staffed, and an advertising team that plans its holiday push in October will be building campaigns while competitors are already collecting the reviews and rank those campaigns would need.

Measurement has to move last. A brand that judges its season on Black Friday and Cyber Monday will miss what happened in October. The whole span, from the first retailer event to the end of December, compared with the same span a year earlier, lets a strong October count toward the season.

When retailers announce their 2022 holiday events, the dates will show how early the season opens. If the first events fall in early October again, the planning calendar should already be set to meet them, and building that calendar across Amazon, Walmart and Target is how we plan holiday seasons for brands.

A0184.title: Walmart Marketplace in 2022 rewards brands that run like sellers
A0184.alt: Packing bench with a parcel on a digital scale, tape gun and stacked cardboard boxes in a blue-walled stockroom.
A0184.ttag: Walmart Marketplace in 2022 rewards brands that run like sellers | Kwontified
A0184.desc: Walmart Marketplace doubled its sellers in 2021, so the offer with the best price and delivery promise now wins. Brands must decide WFS product by product.
A0184.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 1, 2022.
A0184.body:
Walmart Marketplace passed 100,000 sellers in July 2021 and reached nearly 120,000 by late October, doubling in a year, Marketplace Pulse reported. For a brand, that number cuts both ways. More sellers fill the catalog and bring more shoppers, and they also put more offers on the same listings. Once several sellers compete for one product page, the sale goes to the offer with the best mix of price and delivery promise.

That is why Walmart is no longer an easy second channel: in 2022 a brand has to compete on fulfillment speed, price and advertising, and decide product by product whether Walmart Fulfillment Services pays for itself.

How Walmart Marketplace changed in 2021

The growth did not stop in October. By December the marketplace had about 130,000 sellers, according to the firm’s year in review.

Who joined changed too. Walmart opened the marketplace to sellers based outside the U.S. in March 2021. By October it had added about 5,000 sellers from China, and they made up 20% of new sellers that month. Some well-known sellers suspended on Amazon earlier in the year, including Mpow and Aukey, opened storefronts on Walmart, Marketplace Pulse reported.

The catalog grew with the sellers. Walmart said about 160 million items were available on its marketplace, up 21 million in a quarter, EcommerceBytes reported, and Walmart executive Brett Biggs said the company saw high demand from marketplace sellers.

Two other pieces matured at the same time. Walmart Fulfillment Services (WFS), which stores and ships sellers’ products much as Amazon’s fulfillment service does, began to carry more of the marketplace’s volume. And Walmart Connect’s advertising sales grew about 240% over two years, Walmart said on its earnings call, according to a transcript. Walmart still requires approval to sell, so the marketplace remains far smaller than Amazon’s.

How Walmart picks the offer that gets the sale

With few sellers on a listing, a brand could list its range, ship from its own warehouse and expect steady sales. With many, the offer that wins the sale is usually the one with the best combination of price and delivery promise, and some of those competing offers are for the brand’s own products. Walmart does not publish how it chooses which offer to show first, but sellers generally see price and shipping speed weigh heavily.

That makes WFS a pricing decision as much as a logistics one. Products stored with WFS can show faster delivery, and Walmart handles shipping and customer service. The costs are fees, less control over stock and the work of sending inventory to Walmart’s warehouses. Marketplace Pulse noted that WFS makes a seller’s location practically invisible to shoppers, which is why international sellers use it.

Take a home-goods brand that sells a fast-moving storage bin and a slower, bulky shelving unit on Walmart. The bin competes with several similar products, and faster delivery wins the sale, so moving it into WFS lifts conversion enough to cover the fees. The shelving unit sells a few units a week and costs a lot to store, so the brand keeps shipping it from its own warehouse and accepts a slower delivery promise. Same brand, same marketplace, opposite answers. A blanket rule in either direction would have cost it margin on one product or sales on the other.

Advertising follows the same logic. Sponsored Products on Walmart can put a product at the top of search results, but each click costs more as more sellers bid. An ad sends a shopper to the listing; the offer still has to win once the shopper arrives. A brand that relies on advertising alone, without competitive price and delivery, pays for traffic that buys from someone else.

Running Walmart Marketplace like a seller in 2022

The WFS call belongs at the product level. For each product, compare the expected lift in conversion from faster delivery with the WFS fees and storage costs. Fast movers in competitive categories usually justify it; slow, bulky products often do not. Products in WFS still need replenishment, and stock that runs out in Walmart’s warehouses loses its faster delivery promise until it is restocked, so WFS inventory deserves the same lead times and safety stock a brand uses for Amazon.

A brand’s own listings need watching. Checking who else sells its products on Walmart, and at what price, shows where unauthorized or low-priced sellers are taking the sale. Brand registration, consistent pricing across channels and a clear policy on authorized resellers all help. Price discipline cuts both ways: a product priced lower on Walmart than on Amazon can trigger price changes elsewhere, and one priced higher will rarely win the sale against a cheaper seller of the same item.

Search advertising is cheaper to build before the auction fills. Click prices on Walmart are still lower than on Amazon for many searches, and Walmart’s ad business is growing quickly. Keyword data, product page quality and sales history built now will cost less to hold later.

Content needs its own pass. Many brands moved their Amazon content to Walmart with few changes, but the two sites differ in how images, titles and descriptions appear, and product pages written for Walmart’s shoppers and layout convert better.

Watch the share of new sellers using WFS through 2022. If it keeps rising, delivery speed will weigh even more in who gets the sale. The working test for every product stays the same: if its offer would not win the listing without an ad, fix the offer before buying the click. Deciding fulfillment, price and advertising together for each product is how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.
