A0186.crumb: Zalando in 2022 is a platform brands sell…
A0186.title: Zalando in 2022 is a platform brands sell through, not a buyer
A0186.alt: Orange wrapped parcel on a wooden counter between racks of neutral-toned clothing in a sunlit boutique.
A0186.ttag: Zalando in 2022 is a platform brands sell through, not a buyer | Kwontified
A0186.desc: Zalando is turning from a retailer that buys stock into a platform brands sell through. In 2022, choose wholesale, Partner Program or both, product by product.
A0186.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 3, 2022.
A0186.body:
For years a brand sold to Zalando the way it sold to a department store. Zalando’s buyers chose the styles, bought the stock and set the prices, and the brand’s work ended at the warehouse door. That arrangement is giving way. Zalando is turning from a fashion retailer that buys brands’ stock into a platform brands sell through directly, and its Partner Program, where brands list and price their own products, is the part growing fastest. For brands selling in Europe, 2022 is the year to choose how they sell on Zalando, wholesale, as a partner, through their stores or a mix, and to build the operations each route needs.

Zalando grew in 2021, and its partners grew faster

Zalando kept growing as Europe reopened. Its gross merchandise volume (GMV) rose 25.3% to €3.1 billion in the third quarter of 2021, and its active customers rose 30.1% to 46.3 million, according to its third-quarter results. It expected full-year GMV growth of 31% to 36%.

The bigger change was in who does the selling. Partner Program GMV grew more than 100% in the first half of 2021, and close to 4,700 physical stores were selling through its Connected Retail program by mid-year, Zalando reported. Sephora began selling beauty through the Partner Program in Germany in the fourth quarter.

None of this is accidental. Zalando aims to reach more than €30 billion in GMV by 2025 and to raise the Partner Program’s share of GMV to 40%, from 24% in the fourth quarter of 2020, SGI Europe reported.

The map is widening too. Zalando launched in Croatia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia in 2021, opened its Partner Program in all six, and planned Hungary and Romania for 2022, according to the company. It is adding fulfillment centers in Germany and Poland to serve them, according to its announcement.

A platform built one brand at a time

The shift did not happen in one decision. It spread brand by brand, as each one found a reason to try selling directly.

Under the Partner Program, brands send their own stock to Zalando’s warehouses, or ship from their own, and decide what to list and at what price. Zalando earns a commission instead of a margin on stock it owns, and the brand, not Zalando’s buyer, decides which styles reach shoppers in each country. During the lockdowns, brands with closed stores and full warehouses had every reason to try it.

Connected Retail went further. It lets physical stores sell their stock on Zalando, with the store shipping the order, so for a brand with its own shops, store stock becomes online stock across Europe.

Take a Scandinavian outerwear brand that sold to Zalando wholesale for years. Zalando’s buyers took its best-selling jackets but rarely its full range, and marked down unsold stock at the end of the season. In 2021 the brand joined the Partner Program alongside its wholesale account. It listed colors and sizes the buyers had not taken, priced them consistently with its own site, and reached new markets as Zalando opened them. It also took on stock, content and pricing for Zalando itself, work its wholesale team had never done and had to learn quickly.

That last part is where the change lands inside a brand. The wholesale team was organized around a buyer, a line sheet and a delivery window. A partner business runs on daily stock levels, product content in many languages and prices set market by market, which looks more like running a marketplace than like selling to a retailer.

Choosing the route and building for it

The route belongs at the product level. Wholesale suits products where the brand wants Zalando to carry the stock risk. The Partner Program suits products where the brand wants control of price, range and markets. Many brands will use both, and each product needs a clear home so the two routes do not compete.

Running as a partner takes operations that wholesale never asked for. A brand selling directly is responsible for stock levels, product content in many languages and pricing across markets, and teams need to plan for that work before they scale rather than discover it in the first busy season.

Price policy is where the routes collide. A brand that sells the same jacket wholesale and as a partner, at different prices in different markets, can confuse shoppers and undercut its own wholesale account. A single price policy for Zalando, set market by market, avoids that.

New markets reward a focused start. Each country Zalando opens is a chance to test demand without building a local business, but returns, delivery times and local payment preferences differ, so a narrow range that expands as the brand learns carries less risk.

The data is a gain in its own right. Partners see how their own listings perform, which sizes sell in which countries and how often items come back, and that belongs in next season’s range plan as well as in day-to-day Zalando management.

Connected Retail deserves a separate decision. It can turn slow-moving store stock into online sales, but only if store teams can pick and ship orders reliably and the store’s stock records are accurate enough that an online order never lands on an empty shelf.

Zalando’s full-year results on March 1 will show where the partner share of GMV stands. If it keeps rising toward the 2025 goal, Zalando’s buyers will hold less of the range each season, and the brands that sell directly will matter more to it. Setting up the Partner Program and running it day to day across markets is how we help brands sell through Zalando.

A0187.crumb: Amazon ad revenue, reported at last, says…
A0187.title: Amazon ad revenue, reported at last, says costs will keep rising
A0187.alt: Rising stacks of brass coins on a wooden desk with a succulent and pen stand against a pink wall.
A0187.ttag: Amazon ad revenue, reported at last, says costs will keep rising | Kwontified
A0187.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 32% in Q4 2021 while its own store sales fell 1%. Slower growth still means more money per shopper, so plan 2022 for dearer orders.
A0187.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 8, 2022.
A0187.body:
Amazon’s ad growth fell from 88% in the second quarter of 2021 to 33% in the fourth, excluding currency effects. Read quickly, that looks like competition cooling and click prices about to ease. It points the other way. In the same fourth quarter that Amazon ad revenue rose 32%, Amazon’s own online store sales fell 1%. More advertising money chasing roughly the same shoppers raises the cost of each sale, whatever the headline growth rate, so brands should plan 2022 budgets for dearer orders rather than cheaper clicks.

What Amazon ad revenue showed on February 3

Amazon had reported advertising inside a line labeled “other” for years. On February 3 it broke the business out for the first time. Advertising generated $31.2 billion in 2021, with fourth-quarter sales up 32% to $9.7 billion, CNBC reported. That made it larger than Microsoft’s advertising business and larger than the total revenue of Snap or Pinterest. Amazon did not say how profitable it is.

The quarterly path explains the slowdown. Excluding currency effects, ad sales grew 76% in the first quarter and 88% in the second, which included Prime Day, against 33% in the fourth, MediaPost reported. Advertising made up 7% of Amazon’s fourth-quarter sales, up from 6% a year earlier, and sponsored products and brands make up the majority of it, MediaPost reported separately.

Meanwhile, Amazon’s own online store sales fell 1% in the quarter while third-party seller services grew 11%, according to a Raymond James note cited by MediaPost.

Why slower ad growth does not mean cheaper clicks

The hopeful reading has a real basis. Growth did slow sharply, and some of the earlier rate reflected the pandemic, when advertisers rushed online and Prime Day moved between quarters. A slower-growing ad business is less likely to see the extreme jumps in click prices of 2020 and early 2021.

The auction does not price growth rates, though. It prices the money bidding for each search against the shoppers making it. Ad revenue rose 32% while Amazon’s own retail sales fell slightly, so each shopper drew more bids than a year earlier. Every advertiser raising a budget by a reasonable amount, one at a time, adds up to a higher price for all of them.

New money is also arriving. A day before Amazon’s results, Meta said Apple’s privacy changes would cost it about $10 billion in revenue in 2022, CNBC reported. Amazon’s ads are tied to search on its own store and are less exposed to those changes, Axios reported. Some of the money leaving social advertising will bid on the same searches as your brand.

The price rise is already visible. On Amazon, the average cost per click rose 43% during 2021, while conversion stayed between 12% and 13%, Marketplace Pulse reported. Dearer clicks with flat conversion mean dearer orders.

What a 15% rise in click prices does to one budget

Take a brand that spent $50,000 a month on Sponsored Products in late 2021 at an average cost per click of $1.30 and a 12% conversion rate.

Late 20212022, clicks 15% dearer
Average cost per click$1.3015% higher
Conversion rate12%12%
Cost per order$10.83$12.46
Monthly spend for the same orders$50,000$57,500

Conversion holds, so the whole increase lands on the order. To keep the same number of orders, the brand needs about $57,500 a month, or it accepts fewer orders. Slower growth in Amazon’s ad revenue does nothing to that arithmetic.

The change can hide on a return-on-ad-spend dashboard. If the brand’s prices rose with the market, attributed revenue climbs alongside spend, and the ratio barely moves while each order costs more to win. Cost per order shows the shift at once, which is why it belongs in the budget conversation before the ratio does.

Planning Amazon advertising for 2022

Budgets should start from current costs: late-2021 click prices and conversion rates, with an allowance for further increases, rather than 2021 averages. Return on ad spend can stay flat while cost per order rises, especially if prices rise too, so cost per order and units per ad dollar belong beside it in every report.

Conversion is the lever a brand controls. Every improvement in conversion lowers the cost of each order at a given click price, which is why product pages, reviews, pricing and stock all matter more as click prices rise. A page that converts one more shopper in every hundred visits takes back part of the click-price increase without any change to bids, and it keeps paying back as long as the page stays live.

Budgets also need to follow the calendar. Click prices peaked around Prime Day and in December in 2021, Marketplace Pulse reported, and a flat monthly budget will run short in those weeks and sit underused in quieter ones. New formats compete for the same money: Amazon is selling more video, display and streaming television advertising, and those budgets should be set together with search rather than taking from it by default. Walmart, Target and other retailers building ad businesses will face the same forces as they grow.

Amazon’s new disclosure gives brands a yardstick each quarter. If a brand’s ad spend grows much faster than Amazon’s ad revenue, it may be overpaying for its position; if it grows much more slowly, it may be losing share of the searches that matter. Amazon’s first-quarter figure, due in April, will show the underlying pace without Prime Day in either year.

The working rule is simple. If ad dollars on a retailer grow faster than its shoppers, plan for each order to cost more, whatever the growth rate does. Budgets built from current click prices and margins are how we plan Amazon advertising for brands in 2022.

A0189.crumb: Target Plus in 2022 extends a store-first…
A0189.title: Target Plus in 2022 extends a store-first retailer online
A0189.alt: A red wrapped parcel tied with twine beside an open laptop on a wooden counter in a sunlit shop.
A0189.ttag: Target Plus in 2022 extends a store-first retailer online | Kwontified
A0189.desc: Target fulfills more than 95% of its sales through stores, and Target Plus fills the gaps in that range online. Plan it as the online aisle behind the shelf.
A0189.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 10, 2022.
A0189.body:
More than 95% of Target’s third-quarter sales were fulfilled by its stores, whether the guest walked the aisles, collected an order at the counter, waited in a Drive Up bay or had a Shipt shopper bring it home, according to its filing. The store is where Target’s digital business happens. Target Plus, still about 440 sellers, sits at the edge of that model.

It extends the store-led business online by filling gaps in Target’s range. Brands get the most from it when they plan it that way, as the online aisle behind Target’s shelf, with range, returns and service built around how Target’s guests shop.

Target Plus sits inside a store-first business

Target’s growth in 2021 came through its stores. Comparable sales rose 12.7% in the third quarter, with store sales up 9.7% and digital sales up 29%, according to its results. Same-day services, meaning Order Pickup, Drive Up and Shipt, grew nearly 60%.

Target Plus works differently from the rest of that business. Its sellers keep their own stock and handle their own shipping, and guests can bring returns to any Target store. In late 2019 it had nearly 100 sellers offering about 250,000 products, the Star Tribune reported. Two years later the count was about 440, set against roughly 130,000 on Walmart’s marketplace, Marketplace Pulse reported.

So Target Plus has grown about fourfold in two years and remains small by design. It lets Target offer more online without changing what kind of retailer it is.

What Target gets from Target Plus, and what brands get

For Target, the program extends the range without the inventory risk. Target’s buyers choose what fills its shelves and its warehouses. Target Plus lets the website offer sizes, colors and categories the stores could never carry, while sellers carry the stock, and every one of those products appears beside Target’s own brands on Target.com and in its app. Target keeps the guest, the basket and the store visit a return brings; the seller holds the inventory.

For brands, the value is access to Target’s guests on Target’s terms. Guests find Target Plus products in the same search results as everything else, check out in the same basket and can return them at a store. That is the appeal, and it is also the constraint, because the guest’s expectations are set by Target rather than by the seller.

The costs sit on the other side of the ledger. The seller pays to hold the stock, ship each order and absorb the returns a guest brings to the store, while Target supplies the traffic and the trust that make a guest willing to buy from a seller they may never have heard of.

The details show it. A guest who buys a Target Plus item expects it to arrive as reliably as a Drive Up order, and a guest who returns it at a store expects the same courtesy as for any other purchase. A seller that ships late or handles complaints poorly damages Target’s relationship with its guest, which is why Target keeps the program curated.

Take a kitchenware brand that sells its core range to Target wholesale, with its best-selling pans on Target’s shelves. On Target Plus it lists the full cookware sets, the larger sizes and the colors the stores do not stock. Guests who see the pans in store find the rest of the range in the Target app. The brand ships those orders itself, prices them consistently with its other channels and accepts store returns as part of the cost.

The brand learns from it too. Which colors and sizes sell online, and in which regions, tells it what to propose to Target’s buyers for the next store reset. For that brand, Target Plus is the online aisle behind its store shelf rather than a separate business.

Planning Target Plus for 2022 around the store

Range planning starts from the store assortment. Extended sizes, colors, bundles and adjacent products complement what Target already carries. Items that duplicate what Target buys from the brand or from others put its online listings against Target’s own shelves, which is the opposite of what the program is for.

Service has to meet Target’s standard. Delivery promises, cancellation rates and customer service need to match what guests expect from Target itself, and that belongs in staffing and fulfillment plans before the holiday season rather than during it.

Store returns need a budget. They are part of what makes Target Plus attractive to guests, and a brand should agree how returned items are handled before it scales its range.

A brand with an existing vendor relationship at Target can treat Target Plus as part of that relationship. The merchant team that buys for stores will notice how a brand performs online, and a strong Target Plus record can support conversations about wider store distribution. Brands that do not yet sell to Target should be realistic: invitations remain scarce, the program grows slowly, and the best chance belongs to a brand that fits a clear gap in Target’s range and can show reliable operations elsewhere.

Content matters as much as range. Target Plus products compete in the same search results as Target’s own assortment, so complete product pages, strong images and accurate inventory make a real difference to how often they are found.

Target’s digital growth through 2022 will show whether the edge of the store moves. If digital sales keep growing faster than store sales, Target will need more online range, and Target Plus may grow faster than it has so far. Planning that range around the shelf, and running the orders and returns to Target’s standard, is how we manage Target Plus for brands.

A0191.crumb: Amazon’s Q4 ad growth outran its sales…
A0191.title: Amazon’s Q4 ad growth outran its sales, so each sale costs more
A0191.alt: A tall stack of brass coins beside twine-tied paper parcels on an old wooden desk by a window.
A0191.ttag: Amazon’s Q4 ad growth outran its sales, so each sale costs more | Kwontified
A0191.desc: When Amazon demand flattens, brands buy back lost organic sales with ads and bid against each other. Q4 2021 showed it. Budget 2022 for a higher cost per sale.
A0191.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 15, 2022.
A0191.body:
Third-party sellers accounted for 56% of units sold on Amazon in the fourth quarter of 2021, the highest fourth-quarter share on record. In that same quarter Amazon’s own online store sales fell 1%, seller services grew 11% and advertising revenue grew 32%.

The natural expectation is that slower sales should make advertising cheaper, with less money chasing fewer purchases. On Amazon it tends to work the other way. When demand flattens, brands try to buy back the organic sales they are losing, and they bid against each other to do it. That is why brands should plan 2022 for a higher advertising cost per sale and protect conversion and margin rather than chase volume.

Amazon’s Q4 ad growth set against its sales

Amazon reported advertising as its own line for the first time on February 3. Ad sales in the fourth quarter reached $9.7 billion, a rise of 32%, MediaPost reported. Sales from Amazon’s own online stores slipped 1% over the quarter, and third-party seller services, the fees Amazon earns from sellers, rose 11%, figures MediaPost took from a Raymond James note.

Advertising also took a bigger slice of the whole. It was 7% of Amazon’s fourth-quarter sales against 6% a year before, and it drove 20% of Amazon’s total sales growth in the quarter, MediaPost reported in a second piece, citing Wedbush analyst Michael Pachter. The 56% third-party share came from the same report.

One complication sits in the base. Prime Day fell in October 2020 and in June 2021, so the fourth quarter of 2020 held an extra sales event, which flatters the 2020 retail figure and makes 2021’s retail growth look weaker. Even allowing for that, advertising grew far faster than the sales it supports.

How a slowdown pushes brands into the auction

A brand’s Amazon sales come partly from organic search and partly from ads. When demand slows, the organic share falls first. To protect its volume, the brand raises bids and budgets on its most important searches. Its competitors do the same. Each decision is sensible on its own, and together they bid up the price of the same shoppers. The auction does not ask why a brand is bidding: a bid placed to defend lost organic volume counts exactly the same as one placed to grow.

Third-party sellers add to the pressure. Many of them sell the same types of products in the same categories as brands, they now account for more than half of units sold, and most rely on advertising to be found. As their share grows, more of Amazon’s sales depend on winning an auction.

The figures fit that story. Advertising revenue grew about 32% while seller services grew 11%, which in rough terms means sellers spent about a fifth more on advertising for every dollar of fees they paid Amazon. The average Amazon cost per click climbed 43% across 2021 while conversion held between 12% and 13%, according to Marketplace Pulse.

What buying back organic sales costs one brand

Take a pet-supplies brand that sold 10,000 units a month through Amazon in late 2020, a third of them from ads, at $8 of ad spend per ad-driven unit. In late 2021 demand flattened and organic sales slipped. To hold 10,000 units it pushed ad-driven units to 4,000, and because rivals did the same, each one cost $10.

Late 2020Late 2021
Total units a month10,00010,000
Ad-driven unitsabout a third4,000
Ad spend per ad-driven unit$8$10
Monthly ad billabout $26,700$40,000

The brand sold exactly as much and paid far more to do it. It did nothing wrong; it competed in a crowded auction while the market around it stopped growing. Seasonality sharpens the effect. Click prices peaked around Prime Day and again in December in 2021, Marketplace Pulse reported, so a brand recovering lost organic sales in those weeks pays the highest prices of the year to do it.

Planning for a crowded auction in 2022

Budgets should assume each ad-driven sale will cost more in 2022 than it did in 2021, and that assumption deserves a monthly check against actual results. Comparing the cost of each ad-driven sale with the plan every month shows early whether the allowance was too low, while there is still time to move budget between products.

Conversion is the cheapest defense. In a crowded auction the brands that convert best pay least for each sale, and product pages, reviews, price and stock all decide conversion. Organic visibility matters for the same reason: sales from organic search carry no click cost, and products kept in stock, priced well and well reviewed hold more organic position, which reduces how much has to be bought through ads.

Not every search is worth winning at any price. Brands should know which searches bring profitable customers, bid hard for those, and pull back from broad terms where the cost of each sale exceeds the margin. When rivals run out of stock or cut budgets, click prices on shared searches can fall for a while, and teams that track their share of search results can take those openings quickly.

Margin is the final test. A brand that holds volume by spending more on ads than its products earn has not protected its business, so each product needs a break-even advertising cost of sale and every campaign should be judged against it. Amazon’s first-quarter results in April will show whether ad growth again outpaces retail and seller services. The rule for the meantime: if holding volume costs more per unit than the product earns, give up the volume, not the margin. Setting Amazon budgets against margin rather than volume is how we manage advertising costs for brands.

A0192.crumb: Mercado Libre in 2022 rewards brands that…
A0192.title: Mercado Libre in 2022 rewards brands that use its logistics
A0192.alt: A yellow van loaded with cardboard boxes parked outside an open, weathered warehouse with pallets.
A0192.ttag: Mercado Libre in 2022 rewards brands that use its logistics | Kwontified
A0192.desc: Mercado Libre now handles most of its own deliveries and 37% through its warehouses. In 2022, brands that use its logistics will reach buyers fastest.
A0192.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 17, 2022.
A0192.body:
The 2021 holiday season showed discounts shrinking sharply in some categories and growing in others. Costs, stock and demand now differ widely by product. A single discount applied across a range wastes margin on some products and fails to move others. Brands should set promotions product by product, based on margin, stock and how much a discount actually lifts sales.

What the 2021 holiday showed about promotions

Discounts moved in different directions by category. Across the holiday season, electronics were discounted 8% on average, against 21% in 2020, computers 10% against 22%, and sporting goods 6% against 14%, Adobe reported on January 12. Television discounts were unchanged at 11%. Apparel discounts grew to 13% from 11%, and toys to 19% from 14%, according to the same figures.

The reasons were different for each product. Shoppers saw more than 6 billion out-of-stock messages online over the season, up 10% from 2020, TechRadar reported. Where stock was short, retailers had little reason to discount. Where it was plentiful, they discounted more.

Costs are diverging too. Consumer prices rose 7.5% in the year to January, the largest increase since 1982, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on February 10. Amazon’s fulfillment fees rose by an average of 5.2% in January, Benzinga reported, with the increase varying by size and weight.

The bias: repeating the previous year’s promotion

The bias worth naming is calendar habit: running each year’s promotion the way the previous year’s ran, because it worked then.

Many brands plan promotions by event. Prime Day gets 20% off the range. Black Friday gets 25%. The figure is set once and applied to every product, because that is simple to approve and simple to run.

That made more sense when products were similar in cost and supply. It makes less sense now. Two products in the same range may have different freight costs, different fee changes and very different stock positions. The same discount has very different value on each.

A simple, hypothetical example shows the waste. A home-fitness brand runs 20% off its whole range for an event. Its resistance bands are in short supply and sell out at full price anyway, so the discount gives away margin on sales it would have made. Its foam rollers are overstocked, but shoppers are not very price-sensitive, so 20% off lifts sales only slightly. Its yoga mats are well stocked and price-sensitive, and the discount nearly doubles their sales.

One discount produced three outcomes: lost margin, little effect and a real gain. A product-by-product plan would have held the bands at full price, kept the rollers at a modest discount with advertising support, and put the deepest offer on the mats.

Click prices make the waste larger. The average cost per click on Amazon rose 43% during 2021, Marketplace Pulse reported. A brand that pays more to bring shoppers to a discounted product, when the product would have sold anyway, loses twice.

The bias is hard to see because blanket promotions often produce a good total. Sales rise during the event, and the report looks healthy. The margin given away on products that would have sold anyway does not appear in the sales figure.

How brands should set promotions in 2022

Three practices follow.

First, start from margin and stock. Before each event, list each product’s current margin after fees, freight and advertising, and its weeks of stock. Products with thin margin or short stock rarely need a discount. Products with healthy margin and excess stock are the natural candidates.

Second, measure how much a discount lifts sales. Use past events to estimate, for each product, how much sales rose at each discount level. Some products barely respond. Others respond strongly. Put discounts where they change behavior.

Third, choose the type of promotion as well as the depth. A coupon, a bundle, a free gift or a limited-time deal each suits different products. Bundles can move slow sellers alongside popular ones without cutting the popular item’s price.

Advertising should follow the plan. A discount that lifts sales strongly deserves advertising support during the event. One that barely moves sales does not, and spending to promote it wastes budget twice.

Timing matters as well. The 2021 season spread across more days, starting in October. A product that sells out early in the season needs no discount later, while one that lags may need support well before the main event.

Retailer rules matter too. Amazon, Walmart and Target each have their own deal formats, eligibility rules and deadlines. A product-by-product plan should be built early enough to meet them.

Brands should also watch reference prices. Frequent deep discounts teach shoppers to wait for the next one, and can lower the price a retailer’s systems treat as normal. Fewer, better-targeted promotions protect full-price sales between events.

Teams need the right data in one place to do this. Margin, stock, past discount response and advertising cost usually sit in different systems. Bringing them into a single planning sheet for each event is the practical first step.

The signal to watch is margin per unit during events, not sales alone. If event sales rise but margin per unit falls sharply, the promotion bought volume the brand did not need.

What to do

  1. List each product’s margin after fees, freight and advertising, and its weeks of stock, before every event.
  2. Estimate how much past discounts lifted sales for each product.
  3. Set the discount type and depth product by product, and support only the offers that move sales.

We manage promotions and pricing for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target, product by product. If your event discounts are applied across the range, talk to our team.

A0195.crumb: Walmart’s ad growth shows it wants ads in…
A0195.title: Walmart’s ad growth shows it wants ads in every supplier plan
A0195.alt: Five navy binders stand beside a blue shopping basket holding notebooks on a wooden table.
A0195.ttag: Walmart’s ad growth shows it wants ads in every supplier plan | Kwontified
A0195.desc: Walmart books part of its $2.1 billion ad business the way it books supplier funding. Plan Walmart Connect with your buyer, not as a separate ecommerce budget.
A0195.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 24, 2022.
A0195.body:
Walmart’s advertising business reached $2.1 billion in its latest fiscal year, and not all of that money was booked as sales. Walmart recorded $1.6 billion as sales and $0.5 billion as a reduction to cost of sales, depending on the nature of each advertising arrangement, according to its results. That second line is the treatment a retailer usually gives to money its suppliers pay it, and it is a better guide to Walmart’s intentions than the headline figure.

Read together with the rest of the results, it shows a retailer that wants advertising in every supplier’s plan, sitting beside traditional trade spending. Brands that treat Walmart advertising as a separate ecommerce budget are planning for a different retailer. The plan belongs with the buyer relationship and the store business.

Walmart’s ad growth came with far more advertisers

The number of companies buying from Walmart Connect grew faster than the revenue line suggests. Active U.S. advertisers using Walmart Connect increased 136%, Walmart said in the same results.

Walmart is still small next to Amazon, whose advertising brought in $31 billion in 2021, Reuters noted. The pace is what stands out. Walmart Connect’s sales had grown about 240% over two years, the company said on an earlier earnings call, according to a transcript. Executives on that call described selling advertising as a way to help suppliers and marketplace sellers sell more while creating a new profit opportunity for Walmart.

The ecommerce figures explain why the advertising matters to Walmart’s investors. Walmart’s U.S. ecommerce sales grew 1% in the holiday quarter, and 70% over two years. One analyst told Reuters that newer businesses such as Walmart Connect, the marketplace and financial services are asset-light and add to Walmart’s margins.

Walmart’s ad dollars come from the supplier relationship

On Amazon, much of the advertising comes from third-party sellers buying search placements. On Walmart, a large share comes from the consumer brands that already sell to Walmart as suppliers, and those brands have long paid Walmart in other ways: allowances, promotional funding and in-store displays, negotiated with Walmart’s buyers.

The accounting split hints at that link. Some advertising is recorded as sales, as you would expect from a media business. The $0.5 billion recorded against cost of goods is treated the way supplier payments to a retailer are usually treated. Walmart does not say which arrangements fall on which side, but the pattern suggests that some advertising is being bought as part of the broader supplier relationship rather than from a separate media budget.

That is the structure Walmart is building toward. Advertising becomes a normal part of how every supplier does business with it, sitting beside, and sometimes replacing, older forms of trade spending. In return Walmart offers what those older forms could not: measurement that links ads to sales in stores and online, and reach beyond its own sites through Walmart DSP, launched in 2021, according to Walmart.

Data is part of the package as well. Walmart launched Walmart Luminate in 2021, a set of data products for suppliers about shoppers and categories, and executives grouped it with Walmart Connect when describing the businesses they are building, according to the same call.

Take a beverage brand that negotiates its annual plan with its Walmart buyer: shelf space, prices and promotional funding. In 2021 its ecommerce team ran Sponsored Products separately, with a small budget. In 2022 the buyer asks how the brand will support a new flavor launch, and Walmart Connect is part of the answer: search ads, off-site video aimed at past buyers of the category, and in-store screens, measured against store and online sales.

The brand’s choices change with that question. It can fund part of the launch through advertising instead of a deeper price cut, and see which shoppers bought. It can learn which stores responded, which helps in the next negotiation over shelf space. The media plan and the trade plan end up on the same table, in front of the same buyer.

Planning Walmart advertising with the buyer

Once advertising sits inside the supplier relationship, it has to be planned there. Walmart Connect belongs alongside shelf space, pricing and promotions in the annual conversation with the buyer, so that advertising supports the same goals and gets credit in the relationship rather than appearing as an ecommerce line nobody in the room recognizes.

Measurement has to cover the whole of Walmart. A brand that judges campaigns on online sales alone will understate what advertising does for products that sell mostly in stores. Reporting that includes store sales and new buyers is the fairer test, and it is the one Walmart is offering.

The harder conversation is about money already committed elsewhere. If advertising takes budget from older promotional funding, someone has to check which of the two delivers more sales per dollar, and shift the budget accordingly. That check rarely happens on its own, because at many brands the people who negotiate with the Walmart buyer and the people who run the ads rarely plan together.

Without a joint plan, with shared goals and shared reporting, a brand can pay twice for the same result: once in trade funding and again in search ads aimed at the same shoppers. Brands that buy advertising and data together can plan more precisely, provided they are clear about what each costs.

Smaller brands and marketplace sellers will feel the change from the other side. As large suppliers bring bigger budgets into Walmart Connect, search results will get more competitive, and click prices are likely to rise.

Walmart’s own reporting through 2022 will show how far this goes. If it begins to disclose growth rates for Walmart Connect each quarter, advertising will have become a core part of its business with suppliers, and the question for a brand’s leadership is who on the team owns that conversation with the buyer. Planning search, off-site and in-store media alongside the trade budget is how we manage Walmart advertising as part of the supplier plan.

A0197.crumb: Roundel in 2022 pays off most for brands…
A0197.title: Roundel in 2022 pays off most for brands Target already stocks
A0197.alt: Rows of identical kraft boxes fill a dark red shelving unit beneath a blank lit sign in a bright room.
A0197.ttag: Roundel in 2022 pays off most for brands Target already stocks | Kwontified
A0197.desc: Roundel measures ads against Target’s own sales, in stores and online, so its return tracks a brand’s Target distribution. Size the budget to the shelf.
A0197.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 1, 2022.
A0197.body:
Take two snack brands that each put $50,000 into the same Roundel campaign, aimed at the same Target grocery guests. One comes back with strong reported sales in stores and online. The other comes back with far fewer. Both bought the same reach. The difference is what happened after a guest saw the ad, and that depends on where Target stocks each brand.

Roundel, Target’s advertising business, sells access to Target’s guests and measures results against Target’s own sales. Its return therefore follows a brand’s Target distribution, and in 2022 the budget should be sized to that distribution rather than borrowed from the logic of an Amazon plan.

Roundel added store-level measurement in 2021

Target has sold advertising for years. It launched an in-house media company in 2016 and relaunched it as Roundel in 2019, Chain Store Age reported, aiming to become a more aggressive player in digital advertising, the Star Tribune reported.

The business added people and tools in 2021. Target named Sarah Travis, a 13-year Google veteran, president of Roundel in August, and said the business had added programmatic advertising, closed-loop measurement and self-service performance tools, and had consistently beaten its revenue goals since 2019, according to Target. Since May 2021, brands have been able to buy Target Product Ads, its sponsored products, through CitrusAd’s self-serve platform, with SKU-level reporting, Chain Store Age reported.

The retailer behind the ads is what gives them value. In the third quarter, Target’s stores fulfilled more than 95% of its sales, while digital sales grew 29%, according to its results. Target can link an ad a guest saw to a purchase in either place.

Why Roundel’s closed loop rewards distribution

Roundel sells two things. One is reach: Target’s guests, on its own site and app and across other sites through programmatic advertising. The other is measurement, a closed loop from ad to purchase at Target. That second part separates Roundel from a general ad network, and it carries a condition that is easy to miss. The loop can only close where a guest can buy the product.

A brand stocked in most of Target’s stores and online can turn the demand an ad creates into measured sales almost anywhere. A brand sold only online, or in a few stores, cannot. The guest who sees its ad while planning a store visit walks the aisle and finds nothing.

Back to the two snack brands:

Stocked in nearly every Target storeSold only on Target.com
Roundel spend$50,000$50,000
Guest who sees the ad while planning a store tripCan buy it on the next visitCannot find it on the shelf
Guest who sees the ad in the appCan buy online or in storeCan buy online
What Target’s reporting showsStrong sales in stores and onlineFar fewer measured sales
What the brand can take to its buyerWhich stores respondedLittle to show

Neither brand bought bad advertising. The second bought reach that its distribution could not convert, and it also lost the store-level read that the first brand can use in its next shelf conversation. A dollar spent on Roundel by a brand on every Target shelf works harder than the same dollar spent by a brand Target barely carries. The reported return on a Roundel campaign therefore says as much about the brand’s distribution as it says about the creative, the audience or the bids. A team that reads it as a verdict on the ads alone will draw the wrong conclusion.

Where Amazon habits mislead a Roundel plan

Amazon’s sponsored products are measured on Amazon sales over a fixed window, while Roundel’s results include store purchases. A brand that compares the two reported returns directly is comparing different things. Cost per incremental sale is the fairer comparison where a brand can get it.

The Amazon habit also hides the distribution question, because the same Roundel campaign can look strong or weak depending on the shelf behind it. Brands with wide store presence can treat Roundel as a core channel. Brands with limited presence do better starting with Target Product Ads on Target.com and the app, where the products they sell are available.

Self-serve tools change who can use Roundel. Buying Target Product Ads through CitrusAd, with daily reporting, lets smaller brands test sponsored products without a large managed campaign, learn which searches and products convert, and expand once they know.

Planning Roundel spend around the shelf in 2022

The buyer belongs in the plan. Advertising that supports a new item, a seasonal display or a promotion agreed with the Target buyer is easier to justify, and its results feed the next conversation about shelf space.

Timing follows Target’s own calendar. Events such as Deal Days, which Target ran from October 10 to 12, 2021, as Chain Store Age reported, concentrate guest traffic into a few days. Roundel campaigns timed to those events, with products in stock and on promotion, reach guests when they are most ready to buy.

Off-site reach needs the same discipline. Programmatic campaigns that use Target’s data to reach guests on other sites can build demand, but only for products those guests can find at Target. Off-site spend belongs behind the best-distributed products, judged on Target sales rather than clicks. Reporting should include store sales and new guests as well, because for brands that sell mostly in stores, online-only return on ad spend understates what Roundel does.

How Target describes Roundel in its 2022 results will show how central advertising has become to its work with brands. Until then, the rule is simple to apply: before raising a Roundel budget, check how many Target shelves the advertised product sits on, and set the spend in proportion. Matching Target media to Target distribution is how we plan Roundel and Target Product Ads for brands.

A0198.crumb: Instagram shopping in 2022 is built for…
A0198.title: Instagram shopping in 2022 is built for discovery, not checkout
A0198.alt: A smartphone with a glowing purple screen, a vase of wildflowers and a paper bag on a wooden table.
A0198.ttag: Instagram shopping in 2022 is built for discovery, not checkout | Kwontified
A0198.desc: Instagram left shopping off its 2022 priorities in favor of video and creators. Brands should use it to be discovered and close sales where they convert best.
A0198.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 3, 2022.
A0198.body:
Watch how people shop on Instagram: they rarely arrive looking for a product. They scroll, stop on a creator’s video, see something they like, and then save it, ask about it in the comments or look it up somewhere else. That habit raises a question for any brand with an Instagram Shop: who is the shop for?

Instagram has answered it in its own planning. Its stated priorities for 2022 put video, messaging, transparency and creators first, and shopping is not on the list. Brands should treat Instagram in 2022 as the place shoppers discover products through creators and Reels, and send that demand to where they already convert well, rather than building their plans around Instagram checkout.

Instagram shopping slipped down the list in 2021

The push into shopping was real. In late 2020, Instagram’s head, Adam Mosseri, said shopping could earn money both from a cut of each transaction and from ads that prompt people to buy, CNBC reported. In May 2021 the app launched Drops, a section at the top of its Shop tab for limited-edition product launches, ASI reported. It widened who could use shopping tools and added shopping to Reels, Retail Dive reported.

In mid-2021, shopping was still one of Instagram’s four stated priorities, alongside creators, video and messaging, though Mosseri spent most of his time on video, the Motley Fool reported. By December the list had changed. Mosseri’s priorities for 2022 were video, messaging, transparency and creators, Engadget reported. Shopping had dropped off.

The market around it is growing, though slowly next to Asia. U.S. social commerce was expected to reach $36 billion in 2021, up from $26.7 billion in 2020, according to eMarketer figures cited by ASI. That is about a tenth of China’s market, Retail Dive reported, and eMarketer described social commerce as still largely impulse-driven. Meta has other pressures as well. On February 2 it put the 2022 revenue cost of Apple’s privacy changes at about $10 billion, CNBC reported, and its attention is on video and on measuring advertising again.

Discovery and checkout are different jobs

The change in priorities matches the scroll-and-save habit. Instagram is very good at the first half of shopping, putting a product in front of someone who did not know they wanted it. Closing the sale is a different job. It needs product search, delivery promises, returns and trust in the seller, the things marketplaces and a brand’s own site already provide.

The split shows up inside brands too. At many brands, social and ecommerce teams plan separately, which makes it easy to judge an Instagram Shop on the one number it is weakest at, checkout revenue.

Take a skincare brand that sets up an Instagram Shop, tags products in its posts and turns on checkout. Sales through checkout are small. When it works with creators on Reels and links to its own site and its Amazon listing, searches for its brand name on Amazon rise in the following weeks, and its site sees more first-time buyers. Instagram created the demand, and the sales happened elsewhere.

The brand learns which products travel, too. Two of its serums draw most of the saves and comments, while its cleanser, a steady seller elsewhere, draws little interest. It moves its creator budget toward the serums and keeps the cleanser’s advertising on Amazon, where shoppers search for it by name. For that brand, the right measure of Instagram is how much new demand it creates, wherever the sale closes.

Planning Instagram shopping around discovery in 2022

The budget belongs where Instagram is putting its own effort. Creators and Reels are where shoppers discover products, so the work is finding creators whose audiences match the brand’s buyers and giving them products to show rather than scripts to read. Product tags still help shoppers find what they saw, but the link should point to where conversion, delivery and reviews are strongest, whether that is the brand’s own site, Amazon or a retailer.

Measurement has to follow the shopper out of the app. Branded searches on Amazon and the brand’s site, new-customer rates and direct traffic during and after Instagram campaigns tell the story that checkout sales on Instagram alone will understate. Advertising on Instagram needs extra care in 2022, because Meta’s own warning about privacy changes means its ads are harder to measure than they were. Holdout groups or regional splits, where a brand can run them, are a better guide than Meta’s reported conversions alone.

Stock and price decide whether the discovery pays off. A Reel that catches on can send a wave of shoppers to a product within days. The brand needs to know which products its creators will feature and make sure those products are in stock on the linked channels before the content goes live. A shopper who discovers a product on Instagram and then finds it at a different price on every site may buy from none of them, and keeping prices aligned across the brand’s site, Amazon and retailers protects the trust that discovery creates.

The Shop itself is worth keeping tidy. A catalog with accurate prices and stock costs little to maintain, and Instagram may return to shopping when its video work matures. A shared calendar linking creator campaigns to stock and pricing on the channels where sales close keeps demand from arriving at an empty shelf.

Whether Instagram brings shopping back into its stated priorities is the thing to follow through 2022. Until it does, the question for leadership is which team owns the shopper between the save and the sale. Connecting that discovery to sales on Amazon, Walmart, Target and the brand’s own site is how we help brands turn Instagram attention into orders.

A0199.crumb: The true cost of competing on Amazon is…
A0199.title: The true cost of competing on Amazon is about a third of sales
A0199.alt: A sponge cake with a slice cut out sits on a glass cake stand beside a knife on a rustic wooden table.
A0199.ttag: The true cost of competing on Amazon is about a third of sales | Kwontified
A0199.desc: Amazon’s fees, fulfillment and ads took an estimated 34% of seller revenue in 2021. Model the full cost of each unit sold, not the 15% referral fee.
A0199.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 8, 2022.
A0199.body:
Ask a brand what Amazon costs and the answer is often “about 15%,” the referral fee most categories pay. The real figure, counting fulfillment, storage and advertising, was an estimated 34% of third-party sellers’ revenue in 2021, up from 19% in 2014. The increase came through fulfillment and advertising rather than the commission. That is why a brand that budgets from the referral fee can be losing money on products that look healthy in every report it reads.

What the true cost of competing on Amazon adds up to

The Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a group critical of Amazon, estimated that Amazon would collect about $121 billion from sellers in fees and advertising in 2021, about 34% of those sellers’ total revenue, TechCrunch reported. In an earlier report, the group put Amazon’s share at 30% in 2019 and 19% in 2014, according to the report. The estimates rely on Amazon’s reported figures and on assumptions, so they are a guide to direction more than an exact measure.

Amazon’s own changes point the same way. Fulfillment fees rose by an average of 5.2% on January 18, and the off-peak storage fee for standard-size items went from $0.75 to $0.83 per cubic foot, Benzinga reported. Advertising got more expensive as well. Marketplace Pulse put the rise in the average cost per click at 43% over 2021, with conversion holding between 12% and 13% in its year-end review.

Amazon’s results show where the money flows. Advertising brought in $9.7 billion in the fourth quarter, up 32%, while third-party seller services grew 11% and Amazon’s own online store sales fell 1%, MediaPost reported.

The 15% referral fee anchors the estimate

The referral fee is an easy number to hold on to. Most categories pay it, and it has barely moved in years, so it becomes the figure a team quotes for what Amazon costs and the one every later estimate gets measured against.

The other costs never present themselves as one bill. Fulfillment, storage, returns processing and advertising sit in different reports, rise at different times and are often managed by different people. Each looks modest on its own, and no single report shows the total, which is how the anchor survives.

How the costs stack on one unit

Take a brand that sells a $30 kitchen tool through Amazon’s fulfillment service, with advertising running at an advertising cost of sale of 18% across all of the product’s sales:

Cost per unitAmount
Referral fee at 15%$4.50
Fulfillment, small and light item$3.50
Storage, per unit sold$0.30
Advertising at 18% of all sales$5.40
Returns and other small fees$0.50
Amazon’s total$14.20

That total is about 47% of the price. The product costs $8 to make and ship to Amazon’s warehouse, so the brand keeps $7.80, or 26%, before its own overheads.

Now read the same product the way the anchor encourages, with only the referral fee and the product cost. The brand would think it keeps $17.50 per unit, more than twice the real figure, and might cut the price or raise the ad budget on that basis.

The example’s total is higher than the 34% average because advertising and fulfillment weigh more heavily on a low-priced item. That is the useful part of the exercise. The true cost varies widely by product, and only a per-unit model shows the spread.

Size and price sit behind that spread. Fulfillment fees are fixed per unit by size and weight, so they take a much larger share of a $15 item than of a $60 one. Low-priced products often look healthy in revenue reports and lose money once every cost is counted.

Building the per-unit model

The model needs every line in the table for every product: referral fees, fulfillment and storage at current rates, advertising cost per unit sold, returns and any promotion costs. It needs updating whenever Amazon changes a fee, and it belongs with the people who set prices and ad budgets rather than in a finance folder.

Advertising deserves care in the model. Some sales would happen without ads and some would not, so the consistent figure is advertising cost per unit sold across all of a product’s sales, not the advertising cost of ad-attributed sales alone. That puts ads on the same footing as fees and fulfillment.

With the model built, prices and budgets can be set from contribution margin, meaning what the brand keeps after all Amazon costs, rather than from revenue or return on ad spend. Ranking products by contribution margin per unit shows which ones pay. Some will be negative once advertising is included. For those, the options are a higher price, different packaging, less advertising or leaving Amazon for that product.

The same numbers guide channel decisions. A product that keeps 26% on Amazon may keep more on Walmart Marketplace, a brand’s own site or through a retailer, or less once those channels’ own costs are counted. Channels can only be compared fairly when each has a complete per-unit cost.

The model also needs a calendar. Fees change once or twice a year, but advertising costs and return rates move every month, and a product that paid in January may not pay by June, so a quarterly review is the minimum.

The rule that follows is short: if Amazon’s share of your revenue rises each year, as the industry estimates suggest it does for many sellers, prices and product choices have to move with it. A per-unit cost model behind every pricing and advertising decision is how we manage Amazon for brands that want to know what it really costs.

A0201.crumb: Vendor Central in 2022 trades control for…
A0201.title: Vendor Central in 2022 trades control for scale on Amazon’s terms
A0201.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes on a pallet jack sits on a wooden ramp into an open semi-trailer.
A0201.ttag: Vendor Central in 2022 trades control for scale on Amazon’s terms | Kwontified
A0201.desc: Third-party sellers sold 56% of Amazon’s units in late 2021. Vendor Central still offers scale, but brands should plan for Amazon setting the terms.
A0201.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 10, 2022.
A0201.body:
For a brand on Vendor Central, Amazon’s intentions arrive as a purchase order. Amazon decides how many units it wants and when, the brand ships them, and from that point Amazon holds the stock, sets the retail price, ships to customers and handles service. It is the closest thing on Amazon to selling to a traditional retailer.

The purchase orders now come from the smaller side of Amazon. Its own retail business is growing more slowly than its marketplace and accounts for less than half of the units sold on the site. In 2022 Vendor Central still offers scale and simplicity, but on terms Amazon increasingly sets, so brands should treat it as one route among several and keep the option to sell through Seller Central for products where control matters.

Vendor Central now feeds the smaller side of Amazon

The balance between Amazon’s two models has been moving one way. In the fourth quarter of 2021, independent sellers on the marketplace sold 56% of the units bought on Amazon, a record for any fourth quarter, MediaPost reported. Over that quarter Amazon’s online store sales dropped 1% and its seller services revenue rose 11%, according to separate MediaPost reporting. Advertising revenue grew 32%.

Amazon has shown before that it will reshape the vendor side when it suits it. In March 2019, many vendors stopped receiving their usual purchase orders, and some were told their products would do better on the marketplace, Digiday reported. The vendors affected at the time tended to have annual sales on Amazon of $10 million or less, Feedvisor reported.

Read Amazon as an institution and the direction makes sense. Every product sold by a third-party seller carries fees, and most carry advertising too, while a product Amazon buys and resells carries the cost and risk of the inventory. A retailer whose seller services and advertising are growing while its own store sales fall has reason to let the marketplace carry more of the range.

What the vendor arrangement gives and takes

For brands, the appeal is scale and simplicity. A brand sells to Amazon much as it sells to any large retailer, and its products carry the reassurance of being sold by Amazon itself. For Amazon, the arrangement secures the selection that matters most to shoppers, products it can price competitively, keep in stock and fold into its own promotions.

What the brand gives up is control. Amazon decides how much to order and when, and sets the price shoppers see. If Amazon lowers its price to match a competitor, the brand’s other channels can come under pressure. Payment terms, allowances and deductions for operational mistakes are all negotiated with a very large buyer. When Amazon changes its approach, as it did in 2019, a vendor has little say in how or when the change arrives.

Take a small-appliance brand that sells its core range to Amazon through Vendor Central. Amazon orders steadily, the products are always in stock, and sales are strong. Then Amazon cuts the price of the brand’s best-selling blender during a promotion elsewhere, and the brand’s retail partners ask why their price is higher. Later, Amazon orders less of a new model than the brand expected, so it sells out within weeks and loses ranking.

The brand keeps Vendor Central for its core range, where scale matters most. For new and specialist products it sells through Seller Central, where it controls stock and price and can build a product’s sales history before asking Amazon to buy it. The two accounts end up doing different jobs inside the same company, and someone has to decide which product goes where.

Choosing the route product by product

That decision is the real work for 2022. Core, high-volume products often suit Vendor Central. New launches, specialist items and products whose price is sensitive across channels may suit Seller Central better, because the brand keeps the price and the stock in its own hands.

The comparison only works with the full cost in view. Payment terms, allowances, marketing commitments and deductions all reduce what a brand keeps as a vendor, and that total belongs next to the fees and advertising the brand would pay as a seller for the same product. Brands that negotiate their vendor terms without that comparison are negotiating blind.

A working Seller Central account is insurance, even for brands that sell mostly through Vendor Central. An account that is already set up, with listings and fulfillment ready, turns a sudden change in Amazon’s orders into a manageable one.

Advertising applies on both sides. Vendors and sellers can both run sponsored ads, and in either case advertising increasingly decides which products shoppers see. A vendor that relies on Amazon’s orders without supporting its products with advertising may find them losing position to sellers who do.

Content and catalog control matter as well. On Vendor Central, a brand’s product pages are shaped by what it submits to Amazon, but changes can be slower to take effect than on Seller Central, and other sellers can still list against the same product. Checking key pages regularly and correcting errors quickly is part of the job whichever route a brand uses.

Forecasting is the quiet risk. Amazon’s orders follow its own demand forecasts, which can lag a brand’s plans for launches and promotions. Vendors who share their plans with Amazon’s buyers early, and watch order levels closely, are less likely to be caught short.

Amazon’s third-party share of units through 2022 will show where this is heading. If it keeps rising, Amazon’s retail side will matter less to its growth, and vendors should expect more changes to how it buys. That leaves one question for the leadership team: which of our products would we still want Amazon to own if the purchase orders changed next quarter? Running Vendor Central and Seller Central side by side, and deciding which product belongs on each, is how we help brands keep control of their Amazon business.

A0203.crumb: Amazon DSP in 2022 earns its budget only…
A0203.title: Amazon DSP in 2022 earns its budget only when lift is measured
A0203.alt: Two young seedlings of different heights in terracotta pots against a pale blue wall.
A0203.ttag: Amazon DSP in 2022 earns its budget only when lift is measured | Kwontified
A0203.desc: Amazon DSP’s reported returns credit sales that would have happened anyway, most of all in retargeting. Fund it in 2022 on lift measured with a holdout.
A0203.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 15, 2022.
A0203.body:
Amazon DSP retargeting, which shows ads to shoppers who already viewed a brand’s products, reports high returns, and that makes it look like the best place for a DSP budget. The report is answering a narrower question than the one the budget owner is asking. It counts purchases that followed an ad, and many of those shoppers were going to buy anyway. The way to fund DSP in 2022 is on measured lift, the sales the ads actually added, using the brand lift studies and Amazon Marketing Cloud access Amazon expanded in late 2021.

Amazon DSP got better measurement tools in late 2021

Amazon DSP buys display and video ads on and off Amazon using Amazon’s shopper data. The advertising business behind it is now large enough to report on its own: it brought in $31.2 billion in 2021, CNBC reported, and Amazon’s finance chief pointed to sponsored ads, streaming video and measurement as areas of investment.

Measurement is where the tools changed most. At its unBoxed conference in October 2021, Amazon said it would offer brand lift studies within Amazon DSP, surveying opted-in shoppers, and would extend Amazon Marketing Cloud to all DSP customers, Modern Retail reported. Amazon Marketing Cloud, a clean room that returns only aggregated, anonymous results, had been in beta since January 2021, according to Amazon. By the time it left beta, more than 1,000 brand advertisers had used it, AdExchanger reported.

Privacy changes elsewhere raise the value of Amazon’s data. Meta expected Apple’s privacy changes to take about $10 billion out of its 2022 revenue, CNBC reported. Amazon’s audiences come from its own shoppers rather than from tracking across apps.

Why retargeting reports flatter the ads

The case for retargeting is partly right. It reaches shoppers with strong intent, and some of them buy because a reminder reached them at the right moment.

The trouble is who those shoppers are. Many of them viewed the product, added it to a list or bought it before, and a large share were going to buy anyway. Standard attribution credits the ad for any purchase within its window, whether the ad changed the outcome or not. The more likely a shopper was to buy, the more credit the ad collects, so the audiences that need the ad least post the best returns.

A holdout test separates the two. Take a pet-food brand that spends $20,000 a month on DSP retargeting and sees $120,000 in attributed sales, a reported return of 6.0. It withholds the ads from a random tenth of the same audience and compares purchase rates. The holdout group buys at nearly the same rate, and the test shows the ads added about $25,000 in sales, a return of 1.25 on the incremental sales. After product costs, the campaign loses money.

The brand then tests a prospecting campaign aimed at buyers of competing brands who have never bought its products. Reported return is only 2.0, but the holdout shows most of those sales were new, so the incremental return is close to the reported one.

RetargetingProspecting
Reported return6.02.0
What the holdout showedAds added about $25,000 in salesMost sales were new
Return on incremental sales1.25Close to the reported return

The brand moved most of its retargeting budget into prospecting and kept a small retargeting campaign for shoppers who had viewed a product but not bought within the past two weeks. Reported return fell and incremental sales rose. The campaign with the highest reported return had been the least valuable.

Funding Amazon DSP on lift in 2022

Measurement comes before scale. Holdout groups, brand lift studies or Amazon Marketing Cloud analysis can each show what DSP adds, provided the tests run long enough, and on large enough audiences, to trust the results.

Retargeting has a place, especially for considered purchases, but it should be capped. Prospecting toward new-to-brand shoppers, buyers of competing products and relevant interest audiences usually adds more. The scorecard should follow the same logic: new-to-brand purchases, branded search and total sales across Amazon and other channels during campaigns, rather than attributed return alone.

Timing changes what DSP can claim. Prospecting builds demand that converts over weeks, so it works best when it starts well before an event such as Prime Day rather than in the final days. Retargeting near an event mostly collects sales that the event would have produced anyway.

Frequency needs a cap as well. Showing the same shopper the same ad many times a week raises cost without raising sales, and caps only help if someone checks them in reporting.

Off-Amazon reach can help brands that sell elsewhere. DSP can reach Amazon shoppers on other sites and streaming services and send them to a brand’s own site or to retailers, with Amazon Marketing Cloud used to measure the effect. That use is harder to measure than on-Amazon sales, which is why the tests matter more there.

Creative carries more weight than in sponsored ads. DSP ads interrupt shoppers who are not searching, so the message, image and offer must work in a second. Testing two or three creative versions against each other, on the same audience, often changes results more than adjusting bids. A single shared view of new-to-brand sales and total sales during each campaign keeps the DSP, sponsored ads and retail teams judging the channel the same way.

How widely Amazon makes lift measurement available through 2022 will decide how fast budgets move. The more brands can measure incrementality without a large managed budget, the more DSP spending will shift from retargeting to prospecting. Until then the working rule holds: no DSP line gets more money until a holdout has shown what it adds. Building that test into every plan is how we run Amazon DSP on measured lift.

A0204.title: Retailers run superb operations, but retail media grades itself
A0204.alt: A sheet of paper with a gold star sticker on an old school desk, reflected in a small framed mirror.
A0204.ttag: Retailers run superb operations, but retail media grades itself | Kwontified
A0204.desc: Retailers measure every truck and shelf with discipline, yet their ad networks report their own results by their own rules. Ask retail media for the same rigor.
A0204.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 17, 2022.
A0204.body:
Inside a large retailer, a late truck is measured to the minute. Every shelf, truck and order carries a cost the retailer has to control, so its operations teams know, store by store and day by day, what each part of the system costs. The same retailer’s advertising business will report a campaign’s return with few independent checks, using data and rules it chose itself.

That gap is not carelessness. Operations cost the retailer money, while advertising earns it, and the ad businesses grew up inside merchandising relationships where payments were judged loosely. Brands should bring the rigor retailers apply to their own operations to the retail media they buy, which means asking for independent tests and common measures before shifting trade money into ads.

Retail media grew up inside the merchant relationship

The operational discipline shows in the results. Target fulfilled more than 95% of its third-quarter sales through its stores, a network it runs with tight control of stock, labor and delivery, according to its results.

The advertising businesses took a different path. Target relaunched its in-house media company as Roundel in 2019 and has added closed-loop measurement and self-service tools since, according to Target. Walmart renamed its media business Walmart Connect in January 2021, Retail TouchPoints reported. Albertsons, Kroger and others followed with networks of their own, Grocery Dive reported.

Many of these businesses sit close to the merchant teams that buy from brands, and the accounting shows it. Walmart said its global advertising reached $2.1 billion in its latest fiscal year, with $0.5 billion of it recorded as a reduction to cost of sales rather than as revenue, depending on the arrangement, according to its results. That is the treatment usually given to money suppliers pay a retailer.

The arrangement made sense at the start. Brands have long paid retailers for promotions, displays and placement, and those payments were judged as part of the relationship rather than one by one. When retailers began selling digital ads, many brands bought them from the same budgets, through the same people, with the same loose judgment.

The network sets the rules it is graded by

Retailers, in turn, built reporting that showed the value of their ads using their own data and rules. Their closed-loop data is a real strength, because they can see purchases in stores as well as online. The rules, though, are theirs. Each network chooses which sales to credit, over how many days, and whether a view counts as well as a click. A longer window, or credit for a view, raises the reported return without adding a single sale, and each network makes those choices about its own results.

Even within Amazon, the attribution window differs by ad type and account, according to one guide to its reports.

Take a beverage brand whose sales team agrees to shift part of its promotional funding at a grocer into the grocer’s new ad network. The network reports a strong return, counting sales over two weeks after any view. The brand’s own analysts notice that store sales in the campaign weeks were no higher than in the same weeks a year earlier, when the money went to price promotions.

The ads may have worked, or they may have taken credit for sales that would have happened anyway. Without a test, no one can say, and the network’s report is the only number in the room.

Holding retail media to the operations standard

Tests matter more than reports. Holdout tests, matched-store comparisons or other incrementality studies belong before any significant budget moves. Retailers with strong data can run them, and the best networks will welcome the request.

Common measures come next. A brand can define its own attribution window, what counts as a new customer and what counts as a sale, and ask each network to report on those terms where it can, noting the differences where it cannot. Without that, results from two networks cannot sit in the same spreadsheet.

The budget line matters as much as the measure. If retail media comes from trade funds, it should be compared with the promotions it replaces on sales per dollar. If it comes from marketing, it should be compared with other media on the same basis. That only works if the sales team that negotiates with the buyer and the marketing team that buys media agree on the measures before money moves, not after the reports arrive.

None of this damages the relationship. Asking hard questions about results is not a sign of distrust. Retailers that measure their own operations so carefully understand the value of evidence, and brands that bring evidence to the conversation are usually treated as better partners for it.

Contracts are a good place to set expectations. When a brand commits a large budget to a network for a year, it can agree in advance which tests will run, which measures will be reported and how results will shape the following year’s spend. Smaller brands can start more simply. A comparison of sales in campaign weeks against the same weeks before, at the same stores, gives a rough check on what a network reports. It is not a full test, but it beats taking the network’s number on trust.

Which retailers offer independent measurement in 2022 is the thing to follow, because the networks that let brands verify results will earn more of the budget over time. For a brand’s leadership, the useful question is simpler: would we accept this report if it came from our own logistics team? Measuring every network on the same terms is how we help brands hold retail media to account.
