A0205.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud in 2022 answers questions reports cannot
A0205.alt: A brass magnifying glass rests in an open wooden card catalog drawer beside a stack of blank paper.
A0205.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud in 2022 answers questions reports cannot | Kwontified
A0205.desc: Amazon Marketing Cloud lets DSP advertisers query event-level ad data in a clean room. It pays off when brands bring clear questions and an analyst.
A0205.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 22, 2022.
A0205.body:
Say a personal-care brand runs DSP video, DSP display and retargeting on Amazon and wants to know whether the video budget is worth keeping. Its standard reports credit most sales to retargeting, the last touch, so the video line looks like a cost. The reports are not wrong about what they measure. They simply cannot see how the campaigns worked together, and that is the question the budget turns on.

Amazon Marketing Cloud can see it. The clean room, which Amazon opened to all Amazon DSP advertisers in late 2021, lets brands query event-level advertising data about how channels combine and how often shoppers should see an ad. It returns only aggregated results and needs an analyst who writes SQL, so in 2022 it earns its keep on a short list of decisions a brand will actually change, not as a replacement for reporting.

What Amazon Marketing Cloud offers in 2022

Amazon introduced Amazon Marketing Cloud in beta in January 2021. It described a secure, privacy-safe environment in which advertisers analyze pseudonymized signals and receive only aggregated, anonymous outputs, with each instance provisioned to a dedicated AWS account, according to Amazon. Beta users were studying campaign reach and frequency, which combinations of channels drove results, and the total impact of their media.

In October 2021 it left beta. By then more than 1,000 brand advertisers had used it, and advertisers no longer needed their own AWS account, AdExchanger reported. At its unBoxed conference the same month, Amazon said it would extend access to all Amazon DSP customers, Modern Retail reported, and it introduced a way for advertisers to bring their own signals into the clean room, according to Amazon.

The timing fits the money. Advertising on Amazon brought in $31.2 billion in 2021, and Amazon’s finance chief named measurement as an area of investment, CNBC reported. As budgets grow, so does the need to know what each part of them does.

Why event-level data answers what reports cannot

Standard Amazon reports are pre-aggregated. They show what each campaign delivered under Amazon’s attribution rules, one campaign at a time, and they cannot easily show how campaigns interacted. Amazon Marketing Cloud works at the level of events: individual impressions, clicks and purchases, pseudonymized and joined across campaigns. The join is what makes the difference. It lets an analyst ask how many shoppers saw both a DSP video ad and a display ad before buying, or at what number of impressions extra exposure stopped adding sales.

Standard Amazon reportsAmazon Marketing Cloud
Unit of dataTotals per campaignPseudonymized events joined across campaigns
How campaigns interactHard to seeCan be queried directly
Who can read itReady in the consoleNeeds an analyst who writes SQL
LimitsFixed views and attribution rulesAggregated results only; small audiences may return nothing

The cost sits in the last two rows. Queries are written in SQL, results come back only in aggregate, and small audiences or narrow cuts may return nothing at all. The answers are only as useful as the decisions they inform.

Back to the personal-care brand. Its analyst writes a query comparing purchase rates for shoppers who saw video and retargeting with those who saw retargeting alone, and shoppers who saw both bought at a much higher rate. A second query shows that beyond about eight impressions a week, more exposure added almost nothing. The brand keeps its video budget, which reports had undervalued, and lowers its frequency cap, which reports could not show. Two queries changed two decisions.

A third query was less useful. The analyst tried to compare results for a small new product line, and the audience was too small for the clean room to return an answer. Some questions need larger campaigns, or longer time periods, before they can be asked at all.

Weighed against each other, the two sides lean toward using it with a narrow brief: two decisions changed that no standard report could have informed, against one question the data could not yet answer.

Putting Amazon Marketing Cloud to work in 2022

Decisions come before data. The useful starting point is the two or three advertising decisions a brand would change with better evidence, such as channel mix, frequency or the value of upper-funnel media, with queries written for those before anything else gets explored.

Staffing decides whether access turns into answers. The work needs someone who writes SQL and understands advertising. Brands without that skill in-house are better served by a partner who has it than by access that sits unused.

Path analysis shows patterns, not proof. Where a query suggests a channel adds value, a holdout test or brand lift study should confirm it before large budgets shift.

Brands that sell off Amazon can go further. By bringing their own signals into the clean room, such as conversions on their own site, they can see how Amazon media relates to sales elsewhere. That requires careful data work and clear rules about what is shared.

Privacy rules shape what is possible, by design. Because Amazon returns only aggregated results, brands cannot use the clean room to identify individual shoppers or export their behavior, so questions have to be framed around audiences and patterns rather than people. Budget size sets the scale for the same reason: brands spending modestly on DSP should start with broad questions across their whole program before slicing by product or audience.

Each new data source Amazon adds to the clean room in 2022 will widen the questions brands can answer. The rule for now is to write the decision down before writing the query, and to share any result that changes a budget in plain language with the people who set it. Turning clean-room queries into budget decisions is how we run Amazon Marketing Cloud analysis for brands.

A0207.title: Target Plus rewards curation, Walmart Marketplace rewards scale
A0207.alt: A red shelf of ceramics, books and a plant stands beside long blue racks of cardboard boxes in a bright stockroom.
A0207.ttag: Target Plus rewards curation, Walmart Marketplace rewards scale | Kwontified
A0207.desc: Walmart Marketplace ended 2021 with about 130,000 sellers and Target Plus about 440. Each mirrors its retailer, so place each product where it wins.
A0207.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 24, 2022.
A0207.body:
Walmart’s marketplace ended 2021 with about 130,000 sellers, roughly double a year earlier. Target Plus had about 440, Marketplace Pulse reported. Read quickly, the two numbers look like one marketplace racing ahead and the other falling behind. They make more sense as two retailers each behaving like itself.

Target curates a small range that fits its brand. Walmart builds the widest possible selection at low prices. A brand deciding where to sell after Amazon should match each product to the marketplace whose habits it fits, rather than treating the two as interchangeable second channels.

Walmart Marketplace and Target Plus grew in opposite directions

Walmart has been opening the doors. It let sellers based outside the U.S. onto its marketplace in March 2021 and had added about 5,000 sellers from China by October, Marketplace Pulse reported. It put the number of items available at about 160 million, up 21 million in a quarter, EcommerceBytes reported.

Target has kept the door narrow on purpose. Its chief executive has said it will keep curating very carefully, Marketplace Pulse noted. The business behind the marketplace is store-first, with its stores fulfilling more than 95% of what Target sold in the third quarter, according to its results. Target Plus sellers ship their own orders, and shoppers can return items at Target stores, the Star Tribune reported.

What each retailer is after, and what it rewards

Walmart wants selection and low prices. Its shoppers come to find almost anything at a good price, and a bigger catalog serves that promise. The marketplace therefore rewards whatever wins in a crowded catalog: a competitive price, fast delivery through Walmart Fulfillment Services, strong product pages and, increasingly, search advertising. Walmart’s active U.S. advertisers rose 136% in its latest fiscal year, according to its results. The more sellers compete for the same search, the more of them pay to be seen, and that revenue goes to Walmart.

Target wants a range that feels like Target. Its guests come for design, quality and an experience they trust, and a smaller marketplace protects that. Target Plus rewards fit: products that fill gaps in Target’s own range, look right beside its brands, and arrive and return as reliably as Target’s own orders. Target keeps the guest and the store visit a return brings, while the seller carries the stock and the shipping.

Neither approach is better. They suit different products, and each asks different things of the brands that join it.

Take a home brand that makes two lines: everyday storage boxes sold on price, and a smaller collection of designed table linens. On Walmart Marketplace the storage boxes compete well. They are priced sharply, stored with Walmart Fulfillment Services for fast delivery, and supported with sponsored products. The linens struggle there, lost among thousands of cheaper alternatives.

On Target Plus the brand pitches the linens instead. They extend Target’s own home range with colors and sizes it does not carry, and they fit its style. The storage boxes would add little that Target does not already sell.

The brand ends up on both marketplaces with different products on each, and its team learns that the two need different skills. Walmart takes daily attention to price, stock and bids. Target takes careful presentation, reliable service and a relationship with Target’s merchants that develops over time. Each also feeds the brand’s other channels: Walmart’s sales data shows which storage sizes sell best at which prices, and guests’ reviews on Target show which linen colors they want next season.

Choosing product by product in 2022

The sorting question is what wins each product its sales. Products that win on price and speed suit Walmart Marketplace. Products that win on design, fit and the retailer’s endorsement suit Target Plus, if Target will have them.

Each marketplace then sets its own demands. Walmart requires competitive pricing, fast fulfillment and advertising to be found. Target requires an invitation, a clear gap in its range and service to its standard, including store returns.

The two also move at different speeds. Walmart Marketplace requires approval but is open to many sellers, so a brand can start within weeks, while Target Plus is by invitation and a brand may need months to build its case. Starting on Walmart where a product fits, and preparing the Target case in parallel, uses that time well.

Price is where the two strategies can collide. Selling the same product on both marketplaces, and on Amazon, at different prices invites price matching and erodes trust, so products that overlap need one price policy across channels.

Content and advertising follow the same split. A Walmart product page needs a clear price, practical details and images that compare well in a long list of similar items, and sponsored products are often essential for a new product to be found among millions of others. A Target Plus page needs styling and presentation that sit naturally beside Target’s own brands, and a smaller catalog means a well-placed product can be found more easily, though advertising still helps at busy times.

Operations have to match the promise. A brand on Target Plus is representing Target to its guests, and late deliveries or difficult returns reflect on Target as much as on the brand. A brand on Walmart competes with sellers who ship fast and cheaply, so slow fulfillment costs sales directly.

How each marketplace grows in 2022 will decide how much this choice matters. If Walmart keeps adding sellers quickly and Target keeps adding them slowly, the gap between scale and curation will widen. The question for a brand’s leadership then becomes which of its products could win a crowded search and which could earn an invitation. Placing each product where its strengths count is how we run Walmart Marketplace and Target Plus for brands.

A0208.crumb: Most Amazon sales come from fewer…
A0208.title: Most Amazon sales come from fewer keywords than you think
A0208.alt: A row of old iron skeleton keys hangs on a rack, with three bright brass keys caught in a beam of light.
A0208.ttag: Most Amazon sales come from fewer keywords than you think | Kwontified
A0208.desc: Most Amazon ad keywords get under a click a day and drive almost no sales. Fund the few searches that sell for each product and prune the long tail.
A0208.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 29, 2022.
A0208.body:
Most search terms on Amazon, at typical bid levels, get less than one click a day. That finding, from an analysis by the advertising software company Teikametrics, sits awkwardly beside a campaign carrying hundreds of keywords. If most of those terms barely get clicked, a product’s ad sales must be coming from a much shorter list than the campaign suggests. They are, and the long list costs more than it appears to, because it takes budget from the searches that sell.

Why Amazon sales come from fewer keywords

The number of possible searches on Amazon is close to limitless, but most of them get very little traffic. In the Teikametrics analysis, those low-volume keywords each drove, on average, less than 0.001% of a campaign’s revenue, MarTech reported. Only keywords averaging at least three clicks a day drove a share of revenue in line with their cost.

The pattern matters more as clicks get dearer. Amazon’s average cost per click rose 43% during 2021 and conversion held at 12% to 13%, according to Marketplace Pulse’s annual review. When each click costs more, budget spent on keywords that rarely convert is budget taken from those that do.

Searches for a given product tend to cluster around a handful of phrases: the product type, its main feature, its use and the brand name. The long tail is real, but each term in it is rare, and rare terms create a problem beyond their own cost. A keyword with a click every few days never gathers enough clicks to show whether it converts, so it can sit in an account without anyone learning whether it should be there.

Why a long keyword list feels safe

Bidding on every variation of every search a shopper might type feels thorough. Keyword tools make it easy to add hundreds at once, and a long list looks like diligence, because it seems to guarantee the brand will not miss a shopper.

Reach on Amazon, though, depends on winning the searches shoppers actually make. Spreading budget across hundreds of rare terms diverts money from the main searches, so the product loses position where most shoppers look. It also makes the account harder to manage. Every keyword needs a bid, a share of budget and a place in someone’s review, and the main terms get less attention than they need.

Take a brand selling a water bottle through a campaign with 400 keywords and $6,000 a month in spend. Its search term report splits the results like this:

SearchesShare of ad sales
Main searches2582%
Remaining keywords37518%

Most of the 375 had no sale at all in the month. The 25 that mattered were under-funded: the brand’s ads appeared in the top positions for them only part of the day, because the budget ran out in the afternoon.

The brand moves those 25 searches into their own campaign with enough budget to stay visible all day. It keeps an automatic campaign running at a modest budget to find new searches, adds any that prove themselves, and pauses most of the rest. Over the next two months, sales from the main searches rise, total ad spend is unchanged, and the cost of each sale falls.

Building a keyword plan around the searches that sell

The starting point is the short list for each product: the 20 to 50 searches that drive most of its ad sales. The search term report shows which searches produce sales, and Amazon’s Brand Analytics, where a brand has access, shows which searches carry the most volume in the category.

Those searches deserve full funding. Giving them their own campaigns, enough budget to stay visible through the day and bids that hold strong positions puts the money where most shoppers are. A main search that drops out of the top positions every afternoon is one the brand has already paid to learn about and then stopped showing up for.

Automatic campaigns are for discovery rather than coverage. Automatic and broad-match campaigns can find new searches at a controlled budget, with searches that convert moved into the main campaigns and those that waste money added as negatives.

Match types keep the focus. Exact-match keywords on the main searches give the most control over bids and placement. Phrase and broad match on the same terms can catch close variations, but they belong at lower bids so they do not compete with the exact-match campaigns for the same shoppers.

The list needs a monthly review. Search behavior changes with seasons, trends and competitors, and a search that mattered in December may matter less in March.

Product pages count as much as bids. The searches that drive sales should appear naturally in titles, bullet points and descriptions, so the product ranks organically for them too, and a product that wins a search both paid and organic pays less for each sale.

Launches need a wider net at first, because a new product has no search history. Even then, the aim is to find its main searches within weeks and concentrate on them rather than keep hundreds of keywords running indefinitely. Brand searches need a campaign of their own as well. Shoppers searching for a brand by name are already looking for it, so those campaigns usually show high returns, and keeping them apart stops them flattering the category results.

The number to check is the share of ad sales from your top searches. If it is high, concentrate budget there; if sales are spread thinly, the campaigns may be giving most of their budget to keywords that rarely convert. Building campaigns around the searches that actually sell is how we run Amazon advertising for brands.

A0209.crumb: Amazon’s dual role as marketplace and…
A0209.title: Amazon’s dual role as marketplace and rival shapes brand plans
A0209.alt: Six house-shaped kraft boxes in a row before sage, terracotta and cream boxes on a wooden bench.
A0209.ttag: Amazon’s dual role as marketplace and rival shapes brand plans | Kwontified
A0209.desc: Amazon runs the marketplace brands sell on and competes with them through its own retail and brands. Congress is debating limits. Plan for both roles.
A0209.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 31, 2022.
A0209.body:
Look at an Amazon search results page and one company is doing several jobs on it at once. It set the rules for who may sell there. It ranked the results. It sold the sponsored placements at the top. And further down the page it may be selling a product of its own, sometimes against the brands that paid for those placements.

That combination is now in front of Congress, which is debating whether to limit it. Whatever the outcome, brands should plan for Amazon as both landlord and rival: protecting their products and data, building demand Amazon cannot easily redirect, and keeping other channels strong.

Amazon’s dual role grew one business at a time

Amazon did not start as a marketplace. It started as a retailer, buying products and reselling them. The marketplace came later, and by the fourth quarter of 2021 third-party sellers were behind 56% of the units sold on the site, MediaPost reported.

The other roles were added along the way. Amazon became the logistics provider for many sellers through its fulfillment service. It became an advertising platform, earning $31.2 billion in 2021, CNBC reported. It built private-label brands of its own, and in January it announced its first physical clothing store, Amazon Style, CNBC reported.

Each role made sense on its own terms. Taken together, they mean the company that writes the marketplace rules, ranks its search results and sells its advertising also sells products that compete with the brands paying it.

Congress is now debating the dual role

On January 20, the Senate Judiciary Committee voted 16 to 6 to advance the American Innovation and Choice Online Act, which aims to stop dominant platforms from giving their own products an advantage over those of others, S&P Global reported. Amazon has warned third-party sellers that the legislation could harm their ability to sell on its marketplace, Scripps News reported.

It is not clear when, or whether, the bill will reach a vote of the full Senate. The debate itself still shows how central the question has become, and a brand’s plan for Amazon cannot wait for Washington to settle it.

Where the dual role meets a brand’s decisions

For a brand, the dual role shows up in ordinary decisions rather than in hearings. When Amazon’s own retail business buys a brand’s products, it sets the price shoppers see, and that price affects the brand’s other channels. When a brand sells on the marketplace, it competes for the Buy Box and for search position with other sellers and, sometimes, with Amazon. When a category does well, Amazon can see the demand and, in principle, decide to enter it with a product of its own.

Take a brand that sells a popular phone stand on Amazon. Sales grow steadily and the product collects thousands of reviews. A year later a lower-priced stand appears in the same search results, with prominent placement and similar features. Whether it comes from Amazon or from another seller, the brand’s response is the same: it needs reasons for shoppers to choose its product beyond price.

Its next steps are practical. It adds a bundle with a cable and case that the lookalike does not offer, improves its images to show the stand’s build quality, and raises its sponsored ads on searches for its own brand name. It also takes the stand to Walmart Marketplace and its own site, so a change on Amazon touches a smaller share of its sales.

The brands that cope best do not depend on being the only option. They have a name shoppers search for, product details that are hard to copy, and sales across more than one channel.

Planning for landlord and rival

Protection is the floor. Amazon’s brand registration tools, accurate and complete product content, and regular checks on who sells a brand’s products and at what price all reduce how much the landlord’s decisions, or a lookalike’s arrival, can catch a brand off guard.

Demand Amazon cannot easily redirect is the real defense. Shoppers who search for a brand by name are harder to win with a lookalike. That is why brand awareness, reviews, packaging and product features that make a product the one shoppers ask for matter more on a marketplace that is also a competitor. Sponsored placement on a brand’s own searches helps keep lookalikes from taking shoppers who came looking for it.

Other channels change the balance. Walmart Marketplace, Target Plus, retailers’ stores and a brand’s own site reduce how much any one platform’s choices can move the business, and they produce data Amazon does not control.

Pricing across channels needs a policy decided in advance. When Amazon’s own retail business sells a brand’s product, it may lower the price to match others, and that price becomes visible to every shopper and retailer. Brands should know how they will respond and which products they are willing to sell to Amazon’s retail side at all. Data deserves the same care: what a brand shares with any platform, through promotions, product details or advertising, is worth weighing against what it receives back.

None of this is a reason to avoid Amazon. For most brands it remains the largest place to reach shoppers ready to buy, and the point is to sell there knowing that the platform’s interests and the brand’s own overlap without being the same.

If the bill advances in the Senate in 2022, Amazon may change how it promotes its own products, and brands should be ready to adjust; if it stalls, the dual role continues and the same plan applies. The question for a brand’s leadership is how much of next year’s growth depends on a decision Amazon could make without asking. Building strength on Amazon alongside Walmart, Target and a brand’s own channels is how we help brands plan for Amazon’s dual role.

A0211.title: Zalando Fulfillment Solutions will ship brands’ own web orders
A0211.alt: Orange and kraft-wrapped parcels move along roller conveyors in a large, bright fulfillment warehouse.
A0211.ttag: Zalando Fulfillment Solutions will ship brands’ own web orders | Kwontified
A0211.desc: Zalando plans to ship orders from brands’ own sites from its warehouses. One stock pool cuts inventory waste, but it deepens reliance on one partner.
A0211.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 5, 2022.
A0211.body:
Split a brand’s European stock between two warehouses and a familiar problem follows. A size sells out on the brand’s own site while the same size sits unsold in the warehouse that serves Zalando, and at the end of the season the leftovers are in the wrong place. Zalando now plans to ship orders from brands’ own websites and other channels out of its own network, so a brand could hold one pool of stock and sell it everywhere. The pool would cut inventory waste, but it would also make the brand’s whole European business depend on one partner’s warehouses.

What Zalando Fulfillment Solutions offers in 2022

Zalando is growing quickly, and its partner business faster still. Gross merchandise volume rose 34.1% to €14.3 billion in 2021, and its Partner Program and Connected Retail, through which brands and stores sell directly to Zalando’s customers, reached 30% of its fashion store volume, up from 24%, according to Zalando. More than 5,800 brand partners and almost 7,000 stores now sell this way.

Many of those partners already use Zalando’s warehouses. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions handled 51% of Partner Program items in the fourth quarter of 2021, according to its results presentation. In the same presentation, Zalando said it would open the service to channels beyond Zalando, offering one network and one stock pool for a brand’s own online shop and other sales channels. It plans to do so over the next 12 months, Just Style reported.

Zalando expects slower growth in 2022 and will report first-quarter results on May 5, according to its release.

Why one stock pool needs less inventory

Each separate pool of stock has to carry its own safety stock against demand it cannot predict. Each can run out of a size while the other still has it. And each has to be forecast on its own, with more error.

A single pool removes those costs together. A size that sells faster on the brand’s own site than on Zalando ships from the same shelf as the Zalando orders. The brand needs less total stock to offer the same availability, and fewer items end the season unsold in the wrong place.

Take a footwear brand that sells in Germany through Zalando and its own site. It models what a single pool would need:

Split stockSingle pool
Pairs held6,000 for Zalando, 4,000 for its own site9,000
Unsold at season endAbout 900About 500

The pool would hold 1,000 fewer pairs and write off 400 fewer, at the same availability on both channels. Many of today’s leftovers are in sizes that sold out in the other channel, which is exactly the stock a shared shelf would have sold. Valued at the brand’s average cost per pair, the saving is a meaningful share of a season’s margin, before counting the sales it would no longer lose to stock sitting in the wrong warehouse.

What the saving costs in dependence

The other side of the ledger is concentration. If all European orders ship from Zalando’s network, a capacity problem there, a fee change or a dispute affects every channel at once. The brand also gives a large platform more visibility into its full sales pattern.

Weighing the two, the footwear brand’s numbers lean toward pooling, but only part of the way. Its own site would depend on Zalando’s delivery promise and fees, so the brand tests pooling for its core styles in one country and keeps its own warehouse for limited editions and wholesale.

That points to how to evaluate the offer. The stock saving can be modeled before anything moves, by comparing current safety stock and end-of-season leftovers across channels with what a single pool would need. The saving is largest for brands with many sizes and colors, where split pools strand the most stock.

The full cost has to sit beside it. Zalando’s fulfillment and storage fees for web orders, delivery times and returns handling belong next to the brand’s own warehouse costs and the value of the stock it would no longer need. A fallback matters too. Keeping the ability to ship from another warehouse, even at small scale, means a change at Zalando does not stop every channel at once.

Where pooling works first

The starting country matters, because Zalando’s network is strongest where it has its largest warehouses and customer base. A brand pooling stock should start in markets where Zalando’s delivery to its own customers is already fast, and check delivery promises for its own site’s orders in each country before switching.

Returns need particular care in fashion. Return rates are high, and in a single pool a return from any channel goes back into stock that every channel can sell. That speeds resale, but it also means the brand’s own customers’ returns follow Zalando’s processes. Data needs an agreement as well, covering what Zalando can see and use about orders from the brand’s own site and how that information is protected.

The offer is new, and its terms and service levels for outside channels will become clearer through 2022. Brands that test it on a few styles now will know more than those who wait, without putting their whole business at risk.

Pricing will decide how far pooling spreads. If Zalando’s fees for outside orders come close to those for Zalando orders, pooling will make sense for many fashion brands; if they are much higher, it will suit only brands whose stock problem is severe. The working rule is to pool where the modeled saving is larger than the fee gap, and nowhere else yet. Modeling the pool against the fees, country by country, is how we help fashion brands decide on Zalando’s new offer.

A0212.crumb: Decoding Mercado Libre’s fees shows what…
A0212.title: Decoding Mercado Libre’s fees shows what the marketplace wants
A0212.alt: An antique brass balance scale holds a twine-tied paper parcel on one pan and round biscuits on the other.
A0212.ttag: Decoding Mercado Libre’s fees shows what the marketplace wants | Kwontified
A0212.desc: Mercado Libre’s fees are built around free shipping, installments and its own logistics. Brands that read them as signals price better in Latin America.
A0212.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 7, 2022.
A0212.body:
The decision that lands on a brand’s desk when it prepares for Mercado Libre looks like a pricing question. Which listing type, which shipping option, and how close to the free shipping threshold should each product sit? The cheapest answer on paper is the lowest fee, which can be the wrong place to start.

Mercado Libre’s fee structure is built around what buyers in the region value: free shipping, paying in installments and fast delivery from its own network. Its fees reward sellers who offer those things and cost more for sellers who do not. A brand entering Latin America should model each product’s full fee load under each listing and shipping option before setting prices, rather than reading the headline commission alone.

What Mercado Libre’s fees are built around

The marketplace is large and growing. Gross merchandise volume reached $8.0 billion in the fourth quarter of 2021, up 32.2% on a currency-neutral basis, and 287.9 million items were sold, according to its results. Of the 275.9 million items shipped, 89.5% moved through its managed logistics network.

The company is plain about what drives that growth. On its fourth-quarter earnings call it said its free shipping program now delivers over 80% of volume at no cost to buyers. It had 40.5 million unique buyers in the quarter, and more than two-thirds of volume comes from organic traffic, mostly through its app, according to the call transcript. Official brand stores accounted for over 23% of volume.

The fees follow from those priorities. Most marketplace revenue comes from final value fees, charged as a share of each sale, plus flat fees on transactions below a set value and shipping fees net of carrier costs, according to its annual report. Sellers choose between a Classic listing and a Premium listing, which lets buyers pay in installments without interest and carries a higher fee. They also contribute to the cost of free shipping above a set price threshold, according to Mercado Libre’s investor information.

Those fees are moving in 2022. As interest rates rose in Brazil, Mercado Libre said it had begun adjusting installment pricing on the marketplace, offering shorter installment plans on products where longer credit does little for demand. It also said it had started charging sellers for fulfillment in Mexico and Brazil, with no sign so far of sellers pulling back, and that advertising had passed 1% of gross merchandise volume, according to the same call.

What each fee asks of a seller

Read together, the fees work like a set of instructions. The free shipping rule rewards products priced above the threshold, where the marketplace makes free delivery standard. Buyers in the region have come to expect it, and listings without it lose visibility and conversion. Sellers pay part of the cost, so the price has to allow for it.

The Premium listing rewards sellers who offer installments. In markets where many shoppers spread payments over several months, an interest-free installment option can matter as much as the price itself, and the higher fee is Mercado Libre’s charge for financing that convenience.

The fulfillment fees reward sellers who place stock in Mercado Libre’s warehouses. Items held there arrive faster: the company said on its call that items in its fulfillment centers average under 24 hours to delivery, and that close to 60% of all volume arrived the same or next day. Speed lifts ranking and conversion, so the storage fee buys position as well as logistics.

Take a small-appliance brand that lists a coffee grinder in Mexico as a Classic listing, shipped from its own warehouse and priced just below the free shipping threshold to avoid the shipping contribution. Its fees are low, but sales are slow, because the listing offers no installments, no free shipping and slower delivery.

The brand then tests a Premium listing, prices the grinder just above the threshold with free shipping, and moves stock into Mercado Libre’s fulfillment center. Fees per unit rise noticeably. Conversion more than doubles, the product ranks higher, and total margin earned per week rises. It keeps the Classic listing for a cheaper accessory, where buyers rarely use installments and the lower fee leaves more margin.

Higher fees are not always worth paying. The fees and the buyer’s experience are connected, though, and the cheapest fee option can be the most expensive way to sell.

Modeling Mercado Libre’s fees product by product

The model starts with every charge for each product and country: the selling fee for each listing type, shipping contributions above the threshold, per-unit charges for low-priced items, fulfillment and storage fees, and advertising. Rates differ by country and category, so each needs checking.

Listing and shipping options then get tested against each other. Classic against Premium, and own-warehouse delivery against the fulfillment center, compared on margin per week rather than fee per unit.

Thresholds deserve a deliberate choice. A product priced just below the free shipping threshold may sell less than one just above it with free delivery, so each product’s position relative to the line should be a decision rather than an accident.

Currency adds a layer. Fees are charged in local currency, and exchange rates in the region can move quickly, so brands selling from abroad should review fee models and prices more often than they would in a stable market. Advertising sits on top of everything else: Mercado Libre sells sponsored placements, and in competitive categories they add to the fee load from the start rather than as an optional extra.

Official stores deserve a look as well. Brand-owned stores account for a growing share of volume and give shoppers more confidence in authenticity, and for established brands an official store can lift conversion enough to justify the effort of running it.

Mercado Libre has already said installment and fulfillment pricing are changing, and any move in the price line above which delivery costs the buyer nothing can shift many products from one side of it to the other overnight. The question for the leadership team is whether its Latin America prices were set from the fee schedule or from the margin each product earns per week. Building that model country by country is how we help brands price Mercado Libre listings.

A0213.crumb: Walmart shoppers Amazon misses arrive on…
A0213.title: Walmart shoppers Amazon misses arrive on the weekly grocery trip
A0213.alt: Canvas tote bags spill carrots, potatoes, tomatoes, apples and greens beside bread and eggs on a butcher-block counter.
A0213.ttag: Walmart shoppers Amazon misses arrive on the weekly grocery trip | Kwontified
A0213.desc: Walmart reaches shoppers through the weekly grocery trip, in stores and through pickup, that Amazon reaches less often. Plan Walmart around that visit.
A0213.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 12, 2022.
A0213.body:
The natural way to compare Walmart and Amazon is by search: how many people look for a product on each site. On that measure Amazon usually wins, and a brand that plans Walmart as a smaller Amazon will bid on the same category terms and judge them the same way. That comparison misses where Walmart’s reach comes from. Walmart reaches a household that buys groceries every week, lives near a store and watches prices closely, and it reaches that household through the frequency of the trip rather than through search.

Why Walmart shoppers differ from Amazon’s

Walmart’s advantage starts with geography. In 2017, about 90% of Americans lived within 10 miles of a Walmart. That year Amazon cut the price of Prime for shoppers receiving government assistance, an effort to win lower-income households that tended to shop at Walmart, Public Radio East reported.

The income gap between the two shopper bases has persisted. A 2021 Jungle Scout survey compared shoppers who bought online only from Walmart.com with those who bought online only from Amazon, Talk Business & Politics reported:

Walmart.com-only online shoppersAmazon-only online shoppers
Household income below $50,00073%54%
Bought groceries online at that retailer41%20%

Frequency shows up in the same survey: 57% of Walmart-only shoppers bought on Walmart.com weekly or more. And the overlap runs one way, with 57% of Amazon-only online shoppers also shopping in Walmart stores.

Walmart’s results show the pattern online. Its U.S. ecommerce sales grew 1% in its latest quarter but 70% over two years, much of it in grocery pickup and delivery, and its advertising business reached $2.1 billion, according to its results. Inflation reached 7.9% in February, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which makes price-conscious shoppers even more careful.

How frequency creates reach on Walmart

A household that buys groceries at Walmart every week, in the store or through pickup, visits far more often than one that searches Walmart.com for a specific product. Each visit is a chance to see, add and try a product that sits near the groceries in the basket. Search measures how many people look for a product; frequency measures how many times the same household passes it.

Frequency changes what wins a shopper’s attention. On Amazon, a brand competes to appear when a shopper searches for its category. On Walmart, a brand also competes to appear while a shopper builds the weekly basket and adds items they had not planned to buy.

Take a snack brand that copies its Amazon strategy onto Walmart.com. It bids on category searches such as “protein bars” and judges results on return on ad spend, and sales are modest. It then shifts part of the budget to placements that appear while shoppers build grocery pickup orders, and to products that sit alongside items its buyers already purchase weekly. It also checks that its products are in stock in local stores, since pickup orders draw from them. Trial among new households rises, and repeat purchases follow, because the product now appears where those shoppers return every week.

The brand also learns to read its results differently. Return on ad spend for the basket placements is lower than for category search, because they reach shoppers earlier in their decision. The new households they bring in keep buying, though, and their value over three months is far higher than a single campaign’s report shows. The brand did not find more searches. It found the shopping trip.

Planning Walmart around the weekly basket

The plan starts from the basket rather than the search. The products buyers add alongside a brand’s own show where to place promotions and advertising, so they reach shoppers while grocery and essentials orders are being built.

Store stock is part of ecommerce on Walmart. Many online orders are filled from local stores, so a product missing from the shelf is missing from pickup orders too, and store availability affects online sales directly.

Price has to suit the frequent shopper. Walmart’s shoppers compare prices often, and small, steady value, such as the right pack size or a lasting price point, can matter more than a short promotion. Inflation sharpens this. When prices rise, households trade down and shop around more carefully, and brands that are visible, in stock and fairly priced on the weekly trip are well placed to win those shoppers and keep them when prices settle.

Measurement should match the behavior. Repeat purchases and new households matter more on Walmart than a single campaign’s return on ad spend. The share of shoppers who buy a second time within a few weeks is the clearest sign that a product has joined the weekly basket.

Content should suit a quick decision. A shopper adding items to a pickup order scans quickly on a phone, so clear images, the pack size and the price per unit help a product win a place in the basket in the few seconds it gets.

The category a brand sells in sets the ceiling. Grocery, household essentials, health and beauty and pet supplies fit the weekly trip naturally. Brands outside those categories can still reach Walmart’s shoppers, but they should expect more of their sales to come from search and planned purchases, as on Amazon.

Walmart Connect’s placements tied to grocery and pickup will show through 2022 how much of this brands can buy directly. The rule in the meantime is simple: on Walmart, count repeat buyers before you count clicks. Planning Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect around how Walmart shoppers actually shop is how we help brands reach the weekly basket.

A0215.title: Mother’s Day 2022 on marketplaces rewards the delivery date
A0215.alt: A kraft-wrapped gift with a red satin bow and a bouquet of red tulips on sunny stone doorstep steps.
A0215.ttag: Mother’s Day 2022 on marketplaces rewards the delivery date | Kwontified
A0215.desc: Mother’s Day gift shoppers buy late and care most about arrival. In 2022, marketplace sellers win by promising May 8 delivery and making gifts easy to choose.
A0215.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 14, 2022.
A0215.body:
A week before Mother’s Day, the shopper looking at a page of gift candles is not asking which one is cheapest. They are asking which one will arrive in time, and whether it will look like a gift when it does. They often know the person well and the product not at all, and many of them have left it late.

That shopper decides the holiday on marketplaces. With Mother’s Day falling on May 8, 2022, the products that win are the ones that will arrive before the day and are easy to judge as gifts. Brands should plan stock, delivery promises and gift-ready product pages for the final two weeks, rather than relying on discounts alone.

What Mother’s Day 2022 builds on

The 2021 holiday set a record. Consumers planned to spend $28.1 billion on Mother’s Day in 2021, up $1.4 billion from 2020, with an average of $220.48 per person, according to the National Retail Federation. About 83% of adults planned to celebrate.

Online shopping held its place. About 34% of shoppers planned to buy gifts online, while 28% planned to shop at department stores, NRF found. Jewelry accounted for 59% of the year’s increase in spending and electronics for 28%, and shoppers in their late twenties and early thirties planned to spend the most, an average of $367.08. Nearly half planned a special outing, such as brunch.

Prices are higher this spring. Online prices in February were 3.6% above a year earlier, a record, according to Adobe, and apparel was up 16.7%. Gift budgets may stretch less far than in 2021.

Gift shoppers buy against a date

Gift buyers behave differently from people shopping for themselves. They search for a type of gift, such as jewelry, a robe or a plant, rather than a brand, and the calendar does much of their deciding for them. A product with a clear delivery date before May 8 wins over a slightly cheaper one that might arrive after.

They also want reassurance. A gift buyer cannot ask the recipient’s size or taste, so they look for reviews, clear photos, gift wrap and easy returns. A product page that answers “will she like it?” and “can she return it?” converts better than one that only lists features.

Take a candle brand that sells on Amazon and its own site. In 2021 it ran a discount the week before Mother’s Day, then sold out of its best-selling gift set on Amazon five days before the holiday, while plenty of stock sat in its own warehouse.

For 2022 it plans differently. It sends extra gift-set stock to Amazon’s warehouses by mid-April, so the product shows fast delivery through the final week. It adds a gift-ready image showing the packaging, mentions gift notes in the listing and makes returns clear. It advertises on gift searches such as “gifts for mom” rather than only on “candles,” and keeps its discount small.

The discount was never the problem in 2021. Running out of stock was.

Planning stock, pages and spend around May 8

The delivery promise comes first. Gift stock has to reach marketplace warehouses early enough to show delivery before May 8 through the final week. For many products on Amazon that means arriving well before the end of April, since inbound shipments can take time to become available. Walmart and Target add a second route: their gift shoppers can pick up orders in store, which extends the buying window for products held in local stores, so brands sold there should check store stock for gift lines before the final week.

Product pages need to read as gifts. Images of the packaging, gift notes or gift wrap where available, clear sizing and returns, and reviews that speak to gifting all help a shopper who is choosing for someone else. Bundles and gift sets make the choice easier still. Recent gift buyers can help here too, since reviews that mention packaging and arrival time speak directly to late shoppers.

Advertising follows the way gift shoppers search. They look for occasions and types of gift, so terms like “Mother’s Day gifts” and “gifts for mom” belong alongside category terms, with budgets raised in the final ten days, when late shoppers arrive. Timing cuts both ways. Searches for gifts build through late April and peak in the days before the holiday, and gift advertising should come down once delivery before May 8 is no longer possible, because spend after the last delivery date wastes money.

Outings compete for the same budget. With nearly half of shoppers planning a special outing, products that pair with an experience, such as a picnic set or a brunch-ready gift, can benefit from that habit.

Returns come after the holiday. Gifts are returned more often than personal purchases, so brands should expect a rise in returns in mid-May and make sure returned stock is checked and relisted quickly, so it can sell again rather than sit.

Price needs care with prices higher in 2022. Shoppers may hold back on large gifts, and a well-presented gift at a familiar price point may sell better than a deep discount on an expensive item.

NRF’s 2022 Mother’s Day survey will show whether higher prices are holding back gift budgets and how much of the spending is moving online. For a brand’s leadership, the question to settle before then is whether this year’s gift plan starts from the discount calendar or from the last day a parcel can still arrive. Planning a seasonal event backward from the last delivery date, on every marketplace a brand sells through, is how we help brands get gifts there on time.

A0219.crumb: Instagram product tags for all make…
A0219.title: Instagram product tags for all make customers the shop window
A0219.alt: A smartphone on a tripod photographs a shop window displaying handmade ceramic bowls, mugs and vases.
A0219.ttag: Instagram product tags for all make customers the shop window | Kwontified
A0219.desc: Every public US Instagram account can now tag products in feed posts. Brands with clean catalogs and customers who tag turn that into discovery.
A0219.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 21, 2022.
A0219.body:
A new jacket in a mirror photo, a kitchen gadget on a counter, a plant on a shelf: people have always shown off what they buy, and these pictures appear in feeds every day. Friends ask in the comments where it came from, and the answer is often vague or never arrives. Instagram has now opened product tags in feed posts to every public account in the US, so that question can be answered with one tap on the photo itself.

That makes a brand’s own customers part of its shop window, pointing their followers straight to its products, and it strengthens Instagram as a place for discovery rather than checkout. Brands should keep their Instagram catalogs accurate, decide who may tag their products, and encourage customers to tag, instead of relying only on their own posts and paid creators.

What changed with Instagram product tags

Until spring 2022, only brands and approved creators could tag products from a business’s Instagram shop in their posts. On March 22, Instagram said it would extend product tags to all users in the US over the following months, TechCrunch reported. About 1.6 million people already tag brands in their posts each week, Instagram said at the time.

On April 18 the feature went live for all US users with public accounts, for feed posts, with tags in Stories still in development, TechCrunch reported. Brands are notified when someone tags their products, can see the tagged posts, and can choose who is allowed to tag them, PetaPixel reported.

The change fits where Instagram has said it is going. Its head, Adam Mosseri, named video, messaging, transparency and creators as the platform’s priorities for 2022, Engadget reported. Tags from ordinary users fold shopping into the social feed itself, where it had been a separate destination.

A customer’s tag is a recommendation that carries a link

In a store, the window display is something the brand or the retailer arranges and pays for. On Instagram the window now also runs through other people’s living rooms. The person who asked about the jacket sees the product, its price and the brand, and can save it or look it up. A recommendation from someone you know carries more weight than an advertisement, and now it carries a link as well.

Customer photos are more varied and more believable than a brand’s own, and they reach people the brand’s advertising might never find. They are also out of the brand’s hands, which is where the operational work begins.

Take a small homeware brand that sells ceramic planters on its own site and on Amazon. It has an Instagram shop, but its catalog has not been updated in months, and two of its best sellers are missing. When customers begin tagging its planters in photos of their homes, some tags point to products listed as out of stock, and the two best sellers cannot be tagged at all. Interested followers find nothing to buy.

Now suppose the brand updates its catalog, adds the missing products, and starts including a small card in each order asking customers to share and tag their planter. Tagged posts from customers can come to outnumber the brand’s own, and searches for its name on Amazon and on its own site can rise. Its photography budget stays where it was, while the number of images showing its planters in real homes multiplies.

Brands have to be ready before their customers start tagging

The catalog is the first job. Every product a customer might photograph should be taggable, with correct prices, stock and links, because a tag that points to an unavailable product wastes a recommendation. Sellers who work mainly through marketplaces should check one detail. Instagram product tags point to products in a business’s Instagram shop, so a brand that sells mostly through Amazon or a retailer needs a shop set up and connected to its catalog before customers can tag anything. For many marketplace brands, that comes before everything else.

Permissions deserve a deliberate decision rather than a default. Most brands will want to allow anyone to tag, but those with concerns about how their products appear can limit tagging and review tagged posts regularly.

Customers tag more when they are asked. Packaging, order emails or small incentives can carry the request, and the best tagged posts can be featured with permission. That permission matters. A customer’s tagged post is theirs, and a brand that wants to reuse it in its own feed or advertising should ask first and credit the customer, which builds goodwill and encourages more people to tag.

The tone of tagged content will be different from the brand’s own. Customers will post honest photos, not polished ones. That honesty is the value, but it also means problems with products or packaging become visible quickly, so tagged posts work as a feedback channel the brand should read and respond to.

Creators still have a job. Ordinary customers add volume and trust, while creators reach larger audiences and produce content on a plan. The two work together: creators start the conversation and customers keep it going.

Measurement needs a wider lens than Instagram’s own reports. Instagram checkout sales will understate the effect, as many people will buy elsewhere, so brands should track branded searches on Amazon and their own sites, and new customers, alongside the volume of tagged posts.

Whether Instagram extends tags to Stories and Reels for all users in 2022 will decide how far this goes, since each extension would multiply the places a customer’s recommendation can appear. The question for leadership is nearer at hand: if a customer tagged your best seller, would the tag lead anywhere? Keeping the Instagram shop, the catalog and the marketplace listings in step so that it does is how we connect social discovery to sales for brands.

A0220.crumb: Buy with Prime pays only if its…
A0220.title: Buy with Prime pays only if its conversion lift beats its fees
A0220.alt: A brass balance scale weighs a twine-tied parcel against a pan of coins, with a paper shopping bag behind.
A0220.ttag: Buy with Prime pays only if its conversion lift beats its fees | Kwontified
A0220.desc: Buy with Prime puts Amazon’s checkout and delivery on brand sites for a fee. It pays only when the conversion lift covers the added cost on every order.
A0220.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 26, 2022.
A0220.body:
Amazon describes the benefits of Buy with Prime as “conversion-driving,” Chain Store Age reported. It has not published conversion figures. For a brand deciding whether to put Prime checkout and delivery on its own site, that missing number is the whole decision, because the service adds a service fee, payment processing and fulfillment fees to every order that uses it.

Those fees land on the orders a site would have won anyway, while the benefit arrives only on the new ones. Buy with Prime pays only if the extra orders cover the added cost per order across all of them. A brand can work out the conversion lift it needs to break even, then test for that lift on a share of traffic before rolling the service out across its site.

What Buy with Prime costs and offers

Amazon introduced Buy with Prime on April 21. Prime members shopping on a participating merchant’s site can check out with the payment and shipping details in their Amazon account and receive Prime delivery and free returns, Retail TouchPoints reported. The service is invitation-only through 2022, starting with merchants that use Fulfillment by Amazon.

Pricing combines a service fee, a payment processing fee, and fulfillment and storage fees charged per unit, Chain Store Age reported separately.

Fulfillment costs are rising at the same moment. Amazon will add a 5% fuel and inflation surcharge to its fulfillment fees from April 28, about 24 cents per unit on average, UPI reported.

Why Prime checkout could lift conversion

Part of the case is plausible. Prime members trust the delivery promise and do not need to enter payment details, which removes two common reasons shoppers abandon a checkout. Showing a delivery date on the product page may also help shoppers who would otherwise leave to buy on Amazon.

A plausible lift still needs a size. The extra orders have to cover the added cost of every order that uses the service, including the orders that would have happened anyway.

The break-even lift, worked through

Take a skincare brand whose own site converts 2.5% of visitors, with an average order of $60 and a contribution margin of $24 per order before fulfillment. It ships from its own warehouse for about $8 per order. Say Buy with Prime’s service, payment and fulfillment fees together come to about $11 per order, $3 more than its current fulfillment and payment costs. If half its orders switch to Prime checkout, every switching order costs $3 more.

Per 100 visitors, the site earns $40 now: 2.5 orders at $16 each after shipping. With half its orders switching, it earns $36.25 from the same orders, a loss of $3.75.

New orders, each earning about $13 after Prime fees, must close that gap. That takes about 0.29 more orders per 100 visitors, roughly a 12% increase in orders, which moves conversion from 2.5% to about 2.8% just to stand still. If Prime checkout lifts conversion by 15% or more, the service pays. If the lift is smaller, it costs money.

The share of shoppers who switch moves the answer. If most of the site’s visitors are Prime members, more orders move to the higher-cost checkout, and the lift needed to break even rises. If few are, the cost is smaller, and so is the likely benefit.

None of this says the service will fail. The lift may well clear the bar for some brands. Until someone publishes numbers, though, it is something to measure rather than assume.

Testing Buy with Prime before it reaches the whole site

The calculation comes first, with real inputs: your margin per order, your current fulfillment and payment costs, and Amazon’s actual fees. Those give the conversion rise that covers the added cost.

The test comes next. Offer Buy with Prime to a random share of visitors or on a subset of products, and compare conversion and margin per visitor against a control group over several weeks. Track average order value alongside conversion during the test, because if Prime checkout encourages smaller, faster orders, the margin per order may fall even as conversion rises.

Some costs and benefits sit outside the checkout. Returns, customer service and the value of customer data all belong in the comparison, so ask which details your business receives for each order, and whether you can market to those customers later. Returns deserve particular care. Buy with Prime offers free returns, which shoppers value but which add cost when products come back, and brands with high return rates, such as apparel, should build an expected return rate into the break-even calculation instead of assuming every order sticks.

Inventory is the other variable. Orders through Buy with Prime ship from Amazon’s warehouses, so stock placed there serves both Amazon and the brand’s site. That can reduce total inventory needs, but it also ties more of the business to Amazon’s fees, including the new surcharge, and to its capacity limits. Brands that do not use Amazon’s fulfillment network will have to wait, since the first invitations go to merchants already using it. For them, the question for now is whether moving inventory into Amazon’s warehouses would make sense on its own merits, apart from access to Prime checkout.

What invited merchants report will make the break-even question easier for everyone else, if they share conversion results. Until then the rule is simple: if the lift a test measures is below the lift the fees require, the checkout costs money however well shoppers like it. Running that calculation and the test behind it is how we help brands decide where Buy with Prime fits.

A0223.crumb: Pet on Amazon in 2022 rewards brands…
A0223.title: Pet on Amazon in 2022 rewards brands built for repeat orders
A0223.alt: Six plain kraft paper bags stand in a row beside a ceramic bowl of pet kibble on a wooden floor.
A0223.ttag: Pet on Amazon in 2022 rewards brands built for repeat orders | Kwontified
A0223.desc: Pet owners buy the same food and litter again and again. On Amazon in 2022, pet brands win by earning the second order and the subscription after it.
A0223.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 28, 2022.
A0223.body:
Watch a dog owner reorder food and there is almost no shopping involved. It is the same bag in the same size, ideally arriving before the old one runs out, and the real decision was made months earlier, the first time the dog ate it without trouble. Chewy, the category’s online leader, has built its business on that habit and now earns about 70% of its sales from subscriptions.

That habit decides who wins in pet on Amazon in 2022. The first sale matters less than the orders that follow it, so pet brands should build for the repeat order, with subscriptions, consistent stock and pack sizes that suit replenishment, rather than judging success on the first sale alone.

Pet on Amazon follows a record year for the category

The category grew faster than expected in 2021. U.S. pet industry sales reached $123.6 billion, up 13.5%, far above the association’s own forecast of about 6% growth, according to the American Pet Products Association. Spending on food and treats reached $50 billion, up 13.6%, and supplies, live animals and over-the-counter medicines rose 17.8% to $29.8 billion. APPA expects growth to continue in 2022, at a more moderate pace.

Online, the repeat purchase is the business. Chewy’s net sales rose 24.4% to $8.89 billion in its 2021 fiscal year, and sales to customers using Autoship, its subscription service, reached 70.2% of net sales, according to its results. It had 20.7 million active customers.

Prices are climbing as well. Online prices for pet products were 7% higher in March than a year earlier, the 23rd consecutive month of increases, Chain Store Age reported, citing Adobe.

The first bag is a decision, and every bag after it is a habit

Pet owners shop for someone who cannot tell them what they want, and who often reacts badly to change. Once a dog settles on a food, or a cat accepts a litter, owners tend to stick with it, because switching risks an upset stomach or a refused bowl. In a store, that loyalty is easy to miss: the owner walks past every other bag on the shelf to reach the usual one, and nobody records the bags that were never considered.

The habit is easy to keep and annoying to break. Owners want the same product, in the same size, delivered before the bag runs out, and subscriptions fit that pattern closely. Amazon offers Subscribe & Save, and Chewy’s results show how far a subscription model can go when it matches how owners actually buy. A brand that earns a subscription has not made one sale. It has made dozens, as long as it keeps the product in stock and the price fair.

Take a cat food brand that sells well on Amazon but judges its advertising on first purchases. Its return on ad spend looks modest, and its team considers cutting the budget. When it looks at repeat purchases instead, it finds that a large share of new buyers order again within six weeks, and many sign up for Subscribe & Save. Their value over a year is several times the first order, so the advertising that looked modest was building a subscriber base.

The same review turns up a problem. Twice in the past year, its most popular size ran out of stock for a week, and subscribers who could not receive their order switched to another brand. Many did not come back.

It also shows which products bring subscribers. The brand’s large bags attract fewer first-time buyers than its small ones, but buyers who start on the large bag are far more likely to subscribe. So it shifts some advertising toward the large bag for shoppers searching for its exact product type, keeps the small bag for trial, adds stock buffers for its best-selling sizes, and starts tracking subscriptions as its main measure of success.

Building a pet range around the second order

The second order is the figure to report. Track repeat purchase rates and subscriptions for new customers, and judge advertising on customer value over months as well as on the first sale.

Stock is where the habit breaks. Running out of a product that customers buy on repeat sends them looking elsewhere, so the best-selling sizes need extra stock and closer inventory watching than occasional purchases do.

Pack sizes and prices shape the replenishment cycle. Sizes should last a sensible time between orders, Subscribe & Save should be available on core products, and prices should stay consistent so subscribers are not surprised. Increases need particular care. With pet product prices rising, brands may need to raise their own, and subscribers notice a change on a repeat order more than occasional buyers do, so increases are better communicated clearly and without sudden jumps.

New products need a different plan, because launching a new food or treat means persuading owners to risk a change. Smaller trial sizes, strong reviews and clear ingredient information help owners feel safe trying something new.

Reviews carry extra weight in pet. Owners read about other owners’ experiences, especially with food and health products, before risking a change. Brands should make it easy for satisfied buyers to leave reviews and respond helpfully to complaints, since one detailed negative review about a pet’s reaction can deter many buyers.

Supplies and health products behave differently from food. Toys, beds and accessories are bought less often and respond more to discovery and gifting, while over-the-counter health products sit in between, so each part of a range deserves its own goal.

How pet spending holds up as prices rise in 2022 will test all of this. If owners keep buying the same products at higher prices, the repeat model will prove as resilient as it has been.

For a pet brand’s leadership, the useful question is which number the team celebrates at the end of the month: first orders, or the subscribers still ordering. Judging advertising by the subscribers it builds, and keeping their sizes in stock, is how we run Amazon for pet brands.

A0225.crumb: The FBA fuel surcharge hits low-priced…
A0225.title: The FBA fuel surcharge hits low-priced products hardest
A0225.alt: A worn red jerry can beside a stack of twine-tied kraft parcels in a sunlit doorway next to a pink wall.
A0225.ttag: The FBA fuel surcharge hits low-priced products hardest | Kwontified
A0225.desc: Amazon’s 5% FBA fuel and inflation surcharge takes the biggest share of margin on cheap products. Model it product by product and reset ACoS targets.
A0225.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 3, 2022.
A0225.body:
Every seller using Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA) in the U.S. now pays the same 5% fuel and inflation surcharge, in force since April 28, and it does not cost them the same. The surcharge is charged on the fulfillment fee, which follows a product’s size and weight, so a cheap product gives up far more of its margin to it than an expensive product of the same size.

With Amazon reporting heavy cost pressure of its own, sellers should treat the surcharge as part of their cost base for some time. That means modeling it product by product and lowering advertising targets most where it removes the most margin, instead of answering with one account-wide cut.

What the FBA fuel surcharge changes

The surcharge adds 5% to per-unit fulfillment fees, which comes to about 24 cents per unit on average, and Amazon has said the charge is subject to change, UPI reported. It is the first such surcharge Amazon has charged, Bloomberg reported when it was announced on April 13.

It lands on top of January’s changes, which raised fulfillment fees by an average of 5.2% from January 18, EcommerceBytes reported. Amazon described the surcharge as an alternative to a permanent fee increase, Fox Business reported.

The pressure behind it has not eased. On its first-quarter earnings call, Amazon said rising costs, lower warehouse productivity and spare capacity had added about $6 billion of costs in the first quarter, about $2 billion of it from inflation. It expected about $4 billion of these extra costs in the second quarter, according to the call transcript.

Why a 5% surcharge takes the most from cheap products

It is natural to read a 5% surcharge as a 5% problem everywhere, because that is how a charge on the selling price would behave. This one is a percentage of the fulfillment fee, and the fee depends on size and weight rather than price. Two products of the same size pay the same surcharge, whatever they sell for. On a cheap product that fixed amount is a much larger share of the price, and an even larger share of the margin.

Take a kitchen tool, a water bottle and a desk lamp, each with a margin of 25% of price before advertising.

ProductPriceFulfillment feeSurchargeSurcharge as share of priceSurcharge as share of margin
Kitchen tool$12.00$3.50$0.1751.5%5.8%
Water bottle$40.00$5.50$0.2750.7%2.8%
Desk lamp$80.00$9.00$0.450.6%2.3%

The kitchen tool gives up almost 6% of its margin to the surcharge, the lamp about 2%. One rule, applied evenly, lands very unevenly across a catalog.

Break-even ACoS falls furthest where prices are lowest

Advertising targets inherit the same gap. Advertising cost of sale (ACoS) is ad spend divided by attributed sales, and its break-even level is the margin left after product cost and Amazon’s fees, divided by price. Any fee increase lowers that ceiling.

For the kitchen tool, margin before advertising falls from $3.00 to about $2.83 per unit, and break-even ACoS falls from 25% to about 23.5%. A campaign that ran at 24% ACoS and earned a thin profit in March now loses money on every attributed sale.

For the lamp, break-even ACoS moves by about half a point, and most campaigns will not notice. A single account-wide response is therefore the wrong one. Cutting every ACoS target by the same amount overcorrects on expensive products and undercorrects on cheap ones.

Building the surcharge into the cost base

Amazon has framed the surcharge as temporary, and it may be. It has not said when it will end, though, and its own cost picture points the other way. Brands that leave it out of their models while they wait for it to disappear will make pricing and advertising decisions on margins they no longer have.

Low-priced products deserve a closer look at price, packaging and bundles. A small price increase, where the market allows, may recover the surcharge without hurting conversion. A product near the edge of a size tier may move to a cheaper fee band with smaller packaging, which cuts both the fee and the surcharge. Selling two units together spreads one fulfillment fee across a higher price.

Subscription products need the same check. A product sold through Subscribe & Save at a discount already runs on a thinner margin, so the surcharge takes an even larger share of what is left. Each subscription price should be checked against its full cost, surcharge included, before the next round of orders ships.

Finance belongs in the review. A margin model built in January, before the surcharge was announced, now overstates profit on every FBA product. Updating it changes more than advertising targets: it changes which products deserve inventory investment for the second half of the year, and which promotions still make sense at their planned discount.

Merchant fulfillment is worth testing for some products too. Sellers that ship orders themselves do not pay the surcharge, though they carry their own carriers’ fuel charges, which UPS and FedEx had set at 42 and 49 cents per unit respectively as of March 21, UPI reported. That comparison only works product by product.

Amazon’s next fee announcement will settle how long this lasts. If the surcharge is folded into permanent rates, every model built now will already be right. If it ends, brands can raise targets again with a clear record of what it cost them while it lasted. Either way, each product’s ACoS target should come from its own margin after fees rather than from an account average, and rebuilding targets that way, product by product, is how we manage Amazon advertising through fee changes.
