A0226.crumb: Zalando after the boom: slower growth…
A0226.title: Zalando after the boom: slower growth puts partners first
A0226.alt: A twine-tied orange parcel on a wooden side table between two armchairs in a sunlit room with plants and shelves.
A0226.ttag: Zalando after the boom: slower growth puts partners first | Kwontified
A0226.desc: Zalando expects much slower growth in 2022 as European shoppers turn cautious. Partner brands should plan conservatively and supply what Zalando needs.
A0226.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 5, 2022.
A0226.body:
In 2021 a brand could grow on Zalando largely by being present. The platform’s own growth lifted most of the partners selling on it, and a plan needed little more than a stock order and a confident percentage. That lift is fading. Zalando’s growth is set to slow sharply in 2022, and European shoppers have turned cautious faster than its plan assumed.

The channel still matters to the brands on it, for different reasons. In a slower year Zalando will lean harder on its partners for growth, so brands should plan Zalando on conservative volumes, protect their margins, and put effort into the services the platform most needs, instead of budgeting for another year like 2021.

What changed for Zalando partners

2021 was a boom year. Zalando’s gross merchandise volume rose 34.1% to €14.3 billion, and its Partner Program and Connected Retail, where brands sell directly to its customers, reached 30% of its fashion store volume, according to Zalando. More than 5,800 brands now sell directly through it.

For 2022, Zalando set a far lower bar. It forecast gross merchandise volume growth of 16% to 23%, and said that range did not include any potential negative effect from the war in Ukraine, Just Style reported. Its executives expected a more volatile year, citing weakening consumer sentiment, supply chain disruption and inflation, according to a report on its results.

Sentiment has since fallen further. Euro area consumer confidence dropped to -18.7 in March, as the war dragged it well below its long-term average, according to the European Commission. It fell again to -22.0 in April, according to the final figures for the month.

Other online fashion sellers are feeling it. ASOS reported a fall of 87% in first-half profit, to £14.8 million, as revenue rose just 4% to £2 billion, interactive investor reported.

Whether Zalando still earns the investment in a slower year

The decision in front of brand leadership is a plain one. If Zalando’s growth halves, and European shoppers are spending less on fashion, should the brand still put people, stock and budget behind the channel?

The case for staying holds, but it rests on different ground. Growth in 2022 will come from taking share within the platform, and from doing the things Zalando needs from its partners, because the platform’s own growth will carry less of the load.

The partner model shows why partners matter more in a slow year. Through the Partner Program, Zalando adds range without buying stock. Partners carry the inventory risk, pay commission and increasingly use its fulfillment and marketing services. When demand softens, a platform that holds less of its own inventory is better protected, and it has every reason to grow the share of business that partners carry. Zalando has also said it will open its fulfillment service to brands’ own channels over the coming months, deepening that relationship.

For partners, that cuts both ways. Zalando wants their range, their stock and their use of its services. Partners also carry the risk the platform has shifted to them: unsold stock, returns and slower sales sit on the brand’s books, not Zalando’s. A brand weighing the channel has to price both halves: the reach and services Zalando offers, and the stock and returns it now carries on the platform’s behalf.

Take a Scandinavian footwear brand that grew 40% on Zalando in 2021 and built its 2022 plan on 30% growth, with stock ordered to match. In March, with sentiment falling and returns rising, it revises its plan to 10% to 15%.

Rather than cancel stock, it concentrates its range on core styles that sell across markets, moves slow sizes into Zalando’s fulfillment network where they can serve several countries, and shifts marketing spend toward the markets where its sales are holding. It ends the season with less leftover stock than its original plan would have produced, and a stronger position in its two best markets.

Planning Zalando for volumes, returns and markets that may not grow

Volume plans should start low and leave room to rise. Build the 2022 Zalando plan from the lower end of the platform’s own guidance rather than from 2021’s growth, and set stock orders that can flex upward if demand recovers.

Returns and stock are where margin leaks. Fashion returns rise when shoppers are uncertain, and every return costs handling and markdown risk. Return rates deserve a review by style and size before the summer season, so that the fit and content problems behind the worst ones get fixed, with stock kept lean on slow sizes.

The services Zalando most needs are worth using where they pay. Pooling stock in its fulfillment network, using its marketing tools in markets where sales are holding, and keeping range complete all strengthen a brand’s position on the platform, and each should be judged on contribution per market rather than on headline sales.

Country choice matters more in a slow year. Zalando sells across many European markets, and confidence is falling faster in some than in others. A brand selling in many countries should rank them by contribution and focus effort on the few that earn it. Spreading the same effort evenly across every market leaves the strongest ones underserved.

Pricing deserves restraint. Discounting to defend volume trains shoppers to wait, and Zalando’s shoppers can compare prices across thousands of brands in seconds. Targeted offers on overstocked styles do less damage than broad markdowns.

Zalando’s first-quarter results, scheduled for May 5, are the next marker. Whether the company holds or trims its guidance will show how much further partners should lower their own plans. Building that plan market by market, from the low end of the platform’s range, is how we run Zalando for brands across Europe.

A0227.crumb: Amazon’s Q1 2022 ad growth outran the…
A0227.title: Amazon’s Q1 2022 ad growth outran the sales it competes for
A0227.alt: Coins rolling across a worn wooden tabletop toward a small twine-tied brown paper parcel by a window.
A0227.ttag: Amazon’s Q1 2022 ad growth outran the sales it competes for | Kwontified
A0227.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 23% in Q1 2022 while unit sales were flat. More ad money chased the same purchases, so budget for a crowded auction.
A0227.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 10, 2022.
A0227.body:
Amazon’s advertising line missed analysts’ estimates in the first quarter of 2022, and the easy reading is that the auction is finally cooling. The rest of the report points the other way. Ad revenue grew 23% while unit sales were flat and online store sales fell, so more advertising money chased roughly the same number of purchases.

When ad revenue grows faster than the purchases it competes for, the ad spend behind each purchase rises, whatever the headline growth rate. Brands should plan for a crowded auction through 2022 and judge campaigns on cost per order, instead of treating the miss as a sign that clicks will get cheaper.

What Amazon’s Q1 2022 ad growth showed

Amazon reported first-quarter net sales of $116.4 billion, up 7%, according to its results. That was its slowest growth since 2001.

The detail matters more than the total. Advertising sales rose 23% to $7.88 billion. Sales in Amazon’s online stores fell 3%, and unit sales, a measure that excludes cloud contracts and Whole Foods groceries, were flat compared with a year earlier, a first for Amazon, BNN Bloomberg reported.

The ad figure came in below analysts’ expectations of $8.17 billion, CNBC reported. Amazon forecast second-quarter net sales of $116 billion to $121 billion, growth of 3% to 7%, BNN Bloomberg reported.

A missed estimate still leaves the auction tighter

Reading the miss as relief is understandable. Analysts had expected even faster ad growth, and a business that undershoots its forecast looks like a business that is slowing. Yet missing that expectation still left ad revenue growing much faster than sales.

Advertising revenue is, in large part, what brands pay for clicks and impressions on Amazon. If that revenue grows faster than the number of purchases it competes for, the ad spend behind each purchase rises. It shows up as higher cost per click, lower conversion per dollar, or both.

The first-quarter numbers fit that pattern closely. Ad revenue grew 23% and unit sales did not grow at all, so across Amazon as a whole roughly a fifth more advertising money was competing for about the same number of units.

A rough ratio, calculated from the reported growth rates, shows the shift. Advertising revenue equaled about 15% of online store sales in the first quarter of 2022, up from about 12% a year earlier. Online store sales exclude third-party seller fees, so the ratio is only an indicator, but its direction is clear.

Click prices were climbing before the quarter began. Average CPC on Amazon ended 2021 at $1.33, having risen 43% over the year, Marketplace Pulse reported, and nothing in the first-quarter results suggests that trend reversed.

Take a kitchenware brand that kept its Amazon ad budget flat in the first quarter and saw sales slip 5%. Its team assumed demand had softened. A review of the account shows that its cost per click rose 18% from a year earlier while conversion held steady, so the same budget bought fewer clicks and reached fewer shoppers.

That finding changes the brand’s response. Demand had not fallen as much as the brand’s sales suggested; its share of the auction had. Instead of cutting its budget further, as it had planned, the brand moves spend from broad category terms to the searches where it converts best, and keeps its total spend steady into Prime Day.

Budgeting Amazon ads for a crowded auction in 2022

Budgets should start from current costs. Prime Day and second-half budgets belong on first-quarter cost per click and cost per order, not on 2021 averages, because a flat budget in a rising auction buys less reach every month.

Campaigns are better judged on cost per order. Return on ad spend rises with price increases and can hide rising acquisition costs, while cost per order, read alongside units, shows whether the brand is paying more for the same result. A campaign whose return on ad spend held steady while its cost per order climbed has been losing ground the whole time.

Money should go where the brand wins. In a crowded auction, broad keywords become expensive fastest, so budget belongs on the searches where the brand converts best, with branded terms protected and terms cut where cost per order has risen beyond margin.

Costs elsewhere make this more pressing. Amazon reported about $6 billion of extra costs in the first quarter from inflation, lower productivity and spare capacity, according to the call transcript, and sellers now pay a new 5% fuel and inflation surcharge on FBA fees. Higher fees lower the advertising cost each product can afford, just as the auction is getting more expensive.

Category shapes how much of this a brand feels. Advertisers in categories where demand has cooled since the pandemic peak face more competition for fewer shoppers, while everyday categories with steady demand may see smaller increases.

Prime Day will test all of this. If ad revenue keeps growing faster than sales into the event, deal-week click prices will reflect it. Brands that set event budgets from current costs will be ready; those that assume relief will run out early.

Sponsored Products is not the only place costs show up. Display and video placements, sold through Amazon’s demand-side platform and Sponsored Display, compete for the same budgets. A brand that shifts money there to escape rising search costs should measure those placements on the same cost per order, not on reach alone.

Amazon’s second-quarter ad growth, set against its sales growth, is the next reading. If advertising keeps outpacing sales, the auction is still tightening, whatever the headline rate, and each order should be budgeted to cost more. Rebuilding Prime Day plans on first-quarter auction costs is how we plan Amazon advertising for the brands we work with.

A0229.crumb: Inflation is changing what shoppers trade…
A0229.title: Inflation is changing what shoppers trade down on
A0229.alt: A cork-lidded glass jar of preserved apricots beside a tin can in a wire basket on a rustic wooden shelf.
A0229.ttag: Inflation is changing what shoppers trade down on | Kwontified
A0229.desc: With prices up 8.3%, shoppers swap staples, protect small treats and delay big purchases. Brands need to know where each of their products sits.
A0229.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 12, 2022.
A0229.body:
Follow one household through a week of shopping this spring and the price pressure shows up in different places. Store-brand paper towels go into the cart in place of the usual ones. The morning coffee stays the same, bought in a smaller bag. The new blender waits. With consumer prices up 8.3% in a year, shoppers are trading down, but not evenly.

They swap the staples they see as interchangeable, protect the products tied to taste or quality, and postpone larger purchases. A brand’s exposure depends on which of these its products are, so brands should sort their range by how shoppers treat each product and set prices, pack sizes and promotions to match, rather than discounting everything.

What shoppers trade down on in 2022

Prices are still rising fast. U.S. consumer prices rose 8.3% in the year to April, and food bought for the home rose 10.8%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

Online, shoppers are pulling back on bigger purchases. Consumers spent $77.8 billion online in April, up 4.5% from a year earlier, after double-digit growth in January and February, according to Adobe. April spending was $5.28 billion below March, and Adobe said consumers had pulled back on durable goods as borrowing costs and uncertainty rose. Online prices were up 2.9% from a year earlier, and 10 of the 18 categories Adobe tracks saw prices fall from March.

The big brands see the split too. Procter & Gamble raised its sales outlook after price increases, even as shoppers across consumer goods increasingly switched to cheaper brands, Modern Retail reported. Higher-income shoppers have stuck with premium brands despite the increases, Marketplace reported.

Shoppers sort their products before they cut anything

Watch a household under price pressure and the choices look less like a single cut than a sorting exercise.

Some products are treated as interchangeable. Paper towels, rice, batteries, basic cleaning products: if the store brand looks good enough, the shopper switches and rarely misses the old one. For these, price is most of the decision.

A second group is protected. The coffee someone drinks every morning, a skincare product they trust, the pet food their dog will actually eat: shoppers keep buying these, sometimes in smaller packs or less often, because switching feels like a real loss.

Larger purchases are the ones that get postponed. A new blender, a mattress or a television can wait a few months when grocery bills are rising, which is what Adobe’s durable goods figures suggest is happening.

The same shopper sorts products all of these ways in the same week. That is why average trade-down figures mislead brands, because the effect on a given product depends on which group the shopper puts it in.

Take a household brand that sells both a basic dish soap and a premium hand soap on Amazon. In the spring, its dish soap sales fall as shoppers move to cheaper alternatives, while its hand soap holds steady but sells more in single bottles than in multipacks.

Its first instinct is to discount both. On reflection, it does something different. It introduces a larger, lower-cost-per-unit size of the dish soap, competing on value per wash rather than shelf price. It leaves the hand soap’s price alone, adds a single-bottle option to every listing, and stops running deep discounts that would have given away margin to shoppers who were going to buy anyway. Discounting still has its uses; the response that works depends on how shoppers treat the product.

Pricing, pack sizes and promotions for each kind of product

Sorting the range comes first. For each product, the question is whether shoppers treat it as interchangeable, protected or postponable, and sales trends since March, reviews that mention price, and the share of sales on promotion all help answer it.

Where shoppers swap, value per unit wins. For interchangeable products, a better price per unit, a larger size or a bundle often works better than a headline discount, as long as the value is easy to see on the product page.

Where shoppers stay loyal, price is worth protecting. Smaller packs or single units keep shoppers buying protected products, while deep discounts train them to wait. Reviews and clear content remind them why the product is worth what it costs.

Postponable products call for patience more than price cuts. Shoppers delaying a purchase have not decided against it, so these products should stay visible, with financing or bundles where retailers offer them, and stock planned for demand that may return later in the year.

Advertising should follow the sort. Budgets spent defending interchangeable products against cheaper rivals often have the weakest returns now, while protected products may still convert well at steady prices. Rebalancing toward what shoppers still choose usually works better than cutting across the board.

Subscriptions give an early warning. When shoppers skip deliveries or cancel Subscribe & Save orders on a product they used to buy every month, it is often moving from protected to interchangeable in their minds. Brands that track skips and cancellations by product will see the shift before it shows up in total sales, and can respond with a smaller size or a better unit price while the shopper is still deciding.

Marketplace data helps here too. Amazon, Walmart and Target all show search terms and conversion by product, and a rise in searches that include words like “value” or “bulk” in a category is an early sign that shoppers there are trading down.

May’s inflation figure, due in June, will show whether the pressure is easing. If prices keep rising faster than wages, more products will move from protected to interchangeable in shoppers’ minds.

That makes one question worth asking inside every brand now: has anyone sorted the range yet, or is the plan still a single discount calendar for every product? Sorting a range by how shoppers treat it, on each retailer it sells through, is how we help brands set prices and pack sizes as demand shifts.

A0231.crumb: Market share, not sales, is the Amazon…
A0231.title: Market share, not sales, is the Amazon metric that matters
A0231.alt: A lattice-topped peach and blueberry pie with slices missing on a sunlit wooden table with a fork and server.
A0231.ttag: Market share, not sales, is the Amazon metric that matters | Kwontified
A0231.desc: In 2022, Amazon sales growth mostly reflects what categories are doing. Share of category shows whether a brand is winning, so track it every month.
A0231.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 17, 2022.
A0231.body:
Every monthly Amazon report leads with sales growth, and every team reads that number as its own performance. In 2022 the habit misleads in both directions, because a brand’s sales mostly reflect what its category is doing. Online demand is slowing and prices are moving unevenly, so sales can rise while a brand loses ground, or fall while it gains.

The number that separates the brand from its category is share of category sales. Brands should measure it every month, in revenue and in units, and set goals in share as well as in sales.

Why the Amazon market share metric matters more in 2022

The market has changed speed. U.S. online spending grew 12.2% in January and 15.5% in February from a year earlier, then just 4.5% in April, to $77.8 billion, according to Adobe. Durable goods were among the purchases consumers pulled back on, according to Adobe.

Amazon is feeling the slowdown directly. Its online stores sold 3% less in the first quarter than a year earlier, and its unit sales were flat for the first time, BNN Bloomberg reported.

Prices are moving in different directions by category. Online prices rose 2.9% from a year earlier in April, while prices fell from March in 10 of the 18 categories Adobe tracks, according to its price index. Consumer prices overall rose 8.3%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. When demand and prices shift this much, the category’s movement swamps the brand’s own.

Sales growth credits and blames teams for the tide

The pull here is outcome bias: judging a decision, or a team, by the result rather than by the part of the result they controlled. It feels fair, because the result is what reaches the bank account. Nobody sets out to grade a team on the weather; the sales line is simply the number that arrives first and the one finance already tracks.

On Amazon, a brand’s sales growth has two parts. One is what happened to the whole category; the other is what happened to the brand’s share of it. Sales reports combine the two, and teams naturally read the combined number as their own performance.

In 2020 and 2021 that flattered almost everyone. Categories grew fast, so most brands grew, whether or not they gained share. In 2022 it can do the opposite, punishing teams in shrinking categories for a decline they did not cause, and rewarding teams in growing ones for growth that came from the tide.

Take two brands in different categories. In both cases, the share change is the ratio of the brand’s growth to the category’s.

BrandCategory growthBrand sales growthChange in share
Kitchen brand+15%+5%Share fell by about 9%
Home office brand-10%-3%Share rose by about 8%

The kitchen brand’s report shows growth, and its team may be praised. In fact it lost almost a tenth of its position in a category that kept expanding, which usually means a competitor is winning searches, reviews or the Buy Box. The home office brand’s report shows decline, and its budget may be cut. In fact it gained ground while its category shrank, which is exactly what its strategy was meant to do.

Price adds a second layer. A brand that raised prices 8% will show revenue growth even if it sold fewer units, so share measured in units, as well as in revenue, shows whether shoppers are still choosing it.

Measuring Amazon share every month

Category size has to be estimated, because Amazon does not publish category sales. Brands can build the estimate from category data tools, search volume trends and their own position on top searches. Precision matters less than consistency, since the same method every month shows direction.

Share belongs in both revenue and units. Divide the brand’s sales by the category estimate both ways and track the trend monthly. A falling unit share with a rising revenue share usually means price is carrying the results, which rarely lasts.

Goals work better in share. A target such as “hold share in a falling category” or “gain two points of share” judges the team on what it controls. Paired with a sales target, it still lets the business plan its cash and stock.

Share also changes how brands read advertising. Spend that defends share in a shrinking category may look inefficient on return on ad spend while doing its job, and spend that buys sales in a growing category may look efficient while the brand loses ground.

It clarifies the conversation with finance and leadership, too. A board that sees sales down 3% will ask what went wrong. A board that sees sales down 3% in a category down 10% will ask a better question: how did the brand gain ground, and can it keep doing so when the category recovers? The same numbers lead to very different decisions about budget and headcount, depending on which frame comes first.

Share also points to causes. When it falls, the usual reasons are visible on the page: a competitor’s lower price, newer reviews, a lost Buy Box, or stock gaps. Revenue alone never points to any of them. The same method works off Amazon, since brands selling on Walmart and Target face the same slowdown, and share can then be compared across retailers instead of sales alone.

Prime Day will be the next test. Event weeks lift whole categories, so the brands that gain share during the event, and not only sales, are the ones whose plans worked. Reporting each brand’s results against its category, and not only against the prior year, is how we read Amazon performance for the brands we work with.

A0232.crumb: Heritage brands win on Instagram with…
A0232.title: Heritage brands win on Instagram with what they already own
A0232.alt: A smartphone on a tripod photographing a vintage leather suitcase on a wooden floor against a pale blue wall.
A0232.ttag: Heritage brands win on Instagram with what they already own | Kwontified
A0232.desc: Paid social got costlier after Apple’s privacy change. Heritage brands win on Instagram with archives, loyal customers and a name upstarts lack.
A0232.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 19, 2022.
A0232.body:
A familiar bag, a jacket people have worn for decades, a watch their parents owned: when one of these scrolls past on Instagram, the post has almost nothing to explain. The viewer already knows the name, the quality and often the price. For several years that mattered less than it should have, because upstart brands could win on Instagram by buying customers through precisely targeted ads.

Apple’s privacy change made that targeting less accurate and more expensive, and the advantage has moved toward brands with assets that do not depend on it: an archive of recognizable products, customers who post about them, and existing demand for the name. Heritage brands should build their Instagram plans around those assets instead of trying to outspend newer rivals.

What changed for heritage brands on Instagram

The upstart playbook ran on paid social, and its cost has risen. Meta said that Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature would cut its 2022 revenue by about $10 billion, and that the change had made ad targeting less accurate and driving a sale more expensive, CNBC reported. Ecommerce was among the categories most affected, Benzinga reported.

Some heritage brands, meanwhile, are adding customers fast. The company that owns Coach, Kate Spade and Stuart Weitzman recruited more than 1.4 million new customers in North America in its latest quarter, a mid-teens increase. Its digital revenue rose more than 20% and its North American revenue 22%, according to its results, and it raised average prices in each brand’s core category.

Instagram has made customers’ posts more useful too. Since April 18, every U.S. user with a public account can tag products in feed posts, TechCrunch reported. About 1.6 million people were already tagging brands in their posts each week before the change, Instagram said.

The value in a post has moved from targeting to recognition

Ask where the value in an Instagram post comes from and the shift becomes clear. For an upstart, it came mostly from targeting. The brand was unknown, so it paid to find the few thousand people most likely to buy, showed them an ad and measured the sale. When targeting worked well, a small brand could buy its way to scale, and much of what it spent went to the platform that sold the targeting.

For a heritage brand, the value comes mostly from recognition. A shopper scrolling past a familiar bag, jacket or watch already knows what it is. The post does not have to introduce the brand; it only has to remind the shopper why they wanted it, and recognition does not depend on tracking.

When targeting became less precise, the first kind of value lost the most and the second barely changed. Product tags for all users then added a third source that the brand does not pay for at all: customers who already own the product now show it to their followers with a link attached. A heritage brand’s Instagram account starts to work less like a channel for campaigns and more like a display case for an archive, with the customers who love it standing in front.

Take a luggage brand founded decades ago that competes with a younger direct-to-consumer rival built on paid social. In 2021 the rival’s ads became less efficient, and it raised its ad budget to hold sales.

The heritage brand took a different route. It reissued a model from its archive that older customers remembered, posted the original advertisements next to the new version, and invited owners to share photos of their decades-old cases. Those posts, tagged and shared, reached people the brand could no longer target precisely. Its ad budget stayed flat while its branded searches rose.

Planning Instagram around the archive and the customers who own it

The archive is the first place to look. Recognizable products and past campaigns are content an upstart cannot copy, and reissues, anniversaries and side-by-side comparisons give followers a reason to share.

Customers can become the shop window. Owners can be encouraged to post and tag what they already own, and that works provided the Instagram catalog is complete so every tag leads to a product, and the best posts are featured with permission.

Paid spend still has a job, aimed at reach more than retargeting. With precise targeting weaker, broad campaigns that build recognition, especially short video, which Instagram has made a priority, do more work than narrow retargeting of a shrinking pool.

Measurement should match the shift. Branded search on Amazon and Google, direct traffic and new customers matter more than the click-through rate of a single ad. Coach’s parent company led its results with new customers recruited, not ad efficiency.

Timing helps heritage brands as well. Anniversaries, reissues and seasonal returns of classic styles give them a steady calendar of moments that feel natural to share, while an upstart has to invent its own occasions. Planned a year ahead, those moments can carry much of an Instagram calendar without heavy paid support.

Upstarts are not helpless. Many have strong founder stories and loyal early communities. Their cheapest route to growth has become more expensive, though, and they now have to build the recognition heritage brands already hold. Pricing strength tells the same story: a brand that can raise prices while adding customers, as Coach’s owner did, is earning its demand rather than renting it.

How heritage brands’ new customer counts hold up as inflation squeezes budgets will show whether the shift lasts. If recognition keeps bringing in new buyers without heavier advertising, it is structural. Turning an archive and a base of loyal owners into social discovery that ends in a sale is how we help heritage brands sell from Instagram.

A0233.crumb: Walmart’s seller vetting is an advantage…
A0233.title: Walmart’s seller vetting is an advantage only while it holds
A0233.alt: A velvet rope on brass posts across a blue doorway beside a clipboard lectern, leading into a shop with shelves.
A0233.ttag: Walmart’s seller vetting is an advantage only while it holds | Kwontified
A0233.desc: Walmart’s seller vetting builds shopper trust that lifts every listing. As its marketplace doubles, brands should use that edge and guard their listings.
A0233.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 24, 2022.
A0233.body:
A brand that sells the same product on Amazon and Walmart can spend hours each month on Amazon reporting copycat listings, and almost none on Walmart. Walmart has presented its marketplace as more closely vetted than Amazon’s, and that difference shows up in more than enforcement work: a cleaner seller base earns shopper trust, and trust lifts every listing on the site.

The catch is that the advantage belongs to the whole marketplace and lasts only as long as Walmart keeps its bar while the marketplace grows quickly. Brands should use it now, in conversion and in fewer counterfeit rivals, and protect their own listings rather than assume Walmart will stay as clean as it is.

How Walmart seller vetting works and what changed

Walmart’s marketplace is growing fast. It had about 130,000 sellers at the end of 2021, roughly double a year earlier, Marketplace Pulse reported. In March 2021 Walmart began admitting sellers based outside the United States, at a point when it had about 80,000, Caixin reported.

Walmart said the opening would not change its standards. “We do not plan to lower our bar or change our vetting standards,” the head of Walmart Marketplace told Reuters, adding that its teams abroad would vet sellers on their reviews, licensing, reputations and items, according to the report.

The new sellers came quickly. By the end of 2021, Chinese sellers accounted for about one in seven of those joining Walmart’s marketplace, Bloomberg reported. Some had been banned from Amazon, which spent 2021 removing sellers over review abuse, including the well-known accessory brands Aukey and Mpow in May and RavPower in June, Android Authority reported.

Why vetting works like a shared asset

When a marketplace vets sellers well, the average seller is more reliable. Shoppers learn that orders arrive as described, and they buy with less hesitation. That higher trust lifts conversion for everyone on the marketplace, including brands that never had a problem seller in their category.

Shared assets have a familiar weakness, and it is easy to see why a platform might drift. Each additional seller brings Walmart more selection and more commission, and the gain lands with Walmart straight away. The cost of a weaker seller, in lost trust, arrives slowly and is spread across every brand on the site, so no single sale ever looks like the one that did the damage. A town common gets overgrazed the same way: every extra animal pays its owner, and the thinning grass is everybody’s problem.

Walmart faces that pull directly. A bigger catalog helps it compete with Amazon on selection, while a stricter bar protects the trust that makes its marketplace different. Its statements say it will keep the bar; its growth tests whether it can.

For brands, a cleaner marketplace means fewer counterfeit or low-quality listings competing on their own search terms, and shoppers more willing to buy from a third-party listing. If the bar slips later, the brand inherits the problems without having caused them.

Take a kitchenware brand that sells on Amazon and Walmart. On Amazon, it spends time each month reporting copycat listings that use its photos. On Walmart, in early 2021, it found almost none, and its conversion rate there ran higher than on Amazon for the same products.

By early 2022, it notices a few listings on Walmart using its images and similar titles. None are large yet. The brand begins checking its key searches each week and reporting copies promptly, so the problem stays small while it is easy to contain.

Using Walmart’s cleaner marketplace while protecting your listings

The trust is worth using while it is high. Brands that have hesitated to expand on Walmart because of the work involved should weigh the conversion benefit of a cleaner marketplace, which is strongest now.

Your own searches are the early warning. Checking the top searches for your products each week, for listings that copy your images, titles or brand name, and reporting them quickly keeps small problems cheap to fix.

Complete content makes copies easier to spot. Accurate product pages with your own images and details are harder to pass off, and shoppers comparing listings will see the difference.

Advertising is part of the picture as well. Walmart Connect’s search ads let brands appear above copies on their own branded terms, and a brand that already defends those terms will notice quickly when a new seller starts bidding on its name. Branded search reports are often the first place an imitation shows up, before shoppers complain.

Pricing matters too. Unauthorized resellers often compete on price, which can drag a brand’s own listing below its intended price, so monitoring who sells your products, and at what price, protects both margin and the brand’s position. Walmart’s own tools help: brands should register with its brand protection programs where eligible and keep contact details current, so reports reach the right team quickly.

The same logic applies to Target Plus, which admits far fewer sellers, about 440 at the end of 2021 according to Marketplace Pulse. Curated marketplaces trade breadth for trust, and brands benefit most when they understand which side of that trade each marketplace has chosen.

The pull between selection and trust may tighten through 2022, because the fastest way for Walmart to add selection is to admit more sellers. Whether counterfeit complaints rise and enforcement lags, or Walmart keeps removing weak sellers as it adds new ones, will show whether the bar is holding. Watching the searches that matter to a brand every week, on every marketplace it sells through, is how we protect Walmart listings for the brands we work with.

A0235.crumb: Mercado Libre’s growth makes the case for…
A0235.title: Mercado Libre’s growth makes the case for Latin America now
A0235.alt: A yellow delivery scooter parked on a cobbled street lined with purple jacaranda trees and colonial buildings.
A0235.ttag: Mercado Libre’s growth makes the case for Latin America now | Kwontified
A0235.desc: Mercado Libre grew 31.6% in Q1 2022 while Amazon and Zalando slowed. Brands weighing expansion should look at Latin America now, with a staged test.
A0235.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 26, 2022.
A0235.body:
Set the big marketplaces’ first-quarter results for 2022 side by side and one line does not belong. Amazon’s international sales fell about 6%. Zalando’s gross merchandise volume rose just 1.0%. Mercado Libre’s grew 31.6% on a currency-neutral basis, while its delivery network and advertising business kept maturing in ways that make it cheaper for a brand to enter.

For brands weighing international expansion, that gap is the argument for looking at Latin America now. The sensible way in is a staged test in one country, using Mercado Libre’s own fulfillment and advertising, instead of waiting for growth in Europe or the U.S. to return.

What Mercado Libre’s growth looked like in Q1 2022

The numbers stand out against a slowing market. Mercado Libre’s gross merchandise volume reached $7.7 billion in the first quarter, up 31.6% on a currency-neutral basis, with almost 40 million unique buyers and nearly 267 million items sold, according to its results. Its ad revenue nearly doubled, and its fulfillment network handled nearly 40% of volume.

Growth has held up against tough comparisons. Gross merchandise volume has grown above 70% a year on a two-year compound basis, the company said on its earnings call, according to the transcript.

Elsewhere in the industry, growth has stalled. Zalando’s gross merchandise volume rose just 1.0% in the same quarter, according to its results. Amazon’s international sales fell about 6%, the Motley Fool reported.

Latin America runs on a different cycle, and entry costs less than it did

Sales are slowing at home, costs are rising and Europe looks weak, which makes a new region feel like the last thing a leadership team should take on. The case for Latin America rests on its running on a different cycle. Online shopping there started from a smaller base and is still being adopted. A brand that waits for its home market to recover before looking abroad may find that the best time to enter has passed, and that competitors have taken the positions it wanted.

The cost of entry has also fallen. Mercado Libre now delivers most orders through its own network, and stock held in its fulfillment centers reaches shoppers in under 24 hours on average, the company said on its previous earnings call, according to that transcript. A brand no longer needs to build local logistics to offer fast delivery. It needs to put stock in the right warehouse.

Payments belong to the same system. Mercado Libre’s payments arm processed $25.3 billion in the first quarter, up 81.2% on a currency-neutral basis, according to its results. Shoppers who already pay, borrow and save through the platform face little friction when they buy from a new brand there, which shortens the path from first visit to first order.

Mercado Libre’s advertising is maturing as well. With ad revenue nearly doubling, it is building the kind of sponsored search that brands already use on Amazon and Walmart. Early in a platform’s ad business, costs per click are often lower than they will be later, because fewer advertisers compete.

None of this removes the real difficulties. Each country has its own taxes, regulations and currency, prices change quickly where inflation is high, and Mercado Libre has said it is adjusting its installment pricing as interest rates rise in Brazil. Brands that treat Latin America as one market will be surprised.

Take a U.S. personal care brand that decides to test Mexico. It picks its eight best-selling products, registers locally through a partner, and sends stock into Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network. It runs sponsored product ads on its own brand name and two category searches, with a six-month budget it can afford to lose.

After six months, it knows its real costs per order, its return rate and which products travel. It also knows that two products need a local price point to compete. The decision on Brazil, the next and larger market, now rests on its own numbers.

Entering Latin America one country at a time

One country is enough to start. Brazil and Mexico are the region’s largest economies, but they differ in taxes, payment habits and regulation, so a brand learns more from doing one properly than from spreading thin across both.

Mercado Libre’s own services make a test affordable. Fulfillment and advertising on the platform let a brand gauge demand without building local operations, as long as the test is measured on contribution per order rather than on sales alone.

Currency and price need more attention than at home. Prices set in local currency need room to adjust and more frequent review, and installment costs belong in the price wherever shoppers expect to pay over time.

Success should be defined before the test starts: a target contribution per order, a return rate the brand can live with, and a minimum number of repeat buyers. If the test meets those marks, the next country follows. If it misses, the brand has learned cheaply.

Official stores deserve a look. Brand-owned stores accounted for more than 23% of Mercado Libre’s volume at the end of 2021, the company said, and they give shoppers confidence in authenticity, which matters for categories like beauty and electronics.

The calendar is local as well. Peak seasons differ from the U.S., and holidays such as Mexico’s Buen Fin shift demand in ways a U.S. calendar will miss, so a plan built on the local calendar avoids launching just after the moment shoppers were most ready to buy.

Mercado Libre’s second-quarter results will show whether growth holds above 30% while other markets slow, and if it does, the case for entering now gets stronger. A six-month test in one country, run on the platform’s own fulfillment and ads and judged on contribution per order, is how we help brands enter Latin America through Mercado Libre.

A0236.crumb: Amazon DSP off Amazon trades precise…
A0236.title: Amazon DSP off Amazon trades precise audiences for weaker proof
A0236.alt: A wooden recurve bow resting on a fence post in a misty meadow, with an archery target in the distance.
A0236.ttag: Amazon DSP off Amazon trades precise audiences for weaker proof | Kwontified
A0236.desc: Amazon DSP reaches Amazon shoppers on Fire TV, Freevee and Twitch, but its reports miss sales made elsewhere, so set up the holdout before you buy.
A0236.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 31, 2022.
A0236.body:
Take a furniture brand that sells mostly on its own site and through a few retailers, with a small Amazon presence. It buys Amazon DSP video on Fire TV and Freevee, aimed at shoppers Amazon identifies as having moved house or browsing home furnishings. A month later, Amazon’s report shows modest sales on Amazon itself, and the campaign looks weak. Yet most of the brand’s orders happen in places Amazon’s reporting cannot see.

That is the trade a brand makes when it takes Amazon DSP off Amazon. The audiences come from real shopping behavior and hold up well. The proof of what they did is partial. So the outcome has to be defined before the money is spent, and measured with the brand’s own test rather than Amazon’s attribution.

What Amazon DSP off Amazon can buy in 2022

Amazon DSP, the demand-side platform Amazon uses to sell display and video ads, now carries Amazon’s logged-in shoppers well beyond its store. Amazon’s advertising guide to Prime Day 2022 points advertisers to Freevee, Fire TV, live sports on Prime Video and Twitch. It adds that brands which do not sell on Amazon, automotive brands among them, also have an opportunity during the event, according to Amazon Ads.

Amazon is adding more inventory of its own. It renamed its free streaming service IMDb TV as Freevee on April 27, and its exclusive coverage of Thursday Night Football begins on September 15, according to its first-quarter results.

The measurement tools have grown alongside it. In October 2021, Amazon said it would extend Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC), its clean room for matching ad exposure to purchases, to all DSP customers, Modern Retail reported.

Targeting elsewhere has meanwhile lost ground. Meta said Apple’s privacy changes had blunted the accuracy of its ad targeting and made outcomes harder to measure, a hit it sized at about $10 billion in 2022 revenue, CNBC reported.

Amazon’s audiences hold up while its view of the sale shrinks

Amazon builds its audiences from what logged-in shoppers search for, browse and buy, and from what they watch on its streaming services. That signal does not depend on following people across other companies’ apps, so Apple’s changes touch it far less. A brand can reach people who bought a car seat in the past month, or who shop for running gear, while they watch a show on Fire TV.

Measurement runs the other way. Amazon’s reporting connects ad exposure to purchases on Amazon. For a brand that sells mostly there, the loop closes. When the sale happens on the brand’s own site, at Walmart or in a store, Amazon’s reports largely miss it. The ad may have worked, and the dashboard will not show it.

The further a brand’s sales sit from Amazon, the more the trade tilts. Audience quality stays high while the proof thins out. On balance the audiences are still worth buying, provided the measurement plan exists before the first impression, because without one the brand ends up judging a television campaign by a store it barely sells in.

The furniture brand, before launch, had held back a random tenth of its target audience from the ads, and afterward it compared the two groups. Visits to its own site and branded searches were clearly higher among those who saw the ads, and so were online orders from the regions it could match. The campaign worked. Amazon’s dashboard was simply watching the wrong checkout.

Buying Amazon DSP off Amazon with the test already designed

Deciding the outcome has to come before any buying. For a brand that sells mainly on Amazon, purchases on Amazon may be enough to judge the spend. For one that sells elsewhere, the outcome that matters might be site visits, sign-ups or sales in a region, and the plan has to say how the brand will see it.

A control group is the most reliable way to see effects outside Amazon’s reports. Withhold the ads from a random share of the audience, or from comparable regions, and compare the results of the two groups.

Amazon’s own data is what justifies the price. The audiences worth paying for are the ones only Amazon can build: recent purchasers in a category, people shopping for a life event, viewers of its own streaming services. Generic audiences can be bought more cheaply elsewhere.

Pricing needs the same discipline. Streaming TV ads cost more per thousand impressions than most display ads, and premium placements like live sports will cost more still. Each audience’s price is worth setting against what the same reach would cost on another platform.

Frequency needs a cap that covers every placement. Off Amazon, the same viewer can meet a brand’s ad on Fire TV, Freevee and partner sites in the same week. Without one cap across all of them, a campaign can spend heavily on a small group of people who have already seen the message, which looks like reach in the plan and like waste in the results.

AMC helps for sales on Amazon, but it does not see a brand’s own orders unless the brand brings its own data and analysis. Brands planning to rely on it should budget for that work.

How Amazon packages Thursday Night Football for advertisers will show how far this reaches. If it pairs shopping audiences with a large live sports audience, the trade between precise targeting and partial proof will matter to many more brands. The test for any of them is simple. When most of your sales happen away from Amazon, Amazon’s report should never be the only judge of Amazon DSP, and designing that holdout before launch is how we plan and run Amazon DSP for brands.

A0237.crumb: Prime Day 2022 planning needs one owner…
A0237.title: Prime Day 2022 planning needs one owner before the dates arrive
A0237.alt: Three paper-wrapped parcels tied with twine beside an open notebook with a brass key and a leather wallet on a desk.
A0237.ttag: Prime Day 2022 planning needs one owner before the dates arrive | Kwontified
A0237.desc: Amazon says Prime Day 2022 falls in July but has not named the days. Deal, stock and ad budget calls are due in June, so one person should make them all.
A0237.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 2, 2022.
A0237.body:
Amazon has told brands that Prime Day 2022 falls in July, and has not said which days. Inside a brand, that missing date does not pause the work so much as scatter it. E-commerce shortlists deals, finance prices the discounts, supply chain sizes the next shipment to Amazon and marketing drafts a budget, each team on its own calendar. The question in front of leadership is who gets to make those calls together, and the answer should be one person, named before the dates are.

Prime Day 2022 planning starts before Amazon names the dates

Amazon said on April 28 that Prime Day will take place in July in more than 20 countries, in its first-quarter results. It gave no dates. The event returns to its usual month after October 2020 and June 2021.

The stakes are familiar. Prime Day 2021 was the biggest two-day period ever for Amazon’s third-party sellers, and Prime members bought more than 250 million items, GeekWire reported. Adobe estimated that U.S. shoppers spent more than $11 billion online across all retailers during the two days.

Amazon is already courting advertisers for the event. Its advertising guide to Prime Day 2022 steers brands toward ads on Freevee, Fire TV and Twitch as well as inside its store.

The backdrop has changed since 2021. The Bureau of Labor Statistics measured an 8.3% rise in U.S. consumer prices over the year to April. Walmart and Target have both reported general merchandise piling up in their warehouses, so the summer may bring discounting well beyond Amazon.

Working backward from July, the deadlines are already here

Prime Day looks like a two-day event. For the teams behind it, it is a run of deadlines that starts weeks earlier. Deals have to be chosen and submitted in advance, and Amazon reviews them before they run. Stock has to reach Amazon’s warehouses before the event, and inbound shipments can take weeks to check in. Advertising budgets have to be approved, and click costs climb around the event: Marketplace Pulse found that cost per click on Amazon peaked during Prime Day and December in 2021, in its review of the year.

Count backward from a mid-July event and many of these calls land in early June, which means they are due now, while the dates are still unknown.

Four sensible team choices can still lose the best day

At many brands, nobody owns Prime Day outright. E-commerce picks the deals, finance approves the discount, supply chain decides what ships to Amazon and when, and marketing sets the advertising budget. Each team makes a reasonable choice by its own measures, often in its own meeting and on its own timeline.

Those choices depend on each other in ways the org chart does not show. A deep discount on a product that runs out of stock on the first morning wastes both the discount and the ads that point to it. A large ad budget behind shallow deals buys clicks that do not convert. A product sent to Amazon in bulk with no deal and no ads may sit there until autumn, paying storage fees. None of these failures appears in one team’s report; each lives in the gap between two of them.

Take a kitchenware brand whose e-commerce lead picks a 25% deal on its best-selling skillet, its most searched product. Finance approves the deal, and marketing doubles the daily ad budget for the two days. Supply chain, meanwhile, has been told to bring inventory down after a slow spring, and sends Amazon its normal June shipment, sized for an ordinary month.

By midday on the first day, the skillet has sold through its stock. The ads keep running for hours, sending shoppers to a page that says the product is unavailable, and the brand pays for clicks that cannot convert. The skillet also loses the sales momentum that might have lifted its ranking in the weeks after. Every team did its job, and the brand still lost the event’s best day for its best product.

What leadership is really deciding is who holds the authority

More meetings will not close those gaps. The real decision is whether to hand one person authority over deals, stock, budget and timing together, including the duty to say no when they do not fit. That person need not make every call alone. They need to see the whole picture and settle conflicts quickly: if the deal needs more stock, they can ask for it, and if the stock cannot arrive, they can shrink the deal or move it to another product.

In smaller brands, the owner is often the head of e-commerce. In larger ones, it may be a general manager for Amazon. The title matters less than the authority, because someone who can only recommend will watch each team defend its own choice.

With that authority in one place, the pieces start to fit. The products in the event should be the ones that can carry a deal, with healthy margins, enough stock and good reviews, since a deal on a product with weak reviews brings shoppers who do not buy. Depth is a judgment about the year. Deeper deals sell more units, but they also teach shoppers to hold out for the next discount, and in 2022, with other retailers likely to discount excess stock, a modest deal may look less special than it did in 2021.

Stock should be enough to last the event with a margin, tracked by the date a shipment arrives at Amazon rather than the date it leaves the dock, because a shipment that arrives late is as good as one never sent. The budget should allow for higher click costs on the days themselves and in the days just before, when competitors start spending, and it should follow the products that have deals and stock rather than the 2021 total.

When Amazon announces the dates, the calendar will tighten or loosen. A date early in July leaves less time for stock to arrive; a date later in the month gives brands room, and gives other retailers more time to plan competing events. Whichever it is, the owner should already be in the chair, and building that single plan across deals, inventory and advertising is how we help brands prepare for Prime Day.

A0239.crumb: Off-site retail media sells a retailer’s…
A0239.title: Off-site retail media sells a retailer’s data, not its shelf
A0239.alt: A padlocked wooden card-file box beside a wire basket of bread, greens, fruit and a jar on a shop counter.
A0239.ttag: Off-site retail media sells a retailer’s data, not its shelf | Kwontified
A0239.desc: Walmart and Kroger now sell shopper data for ads across the web, but each report sees only its own shelf, so judge off-site retail media on total sales.
A0239.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 7, 2022.
A0239.body:
A cereal brand can now ask a retailer to find the households that bought a rival cereal in the previous month and show them a video ad during a streaming show. Weeks later, the retailer’s report comes back with the sales it saw. It saw only the ones rung up in its own stores and on its own site. A shopper the ad persuaded could have bought anywhere.

That is the catch in off-site retail media. The retailer is selling its data, not its shelf, and its closed-loop report covers only the slice of the effect that lands at that retailer. The bigger that retailer is in a brand’s sales, the more of the truth the report shows. So brands should buy off-site media from the retailers where their sales concentrate, and judge it on total sales across channels.

Off-site retail media in 2022: Walmart and Kroger sell their data beyond their sites

Walmart launched Walmart DSP in August 2021, built with The Trade Desk, Retail Dive reported. It gives advertisers access to inventory across display, streaming, mobile, audio and connected TV, and draws on shopping data from Walmart’s website, app and 4,700 stores. Walmart pitched its ability to connect ads to sales in stores and online as what set it apart from other platforms.

Kroger followed. On October 20, 2021, Kroger Precision Marketing launched the Kroger Private Marketplace, Supermarket News reported. Brands can apply Kroger audience data to campaigns in the ad-buying platform they already use, and optimize against actual retail sales. Kroger’s data arm, 84.51°, says its data covers nearly one in two U.S. households.

The businesses behind these offers are growing. Walmart said growth in Walmart Connect was strong in its first quarter, on its earnings call. The alternatives have weakened over the same stretch: Meta, describing less accurate targeting and harder measurement since Apple’s privacy changes, expected a hit of about $10 billion to its 2022 revenue, CNBC reported.

Retailer data improves targeting, but the report covers one store’s share

The two halves of the product behave differently. Targeting is the strong half. A retailer knows what its shoppers bought, in stores and online, tied to a loyalty card or an account. That is a sturdier signal than the browsing patterns most ad platforms rely on, and it does not depend on tracking people across apps. The cereal brand reaches households that actually bought a rival cereal, not just people who read about breakfast.

Measurement is the narrow half. The retailer can see whether the people who saw the ad later bought the product in its own stores or on its own site, and that closed loop is real. But the ad ran on the open web, away from any shelf. The shopper it persuaded might buy at Walmart, or at Target, at Costco, on Amazon or on the brand’s own site. The retailer’s report sees only its own share.

So the part of the effect a report can see tracks the part of the brand’s sales that run through that retailer. Take a brand that sells 60% of its volume through Walmart: Walmart’s report sees most of what the campaign did. If the same brand sold 15% there, the report would see a small slice, and the campaign would look weaker than it is.

The error also runs the other way. A retailer’s report credits sales from shoppers who would have bought anyway. Off-site campaigns aimed at a retailer’s own past buyers are especially prone to this, because those buyers return regardless of the ad.

A Kroger campaign judged by Kroger’s report and by total sales

Take a snack brand that sells about 20% of its volume through Kroger, and the rest across other grocers, mass retailers and Amazon. It runs a Kroger off-site campaign on streaming video, aimed at households that buy competing snacks. After six weeks, Kroger’s report shows a modest lift in Kroger sales, and on that evidence alone the campaign looks like a poor return.

The brand, however, had held back a set of comparable regions from the campaign. Comparing total sales in the exposed regions with the held-back ones, across every retailer it sells through, it found a lift several times larger than Kroger’s report suggested. Most of the extra sales happened at other stores, which Kroger’s report was never built to count.

Buy where your sales concentrate and judge on total sales

The retailer’s data is strongest for its own shoppers, and its report covers more of the effect when more of a brand’s sales run through it. For a brand that sells mostly through Walmart, Walmart DSP is a natural fit. For a brand spread thin across many retailers, any one closed loop will undercount.

Judging a campaign therefore takes more than the retailer’s report. Regional holdouts or matched markets give the fuller answer, with sales compared across every channel the brand can see, including its own site and syndicated data where it has them. Retailers can also be asked to separate new buyers from repeat ones, and the new buyers deserve more weight.

Price belongs in the same test. Retailer data adds to the cost of each impression, and it is worth paying for only if it reaches buyers that cheaper targeting would miss. Comparing the cost per thousand impressions with and without the retailer’s data, then checking whether the difference shows up in sales, answers that.

Until retailers begin to share results across one another, through clean rooms or industry measurement standards, each report will show only its own slice. The rule for now: before reading a retailer’s off-site report, look up that retailer’s share of your sales, because that share is roughly how much of the campaign the report can see. Measuring the rest across channels is how we run and measure off-site retail media for brands.

A0241.crumb: Home and kitchen on Amazon shifts from…
A0241.title: Home and kitchen on Amazon shifts from setting up to replacing
A0241.alt: A worn, seasoned frying pan next to a shiny new stainless steel pan on a gas stovetop in a kitchen.
A0241.ttag: Home and kitchen on Amazon shifts from setting up to replacing | Kwontified
A0241.desc: Households equipped their homes in 2020 and 2021. In 2022 home and kitchen demand on Amazon is about replacing, so brands should sell the next purchase.
A0241.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 9, 2022.
A0241.body:
For two years, the kitchen was where the money went. People cooking every meal, working from the kitchen table and staying in bought pans, mixers, storage, desks and furniture, much of it online. In 2022 the same households are back on Amazon looking for a replacement lid, a larger stockpot or an attachment for the mixer already on the counter.

That is the shift in home and kitchen on Amazon. Households that equipped their homes in 2020 and 2021 now buy to replace and maintain, and food inflation is pulling money away from general merchandise at the same time. Brands in the category should move their range, product pages and advertising toward the next purchase a household will make, rather than chase first-time buyers who have mostly bought.

Home and kitchen on Amazon in 2022: the setup rush is over

Wayfair gives the clearest view. Its active customers fell 23.4% from a year earlier, to 25.4 million, according to its first-quarter results, even as its chief executive said shoppers were still interested in the home category.

The detail underneath is more telling. Orders per Wayfair customer fell to 1.87 from 1.98, while repeat customers placed 77.7% of orders, up from 74.5%, Home Textiles Today reported. Fewer new people are arriving, and the ones who stay are the ones who already bought.

The big general retailers are seeing the same thing. Target’s customers moved spending away from apparel basics, home goods and electronics, Modern Retail reported. Walmart said food inflation had pulled more dollars away from general merchandise than it expected, according to its earnings call transcript. Food bought for the home cost 10.8% more in April than a year earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said.

Amazon does not report sales by category, so its home business cannot be measured directly. Its shoppers, though, are the same households, facing the same prices at the checkout.

The drop reads better as a change in what households need

It is tempting to call the drop in home sales a slowdown. It is closer to a change in what households are shopping for.

A household that bought a full cookware set in 2020 does not need another one. Over the next few years it needs a replacement lid, a larger stockpot, a better knife, a cleaner that will not scratch the coating. A household that bought a stand mixer needs attachments, not a second mixer. That demand is smaller per order and more frequent, and it is tied to what the household already owns, so the shopper often searches for the brand she bought, or for a product that fits it.

Take a cookware brand whose sales of its ten-piece set fell sharply in early 2022. Its team raises bids on its most competitive search terms, such as “cookware set,” and costs rise while sales do not recover. A closer look shows that sales of single replacement pans, lids and the brand’s own cleaning product are steady or growing, mostly from shoppers who search for the brand by name. The best customers are still buying. They are buying different things.

The reason the bids went up first sits in how the brand plans. Its year was built around the set, which carried the photography, the launch budget, the forecast and the best placement in the brand store. Lids and single pans sat at the bottom of the catalog as support items with thin pages. When demand moved to those support items, the plan, the content and the budget were all still pointed at the set.

So the team moves budget from set-level terms to its replacement items and to ads shown to its past buyers. Total sales still sit below the 2021 peak, but the advertising cost per sale comes down and repeat orders grow.

Selling the next purchase instead of the first

The range is where that work starts. Replacement parts, accessories, upgrades and consumables are the products a household that bought in 2020 will search for in 2022, and if the brand does not offer them, a generic seller will.

Those products then have to be easy to match to what the shopper owns. Accessory pages should say clearly which models they fit, and brand stores on Amazon should group products by what a customer owns, not only by category. A shopper looking for a replacement lid wants to know within seconds that it fits her pan, the way she would hold a lid up to the pot in a store aisle.

Advertising belongs with the owners. Brand-name searches and audiences of past buyers are where much of the 2022 demand sits, while generic category terms, where every seller with excess stock is bidding, are the most expensive place to compete.

Freight costs point the same way. Target said fuel and freight costs ran about $1 billion higher than expected in its first quarter, Bloomberg reported. Full sets and furniture are bulky and cost the most to move, while lids and attachments are small and cheap to ship, so a range that leans toward smaller products helps margin as well as demand.

First-time buyers have not disappeared. People still move house, marry, have children and set up homes, and some of them start on Amazon. They are a smaller share of the market than they were in 2020, though, and they are the share every competitor is fighting over.

Prime Day in July should make the change visible. If sets and big-ticket items need deep discounts to sell while accessories hold their price, the move from setting up to replacing will show on the deals page itself. Planning the range and advertising around that next purchase is how we run home and kitchen brands on Amazon.

A0242.crumb: Amazon Marketing Cloud first steps: match…
A0242.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud first steps: match numbers you trust
A0242.alt: Two brass-framed hourglasses with sand settled at the bottom on a rustic wooden shelf against a pink wall.
A0242.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud first steps: match numbers you trust | Kwontified
A0242.desc: New Amazon Marketing Cloud users should first rebuild numbers they trust from console reports. The gaps show how AMC counts before it answers anything new.
A0242.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 14, 2022.
A0242.body:
Take a brand whose analyst, in her first week with Amazon Marketing Cloud, pulls last quarter’s DSP-attributed purchases and gets a figure 12% below the one in Amazon’s console. The instinct is to ask which number is wrong, and usually the answer is neither, because AMC and the console count the same campaigns by different rules.

That is why a team’s first queries in AMC should reproduce numbers it already trusts. The gaps that turn up, from attribution windows to results withheld for privacy, are the rules every later answer depends on. A team that skips this step will act on new answers it cannot yet read correctly.

Amazon Marketing Cloud first steps in 2022: access is wider than skill

Amazon introduced Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC) in beta in January 2021, describing it on its advertising blog as a secure, privacy-safe environment where advertisers can analyze their campaigns and get back only aggregated, anonymous results. In October 2021, Amazon said it would open the service to all of its DSP customers, Modern Retail reported.

So many more brands now have an AMC instance than have used one. The service works through SQL queries against event-level data. A new user gets a blank workspace and a library of starter queries, not a dashboard.

The calendar raises the stakes. Prime Day falls in July, and Amazon’s advertising guide to the event encourages brands to combine sponsored ads with DSP across Fire TV, Freevee and Twitch. Many teams will want AMC to tell them how those channels worked together, they will want the answer quickly, and they will be tempted to skip the groundwork.

Why AMC and the console disagree

AMC and Amazon’s console reports describe the same campaigns but count them differently. A first-time user who expects them to match will be confused. One who expects a gap, and knows where it comes from, is ready to use AMC. The gaps come from attribution, aggregation and scope.

Source of the gapConsole reportAMCEffect on a familiar number
AttributionApplies Amazon’s standard rules on which purchases an ad gets credit for, and over how many daysThe analyst writes the window and the credit rule into the queryA longer window, or credit only for the last ad seen, gives a different total
AggregationShows every rowReturns only aggregated results; groups that are too small drop outTotals split by many small segments can look short
ScopeOne campaign type at a timeCan combine sponsored ads and DSP eventsA shopper may count once in AMC and twice across two console reports

None of these is an error. A query with a different window answers a different question, and the team needs to know which question it is asking. Rows missing for privacy are a protection built into the service, not a fault in the data. Totals that should add up across channels often do not, because AMC is counting a shopper the console reports count twice. Each difference is predictable, and none is visible until the team sees it on a number it already knows.

The analyst in the opening checks her window first and finds it was shorter than the console’s. She widens it, and the gap closes to 2%. The rest comes from small segments withheld for privacy.

She now knows two rules she will need for every query that follows. Had she started instead with a new question, such as how many Prime Day buyers saw both a DSP ad and a sponsored ad, she would have had no way to tell whether the answer was right.

Reconcile first, then let the starter queries teach the rest

Reconciling comes first. Pick two or three figures the brand already trusts, such as impressions and attributed purchases for one DSP campaign in one month. Reproduce them in AMC, and write down every difference and its cause. A gap that survives every setting the team can change deserves a question to Amazon before anyone builds on it, because an unexplained difference is the one entry the record should never close by assumption.

That record becomes the team’s guide to reading AMC. Keep it short and specific: the figure, the console value, the AMC value, the cause of the gap and the setting that closed it. A new analyst who joins in six months should be able to read it in ten minutes and avoid repeating the same mistakes.

Amazon’s instructional queries are the next step. They cover common questions, such as reach and frequency or how channels overlap. Running them on the brand’s own data, with the reconciliation notes at hand, shows the team how the answers are built before it writes its own.

New questions come last, one at a time, each tied to a decision. “How many Prime Day buyers saw both channels” is useful only if the answer will change how the budget is split for the next event. Questions without a decision attached fill the workspace without changing anything.

Staffing matters as much as sequence. AMC needs an analyst who writes SQL, understands advertising and has time set aside for it. A marketer who borrows an engineer for an afternoon will get queries that run, but not answers the team can defend.

As Amazon adds more ad types and pre-built queries to AMC, each addition will widen what the service can answer and bring new counting rules with it. The rule that holds through all of them is to make AMC reproduce an old number before trusting a new one, and starting from that reconciliation is how we set up Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands.
