A0244.title: Post-pandemic ecommerce habits that stuck save shoppers time
A0244.alt: A paper shopping bag, a shipping box and a brass hourglass on a hallway table near the front door.
A0244.ttag: Post-pandemic ecommerce habits that stuck save shoppers time | Kwontified
A0244.desc: Online shopping kept most of its pandemic gains in 2022. The habits that stuck are the ones that save time, so plan for pickup and repeat orders.
A0244.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 16, 2022.
A0244.body:
Pull into the Drive Up spaces outside a Target store and the habit is plain to see. A car waits, the trunk opens, an order goes in, and the shopper never walks an aisle. Lockdowns taught that routine. It has outlasted them, while many of the things people bought online during those months have not been bought again.

Online shopping has kept most of its pandemic gains in 2022, but not all of them. Shoppers kept the habits that save them time, such as ordering for pickup and reordering staples online, and dropped the ones that only made sense while they were stuck at home. Brands should plan around convenience and repeat purchase, rather than for a return to 2019 or a resumption of 2020’s growth.

Post-pandemic ecommerce habits in 2022: most of the gain held

The numbers describe a market that settled rather than reversed. Before the pandemic, e-commerce made up 11.4% of U.S. retail sales, and in the second quarter of 2020 it jumped to 15.7%, the Census Bureau reported. In the first quarter of 2022 the share was 14.3%, slightly below 14.5% in the fourth quarter of 2021, GlobeSt reported. Most of the jump has held. The peak has not.

Spending is also moving from goods to experiences. In May, the Bureau of Labor Statistics found airline fares 37.8% higher than twelve months before. Sales at online stores fell 1.0% in May while sales at bars and restaurants rose 0.7%, Reuters reported.

What brands need to know is which online habits shoppers kept, and why they kept them.

The habits that stuck are the ones that save time

The first-quarter results from the big retailers point the same way: shoppers held on to what saves them time and let go of what only replaced going out.

Pickup is the clearest case. Target said its same-day services, including Order Pickup, Drive Up and Shipt, grew 8% in its first quarter, with Drive Up growing in the mid-teens on top of more than 120% a year earlier, Drug Store News reported. Shoppers who learned to have an order loaded into the car during lockdowns still use it, because it is faster than walking the aisles.

Walmart shows the same pattern from the other side. Its U.S. e-commerce sales were up 38% on a two-year basis in the first quarter, Supermarket News reported, even as growth over the single year slowed to about 1%. The online grocery and household orders that shoppers adopted in 2020 have largely stayed.

Reordering is the other habit that held. A shopper who found that a favorite coffee or detergent could arrive on a schedule, or with two taps, has little reason to stop. These purchases are frequent, predictable and dull, which is why they suit online so well. Nobody misses the trip to buy paper towels, and once the order is set up, changing it takes more effort than keeping it.

The habits that faded worked differently, because they replaced going out rather than saving time. Shoppers bought home gym equipment instead of going to the gym, and kitchen gadgets instead of going to restaurants. When the gyms and restaurants reopened, much of that demand went back to them.

Take a shopper who, in 2020, ordered groceries for delivery every week, bought a desk and a monitor online, and ordered takeout through an app most nights. By mid-2022 she still orders groceries online, now for pickup on her way home. She has not bought another desk, and she eats out more and orders takeout less. Her online spending has fallen from its peak, but it sits well above where it was in 2019, and it is concentrated in what she buys every week.

Planning for convenience and repeat purchase

Forecasts are the first thing to rebuild. Neither 2019 nor 2020 is coming back. A forecast that assumes online sales will fall to pre-pandemic levels will understock, and one that assumes pandemic growth will resume will overstock, as several large retailers found in May.

Investment belongs where the time-saving habits live. For products bought often, that means subscription options, easy reordering and good availability for pickup at retailers that offer it. Product pages should make it obvious that a product can be collected the same day, or delivered on a schedule.

Advertising follows the same logic. Shoppers who reorder search for the brand by name or go straight to their past orders, so budget that once chased new buyers in a growing channel may work harder protecting those repeat purchases from rivals bidding on the brand’s name. At retailers that offer pickup, ads that show local availability reach the shopper at the moment she plans her trip.

Products that rode the substitution wave need a harder look. Equipment and gadgets that stood in for going out may need a new reason to buy, such as replacement parts, upgrades or a different customer, rather than more advertising behind the old message. The honest test is whether a shopper who already owns the product has a reason to buy again in 2022. If not, the product’s growth now depends on new households, and the plan should say so.

The e-commerce share for the second quarter will be the next reading. If it holds near 14% while spending moves to services, the habits that stuck are durable, and if it falls further, some of what looked like habit was still the pandemic. Building channel and range plans around the week-to-week routine rather than 2020’s spike is how we help brands plan for the way shoppers buy now.

A0246.crumb: Prime Day 2022 forecast: three cases for…
A0246.title: Prime Day 2022 forecast: three cases for sales, clicks and deals
A0246.alt: Three vases of mixed wildflowers, roses and poppies on a wooden windowsill against a pale blue wall.
A0246.ttag: Prime Day 2022 forecast: three cases for sales, clicks and deals | Kwontified
A0246.desc: Prime Day 2022 runs July 12 and 13 amid inflation and swollen inventories. Forecast sales lift, click costs and deal share as three linked cases.
A0246.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 21, 2022.
A0246.body:
A Prime Day forecast usually arrives as one number: what the brand expects to sell over the two days. That number hides the two others that decide whether the event makes money, what the traffic will cost and how much of the volume will go out at a discount. In 2022, with inflation high, early deals starting weeks ahead and retailers clearing excess stock, those numbers can move in ways a single figure cannot show.

So the Prime Day 2022 forecast should be built as three cases, conservative, standard and reach, each a consistent set of assumptions for sales lift, cost per click and deal share. Writing the assumptions down lets a team see which case is arriving while there is still time to act.

The Prime Day 2022 forecast starts from different conditions

Amazon will hold Prime Day on July 12 and 13, with early deals for members from June 21, Fortune reported. For third-party sellers on Amazon, the 2021 event was the biggest two-day period they had ever had, GeekWire reported, and Adobe put U.S. online spending across all retailers over those two days at more than $11 billion.

Prices are higher this time. Consumer prices in the U.S. were 8.6% higher over the year to May, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said, its largest annual increase since 1981. Shoppers have less to spend on discretionary goods, and more reason to wait for a deal.

Demand for goods is softening. Sales at online stores fell 1.0% in May, Reuters reported, and large retailers reported swollen inventories in May, Modern Retail reported. Brands should expect more discounting around the event, on Amazon and off it.

Clicks cost more as well. Amazon’s cost per click climbed 43% over 2021, with its highest points around Prime Day and in December, according to Marketplace Pulse.

Sales lift, click costs and deal share move together

Sales lift is how much each event day sells compared with an ordinary day. Cost per click is what the brand pays for traffic during the event. Deal share is the portion of event sales sold at a discount.

A single sales number feels safer because it is easy to share upward and easy to hold a team to. It fails because the drivers are linked. When competitors discount heavily, a brand’s deals sell more units, but more of its sales come at a lower price, and more sellers bid for the same shoppers, so clicks cost more. When demand is weak, sales lift falls, and so does bidding pressure. Each case therefore has to be a consistent set, and a forecast that pairs high sales lift with low click costs is usually wishful thinking.

Deal share deserves more attention than it usually gets. Sales lift measures revenue, but a dollar sold at a 30% discount earns far less than a dollar sold at full price, so two events with the same sales can leave very different profit behind. Forecasting deal share forces the team to say, before the event, how much margin it will give up for volume.

Take a brand whose ordinary July day sells $10,000 on Amazon. The cases below show the method, not market data, and each brand should build its own from its history.

CaseAssumptionEach event day vs an ordinary dayCost per click vs June averageShare of event sales on deal
ConservativeWeak demand; early deals pull sales forward into late Juneabout 2.5 timesabout 20% higherabout 70%
StandardDemand close to 2021, adjusted for inflationabout 3.5 timesabout 35% higherabout 55%
ReachShoppers who held back in the spring spend during the eventabout 5 timesabout 50% higherabout 45%

In the conservative case the brand discounts to keep pace, which is why its deal share is the highest. In the reach case every competitor bids harder, which pushes click costs up, while demand is strong enough that full-price products sell too, which pulls deal share down.

That makes the reach case less attractive than it looks. Its higher sales arrive with the highest click costs, and for a product with thin margins the extra traffic can cost more than the extra units return. A brand that ranks its cases by revenue will prefer the reach case. Ranked by profit, the standard case can come out ahead, which is why the cases need margin attached before anyone celebrates a big lift.

Writing the assumptions down and watching them

The assumptions belong on paper before the event. The team should agree in advance what each case expects for early-deal sales, click costs in the week before and the share of sales on deal.

Early deals then work as a test. Sales from June 21 onward show which case is taking shape. If early-deal sales run strong and click costs hold, the brand can add budget. If early deals sell weakly while click costs climb, it can protect margin by holding back.

Stock and budget should be set for the standard case, with a plan for the others. Ship enough stock to cover the standard case with a margin, hold back part of the budget, and release it only if the reach case appears.

Click costs in the week of July 4 will give the earliest clear reading. If they already run well above June, bidding pressure is following the reach case, whatever sales do. The rule for the event is never to let the sales case set the bid budget on its own, and building all three cases from a brand’s own history is how we forecast and run Prime Day on Amazon.

A0248.crumb: Mercado Envíos Full rewards fast sellers…
A0248.title: Mercado Envíos Full rewards fast sellers and charges slow ones
A0248.alt: Cobweb-covered boxes on a pallet beside a roller conveyor and yellow bins in a sunlit old warehouse.
A0248.ttag: Mercado Envíos Full rewards fast sellers and charges slow ones | Kwontified
A0248.desc: Mercado Envíos Full lifts conversion and ranking on Mercado Libre, but storage fees now start on arrival. Send the products that sell fast and hold the rest.
A0248.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 23, 2022.
A0248.body:
Put two listings side by side on Mercado Libre: the same product, the same price, the same photos. One of them carries a promise that it arrives tomorrow, because the stock already sits in Mercado Libre’s own warehouse. Mercado Libre says listings like that one typically convert better and, over time, are better rated and ranked. That promise is what Mercado Envíos Full sells to brands.

In 2022 it comes with a new cost. Mercado Libre now charges storage fees from the moment inventory arrives, so Full rewards products that sell quickly and charges the ones that do not. Brands should send their fast sellers, keep slow movers on their own shipping and earn the rest of the catalog in, rather than move everything at once.

Mercado Envíos Full in 2022: speed is the product

Fulfillment handled nearly 40% of Mercado Libre’s shipping volume in the first quarter, and its managed network carries more than 90% of volumes in the region, the company said in its first-quarter letter to shareholders. Almost 55% of shipments arrived on the same or the next day after purchase, with record shipping times in Mexico and Chile.

The company was direct about why Full matters to sellers. Items it fulfills have the fastest shipping on its network, it said, and sellers on fulfillment typically see better conversion because of the better delivery promise.

It is also investing to extend that speed. Mercado Libre announced a $1.48 billion investment in Mexico in 2022 to strengthen its logistics network, Mexico Business News reported.

The same letter carried a change sellers should not miss. Mercado Libre began charging merchants storage fees for fulfillment from the moment inventory arrives, describing the move as a test of its pricing power for the service, and it said Mexico is its most mature market for fulfillment.

Who gains from the delivery promise

The storage fee shows where the value in Full now sits. Mercado Libre has spent heavily to make next-day delivery the default its shoppers expect, and every fulfilled order strengthens that network and the habit behind it. With storage charged from arrival, the platform also earns on each unit while it waits on a shelf. The seller gains only when the unit sells. That split is a reasonable price for the service, but it leaves the seller carrying the risk of choosing the wrong products.

Delivery speed carries more weight in Latin America than many brands expect, and the reason is trust. Many Latin American shoppers grew up with slow and uncertain delivery, and some still treat an online order as a risk. A promise that the product arrives tomorrow, made by Mercado Libre itself, removes much of that doubt. Buyers who might have compared five listings choose the one that arrives first.

Ranking compounds the effect, because Mercado Libre rewards listings that sell and earn good ratings. Faster delivery brings more sales and fewer complaints about late orders, so a product in Full climbs, and once it climbs it gets more traffic, which brings more sales.

That loop only turns if the product sells. A product sitting in a Full warehouse gains nothing from the delivery promise, and now costs money every day it waits.

Take two kitchenware brands entering Mexico with the same 40 products. The first sends its whole range into Full at launch. Its ten best sellers climb quickly and sell through within weeks. The other 30 sell slowly, and three months later most of their stock is still in the warehouse, accruing fees.

The second brand sends only its ten strongest products into Full and ships the rest itself. Its best sellers climb just as quickly. Its slow movers sell at the same pace as before but cost nothing to store, and it adds products to Full one at a time, as each proves it can sell.

Sending the fast sellers and earning the rest in

Speed of sale should decide entry, not how much the brand wants a product to sell. The place to start is with proven sellers, from another market or from the brand’s own shipping on Mercado Libre, because a product’s speed of sale is the best predictor of whether Full will pay.

Shipment size follows from the fee. With storage charged from arrival, smaller and more frequent shipments of a few weeks of demand cost less than one shipment sized for a season, even if they take more planning. Weeks of stock per product in Full is the number to watch, and shipments should slow for any product that builds a backlog.

The list itself should keep moving in both directions. A product that sells well on the brand’s own shipping is a candidate for Full, and a product in Full that stops selling should come back out before its fees outweigh its gains. A monthly review keeps that discipline.

Cash deserves the same attention as fees. Stock in a Full warehouse is stock the brand has already paid to make, ship across borders and clear through customs. A catalog moved into Full all at once ties up that cash in products that may take months to sell, while starting small keeps money free for the products that prove they can move, and for the advertising that helps them climb.

Mexico deserves particular care. As the most mature fulfillment market, it is where the delivery advantage is clearest and competition for fast shipping strongest, and a brand without Full there competes against rivals who have it.

How Mercado Libre prices storage through the rest of 2022 will show how wide the gap becomes. The company has called the fees a test of its pricing power, and if they rise, the distance between fast and slow sellers in Full will widen. Deciding what belongs in Full, product by product, is part of how we launch and run brands on Mercado Libre.

A0249.title: Sponsored Display audiences: what they buy and what they borrow
A0249.alt: A wicker basket of honey jars, mugs and rolled linen beside an empty tagged basket on a wooden table by a window.
A0249.ttag: Sponsored Display audiences: what they buy and what they borrow | Kwontified
A0249.desc: Sponsored Display remarketing borrows sales other ads would win, while in-market audiences buy new demand. Judge each type by a different measure.
A0249.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 28, 2022.
A0249.body:
Take a brand that splits $10,000 a month across two kinds of Sponsored Display audiences. Its views remarketing reports a return of 6 to 1. Its in-market audiences report 2 to 1. On the dashboard, the case for moving everything to remarketing looks obvious, and the holdout test the brand runs next shows why it is not.

Sponsored Display audiences come in two kinds that behave differently. Remarketing reaches shoppers who already viewed or bought a product, while in-market and lifestyle audiences reach shoppers who have not. Remarketing borrows sales that organic listings and other ads would often have won. Prospecting buys new demand that looks weaker on reported returns. Budgets should be split by audience type, and each type judged on its own measure.

Sponsored Display audiences in 2022: remarketing and prospecting in one tool

Amazon launched Sponsored Display audiences in the United States in November 2020 with views remarketing, which reaches shoppers who viewed specific product pages in the past 30 days but did not buy the advertised product, according to its announcement. The targeting draws on Amazon’s own shopping signals.

In April 2021, Amazon added its pre-built audiences, which group shoppers by interests, lifestyle, life stage and what they are shopping for now, Intentwise reported. In October 2021, it added purchases remarketing, which reaches past buyers to encourage repeat purchases, along with custom lookback windows for both remarketing types, according to its launch notice.

On June 23, Amazon made Sponsored Display engagement and conversion signals available in Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC), alongside the Sponsored Products and DSP signals already there, according to a separate notice. For the first time, brands with AMC can see how Sponsored Display audiences overlap with their other ads.

Remarketing returns are high because the audience was already buying

The two families differ in who they reach before any ad runs. Remarketing audiences are selected for intent. A shopper who viewed a product page in the past few days, or bought the product before, is far more likely to buy than an average shopper, ad or no ad, so remarketing campaigns report high returns. Some of those sales are new. Some would have come anyway, through a search, a Sponsored Products ad or the shopper’s order history.

That second group is the borrowed share. The ad touched the sale and the report credits it, but the sale would have happened without it. Picture a shop assistant who greets every customer already queuing at the till and is credited with each sale. The more a campaign concentrates on recent viewers and past buyers, the larger the borrowed share is likely to be.

Prospecting audiences work the other way. In-market and lifestyle audiences reach shoppers who have not engaged with the brand. Fewer of them buy, so reported returns look weaker, but more of the sales they do produce are new, because those shoppers were not on their way to the product.

The brand in the opening tests this directly. It holds out a random share of its remarketing audience for a month, and shoppers in the held-out group buy at nearly the same rate as those who saw the ads, so most of the 6 to 1 was borrowed. A similar test on in-market audiences shows a smaller reported return but a clear gap between the exposed and held-out groups. Those ads were creating demand.

The same test is what would change the conclusion. Had the held-out remarketing group bought at a clearly lower rate than the exposed group, most of the 6 to 1 would have been earned, and the case for shifting budget toward remarketing would stand.

Remarketing still earns a place. Some shoppers who viewed a product would have bought a rival’s instead, and an ad can win them back. What the dashboard cannot say is how many.

Split the budget by audience type and judge each on its own measure

Remarketing and prospecting belong in separate campaigns with separate budgets. Mixed campaigns let the high reported returns of remarketing hide the weaker reported returns of prospecting, and the budget drifts toward the audiences that borrow the most.

The measures differ as well. For remarketing, use lift: hold out a share of the audience, or compare against periods without the campaign, and count only the difference. For prospecting, track the share of sales from new-to-brand customers, and accept a lower reported return in exchange.

AMC is where the overlap becomes countable. With Sponsored Display signals now in AMC, a brand can see how many remarketing conversions came from shoppers who also clicked a Sponsored Products ad or searched for the brand. That overlap is a direct measure of how much is borrowed.

Purchases remarketing needs its own judgment. For a product people reorder, such as a supplement or a pet food, past buyers often return on their own schedule, through their order history or a subscription, and ads to them borrow heavily. For a brand with several products, the same audience can be valuable for selling something new. An ad for a different product to a past buyer is far less likely to be borrowed than an ad for the product she already reorders.

The lookback window changes the borrowed share as well. A shorter window concentrates remarketing on the most recent viewers, who are the most likely to buy anyway. A longer window reaches shoppers who have drifted, where an ad has more room to change the outcome.

As brands run the new AMC queries through the second half of 2022, the size of that overlap will become clearer, and if it proves high, budgets should shift toward prospecting. The working rule is that the closer an audience already is to buying, the more proof its reported return needs, and running that proof is how we plan and measure Sponsored Display for brands.

A0250.crumb: Instagram vs marketplace CAC: count who…
A0250.title: Instagram vs marketplace CAC: count who keeps the customer
A0250.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a smartphone against a small paper shopping bag on a wooden table.
A0250.ttag: Instagram vs marketplace CAC: count who keeps the customer | Kwontified
A0250.desc: Instagram ads can hand a brand a customer it keeps, while marketplace ads sell to searchers the marketplace keeps. Price the customer kept for a year.
A0250.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 30, 2022.
A0250.body:
Put two numbers side by side on a budget slide. Marketing brings a cost per new customer from Instagram, the marketplace team brings a cost per order from Amazon, and the slide treats them as rival prices for the same thing. An Instagram ad finds a shopper who was not yet looking and can turn her into the brand’s own customer. A marketplace ad sells to a shopper already searching, and the marketplace keeps her afterwards. The comparison worth making is what each channel pays for a customer the brand still has a year later.

Instagram vs marketplace CAC in 2022: the two prices moved apart

The prices of the two channels have diverged. Ad impressions across Meta’s apps rose 15% in the first quarter while the average price per ad fell 8%, the company said in its first-quarter results. Part of the reason is weaker targeting: Meta has said that Apple’s privacy changes made its ads less accurate and their results harder to measure, CNBC reported.

Marketplace advertising went the other way. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 23% to $7.88 billion in the first quarter while its online store sales fell 3%, Bloomberg reported. Cost per click on Amazon had already risen 43% during 2021, Marketplace Pulse found.

Instagram has also moved closer to the checkout. On March 22 it opened product tagging to all U.S. users, TechCrunch reported, so shoppers can now tag a brand’s products in their own posts.

Many brands are therefore asking a reasonable question. If Instagram impressions are getting cheaper and marketplace clicks dearer, should budget move to Instagram? That depends on what each channel actually buys, and the two buy very different things.

A search ad rents the shopper; a feed ad can hand her over

A marketplace ad reaches a shopper who is already searching. She typed “linen sheets” into Amazon and the ad put the brand in front of her. The sale was likely to happen somewhere, and the ad decided where. When she buys, Amazon keeps her email, her address and her purchase history. If she wants another set, she will probably search again, and the brand may pay again to be the one she finds.

An Instagram ad reaches someone who was not looking. She was scrolling, saw sheets that caught her eye and tapped through. Fewer people in that position buy, so each first order costs more. When she does buy on the brand’s own site, though, the brand keeps her details. It can email her, invite her back and sell her pillowcases without paying for another ad.

The two costs therefore answer different questions. Marketplace cost per order is the price of capturing a sale already in motion. Instagram acquisition cost is the price of starting a relationship the brand owns. Set side by side on one slide, they look comparable only because both end in a first order.

The arithmetic of a customer kept

Take a bedding brand whose Instagram ads cost $45 per first order, against $15 per order on Amazon. On first orders alone, Amazon looks three times cheaper, which is where a first-order comparison ends.

Now follow the same customers for a year. Half of the brand’s Instagram customers buy again on its own site without further ads, and spend as much as they did the first time. Its Amazon buyers come back too, but mostly through search, where the brand pays for many of the repeat orders all over again. Measured as the cost of a customer kept for a year, the gap narrows sharply, and for the brand’s best products it reverses.

The arithmetic can run the other way. A brand whose Instagram customers rarely come back, or whose products are bought mainly on search, may find that Instagram’s cheap impressions turn into expensive customers.

What a fair comparison asks of each team

Instagram should be judged on the customer it brings in. That means tracking what share of Instagram-acquired customers buy again, and how much they spend, over at least six months. Without that record, Instagram’s acquisition cost will always look high next to a marketplace order.

The marketplace team needs the matching record of its repeat cost. For repeat buyers on Amazon, estimate how many return through paid search and how many through organic listings or their own order history. A marketplace where most repeat orders need another ad is more expensive than its cost per order suggests.

With both records in hand, each channel can be used for the job it does well. Marketplaces capture demand that already exists. Instagram creates demand and builds a list of customers the brand owns. Most brands need both, and the right split depends on repeat behavior, which the cheaper first order says nothing about.

The brand’s own site carries much of the load in this picture. Shoppers who discover a brand on Instagram arrive knowing little about it, so the site has to do the work that reviews and ranking do for a marketplace listing. Clear sizing, fast delivery and a reason to return are what turn an expensive first order into a cheap customer.

Measurement on Instagram needs care in 2022 as well. With targeting and tracking weakened, Instagram’s own reports may undercount the sales its ads cause, especially sales that later happen on a marketplace. Brands that can should test with holdouts or regional splits instead of relying on reported conversions alone.

Whether Meta’s price per ad keeps falling as Reels takes more of Instagram’s time is the next thing to track. Cheaper impressions help only if the customers they find come back, and counting the customers each channel keeps is how we plan social and marketplace budgets for brands.

A0252.title: Walmart Connect in-store screens work before the choice
A0252.alt: An empty blue shopping cart in a bright store aisle lined with shelves of plain-labeled bottles and boxes.
A0252.ttag: Walmart Connect in-store screens work before the choice | Kwontified
A0252.desc: Walmart sells ads on nearly 170,000 store screens. They pay where the screen comes before the shopper’s choice, and stores make the effect easy to test.
A0252.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 5, 2022.
A0252.body:
A self-checkout screen reaches more Walmart shoppers than any aisle display, and for most categories it changes very little about what they buy. Everyone in the lane sees it, but they see it beside a full basket, after every choice on the trip has been made. An ad can only change a purchase it reaches before the decision. That single fact about timing decides which Walmart Connect in-store screens are worth buying, and the stores themselves make it unusually easy to check.

Walmart Connect in-store screens in 2022: reach at the scale of the stores

Walmart opened its stores to advertisers in January 2021, when its media business took the name Walmart Connect. The offer covers TV walls and self-checkout screens, a network of nearly 170,000 digital screens in more than 4,500 stores, and brands can deliver messages by date, time and location, Chain Store Age reported. Its stated goal is to rank among the top ten U.S. advertising platforms within five years, according to its announcement.

Stores are still where most of the shopping happens. On its first-quarter earnings call, Walmart said basket sizes were up while units per basket were down a bit, according to the call transcript, and it described growth in Walmart Connect as strong. At Target, more than 95% of first-quarter sales were fulfilled by stores, according to its results.

So the audience is enormous. It is also shopping while the ads run. The useful question is which of those screens can still change what goes into the cart.

Where the screen sits in the trip decides what it can do

A store screen is sold on how many shoppers pass it. What it can actually do depends on where it sits in the trip.

Start at the end of the trip. The checkout screen reaches every shopper who uses it, after the products are chosen. For most categories an ad there is too late to change what is in the basket. A shopper with a television already in the cart is not going to swap it at the till. The checkout screen can build awareness for the next trip, or prompt a small extra item, but it rarely changes the decision it is shown beside.

A TV wall in the electronics department works the other way. It reaches shoppers while they are still choosing a television, a game or a speaker, in the aisle where that decision happens. An ad there can tip a shopper between two products on the same shelf.

That is why the placement with the most reach is not always the one with the most effect. Self-checkout screens reach more shoppers than any aisle; aisle placements reach fewer of them, at the moment that matters. A plan that buys on reach alone drifts toward the screens that change the least, a little like paying for a shop window that faces only the people walking out.

The same timing sorts categories. Electronics, entertainment and seasonal goods are often bought on the spot in a specific aisle, so screens in or near that aisle sit ahead of the choice. Most groceries are chosen before the trip. There, an in-store screen mostly reaches shoppers who have already decided, and its value lies in the next visit.

Stores turn the question into a test

Stores offer something most online channels do not: clean measurement. Each store is a separate unit with its own sales. A brand can run ads in one group of stores and not in a matched group with similar size, region and sales history, then compare sales of its products between the two. Walmart already sells the link between its ads and the sales that follow, in stores as well as online; it made that pitch when it launched its DSP in August 2021, Retail Dive reported.

Take a games publisher launching a new title. It buys TV wall placements in 200 stores and holds out 200 matched stores. After four weeks, sales of the title are 15% higher in the stores with the ads, and the publisher knows what the screens added without relying on any attribution model. The same money spent on self-checkout screens would have reached far more shoppers, most of whom had finished choosing before they saw the ad.

The test design belongs in the plan before the campaign starts. Agree with Walmart which stores will carry the ads and which will not, matched on size, region and recent sales, and compare sales of the advertised products, and of the category, between the two groups. Store-level tests avoid most of the attribution debates that surround online advertising.

Walmart’s date, time and location targeting makes the comparison easier still. A sunscreen brand can run ads in southern stores during a heat wave, or a grill brand on the weekends before a holiday. Each of those is a natural test as well: compare the stores and days with the ads against the ones without.

Store creative has seconds to work

A screen above a TV wall is seen for seconds, often without sound, by a shopper who is also looking at prices and boxes. The message has to land at a glance: one product, one reason to choose it, and a clear sign of where to find it on the shelf. Video made for streaming, with a slow build and a voiceover, rarely survives the move to a store screen.

If Walmart starts to offer store-level test designs as a standard part of buying in-store media, brands will have one of the most measurable channels in retail media. Until then, buy the screen that comes before the choice and hold out matched stores to prove it, which is how we plan and measure Walmart Connect in-store campaigns.

A0253.crumb: Baby products on Amazon in 2022 are won…
A0253.title: Baby products on Amazon in 2022 are won on availability and trust
A0253.alt: A sunlit nursery with a wooden crib and an open shelf of folded blankets, wooden toys and jars against a blue wall.
A0253.ttag: Baby products on Amazon in 2022 are won on availability and trust | Kwontified
A0253.desc: The 2022 formula shortage taught parents to buy wherever stock exists and to distrust inflated listings. Baby brands on Amazon now win on availability.
A0253.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 7, 2022.
A0253.body:
At the height of the formula shortage, a parent searching Amazon for the brand her baby drank could find it offered only by sellers she had never heard of, at prices far above what she usually paid. Many families in that position bought whatever was in stock, wherever it was, and learned to check the seller’s name before the price. Those habits will outlast the shortage. For baby products on Amazon, being in stock at a fair price from a seller parents trust is now the brand’s main advantage, and the discount comes second.

Baby products on Amazon in 2022: how the shortage unfolded

Abbott recalled some of its powdered infant formula on February 17 after reports of illness in babies who had consumed it, and shut its plant in Sturgis, Michigan, IndustryWeek reported. The national out-of-stock rate for formula reached 43% in the week ending May 8, and several retailers imposed purchase limits, Supermarket News reported.

From there the shortage deepened. The out-of-stock rate rose to 70% in the week ending May 22, Fox Business reported. Abbott expected to restart production in Sturgis on June 4, with product from the plant reaching shelves no earlier than mid-July.

Online, the shortage exposed a different problem. Private sellers were marketing cans at double or triple their normal price, The New York Times reported.

Meanwhile the rest of the baby category held up far better than the home categories around it. At Bed Bath & Beyond, comparable sales at the main banner fell 27% in the quarter to May as spending moved away from the home, while its buybuy BABY stores fell only by mid-single digits, Modern Retail reported.

What a shortage teaches a loyal buyer

Baby products are bought out of need and, very often, out of habit. A parent who has found a formula, a diaper or a bottle that works for her child tends to stay with it, and in most years that loyalty is the category’s great strength.

The shortage broke the habit for many families. With the brand they trusted gone, they bought whatever they could find, wherever they could find it. Some learned that another brand worked just as well. Others learned to check several retailers before every order. New parents, who had no habit to break, formed their first one during the shortage, often with whichever brand happened to be on the shelf.

A parent who has had to hunt once keeps hunting. She compares sellers, watches prices and keeps a second choice in mind. For a baby brand, a stockout used to cost a lost week of sales; now it can cost a loyal customer who has learned to look elsewhere.

The price gouging left its own mark. Parents who saw a can of formula listed at triple its price by a seller they did not know came away wary. They look harder now at who is selling, and many check the seller’s name before they check the price.

A diaper stockout, followed through

Take a diaper brand on Amazon that ran short of its most popular size in May, when demand across the category was erratic. For three weeks its listing showed only third-party sellers at prices well above normal, and reviews from that period mention the price and question whether the product was genuine.

When stock returned, sales recovered, though not all the way. Some parents had switched to a rival that stayed in stock, and they stayed with it. The brand’s June discounts brought back fewer buyers than it expected, because price was never the reason they had left.

Being there, at a fair price, from a seller parents trust

Availability has to come first. Baby brands need forecasts with a wider margin than other categories, safety stock for the products parents depend on, and a weekly look at inventory at Amazon in place of a monthly one. In this category a stockout costs more than the missing sales.

Price and seller integrity come next. The brand, or an authorized seller, should hold the offer on its main products at a fair price. Listings at inflated prices and unauthorized sellers need watching, and Amazon’s brand protection tools are there to act on them. Parents notice who is selling, and they remember it.

Loyal parents also need reasons to stay. Subscription options suit products used on a schedule, like diapers and wipes. Clear product pages that answer safety, ingredient and sizing questions build the kind of trust a discount cannot buy.

Advertising should follow the stock. When a product runs low, its ads should come down before it runs out, so the brand is not paying to send parents to a page with no stock or to a reseller’s inflated offer. When stock returns, brand-name searches should restart first, since that is where returning parents look for the product they used before, and category terms can follow once supply is steady.

Discounts still have a place, particularly for new products and new parents. In a category where trust was shaken, though, a brand that is always there at an honest price earns more than one that is cheapest only some of the time.

Questions for the next supply review

  • How many weeks of cover do our most-needed products hold at Amazon, and who sees that number every week?
  • Who holds the offer on our top listings, and at what price?
  • Which of our ads would keep running if a product went out of stock tomorrow?
  • What do our product pages tell a parent who has never bought from us?

How quickly formula supply recovers in the second half of 2022 is still an open question, and even after it does, expect parents to keep comparing sellers for a long time. Staying in stock, fairly priced and in the right seller’s hands is how we run the Amazon channel for baby and family brands.

A0254.crumb: Target Plus cuts Amazon dependency only…
A0254.title: Target Plus cuts Amazon dependency only where Target shoppers buy
A0254.alt: An abandoned red shopping cart on a gravel path beside a quiet country road lined with hedgerows and trees.
A0254.ttag: Target Plus cuts Amazon dependency only where Target shoppers buy | Kwontified
A0254.desc: Amazon fees and click costs rose in 2022. Target Plus can lower a brand’s exposure to Amazon, but only in categories where Target’s own shoppers buy.
A0254.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 12, 2022.
A0254.body:
From April 28, Amazon’s fulfillment fees carried a new 5% surcharge for fuel and inflation, UPI reported. No seller voted for it, and every seller paid it at once. That is what Amazon dependency costs in practice: the platform’s decisions on fees, click prices and ranking flow straight into a brand’s profit. Target Plus can lower that exposure, but only where Target’s own shoppers bring demand the brand would not have won on Amazon.

Amazon dependency in 2022: costs the brand did not choose

The surcharge was one of several moves against sellers. In the first quarter, Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 23% even as sales in its online stores slipped 3%, Bloomberg reported, so more ad money was chasing flat demand. Click prices had climbed before that: Amazon’s cost per click rose 43% across 2021, Marketplace Pulse found.

Each of those landed on every seller at the same moment. A brand with most of its profit on Amazon had nowhere to absorb them.

Target is one of the alternatives. Target Plus, its invitation-only marketplace, had about 440 sellers at the end of 2021, Marketplace Pulse found in the same review. Target reported digital comparable sales growth of 3.2% in its first quarter (results summary), and its same-day services grew 8%, Drug Store News reported.

The two retailers meet head to head in July. Prime Day runs on July 12 and 13, and Target Deal Days runs from July 11 to 13, Supermarket News reported. For a brand on both sites, the overlap is a small version of the whole question. If its Target buyers are the same people it already reaches on Amazon, it is competing for one July shopper twice. If they are different people, the same week reaches two audiences.

A second channel lowers risk only when its buyers are new

Diversification has one job: to add sales that do not move with Amazon’s decisions. A brand with half its profit elsewhere feels half the shock when Amazon raises a fee or click costs climb.

That arithmetic holds only if the second channel’s sales come from different shoppers. If a brand opens on Target Plus and its Amazon customers simply start buying there instead, it has moved sales without adding any. Its exposure to marketplace fees and retail media prices is barely lower, and it now runs two channels for the same customers. A farmer who buys a second field on the same slope, fed by the same stream, has not spread much risk; both fields flood in the same storm. Only ground with a different water source changes the odds.

So the variable that matters is who shops each channel. Target’s guests are a distinct audience, heavy in categories like home, baby, beauty and household essentials, and loyal to Target’s own stores and app. A brand whose products fit those trips can reach shoppers who would not have found it on Amazon. A brand whose category Target guests rarely buy online will find Target Plus slow, however well it runs the account.

Target’s curation cuts both ways. An invitation-only marketplace limits competition once a brand is in, which helps margins, and it also means the brand must fit Target’s range and standards to get in at all.

Two brands open on Target Plus

Take a home-organization brand that earns 85% of its profit on Amazon. It opens on Target Plus with a focused range of storage products that fit Target’s home aisle. Within a year, Target Plus provides 15% of its profit, most of it from Target guests who did not buy the brand on Amazon. When Amazon’s click costs rise in the fourth quarter, the brand’s total profit falls by less than it would have.

Now take a brand selling niche replacement parts. It opens on Target Plus too, and its Target sales come mostly from shoppers who already knew it from Amazon. Its exposure barely changes.

Both brands pay the same running costs for the second channel: their own listings, their own stock plan, their own customer service and their own advertising. Stock split across two channels can run out on one while sitting idle on the other. Those costs arrive whether the channel brings new shoppers or not. For the parts brand, the channel adds cost and removes almost no risk, which is why new demand is the test that decides the case.

Measure dependency on profit, then grow where demand is new

Dependency is easy to measure in revenue, and revenue can mislead. What matters is the share of profit that rests on one platform’s fees, ranking and advertising prices. A brand with 80% of its revenue on Amazon but strong margins elsewhere may be less exposed than one with 60% and thin margins on its other channels.

Before committing a full range to Target Plus, launch the products that fit Target’s trips and track the share of buyers who are new to the brand. If most are, the channel is adding demand. If most are existing customers, it is moving them.

A ceiling makes the plan concrete. Decide the largest share of profit the brand is willing to have exposed to one platform, and build toward it over time. Diversification takes years rather than a quarter, because new shoppers on a new channel take time to find the brand.

How Target Plus grows its seller base through 2022 is worth following. A wider marketplace brings more reach, but also more competition for the same guests.

The working rule is short. Count dependency in profit dollars, and add a channel only where most of its buyers are new to the brand. That is the test we run when we build channel plans across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0257.title: Zalando Marketing Services is retail media for browsers
A0257.alt: A boutique window with an orange dress, scarf, blazer and woven bag on a quiet cobbled street of stone buildings.
A0257.ttag: Zalando Marketing Services is retail media for browsers | Kwontified
A0257.desc: Zalando shoppers browse more than they search, so Zalando Marketing Services works like paid merchandising. Judge it on full-price sell-through.
A0257.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 14, 2022.
A0257.body:
Zalando’s shoppers often open the app without a product in mind. They scroll through new arrivals, check what a brand they like has added, or open a category to see what is new. They are waiting to be shown something. That habit decides what Zalando Marketing Services is really selling: a place on the front table of a store, which is worth a great deal for a new, well-stocked style and very little for last season’s leftovers. Brands that buy it should judge it the way a merchandiser judges a table, on full-price sell-through.

Zalando Marketing Services and retail media in 2022

Zalando’s advertising business has grown fast. Zalando Marketing Services, known as ZMS, grew its revenue by about 95% in 2021 and contributed around 2% of Zalando’s gross merchandise volume, Coresight Research reported. Zalando expects that share to reach 3% to 4% over the long term.

Its partners are using it more. Partners continued to use ZMS to increase their visibility on the platform and drive sales, Zalando said in its first-quarter results. The same results showed how much the platform itself has slowed: gross merchandise volume of 3.2 billion euros in the first quarter, up 1% from a year earlier, as the economy weighed on demand.

Zalando is not the only European fashion platform selling media. ASOS launched its own advertising business, ASOS Media Group, in September 2020, Coresight noted. European fashion retail is following the path Amazon took in the United States, a few years behind.

When the ad line outgrows the store

A marketplace whose advertising grows faster than its sales is changing who pays for visibility. Zalando’s long-term ambition, an advertising share of 3% to 4% of the volume that passes through it, means a larger slice of every euro a brand earns there goes back to the platform as media. With volume barely growing, those euros come from brands competing harder for the same browsers, and Zalando captures the margin either way.

None of that rules ZMS out for a brand. The return on a placement depends almost entirely on the brand’s side of the transaction: what it chooses to put on the table, and whether it can sell that product at full price once the shopper stops scrolling.

Browsing shoppers respond to what they see

The difference from Amazon starts with the shopper. On Amazon, many shoppers arrive knowing what they want. They type “running shoes, size 10” and compare the results, and advertising there wins the shopper’s query.

On Zalando, a sponsored placement is closer to paying for a spot at the front of a store. It puts a product where browsers will see it. On a phone, that front table is the first rows a shopper sees after opening a category or the new-arrivals feed. Whether they buy depends on whether that product is the one they want at the moment they see it, in the size they need.

So the product chosen for the placement matters more than the bid. A strong new-season style in the sizes shoppers want will sell from a good placement. A style that is running low in key sizes, or that only sells at a discount, will waste it.

Take a sportswear brand that spends its ZMS budget promoting a range of jackets that sold well last season. The jackets get plenty of views, but sales are slow, because many of the popular sizes are gone and the style is no longer new. A competitor promotes a new-season trainer it has stocked deeply, and the placement costs the same. The trainer sells through at full price; the jackets end up in the sale.

Judged on clicks or views, those look like two similar campaigns. Judged on full-price sell-through, one worked and one did not.

Spending ZMS the way a merchandiser would

The choice of what to promote should come from stock and season. New-season products deeply stocked in the sizes shoppers want belong on the table. Styles running low or heading for markdown do not, because the placement will either be wasted or simply speed up a discount.

For brands in Zalando’s partner program, which control their own stock on the platform, the advertising plan and the stock plan should be the same plan, so the products being promoted are the ones the brand can deliver.

Measurement follows from the same logic. Clicks and views show that a placement was seen; sell-through at full price shows that it worked. Compare promoted products against similar ones that were not promoted, over the same weeks.

Timing matters as much as choice. Browsing follows the season: shoppers look hardest at new arrivals in the first weeks after a collection lands, and attention shifts to the sale as the season ends. A placement for a new style is worth most early, while the brand can still sell at full price. Late in the season the same placement mostly competes with markdowns, including the brand’s own, which argues for putting the most ZMS spend behind each collection in its first weeks and easing off as it moves toward clearance.

Price pressure on placements is likely to follow. With Zalando’s volume growing slowly and its advertising growing fast, more brands are bidding for the same browsers, which makes it more important to spend on products that convert and less tempting to buy visibility for its own sake.

Zalando’s second-quarter results on August 4 will show whether ZMS kept growing while the platform stayed flat; if it did, competition for placements will tighten further. Choosing the products, the sizes and the weeks before choosing the bid is how we plan Zalando for fashion brands across the partner program and ZMS.

A0261.title: Back-to-school 2022 starts earlier and finishes later
A0261.alt: A canvas and leather backpack on a wooden desk with a notebook, fountain pen, pencils and books by a sunny window.
A0261.ttag: Back-to-school 2022 starts earlier and finishes later | Kwontified
A0261.desc: Parents started back-to-school shopping early in 2022 to catch deals, then held back the rest. Plan stock and advertising for two peaks instead of one.
A0261.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 21, 2022.
A0261.body:
A backpack bought during a July deal and a pair of sneakers bought the week before term are both back-to-school sales, but they come from different parents in different moods. In 2022 the first kind arrived unusually early. Inflation-conscious parents began shopping in early July to catch deals and spread their costs, and then held back much of the rest until the price, or the need, was right. For brands, back-to-school 2022 is two peaks: one around the July sales and one in late summer.

Back-to-school 2022: record spending, stretched budgets

Spending will be high, mostly because prices are. Deloitte expects parents to spend $34.4 billion on school supplies for children from kindergarten through grade 12, up 5.8% from 2021, or about $661 per student, according to its survey. More than half of parents, 57%, said they were concerned about inflation.

The National Retail Federation expects total back-to-school spending to match the 2021 record of $37 billion, HomePage News reported. Its survey found that 38% of shoppers were cutting back on other spending to pay for school supplies.

The season has started early. As of early July, 56% of shoppers had already begun buying for school and college, NRF found, and Deloitte expects 53% of back-to-school spending to happen by the end of July.

College is a bigger and later market. Deloitte expects back-to-college shoppers to spend $28.3 billion, or about $1,600 per student, and NRF expects back-to-college spending to reach almost $74 billion. College shopping runs closer to move-in day and leans toward electronics and dorm furnishings, so for brands in those categories the late-summer wave matters even more than it does for school supplies.

The aisles parents plan to visit are changing as well. In Deloitte’s survey, 81% of parents named mass merchants as a place they planned to shop, up from 74% in 2021, Supermarket News reported.

Why the season splits in two

A parent stretching a budget behaves like a careful shopper at any sale. When a deal appears on something the child will need, she buys it, even in early July. When the price looks wrong, she waits. The season that results begins with a wave of deal-driven buying around the July sales, pauses, and then picks up again as the school year approaches and the remaining needs become urgent. For a brand, the pause in the middle is the risky stretch, because on a weekly sales report it looks as if the season has already peaked.

The July sales sharpened the pattern. Prime Day and the competing events at Target, Walmart and Best Buy put discounts on backpacks, laptops, headphones and clothing weeks before school, which gave parents who were already planning to shop early a reason to start.

What is left for August is different in kind. Late-summer buying is driven by need: the exact sneakers a growing child now fits, the supplies on the teacher’s list, the item that ran out in July. These shoppers are less sensitive to price, but they need the product to be in stock when they look, and they are often buying against a date on the school calendar.

A school-bag brand caught between the two waves of buying

Take a brand of school bags that planned its season around a single August peak, as in past years. In early July its sales jumped during the Prime Day week as parents bought on deal, and several popular colors sold out. Its next shipment was timed for mid-August.

When need-driven shoppers arrived in August, the colors they wanted were only partly restocked, and some had already bought from a rival. The brand sold more in July than ever before, and less in August than it should have.

Planning stock, deals, messages and listings for two peaks of demand

Stock has to cover both waves. That means enough inventory for deal-driven buying in July, and a second shipment that lands well before the late-summer need. A single delivery timed for August will either miss the first wave or run short in the second.

The message should change between the waves. In July, shoppers respond to price, so deals and deal-led advertising do the work. In August, they respond to availability and fit, so advertising should make clear that the product is in stock, in the right size, and arrives in time for the first day.

The mass merchants deserve a plan of their own, separate from Amazon’s. With more parents planning to shop at Walmart and Target, brands that sell there should have listings, stock and in-store availability ready, and make sure their Amazon plans do not leave those channels short.

Listings carry much of the second wave. Late-summer shoppers often search for a specific size, color or school-list item, so product pages should show sizes in stock, delivery dates before the first day of school and the exact items teachers commonly ask for. A page that answers those questions in seconds wins the parent who is buying under time pressure.

Prices need watching across the brand’s channels too, side by side. With budgets stretched, parents compare prices across retailers before they buy, and a brand priced differently on each channel will lose the sale wherever it looks expensive.

How much of the season’s spending has happened by early August will say which way the second wave leans. A high share means a smaller, more urgent late-summer wave; a low share means parents are still waiting for the right price. Splitting one season into two stock plans, two messages and two sets of listings is how we plan back-to-school across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0262.crumb: Prime Day 2022 results: sales near reach…
A0262.title: Prime Day 2022 results: sales near reach, clicks at reach
A0262.alt: Straw archery target on a grassy field with seven feathered arrows clustered near the center.
A0262.ttag: Prime Day 2022 results: sales near reach, clicks at reach | Kwontified
A0262.desc: Against our June cases, Prime Day 2022 ad sales landed between standard and reach while click costs hit the reach case. Grade each number on its own.
A0262.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 26, 2022.
A0262.body:
In June we set three cases for Prime Day 2022. The first public data on the event puts ad-driven sales between the standard and reach cases, and click costs squarely on the reach case. A brand that grades the event as one number, a win or a miss, will not see that split and where the margin went. Prime Day 2022 results have to be graded one number at a time, with the sales the event added separated from the sales it pulled forward.

Prime Day 2022 results against the forecast

The cases set out in June were multiples of an ordinary day. In the conservative case, each event day sold about 2.5 times an ordinary day and click costs ran about 20% above June. In the standard case, sales ran about 3.5 times and clicks about 35% higher. In the reach case, sales ran about 5 times and clicks about 50% higher.

Across Amazon advertisers on its platform, Skai found that ad-driven sales during the two days of Prime Day were 4.5 times the daily average of the previous 30 days, in its Prime Day analysis. Daily ad spending was 4 times higher. Average cost per click was up 50%, and return on ad spend rose 12% in aggregate, though it varied widely by category.

MeasureConservativeStandardReachPrime Day 2022 (Skai)
Ad-driven sales against an ordinary day2.5 times3.5 times5 times4.5 times
Rise in cost per click20%35%50%50%

Read across each row and the event splits in two. The sales row sits between the standard and reach columns, a good result by any measure. The click-cost row sits on the reach column itself, which is the part of the result that decides margin.

The wider market grew more slowly. Across all retailers, U.S. shoppers spent $11.9 billion online over the two event days, Adobe estimated, up 8.5% from $11 billion in 2021, Fortune reported. Amazon said members bought more than 300 million items, up from about 250 million in 2021, CNBC reported. With consumer prices up 9.1% in the year to June, Adobe’s 8.5% growth was roughly flat in real terms, though online prices and consumer prices are not the same measure.

Why click costs reached the high case before sales did

The June forecast treated the three numbers as moving together. They moved in the same direction, but not by the same amount.

Click prices respond to the number of bidders. On Prime Day nearly every brand with a deal raises its bids, so the price of a click climbs whatever happens to demand. Skai’s data showed advertisers’ daily spending quadrupled, and that alone pushes cost per click toward the high case.

Sales respond to discounts and to shoppers’ budgets. In 2022 shoppers came looking for deals, but with budgets stretched by inflation. They bought heavily, though not without limit, so sales rose strongly without reaching the reach case on average.

The gap between the two is where margin goes. A brand whose click costs rose 50% while its sales rose 3.5 times paid more for each sale than in an ordinary week, even if its reported return held up because deals lifted conversion.

Category mattered more than the average. Skai found that computers and consumer electronics saw spending rise more than ninefold and ad-driven sales more than tenfold, one of the few categories where return on ad spend rose. Lower-priced consumer goods gained a lot of volume, at a lower return.

The averages also hide timing. Same-advertiser spending on Prime Day was up 19% from 2021, but spending in the 30 days before the event was already up 16%, Skai found. The auction was crowded before the event started, which is why the event’s click costs climbed from an already high base.

A kitchenware brand, graded line by line

Take a kitchenware brand that forecast the standard case. Its event-day sales came in at 3.8 times an ordinary day, slightly above standard. Its click costs rose 52%, at the reach case. Its deal share was 65%, between conservative and standard.

On sales alone, the event beat the forecast. On margin it fell short, because the brand paid reach-case prices for standard-case volume.

Grading the event and the weeks around it

Each number gets graded against its own case. For cost per click, sales lift and deal share in turn, note where the result landed and which assumption behind each case held or failed. A single verdict on the event hides the trade-offs. Deal share belongs in the same review, since the share of sales sold on a deal decides how much of the lift was bought with margin.

Added sales and pulled-forward sales need separating. Compare total sales for the weeks before and after the event with the same weeks in an ordinary period. If sales dipped below normal in the week after Prime Day, part of the event’s volume was borrowed from the following weeks rather than added.

Profit is the final grade, ahead of return on ad spend. Calculate margin after discounts and advertising for the event days and the weeks around them. A higher return on ad spend can coexist with lower profit when deals drive conversion.

The holiday season is the next large event, and bidding pressure is likely to be even higher then. If click costs reached the reach case in July, plan for at least that in the fourth quarter. Amazon’s second-quarter results will show how crowded the auction was in the weeks leading up to the event.

Grading each number against the case it was forecast in, and only then adding them up, is how we forecast and review Amazon events for brands.

A0264.crumb: Prime Day 2022 lessons: a shopping week…
A0264.title: Prime Day 2022 lessons: a shopping week, not an Amazon event
A0264.alt: Stone shopfront with three windows displaying red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes and a red bicycle.
A0264.ttag: Prime Day 2022 lessons: a shopping week, not an Amazon event | Kwontified
A0264.desc: Prime Day 2022 showed shoppers waiting for the event and rivals competing in it. It is now a shopping week for all retail, so plan July across every channel.
A0264.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 28, 2022.
A0264.body:
The day before Prime Day 2022 began, Target’s Deal Days had already started. Best Buy and Macy’s were running their own summer sales, and a third of Prime Day buyers would later say they had held off on a purchase until the event arrived. The lasting lesson of Prime Day 2022 is that it has become a shopping week for the whole of retail. Shoppers wait for it and compare prices across retailers while it runs, so brands should plan July the way they plan Black Friday, across every channel they sell on.

Prime Day 2022 lessons: the event spread beyond Amazon

The headline numbers belonged to Amazon. Amazon said Prime members bought more than 300 million items over the two days, against about 250 million in 2021, CNBC reported. Adobe’s tally of online spending at all U.S. retailers in the two days came to $11.9 billion, and the company said the event lifted traffic on competing sites such as Walmart.com and Target.com, Bloomberg reported.

The rivals came prepared. Target ran its Deal Days from July 11 to 13, starting a day before Prime Day, while Best Buy and Macy’s ran “Black Friday in July” sales, Axios reported. Target’s advertisers spent 8% more per day during its event than in the previous 30 days and saw ad-driven sales rise 28%, Skai found.

Shoppers had planned for it too. In Numerator’s survey, 33% of Prime Day buyers said they had waited for the event to buy a specific item at a discount, and 20% said inflation led them to check prices outside Amazon first, Total Retail reported.

The shopper waits for the week, then shops all of it

A shopper who knows deals will arrive on known dates holds her purchases for those dates. A third of Prime Day buyers said they did exactly that. The weeks before the event lose some of their sales, and the event window gains them.

She also shops the whole week rather than one store. With prices high, she compares Amazon with Target, Walmart and Best Buy before she buys. The retailer that hosts the event no longer captures all of the demand it creates; some of it lands with whichever rival has the better price on the day.

That is how Black Friday works: a date every retailer competes on and every shopper plans around. Prime Day is becoming the same kind of date for the summer. The difference is speed: it took Black Friday decades to become an industry fixture, and Prime Day has done much of it in a few years.

Who owns July inside the brand

Prime Day began as an Amazon promotion, so the natural owner of a brand’s July plan has been the Amazon team. The decision in front of leadership now is whether to keep it there or to treat July as a company-wide event, with the Walmart and Target owners, the pricing team and the stock planners in the same plan. Keeping it with the Amazon team is simpler. Moving it gives the Walmart and Target teams a say in the deal calendar, and asks the Amazon team to give up some control of its biggest week.

Take a home brand that sells on Amazon, Target and Walmart and planned its July around Amazon: deep deals, extra stock and a large ad budget there, and nothing special elsewhere. During the week its Amazon sales rose sharply. Its Target listing, priced higher and without a deal, sat next to a rival’s discounted product during Target’s own event, and some Target shoppers who would have bought its product bought the rival’s instead. The brand won on Amazon and lost on Target, in the same week, to the same shoppers.

Planning July like Black Friday, across every channel

The unit of planning becomes the week. Treat the July event window as a shopping week across all retailers, and set deals, stock and advertising for each channel the brand sells on, not just for the host.

Prices have to line up across retailers. Shoppers now compare before they buy. A deal on Amazon and a full price on Target sends the comparison shopper to a rival on Target, or teaches her to buy only on Amazon. Matching offers, or deliberately different products on each channel, protects both.

The weeks around the event need their own assumptions. If shoppers wait for July, the weeks before it will be softer, so budgets and stock plans for June and early July should allow for some demand being held back, and the weeks after should be watched for a dip.

The advertising budget can travel as well. Target’s advertisers saw sales rise far faster than their spending during its event, a sign that its auction was less crowded than Amazon’s on the same days. When every brand concentrates its budget on the host, the rival retailers’ events can buy shoppers more cheaply. A brand that sells on several channels should split its event budget by where each dollar buys the most, not by where the headline event happens to be.

The week should be measured as a whole: total sales and margin across every retailer, for the whole event window and the weeks around it. A brand that reports Amazon alone will miss sales won and lost elsewhere in the same week.

Expect the pattern to spread. If retailers have learned that a summer sales week draws shoppers, more of them will build events of their own, and the retail calendar will carry more fixed sales weeks, each needing its own stock and margin plan. How retailers schedule their autumn promotions will show whether that is happening. One plan for every channel in the event week is how we plan retail events for brands across all three.

A0266.crumb: Amazon’s Q2 2022 results show more ad…
A0266.title: Amazon’s Q2 2022 results show more ad money per sale
A0266.alt: Small kraft paper parcel tied with twine balanced on a stack of coins on a wooden table.
A0266.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2022 results show more ad money per sale | Kwontified
A0266.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue rose 18% in Q2 2022 while its online store sales fell 4%. Ad money per dollar of sales rose about a fifth, so the auction got more crowded.
A0266.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 2, 2022.
A0266.body:
In the second quarter of 2022, Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 18% while sales at its own online stores fell 4%. Put the two lines over each other and advertisers spent about a fifth more for each dollar of Amazon’s online sales than a year earlier, in a quarter without Prime Day. A line that strong is usually read as brands finding more value in Amazon’s shoppers. The arithmetic points mostly to a more crowded auction, which means brands should plan the second half on rising click costs and judge every increase in spend by the sales it actually adds.

Amazon Q2 2022 results: advertising grew while online sales shrank

Net sales rose 7% to $121.2 billion in the second quarter, Axios reported. Sales at Amazon’s online stores fell 4% to about $51 billion, the second quarterly decline in a row. Advertising revenue grew 18% to $8.76 billion, MediaPost reported.

The calendar matters for reading the second quarter of 2022. Prime Day fell in the second quarter in 2021 and in July in 2022. Amazon’s chief financial officer said on the earnings call that Prime Day had added about 400 basis points to Amazon’s revenue growth rate in the second quarter of 2021, according to the call transcript. The 2022 quarter therefore faced a tougher comparison, and advertising still grew by double digits.

Ad growth did slow from the first quarter, when it was 23% against a 3% fall in online store sales, Bloomberg reported. The gap between the two lines stayed wide.

For the third quarter, which includes Prime Day 2022, Amazon guided to net sales of $125 billion to $130 billion, up 13% to 17%, MediaPost reported.

Ad dollars per dollar of sales rose about a fifth

Working back from the reported growth rates gives the year-earlier figures, and the ratio between them.

QuarterAdvertising revenueOnline store salesAdvertising per dollar of online sales
Q2 2021about $7.4 billionabout $53 billionabout 14 cents
Q2 2022$8.76 billionabout $51 billionabout 17 cents

The 2021 figures come from dividing each 2022 figure by its reported growth rate, and the last column divides advertising by online store sales in the same quarter. Going from 14 cents to 17 cents is a rise of about a fifth in one year.

The ratio is imperfect as a measure. Advertising also supports third-party sellers, whose services revenue grew 9%, and the online store line includes only Amazon’s own sales. The direction is still clear: more advertising money is chasing a pool of shoppers that is not growing as fast.

Why the line reads as competition more than value

A strong advertising line looks like evidence that Amazon’s shoppers became worth more to brands. In 2022 the two lines split, and the event data fits a different reading better.

Same-advertiser spending on Amazon in the 30 days before Prime Day was up 16% from 2021, and cost per click during the event rose 50% from the previous 30 days, Skai found. Competition for clicks was already heavy before the event, and more intense during it.

Social advertising points the same way. A day before Amazon reported, Meta said its second-quarter revenue fell 1% to $28.8 billion, its first decline, and that the average price per ad fell 14% while impressions rose 15%, according to its results. Meta described a weak advertising demand environment that it expected to continue into the third quarter. Advertising budgets did not grow everywhere. They grew where the sale happens and can be measured, and Amazon is the largest such place.

So the value reading holds only in part. Advertising is growing because more brands are competing for the same shoppers, and because retail media is where budgets go when measurement elsewhere has weakened. Some of the growth reflects value; much of it reflects competition.

Take a brand whose Amazon sales are flat year over year while its advertising cost per sale has risen from 14 cents to 17 cents, in line with the marketplace ratio. Its campaigns look unchanged, its return on ad spend has fallen, and its team suspects a targeting problem. The real cause is that every rival is spending more for the same shoppers, and no change to its targeting would fix the price of the auction.

Budgeting the second half on current click costs

Second-half budgets should start from current click costs. If cost per click rose through the spring and spiked at Prime Day, the fourth quarter will start from a higher base, and budgets built from 2021 averages will buy fewer clicks than expected.

Every increase in spend should be judged by the sales it adds. Before raising a budget, ask what share of the extra sales would have happened without it; holdouts, matched periods and new-to-brand share all help. A holdout need not be elaborate: pausing a campaign for a set of products in chosen weeks, and comparing their total sales with similar weeks, gives a usable answer. When the auction is crowded, the last dollar of spend is the one most likely to buy a sale the brand would have made anyway.

Brands can also track their own version of Amazon’s ratio: advertising spend per dollar of total sales, organic included, every month. If it rises while total sales stay flat, the brand is buying the same business at a higher price, and the plan should change before the holiday season.

The third quarter will need the same care. With Prime Day back in the quarter, advertising growth may look faster, so compare it with online store growth before reading it as improving demand. Pricing budgets from the auction as it is now is how we plan and measure Amazon advertising for brands.
