A0267.crumb: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2022 is…
A0267.title: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2022 is seasonal again
A0267.alt: Vintage wooden water skis and a worn surfboard leaning against a sunlit stucco garage door.
A0267.ttag: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2022 is seasonal again | Kwontified
A0267.desc: The pandemic rush for bikes, weights and paddles is over, but people kept playing. Sports and outdoors on Amazon now follows each sport’s season again.
A0267.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 4, 2022.
A0267.body:
In the rush, a family that wanted paddleboards for July bought them in March, because March was when they could be found. That scramble is over. Supply has recovered, many households already own the gear they rushed to buy, and the people who took up a sport have kept playing it. So sports and outdoors on Amazon has gone back to the calendar of each sport: gear bought in the weeks before a season starts, consumables bought all through it. Brands should plan stock, deals and advertising by sport season, and clear the excess equipment bought for 2021-level demand before it collides with the next one.

Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2022: the equipment rush ended, the activity stayed

Dick’s Sporting Goods, which describes itself as the largest U.S.-based full-line sporting goods retailer, showed both halves of the story. Its comparable sales fell 8.4% in the first quarter, against a 117% rise a year earlier, according to its results. Sales were still 41% higher than in the same quarter of 2019, and the company expected full-year comparable sales to fall between 2% and 8%.

Its chief executive explained which half was which. The categories that surged during the pandemic, fitness and outdoor equipment including bikes, paddles and golf, had normalized as the company expected, SGB Media reported. People were still running, walking and playing golf. Dick’s inventory was up 40%.

The pressure spread through the summer. Walmart lowered its profit outlook on July 25, saying shoppers were cutting back on discretionary goods and that it would mark down general merchandise more heavily, the Associated Press reported. Nike’s inventories had risen 23% to $8.4 billion, according to its results.

Why the seasons came back

Through 2020 and 2021 the sporting goods calendar stopped working. Bikes sold in November, kayaks sold out in February, and home weights went whenever a delivery date appeared. The usual seasons, when people buy gear in the weeks before they start a sport, flattened into one long rush.

Scarcity drove that rush; the way people play never changed. Stock was short and unpredictable, so shoppers bought whenever they found it. That reason has now gone. The people who kept playing are buying the way they did before: tennis balls and racquets in spring, swimwear and paddles before summer, base layers and snow gear in the autumn.

Consumables and apparel carry more of the demand. A household that bought a bike in 2020 now buys tubes, lights and riding clothes. A new golfer who kept playing buys balls and gloves every season. These purchases are smaller, more frequent and tied to the calendar of the sport.

In a sporting goods store, the season is built into the floor plan: the front tables turn over from bikes to swimwear to skis as the months pass. On Amazon there is no front table to rearrange. The results page reshuffles itself around what shoppers type, so the brand has to do the rearranging itself, in its stock, its listings and its bids.

Two camping brands, one summer

Take an outdoor brand selling camping gear on Amazon that ordered heavily for 2022 on the assumption that demand would keep running as it had in 2021. Tents and stoves sold steadily through the spring, then slowed in late summer as the camping season ended. By August the brand had a warehouse of tents and a season of slow sales ahead.

A competitor had ordered smaller volumes of equipment and more of the consumables campers rebuy each trip: fuel, lanterns, freeze-dried meals. Its sales held through the summer, while the first brand’s tents waited for spring.

Planning by sport season, and clearing 2021’s bets first

Stock should follow the season of each sport rather than a flat monthly forecast. Map each product to the weeks when its sport starts, and time shipments so stock arrives a few weeks before demand rises. Products for a sport whose season has ended should not be restocked until the next one approaches.

Excess equipment needs clearing before it meets the next season. Gear bought for 2021-level demand will compete with new-season stock and with the discounts large retailers are offering. Clearing it with targeted deals in the off-season, or before the next season’s stock arrives, protects the next season’s prices.

The range and the advertising should lean toward what players rebuy. Consumables, apparel and accessories follow the season and repeat each year. Advertising can move with the calendar too, putting budget behind each sport in the weeks before its season, when searches rise, and pulling it back afterward.

Listings should follow the season as well. Before each sport begins, product pages should carry the information players need at that moment: sizing for growing children, compatibility with equipment they already own, delivery dates before the first match or trip. A shopper buying tennis balls in March and a shopper buying a new racquet in April want different answers, and the page that gives them quickly wins the sale.

The weather moves the calendar. Seasonal demand in sports shifts with local conditions: a warm spring brings forward bike and golf purchases, a late snowfall delays winter gear. Brands that adjust shipments and budgets by region and by the actual start of the season, rather than a fixed date, catch more of the peak.

How quickly retailers clear their sporting goods inventories through the autumn is the thing to follow next. If discounts deepen, equipment prices on Amazon will feel the pressure too, and brands should time their own clearance accordingly. Building the range, stock and advertising around how players actually buy is how we run Amazon for sports and outdoor brands.

A0268.crumb: Q4 2022 budget: phase the base, release a…
A0268.title: Q4 2022 budget: phase the base, release a reserve on evidence
A0268.alt: Four glass jars filled with coins on a wooden windowsill overlooking an autumn garden.
A0268.ttag: Q4 2022 budget: phase the base, release a reserve on evidence | Kwontified
A0268.desc: The 2021 holiday season spread out and the 2022 auction is crowded. Phase most of the Q4 budget from October, and hold a reserve to release on weekly results.
A0268.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 9, 2022.
A0268.body:
Cyber Monday 2021 was the first Cyber Monday to shrink: online spending fell 1.4% to $10.7 billion, Fox Business reported. The holiday season as a whole did not shrink with it; spending moved into other weeks. That spread, together with a more crowded auction in 2022, changes how a Q4 2022 budget should be built. Phase most of it across the season from October, and hold a reserve that is released only when weekly results show it will pay.

The Q4 2022 budget starts from a season that spread out

The 2021 holiday season began early. Amazon and Target started holiday deals in early October 2021, as retailers worried about supply chain delays, Fortune reported.

The peak flattened as a result. Online spending during Cyber Week fell 1.4% to $33.9 billion, alongside the Cyber Monday decline. Yet the season as a whole still reached $204.5 billion online, according to Adobe, in its final holiday count. Spending did not fall; it spread across more weeks.

Two forces sharpen the picture for 2022. The auction is more crowded: Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 18% in the second quarter while its online store sales fell 4%, MediaPost reported. And retailers are clearing stock: Walmart said on July 25 that it planned heavier markdowns on general merchandise in the second half, the Associated Press reported.

What a fixed plan buys, and what waiting buys

A fixed phasing plan has one clear advantage: it is simple. A brand decides in August what share of its budget goes to October, November, Cyber Week and December, and spends it.

The weakness is timing: it commits money before the brand knows which weeks will work. In a quiet year that cost is small. In 2022 it is larger, because the most expensive days are known in advance and the best weeks are not.

Event days attract every bidder. Skai measured a 50% jump in Amazon’s cost per click during Prime Day 2022, against the previous 30 days, in its event analysis. Black Friday and Cyber Monday are likely to show the same pattern, and money committed to those days in advance buys clicks at peak prices whatever the result.

The best weeks, meanwhile, are unknowable in August. With shoppers stretched and retailers discounting, demand may arrive early, late or around a particular competitor’s event. A fixed plan pays peak prices with certainty. A reserve accepts a small risk of underspending in exchange for the chance to place money where it returns most.

Holding money back has a cost of its own. Spend that arrives late misses shoppers who bought early, and a reserve that is never released is simply a plan that underspent. A ship’s captain who keeps fuel in reserve until the weather is known faces the same choice: the reserve only earns its keep if it is burned when the storm actually comes. On the 2022 numbers, the balance leans toward keeping some money uncommitted, as long as the rules for spending it are set in advance.

A $200,000 season, phased and held

Take a brand with a $200,000 fourth-quarter budget. It commits 80% as a phased base: about a quarter in October, a third in November before Cyber Week, a quarter in Cyber Week and the rest in December. It holds the remaining 20% as a reserve.

In October its early-season campaigns return well, at click prices below the November peak, so it releases part of the reserve into late October. In Cyber Week click prices jump and returns fall below its threshold, so it holds the rest. In December it releases the remainder behind its best-selling gifts in the last shipping week. The brand ends the season with the same total spend, placed where the evidence pointed.

Setting the base, the reserve and the rules

The base should be phased across the season, not poured into one weekend. Start in October, when shoppers begin and click prices are lower, and keep spend steady through November. Concentrate Cyber Week money on products with real deals and enough stock to last the event.

The reserve needs its rules before the season starts. Decide what weekly return, cost per click or new-to-brand share will release it, and what will hold it back, and write those thresholds down in August, when nobody is under pressure. A threshold written in August is easier to keep than one invented in the middle of Cyber Week, when every dashboard is moving at once.

Review weekly and move fast. Look each week at return, click prices and stock by product. Release reserve where the evidence is strong, hold it where it is not, and pull spend from products that are running out of stock.

The plan should split by channel as well. During Prime Day, Target’s advertisers saw ad-driven sales rise 28% on spending up 8%, Skai found, a sign that rival retailers’ auctions can be less crowded during big events. A brand that sells on Walmart and Target should give each channel its own base and its own share of the reserve, instead of putting the whole holiday plan behind Amazon’s busiest days.

The reserve also needs protecting from habit, because one that drifts into the base as the season gets busy stops being a reserve. Give one person the authority to release it, and require a short written reason each time, so the money moves on evidence rather than nerves.

When retailers announce their first holiday deals will show how early to lean. If they start earlier than in 2021, October deserves a larger share of the base. Budgets that move on weekly evidence are how we plan fourth-quarter advertising across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0270.crumb: Amazon vendor orders in 2022 follow a…
A0270.title: Amazon vendor orders in 2022 follow a fuller warehouse
A0270.alt: Warehouse aisle lined with tall pallet racks of cardboard boxes leading to an open loading dock door.
A0270.ttag: Amazon vendor orders in 2022 follow a fuller warehouse | Kwontified
A0270.desc: Retailers are cutting vendor orders in 2022, and Amazon’s inventory rose 17% in six months as product sales fell. Plan from sell-through, not from POs.
A0270.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 11, 2022.
A0270.body:
A vendor opens Vendor Central in July and finds two numbers pulling apart: units shipped to shoppers are holding steady, and the purchase orders behind them have shrunk or stopped. It reads like a verdict on the brand. Usually it is a verdict on the retailer’s warehouse.

Amazon vendor orders follow the retailer’s inventory, and in 2022 retailers are holding far more stock than they want. Target is cancelling orders outright, and Amazon’s own inventory rose 17% in six months while its product sales fell. Vendors should expect lighter, less regular orders into the autumn and plan from sell-through.

Amazon vendor orders sit downstream of a stock glut

The pattern started at the big-box retailers. Target said on June 7 that it would cancel orders from suppliers, particularly in home goods and clothing, and mark down unwanted stock, the Associated Press reported. Many of those orders had production lead times of nine months. Target cut its expected second-quarter operating margin to about 2%, from 5.3%. Walmart said that 20% of its elevated inventory was product it wished it had never bought, the same AP report noted.

Amazon is in a similar position. Its inventories stood at $38.2 billion at the end of June 2022, up from $32.6 billion at the end of 2021, while its net product sales fell 2.5% in the second quarter, according to its quarterly report. Some of that June stock was bought for Prime Day in July. The direction still matches what Amazon has said about its network: it is looking to sublet at least 10 million square feet of warehouse space after building too much during the pandemic, Bloomberg reported.

A retailer with full warehouses and falling product sales has one simple lever: it buys less.

Why orders fall while products still sell

A retailer orders to bring its stock up to the level its forecast calls for. If it already holds more than that, it orders less, or nothing, until sales bring the stock back down. The order describes the retailer’s warehouse, not the shopper’s basket.

In 2021 the opposite happened. Retailers feared empty shelves, ordered early and ordered big, often months ahead. That stock is now arriving into a market where shoppers have shifted spending to food, fuel and travel. Products ordered for 2021-style demand are sitting in warehouses, and new orders wait until they sell through.

Follow the stock and it becomes clear who is carrying the cost of that misjudgment. Target’s cancellations fell on orders that, in many cases, had nine-month production lead times behind them. A lighter purchase order does the same thing more quietly: the retailer works down its own excess, and the vendor holds the goods, the production capacity and the cash tied up in both until orders return. The retailer’s forecast error becomes the vendor’s inventory problem.

The number that tells a vendor what is really happening is sell-through: how many units the retailer is selling to shoppers each week, and how many weeks of stock it holds. A vendor whose sell-through is steady but whose orders have dropped is watching the retailer work down its excess. A vendor whose sell-through has dropped has a different problem.

A kitchen-tools vendor that read the order instead of the shelf

Take a vendor of kitchen tools selling to Amazon. Its weekly units shipped to shoppers have held steady through the summer, but its purchase orders fell by about half in June and July. Its team assumes demand has collapsed and cuts production. When Amazon’s stock of its items runs down in September, orders return in a rush, and the vendor has nothing to ship. Its items go out of stock just as the holiday season begins.

Planning from sell-through, not from orders

Sell-through and weeks of cover belong on a weekly report. Vendor Central shows units shipped to shoppers and Amazon’s on-hand inventory for each item; dividing one by the other gives the weeks of stock Amazon holds. When cover falls back toward normal levels, orders will return.

Production should follow demand rather than orders. Keep producing to the rate at which shoppers are buying, adjusted for the season, so stock is ready when orders come back, and cut only where sell-through itself has fallen.

Availability needs protecting in the meantime. If Amazon’s stock of an item runs out while orders are still light, the item loses sales and search position. Brands with the option can use other routes to keep items available, such as direct fulfillment or a marketplace listing where their agreement allows it, rather than waiting for orders to recover.

Expect the pause to last into the autumn. Walmart said on July 25 that it expected more pressure on general merchandise in the second half and would mark down more of it to clear stock, the Associated Press reported. Retailers still clearing excess will keep orders light until it is gone. Vendors in home goods, apparel and electronics, the categories hit hardest, should plan for lighter orders through at least the start of the holiday season instead of assuming a quick return to 2021 levels.

The vendor manager is worth a direct conversation. Ask how Amazon sees cover for each key item and what it expects to order for the fourth quarter; a discussion grounded in sell-through tends to be more useful than one about the size of the last purchase order.

Amazon’s inventory at the end of September will show whether the excess is clearing. If it falls while product sales hold, purchase orders should follow. Planning from the shelf rather than the order is how we run Vendor Central accounts for brands.

A0272.title: Walmart Sponsored Products bidding: check the floor first
A0272.alt: Small stack of gold coins on the bottom shelf of a blue bookcase beside a sunlit window.
A0272.ttag: Walmart Sponsored Products bidding: check the floor first | Kwontified
A0272.desc: Walmart Sponsored Products set minimum bids and charge the price you bid. Check each keyword’s break-even CPC against the floor, then tier bids by match type.
A0272.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 16, 2022.
A0272.body:
A $15 kitchen gadget whose broad-match clicks convert at 2% is worth about 7.5 cents a click to a brand that needs a return of 4 on its ad spend. On Amazon that brand could bid close to that value and test. On Walmart it cannot, because the lowest bid a manual campaign accepts is 30 cents. Walmart Sponsored Products bidding starts from two facts that Amazon advertisers often miss: minimum bids, and an auction that charges the price you bid. Work out each keyword’s break-even cost per click before bidding, keep loose keywords on low-priced products out of manual campaigns, and tier bids by match type as Walmart recommends.

Walmart Sponsored Products bidding: the floor and the auction

Walmart’s rules change the arithmetic. Its bid minimums are $0.20 for automatic campaigns and $0.30 for manual ones, and campaigns carry a $100 daily minimum budget, ROI Revolution explained in its guide to the platform. Amazon allows bids as low as a few cents.

The same guide describes Walmart’s auction as first-price: a winning bid of $0.30 pays $0.30 a click. On Amazon, the winner typically pays just above the next-highest bid. In a first-price auction there is no second bidder setting a lower price, so every cent of the bid is paid. To be eligible for search placements, a product must also rank organically within the top 128 results.

Walmart’s own advice is to treat match types differently. Its best-practices guide for its second fiscal quarter of 2022 recommends bidding lowest on broad match, highest on exact match and in between on phrase match, and moving keywords from broad toward exact as they prove they convert, according to Walmart Connect. It also recommends bid multipliers on the page and device types that return best.

Why the Amazon playbook stalls at the floor

Many brands arrive on Walmart with an Amazon playbook: launch broad, bid low, harvest what converts. It is a sensible habit where bids can go as low as the value of the click. On Walmart, the floor sets a price below which no click can be bought.

The number that decides it is break-even cost per click. A click is worth the product’s price, times the share of clicks that convert, divided by the return on ad spend the brand needs. If that value sits below the minimum bid, every click loses money, however good the targeting. The floor works like a cover charge at a club door: worth paying for a guest who will spend, ruinous for one who only wants to look around.

Product and keywordPriceConversion rateReturn neededValue of a clickManual floor
Gadget, broad match$152%4about 7.5 cents30 cents
Gadget, exact match on its own name$1515%4about 56 cents30 cents
$60 item, broad match$602%430 cents30 cents

Take the gadget’s broad keywords first. At about 7.5 cents a click against a 30-cent floor, they cannot pay at any bid the platform allows.

The same brand’s exact-match keyword for its own product name converts 15% of clicks, which makes each click worth about 56 cents. That keyword clears the floor comfortably, and in a first-price auction its bid can be set close to that value.

So the playbook fails for low-priced products and loose keywords. On Amazon, a low bid can buy cheap traffic to test; on Walmart the floor removes that option, and the first-price auction removes the discount a second-price auction would give. Testing broadly costs more per click, so it has to be done more selectively.

It holds better for higher-priced products. A $60 item converting at 2% with the same target is worth 30 cents a click, right at the floor, and above that price broad testing becomes affordable again. Price, more than campaign skill, decides which products can afford broad testing on Walmart.

Setting bids from break-even

Break-even cost per click comes first, for each product and match type, before launch. Use price, expected conversion rate and the return the brand needs. Where break-even sits below $0.30, keep the product out of manual campaigns or limit it to exact match on its strongest terms.

Bids then tier by match type, as Walmart advises: lowest on broad, in the middle on phrase and highest on exact. Because the auction charges what you bid, set exact bids close to their value rather than far above it, and raise them only when position matters.

Automatic campaigns are for finding terms. They carry the lower $0.20 floor and surface search terms the brand had not tried. Terms that convert should move into manual exact-match campaigns, where the bid can be set to their value.

The listing comes before the bid. Because a product must rank in the top 128 organic results to be eligible for search placements, an item with a weak title, few reviews or poor content may not be shown at all, whatever the bid. On Walmart, organic rank is a condition of advertising as well as a complement to it, so check where products rank for their main search terms before raising bids.

Bid multipliers deserve restraint. They raise the effective bid on chosen pages and devices, and in a first-price auction every increase is paid in full, so apply them only where the data shows a higher return.

The share of spend on keywords whose break-even sits below their bid is the number to keep an eye on. If it is rising, the account is buying traffic that cannot pay. Setting bids from break-even rather than habit is how we run Walmart Connect campaigns for brands.

A0273.crumb: Amazon Brand Store: what a flagship needs…
A0273.title: Amazon Brand Store: what a flagship needs in 2022
A0273.alt: Sunlit boutique with arched windows, wooden shelves of ceramics and linens, and a stone display table.
A0273.ttag: Amazon Brand Store: what a flagship needs in 2022 | Kwontified
A0273.desc: Shoppers reach an Amazon Brand Store through the brand’s own ads, follows and searches. Build the flagship around what is new and what fits each of them.
A0273.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 18, 2022.
A0273.body:
A flagship store on a busy street is built to stop strangers: a big window, a story at the door, the whole range on display. An Amazon Brand Store gets a different crowd. Look at the routes in, a brand’s own Sponsored Brands ad, the follow button, a product page the shopper was already on, a search for the brand by name, and most of them carry someone who has already chosen the brand. What that visitor has not chosen is the product. A Store works as a flagship when it answers what is new and what fits, is refreshed on a schedule and is tied to Brand Follow.

The Amazon Brand Store became a place for returning shoppers

Stores are now common. Brands selling on Amazon had launched more than 140,000 of them by October 2021, Amazon said at its Accelerate conference.

The ways shoppers reach them have changed too. Amazon expanded Brand Follow in October 2021 so that shoppers can follow a brand with one button across Stores, Posts and Amazon Live, and may see deals from brands they follow on the Amazon homepage, according to Amazon Ads. There were already more than 20 million follow relationships, and every brand with a Store was enrolled automatically.

Advertising sends shoppers there as well. Shoppers can reach a Store by clicking the brand logo at the bottom of a Sponsored Brands ad’s landing page, Feedvisor reported. And Amazon added scheduled publishing so that brands could keep their Store fresh for returning customers, it said when it released the feature.

Who actually walks into the store

Each of those routes changes the Store’s job. A physical flagship has to stop passersby; an Amazon Store mostly greets people who walked in on purpose. They want to know what is new since their last visit, which product suits their need, and what goes with what they already own.

Many Stores are built for the opposite visitor. They open with a brand film and then lay out every product in a grid, as if the shopper had never heard of the brand. A returning shopper scrolls past a story they already know and has to search the grid for the one product they came for. Some leave to search Amazon instead, where a competitor’s ad is waiting.

That is the quiet cost of a catalog-style Store. It treats its most valuable visitors, the ones who already chose the brand, as strangers who need convincing, and makes them do the work of finding what they came for.

In a good department store, the regular who walks straight to her usual counter is served by someone who remembers what she bought last time. A Store page has no one at the counter. The layout has to do that recognizing, which is why the top of the page matters far more than the brand film below it.

A skincare store, rebuilt for the people who visit it

Take a skincare brand whose Store opens with a long brand story, followed by its full range of 60 products sorted by product type. Most of its visitors are existing customers clicking through from its Sponsored Brands ads. They want the new serum the ad showed them, or a refill of what they already use.

The brand rebuilds the Store around those visitors. The top section shows what is new. The next groups products by skin concern, so a shopper can find what fits, and a third shows the brand’s best sets and refills. The brand story moves to a page of its own. Fewer visitors leave the Store to search, and more of the traffic the brand paid to send there ends in a sale.

Building the flagship around need, freshness and follow

Products belong in groups by need rather than by product type: the problem they solve or the occasion they suit. A shopper who knows the brand is looking for the right product for them, and a need-based layout gets them there faster than a list of everything.

The Store needs a refresh schedule. Change the top of the Store at least with each season and each major event, and use scheduled publishing so updates go live on time. A returning shopper who sees the same page every visit stops coming back to it.

Brand Follow and advertising should be wired in. Make following the brand an obvious action, and point Sponsored Brands traffic to the page that matches the ad rather than the home page. When an ad promotes a new product, its landing page should start with that product.

The cost of sending shoppers there is rising, which raises the price of a Store that loses them. In the second quarter of 2022, Amazon’s ad revenue was up 18% as sales in its online stores dropped 4%, MediaPost reported. When a brand pays more for each click to its Store, a Store that sends a returning customer back to search wastes more of that spend. The Store belongs in the advertising plan, not in a separate brand project.

The Store should be measured against that job: how many visitors come from ads and from follows, how many buy, and which pages they leave from, season by season and page by page. A Store that sends returning shoppers back to search is handing sales to competitors who advertise there.

The share of Store visits that come from repeat shoppers and followers is the figure to follow; as it rises, the case for building around them grows stronger. Designing a Store around the shoppers who actually visit it is how we build and run Amazon Stores for brands.

A0274.crumb: Target Plus advertising in 2022: bid by…
A0274.title: Target Plus advertising in 2022: bid by product, not keyword
A0274.alt: Handmade goods with blank paper tags, including a bottle, soap, tin, dried petals and yarn, on a red shelf.
A0274.ttag: Target Plus advertising in 2022: bid by product, not keyword | Kwontified
A0274.desc: Target Plus ads match each product to searches and charge the price you bid. Set every product’s bid from its own break-even and give Target its own budget.
A0274.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 23, 2022.
A0274.body:
An Amazon seller who opens a Target Plus account in 2022 tends to reach for the familiar kit: a keyword list, match types, a weekly search-term report. Then the campaign screen offers no keyword field to fill. Target’s sponsored products pick the searches themselves from the product’s own data, and the winner pays exactly what it bid, never less than a floor Target sets. That moves the work from keyword research to product-level bids. Set each product’s bid from what a click on it is worth, give Target a budget separate from Amazon’s, and read the results in Target’s own reporting.

Target Plus advertising runs on a product-matched, first-price auction

Roundel, Target’s media business, sells the sponsored products, and they run on Criteo’s retail media technology. Target used Criteo for an exclusive environment it called Private Market, in which ads appear only on target.com, Search Engine Journal explained. The same guide noted that this suited Target Plus sellers, who need to promote products with no presence in stores.

Sponsored products are bought per click in a first-price auction, and they are not keyword-based: each product is matched to searches using data from the retailer’s product feed and site. An advertiser sets a bid for a group of products and can override it for single products, but never below a floor set by the retailer. There was no spend minimum to get access. Target sets floors by category and can change them, so check the current floor in the platform before setting any bid instead of trusting a figure from an earlier season.

Agencies can reach the same inventory through software. In October 2020, Skai said it supported biddable sponsored product ads on Target.com through Roundel, using the Criteo platform’s interface, according to its announcement.

The marketplace is small, though the media business behind it is large. At the end of 2021, Target Plus had about 440 sellers by Marketplace Pulse’s count. Target said Roundel already delivered more than $1 billion in value and that it aimed to double that, WARC reported.

Keyword skill shapes the listing, and bids decide the campaign

Keyword research earns its keep on Amazon because the advertiser chooses what to bid on. On a platform that matches ads from the product’s own data, that choice belongs to the platform. What is left is which products to advertise and how much to bid for each. Keyword work still pays, but it moves upstream into the listing, because the product feed shapes which searches the ad can match.

The instinct to bring the Amazon playbook along is reasonable. Search terms are where most sellers learned retail media, and a search-term report feels like control over where the money goes. On Target, the nearest thing to that control is the product data the platform reads, so hours once spent on match types are better spent on the listing that decides which searches a product can appear against.

The auction type raises the stakes on each bid. In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid, with no discount down to the next bidder’s price. A bid set well above a product’s value is paid in full on every click. So the bid for each product belongs close to what a click on that product is worth, and no higher.

Take a Target Plus seller of home textiles with two products to advertise and a required return on ad spend of 4.

ProductPriceConversion rateValue of one click
Throw blanket$404%40 cents
Pillowcase$123%9 cents

Each value is the price times the conversion rate, divided by the return of 4 the seller needs. A single shared bid of 30 cents gets both products wrong: it underbids for the blanket and overpays on every pillowcase click. If Target’s floor for the category sits above 9 cents, the pillowcase cannot be advertised at a profit at all. Product-level overrides fix both problems. Bid near 40 cents on the blanket, and leave the pillowcase out of the campaign.

For a seller arriving from Amazon, that is the answer: keyword skill helps the listing, but the campaign is won or lost on product-level bids.

Give Target its own budget and its own scorecard

Target’s auction is smaller than Amazon’s and its shoppers are Target’s, so its returns follow their own pattern. Skai’s data from Target’s July Deal Days shows how different the pattern can be: advertisers on its platform spent 8% more per day than over the previous 30 days, and their ad-driven sales grew 28%. A budget copied from the Amazon plan would not reflect that.

Judge results on Target’s own reporting. Compare return by product, adjust bids weekly, and choose an attribution window that matches the one used for other channels, so Target’s results can be compared fairly with the rest of the plan.

The product list deserves the same care as the bids. Advertising works best on products whose listings already convert, and a seller’s best sellers on Target may not match its best sellers on Amazon. Start with the items that already sell on Target. As more sellers join Target Plus, keep an eye on the cost per click for each product; a rising floor or rising prices on key products will show the auction filling up.

The working rule for Target Plus fits in a sentence: no product gets a bid above what its click is worth, and a product whose click is worth less than the floor gets no bid at all. Setting those bids product by product, from each item’s own price and conversion rate, is how we run Target advertising for Target Plus sellers.

A0276.crumb: Winning on Walmart in 2022 without giving…
A0276.title: Winning on Walmart in 2022 without giving up margin
A0276.alt: Sliced sourdough loaf and bread knife on a wooden cutting board against a deep blue wall.
A0276.ttag: Winning on Walmart in 2022 without giving up margin | Kwontified
A0276.desc: Walmart is marking down general merchandise while its shoppers buy value. Brands that win there hold margin with pack sizes and range, not by matching price.
A0276.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 25, 2022.
A0276.body:
Walmart spent the summer of 2022 marking down its own general merchandise, and every brand selling home goods or apparel next to that clearance has had to decide whether to follow it down. Matching each markdown looks like the way to keep the sale. Mostly it hands the brand’s margin to the retailer’s inventory correction. Winning on Walmart in 2022 without giving up margin means competing on format and fit instead: pack sizes and value formats, a range led by what Walmart’s shoppers are buying, and advertising kept disciplined as more brands crowd in.

Winning on Walmart in 2022: growth from value, pressure from markdowns

Walmart’s second-quarter results show where the growth came from. Comparable sales in the United States rose 6.5% and e-commerce grew 12%, but transactions rose only 1% while the average ticket rose 5.5%, according to its earnings release. Walmart said it continued to gain market share in grocery. Its gross profit rate fell 132 basis points, mainly because of markdowns and the mix of sales.

The markdowns were deliberate. In July, Walmart said rising food and fuel prices were pushing shoppers away from discretionary items, particularly clothing, and that it would step up discounts on general merchandise such as home furnishings and electronics, the Associated Press reported. The head of Walmart’s U.S. business later said it had taken deeper markdowns in areas like apparel and home, Talk Business reported.

The advertising side is getting busier at the same time. Walmart’s global advertising business grew nearly 30% in the quarter, led by Walmart Connect, and the number of Walmart Connect advertising customers grew 121% from a year earlier, Talk Business reported.

Matching Walmart’s markdowns pays for the retailer’s correction

Read together, those figures describe a shopper buying fewer and more necessary things. Transactions barely moved while the basket got more expensive, and the growth sat in grocery. The same figures explain the clearance: Walmart is selling down general merchandise that was bought for a different kind of demand.

For a brand that sells home goods or apparel on Walmart, that sets up the decision its leadership is actually weighing: follow the retailer’s prices down, or hold them. Following feels safe, yet in practice it gives up margin on every sale and gains little, because the shopper who buys on price will often pick the clearance item anyway. The brand ends up funding Walmart’s inventory correction with its own margin.

Holding price on the same single item has a cost too, since that item now sits beside cheaper versions of itself. The way out is to stop selling the same item as the clearance rack.

The shopper does not buy on price alone. She also weighs value, meaning what she gets for the money. A larger pack with a lower unit price, a bundle that saves a trip, or a product that does a job the clearance item does not all give her a reason to spend. Each lets her pay a little more per item while paying less per use.

Take a brand of kitchen storage containers that sells a single set on Walmart, priced against marked-down sets from larger brands. Matching their prices would cut its margin by a third. Instead, it lists a larger multi-pack, priced higher in total but lower per container, and a refill pack of lids that no competitor offers. The multi-pack wins the value-seeking shopper without a price cut, and the refill pack brings back customers who already own the set. Its margin per order holds, because the brand is no longer selling the same item as the clearance rack.

Compete with format and range, and keep ad spend disciplined

Value formats do the work a price cut would otherwise do. Larger packs, multi-packs, bundles and refills let a brand show a better unit price without cutting the price of its core item, and they make direct price comparisons harder, which protects margin across channels. They only work if the shopper can see the value at a glance. Put the count and size in the title and the first image, show what is included, and list the pack in the right category so it appears next to the single items it competes with. A value format that looks like any other listing will be compared on total price alone.

The range should follow the shopper Walmart described. Food, consumables and everyday essentials are where Walmart is gaining share. Brands with products in or near those categories should lead with them on Walmart, and treat discretionary items as secondary until demand recovers.

Advertising needs the same discipline. With many more brands advertising on Walmart, click prices will rise. Bid from each product’s break-even, put spending behind value formats and essentials, and avoid paying to advertise items that only sell when discounted.

Prices across channels belong in that conversation too. Walmart shoppers compare, and a product that looks cheaper elsewhere loses the sale and the trust. Value formats help here as well, because a multi-pack on Walmart and a single item on another channel are not the same offer.

So the question to bring to the next pricing review is which of the brand’s items should never have to meet a markdown at all, and what pack, bundle or refill would let them hold their price. Walmart’s general merchandise sales in the third quarter will show how long the pressure lasts: if markdowns ease and those sales stabilize, there will be more room for discretionary items without discounting. Building Walmart ranges, value formats and advertising around how its shoppers buy is the work we do on Walmart Marketplace.

A0277.crumb: FBA restock limits for Q4 2022: give the…
A0277.title: FBA restock limits for Q4 2022: give the space to best sellers
A0277.alt: Twine-tied kraft paper parcels on rustic wooden shelves with cardboard boxes stacked below in a brick storeroom.
A0277.ttag: FBA restock limits for Q4 2022: give the space to best sellers | Kwontified
A0277.desc: Amazon’s Q4 2022 restock limits give FBA sellers at least four months of cover. Treat that space as scarce and give it to the products that earn the most.
A0277.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 30, 2022.
A0277.body:
Four months of inventory sounds like room to spare, and that is the minimum Amazon’s restock limits for the 2022 holiday season allow every FBA seller. The allowance, though, covers a storage type, not a product, so a slow seller and a fast one draw on the same space. Treated as a budget instead of a warehouse to fill, that space should go to the products that earn the most per unit stored. Ship holiday stock early, move slower sellers to your own fulfillment for the season, and rework unit economics for the new holiday peak fee.

FBA restock limits are back, with a peak fee on top

Amazon told sellers on August 29 that it was updating restock limits to prepare for the holiday season. For the standard and apparel storage types, the new limits allow all sellers at least four months of inventory in FBA, taking account of seasonality and scheduled deals, according to the notice posted on its seller forums.

Amazon has also announced its first holiday peak fulfillment fee. From October 15 to January 14, sellers using FBA in the United States and Canada will pay an average of 35 cents more per item sold, the Associated Press reported.

The fee varies by size, Supply Chain Dive reported:

Size tierFee per unit beforeFee per unit in the peak
Small standard, 6 ounces or less$3.07$3.28
Large standard, 2 to 3 pounds$6.08$6.60

That comes on top of the 5% fuel and inflation surcharge Amazon added in April. Amazon said its fulfillment fees remain 70% less expensive on average than comparable two-day shipping.

Why four months of cover still runs short

For a seller shipping steady, fast-selling products, a limit set at four months of cover is generous. The squeeze appears when a range mixes fast and slow products, because the limit applies to the account and storage type, not product by product.

Every unit of a slow seller sits in FBA longer, holding space that a fast seller could have used several times over in the same months. A seller that fills its allowance in proportion to its range will find its best sellers running short in December, while its slower products still sit on the shelf.

Filling the allowance evenly across the range feels prudent. Every product gets a fair share, and nothing is left out. Under a cap, though, each slow unit takes the place of a fast one.

The useful question, then, is which products earn the most per unit of FBA space over the season, which is a narrower test than whether a product is profitable. A product that sells quickly and carries a healthy margin returns far more per cubic foot than a slower product with the same margin.

The peak fee adds weight to that ranking. It raises the cost of every unit shipped through FBA during the season, and as a share of price it falls hardest on cheap items. A low-priced, slow-selling product now costs more to fulfill and uses space that a better seller could have used.

Take a seller with two products. A $30 gift set sells 300 units a month in the holiday period with $8 of margin per unit after fees. A $12 accessory sells 60 units a month with $2 of margin. Per unit stored, the accessory sits five times longer and earns a quarter of the margin.

If both share the same allowance, the gift set runs out in December. Suppose the seller moves the accessory to its own fulfillment for the season and gives the space to the gift set. It keeps its best seller in stock through the peak, at the cost of slower delivery on a product that matters less.

Allocate FBA space like a budget

Start by ranking products on margin per unit of space over the season. Combine each product’s expected holiday sales, its margin after the peak fee, and its size. Fill FBA from the top of that ranking down, and stop when the allowance runs out.

Timing matters as much as the ranking. With limits set as months of cover, the allowance reflects expected sales. Sending fast sellers in September and early October, before the peak, uses the space while it is available. It also reduces the risk of late check-in. Slower sellers can go to your own warehouse or a third-party logistics provider for the season, with slower delivery accepted on products that matter less, and come back to FBA in January if the economics improve.

Advertising should follow the stock. A holiday ad plan that pushes products FBA cannot hold will pay for clicks on items that go out of stock or ship slowly. Put the season’s advertising behind the products at the top of the space ranking, and pull spend from anything moved to slower fulfillment. The same weekly review that tracks stock should release or hold advertising budget, so the two plans move together rather than one undoing the other.

Then rework unit economics with the peak fee. Recalculate margin for every product from October 15 to January 14. Low-priced items may no longer be profitable through FBA at all during the peak, and their prices, pack sizes or fulfillment method may need to change.

Every product faces one test: if it cannot earn its space at holiday margins after the peak fee, it does not get the space. Should Amazon tighten allowances as the season approaches, that ranking decides what stays in stock, and building it product by product is how we plan FBA inventory and fulfillment for brands on Amazon.

A0279.crumb: A second Prime event in October 2022: who…
A0279.title: A second Prime event in October 2022: who decides whether to join
A0279.alt: Two autumn wreaths with mini pumpkins, berries and dried leaves hung on a weathered wooden door.
A0279.ttag: A second Prime event in October 2022: who decides whether to join | Kwontified
A0279.desc: Amazon has not confirmed an October Prime event, yet its deal and stock deadlines arrive first. Brands need one owner who makes the join decision now.
A0279.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 1, 2022.
A0279.body:
Amazon asked some sellers to submit Lightning Deals by July 22 for a fall Prime event it had not dated, and it has still not announced a second Prime event for October 2022. The deadlines keep arriving anyway, and brands therefore have to decide whether to join before the event is confirmed. That decision touches deal depth, inventory and advertising at once. It needs a single owner who weighs all three and decides by the earliest deadline, rather than each team committing on its own.

The second Prime event: what is reported, and what is not

In June, Amazon told some third-party sellers about a “Prime Fall deal event,” a shopping event for Prime members in the fourth quarter, and asked them to submit Lightning Deals by July 22, CNBC reported. The notice gave no dates, and an Amazon spokesperson declined to comment.

Insider later reported leaked documents describing plans for a two-day event in October called the Prime Early Access Sale, as Viral Launch summarized. Another message to sellers set a deal deadline of September 2, and sellers using Amazon’s fulfillment network were told to ship their products by September 12, Value Added Resource reported, citing Insider.

The deadlines are known and the event is not. Amazon has not confirmed the dates, the countries or how the event will be promoted, so brands are being asked to commit before they can see what they are committing to.

Two other changes bear on the decision. Amazon’s August 29 notice to sellers set holiday restock limits at a minimum of four months of inventory in its network, posted on its seller forums. Its first holiday peak fulfillment fee, which averages 35 cents per item, takes effect on October 15, the Associated Press reported.

A decision made in pieces becomes a commitment nobody chose

Where no one owns the whole call, it gets made in pieces. Whoever runs promotions submits the deals. The supply team decides what to ship and when. The advertising lead sets the budget, and finance sees the margin afterwards.

Each piece has its own deadline, and each looks small on its own. A deal submitted in July seemed like an option rather than a commitment. Stock shipped in September looks like ordinary holiday preparation. An advertising budget set in October follows whatever deals were approved.

The order in which Amazon has asked for things matters here. By requesting deals and stock before naming dates, the retailer collects its commitments early and keeps its own options open, which leaves the uncertainty with the brand. Whichever team meets the first deadline makes the first commitment, without anyone having decided that it should.

The pieces add up to a full commitment to an event nobody chose. That is how a brand ends up running deep discounts in October on products it planned to sell at full price in November, or advertising deals on products that did not arrive in time.

The October timing raises the stakes because the event sits so close to the holiday season. A discount in mid-October may pull forward sales that would otherwise have come at full price weeks later. Whether that trade is worth making depends on margin, stock and what the brand expects from November, and no single team sees all three.

Take a home goods brand whose promotions lead submitted three Lightning Deals in July. Its supply team, planning for the holidays, shipped extra stock of all three products. Its advertising lead, seeing the deals approved, planned extra spending for October. Nobody asked whether the brand wanted to sell its best seller at a 25% discount six weeks before Black Friday. Once someone did ask, the answer was no for one product and yes for the other two.

One owner, the earliest deadline, and a call for each product

The owner does not need to do every task. What they hold is the decision: whether the brand joins, with which products and at what depth. The other teams then work to that decision instead of to their own deadlines.

The call has to be made against the earliest deal and shipping deadlines, because those arrive before Amazon confirms the event. Decide with what is known, and set a review for the day the event is announced.

The decision itself runs product by product. For each candidate, weigh the discount against the margin, the stock it needs against the restock limit, and the sales it might pull forward from November. Join with the products where the event adds sales, and hold back the ones where it only moves them.

Staying out is a real option, with its own costs. During July’s Prime Day, average cost per click for Amazon advertisers on Skai’s platform rose about 50%, Skai found. A brand that skips the October event may still face higher click prices while it runs, and competitors’ deals will draw some of its shoppers’ attention. That argues for planning around the event’s days, not necessarily for joining. A brand that sits out can lower bids, protect its stock for November and let the event pass.

The decision belongs on paper. A short note listing the products, discounts, stock and budget gives every team the same plan, and gives the brand something to review after the event.

So the question to put to the team before the September 2 deal deadline is a plain one: who can say no to the October event? If the answer is nobody, the deals submitted in July have already decided for the brand. When Amazon confirms the dates and how widely it will promote the event, that owner should revisit the plan and adjust stock and advertising, the kind of Amazon event planning we do with brands.

A0282.title: Vendor Central chargebacks in a 2022 supply-chain crunch
A0282.alt: Stack of coins on a wooden dock post with a loaded container ship sailing through a misty harbor.
A0282.ttag: Vendor Central chargebacks in a 2022 supply-chain crunch | Kwontified
A0282.desc: Amazon waives its PO on-time chargeback only above a 90% on-time rate. In a congested 2022, a few late shipments can tip a vendor over that line.
A0282.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 6, 2022.
A0282.body:
A vendor that ships 46 of 50 purchase orders on time over four weeks pays nothing for the late ones. Ship 44 of 50 on time and it pays a chargeback on all six.

Vendor Central chargebacks for late purchase orders behave like a threshold rather than a fine per shipment: Amazon waives the on-time chargeback for vendors whose trailing four-week on-time rate is above 90%. In a year of congested ports and unpredictable transit, a few late shipments can push a vendor below that line and expose every late order. Confirm orders against realistic transit times, track the trailing rate weekly, and keep the documents to dispute charges applied in error.

How Vendor Central chargebacks for late orders work

Amazon charges vendors for a range of operational problems: shipments that arrive outside the purchase order window, missing or inaccurate advance shipment notices, carton and labeling errors, and units that were never confirmed. The charges come out of what Amazon pays the vendor instead of being billed separately.

The late-shipment charge is known as PO on-time accuracy. It applies when a shipment does not arrive within the purchase order’s delivery window. For prepaid freight, timeliness is measured against the carrier requested delivery date; for freight Amazon collects, against the freight ready date. Amazon waives the chargeback for vendors whose trailing four-week average on-time rate is above 90%, Chargeflow explained.

That waiver is the part most vendors overlook. A vendor above 90% pays nothing for its occasional late order. A vendor at 88% pays on each late order in the period.

Why a few late shipments now cost more than they used to

In a congested year, the cost of a single late shipment depends less on that shipment than on how close the vendor already is to the line. The threshold turns many small delays into one bill. Each late order costs nothing while the rate stays above 90%, and once it drops below, every late order in the period is charged, including the ones the waiver used to absorb.

Transit has been unusually hard to predict. U.S. container imports set a record against the prior year for the seventh consecutive month in July, and delays moved from the West Coast to major East and Gulf Coast ports, where more ships were waiting offshore, Descartes reported. Congestion at the Port of Los Angeles has eased, but supply-chain problems remain, Fortune reported.

For a vendor, that means more variation in when goods arrive. A vendor that ran at 94% on time in 2021, comfortably above the line, may find that two or three delayed containers in a month take it to 89%. At that point the waiver no longer protects it, and the charges land on every late order, not just the ones that tipped it over.

The pressure also comes from Amazon’s side. Amazon’s quarterly filing shows $38.2 billion of inventory on its books at the end of June, a figure up from $32.6 billion when 2021 closed. A retailer with full warehouses has little reason to be lenient about orders that arrive late.

Take a vendor shipping 50 purchase orders in each of two four-week periods. In the second period, two containers are held at port.

Four-week periodOrders shippedOn timeOn-time rateLate orders charged
First504692%None, the waiver applies
Second, two containers held at port504488%All six

The vendor’s operations barely changed between the two periods. Two held containers moved it from no charges to a charge on all six late orders, not just the two that were delayed at port.

Manage the margin above 90%

Confirmation is where the margin is won. When accepting a purchase order, use the transit times your shipments are actually achieving now, not the ones they achieved in 2021. If a window cannot be met, adjust the confirmation at the start rather than shipping late. A smaller, on-time confirmation protects the rate; a full confirmation that arrives late damages it.

Track the trailing four-week rate every week. Knowing how close you are to 90% tells you how much a single delay will cost. When the rate falls toward the line, move the riskiest shipments to faster lanes or earlier dates, even at some freight cost. Carriers and forwarders can help here: a container held at port is usually known about days before the delivery window closes, and a hold reported as soon as it happens leaves time to adjust confirmations or move other shipments forward.

Keep the documents to dispute charges applied in error. Bills of lading, advance shipment notices, carrier records and proof of delivery are what a dispute rests on. Without them, a charge applied in error usually stays.

Keep shortage claims on a separate line. Shortages, where Amazon pays for fewer units than the vendor invoiced, are a different deduction from operational chargebacks, and both are taken from vendor payments automatically, as Chargeflow noted. Tracked apart, a rise in one cannot hide behind the other. Busy receiving docks make gaps between what was shipped and what was recorded more likely, and the same shipping records that support a chargeback dispute support a shortage dispute.

Review chargebacks by type each month. A rise in one category, such as late orders from one port or labeling errors from one warehouse, points to the fix more directly than the total does.

The working rule is to manage the margin above 90%, because that margin decides what the next late container costs. If your trailing rate is drifting toward 90% in September, it will be harder to hold in November, and recovering chargebacks applied in error while fixing the causes of the rest is work we do for Amazon vendors.

A0283.title: Temu arrives: what an ultra-discount marketplace means for brands
A0283.alt: Wooden crate on a rustic table filled with colorful beads, toy animals, small figurines and an orange toy car.
A0283.ttag: Temu arrives: what an ultra-discount marketplace means for brands | Kwontified
A0283.desc: Temu trades price for patience: deep discounts, 7 to 15 day delivery and an unknown name. Brands are exposed where their shoppers would make that trade.
A0283.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 8, 2022.
A0283.body:
Scroll the women’s dresses on Temu in its first days in the United States and most of them cost under $20, CNBC found. The catch is the wait: delivery can take 7 to 15 business days, from a name few shoppers know yet. Temu’s arrival in September 2022 matters most to brands whose shoppers would trade delivery speed and trust for a lower price. Those brands should map their exposure category by category, defend on the speed, trust and service Temu cannot yet match, and avoid chasing its prices.

What Temu is offering U.S. shoppers

Pinduoduo, the Chinese e-commerce company, launched Temu in the United States on September 1, with no press release or public comment. The site lists clothing, jewelry, pet supplies, and home and garden goods, and most products are likely to ship from overseas, especially China, CNBC reported.

The offer is price. On launch day Temu ran a 20% discount across the site. Dresses sold for as little as $6 or $7 and earrings for less than $1, The Logic reported.

The shopper pays in time instead. Temu says shipping to the United States can take 7 to 15 business days, and it warns shoppers to expect longer deliveries than they are used to, CNBC reported. Shipping is free on orders over $49, and orders below that cost $2.99 to ship, a dollar less than Shein charges, TechNode reported.

The selection is still thin in places, and CNBC found only two products in the men’s wristwatch category. Jacob Cooke of the e-commerce firm WPIC told CNBC that Temu’s main challenges would be building trust and awareness, though it might benefit from relationships with low-cost Chinese manufacturers that have not yet sold in the United States.

Behind the site is a company used to winning on price. Pinduoduo, founded in 2015, has grown into one of China’s biggest e-commerce firms by focusing on lower-income consumers with heavily discounted products, and is worth around $87 billion, CNBC noted. A vendor who sells on Amazon told Nikkei Asia that Temu would run a trial until September 15 before full operations, and that it preferred first vendors with experience on Amazon or Shein, Nikkei reported. Many of Temu’s sellers, in other words, may already compete with brands on Amazon.

Temu takes the purchase that can wait

Temu’s launch terms say plainly what it asks of a shopper: accept a longer wait and an unfamiliar name in exchange for the price. Whether a brand should worry turns on which of its sales come from shoppers willing to accept those terms, and two kinds of purchase are worth separating.

In the first, the shopper knows what she wants, needs it soon, and cares who made it. A replacement phone charger from a known brand, a skincare product she uses every day, a gift that has to arrive by Saturday. Temu has little to offer here. Its prices are low, but it cannot promise the item will arrive this week, and the shopper has no reason yet to trust the seller.

In the second, the shopper is browsing, the item is not urgent, and the brand matters less than the look. A pair of earrings, a summer dress, a set of storage baskets, a phone case. Here, a price that is a fraction of the usual one may be worth a two-week wait.

That second kind of purchase is where Temu will take sales. It is also the kind of purchase that Shein has already been winning, which suggests there are plenty of shoppers willing to make that trade.

A brand’s exposure therefore depends less on its category name than on how its shoppers buy within it. A jewelry brand whose customers buy gifts with a deadline is less exposed than one whose customers buy everyday pieces on impulse. A home brand selling branded appliances is less exposed than one selling unbranded storage.

The effect will show in price perception before it shows in sales. A shopper who sees $7 dresses on a new app may look at a $35 dress on Amazon differently, even if she never orders from Temu.

Defend on what Temu cannot match

The exposure map comes first, built product line by product line. For each line, ask whether a shopper could find a look-alike on Temu for a fraction of the price, and whether she would wait two weeks for it. Lines where both answers are yes need a plan; lines where either answer is no can largely carry on.

The defense is speed, trust and service. Fast delivery, reviews, a clear returns policy and a brand the shopper recognizes are things Temu cannot yet offer, and they only count if the shopper sees them. Put delivery dates, review counts, materials and guarantees where they are visible on your listings.

Chasing Temu’s prices is the losing move. A brand that cuts prices to compete with products shipped directly from manufacturers will lose margin without winning the shoppers who buy on price alone. Where price matters, value formats such as multi-packs or bundles do the job without cutting the core price.

Copies of your own products deserve an early watch. A new marketplace with many first-time sellers may list look-alikes or misuse brand names, and it is easier to report them early.

Advertising will decide how fast this matters. If Temu begins spending heavily to bring shoppers in, its prices will reach many more of your customers, and the exposure map will need revisiting. The question to put to the team is which of your lines would lose a shopper to a two-week wait, and answering it across every marketplace you sell on is how we help brands decide where to compete.

A0284.title: Instagram discovery in crowded categories: show fewer products
A0284.alt: Plain kraft product box on a wooden table between ceramic vases of dried flowers against a pink wall.
A0284.ttag: Instagram discovery in crowded categories: show fewer products | Kwontified
A0284.desc: Instagram now shows more posts from accounts people do not follow. In crowded categories, a few hero products teach that system faster than a full range.
A0284.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 13, 2022.
A0284.body:
On Meta’s earnings call in July, Mark Zuckerberg said that about 15% of what people see in their Facebook feed is now recommended by its artificial intelligence from accounts they do not follow. On Instagram the share is a little higher. He expected those numbers to more than double by the end of 2023, IANS reported. For a brand in a crowded category such as beauty or apparel, that changes the arithmetic of posting.

A recommendation system can only match a brand to strangers after it has seen enough engagement around the same products. The brand that shows a few hero products again and again is therefore likely to reach more new shoppers than the brand that rotates through its whole range.

Instagram discovery now runs through recommendations and tags

The pace is uncertain; the direction is not. Days after the call, users objected to changes that filled their feeds with full-screen video and recommended posts, and Instagram said it would temporarily reduce the number of recommendations, Gigazine reported. A pause in the rollout does not change which way the feed is heading.

Shoppers have also gained a way to point at products. Product tags in feed posts, once reserved for brands and creators, opened on April 18 to everyone in the U.S. whose account is public, TechCrunch reported. Instagram said 1.6 million people tag brands in their posts every week, ChannelX reported, and the company has said product tagging in Stories is in the works. If it arrives, one product could carry tags across feed posts and Stories, from the brand and from its customers alike.

Two things are therefore moving together in 2022. More of what a shopper sees comes from accounts she has never followed, and more of what shoppers post can point to a specific product page.

Why a few hero products teach the system faster

Showing the whole range made sense when most of a feed came from accounts a person had chosen to follow. Followers already knew the brand. A new product each day gave them a reason to keep looking. That logic weakens once the audience that matters is made of strangers, because a stranger meets the brand through whatever the system decided to show her.

A recommendation system decides what to show a stranger by learning which audiences respond to which content. It learns from repeated signals: people who stop on similar posts, save them, tag the same product or buy it. The more often one product appears alongside a strong response, the faster the system learns who else is likely to respond.

In a crowded category every brand is chasing the same strangers, and that is where spreading thin costs the most. A beauty brand that posts a different product every day splits its signals across dozens of items, each with too little engagement for the system to learn much from. A brand that posts its best products repeatedly, in different settings, gives the system a clear picture of who responds to each one.

When shoppers tag a product in their own posts, they multiply the effect, adding signals from audiences the brand does not reach on its own. Customers tag what they own and like, which is usually a brand’s best sellers, so a brand that concentrates on a few hero products also concentrates its customers’ tags on them.

The arithmetic of 40 products against three

Take a skincare brand with 40 products that posts each one roughly once a month. None of them builds much engagement, and few customers tag any single item, so the system receives a long list of faint signals and learns little from any of them.

Now the same brand puts its three best sellers in front of its audience several times a week: in routines, in before-and-after shots, in reposts of customer photos. Those three gather enough saves and tags for the system to find similar shoppers. The rest of the range is then discovered from the brand’s profile, by shoppers who arrived through the heroes.

The cost is visible range: someone scrolling the brand’s feed sees fewer products. The exchange is depth on a few items for reach among people who have never heard of the brand, and for a brand whose growth depends on new customers, depth is the better side of it.

What concentration looks like week to week

Choosing the heroes is a merchandising decision before it is a content decision. The candidates are the items with the strongest reviews, repeat purchases and visual appeal, and the set should rotate with the season rather than with the day.

Every post that shows a hero should tag it, so that each view and save is tied to the same product page. Customer tags take more effort: featuring shoppers’ posts, asking buyers to tag what they bought, and keeping product names and shop listings clear enough that tagging is easy. Those tags carry the brand into audiences it cannot reach alone.

The rest of the range still needs a path. Hero products bring new shoppers to the profile, so the shop, collections and highlights should lead them on. A shopper who arrives for a best-selling serum should find the cleanser and moisturizer that go with it in one or two taps.

Measurement follows the product, not the post. Saves, tags and shop visits for each hero, tracked over a month alongside the share of reach that comes from non-followers, show whether the system is learning. A hero that is not gathering signals should be replaced rather than posted more often. Choosing those few products and reading their signals month by month is how we plan Instagram for brands in crowded categories.

A0286.crumb: Toys on Amazon in 2022: fewer toys…
A0286.title: Toys on Amazon in 2022: fewer toys, higher prices, earlier
A0286.alt: Wooden toy train, pull-along duck and spinning top on a floating shelf against a mint green wall.
A0286.ttag: Toys on Amazon in 2022: fewer toys, higher prices, earlier | Kwontified
A0286.desc: U.S. toy sales grew 2% in early 2022 as units fell 6% and prices rose 8%. On Amazon, that means fewer gifts per family and a season that starts sooner.
A0286.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 15, 2022.
A0286.body:
American families spent a little more on toys in the first half of 2022 and carried fewer of them home. U.S. toy industry sales rose 2% to $11.4 billion, while unit sales fell 6% and the average selling price rose 8% to $11.30, The NPD Group reported. That price rise came on top of increases of 6% in 2021 and 19% the year before.

For toy brands on Amazon, those figures describe a holiday with a shorter gift list. When each toy costs more, each choice carries more weight, and demand gathers around the few products that make the list. The brands that plan stock, price and advertising around their likeliest picks, and get ready earlier than usual, will be better placed than those planning for a repeat of 2021.

Toys on Amazon in 2022: what the first half showed

The growth followed two record years, in which toy sales rose 18% in 2020 and 20% in 2021, the Toy Association noted. NPD’s toy advisor, Juli Lennett, said she expected toys to keep outperforming other general merchandise categories for the rest of the year. Only 6 of the 14 industries NPD tracks grew at all in the first half.

Inside toys, the growth was narrow. Only four of the 11 toy supercategories NPD tracks were up. Plush sales rose 43%, with Squishmallows accounting for seven of the 15 best-selling toys of the period, Kidscreen reported. Sports trading cards drove a 28% rise in the explorative and other toys category, and building sets grew 8% on LEGO Star Wars and Technic.

NPD’s checkout data also showed shoppers making fewer trips to stores for toys and buying less because of higher prices, while turning increasingly to online retailers for cheaper options, Kidscreen reported. That puts Amazon closer to the center of the toy season.

A shorter list concentrates demand on a few toys

When a household buys ten gifts, there is room for the toy that was a maybe. When it buys seven, the maybe drops off. Demand gathers on the items that make the list, usually the ones a child has asked for by name or that a parent already trusts.

On Amazon, that concentration shows up in search results and in the best-seller lists. Shoppers searching for a gift tend to pick from the first products they see, and those products collect the sales and reviews that keep them on top. A toy that misses the shortlist loses more than one sale, because it also loses the reviews that would have helped it the following week.

The growth categories make the same point from the other side. Plush, trading cards and building sets all grew around a few strong properties. A toy brand with one well-known line and several lesser ones is likely to see the well-known line hold up and the rest slow down, even if the range as a whole looked healthy in 2021.

Why 2021 makes a misleading starting point

The obvious base for a holiday plan is last year, and last year was 2021, when toy sales rose 20% on top of an 18% rise in 2020. After two years like that, assuming every line will repeat its 2021 result can feel like caution rather than optimism. The first-half figures point the other way: spending held up only because prices rose, and just four of the 11 supercategories carried the growth.

Take a toy brand with eight products on Amazon: two well-known characters with strong reviews, and six newer items, all of which grew in 2021. In a year of shorter lists, the two characters may sell close to their 2021 level, while the six newer items fall well behind it. If the brand orders stock and plans advertising as though all eight will repeat 2021, it ends the season short of its best sellers and long on the rest.

An earlier season, planned around the likeliest picks

The season is also starting sooner. Amazon told sellers on August 29 that its holiday restock limits would allow at least four months of inventory in its network, according to its seller forum notice. Sellers have also been asked to submit deals and ship stock for a Prime event in October that Amazon has not yet announced, CNBC reported.

Stock is where the shortlist should show first. Most of the holiday inventory belongs behind the items with the strongest demand and reviews, with the rest of the range ordered more cautiously than 2021’s sales would suggest. Advertising follows the same logic: spending on the products that already rank well and convert keeps them at the top of search through the season, while advertising a slow item rarely puts it on a family’s list.

Timing carries more weight than in a normal year. With an October event reported and restock limits in place, holiday stock for the best sellers needs to ship in September and early October, with listings, images and reviews in order before the first deal week, and price deserves the same care. With toy prices already up 8%, a family choosing fewer gifts will notice an increase. Holding prices on the items that carry the most demand, and using bundles or value packs to show more for the money, protects their place on the list.

By early October, the gap between a brand’s best sellers and the rest of its range will show whether the list has already formed. A widening gap is the cue to move stock and advertising toward the leaders before the busiest weeks begin, and reading that gap early, across stock, price and ads on Amazon, is how we plan the holiday season with toy brands.
