A0290.crumb: October Prime event forecast: plan a…
A0290.title: October Prime event forecast: plan a fraction of July
A0290.alt: Layered naked cake topped with figs and berries beside a single cupcake on glass stands against a navy wall.
A0290.ttag: October Prime event forecast: plan a fraction of July | Kwontified
A0290.desc: Amazon has not confirmed an October Prime event, but sellers are preparing for one. Plan it as a fraction of July’s Prime Day, in three cases.
A0290.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 20, 2022.
A0290.body:
Amazon advertisers on Skai’s platform sold 4.5 times as much through ads on July’s Prime Day as on an average day in the 30 days before it. Spending quadrupled, and the average cost per click rose about 50%, Skai reported. Sellers are now preparing for a second members’ event in October that Amazon has not announced, and the easy plan is a copy of July’s.

That plan is likely to overspend. A second event in one year, held weeks before the holidays, should draw less extra demand than July while click prices still rise. The October Prime event forecast belongs in conservative, standard and reach cases, each a fraction of July, with a base budget committed now and the rest released only when Amazon confirms the event and the first day’s results arrive.

The October Prime event forecast starts from what is known

Amazon has not announced an October event. CNBC reported that in June Amazon invited some sellers to put forward Lightning Deals for a “Prime Fall deal event” in the fourth quarter, with a July 22 deadline. Follow-up messages named September 2 as the deal deadline and gave sellers who use Amazon’s fulfillment network until September 12 to ship stock, Value Added Resource reported, citing Insider.

October has worked before. When Prime Day moved to October 13 and 14 in 2020, third-party sellers’ sales passed $3.5 billion, up nearly 60% on the previous year’s event, Amazon said at the time. That event was the only Prime Day of 2020, though, rather than the second of the year.

The backdrop is also tighter than in July. In the year to August, consumer prices were up 8.3%, and core prices, which leave out food and energy, were up 6.3%, First Trust reported.

A smaller lift, bought at a similar price

Copying July is a reasonable instinct. July’s results are the freshest data a brand has, the October deals are already submitted, and the one October Prime Day on record, in 2020, did well. None of those facts describes a second event in the same year, though, and that is the event October 2022 has to be planned for.

Two forces pull against each other. On the sales side, a second event three months after the first, and just weeks before Black Friday, will draw partly on demand that would have come anyway. Some shoppers will buy gifts in October that they would otherwise have bought in November, which is the same demand arriving earlier and at a discount.

On the cost side, click prices are set by how many brands join. If most large advertisers take part, competition for clicks will rise much as it did in July, even if the extra sales are smaller. Put the two together and October looks like a smaller lift bought at a similar price.

The cases below are expressed as a share of the extra ad sales each brand saw on July’s Prime Day, so any brand can apply them to its own results. They are planning ranges, not a prediction. Their job is to size the risk before the money is spent.

CaseShare of July’s extra ad salesClick prices vs normal daysWhat has to happen
Conservative30% to 40%Up 25% to 35%Shoppers treat the event as an early look at holiday deals, not a reason to buy
Standard50% to 60%Up 35% to 45%Amazon promotes it heavily, and deal-seeking shoppers start holiday buying early
Reach70% to 80%Up 45% to 55%The event becomes the real start of the holiday season, much as October 2020 did

In the conservative case, returns on advertising fall well below July’s, because click prices rise faster than sales. In the reach case, they come close. The standard case sits between.

What each case does to a budget

Take a brand whose July Prime Day added $100,000 in ad-driven sales. The October event then adds $35,000 in the conservative case, $55,000 in the standard case and $75,000 in the reach case. A brand that budgets for $100,000 and gets $55,000 will have committed nearly twice the spending its results justify.

The numbers lean toward sizing the base budget to the conservative case. That base covers the deals already submitted and keeps the best sellers visible if the event happens.

More money should follow evidence, and two pieces of it are coming. Amazon’s announcement will show how heavily it plans to promote the event. A confirmation with a long list of deals and heavy promotion points toward the standard case, while a late and quiet one points toward the conservative case. The first day’s results settle the rest. If sales are tracking at the standard case or better, the reserve goes into day two.

November needs protecting as well. Spending October’s budget, or November’s stock, on a reach case that has not appeared leaves a brand short when shoppers come back for the gifts they did not buy in October.

Judge October against a normal week

The event should be measured on its extra sales over a normal October week, not on the two days alone, and the week after belongs in the count. If sales fall below normal once the event ends, part of the lift was pulled forward from later weeks, and the true gain is smaller than the headline. That number, not the event-day total, should set what a brand commits to the next event. A strong two-day total read on its own tends to inflate the plan for whatever comes after it.

Building the normal-week baseline before the event starts is how we forecast Amazon event budgets with brands.

A0291.crumb: Electronics on Amazon in 2022: a category…
A0291.title: Electronics on Amazon in 2022: a category that waits for deals
A0291.alt: Headphone box, a tablet in a canvas sleeve and a blank tag on a wooden shelf by a shop window.
A0291.ttag: Electronics on Amazon in 2022: a category that waits for deals | Kwontified
A0291.desc: Electronics demand fell in 2022 after two strong years, but shoppers still buy when deals appear. On Amazon, the category now lives and dies by its events.
A0291.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 22, 2022.
A0291.body:
Two reports from the summer of 2022 seem to describe different industries. At Best Buy, comparable sales fell 12.1% in the quarter to July 30, against 19.6% growth a year earlier. On Amazon’s Prime Day in July, computers and consumer electronics saw ad-driven sales rise more than tenfold among advertisers on Skai’s platform. Both are accurate. Read together, they explain how electronics on Amazon now behave.

Shoppers who bought heavily in 2020 and 2021 are replacing less and holding out for discounts. Demand sags between events and jumps during them. For brands, that argues for putting stock, deals and advertising behind the event weeks, keeping spending lean in between, and protecting margin by choosing which products to discount.

Electronics on Amazon in 2022: softer demand, deeper discounts

The clearest public read on consumer electronics in 2022 comes from Best Buy. Beyond the drop in comparable sales, revenue fell 12.8% to $10.3 billion, computing and home theater accounted for most of the decline, and operating income fell 53.5%, partly because of heavier promotions, Modern Retail reported.

The company had already warned. In July, its chief executive, Corie Barry, said that as inflation continued and consumer sentiment deteriorated, demand across the consumer electronics industry had softened further, according to the company’s update. Best Buy cut its forecast to a comparable sales decline of about 11% for the year.

On the earnings call, Barry described a promotional environment that was more intense than in 2021, and more than the company had expected, especially where inventory was ample or in excess, according to the transcript. Best Buy’s inventory at the end of the quarter was down 6% from a year earlier but up about 16% from before the pandemic, the transcript shows. The company also expected comparable sales to fall slightly more in the third quarter than in the second, Fortune reported. Neither points to a quick recovery before the holidays.

When the deals arrived, though, electronics shoppers did too. On Prime Day, advertisers in computers and consumer electronics pushed their ad spending up more than ninefold and watched ad-driven sales climb more than tenfold, and the category was among the few where return on ad spend went up, Skai found.

For many shoppers, a new gadget is a choice rather than a need

For a shopper who bought a laptop for working from home, a new television or a pair of headphones in 2020 or 2021, another one in 2022 is a choice rather than a need. A shopper who wants a better monitor can wait, especially with prices rising elsewhere in the household budget. What moves her is a reason to stop waiting: a visible discount, ideally during an event when deals are everywhere she looks.

That is how a category can be weak overall and strong on event days. Best Buy’s results show the overall picture; Prime Day shows the event days. The two fit together if the same shoppers are moving purchases out of ordinary weeks and into the weeks when prices fall.

For brands on Amazon, that changes the shape of the year. Sales between events may run well below 2021, and advertising in those weeks may struggle to pay for itself. Sales during events may hold up or even rise, as long as the brand has a competitive deal and the stock to fill it.

It also changes what discounting does. In a category where retailers are clearing excess inventory, a brand that discounts its whole range will be one of many. A brand that picks a few products for deep, well-timed deals, and keeps the rest at full price, gives shoppers a reason to buy without giving away margin on every sale.

Take a headphones brand with six products on Amazon. If it discounts all six by 15% for the whole of October, sales rise a little and margin falls on every unit. If it instead offers a 30% deal on its best seller during the October event and holds the other five at full price, it wins the event-day shoppers it most wants and keeps its margin on the rest of the range.

A year planned around the event calendar

Event weeks come first in the plan. The products a brand will discount need to be in stock in Amazon’s network before each event, and the deals need planning well ahead, since submission deadlines fall weeks before the event itself. A plan shaped like this will not fit a budget approved in even monthly slices, so the conversation with finance belongs before the first event rather than after it. Ordinary weeks get a leaner budget: bids and budgets held to the levels that pay for themselves, with the larger budget saved for event days, when shoppers are ready to buy.

The choice of what to discount deserves the most thought. Deep deals belong on a few best sellers that bring in new customers, with the rest of the range kept at regular prices, because a smaller number of strong deals stands out more than a long list of modest ones. Competitors’ inventory matters here too. Where rivals hold excess stock, they are likely to discount heavily, and a brand is better off deciding in advance whether to match them on a few products or to compete on reviews, features and delivery instead.

The clearest sign a brand’s shoppers have started waiting is its own sales between events. If those keep falling while event days hold up, the plan should follow the calendar of events rather than the calendar of months, and shaping the budget around those few weeks is how we run Amazon advertising for electronics brands.

A0292.title: Amazon Accelerate 2022: free tools only help if used
A0292.alt: Glossy red metal toolbox on a wooden workbench with chisels, a hammer and wood shavings.
A0292.ttag: Amazon Accelerate 2022: free tools only help if used | Kwontified
A0292.desc: Amazon’s Accelerate 2022 tools are free to every brand, so they create no advantage by themselves. The gain goes to brands that use them on a schedule.
A0292.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 27, 2022.
A0292.body:
Every eligible brand on Amazon can now email its repeat customers, test its bullet points and download its search data, at no cost. That is the puzzle in the tools Amazon announced at Accelerate 2022. A capability every competitor receives on the same day cannot, by itself, put one brand ahead of another. It raises the floor for the whole category.

The edge goes to brands that use the tools more often and more carefully than their rivals, and that comes down to routine. Each tool needs a fixed schedule and an owner: a monthly email to repeat customers, a standing testing calendar for best sellers, and a monthly review of search data against the brand’s own sales.

What Amazon Accelerate 2022 announced

Amazon held Accelerate, its annual seller conference, in Seattle and online on September 14 and 15. For brands, the announcements fall into email, testing and data.

On email, Amazon introduced Tailored Audiences, new audience types in its Customer Engagement tool that let brands email their repeat, recent and high-spend customers at no cost, with Amazon sending the messages, according to its announcement. The tool is in beta and is due to reach all U.S. sellers in early 2023, CNN reported. Amazon also opened Premium A+ Content to all eligible brands, saying it can lift sales by up to 20%.

On testing, Manage Your Experiments now covers bullet points and descriptions as well as titles, main images and A+ content, and can publish the winning version automatically, Amazon said. Amazon said the tool can increase sales by up to 25%.

On data, brands can for the first time download Search Query and Catalog Performance data from the Search Analytics Dashboard, with new detail at the product level, and combine it with their own business data. The Product Opportunity Explorer gains a Customer Reviews Insight feature that summarizes what reviews say about products in a category. For brands looking at Europe, Amazon’s Marketplace Product Guidance now recommends products in high demand for U.S. sellers considering France, Italy and Spain, Amazon said.

Why a free tool raises the floor for everyone

To a brand that had none of these tools the week before, they feel like an advantage, and in absolute terms they are one. The trouble is that sales are won against competitors. When a capability is free to every brand, it changes the baseline, not the ranking. If every brand in a category emails its repeat customers, tests its listings and reads its search data equally well, nobody gains ground.

Advantage goes to the brands that use the tools more often, more carefully or sooner than their rivals. A gym membership handed to every employee does not make the office fitter; the people who keep going, week after week, do.

That part is harder than it sounds. A new tool tends to get an enthusiastic first try and then fade into the list of things nobody owns. The first email to repeat customers goes out and the second does not; one listing test runs and the testing calendar never starts. The search data is downloaded once and filed.

The fade is the opening. A brand that puts each tool on a schedule, with an owner and a review, compounds small gains while competitors drift. A listing test that lifts conversion a few percent is worth little once. Run every month on the best sellers, it adds up.

How a testing calendar compounds over a year

Take a brand with ten best sellers that runs one listing test a month, rotating through the ten and keeping the winners. If half the tests produce a modest lift, every best seller has been tested within a year, and the brand’s listings are measurably better than those of a competitor that tested once in September and stopped.

The order of tests matters. The elements most likely to change conversion, such as main images and bullet points, go first, and winners can publish automatically. A short note on what each test taught keeps the next one from repeating it.

Email follows the same arithmetic. A single message to repeat customers is a promotion. A monthly message, timed to new products, refills or seasons, becomes a habit for the customer and, for the brand, a channel that costs nothing to run. Once Tailored Audiences reaches a brand’s account, the message to repeat and recent customers needs a real reason to buy each time, and opens and sales tracked by message show which reasons work.

Search data and review summaries point to the next test

The search data is most useful as a monthly comparison. Search Query and Catalog Performance data, set beside a brand’s own sales and advertising reports, shows searches where shoppers see the brand’s products but rarely buy. Those listings are the next ones to test, which ties the data review back into the testing calendar.

Review summaries belong before launches. Before a product is added, Customer Reviews Insight shows what shoppers praise and complain about in the category, and the listing and the product can be built around it. For a brand weighing France, Italy or Spain, the Marketplace Product Guidance list gives an evidence-based starting point in place of guesswork.

None of this runs without a name attached. One person responsible for each tool, reporting monthly on how many emails went out, how many tests ran and how many search reviews happened, turns a launch-week enthusiasm into a routine. That count, more than the tools themselves, predicts which brands pull ahead, and setting up that routine is how we run Amazon’s seller tools for brands.

A0294.title: Connecting digital spend to in-store sales in 2022
A0294.alt: Mossy stepping-stone path across a sunny lawn to a small stone shop with its wooden door open.
A0294.ttag: Connecting digital spend to in-store sales in 2022 | Kwontified
A0294.desc: Most retail sales still happen in stores, so a digital ad’s biggest effect can land where online reports cannot see it. Judge retail media on total sales.
A0294.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 29, 2022.
A0294.body:
At a Walmart self-checkout, the screen above the scanner can carry an ad. In January 2021, announcing Walmart Connect as the new name of its ad business, Walmart counted nearly 170,000 screens across more than 4,500 stores, including TV walls and self-checkout, according to its announcement. An ad on that screen can only pay off at the register, yet a report built only from online orders will never see that sale.

Brands that sell in stores should judge digital retail media on its effect on total sales, online and in store. Shoppers move between screens and aisles, and an online-only report undercounts the ads that send people to the shelf. The retailers that run both the ad and the register can join the two, and brands should use that closed-loop data, test it with holdouts, and stop cutting spend that looks weak online but works in the aisle.

Connecting digital spend to in-store sales starts with where shoppers buy

Online shopping is large but still a minority of retail. E-commerce accounted for 14.5% of U.S. retail sales in the second quarter of 2022, the Census Bureau reported. Most purchases still happen in a store.

Retailers with stores have built their advertising businesses around that fact. Walmart described its renamed business as a “closed loop omnichannel media company.” In March 2022, it said it was expanding measurement for all its advertising offerings, including in-store placements, it wrote.

Grocery has gone further. Kroger Precision Marketing joined Roku’s shopper data program in 2020, bringing data from 60 million households across about 2,800 Kroger stores to tie streaming TV ads to in-store and online sales, Grocery Dive reported. Earlier that year, Kroger had added an attribution tool to its self-service advertising platform to show brands the results of their spending across its properties, Grocery Dive noted.

In June 2022, Walmart and Roku began piloting shoppable TV ads, Supermarket News reported. Closed-loop store measurement is not new. What has changed is how many brands can reach it, and how many channels it now covers.

Why online reports undercount ads that drive store sales

Take a shopper who looks up a laundry detergent on her phone at home, compares a few options, and picks one up on her next store trip a few days later. The ad was seen on a screen and the purchase rung up at a register. A report that sees only online orders records an ad with few sales, even when the ad did its job.

In-store screens are the clearest case. An ad on a self-checkout screen can only ever be judged by store sales, and any report that leaves them out will score it at zero.

For a brand that sells mostly online, that gap is small. For a brand whose products are bought mostly in stores, it can be most of the story. A search ad on Walmart’s app that reminds a shopper of a cleaning product she then buys in the aisle has worked, but an online report will show it as a cost with little return.

The retailer that owns the register owns the proof

Store-based retailers stress closed-loop measurement because it is the asset they hold and others do not. They know the ad a shopper saw, through her account, and what she bought, through her card or loyalty number, so they can match the two. That match is what Walmart’s closed-loop description and Kroger’s attribution tool rest on, and it puts the evidence about store sales in the retailer’s hands.

A brand that relies on online figures alone hands that advantage back. It ends up arguing for its store-driving ads with numbers that cannot see the store, and the budget drifts toward whatever looks best online. A brand that asks for the store data, and reads it critically, keeps the decision on its own side of the table.

Reading it critically matters, because the risk runs both ways. Brands that ignore store sales cut ads that were working. Brands that accept every store sale as caused by an ad will overcount, because many shoppers would have bought anyway. Matched sales show that an exposed shopper bought; they do not show that the ad made her buy.

Take a laundry brand whose online report shows that a month of search ads on a retailer’s app drove $20,000 in online sales. The retailer’s closed-loop report shows $80,000 in store sales from shoppers who saw the ads. A holdout test, comparing similar shoppers who did not see the ads, suggests that about $30,000 of those store sales were extra. The true return sits between the online figure and the closed-loop total, and far above what the online report alone suggested.

Measurement belongs in the plan before the campaign

The practical change is to ask for store sales in every retail media report where a retailer offers closed-loop measurement, and to read online and in-store sales side by side so neither is judged alone. Holdouts, run by the retailer or a measurement partner, compare shoppers who saw the ads with similar shoppers who did not; the difference is the sales the ads caused, and it is the number budgets should rest on. Holdouts and store-sales reports are easier to set up at the start of a campaign than to reconstruct afterwards, and the retailer will need time to arrange them.

Before a brand cuts advertising that looks unprofitable online, its store sales deserve a look, because an ad that loses money online may be one of the best in the plan once the aisle is counted. When the ratio of store sales to online sales in the closed-loop reports runs high, the digital ads are mostly working in the aisle, and building budgets on that whole picture is how we measure retail media across online and store sales.

A0296.crumb: Premium A+ content in 2022: when the free…
A0296.title: Premium A+ content in 2022: when the free upgrade pays
A0296.alt: Two kraft boxes on a rustic shelf by a window, one plain and one gift-wrapped with a cream satin bow.
A0296.ttag: Premium A+ content in 2022: when the free upgrade pays | Kwontified
A0296.desc: Premium A+ is free for now, but the content it needs is not. Upgrade where traffic and margin repay production, and test before rolling out.
A0296.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. All channels
A0296.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 4, 2022.
A0296.body:
Amazon says Premium A+ content can increase sales by up to 20%, and for now it charges nothing for the modules. The video, full-width imagery and comparison charts that fill them still cost money to make, and that cost is about the same whether a product sells ten units a month or ten thousand. The return is what varies. Premium A+ content pays on products where traffic, margin and a plausible lift in conversion repay the production cost, and it rarely pays anywhere else.

That turns a free upgrade into a ranking exercise. Brands should clear the eligibility gate once, upgrade the best-trafficked products first, and test each upgrade before rolling it across the range.

What Premium A+ content offers, and who can use it

In August, Amazon opened Premium A+ content to brand owners at no cost during a promotional period, eStore Factory reported. Premium modules include video, full-width imagery, clickable question-and-answer sections, interactive comparison charts, carousels and hotspots.

Eligibility comes with a gate in two parts. Every product a brand owns must carry a published A+ Brand Story, and the brand must have had at least 15 A+ content projects approved in the past 12 months, the same report noted. The promotion is free for now; once Amazon announces a fee, brands will be able to accept or reject it, DEPT explained. At Accelerate in September, Amazon confirmed Premium A+ is available to all eligible brands and gave the up-to-20% figure, according to its announcement.

A fixed cost against a return that scales with traffic

A zero price makes the upgrade look like an easy yes. A brand that pays nothing for the modules feels it has nothing to lose by filling them, and on its best sellers that instinct holds. On the long tail of a catalog it does not. The real bill arrives from the photographer and the video editor, and it arrives for every page.

Better content can only lift conversion among shoppers who reach the page. A product with heavy traffic turns a small lift into many extra sales; a product with light traffic turns the same lift into very few. The cost of the content does not shrink to match.

Amazon’s “up to 20%” is a ceiling. A given product can see much less, or nothing, depending on how much the current page leaves out and how much a shopper needs convincing. Planning on a lift well below the ceiling is safer.

Take a product page with 10,000 visits a month, a 10% conversion rate and a $30 price. A modest 5% relative lift in conversion, well short of Amazon’s ceiling, adds 50 units and $1,500 in sales a month. If the new content costs $3,000 to produce, it repays its cost in sales within two months. It takes longer in margin terms once the cost of goods is counted. The same content on a page with 1,000 visits a month adds five units, and takes nearly two years to pay back.

PageMonthly visitsExtra units a month at a 5% liftPayback on $3,000 of content, in sales
Best seller10,00050Within two months
Long-tail product1,000FiveNearly two years

The eligibility gate carries a cost of its own. A brand with hundreds of products must publish a Brand Story on every one before it can use Premium on any. Brand Story gives shoppers a way to browse the range, so the work is rarely wasted, but it needs planning as a project rather than a box to tick.

The fair comparison is Premium against a better basic page. Sharper images and clearer copy in the standard modules cost less to produce and may capture much of the same lift on products with modest traffic. There is a timing risk as well. The promotion is free now, but a brand that builds its whole catalog around a feature whose price is not yet known is betting on that price.

Rank the catalog before spending on content

The ranking starts with numbers the brand already has. Monthly page visits, conversion and margin for each product give a list, and the upgrade runs down it until a plausible lift no longer repays the cost of the content. The gate gets cleared once, well: a simple Brand Story across the catalog and at least 15 approved A+ projects in the past 12 months, done as one piece of work rather than piecemeal.

Testing comes before any rollout across the range. Manage Your Experiments can test A+ content, so the Premium page can run against the current one on a few best sellers before the range is upgraded, and only the winners stay.

The content itself should answer what shoppers already ask. Reviews and customer questions show what the current page fails to answer, whether size, fit, ingredients or how a product compares with the next one up. Amazon’s new Customer Reviews Insight feature, announced in September, summarizes what reviews say across a category, Amazon said. A question-and-answer module or comparison chart that settles the most common doubt is more likely to lift conversion than a lifestyle image repeating what the main photos already show.

Reusing the content shortens the payback. A product video made for Premium A+ can serve in Sponsored Brands video ads and on social channels, which spreads its cost across more uses. After the first month, the conversion rate on upgraded pages decides the next step: if it moved, the upgrade extends down the list, and if it did not, the content budget goes to better images on the basic page. Ranking pages this way before any content is shot is how we plan Amazon product-page content for brands.

A0297.title: Counterfeit pressure in beauty: brand protection as strategy
A0297.alt: Two cut-glass stoppered bottles, one with pink liquid and one clear, on a stone ledge against a pink wall.
A0297.ttag: Counterfeit pressure in beauty: brand protection as strategy | Kwontified
A0297.desc: Beauty is easy to fake and costly to get wrong, and a fake’s bad review lands on the real listing. Treat brand protection as strategy, not a cleanup.
A0297.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 6, 2022.
A0297.body:
A shopper opens a serum she ordered on Amazon, finds the scent is off and the texture thin, and leaves a one-star review. If that jar came from a counterfeiter, the review still lands on the genuine product’s page, where the next shopper reads it and decides the brand is not as good as she heard. In beauty, a fake costs far more than the sale it took.

That is why brand protection works best as a continuing strategy rather than an occasional cleanup. Beauty products are small, valuable and easy to imitate, and the damage from a fake shows up in the reviews and ratings that every other part of a brand’s Amazon business depends on. Brands should control who sells their products, put Amazon’s protection tools on their most copied items, and read their reviews for signs of fakes before the damage spreads.

Brand protection on Amazon: a stronger, but not complete, defense

Amazon has spent heavily on keeping fakes out. In 2021, it invested more than $900 million and employed more than 12,000 people to protect its store from fraud and counterfeits, up from more than $700 million and 10,000 people in 2020, according to its Brand Protection Report. It stopped more than 2.5 million attempts to create fraudulent selling accounts, and seized and disposed of more than 3 million counterfeit products.

Brands are using the tools. Brand Registry grew to more than 700,000 active brands in 2021, up 40%, while the average number of valid infringement notices each brand submitted fell 25%, Amazon said. Transparency, which places a unique code on each unit, protected more than 500 million product units, the report said. Amazon’s Counterfeit Crimes Unit sued or referred more than 600 criminals for investigation in the United States, Britain, the European Union and China, an increase of more than 300% from 2020.

Beauty has been part of that fight. In 2020, Amazon and KF Beauty jointly sued four companies and 16 individuals for selling counterfeit versions of its WUNDER2 products, using a shell company in Wyoming, with at least one defendant in Shenzhen, BeautyMatter reported. Those figures describe a store working hard at the problem. They do not describe one where a beauty brand can leave the problem to the store.

A fake serum does more harm than a fake handbag

A fake handbag disappoints; a fake serum can hurt. That difference raises the stakes for every beauty listing. The products themselves make easy targets: small, light and valuable, with packaging that can be copied more cheaply than the formula inside.

If the copy is good enough to pass as the real thing, what the shopper experiences is a product that looked right and felt wrong, and the natural conclusion is that the product is weaker than its reputation. She judges the brand, not the seller.

The review outlives the counterfeiter

The bigger cost comes after the sale. When several sellers offer the same product on one listing, a shopper who receives a fake leaves her review on the real product’s page. The next shopper reads it and decides not to buy. A single counterfeit order can cost a brand many later sales, and the review stays long after the counterfeit seller is gone.

Take a skincare brand whose best-selling cleanser is offered by several sellers. One unauthorized seller sources fakes, and over a month a handful of shoppers receive them and leave one-star reviews describing an odd smell and a rash. The brand’s rating slips, conversion falls, and advertising becomes more expensive for every sale, long after the seller is removed.

Seen that way, brand protection is not a legal side task. It guards the reviews, ratings and trust that the rest of the business is built on.

Protection built into how a brand sells

The first line is knowing who sells. A map of every seller offering a brand’s items, marked authorized or not, shows where stock is leaking out of the brand’s own distribution to unauthorized sellers, and closing those leaks leaves fewer places for a fake to enter a listing. The same map should cover every channel that carries the products, not just Amazon, because a counterfeiter removed from one marketplace can reappear on another, and the same evidence can support reports on each.

The strongest tools belong on the most copied products. Brand Registry is the starting point, and Transparency earns its cost on the items counterfeiters target most, usually the best sellers. Coding every unit costs money, so the risk ranking decides where to start.

Reviews are the early warning. Complaints about smell, texture, packaging or reactions that do not match the product are worth reading closely, and test purchases from unfamiliar sellers can confirm a suspicion. Confirmed fakes should go to Amazon quickly with evidence: test-purchase receipts, photos of packaging and lot numbers make reports faster to resolve and stronger if they lead to joint legal action.

A reply on the review, explaining how to recognize the genuine item and offering help, reaches every shopper who reads it after. Where packaging is easy to copy, marks that are harder to imitate, such as batch codes, seals or the Transparency codes shoppers can scan themselves, raise the bar.

Patterns deserve escalation more than single cases. When the same seller, address or listing keeps appearing, a documented case gives Amazon something to act on, and Amazon has shown it will act jointly with brands against organized counterfeiters.

The question for a beauty brand’s leadership is who owns this work week to week, because a sudden drop in a best seller’s rating, with complaints about authenticity, is often the first sign a counterfeiter has found the brand. Giving that watch a clear owner, and pairing it with the seller map, is how we protect beauty brands’ listings and reviews on Amazon.

A0298.crumb: Planning for a cookieless web: retail…
A0298.title: Planning for a cookieless web: retail media’s closed loop
A0298.alt: A coiled natural fiber rope rests on weathered dock planks beside a blue wooden boathouse by the water.
A0298.ttag: Planning for a cookieless web: retail media’s closed loop | Kwontified
A0298.desc: Retail media’s closed loop runs on logged-in shoppers, not cookies, so it gains value as tracking fades. Pay for what it proves, not for what it attributes.
A0298.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 11, 2022.
A0298.body:
Meta has said Apple’s rule requiring apps to ask permission before tracking users would reduce its 2022 revenue by about $10 billion, CNBC reported. Retail media does not depend on that kind of tracking. A retailer’s closed loop runs on signed-in shoppers and its own sales records, so as cookies and app tracking fade, it becomes one of the few places an advertiser can still tie an ad to a purchase.

That makes it more valuable, and the value will not stay with brands for long. Retail media is sold largely by auction, and rising demand raises its price. Brands should move budget toward it only on evidence of incremental sales, buy retailers’ audiences off their own sites with care, and build their own first-party relationships alongside.

The cookieless web is arriving in stages

The signals advertisers have relied on are weakening one at a time. Apple began requiring apps to ask permission before tracking users in 2021. On the web, Google has delayed its plan without abandoning it. On July 27, it said it would begin phasing out third-party cookies in Chrome in the second half of 2024, after earlier targets of 2022 and then 2023, 9to5Google reported. It expects its replacement tools, the Privacy Sandbox, to be generally available by the third quarter of 2023.

Nobody yet knows how well those replacements will measure sales compared with cookies. Until they prove themselves, advertising that can tie an ad to a purchase without cross-site tracking will look safer to budget holders.

Retail media is growing through this. Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 18% to $8.76 billion in the second quarter, MediaPost reported, and Walmart’s global advertising business grew nearly 30%, Talk Business reported.

Why a more valuable loop leaves brands less of the value

A retailer’s closed loop works differently from cookie-based advertising. The shopper is signed in. The retailer sees the ad she was shown and the purchase she made in its own systems, with no need to follow her across other websites. Removing third-party cookies does not break that link. A brand that can no longer tell whether a social ad led to a sale can still see whether a search ad on a retailer’s site did, and budgets tend to follow measurement.

The auction is what turns that advantage into a price. When more brands move budget into the same placements, they bid against each other, and the cost of a click rises until much of the advantage has passed to the retailer. No single brand chose to overpay; each one bid what the better measurement seemed to justify, and together those bids set a higher price. The brands that keep the most of the value are the ones that measure most carefully, not the ones that move first.

The loop also has edges: it sees only purchases made with that retailer. A shopper who sees a brand’s ad on one retailer’s site and buys the product somewhere else, or in a store the retailer cannot match, does not appear. Each retailer’s report is complete within its own walls and blind outside them, so no single loop can tell a brand what its total advertising achieved. A brand selling across several retailers has to compare loops rather than trust any one of them alone.

Attributed sales are not caused sales

A closed loop records that a shopper who saw the ad went on to buy. Whether the ad caused the purchase is a separate question the loop cannot answer on its own. Retail media ads often reach shoppers already searching for the product. A brand that pays for attributed sales without asking how many would have happened anyway will see rising prices hidden behind flattering reports.

Take a brand that moves $50,000 a month from social advertising to a retailer’s search ads because the retailer reports a 4.0 return on ad spend. A holdout test then shows that only half of the attributed sales were extra. The true return is 2.0, which may still beat the social campaign, or may not. The decision rests on the second number, and the first one would have made it for the brand.

Where the budget should move, and where it should not

Proof of incremental sales is the condition for shifting budget toward retail media. Holdout or lift tests from the retailer give the incremental return, and that figure, compared with what the brand’s other channels deliver, shows whether the gap is real.

Retailers’ audiences off their own sites need the same care. Large retailers now sell advertising across other websites, targeted with their shopping data; Walmart partnered with The Trade Desk in 2021 to build its own platform for this, Fox Business reported. That reach is useful, but its measurement depends on how well the retailer can connect an ad seen elsewhere to a purchase on its own site, so it should be tested before it is scaled.

A brand’s own customer list, website and email program are the only signals it fully controls. Retail media data stays with the retailer, so those first-party relationships gain value as everyone else’s tracking weakens.

The price deserves its own line in the report. Cost per click on each retail network, tracked over time, shows when competitors have arrived: if it rises faster than the incremental return, the advantage is passing to the retailer. Chrome’s change is two years away, but Apple’s already applies, and the brands that learn to measure incrementally now keep more of the closed loop’s value later. Planning retail media budgets on that incremental return is how we manage retail media for brands.

A0301.crumb: Cyber Week 2022: who decides, and how the…
A0301.title: Cyber Week 2022: who decides, and how the event sets the calendar
A0301.alt: Wrapped gifts, a leather journal, a mug and a candle sit on a wooden table by a garden window with cane chairs.
A0301.ttag: Cyber Week 2022: who decides, and how the event sets the calendar | Kwontified
A0301.desc: Cyber Week forces deal, stock and budget decisions six weeks before demand is known. Name one owner and decide the three together, from the margin floor up.
A0301.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 13, 2022.
A0301.body:
Black Friday falls on November 25, 2022, and Cyber Monday on November 28. About six weeks before either, a brand selling on Amazon has to settle how deep its deals will go, how much stock will sit in Amazon’s network, and how much it will spend to promote both, without knowing what demand will be. The question in front of leadership is less which numbers to pick than who picks them.

When finance, supply chain and marketing each make one of those calls on their own, the plans rarely fit together. Cyber Week 2022 needs one owner who decides the three together, starting from a margin floor, and who works backward from November 25 to set the date each decision becomes final.

Cyber Week 2022 arrives in a slower, more deal-driven season

The season around the event is expected to be slower than 2021’s. Deloitte forecast that holiday retail sales would rise 4% to 6%, against 15.1% growth in 2021, with e-commerce up 12.8% to 14.3%, according to its forecast. Higher prices mean shoppers will buy fewer gifts for the same money, Fortune reported.

Shoppers are also starting earlier. During Amazon’s October event, 43% of shoppers surveyed had also shopped other early holiday sales, and the average order in the first 30 hours was $45.90, Numerator reported.

The deadlines arrive well before the event. For some sellers, the deadline to submit Lightning Deals for Black Friday fell in early September, eStore Factory reported. Amazon’s holiday peak fulfillment fee, averaging 35 cents per item, starts on October 15, the Associated Press reported, and restock limits shape how much stock can be in Amazon’s network when the event begins.

Three decisions, three natural homes

Each of the three Cyber Week decisions has a natural home inside a brand. Deal depth sits with finance, because it decides the margin the brand gives up. Stock sits with supply chain, because it lives with lead times and inbound dates. The advertising budget sits with marketing, because it owns the biggest media week of the year.

Left to work separately, each team is reasonable on its own terms. Each is also planning for a different week: finance for a deal that protects margin, supply chain for the demand it saw in 2021, marketing for the demand it hopes to create.

The failures that follow are easy to picture. A deep deal on a product sells out on Friday and leaves Cyber Monday with nothing to promote. A large advertising budget sits behind a modest discount that does not move shoppers. Stock arrives for a deal that finance later decides it cannot afford.

Better forecasting will not close that gap, because nobody knows in mid-October what demand will be on November 25. Making the three decisions together will, by sizing all three to the same guess.

Take a brand that offers 30% off its best seller for Cyber Week. Finance approves the discount, but supply chain ordered for a 15% deal and 2021’s demand. The deal sells out by Saturday, the advertising runs on through Cyber Monday against an out-of-stock page, and the brand pays for clicks it cannot convert.

The owner, the margin floor and the backward calendar

That is the decision leadership is really facing: who has the authority to say, in one sentence, this is our deal, this is the stock behind it, and this is the budget to promote it, and who answers for all three. Finance, supply chain and marketing still advise; one person decides.

The decisions run in a fixed order. The brand first agrees the lowest margin it will accept on each product, then sets deal depth above that floor, sizes stock to the demand the deal implies, and sets the budget to promote what the stock can support. Working backward from November 25 gives each decision a final date: deal approval, the last shipment that will reach Amazon’s network in time, and the advertising plan. Those dates are fixed once set.

The owner’s working document can be a single page: the margin floor by product, the stock that can still reach Amazon’s network, and the budget that stock can carry, read side by side rather than in three separate decks.

Stock is the hardest of the three to reverse: a budget can be cut in an afternoon and a deal can sometimes be changed, but stock that misses the last inbound date for Amazon’s network will not arrive in time. A small reserve of budget and, where possible, stock held outside the event plan lets the owner respond if demand runs ahead of the guess or falls short of it.

Every channel, and October as a guide

Amazon is not the only retailer running a Cyber Week, and Target and Walmart have run, or are still running, early holiday events of their own in October 2022. A deal on one marketplace can pull shoppers from another, and stock committed to Amazon’s network cannot easily be moved to fill a Walmart order. The owner needs the plan for each channel side by side, so a deal on one does not quietly starve another.

October is also the best calibration a brand has. Products that responded strongly to a discount during Amazon’s October event, measured against a normal week, are better candidates for a deep Cyber Week deal than products that did not. On Black Friday itself, sell-through on the best seller tells the owner whether the guess was right: if it is running out by midday, budget moves to the products that still have stock before Cyber Monday arrives. Giving one person that call, across deals, stock and advertising, is how we plan Cyber Week with brands.

A0305.title: How installments change Latin American ecommerce economics
A0305.alt: A sliced margherita pizza with tomatoes, mozzarella and basil sits on a wooden board in warm sunlight.
A0305.ttag: How installments change Latin American ecommerce economics | Kwontified
A0305.desc: In Latin America, shoppers judge price by the monthly payment, and someone pays for interest-free installments. Price for the installment, budget its cost.
A0305.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 20, 2022.
A0305.body:
On a Brazilian listing, the price rarely stands alone. Under it sits the offer that shoppers weigh alongside it: twelve payments, “parcelado sem juros,” without interest. In Mexico the same promise reads “meses sin intereses.” A product offered in twelve interest-free payments can feel cheaper than the same product at a lower price paid all at once.

That habit changes the economics of Latin American ecommerce. The interest-free months are free only to the shopper; the cost of financing them is paid by the seller or the marketplace. Brands selling on Mercado Libre should price for the installment, treat the financing fee as part of the product’s cost, and revisit installment terms whenever interest rates move.

Installments in Latin American ecommerce run through the largest marketplace

Mercado Libre is where most brands meet this question first. In the second quarter of 2022, its gross merchandise volume reached $8.6 billion, up 26.2% on a currency-neutral basis, with a record 40.8 million unique buyers, according to its results. Its fintech arm, Mercado Pago, processed $30.2 billion in payments, and its credit portfolio reached about $2.7 billion, Reuters reported.

Financing is built into how the marketplace sells. In its letter to shareholders, Mercado Libre said it had adjusted the financing fees it charges merchants in Brazil at the start of 2022 to reflect higher interest rates, according to the letter. An executive told Bloomberg Línea that the company absorbs much of the rate increase itself and pays sellers in a single installment, Bloomberg Línea reported.

Rates are the reason this matters now: Brazil’s central bank raised its benchmark Selic rate from 2% in March 2021 to 13.75% in August 2022, and held it there on September 21, MercoPress reported.

Household budgets are stretched at the same time. Annual inflation in Brazil was 8.73% in August, well above the central bank’s 3.5% target, AFP reported. When prices rise faster than incomes, spreading a purchase over many months matters more to shoppers, which makes installments harder for sellers to withdraw just as they become more expensive to offer.

Why the monthly figure wins the comparison

The installment offer changes how a listing competes. Two sellers can offer the same item at the same price, and the one with more interest-free months shows the smaller monthly figure. For a shopper whose card limit or monthly budget is tight, the number of months can matter more than the total, and a seller that offers fewer months is asking her to stretch further for the same product.

That is the shelf as the shopper sees it. A department store sorts its floor by price band, while a Mercado Libre search result, read through the installment line, sorts by what each month will cost. A brand that sets its terms without looking at that line is pricing for a comparison its shoppers are not making.

The interest-free month has a price, and the central bank sets it

Interest-free is free only to the shopper. The money still has to be advanced for ten or twelve months, and someone pays for that. On Mercado Libre, sellers who offer interest-free installments pay a financing fee, and the marketplace absorbs part of the cost. When interest rates were near zero, that fee was modest. With Brazil’s benchmark rate above 13%, funding a year of payments costs far more.

An installment offer therefore behaves like a discount whose size depends on the central bank. It raises demand the way a price cut does, and its cost rises and falls with rates. A brand that set its installment terms in 2021 and never revisited them may be giving away much more in 2022 without changing anything on the listing.

Take a kitchen appliance brand selling a product for R$1,200 in Brazil, offered in twelve interest-free payments of R$100. The financing fee for twelve months was 5% of the price when rates were low, about R$60 per unit. With rates higher, the fee for the same twelve months rises to 10%, about R$120. The listing looks identical to shoppers, but the brand’s margin on each unit has fallen by R$60.

Pricing for the payment, and carrying its cost

The pricing decision starts from the monthly figure. A brand decides which installment amount it wants shoppers to see, then sets the price and number of months to reach it, and tests whether more months raise conversion enough to justify what they cost.

The financing fee belongs in product cost, on the same line as fulfillment and marketplace commission, product by product. Every later decision about price, promotion and advertising should start from that true contribution. Terms also need a regular review. When the central bank raises or cuts rates, the cost of every month offered without interest changes, so terms deserve a look each quarter, shortened or lengthened by price tier rather than across the range. Higher-priced items, where the full price is a barrier, usually gain the most from longer terms; on low-priced items the shopper often pays in full anyway, and the fee buys little.

The competitive check is simple to run and easy to skip in a busy quarter. If rivals give shoppers twelve months and a brand gives them six, shoppers see the difference in the monthly figure before they see anything else, so the leading listings in each category deserve a monthly look. Conversion by number of months shows where the line falls: once adding months stops raising conversion, the extra months cost margin without adding sales. Setting price and terms against that line, market by market, is how we run Mercado Libre and other Latin American marketplaces for brands.

A0306.title: Prime Early Access Sale 2022, measured against the forecast
A0306.alt: A brass caliper measures a small twine-tied kraft paper parcel on a wooden table among autumn leaves and acorns.
A0306.ttag: Prime Early Access Sale 2022, measured against the forecast | Kwontified
A0306.desc: Estimates put Amazon’s October event at three-quarters of July’s sales, which lands its extra demand in our standard case. The grade, and what is unknown.
A0306.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 25, 2022.
A0306.body:
Bank of America’s Justin Post estimated that Amazon’s Prime Early Access Sale generated $8 billion in gross merchandise volume, 25% less than the $10.7 billion he estimated for July’s Prime Day, Retail Dive reported. That reads as three-quarters of July. It is not the number a brand should grade its event on.

Once the sales Amazon would have made on any two ordinary days are taken out, the October event’s extra demand lands in the standard case of our forecast, and probably in its lower half. The grade is provisional. Click prices and pulled-forward sales are not yet visible, so brands should grade their own event against a normal October week and wait for November’s first weeks before calling the lift added sales.

What the Prime Early Access Sale 2022 delivered

Amazon itself gave no sales total for the event. It said tens of millions of Prime members shopped the October 11 and 12 event and ordered more than 100 million items from independent sellers, according to its announcement. Numerator put the average order at $46.68, nearly 23% below July’s, Retail Dive noted.

Shoppers were not finished buying, either. Only 29% of shoppers Numerator surveyed said they used the sale to buy holiday gifts, and 95% said they were likely to buy more gifts on Amazon as the season continued, Retail Dive reported.

Our forecast for the event set out three cases. Each was a share of the extra ad sales a brand saw on July’s Prime Day: a conservative case of 30% to 40%, a standard case of 50% to 60%, and a reach case of 70% to 80%.

Why 75% of July does not mean the reach case

The tempting read is to take the Bank of America figure as 75% and call the reach case. The pull is understandable: it is the only hard-looking number available, and it sits right next to the top of the forecast’s range. But a ratio of total sales is not a ratio of extra sales. Both events include the sales Amazon would have made on any two ordinary days, and removing that shared baseline pulls the October event’s share of July’s extra demand below 75%.

How far it falls depends on the baseline, which no public source states. Amazon does not publish it. With illustrative figures only: if a normal two days are worth $4 billion, July added $6.7 billion and October added $4 billion, about 60% of July’s extra demand. If a normal two days are worth $5 billion, July added $5.7 billion and October $3 billion, about 53%.

Normal two days (illustrative)October’s extra demand as a share of July’sWhere it lands
$2 billionAbout 69%Near the reach case
$4 billionAbout 60%Top of the standard case
$5 billionAbout 53%Lower half of the standard case
$6 billionAbout 43%Close to the conservative case

The middle two rows are the likelier ones. Across plausible baselines, the result sits in the standard case, and more likely its lower half than its upper. Only extreme assumptions move it out, and neither the smallest nor the largest baseline in the table seems likely for a business of Amazon’s size. The range is still a reminder that the grade rests on an estimate, not a disclosed figure.

The forecast got the shape right: an October event coming three months after July, and weeks before the holidays, drew less extra demand than the first. What it could not settle in advance was how much less, which is why it gave three cases rather than one.

The two numbers still missing

Neither will be known for weeks. Both could move the grade.

Click prices are the first gap. The forecast expected them to rise 35% to 45% over normal days in the standard case, and no public data on October click prices has appeared yet. If they rose as much as in July, returns on advertising fell further than sales did.

Pull-forward is the second. Some of October’s extra sales would otherwise have come in November. Shoppers’ answers suggest much of the season is still ahead of them. The test is what brands sell in the next three weeks. If sales run below normal after the event, part of the lift was borrowed.

Grading your own event

A brand’s own grade starts from a normal October week, not from July’s totals. Each product’s two event days, set against its average from the weeks before the event, give that brand’s share of extra demand, which is the number the forecast was built on.

Click prices belong in the same grade. The event’s extra ad-driven sales against its extra ad spend capture how far click prices rose, and a brand whose sales landed in the standard case but whose click prices rose like July’s will find its return closer to the conservative case.

The lift is only added sales once the following weeks are in. Sales from October 13 through early November, tracked against the same weeks’ usual pattern, show any dip below normal, and that pulled-forward share comes off before the event is judged.

The result then feeds Cyber Week. A brand whose October lift held up through November has evidence that its deals add demand. A brand whose lift was mostly borrowed should plan smaller deals and keep more stock for the weeks around Black Friday. Quarterly advertising data, due in the coming weeks, will show how much click prices rose during October and complete the grade, and grading events against ordinary weeks rather than headline totals is how we grade Amazon events for brands.

A0308.title: What Prime Early Access Sale 2022 revealed about retail behavior
A0308.alt: Three plain kraft paper shopping bags sit on a wooden park bench beside a path covered in autumn leaves.
A0308.ttag: What Prime Early Access Sale 2022 revealed about retail behavior | Kwontified
A0308.desc: Three retailers ran sales in one October week, and shoppers treated them as one event. A deal is now a cross-retailer decision, so plan it that way.
A0308.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 27, 2022.
A0308.body:
In one October week of 2022, Target’s Deal Days, Walmart’s Rollbacks and More sale and Amazon’s Prime Early Access Sale ran back to back, with Walmart’s overlapping Amazon’s two days. The calendar put three retailers’ events side by side, and the event that carried Amazon’s name was only one door into the same week.

That is the lesson worth keeping. Retailers now compete on the calendar, and shoppers compare across stores within days, so a brand’s deal on one retailer is really a decision about all of them. Each deal belongs in a plan that covers every retailer carrying the product.

Prime Early Access Sale 2022 was one of three sales in a week

The scoreboard has been covered elsewhere. Amazon reported that its two-day event on October 11 and 12 drew tens of millions of Prime members, according to its announcement, and outside estimates put it below July’s Prime Day.

What matters more for planning is what surrounded it. Target ran Deal Days from October 6 to 8, and Walmart held its Rollbacks and More sale from October 10 to 13, overlapping Amazon’s two days, ConsumerAffairs reported. Target also started its holiday price match guarantee on October 6, promising to match its own lower prices through December 24, Fox 32 reported.

Shoppers used all three: in Numerator’s early survey, 43% of Prime Early Access shoppers had also shopped other early holiday events. Baskets were small: orders in the first 30 hours averaged $45.90, and 44% came to $20 or less, Numerator reported. Just 29% reported buying holiday gifts during the sale, Retail Dive reported.

A week of clustered sales becomes one market

When retailers hold events this close together, the week behaves like a single market. A shopper who has already looked at one retailer’s deals can check another’s the same day, and the event’s name gives her no reason to buy in one place rather than another. The retailer that wins her is the one with the right product at the right price when she looks.

The retailers’ own choices fit that reading. Each scheduled its sale near the others, because an event held alone gives shoppers a reason to wait for the rival’s. Target added a price match to remove the fear of buying too early. Walmart’s sale ran across both of Amazon’s days. The calendar itself has become a place where retailers compete.

Inside a brand, that market has no single owner. When each retailer has its own account lead, judged on that retailer’s numbers, nobody is paid to notice that a win on Amazon was a loss at Walmart in the same week. The cross-retailer view needs someone above the account level who is measured on the brand’s total.

What that does to a brand’s deal

For brands, the change is in what a deal is. A brand that offers 30% off on Amazon for two days while its product sits at full price on Walmart and Target has not simply run an Amazon promotion. It has told cross-shoppers where to buy, and it may have pulled sales from its other retailers rather than adding new ones. A brand that discounts everywhere at once may hand back margin on purchases that would have happened at full price anyway.

Take a kitchen brand selling the same blender on Amazon, Walmart and Target. It runs a 25% Amazon deal during the October event and leaves the other retailers unchanged. Its Amazon sales double for two days, but its Walmart and Target sales fall by a third that week as cross-shoppers move. Across all three retailers, the event added much less than the Amazon report suggests.

Pricing across channels also carries scrutiny. California’s attorney general sued Amazon in September, alleging that it penalizes sellers who offer lower prices on other sites; Amazon denied the claims, NPR reported. Whatever the outcome, a brand needs to know how each retailer responds to price differences before it plans event deals.

Planning the week rather than the event

The planning unit is the whole window. When retailers cluster their sales, every event in the window goes on one map, and the brand decides product by product where and when each deal will run. The map can be a single grid, with products down the side, retailers and event days across the top, and the deal depth in each cell, so a gap or a clash shows at a glance.

The scorecard changes with it. An event is judged by its effect on the brand’s sales everywhere, not by one retailer’s report, and if one retailer gained while the others fell, the deal moved demand rather than creating it.

Leading on one retailer can still be the right call, for example to win a best-seller badge or new customers. When it is, the other retailers’ advertising and stock need adjusting for that week. Advertising on the others during the event days may be bidding for shoppers who are about to buy elsewhere. Lower bids there, and a shift of that budget toward the retailer running the deal, keep the spend where the sale will happen. Each retailer’s rules on lower prices elsewhere, and how its price matching works, belong in the same plan, so an event deal does not cause trouble on another channel.

The tell comes from the other stores: if a brand’s sales on other retailers fall during each event while one rises, its shoppers are comparing, and the next event plan should cover every channel at once. Building that plan across Amazon, Walmart and Target together is how we run event deals for brands without one retailer quietly costing another.

A0311.crumb: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2022 changes for…
A0311.title: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2022 changes for advertisers
A0311.alt: An open cardboard box holding a folded knit blanket and dark vase sits on a wooden desk beside a mug and notebook.
A0311.ttag: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2022 changes for advertisers | Kwontified
A0311.desc: unBoxed 2022 made video, setup and analysis easier for every advertiser. When tools are shared, the edge moves to creative and to measurement.
A0311.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 1, 2022.
A0311.body:
Two brands launch new serums on Amazon in the same week. Both accept the recommended daily budget and bidding strategy from the new Sponsored Products presets, and both build their videos from the same Video Builder templates. Their first month looks almost identical, which is the point worth noticing about the tools Amazon announced at unBoxed 2022.

Video templates, preset campaign settings and wider use of Amazon Marketing Cloud make advertising easier for everyone. That is exactly why they stop being an advantage once competitors adopt them. The edge moves to what the tools cannot supply, distinctive creative and rigorous measurement, so presets work best as a floor, real video earns its cost, and analysis belongs in Amazon Marketing Cloud.

What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2022 announced

Amazon Ads held unBoxed in New York in late October, and its announcements on October 26 fell into video, automation, and measurement and reach.

On video, Sponsored Display video creative became available worldwide, and Amazon expanded a public beta of Video Builder, which provides templates for Sponsored Brands and Sponsored Display videos, Amazon Ads said.

On automation, Sponsored Products campaigns with presets now appear in the ads console for new U.S. products, recommending daily budgets and bidding strategies, Amazon Ads said.

On measurement and reach, Amazon Marketing Cloud added Sponsored Display events, more pre-built queries and DSP audience management, and its active customers have quadrupled in a year, MediaPost reported. Sponsored Display is opening to brands that do not sell on Amazon, in a closed beta on Twitch, and digital signage ads in Amazon Fresh stores arrive through Amazon DSP in November.

The business behind them is still growing. Advertising revenue at Amazon climbed 25% to $9.5 billion in the third quarter, GeekWire reported, even as the company forecast slower fourth-quarter sales. It projected fourth-quarter revenue of $140 billion to $148 billion, the slowest holiday growth in its history, The Boston Globe reported. More advertisers chasing slower demand is a recipe for higher prices per sale.

Why easier tools make the race harder to win

For a brand launching its first products, presets genuinely help. They replace guesswork with Amazon’s own recommendation and get a campaign live the same day, and a template turns a video from a production project into an afternoon’s work. The gain is real at the start. It fades as soon as the brand’s competitors take the same shortcut.

When every brand gets a preset budget and bid strategy, campaigns built from presets converge. They bid similarly, on similar terms and with similar budgets. Whatever advantage a brand once had from setting up campaigns well disappears, because everyone now starts from the same recommendation.

Templates work the same way. Video Builder lowers the cost of making a video, which is good for every advertiser. A template any brand can use, though, produces videos that look alike. The brand that wins attention will be the one whose video shows something only it can show: how the product works, what it looks like in use, why it is different.

The advantage therefore moves to two inputs that automation cannot standardize. One is creative: real footage, a clear demonstration, a reason to choose. The other is measurement: the questions a brand asks of its data, and the discipline to act on the answers.

Amazon Marketing Cloud is where that second input lives. It lets advertisers analyze how shoppers moved across ad types before buying, using Amazon’s data in a clean room. Access is widening and the customer count has quadrupled, but the value depends entirely on the questions asked, and two brands with the same access can learn very different things.

Competition is widening too. Sponsored Display for brands that do not sell on Amazon, starting on Twitch, brings new advertisers into display inventory, and more bidders for the same audiences will raise prices for brands that compete only on bids.

How the two serum brands pull apart

Go back to the two skincare brands from the opening. In the second month, one replaces the template with a short video showing the serum’s texture and results, and uses Amazon Marketing Cloud to find that shoppers who saw its video and then searched were twice as likely to buy. It shifts budget accordingly, while the other keeps the presets. By the third month their results have diverged, and the difference came from inputs, not settings.

Presets as a floor, inputs as the edge

A preset is the average recommendation, and a brand’s products are not average. Presets are useful for launching new products quickly, with bids and budgets adjusted from the brand’s own results within the first weeks.

Sponsored Display video and Video Builder are worth using, filled with footage that shows the product. A template is a frame; the content inside it is what differs, and a thirty-second clip of the product in use often says more than a polished brand film.

For brands advertising across Sponsored ads and Amazon DSP, Amazon Marketing Cloud analysis starts best with a few clear questions, such as which ad types new customers saw before buying, with the answers moving budget. Display prices deserve tracking as new advertisers arrive: rising cost per click and cost per thousand impressions without better results mean a brand is competing on bids alone.

The spread between a brand’s results and its competitors’ is the measure to keep. If it narrows as rivals adopt the same tools, the brand is relying on settings; if it widens, its inputs are working. Building that creative and measurement work into an Amazon account is how we run Amazon advertising beyond the presets.

A0312.crumb: Winning a category on Target Plus in…
A0312.title: Winning a category on Target Plus in 2022: own the open tier
A0312.alt: A red bookshelf holds pottery, glass jars of dried herbs, books, a vintage camera and folded textiles beside a houseplant.
A0312.ttag: Winning a category on Target Plus in 2022: own the open tier | Kwontified
A0312.desc: On Target Plus, a brand’s sharpest rival is often Target’s own label, and inflation pushes shoppers toward it. Win the tier the owned brand leaves open.
A0312.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 3, 2022.
A0312.body:
Target’s owned-brand portfolio delivers more than $30 billion in annual sales, and 12 of those brands each generate more than $1 billion, the company said on its second-quarter earnings call. For a brand selling through Target Plus, that portfolio is the neighbor on the digital shelf. Inflation is pushing shoppers toward it.

Winning a category on Target Plus in 2022 means competing less with other marketplace sellers than with Target’s own brands. The brands that hold their ground own a tier the owned brand does not serve, such as specialist, premium or a format Target lacks, rather than chase it on price.

A Target Plus category shares its shelf with the retailer’s own label

Target’s digital business is large and still growing: digital comparable sales rose 9% in the second quarter, and digital penetration reached almost 18% of total sales, Target said on the same call. More than 95% of its second-quarter sales were fulfilled by its stores, according to its results.

The owned brands sit at the center of that assortment. Target is leaning on them. With inflation pressing shoppers, it said it was focused on strong opening price points across every category, including its own brands.

Shoppers are answering that offer. Customers were looking more at Target’s less expensive private-label brands, waiting for discounts and consolidating trips, the Associated Press reported.

Why the owned brand is the real competition

In many categories, Target’s own brand sits on the same digital shelf, clearly priced and familiar from the store. That shapes the competition for a Target Plus seller. On Amazon, a brand fights many sellers on a crowded search results page. On Target Plus, which is invitation-only and curated, there are fewer sellers per category, and the strongest neighbor on the shelf is often the retailer itself.

Inflation sharpens that. When shoppers trade down, they move toward the products that feel safe and good value, and on Target that usually means the owned brand. A Target Plus brand that tries to match it on price is fighting Target’s strongest product on its home ground, with less margin to spend and less visibility in the store.

Target keeps the brands that complete its range

The brands that do well take a different route. They offer what the owned brand does not: a specialist formula, a premium material, a size or pack Target does not carry, or a recognized name the shopper is looking for by brand. They become the step up from the owned brand, or the specialist alternative to it, rather than its rival.

That also explains why Target keeps them. A curated marketplace exists to fill gaps in the retailer’s assortment, and the gap is where the value sits for both sides. A brand that duplicates the owned brand adds little. A brand that completes the category gives Target a reason to feature it.

Take a pet brand on Target Plus selling a mid-priced dog shampoo next to Target’s own brand. It cuts its price to compete and still loses most shoppers to the cheaper owned brand. It then shifts to a sensitive-skin formula with veterinarian-tested claims and a larger size. That makes it the option shoppers choose when the owned brand does not fit their dog. Its sales rise without a price war, and Target gains a product its own range did not offer.

Own a tier the owned brand leaves open

The work starts with a map of the category’s tiers. List what Target’s owned brand offers in your category, at what prices and sizes, and identify what it does not cover: premium, specialist, a format, a size.

Positioning in the open tier happens on the listing. Lead with what makes you different from the owned brand, in the first images and the title, so a shopper scanning the category sees why to step up or across. Then support the difference with proof. Reviews, ratings and clear content matter more on a curated shelf with fewer choices, and your listings should show the claims that justify your price.

The delivery promise has to match too. Target fills most orders from its stores, so its shoppers are used to fast pickup and delivery on owned-brand products. Target Plus sellers ship from their own warehouses, so a slow or uncertain delivery date can lose a shopper who was ready to step up. Keep stock in the right places and shipping times short, especially before holidays.

Price is where brands get pulled back into the fight they should avoid. If you must promote, do it during events, on a few products, to win trial, and return to your normal price afterwards. A permanent price cut against the owned brand rarely ends well.

Target’s advertising should follow the same tier. Advertise on searches and placements where shoppers are looking for what the owned brand does not offer, rather than on the broadest category terms.

Your conversion against category traffic shows whether the position is working. If shoppers view your listing and still choose the owned brand, your difference is not clear enough on the page.

Questions for your next Target Plus review

  1. Which tier in our category does Target’s owned brand leave open, and are our products in it?
  2. Do our first images and titles show why a shopper should step up from the owned brand, or only what the product is?
  3. Where are we promoting against the owned brand outside events, and what is that price cut costing in margin?
  4. How do our delivery dates compare with the pickup and delivery Target shoppers get on owned-brand products?

Making the difference plain, product by product, is how we help brands win categories on Target Plus.
