A0314.title: Cyber Week 2022 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deal share
A0314.alt: An orange windsock on a wooden post flies against a clear blue sky above frosty, snow-covered rolling hills.
A0314.ttag: Cyber Week 2022 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deal share | Kwontified
A0314.desc: Adobe expects Cyber Week 2022 online sales to grow 2.8% after October pulled demand forward. Our ranges for sales lift, click prices and deal share.
A0314.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 8, 2022.
A0314.body:
Cyber Week 2022 will be a slower-growing peak than brands are used to. Adobe expects its online sales to grow only 2.8%. October’s events pulled some spending forward, and discounts are expected at record depth.

Our standard case is a sales lift of 2.5 to 3.5 times a normal day, click prices 30% to 45% above October, and half or more of units sold on deal. Those three numbers rise and fall together; that is the whole planning problem. Set stock, bids and deal depth to the ranges below, not to the 2021 peak.

The Cyber Week 2022 forecast from public data

Adobe expects U.S. online holiday sales from November 1 to December 31 to reach $209.7 billion, up 2.5%, and Cyber Week, from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, to bring in $34.8 billion, up 2.8%, according to Adobe. That puts the week at 16.3% of the season, down from 16.6% in 2021.

Inside the week, Adobe expects Cyber Monday to grow 5.1% to $11.2 billion, Black Friday to grow 1% to $9 billion, and Thanksgiving to fall to $5.1 billion. It expects discounts to reach record highs, and it said early discounting in October would pull up spending that would otherwise have happened around Cyber Week.

October did pull some demand forward. By Bank of America’s estimate, Amazon’s Prime Early Access Sale brought in $8 billion in sales, about three-quarters of July’s Prime Day, Retail Dive reported.

Advertising is crowded and still growing. In the third quarter, Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 25% to $9.5 billion, GeekWire reported. Prime Day in July gave a reading on click prices: Skai’s results had average cost per click up about 50% for the Amazon advertisers it tracks.

Three cases for sales lift, click prices and deal share

Our ranges are for a typical brand advertising on Amazon, comparing the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday with an average day in the four weeks before. They are planning assumptions built from the public data above, not measured results, and each brand should adjust them for its own history.

CaseSales lift vs a normal dayCost per click vs OctoberDeal share of units
Conservative2 to 2.5 timesup 20% to 30%35% to 45%
Standard2.5 to 3.5 timesup 30% to 45%45% to 60%
Reach3.5 to 4.5 timesup 45% to 60%60% to 70%

Sales lift is the multiple of a normal day’s sales during the event. The standard case assumes the event grows little on 2021, consistent with Adobe’s 2.8%, and that October took some of the gifting demand.

Cost per click is measured against October’s average. The standard case assumes bidding below July’s Prime Day peak, because spending is spread over more days, but well above normal as advertisers chase a smaller pool of extra demand.

Deal share is the proportion of units sold at a promotional price. The standard case reflects Adobe’s expectation of record discounts and shoppers who have learned to wait for them.

Extra volume has to pay for the discount and the click

The columns move together. A brand that gets the reach case on sales usually gets it on deal share too, because deep discounts drive the lift. The question is not whether sales rise, but whether the extra sales cover the deeper discounts and higher click prices.

Take a home brand averaging $10,000 a day in the four weeks before, planning for the standard case. At three times a normal day, it expects about $150,000 over the five days. If half of units sell at 25% off and click prices rise 40%, its contribution margin per order falls, and the event pays only if the extra volume more than offsets that.

If the brand lands in the conservative case on sales but the reach case on click prices, it may sell more and earn less than in an ordinary week, which is why the cases must be read together.

The two sides of the deal decision are both real. Shoppers expect deep discounts in 2022, so a shallow deal may not move a product. But a deep deal on every product can turn the event’s extra sales into a loss. The numbers lean toward choosing deal depth by margin, not by habit: deep on the products where volume pays, shallow or none on the rest.

Set stock and bids to the ranges

Stock should be set to the reach case on your best sellers and the standard case elsewhere, because running out during Cyber Week costs the sales and the ranking that carries into December.

Bid caps come from the standard click-price case. Raise bids on your highest-converting terms, cap them where cost per order would exceed your margin, and review them daily from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday.

Judge the event against these ranges afterwards. Compare your lift, click prices and deal share with the cases, and with the four weeks before, then check sales in early December for pull-forward.

Two readings tell you which case you are in: Adobe’s daily figures over the week, and your own click prices on the Monday before Thanksgiving. If prices are already at the top of the standard range then, plan for the reach case on cost.

The Cyber Week checklist

  1. Stock best sellers for the reach case and the rest of the range for the standard case.
  2. Set bid caps from a 30% to 45% rise in click prices, and review them daily through Cyber Monday.
  3. Choose deal depth product by product, by margin, and keep the deepest deals for the products where volume pays.
  4. Grade lift, click prices and deal share against the three cases afterwards, then check early December sales for pull-forward.

Setting those ranges before an event and grading them after it is how we plan Cyber Week stock and budgets with brands.

A0316.title: How Temu’s pricing reshapes ecommerce profitability
A0316.alt: A brass balance scale holds a pile of twine-tied orange parcels on one pan and a few coins on the other.
A0316.ttag: How Temu’s pricing reshapes ecommerce profitability | Kwontified
A0316.desc: Temu’s prices reset what shoppers expect to pay for look-alike goods, and that expectation follows them onto Amazon and Walmart, squeezing margins.
A0316.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 10, 2022.
A0316.body:
Some dresses on Temu were listed for $6 or $7 when the site opened in the United States, and earrings for under $1, The Logic reported. A shopper who has seen a $7 dress carries that reference price onto Amazon and Walmart.

That is how Temu’s pricing reshapes ecommerce profitability: less through the sales it takes than through the expectations it sets. Brands selling look-alike products face price pressure even where Temu is absent. The defense is to make the difference from a cheap alternative visible, not to cut prices to meet it.

Temu pricing reached many shoppers fast

Temu, the U.S. shopping site launched by China’s Pinduoduo, went live on September 1 with a 20% discount across the site and dresses mostly under $20, CNBC reported.

It did not stay obscure for long. On October 17, Temu became the most downloaded shopping app in the United States, MIT Technology Review reported, helped by app-store advertising aimed largely at the United States and Canada.

The shoppers it reached were already stretched. Consumer prices rose 8.2% in the year to September, Reuters reported. At Target, shoppers were looking more at the cheaper private-label brands and waiting for discounts, the retailer said, according to the Associated Press.

A reference price travels to other marketplaces

Shoppers judge whether a price is fair against the lowest price they remember for something similar. Economists call this a reference price. Once a shopper has seen a $7 dress, a $35 dress on Amazon feels expensive in a way it did not before, even if the two are not really comparable in fabric, fit or delivery time.

The pressure is uneven, and it is strongest where products look alike in a photo and the shopper cannot easily see the difference: basic apparel, accessories, phone cases, simple home goods, small kitchen tools. It is weakest where a brand name, a specification or a regulated claim makes the difference obvious, as with skincare carrying clinical claims, branded electronics, or specialist pet and baby products.

So Temu can squeeze a brand’s margin without selling a single competing item. The shopper who never buys on Temu still lowers her idea of what a phone case should cost, and the brand selling phone cases on Amazon sees conversion fall unless it cuts its price or shows why it is worth more.

The difference shoppers forget is the wait. At launch, Temu orders took 7 to 15 business days to arrive, CNBC reported, against two days for many Amazon listings. Shoppers remember the low price long after they have forgotten the wait, which is why a brand that sells fast delivery has to say so plainly rather than assume the shopper will weigh it.

Matching the price is the trap

A brand that matches Temu’s prices is competing against a new marketplace that is spending heavily on discounts and advertising to win customers, backed by a large parent, and the brand will run out of margin first.

Take an accessories brand selling a $24 phone case on Amazon. Its conversion rate falls by a fifth over two months as similar-looking cases appear far cheaper elsewhere. If it cuts to $15 to recover conversion, it loses most of its margin. If instead it leads its listing with drop-test results, a lifetime warranty and two-day delivery, it recovers part of the conversion at full price, because it has given the shopper a reason the cheap case does not offer.

Make the difference visible, not cheaper

The exposure sits in a specific part of the catalog. Look for the products a shopper could mistake for a cheap alternative in a thumbnail. Those are where the reference price will bite first, and where your listing has the least time to make its case.

On those listings, the difference belongs in the first image and the title. Materials, testing, certifications, warranty, delivery speed and the brand name are the reasons a higher price is fair, and they need to sit where a shopper scrolling past a cheaper option will see them. Multipacks, bundles and kits help from the other side: they bring the price of each item closer to what a shopper expects without cutting the price of the core product. That is competing on value per unit rather than price per unit.

Advertising needs the same discipline. The broadest generic terms for look-alike products attract shoppers comparing on price alone, the ones most likely to click and leave. Searches that include your brand, a specification or a use where your difference matters are a better place for the budget.

Watch conversion by product, not just in total. A falling conversion rate on look-alike products, while differentiated products hold, is the early sign that reference prices are moving. Watch, too, how quickly Temu adds categories. Its first range leaned on apparel, accessories and home goods, and if it moves into your category, expect the reference price to follow.

Where to start on look-alike products

  1. List the products in your catalog that a shopper could mistake for a cheap alternative in a thumbnail, and track their conversion rates monthly, product by product.
  2. Lead those listings with visible proof of difference in the first image and the title: materials, testing, warranty, certifications and delivery speed.
  3. Use multipacks, bundles and kits to improve value per unit instead of cutting the price of the core product.
  4. Move advertising for those products off the broadest generic terms and onto searches that name your brand, a specification or a use.

Holding margin while new low-price marketplaces reset what shoppers expect is how we help brands manage Amazon and Walmart.

A0318.crumb: Amazon price increase in inflation: what…
A0318.title: Amazon price increase in inflation: what to test first
A0318.alt: Three speckled white ceramic mugs with blank kraft tags tied to their handles sit on a rustic wooden shelf.
A0318.ttag: Amazon price increase in inflation: what to test first | Kwontified
A0318.desc: On Amazon a price rise hits conversion, ad costs and organic rank at once. Test a few products first, and judge by profit per session, not units.
A0318.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 15, 2022.
A0318.body:
A kitchen brand raises a $20 product to $22 and adds $2 of contribution to every unit. It can still end up earning less than before. The increase lowers conversion, and on Amazon conversion is the input that sets three costs at once.

That is why an Amazon price increase costs more than it appears. A higher price raises the advertising cost of each order and slows the sales that sustain organic rank, so the effects compound. Test increases on a few products first, judge them by profit per session rather than units or revenue, and expect less room in discretionary categories, where prices are now falling, than in staples, where they are still rising.

Amazon price increases meet an inflation that is turning

The pressure to raise prices is real. Consumer prices rose 7.7% in the year to October, the smallest increase since January, and core prices rose 6.3%, the Associated Press reported, via PBS.

Inflation is no longer moving everything the same way, though. From September to October, prices for clothing, used cars and medical care fell, while food price increases slowed, the AP reported. Food was still 10.9% higher than a year earlier, and energy 17.6%, CNN reported.

Shoppers are adjusting their baskets: in Amazon’s October event, 44% of orders were $20 or less, Numerator reported. Target said its shoppers were turning to cheaper private labels and waiting for discounts, the Associated Press reported.

Why a price rise compounds on Amazon

The usual assumption is that a 10% price increase on a product with steady demand adds roughly 10% to revenue per unit and most of that to margin. On Amazon, that is rarely the whole story.

Conversion is the shared input to three things. It sets margin per session, because fewer sessions turn into orders. It sets advertising efficiency, because the cost per click does not fall when conversion does, so the advertising cost of each order rises. And it feeds organic rank, because Amazon’s search results reward products that sell, so slower sales can mean less free traffic the following week.

A price increase that lowers conversion therefore hits all three at once. The margin gained on each unit can be smaller than the margin lost to higher ad costs and lower organic traffic, and the effect is invisible if a brand looks only at the product’s price and cost.

A $2 increase can cost more than it adds

Take the kitchen brand from the start. Its $20 product converts 12% of sessions and earns $8 of contribution per unit before advertising. Its cost per click is $1, so its ad cost per order is about $8.33.

It raises the price to $22, adding $2 of contribution per unit, and conversion falls to 9%. At the same cost per click, its ad cost per order rises to about $11.11. The extra $2 per unit is more than consumed by $2.78 of extra advertising cost, and every advertised order now earns less than before. The comparison that matters sets the $2 gained on the price tag against the $2.78 lost to advertising, and a report of price and cost shows only the first of those numbers.

Organic sales compound the loss. If slower sales cost the product a few places in search results, organic sessions fall too, and the brand earns less in total than it did at $20. The result depends entirely on how much conversion falls, which is why it has to be tested, not assumed.

Test first, and judge by profit per session

A good test changes a few products and leaves the range alone. Choose products that represent different price points and categories, raise their prices, and hold the rest steady as a comparison. Run it for at least two to four weeks, long enough for rank effects to appear.

The measure is profit per session, not units or revenue. Take total contribution after advertising, divide by total sessions, and compare with the period before and with the products you did not change. Revenue can rise while profit per session falls.

Category decides how much room there is. Where prices across the market are still rising, as in food and household staples, shoppers expect increases and conversion may barely move. Where prices are falling, as in apparel, an increase stands out against competitors who are cutting, and conversion may fall sharply. Start where shoppers are least likely to switch. Products bought mostly through searches for your brand name, or with no close substitute on the first page of results, usually lose less conversion to a price increase than generic products competing on price.

A list-price increase is also not the only lever. Smaller pack sizes, multipacks with a lower price per unit, or reduced coupon depth can recover margin with less effect on the price shoppers see first.

Timing matters too. A test that overlaps Cyber Week, from November 24 to 28, will mix the effect of the price with the effect of deals and higher click prices across the market. Wait until early December, or test in January, when demand settles. Watch competitors’ prices during the test as well. If they cut while you raise, your result will exaggerate the loss; if they raise too, it may understate it.

The first week tells you most: compare conversion on the tested products with the comparison products. A drop of more than a few points is an early sign that the increase will not pay, before the rank effect arrives. Testing price against conversion, ad cost and rank together is how we help brands price through inflation on Amazon.

A0319.title: Strategy for Amazon’s first demand contraction in years
A0319.alt: A shopping cart holding paper bags of greens and carrots stands in a bright grocery aisle lined with packaged goods.
A0319.ttag: Strategy for Amazon’s first demand contraction in years | Kwontified
A0319.desc: Amazon’s online store sales fell in two quarters of 2022 while ad revenue kept rising. When demand stops growing, growth becomes a fight for share.
A0319.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 17, 2022.
A0319.body:
In the first quarter of 2022, Amazon’s online store sales fell 3% while its advertising revenue grew 23%, Bloomberg reported. The pattern repeated in the second quarter. Brands are spending more to compete for demand that has stopped expanding.

That is the Amazon demand contraction in one line, and it changes what a sensible plan looks like. With Amazon now cutting its own costs, brands should shift from chasing volume to defending profitable share, keeping the customers they have, and relying less on Amazon’s support.

The Amazon demand contraction in numbers

For most of the past decade, a brand on Amazon could grow simply by keeping up with the marketplace. That changed in 2022.

In the second quarter, online store sales fell 4% while advertising grew 18%, MediaPost reported. In the third, online store sales rose 7%, helped by Prime Day falling in July, while advertising grew 25% to $9.5 billion, according to GeekWire.

Amazon is answering the slowdown inside its own business: it paused new corporate hiring on November 3, citing an unusual economic environment, the Associated Press reported. It also plans to lay off about 10,000 corporate and technology employees, including in its retail division, Fortune reported, citing The New York Times.

The holiday outlook is modest. Amazon’s guidance put fourth-quarter revenue between $140 billion and $148 billion, a range that marks the slowest holiday growth in the company’s history, The Boston Globe reported.

When demand stops growing, every sale is someone’s share

A brand whose advertising is costing more while its sales sit flat or slightly down may not be doing anything wrong. It is feeling the marketplace change shape, and the higher bill reflects that change in the market rather than a mistake inside its own account.

When total demand grows, most sellers can grow at once. When it stops, one seller’s growth comes from another seller’s share. Every brand that wants to grow has to take sales from a competitor, and the main tool for doing so on Amazon is advertising.

The numbers bear that out: advertising revenue grew faster than store sales in each of the first three quarters of 2022, which means sellers as a group were paying more per sale to reach shoppers. Some of that is new advertisers and new formats, but much of it is sellers bidding against each other for the same customers.

Shoppers are changing too. Numerator counted 44% of the orders in Amazon’s October event at $20 or less. Smaller baskets and careful comparison mean each sale is harder to win and worth less, which makes paying more to win it a worse trade.

Amazon’s own cost-cutting adds a second change. Fewer people in retail teams can mean slower support, fewer programs and less help resolving problems. Brands that depend on an Amazon contact to fix listings or approve promotions should plan to do more themselves.

The budget call in front of leadership

The decision this sets up for a leadership team is whether to keep buying growth at the 2021 rate or to defend margin. The behavior that worked in a growing market starts to hurt here. A brand that keeps raising budgets to match its 2021 growth rate pushes up its own costs and its competitors’, and may end the year with more revenue and less profit. A brand that holds its budget may lose share in the short term but keep its margin.

Take a home goods brand that grew 30% in 2021 by expanding advertising across hundreds of keywords. In 2022 it raises its budget again and grows sales 5%, but its advertising cost per order rises by a third. When it cuts the bottom quarter of keywords by profitability, its sales dip slightly and its profit rises, because those terms had been paying for share it did not keep.

Cyber Week is where the choice gets made in practice. The temptation will be to raise budgets to win the event. In a flat market, the extra spend is likely to buy share at a loss, so caps set from profit per order, and a smaller peak if the alternative is an unprofitable one, are the steadier answer.

Defend profitable share and keep customers

The best positions come first. Identify the search terms and products where you earn a profit after advertising, and protect them, then cut spending where you are paying for sales that do not cover their cost.

Keeping customers is the next lever. In a flat market, a returning customer costs far less than a new one. Subscribe & Save where it fits, follow-up audiences in display advertising, and product ranges that give buyers a reason to come back all serve that.

Self-reliance matters more with Amazon trimming its teams. Build the in-house ability to fix listings, manage catalog problems and run promotions without waiting for support. Prune the catalog at the same time: products that sell slowly and need advertising to sell at all are expensive in a contracting market, so consolidate variations and focus stock on what moves.

Other marketplaces deserve a careful look. They may offer growth that Amazon does not, but only where their shoppers buy your category, so test before moving budget and measure profit there by the same standard you use on Amazon.

Advertising cost as a share of sales is the number that tells you whether the plan is working. If it keeps rising while sales stay flat, you are paying more for the same demand, and the plan should change. Adjusting a brand’s Amazon plan to a marketplace that has stopped growing is how we run the channel for brands day to day.

A0320.crumb: Amazon’s returns changes and the cost of…
A0320.title: Amazon’s returns changes and the cost of free returns
A0320.alt: A messy pile of opened shipping boxes, mailers and a tote bag sits on a wooden cabinet against a blue wall.
A0320.ttag: Amazon’s returns changes and the cost of free returns | Kwontified
A0320.desc: Amazon’s extended returns let holiday buyers return until January 31, 2023. Free returns cost more than they look; count them before judging holiday sales.
A0320.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 22, 2022.
A0320.body:
Amazon’s 2022 extended holiday returns window lets most purchases from October 11 to December 25 be returned until January 31, 2023. That moves a large share of holiday returns into January and makes December’s sales look more profitable than they are.

The fix is an accounting habit. Treat each free return as a cost of the sale, set aside expected returns by category, and judge the holiday season only after the window closes.

Amazon returns in the 2022 holiday season

Amazon first told sellers that items bought from October 7 to December 31 could be returned through January 31, 2023. After sellers objected, it narrowed the purchase window to October 11 through December 25, keeping the January 31 deadline, Value Added Resource reported. The new start date includes the Prime Early Access Sale.

Returns were already large before the extension. U.S. retailers expected about $761 billion of merchandise sold in 2021 to be returned, 16.6% of sales, and the online return rate rose to 20.8% from 18.1% in 2020, the National Retail Federation reported. Retailers expected 17.8% of holiday sales to come back.

Some retailers are moving the other way and charging for returns. Zara began charging U.K. shoppers to return online orders in May, and U.S. retailers including J.Crew, at $7.50, and Uniqlo, at $7, charge for mailed returns, RetailWire reported.

Why holiday results look better in January than they are

The pull is to count a sale as finished the day it ships. It feels finished: the revenue is in the report and the stock has left the warehouse. But the shopper still holds a free option to undo it.

A free return is exactly that option. The shopper can send the product back at no cost, and the seller pays for the shipping, the handling and whatever value the product loses. A longer return window extends the option well past the holidays. Shoppers who buy in October can now decide in late January.

More products come back, because the option lasts longer and shoppers have more time to change their minds. They come back later, so December’s reports show the sale and January’s show the refund. And they come back in worse condition for resale, because seasonal products returned after the holidays have lost much of their value, and opened products may not be sellable as new.

Standard sales reports hide all of it. A brand that reviews its holiday results in early January sees strong revenue and a manageable return rate, because many returns have not yet arrived. The true result appears only at the end of February, when the January returns have been processed.

An early report can overstate the season by more than a quarter

Take an apparel brand that sells $500,000 of product on Amazon between October 11 and December 25, at a 30% contribution margin, or $150,000. By early January, 8% of sales have been returned. By the end of January, the total reaches 20%, close to the national online average. The average price is $40, the unit cost $20, handling $6 per return, and a quarter of returned units cannot be resold.

Early JanuaryEnd of January
Returns$40,000$100,000
Contribution lost$12,000$30,000
Handling$6,000$15,000
Unsellable stock$5,000$12,500
Holiday contribution$127,000$92,500

Every line in the later column is larger for one reason: the return rate moved from 8% to 20%, while the price, the unit cost, the handling charge and the unsellable share stayed exactly as they were.

The early report shows $127,000 of holiday contribution. The season’s true contribution is $92,500, more than a quarter below it, and nothing about the brand’s sales changed between the two readings except time.

Set aside returns, then judge the season

Start with a reserve by category: use your own return rates from past seasons, or a cautious estimate where you have none, and reduce holiday revenue and margin by that amount in your planning. Apparel and footwear need a larger reserve than consumables, which shoppers rarely send back.

Report the season twice: once in early January as a provisional view, and once in February after returns are counted. Make decisions about 2023 budgets from the second, after January 31, 2023 has passed.

Put the cost of returns into each product’s margin. A product that sells well but comes back often may earn less than a slower seller that stays sold, so include return handling, lost value and return shipping in contribution, product by product. Adjust advertising results the same way. Attributed sales in your holiday campaigns include orders that will later be returned, so return on ad spend for the season is overstated until January’s returns are subtracted, and products with high return rates deserve lower bids than their headline ROAS suggests.

Some returns can be prevented: clear sizing charts, accurate photos and honest descriptions lower the share of returns that come from mismatched expectations; review return reasons for your top products, and fix the listings behind the most common ones. Returned stock needs a plan as well. Seasonal products returned in late January will be hard to sell, so decide in advance whether to liquidate them, hold them for next season or donate them, and include that cost in the reserve.

Returns by week through January show how much the extension shifted. A sharp rise in the last two weeks of the window tells you how large the 2023 reserve should be, and until those weeks are counted, the early January view is a provisional reading rather than the season’s result. Measuring holiday results after returns rather than before is how we help brands read their Amazon season.

A0321.crumb: What Temu’s launch reveals about its…
A0321.title: What Temu’s launch reveals about its supply chain
A0321.alt: Gantry cranes load orange shipping containers onto a docked cargo ship at a sunny port.
A0321.ttag: What Temu’s launch reveals about its supply chain | Kwontified
A0321.desc: Temu ships most items from overseas in 7 to 15 business days. That model wins on cost and loses on urgency, and this holiday season shows where.
A0321.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 23, 2022.
A0321.body:
Most items a shopper orders from Temu take 7 to 15 business days to arrive. That one line in the launch terms says more about the Temu supply chain than anything the company has explained: products ship from overseas, through suppliers drawn from Pinduoduo’s manufacturer network, rather than from stock held in the United States.

The model trades speed for cost: it wins where shoppers can wait and loses where they cannot. Brands should compete on urgency, reliability and the holiday deadline rather than on price, and watch Temu’s delivery times for the sign that the model is changing.

What is public about the Temu supply chain

Temu has said little about how it works, but its launch terms say a good deal. At its September 1 launch, most items shipped from overseas with a delivery time of 7 to 15 business days, and orders over $49 shipped free, CNBC reported. Orders under $49 carried a $2.99 shipping fee, below Shein’s $3.99, according to TechNode.

The suppliers come from a familiar network. Pinduoduo’s strength in China rests on relationships with low-cost manufacturers, CNBC noted, and Temu recruited vendors with experience selling through Amazon and Shein, Nikkei reported.

Demand followed quickly: on October 17, Temu topped the U.S. download chart for shopping apps, MIT Technology Review reported.

Much is not yet public: how Temu sets prices with its suppliers, who holds stock before an order is placed, and how parcels move from factory to shopper. Claims about those details deserve care until there is better reporting, and plans are better built on what Temu’s terms already show.

What the model does well, and where it breaks

Seen from the shopper’s side, the trade is simple. The price is very low, and the wait is long. For a phone case, a set of storage boxes or a novelty gift with no deadline, many shoppers will accept two or three weeks for a lower price. That is where the model is strongest.

As far as its terms show, the model avoids one of the largest costs in ecommerce: holding stock near the customer. Products appear to wait in the supplier’s country until someone orders them. If so, there is no U.S. warehouse to fill, no stock to mark down at the end of a season, and no inventory tied up in the wrong place.

That same choice makes it slow, and slowness matters more than it seems. Shoppers buying for a date, a birthday, a trip or a holiday cannot wait three weeks. Shoppers replacing something they need now will pay more to have it tomorrow, and shoppers who have been burned by a late order before are less willing to risk it again.

The holiday calendar exposes the wait

Count back 15 business days from Friday, December 23, and a Temu order placed after about December 2 may not arrive before Christmas. At the faster end of its range, the cutoff is about December 14. Brands with stock in U.S. warehouses can promise delivery days later than that, which turns the final weeks of shopping into their strongest period.

Returns are the second place where speed matters. Gift buyers care about what happens if the present is wrong. Amazon’s extended window lets shoppers send back most purchases made between October 11 and December 25 as late as January 31, 2023, Value Added Resource reported. A brand selling through a marketplace with easy, domestic returns can say so in its listings, and a shopper weighing a cheaper gift shipped from overseas may decide the easier exchange is worth the difference.

Take a home brand selling a $25 gift set on Amazon with two-day delivery. In November, it sees conversion slip as shoppers compare it with similar sets on Temu at half the price. In mid-December, its conversion recovers sharply, because the cheaper option can no longer arrive in time. The brand earns more by advertising its delivery date in December than by cutting its price in November.

Compete on time, and watch the delivery promise

The deadline is the thing to sell. In the weeks before a holiday, lead listings and advertising with delivery dates and guaranteed arrival, because shoppers who need a gift by a date will pay for certainty.

That only works with reliable stock. A domestic seller’s edge disappears if it runs out, so protect inventory on gift products through December, when Temu’s delivery times count against it most.

Price is the wrong battlefield, and Temu’s model is built to win on cost. Competing there means giving up the advantage you actually have, and teaching your own shoppers to wait for a lower price instead of paying for speed.

Two things about Temu itself are worth tracking. If its delivery promises shorten from two weeks toward a few days, the company is holding stock closer to shoppers, and the advantage of domestic inventory will narrow. And if it moves into bulky, heavy or urgent products, which are harder to ship across an ocean one order at a time, its supply chain is changing.

Closer to home, your own conversion through December 2022 tells you what your shoppers value. If it rises as the holiday cutoff approaches, speed is part of what they are paying for.

Questions for the December plan

  1. Do our listings and ads for gift products show a delivery date, and is it a date we can keep?
  2. Is stock on our gift products deep enough to last through the holiday cutoff?
  3. Where are we cutting price to meet Temu, and what is that costing us in margin?
  4. Have Temu’s delivery promises or categories moved since launch, and in which of our categories?

Selling speed plainly, where it is the advantage a brand actually has, is how we help brands compete with new marketplaces.

A0326.title: The ESG cost of ultra-low prices, and who ends up paying it
A0326.alt: A worn metal bin overflows with a heap of colorful used clothing spilling onto the floor of a green room.
A0326.ttag: The ESG cost of ultra-low prices, and who ends up paying it | Kwontified
A0326.desc: Ultra-low prices rest partly on costs kept off the price tag. As scrutiny of Shein grows, brands should treat traceability as part of value.
A0326.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 1, 2022.
A0326.body:
A cotton shirt from a direct-from-China retailer can cost a few dollars. The ESG cost of ultra-low prices sits partly in the costs that never reach that price tag: some in opaque supply chains, some in small-parcel shipping that escapes the scrutiny applied to bulk imports.

New evidence about Shein shows those costs beginning to surface. Brands should not race to match those prices. They should treat traceability and compliance as part of the value they sell, and prepare for the scrutiny to widen.

The ESG cost of ultra-low prices, now in view

Prices on these platforms are startling. Temu, which went live in the U.S. on September 1, listed most dresses under $20 at launch and offered 20% off sitewide, CNBC reported. Shein, the larger and older of the two, was expected to sell about $8 billion in the U.S. in 2022, Bloomberg reported.

Bloomberg also published the results of laboratory tests, conducted on two occasions in 2022, which found that garments Shein shipped to the U.S. were made with cotton from China’s Xinjiang region. In a statement, Shein did not dispute the results or say whether it uses Xinjiang cotton.

The law is why that matters. Since June 21, 2022, the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act has presumed that goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang are made with forced labor, and importers must prove otherwise, as Fortune explained when the law took effect. Cotton is exposed: roughly 20% of the world’s supply comes from China, and over 80% of China’s cotton comes from Xinjiang, the same report noted.

Where the costs go when they leave the price tag

The model keeps certain costs out of sight, and the shipping path is the clearest case. Packages worth $800 or less enter the U.S. without import taxes under a rule adopted in 2016, and Customs receives nearly 2 million such packages a day, Fortune reported. Shein’s individual shipments typically fall below that value, Bloomberg noted, so they do not face the scrutiny applied to a retailer’s bulk imports. A brand importing a container of shirts must document where its cotton came from. A retailer sending millions of small parcels rarely faces the same question at the border.

The supply chain itself hides more. Prices this low depend on a large, fast-moving base of small suppliers, which is exactly the kind of chain that is hardest to trace. The lower the price, the less room there is for the audits and testing that traceability requires.

Then there is the product’s short life. Clothes bought for a few dollars are often worn briefly and replaced, so the environmental cost is spread across the volume of goods made, shipped and discarded rather than shown in the price of any one item.

Trace a single order from checkout to doorstep and the pattern is plain. The shopper pays a few dollars and waits; Temu, for example, ships orders from overseas in 7 to 15 business days, according to CNBC. The platform collects the sale and the customer data. The supplier absorbs the pressure to cut its own costs. And the questions about where the cotton came from, and who picked it, are left for someone else to answer later.

None of these costs disappear; they move to workers, to the environment, and eventually to regulators and the brands that sell alongside these platforms. A brand that shares a category with ultra-low-price competitors inherits the comparison, and increasingly the scrutiny, even when its own practices differ.

Matching the price means carrying the risk

Brands tempted to match these prices are making a choice about which costs to carry.

Take an apparel brand selling a cotton shirt for $28, which sees near-identical shirts on Shein and Temu for $8. It could cut corners to get closer, sourcing from cheaper and less traceable mills. That would narrow the gap without closing it, and it would take on the exact risk Bloomberg’s tests just exposed.

The better path for that brand is to make what it pays for visible. If it can show where its cotton comes from, that its suppliers are audited and that its shirt lasts, the $20 gap becomes an explanation instead of a weakness. Some shoppers will still choose the $8 shirt. The ones who stay are more likely to be loyal, and less likely to be lost to the next cheaper app.

Scrutiny is moving toward the brands that share the shelf

Retailers that buy in bulk, such as large department stores and marketplaces, already face documentation demands from customs. As the scrutiny of small-parcel shipping grows, the gap between how the two models are treated may narrow, and brands with clean records will be better placed when it does.

Reputation is only one part of it. Retail partners increasingly ask suppliers to document their sourcing because the law requires them to, and a brand that cannot answer those questions risks losing shelf space, whatever its price.

The rules may also shift, and tighter treatment of small-parcel shipping would change the price gap with direct-from-China platforms, so the debate is worth watching even for brands that never ship that way. The practical work starts now. Map where your cotton and other high-risk materials come from, and keep the evidence on file before a retail partner or regulator asks. Then tell customers in plain language on your listings what your price pays for, from sourcing and auditing to durability.

A brand that can answer the sourcing question in its listings and to its retail partners holds up when the scrutiny arrives, and building channels that do is how we help brands compete against ultra-low prices.

A0324.crumb: What conversational AI like ChatGPT could…
A0324.title: What conversational AI like ChatGPT could mean for product search
A0324.alt: A glowing white lamp, an open laptop and a plain cardboard box sit on a wooden desk against a teal wall.
A0324.ttag: What conversational AI like ChatGPT could mean for product search | Kwontified
A0324.desc: ChatGPT answers in conversation, not a page of results. If shoppers adopt that, fewer products get seen. Prepare product information; hold budgets.
A0324.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 2, 2022.
A0324.body:
A shopper on Amazon who types “rain jacket” sees a page of products, some of them paid placements. A shopper who asks ChatGPT, released on November 30, gets a few sentences. If that second habit spreads, conversational AI would shrink product search from a page of ranked results to a short list of recommendations, and shift visibility from paid placement toward how clearly a product is described in public.

Voice assistants promised a similar change and did not deliver it. Brands should make their product information clear and accurate now, and leave advertising budgets where demand is today.

Conversational AI and product search today

OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free research preview. It interacts in a conversational way, can answer follow-up questions, admit mistakes and challenge incorrect premises, and was trained with human feedback on a model that finished training in early 2022, OpenAI said. OpenAI also warned that it can give answers that sound plausible but are wrong.

It is not a shopping tool: it does not search the web, check prices or link to products, and what it knows stops at its training data. But its format is different from anything most shoppers use to find products today.

Product search today is built on results pages. A shopper types a few words, and Amazon or Google returns many products, some of them paid placements. That model is large: Amazon’s third-quarter advertising revenue came to $9.5 billion, up 25%, GeekWire reported.

A conversation shows fewer products than a results page

A results page shows dozens of products and sells positions among them. A conversation narrows a question over several turns and returns a few answers. If shoppers adopt the conversation, the number of products they see falls sharply.

That changes what earns visibility. On a results page, a brand can buy its way onto the screen with a bid. In a conversation, the products named are the ones the model can describe confidently, which depends on what it learned from public information: descriptions, reviews, comparisons and articles. Clear, consistent, accurate information about a product becomes more valuable than the size of the bid.

For brands, the effect cuts both ways. A conversational answer could send a shopper straight to a product with high intent and no competitors on screen. It could also leave a brand out entirely, with no paid way back in, and it could describe the product wrongly.

Accuracy is the other risk. A model trained on information that ends in early 2022 cannot know about a product launched since, a price changed in November 2022 or a formula updated in the autumn of 2022. If it answers anyway, a shopper may hear an outdated or wrong description of your product, with nothing on the screen to correct it. That makes the accuracy of public information about your products a commercial matter, not just a matter of tidiness.

Take an outdoor brand selling a lightweight rain jacket. On a results page, it competes with forty jackets and pays to appear near the top. In a conversation, a shopper asks for a packable jacket for wet hiking under a certain price, and the answer names three. Whether the brand is one of them depends on whether its weight, waterproof rating and price are stated clearly and consistently across its listings and the reviews written about it.

Alexa is the reason for caution

Amazon spent years building Alexa as a conversational assistant in millions of homes, and shopping by voice never became a major channel. Amazon’s devices unit, which includes Alexa, is on pace to lose about $10 billion in 2022, and the plan to profit from people using the devices has not worked, Business Insider reported. Talking to a machine about products has been possible for years, and shoppers mostly chose not to.

The difference this time may be the quality of the answers, which are fuller and more flexible than a voice assistant’s. Whether that is enough to change how people shop is unknown, and no one should plan as if it were settled.

Prepare the information, keep the budget

Product information is the part to fix now. State the facts a shopper would ask about, such as size, weight, materials, compatibility and use, in plain language, and keep them identical across your own site, Amazon and other retailers.

Then check how you are described: ask a conversational model the questions your customers ask, note whether your category and products are described accurately, and correct the public sources where they are wrong.

Budget is the part to leave alone. Shoppers still buy through results pages, and that is where advertising works today. Revisit the question if conversational tools start sending measurable traffic or sales, and test small before shifting spend.

A link to shopping would change the picture. A conversational tool that can check prices, search current listings or connect to a store would matter far more than one that cannot.

Referral traffic is the test that settles it. If visits begin arriving from conversational tools, the shift has started; until then, it is a possibility, not a channel.

A short audit for conversational search

  1. List the facts a shopper would ask about each product, and check that they read the same on your site, Amazon and other retailers.
  2. Ask a conversational model your customers’ questions, and record where it describes your category or products wrongly.
  3. Correct the public sources behind those errors, starting with your own listings.
  4. Track referral traffic from conversational tools, and keep budget where results pages still deliver sales.

Getting product information ready for AI shopping while protecting the search spend that works now is the job of our AI Agentic Commerce practice.

A0328.title: Cyber Week 2022 results against our forecast: the grade
A0328.alt: A brass caliper measures the top parcel of a stack of twine-tied gift packages against a sage green wall.
A0328.ttag: Cyber Week 2022 results against our forecast: the grade | Kwontified
A0328.desc: Cyber Week 2022 beat Adobe’s forecast, yet the market lift fell in our conservative case and Adobe’s own figures imply a softer December. The grade.
A0328.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 6, 2022.
A0328.body:
Cyber Week 2022 set records in dollars and still produced a smaller lift than we planned for. Online sales rose 4%, against an expected 2.8%. Measured as we defined it, though, the market’s sales lift was about 2.2 times a normal November day, inside our conservative case of 2 to 2.5 times.

Both results are true at once because early November deals had already raised the baseline. Adobe’s own figures also imply the rest of the season will run about 3% below 2021. Grade your own event against the four weeks before it, and judge December separately, before calling the event a success.

Cyber Week 2022 results against the public forecast

Our forecast for the event was built on Adobe’s October outlook, which put Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, at $34.8 billion, a 2.8% rise, and had Thanksgiving slipping to $5.1 billion, according to Adobe. Every day beat it, and Cyber Monday was the largest online shopping day on record, Adobe’s results showed.

PeriodAdobe forecastResultGrowth on 2021
Cyber Week$34.8 billion$35.3 billion4%
Cyber Monday$11.2 billion$11.3 billion5.8%
Black Friday$9 billion$9.12 billion2.3%
Thanksgiving$5.1 billion$5.29 billion2.9%

Amazon’s advertising data points the same way. Sales attributed to Sponsored Products grew 7% from a year earlier in the first half of November and 4% in the week before Thanksgiving, then 29% on Black Friday and 44% on Cyber Monday, Tinuiti reported. Shoppers waited for the event, then bought.

Why the sales lift landed in the conservative case

A beat on the forecast does not mean a big lift. Our ranges set the event’s five days against the average day of the preceding four weeks, with a standard case of 2.5 to 3.5 times.

Adobe’s figures allow a market-level version of that test. Shoppers spent $107.7 billion online from November 1 to 28. Taking out the $35.3 billion of Cyber Week leaves about $72.4 billion over 23 days, or about $3.15 billion a day. Cyber Week averaged about $7.05 billion a day. That is a lift of about 2.2 times, inside our conservative case of 2 to 2.5 times and below the standard case.

The record and the small lift come from the same place. A lift is a ratio, and its denominator was inflated. Retailers discounted early and often in November; Adobe counted eight days above $2 billion before the week began. Those deals raised the baseline, so the event looked smaller relative to it, even as it set records in dollars. “Biggest ever” and “biggest lift” are different measures.

Take the home brand from our forecast: $10,000 of sales on an average day over the preceding four weeks, and a plan for three times that during the event. Suppose it ran a sitewide deal for ten days in early November, so its four-week average rose to $12,000 a day. If the event brought in $150,000 over five days, as planned, its lift would be 2.5 times instead of three.

The dollars arrived exactly as forecast; the ratio shrank, because the baseline had been promotional too. That brand should judge its event in dollars against plan, and use the lift only alongside a note of what the baseline contained.

A brand’s own lift can differ from the market’s. Amazon’s sponsored sales grew far faster on the peak days than the week before, which suggests a sharper lift for advertisers there. But a brand that ran deals through November should expect a lower multiple than in past years, and should not read that as failure.

Click prices, deal share and pull-forward

The other two ranges are harder to grade from public data.

Click prices were forecast against October, and the public data available compares with 2021; still, the direction is clear. On Cyber Monday, cost per click was down from a year earlier for the median advertiser in more than half of the product categories Tinuiti studied. That makes the reach case on cost unlikely and points to the lower half of our range, though each brand should check its own prices against October.

Deal share cannot be graded from public figures. Adobe attributed the result to heavy discounting, and buy now, pay later orders rose 85% from the week before, but no public source measures the share of units sold on deal. That grade belongs to each brand’s own data.

Pull-forward is the most important test, and Adobe’s own numbers already hint at the answer. Spending from November 1 to 28 ran 8.7% ahead of 2021, yet Adobe expects the full season to grow only 2.75%, to $210.1 billion. If both are right, the period from November 29 to December 31 will bring in about $102.4 billion, roughly 3% below the same weeks of 2021. Some of December’s spending has already happened.

Grade the event against the weeks before it, then grade it again against December, after noting how much of November was already on deal and comparing click prices with October product by product. A record week followed by a soft month is a shift in timing, not growth.

How to grade your own Cyber Week

  1. Measure the lift against the average day of the four weeks before the event, and write down how much of that period was already on deal.
  2. Compare event click prices with October, product by product, rather than with last year’s Cyber Week.
  3. Check deal share against your plan using your own unit data, since no public source measures it.
  4. Track December sales against 2021 before deciding whether the event added sales or only moved them.

Grading each event in ranges against your own baseline is how we measure tentpole events for brands.

A0329.title: Cyber Week 2022 shopper behavior: the shopper still waited
A0329.alt: A brown paper shopping bag and a brass hourglass sit on a weathered bench against a sunlit pink wall.
A0329.ttag: Cyber Week 2022 shopper behavior: the shopper still waited | Kwontified
A0329.desc: Retailers spread holiday deals across seven weeks in 2022. Shoppers still waited for Cyber Week, and many went back to stores. What brands should plan for.
A0329.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 8, 2022.
A0329.body:
Target ran seven weeks of Black Friday deals in 2022, three more than the year before. Walmart held deals events on Mondays through November, and Amazon added a second Prime event in October. Then shoppers did most of their buying in five days anyway, and many of them went back to stores to do it.

That is the story of Cyber Week 2022 shopper behavior: the calendar stretched and the shopper did not. Years of deep discounts at the peak taught shoppers that the best price arrives then, and a longer calendar did not unteach it. Brands should treat early events as a way to build consideration, and plan stock and spending for a peak that has not gone away.

Cyber Week 2022 shopper behavior began with a longer calendar

Retailers did their part to spread the season. Target’s seven weeks of deals were three more than in 2021, Axios reported. It also offered a holiday price-match guarantee from October 6 to December 24, promising to refund the difference if a price fell later, according to Axios. Walmart’s three Monday events began online on November 7 and ran ahead of its Cyber Monday sale, Progressive Grocer reported.

The message to shoppers was clear: there is no need to wait. We argued earlier that the holiday peak was turning into a season, and the calendar did become one.

The shopper waited anyway

The buying did not spread as far as the calendar.

Tinuiti’s tracking of Amazon Sponsored Products shows the shape. Attributed sales were up 7% on the prior year through the first half of November and up only 4% in the week before Thanksgiving, before jumping on the event days themselves: 29% on Black Friday, 44% on Cyber Monday, Tinuiti reported. The quiet week before the event is the tell: shoppers who had seen deals for weeks held back just before the days they expected to be best.

Adobe’s figures show the same concentration. The $35.3 billion that shoppers spent online between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday was about a third of the $107.7 billion they spent online from November 1 to 28, Adobe reported. At $11.3 billion, Cyber Monday set a record for a single day of online shopping.

Take a shopper who first sees a discounted air fryer in a Target ad in October. She bookmarks it in early November, watches it on Walmart and Amazon, and buys it on Cyber Monday. Every early event reached her, and none of them closed the sale. That pattern, repeated across many shoppers, is what the week-before dip in the data looks like from the other side.

A habit built at the peak

The habit was not formed in 2022. For more than a decade, the deepest discounts of the year arrived on Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and shoppers learned that buying early often meant paying more. A price-match guarantee answers that fear on paper, but most shoppers never claim a refund. They simply wait, because waiting has worked before.

Money pressure made the habit stronger; with prices rising, shoppers had more reason to hold out for the best deal. Buy now, pay later orders rose 85% during Cyber Week compared with the week before, Adobe said, a sign that many shoppers were stretching budgets to buy at the peak.

The other surprise was the return to stores. A record 196.7 million people shopped over the five days, and the number shopping in stores rose 17% to 122.7 million while online shoppers rose only 2%, the National Retail Federation reported. Curbside pickup fell to 13% of online orders on Thanksgiving and Black Friday at retailers offering it, from 21% a year earlier, Adobe said. Black Friday as an outing came back, after two years when many people avoided crowds.

Independent brands’ own stores had a strong weekend too: merchants on Shopify sold $7.5 billion worldwide from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, up 19% from a year earlier, the Washington Post reported. That figure is global and not directly comparable with Adobe’s U.S. total, which grew 4%. Still, growth of that size suggests that shoppers who wait for the peak do not only wait for the big retailers. They wait for the brands they already know, and buy from them directly when the deal arrives.

What the mismatch costs, and what to plan for

There is a cost to the gap between the calendar and the shopper. A retailer that runs deals for seven weeks pays for promotions, inventory and advertising across all seven, while much of the buying arrives in five days. The brands that sell through those retailers share that cost, in funding for deals and in stock that sits waiting through a slow early November.

Early events do work, but they do different work from the peak, and a plan that judges them by the same measure will undervalue them. They put a product in front of a shopper and into her consideration, so they are better judged by add-to-cart, wish-list and repeat views than by sales alone. The peak is still where much of the buying happens, and stock and advertising budget belong there even when deals run for weeks. For retailers with stores, the weekend is again a store event as much as an online one, which makes their in-store plans part of a brand’s holiday plan.

That cuts against a tempting conclusion. A brand that read the long calendar as the new normal might have spread its budget and stock evenly across November, and run short on the days that mattered most. Planning a brand’s channels around the days its shoppers actually buy is how we run holiday calendars for brands.

A0330.title: The 2023 ecommerce plan: three assumptions to change from 2022
A0330.alt: Brass pocket compasses and a strapped leather journal rest on a rustic wooden table beside a vase of dried stems.
A0330.ttag: The 2023 ecommerce plan: three assumptions to change from 2022 | Kwontified
A0330.desc: Three 2022 assumptions to drop when building a 2023 ecommerce plan: price-led growth, rising click prices and event lifts taken at face value.
A0330.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 13, 2022.
A0330.body:
Take a brand with $10 million in 2022 sales, up 12%. If 7 points of that came from price, units grew about 5%. In 2023, the same unit growth with 2 points of price gives about 7%, or $10.7 million. A plan that carries forward 12% books $11.2 million, and the $500,000 gap is price that is not coming.

That gap is why a 2023 ecommerce plan built on 2022’s assumptions will overstate growth. Much of 2022’s sales growth came from higher prices, and prices are now rising more slowly. Click prices that were expected to keep climbing have flattened, and the events that looked biggest partly moved sales from other weeks. Plan 2023 in units and contribution margin, budget advertising on flat click prices, and count event lifts net of the weeks around them.

The 2023 ecommerce plan starts with price, not demand

The first assumption to drop is that 2022’s revenue growth will repeat. U.S. ecommerce sales in the third quarter of 2022 rose 10.8% from a year earlier, to $265.9 billion, while total retail rose 9.1%, the Census Bureau reported. Those figures are not adjusted for price. Ecommerce accounted for 14.8% of retail, still below the 16.1% first reported for the second quarter of 2020, Axios reported at the time.

Revenue growth is unit growth plus price growth. In the year to October, consumer prices were up 7.7%, down from 8.2% in September, CNN reported, and goods prices were up about 5% from a year earlier, against about 12% earlier in the year, Marketplace reported. When goods inflation falls from double digits to mid single digits, the same unit growth produces far less revenue growth.

The holiday outlook already reflects it; Adobe expects online holiday spending to grow 2.75% to $210.1 billion, according to Adobe. Amazon guided fourth-quarter revenue to $140 billion to $148 billion, growth of 2% to 8%, GeekWire reported.

A revenue plan becomes a purchase plan

The gap does not stay on paper: a revenue plan becomes a purchase plan, and a brand that converts $11.2 million of planned sales into units at current prices orders stock for growth that will not arrive. Retailers learned this in 2022. Target cut prices heavily to clear excess inventory after demand shifted away from the goods it had stocked, the Associated Press reported. A brand that overbuys in the first half of 2023 will face the same choice between storage fees and markdowns.

Planning in units avoids that: start from units sold in 2022 by product, set a unit growth rate from demand evidence such as search volume and repeat purchase, then apply an explicit price assumption. The revenue line becomes an output of the plan rather than its starting point. A price assumption that is written down can be checked each quarter; one buried inside a growth rate cannot.

Click prices have flattened, so the efficiency case changes

The second assumption to drop is steady advertising inflation. Advertising demand is still growing, and GeekWire reported that Amazon’s third-quarter ad business was up 25% at $9.5 billion. But prices per click have stopped rising across the board.

In the third quarter, Sponsored Products cost per click fell from a year earlier in six of the thirteen product categories Tinuiti tracks. On Cyber Monday, the median advertiser paid less per click than a year earlier in more than half of categories, Tinuiti reported. Meta’s cost per thousand impressions fell 29% over the five days of Cyber Week.

That changes the budget arithmetic. A plan that assumed click prices would rise every quarter, as they did for much of 2020 and 2021, sets budgets too high for the same traffic, or targets too low for the same budget. When click prices stop rising, the gains in efficiency that a team reported in 2022 may also reflect the market rather than its own work, and a budget built on those gains carries the same error into 2023.

Flat click prices with slowing sales change the right question too. It is no longer how to afford rising costs, but which spend adds sales that would not have happened anyway. The simplest test is to pause advertising on a matched share of products for two weeks and compare their sales with similar products that kept running.

Events add less than they appear to

The third assumption to drop is that a record event is a record gain. Cyber Week set records in dollars, but its lift over an ordinary November day came to about 2.2 times, as we measured after the event, because early deals raised the baseline. Taken together, Adobe’s numbers point to the remaining weeks of the season coming in about 3% under 2021. October brought a second Prime event from Amazon, and Walmart and Target spread deals across weeks. More events mean more pulled-forward demand.

Goods inflation in the monthly price data is the number to keep reading. If goods prices fall further, revenue growth will slow even if units hold, and the plan should be read in units first.

Four changes to make before the 2023 plan is final

  1. Rebuild the 2023 forecast in units and contribution margin, product by product, with the price assumption set explicitly and conservatively.
  2. Turn the unit plan into a purchase plan only after checking it against search volume and repeat purchase.
  3. Set advertising budgets on flat click prices, and fund increases only where a test shows added sales.
  4. Count each event’s lift net of the weeks before and after it, not against a normal day alone.

Building that plan in ranges and revisiting it each quarter is how we forecast the year with brands.

A0332.title: The year in marketplaces, 2022: three structural shifts
A0332.alt: Tower cranes rise over a large building under construction on a snowy site at dusk, with a city and hills beyond.
A0332.ttag: The year in marketplaces, 2022: three structural shifts | Kwontified
A0332.desc: In 2022, marketplaces became advertising businesses, moved costs and events onto sellers and reached past their own sites. Three shifts brands must plan for.
A0332.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 15, 2022.
A0332.body:
Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 25% in the third quarter of 2022, while the company guided its holiday-quarter revenue to grow between 2% and 8%. That gap sums up the year in marketplaces. Amazon and Walmart grew their advertising far faster than their stores, moved more cost and more events onto the sellers who use them, and pushed their services past their own sites while new low-price marketplaces arrived.

A brand’s marketplace dollar now goes more to advertising, fees and promotions than it did at the start of the year. Planning 2023 starts with following where that dollar goes.

The year in marketplaces: Amazon and Walmart became advertising businesses

The clearest change of the year was where the growth came from; Amazon’s advertising business took in $9.5 billion in that quarter, GeekWire reported. At Walmart, the global advertising business grew more than 30% in the third quarter, led by 40% growth at Walmart Connect in the U.S., while U.S. ecommerce grew 16%, Walmart reported.

When advertising grows faster than sales, each sale carries more advertising cost on average. Some of that buys real new demand. Much of it is brands bidding against each other for the same shoppers on the same search pages. For the marketplace, the result is a high-margin business that grows even when shoppers buy little more. For the brand, it means the price of being seen keeps rising as a share of revenue, even in a year when click prices flattened.

This is a change in the structure of the channel, whatever one thinks of advertising. A marketplace that earns a growing share of its profit from advertising will design its pages, its search results and its programs to sell more of it.

For brands, that turns advertising into a cost of distribution, much like a fee. On a crowded search page, a product that is not advertised may simply not be seen, however good its reviews. The budget question in 2023 is less about whether to advertise than about which products need paid visibility, and how much each one can carry.

Costs and the calendar moved toward the seller

The second shift was who carries the cost of running the marketplace. In April, Amazon put a 5% fuel and inflation surcharge on top of the fulfillment fees paid by U.S. sellers using Fulfillment by Amazon, effective April 28, the first such surcharge in its history, Retail TouchPoints reported. Amazon described it as temporary, but it showed that when the marketplace’s own costs rise, sellers can expect to share them.

Returns moved the same way: under Amazon’s extended holiday policy, most items bought from October 11 to December 25 can be sent back through January 31, 2023, according to Value Added Resource. A longer window helps shoppers buy early, and it leaves sellers carrying the risk of a return for weeks longer than usual.

The event calendar shifted in the same direction. October also brought Amazon’s second Prime event of the year, and Target’s Black Friday deals ran for seven weeks, three more than in 2021, Axios reported. Every event asks brands to fund discounts, stock inventory and raise bids. As we wrote after Cyber Week, shoppers still concentrated their buying at the peak, so more events meant more cost for much the same demand.

Fees, promotional funding, return risk and inventory risk all moved a little further toward the seller over the year. Take one $100 marketplace sale. Suppose that in 2021 a brand spent $8 on advertising, $30 on referral and fulfillment fees and $5 on promotions. In 2022, advertising grows faster than sales and takes $10, the surcharge adds about $1 to fulfillment, and an extra event adds $2 of promotional funding. The brand keeps $5 less of every $100, before any change in returns.

No single change looks large. Together they take a meaningful share of margin, and they all run the same way: from the marketplace’s ledger to the seller’s.

The marketplace moved past its own site, and new ones arrived

The third shift was in where marketplaces operate. In April, Amazon introduced Buy with Prime, which lets merchants offer Prime delivery and checkout on their own websites, initially by invitation for sellers using its fulfillment network, Retail TouchPoints reported. Merchants receive the shopper’s order details, including email address, so they can build direct relationships, Amazon said. Amazon’s logistics and payments are becoming services a brand can rent outside Amazon’s store.

At the other end of the market, a new kind of competitor arrived: Temu opened to U.S. shoppers on September 1 and was the most downloaded shopping app in the U.S. by mid-October, MIT Technology Review reported. Its model, shipping very low-priced goods directly from overseas suppliers, competes with marketplaces on price rather than on speed.

Together these shifts pull in two directions. The established marketplaces are becoming infrastructure that reaches across the web, and the new ones are competing for the shopper who cares most about price. A brand in the middle has to decide where it earns its margin.

Questions for the 2023 marketplace plan

  1. What share of 2022 marketplace sales went to advertising, fees and promotional funding, and how does each compare with 2021?
  2. Which 2023 events are worth joining, judged by what each one added net of the weeks around it?
  3. Where will we build direct customer relationships: on our own site, through programs like Buy with Prime, or both?
  4. Which products need paid visibility to be seen at all, and how much advertising can each one carry?

Running the marketplace channels as one business, and following each dollar through them, is how we manage Amazon and Walmart for brands.

A0334.crumb: Winning the Walmart pickup moment: shelf…
A0334.title: Winning the Walmart pickup moment: shelf first, or ship fast
A0334.alt: A shopping cart full of paper grocery bags stands behind a dark station wagon with its hatch open in a sunny lot.
A0334.ttag: Winning the Walmart pickup moment: shelf first, or ship fast | Kwontified
A0334.desc: Walmart’s online growth runs through store pickup, and pickup orders come from store shelves. The rule: earn the shelf, or win the ship-to-home search.
A0334.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 20, 2022.
A0334.body:
A product can rank first on Walmart.com and still never appear in a pickup basket. Walmart’s online growth now runs heavily through store pickup and delivery, and those orders are filled from the shelves of the shopper’s local store. If the product is not stocked in that store, its listing quality does not matter for that order.

So Walmart.com is not one undivided search. Brands should either earn store distribution and keep it in stock, or compete for the shoppers who choose shipping, and decide product by product which of the two businesses they are in.

Walmart pickup is where its online growth runs

Walmart’s U.S. ecommerce sales grew 16% in its third quarter, adding 0.8 points to comparable sales growth, Supermarket News reported. Walmart said that growth reflected 40% growth in advertising and strength in pickup, delivery, marketplace and fulfillment services.

The network behind it keeps expanding. Walmart now has about 4,600 pickup sites, 300 more than a year earlier, and same-day delivery from more than 3,900 stores, 600 more than a year earlier, the same report said. Its stores are also its fastest warehouses.

Walmart’s pickup service grew out of grocery, and grocery is still its anchor. Its grocery market share kept growing in the quarter, Walmart said in its earnings release. A shopper who orders groceries for pickup every week is building a basket on a schedule, and general merchandise rides along in that basket.

The pickup basket is built from the store shelf

A pickup or same-day delivery order is assembled by store staff from one store’s shelves. Whether a product can be in that order depends on one thing: whether that store has it in stock. Listing quality, reviews and bids do not change that.

Marketplace is the first place this bites. Walmart Marketplace items sold by third-party sellers are not stocked in stores. They ship from the seller’s own warehouse or from Walmart Fulfillment Services, so in our experience across the brands we manage they are not offered for store pickup or same-day delivery from a store.

Store distribution is also local. Suppose a product is carried in 2,000 stores. It is available for pickup to shoppers near those stores and to no one else, and when it runs out on one store’s shelf, it drops out of that store’s pickup orders until it is restocked. For a brand selling to Walmart as a supplier, a store-level stock problem is also an online sales problem.

It can be worse than a lost sale: when an item in a pickup order is out of stock, the shopper is often offered a similar product as a substitute, and the shopper may accept it. A brand that runs out can hand a competitor a trial in a basket the shopper repeats every week, and repeat baskets are where habits form. That is why store-level availability deserves the same daily attention that online teams give to search rank, and why the two teams should look at the same numbers.

The holiday data shows the store-fed stream is a habit more than an event. Adobe’s Cyber Week data shows curbside pickup falling to 13% of online orders at retailers that offer it over Thanksgiving and Black Friday, from 21% a year earlier, Adobe reported. Pickup is strongest in ordinary weeks, when shoppers are restocking.

Two streams of demand on one website

The pickup mechanism splits Walmart.com demand in two, and the two halves reward different things.

Store-fed demandShip-to-home demand
How the shopper buysA pickup or delivery basket from one storeAn item delivered in a day or two
Who can competeItems on that store’s shelfMarketplace sellers and Walmart’s own items
What winsStore distribution and in-store stockFast, reliable shipping and search position
What goes wrongA local out-of-stock and a substituteA slow delivery promise

Each side has a real cost. Store distribution opens the pickup basket. But it brings supplier terms, store-level stock risk and less control over price. Marketplace selling is faster to start and keeps control with the seller, but it competes only for ship-to-home demand.

Take a brand of kitchen storage containers. Sold to Walmart as a supplier and stocked in stores, it can land in a weekly grocery pickup basket as an impulse add, alongside paper towels and cereal. Sold only on Marketplace, it competes for shoppers searching specifically for storage containers to be shipped. Both can work. They are different businesses with different metrics, different costs and different teams.

The kitchen-storage case shows which way to lean: a product that rides along with groceries gains most from the shelf, while one that shoppers search for specifically, to be shipped, can do well on Marketplace alone. Whichever side a product is on, the operating rule is the same. In stores, treat in-store stock as an online metric, because every store that runs out removes you from that store’s pickup orders. On Marketplace only, invest in fast, reliable shipping through Walmart Fulfillment Services or your own network, so your listing qualifies for quick delivery, and target the searches where shoppers are choosing shipping.

Advertising follows the same split. Walmart said sponsored search had its highest ad spend of the year in the third quarter, according to its earnings call. Spend on products that can fulfill the way the shopper is buying, or the click is wasted, however strong the listing behind it. Sorting each product into the right stream before the budget is set is how we run Walmart for brands as one channel with two kinds of demand.
