A0335.title: When Amazon rule changes arrive overnight, who absorbs them
A0335.alt: A worn leather-bound book beside a twine-tied paper parcel on a rustic wooden table by a window.
A0335.ttag: When Amazon rule changes arrive overnight, who absorbs them | Kwontified
A0335.desc: In 2022 Amazon changed fees, returns and events with weeks or days of notice. Why it can, who absorbs the cost, and how brands can be ready next time.
A0335.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 22, 2022.
A0335.body:
On November 17, Amazon told sellers that from January 17, 2023, its fulfillment fees per unit would rise by $0.22 on average, according to Amazon. Referral fees stay the same. The notice landed in the middle of the holiday season, the last of a year of rule changes that arrived with weeks, and sometimes days, of warning.

Amazon can do this because it sets the terms alone, for a marketplace on which brands have come to depend. The cost of each change lands on the sellers with the least time to react. Brands should treat Amazon rule changes as a normal operating risk, with a margin buffer, a monitoring routine and a plan for each kind of change, rather than as a surprise.

Amazon rule changes for sellers in 2022

Look back over the year and the pattern is hard to miss.

In April, Amazon announced a 5% fuel and inflation surcharge on its fulfillment fees, the first in its history, taking effect on April 28, about two weeks after sellers were told, Retail TouchPoints reported.

In October, Amazon first said its extended holiday return window would cover purchases from October 7 to December 31. Within days it narrowed the window to purchases from October 11 to December 25, returnable until January 31, 2023, Value Added Resource reported. Sellers planning their holiday inventory and returns had to adjust twice in the same week.

Amazon also added a second Prime event in October, which asked brands to fund deals and stock inventory for a new date in the calendar.

Then came the 2023 fee notice. Alongside the per-unit increase, the cost of removing inventory from Amazon’s warehouses will nearly double, EcommerceBytes reported. Two months of notice is more than the surcharge got, but it lands when teams have the least time to reprice.

Why sellers have so little room to respond

None of these changes was unusual on its own. What matters is how little room brands have to respond, and that has built up over years.

Third-party sellers now supply nearly 60% of the items sold on Amazon, EcommerceBytes noted in the same report. Many of those brands use Amazon’s fulfillment network because it qualifies their products for Prime delivery, Euronews noted, and many sell more on Amazon than anywhere else.

Each step made sense: Fulfillment by Amazon brought Prime, Prime brought sales, and the sales made Amazon the channel to protect. But each step also moved a little more of the brand’s business onto terms someone else writes.

A marketplace that sets its terms alone can change them when its own costs change, and Amazon has been explicit about that. It described the surcharge as a response to fuel and inflation, and it is cutting costs across the company, including plans announced in November to lay off about 10,000 employees, Retail Dive reported. When its costs rise, a fee change is the quickest lever it has, and sellers are the ones on the other end of it.

Take an apparel brand that ships 20,000 units a month through Amazon’s network. A $0.22 rise in the fulfillment fee is $4,400 a month, or about $53,000 a year, decided by someone else and announced in the busiest weeks of the year. For a brand earning a few dollars of profit per unit, that is not a rounding error. It also arrives alongside higher removal fees, at exactly the moment the brand is deciding what to do with excess holiday stock.

The timing matters as much as the amount. A notice that arrives in November lands in the same weeks as holiday advertising, stock decisions and the year-end conversation with finance, and rule changes do not wait for a quiet week.

Being ready for the next change

Brands cannot stop a marketplace from changing its rules, but they can decide in advance how they will respond.

A margin buffer is the first defense. A product priced so that one fee change wipes out its profit is exposed to every notice Amazon sends, while a cushion of a few percentage points built into pricing turns a crisis into an adjustment.

A monitoring routine comes next. Seller Central notices, fee pages and policy updates arrive constantly, and most are minor. Someone should read them every week, flag the ones that touch fees, returns, inventory or events, and estimate their cost before the effective date.

A plan for each kind of change completes it. If fees rise, decide which products get repriced first and which leave the fulfillment network. If return rules shift, decide how inventory plans change. If a new event appears, apply a standing rule for joining it. Deciding these questions once, calmly, beats deciding them every time under pressure.

Diversification helps too, but it is a longer project; selling on Walmart, Target Plus or a brand’s own site spreads the risk, though each channel has its own rules and its own owner. The aim is to avoid having all of them written by one party.

Before the next seller notice

  1. Calculate what a typical fee change, such as $0.20 per unit, would cost each of your main products over a year.
  2. Name one person to review marketplace notices weekly and price any change before it takes effect.
  3. Write down your response to fee rises, return rule changes and new events, and review it each quarter.
  4. Check which products would lose their profit to a single fee change, and build a buffer into their prices first.

Planning for the next notice before it arrives is how we run marketplace channels for brands.

A0336.crumb: Temu referral economics: what a shared…
A0336.title: Temu referral economics: what a shared discount buys
A0336.alt: Two kraft-paper gifts tied with rust ribbon on a wooden table beside dried flowers in white vases.
A0336.ttag: Temu referral economics: what a shared discount buys | Kwontified
A0336.desc: Temu is reportedly adding Pinduoduo’s share-for-a-discount feature. What a referral buys in place of an ad click, and the rule brands can borrow from it.
A0336.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 27, 2022.
A0336.body:
Temu is reportedly adding the share-for-a-discount feature that helped its parent, Pinduoduo, win users cheaply in China. It replaces paid advertising with shoppers recruiting each other. It works for Temu because a reward made of very cheap goods costs little, and the referred shopper arrives already looking for low prices.

Brands cannot copy the model wholesale. They can borrow its rule: pay for a referral only when the referred customer buys, and judge the program by how many of those customers come back.

The Temu referral plan reversed an ad-first launch

Temu’s U.S. launch came on September 1, with prices low enough to stop a scroll. CNBC reported that most dresses were listed under $20 at launch, and some earrings sold for under $1, according to The Logic.

Its first growth engine was advertising. Chinese outlet LatePost had reported that Temu would not launch a referral feature overseas and would rely on content advertising instead. The app ran ads on iOS in the U.S. and Canada, and by mid-October it topped U.S. downloads among shopping apps, MIT Technology Review reported.

Then the plan changed. TechNode, citing Cailian Press, reported that Temu planned to let shoppers get a lower price by sharing a product link with friends through WhatsApp, Messenger or Facebook. Temu’s daily sales since launch, just over $1.5 million, had been slightly below internal expectations, and that shortfall reportedly prompted the rethink.

How a shared discount replaces an ad click

An ad buys a shopper’s attention at auction prices, and the platform pays whether or not she buys. A referral program pays with a discount or a free item, usually only when the referred shopper signs up or buys. Its cost per new customer is the cost of the reward.

That cost is very low when the reward is a product that costs little to make and ship. A free item worth a few dollars at retail may cost the platform much less. Each shopper who shares a link also reaches friends the platform could not target as precisely with ads, through private messages that carry a personal recommendation.

Take a platform that pays $20 in advertising for each new customer. A referral reward of a free phone case with a retail price of $8, which costs perhaps $2 to make and ship, brings in a new customer for a fraction of that, if the referred shopper buys. The arithmetic favors referral strongly, but only on two conditions: the reward must be cheap to provide, and the referred shopper must spend enough afterwards to matter.

Pinduoduo proved the method in China, where, TechNode noted, it acquired users at very low cost with a similar feature when it launched against Alibaba and JD. The same report noted the downside: the feature drew controversy, including a lawsuit claiming users could never share enough times to earn the promised discount, as the app kept asking for more shares.

The weak point is the second condition. A shopper who arrives for a free item is drawn by the reward. Whether she becomes a customer depends on whether she buys again when nothing is free. A referral program that brings many first orders and few second ones is buying downloads, not customers.

Pay on purchase, judge on return

Most brands cannot copy Temu’s model. Their products cost more to make, so a free item is an expensive reward, and their margins cannot absorb a stream of discounted first orders. A brand selling a $35 product cannot give one away for every referral. The logic behind the model still transfers.

The reward should follow a sale. Tie it to the referred customer’s first purchase, so the brand pays only when a sale happens; a signup or a click alone earns nothing.

Its size should be set against what an ad would cost. If a new customer from advertising costs $25, a referral reward worth less than that, in product cost or credit, is cheaper acquisition by definition.

Take a skincare brand selling that $35 product. Instead of a free item, it offers a $10 credit to the referring customer, paid only when the friend completes a first order. Each referred customer costs $10 in credit, against $25 from advertising, and the credit itself is spent on the brand’s own products. The brand saves on acquisition only if those friends behave like customers, and reward hunters do not.

The cohort is the test. Track whether referred customers buy a second time at the same rate as other customers. If they do not, the program is renting first orders.

The part that drew the lawsuit is the one to avoid. A program that keeps moving the goal, or hides how many shares a reward needs, may win short-term shares but costs trust, and trust is what a brand has that an ultra-low-price app does not.

Temu’s own repeat buying will show how its bet is going. If its referred shoppers keep ordering, the referral economy is building a customer base. If they do not, it is buying attention that will need to be bought again.

Before you fund a referral program

  1. Calculate what a new customer from advertising costs you now, in each channel.
  2. Pay rewards on the referred customer’s first purchase, and keep the reward below that cost.
  3. Compare repeat-purchase rates for referred and non-referred customers before scaling the program.
  4. State the reward terms in full, including how many shares or referrals a reward needs.

Knowing what a referred customer is worth before the reward is set is how we build social and referral programs that bring customers back.

A0339.title: Temu discovery: shoppers browse for deals, they do not search
A0339.alt: A wooden crate of vintage enamel mugs and cutlery with orange bowls on a table on a cobblestone street.
A0339.ttag: Temu discovery: shoppers browse for deals, they do not search | Kwontified
A0339.desc: Temu shoppers find products by browsing deals rather than by searching for them. Why that changes what competes there, and which purchases brands should defend.
A0339.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 29, 2022.
A0339.body:
A shopper who types “rain boots” into Amazon or Walmart.com has a need, a size and probably a price in mind. A shopper who taps an ad for $4 earrings has none of those. She has curiosity, and a few minutes. Temu is built for the second shopper: the one who browses for deals rather than searching for a product.

It buys attention with advertising and keeps it with a stream of very low prices and game-like rewards. The products that win there are the ones that look like bargains at a glance. Brands are competing with Temu for the small, unplanned purchases a shopper makes while scrolling, and they should defend the purchases shoppers make on purpose.

Temu discovery starts with an ad

Most shoppers do not arrive at Temu looking for something. They arrive because something found them. That is a different start from the rain boots shopper’s search on Amazon or Walmart.com.

Temu was downloaded by more than 4.7 million people in its first two months, more than 98% of them in the U.S., and ran ads on more than 1,700 search terms in Apple’s App Store over that time, Appfigures reported. Its growth, the firm concluded, was not organic. The ads were running on iOS mainly in the U.S. and Canada, according to MIT Technology Review.

Inside the app, the deal is the product

Temu’s parent, Pinduoduo, built its business in China on what MIT Technology Review called extremely cheap prices and innovative gimmicks that keep users hooked, and has more than 730 million monthly active users there. The same report described the app as addictive and, at times, manipulative, with incentives to share purchases for steeper discounts.

When our team spent time in the Temu app this autumn, the experience felt closer to a feed than a store. Deals, countdowns and rewards came first. A search box was there, but the app did not seem to expect us to use it. You scroll, something catches your eye because of its price, and you add it to the basket. Then you scroll again.

Take a shopper on a Sunday evening who opens Temu after seeing an ad. Within twenty minutes she has a phone stand, a set of storage bins, two pairs of earrings and a kitchen gadget she had not known existed, for about $30 in total. None of those were on a list. Each one cost little enough that the decision took seconds.

On Temu, that is what discovery means. The shopper is not choosing between brands. She is choosing whether a picture and a price are worth a tap, and a product wins by looking like a bargain.

MIT Technology Review compared Temu more to AliExpress than to Shein, noting that most people go to AliExpress only when they already know they want something inexpensive. Temu’s bet is to make shoppers feel that way more often, by putting the bargain in front of them before they knew they wanted it.

Brands compete with Temu for small, unplanned purchases

This changes the question brands should be asking. The worry is not that a shopper searching for a specific brand on Amazon will defect to Temu. It is that a share of small, unplanned spending (the impulse add, the cheap accessory, the gadget) moves into an app that is built to capture it.

The categories most exposed are the ones where the product can be judged from a photo and a price: accessories, small home goods, phone add-ons, novelty items. Categories where shoppers care about a brand, a fit, an ingredient or a warranty are less exposed, because those shoppers start with a need and search for it.

That split tells a brand where to hold ground. Search-led channels reward clear product information, reviews and a brand name shoppers recognize. Those are the purchases a brand can defend. A discovery feed rewards the lowest price that looks credible in a thumbnail, and most brands cannot win that contest without giving up their margin.

Temu also shows something about attention: a share of shoppers will happily be entertained into buying. Brands that want some of that spending need their own ways to be found without a search, such as social content, creators, gifting moments and bundles that feel like a deal without being a race to the bottom.

The effect will show up first in a brand’s own numbers. Watch sales of the lowest-priced items in impulse-friendly categories, the share of new customers who buy only one low-priced product, and the add-on items that usually ride along in a larger order. If those soften while planned purchases hold steady, the spending is moving to discovery apps instead of a direct competitor, and the answer is different.

Whether discovery shoppers stay is still an open question. A feed full of bargains brings first orders. Whether it brings the same shopper back next month depends on whether the bargains hold up when they arrive.

Questions for the next channel review

  1. Which of our products sell through planned searches, and which through impulse adds that a discovery app could take?
  2. Are the planned purchases protected with strong listings, reviews and branded search, rather than chased with Temu’s prices?
  3. Where will discovery of our own come from for impulse-friendly products: social content, bundles or gifting, priced so the margin survives?
  4. Are our lowest-priced items and one-product new customers softening while planned purchases hold steady?

Sorting a catalog into what shoppers search for and what they stumble on is how we manage brands’ channels across search-led marketplaces and newer discovery apps.

A0341.crumb: The INFORM Act: what marketplaces must…
A0341.title: The INFORM Act: what marketplaces must verify, and when
A0341.alt: A wax-sealed envelope, blank card, brass magnifying glass and stamp on a worn wooden desk.
A0341.ttag: The INFORM Act: what marketplaces must verify, and when | Kwontified
A0341.desc: From June 27, 2023, the INFORM Act puts marketplace sellers on 10-day clocks to verify identity. For brands, the real risk is a notice nobody reads.
A0341.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 3, 2023.
A0341.body:
Ten days is the unit of time that matters in the INFORM Consumers Act, which became law on December 29, 2022, when President Biden signed the year-end spending bill that carried it, the Associated Press reported. A high-volume seller gets 10 days to hand over its identity details, 10 days to recertify them each year, and 10 days after a final notice before the marketplace must stop its sales.

None of the documents involved is hard to produce. The calendar is the hazard. What can hurt a legitimate brand is a request that lands in an inbox no one reads, because the law leaves marketplaces one way to enforce it, suspension, and every reason to use it on schedule. Seller identity therefore needs a named owner and an internal deadline that sits well inside the 10-day window.

What the INFORM Act requires of marketplaces, and from when

The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment. That puts the start date at June 27, 2023. Its detailed terms are in the bill text the House passed in November, recorded in the Congressional Record and carried into law by the spending bill.

Coverage depends on sales activity on the marketplace. A high-volume third-party seller is one that, in any continuous 12 months within the previous 24, made 200 or more separate sales of new or unused consumer products totaling $5,000 or more. Only sales processed through the marketplace count toward that line, so orders on a brand’s own website do not.

For every seller over the line, the marketplace must collect four things: a bank account, contact information that includes a government-issued ID or tax document, a tax ID, and a working email address and phone number.

Four 10-day clocks run from June 27, 2023

The obligations are written as a chain of deadlines. Each link is the same length:

  • A seller that qualifies has 10 days to provide the information.
  • The marketplace has 10 days from receipt to verify it.
  • At least once a year, the marketplace asks the seller to confirm or update its details, and the seller has 10 days to certify.
  • A seller that does not respond gets a notice, and 10 days later the marketplace must suspend its future sales until it complies.

Marketplaces are unlikely to wait for the start date to begin collecting. Spreading the work out avoids a rush of verifications in late June, so requests may arrive in the first half of the year, well before the clocks become mandatory.

Disclosure above $20,000 cuts both ways for brands

A second tier applies to sellers with $20,000 or more in annual gross revenue on a marketplace. Their name, physical address and contact details must be shown to shoppers, either on the product page or in the order confirmation. A seller working from a home address may limit the disclosure to its country and state, but it then has to answer shopper questions promptly or lose that exception.

The same tier closes a gap that drop-shipping resellers have relied on. For sellers above the threshold, the marketplace must tell shoppers when a product was actually supplied by a different seller and, on request, identify that seller. The name on the listing and the business that shipped the box are not always the same, and from June that difference becomes visible.

For a brand, the rule cuts both ways. Its own name and address will be in front of shoppers, so the details on file should be the ones it wants public. Unauthorized resellers above $20,000 lose their anonymity too, which should make them easier to identify and act against.

A few limits complete the picture. Marketplaces may use the collected data only for compliance, unless another law requires otherwise, and must keep it secure. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the Act as a matter of unfair or deceptive practices, state attorneys general may also sue, and conflicting state laws are preempted. A business that supplies a marketplace under an ongoing contract, as a wholesale vendor does, and has provided verified identity information, is not treated as a third-party seller. A brand that sells to Amazon as a vendor and also runs its own seller account is covered for the seller account only.

Why an unread notice, not the paperwork, is the INFORM Act’s real risk

The law puts the duty on the marketplace and hands it a single enforcement tool. A marketplace that wants to stay compliant will send the notice, start the clock and suspend whoever misses it. Waiting gains it nothing, and it has every reason to apply the rule the same way to every seller, large or small.

That turns compliance for a legitimate brand into a question of response time. Take a brand with seller accounts on three marketplaces, opened years ago by an employee who has since left, with seller notices still going to her old address. In June 2023, all three marketplaces send verification requests within a few weeks of each other. If no one sees them, the brand could be suspended on all three channels at once, for a lapse that has nothing to do with what it sells or how it sells it.

The fix is cheap. List every marketplace seller account, its registered contact and the address where notices actually arrive. Give each account one owner, keep current ID, tax, bank and contact documents in one place, and set an internal deadline of five business days for any verification or certification request, tracked like any other compliance task. Seller identity stops being a one-time setup and becomes a maintained record, with five business days of slack before a 10-day clock can bite.

Keeping account contacts, documents and deadlines current across every marketplace is part of how we run marketplace accounts for brands, so an administrative notice never becomes the reason sales stop.

A0342.title: Direct from manufacturer: where retailers can still win
A0342.alt: Palletized cardboard boxes on a roller conveyor leading into an open white van at a warehouse loading dock.
A0342.ttag: Direct from manufacturer: where retailers can still win | Kwontified
A0342.desc: Factory-direct apps strip out the importer, the warehouse and the markup, then hand the shopper waiting and doubt. That is where retailers can still win.
A0342.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 5, 2023.
A0342.body:
Take a shopper choosing a phone case. On a direct-from-factory app it might cost $3 and arrive in two weeks. At a retailer it might cost $12 and be ready for pickup today. If she just cracked her phone, the extra $9 buys two weeks of not waiting. If she is buying a spare, it may not, and both choices are reasonable.

That pair of prices explains most of what selling direct from manufacturer changes. Platforms such as Temu remove the importer, the domestic warehouse and the retailer’s markup, so on a commodity they win the price comparison outright. They also hand back to the shopper the waiting, the doubt about quality and the trouble of returns. Retailers can still win wherever shoppers value time and certainty over the last dollar, and brands should place each product where its shopper’s priorities lie rather than chase the lowest price.

What selling direct from manufacturer takes out of the price

Trace a conventional sale and count who takes a margin. A factory sells to an importer or a brand, which ships goods in bulk, pays duties, stores them in a domestic warehouse and sells them on to a retailer. The retailer adds its markup, holds the inventory and carries the risk that it will not sell. Every handoff adds cost to the price the shopper eventually pays.

The direct model removes most of those handoffs. Temu’s parent, PDD, is known for what it calls next-generation manufacturing, which channels what shoppers want straight to manufacturers to shorten the time it takes to develop products that match demand, TechNode reported. Orders ship from overseas, typically in 7 to 15 business days, according to CNBC.

Shipping each parcel to the shopper also changes the tax bill. Packages worth $800 or less enter the U.S. without import duties, Fortune reported, while a retailer importing the same goods in bulk pays them.

Put together, that is a structural price advantage: no importer’s margin, no domestic warehouse, no duty on small parcels and no retail markup. Shein, an earlier version of the same model in fashion, was expected to sell about $8 billion in the U.S. in 2022, Bloomberg reported.

The shopper pays back in waiting, doubt and returns

The costs the direct model strips out do not all disappear. Some of them move onto the shopper, and they are costs a store used to absorb.

Waiting is the most visible. A retailer keeps stock near the shopper so she can have it today or tomorrow, and Walmart now has about 4,600 pickup sites and same-day delivery from more than 3,900 stores, Supermarket News reported. A direct-from-factory order takes one to three weeks.

Certainty goes next. A retailer stands behind what it sells, and a shopper can see the product on a shelf or lean on a brand she knows. A shopper buying a $4 item from a factory she has never heard of accepts that it may not look like the photo. When it does not, returning something that came from overseas is slow and often not worth the effort for a cheap product, so she absorbs the loss herself.

The retailer carries a cost of its own that the factory avoids: inventory risk. In 2022, Target cut prices heavily to clear stock after demand moved away from the goods it had bought, the Associated Press reported. A platform that lists factory goods and ships to order sidesteps that risk almost entirely.

Where retailers still win, and where each product belongs

On the lowest price for a commodity, retailers will lose, and they should stop trying to win it. The direct model wins there by construction.

Everything the direct model trades away is still open ground. Speed matters for anything a shopper needs this week. Certainty matters for anything that touches skin, food, safety or a child. Easy returns matter for anything with sizes or fit. The store itself has pull again too: in-store traffic rose 17% over Thanksgiving weekend, the National Retail Federation reported.

Fashion is the hard case, and Shein shows why. Shoppers there have been willing to wait a week or two for a new style at a low price, because the product is new and the cost of a mistake is small. Where novelty matters more than speed, the direct model can win even against a retailer with a store down the road. So the line runs less through categories than through purpose: an urgent need, or a want that can wait. A retailer that knows which of its customers are which can decide where to compete on price and where to compete on time, instead of losing on both.

Retailers are borrowing part of the direct model as well. Walmart Marketplace and Target Plus let them offer a wider range without buying the inventory, which is closer to how a platform works than to how a store does.

For brands, the phone case is the whole decision in miniature. Products that win on price alone, with little to separate them from a factory copy, will struggle wherever a direct platform competes, and some of them should be concentrated where a margin can still be earned and accepted as exposed elsewhere. Products that win on speed, trust, fit or a recognized name belong where those qualities show: with retailers, on fast-shipping marketplaces and on the brand’s own site, with delivery times and return terms clear on every listing.

The question worth putting to the team is simple to ask and slow to answer: for each product in the range, is the shopper buying the lowest price, or the certainty of having the right thing this week? Sorting the range that way, channel by channel, is how we decide where each product belongs for the brands we run.

A0343.title: Amazon 2023 fee changes: model them before they reach your margin
A0343.alt: A twine-tied kraft parcel on a vintage brass postal scale beside a dish of coins on a wooden table.
A0343.ttag: Amazon 2023 fee changes: model them before they reach your margin | Kwontified
A0343.desc: A $0.22 rise in Amazon fulfillment fees costs a $10 product twice the ad headroom it costs a $20 one. Rebuild unit economics before January 17.
A0343.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 10, 2023.
A0343.body:
Twenty-two cents sounds like rounding. That is the average rise in Amazon’s fulfillment fee per unit from January 17, and on a $20 product it takes 1.1 points off the most the product can spend on advertising and still break even. On a $10 product the same $0.22 takes off 2.2 points, twice as much.

The difference comes from how a fixed fee meets a price. Every one of Amazon’s 2023 fee changes moves two numbers for each product, the lowest price at which it breaks even and the ceiling on its advertising cost of sale, and per-unit fees move the ceiling furthest on the cheapest products. Brands should rebuild unit economics at the new fees before the effective dates and reset advertising targets from the result, product by product.

What Amazon’s 2023 fee changes include, date by date

Referral fees stay the same, according to Amazon. Most of the rest changes in stages through April.

From January 17, fulfillment fees per unit rise by $0.22 on average, with finer weight tiers, and the separate fuel and inflation surcharge is folded into the standard rates. Off-peak storage rises by $0.04 per cubic foot for standard-size products, and removal and disposal fees go up. The Small and Light program, which carries lower fees, expands from items priced at $10 or less to items at $12 or less.

From February 16, apparel in the large standard size is charged on the greater of actual or dimensional weight.

From April 1, a new storage utilization surcharge applies to sellers holding a lot of inventory relative to their recent weekly sales, about 7.5% of sellers by Amazon’s estimate. From April 15, surcharges rise for inventory stored 271 to 365 days, and new ones start at 180 days, outside apparel, shoes, bags, jewelry and watches.

Not every change is an increase. Some lines move the other way. Amazon is cutting the fee it charges to process customer returns in apparel and shoes by $0.20 per return on average, and doubling the average rebate for eligible products new to its fulfillment network, from 5% to 10% of sales. Other increases run well above the average. Removing a two-pound standard-size item from Amazon’s warehouses goes from $1.14 to $2.20, EcommerceBytes reported.

How a per-unit fee lowers the advertising ceiling

Contribution margin is the money left from each sale after the product cost, the referral fee and the fulfillment fee. Divide it by price and you have the advertising cost of sale at which the product breaks even. Spend more than that on ads and each sale loses money. A fee increase comes straight out of contribution margin, so it lowers that ceiling. Because ad spend often runs several times a brand’s profit, a small move in the ceiling can decide whether the advertising budget makes money at all.

Take two products and add the same $0.22 to each one’s fulfillment fee:

Product AProduct B
Price$20$10
Product cost$6$3
Referral fee$3$1.50
Fulfillment fee$4.50$3.50
Contribution margin$6.50$2.00
Break-even advertising cost of sale32.5%20%
Ceiling after +$0.2231.4%17.8%
Drop1.1 points2.2 points

Product A’s margin falls to $6.28, and its ceiling slips by a little over a point. Product B’s ceiling falls from 20% to 17.8%. Product B gives up twice as many points of advertising headroom from the same few cents, because those cents are a larger share of a smaller price. A fixed per-unit fee always lands hardest on the cheapest products in a range.

The pull, when targets have worked, is to keep them. A team that carries 2022’s advertising targets into 2023 will overspend on exactly the products the fees hit hardest. The Small and Light expansion to $12 offsets some of that for products that fit its size and weight limits.

Storage follows different arithmetic. It ignores price entirely. It is charged on space and time, not on sales, so it lands on slow-moving stock and on brands that send in more than they sell. Under the April surcharges, a product with plenty of inventory and few sales costs more to hold every month it sits.

Rebuild the economics, then reset the targets

The order matters: fees first, ceilings second, targets last. Before January 17, recalculate contribution margin for every product at the new fees and derive its break-even advertising cost of sale. Set advertising targets below the new ceilings, starting with products priced under $15, where the per-unit change bites hardest. Check which products near $12 now qualify for Small and Light, review apparel weights before February 16, and find stock that will be older than 180 days on April 15. Each of those units needs a decision before the surcharge: sell it through, remove it or liquidate it, remembering that removal now costs more.

Leaving Amazon’s fulfillment network is the obvious reaction to higher fees, and it deserves a model before anyone acts on it. Amazon says its fulfillment fees will remain about 30% cheaper on average than standard shipping from other major logistics providers. That is Amazon’s own claim and worth testing against real quotes, product by product, including what the move does to Prime eligibility.

After the changes take effect, the number worth tracking is the gap between each product’s actual advertising cost of sale and its new ceiling. Where that gap is narrow, a small rise in click prices or the next fee change turns a profitable product into a loss, and keeping that gap visible for every product is how we set advertising targets for the brands we manage.

A0345.title: Retail layoffs: what slower ecommerce growth means for brands
A0345.alt: An empty sunlit open-plan office with rows of wooden desks, grey chairs, houseplants and a terracotta wall.
A0345.ttag: Retail layoffs: what slower ecommerce growth means for brands | Kwontified
A0345.desc: Amazon and Shopify staffed up for a pandemic growth rate that faded. Their layoffs point brands to a 2023 of slower growth and platforms that help less.
A0345.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 12, 2023.
A0345.body:
Read the retail layoffs at Amazon and Shopify side by side and they look less like two companies in trouble than like one forecast being taken back. In 2020 and 2021, both bet that the pandemic had pulled shopping online years ahead of schedule, and that it would stay there. Ecommerce has instead drifted back toward its old path, and the people hired for the faster one are being let go.

For brands, the forecast matters more than the headcount. A 2023 plan should assume slower market growth, so most gains will have to be taken from competitors, and leaner platforms that offer less help, so more of the work of running an account will fall to the brand itself.

Retail layoffs follow a forecast that did not hold

On January 4, Amazon said it plans to eliminate just over 18,000 roles, most of them in its Amazon Stores and People, Experience and Technology groups, and that it would begin notifying affected employees from January 18, NBC News reported. Chief executive Andy Jassy pointed to the uncertain economy and to the fact that the company had hired rapidly over several years, Reuters reported.

The hiring before the cuts had been fast. Amazon roughly doubled its workforce, from about 800,000 to about 1.6 million, between the start of the pandemic and the end of 2021, EFE reported.

Shopify had already said the quiet part out loud in July 2022. Its chief executive, Tobi Lütke, wrote that the company had bet the pandemic would permanently move ecommerce’s share of retail five or even ten years ahead, and that it was now clear the bet had not paid off. Shopify cut about 10% of its staff, according to reports of the memo.

The bet looked sound in 2020, and the share fell back

The forecast was reasonable when it was made. In the second quarter of 2020, with stores closed, ecommerce reached 16.1% of U.S. retail sales as first reported, Axios noted at the time. Companies that sell online hired, built warehouses and signed leases for a world in which that share kept climbing.

The share stopped climbing. Ecommerce was 14.8% of retail sales in the third quarter of 2022, the Census Bureau reported, below the 2020 peak. Shoppers went back to stores, and inflation pushed spending toward essentials.

Amazon has acknowledged that it added warehouse workers too quickly as shoppers moved online. The cuts now reaching its corporate teams look like the second stage of the same correction: first the physical capacity, then the people who managed the growth. Across the tech industry, more than 150,000 jobs went in 2022, Reuters noted, citing the tracking site Layoffs.fyi. Few of those companies misjudged what their customers wanted. Most of them misjudged the growth rate.

What leaner platforms leave to the brand

The biggest share of Amazon’s cuts falls in its Stores organization, which runs the retail and seller business. Brands should expect fewer people to call, slower answers to escalations and more reliance on self-service tools and automated decisions. Catching listing errors, chasing reimbursements and resolving policy problems moves further onto the brand’s side of the desk.

The losses are personal as well as procedural. Many of the people leaving Amazon’s Stores teams are the account managers and specialists brands have worked with for years, and what they knew about an account leaves with them. A brand that kept its history in a contact’s memory should write it down now: open cases, contacts, past decisions and who inside the brand owns each account.

The same thinning reaches brands that sell on their own sites. Shopify’s cuts mean the platform many direct-to-consumer brands run on is also planning for slower growth, with a leaner team behind it. The tools will keep working, but brands should expect fewer new features aimed at them and should not assume help will arrive quickly when something breaks.

Platforms that are shedding people will also look for revenue that does not need many of them. Advertising grows without large teams, and so do fees. Brands should expect more of both, and judge each new program by what it actually returns.

Slower growth turns plans into share fights

In a market growing quickly, a brand can grow by keeping pace. In a market growing slowly, most growth has to come from taking share from competitors, which makes the fundamentals matter more than they did during the boom: in-stock rates, listing quality, price position and advertising efficiency.

Take a brand that planned 2023 assuming its Amazon category would grow 15%, as it did during the pandemic. If the category grows 5% instead, the brand’s own 15% target requires taking roughly a tenth more share from competitors than it expected, while getting less support from the platform. By the spring, that plan will look like underperformance, when it is really a forecast problem. The fix is to rebuild the plan on slower category growth and to set targets for share gained, not revenue alone.

There is one opening in all this. Experienced marketplace and ecommerce specialists are on the job market in numbers not seen for years. Brands that were competing with the platforms themselves for that talent in 2021 may now be able to hire people who know exactly how the platforms work from the inside. Those hires belong on the work the platforms are pulling back from: catalog quality, reimbursements and account health.

When the platform answers fewer calls, someone has to know the account well enough not to need it, and building that knowledge on the brand’s side is how we run marketplace accounts with less reliance on platform support.

A0347.crumb: Instagram store traffic: measure it in…
A0347.title: Instagram store traffic: measure it in the store, not the app
A0347.alt: A boutique counter with a kraft shopping bag and glowing pink phone, an open door onto a sunny cobbled street.
A0347.ttag: Instagram store traffic: measure it in the store, not the app | Kwontified
A0347.desc: Instagram is dropping its Shop tab while most U.S. sales still happen in stores. Judge Instagram by store sales in a geo holdout, not by in-app clicks.
A0347.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 17, 2023.
A0347.body:
A shopper sees a skincare product in a Reel on Tuesday and does not tap it. On Saturday she is in a store she visits every week, spots the same bottle on the shelf, recognizes it and buys it. Instagram did its job. Its reports recorded nothing it could claim.

That gap is the whole measurement problem for brands sold in stores. In-app clicks and purchases only see the paths that stay inside the app, so they miss most of what the channel does for a brand whose sales happen at a register. Brands with store distribution should treat Instagram as a way to create demand that shoppers fulfill in stores, and judge it by store sales in geographic holdout tests.

Instagram store traffic matters more as in-app shopping fades

Meta is stepping back from Instagram as a place to check out. Instagram will remove the Shop tab from its main navigation bar in February, and a Meta spokesperson said there will no longer be a dedicated shopping destination, though people can still shop in feed, Reels, Stories, Explore and ads, Retail Dive reported. Meta had already ended live shopping on Facebook on October 1, 2022, according to TechCrunch. The bet now is on the feed and ads as places where people discover things, with less weight on purchases completed inside the apps.

Most buying still happens offline anyway. Census Bureau figures put online sales at 14.8% of U.S. retail in 2022’s third quarter, leaving roughly 85% to physical channels. Over Thanksgiving weekend, in-store shoppers rose 17% from a year earlier while online shoppers rose 2%, the National Retail Federation reported.

For a brand sold at Target, Walmart, Ulta or a regional grocer, that split is the opportunity. Instagram is where a shopper finds out a product exists. The store is often where she buys it.

Why in-app metrics undercount a store-driven brand

Attribution in an app works by following a trail: an impression, a tap, a visit, a purchase, each logged by the same system. Break the trail at any point and the sale drops out of the report. A walk into a store breaks it completely. Judging a store brand’s Instagram by in-app sales is like judging a billboard only by the drivers who phone the number printed on it.

The consequence is predictable. A brand that judges Instagram by clicks or attributed online sales will conclude the channel does not work, cut it, and never connect the decision to store sales that fall away weeks later. The report was accurate about what it measured. It measured the wrong place.

A geographic holdout measures store sales directly

The fix is to measure what the channel is meant to change. In a geographic holdout, a brand chooses comparable markets, runs Instagram advertising in some and not in others, and compares store sales in the two groups over the same weeks. The difference between them is the effect of the advertising.

Take a brand sold in a national pharmacy chain. It picks 20 similar metro areas, runs a six-week Instagram campaign in 10 of them and holds out the other 10. If store sales rise 6% in the test markets and 2% in the holdouts, the campaign added about 4 points of store sales growth, a number no in-app report would have shown. If the two groups move together, the campaign did not change store sales, whatever its click-through rate said.

The method has real costs. A holdout needs enough markets, enough weeks and store-level sales data, often from the retailer, and it means deliberately not advertising in some places for the length of the test. They buy the one answer a store-driven brand actually needs.

Where a full holdout is not possible, lighter options exist. A brand can compare store sales before and after a campaign in matched markets. It can use a retailer’s loyalty-card data to see whether shoppers exposed to ads bought more. Or it can run the lift studies Meta offers on its own platform. Each is weaker than a clean holdout, because something else may have changed at the same time.

On balance the numbers still lean toward measuring imperfectly in the store, because a precise click-through rate answers a question the brand is not asking. An imperfect read of the right outcome beats an exact count of a misleading proxy.

Running Instagram for the shelf

Once store sales are the scorecard, the campaign itself changes shape. Posts and ads should name the retailers that carry the product, so a shopper knows where to find it. Spend belongs in the areas around stores that stock the product, rather than nationwide where many shoppers cannot buy it.

The click should point somewhere useful too. Many retailers offer online ordering with pickup in store, and a link to the retailer’s product page lets a shopper check whether the item is in stock nearby, and reserve it, without leaving the path to the store. That keeps her moving toward the place she is most likely to buy, instead of toward a checkout she may abandon. Creative has to survive the trip as well: the packaging she sees in a Reel should be the packaging she sees in the aisle.

Before Instagram’s budget for 2023 is set, run the holdout and watch the gap between test and holdout markets. A positive, stable gap says keep spending; a flat one points to the creative, the targeting or the distribution, and not to the measurement. Designing that test around the stores where a brand’s products actually sit is how we connect social advertising to store sales.

A0348.title: NRF 2023: what the holiday numbers signaled about retail’s year
A0348.alt: Opened shipping boxes, holiday gift boxes and tangled ribbons piled on a table by a snowy window.
A0348.ttag: NRF 2023: what the holiday numbers signaled about retail’s year | Kwontified
A0348.desc: Holiday sales grew 5.3%, short of NRF’s forecast and below inflation, as groceries rose and electronics fell. What that signals for brands planning 2023.
A0348.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 19, 2023.
A0348.body:
Take a household that, in 2021, bought a new television, a few kitchen gadgets and some furniture, much of it for a home it was spending more time in. In 2022 it spent noticeably more at the grocery store, chose gifts more carefully, waited for deals and skipped the big purchase for the living room. It still shopped, and it still spent. It bought different things, at lower prices where it could find them.

Multiply that household and you have the season NRF’s numbers describe. Holiday sales grew 5.3% in dollars, short of forecast and below the rate of inflation, and spending moved toward groceries and everyday goods and away from home furnishings and electronics. That points to a 2023 in which shoppers keep spending but buy fewer, more necessary things at more promotional prices. Discretionary brands should plan for flat or falling units; essentials brands should plan for growth that comes with price pressure.

NRF 2023 opened on a holiday season that fell short

Retail’s Big Show ran in New York from January 15 to 17, according to the event schedule, and the season the industry brought with it had fallen short. Holiday sales for November and December grew 5.3% from a year earlier to $936.3 billion, short of NRF’s forecast of 6% to 8%, according to NRF.

Sales for the full year grew 7% to $4.9 trillion, meeting its forecast. NRF’s figures exclude autos, gasoline and restaurants and are not adjusted for inflation. That last detail matters more than usual, because with prices climbing a dollar figure can grow while the number of items in shoppers’ bags shrinks.

NRF’s own leaders framed the result carefully. Chief executive Matthew Shay said the previous two years of sales had been unprecedented and that no one thought they were sustainable, and that retailers offered more promotional prices to fit stretched budgets. Chief economist Jack Kleinhenz said early shopping in October likely pulled some sales forward, and that consumers may have pulled back more than hoped. December on its own was softer still in the government’s figures: overall retail sales fell 1.1% from November, NRF noted, citing the Census Bureau.

Where the holiday dollars went

The category detail is where the season’s real story sits. Over November and December, NRF’s figures show grocery and beverage stores up 7.8% and general merchandise stores up 3.8%, while furniture and home furnishings stores slipped 1.1% and electronics and appliance stores dropped 5.7%. Online and other non-store sales climbed 9.5% to $261.6 billion. Read those together and the split is plain: necessities grew, and the big-ticket comforts of the pandemic years shrank. Online growth also came in short of NRF’s forecast of 10% to 12%, so even the channel that carried retail through the pandemic missed its number.

Prices are what change how all of that reads, and they were rising faster than most of those categories. Consumer prices rose 6.5% in the year to December, Yahoo Finance reported, so a holiday that grew 5.3% in dollars means shoppers bought less in real terms. In grocery, rising prices explain much of the gain. In electronics and furniture, dollars fell even before inflation is taken out.

The household in the opening was not staying home, either. A record 196.7 million people shopped over the Thanksgiving weekend, according to NRF. Shoppers turned out in record numbers and spent carefully once they arrived, which is how brands should read the season: plenty of attention, less money behind each visit.

Replacement, promotion and normal online growth will shape 2023

The pandemic categories are still unwinding. Home furnishings and electronics boomed when people were at home, and households now have what they bought, so those categories face a year of replacing rather than adding. A household that bought a television and a sofa in 2021 is unlikely to buy another of either in 2023, whatever the discount. Brands there will be competing for a smaller pool of replacement purchases, and for the shoppers who are moving house or setting one up.

Promotions, meanwhile, are now expected. Part of that is the inventory retailers carried into the second half of 2022: Target marked goods down heavily to work through excess inventory once shoppers stopped wanting what it had ordered, the Associated Press reported, and other retailers did the same. Clearance at that scale teaches shoppers what a normal price looks like. When retailers lean on deals to meet stretched budgets, shoppers learn to wait, so deal events should keep their pull and full-price weeks should stay quieter.

Online growth has settled closer to normal. A 9.5% gain is still faster than stores, but it fell short of forecast and much of it reflects higher prices. Plans that assume online will outgrow stores by a wide margin need a harder look.

What a brand does with that depends on what it sells. A brand in essentials can plan for growth, but should expect much of it to come from price, and should separate price from volume in every report so it can see when units start to slip. A brand in discretionary categories should plan 2023 on flat or lower units, protect margin rather than chase volume, and save its promotional budget for the main deal events shoppers have learned to wait for.

The first question for any leadership team is how its own 2022 holiday looks when restated in units instead of dollars, and whether that matches its category’s direction. Rebuilding a 2023 channel plan around what shoppers are actually buying, not what they paid, is how we read market signals into plans for brands.

A0351.title: Amazon electronics in 2023: a category waiting for replacements
A0351.alt: A cracked smartphone, headphones, a half-closed laptop and a twine-tied parcel on a sunlit wooden desk.
A0351.ttag: Amazon electronics in 2023: a category waiting for replacements | Kwontified
A0351.desc: Shoppers bought their devices early in 2020 and 2021 and now wait to replace them. What a replacement year means for brands selling electronics on Amazon.
A0351.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 26, 2023.
A0351.body:
Look around a home office set up in 2020. The laptop still boots, the monitor still lights up, the webcam still clips to the top of the screen and the headphones still cancel the neighbor’s leaf blower. Almost none of it needs replacing yet, and that is the problem for anyone selling electronics in 2023.

Electronics on Amazon has become a category waiting for replacements. Households bought ahead in 2020 and 2021, and they replace most devices only every three to four years, so demand will be thinner and will bunch around deal events and genuine replacement moments. Brands should plan for a lumpy year, lean on accessories and add-on purchases, and keep older-model inventory from piling up.

Amazon electronics enters 2023 after a down year

U.S. consumer technology sales were expected to end 2022 down 8% from a year earlier and to fall a further 5% in 2023 before flattening in 2024, according to NPD. NPD expected growth to return only in 2025, and noted that revenue would stay above 2019 levels throughout.

The holiday season pointed the same way. Sales at electronics and appliance stores fell 5.7% over November and December while total holiday sales rose 5.3%, the National Retail Federation reported.

The largest specialist felt it first. Best Buy’s comparable sales fell 12.1% in its quarter to July, after rising 19.6% a year earlier, Modern Retail reported. Amazon has pulled back on its own devices as well, with job cuts announced in November that included its devices business, NBC News reported.

Replacement demand follows the retail calendar

In 2020, households set up offices, classrooms and entertainment at home in a matter of months. They bought laptops, monitors, webcams, headphones, televisions and game consoles, many of them earlier than they otherwise would have. Most of those devices still work. NPD’s analysts put the replacement cycle for many technology products at three to four years and in some cases longer, so a household that bought a laptop and a monitor in 2020 has little reason to buy either again in 2023. Demand that would normally have arrived over several years arrived at once, and the years after have less to draw on.

That changes the shape of the category as well as its size. When most purchases are replacements, they happen for specific reasons: a device breaks, a new model offers a real improvement, or a deal makes an early upgrade worth it. Breakages are spread across the year, but improvements arrive with model launches and deals arrive with the retail calendar. A replacement-driven category ends up following the calendars of manufacturers and retailers more closely than the calendar of household needs.

Deal events show it most clearly. Electronics were among the best-selling categories on Prime Day in July 2022, PYMNTS reported. A shopper who has been putting off new headphones waits for the event, buys, and is out of the market for years.

Run that home office forward. Say it held two laptops, a monitor and a pair of noise-canceling headphones bought in 2020. In 2023 one laptop slows down and gets replaced during a spring sale, and the headphones get new ear cushions. Nothing else changes.

A household that was a big customer three years ago is a small one now, and only on the days it has a reason. Multiply it across a category and the plan has to be built for a smaller, choosier customer.

Planning a replacement year on Amazon

The sales curve gets lumpier. Volume will concentrate around Prime Day, the autumn deal events and the holidays, with quieter weeks between, so inventory and advertising belong around those peaks rather than spread evenly into weeks when shoppers have no reason to buy.

Accessories and add-ons hold up better. Households that own devices need cases, cables, chargers, replacement parts, stands and storage. Those purchases are smaller, but they recur, and they follow the installed base the pandemic created. A brand with a strong accessory line can grow in a year when its main device category shrinks.

Older models carry the most risk. Electronics lose value as new models arrive, and a brand that buys for 2021-style demand will be left holding the previous model while prices fall around it. On Amazon, where shoppers compare prices in seconds, an older model’s price is judged against the newest one on the same results page. Every older model needs a sell-through date set before the next model lands, not after.

The shopper changes too. Replacement buyers know what they owned, what they liked and what annoyed them, so they research more and read reviews closely. Listings that compare models plainly, explain what is new and answer the questions an owner of the previous version would ask will convert better than listings written for a first-time buyer. Some shoppers will trade down instead of waiting: Amazon’s Renewed program offers refurbished devices at lower prices, and a brand that sells certified refurbished versions of its own products can keep price-sensitive shoppers in its range without discounting new stock.

There is a quieter opening as well. When a market shrinks, some brands cut advertising across the board. A brand that keeps a steady presence on searches tied to replacement moments, such as a specific model’s replacement battery or a newer version of a device, can win share at lower cost than in a crowded year.

The question for an electronics team is which of its products its customers already own, and what those owners will need next. Planning inventory and advertising around that replacement calendar, instead of 2021’s demand, is how we run electronics brands on Amazon.

A0352.crumb: Amazon streaming TV ads: fund them apart…
A0352.title: Amazon streaming TV ads: fund them apart from Sponsored Ads
A0352.alt: A cozy living room at dusk with a mountain lake on a flat-screen TV and two coin jars on a wooden coffee table.
A0352.ttag: Amazon streaming TV ads: fund them apart from Sponsored Ads | Kwontified
A0352.desc: Amazon now sells streaming TV ads around Thursday Night Football. They create demand that Sponsored Ads later collect, so fund and measure them apart.
A0352.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 31, 2023.
A0352.body:
When a brand runs its first streaming TV campaign on Amazon, two numbers can move in opposite directions. The TV campaign’s reported return on ad spend looks poor. Over the same weeks, branded Sponsored Products campaigns can post some of their best returns of the quarter. The obvious reading is that search works and TV does not, and it is wrong.

Both numbers come from the same shoppers. Amazon streaming TV ads create demand that turns up weeks later as branded searches and first-time buyers, and the search ad collects the credit. Brands should fund streaming TV from its own budget, judge it by the lift in branded search and new-to-brand sales against a holdout, and keep Sponsored Products funded to capture the demand TV creates rather than cutting search to pay for TV.

What Amazon streaming TV ads offer after one NFL season

Amazon’s first season as the exclusive home of Thursday Night Football ended with an average audience of 9.58 million viewers per game by Nielsen’s count, or 11.3 million by Amazon’s own measurement. That compares with 16.2 million the season before, when games also aired on broadcast and cable, TV Technology reported. Nielsen’s 9.6 million average was the lowest for the Thursday package since 2014, according to NextTV.

Smaller did not mean less valuable. Viewers had a median household income of $98,500, 19% higher than the audience for NFL games on traditional networks, and watched an average of 85 minutes per game, according to the same TV Technology report.

Football is only the most visible part of the offer. Amazon also sells video ads on Freevee, its free ad-supported streaming service, and on Twitch, so a brand does not need a football budget to test streaming TV on Amazon. For brands that already sell there, the appeal is plain: the company selling the ad also sells the product, and it can see whether people who saw the ad later searched for and bought the brand in its store.

How a TV ad’s sale ends up credited to search

A television ad reaches a shopper before she has a need. She sees a new air fryer during a game on Thursday. On Sunday she remembers it, opens Amazon and types the brand’s name. She clicks a Sponsored Products ad at the top of the results and buys that afternoon.

In the reports, the sale belongs to the search ad. The TV spot gets nothing, and the search ad is credited with a sale it did not create, like the relay runner who crosses the line and is handed the whole team’s time.

So TV judged by its own return on ad spend looks weak. Search judged by its own return looks stronger than it is. That accounting sets a trap for budgets. A brand that moves money from Sponsored Products to TV, expecting TV to pay for itself, can see search sales fall at exactly the moment TV is creating new interest. If it stops bidding strongly on its own name, a competitor bidding on that name can catch the shopper the TV ad sent.

Take a kitchen appliance brand that spends $100,000 on streaming TV over six weeks in some regions and holds out others. Branded searches on Amazon rise 20% in the regions that saw the ads and 2% in the holdouts, and new-to-brand purchases follow the same pattern. The TV campaign’s own reported return is low. Its real result is the lift in branded search and first-time buyers, and Sponsored Products is where that result gets collected.

Two budgets, one measurement plan

Both sides of the choice are real. Streaming TV reaches people a search ad never will, but it costs more per person reached, and its effect is delayed and partly hidden. Sponsored Products is efficient, but it mostly captures demand that already exists. The numbers lean toward running both, from different budgets: streaming TV from a brand or awareness line, Sponsored Products from the budget that captures existing demand.

Measure TV by what it is supposed to change: branded search volume, new-to-brand purchases and the cost of acquiring a new customer, each compared with a holdout set up before the campaign starts. Keep branded and category search funded during and after the campaign, with branded bids held steady, so the demand TV creates is captured by the brand and not by a rival.

Give the test time. Patience is part of the method. The effect of a TV campaign builds over weeks and fades slowly, so branded search and new-to-brand results deserve a read across at least four to eight weeks after launch, not the morning after the first game. A test judged after one week will almost always look like a failure.

The creative has a job in the search, too. A spot that shows the product clearly and says the brand name plainly gives the viewer the exact words to type later. A clever spot that leaves the brand ambiguous sends her to a generic search, where every competitor is bidding.

Smaller brands should fix the shelf before buying the commercial. A brand whose search advertising is not yet profitable, or whose listings do not convert well, will waste TV money, because the shoppers TV sends will land on pages that do not sell. Strong images, clear titles and enough reviews to reassure a first-time buyer cost less than a television campaign and make every later dollar of TV work harder.

Planning search and video together, with the holdout built in from the first week, is how we design streaming TV tests on Amazon that show what the spots actually did.

A0353.title: Walmart Marketplace in 2023: more sellers, more ads, more work
A0353.alt: A row of market stalls with blue awnings stacked with kraft-wrapped parcels along an old cobbled street.
A0353.ttag: Walmart Marketplace in 2023: more sellers, more ads, more work | Kwontified
A0353.desc: Walmart Marketplace grew fast in 2022, with more sellers, more items and ad revenue up 40%. That makes it a real channel, and one that now takes work to win.
A0353.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 2, 2023.
A0353.body:
About 137,700 sellers were listing on Walmart Marketplace in March 2022, up from about 83,000 a year earlier, by Marketplace Pulse’s estimate, Modern Retail reported. Walmart said at the time that it expected more than 200 million items in its online assortment by the end of the year.

Those numbers made Walmart Marketplace a real channel in 2022, and they also made it a harder one. Every new seller and item competes for the same search results and the same shoppers, and Walmart’s advertising grew about 40% as sellers paid to be seen. A brand entering or expanding there in 2023 should expect to pay for visibility, to need fast fulfillment and strong listings, and to run Walmart as its own business rather than a copy of its Amazon account.

Walmart Marketplace grew up in 2022

By the third quarter, Walmart’s U.S. ecommerce sales were growing 16%, and the company pointed to strength in marketplace and fulfillment services, alongside 40% growth in advertising, Supermarket News reported.

Walmart has also been pulling sellers into its own fulfillment network. Earlier in 2022 it offered new Walmart Fulfillment Services sellers free storage and a discount on fulfillment for their first 90 days, Modern Retail reported. The growth has a clear logic behind it. Walmart’s own inventory is broad but shallow online, and matching Amazon’s selection meant bringing in other sellers, including international ones, to fill the catalog, then giving them a fulfillment service so their products could ship as quickly as Walmart’s own.

Who the crowded catalog serves, and who pays for it

The shopper is the first to gain from all this. A catalog heading toward 200 million items offers more choice, and a fulfillment network that makes third-party products ship like Walmart’s own keeps that choice convenient.

Walmart itself gains next, and in more than one way. More items mean more searches answered on its site, and every crowded results page is a page where a seller has a reason to buy an ad. The 40% growth in advertising is partly the price of that crowding, paid by sellers who want to be found.

The individual seller is where the bill finally lands, in two forms: fewer organic sales and more ad spend. More sellers and more items compete for the same results, and Modern Retail’s headline captured the seller’s view: some sellers joining the marketplace made only a handful of sales. Listing a product on a growing marketplace is no longer enough to be found.

Take a home goods brand that listed 50 products on Walmart in 2021 and saw steady sales with little effort. In 2023 it finds the same products buried below sponsored listings and new competitors offering similar items at lower prices. It has done nothing wrong. The marketplace around it changed, and the approach that worked when the catalog was smaller no longer does. It now needs advertising to be found, faster shipping to convert and sharper listings to stand apart, and each of those costs time and money it did not budget for in 2021.

What a brand needs to win on a crowded Walmart

Visibility now needs its own line in the budget. A Walmart Connect budget belongs in the plan from launch, especially for new products, rather than an expectation that organic search will carry them. Advertising should then be measured against new sales rather than total sales, so the brand pays to be found and not to collect orders it would have had anyway.

Once a shopper finds a product, delivery speed decides whether she buys it. Products that ship quickly and carry Walmart’s fast-delivery signals are more likely to sell. Walmart Fulfillment Services is the simplest route for many brands, though its costs should be compared with the brand’s own network and the cheaper fast option chosen on margin.

Walmart is not a copy of Amazon, and its listings should not be either. Its shoppers, search behavior and store connection differ. Walmart Marketplace items are not available for store pickup, and many Walmart shoppers come for groceries and everyday goods first. The products that fit how those shoppers buy deserve listings written for them, rather than an Amazon catalog copied wholesale.

Walmart is also building an event calendar of its own. For the 2022 holidays it ran three deal events beginning online on November 7, plus Cyber Monday, Progressive Grocer reported. Events concentrate shoppers and advertising demand in short windows, much as they do on Amazon, and inventory, pricing and advertising should be planned for those windows rather than discovered a week before they open.

The crowding has a quieter cost as well. When many sellers list similar or identical products, listings multiply, details drift and shoppers see several versions of the same item at different prices. A brand should check how its own products appear on Walmart, claim and correct its listings and watch for unauthorized sellers offering its goods, because a brand that does not manage its catalog there will find others managing it instead.

Sequence matters most of all. A brand that starts with listings and fulfillment and then adds advertising gets far more from each ad dollar than one that starts with ads on weak pages, because on a crowded marketplace advertising amplifies whatever is already there. The channel is worth the effort: growing traffic, a growing ad business and a parent that wants to win online. The effort has simply grown with it, and doing that work in the right order on Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect is how we run Walmart for the brands we work with.

A0355.title: Amazon Q4 2022 results: ads outgrew sales, and what that means
A0355.alt: A tall stack of gold coins beside three small twine-tied kraft parcels on a wooden desk by a window.
A0355.ttag: Amazon Q4 2022 results: ads outgrew sales, and what that means | Kwontified
A0355.desc: Amazon’s Q4 2022 ad revenue rose 19% while its own store sales fell 2%. Why ads are taking a bigger share of each sale, and how brands should budget for 2023.
A0355.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 7, 2023.
A0355.body:
Late in 2022, Sponsored Products click prices fell from a year earlier in many categories. Tinuiti found declines in six of thirteen categories in the third quarter, and a lower cost per click for the median advertiser on Cyber Monday in more than half of categories, it reported. Amazon’s advertising revenue still grew 19% in the fourth quarter.

Both facts hold because ad revenue is price times volume, and Amazon can grow volume without touching price. In Amazon’s Q4 2022 results, advertising outgrew the company’s own store sales by a wide margin, which means advertising is taking a larger share of every dollar sold on Amazon. Brands should plan 2023 on a total advertising cost that rises as a share of sales, and defend efficiency product by product, rather than expecting the auction to get cheaper.

What Amazon’s Q4 2022 results showed, line by line

Amazon reported fourth-quarter net sales of $149.2 billion, up 9% from a year earlier, MediaPost reported. The lines underneath tell the more useful story, according to EcomCrew’s breakdown of the results:

LineQ4 2022Change from Q4 2021
Online stores (Amazon’s own retail sales)$64.5 billiondown 2%
Third-party seller services (fees from sellers)$36.3 billionup 20%
Advertising services$11.6 billionup 19% (about 23% excluding currency effects)

For the full year, advertising revenue reached $37.8 billion, up 21%, after growing 45% the year before, Intentwise noted. Third-party sellers accounted for a record 59% of units sold in the quarter, Amazon said on its earnings call.

How ad revenue grows while clicks get cheaper

Price is only half of the equation. Amazon does not need to charge more per click to earn more from advertising. It can add ad placements on search and product pages, add formats such as video and streaming, and bring in more advertisers. Each of those raises volume. So the total paid for advertising can climb faster than sales even while the price of a single click holds still or slips.

What matters to a brand is the share of the shopper’s attention that is paid for. When more of the page is sponsored and more sellers are bidding, a brand that holds its ad spend steady will see more of its sales go to rivals that spend more, even if its own cost per click never moves. The odd-looking combination of cheaper clicks and faster ad growth is the auction working as designed. A falling cost per click can sit beside a rising bill, because the brand is buying more clicks just to stand still.

The rough proportions point the same way. Advertising grew 19%. Amazon’s own store sales fell 2%, and seller fees, which track third-party sales and the fees charged on them, grew 20%.

Part of that fee growth came from Amazon raising fees, including a 5% fuel and inflation surcharge on fulfillment from April 2022, Retail TouchPoints reported. Even allowing for that, advertising grew far faster than Amazon’s retail sales and roughly as fast as the seller business it monetizes. The share of each sale that goes to advertising is not shrinking, and on these numbers it is probably growing.

Take a brand whose total advertising cost was 10% of its Amazon sales in 2022. If its category behaves like the marketplace, holding the same share of shoppers’ attention in 2023 may take 11% or 12%, with no rise in its cost per click. Budget at 10% again and its organic sales will slip as sponsored placements multiply around it.

Plan for a rising share, then earn the efficiency back

Total advertising cost of sales, or TACoS, is ad spend divided by all of a product’s sales, ad-attributed and organic together. The 2023 budget belongs on that measure, planned to rise modestly, with any efficiency gain treated as something the team earns rather than something the market hands over. Tracking that share monthly beside cost per click shows whether rising costs come from prices or from spending more to hold position.

Efficiency is still there to be won, product by product. Tighter targeting, less money on searches that never convert and more on products with strong conversion can hold a brand’s overall cost flat while the marketplace rises around it. The gains should be measured and reported at the product level, where they can be seen. The point is to plan for the headwind first and then beat it on purpose, instead of hoping the market supplies the savings.

Which brands feel this most depends on how they sell. With Amazon’s own store sales falling and third-party sellers supplying a record share of units, vendors who sell to Amazon wholesale may see more cautious purchase orders, and may need advertising to keep their products moving through Amazon’s inventory. Sellers, meanwhile, compete with a growing crowd for the same placements. Both end up spending more on advertising, from different directions. The pressure arrives through different doors and lands on the same line of the P&L.

Amazon’s own outlook supports caution. It guided to first-quarter sales growth of 4% to 8%, EcomCrew noted, well below the growth rates of recent years, and slower sales with faster-growing advertising means more brands competing harder for each shopper.

Amazon’s first-quarter report in late April will show whether the gap holds. If advertising again grows several times faster than online store sales, the trend is structural and 2024 budgets should assume it; if the gap narrows, the auction may be near saturation and efficiency gains will be easier to keep. Building budgets on that share, product by product, is how we plan Amazon advertising for the brands we manage.
