A0357.title: The category divide: inflation splits needs from wants
A0357.alt: A wire basket of fresh produce, bread and jars beside an empty open cardboard box on a wooden counter.
A0357.ttag: The category divide: inflation splits needs from wants | Kwontified
A0357.desc: Inflation split retail in 2022: groceries, beauty and essentials grew while electronics and home goods fell. How brands on each side should plan for 2023.
A0357.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 9, 2023.
A0357.body:
In the third quarter of 2022, two retail markets ran side by side inside Target. Beauty, Food and Beverage, and Household Essentials, the categories Target calls its frequency businesses, carried the company’s comparable sales up 2.7%, according to Target, while discretionary aisles stayed soft.

That split is the clearest way to read retail in 2023. Inflation has divided the market into needs, which keep growing in dollars, and wants, which shoppers postpone. A brand should first decide which side of the divide each product line sits on, then plan accordingly: defend volume and price position in needs, and protect margin and timing in wants.

The category divide runs through a single store

On the earnings call, chief executive Brian Cornell said Beauty and Food and Beverage each grew by double digits, while discretionary weakness worsened at the end of the quarter and sales tilted toward promotions, according to the transcript. Target is planning around the divide too. It said it was preparing for a range of fourth-quarter outcomes centered on a low-single-digit decline in comparable sales, given trends that softened late in the third quarter, according to Target.

For a brand on the wants side, that guidance describes the buyer across the table: a retail partner cautious about inventory and keen on promotions. For a brand on the needs side, it describes a retailer leaning on exactly the categories that brand sells, and expecting them to keep the trips coming.

The holiday numbers drew the same line

The whole market looked like Target’s aisles. Across the November and December holiday period, the National Retail Federation’s figures had grocery and beverage store sales 7.8% higher than a year before and health and personal care stores 2.8% higher. On the other side of the line, furniture and home furnishings stores lost 1.1% and electronics and appliance stores lost 5.7%.

Electronics shows the wants side at full scale. NPD’s forecast had U.S. spending on consumer technology finishing 2022 down 8% on the year before, it reported.

A household budget sorts needs from wants

The divide follows the arithmetic of a paycheck. When food prices rise 10.4% in a year, as they did in the twelve months to December, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ figures, the grocery bill takes a larger share of the same income, and something else has to give.

What gives is anything that can wait. A household cannot postpone dinner or laundry detergent. It can postpone a new sofa, a second monitor or a kitchen gadget. Spending on needs therefore grows in dollars, largely because prices rose, while spending on wants falls because shoppers choose to wait.

Take a family in early 2023. The weekly grocery run costs noticeably more than a year ago. Shampoo, toothpaste and cleaning supplies cost more too, and the family still buys them, though more often on promotion or in the store’s own brand. The new television it talked about at Thanksgiving has slipped to “maybe in the summer,” and the patio set is off the list entirely.

That family is reallocating, not cutting back on everything, and the difference matters for anyone reading the sales data. Its total spending may be roughly what it was a year ago; what the money buys has changed. Repeated across millions of households, that reallocation turns one retail market into two, and the brands the family stopped buying from feel it long before any headline about consumer spending does.

Beauty is the instructive exception, and a useful warning against tidy labels. It is technically discretionary, but it behaved like a need in 2022, growing strongly at Target. Small, affordable treats often hold up when larger purchases are postponed, which is a reason to judge a product by how its own shoppers behave rather than by a textbook category label.

Planning each side of the divide

On the needs side, demand is steady but every price is watched. The risk is less that shoppers leave the category than that they switch to a cheaper option, including the retailer’s own brand. Brands there should defend price position carefully, protect in-stock rates and promotional presence, and track units and price position against store brands, so that price-driven growth does not hide a loss of volume.

On the wants side, demand is real but deferred. Shoppers will buy when a reason arrives, often a deal event or a need that can no longer wait. Brands there should protect margin, plan inventory conservatively, concentrate spending on the moments shoppers are waiting for, and avoid chasing volume with discounts that will be hard to reverse.

Advertising should follow the same line. In needs categories, shoppers search and buy all year, so steady spending on the searches that define the category protects share against cheaper alternatives. In wants categories, heavy spending in quiet weeks buys attention from shoppers who are not ready, and budgets work harder concentrated around the events and seasons when those shoppers return.

Some brands sit on both sides of the line, which makes the divide an internal planning problem as well as a market one. A home brand might sell cleaning supplies and decorative pillows, and in 2023 it should run them as two businesses, with different targets, promotion plans and advertising goals, rather than averaging them into one plan that fits neither.

The question to bring to the next planning meeting is which of the brand’s product lines its own shoppers treated as needs in 2022, and which they treated as wants. Sorting the range that way and planning each line on its own terms is how we plan by product line for the brands we run.

A0359.crumb: Target Plus in 2023: an invitation that…
A0359.title: Target Plus in 2023: an invitation that comes with obligations
A0359.alt: A red wax-sealed envelope beside a blank clipboard and red pen on a rustic wooden desk near a window.
A0359.ttag: Target Plus in 2023: an invitation that comes with obligations | Kwontified
A0359.desc: Target Plus stays invite-only, with a few hundred sellers sharing target.com’s traffic. Why that limits competition, and what Target expects in return.
A0359.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 14, 2023.
A0359.body:
Walmart had about 137,700 marketplace sellers in March 2022, by Marketplace Pulse’s estimate, Modern Retail reported. Target Plus had 450, sharing the traffic of one of the most visited retail websites in the U.S. The gap between those two seller counts is the whole economics of selling on Target’s marketplace.

With so few sellers, the seller-against-seller competition that defines Amazon and Walmart barely exists on Target Plus. The price of that calm is an obligation: Target extends its own promise to marketplace items and holds sellers to it. A brand should seek an invitation only if it can meet Target’s standard for service and price, and once inside, it should grow through Target’s own programs rather than by competing on price.

What Target Plus looks like going into 2023

Target launched Target Plus on February 25, 2019 with 30 sellers. Three years on it had 450 sellers offering 250,000 products, having added 180 over the previous year, Marketplace Pulse reported. Target’s chief marketing and digital officer, Cara Sylvester, said it would remain invite-only while Target considers which trusted partners complement its assortment.

Those few hundred sellers share roughly 200 million monthly visits to target.com, by Marketplace Pulse’s estimate. Target’s digital business is large and built on its stores: digital sales grew from $6.8 billion in 2019 to nearly $20 billion in 2021, mostly through store-fulfilled orders, Marketplace Pulse noted. The marketplace is a small addition to that machine, not its engine, and Target has chosen to keep it that way.

How curation trades competition for obligation

On Amazon, a seller competes with many other sellers, often on the same product. On Target Plus, Target chooses who sells and keeps the shelf uncrowded, so a seller faces little competition from other sellers for the shopper’s attention.

The other side of that trade is that Target does not treat marketplace items as someone else’s problem. Its pitch to shoppers is the experience itself. “Because of our trusted and curated assortment, our guests aren’t sifting through thousands of pages of results,” Sylvester said, as Marketplace Pulse noted. Marketplace items appear on target.com alongside Target’s own, so to a guest they are simply part of what Target sells.

In our experience managing Target Plus accounts, Target holds marketplace sellers to that standard in practice: delivery promises, stock accuracy, listing quality and responses to guests are watched closely. A marketplace seller is delivering Target’s promise as well as its own. One that ships late, runs out of stock or handles returns badly damages Target’s relationship with its guests, and because the marketplace runs by invitation, Target can simply decline to keep it. The low competition is earned by meeting a high standard, and kept the same way.

Take a home brand with strong sales on Amazon and its own site. On Amazon it competes with dozens of similar products and spends heavily on advertising to stay visible. Invited to Target Plus, it finds far fewer competitors in its category and a calmer shopping environment.

That calm comes with conditions. The brand must also ship to Target’s standard, keep prices in line with its other channels and keep its listings complete. If it can, Target Plus may become one of its most efficient channels. If it cannot, the invitation is a liability.

Weighed together, the two sides lean toward patience. Fewer rivals is a real advantage, but only for an operation already able to carry Target’s promise; for anyone else, the obligation costs more than the calm is worth.

Qualify first, then grow through Target’s programs

Before chasing an invitation, a brand should audit itself against what a Target guest would expect: fast and reliable delivery, accurate inventory, pricing consistent with other channels, clean product content and responsive service. Target is curating a guest experience, and the brands it wants are the ones that improve it. A brand that would have to cut corners to keep up is better served by waiting until it can meet the bar.

The pitch matters as much as the audit. A brand makes its case in terms of what it adds to Target’s assortment, and category fit strengthens it. In the third quarter of 2022, Target’s growth was led by Beauty, Food and Beverage, and Household Essentials, while discretionary categories were soft, according to Target. Brands in categories where Target’s guests are spending have a stronger case for an invitation and a faster path to sales once they arrive.

Once inside, growth comes from Target’s own tools rather than from out-competing other sellers. Roundel, Target’s advertising business, and the Target Circle loyalty program are the levers, and both belong in the plan from the first month rather than after organic visibility disappoints. Target has said that Circle had 100 million members in 2022, Retail TouchPoints reported, and that Roundel uses that first-party data with its vendors.

There is a longer game too. Marketplace Pulse suggested Target Plus could act as an on-ramp to Target’s physical stores, letting Target test a brand online first. Target has not said it works that way, but a brand that sells well and serves guests reliably on Target Plus is building exactly the record a retailer looks at before giving a brand shelf space.

What would change the calculation is the pace of invitations. Marketplace Pulse’s data show steady but slow growth; if Target starts adding sellers faster, competition inside Target Plus will rise and the calm that makes it valuable will thin. Getting an operation ready for that bar before the invitation arrives is how we prepare brands for Target Plus.

A0360.crumb: Zalando in 2023: from wholesale buyer to…
A0360.title: Zalando in 2023: from wholesale buyer to brand platform
A0360.alt: A bright clothing boutique with neutral garments on wooden racks and a wrapped parcel on a central table.
A0360.ttag: Zalando in 2023: from wholesale buyer to brand platform | Kwontified
A0360.desc: Zalando is moving from buying brands’ stock to hosting brands that sell direct. What that means for fashion brands in Europe, and how to choose a model.
A0360.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 16, 2023.
A0360.body:
Take an outerwear brand that has sold to Zalando wholesale for years. In 2023 its buyer orders more cautiously than before and suggests the brand list its wider range through the Partner Program instead. Around the brand’s own table, the question is no longer how much Zalando will take. It is whether the brand wants to become a seller on Zalando, holding its own stock and setting its own prices.

That conversation follows from where Zalando is heading. It is moving from a wholesale retailer that buys brands’ stock toward a platform where brands sell directly, and partner businesses gained seven points of share in a year toward a goal of half of fashion sales by 2025. Brands selling in Europe should expect more cautious wholesale orders and decide deliberately whether to sell through the Partner Program, where they control price and range but carry the stock and much of the work.

Zalando grew in 2022 while its mix moved toward partners

Zalando grew in the third quarter of 2022 despite weak consumer confidence. Gross merchandise volume rose 7.1% to 3.28 billion euros, revenue rose 2.9% to 2.35 billion euros, and active customers passed 50 million for the first time, up 8%, according to Zalando. Its loyalty program, Zalando Plus, almost tripled its membership.

For brands, the mix matters more than the totals. The share of Zalando’s fashion store sales coming from partner businesses rose by seven percentage points from a year earlier, and Zalando restated its goal of reaching 50% by 2025. Partner businesses are brands and retailers that sell on Zalando with their own stock and prices, rather than selling their goods to Zalando.

Zalando tightened its economics at the same time. It introduced a minimum order value, which it said improved profitability, and expected full-year growth at the lower end of its 3% to 7% range, its third-quarter presentation showed. It also expanded into Hungary and Romania during 2022, reaching 25 markets, Zalando said.

Why Zalando would rather host the stock than buy it

Zalando began as an online retailer in the traditional sense: it bought fashion from brands at wholesale, held the stock and set the prices. That works when demand is predictable. It works less well when demand swings and a retailer is left with inventory nobody wants, which is what many fashion retailers faced in 2022.

The Partner Program moves that risk. A brand lists its own stock on Zalando, sets its own prices and pays Zalando a commission. Zalando gets a wider assortment without buying it; the brand gets direct access to Zalando’s customers and control over how its products are presented.

Two services make the model easier to adopt. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions stores and ships partner stock through Zalando’s logistics network, and Zalando Marketing Services sells advertising to brands on the platform. A brand can now reach Zalando’s customers, store its goods in Zalando’s warehouses and pay Zalando to promote them, all without Zalando owning a single item of its stock.

The climate has hurried the shift along. With consumer confidence at record lows and basket sizes slightly smaller, down about 2% in the year to September by Zalando’s figures, a retailer has good reason to buy less stock up front. The platform model lets Zalando keep its assortment broad while holding less inventory itself.

For the outerwear brand, the new arrangement cuts both ways. It can now sell colors and sizes the buyer would never have taken. It must also hold that stock, price it well and promote it, work that used to sit with Zalando’s buying team.

The decision in the room: wholesale, partner or both

For a leadership team, the choice is no longer whether to be on Zalando but how, and each answer carries a different workload and a different share of the risk.

Wholesale keeps the work simple. Zalando buys the stock and the brand ships a purchase order. In a cautious year, though, orders may be smaller, and the brand has little say over pricing and markdowns once the goods are sold. A useful first step is to set the 2023 orders beside prior years and estimate how much of the range the buyer is no longer taking.

The Partner Program gives control. A brand sets prices, chooses its range and reaches customers in markets it might not otherwise serve. It also carries inventory risk, needs content and pricing discipline, and will often need advertising to stand out, so the range the buyer passes on deserves a model covering stock, fulfillment, commission and advertising before anyone commits.

Geography strengthens the partner case. Zalando’s newer markets in Central and Eastern Europe, including Hungary and Romania, give a brand already selling through Zalando a way to reach shoppers there without building local operations. A wholesale buyer may not stock a brand in every market; a partner decides for itself where its range is offered.

The loyalty program points the same way, and it adds a reason to think about fulfillment early. Zalando Plus members are promised a premium experience, including faster delivery. A partner that stores its stock with Zalando’s fulfillment service is better placed to meet those expectations than one shipping from its own warehouse, which matters more as Plus membership grows.

Many brands will run both: wholesale for proven core products, the Partner Program for broader ranges, new markets and the products the buyer declines. The mistake is drifting into partnership without a plan for stock, pricing and advertising, or clinging to wholesale while the orders shrink. Deciding that split on purpose, with clear pricing rules across every European channel, is how we help brands sell on Zalando.

A0362.title: Amazon rankings: three numbers that measure different things
A0362.alt: An antique brass balance scale, hourglass and pocket compass on a wooden table against a teal wall.
A0362.ttag: Amazon rankings: three numbers that measure different things | Kwontified
A0362.desc: Best Sellers Rank, organic search rank and sponsored position measure different things on Amazon. How each works, and which one fits which decision.
A0362.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 21, 2023.
A0362.body:
A reusable water bottle shows #2 on its product page, in a narrow subcategory for insulated bottles with a particular lid, and the team celebrates. For the broad search “water bottle,” which brings far more shoppers, the same bottle’s organic rank is 38, on the second page. On the searches where it does rank well organically, several sponsored products sit above it. Which number is the real rank?

All of them, because Amazon rankings are at least three different numbers. Best Sellers Rank measures recent sales against a category, organic search rank measures position for one search term, and sponsored position is bought. They often disagree. Best Sellers Rank belongs only in comparisons within a category, visibility should be judged by organic rank weighted by search volume, and paid and organic positions should be reported separately.

What each of the Amazon rankings measures

RankingWhat it measuresWhat moves itFit for
Best Sellers RankRecent sales against other products in the same categorySales, weighted toward the latestSales momentum within one category
Organic search rankUnpaid position for one search termRelevance and performance on that searchVisibility, weighted by search volume
Sponsored positionPaid position on a results or product pageBids and budgetVisibility the brand is renting

Best Sellers Rank is the number on a product page that places it within a category or subcategory. It moves frequently and leans toward the latest sales. It is also relative. A product ranks well because it is outselling the other products in its category at that moment, not because it sells any particular number of units.

Organic search rank is where a product appears, unpaid, when a shopper types a particular search. It is specific to that search and can change from one day to the next, so a product can rank first for one phrase and nowhere for another.

Sponsored position is where a product appears because the brand paid for it, alongside and increasingly above the organic results. Of the first twenty products a shopper sees on an Amazon search, only four were organic results, Marketplace Pulse found, as Modern Retail reported. Marketplace Pulse also noted that few purchases happen beyond the first page of results.

Why one product can hold three different ranks

Best Sellers Rank is relative to the size of a category. Being third in a small subcategory may mean a few dozen sales a day; being third in a large category may mean thousands. Without the category, the rank says nothing about volume. Context is the whole number.

Organic rank depends on the search, and the searches that bring the most shoppers are usually broad and crowded. A product can lead a narrow subcategory, where Best Sellers Rank is easy to win, while sitting deep in the results for the broad search where most shoppers start. Because sponsored placements fill so much of the top of the page, even a strong organic rank can land out of sight: a product ranked fourth organically may be the tenth or twelfth product a shopper actually sees.

Deal events distort the picture further. A strong promotion can lift a product many places in Best Sellers Rank within hours, and the product falls back just as fast when the deal ends, because the rank leans toward the latest sales. Read on the day of a deal, the rank overstates the product’s position; read the week after, it may understate it. Weekly trends are more honest than any single reading.

The pull toward the flattering number is easy to understand. Best Sellers Rank sits on the product page, it is a single figure, and on a good day it looks like a trophy. That is exactly why it gets reported as if it answered questions about visibility it cannot answer. All three numbers are true; the mistake is presenting the first one as the answer to the other two.

One number per decision

Best Sellers Rank fits one job: comparing sales momentum against products that share the same category, tracked as a trend over weeks rather than read hourly. It should never be compared across categories, and it should come off the headline of the report.

Visibility is a job for organic search rank, weighted by search volume. Start with a list of the twenty searches that matter most. Give each its organic position and an estimate of how many shoppers use it. That list says far more about discoverability than any single rank. Rising organic rank on a high-volume search is worth more than a top position on a phrase few people type.

Sponsored and organic positions belong side by side in the report, never merged. When both are folded into one “rank,” a brand cannot tell whether it earned its visibility or rented it, and cannot plan for what happens if it stops paying. Kept separate, they show where advertising is protecting a position the brand already earns and where it is buying visibility the brand lacks, two cases that call for different budgets and different expectations.

The whole thing fits on one page each week. It lists the searches that matter, with estimated volume, organic position and whether the brand also bought a sponsored position on each. It shows Best Sellers Rank trends for the main products against the same few competitors. And it marks any week with a deal or a stock-out. Changes then get read in context, not celebrated or feared.

Building that page, with paid and earned visibility pulled apart, is how we track Amazon visibility for the brands we manage.

A0364.title: Walmart Connect grew 41%: what Walmart now expects from brands
A0364.alt: Rows of blue shopping carts in an empty parking lot beneath a blank billboard and palm trees.
A0364.ttag: Walmart Connect grew 41%: what Walmart now expects from brands | Kwontified
A0364.desc: Walmart Connect grew 41% in the holiday quarter, far faster than sales. What that says about how Walmart now expects brands to compete, and how to plan.
A0364.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 23, 2023.
A0364.body:
Read Walmart’s holiday-quarter results the way a supplier’s sales team would, and one gap jumps off the page. Walmart Connect in the U.S. grew 41%, while Walmart’s U.S. e-commerce sales grew 17%. A retailer does not grow its advertising business more than twice as fast as its online sales by accident. Something about how Walmart makes money is changing, and brands that sell there are part of it.

What it tells brands is that Walmart now expects them to pay for visibility as part of selling there. Brands in 2023 should budget Walmart Connect as a standing cost of the channel, judge it against Walmart’s store and online sales together, and treat it as part of the relationship with Walmart rather than an optional extra.

Walmart Connect outgrew the business it sells against

U.S. comparable sales rose 8.3%, e-commerce sales grew 17%, and Walmart said it continued to gain market share in grocery, according to Walmart. Its global advertising business grew more than 20%, led by that 41% growth at Walmart Connect in the U.S. For the full fiscal year, Walmart said its global advertising business grew nearly 30% to $2.7 billion, led by Walmart Connect and Flipkart Ads.

Underneath the headline sales, the picture was less comfortable. The average ticket rose 6.3% while transactions rose 1.8%, according to the same release, so much of the growth came from higher prices rather than more trips. And the gross profit rate fell 83 basis points, which Walmart attributed mainly to markdowns and the mix of sales.

Put those lines next to each other and the shape of the year becomes clear. Shoppers were paying more per basket and coming in only a little more often, and selling goods was getting less profitable. Advertising was the part of the business moving fastest.

Where the margin sits now

For most of its history, Walmart made money one way: buying goods and selling them for more. Brands paid Walmart through the price of their goods, through promotional funding and through the terms of their supplier agreements. Advertising was a small part of that relationship.

That has changed quickly. Walmart has built an online business with tens of millions of shoppers, a marketplace that brought in thousands of new sellers, and stores that remain its largest asset. Each of those creates places where a brand’s product can be shown to a shopper who is about to buy, and Walmart Connect sells those places.

Follow the money and Walmart’s enthusiasm is easy to understand. Selling goods brings thin margins, as the drop in its gross profit rate showed in this very quarter. Advertising revenue costs little to produce once the audience exists. Every dollar a brand spends on Walmart Connect is worth far more to Walmart’s profit than a dollar of product sales. A supplier’s value to Walmart is starting to include what it spends on Walmart’s media, not only what it sells through Walmart’s shelves.

The growth rates also tell brands where Walmart’s priorities are moving. When advertising grows more than twice as fast as e-commerce, Walmart has a strong reason to make its pages, apps and stores more advertising-friendly. That usually means more sponsored placements and fewer free ones. It also means Walmart’s teams will judge brands partly on how much they help that business grow, in ways no contract spells out.

A snacks brand that has sold through Walmart for years might feel this before it can name it. Its products are on the shelf and on the site, and for a long time its share of searches for its category held up on its own. In 2023 it notices that competitors’ sponsored products now sit above its listings for its own category searches, and Walmart’s merchant team asks about its advertising plans during the annual business review. Nothing in its contract has changed. The terms of competing on Walmart’s shelf have.

What changes in a supplier’s 2023 plan

The budget line is the obvious place to start. Advertising at Walmart belongs in the plan as a standing cost of selling there, sized against expected Walmart sales, not parked in a test budget that has to be argued for each quarter. Brands that sell to Walmart as suppliers and brands that sell through its marketplace face the same pages, so the logic holds for both. Planning Walmart Connect alongside cost of goods, promotions and fulfillment makes the true cost of the channel visible to the people who sign off on it.

Measurement needs to match how Walmart actually sells. Most of Walmart’s sales still happen in stores, and many shoppers browse online before buying in a store. Advertising judged only on online sales will look weaker than it is. Brands should ask what Walmart Connect can report about in-store sales and compare advertised products with similar ones that were not advertised, so the budget conversation rests on the whole effect.

The relationship itself has a new seat at the table. Walmart’s merchants, its media business and its supplier teams increasingly talk to each other. A brand’s advertising plan now sits next to its pricing, promotions and supply performance in how Walmart sees it. A supplier who arrives at the business review with a media plan has a better answer to the question the buyer is now asking.

There is also an opening in the numbers. Walmart’s global advertising business, at $2.7 billion for the year, is still a fraction of Amazon’s, which reached $37.8 billion in 2022, Intentwise noted. Walmart’s sponsored placements are less crowded than Amazon’s, and in many categories fewer brands are bidding. Brands that build their Walmart advertising now, while the auction is still forming, may buy visibility more cheaply than those that arrive once it is as crowded as Amazon’s.

The caution is just as concrete. Advertising cannot fix weak pricing, poor stock or thin content. Walmart’s shoppers in 2023 are trading carefully, as the gap between ticket and transaction growth shows. Paid visibility for a product that is out of stock or priced above its competitors only buys a more expensive disappointment.

So the question for a leadership team is whether its Walmart plan still describes the retailer as it was, a buyer of goods, or as it is becoming, a buyer of goods that also sells the space in front of them. Building that second kind of plan, with media, pricing and supply in one view, is how we run Walmart Connect for suppliers and marketplace sellers.

A0365.crumb: Mercado Libre in 2023: speed and ads…
A0365.title: Mercado Libre in 2023: speed and ads decide who gets seen
A0365.alt: A riderless yellow delivery scooter with a cargo box on a colorful colonial street lined with pastel houses.
A0365.ttag: Mercado Libre in 2023: speed and ads decide who gets seen | Kwontified
A0365.desc: Mercado Libre grew 35% in late 2022, with record fulfillment and fast-rising ads. Why delivery speed and advertising decide visibility, and how to enter.
A0365.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 28, 2023.
A0365.body:
Two brands list comparable products on Mercado Libre in Mexico at the same price, with the same photos and similar reviews. One sells steadily. The other barely moves. The difference usually sits in a warehouse: where the stock is held decides how fast it arrives, and how fast it arrives decides how often it is seen.

On Mercado Libre, speed and advertising decide visibility. Brands entering or expanding there in 2023 should treat the marketplace’s own fulfillment as the price of being seen, budget advertising as a share of sales from launch, and plan country by country rather than for Latin America as one market.

Mercado Libre’s fourth quarter, in five lines

LineQ4 2022
Gross merchandise volume growth, currency-neutral35%
Brazil volume growth22%
Mexico volume growth28%
Share of shipments through Mercado Libre fulfillment43%, a record
Mercado Ads revenue as a share of volume1.4%

Those figures come from Mercado Libre’s letter to shareholders, which also said unique buyers grew more than 20% over 2022. Mexico was its fastest-growing market by volume, helped by a record El Buen Fin sales event, while Argentina showed weaker volume trends.

The last two rows are the ones a brand should circle. Fulfillment, in which Mercado Libre stores and ships sellers’ goods, reached its highest-ever share of shipments. The advertising business, at 1.4% of volume, is more than five times larger than it was three years earlier. The company said it doubled the engineers working on advertising and expected to launch a demand-side platform in 2023.

Scale is no longer the question. Over the full year, Mercado Libre said it shipped more than a billion items and booked more than $10 billion of net revenue, both for the first time.

How delivery speed turns into visibility

Mercado Libre’s promise to shoppers is fast, reliable delivery in markets where that has historically been hard to find. Products stored and shipped through its own network can arrive in a day or two. Products shipped by sellers themselves often take longer.

Shoppers respond to that difference, and the marketplace rewards what shoppers respond to. Faster delivery shows up in the shopping experience, products that convert better earn more visibility, and more visibility brings more sales to convert. A brand that keeps its stock in its own warehouse competes with a handicap, even if its product and price are identical to a rival’s.

Advertising adds a second layer on top of the first. On the earnings call, management said improvements to its advertising platform had increased the presence of ads on product pages, according to the transcript. As Mercado Ads grows, more of the most visible space becomes paid space. A brand that relies on organic visibility alone competes for a shrinking share of the page.

Take a U.S. personal care brand entering Mexico. It lists twenty products, ships from a third-party warehouse and spends nothing on ads. Its listings sit below faster-shipping competitors and below sponsored products, and sales are slow.

The brand then moves its best-selling ten products into Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network and sets an advertising budget at about the marketplace’s own average share of sales. The products now arrive faster, appear more prominently and convert better. The cost per sale rises, but sales rise more.

Sizing the ad budget from day one

Mercado Libre’s own figure, advertising revenue equal to 1.4% of merchandise volume across the marketplace, is a reasonable floor for planning. Say the brand plans for $100,000 of Mercado Libre sales. A budget at the marketplace average comes to $1,400. Treat that as the starting line, not the target, since brands competing for visibility in crowded categories will usually spend more than the average.

The order of spending matters as much as the size. Fulfillment comes first: ship the best sellers into Mercado Libre’s network, then advertise them. Expand the range once you know which products move.

One country at a time

Mexico and Brazil are both growing quickly, with different shoppers, regulations, payment habits and logistics. Argentina’s economy behaves very differently from both. A plan for Latin America as a single market will misjudge all of them. Start with the market where your products, pricing and import logistics fit best, and learn there before expanding.

Brands based outside the region have two ways in. Mercado Libre runs a cross-border program that lets foreign sellers list in its markets and ship from abroad, a lower-cost way to test demand before committing inventory locally. Cross-border delivery is slower, though, so it rarely matches local fulfillment for visibility. Brands that see demand should plan to import and stock locally once a product proves itself.

Currency deserves its own line in the plan. Prices on Mercado Libre are set in local currency, and exchange rates in the region can move sharply within months. A price that is profitable when set can lose its margin before the stock sells. Review prices more often than you would in the U.S., and build a margin buffer into products with long replenishment times.

Local content matters as much as logistics. Listings written for Mexican or Brazilian shoppers, in natural Spanish or Portuguese with local sizes, measurements and terms, convert better than translations of an English listing. Questions from shoppers arrive in the listing itself, and fast, clear answers help the next shopper decide.

Payments help everyone on the platform. Mercado Libre’s payment business, Mercado Pago, had almost 44 million unique active users in the quarter, according to the shareholder letter. Shoppers who already hold money in the wallet buy easily on the marketplace, which helps conversion for every seller there.

The test for any entry plan is simple to state: if a product is not in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network, do not judge it by its ad results yet. Getting the stock, the ads and the country order right is how we launch brands on Mercado Libre.

A0366.title: Roundel in 2023: Target’s ad business moves to the center
A0366.alt: An empty red wooden display unit topped with a blank lightbox sign in a bright, minimal storefront.
A0366.ttag: Roundel in 2023: Target’s ad business moves to the center | Kwontified
A0366.desc: Target says it will put more emphasis and investment behind Roundel and Target Circle in 2023. What that means for vendors and sellers, and how to plan for it.
A0366.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 2, 2023.
A0366.body:
At its meeting with investors on February 28, Target said two things that a vendor should read side by side. It would place additional emphasis and investment behind Target Circle and its Roundel advertising business in 2023. And it would buy discretionary inventory cautiously. One sentence offers vendors more ways to pay Target; the other promises them smaller orders.

Taken together, they move Roundel from a vendor add-on to a central part of how brands keep their place at Target. Brands should plan Roundel budgets alongside their Target sales and inventory plans, insist on measurement that includes store sales, and use Target Circle events deliberately.

What Target said about Roundel at its February 28 meeting

Chief executive Brian Cornell described Target Circle as a program introduced in 2019 that quickly attracted 50 million users and has doubled since, according to the transcript. He said Roundel, Target’s media company, had grown significantly since 2019, with growth and profit potential ahead, and that Target intends to place additional emphasis and advancement toward Circle and Roundel in 2023.

The caution came from the other side of the business. Sales in home and other discretionary categories were still soft, and Target said it was taking a cautious approach to inventory commitments in those areas, Furniture Today reported. The same report said Target is looking to draw more suppliers into Roundel.

Cornell also gave two structural facts that matter for anyone buying ads there. Target’s digital penetration stands at nearly 19%, and more than 95% of all its sales, including digital orders, are fulfilled by its stores.

Roundel rests on two assets Target built for other reasons

One is identity: Target Circle gives Target a way to recognize a large share of its shoppers across stores and its app. A Target executive said Target launched Circle to know more about its guests rather than to drive sales, Retail TouchPoints reported. That knowledge is what lets Roundel target ads and report results.

The other asset is the store, and it is the more unusual one. Because almost all of Target’s sales, including online orders, run through its stores, Target can connect an ad to a purchase whether it happens in an aisle, at the curb or on a doorstep. Few media owners can see the in-store sale at all. Target can.

Put those together and Roundel offers a vendor something a general ad network cannot. It can reach a Target shopper and then show that the same shopper bought the product at Target, in whichever channel the purchase happened.

Why a cautious buyer makes Roundel more central

The timing explains the emphasis. In a year when Target is buying discretionary inventory carefully, advertising is one of the few ways a vendor can help its products sell through faster. Roundel helps Target’s margins, and it gives vendors a lever at the moment shelf space and orders are tight. Those two effects point the same way, which is why the ad business is moving toward the middle of the relationship.

Target’s own brands add pressure from another direction. Target said at the meeting that it would launch or expand more than ten owned brands in 2023 to appeal to value-conscious shoppers, Dow Jones reported. National brands will share more of the shelf and the site with Target’s own products, which usually carry better margins for Target. For a national brand, paid visibility on Target’s pages is one of the few tools it controls in that competition.

Picture how this lands for a home décor vendor. In 2022 its orders shrank as Target cleared excess stock. In 2023 its buyer is cautious again, and the conversation at the business review turns to how the vendor will support sell-through. A Roundel plan focused on its strongest products, tied to a Target Circle event, is a concrete answer to that question. A vendor with no plan leaves the buyer with a harder case to make internally.

Planning Roundel with the rest of the Target business

The Roundel plan belongs in the same document as the Target sales and inventory plan. Advertising for products that are thinly stocked or about to be cut is wasted. Advertising for products Target has committed to, and wants to sell through, strengthens the vendor’s position with the same buyer who is trimming orders elsewhere.

Measurement has to follow the store. Because most Target sales happen in or through stores, judging Roundel on online sales alone will understate it. Ask Roundel how it reports in-store and online results together, and set each advertised product against a similar one that ran without ads, so the result reflects the whole effect.

Target Circle events are where the budget works hardest. Circle offers and events concentrate shoppers’ attention, and a brand that lines up its Roundel spending, promotions and inventory with those moments gets more from each dollar than one that spreads its budget evenly through the year.

Marketplace sellers on Target Plus face the same logic on a smaller stage. Target Plus is small and invitation-only, but its sellers compete on the same pages, and Roundel is the main way to stand out there as well.

None of this replaces the basics. Fill rates, pricing and product quality still decide whether Target wants a brand on its shelves. Advertising strengthens a strong position and rarely rescues a weak one, and a buyer can tell the difference between the two.

The question worth putting to the team before the next Target review is simple: does our Roundel plan follow the products Target has committed to, or the products we wish it had? Building that plan with inventory, Circle timing and store measurement in one place is how we manage Roundel for Target vendors and Target Plus sellers.

A0368.crumb: Hidden search traffic: where your Amazon…
A0368.title: Hidden search traffic: where your Amazon shoppers already are
A0368.alt: A brass magnifying glass on dusty floorboards revealing a faint bootprint, with old books on a shelf behind.
A0368.ttag: Hidden search traffic: where your Amazon shoppers already are | Kwontified
A0368.desc: Amazon’s search query data shows where shoppers who see your product buy it, but too few see it. How to find that hidden search traffic and act on it.
A0368.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 7, 2023.
A0368.body:
When a brand wants more sales on Amazon, the broad category search is the obvious target. It has the most shoppers, so it looks like the most upside, and it is where extra budget tends to go first. Yet the most valuable traffic a brand is missing usually sits somewhere smaller and quieter.

It sits on specific searches where shoppers who see the product buy it at a high rate, but too few see it. Amazon’s Search Query Performance data now makes that gap visible. Brands should rank their searches by the gap between their share of purchases and their share of impressions, and move advertising and listing work toward the searches where that gap is widest.

Where hidden search traffic shows up in Amazon’s data

Amazon said that brands enrolled in Brand Registry would get a Search Analytics Dashboard in early 2022, including a query performance view to help sellers understand the top search terms associated with their products, according to Amazon.

The resulting Search Query Performance dashboard reports, for each search that led shoppers to a brand’s products, the total impressions, clicks, cart adds and purchases across all products, and the brand’s own share of each, Carbon6 explained. The total covers both organic and sponsored results.

That combination is new for most brands. Advertising reports show what happened on searches a brand paid for. This data shows the whole market for each search, and where the brand stands in it, paid or not. A brand can see, for a search it never bid on, how many shoppers bought anything and what share of them bought its product.

A small search can beat a big one

On any search, a brand has a share of what shoppers see (impressions) and a share of what they buy (purchases). If the purchase share is well above the impression share, the brand’s product converts better than the competition once shoppers see it. The bottleneck is visibility, not appeal.

Take a brand of unscented laundry detergent and two of its searches.

SearchImpression sharePurchase share
laundry detergent2%2%
fragrance-free detergent for sensitive skin4%12%

On the broad search, the brand converts at the market average, and visibility there is expensive. On the narrower one, shoppers who see the product choose it three times as often as its visibility would predict. The brand had been raising bids on the broad search. The better move is to raise visibility on the narrow one, through advertising and by making sure the listing speaks directly to that need, and then to look for more searches with the same pattern.

Why would the smaller search be the better investment? On a search like the second, each additional impression is likely to produce sales more efficiently than on a broad search where the brand converts at or below average. That is the hidden traffic: demand the product already wins, on searches where it is under-seen.

These searches are easy to miss. Each one is usually small. They tend to be specific, such as a product type with a size, an ingredient or a use, rather than the broad category term every competitor bids on. No single one looks worth a meeting. Together, though, they can add up to a meaningful share of a category’s sales.

Ranking searches by the gap

Pull your search query data for the past several weeks. For each search, divide the brand’s purchase share by its impression share. Sort from highest to lowest, and focus on searches where the ratio is well above one and the search has enough volume to matter.

On those searches, work on two fronts at once. Raise visibility through targeted advertising, with bids informed by the strong conversion. And improve the listing so the product’s relevance to that search is obvious, in the title, bullets and images. Both work because the product is already the right answer for those shoppers.

Once spending rises, keep watching the ratio. As visibility grows, conversion usually falls somewhat, because more of the shoppers seeing the product are marginal. Keep investing while the purchase share stays comfortably above the impression share, and stop once they meet.

The same lens works in reverse. Searches where the brand’s impression share is well above its purchase share are places where it is seen but not chosen. There, more visibility is wasteful until the listing, price or product fit improves. Cutting spend on those searches often funds the expansion on the others.

The data has limits worth knowing before anyone acts on it. The dashboard covers the searches that led shoppers to a brand’s products, so a search where the brand is almost invisible may not appear at all. Pair it with the search term report from your advertising campaigns, which shows searches where your ads appeared even if few shoppers bought.

The shares also combine organic and sponsored results on the same search. A strong ratio on a search where you already spend heavily may reflect the ads as much as the product. Check how much of your impression share on each search was paid before treating it as untapped demand.

The approach helps small brands most. They rarely win broad searches against large competitors, but they often lead narrow ones where their product fits a specific need, and this data shows them exactly where.

The rule fits on one line: buy visibility where your purchase share already outruns your impression share, and fix the listing where it doesn’t. Running that ranking across a whole catalog, search by search, is how we find hidden search traffic for the brands we manage.

A0370.title: Instagram shopping in 2023: from destination to discovery
A0370.alt: A smartphone with a glowing pink screen beside a eucalyptus vase and kraft paper bag on a wooden table.
A0370.ttag: Instagram shopping in 2023: from destination to discovery | Kwontified
A0370.desc: Instagram removed its Shop tab and is ending live shopping, while Reels viewing doubled. Why Instagram shopping is now about discovery, and how to adjust.
A0370.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 9, 2023.
A0370.body:
A shopper on Instagram watches a creator’s Reel about a moisturizer on Tuesday. She does not tap a product tag. On Saturday she searches for the product on Amazon and buys it. Instagram did the selling, but no Instagram report shows the sale.

That gap between where people discover a product and where they buy it explains the changes Instagram has been making. Instagram is retreating from shopping as a destination: it removed its Shop tab in February and will end product tags in live broadcasts on March 16, while Reels viewing more than doubled in a year. Brands should treat Instagram as a discovery channel, put products into the content and ads where attention is growing, and measure the sales that follow in the stores where shoppers actually buy.

What changed in Instagram shopping

In February, Instagram took its Shop tab out of the row of icons at the bottom of the app, Retail Dive reported. The tab had given shoppers a dedicated place to browse products. Businesses can still run shops on Instagram.

From March 16, 2023, users will no longer be able to tag products in live broadcasts, Business Insider reported. The company said it would focus on features that provide the most value, and continue to invest in shopping across feed, stories, Reels and ads. Facebook had already ended its own live shopping feature on October 1, 2022, TechCrunch reported.

Attention, meanwhile, moved to video. Reels plays across Facebook and Instagram more than doubled over the past year, Mark Zuckerberg said when Meta reported its fourth-quarter results, YourStory reported. Taken together, the changes point the same way: Meta is pulling back from tab-based and live shopping and putting its weight behind short video and ads.

The store Instagram tried to build

Instagram’s shopping push followed a reasonable idea. Many people already found products on Instagram. Brands posted them, creators wore and used them, and followers asked where to buy. A dedicated Shop tab and live shopping were meant to turn that discovery into a destination, so shoppers would go to Instagram to shop, much as they go to a marketplace.

That second step did not take. Shoppers kept using Instagram the way they always had: to be entertained, to follow people and to stumble on things. Few opened the app to shop, and Instagram’s own words point to it. The changes, it said, would let it focus on what provides the most value, and the Shop tab’s place in the navigation bar went back to creating content.

Instagram shopping is not disappearing so much as changing shape. Discovery still happens, and more of it now happens in Reels and ads, where attention is growing. The purchase often happens later and elsewhere, on a brand’s site, on Amazon or in a store, which is exactly the path the moisturizer shopper took. Repeated, that pattern is why Instagram has backed away from building a store and toward building the discovery that leads to one.

Planning for discovery that ends somewhere else

The goal of a post, Reel or ad changes once Instagram is treated as a discovery channel. The job is to make the product memorable and searchable, not to complete a sale inside the app. Clear product names, distinctive visuals and a reason to look the product up later matter more than in-app checkout. Captions and on-screen text that name the product exactly as it appears on the listing make that later search easier.

Content should follow attention into video. With Reels viewing growing fast, product content should increasingly be short, vertical video that shows the product in use. Creator content works well here because it is how people already discover things on Instagram.

Measurement has to move to where the sale happens. If shoppers discover on Instagram and buy elsewhere, Instagram’s own reports will understate its effect. Brands should watch branded search, direct site traffic and marketplace sales around Instagram campaigns, ideally with regional or time-based comparisons, so the moisturizer sale on Saturday gets connected to the Reel on Tuesday.

Ads deserve a larger share of the plan than they had. Organic reach on Instagram depends on the algorithm’s choices, which now favor Reels and recommended content from accounts people do not follow. Paid placements let a brand put a product video in front of the shoppers most likely to want it, and Meta’s ad tools can target and optimize for visits to a brand’s site or a marketplace listing. For discovery that is meant to end in a purchase elsewhere, that is the most reliable bridge.

Links matter for the same reason. Every Reel, Story and ad should make it easy to find the product’s real home, whether a site, an Amazon listing or a store locator. A shopper who has to search for the product after seeing it is a shopper who may never find it.

The existing tools still earn their keep while they last. Shops and product tags help shoppers who do want to tap through, so they should stay in good order. A brand whose Instagram plan depends on in-app checkout, though, should have a second plan ready, because Meta’s own choices show that is not where the platform’s priorities lie.

The broader point reaches past Instagram. A platform succeeds at shopping when shopping fits why people open the app, and on Instagram that reason is discovery. So the question for a brand’s leadership is whether its Instagram reporting can see the Saturday purchase at all, or only the taps that never came. Connecting the two, from the Reel to the marketplace listing, is how we run Instagram for brands that sell elsewhere.

A0371.crumb: Temu in 2023: a price you cannot match…
A0371.title: Temu in 2023: a price you cannot match, and what to do instead
A0371.alt: A leather wallet with a blank kraft tag beside a pile of colorful plastic beads and trinkets with orange price tags.
A0371.ttag: Temu in 2023: a price you cannot match, and what to do instead | Kwontified
A0371.desc: Temu’s prices come from a cost structure U.S. brands cannot copy. Why matching them is a losing game, and how brands should compete on what Temu gives up.
A0371.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 14, 2023.
A0371.body:
A U.S. brand sells a kitchen gadget for $14. A similar unbranded version appears on Temu for $4. The brand’s landed cost is $5 before marketing, so even selling at cost it could not reach Temu’s price. How can anyone sell it for less than the brand pays to land it?

Because Temu’s price comes from a cost structure U.S. brands cannot copy: goods sourced directly from manufacturers, small parcels shipped below the $800 duty threshold, and heavily subsidized marketing. Brands should not try to match Temu on price for undifferentiated products. They should compete on what that structure gives up, which is speed, easy returns, trust and a recognizable brand, while watching the categories where their products overlap with Temu’s.

How Temu reached U.S. shoppers in six months

Temu launched in the U.S. in September 2022, with delivery promised in roughly 7 to 15 business days, CNBC reported. By February it had passed 24 million U.S. downloads and had 13.4 million monthly active users so far that month, ahead of Target’s 9.2 million, according to Sensor Tower data, Modern Retail reported.

It reached that scale quickly, and largely by spending on advertising. In its first two months it bought ads on more than 1,700 search terms in Apple’s App Store, Appfigures reported, and on February 12 it ran its first Super Bowl ad, twice, Adweek reported.

Three costs a brand pays that Temu’s model avoids

Each link in Temu’s chain removes a cost that a domestic brand still carries, and the links add up.

Sourcing is where the chain begins. Temu’s parent, PDD, built its business by connecting shoppers closely with manufacturers in China, TechNode reported. In our observation, Temu controls the price shown to shoppers, while many sellers on the platform are manufacturers supplying goods. There is no importer’s markup and no brand margin in the chain.

Customs is where the gap widens. Packages valued at $800 or less can enter the U.S. without duties, Fortune reported. A brand importing goods by the container pays duty on the whole shipment. A platform shipping each order as its own small parcel generally does not.

Marketing is where the money comes from. Temu is spending heavily to acquire shoppers, and its parent can fund that spending for some time. A brand pays for its own customers and has to make that spending back on each sale.

Put the three together and the gap is structural. No single efficiency a brand can find in its own supply chain closes all three at once.

Why cutting the price feels right and fails

The instinct to match is easy to understand. The two prices sit side by side in a shopper’s mind, and the brand’s team anchors on that comparison: if $14 loses to $4, the obvious lever is the $14.

The arithmetic says otherwise. A brand that cuts its price to compete with Temu only lowers its own margin, and the costs that create the gap are still there. In the gadget case, cutting to $10 would take most of the brand’s margin and still leave it at more than twice Temu’s price. The comparison the brand anchored on has not moved in its favor at all.

Competing on what Temu gives up

Speed is often the most valuable of the things Temu’s structure sacrifices. Temu’s shipping times run to a week or two. A brand that delivers in one or two days through Amazon or its own network wins shoppers who need the product soon, which in many categories is most of them.

Returns and service come next. Shoppers buying at very low prices often accept that returns are difficult. Shoppers spending more expect them to be easy, and clear, simple returns are a reason to pay more.

Trust and brand do the rest. A recognizable brand, consistent quality, real reviews and clear product information reduce the risk of a disappointing purchase. Temu sells many unbranded goods, so a brand that makes its quality visible gives shoppers a reason to choose it.

Overlap decides where any of this matters. Most brands compete with Temu only in part of their range: the low-priced accessories, the commodity items, the products that are hard to tell apart. Those are where the pressure will show. A brand should identify them, decide whether to differentiate them, bundle them with higher-value products or accept lower volume, and watch their sales month by month.

Bundles are one practical response. A single low-priced accessory invites a direct price comparison. The same accessory packaged with a related product, or sold as a set, changes the comparison to one Temu rarely offers, and the brand competes on value per order rather than price per item.

Selling on Temu itself deserves caution. In our observation, a seller on Temu has little control over price. For a U.S. brand that has spent years building its pricing and image, that is usually a poor trade.

Three developments would change this picture. A change to the duty threshold for small parcels would remove one of the three cost advantages at once. Any sign that Temu’s parent is cutting back its marketing spending would show whether shoppers stay without being paid to. And if Temu builds U.S. warehousing and shortens its shipping times, it removes one of the main reasons shoppers pay more elsewhere.

Until then the rule is plain: never answer a structural price gap with a price cut; answer it with the things the structure cannot deliver. Mapping where that gap touches your range, product by product, is how we help brands defend their range against low-priced competition.

A0372.crumb: Vendor Central in 2023: selling to a more…
A0372.title: Vendor Central in 2023: selling to a more cautious Amazon
A0372.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes on a wooden pallet in an empty warehouse with metal shelving behind.
A0372.ttag: Vendor Central in 2023: selling to a more cautious Amazon | Kwontified
A0372.desc: Amazon’s own retail sales fell while its marketplace grew. What a more cautious Amazon buyer means for Vendor Central brands in 2023, and how to respond.
A0372.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 16, 2023.
A0372.body:
When Amazon buys a vendor’s product, it takes on the inventory, the storage and the risk that the stock will not sell. When a third-party seller lists the same product, Amazon collects its fees and the seller keeps the risk. After a year in which Amazon found itself with too much space and too much stock, it is not hard to guess which arrangement looked better from Seattle.

The numbers bear that out. Amazon’s own online store sales fell 2% in the holiday quarter, while third-party sellers reached a record 59% of units. Vendor Central brands should expect a more cautious buyer that orders carefully and presses for better margins. They should respond by tightening their operations, using advertising to support sell-through and deciding deliberately whether to keep part of their range on Seller Central.

Where Vendor Central stands in 2023

Vendor Central is the program through which brands sell their products to Amazon at wholesale, and Amazon resells them as its own retail inventory. Its health depends on Amazon’s retail business, and that business had a difficult 2022.

Amazon took about $2 billion of extra costs in the first quarter of 2022 from excess warehouse and transportation capacity, and its chief financial officer said the company appeared to be overbuilt for current demand, Reuters reported. Amazon also said it was lowering its capital spending for 2022, with less going to fulfillment projects than the year before, the same report noted. A company trimming its warehouse plans is not one looking to hold more inventory, and that is the backdrop to every purchase order a vendor receives in 2023.

By the end of the year, the gap between Amazon’s two retail models was plain. In the fourth quarter, sales in Amazon’s own online stores fell 2% to $64.5 billion, while third-party seller services revenue rose 20%, according to EcomCrew’s breakdown of the results. Of all units sold, a record 59% came from third-party sellers, Amazon said on its earnings call.

Who carries the risk, and why it matters to vendors

Follow the inventory and the incentive becomes clear. On the marketplace, Amazon earns fees without owning the goods. In first-party retail, every unit Amazon buys is a unit it has to store, move and eventually sell or mark down. In a year of too much space, too much stock and slowing growth, that risk looked heavier, and the marketplace looked like the safer way to grow.

So Amazon’s retail team has good reasons to be careful. It orders closer to demand, holds less safety stock, and looks harder at the profitability of each product it buys. Products that are slow-moving, bulky or low-margin for Amazon come under the most pressure.

Vendors experience this as smaller or less predictable purchase orders, tougher negotiations over terms and allowances, and more questions about whether a product earns its place. None of that requires a dramatic announcement. It shows up in the weekly order and the annual negotiation.

Picture a kitchenware vendor that has sold through Vendor Central for years. In 2021 its orders grew steadily. In 2022 they became smaller and less regular, and some products saw no orders for weeks while others ran out of stock.

In its 2023 negotiation, Amazon asks for better terms on its slower products. The vendor’s products did not change. Amazon’s appetite for risk did.

What a vendor still controls

None of the useful responses depends on Amazon changing course, and the most reliable one is operational. A vendor that fills orders completely and on time, ships correctly prepared goods and keeps its product information accurate is cheaper for Amazon to work with. In a cautious year, that reliability carries more weight when Amazon decides which products to keep ordering.

Sell-through is the next lever. When Amazon orders closer to demand, the vendor’s sales to Amazon depend directly on how fast Amazon sells the stock it already has. Advertising and strong product pages speed that up. A vendor that leaves sell-through to Amazon alone is relying on the cautious buyer to be enthusiastic.

The range itself deserves a deliberate split. Some products work well as Amazon-owned inventory: fast-moving, easy to ship and profitable for Amazon. Others may do better on Seller Central, where the brand holds the stock, sets the price and controls availability. Running both programs, with a clear rule for which products go where, gives a brand more control than relying on either alone.

Deductions are where margin quietly leaks. Vendors are paid on terms, and their payments are reduced by shortage claims, chargebacks for preparation or shipping errors, and agreed allowances. In a year when Amazon is pressing for margin, those deductions tend to grow, and not all of them are valid. A vendor that reviews its deductions regularly, disputes the incorrect ones and fixes the operational causes of the rest recovers money it has already earned.

Pricing needs watching for a related reason. On Vendor Central, Amazon sets the retail price. A brand whose products are also sold elsewhere needs to watch how Amazon’s pricing affects its other channels, especially when Amazon is clearing stock.

The next test comes in late April, when Amazon’s results for the first quarter should show whether its own store sales recover or keep shrinking relative to the marketplace. Either way, the question for a vendor’s leadership team is the same: if Amazon’s buyer looked at our account purely as inventory risk, which of our products would it still want to own? Answering that product by product, and running Vendor Central and Seller Central side by side where the answer is mixed, is how we manage hybrid Amazon accounts for brands.

A0374.crumb: Amazon DSP in 2023: buy audiences, judge…
A0374.title: Amazon DSP in 2023: buy audiences, judge it on new customers
A0374.alt: A brown paper-wrapped parcel on a doorstep beside a coir mat, with a blue front door open to a wooden hallway.
A0374.ttag: Amazon DSP in 2023: buy audiences, judge it on new customers | Kwontified
A0374.desc: Amazon DSP’s value lies in Amazon’s shopper audiences, not its placements. When brands should use it, and why to judge it on new customers, not ROAS.
A0374.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 21, 2023.
A0374.body:
A pet food brand’s Sponsored Products campaigns return $5 for every $1 spent. Its Amazon DSP campaign, aimed at shoppers who bought competing brands in the past 90 days, returns $2 on its own attribution. Put those two numbers on one slide and the budget decision makes itself. It is usually the wrong decision.

Amazon DSP’s value lies in the shopper audiences Amazon can build from its own data, not in the placements it buys, and its results show up as reach and new customers rather than search-level return on ad spend. Brands should use it once they need reach beyond search, start with audiences of in-market and lapsed shoppers, and judge it on new-to-brand sales and measured lift. Comparing its return with Sponsored Products leads to the wrong decisions.

What Amazon DSP offers going into 2023

Amazon DSP, its demand-side platform, lets advertisers buy display, video and audio ads on Amazon’s own properties and on other websites and apps, using audiences built from Amazon’s shopping data. At its unBoxed conference in October 2022, Amazon Ads announced a series of updates to help advertisers plan, measure and optimize campaigns across that inventory, according to Amazon.

The places DSP can reach are widening as well. Amazon said advertisers could use Amazon Marketing Cloud to manage DSP audiences across its channels, from Whole Foods to Twitch, MediaPost reported. It also opened digital screens in Amazon Fresh stores to DSP buyers from November 2022, Tinuiti reported.

Measurement is growing alongside it. The customer base of Amazon Marketing Cloud, Amazon’s clean room for analyzing ad exposure and purchases, had quadrupled in a year, Digiday reported ahead of the conference.

Why the $2 campaign can be the better one

Sponsored Products shows ads to shoppers who are already searching. Much of the demand it captures already exists, so its attributed return looks high.

DSP works earlier and later in the shopper’s path. It reaches people who browsed a category but did not buy, people who bought a competing product, and people who bought from the brand months ago. Some of them buy later, and often through a search, where a Sponsored Products ad collects the credit. DSP’s own attributed return therefore undercounts what it does.

The pet food brand’s two campaigns look different once the customer is in the frame:

Sponsored ProductsDSP, competitor buyers
Attributed return per $1 spent$5$2
Share of sales from shoppers new to the brand20%70%

A holdout test also shows branded searches rising among the shoppers who saw the DSP ads. The two campaigns are doing different jobs, and judging them by one number hides the job DSP does best.

So a brand that compares the two on return on ad spend will nearly always cut DSP. That decision feels disciplined, but it removes the one tool that reaches large numbers of new customers, and leaves the brand competing harder and harder for the same searching shoppers. The pet food brand that cut DSP on its first-glance figures would save money in the short run and find fewer new customers in its searches a few months later.

Judging DSP on new customers and lift

The first judgment is about timing. Use DSP once search alone no longer brings enough new customers, usually when a brand is already well covered on its most important searches and wants to grow beyond them.

Start with audiences, not placements. The most productive starting points are shoppers who viewed the brand’s products without buying, shoppers who buy in the category from competitors, and the brand’s own past customers who have not bought in the past six months. Those audiences use exactly the knowledge that makes Amazon’s DSP different from other ad platforms.

Measure it on what it is meant to do. Track the share of DSP sales that come from new-to-brand shoppers, and the cost of each new customer. Where possible, measure lift with holdout groups or with Amazon Marketing Cloud, to see how DSP exposure changes searches and purchases across all of the brand’s ads.

Creative matters more on DSP than in search. A search ad borrows the product’s own listing; a DSP ad has to catch the attention of someone who was not looking. Amazon expanded a public beta of its Video Builder tool at unBoxed, Tinuiti reported, which lowers the cost of producing simple product videos. Brands without video should still start with clear, product-led display ads rather than wait.

Frequency needs a plan as well. A shopper who sees an ad once rarely remembers it. A shopper who sees it twenty times in a week is wasted money and may grow annoyed. Setting a sensible frequency cap, and checking actual frequency in reporting, keeps the budget spread across enough shoppers to matter.

A test needs to be sized honestly. DSP requires creative, audience planning and enough budget to reach shoppers more than once. A brand that spends a small amount for a few weeks will learn little. A planned test over two or three months, with a holdout, is more useful than a series of small experiments.

The money for DSP should come from its own line. A DSP budget taken from Sponsored Products can lower overall sales if search coverage weakens. A DSP budget added to protected search spending can grow the customer base that search later converts.

The working rule: never let a DSP campaign compete with Sponsored Products on a single ROAS column; give it its own column for new customers and lift. Setting up that test, with the holdout built in before the first impression, is how we plan Amazon DSP for the brands we work with.
