A0376.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud in 2023: the bottleneck is the question
A0376.alt: An oak card catalog cabinet with one drawer pulled open, holding a single blank white card.
A0376.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud in 2023: the bottleneck is the question | Kwontified
A0376.desc: Amazon Marketing Cloud’s user base quadrupled in a year. Why the limit on its value is not the data but the questions brands ask, and how to start well.
A0376.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 23, 2023.
A0376.body:
Amazon Marketing Cloud’s customer base quadrupled in a year, and Amazon added new signals and audience features to it in late 2022. For a brand’s leadership team, the decision that follows looks like one about access: should we get in, and who gets the login? Access turns out to be the easy part.

The clean room shifts measurement on Amazon from reports Amazon writes to questions advertisers ask themselves. The limit on its value is now the questions and skills a brand brings, not the data. Brands should start with two or three specific business questions and the people to answer them, rather than with access alone.

What Amazon Marketing Cloud is, and what changed in late 2022

Amazon Marketing Cloud is Amazon’s clean room: a secure environment where an advertiser can analyze its ad exposure and purchase events on Amazon, and join them with its own data, without seeing any individual shopper’s records. Results come back only in aggregate. In practice, the advertiser sees patterns across groups of shoppers, never the shoppers themselves.

Use of it grew sharply in 2022. Its customer base had quadrupled in the past year, Digiday reported in a piece on Amazon’s clean-room push ahead of the unBoxed conference in October.

At the conference itself, the clean room gained Sponsored Display and digital subscription signals, more ready-made instructional queries, and the ability to manage DSP audiences across Amazon’s channels, MediaPost reported. Amazon described the updates as part of a push to help advertisers plan, measure and optimize their campaigns, according to Amazon.

Who asks the questions now

For most of the history of Amazon advertising, measurement came in the form of reports Amazon designed. Each ad type had its own report, each credited sales its own way, and advertisers read what they were given.

A clean room changes who asks the questions. Instead of reading a standard report, an advertiser writes a query. It might ask how many shoppers saw a streaming TV ad and later searched for the brand, how long new customers take to buy again, or how much the audiences for two ad types overlap. Amazon supplies the data; the advertiser supplies the question.

That is why the clean room grew so quickly. Brands spending across several Amazon ad types wanted to know how those types worked together, which no single report could tell them. Streaming TV and DSP are the clearest cases, because their effects show up in other ads’ results, and only a cross-channel view can see them.

The same shift exposes a new constraint. A clean room is only as useful as the questions put to it and the skill of the person writing them. Queries are written in SQL, results need careful reading, and a poorly framed question returns an answer that looks precise and means little.

Picture a home goods brand that gains access to Amazon Marketing Cloud in early 2023. Its team runs a few ready-made queries, produces some interesting charts and then stops, because nobody owns the work and nobody agreed what decision the analysis should change. A year later it has access and no answers. A competitor that started with one question, whether its DSP spending brings in new customers who then buy through search, has an answer and a changed budget.

The decision leadership actually faces

Framed properly, the choice in front of a leadership team is which decisions the clean room should change, and who will own the work. Access follows from that, not the other way round.

Start with the decisions the brand really faces, such as how much to spend on DSP, whether streaming TV ads lift branded searches, or how long new customers take to return. Write each as a question with a clear answer that would change a budget or a plan. A question that could not change a budget, a bid or a plan is a research project, and it can wait.

A good question carries its own decision rule. For example: of the shoppers new to the brand who saw DSP ads in the first quarter, what share bought through a search within 60 days? If that share is high, the brand keeps or grows its DSP budget. If it is low, the brand moves money back to search. Agreeing the rule before running the query keeps the answer from being read to suit whoever asked.

People come next. Someone needs to write and check the queries, and someone needs to translate the answers into decisions. That can be an in-house analyst, an agency or a technology partner. Without both roles, access produces charts rather than changes.

The clean room also works best alongside simpler tests rather than instead of them. A regional holdout or an on-off test answers some questions more directly than any query. A clean room is strongest when it explains how ad types interact and how customers move between them over time.

Privacy shapes the questions too. Because results come back only in aggregate, small or narrowly defined audiences may return no answer at all. That is by design, and it protects shoppers. Brands should frame questions around groups large enough to analyze, rather than trying to see individual shoppers.

As Amazon adds more signals and audience features, the gap between brands that ask good questions and brands that merely have access will widen. The data is becoming something any large advertiser can reach; the questions, and the discipline to act on the answers, belong to the brand. Turning those first two or three questions into queries, rules and budget changes is how we run Amazon Marketing Cloud analysis for the brands we manage.

A0377.crumb: Is a shopping AI a moat? Only if it rests…
A0377.title: Is a shopping AI a moat? Only if it rests on what others lack
A0377.alt: A moated medieval stone castle with round towers reflected in still water at golden hour.
A0377.ttag: Is a shopping AI a moat? Only if it rests on what others lack | Kwontified
A0377.desc: A shopping AI built on a model anyone can license is not a moat. Why the edge lies in data, fulfillment and the customer relationship, and what brands can do.
A0377.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 28, 2023.
A0377.body:
Two online retailers selling outdoor gear launch chat assistants on the same licensed language model in the same quarter. A shopper asks each for a waterproof jacket for a rainy hiking trip. The first compares materials, quotes reviewers and promises delivery by the weekend. The second offers generic advice.

The technology is identical; the answers, and the sales that follow them, are not. A shopping assistant built on a language model that any company can license is therefore not a competitive moat by itself, because a rival can build the same assistant on the same model. The lasting advantage lies in what the assistant draws on and delivers: proprietary product and purchase data, fulfillment and the customer relationship. Brands should prepare by making their product information complete, accurate and structured, so that any assistant can describe their products well.

What has actually shipped in shopping AI

Since ChatGPT’s release in November 2022, retailers and platforms have raced to show what conversational AI can do for shopping. The clearest concrete step came on March 23, when OpenAI announced plugins that let ChatGPT connect to outside services, MediaPost reported. The first plugins came from companies including Expedia, Instacart, KAYAK, Klarna, OpenTable and Shopify.

For someone running a brand’s e-commerce team, the useful part of that announcement is the list, not the technology. Several of the first companies to connect were retailers and shopping services, and they chose to bring their catalogs and services into someone else’s assistant rather than only building their own. That is a statement about where they think shoppers may start, and it is worth taking at face value without assuming anything about how fast shoppers will follow.

Why the model is not the moat

A moat is an advantage competitors cannot easily copy. The language models behind these assistants are available to many companies through licensing. If one retailer builds a shopping assistant on a licensed model, a competitor can build a similar one on the same model within months.

What the competitor cannot copy so easily is what the assistant draws on and what it can do. An assistant’s answers are only as good as the data it can reach: product details, prices, stock, reviews and what similar shoppers bought. Its usefulness depends on what it can complete, such as ordering, delivering and handling returns. Those rest on years of investment in catalogs, logistics and customer relationships. In the jacket example, the first retailer’s edge was its product data, its reviews and its delivery network; the chat window was the same.

So the advantage flows to companies with rich data and strong operations, whatever assistant sits on top. A retailer whose only edge is a clever chat interface has a feature, not a moat.

There is a further risk for retailers. If shoppers start their product searches in a general assistant rather than on a retailer’s site, the assistant owns the first moment of the shopping trip. Retailers that join someone else’s assistant gain reach but give up some of that relationship. Retailers that do not may be left out of the conversation.

By this logic, the largest marketplaces start in the strongest position. They already hold the catalogs, reviews, purchase histories and delivery networks that make an assistant useful. A smaller retailer can match the chat window; it cannot quickly match a decade of purchase data. That does not guarantee the large marketplaces will build the best assistants, but it means the race is less open than the excitement suggests.

What would prove an assistant has become a moat? Shoppers would return to it repeatedly, convert at higher rates than through search, and stay with the retailer even when a rival offers a similar assistant. Those numbers will take time to appear. Until they do, claims that an assistant is a lasting advantage are predictions, not results.

What every assistant will read

Whatever assistants shoppers use, whether a retailer’s own or a general one, they will read product information to answer questions. That is where a brand has real control. A brand cannot choose which assistant a shopper opens, but it can decide what that assistant finds when it looks.

Complete means product titles and descriptions that state what the product is and what it is for, attributes filled in fully and consistently, such as size, material, compatibility and care, and images and specifications that answer common questions. Accurate means the same facts everywhere, so that an assistant reading a brand’s own site, Amazon and other retailers finds no contradictions to resolve.

Reviews matter more in an assistant-led world. Assistants that summarize reviews will surface what customers actually say, and a product with a recurring complaint will hear about it in every summary. Fixing the cause of that complaint is better marketing than any rewritten product description.

Brands should also watch where shopping conversations begin. If general assistants start sending meaningful traffic to retailers, brands will want their products well represented in the catalogs those assistants can reach, much as they once made sure they were well represented in search engines. Tracking where traffic and sales originate through 2023 will show that shift early, if it comes.

None of this requires predicting which assistant wins, or how quickly shoppers will change their habits. The test for any piece of product content is simple: if an assistant read only this page, could it answer the shopper’s next question correctly? Getting a catalog to pass that test is how we prepare brands’ product data for AI shopping assistants.

A0378.crumb: The Amazon Best Seller badge: how it…
A0378.title: The Amazon Best Seller badge: how it shapes competition
A0378.alt: A row of honey jars on a rustic wooden bench with a gold prize rosette ribbon in the center.
A0378.ttag: The Amazon Best Seller badge: how it shapes competition | Kwontified
A0378.desc: Amazon’s Best Seller badge goes to the top seller in every subcategory, and shoppers treat it as a shortcut. How it shapes competition, and how to compete.
A0378.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 30, 2023.
A0378.body:
Scroll an Amazon results page for almost any household product and one listing usually carries a small orange label: Best Seller. Shoppers facing a crowded page and limited time read it as an answer. It is worth asking what that label actually measures, and what it does to the brands competing for it.

Amazon awards a Best Seller badge to the top-selling product in every category and subcategory, and shoppers treat the badge as a shortcut. It rewards the leader with more traffic, which makes leadership self-reinforcing, and that pushes brands toward choosing narrow subcategories and buying short bursts of sales. Brands do better to list in the subcategory that genuinely fits, win the badge through steady sales rather than deal spikes, and track the badge on the searches that matter to them.

How the Amazon Best Seller badge works

The badge is tied to Best Sellers Rank. The product ranked first in a category or subcategory carries a Best Seller label on its product page and in search results. There is one for every category and subcategory on Amazon, Pattern noted, so there are far more badges available than most brands assume.

The badge also brings traffic. A 2018 study by Profitero of 37,000 products found that the Best Seller badge increased a product’s glance views by an average of 45%, a figure Pattern cited in the same article. The study is several years old, and the effect will vary by category, but the direction is clear: shoppers notice the badge and click on it.

Because the badge follows Best Sellers Rank, it moves as rank moves. It reflects recent sales relative to the other products in the same subcategory, as we described in our post on how Amazon rankings work.

A label that feeds its own leader

A small label that says a product is the best seller in its category offers a quick answer to an uncertain choice. Many shoppers take it, especially in categories where products look similar.

That creates a loop. The product with the badge gets more clicks, more clicks bring more sales, and more sales protect its rank and its badge. The leader’s position becomes self-reinforcing, and the second-place product has to outsell a competitor that is being helped by a label.

Brands have found two shortcuts around that loop. One is to choose a narrower subcategory, where a product can rank first more easily. Some of that is sensible, because a product listed in a precise subcategory is easier for shoppers to find. Some of it is gaming, where a product is placed in a subcategory that does not really describe it. Shoppers who browse that subcategory find a product that does not match, and the badge loses meaning for everyone.

The other shortcut is to buy short bursts of sales. A deep discount or a heavy advertising push can lift a product to first place for a few days and win the badge. When the push ends, the rank and the badge often fall away, and the brand has paid for a label it could not keep.

Picture a brand of reusable food storage bags. It runs a deep discount for a week, takes first place in its subcategory and wins the badge. Sales jump. When the discount ends, a competitor with steadier sales retakes first place within days. The brand has spent its margin and is back where it started, while the competitor’s badge was earned by being the product most shoppers kept choosing.

Competing for the badge without renting it

Placement comes first, and the honest choice is also the durable one. Listing in the subcategory that genuinely fits serves shoppers, avoids the risk of a product being moved by Amazon, and puts the product among the competitors shoppers actually compare. A badge earned in the right subcategory is a meaningful signal; one earned in the wrong subcategory rarely brings the right customers.

Steady sales hold the badge where spikes cannot. The badge follows recent sales relative to the subcategory, so consistency matters more than peaks. Reliable stock, competitive pricing, strong reviews and steady advertising on the product’s core searches build the kind of lead a competitor’s one-week discount cannot overturn.

The badge also needs watching where it matters. Brands should know which products in their key searches carry it, including competitors’, and how often it changes hands. A competitor that holds the badge on the brand’s most important searches is taking traffic the brand might otherwise win.

Other labels compete for the same attention. Amazon’s Choice is shown against particular searches rather than categories, and new products can carry a New Release label in their early weeks. A shopper scanning a results page may see several labels at once, and each one changes where the shopper’s eyes go first, so brands should know which appear on their key searches.

Stock deserves a special mention. A product that runs out of stock loses sales, then rank, then the badge, and may take weeks to recover after restocking. Protecting availability on badge-holding products is one of the cheapest ways to keep the advantage.

In the end the badge is a result, not a goal: it marks the product most shoppers choose in its subcategory. Brands that focus on being that product tend to hold the badge, and brands that chase the badge alone tend to rent it. A useful question for the team: which of our badges would we still hold a month after our next promotion ends? Building the catalog placement, pricing and advertising that earn a lasting answer is how we help brands hold the Best Seller badge on Amazon.

A0380.title: Mercado Libre cross-border selling: a test, not a destination
A0380.alt: A twine-tied paper parcel on a wooden footbridge over a river leading to a colorful tropical village.
A0380.ttag: Mercado Libre cross-border selling: a test, not a destination | Kwontified
A0380.desc: Mercado Libre’s cross-border program lets U.S. brands sell in Latin America without importing. Why it works best as a test, and when to stock locally.
A0380.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 4, 2023.
A0380.body:
A U.S. supplement brand lists fifteen products in Mexico through Mercado Libre’s cross-border program. After three months, three sell steadily, eight sell now and then, and four have not sold at all. Is that a disappointing launch? Read correctly, it is a successful experiment: the brand now knows which three products are worth importing.

Cross-border selling lets a U.S. brand reach Latin American shoppers without importing stock, which makes it a cheap way to test demand. Its delivery times, though, cannot match a local network that now delivers most orders within two days, so cross-border listings compete at a structural disadvantage. Brands should treat the program as a time-limited test, with clear criteria for moving proven products into local fulfillment.

Mercado Libre cross-border selling meets a two-day network

Mercado Libre has spent years building a logistics network across its main markets. The share of its merchandise volume delivered within 48 hours rose from an average of 44% in 2019 to almost 80% in 2022, according to its letter to shareholders. Its fulfillment service, which stores and ships sellers’ goods, reached a record 43% of shipments in the fourth quarter.

Growth remains strong across its largest markets. Merchandise volume rose 35% on a currency-neutral basis in the fourth quarter, with Mexico up 28% and Brazil up 22%, the same letter said.

For foreign brands, Mercado Libre offers a cross-border route. In our experience, it lets sellers outside the region list products in markets such as Mexico, Brazil, Chile and Colombia from one account, ship orders from abroad, and receive payment without setting up a local company. Each order travels from the seller’s country to the shopper, rather than from a warehouse in the shopper’s market.

Why a slow listing can still be a useful one

Mercado Libre’s investment in speed has reset what shoppers expect. When most orders arrive within two days, a product that takes a week or more looks slow by comparison. Shoppers hesitate, conversion suffers, and on a marketplace that ranks listings partly by how well they sell, weaker conversion means less prominence. A cross-border listing up against locally stocked alternatives starts behind on both counts.

The same handicap makes the program a clean instrument. Selling from abroad requires no import, no local inventory and no local entity, so a brand can list a range, see which products shoppers buy despite the slower delivery, and learn about pricing, demand and competition at low cost. Demand that survives a speed penalty is strong demand.

That is how to read the supplement brand’s first three months:

Result after three monthsProductsWhat it suggests
Sold steadilythreeDemand strong enough to overcome slow delivery
Sold now and theneightSome interest; cheap to keep testing
Did not sellfourLittle demand at this price and speed

The brand imports the three steady sellers, stores them in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network and keeps the rest listed cross-border. Within weeks, those three deliver faster, appear more prominently and sell several times more. The program did exactly the job it is suited for: it found the products worth importing.

Running the test with exit criteria

Before launching, agree how long the test runs. Three to six months is usually long enough to see which products sell, and short enough to act on the result in the same year.

Agree the graduation threshold at the same time. A simple rule works: products that reach a set number of monthly orders cross-border, despite slower delivery, move into local fulfillment. Writing the number down before the first order arrives keeps the decision from drifting.

Decide, too, what happens to the rest. Products that sell occasionally can stay cross-border at low cost. Products that do not sell should come off, so they do not dilute the brand’s listings.

Currency is where the trade-off bites. In our experience, cross-border sellers set prices and are paid in dollars, which shields them from swings in local currencies during the test. Moving to local stock brings that risk back: prices are set in pesos or reais, and the margin can shrink if the currency weakens before the goods sell. Graduation buys speed and visibility at the cost of currency exposure, and for a proven product the speed is usually worth more. The plan should still carry extra margin on graduated products and a habit of repricing them more often than at home.

Listings deserve the same care in both stages. A test run with machine-translated titles and U.S. sizing will understate demand, because shoppers in Mexico and Brazil respond to listings written in their own language and units, and to quick answers to the questions they post.

Some products should skip the test and go straight to local stock. Items that are heavy, bulky or subject to strict import rules may be expensive or slow to ship cross-border, and fragile goods can suffer in transit, so a cross-border result for them may not be representative. Health, beauty and food products often face import requirements in markets such as Brazil and Mexico, which affect both cross-border shipping and local importation, and brands in those categories should check the rules before listing anything.

Advertising follows the same logic. Spending heavily to promote slow-shipping products is rarely efficient, so a modest budget during the test is enough to get products seen. The larger budget belongs to products after they move into local fulfillment, when faster delivery lets the advertising convert.

The rule, then: run cross-border as an experiment with an end date and a threshold, and let it graduate winners rather than carry the range. Designing that test, and moving its winners into local fulfillment, is how we help brands enter Mercado Libre.

A0381.crumb: Amazon, Shein and Temu: three machines…
A0381.title: Amazon, Shein and Temu: three machines, one contested shelf
A0381.alt: Three twine-tied packages in orange, black and kraft paper on a rustic wooden shelf against a gray wall.
A0381.ttag: Amazon, Shein and Temu: three machines, one contested shelf | Kwontified
A0381.desc: Amazon, Shein and Temu are built differently and compete only on part of the shelf. Where they overlap, how shoppers use each, and where brands should stand.
A0381.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 6, 2023.
A0381.body:
Take one household and a few ordinary purchases. Paper towels and a phone charger come from Amazon, ordered for delivery tomorrow. A summer dress comes from Shein, found while browsing new styles. A set of storage baskets comes from Temu, bought because they were cheap.

Are those three companies competing for that household? Only for part of what it buys. Amazon, Shein and Temu are three different machines: a broad marketplace built on speed, a fashion brand built on small-batch production, and a factory-direct marketplace built on subsidized low prices. They compete head-on only for cheap discretionary goods. Brands should identify which part of their range sits on that contested shelf, defend it on speed, trust and quality rather than price, and recognize that shoppers use each platform for a different job.

Where Amazon, Shein and Temu stand in spring 2023

Amazon remains the largest of the three. In the fourth quarter of 2022, units from third-party sellers reached a record 59% of the total, Amazon said on its earnings call, even as sales in its own online stores fell 2%, according to EcomCrew’s breakdown.

Shein has grown into a large U.S. business in a few years. It was estimated to have made about $8 billion in U.S. sales in 2022, Bloomberg reported, and was valued at roughly $100 billion, Nikkei reported.

Temu is the newest and fastest-growing of the three. Sensor Tower data put it past 24 million U.S. downloads by February 2023, with 13.4 million people using it monthly that month, Modern Retail reported.

The two newcomers share one structural advantage. Both ship many orders as individual parcels from China, and a parcel worth $800 or less can come into the U.S. duty-free, as Fortune has explained.

Three machines built for different jobs

The three grew from quite different starting points, and each still shows its origins.

Amazon built breadth and speed. It sells almost everything, from its own inventory and from millions of sellers, and its advantage is that most of it arrives quickly and returns easily. Shoppers come to Amazon when they know what they want and want it soon.

Shein built a fashion machine. It designs and orders clothing in small batches, watches what sells and reorders the winners. Its advantage is a constant stream of new styles at low prices, and shoppers come to browse what is new, often with no particular item in mind.

Temu built a discount marketplace. It connects shoppers with manufacturers’ goods across many categories and spends heavily to attract them. Its advantage is price, and its app is designed for browsing deals; shoppers come to see what they can get for very little.

The shelf they share

The shelf the three have in common is the cheap discretionary one: inexpensive clothing, accessories, home décor, phone cases, small gadgets and party supplies. There, Shein and Temu compete with each other and with the low-priced end of Amazon. Outside it, the overlap is much smaller. Few shoppers buy laundry detergent on Temu or replacement parts on Shein. For a brand, the real question is how much of its own range sits on that shared shelf, because that is the part of the business exposed to all three at once.

Picture a home décor brand selling decorative pillows for $35 on Amazon. In early 2023 it notices similar-looking pillows on Temu for $9 and on Shein’s home range for $12. Its sales of the simplest designs slip, while its pillows with distinctive fabrics and fills hold steady. The contested shelf took its plainest products, not its best.

The decision on a brand’s table

For a leadership team, the question is less whether these platforms are a threat than which of its products they can reach. Most brands have some products that look interchangeable with cheap alternatives and some that do not. The first group is where Shein and Temu will press, and mapping it is the first piece of work.

Those products are defended on what the newcomers give up. Shein and Temu ship from abroad and take a week or more; their quality varies and returns can be harder. Fast delivery, consistent quality, clear sizing and real reviews are reasons to pay more, and making them prominent on every listing matters more than cutting price.

The longer-term answer is to move more of the range off the contested shelf. Distinctive design, better materials, a recognizable brand and bundles that change the comparison all do that. A pillow that is clearly better is not competing with a $9 one.

Advertising costs feel the contest too. In its first two months, Temu bid on over 1,700 App Store search terms, Appfigures found, and both newcomers spend heavily to reach shoppers. Brands advertising cheap discretionary goods outside Amazon may find those audiences more expensive than a year ago, and should judge that spending on new customers rather than clicks.

Some teams will ask whether to sell on Shein or Temu themselves. For most established brands the answer is caution. Both platforms are built around very low prices, and a brand that appears there invites the comparison it is trying to avoid elsewhere.

Two outside forces deserve a place on the watch list. Any change to the $800 duty threshold would raise Shein’s and Temu’s costs at once, and scrutiny of supply chains, including how cotton is sourced, has already touched Shein. Either could change the economics of the contested shelf quickly. Mapping which products sit on that shelf, and building the listings and range that move them off it, is how we help brands position their range against low-price competitors.

A0382.title: Amazon price perception: the price shoppers actually see
A0382.alt: A cream ceramic vase of eucalyptus with blank paper tags tied on twine, on a wooden table against a blue wall.
A0382.ttag: Amazon price perception: the price shoppers actually see | Kwontified
A0382.desc: Shoppers judge Amazon prices by the cues around them, not the number alone. How reference prices, coupons and unit prices work, and how to manage them.
A0382.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 11, 2023.
A0382.body:
Two coffee brands each sell a 12-ounce bag at $14, and each runs a deal at $11.20. On one product page the deal shows a clear 20% saving. On the other it shows almost nothing. Same price, same deal, same marketplace. Why does one look like a bargain and the other like an ordinary Tuesday?

Because shoppers on Amazon judge a price by the cues around it, not by the number alone. The strikethrough reference price, the coupon badge and the unit price all shape what a price feels like, and the reference price is built from a product’s own recent price history. Frequent discounting erodes the very savings shoppers see. Brands should hold a stable everyday price, use coupons and short deals for visible savings, and keep unit prices comparable across pack sizes.

Why Amazon price perception matters more in 2023

Shoppers are paying close attention to prices. Consumer prices rose 6.0% in the year to February, while retail sales rose 5.4% over the same period, First Trust noted. People are spending more dollars and taking home fewer goods, and they are looking harder at every price.

In that climate, what a price appears to be matters almost as much as what it is. Two products at the same price can feel very different depending on what surrounds the number on the page.

How the reference price turns discounts against you

Amazon surrounds every price with several cues. The strikethrough reference price is the one that matters most here. In our experience, the Was Price Amazon displays reflects the median price customers paid for the product over the previous 90 days, excluding limited-time deals. It is not a number the brand sets; it is built from the brand’s own pricing history.

The coupon works differently. A coupon shows as a badge in search results, before the shopper opens the product page, so it signals a saving at the moment the shopper is choosing which product to click. The unit price does a third job: for products sold in different sizes or pack counts, Amazon often shows a price per ounce, per count or per load, and shoppers comparing a single item with a multipack use it to judge value.

The reference price is where intuition misleads. A brand that discounts often feels it is giving shoppers more reasons to buy. But because the Was Price follows the median price paid, a product that is discounted most of the time drags its own reference down. After a few months of near-constant promotion, the “regular” price shoppers see is the discounted price, and the next promotion shows little or no saving.

That is what separates the two coffee brands. One ran a 20% discount most weeks for three months; the other held its price and saved its deal for once a quarter.

Brand that discounts most weeksBrand that holds its price
Everyday price$14$14
Price customers mostly paid$11.20$14
Deal price$11.20$11.20
Saving the page shows on the dealalmost none20%

The first brand’s median price paid drifted toward $11.20, and the strikethrough reference followed it. The second brand’s reference stayed at $14, so the same $11.20 shows as a clear saving. The brand that discounted less ends up with the more convincing discount, and very different results from the same promotional budget.

Stable everyday price, short visible savings

Hold a stable everyday price for most of the year. That keeps the reference price credible, so each promotion looks like what it is.

Use coupons for routine, visible savings. A coupon badge appears in search results and signals value without changing the product’s underlying price history in the same way that a permanent discount does. A modest coupon can earn the click without training shoppers to expect a lower everyday price.

Keep deals short and purposeful. Limited-time deals around events, launches or slow periods create urgency; running them so often that they become the normal price defeats the purpose.

Check unit prices across pack sizes. A multipack that costs more per unit than the single item sends a confusing signal, and shoppers who compare unit prices will notice. Larger packs should usually offer a lower unit price, or at least not a higher one.

Compare the total, not just the headline. A low price with slow delivery or high shipping can feel worse than a slightly higher price with fast, free delivery, and Prime eligibility is itself a price cue for many shoppers.

Watch your prices elsewhere, too. In our experience, Amazon compares a product’s price with what it finds at other retailers, and a noticeably higher price on Amazon can cost the product its featured offer, the Add to Cart button most shoppers use. A promotion on a brand’s own site that undercuts Amazon can therefore hurt sales on Amazon, and coordinating prices across channels protects both.

Subscribe & Save is a quieter lever for repeat purchases. Its discount appears on the product page as a saving for shoppers willing to commit, without lowering the one-time price, so consumables can keep a stable everyday price while still rewarding loyal customers.

Measure perception, not just price. Track conversion rate alongside price changes, and look at how often your product shows a strikethrough or coupon in search. A product whose conversion falls after a price cut may be suffering from a vanishing reference price rather than a lack of demand.

The rule to apply on Monday: before approving another discount, look at the last 90 days of prices paid and ask what the next deal will show as a saving. Managing that history across a catalog is how we protect price perception for brands on Amazon.

A0385.crumb: Mother’s Day on marketplaces: what gift…
A0385.title: Mother’s Day on marketplaces: what gift shoppers reward
A0385.alt: Ranunculus flowers in an enamel jug beside a gift box with a blue ribbon on a sunny windowsill.
A0385.ttag: Mother’s Day on marketplaces: what gift shoppers reward | Kwontified
A0385.desc: Mother’s Day spending hit a record in 2022, and over a third of shoppers buy online. What gift shoppers reward on marketplaces, and how brands should prepare.
A0385.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 13, 2023.
A0385.body:
In late April, a shopper looking on Amazon for a Mother’s Day present finds two options from skincare brands. One is a single serum at $38, the better value per ounce. The other is a three-piece gift set at $45, shown in a box, with a note that it ships in time. The set wins. It looks like a present, and it removes the guesswork.

Gift shoppers behave differently from everyday shoppers, and Mother’s Day, which set a spending record in 2022 with more than a third of shoppers buying online, rewards products that arrive on time, look like a gift and are easy to choose. Brands selling on marketplaces should secure stock and delivery well before the day, present products as gifts with sets and gift-ready content, and advertise on gift searches in the weeks before May 14.

What Mother’s Day looked like on marketplaces in 2022

Mother’s Day spending reached a record $31.7 billion in 2022, up $3.6 billion from 2021, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey, HomePage News reported. About 84% of U.S. adults planned to celebrate, spending an average of $245.76.

Online shopping led the list of planned venues. More than one in three shoppers, 36%, planned to buy gifts online, ahead of department stores at 30%, National Jeweler reported. For marketplace sellers, that is the number to hold onto: online came ahead of department stores as the place shoppers planned to buy their gifts. Jewelry stood out, with 41% of shoppers planning to give it and spending expected to reach $7 billion.

Gifts also widened beyond physical objects. In the same survey, 27% of shoppers planned to give experiences such as concert or sporting event tickets, the highest since NRF began tracking the category in 2016, HomePage News noted.

Mother’s Day 2023 falls on May 14, and shoppers face higher prices than a year ago. Consumer prices were 6.0% higher in February than a year earlier, First Trust noted. Gift budgets may stretch, but shoppers will want to feel the gift is worth every dollar.

What a gift shopper needs that an everyday shopper does not

The deadline changes the math. An everyday shopper can wait a few days for a better price; a gift shopper cannot miss the day. As Mother’s Day approaches, delivery certainty becomes worth more than a small saving, and products that cannot promise arrival in time lose the sale entirely.

The recipient changes the risk. The shopper is choosing for someone else, often unsure about size, taste or what she already owns. A gift that has to be exchanged is a small disappointment for two people. Products that reduce that uncertainty win: sets, gift-ready packaging, clear sizing and returns that the recipient can use. That is why the boxed set beat the serum in the opening example, even at a higher price.

The way gift shoppers search is different as well. They often search for the occasion rather than the product: “gifts for mom,” “Mother’s Day gift for wife,” “gift set for her.” A brand that only appears for product searches misses the shoppers who have not yet decided what to buy. Those undecided shoppers are exactly the ones a well-presented gift can win.

Reviews carry extra weight for the same reason. A shopper buying for someone else cannot judge the product by using it, so ratings and recent reviews stand in for that judgment. Products with thin or mixed reviews lose gift sales they might win as everyday purchases.

Getting ready for May 14

Stock and delivery come first, because they fail first. Mother’s Day orders peak in the final two weeks, and products that run out or slip outside fast delivery windows during that period lose the most valuable days. Brands should check inventory at fulfillment centers by late April and plan replenishment with a margin for delays.

How the product is presented comes next. Sets and bundles, gift-ready images showing packaging, and copy that names the occasion all help shoppers choose. Where marketplaces allow it, gift messaging and wrapping options are worth enabling. A product that already looks like a present is easier to buy for someone else.

Advertising should follow the occasion searches. In the two to three weeks before May 14, broad searches like “gifts for mom” attract shoppers who are open to suggestion, and advertising on them with gift sets or best sellers reaches buyers a product-only plan would miss. After the last reliable delivery date, budgets should shift back to everyday searches.

Likely gift products deserve a review check before the season starts: enough recent reviews, and no recurring complaint left unaddressed. Returns deserve planning, too. Some gifts come back after the day, often for a different size or color. Making exchanges simple, with stock of the most likely alternatives on hand, turns a return into a kept sale and a satisfied recipient who may buy again for herself.

Brands outside obvious gift categories should not sit the occasion out. Kitchen tools, home goods, wellness products and small electronics all appear in Mother’s Day baskets. The growth of experience gifts also points to an opening for brands that can package a product as an experience, such as a cooking set with a recipe card or a refill plan for a favorite product.

So the question for a brand’s team is a simple one: if a shopper typed “gifts for mom” in the last week of April, would any of our products show up looking like a gift, and arrive in time? Building that seasonal plan across stock, content and advertising is how we prepare brands for Mother’s Day on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0387.crumb: Sponsored Brands video: how a moving ad…
A0387.title: Sponsored Brands video: how a moving ad changes search
A0387.alt: A pink-walled shop with wooden shelves of ceramic cups, linen boxes and jars around a screen showing a blurred garden.
A0387.ttag: Sponsored Brands video: how a moving ad changes search | Kwontified
A0387.desc: Sponsored Brands video plays inside Amazon search results and pulls the eye from static listings. Where that adds sales, and where it buys clicks you had.
A0387.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 18, 2023.
A0387.body:
Take a brand of insulated lunch bags running Sponsored Brands video on two searches. On its own brand name, where the bag already ranks first in the organic results, the video posts a click-through rate three times that of the brand’s other ads. On “lunch bag for work,” where the bag sits 25th, the video’s click-through rate is lower. The second campaign is the one adding sales.

The difference comes from attention. A playing video draws the eye on a page of still images, and what that attention is worth depends on whether the shopper would have found the product anyway. Sponsored Brands video earns its cost on category searches where a product is hard to see, and it should be judged on the sales it adds to a search, not on its click-through rate.

Where Sponsored Brands video appears, and why its numbers look so good

Sponsored Brands video is a short clip that plays silently and automatically, promotes a single product and links to that product’s detail page. The standard Sponsored Brands banner usually sits at the top of the page. The video format mostly does not: its most frequent placements on desktop are within the search results themselves, Bidx observed in a review of its client accounts.

Engagement has been strong. Bidx found a higher click-through rate than standard Sponsored Brands in every account it examined, in some cases twice as high, and lower costs per click, probably because relatively few advertisers were using the format at the time. Results like those explain the growing interest brands have shown in it.

They are also easy to misread. Click-through rate measures how often shoppers who saw an ad clicked it. It says nothing about whether those shoppers would have bought the same product through the organic listing a few rows down.

How a moving ad shifts attention on the results page

A search results page is a grid of still images. A playing video breaks the pattern, the eye goes to it first, and the advertised product collects a larger share of attention than its position alone would earn.

Where that attention comes from decides its value. If the product is otherwise hard to find, on page two or below the fold for a broad search, the video brings in clicks the brand would not have had. If the product already ranks near the top organically, the video mostly intercepts clicks the organic listing would have received, and the brand pays for traffic it would have had for free. In that second case the click-through rate looks excellent for an awkward reason: shoppers who already wanted the product click the most eye-catching version of it.

It is like a shop that stations a greeter at the door and credits the greeter with every regular who walks in. The regulars were coming anyway.

Back to the lunch bags. On the brand-name search, the video’s click-through rate is three times that of the brand’s other ads, yet total sales on the search barely move, because shoppers were finding the bag already. On “lunch bag for work,” the click-through rate is lower, but total sales on the search rise noticeably. The weaker-looking report hides the better result.

Aim the video where your product is hard to see

Category and competitor searches where your product is not already near the top of the organic results are where Sponsored Brands video turns attention into sales you would not otherwise make. Most of the budget belongs there. Organic rank, the position a product holds in the unpaid results for a search, is the number to check before setting any video bid.

Your own branded searches call for restraint. A modest presence can protect your name against competitors who place their own videos on it, while heavy spending there mostly pays for clicks you would have won.

Measuring the difference needs no special tools. Compare total sales on a search, paid and organic together, with and without the video, or run it on some searches and hold it back on similar ones. When total sales rise, the video is adding demand. When they hold steady while paid clicks climb, it is relocating demand you already had.

Rivals’ videos work the same way against you. When a competitor runs video on a search where your product ranks well, its motion pulls attention from your static listing. If total sales on an important search fall while your organic rank holds, a competitor’s video is a likely cause, and that is the moment a modest video of your own earns its cost.

The creative decides more than the bid

Many shoppers scroll past before a video ends, and the sound is off by default, so the product has to be visible and recognizable in the opening seconds. A video that opens on a logo or a lifestyle scene gives away most of the format’s advantage. Clear shots of the product in use, with simple text on screen, do better.

Production need not be expensive. A simple video, made once, can serve many searches for months, and short clips that show the product from a few angles or solving a clear problem are usually enough. Brands that already have product footage for their listings or social channels can often adapt it. Because the video links to a detail page, the product it shows should match the listing exactly; a mismatch wastes the click the video worked to win.

The test for any Sponsored Brands video comes down to one question per search: did total sales go up, or did paid clicks simply replace organic ones? Answering that search by search is how we plan and measure Sponsored Brands video for brands on Amazon.

A0388.crumb: Marketplace brand control: what losing it…
A0388.title: Marketplace brand control: what losing it really costs
A0388.alt: An old wooden slide-lid box among plain cardboard shipping boxes on a sunlit trestle table.
A0388.ttag: Marketplace brand control: what losing it really costs | Kwontified
A0388.desc: On a marketplace, other sellers can change a brand’s price, content and customer experience. Why losing control costs more than sales, and how to win it back.
A0388.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 20, 2023.
A0388.body:
In a department store, a brand’s pans sit on a shelf the brand negotiated, at a price the store agreed to, in packaging the brand designed. On Amazon the same pans sit on a product page that any seller of the product can join, and the price a shopper sees may belong to whichever seller wins the featured offer that week. Marketplaces were built that way on purpose: one product, one page, many sellers, so search stays clean for shoppers.

The consequence is that a brand does not own its own page. Unauthorized sellers, counterfeiters and outside edits can change its price, content and customer experience without its consent. The cost of losing that control reaches well past lost sales, into pricing power with other retailers, customer trust and the brand’s view of its own demand. Brands get it back by enforcing their registration, controlling who distributes their products, and monitoring listings as a standing operation rather than an occasional cleanup.

Marketplace brand control in 2023: what Amazon now catches

Amazon has put heavy investment into the counterfeit side of the problem. In its 2022 Brand Protection Report, the company said it stopped more than 800,000 attempts to create new selling accounts in 2022, down from 2.5 million in 2021 and 6 million in 2020, according to Amazon. It also seized and disposed of more than 6 million counterfeit products, and it said the number of valid notices of infringement filed by brands enrolled in Brand Registry fell by more than 35%.

Behind those results sits a large operation. Amazon said it spent more than $1.2 billion and employed more than 15,000 people to protect customers, brands and partners from fraud and counterfeiting, Retail Insight Network reported.

Those are real improvements, and every brand on the marketplace benefits from them. Counterfeits, though, are only one part of control. Much of what costs brands money comes from sellers offering genuine products the brand never authorized.

What a shared product page costs a brand

Price is where the damage usually starts. An unauthorized seller who bought stock cheaply, from a liquidation or a distributor’s overflow, can undercut the brand’s own price. If that seller wins the featured offer, shoppers see the brand’s product at the lower price, and other retailers see it too. Their buyers then ask a fair question: why hold the brand’s recommended price in their own stores when the product sells for less on Amazon?

Content drifts in quieter ways. Product pages draw on information from several sources, and a page can end up with wrong details, poor images or a title that no longer matches the brand’s naming. Each change makes the product a little harder to find or a little less convincing to buy, and nobody at the brand signed off on any of them.

The customer experience suffers next. A shopper who buys from an unauthorized seller may receive old stock, damaged packaging or poor service, and the complaint and the bad review attach to the brand, not to the seller. Meanwhile the brand loses information it needs: sales made by other sellers are invisible to it, so it loses sight of demand, pricing and customer feedback for its own products.

Take a cookware brand whose pans sell for $80 on Amazon and at department stores. A reseller with surplus stock lists them at $59 and wins the featured offer for several weeks. The brand’s direct sales fall, a department store buyer asks for a price adjustment, and a run of reviews complains about scratched pans from old inventory. The sales loss shows up in the brand’s reports. The damage to its pricing and reputation is larger, and it lasts longer.

How brands take the page back

Registration is the foundation, and it only works when someone uses it. Brand registration on each marketplace gives a brand more authority over its product pages and access to protection tools, and Amazon’s own figures suggest those tools increasingly catch problems before brands have to report them. The tools pay off when a named person reviews listings, files reports and corrects content every week.

Distribution is where most unauthorized stock comes from, which makes it the place to stop it. Genuine products reach unauthorized sellers through gaps in a brand’s own supply chain: distributors selling outside their territory, retailers clearing excess, liquidation channels. Clear reseller agreements, a published pricing policy and tracking of where stock goes close those gaps. Without them, enforcement on the marketplace becomes a constant chase after sellers the brand itself supplied, indirectly.

Monitoring has to be continuous because the page changes continuously. Sellers on each listing, prices, content and reviews move week to week. A brand that checks its main products regularly catches problems while they are small; a brand that checks once a year finds damage that has been building for months.

The same structure applies beyond Amazon. Walmart’s marketplace also lets several sellers offer the same item, and its growing seller base means more potential offers on each product page. Brands expanding to new marketplaces do better setting up control from the start than cleaning up after problems appear.

Not every reseller is a bad actor. Some are authorized partners serving customers the brand does not reach directly, and they belong on the page. What matters is knowing who is selling, at what price and in what condition, and deciding deliberately who stays. A brand with clean listings, consistent prices and authorized sellers is easier for marketplaces to trust, easier for retailers to work with and more convincing to shoppers.

That leaves a leadership team with one question, simple to ask and often hard to answer: who in the company owns what shoppers see on our product page this week, and who would notice if it changed? Making that someone’s daily job, across listings, sellers and prices, is how we run Amazon, Walmart and Target for brands that want their pages back.

A0391.crumb: First-party data: the asset that outlasts…
A0391.title: First-party data: the asset that outlasts the cookie
A0391.alt: A closed wooden keepsake box with a brass latch beside a plate of cookie crumbs on a worn table.
A0391.ttag: First-party data: the asset that outlasts the cookie | Kwontified
A0391.desc: Third-party cookies in Chrome are set to fade from 2024, and retail media grows on logged-in shopper data. Why first-party data matters, and how to build it.
A0391.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 27, 2023.
A0391.body:
A shopper scans her Target Circle account at the register, then reorders the same detergent on Target.com a few weeks later. Without a single cookie, Target knows who she is, what she bought in the store and what she bought online, and it can show her an ad and then see whether she bought the product. That kind of knowledge is what advertising has always wanted, and it is moving out of the browser and into the logged-in account.

The shift rewards whoever owns the login. Google plans to begin phasing out third-party cookies in Chrome in the second half of 2024. Retailers with large logged-in audiences, such as Target with Circle and Walmart with Walmart Connect, are already winning advertising budgets on the strength of their data. Brands should use the time the cookie delay gives them to build first-party relationships of their own, while using retail media to reach the shoppers whose data the retailers hold.

Where first-party data stands in spring 2023

The cookie deadline keeps moving, but it has not gone away. On July 27, 2022, Google said it would extend testing of its replacement technologies and begin phasing out third-party cookies in Chrome in the second half of 2024, 9to5Google reported. The new tools were expected to be generally available by the third quarter of 2023.

The companies with logged-in customers, meanwhile, keep growing their advertising businesses. Target said its Target Circle program had doubled since its launch in 2019, when it quickly reached 50 million members, according to the transcript of its fourth-quarter earnings call. It also said it would put more emphasis behind Circle and its Roundel media business in 2023. Walmart’s U.S. advertising business, Walmart Connect, grew 41% in the holiday quarter, according to Walmart.

How identity moved from the browser to the account

For two decades, much of digital advertising ran on cookies: small files that let advertisers recognize a browser as it moved from site to site. They were imperfect, but they let a brand reach a shopper on one site based on what she had done on another.

That system has been weakening for years. Browsers limited tracking, privacy rules tightened, and mobile platforms began asking users for permission to track them across apps. Google’s planned change to Chrome, the most widely used browser, is the largest step still to come.

As cookies fade, value moves to the companies that know who their customers are because those customers log in. A retailer with a loyalty program knows what each member bought, in store and online, with no cookie involved. It can show that member an ad and then see whether she bought the product. Identity joined to purchase data is what advertisers want, and it is why retail media has grown so quickly.

The same logic works for brands at a smaller scale. A brand that sells directly, runs a loyalty program or asks customers to register a product holds first-party data of its own. It knows who its customers are and can reach them again on its own terms.

Take a kitchen appliance brand that sells mostly through retailers and has leaned on cookie-based retargeting to remind shoppers who visited its site. As that retargeting weakens, the brand adds a product registration with an extended warranty and collects customer emails at the moment of purchase. Within a year it has a direct list of verified owners to use for accessories, replacements and new launches, without depending on anyone else’s data.

Building your own relationships while using the retailers’ data

Every point where customers already touch the brand is a chance to start a relationship. Product registrations, warranties, recipe or how-to content, loyalty programs and direct sales all give customers a reason to share their details, provided the exchange is real. Customers share data when they get something useful back.

Retail media does a different job, and does it well: it reaches shoppers at the moment of purchase, with measurement tied to sales. A retailer’s logged-in data is the strongest identity signal most brands can use, so brands already working with Amazon, Walmart and Target should treat those networks as a central part of their advertising rather than an add-on.

The two are worth connecting where the rules allow. Clean rooms such as Amazon Marketing Cloud let a brand combine its own data with a retailer’s in a privacy-safe way, and brands that bring their own customer lists learn far more from those tools than brands that arrive empty-handed.

Brands that sell only through marketplaces face a particular gap. Marketplaces generally do not pass customer contact details to sellers, so the brand sees the sale but not the buyer. There are still legitimate routes: package inserts inviting customers to register for a warranty or support, where marketplace rules allow them; brand websites with guides worth signing up for; social channels customers choose to follow. Each builds a direct relationship, as long as the brand checks each marketplace’s current rules on inserts and customer contact first.

A brand’s own list also sharpens its measurement. Knowing who its customers are, it can exclude them from campaigns aimed at new shoppers, build audiences that resemble its best customers, and test whether advertising changes what known customers buy. Without its own data, a brand depends entirely on each platform’s view of its results.

That data comes with obligations. Customers expect brands to protect it, use it as promised and respect their choices, and a brand that collects carelessly risks losing the trust that made customers share it in the first place.

The question worth putting to a marketing team is a plain one: if third-party cookies in Chrome were gone tomorrow, which of our customers could we still reach, and how? Building that answer alongside retail media is how we help brands prepare their data and advertising for life after the cookie.

A0393.crumb: Amazon Q1 2023 results: ads grew three…
A0393.title: Amazon Q1 2023 results: ads grew three times faster than retail
A0393.alt: Three stacks of coins beside a twine-tied bundle of brown paper parcels on a wooden table.
A0393.ttag: Amazon Q1 2023 results: ads grew three times faster than retail | Kwontified
A0393.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 21% in Q1 2023 while its retail revenue grew about 6%. What that says about the auction, and how brands should plan for costly clicks.
A0393.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 2, 2023.
A0393.body:
Amazon’s online stores sold $51.1 billion in the first quarter of 2023, flat on a year earlier. Its advertising revenue rose 21% to $9.5 billion over the same period. How does an ad business grow that fast on top of a store that is standing still?

The answer is that brands are paying more for advertising relative to the shopping it sits on. Counting online stores and third-party seller services together, advertising rose from about 10 cents to almost 12 cents for every dollar of that retail revenue. When ad money grows faster than shopping, the auction tightens and the cost of reaching each shopper climbs. Brands should plan for a rising advertising cost per sale, track advertising as a share of total sales, and build the organic strength they do not have to bid for.

Amazon Q1 2023 results: advertising outran the store

Total revenue for the quarter was $127.4 billion, up 9%, GeekWire reported. Online store sales were flat at $51.1 billion, third-party seller services rose 18% to $29.8 billion, and advertising rose 21% to $9.5 billion. A year earlier, advertising had brought in about $7.9 billion, Investing.com reported. Andy Jassy attributed the growth largely to Amazon’s investments in machine learning that help customers see relevant information, according to the company’s statement, the Baker City Herald reported.

MeasureQ1 2022Q1 2023Change
Online stores plus third-party seller servicesabout $76.4 billionabout $80.9 billionabout 6%
Advertising revenueabout $7.9 billion$9.5 billion21%
Advertising per dollar of those retail linesabout 10.3 centsabout 11.7 centsmore than three times the retail growth rate

The quarter extends a pattern. Amazon’s advertising revenue reached $37.8 billion for 2022 as a whole, Intentwise noted, and in both of the last two quarters it has grown far faster than the store. In the fourth quarter of 2022, advertising rose 19% while online store sales fell 2%, EcomCrew reported.

Other ad platforms looked very different. Meta’s advertising revenue rose 4.3% in its first quarter, and Alphabet’s fell by less than 1%, Bidx noted.

What the ratio says about the auction

The ratio in the table is simple to build. Add Amazon’s online store sales and its third-party seller services, a rough measure of the retail activity its ads sit on. Seller services brought in $25.3 billion in the first quarter of 2022, Modern Retail reported, and online store sales were flat across the year. The combined total grew from about $76.4 billion to about $80.9 billion, roughly 6%. Advertising grew 21% over the same period, more than three times as fast, so advertising per dollar of retail revenue rose from about 10.3 cents to about 11.7 cents.

The measure is imperfect. Seller services revenue reflects Amazon’s fees, not sellers’ total sales, and some of Amazon’s advertising runs outside its store. Still, the direction is clear, and it has held across recent quarters.

Two forces can produce that gap, alone or together. More advertisers may be competing for each shopper, which pushes up the price of each click. Or each shopper may see more ads, which spreads attention across more paid placements. Either way, the cost of reaching a shopper rises relative to what that shopper spends.

Take a brand whose Amazon sales were flat from Q1 2022 to Q1 2023. To hold its position as the auction tightened, its advertising spend rose about 14%, in line with the rise in Amazon’s advertising per retail dollar from 10.3 to 11.7 cents. Its advertising as a share of total sales went from 10% to 11.4%. Nothing about the brand changed. The market around it did, and the brand’s margin absorbed the difference without anyone deciding that it should.

Where is the extra competition coming from? In our experience, from three directions at once. More brands are advertising on Amazon, including brands that used to rely on organic sales.

Existing advertisers are spreading into more ad types, from Sponsored Brands video to Sponsored Display and streaming TV. And Amazon has added sponsored placements in more parts of the shopping experience, from search results to product pages. Each adds bidders or ad space.

Plan for a rising cost per sale

Budgets set as a fixed return target slowly squeeze reach in a tightening auction, because the same return gets harder to hit as competition rises. Budgets set as a share of sales, with a clear ceiling, make the trade-off visible to whoever owns the margin.

Return on ad spend can also hold steady while advertising takes a growing share of revenue, if paid sales are replacing organic ones. Advertising as a share of total sales catches that; return on ad spend alone does not. It belongs in the monthly report next to ROAS.

The cheapest sale is still the one you do not bid for. Strong reviews, complete listings, reliable stock and products that rank well on their own searches all reduce what a brand pays for each sale, and they gain value as paid placement gets more expensive. Newer ad types and newer marketplaces often have fewer competitors, too: Walmart Connect, Target Roundel and newer Amazon formats can offer better value while brands are still learning them.

None of this makes advertising less worthwhile. Amazon’s growth shows advertising works well enough for brands to keep spending more on it. The price of participation is rising, though, and the practical test for the second quarter is short: if advertising’s share of your Amazon sales went up while your total sales did not, the auction took the difference. Planning budgets around that number is how we manage Amazon advertising and organic performance together for brands.

A0394.crumb: Beauty on Amazon in 2023: two markets…
A0394.title: Beauty on Amazon in 2023: two markets moving apart
A0394.alt: Glass perfume decanters and apothecary bottles on a rustic wooden shelf against a deep blue wall.
A0394.ttag: Beauty on Amazon in 2023: two markets moving apart | Kwontified
A0394.desc: Prestige beauty grew 15% in 2022 and moved back toward stores, while mass beauty moved online. What that means for beauty brands selling on Amazon in 2023.
A0394.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 4, 2023.
A0394.body:
A shopper testing foundation shades at a beauty counter and a shopper reordering the same shampoo for the fourth time are doing different jobs. In 2022 they increasingly did those jobs in different places. Prestige beauty, the counter-and-sample business, drifted back toward stores, while mass beauty, the restock business, gained share online.

That split decides what Amazon is for in a beauty brand’s plan. On Amazon the category runs mostly on replenishment, reviews and trust rather than on the discovery of luxury brands. Beauty brands should treat it as the place where repeat buyers restock and new buyers check reviews, protect authenticity and pricing closely there, and use stores and social channels for the discovery prestige shoppers still prefer.

Beauty on Amazon and beyond: what 2022 showed

Beauty had a strong year, stronger than almost any other category of discretionary spending. U.S. prestige beauty sales grew 15% to $27.1 billion in 2022, and every prestige category grew by double digits, according to NPD. Makeup rose 18%, skincare 12%, fragrance 11% and hair products 22%, Beauty Packaging reported.

The more useful finding sits underneath the growth. Mass and prestige beauty together grew 11%, but only prestige held up in units, NPD said. The two also moved in opposite directions on where shoppers bought: prestige shifted back toward stores, while online share increased in the mass market.

Some of the growth was price. Revenue rose by double digits, but many brands raised prices during the year, BeautyMatter noted, so units tell a more cautious story than dollars. A beauty brand reading its own Amazon results should make the same separation between price increases and real growth in buyers.

Counterfeiting remains a category worry as well. When Amazon launched its Anti-Counterfeiting Exchange in April, it said it had piloted the program with apparel, home goods and cosmetics stores, where counterfeiting is most common, Reuters reported.

Why the two beauty markets shop differently

The split reflects how people shop for each kind of product, and it has been building for several years.

Prestige beauty is often about discovery and experience. A shopper wants to try a new fragrance, test a foundation shade or get advice from someone behind the counter. Stores do that well, and after two years of restrictions shoppers went back to them. Prestige brands also guard their pricing and image closely, and many have kept a cautious distance from open marketplaces.

Mass beauty is more often about replenishment. A shopper who has found her shampoo, moisturizer or mascara wants to restock it quickly and at a fair price, and online shopping, Amazon in particular, is built for exactly that. Subscribe and Save, fast delivery and a stored order history turn the repeat purchase into a couple of taps.

Reviews sit in the middle of both. Beauty buyers lean heavily on other shoppers’ experiences, especially for skin and hair products where results vary from person to person. On Amazon, a product’s rating and the substance of its reviews often decide whether a new buyer takes the risk at all.

Take a skincare brand sold in specialty stores and on Amazon. Its new serum launches in stores with sampling and advice, where most first purchases happen. Three months later, Amazon sales of the same serum climb, driven mostly by customers reordering. The two channels are doing different jobs, and giving them the same messages and the same budgets would waste money in both.

Running Amazon for the job it actually does

Replenishment is the core of the plan. Existing customers should find and reorder without friction: consistent product names, clear sizes and variations, Subscribe and Save where it fits, and stock that does not run out. Advertising on the brand’s own product searches keeps those repeat customers from being picked off by competitors at the moment they come back.

New buyers arrive with a different question, which is whether the product works for someone like them. Detailed images, full ingredient lists, usage instructions and honest claims answer it. So does fixing the complaints that recur in reviews, whether they concern packaging, texture or results, because the next shopper will read them.

Authenticity and price need closer guarding in beauty than in most categories. Counterfeits and unauthorized sellers are common, so brand registration, controlled distribution and regular monitoring carry more weight. A beauty shopper who receives an expired or fake product blames the brand, and says so in a review.

Shelf life adds an operational wrinkle. Many beauty products carry expiration dates, and products held too long in a marketplace warehouse can reach customers close to expiry. In our experience, brands that send smaller, more frequent shipments of dated products avoid both disposal costs and the reviews that follow a short-dated delivery, which is why planning stock in weeks of cover rather than months matters more here than elsewhere.

Prestige brands weighing Amazon face a real trade-off. Amazon offers reach and convenience, especially for replenishment, but it also exposes a brand to price comparison and resellers unless distribution is tightly controlled. For brands that do sell there, a carefully managed official presence is usually safer than leaving the page to unauthorized sellers.

Discovery still matters; it simply happens somewhere else. Social video, creators and stores introduce new products, and Amazon captures the purchase, especially the second and third ones. The brands that get the most from both make a product easy to find on Amazon once a shopper has met it on a counter or a phone screen.

The question for a beauty leadership team, then, is which of its products are really discovery products and which are restock products, and whether its Amazon plan treats them differently. Drawing that line product by product is part of how we run beauty brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.
