A0395.crumb: Amazon ad goals by funnel stage: one…
A0395.title: Amazon ad goals by funnel stage: one metric cannot judge them all
A0395.alt: A glass funnel in a brass lab stand filled with layers of blue, amber and red glass beads.
A0395.ttag: Amazon ad goals by funnel stage: one metric cannot judge them all | Kwontified
A0395.desc: Amazon ad types reach shoppers at different moments, so judging them all on ROAS starves the ones that create demand. How to match each ad to its own goal.
A0395.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 9, 2023.
A0395.body:
When the Association of National Advertisers asked marketers about retail media, two-thirds said driving sales was their most important objective, and only 12% chose investing in future brand growth, MediaPost reported. On Amazon, that priority usually turns into a single number on every report: return on ad spend. It feels like discipline. Over a year, it can quietly shrink the demand the sales goal depends on.

The reason is where the credit lands. Ads close to the purchase collect the sale, including sales that ads further back in the shopper’s path made possible. Judging every Amazon ad type on return on ad spend therefore favors the ads that capture existing demand and starves the ones that create it. Each funnel stage needs its own measure, and the budget split across stages has to be a decision rather than the result of the highest return winning.

Why Amazon ad goals matter more in 2023

Amazon is now a full-funnel advertising business. Its advertising revenue rose 21% to $9.5 billion in the first quarter of 2023, GeekWire reported. Alongside search ads, Amazon sells display and video through its DSP, streaming TV ads, and audience tools in Amazon Marketing Cloud, as it described at its unBoxed conference in October 2022, according to Amazon.

Most brands still judge that whole range with one number, because return on ad spend is the number every report shows first. It is a good number for some of those ads and a misleading one for others.

How one metric misjudges the funnel

Ads near the purchase, such as Sponsored Products on a brand’s own name or on a product’s exact search, reach shoppers who have largely decided. Their attributed return is high because the sale was likely anyway.

Ads earlier in the path, such as DSP audiences, streaming TV or Sponsored Brands video on broad searches, reach shoppers who have not decided. Some of those shoppers buy later, often after searching for the brand by name, and a search ad takes the credit. The early ad’s own attributed return looks low even when it created the demand.

Judge both on return on ad spend and the budget drifts, quarter after quarter, toward the late ads. The reports look efficient. Meanwhile the pool of new shoppers shrinks, the late ads have less demand to capture, and growth stalls while every dashboard stays green.

Take a snack brand spending $100,000 a quarter. Its branded search campaigns return $8 per dollar; its DSP campaign returns $2. Each quarter the team moves money from DSP to search. A year later DSP is gone, search returns $9, and total sales are down 6%. The branded searches the search ads captured were partly created by the DSP spending that was cut, so the better-looking return arrived with a smaller business.

One goal per stage, written down before launch

Each stage of the funnel can be held to a measure it can actually move. Writing the stage and its measure down before a campaign starts keeps the judgment honest afterward.

StageTypical Amazon ad typesMeasure that fits
AwarenessDSP audiences, streaming TV, broad videoReach among relevant shoppers; share of sales from new-to-brand customers
ConsiderationSponsored Brands and Sponsored Display aimed at category shoppersDetail page views; branded search volume; click-through on category searches
ConversionSponsored Products on high-intent searchesReturn on ad spend; advertising cost of sales
LoyaltyAudiences of past buyersRepeat purchase rate; Subscribe and Save sign-ups

Budgets across stages should then be set on purpose. A common starting point is to protect conversion spending on core searches, fund awareness and consideration as a deliberate share of the total, and review the split each quarter against overall sales growth and new-customer growth.

Attribution windows add a second distortion on top of the first. Different Amazon ad types count sales over different periods after a click or view, and awareness ads often influence purchases that fall outside any window. Comparing reported returns across ad types without adjusting for those differences compares unlike things. In our experience, brands that note each ad type’s window beside its results make fewer mistaken cuts.

Creative should change by stage, too. An awareness ad has to introduce the brand and show why it matters to someone who has never heard of it. A conversion ad only needs to confirm that the product a shopper already wants is right there. Swapping one for the other weakens both.

Smaller brands often ask where to start when the budget cannot cover every stage. The usual sequence is to secure conversion on core searches first, because that protects existing demand, then add one consideration tactic aimed at category searches, and fund awareness only once sales are steady enough to absorb a slower payback.

Reading the stages together

The stages also have to be measured as a system. Rising branded search volume after an awareness campaign, or a higher share of new-to-brand sales, is evidence that the earlier stages are working even when their own return looks thin. Amazon Marketing Cloud and simple holdout tests can show how exposure to earlier ads changes later purchases.

None of this retires return on ad spend. It remains the right measure for conversion ads, and the business still needs its advertising to pay back overall. The working rule is narrower: before cutting any Amazon campaign for a weak return, check which stage it serves and whether branded search and new-to-brand share moved while it ran. Setting those stage goals and reading them together is how we plan full-funnel Amazon advertising for the brands we manage.

A0397.crumb: Amazon account suspensions: why the risk…
A0397.title: Amazon account suspensions: why the risk is rising in 2023
A0397.alt: A red and white boom barrier blocks the entrance to a weathered yellow industrial warehouse yard.
A0397.ttag: Amazon account suspensions: why the risk is rising in 2023 | Kwontified
A0397.desc: A federal law effective June 27 requires marketplaces to suspend sellers who fail verification. Why suspension risk is rising, and how a brand protects itself.
A0397.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 11, 2023.
A0397.body:
The message that can halt a brand’s marketplace business this summer will not look dangerous. It will ask a seller to confirm its bank account, tax identification and contact details, and it will arrive in whichever inbox was attached to the account when someone opened it, years ago, perhaps under a person who has since left. From June 27, marketplaces must suspend high-volume sellers who do not answer within 10 days.

That is why the risk of an account suspension is rising in 2023. Marketplaces are tightening verification and automated enforcement at the same time, and the new federal law adds a way to lose an account that has nothing to do with how the products perform. Account health now needs to be run as an operating discipline, with a named owner, current seller information and an escalation plan written before it is needed.

Why Amazon account suspensions matter more in 2023

The INFORM Consumers Act was signed into law as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 and takes effect 180 days after enactment, on June 27, 2023, Gibson Dunn explained.

It applies to “high-volume” third-party sellers: those with 200 or more sales of new or unused consumer products and $5,000 or more in gross revenue in any continuous 12-month period during the previous 24 months. Marketplaces must collect and verify those sellers’ bank account, contact and tax identification details, and suspend sellers who do not provide the required information or certifications within 10 days. A seller whose annual gross revenue reaches $20,000 or more faces added disclosure requirements on top of that, Gibson Dunn noted.

The Act aims to make it harder to sell stolen and counterfeit goods anonymously. For a legitimate brand, its practical effect is a new administrative route to losing an account, through a missed request for information rather than a policy breach.

Marketplaces are tightening at the front door as well. Amazon’s 2022 Brand Protection Report says the company blocked more than 800,000 attempts to open new selling accounts during that year, according to Amazon.

Suspensions now come from accumulation, not one big mistake

Marketplaces grew by letting many sellers in quickly. As they grew, the problems that came with them, including counterfeits, unsafe products, fake reviews and fraud, drew pressure from regulators, brands and shoppers. The response has been more enforcement, most of it automated. Systems scan listings, reviews, complaints and seller information continuously, and when they find a problem they can remove a listing or restrict an account within hours. That speed protects shoppers, but the notices are often brief, and the path to a human reviewer can be slow.

For a brand, that changes what a suspension is. It is less often the result of one serious violation and more often the result of an accumulation: a cluster of complaints about one product, an expired document, a listing flagged by an automated check, and now an unanswered verification request.

The cost is out of proportion to the cause. While an account is suspended, sales stop, advertising stops and products lose rank. Stock may sit in the marketplace’s warehouses, accruing fees. Even a short suspension can take months to recover from, because rank and sales momentum have to be rebuilt, often with extra advertising.

Take a home goods brand whose finance lead leaves the company. Her successor does not know the marketplace account exists under her predecessor’s email. A verification request goes unanswered, and the account is suspended ten days later. Reinstatement takes three weeks. The brand loses its best-selling month of the season, and its top products take two months to recover their former rank.

Who owns account health?

That scenario is really a question about the org chart, and it belongs on the leadership agenda before something breaks. A seller account sits with whoever opened it, whether an e-commerce manager, a finance analyst or an agency, unless someone deliberately moves it. When that person moves on, the account keeps running and the inbox goes quiet.

Giving account health a named owner changes that. Someone should review account health dashboards, policy notices and performance metrics every week, not only when something goes wrong, because most suspensions are preceded by warnings that nobody read. Seller information has to stay current and reachable too: contact details, bank accounts, tax information and business documents accurate, and notices routed to a shared inbox that more than one person monitors. Under the new law, a missed email can become a suspension.

An escalation plan belongs in the same drawer. The owner should know who drafts an appeal, which documents it needs (invoices, authorization letters, safety certificates) and where they are kept. A brand that can respond fully within a day recovers far faster than one that spends a week finding its paperwork.

Reducing the causes does the rest. Watch for products that draw repeated complaints about quality or authenticity, keep listings accurate, and avoid any review practice that could be read as manipulation. Strong account health is mostly ordinary operations done consistently.

The law’s scope matters for how the job is staffed. It applies to third-party sellers, not to brands selling wholesale to a retailer as a vendor. Many brands run both models, often a vendor account on Amazon and a seller account on Walmart or Target Plus, and the seller accounts are where the new verification risk sits. They are also often the accounts with the least attention, because they were opened later or by a different team. And because the INFORM Consumers Act covers online marketplaces broadly, brands selling on Walmart, Target Plus and elsewhere should expect similar verification requests and similar consequences for missing them.

So the question for the leadership team before June 27 is short: for every marketplace account we sell through, who reads the notices, and who would they call? Answering it account by account, and then running that account health work week to week, is how we protect brands’ marketplace accounts across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0399.title: Walmart first-party vendor: the margin you keep after compliance
A0399.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes in a warehouse beside an antique brass balance scale holding coins and weights.
A0399.ttag: Walmart first-party vendor: the margin you keep after compliance | Kwontified
A0399.desc: As a Walmart first-party vendor, the wholesale price is only the start. Fines and deductions decide the margin you keep. How to model it before you sign.
A0399.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 16, 2023.
A0399.body:
On the term sheet, a first-party Walmart deal has one margin. In the bank account a year later, it has another. The wholesale price sets the first number; everything Walmart takes back after the sale sets the second, and a brand that ships late or short can watch several points of margin disappear without a single price negotiation.

The difference is mostly compliance. Walmart has required suppliers to ship on time and in full 98% of the time since September 2020. Shortfalls carry a fine of 3% of the cost of goods. That fine sits alongside allowances and other deductions that all grow with volume.

So the margin a Walmart first-party vendor keeps depends as much on its operations as on its price. Brands should model the net margin after allowances, fines and deductions, and prove their supply chain can meet Walmart’s standards, before they accept an offer.

How a Walmart first-party vendor relationship works

A brand can sell on Walmart in two main ways. As a marketplace seller, it lists its own products, sets its own prices and ships to customers itself or through Walmart’s fulfillment service. As a first-party vendor, sometimes called a supplier, it sells its products wholesale to Walmart, which owns the inventory, sets the retail price and sells the products online, in stores or both.

The appeal of first-party is scale. Walmart’s buying power can put products into thousands of stores and onto Walmart.com without the brand handling each sale. The cost is control: the brand no longer decides the price shoppers see, and it must meet Walmart’s operating rules.

The best known of those rules is On-Time In-Full. Walmart told suppliers that from September 15, 2020, shipments must be on time and in full 98% of the time, with a fine of 3% of the cost of goods for those that miss, Talk Business reported. Suppliers were meeting a 70% completion rate on average when the rule was announced, Talk Business noted, so the standard was a large step up.

“Cost of goods” here means Walmart’s cost, which is the vendor’s wholesale price. The fine therefore scales with the vendor’s revenue rather than its own production cost, and a 3% charge on a thin-margin product takes a large share of the profit on that order.

Freight terms feed the same calculation. Talk Business noted that suppliers could switch from prepaid freight, where they arrange transport themselves, to collect freight, where Walmart arranges it, in exchange for a reduced price. Collect shifts some delivery risk to Walmart but lowers the wholesale price, so it belongs in the margin model too.

Why compliance decides the margin

A first-party vendor’s revenue is its wholesale price. Its margin is that price minus everything taken back afterward: promotional allowances, compliance fines and other deductions for things like labeling errors or damaged goods. Each of those scales with volume. A brand that ships cleanly keeps most of its wholesale margin; a brand that misses shipping standards loses a slice on every order that falls short, and the slices add up as volume grows.

Take a kitchen brand selling $2 million a year to Walmart at wholesale prices, with a 30% gross margin. If a quarter of its shipments miss On-Time In-Full, the waterfall looks like this:

LineAmount
Gross margin at the wholesale price (30%)$600,000
Promotional allowances (4% of sales)minus $80,000
On-Time In-Full fines (3% on the quarter of shipments that miss)minus $15,000
Labeling and other deductionsminus $25,000
Margin kept$480,000, or 24% of sales

Fix the shipping problems and the $15,000 comes back. Cut the labeling errors and most of the $25,000 does too. The wholesale price never changed; the operations did.

Model the net margin, then prove the supply chain

Before accepting a first-party offer, build the waterfall for your own products: wholesale price, minus cost of goods, minus expected allowances, minus a realistic estimate of fines and deductions in the first year. New vendors usually miss standards more often while they learn Walmart’s requirements, so the first-year estimate deserves a conservative hand.

Then test the supply chain against the standard. Can the brand reliably ship the exact quantities ordered, on the dates required, with correct labels and paperwork? If the answer depends on a single warehouse, a single carrier or one experienced person, the risk is high. A short trial with a limited set of items and stores, where Walmart offers one, finds the weak points more cheaply than a full launch.

The marketplace option belongs in the same comparison. Selling as a marketplace seller keeps pricing control and avoids most first-party fines, but the brand has to manage advertising, fulfillment and customer service itself. For many brands the right answer is a combination: first-party for stores and core products, marketplace for the long tail or for testing new items.

Deductions need a review process from the first purchase order. Every fine and deduction should be checked against shipping records, because some are disputable, and brands that review and dispute invalid charges recover money that brands without a process simply lose. The data that comes with first-party helps here as well: vendors see Walmart’s view of their sales, inventory and forecasts, and brands that use it to anticipate orders rather than react to them ship more reliably and are fined less.

The practical test before signing is one line on a spreadsheet: if a quarter of your shipments missed the standard in year one, what margin would you keep, and would you still take the deal? Building that waterfall, and then running the account so it holds, is how we help brands weigh and manage Walmart first-party and marketplace selling.

A0400.crumb: Amazon Posts in 2023: the free brand feed…
A0400.title: Amazon Posts in 2023: the free brand feed worth running
A0400.alt: A cork mood board of ceramics and textile photos and swatches on a desk with a coffee mug and notebook.
A0400.ttag: Amazon Posts in 2023: the free brand feed worth running | Kwontified
A0400.desc: Amazon Posts is free, sits on product pages and now appears in the Inspire feed. Why it outlasted Amazon’s social experiments, and how a brand should run it.
A0400.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 18, 2023.
A0400.body:
Scroll to the bottom of a best-selling product page in the Amazon app and you may find a strip of lifestyle photos: a skillet on a stovetop, a jacket on a trail, each linking to a product. Some come from the brand whose page it is. Some come from its competitors. That strip is Amazon Posts, and unless someone at the brand is posting, the brand is not the one deciding what goes in it.

Posts has outlasted Amazon’s earlier social experiments because it lives where shopping already happens. It appears on product pages, and since December 2022 it can also appear in the new Inspire feed, without asking shoppers to behave like social media users. Brands should run it as a steady, low-cost organic channel that keeps their products visible on their own pages and in category feeds, while accepting that competitors’ Posts can show up beside theirs.

Where Amazon Posts stands in 2023

Posts lets brands publish image-led content, much like a social feed, that links directly to their products. In December 2022, Amazon said Posts, a cost-free, image-led mobile shopping experience, may now appear in Inspire, according to Amazon Ads. Posts remains in beta and is available to vendors and sellers enrolled in Brand Registry in the U.S. that have an active Store.

Inspire itself launched that month as a short-form video and photo feed in the Amazon app, where shoppers choose interests and browse shoppable content from influencers, brands and other customers, TechCrunch reported.

Why Posts lasted where Spark did not

Amazon has tried social features before. In 2017 it launched Spark, a photo-based feed on which Prime members could post and comment, and it wound Spark down in 2019, Modern Retail recalled. Posts launched in late 2019, the same report noted, and its slots on product pages were already becoming more coveted.

The difference is where each one lived. Spark asked shoppers to visit a separate feed and act like social media users, and few did. Posts appears on product pages, which shoppers visit anyway, and links straight to products. It borrows the look of social media without asking for social behavior.

A shopper meets a Post while doing what she came to do, looking at a product, and needs no new habit to see it. Inspire extends the same idea for shoppers who do want to browse, with a feed that is shoppable by design.

For brands, the result is a free content placement on some of the most valuable pages in online retail, open to any brand willing to supply images regularly. The catch is that the placement is shared. Posts can appear on related product pages, including competitors’, and competitors’ Posts can appear on yours. A brand that does not post leaves that strip, on its own pages, to others.

Take a cookware brand that has never used Posts. A competitor posts steadily, and its images start appearing in the strip at the bottom of the brand’s best-selling product page, so shoppers who scroll down see a rival’s skillet beside the brand’s own. Once the brand begins posting weekly, its own images fill more of that space. Nothing about its listings changed, but the page became more its own.

Running Posts as a weekly habit

Consistency matters more than volume. Posts that keep appearing keep the brand present on its pages and in feeds, and a modest, regular schedule, such as two or three Posts a week, usually works better than a burst of content followed by silence.

The content rarely needs to be new. Lifestyle images from social channels, product shots from campaigns and seasonal imagery can all become Posts with short captions. The real cost is the time to select and upload, which keeps the channel cheap.

Placement deserves more thought than it usually gets. Tag Posts to the product pages where competitors are most active and where the brand most needs to be seen, and refresh those pages with seasonal Posts ahead of key events so they look current.

Some Posts will be rejected at first. Amazon reviews each Post against its content guidelines before it goes live, and images with heavy text, unsupported claims or poor quality are often turned back. Brands that learn the guidelines early waste less time and keep their schedule steady.

Posts also double as a cheap testing ground for advertising creative. An image that draws strong engagement as a Post is a good candidate for Sponsored Brands or display ads, where every impression costs money, so paid budgets can go behind images already shown to attract shoppers.

Followers are a smaller benefit, but a real one. Shoppers can follow a brand’s feed, and followers may see its Posts more often. The numbers are usually modest; they are also shoppers who chose to hear from the brand, which makes them worth growing.

Engagement should be read modestly. Amazon reports impressions, clicks and followers for Posts, which show what content draws attention, but Posts does not replace advertising and its sales impact is hard to isolate. Inspire does raise the value of good visual content: a brand whose Posts are strong lifestyle images may now reach shoppers browsing by interest, before they search for anything, which is a rare opening for organic discovery on Amazon.

The question worth asking inside the brand is simple: who decides what shoppers see at the bottom of our own best-selling page? Making that someone’s weekly job, alongside listings, advertising and the rest of the channel, is part of how we run Amazon for the brands we manage.

A0401.title: AI shopping assistants: what retail leaders must own now
A0401.alt: A small white robotic arm on a wooden desk beside a leather journal and fountain pen in a navy-walled study.
A0401.ttag: AI shopping assistants: what retail leaders must own now | Kwontified
A0401.desc: Amazon is building conversational search and ChatGPT now shops through plugins. When an assistant answers, product data does the selling. What leaders must own.
A0401.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 23, 2023.
A0401.body:
A shopper types a request into a chat window: a quiet blender that can crush ice and fits under a kitchen cabinet. Two blenders of similar quality are on offer. The first has a plain page that states its noise level, height and ice-crushing ability in words. The second has a beautiful page, with its height shown only in an image and its noise level nowhere. An AI assistant answering that request will recommend the first, because it is the only one whose fit it can confirm.

That is the shift AI shopping assistants bring. When an assistant answers a shopping question, it selects and explains products from the information it can read, so a brand’s product data, reviews and stated attributes do the persuading that page design and placement used to do. Amazon is hiring to build conversational search, and ChatGPT has been shopping through plugins since March. Retail leaders should treat structured product information as a strategic asset with an executive owner, not a catalog chore handed to whoever has time.

Where AI shopping assistants stand in May 2023

The change is starting at both ends. On March 23, OpenAI launched plugins for ChatGPT, with early partners including Instacart, Klarna and Shopify, MediaPost reported. Shoppers can now ask ChatGPT for product suggestions and act on them through those services.

Amazon is moving too. Bloomberg reported that Amazon job listings describe “reimagining Amazon Search with an interactive conversational experience,” designed to help customers find answers to product questions, compare products and receive personalized suggestions, VentureBeat reported. An Amazon spokesperson said the company is significantly investing in generative AI across all of its businesses, Business Today reported.

None of this is mainstream shopping behavior yet. Most shoppers still search and browse the way they did a year ago. What has shipped is a set of plugins; Amazon’s plans are visible so far only in its job listings. The largest store and the most popular AI assistant are both building toward it.

How an assistant decides which products to recommend

A conversational assistant answers a question by finding products whose information matches it and summarizing why they fit. For the blender request, it looks for products whose stated attributes cover noise, ice crushing and height. Products with complete, specific and consistent information are more likely to be chosen and more likely to be described well. Products whose details are thin, buried in images or contradictory across sources are harder to match, whatever their page looks like.

To that process, the two blenders look like this:

What the assistant needsFirst blenderSecond blender
Noise levelStated as an attribute; reviews mention quiet operationNot stated anywhere
HeightStated as an attributeShown only in an image
What the assistant can sayRecommends it, with specificsCannot confirm it meets either requirement

Reviews matter in a new way here. An assistant can read hundreds of reviews and summarize what owners say about noise or durability. A product whose reviews confirm its claims gets described with confidence. One whose reviews contradict them gets described with caveats, or skipped.

Give product information an executive owner

Structured product information means attributes stored as labeled fields, such as a decibel rating or a height, rather than buried in sentences or pictures. It is the part of a listing a machine can read without guessing.

At many brands, catalog data sits several levels down, maintained by whoever has time and updated when something breaks. That was tolerable when a well-designed page and good advertising could carry a product. It is less tolerable when an assistant reads the data directly and decides.

The checks a leader should ask for are concrete. Key attributes such as size, materials, compatibility and performance should be stated as text and structured fields, not only in images. Those attributes should match across the brand’s own site, Amazon, Walmart and other retailers. And reviews should confirm the product’s claims rather than reveal gaps the brand ought to fix in the product or the description.

The work those checks reveal is rarely glamorous: filling in fields, standardizing names, correcting contradictions, responding to recurring review themes. It pays off twice. Better data already helps traditional search and conversion, and it positions the brand for assistants as they arrive.

Each retailer adds its own complication. Amazon, Walmart and Target define their own attribute fields, and the same product often ends up described slightly differently in each. Those small differences matter more when an assistant compares sources and finds them in conflict. A single master record of product information, from which each channel’s listing is built, is the most reliable fix.

Assistants also get things wrong. They may misread an attribute, merge two products or repeat an outdated claim. Testing the assistants available today with the questions customers actually ask shows how a brand’s products are described, and where the description is wrong the cause is usually in the source data. Fixing it there corrects every channel that reads it.

The budget question follows from the mechanism. Assistants compress the path from question to purchase, and a brand that relied on being the most visible page may find that being the most accurately described product matters more. That changes how money should be split between advertising, content and product data. None of it requires predicting exactly how fast assistants will spread, because the groundwork is useful either way, and for a catalog of any size it takes months to do well.

A simple test before the next catalog update: ask an assistant the three questions your customers ask most, and see whether your products come back with the right details. Building the product data that passes that test is the work of our AI Agentic Commerce practice.

A0403.crumb: Leaving Amazon: why a brand exit can…
A0403.title: Leaving Amazon: why a brand exit can invite more counterfeits
A0403.alt: A wooden shelf of plain cardboard boxes with an empty gap in the middle, in a blue-walled storeroom.
A0403.ttag: Leaving Amazon: why a brand exit can invite more counterfeits | Kwontified
A0403.desc: Brands that stop selling on Amazon do not leave it. Their products stay, sold by others, and the brand loses its best tools against fakes. What to do instead.
A0403.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 25, 2023.
A0403.body:
In November 2019, Nike said it would stop selling directly to Amazon, ending a two-year pilot, the Associated Press reported. The AP added a detail that mattered more than the headline: shoppers might not notice a difference, because Nike goods would still be available on Amazon from independent sellers. The brand had left. Its products had not.

Nike’s experience shows the pattern. Brands that stop selling on Amazon to escape counterfeits and unauthorized sellers usually find their products still there, sold by others, while they have given up the official presence, the data and the protection tools that work best for brands that participate. An exit tends to leave the counterfeit problem in place with less ability to fight it, so any brand weighing one should first compare it with a managed, tightly controlled presence.

Leaving Amazon: what happened when brands did it

Nike was not the first. Birkenstock had stopped selling directly to Amazon in 2017, unhappy with counterfeits and with how other sellers priced its shoes, the AP noted, and its goods were still available there from third-party sellers.

The difficulty Nike faced was persistent. Third-party sellers whose listings were removed often reappeared under different names, Bloomberg reported at the time, and a consultant quoted in that report made the central point: when a brand walks away, its products do not.

Birkenstock’s own experience bore that out. Its chief executive told The Drum that, by the company’s own data, the way its brand was curated and presented on Amazon declined after it disengaged, The Drum reported.

Who holds the page once the brand is gone

Demand for a known brand on Amazon does not disappear when the brand stops supplying it. Shoppers keep searching, and other sellers keep serving them, with stock obtained through wholesalers, retailers, liquidators or, sometimes, counterfeiters. The question worth asking is who captures that demand once the brand steps back. The resellers take the sales, and the brand is left with the reviews and the reputation that come with them.

When the brand is present, it holds the strongest position on its own product pages. It can register its brand, control listing content, use protection tools and supply genuine stock with full information. When it leaves, those pages remain, but the people managing them are resellers, and the brand’s ability to correct them shrinks. An official seller with a strong offer makes it harder for counterfeits to win sales. Without one, a page may be served by several resellers of varying reliability, and a counterfeit can blend in more easily.

Meanwhile, the tools available to brands that stay have improved. Amazon said in its 2022 Brand Protection Report that valid notices of infringement filed by brands in Brand Registry fell by more than 35% in 2022 as its automated protections improved, according to Amazon. In April it launched an exchange for retailers to share information about confirmed counterfeiters, Retail TouchPoints reported. Those tools work best for brands that are registered, present and engaged.

Take an outdoor apparel brand that leaves Amazon over unauthorized sellers. A year later its jackets are offered by a dozen resellers, some at deep discounts, and reviews mention wrong sizing and suspect quality. The brand has no official listing to anchor the page, sees none of the sales data and has stopped monitoring. The problem it left to escape has grown, and the shoppers who bought those jackets blame the brand.

What to settle before an exit

The first thing to untangle is which problem the brand actually has. Counterfeits, unauthorized resellers of genuine goods and price erosion are related but different, and each has its own fixes, from brand registration and enforcement to distribution agreements and pricing policy. An exit addresses none of them directly.

The choice is also wider than in or out. A brand can sell on Amazon with a narrow, controlled range, strict distribution and active monitoring rather than full participation or none, and for many brands that middle path solves more of the problem than leaving would. Unauthorized sellers of genuine goods get their stock from somewhere, so tracing and closing those distribution leaks reduces the problem on every marketplace at once, whether or not the brand sells on Amazon itself.

There are good reasons a brand might still choose to leave: channel conflict with key retailers, a strategy built around direct sales, or economics that do not work. The decision should be made knowing the brand’s products will likely remain on Amazon either way, which turns the real choice into a question of who controls how they appear.

Timing deserves care. Some brands decide to leave in response to a bad quarter of reseller activity and then find the problem was seasonal or tied to one distributor. Watching the pattern for several months, and tracing where the unauthorized stock came from, often reveals a narrower fix than an exit. Retailer relationships deserve their own check, too: a brand leaving partly to protect other retail partners should find out whether those partners see Amazon prices as the problem, or a handful of resellers that enforcement could remove.

A brand that does leave should not stop watching. Keeping its brand registration, monitoring listings and acting against counterfeits all remain possible without selling directly, and they limit the damage.

For a leadership team weighing an exit, the useful question is not whether to be on Amazon, since the products will be there regardless, but who should be in charge of how they look. Answering that, and then running a controlled presence or protecting the listings from outside, is how we help brands decide how to participate on Amazon.

A0404.crumb: The Target guest in 2023: the trip holds…
A0404.title: The Target guest in 2023: the trip holds, the extras shrink
A0404.alt: A red shopping cart with paper bags, bread and jars in a bulk-food store aisle of wooden shelves.
A0404.ttag: The Target guest in 2023: the trip holds, the extras shrink | Kwontified
A0404.desc: Target traffic rose in early 2023 while digital sales fell. Guests kept the needs trip and dropped the extras, so brands should sell onto that trip.
A0404.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 30, 2023.
A0404.body:
Target’s traffic went up in the first quarter of 2023 and its digital sales went down. Those two numbers look as if they came from different companies. They describe one guest behaving sensibly: still making the trip for shampoo, snacks and detergent, and leaving the candle and the throw pillow on the shelf.

The pattern has a plain cause. Visits anchored by frequency purchases such as beauty, food and household essentials survive a tight budget, because the need does not go away. Discretionary items ride along on those visits, so they are the first thing a guest cuts. For brands selling through Target, the practical answer is to get onto the frequency trip, through placement, bundles, Target Circle offers and Roundel targeting, rather than count on a separate visit for wants.

What Target’s first quarter showed about the Target guest

The headline figures for the quarter, according to Target:

Q1 2023 measureChange
Comparable salesFlat
Comparable store salesUp 0.7%
Comparable digital salesDown 3.4%
TrafficUp 0.9%

Strength in Beauty, Food & Beverage and Household Essentials offset continued softness in discretionary categories, Target said. That softness was deep. Categories including apparel and home posted sales declines ranging from mid single digits to low double digits, CNBC reported. Target cut inventory 16%, including a reduction of more than 25% in discretionary categories, and it expects second-quarter comparable sales to show a low-single-digit decline.

Digital split in two. Same-day services grew by mid-single digits, led by high-single-digit growth in Drive Up, according to Target’s earnings release as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. CEO Brian Cornell explained the weakness in the same terms: fewer packages were shipped to homes, and those deliveries skew toward discretionary items, while same-day pickup orders lean toward everyday needs, CNBC reported. Guests were still ordering, but mostly for pickup on the needs trip.

Why the trip holds while the extras shrink

Many Target trips are built around a need. The guest comes in for diapers and detergent and picks up a new top on the way to the register. When money is tight, the diapers still have to be bought, so the visit still happens. The top was optional, and it is what goes.

Every line in the quarter follows from that. Traffic rose because the needs trip held. Frequency categories grew because they are the reason for the trip. Discretionary categories fell because they depend on the extra spending guests were trimming. And home delivery fell more than same-day pickup, because shoppers ordering for delivery were more likely to be buying wants.

Take a home décor brand sold through Target whose products sell when guests browse the home aisles on a relaxed trip. In early 2023, its sales fall 12%. A storage-bin brand shelved next to the household essentials, and promoted alongside cleaning supplies, falls only 3%. Both are discretionary purchases. The second brand sits on the trip guests are still making; the first depends on browsing they have cut back.

Getting onto the frequency trip

What that means in practice depends on what a brand sells. For frequency brands, the job is to protect the trip. Keep stock reliable, especially for same-day pickup, which held up better than home delivery. Price clearly, because value-conscious guests compare. Use Target Circle offers to reward the visits that are already happening.

For discretionary brands, the job is to attach to the trip. That can mean products positioned near related essentials, bundles that pair a want with a need, smaller price points that fit an add-on budget, or seasonal items tied to the moments guests are already shopping for.

Advertising follows the same logic. Roundel can reach guests based on what they buy, so a discretionary brand can target shoppers of related frequency categories rather than only guests browsing its own category. A storage brand reaching shoppers who just bought cleaning supplies is reaching guests on the right trip.

On Target Plus, the marketplace, the same thinking shapes assortment. Items that complement Target’s own frequency categories tend to fit the guest better than items that compete with them, and Target is selective about what it lets onto the marketplace.

Target Circle puts a large audience on that trip within reach. On its fourth-quarter earnings call, Target said Circle had doubled from the 50 million members it reached soon after its 2019 launch, according to the transcript. Offers through Circle reach guests who already shop Target regularly, which is the audience whose trips are holding.

Two numbers that show which trip a brand is on

Before moving budget or shelf space, find out where your Target sales happen. Look at the share that comes through same-day pickup versus home delivery, then at how basket attachment in your category is changing, meaning how often your product lands in a basket that also holds frequency items. Read together, those two numbers show whether a brand rides the trip or depends on the browsing that is shrinking.

Inventory should be planned for a cautious guest. With Target itself carrying far less discretionary inventory, brands in those categories should expect smaller orders and plan production to avoid excess.

None of this means discretionary demand has disappeared, or that it will stay this weak. Guests are still adding wants, just fewer of them, and when budgets ease the brands still visible on the trip will be first in line. A workable test for any product: if it only sells when a guest has time to browse, it needs a route onto the visit the guest makes anyway. Building that route through placement, bundles and Roundel audiences is how we run Target Plus and Roundel for brands.

A0405.crumb: Prime Day 2023 planning: who decides, and…
A0405.title: Prime Day 2023 planning: who decides, and when it is decided
A0405.alt: A stack of twine-tied paper parcels, a leather folio and a vase of peonies on a farmhouse table by sunny windows.
A0405.ttag: Prime Day 2023 planning: who decides, and when it is decided | Kwontified
A0405.desc: The Prime Day 2023 deal deadline passed in April, before Amazon named the dates. Why the event runs the planning calendar and who should own each call.
A0405.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 1, 2023.
A0405.body:
Ask a brand team when Prime Day 2023 will happen and the honest answer is that nobody outside Amazon knows yet. Ask when the Prime Day deals had to be created, and the answer is precise: April 28, 2023. The event has a firm deadline and no firm date.

That gap explains how the event really works. Prime Day runs the planning calendar weeks before anyone knows its dates, so the decisions that matter most, on deal depth, inventory and advertising budget, are made early and often by different teams. Brands get better results when one person owns the event plan, when decisions follow Amazon’s deadlines rather than the event date, and when the remaining choices are made now.

Prime Day 2023 planning started before the dates existed

Amazon told sellers it was time to prepare for Prime Day 2023, without announcing dates, and said sellers must create their Prime Day deals by April 28, 2023, EcommerceBytes reported. The event was expected in July, as in most recent years.

The 2022 event set a high bar. Prime Day ran on July 12 and 13, 2022, and Prime members bought more than 300 million items worldwide, saving more than $1.7 billion, according to Amazon’s figures as reported by EcommerceBytes. Amazon also held a second event, the Prime Early Access Sale, on October 11 and 12, 2022.

So as of June 1, the deal deadline has passed, the event is probably about six weeks away, and its exact dates are still unannounced. The most important choices were made in spring, when the event still felt distant.

Three teams, three calendars, one event

Prime Day began as a single day of deals and grew into one of the largest shopping events of the year. As it grew, Amazon built a process around it: deal submissions, eligibility checks and inventory requirements, each with its own deadline. Those deadlines come well before the event. Brands that wait for the date announcement to start planning find that several decisions have already been made for them, by default.

The harder problem sits inside the brand. Deal depth is a pricing and margin question, often owned by finance or the commercial team. Inventory is an operations question. Advertising budget belongs to marketing. Each team works to its own calendar, with its own targets, and none of them sees the whole event.

Without one owner, the pieces drift apart: a deal gets approved without enough stock behind it, stock arrives without the advertising to move it, and a budget is set without knowing which products have deals.

Take a kitchenware brand whose commercial team submits deals on six products by the April deadline. Its operations team, planning from its 2022 sales, sends normal stock. Its marketing team sets a Prime Day advertising budget in late June, spread evenly across the range.

On the day, two deal products sell out by midday while advertising keeps spending on products with no deal. Each team did its job well by its own measure. Nobody held the plan, and nobody noticed until the event was underway.

One owner, Amazon’s clock, and the choices still open

The fix starts with a name. One person should own the event: not to make every decision, but to make sure the decisions connect, from which products have deals to whether stock supports them and where advertising goes. In smaller brands, this is often a founder or a channel lead with enough authority to settle disagreements quickly.

That owner plans backward from Amazon’s deadlines, not forward from the event date, because the deadlines arrive first. Deal submissions, inventory arrival and advertising setup each have their own timing. A single calendar that lists them, with an owner beside each, prevents the surprises.

With deals submitted, the open questions for most brands are inventory and advertising. Stock for deal products needs to arrive in time to be available for the event, with a buffer for the days before and after. Advertising plans should concentrate on deal products and the searches that lead to them, with budgets that can rise on the event days.

The days around the event matter as well. Shoppers often search and compare in the week before Prime Day, and some purchases spill into the days after. Advertising that starts a few days early and continues briefly afterward tends to capture more of that demand than a budget confined to the two event days.

The planning year does not end in July either. Amazon added a second Prime event in October 2022, and brands should plan as if a fall event is possible again; deal products, stock positions and advertising lessons from July will feed directly into it. And because the dates may be announced late, any plan that depends on knowing the exact days should have a version for each likely week in July, so the brand can move quickly once Amazon confirms.

Questions for the team before Amazon names the dates

  • Who owns the Prime Day 2023 plan from deal to ad, and do they work from one calendar of deal, inventory and advertising deadlines?
  • Will stock for every deal product arrive in time, with a buffer for the days before and after the event?
  • Is the advertising plan built around deal products, with budgets ready to rise on the event days?
  • Is a review booked within two weeks of the event, comparing deal sales with stock levels, advertising spend with sales by product, and the days before and after with the event itself?

That review is where the next plan starts, and most brands skip it. Putting deals, stock and advertising under one plan, with one owner from April to the post-event review, is how we run Prime Day for brands.

A0407.title: Temu gamification: what retail should copy, and what to avoid
A0407.alt: A vintage wooden prize wheel beside stacked orange paper parcels tied with twine against a peeling yellow wall.
A0407.ttag: Temu gamification: what retail should copy, and what to avoid | Kwontified
A0407.desc: Temu’s spin wheels and games give shoppers a reason to open the app every day. Why that works, and which parts brands and retailers should copy or avoid.
A0407.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 6, 2023.
A0407.body:
Why would a shopping app hand out coupons for spinning a wheel? The spin sells nothing on its own. What it buys is a visit from a shopper who had no reason to open the app that day, and on a marketplace built on cheap products and countdown offers, a visit is worth paying for.

That is the logic of Temu gamification. Spin wheels, timed coupons, games and referral rewards give shoppers a reason to open the app when they have no shopping need, and each visit is another chance to sell. Brands and retailers should take the lesson and leave the mechanics: create genuine reasons to return, such as reorder reminders, loyalty rewards and useful content, and stay away from chance-based games, which raise trust and regulatory risks a brand cannot afford.

How Temu gamification works

Temu has built play into the shopping experience. New and existing users are regularly prompted into flash sales and chance-based games, such as spins that award free items and coupons, CBC reported. One game it described guides new customers through a series of draws that lead to store credit and coupons, which can only be claimed by sharing and promoting the app a set number of times.

Spin wheels and games that reward shoppers with discounts and store credit are a defining feature, 1News reported. An expert it interviewed called the approach the gamification of online shopping, and observed that landing on a big number makes a shopper feel like a winner and want to spin again.

Heavy advertising runs alongside the games. Temu’s Super Bowl campaign in February lifted downloads by 45% on the day it aired, Modern Retail reported, citing Sensor Tower data. Advertising brings a shopper in once. Games and rewards are what keep those new users coming back, day after day.

Unpredictable rewards turn visits into habits

Most shopping apps get opened when the shopper needs something. That caps how often she visits, and every visit depends on a need arising, which the app cannot control.

An app that offers an unpredictable reward for opening it lifts the cap. A daily spin, a game that needs tending or a coupon about to expire gives the shopper a reason to visit with no need at all, and repeated often enough, that becomes a habit. A newspaper’s daily crossword works the same way: it sells no news, but it puts the paper in the reader’s hands every morning.

Each visit then does commercial work. The shopper sees cheap products, limited-time offers and a countdown on the coupon she just won, and some of those visits turn into purchases that would never have happened through need alone. The referral games add a second effect: shoppers recruit other shoppers, and the reward is paid in coupons rather than advertising.

One shopper shows the arithmetic. Take a shopper who buys household items online about twice a month. On a conventional app, she visits about twice a month. On an app with a daily reward, she opens it most days to claim it. If even one visit in ten leads to an impulse purchase, her purchases roughly double, without any change in what she needs.

What brands should copy: real reasons to come back

The lasting lesson from Temu is that visits drive sales, and that brands should give customers genuine reasons to come back between needs.

Brands have plenty of legitimate tools for that. Reorder reminders and subscriptions bring customers back when a product runs out. Loyalty rewards, such as points or member-only offers, give regular customers a reason to check in. Useful content, from how-to guides to seasonal ideas, creates visits around interest rather than chance. On marketplaces, the equivalents are Subscribe and Save, brand follows, Posts and well-timed promotions.

Reminders of any kind need limits. Email, text and app notifications are the legitimate cousins of Temu’s prompts, and they work best when they are timed to a real reason, such as a product running low or a seasonal need. Brands that message too often train customers to ignore them, or to unsubscribe, which removes the channel entirely.

What brands should avoid: chance, and Temu’s price game

The chance-based parts carry costs that are easy to underestimate when the engagement numbers look good. Mechanics that feel like gambling, rewards that turn out smaller than advertised, and rewards that require sharing an app with friends can erode trust quickly. They also draw scrutiny from consumer protection regulators, who look closely at whether advertised rewards are real and whether conditions are clear. A brand built on trust has more to lose from that than a discount marketplace does.

The competitive math points the same way. Temu’s model depends on extremely low prices, heavy advertising and a large catalog. A brand copying its games without its prices gets the friction of gamification without the payoff, and does better competing where Temu is weak: quality, reliability, service and products shoppers trust.

Price comparisons deserve attention for the same reason. Temu’s coupons make its already low prices feel lower still, and shoppers carry that impression to other marketplaces. Brands competing in categories where Temu is active should make their value clear on the page, through quality, materials, warranties and reviews, rather than trying to match a price that includes a game.

Judge it by repeat purchase, not app opens

App opens are exactly what a game is built to raise, which makes them the wrong number for judging one. If a brand adds reasons to return, the measure is repeat purchase and customer lifetime value. Visits only matter if they turn into sales customers are glad they made.

A practical test before adding any engagement feature: name the purchase it should bring back, and track that purchase rather than the visit. Building those reasons to return across Amazon, Walmart, Target and a brand’s own channels is how we grow repeat purchase for brands.

A0408.title: Zalando personalization: how brands get matched to shoppers
A0408.alt: A folded camel wool coat with an orange knit scarf draped over it on a neatly made linen bed.
A0408.ttag: Zalando personalization: how brands get matched to shoppers | Kwontified
A0408.desc: Zalando matches shoppers to products by size, followed brands and now a ChatGPT assistant. What that means for how brands present products on Zalando.
A0408.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 8, 2023.
A0408.body:
Zalando wants a shopper to be able to open its app and type something like “an outfit for a summer wedding” instead of tapping through category filters. The assistant answering her will not browse a rack. It will read product data, and it will choose among the brands whose pages describe a summer wedding outfit well enough to be found.

That is where Zalando personalization is heading. Zalando already matches shoppers to products using what it knows about each customer: size, the brands they follow and their style. Its ChatGPT-powered assistant carries that matching into conversation. Brands on Zalando are increasingly found through the quality of their product data rather than through placement alone, which makes complete attributes, accurate size and fit information and a reason to be followed the core of selling there.

Zalando personalization moves into conversation

On April 19, Zalando said it would launch a first beta version of a fashion assistant powered by ChatGPT across its app and website, according to Zalando. Customers will be able to search Zalando’s assortment using their own words or fashion terms and refine results through ongoing conversation. Zalando described itself as serving about 50 million active customers in 25 markets.

The beta was to reach selected customers in Austria, Germany, Ireland and the United Kingdom by spring, in English and German, PYMNTS reported. Zalando also said it may later combine the assistant with customers’ preferences, such as the brands they follow and products available in their size, to deliver a more personalized selection, Fashion Network reported.

The fitting room that fashion e-commerce never had

Fashion is hard to sell online for a simple reason: shoppers cannot try things on. They worry about size, fit and whether an item will look as it does in the photograph, and that uncertainty drives both hesitation before buying and returns afterward.

Zalando’s answer has been to learn as much as it can about each customer and use it to narrow the choice. A shopper who has bought a certain size from a brand, followed certain labels and returned certain styles tells Zalando a great deal about what she is likely to keep. Showing her products that fit that profile makes buying easier and returning less likely. The personalization, in other words, is Zalando’s substitute for the fitting room.

The assistant adds a new layer to that substitute. Instead of filtering by category and size, a shopper can describe what she wants, from a wedding outfit to a jacket for a rainy city break. The system then has to find products that match a description, not just a filter.

That shifts the work onto the brand’s side of the page. In a filtered catalog, a product needs the right category and size options. In a personalized, conversational one, it needs rich, accurate information that the system can match to a shopper’s words and profile: materials, fit, occasion, style and how sizes run.

Take a knitwear brand on Zalando whose product pages list colors and sizes but describe fit only as “regular” and leave occasion and material details thin. A competitor describes each piece fully, including how sizes run compared with standard measurements. When a shopper asks for a warm, relaxed sweater for weekends, the competitor’s products are easier for the system to match, and its size guidance gives the shopper confidence. The first brand’s sweaters may be just as good. They are harder to find.

What a brand controls on its side of the match

Product data is the first thing to fix. Every attribute Zalando supports, from material and fit to occasion and care, gives its personalization and its assistant something to match, and descriptions should use the words shoppers use rather than internal product codes.

Size and fit information is the part of the page that does the fitting room’s job. Clear guidance on how each item runs, consistent sizing across products and measurements where possible reduce returns and help Zalando recommend the right size. A brand known for reliable sizing is easier to recommend.

Photographs do part of that work too. Those that show fit on a model, with the model’s height and the size worn, help shoppers judge how an item will look on them, and detail shots of fabric and construction answer questions a description cannot. The more a product page answers, the fewer reasons a shopper has to hesitate or send the item back.

Returns are where all of this shows up in the numbers. In fashion, a product that is often returned for poor fit costs the brand twice: once in the lost sale and again in handling. Brands that study their return reasons on Zalando and adjust size guidance or descriptions accordingly usually see the benefit quickly, and their products become easier for Zalando to recommend with confidence.

Then there is the follow. Followed brands are a signal Zalando already uses and plans to use more. Regular new arrivals, distinctive collections and consistent quality all give customers a reason to follow, which in turn brings the brand into more personalized selections.

Who owns the product page

The wider question is who controls that data. Zalando has been encouraging brands to sell directly on its platform rather than only supply it as a wholesaler, and brands that sell directly control their own product data, which makes all of the above easier to carry out.

The assistant itself will change. It is a beta, and Zalando has said it will keep learning from how customers use it. Brands that keep their product information current will benefit as it develops, whatever form it takes. A useful question for the team: if a shopper described your best-selling piece in her own words, would Zalando’s data lead her to it? Answering that for every product in the range is how we run brands on Zalando.

A0409.crumb: Target Plus: how online sales can make…
A0409.title: Target Plus: how online sales can make the case for stores
A0409.alt: A red wrapped gift tied with twine on a rustic wooden table in a shop with shelves of ceramics and goods.
A0409.ttag: Target Plus: how online sales can make the case for stores | Kwontified
A0409.desc: Target Plus lets Target test products online without holding stock. For brands, sales there build the evidence a store buyer looks for. How to use it.
A0409.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 13, 2023.
A0409.body:
Four years after launch, Target Plus had about 650 sellers, and Target was still choosing every one of them by invitation. For a retailer of Target’s reach, keeping the marketplace that small looks like money left on the table. For a brand, the smallness is the useful part.

Target Plus lets Target extend its online assortment without buying or holding inventory, curated to complement what it already sells. That makes it a low-risk test in front of Target’s own guests. The sales, reviews and search demand a product earns there are the kind of evidence a Target buyer weighs when deciding what to carry, so brands on Target Plus should run it as a proof of demand. That means clean operations and clear reporting, rather than treating it as a standalone sales channel.

Target Plus stays small on purpose

Marketplace Pulse reported these seller counts:

Target PlusSellers
At launch, February 25, 201930
Four years laterAbout 650
Added in the previous twelve months190

Target continues to run it on an invitation-only basis, choosing which sellers join. That selectivity is long-standing. When Target Plus launched, Target chose product categories that complemented its own assortment and that customers had been searching for on Target.com, and it invited sellers specifically for their assortment and to protect its brand, the Star Tribune reported. CEO Brian Cornell said in 2020 that Target would continue to curate very carefully and complement its store and online assortment, Marketplace Pulse noted.

The logic holds from Target’s side, because curation protects its brand and keeps the marketplace complementary to its own range. It holds from the seller’s side too. With hundreds of sellers rather than many thousands, an invited brand faces far less marketplace competition on Target.com than it would on an open marketplace, and Marketplace Pulse described Target’s marketplace as the most coveted.

Stores remain Target’s center of gravity. In its first quarter of 2023, comparable store sales rose 0.7% while comparable digital sales fell 3.4%, according to Target.

What a Target buyer is weighing

A buyer deciding what to carry weighs a risk. Putting a product in stores commits shelf space, inventory and distribution, and if guests do not buy it, Target bears the cost. The buyer’s job is to find products guests want before making that commitment.

A marketplace listing on Target’s own site produces evidence at no inventory cost to Target. The seller holds the stock and ships the orders. Target watches how its own guests respond: whether they search for the product, buy it, return it and review it well. A product that sells steadily, earns strong reviews and draws repeat searches on Target Plus has, in effect, been tested on Target’s guests, and that lowers the buyer’s risk.

It does not guarantee a store listing. Store decisions depend on space, category plans and many other factors. What it does give a brand is a much stronger case than a pitch built on sales elsewhere.

Take a home fragrance brand invited to Target Plus. Over a year, its candles sell steadily, average more than four stars across hundreds of reviews and show up in searches on Target.com for its brand name. When the brand meets a Target buyer, it brings that record: sales trends, review themes and the searches that led to its products. Another brand with similar products but only Amazon data has a weaker story, because the buyer cannot see how Target’s own guests responded.

Running Target Plus as a proof of demand

Treat Target Plus as evidence-building, not only as revenue, and manage it that way from the first day.

The operating record is part of the evidence. Target holds Target Plus sellers to its standards for shipping, service and returns, and late shipments, cancellations or poor service weaken the case and can end the invitation. A buyer will reasonably ask whether a brand that struggles with online orders can handle store replenishment.

Reviews from Target’s guests are among the most persuasive evidence a brand can bring, and they have to be built steadily and honestly. Products that solve a clear need, ship reliably and arrive as described earn them.

Demand needs to be driven and measured with the same care. Roundel can bring Target’s guests to the brand’s Target Plus products and shows how they respond. Tracking sales, conversion and branded search over time turns that activity into a record a buyer can read.

Assortment should stay complementary to Target’s own range. Target invites sellers whose products fill gaps, and a brand that offers items Target’s own range lacks is more useful to Target, and more likely to grow there, than one that duplicates what is already on the shelf.

Pricing should stay consistent. Target’s guests compare prices, and a buyer will notice if a product sells for much less on other marketplaces. A brand whose Target Plus price matches its prices elsewhere looks like a dependable partner; one that undercuts itself on another channel raises questions about how it would protect Target’s margins in stores.

Timing matters as much as the record. Store decisions follow category planning cycles, which often run many months ahead of the shelf, and a brand that brings a clear, Target-specific record to the right buyer at the right time is better placed than one that pitches broadly.

A simple test for any brand on Target Plus: if a buyer asked how Target’s guests have responded to your product, you should be able to answer with a year of your own Target.com data, not a slide about Amazon. Building that record through clean operations and Roundel is how we run Target Plus for brands.

A0411.crumb: Apparel on Amazon in 2023: a bigger…
A0411.title: Apparel on Amazon in 2023: a bigger channel, a cautious shopper
A0411.alt: A clothing rack of neutral tagged shirts beside an open shipping box holding a folded grey sweater.
A0411.ttag: Apparel on Amazon in 2023: a bigger channel, a cautious shopper | Kwontified
A0411.desc: Amazon is now the largest U.S. apparel retailer, but clothing demand softened in 2023. What changed in the category and how apparel brands should respond.
A0411.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 15, 2023.
A0411.body:
A dress bought in a store has usually been through the fitting room before it reaches the register. On Amazon there is no fitting room. The size chart, the reviews and the photos have to do that job, and when they fail, the answer arrives later, as a return.

That fitting room problem sits at the center of apparel on Amazon, a category moving in two directions at once. Amazon has become the largest U.S. apparel retailer and is investing in tools such as virtual try-on to address fit. Meanwhile, shoppers cut back on discretionary clothing in 2023, as retailers including Target and Walmart reported declines in apparel and general merchandise. Apparel brands on Amazon should compete on fit confidence, imagery and returns rather than on volume growth, and plan inventory cautiously, while the channel matters more than ever.

How apparel on Amazon became so large

Amazon became the country’s largest apparel retailer in 2021, passing Walmart, and in May 2022 it opened its first physical apparel store, in the Los Angeles area, GeekWire reported.

It has also been working on the category’s oldest problem: shoppers cannot try clothes on, so they hesitate before buying and return more of what they buy. In June 2022, Amazon launched Virtual Try-On for Shoes, an augmented reality feature in its iOS app covering thousands of styles from brands such as New Balance, Adidas and Puma, TechCrunch reported. That followed virtual try-on for athletic shirts that April. Walmart had introduced its own AI-powered try-on feature, using technology from Zeekit, in March 2022, TechCrunch noted.

Taken together, both retailers have signaled to apparel brands that fit is the barrier they are working to remove.

The 2023 apparel shopper buys less, and more carefully

Then the shopper changed course. Inflation has pushed households to spend on needs before wants, and clothing is among the first wants to be cut. Food, household essentials and beauty have held up better, which leaves less of the budget for new clothes.

The major retailers’ spring results show it. At Target, apparel and home were among the categories posting sales declines of anywhere between mid single digits and low double digits in the first quarter, CNBC reported. At Walmart, U.S. general merchandise sales declined by mid single digits, its chief financial officer told investors, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

So apparel brands face an unusual combination. Amazon matters more to apparel than ever, and the company is building tools to make clothing easier to buy there, but the shopper is buying less clothing, and buying it more carefully.

That care shows up in behavior. A shopper buying fewer items wants each one to be right. She reads more reviews, looks harder at images and size guidance, and is less forgiving of a poor fit. Returns hurt more when margins are tight, for brands and for Amazon alike.

Take a women’s activewear brand on Amazon that grew in 2022 by adding styles and colors quickly. In early 2023, its sales flatten, and its returns rise on newer styles with thin size guidance. The brand cuts the slowest styles, adds detailed fit notes and on-model photos to its best sellers, and responds to recurring review complaints about sizing. Its sales do not jump, but its returns fall and its best sellers convert better. In a cautious market, that is progress.

Where apparel brands on Amazon win a cautious year

Fit confidence comes first, because fit decides whether many apparel purchases are kept or returned. Clear size charts, notes on how each item runs, model measurements and the size the model wears all help shoppers choose correctly. Where Amazon offers virtual try-on or other fit tools for a brand’s category, using them adds another reason to trust the purchase.

Images and reviews carry the rest of the fitting room’s work. Apparel shoppers judge by sight, and multiple angles, on-model shots, fabric close-ups and video show what a description cannot. Reviews that confirm fit and quality complete the picture, so recurring complaints should be fixed at the source, in the product or the size guidance.

Range and inventory need more care than in a growth year. Every return costs money, and slow-moving styles tie up stock in a weak market. A narrower range of proven styles, with depth in the right sizes, usually performs better now than a wide range spread thin. Seasons sharpen the risk. A style that misses its season is hard to sell at full price afterward, so planning each season’s stock conservatively, and keeping the ability to reorder winners rather than committing heavily up front, protects margins when demand is uncertain.

Event discounts need discipline too. Summer brings Prime Day and the competing sales around it, and apparel is often discounted heavily in those events. A brand that discounts its best sellers deeply to chase event volume can train shoppers to wait for the next sale. Reserving deeper discounts for slower styles or end-of-season stock, while holding price on proven items, keeps the full-price business healthier. Advertising should follow the same discipline: spending behind best sellers with strong reviews and low returns earns more than spending to launch many new styles while shoppers are cautious.

None of this is a retreat from the channel, whose importance has not changed. The current caution reflects household budgets, and when spending on clothing recovers, the brands with the strongest pages, reviews and fit reputation will be best placed to grow. The question to bring to the next range review is which styles shoppers keep rather than return. Building the season around those styles, from the size chart to the ad budget, is how we run apparel brands on Amazon.
