A0413.title: Prime Day 2023 forecast: sales, click prices and discounts
A0413.alt: A brass rooster weathervane on a terracotta tiled roof against a clear blue sky.
A0413.ttag: Prime Day 2023 forecast: sales, click prices and discounts | Kwontified
A0413.desc: Our Prime Day 2023 forecast in three ranges: online sales, click prices and discount depth, built on 2022 results and stated assumptions brands can test.
A0413.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 20, 2023.
A0413.body:
On Prime Day 2022, the average cost per click on Amazon rose 50% against the previous 30 days, and return on ad spend still rose 12%. Sales simply grew faster than spending. That combination is unlikely to repeat in 2023, because the money chasing Amazon’s shoppers is growing faster than the shoppers’ spending.

Our expectation for Prime Day 2023 is modest growth in online sales, higher click prices on event days and discounts similar to or slightly deeper than in 2022. The ranges below set out conservative, standard and reach cases, built on 2022 results and stated assumptions. Brands should plan budgets and stock to the standard case, protect against the conservative case and keep room to scale into the reach case.

The Prime Day 2023 forecast in three ranges

Amazon has not yet announced the 2023 dates for the event. We assume a two-day event in July, as in 2022.

Measure2022 resultConservativeStandardReach
U.S. online spending across retailers, two event days$11.9 billion$12.4 billion (+4%)$12.7 billion (+7%)$13.1 billion (+10%)
Amazon cost per click, event days vs. prior 30 days+50%+40%+55%+70%
Ad-attributed sales, event days vs. prior 30 days4.5 times3.5 times4.5 times5 times
Typical discount depth in leading categories12% to 15%Similar to 20221 to 3 points deeper3 to 5 points deeper

The 2022 column comes from three sources. U.S. online spending across all retailers during the two Prime Day days reached $11.9 billion in 2022, up 8.5% from 2021, Adobe reported. Discounts were deepest in toys, at 15%, and apparel, at 12%, according to Adobe data reported by Practical Ecommerce.

On the advertising side, daily ad spending on Amazon during the two event days was four times the average of the previous 30 days for advertisers on Skai’s platform, Skai reported. Ad-attributed sales rose 4.5 times, average cost per click rose 50% and return on ad spend rose 12% compared with the previous 30 days. Same-advertiser spending was up 19% on Prime Day 2021.

Why click prices should outrun sales in 2023

Event sales grow with shopper demand and price levels. Click prices on event days rise with the number of advertisers bidding at the same moment. When advertising budgets are growing faster than retail sales, the event-day rise in click prices tends to outpace the rise in sales.

That is the setting in 2023. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 21% in the first quarter, while its online store sales were flat, GeekWire reported. More advertising money is chasing a slower-growing pool of shoppers, so we expect event-day click prices to rise at least as much as in 2022, which is why our standard case sits above the 2022 rise of 50%.

Sales growth, by contrast, should be modest. Consumer prices were still 4.9% higher in April than a year earlier, NPR reported, and retailers report shoppers prioritizing essentials. Our standard case of 7% growth is a little below 2022’s 8.5%, and part of it reflects higher prices rather than more units. Brands should read their own event sales in units as well as dollars for the same reason.

That leaves the 2022 return on ad spend as a poor benchmark. In 2022, return rose 12% on event days because sales rose faster than spending. If click prices rise faster in 2023, the same budget can buy fewer clicks, and event-day returns may be flat or lower even in a good event.

Take a brand that spent $20,000 on event days in 2022 at a return of $5. If click prices rise 55% and conversion holds, that budget buys about 35% fewer clicks. To hold sales, it would need roughly $31,000. To hold return, it would need conversion or order value to improve.

What each case assumes, and the signposts to watch

Each range rests on stated assumptions, and brands should check them against their own data, because category, price point and brand strength all move the numbers. The conservative case assumes cautious shoppers, more competing sales from other retailers, and advertisers holding budgets steady. The standard case assumes demand similar to 2022, slightly higher prices and continued growth in advertising. The reach case assumes stronger demand, deeper discounts that pull purchases forward, and heavier advertising.

The full week matters as well as the two days. Adobe reported that Prime Day week in 2022, with sales running all week, drove $22.4 billion in U.S. online spending, up 6.1%. Brands that plan only for the event days miss much of that demand, and the week before the event is where many shoppers research and compare.

Stock should follow the same logic. Send enough inventory for the standard case, with a buffer on deal products sized toward the reach case, because running out on the event days costs both the sales and the rank built during them. Excess stock after the event is cheaper to manage than a sold-out deal at its peak, especially with a possible fall event ahead.

The signposts arrive once Amazon announces the dates. An early announcement with a long lead-in of early deals points toward the reach case. Strong competing events from Target and other retailers, or weak June retail sales, point toward the conservative case. Click prices in the week before the event are often the clearest early signal of how crowded the auction will be.

The working rule for the budget: set it to the standard case, put a ceiling at the reach case and a floor at the conservative case. Judge the event on total sales across the surrounding weeks rather than event-day return on ad spend alone. Rebuilding these ranges on a brand’s own account data once the dates are confirmed is how we plan Prime Day budgets for brands.

A0415.crumb: Walmart+ for brands: what a membership…
A0415.title: Walmart+ for brands: what a membership changes about shopping
A0415.alt: A paper grocery bag with bread and carrots beside a blank blue card and keys on a wooden table.
A0415.ttag: Walmart+ for brands: what a membership changes about shopping | Kwontified
A0415.desc: Walmart+ has grown every month since its 2020 launch and draws more affluent shoppers to Walmart. What its members expect, and how brands should meet them.
A0415.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 22, 2023.
A0415.body:
A Walmart+ member has already paid for free delivery, so one more order costs her nothing extra to ship, and the order after that costs nothing extra as well. That small piece of arithmetic changes how she shops, what she expects and, increasingly, who she is.

Walmart+ turns occasional Walmart shoppers into members who expect free, fast delivery and come back often. Membership has grown every month since the program launched in 2020, and Walmart is gaining share with higher-income households. For brands, the practical conclusion is to treat members as a distinct and valuable audience: meet their delivery expectations, be present where they reorder and use Walmart’s advertising to reach them.

Walmart+ for brands: a membership that keeps adding members

Walmart launched Walmart+ in September 2020 and has added benefits since. Members were to receive a streaming video subscription at no extra cost from September 2022, alongside benefits such as fuel savings and free delivery, and Walmart+ had seen positive member growth every month since launch, according to Walmart. Walmart does not publish its total membership, so brands have to judge the program by how it changes behavior rather than by its size.

A brand’s own data is the better guide. The share of its Walmart orders that come through pickup and delivery, and how often the same shoppers come back for the same item, say more about the member effect in its category than any headline count.

The program is part of a wider shift in who shops at Walmart. In its first quarter of fiscal 2024, Walmart said it gained market share in grocery, including with higher-income households, and that U.S. ecommerce sales grew 27%, led by pickup and delivery, according to Walmart.

Three things a membership changes

The economics of each trip change first. Once a member has paid for free delivery, every additional order feels free to ship. That encourages smaller, more frequent orders and makes Walmart the default for routine purchases that might otherwise go elsewhere.

Expectations change too, and quickly. A member who pays for fast, free delivery expects it on everything she buys. Products that arrive slowly, cost extra to ship or are unavailable for pickup and delivery feel like a broken promise, and she is more likely to choose an alternative that meets the standard.

And the shopper herself changes. Convenience-led benefits such as home delivery appeal to busy, often higher-income households. Walmart’s own results point to share gains with those households, which brings shoppers to Walmart who may not have bought certain categories there before. For brands, that adds up to an audience worth planning for specifically: frequent, convenience-minded, increasingly affluent, and accustomed to fast delivery.

Take a premium pet food brand selling through Walmart’s marketplace that ships from its own warehouse in four to six days. A competitor sells a similar product through Walmart’s fulfillment service and offers two-day delivery. Members searching for pet food see both, and the competitor’s faster delivery matches what they pay for. The first brand loses sales on delivery speed, with price and quality never entering the decision.

Meeting the member where she reorders

Delivery is the standard a brand is judged against. For marketplace sellers, that usually means fast, reliable shipping, often through Walmart Fulfillment Services, and accurate delivery promises. For suppliers selling to Walmart, it means keeping stock available in the stores and fulfillment centers that serve pickup and delivery orders.

Reorders are where members’ loyalty shows. Members tend to rebuy the same products, and consistent availability, clear product names and sizes that are easy to find again help a brand become part of that routine. Stock-outs are especially costly, because a member who switches once may not switch back, and the replacement brand inherits the routine.

Walmart Connect is the way to reach members before the routine forms. Walmart’s advertising business is growing quickly, with Walmart Connect up nearly 40% in the first quarter, Walmart said, and it lets brands reach shoppers based on what they buy at Walmart. A brand trying to win new members’ routine purchases can target shoppers of related products, much as it would on Amazon.

Price consistency matters as well. Members join Walmart partly for value, and many compare prices with other retailers before they buy. A product priced noticeably higher at Walmart than on Amazon or a brand’s own site loses the comparison and can lose the member’s trust in the brand along with the sale. Keeping prices aligned across channels, and using promotions rather than permanent price gaps to compete, protects both.

The membership shapes the basket in smaller ways. Because delivery is already paid for, members often add items to an order they are already placing, so products that complement everyday essentials, from snacks to household refills, can benefit from being easy to add at the last moment. Walmart also runs promotions aimed at its members, and planning deals and stock around them, as brands do around Amazon’s Prime events, helps a brand reach its most engaged shoppers.

Brands that already sell on Amazon should not assume the same audience. Walmart+ members overlap with Prime members in some ways but shop differently, often combining grocery and household essentials with other purchases in the same order, and assortments and promotions that reflect that combined basket fit better. The question to put to the team is whether your top-selling Walmart products would pass a member’s test on delivery speed, availability and price. Making sure they do is how we run Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect for brands.

A0417.title: Zalando profitability: what the pivot means for partner brands
A0417.alt: A vintage brass balance scale weighing stacks of coins against an orange wrapped parcel on a wooden table.
A0417.ttag: Zalando profitability: what the pivot means for partner brands | Kwontified
A0417.desc: Zalando’s profit is improving faster than its sales as more volume shifts to partner brands. Why that happens, and what it means for brands on Zalando.
A0417.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 27, 2023.
A0417.body:
In the first quarter of 2023, Zalando’s revenue grew 2.3%. Its adjusted earnings, over the same quarter, went from a loss of 52 million euros a year earlier to a loss of 1 million euros. Profit moving that much faster than sales is what happens when a retailer stops owning so much of what it sells.

A growing share of Zalando’s volume now runs through its partner program, where brands hold the inventory and Zalando earns fees. That is the main reason Zalando profitability is recovering faster than its sales, and it means the platform’s economics now reward partner brands that operate efficiently. Brands on Zalando should model their own partner economics, invest in the operations Zalando values, and expect the platform to favor margin over volume through 2023.

Zalando profitability: from a 2022 slump to recovery

Zalando had a difficult 2022. Its gross merchandise volume grew 3% to 14.8 billion euros, revenue was flat at 10.34 billion euros, and adjusted earnings before interest and taxes fell 60.1% to 184.6 million euros, RTÉ reported. The adjusted margin fell from 4.5% to 1.8%, according to Zalando’s results.

For 2023, Zalando guided to adjusted earnings of 280 million to 350 million euros, with revenue between a 1% decline and a 4% increase, and said it would cut several hundred jobs as it focused on profitability, RTÉ reported.

The first quarter showed the shift working. Gross merchandise volume grew 2.8% and revenue 2.3%, while adjusted earnings improved to that loss of 1 million euros, Zalando reported. Its partner business rose 8 points to 39% of gross merchandise volume, and Zalando said it was on track for 50% by 2025.

Why partner volume lifts profit faster than sales

When Zalando sells its own stock, it buys inventory from brands, carries the risk that the stock does not sell, and earns the retail margin on what does. When a partner brand sells through Zalando, the brand owns the stock. Zalando earns a commission and charges for services such as fulfillment and advertising, with far less capital at risk.

Shift volume from the first model to the second, and Zalando’s profit can rise even when total sales barely grow. It holds less inventory, faces fewer markdowns and earns fee income on volume it does not have to finance.

The reporting shows the shift. Partner sales count in full toward gross merchandise volume but appear in revenue only as Zalando’s fees, so volume can grow while revenue stands still. That is what happened in 2022, when volume grew 3% and revenue was flat, and again in the first quarter of 2023, when volume grew slightly faster than revenue. Profit, meanwhile, improved far faster than either.

The off-price business points the same way. Adjusted earnings at Zalando’s off-price segment, which includes its Lounge shopping club, rose from 6.5 million euros to 24.6 million euros in the first quarter, Zalando reported, as more customers bought through the club. Clearing stock through a dedicated channel, rather than through deep discounts on the main store, also protects margins.

The partner model for a brand: more revenue, more risk

For the brand, the same shift has two sides. The inventory risk and much of the operating work move to the brands: partner brands decide what stock to send, manage their pricing and carry the cost of unsold goods.

Take an outerwear brand that sold 2 million euros a year to Zalando at wholesale. As a partner, it sells the same volume to shoppers at retail prices and keeps the difference after Zalando’s commission and fulfillment fees. Its revenue rises, but so does its exposure: if a season’s jackets do not sell, the brand, not Zalando, absorbs the markdown. Its result depends on how well it plans stock and pricing.

The numbers lean toward the partner model for brands that can plan stock and keep returns down, and toward caution for brands that cannot. Modeling the economics honestly settles which one a brand is. Compare the margin it keeps as a partner, after commission, fulfillment, returns and advertising, with what it earns selling at wholesale, and include the cost of carrying stock and the risk of markdowns.

Running partner economics well

A platform focused on profitability favors partners whose stock is available, whose returns are low and whose products convert. Accurate size and fit information reduces returns, one of the largest costs in online fashion, which makes it a strong place to start investing.

Inventory should be planned conservatively. Zalando cut its own discretionary stock exposure by moving volume to partners, and partners should not simply absorb that risk; smaller, more frequent shipments of proven styles protect margins better than large seasonal commitments. Clearance deserves the same planning. Deciding in advance which styles will move to an off-price channel at the end of a season, and at what point, keeps clearance from undermining full-price sales on the main store. A brand that discounts heavily on the main store trains shoppers to wait, while one that clears through a separate channel keeps its regular prices credible.

Zalando’s services should earn their place. Fulfillment and advertising services can raise sales, but each has a cost, and their return deserves the same measurement as any other channel.

Expect a margin-minded partner on the other side of the table. A platform that cut jobs and guided to profit growth will look harder at fees, promotions and which partners earn their place. Brands that run their partner business efficiently will be welcome, and those that rely on heavy discounting may find less support. Building that partner profit model, line by line from commission to carrying cost, is how we help brands weigh the partner model on Zalando.

A0419.title: Footwear on Amazon in 2023: discounts, resellers and fit
A0419.alt: Brown leather oxford shoes on a worn shoebox beside a vintage metal foot measuring device on a wooden bench.
A0419.ttag: Footwear on Amazon in 2023: discounts, resellers and fit | Kwontified
A0419.desc: Footwear in 2023 has too much stock and a careful shopper. How that spills onto Amazon through resellers and discounts, and what shoe brands should do.
A0419.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 29, 2023.
A0419.body:
Foot Locker ended its first quarter of 2023 holding 25% more inventory than a year earlier, and it told investors it was taking more aggressive markdowns to drive demand and clear stock. Those shoes will be sold somewhere. The question for every footwear brand is where, at what price, and by whom.

A good part of the answer is Amazon. Footwear in 2023 is a category with too much inventory and a cautious shopper, and the excess flows onto Amazon through resellers and deep discounts that undercut brands’ own prices. Footwear brands on Amazon should take control of their offers and pricing, compete on fit and size confidence, and plan stock and promotions around a shopper who is buying less and comparing more.

Footwear on Amazon starts with the stock behind the shelf

After strong sneaker sales during the pandemic, retailers ordered heavily. In 2023, shoppers pulled back. Foot Locker, the specialty athletic retailer, reported that comparable sales fell 9.1% in its first quarter and total sales fell 11.4% to $1.93 billion, according to its results. Along with the higher inventory, it lowered its full-year outlook.

Foot Locker cited a changing mix of brands and pressure from lower tax refunds and weaker spending, Modern Retail reported, and it expected promotions to continue at a similar level for the rest of the year.

Excess inventory does not disappear. Some of it is sold through retailers’ own markdowns. Much of the rest moves through off-price channels, liquidators and resellers, and a share of it ends up on marketplaces such as Amazon, often at prices well below what brands want to see.

Who captures the sale when resellers arrive

Follow a discounted pair of shoes onto Amazon and the value splits in ways a brand rarely plans for. The retailer clearing stock recovers some cash. The liquidator and the reseller take a margin on the way through. The shopper gets a lower price. The brand, which built the demand, can end up with the smallest share of the sale, or none at all.

Nike’s experience showed how durable that demand is. When it ended a two-year pilot of selling directly on Amazon in 2019, its products stayed on the site through independent sellers, the Associated Press reported, and Nike has since put more emphasis on its own stores and website. A brand can step back from a marketplace; the shoppers searching for its shoes do not, and resellers fill the gap.

For a brand that stays, the excess stock creates two problems on Amazon. Its products may be offered by resellers at prices lower than its own, which pulls the brand’s own listing down the search results or wins the buy box away from it. And shoppers who see deep discounts come to expect them, which makes full-price sales harder.

Take a running shoe brand with a popular model on Amazon. A retailer clearing excess stock sells several hundred pairs to a liquidator, and within weeks resellers list the shoe at 30% below the brand’s price. The brand’s own offer loses the buy box. Its advertising drives clicks to a listing where a reseller wins the sale, and reviews start to mention the wrong sizes and older colors. The brand is paying to send shoppers to someone else’s offer.

The careful shopper on the other side of the screen

The footwear shopper in 2023 buys fewer pairs, compares prices across sites and reads reviews closely. In footwear, fit is the deciding question. A shoe that runs small or narrow generates returns and poor reviews, and both hurt a listing’s position.

Amazon has tried to address fit directly. In June 2022, it launched virtual try-on for shoes in its app, letting shoppers see sneakers on their own feet through augmented reality, TechCrunch reported. Tools like this help, but they do not replace clear size guidance from the brand itself.

What a footwear brand can still control

Offers and prices come first. Brands should know who is selling their products on Amazon and where the stock comes from. Brand Registry tools, tighter controls on wholesale and distribution agreements, and monitoring of the buy box all help. Where a brand cannot stop discounted stock, it can at least avoid advertising listings where it is not winning the sale.

Fit and size confidence are the brand’s own advantage over a reseller. Clear size charts, notes on how each model fits compared with the brand’s other shoes, width options and images showing the shoe on feet reduce returns and improve reviews, and answering sizing questions on the listing helps too.

Planning for a cautious shopper means narrower assortments focused on proven models, stock levels sized to realistic demand, and promotions concentrated on events such as Prime Day rather than permanent discounts that train shoppers to wait. Prime Day deserves particular care in 2023. With so much discounting already in the market, a deal has to stand out to earn attention, and a brand that discounts its newest models risks resetting shoppers’ sense of their value. Older colorways and models being phased out are usually better candidates for event deals than current best sellers.

Some decisions sit above the listing. Core styles that sell steadily belong on Amazon, while limited releases and premium models may do better through a brand’s own channels, where pricing and presentation are easier to control. Rising returns on a model, reviews that mention fit, or a sudden fall in buy box share are early signs of a problem that is cheaper to fix early.

The question worth asking the team this summer is simple: on our best-selling models, whose offer is the shopper actually buying? Finding out, and taking that sale back through offer control and better fit content, is how we manage footwear brands on Amazon.

A0421.title: Zalando Partner Program: three products, three decisions
A0421.alt: Three kraft cardboard boxes tied with red, yellow and blue ribbons on a sunlit wooden table against a blue wall.
A0421.ttag: Zalando Partner Program: three products, three decisions | Kwontified
A0421.desc: The Zalando Partner Program is really three products: marketplace access, fulfillment and advertising, each priced differently. How to decide on each one.
A0421.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 4, 2023.
A0421.body:
The Zalando Partner Program comes with three price tags. Marketplace access is paid by commission, fulfillment on a cost-plus basis, and advertising by auction. A brand that judges the program by its commission rate alone has looked at one price out of three.

Each part has different economics, which is why the program is best treated as three separate products. Brands should decide on each one on its own merits rather than accepting the bundle, and start with how they will fulfill orders, because that choice shapes the rest.

The Zalando Partner Program in 2023

Zalando’s partner business has become central to its model. Partner sales, through the Partner Program and the Connected Retail program for physical stores, accounted for 36% of Fashion Store gross merchandise volume in the fourth quarter of 2022, up 6 points from a year earlier, Zalando reported. Zalando Fulfillment Solutions shipped 58% of partner items, up 3 points.

The program had more than 5,800 brand partners and almost 7,000 connected stores by the end of 2021, Fashion Network reported. Zalando’s marketing services business, which sells advertising to brands, was equal to about 2% of gross merchandise volume at the end of 2022, according to Zalando’s strategy update.

Zalando prices the three parts differently, according to a presentation to investors:

Part of the programHow Zalando prices itWhat it changes for the brand
Partner Program (marketplace access)CommissionA share of each sale
Zalando Fulfillment SolutionsCost-plusReplaces the brand’s own warehousing and shipping costs
Marketing services (advertising)Auction bidsA variable cost the brand controls

Why each part needs its own test

Each part of the program earns Zalando money in a different way and changes a different line of a brand’s economics. A brand that judges the program as a single deal can overpay for one part while underusing another. Judging each part against its own alternative shows where the program adds value.

Commission sits against the margin a brand earns on other channels. Fulfillment sits against its own warehouse. Advertising sits against not advertising, which is why it needs a test.

Take a German footwear brand selling 1 million euros a year through the Partner Program from its own warehouse. Its commission is set by its agreement, so the open decision is fulfillment. Shipping from its own warehouse costs it a known amount per order and delivers more slowly than Zalando’s network. Moving stock into Zalando’s fulfillment may cost more or less per item, but it can lift sales if faster delivery improves the product’s position. The advertising decision comes last, once the brand knows its margin per order.

Fulfillment shapes everything after it

A brand has three broad options for fulfillment: ship from its own warehouse, use Zalando Fulfillment Solutions, or, for retailers with physical stores, sell store stock through Connected Retail. The right choice depends on the brand’s existing logistics, its volume on Zalando and how many European markets it wants to reach. Zalando’s own goal, set out at its 2021 capital markets day, is for about three-quarters of Partner Program items to ship through its fulfillment service, which suggests the platform will keep making that option more attractive.

For brands with their own stores or retail partners, Connected Retail deserves a closer look. Store stock becomes available to Zalando shoppers, which can turn slow-moving store inventory into online sales without moving it to a warehouse. The cost is control: store stock levels change quickly, and a product shown as available that has just sold in the store creates a cancelled order and a disappointed shopper. Accurate, frequent stock updates are essential.

Market choice belongs in the same decision. Zalando sells across many European countries, and fulfillment through its network can make it practical to reach markets a brand could not serve well from its own warehouse. A brand should still check that its products, sizes and prices suit each market before switching it on, because demand, returns behavior and competition differ from country to country.

Then assortment, then advertising

With fulfillment settled, assortment and pricing determine what the commission buys. Brands should choose which products to offer, in which markets, and at what prices, with commission and returns included in the margin. Fashion returns are high, so a product that sells well but is often returned can lose money after fees.

Advertising comes last. Zalando’s marketing services can raise visibility, but auction-priced advertising is a cost the brand controls, and it should be set against the margin per order established by the earlier choices and measured on incremental sales rather than attributed sales alone. That measurement matters more on Zalando than it might seem. Shoppers often browse many brands before buying, so an ad may be credited with a sale the shopper would have made anyway. Testing advertising on and off for comparable products gives a cleaner read than attribution reports alone.

Taking the decisions in this order prevents a common mistake: spending on advertising to push products whose fulfillment and returns already make them unprofitable.

The decisions also need revisiting as volume grows. A setup that makes sense at small volume, such as shipping from the brand’s own warehouse, may become expensive or slow as orders increase, and a brand that moves into fulfillment too early may pay for capacity it does not use. A review each season keeps the program matched to the business. The rule is short: price each part of the program against its own alternative before signing up for the next one. Working through those three prices with a brand’s own numbers is how we help brands set up the Zalando Partner Program.

A0422.title: Handbags on Amazon in 2023: price discipline wins
A0422.alt: A row of tan, brown and black leather bags with blank tags on a sunlit rustic wooden shelf.
A0422.ttag: Handbags on Amazon in 2023: price discipline wins | Kwontified
A0422.desc: Handbag brands that held price and kept stock tight did well in early 2023. What that means for accessories brands on Amazon, from pricing to discovery.
A0422.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 6, 2023.
A0422.body:
In its fiscal third quarter, the owner of Coach, Kate Spade and Stuart Weitzman described the North American shopper as facing an increasingly challenging backdrop. During that same quarter, it raised the average price at which it sold handbags, in North America as well as globally. A company does not usually push price into a weak consumer. This one did, and its inventory, held close to the prior year’s level, helps explain how.

That is the pattern in handbags and accessories in 2023: the brands doing best are the ones holding price and keeping stock close to demand, while shoppers pull back elsewhere. Accessories brands on Amazon should protect their price and presentation, compete on style discovery rather than discounts, and guard against counterfeits and unauthorized sellers that erode both.

Handbags on Amazon and the results behind the pattern

The clearest picture of the category comes from its largest brands. The owner of Coach, Kate Spade and Stuart Weitzman reported that revenue rose 5% to $1.51 billion in its fiscal third quarter, which ended on April 1, according to its results. Inventory ended the quarter only 2% above the prior year.

Growth across regions was uneven. North America, where shoppers were under more pressure, grew only in the low single digits, and the company described the consumer backdrop there as increasingly challenging while raising the average price at which it sold handbags, according to its earnings call.

By brand, Coach sales rose 7% while Kate Spade sales fell 1%, Chain Store Age reported. The company also said it gained more than 1.2 million new customers in North America, more than half of them from Gen Z and millennial shoppers.

Why tight inventory lets a brand hold its price

The lesson in those numbers is about discipline. A brand that keeps its inventory close to demand does not need to discount to clear it. A brand that does not discount can raise prices, or at least hold them, without teaching shoppers to wait for a sale. And a brand whose prices hold keeps its products looking like something worth paying for.

That discipline did not come easily. After the pandemic, many fashion brands built up stock as supply chains recovered and demand cooled. The brands that cut orders early and managed inventory tightly avoided the heavy markdowns that hit others, footwear among them.

Where price control slips on Amazon

On Amazon, the same logic applies with an extra twist. A handbag brand’s price on Amazon is visible next to every other offer for the same product and next to competing styles. If a reseller or an unauthorized seller lists the brand’s bags at a discount, the brand loses control of its price in the most visible place shoppers compare.

Counterfeits make the problem worse. Handbags and accessories are frequent targets for counterfeiters, and shoppers who receive a fake blame the brand. Amazon’s own figures show the scale. Its 2022 Brand Protection Report said it stopped more than 800,000 attempts in 2022 to create new selling accounts, and that it seized more than 6 million counterfeit products and disposed of them, according to Amazon.

Take a leather goods brand selling a popular tote on Amazon at its full price. An unauthorized seller sources excess stock from a retailer’s clearance and lists the same tote 25% cheaper. Shoppers searching for the tote see the cheaper offer first. The brand’s own listing loses sales, and some shoppers start to wonder whether the full price was ever fair.

How accessories brands hold their price on Amazon

Protecting price and presentation starts with Brand Registry, monitoring who sells the brand’s products, and distribution agreements that limit where wholesale stock can be resold. Strong brand content, including A+ pages and a well-designed brand store, makes the brand’s own listings the clearest place to buy. Brand Registry also lets a brand control the title, images and description on its product pages, so that every seller’s offer appears under the brand’s own presentation rather than a reseller’s version of it. That consistency matters for accessories, where small differences in a photo or a color name can make a genuine product look doubtful.

Style discovery should do the work that discounts would otherwise do. Accessories shoppers browse by look, color and occasion. Images that show bags in use, clear details on size and capacity, and collections grouped by style help shoppers find what they want without a discount to prompt them.

Inventory sent to Amazon should match demand. A brand that sends only the stock it expects to sell avoids the pressure to discount at the end of a season, and smaller, more frequent shipments of proven styles keep prices steady. Product choice matters as well: core styles and everyday accessories suit the channel, while limited editions and the highest-priced pieces may do better through channels where presentation is easier to control.

Younger shoppers deserve particular attention. If a large share of new customers are Gen Z and millennial shoppers, as Coach’s owner reported, then the images, video and social content that reach them matter on Amazon too, where many of them search before they buy.

Prime Day is the test of all this. A deep discount on a core style can reset what shoppers expect to pay for months afterward, while deals on older colors or styles being phased out let a brand take part in the event and still protect its main line. The question for the team before the next event is which of its bags it would be comfortable seeing at a lower price for the rest of the year. Holding that line on Amazon, from seller monitoring to brand content, is how we manage accessories brands on Amazon.

A0423.crumb: Mercado Libre inventory: why fast movers…
A0423.title: Mercado Libre inventory: why fast movers belong in Full
A0423.alt: A sunlit warehouse with cardboard parcels on a curving roller conveyor dropping into yellow bins beside pallets.
A0423.ttag: Mercado Libre inventory: why fast movers belong in Full | Kwontified
A0423.desc: Mercado Libre is pushing sellers into its own fulfillment network. Why centralizing fast-moving stock there pays, and how to decide product by product.
A0423.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 11, 2023.
A0423.body:
Mercado Libre shipped 302 million successful items in the first quarter of 2023, up from 254 million a year earlier. A record 44% of the items it shipped went through its own fulfillment network. For a brand deciding where to hold stock in Latin America, that second figure says more than the first: the marketplace is building its business around delivery from its own warehouses, and it is asking sellers to come along.

The answer for most brands is to move only part of the catalog. Fast-moving products belong in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network in each country they sell in, while slow movers stay in the brand’s own warehouse. The reason is one mechanism. A single pool of stock in a fast network keeps a product’s delivery promise, and that promise is worth most on the products that sell every day.

Mercado Libre inventory is moving into the company’s own network

The marketplace is growing quickly. Gross merchandise volume reached $9.4 billion in the first quarter of 2023, up 43.3% on a currency-neutral basis, and items sold grew almost 16%, the company reported.

Fulfillment sits at the center of that growth. Alongside the record 44% share, Mercado Libre said its delivery times were the fastest across the region, according to its investor presentation. Mexico was its most advanced fulfillment market. In Brazil, fulfillment penetration rose by almost 4 points from a year earlier.

Sellers know the service as Mercado Envíos Full, or simply Full. A seller sends stock to a Mercado Libre warehouse, and the company stores, packs and ships each order. Products stocked this way carry a Full label, which shoppers have learned to read as a promise of fast delivery.

The company was also plain about its order of priorities. On its earnings call, its chief financial officer said the first priority was to keep driving sellers’ use of fulfillment, with higher charges for the service coming later, once other markets reached levels closer to Mexico’s, according to the call transcript.

Split stock breaks the delivery promise

When a product ships from Mercado Libre’s own network, it arrives faster and more reliably. Shoppers see the faster promise and buy more often. The marketplace, which wants that promise kept, gives those products better visibility.

The opposite happens when a brand splits one product’s stock between its own warehouse and Mercado Libre’s network. Each pool is too thin to deliver quickly everywhere. Some orders ship fast and others slowly, so the product’s delivery promise and its ranking both suffer.

A dedicated bus lane works the same way. It pays for itself on the routes that run every few minutes and does little for the route that runs twice a day. Centralizing a fast-moving product in one fast network usually raises its sales by more than the extra fees cost. Slow movers are different. Their stock sits for longer, storage costs mount, and the delivery advantage matters less when few shoppers buy them.

One pan and 80 slow sellers

Take a kitchenware brand selling in Mexico. Its best-selling pan sells 600 units a month, and its other 80 products sell a few units each. Shipped from the brand’s own warehouse, the pan takes three to five days to arrive. Moved into Mercado Libre’s fulfillment, it can arrive the next day in major cities, and its sales rise.

Sent to Full, each of the 80 slow products would sit on a shelf the brand pays for while it waits for an order that comes a few times a month. Kept in the brand’s own warehouse, where storage costs nothing extra, they still sell to the shoppers who want them. The brand gets the delivery advantage where the volume is and avoids paying for it where the volume is not.

Country by country, product by product

Each country is a separate decision. Mercado Libre runs separate operations in Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile and other markets, and stock held in one country cannot serve shoppers in another. A brand selling in several countries needs a fulfillment plan for each, sized to that market’s demand.

The plan starts with a ranking of products by sales velocity in each country. Products that sell steadily every week are candidates for Full; products that sell rarely, or only in one season, usually are not. Stock sizing comes next. Too little stock in the fulfillment network causes stock-outs, which cost the ranking the product built, and too much raises storage costs. A few weeks of cover, refreshed regularly, is a sensible starting point, adjusted for how long replenishment takes to reach each country.

Replenishment has to work around import and customs timing. For brands shipping into Mexico or Brazil from abroad, lead times are long and uncertain. Fast movers need a buffer, and the replenishment plan needs to start well before stock runs low.

The timing argues for moving early. Mercado Libre has said its priority is driving adoption before raising charges, so brands that build their fulfillment operations now do so while the platform is still focused on growing usage, and they will be better placed when its terms change.

Advertising should follow the same logic. Mercado Libre said it launched the first version of a new Ads Console in a test phase in the first quarter of 2023, according to its shareholder letter. As those tools mature, the products worth promoting are the ones that can deliver quickly and stay in stock, which are the fast movers in Full.

The last piece is measurement. Compare sales, delivery times and conversion for each product before and after it moves into fulfillment, with storage and fulfillment fees counted in the margin, and review the split every quarter. A product earns its place in Full when its sales gain covers the fees; when it stops doing so, it goes back to the brand’s own warehouse. Making that call product by product, in every country, is how we run Mercado Libre inventory for brands.

A0426.crumb: Health and household on Amazon: the…
A0426.title: Health and household on Amazon: the price-per-unit shopper
A0426.alt: Three empty glass apothecary bottles, a rolled linen towel and a small bowl on a wooden shelf by green tiles.
A0426.ttag: Health and household on Amazon: the price-per-unit shopper | Kwontified
A0426.desc: P&G raised prices about 10% as volumes slipped. On Amazon, where unit prices sit beside every listing, pack size and loyalty decide who keeps the shopper.
A0426.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 13, 2023.
A0426.body:
Search Amazon for laundry detergent and look just below each price. Many health and household listings carry a second, smaller number: the price per ounce, per load or per count. In a store aisle that figure hides on a shelf tag near the floor. On Amazon it sits next to the headline price, for every brand on the page, including the store brand one row down.

That small number is where the category’s pricing gets judged on Amazon. Health and household shoppers in 2023 are paying higher prices, buying slightly less and comparing more, and Amazon puts the comparison in front of them. The brands that keep the sale manage pack sizes and unit prices on purpose, build repeat purchase through subscriptions, and give shoppers a clear reason not to trade down.

Health and household on Amazon after two years of price rises

The largest household brands have spent two years raising prices to cover higher costs. Procter & Gamble, the maker of Tide, Pampers and Crest, raised prices by about 10% across its categories in the quarter that ended in March, while the volume of products it shipped fell 3%, according to its results.

The pattern varied by category. In fabric and home care, prices rose 13% and volumes fell 5%. In health care, volumes grew 1%. In the United States, organic sales rose 6% with modest growth in units, the company said on its earnings call, according to a transcript.

American shoppers have largely accepted the increases so far. P&G said the share of U.S. sales held by cheaper private label products was stable at about 16%, a sign that shoppers here were not yet trading down in large numbers, the Associated Press reported. Europe looked different. There, shoppers were moving to private label, and the gap between store brands and branded products was widening as store brands delayed their own increases, PYMNTS reported, citing P&G’s chief financial officer.

The pack-size decision is a pricing decision

When costs rise, the choice in front of a household brand’s leadership is rarely framed as a pricing debate. It arrives as a packaging question from operations or finance: do we raise the shelf price, or keep the price and put less in the box? In a store, the second option can pass unnoticed for a while. On Amazon it cannot, because a smaller pack at the same price shows up at once as a higher unit price, right beside the alternatives.

The same arithmetic works in the other direction. A brand that offers a larger pack at a lower unit price can win value-minded shoppers without cutting its everyday price. So the team that sets pack sizes is, whether it knows it or not, setting the brand’s price on Amazon.

Take a vitamin brand selling a 60-count bottle for $15. A cheaper competitor sells a 90-count bottle for $16. On the unit price shown, the competitor costs about 18 cents a capsule and the brand 25 cents. Unless the listing gives shoppers a clear reason to pay more, such as quality, certification or a better formula, the comparison works against the brand on every visit.

What keeps a shopper from trading down

Repeat purchase matters more in this category than almost anywhere else on Amazon. Detergent, vitamins and paper goods are bought again and again, and Amazon’s Subscribe & Save program lets shoppers set up regular deliveries at a discount. A shopper who subscribes is far less likely to compare alternatives each time, which protects the brand’s place in the household routine.

That protection only holds if the product stays in stock, because a subscription that fails to ship is a shopper invited to look elsewhere. The products people use up on a regular schedule are the best candidates, and the subscription discount should be set with the margin in mind, since it applies to every future order.

Cheaper alternatives are always close by. Store brands and lesser-known brands sell similar products at lower prices, and on Amazon they often appear in the same search results and on the brand’s own product page. Clear product content on ingredients, certifications, results and how the product compares helps justify a higher price, and reviews do the rest, because a shopper tempted by the cheaper option often checks whether the brand’s reviews are worth the difference.

Advertising has a defensive job here too. Competitors, including cheaper alternatives, often advertise on searches for a brand’s name and on its product pages, where a shopper about to reorder is easiest to tempt. Brands should advertise on their own branded searches and product pages to keep that space, and watch which competitors appear there. The cost of defending a loyal customer is usually far lower than the cost of winning a new one. Events such as Prime Day belong in the same plan: a shopper who tries a product on a deal and then subscribes is worth far more than one who buys once at a discount.

The gap to watch is in Europe

The private label gap that opened in Europe has not yet appeared in the United States. If it does, the brands best placed to hold their customers will be the ones that already built loyalty and repeat purchase, not the ones that relied on shoppers failing to notice a smaller pack.

Before the next pack change, ask the team a simple question: who checks our unit price against the store brand one row down, and how often? Watching that number, pack by pack and subscription by subscription, is how we run health and household brands on Amazon.

A0429.title: Back-to-school 2023: an earlier, longer season to plan for
A0429.alt: An olive canvas backpack, colored pencils, a jar of pens and blank notebooks on a wooden desk by a window.
A0429.ttag: Back-to-school 2023: an earlier, longer season to plan for | Kwontified
A0429.desc: Back-to-school 2023 starts with Prime Day in July and runs into September. What an earlier, longer season means for a brand’s stock, advertising and price.
A0429.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 20, 2023.
A0429.body:
On the second day of Prime Day 2023, online sales of stationery and office supplies were up 76% compared with an average day in June, Adobe found, Reuters reported. School supplies were selling in a July deal week, weeks before most classrooms open. A plan that treats the season as an August event starts late.

The calendar has moved. Back-to-school 2023 is a record season that begins with Prime Day deals in July and runs into September, with two peaks rather than one. Brands that want their share of it need stock in place by early July and advertising and pricing staged across the whole season, not concentrated in August.

Back-to-school 2023 is bigger, and it starts sooner

Families expect to spend a record $41.5 billion on back-to-school shopping for elementary through high school students in 2023, up from $36.9 billion in 2022, the National Retail Federation reported. Spending on electronics alone is expected to reach a record $15.2 billion, Retail Dive reported.

The start date has crept forward. As of early July, 55% of back-to-school shoppers said they had already started shopping, on par with 2022 but up from 44% in 2019, according to the NRF. Yet 85% said they still had at least half of their shopping left to do.

Shoppers also named online as one of their top destinations for back-to-school purchases, alongside department and discount stores, according to Retail Dive’s report on the survey. That puts Amazon, Walmart and Target at the center of the season, and it makes search ranking and availability on those sites a large part of how a brand competes for the record spending.

A season with two peaks

Two forces stretched the season. Prime Day, held in July, gives families a reason to buy supplies, electronics and clothing weeks before school starts, and other retailers run competing events at the same time. Caution does the rest: shoppers who are watching prices spread their purchases out, buying some items on deal early and waiting on others.

What comes out is a season with two peaks. The first arrives in July, around Prime Day and the competing events, when shoppers buy what is on deal. The second comes in August and runs into September, as school start dates approach and families fill the gaps, often with items they discover they need once classes begin. A planning calendar built around one August spike misses half of that shape.

What an early start asks of stock, advertising and price

For brands, that changes three things, and each one sits with a different team. Stock is a supply chain decision, advertising an e-commerce one, and price may need sign-off from finance or sales. An earlier season only works when all three teams move their dates together, because a well-stocked listing with no budget behind it, or a funded campaign pointing at an empty shelf, wastes the July peak.

Stock has to arrive earlier. A brand that plans for an August peak and ships inventory in late July misses the first peak entirely. On Amazon, products that are out of stock during Prime Day lose both the sales and the search ranking they would have built going into August.

Advertising has to run longer. A brand that concentrates its budget in August misses the shoppers who started in July, and one that spends heavily in July may run short when the second wave arrives. Budgets need to cover both peaks, with room to respond to how each one performs.

Pricing has to be planned across the season. A brand that discounts deeply in July may find shoppers expect the same price in August, while one that holds prices too high early may lose shoppers to competitors running deals.

Take a backpack brand that planned its season around August and landed its stock on Amazon in the last week of July, after Prime Day. Competitors with stock in place would have captured the July buyers. When the brand’s products went live, they would carry little sales history and rank below rivals, and the brand would spend August paying more in advertising to catch up.

The weeks still ahead

Most of the buying is still to come, so availability through September matters more than the July result. Brands should check stock levels after Prime Day, reorder the products that sold through, and keep core items in stock as school start dates arrive in different regions.

August shoppers tend to be filling specific needs, such as a particular calculator or the right size of backpack, which makes advertising on specific product searches work well in this period, alongside broader campaigns. Product content deserves the same attention. Parents buying for a grade or a school supply list search for exact items, such as a graphing calculator model or a backpack that fits a laptop. Titles, images and descriptions that state those details help a product appear in the right searches.

Prices are better held steady than cut. Modest promotions, bundles or coupons keep a brand competitive without resetting what shoppers expect to pay.

The K-12 shopper is not the whole season either. College students and their families are expected to spend $94 billion in 2023, up about $20 billion from 2022, Retail Dive reported. Many college purchases, from dorm furnishings to electronics, come later in August, when move-in dates arrive.

And the 2024 plan starts now, with stock in place before Prime Day, because the 2023 season has shown where it begins. Staging stock, bids and prices across both peaks is how we run back-to-school for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0432.title: Prime Day 2023 lessons: a membership week, not a sale
A0432.alt: A velvet rope between brass posts in front of shelves of kraft-wrapped gift boxes on a teal wall.
A0432.ttag: Prime Day 2023 lessons: a membership week, not a sale | Kwontified
A0432.desc: Prime Day 2023 became a week of competing membership events at Amazon, Walmart and Target. What that shift means for how brands plan the next July event.
A0432.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 27, 2023.
A0432.body:
In the second week of July 2023, a shopper could move from Amazon to Walmart to Target and find the same offer at each: a deal event, built for members. The dates overlapped, the discounts competed, and each retailer asked the shopper to join or stay in its program first.

That overlap is the lesson brands should carry into the next July event. Prime Day has become an industry-wide membership week rather than one retailer’s sale. A brand that plans it as an Amazon event spreads deals evenly where it should choose, and it misses that the audience at each retailer is that retailer’s members.

Prime Day 2023 lessons from three retailers in one week

Amazon held Prime Day on July 11 and 12 and called it its biggest Prime Day ever, with Prime members buying more than 375 million items worldwide, Fox Business reported. The deals were open only to Prime members.

Target ran Target Circle Week from July 9 to 15, with savings of up to 50% for members of its free loyalty program, Fortune reported. Target said more than 100 million people were already members of Target Circle, Value Added Resource reported.

Walmart came back with Walmart+ Week, giving members early access to deals from noon on July 10 and opening the event to other shoppers from July 11 to 13, Value Added Resource reported. Walmart had not held a competing event in July 2022, Chain Store Age reported.

Amazon also pushed the event past its own store. In 2023 it offered Prime Day savings on some brands’ own websites through its Buy with Prime service, along with invite-only deals, GeekWire reported. Independent sellers had their biggest Prime Day, with sales growth that outpaced Amazon’s own retail business, according to Amazon’s figures reported by Fox Business.

Who keeps the value of a membership week

Prime Day began as Amazon’s way of signing up and rewarding Prime members. In 2023, two of its largest rivals copied both the timing and the model, and each event was built around a membership program: paid in the case of Prime and Walmart+, free in the case of Target Circle.

The reason is that a member is worth more than any single week of sales. A member shops more often and is easier to reach with offers, so an event that brings in new members pays off for months afterward. That is why each retailer was willing to discount heavily for a few days. Most of that value stays with the retailer that holds the membership. The brand that supplied the deal gets the sale, and it keeps the customer only if it does something to earn the next order.

The programs also ask different things of shoppers. Prime and Walmart+ charge a fee, so their members have already committed and expect value in return. Target Circle is free, so its event is partly a way to sign up shoppers who have not yet joined. A deal on Amazon or Walmart therefore reaches shoppers who already buy often, while a deal at Target may reach shoppers the retailer is still trying to win. For a brand, the practical question is which of those relationships it can turn into a repeat customer of its own.

Shoppers have adjusted to the pattern. Numerator’s survey found about 52% of households used the event for purchases they had put off until a sale, CNBC reported. Shoppers now plan around the July week, much as they plan around Black Friday.

Planning the next July week across retailers

The event is now multi-retailer, so the first decision is where to play. A brand that plans only for Amazon misses Target’s week-long event and Walmart’s member days, while a brand that runs deep deals everywhere may discount more than it needs to. The better question, retailer by retailer, is where the brand’s shoppers already are and where a deal will win new customers.

Because the audience is members, the week suits winning repeat buyers: through subscriptions on Amazon, for example, or a place in a retailer’s featured member deals. Timing differs too. Target’s event ran for a full week, Walmart’s for parts of four days, and Amazon’s for two, so stock and advertising need to cover the longest window, not only the two Prime Day dates.

Take a home goods brand that sells on Amazon, Walmart and Target and puts its whole deal budget into Prime Day. Target shoppers who see competing brands discounted during Circle Week will choose those brands, and the home goods brand can lose share at Target well beyond the event. Moving even part of that budget to Circle Week would keep the brand in the comparison Target shoppers are making.

Pricing needs watching as well. A deal run on one retailer is visible to shoppers comparing across all three, and retailers watch competitors’ prices closely, so different prices for the same product in the same week can strain retail partnerships and confuse shoppers. Measurement needs the same wide view: judged only on Amazon results, the week may hide sales that moved to Target or Walmart, or credit Prime Day with sales that would have happened elsewhere. Total sales across retailers for the weeks around the event give the truer picture.

The calendar is filling up, too. In October 2022 Amazon held a second Prime event, and if retailers repeat the pattern in the fall, the same planning will apply before the holidays.

The question for the leadership team is who in the company owns that week across all three retailers, rather than one team per retailer. Deciding where deals, stock and budget go across retailers before the dates are announced is how we plan multi-retailer events for brands.

A0430.title: Prime Day 2023 results against our forecast: what we got wrong
A0430.alt: Three wooden arrows in the center of a straw archery target standing in a sunny meadow.
A0430.ttag: Prime Day 2023 results against our forecast: what we got wrong | Kwontified
A0430.desc: We forecast Prime Day 2023 in three ranges. Sales and click prices landed in range; ad sales and returns beat it. The grading, and what we got wrong.
A0430.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 31, 2023.
A0430.body:
Click prices on Amazon rose 58% during Prime Day 2023, more than our standard case, and return on ad spend went up anyway. We had warned it might not. The click prices behaved roughly as we expected; the orders did not. Shoppers filled much larger baskets than we assumed, and each expensive click bought more revenue.

Grading our own forecast gives this picture. Online spending and click prices landed within our ranges, while ad-attributed sales and return on ad spend beat them. Some of the event’s sales were also pulled forward from purchases shoppers had delayed, which matters as much as the miss.

Prime Day 2023 results, graded

Before the event, we published conservative, standard and reach ranges for Prime Day 2023. Against public data, spending, click prices and discount depth all landed inside those ranges, while ad-attributed sales beat even the reach case.

MeasureOur standard caseResultGrade
U.S. online spending across retailers, two days$12.7 billion (+7%)$12.7 billion (+6.1%)Between conservative and standard
Amazon cost per click, vs. prior 30 days+55%+58%Between standard and reach
Ad-attributed sales, vs. prior 30 days4.5 times5.9 timesAbove our reach case of 5 times
Discount depth in leading categories1 to 3 points deeper than 202212% to 14%, similar to 2022Conservative case

Online spending across U.S. retailers rose 6.1% to $12.7 billion over the two days, according to Adobe data reported by Fox Business. Adobe itself had forecast 9.5%. The deepest discounts were 14% on electronics and 12% on apparel and toys, Reuters reported.

The advertising numbers came from Skai’s platform. Amazon ad spending for its advertisers rose 409% compared with the previous 30 days, ad-attributed sales rose 486%, and cost per click rose 58%, compared with 50% in 2022, Marketing Dive reported.

The miss on returns came from basket size

Our biggest miss was on returns. We warned that if click prices rose faster than sales, event-day return on ad spend might be flat or lower. Click prices did rise sharply. Yet return on ad spend rose for Skai’s advertisers, and the gain beat 2022’s, when returns rose 12%, Marketing Dive reported.

Baskets explain it. Skai found the average shopping cart grew 76% during the event compared with the 30 days before it, Marketing Dive reported. Shoppers who had held off on larger purchases, from laptops to appliances, used the event to make them.

Return on ad spend rises when the value of each order grows faster than the cost of the clicks that produce it. Shoppers bought much larger baskets, especially in electronics, so each click produced more revenue, and returns rose even as clicks became more expensive. In ratio terms, the cost of the clicks went up, and the revenue from them went up faster.

We watched the cost side of that ratio and underestimated the order side. Electronics drove much of the change: Skai found that technology sales roughly doubled their average order value compared with the previous 30 days, Marketing Dive reported, while categories such as apparel and groceries saw returns fall. Our forecast assumed baskets similar to 2022, and that assumption carried the error straight through to returns. On event days, click prices and basket size both move, and the second can outweigh the first. That leaves our click-price grade standing but changes what it means: a cost forecast that lands is only half of a return forecast.

The other lesson concerns where the sales came from. Numerator surveyed households and found about 52% bought items during Prime Day that they had been holding off on until they went on sale, CNBC reported. Those purchases were real, but many were delayed from earlier weeks rather than new.

Added sales versus pulled-forward sales

For a brand, the number that matters is the total over the season, not the event-day spike. A sale delayed from June to July adds to Prime Day’s count, but not to the brand’s sales for the summer.

Separating the two takes a wider window. Compare total sales for the eight weeks around the event with the same weeks in 2022, and with the brand’s normal growth rate. If the weeks before Prime Day were weak and the event was strong, some of the event’s sales were pulled forward. If sales after the event stay above normal, the event found new customers.

Take a brand that sold $100,000 on Prime Day 2023, double its 2022 event. If its June sales fell $30,000 below its normal trend while shoppers waited, the event’s true added value is closer to $70,000. If its August sales then rise above trend as new customers reorder, some of that value returns.

The advertising read needs the same care. A return well above the prior 30 days looks strong, but the prior 30 days were themselves depressed by shoppers waiting, so event returns belong next to a normal month, not only the pre-event weeks.

Costs are also climbing outside the event. Skai’s data showed that advertisers’ Prime Day spending rose 65% from a year earlier, and that the event accounted for a little over half of their spending growth so far in 2023, Marketing Dive reported. A brand that budgets the next event on 2022 prices will be short before the event starts.

The rule we are taking into the next forecast: model the basket as carefully as the click, and grade the event on eight weeks of sales rather than two days. Grading event results against the full season is how we measure Prime Day for brands.

A0435.crumb: Amazon category shift: what flat store…
A0435.title: Amazon category shift: what flat store growth is hiding
A0435.alt: Wooden shelves half empty and half stocked with kraft boxes, paper bags and jars with blank labels.
A0435.ttag: Amazon category shift: what flat store growth is hiding | Kwontified
A0435.desc: Amazon’s store sales barely grew in early 2023, but the flat headline hid a move to essentials and cheaper items. How brands should read their own results.
A0435.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 3, 2023.
A0435.body:
A flat line on a quarterly chart invites a flat reading. When Amazon’s online store sales barely moved in the first quarter of 2023, the line on its own said that nothing much had changed for brands selling there. Underneath that line, shoppers were moving a great deal: out of discretionary categories and into essentials and beauty, down to cheaper versions of the things they still bought, and toward independent sellers.

The flat total was an average of several moving parts, and a brand sits in only one of them. The useful question is not how Amazon did, but which way the brand’s own category is moving. Assortment, pricing and investment should follow the answer.

The Amazon category shift behind a flat quarter

Amazon’s online store sales were roughly flat in the first quarter of 2023, while advertising revenue rose 21%, GeekWire reported. Read quickly, that looks like a business standing still.

Amazon described something more specific. Its chief financial officer said the company saw moderated spending in discretionary categories, shifts to lower-priced items, and healthy demand in everyday essentials such as consumables and beauty, according to the earnings call transcript.

The seller mix moved too. Independent sellers accounted for 59% of units sold in the first quarter, up from 55% a year earlier, according to the call.

Three currents under one number

The first current runs from wants to needs. Shoppers squeezed by two years of high prices cut back on discretionary purchases such as home goods, apparel and electronics, while continuing to buy what they use up. Other retailers saw the same thing. Target reported declines in apparel and home in its first quarter, and Procter & Gamble said its prices rose about 10% while volumes fell only 3%, a sign that essentials kept selling even at higher prices.

The second runs toward lower prices inside a category. A shopper who still buys a product type often picks a cheaper version of it: a smaller pack, a store brand, a less expensive model. On Amazon that shows up as shifts to lower-priced items, even in categories that are growing.

The third runs toward independent sellers. Many of the cheaper alternatives come from third-party sellers, including newer brands and sellers based overseas, and as their share of units rises, established brands meet more competition at lower price points in the same search results.

Beauty cuts across all three. It is discretionary in theory, yet shoppers treat many beauty products as small, affordable, everyday purchases, which is why beauty kept growing while other discretionary categories slowed. Each current has been building for months, and none of them shows in the total.

Two brands, one flat number

A flat overall figure hides very different results for different brands. Take two brands whose Amazon sales were flat in the first quarter. One sells vitamins, in a category growing 8%, so flat sales mean it is losing share. The other sells patio furniture, in a category shrinking 10%, so flat sales mean it is gaining share.

In a quarterly review, both slides would show the same line. The vitamin brand should be worried and the patio brand should be pleased, and the same number calls for opposite responses. On the search results page the difference is easy to picture: in the growing category, rivals that are adding sales climb past the vitamin brand, while in the shrinking one the patio brand holds its place as others slip.

That is why a result means little until it is set against the category. Search volume, category rankings and competitor data show the direction a brand is swimming in before anyone decides whether its own number is good or bad.

Reading your own category, and acting on it

Assortment and pricing should move with the shopper. In discretionary categories, that may mean leading with entry-priced products, value bundles or smaller sizes. In essentials, the demand is there to capture, so availability and repeat purchase deserve the attention.

The lower-priced competition needs a deliberate answer. As independent sellers take more of the unit mix, a brand should know which cheaper alternatives appear next to its products, and decide whether to compete on price, on quality, or with a second line at a lower price.

The shift also moves the advertising competition. When shoppers concentrate on essentials and beauty, more brands chase those searches, and click prices in those categories tend to rise faster than in categories where demand has cooled. A discretionary brand may find advertising cheaper than it was a year ago while an essentials brand pays more for the same clicks, and budgets set for the whole account rather than by category can miss both effects.

Investment follows the same logic. Spending heavily to grow in a shrinking category can buy share at a high price, while spending to defend share in a growing category is usually the better return.

The shift may not last. Inflation fell to 3% in June, the Associated Press reported, and if shoppers regain confidence, discretionary categories may recover before the holidays. Brands in those categories should be ready to add stock and advertising quickly if demand returns. Amazon reports its second-quarter results later on August 3, and the overall number will matter less than whether online store sales returned to growth, whether independent sellers took a still larger share of units, and whether the category pattern held.

The question for a leadership team is which current its category is in, and whether its plan was written for that current or for the total. Reading each brand’s results against its own category is how we run Amazon for brands in essentials and discretionary categories.
