A0434.title: Amazon Q2 2023 results: ad dollars outpace the sales they chase
A0434.alt: A line of brass coins leading across a dark wooden table toward a small kraft-wrapped parcel tied with twine.
A0434.ttag: Amazon Q2 2023 results: ad dollars outpace the sales they chase | Kwontified
A0434.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 22% in Q2 2023 while store sales grew 4%. What that gap says about competition for clicks, and how brands should budget for it.
A0434.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 7, 2023.
A0434.body:
Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 22% in the second quarter of 2023. Sales in its online stores grew 4%, and revenue from services for independent sellers grew 18%. Put the ad line over the other two and the result is a simple, uncomfortable number: about 12.5 cents of advertising for every dollar flowing through the store and its sellers, up from about 11.2 cents a year earlier.

No brand decided to pay more for each sale. The auction decided for them. When the total that advertisers bid grows faster than the purchases they bid on, the price of winning each purchase rises, even in a quarter when shoppers are spending. Brands should plan for a rising cost per sale, make each click worth more, and judge their advertising by the sales it adds.

Amazon Q2 2023 results, line by line

Amazon’s revenue rose 11% to $134.4 billion in the second quarter, and sales in its online stores rose 4% to $53 billion, Bloomberg reported. Advertising revenue rose 22% to $10.7 billion, and revenue from services for independent sellers rose 18% to $32.3 billion, Fortune reported.

Independent sellers accounted for 60% of units sold, the highest share ever, Amazon’s chief financial officer said, according to Fortune. Amazon also pointed to new advertising algorithms that help advertisers reach audiences they could not reach before, as the industry moves away from third-party cookies, SiliconANGLE reported.

The first quarter showed the same pattern, with advertising up 21% while online store sales were flat.

How a crowded auction sets the price of a sale

Amazon’s advertising revenue is the total that brands pay for a limited supply of shopper attention. Each advertiser sets its own bids for its own reasons, and no one coordinates them. But every bid lands in the same auctions, and the price of a click is set by the bids around it. When the total grows faster than the sales it competes for, more ad dollars chase each dollar of sales, and the cost of winning a sale through advertising rises for the average brand.

The ratio makes that visible. Divide advertising revenue by online store sales plus seller services revenue.

In the second quarter of 2023, that came to about 12.5 cents of advertising for every dollar. Working backward from the reported growth rates, the same ratio was about 11.2 cents a year earlier. In the first quarter of 2023, it was about 11.7 cents. Each step is small, but together they mean a brand needs more ad money to produce the same sales.

The ratio is rough. Not every ad dollar targets a store sale, and seller services revenue is fees, not sales. The direction still holds: advertising on Amazon is growing faster than the business it advertises into.

Amazon’s growth also stands out against the wider ad market. In the same quarter, Alphabet’s advertising revenue rose 3% to $58.1 billion, the Associated Press reported, and Meta’s revenue rose 11%. Budgets are moving toward advertising sold next to the point of purchase, where results are easiest to attribute, and that money lands in the auctions brands already compete in.

Prime Day showed the same pressure. Cost per click on the event days rose 58% above the previous 30 days, compared with 50% in 2022, and advertisers’ spending was up 65% from a year earlier, Marketing Dive reported, citing Skai data.

Budgeting for a rising cost per sale

In a market where ad dollars grow faster than sales, a brand that keeps its advertising unchanged will pay more for each sale over time. The budget should assume that. A plan built on 2022 efficiency, and on 2022 click prices, will run short before the fourth quarter.

The cost per sale has two halves, and a brand controls the second one. Click prices are set by the auction. What a click earns is set by conversion rate, order value and organic ranking. Better product content, stronger reviews, bundles that raise order value and reliable stock all lower the effective cost per sale even when click prices rise.

Take a brand spending $50,000 a month on Amazon ads at an advertising cost of 20% of sales. If the cost per click rises 10% and nothing else changes, its advertising cost rises to 22% of sales. If it also lifts its conversion rate by 10% through better content and pricing, it can hold its advertising cost near 20%.

Measurement matters more as auctions crowd. More spending goes to clicks on shoppers who would have bought anyway, especially on branded searches, and tests that withhold spending from part of the audience show which ads actually add sales.

Sponsored placements are also taking more of the page. As Amazon adds ad slots in search results and on product pages, organic positions move further down, and a brand that relies only on organic ranking reaches fewer shoppers than it used to. Organic strength and advertising belong in one plan. With 60% of units now sold by third parties, more sellers compete in the same auctions, often for the same searches, so brands should watch which competitors appear on their most valuable searches and product pages.

The fourth quarter is the test. Amazon guided to revenue of $138 billion to $143 billion for the third quarter, Bloomberg reported, and if advertising keeps growing faster than sales into the holidays, the most crowded auctions of the year will be more crowded than in 2022. If a plan assumes last year’s cost per sale, it starts the quarter short. Building that rising cost into the budget, and into the content that offsets it, is how we plan Amazon advertising for brands.

A0436.crumb: Q4 2023 budget: how to phase spend from…
A0436.title: Q4 2023 budget: how to phase spend from October to Cyber Week
A0436.alt: Four glass jars of coins in rising amounts between a small pumpkin and a kraft-wrapped gift on a windowsill.
A0436.ttag: Q4 2023 budget: how to phase spend from October to Cyber Week | Kwontified
A0436.desc: Cyber Week carried about 17% of 2022 holiday online spending in 8% of the days. How to phase a Q4 2023 ad budget across October, November and December.
A0436.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 8, 2023.
A0436.body:
Cyber Week carried about 17% of 2022 holiday online spending in about 8% of the season’s days. That concentration pulls budgets toward it. The other side of the same arithmetic gets less attention: more than four-fifths of the money was spent outside those five days.

So the Q4 2023 budget should follow the sales, not the headlines. Phase spend to the share of sales each period carries, add a premium for the higher click prices of peak days, and protect enough budget for October, early November and December.

The Q4 2023 budget starts with the 2022 calendar

Online holiday spending in the United States reached a record $211.7 billion from November 1 to December 31, 2022, up 3.5% from 2021, Adobe reported. Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, accounted for $35.3 billion of that, up 4%. Shoppers spent more than $3 billion online on 38 separate days.

Inside Cyber Week, Cyber Monday was the biggest day, at $11.3 billion, followed by Black Friday at $9.12 billion and Thanksgiving at $5.29 billion, according to Adobe.

October now carries an event of its own. Amazon’s October 2022 event, the Prime Early Access Sale, was held on October 11 and 12, EcommerceBytes reported. Amazon has not announced whether it will repeat the event in 2023, but brands should plan as if October will carry a sales event of some kind.

Why a budget phased to the peak overspends

On peak days, demand and click prices rise together. Each dollar buys fewer clicks, though more of those clicks convert. In the quieter weeks around the peak, clicks are cheaper, and shoppers are researching and buying steadily. Those clicks still sell. They simply sell at a lower price per click.

A budget phased only to the peak overpays for crowded clicks and underfunds the weeks where advertising is cheapest and most of the season’s sales take place.

Prime Day 2023 showed both sides of that trade. For advertisers on Skai’s platform, cost per click on the two event days ran 58% above the previous 30 days, while ad-attributed sales ran 5.9 times higher, Marketing Dive reported. Peaks can pay, but each click costs more, and the result depends on the weeks before, when shoppers discover and consider products.

The season is also starting earlier. Adobe found that earlier and more frequent discounts in 2022 helped spending pass $3 billion on 20 days by the end of Cyber Monday. Retailers spread their promotions across November rather than saving them for Black Friday, and shoppers followed, so a brand that waits for Thanksgiving to raise budgets misses part of that demand. The weeks before a peak also build the brand’s position for it: sales history, reviews and organic ranking earned in October and early November help products appear higher during Cyber Week, where every position is contested.

Phase to sales share, then adjust for cost

Start by allocating budget in proportion to the share of sales each period carried for your brand in 2022. Then add a premium for the periods when click prices rise most, and hold a reserve to respond to what happens.

Take a brand with a Q4 advertising budget of $300,000. A starting split might look like this:

PeriodShare of budgetAmount
October, including any Prime event20%$60,000
November 1 to the day before Thanksgiving25%$75,000
Cyber Week, Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday25%$75,000
Day after Cyber Monday to mid-December20%$60,000
Mid-December to December 3110%$30,000

Cyber Week gets a larger share of budget than its share of days, because click prices peak, but not so large that the weeks around it go short. Brands should replace these shares with their own 2022 sales pattern. A brand that sells gifts may weight late November and December more heavily. One that sells everyday products may find October and early November carry more than the table assumes. The point of the exercise is the method, which holds either way.

Shipping cutoffs change the shape of December. Sales slow as the last dates for delivery before the holidays pass, so advertising on products that cannot arrive in time should taper, with budget shifting toward gift cards, digital products or items with fast delivery. After the main cutoffs, shoppers who still need gifts turn to fast delivery, store pickup and gift cards, and click prices often ease as competitors cut budgets, so brands with fast-shipping stock can find efficient sales in those last days.

Stock decides whether any of this pays. A budget is only as good as the inventory behind it. Advertising a product that runs out on Cyber Monday wastes the most expensive clicks of the year. Confirm stock for the October and November events before committing the budget that depends on it.

The reserve is the plan’s insurance. Holding back a small share, around a tenth, lets a brand add spending when a product outperforms or a competitor runs out of stock.

Costs are rising underneath the whole plan. Advertising revenue at Amazon grew 22% in the second quarter of 2023, faster than its store sales, Fortune reported, so each 2023 dollar will buy fewer clicks than the same dollar bought in 2022.

The season should be read week by week, with each week’s sales, click prices and return on ad spend set against the same week of 2022 rather than judged only at the end of the quarter. A week that underdelivers in early November is the signal to move budget while there is still time to use it well. Phasing to sales share and pacing week by week is how we build Q4 budgets for brands.

A0438.crumb: AI shopping assistants: the shopper’s new…
A0438.title: AI shopping assistants: the shopper’s new first reader
A0438.alt: A small white robotic arm holding a brass magnifying glass over a cardboard box and blank cards on a wooden table.
A0438.ttag: AI shopping assistants: the shopper’s new first reader | Kwontified
A0438.desc: In 2023 chatbots began turning into shopping assistants that read product pages and reviews for the shopper. What that changes about how a brand gets found.
A0438.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 10, 2023.
A0438.body:
A parent who needs a stroller that folds small enough for a compact car has always done the reading alone: open one listing at a time, squint at the dimensions, scroll the reviews for anyone who mentions a trunk. That parent started getting help in 2023. Ask an AI shopping assistant the same question, and it reads the listings and reviews first, then hands back a short answer.

That shift moves the first reader of a product page from a person to a machine. The brands that do well with it publish complete, consistent product data, collect reviews that describe how a product actually performs, and write content that answers the questions shoppers really ask.

AI shopping assistants arrived in three steps

The change came over a few months. In March, OpenAI let companies build plugins for ChatGPT, with Instacart, Klarna and Shopify among the first, MediaPost reported. A chatbot could now look up real products and help a shopper fill a cart.

In May, Google introduced its Search Generative Experience, a test of answers written by AI at the top of search results, with shopping as one of its main uses. It draws on Google’s Shopping Graph, which holds 35 billion product listings, 1.8 billion of them refreshed every hour, Retail TouchPoints reported.

Days later, Amazon job listings described plans for an interactive, conversational search experience that could answer product questions, compare items and make personalized suggestions, VentureBeat reported. In June, Amazon confirmed it was testing summaries of customer reviews, generated by AI, on some product pages, Business Insider reported.

What a machine reads that a person skims

In traditional search, the shopper types a few keywords, scans a list and opens the listings that look right. Title, main image and price compete for a glance, and a great deal of the listing below the fold is never read at all.

An AI assistant works the other way round. It reads the parts a hurried shopper skips: the attribute fields, the bullet points, the reviews three pages deep. It weighs and summarizes them before a person sees anything, and the shopper may never see most of the products it considered.

The page is judged on different things as a result. A listing that looks appealing but is thin on specifics can be passed over when the assistant is looking for one attribute. Reviews that describe how a product performs give it more to work with than reviews that simply praise. And inconsistent details, such as different dimensions on different sites, make a product harder for a machine to trust.

The shopper’s own habits shift as well. Someone who can ask a detailed question tends to ask a narrower one. Instead of searching a broad category, she describes her situation and expects a short list back, and the few products on that list are there for a reason she stated. A brand that once competed across a full page of results now competes for one of a handful of places in an answer, and the products that miss the cut are never seen at all.

The platforms are competing to own that first question. Google wants shoppers to start in its search, Amazon in its store, and the chatbot makers in a conversation. Whichever one a shopper uses, each assistant draws on the same raw material: the product data brands publish and the reviews customers leave. Improving that material improves a brand’s standing in all of them at once.

Measurement gets harder along the way. A shopper who asks an assistant and then buys may land on a listing without a keyword search, so the usual search reports miss part of how she found the product. Changes in how traffic arrives are worth watching as these tools spread.

Take a luggage brand whose carry-on fits most airline size limits. Its listing calls the bag travel-ready but never states the dimensions in the title or bullets, and its reviews mostly say it is a great bag. A shopper asks an assistant for a carry-on that fits one airline’s limit. The assistant recommends a competitor whose listing gives the exact size and whose reviews mention fitting in overhead bins, and the brand loses a sale it was qualified to win.

The work that pays off on every platform

None of this depends on which assistant wins. Complete, consistent product data comes first. Titles, bullets and attributes should state the facts a shopper might ask about, such as size, materials, compatibility and use, in plain terms. The same facts should be written the same way on every channel where the product sells, because an assistant that finds two different measurements has a reason to recommend something else.

Reviews are the second piece of material. Brands cannot write reviews, but they can encourage customers to share specifics, through follow-up messages and product inserts that ask how the product performed. Amazon’s review summaries, in their test version, drew out themes from what customers wrote, and products whose reviews mention concrete qualities give those summaries more to say.

The third piece is the content around the listing. Brand pages, A+ content and question-and-answer sections should address the questions shoppers actually ask, which a brand can find in its customer service logs, its search terms and its existing reviews.

AI search was still in testing in 2023, and nobody yet knows which assistant shoppers will settle on. The useful question for a team is simpler: could a machine that reads every word of our listing answer the shopper’s question from it? Making sure the answer is yes, listing by listing, is how we prepare product data and content for AI shopping assistants.

A0440.crumb: Temu delivery times: why shoppers wait…
A0440.title: Temu delivery times: why shoppers wait, and where brands win
A0440.alt: A parcel on the doorstep of a thatched stone cottage with roses, beside a winding country lane through green hills.
A0440.ttag: Temu delivery times: why shoppers wait, and where brands win | Kwontified
A0440.desc: Temu’s low prices rest on small parcels shipped straight from China, duty-free and slow to arrive. Why shoppers accept the wait, and where brands still win.
A0440.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 15, 2023.
A0440.body:
A $12 kitchen gadget can reach a shopper by two routes. Imported in bulk into a U.S. warehouse, it pays import duty and storage costs and arrives in a day or two from Amazon. Shipped as a single parcel straight from China, it skips the duty and the warehouse, sells for much less, and takes far longer to arrive. The second route is the one Temu is built on.

That route only wins when the shopper cares more about the price than the wait. Temu’s low prices come from shipping individual parcels under the U.S. duty exemption for small shipments, and the same model makes delivery slow. Brands should compete where speed, certainty and trust matter rather than on Temu’s price, and keep an eye on the policy that makes the model possible.

Temu delivery times begin at the border

The U.S. “de minimis” rule lets packages valued at $800 or less enter the country free of import duties, as long as they are shipped to individuals, and such packages often sidestep the usual customs inspections, Business Day reported.

Temu and Shein lean on that rule heavily. A House select committee found that the two companies are likely responsible for more than 30% of all packages shipped to the United States each day under the provision. They also account for nearly half of all such shipments from China, according to the committee. Together they accounted for almost 600,000 packages a day, The New York Times reported.

The cost difference shows up plainly in what each company pays. The committee’s report said H&M and Gap paid $205 million and $700 million respectively in import duties in 2022, while Shein and Temu, whose packages ship directly to customers, paid nothing.

Two routes, two different costs

Bulk import to a U.S. warehouseDirect-ship parcel from China
Import dutyPaid on every containerNone under the de minimis rule
Domestic warehousingPaid by the brandNot needed
DeliveryFast and predictable from local stockSlower, with more handoffs
Where it winsUrgent, considered or returnable itemsCheap, non-urgent, impulse items

Read the table one column at a time. Every advantage on the right comes from the rules at the border. Every advantage on the left comes from stock that is already in the country.

A parcel shipped directly to a shopper under the exemption pays no import duty and needs no domestic warehouse, so the landed cost of a cheap item falls sharply. But the parcel travels farther and passes through more handoffs, so delivery is slower and less predictable than from a warehouse in the same country. It is the difference between sending freight by slow boat and by express courier: the cheap option is fine until something is needed by a date.

That is the trade, and both sides of it are real. When the item is cheap, the saving is large relative to its price, and when it is not needed soon, the wait costs little. A phone case, a set of kitchen gadgets or a novelty gift fits that description. A replacement charger needed tomorrow, a gift for a birthday this week, or a product where quality and returns matter does not.

For the shopper who wants the gadget eventually, the cheaper parcel wins. For the one cooking dinner this weekend, it does not. Each shopper is making a small bet on patience, and the bet only pays when nothing depends on the date.

The gap behind those prices is structural. A brand that imports in bulk pays duty on every container and carries the cost of the warehouse space that lets it deliver quickly. A direct-ship seller pays neither. No amount of advertising efficiency or supplier negotiation closes a gap that comes from the rules on how goods enter the country, so the numbers lean clearly toward competing on something other than price.

Where brands win against direct shipping

Speed is ground a brand selling from domestic stock already holds. Fast, reliable delivery through Amazon’s fulfillment network, Walmart Fulfillment Services or similar options is an advantage Temu’s model cannot easily match, and the fastest delivery promise belongs on every listing, with the stock to honor it.

Shoppers also pay for certainty about quality. Clear product information, strong reviews, warranties and easy returns give shoppers reasons to pay more, and they matter most in categories where a cheap item that fails is a real cost.

The choice of where to compete sits underneath both. Products that are cheap, generic and non-urgent are exposed to direct-ship pricing. Products that are branded, considered or needed quickly are much less so, and a brand should know which of its products fall into each group before it sets prices or budgets. Each of these is a reason for a shopper to pay more. None of them is a reason to match a lower price.

The policy risk cuts in brands’ favor. A bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced bills in June 2023 that would end de minimis treatment for shipments from China, Business Day reported. If the exemption narrows, Temu’s cost advantage shrinks, and its prices may rise or its delivery model may change.

Temu itself may change too. Like other direct-ship sellers, it may add warehouses closer to shoppers over time, which would speed delivery but add some of the costs it now avoids, and would put it in more direct competition on speed. Until then, the rule for a brand is simple: if a shopper would happily wait to save money on the item, do not fight that sale on price. Sorting products by that test, and competing hard on the rest, is how we help brands compete with Temu on Amazon and Walmart.

A0441.crumb: INFORM Act: the end of anonymous…
A0441.title: INFORM Act: the end of anonymous marketplace sellers
A0441.alt: A blank brass plaque on a navy wooden door beside a blurred shopfront with baskets of goods.
A0441.ttag: INFORM Act: the end of anonymous marketplace sellers | Kwontified
A0441.desc: The INFORM Act, in force since June 27, makes marketplaces verify high-volume sellers. How seller anonymity took hold, and what its end means for brands.
A0441.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 17, 2023.
A0441.body:
A brand manager who found her product listed far below its usual price on a marketplace would click on the seller’s name and learn very little: a store name, a rating, perhaps a short description. If she reported it and the store disappeared, the same goods could reappear with another store name. Anonymity was built into the way marketplaces grew.

The INFORM Consumers Act, in force since June 27, 2023, ends much of that anonymity for high-volume sellers. For brands, the law is a tool and an obligation at once: it makes unauthorized sellers easier to identify and act against, and it holds the brand’s own seller accounts, and those of its partners, to the same rules.

How the INFORM Act answers years of seller anonymity

Marketplaces grew by making selling easy. A seller could open an account, pick a store name and list products, often with limited checks on who stood behind it. That openness gave shoppers an enormous selection, and it gave bad actors room to operate. A counterfeiter shut down under one name could return under another.

The marketplaces built their own defenses. In 2022 alone, Amazon stopped more than 800,000 attempts to open selling accounts before a single product was listed, its 2022 Brand Protection Report says, according to Amazon. Each marketplace set its own rules, though, and no common legal standard said who a seller had to be.

The INFORM Consumers Act supplied one. Congress passed it inside a larger spending bill, and it took effect 180 days later, Gibson Dunn explained.

What the law asks of marketplaces

The law covers “high-volume” third-party sellers, meaning those with at least 200 sales, counting only new or unused consumer products, plus at least $5,000 in gross revenue within any 12 continuous months of the past 24 months. A marketplace has to collect and verify each such seller’s bank account, tax ID and contact information, and suspend a seller who fails to respond within 10 days, Fenwick reported.

Larger sellers face disclosure as well. Any seller whose annual gross revenue on a single marketplace is $20,000 or more must show identifying information to shoppers, and every product listing must give shoppers a way to report suspicious activity. On June 20, the Federal Trade Commission sent letters to 50 online marketplaces reminding them of their obligations, Fenwick noted.

What changes for the people selling your products

The first effect is accountability. A seller who has verified a real bank account and tax identity cannot easily vanish and reappear under a new name, so shutting down a bad actor now lasts.

Visibility follows. Shoppers can see who the largest sellers are, which makes a reputable business easier to tell apart from an unknown one, and over time may favor sellers that trade under a name a shopper can recognize, including brands selling as themselves. A brand that has sold under its own name for years gains a small advantage it did not have before, simply by being recognizable.

The reporting channel is the quieter change. Every listing now carries a way for shoppers to flag something suspicious, which gives brands and their customers one more route to surface counterfeits and unauthorized sellers. A pattern of reports from genuine shoppers is harder for a marketplace to overlook than a single complaint from the brand.

Take a skincare brand that has struggled with an unknown reseller undercutting its prices on Amazon. Before the law, the reseller’s store name told the brand little, and a takedown might simply produce a new account. Now, if the reseller is high volume, its identity has been verified, and if it is large enough, some of that identity shows on its storefront. The brand has a clearer target for a distribution inquiry, a legal letter or a report. None of that removes the need for evidence, but it shortens the search for who is behind the listing.

Putting the new transparency to work

The practical starting point is a map: every seller offering the brand’s products on each marketplace, the identifying information now available for each, and a clear line between authorized sellers and unknown ones. With identities clearer, a brand can trace unauthorized stock back to its source, enforce its distribution agreements, and report counterfeit or suspicious listings through each marketplace’s tools and the new reporting channel.

The obligations land on the brand too. A brand that sells as a third-party seller is a high-volume seller under the law, which means keeping bank, tax and contact details current and answering verification requests quickly, because a missed request can lead to a suspension. Those notices need to reach an inbox someone actually reads, with a named person responsible for answering them, because the account that gets suspended is the one whose verification email sat unopened.

The same rules reach a brand’s authorized partners. Distributors and resellers who sell its products as third-party sellers face the same verification and disclosure requirements, and a distributor suspended over a missed request takes the brand’s products off the shelf with it. Asking authorized sellers to confirm they comply, and writing the requirement into distribution agreements, keeps the law working for the brand.

The law will not end counterfeits by itself, and enforcement depends on how strictly each marketplace applies it. What it removes is one of the oldest advantages bad actors had, the ability to hide. The leadership question is whether anyone on the team knows, seller by seller, who is selling its products. Building that map and keeping it current is how we manage brand protection and seller compliance for brands.

A0442.title: Hyper-personalization: going beyond ‘recommended for you’
A0442.alt: A plaid tweed jacket on a tailor's dress form with a tape measure and pincushion beside a cluttered workbench.
A0442.ttag: Hyper-personalization: going beyond ‘recommended for you’ | Kwontified
A0442.desc: Personalization most often lifts revenue 10% to 15%, McKinsey found. The gains come from tailoring offer, message and timing where shoppers truly differ.
A0442.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 22, 2023.
A0442.body:
Every shopper on a large retail site has scrolled past the grid labeled “recommended for you,” a row of products chosen from what they viewed last week. It is the familiar face of personalization. McKinsey’s research puts the most common revenue lift from personalization at 10% to 15%, and most of that money comes from tailoring the offer, the message and the timing to what a shopper is trying to do. A longer row of products rarely changes that decision.

So the useful question is where tailoring changes what a shopper does. The answer comes down to two conditions: the brand can tell shoppers apart with data it actually holds, and the best response really differs between them. Where both hold, personalization earns its cost. The place most brands can start is first-time versus repeat buyers, on the channels where they can see the difference.

What the evidence says about hyper-personalization

Shoppers have come to expect it: in McKinsey’s 2021 research, 71% of consumers said they expect companies to deliver personalized interactions, and 76% said they get frustrated when that does not happen, McKinsey reported. The same research found that personalization most often drives a revenue lift of 10% to 15%, with results for individual companies ranging from 5% to 25% depending on the sector and how well they execute.

The effect reaches behavior too. In the same survey, 76% of consumers said personalized communications made them more likely to consider a brand, and 78% said such content made them more likely to buy again.

The tools keep getting more capable. In April, Zalando began testing a fashion assistant powered by ChatGPT that lets customers search in their own words. It said it planned to combine the assistant with preferences such as the brands a customer follows and products available in their size, Fashion Network reported.

Two conditions decide whether personalization pays

A personalized experience earns more than a generic one only when two things are true at once. The brand must be able to tell shoppers apart using data it actually has. And the best offer, message or timing must genuinely differ between those shoppers.

Where both conditions are met, personalization pays. Where either fails, it adds cost without return. A brand that personalizes on thin data guesses wrong, and a brand that personalizes where every shopper wants the same thing spends money to deliver the same answer in different packaging.

The recommendation grid clears the first condition easily and often fails the second. It shows more products, but for many shoppers the decision does not turn on seeing more products. It turns on whether the offer fits, whether the message answers the question they arrived with, and whether it reaches them when they are ready to buy.

Take a skincare brand with two kinds of customer. The first-time shopper is unsure which product suits her skin and whether the brand is worth the price. The repeat buyer knows the product and wants to reorder without friction. Show both of them the same recommendations and neither gets what she came for.

A trial size with clear guidance for the first, and a subscription or bundle for the second, speak to the actual decision. The products are the same in both cases; the offer and the message change.

Where tailoring changes the decision

How far a brand can go depends on what it can see. On its own website the scope is broad, because the brand owns the data. On marketplaces the brand sees less, but it still has tools. On Amazon, a brand can tailor its brand store, use audiences built from shopping behavior in its advertising, and offer coupons or deals to specific groups such as repeat customers or brand followers.

The aim is to find the few moments where a tailored response changes what the shopper does, and to invest there before anywhere else. Three of them usually repay the effort.

New and repeat customers are the clearest split, and most channels can tell them apart. Their needs differ sharply: new customers need reassurance and an easy first purchase, while repeat customers need convenience and a reason to stay.

Timing is the next lever. A shopper who bought a product that runs out in 30 days is more likely to respond to a reminder around day 25 than at a random moment. In consumable categories, replenishment timing is one of the clearest wins available.

The message itself rounds out the list. Shoppers who arrive from a search for a specific problem respond to content that addresses that problem. Matching the advertising message and the product page to the search that brought the shopper in is personalization most brands can do now, with the data they already have.

The limits, and the test that keeps personalization honest

Personalization runs into limits on two sides. Shoppers want relevance, but not the sense of being watched, and an offer that reveals too much about what a brand knows can feel intrusive. The data is also getting harder to collect. Google’s stated plan is to phase out Chrome’s third-party cookies during the second half of 2024, 9to5Google reported. Personalization built on a brand’s own customer relationships, and on the audiences retailers provide, will hold up better than personalization built on tracking shoppers across the web.

Measurement decides whether any of it was worth doing. A personalized offer should be tested against a generic one, with a group that does not receive it, so the lift is real and not borrowed from sales that would have happened anyway. A tailored experience that cannot beat the generic version in that comparison has not earned its cost, however clever it looks.

Before building anything, write down three things: the two groups, the data that separates them, and the different response each should get. If any of the three is missing, the generic page will do the same job for less. Working through that list, on a brand’s own site and across its marketplaces, is how we find where personalization pays for brands.

A0444.crumb: AI co-pilots for sales and support: who…
A0444.title: AI co-pilots for sales and support: who gains most
A0444.alt: A white robotic arm beside vintage headphones and a brass service bell on a wooden counter against a yellow wall.
A0444.ttag: AI co-pilots for sales and support: who gains most | Kwontified
A0444.desc: A study of 5,179 support agents found an AI assistant raised productivity 14%, and 34% for newer agents. What that means for brand sales and support teams.
A0444.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 24, 2023.
A0444.body:
A software company gave its customer support agents an AI assistant, but not all at once. It switched the tool on in stages, which meant that for a while some agents answered chats with it and some without, doing the same job. That rollout made customer support one of the first places where generative AI was measured across thousands of workers. The newest agents gained the most. The best ones barely changed.

That pattern matters well beyond call centers. An AI co-pilot spreads the habits of a team’s strongest people to everyone else, so its value sits wherever new people do customer-facing work that experienced colleagues already do well.

What the AI co-pilots study found

The economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond studied 5,179 customer support agents at that company, their working paper shows. The assistant watched each customer chat and suggested responses in real time. Agents stayed in charge of the conversation and could ignore the suggestions.

Access to the tool raised productivity, measured as issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average. For novice and less-skilled agents, the gain was 34%. For the most experienced and skilled agents, the effect was minimal. The researchers also found that AI assistance improved customer sentiment and increased employee retention.

Support was a natural place for this kind of measurement. The first wave of generative AI at work was mostly experiments with drafting emails, summarizing documents and answering internal questions. Support could be measured because its teams already counted how many issues each person resolved and how customers felt afterward.

Why the newest agents gained most

The researchers suggested that the AI model spreads the best practices of more able workers, helping newer agents move down the learning curve faster. The assistant learned what good answers looked like from the strongest agents’ conversations and offered those answers to everyone. An experienced agent already knew them, so the suggestions added little. A new agent did not, and the suggestions closed much of the gap.

That changes how a team is built. A new support or sales person has traditionally needed months to reach full speed, learning from mistakes, manuals and colleagues. A co-pilot compresses that learning. Experienced people do not become less important in the process; they become the source of the practices the tool spreads, and the people who handle the cases it does not cover.

Customers feel that difference too. When every agent can draw on the best answers, the distance between a good conversation and a poor one narrows, and the study’s finding on customer sentiment suggests customers noticed.

Brands already run something like a support desk

Most brands we work with do not run large call centers, yet much of their customer-facing work looks like the support role in the study. On marketplaces they answer buyer messages about orders, sizing, compatibility and returns, often under response-time requirements. They write and update product content. Their account teams field questions from retail buyers, distributors and marketplace partners.

An apparel brand with a small team answering Amazon buyer messages shows how this plays out. Its most experienced member knows how to answer a fit question in a way that heads off a return, and how to handle an angry customer without escalating. A new hire does not. A co-pilot trained on the experienced person’s past replies can suggest those answers to the new hire from the first week, while the experienced person reviews the hardest cases.

The pattern repeats in account work. An experienced account manager knows how to prepare for a retailer review, which numbers a buyer will ask about, and how to frame a request for more promotional support. A newer colleague learns this slowly. A co-pilot that drafts meeting notes, summarizes performance and suggests talking points from the team’s best past work can shorten that learning, while the experienced person still decides what to ask for and when.

What leaders should settle before rolling one out

The study points to where a co-pilot belongs first: wherever new or junior people do repetitive, text-heavy work, such as buyer messaging, review responses and routine partner questions. It also points to what a co-pilot needs. It can only spread what it can learn from, so a brand that has never gathered its best customer replies, product answers and partner communications gives the tool little good material to draw on.

The finding on skilled agents sets a boundary. The tool did little for the people with the most experience, which suggests it does not replace the judgment experience brings: handling an unusual complaint, negotiating with a retailer, deciding when to make an exception. Those calls should stay with experienced people.

Quality needs watching too. A co-pilot that suggests a wrong answer confidently can spread a mistake as quickly as it spreads a good practice, and reviewing a sample of the replies drafted with the tool weekly, especially early on, catches problems before customers do. The same review shows which suggestions agents keep ignoring, and those are the places to check the material the tool learned from. Marketplace rules add one more layer. Buyer messages on Amazon and other marketplaces must follow each platform’s communication policies, a tool that drafts replies must be set up to respect them, and responsibility for what is sent stays with the brand.

The decision in front of leadership, then, is less whether to try a co-pilot than where its newest people spend their first months, and who on the team has the answers worth spreading. Starting with those two lists, across buyer messaging and account work, is how we bring AI co-pilots into marketplace operations for brands.

A0445.title: Amazon coupons: the visible promotion brands often misuse
A0445.alt: Brass scissors on a pile of cut cream paper squares on a worn wooden table by a blue wall.
A0445.ttag: Amazon coupons: the visible promotion brands often misuse | Kwontified
A0445.desc: Amazon coupons cost the discount plus a $0.60 fee on every redemption. Why that fixed fee punishes cheap products, and when a coupon actually earns its cost.
A0445.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 29, 2023.
A0445.body:
A 15% coupon on a $10 product costs the brand 21% of the price every time a shopper uses it. The gap between those two numbers is a fixed $0.60 fee that Amazon charges on each redemption, and it is only the visible part of what a coupon costs. The rest is the discount paid to shoppers who would have bought at full price.

So a coupon earns its cost only where the badge wins buyers who would not otherwise convert, and where the fee is small next to the price. Run by default, on every product, it mostly buys sales the brand already had.

How Amazon coupons work

Coupons have been part of Seller Central since 2017. A seller can offer a percentage or money-off discount, set between 5% and 80% of the product’s lowest price in the previous 30 days, and target all shoppers or specific groups. Each redemption carries a $0.60 fee on top of the discount, and both come out of the coupon’s budget, Viral Launch explained when the feature arrived.

Shoppers see a coupon as a badge in search results and on the product page, and “clip” it to apply the discount at checkout. The coupon’s main appeal is that visibility. A quiet price cut changes a number on the page; a coupon draws the eye.

A fixed fee weighs most on cheap products

The badge raises the share of shoppers who click and buy. But every redemption costs the discount plus the fee, whether or not that shopper needed the incentive. A coupon pays only when the extra buyers it wins outweigh the cost of discounting sales that would have happened anyway.

The fee is the easier cost to miss, because it does not scale with price. The same coupon logic applied to three price points shows how quickly it grows as a share of what the shopper pays:

PriceCouponDiscountFeeCost per redemptionShare of price
$3015%$4.50$0.60$5.1017%
$1015%$1.50$0.60$2.1021%
$820%$1.60$0.60$2.2027.5%

On the $30 product, the fee barely shows next to the discount. On the $8 product, a 20% coupon ends up costing 27.5% of the price. A brand that judges coupons by the discount percentage alone is reading the smaller of the two numbers.

The buyers who did not need the coupon

In a report, the second cost is harder to see. A loyal customer reordering a favorite product will clip a coupon if it is there, because there is no reason not to. The brand pays the discount and the fee on a sale it would have made at full price. On products with many repeat buyers, a large share of redemptions can fall into this group.

A slower cost builds over time. A product that always carries a coupon trains shoppers to expect it. Remove the coupon and conversion can fall below where it was before the coupon started, because the badge has become part of what shoppers see as the normal price.

Where a coupon earns its cost

The useful test is whether the badge changes behavior at a fee the margin can carry. That points coupons toward a short list of situations.

A product launch, or a product with few reviews, is where the badge earns its keep. Shoppers need a nudge to try something unfamiliar, and because most buyers are new, few redemptions are wasted on people who would have bought anyway.

The same logic covers competitive search: where a product sits among close alternatives in search results, the badge can be the difference that wins the click. Targeting helps as well: coupons aimed at specific groups, such as shoppers who have not bought from the brand before, cut the waste on loyal customers. And a coupon can move aging inventory before storage fees rise, where the alternative is a deeper price cut or a removal.

Coupons tend to lose money in the opposite cases: on cheap products, where the fixed fee is a large share of the price, and on established products bought mostly by repeat customers.

The math shifts again once advertising is involved. A coupon raises conversion, which can make the same ad spend more productive, but it also lowers the revenue from each sale. The coupon and the advertising around it should be judged together, comparing profit after the discount, the fee and the ad cost with and without the coupon.

Event timing matters as well. During big sales events, many products in a search carry badges, so a coupon stands out less while costing the same per redemption. A coupon that wins clicks in a quiet week may do little during Cyber Week, when deals are everywhere, so the decision belongs event by event, against the deals already running.

Vendors have a version of the same choice. Brands that sell to Amazon wholesale can also fund coupons, under the terms of their vendor agreements, and the same test applies: whether the badge wins buyers who would not otherwise convert, at a cost the margin can carry.

Measure the coupon, not the redemptions

Redemption counts say how many shoppers clipped the coupon, not how many were won by it. The cleaner measure is to run a coupon for a defined period, compare sales, conversion and profit with a similar period without it, and continue only on that evidence.

Before renewing any coupon, add $0.60 to the discount and divide by the price. If that share is more than the margin can absorb, or most buyers of the product are repeat customers, let the coupon lapse and watch what happens to profit after advertising. Planning promotions and advertising as one budget is how we review Amazon coupons for brands.

A0446.crumb: Amazon’s October event: who decides, and…
A0446.title: Amazon’s October event: who decides, and when
A0446.alt: Stacks of twine-tied kraft parcels with small pumpkins and autumn leaves on a farmhouse dining table.
A0446.ttag: Amazon’s October event: who decides, and when | Kwontified
A0446.desc: Amazon’s October 2022 event drew 28.4% of households to Prime Day’s 34.1%. Why its decisions fall due before it is announced, and who should own them.
A0446.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 31, 2023.
A0446.body:
Amazon added a second Prime event in 2022. It announced the October sale in September 2022, Chain Store Age reported, and the Prime Early Access Sale ran on October 11 and 12, EcommerceBytes reported. Brands had only weeks between the announcement and the event.

The question now in front of leadership teams is whether to commit deals, stock and advertising money to an event that has not yet been confirmed, and who gets to make that call. Finance can fairly ask why margin should be committed to a date nobody has published. Marketing can fairly ask what happens if competitors arrive with deals and stock while the brand waits for confirmation.

The answer is that someone has to make it now, and it should be one person. The October event is smaller than July’s Prime Day, but it opens the holiday season, and the decisions it requires fall due before Amazon announces it.

What the 2022 Amazon October event showed

The event was smaller than Prime Day. According to Numerator’s recap, 28.4% of U.S. households took part, compared with 34.1% for Prime Day 2022. Spend per household was $117 against $177 for Prime Day, and the average order was $50 against $61, Numerator found.

Smaller is still large. The event reached that share of households in two days, at the moment shoppers begin to think about the holidays, and brands should plan as if Amazon will hold an October event again in 2023, even before it confirms the dates.

The category mix was telling. In 2022, toys were the only category with higher shopper participation in the October event than in July, according to Numerator. October shoppers were starting early on gifts and essentials.

Three teams, three reasonable calls

Every major decision for the event has a lead time longer than the gap between announcement and event. Deals must be submitted and approved in advance. Inventory has to be in Amazon’s warehouses before the event, and shipments take weeks to arrive and be received. Budgets for advertising and discounts need approval from people who also manage the rest of the fourth quarter. So the October event is decided in August and early September, by people working from the 2022 pattern rather than a confirmed date.

Those decisions rarely sit in one place.

Marketing wants deals and advertising. Finance wants to protect margin for the holidays. Supply chain wants to avoid shipping stock that then sits unsold. Each makes a reasonable call on its own piece, and the pieces do not always fit. A deal approved without the stock to support it, or stock sent without a deal or advertising to move it, wastes the effort.

Take a home goods brand whose marketing team submits deals for the October event after its supply chain team has already allocated stock to the holiday season. The deals go live with thin inventory, sell out on the first morning, and the products lose ranking just before Black Friday. Nobody in that sequence made a bad decision, and each team could defend its own choice. What was missing was anyone who owned the whole picture.

One owner, one plan, one season

The fix is organizational before it is tactical. One person should be responsible for the October event across deals, inventory and advertising, with the authority to make trade-offs between them. Marketing, finance and supply chain should then settle the October plan together, in a single session before September, so that the deals submitted, the stock sent and the budget approved match. The session has three questions to answer, using the 2022 results: what to discount, what to ship and what to spend.

That owner should plan October as part of the holiday season rather than as a separate promotion. The event is the first step of the fourth quarter. Its results, from deal performance to ranking gains, should feed directly into Black Friday and Cyber Monday plans, and the stock it uses should be counted against holiday needs, not on top of them.

Amazon is not the only retailer in October either. Numerator’s 2022 recap also covered Walmart’s Rollbacks & More event and Target Deal Days, which ran around the same time. Brands that sell across retailers have to decide whether to match offers everywhere or concentrate on one, and that decision belongs to the same owner and the same planning session.

Sizing the plan, and judging it afterward

The evidence should set expectations. The 2022 figures suggest an October event delivers less than July’s Prime Day, and a plan sized like July’s can leave a brand with excess stock and spent budget heading into the busiest weeks of the year.

Product choice follows from what October shoppers were doing. Brands should feature products that suit an early start on gifts and essentials, and hold back those better suited to deeper holiday discounts later. That is a product-by-product decision, made in the same session as the stock plan, rather than a discount across the whole range.

Advertising needs its own plan. Click prices rise on event days as more brands compete, and the days before the event shape which products shoppers already know. The event budget should cover the build-up as well as the two days themselves. The team should also agree in advance how it will judge the result: on profit after discounts and advertising, compared with a normal October week, rather than on event-day sales alone.

The meeting that settles all of this needs one person running it. Holding it in August, with last October’s numbers on the table, is how we plan Amazon’s October event for brands as the opening of their holiday calendar.

A0449.crumb: Amazon mobile search bar test: what it…
A0449.title: Amazon mobile search bar test: what it reveals for brands
A0449.alt: A smartphone with a glowing notification sits in a wooden stand on a rustic desk beside a succulent, cup and notebook.
A0449.ttag: Amazon mobile search bar test: what it reveals for brands | Kwontified
A0449.desc: In June Amazon began testing a search box at the bottom of its app, within reach of a thumb. What it says about mobile search, and how brands should respond.
A0449.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 5, 2023.
A0449.body:
Hold a phone in one hand and try to tap the top of the screen with your thumb. On June 1, Amazon began testing a layout for its shopping app that removes the stretch: the search box moves from the top of the screen to the bottom, GeekWire reported.

It is a small change with a large message. The test shows that Amazon treats search as the center of mobile shopping and will rebuild the app to make searching easier. Sponsored ads and organic ranking both live in search results, so the space brands should design for is the small first screen of mobile results, where titles are cut short and images decide the tap.

What the Amazon mobile search bar test changed

The aim was to keep the search box within easy reach for someone using a phone with one hand. The box stays fixed at the bottom as the shopper scrolls. Amazon said it was testing the layout with select mobile customers in the United States, on both iPhone and Android, and would roll it out to more customers worldwide in the coming months.

Not every shopper welcomed the change, at least at first. Threads on Amazon’s customer forum in June filled with complaints from shoppers who wanted the search box back at the top, Amazon’s forum shows. The purpose of the test is clear enough, whatever its final outcome.

Easier searching pulls shopping into results pages

The easier it is to search, the more often shoppers search rather than browse. Every search produces a results page where sponsored and organic listings compete. A design that makes searching easier therefore shifts more shopping into search results.

Amazon would not spend effort moving a single box unless search were central to how it expects shoppers to use its app. A company that wants shoppers to browse puts recommendations and categories within reach. A company that moves the search box to where the thumb rests is betting that shoppers will search more.

On a phone, those results are cramped. Only a few listings fit on the first screen, and titles are cut short. The main image, the price, the rating and the first words of the title decide which listing a shopper taps. Search results are also where Sponsored Products ads appear and where organic rank is won, so if mobile shopping concentrates further in search, the first screen of mobile results becomes the most valuable space a brand competes for.

What a cut-short title costs

Take a listing whose title reads “Premium Hydrating Face Moisturizer with Hyaluronic Acid, Ceramides and Niacinamide for Dry Sensitive Skin, Fragrance Free, 1.7 oz.” On a desktop, the shopper sees most of it. On a phone, the shopper may see only the first several words, so the size, the skin type and the fragrance-free claim disappear.

A competitor whose title leads with “Fragrance-Free Moisturizer for Sensitive Skin” shows the shopper what she is looking for in the space she can see. Both products may be equally good. Only one of them says so before the cut.

Long titles packed with features made sense on a desktop results page, where most of the title was visible and each extra term described the product a little more fully. The habit is understandable, since it was built for the desktop page. On the phone, the same title spends its first words on adjectives while the answer to the shopper’s actual question waits further along, out of view.

The words a shopper sees before the title is cut short should carry the product type and the attribute that matters most for the search. Brand names and long lists of features can follow. The main image carries even more weight on a small screen. It should show the product clearly, at a size that reads on a phone, and where the rules allow, make the key difference visible, such as the pack size or the variant.

The same logic applies to advertising. Sponsored Products ads at the top of search results are especially valuable on a phone, where the first screen holds so few listings. Brands should review how their ads perform at the top of search, and whether their bids and listings are strong enough to win there.

Check listings where shoppers see them

The team that writes product content usually works on a desktop, while most shoppers see the result on a small screen. Looking at a listing on a phone, the way a shopper does, often reveals problems a desktop view hides.

Amazon’s testing habit deserves its own attention. Amazon runs experiments like this on groups of shoppers all the time, which means two shoppers can see different layouts on the same day. A brand’s sales or click rates can shift because of a test the brand never sees. When mobile performance moves without an obvious cause, an app test is one explanation worth considering before rewriting a listing or changing bids.

Amazon will keep testing its app, and the search box may move again. The direction of these tests, toward faster and easier searching on a phone, is the part brands can plan around, and brands that compete well on the first mobile screen will benefit whichever layout Amazon settles on.

A practical check before the next listing update: open the product on a phone, read only what fits on the first screen, and ask whether a shopper could tell what it is and why it suits her. If not, rewrite the first words and the main image before touching the bids. Making that first screen do its job, for listings and ads together, is how we approach mobile search for brands on Amazon.

A0450.crumb: KPIs for AI shopping: what to measure…
A0450.title: KPIs for AI shopping: what to measure when machines read first
A0450.alt: A brass gauge panel with dials and knobs sits on a wooden shelf beside a small white robotic arm and a potted plant.
A0450.ttag: KPIs for AI shopping: what to measure when machines read first | Kwontified
A0450.desc: As AI assistants start reading product pages for shoppers, clicks and rankings tell less of the story. Four measures brands can start tracking now.
A0450.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 7, 2023.
A0450.body:
A shopper wants a frying pan that works on an induction stove. Instead of scrolling a results page, she asks an assistant, which reads the listings and reviews and names a few pans. If a brand’s pan is not among them, its weekly report will not show a lower click-through rate or a drop in rank. It will show nothing, because the product never reached the stage those numbers measure.

That gap is the reason to rethink KPIs for AI shopping now. Rank, clicks and conversion were built for a shopper who searches, scans and clicks. When a machine reads first, brands also need to measure whether their product information can be read, and whether their products appear in the answers.

How 2023 put a reader between the brand and the shopper

The measures brands rely on were built for a particular way of shopping. A shopper types a search, scans a list of results and clicks, so brands track where they rank, how often shoppers click, and how often those clicks become sales.

In 2023, that pattern started to change. In May, Google began testing answers composed by AI for shopping searches, drawing on a Shopping Graph of 35 billion product listings, Retail TouchPoints reported. Amazon, for its part, confirmed in June that it was testing AI summaries of customer reviews, Business Insider reported. In August, Amazon began rolling those review highlights out more widely, Engadget reported, and the summaries draw only on reviews from verified purchases.

In each case, a machine reads the product information first and presents a short answer. The shopper may see only a handful of products, chosen for reasons she stated, and a summary of what reviewers said in place of the reviews themselves.

Why the existing dashboard cannot see the loss

Ranking and click-through still matter, and brands should keep tracking them. They now measure the end of a process that has gained a new step at the beginning. When an assistant answers a question, it effectively ranks products before the shopper sees any of them, and a product it does not select never gets the chance to rank or be clicked.

Brands have faced this shape of problem before. When search engines arrived, a brand had to be found before it could win a click, and brands learned to measure their visibility in search alongside their sales. Something similar is now needed for assistants.

Take a cookware brand whose sales on a marketplace hold steady while its traffic from searches slowly falls. Its reports show nothing wrong with its listings. Meanwhile a growing share of shoppers in its category ask assistants which pan suits an induction stove, and because its listings never state induction compatibility clearly, the assistant recommends competitors. Every number the brand watches is accurate, and none of them can see the loss.

Four measures to add, none of which needs new technology

MeasureWhat it checksHow to start
Attribute completenessWhether the attributes shoppers ask about (size, material, compatibility, use) are stated clearly in the title, bullets and structured fieldsList the key attributes for each important product and score the share covered
Review specificityWhether reviews describe a concrete attribute or outcome rather than general satisfactionSample reviews and count the specific ones
Presence in AI answersWhich products AI tools recommend for the questions shoppers ask in the categoryPut a fixed list of shopper questions to the available AI tools and record the products named
Traffic without keywordsHow much traffic and how many sales arrive from sources other than keyword searchTrack that share and watch for changes as the tools spread

Review specificity is easy to picture. A review that says “fits a 15-inch laptop” gives an assistant something to work with. A review that says “love it” does not. Presence in AI answers is the one that most resembles the old search report: repeated monthly, the same question list shows whether the brand is gaining or losing ground in the answers.

None of these replaces sales, profit or return on advertising, which remain the measures that count most. They are early signals, meant to show a problem before it reaches the sales line.

Who owns the new measures, and how to keep them simple

The measures are most useful when someone owns them. In many brands, product content belongs to one team, reviews to another and analytics to a third, and these measures cut across all three. Without an owner, each team sees its own piece of the problem, and nobody sees the product that has dropped out of the answers. A practical start is a short monthly review of a brand’s top products, covering attribute completeness, review specificity and presence in a fixed set of AI answers. The review can be done with a spreadsheet and an hour of testing.

It pays to keep the measures simple at first. The tools are changing quickly, and an elaborate measurement system built for the assistants of 2023 may not fit the ones that follow. A few consistent checks, repeated every month, will reveal more than a complex system that is rebuilt every quarter.

The question list deserves the most care. They should come from real shoppers, drawn from customer service logs, reviews and search terms, rather than from the brand’s own view of its products, because an assistant answers the question the shopper asks. A leadership team that wants to know whether this matters yet can ask one thing at the next review: for the shopper questions that matter most in our category, which products does an assistant name? Building that list and the checks around it is how we help brands measure their place in AI shopping.

A0452.title: Amazon 7-Day Deals: the break-even question every brand faces
A0452.alt: A brass balance scale weighs a small wrapped parcel against stacked coins, with kraft-paper packages behind it.
A0452.ttag: Amazon 7-Day Deals: the break-even question every brand faces | Kwontified
A0452.desc: A 7-Day Deal buys a week of visibility for a fee from $300, plus the discount on every sale. How to work out whether it pays, before you run it.
A0452.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 12, 2023.
A0452.body:
Take a product that sells for $40, earns $15 of margin per unit at full price, and normally sells 50 units a week. Put it in a 7-Day Deal at 20% off, and it has to sell 150 units that week just to earn what an ordinary week earns. Selling three times as much would leave the brand exactly where it started.

The fee is the cost everyone sees. The larger cost is the discount handed to every shopper who would have bought at full price. A week-long deal pays only when the lift clears that bar, or when the product comes out of the week ranking higher than it went in, so the break-even belongs on paper before the deal is booked.

How Amazon 7-Day Deals work

Amazon offers sellers two main kinds of featured deal. Lightning Deals run for a few hours with a set number of units. 7-Day Deals run for a full week and do not require the seller to commit a specific number of units, which also gives brands time to promote the deal through their own channels, Search Engine Journal explained. Fees for 7-Day Deals start at $300, and deals running during major events cost more.

Both kinds appear on Amazon’s deals pages, where shoppers browse for discounts, and both put a deal badge on the product listing. That visibility is what the fee pays for. The appeal is easy to see in a sales report, where a deal week shows up as a spike, and a spike looks like success until someone subtracts the units that were coming anyway.

Where the break-even comes from

A deal raises the number of shoppers who see and buy the product during the week. Every unit sold that week carries the discount, though, including the units that would have sold at full price. The extra units therefore have to earn enough margin at the lower price to cover the fee plus the discount given away on baseline sales.

Run the numbers on the $40 product. A 20% deal cuts $8 from the price, so each unit sold during the deal earns $7 instead of $15. The 50 units the brand would have sold anyway now earn $8 less each, a cost of $400. Add the $300 fee and the deal is $700 behind before it sells a single extra unit. At $7 of margin per extra unit, the brand needs 100 extra units to catch up, which takes the week from 50 units to 150.

Deeper discounts raise the bar from both sides at once: they cut the margin on each extra unit and increase what the brand gives away on the baseline. A product with a thin margin can reach the point where no realistic lift covers the cost.

Two ways a deal can pay, and one way it fails

The deal week tells only half the story. A deal can pay through extra profit during the week, which the break-even calculation tests directly. It can also pay through a lasting gain: higher sales during the deal can improve a product’s organic rank, and better rank can raise full-price sales after the deal ends.

The opposite can happen too. A deal can pull sales forward, as shoppers who would have bought next month buy now at a discount. Then the weeks after the deal run weaker than normal, and the deal’s true return is lower than the deal week suggests.

That is why the measurement window should cover at least two weeks before and two weeks after the deal, set against the deal week itself. A deal that lifts the week and leaves the following weeks stronger has earned its place. One that lifts the week and leaves a dip behind has mostly moved sales around the calendar.

What makes a week-long deal worth booking

The products that tend to clear the bar share a profile. They have room to grow, so higher rank would bring new shoppers rather than the same ones. Their margin is wide enough that the discount does not wipe out profit on each unit. And they have enough stock to sell through the week and the weeks after, so a gain in rank is not lost to an out-of-stock.

The same arithmetic decides the choice of deal type. A Lightning Deal costs less and runs for hours, which suits a quick test or a product with a narrow audience. A week-long deal suits a product that benefits from sustained visibility. A coupon carries no flat fee but a cost on every redemption. Running the same break-even calculation for each option, and picking the one with the lowest required lift, turns a habit into a decision.

Event weeks move the numbers. Deals running during major sales events cost more, and many competing products are discounted at the same time, so a deal that clears its break-even in a quiet week may struggle when every listing nearby carries a badge.

Advertising belongs inside the calculation as well. Many brands raise advertising during a deal to send more shoppers to the discounted price. That can lift the week further, but its cost has to be counted against the deal’s return, not reported in a separate line where the deal looks cheaper than it was.

The test before booking is short: multiply the discount by baseline weekly units, add the fee, and divide by the margin left on each deal unit. If the answer is more extra units than the product has ever sold in a week, skip the deal. Doing that calculation for every deal on the calendar, and checking the weeks after, is how we plan Amazon deals for brands.

A0454.crumb: TikTok Shop: your best salesperson may…
A0454.title: TikTok Shop: your best salesperson may not be on payroll
A0454.alt: A phone in a ring light on a tripod faces amber skincare bottles on a wooden desk in a teal room with a monstera.
A0454.ttag: TikTok Shop: your best salesperson may not be on payroll | Kwontified
A0454.desc: TikTok Shop launched in the U.S. with 100,000 creators in its affiliate program. Why creators become a brand’s sales force, and how to manage them like one.
A0454.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 14, 2023.
A0454.body:
A sales manager knows every person on the team: who they are, what they earn on each sale, what they are allowed to say about the product and which accounts they cover. On TikTok Shop, a brand can gain salespeople it has never met. They pick its products, make videos about them and earn a commission when viewers buy, without a contract, a briefing or a hello.

That is the real change in TikTok Shop’s U.S. launch. Creators become a commission-based sales force. Brands should manage them the way they manage a sales team: set commissions deliberately, give creators accurate product information and claims, and choose which creators to support, instead of leaving their presence on the platform to chance.

What TikTok Shop launched, and how its affiliates sell

TikTok officially launched TikTok Shop in the United States on September 12. More than 200,000 sellers had signed up, and more than 100,000 creators had joined its affiliate program, TechCrunch reported.

The affiliate program is the part that changes how brands sell. It lets creators with at least 5,000 followers make videos that link directly to products and earn a commission on what they sell, with those videos appearing in TikTok’s main “For You” feed, the Associated Press reported.

Influencer marketing itself is old news, and brands have paid creators to feature products for years. The structure is what is new. A creator on TikTok Shop does not need a contract with the brand to sell its products. The creator picks a product, makes a video and earns a commission when viewers buy, all inside the app.

A sales force, not a campaign

An advertising campaign is something a brand designs and controls: it chooses the message, the audience and the budget. A sales force is a group of people who represent the brand, each with their own style, paid by results. The brand shapes their behavior through commissions, training and the accounts it assigns, but it cannot script every conversation.

TikTok affiliates behave like the second group. Commissions decide how many creators choose to promote a product. The information creators have shapes what they say about it. And the creators who sell most effectively become, in practice, the brand’s most important salespeople, whether the brand has met them or not.

A sales force brings its own risks, and these come with it. A creator might describe a product inaccurately, overstate what it does, or promote it at a moment the brand did not plan for. A good video can sell out a product in hours. A misleading one can bring returns, complaints and damage to the brand’s reputation.

Take a skincare brand that lists its products on TikTok Shop and opens them to affiliates. A creator it has never heard of posts a video calling its serum a cure for acne, which the brand never claimed. The video spreads, the product sells out, and returns and complaints follow. The brand’s best salesperson that week was not on its payroll, and not on its message either.

Managing affiliates the way a sales manager would

Commission comes first, because the rate decides which creators promote which products. A higher rate on products with wide margins and strong reviews directs attention where the brand wants it, while a uniform rate across the range leaves that choice to the creators.

Then comes information. A good sales manager would never send a new rep to a customer without a product sheet, and affiliates deserve the same: accurate product information, approved claims and examples of good videos. Creators who know what the product does, and what it does not, are less likely to overstate it.

Choosing whom to back matters as much. Brands can identify the creators whose audiences match their customers and whose videos represent the product well, and offer them samples, higher commissions or early access. That turns an open crowd of affiliates into a team the brand has helped to build. It also gives the brand people it can call before a launch or a promotion, the way a sales manager briefs the best reps first.

A sales manager also keeps an ear to the calls. Monitoring the videos that drive sales of a brand’s products, and responding quickly to inaccurate ones, is part of managing any sales force. Disclosure belongs in the same briefing. Creators who earn a commission are promoting the product for pay, and advertising rules require that relationship to be clear to viewers. A promotion that hides a paid relationship can create problems for the brand as well as the creator.

The sales team works beyond the app

A creator’s video can send shoppers to search for the product on Amazon or the brand’s own site, not only to buy inside the app. Brands should watch for jumps in branded searches on other channels after a popular video, and make sure those listings are stocked and ready. Judging affiliates only by their TikTok sales will understate what the best ones are worth.

The scorecard should be kept creator by creator, like a sales manager’s. Sales, returns and the accuracy of each creator’s claims together show who is building the brand and who is only moving units, and where the brand’s commission money is best spent.

Stock is the last part of the picture. A single video can create demand far beyond a normal day, so brands should hold enough inventory for sudden spikes, or limit which products are open to affiliates until they can supply them. Running that program, from commissions to briefings to the stock behind them, alongside the brand’s other marketplaces is how we help brands build a TikTok Shop affiliate team.
