A0458.crumb: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 forecast: sales…
A0458.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deals
A0458.alt: A brass rooster weathervane on a mossy tiled roof as autumn leaves swirl in the wind against a pale sky.
A0458.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deals | Kwontified
A0458.desc: Three forecast ranges for Prime Big Deal Days on October 10 and 11: sales lift, click prices and deal share, from Prime Day 2023 and the 2022 October event.
A0458.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 19, 2023.
A0458.body:
Amazon announced on September 18 that Prime Big Deal Days will run for 48 hours starting at 3 a.m. EDT on October 10, Fox reported. The obvious numbers to reach for are July’s, and July’s are big. Our central estimate is smaller: promoted products selling about four times a normal day, with click prices about 40% higher. The ranges below show how far either side of that the event could land.

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
Sales for promoted products, vs. a normal day2.5 times4 times5 times
Cost per click, vs. the previous 30 days+25%+40%+58%
Share of event sales from products on deal40%55%70%

These are planning ranges, not measured results, and the sections below show the arithmetic and the assumptions behind each column. Brands should set budgets and stock for the standard case, hold a reserve for the reach case, and judge the event against the conservative case rather than against Prime Day.

Where the Prime Big Deal Days 2023 forecast comes from

The starting point is two sets of figures. The first is Prime Day 2023. Advertisers using Skai paid 58% more per click across the two Prime Day 2023 event days than in the previous 30 days, and their ad-attributed sales rose 5.9 times, Marketing Dive reported.

The second is how the 2022 October event compared with July. Numerator’s recap put participation in the October 2022 sale at 28.4% of U.S. households, against 34.1% for July’s Prime Day that year. October shoppers spent $117 per household to July’s $177, with an average order of $50 to July’s $61, Numerator found. On spend per household, the October event delivered about 0.66 of July.

The October event draws fewer shoppers spending less than Prime Day does, so both the extra demand and the extra competition for clicks are smaller. Scaling Prime Day’s observed lift in sales and click prices by the ratio of October to July spending gives a reasonable central estimate. A 5.9-times lift in ad-attributed sales scaled by 0.66 gives about 3.9 times, or roughly four times a normal day. A 58% rise in click prices scaled by 0.66 gives about 38%, or roughly 40%.

What the three cases assume

The conservative case assumes turnout and spending fall short of 2022’s October pattern, with shoppers holding back for later holiday sales as higher gas prices squeeze budgets. The standard case assumes the October event performs relative to July as it did in 2022. The reach case assumes stronger turnout, closer to Prime Day, helped by earlier holiday shopping; its click-price figure is simply Prime Day’s 58%.

The deal-share range is a planning assumption rather than a published figure. It reflects how much of a brand’s event sales would come from products carrying a deal, given that the October event centers on deals.

All three are estimates for promoted products with advertising behind them, not for a brand’s whole catalog. Products without deals or advertising typically see a much smaller lift.

The estimate also moves with category. In 2022, toys were the only category in which more shoppers bought during the October sale than in July, according to Numerator. Shoppers in October lean toward early gifts and household essentials, so categories that fit that pattern may beat these estimates while others fall short. A brand selling toys or giftable items should lean toward the reach case, and a brand in categories that peak in summer should lean toward the conservative one.

Why Prime Day is the wrong yardstick

July’s results are the most recent big event every team has seen, and recent, vivid numbers pull every estimate toward them. That pull is natural, and it can push an October plan wrong in both directions. A team anchored on 5.9 times buys stock and budget for a turnout the 2022 pattern does not support. The same team, judging afterward, calls a perfectly sound October result a disappointment because it missed July.

Forecasts of a single event are uncertain, which is why the ranges are wide. The useful discipline is to decide in advance which number each decision uses. Stock and advertising budgets should support about four times normal daily sales on promoted products, with click prices around 40% higher. The reserve, in advertising money and in knowing which products have the stock to absorb more demand, covers the reach case if the event runs hot. And the verdict afterward should come from the conservative case: an October event that delivers two and a half times normal sales on promoted products, at click prices 25% higher, is a reasonable outcome.

Adjusting before and measuring after

The ranges should be revisited as the event approaches. Early deals, competitor announcements and the click prices seen in the week before October 10 will show whether the event is tracking toward the conservative or the reach case. Budgets can then be adjusted before the two main days, October 10 and 11.

The measurement should take in the days around the event as well. Sales often dip in the days before as shoppers wait for deals, and can stay elevated afterward, so the full picture includes the week before and the week after.

Stock deserves particular care this time. Amazon told sellers that the date for sending inventory in time for the event had already passed when it announced the dates, so the stock already at Amazon sets the ceiling for most brands. Any case that needs more units than are already in Amazon’s warehouses exists only on paper. Building those ranges product by product, and checking them against stock on hand, is how we forecast Prime Big Deal Days for brands.

A0459.crumb: CPG on Amazon: how everyday essentials…
A0459.title: CPG on Amazon: how everyday essentials rewrote the playbook
A0459.alt: Rustic wooden pantry shelves on a sage green wall hold kraft paper packages, an oat box, a jug and folded linens.
A0459.ttag: CPG on Amazon: how everyday essentials rewrote the playbook | Kwontified
A0459.desc: Amazon says everyday essentials are raising basket sizes and how often people shop. Why that turns CPG on Amazon into a game of repeat purchase, not launches.
A0459.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 21, 2023.
A0459.body:
A shopper runs out of dishwasher detergent on Monday evening, orders more on her phone, and has it on Tuesday. She never walks down the store aisle where a brand’s end-cap display and shelf placement used to do the selling. Multiply that small habit across coffee, razor blades and paper towels, and the shape of CPG on Amazon changes: the brand is no longer winning one sale, it is trying to keep winning the next one.

Amazon is building its store around exactly that moment. Faster delivery and more deals are aimed at the frequent, low-priced purchases consumer packaged goods depend on, which makes Amazon a channel where CPG brands win on repeat purchase more than on launches. The brands that do well will organize their Amazon business around replenishment, pack and price design, and staying in stock close to the customer.

What Amazon said, and what it built

Amazon has spelled out the strategy in plain terms. On its second-quarter earnings call on August 3, it said it was growing its selection of everyday essentials, which both increased basket sizes and raised how often customers chose to shop with it, according to the call transcript. It also reported healthy demand across everyday essentials and in categories such as beauty and health and personal care, Campaign Asia reported.

Two investments sit behind that. One is speed: in the second quarter of 2023, more than half of Prime members’ orders in the 60 largest U.S. metro areas arrived the same day or the next day, Campaign Live reported. The other is price, with Amazon saying it offered 144% more deals and coupons in the second quarter than a year earlier.

For most of its history, Amazon was where shoppers went for things they could not easily find nearby, while groceries and household staples were bought in stores, and CPG brands treated Amazon as a secondary channel. The call and the delivery figures show how far that has moved.

Essentials make Amazon a frequency business

Essentials behave differently from other products. A shopper buys a television once every few years. She buys laundry detergent, coffee or razor blades many times a year. For a television, the brand’s task is to win one decision. For detergent, it is to win the first purchase and then keep winning the next one, and the one after that.

Speed changes that second decision. When an essential can arrive tomorrow, ordering it online competes with picking it up at a store, and a shopper who receives Tuesday what she ran out of on Monday has less reason to visit a store at all.

So the value of a customer comes less from a single sale and more from the number of times she comes back. That also raises the cost of failure. A brand that runs out of stock does not lose one sale. It may lose a customer who reorders a competitor and stays with it.

Who holds the repeat customer

Follow the value of that next order and it is clear who has been investing to capture it. Amazon’s speed and deals make Amazon the default place to reorder. Whether the reorder goes to the same brand depends on things the brand controls only partly: whether the product is in stock near the shopper, how its price per unit looks beside the alternatives, and whether the shopper even sees it again.

How a brand sells to Amazon decides how much of that it controls. A brand that sells wholesale to Amazon leaves pricing and stock decisions largely to Amazon, while a brand that sells directly as a seller controls both but carries the inventory risk. In a frequency business, those decisions shape whether loyal customers can reorder when they want to, so the choice deserves a fresh look instead of being treated as settled.

The contest gets sharper with private label. Store brands and lower-priced alternatives sit beside branded products in the same search results, often with a clear price-per-unit advantage. A branded essential needs a reason to cost more that the shopper can see quickly, such as a proven result, a better format or a trusted name, because she is comparing on the first screen.

Take a household cleaning brand that spends most of its Amazon budget on launches and promotions. Its new products sell well in the first month, then fade. Meanwhile, its best seller runs out of stock twice in the quarter, and each time a share of its regular buyers switch. The playbook is built for launches while the customers are buying for replenishment.

A playbook built on the next order

The organizing idea is replenishment. Brands should know how often their customers reorder each product, encourage subscriptions where they fit, and measure success by repeat purchase and customer retention, not only by new sales.

Packs and prices should be designed for the shopper who compares. Shoppers on Amazon often compare price per unit, especially in essentials, so pack sizes, bundles and multi-packs need planning with that comparison in mind, priced so the brand competes on value without eroding its margin.

Stock has to sit close to the customer, because Amazon’s speed depends on inventory near shoppers. That means forecasting demand for core products carefully, keeping best sellers in stock, and counting an out-of-stock as a loss of customers, not just of units.

Advertising and reviews shift in the same direction. In a frequency business, advertising aimed at loyal customers’ own searches often protects repeat purchases that would otherwise go to a competitor, so spending to win new customers has to be balanced with spending to keep existing ones. And because shoppers in essentials often choose quickly between familiar options, a strong rating can decide a close comparison. Product quality, packaging that survives delivery and accurate descriptions are part of keeping customers, since a disappointing first order rarely leads to a second.

The question for a CPG leadership team is which number its Amazon plan is built to move: launch sales, or the share of last quarter’s buyers who ordered again. Rebuilding the plan around the second is how we run Amazon for CPG brands built on repeat purchase.

A0462.title: Amazon Accelerate 2023: what changes for sellers
A0462.alt: A small white robotic arm ties twine on a kraft paper parcel on a wooden packing table with tape and paper rolls.
A0462.ttag: Amazon Accelerate 2023: what changes for sellers | Kwontified
A0462.desc: Accelerate 2023 brought an AI listing tool, Supply Chain by Amazon and Buy with Prime for Shopify. Which to adopt now, which to test, and what each costs.
A0462.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 26, 2023.
A0462.body:
Every service Amazon announced for sellers at Accelerate 2023 does the same two things. It takes work off the seller’s desk, and it moves a little more of the seller’s business into Amazon’s systems. One effect shows up on the next invoice. The other shows up only when the seller wants to leave, or when Amazon changes the terms.

The calculation is simple to state: the value of each service is the saving it offers minus the control it takes and the cost of switching away later. On that scale, the AI listing tool is cheap to try today, while Supply Chain by Amazon and Buy with Prime for Shopify deserve a priced pilot on a slice of volume before they carry more of the business.

What Amazon Accelerate 2023 announced

Amazon used its seller conference on September 13 and 14 to announce a long list of products and features. For brands, three of them matter most.

The first is a generative AI tool for listings. Sellers provide a few details, and the tool drafts a title, bullet points and a description. Amazon cautioned that sellers should review every listing the tool writes for accuracy, SiliconANGLE reported.

Supply Chain by Amazon is an automated set of services to move products from manufacturing locations to customers, using Amazon’s logistics, warehousing, distribution and fulfillment, EcomCrew reported. The service is designed to cover a seller’s inventory across sales channels, not only orders placed on Amazon.

The Buy with Prime app for Shopify lets merchants offer Prime checkout and delivery on their own Shopify stores using inventory in Amazon’s network. It began rolling out to invited merchants and will be available to all U.S. Shopify merchants using Amazon’s fulfillment network by the end of September, Retail TouchPoints reported.

How much control each service asks for

ServiceWhat Amazon takes onWhat moves into Amazon’s systemsHow hard to reverseWhere to start
AI listing toolDrafting titles, bullets and descriptionsLittle beyond the product details enteredEasy: stop using itTest now on a set of products
Buy with Prime for ShopifyCheckout promise and delivery on the brand’s own siteOrders from the brand’s site, routed through Amazon fulfillmentModeratePilot on a limited range
Supply Chain by AmazonMoving stock from factory to customer, across channelsInventory and shipments for every channelSlow and expensivePrice it, then pilot on one channel

None of these is good or bad in itself. The listing tool carries little lock-in of any kind: a brand can use it, edit the results and stop at any time, so the risk is quality, not dependence.

Supply Chain by Amazon sits at the other end. A brand that moves its inventory and its shipments to other channels onto Amazon’s network gains simplicity and possibly lower costs. Amazon then holds its stock for every channel, controls the timing of its deliveries, and sets the fees for both. Moving back is slow and expensive.

Buy with Prime sits somewhere between the two. It can raise conversion on a brand’s own site by offering a delivery promise shoppers already trust, but it routes those orders through Amazon’s fulfillment and ties the brand’s site more closely to Amazon.

Where the hidden cost lands

Take a brand that sells through Amazon, its own Shopify store and Walmart. Moving all three channels onto Amazon’s network might lower its warehouse costs and simplify operations. If Amazon later raises fees or limits capacity during the holidays, every channel is affected at once, and the brand has no second network to fall back on.

That is the cost a fee comparison leaves out. The saving is real and steady. The exposure is concentrated and arrives all at once, which is why the decision needs more than a price check.

A short score helps before adopting any of them. It rests on three things. One is how long it would take to move away if the terms changed. Another is what data or customer relationship the brand would give up. The last is whether a second option would remain in place.

A service that scores well on all three can be adopted quickly. One that scores poorly deserves a longer pilot and a written exit plan before it carries a large share of the business.

Try the light tool now, and pilot the heavy ones

The AI listing tool can be tried now, on a set of products where the brand can compare results with its current listings. Every generated listing should be reviewed for accuracy, required claims and the attributes shoppers search for before it goes live.

The infrastructure services need pricing before anything else. Brands should ask for the full fee structure of Supply Chain by Amazon, including storage, transport and handling, and compare it with what they pay today across all channels.

Only after that comes the pilot. A brand interested in Buy with Prime or Supply Chain by Amazon should start with a limited range or a single channel. It should measure the effect on cost, speed and conversion over a full season, and keep an alternative in place until the results are clear.

The timing of any switch matters as well. Changing fulfillment arrangements just before the holiday season adds risk at the moment a brand can least afford a disruption, so testing in the first quarter of 2024, after the peak, is usually safer than switching now.

The practical rule: adopt what you can drop in a day, and pilot what would take a quarter to unwind. Scoring each new Amazon service against the rest of a brand’s operations is how we help brands weigh Accelerate 2023 announcements.

A0464.title: Conversational commerce in Instagram DMs: the new sales desk
A0464.alt: A smartphone, brass service bell and a twine-tied kraft parcel with lavender rest on a dark wooden counter.
A0464.ttag: Conversational commerce in Instagram DMs: the new sales desk | Kwontified
A0464.desc: A billion people message a business each week on Meta’s apps. Why Instagram DMs are becoming a sales desk, and how brands should staff and measure them.
A0464.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 28, 2023.
A0464.body:
A shopper taps an Instagram ad for a ring and, instead of a product page, lands in a message thread with the brand. She types the question that is stopping her: does it come in a half size, and will it arrive before Saturday? What happens next depends on whether anyone is there to answer.

That is where conversational commerce on Instagram is heading. Shoppers have moved a growing share of their conversations with brands into messaging, so direct messages now work as a sales desk and a service counter at once. Brands that treat the DM inbox as a sales channel, with response standards, clear paths to purchase and measurement of the sales conversations produce, stop leaving those shoppers waiting.

How messaging became a shopping channel

For years, a brand’s Instagram account was a place to post. Shoppers saw products in the feed and in stories, then went elsewhere to buy, and direct messages were for friends. Shopping and conversation lived in separate places.

Meta said in 2022 that one billion people were messaging a business each week across WhatsApp, Messenger and Instagram Direct, whether to ask about products, browse catalogs, seek support or reply to stories, according to Meta. It repeated the figure in September 2023, describing the behavior as accelerating, Meta said.

Advertising has helped push shoppers into those conversations. Meta said in 2022 that tens of millions of conversations were being started every day from ads that click through to a message thread. It also planned to bring recurring notifications, which let businesses follow up with customers who opt in, to Instagram.

A conversation sells differently from a page

On a product page, the brand speaks and the shopper decides alone. In a conversation, the shopper asks the question that is holding her back, such as whether a product comes in her size, works with what she already owns or will arrive in time, and the answer can close the sale.

That makes the inbox part sales desk and part service counter. Some messages come from shoppers ready to buy if they get a quick answer. Others come from customers with a problem. Both affect sales, and both arrive in the same place.

It also puts a price on a slow reply. A shopper who asks a question in a DM is often deciding now, and if the answer comes the next day, she may already have bought elsewhere. Speed of response becomes part of conversion.

Take a jewelry brand that runs Instagram ads leading to its DMs. Shoppers message to ask about sizing and gift wrapping. The brand answers once a day, in a batch, with no link back to the product. Its ads generate plenty of conversations but few sales, and the brand concludes that the ads do not work. The real problem is that its sales desk is closed most of the day.

Running the inbox like a sales channel

The first job is setting response standards, which can start small. A brand should decide how quickly it will answer DMs during the hours shoppers are most active, and staff or automate accordingly. Common questions about sizes, shipping and returns can be answered instantly with saved replies, leaving people for the questions that need judgment.

Every answer to a buying question should then make the next step easy, with a direct link to the product or a way to complete the order. A conversation that ends without a way to buy leaves the sale to chance.

Measurement is what closes the loop on all of it. Brands should track how many conversations they receive, how fast they respond, and how many conversations lead to a purchase. Without that, ads that start conversations are judged only on clicks, which understates or misstates what they produce.

Automation helps, though only within limits. Saved replies and simple automated answers can handle the most common questions at any hour, which matters when shoppers message in the evening or on weekends. The automation should hand the conversation to a person quickly when the question is unusual or the shopper is unhappy. A shopper stuck in a loop of unhelpful automatic replies is more likely to leave than one who waits a little longer for a real answer.

Decisions that sit behind the inbox

A conversation has to send the shopper somewhere to buy. Some brands will link to their own website, some to Instagram’s own checkout where it is available, and some to a marketplace listing such as Amazon. Each choice affects margin, the customer data the brand keeps and how easily it can follow up, so the choice should be deliberate and consistent, not left to whoever answers the message.

Service and sales need to be separated, without losing either. Customers with problems need fast, careful help, and how a brand handles a complaint in a DM can decide whether that customer buys again. Routing service messages to the right people quickly keeps the sales desk from being buried.

Messaging also brings obligations of its own. Shoppers expect their conversations to be handled with care, and follow-up messages should go only to customers who have opted in. A brand that uses DMs for unwanted promotion will lose the trust that makes the channel work.

A leadership team can test its own inbox with one scenario. If a shopper messaged right now asking whether the bestseller ships by the weekend, who would answer, how soon, and would the reply include a way to buy? Building the answer to that question into staffing, routing and reporting is how we help brands run Instagram DMs as a sales channel.

A0466.title: Prime Video ads: what streaming inventory changes for DSP plans
A0466.alt: A navy living room with leather armchairs and a bowl of popcorn on a coffee table facing a TV showing a misty field.
A0466.ttag: Prime Video ads: what streaming inventory changes for DSP plans | Kwontified
A0466.desc: Prime Video adds limited ads in early 2024. Why streaming video fails a search-style ROAS report, and how to budget and test it with a holdout instead.
A0466.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 3, 2023.
A0466.body:
A brand moves part of its search budget into streaming video, then judges both lines on return on ad spend, the same test it has always applied to search. The video’s attributed return comes in low, so after a month the brand cuts it. Its branded searches, which had been rising, fall back. The brand took money from an ad that was working to fund one it measured in a way that could not see its effect.

Prime Video’s move to limited ads in early 2024 will add a large supply of premium streaming inventory that Amazon can connect to shopping behavior, which makes upper-funnel video easier to measure against sales than most television. Brands should give streaming video its own budget instead of taking it from search, and judge it on incremental sales against a control group rather than on the return metrics used for search ads.

What Prime Video ads add to Amazon’s inventory

On September 22, Amazon said Prime Video shows and movies will include limited advertisements starting in early 2024, with an ad-free option for an additional $2.99 a month in the United States, Axios reported. The ads start in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Canada, with France, Italy, Spain, Mexico and Australia following later in the year, Fox reported.

This inventory joins an ad business that is already large and growing. Amazon’s advertising revenue reached $10.7 billion in the second quarter of 2023, up 22%, Campaign Live reported. Amazon pointed to Thursday Night Football, and to the ability for advertisers to tailor their spots by audience, as part of the demand, Campaign Asia reported. Prime Video adds shows and movies to that live sports inventory, with the same link to Amazon’s shopping data.

Why streaming video fails a search-style report

Streaming video reaches shoppers before they search. Its effect shows up later, as more searches and purchases, not as immediate clicks. Because Amazon can link who saw an ad to who later bought, it can measure that delayed effect, but only if the brand compares exposed shoppers with a similar group that did not see the ad.

Search ads are judged on return on ad spend: sales attributed to the ad, divided by its cost. That works for search, because the ad and the purchase sit close together. Video works further back in the decision. A shopper who sees a brand on Prime Video may search for it days later and buy through a search ad, which then takes the credit.

Judged on immediate return, streaming video will usually look weak. Judged on whether exposed shoppers bought more than similar shoppers who were not exposed, it may look very different. The brand that cut its video after a month was reading the first number when the question called for the second.

Fund it apart from search and test it with a holdout

Streaming video serves a different purpose from search, so it should not compete for the same dollars on the same metric. A brand should decide what it wants video to achieve, usually reaching new customers, and fund it for that job.

The test comes with the budget. Run video with a holdout group that does not see the ads, then compare purchases and branded searches between the exposed and unexposed groups. Branded searches belong in the comparison alongside purchases, because a shopper who saw the video may come back through search before she buys. That comparison is the measure of what the video actually added.

The creative also needs separate treatment. Prime Video ads will appear in full-screen viewing, often on a television, and ads made for a phone feed or a product page will not work as well there. Plan video creative designed for that setting rather than reusing assets cut for a feed.

Shopping audiences help only when they reach new buyers

Audience choice is where Amazon’s inventory differs most from traditional television. A television buy reaches whoever happens to be watching a program. Inventory sold through Amazon can be aimed at audiences defined by shopping behavior, such as shoppers who buy in a category but have not bought the brand. That makes it possible to use streaming video to reach the customers a brand most wants to win, and to measure whether it won them.

The same targeting can work against a brand if it is aimed too narrowly. Streaming ads shown only to people who already buy the brand will produce an attractive return, because those people would have bought anyway, but they add little. Both the targeting and the measurement should reflect what upper-funnel video exists to do, which is reach people who are not yet customers.

Watch reach and frequency as closely. A large new supply of inventory makes it easy to show the same ad to the same people too often. Set frequency limits before launch and watch reach as the campaign runs, so the budget finds new viewers rather than repeating to the same ones.

What to settle before the rest of 2024 is budgeted

Several details are still to come from Amazon: how Prime Video inventory will be bought, how it will be priced, and what measurement Amazon will offer. Brands should watch for each of them as Amazon releases them. Early tests, while competition for the inventory is still forming, can give a brand a useful read before budgets are set for the rest of 2024.

A video campaign judged only by the clicks it collects has lost before it airs. Give streaming its own budget, a holdout group and frequency limits before launch, which is how we plan and measure Amazon DSP and streaming campaigns for the brands we manage.

A0467.crumb: The business case for a shopping…
A0467.title: The business case for a shopping assistant in retail
A0467.alt: A cream retro robotic arm reaches toward stacks of coins beside a worn leather wallet on a wooden table.
A0467.ttag: The business case for a shopping assistant in retail | Kwontified
A0467.desc: Instacart, Zalando and Amazon are building AI shopping assistants. The case rests on bigger baskets, earlier influence and cheaper service, not novelty.
A0467.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 5, 2023.
A0467.body:
A shopper asks a home goods retailer’s assistant how to set up a guest room on a budget. Instead of searching for a bed, then sheets, then a lamp, she receives a short list that covers all three. The retailer sells a basket instead of a single item, and the shopper never compared it with another site.

That exchange shows the business case for a shopping assistant in miniature. An assistant can turn a shopper’s open question into a full basket, capture the moment before a search begins, and lower the cost of answering customers. Bigger baskets, earlier influence and cheaper service are why retailers are building them, rather than novelty, and brands should prepare for assistants that recommend complete solutions by making their products easy to combine, compare and explain.

How the shopping assistant business case reached the core of the store

In 2023, several retailers moved from experimenting with chatbots to building assistants into their core shopping experience. On May 31, Instacart began rolling out Ask Instacart, an AI-powered search tool built into its app’s search bar that combines OpenAI’s ChatGPT with Instacart’s own models, TechCrunch reported. The tool draws on Instacart’s catalog of more than a billion items across more than 80,000 retail partner locations, according to Instacart.

In April, Zalando started testing a ChatGPT-powered fashion assistant and said it planned to link it to each customer’s preferences, including the brands followed and the products available in that customer’s size, Fashion Network reported. In May, Amazon job listings described plans for conversational search that could answer questions, compare products and make personalized suggestions, VentureBeat reported.

Each of these assistants is expensive to build, and that raises the obvious question of why the retailers behind them think it pays.

A question carries a bigger basket than a search

A search returns products, while a question returns a solution. A shopper who asks what to make for dinner, or what to wear to a wedding, is asking for several items at once. An assistant that answers with a recipe and its ingredients, or an outfit and its accessories, turns one question into a basket of products, which is exactly what happened with the guest room.

The retailer gets its say before any brand is named

Traditional search begins when the shopper already knows what she wants to buy. An assistant can begin earlier, when she only knows what she wants to do. The retailer gains something valuable from that: a say in the decision before brands and products are even named. In the guest room exchange, the assistant decided which bed, which sheets and which lamp made the list, and the shopper had no reason to look anywhere else. The retailer kept the basket, the customer and the decision in one place.

Cheaper service, and the costs on the other side

Assistants can answer many routine questions that would otherwise reach a customer service team. In a study of customer support agents, an AI assistant raised the number of issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, according to the working paper. Savings like that add up for a large retailer.

The case also has costs on the other side of the ledger, and they explain why retailers are moving carefully. Every answer an assistant gives costs money to generate, more than a traditional search result does. A wrong answer, such as recommending something out of stock or something that does not fit, can cost a sale and some of the shopper’s trust.

That is one reason Instacart limited its assistant to food-related questions. Retailers are building assistants that stay close to their own catalogs, where the answers can be checked, rather than general chatbots that can say anything. Retailers will also measure those assistants differently from search. The useful questions are whether shoppers who use the assistant buy more items per order, return more often and contact customer service less, rather than how many people try it.

Brands now compete to be part of the answer

For brands, the assistant changes what it takes to be chosen. When a shopper searches for a product, a brand competes with the other products in that search. When an assistant builds a solution, the brand competes to be part of the answer, and the assistant chooses products that fit together, that it can explain clearly and that match the shopper’s stated needs.

Brands should describe how their products work with others, including compatible sizes, materials and uses, so an assistant can include them in a complete answer.

Comparison runs on clear attributes, prices and specifications, kept consistent across retailers, which help an assistant decide between options and explain its choice. A product whose key facts are missing is hard to recommend.

The language on the page matters as much as the data. Brands should state plainly what problem a product solves and for whom, in the words a shopper would use, because an assistant builds its answer from that language.

Brands need to know whether they are in the answer

The assistants are still early, but the economics behind them are clear enough that retailers will keep investing, and the brands that are easy to recommend will benefit most.

Brands should watch which retailers are building assistants and test how their products appear in the answers: ask each assistant the questions your customers ask, and record whether your products come up. That check shows quickly whether a brand is part of the solution or missing from it. The question for the team is simple: when a shopper asks for a solution instead of a product, is our product part of what comes back? Getting a catalog ready for that moment is work we do with brands preparing for AI shopping assistants across retailers.

A0468.title: Subscribe & Save: the underused revenue multiplier on Amazon
A0468.alt: Two wire crates of empty glass milk bottles sit on weathered wooden steps beside a sage green wall.
A0468.ttag: Subscribe & Save: the underused revenue multiplier on Amazon | Kwontified
A0468.desc: A 10% Subscribe & Save discount can earn a brand more per customer than a full-price sale. How to find the break-even, and why stockouts end subscriptions.
A0468.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 10, 2023.
A0468.body:
A discount that costs a brand $2.50 on every unit looks like margin leaking away. On Amazon’s Subscribe & Save, that same discount can leave the brand with more money from each customer than a full-price sale would, because it buys something a one-time sale never does: deliveries that keep arriving until something stops them.

Subscribe & Save trades a discount on each order for a stream of repeat deliveries. A subscriber is worth more than a one-time buyer whenever she takes enough deliveries a year to cover the discount, and for most replenishable products that is a low bar. Brands should fund the discount on products customers reorder, set it by the break-even number of deliveries, and protect in-stock rates, because missed deliveries are what end subscriptions.

How Amazon Subscribe & Save discounts work

Subscribe & Save lets shoppers schedule repeat deliveries of products they buy regularly, in exchange for a discount. In 2023, sellers choose to fund a discount of 0%, 5% or 10%. When a customer has five or more subscriptions arriving on the same delivery date, Amazon adds a further 5%, so the shopper can save up to 15%, according to eComEngine. Taking part requires a Fulfillment by Amazon account in good standing.

Many brands treat the program as an afterthought, enrolling products at the lowest discount or leaving them out altogether. That leaves value on the table, because the program changes the economics of a customer and not just of an order.

Why a discount can raise what a customer is worth

A subscriber’s contribution is the discounted margin on each unit multiplied by the number of deliveries she takes. A one-time buyer’s contribution is the full margin multiplied by her purchases, which are usually fewer. The discount pays whenever the extra deliveries outweigh the margin given up.

The deliveries also run on their own. They continue until something stops them, and in practice that is usually one of two things: the shopper cancels, or the product is not available when a delivery is due.

Say a brand sells a $25 product that carries $8 of contribution per unit before any discount. At a 10% discount, the brand gives up $2.50 per unit, leaving $5.50 of contribution on each subscription delivery. A typical one-time buyer who purchases twice a year at full price contributes $16 a year. A typical subscriber who takes five deliveries a year contributes $27.50, more than the one-time buyer despite the discount.

One-time buyerSubscriber at 10% off
Price per unit$25$25 less 10%
Contribution per unit$8$5.50
Orders a yeartwofive
Contribution a year$16$27.50

The break-even is the number of deliveries at which the subscriber matches the one-time buyer: $16 divided by $5.50, or about 2.9 deliveries a year. A product that customers reorder every two or three months clears that bar easily. A product bought once or twice a year does not.

Each brand’s numbers will differ from these illustrative figures, but the structure holds. The right discount depends on how often customers actually reorder, and on the margin available to fund it.

Set the discount by how often customers reorder

Reorder frequency is what decides which products belong in the program. Consumables such as supplements, skin care, pet food and household goods are natural candidates. Products bought rarely, or chosen differently each time, are not.

For each enrolled product, calculate the break-even number of deliveries at 5% and at 10%, compare it with how often customers actually reorder, and choose the level the margin can support. A higher discount usually attracts more subscribers, but it raises the bar each subscriber has to clear.

Delivery frequency matters as much as the discount. Shoppers choose how often their deliveries arrive, and a frequency that does not match how quickly they use the product causes problems either way. If deliveries come too often, product piles up at home and the shopper skips or cancels. If they come too rarely, she runs out and buys elsewhere in between.

Stating clearly on the product page how long a unit typically lasts helps shoppers pick a frequency that fits. A subscription that matches real use is the one most likely to last, and the one that delivers the repeat contribution the discount was meant to buy.

Stockouts and stacked deals end the math early

A subscription that cannot be filled is a subscription at risk. When a product is out of stock on a delivery date, the shopper may skip it, cancel it or buy a competitor instead, and each of those cuts into the deliveries the discount was priced on. In-stock rates for subscribed products deserve priority, especially ahead of busy periods when inventory is tight.

The same care applies to pricing. Because the discount applies to the current price, a temporary price cut or a deal stacks with the subscription discount for every subscriber receiving a delivery at that time. That can turn a planned promotion into a larger cost than expected, so check how a deal stacks before running it.

Measure the program as a customer program rather than a sales channel. The useful questions are how many active subscribers a product has, how long they stay and how much they contribute over a year, not just how many units shipped through Subscribe & Save in the latest month.

For any product, the test is short. If customers reorder it more often than its break-even number of deliveries, fund the discount and keep it in stock; if they do not, leave it out. Finding the products and discount levels that pass is part of how we build Subscribe & Save into a brand’s Amazon plan.

A0471.title: Cyber Week 2023 planning: who decides, and when
A0471.alt: Two wrapped gifts, a pine sprig and a dark hardcover notebook on an oak table with cane-back chairs.
A0471.ttag: Cyber Week 2023 planning: who decides, and when | Kwontified
A0471.desc: Most Cyber Week decisions close weeks before the event. The 2023 Amazon deadlines for deals, inventory and fees, and who in a brand should own each one.
A0471.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 12, 2023.
A0471.body:
An apparel brand submits strong Lightning Deals by September 1. Its operations team, meanwhile, plans inventory around a general holiday forecast, and the stock arrives after October 26. When the deals go live, the brand’s most promoted products are short, and the ad budget it set aside drives shoppers to items it cannot ship quickly.

Cyber Week looks like a single week of selling, but most of its outcome is decided weeks earlier, by a sequence of deadlines for deals, inventory and fees. By mid-October, the deal decisions are already closed. Brands should map the remaining deadlines, give each decision a single owner, and spend the weeks that are left on inventory, pricing, advertising and creative.

The Cyber Week 2023 planning calendar, read backward from November

Black Friday falls on November 24 in 2023, and Cyber Monday on November 27. On Amazon, the deadlines that shape those days arrive much earlier.

The earliest of them has already passed. Amazon set September 1, 2023, as the deadline to submit Lightning Deals for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Cahoot reported. Brands that did not submit by then cannot add a Lightning Deal for those weeks now.

A cost arrives in mid-October. Amazon applies its holiday peak fulfillment fee from October 15, 2023, to January 14, 2024, Bellavix reported. That raises the cost of each unit shipped through the period, which affects the margin available for discounts and advertising.

Inventory has its own date. Amazon recommends that inventory for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deal events arrive at its US fulfillment centers by October 26, according to the same report. Stock that arrives later may not be ready to sell when demand peaks.

Why each deadline lands on a different desk

The event is in late November, so it feels like a November problem. The decisions that matter most, though, fall in September and October, often before a brand has started thinking about the event at all.

Each deadline also belongs to a different part of the business. Deal choices sit with whoever sets prices and margins. Inventory sits with operations and supply, and advertising budgets with marketing. Creative and listing updates may sit with a design team or an agency.

When no one owns the whole sequence, each team works to its own timeline, and the gaps show up in late November as products out of stock, deals without budget behind them, or ads pointing to listings that were never updated. That is what happened to the apparel brand: its deal team and its operations team were each working to a different calendar.

What is still open in mid-October, and who owns it

By mid-October, the deal submissions are behind most brands. What remains is still significant, and each decision needs a single owner.

Inventory leads the list because it takes the longest to fix. Its owner should confirm that stock for promoted products will arrive by October 26, and plan for a buffer, since the October event showed how quickly promoted items can sell.

The pricing owner checks that the prices planned for Cyber Week work with the deals already submitted and with the peak fulfillment fee, and that prices on other retailers will not undercut the Amazon offer. Brands selling on Walmart and Target face the same question on each retailer, often with different deadlines and rules. The pricing owner should hold one view of planned prices and deals across all three retailers, so a discount on one of them does not undercut the offer on another during the same week.

Whoever owns advertising sets budgets for the weeks before, during and after the event, since searches build in the days before Black Friday and continue through Cyber Monday. Budgets that run out early in the week leave the biggest days uncovered.

Creative and listings need an owner of their own. That person updates images, titles and A+ content for promoted products before traffic peaks, so the shoppers the ads bring in find listings that sell.

Measurement also belongs on the list, and it is easiest to settle before the event rather than after. Its owner should decide in advance what normal sales look like for each promoted product, which weeks will serve as the comparison, and which results will count as success. Brands that set these terms only after the event tend to judge it by whichever number looks best, which teaches them little for the following year.

The season runs past Cyber Monday

Shoppers keep buying gifts into December, and the period after the event often carries strong demand at lower advertising costs, as competitors pull back their budgets. Brands that spend everything on the event week can find themselves without stock or budget for the weeks that follow. The person who owns the whole sequence should plan inventory and budgets for the full season, with Cyber Week as its peak rather than its end.

One person should hold the whole sequence

That person does not need to make every decision, but should know every deadline and whether each owner has met it. Prime Big Deal Days in October gave every brand a rehearsal, and the gaps it revealed are the ones to close before Cyber Week. Writing down every remaining deadline, starting with inventory arrival by October 26, is the place to begin, and a review of what went wrong during Prime Big Deal Days shows which gaps to fix first.

A useful question for a leadership team is whether anyone in the building can name every remaining date and the owner of each. Holding that calendar across Amazon and other retailers is part of how we help brands plan and run Cyber Week.

A0475.crumb: Free shipping minimum: why it is becoming…
A0475.title: Free shipping minimum: why it is becoming a member benefit
A0475.alt: A twine-tied cardboard parcel with a blank envelope sits on a coir doormat in front of a pale yellow door.
A0475.ttag: Free shipping minimum: why it is becoming a member benefit | Kwontified
A0475.desc: Retailers are raising free shipping minimums for non-members and keeping shipping free for members. What that means for brands that sell low-priced products.
A0475.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 19, 2023.
A0475.body:
A shopper without Prime adds a $14 lip balm to her Amazon cart. In regions where the minimum for free shipping rises, she now faces a gap of more than $20 before shipping is free. Some shoppers in her position buy two, some add another product, and some leave. Members, meanwhile, buy as before, and the brand sees conversion fall among a group of shoppers it may not track separately at all.

That gap comes from a larger change in how retailers treat shipping. Retailers are turning free shipping from a promise made to every shopper into a benefit reserved for paying members, and raising the minimum order for everyone else. The shift changes the value proposition of shopping online and puts low-priced products at a disadvantage with non-members. Brands should design bundles and multipacks that reach the minimum, and plan pricing and promotion with members as the core audience.

How the free shipping minimum moved in 2023

For most of the last decade, the largest retailers competed by lowering the bar for free shipping. In 2023, the direction reversed.

In March, Amazon raised the minimum order for free delivery from its online grocery business to $150 from $35, and added charges for smaller orders, Reuters reported. Non-Prime shoppers on Amazon generally needed to spend $25 to get free standard shipping, while Walmart and Target, which offer delivery memberships of about $100 a year, required $35 from non-members, according to the same report.

In August, Amazon began testing a $35 minimum for non-Prime shoppers to qualify for free shipping, $10 higher than its usual threshold, Texas Standard reported. Walmart’s $35 threshold for shoppers who are not Walmart+ members was already in place, the report noted.

Retailers are selling a membership, not just delivery

Shipping costs are only part of the pattern, although they matter. It reflects a change in what retailers are selling.

When free shipping was a promise to everyone, it was a cost of doing business, paid for out of margin. As delivery costs rose, that promise became expensive to keep for every order. Retailers had two choices: charge shoppers more for small orders, or reserve the best shipping terms for customers who pay for them in advance.

They are doing both at once. Raising the minimum for non-members pushes those shoppers toward larger baskets or toward a membership, and keeping shipping free for members makes the membership more valuable. Over time, the retailer’s relationship with its best customers shifts from a series of orders to a subscription.

That changes how different products fare on the page. A $40 item clears any threshold on its own. A $12 item does not, and a non-member who wants it has to add more to the basket, pay for shipping, or wait. Many will choose to wait, or to buy it somewhere else. For a member, the price of the item is all that matters.

The decision in the room: whom is the range built for?

For a brand with a low-priced range, this turns into a planning question the leadership team has to answer: is the range designed for members, for everyone, or for both? Each answer leads to different work, and each can be tested on a small part of the range first.

Building baskets is the answer for non-members. Brands with low-priced products should offer bundles, multipacks and sets that reach common thresholds on their own. A three-pack priced near the minimum gives a non-member a reason to buy without hunting for other items.

The other half is planning around members. Members of Prime, Walmart+ and similar programs are increasingly the customers who buy most often and pay least attention to shipping. Brands should make sure their most important products are eligible for member shipping on each retailer, and plan promotions around the events and offers that members see.

Whichever answer a team reaches, it should measure the two groups separately where the data allows. Changes in thresholds affect non-members first. A brand that sees conversion soften on low-priced products should check whether the change is concentrated among shoppers without a membership before concluding that demand has fallen.

Shipping charges and the brand’s own site

Sellers who ship orders themselves face a related choice. On marketplaces that let them set their own shipping charges, they decide whether to absorb the cost, add it to the price, or charge it separately. As retailers make free shipping a member benefit, shoppers compare those options more closely. A seller that charges for shipping on a low-priced item may lose the sale to one whose price already includes it, even if the total is the same. Folding shipping into the price, or reaching the threshold with a multipack, usually reads better to shoppers than a separate charge at checkout.

Brands also need to watch their own websites, because shoppers compare shipping terms across sites and a brand’s own store competes with the retailers that carry its products. If a brand offers free shipping with no minimum on its site while retailers raise theirs, it may win orders it does not expect, and it needs to know whether it can afford them.

Plan for a bar that keeps rising

The direction is unlikely to reverse soon, at least for the largest retailers. Delivery costs are high, and memberships give retailers a reason to keep raising the bar for everyone else. Brands that plan for it will keep their small products selling; those that do not may find their best sellers among members and their losses among everyone else.

Working through bundles, pricing and promotions retailer by retailer is how we help brands adjust a range to new shipping thresholds.

A0476.crumb: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 results: grading…
A0476.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 results: grading our forecast
A0476.alt: A brass caliper leans on a kraft-wrapped parcel on a rustic table surrounded by red and orange maple leaves.
A0476.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2023 results: grading our forecast | Kwontified
A0476.desc: Shopper spend at Prime Big Deal Days matched our forecast while ad sales and click prices came in lower. How to grade the event and separate added sales.
A0476.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 24, 2023.
A0476.body:
Shoppers at Prime Big Deal Days 2023 spent about two-thirds of what they spent in July, close to what our forecast assumed. Advertising did not keep pace with them. Ad-attributed sales and click prices came in lower, toward our conservative case, and none of the headline numbers can show how much of the event’s sales were added rather than pulled forward from the weeks around it.

The grade that follows is mixed, but it is useful. Brands should grade their own results against the forecast ranges they planned for, and measure the weeks around the event, before they set Cyber Week budgets.

Prime Big Deal Days 2023 results against our forecast

Before the event, we set out three cases. Our forecast scaled Prime Day 2023 by how the October 2022 event compared with July. The standard case was roughly four times normal daily sales for promoted products, with click prices about 40% higher than normal. The conservative case was two and a half times, with click prices 25% higher, and the reach case was five times, close to Prime Day. Everything rested on one ratio: we expected the October event to deliver about two-thirds of July’s activity, based on how the 2022 events compared.

MeasureWhat we assumedWhat public data showed
Shopper spend vs JulyAbout two-thirdsAbout 0.68 ($124.09 vs $181.72 per household)
Ad-attributed sales vs JulyAbout two-thirdsAbout 0.55 (45% below, same accounts)
Click pricesAbout 40% above normal (standard case)Premium more muted than the roughly 50% typical of major events

The shopper ratio held. According to Numerator, average household spend during the event was $124.09, compared with $181.72 during July’s Prime Day, Digital Commerce 360 reported. That is about 0.68 of July’s level, close to the two-thirds we assumed. The average order was $53.47, against $58.67 in July.

Advertising results came in below that ratio. On a same-account basis, Skai found that ad spend during the event was 42% below July’s event and ad-attributed sales 45% below, which puts ad sales at about 0.55 of July’s level, according to Skai. Against the October 2022 event, spend rose 41% and ad sales 26%.

Click prices also landed under our standard case. Skai said the cost-per-click premium over the previous 30 days was more muted than the roughly 50% increase it typically sees during major events. That places the event’s click prices toward our conservative case rather than our standard one.

Against October 2022, advertising activity grew. Feedvisor found that ad spend rose 37% and ad sales rose 27% compared with the 2022 event, with the first day accounting for 55% of ad sales across the two days, Feedvisor reported.

Our scaling assumption was right for shoppers and too generous for advertising, where results landed nearer our conservative case. Brands that budgeted for the standard case’s click prices had room to spare. The gap between shopper spending and ad-attributed sales suggests that more of the event’s demand came through deals and organic placements than through ads. Whether sales for promoted products reached four times normal depends on each brand’s own data, which public sources cannot show.

Event-day lift mixes added sales with borrowed ones

One effect matters more than any other when grading an event, including this one. An event’s measured lift combines two kinds of sales: those that would not have happened without the event, and those moved from the days before and after it. A lift measured only over the event days overstates what the event added.

Shoppers who know a sale is coming often wait for it, and shoppers who stock up during it often buy less afterward. Both effects move sales into the event without creating them.

Say a brand’s event days show sales at four times normal. If its sales in the week before the event fell to 80% of normal, and in the week after to 90% of normal, part of the event’s lift came from those weeks. The added sales are the event lift minus the dip around it. The brand still gained from the event, but it gained less than the event days alone suggest.

The way to estimate the gap is to compare the weeks before and after the event with the same weeks in a period without it, adjusted for any underlying trend. If the surrounding weeks were lower than expected, part of the event’s lift was borrowed.

Grade your own event before Cyber Week budgets close

Grade the event against the forecast ranges, and adjust the lift for the weeks around it, before drawing conclusions. Most brands can run the checks from their own sales and advertising reports in an afternoon. Place your event-day results within the conservative, standard and reach ranges you planned for, and record where they fell, as the table above does for our own forecast. Measure the weeks before and after the event against expectations, and subtract any dip from the lift. Then compare your click prices with what you budgeted, since many brands paid less than planned.

The timing matters, because Cyber Week budgets are being finalized now. A brand that saw its October lift mostly borrowed from the surrounding weeks should plan Cyber Week deals more carefully. A brand that paid less for clicks than it budgeted can consider whether to hold that money for Cyber Week or for the December weeks after it.

An event’s result is the lift on the day minus the dip around it, judged against the range you forecast. Grading every event that way is how we measure what Prime Big Deal Days added for the brands we manage.

A0478.crumb: What Prime Big Deal Days 2023 revealed…
A0478.title: What Prime Big Deal Days 2023 revealed about retailer behavior
A0478.alt: Two old shopfronts on a cobbled street display windows stacked with red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes.
A0478.ttag: What Prime Big Deal Days 2023 revealed about retailer behavior | Kwontified
A0478.desc: Walmart and Target scheduled their deal events around Amazon’s, and shoppers bought gifts earlier. Why October is now a three-retailer season for brands.
A0478.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 26, 2023.
A0478.body:
Lay the first half of October 2023 out on a retail calendar and the pattern is hard to miss. Target ran Target Circle Week from October 1 to 7. Walmart ran its Holiday Kickoff deals from October 9 to 12. Amazon’s second October event, Prime Big Deal Days, fell on October 10 and 11, inside Walmart’s window almost exactly. Amazon did not hold the stage alone.

The real result of the event is that calendar. Amazon’s October event now sets the start of the holiday season for the whole market: its competitors scheduled their own events around it, and shoppers started their gift purchases earlier. The lasting lesson is about structure rather than sales totals, and brands should plan October as a three-retailer season, with offers, stock and advertising coordinated across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

How Prime Big Deal Days 2023 reshaped October

Shoppers crossed between the events. In Numerator’s early read of the event, a third of Prime Big Deal Days shoppers said they also shopped or planned to shop the Walmart event, and 27% had shopped Target Circle Week, according to Numerator.

The same research pointed to earlier gift buying. During the event, 20% of Prime Big Deal Days shoppers bought toys and games, up from 16% during July’s Prime Day, Numerator found. More than half of shoppers said they also planned to shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The schedule says more than the scoreboard

Most of the coverage after the event focused on whether it beat the October 2022 event. The more important change is in how retailers now behave around it.

A year ago, Amazon’s October event was a new idea, and its competitors had to decide how to respond. In 2023 they answered by scheduling around it. Walmart placed its event on top of Amazon’s, and Target placed its event the week before. Each retailer chose to compete for the same shoppers in the same fortnight rather than leave October to Amazon.

That changes the shape of the whole holiday season. It used to build toward late November. Now it starts in the first half of October with a cluster of retailer events, pauses, then peaks again at Cyber Week. Shoppers have learned the new rhythm, and the rise in toy purchases suggests that some of them now begin their gift lists in October.

It also changes how shoppers behave during each event. When three retailers run deals in the same days, shoppers compare. A brand’s price on Amazon is judged against its price on Walmart and Target, often within minutes, so the event becomes a contest between offers across several retailers instead of a contest between brands on one.

Take a toy brand that runs a strong deal on Amazon during the event but leaves its Walmart and Target prices unchanged. Shoppers who see the Amazon deal and check the other retailers find the brand more expensive there.

Some buy on Amazon. Others buy a competitor’s product at Walmart, where that competitor ran its own deal. The brand’s results on Amazon look fine, while it has lost share elsewhere without noticing. Its Amazon report never shows the shoppers who left.

One October plan instead of three

The lesson is to plan October as a three-retailer season, with one plan rather than three.

That plan starts with offers. Brands should decide their deals for Amazon, Walmart and Target together, so a discount on one does not leave the brand looking expensive on another during the same week. That does not mean identical prices, but it does mean deliberate ones, checked across all three retailers during each event.

Stock has to be planned for all three as well. Events that overlap draw down inventory on several retailers at once, and a brand that plans stock for Amazon’s event alone may find itself short at Walmart or Target in the days that matter. Inventory forecasts for overlapping events belong on every retailer, not just Amazon.

The same coordination applies to advertising. Retail media budgets on Amazon, Walmart Connect and Target’s Roundel are often set by different teams or at different times. In an October where the events overlap, they should be planned together, with a view of where each dollar reaches shoppers most cheaply.

The structure also lengthens the planning calendar. If the holiday season starts in early October, decisions about deals, inventory and budgets for October have to be made in the summer, alongside the planning for July’s Prime Day. Brands that still treat October as a quiet month before the holidays will find their competitors already in place.

Measure the cluster, not each retailer alone

As the structure changes, measurement has to change with it. A brand that measures its October results on each retailer separately will miss the interaction between them. A strong week on Amazon may have come partly at the expense of Walmart or Target, or partly from shoppers who would have bought from the brand anyway.

The better question is what the brand sold across all three retailers during the cluster of events, compared with the same weeks a year earlier and with the weeks around them. That view shows whether the October season added sales for the brand as a whole, or simply moved them between retailers and between weeks.

None of this makes Cyber Week less important. It remains the peak, but it is now the second peak of a season that starts much earlier, across more retailers, than it used to. Putting one October plan across Amazon, Walmart and Target is how we help brands coordinate their October events.

A0480.crumb: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2023 changes for…
A0480.title: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2023 changes for advertisers
A0480.alt: An open cardboard box glowing with a light bulb inside sits on a sunlit wooden desk among mugs against a navy wall.
A0480.ttag: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2023 changes for advertisers | Kwontified
A0480.desc: Sponsored TV, AI lifestyle images and Sponsored Products on other sites all lower the cost of entry. How to test each without blurring what you measure now.
A0480.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 31, 2023.
A0480.body:
A brand turns on three new Amazon ad options in November. Its Sponsored Products results now include clicks from other sites, which convert less often, and its overall return on ad spend falls. The brand cuts bids, unaware that its on-Amazon search results had not changed at all. The new placements had simply been blended into the old number.

Every main announcement at unBoxed 2023 lowers the cost of entering a format. Sponsored TV removes the minimum spend for streaming ads, an AI tool generates lifestyle images, and Sponsored Products will run on sites beyond Amazon. That brings more advertisers into the same auctions, and it will blur reporting brands rely on today. Advertisers should test each one with its own budget and reporting line, measure it against a holdout, and keep it separate from search results until it proves what it adds.

What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2023 announced

Amazon held unBoxed, its annual advertising conference, in New York from October 24 to 26.

The headline product was Sponsored TV, which lets brands run streaming TV ads with no minimum spend requirement, Modern Retail reported. Amazon also introduced a generative AI tool in beta that creates lifestyle images for ads, and Amazon Publisher Cloud, a clean room for publishers to analyze their audiences with Amazon Ads insights, according to the same report.

Sponsored Products campaigns will also extend to premium apps and websites in the US, including Pinterest, BuzzFeed and Hearst Newspapers, Canopy Management reported.

Cheaper entry changes who competes, and what the reports mean

When a format’s minimum spend or production cost falls, more advertisers enter it. Early tests are cheap, but prices rise as adoption grows. And because the new formats sit inside the same console and reports as search ads, their results can mix into existing numbers, making both harder to read unless they are separated from the start. Each announcement follows that pattern.

Sponsored TV moves streaming video from Amazon’s demand-side platform, where budgets were large, into the self-service console. Brands that could never justify a streaming TV campaign can now test one with a small budget. That is good for testing. It also means many more brands will soon bid for the same streaming audiences.

Creative gets cheaper with the image tool. Lifestyle images, which show a product in use rather than on a plain background, used to require a photo shoot or a designer. Now a brand can generate several versions from an existing photo. More brands will have more creative variations, which raises the standard for everyone.

Sponsored Products on other sites carry search ads beyond Amazon’s own pages. Shoppers on Pinterest or BuzzFeed behave differently from shoppers searching on Amazon: their clicks may convert at different rates, and their purchases may take longer. That is the blending that caught the brand in November.

A separate test for each format

FormatWhat it makes cheaperHow to test it
Sponsored TVStreaming TV with no minimum spendOwn budget, new-customer goals, holdout group
AI lifestyle imagesCreative that used to need a shootControlled comparisons, one change at a time, every image reviewed
Sponsored Products on other sitesReach beyond Amazon’s pagesOff-Amazon placements reported apart from on-Amazon results

Sponsored TV needs a dedicated budget with goals tied to reaching new customers, and a holdout group to measure whether exposed shoppers buy more. A verdict based on immediate return will make it look weak, for the same reason any upper-funnel video does.

The image tool calls for testing generated images against existing creative in controlled comparisons, one variable at a time, and reviewing every image for accuracy before it runs. A generated image that misrepresents a product will cost more in returns and reviews than it gains in clicks.

For Sponsored Products on other sites, watch placement reports closely and, where the controls allow, separate off-Amazon placements from on-Amazon results. From the first week, track the two separately, before the blended number starts driving bid decisions.

Amazon Publisher Cloud matters less to most brands directly, but it points in the same direction. It gives publishers a way to combine their audiences with Amazon’s insights and sell that inventory through Amazon’s demand-side platform. Over time, that adds more places where Amazon-informed ads can run. For advertisers, the practical effect is more inventory to choose from, and more need to know which placements actually add sales.

Pace the tests around Cyber Week

Budget pacing deserves attention as well. New formats often spend unevenly in their first weeks, as Amazon’s systems learn where to place them. A test budget that is too small may never reach enough shoppers to measure, while one that is too large can spend quickly on placements of uncertain value. Set a test budget large enough to reach a measurable audience over several weeks, and cap daily spend so it cannot run away.

Timing matters too. Cyber Week is weeks away, and tests of new formats should not compete with core search budgets during the busiest weeks of the year. A small test now, with a fuller test in the first quarter of 2024 when competition eases, will give clearer results than a rushed launch in late November. For Sponsored TV in particular, plan the main test for early 2024.

None of this argues against the new products. Lower entry costs are good for brands that test well and a risk only for brands that let new formats blur the numbers they already depend on. Setting up those separate tests and reports is how we help brands measure new Amazon ad formats after unBoxed.
