A0481.crumb: Email marketing for brands that sell on…
A0481.title: Email marketing for brands that sell on marketplaces
A0481.alt: Laptop on a rustic wooden desk with a coffee mug, potted plant, twine-tied envelopes and a wrapped parcel.
A0481.ttag: Email marketing for brands that sell on marketplaces | Kwontified
A0481.desc: Marketplaces own the customer relationship, and email is the one channel where the brand owns it. Why email is undervalued beside Amazon, and how to use both.
A0481.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 2, 2023.
A0481.body:
A brand can sell to the same shopper on Amazon again and again and still have no way to tell her about its next product. The marketplace holds her contact details, controls the messages the brand may send, and decides which products she sees next. Every time the brand wants her attention, it pays for it.

Email marketing deserves more weight at marketplace brands than it usually gets, for exactly that reason. Email is the one channel where the brand owns the relationship and can reach customers without paying for each contact. Treated as a revenue channel that works alongside marketplaces, with a list built from every channel the brand controls, it drives repeat purchases wherever customers prefer to buy.

Why email marketing is undervalued for marketplace brands

Email has a long record as one of the highest-returning marketing channels. Litmus put the average return at $36 for every $1 spent in its 2023 State of Email report, according to Litmus.

Yet many brands that sell on Amazon, Walmart and other marketplaces treat email as an afterthought. Their attention goes to retail media, listings and marketplace promotions, where sales are visible and immediate. Email feels like a channel for brands with their own websites rather than for brands whose customers buy elsewhere, and that view misses who owns what.

Who owns the customer, and who gets paid for her attention

On a marketplace, the customer belongs to the marketplace. It holds her contact details and decides which products she sees next, so the brand’s past sales do not give it a way back to her.

That arrangement has costs for the brand. Each time the brand wants that customer’s attention, it pays for it through advertising or promotions, and the marketplace collects the payment. When the brand launches a new product, it starts from scratch with each shopper. When marketplace rules, fees or search results change, it has no other way to reach the customers it has already won.

Email changes that structure. A customer who joins a brand’s email list can be reached directly, as often as she welcomes it, without paying for each contact. The brand owns the relationship, even if the customer still prefers to buy on a marketplace.

Email does not have to pull customers away from marketplaces. A brand can use it to tell customers about a new product, a restock or a promotion, and let them buy wherever they like, including on Amazon. The email does the work of reaching the customer and the marketplace does the work of fulfilling the order, so the brand keeps the relationship while the marketplace keeps the sale.

Take a skin care brand that sells mostly on Amazon and has a small email list from its own website. When it launches a new product, it relies entirely on Amazon advertising to reach shoppers, paying for every click. A competitor with a larger list sends one email to past customers, many of whom search for the product on Amazon and buy it. The competitor’s launch starts with sales and reviews already coming in, while the first brand pays to build them from nothing. Both brands sell on the same marketplace, and only one of them can reach its past customers.

Email feeds what marketplaces reward

A launch that starts with steady sales from past customers tends to earn reviews sooner, and products with sales and reviews usually find it easier to rank in marketplace search. A replenishment reminder that brings a customer back to buy again adds to the sales history that marketplaces use to decide what to show. In that sense, a strong email program does not compete with a brand’s marketplace business. It feeds it.

Building and using the list alongside marketplaces

The list should grow from every channel the brand controls. A brand’s own website, packaging inserts where marketplace rules allow, social media, events and customer service contacts can all invite customers to join, and every sign-up point should give a clear reason to join. The list grows slowly, so the time to start is before it is needed.

The limits come from marketplace rules. Marketplaces limit how brands can contact customers who bought there, and most do not allow brands to use those orders to build an email list. The list should be built from channels the brand controls, with clear permission from each subscriber.

Email earns its keep at particular moments: product launches, restocks of popular items, seasonal promotions and replenishment reminders. A short, useful email at the right time does more than frequent general newsletters, so plan email around those moments and keep each message short and useful.

Wherever the customer buys, the measurement has to follow. If email sends customers to Amazon, its effect will show up as marketplace sales, not website sales. Brands should look for lifts in branded searches and marketplace sales after sends, and use tracking links where marketplaces offer them, so email is credited with what it actually does. Judged on website sales alone, email will look smaller than it is.

The holiday shopper is the place to start

The holiday season is a good time to start building. Shoppers who buy gifts and products during November and December are often open to hearing from a brand they have just discovered. A brand that invites them onto its list now will have a direct line to them in January, when advertising costs fall and many brands go quiet.

Email will not replace marketplace advertising. It gives brands something advertising cannot, a relationship they own, which keeps its value whatever happens to marketplace rules and prices, and building that owned channel alongside the marketplace business is work we do with brands that sell on marketplaces.

A0484.title: Cyber Week 2023 forecast: what Adobe’s season data implies
A0484.alt: Glass jars filled with coins on a frosty windowsill beside kraft-paper wrapped gifts and pine sprigs.
A0484.ttag: Cyber Week 2023 forecast: what Adobe’s season data implies | Kwontified
A0484.desc: Adobe expects Cyber Week to carry 16.8% of holiday spending. What that implies for daily sales and click prices, in three ranges brands can plan against.
A0484.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 7, 2023.
A0484.body:
Cyber Week is five days of a 61-day holiday season, about 8.2% of the calendar, yet Adobe expects it to carry 16.8% of the season’s online spending. That makes the average Cyber Week day worth about 2.05 times an average day of the season.

Put that concentration together with the softer click premium the October event showed, and the standard case for promoted products on the core days is roughly three times normal daily sales, with click prices about 35% higher. Brands should plan stock and budgets around the standard case. They should keep money and units back in case the reach case arrives, and spread spend across Amazon’s longer November 17 to 27 window.

The Cyber Week 2023 forecast in three ranges

The forecast covers the five core days, Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, for products a brand promotes with deals and advertising, compared with a normal day in early November.

CaseDaily sales vs normalCost per click vs normalDeal share of event sales
Conservative2x+20%40%
Standard3x+35%55%
Reach4x+50%70%

The deal-share column is a planning assumption based on how promoted brands typically split event sales between deal and non-deal products, not a published figure. It is the one column in the table that public data cannot supply. Brands should replace it with their own history where they have it.

How a share of spending becomes a daily multiple

When a large share of a season’s spending is concentrated in a few days, that share sets how much each event day exceeds an ordinary day. The click premium then depends on how many advertisers bid in those days relative to the number of shoppers who arrive.

Start with the share of spending. Adobe forecasts that Cyber Week will drive $37.2 billion in online spending, up 5.4%, or 16.8% of a $221.8 billion holiday season, Digital Commerce 360 reported. It expects Cyber Monday alone to reach $12 billion, up 6.1%.

Five days are about 8.2% of the 61-day season, so Cyber Week’s share implies that its average day carries about 2.05 times the season’s average daily spending. Cyber Monday, at $12 billion against a season average of about $3.64 billion a day, runs at about 3.3 times. In other words, the market as a whole runs at roughly twice the season’s average daily pace across the core days, and promoted products should run faster than that.

Those figures are market-wide, covering all online retail. Promoted products, which carry deals and heavier advertising, typically rise more than the market. That is why the standard case puts their lift at three times a normal early-November day, with two times as the conservative case and four times as the reach case.

The October evidence sets the click prices. Skai found that the premium advertisers paid per click during Prime Big Deal Days was softer than the roughly 50% rise it usually sees in major events, according to Skai. The reach case sits at that historical 50%, and the standard case lower, at 35%, to reflect October’s softer premium. If competition during Cyber Week returns to past levels, the reach case applies.

What the ranges mean for one product line

Say a brand sells $10,000 a day of a promoted product line in early November, at $1.00 per click. In the standard case, its core Cyber Week days bring about $30,000 a day in sales, at about $1.35 per click. In the conservative case, that is about $20,000 a day at $1.20 per click. In the reach case, it is about $40,000 a day at $1.50 per click.

The lift arrives differently across Amazon’s longer window. With its Black Friday event starting on November 17, a week before the core days, some demand will arrive early and at lower intensity. We expect the days from November 17 to 22 to run well below the core-day range, perhaps one and a half to two times normal for promoted products, as early shoppers buy ahead of Thanksgiving. The lift should then build through Black Friday, dip slightly over the weekend, and peak on Cyber Monday.

The ranges are wide, and they should be. Each brand’s lift depends on its category, its deals and how its competitors behave. A range exists to plan stock and budgets that cover the likely outcomes, not to predict one number.

Plan for the standard case, judge against the floor

Stock and budgets should cover three times normal daily sales for promoted products across the core days, with a reserve for four times that can be released if early results run hot.

Amazon’s Black Friday event runs from November 17, with a Cyber Monday weekend from November 25 to 27. Budgets set for five days will run out early if they are not paced across eleven. Daily caps help, because they keep spend available for Cyber Monday. Brands that measure only the core days will miss part of the event, and those that spend evenly across all eleven days will overspend before the peak.

A brand that reaches two times normal has met the floor. Judge results against that conservative case and against the weeks before and after the event, not against the reach case. The reach case is the upside, and the floor is the comparison that matters. Replace our deal-share assumption with your own history where you have it.

We will grade this forecast against public data after the event, as we did for Prime Big Deal Days. Applying these ranges to a brand’s own numbers is how we plan Cyber Week stock and budgets for the brands we manage.

A0486.crumb: TikTok Shop and brand growth: discovery…
A0486.title: TikTok Shop and brand growth: discovery replaces the search box
A0486.alt: Smartphone in a ring light photographing a ceramic bottle on a wooden table with vases, books and a magnifying glass.
A0486.ttag: TikTok Shop and brand growth: discovery replaces the search box | Kwontified
A0486.desc: On TikTok, growth comes from creators selling for commission rather than bidding on searches. How that changes brand growth, and why it shows up on Amazon.
A0486.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 9, 2023.
A0486.body:
A shopper scrolling TikTok watches a creator she follows use a serum she has never heard of. She was not looking for it, and nobody bid to reach her. She may buy it in the app, or she may type its name into Amazon, where she already has an account, saved payment details and Prime delivery.

That scroll is how TikTok is changing brand growth: discovery is replacing the search box. Many creators, paid on commission, put products in front of shoppers who were not looking for them, instead of a brand bidding to reach shoppers who already were, and the demand they create often spills onto Amazon and other retailers. Brands should treat creator programs as a sales channel, plan stock for the spillover, and measure TikTok by its effect on branded searches elsewhere as well as by its own sales.

How TikTok Shop changed the path to brand growth

For most of the last decade, brands grew online in a familiar way. Shoppers searched for what they wanted, and brands paid to appear in those searches, on Google and then on Amazon. Growth meant winning more of the searches that already existed.

TikTok works the other way. Its feed shows people videos they did not ask for, chosen by its algorithm, and products appear inside those videos. A shopper discovers a product she was not looking for, often through a creator she follows.

In September 2023, TikTok turned that behavior into a store. It launched TikTok Shop in the United States, with a dedicated shop tab, shoppable videos and live shopping, and an affiliate program that lets creators earn commission on sales, TechCrunch reported. TikTok said more than 200,000 sellers had signed up for the Shop, and more than 100,000 creators for the affiliate program. TikTok has more than 150 million users in the United States, NextShark reported.

Discovery changes what a brand pays for growth

The structure matters because it changes how a brand pays for growth. On a search platform, a brand pays for each click from a shopper already interested in the category. Growth is limited by how many people are searching, and by how much competitors will bid for them.

On TikTok, a brand can pay creators a commission on what they sell. Many creators can feature the same product at once, each reaching a different audience, and the brand pays only when a sale happens. Growth is limited less by existing demand than by how many creators the brand can interest, and how well their videos perform.

Demand gets created this way, rather than captured. A shopper who had never heard of a product sees it, wants it and buys it, sometimes on TikTok itself and often somewhere else.

Much of the demand lands on Amazon

Where that purchase happens is important. A shopper who discovers a product on TikTok may search for it on Amazon, where buying is already easy for her. The demand TikTok created then shows up as a branded search on Amazon, and the sale is credited to Amazon search or advertising.

Take a skin care brand that starts working with creators on TikTok. Its TikTok Shop sales grow slowly, but its branded searches on Amazon double over the same weeks, and its Amazon sales rise with them. If the brand judges TikTok only by TikTok Shop sales, it will conclude the program is small. In fact, it is driving much of its Amazon growth.

Running creators as a sales channel

Commission rates, product samples and the choice of creators should be managed as carefully as an advertising budget. The brands that grow fastest on TikTok tend to work with many creators at once rather than relying on a few. A creator affiliate program with clear commissions and samples is the starting point.

The spillover needs stock ready for it. A product that takes off on TikTok can sell out on Amazon within days, because shoppers go where buying is easiest. TikTok activity is an early signal of demand, and stock and listings on Amazon and other retailers should be ready before the surge arrives.

The measurement has to cover the full effect. That means tracking branded searches and sales on Amazon and other retailers alongside TikTok Shop sales, and looking for the lift that follows creator activity, so TikTok gets credit for the lift it drives. Without that, brands will undervalue a channel that may be doing more for them than its own numbers show.

Rights, logistics and an early test

Content rights deserve attention early. The videos creators make for a brand often outperform the brand’s own advertising, because they look like the rest of the feed. Brands should agree in advance whether they can reuse those videos in their own ads, on TikTok and elsewhere, and on what terms, since a strong creator video the brand cannot reuse is a missed opportunity.

TikTok is also building its own logistics, through a service it calls Fulfilled by TikTok, which stores and ships products for sellers. For brands, that raises the same question Amazon’s fulfillment does: whether the convenience is worth placing more of the business inside one platform. It is worth testing, with a clear view of the costs and of how easily the brand could move its stock elsewhere.

TikTok Shop is new, and its rules, fees and checkout experience are still developing. Brands that test it now, with clear measurement, will learn how discovery works for their products before the channel becomes crowded. Building a creator program that sells on TikTok and lifts every other channel is work we do with brands across TikTok Shop and Amazon.

A0487.crumb: BOGO promotions on Amazon: the break-even…
A0487.title: BOGO promotions on Amazon: the break-even most brands miss
A0487.alt: Two white mugs tied together with twine beside a brass balance scale on a wooden table.
A0487.ttag: BOGO promotions on Amazon: the break-even most brands miss | Kwontified
A0487.desc: A buy-one-get-one offer gives away a whole unit’s cost, so it needs far more new buyers to break even than a coupon. The arithmetic for brands on Amazon.
A0487.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 14, 2023.
A0487.body:
A buy-one-get-one-free offer on a $30 product reads to the shopper like a 50% discount. The brand’s books record a different transaction: the shopper still pays $30, and the brand ships two units instead of one, so the real cost of the promotion is the full cost of the second unit. On a typical product that leaves almost no margin on each order.

That is why BOGO needs nearly all of its orders to come from new buyers to break even, far more than a percentage-off coupon needs. Brands should use it only where new buyers dominate or a second unit has lasting value, and should compare it with a coupon on the same arithmetic before running it.

How BOGO promotions on Amazon work

Amazon sellers can create buy-one-get-one promotions alongside percentage-off promotions, offering a free item with a qualifying purchase, Pattern reported. The offer can be one free unit with one paid unit, or other combinations, such as buy two, get one free.

BOGO is popular in the holiday season because it looks generous. Shoppers see a free item and brands see a way to move more units, and both can be true. What brands tend to misjudge is the cost. It is the full cost of the free unit, not half the price of two.

The arithmetic of a free unit

A free unit costs the brand its full product and fulfillment cost, while the referral fee is charged only on the price the shopper pays. A BOGO order therefore earns little contribution. When the shopper was going to pay full price anyway, the offer turns a profitable order into one that nearly breaks even.

Take a $30 product that costs $12 per unit to make and ship, sold with a 15% referral fee, and set three kinds of order side by side.

OrderShopper paysReferral feeProduct costContribution
Full price$30$4.50$12$13.50
BOGO$30$4.50$24$1.50
25% coupon$22.50$3.38$12$7.13

A full-price order brings in $30, pays a $4.50 referral fee and costs $12 to make and ship, which leaves $13.50. A BOGO order brings in the same $30 and pays the same fee, but the brand ships two units, so the product cost doubles to $24 and the order contributes only $1.50. On the coupon order the shopper pays $22.50, the fee drops to about $3.38, and the brand keeps about $7.13.

Each BOGO order from a shopper who would have bought anyway costs the brand $12 of contribution. Each BOGO order from a genuinely new shopper adds $1.50. The gains from new shoppers have to cover the losses from existing ones before the promotion breaks even, and that requires about 89% of BOGO orders to come from new buyers.

The coupon carries a smaller loss. A shopper who would have bought anyway costs the brand about $6.38, and the coupon breaks even when about 47% of its orders come from new buyers, a far lower bar than BOGO sets.

Each brand’s own numbers will differ, but the structure holds for most products: because BOGO gives away a whole unit’s cost, it needs a much higher share of new buyers than a percentage discount does.

When a free unit pays for itself

There are still cases where BOGO makes sense. A product with a low unit cost relative to its price gives little away with the free unit. A launch is different again, because nearly every buyer is new and the goal is reviews and sales history rather than margin. And some products earn the free unit back later: one half of a pair, a refill, or a starter size that leads to future purchases can bring the shopper back.

Advertising muddies the picture. A BOGO offer usually raises conversion, so ads pointing to the product look more efficient while it runs. The extra orders include many shoppers who would have bought anyway, though, and each of those costs the brand the full $12 in the example. A rising return on ad spend during a BOGO promotion can therefore hide a falling profit. The promotion and its advertising belong in one review, judged on contribution per order rather than on attributed sales.

Offers that pair different products need the same arithmetic. A buy-A-get-B-free offer costs the brand the full unit cost of B. If B is a cheaper product that shoppers rarely buy on their own, the offer can introduce them to it at low cost. If B is a popular item that sells well at full price, the offer gives away sales the brand would have made anyway.

Stockpiling is the quieter cost. A shopper who gets two units now may not buy again for twice as long. For a replenishable product, that can turn a BOGO order into a delay of the next sale, which makes even new buyers less valuable than they appear.

Contribution per order decides between BOGO and a coupon

Set against those cases is the coupon, which needs a far smaller share of new buyers. The decision takes a short calculation. Work out the contribution of a full-price order, a BOGO order and a coupon order for each product you plan to promote. Then estimate how many orders are likely to come from new buyers, and choose the promotion with the lower break-even share.

Keep BOGO for low-cost products, launches and items where a second unit brings shoppers back. For most established products, the numbers will point to the coupon.

Running that arithmetic for every product on the promotion list before Cyber Week is how we help brands choose and price promotions on Amazon.

A0488.crumb: How Temu builds trust: guarantees in…
A0488.title: How Temu builds trust: guarantees in place of brands
A0488.alt: Orange envelope tied with twine, sealed with red wax and a small padlock, on a wooden shelf beside a mug.
A0488.ttag: How Temu builds trust: guarantees in place of brands | Kwontified
A0488.desc: Temu asks shoppers to trust its guarantees, not its products. How free returns and late-delivery credits lower shopper risk, and what brands can learn.
A0488.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 16, 2023.
A0488.body:
A shopper is choosing between a $25 kitchen gadget from a known brand on Amazon and a similar-looking one for $8 on Temu. She suspects the cheaper one may be poorly made. If it is, she can send it back for free, and the worst case is a few weeks’ wait and a trip to the post office. For many shoppers, that is a risk worth taking for a $17 saving.

That small calculation is how Temu sells. It does not ask shoppers to trust its products or its sellers, and many shoppers do not. The platform carries the risk instead, through free returns and credits for late delivery, so a shopper who doubts the quality can still buy because a bad outcome costs her little. Brands competing with Temu should make their own quality visible and back it with guarantees that lower the shopper’s risk, rather than relying on a brand name alone.

How Temu built trust without brands

Most retailers earn trust over time, through familiar brands, consistent quality and a record of delivering what they promise. Temu, which launched in the United States in 2022, had none of those. It sells mostly unbranded products from sellers shoppers have never heard of, shipped from overseas, often at prices low enough to raise doubts on their own.

So its trust had to come from promises the platform itself keeps. In October 2022, Temu said it would give customers a $5 credit if their deliveries arrived late, calling the move a first among major e-commerce providers, according to Temu. It also said buyers could return most new and unused items within 90 days of purchase with no shipping charges and receive a full refund, according to Temu.

The platform pays for the shopper’s risk

A shopper deciding whether to buy weighs two things: how likely she is to be disappointed, and what disappointment will cost her. A brand works on the first. It tells her the product will be good, and a familiar name makes that believable. Temu works on the second. It makes no case that the product will be good; it tells her that if the product is not good she can send it back for free, and that if it is late she will be paid for the wait.

When the cost of a bad outcome is close to zero, the shopper does not need to trust the product much. She can simply try it, and if it disappoints, the platform absorbs the risk. That is why Temu can sell unfamiliar products in large volumes despite widespread doubts about quality.

Someone has to pay for that, and in this case the payer is Temu. Free returns, refunds and credits are expensive, especially on low-priced items shipped across the world. The platform is, in effect, spending money to buy the trust that brands earn over years.

What brands can take from Temu’s guarantees

Brands do not need Temu’s prices to use the lesson. Trust can be built by lowering the shopper’s risk as well as by asking for her confidence.

Visible quality comes first. A shopper comparing a brand’s product with a cheaper one needs to see why it is worth more: materials, dimensions, certifications, and photos that show the details. Reviews that mention durability and quality are especially valuable. A brand that leaves its quality unstated invites comparison on price alone.

Guarantees do the rest of the work Temu’s promises do. Clear return policies, warranties and satisfaction promises lower the shopper’s risk in the same way. On marketplaces the retailer’s own policies often apply, but brands can still state their warranties and guarantees plainly on the listing and make sure they are easy to use.

Brands also benefit from protections they did not create. On Amazon, shoppers already rely on the retailer’s own return policies and protections when they buy from unfamiliar sellers, and a brand that sells through those programs inherits some of that reassurance. The point is to make sure shoppers know it applies, and to add the brand’s own promise on top, rather than assume shoppers will look it up.

Reviews send the same message, written from the shopper’s side. A shopper reading that a product held up after a year of use, or that the brand replaced a faulty item quickly, learns what disappointment would cost her with that brand. Brands should encourage reviews that speak to durability and service, and respond publicly when something goes wrong. A visible record of problems fixed can build more trust than a record of no problems at all.

Some categories need the name more than the refund. For products that must work the first time, such as safety items, children’s goods, or anything a shopper cannot easily return, a known brand still carries more weight than a refund policy. Brands in those categories should make that case directly, explaining on the listing why a known name is the safer choice where a failure matters.

Temu’s model may not last in its current form. Promises on this scale are costly, and scrutiny of the platform is growing. Its approach still shows how much a shopper’s decision depends on what she stands to lose, which is the question a brand team can ask of its own listings: what does a disappointed shopper lose when she buys from us? Brands that lower that cost while making their quality plain can compete with low prices without matching them, and making that case on every listing is how we help brands show their quality across Amazon and other marketplaces.

A0490.title: Privacy-first retail media: why cookie loss favors retailers
A0490.alt: Padlocked shop door opening onto a rustic boutique with a wicker gift basket on a wooden table.
A0490.ttag: Privacy-first retail media: why cookie loss favors retailers | Kwontified
A0490.desc: Chrome begins removing third-party cookies in 2024. Why that strengthens retail media, which measures with its own shopper data, and what brands should do.
A0490.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 21, 2023.
A0490.body:
A brand splits its digital budget between display ads across the web and retail media on Amazon. Both campaigns report results. Once third-party cookies go, the web display campaign can no longer show which buyers saw its ads, and the Amazon campaign still can. In the next budget review, the channel that can prove its results wins money from the one that cannot, even if both work equally well.

That is the likely effect of Google’s plan to remove third-party cookies from Chrome in 2024. Advertising that relies on tracking shoppers across other companies’ websites gets weaker, while retail media stays largely intact, because retailers measure ads with their own logged-in shoppers and purchase records. Budgets are likely to shift toward retailers. Brands should set up retailer clean-room measurement and incrementality baselines now, while cookies still work, so they can see what changes when they go.

Privacy-first retail media and Chrome’s 2024 timeline

Google said it would disable third-party cookies for 1% of Chrome users in the first quarter of 2024, and that its plan to remove them completely in the second half of 2024 remained on track, TechCrunch reported. Google’s original plan had called for phasing out tracking cookies as early as 2022, but the timeline was pushed back twice.

Retailers have been building for that world. At its unBoxed conference in October, Amazon introduced Amazon Publisher Cloud, which lets publishers analyze their own audience signals alongside Amazon Ads insights, Modern Retail reported.

A retailer does not need the cookie

Third-party cookies let an advertiser follow a shopper across sites and connect an ad seen in one place to a purchase in another. Removing them breaks that link for most of the open web. A retailer is in a different position. It knows who its logged-in shoppers are and what they bought, so it can connect its own ads to its own sales without any cross-site tracking.

The difference shows up in targeting and in measurement alike. On targeting, advertisers lose a common way to reach shoppers who visited their site or browsed related products elsewhere. Retailers keep their own version, because they can show ads to shoppers based on what those shoppers searched for and bought on the retailer’s site.

On measurement, advertisers on the open web lose much of their ability to see whether an ad led to a sale. Retail media keeps it, at least for sales on the retailer’s own site. That makes retail media easier to justify in budget discussions at exactly the moment other channels become harder to measure.

The budget review in the opening is a warning as much as a prediction. A channel that can show its results is not necessarily the one adding the most sales.

Baselines to build while cookies still work

Clean rooms are the first tool to learn, starting with the clean-room tools offered by the retailers a brand already sells through. They let a brand analyze how its ads reach and convert shoppers, using the retailer’s data without seeing individual identities. Brands that learn to use them now, with at least one analysis run before the end of the first quarter of 2024, will have the measurement they need once other signals fade.

Holdout tests are what carry the comparison across the change. Before cookies disappear, brands should test their major channels, including retail media, to see what each actually adds. Those results become the baseline for what each channel adds before cookies disappear. Without them, a brand will not know whether a shift in budget toward retailers is justified, or simply driven by better reporting.

First-party relationships sit outside the problem. Email lists, loyalty programs and direct customer relationships do not depend on third-party cookies, so a brand with its own audience, such as an email list or a loyalty program, can keep reaching customers whatever happens to tracking on the open web.

Retailer measurement and incrementality baselines set up while cookies still work are what let a brand see the change when it arrives, and tell a budget shift that is justified from one that is simply driven by better reporting.

Where the retailer advantage stops

The advantage is not limited to Amazon. Walmart, Target and other retailers with large numbers of logged-in shoppers hold the same kind of data, and each is building its own advertising business on it. A brand that sells through several retailers should expect each to offer its own measurement tools, with its own definitions and reports. Comparing results across them will take care, since each retailer measures sales on its own site and may count the same shopper differently.

Another limit is sales that happen off the retailer’s site. A shopper who sees an ad on Amazon and later buys from the brand’s own website, or in a store, may not be counted. Retail media’s measurement is strong inside the retailer and weaker outside it, which is one more reason incremental tests matter.

Brands should also expect retailers to raise their prices as demand shifts toward them. If more advertisers move budget into retail media because it can still be measured, competition for the same placements will rise, and early tests, run before that competition arrives, give a brand a clearer read on what retail media is worth.

The timeline may slip again. Google has delayed before, and regulators are still reviewing the plan, but the direction is clear and the steps that prepare for it are useful in any case. Setting up those baselines with retailer data and incrementality tests is how we help brands measure retail media before the cookies go.

A0491.crumb: Amazon review count experiment: the end…
A0491.title: Amazon review count experiment: the end of review moats
A0491.alt: Stone castle with battlements and towers above a grassy dry moat in golden evening light.
A0491.ttag: Amazon review count experiment: the end of review moats | Kwontified
A0491.desc: Amazon tested hiding review counts in search results. Why a large review count may stop protecting incumbents, and what brands should build instead.
A0491.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 22, 2023.
A0491.body:
Two kitchen products sit side by side in Amazon’s search results, each with a 4.8 average. One has five reviews and the other five thousand, and a shopper scanning the page can tell at a glance which one feels safer. In 2023 Amazon tested search results that take that glance away.

The test showed ratings without review counts, and it threatens an advantage incumbents spent years building. If shoppers cannot compare review counts at a glance, they compare rating quality and recent sales instead. That helps newer products and changes what brands should invest in. Brands should protect their rating quality, keep sales steady, and stop treating review count alone as a defense.

What the Amazon review count experiment showed shoppers

In August, Amazon tested a new way to show ratings on its search pages. Instead of the number of reviews, some search results showed the average star rating and the percentage of reviews rated four stars and above, GeekWire reported. Another version replaced the familiar row of five stars with a single star next to the average rating.

Amazon said in a statement that it was always innovating on behalf of customers to provide the best possible shopping experience. Review counts and full ratings remained on product pages. The test applied to search results, where most shoppers compare products before clicking.

The test was criticized, mostly on the grounds that shoppers rely on the number of reviews to judge how trustworthy a rating is. The two products in the opening make the point: a 4.8 from five reviews and a 4.8 from five thousand do not carry the same weight.

How a review count became a moat

For years, the review count has worked as a moat. A product that has collected thousands of reviews looks safer than a newcomer with a handful, even if both have the same rating. Shoppers scanning a search page use the count as a shortcut for how many other people have bought and liked the product.

In almost every category, that shortcut protects incumbents. A new product, however good, cannot match a review count built over several years, so it has to win shoppers despite looking less proven.

What the page shows once the count is gone

The test changes the comparison. If the count disappears from search results, shoppers look at what remains: the rating, the share of positive reviews, the price and, increasingly, signals of recent sales. Amazon already shows labels on many products indicating how many units were bought in the past month. Those labels and the rating become the main evidence of a product’s standing.

That helps newer products with strong early ratings, and it exposes incumbents whose ratings have slipped over time. A product with 10,000 reviews and a 4.1 average may look worse, side by side, than a newer product with a 4.7 average, once the count is no longer there to tip the balance.

Another change pushes in the same direction. GeekWire’s report also noted that Amazon has started using artificial intelligence to summarize customer reviews, giving shoppers a quick view of what reviewers praise and criticize. A summary draws on what reviews say rather than on how many there are, so a product with fewer reviews but consistent praise for a specific benefit may read better in a summary than a product with many reviews and mixed comments.

Together, the two changes move attention from the quantity of reviews to their content. Shoppers see less of the count and more of what customers actually think. That raises the value of listing details that match what reviewers say, and the cost of recurring complaints that a summary will surface for every shopper to read.

Take a kitchen brand whose best seller has years of reviews but an average that has drifted down, while a competitor’s newer product, with fewer reviews, holds a higher rating. With review counts visible, the incumbent’s count reassures shoppers. Without them, the comparison is rating against rating, and the newcomer wins more clicks.

What brands should build instead of a count

The test may not become permanent. It still shows where Amazon is willing to go, and the response is useful whatever Amazon decides.

Rating quality comes first. Brands should track the average rating and the share of positive reviews for their key products, read the reviews behind any decline promptly, and fix the product or listing issues that cause it. A rating that slips by a few tenths can cost more than a small gap in review count ever did.

Steady sales matter more if recent-sales labels gain weight, because a product that sells consistently will look stronger than one with occasional spikes. Keeping key products in stock is part of that, since a long stockout weakens both the label and the product’s position.

Brands that have treated a large review count as protection should assume competitors can close the gap faster than before, and treat the count as an advantage that can shrink. What holds up is a product shoppers keep rating highly, rather than a number collected years ago.

Brands launching new products can take the opposite lesson. A strong early rating, earned honestly through a good product and a clear listing, may count for more than it used to. Amazon has continued to act against fake reviews, including lawsuits against review brokers, so the only durable path is genuine customer satisfaction.

The question for a brand team is which of its key products would still win the comparison with the count taken away, and working through that answer for each listing is how we help brands protect ratings and visibility on Amazon.

A0494.crumb: Amazon Brand Store: status symbol or…
A0494.title: Amazon Brand Store: status symbol or sales driver?
A0494.alt: Bright minimalist boutique with oak shelves of ceramics and linens and a kraft shopping bag on the counter.
A0494.ttag: Amazon Brand Store: status symbol or sales driver? | Kwontified
A0494.desc: Amazon says updated Brand Stores earn more per visitor. Why that mostly reflects who visits, and how to test whether your store adds sales or just looks good.
A0494.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 28, 2023.
A0494.body:
Amazon reports that followers who visit a brand’s store purchase 54% more units. That looks like proof that a store sells, and a Brand Store does look like a sales driver because its visitors buy more. Most of the gap, though, comes from who visits: shoppers who already know and like the brand.

An Amazon Brand Store pays only when it raises the conversion or basket size of traffic a brand already sends. Brands should test that directly, by sending the same ad traffic to the store and to product pages and comparing the sales, rather than judging the store by its attributed sales per visitor.

What Amazon says about the Amazon Brand Store

Amazon presents Stores as a growth tool. In materials for advertisers, it reported that stores updated within the past 90 days had 11% more repeat visitors and 13.1% higher attributed sales per visitor, based on its internal data from 2022, according to Amazon Ads. The 54% figure for followers comes from the same materials.

Those figures are real, and they explain why so many brands invest in elaborate stores. A polished store also signals that a brand is serious, and for many brands it is as much a statement as a sales channel.

Why store metrics overstate what the store adds

Shoppers who seek out a brand’s store are already more likely to buy than shoppers who land on a single product. Store metrics therefore mix two effects: the effect of the store itself, and the effect of attracting loyal shoppers. A follower who visits the store buys more partly because of the store, and partly because she is a follower.

The same mix appears in store updates. Brands that refresh their stores every 90 days are often the brands that invest more in everything, from listings to advertising to new products. Their stores may perform better because the brands do, and the refresh alone may account for only part of it.

The headline numbers cannot tell you how much a store adds, even when it adds something. To see the store’s own contribution, a brand has to hold the shopper constant and change only where she lands.

Test the Amazon Brand Store against the product page

The cleanest test is one most brands already have the tools for. Sponsored Brands ads can send shoppers to a store or to a product page, so a brand can run the same ad, to similar audiences, with the two destinations and compare sales per click.

Take a brand that sends 1,000 clicks to each destination. Store visitors buy several items, so the basket is larger, but fewer of them buy.

DestinationClicksConversion rateAverage basketSales
Brand Store1,0008%$40$3,200
Product page1,00010%$30$3,000

The store converts 8% of its visitors, but they buy several items, at an average basket of $40. The product page converts 10%, at an average of $30. That puts the store at $3,200 and the product page at $3,000.

The store wins by about 7%, because it raises basket size by more than it lowers conversion. For a brand with a single hero product, the result could easily go the other way: shoppers who land on the product page buy it, while store visitors browse and leave.

Run the comparison before investing heavily. A simple store can be built quickly, tested against product pages, and expanded only if it earns more per click, which means growing it only where it raises basket size or repeat visits enough to beat the product page. None of this requires new tools. The fit with the range matters too. Brands with many related products, where a shopper might buy several, are more likely to benefit, while brands with one or two products may do better sending traffic straight to the product page.

Updates deserve the same treatment. Refreshing a store for a season or a launch can help, but the test is whether sales per click rise; a store that merely looks newer has not passed it.

Costs and the store’s other jobs

A store also has costs, and they belong in the comparison. Design time, photography and the work of keeping pages current all take effort, and a store that is not maintained can show out-of-stock products or outdated offers to the shoppers most likely to buy. A brand that cannot keep a large store current may do better with a smaller one that stays accurate.

The test needs a little care to read. Results can differ by season, by product and by the ad that sends the traffic. A store that loses to the product page for a single best seller may win for a gift-giving search where shoppers want to browse. The most useful approach is to run the comparison for the brand’s main traffic sources separately and to repeat it after major changes, rather than treat one result as permanent.

There are other jobs a store does. It gives followers somewhere to return, and it gives off-Amazon traffic, such as social media links, a branded landing page. Those benefits are real and also measurable, through repeat visits and tagged traffic sources in Amazon’s store reporting. Brands should track both alongside the destination test, so the store’s other contributions are counted rather than assumed.

A store is worth building when it raises the value of traffic the brand already sends, through larger baskets, discovery of other products or repeat visits. When it does not, it is a status symbol. Sending the same Sponsored Brands ad to both destinations and reading sales per click is how we help brands decide where their Amazon traffic should land.

A0495.crumb: Roundel and Target Plus together: how a…
A0495.title: Roundel and Target Plus together: how a curated marketplace works
A0495.alt: Sunlit shop wall with a red floating shelf of ceramic mugs, linen towels, brushes and jars below a wall-mounted screen.
A0495.ttag: Roundel and Target Plus together: how a curated marketplace works | Kwontified
A0495.desc: Target Plus is invite-only, which changes how Roundel advertising works for the brands inside it. Why the two should be planned together, not apart.
A0495.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 30, 2023.
A0495.body:
Take a home goods brand that joins Target Plus with a small range. It runs Roundel ads on its best seller and finds that click prices are lower than on larger marketplaces, because few sellers compete. Encouraged, it adds more products to the marketplace and extends its campaigns to them, building a presence in a category where it faces little direct competition.

That sequence is the system working as designed. Target Plus is a curated, invite-only marketplace, so fewer sellers compete in each category than on open marketplaces. Roundel, Target’s advertising business, reaches shoppers using Target’s own data. For brands inside Target Plus, the marketplace limits the competition and advertising decides who gets seen, so brands should plan their Target Plus assortment and their Roundel campaigns together, rather than as separate channels.

How Roundel and Target Plus took shape

Target began inviting third-party sellers onto its website in 2019, through a program called Target Plus, Mobile Marketing Magazine reported. Sellers had to be invited, and their products would appear on Target.com alongside Target’s own range.

By the end of that year, nearly 100 sellers offered about 250,000 products through the marketplace, and Target said it would be more selective than its competitors, the Star Tribune reported. Joe Kaziukenas of Marketplace Pulse said keeping Target Plus invitation-only was a wise approach, since opening to everyone risked harming the shopping experience.

Target has kept that curated model. Alongside it, Target has built Roundel into an advertising business that lets brands reach Target’s shoppers on Target.com and beyond.

Curation changes what Roundel and Target Plus each do

The structure matters because it shapes the competition a brand faces, and that depends on who is allowed in. On an open marketplace, a brand competes with many sellers offering similar products, including resellers of its own goods and unbranded lookalikes, and advertising there is partly a defense: a brand bids to stay visible against a crowd.

On a curated marketplace the crowd is smaller. Target chooses which sellers join, often to fill gaps in its own range, and a brand inside Target Plus may face only a handful of direct competitors in its category, with few or none selling its own products.

With less crowding, a modest Roundel budget can reach a larger share of the shoppers searching in a category. Advertising then becomes less about defending visibility against a crowd and more about introducing the brand to Target’s shoppers, many of whom may not know it.

The marketplace’s own role changes too. Because Target selects the range, a brand’s place in Target Plus is partly a statement of fit, and the assortment a brand brings to Target matters as much as the advertising behind it.

The planning decision: one system or two channels

For a brand deciding how to enter Target, the choice is whether the marketplace range and the advertising are planned as separate channels, each with its own budget line, or chosen together as one system.

Treating Target Plus and Roundel as one plan starts with the range. The products a brand brings to Target Plus should be the ones it can support with advertising and stock, rather than everything it could list. A large range with no advertising behind it is likely to go unnoticed, even on a curated site.

The lighter competition is worth using early. Brands should test Roundel campaigns while competition in their categories is limited and measure what share of category searches they reach at a modest budget. Where a modest budget wins a large share, it may be worth expanding the range rather than raising bids.

The physical stores and the website connect as well. Target’s shoppers move between its stores and its website, and a brand that sells on Target Plus may, over time, find opportunities to reach shoppers who buy in stores, with Roundel’s audiences helping it understand who those shoppers are.

Curation also protects the brand’s own listings. On a curated marketplace, a brand is less likely to find unauthorized resellers undercutting its prices or lookalike products confusing shoppers, which makes it easier to keep prices consistent and to present the brand as it intends. Advertising money that would go to defending against resellers elsewhere can go instead to reaching new shoppers.

Pricing still needs watching, because Target’s shoppers often compare prices with other retailers, and a brand whose Target Plus prices sit well above its prices elsewhere will struggle to convert the shoppers its advertising brings in. Consistent pricing across retailers makes both the marketplace and the advertising work harder.

The limits of a curated marketplace

A curated marketplace means Target decides who joins and what they may sell, and its standards can be strict. Brands should treat their place as something earned and maintained, by keeping stock reliable, listings accurate and service strong, because the same selection that keeps competitors out applies to them as well.

Measurement also needs care. Roundel reports results within Target’s own systems, which may not match how a brand measures sales elsewhere. Brands should compare Target Plus sales with and without advertising over time, so they can see what Roundel adds instead of relying on attributed figures alone.

For brands used to the crowded economics of open marketplaces, Target’s model can feel unfamiliar. Its structure rewards a different kind of planning: a smaller, chosen range, supported by advertising that reaches shoppers who are new to the brand. The question for the team is whether the Target Plus range and the Roundel budget sit in the same plan, and putting them there is how we help brands sell on Target Plus and advertise through Roundel.

A0497.title: Cyber Week 2023 results: grading our forecast against the data
A0497.alt: Brass vernier caliper measuring a stack of three ribbon-tied gift boxes on a wooden table.
A0497.ttag: Cyber Week 2023 results: grading our forecast against the data | Kwontified
A0497.desc: Public data confirms the market assumption behind our Cyber Week forecast. Why the brand-level grade needs your own data, and how to read it fairly.
A0497.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 5, 2023.
A0497.body:
A forecast built on a ratio can be checked as soon as the inputs to the ratio are published. Ours assumed that an average Cyber Week day would carry about 2.05 times the holiday season’s average daily spending. Adobe’s final figures put it at about 2.09 times, so the market-level assumption behind the forecast held.

That is only half of the grade. Public data cannot say whether a brand’s promoted products reached three times normal sales or what its clicks cost, because those numbers sit in each brand’s own reports. Brands should grade them against their own results, and adjust for the eleven-day Amazon window and the weeks around it before setting plans for 2024.

Cyber Week 2023 results against our forecast

Our forecast started from Adobe’s projection of $37.2 billion in Cyber Week online spending. That would be 16.8% of the $221.8 billion Adobe expected across the whole holiday season. Since the five days make up about 8.2% of a 61-day season, the share works out to the 2.05 multiple. Our standard case then called for promoted products to sell three times their normal daily volume, while click prices ran about 35% higher.

Cyber Week came in at $38 billion, up 7.8% from a year earlier, and Cyber Monday reached a record $12.4 billion, up 9.6%, according to Adobe. Black Friday reached $9.8 billion.

Divide the season forecast by its 61 days and the forecast daily average comes to about $3.64 billion. Against that figure, Cyber Week’s average day of $7.6 billion ran at about 2.09 times, and Cyber Monday at about 3.4 times.

Day or periodSpending per dayMultiple of the forecast season day
Forecast season average$3.64 billion(base)
Cyber Week average day$7.6 billion2.09
Cyber Monday$12.4 billion3.4
Our assumption for a Cyber Week day2.05

Both results are close to what we assumed, if slightly higher. At the level of the whole market, the assumption held.

Why the market grade and the brand grade answer different questions

A market-wide figure can confirm how concentrated spending was in the event days. Each brand’s lift depends on its own deals, stock and advertising, and on how much of its event sales were moved from the days before and after. The market grade and the brand grade answer different questions, so they have to be done separately.

The market grade is the one we can make in public, and it tells us the shape of demand was close to what we planned for. The brand grade, whether promoted products reached three times normal and what clicks actually cost, depends on data each brand holds.

Amazon’s longer event complicates the brand grade. Its Black Friday event ran from November 17 to 27, eleven days rather than five. Some of the demand that would once have arrived on Black Friday arrived earlier. A brand that compares only the five core days with a normal day will understate the event’s total effect and may misread its timing.

Take a brand whose sales rose to 2.5 times normal during the five core days, below our standard case. Looking more closely, it finds that sales also ran at 1.5 times normal during the six earlier days of Amazon’s event. Measured across all eleven days, the event delivered more extra sales than the five-day view suggests. The result was not weak; it was spread out.

How to grade your own Cyber Week

Grade the market and the brand separately, and measure the brand across the whole event window and the weeks around it.

Start with the core days, placing your results within the forecast ranges and recording whether they fell in the conservative, standard or reach case. Then widen the view to the earlier days of Amazon’s event, and compare the full eleven-day window with the same period in 2022. The weeks before and after belong in the check as well, since sales borrowed from early November or early December will show up as a dip around the event.

Click prices deserve a check of their own, kept separate from sales. Compare what you paid on each event day with your plan, and with the days just before the event. Many brands will find that prices rose most on the busiest days and less on the early ones, which matters for how budgets are paced in 2024.

These checks should feed directly into 2024 planning. The share of event sales that came from the earlier days of the window, the true lift after adjusting for borrowed sales, and the actual click premium are the three numbers most likely to change the plan.

Cyber Week next to Prime Big Deal Days

A comparison of Cyber Week with Prime Big Deal Days also helps. In October, shopper spending landed close to our scaling assumption while advertising results came in lower. If the same pattern appeared at Cyber Week for a brand, with strong sales but weaker attributed advertising returns, it suggests that deals and organic visibility carried more of the event than ads did. That is useful to know before setting the balance between deal funding and advertising budgets for the 2024 events.

Cyber Week’s record market figures do not change our earlier view that event advertising is becoming a cost of being present. A bigger market means more shoppers. It also means more advertisers competing for the same shoppers. The brands that measure what they actually added will plan more accurately than those that measure only what they were credited with, and building that measurement around each event is how we help brands grade what their event advertising added.

A0499.crumb: Cyber Week 2023 lessons: how shoppers now…
A0499.title: Cyber Week 2023 lessons: how shoppers now buy
A0499.alt: Laptop, smartphone and a tipped-over paper shopping bag on a window seat overlooking a snowy garden.
A0499.ttag: Cyber Week 2023 lessons: how shoppers now buy | Kwontified
A0499.desc: Cyber Week 2023 ran on phones, deep discounts and short-term credit, across brand stores and marketplaces alike. What that structure means for planning 2024.
A0499.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 7, 2023.
A0499.body:
Take an apparel brand that sold well on Amazon during Cyber Week but saw its own website lag. Looking closer, it finds that most of its site visits came from phones, where its product pages loaded slowly and its offer was buried below the fold. On Amazon, the same shoppers found a clear price and fast checkout. The brand did not lose demand; it lost the sale to its own channel’s weaker mobile experience.

In miniature, that brand’s week is a version of what happened across the whole event. Cyber Week 2023 showed that the holiday peak now runs on phones, deep discounts and short-term credit, spread across brands’ own stores as well as the marketplaces. It rewards brands whose offers are clear on a small screen, whose discounts are planned rather than reactive, and whose sales are measured across every channel. Brands should plan their 2024 events for mobile first, set discount depth deliberately, and judge results across their own stores and the marketplaces together.

What the Cyber Week 2023 lessons rest on

The headline figures for the week were records. Online spending over the week reached $38 billion, 7.8% above the year before, with $12.4 billion of it on Cyber Monday, according to Adobe. Behind those totals, the same report showed how shoppers bought: smartphones drove 51.8% of online sales across the week, up from 49.9% in 2022, and paid search was the largest marketing driver of sales, at 27%.

Discounts were deep, peaking on Cyber Monday at 31% off list price in electronics, 27% in toys and 23% in apparel, HomePage News reported.

Shoppers also stretched their budgets with credit. Buy now, pay later accounted for $940 million of Cyber Monday spending, up 42.5%, The Boston Globe reported.

The spending did not stay on the marketplaces either. Shopify said its merchants set a Black Friday record of $4.1 billion in sales, Fortune reported.

Why the structure matters more than the totals

Taken together, these figures describe a different kind of event from the one many brands still plan for, and each of its features changes what a brand has to get right.

More than half of online sales happened on phones. A shopper on a phone sees less: a smaller image, a shorter title, fewer details before she decides. Offers that need explaining lose to offers that are obvious at a glance.

On a phone, search results are especially compressed, too. Only a few products appear before a shopper scrolls, and the sponsored positions take much of that space. That makes the cost of a top position during the event higher, and its value higher as well, because a shopper on a phone is less likely to scroll far.

With paid search the single largest marketing driver of sales, the shoppers who arrived with a product in mind did most of the buying. That rewards brands that show up when shoppers search for their category, and it puts a premium on the search terms that matter most during the event. Brands that spread their budgets evenly across the year, rather than concentrating them on the searches that peak during the event, may have missed the moments when intent was highest.

With deep discounts across major categories, shoppers learned to expect them. Brands that held back may have kept margin, but they competed against neighbors whose prices were visibly lower.

The rise in buy now, pay later suggests that some of the spending was borrowed against future months. That matters for what comes after: demand in January and February may be softer for brands whose customers stretched to buy in November.

Brands’ own stores set records alongside the marketplaces. A brand that judges Cyber Week only by its Amazon results sees only part of what happened.

Planning the 2024 events around the phone

In that planning, the phone comes first. Product titles, main images and offers should make sense on a small screen without scrolling. Brands should review their key listings and their own store on a phone before every major event, and check how their key products appear on a phone search page during events, not only on a desktop.

Discount depth is a decision to make before the event, not during it. Brands should decide in advance which products will carry deep discounts and which will not, based on margin and on how much the discount actually adds. Reacting to competitors’ prices during the event leads to discounting that costs more than it earns.

Measurement has to reach every channel the shopper actually used. Brands should combine their marketplace results with their own store and other retailers, and look at the weeks after the event as well as the event itself. If credit-funded spending pulled demand forward, the dip will show up in January.

The patterns are unlikely to reverse. Mobile shopping, deep event discounting and flexible payment have each grown for several years, and Cyber Week 2023 was their clearest demonstration so far. Brands that plan for them will capture more of the next peak.

Questions for the 2024 event plan

  • Does every event offer on our key listings and our own store make sense on a phone, without scrolling?
  • Which products will carry deep discounts, decided product by product before each event on margin and incremental sales?
  • Do our event results combine our own store, the marketplaces and other retailers in one view?
  • Who is watching January for the demand that credit may have pulled forward?

Putting those answers into one plan for every channel is how we help brands prepare for the 2024 event calendar.

A0500.title: Amazon low-inventory-level fee: the arithmetic of running lean
A0500.alt: Two cardboard boxes and a brass dish of coins on a mostly empty metal warehouse shelf.
A0500.ttag: Amazon low-inventory-level fee: the arithmetic of running lean | Kwontified
A0500.desc: From April 2024, holding too little stock at Amazon costs a fee on every unit sold. Why extra cover is usually cheaper than the fee, and how to find your level.
A0500.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 12, 2023.
A0500.body:
Starting April 1, 2024, a brand that keeps its Amazon stock lean pays for it on every unit it sells. Amazon’s low-inventory-level fee charges on each unit sold while a standard-size product carries less than about four weeks of supply. The cost of running lean now grows with sales volume, while the cost of carrying extra stock grows only with the extra units held.

That difference decides the answer. For most products, a little more cover is far cheaper than the fee. Brands should calculate both costs for each product and set their target cover from the comparison, not from habit.

How the Amazon low-inventory-level fee works

On December 5, Amazon outlined its 2024 fee changes for US sellers, Value Added Resource reported. The new low-inventory-level fee applies to standard-size products that carry consistently low inventory relative to unit sales. Amazon said sellers can avoid it by maintaining more than four weeks of inventory relative to sales, starting April 1, 2024.

Amazon also said it would reduce non-peak monthly storage fees for standard-size products from an average of $0.87 to $0.78 per cubic foot, from January through September. The two changes point the same way. Amazon wants sellers to hold more stock in its network, and it is making that cheaper while making the alternative more expensive.

Fee or extra stock: why the fee usually costs more

The fee is charged per unit sold while cover is short, so it grows with every sale. Storage on the extra units, plus the cash tied up in them, is what holding an extra two weeks of stock costs. For compact, fast-selling products, that holding cost is small, and for most of them the fee outweighs it by a wide margin.

Take a product that takes up 0.1 cubic feet, costs $10 to make, and sells 100 units a week, or about 400 a month. Say the brand normally holds two weeks of cover and is charged a fee of $0.30 per unit sold. That fee is a figure chosen for illustration: Amazon has published the fee’s structure, and actual per-unit amounts vary by product.

Monthly costRunning leanTwo more weeks of cover
Low-inventory-level fee$0.30 on 400 units = $120avoided
Storage on 200 extra unitsnone20 cubic feet at $0.78 = $15.60
Cash tied up in 200 extra unitsnone$2,000 at 10% a year = $16.67
Total$120about $32

Running lean costs $0.30 on 400 units, or $120 a month. Holding two more weeks of cover means 200 extra units. Their storage, at 20 cubic feet and $0.78 per cubic foot, costs $15.60 a month, and the cash tied up in them, $2,000 at a 10% annual cost of capital, costs about $16.67 a month. Together, that is about $32.

In this example, running lean costs nearly four times as much as holding enough stock to avoid the fee.

The other side of the trade has real weight for some products. Bulky items take up more space, so their storage costs more. Slow sellers pay little in fees, because the fee scales with sales. Expensive products tie up more cash per unit. For those, the answer may differ, which is why the calculation should be made product by product.

For compact, fast-selling products like the one in the example, the numbers lean toward holding the stock.

How to set cover after the fee

Calculate the fee and the holding cost for each standard-size product, and set target cover from the comparison.

Start with the fastest sellers. Because the fee scales with sales, the products that sell most are the ones where running lean costs most, and they are where brands should review their cover first.

Both sides of the comparison need all their costs counted. Holding cost includes storage, the cash tied up in stock, and the risk of aged-inventory surcharges if stock sits too long. The fee side includes the fee itself and the risk of running out, which costs sales and search position.

Reorder timing should follow the new threshold. Four weeks of cover at Amazon has to be measured against the time it takes to restock, including Amazon’s own receiving times. Brands with long supply chains need to reorder earlier than before to stay above the line.

Seasonality matters too. The reduced storage rate applies from January through September. Storage in the final quarter of the year costs more, so the balance between holding stock and paying the fee shifts during the holiday months. Brands should run the comparison separately for the peak season, when higher storage costs and higher sales volumes both come into play.

It also helps to aim a little above the threshold, rather than exactly at it. Sales vary from week to week, and a product that sits at four weeks of cover on average will dip below it in its busiest weeks. A buffer of a week or so above the line costs little in storage and avoids paying the fee during the very weeks when sales, and therefore the fee, are highest.

The other 2024 changes interact with the fee as well. A new inbound placement fee from March 1 rewards shipping to several locations rather than one, and fulfillment fees fall from April 15. The net effect on each product depends on all three, and on how a brand changes its shipping and stock levels in response.

The new structure is more complex, but its direction is clear: Amazon is charging for behavior that makes its network less efficient. For most brands, the cheapest response is to hold a little more stock, in the right places, rather than pay to run lean. Working out that level for each product is how we help brands set inventory cover for Amazon’s 2024 fees.

A0502.title: The year in marketplaces 2023: venues became managed systems
A0502.alt: Row of lever frames inside a railway signal box with windows overlooking tracks and semaphore signals.
A0502.ttag: The year in marketplaces 2023: venues became managed systems | Kwontified
A0502.desc: In 2023, marketplaces set more of the terms: fees tied to seller behavior, longer events, changed search signals. What that shift means for brands in 2024.
A0502.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 14, 2023.
A0502.body:
Plan 2024 for a brand that sells on Amazon, Walmart and TikTok Shop, and the three marketplaces give three different answers. On Amazon, the brand’s best move is to hold enough stock to avoid the new fee and to plan around Amazon’s event calendar. On TikTok Shop, it is to work with creators who can show the product in use. On Walmart, it is to align offers with member-first events. The same brand needs three different operating plans, each built around a different platform’s incentives.

That is what the year changed. In 2023, the major marketplaces moved from open venues, where sellers competed on listings and price, toward managed systems, where the platform sets more of the terms. They did it through fees tied to seller behavior, longer platform-run events, curated or guaranteed models, and changes to the signals shoppers see. A brand’s advantage shifts from optimizing listings to operating well within each platform’s rules, so brands should plan 2024 around each marketplace’s incentives, not just its audience.

What the year in marketplaces 2023 changed

Fees began to respond to how sellers behave. Amazon’s 2024 fee changes, outlined on December 5, split charges into inbound and outbound services and added a low-inventory-level fee for products that carry too little stock relative to sales, Value Added Resource reported. Amazon said the changes create incentives for sellers to use its network more efficiently. Fees no longer just price a service; they steer how sellers ship and stock.

The events grew longer, and the platforms ran them. Amazon ran a second Prime event in October, and its Black Friday event lasted eleven days, from November 17 to 27, HomePage News reported. The platform, rather than the seller, increasingly decides when demand peaks.

The range of marketplace models widened. TikTok launched TikTok Shop in the United States in September, with an affiliate program for creators, TechCrunch reported. Temu grew on platform guarantees, such as free returns within 90 days, according to Temu. Target, for its part, kept its marketplace invitation-only. Each model sets its own rules for who sells and for how shoppers decide.

Even what shoppers see on the page changed. In August, Amazon tested search results that showed a rating and the share of positive reviews in place of the review count, GeekWire reported. The platform can change, in a test, signals that brands had spent years building.

Who holds the control now

The common thread running through all four changes is control. In each case, the platform decided more of what determines a seller’s results: what it pays, when demand arrives, who it competes with, and how shoppers judge it.

In an open venue, a brand’s advantage came largely from listing work: better titles, better images, more reviews, sharper prices. Those still matter.

In a managed system, though, the platform’s rules can raise or lower their value overnight. A large review count is worth less if the count is hidden. Lean inventory is worth less if it triggers a fee. A carefully planned promotion matters less if the platform moves the event.

That shifts the advantage toward operating well within the rules. A brand that understands how each platform’s fees, events and signals work, and adjusts quickly when they change, will do better than one that optimizes listings in isolation.

The shift also raises the cost of surprise. When platforms change terms more often, brands that monitor announcements and test changes quickly gain ground on brands that find out at the end of a quarter. Operating discipline, more than any single tactic, becomes the advantage.

Regulators are paying attention to the same shift. When platforms set more of the terms, questions about how those terms are set, and whether sellers can reasonably avoid them, become questions of competition policy as well as business. Brands should expect more scrutiny of marketplace fees and rules in 2024, and possibly some changes as a result. That is one more reason to watch platform announcements closely, since the rules may move from either direction, through the platform’s own choices or through pressure from outside it.

None of this makes marketplaces less attractive. They still bring the shoppers. But a brand that treats them as neutral shelves will be surprised more often in 2024 than one that treats them as systems with their own goals.

Planning 2024 around each platform’s incentives

The 2024 plan starts with a map of incentives. For every marketplace a brand sells on, it should list what the platform rewards and penalizes: fees, event timing, signals in search, rules on who can sell. That list is the base of the 2024 channel plan, and it will look different for each platform.

Operations need room to move when the rules do. Inventory, pricing and advertising should be able to change quickly when a platform’s rules change, whether that is a fee, an event date or a search signal. Brands should keep a short list of the changes most likely to affect them and a plan for each.

Spreading sales across channels helps where it reduces dependence on one platform. A brand that depends entirely on one platform’s rules carries that platform’s risk. Selling across several marketplaces, and through its own store, spreads that risk, as long as each channel is run on its own terms rather than as a copy of the others.

The question for a brand’s leadership is whose rules its 2024 plan was written around, and building a separate operating plan for each marketplace is how we help brands plan their 2024 channels.
