A0504.title: 2024 marketplace plan: four assumptions to change from 2023
A0504.alt: Four brass compasses lined up beside a worn leather journal on a rustic wooden table.
A0504.ttag: 2024 marketplace plan: four assumptions to change from 2023 | Kwontified
A0504.desc: Many 2024 plans copy 2023 with a growth rate added. Four assumptions that 2023 showed to be wrong: event timing, click prices, inventory and measurement.
A0504.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 19, 2023.
A0504.body:
Copy the 2023 plan, add a growth rate, and the 2024 plan is finished. Many 2024 plans are built exactly that way. But 2023 changed four assumptions such plans rely on: that demand peaks on a few fixed days, that event click prices are a temporary premium, that lean inventory is always cheaper, and that platform reports measure what advertising adds.

A plan rolled forward from 2023 carries those assumptions into a year whose rules have changed, so the errors compound. Brands should rebuild those four parts of the plan from the 2023 evidence, rather than roll them forward, and keep the parts that did not change.

Why a 2024 marketplace plan cannot simply roll forward

The overall market is not the problem. Adobe expected online holiday spending to grow 4.8% to $221.8 billion, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Cyber Week then came in at $38 billion, slightly above that forecast, according to Adobe. As a starting point, steady growth is reasonable.

The problems lie in the structure underneath it, in four places where 2023 changed the rules. A plan that rebuilds the assumptions that changed, and keeps the ones that did not, starts from the conditions the brand will actually face.

Assumption carried from 2023What 2023 showedWhat the 2024 plan does instead
Demand peaks on a few fixed daysLonger events and a second Prime eventMaps every event window and spreads budget and stock
Event click prices are a temporary premiumEvent returns below the scaling assumptionBudgets the click premium as a line
Lean inventory is always cheaperA fee on low stock from April 2024Sets target cover above four weeks
Platform reports measure what ads addChrome cookie removal planned; new formats measured poorlyRuns a measurement program with holdouts

The event calendar is longer than the plan assumes

Amazon’s calendar now holds a second Prime event, in October, and a Black Friday event that lasted from November 17 to 27, eleven days in all, as HomePage News reported. A plan that concentrates budget and stock on Black Friday and Cyber Monday will be short in the earlier days of each event. The 2024 plan should map every event window, including the early-access days, and spread budget and stock across them.

The click premium belongs in the budget

As more advertisers competed for the same shoppers, our reviews of the year’s events found advertising returns lower than the scaling assumption suggested. We now treat the click premium as a cost of being present, and the 2024 plan should budget for it explicitly.

Take a brand that spends $10,000 on an event and assumes click prices will rise 35%. The same clicks now cost $13,500.

If the brand’s promoted sales triple, its advertising still earns more than it costs, since sales grow about 2.2 times faster than the click price. But if the brand budgets $10,000 and expects the same number of clicks, it will run out before the event ends. The premium is a line in the plan, not a surprise to manage.

Lean inventory now carries a fee

Amazon’s low-inventory-level fee, starting April 1, 2024, charges standard-size products whose supply falls below about four weeks of sales, Value Added Resource reported. Amazon also cut non-peak storage fees. For most fast-selling products, holding a little more stock is now cheaper than the fee. The 2024 plan should set target cover above four weeks for those products, with reorder timing to match.

Platform reports will measure less

Google plans to begin removing third-party cookies from Chrome in 2024, TechCrunch reported, and retailers are expanding into formats whose effects their own reports measure poorly. The 2024 plan should include a measurement program: holdout tests on major channels, a view of total sales across channels, and clear rules for which results count.

Keep what 2023 confirmed, rebuild what it changed

The answer to a rolled-forward plan is to keep the assumptions 2023 confirmed and rebuild the four it changed. In practice, that means four sections in the plan that did not exist, or looked different, a year ago:

  • An event calendar with every window and its budget.
  • A click-price assumption for each event, written into the budget.
  • A target cover for each standard-size product, set from the fee and the holding cost.
  • A measurement plan, with the tests the brand will run and the dates it will run them.

Each section has an owner and a review date. Assumptions that are written down can be checked; assumptions that are carried forward silently cannot.

Brands should also leave room for what they cannot plan. Platforms changed their rules several times in 2023, and they will again. A plan with a reserve of budget and a short list of likely changes, each with a response, will handle those moves better than one that commits everything in January.

The plan gets stronger with a midyear review. By July 2024, the brand will have results from the first quarter under the new fees, the first events of the year and at least one round of holdout tests. Those results should be compared with the assumptions written into the plan, and the plan adjusted where they differ. A plan reviewed against evidence twice a year will drift less than one checked only at year end. The review should record which assumptions held and which did not, so the 2025 plan starts from a written history rather than from memory.

None of this requires a bigger plan. It requires a more honest one, built on what 2023 actually showed rather than on what the 2022 plan assumed, and writing those four sections from the evidence is how we help brands rebuild their 2024 plan.

A0505.crumb: The end of the search bar? Why it is…
A0505.title: The end of the search bar? Why it is changing shape instead
A0505.alt: Fabric smart speaker, smartphone and a camera lens side by side on a worn wooden table against a teal wall.
A0505.ttag: The end of the search bar? Why it is changing shape instead | Kwontified
A0505.desc: Shoppers are starting to ask questions and browse feeds instead of typing keywords. Why the search bar is changing shape, and what product data now has to do.
A0505.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 21, 2023.
A0505.body:
Take an outdoor brand whose water bottle ranks well for keyword searches because its title is full of the right terms. When a shopper asks an assistant for a bottle that keeps ice for a full day, the brand’s product does not appear, because its listing never states how long it keeps drinks cold. A competitor that lists the figure, along with its weight and base width, is recommended instead. Nothing about keyword search changed. The question simply asked for information the brand had not provided.

That is how the search bar is changing. It is not ending: paid search still drove more online sales than any other marketing channel at Cyber Week 2023. But shoppers are beginning to ask questions of AI assistants and browse feeds as well as type keywords. Product information now has to answer questions and describe uses, as well as match keywords, so brands should rebuild their product data around the questions shoppers ask while keeping their keyword search work strong.

Where the idea of the end of the search bar came from

The idea that the search bar is ending grew through 2023, as new ways of finding products appeared.

Instacart launched Ask Instacart in May, an AI tool built into its app that answers questions such as what to cook or what goes with a dish, TechCrunch reported. A shopper no longer has to know what to type; she can ask.

Amazon, for its part, started summarizing customer reviews with artificial intelligence, so shoppers see at a glance what reviewers praise and what they criticize, GeekWire reported. The summary answers a question the shopper did not have to type.

In September, TikTok Shop opened in the United States and turned a feed into a place to buy, TechCrunch reported. On a feed, a shopper discovers a product before she searches for it.

Yet keyword search remains the largest single driver of online sales. Paid search accounted for 27% of online sales across Cyber Week, more than any other marketing channel, according to Adobe. The search bar has not gone anywhere; it now has company.

Why the shape of search matters for product data

The difference between a keyword and a question is a difference in what a product listing has to do.

A keyword search matches words. A shopper types “insulated water bottle,” and the system returns products whose titles and descriptions contain those words. Brands have spent years learning to place the right words in the right places.

A question asks for judgment. A shopper asks an assistant what bottle keeps drinks cold on a long hike, or which one fits in a car cup holder. The assistant has to find products that answer that question, which means it needs to know facts the listing may not state: how long the bottle keeps drinks cold, how wide its base is, how much it weighs.

Again, a feed works differently. On a feed, a product is shown to shoppers who did not ask for it, based on what similar shoppers liked. What matters is how well the product’s content shows its use, often through video, and how quickly it earns a response.

The same product now needs three kinds of description: words for keyword search, facts and uses for questions, and demonstrations for feeds. The water bottle that lost the recommendation had the first and lacked the second.

Building product data for questions as well as keywords

The work starts with the facts shoppers ask about. For each key product, a brand should list the questions shoppers most often ask, from reviews, customer service and questions on the product page, and make sure the listing answers each one clearly and specifically.

Uses deserve as much space as features. A feature tells a shopper what a product is, and a use tells her when it helps. Assistants answering questions draw on both, so listings that describe situations, such as long hikes, small kitchens or sensitive skin, give them more to work with. Each key listing should say when and how the product is used, alongside what it is.

Keyword work still has to stay strong. Most shoppers still search by keyword, and paid search still drives a large share of sales. Building for questions should add to keyword work, not replace it. That includes search advertising as well as keyword optimization, since keyword search still drives the largest share of sales.

Structured information matters as much as prose. Many systems read a product’s attributes, such as size, material, capacity and compatibility, directly from the fields a retailer provides, rather than from the description. Brands should fill those fields completely and consistently across retailers. A missing attribute is invisible to a system that filters on it, however well the description is written.

In this shape of search, review content matters more, too. If assistants and summaries draw on what customers say, then recurring complaints and praise become part of how a product is described to new shoppers. Brands should read reviews as product information, and fix the issues that show up most often.

None of this requires a brand to predict which interface will win. Facts, uses and demonstrations make a listing stronger for keyword search, for questions and for feeds alike, and brands that build them now will be ready for however shoppers choose to search in 2024. The question for a brand team is how many of its key listings could answer a shopper’s question as they stand, and reviewing them question by question is how we help brands prepare product data for every way shoppers search.

A0506.crumb: Social promo codes on Amazon: the…
A0506.title: Social promo codes on Amazon: the off-Amazon handshake
A0506.alt: Smartphone, blank white card and a ribbon-tied kraft gift box on a wooden table by a pink wall.
A0506.ttag: Social promo codes on Amazon: the off-Amazon handshake | Kwontified
A0506.desc: A promo code shared on social media links an outside audience to an Amazon sale. How the referral bonus offsets part of the discount, and how to measure it.
A0506.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 26, 2023.
A0506.body:
A 20% code on a product that sells for $30 gives away $6 on every sale. Send the same sale through a tagged link, where it qualifies for an average referral bonus of 10%, and the brand gets about $3 of it back. The discount that looked like 20% now costs about 10% of the price.

A promo code shared on social media works as a handshake between an audience a brand built off Amazon and a sale on Amazon. When the traffic is tagged for Amazon’s Brand Referral Bonus, the bonus, which averages 10% of qualifying sales, can offset about half of a 20% discount. Brands should offer codes only on traffic they bring themselves, tag every link, and compare code redemptions with attributed sales to see what the code actually adds.

How social promo codes on Amazon fit the off-Amazon picture

Amazon pays brands to send it traffic. When brands direct non-Amazon marketing traffic to Amazon, they earn a bonus averaging 10% of the purchase price. The bonus covers the promoted product and the brand’s other products the shopper buys, Amazon said when it described the program in 2021. The bonus is tracked through tagged links.

Many brands pair that traffic with a promo code shared on social media, in a creator’s post, a brand’s own story or an email to followers. The code gives the audience a reason to act now, and it gives the brand a second way to see where sales came from.

Why the code and the bonus belong together

A code ties a sale to a specific audience in a way a link alone cannot. Shoppers who redeem it identify where they came from even if they did not click the link, for example if they saw a post on one device and bought on another. Meanwhile, the referral bonus returns part of the sale on tagged traffic. So the true cost of the discount is the discount minus the bonus, and the true value is the redemptions that would not have happened without the code.

Per sale of a $30 productCode on untagged trafficCode on tagged traffic
Discount at 20%$6$6
Referral bonus at an average 10%noneabout $3
Net cost of the discount$6about $3

That changes the decision. A 20% discount that looks expensive on its own may cost about half that much once the bonus is counted, but only on traffic the brand brought and tagged. Codes that spread to coupon sites and are redeemed by shoppers who would have bought anyway earn no bonus and add little.

The insight lies in comparing the two signals. Tagged links show clicks and attributed sales, while code redemptions show who acted on the offer. If redemptions run well above attributed sales, the audience is buying through paths the tags miss, which suggests the brand’s off-Amazon marketing is doing more than the reports show. If redemptions run well below, the code may be leaking to shoppers outside the intended audience.

How to run codes as a measured channel

Offer codes only on traffic you bring, tag every link, and judge each code by the sales it adds. In practice, that means a separate code for each creator or campaign, with an expiry date and a usage limit, and a tag on every off-Amazon link, so tagged sales qualify for the Brand Referral Bonus. It also means a regular comparison of code redemptions with attributed sales.

Specific codes make that possible. A separate code for each creator or campaign shows which audiences respond, while a single code shared everywhere reveals little and leaks quickly.

Every link needs its tag. Without a tag, the brand earns no referral bonus and loses the attributed view of clicks and sales, so every post, email and creator link should carry its own tag.

The risk to watch is leakage. If a code begins to appear on coupon sites, redemptions will rise while the share coming from the intended audience falls. Brands should set expiry dates and usage limits, and retire codes that spread beyond their purpose.

Creator codes deserve particular care. A creator’s audience trusts the creator, so a code shared in a genuine post can convert far better than a brand’s own advertising. But creators often share codes widely, and their followers share them further. A separate, time-limited code for each creator keeps the measurement clean and limits how far the discount travels.

Where the arithmetic needs adjusting

The bonus is a credit, not cash. It reduces the referral fees a brand pays Amazon, so its value depends on the brand having enough fees to offset. For most brands selling at volume this is not a constraint, but small brands should check how the credit is applied before counting it in their arithmetic. The bonus rate also varies by category, so the 10% average may be higher or lower for a given product.

Price perception matters as well. Frequent discounting can teach followers to wait for a code. Codes work best when they are tied to a moment, such as a launch or a creator’s first post, rather than offered constantly.

On all of this, margin still sets the limit. For a product with a thin margin, even the net cost of a discount after the bonus may be too high. Brands should run the arithmetic for each product before choosing the discount depth, with the bonus rate for that product’s category rather than the average. Comparing redemptions with attributed sales each month, code by code, is how we help brands measure what their promo codes add on Amazon.

A0508.title: Walmart DSP and off-site audiences: reaching shoppers early
A0508.alt: Vintage blue delivery van parked on a misty country lane near a stone farmhouse with a smoking chimney.
A0508.ttag: Walmart DSP and off-site audiences: reaching shoppers early | Kwontified
A0508.desc: Walmart’s DSP carries its shopper data to ads off Walmart’s own sites, and can connect them to store purchases. How that changes what off-site ads can do.
A0508.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 28, 2023.
A0508.body:
Take a household goods brand that sells mostly in Walmart stores. Its on-site search ads look modest, because few of its shoppers search Walmart.com for its products. When it runs off-site campaigns to Walmart audiences who have bought in its category, it finds that store sales rise among shoppers who saw the ads, even though online attributed sales barely move. Judged on online results alone, the campaign looks weak. Judged on combined results, it is the brand’s most effective Walmart advertising.

The difference comes from what Walmart’s DSP can see. It carries Walmart’s shopper data to advertising across the wider web, streaming and connected TV, and it can connect an ad seen off Walmart’s sites to a later purchase, including in a store. Off-site Walmart audiences can therefore reach shoppers before they walk in, and can be measured on sales an online-only view would miss. Brands should judge Walmart’s off-site advertising on combined store and online results, and coordinate it with their on-site search.

Where the Walmart DSP came from

Walmart renamed its media business Walmart Connect in January 2021 and set out a plan to use its first-party shopper data to drive advertising outside its own sites, Walmart said at the time. It also opened in-store advertising on nearly 170,000 digital screens across more than 4,500 stores.

In August 2021, Walmart launched Walmart DSP, a demand-side platform built with The Trade Desk, according to Walmart. It lets advertisers reach audiences built from Walmart’s past-purchase and predictive segments across display, streaming video, mobile, audio and connected TV. Before then, Walmart’s off-site advertising had been available only as a managed service.

The store connection was central from the start. If a shopper sees an ad online and later buys the item in a store, Walmart can connect the two, Janey Whiteside, then Walmart’s chief customer officer, told CNBC, something advertisers had not historically been able to do.

Why the store connection changes off-site advertising

The structure matters because of where Walmart’s shoppers buy. Much of Walmart’s business happens in its stores. A shopper may see an ad on her phone or television, then buy the product during her weekly trip days later. For most off-site advertising, that sale is invisible: the ad ran on one screen and the purchase happened at a register.

Walmart’s DSP closes that gap in measurement. Because Walmart knows what its shoppers buy, both online and in stores, it can show whether people who saw an ad went on to buy, wherever they bought. That gives off-site advertising a way to prove itself that most of the open web lacks, especially as third-party cookies fade.

The timing of advertising changes too. On-site search reaches shoppers who are already looking. Off-site audiences reach them earlier, before they search, and sometimes before they leave home. For products bought mostly in stores, that earlier reach may matter more than any placement on Walmart’s website.

Using Walmart’s off-site audiences the way its shoppers buy

The lesson is to measure Walmart’s off-site advertising the way Walmart’s shoppers behave: across stores and online. Brands should ask for results that include store purchases, and judge off-site campaigns on those rather than on online sales alone, particularly for products bought mostly in stores.

The choice of audience deserves deliberate thought. Past-purchase audiences reach shoppers who already know the category, while predictive audiences reach shoppers likely to buy soon. Brands should test both and compare how each lifts sales, rather than defaulting to the broadest reach. Testing each audience separately is what makes the sales lift from each one comparable.

On-site search has to be ready for what off-site advertising starts. Off-site ads can raise searches on Walmart.com among shoppers who saw them. Brands should watch whether branded and category searches rise during off-site campaigns, and make sure their on-site search ads and listings are ready to capture that demand.

In-store screens extend the same idea to the last moment before purchase. Walmart’s screens reach shoppers inside the store, close to the shelf, and can carry messages timed to a date, time or region. A brand that runs off-site audiences before the trip and in-store screens during it is covering the whole path, from first exposure at home to the final choice in the aisle.

How Walmart’s DSP differs from Amazon’s

Brands that already run Amazon’s DSP will find the structure familiar, since both retailers use their shopper data to reach audiences off their own sites. The store is the difference. Amazon’s purchases happen mostly online. Walmart’s happen largely in stores, so its off-site measurement covers a kind of sale that online-only retailers cannot see. Brands should not assume that results from one retailer’s DSP predict results from the other.

Brands should weigh the operating cost of a DSP too. Running a self-serve DSP takes skills many brands do not have in-house, and agencies often charge for the work. A managed service may suit smaller budgets, while larger ones may justify the control a self-serve platform offers. Either way, the store connection is the reason to use Walmart’s data rather than a general-purpose platform.

Even with the store connection, measurement still deserves scrutiny. Walmart reports results from its own data, as every retailer does. Holdout tests, where some shoppers are kept from seeing ads, remain the clearest way to see what the advertising adds, in stores as well as online. The question for a brand that sells mostly in Walmart’s aisles is whether its off-site budget is judged at the register, and building that combined view is how we help brands plan Walmart advertising across stores and online.

A0510.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud as strategic intelligence, not a report
A0510.alt: Antique brass compass, dividers and a leather-bound spyglass on blank paper atop a wooden desk.
A0510.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud as strategic intelligence, not a report | Kwontified
A0510.desc: Most brands use Amazon Marketing Cloud for bigger reports. Its real value is answering questions about the path to purchase that shape the media mix.
A0510.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 2, 2024.
A0510.body:
A Sponsored Products report can tell a brand which ad got credit for a sale. It cannot tell the brand that the same shopper had already seen two of its Sponsored Brands ads and a streaming TV spot before she searched. That gap is the reason to bother with Amazon Marketing Cloud. Run as a bigger reporting tool, it restates what the console already says at greater length. Pointed at a handful of questions about the path to purchase, it can reshape the media mix, frequency and audience choices, as long as each answer is treated as a lead for a test.

The brands that get value from it start with three or four business questions whose answers would change a budget decision, write queries to answer them, and use the results to decide what to test next. They do not read a query result as proof of what the advertising added.

What Amazon Marketing Cloud holds that the console does not

Amazon Marketing Cloud is a privacy-safe, cloud-based clean room in which advertisers can analyze pseudonymized signals, including Amazon Ads events and their own inputs, Amazon Ads said when it released new training material and noted paid features in beta. Results come back only in aggregate.

Amazon has also added the ability to build custom audiences in Amazon Marketing Cloud using SQL queries and to activate them in Amazon DSP campaigns, according to Amazon Ads. Its examples included shoppers who viewed a product page several times after seeing an ad, and past buyers with no recent engagement.

Judge the product by those two capabilities rather than by the word “intelligence” in anyone’s pitch deck. One lets a brand query the order of events. The other lets it act on what the query finds.

Credit and sequence are different questions

Standard reports work one ad and one sale at a time. Each conversion is credited to an ad, so the question they answer is which ad got credit. A clean room that holds event-level records of the ads a shopper saw and the actions she took can show the order of exposures and actions before a purchase. That answers how the formats work together.

Those are strategic questions, and the console cannot reach them. A brand can learn how many times shoppers typically see its ads before buying, and whether shoppers who see a streaming TV ad search for the brand more often afterward. It can see which combinations of Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands and display come before purchases by new customers. It can measure how long after a first exposure a typical purchase happens. Standard reports cannot show any of this, because they look at one ad and one sale at a time.

Why every pattern needs a holdout behind it

Shoppers who see more ads also differ from those who see fewer. They may be more engaged with the category, or closer to buying already, which is partly why the ads reached them so often. A pattern in Amazon Marketing Cloud suggests where to test. It does not prove cause.

Take a brand that finds shoppers who saw both its Sponsored Brands and Sponsored Products ads converted at 6%, against 3% for those who saw only Sponsored Products. It is tempting to conclude that adding Sponsored Brands doubles conversion. The shoppers who saw both formats were probably searching more often, though, and searching more often is itself a sign of intent. The finding is a strong reason to run a holdout test on Sponsored Brands. It is no reason to double the Sponsored Brands budget.

Questions worth a query

A good question is one whose answer would move money. Knowing that most buyers saw an ad three times is interesting. Knowing that buyers who saw it five or more times converted no better than those who saw it three times is useful, because it suggests a frequency cap that could free budget. Before running a query, write down what you would change if the answer came out one way or the other.

Three or four questions about the path to purchase, chosen because their answers would change a budget decision, are worth more than dozens of reports. Frequency, the order of formats, time to purchase and the path of new-to-brand customers are good candidates for that short list.

When a query suggests a format or a frequency level works, the next step is a holdout test or a controlled change in spend. The query points to the opportunity; the test confirms it. Custom audiences then let a brand reach the groups its analysis identifies, such as shoppers who viewed a product several times without buying, or lapsed customers. Each of those audiences should be measured against a holdout too, so the brand can see what reaching it adds.

What the work costs, and whose data it is

Brands should budget for the work. Queries require SQL skills and an understanding of how the data is structured, and Amazon applies minimum thresholds to protect privacy, which limits analysis on small audiences. For a brand without those skills in-house, it is better to answer a few questions well than to run many queries poorly.

It is also worth remembering whose data this is. Amazon Marketing Cloud is Amazon’s environment, built on Amazon’s records of its own ads. It is a powerful way to understand those ads, and it should sit alongside a brand’s own measurement rather than replace it.

Brands that already run holdout tests get more from Amazon Marketing Cloud than those that do not, because the two answer different halves of the same question. The queries show where to look and the tests show what is real. A brand with both can move budget with far more confidence than one relying on standard reports alone.

So keep one rule: no Amazon Marketing Cloud finding moves a budget line until a holdout has confirmed it. Pairing each query with its test is how we turn Amazon Marketing Cloud findings into media-mix decisions.

A0511.crumb: TikTok Shop and DTC acquisition: who owns…
A0511.title: TikTok Shop and DTC acquisition: who owns the customer?
A0511.alt: Kraft-wrapped parcel with teal and pink ribbon and an old key on a stone doorstep beside a potted geranium.
A0511.ttag: TikTok Shop and DTC acquisition: who owns the customer? | Kwontified
A0511.desc: TikTok Shop moves the first purchase inside TikTok’s app. That can make acquisition cheaper, but it changes who holds the customer relationship afterward.
A0511.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 4, 2024.
A0511.body:
For a decade, the direct-to-consumer playbook has had a fixed shape. A brand bought ads on social media, sent shoppers to its own website, and came away with a first order and an email address. The website was the front door, and the customer relationship began the moment someone walked through it. TikTok Shop moves that first purchase inside TikTok’s app, paid for largely through creator commissions rather than clicks. The first order can get cheaper, and TikTok keeps more of what follows it.

Who owns the customer, then? Increasingly, the platform. That is a trade a brand can choose to make, as long as it values TikTok Shop buyers differently from the buyers it acquires on its own site and plans how a first TikTok order becomes a lasting relationship.

How TikTok Shop DTC acquisition works

TikTok Shop launched in the United States in September 2023 with more than 200,000 sellers and an affiliate program in which more than 100,000 creators earn commission on the products they promote, TechCrunch reported. A shopper can see a product in a video and buy it without leaving the app.

The sale is still the brand’s. The purchase, though, runs through TikTok’s checkout, and TikTok decides what the brand sees about the buyer. On a brand’s own site, that buyer becomes a customer the brand can email again, offer a subscription to and learn from. On a platform’s checkout, the brand typically receives what it needs to fulfill the order, while the platform keeps the ongoing relationship. Reaching that buyer again usually means going back through TikTok, and paying TikTok to do it.

The way acquisition is paid for shifts too. On the old path a brand paid for clicks and hoped they converted on its site. On TikTok Shop much of the cost is a commission to the creator, paid only when a sale happens. The brand pays for results rather than attention, which can make the first order cheaper and easier to predict.

Where the value of a customer ends up

Follow the money past the first order and the trade becomes clearer. Take a skincare brand that spends about $40 in social advertising to acquire a buyer on its own site, and gets an email address with the order. On TikTok Shop, it pays a creator 15% of a $40 order, or $6, plus the platform’s fees. On the first order, TikTok wins by a wide margin.

Now suppose 30% of the brand’s site customers buy again within a year through email, at about $15 of margin each. That relationship is worth about $4.50 per acquired customer in the first year alone, and more over time. On TikTok, the brand has to pay again, through ads or commissions, to win the same repeat purchase. The commission that made the first order cheap comes back on the second.

The arithmetic is kept small on purpose, and what it leaves out matters. It ignores the platform’s fees on the TikTok side and any value beyond the first year on the site side. Both omissions push the same way: the site customer is worth more, relative to the TikTok buyer, than the first-order comparison suggests.

Neither path wins in every case. For a product people buy once, the cheaper first order carries the decision. For a product people buy again and again, owning the relationship can matter more than what the first order cost. Gifts and impulse items suit TikTok Shop well. Products with strong repeat purchase may sell better where the brand keeps the relationship, or on TikTok with a clear invitation to buy again directly.

The parts of the experience the brand no longer sets

Service and returns follow the same structure as the data. When an order is placed on TikTok’s checkout, the platform’s policies shape how returns and complaints are handled, so a buyer’s experience of the brand depends partly on rules the brand does not write. Reading those policies closely matters, and so does keeping stock and shipping times reliable, because the first TikTok order is the brand’s chance to earn a second one.

Creators deserve the same care a brand once gave its sales team, because on TikTok Shop they effectively are the sales force. Steady relationships with a group of creators who fit the brand will produce more consistent results than chasing whoever is trending that week.

The trap is to judge the channel on one number, cost per first order, where TikTok will look excellent. The better comparison is the expected value of a customer over a year in each channel, repeat purchases included, set against what it cost to acquire them. Packaging inserts, product registration, warranties and loyalty offers can then invite TikTok buyers to connect with the brand directly, within the platform’s rules. A brand that converts even a share of them into its own customers gets the cheaper first order and keeps part of the relationship.

Measurement has to cover more than TikTok, too. TikTok Shop may also raise searches for the brand on Amazon and on its own site, so watching those channels during TikTok campaigns is how a brand sees value that shows up elsewhere.

TikTok Shop is new, and its rules and fees may change as it grows. The brands that test it now while measuring the full value of each customer it brings will decide how far to rely on it with evidence rather than enthusiasm. The question worth putting to the growth team is simple: what is a TikTok Shop buyer worth to us twelve months after the first order? Answering it channel by channel is part of how we plan and measure TikTok Shop for brands.

A0512.crumb: Amazon 2024 fee changes: model them per…
A0512.title: Amazon 2024 fee changes: model them per product before April
A0512.alt: Four brass balance scales on a wooden sideboard holding oil, lavender, soap, cinnamon, sage and a salt crystal.
A0512.ttag: Amazon 2024 fee changes: model them per product before April | Kwontified
A0512.desc: Amazon’s 2024 fee changes average out to small numbers, but they move each product differently. Why brands should model them product by product before April.
A0512.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 9, 2024.
A0512.body:
Add up the two largest averages in Amazon’s 2024 fee changes and you get a rounding error. A new inbound placement fee averages $0.27 per standard-size unit, fulfillment fees fall by an average of $0.20, and the net is about seven cents a unit. A brand that stops there will plan for almost nothing. It will also misjudge individual products, because each change is triggered by a different product trait: size, price, category, return rate and how the brand ships. Some products gain more than a dollar per unit while others lose margin.

That is why the changes need to be modeled product by product, before each one takes effect, rather than applied to the whole range as averages.

What the Amazon 2024 fee changes include

Amazon set out its 2024 changes to US referral and fulfillment fees, Value Added Resource reported. Five matter for most brands, and they arrive on different dates.

ChangeStartsTriggered by
Apparel referral fee: 17% to 5% under $15, 17% to 10% from $15 to $20January 15Category and price
Inbound placement service fee, average $0.27 per unit, lower or none when shipping to several locationsMarch 1Size tier and shipping pattern
Low-inventory-level fee, under about four weeks of stockApril 1Size tier and cover
Fulfillment fees, down an average of $0.20 per unitApril 15Size tier
Returns processing fee for the highest return rates in a category, outside apparel and shoesJune 1Return rate and category

The placement, low-inventory and fulfillment changes apply to standard-size products. The placement fee is lower, or zero, for brands that send shipments to several locations rather than one.

One average, two very different products

Every row in that table keys on a different trait. The net effect on any one product depends on which traits it has, and those traits are spread unevenly across a range. A small average can therefore sit on top of large gains for some products and real losses for others.

Take two products from the same brand. One is a $14 apparel item. Its referral fee falls from 17% to 5%, or from $2.38 to $0.70, a saving of $1.68 per unit. If the brand ships to several locations, it may avoid most of the placement fee, and the fulfillment fee falls. This product’s margin improves by well over a dollar.

The other is a $30 home product with a high return rate, shipped to a single location and often low on stock. It pays the placement fee, may pay the low-inventory-level fee, and from June may pay the returns processing fee. Its fulfillment fee falls by about the average. On balance, it loses margin.

Apply the averages, a $0.27 placement fee against a $0.20 fulfillment saving, and the brand concludes its fees rise by about seven cents a unit. That conclusion is wrong for both products. Seven cents is simply the difference between two averages, and it may describe very few of the items the brand actually sells. The figure is real arithmetic. It is just the wrong unit of analysis for a pricing decision.

Building the per-product model

Most of the work is tagging. Each product needs the traits that trigger each change: size tier, price, category, return rate, typical cover and how it is shipped. Once those are known, the arithmetic is simple. The output that matters is the net change per unit for each product, and from it the new break-even price.

A product whose break-even rises above its current price needs a decision before April: raise the price, change how it is shipped, hold more stock, or reduce advertising on it. Several of the triggers are within the brand’s control. Shipping to several locations, holding more than four weeks of stock and reducing returns through better listings all lower fees, and for many products changing behavior is cheaper than absorbing the fee.

The order of work follows the calendar. The apparel referral cut arrives first, in January. The placement fee follows in March, the low-inventory-level fee and fulfillment changes in April, and the returns processing fee in June. Each product’s model should be finished ahead of the date of the change that hits it, so pricing and operations can adjust in time.

Advertising targets should move with the fees. A product whose margin improves can support a higher advertising cost per sale. One whose margin shrinks needs a lower target, or it will lose money on every advertised order. Updating targets product by product, alongside the fee model, keeps advertising aligned with the new economics.

Checking the model against the bill

After each change takes effect, compare the model with what Amazon actually charged. Amazon’s own reports show the fees applied to each product, and the comparison reveals errors in the product traits or misunderstandings of how a fee works. A model checked against reality after the March and April changes will be far more reliable for the rest of the year.

The changes also belong in pricing conversations with retail partners and distributors. If Amazon’s fees move a product’s margin significantly, the brand’s pricing elsewhere may need to move as well, to keep prices consistent across channels.

For apparel brands selling low-priced items, 2024 may bring a meaningful margin gain. For brands with bulky, high-return products shipped to one location, it may bring the opposite. The rule is short: if a fee change has an average, ignore it and price the product in front of you. Running that model across a catalog, and resetting prices and ad targets from it, is how we help brands absorb Amazon’s 2024 fee changes.

A0514.title: Curated marketplace brand protection: gates versus policing
A0514.alt: Padlocked wrought-iron gate opening onto a formal garden with a gravel path, stone bench and flowering borders.
A0514.ttag: Curated marketplace brand protection: gates versus policing | Kwontified
A0514.desc: Open marketplaces protect brands by policing sellers after they arrive. Curated ones protect them by choosing who gets in. What each model asks of the brand.
A0514.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 11, 2024.
A0514.body:
A department store decides which brands get a counter before the doors open. A street market rents a stall to almost anyone, then pays guards to walk the aisles. Marketplaces protect brands in the same two ways. Open marketplaces police sellers after they arrive, and curated marketplaces choose who gets in. The choice decides who does the protection work, and for a brand selling through both, how much of that work lands on its own team.

Policing asks the brand to enroll, monitor and report. A gate does most of that work for it, but asks the brand to earn its place and keep it. So the useful question is which product lines belong behind a gate, and how many people each open channel needs for policing that never really stops.

What curated marketplace brand protection looks like next to policing

Amazon is the clearest example of protection by policing. In its Brand Protection Report, Amazon said it stopped more than 800,000 attempts by bad actors to create new selling accounts in 2022, down from 2.5 million in 2021 and 6 million in 2020. It also seized and disposed of more than 6 million counterfeit products, HomePage News reported. Those numbers show the scale of the effort and the scale of the problem an open marketplace has to manage at the same time: even the improved figure is more than 800,000 attempts in a single year.

Target Plus is the clearest example of protection by a gate. When it launched in 2019, Target said it would be more selective than its competitors, and nearly 100 sellers offered about 250,000 products by the end of that year, the Star Tribune reported. Joe Kaziukenas of Marketplace Pulse said invitation-only was a wise approach, since opening to everyone risked harming the shopping experience.

Where the protection work lands

On an open marketplace, anyone who passes the platform’s checks can sell. Most sellers are legitimate, but the platform cannot know in advance which will copy a listing, sell counterfeits or undercut a brand’s price with diverted stock. So it polices: it screens new accounts, filters listings and gives brands tools to report problems. The brand’s share of the work is to enroll in those programs, watch its listings and act when something goes wrong.

On a curated marketplace, the platform decides who sells before anything is listed. Counterfeits and unauthorized resellers are much less likely to appear, because they are unlikely to be invited. The brand’s share of the protection work shrinks, and a different job appears in its place: winning a place and keeping it, by meeting the platform’s standards for quality, service and stock.

Neither model comes free. Policing costs the brand time and attention. A gate costs it some control, since the platform decides whether it may sell at all and on what terms.

Take a premium skincare brand selling in both kinds of store. On the open marketplace it finds sellers offering its products at a discount, some of the stock diverted from overseas distributors and a few units counterfeit. It enrolls in the platform’s protection programs and reports problems weekly, and the work never ends. On the curated marketplace it sells alongside a small number of chosen sellers, none of them offering its products, and its prices hold. The protection there came from the gate rather than from anything the brand’s team did.

Deciding which product lines go behind a gate

Problems are rarely spread evenly across a range, so the starting point is a map of where counterfeits, unauthorized resellers and price undercutting show up, by channel and by product. The map shows which lines need the strongest protection. Premium products, those with strong brand value or a history of counterfeiting, benefit most from curated channels. Products with less brand premium may do well on open marketplaces, where reach is larger and the cost of policing is easier to justify.

On open marketplaces, protection does not run itself. Brands that enroll in the platform’s protection programs, monitor listings regularly and keep records of what they report keep their listings in far better shape, provided they treat it as an ongoing job rather than an occasional clean-up.

Product-level authentication adds a further layer. Some brands put a unique code on each unit, which platforms or shoppers can check before a sale. The codes make counterfeits harder to sell on open marketplaces and give brands evidence when they report a problem. They add cost and setup work, so they suit products where counterfeiting is a real risk rather than every line. For those products, authentication can make an open marketplace behave a little more like a curated one.

Distribution practices matter on both sides of the divide. Many unauthorized sellers get their stock from a brand’s own distributors or wholesale partners. Clear distribution agreements, and checks on where products end up, reduce the problem at its source, whichever marketplace a brand sells through.

Questions for the next channel review

  • Where did counterfeits, unauthorized resellers and undercut prices appear, line by line and channel by channel?
  • Which of our most vulnerable lines could move behind a gate, and how much reach would we give up?
  • Who owns policing on each open marketplace, and how many hours a week does it actually take?
  • If a curated channel we rely on widened its gate, how quickly could we start policing there?

A platform that is selective at launch may open up as it grows, which is why the last question deserves a standing place on the agenda. Watching how sellers are admitted, and keeping the policing habit ready, is part of how we protect brands’ listings and prices across open and curated marketplaces.

A0516.crumb: Amazon Brand Analytics: the funnel view…
A0516.title: Amazon Brand Analytics: the funnel view every leader needs
A0516.alt: Glass marbles funneling one by one through a lab funnel on a brass stand into a ceramic bowl.
A0516.ttag: Amazon Brand Analytics: the funnel view every leader needs | Kwontified
A0516.desc: Amazon Brand Analytics shows a brand’s share at each stage of the search funnel. Comparing the shares shows where shoppers are lost, and which team should act.
A0516.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 16, 2024.
A0516.body:
Take a brand that holds 20% of impressions for its main search term on Amazon, 10% of clicks and 12% of purchases. Is that a good month? The purchase share alone cannot say. Put the three numbers in order, though, and the problem is obvious: the brand’s share halves between being seen and being clicked, then recovers slightly once shoppers reach the product page.

Shoppers see the brand and pass it over, and those who do click buy at a better-than-average rate. That is the case for the funnel view in Amazon Brand Analytics.

Comparing a brand’s share at each stage of the search funnel shows where shoppers are lost, which turns a report into a diagnosis that tells leaders which team should act.

What Amazon Brand Analytics shows by stage

Amazon announced a Search Analytics Dashboard that would be available in the United States in early 2022 at no charge to sellers enrolled in Brand Registry, according to Amazon. Amazon said the tool would help sellers understand the top search terms associated with their products and analyze the price competitiveness of their products.

The Search Query Performance dashboard that resulted shows, for each query, the total number of impressions, clicks, cart adds and purchases, along with the brand’s share of each, SPS Commerce explained. For the first time, brands could see their position at each stage of the search funnel using Amazon’s own data.

Each stage belongs to a different team

Each stage of the funnel depends on a different part of the business. A drop in share between two stages therefore points to the part responsible.

StageExample shareA drop arriving at this stage points toWho owns it
Impressions20%Search visibility and advertisingAdvertising and search
Clicks10%What shoppers see in results: main image, title, price, ratingContent and pricing
Purchases12%The product page, the price after a closer look, availabilityListing, pricing and supply

Low impression share means the brand is not showing up often enough. A fall from impressions to clicks points to the results page. A fall from clicks to purchases points to the product page, the price after a closer look, or stock.

Read the example through that table. A share that rises from 10% of clicks to 12% of purchases means the brand converts its own clicks at a higher rate than the query as a whole. The product page is not the problem.

The problem sits in what shoppers see before they click: perhaps the main image, the price shown in results, or the rating. Spending more on advertising would raise impressions further without fixing the step where shoppers are lost. Advertising is the easiest lever to pull, and in this pattern it is the wrong one.

A different pattern points elsewhere. A brand with strong click share but weak purchase share has a product page, price or stock problem. A brand with low impression share throughout has a visibility problem, which advertising and listing relevance can address.

The cart-add stage adds a further clue. A brand whose cart-add share is strong but whose purchase share is weaker may be losing shoppers at checkout, often to a lower price elsewhere, a slower delivery date, or a competitor’s coupon that appears late. That pattern points to price and delivery promises rather than to the product page itself.

Reading the shares without fooling yourself

During events and holidays, shares can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the brand, as competitors run deals or pause advertising. Comparing each month with the same month a year earlier, as well as with the month before, separates real changes from seasonal ones.

A share also only means something relative to the category. If total clicks for a query fall, a stable click share still means fewer clicks for the brand. Reading shares alongside total counts keeps the picture honest.

Brand Analytics has limits too. It covers Amazon’s own search results and the queries associated with a brand’s products, and it does not explain why shoppers behave as they do. It is available only to brands enrolled in Brand Registry. Within those limits, it gives leaders a view of the funnel that no external tool can match, because it uses Amazon’s records of what shoppers actually saw and did.

A monthly review that fits on one page

Leaders do not need to read every row. A short list of high-volume and high-value queries, including category terms and branded terms, is enough; reviewing hundreds buries the signal. The two kinds of term answer different questions. Category terms show how the brand competes for shoppers who have not chosen a brand yet, and branded terms show how well it keeps the shoppers who already have. For each query, a one-page view shows share at each stage and the change from the prior month.

The discipline is to compare stages rather than totals. A rising purchase share is good news, but the funnel shows why it rose, and where share is gained or lost between stages is what points to a cause. Each finding then needs an owner. A visibility problem belongs to advertising and search teams, a click problem to content and pricing, a purchase problem to listing, pricing and supply. Without an owner, findings stay in reports. Once one is named, the following month’s review should check whether the share between those two stages moved.

The rule fits in a sentence: find the biggest drop in share between two adjacent stages, and hand it to the team that owns the later one. Building that monthly funnel view for a brand’s top queries is how we turn Brand Analytics into decisions for each team.

A0517.title: What NRF 2024 signaled: retailers are building the AI layer
A0517.alt: A touchscreen display on a white pedestal in a bright glass-walled lobby overlooking a snowy landscape.
A0517.ttag: What NRF 2024 signaled: retailers are building the AI layer | Kwontified
A0517.desc: Generative AI dominated NRF 2024 as retailers moved it into service, merchandising and marketing. Why that puts retailer AI between brands and shoppers.
A0517.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 18, 2024.
A0517.body:
The agenda gave the story away before the doors opened. The National Retail Federation had booked Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff and Walmart U.S. chief executive John Furner for a fireside chat on AI and its effect on business, according to NRF. By the time the show ran in New York from January 14 to 16, retailers were talking less about experiments and more about where generative AI already sat in their operations.

For brands, the point is practical. When a retailer runs AI in customer service, merchandising and marketing, more of what shoppers see about a brand’s products is selected, summarized and presented by systems the retailer runs. Each retailer’s AI becomes a new layer between the brand and the shopper. Brands that supply that layer with good data, and watch what it says, will be presented better than those that assume the listing they wrote is what shoppers read.

What NRF 2024 showed about where AI is going

Generative AI dominated the show, with retailers saying they were folding it into customer service, merchandising and marketing, Modern Retail reported. A survey Google shared at the event found that 81% of retail decision makers felt urgency to adopt generative AI.

The tone had changed from a year earlier. In 2023, retailers were asking what generative AI could do. In 2024, they were describing where they were putting it to work, and the three places they named are the three places a shopper meets a product.

How the layer sits between brand and shopper

When a retailer uses AI in customer service, it answers shoppers’ questions about products. In merchandising, it decides which products to feature and how to group them. In marketing, it writes or adapts the descriptions and messages shoppers see. In each case the retailer’s system sits between the brand and the shopper. The brand still supplies the product and its information, but the shopper increasingly meets that information after a retailer’s system has selected, summarized or rewritten it.

For years, a brand could write a listing and expect shoppers to read it largely as written. In a store run partly by AI, the listing becomes raw material. What shoppers read may be a summary, an answer to their question, or a comparison with other products, produced by the retailer.

Take a home goods brand whose product page carefully explains why its blender is quieter than competitors’. A shopper asks a retailer’s assistant which blender is best for an early-morning smoothie without waking the house. If the assistant draws on structured data that lacks a noise rating, and on reviews that rarely mention noise, it may recommend a competitor whose listing states a decibel level. In an aisle, the brand would at least have had its box, with the claim printed on the front. The assistant reads fields, and the brand’s best argument never reaches the shopper.

The ownership question inside the brand

That example lands on a decision e-commerce leaders now face, and it is less technical than it sounds: who owns how a product is described once a retailer’s system is doing the describing? The content team writes listings. The e-commerce team manages the retailer. Checking what a retailer’s assistant says about the range, and tracing a wrong answer back to the data behind it, fits neatly into neither job.

Whoever takes it on starts with the data that retailer systems actually use. Structured attributes, specifications and clear claims are what AI systems can read and compare reliably, so every attribute field a retailer offers should be complete and accurate, and the most important claims should appear as data, not only as marketing text. The same owner should regularly ask retailer tools the questions shoppers ask and read the answers. Where the presentation is wrong or weak, the fix usually lies in the data or the reviews behind it.

The layer will not look the same at every retailer. Each is building its own tools, trained on its own catalog and reviews, with its own rules about what to show. A product presented well by one retailer’s assistant may be presented poorly by another’s, because the data behind it differs, so each retailer has to be checked separately. That makes a single, accurate source of attributes and claims, sent to every retailer, more valuable than it has ever been, since it reduces the chance that one system works from outdated or incomplete information.

Many retailers are still building these systems and want better product data. Brands that offer it, and that ask how their products are being represented, are more likely to be presented well than those that wait. AI systems can also make mistakes, summarizing a product inaccurately or recommending it for the wrong use, so keeping a record of what turns up and raising errors with retailers promptly matters. A wrong answer repeated to many shoppers can cost sales quietly.

Where retail media and the basics fit

Several sessions at NRF focused on retailers’ advertising businesses. As retailer AI shapes more of the shopping experience, advertising placements will increasingly sit inside or alongside AI-driven pages. Brands should expect new ad formats tied to these tools, and measure them as carefully as any other placement on a retailer’s site.

None of this replaces the basics. Clear listings, good reviews and reliable stock still matter, but in 2024 they will increasingly be read by a retailer’s system before they are read by a shopper. Asking each retailer’s tools what they say about a range, and fixing the data behind the answers, is how we help brands prepare product data for retailer AI.

A0518.crumb: Reels and Stories for product launches…
A0518.title: Reels and Stories for product launches: reach first, then convert
A0518.alt: A smartphone on a small tripod filming a ceramic vase against a pastel paper backdrop, lit by a ring light.
A0518.ttag: Reels and Stories for product launches: reach first, then convert | Kwontified
A0518.desc: Reels reach people who do not follow a brand. Stories reach those who do. Why a product launch should use them in sequence, and how to measure each.
A0518.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 23, 2024.
A0518.body:
A brand posts a Reel and a Story for the same launch. The Reel brings 1,000 visits to the product page and the Story brings 300. By the end of launch day the Story has produced more orders. Which one worked?

Both did, at different jobs. Reels are shown widely to people who do not follow the brand, while Stories mostly reach existing followers, so the two formats sit at opposite ends of the launch. Use Reels before and during the launch to build an audience that knows the product, and Stories at launch to convert the followers most ready to buy. Then measure each format on its own job rather than judging both by sales.

How Reels and Stories for product launches reach different people

Short video has become the main way Meta’s apps distribute content. Reels reached more than 200 billion daily views across Facebook and Instagram, up from 140 billion the previous October, Tubefilter reported, citing Meta’s earnings for the second quarter of 2023.

That scale changes how launches reach people. A brand’s Reel can be shown to many people who have never followed it, chosen by Meta’s recommendations rather than by the brand’s follower list. Stories work differently. They sit at the top of the app for people who already follow the brand, and they disappear after a day.

Because Reels are distributed largely by recommendation to people outside a brand’s following, they produce wide reach at a low rate of action. Stories appear mainly to followers who already know the brand, so they produce narrow reach at a high rate of action. Each fails when asked to do the other’s job.

The arithmetic of reach against conversion

Take the launch from the opening and put numbers on both sides.

FormatPeople reachedTap to product pageVisitsVisitors who buyOrders
Reel50,0002%1,0002%about 20
Story on launch day5,0006%3008%about 24

Judged by visits alone, the Reel wins. Judged by orders, the Story wins, producing more sales from a much smaller audience because its viewers already knew and trusted the brand.

Both sides of that trade are real. The Reel introduced the product to 50,000 people, many of whom may buy later, follow the brand, or search for the product elsewhere. The Story turned existing interest into sales on the day. The numbers lean toward running both in sequence rather than choosing one, because a launch that used only one format would miss half the work: either the audience that buys later, or the orders on the day.

Sequencing the launch window

Reels need a head start in the calendar. Teasers, behind-the-scenes clips and early demonstrations give the recommendation system time to find interested viewers, and give those viewers time to follow or remember the brand. A Reel posted on launch day alone has little time to build an audience before the moment of sale. Creators fit the same slot. A creator’s Reel reaches that creator’s audience, which may be far larger than the brand’s, so creator content should land before launch, when the goal is awareness, rather than only on launch day.

Stories belong to launch day and the days after. They suit announcements, countdowns and direct links to buy, because the audience already cares. A series of Stories across the launch window, each with a clear path to the product, keeps the launch in front of followers while it matters. Frequency needs a limit, though. Followers who see too many launch Stories may skip them, or stop watching the brand’s Stories altogether, so a short, planned series works better than a burst on a single day.

The creative should differ too. A Reel has to earn attention from someone who has never heard of the brand, so it needs to show the product’s point in the first seconds, without assuming any background. A Story speaks to people who already know the brand and can be direct: the new product, the price, the link. Using the same video in both places usually serves one audience well and the other poorly.

Paid support can extend both. Boosting the best-performing Reels widens reach among people similar to those who engaged, while advertising to people who watched the Reels brings them back at the moment of launch. Both work better when the organic sequence is already in place.

Scoring each format on its own job

Reels should be judged on reach among non-followers, new followers gained and the rise in searches for the product. Stories should be judged on taps and sales. Judging Reels by direct sales alone will undervalue them, and judging Stories by reach will undervalue them in the other direction.

Set that scorecard before the first post goes up. Once the launch is live, the team will see sales by format, and the Reels will look weak on that view because many of the people they reached have not bought yet. Writing down what each format is for, before the numbers arrive, is what keeps the Reels budget from being cut halfway through the launch.

Sales may not happen on Instagram at all. Many viewers will buy through Amazon, the brand’s own store or another retailer. Watching searches and sales across those channels during the launch, and using tracked links where possible, makes the effect of the Reels and Stories visible wherever the purchase happens.

The rule for the next launch: give Reels the weeks before, give Stories the days after, and never grade one by the other’s scorecard. Planning that sequence across Instagram and the marketplaces where launch buyers actually check out is how we run product launches for brands.

A0520.crumb: Amazon private label in health and…
A0520.title: Amazon private label in health and household: where it stays
A0520.alt: A row of white bottles beside amber, blue, and green glass bottles on a wooden shelf against a pale yellow wall.
A0520.ttag: Amazon private label in health and household: where it stays | Kwontified
A0520.desc: Amazon cut dozens of house brands in 2023, mostly in clothing and furniture, but kept its broad ones. Why everyday categories stay exposed, and how to compete.
A0520.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 25, 2024.
A0520.body:
Every supermarket has a shelf where the store brand sits beside the national one, often a little cheaper, with packaging that looks just familiar enough, and the retailer decides how close to eye level it goes. In 2023 Amazon pruned its own version of that shelf hard, cutting its house brands from 45 to fewer than 20, mostly in categories where shoppers choose by style, such as clothing and furniture. It kept the broad brands, Amazon Basics among them, that fit categories where shoppers choose by price and by trust in a familiar name.

For a brand in everyday health and household products, the retreat changes less than the headline suggests. Amazon’s own products are likely to remain competitors on those shelves, and the way to compete is on what a store brand cannot easily match: specific benefits, formulations and the loyalty that brings repeat purchases.

How Amazon private label in health and household took shape

Amazon built a large private-label business over the last decade. In 2020 it had about 243,000 products across 45 house brands, but private label accounted for only about 1% of its sales, PYMNTS reported, citing The Wall Street Journal.

Then it pulled back sharply. Amazon eliminated 27 of its 30 clothing brands and cut its house brands to fewer than 20, while keeping Amazon Basics and Amazon Essentials, according to the same report. Amazon also said it planned to move some popular items under those existing brands, Retail Dive reported.

Everyday categories were already where Amazon’s private label held a share. Retail Dive cited a Numerator report putting Amazon’s private label share at 3% in household, health and beauty, and grocery.

Why style categories emptied and everyday ones did not

The pattern behind the cuts shows where private label stays. In clothing and furniture, shoppers choose by style. A house brand has to compete on design and fashion, which change quickly and are hard to win across a large range. Many of Amazon’s house brands in those categories did not resonate with shoppers, and they were the ones cut.

In everyday health and household categories, shoppers often choose by price and by trust in a familiar name. Batteries, paper goods, basic supplements and cleaning products are bought repeatedly, and many shoppers see little difference between brands. A broad store brand like Amazon Basics fits that behavior well: it signals reliability and value, and Amazon can place it prominently. That is the supermarket shelf again, with the retailer deciding where its own product sits.

So the retreat from style categories is no retreat from everyday ones. Consolidating products under a few broad brands may even strengthen Amazon’s position where those brands already do well.

Take a household cleaning brand whose best seller is a plain, unscented surface spray. A store brand can match that product closely at a lower price, and shoppers buying on price may switch. The same brand’s specialized spray, made for one particular surface, with a clear benefit and loyal reviewers, is much harder to match, because shoppers buy it for what it does as well as for what it costs.

Where a national brand can still win the shelf

Start by checking which key searches show Amazon’s house brands, and how prominently. That map shows where price-driven competition is strongest. Products that solve a particular problem, use a distinctive formulation or meet a specific need are harder for a broad store brand to copy. Their listings and advertising should make those benefits plain, instead of leaning on general claims a store brand can just as easily make about itself.

In everyday categories the second order matters as much as the first. Subscription offers, larger sizes and bundles reward loyalty, and reviews that describe specific results build trust a store brand cannot borrow. Subscriptions deserve particular attention. Shoppers who subscribe to a product tend to keep buying it without comparing alternatives each time, so a brand that wins the subscription wins a stream of repeat orders that a store brand’s lower price cannot easily interrupt. Encouraging subscriptions on everyday products, with a modest discount and reliable stock, is one of the strongest defenses a brand has.

Price still matters, and brands should know where they stand. A brand priced far above a comparable store brand needs a clear reason for the difference. Where no such reason exists, the gap is a risk, and the choice is to narrow it or to move the range toward products that justify it. Advertising can protect the most exposed products in the meantime. Defending branded searches, and the searches where house brands appear most often, keeps the brand visible at the moment a shopper might switch, and that spend should be judged on whether it holds share rather than only on the returns it reports.

The position differs for vendors and sellers. A vendor selling to Amazon wholesale competes with Amazon’s own brands on a shelf Amazon controls, and its terms may be affected by Amazon’s broader product plans. A seller controls its own pricing and stock but faces the same search results. Both should watch how house brands are placed in their categories over time, since placement can change faster than prices.

Regulatory attention may shape how Amazon promotes its own products in the years ahead. Planning on that, though, means planning on someone else’s timetable. In the aisles where shoppers reach for whatever looks familiar and costs less, the store brand is a permanent neighbor, and mapping where it sits in each category is how we help brands compete with Amazon’s own products.

A0524.crumb: TikTok and beauty’s holiday on Amazon…
A0524.title: TikTok and beauty’s holiday on Amazon: demand made elsewhere
A0524.alt: A phone in a ring light on a stool, aimed at red lipsticks and cloth-wrapped gifts on a terracotta ledge.
A0524.ttag: TikTok and beauty’s holiday on Amazon: demand made elsewhere | Kwontified
A0524.desc: In beauty, TikTok increasingly creates holiday demand while Amazon captures the sale. Why brands unprepared on Amazon lose that demand, and what to fix first.
A0524.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 1, 2024.
A0524.body:
Take a skincare brand whose serum turns up in a widely shared video in November. Shoppers go to Amazon and type in what they heard. The brand’s listing uses a technical product name the video never mentions, so many of those searches land on a lookalike instead. The shoppers who do find the real listing buy it out within a week. The brand earned the attention, and much of the holiday demand went to someone else.

That is the shape of beauty’s holiday now. TikTok increasingly creates the demand and Amazon captures the purchase, so a brand’s holiday result on Amazon can depend on attention it earned somewhere else. Brands that plan TikTok activity and Amazon readiness together, with stock, listings and branded search ready before the videos spread, keep that demand. Brands that do not lose it to resellers, lookalikes and stockouts.

How TikTok beauty demand reaches Amazon at the holiday

The link between the two is not new. Beauty products that went viral on TikTok saw average month-on-month sales growth of 85.3% on Amazon, according to a Similarweb analysis, YPulse reported.

What has changed is how much of the holiday season runs through that path. TikTok users are 1.5 times more likely than non-users to spend on beauty and personal care products during the holiday season, according to TikTok data cited in a Similarweb and Statista analysis, ChannelX reported.

Beauty suits short video unusually well. A product can be shown working in seconds, on a real face or real hair, with a result shoppers can judge for themselves. And when a shopper decides to buy during the holidays, fast delivery matters for gifts, which sends many of them to Amazon. At a department store beauty counter, the person who demonstrated the serum also rang up the sale. Here the demonstration happens in one company’s app and the till sits in another’s, and the brand has to manage the gap between them.

Why demand made elsewhere leaks away

A brand can earn attention on TikTok without controlling where the purchase happens. What shoppers find when they search on Amazon depends on how ready the brand is. If the listing is clear, in stock and easy to find, the demand turns into the brand’s sales. If it is not, the demand goes to a reseller offering the product at a markup, to a lookalike with a similar name and image, or to a competitor that appears first in the results.

Consider a brand where the social team briefs creators and a separate e-commerce team runs Amazon. Each can do its job well and the demand still leaks.

The creator brief follows the social calendar. The stock plan was set earlier, against last year’s sales. The listing copy was written before anyone knew what the videos would call the product. Nobody failed; the plan simply had no place where the two calendars met.

That makes a brand’s holiday result on Amazon partly a measure of its preparation for attention it may not have planned. A product that goes viral in early December can sell out in days, and a stockout during the holiday peak can mean the demand is gone by the time new stock arrives.

Viral products also attract copies, often with similar images and names. Enrolling in brand protection programs and reporting copies quickly limits how much demand they divert.

Gift buyers and a second checkout

Gifting adds another layer. During the holidays many beauty purchases are gifts, and gift buyers often know only what they saw in a video, not the exact product name or shade. Listings that make the product easy to recognize, with an image that matches what appeared in videos and clear options for sets and gift sizes, help those shoppers buy the right thing quickly. Gift sets and bundles can also lift the value of each order at the moment demand is highest.

The arrival of TikTok Shop in the United States in 2023 adds a second path. Some shoppers now buy directly in the app, while others still search on Amazon. Brands active on both should expect demand to split between them, and should make sure neither channel runs out of stock while the other has plenty. Watching both together during the holiday gives the clearest view of total demand.

The pattern goes beyond the holiday, since TikTok will keep creating beauty demand throughout the year. The holiday is simply when being unprepared costs most, because shoppers want products quickly and stockouts are hardest to recover from.

Before the next peak

Four checks, owned jointly by whoever runs social and whoever runs Amazon:

  • Add the words creators and shoppers actually use for a product, its nickname, its benefit or its shade name, to the Amazon listing, so people searching in their own language find it.
  • Hold a stock buffer on products being promoted by creators or already gaining views. A viral moment cannot be planned precisely, but the products most likely to have one can be identified and protected.
  • Advertise on branded searches through the holiday period, so the real product appears first, ahead of lookalikes and resellers.
  • Watch TikTok mentions and Amazon branded searches side by side. A rise in one usually comes before a rise in the other, which leaves a few days to adjust stock and advertising.

A brand that has done those four things can treat a viral video as good news rather than an emergency. Connecting what happens on TikTok to what happens on the Amazon shelf is how we prepare beauty brands for demand they did not plan.
