A0526.crumb: Amazon Rufus arrives: what it will read…
A0526.title: Amazon Rufus arrives: what it will read on your listing
A0526.alt: A small white robotic arm holds a brass magnifying glass over a plain white box and blank cards on a wooden table.
A0526.ttag: Amazon Rufus arrives: what it will read on your listing | Kwontified
A0526.desc: Rufus answers shoppers from listings, reviews and answered questions. Why gaps in a listing get filled by reviews, and how to measure your question coverage.
A0526.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 6, 2024.
A0526.body:
Say a shopper asks Amazon’s new assistant whether a stand mixer is loud. The listing says nothing about noise. The answer still arrives, because Rufus finds it somewhere else: in a review, or in an old answered question from a buyer whose unit rattled. That is the new arithmetic of a product page. Every question a listing leaves unanswered gets answered from reviews and questions the brand does not control, and those tend to dwell on problems.

So the number that now matters is the share of shoppers’ common questions a listing answers directly. Measure it on key products, raise it, and treat it as a measure of how much of each Rufus answer the brand controls.

What Amazon Rufus reads, according to Amazon

Amazon introduced Rufus in beta on February 1, to a small subset of customers in its mobile app, with a wider US rollout planned over the coming weeks, according to Amazon. Amazon gave examples of the questions shoppers can ask on a product page, such as whether a jacket is machine washable, and said Rufus generates answers from listing details, customer reviews and community questions and answers.

The assistant was trained on the product catalog, shopper reviews and the customer questions and answers section, SiliconANGLE reported. Amazon also cautioned that the technology would not always get answers exactly right.

That turns the listing into a source document, read by a machine on the shopper’s behalf. A shopper who asks Rufus a question reads an answer assembled from what the page and its reviews say, instead of reading the page itself.

Gaps in the listing get filled by reviews

Rufus generates an answer from whatever available source states the relevant fact. When the listing is silent, it falls back on reviews and answered questions. Those are written by shoppers, skew toward problems and vary in accuracy. Of the three sources, only the listing belongs to the brand. The share of common questions the listing answers directly therefore decides how much of each answer reflects the brand’s own account of its product.

An audit makes this concrete. Take a kitchen appliance and list 20 questions shoppers commonly ask about it: dimensions, wattage, noise, cleaning, warranty, what comes in the box, and so on. Then check the listing for each one.

Answered by the listingLeft to reviews and Q&AQuestion coverage
Before8 of 201240%
After16 of 20480%

At 40%, Rufus has to look elsewhere for 12 answers. Some will come from helpful reviews. Others will come from a review describing one unit that failed, or from an answered question that is no longer accurate, and the brand has no say in which.

At 80%, only 4 questions depend on reviews and answered questions, and the brand’s own account shapes most answers. The listing has not grown for its own sake. It has become complete on the things shoppers actually ask.

Raising coverage without padding the page

Start with the products that carry the most sales or the most returns, since those are where a wrong answer costs most. The question list should come from real sources: customer questions on the product page, reviews that mention confusion, returns reasons and customer service inquiries. It should reflect what shoppers ask, which is rarely the same as the brand’s preferred talking points.

Answers belong in plain text. Facts go in the bullets, the description and the structured attributes Amazon offers, stated in the words shoppers use. A fact hidden in an image may not be read, and a fact wrapped in marketing language may be read less reliably than a plain statement.

Brands can also answer customer questions on their own listings, and few parts of the page are as directly under their control. Clear, accurate answers to common questions give Rufus a reliable source, and correcting outdated answers removes a source of error.

Variations and bundles need the same care. When a product comes in several sizes, colors or pack counts, shoppers ask which one fits their need, and the answer depends on whether each variation states its differences. A listing family where every variation shares the same bullets leaves Rufus unable to tell shoppers which option to choose, so the distinguishing facts, such as capacity, dimensions or quantity, should be stated for each one.

Reviews still matter, and the brand cannot write them. Recurring complaints usually point to a real issue in the product, the packaging or the expectations the listing sets. Fixing the issue, and stating the relevant fact clearly in the listing, reduces how often the complaint becomes the answer.

Testing the assistant directly

As Rufus reaches more accounts, ask it the questions on the audit list and read the answers. That shows where coverage is weak and where Rufus may be wrong, and errors worth raising with Amazon turn up quickly this way.

Advertising may change as well. Amazon has not said how ads will appear around Rufus answers, but as more shopping runs through the assistant, sponsored placements tied to it are likely. Brands with complete listings will be better placed to use them, because the answers next to their ads will be accurate. The same work pays off away from Rufus too: complete, plain listings convert better with shoppers who read the page themselves, and they reduce returns from mismatched expectations.

The rule to carry into every listing review: count the questions, count the answers, and treat any coverage below the level you would accept from a salesperson as a gap the reviews will fill. Running that audit across a catalog is how we prepare listings for AI shopping assistants.

A0527.crumb: Brand power in Amazon Home & Kitchen…
A0527.title: Brand power in Amazon Home & Kitchen without leaning on ads
A0527.alt: A worn cream enameled Dutch oven on a gas stove beside a cutting board, utensil crock, and potted herb.
A0527.ttag: Brand power in Amazon Home & Kitchen without leaning on ads | Kwontified
A0527.desc: Home & Kitchen shoppers mostly search by function, not brand, so brand power there is built on Amazon itself. How reviews, rank and repeat buyers create it.
A0527.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 8, 2024.
A0527.body:
On a department store’s housewares floor, the cookware brands each get a bay of their own, with the name printed above the shelf. Shoppers walk past the names before they reach the pans. Search Amazon for a nonstick pan and the order runs the other way: the grid shows pans, and the brand is the small print under each photo. In Home & Kitchen, most shoppers search for what a product does rather than who makes it.

That changes where brand power comes from. In this category it is rarely carried in from outside; it is built on Amazon itself, through reviews, search rank, a recognizable product line and buyers who come back by name. The measure of it is how many shoppers search for the brand by name, and the aim is advertising that defends a position instead of renting one.

How Amazon Home & Kitchen brands built power on the platform

Home & Kitchen is one of the largest parts of Amazon’s store. Kitchen and dining alone ranged between $1 billion and $2.4 billion in monthly sales on Amazon in 2021 and 2022, according to YipitData. During Prime Day in July 2023, Home & Kitchen brought in $2.5 billion in sales, up 3% from the previous year, according to Similarweb.

The category’s leading brands show how power is built there. Zinus was the largest furniture brand on Amazon, with more than $480 million in sales from January to October 2022, about 6% of total furniture sales on the retailer, YipitData found. Zinus is not a name most shoppers knew from shopping malls or television. It became large largely on Amazon.

Who keeps the value of a search

The reason sits in how people shop for the home. A shopper looking for a mattress, a set of storage bins or a nonstick pan usually searches for the product, not a brand. Many home products are bought rarely, and few shoppers have a favorite brand of shower caddy.

Follow the money on those generic searches. The first sale goes to whichever product looks most convincing on the results page: strong reviews, a clear image, a good price and fast delivery. Advertising can buy a place on that page. The price of the place is set in an auction that Amazon runs, so a brand that wins every sale through generic ads hands part of its margin back to the auction each time. Without the underlying strengths, the ads buy visits that do not convert, and the brand stays invisible once they stop.

Branded searches split the value differently. A shopper who likes a product may come back to the same brand for a matching item, a replacement or a gift, and search for it by name. Over time, a growing share of the brand’s traffic arrives through those searches. That share is the clearest sign that the brand, and not only the product, has a position, and it is the part of demand where the brand keeps more of what the sale is worth.

Take a cookware brand that, two years ago, made nearly all its sales from generic searches such as frying pan, won through advertising and price. It builds a matching line, earns strong reviews and puts a card in each box pointing to the rest of the range. Over time, a meaningful share of its traffic comes from shoppers typing its name, and its advertising protects that traffic rather than paying for every visit.

How a home brand earns searches for its name

Amazon’s Brand Analytics shows how often shoppers search for a brand’s name and how the brand performs on those searches. Tracking that branded search share over time shows whether the brand is building a position or relying on ads to rent one, and it is the number worth putting in front of leadership each quarter.

A line does more than a single product. Shoppers who return for matching or related items are the source of most branded searches in home goods, and a coherent range, with consistent design and naming, gives them a reason to search for the brand. Reviews that praise durability, design or service build trust that carries across the range, so a shopper who trusts one product is more willing to try another.

Packaging and inserts matter for the same reason. Many home products arrive in plain shipping boxes, and the moment of unboxing may be the brand’s only chance to be remembered. A simple card pointing to the rest of the range, within Amazon’s rules on what inserts may say, turns a one-time buyer into a possible repeat one. A Brand Store that groups the range by room or use then gives returning shoppers a place to find the matching item they came back for, and it works best once the brand has enough recognition for shoppers to look for it.

Timing helps the name stick as well. Home purchases cluster around moves, holidays and seasonal changes, and many products are replaced after a few years. A brand that is remembered when the shopper next moves house or replaces a worn-out item can win that sale without competing on the generic search at all. Keeping product names stable and the brand’s look consistent makes that recall easier, since a shopper searching years later needs to recognize what they bought.

Advertising still has a role, especially for new products and generic searches. But a home brand whose advertising carries all its traffic is exposed to rising click prices and to any competitor willing to bid more. Branded search is the part of demand it does not have to win again every day, and raising that share is how we build lasting positions for home brands on Amazon.

A0528.crumb: Amazon’s Q4 2023 results: what ad revenue…
A0528.title: Amazon’s Q4 2023 results: what ad revenue says about clicks
A0528.alt: A wooden gavel in front of holders filled with blank wooden bidding paddles on a sunlit table by a window.
A0528.ttag: Amazon’s Q4 2023 results: what ad revenue says about clicks | Kwontified
A0528.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 27% in Q4 2023 while online store sales grew 9%. What that gap says about competition for clicks, and how to plan for it.
A0528.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 13, 2024.
A0528.body:
Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 27% in the fourth quarter of 2023. Its online store sales grew 9%. Those two numbers describe the same shoppers from two sides: one is what advertisers paid to reach them, the other is what they bought. When the first grows much faster than the second, more money is chasing each dollar of sales.

The consequence for a brand is simple to state and easy to miss in a dashboard. A brand that holds its share of attention on Amazon will see its advertising cost as a share of sales rise. So plan 2024 budgets on rising cost per sale, judge spending on what its last dollar returns, and watch total advertising cost of sales rather than reported returns alone.

What Amazon’s Q4 2023 results showed

Amazon reported record fourth-quarter revenue of $169.9 billion, up 14%, GeekWire reported. The lines that matter for brands moved at different speeds.

LineQ4 2023 revenueGrowth
Online stores (Amazon’s own retail sales)$70.5 billion9%
Third-party seller services (fees sellers pay Amazon)$43.5 billion20%
Advertising$14.6 billion27%

Advertising outgrew both measures of the retail business it sits on, and that gap, more than the headline total, is what a brand’s budget has to absorb.

How the auction turns the gap into a price

Advertising revenue is what all advertisers together pay to compete for shoppers’ purchases. When it grows faster than the sales available to win, the average amount paid per dollar of sales rises. A brand that holds its share of attention sees its own advertising cost as a share of sales rise in proportion to the gap.

The reported figures let you size the gap. Working back from the growth rates means dividing each fourth-quarter figure by one plus its growth rate. Done that way, advertising revenue a year earlier was about $11.5 billion against online store sales of about $64.7 billion, or about 17.8%. In the fourth quarter of 2023 it was $14.6 billion against $70.5 billion, or about 20.7%. Over the year, the ratio of advertising to online store sales rose by a factor of about 1.165.

Now take a brand that spent 10% of its Amazon sales on advertising in late 2022 and wants to keep its share of attention. If its costs moved with the market, it would need to spend about 11.7% of sales a year later to hold the same position.

The odd part is that nobody in this auction is behaving badly. Much of the extra money comes from sellers and vendors moving budget from other channels into Amazon, because Amazon ads sit close to purchase and report results quickly. Each of those moves is sensible on its own. Together they put more bidders into the same auctions, and the price of a sale rises for everyone. A brand’s results can weaken even when nothing about its products or listings has changed, simply because rivals are spending more on the same searches.

What the comparison overstates, and what it does not

Online store revenue excludes sales by third-party sellers, who also buy ads. Third-party seller services grew 20%, much faster than online stores, so the sales base advertisers compete for grew faster than 9%. Even so, advertising outgrew it. Amazon’s advertising line also includes more than sponsored search ads, such as display and video, so not all of the growth falls on search clicks.

The direction still holds. More advertising money is competing for each dollar of sales than a year earlier, and Amazon’s finance chief said on the results call that the company expected the acceleration to continue in 2024, Campaign Asia reported.

New inventory is the variable worth watching. Amazon began showing ads on Prime Video in late January. New supply can ease pressure on search placements if some budgets move to it, or add to costs if advertisers simply spend more overall. Category matters too, because growth in advertising is not spread evenly and some categories will see costs rise much faster than the average. A brand’s own cost per click and cost per sale, tracked over time, says more than the company-wide figure.

Budgeting for a rising price per sale

Total advertising cost of sales is the measure to budget on. Advertising spend divided by total sales, including sales not credited to ads, shows whether advertising is becoming more expensive relative to the business. Reported return on ad spend can stay flat while total cost of sales rises, if ads are taking credit for sales that would have happened anyway. Tracking it monthly matters, because a quarterly view can hide a rise that started weeks earlier.

Spending should be judged at the margin. As costs rise, the last dollars in each campaign earn the least. Lowering bids on the least efficient terms and products, and seeing how much sales actually fall, shows where spend was doing little; where sales hold, the money can go elsewhere.

Some sales are cheaper to win than others, and a rising auction price makes the difference worth more each quarter. Strong listings, reviews and branded demand convert at lower cost, and investment there reduces how much a brand must pay in the auction for each sale.

None of this means Amazon advertising has stopped working. It still reaches shoppers close to purchase. But the price of that reach is rising faster than the sales behind it. The rule for 2024 follows from the table: if your advertising cost of sales is flat while the market’s ratio climbs, check whether you are losing share before you celebrate. Rebuilding a 2024 plan on marginal returns is how we budget Amazon advertising as click prices rise.

A0530.crumb: The state of Walmart Marketplace for…
A0530.title: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands, 2024
A0530.alt: Cardboard delivery boxes and a blue tote on a sunny front porch beside a yellow door and potted geraniums.
A0530.ttag: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands, 2024 | Kwontified
A0530.desc: Walmart’s ecommerce grew 24% on everyday shopping while its marketplace assortment doubled. What that means for brands selling there in 2024.
A0530.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 15, 2024.
A0530.body:
Think of a Walmart order placed in the app: milk, paper towels, a refill of vitamins, a pickup slot for Saturday morning. The shopper knows the list before opening the app and gets through it quickly. Trips like that, store-fulfilled pickup and delivery of everyday goods, are the engine of Walmart’s online growth, and they are also the main thing a brand has to understand before selling on Walmart Marketplace.

In 2024 the marketplace is larger and more crowded than it was, and shoppers arrive for needs rather than to browse. The brands that do well there fit the everyday basket, ship as fast as Walmart’s own items, and use advertising to reach shoppers who did not come looking for them.

Where Walmart Marketplace for brands stands in 2024

Walmart’s ecommerce grew quickly through 2023. In the quarter ending in October, Walmart U.S. ecommerce sales rose 24%, led by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, and Walmart Connect advertising sales rose 26%, according to Walmart. Sales strength was led by grocery and health and wellness, while general merchandise sales declined modestly.

The marketplace grew faster still in assortment. On the earnings call, Walmart chief executive Doug McMillon said the company had more than doubled the number of items on its U.S. marketplace since the beginning of the previous year, according to a transcript. He added that Walmart had held its first Marketplace Seller Summit in September, and described the marketplace as an engine that pulls other businesses, such as fulfillment and advertising, along with it.

Walmart also said it would expand next-day and two-day shipping to nearly 90% of the United States, including marketplace items shipped by Walmart Fulfillment Services, PYMNTS reported.

A needs-based shopper in a crowded marketplace

The restock trip explains most of what brands experience on Walmart. Many shoppers arrive to replenish groceries and household needs, often for pickup or delivery. They know what they want and shop quickly, unlike someone browsing for something new.

For brands in general merchandise, this cuts both ways. Walmart brings an enormous number of regular shoppers to its site and app. But those shoppers did not come for a new lamp or a set of headphones, and general merchandise was the soft part of Walmart’s results. A brand in those categories has to catch shoppers on a trip planned for something else.

The marketplace’s growth adds a second pressure, and it lands hardest on brands arriving now. With more than twice as many items as before, more sellers compete for the same searches. Walmart’s marketplace now looks more like Amazon’s: crowded, served by Walmart’s own fulfillment network, and increasingly reached through paid placement.

Take a kitchen brand selling on Walmart for the first time, with products that sell steadily on Amazon. On Walmart its listings get few views, because shoppers searching for groceries rarely search for its category, and its products ship more slowly than similar items fulfilled by Walmart. Sales start to grow only when it moves stock into Walmart’s fulfillment network, prices to match the everyday shopper’s expectations and advertises on the searches its buyers make.

What fitting the trip looks like in practice

Speed is the first thing shoppers notice, and the easiest gap to see from the outside. People used to fast pickup and delivery expect marketplace items to arrive quickly too, so using Walmart Fulfillment Services, or matching its speed through another network, keeps products competitive with Walmart’s own assortment.

The basket comes next. Products that complement what shoppers already buy, such as household goods, health and wellness items, or smaller everyday versions of a brand’s range, are easier to sell on a needs-based trip, and a brand can lead with those and expand from there. Walmart Connect then does the work the shopper’s list will not. It is growing quickly because advertisers can reach shoppers on trips planned for something else. Search ads on related terms and display placements can put a brand in front of shoppers who would not have searched for it.

Price matters more on Walmart than on many marketplaces. Shoppers come expecting everyday low prices, and listings priced well above comparable items struggle. The useful comparison is against similar products on Walmart, not only against the brand’s own prices elsewhere, since that is the shelf the shopper is actually looking at.

The operating basics that decide whether growth sticks

Operations deserve attention before growth. Walmart holds marketplace sellers to performance standards on shipping times, cancellations and responsiveness, and sellers who fall short can lose visibility or selling privileges. A brand that expands quickly without the operations to match risks undoing its progress, so a focused range the brand can fulfill reliably is a safer start than listing everything at once.

Reviews take a while to accumulate. A product with hundreds of reviews on Amazon may launch on Walmart with none, and shoppers there will treat it as new. Planning for a slower start on newly listed products, and using Walmart’s review programs where eligible, builds early trust. Content matters as well: listings that are thin, or carried over unedited from another marketplace, convert poorly, while complete titles, images and attributes help both shoppers and Walmart’s search.

Walmart is not yet as large an online marketplace as Amazon, and the investment should be sized accordingly. But it is growing, it brings shoppers Amazon does not always reach, and its services make it easier to operate than a few years ago. A brand that earns a place in the Saturday pickup order has earned something durable, and working out which products belong in that order is how we build brands’ businesses on Walmart Marketplace.

A0533.crumb: Why premium pricing and big brands win…
A0533.title: Why premium pricing and big brands win launches on Amazon
A0533.alt: A navy gift box with gold trim on a blue velvet pedestal, with stacked cardboard boxes in dramatic light behind.
A0533.ttag: Why premium pricing and big brands win launches on Amazon | Kwontified
A0533.desc: A new product on Amazon has to buy its early clicks. Why products with more profit per sale, and brands shoppers already know, can afford to win that race.
A0533.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 20, 2024.
A0533.body:
Two new products launch in the same Amazon category. Both convert 10% of the shoppers who click, and both carry a 30% margin before advertising. In a contested search where clicks cost around $1, one of them can advertise profitably and the other cannot advertise at all without losing money on every sale. The only difference is the price tag.

That gap is set by a single ceiling. The most a brand can afford to pay for a click is its profit per sale times its conversion rate, and a new product has to buy its early sales through advertising before it earns organic rank. Products with more profit per sale, and brands whose names shoppers already search for, can bid more and convert better during launch. Smaller brands launching lower-priced products should narrow the race they enter, and concentrate spend on the few searches they can afford to win.

Why launches on Amazon got more expensive

Launches now happen in a busier auction. In the fourth quarter of 2023, Amazon’s online store sales grew 9% and its advertising revenue grew 27%, GeekWire reported. Every dollar a shopper spends now has more ad money chasing it, and a new product enters that auction with no reviews and no sales history.

Established products can fall back on organic rank and repeat buyers. A new product depends on what it can afford to pay for attention, which is where price and brand start to matter.

The bid ceiling, product by product

A product that earns more on each sale, or converts better because shoppers recognize the brand, can pay more for each click and still break even. The products that can pay most win the early placements, and those placements build the sales history that organic rank depends on.

PriceProfit per sale at 30%Break-even cost per click at 10% conversion
Premium product$40$12$1.20
Lower-priced product$15$4.50$0.45

Paying $1.20 for a click that converts one time in ten means paying $12 for each sale, which is exactly the profit that sale earns; that is what break-even means here. The premium product can outbid the cheaper one by more than 2.6 times for the same click. At around $1 a click, the $40 product competes profitably and the $15 product loses money on every sale it buys.

Brand recognition widens the gap. A shopper who recognizes a brand is more likely to click its ad and buy. If a known brand converts at 14% instead of 10%, its ceiling rises by 40% without any change in price. Big brands also bring branded searches with them, which convert well and cost little, and those early sales feed the history that organic rank rewards. None of that is available to a brand shoppers have not heard of yet.

The same arithmetic explains why launches by smaller brands often stall. They enter the same broad searches as larger competitors, pay prices their margins cannot support, and stop advertising before the product has built enough history to rank on its own.

Choosing a race the margin can pay for

Work out the ceiling before launch. Profit per sale times an expected conversion rate gives the most the brand can pay per click, and searches where typical click prices sit well above that ceiling are not worth entering at launch. Writing the ceiling next to each target search in the launch plan means the comparison is made before money is spent rather than after.

Specific searches are where a smaller brand can compete. Longer, more specific searches usually cost less per click and convert better, because the shopper knows what they want, and a product that matches a specific need can win them even against larger brands.

Profit per sale can sometimes be raised. Bundles, larger pack sizes and multi-unit offers lift the value of each order, which raises the ceiling. A product that sells for $15 alone may justify a launch as a $30 two-pack.

Spending above break-even can be a deliberate choice. Many launches run at a loss for a period to build sales history and reviews, and that can be sensible, as long as it is a decision with a budget and an end date rather than a drift. Setting the amount the brand is willing to lose to reach a target rank makes the decision explicit.

Reviews deserve early attention for the same reason. A product with a handful of good reviews converts better than one with none, which raises its ceiling without any change in price, and enrolling eligible products in Amazon’s review programs at launch closes that gap sooner. Off-Amazon demand helps too. A brand that drives shoppers to search for it by name, through social media, email or press, gives its launch a stream of cheap, high-converting sales that do not depend on winning the auction.

Timing is the last lever, and often the cheapest to pull. Launching just before a busy period puts a new product into the most expensive auctions of the year. Launching in a quieter month gives it time to build history while click prices are lower, so it enters the busy season with reviews and rank already in place.

Smaller brands can launch successfully; they just cannot win by playing the same game as the largest brands in the category. The rule is one line of arithmetic: if a search’s typical click price is above profit per sale times conversion rate, leave it for later. Setting those ceilings and choosing launch searches to match is how we plan Amazon launches that fit a brand’s margins.

A0534.crumb: Walmart buys a TV maker: what it says…
A0534.title: Walmart buys a TV maker: what it says about the ad business
A0534.alt: A wire basket of groceries on a sofa arm in a cozy living room facing a glowing TV, plants, and bookshelves.
A0534.ttag: Walmart buys a TV maker: what it says about the ad business | Kwontified
A0534.desc: Vizio sells TVs but earns most of its gross profit from ads. Why Walmart bought it, and what the deal says about how retailers now see advertising.
A0534.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 22, 2024.
A0534.body:
On a Walmart shelf, a Vizio television is one of the cheaper ways to fill a living room wall. The price tag, it turns out, is not where Vizio makes most of its money. It earns the larger part of its gross profit after the sale, from the advertising shown on the screen while people watch. So when Walmart agreed to buy Vizio, it was buying an advertising business that happens to ship in a box.

The deal shows how retailers have come to see their own businesses. The product or the store is the way in, and advertising is where much of the profit is made. For brands, that points to more screens, formats and data for sale, and to retail media as a lasting cost of selling through those retailers rather than a passing opportunity.

Why Walmart buys a TV maker now

Walmart announced the deal on February 20, alongside its fourth-quarter results. It agreed to acquire Vizio for about $2.3 billion to accelerate its advertising business, Walmart Connect, through Vizio’s SmartCast television operating system, according to Walmart. Walmart said Vizio’s Platform+ business, which consists largely of advertising, now accounts for a majority of Vizio’s gross profit.

Walmart’s own advertising business is growing quickly. Its global advertising business grew about 33% in the fourth quarter, including 22% for Walmart Connect in the United States, and about 28% for the full year to reach $3.4 billion, Walmart reported. Its global ecommerce sales grew 23% in the quarter and passed $100 billion for the year.

Where the margin in a cheap television sits

Follow the money in the Vizio model. The television is sold, often at a low price, and the profit arrives later, from what happens on the screen. The hardware is the way into the home; the advertising is the business.

Retailers have learned the same lesson. Selling goods at low margins brings shoppers to a store or website. Selling advertising to the brands that want those shoppers’ attention earns much more on each dollar. Advertising, in other words, helps pay for the low prices that bring shoppers in, and the brands buying the ads are the ones funding it.

Walmart now wants that model in the living room as well as the store. Vizio gives it a screen in millions of homes, and Walmart’s purchase data can tell advertisers whether people who saw an ad later bought the product. Who captures the value in that arrangement is plain enough: the company that owns the screen, the shopper data and the checkout gets paid at every step.

How far Walmart has to go, and what it has that Amazon lacks

Scale shows how much room there is to grow. Walmart’s advertising business reached $3.4 billion for its full fiscal year, while Amazon took in $14.6 billion from advertising in the fourth quarter of 2023 alone, GeekWire reported. Walmart has a long way to go to match Amazon, and buying Vizio is one way to close the gap faster.

Walmart’s business also differs from Amazon’s in a way that shapes its media. Most of Walmart’s sales still happen in physical stores, and its ecommerce growth has been led by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery. That gives Walmart data on in-store purchases that few online advertisers can match. A television ad shown through Vizio could, in principle, be measured against purchases made in a Walmart store the following week. Many brands have wanted that kind of measurement for years, and it explains why Walmart sees value in owning the screen.

What brands should do with the signal

Plan retail media as a cost of doing business. As retailers rely more on advertising for profit, they will offer more ways for brands to pay for visibility, and the brands that do not pay may find themselves less visible. Retail media belongs in the budget alongside other selling costs, not as an occasional extra.

New formats should be judged on what they add. Connected TV ads sold by retailers, with sales measured against the retailer’s own data, will sound compelling, but each retailer will measure results in ways that favor its own media. Comparisons with control groups, and a look at total sales rather than attributed ones, keep the claims honest. Spending should also stay in proportion to where a brand’s sales actually happen. A brand that sells mostly on Amazon should not shift large budgets to Walmart’s new screens just because they are new, and the reverse holds too.

Shoppers will notice the change in their own living rooms. A television that shows ads chosen using shopping data, from the same company that sold the shopper the television, is a new kind of experience. Some shoppers will accept it in exchange for low prices and free content; others may object. The brand, and not only the retailer, is what the viewer sees, so placement in these settings deserves thought.

The money has to come from somewhere, too. Much retail media spending comes from budgets that once went to trade promotions, traditional TV or other channels, and as retailers add formats, brands will face more requests from their retail partners to spend. A clear view of what each channel returns makes those conversations easier.

The deal is not yet complete and needs regulatory clearance, but the motive behind it does not depend on the outcome. Retailers want to be media companies because media pays better than retail, and a brand that understands that negotiates from a stronger position with every retailer it sells through. Deciding how much to spend with each of them is how we plan retail media across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0538.crumb: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants…
A0538.title: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands in 2024
A0538.alt: A store aisle of blue shelves stocked with plain kraft bags, white boxes, and unlabeled jars.
A0538.ttag: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands in 2024 | Kwontified
A0538.desc: Walmart’s CEO calls its marketplace an engine that pulls sellers into fulfillment and ads. What that reveals about the brands Walmart will reward in 2024.
A0538.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 29, 2024.
A0538.body:
When Walmart’s chief executive, Doug McMillon, talks about the company’s marketplace, he describes an engine that pulls other businesses along with it. As more sellers find customers on the marketplace, he said, they will want to use services like Walmart’s fulfillment and its advertising business, PYMNTS reported. It is a plain statement of what Walmart wants from the brands that sell through it.

Read that way, Walmart’s fast-growing ad business is the visible end of a chain, and the chain tells brands what Walmart will reward: sellers who commit to assortment, fulfillment and media together. How deeply to commit to Walmart in 2024 is therefore a decision to make on purpose. Drifting into a partial presence earns little of what Walmart hands out.

Where Walmart ad growth comes from

Walmart’s advertising grew quickly through its fiscal year. Its global advertising business grew about 28% to reach $3.4 billion, and Walmart Connect in the United States grew 22% in the fourth quarter, according to Walmart’s results. Walmart’s ecommerce sales passed $100 billion for the year.

Those figures sit at the end of a sequence that every seller walks through. A seller that lists products on Walmart earns Walmart a commission. A seller that also stores its stock with Walmart Fulfillment Services pays fulfillment fees, and its products qualify for faster delivery promises. A seller that also advertises with Walmart Connect pays for visibility. Each step deepens the relationship and adds to Walmart’s revenue.

What the flywheel rewards on the page

Treat Walmart as an institution with incentives and the pattern is easy to see. It is building a set of connected services rather than a marketplace alone, and it benefits most when sellers use all of them. Its systems will tend to favor the sellers who take each step. Faster delivery badges help products convert, and advertising puts products in front of shoppers who would not otherwise see them. A seller that uses neither is competing without the tools Walmart gives its committed sellers.

Take two brands that list similar products on Walmart. The first lists a handful of items, ships from its own warehouse with slower delivery, and does not advertise. The second lists its full range, uses Walmart’s fulfillment and runs search ads on its main products. Both are on Walmart. Only the second is really in the flywheel, and it is the one Walmart’s systems will tend to show.

In a physical store, the gap between those two brands would look like the difference between a full bay at eye level and a few facings near the floor. Online it shows up in quieter places: the delivery promise printed under the product, and how far down the results page a shopper has to scroll to find it.

How far to commit, and in what order

Whether Walmart is a priority channel comes before anything else. For some brands, Walmart’s shoppers and categories are a strong fit, and a full commitment makes sense. For others, Walmart is a smaller opportunity, and a limited presence, chosen deliberately, is better than a half-hearted attempt at everything.

A brand that does choose Walmart does better committing in sequence. It can start with a focused range, move those products into Walmart’s fulfillment network, and advertise once its listings and delivery are competitive. Advertising products that ship slowly or have thin listings wastes money.

Judging the channel means adding up the whole relationship. Commissions, fulfillment fees and advertising costs together determine whether Walmart is profitable for a brand. Looking at each piece alone can make the channel look better or worse than it is. Strong advertising returns can hide fulfillment fees that eat the margin, and fees that look high in isolation can pay for themselves through the faster delivery promise they buy.

Brands that already sell heavily on Amazon have a useful reference here, and a trap. Many of the same choices apply on Walmart: whether to use the marketplace’s fulfillment, how much to advertise, how broad a range to list. But Walmart’s shoppers, categories and costs differ, so the answers may differ too, and an Amazon setup copied straight onto Walmart carries Amazon’s assumptions with it.

Reading Walmart’s signals through 2024

The advertising side should keep growing. Walmart’s agreement to buy Vizio, announced alongside its results, shows how much it wants to expand Walmart Connect. Brands selling on Walmart will see more advertising options, and more encouragement to use them.

Walmart also announces new seller programs, fulfillment options and advertising formats through the year, and each one tells brands where it wants growth. A new advertising format usually comes with early incentives or less competition. A new fulfillment option often brings better delivery promises for early adopters. Brands that watch for these changes and test them early tend to get more from Walmart than those that wait for others to prove them.

Timing matters for the same reason. Walmart’s marketplace is growing quickly and adding sellers, which means the cost of establishing a position there is likely to rise. Brands that commit early may find it easier to build reviews and rank than those that wait, because early sellers face fewer competitors on each search.

Walmart’s interests and a brand’s interests overlap without being the same. Walmart benefits from every service a seller uses, while a brand benefits only from the ones that earn back their cost. The question worth putting to the leadership team is how far into the flywheel the brand’s own numbers justify going, reviewed each quarter as costs and results change. Answering it with one plan for range, fulfillment and media is how we run Walmart as a channel for brands.

A0540.crumb: What reaching number one on Amazon is…
A0540.title: What reaching number one on Amazon is actually worth
A0540.alt: A gold award rosette ribbon beside a small ceramic vase on a sunlit wooden shelf against a terracotta wall.
A0540.ttag: What reaching number one on Amazon is actually worth | Kwontified
A0540.desc: The top Amazon search slots take most of the clicks, yet first place is only worth the profit it adds over your current rank, minus what it costs to hold.
A0540.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 5, 2024.
A0540.body:
The first three items on an Amazon search results page get about 64% of clicks, according to a former Amazon employee turned consultant, The Markup reported. With a figure like that in the room, reaching number one looks like the only goal worth setting.

What first place is worth to a brand, though, is not the clicks it collects. It is the extra profit first place brings over the position the product already holds, minus what it costs to hold the top spot. On searches a brand would win anyway, or where ads crowd the top of the page, that difference can be negative, so each position needs a price before anyone pays for it.

Why number one on Amazon looks so valuable

Position drives clicks, and the evidence is solid. Analyzing results from more than 2,000 Amazon searches, researchers at University College London found that a product’s position strongly shapes whether shoppers click on it, according to their working paper. Among the top five results, where typically four are advertisements, they found that neither lower relevance nor higher price significantly swayed shoppers’ choices.

That second finding cuts two ways. It confirms that the attention sits at the top of the page. It also shows that the top of the page is increasingly paid space, so a product that reaches number one in the organic results may still sit below several ads.

Anyone who reads those click shares as profit will conclude that first place is always worth chasing. The belief is reasonable as far as it goes. It stops working once the question becomes what the move adds, rather than what the destination earns.

A position is worth the gain over where you stand

The value of a search position equals the extra clicks it brings over the current position, multiplied by conversion rate and profit per sale. Holding a higher position costs money, through ads, discounts or bids. First place is worth having only where the extra profit exceeds the cost of holding it.

Take a search that produces 10,000 clicks a month, where the first position gets 30% of those clicks and the fourth position gets 8%. At first place, a product gets 3,000 clicks. At a 10% conversion rate and $12 of profit per sale, that is 300 orders and $3,600 of profit a month. At fourth place, the same product gets 800 clicks, 80 orders and $960 of profit.

The difference is $2,640 a month. That is what first place is worth over fourth on this search, and no more. If holding first place costs $3,000 a month in ads and discounts, chasing it loses money. If it costs $1,000, the move pays. A team that compared either cost with the full $3,600 would have approved both.

What changes the answer from one search to the next

The same arithmetic gives different answers on different searches. On a brand’s own name, shoppers will find it anyway, so the extra clicks from first place are small. On a broad, competitive search, first place may cost far more than the extra profit it brings. The best value often sits on specific searches where the product fits closely and competition is lighter.

Ads above the organic results move the numbers as well. If several sponsored products sit above the top organic result, organic first place may earn far fewer clicks than the figures above suggest. On those searches a sponsored position may be the only way to reach the top of the page, and the calculation becomes ad cost against extra profit, with organic rank out of it. Look at the actual page for each important search, on both desktop and mobile, before deciding what first place means there.

Some value is harder to count. A product at the top of a busy search is seen by many shoppers who do not click, and some of them may search for the brand later or buy another of its products. That halo is real, but it is also easy to overstate. Measure branded searches and sales of related products before and after a move up, rather than assume it.

Organic rank also builds on itself. A product that sells more ranks higher, which helps it sell more, so spending to reach a higher position can be worth more than one month’s numbers show if the product holds its place afterward. That argument deserves a time limit and a test before it gets a budget.

Pricing the position before paying for it

The inputs are already in the account. Amazon’s Brand Analytics and search query reports show how a product performs on its most important searches, which gives the current position and the clicks it brings. From there, the gain to estimate is how much more a higher position would earn than the current one, using conversion rate and profit per sale. Set that gain against what the ads, coupons or lower prices needed to get there would cost. Where the cost is larger, the brand is better off where it is.

The top of the page keeps changing. Amazon adds and rearranges ad placements, and competitors move in and out, so a position worth buying in one quarter may not be worth it in the next. Pay to move up only where the profit added over the current position beats the price of getting there, and rerun the numbers on the most important searches each quarter. Number one is a good outcome, and it is not always a good investment; putting a price on each position across a brand’s main searches is how we decide where Amazon ad budgets go.

A0541.crumb: The Amazon content divide reshaping who…
A0541.title: The Amazon content divide reshaping who succeeds
A0541.alt: Side-by-side shots of a kraft box: one styled with a mug, dried oranges, and a succulent, the other plain on bare wood.
A0541.ttag: The Amazon content divide reshaping who succeeds | Kwontified
A0541.desc: Rich Amazon listings convert better, rank better and now feed Amazon’s AI answers, so the gap with thin listings widens. Where brands should start closing it.
A0541.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 7, 2024.
A0541.body:
Put two water bottle listings side by side on Amazon. One has clear photos of every color, a size comparison chart, a short video showing the lid and a plain list of materials. The other has three photos and a few lines of text. A shopper who asks Amazon’s new shopping assistant whether each bottle fits a car cup holder gets a clear answer about the first and a guess about the second.

That exchange is the content divide at the scale of a single search. Brands with rich, complete product content are pulling away from brands with thin listings, because better content raises conversion, higher conversion supports rank, and Amazon’s AI tools now read that same content to answer shoppers. The advantage compounds each year. A brand with thin listings should treat content as a core investment, starting with its best-selling products.

Where the Amazon content divide began

For a long time the case for a better product page was made as a sales lift. At its Accelerate seller conference in September 2022, Amazon said brands that create A+ Content, the enhanced section of a product page, see a sales lift of about 8%. It added that Premium A+ Content increased sales by up to 20% in limited tests, Teikametrics reported, and Amazon also opened Premium A+ Content to more brand owners.

Framed that way, content was a percentage a brand could add on top of a listing once the product was live. That framing stopped fitting when the content gained a second reader. Amazon added an AI tool that summarizes the reviews on product pages, and on February 1 introduced Rufus, a shopping assistant that answers questions using listing details, reviews and community questions and answers, according to Amazon. A product page is now read by a shopper deciding whether to buy and by a system deciding what to say about the product.

Why each advantage feeds the next

A brand with clear images, complete details, comparison charts and video converts more of the shoppers who reach its page. Higher conversion means more sales from the same traffic, and sales history helps a product rank. A higher rank brings more traffic, which brings more sales and more reviews.

The AI step lengthens that chain. When Rufus answers a shopper’s question, it draws on what the listing and reviews say. A listing that states materials, sizes and uses plainly gives Rufus good material. A thin listing leaves Rufus to rely on reviews, which may be incomplete or negative.

For the brand with thin content, the chain runs the other way. Fewer shoppers convert, rank slips, and AI answers about its products are vaguer. Each year, the gap is wider than the year before.

Closing the gap, starting with the best sellers

Improving content on the products that already drive most sales returns the most, so those pages deserve the first audit. Check each one against what shoppers ask and what competitors show.

Every page now has two readers to serve. Shoppers need images and stories that help them decide, while Amazon’s systems need plain facts they can read and compare. Strong visuals, with every important fact also stated in text, serve both at once.

Content also ages as the category moves around it. Products change, competitors improve, and shoppers raise new questions, so a page built once and left alone falls behind. Pages for the main products need regular review, especially after new reviews reveal confusion or complaints.

Testing settles arguments that would otherwise come down to taste. Amazon lets brands test different versions of their A+ Content against each other, which shows which images, layouts and messages actually lift sales.

Video deserves particular attention on those pages. A short clip of a product in use answers questions that photos cannot, such as how a lid opens, how a fabric moves or how large an item looks in a hand. Many brands still have no video on their main pages, which makes it one of the clearest gaps to close. A simple, well-lit demonstration often does more than an expensive production.

Why the divide reaches past the product page

Content works at the brand level too, not only product by product. A Brand Story section and a well-organized Brand Store help shoppers understand the range and move from one product to another. Brands with several related products gain the most, because a shopper who trusts one product page is more likely to try a second if the brand’s pages look and read consistently.

This is also ground where smaller brands can compete. Content takes effort, but it does not require a large advertising budget. A small brand with the best page in its niche can convert better than a larger brand with a thin one, and that advantage holds even when its ad spend is lower.

Content protects advertising as well. An ad can deliver a shopper to the page; whether that shopper buys is settled by what the page shows. A brand that spends on ads while its content is thin pays for clicks that do not convert. Fixing content first makes every advertising dollar work harder, and often lowers the cost of each sale without any change to bids.

The same divide is likely to grow on other retailers. Walmart and Target are building their own AI tools, and they will read product content the same way, so the facts and images a brand builds now can be adapted for each retailer. The question for a leadership team is whether product content has an owner and a budget of its own, or still gets finished when someone has a spare afternoon. Giving it both, beginning with the top sellers, is how we run Amazon content as part of the channel.

A0535.crumb: Amazon’s March sale: forecast lift, click…
A0535.title: Amazon’s March sale: forecast lift, click prices and deal share
A0535.alt: A terracotta pot of daffodils beside twine-tied cardboard parcels on a stone doorstep against a navy wall.
A0535.ttag: Amazon’s March sale: forecast lift, click prices and deal share | Kwontified
A0535.desc: A first-time Amazon event has no history, so plan its sales lift, click prices and deal share as ranges and size the budget to survive the low case.
A0535.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 12, 2024.
A0535.body:
A forecast with one number in it feels more useful than a forecast with three. For Amazon’s March sale it is less useful, because nobody has run this event before. Amazon has invited sellers to submit deals for a sale built around home, outdoor, beauty, fashion, pets and travel. A first-time event has no history to work from.

The sound plan is a set of ranges for sales lift, click prices and deal share. Budgets should hold at the low end, and stock should be able to scale toward the high end. One result does not depend on which case arrives: advertising cost as a share of sales goes up in all of them.

The pull toward a single figure is easy to understand. Finance wants one line for the plan, the purchase order needs a quantity, and a range can look like an analyst who will not commit. Once a number sits in the deck, every later decision gets measured against it. For an event with no track record, that number has nothing underneath it. A range commits to more than a point does, because it says how far off the plan can be and still work.

What is known about Amazon’s March sale

Amazon has told sellers it is accepting deal submissions for a 2024 March sale, with deals selected for the week of March 18 to March 24, EcommerceBytes reported. According to the invitation, the sale will focus on Outdoor & Garden, Home, Beauty & Fashion, Pets, Travel and other seasonally relevant categories.

Shoppers have not been told yet. Amazon has not announced the event publicly. Its name, its length and whether it is open to all customers could still change. The categories and the dates in the invitation are the firm ground for planning, and the rest waits until Amazon confirms it.

Prime Day and Prime Big Deal Days have years of history behind them, so a brand can look back at its own past events and set a range with some confidence. A March sale has none. Any single estimate of its effect would be a guess presented as a number.

Why click prices push advertising cost up in every case

During a sale, sales lift and click prices rise together, because more advertisers compete for the same shoppers. When click prices rise, spend grows faster than sales. Total advertising cost of sales therefore increases in every plausible scenario. A single-point forecast hides how much the cost of the extra sales can vary.

Take a brand that normally sells $20,000 a week on Amazon and spends $3,000 a week on advertising, an advertising cost of sales of 15%. Assume it keeps its share of clicks during the sale, so its spend grows with its sales and with the price of each click.

CaseSales liftClick price riseWeekly salesAd spendAdvertising cost of sales
Normal weeknonenone$20,000$3,00015%
Low1.3 times10%$26,000$4,29016.5%
Middle1.6 times20%$32,000$5,76018%
Highsales double30%$40,000$7,80019.5%

Every case brings more sales, and every case costs more per dollar of sales than a normal week. The plan should be built on the spread from 16.5% to 19.5%, since the middle figure on its own says nothing about how thin the low case could feel or how expensive the high case could get.

Deal share adds a third range. If the brand runs a discount during the sale, some of its units sell at the lower price. Nobody knows in advance how many. A cautious case might put a third of sale-week units on the deal and a strong one well over half; the margin should be checked at each level. A deal that leaves acceptable margin when it carries a small share of volume can turn costly once it carries most of the week.

Budget for the low case, stock for the middle

A budget ceiling tied to advertising cost of sales does most of the work. Decide before the event the highest share of sales the brand will spend, and cap spending there. Because the cap is a share rather than a fixed sum, it flexes on its own: if sales come in high, it allows more spend, and if they come in low, it limits the loss.

Stock follows different logic, since running out during a sale wastes the advertising that brought shoppers to the page. Holding enough for the middle scenario overall, with extra on the products most likely to sell through, protects the top sellers without staking the whole order on the high case.

Deal selection should follow the invitation. Amazon named specific categories, and products in those categories are more likely to be featured and to benefit from the event’s traffic. Products outside them may pay the higher click prices without the same lift.

Bids, pacing and the weeks either side

Click prices often rise most on the first day of an event and in its final hours, when competitors push hardest. Raise bids gradually into the event and watch hourly costs on the busiest days. That keeps spending closer to plan than setting high bids for the whole week. Branded searches should stay well funded throughout, since shoppers who arrive looking for the brand by name are the cheapest sales of the event.

The days around the sale belong in the reading too. Many shoppers delay purchases before a sale and slow down after it, so the sale week alone overstates what the event added. Comparing the full period, including the week before and the week after, with a normal period gives a truer picture.

Write the low, middle and high cases down before the sale starts, then record afterward where each result fell within its range. That record turns the next March sale from a guess into a forecast, and building those ranges ahead of each Amazon event is how we plan event budgets that hold at the low end.

A0542.crumb: When branded search becomes a misleading…
A0542.title: When branded search becomes a misleading metric on Amazon
A0542.alt: A brass magnifying glass leaning on a wooden table beside stacked coins, with a small cardboard box behind.
A0542.ttag: When branded search becomes a misleading metric on Amazon | Kwontified
A0542.desc: Branded search ads report the best returns on Amazon because they mostly collect sales already coming. How to test what they add and where defense pays.
A0542.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 12, 2024.
A0542.body:
Take a campaign that spends $1,000 a month on a brand’s own name and reports $12,000 in attributed sales. A return of 12 times spend makes it the best line in the account, and nobody asks it to defend its budget. Now suppose the brand pauses it on searches where no competitor appears, and its total sales fall by only $1,500 a month. The campaign was adding $1,500 in sales for $1,000 of spend, a real return of 1.5 times.

That gap is the trouble with branded search as a metric. Ads on a brand’s own name mostly capture sales that would have happened anyway, and branded volume moves for reasons unrelated to brand strength. Brands should test what branded ads actually add, defend their name where competitors bid on it, and read branded volume alongside the causes that move it.

Why branded search looks so strong

The appeal is easy to see. Shoppers who type a brand’s name are ready to buy, so ads on those searches convert at high rates and report high returns. Branded search volume also rises when a brand is doing well, so it looks like a natural measure of brand health. Both readings are sensible on their face, which is why the campaign in the opening example keeps its budget year after year.

What the eBay experiments found

The best evidence comes from outside Amazon. In a series of large experiments at eBay, researchers found that ads on brand keywords had no measurable short-term benefit, according to their working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research. When eBay stopped those ads, nearly all the traffic they had brought arrived through free search results instead.

The same research found a pattern that matters beyond brand terms. On non-brand searches, ads did influence new and infrequent users, but frequent users, whose buying the ads barely changed, accounted for most of the spending. The ads worked best on the shoppers who knew the advertiser least.

The study covered search engines rather than Amazon, and Amazon differs in an important way, as the section on defense explains. The underlying behavior carries over all the same. A shopper who searches for a brand by name usually finds it with or without an ad.

Why branded returns mislead

A shopper who searches for a brand by name has already decided to look for it. An ad on that search gets credit for a purchase the shopper was likely to make anyway, which inflates reported returns. Paying for those clicks where nobody else is bidding is a little like tipping the doorman for every customer who was already walking in.

The only way to separate the ad’s effect from the shopper’s intent is to compare sales with and without the ad, which is what the pause in the opening example does. The 1.5 times return is still positive, but it is a very different number from 12. A brand that judges its account by blended returns will overvalue branded campaigns and may underinvest in the campaigns that bring new customers.

Defend where competitors bid, and test the rest

Amazon’s nuance is competition on the brand’s own name. On Amazon, competitors can bid on a brand’s name and place their products above the brand’s own listing. Where that happens, a branded ad keeps shoppers from being diverted, and its value is real. Where no competitor bids, the ad mostly pays for sales the brand would get anyway. Branded ads earn their place as defense; growth has to come from somewhere else.

Each important branded search needs a look at the actual results page. If competitors appear, defending the search is likely worth paying for. If they do not, a pause test shows what the ad adds.

A pause test needs more care than it first appears to. It should run long enough to see past daily swings, cover searches where competitors are genuinely absent, and be watched for any change in competitor behavior during the test. A competitor that starts bidding while the brand’s ad is paused changes the result, and the ad should go back on if that happens.

Reporting needs the same discipline. Branded returns flatter the overall numbers, so branded and non-branded campaigns belong on separate lines. Only then does the account show how well the brand is reaching new shoppers.

The logic extends to audiences on Amazon. Ads shown to a brand’s past buyers, or to shoppers already viewing its products, will report strong returns for the same reason branded search does: many of those shoppers were going to buy. Those campaigns deserve the same testing before they claim a large share of budget.

Reading branded volume without over-reading it

Branded searches rise when off-Amazon advertising, press coverage or promotions send shoppers looking. They can fall when shoppers find products through other routes, such as Amazon’s new Rufus assistant. A change in branded volume is a signal to investigate, not proof that brand strength has changed.

Over long periods the number is still useful, since a brand that more shoppers seek by name is usually a stronger brand. In any month or quarter, the number reflects many causes besides brand strength.

Budget should follow what the tests show. If branded ads add little on most searches, the money is better spent reaching shoppers who do not yet know the brand, where advertising creates sales rather than collecting them. The working rule is simple enough to apply this week: defend the name wherever a competitor sits above it, and make every other branded dollar earn its place through a pause test. Running those tests and moving the budget they release is how we measure what Amazon brand ads add.

A0544.crumb: Home and kitchen on Amazon: the 2024…
A0544.title: Home and kitchen on Amazon: the 2024 playbook
A0544.alt: Nested copper saucepans beside ceramic bowls, linen towels, a wooden spoon, and rosemary on a sunny kitchen counter.
A0544.ttag: Home and kitchen on Amazon: the 2024 playbook | Kwontified
A0544.desc: New fees, rising click prices and AI shopping tools reach home and kitchen in 2024. The order in which brands should fix cost, stock, content and ads.
A0544.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 14, 2024.
A0544.body:
For home and kitchen brands, the first date on the 2024 Amazon calendar that mattered had nothing to do with shoppers. On March 1, a new inbound placement fee started applying to inventory sent to Amazon, and two more fee changes follow in April. They weigh most on large, slow-moving items, and many home products are exactly that. Competition for clicks keeps rising at the same time, and AI tools now read product content to answer shoppers.

The plan that holds up through the year works in order. Fix the cost of each product first, then time stock and promotions to the category’s seasons, then strengthen content, and only then scale advertising. Taking those steps out of order means paying to advertise products whose economics or pages are not ready for the traffic.

Home and kitchen on Amazon is big, and costlier to sell in

The category is large. Across 2021 and 2022, monthly Amazon sales in kitchen and dining alone moved between $1 billion and $2.4 billion, YipitData figures show. Over Prime Day in July 2023, Home & Kitchen took $2.5 billion in sales by Similarweb’s count.

The cost of selling there is changing on a fixed timetable. Amazon’s 2024 fee changes arrive in three steps, Value Added Resource reported:

DateWhat changesWhere home and kitchen feels it
March 1New inbound placement fee, charged 45 days after inventory is receivedLarge items sent in volume
April 1Low-inventory-level fee for standard-size productsFast sellers that run low in season
April 15New fulfillment rates take effectHeavy products where fulfillment is a big share of price

Sellers can avoid the low-inventory fee by holding more than four weeks of stock.

Advertising is getting more expensive too. In the fourth quarter of 2023, Amazon’s ad revenue was up 27% against 9% growth in its online store sales, GeekWire reported.

Why product cost comes first

Home and kitchen has a particular cost structure. Many products are large, heavy or slow to sell, which makes fulfillment and storage a bigger share of their price than in categories like beauty. When fees change, home brands feel it more, and a product that loses money after the new fees will lose more once it is advertised.

So the year starts with profit per product, recalculated under the 2024 fees: the inbound placement fee, the new fulfillment rates and, for standard-size items, the low-inventory fee. Products that no longer earn a profit need a new price, a new pack size or a different fulfillment approach. The work has to be done item by item rather than as an average for the range, since a profitable range can hide individual products that lose money on every order.

Bundles and multi-packs belong in that conversation. Selling items together can raise the value of each order, spreading fulfillment and inbound costs over more revenue. That matters most for lower-priced products, where fees take a larger share.

Seasons, stock and the event calendar

Home shopping is strongly seasonal. Spring cleaning, outdoor living, moving season, back to school and the holidays each lift different products, and stock and promotions timed to those moments earn more than the same spend spread evenly. Mapping which products peak in spring, summer, back to school and the holidays lets stock arrive before each peak. It also helps avoid the low-inventory fee on products that sell quickly in season.

Inventory deserves particular care in this category. The low-inventory fee encourages holding more stock, while storage costs penalize holding too much, especially for bulky items. The balance has to be struck product by product.

Amazon’s own events shape the calendar as well. Prime Day and the fall Prime event have long been the category’s biggest moments, and sellers have now been asked to put forward deals for an Amazon sale in March that leans partly on home and outdoor products. Brands should decide early which events they will join, which products they will feature and how deep a discount each product can afford under the new fees. Joining every event with every product is rarely the best use of margin.

Content and returns before advertising

Home shoppers want dimensions, materials, capacity and care instructions stated plainly, along with images that show scale. Video of a product in use is often the clearest way to answer their questions. A home product whose page lacks those details will waste the clicks advertising buys, and Amazon’s new Rufus assistant will have little to say about it.

Returns are where thin content shows up on the profit line. Home products are often returned because they arrive damaged, look different in person or do not fit the space a shopper had in mind. Each return costs shipping, handling and sometimes the product itself. Clear dimensions, honest images that show scale and sturdy packaging reduce returns more cheaply than any fee change can be absorbed. Reading the return reasons for the top products each month, and fixing the most common causes, keeps that cost in view.

Advertising comes last, once costs are fixed, stock is planned and pages are complete, because each advertising dollar then goes further. Spend belongs on the specific searches where the products fit closely, and branded campaigns deserve a test before anyone assumes they add sales.

The plan itself needs a review each quarter. Fees, competition and seasons all change, and a plan built in March will need adjustment before the holidays, when the category’s largest sales and highest costs arrive together. The question worth bringing to that first review is which products still earn their place under the new fees, and building the year around the answer is how we run Amazon for home and kitchen brands.
