A0546.crumb: The state of Target Plus for brands…
A0546.title: The state of Target Plus for brands heading into 2024
A0546.alt: A ceramic vase of eucalyptus, folded linen, a mug, and a leather journal on a rustic shelf against a red wall.
A0546.ttag: The state of Target Plus for brands heading into 2024 | Kwontified
A0546.desc: Target’s online growth runs through its stores, while Target Plus items ship from sellers. Why Target Plus suits products Target does not stock.
A0546.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 19, 2024.
A0546.body:
Target’s digital comparable sales fell 4.8% for the full 2023 fiscal year, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Over the same year, Target reported more than $500 million in sales growth in same-day services, led by double-digit growth in Drive Up. Online shrank and online grew, depending on which online you count.

The difference is the store. Target’s online growth runs through orders its stores fill, and Target Plus items ship from the sellers themselves, so they cannot use those services. In 2024, Target Plus works best as a way to extend Target’s range with products its stores do not carry. As a second shelf for items Target already stocks, it has little to offer the shoppers driving that growth. Brands should choose products on that basis, and judge the channel on whether those products reach Target’s shoppers.

What the numbers say about Target Plus for brands

Target’s online sales are large but grew unevenly in 2023. In the fourth quarter, digital comparable sales fell 0.7%, while online sales accounted for 21.3% of total sales, according to the same report. For the full year, online accounted for 18.3% of sales, on total revenue of $107.41 billion.

If online sales were 18.3% of $107.41 billion, Target’s online business was roughly $19.7 billion in fiscal 2023. That is a large audience. Much of it, though, is shoppers ordering items for pickup or same-day delivery from a nearby store.

Target Plus, its marketplace, has always been selective. When it launched in 2019, Target invited sellers rather than opening to all, and by the end of that year it had nearly 100 sellers, the Star Tribune reported.

Why marketplace items compete with store stock

Target’s shoppers increasingly use its stores to receive online orders the same day. That favors items held in Target’s own stores. Target Plus items ship from the seller and compete on delivery time with that store stock. Marketplace products therefore win where Target’s stores leave a gap in the range, and struggle where they duplicate items a shopper can pick up within hours.

Take a common kitchen item. A shopper can usually get it from Target’s own stock the same day, so a marketplace version shipped from a warehouse in several days has little to offer that shopper. A product Target does not stock at all, such as a specialized size, a niche design or an extended color range, faces no such competition.

That is where Target Plus earns its place. It lets Target offer more than its stores can hold, and it rewards brands whose products fill those gaps.

One change would alter this reading. Target Plus items cannot use Drive Up or same-day pickup, and that limit is what pushes them toward range extension. If Target ever let marketplace items flow through its store services, duplicates would compete on equal terms and the calculation would need redoing. Until it does, the delivery gap is the fact to plan around.

Choosing products and running the channel

Mapping the brand’s range against Target’s own shelves comes first. Products Target already stocks in stores, whether from the brand or a competitor, will compete with same-day pickup. Products it does not stock have room to grow.

Delivery and service decide whether range alone is enough. Target Plus is selective, and sellers must keep up with its expectations on shipping times and customer service. A brand that ships slowly loses the advantage that range can give.

A seller on Target Plus ships orders itself or through a third-party warehouse, and its delivery promise is what Target’s shoppers see beside the store stock. Faster, reliable shipping narrows the gap with same-day pickup, especially for products Target does not carry, where the shopper has no nearby alternative anyway. Delivery promises are worth testing against conversion.

Shoppers who arrive looking for store items need an introduction to the extended range. Target’s media business, Roundel, can show marketplace products to Target shoppers who would otherwise never come across them. The loyalty program works alongside it: many Target shoppers are members of Target Circle and tend to shop Target often, and products that appear in Target’s promotions and member offers can reach those regular shoppers in a way a listing alone cannot.

Price consistency matters on Target. Its shoppers expect fair prices, and a brand that prices higher on Target Plus than elsewhere will struggle to convert.

Judging the channel follows from the same logic. The measure that matters is whether the range-extension products are being found and bought by Target’s shoppers, so sales of the products Target does not stock deserve their own line in the report, apart from any duplicates the brand also lists.

Sizing Target Plus realistically

The channel’s selectivity is an advantage. With fewer sellers than open marketplaces, Target Plus has less price undercutting and fewer lookalike listings, so a brand that earns a place there competes in a calmer environment than on Amazon or Walmart.

Scale is the other side of that selectivity. Target Plus is smaller than Amazon’s or Walmart’s marketplaces, and growth depends on Target’s own digital trends. It is best treated as a focused channel for the right products rather than a primary engine of growth.

Getting in takes patience as well. Because Target Plus is invitation-based, brands usually need to show a strong product range, reliable operations and a fit with Target’s shoppers before they are accepted. A prepared case, with clear evidence of demand and service standards, improves the odds.

The test for any product is short. If a shopper can pick it up at a nearby Target this afternoon, it will struggle on Target Plus; if they cannot, it has a chance. Running that test across a brand’s range, and then operating the products that pass it, is how we build a Target Plus presence for brands.

A0547.crumb: Grocery on Amazon: interest is outrunning…
A0547.title: Grocery on Amazon: interest is outrunning growth
A0547.alt: A paper grocery bag of carrots and greens beside a bowl of produce with a magnifying glass on a wooden table.
A0547.ttag: Grocery on Amazon: interest is outrunning growth | Kwontified
A0547.desc: Amazon keeps rewriting what it charges for grocery delivery, a sign interest is outrunning profitable growth. Where grocery brands should build instead.
A0547.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 21, 2024.
A0547.body:
A Prime member who orders groceries from Amazon has watched the rules change more than once. Free Amazon Fresh delivery used to start at orders above $35. In 2023 the free-delivery threshold rose to $150, then came back down to $100 in October. In December, Amazon began testing a $9.99-a-month subscription for Prime members in three cities, with free Fresh and Whole Foods delivery on orders over $35.

A retailer that keeps rewriting its prices is telling its suppliers something. In this case, interest in grocery on Amazon is outrunning the growth Amazon can make pay. Grocery brands should build on the stable part of the channel, which means shelf-stable products, repeat buying and bundles shipped through Amazon’s main store, and keep fresh delivery models that are still changing out of the foundation of their plans.

How grocery on Amazon got here

Amazon has wanted to be a grocery destination for years. It bought Whole Foods Market in 2017 for $13.7 billion and has since launched its own Amazon Fresh stores, CNBC reported. The way it charges for delivery has kept moving. In 2021, Amazon introduced a service fee for Whole Foods delivery orders, and the Fresh thresholds then rose and fell before the subscription test began, according to the same report.

Why the changes signal a gap

Grocery delivery is expensive to run. Orders are bulky, often perishable and frequently small, and shoppers expect them quickly. Each change in fees or thresholds is an attempt to make the numbers work, whether through larger orders, regular customers or a fee that covers the cost.

Read as an institution, Amazon is showing both its ambition and its limit. Shoppers clearly want convenient grocery delivery, and Amazon clearly wants to provide it. The version shoppers want most, small orders delivered free and fast, is the version that costs the most to run. That is what interest outrunning growth looks like from the outside.

The rest of Amazon grocery is steadier. Shelf-stable products such as snacks, pantry staples, coffee and household consumables ship through Amazon’s main store and fulfillment network, alongside everything else Amazon sells. Shoppers buy them in larger quantities, often on repeat, and they do not depend on a fresh delivery model. Nothing about how those products reach the shopper changes when a delivery threshold moves.

The decision in front of a grocery brand’s leadership

For the leadership of a grocery brand, the real question is how much of the Amazon plan to hang on fresh delivery. The case for leaning in is easy to make: Amazon is clearly investing, and if its subscription test expands, it could make fresh and chilled products more accessible to more shoppers. The case for holding back is the record. A brand that builds its plan around one fee structure may find it changed within months, along with the shopping behavior that structure encouraged.

Take a snack brand that sells well in grocery stores and wants to grow on Amazon. If it plans around fresh delivery promotions, its results swing with every change in Amazon’s fees. If it focuses on multipacks of its shelf-stable snacks, sold through Amazon’s main store with subscription discounts, it builds a steadier base of repeat buyers.

Fresh delivery is still worth following closely. Brands with perishable products should track the subscription test and be ready to act, without making it the center of their plan until the model settles.

Building on the stable part of the channel

The range should lead with shelf-stable products. Products that ship well and store well fit Amazon’s main fulfillment network, where costs and delivery are predictable.

Repeat buying is where the steady growth comes from. Subscribe & Save, larger pack sizes and variety bundles suit how shoppers restock pantry goods, and a shopper who subscribes keeps buying without comparing alternatives each time.

Pricing should be built around the pack rather than the unit. Grocery shoppers on Amazon often compare cost per ounce or per item, so multipacks that offer clear value per unit convert better than single items priced to match a store shelf. Fees push in the same direction. Low-priced pantry items carry Amazon’s fulfillment fees like any other product, and on a single inexpensive item those fees can take most of the margin. In packs and bundles the fees are spread over more value, and each order earns enough to cover them.

Shoppers’ habits support the same plan. Many households split grocery shopping between a weekly store trip for fresh food and occasional online orders for heavy or bulky staples, and Amazon fits the second habit well. Cases of drinks, large packs of paper goods and bulk snacks match how shoppers already use Amazon for groceries.

Products with short dates need a separate check. Items with short dates or temperature limits can be damaged or expire in a general fulfillment network, so brands should confirm that their products meet Amazon’s requirements for expiration-dated items before listing them widely, and plan stock so older units sell first.

Advertising in pantry categories calls for restraint. Those categories are competitive, and many shoppers buy the same brands again and again. Ads work best on new products and on bringing in first-time buyers, who may then subscribe. Heavy spending to reach shoppers who already buy the brand every month mostly pays for orders that were coming regardless.

Amazon may keep adjusting its grocery terms for some time, and nobody outside the company knows where they will settle. The pantry business underneath does not have to wait for that answer, and building it pack by pack and subscriber by subscriber is how we grow grocery brands on Amazon.

A0548.crumb: The state of Zalando for brands heading…
A0548.title: The state of Zalando for brands heading into 2024
A0548.alt: A white clothing rack of brown and tan coats above a wrapped parcel on a herringbone floor in a bright room.
A0548.ttag: The state of Zalando for brands heading into 2024 | Kwontified
A0548.desc: Zalando is shifting from buying stock to hosting brands that sell directly. When the Partner Program beats wholesale, worked out as a break-even sell-through.
A0548.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 26, 2024.
A0548.body:
Zalando’s gross merchandise volume fell 1.1% in 2023. Over the same stretch, the share of its Fashion Store GMV running through the Partner Program, where brands sell directly, climbed to 39.2% by the fourth quarter. A shrinking platform with a growing partner business looks like a contradiction until you ask who owns the stock.

Under wholesale, Zalando owns it and carries the risk of what does not sell. Under the Partner Program, the brand owns it, and it earns a higher margin in exchange for carrying the risk. Brands selling on Zalando in 2024 face that choice between the certainty of wholesale and the margin of selling directly. They should make it by calculating the sell-through rate at which the partner model beats wholesale, product by product, rather than by preference.

Why Zalando for brands looks different in 2024

Zalando had a difficult 2023. Its gross merchandise volume fell 1.1% to €14.6 billion and its revenue fell 1.9% to €10.1 billion, while adjusted operating profit rose to €350 million, FashionUnited reported. Active customers fell to 49.6 million from 51.2 million, according to a report on the same results.

The partner business moved the other way. In the fourth quarter, the Partner Program’s share of Fashion Store GMV rose 2.8 percentage points to 39.2%, and 62% of partner items were shipped by Zalando Fulfilment Solutions, up 4 percentage points, FashionUnited reported. Wholesale still accounts for the remaining 60.8% of Fashion Store GMV, but Zalando is selling less of its own stock and hosting more of brands’ stock. It expects GMV and revenue to grow 0% to 5% in 2024.

Wholesale against the Partner Program, in one jacket

Under wholesale, Zalando buys a brand’s stock and carries the risk of unsold items. Under the Partner Program, the brand keeps ownership, earns a larger share of each sale after commission and fulfillment costs, and carries the risk itself. The partner model therefore pays more only above a break-even sell-through rate, and that rate depends on the gap between the wholesale price and the brand’s net per unit.

Take a jacket that retails for €100. Under wholesale, Zalando buys 100 units at €45 each, paying the brand €4,500 regardless of how many sell. Under the Partner Program, suppose commission and fulfillment costs total 35% of the retail price, so the brand nets €65 on each jacket sold, and it places the same 100 units.

ModelJackets soldBrand receivesUnsold jackets
Wholesalehowever many sell€4,500carried by Zalando
Partner Program, stronger season70€4,550owned by the brand
Partner Program, weaker season60€3,90040, owned by the brand

The break-even is about 69% sell-through. Above that, the partner model pays more. Below it, wholesale was the better deal. These numbers are illustrative, and actual commission rates and fulfillment costs vary, but the structure holds: the partner model rewards products the brand can sell through reliably and penalizes those it cannot.

Both sides of the choice

The case for wholesale is certainty. The €4,500 arrives whether the jackets sell or not, and the decision to mark down belongs to Zalando. The case for the Partner Program is margin and control: €65 a unit against €45, plus more say over pricing, range and timing. Some brands value that control enough to accept somewhat lower expected returns, especially when protecting their prices across channels matters.

Markdowns move the break-even line, and they are easy to leave out of the model. Under wholesale, Zalando decides when to discount the stock it owns; under the Partner Program, the brand decides. A brand that discounts late in the season to clear stock will earn less than €65 on those units, which raises the sell-through it needs at full price. The model should include the share of units likely to sell at a discount, not only the share that sells at all.

Every partner cost belongs in the same calculation. Commission, Zalando’s fulfillment fees, returns handling and the cost of unsold stock all count, and returns deserve particular care in fashion, where many orders come back.

Geography adds a further layer. Zalando sells across many countries, and demand for the same product can differ widely between them. Under wholesale, Zalando decides where stock goes. Under the Partner Program, the brand chooses which markets to sell in and how much stock to commit, which helps brands with a strong position in particular countries and adds work for those without.

Fulfillment narrows one of the gaps. With most partner items shipped through Zalando’s own fulfillment, brands using it gain the same delivery promises as Zalando’s own stock, while brands shipping from their own warehouses should compare delivery speed carefully. Zalando has also grouped its fulfillment and other brand services under the ZEOS name and plans to grow them in 2024. Brands should watch whether those services become a cheaper way to reach shoppers across Europe than running their own networks.

Where the numbers lean

On balance, the numbers lean toward a split made style by style. Core styles with steady demand often sell through at high rates and clear the break-even comfortably, so they suit the partner model. Fashion items with uncertain demand may fall below it, and for those, wholesale leaves the risk with Zalando. Online fashion demand was weak in 2023 and Zalando expects only modest growth in 2024, so any move into the partner model should be sized to that outlook, starting with the styles most likely to sell through.

The working rule takes one division per style: divide the wholesale price by the net per unit under the Partner Program, and move the style across only when its real sell-through clears that line with room to spare. Building that model across a full range is how we help brands choose how to sell on Zalando.

A0550.crumb: Apparel on Amazon: winning in a difficult…
A0550.title: Apparel on Amazon: winning in a difficult category
A0550.alt: An open shipping box of clothes beside stacks of folded sweaters and shirts on a wooden bench by a pink wall.
A0550.ttag: Apparel on Amazon: winning in a difficult category | Kwontified
A0550.desc: Amazon charges a fee on every returned apparel unit and cut most of its own clothing brands. Why fit and returns decide who wins apparel on Amazon.
A0550.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 28, 2024.
A0550.body:
A shopper who is unsure about a pair of jeans on Amazon has an easy way out: order two sizes and send one back. In a fitting room, the same shopper would try both and leave one on the hook at no cost to anyone. Online, the second pair travels to the door and back again, and someone pays for the trip.

That habit is why apparel is one of Amazon’s hardest categories. Shoppers cannot try clothes on, so returns are frequent and costly. Amazon already charges a processing fee on every returned apparel unit, and even Amazon cut most of its own clothing brands in 2023. Apparel brands win on Amazon by reducing returns and selling what shoppers can buy with confidence, and fit information and range choice are their main levers. Reach on its own does not get them there.

How apparel on Amazon became so demanding

Amazon has tried hard in clothing. In 2023 it pulled back, eliminating 27 of its 30 clothing brands as it cut its house brands overall, PYMNTS reported, citing The Wall Street Journal. Amazon had the data, the traffic and the placement, and still found most of its own clothing lines not worth keeping.

Returns are a large part of why the category is hard. Amazon charges a returns processing fee on apparel and shoes for each customer-returned unit, and said in its 2024 fee changes that those fees would remain unchanged on average, according to a fee guide. From June 1, 2024, Amazon will extend a returns processing fee to high-return products in other categories, the same guide noted. Apparel brands already pay for returns in a way that most other categories are only now starting to.

Why fit decides who keeps the sale

A shopper buying a phone charger knows what will arrive. A shopper buying jeans does not know how they will fit, how the fabric will feel or whether the color matches the photo, which is exactly why ordering two sizes feels sensible.

Each return costs the brand twice. It loses the sale, and it pays the processing fee and the cost of handling the returned item. Returns can also hurt the listing, since products with frequent returns may be flagged to shoppers and draw negative reviews about fit.

That is why reach alone does not win in apparel. Advertising can bring many shoppers to a listing, but if a large share of the resulting orders come back, the brand pays for clicks, sales and returns, and keeps little.

Take the same pair of trousers listed two ways. The first listing offers a standard size chart and a single photo of a model. The second offers measurements for each size, notes on whether the trousers run large or small, photos on models of different heights and a plain description of the fabric’s stretch. The second listing sells to fewer undecided shoppers but keeps far more of its sales.

Where apparel brands can win

Fit information has to be unmistakable. Measurements for each size, clear notes on how items run, fabric details and photos that show how garments look on different bodies all help shoppers choose the right size the first time. Answering common fit questions in the listing and in customer questions reduces the guesswork further.

Range choice matters as much as the listing. Basics and replenishable items, such as socks, underwear, t-shirts and simple activewear, are easier to buy online with confidence than fashion pieces that depend on fit and style. Brands can lead on Amazon with those items and keep more fit-sensitive pieces for channels where shoppers can try them on. Variations call for the same discipline, because offering every color in every size multiplies stock and returns. An Amazon range works best when it is focused on the sizes and colors that sell through reliably.

Return reasons are among the most useful reports a brand receives. Amazon shows sellers why items come back. When many returns cite size, the fix may be better guidance or a different size range. When they cite quality or color, the fix may be in the product or the photos.

Reviews carry special weight in apparel, because shoppers read them for fit advice more than for quality alone. Repeated comments about sizing belong in the listing, so that new shoppers benefit from what earlier buyers learned.

Seasons, channels and the ad budget

Seasons add pressure. Apparel demand shifts quickly with the weather and the calendar, and stock left over at the end of a season loses value fast. Under Amazon’s fees, unsold apparel also costs money to store. Smaller, more frequent shipments suit seasonal items, with larger quantities kept for year-round basics.

Amazon is also one channel among several for most apparel brands. Shoppers who want to feel a fabric or try a fit may prefer a store, a brand’s own site with generous returns, or a specialist retailer. A brand does not need its whole range on Amazon to succeed there, and choosing the products that suit how Amazon shoppers buy is often more profitable than listing everything.

Advertising should follow the same logic. Most of the spend belongs on products with low return rates, where each sale is likely to stick, and fit-sensitive items deserve a test before their budgets grow.

Amazon’s own retreat is the plainest lesson the category offers. With every advantage a seller could ask for, it still kept only a handful of its clothing brands. The apparel brands that last on Amazon are the ones whose shoppers keep what they order, and building listings and ranges around that is how we run apparel on Amazon for brands.

A0553.crumb: The ad war in arts, crafts and sewing on…
A0553.title: The ad war in arts, crafts and sewing on Amazon
A0553.alt: Rolls of natural linen fabric, yarn balls, thread spools and vintage scissors against a sage green wall.
A0553.ttag: The ad war in arts, crafts and sewing on Amazon | Kwontified
A0553.desc: Joann’s bankruptcy pushes crafting further online, into a category of cheap items and crowded ads. Why order value decides who can afford to win the clicks.
A0553.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 2, 2024.
A0553.body:
A spool of thread that sells for $8 on Amazon can afford to pay about $0.29 for a click before its advertising stops breaking even. A sewing starter kit at $30 can pay about $1.08 for the same click. As craft shopping moves online, that gap decides who gets seen.

The demand leaving specialist craft stores lands in a category full of low-priced items and many sellers, where revenue per click is small and competition for ads is intense. The brands that can afford to win are those that raise the value of each order through kits, bundles and multi-packs. Craft brands should build their Amazon range and advertising around order value rather than around single low-priced items.

Why arts, crafts and sewing are moving online

The clearest signal came in March 2024. Joann, the fabric and craft retailer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on March 18 and said it had secured $132 million in new financing, while keeping its roughly 800 stores and website open, Digital Commerce 360 reported. The same report showed where Joann’s sales were heading. In its most recent reported quarter, net sales fell 4.1% while ecommerce sales grew 11.5%, reaching 13.1% of total sales.

The pressure came from several directions. Consumers had stepped back from at-home crafting after the pandemic, and rivals such as Hobby Lobby offered lower prices, while casual crafters could find supplies at stores such as Target, the Associated Press reported.

Crafters who shift online often go where the selection is widest. On Amazon, that means a category crowded with sellers offering yarn, fabric, paints, beads and tools, many at low prices.

The bid ceiling in a low-price category

A click is worth, at most, what a sale earns multiplied by the share of clicks that turn into sales. In a category of low-priced items, that affordable bid is small. When many sellers compete for the same searches, only products with higher order value can bid enough to win placements while staying profitable.

Low-priced items look like the easy ones to advertise. Shoppers add a spool of thread to the basket without much thought, so conversion can be healthy, and a cheap product seems to carry little risk. The trouble is that conversion multiplies whatever profit the sale earns, and a good rate applied to a small profit still leaves a small ceiling.

Run the two products from the opening through that calculation, each with a 30% margin before advertising and a 12% conversion rate.

ProductPriceProfit per saleMost it can pay per click
Single spool of thread$8$2.40about $0.29
Sewing starter kit$30$9about $1.08

The kit can bid about 3.75 times as much for the same click. On a contested search where clicks cost more than $0.29, the single spool cannot advertise profitably at all, while the kit still can. The ad war in crafts goes to the brands whose orders are large enough to pay for the attention, whatever the size of their catalog.

The ceiling is only half of the comparison. The other half is what clicks on a given search actually cost, which the search term report shows. Products whose ceilings sit well above that cost can advertise there; products whose ceilings sit below it are paying for clicks that cannot earn back their price.

What raises order value

Kits and bundles should lead the advertising. Starter kits, project kits and curated bundles raise order value and suit crafters who want everything for a project in one purchase, and they stand out from single-item listings.

Supplies earn their place in advertising as multi-packs. Thread, needles, paint and beads sell well in sets of colors or sizes, and a multi-pack lifts the order value of items that would be too cheap to advertise alone.

Single items can still earn their keep without ads. Low-priced replacement items matter, especially to repeat customers, and they can earn sales through good listings and brand searches without carrying advertising costs they cannot support.

Repeat buying changes the arithmetic for the first order. Crafters return for supplies as they finish projects, so a brand that wins a customer with a kit can sell refills and add-ons later, often without paying for a new click. That repeat value can justify spending more to win the first order, as long as the brand measures it.

Brand-level ads help broad ranges. Ads that show a brand’s logo and several products at once let a shopper see a range of colors or supplies in one place. That can raise the chance a click turns into a larger order, because the shopper lands on a page built to sell more than one item.

Lookalikes, content and seasons

Lookalike sellers are a constant presence in this category. Many craft products are easy to copy, and sellers with very low costs can undercut on price. A brand cannot win that contest on price alone. It wins on quality the shopper can see, clear branding and the kits and bundles a low-cost copier is less likely to offer.

Content raises the ceiling itself. Clear photos of finished projects, color charts and plain descriptions of materials help shoppers choose among many similar listings, and they raise conversion, which raises the affordable bid.

Crafting demand rises around holidays, back to school and gift-giving periods, and click prices rise with it. Kits and bundles belong in those moments, and spend on low-value items should hold back when competition peaks.

Competition is likely to stay intense as more crafters shop online and more sellers follow them. The working rule for any craft range is to calculate each product’s bid ceiling from its profit and its conversion, and stop advertising anything whose ceiling sits below what its searches cost. Shaping the range so the advertised products clear that bar is how we run Amazon advertising for craft brands.

A0554.crumb: Where the Amazon Small Business badge…
A0554.title: Where the Amazon Small Business badge matters most
A0554.alt: A glazed ceramic bowl nestled in shredded paper inside a cardboard box on a pottery studio workbench.
A0554.ttag: Where the Amazon Small Business badge matters most | Kwontified
A0554.desc: Amazon’s Small Business badge helps where shoppers care who made a product and barely registers where they do not. Where it counts and how to use it well.
A0554.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 4, 2024.
A0554.body:
When an Amazon search includes products from eligible small businesses, the shopper can narrow the results to those brands with a single filter. The shoppers who use it have chosen deliberately to see small businesses. That choice is most common when they are buying a gift, a handmade piece or something for the home, where who made it is part of the purchase.

That is where the Small Business badge earns its keep. The wish to support small brands shapes decisions mainly in categories where the maker matters, such as gifts, handmade goods, home decor and independent beauty, and it barely registers in commodity categories. Eligible brands should build on the badge in those categories and treat it as a minor tiebreaker elsewhere. It is not a general growth lever.

What the Amazon Small Business badge is

Amazon introduced the badge ahead of Prime Day 2022, to help shoppers find products from small business brands and artisans on product pages and in search results, according to Amazon. During the lead-up to that Prime Day, shoppers spent more than $3 billion on more than 100 million small business items included in a related sweepstakes, Amazon said.

To qualify, brands need to be registered in Amazon’s Brand Registry or Amazon Handmade, and products from eligible small businesses receive the badge automatically, ChannelX reported. The search filter came later. Amazon introduced it in July 2023, and it appears when a search includes eligible products, EcommerceBytes reported.

Why the badge matters more in some categories

Some purchases carry meaning beyond the product. A shopper buying a gift, a handmade candle or a piece of art for the home often cares who made it, and a small business story adds to the product’s appeal. In those moments, a badge that signals a small maker can tip the decision.

Other purchases carry no such meaning. A shopper buying batteries, printer paper or a phone cable wants the right specification at the right price, delivered quickly. Few shoppers in those categories filter by business size, and a badge rarely changes their choice.

Read as a signal from the retailer, the badge and the filter suggest that Amazon wants independent makers to see it as a place where their story can be told. It also wants the shoppers who care about that story to act on it without leaving Amazon. That aim lines up with a brand’s interest only where shoppers actually care, which is why the category matters more than the badge.

Take two eligible small brands. One makes hand-poured candles and sells them as gifts. The other makes generic phone chargers.

For the candle maker, the badge reinforces a story shoppers already want to support, and it appears in a filter gift shoppers actually use. For the charger maker, the badge sits unnoticed next to price and delivery speed, which decide the sale. At a craft fair, the maker’s name on the stall is half the pitch; at an electronics counter, nobody asks who made the cable.

Putting the badge to work where it counts

The same line can run through a single brand’s range. A maker that sells boxed gift sets and plain refills will find the badge doing real work on the gift set, where the buyer is choosing for someone else. It does very little on the refill, which a loyal customer reorders without a second look. Planning content and spend product by product follows from that.

A missing badge helps nobody, so enrollment comes first. Brands that qualify should make sure they are registered and that the badge actually appears on their products, since it cannot help even in the categories where it matters most if shoppers never see it.

In gifts, home decor, handmade and independent beauty, the badge works best alongside listing content that explains who makes the product and why. A Brand Story section and images of the making process give the badge something to point to. Advertising can carry the same story further. Ads that show a brand’s logo and maker story reach shoppers who have not yet found the filter, and they work best in the same gift and home categories where the badge counts.

Timing matters as well. The badge and filter count most when shoppers are buying for others, around holidays, Mother’s Day and other gifting occasions, so gift-ready products with clear gift options should be well stocked and featured then. Amazon has also run programs that spotlight small businesses around major events. Qualifying brands should look for those each season, since they can bring traffic the badge alone would not.

Amazon offers other badges that signal who is behind a brand, and some shoppers look for them in the same way. Brands that qualify for more than one should check that each appears correctly and tell a consistent story across them, rather than relying on any single badge.

Keeping the badge in proportion

The badge does not replace good listings, competitive prices or fast delivery. In categories where shoppers decide on specification and price, those factors decide the sale, badge or not.

Nor does the badge say anything about quality on its own. Shoppers who support small businesses still expect products to arrive as described. A small brand that disappoints them loses the goodwill the badge helped earn, so reviews and reliability matter as much as ever.

Whether the badge is helping a given product is something a brand can read from its own numbers, by comparing conversion before and after enrollment or across products in different categories. The question worth putting to the team is which of its products shoppers would buy partly because of who made them. Putting the small business story behind exactly those products is how we help independent brands sell on Amazon.

A0555.title: Walmart Connect beyond search: when display makes sense
A0555.alt: A blank white roadside billboard on wooden legs in tall grass beside a highway under a deep blue sky.
A0555.ttag: Walmart Connect beyond search: when display makes sense | Kwontified
A0555.desc: Walmart is opening auction-based display to brands of all sizes. Display pays only when it reaches shoppers search would miss, and a holdout test shows it.
A0555.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 9, 2024.
A0555.body:
Walmart said on April 1 that its onsite display advertising is becoming primarily programmatic and auction-based, and that it would be available to brands of all sizes starting in April 2024, according to Walmart. More brands will soon be able to buy display on Walmart, and many will be tempted to try it.

The announcement is about access. It cannot tell any one brand whether display will add sales, and the console’s reported returns cannot either. Display pays only when it reaches shoppers that search would not have reached anyway. It suits launches, products shoppers research before buying, and brands whose search coverage is already near its ceiling. Brands should test display against holdout groups, and judge it on added sales rather than reported sales, before moving budget from search.

What the Walmart Connect display change does

Auction buying is not entirely new at Walmart. It introduced auction bidding for self-serve display campaigns in March 2023, letting advertisers bid on available onsite display inventory, according to Walmart Connect. The latest announcement makes the auction the main way onsite display is sold and widens who can take part.

The business behind it is growing quickly. In the fourth quarter of its fiscal year, US sales at Walmart Connect were up 22%, Walmart reported.

Judged by what it does, the change gives more brands a way into more inventory, with prices set by bidding. What it does not do is change who sees a display ad or why they buy. That question decides whether display earns its budget, and only a test answers it.

Why display’s reported returns run ahead of its real ones

Display reaches shoppers earlier and more broadly than search. Many shoppers who see a display ad would have bought anyway, through search or habit, so reported display returns include sales display did not cause. Display earns its budget only where the sales it adds, multiplied by profit margin, exceed what it costs.

Take a display campaign on Walmart that spends $5,000 and is credited with $20,000 in attributed sales, four times what it cost. Now suppose a holdout test shows that only $6,000 of those sales would not have happened without the ads. The real return is 1.2 times spend. At a 30% profit margin, $6,000 of added sales earns $1,800, well short of the $5,000 the campaign cost.

To break even at that margin, the campaign would need to add about $16,667 in sales. The reported $20,000 looked like a success, and the added $6,000 showed a loss. Display can still work for this brand. The reported number alone simply cannot say whether it did.

Where display reaches shoppers search cannot

A launch is the clearest case. A new product has no search history and few shoppers looking for it by name, so display can introduce it to shoppers browsing related products who would not have found it through search alone.

Products that shoppers research before buying fit as well. Small appliances or furniture involve several visits before a decision, and display can keep a brand in view during that research, when search alone may catch the shopper only at the end.

A search program near its ceiling opens the same door. When a brand already wins most of the searches it can afford, more search spending brings little. Display can reach shoppers beyond those searches, where the next dollar may work harder.

Audience choice decides how much of that potential is real. Display pointed only at past buyers, or at shoppers already looking at the brand’s products, will post flattering returns, since a good share of those people had their purchase in mind before the ad appeared. Display aimed at shoppers of related categories, who have not yet met the brand, is where it can add the most.

Running a display test on Walmart

Every campaign needs a holdout. Comparing shoppers who could have seen the ads with similar shoppers who did not shows what the ads added. Without that comparison, reported returns will flatter the campaign.

A budget cap and a clear goal keep the test honest. A launch campaign might aim at new-to-brand buyers, while a defensive campaign might aim at holding share on a category page, and each needs its own measure.

Auction prices need watching once more brands can bid, because display prices will rise in busy periods. The arrival of non-endemic advertisers, brands that do not sell at Walmart, adds a further competitor for the same placements. Their budgets come from outside retail, and they may bid on audiences rather than products. Bids should follow what each placement returns, and peak prices for low-value impressions are worth declining.

Frequency deserves a limit too. A shopper who sees the same display ad many times in a week is unlikely to respond more on the tenth view than on the third. Capping how often each shopper sees an ad keeps spending on fresh reach, and it reduces the chance that shoppers grow tired of the brand.

Creative carries more weight in display than in search. A search ad answers a shopper’s query, while a display ad has to catch attention from a shopper who was not looking for the product. Clear images, a simple message and a reason to click separate an ad that is seen from one that is skipped.

Brands that already run display on Amazon can learn faster by testing on both retailers at once, then moving budget toward the one whose shoppers respond with added sales.

Hold the new auction to the standard any new ad product should meet. Judge it by the sales it adds in a holdout, multiplied by margin, and move budget from search only when that figure covers the cost. Designing the holdout before the first dollar goes in is how we test Walmart Connect display for brands.

A0557.crumb: Electronics on Amazon: selling into a…
A0557.title: Electronics on Amazon: selling into a maturing category
A0557.alt: Over-ear headphones, a smartphone and a tablet on a wooden desk beside cardboard shipping boxes.
A0557.ttag: Electronics on Amazon: selling into a maturing category | Kwontified
A0557.desc: US tech spending fell 10% in 2023, and growth now depends on replacements. Why electronics on Amazon is won at the upgrade moment, and how brands compete.
A0557.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 11, 2024.
A0557.body:
Most people scrolling Amazon’s results for headphones, a laptop or a television already own one. They are there because something broke, wore out or fell behind what they need, and they read every listing with the old device in mind. That shopper now sits at the center of the electronics business.

Consumer electronics has become a mature, replacement-driven market. Spending fell in 2023, fewer new products are arriving, and older buyers account for more of the spending. Electronics brands on Amazon win by meeting shoppers at the moment they upgrade or replace a device, with clear comparisons, compatibility details and accessories. The launch excitement that drove the category in earlier years can no longer carry it.

What the numbers say about electronics on Amazon

The pandemic pulled years of electronics buying forward. Households bought laptops, monitors, headphones and televisions for working and learning at home, and then demand fell back.

Total US spending on technology products declined 10% in 2023, and just 12% of tech categories grew in both dollars and units, Retail Brew reported, citing Circana data shared at CES. Two other shifts stand out, the first from the same Circana figures and the second reported by etcentric.

Measure20212023
New products as a share of tech items sold17.8%12.6%
Share of tech spending from consumers aged 55 and older31%35%

Younger buyers moved the other way, with the share from 18- to 24-year-olds falling to 6%. Circana expects a modest recovery. It forecast that US consumer technology sales would grow 2% in 2024, as consumers replace devices bought during the pandemic, according to a report.

Why the upgrade moment decides sales

Shopping behavior in a mature category differs from a growing one. In a growing category, many shoppers are buying a type of product for the first time, and excitement about what is new drives demand. In a mature category, most shoppers already own the product, and they buy when something breaks, wears out or falls behind what they need.

That makes the purchase practical. A shopper replacing headphones wants to know how the new pair compares to the old one, whether it works with their phone and whether it is worth the price. A shopper upgrading a laptop wants clear specifications and an honest sense of what will improve.

Older buyers sharpen that pattern. They tend to research carefully, read reviews and value reliability and support, and flashy launch messaging matters less to them than clear answers.

Take two headphone listings. One leads with excitement about a new design. The other explains, in plain terms, how the headphones compare with the previous model, which devices they pair with, how long the battery lasts and what the warranty covers. In a replacement market, the second listing answers the questions shoppers are actually asking.

Selling to the upgrade moment

Comparison is the first thing a replacing shopper looks for. Comparison charts across a brand’s own range, clear model numbers and plain explanations of what changed between generations all help, and A+ content is well suited to that job.

Compatibility is often the deciding question in electronics. Whether a product works with a particular phone, computer or system should be stated clearly, and common questions answered in the listing and in customer questions, which prevents lost sales and returns.

The installed base is a business of its own. A mature category has a large base of existing devices that need cases, cables, chargers, mounts and replacement parts. These purchases recur and often face less competition than the main device.

Bundles push in the same direction. A device sold with the accessories most buyers add later, such as a case or a spare cable, raises the order value and saves shoppers a second search. It also sets a listing apart from similar devices sold alone at a lower price.

Reviews carry particular weight, because shoppers look for evidence that a product works reliably over time. Recurring problems flagged in reviews deserve quick fixes and, where possible, a response.

Price competition is intense in mature categories, where many sellers offer similar products and shoppers compare closely. A brand that cannot be the cheapest needs clear reasons to pay more: better warranties, support, build quality or features that matter to the buyer. Refurbished and renewed products compete in the same searches, since shoppers replacing a device will often consider a cheaper renewed version of a well-known model. Knowing where renewed versions of a brand’s own products appear, and making the case for buying new through warranty, condition and support, beats ignoring them.

Safety and returns need attention too. Electronics with batteries or power adapters face stricter rules and closer scrutiny from shoppers, and returns are costly when products arrive damaged or do not work as expected. Clear setup guidance and honest specifications reduce returns as much as any packaging change.

Advertising follows the same logic. Searches that signal replacement or upgrade, such as a model name followed by a newer generation, show a shopper ready to buy, and they deserve priority over broad category searches, where many shoppers are only browsing. Replacement purchases also cluster around back to school, the holiday season and new product releases from major device makers, so stock and advertising belong around those moments.

The question for an electronics team is whether its listings are written for the shopper who has never owned the product or for the one holding the old version. On Amazon, most of the time, it is the second, and building listings, accessories and ad plans around that shopper is how we run electronics on Amazon for brands.

A0559.crumb: Predicting competitor ad spend on Amazon…
A0559.title: Predicting competitor ad spend on Amazon before it hits you
A0559.alt: Vintage black binoculars on a worn wooden windowsill overlooking a sunlit cobblestone street of old stone shopfronts.
A0559.ttag: Predicting competitor ad spend on Amazon before it hits you | Kwontified
A0559.desc: You cannot see a competitor’s Amazon ad budget, but you can estimate it as a range and see a rise coming. How to build the estimate and what to do with it.
A0559.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 16, 2024.
A0559.body:
A brand’s click prices on its best search can jump in a week when its own budget has not moved at all. The price of a click on Amazon depends less on a brand’s own plans than on what competitors decide to spend, and no brand can see a competitor’s budget.

It can estimate that spend within a useful range, though, from how often the competitor appears on key searches and what those clicks cost. It can also predict when the spend will rise, from signals such as launches, stock levels and sale events. A brand that forecasts competitive pressure as a range, and adjusts its own bids and budgets before the pressure arrives, avoids reacting after costs have already risen.

Why competitor ad spend on Amazon matters more each year

Advertising on Amazon keeps growing. Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 27% to $14.6 billion in the fourth quarter of 2023, GeekWire reported. Every dollar of that growth is spent by brands competing for the same shoppers.

A competitor that raises its budget on a shared search pushes up the price for everyone bidding on it. A brand that sees that coming can plan for it. A brand that does not finds out when its costs jump and its sales slip.

It is tempting to treat those jumps as weather. The auction is sealed, nobody announces a budget increase, and the rise shows up as a line on a report after the money is spent. But a competitor’s spend is built from parts a brand can watch, and those parts usually move before the price does.

Estimating a budget you cannot see

A competitor’s spend on a search equals the clicks it receives times the price of each click. Clicks depend on search volume, how often the competitor’s ad appears and how often shoppers click it. Those inputs can be observed or estimated but never known exactly, so they produce a range rather than a single figure.

Take a search term that gets 50,000 searches a month. Suppose a competitor’s ad holds the top sponsored position on 60% of those searches, shoppers click it 1.5% of the time and each click costs $1.40. That gives about 450 clicks a month and about $630 in spend on that search. If the competitor runs similar campaigns across 40 comparable searches, its monthly spend is roughly $25,200.

The click rate is the least certain input. If it is 1% rather than 1.5%, spend on the search falls to about $420. At 2%, it rises to about $840. Across the 40 searches, that is a range of about $16,800 to $33,600 a month.

A range that wide still earns its keep. It tells a brand whether a competitor is spending a few thousand dollars or tens of thousands, and whether a planned budget can realistically compete. The estimate is only as good as its inputs, and search volumes and click rates vary by category and season. It needs refreshing each quarter and checking against what the brand sees in its own campaigns.

The estimate also has a blind spot. It says roughly how much a rival is spending, not why. A competitor may be buying share it intends to keep, testing a search for a few weeks or clearing stock before a new model arrives, and each calls for a different response. Watching what happens around the spend helps tell those cases apart.

The signals that come before a rise

A launch is the most reliable warning. When a competitor lists a new product, it usually advertises heavily to build sales history, so a new listing on a brand’s key searches is a reason to expect higher click prices there in the following weeks.

Stock tells a quieter story. A competitor that has run low on stock often pulls back advertising, and returns hard when stock is replenished. Watching whether a competitor’s main products are in stock helps predict when it will come back to the auction.

The event calendar is the most predictable signal of all. Competitors raise budgets ahead of and during Prime Day, other Amazon events and holidays, and click prices on shared searches usually rise during those periods. Planning for that beats discovering it on the first morning.

A competitor bidding on a brand’s own name is a signal of a different kind. It is usually trying to capture shoppers who were already looking for that brand, and those shoppers are the most likely to buy, so the name deserves defending.

Turning the forecast into decisions

A short list of searches is enough. Tracking the 20 to 40 that drive most of a brand’s sales, and who appears on them, gives a clear picture of competitive pressure without watching every search.

Position and price should be read together. If a brand’s own ads appear less often while click prices rise, a competitor is likely spending more. Either signal alone can mislead, because prices also rise with seasonal demand.

Budgets for contested searches belong in the plan before an event starts. Deciding in advance how much the brand is willing to pay on each one, and where it will hold back, keeps the auction from making that decision instead.

Some things stay out of reach. A competitor with deeper pockets may outspend a brand on a search for a period, and sometimes the right response is to step back on that search, protect margin and compete where the rival is weaker. When a rival’s estimated spend on a search sits well above what a brand can profitably match, the better move is to shift budget elsewhere before the auction forces it. Building those estimates, and the budget plan around them, is how we plan Amazon ad budgets against the competition.

A0560.title: Mother’s Day 2024 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards
A0560.alt: A kraft-paper gift box tied with a linen ribbon and blank tag beside a vase of pink tulips on a rustic table.
A0560.ttag: Mother’s Day 2024 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards | Kwontified
A0560.desc: Online only tied department stores for Mother’s Day gifts in 2023. What gift shoppers reward on marketplaces, and how sellers can prepare for May 12.
A0560.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 18, 2024.
A0560.body:
A shopper buying a candle for herself checks the price, the scent and the reviews, then clicks buy. The same shopper buying that candle for her mother in early May checks something else first: the delivery date. Then she goes back to the photos and wonders whether it will look like a present when it lands on the doorstep, or like something pulled off a warehouse shelf.

Those second thoughts explain a result that surprises many marketplace sellers. In 2023, online shopping only tied department stores as the place Americans planned to buy Mother’s Day gifts. Gift shoppers weigh care and certain delivery as heavily as price, so sellers win this holiday by making products look like gifts, getting them there on time and putting their effort where gift spending concentrates. Discounting does less of the work than it does on an ordinary sale weekend.

What Mother’s Day on marketplaces is up against

Mother’s Day spending reached a record in 2023. Shoppers planned to spend $35.7 billion, or $274.02 per person, with 84% of US adults expecting to celebrate, Fashion Network reported, citing the National Retail Federation’s annual survey. Shoppers aged 35 to 44 planned to spend the most, an average of $382.26.

The money clusters in a handful of categories. Jewelry led at $7.8 billion, followed by special outings at $5.6 billion and electronics at $4 billion, National Jeweler reported.

The destination figures in that report are the ones a marketplace team should pin above the desk. Online and department stores tied as the top destinations at 34% each, with specialty stores at 30%, local and small businesses at 24% and discount stores at 23%. For a holiday built almost entirely on gifts, the online channel’s lead over the store counter was zero. Mother’s Day falls on May 12 in 2024, so the buying window is already open.

Why a gift shopper decides differently

A gift carries a message, and the shopper is buying the message as much as the object. She wants something that looks chosen with care, arrives in good shape and turns up before the day. A late delivery cannot be fixed with a refund, because by then the gift has already failed.

That changes what decides the sale. For everyday purchases, price and speed lead. For a Mother’s Day gift, presentation and certainty count just as much, and a shopper may pay more, or go to a store, to be sure the present will be right and on time. A store settles both worries by putting the gift in her hands before she leaves. A listing has to settle them with photographs and a delivery promise.

Marketplaces can compete on those terms, though only when sellers make the gift obvious. A product photographed alone on a white background under a technical title does not read as a present. The same product shown wrapped, beside a card, with a clear note that it will arrive before the holiday, does.

Take a candle brand with two listings for the same product. One shows the candle by itself, with a title that lists its size and scent. The other shows it in gift packaging next to a card, with “Mother’s Day gift” in the images and a plain delivery promise. Both sell the same wax and wick. Only the second speaks to what the gift shopper is anxious about.

Working back from May 12

Listing work comes first, because it takes longest to change. Gift-oriented images, gift sets and bundles, and visible options for wrapping or a message help a shopper see the product as a present. Titles and images can name the occasion without crowding out what the product actually is.

Stock comes next. Inventory placed well before the holiday is what lets a product show fast delivery in the final week, when the delivery estimate often decides the click. Sellers should watch those estimates as the date approaches and move advertising toward the products that will still arrive in time.

Advertising follows the search curve. Gift searches rise in the weeks before the holiday and peak in the final days, so budgets should climb with them. Once a product can no longer arrive by May 12, its clicks lead to late orders, and the spend on it should come down instead of running to the end.

The final days need a plan of their own. Shoppers who leave it late look for gifts that can arrive quickly or be sent digitally, so gift cards, digital gifts and products with same-day or next-day delivery catch the buyers that physical items can no longer reach. Walmart and Target shoppers also buy Mother’s Day gifts online, and both retailers offer store pickup, which gives a late shopper a way to collect a gift the same day. Brands selling on those marketplaces should make sure their gift-ready products are stocked and visible there as well.

The holiday also leaves something behind. Gift sets and occasion packaging lose their appeal quickly once the date passes. Ordering them in smaller quantities, and keeping the core product available without holiday packaging, limits the stock that has to be cleared at a discount afterward.

Where gift spending goes, and what it does not reward

Category decides how hard to push. Jewelry, beauty, home and flowers or plants draw much of the holiday’s gifting, and brands in those categories should plan their biggest effort of the spring around it. Brands elsewhere can still present a product as a gift where it honestly fits, without rebuilding their calendar.

Discounts matter less than usual. Gift shoppers care about value, but a steep price cut can make a present look less special, which is the opposite of what the buyer wants to hand over. A modest offer or a free gift set often works better than a deep markdown.

Reviews carry extra weight for a related reason. A shopper buying for someone else cannot judge the product personally, so reviews that mention gifting, packaging and how the recipient reacted reassure her in a way a star rating alone cannot.

So the useful question for a marketplace team in late April is a plain one: would its best listings pass for a present on someone’s doorstep? If the answer is no, the photographs and the delivery plan need attention before the budget does, and getting those ready for gifting occasions on Amazon, Walmart and Target is how we prepare brands for Mother’s Day.

A0561.title: Amazon coupons as a search-ranking investment: when they pay
A0561.alt: Brass scissors, a fan of blank cream cards and a small kraft mailer box on a worn wooden table by a window.
A0561.ttag: Amazon coupons as a search-ranking investment: when they pay | Kwontified
A0561.desc: A coupon on Amazon is worth running for rank only if the organic sales it earns afterward exceed what it cost. How to work out that payback before you spend.
A0561.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 23, 2024.
A0561.body:
While a coupon is running, the dashboard nearly always looks good. More shoppers click the listing, more of them buy, and the sales line climbs for as long as the badge is up. None of that says whether the coupon was worth its cost. That gets settled later, after the badge comes off, by a single question: did the product keep the organic rank the coupon helped it reach?

A coupon pays as a ranking investment only when the extra organic sales it leaves behind, multiplied by margin, exceed what it cost in discounts and redemption fees. That makes a coupon a time-limited investment with a payback to measure. It belongs on products where rank is close to moving, and it should stop where the ranking gain fades.

How Amazon coupons are supposed to buy search rank

Coupons on Amazon appear as a badge in search results and on product pages, and shoppers clip them to receive the discount at checkout. In the United States, the standard fee is $0.60 per redemption, charged on top of the discount itself, according to a coupon guide from eComEngine.

Many brands run coupons for a reason beyond the immediate sale, and the reasoning is sound as far as it goes. The badge raises click-through in search, and the lower effective price raises conversion. Together they push up sales velocity, and a product that sells faster tends to rank higher in organic search. A coupon that lifts sales for a few weeks can move a product up the results, where it keeps selling after the coupon ends.

What that chain leaves out is duration. The discount is paid in full while the coupon runs. The ranking benefit is paid back slowly, one organic sale at a time, and only for as long as the new position holds.

The payback arithmetic on one coupon

Take a $30 product carrying a 15% coupon. Each redemption costs $4.50 in discount plus the $0.60 fee, or $5.10. Say the coupon runs for four weeks and is redeemed 600 times. Its total cost is $3,060. At a 30% margin, each organic sale afterward earns $9 a unit.

Now follow the product for the 60 days after the coupon ends, under two outcomes.

After the coupon endsExtra organic sales a dayExtra sales over 60 daysMargin earned
Rank gain holds10600$5,400
Rank gain fades3180$1,620

When the higher rank holds, the coupon earns back comfortably more than the $3,060 it cost. When the gain fades, it recovers about half. Break-even in this example sits at about 5.7 extra organic sales a day over the same period.

Both rows begin with an identical coupon, discount and fee. The only thing that changes the verdict is how long the rank gain survives without the badge, which is why the decision belongs before launch and the measurement belongs after.

Where a coupon can actually move rank

Position in the results matters most, because a product ranked just below the first page, or just below the top positions, may need only a modest lift in velocity to climb. A product far down the results may need more velocity than any coupon can buy.

Conversion once a shopper lands on the listing matters next. A coupon helps most when shoppers who find the product tend to buy it. If conversion is weak because of the listing or its reviews, the coupon pays for clicks, and the product slips back once the discount is gone.

The category sets the ceiling. Where every competitor runs a coupon, one more badge stands out less and the ranking effect shrinks. Where coupons are rare, the badge draws the eye.

Price level belongs in the same check. The $0.60 fee is fixed per redemption, so on an inexpensive item it can take a large share of the margin. Coupons work best as ranking investments on products priced high enough for the fee to matter less.

Measuring what the coupon returned

A payback cannot be measured without a baseline. Rank and organic sales need recording before, during and after the coupon, or there is no way to tell whether a gain came from the coupon or from the season.

The return should count only added sales. Some shoppers who clip a coupon would have bought anyway, and their redemptions cost the discount without adding a sale, which lowers the coupon’s real return below what the redemption count suggests.

Advertising should move with the coupon. Because a coupon raises conversion, the same clicks become more valuable while it runs, so bids can rise modestly for the coupon period and return to normal when it ends, instead of sitting unchanged throughout.

Reviews are a quieter return. More sales during a coupon usually bring more reviews afterward, and a product with more recent reviews tends to convert better. That effect is harder to measure than rank, but it belongs in the calculation for a product short of reviews.

Repetition carries its own cost. A product that always carries a coupon trains shoppers to expect one, and the badge stops signaling a deal. Coupons work better in bursts with a stated goal than left on indefinitely.

The test to apply before launch is simple to write down: the break-even daily gain in organic sales, worked out from the discount, the fee and the margin, which was 5.7 a day in the example above. If organic sales fall back to where they were within a few weeks of the coupon ending, the coupon missed that number, and repeating it on the same product spends margin for nothing. Setting that bar before the badge goes up, and checking it 60 days after it comes down, is how we measure what coupons return for brands on Amazon.

A0564.crumb: Seller reputation is the critical asset…
A0564.title: Seller reputation is the critical asset on Mercado Libre
A0564.alt: Five brass stars on a weathered wooden beam above a textile stall on a colorful cobblestone market street.
A0564.ttag: Seller reputation is the critical asset on Mercado Libre | Kwontified
A0564.desc: On Mercado Libre, every shopper sees a seller’s reputation as a color, and it shapes visibility. Why it matters so much, and how brands protect it as they grow.
A0564.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 25, 2024.
A0564.body:
Two listings for the same pair of running shoes sit next to each other on Mercado Libre. The price is close, the photos come from the same brand kit, and the delivery estimates match. Under one seller’s name the reputation thermometer shows green. Under the other’s it shows orange. A shopper who has never bought from either does not need to read further to decide.

That small colored bar carries a great deal of weight on Mercado Libre. It is built from claims, cancellations and late shipments, every shopper sees it, and it shapes how visible a seller is. In a fast-growing market where many buyers are still learning to trust online sellers, reputation is the most valuable asset a brand has there, and it should be protected through reliable stock and fulfillment before the brand spends heavily on growth.

How Mercado Libre seller reputation is measured

Mercado Libre’s developer documentation describes each seller’s reputation as a thermometer level shown by color, together with a MercadoLíder status for top sellers, according to Mercado Libre. The documentation lists three measures behind the color: claims from buyers, cancellations by the seller and late shipments.

The thresholds are tight. On claims, a seller stays at light green or above with a claims rate of 2% or less, falls to yellow above 2%, to orange above 4% and to red above 7%. Because the color reflects recent performance over a rolling period, a bad stretch can mark a seller for months, even after the cause is fixed.

Why trust carries so much weight on this marketplace

Mercado Libre is growing quickly. Gross merchandise volume for the fourth quarter of 2023 reached $13.5 billion, up 39.9% on a 29% rise in items sold, and its unique active buyers reached almost 85 million for the year, the company reported. Its fulfillment network shipped 650 million items in 2023, 45% more than the year before, according to its shareholder letter.

Growth on that scale brings in shoppers who are new to buying online. In many Latin American markets, ecommerce is younger than in the United States, and many shoppers worry about whether a seller will deliver what was promised. A clear, visible signal of reliability answers that worry directly, which is why many shoppers will pay a little more to buy from the green seller in the opening example.

The color also decides who gets seen in the first place. Sellers with stronger reputations are favored in Mercado Libre’s results and qualify for MercadoLíder status, which adds a badge of its own. A weaker reputation therefore costs a seller twice: fewer shoppers see the listing, and fewer of those who do are willing to trust it.

The marketplace owns the signal

The value in this arrangement sits with Mercado Libre. The seller earns the reputation through its own stock, shipping and service, but the marketplace sets the thresholds, measures the results and decides how the color affects visibility. A brand cannot take its green thermometer to another site, and it cannot carry it across borders either. Mercado Libre operates separately in each country, so a strong reputation in Mexico does not follow a brand into Brazil, and each new market starts the count again.

Payments tighten the same loop. Many purchases are paid through Mercado Pago, the company’s own payment service, which holds buyer protection in the same system that records claims. A buyer who opens a claim is using a protection the platform built to make online shopping feel safe, and every claim counts against the seller. Avoiding the causes of claims is worth more than winning disputes after they arise.

For a brand, the practical meaning is that the most valuable thing it builds on Mercado Libre is an asset it does not control and cannot move. That argues for guarding it carefully from the first order.

Protecting the color before buying growth

Take a brand that enters Mercado Libre with a strong product but thin stock. A busy week sells through its inventory, and it cancels a handful of orders it cannot fill. Claims and cancellations rise together, the color slips, and its listings lose visibility just as demand was building.

Accurate stock would have prevented that story. Cancellations caused by selling items that are out of stock are among the easiest reputation problems to avoid, and brands should sync inventory carefully across channels and keep a buffer on Mercado Libre.

Fulfillment carries the late-shipment measure. Mercado Libre’s own fulfillment network gives sellers faster, more predictable delivery than many can manage alone, and it reduces the risk of a shipment arriving late.

Service decides whether a problem becomes a claim. A fast and fair response to a buyer’s issue can keep a claim from being opened at all, so customer service for Mercado Libre needs staffing in the local language, with replies inside hours rather than days.

Listings do their part as well. Clear titles, accurate specifications and good photos reduce the claims that arise when a product does not match what the buyer expected.

Advertising comes last in this sequence. Mercado Libre has a growing advertising business, and brands can buy ads to bring shoppers to their listings, but those ads send people to the same listing that shows the seller’s color. A brand with a yellow or orange thermometer pays for clicks from shoppers who may hesitate at the final step, and a brand that advertises heavily before its fulfillment is reliable risks taking more orders than it can serve well.

The order of spending is the real decision for a leadership team entering the region: reputation in each country first, then the media budget that rides on it. Building that foundation market by market is how we help brands grow on Mercado Libre.
