A0566.title: Planning TikTok Shop under a divest-or-ban law
A0566.alt: A smartphone in a ring light stand beside an open cardboard box of books and a kraft envelope against a teal wall.
A0566.ttag: Planning TikTok Shop under a divest-or-ban law | Kwontified
A0566.desc: TikTok Shop now has a legal deadline and no known ending. Brands can keep selling there while building creators, content and demand that outlast the app.
A0566.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 2, 2024.
A0566.body:
A shopper scrolling TikTok stops on a creator’s video about a product she has never looked for, taps through and buys it without leaving the app. Nobody searched for anything. For a growing number of brands that kind of purchase has become a real sales line, and it now sits on a channel with a legal deadline but no known ending.

The question for a leadership team is how much to build on a channel that may be sold, banned or tied up in court. The answer is to keep selling there while it pays and to hold new TikTok-only commitments to what pays back inside the window. Everything else should go into assets that outlast any outcome: creator relationships, reusable content and demand on other channels.

TikTok Shop grew fast enough to matter

TikTok Shop opened to American shoppers in September 2023, and it grew quickly. More than 500,000 merchants were selling to US shoppers by the end of 2023, more than double the number three months earlier, and the platform had more than 15 million sellers worldwide, Retail Brew reported, citing TikTok’s first Shop safety report. As of January, TikTok Shop had a US sales run rate of $3 billion, according to the same report.

Then the rules changed. President Biden signed a law on April 24 requiring ByteDance to sell TikTok or face a US ban, with a possible 90-day extension, and TikTok said it would challenge the law in court, SiliconANGLE reported. The law starts a 270-day clock, according to Techmeme’s roundup of the coverage, which points to a deadline in January 2025.

What a ban would actually take away

Shopping on TikTok works differently from shopping on a marketplace. Many TikTok shoppers are not looking for a product at all. They come across it in a video from a creator they follow, often on impulse, and that moment of discovery is what TikTok really offers a brand. It is also the hardest part to replace.

The difference is easier to see in store terms. A brand that loses Amazon traffic is like a brand that lost a good aisle position: shoppers still come in for the category, and better listings or advertising can win them back. A brand that loses TikTok loses something closer to the display by the entrance, the one that stopped people who came in for something else. Those shoppers may still want the product, but they will need another way to find it.

So the risk reaches past TikTok Shop’s own sales line. Discovery on TikTok feeds demand on every other channel, and losing it would show up later as softer searches on Amazon, Walmart and a brand’s own site.

One plan for three endings

Brands have to plan for three outcomes. If TikTok is sold, TikTok Shop may continue under new owners, possibly with new rules. If it is banned, the channel disappears and brands need their audiences somewhere else. If the legal fight runs long, the uncertainty may last well into 2025, and brands will have to keep operating without knowing how it ends.

A plan that holds up in all three is safer than one that bets on a single result, and it starts with matching spending to the window. Spending that pays back quickly, such as creator commissions and short promotions, still makes sense. Commitments tied only to TikTok, such as large inventory set aside for TikTok Shop fulfillment or multi-year creator contracts, carry more risk than they did before the law.

The rest of the effort belongs in what travels. Creator relationships can move to other platforms, and video made for TikTok can run again on Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. Awareness built on TikTok also shows up as searches elsewhere: products that go viral there often see searches rise on Amazon, Walmart and brand sites. Listings on those sites should be strong and well stocked, so the demand TikTok creates is not picked up by a competitor.

Creators deserve particular attention, because many of them are planning for life after TikTok as well. A brand that works with a creator across several platforms keeps that partnership whatever happens to the app. Other retailers stand to gain if TikTok’s reach shrinks, and Amazon, Walmart and other platforms have been building their own video and creator tools. A brand with strong listings and creator content on those platforms will be ready if shoppers and creators move there, instead of building a presence from nothing.

Who owns the customer when the sale happens inside the app

Sales made through TikTok Shop happen inside TikTok’s systems, and brands typically have less direct access to those customers than they do on their own sites. That gap existed before the law, but the law makes it expensive. Packaging inserts and post-purchase messages, where the platform allows them, can invite TikTok buyers onto an email list or to follow the brand elsewhere, so the relationship does not depend on the app alone.

Measurement tells a team how urgent all of this is. A brand should know how much of its total sales, and how many of its new customers, come through TikTok. One that finds TikTok drives a small share can keep investing calmly. One that finds it drives most of its growth should diversify faster.

The holiday season will test the plan

Brands planning for late 2024 should treat TikTok as a strong channel for that season, while preparing alternatives that can carry the load if the outcome in early 2025 goes against the app. The plan also deserves a fresh look each quarter as the court case and any sale talks develop, with the reliance on TikTok adjusted as the picture becomes clearer.

The question to put to the team is a plain one: if TikTok Shop went dark after the holidays, which of our creators, our videos and our customers would we still have? A good answer takes time to build, and a contingency plan that spans social commerce and the marketplaces is how we help brands keep selling through the uncertainty.

A0568.crumb: Amazon’s Q1 2024 results: what ad growth…
A0568.title: Amazon’s Q1 2024 results: what ad growth says about clicks
A0568.alt: A wooden gavel and a stack of coins on a table beside rows of small upright cardboard boxes.
A0568.ttag: Amazon’s Q1 2024 results: what ad growth says about clicks | Kwontified
A0568.desc: Amazon ad revenue grew 24% in Q1 2024 against 13% for the whole company. For brands, that gap means a pricier auction and a higher cost for each sale.
A0568.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 7, 2024.
A0568.body:
Amazon’s advertising business grew almost twice as fast as Amazon in the first quarter of 2024. Ad revenue rose 24%, while total revenue rose 13% excluding currency effects. On an earnings slide that is a growth story. For a brand that buys clicks, it is a price signal.

When ad spending grows faster than the shopping it competes for, more advertiser money chases each sale, and the auction turns that gap into a higher cost per sale. Brands should expect click prices to keep rising faster than their sales. The way to protect efficiency is to raise what each click is worth and to concentrate spend where they can win, instead of raising budgets to hold position on every search.

What Amazon’s Q1 2024 results showed

LineQ1 2024 revenueGrowth
Advertising services$11.8 billion (from $9.5 billion)24%
Third-party seller services$34.5 billion16%
Total revenue$143.3 billion13% excluding currency effects

Amazon reported first-quarter revenue of $143.3 billion, and its advertising services revenue rose 24% to $11.8 billion from $9.5 billion a year earlier, the Motley Fool reported. Third-party seller services, which include commissions and fulfillment fees, grew 16% to $34.5 billion, according to CNBC’s report of the results.

On the earnings call, Amazon said overall revenue was up 13% excluding currency effects. It described shoppers as still buying but cautious, trading down on price when they can and seeking out deals, according to the call transcript, and it noted its first Big Spring Sale in the quarter.

Nobody raises the price of a click on purpose

No one at Amazon sets the price of a sponsored click, and no advertiser sets out to pay more for one. Each brand bids what a click seems worth to it, and when rivals bid a little higher, it raises its own bid a little to keep its place. Every one of those decisions is reasonable. Added together, with more advertiser dollars arriving each quarter than new shopping, they produce a rising price that none of the bidders chose.

Cautious shoppers push from the other side. When shoppers compare prices and wait for deals, they convert less readily, so each click is worth less to the brand paying for it. The cost of each advertised sale rises from both directions at once.

Amazon’s ad revenue is not a direct measure of click prices. It includes Prime Video ads and other formats, and Amazon’s mix of advertisers changes over time. Still, the gap between ad growth and revenue growth is wide enough to show the direction.

The arithmetic behind that direction fits in a few lines. If advertising grows 24% while overall revenue grows 13%, advertising is growing about 10% faster than the business it sits on. Take a brand whose click prices rose in line with that gap. If it spends $10,000 a month to hold its share of clicks, it would need about $10,970 for the same share.

Now put the cautious shopper back into the same example. If its shoppers convert slightly less often while they shop around, the brand gets fewer sales from those same clicks. Its cost per sale rises faster than its click prices, and its return on ad spend falls even though nothing in its campaigns changed.

Raise the value of a click instead of buying position everywhere

A brand that converts more of its clicks into sales can afford to pay more for each one, which makes conversion the first defense in a crowded auction. Better images, clearer listings, stronger reviews and competitive prices all lift it, and in a cautious market clear value per unit carries extra weight. Amazon said shoppers are seeking deals, so coupons, multipacks or event pricing may convert better for now. Each deal still has to be measured against its cost rather than run on every product.

Concentration is the second defense. A brand that tries to hold position on every search pays the rising price everywhere. One that focuses on the searches where it converts best, and steps back from contested generic searches where it rarely wins, spends less for more of its sales. Sponsored Brands and video placements reach shoppers earlier and can be priced differently from product ads on the most contested searches, so part of the budget may work harder there.

Other retailers belong in the same comparison. Walmart and Target are building their own ad businesses, and in some categories their auctions are less crowded than Amazon’s. A modest test budget elsewhere shows whether the same shoppers can be reached for less. Prime Video ads add a new form of competition as well: Amazon is now selling streaming TV ads that it can tie to product sales, and large brands with video budgets may move some spending there. That could ease search competition or tighten it, and it is worth watching as that market grows.

Read profit, not reported return

Rising click prices can hide behind reported returns that still look acceptable. What matters is what advertising adds after margin, and how many of the reported sales would have happened anyway. Planning should assume the trend continues: click prices that rose faster than sales in the first quarter are likely to keep rising, especially around Prime Day and the holiday season, so budgets for those periods need the higher costs built in.

When a platform’s ad revenue grows faster than its sales, budget for a higher cost per sale before the next event, and pay for it by lifting conversion rather than by bidding up every search. Finding the searches where a brand’s clicks still convert well enough to pay is how we run Amazon advertising as the auction gets more crowded.

A0570.crumb: What Amazon’s private label retreat means…
A0570.title: What Amazon’s private label retreat means for brands
A0570.alt: Plain white boxes beside colorful patterned jars, tins and boxes on a sunlit wooden shop shelf.
A0570.ttag: What Amazon’s private label retreat means for brands | Kwontified
A0570.desc: Amazon cut most of its house brands, yet they were never a large share of its sales. The space they leave goes mostly to independent sellers, not to brands.
A0570.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 9, 2024.
A0570.body:
For a few years Amazon looked like it was building a department store’s worth of its own labels, and the size of the effort made those labels easy to read as a threat to every brand on the site. As of 2020, its private label business had 243,000 products across 45 house brands, Retail TouchPoints reported, citing The Wall Street Journal. Then Amazon pulled back. It began scaling back in July 2022 after disappointing sales and scrutiny from lawmakers, and in 2023 it eliminated 27 of its 30 clothing brands and two furniture brands, leaving fewer than 20 house brands, according to the same report.

Amazon Basics and Amazon Essentials remained. Brands that sold next to the labels that went might read the cuts as a windfall, and they should not. Amazon’s house brands were a small business that shoppers mostly passed over, so their retreat frees little demand, and the space goes mostly to independent sellers. The brands that gain will be the ones that compete with that field of sellers, while still expecting Amazon Basics in commodity categories.

Amazon private label was always a small business

The scale was modest from the start. Total sales by Amazon’s private label brands in 2022 were estimated at under $1 billion, excluding Echo devices and Whole Foods grocery brands, compared with about $220 billion in total, Modern Retail reported, citing Marketplace Pulse.

Read Amazon as an institution and the retreat looks less like a change of heart than a correction. Shoppers did not seek out most of its house brands, particularly in fashion and furniture. They bought on price, reviews and convenience, and in many categories they found plenty of alternatives from independent sellers. Amazon’s own statement on the cuts said as much: customers seek out its biggest brands, such as Amazon Basics and Amazon Essentials.

As a signal of what Amazon wants, the cuts point back to the marketplace: the company kept the labels shoppers chose and left the rest of the assortment to independent sellers. The labels that disappeared were, in many cases, the ones shoppers were already passing over. The people who bought them were mostly looking for a good product at a fair price, and plenty of other sellers already offered that.

Why the fashion labels never found their customer

Clothing depends on style, fit and a sense of who the brand is for. In a department store a house label gets a fixture, a sign and a sales associate who can explain what it stands for. On a search results page it is one tile among many, the same size as the seller’s listing next to it. Amazon’s labels offered low prices, but few shoppers knew what most of them stood for, and many never noticed them among pages of similar listings.

That is where established brands hold a real advantage. A brand with a clear identity, consistent quality and a history of good reviews has something a house brand, however well placed, found hard to build. In categories crowded with similar products from many sellers, shoppers lean on reviews and product information to tell the options apart, and brands that invest in both stand out.

Who takes the space Amazon left

The space goes to whoever competes best for those shoppers. In most categories that means a large field of independent sellers, many with low prices and fast-moving product lines. Established brands gain a little shelf space, and so does everyone else.

Take an apparel brand that expected Amazon’s clothing cuts to lift its sales. A few months later its key searches are no less crowded than before. The competitors have simply changed, and the newcomers are independent sellers offering similar styles at lower prices. The house brands are gone, but the competition is not.

The practical response is to watch who fills the gap. A brand in a category Amazon exited should track which sellers are growing on its key searches and adjust pricing and advertising to compete with them rather than with Amazon. More competitors usually means more bidders, so click prices on those searches deserve a close eye as new sellers move in, and the budget belongs on the searches where the brand’s name gives it an edge.

Commodity categories are the exception. Amazon kept Amazon Basics, which sells items such as batteries, cables and household staples, where shoppers value a trusted low-price option. Brands there still compete with Amazon directly, against a competitor with deep knowledge of the category and strong placement, and they need to give shoppers a clear reason to choose a branded product.

The retreat is Amazon’s, not the industry’s

Other retailers are moving the other way. Walmart and Target continue to invest in their own private labels, which play a large role in their stores and on their websites. A brand selling there should not read Amazon’s retreat as a general trend, because on Walmart and Target house brands remain a real competitor to plan for.

Amazon’s own rules may keep moving too. The retreat came amid regulatory scrutiny, and the company has continued to face questions about how it treats sellers. The rules governing Amazon’s own products and placements shape how competition works on the platform, so changes there deserve the same attention as a new competitor.

When the team reviews a category Amazon has left, the useful question is who took the shelf and whether the listing gives a shopper a reason to pick the brand over that seller. Keeping track of who a brand really competes with as Amazon’s categories change is how we help brands hold their place on Amazon.

A0571.crumb: Why many top brands under-invest in…
A0571.title: Why many top brands under-invest in Amazon ads
A0571.alt: A navy and gold shopfront window displaying a single ceramic vase on a stone plinth on a quiet city street.
A0571.ttag: Why many top brands under-invest in Amazon ads | Kwontified
A0571.desc: Strong brands often under-fund Amazon category search because their reports never show the new customers a competitor wins. How to see that cost and fund it.
A0571.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 14, 2024.
A0571.body:
A well-known brand opens its Amazon advertising report and finds a healthy return on a modest budget. Nothing in the report suggests a problem. The report is accurate about what it measures and silent about what it misses: the shoppers who searched the category, saw a competitor’s ad first and never met the brand at all.

That silence is why many strong brands under-invest in Amazon ads. Category advertising should be split from branded advertising, judged on the new customers it wins and what they are worth over time, and paid for as customer acquisition rather than as a cost of this month’s sales.

Why Amazon ads get funded like a sales cost

Brands have long spent less on Amazon than their confidence in it would suggest. In a survey reported by Modern Retail, only 7% of brands said they spent a large or very large portion of their marketing budget on Amazon and other retail sites such as Walmart, Target and eBay.

The auction did not wait for them. Advertising on Amazon kept growing, with revenue up 24% to $11.8 billion in the first quarter of 2024, the Motley Fool reported. Competitors are spending more, and the searches a brand leaves uncontested are increasingly won by someone else.

The habits that keep strong brands under-funded each start from something true. Branded search ads often add little, because shoppers searching for a brand by name would usually find it anyway, and teams that learn this lesson are right to keep branded spend lean. The trouble comes when the same lesson is stretched to category search, where the shopper has not chosen a brand yet and the ad can change who wins the sale.

Where the money sits does the rest. When Amazon advertising is funded from a sales or trade budget, it is judged against short-term sales, and spending to win new customers who pay back over months looks expensive by that yardstick. Brand confidence adds a final push. Well-known brands assume shoppers will find them, and many shoppers do, but many others search for a kind of product, compare what appears and choose from that page.

The customers a report cannot show

An advertising report records what the ads cost and the sales they are credited with. It has no line for the customers a brand never reached. A brand that spends little on category searches therefore sees respectable returns, while competitors win the new shoppers who search by category rather than by brand. That loss compounds, because each of those customers would have bought again.

Take a category search that gets 1 million searches a month. Say shoppers click 2% of the ads they see, and 10% of those clicks become purchases. The only difference between the two brands below is how often their ads appear.

Strong brandCompetitor
Share of searches showing its ad20%60%
New customers each monthabout 400about 1,200

The strong brand’s report shows a decent return on its spend. It does not show the 800 extra customers the competitor won. If each new customer is worth $90 over the following year through repeat purchases, those 800 customers are worth about $72,000 a month in future value to the competitor, and the strong brand never sees that number anywhere in its advertising report.

Fund category search as customer acquisition

The first change is structural: separate branded and category campaigns. Branded ads can be kept lean and tested for what they add. Category ads should be measured on new-to-brand customers, not only on their immediate return.

Lifetime value turns that measurement into a budget. A brand that knows what a new customer is worth over a year can decide how much it can afford to pay to win one, and that number is usually higher than the short-term return suggests, especially for products people buy repeatedly. The right level differs by brand. One with strong repeat purchase can pay more for a new customer than one whose customers buy once.

The decision also belongs in a different budget. Category advertising that wins new customers fits a marketing or growth budget, judged on acquisition, better than a trade budget judged on the current month’s sales.

Measurement needs care. Not every new-to-brand sale is truly new, and some would have happened anyway. Holdout tests and comparisons across similar periods help separate the customers advertising actually won from those who would have arrived regardless. The same tests say what would change the plan: if a holdout shows category ads mostly reach shoppers who would have bought the brand anyway, the case for more spend weakens, and if new-to-brand customers keep coming back, it gets stronger.

Share of category searches is worth tracking alongside those tests. A slow decline in how often a brand appears on the searches that matter is an early warning that competitors are taking new customers, long before it shows up in total sales.

Creative and content carry part of the load. A shopper who has not chosen a brand compares whatever appears on the page, and strong images, clear benefits and good reviews raise the chance that a category click becomes a first purchase, which lowers the cost of each new customer.

A practical check for the next budget meeting: if a brand appears on only a minority of the category searches where new customers start, a healthy return in its report is measuring a small budget. The customers it is missing are showing up in someone else’s numbers. Putting a value on those searches is how we help brands size their Amazon ad investment.

A0572.title: Amazon’s two-speed economy: why the middle is squeezed
A0572.alt: A ribboned gift box, a creased shipping box and a crushed carton lined up in an old wooden vise on a workbench.
A0572.ttag: Amazon’s two-speed economy: why the middle is squeezed | Kwontified
A0572.desc: Shoppers are splitting into bargain hunters and convenience buyers, and on Amazon both meet on one page. Mid-priced brands with no clear lane lose both.
A0572.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 16, 2024.
A0572.body:
Take a search for kitchen knife sets on Amazon. One brand sells a larger set at a lower price per knife, and its listing talks about savings. Another sells better materials with a warranty and polished images. A third sits between them on price, with a listing that could describe either. In 2024 that third brand has the hardest job on the page.

Shoppers are splitting into two speeds. Budget-pressed households are trading down for the lowest prices, while higher-income households spend on convenience and quality, and both groups shop the same Amazon search pages. Mid-priced brands without a clear reason to be chosen get squeezed from both sides. The way out is to pick a lane for each product, clear value or clear premium, and make that position obvious in price, pack size and listing.

How Amazon’s two-speed economy took shape

The split shows up in what retailers told investors. Amazon’s first-quarter call painted its customers as cautious: they kept buying, but they traded down on price where possible and went looking for deals, as the call transcript shows.

Walmart described the other side. In its fourth-quarter results, it reported share gains in grocery and general merchandise primarily among higher-income households, while its general merchandise sales declined modestly, according to Walmart. Its chief financial officer said two-thirds of the quarter’s general merchandise share gain came through households earning more than $100,000 and through digital channels, Business Insider reported.

Read side by side, the two reports describe one economy from opposite ends. Amazon is talking about shoppers who stretch every dollar. Walmart is talking about shoppers who are still spending but choosing where and how, often paying for convenience and speed. A brand that sells on both retailers is selling to both groups at once.

Why the middle of the page gets squeezed

A budget-pressed shopper searching on Amazon sorts by price, looks for multipacks and deals, and often picks the cheapest acceptable option. A higher-income shopper on the same page looks for quality, reviews, fast delivery and a brand they trust, and will pay more for them. A mid-priced product with no clear identity serves neither well. It is too expensive for the first shopper and not distinctive enough for the second. In a growing economy that middle ground can still sell, but in a split economy it loses shoppers at both ends.

Amazon sharpens the effect because both groups see the same results. In a store, a mid-priced product can lean on the shelf around it, with the value line below it and the premium line above it explaining where it sits. On a results page, a low-cost seller and a premium brand appear side by side, the shopper chooses quickly, and products that do not signal which group they are for get passed over.

Pressure at the value end is rising too. Platforms such as Temu, and low-cost sellers on Amazon itself, give budget shoppers more options at very low prices. A value brand cannot always match them on price, so it has to win on reliability, delivery speed and reviews, the things budget shoppers still care about when a purchase must work.

Picking a lane, product by product

The first decision is which shopper each product is for. Some brands will serve both groups well with clearly different products, a value line and a premium line, each positioned on its own terms. Others will choose one lane for the whole range. What does not work is a range where nobody can say which shopper a product was made for.

Value products need the saving to be visible. Multipacks, larger sizes and a clear cost per unit help budget-pressed shoppers see it. Coupons and event deals can help, as long as they are measured against their cost. Premium products need the quality to be visible instead: strong images, detailed descriptions, warranties, reviews that mention durability and a clear brand story justify a higher price to shoppers willing to pay it.

Amazon itself serves both lanes. Its deal events and low-price options speak to budget shoppers, while Prime’s fast delivery speaks to shoppers who value convenience. Brands can use the same split, with event deals and coupons for value products and fast delivery and strong content for premium ones. The mistake is using one approach for every product in the range.

Advertising should follow the same choice. Value products should bid on searches where shoppers compare prices, such as category terms with words like “pack” or “bulk.” Premium products should bid where shoppers look for quality, such as searches that include materials, features or brand names. Delivery speed matters to both groups in different ways. Higher-income shoppers will pay for fast delivery, while budget shoppers may wait longer for a lower price, so premium products should be stocked for the fastest delivery options.

The price-tier review that shows where shoppers are moving

It is too early to say how long the split lasts. If the economy strengthens, the middle may recover. If pressure on lower-income households grows, value products may need to become sharper still. A quarterly review of sales by price tier shows which way shoppers are moving, and gives a brand time to adjust pack sizes, prices and advertising before the shift shows up in total sales.

The question for the next range review is whether the team can say, for each product, which of the two shoppers it is for. The products nobody can place are the ones a split market finds first, and positioning a range for both kinds of Amazon shopper is how we help brands choose their lane.

A0574.crumb: When more advertising earned less: the…
A0574.title: When more advertising earned less: the pet event paradox
A0574.alt: An empty linen pet bed and an overflowing bowl of dry kibble on a sunlit wooden floor against a mint wall.
A0574.ttag: When more advertising earned less: the pet event paradox | Kwontified
A0574.desc: Amazon’s Pet Day pulls forward pet food and litter that shoppers would have bought weeks later. Why doubling event ad spend can earn less, and how to budget it.
A0574.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 21, 2024.
A0574.body:
The advertising report from a deal event is usually one of the best-looking pages a pet brand sees all quarter. Traffic is up, attributed sales are up and the returns look strong, so the case for spending more next time seems to make itself. For pet food and litter, that report overstates what the ads added, because much of what shoppers bought during the event was food, litter and supplies they would have bought within weeks anyway.

Doubling advertising for an event like Amazon’s Pet Day often buys sales pulled forward from later rather than new sales, and it buys them at peak click prices. Pet brands should judge event budgets on the sales they add across the event and the weeks after, not on the sales attributed during it, and put the extra money on the products and shoppers the event really adds.

How Amazon’s Pet Day became a pet event test for advertising

Amazon ran Pet Day on May 7 and 8, a 48-hour event open to all customers rather than only Prime members, with early deals starting April 23, Supermarket News reported. Deals covered brands including Purina, Merrick and Blue Buffalo, the report said.

Events like this pull budgets toward them. Traffic rises, competitors bid aggressively and attributed sales jump. The event-day numbers are vivid and recent, and they sit on top of the pile when the next budget is set.

That is a very human way to read a report: the latest and most dramatic figure gets the most weight, while the quieter weeks after the event, where the cost appears, are easy to leave out of the same review. Nobody is being careless. The report simply puts the gain on one page and the cost on another.

Why the extra spend borrows from next month

During a deal event, replenishment shoppers stock up early on products they would have bought soon anyway, so part of the event’s extra volume is borrowed from the following weeks. Click prices rise at the same time, because many advertisers are bidding at once. Extra spend during the event can therefore produce sales that look strong in the moment and add little once the dip afterward is counted.

Take a pet food brand that normally spends $2,000 a day on advertising and earns $10,000 a day in attributed sales. For the two days of the event, it doubles spend to $4,000 a day, and attributed sales rise to $16,000 a day.

Across the event, that is $4,000 of extra spend and $12,000 of extra sales. At a 30% margin those sales earn $3,600, which is already less than the extra spend.

Then come the weeks after. Many of those buyers stocked up on food they would have bought in the next few weeks, and say the brand’s sales over that stretch fall by $8,000 as a result. The truly added sales are only $4,000, earning $1,200 at the same margin, against $4,000 of extra spend. The brand loses $2,800 on the extra advertising, despite an event that looked strong in every report produced while it ran.

The more a category runs on replenishment, the more an event borrows from the future, and the less the extra advertising adds.

What the event report can and cannot tell you

The most useful number is the one after the event. Comparing sales in the following weeks with a normal baseline shows how much of the event’s volume was pulled forward, and a sharp drop after a big event is the clearest sign that it was.

Amazon’s own reporting helps with the other half. Its advertising reports show how many event buyers were new to the brand, a useful first signal of what the event added. A high share of new-to-brand buyers suggests real growth. A low share suggests the event mostly served existing customers who would have bought anyway, and that extra spend should be trimmed next time.

Subscriptions need a separate look. Shoppers on Subscribe & Save may adjust deliveries around an event, shifting purchases rather than adding them, so brands should check whether subscription volume dips afterward and whether some subscribers skip a delivery after stocking up.

Where pet event money belongs

The split that matters is between replenishment and discovery. Food, litter and treats bought by existing customers are mostly pulled forward. Toys, beds, accessories and new products bought by new customers are more likely to be genuinely added, and that second group is where extra event spend belongs. Shoppers who are new to a brand, buy during the event and then keep buying add real value, which makes new-to-brand customers a better measure of an event than total event sales.

Discounts follow the same logic. A deal on food that loyal customers would have bought at full price gives away margin on sales that were coming anyway, so deep discounts on core replenishment products deserve limits, with deals used mainly on items that attract new buyers.

The pattern carries over to Prime Day, which Amazon has held in July in recent years. Prime Day covers far more categories, but replenishment products behave the same way there. A brand that learns from Pet Day what share of its event volume is pulled forward can set its Prime Day budget by product instead of doubling spend everywhere.

None of this argues for skipping Pet Day. Events bring in shoppers, and some of them become loyal customers. The test before doubling any event budget is to measure sales across the event and the weeks after, against a normal baseline, and spend more only where that number grew. Measuring that full window is how we help pet brands plan events that add sales.

A0576.crumb: Why Amazon’s record seller share signals…
A0576.title: Why Amazon’s record seller share signals trouble for vendors
A0576.alt: A cluster of taped cardboard parcels in a patch of light on a warehouse floor beside pallets of stacked boxes.
A0576.ttag: Why Amazon’s record seller share signals trouble for vendors | Kwontified
A0576.desc: Third-party sellers reached a record 61% of Amazon units in early 2024. Why that leaves vendors on the slower half of the store, and what 1P brands should do.
A0576.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 23, 2024.
A0576.body:
Amazon runs two businesses in one store, and a shopper can rarely tell which one she is buying from. In the first, Amazon buys products from brands, known as vendors, and resells them. In the second, independent sellers list and sell their own products and pay Amazon fees for the marketplace, fulfillment and advertising. The page looks the same either way. Underneath it, the two businesses are growing at very different speeds.

Third-party sellers reached a record 61% of Amazon’s paid units in the first quarter of 2024, and the marketplace side is growing much faster than the side where Amazon buys and resells. Brands that sell mainly as vendors are on the slower-growing half of the platform. They should build the ability to sell some products directly as sellers, rather than relying on vendor orders alone.

How Amazon’s seller share reached a record

Third-party sellers accounted for 61% of Amazon’s paid units in the first quarter of 2024, up from 59% a year earlier, and revenue from third-party seller services grew 16% excluding currency effects, Yahoo Finance reported from the results. Worldwide paid units grew 12%, EcommerceBytes reported.

Put those figures together and the growth rates separate sharply. If total units grew 12% and the seller share rose from 59% to 61%, units sold by third-party sellers grew about 16%, while units Amazon sold itself grew about 6.5%. The vendor side is still growing, but at well under half the pace of the marketplace. If that gap persists, the share of Amazon’s units sold by vendors will keep shrinking each year.

Who keeps the value on each side of the store

When Amazon buys from a vendor, it takes on inventory risk and earns a retail margin. When a seller lists a product, Amazon earns fees without owning the stock. As the marketplace grows faster, more of Amazon’s attention, investment and growth comes from the side where it carries less risk and still collects on every sale. The seller carries the inventory, and Amazon keeps a share of the transaction either way.

Read as a statement of priorities, the record share says that Amazon’s growth now comes more from hosting other companies’ inventory and charging for the services around it. A brand that wants Amazon’s attention will increasingly earn it the way sellers do, through the stock, prices and advertising it controls itself.

Vendors feel that shift in their terms as well as their volumes. Each year, vendors negotiate allowances, marketing contributions and payment terms with Amazon, and those costs come out of the wholesale price. As the vendor side grows more slowly, Amazon has less reason to ease those terms. A brand should calculate its true net margin as a vendor, after all allowances and deductions, before deciding how much of its range to keep in that model.

The economics of the other model are different, not simply better. Vendors receive a wholesale price and leave retail pricing to Amazon. Sellers keep more of the retail price but pay fees for fulfillment, referral and storage. The two only become comparable product by product, once a brand counts the cost of its own time and inventory risk.

What a vendor controls, and what it does not

A vendor depends on Amazon’s purchase orders, which follow Amazon’s own forecasts and inventory plans. When Amazon is cautious, orders shrink. When the marketplace is growing faster, a vendor’s competitors in the same category may increasingly be sellers who control their own stock, pricing and promotions.

Shoppers do not see much difference. A product listed by a seller and one sold by Amazon look similar on the page, and both can carry fast delivery. What matters to the shopper is price, availability and reviews, and whoever controls those three most reliably tends to win the sale.

Take a household goods brand that sells only as a vendor. During a quarter when Amazon orders conservatively, its products go out of stock for several weeks. A competitor selling as a third-party seller keeps its products in stock, runs a coupon and wins the searches the vendor’s products would have captured. The vendor did nothing wrong. It simply had far less control over the outcome than its competitor.

Advertising follows the same line. A vendor’s ads depend on Amazon keeping the product in stock, while a seller can align advertising with its own inventory, which is one more reason many brands move fast-changing products to the seller model.

Choosing the model product by product

Vendor relationships are not failing, but relying on them alone leaves a brand on the slower half of the platform with less control. Brands that have only sold as vendors can set up a seller account and learn to manage inventory, pricing and promotions directly, even if most sales stay in the vendor model.

The split works best by product. Fast-moving core products with steady demand may suit the vendor model, where Amazon handles stock. New launches, seasonal items and products Amazon orders inconsistently may do better sold directly, where the brand controls availability. Out-of-stock periods are the most common way vendors lose ground to sellers, so the brand should watch Amazon’s orders closely, flag shortfalls early and, where it can, fill gaps through a seller account instead of leaving products unavailable.

Running both models for the same product can create conflicts over price and listing control. A clear rule about which products go through which model, reviewed each quarter, keeps those conflicts small.

The question for the leadership team is which half of Amazon each product line is on, and whether the team has the skills to move it if it needs to. Running both sides of the store, vendor and seller, is how we help brands keep control on Amazon.

A0577.crumb: AR try-on and the return-rate problem in…
A0577.title: AR try-on and the return-rate problem in social shopping
A0577.alt: A linen dress on a hanger beside a floor mirror, a phone on a stand and an open shipping box in a sage-green room.
A0577.ttag: AR try-on and the return-rate problem in social shopping | Kwontified
A0577.desc: Online orders come back far more often than store purchases. AR try-on cuts only the returns caused by how a product looks, so it pays in some categories only.
A0577.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 28, 2024.
A0577.body:
Online purchases come back far more often than store purchases, and AR try-on is often sold as the fix. It can only fix one kind of return. Augmented reality shows a shopper how a lipstick shade or a pair of frames looks on her face before she buys, which removes surprises about color and style. It cannot tell her how a jacket fits, how a fabric feels or how well a product is made.

So AR is worth its cost only where appearance drives returns: makeup shades, eyewear, accessories. Where size drives returns, fit data and better descriptions do more. Brands selling through social shopping should find out which kind of return they have before they pay for the technology.

Why AR try-on is pitched against returns

Returns are expensive and growing. US shoppers returned $743 billion of merchandise in 2023, or 14.5% of sales. Online purchases came back at a rate of 17.6%, about $247 billion, compared with about 10% for purchases made and returned in stores, the National Retail Federation reported with Appriss Retail.

The gap has an obvious cause. A shopper in a store can see, touch and try a product, and a shopper scrolling a social feed cannot. AR try-on, which overlays a product on a live camera image of the shopper or their room, promises to close part of that gap, and social platforms and beauty brands have adopted it for exactly that reason. The pitch is reasonable. The trouble is that it is usually made about returns in general, when the tool reaches only a slice of them.

AR’s value is a share times a cost

What AR can save equals the share of returns caused by appearance, multiplied by the cost of each return it prevents. Everything else in the return pile is out of its reach.

Take a brand that receives 1,000 orders through social shopping with an 18% return rate. That is 180 returns. Say 30% of those, or 54, happen because the product looked different from what the shopper expected, and AR try-on halves those appearance returns, preventing 27.

Returns per 1,000 ordersReturn rate
Without AR try-on18018%
With AR try-on153about 15.3%

At $15 per return, covering shipping, handling and lost resale value, that saves about $405 for every 1,000 orders. Total returns fall by 15%. That is a real saving, but a bounded one. The other 126 returns, driven by size, fit, quality or a change of mind, are untouched.

The same arithmetic tells you how to read any vendor’s claims. A brand whose returns are mostly about fit will see much less from AR, because the share it can reach is small. A brand whose returns are mostly about shade or style will see more. The question to ask before any demo is what share of your returns AR could possibly touch. A test is what would change the estimate: if shoppers who used try-on return appearance items about as often as everyone else, the assumption that AR halves those returns was wrong.

Reading return reasons before buying the tool

The first step costs nothing: sort returns into appearance, fit, quality and other causes. The appearance share tells you the ceiling on what AR can save before any money is spent.

Then match the tool to the problem. AR suits makeup shades, hair color, eyewear, jewelry, watches and furniture placement, where seeing the product on the shopper or in the room answers the main question. Apparel sizing needs fit guidance, measurements and reviews that describe fit, which AR does not provide. Some products gain little from AR at all. Items bought mainly on function, such as kitchen tools or cables, rarely come back because of how they look, however impressive the feature seems in a demo.

Measure AR on returns and conversion together. Shoppers who can see a product on themselves may buy with more confidence, so AR can lift conversion as well as cut returns. A test that compares shoppers who used try-on with similar shoppers who did not shows both effects.

Social shopping strengthens the case in some categories. Shoppers on Instagram and similar platforms often buy on impulse after seeing a product in a creator’s video, which raises the chance of a gap between expectation and reality. For appearance-driven products, AR adds a quick check before the purchase.

The cheaper fixes come first

Content still does much of the work. Clear photos in natural light, true-to-life color, shade comparisons and videos of the product on different people reduce appearance surprises even without AR, and for many brands improving them is cheaper and nearly as effective. Building and maintaining AR assets for many products takes time and money, so the sensible order is to start with the products where appearance returns are highest and expand only if the savings justify it.

Return policies interact with all of this. Generous return policies that cost the shopper nothing encourage shoppers to order several options and send back the rest, a habit no try-on tool fully changes. It is worth checking whether a policy invites that kind of bracket buying, and whether clearer guidance at the point of purchase could reduce it, before investing in new technology. Fraud is a separate problem again: NRF also reported significant losses from return fraud, which AR does nothing to address.

The rule is short. Fund AR up to the value of the appearance returns it can reach, and put the rest of the returns budget into fit, content and policy. Working out where AR will pay across social and marketplace channels is how we help brands cut costly returns.

A0578.title: Winning Amazon’s baby products category as births decline
A0578.alt: A wooden crib with folded knit blankets beside a dresser holding baby bottles and toys in a sunlit blue nursery.
A0578.ttag: Winning Amazon’s baby products category as births decline | Kwontified
A0578.desc: US births fell 2% in 2023, so the baby category’s pool of new parents is shrinking. Why trust, registries and repeat buying now decide who wins on Amazon.
A0578.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 30, 2024.
A0578.body:
Months before a due date, an expectant parent sits down with a laptop and starts a baby registry: a car seat, a stroller, bottles, a monitor, a first box of diapers. Each choice takes longer than it would for almost anything else in the house, because each one feels like a safety decision. Once the list is shared, friends and family buy from it, so a handful of brand decisions made at that laptop turn into sales from several buyers at once.

That registry is where Amazon’s baby products category is now won, because the category itself is shrinking. US births fell 2% in 2023 to about 3.59 million, so brands grow mainly by winning a larger share of each family rather than by riding a growing market. They should compete on the trust, safety signals and registry presence that careful new parents rely on, then build repeat buying in the consumables families purchase for years.

How Amazon baby products became a share game

The customer pool for baby products is set by births, and births are falling. There were 3,591,328 births in the United States in 2023, down 2% from 2022, and the general fertility rate fell 3% to a historic low, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported. From 2014 to 2020, the rate had declined about 2% a year, the CDC said. The number fell from about 3.66 million in 2022, ABC News reported, and births continue to shift toward older mothers.

For a brand, the consequence is plain. Fewer babies means fewer new families entering the category each year, and total demand for diapers, bottles, strollers and car seats does not grow on its own. A brand that wants to grow has to win families from competitors or sell more to each family it already serves.

Why careful parents decide the category

Shopping behavior in the baby category is unusual. Many buyers are first-time parents, and a growing share are older and more established. They research heavily, read reviews closely and care intensely about safety. A mistake with a car seat or a sleep product feels far more serious than a mistake with a kitchen gadget.

In a store, a nervous parent can pick up a car seat, pull on the straps and ask someone how it installs. On Amazon the listing has to do all of that work. Parents look for safety certifications, clear materials information, consistent reviews and brands other parents recommend. Price matters, but rarely more than confidence.

Registries concentrate the decision. Many parents build a registry months before the birth, choosing the brands they want for the first year, and a brand that makes it onto the list gains sales from several buyers at once. A brand that is left off is often never considered.

Take two stroller brands with similar products and prices. One has detailed safety information, clear photos of every feature, a strong review history and products that are easy to add to a registry. The other has a thin listing. Expectant parents comparing the two during registry planning choose the first, and the decision holds for months of gifts that follow.

Winning the registry decision

Safety and trust have to be obvious. Certifications, materials, age ranges and safety features belong in titles, images and descriptions, so parents never have to hunt for the information that matters most to them. Reviews deserve the same care. Parents read negative reviews closely, especially any that mention safety, so a brand should respond quickly, fix recurring problems and make sure its product information answers the questions reviews raise.

Being registry-ready is a supply question as much as a content one. Products should be in stock, clearly described and easy to add to registries, with variations named consistently, and brands should watch registry timing, since parents often build lists well before a due date. Advertising can follow the same calendar, with durable goods promoted during registry research and consumables once the baby arrives.

Compliance sits underneath all of it. Baby products face strict safety rules, and listings that lack required information or documentation can be removed, so certifications have to stay current and records ready.

Growing within each family

Diapers, wipes, formula and other consumables are bought for years. Subscribe & Save, multipacks and size progressions help a family that chooses a brand early keep buying it as the baby grows. Starter sets that combine bottles, accessories or care products suit new parents who want to buy what they need in one step, and they make a brand’s range easier to choose as a whole.

Gift buyers are a second audience. Grandparents, friends and colleagues buy from registries and for baby showers, often with little knowledge of the category, so they rely on the parents’ list and on clear, reassuring listings. Gift-ready options, such as sets that arrive well packaged, help a brand win those purchases too.

Second and later children change the pattern again. Parents who already have one child often reuse durable items and buy mainly consumables and replacements, and they choose faster. Brands that earned trust the first time hold a strong advantage, since experienced parents tend to buy again from brands that served them well. Range extends that advantage: a brand that sells feeding products can add teething, bath or travel items the same family needs at later stages, giving a satisfied family another reason not to search again.

The question for a leadership team in this category is how many families the brand won at the registry, and how many of those are still buying from it a year later. Growing that share one family at a time is how we help baby brands grow on Amazon.

A0580.crumb: AI in post-purchase support: automate the…
A0580.title: AI in post-purchase support: automate the routine first
A0580.alt: A small white robotic arm picking a paper-wrapped parcel from a wooden crate beside a brass service bell.
A0580.ttag: AI in post-purchase support: automate the routine first | Kwontified
A0580.desc: Klarna’s AI assistant handled two-thirds of its chats in one month. Why AI pays on routine post-purchase questions, and where failures cost more than it saves.
A0580.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 4, 2024.
A0580.body:
Klarna’s AI assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, two-thirds of the company’s customer service chats and the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents. Figures like that make every support budget look oversized. They also leave out the conversations the assistant did not handle, and those are the ones that decide whether AI support saves money or loses customers.

AI assistants can now resolve routine post-purchase questions, such as order status, returns and refunds, faster and far more cheaply than people. Their value depends on how much of the contact volume is routine and on how quickly the hard cases reach a person. Brands should automate the routine questions, route complex and emotional cases to people fast, and judge AI support on repeat contacts and loyalty rather than on cost per contact alone.

What Klarna’s results show about AI in post-purchase support

Klarna, the payments company, said its AI assistant, built with OpenAI, had handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month. That was two-thirds of its customer service chats and the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents, with customer satisfaction on par with human agents, according to Klarna’s announcement. Customers resolved their issues in under 2 minutes, compared with 11 minutes before, and Klarna estimated the assistant would add $40 million to its profit in 2024, tech.eu reported. Much of the work involved refunds, returns and payment questions.

Judged by what the assistant does rather than by the launch figures, the picture is more specific. An analysis by The Pragmatic Engineer noted that the assistant passes more complex questions to human agents. The routine work moved to AI, and the hard work stayed with people. That is the design that makes the headline numbers possible, and it is the part a brand has to copy. The same analysis noted Klarna’s statement that the assistant communicates in more than 35 languages.

Net value is the saving minus what the AI gets wrong

An AI assistant answers routine questions at a fraction of a person’s cost, so the saving scales with the share of contacts that are routine. Each case it handles badly costs a second contact and some of the customer’s goodwill. The net value of AI support is therefore its saving on routine contacts minus the cost of its failures, including purchases the customer no longer makes.

Take a brand that receives 10,000 support contacts a month. Say 65% are routine, such as order tracking or return requests, and the AI handles each for $0.50 compared with $5 for a person. Automating those 6,500 contacts saves $29,250 a month.

Now say the AI mishandles 5% of them. Those 325 customers contact the brand again and reach a person, adding $1,625 in cost, which leaves a net saving of $27,625. Those customers also had a worse experience, and if each failed contact costs the brand $40 of future margin, that is another $13,000. The net saving falls to about $14,625, roughly half the headline figure.

The saving is real, and so is the cost of getting the hard cases wrong, which rarely appears in a support dashboard. Those dashboards count tickets closed and minutes saved but not orders that never came.

Automate by contact type and guard the handoff

Contacts sort by type before they sort by cost. Order status, delivery dates, return labels and refund timing suit AI well. Damaged goods, disputes, safety concerns and upset customers need a person who can use judgment.

The handoff decides how much the failures cost. A customer whose question the AI cannot solve should reach a person quickly, without repeating the whole story. A slow or hidden route to a human turns a small problem into a lost customer, which is exactly the $40 line in the example.

The measure that counts is what customers do next. Repeat contacts, satisfaction scores and whether customers buy again tell a brand whether AI support is working. Cost per contact alone can look excellent while loyalty erodes underneath it. Reading a sample of AI conversations each week shows where answers are wrong, where customers get stuck and which questions should be routed differently.

Policy has to come before automation. An assistant can only apply the return and refund rules it is given. Clear, consistent policies make its answers more accurate and reduce the cases that need judgment, while vague rules produce vague answers, and customers notice quickly when the assistant contradicts what a person told them last week.

Where the saving is largest for marketplace brands

Which channel the order came through changes the picture. On Amazon, much post-purchase support for orders fulfilled by Amazon runs through Amazon itself. On a brand’s own site, on Walmart or Target marketplaces when the brand ships orders itself, and on TikTok Shop, the brand handles more of it, and those are the places where AI support can save the most.

Coverage is a further benefit. An assistant answers at any hour and in many languages, which matters for brands selling across time zones and countries, and for a brand expanding to marketplaces abroad it can make support possible where hiring local teams is not. Support conversations are also a source of insight: the questions customers ask after buying show where listings are unclear, where products disappoint and where delivery promises fail. Feeding those patterns back into product pages, packaging and policies cuts contacts at the source, which saves more than automating them.

Before switching an assistant on, count the routine share of contacts and price a failed contact in lost margin, not just in a second ticket. If the net saving survives that arithmetic, automate. Running that check across a brand’s own site and its marketplaces is how we help brands decide what to automate.

A0581.crumb: Who decides Prime Day 2024, and how it…
A0581.title: Who decides Prime Day 2024, and how it runs the planning calendar
A0581.alt: A stack of string-tied paper parcels and a leather journal on a wooden table by a sunny garden window.
A0581.ttag: Who decides Prime Day 2024, and how it runs the planning calendar | Kwontified
A0581.desc: Amazon’s Prime Day deadlines arrive months before the event and split decisions across teams. Who should own Prime Day 2024, and what is still open in June.
A0581.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 6, 2024.
A0581.body:
In early June, a leadership team asks how Prime Day is shaping up, and the answer arrives in three parts. Finance has a view on deal depth, operations on stock, marketing on the advertising budget. Each view is reasonable. None of those teams owns the whole event, and by this point much of it has already been settled by Amazon’s calendar rather than by any of them.

Prime Day has grown into Amazon’s biggest event of the year, and its deal and inventory deadlines now fall months before the event, splitting the decisions across finance, operations and marketing. By early June, much of a brand’s Prime Day 2024 is already decided. Brands should give the event a single owner, plan backward from Amazon’s deadlines and use the decisions still open, inventory and advertising, to protect margin.

How Prime Day 2024 planning took over the calendar

Prime Day keeps getting bigger. In 2023, Prime members bought more than 375 million items worldwide and saved more than $2.5 billion, and US online spending across the two days reached $12.7 billion, up 6.1%, according to Adobe Analytics, Retail TouchPoints reported. Shoppers had bought about 300 million items during the 2022 event, CNN reported.

As the event has grown, its planning has moved earlier. Amazon published a schedule in April with US deadlines of April 12 for Prime Exclusive Top Deals and May 3 for Prime Exclusive Lightning Deals and Best Deals. It also set an FBA inventory cutoff of June 20 for sellers in the United States, eStore Factory reported. Vendors faced the same June 20 cutoff for inbound inventory.

Amazon had not announced the 2024 event dates by early June, and recent Prime Days have been held in July. The deadlines arrived anyway, months ahead of an event without a date. Read as an institution, Amazon is doing what any host of a large event does: it locks in its deals and its stock early enough to run the show. Those dates were never built around a brand’s own approval cycle.

Why the decisions fall between teams

Each major Prime Day decision belongs to a different part of a brand. Deal depth affects margin, so finance cares about it. Inventory affects cash and warehouse capacity, so operations owns it. Advertising budgets sit with marketing or a retail media team. Each team works on its own calendar, and Amazon’s deadlines do not wait for any of them.

When no one owns the whole event, the pieces drift apart. Finance approves a deal after the submission deadline. Operations ships stock for a forecast that assumed a bigger deal. Marketing sets a budget without knowing which products will carry a deal badge. The event happens, but not as anyone planned it, and no one can say afterward which decision cost the most.

Take a home brand whose marketing team planned heavy Prime Day advertising on a best-selling product. The deal submission passed in early May while finance was still reviewing the discount, so the product has no deal. Operations, expecting the deal, shipped extra stock. The brand now holds more inventory than it can sell at full price, and an ad budget aimed at a product without the badge shoppers look for.

One owner, working backward from Amazon’s deadlines

The debate in the room usually sounds like a question about discounts or budgets. Underneath, it is a question about ownership. One person should hold the plan, the deadlines and the trade-offs between deal depth, stock and spend. That person does not make every decision, but makes sure each one is made on time, which means listing every Amazon deadline for the event and setting an internal deadline ahead of each, so approvals happen before submissions are due.

Vendors and sellers face this differently. Sellers submit their own deals and control their own stock. Vendors negotiate deals with Amazon and depend on Amazon’s purchase orders to have inventory in place, so a vendor brand’s owner has to coordinate with Amazon’s buying team as well as internal teams, which makes early decisions even more important.

What is still open in June

By early June, deal submissions for the main deal types have closed. Inventory can still reach Amazon before the June 20 cutoff, though, and advertising budgets, bids and coupons can still be adjusted. Those choices decide much of the event’s profit.

Inventory deserves the closest attention now. Too little stock means lost sales and wasted advertising during the event, and too much means stock that must be sold at a discount afterward. Shipments should be sized to the deals a brand actually has, not the ones it hoped for. Advertising should follow the same deals. Products with deal badges usually convert better during the event and can justify higher bids, while products without deals may convert less well against discounted competitors.

Deal fees belong in the calculation as well. Amazon charges fees for several deal types, and a deal that looks attractive on discount alone can lose money once fees and advertising are counted. A deal that loses money on every unit does not become profitable because it sells more units.

After the event, the review should happen while the details are fresh, with the decisions and deadlines recorded for the 2025 event. Prime Big Deal Days, which Amazon has held each October since 2022, uses the same structure, so the lessons apply within months.

The question a chief executive can put to the team this week is simple: who can say which of our Prime Day decisions are already locked, and who is making the ones that are not? Holding deals, stock and advertising in one plan is how we help brands run Prime Day.

A0582.crumb: Why most Amazon searches never become…
A0582.title: Why most Amazon searches never become clicks for your brand
A0582.alt: Dusty boot prints on a cracked pavement in front of an old wooden shopfront on a quiet brick street.
A0582.ttag: Why most Amazon searches never become clicks for your brand | Kwontified
A0582.desc: Many Amazon searches end with no click, and most clicks go to the top few results. Why being shown is not being chosen, and how to close the gap to clicks.
A0582.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 11, 2024.
A0582.body:
A brand opens its search report and finds its products on a healthy share of the results for its most important search. Its sales from that search are far smaller than that share would suggest. Nothing is wrong with the report. Being shown and being chosen are two separate events, and an Amazon search page pulls them a long way apart.

Many Amazon searches end without a click on any result, and the clicks that do happen go mostly to the top few listings. Brands should judge their search presence on click share relative to impression share. When shoppers see a product but do not click it, the fix is usually the main image, the price, the reviews or the position on the page.

How Amazon searches turn into clicks

A search on Amazon produces a page of sponsored and organic results, and the shopper scans it, often in a few seconds. Some click a listing. Many refine the search, add a word, sort by price or leave. Every search is an opportunity, but only some become a click on anything at all.

The clicks that do happen are concentrated. About 64% of clicks on an Amazon search page go to the top three items, a former Amazon consultant estimated in reporting by The Markup. Products further down the page share what is left.

Impression share became the headline number for understandable reasons. It is easy to count, it moves when budgets move, and on a page where position matters it looks like the goal. Amazon’s Brand Analytics now shows the rest of the funnel. Its Search Query Performance view lays out each search a brand cares about stage by stage, from the times shoppers saw results to the clicks, cart adds and orders that followed, with the slice of every stage that went to the brand. That makes the gap between being seen and being chosen visible.

Being shown is not being chosen

Take a search that gets 10,000 searches a month. Say 55% of those searches produce a click on some result, about 5,500 clicks, and the other 4,500 end with a refinement or no click at all. A brand’s products account for 20% of impressions on that search but only 8% of clicks.

Impression shareClick shareClicksPurchases at a 12% conversion rate
The brand as it stands20%8%440about 53
If clicks matched impressions20%20%1,100about 132

The brand is being shown, and it is not being chosen. Buying more impressions does not fix that, because each extra impression converts to clicks at the same weak rate until the listing itself starts winning the click.

Reading the funnel one search at a time

The comparison works search by search. For its top searches, a brand should line up impression share, click share, cart add share and purchase share. Where click share falls well below impression share, shoppers are seeing the product and passing it over.

The later stages tell a different story. A product that wins clicks but loses at the cart or purchase stage has another problem, such as price, the reviews shoppers read on the detail page or content that does not answer their questions. Searches with many clicks and few purchases deserve particular care. They may be searches where shoppers browse heavily before buying elsewhere, or where the results do not match what they want, and they can cost a lot in advertising without returning much.

Click share also moves on its own as competitors change prices, run deals or improve their images. A monthly review of the top searches catches those shifts before they show up in total sales.

Click share has limits as a measure too. It says nothing about whether the clicks were profitable, and on a search where the product is a poor match for what shoppers want, a low click share may be the right outcome. The comparison matters most on the searches a brand should win, such as its core category terms and its own name.

Image, price, badges and position decide the click

On a search page, a shopper sees the main image, title, price, star rating, review count and delivery promise, and those few elements decide the click. A clearer main image, a sharper title, a competitive price or more reviews can raise click share without any change in position. Deal badges, coupons and labels such as best seller or Amazon’s Choice change how a listing looks beside its neighbors and can lift click share on their own.

Mobile tightens all of this. On a phone, a shopper sees only a few results before scrolling, and the main image fills much of the screen, so a listing that looks acceptable on a desktop page can be passed over entirely. Main images and titles should be judged on a phone. The page is crowded as well, with sponsored listings, brand banners, video ads and recommendation rows competing with organic results for the same few seconds, which is why a strong organic rank alone does not guarantee clicks.

Position is the last lever. Because clicks concentrate at the top, moving from the middle of the page into the first few results can change outcomes more than any listing change, and advertising can buy that position on searches where the product converts well once clicked.

When click share runs well below impression share on a search, fix the listing before paying for more impressions; when the two match but the product sits low on the page, pay for position. Reading that funnel search by search is how we help brands turn Amazon search visibility into sales.
