A0584.title: How viral social brands disrupt traditional retail planning
A0584.alt: A coral box crashing into a corkboard, scattering blank pinned notes and pushpins onto a wooden shelf.
A0584.ttag: How viral social brands disrupt traditional retail planning | Kwontified
A0584.desc: Viral brands like Stanley build demand on social media faster than retail plans can follow. What breaks when the spike lands, and how to plan around it.
A0584.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 13, 2024.
A0584.body:
Around New Year’s Day, Target released exclusive Stanley tumblers in new colors, and they sold out within minutes in stores across the country. No buyer’s forecast had a line for that kind of rush. The demand had been building on TikTok, where the hashtag for Stanley cups had 6.7 billion views, Modern Retail reported. By the time it reached the shelf, it arrived all at once.

That is the problem viral social brands pose for retail planning. Demand forms on social platforms faster than store buyers and marketplace stock plans can register it, and it lands in spikes instead of steady growth. The brands that cope plan supply for the spike, stay available wherever shoppers search, and treat each viral moment as temporary rather than as a new baseline.

How viral social brands outrun the planning calendar

Stanley’s Quencher is the clearest case, partly because its early history was so unremarkable. The tumbler sold so poorly at first that by 2019 the company had stopped restocking and marketing it, CNBC reported. Then a shopping-focused online business persuaded Stanley to let it sell the cup to its audience, and demand took off. Stanley’s revenue grew from $73 million in 2019 to $194 million in 2021 and $402 million in 2022, and was expected to reach about $750 million in 2023, the same report said.

Social media carried much of that growth, and social platforms are turning into places to buy as well as to discover. TikTok Shop had more than 500,000 US merchants by the end of 2023 and a US sales run rate of $3 billion as of January, Retail Brew reported. For a brand, that means the place where demand is created and the places where it gets fulfilled are drifting further apart.

Retail planning was built for gradual change

Retail planning keeps a slow and sensible rhythm. Store buyers set assortments and orders months ahead, working from past sales and category trends. Marketplace sellers forecast stock from recent velocity. Both systems assume demand changes gradually, and most weeks that assumption holds.

Viral demand does not behave that way. A product can go from steady sales to a sellout within days because a video spreads or a creator features it. Shoppers who see it on social media then search for it wherever they shop: in stores, on Amazon, on Walmart, on the brand’s own site. Stock runs out where demand lands, and shoppers who cannot find the product buy a lookalike or give up.

Retailers react to the same signal in their own way. Seeing the rush, they move to secure exclusives and limited editions, which can concentrate demand even further on a few shelves and a few days.

The reporting cycle adds a delay of its own. A buyer’s sales report shows what sold last week, not what is spreading on social media this week, so by the time a viral product appears in the numbers the moment may already be peaking. Brands that watch social signals directly, such as views, creator posts and search interest, can see demand coming before retail systems register it.

The risk on the way down

A spike creates a second problem when it ends. A brand that orders inventory to match the peak may find demand has moved on by the time the stock arrives, because viral attention fades as quickly as it rises.

Take a home brand whose product goes viral on TikTok. Within a week, its Amazon listing sells out and searches for its name triple. Shoppers who search on Walmart find a competitor’s similar product instead. The brand rushes a large production run, which arrives two months later, just as the trend cools, and it now holds more stock than steady demand can absorb.

Every part of that story is a planning decision made with last month’s information. The listing ran out because the stock plan followed velocity. The Walmart shoppers went to a rival because the product was hard to find there. The oversized order came from treating the peak as the new normal.

Plan for the spike, then for the fade

The supply side starts with flexibility. Brands with products that could go viral are better served by flexible capacity, safety stock on the items most likely to spike and fast restocking options than by one large order sized to a guess. Smaller, more frequent production runs reduce the risk of being caught with too much or too little.

Availability matters as much as quantity. Viral attention sends shoppers to many retailers at once, so the product needs to be listed, stocked and easy to find on the marketplaces its customers use, with brand searches on those marketplaces defended by advertising where needed.

Patience protects the balance sheet. A viral spike is not a new baseline, and judging demand a few weeks after the peak, before committing to large orders, keeps a brand from building inventory for a moment that has passed. The lasting business is built from the customers the moment brought in.

Limited editions deserve particular care. Scarcity can fuel attention, as Stanley’s colors at Target showed, but deliberate scarcity works only when a brand can deliver what it promises. Repeated sellouts without restocks frustrate shoppers and push them toward alternatives.

Retail partners need to be kept close. Retailers that see a product take off will want stock and sometimes exclusives, and those deals have to be weighed against the brand’s own marketplace presence, so that one exclusive does not leave shoppers elsewhere empty-handed.

The content that started the wave is worth keeping. The videos that drive viral demand can be reused as product content on marketplace listings, where shoppers who arrive from social media want to see the product as they first saw it.

The question worth asking inside a brand is who sees the video before the sales report does, and whether that person has any say over the next production order. Closing that gap, and keeping listings stocked across retailers while the moment lasts, is part of how we run marketplace channels day to day for brands.

A0586.crumb: Why the Best Seller badge pays in one…
A0586.title: Why the Best Seller badge pays in one category, not another
A0586.alt: An orange award rosette pinned to a rustic wall shelf holding ceramics, an amber bottle, a jar of tea and soap bars.
A0586.ttag: Why the Best Seller badge pays in one category, not another | Kwontified
A0586.desc: The Best Seller badge lifts Amazon traffic, but what it is worth depends on the category and on what it costs to hold. How to put a daily value on it.
A0586.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 18, 2024.
A0586.body:
Amazon’s Best Seller badge can lift a product’s traffic sharply, and chasing it can still leave a brand with less margin than before. Both outcomes come from the same small label. The badge does two things that vary by category: it moves shoppers who are choosing, and it costs something to keep.

The badge is worth chasing where shoppers pick among lookalike products and the rank that earns it can be held cheaply. It is worth little where shoppers buy by brand, or where holding it takes deep price cuts. Its value is the extra visits it brings, times conversion and margin, minus the cost of holding the rank. Brands should put a daily figure on that before spending to win it.

How the Best Seller badge is awarded, and what it moves

Amazon gives the Best Seller badge to the top-selling product in each category and subcategory, so there is one badge for every category and subcategory, Pattern explained. Best Seller Rank is updated hourly, based on recent and historical sales.

The badge does move shoppers. In a study of 37,000 products, Best Seller badges increased a product’s glance views by an average of 45%, while Amazon’s Choice badges had a greater effect on conversion, raising it by 25% on average, Profitero found.

A 45% lift in traffic is the kind of number that ends a meeting. It is easy to see why teams chase the badge on its strength. But it is an average across many categories, and an average hides the spread that decides whether the badge pays for a particular product.

The badge’s value is traffic times margin, minus the cost of holding rank

The badge raises traffic by signaling popularity. The extra visits turn into money only through conversion and margin, and the rank that earns the badge has a price of its own, usually paid in coupons, discounts or advertising. Both sides of that ledger change from category to category.

The traffic side is large where shoppers rely on cues to choose among similar products. It is small where they already know which brand they want. The cost side depends on how hard competitors fight for the top spot.

Take two products, each receiving 1,000 product page views a day. The first is a phone cable in a category full of near-identical listings, converting at 10% with a $4 margin per sale. Say the badge adds the average 45% in traffic. The second is a premium skincare product in a category where shoppers buy by brand, converting at 8% with a $20 margin, and the badge adds only 5%.

Phone cablePremium skincare
Daily product page views1,0001,000
Conversion rate10%8%
Margin per sale$4$20
Traffic lift from the badge45% (views to 1,450)5%
Daily sales, without and with the badge100 to 14580 to 84
Extra margin per day$180$80
Cost of holding the badge$0.50 coupon on every sale, about $72.50 a day$5 discount on every sale against strong competitors, $420 a day
Net value per dayabout $107.50minus $340

The cable earns about $107.50 a day from the badge. The skincare product loses $340 a day holding it, even though it earns far more on every sale. Same badge, opposite conclusions, and the difference comes from how shoppers choose and what it costs to stay on top.

Both sides of the trade are real. The badge brings extra visits without a matching ad bill, and in a crowded category it can be the cue that tips a shopper choosing among lookalikes. Holding it can also cost more than it brings. The numbers lean toward chasing it in commodity-like categories and leaving it alone in categories where reputation decides the sale.

Where the badge earns its keep

The category comes first. Where products look alike and shoppers lack strong brand preferences, cues such as the badge carry weight. Where shoppers know the brands and buy on reputation, the badge adds less, and the money spent defending it would do more elsewhere.

The cost of holding the badge needs to be counted over weeks. Winning it once is different from keeping it, so the discounts, coupons and advertising needed to stay at the top of the category over time belong in the calculation, along with the push to get there.

Subcategories can change the arithmetic. Because there is a badge for every subcategory, a product may win one in a narrower subcategory more cheaply than in a broad one. That can be worthwhile if shoppers actually browse or search that subcategory, and pointless if they do not.

Views have to be followed through to sales. The 45% average lift measures glance views, and a badge that brings browsers who do not buy adds little margin. Advertising interacts with the badge as well. Products that already carry it enjoy extra traffic, so heavy ad spend on them may buy less than spend on products that convert well but lack visibility. Profitero’s study made the same point about where ad dollars do the most.

The badge can disappear quickly. Because Best Seller Rank updates hourly, a competitor’s deal or a stockout can move the badge to another product within a day. It has to be earned continuously, and its cost should be planned that way instead of assuming a single push secures it.

Amazon’s Choice is a separate signal. Profitero found it affected conversion more than traffic, and it is tied to specific searches rather than to category sales. A product may benefit from one badge and not the other, so each deserves its own estimate.

Price wars are the main risk. In crowded categories, competitors may chase the badge too, and a contest fought with discounts can lower prices across the whole category. Setting a limit on what the brand will spend to hold the badge, and stepping back when competitors push beyond it, keeps a badge contest from becoming a margin contest.

The working rule fits on one line: if the extra margin the badge brings each day does not cover the daily cost of keeping it, let a competitor have it. Putting that daily figure on rank, category by category, is part of how we run and measure Amazon advertising for brands.

A0587.crumb: Self-serve or managed: choosing how to…
A0587.title: Self-serve or managed: choosing how to buy retail media
A0587.alt: A self-checkout kiosk beside a wooden shop counter with a brass bell in a bright grocery with produce crates.
A0587.ttag: Self-serve or managed: choosing how to buy retail media | Kwontified
A0587.desc: Retail media networks are opening self-serve buying to more brands. How spend, skill and data access decide between self-serve and managed, network by network.
A0587.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 20, 2024.
A0587.body:
On April 1, Walmart said its onsite display advertising would become primarily programmatic and auction-based, that it was opening access to brands of all sizes and that it was investing more in self-serve tools, according to Walmart. Marketplace sellers were among its fastest-growing advertisers, the company said. Read as an institution, Walmart was telling brands something about who it expects to be doing the buying.

For a brand, that turns a settled habit into a live decision. Buying ads directly through self-serve tools and paying for a managed service now sit side by side on more networks, and the right choice depends on spend, in-house skill and how much control and data the brand needs. Smaller budgets often do better with managed help, larger ones usually justify building self-serve capability, and the decision belongs to each network rather than to the portfolio as a whole.

How self-serve or managed retail media became a real choice

For years, many retail media networks sold most of their advertising through managed services. A retailer’s team, or a partner, planned campaigns and ran them on the brand’s behalf. Self-serve tools existed, but often for a narrow set of ad types.

Amazon has long been the reference point. Its search ads, such as Sponsored Products, have always been self-serve, which is one reason so many brands built in-house skills there first. Its display and video buying through Amazon DSP can be run either by the brand or with Amazon’s managed help.

Other networks have moved in similar directions, adding self-serve consoles and auction buying alongside their managed teams. The result is a real choice on more networks: run campaigns directly, pay for a managed service or combine the two.

What a managed fee costs as budgets grow

Managed services provide expertise, planning and execution, usually for a fee or a minimum commitment. Self-serve gives a brand direct control, faster changes and closer access to performance data, but it needs people with the skill and time to run it. Spend tilts the balance more than anything else, because a fee charged as a share of spend grows with the budget while the cost of an in-house team grows more slowly.

Take a brand comparing a managed service that charges 15% of spend with running self-serve in house. At $20,000 a month, the managed fee is $3,000. Running it in house might take 40 hours of analyst time a month, which at $60 an hour is $2,400. The gap is only $600, and the managed team may bring expertise the brand lacks.

At $100,000 a month, the managed fee is $15,000. Running the same work in house might take 80 hours, or $4,800, so self-serve saves $10,200 a month, more than enough to fund the skills it requires.

The arithmetic holds only if the in-house hours are real. Self-serve works when the people running it know the tools and can watch campaigns closely, and a brand without that capacity may lose more through poor execution than it saves in fees. On networks where a brand spends heavily, building self-serve capability usually pays. On smaller networks, managed help may cost less than learning another console.

Control counts as well. Self-serve lets a brand adjust bids, budgets and targeting daily, react to stock problems and test ideas quickly. Managed services can be slower to change, which matters during events or when inventory is tight.

Who keeps what the campaigns teach

The fee is the visible cost. The less visible one is where the learning ends up. Running campaigns directly often gives brands more detailed reporting and a clearer view of what works, and that knowledge builds over time and carries across networks. A brand that learns which audiences and searches convert on one network can apply the lesson on the next, which is harder when every insight sits inside someone else’s reports.

That is why the question of who holds the accounts and the reporting matters as much as the fee. Managed services may come with minimum commitments, fixed fees or terms that make it hard to switch. A brand should know how long it is committed and what happens to its campaigns, data and creative if it moves to self-serve later.

Creative belongs in the same comparison. Display and video campaigns need regular new images and videos. A managed service may include creative support, while self-serve leaves the brand to produce it.

Partners can sit between the two models. Agencies with experience across networks can run self-serve campaigns for a brand, giving it control and data access without building every skill internally, provided the brand keeps ownership of its accounts and data.

Many brands end up with a hybrid. They run search ads themselves, where daily control matters, and use managed help for display, video or offsite campaigns that need more planning and creative work.

Questions to settle for each network

The networks keep changing their tools, minimums and ad types, so the answer needs revisiting every year. A network that mainly offered managed buying in 2023 may now support self-serve, as Walmart’s shift shows. For each network on the plan, a leadership team can work through four questions:

  • How much do we spend here, and at that level does a percentage fee cost more than the people self-serve would need?
  • Do we have someone with the skill and the hours to watch these campaigns closely, or would poor execution cost more than the fee saves?
  • Under either model, do we get detailed reporting and keep ownership of the account, so we can switch later without starting over?
  • What do the contract terms and the creative workload add to the real cost?

Making that call network by network, and running the campaigns under whichever model wins, is how we work with brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target advertising.

A0589.title: Prime Day 2024 forecast: ranges for sales, clicks and deals
A0589.alt: Brass rooster weathervane with an arrow atop a mossy red clay tile roof against a pale blue sky.
A0589.ttag: Prime Day 2024 forecast: ranges for sales, clicks and deals | Kwontified
A0589.desc: Our Prime Day 2024 forecast in three cases for market spending, promoted-product sales, click prices and deal share, and the assumptions behind each.
A0589.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 25, 2024.
A0589.body:
Every Prime Day forecast starts from last year’s number. For 2023 that number was $12.7 billion: US online spending across the two days of the event, up 6.1% from 2022, according to Adobe Analytics, Retail TouchPoints reported. The event’s market growth has settled into single digits, and that figure describes the market as a whole. It does not tell you what happens to a promoted product, where the lift and the click prices are several times larger than the market’s.

Our Prime Day 2024 forecast puts market growth at about 7% in the standard case. Promoted products should see roughly three times their normal daily sales, at click prices about 35% higher. The planning answer follows from the spread: stock and budgets for the standard case, a reserve for the reach case, and results judged against the conservative case.

The Prime Day 2024 forecast in three cases

  • Conservative: US online spend of about $13.2 billion (up 4%), promoted products at 2x normal daily sales, click prices up 20%, deal share of 40%.
  • Standard: about $13.6 billion (up 7%), promoted products at 3x, click prices up 35%, deal share of 55%.
  • Reach: about $14.0 billion (up 10%), promoted products at 4x, click prices up 50%, deal share of 70%.

The deal-share range is a planning assumption drawn from our own work with brands rather than a published figure. Each brand should swap in its own history.

Why promoted products move so much more than the market

Market growth sets the size of the event. Promoted products rise much further than the market because deals and heavier advertising pull shoppers toward a small set of listings. Click prices rise because many advertisers bid in the same short window for the same shoppers. The forecast therefore scales from 2023’s spending and growth, adjusts for more cautious shoppers in 2024, and then applies event lift and click premiums drawn from past events.

The market cases are simple multiples of last year’s figure. The standard case assumes growth similar to 2023’s, about 7%, which gives about $13.6 billion. The conservative case, at 4%, reflects weaker shoppers. The reach case, at 10%, reflects a stronger response to deals.

Shoppers are cautious going in. Consumer sentiment fell in early June to 65.6, its lowest level since November, according to the University of Michigan’s preliminary survey, Anadolu Agency reported. Spending adjusted for inflation slipped 0.1% in April, PNC noted. Cautious shoppers tend to wait for deals, which supports event demand but caps how much they spend.

Click prices carry the second half of the forecast. Skai has found that click prices typically rise about 50% during major shopping events, though the premium was more muted during Amazon’s October 2023 event, according to Skai. We set the reach case at that historical 50% and the standard case at 35%.

Take a brand that sells $10,000 a day of a promoted product line in a normal week, paying $1.00 per click. In the standard case, its event days bring about $30,000 a day at about $1.35 per click. The conservative case gives about $20,000 a day at $1.20, and the reach case about $40,000 a day at $1.50. Sales triple in the middle case, and every click costs more on the way there.

Turning the ranges into a plan

The ranges are wide on purpose. Each brand’s result depends on its category, its deals and its competitors, so the job is to cover the likely outcomes with stock and budget rather than to bet on one number.

Stock and budgets should cover about three times normal daily sales for promoted products, the standard case, with a reserve that can be released if early results run hot toward the reach case. Bids that work in a normal week will lose position during the event, so raising bids on the best-converting searches before the event begins, and watching closely during the first hours, keeps those listings visible when click prices climb.

The conservative case is the floor for judging results. A brand that reaches twice its normal daily sales has met it. As we have argued before, results should also be checked against the weeks after the event, since replenishment categories often borrow sales from them.

Timing affects the shape of demand. Whenever Amazon schedules the event, most likely in July as in recent years, early deals and advertising before the event will pull some demand forward. Brands should expect a smaller lift in the days just before the event and plan budgets across the whole period.

Inventory sets a hard limit. Stock for the event had to reach Amazon’s warehouses by the June 20 cutoff Amazon set in its 2024 schedule, so most brands’ supply for the event is now fixed. Where that stock covers less than the standard lift, trimming budgets keeps the product from selling out on the first day and leaving advertising running on an empty listing.

Products without deals face a different picture. They compete against discounted rivals at higher click prices, so their lift is often smaller than the standard case, and some may see lower sales. They deserve their own, lower targets.

Profit is the last check on all of it. A brand that hits the reach case on sales but pays reach-case click prices and gives away its deepest discount may earn less than it did in a quiet week. Margin after discounts, fees and advertising, worked out for each case before the event, tells a brand which outcome is actually good for it.

The rule we would apply: plan to the standard case, judge against the conservative one, and treat the reach case as a reserve you release only when the first hours earn it. Building those cases from a brand’s own numbers is how we plan and run Prime Day advertising for brands.

A0591.crumb: When a Super Bowl ad becomes a…
A0591.title: When a Super Bowl ad becomes a competitor’s payday
A0591.alt: Navy living room with a retro TV showing football, a bowl of pretzels and a twine-tied parcel on a wooden table.
A0591.ttag: When a Super Bowl ad becomes a competitor’s payday | Kwontified
A0591.desc: A big TV ad sends shoppers to search on Amazon and Walmart, where rivals can bid for the demand it created. Why the advertiser has to defend retail search.
A0591.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 27, 2024.
A0591.body:
When the DTC soap brand Dr. Squatch ran a Super Bowl ad in 2021, its name became one of the top searched terms on Amazon during the game, Modern Retail reported. The response to the ad showed up in a store’s search box, during the game itself.

That habit changes who benefits from a Super Bowl ad. The demand a big TV campaign creates now lands on retail sites like Amazon and Walmart, on a results page where any brand can buy a place beside the advertiser. A brand that does not defend its own name and its category searches lets competitors collect part of what it paid for, which makes retail search the second half of every large awareness campaign.

What a Super Bowl ad buys, and where the response goes

The first half is expensive. A 30-second spot during the 2024 game cost $7 million, about the same as in 2023 and well above the $4.5 million of 2019, CBS News reported. For that money, a brand gets half a minute of national attention and a surge of curiosity about its name and its category.

Much of the response to those ads now happens in search. Many viewers search on a retail site rather than visiting the brand directly, so the brand’s own site, the destination its marketing team planned for, is not always where the curiosity lands.

The same Modern Retail report described a smaller brand taking the other side of that trade. Ollie, a dog food company, decided a Super Bowl ad did not make sense for a business its size while some of its competitors were advertising in the game. It ran its own promotion during the game instead, aimed at shoppers searching for alternatives. Its branded search terms rose by 20% to 30%, and sales conversion jumped 24% during the 24-hour promotion, the company told Modern Retail.

A retail results page sells to whoever bids

Read the retailer as an institution and the opportunity for rivals is easy to see. Retailers sell the sponsored places on their search pages, and a search prompted by one brand’s ad is open to every brand that bids on it. Search results include sponsored listings that any advertiser can bid for, including competitors.

So the advertiser pays to create demand, and the demand arrives on a page it does not control. Rivals that bid on the advertiser’s brand name or category searches can appear beside or above it, with lower prices or deals. A shopper who searched because of the ad may never notice that the first listing belongs to someone else.

Take a brand whose game-day ad sends 50,000 extra shoppers to search on a retail site. Say 55% of those searches produce a click, about 27,500 clicks. If the brand captures only 40% of them because competitors are bidding aggressively, it gets 11,000 clicks and rivals get 16,500.

Defending those searches is cheap by comparison. Retail search clicks cost about $1.60 on Walmart, according to a media executive’s estimate cited by Digiday. At that price, buying 20,000 clicks would cost $32,000, less than half of one percent of the $7 million TV spot.

Every large awareness push needs a search plan behind it

The same logic reaches well beyond the Super Bowl and beyond television. A TV campaign, a viral moment or a major press story all create search demand that competitors can capture, and the brand that paid for the attention has the most to lose.

Defense starts with bids and budgets. A brand running a large awareness campaign should raise them on its own name and its main category searches on Amazon, Walmart and other retailers, during the campaign and after it. The products need to be ready as well. Shoppers arriving from a TV ad expect to find the product they saw, in stock, with clear images and reviews, and a product that is out of stock or hard to find hands the sale to a competitor.

Timing deserves a line in the plan. Search demand from a TV ad arrives during and shortly after it airs, so budgets that cap out early in the day or run dry before the evening can leave the field open when demand peaks. The demand does not vanish after the game either. Strong campaigns often lift branded searches for days or weeks afterward, as people who saw the ad remember it later, which argues for tapering defensive budgets as search volume returns to normal instead of switching them off at once.

For smaller brands, the logic runs in reverse, as Ollie’s approach shows. When a larger rival runs a big campaign, its category searches become busier, and a well-targeted promotion with competitive offers can win some of those shoppers. Bidding on a rival’s brand name is legal on most retail sites, but it carries risks: it can raise costs for both brands, invite retaliation and annoy shoppers who wanted the original brand. Many brands focus on category searches during a rival’s campaign, where shoppers are still choosing.

Measurement should follow the search. Comparing branded and category search volume, share of clicks and sales during and after the campaign shows how much of the created demand actually reached the advertiser, and how much went to the brands beside it. Retailers’ own display and video advertising can then reach shoppers who saw the TV ad, closing the loop between awareness and purchase.

The question for a marketing leadership team is simple to ask and often hard to answer: when the big spot airs, who owns the retail search budget that night, and do they know it is coming? Lining those two plans up is part of how we run retail search advertising alongside brand campaigns.

A0593.title: Temu’s logistics and global distribution: what the shift means
A0593.alt: Cargo ship docked beside stacked orange shipping containers and a gantry crane at a sunny port.
A0593.ttag: Temu’s logistics and global distribution: what the shift means | Kwontified
A0593.desc: Temu built its US business on duty-free parcels from China and is now adding local warehouses. How the landed-cost math works, and what it means for brands.
A0593.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 2, 2024.
A0593.body:
A platform whose whole pitch is the lowest price has started shipping some goods in a way that costs more per item. Temu built its US business on small parcels flown from China under the duty-free de minimis rule, and it now lets merchants sell from warehouses inside the country. On a cost sheet that looks like a step backward.

It is a sensible step once you price the two routes side by side. Temu’s logistics have favored direct parcels because, for cheap and light items, a parcel that pays no import duty lands cheaper than bulk stock that does. That edge comes with slow delivery, it does not reach heavier goods, and it rests on a rule that is under pressure. Local inventory buys speed and range. Brands competing with Temu should compare landed cost and delivery time item by item.

Temu’s logistics run on a customs threshold

Under the US de minimis provision, packages valued at $800 or less can enter the country without import duties. Temu and Shein together are likely responsible for more than 30% of all packages shipped to the United States daily under that provision, about 600,000 a day, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party found.

The volume has grown fast. More than 1 billion de minimis packages entered the United States in 2023, up from 134 million in 2015, Fortune reported, citing customs data.

The second route arrived in March 2024. Temu launched a model in the United States for merchants holding inventory in overseas warehouses, aimed at faster delivery and at larger items previously limited by air freight, Caixin Global reported. The shift also helps platforms respond to scrutiny of air freight and de minimis rules, the report said, noting that the Department of Homeland Security announced a crackdown on small package shipments in April.

The landed-cost arithmetic of two routes

Landed cost is everything it takes to get an item to the shopper’s door: freight, duty, warehousing and delivery. A parcel shipped directly from China under de minimis pays air freight and no duty. Stock imported in bulk pays a little freight per item, then duty, then the cost of holding it in a US warehouse and delivering it. For cheap, light items, the missing duty line is enough to make the slow route cheaper.

Take a $10 item and three ways of getting it to a US shopper.

Direct parcel under de minimisUS warehouseDirect parcel without de minimis
Item$10$10$10
Freight$3 by air$0.50 in bulk$3 by air
Duty (say a 25% rate)none$2.50$2.50
Warehousing and delivery, or customs processingnone$4$1
Landed costabout $13about $17about $16.50
Deliveryperhaps 7 to 10 daysperhaps 2 daysperhaps 7 to 10 days

With the exemption in place, the direct route is $4 cheaper and much slower. Remove the exemption, so the direct parcel pays the same $2.50 in duty plus, say, $1 in customs processing, and the gap shrinks to $0.50 while the local route still delivers days faster.

That is the logic behind the warehouses. Temu’s cost edge on small parcels is real, but it depends on a threshold that regulators are examining, and it never extended to heavy or bulky goods that are expensive to fly. Local inventory gives up part of the edge on cheap items in exchange for speed, for larger products and for a route that does not depend on the threshold.

Where brands meet Temu, item by item

The direct competition is sharpest on cheap, light products that ship easily in small parcels, where Temu’s cost edge is strongest. Heavy, bulky or higher-priced items are where it has been weakest, though local warehouses narrow that gap. Sorting a catalog along those lines shows which products face the platform’s prices head on.

Speed is the counterweight. Fast, reliable delivery is an advantage for brands with US inventory on Amazon, Walmart and their own sites. Shoppers who want a product this week often pay more for it.

Returns favor the local route too. Sending a cheap item back to China rarely makes sense, so cross-border sellers often refund without a return, which costs margin, or ask shoppers to absorb the trouble. Local inventory makes returns, exchanges and replacements far simpler. That convenience matters to shoppers buying anything they might need to send back.

The rules deserve their own model. Changes to de minimis, customs enforcement or tariffs could shift the cost balance quickly, and a brand that has worked out its price position under each scenario will not be surprised by any of them.

Temu’s local presence is also a channel. US-based sellers can now list on Temu while shipping from their own warehouses, and for some brands, especially those with value-focused products, that is worth a test, weighed against the platform’s pricing pressure.

The same pattern is playing out beyond the United States. Cross-border platforms selling into Europe face their own customs thresholds and growing scrutiny, and local warehousing offers the same trade of cost for speed there. Expect the competitive picture to shift market by market as rules change. Quality and trust remain open questions for shoppers everywhere: Temu’s low prices attract buyers, while slow delivery and uncertain quality push others back toward familiar retailers.

A workable rule: for any product under direct price pressure, write down both landed costs and both delivery times, then recalculate with the duty line restored. If you still lose on cost and win on speed, sell the speed. We run that comparison across Amazon, Walmart, Temu and a brand’s own site as part of operating marketplace channels for brands.

A0594.title: When Climate Pledge Friendly actually drives sales
A0594.alt: Kraft paper parcel tied with twine and a rosemary sprig beside amber and clear glass bottles on a rustic shelf.
A0594.ttag: When Climate Pledge Friendly actually drives sales | Kwontified
A0594.desc: Climate Pledge Friendly brings certified products extra Amazon traffic, but whether it pays depends on how shoppers in a category choose. When to certify.
A0594.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 4, 2024.
A0594.body:
Search Amazon for laundry detergent or baby wipes and some listings carry a small green leaf beside the title. That is the Climate Pledge Friendly badge, and in the categories where shoppers read ingredient lists and packaging claims before they buy, it sits exactly where they are looking. Search for a phone charger and the same leaf is easy to scroll past.

The badge does bring extra traffic to certified products. What it is worth depends on how much shoppers in a category look for sustainability cues, and on what certification costs every year. The decision on a leadership team’s table is whether that recurring cost buys a real change in how its shoppers choose. Where they compare on sustainability and the certification is affordable, it usually does. Elsewhere, Climate Pledge Friendly is a modest bonus.

What Climate Pledge Friendly delivers on average

Amazon created Climate Pledge Friendly to help shoppers find products with sustainability certifications. Products qualify through recognized third-party certifications or Amazon’s own standards, and carry a badge and leaf icon in search results and on product pages.

The program has grown quickly. As of April 2023, Amazon reported 550,000 certified products, up 72% from 2021, and 800 million badged products sold, up 121% from 2021, according to figures relayed by the textile certifier Hohenstein. Badged products received about 10% more traffic through search, product pages and recommendations, and top Amazon partners saw a 15% sales lift, the same figures showed.

Those are averages across many categories, and the 15% lift describes top partners rather than typical ones. They show that the badge can matter. They say much less about whether it will matter for a particular shelf.

Shoppers decide whether the leaf counts

In some categories a meaningful share of shoppers actively look for sustainability. Household cleaning products, baby care, personal care and apparel are common examples, where ingredients, materials and environmental claims are part of how people choose. A trusted badge helps a product stand out among similar listings there, in the same way an organic seal does on a grocery shelf.

In other categories, shoppers rarely consider sustainability when choosing. They decide on price, function, delivery speed and reviews, and a badge may earn a few extra clicks without changing the purchase.

The cost side does not vary with the shopper. Amazon does not charge to join the program, but third-party certifications usually involve fees, audits and ongoing compliance work, and a brand pays those costs every year whether or not its shoppers care. A certification renewed every year for a product whose shoppers never notice the leaf is a cost with no return.

Take a product with $200,000 in annual Amazon sales and a 30% margin, with certification costing $5,000 a year. In a category where shoppers look for sustainability, a 10% sales lift adds $20,000 in sales and $6,000 in margin, a net gain of $1,000 after the certification cost. In a category where shoppers do not care, a 2% lift adds $1,200 in margin, a net loss of $3,800. The fee is identical in both cases; only the shoppers differ.

Ways to make the certification cheaper

Many brands already hold certifications for other retailers or markets that also qualify for the badge. In that case the extra cost is small and the badge is close to free, which makes those products the natural place to start.

Amazon’s own certifications offer another path. Compact by Design, which recognizes products that ship efficiently with less packaging and air, can qualify products without a separate third-party audit for some categories. For brands already working to reduce packaging, it can be the cheapest way to earn the badge.

Range and reach change the math as well. Certifying a whole product line under one standard spreads the cost across many products, which can make the badge worthwhile even where the lift on each product is modest. Other retailers run similar programs, and one certification may support sustainability labels on several sites at once.

Price deserves caution. Some shoppers will pay a little more for a certified product, but many will not, and in categories where shoppers mostly compare on price the badge is unlikely to justify a premium. Claims need the same care. Sustainability messages should match the certification and avoid overstatement, because shoppers who care about sustainability often read claims closely, and vague or exaggerated wording can damage trust faster than the badge builds it.

The leaf is also one signal among many. Clear product information, honest descriptions of materials and packaging, and good reviews matter as much to sustainability-minded shoppers as the icon itself.

Before the certification budget is approved

  • Read the category’s reviews, questions and search terms for mentions of sustainability, materials or ingredients.
  • Put the full cost on one line: fees, audits, product changes and the time needed to stay compliant, set against a realistic lift for the category rather than the program average.
  • Start with products that already hold a qualifying certification, or that could qualify through Compact by Design.

Measurement should be planned before the badge goes live. A brand can compare a certified product’s traffic and conversion in the months before and after the badge appears, against similar uncertified products in its range over the same period. That comparison shows whether the badge is doing anything in the category, instead of leaning on program averages.

Knowing whether the leaf is doing any work on a brand’s own shelf, and weighing it against the other programs a listing can join, is part of how we run Amazon channels for brands day to day.

A0595.crumb: AI content automation for catalogs: where…
A0595.title: AI content automation for catalogs: where review pays
A0595.alt: Small white robotic arm lifting a blank card from a stack beside a brass magnifying glass on a wooden desk.
A0595.ttag: AI content automation for catalogs: where review pays | Kwontified
A0595.desc: Amazon says more than 100,000 sellers have used its AI listing tools. Why AI makes catalog drafts cheap, why review becomes the bottleneck, and where it pays.
A0595.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 9, 2024.
A0595.body:
More than 100,000 of Amazon’s selling partners had used one or more of its generative AI listing tools, and sellers accepted the suggested attributes nearly 80% of the time with minimal edits, Amazon said. If a first draft of a listing now costs almost nothing, the bottleneck in catalog work has moved somewhere else. It now sits in the step that comes after the draft.

AI content automation moves the cost of catalog work from writing to review. The draft is cheap. Checking it is not, and skipping the check is the expensive option, because errors now scale as fast as output. Brands should automate first drafts and attributes across the catalog and keep human review on claims, compliance and the details that set each product apart.

How AI content automation reached the listing page

Amazon has built generative AI directly into listing creation. Sellers can describe a product in a few words or upload an image, and the tools draft titles, descriptions and attributes. Amazon also said it had compared content its AI tools wrote with other content and found improvements in clarity, accuracy and detail.

The company added a tool that creates an Amazon listing from the URL of a product page on a seller’s own website, rolling out in English to US sellers, TechCrunch reported. Amazon encouraged sellers to review the drafted content before submitting it, Digital Commerce 360 reported. That advice is the part of the announcement most worth reading twice.

Images are on the same path. In October 2023, Amazon rolled out a tool for advertisers to generate product image backgrounds from text prompts, and said a contextual background could produce a 40% higher click-through rate than a plain white one, TechCrunch noted in the same report. Visual content, once expensive to produce for every product, is becoming cheap to vary and test.

Review becomes the step that decides the return

AI drafts titles, descriptions and attributes in seconds, so the cost of creating each listing falls toward the cost of checking it. The same speed lets a mistake spread across thousands of listings at once. The net value of automation is the drafting time saved minus the cost of the errors that reach shoppers, which makes the review step, and how well it is staffed, the thing that decides whether the switch pays.

Take a brand updating 2,000 listings. Written by hand at about 2 hours each and $40 an hour, the work costs about $160,000. With AI drafting and 20 minutes of human review per listing, it costs about $26,667, a saving of about $133,333.

Now skip the review, and say 5% of the drafts contain an error that matters, such as a wrong size, an unsupported claim or a missing compliance detail. That is 100 flawed listings. At about $500 each in lost sales, returns and fixes before the error is caught, the damage is about $50,000.

Written by handAI draft plus reviewAI draft, no review
Human time per listingabout 2 hours20 minutesnone
Labor cost at $40 an hourabout $160,000about $26,667none
Flawed listings that go livenot estimatednot estimated100 (5% of drafts)
Cost of those flaws at $500 eachnot estimatednot estimatedabout $50,000

The unreviewed route costs nearly twice what reviewing everything would have. Automation pays; unreviewed automation pays less, and carries risks that a spreadsheet does not show, such as compliance problems, damaged reviews and listings that Amazon may suppress until they are fixed.

Where people still earn their time

Repetitive work is where AI belongs. Attributes, bullet structure, size and color details, and first drafts of descriptions are well suited to it. Filling missing attributes alone can improve how products appear in filtered searches.

Risk is where a person belongs. Claims about health, safety, performance or materials, regulated categories and anything with legal exposure need someone who knows the product. AI can state things confidently that are not true. The same goes for what makes a product different. AI drafts tend toward the generic, and the details that set a product apart, such as a specific material, a design choice or a real customer benefit, often have to be added by people who know why shoppers choose it.

Source data sets the ceiling on quality. AI working from accurate product specifications produces better listings than AI working from a vague description, so a clean, complete product information record fed into the tools beats asking the AI to infer details. Ownership matters as much. Someone on the team should approve machine-drafted content before it goes live, with a checklist for the claims and details that must be verified. Without a named owner, review tends to be skipped when deadlines press.

A brand selling on Amazon, Walmart and its own site should make sure the drafted content for each channel draws on the same facts, so shoppers do not see conflicting claims. Machines are reading listings too. AI shopping assistants and search systems draw on product titles, attributes and descriptions to answer shoppers’ questions, and thin or wrong attributes can leave a product out of those answers altogether.

Conversion, return rates and search visibility, compared before and after each update built on AI drafts, product by product, show where the content improved and where it needs work.

The rule: budget the review before you budget the drafting, and never let an AI draft go live on a claim no one has checked. Building that workflow, so a catalog is ready for both shoppers and the AI systems reading it, is the work of our AI Agentic Commerce practice.

A0597.crumb: Is it too late for new brands to win on…
A0597.title: Is it too late for new brands to win on Amazon?
A0597.alt: Young staked sapling with a wire guard planted in front of mature apple trees in a sunny orchard.
A0597.ttag: Is it too late for new brands to win on Amazon? | Kwontified
A0597.desc: Established brands hold the reviews, rank and data on Amazon, and the profit gap is widening. Why it is not too late for new brands, and where they still win.
A0597.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 11, 2024.
A0597.body:
Ask a room of Amazon sellers whether 2023 was more profitable than the year before, and the answer depends on the size of the company answering. In Jungle Scout’s survey, 62% of enterprise brands reported higher profits in 2023 than in 2022. Among small and midsize sellers, only 27% did. It is not too late for new brands on Amazon, but the route in has changed. The openings now sit where established brands are weak, in narrow needs, new product forms and demand built off Amazon, and they take a funded first year to reach.

That changes the question a founder should be asking. Whether to launch matters less than where to stand, and whether the plan can carry a year of advertising and patience before the profit arrives.

How the gap for new brands on Amazon opened

Jungle Scout surveyed nearly 2,000 Amazon sellers and businesses between December 1, 2023 and January 3, 2024, from solo sellers to enterprise brands, for its State of the Amazon Seller 2024 report. The profit split by size comes from that report as summarized by Fit Small Business. The same report found that 58% of sellers became profitable in under a year, while 22% said they had never been profitable.

Those numbers describe a harder average path and larger players pulling ahead. They do not describe a closed door. Most sellers in the survey reached profit inside a year, and the ones that never did are the minority a launch plan is meant to avoid.

The marketplace rewards whoever started earlier

Amazon rewards products that already sell. Sales lift a product’s rank, rank brings visibility, visibility brings more sales and reviews, and reviews raise conversion. Each turn of that cycle helps the brand that got there first, much as the end-cap in a supermarket tends to stay with the brand that has filled it for years.

Advertising adds to the advantage. As more brands compete for the same searches, click prices rise. An established brand can pay those prices because its listings convert well and its customers come back. A new brand pays the same price for a click that converts less often, because it has fewer reviews and no reputation yet.

The data runs the same way. Established brands know which searches convert, which products sell together and how demand moves through the year, while a new brand has to learn all of it, often by spending money on what does not work.

The cycle has gaps, though, and they are predictable. Established brands tend to defend broad, high-volume searches and their best-selling products. They are slower to serve narrow needs, new product forms or shoppers who arrive from outside Amazon.

Take a new kitchen brand. Competing head-on for the search “frying pan,” it faces dozens of established brands with thousands of reviews. Focused instead on a specific need, such as a pan designed for a cooking style larger brands do not cater to, it competes in a smaller market where its product is the best answer and its reviews can quickly match the competition.

Where a new brand can still take ground

A narrow start is the strongest opening. A new brand does best where it can be the clear best option for a specific need, and a lead held there can later be widened into neighboring needs and searches.

Demand built outside Amazon changes the economics of arrival. Brands that build an audience on social media, through creators or through their own sites arrive on Amazon with shoppers already looking for them, and branded searches are cheaper to win and convert better than broad category searches.

The first year needs its own budget. Launch costs include advertising at low conversion rates, early reviews and inventory before demand is proven, and brands that plan for a year before profit are more likely to reach it than those expecting quick returns.

The product itself carries more weight than any tactic. A genuinely better or different product earns reviews and repeat purchases that no advertising budget can buy, which is why the money belongs in the product first and the marketing second.

Early reviews deserve a plan. Amazon’s Vine program lets brands give products to trusted reviewers, which can help a new listing gather honest reviews faster. Any shortcut that breaks Amazon’s rules is a bad trade, since review abuse can end a new brand before it starts. Registering the brand with Amazon from the first day gives access to better content tools, advertising options and protection against others listing on the brand’s products.

Selling beyond Amazon reduces the risk. A new brand that sells through its own site, Walmart or social commerce is less dependent on one marketplace’s rules and costs, and can test demand in more than one place. Speed helps as well: smaller brands can change products, packaging and messaging faster than large ones, and quick answers to reviews and shopper questions can turn early customers into advocates.

Waiting carries a cost that rarely shows up in a plan. Each month a brand delays, incumbents gather more reviews and data in the niches it might have entered. A brand with a clear product and a funded plan is usually better off starting in a narrow niche than waiting for a perfect moment.

The signal worth watching inside a young brand is where its first reviews come from: a broad search it is renting with ad spend, or a specific need it owns. Helping new brands pick that ground and run the first year on Amazon is part of how we operate marketplace channels for growing brands.

A0599.crumb: How creator content earns pricing power…
A0599.title: How creator content earns pricing power on TikTok Shop
A0599.alt: Smartphone on a ring light recording a frosted bottle displayed on a pink velvet riser against a blush wall.
A0599.ttag: How creator content earns pricing power on TikTok Shop | Kwontified
A0599.desc: TikTok Shop’s referral fee reached 8% in July as subsidies faded. Why creator content that explains a product holds price, and why discounts now cost more.
A0599.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. TikTok Shop
A0599.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 16, 2024.
A0599.body:
A 20% discount on TikTok Shop can take far more than 20% out of the profit on each sale. Many sellers built their early volume on the platform’s deals, when discounts were cheap to run and some were partly paid for by TikTok itself. The fee schedule has changed since then, and the arithmetic has changed with it.

Creator content is the way out. On TikTok Shop, shoppers meet a product through a creator’s video rather than a page of competing listings, so content that shows why a product is different lets a brand hold its price. With the referral fee rising to 8% and merchant subsidies pulling back, discount-driven sales cost more than they did, and full-price sales earned by content are worth more.

How creator content became the price setter on TikTok Shop

TikTok Shop launched in the United States with low fees and generous support for sellers. Its referral fee was 2% plus 30 cents per order, rising to 6% on April 1 and 8% on July 1, according to a note to sellers cited by The Information, Tubefilter reported. TikTok was also reducing merchant subsidies, and it wanted to grow its US shop business tenfold in 2024, the same report said, citing Bloomberg.

The platform’s growth has been fast. TikTok Shop counted more than 500,000 US merchants at the close of 2023, and its US sales run rate stood at $3 billion as of January, Retail Brew reported. Much of that early growth was helped by discounts, some funded by the platform, and shoppers grew used to low prices. As fees rise and subsidies fade, the question becomes what makes a shopper pay full price.

Why a discount costs more than it looks

A creator video presents one product and its benefits without the side-by-side price comparison of a search results page. Shoppers judge the price against the value the video shows, rather than against the cheaper alternatives one row down, and that is where pricing power comes from.

A discount works against it. Fees and creator commissions on TikTok Shop are percentages of the sale, so they shrink when the price drops. The cost of the product itself does not, and it takes a larger share of what is left.

Take a $40 product that costs $16 to make and deliver. At the 8% fee and an assumed 15% creator commission, a full-price sale leaves $14.80 in margin. Discount the price by 20%, to $32, and the fee and commission fall slightly while the product still costs $16. The sale leaves $8.64, and the brand would need about 71% more sales just to earn the same profit.

Discounts stay popular anyway, and the reason is a familiar pull. Units sold and revenue show up on the dashboard the next morning, while margin shows up later and in another report. A promotion that lifts orders sharply looks like a win in the first view and a loss in the second, and teams tend to trust the number they see first. As fees rise, that gap widens, because every percentage-based cost falls on a smaller margin.

That is what pricing power is worth in this example. Content that justifies $40 earns more than a discount that sells many more units at $32, and the difference grows with every increase in the fee.

Content that earns the full price

The strongest briefs to creators are about value. Videos that show the problem a product solves, how it compares with what shoppers use now and what makes it different produce shoppers who are less sensitive to price and less likely to go looking for a cheaper version elsewhere. Creators matter as much as briefs: those whose audiences trust them in a category, and who use the product honestly, persuade better than broad reach alone.

Discounts still have jobs. Launches, events and clearing inventory are reasons to discount. Routine discounts to keep volume up train shoppers to wait and erode margin as fees rise.

Commission is part of the price. Higher commissions attract more creators but take a larger share of each sale, so commissions should reward the creators who drive full-price sales and be reviewed as fees change.

Live shopping strengthens the effect. In a live stream, a creator can answer questions, demonstrate the product and respond to doubts in real time, which is hard to match on a search page and often supports full-price sales better than a short video.

Returns belong in the calculation too. Products sold on impulse through entertaining content can come back more often than products bought after careful research. Content that sets accurate expectations about size, color and use protects margin twice, supporting the price and reducing returns.

Measurement should follow margin, not orders. Sales, discount depth and margin after fees and commissions, tracked by creator and by video, show which content earns full-price sales and which only moves discounted volume.

Platform risk argues for portable advantages. The law passed in April requiring TikTok’s sale or a ban means TikTok Shop is best treated as one channel among several. Pricing power earned through content travels to other platforms more easily than volume built on platform-funded discounts. Shoppers who see a product on TikTok often search for it elsewhere, including on Amazon, where the same videos can support the same price in listings and ads.

The rule worth keeping: before approving any TikTok Shop discount, work out the margin after the fee and creator commission at the discounted price, and ask how many more sales it would take to stand still. Putting the budget behind the content that earns full price is part of how we run TikTok Shop for brands.

A0601.crumb: Outdoor’s spring season on Amazon: casual…
A0601.title: Outdoor’s spring season on Amazon: casual gear leads a soft year
A0601.alt: Two blue striped deck chairs on a sunny lawn beside a vintage cooler and canvas tote in a flowering garden.
A0601.ttag: Outdoor’s spring season on Amazon: casual gear leads a soft year | Kwontified
A0601.desc: The US outdoor market shrank 3% in 2023 as casual products gained. Why outdoor brands on Amazon should plan the year around the spring window and everyday use.
A0601.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 18, 2024.
A0601.body:
One standout in outdoor retail over the past year was not built for a mountain. Sales of Stanley’s 40-ounce Quencher, a drinks tumbler, rose 572% from April 2023 to March 2024, while snow sports equipment fell by double digits over the 2023 to 2024 season, Circana said at its outdoor retail awards, Shop Eat Surf reported. The outdoor buyer has changed from someone preparing for an expedition to someone preparing for a weekend.

That shift lands in a market that is shrinking, and in a category whose demand gathers in a few spring and early summer months. For outdoor on Amazon, the plan follows from both facts: build the year around the spring window, and sell versatility and everyday use, because technical features alone carry less of the load in a soft year.

How outdoor on Amazon changed after the pandemic boom

The outdoor market boomed during the pandemic and has been cooling since. Total US outdoor retail sales fell 3% to $27.5 billion in 2023, with declines across all three retail channels, the Outdoor Industry Association reported, drawing on Circana data. An expanding market for casual products drove changes in the sales mix, the report said.

On Amazon, the pattern is easy to recognize. Products that fit into everyday life, such as bottles, chairs, coolers and versatile apparel, are holding up better than specialized gear for serious enthusiasts. A camping chair now competes as much on whether it suits a kids’ soccer game as on its weight rating.

Listings have to follow that buyer. Casual shoppers want to see how a product fits their weekends, and images and titles built only around technical ratings speak to a smaller audience than they did while the market was growing.

A soft market makes the spring window decisive

Outdoor purchases follow the weather and the calendar. Shoppers plan camping trips, hikes, beach days and backyard summers in the spring, and they buy the gear just before they need it, so much of a year’s demand for many outdoor products arrives in a few months.

When overall demand is growing, a brand can miss part of that season and still have a good year. When demand is flat or falling, the brands that are ready for the spring window, with stock, content and advertising in place, take a larger share of a smaller market.

The casual shift reinforces the timing. Casual buyers are less likely to research technical specifications months ahead. They buy when the occasion arrives, often based on what looks useful, well reviewed and available quickly.

Take two camping chair brands. One emphasizes weight and materials and advertises evenly through the year. The other shows its chair at a backyard barbecue, a kids’ soccer game and a beach, stocks heavily for April through June and concentrates advertising in those months. In a soft market, the second brand wins more of the season’s buyers, even if the first makes the better chair.

Search behavior shifts across the same window. Early in spring, shoppers search broadly, for ideas such as camping gear or beach essentials, and closer to their trips they search for specific items. Broad searches early win consideration, and specific ones later win the sale.

Advertising follows the same curve. Budgets that rise ahead of and during the spring and early summer, when shoppers are searching, and fall back afterward put money where the demand is. Spending evenly through the year wastes money in the quiet months and leaves the weeks that decide the year underfunded.

Reviews carry extra weight with this buyer. People buying a tent or a cooler once every few years lean heavily on reviews and photos from other customers, so reviews from early-season buyers help convert the larger wave of shoppers that follows. Bundles suit the same shopper: someone preparing for a first camping trip or a beach season often wants several items at once, and sets that combine chairs, coolers or accessories make the choice easier and raise order value.

Technical gear still has a place. Serious enthusiasts remain a loyal, higher-spending audience, and brands that serve them should keep their technical content strong while adding everyday uses to reach the larger casual market.

The outdoor year, planned backward from spring

Before the season, inventory should reach Amazon’s warehouses well before shoppers start planning their summers, with listings updated first. Running out of stock in May costs sales that cannot be recovered later, because the shopper who needed a tent for June will have bought one elsewhere.

As shoppers start planning, images, titles and descriptions should show products in ordinary situations as well as on mountaintops, and advertising budgets should rise ahead of the spring and early summer searches.

At the height of the season, Prime Day falls in the middle of the outdoor season, which makes it a natural moment for deals on summer products aimed at shoppers still preparing for trips and backyard gatherings. Returns need attention now in apparel and footwear, where fit problems drive many of them and a returned jacket in June may not sell again until the next season. Clear sizing guidance and honest descriptions protect margin during the busiest months.

After summer, budgets fall back, and the quiet months become the time to review what sold, adjust the range and plan next spring’s stock, rather than discounting heavily to clear inventory.

A brand that can say, by the first warm weekend, which of its products a casual buyer would reach for and whether they are stocked, priced and visible, is ready for the year. Building that seasonal calendar, and running it through each spring, is part of the marketplace work we do for outdoor brands.

A0605.title: Back-to-school 2024: what an earlier season does to planning
A0605.alt: Olive canvas backpack, notebooks, ruler and colored pencils on a wooden desk beside a desk fan and wildflowers.
A0605.ttag: Back-to-school 2024: what an earlier season does to planning | Kwontified
A0605.desc: More than half of back-to-school shoppers began buying by early July, around Prime Day. Why the season now comes in two waves, and how to plan for both.
A0605.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 25, 2024.
A0605.body:
In the middle of July, with school still weeks away for most families, back-to-school spending online rose 216% across July 16 and 17 compared with daily levels in June, Adobe reported. Those were the two days of Prime Day, and the school season showed up inside a deal event built for everything else.

That early burst is only half of back-to-school 2024. Most families still had much of their buying left for August, when supply lists arrive and children try on clothes. The season now comes in two waves, an early one driven by deals and a later one driven by need, and brands that stock and advertise early have to keep enough budget and inventory back for the second.

How back-to-school 2024 moved into July

The season has been creeping earlier for years, and July’s deal events have pulled it further forward. As of early July, 55% of back-to-school and college shoppers had already begun buying for the coming school year. And 85% said they would use Prime Day and other retailer sales in July, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey, Vision Monday reported.

The same survey found that more than 86% still had at least half of their purchases left to make. Families with children in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $874.68, about $15 less than in 2023, with total spending expected near $39 billion.

Read together, the figures describe a household that starts early and finishes late. July’s deal events give families a reason to begin, and the school calendar decides when they finish.

Two waves that reward different things

In July, families buy what they know they will need and what is on sale: backpacks, basic supplies, electronics and clothing for growing children. Many other purchases depend on information that arrives later. Schools send supply lists, children try on clothes, and families find out what they forgot. Those purchases happen in August, closer to the first day of school, and they depend more on availability and convenience than on deals.

The July waveThe August wave
What drives itDeal events and items families know they needSupply lists, fittings and things forgotten
What it rewardsPrice and visibility during the eventsBeing in stock, ranking for specific searches, fast delivery
How shoppers searchBroadly, for backpacks or school suppliesFor specific items on their lists
What the listing should sayThe dealThe exact size, item and delivery date

The two waves often involve different products as well as different moods. A family that bought a backpack on sale in July may come back in August for an item named on the teacher’s list, and the brand that won the first purchase has no claim on the second. Searches change in the same way, so broad terms deserve budget in July and the specific ones through August.

A brand that plans for only one wave misses the other. One that spends heavily in July, runs out of popular items and pulls back its advertising may find itself absent when the need-driven shoppers arrive. One that waits for August misses the early buyers, who have already bought elsewhere.

Take a backpack brand that discounts deeply for Prime Day, sells through most of its popular colors and reduces advertising afterward. In August, when families shop with school lists in hand, its best sellers are out of stock and competitors take the searches. The July sales looked strong, but the season as a whole fell short.

Planning a season that runs from July into September

Inventory has to cover the whole season. Plans should cover the July surge and the August wave, with enough of the best sellers to stay available through the start of school, because running out in early August costs sales that discounts in July cannot make up.

The advertising budget needs the same shape. Spend should rise for the July deal events and stay strong into August, since the second wave often converts well: shoppers know exactly what they need and are ready to buy. Messages shift with the wave, from price in July to specific needs, sizes and fast delivery in August. Listings and ads should change with them rather than carrying the Prime Day copy into the weeks when shoppers want a size chart and a delivery date.

The calendar is regional, too. Schools in parts of the South begin in early August, while many in the Northeast start after Labor Day, so a brand selling nationally faces a rolling season and a reason to keep stock and advertising running longer. College shoppers add a third pattern. Students heading to campus often buy later and in larger amounts, for dorm furnishings and electronics, which can extend the season into late August and September.

Price sensitivity remains high. With families planning to spend slightly less than in 2023, value messages and bundles that cover several needs at once can help win both waves.

The first wave also feeds the second. Families who buy in July leave reviews and photos by early August, just as the need-driven shoppers arrive, so reviews from early buyers improve conversion for the busier weeks that follow. Returns rise with clothing and shoes, since children’s sizes are hard to judge in advance, and clear size guides and easy exchanges protect margin at the peak.

The useful question for a team reviewing its July numbers is what share of its best sellers will still be in stock, and still advertised, on the second Monday of August. Planning the whole season, not just the event that opens it, is part of how we run Amazon, Walmart and Target channels for brands.
