A0606.title: Prime Day 2024 results, measured against our forecast
A0606.alt: Brown paper parcel tied with twine, topped with a brass caliper and lavender, near a fruit bowl and old books.
A0606.ttag: Prime Day 2024 results, measured against our forecast | Kwontified
A0606.desc: Prime Day 2024 spending beat our reach case. What public data can and cannot grade yet, and how brands should separate added sales from pulled-forward sales.
A0606.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 30, 2024.
A0606.body:
A forecast that comes in just above its own highest range sounds like a forecaster’s good week. Our June forecast set three ranges for US online spending over the two event days. They were about $13.2 billion in the conservative case, $13.6 billion in the standard case and $14 billion in the reach case, scaled from 2023’s $12.7 billion. The market beat all three.

That is the easy number to grade, and the least useful one for a brand. A market total says how many shoppers turned up across every retailer; it says nothing about what any one listing paid to win them or gave up afterward. Prime Day 2024 results that matter to an individual brand, its click premiums, its promoted-product lift and the demand it pulled forward from the weeks after, show up only in its own data and only over several weeks. The honest way to grade the event is against the forecast ranges, with the post-event dip netted out first.

How Prime Day 2024 results measured up so far

US online spending across retailers reached $14.2 billion over July 16 and 17, up 11% from a year earlier, Adobe reported. Our reach case assumed 10% growth, so we underestimated the market by about $200 million, or one percentage point of growth.

Other early signals were mixed. Amazon said the event set records for sales and items sold, though the average household spent about $152 on Amazon during the event, down slightly from 2023, according to Numerator data cited by Transport Topics. On the advertising side, Sponsored Products spending rose about 20% from a year earlier and click prices rose more than 10%, Pacvue reported.

Two forces probably explain the stronger market. Back-to-school shopping arrived early, with related online spending up 216% during the event compared with daily levels in June, Adobe said. And the event drew shoppers across retailers, since Walmart and Target ran their own sales in the same weeks. Neither was fully reflected in our June ranges.

Why most of the forecast cannot be graded yet

Market spending is measured across all retailers within days. A brand’s event result depends on its own click prices, its deals and the sales it borrowed from the weeks after, and those appear only once post-event sales return to a normal level. True added sales equal the event lift minus the post-event shortfall, both measured against the same normal baseline.

That limits what can be graded so soon after the event. Our click-price ranges compared event days with a normal week. Pacvue’s figure compares event days with the same event a year earlier. The baselines differ, so the public number can neither confirm nor reject our click ranges. The same is true of promoted-product lift and deal share, which vary by brand.

A brand can grade its own click premium now, by comparing its event-day cost per click with its own normal week, and it can set its promoted lift against its own baseline. What it cannot do yet is net out the weeks after, and that is the part that decides whether the event paid.

Go back to the brand from our June forecast, which sold $10,000 a day of a promoted line in a normal week. Say it sold $27,000 a day during the event, just below our standard case of three times normal. The two event days added $34,000 above normal.

Then say its sales ran 10% below normal for the 14 days after the event, as shoppers who had stocked up stayed away. That shortfall is $14,000. The true added sales are $20,000, and about 41% of the apparent event lift was borrowed from the weeks after.

The event still paid for this brand, by much less than the event days suggested. Reported on the event days alone, it would have looked about 70% more successful than it was. The full picture will not be clear until mid-August.

Grading your own Prime Day

The first thing to settle is the baseline. The average daily sales from the weeks before early deals began make a fairer base than the pre-event week, which is often depressed as shoppers wait.

The dip has to run its course next. Daily sales tracked for three to four weeks after the event, until they return to the baseline, show the shortfall to subtract. Replenishment categories, such as pet food and household supplies, usually show the deepest dips.

Margin comes last, and decides the grade. Discounts, fees and the higher click costs come off the added sales, so the result reflects profit; a strong revenue result can still be a weak profit result.

Products without deals deserve their own review. Our forecast warned that they would face discounted rivals while paying more for each click, and any sales they lost during the event count against its overall result. Lower spending per household alongside record items sold also suggests shoppers bought cheaper items or took deeper deals, so a falling average order value is worth checking even where unit sales rose.

Our miss on market spending carries its own lesson. Shoppers responded to deals more strongly than sentiment surveys suggested, which is worth remembering when planning the October event and the holidays. Cautious shoppers still buy when the deal is right. We will publish a fuller review once post-event data has settled, including what the event revealed about how brands and retailers behaved.

The rule for this week: do not grade Prime Day until the dip has ended, and grade it on margin against your own baseline, not on the market’s 11%. Grading every tentpole event that way is the measurement work we do around Prime Day advertising for brands.

A0607.title: Prime Day 2024 lessons: what shoppers, rivals and brands did
A0607.alt: Three shop windows on a stone street filled with stacked red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes.
A0607.ttag: Prime Day 2024 lessons: what shoppers, rivals and brands did | Kwontified
A0607.desc: Prime Day 2024 showed shoppers stocking up on staples, rivals running their own sales and brands crowding Amazon’s auctions. What that means for planning July.
A0607.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 1, 2024.
A0607.body:
Among the top sellers of Prime Day 2024, alongside Amazon’s Fire TV Stick, were protein shakes and Glad trash bags, according to Numerator, which tracked 35,588 households. Trash bags and protein shakes are not impulse upgrades. Households buy them every few weeks, and a list of top sellers that includes them describes shoppers using the event to fill the cupboard at a discount.

That is the first of three behaviors that now define the event. Shoppers stock up on staples as well as buying upgrades. Rival retailers have turned Prime Day into a July season, even as Amazon’s share of online spending still jumps for 48 hours. And brands concentrate their advertising in the same window. Brands should plan Prime Day as part of a multi-retailer July season, and treat staples sales during the event as partly borrowed from the weeks after.

How the Prime Day 2024 lessons took shape

The headline numbers were strong. US shoppers spent $14.2 billion online across all retailers during the two days, up 11%, according to Adobe, and Amazon said the event set a record for items sold, Bloomberg reported in a story carried by Transport Topics.

The details were more revealing. Numerator put the typical household’s Amazon spend over the two days at about $152, a little below its 2023 figure. Record item counts with a smaller basket per home point the same way as the trash bags: shoppers bought more things, and cheaper ones, at deal prices. Upgrades still sold, and the Fire TV Stick on the same list is a reminder that the event does both jobs at once.

Stocking up has a consequence that does not show in the event-day numbers. A household that buys three months of trash bags in July does not buy them in August, so for staples brands a large part of the event’s sales is borrowed from the weeks that follow.

Who captures the July shopper

Walmart ran its Walmart Deals event from July 8 to 11, and Target ran Target Circle Week from July 7 to 13. Adobe measures spending across all retailers precisely because rivals offer their own deals and shoppers compare sites, Bloomberg noted. The result is a July shopping season with several hosts.

Amazon still captures the peak. It takes about 60% of all online spending on Prime Day, compared with about 40% on a typical day, according to eMarketer, as cited in the same report. Shoppers spread their buying across retailers over the month, then concentrate on Amazon for 48 hours. Each retailer is competing for the same household’s July budget, and Amazon’s event concentrates that budget into its own two days.

For brands, the question is where they stand when that money moves. A brand that sells only on Amazon catches the peak and misses the rest of the season. One that sells across retailers can catch both, and is less exposed to a single host’s terms.

The membership base behind the peak keeps growing. With about 180 million Prime members in the United States as of March, up 8% from a year earlier according to Consumer Intelligence Research Partners, as cited in the same report, the audience for Amazon’s exclusive deals keeps getting larger.

Brands crowded into the same two days

Pacvue’s figures show advertisers leaning in hard: average daily Sponsored Products spend during the event was about 20% above the prior year’s event, and the price of a click climbed by more than 10%, Pacvue reported. When many brands bid for the same shoppers in the same 48 hours, the cost of reaching them rises for everyone, and the higher prices flow to the platform that runs the auction.

Take a household cleaning brand that sells only on Amazon, discounts heavily for Prime Day and spends most of its July advertising budget in the two event days. Its event sales look excellent. Its customers stocked up, though, so August sales fall, and it was absent from Walmart and Target when shoppers browsed their deals earlier in the month. Over the full season, it did less well than its event days suggested.

What July should look like next year

Planning across retailers is the first change. Brands selling on Walmart and Target should run deals during those retailers’ events as well as during Prime Day, because many shoppers compare prices across sites before buying, and a brand missing from one retailer’s event loses those shoppers to rivals.

Staples and upgrades need different yardsticks. For staples, a post-event dip is likely, and the event deserves to be judged over six to eight weeks. For upgrades, such as electronics and small appliances, the event more often brings genuinely new purchases.

Advertising can be spread across the month. Shoppers can be reached earlier in July, when competition is lower and click prices are cheaper, with part of the budget saved for the peak. Subscribe and Save offers a way to keep the stock-up buyer. A shopper who discovers a staples brand during the event can be encouraged to subscribe, which turns a one-time stock-up into repeat purchases and changes the event from borrowing future sales to securing them.

The October event will test these lessons again. The question to put to a team before it is which products gained new customers in July and which mainly sold to shoppers who would have bought anyway. That answer decides which products deserve the deepest discounts next time and which can hold their price. Working through it across Amazon, Walmart and Target is the cross-retailer planning we do when we operate marketplace channels for brands.

A0609.crumb: Amazon’s Q2 2024 results: what ad revenue…
A0609.title: Amazon’s Q2 2024 results: what ad revenue says about clicks
A0609.alt: Row of stacked cardboard boxes lined up beside a steel turnstile in a sunlit lobby with a copper wall.
A0609.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2024 results: what ad revenue says about clicks | Kwontified
A0609.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 20% in Q2 2024, twice its sales growth. Why the auction is more crowded, why average cost per sale held, and who paid more.
A0609.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 6, 2024.
A0609.body:
Advertising grew about twice as fast as everything else Amazon sold in the second quarter of 2024: ad revenue up 20%, total sales up 10%. Read quickly, that sounds like brands paying more for every sale they win on Amazon. For the average advertiser, they were not. Click prices rose, conversion rates rose about as fast, and the cost of winning a sale held steady.

The average hides the real result. Amazon’s Q2 2024 results describe a more crowded auction, and in a crowded auction the brands whose conversion kept pace paid no more per sale while the brands whose conversion stalled paid more for every order. The number to check is a brand’s own cost per order, not the market’s click price.

How Amazon’s Q2 2024 results compared ad revenue with sales

Amazon’s advertising business brought in $12.77 billion in the second quarter, up 20% from a year earlier but short of analysts’ estimates of $13 billion, CNBC reported. Total sales were $147.98 billion, also slightly below estimates.

Total sales grew 10%, from $134.4 billion a year earlier, Storyboard18 reported. Advertising grew about twice as fast. Set against ad revenue of $10.6 billion in the second quarter of 2023, advertising rose from about 7.9% of Amazon’s sales to about 8.6%.

Growth slowed from the first quarter, when Amazon’s advertising revenue had grown 24% to $11.8 billion, Motley Fool reported. A drop to 20% is still fast growth, though it suggests the pace at which advertisers are adding budget has eased slightly.

Part of the ad growth now comes from Prime Video, which began showing ads in January, Variety reported. Video ads are not search clicks, so growth in sponsored search ads alone may be somewhat lower than 20%. The company was also cautious about the months ahead. Amazon said consumers remained careful with spending, and its forecast for the third quarter fell below Wall Street targets, Reuters reported, as cited by Gigazine.

Why a pricier auction need not mean a pricier sale

When ad revenue grows faster than sales, advertisers are spending more for each dollar of sales on the platform, which pushes click prices up. The cost of a sale, though, is the click price divided by the conversion rate. If conversion rises as fast as click prices, the cost per sale stays flat, and only brands whose conversion lags see it rise. A rising click price, on its own, says little about whether advertising got more expensive for any particular brand.

Market data from the same quarter fits that pattern. Retail media click prices rose 12% from a year earlier in the second quarter, while conversion rates also grew 12% and total conversions grew 18%, according to Skai’s quarterly trends report.

Take a brand paying $1.00 a click and converting 10% of clicks, a cost of $10 per order. Its click price rises 12% to $1.12.

Click priceConversion rateCost per order
Before$1.0010%$10
Conversion kept pace$1.1211.2%$10
Conversion stood still$1.1210%$11.20

Same auction, same click price, two different businesses. Some brands improved their listings, reviews and targeting and kept their costs flat. Others paid the higher click prices without converting better, and their cost per sale rose. When everyone’s click prices rise together, conversion is what separates the brands that hold their costs from the rest.

Reading the crowded auction from your own account

Cost per order is the ratio to watch. Click prices are rising for everyone; whether a brand’s cost per order rises depends on its own conversion. Better images, clearer titles, stronger reviews and accurate attributes raise conversion and offset rising click prices, and each improvement compounds across every ad dollar while also lifting sales from shoppers who arrive without clicking an ad.

Where conversion is weakest, costs rise first. Searches and placements with low conversion become more expensive as click prices climb, and trimming them before cutting broad budgets keeps the remaining money where each click is most likely to become a sale.

Amazon is not the only crowded auction. Walmart’s advertising business grew 26% in its most recent quarter, according to Walmart, faster than Amazon’s. As budgets spread across retailers, comparing cost per sale between them shows where a brand’s conversion is strongest. Measurement windows matter in that comparison. Amazon attributes sales to ads over a set period after a click, so cost per sale depends on that window, and a comparison across retailers with different windows will favor whichever network counts more sales.

Video changes the mix. With Prime Video ads available, some advertisers are shifting money from search to video, which may ease pressure on some search auctions while adding a channel that is harder to measure directly. Holdout tests tell more about it than attributed sales alone, because a video viewer who later buys through a search ad can be counted by either channel, or by both.

The second half deserves caution. If shoppers stay careful, conversion gains may slow while click prices keep rising, especially around the October event and the holidays. That is the combination that turns a flat cost per sale into a rising one. It tends to show up in weekly numbers well before it shows up in a quarterly review, which is why bids are best adjusted before rising costs eat into margin rather than after.

The rule for the fourth quarter: watch cost per order weekly, and when it rises faster than click prices, fix conversion before raising bids. Managing Amazon advertising on cost per sale rather than click price is how we run retail media for brands.

A0610.crumb: Pet supplies on Amazon: where the growth…
A0610.title: Pet supplies on Amazon: where the growth really comes from
A0610.alt: Dog bed, ceramic bowls, leather leash and a burlap food sack by an open door to a sunny garden.
A0610.ttag: Pet supplies on Amazon: where the growth really comes from | Kwontified
A0610.desc: US pet spending will grow about 2% in 2024, yet pet keeps growing online. Why the reorder decides which brands win on Amazon, and how to defend it.
A0610.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 8, 2024.
A0610.body:
A pet store can keep the dog food at the back, so every regular customer walks past the treats, the toys and the beds to reach the bag she came for. Amazon has no back of the store. A household that has bought the same bag before can reorder it from its order history without seeing anything else on the way.

In a market that is barely growing, the difference matters. US pet spending is forecast to rise about 2% in 2024, yet pet remains a growth category online, because most of the money goes on food and health products that households buy again and again. For a brand selling pet supplies on Amazon, growth comes from winning those repeat orders away from stores and rivals, which makes subscriptions, early reviews and the defense of each customer’s next order worth more than any single sale.

How pet supplies on Amazon became a repeat business

It is a large, mature market. US pet industry spending reached $147 billion in 2023 and is forecast to reach $150.6 billion in 2024, according to the American Pet Products Association. That forecast implies growth of about 2.4%.

Most of that money buys things that run out. Pet food and treats accounted for $64.4 billion of 2023 spending, and supplies, live animals and over-the-counter medicine for another $32 billion, the association said. About 66% of US households, or 86.9 million, own a pet: a very large base of customers who place the same order every few weeks.

Chewy, the online pet leader, shows what that looks like for a retailer built on it. Its first-quarter net sales were $2.88 billion, up 3.1%, according to the company’s first-quarter results. Customers on its Autoship subscription accounted for $2.2 billion, or 77.6% of sales, and about 85% of sales came from consumables and health products, the company told analysts, Pet Food Processing reported. Total sales barely moved, yet most of them arrived on a schedule the customer had already set.

A pet household is worth years of orders

Pet owners are creatures of habit, and with good reason. A household with a dog buys food every few weeks, often the same brand for years. Once it has settled on what to buy and where, it rarely changes without a trigger: a price jump, a stockout or a change in the animal’s health.

Take a household buying a $50 bag of dog food every six weeks. That is about 8.7 orders and roughly $433 a year, or about $867 over two years. The brand that wins the first order has a claim on every reorder that follows, for as long as nothing gives the household a reason to look elsewhere.

With that arithmetic in mind, a brand should read its advertising and its discounts differently. Paying more to win a first order can pay back many times over if the customer stays. Losing a customer to a rival or to a store costs every future order, not just one sale.

The same arithmetic explains how a slow market can produce a fast-growing online channel. Part of the growth online is households moving their repeat purchases out of stores, and each household that moves brings years of orders with it. Chewy’s results show the same pattern from the other side. Its sales grew slowly overall, but subscriptions grew faster, because existing customers kept buying while new ones were harder to win.

Where pet brands win or lose the next order

The reorder is the moment to protect, and Subscribe and Save is the simplest protection Amazon offers. It lets shoppers set up regular deliveries, often with a discount, so the next order happens without a fresh search. Consumable products belong in it, and listings and advertising should make the option easy to see.

Advertising targets need the same long view. For food and treats, a brand can accept a higher cost for a first order, as long as repeat purchases make up for it, and that only works if someone tracks how often first-time buyers come back. Rivals, meanwhile, advertise on a brand’s own name and product pages, and a loyal customer is most exposed at the moment she searches to reorder. Protecting branded searches keeps her from being picked off at that moment.

Events work differently in pet. Prime Day and Amazon’s Pet Day bring discounts that encourage stocking up, and as we have argued before, that can pull orders forward rather than add new ones. In pet, the better use of an event is to win new subscribers, not to sell extra bags to the households that would have bought anyway.

Trust carries extra weight with pet owners. They worry about ingredients, safety and how their animals will react to something new. Clear ingredient information and strong reviews lower the risk of switching, and the risk of switching is the main barrier to winning a new customer.

The practical details of a heavy, recurring purchase decide a surprising number of reorders. Several bag sizes and multipacks let households match their usage and stock up when it suits them, and larger sizes often carry better margins while cutting the number of reorder moments at which a rival can step in. A household that runs out of food before the next delivery arrives may buy elsewhere and never come back, so healthy inventory in Amazon’s warehouses, especially for best sellers, protects the subscription base.

Packaging matters too: bags that split in transit and litter that leaks bring complaints and returns, and packaging designed for shipping rather than for a store shelf protects both reviews and margin.

Health products are a growing part of the mix. Over-the-counter medicine, supplements and wellness products often sell at higher prices and are bought regularly, which makes them valuable for brands that can earn a pet owner’s trust.

Brands no longer compete for pet shoppers on Amazon alone. Chewy has built its own sponsored ads business, so brands now bid for the same households on several retail media networks. Comparing the cost of a new customer across those networks shows where the next dollar should go.

A pet business planned around the reorder asks different questions at the planning table. Instead of how many bags the next event will move, the leadership team asks how many households the brand added to its regular rotation each quarter. It also asks how many it lost to the store down the road or to a rival’s ad at the moment of reorder. Those are the numbers we build Amazon channel management for pet brands around.

A0611.crumb: Q4 2024 budget: how to phase spend from…
A0611.title: Q4 2024 budget: how to phase spend from October to Cyber Week
A0611.alt: Four glass jars filling up with coins in rising order on a windowsill between a small pumpkin and a wrapped gift.
A0611.ttag: Q4 2024 budget: how to phase spend from October to Cyber Week | Kwontified
A0611.desc: Cyber Week took about 17% of 2023 holiday online spending in five days, and 2024 has five fewer days before Christmas. How to phase a Q4 budget by demand.
A0611.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 13, 2024.
A0611.body:
Cyber Week lasted five of the 61 days in the 2023 holiday season and carried about 17% of its online spending. A budget spread evenly across those 61 days gives each of the five busiest days the same money as a quiet weekday in early November. The 2024 calendar makes that mismatch worse, with five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas.

The answer is to phase a Q4 2024 budget by each period’s share of demand per day, not by the calendar, and to keep a reserve for the days that run hot. The arithmetic behind it is one line: a period’s daily budget is the total budget times the period’s share of demand, divided by the number of days it lasts.

How Q4 2024 budget planning starts from the 2023 curve

US shoppers spent $222.1 billion online from November 1 to December 31, 2023, up 4.9%, according to Adobe data that Chain Store Age reported. November accounted for $123.5 billion and December for $98.6 billion.

The peak was sharp and short. Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, brought in $38 billion, up 7.8%, according to Adobe. Cyber Monday alone took $12.4 billion, Black Friday $9.8 billion and Thanksgiving Day $5.6 billion.

Set side by side, those figures put about 17% of the season’s online spending in about 8% of its days. Per day, Cyber Week ran at roughly twice the season’s average rate.

The calendar for 2024 is tighter. Thanksgiving falls on November 28, five days later than in 2023, which leaves 27 days between Thanksgiving and Christmas compared with 32 the year before.

Why an even split runs out of money on Black Friday

An even split feels safe, because no single day can blow through the budget. That same safety means the plan never spends enough on the days when shoppers are most ready to buy.

Take a brand whose sales follow the market pattern, planning $60,000 for November and December. Its Cyber Week share, about 17%, is roughly $10,300 across five days, or about $2,050 a day. The other 56 days share the remaining $49,700, about $890 a day.

PlanDaysBudgetPer day
Phased: Cyber Weekfive$10,300$2,050
Phased: all other days56$49,700$890
Even split61$60,000$980

On the even plan, every day gets about $980. The brand would overspend on quiet days and run out of budget by midday on Black Friday, the day the phased plan was built to fund.

A shorter December changes the arithmetic again. With five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas, the same December budget has fewer days in which to be spent. Daily budgets have to rise, or part of the money will go unspent before the gifting deadline.

Phasing commits money, a reserve keeps it free

Phasing and a reserve pull in opposite directions, and both have a real case. Phasing commits money to the days the curve says will matter, which is where demand should be. A reserve keeps money uncommitted for the days that beat the curve, at the cost of earning nothing while it waits. A curve built from 2023 describes the market, not your brand’s Black Friday in 2024.

The numbers lean toward a modest reserve. Keep about 10% to 15% of the budget unallocated and release it on days that run hot, as with Prime Day. Black Friday and Cyber Monday often exceed plans, and running out of budget on those days costs sales that cannot be recovered later.

Start the phasing from your own sales pattern, not the market’s. Market data shows the shape of the season, but categories differ: gifts peak later, and everyday staples may peak during deal events. Calculate each period’s share of your own Q4 2023 sales and phase the 2024 budget to match.

October needs its own line. Amazon held a Prime Big Deal Days event in October 2023, and if it repeats the event in 2024, holiday shopping will start early. Set aside budget for it once dates are announced, but keep the bulk of the quarter’s spend for November and December, when demand is highest.

What changes the plan once the season starts

Click prices rise with demand. During Cyber Week more advertisers compete for the same shoppers, so each dollar buys fewer clicks. Higher daily budgets are still worth it if conversion rises, as it usually does on peak days, which is why cost per order, not spend, is the number to watch each day.

Inventory sets the ceiling on all of this. A bigger Cyber Week budget only works if the products are in stock, so check that holiday inventory will reach Amazon’s warehouses in time, and trim budgets for products that may sell out.

Walmart’s and Target’s curves look similar, but they run their own holiday events, sometimes on different dates. A brand selling across retailers should phase each retailer’s budget to that retailer’s own event calendar rather than copying the Amazon plan.

Phasing is a starting point, not a fixed schedule. From October onward, compare actual sales and cost per order with the plan each week, and move money between periods when demand runs ahead of or behind it. After Christmas demand drops but does not vanish: gift card redemptions and exchanges after returns create a smaller wave in the last week of December, which deserves a modest budget rather than none.

A day’s budget should follow its share of demand, not its share of the calendar, and anything you are unsure of belongs in the reserve rather than in an even split. Building that curve from a brand’s own Q4 history is where we start when we phase Q4 retail media budgets across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0613.crumb: Office products on Amazon: a category…
A0613.title: Office products on Amazon: a category worth a second look
A0613.alt: Wooden desk organizer holding notebooks, pencils, pens and clips beside a jade plant and mug on a rustic desk.
A0613.ttag: Office products on Amazon: a category worth a second look | Kwontified
A0613.desc: Office Depot ran 58 fewer stores and its sales fell 12%, while office products led Prime Day’s day-two sales gains. Why the category deserves a second look.
A0613.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 15, 2024.
A0613.body:
When an office superstore closes, the need it served stays behind. The people who bought printer paper, toner and labels there still run out of them, and they still have to buy them somewhere. Only the shelf has gone.

For a brand that has sold through those shelves for years, that raises a practical question for the leadership team: keep treating Amazon as an afterthought, or fund it as the place the demand is going. The evidence leans toward the second. Office products look like a dull, shrinking category, but the shrinking is happening in stores. Brands that treat office products on Amazon as a growth opportunity, with complete listings, subscriptions for supplies and attention to business buyers, can pick up the demand that stores are losing.

How office products on Amazon came back into view

The store channel is where the category is contracting. Office Depot’s division sales fell 12% to $799 million in the second quarter, and comparable store sales fell 7%, as it operated 58 fewer stores than a year earlier, the ODP Corporation said in its second-quarter results. The company ended the quarter with 894 stores, Digital Commerce 360 noted, and ODP’s total sales fell 10% to $1.7 billion.

Not all of that decline comes from shoppers moving online. ODP pointed to cautious business spending and softer consumer activity, and said its own online sales also fell. But each closed store removes an option from its neighborhood, and shoppers who still need paper, ink and desk supplies will buy them somewhere.

The category also showed how strongly it responds to a deal. On the second day of Prime Day, office products saw the largest increase in average sales of any category Pacvue tracked, up 136%, according to Pacvue’s Prime Day review.

Why demand follows a closing store online

Office supplies are practical, repeat purchases. People buy them when they run out, not because they enjoy browsing, and when the nearby store closes the easiest substitute is to order online, often from a marketplace that already holds the household’s account.

Home offices add to that demand. Many people now work from home at least part of the time, and they buy supplies, chairs, desks and organizers for their own use rather than relying on an employer’s supply cupboard. Those purchases tend to happen online. Small businesses behave much the same way. Without a corporate purchasing contract, a small office buys supplies the way a household does, quickly and online, choosing reliable delivery and good prices, and once it finds a dependable source it tends to reorder from it again and again.

In a superstore, a brand’s paper sat on a shelf any shopper walking the aisle could see. On Amazon, a shopper filters by size, count or compatibility, and a listing without those details never enters the results at all. The category’s dull reputation helps here: fewer brands compete hard for attention in office products than in beauty or electronics, so a brand willing to invest in good listings and advertising may find less crowded searches than in more fashionable categories.

Take a brand selling printer paper and filing supplies that has relied on office superstores for years and treated Amazon as an afterthought. As stores close, its store sales fall while shoppers search for the same products online, where its listings are thin and its advertising minimal. A competitor that invested online picks up the customers the store lost, and keeps them as they reorder.

The decision in front of the brand team

The debate in the planning meeting can look like a channel question: protect the superstore relationship, or move money to Amazon. The more useful version asks where the brand’s existing buyers will go when their store closes, and whether the brand will be there to meet them.

The listing is where a yes begins. Office products are bought on specifications (sizes, counts, compatibility and materials), and complete, accurate attributes help products appear in filtered searches and reduce returns. Compatibility deserves particular care, because ink, toner and accessories that do not fit a shopper’s printer or device come back quickly, so clear compatibility information on every listing protects both margin and reviews.

Reordering should take no effort. Paper, ink, labels and other consumables suit Subscribe and Save, and multipacks that match how households and small offices actually use them make the next order easier than a trip to a store. Business buyers want more: bulk pricing, invoices and reliable delivery. A brand’s offers on Amazon should work for business purchasing, with clear pack sizes and quantity discounts.

Private label competes for the same shopper. Amazon and other retailers sell their own basic office supplies at low prices. A branded product needs a clear reason to be chosen, such as better quality, a distinctive design or a specific use, and the listing should make that reason obvious. A strong record of reviews about durability and reliability helps a branded product justify a higher price in a category full of low-priced alternatives. Bundles help too: sets for a new home office or a classroom, combining items buyers would otherwise purchase separately, give shoppers convenience and give the brand a reason to be chosen over single-item rivals.

Advertising should start with specific searches. Shoppers looking for office products often search for exact items, such as a particular pen type or label size. Those searches convert well and cost less than broad terms, which makes them the natural place to begin before expanding.

The calendar brings two peaks: back-to-school, when students and parents buy supplies, and January, when offices restock for the new year. Budgets and inventory should follow both. Furniture needs its own plan, because desks and chairs are larger, higher-priced purchases that depend on reviews, photos and assembly information, and they carry higher shipping costs that belong in the price.

A brand team that takes the second look ends up asking a different question at the next planning meeting. Not how much the superstore will order for back-to-school, but how many of the shoppers it used to serve are now searching on Amazon, and what they find when they do. Answering that question is the day-to-day work of running office products on Amazon, Walmart and Target that we do for brands.

A0615.crumb: Why brand still matters in unbranded…
A0615.title: Why brand still matters in unbranded search on Amazon
A0615.alt: Glass jars of pickled vegetables and dried herbs on a wooden pantry shelf against a navy wall.
A0615.ttag: Why brand still matters in unbranded search on Amazon | Kwontified
A0615.desc: About 77% of Amazon searches name no brand, yet shoppers still click names they know. How recognition cuts the cost of winning a generic search on Amazon.
A0615.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 20, 2024.
A0615.body:
About 77% of Amazon searches name no brand at all. Taken at face value, the figure makes brand building a sideshow on Amazon: if shoppers type a product rather than a name, the auction should reward bids and relevance, and reputation should hardly matter. It does not work out that way. Shoppers scanning generic results still favor names they recognize.

Recognition works through two numbers every advertiser already watches. At the same bid, a known brand earns more clicks per impression and more orders per click, so it pays less for each sale. That makes brand building one of the cheapest ways to improve performance advertising on Amazon, not a separate activity that competes with it for budget.

How unbranded search came to dominate Amazon

Most Amazon shoppers search for what they need rather than for who makes it, and let the results guide them. In June 2024, 22.9% of Amazon US searches included a brand name, up slightly from 22.6% a year earlier, according to PMG’s analysis. That leaves about 77% of searches unbranded, although PMG found the branded share rising more sharply in popular categories.

The way brands advertise has followed that split. Because most searches are generic, much of the budget goes to winning them, and many brands treat awareness as a separate activity that is harder to measure. The two are closer than the budget lines suggest. A generic search is not a blank slate for the shopper, who arrives with memories of brands seen elsewhere, and those memories shape what she clicks.

Why recognition lowers the cost of a generic sale

On an unbranded search, shoppers compare several similar products in a few seconds, and recognition tilts that comparison. At the same bid, a known brand gets more clicks per impression and more orders per click. That lowers its cost per order, and because Amazon rewards products that sell, it also improves the brand’s organic rank for the same search.

Take two water bottle brands, each bidding $1.20 a click on the same unbranded search. The known brand earns a 0.6% click-through rate and converts 15% of clicks. The unknown brand earns 0.4% and converts 10%. Over 10,000 impressions the results look like this:

Over 10,000 impressionsKnown brandUnknown brand
Click-through rate0.6%0.4%
Clicks6040
Conversion rate15%10%
Orders94
Ad cost$72$48
Cost per orderabout $8about $12

The known brand wins more than twice as many orders at two-thirds the cost per order, from an identical bid. Nothing in its campaign settings explains the gap. The difference sits in the shopper’s head before the search begins.

Over time, the gap compounds. More orders improve the known brand’s sales rank, which earns it more organic visibility, which brings more orders without any additional ad spend.

How brands should build recognition that pays

Treat recognition as an input to search performance, and invest in it where it changes how shoppers choose in generic results.

Consistency comes first. Packaging, logo, product names and main images should look the same across Amazon, social media and stores, because recognition depends on shoppers seeing the same thing repeatedly. A product that looks different everywhere earns less of it.

Much of that recognition gets built off Amazon. Social media, creators, television and stores create the memories shoppers bring to a generic search. The payoff often shows up on Amazon as higher click-through and conversion on unbranded terms, even when no report credits it to the channel that created it.

That makes the link worth measuring directly. Track click-through and conversion rates on your most important unbranded searches over time. Rising rates at stable prices suggest that brand building is working, even when branded search volume barely moves.

Amazon’s own brand ads help on the same searches. Sponsored Brands ads show a logo, headline and several products together at the top of results, building recognition on the generic searches where most shoppers start. Reviews do similar work: a product with many strong reviews signals that other shoppers chose it, which functions much like a familiar name for a shopper who has never heard of the company.

Branded search is still worth defending, even with unbranded searches in the majority. As awareness grows, more shoppers search by name, and competitors often bid on those searches. Protecting branded terms keeps the demand that brand building creates.

New brands are not locked out. A brand without recognition can borrow some of its benefits through strong reviews, clear main images, distinctive design and a price that invites a first try. Each early customer with a good experience adds to the recognition that later shoppers bring.

AI shopping assistants raise the stakes. Amazon made its Rufus assistant available to all US customers on July 12, Bloomberg reported. A shopper who asks an assistant for a recommendation may get a short list rather than a page of results, and brands that are well known, well reviewed and clearly described are more likely to appear on it.

Budgets should reflect that link as well. When brand building lifts unbranded performance, part of the return from awareness spending shows up in search results, so a brand deciding how much to spend on awareness should count that effect, not just direct sales from the awareness channel. The effect varies by category: recognition matters most where shoppers care about quality, safety or style, and price may dominate in simple commodity categories.

The test is simple to run on your own account. If click-through and conversion on your top generic searches rise while prices hold steady, the brand spending is paying for itself inside the search results, whatever the awareness report says. Reading those two numbers alongside the awareness plan is how we run Amazon advertising and brand building as one budget.

A0616.crumb: How manufacturer brands from China built…
A0616.title: How manufacturer brands from China built loyalty on Amazon
A0616.alt: Wall of stacked sage green boxes in a sunlit brick loft with tall factory windows and potted plants.
A0616.ttag: How manufacturer brands from China built loyalty on Amazon | Kwontified
A0616.desc: Nearly half of Amazon’s top US sellers are China-based, and the best now run real brands. How they won loyalty through reviews, and what older brands can learn.
A0616.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 22, 2024.
A0616.body:
In a store, a brand’s heritage is visible before the shopper reads a word: the shelf position, the end-cap, the packaging that has sat in the same aisle for years. On an Amazon results page, all of that history shrinks to a thumbnail, a star rating and a review count, the same things every rival gets.

That flattened shelf is where China-based sellers came to make up nearly half of Amazon’s top US sellers, and where the best of them turned from anonymous factories into brands that shoppers return to. They owned product development, fixed what reviews complained about faster than anyone else and built names designed for the search page. Established brands that lean on heritage and store presence to defend a category are defending with assets the results page barely shows.

How manufacturer brands from China moved from sellers to brands

China-based sellers represent nearly 50% of the top 10,000 sellers on Amazon’s US marketplace, according to Marketplace Pulse research. That share has risen steadily over the past decade, as more manufacturers sold directly to US shoppers.

Many of those sellers started out as factories or trading companies selling generic goods under forgettable names. Some stayed that way, competing only on price and disappearing when a cheaper rival arrived. A growing group built brands that shoppers seek out and come back to.

Anker is the clearest example of that shift. Anker Innovations, based in China, reported 2023 revenue of more than $2.41 billion, up 23%, with nearly half coming from the United States, and spent about $38 million on US advertising, according to the Chinesellers newsletter’s summary of its financial report. Its Amazon store, AnkerDirect, ranked second among all US sellers by positive reviews in Marketplace Pulse’s updated top 100 list, the same newsletter reported.

Why these brands earned loyalty

Most Amazon shoppers look for the thing they need, not for a brand, and in that setting the products that win are the ones with the best mix of price, reviews and features. A manufacturer close to the factory can improve all three faster than a brand that relies on outside suppliers and long product cycles. The advantage is organizational as much as technical: the people reading the reviews work for the same company as the people who can change the product.

The leading Chinese brands used that advantage deliberately. They watched reviews closely, found the complaints shoppers repeated and released improved versions quickly. Each improvement raised ratings, which raised conversion, which raised sales rank, and over time shoppers began to recognize the brand that kept delivering. Loyalty followed the repairs.

Their brands were also native to Amazon. Product images, names, packaging and listings were designed for the search results page, not for a store shelf. Several created separate brands for different categories, each with a clear identity, rather than putting one name on everything.

Take an established kitchen brand with decades of store presence. A manufacturer brand launches a competing product on Amazon, reads the reviews of both, fixes the main complaint about the established brand’s product within months and prices slightly lower. The established brand, working on an annual product cycle, keeps selling the version shoppers have been criticizing. Within a year, the newcomer leads the category’s search results, and nobody at the established brand made a decision that looked wrong at the time.

What established brands can take from them

Heritage does not defend a category on Amazon. Product quality, responsiveness and reviews do, and they have to be earned again with every release.

The reviews are the cheapest product research a brand will ever get. Reading your own ratings and your competitors’ regularly, listing the complaints that repeat and deciding which can be fixed turns a public comment section into a product roadmap. Competitors are already reading them.

Product cycles need to shorten where it matters. Not every product needs constant updates, but in categories where competitors improve quickly, waiting a year to fix a known problem hands share to rivals. The listing needs the same attention: main images, titles and product names should communicate the product’s advantage at thumbnail size, where most shoppers first meet it.

Customer service belongs to the brand as much as the product does. The strongest manufacturer brands answer questions quickly, replace faulty products without argument and treat negative reviews as problems to solve. That responsiveness turns a disappointed buyer into a loyal one and shows other shoppers that the brand stands behind what it sells.

Breadth builds recognition, and separate names manage risk. A shopper who has a good experience with one product is more likely to choose the same brand for a related one. Manufacturer brands build families of related products, such as chargers, cables and power banks, that turn one purchase into several. By running distinct brands for distinct categories, some manufacturers keep each identity clear and protect the others if one product line struggles. An established brand stretching one name across unrelated categories may dilute what that name means.

Brand protection matters too. Established brands face sellers who copy designs or use similar names. Registering the brand with Amazon and monitoring listings helps guard against imitation, though it is no substitute for a better product.

Price is not the whole story, and treating these competitors as low-quality imitators underestimates them. The most successful manufacturer brands offer features and quality that match or exceed established brands at a competitive price, then earn loyalty through consistency. Many invest heavily in research, design and customer service, and the brands they are building are meant to last.

The question worth putting to a leadership team is who in the company reads the reviews, and how long it takes for what they find to reach the product. If that path runs through several departments and an annual calendar, it is longer than the one at the manufacturer brands winning on Amazon. Shortening it on the Amazon side is part of the channel management work we do for established brands.

A0617.crumb: Why big brands leave their own search…
A0617.title: Why big brands leave their own search terms undefended
A0617.alt: Open wrought iron gates between ivy-covered stone pillars reveal a gravel drive winding to a country house.
A0617.ttag: Why big brands leave their own search terms undefended | Kwontified
A0617.desc: Rivals can buy the top slot on a big brand’s own name on Amazon. Why large brands leave branded search undefended, and why defense usually pays for itself.
A0617.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 27, 2024.
A0617.body:
A shopper types a well-known brand’s name into Amazon, and the first product she sees belongs to a rival. Big brands often allow it. Their reasoning sounds airtight: the shopper asked for us by name, our organic listing is right there, and paying for that click would mean paying for a sale we already have.

The sale is not theirs until the shopper buys. Rivals can buy the top placements on a brand’s branded search terms and divert part of that demand, while the brand itself can hold those placements cheaply because branded clicks cost it little and convert well. Defending them usually costs far less than the sales lost, even after allowing for clicks the brand would have won anyway.

How branded search terms became a target

Branded searches are a minority of Amazon searches, but a valuable and growing one. Searches that include a brand name rose to 22.9% of Amazon US searches in June 2024, from 22.6% a year earlier, with sharper increases in popular categories. PMG advised brands to track branded search volume for themselves and their competitors, including competitor placements on their own terms.

For established brands, those placements are the real problem. On Amazon, any advertiser can bid on another brand’s name, subject to Amazon’s ad policies. A shopper who types a famous name may see a rival’s sponsored product or brand ad at the top of the page, above the brand’s own listing.

Why large brands talk themselves out of defense

Many large brands do not respond at all, and their reasons are easy to understand. Some believe their organic rank is strong enough. Some see paying for their own name as wasteful. Others have teams measured on new-customer growth, which makes defensive spending look unproductive on the scorecard.

Behind all three sits one mental pull: treating demand the brand created as demand the brand already holds. A sale feels settled the moment a shopper types your name, so money spent to protect it feels like money thrown away. The results page does not share that feeling. It shows the shopper whoever won the top placement, and a shopper who has settled on a product type can still be drawn to a rival sitting one row above the brand she asked for.

Why branded search defense is cheap insurance

A shopper searching for a brand by name has usually already decided, so these searches convert at high rates. That is exactly what makes them valuable to rivals. The brand, meanwhile, pays little to hold the top position, because its relevance to the search is high. The cost of defense is small next to the sales a rival can divert.

Take a brand that receives 100,000 branded searches a month. Undefended, rivals’ ads divert 8% of those shoppers, or 8,000 people. If they would have converted at 12% with a $30 average order, the brand loses 960 orders, about $28,800 in sales a month.

Defending the term costs, say, 15,000 clicks at $0.40 each, or $6,000 a month. The sales at risk are 4.8 times the cost of defense.

Cannibalization is the honest counterweight. Some of those defensive clicks would have reached the brand’s organic listing for free. Even if half the spend went to shoppers the brand would have won anyway, the effective cost of protecting its sales is about $12,000, still well below the $28,800 at risk.

How to defend without overpaying

Defend branded searches by default, measure the effect and spend only as much as protection requires.

Start by watching who is bidding. Search your own brand and main product names regularly, and use brand analytics to see which rivals appear and how often. Defense matters most where competitors are active. It also matters more the bigger the brand is: a large brand receives more branded searches, those searches are more attractive to rivals, and a small percentage diverted from a large brand is a large number of sales.

Use the formats that hold the page. Sponsored Brands ads at the top of results show the brand’s logo and several products in the most visible position, and Sponsored Products ads on the brand’s own name and product names add coverage further down. Bids can stay low. Because branded searches are highly relevant to the brand’s own products, it usually wins top placement at a lower cost per click than rivals do, so start with modest bids and raise them only where rivals keep winning the top spot.

Product pages need the same protection. Rivals also advertise on a brand’s product detail pages, and running ads on your own pages, with listings that are complete and well reviewed, makes it harder for shoppers to be drawn away at the last step.

Then test what the defense buys. Pause it on some terms or in some weeks, and compare total sales, organic plus paid, with similar periods when it was on. That shows how much of the spend protects sales and how much simply buys clicks the brand would have won anyway. Brand analytics add a running measure: the share of clicks and purchases on a brand’s own search terms that go to the brand. A falling share, even with steady branded search volume, signals that rivals are taking more of the demand the brand created.

Defense should move with brand building. Television, social media and creator campaigns increase branded searches on Amazon, so defense should rise while they run, or competitors capture the demand those campaigns create at the moment of purchase. The same exposure exists elsewhere: Walmart and Target also let advertisers bid on searches that include a rival’s name, and a brand well defended on Amazon may be open on both.

A workable rule for a large brand is to assume its name is contested until a pause test shows otherwise, and to let the test, not the feeling of ownership, set the budget. Running that test and the defense behind it is part of how we manage branded search on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0619.crumb: Who decides Amazon’s October deal event…
A0619.title: Who decides Amazon’s October deal event and its calendar
A0619.alt: Stack of twine-tied brown paper parcels on a wooden dining table before French doors to an autumn garden.
A0619.ttag: Who decides Amazon’s October deal event and its calendar | Kwontified
A0619.desc: Deal submissions for Amazon’s fall Prime event closed in August, before any dates were set. Why the decision belongs to the people who own margin and inventory.
A0619.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 29, 2024.
A0619.body:
By the time Amazon announces the dates of its October deal event, the decisions that matter have already been made or missed. For the fall Prime deal event, Best Deals submissions were due on August 8, and inventory for Fulfillment by Amazon had to arrive by September 12, while the event itself was still undated.

The calendar settles the question of who should decide. Whether to take part, with which products and at what discount, is a question for the people who control margin and inventory, working to a timeline that runs backward from mid-September. The marketing team planning October advertising arrives too late to make it.

How the Amazon October deal event took shape

Amazon added a second Prime event in October in 2022, and in 2023 it ran as Prime Big Deal Days on October 10 and 11, according to Skai’s review of the event. Because the event falls in October, it is easy to file it with October’s advertising plans and treat it as a media moment that starts when the dates are announced.

Sellers widely expected another October event in 2024, though Amazon had not yet announced the dates, SellerBites reported. The deadlines did not wait for the announcement. The submission deadline for Best Deals was August 8, Lightning Deals were due in September and the inventory cutoff for Fulfillment by Amazon was September 12, according to a seller guide to the fall event.

The calendar runs backward from September

Read backward, the timeline shows where each decision sits. The September 12 inventory cutoff means the extra stock has to be produced and shipped in July and August. The Lightning Deals deadline in September leaves a little room for late additions. The August 8 deadline for Best Deals, the most visible deal type, is the real decision point, and it falls weeks before anyone outside Amazon knows the event dates.

A brand that waits for the dates before deciding has already missed the main deal deadline, and is left with fewer and less visible options.

Why the decision belongs to margin and inventory owners

A deal commits a brand to a discount, which is a margin decision. It needs extra inventory at Amazon’s warehouses by the cutoff, which is a supply chain decision. And it has to fit the fourth quarter as a whole, which is a planning decision. Advertising matters too, but it comes last, once the deals and the stock are settled.

When marketing teams own the event, those earlier decisions are often made by default. Discounts are set to match the previous year’s, inventory is whatever happens to be available, and the event’s place in the holiday plan goes unexamined. The result can be deals that cut margin without adding sales, or deals that sell out on the first morning.

The October event also has an awkward place in the calendar. It arrives before Black Friday and Cyber Monday, when many shoppers are starting holiday purchases early. A deal in October may bring forward sales that would otherwise have happened in November at full price, or it may win early holiday shoppers who would have bought from a rival, and which effect dominates depends on the category.

Take a home goods brand whose marketing team decides in mid-September to join the October event. The deal deadlines have passed and the inventory cutoff is days away, so it runs a coupon instead, ships extra stock late and runs short during the event. A competitor that decided in early August secured its deals, shipped on time and captured the early holiday shoppers.

Running the October event as a margin decision

Decide by early August. That means reviewing the previous year’s October results, choosing which products to discount and by how much, and submitting deals before the main deadline. Inventory follows the same clock: extra stock for the event must reach Amazon’s warehouses before the mid-September cutoff, so production and shipping decisions belong in July and August.

The event belongs inside the quarter, not beside it. October deals should be planned alongside Black Friday, Cyber Monday and December, so that discounts and inventory are spread sensibly across the season rather than spent all at once. Walmart and Target have run their own October deal events in recent years, timed close to Amazon’s, and a brand selling across retailers should decide on all of them together so that discounts and stock stay consistent and no retailer undercuts another.

Deal types differ in cost and reach. Featured deals with large discounts reach the most shoppers but cost the most margin, while coupons and Prime-exclusive discounts are cheaper, easier to set up and in some cases can be added closer to the event. The deal type should match the product’s margin and the goal.

Category decides whether to take part at all. For gifts and seasonal products, October is an early holiday moment. For everyday staples, an October deal mostly pulls forward sales from the weeks after.

October doubles as a rehearsal. It tests deal types, advertising budgets and inventory processes before Black Friday, and brands that review what worked within days of the event can still adjust their November plans. The test of an October deal is not the event’s sales but the quarter’s margin, including any dip in November that the deal caused.

None of this works without one owner. One person should be responsible for the event decision, with finance, supply chain and marketing contributing; without that person, the deadlines pass while each team waits for the others. The question to put to the leadership team in July is simple: whose name is on the October decision, and do they own the margin it spends? Setting that calendar and running it across retailers sits at the center of how we manage the fourth quarter for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0621.crumb: Why winning on Amazon isn’t always about…
A0621.title: Why winning on Amazon isn’t always about being cheapest
A0621.alt: Brown leather satchel on a stone pedestal beside a wicker basket of canvas tote bags against a pink wall.
A0621.ttag: Why winning on Amazon isn’t always about being cheapest | Kwontified
A0621.desc: A 10% price cut on Amazon can need 32% more sales just to stand still, and most shoppers weigh reviews as well as price. When to cut, and what to fix instead.
A0621.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 3, 2024.
A0621.body:
Take a $25 product that earns $8.75 a unit after costs and Amazon’s referral fee. Cut its price by 10% and it has to sell 32% more units just to earn the same profit. The discount is 10%; the sales lift it needs is far larger.

That gap is why winning on Amazon is not always about being cheapest. A price cut takes margin from every unit, including the units that would have sold anyway, while the extra sales it brings are uncertain. Brands should cut prices only where the arithmetic shows enough added volume, and otherwise compete on what raises conversion without lowering margin: reviews, content and delivery speed.

How price came to dominate thinking about winning on Amazon

Price clearly matters to Amazon’s shoppers. In the first quarter of 2024, 71% of Amazon shoppers looked for the lowest price while browsing the site, according to Jungle Scout’s quarterly survey of 1,000 US consumers, eMarketer reported.

Price is not the only thing shoppers weigh. The same survey, conducted from February 21 to 23, found that 64% of consumers are influenced by products with the best ratings and reviews, according to Jungle Scout’s report.

The two findings fit together once you see how shoppers use them. Shoppers look for a good price among products they trust, and a product that is cheapest but poorly reviewed often loses to one that costs a little more and has strong reviews. Price gets a product considered. Trust gets it bought.

Why a price cut needs more volume than it seems

A price cut reduces the margin on every unit sold. It pays only if it adds enough new units to make up for the margin given away on all the others, and because the product’s cost does not fall with the price, the margin shrinks faster than the price does. Improving conversion through reviews and content works the other way: it adds sales without reducing the margin on each one.

Back to the $25 product. It costs $12.50 to make and deliver, and Amazon takes a 15% referral fee, so each unit earns $8.75 at full price. Cut the price by 10%, to $22.50, and the referral fee falls slightly, but the product still costs $12.50. Each unit now earns about $6.63.

Full priceAfter a 10% cut
Price$25$22.50
Cost to make and deliver$12.50$12.50
Referral fee15%15%
Margin per unit$8.75about $6.63

Dividing the old margin by the new one gives the break-even: the brand needs 32% more units to earn the same profit. Suppose the cut lifts sales by 15%, a healthy response in most categories. On a base of 1,000 units, profit falls from $8,750 to about $7,619, a loss of about $1,131. The product sells more and earns less, and shoppers have learned to expect the lower price.

Compete on conversion before price

Cut price only where the expected lift exceeds the break-even volume, and invest first in the things that raise conversion without touching margin.

That starts with the break-even calculation itself, made before any price change, using the product’s real costs and fees. If the lift a discount needs is unrealistic for the category, the discount is a loss.

Reviews and ratings are the next lever. Since most shoppers weigh reviews, raising a product’s rating or review count can lift conversion more cheaply than a price cut, and both programs that encourage honest reviews and fixes to the issues customers complain about help. Content and delivery do similar work. Clear images, complete details and fast delivery reduce the doubts that push shoppers toward the cheaper option, and each raises conversion at the existing price.

Price still decides the sale where shoppers compare identical products. For commodity items with many near-identical sellers, small price differences can settle both the sale and the Buy Box, so those products need competitive prices. Even there, check the arithmetic before cutting further.

Planned deals still have a role to play. Short, planned discounts during events can win new customers and reviews, and because they end on a set date, the full price returns afterward. The damage comes from permanent cuts made in response to every competitor move, which erode margin without building anything lasting. When several sellers follow each other’s cuts automatically, prices fall until margins disappear, so set floors below which you will not follow, based on the break-even arithmetic.

Test a price before committing to it. Change a price for a few weeks and compare units, conversion and profit with similar periods, while watching competitors’ prices. A short test costs far less than a permanent cut that turns out not to pay.

Price and advertising also interact with each other. A lower price can raise conversion on ads, which lowers the advertising cost of each sale, and that effect belongs in the calculation. It rarely makes up for a large loss of margin on every unit, including the units that were never advertised. Large price gaps between Amazon, Walmart and a brand’s own site carry their own costs as well: they can trigger price matching, strain retailer relationships and confuse shoppers.

Some brands price above competitors deliberately and win through quality, design and reputation. On Amazon that works when reviews and content clearly justify the difference. A premium price with weak reviews simply loses.

Before the next price cut, divide the current margin per unit by the margin after the cut, and ask whether the category can really deliver that much extra volume. If it cannot, the money belongs in the listing. Running that check across a catalog before every pricing move is part of how we manage pricing and listings on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0622.crumb: Temu’s marketing blitz and what it means…
A0622.title: Temu’s marketing blitz and what it means for your growth plan
A0622.alt: Rows of blank orange posters pasted along an old stone wall on a cobbled street.
A0622.ttag: Temu’s marketing blitz and what it means for your growth plan | Kwontified
A0622.desc: Temu bought US attention on a huge scale, from Super Bowl spots to $15 million in giveaways. Who pays for that attention, and where brands should compete.
A0622.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 5, 2024.
A0622.body:
During the Super Bowl in February 2024, Temu bought spots that sold for $6.5 million to $7 million per 30 seconds and backed them with more than $15 million in coupons and giveaways. For a brand selling household goods or accessories, the game was a reminder that a rival with very different economics was buying the same shoppers’ attention, at a scale no ordinary marketing budget can match.

The useful question is what that spending does to everyone else’s growth plan. Attention bought this way fades unless it is constantly refueled, and while it lasts it raises the price of reaching the same shoppers. Brands should not try to match Temu’s spending or prices in commodity categories. They should plan for more expensive advertising during Temu’s heavy periods and compete on trust, quality and speed, which Temu’s model struggles to offer.

How Temu marketing reached every screen

Temu arrived fast and spent heavily from the start. It launched in the United States in September 2022 and returned to the Super Bowl in February 2024 with an ad campaign that included the coupons and giveaways, CNN reported.

The spending built a large audience. Temu had about 70 million monthly active users in the United States, up from 13 million a year earlier, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN, SlashGear reported.

But the interest needed constant support. Online searches for Temu had been declining since the previous July, before spiking during its Super Bowl ads, Business Insider reported.

The cost is now showing. Temu’s parent company warned in August that competition was intensifying and that profitability would likely be affected as it continued to invest, after its shares fell 28%, the Motley Fool reported.

Who pays for Temu’s attention

Follow the money from a Temu campaign and part of the bill lands on other advertisers. When one advertiser spends heavily on social media and search, it bids up the price of reaching shoppers in those auctions. The platforms collect the higher prices, and brands targeting the same people, especially young, price-conscious shoppers, pay more for each impression and click during Temu’s heavy periods.

Temu also shapes what shoppers think a fair price is. Constant ads for very cheap products teach shoppers that many everyday items should cost a few dollars, even when the cheap versions are lower in quality or slower to arrive. Brands selling similar products at normal prices then have to explain why theirs are worth more.

The model has limits, though. Attention bought through heavy advertising and giveaways has to be bought again and again, as the fall in search interest before the Super Bowl showed. Long delivery times and inconsistent quality, common complaints about ultra-low-price platforms, make repeat buying harder to sustain. What Temu rents, a brand with loyal customers owns.

Take a home goods brand that sees cheap versions of its products advertised constantly on Temu and considers cutting prices to match. If it does, it loses margin on every sale and still cannot match Temu’s costs. If instead it emphasizes quality, warranties and two-day delivery on Amazon, it wins the shoppers who want the product to last and arrive quickly, and it keeps its margin. The second path is slower, and it is the one that builds repeat customers.

Where brands should compete instead

The answer is to stay out of Temu’s game and play on ground where a brand’s strengths count.

In categories where Temu sells near-identical goods for a few dollars, a price war is unwinnable, so compete where the product is clearly different or better. Some categories are more exposed than others. Low-cost accessories, small household items and fast fashion compete most directly with Temu, while higher-value, regulated or quality-sensitive products, such as baby goods and health products, are less exposed.

Plan for the expensive stretches. When Temu spends heavily, especially before major events and the holidays, social and search advertising can cost more. Brands can compare their cost per click and cost per thousand impressions on social platforms before, during and after Temu’s major campaigns, and if costs rise sharply, the data supports moving budget to channels where Temu’s bidding matters less.

Retail media is the obvious counterweight. On Amazon and Walmart, shoppers are already searching for products, and Temu does not compete in those auctions. Budgets moved from social media to retail search can reach shoppers closer to buying, at more stable prices.

Sell what Temu cannot easily offer. Fast delivery, reliable quality, clear return policies and genuine reviews all matter to shoppers who have had a disappointing experience with ultra-cheap goods, and listings and ads should make those advantages obvious. Temu’s shoppers are not lost causes either. Many shop on several platforms, and a shopper who buys cheap items on Temu may still choose a trusted brand on Amazon for products where quality matters.

Temu itself is also changing its model. It began moving toward local warehouses in the United States in early 2024, Caixin reported, which could shorten delivery times, so brands that compete on speed should keep improving. Regulation may also shift the field. Scrutiny of the de minimis rule, which lets low-value parcels enter the United States without duties, could raise Temu’s costs if the rules change, but a growth plan should not depend on the outcome.

What deserves a close eye is not Temu’s next campaign but your own cost per click while it runs. If it climbs every time Temu spends, the plan needs a channel where Temu does not bid. Building that plan across Amazon, Walmart and Target is the channel management work we do for brands facing low-price platforms.
