A0624.title: Why dominating sales doesn’t guarantee search visibility
A0624.alt: Two tall stacks of taped cardboard boxes beside a dark velvet curtain in an empty blue-gray room.
A0624.ttag: Why dominating sales doesn’t guarantee search visibility | Kwontified
A0624.desc: A category best-seller on Amazon can be missing from most of the searches its shoppers type. Why ranking works search by search, and how to find the gaps.
A0624.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 10, 2024.
A0624.body:
A brand can lead its category in sales and still be missing from most of the searches its shoppers type. That looks like a contradiction until you remember that Amazon does not rank products once. It ranks them search by search, on relevance and performance for each query, and sponsored listings take the top positions on many of those searches.

So sales rank and search visibility measure different things. A product can sell heavily through a handful of searches it already wins and barely exist on the rest. Brands should measure their visibility across all the searches that matter, not just their sales rank, and close the gaps where their products belong but do not appear.

How search visibility drifted from sales rank

Sales rank is easy to see, so brands watch it closely. Shoppers, though, do not browse by sales rank; they search. About 77% of Amazon US searches in June 2024 did not include a brand name, PMG reported, which means most shoppers start with a description of what they need.

Position on those searches matters a great deal. Shoppers gave about 64% of their clicks to the first three items on a results page, in the estimate of a former Amazon consultant quoted by The Markup. That figure is several years old, but the principle holds: a product that is not near the top of a search is barely seen on it.

A brand’s growth therefore depends on how many searches it appears on, and where. Sales rank does not tell you that.

Why a best-seller can be invisible

Amazon decides what to show for each search separately, weighing how relevant a product is to that query and how well it has performed for it. A product that sells mostly through a few searches it already wins builds a strong record there and little anywhere else. The ranking is doing exactly what it was built to do; it simply has no reason to show the product on searches where it has never sold. Meanwhile, ads occupy the top positions on many searches. Overall sales rank says little about how often a product is seen across the full range of relevant searches.

Take a brand that leads its category, selling 1,500 units a week. Shoppers make about 200,000 searches a week that are relevant to its product, but the brand appears on the first page for searches totaling only 60,000 of those, about 30%. Most of its sales come from its own name and a handful of core terms.

That leaves 140,000 relevant searches a week where the brand is effectively absent. If 10% of those searches end in a purchase and the brand could win just 5% of those buyers, it would add about 700 units a week, roughly 47% more than it sells now.

The sales rank says the brand is winning. The search data says most of the market never sees it.

How to measure and close visibility gaps

Measure visibility across the full set of relevant searches, and invest where products should appear but do not.

Start by mapping the searches that matter. List the searches shoppers use for your products, including descriptive, problem-based and competitor terms, using Amazon’s brand analytics and search term reports. That list defines the market the brand is actually competing for.

Then measure share by search. For each important search, track how often your products appear, at what position and with what share of clicks and purchases. Amazon’s search query reports make much of this visible for brand owners. Where a product is relevant but missing, the fixes include adding the right terms to titles and details, improving images and reviews to raise conversion, and using sponsored ads to earn early sales that build a record for that search.

Ads and organic results are linked here. Advertising on searches where a product is weak can generate the clicks and sales that help it rank organically over time, so watch whether organic position improves as a result, and reduce ad spend where it does.

Visibility is a relative measure. A brand’s position on a search depends on competitors’ listings and bids as well as its own, and rivals that improve their content or raise their bids can push a best-seller down without any change on its side. That is why visibility needs regular measurement: search patterns shift with seasons, trends and competitors’ moves, and the list of important searches and the brand’s share on each should be refreshed monthly.

The same gap appears on other retailers. Walmart and Target also rank products search by search, and a brand’s position can differ widely between marketplaces, so a brand that tracks visibility on Amazon should track it on each of them. AI shopping assistants raise the stakes further. When a shopper asks an assistant for a recommendation instead of scrolling a results page, only a few products are named, and brands that are visible and well reviewed across many related searches are more likely to be among them.

Doing nothing has a cost of its own. A brand that dominates a few searches and ignores the rest may see its sales hold steady for a time, while competitors build sales records on the searches it is missing. When shoppers’ habits shift, those competitors are already in position.

Not every search is worth winning. Broad terms with low purchase intent can be expensive to rank on and convert poorly, so focus on searches where shoppers are likely to buy and where the product genuinely fits.

Once a quarter, compare the number of relevant searches your best-seller appears on with the number shoppers actually use, and treat the difference as the size of the opportunity rather than as noise. Measuring that gap on every marketplace is part of how we run retail media and search for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0626.crumb: Predictive supply chains and AI: why…
A0626.title: Predictive supply chains and AI: why stock position sells
A0626.alt: A white robotic arm stacks cardboard boxes on pallets beside tall shelving near an open warehouse loading dock.
A0626.ttag: Predictive supply chains and AI: why stock position sells | Kwontified
A0626.desc: Amazon predicts where demand will appear and places stock across eight regions, while AI assistants change discovery. Why a brand’s stock position now sells.
A0626.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 12, 2024.
A0626.body:
When the decision about the next shipment to Amazon sits with operations and the Amazon sales number sits with e-commerce, two teams are managing the same lever without seeing each other’s data. On Amazon, that separation has stopped making sense. Where a brand’s stock sits now shapes how fast Amazon promises to deliver it, how often shoppers buy it and how prominently it appears.

Amazon has built a supply chain that predicts where demand will appear and places inventory across eight regions to deliver faster, and AI shopping assistants are changing how shoppers discover products. Together they turn a brand’s stock position in each region into a sales lever. Brands should forecast and replenish as active participants in that predictive system rather than treat inventory as a back-office task.

How predictive supply chains took hold at Amazon

Amazon rebuilt its US fulfillment network around regions over 2022 and 2023. It created eight interconnected regions covering smaller geographic areas, CEO Andy Jassy wrote in his letter to shareholders, Supply Chain Dive reported. The company was also developing machine learning algorithms to predict what customers in different parts of the country would need, so the right inventory would be in the right regions at the right time, Chain Store Age reported.

The change showed up fast. More than 76% of the orders Amazon fulfilled came from within the customer’s region, the company said, EcommerceBytes reported.

The results showed up in the next set of numbers. In 2023, Amazon delivered more than 4 billion items in the United States the same or next day. Its US cost to serve fell by more than $0.45 per unit, Jassy wrote in his next shareholder letter, as reported by CNBC via EMEA Tribune. He named inventory placement as an area of focus for 2024.

Shopping itself is changing as AI enters the search for products. Amazon made its AI shopping assistant, Rufus, available to US customers nationwide on July 12, Bloomberg reported.

Why stock position now affects sales

The structure of the system explains why inventory has moved from the back office to the front. When stock is close to a shopper, Amazon can promise faster delivery, and faster delivery promises help shoppers decide. Amazon said in 2023 that items closer to customers would rank higher in search results, CNN reported.

A brand that is in stock nationally but thin in some regions can therefore see slower delivery promises, lower conversion and weaker visibility in those regions, without any change to its listing or advertising. In a store, a product on the shelf is a product the shopper can take home today. On Amazon, a product sitting in a warehouse on the other side of the country is, for the shopper looking at a slower delivery date, a weaker product.

AI assistants add a further layer. When a shopper wants a recommendation from an assistant, the answer is likely to favor products that are relevant, well reviewed and available to deliver quickly. A product missing from a shopper’s region, or slow to arrive there, is less likely to be the one recommended.

Take a home fitness brand that sends most of its stock to Amazon in one large shipment each quarter. The stock lands in a few warehouses, and Amazon redistributes it over time. For several weeks after each shipment, shoppers on the other side of the country see longer delivery times, and sales there lag. A competitor that sends smaller, more frequent shipments keeps its delivery promise fast everywhere and wins those shoppers.

How brands should work with a predictive system

The practical change is to treat inventory as part of the sales plan and to feed Amazon’s system the stock it needs to place products well.

That starts with forecasting at the right level: demand by product and season, shared realistically with operations teams, so stock arrives before demand rises rather than after. It continues with replenishment. Smaller, more frequent shipments give Amazon more chances to place stock close to shoppers and reduce the weeks when some regions run thin. And it needs someone to watch the delivery promises by region, because the delivery dates shown to shoppers in different parts of the country often explain uneven sales better than any ad report.

Events need extra lead time. Before major deal events and the holidays, stock must arrive early enough for Amazon to spread it across regions, or products end up in stock nationally but slow to deliver where demand spikes.

Listings must be ready for AI as well. Shopping assistants rely on clear, complete product information, and accurate attributes, sizes and use cases help them match products to questions, which matters as much as having the stock in place.

Amazon’s own signals deserve a close look. Its inventory tools show recommended replenishment quantities, restock limits and inventory health. They are not perfect, but they reflect the same predictions that drive placement, and brands that ignore them often find themselves out of step with the system.

New and slow-moving products need care. Amazon’s predictions rely on sales history, so a new product has little to go on; send enough stock for a launch to be placed sensibly, and avoid overloading slow sellers that tie up capacity and storage fees. Costs need watching too, since inbound shipping, storage and placement choices all affect margin, and the cost of more frequent, better-distributed shipments should be weighed against the sales they protect, product by product.

Other retailers are heading the same way. Walmart and Target also invest in faster delivery from stock positioned near shoppers, and brands selling across retailers should plan stock where each retailer’s demand is growing.

What a leadership team needs to know is whether the people who decide shipment size and timing see the same regional sales and delivery data as the people who own Amazon revenue. For brands selling on Amazon, Walmart and Target, bringing those two views into one plan is where our channel management starts.

A0629.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2024 forecast: lift, CPC and deal ranges
A0629.alt: A brass rooster weathervane on a red tiled roof as autumn oak leaves blow across a cloudy sky.
A0629.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2024 forecast: lift, CPC and deal ranges | Kwontified
A0629.desc: Prime Big Deal Days runs October 8 and 9. Conservative, standard and reach ranges for sales lift, click prices and deal share, scaled down from July’s event.
A0629.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 18, 2024.
A0629.body:
Amazon confirmed on September 17 that Prime Big Deal Days will run on October 8 and 9, EcommerceBytes reported. That leaves brands three weeks to set budgets for a 48-hour event whose deals and inventory are already locked in. The ranges below are our Prime Big Deal Days 2024 forecast for a promoted product line.

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
Sales on promoted products, vs normal day1.5x2x2.5x
Click prices, vs normal week+15%+25%+35%
Share of event sales on deal products35%45%55%

The October event is likely to deliver a smaller lift than July’s Prime Day, because it has drawn fewer households and lower spending per household. Click prices fall by less, because advertisers still crowd their budgets into the same two days. Plan for the standard case, keep a reserve for the reach case and decide within the first hours which range is playing out.

Each row answers a different planning question. The lift row sets the budget and the inventory check for promoted products. The click-price row sets the cost side of the margin check. A sale that costs 25% more to win has to clear a higher bar. The deal-share row says how much of the event’s sales will come from discounted items, which decides how much margin the event gives away even when the sales target is met.

How the Prime Big Deal Days 2024 forecast scales from 2023

The best guide to the event’s scale is the 2023 October event. During Prime Big Deal Days on October 10 and 11, 2023, the average order was $53.47 and the average household spent about $124.09, compared with $181.72 during July’s Prime Day, according to Numerator, Digital Commerce 360 reported. That is about 68% of July’s spending per household.

Participation in the fall event was lower too. In October 2022, 28% of US households shopped Amazon’s fall event, compared with 34% for July’s Prime Day that year, Numerator said. That is about 82% of July’s households.

An event’s lift for a brand depends on how many shoppers take part and how much each spends, and on both counts October has run behind July. The same deals therefore produce a smaller lift. Click prices respond to something else: the crowd of advertisers bidding together in a short window. That is why October needs smaller sales expectations but not proportionally smaller cost expectations.

The lift ranges are about two-thirds of the ranges we used for Prime Day in July, in line with the 2023 gap in spending per household. The click-price ranges are lower than July’s but not by as much, since bidding still crowds into 48 hours. The deal-share ranges are planning assumptions rather than measured figures, and brands should replace them with their own history.

What the ranges mean for a promoted line

Take the brand from our Prime Day forecast again: in a normal week, its promoted line sells $10,000 a day. In the conservative case it sells $15,000 a day during the event, adding $10,000 over the two days. In the standard case, $20,000 a day adds $20,000. In the reach case, $25,000 a day adds $30,000. A click that normally costs $1.00 would cost $1.15, $1.25 or $1.35.

Those are gross additions, counted before any dip after the event. The true result is the event lift minus the shortfall in the weeks that follow, both measured against the same normal baseline, which is the same test we applied to Prime Day.

Planning inside the ranges

Set the budget for the standard case: about twice normal sales on promoted products, at click prices about 25% above a normal week, and check that the margin still works at those costs. Hold 10% to 15% of the event budget unallocated, to release if the first hours run toward the reach case. Then watch the first six hours: compare sales and click prices with the three ranges early on October 8, and shift budget toward the products and searches that are outperforming.

If the first hours track the conservative case instead, the reserve does not have to be spent at all; it can roll into the November plan rather than being forced into a slow event.

Staples deserve particular caution. Amazon is promoting everyday essentials, and stocking up on staples pulls sales from the weeks after, so brands selling replenishable products should judge the event over six to eight weeks. Gift categories behave differently: with Thanksgiving falling on November 28, October is an early chance to reach gift shoppers, and gift categories may run closer to the reach case.

Target’s Circle Week, from October 6 to 12, overlaps the event, so brands selling on both should keep prices consistent and watch whether shoppers split their spending. Walmart is likely to respond too. It has run its own October deal events in recent years, often timed close to Amazon’s, and brands selling on Walmart should be ready to match Amazon deals there, or decide in advance not to.

We will grade these ranges after the event, as we did after Prime Day. The grading will compare each brand’s event-day lift, click prices and deal share with the three ranges, then subtract any shortfall in the following weeks before calling the event a success. If results land outside the ranges, we will say so and adjust the November plans.

For the next three weeks, the working rule is simple to state: fund the standard case, hold the reserve, and let the first six hours of October 8, not the plan, decide where the reserve goes. Setting and grading those budgets is part of how we plan event advertising on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0630.crumb: Sports and outdoors: resetting a stalled…
A0630.title: Sports and outdoors: resetting a stalled strategy
A0630.alt: Two vintage bicycles, wooden rackets, leather balls and helmets hang on pegs against a sage green wall.
A0630.ttag: Sports and outdoors: resetting a stalled strategy | Kwontified
A0630.desc: Sports and outdoors has not stopped growing; the growth moved to casual products, distinctive retailers and new channels. Where a stalled brand should reset.
A0630.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 19, 2024.
A0630.body:
When sales at a sports and outdoors brand go flat, the leadership team faces two options: wait for the category to come back, or move money and attention now. The category numbers make waiting sound sensible, and they mislead, because sports and outdoors has not stopped growing. The growth has moved, toward casual and performance products, toward retailers that give shoppers a reason to visit and toward the channels where shoppers now buy. A brand whose sales have stalled should follow it.

Why a sports and outdoors strategy built on the old mix stalls

The broad numbers look flat or worse. In 2023, US outdoor retail sales fell 3% to $27.5 billion, and casual products drove the changes in the sales mix, the Outdoor Industry Association and Circana reported.

Even the largest brand has stumbled. Nike’s revenue fell 2% to $12.6 billion in the quarter ended May 31, with its direct-to-consumer sales down 8% and wholesale up 5%, according to its quarterly results. Nike expects revenue to decline by mid-single digits in its 2025 fiscal year, the Motley Fool reported. Inside that total, its lifestyle products declined while its sport performance products grew, RTTNews reported.

Yet some players are growing fast. Dick’s Sporting Goods reported comparable sales growth of 4.5% in its second quarter, with net sales up 7.8% to $3.47 billion, and it raised its full-year outlook, according to its results.

The gaps inside outdoor are wider still. Sales of Stanley’s 40-ounce Quencher tumbler rose 572% over the year to March 2024, while snow equipment fell by double digits in the 2023 to 2024 season, according to Circana data that Shop Eat Surf reported.

Growth moved to everyday use, distinctive retailers and new channels

Shoppers have changed what they buy outdoor products for. Casual use now drives much of the buying, so products that fit everyday life, such as drinkware and versatile apparel, grow while specialist gear depends on weather and seasons. Performance products with clear benefits still sell, while lifestyle products that rely on fashion cycles can fade quickly.

Retailers have split as well, and the ones that give shoppers a reason to visit, through experiences, assortment or service, are taking share, as the Dick’s results show. Brands that sell mostly through weaker channels feel the stall more sharply. For a brand, choosing which retailers to grow with has become part of the strategy.

Channels have shifted most of all. Nike’s direct sales fell while its wholesale sales rose, a sign that even the strongest brand cannot rely on its own stores and sites alone. Shoppers buy where it is convenient, which increasingly includes marketplaces such as Amazon. Private labels compete in the middle of the range too: retailers and marketplaces offer their own basic athletic and outdoor products at lower prices, and brands without a clear performance or design advantage are the most exposed.

Take an outdoor apparel brand whose sales have been flat for two years. Its total masks two trends, a growing line of casual layers and a shrinking line of technical ski wear. Its marketing still centers on the ski line, and it sells mostly through specialty stores. The brand is not stalled; its strategy is aimed at the part of the business that is shrinking. Split by line, its flat total would show a growing business inside a shrinking one, with the marketing pointed at the wrong half.

The decision in the room is where the next dollar goes

Framed as wait or reset, the choice sounds like a bet on the category. In practice it is a question of allocation: which lines, retailers and searches get the next dollar of inventory and advertising.

That question starts with splitting the numbers. Break sales down by product line, use case and channel, and find which parts are growing and which are shrinking. Flat totals often hide strong growth in one area and steady decline in another, and a planning meeting cannot make a good call until both are on the table.

Marketplace data reveals demand early, and Amazon’s search data shows what shoppers are looking for in each category, often before trends appear in store sales, so a brand can spot growing segments early and check where its growing products sell best. Effort should then shift toward those channels, marketplaces included.

Advertising is usually the slowest budget to move, because it tends to stay with the products that sold best in the past. A reset shifts it toward the lines and searches that are growing, and judges results by the growth of those lines, not the category as a whole. Seasonality needs the same line-by-line view. Outdoor and sporting goods swing with weather and seasons, so inventory and advertising should be planned around the peak periods for each line.

Growing lines also need a faster product rhythm. In fast-moving segments, shoppers reward new colors, sizes and features, which calls for regular updates instead of long cycles. Retail partners can speed up that learning: brands sold at fast-growing retailers such as Dick’s can use those relationships to test new products and learn what shoppers respond to, then apply the lessons online.

The harder half of the conversation is what to stop. A reset is as much about subtraction as addition. Lines that have declined for several seasons, with no sign of recovery, tie up inventory, advertising and attention, and the team needs clear rules for when to reduce or drop them.

Nike’s experience shows that size does not protect against a shift in what shoppers want or where they buy, and smaller brands that move quickly can win share during a reset. Following that growth line by line across Amazon, Walmart and Target is the day-to-day work we do for sports and outdoor brands.

A0632.title: What Amazon Accelerate 2024 changes for sellers
A0632.alt: A small white robotic arm grips a kraft-paper parcel on a wooden table beside twine, mugs and a succulent.
A0632.ttag: What Amazon Accelerate 2024 changes for sellers | Kwontified
A0632.desc: Accelerate 2024 pushed Amazon into sellers’ supply chains, content and off-Amazon sales. What its 20% average sales claim is worth on your own catalog.
A0632.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 24, 2024.
A0632.body:
Amazon says its supply chain services are increasing sales by an average of 20% through faster delivery, according to PPC Land’s report. That is the headline benefit attached to the largest news from Accelerate. Like every average, it describes sellers in general rather than any one catalog.

The conference extended Amazon’s role from storefront to supply chain, content and off-Amazon selling. Each new service is worth adopting where a test on part of the business shows the gain covers the cost. Start with the fully managed supply chain and the AI content tools, and keep an alternative for any function that would be hard to replace.

What Amazon Accelerate 2024 announced

According to the same report, Amazon launched a fully managed version of Supply Chain by Amazon, available to all US sellers for domestic pickups in October. Amazon is also quadrupling the capacity of its warehousing and distribution service in the United States in 2024, and sellers who use the full package get lower storage and transport rates.

Amazon’s logistics also extend beyond its own store. It announced on September 18 that its Multi-Channel Distribution service can now apply custom labels, so sellers can send stock from one inventory pool to other marketplaces, wholesalers and their own stores. Its Multi-Channel Fulfillment service made standard delivery 40% faster at no extra cost, and PayPal is now available at checkout for brands using Buy with Prime on their own sites.

AI tools for content and analysis completed the set. Amazon launched a beta of Project Amelia, an AI selling assistant inside Seller Central, GeekWire reported, and introduced Video Generator, which turns product images into video ads, Modern Retail reported.

Bundled services save steps and add dependence

Amazon’s new services bundle steps that sellers used to manage separately. That can cut cost and speed up delivery, which raises conversion. Each step handed to Amazon also deepens dependence on one partner. The published benefits are averages across sellers that may not hold for a given catalog. So the gain has to be measured on a seller’s own products before it is assumed.

An average lift describes sellers as a group. It says nothing about how the gain is spread among them. A seller whose products already arrive quickly has less delivery speed left to gain, while one whose stock often runs short or ships slowly may have more. The same figure can be generous for one catalog and modest for another. What should settle the decision is the seller’s own before-and-after numbers on comparable products, and that is why the test comes before the commitment.

The full-package discounts show both sides at once. They are real savings, and they are also an incentive to consolidate, so the comparison that matters is the full package against current costs, not the discounted line items. New services often launch with attractive pricing that changes later, which is why the number to track is the full cost per unit, including storage, transport and fulfillment.

What the 20% claim is worth on one catalog

Take a brand selling $200,000 a month on Amazon, with 60% of its sales coming from products that could move to the fully managed supply chain. The table puts Amazon’s average next to a result half as strong, at a 30% contribution margin.

Lift on eligible productsExtra sales per monthExtra profit per month
Amazon’s average, 20%$24,000$7,200
Half the average$12,000$3,600

The profit column works as a ceiling: it is the most the service could add in extra cost and still pay for itself. A seller who knows its current logistics costs can make that comparison in a single month, and the answer differs between a catalog that already ships fast and one that does not.

Test on part of the catalog before the holiday peak

When pickups open in October, move a set of products to the managed supply chain and compare delivery promises, conversion, stockouts and total cost with similar products left on the current setup. Avoid moving everything before the holiday peak, when a problem would be most costly. October pickups arrive just before the busiest weeks of the year, so the test on a small set should finish before peak inventory is committed to a new process.

AI content deserves the same kind of trial. Use Video Generator on a few products with strong images, and use AI listing tools with a human check on claims, sizes and compatibility, then compare results with existing ads and listings before expanding. Buy with Prime and Multi-Channel Fulfillment need a separate check of their own. Brands with their own sites should test whether faster Multi-Channel Fulfillment and Buy with Prime raise conversion there, and whether one inventory pool reduces stock needs across channels.

Advertising may follow the logistics. When Amazon handles a brand’s freight, storage and fulfillment, it also knows more about the brand’s stock and delivery speed. Brands should expect Amazon to connect those services with advertising and placement over time, and watch how in-stock rates and delivery promises affect their ad results. None of that was announced at Accelerate; it is the direction the incentives point.

A brand that moves its freight, storage, fulfillment and site checkout to Amazon gains simplicity but loses bargaining power. For each critical function, keep at least one working alternative and the data to switch if terms change. The test for any Accelerate service is the brand’s own conversion, delivery promise and cost per unit before and after, with Amazon’s averages as the starting point. Running that comparison across the supply chain and the ad account is how we work out with brands which of the new services to adopt.

A0634.title: Instagram’s algorithm as a visual merchandiser for brands
A0634.alt: A shop window in a pink wall displays handmade ceramic bowls and vases in a grid of wooden cubbies.
A0634.ttag: Instagram’s algorithm as a visual merchandiser for brands | Kwontified
A0634.desc: Instagram decides which posts reach new people the way a merchandiser picks window displays. How its 2024 ranking changes reward original brand content.
A0634.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 26, 2024.
A0634.body:
In a department store, someone decides what goes in the front window and on the tables by the door. Products that draw people in earn more space, and the ones shoppers walk past get moved to the back. Instagram’s recommendation system makes the same call for every post a brand publishes. It tests each post with a small audience, then decides how widely to show it to people who do not follow the account. Its 2024 changes give original content and smaller accounts a fairer test, so a brand now earns the window with original posts that people respond to.

Instagram’s algorithm changed its window rules in 2024

Instagram announced a set of ranking changes on April 30. It said it would give smaller creators more distribution, replace reposted content with the original in its recommendations, add labels to reposts that link to the original creator and remove content aggregators from recommendations, TechCrunch reported.

The company gave its reason plainly. Historically, creators with large followings and aggregators of reposted content had received more reach in recommendations than smaller, original creators, Instagram said in announcing the changes, which would roll out over the following months, Engadget reported.

For brands, the change matters because recommendations now drive much of what people see. Posts reach followers, but they also appear in the Reels feed, Explore and suggested posts for people who have never heard of the brand. That second audience is where growth comes from, and it is the audience the merchandiser controls.

Read as a statement of what Instagram wants, the April changes are plain. A platform that let aggregators and large accounts collect more reach than the people who made the work now says it will correct that. It is telling brands how it wants the window filled: with work made for the platform by the people who made it. A brand team that keeps score by follower growth alone is keeping score by the older rules.

How the merchandiser decides what earns space

A new post is shown first to a limited group. If people watch, like, comment and share it with friends, the system shows it to more people; if they scroll past, it stops there. The decision depends on how people respond relative to how many saw the post, not on the size of the account that made it.

The 2024 changes make that test fairer. Smaller accounts get a better chance at the window, and reposted content no longer takes space from the original. A brand that relied on reposting creators’ videos, or on the reach of a large follower count, will find that both count for less.

Take a skincare brand that fills its account with reposted customer videos. Under the new rules, its reposts may be labeled or replaced by the originals in recommendations, sending attention to the customers’ accounts instead. A competitor that films its own short demonstrations, and pays creators to make original content for its account, keeps the window space.

Followers still count, though differently. Posts reach followers first, so a loyal following that responds quickly gives each new post a strong start in its test. A large following that ignores the brand’s posts does the opposite.

The store comparison has one limit worth keeping in mind. A store merchandiser dresses one window for a season, while Instagram runs its test on each post a brand publishes, so no brand keeps the window for long. Each post starts again with a limited group, and past success buys only the strong start that a responsive following provides.

Dressing the window with original work

The work starts with original content. Brands should film and design their own posts, and when they want creator content, commission it or collaborate rather than repost it. Collaborative posts, shared between a brand and a creator, let both accounts benefit.

Response rate is the measure that matches what the system rewards. Look at likes, comments, saves and shares relative to reach, not total counts. A post seen by fewer people but shared widely is a stronger signal than a post seen by many and ignored. Account insights show reach from followers and non-followers, shares and saves for each post, so a brand can see which posts reached new people and make more of what worked.

In a crowded feed, the opening frame decides whether people stop. Clear products, faces and motion at the start help a post pass the first test. Posting more often does not help if each post performs poorly in that test, so the pace should be one the team can sustain with original, well-made content. A consistent look, in colors, settings and style, lets each new post build on the last for shoppers who see the brand repeatedly in recommendations.

What happens after the window

Shopping links follow attention. Product tags and shopping features help turn interest into sales, but only after a post has earned attention; they are the step after the window, not a substitute for it. Paid promotion is a separate decision. Ads can extend a post’s reach, but posts that perform well organically usually make better ads, so it pays to test which original posts earn the strongest response before putting budget behind them.

The best visuals can also travel beyond Instagram. Images and videos that perform well on Instagram often work as marketplace content too, and a brand can test creative ideas there, then use the best in Amazon listings and ads, where they reach shoppers closer to buying. Treating each post as a window display, and moving the winners onto the shelf, is how we plan social commerce for brands across Instagram, TikTok and the major marketplaces.

A0636.crumb: What search trends reveal about the…
A0636.title: What search trends reveal about the Amazon shopper
A0636.alt: A brass magnifying glass is held up before a wooden shelf of labeled ceramic jars and folded linens.
A0636.ttag: What search trends reveal about the Amazon shopper | Kwontified
A0636.desc: A brand can grow its Amazon sales while losing share of the searches that matter. How to read search volume, wording and funnel share before sales reports do.
A0636.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 1, 2024.
A0636.body:
Take a brand whose purchases on its most important Amazon search rose 5% in a year, from 240 a month to 252. The sales report calls that growth. The search data says otherwise: purchases on that search from all sellers rose 40%, from 2,000 a month to 2,800, and the brand’s share fell from 12% to 9%. Shoppers search before they buy, so changes in search volume, in the words shoppers use and in a brand’s share at each step from impression to purchase show shifts in demand and competition before sales reports do. A growing market can hide a brand that is losing ground.

Search trends became visible to brands in 2022

For years, brands could see their own sales but little of the searches that led shoppers to them. That changed when Amazon added search dashboards to Brand Analytics in 2022, giving brand owners a view of each query from impression through click and cart add to purchase, as the Playbook for Amazon podcast noted.

Those dashboards show more than volume. For each search, a brand can compare its own share with the totals across all sellers, step by step, from impressions and clicks to cart adds and purchases. With those shares in hand, a brand sees where shoppers stop choosing it.

The searches themselves are changing too. In June 2024, about 77% of US searches at Amazon did not include a brand name, while branded searches rose slightly to 22.9%, PMG reported. Shoppers mostly still describe the need instead of the brand. AI assistants are stretching those descriptions: shoppers who ask questions of Amazon’s Rufus assistant, launched to all US customers in July, phrase their needs as full questions rather than short keywords.

Search runs ahead of sales because every purchase starts with one

Sales reports earn their trust honestly. They count real orders, they reconcile with finance, and a rising line is hard to argue with. What they cannot show is the denominator: how many purchases the brand could have had on the same searches. Search data fills that gap.

Every purchase on Amazon starts with a search or a browse. So search volume rises before sales in a growing category, and the words shoppers use reveal the needs they are trying to meet. A brand’s share of impressions, clicks, cart adds and purchases on each search shows where it wins and loses. Sales growth alone can mask a falling share when the whole search is growing faster.

The brand from the opening shows how far apart the two views can drift.

On one important searchBeforeAfter
Purchases per month, all sellers2,0002,800
Brand’s share of purchases12%9%
Brand’s purchases per month240252

Had it kept its 12% share, it would have made 336 sales a month. It lost 84 sales a month to competitors while appearing to grow.

The funnel locates the loss. If the brand’s share of impressions held steady but its share of clicks fell, its main image or price is losing shoppers’ attention. If clicks held but purchases fell, the listing, reviews or delivery promise is losing them at the end. Competitors always show up in the same data: when a brand’s share falls on a search, someone else’s rises, and checking which products appear at the top of that search usually reveals who is winning and why.

Reading search data every month

Share is the number to track, not sales alone. For the searches that drive most of a brand’s sales, review share of impressions, clicks, cart adds and purchases every month. Falling share on a growing search is an early warning that sales reports will not show for months. A monthly review of share on the top searches, with a quarterly look at new and rising phrases, catches most shifts early without overwhelming a team with data.

The words carry their own signal. New phrases, rising descriptive terms and changes in how shoppers describe a need often signal new demand. A brand that notices “travel size” or “fragrance free” rising in its category can adjust products and listings before competitors do. Longer, problem-based searches deserve the same attention, and listings should answer the questions shoppers ask. A question names the problem a product has to solve, which is more than a two-word keyword ever told a brand.

Seasonal timing shows up in search as well. Search volume often rises weeks before seasonal sales peak, and that lead time is enough to build inventory, refresh listings and set advertising budgets. Waiting for the sales report to confirm a peak spends that lead time.

The ad reports add detail of their own. Search term reports from sponsored ads show which searches lead to sales from ads. Combined with organic share, they show whether advertising is winning new shoppers or simply buying sales the brand would have made anyway. Walmart and Target also provide search and performance data to brands, and reading it the same way lets a brand compare its position across retailers.

The same trends matter to product, packaging and sales teams as well as advertisers. Rising demand for a size, scent or feature that a brand does not offer is a product decision, not an advertising one. The data has limits: it shows what shoppers type, not everything they want, and new needs sometimes appear in reviews and social media before they reach search, so it belongs alongside reviews and customer feedback.

A brand that judges itself by share of the searches that matter, and reads each step of the funnel for the cause, sees the decline while its sales report still shows growth. Building that monthly share view across Amazon, Walmart and Target is how we read search data for brands.

A0637.title: Measuring TikTok Shop beyond last-click attribution
A0637.alt: A cardboard parcel waits on the step of a stone cottage with a blue door, wisteria and a lush cottage garden.
A0637.ttag: Measuring TikTok Shop beyond last-click attribution | Kwontified
A0637.desc: TikTok creates demand that often converts on Amazon and brand sites, where its own dashboard cannot see it. How brands should measure what TikTok Shop drives.
A0637.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 3, 2024.
A0637.body:
A shopper sees a product in a TikTok video, closes the app and buys it on Amazon a few days later. TikTok’s dashboard records a view. Amazon records a sale, often from a search for the brand’s name. Neither report connects the two, and a budget meeting that sees both side by side is looking at two halves of one story.

So TikTok Shop’s own reports and last-click attribution capture only part of the demand TikTok creates. The fair way to judge it is by the total sales it causes, wherever they happen.

Why TikTok Shop measurement misses demand it creates

TikTok Shop has grown quickly since its US launch. It had more than 500,000 US merchants at the end of 2023 and reached a $3 billion annual run rate in the United States in January 2024, Retail Brew reported.

Its reporting shows what happens inside TikTok: views, clicks and purchases made in the app. That view is useful and still misses shoppers who watch a video, then search for the product on Amazon or visit the brand’s own site days later.

Last-click attribution has the same blind spot. In analytics tools, sales influenced by TikTok often appear as direct visits rather than TikTok, and last-click measurement continued to undervalue paid social in early 2024, the measurement firm Fospha reported. TikTok made up about 10% of the average brand’s channel mix in its data.

The demand starts on TikTok and the sale lands elsewhere

TikTok is a place for discovery. Many shoppers see a product in a video but prefer to buy where they already have an account, trust the delivery or can compare prices, which often means Amazon. The video creates the interest and the purchase happens somewhere else, and each platform’s report credits only its own part.

Follow where the value lands and the split is lopsided. The brand pays for the content and the ad on TikTok, while the marketplace collects the transaction, the review and the search data that come with it. A brand that judges each channel by its own dashboard ends up rewarding the channel that closed the sale and starving the one that started it.

The available tests point to a meaningful effect on Amazon. The baby products brand Newton Baby ran a test that compared regions with and without TikTok ads. It found its TikTok ads lifted sales on its own site by 4.14% and on Amazon by 5.11%, according to a case study by Haus, the measurement firm. The brand found TikTok ads were more effective at driving Amazon sales than its Amazon advertising program.

Take a brand spending $5,000 a month on TikTok. Its TikTok Shop dashboard shows $10,000 in sales, a return of 2 to 1, which looks marginal. A test comparing regions with and without TikTok ads shows another $8,000 a month in Amazon sales caused by the same spending. The full return is $18,000, or 3.6 to 1, and the decision to cut TikTok would have been a mistake.

Measuring the whole path from video to purchase

Holdout tests settle the question most directly. A brand can turn TikTok advertising off in some regions or for some periods and compare total sales, across TikTok Shop, Amazon, its own site and stores, with regions or periods where it stayed on. The difference is TikTok’s true effect, wherever the sales happened. Shoppers who discover a product on TikTok may not buy for days or weeks, so tests should run long enough, usually several weeks, to capture purchases that happen after the first view.

Branded search on Amazon gives a faster read between tests. When TikTok content takes off, searches for the brand’s name and products on Amazon often rise, and Amazon’s search data lets brand owners track them. Amazon Attribution links in TikTok bios and creator content show some of the traffic sent to Amazon. They will not capture everyone, but they add evidence alongside tests and search data.

A large part of the effect comes from creators. Content from creators often travels further than brand ads, and shoppers trust it more, so creator programs belong in the tests, not just paid ads, since both feed the same demand. Budget is easier to judge when it is split by role: TikTok Shop ads and live selling capture sales inside the app, while broader content builds demand that may convert elsewhere. Each should be judged by the outcome it is meant to drive, rather than holding both to TikTok Shop sales alone.

The opposite error matters too. Not every rise in Amazon sales comes from TikTok. Seasonality, promotions and other advertising also matter, which is why tests beat assumptions. A rise in Amazon sales that coincides with a price cut or a deal event proves little on its own.

Getting ready where the sale lands

If TikTok sends shoppers to Amazon, the Amazon listing must be ready: in stock, well reviewed and easy to find. Brands should also defend branded searches there, so competitors do not capture the demand TikTok created. Shoppers comparing a product on TikTok Shop and Amazon notice price gaps, and consistent prices with enough inventory on both prevent lost sales.

The same conversation has to cover platform risk. TikTok’s future in the United States remains uncertain after the April 2024 law requiring its sale or a ban. Brands should value its effect accurately, but avoid depending on it so heavily that a shutdown would leave a gap they cannot fill.

The question for a leadership team is which report its TikTok budget is being judged on, and whether anyone is counting the Amazon sales TikTok started. Setting up that cross-channel test is part of how we measure social commerce for brands across TikTok, Instagram and the major marketplaces.

A0639.crumb: The hidden costs of Amazon’s push for low…
A0639.title: The hidden costs of Amazon’s push for low prices
A0639.alt: A stoneware pot with a blank coral price tag sits on a rustic wooden shelf with coins tucked in a crack below.
A0639.ttag: The hidden costs of Amazon’s push for low prices | Kwontified
A0639.desc: A discount on your own site can cost more in lost Amazon sales than it earns. How Amazon’s push for low prices sets a price floor across every channel.
A0639.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 8, 2024.
A0639.body:
A brand sells $50,000 a week on Amazon. It runs a 20% discount on its own website for a week, expecting to add $8,000 in sales there. Amazon detects the lower price and stops featuring the brand’s offer, and its Amazon sales fall 30% for the week. The promotion that was meant to add sales takes them away.

Amazon’s push for low prices reaches beyond its own store: its pricing rules can penalize a brand on Amazon for offering a lower price elsewhere, while its plans for more low-priced selection add competition from below. A price change on any channel is a decision for every channel.

Amazon low prices sit at the center of its retail strategy

In his annual letter to shareholders, CEO Andy Jassy said lower costs let Amazon add more selection at lower average selling prices, putting it in consideration for more purchases, as coverage of the letter reported.

Amazon’s pricing rules extend that goal to other channels. The Federal Trade Commission’s lawsuit against Amazon, filed in September 2023, alleges that Amazon uses anti-discounting tactics that punish sellers for offering lower prices elsewhere, according to the FTC’s announcement. Amazon disputes the allegations, and the case is ongoing.

Amazon is also adding competition at the bottom of the market. It announced plans in June for a discount storefront of unbranded items, many priced under $20 and shipped directly from China, VC Post reported. The move followed a report by The Information, Retail TouchPoints noted.

The reason for those rules is easy to read. Low prices build shopper trust, and shoppers who trust that Amazon has the best price search there first. Every lower price elsewhere weakens that habit, so Amazon has a strong incentive to match or penalize it. The discount storefront applies the same logic to the cheapest end of the catalog.

Why a discount elsewhere can cost you on Amazon

Amazon can stop featuring an offer when it finds the same product priced lower elsewhere. So a discount on a brand’s own site or at another retailer can reduce its Amazon sales, and the lowest price a brand offers anywhere tends to become its effective price everywhere. As Amazon adds lower-priced selection, that floor keeps moving down.

The opening brand’s week looks like this, line by line.

LineSales for the week
Added on the brand’s own site$8,000
Lost on Amazon, 30% of $50,000$15,000
Net loss$7,000

The promotion costs the brand $7,000 in sales before counting the margin it gave up on the discounted orders.

None of that shows up as a cause in the sales report. The week’s Amazon sales simply fall, and nothing in the report says a discount elsewhere triggered it. A team that sees the drop without checking offer status may blame advertising or seasonality and cut the wrong budget.

The same pressure comes from other retailers. Walmart and Target also compare prices across the web and adjust their own, so a deep discount in one place can set off a chain of matching that lowers a brand’s prices everywhere for longer than intended. Third-party sellers who discount a brand’s products elsewhere can trigger the same effect, which is why controlling distribution and monitoring unauthorized sellers protects both price and offer status.

Match the price or hold it: both have a cost

Matching a lower price protects the featured offer and the Amazon sales behind it. Its cost is margin, and once matched, the lower price tends to spread to every channel. Holding a higher price protects margin, at the risk of the offer and the sales that go with it. Brands that sell to retailers wholesale face another cost on the matching side: a retailer that sees a lower price on the brand’s own site or on Amazon may demand support payments or reduce orders.

The numbers lean toward deciding product by product. Every brand should know, for each product, the lowest price at which it still earns an acceptable margin on every channel. That number makes it easier to say no to discounts that would spread. If a competitor’s lower price is permanent and shoppers clearly prefer it, holding a higher price may cost more than matching, so sometimes matching is right. In categories facing the new discount storefront and ultra-low-price rivals, brands should decide which products need to compete on price and which can win on quality, because fighting everywhere erodes margin across the whole range.

Where a brand wants to win shoppers on its own site, exclusive value works better than a lower listed price. Bundles, gifts with purchase and loyalty rewards can attract shoppers without a lower price for the same product. A bundle has no single listed price to compare, which is what makes it the safer lever.

The remaining gaps are about timing and monitoring. Run discounts on the brand’s own site and at other retailers on the same dates and terms as Amazon, or confirm in advance that the difference will not affect the Amazon offers. During any promotion, check daily whether the Amazon offers are still featured, and end or adjust discounts elsewhere quickly if they are not. Deal events lower prices on Amazon for a few days, and some brands match them elsewhere; planning those matches in advance avoids accidental price conflicts before and after the event.

The outcome of the FTC case could change how Amazon treats lower prices elsewhere. Brands should follow it, but plan for the rules as Amazon applies them now. Until then, the working test is simple: plan prices across all channels at once, and never assume a discount elsewhere stays elsewhere. Setting those prices across Amazon, Walmart, Target and a brand’s own site is part of how we run cross-channel pricing for brands.

A0642.crumb: The state of Mercado Libre for brands in…
A0642.title: The state of Mercado Libre for brands in 2024
A0642.alt: A yellow delivery motorcycle with a cargo box is parked on a cobblestone street lined with colorful colonial houses.
A0642.ttag: The state of Mercado Libre for brands in 2024 | Kwontified
A0642.desc: Mercado Libre grew revenue 42% and unique buyers 19% in mid-2024, with faster delivery and a young ad business. What it rewards in brands that enter now.
A0642.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 10, 2024.
A0642.body:
A US home goods brand that sells well on Amazon and looks at Latin America runs into three questions: tax, language and delivery. They are fair questions, and they can end the conversation before anyone looks at what Mercado Libre has built. Its buyer growth is at its fastest pace since 2021, its own fulfillment is speeding up delivery and its advertising business is growing fast from a small base. Brands that enter now can build position while attention is still relatively affordable, through official stores that use its fulfillment and local partners who handle tax and language.

What Mercado Libre for brands looks like in 2024

The business is large and still growing. Mercado Libre’s revenue rose 42% to $5.1 billion in the second quarter of 2024, and the value of goods sold on its marketplace rose 20% to $12.6 billion, or 83% excluding currency effects, according to the company’s shareholder letter.

Unique buyers grew 19% from a year earlier, the fastest pace since the second quarter of 2021, which the company attributed to bringing offline shopping online.

Delivery is getting faster as well: the share of orders shipped through Mercado Libre’s own fulfillment rose 8 percentage points in Brazil. The company also opened a fulfillment center in Texas so US sellers can reach buyers in Mexico, according to the same letter.

Advertising is young but growing. Ad revenue equaled 2% of the value of goods sold and grew 51% from a year earlier, the company said, adding that more external display and video partnerships were coming for its ad business, Mercado Ads. For a brand used to Amazon’s crowded auctions, that is an unusual starting position.

Mercado Libre rewards what makes a first purchase feel safe

Read Mercado Libre as an institution and its priorities are plain: it is investing in the things that make a first online purchase feel safe. Online shopping in Latin America is still well below levels in the United States, so many shoppers are buying online for the first time or buying new categories. Brands that are present and well reviewed as those habits form can become the default choice.

Fulfillment is the clearest signal. As on Amazon, products stored in Mercado Libre’s warehouses can promise faster delivery, which lifts conversion, and the jump in fulfillment use in Brazil shows sellers responding. Reputation counts as well. Mercado Libre shows each seller’s reputation based on delivery, cancellations and complaints, and a poor record lowers visibility and trust, so operational reliability matters from the first order. Payments complete the picture: Mercado Pago, its payments arm, offers installment options that many shoppers in the region expect for larger purchases.

On a Mercado Libre results page, the delivery promise, the seller’s reputation and whether the store is official all sit next to the price. Those are the same things the marketplace is investing in, which tells a brand where its own effort will pay back first.

The ad auction is still affordable by comparison. With ad revenue at 2% of the value of goods sold, fewer brands are competing for sponsored placements than on more mature marketplaces. That gap is likely to narrow as more brands arrive, and competition is rising from outside too: Amazon, Shopee and the Chinese cross-border platforms all compete for Latin American shoppers. Mercado Libre’s lead in logistics and payments is large, but brands should expect more rivals in their categories over time, which is another reason to establish position early.

Entering one country at a time

For the home goods brand, the route is less daunting than the three questions suggest. Mercado Libre’s Texas fulfillment center can reach Mexico, a local partner can handle tax and listings, and early advertising can test demand without building local operations. None of those steps needs a local office, and each can be reversed if demand does not show up.

An official brand store comes first, because it helps shoppers trust that products are genuine, which matters in categories with counterfeits and resellers. Storing inventory in Mercado Libre’s warehouses, or using the Texas route for Mexico, gives products faster delivery promises and better visibility. Taxes, import rules, payments, returns and language differ by country, and partners who know Mexico, Brazil or other markets prevent costly mistakes.

Mexico and Brazil are the largest opportunities but differ in rules, languages and logistics, so brands should prove the model in one before expanding. The category matters as much as the country. Products that are light, durable and easy to explain travel well across borders, while bulky, fragile or heavily regulated products face higher costs and more paperwork and suit brands with local operations.

The listing work deserves the same care. Machine translation is a starting point, not a finished listing; titles, sizes, measurements and product benefits should read naturally to local shoppers. Exchange rates and local inflation affect pricing, so prices need review more often than on US marketplaces. Returns and customer questions need an owner in each country, decided in advance, along with the language they will be handled in.

Brands that already sell well on Amazon start with useful content, reviews and data. Many of the same images, product details and lessons on pricing carry over, with local adjustment. As Mercado Ads adds display and video partnerships beyond its own site, brands will be able to reach shoppers before they start searching, and early tests can show whether that reach adds sales or simply repeats it.

A leadership team has to settle whether it will judge the channel like any other: sales, margin after fees and logistics, and advertising return by country, compared with the brand’s other channels before scaling. Answering it country by country is how we help brands plan an entry onto Mercado Libre.

A0644.crumb: The state of Target’s Roundel for brands…
A0644.title: The state of Target’s Roundel for brands in 2024
A0644.alt: A red wooden store display holds stoneware bowls, linen towels, glass jars and wooden spoons under a blank lightbox sign.
A0644.ttag: The state of Target’s Roundel for brands in 2024 | Kwontified
A0644.desc: Roundel is a $1.5 billion ad business built on 100 million Target Circle members. Why brands should judge it on store and online sales together.
A0644.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 15, 2024.
A0644.body:
Target values its ad business, Roundel, at more than $1.5 billion a year. Yet judged on online return alone, a Roundel campaign can look middling next to Amazon advertising. The online number leaves out where most of Target’s sales happen: in stores. Roundel is built on loyalty data from more than 100 million members who shop in both places, and it now offers self-service sponsored product ads, so brands should judge it on total sales, including the in-store sales its data can measure. They should also keep in mind that its reach is smaller than Amazon’s.

Roundel for brands in 2024: a loyalty-data business

Roundel has grown quickly over the past few years. A Target executive said in March that Roundel had become a business worth more than $1.5 billion a year, Benzinga reported. The ad business grew more than 20% in 2023, according to a transcript of Target’s March investor meeting.

Its data comes from Target’s loyalty program, which links store and online shopping. Target Circle has more than 100 million members, and in April Target added a paid tier, Target Circle 360, offering same-day delivery for an introductory $49 a year, the Associated Press reported.

Access has also improved for smaller brands. Roundel Media Studio, a self-service platform for buying and managing Target Product Ads, Target’s sponsored product format, became available in 2024, according to a guide from the agency Tinuiti. Marketplace sellers on Target Plus can use Target Product Ads to promote their listings too, which helps newer brands build visibility on Target’s site.

Store sales change the return

Most of Target’s sales happen in stores, and its loyalty program links shoppers’ store and online purchases. So ads on Target’s site and app can be measured against sales in both places, and a campaign that looks average on online return alone can be strong once in-store sales are counted.

The online return earns its place in most reports honestly. It arrives fast, it comes from the same click data every platform shares, and it compares neatly with Amazon. Its blind spot is specific to a retailer like Target: a shopper who sees a Target Product Ad in the app and buys the item in a store later in the week counts as nothing online.

Take a brand that spends $10,000 on Roundel in a month. Online, it records $30,000 in sales from those ads, which trails its Amazon advertising. Roundel’s measurement also shows $20,000 in store sales from shoppers who saw the ads.

What is countedSales from $10,000 of adsReturn
Online sales only$30,0003 to 1
Online plus store sales$50,0005 to 1

A brand that cut Roundel based on online results alone would have cut one of its better investments.

What would change that conclusion is evidence that the store sales would have happened anyway. A loyal Target shopper who buys the same detergent every month may see the ad and buy as usual, and the loyalty match still credits the ad. The in-store number needs the brand’s own test before it settles a budget. Brands with limited store distribution should expect a smaller in-store effect, since Roundel works best for products stocked in Target stores and on its site.

The same match that makes the store number possible also sets its limits. Attributing store sales to online ads relies on matching loyalty members, which does not capture every shopper. Roundel’s reporting belongs alongside the brand’s own tests, such as comparing periods with and without spending. Walmart’s US advertising business grew 30% in its latest quarter, Walmart reported, and it also links store and online sales, so brands that sell heavily in stores should weigh Roundel and Walmart Connect against each other on the same total-sales basis.

Sizing the budget to Target’s reach

Target’s audience is large but smaller than Amazon’s. That limits how much budget Roundel can absorb, so spending should rise gradually while the team watches for falling returns, rather than assuming Roundel can take an Amazon-sized budget. A return that falls as spend rises is the sign that the reachable audience is running out.

Self-service Target Product Ads are the place to start. Buying them through Roundel Media Studio gives brands direct control over bids and products, similar to sponsored ads on other marketplaces. Fewer advertisers compete on Target’s site than on Amazon for many searches, which can mean lower click prices, so bids deserve their own tests on the most important searches rather than a copy of the Amazon bids.

Target Circle data lets advertisers reach shoppers based on their purchases at Target. That targeting is Roundel’s distinctive advantage, especially for brands that sell mostly in stores. Roundel also offers advertising on other websites and channels using Target’s shopper data. Those campaigns are harder to measure than sponsored product ads, so they need clear control groups before they scale.

Traffic at Target concentrates around Target Circle Week and holiday promotions, and Roundel budgets should rise around those events in line with deals and inventory. Holiday competition for placements rises in a few weeks, so the fourth-quarter budget and product list should be set well before November, matched to store inventory. Creative needs the same attention: Target’s audience responds to design and value together, and images and copy that work on Amazon may need adjustment for Target’s style.

Across all of it, one rule holds. Ask Roundel for reporting that includes in-store sales, compare that total with other retail media on a like-for-like basis, and let the budget grow only as fast as the return holds. Building that comparison across Target, Amazon and Walmart is how we plan and measure Roundel for brands.

A0646.title: Who decides Cyber Week 2024 participation, and by when
A0646.alt: Kraft-wrapped gifts with ribbons, a pine sprig, a brown book and mugs sit on a rustic wooden table.
A0646.ttag: Who decides Cyber Week 2024 participation, and by when | Kwontified
A0646.desc: Amazon’s Black Friday inventory deadline is October 19, a week earlier than in 2023. Who should own Cyber Week decisions, and which choices are still open.
A0646.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 17, 2024.
A0646.body:
Amazon set October 19 as the date inventory must arrive to be ready for Black Friday, a week earlier than in 2023. That date settles a question many planning calendars leave for later: who actually decides whether a product takes part in Cyber Week. On Amazon, the answer is whoever controls margin and stock, weeks before marketing plans the event. Brands should name one owner and settle a tier for each product now, and where deal deadlines have passed, use the options still open, such as coupons and advertising.

How Cyber Week 2024 decisions moved earlier

The deadline has moved forward by a full week. Amazon told sellers that inventory must reach its fulfillment centers by October 19, 2024, to be ready for Prime delivery by Black Friday, a week earlier than the October 26 deadline in 2023, Logistics Manager reported. Amazon recommended sending holiday inventory in August and September.

The stakes are large. Cyber Week drove $38 billion in US online spending in 2023, up 7.8% from 2022, according to the same report. Amazon said its US customers bought more than 500 million items from independent sellers during the 2023 Black Friday and Cyber Monday period. Black Friday falls on November 29, 2024.

The holiday calendar is crowded as well. Amazon’s October event, Prime Big Deal Days, ran on October 8 and 9, only seven weeks before Black Friday, and for many brands the inventory and deal decisions for both events overlapped.

Three decisions, and only one belongs to marketing

Cyber Week participation is three separate decisions, owned by different people. Whether a product runs a discount, and how deep, is a margin decision. It belongs to whoever owns pricing and profit, usually finance or the channel lead. Whether enough inventory reaches Amazon’s warehouses by October 19 is a supply chain decision, and it was largely settled when purchase orders and shipments were planned over the summer. How much to spend on advertising, and on which products, is the marketing decision, and it comes last because it depends on the other two.

When marketing owns the whole event, it often discovers too late that stock is short or the deal deadline has passed. When finance and supply chain decide first, marketing can plan spending around products that are ready. The order in which those three conversations happen inside a brand tells you more about its Cyber Week than any media plan does.

The decision in the room: one owner and a tier for every product

The practical step is to name one owner for Cyber Week, with finance, supply chain and marketing contributing, and to place every product in a tier. In practice that is a short meeting with the three owners in it rather than a crowded one. They are the person who owns profit, the person who owns inventory and the person who owns the media budget, each bringing the same product list. The tiers are:

  • Full participation, for products with healthy margins and stock already at Amazon: deals, coupons and higher advertising budgets.
  • Advertise without a deal, for products with good stock but thin margins, which can benefit from the extra traffic through advertising alone, without discounts that erase profit.
  • Protect and wait, for products with low stock, which keep their prices and limit advertising so they do not sell out before the end of the season.

The evidence for those tiers is already on the table. Results from Prime Big Deal Days show which products respond to deals and which do not, and they are a better guide than repeating the 2023 plan. Deals on Amazon are often compared with recent prices, so a discount in October can affect what counts as a deal in November, and the owner should check how October prices shape the Cyber Week options.

Where deal deadlines have passed, coupons and advertising can still lift visibility during the event. They get less prominence than headline deals and are still far better than nothing. If shipments will miss the October 19 date, plan for products to arrive later in the season; inventory that arrives in early December can still serve the weeks before Christmas.

The cost side needs the same discipline. Deals on Amazon carry fees, and discounts reduce margin on every unit sold, so the extra sales a deal is expected to bring should be weighed against the full cost, including fees, discounts and advertising. Competition for sponsored placements rises sharply during Cyber Week, so the same budget buys fewer clicks; budgets should rise only for products that convert well, with bids kept disciplined on the rest. Advertising that drives traffic to products about to run out wastes money, which is why budgets belong to the first two tiers and need a daily review during the week.

Listings and other channels round out the plan. Images, titles and reviews matter more when traffic peaks, and changes made during Cyber Week can take time to appear and may introduce errors at the worst moment, so updates should be finished before the event. Walmart, Target and other retailers run competing events in the same weeks, and prices and promotions should be planned together so a deal on one channel does not undercut another.

The last piece is deciding, before the event, how it will be judged: total sales and profit over the weeks around Cyber Week, compared with a normal period, rather than sales on the busiest days alone. The question for a CEO in October is simple to ask and harder to answer: who in the company owns Cyber Week, and did they decide before October 19 or after it? Settling that owner and the product tiers is part of how we run holiday events for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.
