A0647.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2024 measured: forecast against results
A0647.alt: A brass caliper leans against a twine-tied kraft parcel resting on scattered autumn maple leaves.
A0647.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2024 measured: forecast against results | Kwontified
A0647.desc: Click prices hit the top of our Prime Big Deal Days range while order values fell from 2023. How the forecast held up, and what it means for Cyber Week budgets.
A0647.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 22, 2024.
A0647.body:
One number in the early Prime Big Deal Days data flatters any forecaster. Advertiser revenue from ads rose 258%, or about 3.6 times normal, which sits above the top of our sales range. It is also the number most likely to lead a team astray. Click prices landed at the top of our forecast range, sales rose roughly in line with ad spending, and order values and returns on ad spend fell from 2023. The event was busier but less profitable per dollar, and Cyber Week budgets should be built on reach-case click prices and lower order values rather than the standard case.

How Prime Big Deal Days 2024 results compare with the forecast

Our forecast set three ranges. Sales on promoted products would run 1.5 to 2.5 times a normal day, with 2 times as the standard case. Click prices would run 15% to 35% above a normal week, with 25% as the standard case. The share of event sales on deal products was labeled a planning assumption.

MeasureOur range (standard case)What the data showed
Click prices against normal15% to 35% (25%)35% above the previous 30 days
Sales on promoted products1.5 to 2.5 times (2 times)Ad revenue about 3.6 times; total sales not public
Share of sales on dealsPlanning assumptionNot public

Click prices landed at the top. Across advertisers on its platform, the software company Skai found average click prices rose 35% during the event compared with the previous 30 days, as clicks rose 152% and ad spending rose 250%, according to its recap. Advertiser revenue from ads rose 258%, Skai found.

Compared with 2023, efficiency fell. Among advertisers active in both years, click prices rose 15%, average order value fell 20% and return on ad spend fell 29%, according to the same analysis. Other data points the same way. Sales at clients of the agency Momentum Commerce rose 42% from 2023, but day-two sales were 32% below July’s Prime Day, and Salesforce found US discounts averaged 21%, up 14% from 2023, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Why busier did not mean more profitable

Ad-attributed sales and ad spending rose by almost the same multiple during the event, about 3.6 times against 3.5 times. So the event added volume without improving efficiency. With click prices up and order values down a fifth from 2023, each dollar of advertising bought less revenue than the year before.

The brand from our forecast makes the cost concrete. In a normal week, it sells $10,000 a day of a promoted line and buys 1,500 clicks at $1.00, so advertising costs 15% of sales. During the event, sales double to $20,000, the standard case, and clicks double to 3,000. At reach-case click prices of $1.35, advertising costs $4,050 a day, or about 20% of sales. The brand sold more, but each sale cost a third more to win.

The pull of the flattering number

The 258% figure invites a conclusion the data does not support. It is the number a forecaster wants to see, and it is easy to read as proof that sales beat the range. But it measures advertised sales among brands that spent heavily, not total sales on promoted products. Ad-attributed sales above our range do not mean total sales on promoted products beat it, and brands should compare their own total sales on promoted products, not ad reports, against the ranges. The same pull works in reverse after a disappointing event, when the worst number in a recap gets all the attention.

The honest grade is a mixed one. The ranges held in direction. We expected October to deliver less than July, and it did: Skai found the October event’s effect on spending and sales was about half of July’s Prime Day. We expected click prices to rise more than sales efficiency, and they did.

Our standard cost case, though, was too gentle for this event. We told brands to budget for click prices about 25% above normal and to hold a reserve for the reach case, and the aggregate data shows the reach case was the right planning assumption.

Some of the forecast cannot be graded yet. It promised to subtract any shortfall in the weeks following the event, and two weeks of data is too early to judge that from public sources, so brands should check their own sales for the rest of October. Public data also does not show what share of each brand’s event sales came from deal products. Brands should measure it from their own reports and replace our planning assumption with that history. A forecast is a set of ranges because nobody sees an event before it happens, and its grade deserves the same humility.

What October means for Cyber Week budgets

The reserve was the right tool. Brands that held part of their budget back and released it once the first hours showed reach-case click prices could keep their best products visible without overspending on the rest. For Cyber Week, a reserve tied to first-day results remains the right tool.

Brands should assume click prices at least 35% above a normal week during Cyber Week, when competition is usually stronger than in October, and check that margins still work at that cost. With order values down a fifth from 2023, they should not assume shoppers will buy more expensive items; bundles and multi-packs can help raise order values where products allow.

Profit, not volume, is the test that settles the event. Budget Cyber Week for reach-case click prices and lower order values, and measure it on contribution margin after discounts, fees and advertising, compared with a normal week, rather than on sales or ad-attributed revenue alone. Grading each event against a written forecast is how we plan holiday budgets for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0649.crumb: What Prime Big Deal Days 2024 revealed…
A0649.title: What Prime Big Deal Days 2024 revealed about how retail behaves
A0649.alt: Three shop windows display stacks of red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes above a leaf-strewn sidewalk.
A0649.ttag: What Prime Big Deal Days 2024 revealed about how retail behaves | Kwontified
A0649.desc: Walmart and Target stacked their events on Amazon’s, yet US online sales elsewhere fell as discounts deepened. What the week showed about how retail behaves.
A0649.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 24, 2024.
A0649.body:
For two days in October, Amazon, Walmart and Target all ran deal events at once. Amazon held Prime Big Deal Days, Walmart started its own event the same day and Target Circle Week was already under way. Amazon now sets the retail calendar, and its rivals place their events on top of it rather than apart from it. Yet US online sales outside Amazon fell during the event while brands discounted more deeply. The lesson for brands is to plan each retailer’s event on its own terms, use the longer rival windows after Amazon’s days end and stop matching every discount everywhere.

Prime Big Deal Days 2024 drew rivals into the same week

Rivals clustered tightly around Amazon’s chosen dates. Walmart held its Holiday Deals event from October 8 to 13, starting the same day as Amazon’s two-day event and running four days longer, EcommerceBytes reported. Target scheduled Target Circle Week for October 6 to 12, according to a Home Page News report.

Overlapping did not pull shoppers away from Amazon. US online retail sales outside Amazon declined during Prime Big Deal Days, while European online sales outside Amazon grew 9%, according to Salesforce data reported by Digital Commerce 360.

Brands competed on price instead. Salesforce found US discounts during the event averaged 21%, up 14% from 2023, according to the same report. Among advertisers on its platform active in both years, Skai found average order value fell 20% from 2023, according to its recap, and average click prices on Amazon rose 35% against the previous 30 days during the event.

Why everyone ends up in the same week

The behavior is easy to explain once the incentives are laid out side by side. Amazon’s event draws shoppers into a buying mood. Rival retailers worry that if they stay quiet, those shoppers will buy everything on Amazon, so they schedule events in the same week to give shoppers a reason to compare. Each retailer also used its event to promote its own membership, with early access or exclusive deals for members, which tells you what each one was really competing for.

The dates say something about what each retailer wanted. Walmart ran longer than Amazon, which gives a shopper who missed Amazon’s two days a reason to keep looking. Target started earlier, catching shoppers before Amazon’s event began. Neither was trying to beat Amazon on its own days; each was trying to own the days around them.

Brands follow the same logic one level down. With every retailer promoting at once, brands feel they must offer deals everywhere, or risk losing sales to rivals who do, and discounts deepen across channels, not just on Amazon. When every brand concentrates spending into the same days, click prices rise as well.

Shoppers, meanwhile, go where the event is loudest. In the United States, that was Amazon. The rival events gave deal-hunters more options, but the data suggests they did not draw much spending away from Amazon during the two days that mattered most. Europe behaved differently: online sales outside Amazon grew there during the event, which suggests shoppers spread their spending more widely.

The result is a week in which retailers and brands spend more on promotions without clearly expanding total spending. The winners are the shoppers who compare prices, and the retailer that set the date. Retailers have every reason to keep placing events around Amazon’s dates, so brands should expect the clustering to continue and plan for it each year rather than reacting to each announcement.

Planning each retailer’s event on its own terms

Walmart’s event ran four days after Amazon’s ended, and Target’s ran three. Those later days are a chance to reach shoppers once Amazon’s event is over, when advertising competition on rival sites may ease, and brands that spread spending across the longer rival windows can avoid some of the peak in click prices. Walmart Connect and Roundel budgets for the week should be set by each retailer’s expected traffic and returns, not as a fixed share of the Amazon budget, and some brands will find their best returns of the week on a rival site.

Not every retailer needs the same deal. A deeper discount where a product sells best, and steady prices elsewhere, can protect margin without losing the shoppers who matter most. With three or more retailers running events in the same week, shoppers can compare prices easily, so any price difference will be noticed and prices across retailers belong in one plan. Members of each retailer’s program behave differently too, and deals and advertising can be aimed at the shoppers each retailer values most.

The measurement question is easy to skip. A week with three overlapping events produces three sets of results that look comparable and are not. Setting Walmart’s six days against Amazon’s two mixes different shoppers, different traffic and different event lengths.

Stores are part of the same week. Walmart’s deals also reached its stores, and Target’s event runs through its stores as well, so brands with strong store distribution should coordinate online deals with in-store pricing. A brand’s results on Walmart or Target during the week should be judged against that retailer’s normal sales, not against Amazon’s event, because shoppers and traffic differ. Brands selling in Europe should set their event budgets with the European pattern in mind.

The same retailers will cluster again around Black Friday. The October results already show which retailer worked best for which products, and a brand that has read them can place its holiday deals more precisely. Reading each retailer’s week on its own terms, then carrying that into Cyber Week, is how we plan holiday events for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0650.crumb: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2024 changes for…
A0650.title: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2024 changes for advertisers
A0650.alt: An open, well-worn cardboard box with a warm glow inside sits on a wooden table beside mugs and an old book.
A0650.ttag: What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2024 changes for advertisers | Kwontified
A0650.desc: unBoxed 2024 pushed more automation into how Amazon ads are bought, made and measured. Where the advertiser’s edge moves, and why independent tests matter more.
A0650.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 29, 2024.
A0650.body:
Nothing about a brand’s sales changes when Amazon changes how it credits them. Yet a brand selling $100,000 a month could see its Amazon DSP return triple on paper under a new attribution model, and the report alone would tempt its team to triple the budget. That is the risk inside the most consequential announcement at unBoxed 2024.

Amazon Ads used the event to automate more of how ads are bought, made and measured. That shifts the advertiser’s advantage from manual bidding to the inputs the systems use and to independent checks on their results. Brands should control those inputs, test the new tools against holdouts and keep a new attribution model from moving budgets on its own.

What Amazon Ads unBoxed 2024 announced

Buying became more automated across Amazon’s own sites and partner channels. Amazon said a consolidated display buying feature in Amazon DSP cut campaign setup time by 75% in early tests, and that its automated Performance+ feature improved customer acquisition costs by 51% on average, PPC Land reported from the October 15 announcements. Amazon also put its US monthly ad-supported audience at more than 275 million customers.

Bidding gained audience signals. Amazon introduced audience bid boosting for Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands, which raises bids for shoppers in chosen audiences, PPC Land reported separately. Creative became automated too: Amazon launched AI creative studio, a self-service tool that turns product images into display and video ads, according to Amazon Ads’ announcement. Amazon also introduced a managed service that plans full-funnel media for new product launches, Swipe Insight reported.

Measurement will change, perhaps more than anything else announced. Amazon will begin testing multi-touch attribution later in 2024, with full rollout planned for 2025, according to the same PPC Land report.

Shared automation raises the baseline, not the edge

Automated bidding and AI creative tools make the same decisions for every advertiser that uses them. So they raise the baseline without creating an edge. Two brands using the same automated bidding on the same searches end up bidding by the same logic; what differs is what each one feeds it. An attribution model built by the seller of the ads, meanwhile, decides how much credit each ad receives. A brand’s edge therefore comes from better inputs, and its protection comes from measuring results outside the platform’s own reports.

Audiences built from the brand’s own data, strong product images and accurate margins by product give automated systems better material than competitors provide. Automated bidding works toward the goal it is given, so cost limits and goals tied to profit, not just sales, keep it from buying volume at any price.

When the credit moves, the sales do not

Take a brand that sells $100,000 in a month. It spends $20,000 on Sponsored Products and $10,000 on Amazon DSP. Under last-click reporting, Sponsored Products receive credit for $80,000 in sales and DSP for $10,000. Under a multi-touch model, credit shifts toward the display ads seen earlier.

ReportSponsored Products creditAmazon DSP credit
Last click$80,000, a return of 4 to 1$10,000, a return of 1 to 1
Multi-touch$60,000, a return of 3 to 1$30,000, a return of 3 to 1

Nothing about the brand’s sales has changed. Only the credit moved, yet a team reading the new report would be tempted to triple its DSP budget.

Last click has a real virtue. It is simple, it is consistent from month to month, and everyone in the room knows its bias: it favors the ad closest to the purchase. A multi-touch model spreads credit by rules that Amazon writes. The rules may be sensible, but they are still the seller’s rules, and a brand cannot audit them from the report. When multi-touch reporting arrives, it belongs next to last-click reporting and holdout results, and budget should move only when independent tests agree with the new model’s direction.

Testing the new tools before they move budget

Before scaling Performance+, audience bid boosting or AI creative, run them against a control: a matched set of products, regions or periods without the new feature, judged on total sales rather than the feature’s own reports. Automated bidding and new audience features often need several weeks of data before they perform well, so tests should run long enough to get past that learning period instead of being judged on the first few days. A feature that cannot beat its own control on total sales has not earned a larger budget.

Ads made with AI tools are fast and cheap, but they can drift from brand standards or make claims the brand cannot support. Every generated ad should be reviewed before it runs. If every brand can now produce video and display ads cheaply, more of them will, and the cost of reaching shoppers on Amazon’s sites and partner channels may rise as a result. Smaller advertisers may gain most: AI creative tools give brands without design budgets access to video and display ads they could not produce before, and their first test is whether those ads add sales at all.

The launch service can help brands without launch expertise. Its results should still be judged against a comparable launch run without it, not only against Amazon’s reporting. As setup and bidding become automated, the most valuable work shifts to analysis, testing and creative direction. Faster setup in Amazon DSP frees time that belongs to testing and analysis, not to launching more campaigns that nobody measures.

Control the inputs the systems use, and verify their outputs with your own tests before moving budget. The tools will keep changing from one unBoxed to the next, and that rule will not. Running those holdouts next to Amazon’s own reporting is how we measure Amazon advertising independently for brands.

A0651.crumb: What one skincare rivalry teaches about…
A0651.title: What one skincare rivalry teaches about the digital shelf
A0651.alt: Two unlabeled cream skincare jars sit on a weathered wooden shelf against green tiles beside a towel and plant.
A0651.ttag: What one skincare rivalry teaches about the digital shelf | Kwontified
A0651.desc: CeraVe led Cetaphil on Amazon because shoppers searched its name, while Cetaphil paid for visibility. What that rivalry shows about holding the digital shelf.
A0651.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 31, 2024.
A0651.body:
In April 2024, Amazon shoppers searched for CeraVe by name about 5.8 million times and for Cetaphil about 1.5 million times, according to estimates from the agency PMG’s analytics platform. That is 3.9 searches for CeraVe for every one for its rival, and the sales followed the searches: an estimated $22.6 million for CeraVe that month against $8.3 million for Cetaphil.

The rivalry shows that the digital shelf is won mainly by shoppers who ask for a brand by name. Paid placements can borrow from that demand but cannot replace it, and even a leader’s demand erodes once it stops giving shoppers something new. Brands should measure their share of branded search, fix their best-selling listings before buying visibility, and keep renewing the reasons shoppers ask for them.

How CeraVe and Cetaphil built their digital shelf positions

CeraVe’s lead came from demand. Over the previous 12 months, PMG estimated about 38 million branded searches for CeraVe and 12.2 million for Cetaphil.

Cetaphil bought its visibility instead. It increased its share of paid placements from August 2023, while CeraVe relied more on organic positions, and it ran Sponsored Brands ads on searches for CeraVe’s own name, PMG found. The weak point sat further down the funnel. Cetaphil’s best-selling product, its large daily facial cleanser, was less well positioned on Amazon than CeraVe’s top products, so the traffic it paid for landed on a page that was not winning on its own.

In each case the positions differ in who owns the shopper. CeraVe’s customers came to it by name, so the relationship belonged to the brand. Cetaphil paid for placements in front of shoppers who had searched for CeraVe’s name, and many of those shoppers still belonged to the brand they had asked for.

Then the leader began to slow. L’Oréal’s chief executive said the United States was the biggest cause of a slowdown in its dermatological skincare business, citing Gen Z shoppers trying other brands and a lack of newness from CeraVe, Retail Brew reported. Galderma, Cetaphil’s owner, said Cetaphil lagged in the United States as well, and that it was adding a new exfoliating line promoted by a Gen Z influencer.

Why demand beats placement, until it fades

The numbers have a familiar behavior behind them. Shoppers who already want a brand search for it by name, and those searches convert well. A brand with nearly four times its rival’s branded searches starts each day with an advantage that ads alone cannot match.

Paid placements let a challenger borrow some of that traffic. Ads on a rival’s brand name reach shoppers at the moment of choice, but those shoppers came looking for the other brand, and many of them will still buy it. Conquesting works best when the challenger’s product page gives them a strong reason to switch, and Cetaphil’s top listing did not.

The leader’s position is not permanent either. Branded search reflects reasons to ask for a brand: recommendations, new products, social conversation. When those reasons fade, as L’Oréal said happened with newness at CeraVe, younger shoppers try alternatives and the search lead narrows. If younger shoppers try new brands more readily, established brands have to show up where those shoppers discover products, social media included, and not only in search results.

Where the digital shelf is held

Share is the number to read before sales. CeraVe held an estimated 0.8% of the category on Amazon against Cetaphil’s 0.3%, PMG found, in a category with thousands of brands. Even the leader holds a small slice, so small changes in branded search can move rankings quickly. That makes branded search share, tracked month by month against the closest competitors, the clearest early sign of whether a brand is gaining or losing ground. Ratings deserve the same weekly attention on the top products, because a drop in average rating or a rise in complaints often shows up before sales fall, and rivals notice it too.

The listing has to work before visibility is worth buying. Images, titles, reviews and pack sizes on a brand’s best-sellers decide whether paid traffic converts, and advertising a weak listing wastes money.

Reviews compound: a product with more reviews and higher ratings converts better, which brings more sales and more reviews, so the cycle favors whichever brand reaches the top first. A challenger does better to concentrate review-building on one or two hero products than to spread the effort across the whole range. Price per unit matters as much as price, since shoppers comparing skincare on Amazon often look at the price per ounce, and a pack size that makes that comparison favorable can win a shopper even when the headline price is higher.

Search ads play defense for the leader and offense for the challenger. Leaders should run ads on their own brand searches when rivals target them, so a competitor cannot take the top placement for free. Challengers should target a rival’s searches only with products that offer a clear reason to switch, such as a better price per ounce, a different format or stronger reviews. Neither move replaces the slower work of renewing demand through new products, fresh formats and creator content, and a leader that stops doing that work gives challengers an opening.

The shelf itself is also moving. Retail Brew noted that drugstore chains were closing locations while Walmart and Amazon gained staple purchases. More of a skincare brand’s shelf is becoming digital, which argues for planning merchandising across Amazon, Walmart and Target together rather than one retailer at a time.

For a leadership team, the question is which side of the CeraVe and Cetaphil story its own brand is on. Is the search bar sending it shoppers who ask for it by name, or is it paying to stand in front of someone else’s? Measuring that share and fixing the listings it points to is how we run the digital shelf for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0653.crumb: Amazon’s Q3 2024 results: what ad revenue…
A0653.title: Amazon’s Q3 2024 results: what ad revenue says about clicks
A0653.alt: A wooden gavel rests on its sound block in front of rows of small plain cardboard boxes on a rustic table.
A0653.ttag: Amazon’s Q3 2024 results: what ad revenue says about clicks | Kwontified
A0653.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 19% in Q3 2024 while online store sales grew 7%. What that gap says about the price of a click, and how to budget for 2025.
A0653.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 5, 2024.
A0653.body:
A brand can change nothing about its products, grow in line with Amazon, and still watch its margin shrink. Amazon’s third quarter of 2024 shows how. Advertising revenue grew 19%, while sales in Amazon’s own online stores grew 7%, so each dollar of sales on Amazon now carries more advertising cost than it did a year earlier.

The gap comes from the auction, and it changes what a sensible budget looks like. Brands that plan 2025 on 2024’s ratio of ad spending to sales are planning on a price that has already moved. The better plan assumes a rising advertising cost per sale and decides in advance how conversion, organic rank and spending discipline will offset it.

Amazon Q3 2024 results put advertising ahead of every retail line

Advertising grew fastest of all the lines that touch a brand’s sales, GeekWire reported:

Line, third quarter of 2024RevenueGrowth from a year earlier
Advertising$14.3 billion19%
Online stores (Amazon’s own retail sales)$61.4 billion7%
Third-party seller services$37.8 billion10%
Total revenue$158.9 billion11%

Retail grew more slowly than the advertising sold against it. Revenue from Amazon’s online stores rose 7% to $61.4 billion, revenue from services to third-party sellers rose 10% to $37.8 billion, and total revenue rose 11% to $158.9 billion.

Third-party sellers accounted for more than 60% of units sold. Chief executive Andy Jassy said advertising growth was driven by strong demand for Sponsored Products, with early momentum in Prime Video ads, according to a transcript of the earnings call. He also said the stores business grew sales 9% in the North America segment. Even there, advertising grew about twice as fast.

The fee line did not move the same way. Third-party seller services, which include the fees sellers pay Amazon, grew 10%, close to retail growth. That suggests the faster-rising cost for most brands is advertising, not fulfillment and referral fees.

Put the lines together and advertising now comes to about 14.4% of combined online store and third-party seller services revenue, up from about 13.1% a year earlier, based on the reported figures and growth rates.

Why faster ad growth makes each sale cost more

Advertising revenue is what brands pay to compete for placements on Amazon’s pages. Retail sales measure what shoppers buy there. When the first grows more than twice as fast as online store sales, brands are paying more for each sale on average, and the cost of standing still goes up unless conversion or organic visibility improves.

Some of the growth comes from new inventory, such as Prime Video ads, rather than higher prices for search placements. But Sponsored Products, the ads brands use most, led the growth, which points to more competition in search results. Averages also hide the spread: large brands with strong organic rank may see little change, while brands that rely on ads for most of their sales feel the full increase.

Take a brand that spends 15% of its Amazon sales on advertising. Over the following 12 months, its sales grow 8%, close to Amazon’s retail growth. To keep the same visibility, its ad spending grows 19%, in line with Amazon’s ad revenue.

Its advertising now costs about 16.5% of sales. Both lines grew, and the ad line simply grew faster. Nothing about the brand’s products changed, yet its margin fell by 1.5 percentage points because the auction got more crowded.

That is the part that looks irrational from inside one account. The brand made no change of its own; the higher cost came from a more crowded auction.

Budget 2025 for a more crowded auction

Plan for advertising to cost a larger share of sales in 2025, and decide in advance how the brand will offset it. Model the year with advertising costs growing faster than sales, and check that margins hold at a higher ratio of ad spending to sales.

Conversion is the most direct offset. Better images, reviews, prices and delivery promises turn more clicks into sales, and a higher conversion rate offsets higher click prices directly. Organic rank works more slowly: products that rank well without ads depend less on the auction, and strong sales history, reviews and relevant listings reduce how much a brand must pay to stay visible.

Rising click prices also raise the cost of ads that add nothing. Ads on a brand’s own name that would win the sale anyway, and ads on searches that rarely convert, become more expensive, so test whether they add sales before keeping them. New formats such as Prime Video ads reach shoppers before they search; they may be worth testing, but judge them on added sales, not on the platform’s own reports. Some advertising builds awareness that pays back over months, so label that spending separately and a rising ratio caused by deliberate investment will not be confused with rising click prices.

Timing matters too. Amazon guided fourth-quarter revenue to $181.5 billion to $188.5 billion, according to GeekWire, and the holiday season concentrates competition, so click prices are likely to be highest when brands most want visibility. Walmart Connect and Roundel are growing as well, but their auctions are generally less crowded than Amazon’s, which makes cost per sale across retailers worth comparing before an Amazon budget goes up.

The test that settles it is your own ratio. Calculate advertising cost as a share of Amazon sales for each quarter of 2023 and 2024. If that ratio is rising faster than the market’s, the brand is losing ground in the auction, not just paying the market rate. Building that ratio into the 2025 plan is how we budget Amazon advertising against margin for brands.

A0654.crumb: The gifting gap between Mother’s Day and…
A0654.title: The gifting gap between Mother’s Day and Father’s Day
A0654.alt: A cream gift box with a pink satin bow and blush flowers sits beside a twine-tied kraft box on a wooden shelf.
A0654.ttag: The gifting gap between Mother’s Day and Father’s Day | Kwontified
A0654.desc: Shoppers planned $33.5 billion for Mother’s Day 2024 and $22.4 billion for Father’s Day. What the gap says about gift shoppers, and how to sell to them.
A0654.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 7, 2024.
A0654.body:
Shoppers planned to spend $33.5 billion on Mother’s Day in 2024 and $22.4 billion on Father’s Day, according to National Retail Federation surveys reported by PYMNTS. That is about half as much again for mothers as for fathers.

The gap reflects how differently people shop for men: Mother’s Day comes with settled gift traditions, while Father’s Day comes with fewer of them and more uncertainty. Brands that sell to men can close part of that gap by making their products easy to choose as gifts, with gift-ready bundles, clear gift language and dependable delivery dates. That matters now, because the same uncertainty returns in the holiday season.

The Father’s Day gifting gap in the 2024 numbers

Both holidays slipped from records. Father’s Day spending was projected at $22.4 billion, below 2023’s record of $22.9 billion, and Mother’s Day spending at $33.5 billion, below its 2023 record of $35.7 billion. Father’s Day shoppers planned to spend $189.81 on average, down from $196.23 a year earlier. Shoppers seem to have trimmed gift budgets across the board, yet the distance between the two holidays stayed wide.

The gap holds per person too. Mother’s Day shoppers planned to spend $254.04 on average, and flowers were expected to be the most popular gift, chosen by nearly three-quarters of consumers, Fox Business reported. That is about $64 more per shopper than for Father’s Day, or roughly 34% more.

The gifts themselves differ in kind as well as in size. For Father’s Day, the largest category of spending was special outings, at $4.5 billion, and nearly half of shoppers said they wanted something unique, according to the same report. The shoppers themselves vary. Half planned to buy for a father or stepfather and 26% for a husband, PYMNTS reported, and consumers aged 25 to 34 were the biggest spenders, at $275.67 on average, according to Retail Insight Network.

Why shoppers spend less, and differently, on men

Mother’s Day has its traditions: flowers, jewelry, brunch, cards. Shoppers know what a good gift looks like, so they buy with confidence and often trade up. Father’s Day has fewer of those traditions. Shoppers are less sure what to buy, so many fall back on cards, gift cards or outings rather than products, and the ones searching for something unique without knowing what it is reward whichever brand makes the choice easy.

That uncertainty shows up in how they search. Shoppers often type broad phrases such as gifts for dad or gifts for men rather than a specific product. The listings that appear for those searches, and that clearly signal they make good gifts, capture spending that would otherwise go to a gift card.

The same shopper comes back for the holiday season. Men are often described as hard to shop for, and the people buying for them face the same doubt in December as in June. Whatever a brand learns about selling to that doubt around Father’s Day carries straight into the peak weeks.

What a gift-ready product page has to do

The gift shopper is buying reassurance, and a men’s product page has to supply it. Many men’s products are sold only as single items, which makes them harder to pick as gifts; bundles, gift sets and products in gift packaging remove the shopper’s doubt about whether the product is a proper present. Titles, bullet points and images should say plainly who the product suits and why it makes a good gift, which helps the listing appear for broad gift searches and convinces the uncertain shopper once they arrive.

Delivery belongs on the same list. Gift shoppers need products to arrive on time, so stock in Amazon’s warehouses and clear delivery dates matter more for gifts than for everyday purchases. Reviews carry extra weight because the buyer cannot judge the product for themselves, and reviews that mention gifting, or that come from people who bought the product for someone else, are especially persuasive. Clear price points help too, since an uncertain shopper often sets a budget first and then looks for something under a set amount.

The way people spent on Father’s Day also points to experiences. Outings took the largest share, so products that create an experience, such as kits, classes or subscriptions, fit that preference better than another object. The biggest spenders were shoppers aged 25 to 34, which argues for listings, images and advertising that reflect what that group values and where it discovers products, social media included.

Advertising follows the same logic. Broad searches such as gifts for men, gifts for dad and stocking stuffers attract shoppers who have not chosen a product yet. That makes them worth bidding on in the weeks before a holiday, as long as gift-focused listings are ready to convert the shoppers they bring.

Questions to settle before the holiday gift weeks

  • Which of our men’s products sell only as single items, and which could become a gift set or a gift-ready version first?
  • Do the titles, bullets and images on those products say who they suit and why they make a good gift?
  • Are we bidding on broad searches such as gifts for men, gifts for dad and stocking stuffers in the weeks before the holiday, with gift-focused listings and stock in place?
  • What does our own data show when we compare sales of men’s products in the weeks before Father’s Day with the weeks before Mother’s Day and with the holiday season, and which products rose most?

The products that rise most before Father’s Day are the strongest candidates for holiday gift promotion, and preparing their gift sets, gift language and stock before the peak weeks is how we plan gifting seasons for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0659.crumb: The state of Instagram shopping for…
A0659.title: The state of Instagram shopping for brands in 2024
A0659.alt: Smartphone with a pink gradient screen beside a ceramic vase of dried stems and a kraft paper bag on a wooden table.
A0659.ttag: The state of Instagram shopping for brands in 2024 | Kwontified
A0659.desc: Meta made in-app checkout mandatory for US Instagram Shops in 2024, while Amazon closes sales inside Instagram ads. Where brands should let the sale end.
A0659.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 14, 2024.
A0659.body:
People open Instagram to be entertained and inspired, not usually to buy. They see a product in a creator’s video or a brand’s post, and many of them go somewhere else to compare and purchase, often to Amazon, where their payment details and delivery promises are already set. In 2024, Meta built its shopping business around both halves of that habit.

One track is Meta’s own in-app checkout, now required for US Shops. The other is partnerships that let retailers such as Amazon close sales inside Instagram ads. At the same time, Instagram’s ranking changes reward original content. For brands, that makes Instagram first a place where shoppers discover products, and it leaves them with a decision to make on purpose: where the sale should be completed.

How Instagram shopping for brands changed in 2024

Meta pushed checkout inside the app. In April 2023, Meta said that from April 24, 2024, US Shops on Facebook and Instagram without in-app checkout would no longer be accessible, TechCrunch reported. Shops that sent shoppers to a brand’s own website to pay would disappear.

Meta also let retailers close sales in its apps. Since November 2023, Facebook and Instagram users who link their Amazon accounts can buy from Amazon product ads without leaving the app, according to TechCrunch.

Then Instagram changed what it shows to people who do not follow a brand. On April 30, 2024, it said it was updating its ranking to give smaller creators more chances to reach new audiences and to favor original content over reposts in its recommendations, TechCrunch reported.

Instagram’s competition works from a different model. TikTok Shop keeps discovery and purchase in one app. Its US merchants numbered more than 500,000 at the close of 2023, and by January 2024 its annual run rate in the United States had reached $3 billion, Retail Brew reported. Instagram’s in-app checkout is Meta’s answer to that model.

Why Instagram works more like a shop window than a store

That shopping habit holds across categories, and it explains the shape of Meta’s business. Its two tracks read as two answers to the same shopper. In-app checkout tries to capture the sale on the spot, which suits impulse purchases and brands without a strong marketplace presence. The Amazon partnership accepts that many shoppers prefer to buy where they already trust the checkout, and lets Instagram earn from the ad rather than the sale.

Both tracks feel the ranking change. If original content from smaller creators gets more distribution, brands that work with many creators producing original posts gain reach, while brands that rely on reposted or aggregated content lose it. A brand that keeps recycling its own assets gives the new ranking little to reward. Reels are where Instagram shows content to people who do not yet follow a brand, and product demonstrations, before-and-after results and creator reviews in short video reach new shoppers more reliably than static posts.

The checkout decision, product by product

For a brand, the Instagram decision is a choice between three destinations for the same shopper: the app’s own checkout, Amazon, or the brand’s website. In-app checkout keeps the shopper in Instagram but carries selling fees and gives the brand less control over the customer relationship and less customer data. Sending shoppers to Amazon uses delivery and reviews they already trust.

The answer can differ by product, and no single path fits every item in a range. A brand should pick the path that fits each product’s margin and the customer data it needs, and compare the fees and the data it gives up with the conversion gains before moving sales into the app. For brands with strong Amazon listings, ads that let shoppers buy through Amazon inside Instagram may convert better than ads that send them elsewhere, and a simple test against existing ads shows which works.

The details have to match whichever path a product takes. Shoppers who discover a product on Instagram and search for it on Amazon expect the same name, images and price, and inconsistent listings lose them at the moment of purchase.

What to fund on Instagram, and how to judge it

Original creator content is the investment the ranking change rewards. Brands should brief creators to produce their own content rather than reposting brand assets, and work with more smaller creators rather than a few large ones. Partnerships must be disclosed, and creators need clear guidance on the claims they can make; original content works best when creators have freedom within clear limits.

Discovery matters most when shoppers do not know a product yet, so new launches and holiday gift ideas suit Instagram better than routine replenishment. With the holiday season under way, Instagram is where many shoppers look for gift ideas, which argues for gift-focused creator content now, linked to products that are stocked and ready to ship.

Measurement has to follow the shopper out of the app, and past the last tap inside it. Much of Instagram’s effect shows up as searches and sales on Amazon or on a brand’s own site, so campaigns should be judged on branded search and total sales across channels, not on in-app sales alone. Followers, email sign-ups and customers who buy through in-app checkout can be reached again, so each campaign should collect what it can and the next one does not start from zero.

Instagram creates the demand, and the brand decides where that demand turns into a sale. The question for the leadership team is a practical one: for each product we promote on Instagram, where should the sale end, and are we measuring the sales that land somewhere else? Connecting that discovery to marketplace sales is how we run Instagram shopping alongside Amazon for brands.

A0656.crumb: Cyber Week 2024 forecast: sales lift, CPC…
A0656.title: Cyber Week 2024 forecast: sales lift, CPC and deal share ranges
A0656.alt: Glass jars partly filled with coins sit on a frosted windowsill before kraft-wrapped gifts tied with twine and greenery.
A0656.ttag: Cyber Week 2024 forecast: sales lift, CPC and deal share ranges | Kwontified
A0656.desc: Three ranges for Cyber Week 2024 spending, promoted sales, click prices and deal share, set after October pushed click prices to the top of our range.
A0656.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 15, 2024.
A0656.body:
In our grading of October’s Prime Big Deal Days, click prices rose 35% against the previous 30 days, the top of our range, while order values fell 20% from 2023, based on Skai’s data. Costs went to the ceiling of our range at the same time as baskets shrank, and a forecaster should not ignore that pairing.

The Cyber Week forecast starts from that result. The sales lift is likely to look like July’s Prime Day, but the click prices are likely to be the highest of any event in 2024. Brands should budget for reach-case click prices, plan sales around the standard case and judge the event on profit across the full 12 days.

The Cyber Week 2024 forecast in three ranges

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
US online Cyber Week spending$39.9 billion (+5%)$40.6 billion (+7%)$41.4 billion (+9%)
Sales on promoted products, peak days vs normal day2x3x4x
Click prices, vs normal week+25%+40%+55%

The market will be large. The spending range brackets Adobe’s forecast around 2023’s $38 billion. Adobe expected US online spending during Cyber Week (Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, five days in all) to reach $40.6 billion, up 7% and 16.9% of the holiday season, Retail TouchPoints reported. It expected Cyber Monday to reach $13.2 billion, up 6.1%, and the deepest discounts of the season to fall in Cyber Week.

The sales ranges match our July forecast, because Cyber Week gift demand is at least as strong as Prime Day for most categories. The click-price ranges sit higher than July’s and October’s. For deal products’ share of event sales, we use planning assumptions of 40% in the conservative case, 55% in the standard case and 70% in the reach case. They are not measured figures. Brands should swap in their own history from July and October.

The event calendar is already set. Amazon’s Black Friday Week runs from November 21 to 29 and its Cyber Monday event from November 29 to December 2, according to its announcement, with daily deal drops spreading traffic across the 12 days.

Why the cost side needs the cautious assumption

Cyber Week concentrates the year’s biggest gift demand into a few days, which raises sales more than October’s event did. But it also draws the heaviest advertising of the year into the same auctions. Click prices therefore rise faster than sales unless conversion improves, and the cost side deserves a more cautious assumption than the sales side.

Take a promoted line that sells $10,000 a day in a normal week. Its brand buys 1,500 clicks at $1.00, so advertising comes to 15% of sales. On peak days in the standard case, sales triple to $30,000 and clicks triple to 4,500 at $1.40, so advertising costs $6,300, or 21% of sales. In the conservative case, costs reach about 19% of sales. In the reach case, with sales four times normal and clicks at $1.55, they reach about 23%.

Even the best case costs more per sale than a normal week.

Budget the reach case across all 12 days

Budget for the reach case on cost, plan sales around the standard case and decide in advance what profit the event must deliver. Before the event, set a margin floor for each promoted product. The floor is the highest ad cost as a share of sales the product can bear after discounts and fees. Pause or reduce spending on products that cross it, and decide that rule before the first deal goes live.

Pacing matters because Amazon’s daily deal drops spread traffic across the event. Keep budget available for the final weekend and Cyber Monday rather than spending it in the first days. Hold 10% to 15% of the event budget unallocated as a reserve. Release it on the products that convert best once the first peak day shows which range is playing out, so the reserve follows evidence from the event rather than the plan made before it.

The first peak day is the one to watch. Black Friday will show whether click prices are tracking the standard or reach case, so compare your own results with the ranges that day and adjust for the weekend.

The deal mix decides the margin. If deal products carry most of the event’s sales, margins fall with them, so check how much event revenue comes from discounted products and limit discounts to products that still earn a profit at the deal price. October’s order values fell from 2023, which argues for bundles and gift sets where products allow, since they can lift order values.

Stock needs the same attention. Products that sell fastest in the first days can run out before Cyber Monday, so watch stock daily and shift advertising away from products about to sell out.

Other retailers belong in the same plan. Walmart and Target run their own holiday events alongside Amazon’s, and prices and promotions on all three should be planned as one, so a deal on one site does not undercut another, with budgets following each retailer’s own returns. With only 27 days between Thanksgiving and Christmas, set December promotions and stock before Cyber Week ends.

After the event we will grade these ranges the way we graded July and October, setting each brand’s lift, click prices and deal share against them. Until then the working rule is simple: assume click prices run about 55% above a normal week, and only spend at that price where the margin floor still holds. Setting those floors product by product is how we forecast and run brands’ holiday events on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0661.crumb: The state of Temu for brands in 2024…
A0661.title: The state of Temu for brands in 2024: price parity comes first
A0661.alt: Antique brass balance scale holding two peach and brown boxes against a blue-gray wall.
A0661.ttag: The state of Temu for brands in 2024: price parity comes first | Kwontified
A0661.desc: Temu opened to sellers with US warehouses in 2024 as the duty-free parcel rule came under threat. When joining helps a brand and when it risks Amazon sales.
A0661.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 19, 2024.
A0661.body:
Say a brand sells $20,000 a month of one product on Amazon at $20. It lists the same product on Temu at $17 and sells $1,700 a month there. If Amazon stops featuring the brand’s offer for one week, and Amazon sales fall by a quarter for that month, the brand loses about $5,000 on Amazon, roughly three months of its Temu sales.

The case for caution comes from that arithmetic. Temu grew by setting prices itself and shipping parcels directly from China under the duty-free import rule, and in 2024 it began adding sellers with US warehouses as that rule came under threat. For most brands, Temu is first a price anchor that shapes what shoppers expect to pay. Joining makes sense only through the local-warehouse model, and only for products where the brand can hold the same price it charges on Amazon.

How Temu’s model for brands changed in 2024

Temu’s original model put the platform in charge. Factories act as merchants and ship products to Temu warehouses in China, which are then delivered directly to shoppers in the United States, the AP reported. Marketplace Pulse estimated Temu then had more than 100,000 merchants based in China, and in the same report Temu confirmed it was opening its platform to US and European sellers.

By March, Temu was inviting sellers with US-based warehouses, though early adopters were mostly Chinese sellers with American storage rather than US brands, Benzinga reported, citing Marketplace Pulse.

The rule behind the original model came under pressure in September. US law exempts shipments under $800 from import tax, and more than 1 billion such packages entered the country in 2023, compared with 140 million a decade earlier, NPR reported. The White House proposed rules to stop the exemption from applying to goods that face certain tariffs, including most clothes and textiles shipped from China. Temu said its growth did not depend on the exemption, and the timeline for the rules was unclear.

Who sets the price in each Temu model

The difference between Temu’s two models is who controls price and stock, and that is the difference a brand has to weigh. In the original model, Temu sets the retail price and handles delivery. A factory supplies products at an agreed cost, and Temu decides what shoppers pay. That works for unbranded goods sold mainly on price. It does not suit brands, which need to control how their products are priced and presented.

In the local-warehouse model, the seller holds stock in the United States and ships orders itself. That gives faster delivery and more control, and it does not rely on the duty-free rule. It is the only version of Temu that fits how most brands operate, because it lets the brand decide what shoppers pay and how quickly they receive it.

The trade-off for a brand already on Amazon

Both sides of that opening arithmetic are real. Temu adds sales, $1,700 a month in that example. The cost sits on Amazon. If Amazon finds the same product offered at a meaningfully lower price elsewhere, it can stop showing that product’s offer in the main buy position on its product page, which can sharply cut sales. One lost week of that position wipes out about three months of the Temu gain.

Those numbers point one way. List on Temu only at the same price as on Amazon, or only products not sold on Amazon at all. Bundles or sizes made only for Temu are one way to do that without creating a direct price comparison.

Most brands will not sell on Temu, and it still affects them. Shoppers who see similar-looking products at very low prices on Temu bring that reference point to Amazon, whether or not they ever buy on Temu. Brands selling simple products that are easy to copy feel the most pressure, and Amazon’s own response, its new low-price Haul storefront, shows the pressure is real.

The answer is to compete on what Temu’s original model does not offer, fast delivery, clear brand identity, reliable quality and strong reviews, and to make those visible in images, titles and descriptions. The first thing worth checking is whether Temu listings that resemble your products appear for your key searches, and at what prices.

Four checks before listing on Temu

  1. Price. Can the brand sell on Temu at the same price as on Amazon, after Temu’s fees, and still make money? If not, it should not list.
  2. Fulfillment. Does the brand have US stock and the ability to ship orders quickly from its own or a partner’s warehouse? The local-warehouse model depends on it.
  3. Product fit. Products that shoppers compare mainly on price may sell on Temu but put the brand’s prices elsewhere at risk. Products with clear brand value are safer but may sell less on a discount-focused site.
  4. The rules. The proposed changes to duty-free imports could shift Temu’s model further toward local sellers, so watch how those rules develop before making large commitments.

We are watching whether Temu opens fully to US sellers and how many established brands join. A change to the import-tax exemption for parcels under $800 would raise the cost of shipping directly from China. We are also watching whether Temu’s prices hold up as more of its sales come from US warehouses. Each of these will tell brands more about whether Temu becomes a sales channel in its own right or stays mainly a price reference.

Until then the rule is parity or nothing. Deciding where each product sells, and holding its price across those channels, is how we run marketplace channels for brands.

A0662.crumb: Amazon Haul and the low-price anchor…
A0662.title: Amazon Haul and the low-price anchor: what it means for brands
A0662.alt: Large iron anchor leaning on a blue wall beside wooden bins of rope, twine and marine hardware with blank tags.
A0662.ttag: Amazon Haul and the low-price anchor: what it means for brands | Kwontified
A0662.desc: Amazon Haul puts items mostly under $10 inside Amazon’s app, behind its own search and cart. How that shapes what shoppers expect brands to charge.
A0662.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 21, 2024.
A0662.body:
Picture a department store that opens a dollar aisle with its own entrance and its own checkout lane. Shoppers can walk in and fill a basket without passing the full-price floor, but they now know what a cheap version of almost anything costs. Amazon Haul works much the same way: a storefront of items mostly priced at $10 or less, inside Amazon’s app, behind its own search, cart and checkout.

That design sets a new low reference price for shoppers while keeping most of the comparison away from the main store. The anchor will bite hardest on simple, easily copied products, and brands should respond by making their value visible rather than by cutting price.

How Amazon Haul arrived and how it is built

Amazon launched Haul on November 13, in a beta version for shoppers using its app or mobile browsers. Every item is priced at $20 or less, with delivery in one to two weeks and a $3.99 shipping fee waived on orders over $25, Bloomberg reported.

Amazon’s own description added how Haul is built. It has its own shopping experience, search, cart and checkout. Most items are priced at $10 or under, and shoppers get 5% off orders of $50 or more and 10% off orders of $75 or more, according to Amazon’s description quoted by Betanews.

Haul’s target is easy to read. Temu grew by offering very low prices in exchange for slower delivery, and Amazon built Haul to keep those shoppers inside its own app. It also says something about where Amazon is heading: a separate experience inside the main app, built around slower and cheaper delivery rather than speed. If it succeeds, Amazon may extend the idea to more categories, which would widen the range of prices shoppers see without leaving the app.

How a low-price anchor shapes what shoppers expect

Shoppers judge prices against a reference point, usually the prices they have seen for similar items, and that reference is an anchor. Take a shopper who sees a phone case for $3 or a pair of earrings for $5. A $15 version then starts to look expensive, even if it is better made.

Before Haul, that anchor sat mostly outside Amazon, on Temu and Shein. Now it sits inside the same app shoppers use for everything else, and some shoppers who browse Haul will carry its prices back to the main store.

Haul’s design limits the effect. Because Haul has its own search and cart, a shopper searching the main store for a phone case does not see Haul items mixed into the results; the two experiences sit side by side rather than on top of each other. Amazon appears to want Haul’s low prices to attract shoppers without dragging down prices across its main store, where most branded products sell.

The shopper’s mission matters too. Shoppers come to Amazon with a specific need and want it delivered quickly. Haul serves a different mission, browsing for cheap finds and accepting a wait, and those missions rarely compete for the same purchase. A shopper who needs a charger tomorrow will not wait two weeks to save a few dollars.

Where the anchor bites, and what brands can do about it

The pressure falls on simple, easily copied products. Phone cases, basic jewelry, home decor and small accessories are exactly what Haul sells, and brands in those categories will see more shoppers questioning their prices. It falls least on products where quality, safety or brand trust matter. Skincare, supplements, baby products and electronics with warranties are harder to replace with a cheap alternative, and shoppers are wary of saving a few dollars on them.

The tempting response, cutting price to match, is the wrong one. A brand that drops its price toward Haul levels teaches shoppers that its old price was too high and gives up margin it cannot easily recover. Making value visible works better: show what the shopper gets for the extra cost, from materials, durability and safety testing to fast delivery and reviews from real customers. Images that show quality up close and titles that state the difference clearly help shoppers justify paying more.

Bundles help too, especially for small accessories. A set of three phone cases at a price per case closer to Haul’s, delivered tomorrow, competes on value without lowering the price of a single case. Clear product tiers do a similar job. A brand selling both fast-moving basics and premium lines can price the basics competitively while keeping the premium products clearly positioned above them, rather than letting one price signal cover everything.

The early warnings are in the brand’s own data. Start by identifying which products resemble items sold on Haul, then read how shoppers’ reviews of those products talk about price. Comments that a product is “not worth the price” often rise when a cheaper reference appears, and they are a sign that the brand needs to explain its value better. Conversion on the most exposed products deserves the same watch through the holiday season: a drop in conversion with steady traffic suggests shoppers are seeing the product but hesitating at the price, which calls for clearer value messaging rather than more advertising.

The calendar sharpens all of this. Haul launched just over a week before Amazon’s Black Friday Week, when gift shoppers are browsing widely and comparing prices more than usual. Stocking stuffers and small gifts are exactly the kind of items Haul offers, so brands selling them should expect sharper comparison through December, and showing value on those listings before the gift weeks is how we protect price for brands on Amazon.

A0663.crumb: The state of TikTok Shop for brands in…
A0663.title: The state of TikTok Shop for brands in 2024: count the full cost
A0663.alt: Phone on a wooden stand beside a ribbon-tied gift box, rising stacks of coins and a small ceramic dish on a table.
A0663.ttag: The state of TikTok Shop for brands in 2024: count the full cost | Kwontified
A0663.desc: TikTok Shop raised its seller fee to 8% in 2024 and faces a January 2025 sale-or-ban deadline. How brands should count the full cost of a sale and limit risk.
A0663.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 26, 2024.
A0663.body:
An 8% seller fee looks cheap next to a marketplace referral fee. On a $30 product sold through TikTok Shop, it comes to $2.40. Add the creator’s commission, the samples and the paid promotion behind the video that made the sale, and in this worked example the cost reaches $9.90, or 33% of the price.

TikTok Shop grew quickly by selling through creators, and in 2024 it raised its seller fee and came under a sale-or-ban deadline set for January 2025. Brands should judge it on the full cost of a sale and on the new customers it brings, and they should keep their investment portable, building content and customer relationships they can use on other channels.

How TikTok Shop for brands changed in 2024

TikTok Shop raised its fees. Its commission on US sales rose from 2% to 6% on April 1 and to 8% on July 1, with a smaller cut for some pricier items, Retail Brew reported.

Growth continued through the fee increases. Its US merchant base passed 500,000 by the end of 2023, and its US business was running at $3 billion a year by January 2024, according to a later Retail Brew report.

Its future also became uncertain. On April 24, 2024, President Biden signed a law requiring TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, to sell the app within nine months or face a ban, with a possible three-month extension if a sale is in progress, NPR reported. TikTok said it would fight the law in court. The nine-month period ends around January 20, 2025, and the app has about 170 million US users, according to the Christian Science Monitor.

Why the headline fee understates the cost of a sale

TikTok Shop works differently from a search marketplace. On Amazon, most shoppers arrive looking for a product. On TikTok, most shoppers discover products in creator videos and live streams they were not expecting to see, and that changes what a sale costs.

The referral fee is only where the cost starts. Most TikTok Shop sales come through creators who earn a commission on what they sell. Brands also send free samples to creators, often many more than end up posting, and they frequently pay to promote the best videos so they reach more people. Say a brand sells a $30 product with a 15% creator commission, and samples and paid promotion add another $3.00 per sale:

Cost of one sale on a $30 productAmount
Referral fee (8%)$2.40
Creator commission (15%)$4.50
Samples and paid promotion$3.00
Total$9.90, or 33% of the price

The comparison that matters is with the full cost of a sale on Amazon, not with Amazon’s referral fee alone. A brand paying a 15% referral fee on Amazon and spending another 15% of sales on advertising pays about 30% in total. On that basis, TikTok Shop’s low headline fee does not make it cheaper. Its value has to come from reaching shoppers who would not have found the product otherwise.

Commission rates are the lever brands control most directly. Higher commissions attract more creators, but they raise the cost of every sale those creators drive. Rates should follow product margin: more on products that can afford it, modest where margins are thin.

The first tests should stay small. A brand new to TikTok Shop can begin with a handful of products that photograph well, demonstrate easily on video and carry healthy margins. Running those for a few months shows the real cost of a sale before the brand commits more stock or budget.

How brands should manage TikTok Shop’s risk

The legal deadline is the second thing to weigh. Nobody knows whether TikTok will be sold, banned, or kept running by court challenges and extensions. A brand cannot plan around a single outcome, but it can limit what it would lose.

The defense is to keep the investment portable. Creator videos can be reused as ads on Instagram, YouTube and Amazon, so brands should secure the rights to use them beyond TikTok. Customers who buy through TikTok Shop should be invited to follow the brand elsewhere, sign up for email or find the product on Amazon, and creator relationships built on TikTok often carry over to other platforms.

TikTok Shop’s share of sales needs the same discipline. A brand that depends on TikTok Shop for a large share of its revenue faces real risk if the app is disrupted, while a brand that uses it as one source of new customers among several is better protected.

Live shopping is worth testing on its own terms: live streams can sell large volumes in a short window, but they need preparation, a confident host and stock ready to ship, so treat them as events with their own budgets and results. Inventory needs the same care, because TikTok Shop sales can spike when a video spreads and then fall just as quickly. Keep enough stock to meet a spike without building large inventory that depends on TikTok demand alone.

Measurement should also take in the other channels. A TikTok video often drives searches and sales on Amazon as well as purchases in TikTok Shop, so track branded search and sales on Amazon during TikTok campaigns and credit TikTok for the full effect rather than only its direct sales.

The rule is to count every part of the cost before the first video goes live, and to keep each piece of content, each customer and each creator relationship usable somewhere else. Working out that full cost against a brand’s Amazon numbers is how we help brands decide where each sale should happen.

A0664.title: The state of Vendor Central for brands in 2024: be ready for both
A0664.alt: Green warehouse loading docks, one with a shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes and one with a cage cart full of parcels.
A0664.ttag: The state of Vendor Central for brands in 2024: be ready for both | Kwontified
A0664.desc: Amazon ended many Vendor Central relationships in 2024 as its marketplace grew faster than its own retail sales. How brands should prepare for both 1P and 3P.
A0664.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 27, 2024.
A0664.body:
In September 2024, many Amazon vendors learned that their wholesale relationship had an end date. A significant number were told their vendor relationships would end by November 9, 2024, after which Amazon would no longer buy their products under the wholesale model, SPS Commerce reported.

Read alongside Amazon’s results, where the marketplace kept growing faster than Amazon’s own retail sales, the terminations show Amazon reserving Vendor Central for the brands it most wants to buy from directly. Every vendor should prepare to sell through Seller Central as well, keep control of its catalog and plan for the change in cash flow before Amazon makes the choice for it.

How Vendor Central for brands changed in 2024

The notice periods were not the same for everyone. Some brands received two to three months’ notice, while overseas vendors were given six months, and switching to selling as a third-party seller on Amazon’s marketplace was the main option for affected vendors, Retail Brew reported. Experts quoted in that report advised vendors relying only on Vendor Central to diversify. The length of the notice decided how much of that work a brand could finish before its purchase orders stopped.

The third-quarter numbers point in the same direction. Amazon’s online stores revenue, which includes the products it buys and resells, grew 7% in the third quarter of 2024 to $61.4 billion. Its revenue from services to third-party sellers grew faster, by 10% to $37.8 billion, according to GeekWire.

Why Amazon is narrowing its vendor base

Follow the risk and the margin. When Amazon buys from a vendor, it holds the inventory, sets the retail price and carries the risk of unsold stock. When a brand sells through the marketplace, the brand holds those risks and Amazon earns fees. For many products, the marketplace is simply the better deal for Amazon: it earns fees without tying up money in inventory or managing purchase orders with thousands of suppliers.

Amazon keeps the wholesale model where it adds the most value: large brands, fast-moving products and categories where controlling price and availability matters to its customers. That points to who is most at risk, vendor relationships where the cost of managing the account outweighs the benefit of buying directly. For those brands, the decision is less about performance than about fit with Amazon’s model.

This pattern is likely to last. With the marketplace growing faster than Amazon’s own retail sales, the wholesale side will keep competing for Amazon’s attention and resources, and vendors who remain should expect closer scrutiny of their profitability to Amazon.

How vendors should prepare for both models

The practical answer is to be ready for both models, whichever one a brand uses today. A brand that already has a Seller Central account, knows its fees and has tested shipping to Amazon’s warehouses can move quickly if purchase orders slow or stop; a brand starting from nothing loses weeks of sales. Registering with Amazon’s Brand Registry puts the brand, rather than any seller, in control of its product pages, and that protection holds whether Amazon buys from the brand or the brand sells directly. It is the one step that pays off under either model.

Cash flow changes shape with the model. Under Vendor Central, Amazon pays invoices on agreed terms, after deducting chargebacks and other costs. Under Seller Central, the brand buys and ships its own inventory and receives payment as products sell, so the move changes when money comes in and how much working capital the brand needs.

Control of the retail price shifts as well. Under Vendor Central, Amazon sets the retail price, sometimes lower than the brand would choose. Under Seller Central, the brand sets the price but carries the fees and advertising costs. Both are worth modeling before deciding which products belong where.

A vendor that stays should look hard at its own record. Shipping accuracy, labeling and on-time delivery all count, and chargebacks for compliance errors and disputes over shortages reduce what a vendor earns and make the account less attractive to Amazon. The relationship with Amazon’s vendor team needs care as well: know who manages the account, raise problems early and come to annual negotiations with clear data on sales, margins and compliance. A vendor that shows it is profitable and easy to work with is harder to drop.

Many brands will end up with a mix. Some products may suit Vendor Central, where Amazon handles demand planning and pricing, and others may do better through Seller Central, where the brand controls price, stock and promotions. Planning that split product by product is better than waiting for Amazon to decide. Data access changes with the model too, since vendors and sellers see different reports, and brands moving between models should make sure they keep the sales, traffic and search data they rely on for planning. Advertising continues either way, so advertising plans should be set up to move with the products rather than depend on one model.

Vendors that already received a termination notice face a shorter list. They should list their products through Seller Central before purchase orders stop, send inventory to Amazon’s warehouses early so listings stay in stock, and watch for other sellers offering their products at lower prices while the transition happens.

For the leadership team, the blunt question is this: if the purchase orders stopped next month, how many weeks would it take us to sell the same products ourselves? Running Vendor Central, Seller Central or a mix of both, product by product, with the switch rehearsed before it is needed, is how we keep brands ready for either model.
