A0669.crumb: The end of the branded search tax: test…
A0669.title: The end of the branded search tax: test before you defend
A0669.alt: Empty wooden checkpoint booth with a raised red and white barrier on a country road through green hills.
A0669.ttag: The end of the branded search tax: test before you defend | Kwontified
A0669.desc: Branded search ads report high returns because the shoppers who click them already chose the brand. How to test them and keep only the defense that pays.
A0669.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 3, 2024.
A0669.body:
Many brands pay every month to advertise on their own brand name, and the reports make it look like the best money they spend. A shopper searches for the brand, clicks the brand’s ad and buys. The report credits the ad with the sale, and the return on spending is often many times higher than on any other campaign. The shoppers who see those ads were already looking for the brand, so the brand does not know whether the ads add sales.

Better measurement is making that blind spending unnecessary. Brands should test branded ads against a comparison group, and keep paying only where competitors bid on their name or where their own listings would otherwise lose the sale.

Why branded search became a habit, and why that is changing

Branded search advertising became routine for a simple reason: it looks excellent in reports. The risk behind it is real, which is why brands pay. Competitors do bid on rival brand names. From August 2023, Cetaphil increased its share of paid placements in skincare, including ads on CeraVe’s brand searches on Amazon, PMG reported. A brand that leaves its name undefended can lose shoppers who were looking for it.

What is changing is measurement. At its unBoxed event in October, Amazon Ads said it would begin testing a multi-touch attribution model later in 2024, with full rollout in 2025, according to PPC Land. Amazon Marketing Cloud and simple tests that pause ads for some shoppers or some periods already let brands compare what happens with and without branded ads.

Why branded ads report more than they add

Shoppers searching for a brand by name have already decided what they want. Many would click the brand’s own listing just below the ad and buy anyway. When the ad appears, the report credits the ad. When it does not, the same sale arrives through the organic listing.

So the reported return measures sales that happened near the ad, not sales the ad caused. The number that matters is how many of those sales would have been lost without the ad.

Take a brand spending $10,000 a month on its own brand name, with $100,000 in reported sales: a 10-to-1 return. A test that pauses the ads for a comparison group finds that 70% of those sales would have happened anyway through the organic listing. The ads added $30,000 in sales, a 3-to-1 return. That may still be worth paying for, but it is very different from 10-to-1, and it changes how much the brand should spend.

Judge branded ads on the sales they add, measured against a comparison group, not on reported return.

Alternating weeks are enough to run the test

A brand can pause branded ads on alternating weeks for a month or two and compare total brand sales, not just ad-attributed sales, between the weeks with and without ads. Amazon Marketing Cloud lets brands with access look more precisely at whether shoppers who saw branded ads bought more than similar shoppers who did not. Either way, the measure is total sales of the brand’s products, because that captures the sales that shift between ads and organic listings.

During the test, brands should also watch organic rank. If a product’s organic position drops sharply when ads pause, the ads may have been supporting its rank, and the test should run long enough to see that effect.

When to defend a brand name, and when to stop paying

The test usually shows one of two situations. Where competitors bid on the brand’s name, they take the top positions when the brand’s ads pause, and some shoppers buy their products instead. Those branded ads protect real sales, and the brand should keep paying at bids high enough to hold the top position.

Where nobody else bids on the name, or the brand’s organic listings already appear at the top, sales barely change when the ads pause. The brand is paying for sales it would have won anyway, and it should cut spending sharply or stop.

Most brands will find a mix. Some brand searches attract competitors and need defending. Others, often longer searches that include the brand name and a specific product, attract no competition and need little or no spending.

Ad type matters as well: brand ads at the top of search results, which show a brand’s logo and several products, often protect a brand’s name more visibly than single-product ads. Testing each type separately shows which one does the defending.

Product mix matters too. A brand’s best-known products may rank first for its name without help, while newer products need ads to appear on branded searches. Testing by product shows where ads still add sales.

Timing also matters: competitors bid on rival brand names more heavily during big events, when shoppers are comparing; a brand might need full defense during Prime Day or Cyber Week and far less in quieter months.

Where the savings should go

Budget that no longer pays for sales the brand would have won anyway can fund advertising that reaches new shoppers, such as category searches where the brand competes for customers who have not chosen it yet.

The work starts with a list of every brand-name search campaign and what it costs each month. Then comes the test: pause branded ads for a comparison group or set of periods, and measure the sales that disappear. Keep paying where competitors take the sales during the pause, and move the rest of the budget to searches that reach new shoppers. Testing advertising and moving budget to what adds sales is how we help brands stop paying for sales they would win anyway.

A0670.crumb: Preparing for an Amazon without review…
A0670.title: Preparing for an Amazon without review counts in search
A0670.alt: Gold star pins scattered on a wooden shelf beside a kraft box and an empty wooden plaque against a mustard wall.
A0670.ttag: Preparing for an Amazon without review counts in search | Kwontified
A0670.desc: Amazon tested search results without star ratings or review counts in 2024. The signals shoppers fall back on instead, and how brands should prepare listings.
A0670.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 5, 2024.
A0670.body:
Take a shopper scanning a page of Amazon results who sees one product with 20,000 reviews and another with 200. They assume the first is safer. The count tells them how many other people bought and were satisfied, without reading a word. In 2024, Amazon tested search results without star ratings or review counts, and at one point removed review counts from 15.6% of top searches.

The test shows Amazon is willing to weaken a signal shoppers have long used as a shortcut for trust. So brands should prepare by strengthening the signals shoppers would rely on instead: the main image, a recognizable brand, the content of reviews on the product page and visible sales momentum.

How Amazon review counts disappeared from some searches in 2024

In August, Amazon confirmed it was testing product search results that do not show star ratings or the number of reviews, Fortune reported. Amazon called it a limited test on a small set of products, said it aimed to make results more compact and easier to browse, and noted that ratings and review totals remained on product pages.

The test briefly grew much larger. On August 14, 2024, 15.6% of the top one million Amazon US search terms displayed no review counts, before the level came back down in the following days, PMG reported.

The tests fit a longer pattern. Amazon has added one-tap ratings, which let verified buyers rate a product without writing a review, and summaries of reviews written by AI on product pages, according to the same Fortune report. Each change reduces how much shoppers depend on the raw count.

What shoppers look for when the count is gone

Remove the count, and shoppers look for other shortcuts, several of which are already on the page.

The main image carries more weight. With fewer numbers to compare, shoppers judge more by what the product looks like and how clearly the image shows what they will get.

A recognizable brand matters more. Shoppers who cannot see review counts fall back on names they know, and that favors brands with recognition built outside Amazon.

Sales signals take on a larger role. Amazon already shows labels such as how many units of a product were bought in the past month and tags for best sellers. Without review counts, those labels become one of the few remaining ways to see what other shoppers chose.

The product page becomes the place where trust is decided. Shoppers still find star ratings, review totals and review summaries once they click. More of the decision moves from the search page to the product page.

Who gains and who loses when counts are hidden

The change would cut both ways. Established brands with large review counts would lose an advantage. Their thousands of reviews would no longer set them apart at a glance, and the strongest moat many established brands have on Amazon would be partly hidden.

Newer brands would gain a fairer start. A new product with a few strong reviews would no longer look weaker next to a rival with years of accumulated reviews. Launches could compete more on product and presentation.

Preparing listings for a search page with fewer numbers

Either way, brands should prepare for review counts to matter less in search, whether Amazon makes the change permanent or keeps testing. Preparing costs little, because every step also improves listings under today’s display.

Preparation starts with the main image. It should show the product clearly, at a size that reads well on a phone, and make the product’s main benefit obvious without needing text. The brand should be visible too: a clear logo or brand name on packaging and in images helps shoppers recognize the brand at a glance, especially those who know it from outside Amazon.

Titles need sharpening as well. With fewer numbers on the search page, the title does more of the work of telling shoppers what the product is and why it suits them. Titles should lead with the product type and main benefit, not a long list of keywords.

The product page needs strengthening as well. Since trust is decided there, images, descriptions and the content of reviews matter more. Brands should read their reviews, fix the problems customers mention and make sure the review summary reflects the product’s strengths. Add video where possible. Product videos on the detail page help shoppers who click through without a count to reassure them, by showing the product in use and answering common questions.

Advertising deserves a check too. If review counts disappear from search, sponsored placements lose one of the signals that made them persuasive. Brands should watch whether conversion on sponsored results changes and adjust bids for products that rely heavily on their review lead.

Sales momentum has to stay steady as well. Labels showing recent purchases depend on consistent sales, and running out of stock or letting advertising lapse can weaken those labels when they matter most.

Click data from search gives the early warning. If a product’s share of clicks from search pages drops while its traffic stays steady, the change may be affecting it, and the main image and title deserve attention first.

The routine itself is short. Review the main images on a phone screen and make the product and brand obvious at a glance. Read the recent reviews, fix the problems they raise and check what Amazon’s review summary says. Track click-through rates from search on the top products, so the brand can see quickly if the display changes. Strengthening listings and protecting conversion as Amazon changes its search page is how we help brands prepare for a page with fewer numbers.

A0671.title: Cyber Week 2024 measured: the result against the forecast
A0671.alt: Brass vernier caliper resting on twine-tied wrapped parcels in blue, cream and kraft paper on a wooden table.
A0671.ttag: Cyber Week 2024 measured: the result against the forecast | Kwontified
A0671.desc: Cyber Week 2024 spending landed between our standard and reach cases and click prices on the standard case, but early buying moved sales out of the peak days.
A0671.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 10, 2024.
A0671.body:
US online spending across Cyber Week 2024 reached $41.1 billion, up 8.2% from 2023, Adobe reported. That landed between our standard and reach cases, and click prices landed on our standard case. But shoppers bought earlier than in 2023, which moved sales into the days before the event.

So brands should judge Cyber Week on the full season rather than the peak days, and separate the sales the event added from the sales it pulled forward.

How the Cyber Week 2024 results compared with the forecast

Before the event, we set three ranges for Cyber Week 2024. Cyber Week here means the five days that run from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, and the ranges covered spending, click prices, the sales lift on promoted products and the share of sales from deals. For US online spending, our ranges ran from $39.9 billion (conservative) through $40.6 billion (standard) to $41.4 billion (reach). The result landed between standard and reach, closer to reach.

Click prices landed on our standard case. Across retail media, click prices on Black Friday rose 39% and on Cyber Monday 41% compared with the November daily average, Skai reported. Our ranges were 25%, 40% and 55% above a normal week. A rise of 39% on Black Friday and 41% on Cyber Monday lands on the 40% standard case.

MeasureConservativeStandardReachResult
Cyber Week online spending, US$39.9 billion$40.6 billion$41.4 billion$41.1 billion
Click prices, vs normal period+25%+40%+55%+39% to +41%
Sales lift on promoted products, vs a normal daytwo timesthree timesfour timesNot public; brand data
Share of event sales from deal productsPlanning assumptionPlanning assumptionPlanning assumptionNot measured

A second source points the same way. Salesforce put US Cyber Week online spending at $76 billion, up 7%, TechCrunch reported. The two firms measure differently, so the totals differ, but both show growth of 7% to 8%, in line with our standard and reach cases.

The click-price result matters most for budgets. Brands that budgeted for the reach case, as we recommended, had room to spare. Brands that budgeted for a rise of 25% or less ran short on the peak days, when competition for clicks was highest.

Two of our measures cannot be graded from public data. The sales lift on promoted products, which we set at two, three and four times a normal day, depends on each brand’s own results. And the share of event sales from deal products was a planning assumption, not a measured figure. Brands should grade both against their own data.

Early buying moved sales out of the event days

The most important finding is about timing. Adobe’s lead analyst said growth was stronger on Thanksgiving and Black Friday than on Cyber Monday, as early discounts persuaded shoppers to buy sooner, according to the Adobe report.

Skai saw the same pattern in its clients’ retail media results. Its data showed slightly lower daily sales volumes during the five days than a year earlier, while activity before Thanksgiving lifted conversions significantly. Skai suggested that the longer selling window could offset the lower daily volumes.

When deals start before the main event, some sales that would have happened on the peak days happen earlier instead. A lift measured only on the event days misses that shift.

Take a brand that normally sells $10,000 a day and sells 3 times that during the 12-day event, $360,000 in all. Compared with a normal 12 days, the event appears to add $240,000. But if sales in the two weeks before the event ran 10% below normal as shoppers waited, and the two weeks after ran 20% below normal as demand was used up, the brand lost $14,000 and $28,000 in those weeks. The event really added $198,000, about 83% of the apparent lift.

In 2024 the shift ran partly the other way. Early deals pulled sales into the weeks before the event rather than holding them back. Either way, the event days alone give a misleading picture.

Grading a brand’s own Cyber Week on the full season

Judge Cyber Week on the full season, from early November through December, compared with the same period a year earlier, rather than on the event days alone. Brands can run that grade in four steps.

Start with totals. Compare total sales for November and December with 2023, not just the sales on the Cyber Week days. That captures sales that moved earlier or later. Then measure the weeks around the event, the two weeks before and the two weeks after it. Sales that dip before or after the event show how much of its lift was moved rather than added.

Next, grade click prices against the ranges. Brands whose click prices rose well above 40% against a normal week paid more than the market and should review which campaigns drove it.

The last step checks margins on deal products. Sales at discounted prices carry less profit, so the share of event sales on deals determines how much the event really earned. Brands that tracked their July and October deal share can now compare all three events.

Our own forecast gets the same treatment. Our spending range held, and our click-price range was accurate. The forecast missed the timing shift, which is where the real lesson sits. For 2025, we will forecast the full season rather than the event days, and treat early-November deals as part of the event. Measuring what events really add, across the weeks before and after as well as the peak, is how we help brands grade Cyber Week.

A0673.crumb: What Cyber Week 2024 revealed about brand…
A0673.title: What Cyber Week 2024 revealed about brand and retailer behavior
A0673.alt: Three frosted shop windows on a snowy street showing red, blue and gold wrapped gift displays.
A0673.ttag: What Cyber Week 2024 revealed about brand and retailer behavior | Kwontified
A0673.desc: Cyber Week 2024 ran online, over 12 days, with independent sellers supplying most of Amazon’s sales. What that reveals about how the event now works for brands.
A0673.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 12, 2024.
A0673.body:
On Black Friday 2024, online retail sales rose 14.6% while in-store sales rose 0.7%, according to Mastercard SpendingPulse data reported by PYMNTS. On Amazon, more than 60% of sales during its holiday event came from independent sellers. Cyber Week 2024 showed that the event now runs online, over many days, and largely through independent sellers rather than the retailer itself.

So brands should treat Cyber Week as a season they compete in against other brands, planned and measured from early November, rather than as a few peak days the retailer runs for them.

Where Cyber Week 2024 happened: online, on phones and over 12 days

The event moved further online. Beyond the Black Friday gap between online and in-store growth, Mastercard said Black Friday has become a window of time for shoppers rather than a single day.

It stretched across the calendar as well. Amazon’s Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday event ran 12 days, from November 21 through December 2, and was its biggest ever compared with the same 12-day period in prior years, Amazon announced. Amazon said further deals would run from December 3 to 14.

Much of it happened on phones. On Cyber Monday, 57% of online sales came through a mobile device, representing $7.6 billion in spending, Adobe reported. The event is now shopped mostly on small screens, often in short sessions.

And the event ran through independent sellers. More than 60% of sales in Amazon’s store during the event came from independent sellers, most of them small and medium-sized businesses, according to Amazon’s announcement.

How brands and retailers behaved differently in 2024

The retailer’s role has changed, at least on Amazon. There, most event sales came from independent sellers setting their own deals, not from Amazon buying stock and discounting it. The retailer provides the stage, the traffic and the event dates. Brands and sellers provide the deals.

Shoppers responded by buying earlier. In the same Adobe report, its lead analyst put the stronger growth on Thanksgiving and Black Friday, ahead of Cyber Monday, down to early discounts that persuaded shoppers to buy sooner.

Advertisers also kept spending after the peak days. Retail media spending did not fade after Cyber Monday, particularly on Amazon, and stayed elevated in the days that followed, Skai reported. Brands kept spending because shoppers kept buying.

Put together, the behavior shows a different event from the one many plans still assume. The retailer sets the window and hosts the traffic. Brands compete with each other inside it, mostly online, across nearly two weeks, with shoppers moving when the right deal appears.

What the new shape of Cyber Week means for brands

When independent sellers and brands supply most of the deals, a brand’s main rivals during Cyber Week are other brands in its category, not the retailer. Its price, placement and advertising are judged against theirs, and that is the benchmark to use when reviewing the event.

Timing follows from the length. A 12-day event with deals before and after it rewards brands that plan the whole season. Budgets, stock and promotions need to cover early November through mid-December, with extra weight on the peak days rather than everything concentrated in them.

Measurement has to stretch the same way. If shoppers buy earlier and advertisers keep spending after Cyber Monday, judging the event on its five core days misses much of what happened. Brands should compare November and December as a whole with 2023.

Channels have shifted too. With Black Friday growing so much faster online, the online plan is the main plan for most brands. Store promotions still matter for brands sold in stores, but they are no longer where growth comes from.

Preparation matters more than reaction. In an event this long, run largely by sellers, the brands that do well are the ones with stock in place, deals set and advertising planned before the first day. Retailers no longer run the event for them.

The checks that the longer, phone-sized season adds

Mobile deserves its own check. If most event sales happen on phones, product images, titles and deal badges need to work at phone size. A deal that is clear on a desktop page can be easy to miss on a small screen, and shoppers moving quickly between apps rarely look twice.

Retailer events beyond Amazon follow the same pattern. Walmart and Target run their own holiday deals around Amazon’s dates, so a brand selling on several sites is effectively running several overlapping events at once, and needs one plan that covers all of them.

Stock planning has to follow the longer season. With Amazon running further deals from December 3 to 14, demand did not stop on Cyber Monday. Brands that sold out of their best products during the 12-day event missed the weeks after it, when gift shoppers were still buying.

The final review looks at which deals actually drew new customers. A long event with many sellers competing on price can attract shoppers who buy only on discount. Knowing which products brought in customers who return at full price helps brands decide which deals to repeat.

That puts a different question in front of the leadership team planning the 2025 holiday season. Is the plan built for early November to mid-December, with the peak days inside it rather than at its center alone? The brand’s prices, placement and advertising should be benchmarked against the competing brands in the category rather than the retailer, and November and December measured together against 2023, with a review of which deals brought customers who returned. Planning and measuring the full holiday season, from the first early deal to the last gift order, is how we help brands compete inside Cyber Week.

A0675.crumb: The 2025 plan: the assumptions to change…
A0675.title: The 2025 plan: the assumptions to change from 2024
A0675.alt: Leather-bound notebook with a pencil and a brass compass on a worn wooden desk by a window.
A0675.ttag: The 2025 plan: the assumptions to change from 2024 | Kwontified
A0675.desc: Five planning assumptions that 2024 proved wrong, from ad costs and event timing to attribution and channel risk, and what to use instead for 2025.
A0675.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 17, 2024.
A0675.body:
In the third quarter of 2024, Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 19% to $14.3 billion, while its online stores revenue rose 7%, GeekWire reported. Advertising grew faster than the sales it sits on. It was not the only assumption behind 2024 plans that stopped holding. Events spread over weeks rather than days, low-price competition moved inside Amazon and measurement is about to change.

So brands should build 2025 plans on ranges rather than single figures, budget advertising cost as a rising share of sales, plan events as seasons and keep a test group to check what each channel adds.

What changed in 2024 that a 2025 plan must reflect

Click prices rose sharply at every major event. During Prime Big Deal Days in October, click prices rose 35% against the previous 30 days, Skai reported. During Cyber Week, retail media click prices rose 39% on Black Friday and 41% on Cyber Monday against the November daily average, according to Skai’s Cyber Five data.

Events stretched out as well. Amazon’s holiday deal event, Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday, ran for 12 days, according to Amazon’s announcement. Shoppers also bought earlier: Thanksgiving and Black Friday grew faster than Cyber Monday, Adobe reported.

Measurement is about to shift as well. Amazon Ads said it would test a multi-touch attribution model in late 2024 and roll it out fully in 2025, PPC Land reported.

Five assumptions to change for 2025

A plan that copies the previous year’s averages assumes the system that produced them is unchanged. In 2024 several parts of the system changed, so the averages mislead.

Assumption in 2024 plansWhat 2024 showedWhat to plan for in 2025
Advertising cost holds steady as a share of salesAd revenue up 19%, online stores up 7%A rising share, with an offset decided in advance
Events are a few peak daysA 12-day holiday event, with deals before and afterEach event as a season
Event click prices rise modestlyUp 35% and 39% to 41% at the autumn eventsIncreases of 35% to 55%, with a limit per product
Low-price competition sits outside AmazonHaul and Temu’s US sellers inside the same appA price or quality role for each product
Reported results show what advertising addsA new attribution model arriving in 2025A test group to judge each channel

The first assumption to drop is that advertising cost holds steady as a share of sales. When advertising grows more than twice as fast as sales, the average cost of each sale rises. Take a brand spending 15% of its sales on ads. If its sales grow 8% and its ad spending must grow 19% to hold its position, its ad cost rises to about 16.5% of sales. Plan for a rising share and decide in advance how to offset it.

Events now need a season’s plan. In 2024 the holiday event ran 12 days on Amazon, with deals before and after, so budgets, stock and promotions should cover the weeks around each event. Click prices rose by more than a third against normal periods at both of 2024’s autumn events. Budget event advertising for increases of 35% to 55%, and set a limit on what each product can bear.

Price competition has moved closer. With Amazon’s Haul storefront and Temu adding US sellers, simple products face price pressure inside the same app. Brands should decide which products compete on price and which on quality, and plan prices accordingly.

Reported returns are about to move on their own. With a new attribution model arriving in 2025, reported returns will shift between campaigns without total sales changing. Keep a test group, such as paused weeks or regions, so the brand can judge each channel on the sales it actually adds.

How to build the 2025 plan on ranges

Replace each single figure in the plan with a range, and test which end of the range the brand is tracking. For sales, advertising cost and event results, set conservative, standard and reach figures. Budget costs on the reach case and sales on the standard case, as we did for each 2024 event.

The plan needs a quarterly review. Compare actual results with the three cases each quarter, and move budgets when the brand is clearly tracking one end of the range. Protect the test group as well. Commit a small share of budget, or a set of weeks, to testing what advertising adds, and keep it even when results look good. That test is what tells the brand whether its reported returns can be trusted.

Start with the assumptions that moved most. For most brands, advertising cost and event click prices changed more in 2024 than anything else, so those are the first figures to revise. Sales growth, by contrast, landed close to the forecasts for the events we tracked, and can often carry forward with smaller changes.

Inventory plans need the same treatment. If events stretch over weeks and shoppers buy earlier, stock has to arrive earlier and last longer. A plan that times inventory for a few peak days will run short before the season ends.

Channel risk belongs in the plan too. TikTok faces a sale-or-ban deadline in January 2025, and Amazon ended many vendor relationships in 2024. Brands should know what share of sales each channel carries and what they would do if one changed suddenly.

The plan should also name an owner for each assumption. Someone should be responsible for watching click prices, someone for event timing and someone for measurement, so changes are spotted early rather than at year-end. A 2025 budget rebuilt with advertising cost rising as a share of sales, events planned as seasons and a test group set aside now is how we help brands plan on ranges.

A0676.title: The year in marketplaces, 2024: the structural shifts
A0676.alt: Tower cranes over concrete frames of large warehouses under construction at sunrise, with sunbeams and mist.
A0676.ttag: The year in marketplaces, 2024: the structural shifts | Kwontified
A0676.desc: Three structural shifts reshaped marketplaces in 2024: sellers over wholesale, local stock as the entry ticket and advertising as the business model.
A0676.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 19, 2024.
A0676.body:
In September 2024, many of Amazon’s wholesale vendors were told their relationships would end by November 9 and that Amazon would stop buying their products after that date, SPS Commerce reported. It was one sign of three structural shifts that reshaped marketplaces in 2024. Platforms moved further from buying stock toward hosting sellers. Holding stock close to shoppers became the price of competing. And advertising became central to how marketplaces earn money.

So brands entering 2025 should plan to act as sellers, invest in local fulfillment and treat advertising as a fixed cost of selling rather than an optional extra.

The year in marketplaces: from buying stock to hosting sellers

The first shift is about who owns the inventory. Marketplaces increasingly prefer to host sellers who carry their own stock rather than buy it themselves.

Amazon shows it most clearly, in its results as well as in those vendor notices. In the third quarter of 2024, its third-party seller services revenue grew 10% to $37.8 billion, while revenue from its own online stores rose 7%, GeekWire reported.

The holiday season confirmed the shift. Independent sellers accounted for more than 60% of the sales made in Amazon’s store during its 12-day Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday event, Amazon announced.

Hosting sellers lets a marketplace grow selection without taking on inventory risk, and earn fees on every sale. For brands, it means more of the work of selling, including pricing, stock and promotion, sits with them.

Why local stock became the entry ticket

The second shift is about where stock sits. In 2024, marketplaces pushed sellers to hold inventory near shoppers, so orders arrive quickly.

Temu, a discount app built on shipping parcels from China, moved toward local stock. It began inviting sellers with US warehouses in March, Benzinga reported, and in November it opened to US sellers without an invitation, saying sellers could ship from US warehouses, Modern Retail reported.

Mercado Libre, which serves shoppers across Latin America, moved the same way. In the second quarter of 2024, the share of orders it fulfilled itself rose by 8 percentage points in Brazil from a year earlier, according to its shareholder letter. It also opened a warehouse in Texas to help US sellers reach shoppers in Mexico.

The pattern is consistent across very different platforms, from a discount app built on cross-border parcels to a marketplace serving shoppers across Latin America. Fast delivery wins shoppers, and fast delivery requires stock nearby. Whatever their price, brands that cannot hold inventory close to shoppers in each market will find it harder to compete.

How advertising became the marketplace business model

The third shift is about how marketplaces make money. Advertising grew faster than sales across the major platforms in 2024.

In the third quarter, Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 19% to $14.3 billion, more than twice the growth of its online stores, according to the same GeekWire report. Walmart Connect, Walmart’s US advertising business, grew 26% in the third quarter, Walmart said when it completed its acquisition of Vizio on December 3. Mercado Libre’s advertising revenue reached 2.0% of the value of goods sold on its platform in the second quarter, up 51%, according to its shareholder letter.

When advertising grows faster than sales, it becomes a larger share of what it costs a brand to sell. Paid placements take more of the visible space on search and product pages. Without them, organic visibility gets harder to win.

Brands that treat advertising as optional, switching it on for launches and off in quiet months, lose ground to brands that budget it as a steady cost of selling. Advertising is no longer a lever brands pull now and then; it has become part of the price of being on the shelf.

How the three shifts work together

The three shifts also reinforce each other. Marketplaces that host more sellers have more brands competing for the same placements, which raises demand for advertising. Sellers that hold local stock can promise fast delivery, which makes their ads convert better and justifies higher bids. Each shift makes the others stronger.

The shifts land differently by brand size. Smaller brands gain access, because marketplaces that host sellers make it easier to list without a wholesale deal. But they also carry more of the cost and risk of stock and advertising than they would as vendors. Larger brands keep more negotiating power, yet face the same pressure to hold stock locally and advertise steadily.

International selling follows the same rules. A brand expanding to Mexico or Brazil through Mercado Libre faces the same three requirements as on Amazon in the United States: act as the seller, hold stock in the market and plan steady advertising from the start.

Not everything changed. Shoppers still chose on price, delivery speed and reviews, and the brands with clear products and strong listings still won the most sales. What the shifts changed was the cost and structure of competing. These were not one-off decisions by a single platform. Several marketplaces arrived at the same structure independently in the same year, which is why these changes are likely to last.

For a brand planning 2025, that means planning as a seller on each marketplace, owning pricing, stock and promotion even where wholesale relationships remain. It means holding inventory close to shoppers in each market, using the marketplace’s own fulfillment where it is offered. And it means budgeting advertising as a steady share of sales across the year, not as a switch for launches and events. Selling across marketplaces as these structures change is how we help brands plan the year ahead.

A0677.crumb: Why premium brands should rethink generic…
A0677.title: Why premium brands should rethink generic holiday search
A0677.alt: Black gift box with a satin bow among kraft-wrapped presents, pine garland and string lights on a wooden shelf.
A0677.ttag: Why premium brands should rethink generic holiday search | Kwontified
A0677.desc: Generic holiday searches carry the season’s highest click prices and the most price-driven shoppers. Why premium brands overpay there, and what to bid on.
A0677.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 24, 2024.
A0677.body:
Searches such as “gifts for her” or “gifts for dad” draw many advertisers at once, because they appear in every category, and the shoppers making them have not yet chosen a product or a price level. Generic holiday searches carry the season’s highest click prices and attract shoppers comparing many options on price. So a premium product converts poorly there, and each sale costs far more than on specific searches.

Premium brands should shift holiday budget toward searches that signal quality, category and intent, cap spending on broad gift terms and judge any generic spending on the new customers it brings rather than its return.

How generic holiday search got more expensive in 2024

Holiday click prices rose sharply. On Black Friday, retail media click prices ran 39% above the November daily average, and on Cyber Monday they ran 41% above it, Skai reported. Some categories paid more: Home & Garden saw a 63% click-price premium on Black Friday, and apparel and beauty saw higher click prices on Cyber Monday, according to the same report.

Price pressure grew at the same time. Amazon launched Haul, a storefront of items priced at $20 or less, on November 13, Bloomberg reported. And shoppers bought earlier when early discounts were strong, Adobe reported. Generic gift searches sit where those pressures meet.

Why premium products lose on generic searches

A shopper searching a broad gift term is comparing many options across categories and prices. Faced with a wide range, many choose a cheaper item. A premium product competes in that auction at the same click price as everyone else but converts at a lower rate, because it costs more than most of what the shopper is seeing.

Take a premium brand that sells a $90 product. On a specific search, such as the product type plus a quality term, it pays $1.50 a click during the season and converts 10% of clicks, so each sale costs $15 in advertising. On a broad gift search, it pays $2.50 a click and converts 3%, so each sale costs about $83, nearly the full price of the product.

SearchClick priceConversionAd cost per sale of a $90 product
Specific: product type plus a quality term$1.5010%$15
Broad gift search$2.503%about $83

The specific search delivers a sale for about a fifth of the cost. And the broad search, even when it wins a sale, often wins one that the brand’s margin cannot support.

Premium brands should bid on searches that already signal what the shopper wants, and limit broad gift terms to a capped budget judged on new customers.

Where a premium brand’s holiday search budget should go

Specific searches should carry most of the budget. Searches that name the product type, a material, a feature or a quality signal attract shoppers who have already narrowed their choice. Premium products convert better there because the shopper is looking for what they offer.

The next priority is the brand’s own audience. Shoppers who have viewed or bought from the brand before convert far better than strangers on broad searches, and holiday budgets for premium brands should weight returning shoppers and people who searched the brand name.

Broad gift terms need their own cap. If a brand does bid on generic gift searches, it should set a fixed budget and a bid ceiling, so a few expensive days do not consume the season’s budget.

Those terms should also be judged on new customers. Generic searches can introduce a brand to shoppers who later return at full price. That value is real but slow, so brands should measure the share of new customers those searches bring rather than their return on the day.

Amazon’s new-to-brand reporting helps here. Its advertising reports show how many sales came from customers who had not bought from the brand in the past year. Brands can use that figure to decide whether broad gift searches are introducing new customers or just buying sales at high prices.

Video and display deserve a look for discovery as well. If the goal of broad holiday spending is to introduce the brand, formats built for discovery, such as video ads, often show the product’s quality better than a small search listing among dozens of cheaper items.

Making the premium case on every holiday search

On any holiday search, a premium product needs its images and title to show why it costs more: materials, durability, design or a recognizable brand. Without that, it competes on price and loses. Cutting price to win generic gift searches teaches shoppers to wait for deals and erodes the premium position, while bundles and gift sets add value without lowering the price of the core product.

The calendar matters as well. Click prices on broad gift searches peak around the big event days, and premium brands can shift budget to the quieter weeks before and after, when gift shoppers are still searching but competition is lighter. The weeks after Christmas deserve a plan too. Shoppers with gift cards and returns are back in late December and early January, often looking for specific items rather than browsing gift lists. Those searches suit premium products well and usually cost less than the peak days.

Make sure the images and titles show why the product costs more before spending on any holiday search. Split the holiday search budget into specific searches, returning shoppers and broad gift terms, and weight it toward the first two. Then set a fixed budget and a bid ceiling on broad gift searches, and track the new customers they bring. Spending holiday budgets where they pay back is how we help premium brands through the season.

A0679.title: How manufacturer brands are reshaping Amazon’s competition
A0679.alt: Cardboard boxes on roller conveyors leading out of open warehouse loading bay doors in bright sunlight.
A0679.ttag: How manufacturer brands are reshaping Amazon’s competition | Kwontified
A0679.desc: Amazon’s own brands lost share, vendors were pushed to sell directly and resellers faced new pressure in 2024. How brand-against-brand competition works.
A0679.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 26, 2024.
A0679.body:
Competition on Amazon is shifting. It used to be a three-way contest between Amazon’s own brands, resellers and manufacturers. In 2024 it moved toward manufacturer brands competing directly with each other. Amazon’s private label share fell, wholesale vendors were pushed to sell for themselves and resellers faced new pressure.

So manufacturer brands should run their Amazon business as operators who control distribution, price and content, rather than as suppliers who hand those decisions to others.

How the shelf changed for manufacturer brands on Amazon in 2024

Amazon’s own brands pulled back. In the first quarter of 2024, Amazon’s private label brands took 0.9% of its US retail revenue, down from 1.0% a year earlier, with declines in 16 of the top 20 physical goods categories, PMG reported. PMG measured that as a 6% drop in share, even though those brands still sold more than $1 billion in the quarter.

Wholesale relationships narrowed at the same time. In September, many vendors were told their relationships would end on November 9, and that after that date Amazon would no longer buy their products, SPS Commerce reported. Those brands had to choose between selling through Amazon’s marketplace themselves or leaving it to others.

The reseller picture shifted too. After Amazon cut referral fees on low-priced clothing in January, more resellers found it profitable to list cheap apparel. As a result, brands that sell wholesale to Amazon became more likely to lose the main buy position to resellers undercutting Amazon’s price, Modern Retail reported.

Why competition is becoming brand against brand

When Amazon promotes its own brands less, the space they gave up on search pages goes to other brands. When Amazon buys less stock directly, the brands themselves become the sellers. And when resellers compete on price for the same products, brands that control their own listings hold the advantage.

Put those changes together, and the main competitor for a manufacturer brand on Amazon is increasingly another manufacturer brand. Two brands in the same category now fight over the same placements, the same searches and the same shoppers, with fewer intermediaries between them.

That changes what wins in a category. In a contest between brands, the advantages are the ones brands control: product quality, clear listings, reviews, stock and advertising. A brand cannot rely on Amazon’s buyers to promote it, or on resellers to keep it in stock. It has to do that work itself.

How manufacturer brands should operate on Amazon

Control over a brand’s Amazon business starts with distribution. Brands should know who sells their products on Amazon and where those sellers get their stock. Tightening distribution, so that only authorized sellers can list the brand, protects price and the main buy position.

Owning the listing is the second piece of control. Brands should register with Brand Registry, so they control product pages, images and descriptions. That control matters whether the brand sells through Vendor Central, Seller Central or both. Price needs the same deliberate handling: in a market where resellers can undercut a wholesale price, brands need a clear policy on the prices they want shoppers to see, and the ability to enforce it with their distributors.

Advertising, too, becomes a contest against other brands, not just against Amazon. With more manufacturer brands competing for the same searches, brands should know which competitors appear on their key searches and on their own product pages, and plan bids and placements accordingly. They should also watch what space opens up. As Amazon’s own brands give up share, categories where they were strong, such as household basics, leave room for other brands, and those openings favor brands that move quickly with stock and advertising.

Measurement should follow the competition. Brands should track their share of their category’s searches and sales against named competitors, not just their own growth. Amazon’s brand analytics tools show which brands shoppers click and buy for each search, and a brand losing ground to a rival there will see it before it shows in total sales.

Content needs the same attention. When competitors sit side by side on a search page, the brand with clearer images, a sharper title and better answers to shoppers’ questions wins the click. Brands should review their listings against their closest competitors’ at least once a quarter.

The longest-lasting investment goes into what competitors cannot copy easily. Product design, a recognizable name and a record of strong reviews take years to build. In a market with fewer intermediaries, those are the advantages that last.

The decision on the leadership team’s table

There is a cost to this shift. Acting as an operator takes people, systems and capital that a wholesale relationship did not require. Brands that are not ready to carry stock, manage listings and run advertising themselves may need help, or may choose to keep some products with Amazon as a vendor while selling others directly.

That makes the mix of Vendor Central and Seller Central the decision in front of the leadership team, and every brand should review it. Selling directly gives more control over price and stock, while selling wholesale hands those decisions to Amazon. In a brand-against-brand market, many brands will want direct control over their most important products.

The groundwork is the same either way. Map who sells the brand’s products on Amazon and tighten distribution to authorized sellers. Confirm control of the product pages through Brand Registry, and set a clear pricing policy. List the competing brands on the top searches and plan advertising against them, not just against Amazon. Running Amazon as an operator is how we help manufacturer brands compete brand against brand.

A0680.crumb: Why a single keyword strategy sabotages…
A0680.title: Why a single keyword strategy sabotages growth
A0680.alt: Ring of worn brass and steel keys lying in sunlight on a concrete step beside a blue wall.
A0680.ttag: Why a single keyword strategy sabotages growth | Kwontified
A0680.desc: Pouring budget into one big search term buys each extra sale at a rising cost. Why single-keyword strategies stall growth, and how to build a portfolio instead.
A0680.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 31, 2024.
A0680.body:
A brand finds one search term that drives most of its sales, often the broadest description of its product. It works, so the brand puts more money behind it, raising bids to hold the top position. The habit is easy to understand, and it gets steadily more expensive: brands that concentrate advertising on one or a few big search terms pay a rising price for each extra sale.

Every search has a limited pool of shoppers, and higher bids mostly buy the same clicks at a higher cost. So brands should judge spending on the cost of the next sale rather than the average. And they should spread budget across a portfolio of specific searches, where extra money still reaches new shoppers.

How a single keyword strategy becomes more expensive

The auction makes concentration steadily more expensive. Amazon’s ad business grew faster than its store: in the third quarter of 2024, advertising revenue rose 19% to $14.3 billion against 7% growth in online stores revenue, GeekWire reported. More advertising money chasing slower-growing sales means more competition for each search.

The biggest searches feel the pressure most. They attract the most advertisers, and at peak times their click prices jump. Against the November average, retail media click prices were up 39% on Black Friday during Cyber Week and 41% on Cyber Monday, Skai reported.

Why the next sale costs more than the average

A search term has a limited number of shoppers. Once a brand appears near the top for most of them, a higher bid cannot find many more. It mostly pays more for the same clicks, plus a few extra from a slightly higher position.

Take a brand that bids $1.00 a click on its main search term, buys 1,000 clicks a month and converts 10%, so it spends $1,000 for 100 sales, or $10 a sale. To grow, it raises its bid to $1.50. Its clicks rise to 1,300, because the search has few shoppers left to reach, and it spends $1,950 for 130 sales.

The average cost per sale rose to $15. But the 30 extra sales cost $950, or about $32 each. That is the true price of growth on that search, and it is more than three times the original.

Now spend the same $950 elsewhere. Spread across ten specific searches at $0.80 a click and converting 8%, it buys about 1,190 clicks and 95 sales, at $10 each. The portfolio grows sales three times as much for the same money.

OptionClick priceClicksConversionSpendSalesCost per sale
Main term, starting bid$1.001,00010%$1,000100$10
Main term, higher bid$1.501,30010%$1,950130$15 average
Extra sales from the higher bid$95030about $32
Same $950 across ten specific searches$0.80about 1,1908%$95095$10

Judge each increase in spending on the cost of the extra sales it buys, and move money to the searches where that cost is lowest.

How to build a keyword portfolio

Start by measuring the cost of the next sale. For the biggest searches, compare results at different bid levels and work out what the extra sales cost. Where that figure is far above the average, the search is saturated.

Then group searches into tiers by how specific they are. Broad, high-volume terms define the category. More specific searches name features, uses or sizes. The long tail holds precise searches, each small but cheap and often highly relevant.

Set budgets by tier, not by habit. Keep enough on the broad terms to hold a reasonable position, but stop raising bids once the cost of extra sales climbs steeply. Put the growth budget into the specific and long-tail tiers, where extra money still reaches new shoppers.

New searches should come in continuously. The search terms report shows what shoppers actually typed before clicking a brand’s ads, and new, relevant searches found there are candidates for the portfolio. Match types do different jobs: broad matching finds new searches shoppers use, while exact matching controls cost on searches that already work. A portfolio needs both, broad campaigns to discover and exact campaigns to scale what the discovery finds.

Keeping the portfolio clean as it grows

Negative keywords guard the budget. Searches that bring clicks but never sales drain the budget a portfolio needs, and excluding them keeps money on searches that convert. Each search should also point at the right product. A search that suits one product in a range may not suit another, so brands should point each search at the product most likely to convert, rather than advertising the whole range on every term.

Duplicate bids cost money too. When several campaigns bid on the same search, the brand competes against itself. Each search should have one home in the account, so budgets and bids are clear.

The portfolio also needs a regular review. A search that was cheap last quarter may attract competitors, and a saturated one may ease when a rival pulls back. A monthly review of the cost of extra sales by tier keeps the portfolio balanced.

Seasonal swings change the mix as well. Broad terms become far more expensive around big events, while specific searches often stay steadier. Shifting the mix toward specific searches during peaks protects the budget without giving up visibility.

The brand name sits outside the portfolio. Searches for the brand itself behave differently and should be managed on their own, tested for whether ads add sales rather than mixed into the growth portfolio.

The first number to pull is the cost of extra sales on the three biggest search terms, not just their average cost per sale. Next come the tiers, broad, specific and long-tail, with a budget for each. Moving growth budget from saturated broad terms to the specific searches where extra money still reaches new shoppers is how we help brands build keyword portfolios that keep growing.

A0681.title: What Mercado Libre’s investments signal for brands
A0681.alt: Vintage yellow van parked beside shrink-wrapped pallets of boxes outside an ochre warehouse with palms and hills.
A0681.ttag: What Mercado Libre’s investments signal for brands | Kwontified
A0681.desc: Mercado Libre spent 2024 building warehouses, credit and advertising, and took lower profit to do it. What that signals for brands selling in Latin America.
A0681.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 2, 2025.
A0681.body:
In the third quarter of 2024, Mercado Libre earned $397 million, below the average analyst estimate of $513 million. The gap traces back to lending. Its credit book grew 77% to $6 billion, and the provisions it set aside for those loans cut into net income, Bloomberg reported. A company that accepts an earnings miss to keep extending credit is showing, in its own accounts, how it weighs the next quarter against the next several years.

That choice runs through everything Mercado Libre did in 2024. It spent the year building infrastructure Latin American commerce still lacks, from warehouses and fast delivery to consumer credit and advertising, and took lower profit to pay for it. The bet is on long-term share of a region that is still moving online. For brands, the practical reading is that fulfillment through its network has become the entry ticket, advertising belongs in the plan from launch, and the delivery bar will keep rising.

How Mercado Libre’s investments added up over 2024

The spending plan was public early. In March, Mercado Libre said it would invest a record 23 billion reais, about $4.6 billion, in Brazil in 2024, Reuters reported. That was 21.1% more than in 2023, and it compared with 2 billion reais in 2019. Logistics was the main focus, with the rest going to technology, to Mercado Pago, its financial services arm, and to new tools for its advertising business, Mercado Ads.

By the third quarter the money had turned into buildings and delivery times. Mercado Libre opened five fulfillment centers in Brazil and one in Mexico during the quarter. More than 94% of shipments ran through its own managed network, and 75% of deliveries arrived in less than 48 hours, according to its third-quarter results.

The shoppers came with it. Unique buyers rose 21% to nearly 61 million, and the share of shipments handled through its fulfillment centers reached 53%, according to the company’s results release. Gross merchandise value reached $12.9 billion, with growth of 34% in Brazil and 27% in Mexico in local currency.

Why a marketplace in Latin America builds its own roads

The behavior makes sense once you look at what the region is missing. In much of Latin America, the services online shopping depends on, such as reliable fast delivery, widely available credit and established digital advertising, are less developed than in the United States. A marketplace that wants to grow there cannot wait for someone else to supply them. So Mercado Libre supplies them itself.

Each piece feeds the next. Fast delivery brings shoppers online and keeps them coming back. Credit lets them buy more and buy sooner. Advertising turns that growing traffic into revenue from brands that want to reach those shoppers, which is why Mercado Ads revenue rising 37% in the third quarter, as Benzinga reported, belongs in the same story as the warehouses and the loan book.

Follow the value through that loop and it settles in one place. When the marketplace owns the warehouse, the delivery promise, the shopper’s line of credit and the ad auction, it decides how fast shoppers expect a parcel to arrive, sees how they pay, and sells brands access to the traffic it built. For a brand, that is mostly useful for now, because the platform is doing infrastructure work no single seller could afford country by country. It also means the terms a brand competes on are written inside Mercado Libre’s buildings.

The willingness to take lower profit is the clearest signal of intent. A company that spends ahead of demand, and accepts a miss on earnings to fund credit and logistics, expects the region’s shift online to continue for years. It is building for share, and the next quarter comes second.

What Mercado Libre’s network asks of brands that sell there

Delivery speed is where a brand feels the build-out first. With more than half of shipments moving through Mercado Libre’s own fulfillment centers and most deliveries arriving within two days, shoppers come to expect that speed. Brands that ship slowly from their own warehouses look worse in search results and on product pages. Each new fulfillment center shortens delivery times in more cities, and shoppers’ expectations rise with them, so stock belongs in the regions where delivery is fastest.

Advertising has to be in the launch plan rather than added later. With Mercado Ads growing quickly, more brands are competing for paid placements, and a brand that arrives without an advertising budget will struggle to be seen next to competitors who brought one.

Latin America also behaves as several markets that share a platform. Growth rates, delivery networks and shopper habits differ between Brazil, Mexico and the rest of the region, which argues for planning stock, prices and budgets country by country. Credit adds another local layer, especially for larger purchases. When more shoppers can pay over time through the platform, higher-priced items become easier to sell, so it is worth checking how payment options appear on each listing and whether prices suit the way shoppers in each country pay.

For US brands, there is a softer way in. Mercado Libre opened a warehouse in Texas to help US sellers reach shoppers in Mexico, according to its second-quarter shareholder letter. That offers a way to test demand in Mexico before committing stock inside the country, though delivery from Texas will not match the times from local warehouses.

Reviews and ratings carry as much weight there as anywhere. Shoppers who are new to buying online rely heavily on what other buyers say, so the first reviews after launch need a plan of their own. So does local readiness: listings in the right language, products registered under each country’s rules, and customer service that answers quickly. The infrastructure Mercado Libre is building rewards brands that arrive prepared.

There are risks on the platform’s side. Its spending depends on continued growth and on its credit performing well, so any slowdown is worth watching for, even while the investments make the network stronger for the sellers who use it.

The question worth putting to a leadership team weighing Latin America, then, is which countries the brand can stock, advertise and serve well enough to keep up with a delivery promise Mercado Libre keeps raising. Answering it one country at a time, from the first stock transfer to the first campaign, is how we launch and run brands on Mercado Libre.

A0683.crumb: What shifting search trends reveal about…
A0683.title: What shifting search trends reveal about the Q4 shopper
A0683.alt: Brass magnifying glass on twine-tied kraft parcels with dried berries on a windowsill overlooking a garden.
A0683.ttag: What shifting search trends reveal about the Q4 shopper | Kwontified
A0683.desc: The 2024 holiday shopper searched in phases, deals early and urgency late. Why budgets spread evenly or pinned to one peak miss that, and how to plan by phase.
A0683.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 7, 2025.
A0683.body:
The last five days of the 2024 holiday season accounted for 10% of all holiday spending, according to Mastercard SpendingPulse. A Q4 budget spread evenly across the season gives those days the same daily amount as the quiet weeks of early December, and a budget pinned to Cyber Monday misses them altogether. Both plans treat a search as a search, whatever the date.

Neither matches how the 2024 holiday shopper behaved. That shopper searched in phases: hunting for deals during the promotional events, then buying urgently in the final days. The same query carried a different shopper, and a different value per click, depending on when it was typed. Q4 budgets work better when they follow those phases of intent than when they follow the calendar evenly or bet everything on one peak.

Q4 shopper search trends in 2024 put value first and urgency last

The season was led online. US retail sales rose 3.8% from November 1 to December 24, with online sales up 6.7% and in-store sales up 2.9%, according to Mastercard SpendingPulse. Mastercard’s chief economist described a consumer driven by a search for value, with online spending concentrated in the biggest promotional periods.

Deals pulled shoppers forward in the calendar. Growth was stronger on Thanksgiving and Black Friday than on Cyber Monday, as early discounts persuaded shoppers to buy sooner, Adobe reported. Activity before Thanksgiving also lifted conversions significantly, Skai found.

Then the end of the season compressed. With fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas than in 2023, shoppers who had not finished their lists bought late and fast.

Why the same search is worth more on some days than others

A search for a product type attracts different people at different points in the season. During a promotional event, many of the shoppers typing it are comparing deals across brands and will buy whichever discount is best. In the final days, many need the product now and will pay for whatever can arrive in time.

That changes what each click is worth. A deal-seeker clicks often and converts when the price is right. A last-minute shopper clicks less but converts quickly, as long as delivery is fast. An even budget pays for clicks in the weak-intent weeks and runs short in the strongest ones. Concentrating on Cyber Monday loses the early deal-seekers and the late buyers alike.

Take a brand spending $1,000 a day through the season and converting 6% of clicks on its main searches. During the final five days its conversion rate rises to 10%, because shoppers are ready to buy, but the daily budget runs out by midday. Say the brand moves $2,000 from four quieter mid-December days into those final five. It buys the same clicks at a 10% conversion rate instead of 6%, which is about two-thirds more sales from the same money, assuming click prices are similar.

Nothing about the brand, the product or the bid changed in that example. Only the timing of the money did.

Planning the 2025 season by phase of intent

The practical answer is to split the season into phases, each with its own goal, its own budget and its own message.

PhaseWho is searchingWhat the ad leads with
Early NovemberShoppers drawn in by early deals ahead of the big weekendThe deal, with listings and prices already live
Promotional event weeksDeal-seekers comparing discounts across brandsThe deal
Early and mid DecemberSteady shoppers, often at lower click pricesSpecific products, building visibility before the rush
Final days before shipping cutoffsShoppers who need it nowDelivery: arrives by Christmas, in stock, fast shipping
Week after ChristmasShoppers with gift cards and returnsThe specific product

Early November belongs in the plan. Early deals drew shoppers ahead of the big weekend in 2024, so listings, prices and advertising should be ready at the start of November rather than in the week of Thanksgiving.

The search mix moves with the phases as well. Broad gift searches peak during the promotional weeks, while brand and specific product searches carry more of the final days, as shoppers return to what they already decided to buy. Bids should follow that shift, and the quieter weeks of early and mid December are the time to build visibility on specific searches before competition returns for the final rush.

Delivery cutoffs decide the late phase. Late-season demand depends on whether a product can arrive in time, so each brand needs its own shipping deadline on each marketplace, with budget moving to products that can still arrive and away from those that cannot. Shoppers in a hurry often buy on their phones, so images, titles and delivery promises have to read clearly on a small screen. And stock has to survive the promotional weeks: a brand that sells out early misses the final days, when shoppers convert fastest, so the inventory plan should reserve units for the late surge.

The channel split matters too. With online sales growing more than twice as fast as store sales, brands sold in both channels should expect more of their holiday demand to arrive through searches. Advertising should be planned for that demand, instead of treating online as a supplement to in-store promotions.

Measurement should follow the same lines. Comparing each phase with the same phase in 2023 shows where intent rose or fell and where the 2025 budget should move.

A quick check on any Q4 plan: if the daily budget for the last five days before your delivery cutoffs is no larger than an average day in early December, the plan is following the calendar instead of the shopper. Rebuilding that plan phase by phase, budget, bids and message together, is how we plan holiday retail media for brands.

A0685.title: How mid-market retail media networks compete for brand budgets
A0685.alt: Empty market stalls with striped red, blue and yellow awnings lining a cobbled street beside an ornate stone building.
A0685.ttag: How mid-market retail media networks compete for brand budgets | Kwontified
A0685.desc: Amazon and Walmart will take more than 84% of US retail media spending in 2025. How smaller networks compete for the rest, and how brands should test them.
A0685.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 9, 2025.
A0685.body:
A mid-sized retailer pitching its media network to a brand cannot open with reach. Amazon and Walmart are expected to take more than 84% of US retail media spending in 2025, and the share left for every other network rose by less than one percentage point between 2019 and 2024. Whatever a smaller network sells, it has to be something the two leaders cannot offer.

In practice that comes down to shoppers who are already in a category, physical stores, and the retailer’s own customer data. They are real advantages, and narrow ones. For a brand, the sensible response is to keep core budgets with Amazon and Walmart and to test smaller networks only where its own customers already shop, judging each one on the sales it adds rather than the reach it reports.

Mid-market retail media networks compete for what the leaders leave

The concentration is stark in the forecasts. Amazon and Walmart combined will take more than 84% of all retail media ad spending in 2025, according to an eMarketer report cited by Business Insider, and the share going to every other network has hardly changed since 2019.

The market as a whole is still growing fast. US omnichannel retail media spending rose 20.4% to $52.3 billion in 2024, and Amazon alone holds a share of about 75%, according to eMarketer figures reported by invidis. The same analysis found that most small and medium-sized retailers’ networks do not reach enough shoppers to generate significant sales for advertisers.

Meanwhile the leaders kept pulling away. Walmart Connect grew 26% in the third quarter of 2024, Walmart said, and Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 19% to $14.3 billion, GeekWire reported. A brand team looking at those numbers sees two networks growing fast from a large base, and a long list of others asking for a slice of the remainder.

What a smaller network can sell that Amazon and Walmart cannot

Seen from the retailer’s side, the media network is a way to earn more from assets it already has. A mid-sized retailer cannot match Amazon’s traffic or Walmart’s reach, so its network has to package something brands cannot buy from either of them, and the strongest packages start from what the retailer already does well.

Category focus is the most obvious of those assets. A retailer built around home improvement, beauty or pet supplies sees shoppers who are already in the market for those products, and for a brand in that category, those shoppers can be worth more per impression than a broad audience somewhere else. The narrowness that limits the network’s reach is the same thing that makes its audience useful.

Stores are an asset too, though the slowest to turn into media. Large store networks are a genuine advantage, and retailers such as CVS, 7-Eleven and Hy-Vee are expanding advertising screens inside their stores, according to the invidis analysis. The cost of installing those screens is the main obstacle, which is why in-store networks are growing slowly.

Loyalty data completes the set. Retailers with loyalty programs know what their shoppers buy, online and in stores. They can use that information to target ads elsewhere on the internet and to show brands whether those ads led to sales.

Target shows what a network looks like when it combines all three. Its Roundel business sits on the shopping data of Target Circle members and on Target’s stores, and a Target executive described Roundel as a business of more than $1.5 billion a year, Benzinga reported. That is substantial. Even so, Target is competing for a small share of the budget next to the two leaders, which says a good deal about how hard the climb is for retailers with less to offer.

How a brand should test the rest of the market

Core budgets belong with Amazon and Walmart, because that is where most of the shoppers and most of the measurable sales are. Money for smaller networks should come from a budget already set aside for testing, never from campaigns that are proven.

Where to test follows from where the brand already sells. A beauty brand sold heavily at a beauty retailer has a natural reason to try that retailer’s network; a brand with little presence at a retailer gains little from advertising there. Searches, audiences and messages that work on Amazon and Walmart make a sensible starting point, because shoppers often behave similarly across retailers in the same category. The images and copy that work there can usually be adapted to each smaller network’s formats instead of being produced from scratch.

How to judge is the harder conversation. Smaller networks often report reach and impressions, and those numbers say little about whether the ads moved product. Brands should ask for results that show added sales, ideally compared against a group of shoppers who did not see the ads, and should agree on that measurement before buying. Networks that can link ads to purchases online and in stores give more useful answers than networks that report only clicks.

Every network also brings its own tools, reports and contacts, and testing several at once can stretch a team thin. Starting with one or two networks that fit the brand’s customers best keeps the work manageable. In-store media deserves particular care before large budgets go in: screens can reach shoppers at the moment they choose, but measurement is harder, and the brands sold heavily in physical stores have the most to gain from a test.

Brands also have some bargaining power here. Smaller networks want to win budget from the leaders, which leaves room to ask for added value in exchange for a trial, such as extra placements, better reporting or shared results. Then the quarterly review does the sorting: a network that adds sales earns a larger share of the testing budget, and one that does not is dropped.

Before the next network pitch reaches the leadership team, the question to ask is whether the brand’s customers already shop at that retailer, and whether the network will show which sales its ads added. Holding every network to that standard, from the first test to the quarterly review, is how we run retail media for brands beyond Amazon and Walmart.
