A0686.title: Amazon’s 2025 fees: model them before they reach the margin
A0686.alt: Twine-tied kraft parcel with a blank tag on a vintage brass dial scale beside a dish of coins and buttons.
A0686.ttag: Amazon’s 2025 fees: model them before they reach the margin | Kwontified
A0686.desc: Amazon froze its 2025 referral and FBA rates, but fees tied to stock and shipments still move each product’s margin and the most it can spend on ads.
A0686.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 14, 2025.
A0686.body:
Amazon’s fee notice for 2025 said what sellers hoped to hear: no increase to US referral and FBA fees, and no new fee types. Yet a product can still lose margin in 2025 without any headline rate moving, because several of the fees a brand pays depend on how it stocks and ships. That margin is also the ceiling on what the product can spend on advertising. A freeze on rates, in other words, is not a freeze on bids.

The useful response is to model fees product by product, recalculate the break-even advertising cost for each one, and set prices and bids against that number instead of assuming nothing changed.

What Amazon’s 2025 fees changed and what they left alone

The headline was a freeze. Amazon said it would not increase US referral and FBA fees in 2025 and would not introduce any new fee types, while lowering some fees and adding benefits, in its announcement to sellers.

A few fees came down. Amazon is lowering inbound placement service fees for large bulky products by an average of $0.58 per unit for shipments with minimal splits, effective January 15, 2025, Chain Store Age reported. It is also waiving inbound placement fees for up to 100 units of qualifying new products in shipments created between December 1, 2024, and March 31, 2025, Helium 10 reported.

What stayed matters as much. The fees Amazon introduced in 2024, such as the inbound placement fee, the low-inventory-level fee and the returns processing fee for products with high return rates, remain in place. Those charges depend on operations, so two brands paying identical referral and FBA rates can end up with very different fee bills.

Why every fee change moves the advertising ceiling

Every product has a margin before advertising: its price, minus the cost of the product, minus Amazon’s fees. That margin is the most the brand can spend on advertising for each sale before it starts losing money. Change a fee and the ceiling moves with it.

Take a $40 product that costs $14 to make and ship to Amazon. The referral fee at 15% is $6 and the FBA fee is $7, which leaves $13 before other charges. If inbound placement and storage add $1, the margin before advertising is $12, or 30% of the price, so the brand can spend up to 30% of each sale on advertising and break even.

Now let operations add their share. The product runs low on stock and triggers a low-inventory fee of $0.36 per unit, and a split shipment adds $0.30 in placement fees.

Per unitBefore operational feesWith operational fees
Price$40$40
Product cost$14$14
Referral fee (15%)$6$6
FBA fee$7$7
Left before other charges$13$13
Inbound placement and storage$1$1
Low-inventory feenot charged$0.36
Extra placement from a split shipmentnot charged$0.30
Margin before advertising$12$11.34
Break-even advertising cost30%about 28%

The margin falls to $11.34, about 28% of the price, and the break-even advertising cost drops by nearly two percentage points. A brand that keeps bidding as before is now losing money on more of its sales, with no change in Amazon’s headline rates. A gap of nearly two points sounds small until it applies to every click in the account.

How to model Amazon’s 2025 fees before they reach the margin

The model starts with each important product. It needs the list price, product cost, referral fee, FBA fee, and the operational fees that product actually incurs. The referral and FBA fees are easy to find; the operational ones are the lines that slip out of a spreadsheet. Divide the margin before advertising by the price. The result is the most each product can spend on advertising per sale and still break even.

Products with thin margins need tight bids, and products with wide margins can support more growth spending. Break-even is a ceiling, though, and advertising at break-even earns nothing. A target a few points below it leaves room for profit and for fees that vary month to month.

Operations is where a brand can act on its fees. Brands selling large, bulky products should check whether their shipments qualify for the lower inbound placement fees, and brands launching new products should use the waiver for new selection before March 31. Low-inventory fees reward steady stock levels. Split shipments raise placement fees. Better inventory planning lowers fees and raises the advertising ceiling at the same time.

Returns belong in the same review: products with high return rates can incur returns processing fees, and fixing the causes, such as unclear sizing or inaccurate images, protects the margin and the customer experience together.

When a product’s fees do rise, the brand has two levers. It can raise the price or lower its advertising target. Which one protects more profit depends on how sensitive shoppers are to that product’s price, and running both through the model shows the answer before either change goes live.

The calendar needs its own version. Amazon charges higher fulfillment fees during the holiday peak, which lowers the margin exactly when click prices are highest. Holiday bids should come from a peak-season model with that lower ceiling built in.

Fees, prices and product costs all move, which makes a quarterly review the minimum for keeping the break-even advertising cost current. And because pricing, inventory and advertising decisions all draw on the same margin, the model works best as one shared file, so a change in one team’s area does not quietly undo another team’s plan.

A workable rule for Monday: no product’s bid target should be set until someone can say what its margin before advertising is under the 2025 fees, including the operational ones. Building that model and running the account against it is how we manage Amazon for brands, from fees through bids.

A0687.crumb: Customer service as conversion on TikTok…
A0687.title: Customer service as conversion on TikTok Shop
A0687.alt: Open mailer box with teal and pink tissue and a ribbon-tied blank card beside a phone on a wooden stand.
A0687.ttag: Customer service as conversion on TikTok Shop | Kwontified
A0687.desc: On TikTok Shop, buyers decide fast and judge sellers by their service record. Why service shapes conversion and visibility, and how brands should staff for it.
A0687.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. TikTok Shop
A0687.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 16, 2025.
A0687.body:
Watch a TikTok Shop live stream for a few minutes and the comments fill with questions: whether it runs small, when it will arrive, whether it will work on dry skin. Each of those questions is a shopper standing at the checkout, and whoever answers it, the host, a chat agent or nobody, decides whether the sale happens. On TikTok Shop, customer service sits inside the purchase, before the order exists.

That puts brands in front of an awkward budgeting question. If service reports as a cost center, judged on tickets closed and money saved, while the TikTok Shop team is judged on sales, the two are pulling against each other. Shoppers on the platform buy quickly from videos and live streams, ask before they commit and see each seller’s service record through its score and badges. So service on TikTok Shop is part of how a product sells, and brands get more from it when they staff, measure and plan it as a conversion function.

How TikTok Shop customer service shapes what sells

TikTok Shop grew quickly as a channel. It had more than 500,000 US merchants by the end of 2023 and a $3 billion annual run rate in the United States by January 2024, Retail Brew reported.

It also grades its sellers closely, and service is written into the grade. TikTok Shop’s Shop Performance Score rates sellers on product satisfaction, fulfillment and logistics, and customer service, and sellers who keep a score of 4.5 or higher can earn a Star Shop badge, according to Tabcut. Service is one of the three things that decide how a shop is judged, which tells you what the platform wants from the brands that sell there.

The platform’s future in the United States is uncertain. A law requiring TikTok’s sale or ban takes effect on January 19, and the Supreme Court scheduled arguments for January 10, the AP reported when the court agreed to take the case. Whatever the court decides, the lesson about service applies to any platform that sells through content.

Why a reply becomes part of the sale

On a search marketplace, a shopper arrives looking for a product, compares listings and reads reviews before buying. On TikTok Shop, a shopper sees a product in a video or live stream, often for the first time, and decides within moments. A decision that fast leaves questions open about size, delivery timing or whether the product suits the person watching. A shopper who gets a quick, clear answer often buys. A shopper who waits usually scrolls on, and the moment is gone.

In a live stream, the host’s answers to comments can move viewers from interest to purchase. In a chat, a seller’s response can settle the doubt that stood between a shopper and checkout. Neither looks like customer service in the old sense, yet both are the service team’s work happening at the most valuable moment in the funnel.

Service also shapes what future shoppers see. A shop’s rating and badges appear to buyers, and a strong service record earns recognition that signals trust. Poor service lowers the score, which can limit visibility and access to promotions, so each slow reply or unresolved complaint makes the next sale harder.

The pattern compounds over time. Good service earns better ratings, better ratings earn more visibility and trust, and more visibility brings more shoppers with more questions. A brand that treats service as a cost to minimize falls behind one that treats it as a sales tool.

Running service as a sales channel

Coverage hours are the first thing to change. Questions arrive fastest during live streams and after a video spreads, so service coverage belongs on the content calendar, with people ready to answer when traffic peaks rather than during standard support hours.

Many questions repeat: sizing, shipping times, ingredients, returns. The cheapest answer is the one a shopper never has to ask for, which means putting those answers in product details, video captions and pinned comments. In live streams, the host is the first line of service, so hosts and creators need to know the product, its limits and the return policy well enough to answer accurately without promising what the brand cannot deliver.

Problems need the same urgency. Complaints and return requests affect a shop’s score, and fast, fair resolutions protect the rating and often turn an unhappy buyer into a returning one. Shoppers buying on impulse want to know they can send a product back, so a clear, easy return policy, stated in the listing and repeated in live streams, reduces hesitation and lowers complaints when a product does not suit. Reviews belong to the same job: early reviews shape how new shoppers judge a product they have just discovered, and following up with buyers, resolving problems before they turn into negative reviews and responding to concerns publicly all help.

Creators add a wrinkle. When affiliates and creators sell a brand’s products, buyers still contact the shop with their questions, so creators need to know where to send buyers, and the brand’s service team needs to be ready for the volume a successful video can bring. Many of those questions are about delivery, which is why service works best when it is connected to accurate stock and shipping data that prevent complaints and cancellations before they reach the score.

Measurement is where the org chart shows. Response speed, how often chats end in a purchase and how service ratings move belong alongside conversion and advertising results, in the same weekly report, instead of in a separate support summary. The shop’s performance score deserves a weekly look as well, with attention on whichever part, product satisfaction, fulfillment or service, is pulling it down, because fixing the weakest part first usually lifts the score fastest.

None of this is wasted if TikTok’s future in the United States changes. Fast replies, clear product answers and trained hosts carry over to every other platform that sells through content, including Instagram and live shopping on marketplaces.

So the question for the leadership team is a structural one: who owns the reply that closes the sale, and which number are they judged on? Building that function around the content calendar and the shop score is how we run TikTok Shop for brands as a sales channel.

A0690.title: What Target’s sortation centers signal for brands
A0690.alt: Curved roller conveyors carrying parcels toward a row of red sorting bins in a sunlit brick warehouse.
A0690.ttag: What Target’s sortation centers signal for brands | Kwontified
A0690.desc: Target’s sortation centers take parcel sorting out of store backrooms and batch it for delivery. What that means for speed, cost and the brands Target sells.
A0690.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 21, 2025.
A0690.body:
Adding a stop to a delivery chain ought to slow it down. Target added one, a sortation center between its stores and its customers’ doors, and its next-day deliveries rose by more than 150%. The extra step works because it changes how parcels share a route: batched together, each one travels faster and costs less. And when a retailer makes fast delivery cheap, shoppers learn to expect it, which means brands selling through Target, as vendors or as Target Plus sellers, need to plan stock and fulfillment for that speed.

How Target sortation centers fit the stores-as-hubs model

Target fulfills almost everything from its own stores, a model it calls stores as hubs. Stores fulfill more than 96% of Target’s total sales, and sortation centers sit downstream of those stores, sorting, batching and routing the orders they ship to local delivery partners, Trade & Industry Development reported.

The network is growing steadily. Target opened its eleventh sortation center, in Detroit, in 2024. In 2023 it had announced a $100 million investment to build at least 15 such facilities by 2026, according to the same report, and Target said sortation centers have increased the number of next-day deliveries by more than 150%.

The results reached the income statement in the third quarter. Target’s digital sales grew nearly 11%, and its ship-to-home business grew as the company moved more shipments through sortation centers to increase speed and reliability and lower costs, executives said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. Same-day delivery with Target Circle 360 grew nearly 20%, according to Target’s third-quarter results.

Why one more stop makes delivery faster and cheaper

Start with a store shipping online orders on its own. Store staff pick, pack and hand off each parcel to a carrier, often a few at a time. That ties up backroom space and labor, and it produces scattered deliveries: a handful of parcels from one store, bound for addresses spread across a metro area.

A sortation center changes the flow. Stores still pick and pack, then send their parcels to the center, which sorts packages from many stores together and groups them by neighborhood. Drivers carry more parcels on each route, to addresses closer together.

It works like a school bus against every parent driving their own child to class. The bus adds a vehicle and a schedule to the system, yet the miles driven per child fall, and the arrival time becomes predictable.

Speed rises because parcels move on scheduled routes instead of waiting for carrier pickups, so more orders can arrive the next day. Cost falls because each delivery shares its route with more parcels. Target’s report of more than 150% growth in next-day deliveries reflects both effects at once. What looks like an extra handoff is the step that lets the rest of the chain run full.

The consequence for brands follows from the economics. When a retailer lowers the cost of fast delivery, it raises the speed shoppers expect from it, and products on its site are judged against that speed.

What faster Target delivery changes for vendors and sellers

For vendors, the effect runs through store inventory. Because Target ships from stores, a product’s delivery speed depends on whether nearby stores have it in stock. Products well distributed across stores in markets with sortation centers can be offered faster, so vendors should work with Target to keep stock deep in the stores that feed those centers.

For Target Plus sellers, the effect runs through comparison. They ship from their own warehouses, not from Target’s stores. As more of Target’s own products arrive the next day, a Target Plus listing that takes several days to deliver looks slower next to them, and sellers should check their delivery promises against what shoppers see on Target’s own items.

Advertising sits downstream of the same change. Roundel, Target’s advertising business, grew at a mid-teens rate in the third quarter, according to the earnings call. When fast delivery helps a product convert, advertising on that product works harder, which argues for weighting Roundel spending toward products that can be delivered quickly in the markets a brand targets.

Not every product rides the faster routes. Items that are oversized, fragile or slow-selling in a given store may still ship more slowly. Brands should check which of their products qualify for the fastest delivery options and, where possible, adjust packaging or store distribution so more of them do.

Measurement should follow speed. Tracking how delivery promises differ across markets, and whether conversion rises where next-day delivery is available, shows where deeper stock pays for itself. Target’s own events, such as Target Circle Week, draw large traffic in short windows, and products that can arrive quickly convert better during them, so stock and delivery eligibility deserve a check before each one. The holiday season raises the stakes further: faster delivery lets shoppers order later before gift deadlines, and brands whose products can arrive the next day in major markets can keep selling after slower products have stopped shipping in time.

Other large retailers are moving the same way, with fast delivery from local stock becoming the standard, so the discipline a brand builds for Target carries over. Target’s network will keep expanding toward its goal of at least 15 sortation centers, bringing faster delivery to more markets.

A practical test for each Target product: if it cannot arrive the next day in the markets a sortation center serves, find out whether the cause is store stock, packaging or eligibility before spending more on Roundel to sell it there. Working through that list market by market is how we run Target and Roundel for brands.

A0692.title: What NRF 2025 signaled about retail’s year ahead
A0692.alt: Black cylindrical speaker and a wicker basket on a white round plinth in a glass-walled hall with snow outside.
A0692.ttag: What NRF 2025 signaled about retail’s year ahead | Kwontified
A0692.desc: AI, retail media and the store dominated NRF 2025. What the show signaled about how retailers will behave this year and what they will ask of brands.
A0692.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 23, 2025.
A0692.body:
Roughly one-third of the nearly 100 exhibitor “Big Ideas” sessions at NRF 2025 had AI in the title. Look at what retailers said they were using it for, though, and a quieter pattern shows through. Much of the AI was aimed inward, at forecasting, promotion planning, new product introductions and the work of store staff, well before anything a shopper would notice.

That inward turn, together with the spread of retail media and a new way of thinking about the store, tells brands what retailers will ask of them in 2025. They will want cleaner product data, content that AI tools can use, and advertising budgets they can measure, and the brands that prepare those three things early will find the conversations easier.

How NRF 2025 framed retail’s priorities

By any measure the show was large. Retail’s Big Show returned to New York’s Javits Center from January 12 to 14 with more than 1,000 exhibitors and 175 sessions, and a pre-show program on retail media networks, Retail TouchPoints reported in its preview.

About 40,000 attendees heard a continuous focus on AI, and AI agents that carry out tasks on their own were a leading theme, according to a recap by SymphonyAI. SymphonyAI sells AI software to retailers, so its emphasis is unsurprising, but other accounts described the same focus. Retail executives discussed generative AI, personalization and the store experience, according to a summary of the show’s notable quotes, which put the store back in the conversation alongside the technology.

Why retailers are pointing AI at themselves first

The behavior beneath the themes is consistent. Retailers are applying AI first to their own work: forecasting demand, planning promotions, helping store staff and introducing new products. Those uses save money and time inside the company, where the savings show up on the retailer’s own results, well before they change what shoppers see.

That ordering matters to brands because every one of those systems runs on product data. When a retailer’s tools decide what to stock, promote or recommend, products with complete, accurate and consistent data are easier for them to use. Gaps in a brand’s data become gaps in how the retailer treats its products, and the product simply surfaces less often.

Retail media keeps spreading along the same logic. With retail media featured before the show even opened, more retailers are building advertising businesses on their shopper data and stores, and each new network arrives with its own request for budget, its own tools and its own reporting. That fits the shape of the market: Amazon and Walmart still take most retail media spending, and smaller networks compete on specific shoppers, stores and their own data. The attention retail media drew at NRF suggests more retailers will launch networks in 2025, even as the leaders hold their share.

The store is being rethought as well. Retailers see stores as places to shop, as sources of fulfillment and increasingly as media spaces, with screens and in-store advertising. A brand’s presence in a store is becoming something it may be asked to pay for, as well as something it stocks.

What NRF 2025 means for the brands that sell to retailers

Product data sits at the top of the list. The information brands send to retailers, such as titles, descriptions, attributes, images and sizes, needs to be complete and consistent across every retailer, because clean data becomes a competitive advantage as retailers lean on AI to plan and recommend. The same tools reach the shop floor: AI that helps associates answer questions and find products depends on accurate product information, and a brand whose details are clear in the retailer’s systems is easier for staff to recommend.

Content comes next, written for the systems that now read it. Shopping assistants and recommendation systems draw on product details and reviews, so product information that answers shoppers’ real questions clearly is what those systems will surface.

Advertising needs agreed measurement before money moves. With more retailers asking for budgets, brands should settle in advance how each network will show results, ideally the sales it adds rather than only clicks or impressions. Networks that can prove results deserve a share of the budget; those that cannot should earn it through tests.

Retailers’ own data shifts the balance of the relationship. Loyalty programs and shopper data give retailers more power to decide which products to feature, and new AI tools let them plan promotions, stock and advertising more precisely. Brands that share forecasts, launch plans and promotional calendars early give those systems better inputs and tend to get better outcomes in return, while brands that only supply products leave the retailer’s systems to fill in the gaps.

Promotion planning was among the AI uses highlighted at the show. Tools built for it will make retailers sharper about which deals they run and which brands fund them, so brands should expect more precise questions about promotional spending and what it delivers.

The store belongs in the digital plan too. Store stock now drives fast delivery, and store screens are becoming advertising space, so a brand’s online and in-store plans with a retailer increasingly belong in one conversation.

Some caution is warranted. Trade shows highlight what vendors are selling, and many AI tools discussed at NRF are still early. Brands should prepare for the direction without assuming every promise will arrive in 2025.

The question worth bringing back from New York is a plain one: if a retailer’s planning system looked at our product data tomorrow, what would it conclude about us? Getting that answer right across every retailer, from the attribute file to the measurement plan for each new network, is how we run marketplaces and retail partnerships for brands.

A0694.title: First-party data from shopping conversations for brands
A0694.alt: Small fabric smart speaker beside an open notebook and pencil on a wooden kitchen counter with a basil plant.
A0694.ttag: First-party data from shopping conversations for brands | Kwontified
A0694.desc: Shoppers increasingly ask AI assistants what they need. Retailers keep most of that data, so brands should build their own from the questions they can see.
A0694.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 30, 2025.
A0694.body:
Typed into a search bar, a shopper’s need is two words: “running shoes.” Said to an AI assistant, the same need becomes a paragraph about a first half marathon, wide feet and mostly paved roads. The second version carries the reasons behind the purchase, which is exactly what a brand wants to know and exactly what it rarely gets to see.

Shoppers are increasingly asking AI assistants and chat tools what they need, in their own words, and those shopping conversations reveal intent far more directly than search keywords. Retailers keep most of that conversation data. So brands need a first-party record of their own, built from service chats, reviews, product questions and social comments, and used to write product content that answers what shoppers actually ask.

How shopping conversations spread in 2024

Amazon made its assistant widely available in 2024. It extended Rufus, its generative AI shopping assistant, to all US customers in its shopping app, and said the tool had already received tens of millions of questions from customers, Retail Dive reported.

Shoppers are also arriving from AI tools outside the retailers. During the 2024 holiday season, traffic to retail sites from generative AI chat tools rose 1,300% from a year earlier, and by 1,950% on Cyber Monday, Adobe reported, while noting that the base of users remains modest.

Shoppers who try these tools tend to like them. In Adobe’s survey of 5,000 US consumers, 7 in 10 of those who had used generative AI for shopping said it improved their experience. They used it most to find deals, to find specific items quickly and to get brand recommendations.

Who holds the transcript

Search data shows what people typed. A conversation shows the problem a shopper is trying to solve, the comparisons they are making and the doubt that stops them buying, and that makes it some of the most useful information about demand a brand could ask for.

The institution that collects it, though, is the retailer. When a shopper asks Amazon’s assistant a question, Amazon sees the conversation and the brand does not. The richest new source of shopper intent sits inside the retailer’s system, and brands receive at most a summary. The best record of why people buy a brand’s products is being written somewhere the brand cannot read. That is a reasonable arrangement from the retailer’s side, since the conversation happens on its property.

What brands can change is how they treat the conversations they already hold. Most of those sit in departments that seldom compare notes.

The conversation record a brand already owns

Customer service is the obvious place to start. Chats, emails and calls are full of questions in shoppers’ own words, about whether a product fits, how to use it and why it arrived late. Tagging and reviewing those questions regularly turns them from tickets to close into a record of demand.

Reviews explain what buyers expected and whether the product delivered, and their patterns, such as repeated comments about size or a confusing feature, show what product pages fail to explain. The questions shoppers ask on product pages, and the answers they receive, are a direct record of what was unclear before purchase. Comments on videos and live streams, especially on platforms that sell through content, show what shoppers wonder about when they first discover a product.

None of these sources is new; reading them together is. A simple shared log of the most common questions, updated monthly, shows which doubts come up most and whether they are changing.

The log earns its keep on the product page. Titles, descriptions, images and answers should address the questions that come up most often. When a shopper asks an assistant about a product, the assistant draws on the information the brand has provided, and content that already answers real questions is more likely to be used in the reply. Retailers’ search reports add a second layer: comparing the terms shoppers use to find a brand’s products with the questions in the log shows where shoppers’ language differs from the brand’s own, and which words the pages should use.

Changes should be measured. After rewriting a product page to answer common questions, brands should track whether conversion rises, whether returns fall and whether the same questions appear less often in service chats. Together those three readings show whether the content now answers what shoppers wanted to know.

Advertising will feel the shift too. As more shopping starts in conversations, the products an assistant mentions first gain an advantage. Clear, complete product information makes a product easier to recommend, and advertising alone cannot make up for a page that leaves shoppers’ questions unanswered.

The log also belongs in product decisions. Repeated questions about sizing, durability or ingredients can point to changes in the product itself, and to more than a better description. Customer service, marketing and product teams each hold part of the conversation record, and a monthly review that brings them together turns scattered questions into decisions about content, product and service.

Privacy sets the limits on all of this. Brands must handle customer information carefully, use it only in ways customers would expect and follow privacy rules in each market. The aim is to understand common questions, never to track individual shoppers.

The retailer will keep the transcript of the conversation on its site. The brand can still own the answer, and a team that knows the questions its shoppers ask most is already ahead of one waiting for a summary. Building that record and turning it into content assistants can use is the work of our AI Agentic Commerce practice.

A0696.crumb: The state of Walmart Marketplace for…
A0696.title: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands in 2025
A0696.alt: A row of blue shopping carts lined up along a yellow curb in an empty parking lot, one holding a cardboard box.
A0696.ttag: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands in 2025 | Kwontified
A0696.desc: Walmart Marketplace grew 42% in late 2024 and is nearing 700 million items. Why speed and price now decide who wins on Walmart, and how brands should respond.
A0696.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 4, 2025.
A0696.body:
A product page on Walmart has one featured offer, and the number of items competing for pages like it is approaching 700 million. Walmart Marketplace grew 42% in late 2024, and its number of sellers grew by double digits. When that many offers chase each search, Walmart has to choose, and its choice keeps landing on the offer that arrives fastest at a competitive price.

For brands, that turns two operational questions into the main growth levers. Meeting Walmart’s fast-delivery standard, through Walmart Fulfillment Services or an equivalent, and keeping prices competitive across channels come before any spending on growth, and advertising becomes part of the cost of being found.

How Walmart Marketplace for brands grew in 2024

In the third quarter of Walmart’s fiscal 2025, which ended October 31, 2024, Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Fulfillment Services grew 42% in the United States, the fifth straight quarter of growth above 30%, Digital Commerce 360 reported. The number of sellers grew by double digits, and the number of items listed was approaching 700 million.

Walmart’s online business grew with it. Walmart US e-commerce sales grew 22% in the quarter, and Walmart Connect, its advertising business, grew 26%, RTTNews reported.

Delivery got more efficient at the same time. Orders per delivery rose 20% as Walmart expanded store-fulfilled delivery, according to the Digital Commerce 360 report. Walmart is building the delivery network that makes fast shipping cheaper to offer.

Why speed and price decide the featured offer

When a marketplace adds sellers and items faster than shoppers arrive, more offers compete for each search and each product page. Walmart has to decide which offers to show first and which seller wins the featured offer, the main buy position on a product page.

Speed is one deciding factor. Offers that can arrive in two days or less, especially those fulfilled through Walmart Fulfillment Services, carry fast-delivery labels that shoppers notice. Price is the other. Walmart’s identity rests on low prices, and offers priced above what shoppers can find elsewhere are less likely to be featured.

Take a brand selling a product on Walmart that ships from its own warehouse in 4 to 5 days. A competing seller lists a similar product at the same price, fulfilled through Walmart’s network with 2-day delivery. Shoppers see the faster offer with its fast-delivery label, and many choose it. The brand’s product has the same price and the same quality, and it loses the sale on speed.

Reverse the setup and the result holds. If the brand’s price is higher than the same product’s price on another site, Walmart is less likely to feature its offer at all, however fast it ships. A brand needs both to compete, and neither one makes up for the other.

The fulfillment trade-off, and which way it leans

The first decision is how to reach two-day delivery. Walmart Fulfillment Services carries a fulfillment fee; meeting two-day delivery from the brand’s own warehouses or a third-party partner avoids that fee but has to hit the same standard every day. Both are real options. For most products, though, the fast-delivery label is worth more than the fulfillment fee, because the label is what the shopper sees at the moment of choosing between two otherwise similar offers. The fee shows up on every invoice, while the cost of a missing label shows up only as sales that went to someone else.

Stock is the hidden half of that decision. Fast delivery depends on stock being available where Walmart expects it, and running out removes the fast-delivery label and can hand the featured offer to a competitor.

How brands should operate on Walmart Marketplace in 2025

Price checks come next. A product priced higher on Walmart than on the brand’s own site or another marketplace risks losing visibility, and a product priced lower elsewhere can pull Walmart’s price down with it, so the comparison needs doing for every key product.

The listing itself needs protecting. With more sellers on the platform, brands should make sure they control their product pages, with accurate content, images and attributes, and that unauthorized sellers do not undercut them. Walmart’s search relies heavily on product attributes, such as size, color, material and use, so listings with complete, accurate attributes are easier to find through filters and search. Every relevant attribute should be filled for Walmart, rather than copying content over from another marketplace.

Advertising belongs in the launch budget. With Walmart Connect growing and more sellers competing for each search, sponsored placements take a growing share of visibility, and brands should track how much of their Walmart sales advertising supports. New listings also need a plan for their first reviews, through follow-up with early buyers and Walmart’s own review programs where eligible, because a product without reviews struggles against established competitors. The cleanest launches go live with fast delivery, a competitive price, complete content and advertising ready on the first day.

With nearly 700 million items listed, a brand’s whole catalog will not compete equally, so fulfillment, pricing work and advertising should go first to the products that sell best or matter most. Featured-offer share on those products is the number to watch: how often the brand wins the main buy position, and why it loses when it does. Speed and price usually explain most of the gap. A quarterly review of speed, price, featured-offer share and advertising returns keeps the plan current on a marketplace that is changing this fast.

The rule for 2025 is simple to state. On Walmart, meet the fast-delivery standard and match prices across channels before spending another dollar on growth. Putting those two in place first, then building advertising on top, is how we run Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect for brands.

A0697.crumb: The state of Zalando for brands in 2025…
A0697.title: The state of Zalando for brands in 2025: from store to ecosystem
A0697.alt: A sunlit boutique with hanging clothing racks, wooden shoe displays, rust-colored armchairs and potted plants.
A0697.ttag: The state of Zalando for brands in 2025: from store to ecosystem | Kwontified
A0697.desc: Zalando agreed to buy About You and is building services that run brands’ online business across Europe. What its shift from store to platform means for brands.
A0697.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 6, 2025.
A0697.body:
A fashion brand that wants to sell online across Europe inherits a long list of local problems: different languages, payment methods, delivery networks and return habits in each country it enters. Zalando’s plan for 2025 is to be the company that solves that list once, for many brands at the same time. With its purchase of About You it will run two consumer storefronts, and with its own e-commerce operating system it is building services that run brands’ online business well beyond its own site.

That turns Zalando from one online store into a European fashion platform with several parts, and it changes what brands are negotiating with. More of the market will run through one partner. Brands selling in Europe need to decide where they sit in each storefront, and how much of their European operations they are willing to place on Zalando’s infrastructure.

How Zalando for brands changed going into 2025

The biggest move was the About You deal. On December 11, 2024, Zalando announced a voluntary public offer of 6.50 euros per share for About You, worth about 1.1 billion euros and a premium of 107% to About You’s three-month average share price, according to Zalando’s investor presentation. Shareholders holding about 73% of About You’s shares agreed to sell, and Zalando expects to close the deal in summer 2025 after regulatory approval. It published the formal offer on January 20, 2025.

The deal sits inside a wider strategy. Zalando said the combined group aims to cover a larger share of the 450-billion-euro European fashion market, with a dual-brand approach in which Zalando and About You serve shoppers as separate storefronts, according to the companies’ joint announcement.

The business-facing side is growing too. About You’s software unit, SCAYLE, complements Zalando’s e-commerce operating system, ZEOS, which helps brands and retailers manage their online business across Europe through one platform covering logistics, software and service, according to the investor presentation. The companies expect combined sales to grow 5% to 10% a year until 2028 and aim for about 100 million euros a year in added operating profit from combining the two businesses, Silicon Canals reported.

Why Zalando is building a platform rather than a bigger store

European fashion e-commerce is fragmented across countries, languages, payment methods and delivery networks, and a brand selling across the continent faces dozens of local challenges. A company that solves those challenges once, for many brands, holds a strong position, and Zalando is building on both sides of it.

For shoppers, it now plans two storefronts with different styles and audiences, which lets it reach more of the market without blurring either name. For brands, it is building the logistics and software they need to sell across Europe, on Zalando and also on their own sites and other channels.

Follow the value through that design and it gathers in Zalando’s hands. A brand that uses Zalando’s storefronts to reach shoppers, its warehouses to ship and its software to run its own site has handed one partner its European customers, its stock and much of the data about both. In return it gets speed and reach it could not build alone, which is a real trade.

The relationship changes shape along the way. A store that buys or lists a brand’s products becomes a platform that many brands use to run their European online business, and Zalando gains a larger share of the market and a deeper hold on each brand as a result.

The decisions Zalando’s shift puts in front of brands

Concentration comes first. With About You inside the same group, more of Europe’s online fashion market will run through one company, and brands should expect that partner to carry more weight in negotiations over terms, visibility and fees.

Then there is the question of where a brand belongs. A brand may fit Zalando’s audience, About You’s, or both, and presentation should differ between them rather than assuming both storefronts will treat a brand the same way. Brands already selling on About You should expect changes as the deal closes and integration follows, which will take longer than the summer, and should stay close to their account contacts.

Infrastructure is perhaps the biggest decision for a brand new to Europe. Zalando’s logistics and software services can make expansion easier, especially for brands without their own operations there, but placing fulfillment and software with one partner also deepens reliance on it. The choice is speed of entry against control, and it is worth making country by country, because Europe does not behave as one market. Some countries will justify local stock and others can be served cross-border.

How a brand sells matters as much as where. Zalando works with brands both as a wholesale buyer and through its partner program, in which brands list and price their own stock. The partner route gives more control over price and assortment, while wholesale shifts stock risk to Zalando, and many brands use both, product by product.

Returns deserve their own plan. Online fashion in Europe sees high return rates, and shoppers expect easy, free returns in many markets, so returns belong in pricing and stock plans from the start, with sizing guidance and accurate images doing the work of keeping them down. Advertising is part of the cost as well. Zalando sells marketing services that help brands stand out across its storefronts, and as more brands compete for attention in fewer, larger storefronts, paid visibility takes a larger share of the cost of selling there.

Rules and content close the list. European regulation on product safety, labeling and sustainability claims is tightening, and product information should meet the rules in each market before a brand scales. Product information, sizing guidance and returns policies also need to work across languages and national rules, which matters more when shoppers can compare a brand across two storefronts owned by the same group.

The question for a leadership team planning Europe is how much of the continent it wants to rent from one landlord, and on what terms it would move out. Answering it storefront by storefront and country by country is how we launch and operate brands on Zalando.

A0698.crumb: Amazon’s Q4 2024 results: ad growth and…
A0698.title: Amazon’s Q4 2024 results: ad growth and competition for clicks
A0698.alt: A wooden gavel resting on its block in front of descending cardboard boxes against a blue wall.
A0698.ttag: Amazon’s Q4 2024 results: ad growth and competition for clicks | Kwontified
A0698.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 18% in Q4 2024 while its online stores grew 7%. What that gap says about competition for clicks, and how brands should budget for 2025.
A0698.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 11, 2025.
A0698.body:
Divide Amazon’s advertising revenue by the retail revenue it sits on top of, and the fourth quarter of 2024 gives a figure of about 14.1%. A year earlier the same ratio was about 12.8%. No brand’s ad console shows that number, but it describes the market every brand is bidding in: it now takes more advertising to win the same sale.

The cause is competition for clicks. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 18% in the quarter while its online stores grew 7.1% and third-party seller services grew 9%, so advertising took a larger share of what brands spend to sell on Amazon for another quarter. Brands budgeting for 2025 should plan advertising as a rising share of sales, protect the searches that matter most and test what each increase actually adds.

What Amazon’s Q4 2024 results showed

Q4 2024RevenueGrowth
Advertising services$17.3 billion18%
Third-party seller services$47.5 billion9%
Online stores$75.6 billion7.1%

Those are Amazon’s reported results for the quarter. Advertising kept outpacing retail, as it has for some time.

The advertising business is now very large. It is running at a $69 billion annual rate, more than double the $29 billion of four years earlier, and sponsored products remain its largest part, Amazon’s chief executive said on the company’s earnings call. Third-party sellers made up 61% of the items Amazon sold in 2024, their highest annual share, according to the same call, and more sellers on the platform means more bidders for the same searches.

The gap has persisted across quarters. In the third quarter, advertising grew 19% while online stores grew 7%, and the fourth quarter carried the same pattern through the holiday season.

Why faster ad growth means each sale costs more to win

Advertising revenue is what brands and sellers pay Amazon to be seen. Retail sales are what shoppers spend. When the first grows faster than the second, brands are paying more for each dollar of sales they win through the same store.

The ratio in the opening makes that visible. Using Amazon’s reported figures, advertising revenue was about 14.1% of online store and third-party seller services revenue combined in the fourth quarter of 2024. Working back from the growth rates, it was about 12.8% a year earlier. That is a rough measure, since not every ad dollar maps to a retail dollar, but the direction is clear: advertising is taking a larger slice of the retail business it supports.

The engine underneath is the auction. More sellers and more brands bid for the same searches, and the auction prices those searches higher. A brand that holds its advertising budget flat as a share of sales will see its visibility shrink as rivals spend more.

Take a brand that spent 15% of its Amazon sales on advertising in late 2023. If its costs rose in line with Amazon’s ratio, it would need about 16.4% of sales to hold the same position a year later. Kept at 15%, it would have slipped behind competitors that absorbed the increase, without any visible change in its own campaigns to explain why.

That is why a flat budget in a rising market can look like a performance problem. The campaigns, bids and products are unchanged; the auction around them has moved, and the same money now buys fewer of the clicks that used to turn into sales.

How brands should budget Amazon advertising in 2025

A rising share needs planning from the start. A 2025 budget should allow advertising cost to rise as a share of sales and settle in advance where that money comes from, whether higher prices, lower other costs or a thinner margin on some products.

Not every search is worth defending at any price. The searches that bring most of a brand’s profitable sales deserve protection first, instead of spreading rising costs evenly across every term. And with competition rising, it is easy to spend more just to stand still, so each budget increase should be tested with comparison periods or groups. That is how a brand learns when more spending buys growth and when it only holds position.

Conversion is often the cheapest lever available. A product page that converts more of the clicks it gets is the best defense against rising click prices: better images, clearer titles and stronger reviews lower the cost of each sale without raising bids. Each gain in conversion offsets part of the rise in click prices without any extra spend.

The ad format mix spreads the pressure. Sponsored product ads carry most of the spending, so they feel competition first. Brand ads, video and display reach shoppers earlier in their search and can cost less per new customer, and a broader mix keeps rising costs from concentrating on the most crowded placements.

Season distorts every reading. The fourth quarter includes the holiday peak, when competition is highest, so a brand’s own fourth quarter should be compared with the same period a year earlier and never with quieter months before concluding that costs are rising faster than expected. Third-party competition deserves the same attention: with third-party seller services still growing and independent sellers supplying a large share of what Amazon sells, tracking which competitors appear on key searches, and how that changes, shows where the pressure is coming from.

Amazon’s own quarterly figures make a useful benchmark. Comparing a brand’s advertising share of sales with Amazon’s trend each quarter shows whether the brand is keeping pace, falling behind or overspending.

The rule for 2025 fits on one line: if your advertising share of sales is flat while Amazon’s ad revenue grows faster than its retail revenue, you are losing ground, and the only question is where. Finding that answer search by search, and testing each increase before it becomes permanent, is how we plan and run Amazon advertising budgets for brands.

A0700.crumb: The state of Target Plus for brands in…
A0700.title: The state of Target Plus for brands in 2025: curation decides
A0700.alt: A red wooden shelf holding dried flowers in a ceramic vase, an amber jar, and a bar of soap on a linen cloth.
A0700.ttag: The state of Target Plus for brands in 2025: curation decides | Kwontified
A0700.desc: Target Plus doubled its sellers and items in a year but stays invite-only and curated. What that means for brands that want in, and for those already there.
A0700.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 13, 2025.
A0700.body:
On Amazon or Walmart, a brand that wants to sell lists its products first and fights for the featured offer afterwards, against every reseller and copycat on the same page. Target Plus runs the other way round. Target decides who sells, often allowing just one seller for a given item, so the contest happens before a listing exists and is settled by an invitation.

That matters more as the marketplace grows. Target Plus more than doubled its sellers and items in the year to mid-2024 and opened a route for Shopify merchants, but it remains invite-only and curated. Brands compete to be chosen, and the ones that get in will have proved reliable delivery, clean content and steady demand before they applied. For some, a place on Target Plus may also be a path into Target’s stores.

How Target Plus for brands grew in 2024

The marketplace grew quickly from a small base. Target Plus offered more than 2 million items from more than 1,200 sellers, after Target more than doubled the number of sellers and products over the previous year, Fortune reported. Target called it one of the fastest-growing parts of its business.

It is still small by comparison. Amazon said in 2022 that it had 2 million merchants selling on its platform, and Walmart’s marketplace sold about 420 million items, according to the same Fortune report. By November, Walmart’s count was approaching 700 million items, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Target Plus is a fraction of either.

The model stayed curated. Target said it would keep its invite-only approach and continue vetting sellers, and that curating selection, for example by allowing only one vendor to offer a given item, helps it stand out and build trust, according to Fortune.

And a new route opened. Target partnered with Shopify so that US-based Shopify merchants can apply to sell through Target Plus, and in some cases in Target’s physical stores, Retail TouchPoints reported.

What curation says about Target as an institution

Target’s reasons are easiest to see from inside the company. Its identity rests on a curated, trustworthy shopping experience, the feeling that what is on the shelf was chosen. A marketplace that let anyone sell would invite the problems open marketplaces face, such as counterfeits and inconsistent service, and those problems would land on Target’s name. Curation lets Target add selection while protecting the brand it has built.

That shifts what matters for the brands involved. On an open marketplace, a brand fights resellers and copycats on every listing. On Target Plus, a brand that gets in faces less of that, but it has to earn the place by meeting Target’s standards for quality, delivery and service, and keep meeting them.

The Shopify partnership shows how Target intends to grow inside that model. Instead of opening the doors, it is building a pipeline of vetted, growing brands, many of them direct-to-consumer companies with loyal followings, and inviting them in. Growth comes more slowly that way, but on Target’s terms.

Getting into Target Plus, and staying there

For a brand that wants in, the case is built on its existing channels. Target looks for sellers that deliver consistently and serve customers well, so fast, accurate shipping, low cancellation rates and strong reviews elsewhere are the evidence. Product information, images and descriptions should already meet the standard shoppers expect from Target’s own pages, because a brand that looks polished on its own site and other marketplaces makes a stronger case. Demand counts too: a growing customer base and strong sales elsewhere give Target a reason to add a brand, and for Shopify merchants the new partnership offers a direct way to apply.

The proposal itself should be focused. A curated marketplace rewards a tight assortment, so leading with the products that sell most reliably and fit Target’s audience is stronger than offering the whole catalog at once.

For brands already on Target Plus, the job is to protect the place. Missed deliveries, poor reviews or slow service can cost a curated seller its spot, and Target’s standards are better treated as the floor than as the goal.

Delivery speed needs particular care. Target Plus sellers ship from their own warehouses, while Target’s own products increasingly arrive the next day through its sortation centers. A Target Plus listing that takes a week to arrive looks slow beside Target’s own items on the same page.

Pricing should stay consistent with other channels. Target’s shoppers expect fair prices, and a product priced well above what it costs elsewhere looks out of place among goods Target has chosen. Advertising still has a role, even with less direct competition on each item: Roundel, Target’s advertising business, lets Target Plus sellers reach Target’s shoppers, and brands still compete for attention across the category.

The store question sits behind all of this. Target has said some marketplace brands may reach its physical stores, and a strong record on Target Plus is one way to make that case.

There are limits worth keeping in view. Target Plus remains small next to Amazon and Walmart, and no brand can count on an invitation, so Target Plus works as one channel among several in 2025, alongside the larger marketplaces rather than in place of them.

A leadership team weighing Target Plus can test its readiness against Target’s own reason for curating: would our delivery record, reviews and product pages make Target look more trustworthy, or less? Building that record, and then running the Target Plus listing and its Roundel campaigns once the invitation comes, is how we help brands earn and keep a place at Target.

A0702.title: Five data-backed truths for the 2025 Amazon plan
A0702.alt: Five brass pocket compasses in a row beside a worn leather notebook on a wooden table.
A0702.ttag: Five data-backed truths for the 2025 Amazon plan | Kwontified
A0702.desc: The final 2024 numbers are in. Five facts from Amazon’s results, the holiday season and the 2025 fee changes, and the planning rule each one implies.
A0702.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 18, 2025.
A0702.body:
Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 18% in the fourth quarter of 2024. Its online stores grew 7.1%. A plan that carries last year’s assumptions into 2025 is quietly betting that gap has closed, and the final 2024 numbers say it has not. They say four other things as well, about sellers, holiday timing, fees and AI shopping, and each one changes how much margin a brand has left to bid with.

So the 2025 Amazon plan should start from five facts, each with one planning rule attached, and from the fact that the five rules reinforce each other when they are applied together.

What the 2024 data showedThe rule it implies
Advertising grew more than twice as fast as the online storeBudget advertising as a rising share of sales
Third-party sellers supplied a record share of itemsExpect more competitors on every important search
Holiday demand came earlier and in burstsBudget each big event by phase
Headline fees froze, operational fees did notModel fees product by product before setting bids
AI shopping tools grew from a small baseWrite product content that answers shoppers’ questions

The 2025 Amazon plan starts with the cost of being seen

Advertising is outgrowing the store. Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 18% to $17.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2024, while online store sales rose 7.1%, according to Amazon’s reported results. When advertising revenue grows faster than the store it sits on, every dollar of sales won there costs more in advertising. Keeping the ad budget at a fixed percentage of sales then means slowly losing visibility to rivals that spend more.

By our estimate, advertising rose to about 14.1% of Amazon’s store and seller services revenue in the fourth quarter, from about 12.8% a year earlier. A 2025 budget should therefore let advertising’s share of sales climb, with the funding agreed up front: a price rise, savings elsewhere in the P&L, or accepting less margin on selected products.

The bidders are multiplying too. Third-party sellers accounted for 61% of items sold on Amazon in 2024, the highest annual share yet, Amazon’s chief executive said on the fourth-quarter earnings call. More sellers means more bidders for the same searches and more offers on the same product pages. The practical answer is to expect more competitors on every important search, protect the searches that bring most of the profitable sales, and track who appears on them each month.

Timing and fees change the arithmetic underneath

Holiday demand moved earlier and arrived in bursts. US shoppers spent $241.4 billion online from November 1 to December 31, up 8.7%, and Black Friday grew faster than Cyber Monday as shoppers embraced earlier deals, Adobe reported.

The last five days of the season accounted for 10% of holiday spending, according to Mastercard SpendingPulse. Shoppers bought in three bursts: early deals, the event weekend and the final rush. Budgets for each big event should follow those phases, from the early window through the last days before delivery cutoffs, instead of spreading evenly or pinning everything to one day.

Headline fees froze, but margins did not. Amazon committed to no increase in US referral or FBA fees for 2025, and no new fee types, in its announcement to sellers. Fees tied to stock levels, shipment splits and returns remain, and a product’s margin before advertising sets the most it can spend on ads. Those fees move that margin, so fees need modeling product by product, with each product’s break-even advertising cost recalculated and bids set against it.

Take a brand whose 2024 plan held advertising at 15% of sales, spread event budgets evenly and ignored operational fees. Each of those choices now works against it. The ad share is too low for a market where advertising outgrows sales. The even spread misses the early and late surges. And the unmodeled fees overstate the margin, so bids run above what products can afford, which means the brand is underspending where it matters and overbidding where it cannot afford to.

AI shopping changes what the product page is for

AI shopping tools grew from a small base. Visits that generative AI chat tools sent to retail sites rose 1,300% during the 2024 holiday season, and by 1,950% on Cyber Monday, though from a modest base, according to the same Adobe report. Amazon’s own assistant, Rufus, had fielded tens of millions of customer questions by the time it reached all US customers, Retail Dive reported. Assistants answer shoppers’ questions using the information brands provide on their pages, so titles, descriptions and answers should be rewritten around the questions shoppers actually ask.

Why the five rules work better together

A plan that applies all five rules is not more expensive by default. It moves money to where it works: protected searches, peak phases and products with room in their margin, and it funds some of that by cutting spend on searches that no longer pay back and on even, all-season coverage.

The rules also feed each other. Rising competition raises advertising cost, which makes fee modeling more important, because the margin left for advertising decides how far a brand can bid. Content that converts better lowers the cost of every click. A brand that acts on one rule in isolation leaves value on the table, while one that acts on all five compounds the gains.

Keeping the plan current matters as much as writing it. Amazon reports advertising and retail growth every quarter, and event results arrive within days. Each rule deserves a quarterly check against that new data: whether the advertising share is keeping pace, which competitors have arrived on key searches, how phase budgets performed and whether fee models still match what the brand pays.

A plan passes the 2025 test if every bid can be traced back to a product margin that already includes this year’s fees and this year’s cost of being seen. Building that plan, and rechecking it each quarter, is how we run Amazon for brands across ads, fees and content.

A0703.crumb: Mercado Libre for brands in 2025: the…
A0703.title: Mercado Libre for brands in 2025: the case for local stock
A0703.alt: A sunlit stockroom with wooden shelves of cardboard boxes and folded clothes, and a yellow hand truck.
A0703.ttag: Mercado Libre for brands in 2025: the case for local stock | Kwontified
A0703.desc: Cheap cross-border sellers are pushing into Latin America, but Brazil’s import tax and Mercado Libre’s network favor brands that keep stock in the country.
A0703.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 20, 2025.
A0703.body:
Two very different parcels compete for the same shopper in Latin America. One is cheap and ships from overseas. The other costs more, sits in a warehouse inside the country and arrives in a day or two through Mercado Libre’s own network. Price is the first parcel’s whole argument. In 2024, Brazil changed that price, and the second parcel’s advantages started to count for more.

Mercado Libre enters 2025 facing low-price rivals that ship cross-border into the region, but its strengths are local stock and fast delivery, and Brazil’s new 20% tax on imported purchases of up to $50 narrowed the price gap there. Brands selling on Mercado Libre should compete on speed, local inventory and trust rather than on price, and plan country by country, because the rules and the rivals differ from market to market.

How the market for Mercado Libre for brands changed in 2024

The region kept growing. E-commerce in Latin America was expected to grow 6.55% to $194.7 billion in 2024, according to a ResearchAndMarkets report, which also noted that Temu operated in Chile and Mexico and that Shein planned to add warehouse capacity in Mexico.

Mercado Libre grew faster than that regional forecast. In the third quarter of 2024, its gross merchandise value rose, in local-currency terms, 34% in Brazil and 27% in Mexico, and unique buyers rose 21% to nearly 61 million, according to the company’s results release.

Brazil, meanwhile, changed the rules for cheap imports. President Lula signed a law on June 27, 2024, setting a 20% import tax on international online purchases of up to $50, TecMundo reported. The tax took effect on August 1, on top of the state sales tax already charged, according to TecMundo.

What each business model rewards

Cross-border sellers compete on price, shipping low-cost goods directly from overseas. Mercado Libre competes on speed and reliability, with stock held in the country and delivered through its own network. Each model has a strength the other lacks, and a government that taxes one of them moves the line between the two.

That is what happened in Brazil. A 20% charge on small imported purchases, plus state tax, raises the price of the cheapest cross-border goods. The gap between a cheap import and a locally stocked product delivered in a day or two narrows, and speed carries more weight in the shopper’s decision.

Mexico is a different case. Shein’s plans for more warehouse capacity there suggest cross-border rivals are moving toward local stock themselves. Where they do, they compete directly with Mercado Libre’s own advantages, and brands face rivals that are both cheap and fast.

Shoppers’ habits reinforce the pattern. Many shoppers in the region are still new to buying online, and trust matters to them. A product delivered quickly by a familiar platform, with clear returns and local customer service, feels safer than a parcel shipped from overseas, which gives brands that invest in being local something a cross-border seller finds hard to copy.

Competing on Mercado Libre without competing on price

Price alone is a weak place for most brands to stand. Competing with ultra-low-cost imports on price is a losing game for them; the stronger ground is what cross-border sellers struggle to match, which is speed, authenticity, quality and service. Fast delivery from local inventory, through Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network, is the clearest of those advantages, and a brand that ships from abroad gives it up.

Planning has to happen country by country. Brazil now taxes small imports, while Mexico is seeing cross-border rivals build local warehouses, so a plan that works in one may not work in the other. Where to hold stock and how to price are decisions for each market. So is tracking policy: import taxes and trade rules in the region shift with politics, and a change in tax can quickly move the balance between local and cross-border sellers.

Trust needs to be visible on every listing. Clear product information, genuine reviews, authorized selling and responsive service help shoppers choose a brand over a cheaper unknown. Content should be local too: listings in the right language, with sizing and product details written for each market, because translated copy from a US listing rarely meets that bar.

Advertising grows more important as competition rises. With more sellers and rivals in the region, paid visibility on Mercado Libre matters more, and it works best planned from launch and focused on the searches where a brand’s speed and trust give it an edge.

Fashion faces the sharpest pressure. Low-cost apparel and accessories are where cross-border sellers have been strongest, so brands in those categories should lean hardest on quality, fit information and fast delivery to stand apart. Price still matters in some other categories as well: in fast-moving, low-cost lines, shoppers may tolerate slower delivery to save money, and brands there should test where their price must sit rather than assume speed alone will carry them.

US brands have a middle path into Mexico. A Texas warehouse that Mercado Libre opened gives US sellers a route to Mexican shoppers, according to its second-quarter shareholder letter, which offers a way to test demand before committing stock inside the country. For brands entering the region for the first time, the best starting points are the markets where local stock and fast delivery already set the standard, because there a new brand competes on its strengths.

For a leadership team, the useful question is which of the two parcels the brand wants to be: the cheap one from far away, or the one already in the country when the shopper clicks. Holding stock where the shopper is, and running the listings and ads around it, is how we help brands sell on Mercado Libre.

A0704.crumb: Alexa+ and the rise of the shopping…
A0704.title: Alexa+ and the rise of the shopping assistant that acts
A0704.alt: A smart speaker beside a paper grocery bag of greens, tomatoes, bananas and bread on a wooden kitchen table.
A0704.ttag: Alexa+ and the rise of the shopping assistant that acts | Kwontified
A0704.desc: Alexa+ can order groceries and book services. Why an assistant that acts narrows choice to one product, and what brands must do to be the one it picks.
A0704.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 27, 2025.
A0704.body:
A search results page has room for a fifth-place brand. Shoppers scroll, compare and sometimes pick the option a few rows down. An assistant asked to “reorder paper towels” has room for one answer, and that difference is what makes Alexa+, which Amazon introduced on February 26, 2025, more than a better voice assistant.

Alexa+ moves Amazon’s assistant from answering to acting. An assistant that completes a purchase usually picks one product instead of laying out a page of options, so brands start competing to be its choice. That rewards products shoppers already buy, clear product information, steady stock and fast delivery, and it means brands now need to build for being the default as well as for being visible in search.

What the Alexa+ shopping assistant can do so far

In demonstrations, Alexa+ ordered groceries from Amazon Fresh and carried out tasks in other services, booking Uber trips, finding concert tickets and making restaurant reservations, SiliconANGLE reported. It costs $19.99 a month, and Prime members get it free.

It is built to take steps, beyond replying. Alexa+ can carry out multi-step actions and draws on models available through Amazon Bedrock, eWeek reported. Early access starts in March and will work on almost every Alexa device Amazon has shipped, Engadget reported.

It is worth separating what was shown from what is shipping. The demonstrations are what Amazon chose to show at launch; early access has not yet begun, and how well the assistant handles a messy real-world shopping request is still to be seen. What is already settled is the distribution. Because Alexa+ is free for Prime members, Amazon can put it in front of its most loyal shoppers from the start, rather than waiting for people to pay for it.

It also lands on ground that is already moving. When Rufus, Amazon’s shopping assistant, was extended to every US customer, it had already taken in tens of millions of questions from shoppers, Retail Dive reported. And visits to retail sites referred by AI chat tools rose 1,300% during the 2024 holiday season, from a modest base, Adobe reported.

Why an assistant that acts narrows the choice to one

A search page shows a shopper many products and lets the shopper choose. Brands compete to appear high on that page, and even a brand in fifth place can win some sales.

An assistant that completes a purchase works differently. Asked to reorder paper towels or buy a birthday gift, it usually picks one product, drawing on what it knows: what the shopper bought before, what the product page says, whether the item is in stock and how fast it can arrive.

Take a brand that wins 10% of the clicks in its category on a search page, behind two larger rivals. If shoppers start reordering through an assistant, that 10% does not carry over as 10%. For shoppers who already buy the brand, the assistant may pick it every time. For shoppers who do not, it may never appear at all. Share becomes more concentrated: brands that are already chosen gain, and brands that relied on being one option among many lose.

For the people on a brand team, that changes the job description. The search team’s question is how high the product ranks. An assistant asks something else, whether the product is the one it already trusts for this shopper, and that is a question about repeat purchase, data quality and operations as much as about advertising.

How brands should prepare for assistants that act

Repeat purchase is the place to start. Assistants lean on what a shopper bought before, so brands in categories people buy repeatedly should invest in winning the first purchase and in subscription options, so they become the default when the shopper asks again.

Product information has to be unmistakable. An assistant needs to know exactly what a product is, what size it comes in and who it suits, and clear titles, complete attributes and plain descriptions make a product easier to select correctly. Shoppers will also ask assistants which product suits them before buying, so pages that answer common questions about fit, use and comparison give the assistant what it needs to recommend a brand with confidence.

Operations decide eligibility. An assistant is unlikely to pick a product that is out of stock or slow to arrive, and running out does more than lose a day of sales; it can hand the default to a competitor. For a Prime member asking an assistant to buy something, fast delivery is part of the expectation, so products that are eligible for Prime and arrive quickly are more likely to be chosen. Reviews feed the same choice: ratings signal quality to shoppers and give assistants evidence when choosing between products.

Measurement should shift with the behavior. As assistant shopping grows, repeat purchase rates, subscription sign-ups and the share of orders from returning customers become more important, and they belong next to search rankings in every review.

Exposure will differ by category. Assistants are most likely to take over repeat purchases of familiar items, such as household staples, where shoppers already know what they want. Considered purchases, such as a new skincare routine or a piece of furniture, will still involve comparison and research for some time, so each brand should judge how exposed its own categories are.

Advertising remains the open question. Amazon has not said how sponsored products will appear in Alexa+ answers. If paid placement enters assistant replies, the value of the top spot could rise sharply, because there may be only one spot, and brands should follow how Amazon handles this as Alexa+ rolls out. Search does not go away in the meantime: Alexa+ is rolling out gradually, and most shopping will still start with search for some time.

A simple test for each product: if a loyal customer asked an assistant to reorder it tomorrow, would the assistant have the stock, the delivery promise and the product facts it needs to say yes? Getting every important product to yes is what our AI Agentic Commerce practice works on with brands.
