A0707.crumb: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants…
A0707.title: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands in 2025
A0707.alt: A blue store shelving unit stocked with brown and white boxes beside a stack of yellow shopping baskets.
A0707.ttag: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands in 2025 | Kwontified
A0707.desc: Walmart’s ad business grew 27% to $4.4 billion, helped by more sellers who advertise. Where that money goes, and what Walmart now wants from brands.
A0707.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 27, 2025.
A0707.body:
For most brands, Walmart has long meant a buyer: the person who decides how many cases to take, which shelf they sit on and what margin Walmart keeps. The results Walmart reported for its latest fiscal year describe a different counterpart. Its advertising business grew 27% to $4.4 billion over the year, and Walmart Connect in the US grew 24%, helped by a 50% rise in the number of marketplace sellers who advertise.

Those figures say what Walmart wants from a brand in 2025: more of its range sold through the marketplace, advertising bought as a seller as well as a supplier, and media planned across Walmart’s site, its stores and, soon, television screens. Each of those requests moves a brand’s spending into the parts of Walmart that earn the most. Brands that treat Walmart as a growing media partner, and not only as a retail account, are reading the company the way it now reads itself.

Walmart ad growth came from sellers as much as from suppliers

Walmart’s earnings release put global advertising growth for the fourth quarter at 29%, including the 24% for Walmart Connect in the US, on the way to the full-year 27% and $4.4 billion. The same release credits that US growth in part to the 50% increase in marketplace sellers who advertise. In the US, Walmart’s e-commerce sales were up 20% for the quarter, reflecting strength in pickup and delivery, advertising and the marketplace.

Online now makes up a larger share of the whole company. E-commerce accounts for 18% of Walmart’s sales globally, executives said on the earnings call, and Walmart US executives said they plan to use Vizio’s television operating system to give sellers and suppliers more ways to place advertising. Walmart completed its Vizio acquisition in December, as we reported at the time.

Where the margin goes when a brand advertises on Walmart

Advertising is among Walmart’s higher-margin businesses, alongside membership and the marketplace, and executives described those businesses as part of why profit is growing faster than sales. That gives Walmart every reason to grow them together, and the three feed one another. More marketplace sellers bring more products, which bring more shoppers searching for them, and more sellers competing for those shoppers creates more demand for advertising. The 50% rise in seller advertisers is that loop turning.

Look at the same loop from the brand’s side of the table. A supplier that sells cases to a store buyer gives Walmart a retail margin on the product. The same brand selling more of its range on the marketplace, and buying Walmart Connect ads so shoppers find it there, also hands Walmart advertising revenue from the very business executives point to when they explain profit growth. Walmart keeps the data as well. It can link an ad to a purchase in its stores or on its website, which makes Walmart the party that knows best what the brand’s spending achieved.

Vizio carries the same logic into the living room. Walmart’s executives plan to connect Vizio’s television platform to Walmart Connect, which would let brands reach shoppers on their TV screens and measure the result in Walmart’s stores and website. Put together, Walmart is building something closer to a media business with a store attached, one that sells reach, data and placement across many screens as well as buying product and taking a margin on it.

What that asks of a brand’s Walmart plan

Assortment is the first thing Walmart is asking for. A brand that sells only a narrow line through Walmart’s stores can add more of its range through the marketplace and reach online shoppers without needing shelf space. Those products should have Walmart Connect advertising planned from launch, not added as an afterthought, and their listings deserve attention before any budget rises. Advertising sends shoppers to product pages, and pages with complete attributes, clear images and strong reviews convert more of that traffic.

More seller advertisers also means more brands bidding for the same searches. Click prices on Walmart are likely to rise as the network grows, so the searches that matter most to a brand need protecting, and costs need tracking closely. With search ads on the site, display across Walmart’s properties and television through Vizio coming, a brand can plan Walmart campaigns that meet shoppers at several points and judge each one by the sales it adds. The measurement to ask Walmart for is the link between ads and purchases in stores and online, which also lets a brand compare Walmart’s results with other networks.

Scale keeps Amazon at the center of most plans. Amazon’s advertising revenue was $17.3 billion in its fourth quarter alone, according to Amazon’s reported results, nearly four times Walmart’s advertising for the whole year. An eMarketer forecast cited by Business Insider expects the two together to capture more than 84% of what US advertisers spend on retail media in 2025. That makes Walmart the clear second network, growing faster from a smaller base, and for most brands the sensible plan keeps Amazon at the core while Walmart’s share of the budget grows as results justify it.

The cautions are real. Walmart’s media business is still much smaller than Amazon’s, and some of its newer tools, such as television advertising through Vizio, are not yet fully in place, so new formats call for tests with measured budgets rather than large shifts at once. Suppliers also have two sides of their own business to connect. Store buyers and the Walmart Connect team work toward related goals, and a brand that coordinates its in-store plans with its advertising plans is likely to get more from both.

Four questions for the next Walmart planning meeting

  1. Which of our products sell only in Walmart’s stores, and which could reach online shoppers through the marketplace?
  2. Does every marketplace product have Walmart Connect advertising planned from launch, with our most important searches protected?
  3. Have we asked Walmart for measurement that links our ads to store and online sales?
  4. Do the people who sell to Walmart’s store buyers and the people who buy its media see each other’s plans?

Walmart’s results show where it intends to earn its growth, and the answers to those four questions decide how much of that growth a brand shares in. Putting the marketplace, the media budget and the store relationship into one plan is how we run Walmart for brands as both a marketplace and a media partner.

A0710.title: Big Spring Sale 2025 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deal share
A0710.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes beside a jar of orange and yellow tulips and a watering can on a porch table.
A0710.ttag: Big Spring Sale 2025 forecast: sales lift, CPCs and deal share | Kwontified
A0710.desc: Amazon’s 2024 spring sale lifted sales about 3% to 6%, far below Prime events. Our 2025 ranges for sales lift, click prices and deal share, and how to budget.
A0710.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 4, 2025.
A0710.body:
Amazon’s first Big Spring Sale, held March 20 to 25, 2024, lifted sales by 3.1% against the average of the trailing four weeks. Measured the same way, Amazon’s October 2023 Prime Big Deal Days had lifted them by 23%. Both carry Amazon’s event branding, and they sit on very different scales.

Our 2025 forecast follows from that gap: a sales lift of 2% to 7%, click-price increases of 5% to 20%, and deal-driven sales making up 15% to 35% of event sales. The expensive mistake is to budget the spring event as a smaller Prime Day. Advertisers who plan a second-tier event like a tentpole push click prices up faster than its lift can pay for. The plan that works is a modest budget increase with selective deals.

The Big Spring Sale 2025 forecast in three ranges

Amazon has not yet announced dates for a 2025 spring sale. The ranges below assume it repeats the event in late March.

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
Sales lift vs trailing four weeks2%4%7%
Click-price increase vs prior 30 days5%10%20%
Deal-driven share of event sales15%25%35%

The sales lift range brackets 2024’s results. The conservative case assumes a smaller lift than 2024’s 3.1% as the event loses novelty. The standard case assumes slight growth. The reach case assumes a lift close to 2024’s year-on-year figure, if Amazon promotes the event more heavily.

The click-price range is an assumption, since no one has published a measured figure for the spring event. We set it well below the 35% rise in Amazon click prices during Prime Big Deal Days in October 2024, which Skai reported, because the spring event draws fewer shoppers. The deal share is a Kwontified planning assumption, based on how deal sales typically compare with total sales during smaller Amazon events, and of the three ranges it is the least certain.

Categories will scatter around these figures. Amazon focused the 2024 event on seasonal goods. That means categories such as outdoor and garden, home, beauty and fashion are likely to see lifts at the top of the range, while categories with little seasonal demand in March may see almost none. Each brand should find its own place within the range by category instead of planning to the average.

What the 2024 spring sale showed, measured two ways

The 3.1% lift comes from Earnest credit card data reported by Chain Store Age, and it compares the event with the weeks just before it. A year-on-year view looked better. Amazon US sales rose 5.9% from a year earlier during the event, and an average of 3.7% of products carried a Limited Time Deal tag, according to Momentum Commerce analysis published by PMG.

Baskets were smaller than at Prime events. Big Spring Sale shoppers spent 32% less on average than at the most recent Prime Days sale and bought about six items each, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence survey of 7,426 US consumers in March 2024.

Those two lift figures answer different questions, and a plan needs both. Comparing event sales with the trailing four weeks shows the lift the event created. Comparing them with the same week a year earlier shows whether the brand grew. In 2024 the answers were about 3% on one measure and about 6% on the other, which is why a recap that quotes only one of them should be read with care.

Why a Prime-sized budget loses money in a spring-sized event

A second-tier event draws fewer shoppers and smaller baskets than a Prime event, so its sales lift is modest. Advertisers who plan it like Prime Day raise bids and budgets anyway, which pushes click prices up. A budget sized for a big event then pays more per sale than the lift justifies.

Take a brand that normally sells $100,000 a week on Amazon. At the standard case, a 4% lift adds $4,000 in sales. If the brand doubles its usual $10,000 weekly advertising budget for the event, the extra $10,000 buys about $4,000 of added sales, a heavy loss on the increase. Raising the budget by 10% to 20%, which is $1,000 to $2,000 on that base, matches the opportunity far better.

Running a week-long event to its size

A seven-day sale spreads shoppers across several days, unlike a two-day Prime event, so the budget has to be paced. Watch the first two days closely and shift spend toward the products and searches that respond, instead of fixing the whole week’s budget in advance. Bid ceilings for the event week keep rising click prices from outrunning the small lift.

Deals earn their place only on some products: where they bring in new customers or move seasonal stock. A modest lift does not call for deep inventory builds, but a brand running deals on seasonal products should make sure stock covers the event and the weeks after, when spring demand continues.

New customers are where a small event can still pay back over time. The 2024 sale was open to all shoppers, beyond Prime members, which brings in people who rarely buy during Prime events. Track how many event buyers are new to the brand.

Timing may still move. If Amazon announces different dates, or a shorter or longer event, the ranges still apply to the event week. Keep budgets ready to move, and set bid ceilings once dates are confirmed.

The rule for the spring sale is to budget it to the size of its expected lift and to run deals only where they win new customers or clear seasonal stock. Sizing each Amazon event to its real opportunity, before the bids go up, is how we plan event budgets for brands.

A0711.crumb: How an activewear brand can win a war of…
A0711.title: How an activewear brand can win a war of attrition on Amazon
A0711.alt: A muddy pair of blue running shoes next to a clean white pair and navy track pants on a wooden bench.
A0711.ttag: How an activewear brand can win a war of attrition on Amazon | Kwontified
A0711.desc: Cheap apparel and rising click prices turned activewear on Amazon into a war of attrition. How a brand outlasts rivals by narrowing to its strongest products.
A0711.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 6, 2025.
A0711.body:
An activewear team on Amazon can open its main search and find a cheaper pair of leggings sitting beside its own, and the question in the next meeting is whether to match the price. Through 2024 that question got harder to avoid, and a brand that answered yes every time was spending margin it would need later.

Activewear on Amazon has become a war of attrition. Cheap clothing is growing fast after fee cuts, new low-price storefronts are arriving, and rising click prices squeeze every brand’s margin. The brands that win are the ones that outlast their rivals by narrowing to their strongest products, protecting margin and building reviews rather than matching every discount. A brand in a crowded apparel category should plan to endure instead of trying to win each price fight.

Why an activewear brand on Amazon now fights a war of attrition

Fastest growth came at the low end of the market. Sales of clothing items priced under $20 on Amazon rose 27% from mid-January to the end of August 2024, compared with 5% growth in the same period a year earlier, according to Momentum Commerce data reported by Modern Retail. The jump followed Amazon’s fee cuts on low-priced apparel.

Then came new low-price competition. Amazon launched Haul, a storefront of items priced at $20 or less, in November 2024, Bloomberg reported. Basic activewear, such as leggings and t-shirts, fits inside that price range easily.

Advertising also got more expensive. In the fourth quarter of 2024, Amazon’s ad revenue was up 18% against 7.1% for its online stores, according to Amazon’s reported results. When advertising outgrows sales, each sale costs more to win.

How attrition picks its winners

A crowded category with cheap competitors and rising advertising costs squeezes every brand’s margin at the same time. Brands respond by discounting to keep sales, which lowers margins further, until some can no longer afford to compete and pull back. The winner is rarely the brand with the lowest price on any given day. It is the brand still investing when weaker rivals have exhausted their margin and stepped away, which leaves more shoppers and lower click prices for those who remain.

Take a mid-priced activewear brand with forty products on Amazon that spends a year matching competitors’ discounts across its whole range and advertising every product. Its sales hold, but its margin after advertising falls sharply, and half its products end up losing money. Now say it changes course. It narrows its advertising to its eight best products, the ones with the strongest reviews and the most repeat buyers, stops matching discounts on the rest and lets slower items sell at full price or not at all. The effort that used to go into price matching goes into reviews, sizing information and images for the core eight.

Narrowing has a cost, because some loyal buyers of the dropped products will go elsewhere, and total sales may dip slightly. What the brand gets back is margin, and with it the ability to keep bidding. If lower-priced rivals cut their advertising, click prices on its core searches ease, and the brand holds its position on the searches that matter while competitors are pulling away from them.

Building a range that can outlast the price fight

Endurance starts with knowing the margin on every product after advertising and fees, because a war of attrition is won by the brand that can afford to keep going, and that depends on margin more than revenue. Once those numbers are on the table, narrowing to strength stops feeling like retreat. Advertising belongs on the products that convert best and earn repeat buyers, and money spent defending products that lose money is money the core cannot use.

The discount spiral is the trap to stay out of. Matching every competitor’s price cut drains margin and teaches shoppers to wait for deals, so discounts work best when they are selective, on products and moments where they win new customers. Big sale events test that discipline hardest, since they tempt a brand to discount everything to stay visible. A brand in a war of attrition can pick a few products where a deal brings in new customers and let the rest sit out.

What cheap rivals cannot copy is where the long-term money goes. Reviews, accurate sizing, quality materials and a recognizable brand give shoppers a reason to pay more, and those advantages take time to build but last through price fights. Watching the field matters too: tracking which competitors advertise on the key searches, and whether click prices are easing, shows when a rival is pulling back, which is the moment to hold or grow position.

Inventory should follow the narrowing. Products that no longer get advertising support should be reordered cautiously, so cash is not tied up in slow stock, while products in the core should rarely run out, because a stockout hands their searches to a rival. Other channels relieve the pressure as well. A brand with its own site, wholesale partners or other marketplaces is less dependent on winning every Amazon price fight, and it can carry full-price customers through periods of heavy competition.

The strategy has limits. A brand without a clear quality or brand advantage may not be able to outlast cheaper rivals, and some categories may simply move to lower prices. Before choosing to endure, a brand has to be honest about whether its products can command a premium.

For the brands that can, the picture at the end of a price war is a short list of products still bidding on their core searches after the cheaper listings have gone quiet. Choosing that list, and running the margin math behind it, is how we manage apparel brands on Amazon without giving away the margin.

A0712.crumb: Roundel for brands in 2025: more ad…
A0712.title: Roundel for brands in 2025: more ad money, same shoppers
A0712.alt: A bright store aisle lined with shelves of neutral packaged goods and digital screens, with a red basket on the floor.
A0712.ttag: Roundel for brands in 2025: more ad money, same shoppers | Kwontified
A0712.desc: Target plans to double Roundel by 2030 while its own sales slipped in 2024. Why more ad money chasing the same shoppers raises costs, and how to judge it.
A0712.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 11, 2025.
A0712.body:
Target wants Roundel, its in-house media business, to be twice its current size by 2030. Roundel drove more than $2 billion in value in 2024. In the same year Target’s net sales fell 0.8% to $106.6 billion. When an ad business doubles on top of a store whose sales are flat, much of that growth arrives as more advertising money competing for roughly the same shoppers.

That is the number brands should plan around. When ad demand grows faster than the audience it buys, the cost of reaching each shopper rises, and a brand that keeps its Roundel budget flat reaches fewer people each year. Roundel for brands in 2025 is still worth buying, but it has to be judged by the sales a brand’s own ads add, using Target Circle data to aim spending more precisely and negotiating commitments against measured results.

What Target said about Roundel for brands

Target set out the plan on March 4, 2025. It aims to double Roundel, which drove more than $2 billion in value in 2024, by adding hundreds more vendor partners each year and integrating Roundel further with Target Plus, its marketplace, and Target Circle, its loyalty program, Retail TouchPoints reported. The same plan aims to grow Target Plus sales from about $1 billion in 2024 to more than $5 billion by 2030.

Executives put Roundel’s 2024 growth at a mid-teens rate, and Target Circle added 13 million members during the year, they said on the company’s earnings call. Target’s own sales did not keep pace: net sales fell 0.8% to $106.6 billion in its 2024 fiscal year, according to the same Retail TouchPoints report.

Why a big headline number pulls budgets the wrong way

Target chose its word carefully. It describes Roundel’s $2 billion as the value Roundel drove, a measure that can include more than ad revenue alone. Brands should not read it as the size of the auction they bid in.

The mistake is easy to make because the figure is the first one anyone sees. A large, fast-growing number becomes the anchor for the budget conversation: the network is growing, so spending more there must be keeping up. Network growth describes Target’s business, though. It says nothing about what the next dollar of a particular brand’s spend will return, and when the growth comes from more advertisers rather than more shoppers, it points the other way.

How more ad money for the same shoppers raises the cost

An advertising network sells access to a retailer’s shoppers. When the retailer’s sales and traffic grow slowly while its advertising business grows fast, more advertising money competes for roughly the same people. Each placement, each audience and each search is bid for by more brands with bigger budgets. A brand that keeps spending the same amount reaches fewer shoppers, and a brand that keeps reaching the same shoppers pays more.

Take a brand that spends $100,000 a year on Roundel and reaches a given number of Target shoppers. If Roundel’s ad business grows 15% a year while Target’s shopper base stays flat, competing demand for the same shoppers rises by roughly that much. To reach the same shoppers at the same frequency, the brand might need to spend close to $115,000 the following year, with no guarantee of added sales.

The same pressure shows up on Amazon and Walmart, whose advertising businesses have also grown faster than their retail sales, so Roundel is following the pattern of the larger networks. That is no reason to avoid it. Target’s shoppers and its Circle data are valuable, and Roundel can reach them online and in stores. It is a reason to measure carefully.

Judging Roundel by what it adds

The first thing to ask Roundel for is results that show the sales a brand’s ads added, compared against shoppers who did not see them, across Target’s website and stores. That measure, more than clicks or reach, decides whether spending deserves to grow. Brands sold heavily in Target’s stores should ask how in-store results are measured, since that may be where much of the added value shows up.

Target Circle is the precision tool. With 13 million members added in 2024, Target can help brands reach shoppers by what they buy. That lets spending concentrate on the shoppers most likely to buy instead of broad audiences. Creative needs the same care as targeting: as more brands compete for the same shoppers, ads that look like every other brand’s are easy to ignore, so images and messages should be refreshed often and tested for which ones lift sales.

Vendor commitments should follow results as well. Vendors that sell to Target often fund advertising as part of the relationship. With Target planning to add hundreds of vendor partners to Roundel each year, that money should be tied to measured results instead of reach a brand cannot connect to sales. As Target grows its marketplace toward $5 billion and links Roundel to it, brands on Target Plus will gain more ways to advertise and should plan advertising alongside their marketplace launch.

Cost needs its own line in the quarterly review. Track what it costs to reach target shoppers on Roundel each quarter. If that cost rises faster than the sales it supports, move budget to better-performing placements or channels. Amazon and Walmart are larger, while Roundel offers Target’s distinct shoppers and loyalty data. Compare Roundel’s added sales per dollar with what the same money earns elsewhere before deciding how much to move.

The rule for 2025 is to judge Roundel by the sales your ads add, never by the network’s growth or the reach it reports. Measuring that number on Target’s site and in its stores, and setting the budget from it, is how we plan and measure Roundel spending for brands.

A0714.title: Instagram shopping for brands in 2025: the ad system is the store
A0714.alt: A smartphone on a wire stand beside a twine-wrapped parcel, paper bag and dried flowers on a wooden table.
A0714.ttag: Instagram shopping for brands in 2025: the ad system is the store | Kwontified
A0714.desc: Meta’s automated shopping ads passed a $20 billion run rate as ad prices rose 14%. Why Instagram shopping runs through the ad system, and what brands control.
A0714.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 13, 2025.
A0714.body:
Shoppers on Instagram rarely go looking for a store. They scroll, a product turns up in a post, a Reel or an ad, and they decide in the moment whether to tap. Whatever put the product in front of them at that moment is, in practice, the store, and on Instagram that is now Meta’s automated ad system far more than any shop storefront.

The numbers show where the shelf moved. Meta’s Advantage+ Shopping campaigns passed a $20 billion annual run rate in the fourth quarter of 2024, while the average price per ad rose 14%. With the system choosing who sees what, a brand still controls two things, its creative and where the sale happens, and as costs rise it should judge Instagram on sales per dollar.

How Instagram shopping for brands moved into the ad system

The storefront rules tightened first. From April 24, 2024, US shops on Instagram and Facebook that did not use Meta’s in-app checkout were no longer accessible, TechCrunch reported. Brands either moved to Meta’s checkout or relied on ads that send shoppers somewhere else to buy.

Then the ad system grew around them. Meta’s automated Advantage+ Shopping campaigns surpassed that $20 billion run rate in the fourth quarter of 2024, up 70% from a year earlier. More than 4 million advertisers used at least one of Meta’s generative AI ad creative tools, up from 1 million six months before, afaqs reported after Meta’s results.

The ads themselves got more expensive. Ad impressions across Meta’s apps grew 6% in the fourth quarter while the average price per ad rose 14%, according to Meta’s fourth-quarter results.

The decision the ad system leaves on the table

Meta built its system around in-the-moment discovery. Automated campaigns decide which shoppers see which products, in which format and at what price, with less manual targeting from the brand. The brand supplies the products, the creative and the budget, and the system does the rest. That shifts where control sits: the audience and the placement are mostly Meta’s call now.

What stays with the brand is a decision that belongs with its leadership team: when a shopper taps, where should the purchase happen? Meta’s checkout keeps shoppers in the app but gives the brand less customer data. The brand’s own site keeps the relationship but adds a step. Amazon offers a trusted checkout but a weaker direct relationship, and the option is real: Meta has let shoppers buy from Amazon inside its apps through Amazon’s ads since November 2023, TechCrunch reported.

There is no single right answer, so the useful way to settle it is product by product, on margin and repeat purchase. A product people reorder often may earn more when the sale lands on the brand’s own site, where the next order can be won through email, while a product bought once may sell more easily through a checkout the shopper already trusts.

Rising ad prices raise the stakes of both choices. When each ad costs more and more brands rely on the same automated system, the brands whose creative persuades best win the most sales for the money. The brands that route each sale to the right place keep more of what those sales are worth.

Running Instagram when the store is an algorithm

Creative is the main lever left. With automation handling targeting, the images and videos a brand supplies decide most of what the system can do with it, so brands need more variations, tested often, with the tired ones retired. Creators help where they fit the brand, because their content often feels more natural in a feed than polished brand ads and gives the system more varied creative to work with.

The system also learns from what it is fed. Automated campaigns draw on product catalogs and purchase signals, so accurate catalogs, clear product data and reliable purchase tracking help it find buyers. Catalog and creative have to move together: when a product goes out of stock or a price changes, the ads built around it should change too. The system will keep promoting whatever it is given, which is why someone should review which products it is pushing and pause those that cannot be delivered profitably.

Measurement has to widen as prices climb. Instagram belongs on the sales its ads add, judged against what the same budget earns elsewhere, rather than on reach or engagement. Many shoppers who discover a product on Instagram buy it later on Amazon or in a store. A brand can look for that effect, for example by comparing Amazon sales of a product during and after an Instagram campaign, before judging Instagram on in-app results alone.

Costs will move with the calendar and with competitors. Ad prices on Meta tend to rise when many advertisers compete at once, around holidays and big sale events, so budgets and expectations belong by season instead of on an assumption of steady costs. With TikTok’s future in the United States uncertain, some brands may shift social budgets toward Instagram, and if they do, competition there could rise further; nobody should plan on 2024 prices holding.

Instagram is a powerful place to be discovered, but the brand does not own the audience there. Email and the brand’s own site are where discovery turns into a relationship the brand controls, and they deserve investment alongside the ad budget.

A leadership team that settles where each product’s sale should happen, and funds the creative to earn it, has taken back most of what the algorithm left open. Making those calls product by product, across Meta’s checkout, a brand’s own site and Amazon, is how we run social commerce for brands on Instagram.

A0716.crumb: Temu for brands in 2025: tariffs push it…
A0716.title: Temu for brands in 2025: tariffs push it toward local stock
A0716.alt: A sunlit warehouse with a tagged wooden crate, boxes on pallets, and shelves of orange storage bins.
A0716.ttag: Temu for brands in 2025: tariffs push it toward local stock | Kwontified
A0716.desc: Tariffs and the threat to duty-free parcels are pushing Temu toward US warehouses. Why that narrows its price edge, and what it means for brands selling there.
A0716.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 18, 2025.
A0716.body:
Temu’s prices in the US were built on a customs rule. A single parcel shipped from a factory in China was worth so little that it entered without duty, and US customs was handling millions of low-value parcels a day. Early in 2025 that rule started to wobble just as tariffs on Chinese goods rose, and the cheapest way for Temu to reach a US shopper began to look like the way Amazon does it: stock already sitting in a US warehouse.

Local warehouses already supplied about a fifth of Temu’s US sales. As that share grows, Temu delivers faster but loses some of its price edge, so it starts to behave like the marketplaces it set out to undercut. Temu for brands is therefore less a bargain bin than a marketplace converging on its rivals, best judged on consistent prices, locally stocked goods and shopper fit.

What changed for Temu for brands in early 2025

Tariffs on Chinese goods rose twice within a month. A 10% tariff on goods from China took effect on February 4, Geodis noted in a customs update, and the rate rose to 20% on March 4, according to a RetailStat analysis.

The duty-free rule moved at the same time. The administration moved to end duty-free treatment for low-value parcels from China, then paused the change to give agencies time to handle the volume, the AP reported. The volume behind that pause is large: US customs processed more than 4 million such parcels a day in 2024, with Shein and Temu accounting for more than 30% of them, ABC reported.

Temu was already shifting. About 20% of its US sales were shipped from local sellers rather than directly from China, according to Marketplace Pulse estimates cited by Reuters. Two China-based sellers said half the products they sold to the US by the end of 2024 went to US warehouses first, and Temu was shipping more goods by sea. Analysts at Nomura estimated that duty-free parcel shipments to the US could fall by 60% if the exemption ends, according to the same Reuters report.

The app showed the shift too. Temu was prominently promoting products shipped from US warehouses, RetailWire reported.

Why tariffs make Temu look more like its rivals

Temu’s original model shipped individual parcels from factories in China directly to US shoppers. Because each parcel was worth little, it entered without duty. Prices stayed very low, and the cost was slow delivery.

Tariffs and the threat to duty-free treatment raise the cost of that model. Goods shipped in bulk to US warehouses pay duty once on a larger shipment and then reach shoppers quickly. As the parcel model gets more expensive, the warehouse model becomes relatively more attractive, even though it pays the tariff too.

Take a small item that costs $4 to make and ships as a single parcel. Without duty, it can sell for very little. If duty-free treatment ends and a 20% tariff applies, the import cost rises, and putting each parcel through customs one at a time adds cost and delay. The same item shipped in bulk to a US warehouse pays the tariff as well, but spreads the handling across thousands of units and arrives in days instead of weeks.

What follows is convergence on the rest of the market. Temu’s goods arrive faster, but its price edge over Amazon, Walmart and Amazon’s own low-price Haul storefront narrows. Temu ends up competing on the same ground as the marketplaces it set out to undercut.

How brands should approach Temu in 2025

Pricing is the first test for any brand there. As Temu competes more directly with other marketplaces, a product priced much lower on Temu than elsewhere risks undercutting a brand’s other channels and its standing with marketplaces that watch prices. Temu prices belong within the brand’s normal range.

Brands that do sell there should sell from local inventory. Temu is promoting goods shipped from US warehouses, and local stock delivers faster and fits where Temu is steering shoppers. Temu also opened its marketplace to US-based sellers without an invitation in November 2024, Modern Retail reported. As it leans on local stock, brands with US inventory are the sellers it is trying to attract, which may give them better terms and visibility than they would have had a year earlier.

The rules themselves need watching. Tariff rates and the duty-free exemption were both changing in early 2025, and each change shifts the cost of selling and the prices competitors can offer. If cross-border parcels get more expensive, the cheapest imported goods may rise in price, which could give brands selling locally stocked products a little more room in low-price categories.

Brand protection works the same way it does anywhere else. Check whether unauthorized sellers are listing the brand’s products on Temu, and handle them as on any other marketplace.

Fit is the last question, and for many brands the deciding one. Temu’s shoppers may not match a premium brand’s customers, and convergence does not make Temu right for every brand; it makes Temu easier to judge on the same terms as other marketplaces. A brand unsure whether Temu’s shoppers will buy can start with a few items from local stock, especially in categories new to the brand, compare results with other channels and expand only if the margin holds.

The rule that follows from the mechanism: treat Temu as a marketplace converging on its rivals, and plan for it on price consistency and local stock instead of extreme discounting. Working out which marketplaces fit a brand’s products and prices, Temu included, is how we manage channels for brands across marketplaces.

A0717.crumb: TikTok Shop for brands in 2025: big…
A0717.title: TikTok Shop for brands in 2025: big moments, uncertain future
A0717.alt: A smartphone mounted in a ring light on a small table between teal velvet armchairs in a lamp-lit lounge.
A0717.ttag: TikTok Shop for brands in 2025: big moments, uncertain future | Kwontified
A0717.desc: TikTok Shop tripled Black Friday sales to over $100 million while its US future rests on April 5. How brands should run a channel built on big moments.
A0717.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 20, 2025.
A0717.body:
On Black Friday 2024, US shoppers joined more than 30,000 live shopping streams on TikTok, and one hair-care brand reached $1 million in sales within two hours of going live. TikTok Shop sells in bursts, around live streams, creators and big shopping days, and that rhythm is the first thing a brand has to plan around.

The second is the calendar of a law. The app’s US future hangs on an April 5 deadline, and social commerce is still a small share of American online sales. Together those facts point to one way of running TikTok Shop for brands in 2025: as an event and creator channel with limited stock commitments and content that can travel, rather than as a steady base of sales.

How TikTok Shop for brands performed into 2025

Black Friday was the biggest moment so far. TikTok Shop’s US sales on Black Friday 2024 tripled to more than $100 million, and the number of shoppers between Black Friday and Cyber Monday rose 165% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported. The 30,000 live streams and the hair-care brand’s $1 million in two hours come from a Benzinga report, and they show where the sales came from: live selling.

Scale keeps it in perspective. TikTok Shop’s Black Friday sales were a small piece of the more than $10 billion spent online that day, and social commerce makes up around 5% of US e-commerce sales, an analyst at Mintel told Marketplace.

Then there is the law. After the app briefly went dark in January, President Trump ordered a 75-day pause in enforcement of the sale-or-ban law on January 20, TechCrunch reported. That pause runs to April 5.

Why demand on TikTok Shop arrives in bursts

On TikTok, shoppers do not arrive looking for a product. They arrive to watch, and they buy when a video or a live stream catches them at the right moment. Sales follow attention, and attention clusters around creators, live events and big shopping days. A search marketplace works differently: on Amazon, demand for a product is fairly steady, because shoppers search for it whenever they need it. On TikTok Shop, a product can sell thousands of units during one live stream and very few the following week.

The way orders are fulfilled adds risk to that pattern. Merchants fulfill most TikTok Shop orders themselves, sometimes through third parties or TikTok’s own fulfillment services, Reuters reported. A brand that builds stock for a burst of demand carries that stock if the moment does not come, or if the app goes dark.

Running a channel built on moments

The calendar should be built around the bursts. Live streams, creator partnerships and shopping events are where effort and stock belong, and the right creators are chosen by their record of sales rather than their follower counts, with rights agreed up front to reuse the content elsewhere. Videos made for TikTok can work on Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts and marketplace listings, so content planned with those uses in mind keeps its value whatever happens to the app.

Stock commitments should stay light. With demand arriving in bursts and the app’s future uncertain, deep inventory dedicated to TikTok Shop is where the risk concentrates. Sharing stock with other channels, or using fulfillment that serves several channels, reduces that risk. The live moments themselves need people: a stream that sells well brings a rush of questions and orders, and a team ready to answer shoppers and ship quickly keeps a strong event from ending in delays and poor reviews.

The full cost has to be counted. TikTok Shop raised its commission on most US sales from 2% to 8% in stages during 2024, with the higher rate taking effect on July 1, Retail Brew reported. Creator commissions, live-stream production and fulfillment come on top, and a burst of sales can look profitable until those costs are added up.

Product choice matters more here than on a search marketplace. Home goods, fashion and beauty were among the most popular categories on Black Friday, according to the same Benzinga report, and products that can be shown working in a short video or a live demonstration tend to sell best. A brand does better leading with those than putting its whole catalog in front of a camera. Event offers need the same discipline: deep discounts during a live stream can pull a brand’s prices below what it charges elsewhere, so offers should feel special without undercutting its pricing on Amazon or its own site.

Every TikTok Shop buyer is also a relationship worth moving somewhere safer. Inviting buyers to follow the brand elsewhere or join an email list means the relationship survives whatever happens to the app.

Measurement has to match the rhythm. Average weekly sales understate a channel built on bursts, so each event and live stream deserves its own reading, on sales and new customers, set against the cost of the content and stock behind it.

A plan for each April 5 outcome beats waiting for one

A sale of TikTok’s US business, a further delay or a ban would each change the channel’s prospects, and a brand that waits for the outcome before deciding what to do leaves itself little time to act. The teams that are ready will have walked through all three before the deadline: which creators and content move to other platforms, how much stock is exposed, and which buyers they can still reach by email.

The picture to aim for is a channel that can have a record night without leaving the brand exposed the morning after. Running TikTok Shop around its moments, with stock and content that can move, is how we operate social commerce for brands through an uncertain year.

A0718.crumb: Vendor Central for brands in 2025: who…
A0718.title: Vendor Central for brands in 2025: who absorbs rising costs
A0718.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a twine-wrapped parcel against stacks of coins on a wooden table.
A0718.ttag: Vendor Central for brands in 2025: who absorbs rising costs | Kwontified
A0718.desc: Under Vendor Central, Amazon sets the price and the vendor absorbs rising costs. With tariffs up in 2025, why that matters and how to split 1P and 3P.
A0718.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 25, 2025.
A0718.body:
When a tariff goes up, someone pays it before anyone else notices. On Vendor Central, that someone is usually the brand. Amazon buys at a negotiated cost price and sets the retail price itself, so when a vendor’s costs rise, as tariffs on Chinese goods have made them in 2025, the vendor absorbs the increase until it can renegotiate.

A seller on Seller Central can change its own price the same day. That difference was easy to ignore while costs held still. With costs rising, it becomes the deciding factor in where each product should sit, and Vendor Central for brands in 2025 is best treated as one of two homes, chosen product by product after the cost increases have been modeled.

What changed for Vendor Central for brands going into 2025

Amazon narrowed its wholesale base in 2024. Many vendors were told their relationships would end by November 9, after which Amazon would no longer buy their products wholesale, SPS Commerce reported. Some received two to three months’ notice and could switch to selling directly, Retail Brew reported.

Third-party selling kept growing faster than Amazon’s own retail. Amazon’s fourth-quarter 2024 figures show seller services revenue up 9% against 7.1% for its own online stores, according to Amazon’s reported results. On the earnings call, Amazon’s chief executive put the third-party share of units sold in 2024 at 61%, its highest annual share.

Costs then rose in early 2025. The tariff on goods from China rose to 20% on March 4, doubling the 10% rate that took effect in February, according to a RetailStat analysis.

Who carries a cost increase under each model

A vendor sells to Amazon at an agreed cost price, and Amazon decides what to charge shoppers. If the vendor’s own costs rise, from tariffs, freight or materials, the cost price it receives does not change until the vendor negotiates a new one. Until then, the vendor’s margin shrinks.

A seller sets the price shoppers pay. If its costs rise, it can raise the price the same day. It then accepts whatever effect that has on sales. It carries more operational work, but it holds the lever that matters most when costs move.

Vendor Central (1P)Seller Central (3P)
Who sets the retail priceAmazonThe brand
When the brand’s costs riseThe vendor absorbs them until it renegotiatesThe seller can reprice the same day
Who holds the inventoryAmazon buys and holds the stockThe brand holds its own stock at Amazon

Take an item a vendor imports from China for $6 and sells to Amazon at a cost price of $12, after paying freight and duty. When the tariff on that item rises by 10 percentage points, the vendor’s duty rises by $0.60. If the vendor cannot renegotiate quickly, that $0.60 comes straight out of its margin on every unit Amazon orders. A seller with the same product could raise its price by a similar amount and keep its margin, if shoppers accept the new price.

Both models have a real case, and costs tip the balance

Vendor Central still earns its place. Amazon handles much of the work, buying the stock and running the retail side, and products that sell well with healthy margins are worth keeping there. Seller Central gives price control at the cost of more operations and more cash tied up. Brands selling directly carry their own inventory at Amazon, so moving a product from Vendor Central to Seller Central changes working capital, and that change needs planning before the switch.

With costs flat, those two sides can balance out. With costs rising, the numbers lean toward whichever model lets the brand pass an increase on, which is why the decision belongs at the product level. Products with stable costs and steady demand may suit Vendor Central. Products exposed to rising costs, or where the brand wants control over price, may suit Seller Central. Many brands already run a split, selling some products to Amazon wholesale and others directly.

A cost model comes before any move between 1P and 3P

Start with a cost model. Calculating how tariffs and other increases change the margin on each product under its current cost price shows which products are under the most pressure. Vendors with products in that group should bring the evidence to their next negotiation with Amazon, since clear numbers make a stronger case than general claims about rising costs. The same logic reaches beyond tariffs, because freight, materials and labor costs also move.

Watch the price shoppers see. On Vendor Central, Amazon may lower the retail price to match competitors and then press the vendor for better terms, so tracking retail prices on Amazon prepares a brand for those conversations. Pricing changes also belong in one decision across channels: a cost increase that squeezes margin on Amazon also affects the brand’s own site and other marketplaces, and a move on one channel can create gaps that shoppers or other retailers notice.

Be ready to switch. Amazon ended many wholesale relationships in 2024 with limited notice, so brands still on Vendor Central should keep a Seller Central account set up and their listings protected through Brand Registry. Finance belongs in the room early, because splitting products between wholesale and direct selling changes revenue recognition, cash flow and inventory accounting.

The rule for a year of rising costs: the model that lets a brand pass an increase on is worth more than it was, so place each product where it earns the most and keep the option to move it. Building that product-by-product split between Vendor and Seller Central is how we run Amazon channel management for brands under cost pressure.

A0720.crumb: Amazon DSP for brands in 2025: the system…
A0720.title: Amazon DSP for brands in 2025: the system behind Prime Video ads
A0720.alt: A navy living room at dusk with a wall TV showing mountains, a floor lamp, and popcorn and glasses on a table.
A0720.ttag: Amazon DSP for brands in 2025: the system behind Prime Video ads | Kwontified
A0720.desc: Prime Video ads reached 200 million viewers a month after Amazon switched them on by default. Why Amazon DSP now buys TV, and how brands should test it.
A0720.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 27, 2025.
A0720.body:
Rival streaming services built their ad audiences by launching separate ad-supported plans and waiting for viewers to sign up. Amazon skipped the waiting. On January 29, 2024, it began showing limited ads in Prime Video shows and movies for all Prime customers, unless they paid extra to remove them, and every viewer who did not pay joined the ad-supported audience.

That one decision gave Amazon one of the largest ad-supported streaming audiences almost overnight, and Amazon DSP is how brands reach it and connect it to sales on Amazon. The tool many teams still file under display and retargeting has become Amazon’s system for buying television. Amazon DSP for brands in 2025 belongs in the streaming TV plan, tested for the sales it adds before any budget scales.

How Amazon DSP for brands changed with Prime Video

The default did the work. Where rivals asked viewers to opt into a cheaper tier, Amazon included ads for all Prime customers, StreamTV Insider reported.

The scale followed within months. Amazon said at its first upfront presentation in May 2024 that Prime Video had a monthly ad-supported reach of more than 200 million viewers worldwide, and its wider streaming TV offering reached more than 175 million customers a month, Advanced Television reported. About 115 million of Prime Video’s ad-supported viewers were in the United States, Deadline reported from the event.

The business around it kept growing too. For the last three months of 2024, Amazon booked $17.3 billion of ad revenue, 18% more than a year before, according to Amazon’s reported results.

Why the default made DSP a TV-buying system

An audience that size needs a way to be bought. Amazon DSP, its tool for buying ads across Amazon’s properties and other websites and apps, became the main route for brands to buy Prime Video placements programmatically and to target viewers using what Amazon knows about their shopping. DSP was once mostly a tool for display ads and for retargeting shoppers who had viewed a product. It is now also how many brands buy television.

The link to shopping is what sets it apart. A brand buying television through other channels usually cannot see whether an ad led to a sale. Through Amazon, a brand can connect streaming TV exposure to purchases on Amazon, at least for the products it sells there.

Trace where the value settles and Amazon sits at every point. It owns the audience, which it gathered by default rather than by persuasion; it owns the shopping data used to target that audience; and it owns the record of what was bought afterwards. For a brand, that combination is useful, because few other TV buys come with a sales receipt attached. It also defines the limits of the receipt. Amazon’s measurement sees sales on Amazon, so a brand that sells heavily through other retailers or its own site sees only part of what its television spend did.

Testing streaming TV before scaling it

Streaming TV fits inside the Amazon plan. Brands that already advertise on Amazon can reach Prime Video viewers with the same shopping-based audiences they use elsewhere, so television becomes an extension of their Amazon advertising instead of a separate budget. Amazon’s streaming reach also spans Twitch, Fire TV and its free streaming services, according to the same Deadline report, and DSP can plan across those placements instead of treating Prime Video as the only option.

Reach is the easy part to buy, and it is a different thing from new customers. Tests that compare sales among viewers who saw an ad with similar shoppers who did not should come before any large commitment. Streaming TV can absorb money quickly, so a brand new to it is better off with a fixed test budget, run long enough to measure, scaling only the audiences and creative that show added sales. Television ads often influence purchases days or weeks after viewing, which means the measurement window has to be long enough to catch that delay.

New-to-brand sales are the number to watch. The value of streaming TV often lies in reaching people who have not bought the brand before, and total sales from DSP campaigns can include existing customers who would have bought anyway. Audience choice shapes that number. Amazon can target viewers by what they have bought or browsed, which can make television more efficient, but an audience drawn too narrowly defeats the point of reaching new customers, so a mix of broad and targeted audiences deserves testing.

Creative made for a product page will not carry a television spot. Video ads for Prime Video need to work on a big screen, often with the sound on, and tell a story in a short time. Viewers who see the same ad too often grow tired of it, so frequency limits and regular creative refreshes belong in the plan from the start.

Size matters too. Streaming TV works best for brands with enough sales and distribution to benefit from wide awareness, and smaller brands may get more from DSP’s retargeting and Amazon audience targeting than from television reach. Brands running both TV and search should also watch whether television raises searches for the brand on Amazon, and make sure their search ads are ready to capture that interest.

The leadership question is less whether to buy Prime Video than how much of the answer to accept from the party that sold the audience. Building the test, reading Amazon’s numbers alongside the brand’s own and scaling only what adds customers is how we plan and measure Amazon DSP for brands, streaming TV included.

A0722.crumb: Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands in…
A0722.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands in 2025: past the last click
A0722.alt: A brown paper parcel on the doorstep of a cottage at the end of a stone path through a sunny flower garden.
A0722.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands in 2025: past the last click | Kwontified
A0722.desc: A last-click report hands every sale to the final search ad. Amazon Marketing Cloud shows the whole path, so brands can fund each ad by what it adds.
A0722.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 1, 2025.
A0722.body:
Open a standard Amazon ad report and the whole sale belongs to the search ad the shopper clicked just before buying. The streaming TV spot she watched on Monday and the display ad she saw on Wednesday earn little or nothing. Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands exists to fix that accounting. Between October 2024 and early 2025 it became easier to use and open to more advertisers, and its value is the full path it shows: which ads a buyer saw, in what order, before the click that gets the credit.

Seeing that path changes how a brand spends. It stops paying only for the last touch, measures what each ad type adds, and bids more for shoppers its other ads have already reached.

What changed for Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands

The first change was access. After Amazon’s unBoxed conference in October 2024, Amazon Marketing Cloud became available to brands that advertise only through sponsored ads, not just to those using Amazon’s DSP, Flywheel reported.

Audiences built in it also reached search ads. Advertisers using Amazon Marketing Cloud can now adjust their Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands bids for shoppers who have seen their streaming TV ads, Amazon announced.

The tool also became easier to query. At CES on January 15, 2025, Amazon introduced a generator that turns plain-language descriptions into the database queries Amazon Marketing Cloud requires, PPC Land reported. Before, using it well meant writing those queries by hand.

Why a last-click report misjudges each ad

Follow one shopper through a week. She sees a brand’s streaming TV ad on Monday and a display ad on Wednesday, then on Friday searches for the brand, clicks a search ad and buys. A standard report credits the sale to the search ad, the last thing she clicked.

That flatters search. It flatters searches for the brand’s own name most of all. Many shoppers who type a brand name already intended to buy it. Meanwhile the TV and display ads that created the intent get little or no credit.

Brands that budget on those reports drift in one direction. Money moves toward the last click and away from the ads that created demand. Over time the demand-creating ads shrink, fewer shoppers arrive searching for the brand, and search results weaken too. It works like a relay team that pays only the runner who crosses the line: the anchor leg looks brilliant, the early legs look like cost, and the team gets slower every season it follows the payroll.

Amazon Marketing Cloud lets a brand see the whole path for its own ads. It can show how many buyers saw a TV or display ad before clicking a search ad, and how their buying compares with shoppers who saw none.

Take a brand whose reports show branded search ads returning $8 in sales for every $1 spent, and streaming TV returning $1. Amazon Marketing Cloud shows that most branded-search buyers had seen the brand’s TV ads first, and that shoppers exposed to TV converted on search at twice the rate of those who were not. The TV ads were creating much of the demand that search was collecting. Judged by contribution across the path, rather than by what each ad collected at the end, the budget would move the other way.

Reading the path before moving the budget

The first analysis is the overlap between ad types: how many buyers saw more than one kind of ad, and in what order. That alone often changes how a brand views its search results. From there, brands running streaming TV or display should compare buying among shoppers who saw those ads with similar shoppers who did not, which shows what the ads add rather than what they were credited with.

Branded search deserves its own check. A brand can test how much of its branded search sales would happen without the ads, for example by reducing bids on some branded terms for a period and watching sales, and Amazon Marketing Cloud helps read the result. The new bid adjustments work in the opposite direction: they let a brand bid more for shoppers who have seen its TV or display ads, when those shoppers convert better, which links spending across the funnel.

The plain-language generator makes all of this more accessible, but someone who understands the data should review generated queries before decisions rely on them. Brands with direct sales or loyalty programs can go further, because Amazon Marketing Cloud lets advertisers combine their own customer data with Amazon’s ad data in a privacy-safe way and see how Amazon ads reach existing customers.

Limits, reruns and the other networks

Amazon Marketing Cloud reports only on groups of shoppers above a minimum size, to protect privacy. Smaller brands may find some questions cannot be answered at their scale, which is worth knowing before a study is planned around them.

Shopping paths also change with seasons, events and new ad formats. A single study is not a permanent answer; the main analyses are worth rerunning each quarter and before big events.

Walmart, Target and other retail networks report on the last click as well. Asking each of them for evidence of what their ads add keeps budgets moving between networks on comparable measures.

The rule for Monday is a question to put to any report before a dollar moves: would this sale have happened without this ad? A last-click report cannot answer it, while a path analysis or a branded bid test can, and building those analyses before budgets shift is how we set up Amazon Marketing Cloud measurement for brands.

A0724.crumb: How a kitchen brand can win a crowded…
A0724.title: How a kitchen brand can win a crowded category in thirty days
A0724.alt: A copper saucepan in front of stacked steel and cast iron pans on a rustic wooden shelf.
A0724.ttag: How a kitchen brand can win a crowded category in thirty days | Kwontified
A0724.desc: On a crowded Amazon kitchen page, a new product’s first month sets its rank and reviews. Why launch budgets belong in those weeks, and what to have ready.
A0724.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 3, 2025.
A0724.body:
Type “chef knife” into Amazon and the first screen is a wall of established products, many carrying thousands of reviews and ranked on long sales histories. A new knife, however well made, arrives with neither. For a kitchen brand launching into that page, the first weeks largely decide the product’s course, because Amazon’s ranking reflects recent and past sales, reviews accumulate on early buyers, and rivals respond to any newcomer that gains ground.

The launch plan should follow that calendar. Stock, advertising and review-building concentrated into the first month do the work; the same effort spread evenly over a quarter arrives after the race has been run.

How a kitchen brand’s launch on Amazon gains or loses ground

Amazon’s ranking rewards early momentum. Its Best Sellers Rank is based on a product’s sales, updated hourly and reflecting both recent and historical sales, Helium 10 explained. A product that sells steadily from its first days climbs and stays visible, while one that starts slowly has to overcome its own weak history.

Getting a new product into Amazon’s warehouses has become cheaper. Amazon waived inbound placement fees on up to 100 units for new products shipped between December 1, 2024 and March 31, 2025, Helium 10 reported. Programs like that lower the cost of stocking a launch quickly.

Being seen on the page, meanwhile, costs more each year. In the fourth quarter of 2024, Amazon’s reported results showed ad revenue up 18%, a faster pace than its online stores. In crowded categories, a newcomer pays more for each click than it would have a few years ago.

Why the first month decides so much

Kitchen categories, from knives to small appliances, are crowded with established products carrying thousands of reviews. Shoppers choose among the first few results, and those results favor products with proven sales and strong ratings. A department store buyer can put a new knife on an end cap the day it arrives. On Amazon nobody hands out the end cap; the page gives it to whatever already has sales and ratings behind it.

A new product starts with neither of those, and its early weeks are the only time it can build both at once. Sales lift its rank, the rank brings more visibility, and the visibility brings more sales. Early buyers leave the first reviews, which reassure the buyers who come after them.

Established rivals notice quickly. When a newcomer starts taking sales, established brands often respond with deals or higher bids. A newcomer that has already built rank and reviews by then is much harder to push back, and one without them may need to spend heavily just to stay visible.

One chef’s knife, two launch plans

Take a brand launching a premium chef’s knife into a category where the top results carry thousands of reviews. Say its first plan spreads a modest advertising budget evenly over three months and ships stock in small batches. After a month, the knife has few sales, few reviews and a rank that keeps it off the first page.

Now give the same knife a concentrated plan. The brand ships enough stock for the full first month in one go, so it never runs out. It spends most of its first-quarter advertising budget in the first four weeks, aimed at a small set of specific searches rather than the most competitive broad terms. It also works to earn early reviews through Amazon’s approved programs and a clear product page.

By the end of the month, the knife ranks on the first page for its specific searches, carries enough reviews to compete, and can reduce advertising while keeping sales. The total budget is unchanged; only its timing moved.

Planning the first thirty days of a launch

Stock and money come first, because running out early stalls rank and wastes the advertising that brought shoppers to the page. Enough inventory to cover the whole launch period, with no gap, protects everything else. Advertising works best front-loaded, building sales history when it matters most, with a planned taper once rank and reviews hold.

Where to compete matters as much as how much to spend. Broad terms like “chef knife” are dominated by established products, while narrower searches, such as a particular steel or handle style, give a newcomer somewhere to win first.

The page has to be finished before launch day. Images, titles and descriptions that answer shoppers’ questions convert more of the expensive early traffic. Reviews must come from genuine buyers through Amazon’s approved programs; incentives that break Amazon’s rules can cost the product its listing.

The first two weeks show whether the plan is working. Daily sales, conversion rate and search position all move early, and a product that converts poorly even with heavy traffic usually has a page or price problem to fix before more money goes in. The calendar matters too. Launching just before a big sale event means competing with deep discounts from established products, so a launch should come early enough to build rank before the event, or wait until after it.

None of this rescues a product shoppers do not want. A concentrated launch costs more up front and can still fail, which is why demand and price deserve a test before a launch budget is committed.

For a leadership team signing off on a kitchen launch, the useful question is less how large the budget is than how much of it lands in the first four weeks. The next is whether the stock, the page and the review plan are ready to meet it. Lining those pieces up before the first unit ships is how we manage Amazon launches in crowded categories.

A0725.crumb: Pricing through tariffs: what to test…
A0725.title: Pricing through tariffs: what to test before you raise prices
A0725.alt: Three cork-lidded ceramic jars with blank kraft tags beside a brass balance scale on a wooden shelf.
A0725.ttag: Pricing through tariffs: what to test before you raise prices | Kwontified
A0725.desc: A tariff-driven price rise on Amazon also lowers conversion, ad efficiency and rank. How to find each product’s break-even and test before raising prices.
A0725.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 8, 2025.
A0725.body:
When a tariff lands, the reflex is to pass the cost through. On most websites a price increase loses some shoppers and that is the whole effect. On Amazon it is only the start, because lower conversion also raises the advertising cost of each sale and weakens search rank. The tariffs that took effect on April 5 raise landed costs for most imported goods, so the first job is to calculate each product’s break-even sales loss and test a few increases before raising prices across the range.

Where a straight increase would cost too much volume, other levers exist: smaller discounts and different pack sizes raise what a shopper pays without moving the list price.

Why pricing through tariffs is now urgent

Landed costs rose in a matter of days. A 10% baseline tariff on imports from nearly all countries took effect at 12:01 a.m. on April 5, Business Today reported. Higher rates for about 60 countries, including 34% for China, 20% for the European Union and 46% for Vietnam, are due to follow on April 9, according to a Thompson Coburn trade alert.

Chinese goods were already more expensive. A RetailStat analysis puts the tariff on goods from China at 20% from March 4, and the new rates come on top of it.

Shoppers are in a weak position to absorb increases. Retail sales rose just 0.2% in February, after a revised 1.2% decline in January, Greenleaf Trust reported.

Hold the price or raise it: the break-even

Take a product that sells for $30, sells 1,000 units a month and earns $8 per unit after costs and fees. A tariff adds $1.50 to its cost. The brand has two clean options.

OptionPriceMargin per unitWhat it takes to earn the same
Hold the price$30$6.50$6,500 a month at 1,000 units
Raise the price$31.50$8about 813 units a month

Holding the price leaves demand where it was and gives up margin: $6.50 per unit, or $6,500 a month. Raising it to $31.50 keeps the $8 margin, and the increase pays off as long as monthly sales stay above about 813 units, a drop of no more than about 19%.

Each option has a real price. Holding protects conversion, ad efficiency and rank, at a known cost in margin. Raising protects margin, at a cost in volume that is harder to know in advance. On a simple calculation the increase looks safe. The question is whether the simple calculation is right.

Why the real sales loss runs past the simple one

A price increase removes some buyers, so conversion falls. Each click on an ad costs about the same as before, but fewer clicks turn into sales, so the advertising cost of each sale rises. Lower sales also weaken a product’s search rank, which reduces the free traffic it gets. The volume lost to a price increase compounds.

That is why a shopper survey or a single week’s test can understate the damage. If the higher price also raises the advertising cost per sale and costs the product search position, the real sales loss can run past what those methods suggest. The break-even line stays at 813 units; the risk of crossing it is higher than the simple calculation implies.

The numbers lean toward raising, but not everywhere at once. Products with a large cushion between their expected loss and their break-even are the safest place to start, and the full effect, including advertising cost and rank, should be measured on a few products before an increase goes across the range.

What to test before you raise prices

The first test should be small. Raise prices on a handful of products with different characteristics, then watch conversion, advertising cost per sale and search position for two to three weeks. That shows how shoppers in each category respond. The test has to run in ordinary weeks: one held during a sale event or a competitor’s stockout will mislead, and the result should be compared against the same products’ recent history so it reflects the price change rather than outside noise.

Customer loyalty should decide the order. Products with strong reviews and loyal buyers usually tolerate increases better than products competing mainly on price, so they are the natural first candidates. Where the cushion is thin, softer levers protect margin without touching the list price. Reducing the depth or frequency of discounts raises the average price paid, and a larger pack at a better unit price can also hold margin.

Competitors shape the outcome as well. If rivals importing from the same countries raise prices, a brand that holds may gain share; if they hold, a brand that raises alone may lose it. Tracking competitor prices weekly while tariffs settle turns that into a decision rather than a surprise.

Timing and channels matter too. Inventory bought before the new tariffs carries the old cost, so a brand can sell through that stock at current prices and plan increases for when higher-cost inventory arrives, which spreads the change and gives time to see how competitors move. Prices raised on Amazon but not on the brand’s own site or other marketplaces create gaps that hurt the brand’s standing with Amazon. A product priced noticeably higher on Amazon than elsewhere can lose its featured offer, which removes most of its sales. Increases should be planned across channels together.

Vendors face a different version of the problem. Brands selling to Amazon wholesale cannot set the retail price, so their test sits in the cost price negotiation, supported by evidence of the tariff’s effect on each product.

The rule to carry into Monday’s pricing meeting is simple: no product gets a tariff increase until someone can state its break-even sales loss and point to a test that measured conversion, ad cost per sale and rank together. Working through those numbers product by product is how we help brands price through cost changes on Amazon.
