A0727.title: One-to-one campaigns with conversational AI: where to run them
A0727.alt: A smartphone, a wax-sealed envelope, eyeglasses and a mug of dried flowers on a wooden table.
A0727.ttag: One-to-one campaigns with conversational AI: where to run them | Kwontified
A0727.desc: AI influenced 19% of online holiday orders in 2024. Shopping conversations make one-to-one campaigns possible, but brands own only some of them.
A0727.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 10, 2025.
A0727.body:
A shopper opens a chat window and types that she needs a gift for a runner, on a modest budget. In one sentence she has told the seller what personalization used to guess at. That habit of saying what you want, rather than browsing for it, is what makes one-to-one campaigns with conversational AI possible, and during the 2024 holidays AI tools influenced 19% of online orders through recommendations, targeted offers and conversational support.

The catch is who owns those conversations. Many of the most valuable shopping conversations happen inside the platforms, where a brand cannot run a campaign at all. The practical answer is to run one-to-one campaigns where the brand controls the conversation, on its own site and messaging channels, and to shape the platform conversations through the product information it supplies.

How one-to-one campaigns with conversational AI reached scale

The scale arrived in the 2024 holiday season. AI and agents influenced $229 billion, or 19%, of global online orders during the season through product recommendations, targeted offers and conversational customer service, according to Salesforce’s holiday shopping data. Shoppers used AI-powered chat for customer service 42% more than in the 2023 season, the same data showed.

Shoppers also brought AI to their searches. Generative AI chat tools sent 1,300% more visits to retail sites during the season, from a modest base, and seven in ten shoppers who had used such tools said they improved their experience, Adobe reported.

The platforms built assistants of their own. Amazon opened its Rufus assistant to all US customers after it had already fielded tens of millions of questions, Retail Dive reported. On February 26, 2025, Amazon introduced Alexa+, which can complete purchases on a shopper’s behalf, SiliconANGLE reported.

Who owns the shopping conversation

For years, personalization meant inference: showing products based on what similar shoppers bought. A conversation removes much of that guessing, and it changes what a campaign can be. A traditional campaign sends the same message to a segment. A conversational one can answer each shopper’s actual question with a product, an explanation and, where it makes sense, an offer suited to that person.

The opportunity, though, is split down the middle. A shopper asking Rufus or Alexa+ for a recommendation is talking to Amazon, and the brand whose product she ends up buying was never in the room. It cannot run a campaign inside that conversation. It can only influence what the assistant knows about its products.

Where the brand does own the conversation, on its own website, in its customer service chat or in messaging apps, it can do much more. It can remember past purchases, offer a tailored discount or follow up after delivery.

So the decision on the leadership team’s table is an allocation question with two columns. One column is the conversations the brand can own and should build campaigns inside. The other is the conversations it can only inform, where the work is product information rather than messaging. Filing both under one AI budget hides the difference between them.

Where brands can run one-to-one campaigns

The brand’s own site is the natural starting point. An AI assistant there can answer product questions, recommend items based on a shopper’s stated needs and offer help at the moment of hesitation. The questions the customer service team answers most often are where it should begin.

Customer service itself is a selling moment. Salesforce’s figures show shoppers using AI chat for service more than a season earlier, and a shopper asking about an order may welcome a recommendation for a related product. Brands with permission to contact customers can extend the same approach to messaging apps and email, replying to questions or tailoring follow-ups to what each customer has bought and asked.

On the platforms, influence runs through product information. Titles, descriptions and answers that address real shopper questions give assistants what they need to recommend the right product.

Behind every one of these sits an answer library. Conversational tools are only as good as the information behind them, so approved answers on sizing, materials, care, compatibility and policies belong in place before launch, so the assistant responds accurately and consistently. Some conversations, such as complaints, complex orders or sensitive requests, are better handled by people, and clear rules for passing them from the assistant to a member of staff keep that handover smooth.

Trust and voice need the same care. Shoppers notice when an assistant pushes products that do not fit their question, so recommendations should be honest and offers should not feel manipulative. An assistant that sounds generic undoes years of brand building; clear guidance on tone lets a shopper hear the same brand in a chat as on the product page. Privacy is the third guardrail. One-to-one campaigns rely on what a brand knows about each customer, which means collecting only what is needed, explaining how it is used and following the rules in every market the brand sells in.

Measurement works best when the first assistant is small. One that answers a few common questions well is worth more than one that tries to do everything and frustrates shoppers, and the measure is whether conversations lead to purchases and fewer returns, not how many take place. Salesforce noted that online holiday returns rose sharply in 2024. Conversations that help a shopper choose the right size or model the first time can bring returns down, which is one of the clearest ways to show the value.

The question for a CEO to put to the team is which of the brand’s customer conversations it actually owns, and whether the budget follows that answer. Preparing the answer library and product content that both kinds of conversation draw on is what our AI agentic commerce practice does for brands.

A0729.crumb: How Temu uses data, and what it means for…
A0729.title: How Temu uses data, and what it means for brand pricing
A0729.alt: A magnifying glass resting on a wooden tray of sorted toy figures, marbles and trinkets beside orange peels.
A0729.ttag: How Temu uses data, and what it means for brand pricing | Kwontified
A0729.desc: Temu sets prices itself, feeds shopper demand back to factories and favors the cheapest supplier. Why that compresses prices, and how brands should respond.
A0729.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 15, 2025.
A0729.body:
A Temu price can look like a mistake. A kitchen storage set that a brand sells for $30 on Amazon shows up in the Temu app as a close substitute for $12, and the obvious question is who is losing money. The more useful question for a brand is how that price got set. Temu uses shopper data to decide which products to promote and to relay demand to manufacturers, and under its managed model it sets the retail price itself and favors the cheapest supplier for each item.

Put those together and prices in targeted categories move toward the lowest supplier cost. Brands should assume that compression wherever Temu can source a close substitute, compete on what Temu cannot copy, and price any Temu listings with that pressure in mind.

How Temu uses data across its model

Demand flows back to the factories. Temu uses a reverse-manufacturing model that relays customer feedback directly to manufacturers, and it offers free shipping and returns through its parent company PDD Holdings’ network of suppliers and shipping partners, ECDB reported.

Temu also sets the price. Under its fully managed model, merchants agree on a selling price with Temu and ship goods to its warehouse. Temu then sets the consumer price, handles shipping, marketing and customer service, and uses the cheapest supplier, Tech Buzz China reported.

The model is now shifting toward local stock. Marketplace Pulse estimated that local sellers, not Chinese warehouses, shipped about 20% of Temu’s US sales, in figures cited by Reuters. Tariffs and the threat to duty-free parcels had raised the cost of shipping from China.

Why price control turns demand data into lower prices

Temu sees what millions of shoppers click, add to cart and buy. That tells it which products are in demand, and at what prices, almost in real time. It uses the signal to decide which items to promote in its app and passes it back to manufacturers, who can make more of what sells.

On its own, that is just good merchandising. The second half is what moves prices.

Because Temu sets the retail price and chooses among suppliers, demand data becomes pricing power. When several suppliers can make a similar item, Temu can favor the one with the lowest price. Suppliers compete to be chosen and prices drift toward the lowest cost any of them can accept. It behaves like a reverse auction that never closes: each round the lowest offer wins the placement, and each losing supplier has a reason to bid lower next time.

Go back to the storage set. Temu’s data shows strong demand for sets like it, several factories can make a close substitute, and Temu lists the cheapest at $12. Shoppers who see the two side by side, or who arrive at Amazon having seen Temu’s price, now judge the brand’s set against $12. Unless the brand gives them a reason to pay $30, its sales fall.

The pressure is strongest where products are easy to copy and hard to tell apart, and weakest where quality, brand trust, fit or service clearly differ. It also spreads beyond Temu. Shoppers carry prices in their heads, and once a low price for a similar item is common on one platform, it shapes what they expect to pay on others, including Amazon and a brand’s own site. A brand does not have to sell on Temu to feel its pricing.

Where the pressure lands, and how to answer it

The exposure map comes first: the products in the range with close, cheap substitutes, and which of those are already sold on Temu. That is where price pressure lands first. Temu’s app pushes the products its data says are selling, so the items it promotes in a brand’s categories are a running signal of where it expects demand and where the pressure will follow.

The defense is whatever cannot be copied. Proven quality, materials, safety certifications, warranties, sizing accuracy and service are what justify a higher price, and each of them belongs on every product page where a shopper can see it. Matching Temu’s prices on commodity products usually destroys margin. A brand is better off accepting the loss of some price-driven shoppers in those categories and focusing on the ones who value what it offers. Some brands answer with a simpler, cheaper value line under their own name, which can work if it is clearly different from the main range and does not pull buyers down from it.

Brands that sell on Temu face a separate question. Under the managed model, Temu, not the brand, sets the retail price. It pays to understand which selling model a brand is joining, and how much pricing control it keeps, before committing products. Elsewhere, retail partners notice when a brand’s products appear much cheaper on another site, which makes consistent pricing across Amazon, Walmart, Target and the brand’s own site worth protecting even as Temu pushes substitutes lower.

The shift to local stock raises the stakes. As Temu moves toward goods held in US warehouses, delivery gets faster and the gap with Amazon narrows, so Temu is likely to become a more direct competitor on speed as well as price.

Temu’s edge is its view of demand, and brands hold a version of that too: sales, reviews, returns and customer questions across their channels. The working rule is to decide which products to build, defend or drop on that data, and to stop defending on price any product a factory can copy for $12. Mapping that exposure across a catalog is how we help brands hold margin against low-price marketplaces.

A0730.title: Mother’s Day 2025 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards
A0730.alt: A paper-wrapped bouquet of pink and white peonies beside a small twine-tied gift box on a sunlit wooden table.
A0730.ttag: Mother’s Day 2025 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards | Kwontified
A0730.desc: Gift shoppers buy for someone else, against a deadline, and want something meaningful. What Mother’s Day 2025 rewards on marketplaces, and how to prepare.
A0730.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 17, 2025.
A0730.body:
Someone buying a Mother’s Day gift reads a product page like an inspector. She checks the delivery date, studies the photos of what actually arrives in the box and scans the reviews for anyone who bought it as a gift. She is guessing at another person’s taste, against a date that will not move, and whatever she sends will say something about her.

That caution is the whole game for Mother’s Day 2025 on marketplaces, where online was the top place to shop for the holiday in 2024. What the holiday rewards is a brand that makes the gift decision feel safe: delivery before the day, content that helps a giver choose, and products that arrive ready to give.

What Mother’s Day 2025 on marketplaces builds on

The occasion is large enough to deserve its own plan. Consumers planned to spend $33.5 billion on Mother’s Day in 2024, the second-highest total in the survey’s history, and those celebrating planned to spend an average of about $254, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey.

Online shopping led the field. It was the most popular destination for Mother’s Day gifts, cited by 35% of shoppers, ahead of department stores at 32% and specialty stores at 29%, according to the same survey. Meaning mattered more than it used to: more shoppers than in past years wanted gifts that were unique or different, at 48%, or that would create a special memory, at 43%.

The money concentrated in a few categories:

CategoryPlanned Mother’s Day spending, 2024
Jewelry$7 billion
Special outings$5.9 billion
Electronics$3.5 billion
Flowers$3.2 billion

In 2025, Mother’s Day falls on Sunday, May 11.

Why a gift buyer shops differently

A shopper buying for herself knows what she wants and can send it back if it disappoints. A gift buyer is guessing about someone else, and a gift that arrives late or looks cheap reflects on the giver. That makes her cautious in specific ways. She leans on reviews that mention gifting, looks for clear photos of what arrives, checks delivery dates closely and abandons products that cannot arrive in time.

The deadline shapes everything else. Gift demand builds in the weeks before the holiday and peaks in the final days, when delivery promises decide which products still qualify. On a marketplace, a product showing guaranteed delivery before Sunday wins shoppers that a slower one loses, however good it is. In a department store the gift is in the bag at the register; online, the promise on the page is the product until the box arrives.

The wish for something unique pulls the other way. Shoppers want something that feels personal, yet they are buying on platforms built for side-by-side comparison. The brands that do well offer products that stand out from generic options while still being easy to evaluate and trust.

Getting the stock, the page and the budget ready

Stock is the first thing to settle. Gift-friendly products need to sit in Amazon’s and other marketplaces’ warehouses well before the holiday, so they show fast delivery when demand peaks. Brands selling on Walmart, Target and other retailers face the same test on each, because those retailers run Mother’s Day promotions too and gift shoppers compare across them; prices should stay consistent from one to the next.

The page has to show the gift. Images that show the packaging, what is inside and the product in use answer the giver’s first question, and a plain statement of what arrives keeps her from being surprised. Titles and descriptions can say who the product suits and why it makes a thoughtful gift without stuffing in holiday keywords, and answers on sizing and care reduce hesitation. Gift sets, bundles and products that arrive presentable save the giver effort, and gift-wrap or gift-message options should be easy to find.

Search behaves differently in the run-up. Gift shoppers often search by recipient and occasion, such as “gifts for mom”, rather than by product, so the useful step is to check which of those searches already bring a brand sales and include them in the season’s advertising. Spending should rise as the holiday approaches, peak in the final week while delivery is still possible, then fall away once products can no longer arrive in time.

Margin needs protecting in 2025 as well. New tariffs announced in April raise costs for many imported products, which argues against deep Mother’s Day discounts on goods whose costs have just risen and for leaning on gifting value instead.

Reviews and returns deserve daily attention. Gift shoppers read recent reviews carefully, and a run of complaints about damaged packaging or late delivery just before the holiday can cost a product its best weeks. Some gifts will not fit or suit the recipient, and a clear, easy exchange policy reassures the giver at the point of purchase and can turn a potential return into a second sale.

The category is wider than jewelry and flowers. Kitchen, home, fitness and personal care products all become Mother’s Day gifts when presented that way, and a brand’s own reviews and search terms show whether shoppers already buy its products as gifts.

The last opportunity arrives after the day itself. A gift recipient is a potential customer, and clear branding on the packaging and inserts can turn the gift into her first purchase. The signal worth watching afterwards is how many recipients come back as customers, and making sure each marketplace is stocked, priced and presented for the whole gifting season is how we run seasonal events across marketplaces for brands.

A0733.crumb: Live shopping and video on Mercado Libre…
A0733.title: Live shopping and video on Mercado Libre: discovery moves inside
A0733.alt: Market stall piled with colorful woven textiles, baskets, pottery, fruit and flowers, with a phone filming on a tripod.
A0733.ttag: Live shopping and video on Mercado Libre: discovery moves inside | Kwontified
A0733.desc: Mercado Libre added short seller videos, a free streaming service and live commerce tests. Why it is pulling discovery inside, and what brands should do.
A0733.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. Mercado Libre
A0733.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 24, 2025.
A0733.body:
For years the path to a purchase on Mercado Libre could start somewhere else entirely. A shopper in São Paulo or Guadalajara would see a blender or a serum demonstrated in a video on a social app, then open Mercado Libre to search for it and buy. The marketplace collected the sale; the attention had already been spent elsewhere.

Mercado Libre is changing that. It has added short seller videos watched by more than 27 million users, a free ad-supported streaming service and tests of live commerce, and together they pull product discovery inside its own marketplace. For brands selling there, live shopping and video on Mercado Libre now belong in every listing plan, alongside video advertising through Mercado Ads and preparation for live selling as it spreads.

How live shopping and video on Mercado Libre reached the marketplace

Short seller videos were the first piece. Mercado Libre launched Mercado Clips, a section where sellers create and share short videos of their products, in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia. More than 27 million users had watched videos there, for more than 3 million hours, Forbes Colombia reported. The company said the videos help sellers show how products look and work, reducing returns.

A streaming service followed. Mercado Play, a free streaming service supported by advertising rather than subscriptions, was available in seven countries with more than 1,200 titles, and users watched an average of 39 minutes a day, according to the same report.

The company has kept building. In 2024 it continued to scale Mercado Play, which it describes as a new platform for video advertising alongside the other formats available through Mercado Ads, according to its annual report for that year.

Live selling is still in testing. Mercado Libre had begun trials of live commerce, or selling through live broadcasts, in Brazil, a company executive told Forbes Colombia, describing it as something likely to come to Mercado Libre in the future.

Who keeps the attention when discovery moves inside

Shoppers in Latin America watch a great deal of online video, and much product discovery happens there, on apps where a brand or creator shows a product in use. As long as that discovery happened on social apps, Mercado Libre sat at the end of the shopping process, collecting the sale but not the attention.

Each piece of the video push moves something Mercado Libre did not hold back inside its walls. The attention a shopper spends watching now happens on its platform. Videos link directly to listings, so the path from watching to buying is short and the marketplace sees every step of it. Mercado Ads can sell video placements that reach viewers using Mercado Libre’s shopping data, so the advertising money that once paid for discovery elsewhere has somewhere to go on the marketplace itself. And content that keeps users in the app gives Mercado Libre more chances to show them products.

Brands gain something real from the trade: a viewer who can buy in a tap, and a seller video that answers questions before they turn into returns. What they give up is the separate stage where a brand could win attention cheaply off the marketplace and then collect the sale on it. The pattern resembles moves by other large marketplaces, which have built their own version of a new way of shopping inside their walls rather than leaving it to others.

Getting listings, ads and presenters ready

Video on the listing is the first job. Short videos that show a product in use, its size and how it works help shoppers decide and can reduce returns, and the best place to start is the best-selling products and those that draw the most questions or returns. Each market needs its own version.

Shoppers in Brazil watch in Portuguese and shoppers in Mexico in Spanish, with different expectations and references, so video should be produced or adapted for each country rather than reused everywhere. Brands with content made for Instagram or TikTok have a head start, as long as the clips are reformatted, translated where needed and linked to the right listing.

Video advertising deserves a real test. With Mercado Play serving video ads through Mercado Ads, brands can reach shoppers while they watch, and those ads should run alongside product ads and be judged by the sales they add. Mercado Libre’s reporting should show whether listings with video convert better or see fewer returns, and video is worth extending to more products only where it pays.

Live selling needs preparation before it arrives. It suits products that benefit from demonstration, such as beauty, kitchen and electronics, and the useful work now is deciding which products fit and who would present them. Local creators already know how to present products to audiences in each market and can make videos for Mercado Clips or host live sessions, as long as the content links back to the brand’s listings. Big sale events in Latin America, such as Hot Sale in Mexico and Black Friday across the region, draw heavy traffic, and video and live sessions prepared for those periods reach shoppers when they are most ready to buy.

Two disciplines hold it together. Videos should show products as they are, because exaggeration leads to disappointment and returns that undo the benefit. And search still matters: many shoppers search before buying, so titles and descriptions should match what the video shows, letting a viewer find and recognize the product.

The signal worth watching through 2025 is when live selling moves from tests in Brazil to the other markets, because that is the moment a brand’s presenters and products need to be ready. Building that video and live plan market by market is how we run Mercado Libre for brands across Latin America.

A0735.title: Walmart Connect self-serve display: who competes now, and how
A0735.alt: Silver laptop and mug on a wooden ledge on a sunny rooftop, facing a large blank billboard under a clear sky.
A0735.ttag: Walmart Connect self-serve display: who competes now, and how | Kwontified
A0735.desc: Walmart opened onsite display to sellers of all sizes through self-serve auctions. Why that changes who competes for display, and how brands should run it.
A0735.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 1, 2025.
A0735.body:
Display advertising on Walmart used to be a conversation. A large supplier described its goals to Walmart’s team, a package was negotiated, and Walmart planned and placed the ads. The marketplace seller running a handful of search campaigns was not part of that conversation at all.

Since April 2024 that seller can bid for the same onsite placements. Walmart moved its onsite display toward self-serve, auction-based buying open to brands and marketplace sellers of all sizes, while seller advertisers kept growing fast. Walmart Connect self-serve display is now a competitive auction that brands run themselves, and it rewards the habits of search: tight audiences, fresh creative and measurement of the sales the ads add.

How Walmart Connect self-serve display opened up

The idea has a long history at Walmart. In February 2021, Walmart announced plans for a display self-serve platform alongside its acquisition of Thunder, an advertising technology company meant to shorten the time between an idea for an ad and the ad going live, according to the company’s announcement.

The opening came in 2024. Walmart said its onsite display business was becoming primarily programmatic and auction-based, with greater access and control, available to brands of all sizes starting in April, in a post by Walmart Connect. Marketplace sellers gained access to onsite display through the self-service platform for the first time, Marketing Dive reported.

Sellers drove much of the growth. Marketplace sellers were Walmart Connect’s fastest-growing advertisers, with their search advertising spending up 63% in 2023 and doubling on the self-serve platform, according to the same Walmart post. In its latest fiscal year, Walmart Connect’s US advertising sales rose 24%, helped by a 50% rise in marketplace sellers running ads, Walmart said in its earnings release.

What changes when display becomes an auction

Self-serve auctions change who takes part and how. Any eligible brand or seller can now bid for display placements, set its own audiences and change campaigns quickly. Display starts to behave like search: a continuous auction in which many advertisers compete for the same shoppers.

The people at the auction change as well. Sellers who learned Walmart advertising through search now extend into display. Large suppliers that once had display largely to themselves face more competitors, and the figures show how quickly they are arriving: seller search spending rose 63% in 2023, and the number of sellers who advertise grew 50% in Walmart’s latest fiscal year. Many of them learned the auction on search first. Because the auction rewards relevance and performance, the advertisers who manage their campaigns closely tend to win the best placements at the best prices, whatever their size.

Control comes with responsibility. A managed campaign has Walmart’s team watching it, and a self-serve campaign succeeds or fails on how well the brand sets its audiences, creative and budgets. Inside a brand, that moves display from the media plan negotiated once a year into the daily work of whoever runs Walmart search, which may be a different team with a different budget line. Walmart still offers managed services for larger campaigns, and brands with complex needs, such as integrated in-store and online programs, may combine self-serve display with managed support.

Running Walmart display the way search is run

Every campaign needs a stated goal before it gets a bid. Display can introduce a brand to new shoppers, remind past buyers or support a product launch, and each of those calls for different audiences and different measures. Walmart can target shoppers based on what they buy, so a few well-defined audiences, such as buyers in a related category, will teach more than budget spread broadly. Brands that know who their best customers are can use that knowledge to choose Walmart audiences that resemble them rather than starting from scratch.

Creative wears out faster in an auction, because ads that shoppers ignore become expensive. Several versions of each display ad, with weak performers replaced quickly, keep costs in check. The product page matters as much as the ad. Every display click lands on a product page, and a page with complete information, strong images and good reviews converts more of that traffic, which also improves performance in the auction.

Measurement has to reach past the click. Display often works earlier in the shopping process than search, so the right comparison is whether exposed shoppers go on to buy against similar shoppers who were not reached. Display can also raise searches for a brand on Walmart, which means search campaigns should be ready to capture the added interest. Placement reports show which spots on Walmart’s site and app bring results, and spending should follow them rather than spreading evenly across every placement.

Costs will move as the auction fills. As more sellers and brands bid for display, costs are likely to rise, so cost per sale is worth tracking over time, with budget shifted if display stops paying back. Walmart’s big events, such as its Deals weeks and the holiday season, bring more shoppers and more advertisers, and display budgets and creative for those periods belong in the plan well in advance. For a brand new to Walmart display, a limited test on a few products and audiences, run for several weeks and scaled only where it works, is safer than a large commitment at once.

The question for a leadership team is who inside the company now owns Walmart display, and whether that team has the creative, the audiences and the measurement to compete in an auction every day. Setting that up and running it alongside Walmart search is how we manage Walmart Connect display for brands.

A0734.title: Amazon’s Q1 2025 results: the auction keeps getting more crowded
A0734.alt: Rows of wooden paddle boards leaning against a dark blue wall behind a rustic table with an auction gavel.
A0734.ttag: Amazon’s Q1 2025 results: the auction keeps getting more crowded | Kwontified
A0734.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 18% in Q1 2025 while online stores grew 5%. Why that means more money chasing each click, and how brands should budget for it.
A0734.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 2, 2025.
A0734.body:
In the first quarter of 2025, the money brands paid Amazon for ads grew faster than the sales those ads compete for: advertising revenue rose 18%, against 5% for online stores and 6% for third-party seller services. When the money spent to win a sale grows faster than the sales, the average cost of winning one goes up.

Read that way, Amazon’s Q1 2025 results carry a budget message for any brand buying its ads. Advertising is set to take a larger share of sales, and efficiency has to be defended campaign by campaign. Tariff-driven price increases that have not yet reached the shelf will add to the pressure.

What Amazon’s Q1 2025 results showed

Advertising led the quarter again. TheWrap reported the quarter’s segment results:

SegmentQ1 2025 revenueGrowth
Advertising services$13.9 billion18% (19% excluding currency effects)
Online stores$57.41 billion5%
Third-party seller services$36.5 billion6%

The outlook for the next quarter was cautious. Amazon expected second-quarter net sales of $159 billion to $164 billion, growth of 7% to 11%. Management said some of its strength reflected stock bought ahead of tariffs and that most sellers had not yet changed their prices, according to the same report.

None of this is a one-quarter story. In the fourth quarter of 2024, Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 18% while its online stores grew about 7%, according to Amazon’s reported results.

More advertising money behind each dollar of sales

Advertisers on Amazon compete for clicks from shoppers. If total advertising spending grows faster than the sales those shoppers make, each dollar of sales attracts more advertising money, and unless ads become more efficient, the average advertiser’s cost of winning a sale rises.

The first-quarter numbers put a size on it. Online stores and third-party seller services together grew about 5.4% by our calculation. Advertising grew 18%. If advertising money grows 18% while the sales it competes for grow 5.4%, advertising per dollar of those sales rises by about 12%.

Take a brand that spends 10% of its Amazon sales on advertising. If its costs moved with the market, and its ads did not become more efficient, it would need to spend about 11.2% of sales a year later to hold the same position.

That figure is an average, not a forecast for any one brand, and it carries real limits. Some of Amazon’s advertising growth comes from new formats, such as video, and from advertisers outside retail, which do not compete for the same sponsored product clicks. The effect is also uneven. Crowded categories with many sellers, such as supplements, beauty and home goods, tend to feel rising costs first, while categories with fewer advertisers may see little change, so a brand’s own cost trend belongs next to its category’s, not just Amazon’s totals. The direction, though, has held for several quarters.

The ratio a budget anchors on

The hard part is psychological. It is tempting to start an annual plan from last year’s advertising-to-sales ratio, because it is the last number that worked and the easiest one to defend in a budget meeting. That anchor quietly assumes the auction stands still. When costs per sale drift upward, a plan anchored on the old ratio does not fail loudly; it loses position slowly, and the shortfall is easy to blame on creative or seasonality. Nobody can say exactly where costs will land in a given category, which is the honest reason to plan for a range and revisit it, instead of holding the 2024 ratio and being surprised.

Efficiency targets set at the start of the year may no longer fit by the second quarter. Reviewing them each quarter against what the market is doing keeps the anchor from setting itself.

Where the money should go as the auction fills

Rising costs make it harder to justify campaigns that mostly capture sales a brand would have made anyway. The first test is which campaigns add sales, starting with ads on the brand’s own name. Amazon Marketing Cloud lets brands with the data and skills see which ads come before purchases across formats and separate campaigns that add sales from those that do not. Waste gets more expensive in a crowded auction too, which makes regular reviews of search terms and placements, and cuts to those that do not convert, worth more than they were a year ago.

Budget should move toward what the auction rewards. Campaigns built around specific, high-converting searches and products with strong reviews tend to win clicks at lower cost. Higher conversion also lowers the cost of each sale from the same clicks, which makes better images, clearer information and stronger reviews the cheapest offset to rising click prices. Amazon’s video and streaming formats give brands more ways to reach shoppers and deserve testing on the same terms as sponsored ads: by the sales they add.

Prices are the next pressure point. Management’s comment that most sellers had not yet raised prices suggests increases are coming as higher-cost stock arrives. When they do, conversion may fall, which raises advertising cost per sale further, so price and advertising changes need to be planned together. Uncertainty about tariffs and shopper demand is high, which argues for plans flexible enough to cut or shift spending quickly if demand weakens.

Walmart’s advertising has also grown quickly, but from a smaller base, and brands selling on several marketplaces can compare costs per sale across them and move budget toward where each dollar works hardest.

The rule for the next budget cycle: plan Amazon advertising on a rising cost per sale, judge it on efficiency rather than spend growth, and rebuild the ratio every quarter instead of inheriting last year’s. Doing that work against each campaign’s real contribution is how we run Amazon advertising for brands as the auction gets more crowded.

A0738.crumb: The end of de minimis for China: what…
A0738.title: The end of de minimis for China: what cross-border sellers pay
A0738.alt: Kraft-paper parcels tied with twine and blank tags beside a brass wax seal stamp on a worn wooden table.
A0738.ttag: The end of de minimis for China: what cross-border sellers pay | Kwontified
A0738.desc: Parcels from China now owe 120% of their value or $100 each. Why that moves cross-border sellers into US warehouses and into the same search results as brands.
A0738.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 6, 2025.
A0738.body:
Take an item that sells for $15 and costs its seller $5 at the factory. Until May 2, a shopper’s order for it could travel by mail from China to a US doorstep without paying any duty. Now that one parcel owes $18, which is 120% of its $15 value, or a flat $100 per package. Brought in by the container load instead, the same item pays its tariff on the $5 factory value, however high that tariff rate is.

That gap decides where cross-border sellers keep their stock. Shipping single orders from China has become far more expensive than importing in bulk, so the sellers who built a business on mailed parcels will move inventory into US warehouses. Brands should expect those rivals back with higher prices and faster delivery, competing directly on Amazon and Walmart instead of from a separate low-price channel.

What the end of de minimis for China changed on May 2

The exemption closed for goods from China and Hong Kong on May 2. From 12:01 a.m. Eastern time that day, goods from either place valued at $800 or less stopped qualifying for duty-free entry, Barnes Richardson reported, describing the customs notice that put the change into effect.

The parcel charges are steep. Postal shipments that would have qualified face a duty of 120% of the package’s value or a flat $100 per package, and the flat amount rises to $200 on June 1, according to the same report.

The volume at stake is large. Before the change, more than four million parcels a day came into the United States under the exemption, and more than 30% of that flow belonged to two companies, Shein and Temu, ABC reported.

A duty on every parcel against a tariff on every container

The two charges fall on different numbers. A duty on each parcel hits every order separately, at roughly the price the shopper paid. A tariff on goods imported in bulk is paid once per shipment, on what the seller paid the factory, which is usually far below the retail price.

Run the opening item through both routes. Mailed one at a time, it carries $18 of duty on a $15 sale before the seller has paid for postage. Shipped in bulk, the tariff is a percentage of $5. For most low-cost goods, sending individual parcels from China stops making sense, and importing in bulk to hold stock in US warehouses becomes the cheaper route even after tariffs.

The flat option does not rescue the parcel model either. At $100 per package, and $200 from June 1, the flat duty is many times the price of most low-cost items. Sellers will pick whichever charge is lower, but neither leaves room for very cheap goods shipped one order at a time.

Moving to bulk changes the seller as well as the route. Its costs rise, because it now pays tariffs and US warehousing. Its delivery gets faster, because the stock already sits in the country. And it moves under the same rules and into the same channels that domestic sellers use, which is where brands meet it.

Cheap rivals come back pricier, faster and closer

Prices in crowded categories are likely to climb. A seller paying tariffs and warehouse fees cannot match the price it charged when a parcel crossed the border duty-free, so in categories full of very low-priced listings the floor should move up.

Speed stops being a brand’s advantage. Goods held in US warehouses arrive in days, not weeks, and a brand that counted on faster delivery to beat cross-border listings should not count on that lasting.

The competition moves onto the same shelf. Sellers holding US stock can use the same fulfillment programs as domestic brands, and some will appear in the same search results on Amazon and Walmart rather than on separate low-price platforms. The platforms themselves were already adjusting: by Marketplace Pulse’s estimate, about 20% of Temu’s US sales shipped from local sellers, a figure cited by Reuters. Amazon Haul, which depends on low-cost goods, may also see its prices change.

Their product ranges should narrow too. Importing in bulk means paying for stock before it sells. Cross-border sellers that tested thousands of items cheaply, shipping only what found a buyer, will likely carry fewer products and concentrate on proven sellers. In some categories that means fewer rivals, each of them stronger.

Where brands gain room, and where they are exposed

The rebuild opens a window. While cross-border rivals rework their supply chains and their prices rise, brands have a chance to win back shoppers, and the reviews and repeat purchases earned in that period are what keep those shoppers once rivals settle. A brand that discounted to stay near very cheap listings may also find room to recover margin as those rivals’ costs go up.

Some brands carry the same exposure. A brand that ships orders straight from China to customers, through its own site for example, owes the same parcel duties, and should work out the new cost of each order before deciding whether to import in bulk instead.

The rates are not settled. Duty rates on parcels from China changed several times in April, and further changes are possible, so rates deserve a fresh check before any large stock or pricing decision. The change also covers only China and Hong Kong. Cross-border sellers in other countries can still ship parcels in without duty for now, and some may move their sourcing there, which means some listings will move rather than disappear.

A rule for reading your category: when the duty falls on each parcel instead of each container, treat the cheap seller as a future US-stocked rival with a higher price and a faster promise. Plan your pricing against that seller, not the old one. Watching how those rivals reprice and restock across Amazon and Walmart is part of how we run marketplace channels for brands.

A0739.title: The organization video commerce requires, and how to build it
A0739.alt: Home photo studio in a blue room with two softbox lights, a linen backdrop and ceramic vases on a trestle table.
A0739.ttag: The organization video commerce requires, and how to build it | Kwontified
A0739.desc: Video commerce turns content, selling and fulfillment into one moment. Why it needs its own organization, and how brands can build one without a big team.
A0739.kicker: Article. Creative and conversion. All channels
A0739.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 8, 2025.
A0739.body:
On Black Friday 2024, more than 30,000 live streams ran on TikTok Shop, and one beauty brand made $1 million within two hours of going live, Benzinga reported. Picture what those two hours asked of the brand behind them. It needed someone on camera who knew the product cold and an offer approved in advance. It also needed stock that did not run out halfway through, and a service team answering questions while the stream was still live.

Most brands are not organized to deliver that combination, because their departments were built to work one after another. Video commerce asks them to work at once. The brands that win there run it as a single operation, with one owner, a steady flow of content, reliable presenters and creators, and operations that can respond within hours. A campaign handed to the social media team will not get them there.

Why the organization video commerce requires looks different

The sales moments are sharp. Over the same Black Friday 2024, US sales on TikTok Shop more than tripled to over $100 million, Bloomberg reported. Spikes of that size do not wait for a monthly marketing calendar to catch up.

The operations sit with the brand. On TikTok Shop, merchants often ship orders themselves, at times through third parties or through fulfillment services run by TikTok, Reuters reported. So the warehouse and the service desk are part of the channel’s performance in a way they rarely are when a retailer ships the order.

And the format is spreading beyond social apps. Mercado Libre’s short seller videos, Mercado Clips, had been watched by more than 27 million users, Forbes Colombia reported. Video is becoming part of how products are sold on marketplaces, as well as how they are advertised.

Departments built for sequence meet a channel that runs all at once

In traditional e-commerce, marketing builds demand over weeks and operations fulfill it at a steady pace. Teams can hand work along a line: the brand team signs off the creative, e-commerce loads the listing, supply chain plans the stock, and customer service hears about the launch when the first emails arrive. Each department keeps its own calendar, and the sequence holds because demand arrives slowly enough for it to.

Video compresses that line into a single moment. A live stream or a clip that catches on creates demand within hours, and the content, the offer, the stock and the customer service all have to be ready together. Shoppers buying through video act on impulse and expect fast delivery and quick answers, so a stockout or a slow reply during a spike loses sales that do not come back later. The brand that runs those functions as separate departments, each waiting on the others, misses the moment.

The skills differ too. A video that sells needs quick turnaround, comfort on camera and a direct way of explaining the product, which is a different craft from producing a brand advertisement, and few traditional marketing teams have all of it in place. The content also never stops. Video platforms reward a steady flow of new posts, and a brand that produces a burst for a launch and then goes quiet loses visibility quickly.

The decision on the table is who owns it

The question leadership teams are actually weighing is whether video commerce belongs inside an existing department or needs an owner of its own. Handing it to social media keeps the org chart tidy, but the social team rarely controls the offer, the stock or the service queue. Handing it to e-commerce puts it next to the listings, but far from the creators. Either way, each department ends up waiting for the others during the hours that matter.

The brands that move fastest give one person responsibility for video commerce results across content, offers, stock and service, with the authority to make quick calls. That owner also needs a single budget. Video commerce spending mixes production, creator fees, platform commissions and advertising, and when those sit in four departmental budgets, money cannot move to whatever is working while it is still working.

Around the owner, the organization is mostly about rhythm and people. A steady weekly output of videos, mixing product demonstrations, answers to common questions and seasonal content, replaces the occasional campaign. Live selling depends on presenters who know the products and can hold an audience, whether they are trained staff, creators or both, and they need to be available on a schedule. Creators bring audiences and credibility, so lasting relationships with a group who fit the brand, on clear terms for pay, content and disclosure, are worth more than one-off posts.

Operations, measurement and the wider team

The warehouse and the service desk have to be on alert. Stock levels, fulfillment capacity and customer service staffing belong in the plan for every live event and big moment, and the brand should know in advance how much it can ship in a day if a video takes off. The people in customer service, the warehouse and finance need to know when those moments are planned and what they mean for their work, and a short briefing before each major live event lets them prepare.

Measurement has to be fast as well. Sales, returns and questions from each video and live session should be tracked within days, so the team can repeat what works and drop what does not. The same discipline applies to the format mix. Short videos build steady visibility while live sessions create spikes, and most brands need both. The right balance depends on the products and the audience, which is a reason to test and adjust rather than copy another brand’s approach.

None of this requires a large team on day one. A small group with clear ownership, a modest weekly production plan and a few trusted creators can learn what works before the brand invests more.

Two risks belong in the plan from the start. Video commerce runs on platforms whose rules and status can change quickly, as TikTok’s uncertain position in the United States has shown. Effort spread across more than one platform, plus customer relationships the brand keeps for itself, protects against a single change wiping out the channel. And many shoppers who discover a product through video still buy it on Amazon or Walmart, so marketplace listings, prices and stock need to be ready for the traffic a video creates.

For a leadership team deciding where video commerce sits, the useful question is which single person would be accountable if a stream sold out in its first hour, and whether that person could have approved the restock. Building that ownership, alongside the shop operations behind it, is how we run TikTok Shop and Instagram Shop for brands.

A0740.crumb: Price strategy in an era of…
A0740.title: Price strategy in an era of contradictions: separate what lasts
A0740.alt: Two plain white mugs with blank kraft tags on a rustic wooden shelf beside dried flowers and old books.
A0740.ttag: Price strategy in an era of contradictions: separate what lasts | Kwontified
A0740.desc: China tariffs went from 145% to 30% in a month. Why brands should move list prices only for lasting costs and absorb temporary swings with reversible tools.
A0740.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 13, 2025.
A0740.body:
Within a single month, the US tariff on Chinese goods rose to 145% and was then cut to 30% for 90 days. A brand that repriced on the way up now has to decide whether to reprice on the way down, and either answer costs it something. The cheaper course was available all along: keep list prices for cost changes that will last, and absorb the temporary ones with promotions and spending that can be switched off.

That is the core of price strategy in an era of contradictions. Some costs are swinging hard in both directions, others are rising steadily, and shoppers are cautious yet still spending. Each needs a different tool, and the list price is the one tool that is expensive to move twice.

Why price strategy in an era of contradictions is hard

The costs moved in opposite directions. On May 12, the United States agreed to cut its tariff on Chinese goods from 145% to 30%, and China agreed to cut its tariff on US goods from 125% to 10%, for a 90-day pause to continue talks, the AP reported.

Advertising costs, by contrast, only climbed. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 18% in the first quarter while its online stores grew 5%, TheWrap reported, which means more advertising money chasing each sale.

Shoppers, meanwhile, sent mixed signals. Consumer spending growth slowed to 1.8% in the first quarter from 4%, Axios reported. Yet consumers still expected to spend $34.1 billion on Mother’s Day, up from $33.5 billion a year earlier, the National Retail Federation said.

A list price is an anchor, and anchors are expensive to move twice

Shoppers remember a list price and compare against it. Marketplaces show price history, judge discounts against recent prices and use price when deciding which offer to feature. A change to the list price ripples through all of those at once.

Raise it and lower it again a few weeks later, and the brand has taught shoppers that its prices move with the news. Lower it and raise it again, and shoppers see an increase that looks like opportunism. Either way, trust and conversion take the hit.

A coupon, a temporary discount or a change in advertising spend works differently. Each can be switched on and off without touching the price shoppers anchor on.

Take a brand that, facing a 145% tariff on its Chinese-made products in April, raised list prices by 15%. A month later the rate falls to 30% for 90 days. Cutting prices back now reads as a correction, and keeping them high risks losing shoppers to rivals who held their prices. Had the brand absorbed the April spike by trimming promotions and running leaner advertising, it could simply restore both now, with its list price untouched.

The trade-off between repricing and absorbing

Both sides of the choice are real. Absorbing a cost through fewer promotions and lighter advertising protects the anchor. It also gives up sales and visibility while the cost lasts, and no brand can absorb a durable increase forever. Repricing protects margin at once. Every reversal, though, spends some of the trust the list price carries.

The numbers in this market lean toward caution with list prices: a rate that moved from 145% to 30% within a month, and is set for only 90 days, is a poor basis for a price shoppers will remember.

The lean changes with the cost. Sorting each change by how long it is likely to last points to the tool:

Cost changeLikely to last?Tool
Supplier price increases, wage costs, permanent duty changesUsuallyA measured list price increase, tested on a few products first
China tariff rate during the 90-day pauseUncertainDiscount depth, promotion frequency, advertising on low-margin products
The 30% China rate that remains after the cutMore likelyA modest list price change on affected products
Rising advertising costsA lasting trendPricing and margin plans over time, beyond the quarterly budget

The residual rate deserves its own line. Even after the cut, goods from China face a higher tariff than at the start of the year, and that part of the cost is more likely to last.

The 90-day clock also argues for two plans for China-made products: one if the 30% rate holds or falls further, one if it rises again when the pause ends. With both ready, the brand acts on facts when the clock runs out rather than reacting to headlines, and avoids locking in prices that assume the current rate is permanent.

Reading shoppers, rivals and retailers

Cautious shoppers still spend on occasions and on products they value, as the Mother’s Day forecast shows. That argues for protecting prices on products with strong loyalty and using promotions where shoppers are most price-sensitive.

Competitors will not move together. Some will cut prices immediately after the tariff cut, others will hold, and the category’s response over the next few weeks is worth watching before deciding whether to follow.

Vendors face the same problem in a different form. Brands that sell to Amazon or Walmart at negotiated cost prices cannot set retail prices directly, so the same separation belongs in cost negotiations: lasting changes in what they ask retailers to accept, temporary ones handled elsewhere. And brands selling across several marketplaces and their own sites should keep list prices aligned, so a temporary adjustment in one place does not open gaps in another.

The test before any price change: if the cost behind it could reverse within months, use a tool you can switch off, and save the list price for costs you expect to carry for a year or more. Sorting those changes product by product, across every channel a brand sells in, is part of how we run marketplace pricing and operations for brands.

A0742.crumb: The data Target gives its marketplace…
A0742.title: The data Target gives its marketplace partners, and how to use it
A0742.alt: Brass magnifying glass, open blank book and small red wire shopping basket on a worn wooden table.
A0742.ttag: The data Target gives its marketplace partners, and how to use it | Kwontified
A0742.desc: Target shares shopper insight with partners mainly through Roundel’s ads and measurement tools. Why that shapes what brands learn, and how to use it well.
A0742.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 15, 2025.
A0742.body:
Sit with a Target Plus seller that has never bought an ad and look at what it can see: its listings, its orders, its own sales. Then sit with one that runs campaigns through Roundel. The second seller can see which audiences responded, which products sold and whether the sales came from shoppers its ads reached. Both sell on the same marketplace. Only one is learning who Target’s shoppers are.

That gap is by design. Target holds rich first-party data, and it shares insight with partners mainly through Roundel’s advertising, audience and closed-loop measurement tools rather than as raw data. Brands on Target Plus should treat Roundel reporting as a research tool as well as a media channel, and build campaigns partly to learn.

What data Target gives its marketplace partners

The data behind Roundel is large. Target’s retail media business draws on first-party data from the tens of millions of shoppers who visit Target weekly in stores and online, and from its Circle loyalty program of 100 million members, Retail Dive reported. Its self-service tools include Media Studio for buying ads and Kiosk for campaign reporting and measurement, according to the same report.

Access runs through advertising. Roundel Media Studio gives advertisers self-service access to Target Product Ads, with closed-loop sales attribution and access through Target’s Partners Online portal, Tinuiti explained.

The marketplace itself is selective. Target Plus listed more than 2 million items, sold by more than 1,200 sellers, and still admitted sellers by invitation only, Fortune reported. And Target intends to tie the pieces closer together: in March 2025 it said it planned to double Roundel by 2030 and to integrate it more closely with Target Plus and Target Circle, Retail TouchPoints reported.

Why Target shares insight through its media business

Read Target as an institution and the pattern makes sense. Retailers treat their shopper data as one of their most valuable assets. Handing it over as raw data puts shopper privacy at risk and gives away the advantage the data creates. Sharing insight through advertising and measurement lets the retailer keep control while still giving partners something they can use, and it ties that insight to the part of the business Target is working to grow.

That choice shapes what each brand learns. A brand advertising through Roundel builds a picture of Target’s shoppers over time: who buys its category, what else they buy, how they respond to offers. A brand that treats Roundel only as a cost center never sees that picture, and one that does not advertise at all sees mainly its own orders.

The two halves of a seller’s Target business also sit apart. Listings and orders are managed through Target’s partner tools, advertising through Roundel, and the richer view of shoppers lives on the advertising side. Closed-loop measurement is the most valuable part of it. Because Target can connect ads to purchases in its own stores and online, a brand can see whether its advertising led to sales instead of guessing, which is rare across advertising channels and worth using deliberately.

Turning Roundel into a research tool

The habit that changes the most is deciding, before each campaign, what the brand wants to learn: which shopper groups respond, which products draw new customers, or how a promotion changes sales. A campaign designed around one of those questions answers it; a campaign designed only to spend its budget answers none.

Audiences are the natural place to start testing. Roundel’s audiences draw on Target Circle data, and comparing a few of them side by side shows which shoppers are most valuable to a particular brand at Target. The reporting rewards a careful reader, too. Beyond immediate sales, it is worth looking at new-to-brand customers, repeat purchases and halo sales of other products wherever the reporting shows them. The new-to-brand share deserves particular attention, because Target’s audience tends to differ from Amazon’s and Walmart’s, and a high share suggests Target is reaching shoppers the brand does not reach elsewhere.

The marketplace data belongs in the same analysis. Combining Roundel results with Target Plus order data shows which products and prices work best for Target’s shoppers, and timing adds another layer. Shoppers behave differently around back-to-school, Target Circle Week and the holidays, so comparing results across those periods tells a brand when its products sell best at Target, not just whether they sell.

What a brand learns at Target can travel. The findings can inform product ranges, pricing and creative on other channels, especially for shoppers who move between several retailers.

Budgets, records and the limits of what Target shares

Learning needs its own line in the budget. Some spending should go toward tests whose main purpose is insight, and a small, well-designed test that shows which audiences respond can guide much larger spending later. Roundel also offers managed support alongside its self-service tools, and brands with complex questions can ask their Roundel contacts for deeper analysis, especially before major seasons.

Keeping a record matters as much as running the test. Lessons from one campaign are easy to lose by the next season, and a simple log of what each test showed lets a brand’s understanding of Target’s shoppers build year after year instead of starting over.

The limits matter as well. Target’s data is shared under its rules, and brands should use the insights within those rules and not expect access to individual shopper information. Expectations about scale should stay realistic too: Target Plus is invitation-only and smaller than the Amazon and Walmart marketplaces, so the data is valuable while the sales volume is different, and budgets should reflect both.

The question worth asking after every Roundel campaign is what the brand now knows about Target’s shoppers that it did not know before, and where that answer is written down. Designing campaigns that sell on Target Plus and answer that question is how we run Target Plus and Roundel for brands.

A0744.title: Planning promotions on Walmart without destroying margin
A0744.alt: Wooden shop shelves against a blue wall with tagged jars, stoneware bottles, folded linens and a brass scale.
A0744.ttag: Planning promotions on Walmart without destroying margin | Kwontified
A0744.desc: On Walmart, a deep discount on any channel can become the price your normal Walmart price is judged against. How to plan promotions that sell and keep margin.
A0744.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 20, 2025.
A0744.body:
A $40 product that earns $14 a unit after costs and fees goes on promotion at 25% off. The price drops by $10, the margin by the same $10, and each sale now earns $4. To bring home the same total margin, the promotion has to sell 3.5 times as many units as the brand would have sold at full price. Few promotions do.

On Walmart that arithmetic is only half the bill. Walmart’s pricing rules compare a seller’s price with prices offered now or in the weeks before, on Walmart and elsewhere, so a deep discount on any channel can leave the normal Walmart price looking too high once the promotion ends. Promotions on Walmart work best shallow and short, coordinated across every channel, and after advertising and visibility have been tried first.

Why promotions on Walmart need a plan now

Walmart is growing fast as a place to sell and to advertise. Its US e-commerce sales rose 21% in the first quarter, and Walmart Connect advertising in the US grew 31%, Walmart said in its earnings release.

Costs are under pressure at the same time. Tariffs on goods from China were cut to 30% from 145% for 90 days, the AP reported, but remain far above where they started the year. With margins on many products already thinner, a discount that was affordable a year ago may not be now.

Walmart also polices its marketplace prices. Its seller guidance explains that offers priced far above prices offered for the same item, now or in the weeks before, on Walmart or on competing sites, can be unpublished. Offers priced somewhat higher can lose their Add to Cart button.

The low price stays on the record after the promotion ends

The discount is the cost everyone sees: each promoted sale earns less, which the opening example puts at $10 a unit. The cost that hides is the record. A promotional price becomes part of the price history that Walmart, shoppers and rival sellers compare against.

On Walmart, the pricing rules make that hidden cost sharper. If a brand runs a deep discount on its own site or on another marketplace, that low price can become the benchmark its normal Walmart price is judged against. When the promotion ends, the normal price may look too high and the listing can lose visibility, which turns a short sale into a longer slump.

Brands that also sell through Walmart’s own buying team carry one more exposure. Deep marketplace discounts can complicate cost conversations with a retailer that watches market prices closely.

Put together, these explain why deep promotions on Walmart so often disappoint. The sales lift shows up in the report, while the lost margin and the pricing aftermath do not.

It is easy to see why the deep discount keeps winning the planning meeting. The lift is visible and easy to chart, and it answers the plainest question in the room, which is whether sales went up. The margin given away is spread across every unit sold, and the benchmark problem shows up afterward, as a listing that struggles at its normal price, when the promotion is no longer the obvious suspect. A plan that judges promotions on margin and on the listing’s health afterward, instead of on the lift alone, corrects for both.

Setting the depth and the length

The break-even comes before any other decision. For each product, work out how many extra units a given discount must generate to match the margin of selling at full price, as in the opening example. If the answer looks unrealistic, the promotion is too deep. Smaller discounts lose less margin per unit and leave a less damaging benchmark behind, so modest depths deserve a test before deeper ones.

Length matters for the same reason. A short promotion tied to a clear moment, such as a seasonal event, limits the time a low price sits in the record. Walmart runs its own sale events during the year, and deciding in advance which products to include and at what depth beats joining every event by default.

Product choice decides whether the margin comes back. Promotions work best on products where a lower price brings in new buyers who return at full price, and worst on products bought by loyal customers who would have paid full price anyway. That makes new buyers the measure to watch: a promotion that mostly sells to existing customers at a lower price loses money, so track how many promotion buyers are new and whether they come back at full price later.

Coordinating the price everywhere it shows

Because Walmart’s rules look across the market, the plan has to as well. A deep promotion on a brand’s own site or another marketplace can affect its Walmart listing, so promotions on all channels belong in one plan instead of one per team. Knowing how the brand’s prices compare with rivals’ before and after each promotion closes the loop.

Visibility comes before discounting. Walmart’s advertising and onsite placements can raise sales without changing the price, and advertising support is worth testing before reaching for a cut. Bundles and gifts with purchase work the same way, adding value at the same price so the visible price of the main product stays put.

Stock has to be ready. A promotion that sells out early wastes advertising and can hurt the listing’s standing, so stock levels at Walmart’s warehouses or the brand’s own deserve a check before any discount starts. Afterward, the listing needs one more look: whether it stays visible at the normal price, and how quickly sales recover. A promotion that leaves the listing struggling cost more than it seemed.

The test before any Walmart promotion: if the break-even lift looks out of reach, or the discount would set a benchmark lower than the normal price can live with, cut the depth or skip the discount and buy visibility instead. Running that math for each listing, with every channel’s prices in view, is how we plan Walmart promotions for brands that need the margin back.

A0745.title: Health and household shopper psychology: refill or research
A0745.alt: White liquid pouring from a refill pouch into a glass bottle on green tiles, beside a magnifying glass and frosted bottle.
A0745.ttag: Health and household shopper psychology: refill or research | Kwontified
A0745.desc: Health and household shoppers either refill on autopilot or research hard before trying something new. Why the split matters, and how to sell to both of them.
A0745.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 22, 2025.
A0745.body:
Watch someone reorder paper towels on Amazon and the whole decision takes seconds: the same brand, the same pack, a tap on the reorder button. Watch the same person consider a new supplement and they read the ingredient list, scroll through reviews, check the questions section and may leave and come back before buying. Both purchases sit in the same health and household category. They are made by what amounts to two different shoppers.

That split is the most useful thing to understand about health and household shopper psychology. One shopper refills familiar products on price and convenience; the other researches carefully before trusting something new. Brands that run one strategy across the whole category serve both of them poorly, and the ones that run separate playbooks for refill and discovery serve each on its own terms.

Health and household shopper psychology in a cautious year

Essentials are carrying a large share of online growth. In the first quarter, everyday essentials outgrew the rest of Amazon’s business by more than two to one. They also accounted for one out of every three units sold on Amazon in the United States, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy said, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Walmart saw the same pattern. Its US comparable sales grew 4.5%, with strong growth in health and wellness and in grocery, Walmart said in its first-quarter earnings release.

All of this happened against a cautious backdrop. Growth in consumer spending eased from 4% at the end of 2024 to 1.8% in the first quarter, Axios reported. When budgets tighten, shoppers protect necessities and cut elsewhere, which puts this category’s two buying modes under pressure from opposite sides.

One aisle, two shoppers

Much of health and household is bought again and again: detergent, paper towels, toothpaste, the vitamins a shopper already trusts. For these, the decision is made once. After that, the shopper wants the same product at a fair price, delivered without effort, and resents having to think about it.

The same aisle also holds products shoppers think hard about, such as a new supplement, a skin treatment or a cleaning product for a sensitive household. Those get researched. Shoppers read ingredients, compare reviews and look for signs of safety and credibility before they try something new, and they resent being rushed.

Caution sharpens both habits. Refill shoppers become more sensitive to price on the products they buy most often, and some switch to cheaper options or store brands. Meanwhile, researching shoppers become more reluctant to experiment, so a new product needs an even stronger reason to be tried.

Marketplaces already serve both modes, in different places on the page:

Refill shopperResearching shopper
WantsSpeed, reliability, a fair and steady priceInformation, reassurance, proof of safety
Served bySubscriptions, reorder buttons, saved listsSearch, reviews, product detail, questions and answers
Lost byA stockout or a price jumpA thin page or an unanswered doubt
Measured byRepeat purchase and subscription retentionNew-to-brand customers and conversion on new products

A brand’s products also move between the two columns. A new product starts in research mode, and once a shopper trusts it, it moves into refill mode. The business is built on that move: the first purchase costs the most to win, and the repeat purchases pay for it.

Running a refill playbook and a discovery playbook

Sorting the range comes first. Repeat purchase rates, subscription share and search behavior show which products are mostly refilled and which are mostly researched, and the two lists deserve different plans.

For refill products, the job is to make reordering effortless and hard to interrupt. That means encouraging subscriptions where marketplaces offer them, keeping stock reliable and pricing consistently, because a stockout sends a loyal refiller to a rival who may keep them. Competitors advertise on a brand’s own product pages and search terms, so the best-selling refill products need defending with advertising on the brand name and on those pages, especially in crowded categories.

Refill shoppers also notice price changes on what they buy often. With tariffs raising some costs, increases on high-frequency refill products carry more risk than increases on lower-frequency items, which are the safer place to move first.

For researched products, the job is earning trust. Clear ingredient information, credible claims, strong images and answers to common questions do most of that work, and reviews from verified buyers matter most. Advertising should reach shoppers searching for a problem or a need, not only the brand name. Health products also face rules on what they can claim, and pages and ads that stay within those rules protect the listing, because a removed listing loses both kinds of shopper at once.

The move from trial to habit is where the two playbooks meet. Smaller trial sizes, bundles with known products or a modest first-purchase incentive lower the risk of trying something new, and the second purchase, often the hardest, deserves its own push. The refill moment works in the other direction too: a shopper reordering a trusted product is a good audience for a related one, reached through bundles, links on product pages or advertising on the brand’s own refill pages.

Seasons add a rhythm to both. Some needs rise at predictable times, such as cold and allergy seasons or back-to-school, and stock and advertising prepared for those periods meet researching shoppers when they are most active.

Two scorecards instead of one average

The last change is in the reporting. Refill success shows up in repeat purchase and subscription retention; discovery success shows up in new-to-brand customers and conversion on new products. A single blended number for the category hides both.

A useful question for the next category review is which of the brand’s products sit in each column, and whether each one is being managed, measured and priced for the shopper it actually has. Splitting a range that way, then managing each half on Amazon and Walmart, is how we run health and household brands’ marketplace channels.
