A0746.title: Structuring creator partnerships for sales: pay for what you want
A0746.alt: Phone on a ring light beside a brass balance scale weighing coins against an amber dropper bottle on a wooden table.
A0746.ttag: Structuring creator partnerships for sales: pay for what you want | Kwontified
A0746.desc: Flat fees buy reach and commissions buy sales. Why the way brands pay creators shapes what creators deliver, and how to structure partnerships that sell.
A0746.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 27, 2025.
A0746.body:
A creator quotes $1,000 for a video about a $40 product that earns the brand $15 a unit. The alternative is a 15% commission, $6 on every sale. If the video goes on to sell 500 units, the commission costs $3,000, far more than the flat fee. The commission still looks like the worse deal right up until you ask how many videos sell 500 units.

The flat fee buys content whether it sells or not; the commission buys only sales. That difference in what the brand pays for changes what the creator delivers, and it is why brands chasing sales should lead with commissions, add flat fees only for creators with a record of converting, and measure results creator by creator.

The tools for structuring creator partnerships for sales now sit inside marketplaces

Brands no longer have to build commission deals by hand. Amazon’s Creator Connections program lets brands set up campaigns that creators in Amazon’s affiliate and influencer programs can join, setting a budget, a commission rate and the products to promote, Stack Influence explained. Creators can also post rate cards showing what they charge for content or the minimum commission they accept, according to the same explanation.

Live selling showed how much a creator can move. TikTok Shop hosted more than 30,000 live streams over Black Friday 2024, and a single beauty brand took in $1 million in the first two hours after its stream started, according to Benzinga.

A creator does more of what the payment rewards

A flat fee pays for a post or a video. The creator earns the same whether the content sells one unit or a thousand, so the sensible thing for the creator to make is content their audience enjoys, which may or may not lead to purchases. Nothing about that is cynical. It is what the contract asks for.

A commission pays only when shoppers buy through the creator’s link. The incentive moves to products that convert and to content that drives purchases, and creators paid this way tend to choose products carefully, because their time pays off only if shoppers buy.

Run the opening numbers both ways. To recover a $1,000 flat fee at $15 of margin a unit, the video has to sell about 67 units before the brand earns anything. At a 15% commission, the brand pays $6 a sale and pays nothing when nothing sells. If the video sells 30 units, the flat fee loses money, while the commission costs $180 and the brand keeps the rest of its margin. If it sells 500, the flat fee was a bargain and the commission costs $3,000.

That is why the arrangement that costs more in the best case is the safer one to start with. The commission’s worst case is a small bill on a small result. The flat fee’s worst case is the whole fee on no result, and nobody knows in advance which videos will be the 500-unit ones. Flat fees pay off with creators who convert reliably, which is something a brand can only know after it has seen them sell.

Tracking windows bend the arithmetic a little. Commission programs credit sales only within a set period after a shopper clicks the creator’s link, so content that inspires a purchase days later may not be credited. That matters when judging creators whose audiences take time to decide.

Commissions first, flat fees earned

Commission programs, Amazon’s included, let a brand pay only for results. The rate has to be high enough to interest creators and low enough to leave margin after fees and costs. Finding that point means starting at a rate that keeps a healthy margin, watching how many creators join and how they perform, and adjusting. Too low a rate attracts no one; too high a rate gives away margin.

Product choice follows from the incentive. Creators paid on commission favor products that convert well, so the strongest products, with good reviews and clear benefits, belong in the program. Slow sellers that a brand hopes creators will rescue do not.

Flat fees become sensible once a creator has shown they drive sales. A hybrid, a modest flat fee plus a commission, shares the risk between the brand and the creator. Discount codes and creator-exclusive offers can lift conversion, but they cut margin too, and any discount belongs in the break-even calculation alongside the fee.

Measuring creators one at a time

Campaign totals hide which creators work. Tracking sales, conversion and returns for each creator shows who is worth keeping, and the same view catches a quieter problem: some affiliates target shoppers already searching for the brand by name, earning commissions on sales the brand would have made anyway. Creators who bring new shoppers deserve the preference.

Over time, the measurement also shows which content lasts. Some keeps selling for months and some fades in days, and noting which formats and creators produce lasting results is how a brand builds a smaller group of long-term partners. Creators who know a brand’s products well make more convincing content, and that group often outperforms many one-time posts.

The operating basics sit around all of this. Every creator needs a clear brief covering the product’s key benefits, which claims are allowed and what disclosure is required, because the brand remains responsible for claims made about its products. Creators must make clear when content is paid or rewarded, so disclosure belongs in every agreement, with checks that creators follow it. And because a creator’s video can drive a sudden spike, the products creators will feature need enough stock to meet demand.

A practical test for any creator deal: if the brand cannot say how many units the content must sell to cover its cost, it is paying for content rather than sales, and the deal should start as a commission. Setting up those programs and the per-creator reporting behind them is how we build creator programs that sell on Amazon and social platforms.

A0748.crumb: Four days instead of two: who decides…
A0748.title: Four days instead of two: who decides Prime Day participation now
A0748.alt: Four navy-striped deck chairs on a sunny terrace beside a pink wall, overlooking a turquoise sea.
A0748.ttag: Four days instead of two: who decides Prime Day participation now | Kwontified
A0748.desc: Prime Day 2025 doubles to four days, and Amazon gives extra placement to deals of 40% or more. Why that moves the decision beyond the marketplace team.
A0748.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 29, 2025.
A0748.body:
With a two-day Prime Day, the plan could live with the marketplace team: pick a handful of deals, send the stock, spend hard for 48 hours, report the results. Finance and operations could sign off at the edges. That arrangement worked because the event was short enough to treat as a burst.

Amazon has now told sellers that Prime Day 2025 will run four days instead of two, and that deals of 40% or more will receive expanded placement. Participation stops being a single marketplace decision and becomes a cross-functional one about margin, stock and the pacing of advertising. Brands should bring finance, operations and advertising into Prime Day decisions while deal depth, stock and budgets can still be set.

What changed in Prime Day participation for 2025

The event itself is doubling in length. Amazon is extending Prime Day to four days in 2025, the longest in its history, according to an internal memo to third-party sellers reported by Modern Retail. The memo told sellers that two days simply was not long enough, and the exact dates had not been disclosed.

Discount depth now buys visibility. Sellers can offer Prime-exclusive Best Deals, Lightning Deals, member coupons and price discounts, and deals of 40% or more will receive expanded placement across Amazon’s site, according to the same report.

The stakes are large. Shoppers spent $14.2 billion online during the two-day Prime Day in 2024, according to Adobe Analytics figures cited in the same report, and independent sellers account for about 60% of sales on Amazon.

A campaign, not a burst

A two-day event let brands choose a few deals, stock up and spend heavily for 48 hours, and the marketplace team could make most of those calls on its own. Four days is a campaign. Stock has to last twice as long, and advertising budgets have to be paced across days instead of spent in a rush. Deals have to be chosen with the longer window in mind, because a deep discount held for four days costs more margin than one held for two.

Shoppers may behave differently too. With four days, they have more time to compare and less pressure to buy on the first day, so demand may spread more evenly, with peaks on the first and last days.

Who gains from the 40% line

Follow the placement and a second decision-maker appears: Amazon. By rewarding deep discounts with more visibility, Amazon effectively decides which deals shoppers see most. A brand that will not go to 40% can still take part, but with less placement, which means the retailer sets the price of attention and the brand pays it in margin.

Amazon’s reasons are not hard to read. Rival retailers have built their own summer sales around Prime Day, and a longer event helps Amazon hold shoppers’ attention for more of that period. For brands, that brings more traffic to compete for, and also more days on which rivals can undercut a deal. The value of the longer event flows first to whoever controls the placement; brands keep their share only if they decide deliberately what the visibility is worth to them.

That makes participation a business decision rather than a marketplace one. Finance has to decide whether deep discounts are affordable, especially with tariffs raising costs. Operations has to decide whether stock can cover four days of demand. Advertising has to decide how to pace spending across a longer event.

Deciding with the whole table

The first change is naming who decides deal depth, stock and budget, and bringing finance and operations in before deal choices are final. Once that group exists, the deal economics become its first agenda item: for each candidate product, the margin at the planned discount, including any deal fees, and the sales lift needed to make it worthwhile. Products that cannot afford a 40% discount are candidates for smaller deals or none.

Stock is the operations question. It has to arrive at Amazon’s warehouses in time and cover four days, which means planning for higher demand than the 2024 two-day event while avoiding excess that ties up cash afterward. Advertising is the pacing question: budgets for each day, with room to shift spending toward the days and products that perform best, and a build-up in the days before the event. Products not on deal still need visibility, and full-price items can benefit from the traffic the event brings. Because a longer event means shoppers may see the same ads many times, several creative versions, refreshed during the event, keep fatigue down.

The decision also reaches beyond Amazon. Walmart and Target often run competing events around the same time, and pricing across channels has to be settled so a deep Amazon deal does not create problems elsewhere. Some products should sit out altogether: for items with thin margins or loyal buyers who pay full price, advertising without a deal may be the better choice.

The weeks on either side of the event need a plan as well. Shoppers often research and save items before a big event, so stronger product pages, more reviews and wider awareness put a brand on their lists before deals go live. Afterward, shoppers who discovered the brand during Prime Day can become repeat buyers through follow-up promotions, bundles or advertising aimed at recent buyers.

The exact dates are still open. Amazon had not announced them when it told sellers about the longer event, so plans should be built around the likely July window and adjusted once the dates are confirmed.

The question for the next planning meeting is who in the room can say yes to a 40% discount. The follow-up is whether that person has seen the margin, the stock plan and the advertising budget that come with it. Bringing those three together for every tentpole event is how we run Prime Day across deals, stock and advertising for brands.

A0750.title: When ‘Made in America’ search interest doesn’t equal sales
A0750.alt: Footprints in fresh snow along a quiet village street of old stone buildings with weathered wooden doors.
A0750.ttag: When ‘Made in America’ search interest doesn’t equal sales | Kwontified
A0750.desc: Searches for Made in USA nearly doubled in 2025, but most shoppers will not pay much more. Why interest does not become sales, and when the claim is worth it.
A0750.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 3, 2025.
A0750.body:
Searches for “Made in USA” nearly doubled in early 2025 as tariffs dominated the news, yet the most common answer in a survey by the same research firm was that shoppers would not pay more for American-made goods. Both findings can be true at once. A search costs the shopper nothing; a purchase costs money, and the price premium decides how much of the interest survives the trip from one to the other.

So Made in America search interest is a reading of curiosity, not of demand. Brands should lean on a “Made in USA” claim only where the price gap to imports is small and the claim is fully provable, and they should measure sales, not searches, before investing in it.

How Made in America search interest surged

Interest in American-made goods rose fast. Searches for the term “Made in USA” nearly doubled since early 2025, according to an analysis of Google Trends data by Trace One, a product software company, WGNS reported. In Trace One’s April survey, 43% of Americans said their interest in American-made goods had increased over the past year.

Willingness to pay was weaker. The most common response in the same survey was an unwillingness to pay more for American-made goods, and the share willing to pay a premium fell as the premium rose, according to the same report.

Marketers noticed the interest anyway. Tariffs have sparked a surge in “made in USA” marketing, with one survey finding 40% of Americans saying they would pay more for American-made products, Modern Retail reported. Legal experts quoted in the same report warned that such claims must be accurate.

What a search says and what a purchase says

A search or a survey answer reveals what a shopper would like, all else being equal. A purchase reveals what the shopper will actually do when all else is not equal, and the main thing that is not equal is price. When an American-made product costs only slightly more than an import, many interested shoppers will choose it. As the premium grows, the share who follow through falls quickly.

Two price gaps show how quickly:

CaseAmerican-madeComparable importPremium
Wide gap$30$2050%
Narrow gap$24$22about 9%

In the wide case, interest in the American-made version may be high, but few shoppers will pay half as much again. In the narrow case, many more of the interested shoppers will act. The claim is the same in both rows. The premium is what changes the outcome.

Search volume adds a second gap. Many shoppers who search for American-made products are researching, not buying that day. Some will buy later, some will buy an import after comparing prices, and some will never buy at all, yet the search count treats all of them the same.

Tariffs can narrow the price gap by raising import prices, which is why the interest feels like it should convert. But they also raise costs for many domestic makers that use imported parts or materials, so the gap does not always close as much as the headlines suggest.

It is easy to see why a chart of rising searches persuades a planning meeting. It is current, it points in one direction, and it seems to measure shoppers rather than opinions. But a search is still a stated preference, only a quieter one than a survey answer. The number that would change the decision is different: conversion on listings that carry the claim, compared with similar listings that do not, at the price gap the brand actually has. Until that number moves, the search chart describes what shoppers are curious about, which is useful for content and targeting and weak as a forecast of revenue.

Where the claim earns its place

The price comparison comes first. Set each American-made product against the closest imported alternative: where the premium is modest, the claim can tip the decision, and where it is large, the claim alone will not. Pricing should stay on costs and competition, too. Raising prices on American-made products while interest is high risks losing exactly the shoppers who were willing to try them at a modest premium.

The claim has to be true before it goes anywhere. “Made in USA” claims must be accurate and supportable, so brands should confirm what their products qualify for, including where components come from, and seek advice where the answer is unclear. Marketplaces add their own requirements for origin claims in titles, images and descriptions, and checking each marketplace’s rules first keeps a well-meant update from getting a product suppressed.

Testing settles the rest. Add the claim to titles, images or advertising on some products and compare sales and conversion with products that do not feature it. Interest also varies by region and group, so advertising aimed at shoppers searching for American-made products deserves a test against the brand’s usual targeting. Categories where safety or quality is closely tied to origin, such as food and tools, are the natural place to test first.

The claim works best alongside quality, reviews and value; a product that is American-made but weaker on the basics will not win on origin alone. And news-driven search spikes can fade when the news moves on, which argues against building large commitments, such as new product lines, on a surge that may not last. A decision to move production to the United States belongs on costs, quality and tariff risk over years, not on a few months of searches.

The rule for reading this kind of interest: count it only when it shows up in conversion at the brand’s actual price gap, and treat everything else as curiosity. Putting claims like this one through a sales test before they reach every listing is how we manage Amazon and Walmart listings for brands.

A0751.title: Zalando and circular fashion: when circularity becomes a cost
A0751.alt: Rack of vintage denim jackets beside an open suitcase of sewing supplies and a tag gun on a wooden stool.
A0751.ttag: Zalando and circular fashion: when circularity becomes a cost | Kwontified
A0751.desc: The EU agreed that fashion brands will pay to collect and recycle their products, with fees tied to circular design. Why that changes selling on Zalando.
A0751.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 5, 2025.
A0751.body:
For years, circularity in fashion lived in the sustainability report and the campaign calendar: a resale pilot here, a recycled-fabric capsule there. Brands chose whether to offer resale, repairs or recycled materials, the benefit was mainly reputational, and few faced any direct cost for what happened to a jacket after it sold.

That is changing in Europe. The EU has agreed that textile producers and fashion brands will pay to collect, sort, reuse and recycle their products, and the fees will eventually depend on how circular the designs are. Zalando, meanwhile, has spent years building pre-owned and circularity programs. Circular fashion is becoming a cost of selling, and brands on Zalando should prepare their product data, durability evidence and a view on resale before the fees arrive.

How Zalando and circular fashion got here

Zalando moved well before the regulators did. It introduced new business models for circularity across the product life cycle, including scaling its pre-owned offering, piloting repairs and designing for circularity, with the aim of extending the life of at least 50 million fashion items by 2023, Fibre2Fashion reported. Its pre-owned experience let customers buy or trade in like-new fashion.

Regulation has since caught up. The European Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement under which each member state will set up an extended producer responsibility scheme for textiles and footwear, making producers responsible for managing post-consumer textiles, Just Style reported.

The money will follow the design. Textile producers and fashion brands will pay fees to finance the collection and recycling of used textiles, and those fees will in future be adjusted based on how circular and sustainable their product designs are, Landbell Group explained.

From reputation to cost of goods

Producer responsibility moves what used to be a voluntary choice into the cost of goods. When brands pay for collecting and recycling what they sell, the end of a product’s life becomes part of its cost. When the fee varies with how circular the design is, durable, repairable and recyclable products become cheaper to sell than disposable ones, and the conversation moves from the sustainability team’s agenda to the margin review.

Platforms sit in the middle of this. Zalando already connects brands with customers who buy, trade in and resell. As the rules take effect, platforms like Zalando are likely to need more information from brands about materials and durability, and to offer more ways for customers to pass products on. A pre-owned offering also does something for shoppers. It gives price-conscious buyers access to brands they might not buy new, and gives owners a reason to keep items in good condition, which can widen a brand’s audience while keeping its products in use longer.

The competitive picture shifts with it. Brands that can show durable, repairable products may face lower fees and win shoppers who care about longevity. Brands built on cheap, short-lived items will face higher costs, which may narrow the price gap between them and better-made rivals.

The change also brings a good deal of new work. Brands will need data on what their products are made of, how long they last and how they can be repaired or recycled, and many do not hold that information in a usable form.

What preparing for the fees looks like

Product data is the foundation. Material composition, origin and care information for every product, held in a structured way, lets a brand supply it to platforms and compliance schemes when asked instead of assembling it under deadline.

Durability needs evidence behind it. Products that last longer will benefit as fees reward circular design, so testing and recording durability where possible, and making quality visible to shoppers, turns a design virtue into something a scheme and a customer can both see. Design itself takes the longest to change: fewer mixed materials, easier repairs and longer life have to be built into collections well before fees apply.

Resale is a decision, not a default. A brand can take part in platform resale programs, run its own or partner with specialists. Resale can bring new shoppers, but it needs careful pricing so it does not undercut new products. Repair belongs in the same conversation; offering it directly or through partners can extend product life and build loyalty, and is worth testing on the most expensive or durable lines.

Returns are part of the same arithmetic. Fashion has high return rates, and many returns stem from poor fit or unclear product information. Cutting returns reduces waste and cost at the same time, which matters more once end-of-life costs are on the bill.

Budgets, timing and claims across Europe

Fees will vary by country as each member state sets up its scheme, so brands selling across Europe need a cost estimate for each market and a way to follow how each scheme develops. The agreement is provisional, and schemes will arrive country by country over the coming years; brands should watch their main markets rather than wait for a single EU-wide date.

The rules also reach beyond Zalando. They apply to brands selling in the EU through any channel, including their own sites and other marketplaces, which argues for one approach that works across every European channel. And the story has to stay honest: sustainability claims face growing scrutiny in Europe, so brands should make only claims they can support with evidence.

The question for a brand’s next European planning meeting is who owns the end-of-life cost of its products, and whether that person has the material data to estimate it. Preparing catalogs and listings for those rules, on Zalando and the other European marketplaces, is how we launch and run European marketplaces for brands.

A0752.crumb: Being found in a GPT-first shopping…
A0752.title: Being found in a GPT-first shopping world: fewer slots, no bids
A0752.alt: Floating oak shelf on a pale green wall holding a stoneware vase, a corked amber bottle and a folded linen towel.
A0752.ttag: Being found in a GPT-first shopping world: fewer slots, no bids | Kwontified
A0752.desc: ChatGPT now shows shoppers products, prices and buy links, chosen without ads. Why fewer slots and no bids change how brands get found, and what to fix first.
A0752.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 10, 2025.
A0752.body:
A shopper searching a marketplace for a blender may see 20 or more products on the first page, several of them sponsored. The same shopper asking an AI assistant may see three to five. A blender that would have ranked eighth on the marketplace page still had a chance at a click. In a five-product answer, it does not appear at all, and there is no bid it can place to get in.

That is the practical change behind being found in GPT-first shopping. OpenAI has started showing shoppers products, prices, reviews and buy links in ChatGPT, chosen independently rather than sold as ads, and traffic from AI tools to US retail sites has risen sharply. Getting found now depends on being a product the assistant can describe with confidence. For a brand team, that means complete and consistent product information everywhere, independent reviews and mentions, and AI referrals tracked as a channel of their own.

What has shipped in GPT-first shopping so far

The traffic is growing quickly, from a small base. Traffic to US retail websites from generative AI sources rose 1,300% during the 2024 holiday season compared with the year before, and in February 2025 it was up 1,200% compared with July 2024, Adobe reported.

The assistants are being built for shopping. OpenAI began rolling out features in ChatGPT that make it easier to find, compare and buy products, including improved product results, visual details, pricing, reviews and direct links to buy, PYMNTS reported. OpenAI said product results are chosen independently and are not ads.

Those are the shipped facts. What follows is the logic of the format, not a description of how any assistant ranks products.

Fewer slots, chosen without bids

A search engine or marketplace shows a long page of results, usually with paid placements near the top, and a brand that ranks poorly can still buy its way onto the page. An assistant answers differently. It gives a short answer, often naming only a few products, chosen from the information it can find and trust. If the results are not ads, a brand cannot simply pay to appear.

Marketplace search pageAssistant answer
Products shown20 or moreThree to five
Paid placementSeveral sponsored slotsNone; results are not ads
A product ranked eighthStill on the pageNot named
What earns the slotRanking, or a bidInformation the assistant can describe and trust

Fewer slots concentrate visibility. The few products an assistant names win a large share of attention, and the rest are invisible. Because the choice rests on information rather than bids, the products chosen tend to be the ones with clear specifications, consistent details, credible reviews and independent mentions.

There is a second effect, and it favors incumbents. Assistants rely on what has been written about a product, so established products with many reviews and mentions start ahead. New products and smaller brands have to work harder to build the record an assistant needs before it will recommend them.

What a brand team actually changes

Most of the work is product information, which is less exotic than the headlines suggest. Assistants draw on what they can read, so product pages on the brand’s own site and on marketplaces should state specifications, materials, dimensions, uses and compatibility clearly and in plain language. The details should match everywhere: different names, specifications or prices on different sites create doubt for shoppers and assistants alike. Pages should also say who a product is for and what problem it solves, because shoppers ask assistants which product suits a particular need.

Marketplace listings belong in the same review. Assistants may draw on them as well as on brand sites, so marketplace titles, bullet points and images should carry the same complete information as the brand’s own pages. The site itself should load reliably and present information in a form automated tools can read, including structured product data.

The corroboration is harder to manufacture, which is the point. Reviews, expert comparisons and editorial coverage give assistants reasons to trust a product, and genuine reviews from verified buyers are among the details assistants show. Shortcuts work against a brand here: keyword stuffing and misleading claims confuse shoppers and damage trust, and assistants that compare sources may pass over products whose details conflict.

For the people on a brand team, the bigger adjustment is ownership. The content team that writes product pages, the marketplace team that manages listings and whoever handles reviews and press coverage all feed the same answer now, and none of them has a bid to raise when the brand goes unmentioned. Someone has to own what an assistant says about the brand’s products, and check it the way an ads manager checks a search term report.

Measuring a channel that has no bid

Results that are not ads come without an ad console’s reporting, so measurement has to be built. Traffic arriving from AI tools can be identified in analytics and followed through to conversion. And the simplest audit is direct: ask the leading assistants the questions shoppers ask, regularly, and record which products are named, where rivals appear and which details the assistant uses.

The landing page still decides the sale. Assistants often send shoppers to marketplaces and retailers, and a recommended product that has run out of stock, or sits on a weak listing, loses the sale anyway. Proportion matters as well. AI shopping traffic is growing fast but remains small next to search and marketplaces, so it is a channel to prepare for alongside search and advertising, not a replacement for them.

The rule for assistant-led shopping: a brand is found by being the most clearly described and best corroborated option, not by outbidding rivals. Getting catalogs and content ready for assistants to read and repeat accurately is how our AI Agentic Commerce practice prepares brands for AI shopping.

A0754.title: Beauty on Amazon needs a subcategory-first approach
A0754.alt: Glass trays of lipsticks, dropper serum bottles and perfume bottles on a wooden dresser against a navy wall.
A0754.ttag: Beauty on Amazon needs a subcategory-first approach | Kwontified
A0754.desc: Skin care grew 26% on Amazon in 2024 while fragrance grew 14%. Why beauty on Amazon behaves like several markets, and how brands should plan by subcategory.
A0754.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 12, 2025.
A0754.body:
Walk through a beauty hall and the store does the sorting for you. Fragrance has testers and a counter of its own, skin care has advisers who ask about your routine, and makeup has shade walls and mirrors. Each subcategory gets the setting its shoppers need to decide. On Amazon, the same products sit in one category, reached through the same search bar, and it is easy to plan them with one strategy.

The numbers say that strategy misses. Skin care on Amazon grew 26% in 2024 and made up a third of beauty sales there, while fragrance grew 14% and struggles with sampling. Beauty on Amazon behaves like several markets, each running on a different kind of shopper decision, and brands do better when strategy, content and advertising are set subcategory by subcategory.

How beauty on Amazon grew, and where it grew unevenly

Amazon became a beauty destination quickly. Analysts at Morgan Stanley forecast that Amazon would overtake Walmart as the largest US beauty retailer by 2025, with about 14.5% of the market, Business Standard reported. Premium brands followed: more than 300 beauty brands joined Amazon’s premium beauty store in 2024, Glossy reported.

The growth was not even. Skin care sales on Amazon grew 26% from 2023 to 2024 and made up a third of the platform’s beauty sales, while fragrance grew a more modest 14%, according to data from Front Row cited in the same report. Fragrance faced hurdles such as the lack of sampling. In some places demand ran ahead of sales. Searches for “fragrance” in Amazon’s beauty category rose 35% in 2024 to 1.1 million, and men’s fragrance sales grew 19% compared with 14% for women’s.

The wider market showed similar splits. Prestige beauty sales in the United States grew 7% to $33.9 billion in 2024, with fragrance up 12% and lip makeup up 19%, Circana reported.

Each subcategory runs on a different decision

Skin care suits Amazon well. Shoppers research ingredients and results, read reviews closely and, once a product works, buy it again. Detailed information and repeat purchase are what Amazon does best, and skin care rewards both.

Fragrance is harder, because scent cannot be judged on a screen. Shoppers who know a fragrance will reorder it online, but discovering a new one usually needs a sample or a store visit. That is why searches can grow faster than sales: the interest is there, the confidence is not.

Makeup sits in between. Shade and finish matter, and a wrong shade means a return, so shoppers need help matching products to their skin tone and preferences, which images, swatches and reviews from similar shoppers can provide. Hair care and tools follow their own patterns: treatments are researched like skin care, and tools are compared on features and price like electronics.

Reviews do different jobs in each. Skin care shoppers look for reviews that describe results over weeks. Makeup shoppers look for reviewers with similar skin tones. In fragrance, reviews struggle to convey a scent, so shoppers lean on comparisons with fragrances they already know. Each subcategory has its own path to a first purchase and its own reasons for a repeat.

One beauty plan or several

The decision leadership teams actually face is whether beauty on Amazon gets one plan or several. One plan is simpler to budget and report, and it lets a strong skin care line carry the whole category’s numbers. Several plans cost more attention, but they are the only way to see whether fragrance is underperforming because of the product or because it is being sold like skin care.

The case for several starts with mapping the range by how shoppers decide and setting separate goals and budgets for each group. From there, the content follows the decision. Skin care needs evidence: ingredients, concentrations and expected results explained clearly, reviews that describe outcomes, and subscriptions where available to encourage the repeat.

Fragrance needs discovery aids: scents described in specific terms, comparisons with well-known references where accurate, and travel sizes or sets that lower the cost of trying, with advertising aimed at shoppers searching for scent families and occasions as well as brand names. Makeup needs matching: shades shown on a range of skin tones, clear swatches, and finish and coverage described precisely to cut returns.

Advertising splits the same way. Search terms, competitors and costs differ between skin care, fragrance and makeup, so separate campaigns judged against their own benchmarks show what a blended campaign hides. Search data is also the best guide to language, from ingredient names in skin care to scent notes in fragrance, and those terms belong in titles, bullet points and ads.

Calendars, growth pockets and the premium shelf

The fastest growth often sits inside a subcategory. Men’s fragrance and lip products grew faster than their categories, and similar pockets may exist in a brand’s own range. Timing differs too: fragrance and gift sets sell heavily around holidays and occasions such as Mother’s Day, while skin care sells more steadily, so stock and advertising should follow each subcategory’s own calendar. Bundles that pair a known product with a new one can introduce shoppers to more of a range, designed around how each subcategory is bought.

For premium brands, consistent pricing and controlled distribution matter, which means watching for unauthorized sellers and keeping listings accurate.

The question to put to the team is whether the beauty report shows repeat rate, return rate and conversion for each subcategory, or one number that lets skin care hide fragrance. Building plans that sell each subcategory the way its shoppers decide is how we run Amazon for beauty brands.

A0757.crumb: Prime Day 2025 forecast: what four days…
A0757.title: Prime Day 2025 forecast: what four days does to the ranges
A0757.alt: Four brass hourglasses of decreasing size on a sunlit wooden table by a window, with dried flowers and old books.
A0757.ttag: Prime Day 2025 forecast: what four days does to the ranges | Kwontified
A0757.desc: Prime Day 2025 doubles to four days, but sales won’t double. Our conservative, standard and reach ranges, their assumptions, and what they mean for stock.
A0757.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 17, 2025.
A0757.body:
Our ranges put US online spending over the four days of Prime Day 2025 at about 1.3 to 1.6 times the 2024 two-day level, not double it:

ScenarioEach added day drawsFour-day totalMultiple of 2024
Conservative25% of a core dayabout $18.8 billion1.32
Standard40% of a core dayabout $21.1 billion1.48
Reach55% of a core dayabout $23.3 billion1.64

Amazon is doubling the event’s length, but shoppers arrive with fixed budgets, and urgency fades when the deals will still be there tomorrow. The two added days should add far less than the first two. Brands should plan stock and advertising for that range rather than for twice their 2024 results.

Where the Prime Day 2025 forecast starts

Amazon told sellers that Prime Day 2025 would run four days instead of two, according to an internal memo reported by Modern Retail.

The base is the 2024 event. Over the two days of Prime Day 2024, US shoppers spent $14.2 billion online, by Adobe Analytics’ count as cited in the same Modern Retail piece. That figure covers spending across online retailers, not Amazon alone.

Growth is modest. Amazon’s online store sales grew 6% in the first quarter of 2025, Digital Commerce 360 reported, and we use that as the growth assumption for the core two days.

Why the added days add less

Most shoppers arrive at a sale with a rough idea of what they will buy and how much they will spend. A longer event gives them more time to buy, but not much more money, and the urgency that drives a short sale weakens when shoppers know the deals will last. Some shoppers who would have bought on day one wait until day three. Some new buying does happen, because more time reaches more shoppers and new deals appear each day. The net effect is that the added days draw less spending than the core days.

The model behind the table is simple. Grow the 2024 base of $14.2 billion by 6%, which gives about $15.05 billion for the two core days, or about $7.53 billion a day. Then assume each added day draws a share of a core day’s spending: 25% in the conservative case, 40% in the standard case and 55% in the reach case. Adding the two extra days at those shares produces totals of about $18.8 billion, $21.1 billion and $23.3 billion. Those are 1.32, 1.48 and 1.64 times 2024.

These are ranges built on stated assumptions, not a prediction of a precise figure. They will move with consumer confidence, tariff-driven prices and how heavily retailers promote. Tariffs push both ways: higher prices on some imported goods may hold spending back, while shoppers looking for relief from higher prices may wait for the event and buy more during it.

It is tempting to read a longer event as a bigger one in proportion, because the calendar is the most visible thing that changed. The budget each shopper brings is what did not change, and it is the better guide.

The event itself will show which range applies. If day three draws more than half of a core day, the reach case is in play. If it falls below a quarter of a core day, the conservative case is more likely. Watching the shape of the event day by day tells a brand which plan to follow.

Stock, pacing and the extremes

Stock should follow the range. A brand can take its 2024 Prime Day unit sales and plan for roughly 1.3 to 1.6 times that volume, adjusted for its own growth, instead of doubling. Doubling risks excess stock that ties up cash after the event.

A brand’s own multiple can differ from the market’s. Products featured in themed or daily deals may see more than the average lift on those days, while products not on deal may see less, so each brand should adjust the range using its own 2024 results and deal plan. Margin needs the same care. Doubling the length of a deal doubles the days of discount it carries, and the expected lift has to cover that longer discount.

Advertising should follow the curve rather than an even split. If the added days draw less, budgets belong weighted toward the first days and the final day, with money shifted during the event toward what performs. Some shoppers will delay purchases, so soft day-one results are not a reason to cut advertising early; part of that demand may arrive later.

The extremes deserve a plan before the event starts. The conservative and reach cases differ by several billion dollars, so a brand should know which products it would restock quickly if demand runs high and how it would limit spending if demand runs low.

Reading the result afterward

Measurement should cover the whole window. Total four-day results belong against the plan, rather than each day against a two-day benchmark, and the way sales spread across the days is the input for planning 2026. The halo belongs in the count as well: Prime Day lifts sales of products not on deal and the weeks around the event, so full-price sales and the days before and after are part of the result.

The rule for a longer event: it lifts total sales by far less than its added length, so plan for a multiple well below two and let the shape of day three tell you which end of the range you are in. Building ranges like these for a brand’s own account, and pacing stock and spend against them, is how we forecast and run Prime Day advertising for brands.

A0758.crumb: Why category-level strategy is the path…
A0758.title: Why category-level strategy is the path forward for brands
A0758.alt: Inside a sunny wooden greenhouse with trays of lettuce, tomato and herb seedlings on benches against a blue wall.
A0758.ttag: Why category-level strategy is the path forward for brands | Kwontified
A0758.desc: Growth, competition and ad costs differ sharply by category on Amazon and Walmart. Why brand-wide averages mislead, and how to plan category by category.
A0758.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 19, 2025.
A0758.body:
Take a brand whose marketplace sales rose 8%, with advertising costs holding at 12% of sales. In the quarterly review, that line gets a nod and the meeting moves on. Now split the same business in two. Half its sales sit in a category growing 20%, half in one shrinking 4%, so the two categories together grew 8%. The brand grew 16% in the fast category and held flat in the slow one.

The total said nothing needed to change. The categories say something else: the brand is losing ground where demand is booming and winning where demand is falling. That is the case for category-level strategy. Growth, competition and advertising costs differ sharply from one category to the next on Amazon and Walmart. Brands that set plans, benchmarks and budgets category by category, judged against the category rather than their own history, can see what a brand-wide average hides.

Why category-level strategy matters more in 2025

This year’s marketplace growth is concentrated in a few places. On Amazon, everyday essentials expanded at more than double the pace of everything else in the first quarter. They also accounted for one in every three units sold in the United States, the company’s chief executive said, as Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Walmart’s quarter had the same lopsided shape. US comparable sales grew 4.5%, led by health and wellness and by grocery, according to Walmart’s first-quarter earnings release.

The splits run inside categories too. In beauty on Amazon, skin care sales grew 26% from 2023 to 2024 against 14% for fragrance, in Front Row data cited by Glossy. Across US prestige beauty, the whole market grew 7% while fragrance grew 12% and lip makeup 19%, Circana reported.

What a brand-wide total hides

A brand that sells across several categories usually sees one total, and that total blends categories that behave very differently. A fast-growing category can make a brand look healthy while it loses share, because the category is rising faster than the brand. A slow one can make a brand look weak while it gains share. Neither shows up in the blended line, which is why the brand in the opening example was told to change nothing when it needed to fix one category and invest in the other.

Competition is uneven in the same way. Some categories are crowded with sellers bidding on the same searches, which pushes advertising costs up, while others have few strong competitors. A single advertising target applied across all of them will overspend in some and underspend in others.

Shoppers behave differently by category as well. Essentials are reordered on price and convenience, considered purchases are researched, and gifts peak around occasions. The product page, price and advertising that suit one category can be wrong for the next.

And the marketplaces themselves are built this way. Amazon and Walmart rank products, set fees and report data by category, and shoppers browse and search within categories. A brand that plans by category is matching the structure the retailer and the shopper already use; a brand that plans by total is working against it.

The habit of planning by total is easy to understand. The total is what the profit and loss statement shows, what the annual target is written against and what leadership asks about first, so it becomes the number teams manage to. Category results, by contrast, take work to assemble and need someone to own them. The blended line wins by default, not because anyone decided it tells the truth about the business.

Building the plan category by category

The work starts with a split. Sales, advertising and margin need breaking out into the categories and subcategories the brand competes in, using the marketplace’s own category structure where possible. Once the split exists, the key number changes from growth to share: whether the brand is growing faster or slower than each category, estimated from search share, sales rank and marketplace category reports.

Benchmarks follow the category. Advertising cost targets, conversion rates and return rates belong against each category’s own norms, not a brand-wide average. Budget follows opportunity: more money where the brand is gaining share at acceptable cost, less where it is losing share at high cost, instead of an even spread. The playbook for product pages, pricing, promotions and advertising should be shaped by how each category’s shoppers decide, and the category’s own search language is the best guide to the words in titles, content and ads.

The categories themselves keep moving. They rise and fall with seasons, prices and trends, which argues for a monthly review and budgets that can move with conditions.

People, connections and new ground

Structure inside the brand matters as much as the plan. Where possible, someone should own each major category, responsible for its share, margin and plan, and leadership reporting should show share and margin by category alongside the totals, because category results give a clearer picture than the brand line.

The categories in a range are also connected. Some shoppers move across a brand’s range, from a cleanser to a moisturizer for example, and the categories that lead shoppers into others deserve protection even where their own margins are lower. Emerging categories can grow quickly before competition arrives, so a small testing budget in categories where the brand is new, judged on share gained rather than immediate profit, keeps the plan from looking only backward.

The question for the next quarterly review is which of the brand’s categories it is gaining share in, and whether anyone in the room can answer without first blending them into one number. Building plans at that level across Amazon, Walmart and Target is how we run marketplace categories for brands.

A0759.crumb: Live shopping events on TikTok: when a…
A0759.title: Live shopping events on TikTok: when a session pays for itself
A0759.alt: Phone on a mini tripod filming lit beeswax candles on a rustic table beside an open cash box full of coins.
A0759.ttag: Live shopping events on TikTok: when a session pays for itself | Kwontified
A0759.desc: Only four of 4 million TikTok Shop live sessions topped $1 million in 2024. Why live selling has fixed costs and uneven returns, and when a session pays off.
A0759.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 24, 2025.
A0759.body:
Influencers ran 4 million live sessions on TikTok Shop in the United States in 2024, and only four of them sold more than $1 million. The best one reached $2.1 million over 14 hours. Those four sessions are the ones people talk about, and they are a poor guide to what a typical session earns.

Live shopping events on TikTok have a simple economic shape: the cost of a session is largely fixed, while its sales depend on how many people watch and what share of them buy. That makes the audience a session needs to break even the number to know before planning one. Brands should test with short, inexpensive sessions and scale live selling only where the audience reliably clears that bar.

What live shopping events on TikTok add up to

TikTok Shop grew fast. Its US gross merchandise value reached $9 billion in 2024, making the United States its largest market, according to a report by Momentum Works and Tabcut covered by TechNode.

Live selling is the smallest slice. Videos contributed 58% of US sales, shop pages 32% and live streams 10%, according to the same report, which is also the source of the session counts above.

Peak days show the upside. Black Friday 2024 brought more than 30,000 live streams to TikTok Shop, and a beauty brand passed $1 million in sales inside two hours of starting its stream, Benzinga reported.

A fixed cost against an audience-sized return

A live session costs roughly the same whether ten people watch or ten thousand: a host, a producer, samples, a set and hours on air. Its sales rise with the number of viewers and the share who buy. That combination produces very uneven results. Live sales of about $900 million across 4 million sessions works out to an average of about $225 per session by our calculation, and because a few big sessions pull that average up, the typical session earns less.

Take a four-hour session that costs $1,500 for the host, production and samples, with a product earning $12 of margin per unit sold. The session needs 125 units to break even, or about 31 an hour. If 1% of viewers buy, that takes about 3,125 viewers an hour.

Viewers an hourUnits sold (1% buy)Margin earnedAgainst a $1,500 cost
1,000about 40$480Loses money
5,000about 200$2,400Makes money

The same session, with the same host and the same product, loses money in one row and makes money in the other. Audience is the hard part. A brand starting live selling on its own account usually begins with few viewers, because the audience comes from followers, the platform’s recommendations and any creators involved. Conversion matters too, but a session cannot convert viewers it never reaches, which is why the biggest sessions are concentrated among a few hosts with large followings.

The session everyone remembers

The pull toward live selling usually starts with a story like the Black Friday beauty brand. It is vivid, recent and easy to retell, so it becomes the reference point for what a session can do, while the millions of sessions that sold little leave no story behind. Planning from the memorable outcome instead of the typical one is how a brand ends up funding a studio before it has an audience.

The average of about $225 a session is less exciting to repeat in a meeting. It is also much closer to what a new account should expect from its first sessions, and it is the number the break-even has to beat. Nobody can say in advance which session will catch on, which is the honest reason to start small and let the numbers decide.

Running sessions that can pay back

The break-even audience comes first. Before planning a session, estimate its full cost and the margin per unit, including TikTok Shop’s commissions and any time-limited offer. Then work out the viewers and conversion needed to cover it. Short sessions with a single host and simple production cost less and show quickly whether an audience exists, so several of those belong ahead of any larger event.

An audience can also be borrowed. Creators with established followings bring viewers a new brand account lacks, and partnering with creators whose audiences match the brand’s customers, paid in ways tied to sales where possible, changes the viewer count the arithmetic depends on. Products matter as well: live selling suits products a host can demonstrate on camera, such as beauty, kitchen tools or gadgets. Meanwhile, products that sell easily from a photo may not need a host at all. Large moments such as Black Friday draw bigger audiences, which is where live spending belongs.

Each session should be tracked against its own break-even: viewers, conversion, sales and cost. Host and time of day are variables to test, since the same product can sell very differently with a different host or at a different hour. Clips cut from a session can run as short videos, which drive most TikTok Shop sales, spreading the session’s cost across more sales. Stock has to cover a spike, and the platform’s rules on claims and offers apply on air as much as in a listing.

A dollar spent on live selling could instead fund short videos or advertising, so the sales each channel returns per dollar belong side by side before budget moves toward live. Video still drives most of TikTok Shop’s sales, and live works best as an addition to a strong video program.

The rule before booking a host: if you cannot name where the 3,125 viewers an hour will come from, run the short test instead of the big event. Building those tests, and the video program around them, is how we build TikTok Shop live and video programs.

A0761.title: Earning category leadership at Walmart: be the dependable choice
A0761.alt: Rows of identical blue corked ceramic bottles filling two shelves of a painted blue wooden shelving unit.
A0761.ttag: Earning category leadership at Walmart: be the dependable choice | Kwontified
A0761.desc: Walmart’s US e-commerce grew 21% and its ad business 31% in early 2025. Why category leadership there goes to the dependable product, and how brands earn it.
A0761.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 26, 2025.
A0761.body:
Watch someone reorder dog food or paper towels on Walmart’s app and the search hardly matters. They type the category, look for the bag they bought the time before, check that it arrives soon at roughly the price they remember, and check out. That small ritual raises a question for any brand trying to lead a Walmart category: what does the shelf reward when the shopper mostly wants the same thing again?

The answer is dependability: category leadership at Walmart goes to the product that is reliably in stock, fairly priced and quick to arrive, more than to the newest or most heavily promoted one. Brands that build stock, price, delivery speed and advertising around being that dependable choice earn the position; brands that treat Walmart as one more place to push a launch tend to rent it.

Category leadership at Walmart is getting more valuable and more contested

The channel is growing quickly. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales grew 21% in its first quarter, while its advertising arm, Walmart Connect, grew 31% in the United States, according to Walmart’s first-quarter earnings release. Comparable sales in the US were up 4.5%, with health and wellness and grocery in front: the everyday categories that shoppers come back to week after week.

The shelf is also getting more crowded. In the prior quarter, Walmart Connect grew 24% in the United States, helped by 50% growth in the number of marketplace sellers advertising, Walmart said in its fourth-quarter earnings release.

Follow the money in those two releases and the incentives line up plainly. More sellers bidding for the same searches means more advertising revenue for Walmart, while the shopper still buys whichever product shows up in stock at a fair price. The seller whose item disappoints on price or delivery still pays for the click and loses the sale. As visibility gets more expensive, the cost of being undependable lands on the advertising invoice.

Delivery is moving closer to the shopper, too. Walmart is adding drone delivery at 100 stores across five metro areas, building on existing operations in Arkansas and Texas, Bloomberg reported. Frequently ordered items include fresh fruit, eggs and pet food, which is to say the reorder basket.

Why the dependable product ends up leading

Walmart has built its offer around everyday low prices and fast delivery, and its marketplace behaves the same way. Products that are in stock, priced competitively and fulfilled quickly are well placed to win visibility and the sale. A product that is often out of stock or priced above its rivals loses ground, however good it is.

From there the advantage compounds. A product that is reliably available and fairly priced earns sales, reviews and repeat purchases, and those in turn support its position in search. An unreliable product loses each of them in sequence. Reviews matter more than they look. A shopper choosing quickly between two similar items leans on the rating and the number of reviews, so products that keep meeting expectations build that record, while a product with quality problems takes a long time to recover it.

The stores add a physical dimension. Walmart’s thousands of stores serve as pickup points and local fulfillment hubs, and drone delivery now runs from some of them. Stock positioned where shoppers live can reach them faster than stock shipped from a distant warehouse, so speed depends on place as much as on process.

That makes Walmart unlike the channels built on discovery. On social platforms a new product can break through on one viral moment. At Walmart the dependable product tends to win steadily, and the leader holds its place through consistency.

What being dependable asks of a brand

Dependability is hard to own because it crosses teams. The demand forecast, the price file and the advertising budget can sit with three different people, each judged on a different number, and the shopper experiences all three at once.

Stock is where dependability starts. Leading products need careful demand forecasts and enough inventory to stay available through peaks, and Walmart Fulfillment Services can help products qualify for faster delivery options, which shoppers increasingly expect. Walmart’s deal events need the same planning, so that a promotion does not leave the item out of stock the week after.

Price needs to be competitive and steady. That means watching rival prices, staying in line with them and avoiding the large swings that erode a reorder shopper’s trust. Where tariffs raise costs, increases deserve a plan rather than a surprise.

The listing has to carry the decision. Clear titles, complete details, good images and steady reviews help a product convert and support its search position. Other sellers may offer the same product, so the content shoppers see should be accurate and unauthorized sellers should not undercut its price or service.

Advertising then amplifies what already works. Walmart offers sponsored search and display advertising, including self-serve options for marketplace sellers. Search ads suit purchase-ready shoppers and display reaches them earlier. Spend belongs on products that are in stock and competitively priced, along with protecting the brand’s own searches from rivals. Making reordering easy and keeping the product experience consistent brings the shopper back without paying for the click again.

The scoreboard has to change as well. Share of category sales and search shows whether a brand is gaining leadership in a way its own growth rate cannot. The current leaders in each category reveal what Walmart shoppers value through their prices, delivery promises, reviews and content. As the marketplace keeps adding sellers and items, searches where shoppers find few strong options are often a faster route to leadership than a head-on fight with an established leader.

The question to take into the next planning meeting

Ask the team which of your leading Walmart products a shopper would have found out of stock, priced above a rival or slow to arrive, and who in the building owns fixing it. If no single person can answer, the category is being led by someone else’s reliability. Getting stock, price, speed and advertising to work as one system is the job we take on when we manage a brand’s Walmart selling and advertising together.

A0763.crumb: When winning on Amazon means losing…
A0763.title: When winning on Amazon means losing money: the unit math
A0763.alt: Small gold trophy cup beside an open leather wallet, old papers and books on a sunlit wooden desk.
A0763.ttag: When winning on Amazon means losing money: the unit math | Kwontified
A0763.desc: Amazon sales and rank can climb while every unit loses money. Why heavier ads and deeper discounts erode margin, and the limit that keeps growth profitable.
A0763.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 1, 2025.
A0763.body:
A brand selling 1,800 units a month on Amazon can be worse off than the same brand selling 1,000. The bigger number arrives with a better rank and a busier dashboard, and in the example below it also arrives with a loss of $2,700 a month, where the smaller number was earning $4,500. Amazon’s fees did not change between the two. The cost of each extra unit did.

Fees and product cost are fixed per unit, but the advertising and discounts needed to sell one more unit rise as a brand pushes harder. So total profit can fall while sales and rank climb. The fix is to judge Amazon growth by contribution profit after advertising, product by product, and to set a ceiling on advertising cost and discount depth for each item.

Why winning on Amazon can mean losing money as ads take a bigger share

Advertising is a growing share of what Amazon earns. In the first quarter of 2025 its advertising revenue grew 18%, well ahead of third-party seller services at 6% and online stores at 5%, TheWrap reported. The pattern held a quarter earlier: in the fourth quarter of 2024, advertising also grew 18% while online stores grew about 7%, according to Amazon’s fourth-quarter results.

When advertising grows faster than the sales it competes for, the cost of winning each sale tends to rise. For a brand chasing rank and share, that widens the distance between growing sales and growing profit.

The unit math of a push for rank

Take a product priced at $30. Amazon’s referral fee at 15% is $4.50, fulfillment costs $6 and the product costs $9 to make. That leaves $10.50 a unit, or 35% of the price, before any advertising.

In its steady state, half of the product’s sales come through ads at an advertising cost of 40% of those sales. That averages out to $6 of advertising per unit, leaving $4.50 of profit, or 15% of the price. At 1,000 units a month, the product earns $4,500.

Then the brand pushes for rank. It bids higher and more broadly, so 70% of sales come through ads at an advertising cost of 50%. Advertising now costs $10.50 per unit, the whole of the profit before advertising, and each unit earns nothing. Sales climb to 1,500 units while monthly profit falls to zero.

Next it adds a 10% discount, taking the price to $27. Profit before advertising drops to $7.95, advertising costs $9.45 per unit, and each unit loses $1.50. Sales reach 1,800 units, 80% more than in the steady state, and the product loses $2,700 a month.

Per unit unless statedSteady statePush for rankPush plus 10% discount
Price$30$30$27
Share of sales through ads50%70%70%
Advertising cost of those sales40%50%50%
Profit before advertising$10.50$10.50$7.95
Advertising cost$6$10.50$9.45
Profit after advertising$4.50nothingloss of $1.50
Units a month1,0001,5001,800
Profit a month$4,500zeroloss of $2,700

Units rise with each step to the right across the table, and the bottom row falls with each of the same steps.

Why the push keeps looking like progress

Sales and rank are visible every day, while profit after advertising often appears only in a monthly report, if at all. Teams rewarded on sales growth or on advertising return per campaign can hit their targets while the business loses money, which makes the measures, more than the effort, the source of the problem.

Attribution flatters the push as well. Advertising reports credit ads with sales that might have happened anyway, especially on searches for the brand’s own name, so a campaign that looks efficient may be buying sales the brand already had. Testing whether higher bids or deeper discounts bring sales that would not otherwise happen is the only way to know, and often they buy sales the brand would have made regardless.

Rank does have real value, which is what makes the push tempting. Higher rank brings more organic sales, and that can justify some investment. For a new product, a push with a time limit, a goal and a payback test can be a deliberate investment, provided organic sales actually rise enough to pay it back. Pushing an established product indefinitely is usually a leak.

Guardrails that keep Amazon growth paid for

Contribution comes first, calculated for every product: the profit after fees, product cost, advertising, discounts and returns. Products with high return rates lose more money than their sales figures suggest, and totals or average advertising cost hide the products that lose money.

Each product then needs its own ceiling on advertising cost and discount depth, set from its margin. A thin-margin item cannot sustain the spending a rich-margin item can. Alongside the per-product view, advertising cost as a share of all sales, including those the ads did not drive, shows whether the brand is buying its growth; a rising share is the warning.

Price needs a floor. Discounts that become permanent reset shoppers’ expectations and make the return to full price harder, so each product should carry a minimum price, with deeper cuts kept to short, planned events. Fee assumptions need regular checks too, because Amazon’s fees change over time and differ by size, weight and category.

The reporting has to show it. Leadership reports that put contribution profit next to sales and rank make growth that loses money visible before the month closes.

A test to apply on Monday: if a product’s profit per unit after advertising is falling while its units rise, the extra units are being bought, and the next push will cost more than the last one did. Putting contribution profit beside every campaign is how we manage Amazon ads for brands that need growth to pay for itself.

A0764.title: After de minimis: how cross-border sellers are rebuilding
A0764.alt: Bright warehouse loading dock with open shipping containers, cardboard boxes on roller conveyors and stacked pallets.
A0764.ttag: After de minimis: how cross-border sellers are rebuilding | Kwontified
A0764.desc: Since duty-free parcels from China ended, Temu moved all US sales to local sellers and warehouses. How cross-border rivals are rebuilding, and what that means.
A0764.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 3, 2025.
A0764.body:
For years the cheapest products on an American phone screen travelled the same way: one parcel at a time, from a factory in China to a front door, entering duty-free because each box was worth too little to tax. That route closed on May 2. For brands, the useful question is less what the cross-border platforms lost than what they turned into.

They turned into something closer to a domestic seller. After de minimis, cross-border sellers are rebuilding around bulk imports held in US warehouses, as Temu did when it moved all US sales to locally based sellers. That trades the cheapest-parcel advantage for faster delivery, duty paid up front and inventory risk. Brands should reset their price watch and competitive plans around these warehouse-stocked rivals rather than the parcel shippers they replaced.

How cross-border sellers began rebuilding after de minimis

The rule ended overnight. From 12:01 a.m. on May 2, goods from China and Hong Kong valued at $800 or less no longer entered the United States duty-free, Barnes Richardson reported. After a US-China agreement, the duty on postal parcels was cut to 54% from 120%, with a $100 flat fee kept, RTÉ reported. Even at the lower rate, sending single parcels from China remains costly.

The largest player moved within hours of the change. Temu stopped shipping products directly from China to the United States, and a spokesperson said all US sales are now handled by locally based sellers with orders fulfilled from within the country, TechCrunch reported. Shoppers had earlier seen import charges of 130% to 150% added to their bills, according to the same report.

The groundwork had been laid well before May. Temu and Shein had spent years expanding US warehouses, and in February Temu began asking supplier factories to ship items in bulk to US warehouses, CNN reported, citing Bloomberg. Local fulfillment does not mean local manufacturing, the same report noted.

Two supply chains produce two different competitors

The old model shipped one parcel at a time from a factory to a shopper. Each parcel entered duty-free, which made very low prices possible, but delivery was slow and the seller held little stock in the United States. A seller could list thousands of items and let demand sort them out, because an unsold item cost almost nothing to carry.

The new model ships goods in bulk to US warehouses and pays duty on the whole shipment when it enters. Delivery gets faster, since the goods already sit near the shopper. In exchange the seller pays duty before it sells anything, holds stock and has to guess demand in advance.

That changes how the rival behaves. A seller holding inventory cannot test thousands of products cheaply, because each one ties up money in a warehouse, so assortments narrow toward proven sellers. Prices rise to cover duty and storage. Unsold stock becomes a cost, which pushes sellers to discount slow items to clear space.

Shoppers see the difference on the screen. Items that once came only by slow parcel now arrive in days, while some cheap listings disappear or show as out of stock. Shoppers who came for the lowest prices may find fewer of them; those who valued speed find more to like.

The pressure on price has eased without going away. Bulk imports pay duty on their declared value, usually well under what the item sells for, so warehouse-stocked sellers can still undercut brands with higher costs. The gap has narrowed, and it is still there.

Where brands now meet these rivals

The meeting point is moving onto the marketplaces brands already sell on. Many of the same factory-direct products are likely to appear on Amazon and Walmart through warehouse-stocked sellers, and as more sellers shift stock into the United States, more of them may list there. Temu moved first and most visibly, but Shein and other sellers built on cheap parcels face the same pressure, and some had been stocking US warehouses for some time.

Delivery speed stops being a reliable edge. As cross-border sellers ship from US warehouses, their delivery times approach those of established brands, and a brand that leaned on faster delivery as its answer to cheap imports needs another way to stand apart.

Inventory, though, makes some things harder for these rivals. Sellers paying to hold stock favor proven, fast-moving products, which leaves room for breadth, newness and niche products that are uneconomic for a bulk importer to carry. Trust is the other opening: warehouse-stocked rivals may still be unknown names, so a brand’s quality, reviews and service count for more when price alone is a smaller advantage than it was.

Some exposure sits inside the brand. A brand that shipped directly from China to its own customers now faces the same choice as Temu’s sellers: pay higher duties on every parcel or move stock to US warehouses, and the cheaper answer can differ product by product. Factory-direct sellers also sometimes sell close copies of successful products, which makes listing monitoring and the marketplaces’ brand-protection tools part of the response.

What to watch in your own categories

  • Which rivals now undercut you on price, and whether they ship from US warehouses or still send parcels.
  • New cross-border sellers and close copies appearing on Amazon and Walmart in your categories.
  • Delivery promises from those rivals closing in on your own.
  • Further rule changes, including for low-value parcels from other countries, which argue for keeping sourcing and pricing plans flexible.

The rivals that matter most now look more like the sellers brands already know, and they need watching listing by listing across marketplaces. That watch, kept alongside the listings themselves, is part of how we operate Amazon and Walmart channels for brands.
