A0765.crumb: How Amazon’s new fee structure ends easy…
A0765.title: How Amazon’s new fee structure ends easy discounting
A0765.alt: Red paper price tag being cut in two by brass scissors on a worn wooden tabletop.
A0765.ttag: How Amazon’s new fee structure ends easy discounting | Kwontified
A0765.desc: Since June 2, Amazon charges coupons and deals a share of sales instead of flat fees. Why that ends always-on discounting, and when a promotion still pays.
A0765.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 8, 2025.
A0765.body:
Take a coupon on a $40 product that sells 1,000 units. Under Amazon’s old fees it cost $600; since June 2, the same coupon on the same product costs $1,005. The discount is unchanged and so is the product. What changed is the fee on each extra unit the promotion sells.

Under the old flat fees, the last unit through a promotion carried no extra fee. Always-on coupons and long deals were cheap to leave running. Amazon’s new fee structure charges coupons and deals a share of promotion sales on top of a smaller fixed fee, so a promotion’s cost now rises with every unit it sells. Standing coupons on higher-priced products and long Best Deals get more expensive, short tests get cheaper, and each promotion is best priced as a share of the sales it drives.

What changed in Amazon’s new fee structure

Amazon said it would move to a performance-based fee structure for deals and coupons, effective June 2, 2025, Helium 10 reported.

The old fees were flat: $150 for a Lightning Deal, $300 for a Best Deal and $0.60 per unit redeemed for coupons, Modern Retail reported after Amazon’s March 20 announcement. Under the new model, Lightning and Best Deals cost $70 per day plus 1% of the sales driven by the deal, capped at $2,000, and coupons cost $5 each plus 2.5% of coupon sales, according to the same report. Fees for Prime Day and other peak events stay flat.

Why a flat fee made discounting look free

Under a flat fee, once a brand had paid for a promotion, every extra unit sold cost nothing more in fees. The longer a coupon ran and the more it sold, the lower its fee per unit, so the arithmetic quietly rewarded leaving promotions switched on.

The new structure sends a share of every promoted sale to Amazon. The more a promotion sells, the more it costs, and the free extra unit is gone.

At first glance Amazon is doing two contradictory things, cutting the fee on some promotions while raising it on others. The logic holds together once you look at which promotions get cheaper. Tying fees to sales lets Amazon share in the value of promotions that work while lowering the barrier for a seller to try one. It also discourages promotions that run on autopilot, which can crowd deal pages without adding much for shoppers.

The arithmetic for coupons and deals

Coupons first. The old fee of $0.60 per unit equals 2.5% of a $24 price, so for any product priced above $24 the new coupon fee costs more per unit than the old one did. On the $40 product, 1,000 units generate $40,000 of sales, and the coupon costs $1,005 under the new fees against $600 under the old. Folded into the discount, a 10% coupon on that product now costs about 12.5% of coupon sales.

Deals cut the other way at small sizes. A one-day Lightning Deal that sells $3,000 now costs $100, less than the old $150. One that sells $20,000 costs $270. The two structures break even at $8,000 of sales.

Length is where the cost builds. A seven-day Best Deal now carries $490 in daily fees before any share of sales, and if it sells $50,000 the total comes to $990, compared with $300 before.

Two edges of the new schedule matter for planning. The variable fee is capped at $2,000 per deal, so very large deals cost relatively less, and brands with high-volume deals should know where they cross the cap. At the other end, for products that sell only a few units a day, the $70 daily fee can exceed any likely gain, which argues for keeping deals to products with enough demand to cover it.

Running promotions that still pay

Every promotion now needs its fee in the calculation, as a share of sales, alongside the discount itself and any advertising behind it. Standing coupons are the place to start. A coupon left running indefinitely on a product priced above $24 now costs more than it did. Does it bring sales that would not happen without it? Rising fees make that incrementality question more pressing, because a promotion that only sells what the brand would have sold anyway now pays Amazon a share of those sales too.

Short deals have become the cheap way to learn. Lower daily fees make one- or two-day tests of products, prices and discount depths cheaper than before. Week-long Best Deals are left for specific purposes, such as clearing stock or launching a product. Each needs a measurable target that justifies the higher cost.

The tool should match the price. Coupons now suit lower-priced products, where 2.5% of sales is less than the old per-unit fee; on higher-priced products a short deal or a simple price cut may cost less in fees than a standing coupon. Stacking needs a second look as well. Coupons, deals and price discounts can combine on one product, and each layer now carries its own fee, so the total matters more than any single layer.

Peak events sit outside all of this. Prime Day and other peak events keep flat fees, so the old logic still applies there, and a large deal during a peak event can still spread its fee over many units.

There is a pricing benefit in fewer standing discounts, too: shoppers who rarely see a coupon are more likely to read the full price as the real one, and promotions work better as events than as a permanent second price.

The test for any coupon still running: if the product is priced above $24 and nobody can show the sales the coupon adds, it now costs more than it used to and should come off. Building the promotion calendar around those fees is part of how we run Amazon promotions and advertising together for brands.

A0767.crumb: Walmart Connect after Vizio: what TV…
A0767.title: Walmart Connect after Vizio: what TV inventory adds for brands
A0767.alt: Pink living room at dusk with a glowing blank TV, linen sofa, grocery bag of vegetables and a patterned rug.
A0767.ttag: Walmart Connect after Vizio: what TV inventory adds for brands | Kwontified
A0767.desc: Walmart’s ad business grew 50% in early 2025 with Vizio included. Why linking TV screens to shopping data changes TV advertising for brands, and its limits.
A0767.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 10, 2025.
A0767.body:
Switch on a Vizio television and the home screen that greets you belongs to a company owned by Walmart. Walmart completed its $2.3 billion all-cash acquisition of Vizio on December 3, 2024, to help grow its advertising business, TechCrunch reported. For a brand, that screen raises a budgeting question: should money that used to buy TV for awareness now be bought through a retailer and judged on what shoppers purchase?

For brands that sell heavily at Walmart, it is worth testing. Walmart Connect after Vizio can target TV ads with shopping data and measure them against purchases at Walmart, which pulls part of brand advertising into retail media. The test should be sized for what the offer is now: early, partial in reach and measured only at one retailer.

What Walmart Connect after Vizio looks like

The platform came with an audience. Vizio’s SmartCast operating system had more than 19 million active accounts, up about 400% since 2018, and its Platform+ segment, largely advertising, accounted for all of Vizio’s gross profit, Walmart said in its announcement of the deal’s completion. Walmart said the deal would bring new ways for advertisers to reach customers through Walmart Connect.

The advertising numbers moved quickly after the close. Walmart’s global advertising business grew 50% in its first quarter, boosted by Vizio, and 27% on a comparable basis without it, its chief financial officer said, Marketing Dive reported. Walmart Connect, the US retail media business, which did not yet include Vizio, grew 31%.

Integration has started. At its April investor day, Walmart unveiled a beta offering that gives advertisers direct access to Vizio’s connected TV inventory, eMarketer reported.

The gap between those two growth rates shows how much the deal changed the business. Growth of 27% without Vizio and 50% with it suggests Vizio added a large share of the quarter’s advertising growth. That reflects new inventory joining Walmart’s business, and it gives Walmart a much bigger offer to put in front of brands.

Why a TV screen changes what a retailer can sell

Traditional TV advertising reaches large audiences but struggles to show which sales it caused. Retail media shows sales but has mostly lived on the retailer’s own website and app, close to the moment of purchase. The two have been bought for different reasons and judged on different numbers.

Vizio puts both under one owner. Walmart now controls a TV operating system in millions of homes along with the shopping data of a very large retailer, which allows TV ads to be targeted with that data and measured against purchases at Walmart. Many shoppers see a product on TV and buy it later in a store or online; linking the two lets a brand see that path rather than guess at it.

Read as an institution, Walmart is telling brands where it wants their money to sit. Budgets that once went to national TV for awareness can now be partly placed through a retailer and judged on sales. For a brand sold heavily at Walmart, that makes TV more accountable, and it gives the retailer a claim on money that used to sit outside retail media.

There is a competitive reading as well. Amazon has long combined streaming video advertising with shopping data, and Walmart’s move brings a second large retailer into that space, which may give brands more choice and better terms over time.

The limits a planning team should price in

Vizio’s audience is large but not universal. It reaches homes with Vizio TVs or SmartCast, not every viewer. Measurement covers purchases at Walmart, so for a brand sold widely it can understate the effect: a shopper who sees the ad and then buys on Amazon or at another store does not appear in Walmart’s reporting. And the offering is new, still being integrated with Walmart Connect, so targeting, inventory and measurement will keep changing.

Those limits shape the test. A controlled test with a clear goal, and a comparison group where possible, comes before any large commitment, funded from a test budget with an end date rather than taken from proven search advertising. Products with strong distribution and availability at Walmart are the right candidates, since that is where the measurement can see results. The scorecard should look past the last click to new-to-brand customers, total sales lift and repeat purchases at Walmart, with total sales trends across channels as the check on what Walmart’s numbers cannot see.

The rest of the media plan needs to know about it. Brands already buying streaming or traditional TV should avoid overlap and compare cost per new customer across channels. And the basics at Walmart have to be ready before a campaign airs. TV that sends shoppers to an unavailable or poorly presented listing wastes the money. A shopper who sees the brand on TV and later searches Walmart should find the brand’s own product page and search ads waiting, not a rival’s, so stock, pricing and pages need to be in order first.

The decision in the budget meeting

The question for the leadership team is less whether TV through Walmart works in general than whether the brand’s Walmart business is strong enough to make a retailer-measured TV test readable. A second question follows quickly: who owns the result when the brand team holds the TV budget and the e-commerce team holds Walmart? The answer may change as Walmart folds Vizio into Walmart Connect, so the plan deserves a fresh look as targeting, inventory and measurement develop. Settling that ownership before the test runs, and planning search, display and TV on Walmart as one budget, is how we plan Walmart Connect for brands.

A0770.title: Best Seller Rank volatility and what it means for brands
A0770.alt: Handmade wooden spinning top balanced on its brass tip on a rustic table, with other tops lying around it.
A0770.ttag: Best Seller Rank volatility and what it means for brands | Kwontified
A0770.desc: Amazon’s Best Seller Rank updates hourly and moves with rivals’ sales as well as yours. Why rank swings mislead after Prime Day, and what to track instead.
A0770.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 15, 2025.
A0770.body:
Prime Day 2025 drove an estimated $24.1 billion in US online spending over four days, up 30.3% from 2024, according to Adobe figures reported by Barron’s. Somewhere in that surge, a product that sold exactly as many units as it did the week before can watch its Best Seller Rank slide. Nothing went wrong with the product. Its neighbors sold more.

Best Seller Rank volatility comes from what the number is: a relative position, weighted toward recent sales, on a sales curve that is steep at the top and flat further down. It moves with competitors’ sales and with one-day spikes as much as with a brand’s own demand. Units, share of category sales and conversion tell a brand whether demand changed; rank, read over weeks, gives at most a rough trend.

Where Best Seller Rank volatility comes from

Amazon describes the calculation in a single sentence. Its Best Sellers calculation is based on Amazon sales and is updated hourly to reflect recent and historical sales of every item sold on Amazon, according to Amazon’s definition quoted by Helium 10.

Several properties follow from that definition and the way categories are shaped. Rank is a position, not a quantity, so it depends on how a product’s recent sales compare with every other product in its category. It can change when the brand’s own sales change, and also when competitors’ sales change while the brand’s stay put. Because recent sales count heavily, a single strong or weak day can move rank more than a steady trend does.

The shape of the category does the rest. In most categories, sales fall steeply as rank rises: the top few products sell far more than those ranked a little lower. Further down, many products sell similar amounts, so a small change in units moves a product past many others.

How a steady product’s rank swings

Take a category where the product at rank 50 sells about 20 units a day, rank 100 about 10 and rank 200 about 5. A product selling 10 a day sits near rank 100.

On its own deal day it sells 40, enough to jump well inside the top 50. When the deal ends, it drifts back toward rank 100, and its long-run demand never changed.

Now run it the other way. The product keeps selling 10 a day, but during an event many competitors run deals and sell more. Its rank slips toward 150 or 200 although its own sales are unchanged, and a team watching rank sees a decline that did not happen.

SituationOwn units a dayCompetitorsApproximate rankChange in the product’s demand
Ordinary day10No dealsNear 100None
Own deal day40No dealsInside the top 50A one-day spike
Competitors’ event10Running dealsToward 150 or 200None

Only the middle row reflects anything the brand did, and even that one fades the next day. The other two rows show the same product, with the same demand, at two very different ranks.

Rank also feels like a verdict, which is why it gets over-read. It is public, it updates constantly and it is easy to compare with rivals, so it is tempting to treat it as a score. A score that moves when competitors act, regardless of what the brand does, is a poor basis for decisions.

What to track instead of rank

The first measure is plain unit sales. Daily and weekly units, set against the matching days or weeks of the prior year, show whether demand changed, which rank on its own cannot. Where a brand can estimate the size of its category, share of category sales shows whether it is gaining or losing ground against rivals, the thing rank tries and often fails to show. Changes in traffic, or in the share of visitors who buy, explain sales movements better than rank does.

Rank still has uses if it is read slowly. Hourly or daily moves are mostly noise, and a smoothed trend over several weeks says more. Around Prime Day and other events, rank will move sharply for reasons that have little to do with lasting demand, so the sensible reading waits for it to settle. Ranks are only comparable within a category: a rank of 500 in a large category may mean far more sales than a rank of 50 in a small one. Rival sales estimates built on rank inherit its volatility, so averages over time beat single readings.

The expensive mistake is chasing rank with money. Cutting prices or raising advertising to recover a rank that fell because competitors ran deals spends money on a problem that may not exist. The warning signs that do deserve action are a sustained fall in units, a drop in conversion and the loss of the Buy Box, and those are the measures worth alerts.

Rank does matter, but only indirectly. Products that sell well tend to gain visibility, and a strong sales trend can support organic placement, but that benefit comes from the sales themselves, which is where the investment belongs. Executives often watch rank because it is visible, so reporting units, share and conversion beside it keeps a swing in rank from driving a hasty decision.

The rule for the week after any event: before anyone acts on a falling rank, check whether units fell. If they did not, the rank is reporting on your competitors. Separating real demand changes from rank noise is part of how we run Amazon channels for brands.

A0771.title: Back-to-school 2025: what an earlier season does to planning
A0771.alt: Olive canvas backpack, notebooks, pencils and a jar of pens on a linen-covered table near a window with a desk fan.
A0771.ttag: Back-to-school 2025: what an earlier season does to planning | Kwontified
A0771.desc: Two-thirds of back-to-school shoppers had started buying by early July 2025. How an earlier, longer season changes stock, advertising and pricing plans.
A0771.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 17, 2025.
A0771.body:
For years the back-to-school calendar inside many brand teams has been built around August: the school lists arrive, families head to the store, the season peaks in the last weeks before the first bell. In back-to-school 2025, two-thirds of shoppers had started buying before that calendar was meant to begin.

The season has stretched rather than shifted. Shoppers worried about tariff-driven price rises started in July, helped along by the summer deal events, and many still had most of their buying ahead of them. The result is a longer, flatter season with more price comparison along the way. Brands should be stocked and advertising by early July, pace both through September and judge the season as a whole rather than month by month.

How back-to-school 2025 started early

Two-thirds (67%) of back-to-school shoppers had already begun buying for the coming school year as of early July, the National Retail Federation said in its annual survey. That was up from 55% a year earlier and the highest share since the NRF began tracking early shopping in 2018. The survey covered 7,581 consumers from July 1 to 7.

Prices drove much of it. Half (51%) of back-to-school families were shopping earlier than in 2024 specifically out of concern that tariffs would raise prices, according to the same release.

Shoppers were also hunting for value. Discount stores rose five percentage points in popularity as a destination, Homepage News reported, citing the NRF. Budgets were restrained as well: Deloitte expected spending of about $570 per child, with shoppers focused on essentials, and found that four in 10 consumers showed signs of value-seeking, NBC Los Angeles reported.

The summer events gave those worries somewhere to go. Prime Day, Walmart Deals and Target Circle Week all ran in early July 2025, with back-to-school deals among their offers, so a family that wanted school supplies and clothing at a discount had every reason to buy early.

Why the season stretches instead of moving

When shoppers expect higher prices later, they buy sooner, and that pulls part of the season’s demand into July while many brands are still planning for August. An earlier start is not an earlier finish, though. Families who began in July still had most of their buying left, and many will keep shopping through August and into September as school lists arrive and needs become clear.

Value-seeking changes the path through those weeks. A shopper who compares prices across retailers and is willing to switch brands is harder to keep, and a brand that wins the first purchase in July can lose the second in August to a cheaper rival. Peak weeks still matter, but they carry less of the total, and the brands that do best are present and competitive throughout.

Some of the July spending was probably moved rather than added, replacing purchases that would otherwise have landed in August. A strong July can therefore make August look weak against 2024 without any loss of demand, which is why a month-by-month scorecard misreads this kind of season.

Planning the season backward from early July

Spring is now decision season. Orders, creative and promotional calendars need to be settled before most brands have traditionally begun back-to-school planning, because a brand that decides late will find shoppers already buying. Plans for 2026 should assume a start at least as early.

Early July is the start line. Stock should be in place and advertising running then, not in late July. Inventory needs to cover sustained demand from July through September rather than a single peak, with weekly sell-through checks and early replenishment of fast-moving items. Advertising should be paced across the longer window, weighted toward the summer events and the final weeks before school starts; spending everything early leaves a brand absent when late shoppers arrive.

August is where value decides the sale. With shoppers comparing prices and switching brands, prices and promotions need to be competitive on the items shoppers compare most, such as supplies and basics. Leading with must-have items and clear value works better than premium extras when budgets are focused on essentials, and bundles and multipacks help a family stretch the budget. Discount stores gained ground, so brands already in those channels should support them, and brands outside them should ask whether their range fits value-focused shoppers.

Rising costs complicate the middle of the season. They may push a brand to raise prices mid-season, and any increase has to be weighed against losing value-seeking shoppers. Running out of a key item at the moment shoppers are ready to buy is the other risk to manage in the same weeks.

Retention runs through all of it. A shopper who buys once may switch next time, so reviews, subscriptions for consumables and clear product information that makes the brand easy to choose again are worth the effort before the season ends.

September is for the scorecard. Comparing July through September combined with the same months of 2024, rather than judging each month alone, reads a strong July and a softer August correctly.

The question for the post-season review

When the team sits down after the season, the first question is whether the plan was built for the season shoppers actually ran or for the August peak on last year’s calendar. The follow-up questions are practical ones: which items ran short in the weeks shoppers were ready, which advertising was spent before the late shoppers arrived, and whether anyone is already setting the start date for the 2026 season. Building that longer season across Amazon, Walmart and Target, with stock and spend paced to it, is how we plan seasonal advertising for brands.

A0772.title: Prime Day 2025, measured: the result against our forecast
A0772.alt: Brass vernier caliper measuring a small kraft-paper gift tied with twine and dried flowers on a worn wooden table.
A0772.ttag: Prime Day 2025, measured: the result against our forecast | Kwontified
A0772.desc: Prime Day 2025 drew $24.1 billion online, just above our reach case. How we graded the forecast, and why added and pulled-forward sales need separating.
A0772.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 22, 2025.
A0772.body:
In June we published three cases for a four-day Prime Day. The actual landed above the highest of them. Prime Day 2025 drew an estimated $24.1 billion in US online spending, about 3% above our reach case, with the two added days drawing about 60% of a core day’s spending against the 55% we allowed.

Missing high is still a miss, and it is worth saying how. We had the shape right and the top of the range too low. The bigger lesson sits in the total itself: four days of sales mix the demand the event created with demand it moved from the days around it. Brands grading their own Prime Day should use a wider window, compared with the same window a year earlier.

How the Prime Day 2025 result compared with our cases

The headline was a record. Online spending across US retailers reached $24.1 billion from July 8 to 11, above Adobe’s own forecast, Reuters reported. The total was up 30.3% from 2024, according to Adobe data reported by Barron’s. The base was much smaller: the two-day 2024 event drew $14.2 billion in US online spending, according to Adobe figures cited by Chain Store Age.

Our June forecast started from that $14.2 billion base and grew it by 6% for the two core days, giving about $15.05 billion. It then assumed each added day would draw a share of a core day’s spending.

CaseAdded day as a share of a core dayFour-day total
Conservative25%about $18.8 billion
Standard40%about $21.1 billion
Reach55%about $23.3 billion
Resultabout 60% (implied)$24.1 billion

The result landed about $0.8 billion, or 3.3%, above the reach case. Holding the core-day assumption fixed, the added days drew about 60% of a core day. Either they were stronger than we allowed, or the core days grew faster than 6%, or both, and public figures do not let us separate the two.

The shape held. We argued that four days would not double the total, and $24.1 billion is about 1.7 times the 2024 base. We argued that spending per day would fall, and it did, to about $6.0 billion a day in 2025 against about $7.1 billion in 2024.

The upside is where we were wrong. Shoppers responded to the longer event more strongly than the reach case assumed, and the range was too narrow at the top. The pull behind that is a familiar one: a forecast anchored on last year’s two-day event tends to set its high case a step above that base rather than far enough. One result is one data point, though, and the opposite mistake would be to treat 2025 as the new baseline.

Why a four-day total overstates what the event created

When an event gets longer, it adds sales on the new days. Some of that demand would have happened on nearby days anyway: shoppers who see a sale coming wait for it, and shoppers who buy during it may buy less afterward. A four-day total therefore mixes demand the event created with demand it moved.

Adobe’s comparison hints at the size of the shift. Its 30.3% growth appears to compare the four days of 2025 with a comparable four-day window in 2024; if so, that window totaled about $18.5 billion. Take out the $14.2 billion from the two 2024 event days, and the two ordinary days in that window ran about $2.15 billion each.

In 2025 those two days were event days. At about 60% of a core day each, they brought in far more than the roughly $2.15 billion an ordinary July day would. Part of that gap is new demand, and part is demand moved from the days just before and after the event. Public figures cannot show the split, which is exactly why the four-day total is the wrong measure of what the event created. The better measure compares a wider window, such as two weeks before through two weeks after, with the same window a year earlier.

Grading your own Prime Day

The window comes first: sales from late June through late July against the same weeks of 2024, rather than four event days against two.

Inside that window, a few readings separate added demand from moved demand. Full-price sales in the weeks around the event, compared with the same weeks a year earlier, show whether deep-discount sales replaced purchases that would have happened at full price. The week after the event matters too; a sharp slump suggests demand was pulled forward, and the time sales take to return to normal shows how much. Sales to customers new to the brand are more likely to be added than moved, so new-to-brand sales deserve their own line.

Revenue over four days is also the wrong scoreboard for the business. Deals, fees and advertising during the event cost money, so the comparison that counts is profit over the wider window.

October deserves the same thinking. Amazon’s fall event will follow the same logic, so the added days may draw strongly again. Stock and budgets should still be planned for demand that also moves out of the weeks around the event, rather than on the assumption that every event sale is new. For our part, we will widen our range for future multi-day events.

The rule we are applying to our own forecast applies to any brand’s review: grade the event over a wider window than the event itself, against the same window a year earlier, and treat any single year as one data point. Setting up that window before the event starts is how we measure what tentpole events add for brands.

A0774.crumb: What Prime Day 2025 revealed about brands…
A0774.title: What Prime Day 2025 revealed about brands and retailers
A0774.alt: Red, blue and yellow paper shopping bags standing on a sunlit wooden table against a slate wall.
A0774.ttag: What Prime Day 2025 revealed about brands and retailers | Kwontified
A0774.desc: Prime Day 2025 showed platforms setting the calendar, rivals stacking sales around it and brands paying to join everywhere. What it means for planning.
A0774.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 24, 2025.
A0774.body:
In the second week of July 2025, a shopper could keep three sales open in three browser tabs. Target Circle Week ran from July 6 to 12, Walmart Deals from July 8 to 13, and Prime Day from July 8 to 11. For the brands selling in all three stores, the overlap raised a question that matters more than the sales total: who designed this week, and who paid for it?

What Prime Day 2025 revealed is a structure. The platform sets the calendar, rival retailers stack their own sales around it, and brands pay to take part everywhere at once through discounts, fees and advertising. That shifts costs and choices onto brands, and the brands that come out ahead decide deliberately where and how deeply to join each event instead of following every retailer’s lead.

What Prime Day 2025 revealed about who sets the calendar

Amazon wrote the rules before anyone else moved. In March it told sellers that Prime Day 2025 would double in length to four days, and that deals of 40% or more would receive expanded placement, according to a memo reported by Modern Retail.

Its rivals then built their own calendars around that decision, scheduling Target Circle Week and Walmart Deals to overlap Prime Day, Supermarket News reported. The combined week was large: shoppers spent $24.1 billion online with US retailers over July 8 to 11, more than Adobe itself had forecast, Reuters reported.

The cost of joining changed as well. From June 2, Amazon replaced flat fees for deals and coupons with a smaller fixed fee plus a share of the sales each promotion drives, Helium 10 reported.

Who gains from the overlap, and who pays

Amazon chose the dates, the length and the rules for which deals got the best placement, and every other participant reacted to those choices. Rival retailers did not pick a quiet week of their own. They scheduled sales on top of Amazon’s, betting that shoppers primed by Prime Day would compare prices across stores, and a single event became a summer sales week across the largest US retailers.

Shoppers adapted to the new shape of the week. With overlapping sales and a longer window, they had more reason to wait for the event and to compare across retailers once it began. Our own grading of the result found spending per day lower than in 2024, consistent with shoppers spreading purchases across a longer window.

Follow the value and the incentives line up. The platform designs the event to suit its goals: more members, more traffic and, with fees now tied to deal sales, more revenue from promotions. Walmart and Target gain from the overlap too, advertising deals to shoppers already in a buying mood without having to create that mood, which costs less than building a rival event from nothing.

Brands carry much of the cost. A brand sold at Amazon, Walmart and Target faced three overlapping events, each with its own deal rules, placement and fees. Joining all three meant discounting in three places at once; sitting one out meant risking lost visibility while rivals discounted. Brands absorb the discounts, fees and higher advertising costs while having little say in the design.

Events still do real work for brands. They bring in new customers, clear stock and lift sales, and a brand that skips one can lose ground to rivals that join. The loss is not the same in every channel or for every product, though, and the structure tilts the decision toward joining everything, everywhere, at maximum depth, which is rarely the most profitable choice. Careful measurement shows where joining pays and where it does not.

Deciding where to join and how deeply

The decision works best channel by channel and product by product, rather than on the assumption that a brand must take part everywhere. Depth deserves the same deliberation. The deepest discounts earned the best placement on Amazon, and the question is whether that placement brings enough new customers to justify the margin given up.

Overlapping events also make staggering possible. With rivals running sales in the same week, a brand does not need its deepest discount in every store at once; it can lead in one channel and hold price in another. Frequent deep discounts across every retailer teach shoppers to wait, so keeping events as events, rather than a permanent second price, protects full price everywhere else in the year.

Stock needs a channel plan of its own. Overlapping events can drain inventory in one store while another sits full, so allocating stock to each channel on its expected event demand, with a reserve for whichever sells fastest, keeps a promotion from becoming a stockout.

The scorecard has to match the structure. Discounts, deal fees, coupon fees and higher advertising costs all rise during events, so each event is judged on profit after all of them. Total sales across Amazon, Walmart and Target over the weeks around each event, measured against those weeks in 2024, show what the events added overall.

Events also give brands something to bargain with. Retailers want strong deals for their events, and a brand that plans early can trade deal depth for better placement, marketing support or terms rather than giving discounts away.

What to settle before October

Amazon’s fall event and the rival responses are likely to follow the same pattern. The question to put to the team now is simple: for each retailer and each lead product, are we joining because it pays, or because the calendar was set for us? Setting that channel-by-channel plan early, while the choices are still open, is how we plan retail events for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0776.crumb: Making sense of the retail media…
A0776.title: Making sense of the retail media explosion beyond Amazon
A0776.alt: Sunlit blue corridor lined with rows of colorful old metal mailboxes opposite tall arched windows.
A0776.ttag: Making sense of the retail media explosion beyond Amazon | Kwontified
A0776.desc: Dozens of retailers now sell ads, yet Amazon and Walmart take over 84% of US retail media spending. How brands should choose which other networks get budget.
A0776.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 31, 2025.
A0776.body:
The list of retailers that sell advertising now runs from grocers and drugstores to delivery apps and home improvement chains, and each of them is asking brands for a share of the advertising budget. For a brand team, the volume of pitches makes it feel as if the money has already moved. It has not.

The retail media explosion is in the number of networks, not in their share of spending. Amazon and Walmart are expected to hold more than 84% of what brands spend on US retail media in 2025, while all the other networks together gained less than a point of share in five years. Brands should treat Amazon and Walmart as the core and add other networks only where their own sales, a network’s unique shopper data and credible measurement justify it.

How retail media beyond Amazon grew, and where the money went

The two leaders kept growing. Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 18% in the first quarter of 2025, TheWrap reported. Walmart Connect, Walmart’s US retail media business, grew 31% in the same period, Marketing Dive reported.

Everyone else grew in number more than in share. An eMarketer forecast expected Amazon and Walmart together to take more than 84% of every US retail media dollar in 2025, as summarized by Sixteen:Nine. Between 2019 and 2024, all the other retail media networks combined added less than one percentage point of share, according to the same summary.

The result is two giants and a long tail. The grocers, drugstores, delivery apps and home improvement chains now selling advertising compete for a small and slowly growing share of budgets.

Why the long tail stays small

Retail media works best where shoppers already search and buy in large numbers, because that is where ads reach people ready to purchase and where results can be measured against sales. Amazon and Walmart have the most shoppers, the most searches and the most products, so they offer the most of what advertisers are paying for.

Smaller networks face a harder path. Each has fewer shoppers, and many sell a narrower range of products, so their ads reach fewer people and their measurement covers only purchases in their own stores. Every new network also brings another set of tools, reports and staff time on the brand’s side.

Inside the brand, budgets tend to follow sales. A brand that sells most of its online volume through Amazon and Walmart puts most of its retail media budget there, which leaves little for smaller networks unless they offer something distinctive. Nobody has to decide to starve the long tail; the budget process does it by default.

Some smaller networks do offer something distinctive, and it is usually data. A grocer’s loyalty card shows what households buy in stores every week. A delivery app sees meals and groceries ordered on demand. For brands sold heavily in those places, that view of the shopper can be worth paying for.

Off-site advertising complicates the picture. Many networks now sell ads that run outside their own stores, on other websites, apps and TV, targeted with their shopper data. That widens their reach but weakens the link between an ad and a sale in their store, which was retail media’s main advantage in the first place.

It is possible that the giants’ share partly reflects where brands have always spent, and that some smaller networks would perform better if given a fair chance. The way to find out is to test them on clear terms rather than to assume they will work or that they will not.

How to choose networks beyond Amazon and Walmart

Sales are the starting point. Ranking retailers by how much of the brand’s sales each one drives shows where budget can earn a return; a network attached to a retailer that sells little of the brand’s product rarely deserves much. For most brands that ranking puts Amazon and Walmart first, and their budgets get set before anything else. With Walmart Connect growing faster than Amazon’s advertising, brands selling well at Walmart should also check whether their budget there has kept pace.

Beyond the core, a network earns a test when it offers shopper data or audiences the brand cannot reach elsewhere, such as in-store purchase history. Measurement decides whether the test means anything. The questions are how the network measures results, whether it can show sales that would not have happened anyway, and whether it covers in-store as well as online purchases. Credible looks specific: a test with a holdout group that sees no ads, sales from new customers reported separately, and results shared at product level. Networks that offer only attributed sales totals deserve more caution.

Trials need terms of their own: a fixed budget, a clear goal and a set end date, with scale reserved for the networks that clear the bar. The hidden costs belong in that judgment too, since each network adds tools, reports and staff time. Smaller networks need advertisers, which gives a brand room to ask for better terms, data access or added support in return for a test.

The mix deserves a fresh look every year. Networks change quickly, and one that was not worth testing in 2024 may be worth testing in 2025 as a brand’s sales and the networks themselves change.

The question to bring to the next pitch

When the next network presents, the useful question is not how many shoppers it reaches but what it can show the brand that Amazon and Walmart cannot, and how it will prove the sales were added. Running that test discipline across every network a brand is offered is how we decide where retail media budgets belong.

A0778.crumb: Amazon’s Q2 2025 ad revenue and the…
A0778.title: Amazon’s Q2 2025 ad revenue and the competition for clicks
A0778.alt: A row of open cardboard boxes lined up along a teal wall in an empty room with a bright window.
A0778.ttag: Amazon’s Q2 2025 ad revenue and the competition for clicks | Kwontified
A0778.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 23% in Q2 2025 while online store sales grew 11%. Why that gap means a more crowded auction, and how brands should budget for it.
A0778.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 5, 2025.
A0778.body:
Amazon’s online store sales grew 11% in the second quarter of 2025. Its advertising revenue grew 23%. When the money spent to influence purchases grows much faster than the purchases themselves, someone is paying more for each sale, and in a self-serve auction that someone is the advertiser.

Amazon’s Q2 2025 ad revenue says the auction got more crowded: more bidders, or higher bids, for the same clicks. The practical answer is a budget that expects each sale to carry more advertising cost, with profit protected through conversion, targeting and organic strength rather than by bidding more.

What Amazon’s Q2 2025 ad revenue showed

Advertising led the quarter again. Amazon’s advertising segment brought in $15.6 billion in the second quarter, up 23% from a year earlier, Fortune reported. Online store sales grew 11% to $61.5 billion, and third-party seller services rose 11% to $40.3 billion, according to the same report. On the earnings call, Amazon put advertising growth at 22%, according to a transcript published by Investing.com.

The gap has held all year. In the first quarter, advertising revenue rose 18% while online stores grew 5%, TheWrap reported. Store growth picked up in the second quarter, and advertising grew faster still, which suggests more shoppers and more sales were not enough to absorb the extra advertising money.

Why the gap shows up as a higher price per click

Amazon sells most of its advertising through auctions. When more advertisers bid, or bid higher, for the same searches and placements, prices rise. When ad revenue outruns the store sales it is chasing, advertisers as a group are paying more to influence each dollar of sales.

A rough ratio makes the point. A year earlier, Amazon earned about 22.9 cents of advertising revenue for every dollar of online store sales; in the second quarter of 2025 it earned about 25.4 cents. The measure is imperfect, since advertising revenue includes video and other ads and online store sales exclude third-party sales. Its direction still matches what advertisers report, which is more competition for clicks.

Take a brand that spends 10% of its sales on advertising. If its advertising costs rise in line with Amazon’s 23% and its sales grow in line with Amazon’s 11%, its advertising cost rises to about 11.1% of sales. The brand sells more and keeps less of each sale.

MeasureA year earlierSecond quarter of 2025
Amazon advertising revenue per dollar of online store salesabout 22.9 centsabout 25.4 cents
Example brand’s advertising cost as a share of sales10%about 11.1%

Both rows move the same way for the same reason. The brand does not have to change anything for its share of sales spent on ads to climb; the auction does it as long as advertising money keeps growing faster than the sales it chases.

Some of the growth may come from new placements, such as more sponsored listings and video, rather than higher prices for existing ones, and more inventory can ease price pressure. The persistent gap between advertising growth and sales growth suggests competition is still rising anyway.

A brand can check which side of this it sits on in its own data. If cost per click rose faster than conversion rate, or advertising cost of sales rose while sales grew, the brand is feeling the crowded auction. If its advertising cost of sales held steady, it is probably gaining through conversion or targeting. Bidding alone cannot hold both the brand’s share of visibility and its profit when prices climb; one of them gives.

Where the margin comes back from

Budgets come first. Targets for total advertising cost of sales should assume rising prices instead of 2024’s efficiency, so a rising ratio reads as the market rather than a failure.

Conversion is the cheapest defense. A listing that converts better turns the same clicks into more sales, and better images, clearer titles, strong reviews and competitive prices all lower the effective cost of every click. Precision comes next: shifting spend toward the searches and audiences that convert best, and cutting terms that draw clicks but few sales, matters more when broad bidding pays the highest prices.

Organic strength reduces the bill. Products that rank well without advertising need less paid support, and sales history, availability and listing quality all help organic placement. On branded searches, bidding where rivals compete for the brand’s own terms makes sense, while paying heavily for shoppers who would find the brand anyway does not.

As costs rise, the gap between attributed sales and the sales ads truly created matters more, so incrementality tests deserve a place in the plan. Newer formats such as video may offer lower prices while competition is lighter and are worth testing against the cost of search ads. Brands with strong sales elsewhere should also check whether Walmart or other networks offer better returns at the margin.

The fall needs its own budget logic. The second quarter did not include Prime Day, which fell in July, and Amazon’s fall event was held in October in both 2023 and 2024. Event weeks bring the most bidders of all, so event budgets should assume higher prices per click and name in advance which products and terms deserve the extra spend. Prices need the same review, because rising advertising costs alongside fees squeeze margins.

The test to run before raising any bid: if the brand’s advertising cost of sales rose while its conversion rate did not, the money is going to the auction, and the next dollar belongs in the listing. Holding that line campaign by campaign is how we keep Amazon advertising profitable as auctions get more crowded.

A0779.crumb: Why perfect ratings don’t win launches…
A0779.title: Why perfect ratings don’t win launches anymore
A0779.alt: Five gold stars lined up on a rustic wooden shelf beside a plain shipping box against a mustard wall.
A0779.ttag: Why perfect ratings don’t win launches anymore | Kwontified
A0779.desc: Shoppers buy most at 4.2 to 4.5 stars, and fake reviews now carry federal penalties. Why a perfect launch rating is a warning sign, and what wins instead.
A0779.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 7, 2025.
A0779.body:
Some new product pages give away how the launch was run before a shopper reads a word: a few dozen reviews, every one of them five stars. Inside the brand, that page can look like a win on the launch dashboard. To the shopper deciding whether to spend money, it raises a simpler question: are these real?

Shoppers have long been most likely to buy products rated a little below perfect, and since October 2024 a federal rule has penalized fake and suppressed reviews. Together those make a near-perfect rating on a new product read as a warning sign rather than a strength. Launches are won with credible review volume, honest detail and strong content, not with a flawless score.

How perfect ratings lost their pull with shoppers

Shoppers have distrusted perfection for a long time. Across more than 40 categories, purchase likelihood peaks when a product’s average rating is between 4.2 and 4.5 stars and falls as ratings approach a perfect 5, according to a study by Northwestern University’s Spiegel Research Center using PowerReviews data. Negative reviews help establish trust, the center found, citing earlier PowerReviews research that 82% of shoppers seek them out. The study dates from around 2015, but its finding has held up as a reference point for the industry.

The same study found that star ratings matter most for expensive products in high-consideration categories, because reviews reduce the risk of a costly mistake. For a premium launch, shoppers read reviews closely, and a suspiciously perfect score can cost more sales than it wins.

How the rules changed the cost of chasing five stars

The Federal Trade Commission announced a final rule on August 14, 2024, banning fake reviews, the buying and selling of reviews, undisclosed insider reviews and the suppression of negative reviews, with fake reviews written by AI covered too, Mintz reported. The rule took effect on October 21, 2024, and lets the FTC seek civil penalties of up to $51,744 per violation, Mondaq reported.

Before the rule, aggressive review tactics carried reputational risk. Now they carry legal risk as well. A brand that once pushed for a flawless launch rating through incentives or by filtering out complaints now faces real penalties, which makes the honest path the safe one too.

Why a perfect launch rating looks suspicious

Shoppers use reviews to judge risk, and experienced shoppers know that genuine customers rarely agree perfectly. A small share of critical reviews makes the rest more believable, because it shows the brand let unhappy buyers speak and gives the next shopper a sense of what could go wrong. A page with no criticism at all removes that evidence and leaves the shopper guessing.

New products are where this bites hardest. An established product has years of reviews, so a high rating rests on a large base. A new product has few reviews and each one carries more weight, so a perfect score from a small base looks less like quality and more like curation.

The first critical review is the moment many launches go wrong. The instinct inside the brand is to bury it under positive ones, and shoppers can read that pattern as easily as the brand can. A brand that answers the criticism openly usually earns more trust than one that drowns it out.

None of this argues for aiming low. A higher rating still beats a much lower one, and ratings below 4 can hurt badly. What has changed is the goal. A launch used to be judged partly on how close its rating came to perfect; now shoppers and regulators both reward authenticity, and what wins is enough credible reviews to make the rating meaningful, with the detail that helps a shopper decide.

What a credible launch looks like

Volume matters more than perfection. The work is gathering enough genuine reviews to make a rating credible, through approved programs such as a retailer’s early-reviewer program where one exists. Review requests should go to every buyer in the same way; asking only satisfied customers, or filtering complaints, risks breaking the FTC rule. Reviews from employees, family or partners must be disclosed under the rule, and the simplest policy is to keep them out entirely.

Criticism is information. A thoughtful reply to a critical review shows care and helps the next shopper, and the brand can fix real problems and explain misunderstandings. Many critical reviews come from mismatched expectations about size, fit, use or ingredients, so clear images, specifications and answers in the listing prevent a share of them before they are written. Early critical reviews are also free product feedback, and a brand that fixes problems quickly can lift both its rating and its credibility.

Partners need checking as well. Any agency, tool or program used for reviews should follow the FTC rule, because the brand can bear the consequences of a partner’s tactics.

The number to put on the launch dashboard

Take two launches: one converting well at 4.4 stars, the other stuck at 5.0 with few sales. The first is doing better, and a dashboard that celebrates the second is measuring the wrong thing. The question for the launch review is whether the team can show how the rating and reviews are moving sales, rather than the rating alone.

Three checks belong beside it. The product needs enough genuine reviews for a shopper to trust the average. Requests should have gone to every buyer in the same way. And the first critical review should have had an open answer from the brand, not an attempt to bury it. Planning a launch around that measure from the first review request onward is how we run product launches for brands.

A0780.title: Q4 2025 budget: phasing spend from October through Cyber Week
A0780.alt: Glass jars of coins in rising sizes on a windowsill between a small pumpkin and a twine-wrapped gift.
A0780.ttag: Q4 2025 budget: phasing spend from October through Cyber Week | Kwontified
A0780.desc: Cyber Week drove 17% of 2024 holiday online spending in five days. How to phase a Q4 2025 ad budget from October to Cyber Week by sales and efficiency.
A0780.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 12, 2025.
A0780.body:
Five days out of 61 produced about 17% of the 2024 holiday season’s online spending. That is the case for putting the biggest share of a Q4 budget into Cyber Week, and it is right as far as it goes. The catch is that every other advertiser reads the same number, so the price of each click rises with the crowd.

A peak dollar pays only where conversion rises faster than cost per click. The Q4 2025 budget should therefore follow expected sales adjusted for efficiency, building from October through Cyber Week, with each period capped where the next dollar stops earning its target.

What the 2024 season says about the Q4 2025 budget

The season was large. From November 1 to December 31, 2024, US consumers spent $241.4 billion online, up 8.7%, according to Adobe data reported by Homepage News. Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, brought in $41.1 billion, up 8.2%, and Cyber Monday alone drove $13.3 billion, according to the same report. Black Friday reached $10.8 billion and Thanksgiving $6.1 billion, according to Adobe figures reported by MT Newswires.

The plan has to absorb how unevenly that money arrived. Cyber Week accounted for about 17% of the season’s online spending in five of its 61 days. Each Cyber Week day averaged about $8.2 billion in spending, against about $3.6 billion on the other days of the season, roughly 2.3 times as much.

More shoppers, and a higher price to reach them

More shoppers buy during peak weeks, so more advertising budget belongs there. Advertisers know this, though, and they bid more for the same placements, so the price of each click rises alongside demand. Whether a peak week pays depends on which rises faster. If conversion outpaces cost per click, each advertising dollar earns more. If cost per click outpaces conversion, each dollar earns less, even though sales are higher.

Take a brand whose cost per click rises 40% during Cyber Week. If its conversion rate rises 60%, its efficiency improves by a factor of about 1.14, so it gets more sales per dollar. If its conversion rate rises only 20%, its efficiency falls to about 0.86 of normal: fewer sales per dollar in a busier week.

Both paths through that choice carry a real cost. Spending heavily in the peak buys share of the biggest days, and a brand that holds back can watch rivals take the traffic. Spending heavily where efficiency falls buys sales at a worse price than the same money would earn earlier in the quarter. The numbers lean toward funding the peak in proportion to the brand’s own conversion history, not in proportion to the calendar.

The same logic runs across products. A brand’s best-selling products often see the steepest rise in click prices, because rivals target the same searches, while smaller products may see smaller price rises and better efficiency. A good plan phases budget by product as well as by week.

Competition sharpens all of this in 2025. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew faster than its store sales through the first half of 2025, as our post on its second-quarter results showed, which suggests peak-week click prices will be higher than in 2024. The plan should assume that, not 2024’s prices.

Phasing the quarter week by week

The starting point is the brand’s own 2024 curve: sales and advertising efficiency mapped week by week from October through December, showing where demand rose and whether efficiency rose with it.

October is built around Amazon’s fall event. Amazon held its fall deal event in October in 2023 and 2024, and budgeting for the event and the days around it can lift sales and build reviews and sales history ahead of the holidays. The weeks before Thanksgiving are a chance to grow awareness and capture early shoppers at lower prices per click than Cyber Week, and spending there can lift organic rank and build audiences to retarget later.

Cyber Week gets the highest daily budget, at a level set by the brand’s own history of conversion against cost per click. Products that convert strongly during deals warrant more; products that do not should be held back. Daily budgets need to be high enough to stay live through peak hours, because a budget that runs out by midday misses the evening, with caps tied to returns rather than to habit.

The December tail depends on shipping cutoffs. Advertising should run through the last reliable delivery dates, then shift toward products with faster delivery, or toward gift cards, which a shopper who missed the cutoff can still give on the day.

Creative and listings, including images, video and deal pages, should be ready before October, because changes made during peak weeks can take time to approve and miss the busiest days. A reserve kept unallocated can move toward whatever is converting best as results come in. Peak budgets should be tied to inventory, since advertising products that sell out wastes money and can hurt rank.

Walmart and Target run their own events, so marginal returns are worth comparing across channels, with budget shifted to wherever the next dollar earns most. And because peak weeks pull some demand from nearby weeks, the quarter is judged on total profit from October through December rather than on Cyber Week alone. A Cyber Week that looks brilliant in isolation may simply have borrowed sales from the weeks around it.

Fund every period in the plan by expected sales adjusted for efficiency, and stop adding budget where the return on the next dollar falls below target. Phasing a quarter that way, product by product, is how we plan Q4 advertising budgets for brands.

A0782.crumb: Why product data quality is now an…
A0782.title: Why product data quality is now an advertising decision
A0782.alt: Open oak filing cabinet drawer full of pastel hanging folders in a sunlit room with a wicker basket.
A0782.ttag: Why product data quality is now an advertising decision | Kwontified
A0782.desc: AI shopping assistants and ad systems both read product listings. Why product data quality now decides where brands appear, and why it belongs in the ad budget.
A0782.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 14, 2025.
A0782.body:
A shopper who once scrolled a page of results now often types a question instead: which of these is easiest to clean, which fits a small kitchen, which is safe for sensitive skin. Whatever answers that question replies from what the listing and its reviews say. A product whose listing never mentions the feature is less likely to be named, however good it is.

Ad systems read the same listing. That puts product data quality in a new place. It decides where a brand’s products are recommended and where its ads appear, which makes it an advertising decision, with a place in the media plan and its budget.

Product data quality now feeds the answer and the ad

The assistants arrived inside the store first. Amazon made its AI shopping assistant, Rufus, available to all US customers in its app after testing it with tens of millions of questions, Swipe Insight reported. Rufus answers product questions using product listing details, customer reviews and community Q&As, according to the same report. In effect the assistant reads the page for the shopper.

Shoppers took the habit outside the store as well. Traffic to US retail sites from generative AI sources rose 1,200% between July 2024 and February 2025, Adobe reported. In April, OpenAI began showing products and buy links in ChatGPT, saying the results were chosen independently and were not ads, PYMNTS reported. For anyone holding a media budget, that last detail is the uncomfortable one. A brand cannot bid its way into that answer; what it can shape is the information available about its product.

Advertising works from the same material. Automated targeting on retail platforms matches ads to searches and products partly by reading listing titles, descriptions and attributes. A listing with incomplete or vague data gives the system less to match on, so ads show for fewer relevant searches or for the wrong ones. The title, bullets, attributes and images now feed organic search, AI answers and ad matching at once. Improving them lifts all three; neglecting them weakens all three, and no amount of bidding fully makes up for it.

The listing sits with one team and the budget with another

The org chart has not moved as fast as the shopper. At many brands, listings belong to a catalog or e-commerce operations team, while advertising belongs to a media team with its own budget and its own targets. Each team is doing the job it was given. The trouble sits in the queue between them: data fixes wait their turn while media spending continues, and the brand pays to send traffic to listings that cannot answer the questions shoppers arrive with.

The split shows up in the reports each team reads. The media team sees irrelevant search terms in its ad reports. The catalog team may never see those reports at all, although an irrelevant search term can point to a listing the system misread. When nobody owns that connection, the same gap keeps getting paid for.

Media teams will answer that advertising still buys placement that data alone cannot, and they are right about that. Placement pays only if the listing converts and if the system can match the ad to the right shopper, though, and both depend on the data. Product data has become the input that decides where a product shows up, in answers and in ads.

What changes when product data is funded like media

Start with who pays. When a listing fix will raise conversion and improve ad matching, it deserves funding alongside media, and the fair comparison is between a data improvement and the next increment of ad spending. Put that way, the listing stops being a catalog chore and becomes a line in the media plan.

The work itself starts from the shopper’s questions rather than from keyword lists. List the questions shoppers ask in the category, drawn from reviews, Q&As and search terms, and check whether each listing answers them clearly. Recurring questions in reviews and Q&As point to missing information, and the answer belongs on the listing itself. Assistants interpret content rather than counting words, so titles and bullets should state plainly what the product is, who it is for and what makes it different.

Structured fields carry more weight than they used to. Size, material, ingredients, compatibility and use case are easy for systems to read, and missing attributes leave products out of filtered searches and AI answers. Images and video count as data too. Pictures that show size, use and key features answer questions before shoppers ask them, and text on images or in captions can carry details that are hard to fit in bullets. Every claim in the visuals should also be stated in text, where systems can read it.

Consistency across channels is the last piece of the work. Conflicting details between Amazon, Walmart, a brand’s own site and other sources confuse both shoppers and AI systems, which is the case for keeping one accurate source of product data.

Where to begin is the easy part. Fix the listings of the top sellers and the most advertised products first, where better data pays back fastest, and have the catalog and advertising teams review those products together so that what the ad reports reveal turns into listing fixes. Track conversion, ad relevance and the share of searches where the products appear, before and after each change, to show what data quality returns.

The harder question belongs to the leadership team: when did anyone last read your top listings the way an assistant reads them, and whose budget would pay to fix what they found? Putting catalog and media on the same plan is how we run a brand’s marketplace channels day to day.

A0784.crumb: Brand integrity on TikTok Shop: control…
A0784.title: Brand integrity on TikTok Shop: control who sells and who earns
A0784.alt: Leather handbags displayed on glass shelves inside a locked glass cabinet with a brass key in the lock.
A0784.ttag: Brand integrity on TikTok Shop: control who sells and who earns | Kwontified
A0784.desc: On TikTok Shop, creators promote whichever seller pays them most. Why that invites undercutting and fakes, and how brands keep control of who sells.
A0784.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 19, 2025.
A0784.body:
A creator about to post a video for a popular product often has more than one listing to tag. Take two listings for the same product. The brand’s own shop sells the product at $30 and pays creators a 10% commission. An unauthorized seller lists the same product at $25 and pays 20%.

Brand’s own shopUnauthorized seller
Price to the shopper$30$25
Creator commission rate10%20%
Creator earns per sale$3$5

The creator earns $5 a sale instead of $3, and the lower price converts better too. Unless the brand acts, its traffic flows to the other seller. That comparison decides brand integrity on TikTok Shop. The platform removes fakes by the million, but creators still earn commission from whichever seller lists a product, so whoever controls the best offer controls the traffic.

How TikTok Shop polices brand integrity, and where that stops

The platform enforces heavily. TikTok Shop’s first intellectual property report showed that 5,240,184 products were rejected from going live and 497,026 were removed from livestreams between July 2023 and June 2024, Interaksyon reported. For branded products, TikTok Shop requires sellers to obtain a letter of authorization from the brand owner or authorized resellers, according to the same report.

Enforcement kept growing after that. Between July and December 2024, TikTok Shop prevented more than 7.5 million products from being listed for intellectual property violations, according to its safety report as summarized by MediaPost. It also removed e-commerce features from more than 700,000 creators and removed more than 450,000 sellers, according to the same report.

Enforcement on that scale addresses fakes, and it is tempting to stop there. It does not touch the arithmetic in the table. Authorized or semi-authorized sellers can still undercut each other on a genuine product, and enforcement often follows a report rather than preventing the problem. Removing fakes does not decide what a genuine product sells for, or which seller a creator tags.

Creators follow the commission

On TikTok Shop, creators promote products and earn a commission on what they sell, and they can usually choose which seller’s listing to promote. Their incentive is to pick the listing that pays them the most, or the one that converts best because its price is lowest.

That makes a brand’s best-known product the most attractive target for other sellers, since it is the one creators most want to promote. A creator choosing which listing to tag sees the price, the commission and perhaps the seller’s rating. A fast-moving creator posting many videos a week will rarely check who the seller is, so the listing that pays more and sells faster wins by default.

The cost to the brand compounds. Each sale through an unauthorized seller is a sale the brand did not make, at a price that resets what shoppers expect to pay. If the product is fake, the brand’s reputation takes the damage as well. And if enough creators switch, the brand’s own shop loses the sales history that helps it rank, which makes it less attractive to the next creator who goes looking for a listing.

Letters of authorization decide who sells

Supply is the lever a brand holds most directly. Brands should register their trademarks in TikTok Shop’s intellectual property tools and use them to report infringing listings quickly. Because branded products require authorization, letters of authorization are the gate: issue them only to sellers the brand approves, track who holds them, and withdraw them from sellers who break pricing or quality rules.

Brands that sell through distributors also need clear policies on minimum advertised prices and on which channels resellers may use, and they need to act when those policies are broken. Unauthorized sellers often buy stock from other retailers or distributors, so tracing where leaked stock comes from closes the gap at its source.

Speed matters as much as the rules. A takedown that comes weeks late lets an unauthorized seller keep the sales history it built, which is why someone should own the job of reviewing and reporting violations each week.

That person needs eyes on three places. TikTok Shop search shows who is selling the product and at what price. Creator videos reveal the ones promoting unauthorized sellers. Reviews carry the complaints about quality, packaging or smell that often signal fakes worth investigating and reporting.

Viral moments attract copycats fast, so monitoring and reporting have to be in place before a product takes off, not after.

Making the brand’s shop the best offer

Control of supply only narrows the field. Even with every unauthorized listing gone, authorized sellers can still compete for the same creators, so the table still has to favor the brand. Brands should offer competitive commissions, free samples and exclusive content through their own shop, so creators have every reason to promote it.

Creators who work directly with a brand, on agreed terms and with support, are also less likely to switch to a rival seller for a slightly higher commission. Direct relationships change the comparison in the table, because the creator is weighing a partner against a stranger instead of $3 against $5. A creator with a standing arrangement has something to lose by tagging the cheaper listing; a creator without one has only the commission to look at.

Whether all of this is working is visible in one number, the share of a product’s TikTok Shop sales that go through the brand’s own shop rather than other sellers. A falling share is the earliest sign that creators are being drawn elsewhere. Tracking that share, and treating any decline as a pricing or commission problem to fix, is how we manage TikTok Shop for brands that want control of their sellers.
