A0785.crumb: AI and personalization on Target Plus: a…
A0785.title: AI and personalization on Target Plus: a curated marketplace
A0785.alt: White robotic arm placing a red wrapped gift onto a book on a wooden wall shelf beside a small vase.
A0785.ttag: AI and personalization on Target Plus: a curated marketplace | Kwontified
A0785.desc: Target plans to grow Target Plus fivefold by 2030 with AI-driven personalization and loyalty data. What that means for brands on a curated marketplace.
A0785.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 21, 2025.
A0785.body:
Walk into a Target and the store has already made most of the choices for you. The endcaps, the seasonal tables and the narrow run of brands on each shelf are an edit. Target Plus, the retailer’s online marketplace, works the same way: sellers join by invitation, and the assortment stays close to what Target already sells.

What changes is the scale Target now wants from that edit. The retailer plans to grow Target Plus from about $1 billion in sales to more than $5 billion, while using AI to personalize search and offers around its Circle loyalty program. On a marketplace built like that, reach goes to the products Target’s personalization chooses to show, so the brands that grow will be the ones that give those systems the most to work with.

How AI and personalization on Target Plus fit Target’s plan

Target set out its plan in March 2025. Its priorities include using AI to improve search and data-driven personalization, a dramatic expansion of Target Plus and a doubling of the value generated by its Roundel media business, Retail TouchPoints reported.

The marketplace targets are large. Target plans to increase Target Plus from about $1 billion in 2024 sales to more than $5 billion by the end of the decade, adding brands such as Peloton, Daily Harvest and Honest Baby Clothing, according to the same report. Advertising is tied in as well. In 2024 Roundel drove more than $2 billion in value, and Target plans to double it, partly by creating more personalized connections and integrating further with Target Plus and the Target Circle loyalty program, according to the same report.

Read those three priorities together and they describe one machine. Circle tells Target what households buy in stores and online. AI search and personalization use that knowledge to decide which products a shopper sees. Roundel sells brands access to the same shoppers. The data that connects all three is Target’s.

A curated marketplace rewards fit over volume

Target Plus admits sellers by invitation only. Target chooses which sellers and brands join, rather than opening the doors to anyone, which keeps the assortment narrower and more consistent with the rest of the store. On a huge open marketplace, shoppers search through millions of options and ranking does much of the work. On a curated marketplace, the retailer can do more of the choosing, suggesting products based on what a shopper has bought, what they browse and what they earn rewards on through Circle.

Target’s shoppers lean toward that kind of help. Many come to browse and discover rather than to find a single item at the lowest price, which makes recommendation and personalization more powerful than on a store built around price comparison. Price works differently as a result. On an open marketplace the lowest price often wins the sale; on a curated one, shoppers compare fewer options and weigh quality, style and trust alongside price. That gives brands more room to hold price, as long as the product clearly fits what Target’s shoppers came for.

So the path to reach changes shape. On an open marketplace, a brand grows by listing more products and bidding more. On Target Plus, it grows by being the kind of product Target’s personalization chooses to show, to the shoppers most likely to want it. Brands sold through Target Plus can reach Circle shoppers when Target’s systems judge them a good match, and through Roundel when they pay to.

Target keeps the loyalty data, the shopper relationship and the media revenue from that loop, while the brand gets access to a high-intent audience on Target’s terms. It is a different deal from an open marketplace, and it should be judged on its own numbers. Target Plus is still small, at about $1 billion in 2024, and its plans run to 2030, so it belongs in the plan as a growing channel with specific rules rather than as a replacement for larger marketplaces.

What brands bring to Target’s edit

Fit comes before everything else. Brands should offer products that suit Target’s style and its discovery-led shoppers, and show how they complement what Target already sells. Brands new to Target Plus should launch with a focused range of the products that fit Target’s shoppers most closely, learning how personalization treats them and expanding from there.

Target’s systems need material to work with. Personalization and AI-driven search depend on detailed, accurate product information, so every attribute should be complete, use cases described clearly and images strong. Personalization systems often favor products with a track record of satisfied buyers, which makes early, genuine reviews gathered through approved programs part of the launch. Shoppers who see a product on Target Plus may check it elsewhere too, so prices, product details and images need to match across channels if the comparison is not to cost the sale.

Roundel is where the loyalty data becomes reachable. It can target shoppers using Target’s first-party data, and campaigns aimed at Circle audiences most likely to buy the category are the natural first test. Target Circle Week and seasonal moments drive traffic and personalization, so promotions and stock should line up with Target’s events.

A curated marketplace also notices how a brand operates. Late deliveries, stock-outs and poor service undermine it, and Target holds sellers to high standards, which turns fulfillment into part of the marketing. Working closely with Target’s team matters more here than on an open marketplace: sharing plans, product launches and performance openly. Measurement shifts as well. Because personalization shapes visibility, the useful number is how often products are recommended and to whom, where Target’s reporting allows, alongside search rank.

The question for a leadership team weighing Target Plus is less about the channel’s current size than about whether the brand is the kind of product Target’s machine wants to show. Answering it honestly, assortment first, is how we help brands plan a Target Plus launch alongside Roundel.

A0786.title: Shared insights between retailers and brands: what the data buys
A0786.alt: Open blank notebook with red and blue pens between two cups of coffee on a wooden cafe table by a window.
A0786.ttag: Shared insights between retailers and brands: what the data buys | Kwontified
A0786.desc: Retailers share shopper data with brands in tiers, keeping raw data and releasing answers. Why insight access is worth negotiating, and how to use it.
A0786.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 26, 2025.
A0786.body:
Shopper data is one of the most valuable things a retailer owns, and yet retailers keep offering it to the brands they sell. Walmart has given suppliers a basic version of its insights service at no added cost. Why would a retailer hand over its best asset?

It doesn’t. Retailers keep the raw data and release answers to questions, in tiers, with the deeper tiers costing more or tied to advertising. The giveaway is a sales tool: insight helps brands spend more effectively on the retailer’s own media, which is exactly what the retailer wants. For a brand, the value of shared insights depends on which tier it can reach and on how good its questions are.

How shared insights between retailers and brands are packaged

Walmart’s service shows the pattern. In October 2024, Walmart said its supplier insights service, Luminate, would be renamed Scintilla, and it opened Insights Activation, which applies those insights to display campaigns on Walmart Connect, to all charter subscribers, Talk Business & Politics reported. The basic form of Luminate came at no added cost to suppliers, while the charter version required a subscription, according to the same report. Walmart rebranded Luminate as Scintilla on February 5, 2025, 8th & Walton reported.

The free layer reports and the paid layer explains shoppers, while the activation feature links the paid layer straight to the retailer’s ad business. That last step makes the logic visible. The insight and the media buy sit side by side because each makes the other more likely.

Answers, not records, released in tiers

Retailers rarely hand data over. They share answers: how many shoppers bought a brand, how often they returned, what else they bought, which rivals they switched from. Those answers come from privacy-safe systems that release aggregates rather than individual records, and the retailer decides what each tier reveals. Basic reporting often comes free, covering sales and inventory. Deeper insight into shopper behavior, switching and audiences often comes through paid subscriptions or is tied to advertising spend.

Seen from the retailer’s side, every part of that design is rational. Insight helps brands spend more effectively on the retailer’s media, stock the right products and run better promotions, and all of that grows the retailer’s sales and advertising revenue. Insight is, in part, a tool to keep brands investing. Charging for the deeper tiers, or bundling them with spend, also tends to route the most useful answers to the brands that already invest most.

Privacy rules then shape what comes back. Systems that release aggregates usually set minimum group sizes, so small audiences or narrow questions may return no answer at all. Brands with smaller sales at a retailer may find the deepest insights less useful, because their groups of buyers are too small to report on.

What one answer can be worth

The case for paying rests on arithmetic like this. Take a brand with 10,000 first-time buyers a year at a retailer. Deeper insight shows its repeat rate is 25%, against a category rate of 35%. Targeted follow-up that closes half of that gap adds 5 points of repeat purchase.

StepFigure
First-time buyers a year10,000
Brand’s repeat rate25%
Category repeat rate35%
Repeat rate gained by closing half the gap5 points
Additional repeat buyers500
Value at $40 per repeat purchase$20,000 a year

That is about $20,000 a year from one insight, before counting what those customers buy later. The same insight is worth nothing if no one acts on it. Paying for deeper insight costs money; not paying leaves a brand deciding with less information than rivals who do. Even the deepest tier is only worth the question asked and the action taken.

An insight drawn from aggregated data can also mislead if the group behind it differs from the shoppers a brand targets. That is why a small test belongs between the insight and any large budget change: a targeted campaign, a pack size change, a price change or a new product placement, with the result tracked.

Buying insight like a media line

Brands committing significant budgets are in a position to ask for more than placements, because retailers want advertising and promotional investment. Insight access, data support or analytical help can be part of that deal, which starts with knowing what each retailer’s free and paid tiers reveal and what deeper access would add.

The questions come before the dashboards. Decide what the team needs to know, such as why buyers lapse, where they come from or what they buy instead, and then find the insight that answers it. Each retailer shares different data in different ways, so comparing what a brand learns at Amazon, Walmart and Target shows which patterns hold across channels. Brands with their own customer data can learn more by comparing it with retailer insights, within each retailer’s privacy rules.

Insight platforms reward teams who can ask precise questions and read aggregated data correctly, so the skill is worth investing in, through analysts or partners. Insights also lose value when they live in one person’s inbox; a simple log of each question, the answer and the action taken carries lessons across seasons and staff changes. Retailers also value brands that bring ideas backed by data, and sharing a category trend a brand has spotted can strengthen the relationship and open further access.

The test for every paid tier is the one in the table: compare its cost with the value of the decisions it improves, and drop any tier that does not pay. Running that comparison retailer by retailer is how we measure what retailer insights are worth to brands.

A0788.crumb: Prime Big Deal Days 2025: who decides…
A0788.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2025: who decides, and when
A0788.alt: Stack of kraft-paper parcels and a leather folio on a wooden table between two chairs by autumn windows.
A0788.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2025: who decides, and when | Kwontified
A0788.desc: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 deal submissions close September 12, weeks before the October event. Who should decide deal depth, stock and budget, and when.
A0788.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Aug 28, 2025.
A0788.body:
The decision about a brand’s October deals usually gets made by whoever owns the deal submission when the window opens. At many brands that is a marketplace or e-commerce manager, working through a list of products and discount levels in late summer, weeks before finance, operations or the advertising team have looked at the event. Nobody planned it that way; the deadline arranged it.

For Prime Big Deal Days 2025, that deadline is September 12. Deal depth, inventory and budget all get settled by then, which makes the first question who decides, and how early they start.

How Prime Big Deal Days 2025 sets the calendar

Submissions for Prime Big Deal Days Best Deals and Lightning Deals are open and close on September 12, EcommerceBytes reported, as Amazon published its holiday schedule for sellers. For Prime Day and other peak events, Amazon kept deal fees flat at $500 for a Lightning Deal and $1,000 for a Best Deal, even as it moved everyday deals to performance-based fees, Modern Retail reported after Amazon’s March 2025 announcement.

Amazon sets deadlines for deals and stock well ahead of an event so that it can run, and those deadlines fall weeks before the shopping does. A brand that wants a deal in October has to commit its price, its units and its stock in late summer, often before it has fully reviewed how Prime Day went in July.

The person who owns the deadline makes the call

Organizations bend around a deadline like that. The person who owns the deal submission faces the first deadline and makes the first decision. Finance may not see the discount until it has been submitted, and operations may learn the unit commitment only when stock needs to move. Advertising may plan its budget after the deal is already fixed. Each team then inherits a choice it did not make and works around it.

The mistakes that follow are predictable. Deals are set at a depth that wins placement but loses money once fees and advertising are counted. Stock is committed to Amazon that would have sold better in another channel. Advertising budgets are set without knowing which products will carry deals.

Take a product that sells at $40 with a $14 margin. A 30% deal cuts the price to $28 and the margin to $2. If the deal sells 400 units, the $1,000 Best Deal fee alone takes $2.50 per unit, which turns the margin negative before a dollar of advertising. A marketplace manager chasing placement might submit that deal. Finance, looking at the same numbers, might not.

None of this is careless behavior. Deadlines reward whoever acts first, and no single team owns the whole decision. Speed matters too, and the obvious fix, a committee, can miss a deadline as easily as it can improve a choice. What the October event needs is a clear owner with a short, agreed process, because the decision touches margin, inventory and advertising at once.

The event calendar is running the planning year

The wider view shows the same pattern across the season. The October event, Black Friday and Cyber Monday all have their own deadlines, and each decision shapes the next. A deep discount in October can set shoppers’ price expectations for November, and stock used in October may not be replaced in time for Cyber Week. Walmart and Target often schedule their own events near Amazon’s, which adds a further question about where to lead with deals and where to hold price, as opposed to matching everywhere.

At that point the retailer’s event calendar is effectively setting the brand’s planning year. Each choice looks small inside a single submission form; added together across the season, those choices decide how much of the brand’s holiday business runs at a discount, and in which channel. A brand keeps control by treating the deadlines as inputs to its own calendar rather than as the calendar itself.

That starts with one person who owns the brand’s participation decision across deal depth, units, stock and advertising, with the authority to bring in finance, operations and advertising. The owner lists every Amazon deadline for the October event and the holiday events after it, then sets internal decision dates a week or more earlier. Prime Day results should shape the October plan, so the first internal date is a review of which July deals paid, which pulled demand forward and which products ran short.

Each function then decides its own part against those dates. Finance confirms the margin after the discount, the flat peak-event deal fee and expected advertising costs before any deal is submitted. Operations decides how many units to send to Amazon for the event, given demand in other channels and the risk of stock-outs before Cyber Week. The advertising team learns which products carry deals and builds budgets around them, with extra support where deals and advertising together drive new customers. October, Black Friday and Cyber Monday are decided together, so discounts, stock and budgets work across the season instead of event by event.

A one-page plan listing each product, its deal, its units and its advertising budget lets everyone work from the same numbers and makes the post-event review easier. It also leaves room for a fallback: if the review shows a product should not join, the owner can withdraw or adjust it before the event, within Amazon’s rules.

One question belongs on the next planning agenda. When the September 12 window closes, who will have decided your October discounts, and will finance have seen them first? Running October and the holiday season as one calendar is how we plan Amazon deal events with brands.

A0791.crumb: Sustainable products as a premium on…
A0791.title: Sustainable products as a premium on Mercado Libre: when it holds
A0791.alt: Wooden street stall with crates of fresh produce and glass bottles on a cobblestone lane of colorful old buildings.
A0791.ttag: Sustainable products as a premium on Mercado Libre: when it holds | Kwontified
A0791.desc: Sustainable product sales on Mercado Libre grew 26% while the catalog grew 48%, so a green price premium now holds only where the proof is easy to see.
A0791.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 2, 2025.
A0791.body:
Sales in Mercado Libre’s Sustainable Products categories grew 26% in the first half of 2024. Over the same stretch, the catalog behind them grew 48%. For a brand that prices a recycled or organic product above the standard version, those two numbers point in different directions: shoppers are arriving, but sellers are arriving faster.

That gap decides whether a sustainability premium holds. It holds for products that are verified, clearly different and easy to find, and it erodes for everything else as the section fills.

Demand for sustainable products on Mercado Libre is real

Start with the case for charging more, because it is a good one. Sales in the Sustainable Products categories grew 26% compared with the same period of 2023, and more than 4.8 million products with a positive impact sold across the region, Forbes Argentina reported. More than 2.7 million buyers bought them, up 27%.

Some categories did far better than the average. Sustainable fashion was the fastest-growing category in Latin America in that tracking, with units sold up 92% and buyers up 91%.

A pricing team looking at those figures would reasonably conclude that the premium is safe. More buyers are looking for the badge, a dedicated section gathers them in one place, and many of them will pay more for a product they trust is better for the environment. That reasoning gets the shoppers right and leaves out the shelf.

The section is filling faster than it is selling

The Sustainable Products catalog expanded by 48% across the region, according to the same report, and the number of entrepreneurs offering such products rose 9%. Put the two growth rates side by side: 1.26 divided by 1.48 is about 0.85. On average, each listing in the section captured roughly 15% less of the demand than a year earlier.

That measure is rough by design, and it should be read that way. The sales figure and the catalog figure count different things, units in one case and listings in the other, so treat the 15% as a direction rather than a precise result. The direction is still plain: more sellers are sharing each shopper.

Think of a weekend market where the organic stalls multiply faster than the shoppers who come for organic produce. Every stall still sells something, but each one sees fewer of those shoppers, and the stallholders start watching each other’s prices.

The same thing happens on the screen. A shopper choosing between several recycled-fabric t-shirts in the section compares price, reviews and delivery speed, just as in any other category. In a thin section the label set the product apart; in a crowded one it is merely the entry ticket.

Take a sustainable t-shirt priced at a 20% premium over a standard shirt. A similar shirt joins the section at a 5% premium. A shopper who sees little difference between the two buys the cheaper one, so the first shirt keeps only the shoppers who can see why it costs more. Its premium survives exactly as far as that difference is visible.

Proof is what separates one green label from the next

Sustainability claims are hard for shoppers to check for themselves. In a crowded section, vague claims start to look alike, and shoppers grow wary of all of them at once. A product with a named certification or a stated share of recycled material stands apart. A product relying on loose wording drifts toward competing on price. Shoppers paying more want proof, and a crowded section gives them every reason to ask for it.

The buyers in this section are not indifferent to price. They want a product that is better for the environment and good value at the same time, which makes clear proof and visible quality the deciding factors when two sustainable products sit side by side.

Pricing a sustainability premium on Mercado Libre

The first job is evidence. Hold certifications or clear documentation for every sustainability claim, and state it precisely in the listing: the material, the share recycled, the certification held. Use images and short descriptions to show how the product was made, rather than relying on a badge alone, and make sure the product qualifies for the sustainable section with complete data so it surfaces in searches and filters.

Differentiation beyond the label matters as much as the proof. Quality, design, fit and durability still decide close calls, and products that are sustainable and clearly better on those grounds hold their premium longest. Reviews that mention quality and durability support the price, so encourage genuine reviews from early buyers. Delivery matters too: shoppers paying more expect accurate listings, fast delivery and easy returns, and Mercado Libre’s fulfillment options can help where they improve delivery speed in a market.

Price discipline is where the crowding bites first. As the section fills, track the prices of similar products and decide where a premium can hold and where the product needs to compete. Categories where demand is outpacing supply, as sustainable fashion did during 2024, leave more room than crowded ones. Mercado Libre spans several countries with different incomes and preferences, so test the premium shoppers will accept in each market rather than setting one price everywhere. Compare sales and margin at different price points, and pick the premium that maximizes profit rather than the highest one shoppers will tolerate.

Before raising a price, check whether your category’s listings are growing faster than its sales. If they are, price for the proof a shopper can see on the page, because the label alone is now shared by every product around you.

Setting that premium market by market, with the listing evidence to back it, is how we operate Mercado Libre stores for consumer brands.

A0792.title: Walmart as a replenishment channel: winning the repeat basket
A0792.alt: Rows of clipped kraft-paper bags on wooden shelves beside an empty blue wicker basket by a window.
A0792.ttag: Walmart as a replenishment channel: winning the repeat basket | Kwontified
A0792.desc: Walmart store-fulfilled delivery sales grew nearly 50% as households restock from nearby shelves. The brands that win there plan for the second purchase.
A0792.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 4, 2025.
A0792.body:
A household runs low on dish soap. Someone opens the Walmart app, taps the bottle they bought last time, and a nearby store picks it off the shelf for delivery. Nobody searched the category, compared brands or read a review. Walmart’s second-quarter results suggest that small ritual now sits near the center of its online business: sales through store-fulfilled delivery channels grew nearly 50%, with about a third of those orders expedited.

That makes Walmart a replenishment channel, where share is decided by whether the shopper buys the same product again. Brands win the repeat basket there through local availability, the right pack sizes and visibility at the moment of reorder, and a Walmart plan organized around the first purchase misses where the channel is won.

How Walmart became a replenishment channel

In the second quarter, US e-commerce sales at Walmart grew 26%, reflecting strength in store-fulfilled delivery, advertising and marketplace, the company said in its earnings release. Membership grew alongside it, and global membership income rose 15.3%, according to the same release.

Those numbers describe the institution. Walmart built its online business on top of its stores, so a delivery order is filled from the shelves of a nearby store, and what the shopper can get depends on what that store holds. Membership reinforces the pattern. Members who pay for free delivery have a reason to order often, in smaller baskets, rather than plan one large trip, and every one of those smaller orders is a chance to stay with a brand or switch away from it.

Those baskets fill mostly with familiar items: detergent, diapers, pet food, snacks, toiletries. A shopper who is running low wants the usual item, delivered quickly, without starting a search from scratch. Fast delivery from the local store turns Walmart into an extension of the household pantry.

Walmart’s growth figures cover the whole business, not any one category, so a brand should check whether its own categories show the same reorder pattern before it reshapes a plan around it.

The decision on the table is the first purchase or the second

When a brand team sits down to set its Walmart plan, the debate tends to be about trial: how much to spend on launch support, which items to push into search, what the first-order promotion should be. The replenishment pattern asks the leadership team a different question. Is the money there to win a shopper once, or to win the same shopper on every restock?

On a discovery-led marketplace, brands compete to be found. In a replenishment channel, they compete to be reordered. The first purchase still matters, but share is settled later, each time the household runs low and opens the app again.

That moves the places where brands lose. A product out of stock at the local store loses the reorder to whatever the shelf has. A pack size that runs out at the wrong moment loses to a rival’s larger pack. A product that drops out of the shopper’s usual list has to be found again, and may not be.

Take a brand that gains 1,000 new buyers a month at Walmart, and a rival with the same trial that wins back 5 points more of its buyers each cycle. Over a year of monthly restocks, the rival’s base of regular buyers grows noticeably faster without spending more on trial. Small differences in repeat rate turn into large differences in share, and none of them show up in a launch report.

Where the repeat basket is won at Walmart

Availability comes first, because the shelf is the warehouse. Monitor in-stock rates by store and work with Walmart to fix gaps in high-demand areas. Check that items are not frequently substituted or missing in delivery orders, since expedited delivery rewards products that stores carry and pick reliably. Store-fulfilled orders draw on the same shelves as in-store shoppers, so store execution and online availability are one problem with one owner.

The product itself should fit the household’s cycle. Offer pack sizes that match how often a family uses the item, and test larger packs that stretch the gap before the shopper has to choose again. Keep prices steady, because replenishment shoppers notice jumps on items they buy often, and a sharp swing pushes regular buyers to try something else. Brands with related products can make them easy to buy together, so one reorder brings in more of the basket.

Being easy to reorder is a merchandising job. Products should appear consistently in search and in the places shoppers return to reorder, with clear names and images so the shopper recognizes the usual item at a glance. Reviews matter less to someone buying the same detergent again, but they matter to the first-time buyer, so keep them current and give that buyer a reason to come back.

Advertising can serve retention as well as trial. Walmart Connect can reach past buyers, and campaigns timed to when they are likely to run low are worth testing. The moment of reorder is also when rivals’ ads and promotions catch a shopper, so know which competitors take your reorders and answer with targeted offers.

All of this rests on one measure. Track how often first-time buyers come back and how quickly, using Walmart’s supplier insights where available, and treat repeat rate as a core number in the Walmart review rather than a footnote to new-buyer growth.

One question for the team is simple to ask and harder to answer: of the shoppers who bought from us at Walmart, how many came back, and which store gaps cost us the ones who did not? Answering it store by store and reorder by reorder is how we manage Walmart for brands, from store-level stock to Walmart Connect.

A0794.crumb: Build, buy or partner for shopping AI…
A0794.title: Build, buy or partner for shopping AI: where the return is
A0794.alt: An old brass skeleton key, a single modern key and a key ring with two keys on a worn wooden table.
A0794.ttag: Build, buy or partner for shopping AI: where the return is | Kwontified
A0794.desc: Shoppers use AI assistants run by retailers and chat apps, not brands. Most brands should partner and buy tools, and build only where they own the traffic.
A0794.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 9, 2025.
A0794.body:
Take a brand that sells 90% of its volume through retailers and 10% through its own site. If it builds an AI shopping assistant, the assistant can live only on that site, so it can influence at most the 10%. The other 90% is shaped by assistants the brand does not run: Amazon’s, other retailers’ and the general chat tools, all of which answer from product listings, reviews and data.

That arithmetic settles most of the build question. For most brands, the better return comes from partnering with the assistants shoppers already use, which means making products easy for those systems to understand. After that comes buying tools for content and measurement, and building only where the brand owns enough traffic to justify the cost.

Why build, buy or partner for shopping AI is now a real choice

Retailers put assistants inside their stores first. Rufus, Amazon’s AI shopping assistant, is open to every US customer in the Amazon app, and it builds its answers from material sellers and shoppers have already written: listing details, community Q&As and customer reviews, Swipe Insight reported.

General AI tools are sending shoppers to stores as well. Visits from generative AI sources to US retail sites climbed 1,200% from July 2024 to February 2025, according to Adobe’s analytics data. Chat tools now recommend products on their own, too. ChatGPT shows products with buy links, and OpenAI says it picks those results independently and does not sell them as ads, PYMNTS reported.

For anyone on a brand team, the useful split is between what has shipped and what is still a demo. Rufus answering questions inside the Amazon app has shipped. Product results inside ChatGPT have shipped.

Both read the same raw material a brand already produces: titles, attributes, images, reviews and answers to shopper questions. That means the person who fills in product attributes is now writing for a machine reader as well as a human one. That makes the AI question the content owner’s problem as much as the developer’s.

Reach sets the ceiling on an owned assistant

A shopping assistant is only useful if shoppers open it, and shoppers open the ones built into the places they already shop and search. A brand that builds its own assistant can put it only on its own website or app. It reaches the shoppers who already visit the brand, which is often a small share of total sales for a brand that sells mainly through retailers.

Cost points the same way. Building an assistant means paying for models, data integration, testing and ongoing upkeep, and fixing it when it gives wrong answers about the brand’s own products. Those costs stay roughly fixed whether the assistant serves a thousand shoppers or a million, so for a brand with a small direct audience the cost per shopper reached is high.

Back to the brand with the 90/10 split. An owned assistant can improve, at best, how the 10% buys. Better product data can improve how every assistant treats the 90%. Even a modest gain across the larger share is likely to outweigh a strong gain on the smaller one.

OptionWhat it asks of the brandWhose shoppers it reaches
PartnerComplete product data, consistent details across channels, answers to the questions shoppers askShoppers using Rufus, retailer search and chat assistants
BuyTools to write and test listings, monitor reviews and track how products appear in AI answersThe same shoppers, through better data, at lower cost than building
BuildModels, data integration, testing and upkeepOnly visitors to the brand’s own site or app

Partnering needs no software, but it does need discipline: complete product data, consistent details across channels and answers to the questions shoppers actually ask. That work also improves ordinary search and conversion, so it pays off even if the assistants themselves change.

How brands should decide

Start with where sales come from. Know what share comes through each retailer and through your own site, because that share sets the ceiling on what an owned assistant can influence.

Then make product data legible. Assistants answer from listings, attributes and reviews, so complete every attribute, describe use cases plainly and keep product details consistent across channels. Collect the questions shoppers ask in reviews, Q&As and search terms, and make sure listings answer them clearly. Assistants repeat what they read, so correct errors in listings and third-party content quickly before they spread through AI answers.

Buying tools is usually the cheaper route. Software that helps write and test listings, monitor reviews and track how products appear in AI answers is generally faster to put in place than anything built from scratch. Alongside it, ask the leading assistants about your category and products on a regular schedule, and record whether and how your products appear.

There is still a place for building. Brands with large direct-to-consumer audiences may benefit from their own assistant for customer service or product guidance, and others should consider one only after the partner and buy steps are working. Each retailer also decides how its assistant uses product data and advertising, so follow how Amazon, Walmart and Target change their assistants and adjust listings and ad plans as those systems evolve. Revisit the build, buy or partner choice as the assistants change and as your own channel mix shifts.

The rule fits on a sticky note: partner first, buy tools second, and build only where you own the traffic. Preparing product data for the assistants shoppers already open is where our AI Agentic Commerce practice starts with a brand.

A0796.title: Is Zalando’s sustainability a differentiator? Less than it was
A0796.alt: Wooden clothing rack of earth-toned shirts with blank green tags in a sunlit room beside an armchair.
A0796.ttag: Is Zalando’s sustainability a differentiator? Less than it was | Kwontified
A0796.desc: Zalando made sustainability visible early, then missed its 25% target for 2023. Why its sustainability flag now works as a baseline more than a way to stand out
A0796.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 11, 2025.
A0796.body:
A shopper browsing Zalando can narrow any category to products the platform marks as more sustainable, with a small flag on each one that qualifies. Zalando built that flag and filter into its store early, at a time when few large fashion platforms made sustainability so visible, and for a while it gave brands with qualifying products an easy way to stand out. Then the platform missed its own target for sustainable sales in 2023.

That miss says something about the flag itself. On Zalando, sustainability has moved from a differentiator to a baseline: brands need to meet the flag criteria to be found by the shoppers who care, and then compete on fit, quality and price like everyone else.

How Zalando sustainability became part of the store

Zalando set an ambitious number early. It raised its target for gross merchandise volume generated by more sustainable products from 20% to 25% by 2023, after reaching 16% in 2020, up from 6.7% in 2019, Just Style reported. It also tripled its sustainable assortment to 80,000 products and gave shoppers a sustainability filter and a product flag to find them, according to the same report.

The goal proved hard to reach. Zalando’s 2023 sustainability report listed the 25% target among its notable misses, Sourcing Journal reported.

Why the flag stands out less than it did

The early advantage came from scarcity. When few large fashion platforms put sustainability front and center, a brand with qualifying products had something its rivals did not, and shoppers who cared about it had a simple way to find those products in a crowded catalog.

Shopper behavior then set a ceiling. The share rose fast at first, from 6.7% to 16% in a year, as interested shoppers found the products. Moving beyond that meant persuading shoppers who choose mainly on style, fit and price, and those shoppers did not switch in large enough numbers to reach 25%. That suggests sustainability works for many of them as a tiebreaker rather than as a reason to buy.

From the other side, competition narrowed the gap. As more brands qualified, flagged products stopped being rare, and a flag that appears on many products in a category tells a shopper less about any one of them.

Regulation pushes the same way. European rules on product design and environmental claims are tightening, which moves brands toward verified claims and common standards. Once every brand has to document sustainability in the same terms, it becomes harder to use as a point of difference.

Put together, the role has changed, and it has changed in a way that matters for planning. Sustainability on Zalando is now a condition for being considered by the shoppers who filter for it. A brand without qualifying products risks being filtered out by those shoppers; a brand with them gains less than it once did.

Where the new difference is coming from

Durability, repair and resale give brands ways to show sustainability that a material flag cannot. A jacket that holds its value on resale, or a pair of boots that comes with repair support, offers something a shopper can see more easily than a percentage of recycled fiber.

Returns belong in the same conversation. Fashion returns carry an environmental cost and a financial one, and brands whose sizing and imagery cut returns can point to a practical benefit that shoppers and platforms both value. That is a sustainability story told through operations rather than a badge, and it is one a shopper experiences directly when the first order fits.

Sustainability still matters to a meaningful share of Zalando’s shoppers, and it can decide between two otherwise similar products. It simply no longer sets a brand apart on its own.

Treating sustainability on Zalando as a baseline

Qualifying is the floor. Where it is practical, products that meet Zalando’s criteria should carry the flag, with the documentation the platform requires, so they appear when shoppers filter. Make sure the best qualifying products, not only the cheapest, show up for those deliberate shoppers. Every claim needs clear evidence for materials and processes, both to meet Zalando’s standards and to prepare for stricter European rules. A precise claim (the share of recycled fiber, a named certification) persuades the shoppers who care more than a generic badge does.

The competition itself happens on fit, quality and style. Many shoppers still choose on how a product looks, fits and lasts, so size guidance, product imagery and quality that reduce returns and build repeat buyers carry more weight than the flag. Pricing follows the market: a sustainable product priced well above similar flagged items needs a clear reason, such as better design or longer wear, to justify the gap. Lower return rates can sit inside the sustainability story, since products that last and fit well support both the claim and the margin.

Measurement keeps the debate honest: compare how flagged and unflagged products perform on Zalando, including conversion and returns, to see where sustainability is earning its place. Zalando Marketing Services can put products in front of interested shoppers, so test whether sustainability messaging improves results in your categories before leaning on it. And because shoppers who see a claim on Zalando may check it elsewhere, keep claims consistent across your own site and other retailers.

The question for a European leadership team is whether its Zalando plan still treats the flag as the headline, or as the price of admission it has become. Building a Zalando assortment that clears the bar and then wins on fit and quality is how we grow brands on Zalando and other European marketplaces.

A0799.crumb: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast: sales…
A0799.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast: sales lift, CPC and deal share
A0799.alt: Brass rooster weathervane on a clay-tiled roof with autumn maple leaves blowing across a blue sky.
A0799.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast: sales lift, CPC and deal share | Kwontified
A0799.desc: Our Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast: conservative, standard and reach ranges for ad-driven sales lift, CPC and deal share, and the assumptions behind them.
A0799.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 17, 2025.
A0799.body:
In 2024, advertisers on Amazon’s October event lifted average daily ad spending 250% against the previous 30 days, and ad-attributed revenue rose 258%. Clicks got dearer at the same time, with average cost per click up about 35%. The event made sales easier to find and each click harder to win, both at once.

That pattern is the basis for our forecast. Prime Big Deal Days 2025 runs October 7 to 8, and we expect ad-driven sales lift of 200% to 300%, CPC increases of 30% to 50% and a deal share of 35% to 55% of event sales. Set budgets and judge results against those ranges, not a single number.

The Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast in three cases

Each range is measured against the brand’s own average day in the 30 days before the event. These are our assumptions, not reported figures, and they are built from the 2024 event and the trend since 2023. Read the standard case as the plan and the outer cases as the edges a budget should be ready for.

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
Ad-driven sales lift200%250%300%
CPC increase30%40%50%
Deal share of event sales35%45%55%

Amazon will run Prime Big Deal Days on October 7 and 8 in the US and 17 other countries, Homepage News reported.

What the 2024 event says about the ranges

The baseline comes from Skai’s analysis of advertisers on its platform. Average daily ad spending during Prime Big Deal Days 2024 rose 250% against the previous 30 days, up from a 212% lift in 2023. Clicks rose 152% and average cost per click about 35%, while conversions rose 165% and ad-attributed revenue 258%. The October event is also smaller than July’s: its effect on spending and sales was about half that of Prime Day, according to the same analysis.

The cause sits in the calendar. The event compresses shopper demand into two days, and advertisers know it, so they raise budgets and bids at the same moment. Clicks rise sharply, but so does competition for each one, which pushes cost per click up.

That is why the event can lift sales strongly while making each sale more expensive to win through ads. In 2024, ad-driven revenue rose about as fast as spending, so return on ad spend held roughly level against the prior month even as clicks became more costly.

Competition is also rising from one event to the next, which is why the forecast leans higher on cost than on sales. The spending lift grew from 212% in 2023 to 250% in 2024, and the cost-per-click lift from about 28% to about 35%, according to Skai. More advertisers are treating the October event as a major moment, and that bids up prices.

The assumptions behind each case

For ad-driven sales lift, the standard case of 250% assumes a result close to 2024’s 258%. The conservative case allows for tariff pressure on prices and for shopper caution, with inflation at 2.9% in August. The reach case allows for wider participation after a strong July event, when shoppers showed they would turn up for a longer Prime Day.

For cost per click, the 30%, 40% and 50% increases follow from the trend. Higher competition each year points to a further rise from 2024’s roughly 35%, and brands bidding on broad, popular terms should expect the higher end.

For deal share, the range covers how much of a brand’s event sales will come from products with an Amazon deal, which matters because deals drive conversion during the two days. Brands that submitted fewer deals before the September 12 deadline should expect the lower end, while brands with deals on their best sellers may reach the top of the range.

Take a brand that spends $1,000 a day on ads at a CPC of $1.50 in the month before the event. At a 40% CPC rise, event clicks cost $2.10. If it spends 3.5 times its usual budget, as advertisers did in 2024, it spends $3,500 a day and buys about 1,670 clicks, against about 670 on a normal day. That is roughly 2.5 times the clicks for 3.5 times the money, and the gap is what the event’s higher conversion has to cover.

Budget and bid triggers for October 7 and 8

Budgets should sit on the standard case, with room for the reach case approved in advance, so they do not run out early on October 7. Put the largest share of event spending behind products with accepted deals, since deals drive conversion during the event.

Bids need the CPC rise built in. Raise bids on your most important terms to stay visible, and cap bids on terms that rarely convert. Shoppers research before the event and buy after it, so keep budgets steady on October 6 and 9 rather than cutting straight back.

Stock has to match the lift. A 250% sales lift on a product with thin stock can end in a stock-out on the first day, so confirm cover for the reach case on top products. Ads capture only part of an event’s sales, so track total sales lift alongside ad-attributed lift to see how much of the demand arrived without paid clicks.

After October 8, set your lift, CPC and deal share beside the three ranges and note which assumptions held. A result inside the range means the plan worked; a result outside it tells you which assumption to change before the next event. Building that plan, and grading the event against it afterward, is how we plan and measure Amazon tentpole events with brands.

A0800.crumb: Why Temu may help premium brands, and…
A0800.title: Why Temu may help premium brands, and where it still hurts
A0800.alt: Plastic grocery bag beside a brown leather handbag on a marble windowsill.
A0800.ttag: Why Temu may help premium brands, and where it still hurts | Kwontified
A0800.desc: Temu sets the floor for cheap online goods, which can make a premium brand’s value easier to see. Where that contrast helps, where it hurts, and what to change.
A0800.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 18, 2025.
A0800.body:
Watch how a household shops across a single week. Party supplies, a phone case and a set of storage bins come from the cheapest listing anyone can find, on a site like Temu. The same household then pays full price for a moisturizer it trusts, a car seat, or the running shoes someone wears every day. Shoppers do not spend evenly, and Temu has made the cheap end of that split easy to see.

For premium brands, that visible floor can help, because it sharpens the contrast that justifies a higher price. It helps only where a brand makes its quality easy to see, and Temu’s return to the ad auctions after its spring 2025 pullback means the cost of reaching shoppers is climbing back too.

How Temu shaped the market for premium brands

Temu advertised heavily, then pulled back hard. Its average daily US ad spend on six major social and video platforms fell 31% in the two weeks from March 31 to April 13, against the previous 30 days. The 31% figure comes from Sensor Tower estimates reported by Reuters, covering Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snap, X and YouTube. Temu also sharply reduced its Google Shopping ads from April 12, according to Tinuiti, Reuters reported.

Then it came back. Temu was running about 1,100 active Meta ads and its parent had about 700 active Google ads in the US by late July, up from six Google ads in mid-April, Modern Retail reported. Daily active users rose 17.2% month over month in July but remained 49.5% below March levels, according to the same report.

Why a price floor can work in a premium brand’s favor

Many shoppers economize on items they see as disposable and spend more where quality, safety or the brand matters to them. Temu sharpens that split. By setting a visible floor for what cheap looks like, it makes the difference between a throwaway item and a well-made one easier to point to. A premium brand that explains why its product lasts, fits or performs better gains a clear point of comparison.

The same shopper often plays both roles. Someone who buys cheap party supplies on Temu may buy premium skincare on Amazon the same week. Premium brands do not need to win every purchase that shopper makes, only the ones where quality matters to them.

That is also where Temu still hurts, and it is worth being honest about how much of a catalog sits in that zone. In categories where shoppers cannot easily see a quality difference, or where the cheap version is good enough, premium brands lose sales to Temu. The help is real only where the brand can make its value visible.

Who captured the value when Temu stepped back

The spring pullback showed how the economics of shared ad auctions work. When a large, aggressive bidder leaves, the advertisers who remain face less competition for the same clicks. During the pullback, some of the value Temu had been paying into those auctions went to the brands that stayed, in the form of easier access to the same shoppers.

The return moves that value back. Temu’s ads came back over the summer, so premium brands are again sharing auctions with a bidder whose goal is volume at low prices, and the platforms that sell those clicks gain from the renewed competition. Brands that bid on broad, generic terms meet that competition most directly, because those are the terms where a low-cost seller and a premium one chase the same search.

Temu’s future in the US also depends on trade policy that keeps changing, and its users fell sharply after tariffs took effect. A plan built around Temu’s presence or its absence will be wrong for part of the year.

What premium brands can change now

The most useful first exercise is sorting products by how visible their quality is. Some products a shopper can judge as better at a glance; others look much like cheaper versions. The first group benefits from the contrast, and the second needs more explanation or a different position. Within that sort, listings carry the argument: images, materials, certifications and comparisons should make the difference obvious in seconds. Reviews that say a product lasted, fit well or worked as promised are the evidence premium shoppers look for, so encourage genuine ones.

Ad spending follows the same logic. Generic terms attract shoppers comparing on price, where Temu and other low-cost sellers compete hardest, so concentrate spending on branded, specific and quality-led search terms. Track cost per click on your main terms and adjust bids if a returning low-cost bidder pushes prices up. Check which products appear in searches alongside Temu listings and track their conversion separately, to see where the contrast helps and where it costs sales.

Price is where discipline matters most. Cutting prices to match Temu weakens the contrast that makes premium products appealing, so promote through value-adds, bundles or loyalty offers rather than deep cuts. In categories where cheap alternatives are good enough for many shoppers, decide deliberately whether to answer with a value line or to focus on the segments where quality matters most. And keep the brand story clear on your own site and social channels, because shoppers who discover a premium brand on a marketplace may look it up later.

The question to take back to the team is which of your products a shopper could tell apart from a Temu version at a glance, and what you are spending to sell the ones they could not. Answering that across Amazon, Walmart and the rest of the shelf is how we help premium brands hold their price against low-cost rivals.

A0802.title: What Amazon Accelerate 2025 changes for sellers
A0802.alt: White robotic arm pressing on a kraft-paper parcel on a wooden packing table with paper rolls, tape and envelopes.
A0802.ttag: What Amazon Accelerate 2025 changes for sellers | Kwontified
A0802.desc: Amazon Accelerate 2025 ended FBA commingling, opened fulfillment to Walmart and Shopify orders and let Seller Assistant act. What each change saves and risks.
A0802.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 23, 2025.
A0802.body:
One change from Amazon Accelerate 2025 comes with a dollar figure attached, and it is about a sticker. Brand owners will no longer need to put an FBA label on products that carry a manufacturer barcode, a change Amazon expects to save sellers about $600 million a year, according to its post on the Selling Partners site. The sticker goes because commingling goes, and that is the pattern across the event: each change moves a cost or a risk from one place to another.

Three changes matter most for a brand. Commingling ends within FBA. Amazon’s fulfillment network opens to Walmart, Shopify and SHEIN orders, so one pool of stock can serve several channels. Seller Assistant gains the power to act with permission. The first gives brand owners control of their own units, the second cuts the safety stock a multichannel brand carries, and the third turns every permission into a decision about risk.

What Amazon Accelerate 2025 announced

Amazon will end commingling within FBA, and brand owners will no longer need to apply an FBA sticker to products with a manufacturer barcode. Amazon puts the saving at about $600 million a year.

Fulfillment opens to other channels. Amazon announced partnerships with Walmart, Shopify and SHEIN through Multi-Channel Fulfillment, and said that moving from multiple inventory pools to one lets businesses run with leaner inventory while keeping consistent in-stock levels. Sellers using Multi-Channel Fulfillment reported nearly 19% higher sales on average after adding it to off-Amazon channels, Amazon said.

Seller Assistant can now set goals, develop strategies and, with permission, take action on behalf of sellers. The enhanced version is available to all US sellers at no additional cost, PPC Land reported. Amazon also introduced Custom Analytics, which combines more than 100 metrics in one free tool, and shoppable A+ Content.

Ending commingling trades some speed for control

Commingling let Amazon store identical products from different sellers together and ship them interchangeably, so a shopper buying from one seller might receive a unit sent in by another. That helped Amazon ship faster from nearby stock. It also meant a brand’s customer could receive a counterfeit or damaged unit from someone else’s inventory.

Ending commingling ties each unit to the seller who sent it, and both sides of that trade are real. Brand owners gain control and lower counterfeit risk. Amazon gives up some flexibility in shipping the nearest identical unit, which may matter for delivery speed on some products. For a brand owner the balance leans toward control: the cost is a possible delay on some products, and the gain is that every unit a customer receives came from the brand’s own stock.

The picture differs for resellers. Sellers who do not own the brand they sell may still need to label their own units, so the savings fall mainly to brand owners. For brands, separate inventory also makes it easier to trace which seller sent a problem unit, which strengthens their hand against unauthorized or careless resellers.

One pool of stock needs less safety stock than three

The arithmetic sits in pooling, which works the other way from commingling. When a brand holds separate stock for Amazon, Walmart and its own site, each pool needs its own safety buffer against demand swings. One shared pool needs less, because swings in different channels partly offset each other.

Take a brand whose three channels each need 300 units of safety stock. Held separately, that is 900 units. A common approximation in inventory planning, the square-root rule, says safety stock for a combined pool rises with the square root of the number of pools, so one pool might need about 520 units, roughly 300 times the square root of 3. That frees about 380 units of cash tied up in stock, if demand in the channels is not perfectly correlated.

That condition decides the whole result. If demand in every channel rises and falls together, the offset disappears and the pooled buffer drifts back toward 900 units. Pooling also has a cost of its own: stock held in one network makes a brand more dependent on that network, so high-volume channels deserve a fallback.

An assistant that can act changes what a mistake costs

A tool that only advises cannot break anything. A tool that can act with permission can change prices, listings or ads, and every permission a seller grants is a decision about risk.

Grant permissions in order of what a mistake costs, from the cheapest possible one to the most expensive. Start with monitoring and alerts, then allow low-risk actions, and keep pricing and advertising changes under human approval until the results earn trust. Keep a record of every action the assistant takes and review it weekly. The review catches mistakes early, so permissions can be widened with evidence rather than optimism.

Barcodes first, then pooling, then permissions

Brand owners should confirm that every product has a valid manufacturer barcode registered correctly and plan when to stop applying FBA labels. As commingling ends, track delivery promises and conversion on key products, in case separate inventory affects speed in some regions. Brands paying for FBA label services or prep work can estimate what stickerless inventory saves them and use the savings to fund other priorities.

Multi-Channel Fulfillment for Walmart or Shopify orders suits products with steady demand. Start there, compare costs with current fulfillment and check delivery times against each channel’s requirements. Compare Custom Analytics with current reports and retire duplicate work, and test shoppable A+ Content on top products.

The order matters as much as the changes: switch to manufacturer barcodes, pool stock only where demand is steady and grant the assistant permissions one area at a time. Sequencing those moves across Amazon and the channels around it is part of how we run the channel day to day for brands.

A0804.title: Using Instagram data for product development, before you build
A0804.alt: Rustic wooden table with linen fabric swatches, sketches on paper, a mug, thread spool, scissors and a phone.
A0804.ttag: Using Instagram data for product development, before you build | Kwontified
A0804.desc: Instagram shows demand for a product before it exists, in saves, comments and trial reels. How to read those signals and confirm them with marketplace search.
A0804.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 25, 2025.
A0804.body:
Open the comments under a brand’s product post on Instagram and part of a product roadmap can be sitting there. Someone asks whether it comes in a larger size. Someone tags a friend. Someone wants to know if the scent will ever come in a travel version, and a few posts later another person asks the same thing. None of it shows up in a sales report, because the product those people are asking for does not exist yet.

Instagram works as an early demand test for exactly that reason. Saves, shares, comments and reach among non-followers say something about interest before a brand commits to production. The signals are a first filter, though, not a verdict, and they only become useful once marketplace search and sales data confirm them and once they reach the people who decide what gets built.

Instagram data for product development works because discovery moved to social

Nearly 8 in 10 shoppers discover new products through social media, and 96% of those discoveries happen on Meta’s platforms, according to a Meta-commissioned study by GWI of internet users in India, exchange4media reported. The study covered one market, but it shows how central social discovery has become.

Instagram also gave brands a way to test an idea on strangers. In December 2024 it began rolling out trial reels, which are shown to non-followers and do not appear on a creator’s main grid or reels tab, TechCrunch reported. Engagement results such as views, likes, shares and comments appear within 24 hours, Swipe Insight reported.

What a save or a comment says that a sales report cannot

On Instagram, people react to products before they buy them. They save posts they want to come back to, share them with friends, tag people in comments and ask questions about sizes, colors and prices. A save or a share signals stronger intent than a like, so comparing them across posts shows which products or features interest people most. Comments carry the detail: repeated requests for a larger size, a travel version or a different scent point to demand the current range does not meet. Direct messages add the questions shoppers would rather not ask in public, about sizes, ingredients or availability, and those point to gaps as well.

Brands can see all of this on their own posts, and they can read the comments on creators’ and competitors’ posts too. Creators hear directly from their audiences, so asking partners what their followers request is another way into the same evidence. Trial reels close the last gap. Because they go to people who do not already follow the brand, they avoid the bias of loyal fans.

That makes Instagram a cheap first test. A brand can post a concept, a prototype or two color options and see which draws more saves and questions.

Take a skincare brand weighing two new scents. It posts each one as a trial reel to non-followers, and after 24 hours one scent has twice the saves and three times the comments asking when it will launch. That does not prove the scent will sell. It tells the brand which one to check against search data first, before any money goes into production.

Where the Instagram signal misleads

The people who comment and save are more engaged than average shoppers, and engaged commenters skew younger and more enthusiastic than many buyers. A post can also draw attention for reasons unrelated to the product, such as the music or a creator’s personality. Interest on Instagram does not always turn into purchases on Amazon or Walmart, so a brand has to weigh what it sees against the profile of its actual customers.

Marketplace data is the second filter for that reason. Search terms on Amazon and Walmart show what shoppers actually look for when they are ready to buy. Before committing, a brand can check search volume and trends for the product or feature and look at how competitors’ similar products sell. An idea that draws strong interest on Instagram and matches real search demand is far more promising than one with only social buzz.

A purchase is the last check. A limited run or a pre-order tests real buying rather than interest, and early sales settle what the first two filters could only suggest. So the sequence has three stages: Instagram finds and shapes ideas early and cheaply, marketplace search confirms whether the demand is large enough to act on, and a small launch proves it.

Who in the company hears what shoppers are asking for

The method is simple; where the evidence lands is harder. Comments, saves and messages arrive in the social account, while the decision about what to build sits with product, and the search data sits with whoever runs the marketplaces. If nobody carries the requests across, the brand ends up with a full inbox and a roadmap that never heard from it.

Mostly, the fix is a set of habits. Collect comments on brand, creator and competitor posts, and tag the recurring requests and complaints so a pattern is visible rather than anecdotal. Share a short monthly summary of what shoppers are asking for with product, marketing and marketplace teams alike. Keep a record of which ideas came from Instagram, how they performed in testing and what sold, so the brand learns which signals predict success in its category. And when a product launches, tell the people who asked for it, through the same posts and creators, which turns early interest into first buyers.

A useful question for the next product review is who in the company read last month’s comments, and whether that person was in the room when the range was decided. Connecting what shoppers say on Instagram to what they search for on Amazon and Walmart is the social commerce work we do with brands.

A0806.crumb: How a four-day Prime Day changed bidding…
A0806.title: How a four-day Prime Day changed bidding and pacing
A0806.alt: A wooden metronome beside four stacks of twine-tied kraft paper parcels on a wooden desk with a succulent and books.
A0806.ttag: How a four-day Prime Day changed bidding and pacing | Kwontified
A0806.desc: Prime Day 2025 ran four days, and cost per click fell as shoppers and advertisers spread out. Why that happened and how to pace budgets by day and hour.
A0806.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Sep 30, 2025.
A0806.body:
Prime Day 2025 stretched to four days, and clicks got cheaper. Average cost per click fell 11% year over year during the event, after rising 12% during Prime Day 2024, Tinuiti reported.

A bigger event with lower prices looks backward. Watch the auction hour by hour and it makes sense. Shoppers and advertisers spread across more hours, and fewer bidders fought over any single click. The budget that won was the one still standing on the last evening.

What the data shows about four-day Prime Day bidding and pacing

Totals rose while daily figures fell. Brands’ total average sales rose 34% and total ad spend 48% year over year, but average daily sales fell 33% and average daily ad spend 26%, according to Pacvue’s analysis of Prime Day 2025.

Shopping clustered at the ends of the event. Shoppers favored early morning on the first day and made a final push on the evening of the fourth, with steadier mid-day buying on days two and three, according to Pacvue data reported by Chain Store Age. Amazon ad spend ran 172% above the lead-in period’s daily average, according to the same report.

The cheaper clicks showed up late in the event as well. In days three and four, cost per click was 16.2% lower than on the second day of 2024, according to Skai’s analysis of its advertisers. Amazon DSP grew from 13.6% of the ad mix on day one to 17.9% on day three, according to the same analysis.

The same demand, spread over more hours

The old expectation made sense. In two-day events, everyone bid hard at once and cost per click rose, so a bigger event looked like it should mean a more expensive one.

That reasoning treats event length as extra demand. It isn’t. A longer event does not create twice the shoppers; it spreads them over more hours, and advertisers spread their budgets the same way. Fewer advertisers compete hard in any one hour, so the auction for each click is less intense.

Pacvue’s numbers fit that picture. Total sales rose 34% while average daily sales fell 33%, so the shoppers came, just at a slower rate per day.

In four days the pressure eased, and advertisers who paced their budgets bought more clicks for the money. The same spreading changes what wastes money. A brand that spent most of its budget in the first hours of day one paid for the most contested clicks and had less left for the final push on day four, when shoppers returned to buy. A brand that paced its budget across the days bought clicks when they were cheaper and kept power for the end.

Front-loading buys fewer clicks with the same $10,000

Take a brand with $10,000 to spend, where day-one clicks cost $2.00 and later clicks cost $1.70.

PlanDay oneDays two to fourTotal clicks
Front-loaded$6,000 at $2.00 = 3,000 clicks$4,000 at $1.70 = about 2,350 clicksabout 5,350
Paced$2,500 at $2.00 = 1,250 clicks$2,500 each day at $1.70 = about 4,410 clicksabout 5,660

Spending $6,000 on day one buys 3,000 clicks and leaves $4,000, or about 2,350 clicks, for the next three days. Spending $2,500 each day instead buys 1,250 clicks on day one and about 4,410 over the following three days. That is about 5,660 clicks in total against about 5,350, and the paced brand still has full budget on the evening of day four, when shoppers return to buy.

The gap in clicks is the smaller half of the argument. The larger half is timing: the front-loaded brand runs thin exactly when the evening push arrives, while the paced brand arrives at that hour with a full day’s budget.

Setting bids and budgets for a long event

Plan the budget by day rather than as a single event total that can run out early, weighted toward the first and last days. Within each day, raise bids and budgets for the windows shoppers favored, early morning on day one and the evening of the last day, and keep the middle hours steadier. Hold back part of the budget for the final day, and release it only if the early days run under plan.

Bids deserve the attention that budgets get. Track cost per click by hour and adjust bids when prices fall or rise, rather than setting bids once for the whole event. Shoppers searching for a brand by name are likely to buy whenever they search, so keep branded bids steady across the event and concentrate pacing decisions on broader category terms, where competition and price swings are greater. DSP’s growing share on days two and three suggests advertisers used it to keep reaching shoppers between peaks, and brands with DSP access should consider it for remarketing during the event.

Two checks keep the plan intact. A brand that paces its budget well can still lose day four if its best sellers run out, so check stock levels each evening and shift budget away from products running low. And because daily figures fell even as totals rose, judge the event on total sales and profit across all days, not on how the first day compared with 2024’s. Afterward, compare your own sales and cost per click by hour with the overall pattern, to see where your shoppers differ and set better weights for the next event.

October brings a different auction. Prime Big Deal Days runs two days, so competition will be more concentrated, and brands should expect higher cost per click than in July and plan accordingly.

The test for any event budget is simple: if it cannot buy a click on the final evening, it was spent too early. Pacing by day and by hour, with a reserve for that last push, is how we bid and pace Amazon events for brands.
