A0807.crumb: Building a creator-led sales force on…
A0807.title: Building a creator-led sales force on commission
A0807.alt: Five smartphones in wooden stands lined up on a wooden table with coins, a key dish, a jar and potted plants.
A0807.ttag: Building a creator-led sales force on commission | Kwontified
A0807.desc: Amazon Creator Connections lets brands pay creators only when they sell. That makes creators a sales force, and it changes who should manage them and how.
A0807.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 2, 2025.
A0807.body:
A creator holds a product up to the camera, shows what it does and leaves a link. The shopper who taps that link often finishes the purchase somewhere else. Many shoppers now begin on TikTok and Instagram and then click through to Amazon to buy, Intentwise noted. Paid a fixed fee for a post, the creator in that chain draws on the marketing budget whether anything sells or not.

Commission programs such as Amazon’s Creator Connections change that. Brands can now pay creators only when they sell, which turns creators into a variable-cost sales force. The brands that get the most from it will manage creators the way they would manage any sales team: with recruiting, briefing, samples, commissions set by margin and results tracked creator by creator.

How Creator Connections makes a creator-led sales force possible

Through Creator Connections, brands set a budget, a timeline and a commission rate for a campaign, and eligible creators choose whether to join, according to Intentwise. Commissions start at about 10%, the minimum budget is $15,000, and brands pay only when products sell. Amazon reports the sales each campaign generated, which ties social promotion directly to marketplace sales.

The brand also picks its partners. It can set how many creators it wants, up to 50 per campaign, along with creator interests, budget, commission rate and products, Stack Influence reported.

The reason the model works sits with the shopper. People trust those they follow more than they trust brand advertising, and a creator who uses a product and explains it can move a shopper from interest to purchase in a way a banner rarely does.

A commission moves creators from the marketing line to the sales line

The decision a leadership team now faces is where creators belong. Paying a creator a flat fee for a post is a marketing cost whether or not anything sells. Paying a commission on each sale makes the creator a variable cost, like a commission-based sales rep, and the brand spends more only when creators sell more. On the invoice the money looks the same. The difference is which team should be accountable for it, and what that team should be asked to report.

Treat it as a sales cost and the management follows. A sales team needs recruiting, training, tools, incentives and reporting, and so does a creator program. Brands that simply post a campaign and wait tend to get uneven results, because the best creators choose campaigns that are easy to sell and well supported. A program that nobody recruits for, briefs or follows up on is competing for those creators with programs that do.

Setting the commission is a pricing decision

A commission has to clear two bars at once: it must attract good creators, and it must still leave the brand a margin once advertising and fees are paid. Different products deserve different rates, depending on margin and on how much help they need to sell.

Take a product that sells for $40, with $12 of profit after costs, fees and advertising. A 15% commission costs $6 per sale, which leaves $6 of profit on each creator-driven order. A 25% commission would cost $10 and leave $2. That thinner margin may still be worth paying for new customers who buy again, but only if the brand knows its repeat rate.

Whether the product suits creators matters as much as the rate. Not every product sells well through creators. Products that are visual, demonstrable or solve a clear problem tend to do best, while commodity items with little to show may not justify a program at all.

Running creators like a sales team

The work begins with choosing the range, favoring products that demonstrate well on video and have enough margin to fund a meaningful commission. Each rate then sits within what that product can afford after costs, advertising and fees, higher for products that need more help. Rather than waiting for creators to opt in, identify creators whose audiences match your buyers and invite them, starting with a small group.

Next, equip the creators. Creators need the key product facts, what makes the product different and which claims they may and may not make; a short brief improves both sales and compliance. Creators cannot sell what they have not used, so budget for samples and ship them promptly. Insist that every creator discloses the commercial relationship clearly, and review content for accurate claims, because brands are responsible for what is said about their products and a creator who exaggerates can create legal and reputational trouble.

The rest is the discipline of any sales operation. Track results creator by creator, to see who drives sales and at what cost, and focus support on those who perform. Creator content often sends shoppers to search for a brand by name, so track branded search on Amazon alongside campaign sales to see the full effect.

Make sure the products creators push have strong listings and advertising support, so the shoppers who arrive convert. Schedule campaigns ahead of seasonal peaks and major events, so creator traffic lands when listings and stock are ready. And keep the creators who sell well repeatedly, since they are worth more than a large number of one-time partners; reward them with higher commissions, early access and products no other creator gets.

The resulting structure is a hybrid. Creators supply reach and trust, marketplaces supply checkout and measurement, and commission programs connect the two. The question worth putting to the team before the next campaign: who owns the creators, and is that person measured on what they sell? Connecting creators to marketplace sales is part of how we run social commerce for brands.

A0809.crumb: Buying inside ChatGPT: what an agent…
A0809.title: Buying inside ChatGPT: what an agent needs from your catalog
A0809.alt: A small white robotic arm lifts a blank index card from a wooden card catalog drawer.
A0809.ttag: Buying inside ChatGPT: what an agent needs from your catalog | Kwontified
A0809.desc: ChatGPT ranks products on relevance and compares merchants on price, stock, quality and seller status. What an AI agent needs to read in your catalog.
A0809.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 7, 2025.
A0809.body:
On Amazon, a product with thin data can still buy its way onto the first screen. In ChatGPT’s product results there is no ad slot to buy, at least for now. Products are ranked on relevance to the user’s query and context, and items with Instant Checkout do not get a boost in the rankings, OpenAI said, as Nairametrics reported. So the question for a brand is no longer how much visibility costs. It is whether an agent can read the catalog well enough to pick the product, and then pick the brand as the place to buy it.

How buying inside ChatGPT works

Instant Checkout lets US users with Free, Plus and Pro accounts buy single items from Etsy merchants, with Shopify stores to follow. It runs on the Agentic Commerce Protocol, which OpenAI open-sourced with Stripe, SiliconANGLE reported. Orders are passed to the retailer, which processes them through its own systems, according to the same report. Merchants other than Etsy and Shopify sellers can apply through OpenAI’s merchant portal, according to Nairametrics.

For brands, the most important detail is how ChatGPT chooses between merchants. When ranking multiple merchants that sell the same product, it considers availability, price, quality, whether a merchant is the primary seller and whether Instant Checkout is enabled, OpenAI said, as Thurrott reported.

Those are OpenAI’s own stated factors, and they are worth taking at face value rather than reading more into the launch. They describe a system that compares data. Nothing in them describes a way to pay for position.

Brands that grew up on marketplaces have good reason to reach for the ad budget first. On Amazon, advertising can buy visibility for a product with thin data, which makes spend the obvious fix for a weak listing. An agent removes that fix. Whatever a brand spends elsewhere, the agent still has to find the answer to the shopper’s question in the product data, and it still has to find a merchant it can trust to deliver.

An agent makes two choices, and both read data

An agent answering a shopping question has two jobs. It decides which products fit the request, which depends on how well product data describes what each item is and does. Then it decides which merchant to send the shopper to, which depends on price, stock, quality signals and who the seller is.

Vague listings lose at the first choice. A product the agent cannot understand is simply not chosen. Variants make this harder than it looks: a shirt that comes in six sizes and four colors is 24 purchasable items, and an agent that cannot tell which size is in stock may recommend a product the shopper cannot buy.

Stale data loses at the second. An agent that recommends a product shown in stock at one price, only for the shopper to find it unavailable or more expensive, loses trust, so merchants whose data is current are likely to fare better over time. Quality is judged from signals, because the agent cannot touch the product. It relies on what it can read: reviews, ratings, return policies and how consistently the product is described across sources. Brands with thin or conflicting information look riskier to recommend.

The primary-seller factor is where brands win or lose

Of the merchant factors, the primary-seller test matters most for brands. If a brand’s products are sold by many resellers, and the brand itself is not a clear primary seller, an agent may send shoppers to a reseller with a lower price. The brand then loses control of price and of the customer relationship on its own product.

Take a shopper who asks for a waterproof hiking boot under $150. A brand whose listing states waterproofing, weight and price clearly, and shows stock, is a candidate. A rival whose data omits waterproofing is not, however good its boots are. That settles the first choice. For the second, among the merchants selling the brand’s boot, the brand selling directly at the list price with stock and checkout enabled is better placed than a reseller with stale stock data.

Getting the catalog ready for an agent

Write product data for questions rather than keywords. Agents match products to questions about use, size, materials and fit, so state those facts plainly in titles, descriptions and attributes, and make every variant’s details and stock clear. Keep price and availability current on your own site and feeds, so agents see accurate information. Provide a clean main image and supporting images that show the product’s key features, since shoppers deciding inside a chat still look at pictures before they buy. Keep return, shipping and warranty information visible as well, because it helps shoppers trust a recommended merchant and helps the agent judge quality.

Next, claim the seller position. Make clear on your own site that you are the primary seller of your products, with consistent identifiers such as GTINs across channels. Check whether authorized resellers undercut you on price or show inaccurate data, because agents compare merchants directly.

Checkout is a decision rather than a default. Brands on Shopify or Stripe should weigh whether to enable Instant Checkout, considering fees, fraud controls and how orders flow into their systems. Whatever they choose, measure visits and orders arriving from ChatGPT separately, to learn what the channel delivers.

The most useful test costs nothing. Ask ChatGPT the questions your shoppers ask, see which products and merchants it recommends, and fix the data gaps that keep your products out. If the agent cannot answer a shopper’s question from your catalog, it will answer it from someone else’s. Making the catalog complete and current, and owning the primary-seller position on every channel an agent reads, is part of how we manage catalogs and channels for brands.

A0814.crumb: Is Temu a threat or an opportunity for…
A0814.title: Is Temu a threat or an opportunity for mid-market brands?
A0814.alt: A lone orange pawn stands apart from wooden chess pieces on a worn chessboard by a window.
A0814.ttag: Is Temu a threat or an opportunity for mid-market brands? | Kwontified
A0814.desc: Temu now sells only US-warehoused goods from local sellers, which narrows its price edge. Where it still threatens mid-market brands and where it is a channel.
A0814.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 14, 2025.
A0814.body:
Take a generic kitchen item that once reached a Temu shopper for $3 in total cost. Imported in bulk with a 30% duty, stored for $0.50 and shipped domestically for $1.00, the same item might cost about $5.40.

Temu forced that change on itself in May 2025, when it stopped shipping cheap parcels directly from China and began selling only goods held in US warehouses by local sellers. The new costs narrow its price edge, and the local-seller model opens its marketplace to US brands. For a mid-market brand, Temu is now a threat where products are generic and a possible channel for value lines and surplus stock where the brand controls assortment and price.

How Temu changed its model, and why mid-market brands should care

Temu’s US site began showing only products held in US warehouses, with goods shipped from China listed as out of stock, TechCrunch reported. In the company’s account, every US sale now went through sellers based in the country, who filled orders domestically. A spokesperson added that Temu’s pricing for US consumers remained unchanged, according to the same report.

The shift had been prepared. Temu had asked Chinese factories in February to ship goods in bulk to American warehouses, and it was actively recruiting US merchants, Bloomberg reported, as The Peninsula published.

Then the wider rules tightened. Duty-free treatment for low-value shipments ended for all countries on August 29, 2025, Thompson Coburn noted, so shipping small parcels from other low-cost countries is no longer a way around the change.

Temu also went back to buying attention. It was running about 1,100 active Meta ads by late July, and its parent about 700 active Google ads, up from six in mid-April, Modern Retail reported.

Why the old price edge was so wide

Small parcels shipped straight from Chinese factories entered the US without duty and skipped domestic warehouses. That cut costs to the bone and let Temu price far below brands that imported in bulk, paid duty and stored stock locally. A mid-market brand comparing shelf prices was never comparing like with like; it was comparing its own landed cost with a parcel that had avoided most of the lines on its cost sheet.

Those lines come back with the new model. Goods imported in bulk pay duty. They sit in US warehouses that charge rent and labor, and they ship through domestic carriers. Those are the same costs mid-market brands already carry.

What the new model does to the price gap

Cost lineDirect parcel modelUS warehouse model
Product and duty$3 total, no duty$3 plus 30% duty
Storagenone$0.50
Domestic deliverynone$1.00
Total cost per unit$3about $5.40
Gap to a $12 brand versionfour timescloser to two times

A mid-market brand selling a better version of that item at $12 faced a price gap of four times. Now the gap is closer to two times. Temu remains cheaper, but the difference is easier to justify with quality. That is the core of the threat assessment: the more generic the product, the less a narrower gap helps, because shoppers who see no difference will still take the cheaper one.

The arithmetic is sensitive to its inputs. A higher duty rate, a longer stay in storage or a heavier item would push the warehouse cost up further. A lighter item or a lower rate would pull it down. The direction holds either way, because every line the old parcel skipped now has a price.

Local stock also changes delivery. Goods held in US warehouses can reach shoppers in days rather than the weeks that cross-border parcels often took. That removes one of the clearest reasons shoppers chose mid-market brands on Amazon or Walmart over Temu, which was faster arrival, and brands can no longer rely on speed alone to justify their price.

The open door cuts both ways

A marketplace recruiting local sellers is a marketplace brands can join. Selling on Temu may reach price-focused shoppers a brand does not reach elsewhere, but it risks associating the brand with the lowest prices and drawing sales away from other channels. Which way it cuts depends on the line. For value lines, end-of-season stock or surplus inventory, Temu may offer a way to sell without discounting on main channels, and a separate assortment is the safer test than the core range.

Deciding product by product

Start by sorting products by how generic they are. Where shoppers see little difference between a brand’s version and a cheaper one, the pressure from Temu is greatest, and those products need a clearer quality case or a lower-cost line. Then recheck the gap: compare prices with Temu’s current local-warehouse prices on overlapping products, since the gap may have narrowed, and adjust messaging where quality now justifies the difference.

A brand that does sell on Temu should keep Temu prices consistent with its pricing policy, so it does not undercut its own listings on Amazon, Walmart or its site. Local sellers on Temu may also list a brand’s products without permission, so monitor Temu and enforce seller policies. With Temu shipping from US stock, check that delivery promises on key products remain competitive, especially for items shoppers need quickly.

Temu’s return to advertising adds competition on broad search and social terms, so watch cost per click on generic terms and shift spend toward branded and specific searches. And because Temu’s model shifted with trade rules, it may shift again as tariff rates and import rules continue to move; review the Temu plan whenever tariffs or import rules change.

The working rule is brief. Treat Temu as a threat on generic products, compete on quality where its price edge has narrowed, and consider it as a channel only for lines where the brand controls assortment and price. Deciding which lines belong where, channel by channel, is how we help mid-market brands choose where to sell.

A0815.title: Cyber Week 2025 planning: who decides, and when
A0815.alt: A leather journal and stacked kraft-wrapped parcels on a pine dining table by garden doors, with evergreen sprigs in a vase.
A0815.ttag: Cyber Week 2025 planning: who decides, and when | Kwontified
A0815.desc: Amazon’s Cyber Week 2025 deadlines force deal, stock and budget decisions in October, owned by different teams. Who should own each one, and by when.
A0815.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 16, 2025.
A0815.body:
Amazon’s form for a Black Friday and Cyber Monday Lightning Deal asks for a discount of at least 20% and a $500 fee, and the window to submit it closes on October 28. The marketplace team fills it in. But the discount is a finance decision, the stock behind it is a supply chain decision, and the advertising that brings shoppers to it is a marketing decision, each on its own clock. Most of those clocks run out in October.

So the decisions that shape Cyber Week are made about six weeks before it starts, by different teams. The useful planning question is less what to promote than who decides each piece, and by when. A brand that gives every decision an owner and a date now is planning the event; a brand that treats it as a November problem is reacting to it.

Cyber Week 2025 planning runs on October deadlines

Submissions for Black Friday and Cyber Monday Week Best Deals and Lightning Deals close October 28, EcommerceBytes reported. The deals carry minimums and fees: Best Deals require at least a 15% discount and a $1,000 fee, and Lightning Deals at least 20% and a $500 fee, according to a Bellavix summary.

The stock deadlines come even earlier. For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, inventory sent through Amazon Warehousing and Distribution was due by October 9, and inventory sent directly to FBA by October 20 to 30, depending on the shipment option, according to the same summary.

Shoppers expect deals across a long holiday window, and Amazon lines up its events to meet that expectation, which means it needs deals submitted, approved and stocked well ahead. By mid-October the important choices are already being locked: which products get deals, how deep the discounts go, how much stock arrives and when. In November, brands mostly execute choices made weeks earlier.

Each decision belongs to a different team

Each piece has a different holder. Deal depth is a finance decision, because it sets margin. Stock is a supply chain decision, because it depends on production and shipping. Advertising budgets belong to marketing, and submissions and listings belong to the marketplace team. Each of those teams can do its own job well and the event can still fail, because the decisions depend on one another and nobody is responsible for the order they happen in.

Take a brand whose marketplace manager wants a Lightning Deal on a top product at 20% off. Finance has not approved the margin. Supply chain has not shipped extra units. By October 28 the deal is submitted, but the stock arrives after the inbound deadline, and the product runs out on the first day of the event. Each team did its part; no one owned the sequence.

Where the teams collide

Teams will also disagree. Finance may want shallower discounts than the marketplace team, and supply chain may not be able to promise the stock marketing wants to promote. Those conflicts are normal. What hurts is discovering them after a deadline, when the only options left are to drop a deal or to run short.

The calendar also reaches beyond Amazon. Walmart and Target run their own holiday events, and shoppers compare across them. A brand that sets deep discounts on Amazon but not elsewhere may shift sales between channels rather than add them, or face pressure to match prices everywhere.

And not every product belongs on deal. Products with thin margins, limited stock or strong full-price demand may do better without deep discounts, supported by advertising instead. That is a decision too, and it needs an owner as much as the deals do.

A calendar with one owner and fixed dates

The arrangement that works is a cross-team plan built on the event’s own deadlines, with one person who owns the Cyber Week calendar and chases each decision to its date. Finance approves which products can carry a deal and how deep, after fees and advertising. Supply chain confirms which deal products will reach fulfillment centers by October 20 to 30 and flags any at risk. The marketplace team submits approved deals early, leaving time to fix rejections before the October 28 window closes.

Marketing sets advertising budgets by day for the event, weighted toward peak days, with a reserve for strong performers. Images, titles and content on deal products get refreshed before traffic arrives, and full-price products get their own plan, using advertising and coupons where they fit.

The owner’s other job is to surface conflict early. One meeting in mid-October, with finance, supply chain, marketing and the marketplace team in the same room, can settle disagreements on deal depth, stock and budgets before the deadlines force a choice. The same meeting is the place to align deal plans for Walmart and Target, so discounts and stock across channels support each other rather than compete. It is also where the teams agree how the event will be judged: total sales, profit, new customers and stock left over, so every team decides against the same goals.

The plan closes with two dates. About a week before the event, the owner confirms that deals, stock, budgets and listings are ready. And a review booked for the week after Cyber Monday captures the lessons on deals, stock and advertising while they are fresh, so they feed next year’s plan.

The question to put to the team before the next planning meeting is a short one: who owns Cyber Week, and what does each team have to decide before October 28? Holding that calendar together, across the deals and the advertising behind them, is part of how we plan holiday events with brands.

A0812.crumb: Why Walmart wants to be inside ChatGPT…
A0812.title: Why Walmart wants to be inside ChatGPT, and what brands gain
A0812.alt: A smartphone in a blue case on a butcher-block counter beside a blue basket of bread, artichokes and lemons.
A0812.ttag: Why Walmart wants to be inside ChatGPT, and what brands gain | Kwontified
A0812.desc: Walmart will sell through ChatGPT’s Instant Checkout. Why the challenger to Amazon wants to meet shoppers inside an assistant, and what it means for brands.
A0812.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 17, 2025.
A0812.body:
Picture a shopper who asks ChatGPT for a weeknight dinner plan and a shopping list. The assistant suggests recipes and offers to buy the ingredients and a pack of paper towels from Walmart, for delivery that evening. She never opens Walmart’s site or app, and Walmart still makes the sale. For a retailer with its own site, app and ad business, that is an unusual arrangement, and it raises a fair question about why Walmart would sign up for it.

The answer has to do with where Walmart stands. Shoppers are beginning to start their shopping in AI assistants. As the challenger to Amazon online, Walmart gains more by meeting them there than by trying to pull them back to its own site, especially for the everyday replenishment it does best. For brands on Walmart, that turns listings into data an assistant will read, with repeat-purchase products as the first test.

What Walmart inside ChatGPT will look like

Walmart announced the partnership on October 14, 2025. It will join Shopify, Etsy and Salesforce in linking its catalog to ChatGPT’s Instant Checkout, with the integration taking effect later this fall for Walmart and Sam’s Club, Retail TouchPoints reported. The feature will offer a wide range of Walmart items as well as clothing, entertainment and food from third-party sellers, a Walmart spokesperson said, as CNN reported.

Everyday shopping was the frame Walmart chose for the move. Customers will be able to plan meals, restock household items and find new products, Walmart said, as Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Walmart came to the deal with momentum. Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 26% in the second quarter, and store-fulfilled delivery sales grew nearly 50%, Walmart said in its results release. Its global advertising business grew 46%, including Vizio, according to the same release.

Why a challenger wants a neutral starting point

Shoppers are starting to ask AI assistants what to buy, much as they once started with a search engine, and a retailer that is not present when the question is asked may not be considered at all. That alone would explain a partnership. It does not explain why Walmart moved early.

Walmart’s position explains the timing. On its own site, Walmart competes with Amazon for shoppers who already know where they want to buy. Inside a general assistant, every retailer starts closer to equal, and for the challenger a neutral starting point is an opportunity rather than a threat. Walmart’s strengths also suit the format. Meal planning and restocking are repeat purchases where price, availability and fast delivery matter most, and Walmart’s store network and growing delivery business are built for exactly those needs.

Who keeps what when the assistant does the shopping

Follow the pieces of value and the deal looks less like a concession. A shopper who buys Walmart products inside ChatGPT still becomes a Walmart customer, with the order fulfilled by Walmart, so the retailer keeps the transaction while the assistant handles discovery. In effect Walmart acts as a supplier to the assistant: it supplies the products, prices and delivery, and the assistant supplies the shopper.

Walmart also kept its own front door. In announcing the partnership, it pointed to its AI shopping assistant Sparky and other uses of AI at Walmart and Sam’s Club, the Associated Press reported. Sparky serves shoppers who are already on Walmart’s app; ChatGPT reaches shoppers who are not. Walmart is covering shoppers inside its own app and outside it, rather than betting on one.

What Walmart gives up is real. It cedes some control of the shopping experience, and its own advertising business depends on shoppers browsing Walmart’s site and app, so purchases made inside ChatGPT may see fewer of Walmart’s ads. That trade-off suggests Walmart judged the reach worth more than the ad impressions it might lose.

For brands, the same shift moves value toward whoever has the clearest, most complete product data, because that is what the assistant reads when it builds the list. Brands sit between the two sides. They supply the listings that both Walmart and the assistant depend on, and they pay for Walmart Connect ads that may reach fewer shoppers if the assistant takes over more of the browsing.

What brands on Walmart should change

Treat Walmart listings as agent-ready data. Titles, attributes, sizes and ingredients should be complete and accurate, because an assistant reads them to decide what fits. Start with repeat-purchase products: household essentials, pantry items and personal care are the likeliest early winners, so make sure those items are in stock and well described. Keep price and stock current on Walmart, since an assistant that recommends an out-of-stock or mispriced item loses trust. Brands selling through Walmart’s marketplace should check that their items carry complete data, since third-party products are included.

Shopping lists change what a listing has to do. Meal planning produces baskets of several items at once, so brands whose products often appear together, such as pasta and sauce, should check that each is well described and the assistant can include them in the same list. Make sure the descriptions, claims and images on Walmart are the version you want repeated, because assistants summarize product information. The same work pays off twice: Sparky reads the same listings, so improvements made for ChatGPT should also help shoppers who ask Sparky for products on Walmart’s app.

The last piece is measurement. If more shopping happens inside ChatGPT, fewer shoppers may see Walmart Connect ads, so track whether ad-driven sales shift as the feature rolls out, and look for changes in Walmart order patterns once the integration launches, separating them where possible.

One thing to watch through the holiday season is whether repeat-purchase orders on Walmart start arriving without a matching rise in site visits. Getting a Walmart catalog ready for the assistants that will read it is part of how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

A0817.crumb: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 results against…
A0817.title: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 results against our forecast
A0817.alt: Three wooden arrows in the bullseye of a straw archery target on grass covered with autumn leaves.
A0817.ttag: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 results against our forecast | Kwontified
A0817.desc: We graded our Prime Big Deal Days 2025 forecast against early results. Clicks cost less than we expected, baskets shrank, and deal share needs brand data.
A0817.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 21, 2025.
A0817.body:
Clicks on Amazon during Prime Big Deal Days 2025 cost about what they did a year earlier, and return on ad spend still did not improve. Among advertisers active in both years, cost per click stayed steady, but average order value fell 11%, from $43.47 to $38.72, according to Skai’s analysis. Cheaper clicks than we expected met smaller baskets than we expected, and the two cancelled out.

In short, that is what grading our own forecast shows. We overestimated bidding pressure and had no assumption at all for basket size. The public data cannot grade our sales-lift or deal-share ranges, which brands have to measure with their own numbers. For Cyber Week, the lesson is to lower the cost-per-click range and add a range for order value.

What the Prime Big Deal Days 2025 results show

Spending across the market grew modestly. Adobe’s data put online spending at US retailers during the event at $9.1 billion, up 7.3% from 2024, as Retail Brew reported and Skai cited. Adobe had forecast a 6.2% rise to $9 billion before the event, Retail TouchPoints reported, so the result came in slightly ahead.

The shoppers who did come were cautious. Nearly half, 48%, said tariffs affected their purchase decisions, and 61% said they also shopped Prime Day in July, Numerator reported.

On the advertising side, the picture held steady. Among advertisers active in both years, US Amazon ad spending rose nearly 7%, and conversion rates held stable alongside the steady cost per click, Skai found. Click-through rate rose from 0.22% to 0.39%, and return on ad spend was flat or slightly down as a result of the smaller baskets. Amazon DSP clicks rose 26%.

Grading the forecast range by range

Forecast elementOur ranges (conservative, standard, reach)What the public data showsGrade
Ad-driven sales lift vs the pre-event month200%, 250%, 300%Not reported; public figures are year over yearBrands grade with their own data
Cost per click vs the pre-event monthup 30%, 40%, 50%Steady year over year among the same advertisersLikely too high
Deal share of event sales35%, 45%, 55%No public sourceBrands grade with their own data
Average order valueNo assumptionDown 11%, $43.47 to $38.72Missing, and the bigger gap

The public figures compare year over year, not against the pre-event month, so they do not test our cost-per-click range exactly. But steady year-over-year cost per click suggests the event-day premium did not climb the way we assumed, and our range was likely too high. Sales lift is a different measurement altogether: our range set each brand’s event days against its own pre-event month, while public figures measure the market year over year. No public source reports the share of event sales from deal products either.

Why we expected dearer clicks

We assumed competition would keep rising, as it had from 2023 to 2024. Instead, ad spend grew only about 7% year over year and cost per click held steady. The pull behind the miss is a familiar one: the most recent change feels like the trend, so a forecaster extends it. One year of rising costs is a data point about that year’s auction, not a law about the next one, and the honest response is a wider range and a lower midpoint rather than a confident correction in the other direction.

The direction of demand is what we got right. We expected shoppers to show up despite cost pressure, and they did, with spending above Adobe’s own forecast. The standard case also allowed for tariff pressure and shopper caution, which proved to be the defining feature of the event.

Cheap clicks, flat returns: the basket effect

Return on ad spend is revenue per click divided by cost per click. Clicks were cheaper than we expected, yet return on ad spend did not improve, because each converted click brought in less revenue when average order value fell 11%. Engagement moved the other way: click-through rates rose sharply while conversion held flat, so shoppers were looking and comparing more without buying more per visit. That fits cautious shoppers who browse widely before committing.

Take a brand that forecast a 250% sales lift and a 40% cost-per-click rise. Its own data shows a 230% lift and a 20% cost-per-click rise, but order value down 10%. Lift landed inside the range, cost per click came in below it, and revenue per click fell because of smaller baskets. Graded honestly, that brand got one range right, one wrong in its favor, and missed a variable it never forecast.

Carrying the lessons into Cyber Week

Grade your own event first. Compare lift, cost per click and deal share with the ranges you planned, and note which assumptions held. Then fix the model. Cyber Week forecasts need a range for average order value, since smaller baskets can flatten return on ad spend even when clicks are cheap. Cyber Week bids should be planned on the evidence that event cost per click held steady, rather than on a steep climb.

Work on the basket directly. Bundles, multipacks and spend thresholds can lift order value, so test them on deal products before Black Friday. Smaller baskets also suggest shoppers bought practical items on deal, which makes it worth checking whether deep discounts on big-ticket items moved volume or shallower deals on essentials did more. With nearly half of shoppers citing tariffs, lead Cyber Week messaging with value, durability and practical gifting rather than aspiration.

Two checks finish the review. Compare sales in the weeks after the event with the same weeks in 2024, to see whether October deals took sales from November. And with DSP engagement rising, test upper-funnel campaigns ahead of Cyber Week.

The rule we are taking forward is simple: grade forecasts with your own data, and separate price effects from basket effects before deciding whether an event worked. Building those ranges and grading them afterward is how we measure Amazon events with brands.

A0819.crumb: What Prime Big Deal Days 2025 revealed…
A0819.title: What Prime Big Deal Days 2025 revealed about retailers and brands
A0819.alt: Three shop bay windows filled with red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes and autumn leaves along a brick street.
A0819.ttag: What Prime Big Deal Days 2025 revealed about retailers and brands | Kwontified
A0819.desc: Prime Big Deal Days 2025 turned into an industry week, with Target, Walmart and Best Buy selling around it and shoppers moving between them. What brands learn.
A0819.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 23, 2025.
A0819.body:
In the first half of October, a shopper with a Prime membership, a Target Circle account and the Walmart app could work three sales at once. Target Circle Week ran from October 5 to 11, around Amazon’s October 7 to 8 event, and Walmart’s sale ran from October 7 to 12. Best Buy had already opened member deals on September 28, running to October 5. Plenty of shoppers did move between them, which raises the question every brand team should now be asking: whose event was it?

The answer from Prime Big Deal Days 2025 is that the event belonged to the whole industry. Amazon anchored the week, but the market was every retailer a brand sells through. Brands that plan October as a cross-retailer week, with deliberate choices about which deals go where, will get more from it than brands that plan an Amazon event and treat the rest as spillover.

How Prime Big Deal Days 2025 became an industry week

The dates above come from Retail TouchPoints, which tracked how the rivals scheduled around Amazon. The retailers also chose different rules. Walmart’s sale did not require a membership, unlike the events from Amazon, Target and Best Buy, according to the same report. Target’s program is free to join, while Amazon’s requires paid Prime. Target offered 20,000 new items, twice as many as in 2024, with more than half exclusive to Target.

Delivery speed was part of the offer as well. Target said it would expand next-day delivery to 35 top US markets by the end of October, so retailers competed on delivery as well as price.

The shoppers followed the deals across sites. Among Prime Big Deal Days buyers, 36% said they shopped or planned to shop Walmart’s deals and 27% said they shopped Target Circle Week, Numerator reported. Average spend per order on Amazon was $45.42, according to the same release.

Each retailer chose a different lever

Shoppers no longer treat one retailer’s sale as the whole event. They compare prices across sites, buy what is cheapest or most convenient, and use each retailer’s deals for different needs. Each retailer picked its own way to compete.

Amazon and Target use membership to make deals exclusive and reward loyalty. Walmart dropped the membership requirement to widen its audience. Target leaned on exclusive products that cannot be compared directly, and Best Buy went first to catch early shoppers. Target added delivery speed to the list with its next-day expansion.

Read as institutions, those choices say what each retailer is protecting. A membership-gated event concentrates loyal, frequent shoppers. An open event reaches people who have not joined any program. An exclusive assortment avoids head-to-head price comparison altogether. For a brand, each lever is a different audience and a different kind of opportunity.

What cross-shopping does to a brand’s deal plan

The difficulty is that a deal no longer lives on one shelf. A deal offered only on Amazon may pull sales from the brand’s own Walmart and Target listings rather than adding new ones. A deal offered everywhere at the same depth gives shoppers no reason to choose one retailer, and squeezes margin across all of them.

Take a brand that ran a 25% deal on its best seller on Amazon and no deal on Walmart or Target. Amazon sales jumped, but Walmart sales of the same item fell during the week, and some loyal Target shoppers waited for a better price. Total sales rose less than the Amazon numbers suggested, and the team that reported only the Amazon result would have called the week a success. That is a measurement problem as much as a pricing one, because the loss shows up in a different retailer’s report.

Loyalty still counts for something. Most Prime Big Deal Days shoppers, 84%, said they would definitely or probably shop on Amazon again for holiday items in the next three months, according to Numerator. Shoppers compare across retailers, but they also return to the ones they trust, which makes each event a chance to win the next purchase as well as this one.

None of this means matching everywhere. Not every brand sells on every retailer, and not every product needs a deal on each. The point is to decide deliberately.

Planning the next event week across retailers

The plan starts with a map: as soon as retailer events are announced, list every one in the window, with dates, membership rules and deal formats. Then assign deals by retailer, based on each retailer’s audience, so deals add sales rather than move them. Bundles, sizes or colors exclusive to one retailer avoid direct price comparison and suit retailers that value exclusives, such as Target. Where the same item sells everywhere, avoid deep price gaps between retailers, which push shoppers to the cheapest site and squeeze margin.

The supporting plans for ads, delivery and stock have to cross channels too. Budgets on Amazon, Walmart Connect and Roundel should be planned together, so the brand does not bid against itself for the same shopper. With retailers competing on speed, check that deal products show fast delivery on each retailer, since a slower promise can lose a shopper who is comparing. And allocate stock for the whole week, because a deal that sells out on one retailer may leave the brand short elsewhere.

Judge the week on total sales and profit across all channels, not on Amazon results alone, and compare sales by retailer during and after the event to see which deals added new buyers and which only moved existing ones.

Before the next event, ask who owns the week rather than who owns Amazon. Planning one event across Amazon, Walmart and Target, with the deals, ads and stock to match, is part of how we run retail channels for brands.

A0821.crumb: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2025…
A0821.title: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2025: more players, higher costs
A0821.alt: A green gear room with bikes hung on a wall rack, a wooden kayak overhead, backpacks, boots, paddles and climbing gear.
A0821.ttag: Sports and outdoors on Amazon in 2025: more players, higher costs | Kwontified
A0821.desc: Record sports participation, led by pickleball, is meeting tariff-driven costs on imported gear. Where sports and outdoors sellers on Amazon gain and lose.
A0821.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Oct 30, 2025.
A0821.body:
Think about what a first-time pickleball player buys: a paddle, balls, a bag, court shoes, maybe a set of accessories, all at once, by someone who owned none of it before. There were 19.8 million pickleball participants in the US in 2024, up 45.8% from 2023 and 311% from three years earlier, according to the Sports & Fitness Industry Association. Players like that are the reason the category is growing. The same category is also paying more for much of what it imports.

So sports and outdoors on Amazon entered 2025 with record participation and a cost problem at the same time. The growth is real but uneven. Sellers who follow participation into new products, while protecting margin on the equipment most exposed to tariffs, will come through it in better shape than sellers who treat the category as one market.

Sports and outdoors on Amazon grew on participation

A record 247.1 million Americans, or 80%, participated in at least one sport or fitness activity in 2024, an increase of 25.4 million since 2019, the SFIA said in its participation report. Pickleball was the fastest-growing sport for the fourth year in a row, and racquet sports as a whole kept growing, according to the same report.

Big sporting events add to that pull. The SFIA said the 2024 Paris Olympics produced a clear bounce in participation for several sports. Moments like these can send new players looking for gear.

The industry’s main worry is cost. The industry grew 2.9% in 2024, and executives named tariffs as their top concern heading into the second half of 2025, according to the SFIA’s state of the industry report, as Recreation Management reported.

Why the category grows at two speeds

More people playing more sports means more buyers of equipment, apparel and accessories. Newer sports bring first-time buyers who need everything, and an online marketplace lets them compare options quickly. Participation also shifts what people buy over time. A player who moves from casual to regular play upgrades equipment, buys replacements and adds accessories, so a fast-growing sport creates a ladder of purchases, from starter sets to premium gear.

The cost side works differently. Much sports equipment is manufactured abroad, so tariffs raise landed costs for many sellers. Size and weight add another layer: many sports and outdoors products are bulky, such as tents, coolers, bikes and fitness equipment, and fulfillment and storage fees take a larger share of the price for these items than for small accessories. That squeezes margin further when import costs rise.

The result is growth that follows participation and margin pressure that follows import exposure. Categories tied to rising participation, such as racquet sports, can grow despite higher costs, because demand is expanding. Mature categories with flat participation have less room to absorb price increases. Both forces act on the same catalog at once, so a seller has to read them product by product.

The decision in the room: where to raise prices

For a leadership team in this category, the practical question is not whether tariffs hurt but where to take the increase. Brands must choose between raising prices, absorbing costs or changing suppliers, and each choice affects sales on a price-sensitive marketplace.

Take a seller with pickleball paddles and camping chairs, both imported. Paddle demand is rising, so a modest price increase barely slows sales. Camping chair demand is flat, so the same increase pushes shoppers to cheaper rivals. The same tariff hits the two products very differently, which is why a single company-wide pricing decision can be wrong for part of the range.

One caution belongs in that meeting. Participation data counts people who play at least once. Casual participants spend far less than regular players, so headline growth overstates the spending boost, and a team that prices every growing sport as if it were full of committed players will overreach.

Building the range around the new player

The work starts with a map of the range. Identify which sports in the catalog are growing, and check whether the range covers starter, intermediate and premium buyers in each. New players buy starter sets and then upgrade, so offer clear paths from first purchase to premium gear and use bundles to start the ladder. First-time buyers also need guidance on size, weight and skill level; clear listings with comparison charts help them choose and reduce returns.

The cost work runs product by product. List which products are most exposed to tariffs, by origin and margin, and decide for each whether to raise prices, absorb costs or change sourcing, testing increases first where demand is rising. Where tariff rates may change, plan purchase orders and inbound timing carefully, balancing the cost of holding extra stock against the risk of paying higher duties later. On large products, check fulfillment and storage costs and consider bundles, packaging changes or other channels where fees eat too much margin.

Timing and feedback complete the picture. Outdoor products swing with weather and seasons, so time stock and advertising to each sport’s season rather than to a single holiday plan. Beginners and experienced players judge products differently, so read reviews for complaints from each group and adjust listings or products to match. Fast-growing sports also have active online communities and creators; working with them reaches new players where they learn about the sport.

The question to bring to the next pricing review is which products in the range sit on rising participation and which sit on flat demand, because the answer decides where an increase will hold. Making that call across Amazon, Walmart and Target is part of how we run the sports and outdoors channel for brands.

A0825.title: Amazon Q3 2025 advertising revenue and the competition for clicks
A0825.alt: A long line of cardboard boxes queued along steel railings toward a metal turnstile in a yellow-walled hall.
A0825.ttag: Amazon Q3 2025 advertising revenue and the competition for clicks | Kwontified
A0825.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew 23.5% in Q3 2025, more than twice the pace of its online store sales. What the gap says about competition for clicks and ad budgets.
A0825.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 4, 2025.
A0825.body:
Advertising revenue at Amazon rose 23.5% in the third quarter of 2025, while its online store sales rose 9.8%. If shoppers bought 9.8% more through Amazon’s own store, why did advertisers pay 23.5% more?

Part of the answer is new ad inventory away from the store pages. The rest is a more crowded auction, in which more advertisers chase each shopper and more ad dollars sit behind every retail dollar. For a brand, that means growth and rising ad costs can arrive together, and the only way to see it is to measure advertising against total sales.

What Amazon’s Q3 2025 advertising revenue showed

Business lineQ3 2025 revenueGrowth year over year
Advertising services$17.7 billion23.5%
Online stores$67.41 billion9.8%
Third-party seller services$42.49 billion12.2%

The figures come from a summary of Amazon’s third-quarter results. The ad business outpaced the online stores by more than twice, and it did so from a larger base. At 23.5% growth, the $17.7 billion figure implies advertising revenue of about $14.3 billion in the third quarter of 2024, so Amazon added roughly $3.4 billion of quarterly ad revenue in a year.

Third-party seller services grew faster than Amazon’s own online store sales, which suggests sellers are both selling more and paying more for services such as fulfillment and advertising. The marketplace is strong, and the advertisers in it are spending into that strength.

More ad dollars behind each retail dollar

Advertising revenue measures what advertisers pay Amazon. Online store sales measure what Amazon sells directly. When advertising grows more than twice as fast, one of two things is happening. Either advertisers are paying more to win each sale, or Amazon is selling more advertising that does not sit on its store pages, such as Prime Video, Twitch and ads on other sites. In practice it is some of both.

A rough ratio makes the trend visible. Advertising equaled about 26% of online store sales in the third quarter of 2025, up from about 23% a year earlier, based on the reported figures. The comparison is imperfect, because third-party sales are not in the online stores line and some advertising runs off Amazon, but the direction is clear.

The on-site part of the story is about who is bidding. More sellers, more brands and more categories competing for the same searches raise the price of each click. Even if shopper demand grows, the number of advertisers chasing each shopper can grow faster. That is why Amazon can report strong shopper demand and a healthy marketplace while the cost of reaching shoppers through ads rises faster than sales.

The off-site growth softens that picture. Some of Amazon’s ad growth comes from formats such as Prime Video ads and DSP, which add new inventory rather than raising the price of search clicks, so not all of the gap means pricier search ads. For brands buying Sponsored Products, though, competition for the same search results keeps rising.

What the gap looks like inside one brand

Take a brand whose sales grew 10% in 2025, in line with Amazon’s online stores, while its ad spend grew 23%, in line with Amazon’s ad revenue. If advertising started at 10% of its sales, it ends the year at about 11.2%. Its ad line grew more than twice as fast as its sales line, the same pattern Amazon’s own numbers show. The brand grew, but each dollar of sales cost more in advertising, and a report built only on return on ad spend would never show it.

Company-wide figures describe the average across millions of advertisers, so this is a direction, not a forecast for any one account. A brand in a quiet category may see flat costs while a brand in a crowded one sees costs climb much faster. Each brand should check its own trend before drawing a conclusion from Amazon’s.

Keeping ad costs from outrunning sales

The first fix is measuring the right ratio. Return on ad spend alone hides the trend, so watch advertising cost against total sales, including organic, every month. Judge Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, DSP and streaming ads each against its own goal rather than blending them into one number, because they do different jobs.

On search, defend efficiency. Prune keywords that rarely convert, harvest search terms that do, and shift spend toward branded and specific terms where competition is lower. Look for periods and placements where competition is lighter and buy there; cost per click held steady during Prime Big Deal Days among advertisers Skai tracked, according to its October analysis. Track share of voice as well as cost, meaning how often products appear in sponsored and organic results for key searches. Rising costs matter less if share of voice holds, and more if a brand pays more and appears less.

Reduce the dependence on auctions where you can. Strong listings, reviews and stock lift organic rank, and every sale won organically is one that does not need an auction. If off-site formats are where Amazon is adding inventory, test them with clear goals for new customers and branded search rather than simply moving budget. Amazon also introduced AI tools for building ads in Creative Studio in September, PPC Land reported; they can save time, but review what they produce before it goes live.

The first test of all this is Cyber Week. Set holiday budgets as a share of expected sales, with a ceiling, so rising costs during the busiest weeks do not erase margin.

The rule we use is to track advertising against total sales, separate search from off-site media, and keep the efficiency gains you earn. Holding that line through a quarter like this one is how we manage Amazon ad budgets for brands.

A0826.crumb: Who gets to shop for the shopper: Amazon…
A0826.title: Who gets to shop for the shopper: Amazon versus the agents
A0826.alt: A white robotic arm holds a wire shopping basket of bread and jars in front of shelves of glass jars and linens.
A0826.ttag: Who gets to shop for the shopper: Amazon versus the agents | Kwontified
A0826.desc: Amazon’s suit against Perplexity asks who may act for a shopper inside a store. What the fight over AI agents means for brands on Amazon and beyond.
A0826.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 6, 2025.
A0826.body:
A shopper asks her assistant to reorder her usual detergent at the best price. If the assistant can shop at Walmart openly but is blocked at Amazon, it buys from Walmart. The brand still makes the sale, but on a different retailer, and Amazon loses the order without the shopper ever deciding against it. Amazon’s lawsuit against Perplexity concerns errands like that one, and it turns a technical question into a policy one: who may act for a shopper inside a store.

Shoppers want to delegate, and retailers want control. The likely settlement is agents that identify themselves and stores that set the terms. Brands should expect agent shopping to flow to the retailers that welcome it, and should prepare their listings both for Amazon’s own assistants and for the outside agents that compare stores.

How Amazon versus AI shopping agents reached court

The dispute moved to court on November 4, when Amazon sued Perplexity in San Francisco federal court to stop its Comet browser agent from making purchases on Amazon for users, Bloomberg reported. Amazon accuses Perplexity of computer fraud for failing to disclose when Comet is shopping on a real person’s behalf, according to the complaint as Bloomberg reported it.

Perplexity pushed back the same day. In a statement titled “Bullying is Not Innovation,” the company said it had received an aggressive legal threat from Amazon seeking to stop Comet users from using AI assistants on Amazon, Investing.com reported, citing Reuters.

The suit follows earlier signals. Through its robots.txt file, Amazon had already asked crawlers from Perplexity, Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Project Mariner agents, among others, to stay off its site, Modern Retail reported. Amazon is also offering its own answer to the outside agents. Its new Help Me Decide feature uses a shopper’s searches, browsing and purchase history to recommend a product and explain why, TechCrunch reported.

Walmart has taken a different path. It said on October 14 that it would let shoppers buy its products inside ChatGPT, with the feature due this fall, Retail TouchPoints reported. So one retailer has gone to court to keep an outside agent away from its checkout, while another has invited a chat assistant to sell its products.

Why the question is who acts for the shopper

Shoppers supply the pressure. They increasingly want software to do the tedious parts of buying: compare options, find the best price, reorder what they always buy. An agent that can do this across stores is genuinely useful.

The resistance comes from what a store is. A store is more than a warehouse with a checkout. Its search results, product pages and recommendations are where it earns advertising revenue and builds loyalty. An outside agent that buys without browsing skips all of that, and the store loses control of the experience it built.

Each side has a fair point. Perplexity argues that the shopper, not the store, should choose the tools they use. Amazon argues that software acting in its store should say what it is and follow its rules. Both claims are about trust: shoppers trusting their agent, and stores trusting who is in their aisles.

That points to disclosure as the middle ground. Agents that identify themselves, in stores that set clear terms for what agents may do, would let both sides keep something. Retailers could welcome agents that respect their rules and block those that hide. The structure that emerges is a split market, in which some retailers welcome outside agents under terms and others keep them out and offer their own assistants instead.

None of this is settled. The case is at an early stage, and a court may take months to rule. Retailers’ positions may also shift as agent shopping grows. Brands should watch the direction rather than bet on a specific outcome.

Getting a catalog ready for two kinds of shopper

The groundwork is listings that any reader, human or software, can use. Complete titles, attributes, prices and stock help both outside agents and retailers’ own assistants recommend a product. Reviews and ratings belong in the same effort, because agents and assistants alike lean on quality signals, so review programs should stay active on every major retailer.

Distribution comes next. A brand should know which of its retailers allow outside agents and which rely on their own assistants, so it understands where agent-driven sales can come from. Price consistency matters more once agents are comparing across stores: wide gaps between retailers push agent orders to the cheapest one, which can reshape a brand’s channel mix without warning.

Discovery splits along the same line. Inside Amazon, products are found by Amazon’s search and assistants; outside, they may be found by agents comparing stores. Content and pricing have to be planned for both.

Amazon’s own assistants deserve separate attention, since they will shape what shoppers see inside Amazon. Brands should test how their products appear in Amazon’s assistant answers and fix the gaps they find.

Account access needs its own policy. Agents that log in to shoppers’ accounts raise questions about security and about responsibility for mistaken orders. Brands should make returns and order policies clear, since agent errors may land on their customer service teams.

Measurement and the court case keep the picture current. Where possible, brands should measure orders that arrive from AI assistants separately, to see how much agent shopping is growing, and they should follow the case. Its outcome will set expectations for what agents may do in stores, which affects how brands plan their channels.

The question to put to the team

The useful question is which retailers your products would be bought from if an assistant did the shopping, and whether your listings, prices and reviews hold up in each of them. Preparing a catalog for the shopper who browses Amazon and the one who sends an agent instead is how we get brands ready for AI shopping across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0828.crumb: Cyber Week 2025 forecast: plan by day…
A0828.title: Cyber Week 2025 forecast: plan by day type, not by event
A0828.alt: Seven glass jars holding varying amounts of coins on a wooden ledge in front of ribbon-wrapped holiday gifts.
A0828.ttag: Cyber Week 2025 forecast: plan by day type, not by event | Kwontified
A0828.desc: Ranges for daily lift, cost per click, deal share and order value across Amazon’s 12-day Cyber Week 2025, and why budgets should be planned by day type.
A0828.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 11, 2025.
A0828.body:
Amazon’s Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday deal events run from November 20 through December 1, Amazon said in a release. Twelve days of selling make a window that behaves like two events in one: a long, steady middle and two crowded peaks on Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Our forecast ranges, including a new one for order value, are built around that shape. The practical answer for budgets is to plan by day type and to grade results against ranges, not against one event-wide number.

The Cyber Week 2025 forecast in four ranges

The ranges below are Kwontified assumptions for a typical brand advertising on Amazon, measured against its own average in the 30 days before November 20.

MeasureConservativeStandardReach
Average daily ad-attributed sales lift across the window80%120%160%
Cost per click increase against the pre-event month15%25%35%
Deal share of event sales30%40%50%
Average order value against the same window in 20245% declineno change5% rise

Peak days will run well above the lift averages, and middle days below. We have lowered the cost-per-click ranges from our October assumptions, after Prime Big Deal Days passed with cost per click steady. Deal share depends on how much of a brand’s catalog carries accepted deals. The order value range is new: we added it after smaller baskets flattened returns in October.

What last year and October say

The 2024 event set the baseline. During the Cyber 5 in 2024, Amazon ad spend rose 25% year over year and cost per click rose 13%, with Sponsored Brands cost per click up 20%, according to Pacvue’s Cyber 5 benchmark. Brands spent more in the lead-up and on Black Friday than on Cyber Monday, according to the same report.

Upper-funnel ads mattered at the peaks. New-to-brand shoppers accounted for 68% of Amazon DSP sales on Black Friday 2024 and 63% on Cyber Monday, Pacvue found.

The fresher signal came in October. During Prime Big Deal Days 2025, cost per click held steady year over year, average order value fell 11% and return on ad spend was flat, according to Skai’s analysis. That is the reason the cost-per-click ranges came down and the order value range went in.

Why a 12-day event needs forecasts by day type

Twelve days spread the same shoppers over more time. The average daily lift is lower than in a two-day event, and bidding on ordinary days eases. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain peaks, where shoppers and advertisers crowd in together.

So the event as a whole may look less intense than a short sale, while the two peak days are as competitive as ever. Each advertiser’s choice to concentrate on the same two days is what keeps those days expensive, even as the long middle gets cheaper. A single event-wide forecast averages the two together and hides the pattern that matters most for budgets. The gap between the average day and the peak day is the case for planning by day type.

Thanksgiving itself adds a wrinkle. Some shoppers browse on Thanksgiving Day and buy the next morning, so clicks can rise a day before orders do. Brands that judge Thanksgiving on same-day return on ad spend may cut spend just before the payoff arrives.

Take a brand that spends $1,000 a day before the event, with cost per click of $1.00. In the standard case, its cost per click rises to about $1.25. If it raises spend to $1,800 a day, it buys about 1,440 clicks a day against 1,000 before, and needs sales lift of at least 80% just to hold return on ad spend steady. The extra clicks are real, but they cost more each, and the lift has to cover the whole increase in spend before the event adds anything. On a peak day, where cost per click is higher still, the same arithmetic asks even more of the lift.

How brands should plan Cyber Week budgets

Start by splitting the window. Brands should plan separate budgets for the early days, the middle days, Black Friday weekend and Cyber Monday, rather than one daily figure. Black Friday and Cyber Monday deserve the largest daily budgets, with bids that can rise when competition does. The middle days earn their place too. Ordinary days in a long window often bring cheaper clicks, so brands should keep steady spend there, especially on products with strong conversion.

Order value needs watching alongside sales. If baskets shrink, return on ad spend can fall even when clicks are cheap, so brands should push bundles and multipacks on deal products. Branded terms need protecting as well. Competitors bid on brand names during peaks, and brands should keep branded campaigns funded every day of the window, since those shoppers are the most likely to buy.

Brands should hold part of the budget in reserve for products that outperform, and for the final push on Cyber Monday. Stock deserves a daily check, because a 12-day event can drain inventory before the peaks arrive; brands should shift spend away from products running low.

New shoppers are the case for DSP. With most DSP sales on peak days coming from new-to-brand customers in 2024, brands with DSP access should plan audience campaigns in the lead-up and through the peaks.

Grade it by day type

After December 1, brands should compare their results with these ranges by day type, as we did after October. The rule for the 12 days of the window is short: forecast by day type, budget for higher cost per click on the peak days, expect it to rise 15% to 35% against the pre-event month, and measure order value alongside sales. Building that plan before the window opens, and grading it after, is how we forecast and pace Amazon events for brands.

A0832.crumb: Toys on Amazon in 2025: growth, licenses…
A0832.title: Toys on Amazon in 2025: growth, licenses and tariff pressure
A0832.alt: Colorful wooden toy blocks and a toy train on a wood floor in front of stacked wooden crates against a blue wall.
A0832.ttag: Toys on Amazon in 2025: growth, licenses and tariff pressure | Kwontified
A0832.desc: US toy sales grew in 2025 on licensed toys, collectibles and adult buyers as tariffs on Chinese imports raised costs. What changed for toy sellers on Amazon.
A0832.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 13, 2025.
A0832.body:
Shoppers search for the characters, teams and franchises they love, and in 2025 that habit carried the US toy business. Licensed toys accounted for 37% of US toy sales in the first half and grew 18%, according to Circana’s figures. A product tied to a popular license gets found and chosen more easily than a generic one, and the sales data shows it.

The category returned to growth on licensed toys, collectibles and adult buyers. At the same time, nearly 80% of imported toys come from China and face tariff pressure. Toy sellers on Amazon should lean into the licenses and price points that are growing, protect margin on tariff-exposed lines, and plan the holiday season around a shopper who is buying but watching prices closely.

How toys on Amazon changed in 2025

Sales grew after two weak years. From January through June 2025, US toy dollar sales rose 6%, units rose 3% and average selling price rose 3%, Circana reported, as The Toy Association published. The average toy price was $11.11, Kidscreen reported. Most of the year was still ahead at midyear: the second half typically accounts for more than 60% of annual toy sales, according to the same Toy Association release.

Collectibles became a growth engine. Global collectibles sales rose 35% in the first half, as toy makers used social media to promote them, according to the same release.

Growth continued into the fall. The US toy industry posted a solid third quarter, with the steepest declines in outdoor and sports toys and in plush and dolls, License Global reported. Circana’s Juli Lennett said shoppers’ willingness to absorb tariffs would be the key factor in the fourth quarter, according to the same report.

That willingness matters because of where the toys come from. Nearly 80% of toys imported into the US come from China, Retail Dive reported, which makes tariffs the main risk to the season.

Why the toy category is growing unevenly

Toys are emotional purchases, and shoppers keep buying them for gifts and for themselves even when budgets are tight. Adults collecting toys and buying for themselves have become a meaningful source of growth. Licenses then concentrate that demand on the products shoppers already know by name, which is why licensed toys grew so quickly.

Costs behave differently, landing across the whole category. With most imported toys made in China, tariffs raise landed costs everywhere. Sellers must decide whether to raise prices, absorb costs or move production, and each choice affects sales in a season when shoppers compare prices closely.

The question underneath every one of those decisions is who ends up paying the tariff. Take a seller with a licensed figure at $24.99 and a generic plush at $14.99, both made in China. A tariff adds $2 to each.

The licensed figure can carry a modest price increase because shoppers search for it by name, so the shopper pays. The generic plush cannot, because shoppers can find a similar one for less, so the seller pays out of margin. The same tariff squeezes one product far more than the other.

That is why growth looks uneven. Licensed toys and collectibles grow, while categories such as outdoor toys and plush lose ground, and price increases land differently depending on whether a product has a reason to command a premium. Licenses, collectibles and products with a reason to be chosen by name can absorb cost pressure. Generic products in declining categories face the hardest squeeze.

The first-half numbers carry a caution. Strong first-half sales may partly reflect retailers and shoppers buying early ahead of expected price increases. Holiday results will show whether demand holds once higher prices reach shelves.

What toy sellers on Amazon should do before the holidays

Put the effort where the demand is. Sellers should prioritize stock, listings and advertising on licensed products and collectibles, where demand is strongest. Adult buyers deserve their own attention in the listing itself: collectors and adults buying for themselves search differently from parents, so sellers should include collector details, such as edition, series and condition.

Price by brand power, and know the exposure first. Sellers should list which products are made in China and how much margin each carries, then decide product by product how to respond. Products shoppers search for by name can carry modest increases. Generic products may need to hold price, with costs absorbed or offset elsewhere.

Stock for the holidays needs care. With more than 60% of sales in the second half, running out during the holiday peak is costly, and sellers should confirm inventory for top products through December. Value messaging belongs in the same plan, because shoppers watching prices respond to bundles, gift sets and clear value messaging; sellers should feature these on deal days.

Advertising should follow the calendar. Amazon has set its Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday events for November 20 through December 1, according to its release. Toy sellers should weight advertising toward that window and the weeks before Christmas, when gift searches peak.

The season also calls for two protections. Popular licenses attract counterfeit and unauthorized sellers, so licensed brands should monitor their listings closely during the holidays and report infringing offers quickly. Gift buyers rely on reviews and ratings, so sellers should address product complaints quickly and keep ratings strong when traffic peaks.

The tariff question will be answered at the checkout in the fourth quarter, one product at a time, as shoppers decide which price increases they accept. Sorting a catalog by license strength and tariff exposure before that happens is how we help toy brands grow on Amazon, Walmart and Target.
