A0834.title: What Amazon unBoxed 2025 changes for advertisers
A0834.alt: An open cardboard box with crumpled paper glowing warmly inside, on a wooden table beside a mug and linen cloth.
A0834.ttag: What Amazon unBoxed 2025 changes for advertisers | Kwontified
A0834.desc: unBoxed 2025 put Sponsored Ads and Amazon DSP in one Campaign Manager with AI agents. Why shared data pulls budgets up the funnel, and how to keep control.
A0834.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 18, 2025.
A0834.body:
In separate consoles, a search click that closes a sale gets the credit, and the DSP ad the shopper saw days earlier sits in another report. Put both in one platform with one view and they appear side by side. DSP’s role becomes visible, and DSP starts to look more valuable. Nothing about the shopper changed; only the report did.

That is what unBoxed 2025 did when it put Sponsored Ads and Amazon DSP into one Campaign Manager, with unified reporting and AI agents. It will pull budgets up the funnel. But Amazon both sells and measures both ad types, so brands should keep budgets split by objective, prove DSP’s value with incrementality tests and decide deliberately what agents may change.

Amazon unBoxed 2025 changes for advertisers start with one console

Amazon launched a beta of a revamped Campaign Manager that brings Sponsored Ads and Amazon DSP into a single platform, with an “All View” that combines their performance data in one workspace, PPC Land reported. A broader rollout to all advertisers is planned, according to the same report.

The console arrived with AI agents attached. Amazon introduced an Ads Agent and a Creative Agent alongside the unified Campaign Manager, and positioned the tools as transparent rather than fully automated, The Drum reported.

Reporting moved the same way. A new reporting experience in open beta lets advertisers combine data across ad products, accounts and countries, with daily data for 15 months, PPC Land reported. Outside AI tools can now connect too, through a server Amazon opened in closed beta on November 13, according to a separate PPC Land report.

Why one view moves money toward DSP

The shift toward DSP has already started. Among advertisers Skai tracked, Amazon DSP clicks rose 26% year over year during Prime Big Deal Days in October, according to Skai’s analysis. DSP also reaches new customers. On Black Friday 2024, 68% of DSP sales went to new-to-brand shoppers, according to Pacvue’s Cyber 5 benchmark.

That visibility will move money. Advertisers who see DSP touching many of their converting shoppers will shift budget toward it, and Amazon’s own recommendations, built into the same workspace, will tend to point the same way.

The catch is that better visibility can make measurement look more certain than it is. When a shopper sees a DSP ad and then clicks a search ad, both may claim the sale. The platform that sells both ad types also decides how credit is shared. Overlapping credit can make the combined return look better than the real lift. A sale that both ad types claim shows up in the totals once for each of them.

Take a brand that spends $50,000 a month, 90% on Sponsored Ads and 10% on DSP. In the unified view, 40% of its converting shoppers saw a DSP ad first. That looks like a case for more DSP. But many of those shoppers were already searching for the brand, and without a test the brand cannot tell how many extra sales DSP created. The 40% describes who saw an ad, not who was persuaded by it.

None of this argues against DSP. DSP can genuinely create demand, especially among shoppers who have never bought from a brand, and unified data is a real improvement over guessing. The point is to verify the gain with a test before moving large budgets.

How advertisers should respond to the new console

Budget structure is the place to start. Brands should keep separate budgets for capturing demand through search and creating demand through DSP and streaming, each with its own goal. Before shifting money between them, brands should run holdout or geography-based tests to measure how many extra sales DSP drives, rather than relying on attribution in the unified view. That is the same view that makes DSP look strong in the first place.

The number to check is double counting. Brands should compare total sales with the sum of attributed sales across ad types; a large gap suggests credit is being counted twice. DSP itself is best judged on new customers. New-to-brand sales and branded search growth show whether DSP is reaching people who would not otherwise buy, and brands should track both alongside attributed return.

The agents need permissions before they need trust. Ads Agent and outside tools connected through Amazon’s server can create and change campaigns, so brands should start with read-only access and require human approval for budget and bid changes. Creative from Creative Agent deserves the same care: AI-built ads can save time, but brands should check claims, imagery and brand standards before anything goes live, especially in regulated categories.

The platform changes workflows as well. Agencies managing many accounts will gain from one login and one view, and brands should agree with their agencies how budgets, approvals and reporting will work in the new platform. Campaign Manager is rolling out over time, so brands should map how their current campaigns, naming and reporting will carry over, so nothing breaks mid-season.

The new reports earn their keep immediately. Fifteen months of daily data makes it easier to compare Cyber Week with 2024, and brands should build year-over-year views by day now. The holiday window is the first large test of the new tools. Once the event ends, brands should review what the unified view and agents got right and wrong, before committing more budget to them.

The test before the shift

The rule is short: split budgets by objective, prove DSP with an incrementality test before the unified view moves the money, and give the agents read-only access until a person signs off on budgets and bids. Measuring what DSP adds on top of search is how we plan and measure Amazon advertising across the funnel.

A0835.title: Electronics on Amazon in 2025: early buying, then caution
A0835.alt: Leather headphones on a tablet beside a vintage film camera and a plain cardboard box on a wooden table.
A0835.ttag: Electronics on Amazon in 2025: early buying, then caution | Kwontified
A0835.desc: Shoppers bought electronics early in 2025 to beat tariffs, then slowed and traded down. What changed on Amazon, and how sellers should plan the holiday.
A0835.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 20, 2025.
A0835.body:
Picture a pair of wireless earbuds that sold strongly in spring, when shoppers were buying early. By fall, the same $79 model sits on the results page next to a $49 rival and the 2024 version on discount. Without a clear reason to pay more, the seller loses the sale or discounts into its margin.

That one page holds the whole electronics year. Shoppers bought early in 2025 to get ahead of tariff-driven price increases, which lifted the first half and left the second half softer, with shoppers trading down. Electronics sellers on Amazon should expect a cautious holiday, compete on value and clear comparisons, and protect margin on the products most exposed to tariffs.

How electronics on Amazon changed in 2025

The year started with optimism. The Consumer Technology Association forecast record US consumer technology revenue of $537 billion in 2025, up 3.2%, in a release that also warned tariffs could reduce US consumers’ purchasing power for technology by $90 billion to $143 billion.

Then shoppers started buying ahead of the tariffs. Consumer technology retail dollar sales grew 1.5% in the first half of 2025, partly because shoppers pulled forward purchases in anticipation of tariffs, Circana data showed, as RetailWire reported. Circana cut its full-year forecast to a 1% gain from 1.6%, citing signs of shoppers trading down, according to the same report.

The price pressure was large on paper. A study for the CTA estimated that tariffs would raise average retail prices for smartphones by 31%, laptops and tablets by 34% and video game consoles by 69%, according to the study’s summary.

Computers were the strongest part of the year. Early on, the PC market entered a refresh cycle, with a strong emphasis on IT products, Circana’s Paul Gagnon said, according to RetailWire. Replacement needs helped too. Microsoft ended standard support for Windows 10 in October 2025, which gave many households and small businesses a reason to replace older PCs during the year. Replacement purchases are harder to delay than upgrades, which helps explain why computers held up better than other categories.

Why the electronics year split in two

When shoppers expect prices to rise, they buy sooner. That moves sales from later months into earlier ones, so the first half looks strong and the second half has fewer shoppers left who need to buy. Much of the demand did not disappear; it arrived earlier. The ones who still buy later in the year look for lower-priced models, older generations or deals, and premium products meet more resistance.

From the other side, costs add pressure. Most consumer electronics are manufactured abroad, so tariffs raise landed costs. Sellers face a choice among raising prices, absorbing costs and changing suppliers, in a category where shoppers compare specifications and prices closely.

And the comparison is easy to make. Reviews, comparison sites and AI assistants let shoppers check specifications and prices across sellers in seconds. A product without a clear advantage in that comparison loses the sale to whichever rival is cheapest, which is exactly what happens to the $79 earbuds when nothing on the page explains why they cost more than the $49 pair.

Holiday gifting complicates that picture. Gifts can still lift electronics, and new products with real improvements can overcome price resistance. The softness applies most to products shoppers can delay or replace with cheaper options.

What emerges is a two-speed category. Products with strong reasons to buy, such as new features or replacement needs, hold up. Discretionary upgrades face the most caution.

What electronics sellers on Amazon should do this holiday

Planning has to come before promotion. Sellers should set forecasts and stock with the first-half pull-forward in mind, rather than extending early-year growth into the holiday. Gift-ready stock still matters inside that cautious plan: electronics are popular gifts, gift buyers want fast delivery close to the holidays, and sellers should keep top products in stock through mid-December, when last-minute buyers arrive.

Value is the argument to win. Bundles, accessories included in the box and clear warranty terms give shoppers reasons to choose one product over a cheaper rival. Shoppers buying a laptop, phone or console often need cases, cables, chargers or controllers, so sellers should bundle or cross-promote accessories, which carry better margins and lift order value.

The listing has to carry the comparison. Electronics shoppers compare specifications, so sellers should present key specifications clearly in titles, bullets and comparison charts, so shoppers see the difference. Clear listings and accurate compatibility information also reduce costly returns after the holidays, since electronics carry higher return rates when expectations are not met.

Pricing calls for a product-by-product map. Sellers should list products by origin and margin and decide product by product how to respond, starting with the most price-sensitive items. Older models belong in the same exercise: previous generations can serve shoppers who are trading down, and sellers should price them deliberately, rather than letting them undercut new models by accident.

The plan ends with timing and control. Amazon’s Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday events run from November 20 to December 1, according to Amazon’s release, and electronics sellers should weight spend toward those days, when deal-seeking shoppers are most active. Electronics also attract many resellers, so brands should monitor who is winning the Buy Box on their products and act on unauthorized sellers before peak days.

The earbuds on that fall results page need a listing that answers one question before the shopper asks it: why this pair, at this price, instead of the cheaper one beside it. Building that answer into every listing, product by product, is how we help electronics brands grow on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0836.crumb: Apparel and CPG on Target Plus: where the…
A0836.title: Apparel and CPG on Target Plus: where the marketplace fits
A0836.alt: Folded knit sweaters stacked on a red wooden bench beside ceramic mugs, mason jars and linen napkins by a sunny window.
A0836.ttag: Apparel and CPG on Target Plus: where the marketplace fits | Kwontified
A0836.desc: Target Plus GMV grew nearly 50% while Target’s stores struggled. Why the marketplace grows, and how apparel and CPG brands should use it alongside stores.
A0836.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 25, 2025.
A0836.body:
Target’s comparable sales fell 2.7% in the third quarter of 2025. In the same quarter, Target Plus, its third-party marketplace, grew gross merchandise value nearly 50%. The stores are struggling, the marketplace is growing fast, and the two numbers are connected.

The marketplace lets Target widen its assortment without holding the inventory. That makes it most useful exactly where Target’s own buying is cautious. Apparel and consumer goods brands should use Target Plus to sell what stores do not carry, keep their offers distinct from their in-store range and support listings with Roundel advertising.

How apparel and CPG on Target Plus fit Target’s results

Target Plus gross merchandise value grew nearly 50% in the third quarter, and Roundel saw double-digit growth, Target said in its results summary. Comparable sales fell 2.7%, according to the same summary.

Discretionary categories were where the softness sat. Food and beverage and hardlines grew, offset by continued softness across the broader discretionary portfolio, and non-merchandise sales grew nearly 18%, with Roundel, membership and marketplace revenue all growing double digits, Target said in its earnings release.

Target has set a goal for the marketplace. Executives laid out plans to grow Target Plus from more than $1 billion in gross merchandise value to more than $5 billion within five years, Modern Retail reported.

Curation is the model. Target Plus is invite-only, and Target has limited some items to a single seller as a way to stand out, Fortune reported.

Why a marketplace grows when stores are cautious

When a retailer’s own buying turns cautious, it carries fewer sizes, colors and pack options in stores and in its own inventory. A marketplace fills that gap with products sold by partners, who hold the stock. Target earns commissions and advertising revenue without the inventory risk.

That explains the divergence in the quarter. Target can tighten its own merchandise in soft categories while letting the marketplace widen the range online, so the marketplace grows fastest precisely when owned inventory is constrained.

Curation changes the economics for brands, and it cuts both ways. On open marketplaces, many sellers can list the same item, and brands fight resellers for the sale. On Target Plus, an invited brand often faces far less competition on its own products. Fewer brands get in, but those that do face a calmer shelf. For brands that fit Target’s assortment, the trade favors getting in.

Apparel and consumer goods use the gap differently. Apparel brands can offer extended sizes, extra colors and styles that stores do not stock. Consumer goods brands can offer larger packs, bundles and items outside the in-store planogram. Two brands show the pattern:

BrandIn Target storesOn Target Plus
Apparel brandfive of its styles in core sizesthose styles in extended sizes, plus eight more styles
Consumer goods brandits single bottlesa four-pack and a gift bundle that stores do not stock

For the apparel brand, shoppers who cannot find their size in store, or want more choice, buy through the marketplace, and the brand adds sales without competing against its own in-store range. For the consumer goods brand, shoppers who want to stock up find the larger pack online, and the brand avoids undercutting its own shelf.

Scale is the limit to keep in view. Even at $5 billion, Target’s marketplace would be small next to Amazon’s $156 billion in third-party seller services in 2024, according to the same Modern Retail report. Target Plus is a valuable addition for brands that fit rather than a replacement for larger marketplaces.

Delivery expectations are rising too. Target said next-day shipping now reaches more than half of the US population, according to its earnings release. Marketplace sellers will be judged against that standard, so slow shipping will stand out.

What apparel and CPG brands should do on Target Plus

Mapping the gap comes before any listing. Brands should list what Target stores and Target-owned online inventory carry, and identify the sizes, colors, packs and products that are missing. Brands new to Target Plus should begin with a small set of products that fill clear gaps, then expand as they learn what sells.

Pricing has to respect the wholesale side. Marketplace prices that undercut a brand’s in-store items create conflict with Target’s buyers, so brands should price marketplace items consistently with their wholesale relationship.

Whether the listings hold up is a question of operations. Target expects reliable fulfillment and service, and brands should confirm shipping speed, stock accuracy and returns handling before scaling. Marketplace stock sits in the brand’s own warehouse or with its logistics partner. Brands should forecast Target Plus demand on its own, so a marketplace surge does not drain stock meant for other channels. Target shoppers expect clean imagery and consistent product information, and brands should adapt listings to Target’s style rather than copying content from other marketplaces.

Visibility comes from Roundel and the calendar. Marketplace items need it, so brands should use Roundel advertising to reach shoppers searching for extended sizes or bundles. Target’s events, such as Circle Week and holiday moments, draw shoppers who are already loyal, and brands should plan marketplace deals around them.

The sales data is worth sharing. Marketplace sales reveal unmet demand, and brands that share what sells with their Target buyers can strengthen the case for in-store placement.

The rule for Target Plus is simple to state: sell what stores do not carry, keep offers distinct from the in-store range, and support listings with Roundel advertising. Finding those gaps and running the listings and Roundel campaigns that fill them is how we help brands sell and advertise on Target Plus.

A0837.title: Beauty on Amazon in 2025: value, fragrance and converging tiers
A0837.alt: Vintage glass perfume bottles on a mirrored silver tray atop a wooden dresser in warm sunlight.
A0837.ttag: Beauty on Amazon in 2025: value, fragrance and converging tiers | Kwontified
A0837.desc: Mass beauty outgrew prestige in 2025 and fragrance led. On Amazon both tiers share one shelf, so beauty brands win on proof, entry sizes and price control.
A0837.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Nov 26, 2025.
A0837.body:
In a physical store, prestige beauty has its own counters and mass beauty has its own aisles, and the separation tells the shopper what each tier is worth. On Amazon that separation is gone. A $15 serum and a $65 serum appear side by side in the same search results, and the shopper compares them on ingredients, reviews and price.

That shared shelf is where beauty shoppers in 2025 rewarded efficacy at a fair price. Mass outgrew prestige, fragrance led growth and the line between the two tiers blurred, which suits Amazon, where both tiers meet on one shelf. Beauty brands on Amazon should compete on proof and value, use smaller sizes and fragrance to win new buyers, and give shoppers clear reasons to pay more for prestige products.

How beauty on Amazon changed in 2025

In the first half of 2025, US prestige beauty sales grew 2% to $16 billion, while mass sales grew 4% to $34.6 billion, according to Circana’s first-half report.

Fragrance led that growth. Prestige fragrance sales rose 6% to $3.9 billion, and fragrance was the fastest-growing mass category, up 17%, according to the same report. Within the category, mini and travel-size fragrances grew 15% in units, nearly four times the rate of other sizes, Circana said, as Chain Drug Review reported.

Skincare moved in two directions at once. Prestige skincare sales fell 1% to $4.6 billion, which Circana attributed mainly to declines in facial skincare sold in physical stores, while masstige brands grew by double digits. Hair care grew too: prestige hair sales rose 6% to $2.3 billion, with growth in every segment and a double-digit lift in styling products, according to Circana’s release. Treatments and styling are categories where shoppers search for specific problems, which suits online discovery.

Underneath those category numbers sits a question about price. Only 14% of US beauty buyers believe that higher prices mean better quality, said Larissa Jensen, Circana’s global beauty industry advisor, adding that the mass and prestige markets are converging, as Personal Care Magazine reported.

Why value now decides beauty purchases

Beauty shoppers research ingredients, read reviews and watch creators test products. When they can judge results for themselves, a high price is no longer enough to signal quality. What wins is value, meaning visible results at a fair price.

That habit favors online channels. Physical stores separate prestige counters from mass aisles, while online, especially on Amazon, both tiers sit in the same search results, the $15 serum a scroll away from the $65 one.

Take a skincare brand whose $58 moisturizer competes in search with a $22 masstige rival. Shoppers who cannot see a clear difference choose the cheaper one, and the brand’s ad spend buys clicks that do not convert. When the brand adds clinical results, ingredient explanations and a $19 travel size, more shoppers try it, and some trade up to the full size.

Smaller sizes lower the barrier in the same way across the category. Minis and travel sizes let shoppers try a prestige product without committing to the full price. They work as an entry point, especially in fragrance, where shoppers want to test a scent.

Gifting adds a second engine. Beauty sells strongly as a gift in the fourth quarter, when shoppers buy sets for others rather than single products for themselves. Brands that rely on one-off purchases through the year should plan holiday assortments separately, with sets that look like gifts and ship quickly.

Proof has to do the work the store counter used to do

What emerges is a single shelf holding two tiers. Brands win by showing why they are worth the price, rather than relying on a store counter to say it for them. On the listing, that means clinical results, ingredient benefits and before-and-after evidence where allowed, so shoppers can judge efficacy.

Reviews and creators carry the rest of the proof. Ratings and reviews weigh heavily with beauty shoppers: review programs should stay active, and quality complaints should get a quick response. Shoppers also trust creators who test products on camera, and briefing creators on the evidence behind claims supports both sales and compliance.

Entry sizes and fragrance are how a brand recruits its next buyers. Minis, travel sizes and discovery sets let shoppers try products at a lower price and can lead to full-size purchases. Fragrance is growing in both tiers, and brands with scents should use samplers and gift sets to reach new buyers. Gift sets and value bundles sell strongly in the holiday window and deserve a featured place during Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday.

The buyers a brand already has deserve the same attention. Cleansers, moisturizers and hair care are bought again and again. Subscribe & Save belongs on those replenishable items, priced to keep loyal buyers coming back. Beauty shoppers also often search for a concern, such as dry skin, frizz or dark spots, and including those problems in titles, bullets and keywords puts products in front of shoppers who describe what they want to fix.

For prestige brands, the Amazon question is about price control

Prestige brands also guard their image and distribution, and some choose not to sell broadly on Amazon. That is the decision in front of a prestige leadership team: whether to sell there at all. Those that do must manage pricing and resellers carefully to protect brand equity, which means monitoring who sells their products and at what price, since unauthorized discounting erodes prestige positioning.

Getting listings, reviews, entry sizes, holiday sets and reseller pricing to pull in one direction, on Amazon as well as Walmart and Target, is the work we take on when we run the channel for beauty brands.

A0841.title: Temu’s data-for-discount model, and why brands should not copy it
A0841.alt: Paper bag spilling vintage toys, trinkets and blank price tags onto a wooden table beside a magnifying glass.
A0841.ttag: Temu’s data-for-discount model, and why brands should not copy it | Kwontified
A0841.desc: Temu’s spin-to-win discounts buy engagement and data, and states have sued over its data practices. Why brands should compete on trust instead of copying it.
A0841.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 2, 2025.
A0841.body:
A spin-to-win wheel on Temu looks like a price cut. It works more like a payment. The shopper gets a discount or a credit, and Temu gets what it values: the app opened, a longer visit, notifications accepted and friends invited. Each of those actions produces engagement and data, which lowers Temu’s cost of acquiring and retargeting shoppers.

That is a model brands should not copy. Several states have sued over Temu’s data practices, and most brands lack the breadth of future purchases that makes the subsidy pay. The better route is to compete on trust, clear value and first-party relationships that shoppers knowingly choose.

How Temu’s data-for-discount model works

Temu’s rapid adoption has been driven by gamified shopping, including spin-to-win wheels, flash sales and constant notifications about limited-time deals, the Consumer Federation of America said in a holiday shopping report. The report notes that state complaints describe these techniques as encouraging impulsive purchases.

The data side has drawn lawsuits. Nebraska’s attorney general sued Temu, alleging that it unlawfully harvests data, including from children, and uses deceptive practices to encourage purchases, according to the office’s release. Kentucky’s attorney general sued in July, alleging that the app collects data well beyond what its operations need, including location data, Bloomberg Law reported. Arkansas filed the first state lawsuit in June 2024, PIRG reported.

The concerns go beyond data. In August 2024, attorneys general from 21 states raised concerns that Temu does not adequately warn consumers about product dangers or safety recalls, according to the Consumer Federation of America report.

Temu disputes the claims and has said the Kentucky allegations are based on misinformation and are unfounded, and that it will defend itself, according to PIRG. None of the allegations has been proven in court.

The discount is paying for attention and data

Temu uses game-style discounts and credits to buy engagement and data, and that data has value beyond one order. It helps a platform target offers, bring shoppers back and acquire new customers through referrals at lower cost than paid advertising. The discount becomes an acquisition and retention expense, recovered over many future purchases.

Most brands cannot fund that subsidy. A brand selling one product line on Amazon, Walmart or its own site does not have a platform’s breadth of future purchases to spread the cost across. Matching Temu on discounts alone means giving away margin without the long-term return that makes the subsidy work for Temu.

The model also carries risk. Aggressive data collection and pressure tactics can draw legal action and damage trust, as the state lawsuits show, and the cheap engagement comes with legal and reputational exposure attached.

Two ways a brand could ask for the same customer

Take a brand that copies Temu’s tactics with a spin-to-win popup offering up to 40% off in exchange for an email, phone number and app download. Then put it beside the same brand taking a different path: members get 10% off every order, early access to new products and free returns, in exchange for an account with clear permission to send offers.

Spin-to-win popupMember program
OfferUp to 40% off10% off every order, early access, free returns
What the shopper givesEmail, phone number, app downloadAn account with clear permission to send offers
Sign-upsRiseFewer at first
What happens nextMany take the discount once and leave; customers learn to wait for the next gameThose who sign up buy again
What the brand ends up withLower margin and shallow dataKnowledge of what customers actually want

The popup’s sign-ups rise while its margin falls. The member program starts with fewer sign-ups, but the shoppers who join buy again, and the brand learns what they actually want.

Not every gamified promotion is harmful, and many legitimate retailers use loyalty points and limited-time deals. The difference lies in transparency: shoppers should know what they are giving and what they get in return.

How brands should compete with Temu instead

Trust is where brands should compete: shoppers worried about quality and data are a real audience, and return policies, product origins and data practices should be clear and easy to find. The same openness belongs in how brands ask for data: they should explain what they collect and why, and offer a clear benefit, such as early access or personalized recommendations, in return. Data that shoppers give knowingly is more accurate and more durable than data taken quietly.

Loyalty should be rewarded instead of luck. Points, member pricing and subscriptions reward repeat purchases and build lasting relationships, unlike one-time games that attract deal hunters.

Value and quality have to be visible on the page. Shoppers comparing a brand with a cheaper copy need a reason to pay more. Listings should show materials, durability and warranty terms plainly, alongside clear photos, accurate descriptions and verified reviews, which address the concerns raised about low-cost platforms.

On price, brands do not need to match Temu across the board. They should identify entry-level products where price matters most and compete there, while protecting margin elsewhere. Copies are a separate threat: several state complaints raise counterfeiting concerns, and brands should monitor marketplaces for copies of their products and act quickly. Data privacy rules are tightening too, and brands should review their own data collection against current state laws before expanding marketing programs.

Measuring customers over time is the test that settles it. A discount that wins one order can look efficient in a monthly report. Every promotion deserves to be judged by repeat purchase and lifetime value, which reveal whether a tactic builds customers or rents them. Holding every promotion on Amazon, Walmart and Target to that standard is the discipline we bring when we compete for brands without racing to the bottom on price.

A0842.title: Apparel on Amazon in 2025: tariffs, prices and discounts
A0842.alt: Rolling clothing rack of wool coats with hang tags in a sunlit navy-walled room with wooden floors.
A0842.ttag: Apparel on Amazon in 2025: tariffs, prices and discounts | Kwontified
A0842.desc: Nearly all US clothing is imported, so 2025 tariffs raised apparel costs, yet shoppers still bought on deep discounts. How Amazon sellers can protect margin.
A0842.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 4, 2025.
A0842.body:
Take an apparel brand selling a $40 sweater on Amazon. Before tariffs it cost $14 to land; after, $18. Sold at 25% off during Cyber Week, it brings in $30, leaving $12 before fees and advertising, down from $16. The event page fills with orders and each one earns far less.

The whole apparel year sits inside that sweater. Nearly all clothing sold in the US is imported, so 2025 tariffs raised apparel costs and began lifting prices, and shoppers still kept buying when holiday discounts arrived. Apparel sellers on Amazon should protect margin through assortment and sourcing choices, reserve deep discounts for the moments that drive volume, and use clear fit and quality information to win shoppers who are paying more.

How apparel on Amazon changed in 2025

The exposure starts with where clothes are made. About 97% of the clothes and shoes bought in the US are imported, mostly from Asia, the American Apparel & Footwear Association said, as the Associated Press reported.

Prices then began to move. Apparel prices rose 0.4% between May and June, the first increase since the tariff announcements, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, as Business of Fashion reported. Forecasts pointed higher still: Yale’s Budget Lab estimated that 2025 tariffs could raise apparel prices by 36.2% in the short run, Fibre2Fashion reported.

Higher prices did not stop the holiday. Online apparel spending reached $2.6 billion on Cyber Monday, up 5.2%, with apparel discounts peaking at 25% off listed prices, according to Adobe’s Cyber Monday data.

Low-cost rivals also lost an advantage. The US ended duty-free treatment for low-value imports from all countries in August 2025, which removed a cost edge that ultra-cheap fashion platforms had relied on to ship small parcels directly to shoppers. That narrowed the price gap between those platforms and brands selling through Amazon’s fulfillment network.

Why apparel sellers are squeezed from both sides

Two forces meet in apparel in 2025: a cost structure built almost entirely on imports, and shoppers who have learned to wait for deals. When nearly every garment is imported, tariffs raise costs across the category at once. Sellers cannot easily switch to domestic production, and moving factories between countries takes time.

Shoppers who have seen prices rise wait for deals. When discounts arrive, they buy, which lifts sales during events. Outside those moments, they hold back or trade down.

That leaves sellers squeezed from both sides. Costs rise on every unit, while shoppers expect deep discounts at the moments when most volume happens. Margin falls unless sellers manage both sides deliberately, and the sweater shows the result. At 25% off, the $40 sweater brings in $30, and an $18 landed cost leaves $12 where the old $14 cost left $16. Volume rises during the event, but each sale earns far less.

Trading down happens inside the category as well. When prices rise, many shoppers move toward basics, value brands and multipacks rather than leaving the category altogether. Brands with a strong entry-level line hold onto those shoppers, while brands with only premium items lose them to cheaper alternatives.

None of this has played out evenly. Tariff rates changed repeatedly during 2025, and many brands moved production or absorbed costs, so the effect on shelf prices has been smaller and slower than early forecasts. Results vary widely by product and origin.

What emerges is a margin problem more than a demand problem. Shoppers still want clothing. The question is how much each sale earns.

Margin is decided by the product, not the category

The work starts with landed cost by product. Sellers should update cost with current tariffs and origin, and identify which items still earn margin at full price and on discount. That calculation shows which products can carry a discount and which cannot, and it then shapes the assortment: products with strong margins can carry deep event discounts, while thin-margin products should be discounted less or not at all. Where feasible, sellers should compare production costs across countries and plan shifts for future seasons.

Deep discounts belong to peak moments. Event days drive volume, and sellers should avoid running constant discounts that teach shoppers to wait. Clicks also cost more during peak days, and event spend should concentrate on products with enough margin to carry both the discount and the higher cost of traffic. Multipacks of basics, such as socks, underwear and T-shirts, suit shoppers trading down and let sellers protect per-unit margin while offering a lower price per item.

When popular sizes run out mid-event, the ad spend that pulled shoppers onto the listing is wasted. Sellers should check size-level inventory before every major event.

Fit and quality information protect what the discount leaves

Fit problems drive apparel returns, which hurt margin. Clear size charts, fit notes and customer photos help shoppers choose the right size. Video and creator content show how a garment fits and moves better than still images, and short videos on best-selling listings also help reduce size-related returns.

Shoppers paying more want to know why. Listings should show fabric, construction and care details clearly.

The calendar matters too. Launching new styles just before peak events gives them little time to gather reviews, and sellers should launch new lines earlier in the season and use events to sell proven products. Apparel returns and clearance follow the holidays, and markdowns for unsold seasonal stock should be planned early, so clearance does not erode margins on core products.

Treating apparel as a margin problem, product by product, from landed cost through the January markdown, is the work we do when we run Amazon, Walmart and Target for apparel brands.

A0843.crumb: Cyber Week 2025 against our forecast: the…
A0843.title: Cyber Week 2025 against our forecast: the day-type call held
A0843.alt: Stack of kraft-wrapped gift boxes tied with twine, a brass caliper and a pine sprig on a wooden table.
A0843.ttag: Cyber Week 2025 against our forecast: the day-type call held | Kwontified
A0843.desc: Grading our Cyber Week 2025 forecast with public data: the day-type pattern held and cost pressure eased, while the numeric ranges await brand-level data.
A0843.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 9, 2025.
A0843.body:
Shoppers set a spending record over Cyber Week, yet the cost of an Amazon click rose far less than a year earlier. In 2024, Amazon cost per click rose 13% year over year during the Cyber 5. In 2025 the implied rise was about 3%, so cost pressure on Amazon was far lower than a year earlier.

Graded against that public data, the central call of our forecast held. Performance differed sharply by day type: Black Friday concentrated revenue, the weekend was cheaper and Cyber Monday converted best. Our numeric ranges were measured against each brand’s own pre-event month, so they can only be graded with brand-level data. Brands should keep budgeting by day type and grade their own results against the ranges.

What the Cyber Week 2025 results showed

US shoppers spent $44.2 billion online over the five days that run from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, up 7.7%, according to Adobe’s results. Black Friday grew 9.1% and Cyber Monday 7.1%, according to the same data.

Amazon advertising grew more modestly. Among advertisers Skai tracked, Amazon ad spend rose 12% over the Cyber 5, clicks rose 9% and conversions rose 4%, according to Skai’s analysis. Spend growing slightly faster than clicks implies cost per click rose about 3% year over year.

The same analysis shows that the days did not behave alike:

Day typeWhat Skai’s data showed
Black Friday30% of five-day Sponsored Products revenue; the highest cost per click
The weekendCost per click 10% to 15% below Black Friday
Cyber MondayThe highest conversion rate; Amazon DSP converted best

Amazon DSP spend rose 39% over the period, and Walmart Connect stood out too. Among Skai’s advertisers, Walmart Connect spending rose 52%, with conversion rates more than double Amazon’s baseline and cost per click about 40% below Amazon’s. Walmart’s five days were also more even, with Black Friday producing 25% of the total.

Our day-type call held, and costs came in lower

Our central call split the 12-day event in two: a long, steady stretch in the middle, with Black Friday and Cyber Monday as its crowded peaks. The public data supports it. Black Friday drew the most revenue at the highest cost, the weekend offered cheaper traffic with conversion rates close to Black Friday’s, and Cyber Monday converted best. Brands that budgeted the same amount every day left value on the table.

Cost pressure was lighter than we planned for. The 13% rise in 2024 comes from Pacvue’s benchmark data for that year’s Cyber 5; in 2025, the implied rise was about 3%. Our cost-per-click range of 15% to 35% measured event days against each brand’s pre-event month, not against 2024, so the two numbers are not directly comparable. But the softer year-over-year picture suggests most brands landed nearer the conservative end of our range.

A longer event made the two peaks more valuable, which sounds backward until you follow the money. With demand spread over 12 days, the two peak days still carried a large share of revenue, while the cheaper middle let disciplined brands buy traffic at lower cost. The event rewarded brands that treated days differently.

Four ranges still need each brand’s own data

The four are average daily sales lift, deal share of event sales, order value measured against 2024, and the cost-per-click change from the pre-event month, and each was defined against the brand’s own history. Public benchmarks report year-over-year totals across many advertisers, which cannot grade those ranges. We will grade them with brand-level results and publish what we learn.

Take a brand that spent $1,000 a day at $1.00 per click before the event. During the event, its cost per click averaged $1.18 against the pre-event month, a rise of 18%, inside our conservative-to-standard band. Its Black Friday cost per click ran $1.32, while weekend clicks cost $1.12, a gap that matches the public pattern of an expensive Black Friday and a cheaper weekend. Grading by day type tells the brand where its money worked hardest.

Skai’s data covers advertisers on its platform, not every brand on Amazon, and different benchmarks will show different numbers. Brand-level results will vary widely by category and deal participation, which is why the public figures check the pattern but cannot grade the numbers.

Grading your own Cyber Week, day by day

Set each day’s cost per click, sales lift, deal share and order value beside the same figures from the month before the event, using our ranges as a guide, and write the results down now, which makes the next forecast sharper. Review Black Friday, the weekend and Cyber Monday separately, since each played a different role; a strong event average can hide an expensive Black Friday or a missed weekend opportunity.

The weeks after the event deserve a budget too. Many advertisers spend most of their budgets by Cyber Monday, which can leave cheaper traffic in the weeks that follow, and brands should maintain steady budgets through mid-December. DSP spend and clicks grew sharply among Skai’s advertisers, and brands that used DSP should check how many new customers it reached, as well as how many shoppers it retargeted.

Walmart deserves a second look before the 2026 plan is set. Lower costs and strong conversion on Walmart Connect make it worth testing for brands that sell there, and comparing cost per sale across both retailers belongs before 2026 budgets are set. Those 2026 event budgets should be built by day type from the start.

Budget by day type, and grade results against ranges rather than a single event-wide number. Grading every event that way, on Amazon and Walmart alike, is how we plan and measure retail events for brands.

A0845.title: What Cyber Week 2025 revealed about brands and retailers
A0845.alt: Three snowy storefront windows with red, blue and gold holiday displays on a stone building.
A0845.ttag: What Cyber Week 2025 revealed about brands and retailers | Kwontified
A0845.desc: Cyber Week 2025 showed retailers stretching events earlier and brands pacing budgets with more discipline. What that behavior means for planning in 2026.
A0845.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 11, 2025.
A0845.body:
The holiday used to be one frantic weekend. In 2025 Amazon stretched its holiday deal events, Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday, across 12 days, running November 20 through December 1, as Amazon announced. Brands spent the weeks around it pacing their budgets instead of emptying them on two days.

That is what Cyber Week 2025 revealed. Retailers stretched deals earlier and longer, while brands paced budgets with more discipline and moved money toward newer channels. The holiday is becoming a managed season of distinct days rather than one frantic weekend, and brands should plan by day type, start earlier and spread spend across retailers and formats.

Cyber Week 2025 showed shoppers following the early deals

Black Friday outgrew Cyber Monday for the second season in a row as shoppers embraced early, competitive deals, according to Adobe’s holiday data. Online spending over the five days reached $44.2 billion, up 7.7%.

Shoppers were managing budgets of their own. Buy now, pay later drove $1.03 billion of Cyber Monday spending, and 57.5% of Cyber Monday online sales came through mobile devices, according to Adobe. Shoppers spread payments and shopped from their phones throughout the event.

Brands paced the season instead of sprinting through it

Brands paced with more discipline than in the seasons they had learned from. Retail media spending stayed close to normal levels in early November, accelerated in a controlled way from mid-month and ramped up in the week before the event, Skai reported. On the event days, spending reached more than triple baseline levels on Black Friday and stayed near triple on Cyber Monday, according to the same analysis.

Money also moved toward newer channels. Amazon DSP spending among Skai’s advertisers rose 39% and Walmart Connect spending rose 52%, while some brands pulled back on Facebook and moved budget to Amazon DSP, according to the same analysis. Some of the new DSP money came straight out of social budgets.

The retailers did not behave alike either. Black Friday produced 30% of five-day Amazon Sponsored Products revenue, while on Walmart Connect, Black Friday produced 25% and all five days performed within 20% of each other, according to Skai. Thanksgiving delivered Amazon’s lowest cost per click of the period.

Advertisers had learned from earlier years that spending heavily too soon drains budgets before the peak, while spending everything on two days pays the highest prices. Controlled pacing lets brands stay visible across a longer window without wasting money. Channel choices reflect the same discipline. As Amazon’s search auctions mature, brands look for reach and cost advantages elsewhere: in Amazon DSP, which reaches shoppers beyond search results, and in Walmart Connect, which offered lower costs among Skai’s advertisers.

Take a brand that in 2024 spent half its holiday budget on Black Friday and Cyber Monday and ran out of stock on the weekend. In 2025, it ramped spend from mid-November, kept steady budgets on the weekend and tested Walmart. Its total spend was similar, but more of it bought traffic at lower prices. The difference came from pacing and channel mix rather than a bigger budget.

Those figures come from advertisers on Skai’s platform, who may plan more carefully than average. Many brands still spent heavily and late, and results varied widely by category.

Longer events give retailers more days and more ad inventory to sell

The shape of the season starts with the retailer’s interest. Retailers started earlier, and brands planned around the calendar the retailer set. Longer events let retailers spread demand, reduce strain on fulfillment and give more shoppers a reason to visit across more days. Earlier deals also capture shoppers before competitors do. And a longer event gives a retailer more selling days and more advertising inventory to sell, which is why retailers are unlikely to reverse course and why brands should expect holiday windows to stay long or grow longer in 2026.

The pattern that emerges is a season with distinct roles for each day: early weeks for building awareness, Thanksgiving for efficient entry, Black Friday for volume, the weekend for value and Cyber Monday for conversion. Planning by day type follows directly from that pattern.

Planning the 2026 season by phase

The practical change is to plan a season instead of a weekend. A season needs a plan that starts in early November and assigns a role to each phase. It also needs more stock than a weekend: a 12-day event spreads demand across more days, and inventory planned for the full window and checked daily keeps the peak days from arriving with empty shelves. Shoppers responded to early deals, and brands should have stock, deals and creative ready when retailers open their events.

Daily budgets that ramp gradually, with reserves held for the peak days, belong in the plan as well, following the pattern Skai saw. Upper-funnel media belongs early: DSP and streaming ads can build awareness in the weeks before the event, so shoppers already know the brand when deals arrive and are more likely to choose it over an unfamiliar rival.

The retailers beyond Amazon deserve their own plan. Walmart and Target each behave differently during the holiday, and brands should test those channels while costs there are still lower. The season also does not end on Monday. Many advertisers have spent most of their budgets by then, and brands that stay active into December can reach late shoppers at lower cost, including gift buyers who wait until the final shipping deadlines.

With most Cyber Monday sales on phones, images, titles and deal badges need to be legible on a phone. Before 2026 budgets are set, brands should compare their pacing and results by day with these patterns, and that review is where we start when we build holiday plans by day and channel for brands.

A0847.crumb: The 2026 plan: the assumptions to change…
A0847.title: The 2026 plan: the assumptions to change from 2025
A0847.alt: Leather journal, brass compass, pencil and sharpener on a wooden desk by a snowy window.
A0847.ttag: The 2026 plan: the assumptions to change from 2025 | Kwontified
A0847.desc: Five planning assumptions that 2025 broke, from ever-rising cost per click to Amazon-only budgets, and how brands should reset their 2026 retail media plan.
A0847.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 16, 2025.
A0847.body:
Most annual plans start from the previous year’s numbers and adjust them. That works when the market is stable. In 2025 it was not: cost per click held steady, baskets shrank, events stretched into seasons, Amazon search lost its monopoly on budgets and AI agents began to shop.

A 2026 plan built by nudging 2025 figures carries those broken assumptions into every budget line, and the errors compound across a year. Brands should reset each input explicitly in their 2026 retail media plans rather than carrying 2025 habits forward.

What 2025 did to the inputs behind the 2026 plan

Costs stopped climbing in 2025. Cost per click during October’s Prime Big Deal Days was flat against the prior year, while average order value fell 11%, according to Skai’s event analysis. Over the Cyber 5, Amazon ad spend rose 12% while clicks rose 9%, which implies cost per click rose only about 3%, according to Skai’s later analysis. In 2024, Cyber 5 cost per click had risen 13%, according to Pacvue’s benchmark.

Events stretched out over more days. Amazon ran its holiday deal events for 12 days, from November 20 to December 1, as Amazon announced in its release. Budgets spread out with them: among Skai’s advertisers, Amazon DSP spending rose 39% and Walmart Connect spending rose 52% over the Cyber 5.

AI shopping agents arrived as well. Walmart opened its catalog to purchases inside ChatGPT, Retail TouchPoints reported, and Amazon sued Perplexity to stop its agent shopping on Amazon, Bloomberg reported.

Five assumptions a 2025-based plan carries forward

Old assumptionWhat 2025 showedWhat the 2026 plan should do
Cost per click always risesCosts held steady or rose only slightly at major eventsStop adding a standard yearly increase
Basket size holdsSmaller baskets in October meant cheaper clicks did not translate into better returnsForecast order value as a separate input
The holiday is one weekendA 12-day event spreads demand across distinct daysBudget by day type and by phase
Amazon search is the whole planDSP and Walmart Connect grew fastestTest cheaper or incremental reach outside Amazon search
Shoppers arrive on the retailer’s siteSome shopping now begins in AI assistantsTreat product data and catalog quality as plan work

Many plans add a standard increase to cost per click every year, and plans that assumed steep increases in 2025 set budgets too low for the clicks they could actually buy, or bid too timidly. Plans that put almost everything into Amazon search left cheaper or incremental reach untested. And catalog quality affects how agents find and recommend products.

Order value deserves its own line. Smaller baskets in October meant that cheaper clicks did not translate into better returns. A plan that forecasts order value separately sees that, where a plan assuming it stays flat does not.

The holiday row is the easiest to see: a 12-day event spreads demand across distinct days, and plans should budget by day type and by phase rather than for one weekend. The last row is the newest. Some shopping now begins in AI assistants, which puts product data and catalog work inside the plan rather than beside it.

A sixth input sits outside advertising. Tariffs changed product costs across categories in 2025. Apparel is the clearest case: the American Apparel & Footwear Association puts the share of US clothing and footwear purchases that come from imports at about 97%, as the Associated Press reported. Advertising targets built on 2024 margins will push spend onto products that no longer earn enough to carry it, and plans should start from current landed cost by product.

Steady costs can still make returns look worse

When cost per click is steady but baskets shrink, a plan that expected higher costs and stable baskets will misread the result. The problem is in the basket, while the plan blames the bid.

Take a brand whose 2025 plan assumed cost per click would rise 15% and order value would hold. In practice, cost per click held steady and order value fell 10%. Its return on ad spend fell, and the team cut bids, treating a basket problem as a cost problem. The real fix was bundles and multipacks to raise order value.

The 2025 patterns may not repeat. Costs could rise again in 2026 as more advertisers adopt AI tools and automated bidding. The point is to reset assumptions with current evidence, and to avoid replacing one fixed assumption with another.

Building the 2026 plan on fresh inputs

The starting point is a list of every assumption in the 2025 plan, each one checked against what 2025 actually delivered.

Cost per click, conversion rate and order value belong on separate lines, so a brand can see which one moves. Each input should carry conservative, standard and reach cases, with results graded against them during the year. Each major event gets a budget by phase and day type, with reserves for peak days.

Budget should be set aside to test DSP, Walmart Connect and other retailers, with clear measures of incremental sales. Catalog accuracy and completeness deserve their own planning line, since they affect agents, retailers’ own AI tools and shoppers alike; missing specifications or inconsistent prices can keep a product out of an assistant’s recommendations entirely.

The finished plan also needs reopening. Brands should revisit each assumption every quarter and adjust budgets when evidence changes, and Prime Day, the fall events and Cyber Week each offer a natural checkpoint for comparing results with the plan.

The rule for 2026 is to reset each planning input explicitly from current evidence before setting budgets. Stress-testing those inputs before the budget is locked is the work we do when we build retail media plans for brands.

A0848.title: The year in marketplaces, 2025: the structural shifts
A0848.alt: Large warehouse construction site with tower cranes and steel framing at sunrise, city skyline beyond.
A0848.ttag: The year in marketplaces, 2025: the structural shifts | Kwontified
A0848.desc: In 2025 Walmart and Target grew into real marketplaces, cheap cross-border parcels lost an edge, agents arrived and delivery sped up. What it means for 2026.
A0848.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 18, 2025.
A0848.body:
Follow a brand through 2025. At the start of the year it sold almost entirely on Amazon. By the end of the year it had joined Walmart Marketplace, tested Walmart Connect, been invited to Target Plus and cleaned up its product data for AI assistants. Its Amazon business still led, but more of its new growth came from other retailers.

Four structural shifts run through that brand’s year. Every major retailer became a marketplace and an advertising network, cheap cross-border parcels lost their tariff advantage, retailers chose sides on AI shopping agents, and fast delivery became the standard. For 2026, brands should treat Walmart and Target as real marketplace channels, plan for agents and meet faster delivery expectations. Each of those shifts shows up in the year’s results.

The year in marketplaces 2025 made Walmart and Target real channels

Through the year, Walmart’s marketplace kept growing. In the third quarter, Walmart grew its US e-commerce sales 28%, and Walmart Connect advertising sales grew 33%, excluding VIZIO, the company said in its earnings release. US marketplace sales grew 17%, CEO Doug McMillon said on the earnings call, as PYMNTS reported.

The mix of what sells there broadened as well. Walmart marketplace categories such as apparel, electronics and toys grew more than 40%, according to the same PYMNTS report. Categories once associated with specialty retailers and Amazon are now growing quickly on Walmart.

At Target, the marketplace picked up speed. Target said in its results summary that Target Plus grew its gross merchandise value nearly 50% in the third quarter. The retailer’s plan, as Modern Retail reported, is to take the marketplace within five years from more than $1 billion of gross merchandise value to more than $5 billion.

Amazon’s advertising, meanwhile, grew faster than its store. According to Amazon’s reported results, advertising revenue at Amazon rose 23.5% to $17.7 billion in the third quarter.

And shopping agents arrived. Walmart enabled purchases inside ChatGPT, Retail TouchPoints reported, while Amazon sued Perplexity to stop its agent from shopping on Amazon, as Bloomberg reported.

Every retailer wanted a marketplace and an ad network

Marketplaces let retailers widen their assortment without holding inventory, and advertising earns money from the sellers who join. Walmart and Target both grew advertising alongside their marketplaces in 2025, and the model Amazon built over two decades became the standard for large retailers.

The reason the two move together is that advertising follows sellers. When a marketplace adds sellers, competition for search placement rises, and sellers pay for visibility. That is why marketplace growth and advertising growth arrived together at Walmart and Target. For a brand, a growing marketplace soon becomes a growing auction, so early entrants pay less for traffic. Walmart’s results point the same way: its advertising grew faster than its marketplace sales, as more sellers paid to stand out in a larger catalog.

Tariffs, agents and delivery speed redrew the field

The cheap cross-border parcel came to an end. In August 2025 the US stopped letting low-value imports from any country enter duty free. Platforms that shipped small parcels directly from overseas lost a cost advantage, and sellers using domestic warehouses and marketplace fulfillment gained ground.

On agents, the retailers split into two groups: those that welcome outside AI shoppers, and those that keep them out and build their own. That choice will shape where agent-led purchases flow.

Delivery speed became the standard as well. Walmart’s sales through expedited store-fulfilled delivery grew nearly 70%, according to its earnings release, and Target said its next-day shipping now covers more than half of the US population. Marketplace sellers are judged against those delivery promises.

Amazon remains far larger than any other US marketplace, and many brands will continue to earn most of their marketplace sales there. Diversifying makes sense only where a brand can meet each retailer’s standards for content, stock and delivery. What emerges is a field with more real choices than before: several retailers now offer both reach and advertising, and each sets its own rules.

Brands should plan 2026 across marketplaces

Walmart belongs in the plan as a core channel rather than an extension of the Amazon account. Brands should run Walmart Marketplace and Walmart Connect with dedicated plans, budgets and reporting, separate from Amazon. Target Plus works by invitation. Brands that fit Target’s curated model should map the products its stores do not carry and request invitations.

Brands should keep product data complete and consistent everywhere, since AI shoppers read listings rather than ads, and retailers that welcome agents will route those orders to whichever seller offers the clearest, most accurate information. Brands should also review fulfillment speed on each marketplace and use retailer fulfillment programs where they improve the delivery promise shown to shoppers.

The lower-cost rivals that moved stock into domestic warehouses remain competitive. Brands should track them in search results and protect their positions on key products.

Listings on Walmart and Target often lag behind Amazon in images, specifications and descriptions. Brands should bring every retailer’s listings to the same standard, since weaker content wastes the advertising that sends shoppers there. A shopper who clicks a Walmart ad and lands on a thin listing is a click the brand paid for and the page lost. Return on ad spend and conversion rates also differ by retailer. Brands should set separate targets for each one rather than applying Amazon’s benchmarks everywhere.

The brand that started 2025 on Amazon alone ends it selling through several retailers, each with its own rules for content, stock and delivery. Running each of those channels on its own plan and its own targets is the work we take on for brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0849.title: TikTok Shop analytics as competitive intelligence
A0849.alt: Vintage black binoculars beside a smartphone with a blank screen on a wooden table against a terracotta wall.
A0849.ttag: TikTok Shop analytics as competitive intelligence | Kwontified
A0849.desc: TikTok Shop shows sales counts that Amazon hides, which makes it an early warning system for competitors, prices and creators. How to read it, and its limits.
A0849.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 23, 2025.
A0849.body:
Open a TikTok Shop product page and it tells you how many units have sold. An Amazon listing tells you nothing of the kind. That one difference turns TikTok Shop into an early warning system for rising competitors, products, price points and creators, including for brands that sell only on Amazon.

The catch is that the numbers are estimates. Brands should monitor TikTok Shop analytics regularly, treat third-party figures as directional, and confirm each signal with Amazon search data before shifting budget or inventory.

TikTok Shop analytics matter because the channel reached real scale

Over the four days from Black Friday to Cyber Monday 2025, TikTok Shop’s US sales exceeded $500 million, with nearly 50% more shoppers buying than in the 2024 campaign, TikTok said in an announcement. Sellers hosting livestreams saw sales grow 84%, according to the same announcement.

Established brands are growing there too. Brands with more than $10 million in annual revenue grew their TikTok Shop sales 76% during the 2025 campaign compared with 2024, according to TikTok’s announcement, as GCI Magazine reported. A TikTok spokesperson called the $500 million a record, Modern Retail reported, and Pop Mart had one of the most popular livestreams of the event.

The growth did not start with the holiday. US TikTok Shop sales rose about 120% year over year in the first half of 2025, according to FastMoss’s mid-year report.

Visible sales counts make competitors readable

TikTok Shop product pages show how many units have sold. Third-party analytics tools collect those counts over time and turn them into estimated sales by product, by shop and by creator. Amazon does not publish sales counts, so the same view of a competitor is much harder to get there.

Amazon’s tools for brand owners work differently. Search reports for brand owners show which queries shoppers use and how often they click and buy that brand’s products, but they do not show a competitor’s sales. TikTok Shop data fills that gap with estimates that, however rough, point to who is winning.

That visibility has value because demand moves between platforms. A product that takes off in a creator’s video often sends shoppers to search for it, or for something like it, on Amazon and other retailers. Momentum that appears on TikTok Shop can show up in Amazon search weeks later.

A brand with no TikTok Shop presence still has a reason to watch the channel closely. Watching a store you do not sell in looks like wasted effort. It stops looking that way once you see what the data shows: which competitors are gaining attention, which price points are moving and which creators are driving sales in the category, whether or not the brand plans to sell there.

Take a skincare brand that sells only on Amazon. A tracking tool shows a competitor’s $24 serum climbing fast on TikTok Shop, driven by three mid-sized creators. The brand checks Amazon search data and sees queries for the ingredient rising. It adds the ingredient to its listing copy, bids on the rising terms and contacts creators in the same niche before the competitor reaches Amazon. The signal came from TikTok Shop, but every decision the brand made rested on its own Amazon data.

What the estimates cannot tell you

Third-party estimates are imprecise. Sales counts can include returns, bundles or promotional spikes, and different tools report different numbers. A single viral video can create a burst that fades within days. That puts the figures in the directional column: useful for spotting movement, too rough for sizing it.

The data also cannot show what the sales cost. A product selling thousands of units may be losing money on commissions to creators, discounts and advertising. Brands should read rising sales as proof of demand, rather than as proof that the competitor’s model is profitable or worth copying.

How brands should use TikTok Shop data each week

The weekly review starts with the category’s top sellers: competitors’ fastest-growing products and the creators behind them. Those same tools show which creators drive sales in a category. Brands should build a list of creators to partner with from that data, whether or not they sell on TikTok Shop.

Price is the next thing to read. TikTok Shop reveals which prices convert for impulse buyers. Brands should compare those price points with their own entry products on Amazon, and consider a smaller size or bundle where they have no product near the winning price.

Brands should separate trends from spikes. They should look for growth that lasts two to three weeks and spreads across several creators before treating it as a trend. A single viral video rarely changes demand for long. Before acting, they should check Amazon search query data and their own search term reports for matching movement. When a trend is confirmed, inventory, listing copy and advertising should be ready for the search demand that may follow.

Livestreams deserve their own look. Livestream sales grew fastest during the holiday. Brands should review which products and formats succeed in live selling in their category, and note which hosts and demonstrations hold viewers long enough to buy.

The same analytics also reveal unauthorized sellers and copies of a brand’s products. TikTok said it proactively rejected more than 40 million products from January to June 2025 for intellectual property violations, according to its announcement. Brands should still monitor for copies and act through TikTok Shop’s reporting tools.

The rule that ties it together is short: treat TikTok Shop data as an early warning, and confirm each signal with Amazon search data before acting. Reading those signals next to a brand’s Amazon search reports is part of how we run Amazon and TikTok Shop channels for brands.

A0850.crumb: How Walmart search differs from Amazon’s…
A0850.title: How Walmart search differs from Amazon’s, and what to fix
A0850.alt: Blank wooden signpost with one blue arm at a village road junction lined with stone cottages.
A0850.ttag: How Walmart search differs from Amazon’s, and what to fix | Kwontified
A0850.desc: Walmart scores listings on content, price against other sites, shipping, stock and reviews. Why Amazon listings copied to Walmart underperform, and what to fix.
A0850.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 24, 2025.
A0850.body:
A brand copies its Amazon listing to Walmart: the same title, the same bullets, the same images. To the team that uploaded it, the listing looks complete. On Walmart it scores poorly, and the reason is that Walmart search grades the whole offer.

Walmart scores each listing on content, price compared with other websites, shipping, stock and reviews, while Amazon publishes no comparable score. That is why listings copied from Amazon tend to underperform on Walmart. Brands should rebuild content for Walmart’s standards, keep prices at parity across retailers and treat delivery speed and stock as search factors.

Walmart search vs Amazon search starts with a published score

Walmart tells sellers what it grades. Its Listing Quality score is built from five components: content quality, price competitiveness, shipping, published and in-stock status, and ratings and reviews, according to Walmart’s Marketplace Learn guide for sellers.

The price component looks beyond Walmart. It compares a seller’s own price with similar products on external websites, excluding Walmart-funded incentives, and reflects the share of customer impressions where the offer is price competitive, according to Walmart’s seller FAQs. Content has its own standard as well: content quality measures the effectiveness of an item’s name, description, key features and images, according to the Listing Quality guide.

Whose content shows is a matter of ownership. When several sellers offer the same item, Walmart determines the best available content unless a brand owner or authorized reseller provides it, according to the same FAQs. Brands that do not establish ownership may find another seller’s content on their own product page.

The marketplace these listings compete in is growing. On the third-quarter earnings call, CEO Doug McMillon said Walmart’s US marketplace sales grew 17%, as PYMNTS reported.

A store’s habits shaped how Walmart grades a listing

Walmart grew as a store, where shoppers expect everyday low prices, items on the shelf and a clear label. That heritage shows in its marketplace search. It checks whether the offer is complete, fairly priced, in stock and quick to arrive, much as a shopper would size up a shelf tag in an aisle.

Amazon’s approach evolved differently from Walmart’s. Amazon does not publish a comparable listing score, and its search is widely understood to lean heavily on relevance and sales performance. A product that sells well tends to rank well, which rewards momentum. On Amazon, a brand can sometimes overcome weak content with strong sales and advertising; on Walmart, the weak content itself lowers the score.

That difference surfaces the moment a brand copies its Amazon listing to Walmart. Titles and bullets written for Amazon may not match Walmart’s content standards, attributes Walmart uses for filters may be missing, and a price that is lower on Amazon lowers the Walmart price score. The listing looks complete to the brand but scores poorly on Walmart.

Take a brand that lists a $34.99 blender on Walmart using its Amazon content. On Amazon, the same blender sells for $29.99 during a promotion. Walmart’s price score drops, several attributes are blank and shipping takes five days. The listing ranks low despite strong Amazon sales. After the brand fills the attributes, aligns its prices and moves the item to faster fulfillment, its Walmart ranking improves.

Another reader has arrived: AI assistants. Walmart introduced its Sparky shopping assistant in June 2025, which answers questions and summarizes reviews inside the Walmart app. Assistants like Sparky draw on the same product data that search uses, so complete attributes and accurate descriptions help listings appear in answers as well as in search results.

Walmart does not publish exactly how much each component affects search ranking, and third-party guides disagree on the weights. The Listing Quality score is best treated as Walmart’s own checklist for what it values, rather than a formula. Read that way, the two retailers are two different graders: Amazon largely rewards what sells, and Walmart rewards what looks like a good offer to a value-minded shopper.

What brands should change for Walmart search

The rebuild starts with content written for Walmart. Brands should write titles, key features and descriptions to Walmart’s style guides rather than pasting Amazon copy, and register with Walmart’s brand program so their own content appears on their product pages instead of content supplied by resellers. Walmart’s filters and browse pages rely on product attributes, so brands should complete every relevant field; blank attributes can keep items out of filtered results.

Price and promotions need a cross-retailer view. Because Walmart compares prices with other websites, brands should avoid running deeper discounts elsewhere that lower their Walmart score, and plan promotions across retailers.

Delivery, stock and reviews are part of the grade too. Shipping speed is part of the score, so brands should use Walmart Fulfillment Services or faster shipping options where they improve delivery promises. Published and in-stock status is scored too. Walmart inventory deserves the same close monitoring as Amazon inventory, especially before events, when a stockout costs both sales and search position. Ratings and reviews are scored as well, and brands should use Walmart’s review programs to build a solid base of reviews on their key items.

Walmart’s Listing Quality dashboard shows what to fix item by item. Brands should review it monthly and prioritize their best-selling products, since small gains on high-traffic items move the most sales. Walmart Connect sponsored placements can lift visibility while organic scores improve, but ads work best on listings that already score well and convert the traffic they receive.

The brand that copied its Amazon listing was writing for one grader and being scored by another. Rebuilding each listing to the retailer’s own standard is part of the work we do running Walmart Marketplace alongside Amazon for brands.
