A0852.crumb: Trust, privacy and ethical AI in…
A0852.title: Trust, privacy and ethical AI in commerce: why it pays
A0852.alt: Brass padlock and old key resting on a leather portfolio on a wooden desk by a window.
A0852.ttag: Trust, privacy and ethical AI in commerce: why it pays | Kwontified
A0852.desc: When AI agents shop for people, trust decides which brands get recommended. Why disclosure, consented data and accurate product details now carry real weight.
A0852.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 30, 2025.
A0852.body:
Trust in AI shopping recommendations rose to 86% of users, up from 46% in May, and 17% of consumers had used an AI assistant for product searches in the past year, according to Salesforce research, as Fibre2Fashion reported. Those figures describe shoppers handing more of the choosing to software, and that changes what a brand’s honesty is worth.

As AI agents begin to recommend and buy products for shoppers, trust becomes a commercial asset. Systems and shoppers alike reward clear disclosure, consented data and accurate product information, and they punish the opposite. Brands should label sponsored and automated activity, collect data openly and keep product claims verifiable. The case for that restraint is commercial as well as ethical.

Ethical AI in commerce became a business issue in 2025

Disclosure turned into a legal question. Amazon sued Perplexity to stop its Comet agent from making purchases on Amazon, accusing it of failing to disclose when the agent shops on a person’s behalf, Bloomberg reported.

Data practices drew lawsuits too. In Nebraska, the attorney general’s lawsuit against Temu alleges unlawful data harvesting and deceptive practices that encourage purchases, as the attorney general’s release sets out. Temu disputes the allegations, which have not been proven in court.

Retailers began acting as gatekeepers. Walmart chose to let shoppers buy its products inside ChatGPT, Retail TouchPoints reported, while Amazon chose to fight an outside agent in court. Each retailer is deciding which automated shoppers it trusts and on what terms.

Pressure tactics drew scrutiny as well. A Consumer Federation of America report found that spin-to-win wheels, flash sales and a steady stream of notifications encourage impulsive purchases.

Delegated shopping runs on trust at every step

When a shopper asks an assistant to find or buy something, the shopper hands over judgment. The assistant, in turn, relies on product data, reviews and prices it cannot independently verify. Both steps depend on trust. The shopper trusts the assistant, and the assistant trusts the brand’s data.

That makes trustworthy inputs valuable. Assistants that recommend products with inaccurate claims or hidden problems lose the trust that makes people use them. Every disappointing product an assistant suggests spends some of that trust. Over time, the systems doing the choosing will favor sources whose information holds up, and penalize those whose information does not.

Disclosure runs through the whole chain. Shoppers want to know when a recommendation is paid, when an agent is acting for them and what data is collected. Retailers want to know when an agent is on their site. The Amazon and Perplexity dispute shows that undisclosed automation is now a commercial and legal issue.

Reviews sit at the center of it. Assistants summarize reviews to answer shoppers’ questions, which makes the honesty of reviews more important. The Federal Trade Commission’s rule banning fake reviews and testimonials took effect in October 2024, so manufactured reviews now carry legal risk as well as the risk of misleading the assistants that read them.

Restraint can also be a growth strategy. Collecting less data, labeling ads plainly and avoiding pressure tactics may lower short-term conversion. The cost of those choices can show up first, and the benefit later. In a market where agents and shoppers screen for trustworthy sources, those choices can increase how often a brand is recommended.

Take a brand whose product page claims a jacket is fully waterproof, while reviews mention leaks. An assistant summarizing reviews flags the mismatch, and the brand stops appearing in answers about waterproof jackets. A competitor with a more modest, accurate claim and consistent reviews takes its place. The brand lost the recommendation on the gap between its claim and its reviews.

Rules for AI in commerce are still forming, and many shoppers still choose on price and convenience above all. Trust will not save a product that is uncompetitive. It is a necessary condition rather than a complete strategy.

How brands should build trust into AI-era commerce

Brands should start with claims and labels: back product claims with evidence and remove claims that reviews or testing contradict. They should also make sure sponsored products, influencer partnerships and affiliate links are clearly disclosed.

Data and automation need the same openness. Brands should explain what data they collect, why and what shoppers get in return, and avoid collecting more than they need. Data gathered openly is also more accurate, because shoppers who choose to share it have a reason to keep it current. When a brand uses AI to answer customers, write content or set prices, it should say so where customers would expect to know, and give them an easy way to reach a person.

Reviews and urgency call for the same restraint. Brands should never buy, write or filter reviews to hide criticism, and should respond to complaints in public where shoppers and assistants can see the answer. They should favor clear value over artificial urgency, countdowns that reset or games designed to force quick decisions.

Privacy and AI laws vary by state and are changing quickly. Brands should review data collection and AI use with counsel before scaling new programs.

Brands should also check how assistants describe their products and correct inaccurate information at the source, in their own listings and content. Assistants repeat what they find, so errors in a brand’s own pages travel quickly. A wrong specification on a product page can become the wrong answer in an assistant’s reply.

The rule is to treat trust as an operating discipline, with disclosure, consent and accuracy built into daily work. Clearly labeled ads sent to accurate listings are how we run retail media for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0853.crumb: Why global brands choose Zalando over…
A0853.title: Why global brands choose Zalando over pure direct sales in Europe
A0853.alt: Orange parcel tied with string on the stone steps of a Georgian townhouse beside a cobbled street.
A0853.ttag: Why global brands choose Zalando over pure direct sales in Europe | Kwontified
A0853.desc: Zalando reaches 61.4 million active customers after combining with ABOUT YOU. Why global brands use it to enter Europe instead of building direct sales first.
A0853.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Dec 31, 2025.
A0853.body:
A US apparel brand looking at Europe sees a map of separate markets. Germany, France and the Netherlands each have their own language, payment habits, return expectations and delivery networks, and a direct site has to solve all of them country by country, often with separate sites, payment providers and carriers.

That is why global brands increasingly enter Europe through Zalando rather than pure direct sales. One connection reaches more than 61 million active customers across many countries, with local payments, returns and logistics already solved, and partner models let brands keep control of price and assortment. Brands should use Zalando to reach scale quickly and keep their own sites for loyal customers and brand building.

Zalando for global brands is now one connection to 61.4 million customers

Zalando got bigger in 2025. It completed its combination with ABOUT YOU in July 2025, and its combined active customer base reached 61.4 million, the company said in its third-quarter results. Gross merchandise volume grew 21.6% to 4.2 billion euros in the quarter, according to the same release.

Revenue grew faster than volume. It rose 26.5% to 3 billion euros in the quarter, and the average basket over the prior 12 months was 61.80 euros, according to the same release. Those are the economics of a platform where shoppers buy several items per order and return what does not fit.

The two audiences overlap only partly. More than 5 million customers use both the Zalando and ABOUT YOU platforms, according to the same release, which means most customers shop on only one of the two.

The list of partner brands runs long. Zalando works with more than 7,000 partner brands, as Retail Insight Network reported.

Zalando also sells services to those brands. Its business-to-business revenue, which includes logistics and software services for brands, rose 15.6% to 277 million euros in the third quarter, Fibre2Fashion reported. Advertising is part of that offer. Zalando reported strong revenue growth in its business-to-business segment and in Zalando Marketing Services, its advertising business, in the first nine months of 2025, according to its quarterly statement. Brands selling on Zalando can buy visibility on the same platform, as they do with retail media in the US.

Europe is many markets, and Zalando has already done the build-out

Europe is not one market, and that fact shapes the choice. Zalando has already solved the country-by-country problems a direct site would face. A single connection gives a brand access to shoppers across its European markets, with local payment methods, free returns and delivery that shoppers already trust. That removes years of build-out for a brand from outside Europe.

Shopping habits lead to the same place. European fashion shoppers often start on multi-brand platforms, where they compare brands and rely on familiar return policies. A brand that is absent from those platforms is absent from much of the browsing that leads to purchase.

Control is less of a sacrifice than it once was. Under partner models, brands sell directly to Zalando’s customers, set their own prices and choose their assortment, rather than handing everything to a wholesale buyer.

Go back to the US apparel brand. Building direct sites for Germany, France and the Netherlands would require translation, local payment options, a returns hub and months of marketing to build traffic. Listing with Zalando, it reaches shoppers in those countries and others within a single launch, then uses sales data to decide which countries deserve their own direct investment.

The platform keeps its share of the value. Zalando charges commissions and requires brands to meet its content and service standards, and brands that sell heavily on a platform also give up some direct customer relationships and data. Zalando collects the commissions and part of the customer relationship, and the brand gets reach that would otherwise take years to build. A marketplace is a route to scale, while a brand’s own site remains the home for loyalty and storytelling. What emerges is a combined approach: Zalando provides reach and logistics across Europe, while direct sales deepen relationships in the markets that matter most.

How global brands should approach Zalando

Reach comes from the platform. Brands entering Europe should use Zalando to test demand across countries before committing money to separate direct sites, and compare selling through Zalando’s partner model with traditional wholesale, weighing control of price and assortment against the operational effort each requires.

The listing has to feel local. Zalando shoppers expect product information in their own language and sizing in local formats. Brands should invest in translation and size guides, since accurate sizing also reduces returns, which protects margin in every country. European fashion shoppers return items often. Brands should build return rates into pricing and choose logistics that handle returns efficiently, ideally with stock held inside Europe so returned items can be resold quickly.

Sales by country, size and style reveal where demand is strongest. Brands should use that data to decide where to build direct sales next, and which styles to lead with in each country. Brands should keep their own sites focused on loyalty programs, exclusive products and the kind of storytelling that a multi-brand platform cannot provide.

Brands should use Zalando’s marketing services to support launches and key seasons, and measure the results with the same discipline they apply to Amazon advertising. Large price gaps between Zalando and a brand’s own site confuse shoppers and erode trust. Brands should set consistent prices and use promotions deliberately.

For the brand looking at that map of separate markets, Zalando turns many launches into one. Launching and running Zalando for brands entering Europe is part of the work we do across Europe and the Americas.

A0855.crumb: Why the last ad dollar earns less than…
A0855.title: Why the last ad dollar earns less than the average one
A0855.alt: Five drinking glasses in a row on a marble counter, each holding progressively less water.
A0855.ttag: Why the last ad dollar earns less than the average one | Kwontified
A0855.desc: Average ROAS hides diminishing returns. The last ad dollar earns far less than the average one, so 2026 budgets should follow marginal return.
A0855.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 6, 2026.
A0855.body:
Every campaign report leads with one return on ad spend (ROAS), averaged across all the money the campaign spent. Over the 2025 Cyber 5, Amazon ad spend among the advertisers Skai tracks rose 12% while conversions rose only 4%, according to Skai’s analysis. More money bought proportionally fewer sales. That is diminishing returns seen from the outside, and it means the last ad dollar earns less than the average one.

The reason is the order in which ad money finds shoppers: the first dollars reach the likeliest buyers, and each dollar after them reaches someone less certain at a higher price. So the budget question for 2026 is a campaign-by-campaign one. What does the next dollar earn, its marginal return, and is that above the point where the sale stops paying for the ad?

The last ad dollar buys the least likely shopper

A campaign that spends $10,000 and earns $50,000 in attributed sales reports a ROAS of 5. That number describes all the dollars together. It cannot tell you what the next $1,000 will earn.

When a brand starts spending, its ads reach the most likely buyers first: people searching for the brand’s name, shoppers already on its product pages, and searches that closely match its products. Those clicks are cheap relative to the sales they produce. As spending rises, those easy sales are taken. Each additional dollar reaches shoppers who are less certain, searches that match less closely and placements that cost more. Conversion rates fall and costs rise, so the return on each new dollar declines.

The average hides that decline. Because the early dollars earn so much, the average stays high even when the last dollars barely break even. A team that watches only the average keeps adding money long after the next dollar has stopped paying for itself, and nothing on the dashboard turns red.

Shrinking baskets push the line closer. During Prime Big Deal Days in October 2025, cost per click held steady while average order value fell 11%, in Skai’s event analysis. The click cost the same and the sale behind it was worth less. When each sale is worth less, the last dollars of spend cross the break-even line sooner.

Why a high-ROAS campaign can be the wrong home for new money

The logic that follows looks backward at first. A campaign with a high average return can be the worst place for the next dollar, and a campaign with a modest average can be the best.

Take a brand running two campaigns at $5,000 a month each. The branded campaign earns $60,000, a return of 12. The category campaign earns $15,000, a return of 3. Now raise each budget to $6,000.

CampaignMonthly spendAttributed salesAverage returnSpend raised toSales afterSales from the extra $1,000
Branded$5,000$60,00012$6,000$61,000$1,000
Category$5,000$15,0003$6,000$17,500$2,500

The branded campaign already captures nearly every search for the brand’s name, so the extra $1,000 mostly raises the price of clicks it would have won anyway. It earned $1,000. The category campaign still had shoppers it had not reached, and its extra $1,000 earned $2,500. The campaign with the lower average was the better home for the next dollar.

Profit sets the stopping point. With a 40% contribution margin, each additional dollar of advertising has to bring in at least $2.50 in sales to break even. Below that, the next dollar loses money even while the campaign’s average return still looks healthy. Every brand should work out its own break-even return and treat it as the floor for every increment of spend.

The same logic runs across retailers. Among Skai’s advertisers, Walmart Connect cost per click ran about 40% below Amazon’s during the Cyber 5, in the same Skai analysis of the week. A brand that has saturated its Amazon search campaigns may find its next dollar earns more on Walmart, even if its Amazon average looks stronger. The money should go wherever the marginal return is highest: across campaigns, across days and across retailers.

What marginal return data can and cannot tell you

Marginal return is harder to measure than the average. Attribution overstates some campaigns, and a small budget change can produce noisy results for a few weeks. The aim is an estimate good enough to improve the next decision, which is a lower bar than a perfect number and a much higher one than the average alone.

The cleanest estimate comes from changing one thing at a time. Raise or lower the budget on a single campaign by a set amount for a few weeks, and measure the change in sales alongside the change in average return. If sales barely move, the campaign was near its ceiling. Impression share points the same way: a campaign that already wins most of the available impressions has little room to grow, and extra spend there mostly bids up its own clicks.

Branded and non-branded campaigns belong in separate columns. Branded campaigns often show the highest averages and the lowest marginal returns, and blending them with prospecting campaigns hides both facts. Where a brand can run them, holdout and geography tests go further, because they show how many sales the advertising actually adds rather than how many it was credited with.

Marginal returns also move. Seasons, competitors and stock levels shift the slope, so the estimate should be refreshed every month and again before and after each major event. The report worth asking a team or an agency for is the slope itself: what the last increment of spend earned, printed next to the average.

Each budget increment goes where the next dollar earns most

Allocate the 2026 budget in steps. Give each next increment to the campaign whose next dollar is expected to earn the most, then recheck, and stop when the next dollar falls below the brand’s break-even return. Finding that slope campaign by campaign, on Amazon, Walmart and Target, is the budget work we do for brands every month.

A0856.title: Retail media consolidation: why brands should fund three networks
A0856.alt: Three potted olive trees and rows of seedlings in terracotta pots inside a sunny conservatory.
A0856.ttag: Retail media consolidation: why brands should fund three networks | Kwontified
A0856.desc: Amazon and Walmart are forecast to take nearly 90% of new US retail media dollars in 2026. Most brands should fund three networks well, not many thinly.
A0856.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 8, 2026.
A0856.body:
The renewal meeting for a small retail media network tends to turn on one question from the person who owns the budget: can you show the sales this spend added? Brands that tested many networks in 2023 and 2024 often found the smaller ones could not answer it clearly. So budget holders started asking for proof before renewing, and the money flowed back to the networks that could provide it.

Add that habit up across an industry and you get consolidation. Amazon and Walmart are forecast to capture nearly 90% of new US retail media dollars in 2026. For most brands the right response is to fund three networks well: Amazon, Walmart and the one network where their category and their shoppers concentrate. Spreading a budget thinly across many networks costs more in data, staff and measurement than it returns.

Retail media consolidation is running toward two networks

The two leaders were already far ahead. Amazon and Walmart accounted for 84.2% of US retail media ad spending in 2024, with Amazon alone taking more than three-quarters, according to EMARKETER’s outlook.

The gap is widening. US retail media ad spending reached an estimated $58.79 billion in 2025. Of the $10.53 billion in additional spending forecast for 2026, $9.42 billion, or more than 89%, will go to Amazon Ads and Walmart Connect, according to EMARKETER’s H2 2025 forecast. The same report forecast Walmart Connect to earn $4.75 billion in 2025, an 8.1% share. Walmart’s own numbers point the same way: Walmart Connect advertising sales in the US grew 33%, excluding VIZIO, in the company’s third quarter, according to its earnings release.

Third place is growing too. Target said Roundel achieved double-digit growth in its third quarter, alongside nearly 50% growth in Target Plus gross merchandise value, in its results summary. A strong specialist network can keep growing even while the two leaders take most of the new money.

The concentration has a plain cause. Amazon and Walmart have the most shoppers, the most first-party purchase data and the most mature self-service tools. Advertisers go where the shoppers are and where results are easiest to measure, and every dollar that follows that logic makes the leaders’ measurement and tools better still.

Every extra network brings its own overhead

Inside a brand, the cost of a network rarely shows up on the media line. Every additional network needs its own setup, creative, reporting, data connections and staff time. A brand spending modestly on six networks pays six sets of overhead and learns little from any of them, because each one gets too little money to produce a result anyone can read.

Take a brand that spends $600,000 a year across Amazon, Walmart and four smaller networks. Each of the four receives $15,000, and none produces results large enough to measure reliably. Move that $60,000 to Roundel, where the brand’s products already sell well, and one network finally has enough spend to test properly and show what works.

Funding properly means more than switching a network on. A network needs enough budget to cover the brand’s main products, test creative and run at least one incrementality test a year. Below that level the results are too noisy to guide a decision, and the network’s overhead eats much of whatever value it creates. The discipline that follows is a minimum budget per network, set in advance, and a refusal to activate any network the brand cannot fund at that level.

The people feel it before the spreadsheet does. Every network has its own interface, reporting quirks and account contacts. A specialist responsible for three networks can learn each one deeply; spread across many, the same person spends more of the week reconciling dashboards than improving campaigns. Concentration tends to improve results faster than adding another platform to an already crowded workload.

The value of concentration flows back to the brand

Follow where the advantage goes when a brand concentrates. A brand that is a meaningful advertiser on three networks gets more attention from account teams, earlier access to new tools and better support than a brand spread thinly across many. The networks capture most of the new money, but the brand that concentrates captures something too: a seat closer to the front of each retailer’s line.

That is also why the third network deserves a real choice rather than a default. For many lifestyle brands it will be Target. Some smaller networks offer value the leaders cannot: grocery networks reach shoppers at the moment of a weekly shop, and specialty retailers reach audiences that Amazon and Walmart do not. For a brand in those categories, the third network may be one of them instead.

The choice starts with sales. Rank networks by how much of the brand’s own retail sales flow through each retailer, since retail media works best where the products already sell. Fund Amazon and Walmart with budgets large enough to test and improve, not token amounts. Require incremental sales measurement from every network before increasing spend, and walk away from networks that cannot provide it.

Networks outside the three get money only for defined tests with clear success criteria, or none at all. One reporting system across all three makes the comparison fair, cuts staff time and shows where the next dollar earns most across retailers rather than within each one. Retailers’ sales and networks’ capabilities change, so the third seat should be reopened once a year.

Questions for the 2026 network review

  • Which network carries the largest share of our retail sales after Amazon and Walmart, and does our media plan reflect it?
  • What is our minimum budget for a network to be measurable, and which networks sit below it?
  • Which networks gave us incremental sales measurement in 2025, and which only gave us attributed sales?
  • If we moved the money from our smallest networks into one, which one would it be?

When those answers are on the table, the renewal meeting gets shorter, and choosing and running those three networks is the work we do with brands across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0857.title: Amazon’s 2026 fees: model them before they reach the margin
A0857.alt: Kraft-paper parcel on a vintage brass postal scale beside packing tape and loose coins on a wooden table.
A0857.ttag: Amazon’s 2026 fees: model them before they reach the margin | Kwontified
A0857.desc: Amazon’s 2026 FBA increase averages $0.08 per unit, but small items priced $10 to $50 pay $0.25. Model the fees product by product before January 15.
A0857.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 13, 2026.
A0857.body:
Amazon’s FBA fees rise by an average of $0.08 per unit sold in 2026, less than 0.5% of an average item’s selling price, Amazon said in its announcement to sellers. A small standard-size product priced between $10 and $50 pays $0.25 a unit, roughly three times that. Both numbers are correct, and the gap between them is the whole story of this year’s fee change. The average is spread across every unit Amazon ships, and the bill a brand actually pays depends on its own mix of sizes and prices.

That is why the headline is a poor planning number. The useful exercise is to model the change product by product before it takes effect on January 15, find the items where a small increase takes a large share of the margin, and act on price, packaging or inventory there first.

What Amazon’s 2026 fees change, tier by tier

The overall change is modest. It follows a year with no increase in US referral and FBA fees in 2025, and Amazon added no new FBA fee types, according to the same announcement. The changes take effect on January 15, 2026, with no general increase to referral fees, Jay Group reported.

The detail is where the spread shows. For small standard-size products, the increase depends on the selling price, according to a fee breakdown by eFulfillment Service:

Small standard-size product pricedFBA fee increase per unit
Below $10$0.12
$10 to $50$0.25
Above $50$0.51
Amazon’s average across all units$0.08

Every tier in that table sits above the average. That is how averages over a mix behave: some tiers see little or no change, and they pull the average down for everyone. A beauty or accessories brand whose catalog is mostly small items between $10 and $50 faces $0.25 a unit. A brand with few products in that tier may pay less than the average.

Two other changes matter for planning. The update also covers fees for Multi-Channel Fulfillment, which ships orders from other sales channels through Amazon’s network, and for Buy with Prime, according to the same Jay Group report. And starting in 2026, Amazon calculates the low-inventory-level fee at the individual seller product level rather than the parent product level, applying it only when that product’s inventory falls below 28 days of supply, according to the eFulfillment breakdown.

A quarter per unit hits thin-margin best sellers hardest

Small fee changes hurt most on products that look healthy. A product with a strong sales rank and a thin margin can lose much of its profit to a quarter per unit, while a slower product with a wide margin absorbs the same increase without anyone noticing.

Take a brand selling a $16 small standard-size cleanser, moving 20,000 units a month. Its contribution margin after fees and advertising is $1.40 per unit. The $0.25 increase cuts that margin by 18%, or $5,000 a month. The brand’s average fee change looks trivial, and its best seller now earns noticeably less.

The low-inventory change adds a second exposure. Because stock is now measured at the individual product level, a brand that lets one size or color run low can pay the fee on that variation even when the parent product as a whole is well stocked.

Timing makes all of this worse if it is ignored. Fees reset in January, just as many brands set annual prices and advertising budgets. A plan built on 2025 fees carries the old margin into every forecast for the year, so the product-level review belongs in the first weeks of January, before budgets lock.

Perspective helps here too. The 2026 increases are smaller than many carriers’ annual rate increases, and some brands will see little effect. The job is to find the products where the change matters, rather than to assume the worst across the catalog and reprice everything at once, which would cost conversion on products that never needed it.

The January fee review, product by product

Start with Amazon’s own tools. The Revenue Calculator and the Fee and Economics Preview report, which Amazon is updating with 2026 rates, give old and new fees for every product. Sort the results by the dollar effect on contribution margin, not by the size of the fee change, and work from the top.

For the products at the top of that list, three levers are available. Packaging comes first, because a small change in dimensions or weight can move a product into a cheaper tier. Price comes next, through modest tests on products with strong demand, with conversion watched closely. Inventory is the third: under the new low-inventory rules, each size and color needs to stay above the 28-day threshold on its own.

Advertising targets have to move with the margin. A lower margin raises the return on ad spend a product needs to break even, so campaigns for affected products need new targets, or they keep spending where the next sale no longer pays. Brands that use Multi-Channel Fulfillment for their own websites or other marketplaces should also rerun the shipping cost in those channels, since a higher cost per order there lowers margin outside Amazon. Seasonal surcharges and storage costs change through the year as well, so the review is worth repeating each quarter, starting after the holiday peak fee period.

The test for whether the work is done is simple: every product has a 2026 margin and an advertising target built on 2026 fees before January 15. Running that model alongside pricing and ad targets is how we manage Amazon fees for brands.

A0859.crumb: Who owns the marketplace channel inside a…
A0859.title: Who owns the marketplace channel inside a brand
A0859.alt: Bright conference room with a long live-edge walnut table, cane chairs, leather lounge chairs and plants.
A0859.ttag: Who owns the marketplace channel inside a brand | Kwontified
A0859.desc: Retail media money still comes largely from trade and shopper budgets, and marketplace work is split across four teams. Brands need one accountable owner.
A0859.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 15, 2026.
A0859.body:
Take a consumer goods brand whose sales team owns Amazon Vendor Central, whose e-commerce team owns the listings, whose agency runs advertising on a marketing budget, and whose supply chain team manages inventory. A top product goes out of stock during a promotion. The agency keeps spending, the listing team cannot change anything without approval, and sales learns about the problem at the monthly review. Every team did its job, and the brand still lost the sale.

The question that scene raises is who was responsible for the product page that week, and in a structure like that one the honest answer is nobody in particular. The marketplace channel is split across sales, trade, marketing and e-commerce, and retail media budgets are still drawn largely from trade and shopper marketing. Brands need one accountable owner for listings, pricing, inventory and advertising, with a shared profit target and the freedom to move budget to what proves incremental.

Who owns the marketplace channel today: four teams and two budgets

The money is the place to start. Of US retail media spending, 36% comes from existing trade marketing budgets and 26% from shopper marketing budgets, with the rest typically from marketing teams, according to a Forrester survey that Digiday reported. Retail budgets generally sit with sales teams and national budgets with marketing and media teams, which creates tension over who controls retail media, according to the same report. Sales teams also use retail media spending as bargaining power in their annual negotiations with retailers.

Measurement inherits the split. Forrester analyst Nikhil Lai asked whether evaluating Walmart Connect should include slotting fees, trade promotions, fines and the other costs of participating, or only the cost of media, according to the Digiday report. The question has no single answer when each cost sits in a different department’s budget. Agencies told Digiday they are pushing clients to centralize retail media under marketing teams, which have a broader view.

The brands further along are moving to a different shape. Most start with retail media inside e-commerce and are shifting to hybrid teams, and leading brands appoint heads of commerce media to unify media, sales and marketing, according to a panel recap from Skai’s ShopAble 2025 event.

The budget line decides the behavior

Each of those teams is doing what it is paid to do. Sales wants to keep retailers happy and win shelf space, and trade marketing wants promotions that move volume. Brand marketing wants consistent messaging and reach. E-commerce wants traffic and conversion. None of these goals is wrong, yet they pull in different directions, and the marketplace is the one place where they all land on the same product page.

On that page the levers interact. A listing change affects conversion, which affects advertising efficiency. A price change affects the Buy Box, which affects both sales and advertising. A stockout wastes the advertising that sent shoppers to the page. When a different team owns each lever, problems surface late and fixes take weeks, because every fix needs a meeting between people with different targets.

Where the money comes from makes it harder still. Spending drawn from trade budgets often arrives with commitments to the retailer attached, which makes it hard to move on performance. A brand may keep funding a network that underperforms because the sales team promised the spend in negotiations, and nobody in the room has the authority to take it back.

The problem grows with every marketplace added. A brand selling on Amazon, Walmart and Target, with retail media on each, may have a dozen people touching the channel across five departments. Without a single owner nobody sees the whole picture, and each retailer is managed as a separate project rather than as one channel with shared lessons.

No single structure suits every brand. A small brand may run the whole channel with one person, while a large manufacturer must coordinate across divisions and retailers. What carries across sizes is clear accountability; the organization chart can vary.

What a single owner changes

The role that resolves the scene at the top is a head of marketplaces or commerce, accountable for marketplace sales and profit, with authority over listings, pricing, inventory planning and advertising. That person does not need to do all the work. They need to make the final call when teams disagree, and they need specialists in each area who answer to the channel’s result.

The teams contributing to the channel then share one profit target, so sales volume, advertising efficiency and margin are judged together rather than in four separate reviews. Retail media money can move to the networks and tactics that prove incremental instead of being locked by commitments made in separate negotiations. And payments that secure distribution are separated from advertising that drives demand, so each is measured on its own terms. Each retailer is judged on the total cost of doing business there, including trade payments, promotions, fees and advertising, rather than on advertising alone.

The working rhythm changes with it. A short weekly review across sales, e-commerce, advertising and supply chain catches stockouts, pricing problems and listing issues before they cost a month of sales. One dashboard showing sales, advertising, inventory and profit ends the argument about whose report is right. Agencies running advertising see inventory and pricing data too, so they can pause spending when a product goes out of stock instead of finding out at the monthly review.

For a leadership team, the useful test is to replay the stockout and ask which single person would have known first and had the authority to stop the spend. If the answer takes more than one name, ownership is still split, and running the channel as one business across Amazon, Walmart and Target is the work we take on for brands.

A0861.crumb: Reach and frequency on Amazon DSP: the…
A0861.title: Reach and frequency on Amazon DSP: the two numbers to watch
A0861.alt: Row of identical blank coral posters pasted along a sunlit brick wall beside a paved sidewalk.
A0861.ttag: Reach and frequency on Amazon DSP: the two numbers to watch | Kwontified
A0861.desc: Amazon DSP budgets drift toward the same shoppers, so ROAS rises while reach stalls. Reach and frequency show the waste, and both can be capped.
A0861.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 20, 2026.
A0861.body:
A DSP campaign’s return on ad spend (ROAS) climbs for three months in a row, and the brand’s count of new customers barely moves. Both facts come from the same cause. Amazon DSP campaigns optimize toward conversions, the shoppers likeliest to convert are the ones who already know the brand, and so the budget drifts toward showing more ads to the same households. ROAS rises because those shoppers were close to buying anyway.

Two numbers expose the drift that ROAS hides: reach, the count of unique households that saw the ads, and frequency, the average number of times each household saw them. Brands that track Amazon DSP reach and frequency, cap frequency across campaigns and judge DSP on new households reached will see where the money is circling.

Amazon DSP reach and frequency tools have caught up with the spend

DSP budgets are growing. Among the advertisers Skai tracks, Amazon DSP spending rose 39% over the 2025 Cyber 5, according to Skai’s analysis.

The controls to manage it are already in the console. Advertisers using Amazon DSP’s frequency cap controls saved up to 26% of their campaign budgets from duplicate impressions and drove up to 21% incremental reach, Amazon said in its unBoxed 2024 announcement. Frequency groups, launched in October 2023, let an advertiser set one frequency cap across several orders, and on December 23, 2024, Amazon added reporting of deduplicated reach and frequency across those orders, PPC Land reported. Advertisers using frequency groups achieved an average 6% increase in unique reach, according to Amazon data cited in the same report.

Goals can now be set directly. Amazon DSP’s goal-based bidding, launched on September 19, 2024, lets advertisers set reach and frequency goals for brand campaigns and optimizes bids toward them, PPC Land reported. Unified reporting, announced at unBoxed in November 2025, combines data across ad products with 15 months of daily history, according to PPC Land’s coverage, which makes a reach trend far easier to follow over time.

Why optimization keeps finding the same shoppers

An algorithm told to maximize conversions learns quickly that shoppers who viewed the brand’s products, or bought from it before, convert best. It shows them more ads because those impressions produce the most visible sales. Nothing is broken. The system is doing exactly what it was asked.

The cost shows up in the two numbers. Frequency rises as the same households see the brand again and again, while reach stops growing. Rising frequency with flat reach means the budget is circling the same people: the brand is paying to remind its existing audience rather than to find new customers.

Take a brand spending $40,000 a month on DSP. Over three months its reach stays near 800,000 households while frequency climbs from 6 to 14, and its ROAS rises. Then it applies a frequency group cap of 8 across all orders.

Before the capAfter a frequency group cap of 8
Monthly DSP spend$40,000$40,000
Households reachednear 800,0001.2 million
Average frequencyclimbed from 6 to 14capped at 8
ROASrisingfalling
New-to-brand salesbaselinerising

ROAS falls after the cap, and that is the result the brand wanted. New shoppers convert more slowly than shoppers who were already on the product page, so their attributed return is lower in the month they first see an ad, but they are the audience that drives future sales.

The drift compounds if nobody stops it. Retargeting pools shrink when reach stalls, because fewer new shoppers enter the funnel in the first place. A brand that spends heavily on retargeting can find its audiences thinning a few months later, with cost per sale rising even though nothing obvious changed in the account.

Repetition has a price and a purpose

The case for frequency is real. Some repetition helps, especially for high-consideration products where shoppers need several exposures before buying, and the right frequency varies by category and price. The case against is just as real: past the point where another exposure changes a decision, each impression is a duplicate the budget pays for twice.

The numbers lean toward choosing frequency deliberately. Amazon’s own figures (up to 26% of budget saved from duplicate impressions, and an average 6% gain in unique reach from frequency groups) show what default settings leave on the table. Letting optimization set frequency by default puts the brand on the wrong side of that trade.

How to manage DSP reach and frequency each month

Deduplicated reach and average frequency belong in the monthly report for all DSP spending, next to the campaign-level metrics. Frequency groups should apply one cap across orders, so that separate campaigns do not stack exposures on the same households. Prospecting and retargeting need their own budgets and goals, or one quietly absorbs the other’s money.

The outcome measures follow from the purpose. New-to-brand sales and branded search growth show whether reach is turning into new demand, which is the reason most DSP budgets exist. Cost per additional household reached, compared across campaigns and months, shows where reach is cheap. A few weeks of testing different caps, comparing new-to-brand sales and incremental lift, settles the right frequency for a product better than any rule copied from another category.

For campaigns meant to find new audiences, goal-based bidding with explicit reach and frequency targets points the algorithm at breadth rather than repeat conversions. Combined exposure with Sponsored Ads is worth reviewing too, since many DSP shoppers also see a brand’s search ads, and heavy repetition across both channels can annoy shoppers without adding sales. Holdout tests then show how many sales DSP actually adds, which matters most for budgets weighted toward retargeting.

The working rule: in any month when frequency rises and reach does not, the next dollar should go to new households, whatever ROAS says. Reading those two numbers alongside Sponsored Ads is how we plan Amazon DSP for brands.

A0862.title: What NRF 2026 signaled about retail’s year ahead
A0862.alt: Smart speaker beside a wicker basket of groceries on a white plinth in a bright atrium overlooking snow.
A0862.ttag: What NRF 2026 signaled about retail’s year ahead | Kwontified
A0862.desc: NRF 2026 put AI shopping agents at the center of retail, from Google’s shopping protocol to Walmart in Gemini, after a holiday that grew 4.1%.
A0862.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 22, 2026.
A0862.body:
Walmart’s incoming CEO, John Furner, chose NRF 2026 to compare agentic AI to the impact search had on e-commerce, as Walmart unveiled an agent-led shopping experience inside Google’s Gemini, Mass Market Retailers reported. When Walmart frames a technology that way at NRF and unveils a product to match, it is telling its suppliers where it expects the next shift in how people shop to come from.

The rest of the show said the same thing: AI shopping agents are becoming retail infrastructure rather than an experiment. The year ahead favors brands whose product data an agent can read, whose prices hold together across retailers, and who try the seller tools that retailers are now building around agents.

NRF 2026 put shopping agents at the center of the show

Google set out to write the standard. It announced the Universal Commerce Protocol, a standard for shopping through AI agents developed with retailers including Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target and Walmart, the National Retail Federation reported. Google also launched Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience, an agentic shopping solution, along with a Customer Experience Agent Studio, Grocery Dive reported.

Walmart’s announcement reached in two directions at once. Alongside the shopper experience in Gemini, it described agents that help marketplace sellers and suppliers list products and build campaigns, according to the same Mass Market Retailers report. The same technology is being pointed at the customer and at the brand.

A strong holiday, built by careful shoppers

The announcements landed on top of a good season. US holiday retail sales grew 4.1% from November 1 through December 31, near the top of NRF’s forecast of 3.7% to 4.2% and above $1 trillion, the federation said in its holiday results. Online spending reached a record $257.8 billion, up 6.8%, according to Adobe’s holiday data. Retail sales for all of 2025 grew 4.93% over 2024, and a late Thanksgiving pushed Cyber Monday into December, according to the same NRF release.

The growth came with a careful shopper attached. Discounts and flexible payment options drove much of it, which leaves brands planning 2026 for customers who spend but compare before they buy.

What the retailers’ moves say they want from brands

Read the announcements as statements of intent rather than product news. A year ago, AI shopping agents were experiments, and each retailer connected to each assistant in its own way. A shared protocol lowers the cost of connecting, which lets more retailers and more assistants work together, and that is the step that turns a novelty into infrastructure. Shoppers already ask assistants for recommendations. When the assistant can also complete the purchase inside the conversation, the path from question to order shortens, and the retailer’s own website matters less in that moment.

Walmart’s seller and supplier agents say something about the other side of the relationship. The same technology is going to change how brands work with retailers, from listing products to building campaigns, and brands may spend less time on manual setup and more on deciding what the agents are allowed to do.

Take a home goods brand that, in 2025, drew most of its Walmart sales from shoppers searching on Walmart’s site. In 2026, a growing share arrives through assistants that read its product data directly. If it kept its attributes complete and its prices consistent, it shows up in those answers; a competitor with gaps in its listings does not. The advantage goes to preparation more than size, since a shared protocol lets a brand selling through Shopify or a marketplace appear alongside much larger competitors when its data is complete.

Advertising will follow, slowly. Google sells search advertising and now also builds agent shopping tools, while retailers sell retail media and open their catalogs to assistants. How brands pay for visibility inside those conversations is likely to become one of the year’s central questions, even if the answers arrive gradually. Conference announcements often run ahead of shopper behavior, too. Most purchases in 2026 will still happen on retailers’ own sites and apps, and many agent features will roll out in stages, so the signal is about direction more than immediate volume.

Preparing the catalog for the agent layer

The retail year that emerges has two layers: the familiar store and search experience, and a growing agent layer that depends on clean, consistent product data. Most of the work for the second layer is unglamorous. Every attribute completed, descriptions kept accurate, specifications consistent across retailers, because agents read structured data, and a blank field is a fact they cannot use.

Price discipline matters more once software is doing the comparing. Agents compare prices across sellers and retailers in seconds, and large gaps between retailers can steer agent-led purchases away from a brand’s preferred channels. With a holiday built on discounts behind it, the harder task for 2026 is protecting margin on key products while staying competitive.

The new seller tools deserve an early, small trial: a handful of products, a clear rule for what the agent may change, and a person reviewing every decision that touches price or spend. Brands should also ask retailers for reporting on orders that arrive through assistants, so the share can be tracked as it grows, and be ready to test paid placements inside agent experiences with small budgets and clear measurement when they appear.

The question for a leadership team after NRF 2026 is a plain one: if an assistant read our product data on Walmart and Target tonight, would it find enough to recommend us? Getting catalogs, pricing and advertising to the point where the answer is yes is part of how we run Amazon, Walmart and Target channels for brands.

A0865.title: Counterfeit and brand-safety risk on Instagram
A0865.alt: Two tan leather bifold wallets, one new and one worn, side by side on a pale wooden table.
A0865.ttag: Counterfeit and brand-safety risk on Instagram | Kwontified
A0865.desc: Reuters reported Meta’s own estimates put scam and banned-goods ads at about 10% of its 2024 revenue. Impersonation on Instagram is a brand problem too.
A0865.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jan 29, 2026.
A0865.body:
A shopper scrolling Instagram sees a familiar logo, a discount and a polished product image, and taps through before checking who is selling. On a feed built for impulse buying, that is ordinary behavior, and it is exactly the behavior counterfeit sellers are built around. They run impersonation ads and lookalike accounts that borrow a brand’s name for long enough to take the order.

Meta’s own internal estimates, reported by Reuters, suggest scam and banned-goods advertising on its platforms is large. A brand cannot outsource the problem to the platform. It has to monitor for misuse of its name, make its official shop easy to verify and tell customers plainly where genuine products are sold.

How large counterfeit risk on Instagram has become

Meta internally projected that about 10% of its 2024 revenue, or $16 billion, would come from advertising for scams and banned goods, according to company documents reviewed by Reuters and reported by the news agency. A December 2024 document estimated that Meta’s platforms showed users about 15 billion higher-risk scam ads a day, according to PYMNTS’s summary of the Reuters reporting.

Brands are named in the problem directly. Internal slides estimated that Meta earned about $3.5 billion every six months from higher-risk scam ads, including those that impersonate brands and public figures, MediaNama reported.

Meta disputes the framing. A Meta spokesman said the documents present a selective view that distorts its approach, and that the 10% estimate was rough and overly inclusive, according to the reporting. Meta said it had reduced user reports of scam ads globally by 58% over 18 months and removed more than 134 million pieces of scam ad content in 2025, according to the same reports.

Why impersonation is cheap and enforcement is slow

The economics favor the impersonator. Creating an account and running ads takes little effort, while removing them takes reports, reviews and time. A counterfeit seller can launch new accounts faster than a brand can report old ones, and every removal resets the clock rather than ending the game.

The platform’s thresholds lengthen that window. Suspicious advertisers were often banned only when Meta’s systems predicted fraud with 95% certainty, while others were charged higher ad rates as a deterrent, TechCentral reported, citing the Reuters documents. An April 2025 internal review found it was easier to advertise scams on Meta’s platforms than on Google, according to MediaNama’s report. Read for its incentives, charging a suspected scammer more instead of removing it prices the risk rather than refusing it, and a brand should plan on that basis.

Personalization then amplifies whatever gets through. Users who click on scam ads are likely to see more of them because of Meta’s ad-personalization system, according to the internal documents cited in the Reuters report. A shopper who clicks one fake offer may soon see several more, each looking like a new and separate deal.

The damage lands on the brand that never sold the item

Take a skincare brand whose best-selling serum appears in an Instagram ad at half price, run by a lookalike account that copies its name and photos. Hundreds of shoppers buy, receive a fake product and post complaints tagging the real brand. Customer service fields angry messages, and the brand’s ratings on other channels suffer before anyone inside realizes what happened.

The shopper who received the fake usually blames the name in the ad. Reviews, complaints and returns follow the real brand, even though it never sold the item, and those complaints can stay visible long after the counterfeit account is gone.

The Reuters reporting covers scam and banned-goods advertising broadly, and counterfeits are only one part of it. Meta disputes how the estimates should be read, and the share of impersonation that touches any single brand is unknown. The direction is clear enough to justify active monitoring all the same.

The brand-protection decision on the leadership table

The decision in front of a leadership team is who owns this and what it is worth spending. Platforms enforce their rules, but only the brand can watch for misuse of its own name and give shoppers a reliable way to find the real thing, so the responsibility is shared whether or not anyone has been assigned it.

In practice that means continuous monitoring: regular searches for ads and accounts using the brand’s name, logo or product images, and use of Meta’s brand rights protection tools to report infringing content. A verified account and a clearly linked shop make the real brand easy to recognize when lookalikes copy its name and photos. The brand’s own ads should be recognizable too, with consistent visuals, a verified handle and links only to official pages. A published list of official stores and authorized retailers, on the website and the social profiles, gives shoppers somewhere to check, and it is worth repeating in posts during peak seasons.

When fakes surface, the response should be quick and public: report them, warn followers and answer confused customers so the record is clear for anyone who searches later. Support teams need to recognize counterfeit complaints, explain where genuine products are sold and collect the details that help with reports. Counterfeit sellers often work across several platforms at once, so the same information belongs with the teams running Amazon, Walmart and TikTok Shop. Impersonation tends to rise around holidays and major sales, when shoppers expect deep discounts, which is when monitoring should increase. Records of infringing ads, accounts and complaints support platform reports and, if it comes to that, legal action.

The question to put to the team is simple: if a lookalike account started selling our best seller on Instagram tomorrow, who would see it first, and how many days would pass before the ad came down? Closing that gap across Instagram and the marketplaces is part of how we sell and protect products for brands.

A0869.crumb: The state of Walmart Marketplace for…
A0869.title: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands, 2026
A0869.alt: Shopping cart holding a cardboard box and a tote of bread and greens in a sunny parking lot by a blue wall.
A0869.ttag: The state of Walmart Marketplace for brands, 2026 | Kwontified
A0869.desc: Walmart’s US e-commerce grew 28% and its marketplace 17% in late 2025, and it now sells through ChatGPT and Gemini. Brands need a Walmart plan of its own.
A0869.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 5, 2026.
A0869.body:
The weekly Walmart order starts with groceries and household staples, and more and more often it picks up something from another category on the way to checkout. Every one of those habits, formed around essentials, is a chance for a brand that has never sold a carton of milk to be discovered. That is the quiet engine behind Walmart’s marketplace, and it is why the channel deserves more than a copy of a brand’s Amazon catalog.

Walmart Marketplace enters 2026 as a fast-growing second channel for brands, now reachable through ChatGPT and Gemini as well as Walmart’s own site and app. It rewards brands that run it with its own content, pricing, fulfillment and advertising plan.

Walmart Marketplace for brands now has the growth to justify its own plan

Online sales are growing fast. Walmart US e-commerce sales grew 28% in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, and Walmart Connect advertising grew 33%, excluding VIZIO, the company said in its earnings release. The marketplace is a large part of that growth: Walmart’s US marketplace grew 17% in the quarter, and many marketplace categories grew more than 40%, PYMNTS reported. Sales through expedited store-fulfilled delivery grew nearly 70% in the quarter, according to Walmart’s release.

Advertisers have followed the shoppers. Walmart Connect spending was up 52% during the 2025 Cyber 5 for the advertisers in Skai’s data. Walmart Connect was forecast to earn $4.75 billion in US retail media in 2025, an 8.1% share, according to EMARKETER’s H2 2025 forecast.

AI shopping has arrived as well. Walmart announced Instant Checkout in ChatGPT in October 2025, Retail TouchPoints reported, and in January 2026 it unveiled an agent-led shopping experience inside Google Gemini, Mass Market Retailers reported.

Walmart grades listings by its own rules

Read Walmart as an institution and the marketplace makes sense. It combines a huge store network with an expanding online assortment, and third-party sellers fill gaps in its own inventory. That lets Walmart offer more choice without holding more stock, and it gives brands access to Walmart’s shoppers without a wholesale relationship. Fast delivery, including store-based fulfillment, makes online orders feel as convenient as Amazon’s for many households.

What Walmart measures tells a brand what it wants. Walmart scores listings on a Listing Quality measure with five components, including content, price competitiveness and reviews, and it compares sellers’ prices with those on external websites, according to its Marketplace Learn guide. A retailer that grades sellers on how their prices compare off the site is telling brands that it intends to be the price shoppers trust. Brands that copy their Amazon content and pricing into that system often underperform.

Take a home goods brand that lists on Walmart by copying its Amazon listings, and sells little. It rewrites the content to Walmart’s guidelines, matches prices to its other channels and enrolls in Walmart Fulfillment Services. Sales start to grow steadily, and its Walmart Connect campaigns turn profitable once the listings convert. Nothing about the products changed; the brand simply started speaking the retailer’s language.

Reviews take longer to fix. Many brands start on Walmart with few reviews even when their Amazon listings have thousands. Walmart’s review programs and steady sales close the gap, but conversion should be expected to lag at first. A plan that judges Walmart by Amazon’s conversion rate in its first months can cut the channel’s budget before the reviews have had time to arrive.

The store sets the delivery bar for every seller

Walmart’s advantage is the store. Store-fulfilled delivery lets it promise fast shipping on many products from locations close to shoppers. Marketplace sellers do not use those stores directly, but they are judged against the delivery speed shoppers come to expect, which raises the bar for every seller on the site. Walmart Fulfillment Services lets sellers store inventory in Walmart’s network for fast shipping, which helps listings qualify for faster delivery promises. For a brand that cannot use it, reliable shipping times and accurate inventory matter even more.

The marketplace remains much smaller than Amazon for most brands, and some categories sell better in Walmart’s stores than online. The opportunity varies by product, price point and shopper. What emerges for most brands selling in the US is a two-marketplace plan: Amazon as the largest channel, and Walmart as a growing second one with rules of its own.

What a Walmart-specific plan covers in 2026

The plan starts with listings written to Walmart’s guidelines, with every attribute filled, and with Listing Quality scores checked regularly so the lowest-scoring products are fixed first. Prices need watching across every channel, because Walmart’s search rewards price competitiveness against other sites, and a gap that looks harmless on a spreadsheet can cost visibility. Walmart Fulfillment Services belongs wherever it fits, and review programs belong on new listings from the start.

Advertising comes after the listings are strong. Sponsored Products on the best-converting items is the place to begin, with other formats added as returns become clear. Walmart runs its own deal events, and Walmart Connect spending rises sharply around them, so inventory, prices and campaigns for those events deserve the same preparation a brand gives Prime Day. With Walmart selling through ChatGPT and Gemini, complete product data and consistent pricing matter even more, since assistants read listings directly and compare prices across sellers. And Walmart’s results should be reported on their own, with goals that reflect a smaller but faster-growing business.

The question for a leadership team is whether Walmart has its own owner and its own targets, or still lives as a line inside the Amazon report. Building that second channel properly, alongside Amazon, is the work we do for brands on Walmart Marketplace.

A0868.crumb: Amazon’s Q4 2025 ad revenue and the fight…
A0868.title: Amazon’s Q4 2025 ad revenue and the fight for clicks
A0868.alt: Pile of pastel lidded gift boxes stacked on a small white pedestal table near a window.
A0868.ttag: Amazon’s Q4 2025 ad revenue and the fight for clicks | Kwontified
A0868.desc: Amazon’s Q4 2025 ad revenue rose 23% to $21.3 billion, more than twice its North America sales growth. Brands are paying more for each sale they win.
A0868.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 6, 2026.
A0868.body:
In the fourth quarter of 2025, Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 23%. Its North America sales grew 10%. Advertising revenue is what brands collectively pay Amazon for visibility, and retail sales are what shoppers buy. When the first grows more than twice as fast as the second, brands as a group are paying more for each dollar of sales they win.

That gap is the most useful number in the quarter for anyone who buys Amazon ads. It says the competition for clicks is still rising. It does not say how much of that pressure reaches any one brand, which is why the response starts with each brand’s own cost per sale.

Amazon’s Q4 2025 ad revenue, against the rest of the business

The headline figures, from TheWrap’s report on the results and a MarketBeat summary of the earnings call:

Fourth quarter of 2025RevenueGrowth
Advertising services$21.3 billion23%
Total company$213.4 billion14%
North America segment$127.1 billion10%
Subscription services, including Prime$13.1 billion14%

The year was large too. Advertising contributed more than $12 billion of incremental revenue for Amazon in 2025, CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call, according to the MarketBeat summary. Features such as Rufus and Prime Video ads contributed meaningfully to advertising, according to the same summary.

Investment is rising sharply. Amazon expects about $200 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, citing opportunities in AI, chips, robotics and satellites, TheWrap reported. Much of that spending supports the AI systems that increasingly power Amazon’s advertising tools, from campaign agents to shopping assistants. For the first quarter of 2026, Amazon guided net sales of $173.5 billion to $178.5 billion, growth of 11% to 15%. A growing Prime base gives advertisers more shoppers to reach, and gives Amazon more reasons to sell ads against that audience.

Why ads growing faster than sales means a costlier click

Two forces open the gap. More advertisers compete for the same prominent placements in search results, which pushes prices up. Amazon also keeps adding inventory, such as Prime Video ads and display placements across the web, which brings in spending that is not tied to search at all.

The second force matters for how the number is read. Because part of Amazon’s ad growth comes from formats beyond search, the gap overstates the pressure on search costs alone. The direction still holds: more money is chasing the shopper’s attention, and a brand that stands still in its bidding will slowly lose visibility to brands that do not.

Rising ad revenue also does not mean rising costs for every brand. Search costs held steady at some 2025 events while newer formats absorbed a growing share of budgets. A brand that tracks its own cost per click and cost per sale can see whether the market’s pressure is reaching it, instead of assuming the market average applies.

Take a brand whose Amazon sales grew 8% in 2025 while its advertising spend grew 20% to defend its search positions. Its advertising cost per sale rose by about 11%. The brand assumed the increase was unavoidable.

A closer look showed that much of it came from bidding up its own brand terms, where it already ranked first organically. Part of the rise was the market. Part of it was the brand competing with itself.

Company-wide figures mix many categories, regions and ad formats, and they cannot show what any single brand pays. The comparison of ad growth with sales growth is a signal of direction, not a measure of anyone’s cost.

What to check before setting 2026 budgets

Cost per sale is the number to watch. Advertising cost per dollar of sales, followed over time and broken out by campaign type, shows whether competition is raising a brand’s costs and where. Branded search deserves its own line, because bidding on a brand’s own name often absorbs rising costs without adding many sales, and it is worth testing how much of that spend is incremental. Holdout tests and new-to-brand metrics do the same job across the account, separating spending that creates sales from spending that only claims them.

Cost per sale has limits of its own. It rises when a brand moves budget into prospecting, where clicks convert more slowly, and it falls when a brand leans on branded terms that would have sold anyway. Read alone, it can reward the wrong campaigns, so it belongs next to new-to-brand sales in the same report.

Thinner competition is worth looking for. Prime Video and other video ads face different competition from search, and brands with suitable creative can test them with clear goals and a count of new customers reached. Walmart Connect and other networks often offer lower costs per click, so cost per sale belongs in a comparison across retailers before budgets are set. Amazon’s spring and summer events will draw the same rising competition, and their budgets should be built on current cost data rather than 2025 averages.

Two longer-term defenses round it out. As Amazon invests in AI that builds and manages campaigns, those tools deserve a test with clear goals and spending limits, compared against campaigns managed by people. And strong listings, reviews and reliable stock help a brand rank without paying for every click, which reduces its dependence on rising ad prices over time.

The rule for 2026: if a brand’s ad spend is growing faster than its sales, find out whether the market or the brand’s own bidding is causing it before raising the budget again. Separating the two, campaign by campaign, is the kind of advertising measurement we carry out for brands on Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0870.crumb: Amazon’s Ads MCP server: what an AI agent…
A0870.title: Amazon’s Ads MCP server: what an AI agent can now do
A0870.alt: Small robotic arm gripping a knob on a vintage brass control panel on a wooden table.
A0870.ttag: Amazon’s Ads MCP server: what an AI agent can now do | Kwontified
A0870.desc: Amazon’s Ads MCP server lets AI agents pull reports, change budgets and build Sponsored Products campaigns from one prompt. People should still own the rules.
A0870.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 10, 2026.
A0870.body:
Raising a campaign budget in Amazon Ads used to mean logging in, finding the campaign, typing a number and checking the result. One of Amazon’s documented examples for its Ads MCP server does the same thing with a sentence: an instruction asking an AI agent to increase a campaign budget to $500. When an action costs a sentence instead of a session in the console, a team makes more of them, and the wrong ones travel exactly as fast as the right ones.

That is the real change behind the Amazon Ads MCP server, which entered open beta on February 2, 2026. Execution gets cheap. Brands should hand that execution to agents and keep the goals, the approvals and the measurement with people, because those are the parts that decide whether faster means better.

What the Amazon Ads MCP server can do

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the industry protocol through which assistants such as Claude or ChatGPT connect to Amazon’s advertising tools. Through Amazon’s server, agents can query campaign performance, list advertising accounts, show recent invoices and generate campaign reports from plain-language requests, according to Amazon’s documented examples cited by PPC Land.

The server changes things as well as reading them. Beyond budget changes, one tool creates an end-to-end Sponsored Products campaign in a single workflow, handling the campaign, ad groups and ads, and produces a ready-to-launch campaign that only needs review and approval, according to the report. Another tool expands existing campaigns to a new country with a single prompt.

Those pre-built tools are what make the difference. Traditional APIs expose capabilities one at a time, so an agent has to piece the steps together, and a task such as launching in a new country can involve dozens of manual steps, according to the PPC Land report. Amazon’s tools bundle those steps into complete workflows.

The server is open to many assistants. Advertisers can connect Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Amazon Q, Amazon Bedrock and other compatible applications, and Amazon does not own or operate the AI models that connect, according to the report. The server currently exposes tools, with resources and prompts planned for later releases. It sits beside Amazon’s own Ads Agent, launched inside the advertising console at unBoxed in November 2025; the MCP server extends similar capabilities to the assistants and tools brands and agencies already work with.

Why cheaper actions scale mistakes too

Friction used to do quiet work in an ad account. Every change took time, and that time slowed bad decisions as well as good ones. An agent removes the friction, so a brand will make more changes, faster.

Speed has no opinion about direction. An instruction the agent misreads, a wrong account identifier or a vague request can change many campaigns at once. A change a person would have made to one campaign can reach every campaign in the account before anyone looks. Security researchers have also warned that MCP implementations can be vulnerable to attacks such as tool poisoning, according to the same PPC Land report.

So the agent’s value depends less on the agent than on the instructions around it. Take two teams that both ask an agent to raise budgets on their best campaigns. The first leaves “best” undefined. The agent reads it as highest attributed return on ad spend and raises budgets on branded campaigns that were already capturing nearly every brand search. Spend rises, and sales barely move.

The second team gives the agent a written rule: raise budgets only where impression share is below 70% and the product is in stock. Its spend grows where it can still buy sales. The two agents were identical. The rules were not.

Plenty of agent projects disappoint for reasons that have little to do with the model. Gartner predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of costs, unclear value and weak risk controls, according to the PPC Land report. The payoff depends on how carefully the tool is deployed.

Roles shift as a result. Specialists spend less time clicking through settings and more time writing rules, reviewing changes and testing ideas. A team trained for that shift will get more from an agent than a team that simply adds one to an unchanged process.

Five controls to set before an agent touches spend

  1. Start with reading. Let agents pull reports and answer questions first; it carries little risk and builds familiarity before any change is allowed.
  2. Write the rules down. Goals, budget limits, bidding rules and products to avoid should exist in writing before an agent changes anything.
  3. Require sign-off on money. Budget increases, new campaigns and expansions to new countries need a person’s approval, and every campaign the build tool prepares gets its keywords, bids and budgets checked before launch.
  4. Log every action. A record of what agents changed, compared weekly with results, is how a team learns which instructions worked.
  5. Measure independently. Agents should not grade their own work, so results belong in the brand’s own reporting and incrementality tests.

Two housekeeping decisions sit behind the list. Some teams will prefer Amazon’s in-console agent and others their own assistant connected through the MCP server, and each option puts data and control in a different place, so the choice should be deliberate. And every agency, tool and assistant connected to the account should be known, with access removed when it is no longer needed.

The rule that holds it together is short: delegate execution, keep judgment. Writing those rules and limits into an Amazon Ads account is part of how we run retail media for brands.
