A0872.crumb: The state of Target Plus for brands…
A0872.title: The state of Target Plus for brands, 2026: small but growing
A0872.alt: Stoneware vases and bowls, a linen cloth and a potted olive tree on a rustic bench against a red wall.
A0872.ttag: The state of Target Plus for brands, 2026: small but growing | Kwontified
A0872.desc: Target Plus grew nearly 50% in late 2025 while Target’s store sales fell. What the curated, invite-only marketplace offers brands, and who should apply.
A0872.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 12, 2026.
A0872.body:
In a Target store, an apparel brand might hold five styles on the shelf, in the sizes and colors the buyer picked for that season. Online, through Target Plus, the same brand can list eight more styles in a wider run of sizes and colors, shipped directly to the shopper, and the sales from those extra styles become its argument for wider store placement the following season. That is the role Target’s marketplace plays for a brand like this one: an extension of the shelf, not a replacement for Amazon.

It is also growing fast while Target’s comparable sales fall. Target Plus enters 2026 as a small, curated, invite-only marketplace, and brands whose products and price points fit Target’s shopper should pursue an invitation and use it to extend their assortment and test products, with expectations in line with its scale.

Target Plus for brands is growing while the stores are not

Target Plus gross merchandise value grew nearly 50% in the third quarter of 2025, and Roundel, Target’s retail media network, grew at a double-digit rate, while comparable sales fell 2.7%, Target said in its results summary. Non-merchandise sales, which include advertising and marketplace revenue, grew about 18% in the quarter, and next-day shipping reached more than half of the US population, according to its earnings release.

The shoppers behind those numbers were selective. Target’s food and beverage and hardlines categories grew in the quarter while discretionary categories softened, according to the same release. People kept visiting for essentials and held back on some discretionary purchases, which matters for a brand choosing which products to list.

The ambition is large relative to the starting point. Target aims to grow Target Plus from more than $1 billion in gross merchandise value to more than $5 billion within five years, Modern Retail reported. The model is curated: Target Plus is invite-only, and Target partnered with Shopify to bring more merchants into the program, Fortune reported.

Who captures the value in a curated marketplace

Follow the value and the design becomes clear. Target Plus lets Target offer more products online without buying and storing them. Sellers ship directly to shoppers, while Target decides which sellers and products appear. Target gets a wider assortment, a marketplace revenue line and, through Roundel, an advertising line, without carrying the inventory risk.

The brand’s side of the bargain is access and calm. Because Target admits sellers by invitation, the marketplace avoids the crowded listings and price wars of open marketplaces, and shoppers see fewer sellers and more consistent quality. A brand admitted to Target Plus often faces fewer direct competitors on the same product than it would on an open marketplace, which makes pricing and content easier to manage. The same curation cuts the other way: Target can remove sellers who fall short of its standards.

Data is the quieter benefit. The apparel brand with eight extra styles online learns which of them Target’s shoppers actually buy, and that evidence belongs to the conversation with its Target store buyer. Roundel lets Target Plus sellers promote those listings to Target’s shoppers, so the brand can give a new style visibility instead of waiting for it to be found.

Delivery is where Target sets the terms. With next-day shipping available to more than half of the US population, Target’s shoppers expect fast delivery from every seller. A marketplace seller that ships slowly stands out for the wrong reasons, and its listings may lose visibility as a result.

Small by design, at least for now

Even at $5 billion, Target Plus would remain far smaller than Amazon’s third-party business, which generated $156 billion in seller services revenue in 2024, according to the Modern Retail report. Target Plus is rarely a brand’s largest channel. Its value is reach to Target’s loyal shoppers, room to extend an assortment beyond what Target buys for its stores, and a place to test new products before a wider wholesale push.

Invitations are selective, and many brands will not be admitted. Even for those that are, the decline in comparable sales shows that Target’s overall traffic has been under pressure, so marketplace growth does not guarantee strong results for every seller.

The Shopify partnership matters most for smaller brands. By working with Shopify to recruit merchants, Target opened a path for brands that sell mainly through their own websites, which can bring an existing catalog to Target’s shoppers with less setup than building a wholesale relationship from scratch.

Deciding whether to pursue an invitation

Fit comes before anything else: products, price points and style that match Target’s shopper. Operations follow, since Target expects fast, reliable fulfillment and a brand should know it can meet the shipping standard before applying. A brand that already has wholesale placement at Target should use the marketplace for complementary products, sizes and colors, and coordinate with its wholesale team so the listings support the store relationship instead of competing with it.

Once in, the work is familiar. Roundel budget gives new listings visibility. Prices stay consistent with other channels, because Target’s shoppers compare prices with other retailers and a gap hurts both conversion and the wholesale relationship. Inventory and Roundel budgets get built around Target’s busiest windows, including back-to-school and the holidays. And Target Plus is judged on its own goals, such as reach to new shoppers and assortment testing, rather than on volume set against Amazon.

The question worth asking inside a brand is which of its products Target’s buyer passed over, and whether Target’s shoppers would have bought them anyway. Answering it on Target Plus, alongside Amazon and Walmart, is work we take on for brands.

A0874.crumb: The state of Zalando for brands, 2026…
A0874.title: The state of Zalando for brands, 2026: scale, control and returns
A0874.alt: Folded knit sweaters in an open tissue-lined shipping box on a wooden table, a camel coat hanging behind.
A0874.ttag: The state of Zalando for brands, 2026: scale, control and returns | Kwontified
A0874.desc: Zalando reached 61.4 million active customers after ABOUT YOU. Selling direct to its shoppers can beat wholesale for brands, if returns are managed.
A0874.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 17, 2026.
A0874.body:
Selling to Zalando wholesale feels safe. Zalando buys the product at a discount, sets the price, and carries the unsold stock and much of the cost of returns. Selling the same product directly to Zalando’s shoppers through the partner model hands the brand the price, the assortment and a larger share of each sale, along with the risk. Which model pays more is decided mostly by a number that sits in neither contract: the share of items shoppers send back.

That matters more now that the audience is bigger. After combining with ABOUT YOU, Zalando has more than 61 million active customers. Selling directly to them can earn a brand more per item than wholesale, but only when returns are managed, which is why the choice between wholesale and the partner model belongs at the level of each product.

Zalando for brands in 2026: a larger audience and more services

Zalando completed its combination with ABOUT YOU in July 2025, and the group’s active customers reached 61.4 million, the company said in its third-quarter results. Gross merchandise volume grew 21.6% to 4.2 billion euros in the quarter. The two audiences overlap only partly: more than 5 million customers use both platforms, according to the same release, so most shop on only one of the two. The average basket over the prior 12 months was 61.80 euros.

The supply side is crowded. Zalando works with more than 7,000 partner brands, Retail Insight Network reported.

Services for brands are growing too. Zalando’s business-to-business revenue, which includes logistics and software services for brands, rose 15.6% to 277 million euros in the third quarter, Fibre2Fashion reported. Zalando also reported strong growth in Zalando Marketing Services, its advertising business, over the first nine months of 2025, according to its quarterly statement.

Who carries the risk under each model

Under wholesale, Zalando buys a brand’s products at a discount and sells them at prices it sets. It carries the risk of unsold stock and absorbs much of the cost of returns. Under the partner model, the brand sells directly to Zalando’s shoppers. It sets prices, chooses the assortment and keeps a larger share of each sale after Zalando’s commission, and it also carries the unsold stock and more of the cost when shoppers send items back.

Returns decide the outcome. European fashion shoppers return often, especially over sizing, and a product with high returns can lose much of its extra margin under the partner model while a product with low returns keeps it.

Take a brand selling a 100-euro jacket. Under wholesale it receives 45 euros per jacket with no returns risk. Under the partner model, assume it keeps 70 euros per sale after commission but pays 12 euros in handling for every returned item. The rates are assumptions for the arithmetic, not Zalando’s terms.

100-euro jacketWholesalePartner model, 30% returnsPartner model, 60% returns
Brand receives per sale45 euros70 euros70 euros
Handling per returned itemZalando’s cost12 euros12 euros
Net per jacket kept45 eurosabout 65 eurosabout 52 euros

At a 30% return rate, the partner model nets about 65 euros per jacket kept. At a 60% return rate, it falls to about 52 euros, and that is before counting unsold stock. Both still beat wholesale in this example, but the gap shrinks fast as returns climb, and the shape holds whatever the exact terms: returns decide which model pays.

The case for wholesale, and where the numbers lean

The trade-off has two real sides. Wholesale feels safer, and for some products it is. Unsold stock is the second cost of selling direct: under the partner model it stays with the brand, so quantities have to be planned carefully and slow sellers cleared through the brand’s own markdowns. Under wholesale, the retailer makes those calls. A brand with strong demand planning handles that well; a brand without it can give back the margin it gained.

The partner model has an advantage the table cannot show. Selling directly gives a brand clearer information on which sizes, colors and markets sell, and at what prices, which helps it plan production, set prices in other channels and decide where to build direct sales in Europe.

The numbers lean toward the partner model for products with steady demand and low returns, where it can earn noticeably more per item while giving the brand control over price and data. They lean toward wholesale for high-return fashion items, where Zalando carries more of the risk. Many brands use both models at once, and Zalando’s terms vary by brand and category, so the comparison has to run on the brand’s actual contracts and return data rather than on general assumptions.

What to model before the next season

Each product needs its own comparison of wholesale and partner economics, using real return rates by size and category and the cost of unsold stock at the end of each season. Sizing comes first among the fixes, because accurate size guides and fit information reduce returns, which improves partner-model margins most of all; return reasons reviewed by product each month show which listings to fix.

Zalando’s business-to-business services can store and ship a brand’s stock across channels, which may lower costs for a brand selling in several European markets. Zalando Marketing Services can support partner-model launches, measured against the margin each product earns. Prices need to stay coherent across markets, since shoppers in different European countries compare across borders. And with ABOUT YOU now part of the group, each platform’s shoppers deserve their own check on assortment and imagery.

The rule is simple to state: below the return rate where the partner model stops beating wholesale, sell direct; above it, let Zalando carry the risk. Finding that line product by product, alongside a brand’s US marketplaces, is part of how we run Zalando for brands.

A0875.crumb: The state of Mercado Libre for brands…
A0875.title: The state of Mercado Libre for brands, 2026: growth and logistics
A0875.alt: A yellow vintage scooter with a large delivery box parked on a cobblestone street lined with colorful old buildings.
A0875.ttag: The state of Mercado Libre for brands, 2026: growth and logistics | Kwontified
A0875.desc: Mercado Libre’s sales grew 28% and its ad revenue 56% in late 2025, built on fast delivery. What its marketplace offers brands entering Latin America in 2026.
A0875.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 19, 2026.
A0875.body:
A US beauty brand that wants to sell directly to shoppers in Brazil through its own website has three problems before its first order ships: local payments, tax handling and a delivery partner. In Latin America those have long been the hardest parts of selling online. Mercado Libre’s business is built around exactly those three, with a marketplace, a payments system in Mercado Pago and its own logistics network under one roof.

That is why Mercado Libre enters 2026 as the main channel for brands entering the region. Its sales are up 28%, unique buyers number almost 77 million and ad revenue is up 56%, all resting on a network that makes fast delivery the norm. A brand arriving now should start with Brazil and Mexico, use Mercado Libre’s fulfillment and add Mercado Ads once its listings convert.

Mercado Libre for brands: the numbers behind the growth

Gross merchandise volume rose 28% to $16.5 billion in the third quarter of 2025, or 35% excluding currency effects, and unique buyers grew 26% to almost 77 million, according to Mercado Libre’s third-quarter release. Ads revenue grew 56%, or 63% excluding currency effects, with display and video revenue almost doubling, according to the same release.

The logistics numbers explain the rest. Mercado Libre increased its fulfillment capacity by 41% in the quarter, and items sold rose 39% to 635 million units, with 80% of fast deliveries made within 48 hours, the company said in the release.

Payments widen the reach of all of this. Mercado Pago’s net revenue grew 49% to $3.2 billion in the quarter, and total payment volume surpassed $71 billion, according to the same release. Its monthly active users reached 72 million, the company said on its news site.

Payments, logistics and a marketplace under one roof

Read Mercado Libre as an institution and its advantage is plain. Owning the marketplace, the way people pay and the trucks that deliver gives it control over the three things that have long been hardest about selling online in the region. Competitors that own only one of them struggle to match the experience.

Shopper behavior compounds the structural advantage. People return to the platform they trust to deliver quickly and handle payment safely. Lower free shipping thresholds bring in more buyers, and more buyers attract more sellers and advertisers, which in turn gives shoppers more reasons to come back. Shoppers who already trust Mercado Pago have one less reason to hesitate at checkout.

For brands, logistics changes the job. Fast delivery is now expected, and listings that cannot meet it lose ground. A brand that stores stock in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment network inherits the same delivery promises that drive the platform’s growth, a shortcut a standalone website cannot easily match.

Advertising is reaching past the marketplace too. Mercado Ads added premium inventory through partnerships with Roku and HBO in the quarter, according to the release. That combines the marketplace’s purchase data with placements such as streaming television, so a brand can reach shoppers before they search and still measure the sales on the marketplace itself.

What each country asks of a brand

The largest markets are surging. In Brazil, lowering the free shipping threshold accelerated growth in items sold to 42% and currency-neutral sales to 34%. In Mexico, items sold also grew 42% and currency-neutral sales grew 34%, according to the release. Even Argentina held up: despite a challenging economy, items sold there grew 34% and currency-neutral sales grew 44%.

Each country still has its own rules, taxes and currency risks. Argentina’s economy has been volatile, and cross-border selling into Brazil and Mexico involves import requirements that can slow a launch. Brands need local expertise or partners to handle product registrations, import rules and taxes before the first listing goes live.

Localization goes further than translation. Listings need Portuguese for Brazil and Spanish for the other markets, with local sizing, measurements and product details. Prices should reflect local competition, taxes and free shipping thresholds, rather than a straight conversion of US prices, and they need reviewing as currencies move. Each country also has its own peak shopping periods, which differ from the US calendar, so stock, prices and advertising have to be prepared market by market.

A 2026 entry plan starts with fulfillment, not a website

Go back to the beauty brand. Instead of building payments, tax handling and delivery for its own site, it lists on Mercado Libre, stores stock in Mercado Libre’s fulfillment centers and reaches Brazilian shoppers with fast delivery from the first week. It launches with a focused set of products so reviews can build before the range expands. Once listings convert, it adds Mercado Ads, starting with product ads and moving into display and video as results become clear.

The order of those steps matters as much as the steps. Brazil and Mexico come first, as the largest and fastest-growing markets, before smaller countries in the region. Fulfillment comes first among the operational choices, starting with best sellers, because fast delivery drives both ranking and conversion. And results are tracked country by country, since each market behaves differently in sales, advertising and delivery. A brand that reports Latin America as one line will miss the country where its listings convert and the one where they stall, and is likely to move money too late in both.

The question for a leadership team considering the region is which of the three problems it would rather solve itself, and at what cost, when one platform has already solved all of them. Launching and operating Mercado Libre alongside a brand’s US and European marketplaces is part of how we help brands enter Latin America.

A0876.crumb: The state of Roundel for brands, 2026…
A0876.title: The state of Roundel for brands, 2026: growth Target needs
A0876.alt: Red wooden shelves holding white ceramic vases, bowls and folded linens beneath a glowing wall screen in a sunlit room.
A0876.ttag: The state of Roundel for brands, 2026: growth Target needs | Kwontified
A0876.desc: Target plans to double Roundel by 2030 while its store sales fall. That puts pressure on brands to fund media, so judge Roundel spend on proven sales lift.
A0876.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 24, 2026.
A0876.body:
Target’s comparable sales fell 2.7% in the third quarter of 2025. In the same quarter Roundel, the company’s retail media business, posted double-digit growth, and Target plans to double Roundel by 2030. A media business can grow faster than the store it sells access to, but only by earning more from each shopper who walks through it.

That arithmetic is the most important fact about Roundel for brands in 2026. More money per shopper means rising costs to reach each one and steady pressure on suppliers to fund media. Roundel spending should be judged on proven sales lift, kept separate from the commercial relationship with Target, and expanded into new formats only where they show results.

Roundel for brands: where the network stands

Target plans to double the size of Roundel by 2030, after the media business drove nearly $2 billion in value in 2024, the company said in its strategic plan announcement. That value figure is broader than revenue: it includes direct ad revenue as well as contributions that offset cost of sales and operating expenses, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Roundel measureFigureSource
Value driven, 2024nearly $2 billionTarget
Target advertising revenue, 2024$649 million, up about 24%Marketing Dive
Roundel revenue, fourth quarter of fiscal 2024$190 million, up nearly 14%Marketing Dive
Target Product Ads sales growth, 2024more than 35%Digital Commerce 360
Roundel teammore than 800 peopleDigital Commerce 360

The revenue figures come from Marketing Dive’s report. The rest of the scale shows in the tools. Target added a self-service platform, Roundel Media Studio, a second-price auction model and Precision Plus, a buying solution built on Target’s first-party data. It also planned to test in-store formats such as demos, sampling and digital signage in 2025, according to the Digital Commerce 360 report.

Growth continued while the stores slowed. Target’s results summary for the third quarter of 2025 put the two side by side: double-digit growth for Roundel, and a 2.7% decline in comparable sales. Roundel is also moving into AI assistants: Target became one of the first retailers to test contextual ads in ChatGPT, with Roundel offering brand partners a chance to take part, Supermarket News reported.

What doubling media on a flat shopper base does to price

A retail media network earns money from brands that want to reach a retailer’s shoppers. If the number of shoppers grows slowly while media revenue has to double, the network must earn more from each shopper. It has three ways to do that: add placements, raise prices and draw in more advertisers. All three land on the brand’s cost to reach a Target shopper.

The pressure also travels through the commercial relationship. Brands that sell to Target wholesale often find media spending tied, formally or informally, to their dealings with the retailer, and when the retailer needs media growth, its buyers have reasons to encourage it.

None of that makes Roundel a poor buy. The network’s growth can reflect real strength in its tools and data and still deliver weaker returns for a particular brand. Both can be true at once, which is why the network’s growth is not evidence of value for any one advertiser.

Take a home brand whose Target sales are flat while its Roundel budget rose 30% at the buyer’s encouragement. Attributed returns look acceptable. A holdout test then shows that half the attributed sales would have happened anyway. The brand moves budget toward Target Product Ads on new items, where the test shows real lift, and cuts broad awareness spending. Its Roundel total may barely change; what it buys changes completely.

Attributed return answers a narrower question than it appears to. It counts sales that followed an ad, including sales from shoppers who were already loyal to the brand and already shopping at Target. On a network built around a retailer’s own regular customers, that overlap can be large, which is why the holdout result matters more on Roundel than the dashboard figure.

Target’s leadership has given brands an argument to use. Michael Fiddelke, then Target’s chief operating officer, told investors at the March 2025 meeting that retail is about product and that the best product at the best value wins, according to NBC’s report on the meeting. A retailer focused on winning back shoppers will want its media business to support that goal, which gives a brand room to ask for spending tied to sales.

Buying Roundel on evidence in 2026

Roundel has genuine strengths: Target’s first-party data, loyal shoppers and growing self-service tools. For many brands it remains an essential channel. The discipline is in how it is bought.

Holdout or geographic tests on major campaigns show how many sales Roundel actually adds, and that result is the brand’s best evidence when a buyer encourages higher spending; any increase should be tied to measurable goals. Advertising that drives demand belongs in a different column from payments that support the commercial relationship, each measured on its own terms. Roundel Media Studio gives more control over bids and budgets and suits search and product ads, where results are easiest to measure. Precision Plus and Target’s audience data can sharpen targeting, but they earn their cost only if a test shows the lift.

The ChatGPT pilot and the in-store formats are early, and they deserve small budgets with clear goals. Brands selling through Target Plus should use Roundel to support new listings, which is often where advertising adds the most.

The rule for a doubling network: every Roundel dollar should be able to point to a test that shows it added sales. Running that test alongside Amazon and Walmart advertising is how we measure Roundel for brands.

A0879.crumb: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants…
A0879.title: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands
A0879.alt: A store aisle with blue-lit shelves of unlabeled kraft boxes, bags and glass bottles, and a yellow crate on the floor.
A0879.ttag: What Walmart’s ad growth says it wants from brands | Kwontified
A0879.desc: Walmart Connect grew 41% and marketplace categories over 40% in Walmart’s latest quarter. What those results show Walmart wants from brands in 2026.
A0879.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Feb 26, 2026.
A0879.body:
In Walmart’s latest quarter, 35% of the orders it filled from its stores reached the shopper in under three hours, executives said on the earnings call. A shopper who gets a third of their orders that fast starts to expect it of everything on the site, including the items sold by brands through the marketplace. That expectation is one of several things Walmart’s results quietly ask of the brands that sell there.

Read the quarter as a list of requests and it is unusually clear. Walmart wants brands to broaden its online assortment in the categories where it is pushing, to match its delivery speed, to fund growth through advertising and to keep their listings readable by machines. Brands that expand their Walmart catalogs, meet fast delivery and build Walmart Connect into the annual plan are giving Walmart what it is asking for.

Walmart’s ad growth outpaced the rest of the business

Walmart Connect sales in the US grew 41%, excluding VIZIO, and the global advertising business grew 37% including VIZIO, Walmart said in its fourth-quarter release. Revenue rose 5.6% to $190.7 billion, global e-commerce sales grew 24% and membership fee revenue grew 15.1%, according to the same release.

Online sales kept climbing through the holiday quarter. Walmart US e-commerce sales grew 27%, sales through expedited store-fulfilled delivery grew more than 50% and comparable sales grew 4.6%. Marketplace categories such as cook-and-dine, fashion and home decor grew more than 40%, executives said on the call.

The pace for the whole company ahead is steadier. Walmart guided fiscal 2027 net sales growth of 3.5% to 4.5% in constant currency, according to the release. With total sales growing at that rate, the faster-growing parts of the business (advertising, marketplace and membership) carry more of Walmart’s ambitions.

Four things Walmart is asking brands for

Breadth is the first request on the list. Walmart’s marketplace growth is strongest in categories where it has historically been weaker online, such as fashion and home, and executives said on the call that the company is investing for growth over immediate profitability in those categories. A retailer that accepts thinner profit to grow a category is telling suppliers in that category that it wants them now.

Speed is the second request. With a third of store-fulfilled orders arriving in under three hours, Walmart’s shoppers carry that expectation to everything they buy there, and marketplace sellers are judged against it. That is why fulfillment through Walmart’s network matters more each quarter.

Advertising is the third, and it funds the rest. Advertising growing faster than sales means brands are spending more to be seen on Walmart and that more brands are competing for the same shoppers. Walmart uses that income to support low prices and fast delivery, so brands that advertise are helping to pay for the experience that brings shoppers back.

The fourth request is the newest one. Executives said customer engagement with Sparky, Walmart’s shopping assistant, is rising, according to the call transcript. An assistant that recommends products needs complete product data, which adds listings that machines can read and trust to the list.

The budget decision on the leadership table

The decision these results put in front of a leadership team is how much of next year’s retail media money should move toward Walmart. Framing it as a fixed share of the Amazon budget starts from the wrong place, because the two retailers are now growing their ad businesses at very different rates. Amazon’s advertising revenue grew 23% in the fourth quarter of 2025, TheWrap reported, while Walmart Connect grew 41%. Walmart is growing from a smaller base, but the comparison suggests advertisers are shifting more of their attention, and budgets, toward it.

Company results describe the whole marketplace rather than any one brand, though. Some categories will not benefit from Walmart’s push, and advertising costs rise as more brands compete, so a test on a handful of items should come before any large commitment.

Take a home decor brand that sold a narrow range on Walmart and saw little growth. It expanded its catalog into the categories Walmart is pushing, enrolled its best sellers in Walmart Fulfillment Services and launched Walmart Connect campaigns on new items. Its listings appeared more often in search and converted better. Each of those steps answered one of Walmart’s requests, and the search results rewarded the brand for answering them.

In practice, the response comes down to a short set of moves. Brands with products in fashion, home and kitchen should broaden their Walmart catalogs where Walmart is investing, and build reviews and visibility early, before more sellers and advertisers arrive. Best sellers belong in Walmart Fulfillment Services or on reliable fast shipping, so listings qualify for faster delivery promises and keep their search placement.

Walmart Connect belongs in the annual plan alongside Amazon, starting with Sponsored Products on new and high-margin items, with off-site, video and in-store options tested on a small scale and kept only where they prove incremental sales. Attributes and descriptions on the most important items deserve an audit, since Sparky and Walmart’s partnerships with ChatGPT and Gemini read product data directly.

The budget itself should follow cost per sale on Walmart and Amazon, with money moving toward whichever delivers more for the next dollar, instead of Walmart being set as a fixed share of Amazon. And Walmart’s sales, advertising costs and delivery performance should be tracked on their own, so each quarter’s growth can be confirmed as profitable. Making that call with real numbers on both retailers is part of how we plan Walmart Connect for brands.

A0881.title: Amazon Big Spring Sale 2026 forecast: lift, CPCs, deal share
A0881.alt: A cardboard box beside potted red and yellow tulips, a watering can and garden gloves on a weathered green porch.
A0881.ttag: Amazon Big Spring Sale 2026 forecast: lift, CPCs, deal share | Kwontified
A0881.desc: Amazon’s spring event barely moves the whole market, yet brands with deals can see far more. Our 2026 forecast ranges for sales lift, CPCs and deal share.
A0881.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 3, 2026.
A0881.body:
Amazon’s first Big Spring Sale, held March 20 to 25, 2024, lifted sales by 3.1% against the average of the trailing four weeks, according to Earnest credit card data that HomePage News reported. That is a small number for an event with Amazon’s name on it. Yet a 3% market lift can coexist with a 30% lift for a single brand that ran a deal that week.

The market average is the wrong planning number. The Big Spring Sale lifts Amazon’s overall sales only slightly, but brands that run deals and advertise into it can see a far larger lift at a modest rise in click costs. That is the basis for the ranges below, and for sizing stock and budgets around them.

The Amazon Big Spring Sale 2026 forecast, in three scenarios

For brands that run deals and advertise into the event, our forecast compares event sales with the prior month in conservative, standard and reach scenarios. The standard case is the reference figure.

Measure, vs prior monthConservativeStandardReach
Sales lift15%25%40%
Cost per clickup 5%up 10%up 20%
Deal-priced items, share of event sales25%35%45%

Brands in categories with strong spring demand, such as home, garden and seasonal apparel, should lean toward the higher end. Brands in categories with little seasonal demand should plan for the conservative case.

These are forecasts rather than guarantees. The event’s timing relative to Easter, Amazon’s promotion of it and each brand’s discount depth will move results, so the ranges work as planning inputs to be updated as the event approaches.

What the market data says about the event

The lift is modest by Amazon’s own standards. Prime Big Deal Days in October 2023 generated a 23% lift on the same trailing-four-week basis, according to the same report, so the spring event moved the market by a fraction of what the fall event did.

The event has also grown longer. The 2025 Big Spring Sale ran for seven days, from March 25 to March 31, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Amazon had not announced 2026 dates when these ranges were set, but a late-March event of similar length is the likely pattern.

Click costs can stay steady at smaller events. When Skai looked at the fall event, Prime Big Deal Days in October 2025, it found average order value down 11% and cost per click flat. Fewer advertisers bid aggressively at a spring event than at Prime Day, which is why the cost ranges above sit well below the lift ranges.

Why a 3% market lift and a 30% brand lift fit together

The Big Spring Sale is a smaller, less publicized event than Prime Day. Many shoppers do not plan around it, so total spending rises only a little. The shoppers who do arrive find deals concentrated among a limited set of brands, and those brands capture most of the extra demand.

An average across every product on Amazon is mostly an average of products that had no deal that week. Their sales barely move, or slip as shoppers trade over to a discounted competitor. Mix the flat listings with the discounted ones and the market reads 3%; look only at the discounted listings that were also advertised and the picture changes. A brand’s own result depends on whether it gave shoppers a reason to buy that week.

That also explains why the event is efficient for those who join it. Demand concentrates on deal items while competition for clicks stays thin, so the cost of reaching an event shopper rises far less than the sales on offer. Easter can tilt the picture further in years when it falls close to the event, lifting seasonal categories such as toys, candy and home decor, so brands in those categories should check the gap between the two dates.

Brands without deals face a different calculation. They can still advertise during the event, but they compete for attention against discounted products. For them, holding budgets steady and protecting branded search is usually wiser than raising bids to chase shoppers looking for deals. The ranges in the table assume a deal and advertising behind each item, so they are not the right yardstick for a brand that sits the event out.

Preparing stock, budget and margin for the sale

Deals come first, because Amazon sets deadlines for event deals ahead of the sale. Brands should choose which items get a discount and submit them well before the cutoff. Then they should raise advertising budgets for those items in the days before and throughout the event, using the cost ranges above to avoid running out of budget mid-sale.

Stock is the constraint that ends events early. A 25% to 40% lift on deal items can empty inventory before the event ends, so stock levels for deal items belong next to the forecast in the same planning sheet. Margin needs the same check: discounts and higher click costs both reduce it, and each deal item should still be profitable at the forecast click costs.

The days after matter too. Sales often dip briefly after an event as shoppers who bought early stop searching. Budgets should stay steady through that short lull, rather than being cut sharply when the event ends.

Finally, measure against the right baseline. Comparing event sales with the prior four weeks uses the same basis as the market data, which lets a brand set its own result beside the 3.1% market figure and keep a clean record for the next event. Plan for a brand-level lift well above the market average, but only where the listing gives shoppers a reason to buy; building that plan on a brand’s own deal and stock data is how we plan Amazon events for brands.

A0883.crumb: The state of Instagram shopping for…
A0883.title: The state of Instagram shopping for brands, 2026: discovery first
A0883.alt: A smartphone on a stand photographs a ceramic vase of wildflowers set on peach paper against a pink wall.
A0883.ttag: The state of Instagram shopping for brands, 2026: discovery first | Kwontified
A0883.desc: Instagram shopping in 2026 is a discovery channel that sends buyers elsewhere. What Meta’s results say about Reels, conversion ads and agentic shopping.
A0883.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 5, 2026.
A0883.body:
Watch someone shop on Instagram and they rarely look like they are shopping. They are thumbing through Reels, half watching a creator’s morning routine, when a serum appears in the creator’s hand. They pause, tap through to the brand’s profile, and later they buy it, often on the brand’s own site or on Amazon. Instagram did the selling, and the sale was recorded somewhere else.

That pattern is the state of Instagram shopping in 2026. It works as a discovery and advertising channel that sends shoppers to brand sites and marketplaces, carried by fast-growing Reels viewing, ads that convert better and agentic shopping tools still to come. The brands that do well there treat it that way: they invest in Reels and creator content, run conversion ads tied to complete product catalogs and guard against the brand-safety risks that come with a large audience.

Instagram shopping for brands rests on an enormous, growing audience

More than 3.5 billion people use at least one of Meta’s apps every day, with Instagram just shy of 2 billion daily users, Mark Zuckerberg said in Meta’s fourth-quarter prepared remarks. The advertising business built on that audience keeps growing. Meta’s Family of Apps ad revenue reached $58.1 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 24%, as ad impressions rose 18% and the average price per ad rose 6%, according to the same remarks.

Reels is where the growth sits. Instagram Reels watch time rose more than 30% year over year in the US, and 75% of Instagram recommendations in the US now come from original posts, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said on the call, MarketBeat reported. The ads are converting better too: a new model launched across Instagram Feed, Stories and Reels lifted conversion rates by 3% in the quarter, according to the same report. And Zuckerberg said new agentic shopping tools will allow people to find specific products from businesses in Meta’s catalog, according to the prepared remarks.

The sale lands somewhere else, and so does the credit

Most shoppers on Instagram are not searching for a product. They are watching Reels and scrolling feeds, and they discover products through creators, brands and ads along the way. Instagram’s role is to create demand that shoppers then complete elsewhere, and for most brands that means the brand’s own site or a marketplace.

That is where the organizational trouble starts. A channel whose results show up in other places complicates measurement, because the account that pays for Instagram is not the one that records the sale. When budgets are set on in-app results alone, Instagram looks weaker than it is, and the marketplace looks stronger.

Meta’s push toward original posts in recommendations adds another twist. It rewards brands and creators who publish their own content, rather than reposting others’ material, so brands that produce consistent original Reels reach more people without paying for every view. At the same time, as Meta’s ads convert better, more brands treat Instagram as a performance channel rather than an awareness channel. That raises competition for the same audiences, which shows up in the rising price per ad.

Take a skincare brand that posted product photos and saw little reach. After shifting to short, original Reels showing the product in use, partnering with a few creators and running conversion ads tied to its product catalog, its Instagram-driven sales rose, most of them completed on its own site and on Amazon. A report that looked only inside Instagram would have missed most of what changed.

Catalogs decide who appears when the shopping tools arrive

Agentic shopping could change the path from discovery to purchase. If Meta’s shopping tools help people find specific products from catalogs, complete and accurate product data will decide which brands appear. Brands that keep their catalogs current will be ready; brands that treat the catalog as a one-time setup task will find out late.

A large audience also draws counterfeiters

Instagram carries brand-safety risk alongside its reach. Internal Meta documents projected that ads for scams and banned goods would bring in about 10% of the company’s 2024 revenue, roughly $16 billion, Reuters reported in a story carried by Khaleej Times; Meta disputed the characterization. Meta’s platforms show users an estimated 15 billion higher-risk scam ads every day, PYMNTS reported, citing the same internal documents. Counterfeit sellers and impersonators can target the same audiences legitimate brands want.

Running Instagram as the start of the sale

The brands that get this right organize around Instagram’s real job. Short, original video is where attention and recommendations are growing, so they publish Reels regularly, show products in use and test several hooks in the first seconds, since that is where viewers decide whether to keep watching. They partner with creators whose followers match their customers, agree on usage rights up front and use that content in ads where permitted. Creator video often outperforms polished brand content in Reels, because it looks like the posts people already watch.

On the paid side, they connect product catalogs to Meta’s ad tools and run conversion campaigns that send shoppers to the best place to buy. Accurate product titles, prices, images and availability help those ads perform and prepare the catalog for agentic shopping as it rolls out. Meta’s automated campaign tools find buyers efficiently, but they work best with accurate catalogs, clear conversion goals and regular review of where ads appear.

The budget conversation changes as well. Instagram budgets set on the sales lift seen across all channels, with an accepted share of that lift appearing on Amazon and the brand’s own site, give a fairer picture than budgets set on in-app conversions. That depends on tracking how Instagram activity lifts sales on owned sites and marketplaces, including Amazon, rather than judging Instagram on in-app results alone.

And the brand needs guarding. Monitoring for impersonators and counterfeit ads, reporting them quickly and protecting trademarks are part of the cost of the channel. Registering trademarks with Meta’s brand protection tools makes reports faster and more likely to succeed.

The question worth putting to the team is simple: who owns the sale that Instagram starts and Amazon finishes? Connecting that discovery to what happens on a brand’s own site and marketplaces is how we run the channel for brands.

A0884.crumb: The state of Temu for brands, 2026: a…
A0884.title: The state of Temu for brands, 2026: a marketplace remade
A0884.alt: A pallet of stacked cardboard boxes in a bright warehouse lined with shelves of orange storage bins.
A0884.ttag: The state of Temu for brands, 2026: a marketplace remade | Kwontified
A0884.desc: Losing the de minimis exemption turned Temu from a cheap-import channel into a marketplace of US-stocked sellers. What that shift means for brands in 2026.
A0884.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 10, 2026.
A0884.body:
Temu’s US daily users fell 58% after the de minimis exemption ended on May 2, 2025, and the company cut its US advertising spending, RetailWire reported. PDD’s first-quarter net income fell 47%, according to the same report. A drop that steep from one customs rule says the rule was carrying the business model.

It was. Temu’s low prices depended on shipping small parcels duty-free straight from factories. With the exemption gone, Temu moved toward sellers holding stock in US warehouses, which removed much of its price advantage and left a marketplace competing on more equal terms. For brands, that makes Temu a channel to monitor for unauthorized sellers and price undercutting rather than a priority, and a place to test only with commodity products.

Temu for brands: how the model changed

The old model rested on an exemption. Temu shipped low-value parcels from China directly to US shoppers, and packages under $800 entered the US duty-free. Shares of Temu’s parent, PDD Holdings, fell when the US moved to end that exemption, CNBC reported.

Temu runs two seller models. In the original one, factories ship goods to Temu, which sets prices and handles marketing and delivery. In the newer one, sellers keep stock in local warehouses and keep more control over fulfillment, while Temu still owns the storefront.

WhenWhat happenedSource
March 2024Temu begins courting sellers with US warehouse stockReuters
End of 2024Local warehouses at 20% or more of Temu’s US salesCiti, via CNBC
May 2, 2025De minimis exemption endsRetailWire
After the exemptionUS daily users down 58%; PDD first-quarter net income down 47%RetailWire

The shift to local sellers had already started before the rule changed. About 20% of Temu’s US sales were shipped from local sellers rather than directly from China within months of Temu inviting sellers with US warehouse stock, according to Marketplace Pulse estimates, Reuters reported. Temu began courting those sellers in March 2024, according to the Reuters report. Citi analysts similarly estimated that local warehouses contributed 20% or more of Temu’s US sales by the end of 2024, according to the CNBC report.

Why landed cost now looks like everyone else’s

When the exemption ended, small parcels faced tariffs and customs checks. Temu moved toward sellers who import in bulk and hold stock in US warehouses, the same model Amazon and Walmart sellers use.

That model carries the same costs. Sellers holding US stock pay import duties, warehouse costs and domestic shipping. Their prices rise toward those on other marketplaces. Temu still offers low prices, but the gap that defined it has narrowed.

Advertising tells the same story from the demand side. Temu’s heavy spending on digital ads had driven its growth. Bank of America analysts expected the end of the exemption to dampen that spending, according to the CNBC report, and Temu did cut US ad spending afterward. Fewer ads and smaller price gaps leave shoppers with less reason to choose Temu over Amazon or Walmart. Some will stay out of familiarity, but the pull has weakened.

For brands the margin math is thin. A brand selling on Temu competes against low-priced alternatives and often against its own resellers. After marketplace fees, shipping and promotions, many branded products earn less there than on Amazon or a brand’s own site.

A smaller Temu can still move a brand’s prices

A weaker Temu can still create problems. As Temu recruits US sellers, some of them may list branded products they bought elsewhere, at prices below a brand’s preferred level. If other retailers’ price-matching systems notice, a small marketplace can pull a brand’s pricing down everywhere.

Take a kitchen brand that never sold on Temu. A reseller with US stock lists its best-selling product there below the brand’s minimum advertised price. Within days, other marketplaces adjust, and the brand loses its Buy Box on Amazon until the Temu listing is removed. The brand made no decision about Temu at all, and Temu still set its price for a while.

Temu also remains large and keeps adapting, recruiting more sellers with local stock, and trade rules could change again. That argues for watching it closely rather than dismissing it.

In 2026, most of the Temu work is defensive

Brands should check Temu regularly for their products and identify unauthorized sellers, ideally with the same tools they use to watch Amazon and Walmart. Minimum advertised price policies should apply to Temu sellers too, with quick action when listings undercut them. Counterfeit or infringing listings go through Temu’s reporting procedures, with a record kept of every report.

Distribution agreements are the upstream fix. Tightening them so authorized resellers cannot sell on marketplaces the brand has not approved cuts off the supply that feeds unwanted listings. Large retail customers watch marketplace prices closely, so key partners should hear how the brand handles Temu before a low listing there damages a wholesale relationship.

Selling on Temu directly is a narrower question. Brands considering it should start with low-priced, high-volume items that will not damage pricing elsewhere. Before listing, they should compare Temu’s fees, required discounts and shipping costs with the margin they earn elsewhere, and list only where the result is clearly positive. Tariff and import rules shape Temu’s prices, so changes that could restore or remove its advantage belong on the watch list.

The practical test is simple: if a Temu listing would sell below the price that holds your Buy Box elsewhere, it is a pricing problem before it is a sales channel. Finding those listings and fixing the distribution behind them is how we protect pricing for brands across marketplaces.

A0887.crumb: The state of TikTok Shop for brands…
A0887.title: The state of TikTok Shop for brands, 2026: steadier and bigger
A0887.alt: A phone on a wooden stand beside dropper bottles and ribbon-tied kraft paper parcels on a white table by a window.
A0887.ttag: The state of TikTok Shop for brands, 2026: steadier and bigger | Kwontified
A0887.desc: TikTok Shop’s US sales reached an estimated $15.1 billion in 2025 and its ownership is now settled. What brands should expect from the channel in 2026.
A0887.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 12, 2026.
A0887.body:
Over the four days from Black Friday to Cyber Monday 2025, TikTok Shop’s US sales exceeded $500 million, the company said in a newsroom post. On TikTok, much of that selling happens away from brand accounts: through affiliate creators showing products in their own videos, through livestream hosts, and through the automated ads the platform now requires merchants to use.

That is the state of TikTok Shop for brands in 2026: larger and on firmer footing, with its US ownership settled, but with growth concentrated among the sellers who invest in creators, live shopping and the platform’s own advertising. Brands that treat it as a real sales channel, build creator programs and plan for the holiday peak are the ones the numbers favor.

TikTok Shop for brands is now a $15 billion US channel

TikTok Shop generated an estimated $15.1 billion in US gross merchandise value in 2025, up 68% from $9 billion in 2024, according to a report by Momentum Works and Tabcut, DealStreetAsia reported. The platform counted 803,500 US stores and 15.4 million influencers, according to the same report.

TikTok Shop’s sales calendar is lopsided toward the holidays. November and December generated roughly 30% of TikTok Shop’s 2025 US sales, according to the report. Live shopping carried much of that peak: sales from livestreams rose 84% during the 2025 Black Friday campaign compared with the previous year, and nearly 50% more US shoppers bought something on TikTok Shop, according to TikTok’s data, reported by SDI.

The US business also sits inside a much larger one. TikTok Shop’s global sales nearly doubled to $64.3 billion in 2025, and Southeast Asia doubled to $45.6 billion, according to the Momentum Works report. Methods and formats that work in Asia, especially live shopping, often arrive in the US later. And the ownership question that hung over the US platform is settled: TikTok’s US joint venture was finalized on January 22, 2026, with more than 200 million Americans using the app, SiliconANGLE reported.

Who keeps the money from a TikTok Shop sale

Discovery drives the sale on TikTok. Shoppers there are watching videos, and products reach them through creators and brand content. Unlike Instagram, TikTok lets many of those shoppers buy without leaving the app, which brings discovery and purchase together in one place, and puts the platform in the middle of both.

Follow a single sale and the value splits several ways. With 15.4 million influencers on the platform, much of TikTok Shop’s selling happens through affiliate creators who earn commission on sales, so the creator who made the video keeps a share of every order it drives. The platform keeps another share through advertising: TikTok has required merchants to use GMV Max, its automated campaign product, and offered incentives to boost holiday sales, Digiday reported. Brands that sell on TikTok Shop increasingly pay to be seen. Discounts and free samples come out of the same sale before the brand counts its margin.

That split is why growth is uneven. Hundreds of thousands of stores compete for attention, but sales concentrate among sellers with strong creator networks and live shopping programs. Six US live sessions exceeded $1 million in sales in 2025, up from four in 2024, according to the Momentum Works report. The brands that win are the ones that have built relationships with the people who hold the audience.

The report describes TikTok Shop’s US business as settling into a steadier growth phase, and the platform depends heavily on promotions, incentives and holiday spikes. Margins can be thin once creator commissions, discounts and advertising are counted, so profitability needs tracking as closely as sales.

Rules matter more as the channel grows. Creators speak for brands in their own words, and product claims made in a video carry the same weight as claims on a label. Categories such as beauty, supplements and children’s products face particular scrutiny.

Take a haircare brand that opened a TikTok Shop and posted its own videos, with modest results. After recruiting 200 creators through the affiliate program, running weekly livestreams and adding GMV Max campaigns before the holidays, its TikTok Shop sales grew several times over, with the largest gains in November. Each of those steps paid someone other than the brand, which is exactly why the brand’s profit line deserved as much attention as its sales line.

Running TikTok Shop as a sales channel in 2026

The creator program comes first. Brands should recruit creators whose audiences match their customers, set clear commission rates and supply samples and talking points. Sending free products to creators drives content but costs money, so it pays to track which creators turn samples into sales and focus on them. Creators also need approved claims, with content reviewed for accuracy, especially in regulated categories.

Live shopping deserves a schedule rather than an occasional slot. Regular livestreams with hosts who know the product convert well, especially during major events. A weekly cadence is a reasonable start, with different hosts and formats tested and the times that sell expanded.

On TikTok Shop, the holiday peak sets the whole year. With much of the year’s sales arriving in November and December, stock, creator content and budgets need preparing months ahead, and the best creators need booking early, before competing brands fill their calendars.

GMV Max needs a human watching it. TikTok’s automated campaigns can run, but someone should watch costs, margins and which products receive spend, and move budget away from items that sell only at a loss.

The measure that matters is profit. TikTok Shop should be judged after creator commissions, discounts, fees and advertising, rather than on sales alone. A product that sells well at a loss is a marketing cost, and should be budgeted that way. TikTok activity often lifts searches on Amazon and other marketplaces too, so tracking that effect and coordinating pricing across channels belongs in the same review.

The question for a brand’s leadership is who on the team owns the creator relationships, because on TikTok Shop that is where the sales are decided. Building that program alongside a brand’s marketplace channels is how we run TikTok Shop for brands.

A0889.crumb: The state of Vendor Central for brands…
A0889.title: The state of Vendor Central for brands, 2026: margin by the item
A0889.alt: A brass balance scale weighing a jar of dried herbs against stacks of coins on a wooden table.
A0889.ttag: The state of Vendor Central for brands, 2026: margin by the item | Kwontified
A0889.desc: Amazon asks most vendors for lower cost prices because it will not raise shelf prices. Why that makes Vendor Central an item-by-item call for brands in 2026.
A0889.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 17, 2026.
A0889.body:
In a February 2025 survey of 203 first-party vendors, 64% said Amazon had asked them to lower their cost prices, according to Statista’s summary of the Consulterce study. When most vendors get the same request in the same season, the request is a policy showing through rather than a negotiating style.

Amazon matches competitors’ prices, so it cannot take margin from shoppers. It seeks margin from vendors instead, and most vendors face cost price reduction requests and rising trade terms every year. That turns Vendor Central into an item-by-item decision rather than an all-or-nothing one: model each item’s margin after all terms, keep it where it earns the most, and keep a working Seller Central account for the items that belong there.

Vendor Central for brands: the pressure in 2025

The cost requests came with rising terms. Half of vendors expected Amazon’s trade terms to increase in their 2025 negotiations, and 64% faced cost price decrease requests, Martin Heubel of Consulterce wrote in an analysis of the study published by Kamcity.

Amazon has also trimmed its vendor base. Amazon cut ties with many small vendors in 2024, pushing them toward Seller Central or a hybrid model, ChannelEngine reported. Taken together, the survey and the cuts describe a retailer asking more of the vendors it keeps and keeping fewer of the small ones.

Why a price-matching retailer takes margin from its suppliers

Amazon’s retail business matches the lowest prices it finds elsewhere. That keeps shoppers loyal, but it means Amazon cannot raise prices to protect its margin. When costs rise or prices fall, the margin has to come from somewhere else, and vendors are the obvious source.

The requests use a small set of levers. Amazon asks for lower cost prices, higher co-op and other trade terms, and contributions to cover items that lose money at matched prices. Items that remain unprofitable can lose their purchase orders or their Buy Box.

The scorecard behind those requests is item margin. Amazon’s retail teams judge each vendor by net pure product margin, often called Net PPM, which captures what Amazon keeps from a vendor’s products after its price, the vendor’s cost price and the money the vendor contributes. When that number falls, negotiations follow.

That makes the pressure structural. It does not end with one negotiation, because the reason for it, Amazon’s pricing policy, does not change. Every year brings new requests, especially when tariffs or other costs push vendors to seek higher prices.

Vendor Central or Seller Central, item by item

The obvious reaction is to leave Vendor Central entirely, and it is rarely the right one. For many large brands, Amazon’s purchasing scale and the shopper trust of “sold by Amazon” still justify the lower margin on core items. The mistake is treating the decision as all or nothing, when the economics differ by item.

Each side of the choice has real weight:

Vendor CentralSeller Central
OrdersLarge purchase orders from AmazonThe brand sells each unit itself
FulfillmentAmazon-runThe brand’s responsibility
Price and contentAmazon sets the shelf priceThe brand controls price, inventory and content
CashPaid on terms after Amazon buys the stockPaid after each sale

Take a household brand whose top 30 items sell in high volume and earn acceptable margins after terms through Vendor Central. Another 50 items lose money after Amazon’s price matching and trade terms. The brand keeps the top items in Vendor Central, moves the weaker ones to Seller Central at prices it controls and uses its Seller Central account as evidence in the next negotiation that it has a real alternative.

Running both models takes work, which is the cost on the other side of the ledger. A brand selling the same item through both channels can confuse pricing and lose the Buy Box. Hybrid models need clear rules about which items go where, and discipline about pricing. On balance the numbers lean toward the hybrid, but only for brands willing to run it with those rules in place.

A hybrid works only with margin data and clear rules

The starting point is margin after all terms. Each item’s profit should be calculated after the cost price, co-op, freight allowances, chargebacks and advertising, rather than judging Vendor Central on gross sales. Items with strong volume and acceptable margin stay in Vendor Central. Items that lose money after terms move to Seller Central or leave Amazon.

Seller Central has to be ready before it is needed. A working account gives a brand somewhere to move items quickly and shows Amazon that the brand has options, so listings, fulfillment and advertising belong set up there even for items currently sold through Vendor Central. Brands running both models should assign each item to one channel where possible, and avoid competing with Amazon on the same listing.

Negotiations go better with data. Item-level profit, sales growth and market evidence belong in every annual negotiation, along with a willingness to resist cost reductions that make items unprofitable. When tariffs raise costs, documenting the increase and preparing cost-increase requests early helps, though approval is not guaranteed.

Price parity needs a standing watch, because Amazon’s price matching responds to lower prices elsewhere, and a low price at another retailer can trigger losses on Amazon. So do purchase orders: Amazon’s ordering can change quickly, and shrinking orders on an item are the cue to prepare its Seller Central listing before they stop. Moving items between the two models also changes when the money arrives, so the cash effect belongs in the model.

The rule for 2026 is to decide item by item, on margin after all of Amazon’s terms. Building that item-level view across both accounts is how we manage Vendor Central and Seller Central for brands.

A0890.title: The state of Amazon DSP for brands, 2026: one console, more reach
A0890.alt: A dark navy living room at dusk with a cream sofa, wooden coffee table and a wall screen showing misty mountains.
A0890.ttag: The state of Amazon DSP for brands, 2026: one console, more reach | Kwontified
A0890.desc: Amazon DSP now shares one console with sponsored ads and reaches Prime Video, Netflix and Spotify audiences. How brands should put it to work in 2026.
A0890.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 19, 2026.
A0890.body:
Amazon DSP used to live behind its own login. The team that ran sponsored ads worked in the advertising console, and DSP, Amazon’s programmatic display and video platform, needed a separate account, and a separate account can easily become a separate owner and a separate budget line. Amazon’s new unified Campaign Manager ends that split: it brings the advertising console and Amazon DSP together in one platform, removing the need for separate accounts, Amazon said in its unBoxed Toronto recap.

A shared console changes who can plan DSP and how. Amazon DSP enters 2026 as a full-funnel buying platform: it sits beside sponsored ads, reaches premium streaming audiences including Netflix and Spotify, and offers automated campaigns. The brands that get value from it will use it for audiences search ads cannot reach, apply frequency limits and guardrails to automation, and judge it on incremental sales rather than attributed returns.

Amazon DSP for brands is growing inside a growing ad business

Spending on the platform is rising quickly. Amazon DSP spending rose 39% during Cyber 5 in 2025, according to Skai’s analysis. The ad business around it keeps expanding too: Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 23% in the fourth quarter of 2025, to $21.3 billion, according to TheWrap’s earnings report. Executives said Prime Video ads contributed meaningfully to growth, according to MarketBeat’s summary of the call.

The reach now extends past Amazon’s own properties. Amazon DSP offers direct integrations with Netflix and Spotify, according to the same unBoxed recap. Reporting has been pulled together as well: Amazon launched unified reporting across its ad products in November 2025, giving advertisers 15 months of daily data, PPC Land reported.

Automation is the other big change. Amazon reported that advertisers using Brand+ saw 71% more product detail page views, and that brands selling in its store that combined Brand+ with Performance+ achieved a 34% boost in return on ad spend, according to the recap. Brand+ users also saw a 42% increase in brand discovery among new customers and 64% more purchases, and brands not selling in Amazon’s store that combined the two products saw a 68% improvement in cost per acquisition, Amazon said. These are Amazon’s own figures, and they describe Amazon’s products in Amazon’s words.

What DSP reaches that search cannot

Search ads reach shoppers who are already looking. DSP reaches people earlier, while they watch Prime Video, stream music or browse other sites, and for brands that need new customers, that reach is the reason to buy it. Amazon’s shopping data is what makes the reach useful: DSP campaigns can target shoppers based on what they browse and buy on Amazon, then measure whether those shoppers later buy the brand’s products. Few other media platforms can connect viewing and purchasing so closely.

Consolidation lowers the barrier to entry. With DSP and sponsored ads in one console, brands that once found DSP too complex can now plan both together. DSP also serves brands beyond Amazon’s store: brands that sell elsewhere can use Amazon’s audiences to reach shoppers and send them to their own sites or other retailers. That widens the pool of advertisers competing for the same audiences.

As reach grows, frequency is where budget leaks. Advertisers using Amazon’s frequency controls saved up to 26% of their budgets and reached up to 21% more unique shoppers, Amazon said in an announcement of the controls. Without such limits, DSP budgets can be spent showing the same ads to the same people.

Take a pet food brand that relied on search ads and saw sales plateau. It added a DSP campaign reaching dog owners who had not bought from it, capped how often each person saw the ad and measured new-to-brand sales. Its customer base grew, and later search ads converted better among shoppers who had seen the DSP ads. The search team’s numbers improved because of money the DSP line spent, which is exactly the kind of credit a single console makes easier to see.

The limits of Amazon’s own scorecard

DSP attribution can overstate results, because it credits sales from shoppers who might have bought anyway. Automated campaigns also give Amazon more control over where money goes. Amazon’s own performance claims should be tested rather than assumed, and the figures from the recap belong in that category until a brand’s own test confirms them.

Putting DSP to work in 2026

The goal comes before the campaign. A brand should decide whether DSP is for reaching new customers, bringing back past buyers or building awareness, and set measures that match. A campaign aimed at new customers is judged on new-to-brand sales, while a remarketing campaign is judged on incremental repeat purchases. DSP adds the most when it finds shoppers who are not yet searching for the brand, such as buyers of related products or past customers who have not returned.

Discipline is what keeps the spend honest. Caps on how often each person sees an ad, with frequency reports reviewed regularly and caps tightened when reach stops growing, protect the budget. Brand+ and Performance+ can save time, but they need budgets, exclusions and goals set by the brand, and a weekly review of where spending goes. Prime Video, Netflix and Spotify inventory can reach valuable audiences, and each deserves a test with clear measures before it scales. Streaming ads need video made for television, while display ads need clear product images and messages, so one asset reused everywhere shortchanges both.

Measurement is what settles the argument. Holdout or geographic tests show how many sales DSP adds, which attributed returns alone cannot. And with both now managed in one console, budgets and audiences can be coordinated so DSP feeds search and search captures the demand DSP creates.

The question for leadership is whether DSP and search now have one owner, or still two. Planning and measuring the two together is how we run Amazon DSP for brands.

A0891.title: Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands, 2026: questions win
A0891.alt: A brass magnifying glass resting on blank index cards in an open wooden card catalog drawer.
A0891.ttag: Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands, 2026: questions win | Kwontified
A0891.desc: Amazon Marketing Cloud is now open to every sponsored ads advertiser. Why access no longer sets brands apart, and where the edge from AMC sits in 2026.
A0891.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 24, 2026.
A0891.body:
Every brand running sponsored ads can now open Amazon Marketing Cloud, the clean room where Amazon lets advertisers analyze how shoppers move from ad exposure to purchase. Two brands in the same category, with the same templates and the same AI assistant, will still get very different value from it. Why?

Because access was the advantage, and access is gone as a differentiator. When everyone holds the same tool, the edge moves to the brands that ask questions tied to real decisions and turn the answers into audiences, bids and budgets. The practical work is a short list of decision questions, findings that are acted on, and results that are measured.

Amazon Marketing Cloud for brands is now open to all

Amazon launched direct, self-service access to Amazon Marketing Cloud for sponsored ads advertisers within the Amazon Ads console on September 16, 2025, PPC Land reported. Previously, sponsored ads advertisers needed partner relationships or account representatives to gain access, according to the report. Audiences built in Amazon Marketing Cloud can be activated directly through Amazon DSP, the same report said.

The change covers every sponsored ads format. Anyone running Sponsored Products, Sponsored Display, Sponsored Brands or Sponsored TV campaigns can now use the clean room and combine their own data with Amazon’s shopping, browsing and streaming signals, Marketing Dive reported.

AI is lowering the skill barrier too. Amazon showcased Ads Agent in Amazon Marketing Cloud, an assistant that lets advertisers ask business questions in plain English to build audiences and receive insights without writing SQL, according to Amazon’s recap of unBoxed Toronto. Beta users saw a median 18% reduction in cost per thousand impressions and 16% reduction in cost per acquisition, Amazon said, figures that come from Amazon itself rather than an independent test.

What happens to an edge when everyone has the tool

Amazon Marketing Cloud works on privacy-safe, aggregated data. For years, access was limited: brands with DSP campaigns or specialist partners could use it, and most sponsored ads advertisers could not. That gap was the edge. Brands that could see paths to purchase, overlap between campaigns and the value of new customers made better decisions than brands relying on standard reports.

Opening access removes that edge. When every sponsored ads advertiser can run the same templates and ask the same AI assistant, simply having Amazon Marketing Cloud no longer distinguishes anyone. The tool became more valuable to the market as a whole and less valuable as a source of advantage for any single brand. A library card works the same way. Once every resident has one, the card says nothing about who reads well; the value goes to the people who walk in knowing what they are looking for.

What stays scarce is judgment: knowing which questions matter, interpreting the answers correctly and changing budgets, bids and audiences as a result. The role of specialists shifts with it. Agencies and analysts who once sold access must now sell that judgment, and brands should hire for it rather than for technical access alone.

A good AMC question ends in a decision

Good questions are specific, and each answer points to something a brand would change:

QuestionDecision it informs
How many purchases follow a Sponsored Brands view within 14 days?How much to credit, and fund, Sponsored Brands
Which audiences buy a second product within 60 days?Which audiences deserve remarketing
How much overlap exists between two campaigns?Where to cut duplicated spend

Take a supplement brand that opened Amazon Marketing Cloud, ran several templates and produced reports nobody acted on. It then defined three decisions it needed to make: how much to spend on new customers, which campaigns overlapped and which audiences deserved remarketing. Each analysis answered one decision, and each answer changed a budget or an audience. Within a quarter, its spending shifted toward campaigns that brought in new customers. Nothing about its access had changed between the two attempts; only the questions had.

The method has limits worth stating plainly. Amazon Marketing Cloud shows aggregated data, which limits detail, and its results reflect Amazon’s own measurement. Findings that would move large budgets deserve an experiment before the money moves.

Turning answers into budgets, bids and audiences

The work starts with the few budget, audience and bidding decisions a brand makes most often, and the question each one depends on. Amazon’s no-code templates and Ads Agent can answer many common questions without SQL; they are fast, and their results are worth checking against standard reports. A question that would not change any decision produces a report, and reports were never the scarce part of retail media.

Findings need somewhere to go, or the reports pile up unread. Insights become audiences, such as shoppers who viewed but did not buy, activated through DSP or sponsored ads. New-to-brand value over time sets acquisition budgets. Campaign overlap shows where duplication can be removed and the savings moved to campaigns that reach people the brand has not yet reached. Brands with their own customer data can add it to the clean room, following Amazon’s privacy rules, to see which ads bring in their best customers.

What keeps the habit alive is ownership. Analysis without an owner rarely changes anything, so one person should be responsible for turning findings into actions. A saved library of the questions and queries that informed decisions lets the team rerun them each month or quarter and compare results, since shopper behavior and campaigns change.

The test for any AMC query is whether its answer could change a budget, a bid or an audience; if it could not, it is not worth running. Building that list of decision questions and acting on the answers is how we put Amazon Marketing Cloud to work for brands.
