A0893.title: AI-driven retail media buying: what brands still decide
A0893.alt: A white robotic arm moves a pawn on a wooden chessboard, with a dark king in sharp focus in the foreground.
A0893.ttag: AI-driven retail media buying: what brands still decide | Kwontified
A0893.desc: Amazon, Walmart, TikTok and Meta are handing campaign work to AI agents. What that changes for brands, and which decisions should stay with people.
A0893.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 26, 2026.
A0893.body:
Open Amazon’s advertising console and there is now an assistant waiting in it. Ads Agent launched inside the console in November 2025, and it will take a request in plain language and turn it into work that used to take many manual steps. Walmart, TikTok and Meta are building or requiring the same kind of help. The console screens that campaign managers worked inside are turning into a conversation.

That changes what the brand’s people are for. Retail media buying is moving from manual bidding to AI agents across Amazon, Walmart, TikTok and Meta, and the brand’s job is shifting from operating campaigns to setting goals, supplying clean product data, defining guardrails and checking results independently. The tools deserve adoption where they save time; budget limits, approvals and incrementality tests belong in human hands.

AI-driven retail media buying is arriving on every major platform

Amazon has opened its ads to outside agents. Amazon Ads opened its MCP server, which lets AI agents query performance, pull reports and build Sponsored Products campaigns that still need review and approval before launch, in open beta on February 2, 2026, PPC Land reported. Inside Amazon Marketing Cloud, Ads Agent answers business questions put to it in plain English, and Creative Agent produces video and display ads through conversation, Amazon said in its recap of unBoxed Toronto.

Walmart is moving the same way. It expanded Marty, an AI assistant that analyzes sponsored search campaigns and recommends bids and keywords, and expects to make it available to all advertisers buying search ads in the first half of 2026, B&T reported.

Some platforms have stopped making automation optional. TikTok Shop merchants have been required to run GMV Max, TikTok’s automated campaign product, Digiday reported. Meta made automated campaigns the default for sales, leads and app objectives, while keeping manual controls, PPC Land reported after Meta’s fourth-quarter results.

Why the platforms want the machines in charge

Scale made manual work hard to sustain. Retail media accounts now span thousands of keywords, products and audiences across several retailers, and no team can adjust every bid by hand every day, so platforms built systems that do it continuously. Tasks that once took dozens of manual steps, such as launching campaigns in a new country, can become a single request.

The platforms also gain from automation, and it helps to be clear about how. Automated campaigns spend budgets fully and find inventory that manual campaigns miss. That serves advertisers when the systems work well, and it serves the platforms regardless, because more of each budget gets spent. Platform automation is often good at what it measures, such as attributed sales, and weaker at what it does not, such as profit or incremental growth.

Agents bring outside models into the account as well. Amazon’s MCP server lets advertisers connect assistants built on models such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, and Amazon does not own or operate those models, according to the PPC Land report. Security researchers have documented vulnerabilities in such connections, including tool poisoning, in which a malicious tool feeds an agent harmful instructions, the report noted.

Analysts expect a large share of agentic projects to stall. Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects would be canceled by the end of 2027, according to the same report. Tools that act quickly can also make mistakes quickly, and an agent that can launch a campaign can launch the wrong one just as fast.

Take a beauty brand that moved most of its Amazon and Walmart campaigns to automated bidding and used an AI assistant to build new campaigns. Sales rose, but a review found that much of the new spending went to its own branded searches, which it would have won anyway. It set budget limits on branded campaigns, required approval for new campaigns and ran a holdout test, and its results became easier to trust.

The decision on the leadership agenda: what to hand over

The decision in front of a brand’s leadership is not whether to use these tools; the platforms have largely settled that. It is which decisions to hand to the machines and which to keep, and the answer reshapes the e-commerce team from operators into supervisors.

Goals stay with people. Automated systems need to be told what matters, such as new-to-brand sales or profit targets, rather than accepting default goals. A system told to maximize attributed sales will find the easiest sales, which are often the ones a brand would have made anyway. The inputs stay with people too, because automated systems work only as well as the product data, prices and inventory information they receive, and catalogs have to be kept accurate and current.

Limits are set before the switch is flipped. Budget caps, exclusions and limits on branded spending belong in place before automation runs. New campaigns, large budget increases and entries into new markets should require human approval, even when an agent builds them. Access needs the same care: deciding which people and agents can change campaigns, using separate permissions for read-only analysis and recording what each agent changes.

Results get checked by someone other than the system that produced them. Holdout and geographic tests show what automation adds, which platform-reported results cannot. When several automated systems run at once across retailers, they can compete for the same shoppers and push up each other’s costs, so overlapping budgets need reviewing and priorities set between channels.

That leaves a hiring question for the leadership team: whether the team has people who can set goals, read results and question the systems, rather than only operate consoles. Setting up that supervision across Amazon, Walmart and other retailers is how we run AI-driven buying for brands.

A0894.crumb: Avoiding a premature shopping AI rollout…
A0894.title: Avoiding a premature shopping AI rollout: lessons from Walmart
A0894.alt: A blue and white self-service kiosk with paper covering its screen stands in an empty store with bare shelves.
A0894.ttag: Avoiding a premature shopping AI rollout: lessons from Walmart | Kwontified
A0894.desc: Walmart found purchases inside ChatGPT converted at one-third the rate of its own site. Why brands should first build what every AI shopping surface can use.
A0894.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Mar 31, 2026.
A0894.body:
Walmart put around 200,000 products into ChatGPT’s checkout and found that purchases completed inside the chat converted at roughly one-third the rate of shoppers who clicked through to Walmart’s own site. The retailer and the products were the same in both cases. What changed was where the shopper paid.

That result carries the lesson. Shoppers use AI to discover products, but they still prefer to buy where they trust the checkout. For brands, the expensive mistake would be rebuilding around any single AI surface’s checkout. The better spend goes on accurate product data and strong retailer listings that every AI assistant can use, with new surfaces tested in small, measured steps.

What Walmart’s test says about a premature shopping AI rollout

Walmart’s test was not a small pilot. In November 2025, Walmart made around 200,000 products available through OpenAI’s Instant Checkout, letting shoppers complete purchases in ChatGPT without visiting Walmart.com, MarTech reported. Purchases completed directly inside ChatGPT converted at roughly one-third the rate of transactions where shoppers clicked through to Walmart’s site, meaning moving checkout into the AI interface cut conversion by about 66%, according to the same report.

Walmart has since changed course. Daniel Danker, Walmart’s executive vice president of product and design, described the in-chat experience as “unsatisfying,” and the company is already pulling back, MarTech reported. OpenAI has begun phasing out Instant Checkout in favor of checkout experiences controlled by merchants, according to the report.

The next step hands the sale back to the retailer. Walmart plans to embed its own assistant, Sparky, inside ChatGPT, letting shoppers log into their Walmart accounts, sync carts and complete purchases within Walmart’s own system, with a similar integration expected for Google Gemini, according to the MarTech report.

Discovery through AI was never the problem. In January 2026, Walmart and Google unveiled an agent-led shopping experience in Gemini, Mass Market Retailers reported. The lesson from ChatGPT concerned where the purchase happened, rather than whether shoppers found products through AI.

Why discovery moves faster than trust

Shoppers adopt new tools for research quickly, because asking an assistant costs nothing. Paying is a different matter. Shoppers want saved payment details, familiar delivery promises, easy returns and the ability to add other items to a basket, and those habits are tied to retailers they already trust.

So the purchase lags well behind discovery for now. AI assistants can send shoppers to products, but forcing the transaction inside a new interface asks shoppers to trust a checkout they have not used before. Many decline. Walmart’s fix confirms the point: its new approach keeps discovery inside the assistant while moving the purchase back into Walmart’s own account, cart and checkout. The assistant becomes a doorway to a trusted store, rather than a replacement for it.

That has a cost for brands that move early. Building custom integrations, feeds or content for one AI surface’s checkout takes money and time. If shoppers do not buy there, the investment earns little, and the surface may change, as Walmart’s experience shows.

The pull of the new surface

The urge to build for the newest surface is understandable. A launch from a major AI company feels like the start of a land grab, and nobody wants to be the brand that arrived late. That fear of missing the moment makes a dedicated integration look like strategy, when it is often a bet on one interface’s checkout before shoppers have shown they will use it. Walmart made a version of that bet across a catalog of that size and is now unwinding it.

The best preparation for AI shopping looks unglamorous. Complete product titles, accurate attributes, current prices, reliable stock levels and strong reviews on major retailers help every AI assistant recommend a product, whichever surface wins. Those investments pay off on the retail sites shoppers use now as well.

Take an apparel brand that planned to build a dedicated integration for checkout inside an AI assistant. Instead, it spent the budget cleaning product data across Amazon, Walmart and its own site, adding sizes, materials and fit details. When shoppers began asking assistants for recommendations, its products appeared more often, and the sales flowed through retailers that already converted well.

Waiting too long carries its own risk. AI shopping surfaces will improve, and early testers learn faster. The answer is to test with small budgets and clear measures, rather than avoid AI surfaces entirely.

Building for every AI surface in 2026

The product data has to come before anything else. Titles, attributes, images and descriptions should be complete across every retailer and the brand’s own site, since assistants rely on that data to match products to shoppers’ questions. Missing sizes, materials or use cases can keep a product out of an answer entirely. Listings where shoppers actually buy deserve the same care. Reviews, stock and prices on Amazon, Walmart and other retailers matter more as AI sends shoppers there, and where assistants hand shoppers to retailers they already use, brands benefit from those retailers’ trust and conversion.

New surfaces get small tests with clear goals and limited budgets, and a test that does not convert gets stopped. Tracking how AI-referred shoppers behave and where they buy matters more than assuming purchases will move into the assistant. New surfaces may also bring new fees or advertising costs, which should be modeled before scaling and compared with the cost of reaching the same shoppers through existing retailers. AI shopping is changing quickly, so a quarterly review of new options beats an early commitment to one.

The rule is to invest first in what every AI surface needs, and to test new checkouts in small steps. Getting a catalog ready for AI shopping agents across retailers is how we prepare brands for agentic commerce.

A0895.crumb: Footwear on Amazon in 2026: what changed…
A0895.title: Footwear on Amazon in 2026: what changed in the category
A0895.alt: A pair of white leather sneakers on tissue paper in an open cardboard shoebox on a wooden floor.
A0895.ttag: Footwear on Amazon in 2026: what changed in the category | Kwontified
A0895.desc: Nike’s return to Amazon and tariff-driven price increases reshaped footwear on Amazon. What the category looks like in 2026 and where brands should act.
A0895.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 2, 2026.
A0895.body:
Until 2025, a shopper looking for Nike shoes on Amazon was buying from independent merchants rather than from Nike. The listings, the prices and the content belonged to whoever held the stock. That shelf is being rebuilt. Nike announced in May 2025 that it would return to selling on Amazon for the first time since 2019. Amazon told some of those merchants it would stop them selling certain Nike products from July 19, because it was working with Nike directly, Reuters reported.

That one decision sums up how the category moved. Footwear on Amazon has shifted from a category shaped by resellers to one where major brands sell directly, and at the same time tariffs pushed prices up. The brands that do well in 2026 take control of their own listings and authorized sellers, invest in size and fit information that reduces returns, and set prices with tariff costs in mind.

What changed for footwear on Amazon

ChangeDetailSource
Nike returnsFirst time selling on Amazon since 2019; merchant restrictions from July 19Reuters
Nike’s pull on AmazonTop-selling apparel brand; 38% of Amazon apparel shoppers reported recent Nike purchasesCoresight Research, via Modern Retail
Nike price increasesAdult apparel and equipment up $2 to $10; footwear priced $100 to $150 up $5Reuters
Sourcing exposureAbout half of Nike’s footwear made in China and VietnamNBC News, via RetailWire
Where search startsMore than a third of consumers begin their footwear search on AmazonAlixPartners and FDRA, 2024

Amazon confirmed the relationship in an email telling sellers it was working directly with Nike to source its products. A May 2025 Coresight Research survey ranked Nike as the top-selling apparel brand on Amazon, with 38% of Amazon apparel shoppers reporting recent Nike purchases, Modern Retail reported.

Prices moved in the same months. Nike raised prices on adult apparel and equipment by $2 to $10, and on footwear priced between $100 and $150 by $5, the Reuters report said. About half of Nike’s footwear is made in China and Vietnam, RetailWire reported, citing NBC News. And shoppers start on Amazon: more than a third of consumers begin their footwear search there, according to a 2024 survey by AlixPartners and the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America, cited by TipRanks.

Why the brands that left came back

Counterfeits drove the earlier exits. When Nike left in 2019, several brands, including the shoemaker Birkenstock, also cut ties with Amazon over concerns about counterfeit products on its third-party marketplace, CNBC reported. Nike’s return signaled that brands now see more risk in staying away.

The logic is easy to see from the shelf. When brands left Amazon, their products often stayed on the site through resellers, at prices and with content the brands did not control. Staying away did not keep shoppers away; it only handed the listings to others. Amazon, for its part, has worked to bring well-known brands into direct relationships, and limiting unauthorized sellers gives brands a reason to return. For a brand, that means a cleaner shelf, with fewer competing sellers on its own products.

Tariffs raised the stakes for everyone. Footwear depends heavily on Asian manufacturing, so tariffs hit the category hard. Price increases test how much shoppers will pay, and Amazon’s price transparency makes any gap with other retailers visible quickly.

Returns remain the hidden cost in footwear. Shoes are bought by size and fit, and wrong sizes come back. Listings with clear size guidance, fit notes and good images lower returns, which protects margin as prices rise.

Take a running shoe brand whose shoes sold on Amazon mainly through resellers with inconsistent pricing and thin content. After moving to direct selling, enrolling in brand protection, adding detailed fit guidance and setting prices that reflected tariff costs, it saw fewer returns and steadier sales, and resellers lost the Buy Box on its core styles.

Selling directly has costs of its own. It brings fees, advertising costs and pressure on price, and brands that relied on full-price wholesale partners may see tension if Amazon prices fall. Pricing has to be planned across all channels together.

Running a footwear brand on Amazon in 2026

Control of the listing comes first. That means registering the brand, owning the product content and working to remove unauthorized sellers. The choice of selling model follows from it: Vendor Central, Seller Central or both, decided on margin after Amazon’s terms and on how much control the brand needs over price.

Fit information is the work that is specific to footwear. Size charts, fit notes, width options and customer fit feedback reduce returns and build trust, and a brand should compare its sizing with major competitors and say clearly whether a style runs large or small. New styles start without reviews, and shoppers rely on reviews for fit, so Amazon’s review programs belong in every launch plan, with fit feedback answered quickly.

Pricing needs a model by style. Brands should work out how tariff costs affect each one and decide where to raise prices, where to absorb costs and where to change sourcing. Prices also need to stay consistent across channels, because large gaps between Amazon and other retailers damage relationships and invite price matching.

Inventory runs by size as much as by style. Footwear sells in many sizes, the most popular ones need to stay in stock because missing sizes lose sales and rankings, and sales data by size should drive reorders. Advertising belongs on the best styles and new launches, with branded search protected from competitors and resellers that bid on brand names. Sandals, boots and back-to-school styles follow the calendar, so stock and advertising need timing to each season.

The shelf Nike walked back onto rewards the brand that controls its listing, its sizes and its price. Building that on Amazon while protecting pricing across other channels is how we run footwear brands on Amazon.

A0897.crumb: Categories winning on TikTok Shop, and…
A0897.title: Categories winning on TikTok Shop, and the traits behind them
A0897.alt: A flat lay of lipstick, a powder compact, a folded peach blouse and beige sneakers on a coral background.
A0897.ttag: Categories winning on TikTok Shop, and the traits behind them | Kwontified
A0897.desc: Beauty and personal care lead TikTok Shop, then womenswear and sports and outdoors. Three product traits explain why, and how brands can test their own fit.
A0897.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 7, 2026.
A0897.body:
Beauty and personal care topped US sales on TikTok Shop in 2025, followed by women’s wear and underwear and then sports and outdoors. On a search-led marketplace, a big category means a lot of shoppers typing its name into a search box. TikTok Shop sells differently, and its ranking has a different cause.

Most sales there begin with a short video shown to someone who was not searching. That favors products that show their value in seconds, cost little enough to buy on impulse and get bought again. Brands should judge their TikTok Shop fit by those three traits rather than by category size, and choose which products to push there accordingly.

The categories winning on TikTok Shop held steady in 2025

The ranking comes from Momentum Works and Tabcut, whose estimates of the US business DealStreetAsia covered. TikTok Shop’s US sales reached an estimated $15.1 billion in 2025, up 68%, according to the same report.

Selling formats shifted at the same time. Live selling’s share of US TikTok Shop sales rose from 10% to 14% in 2025, and the Shop tab’s share rose from 32% to 36%, TechNode Global reported.

Growth reached every category. In the first half of 2025, all categories grew, kids’ fashion grew fastest, food and beverages saw the largest average price increase and beauty products joined supplements among the top-selling items, according to a Momentum Works summary of its report.

Why an unsought video rewards three product traits

A shopper scrolling TikTok did not ask to see the product. It has seconds to prove itself, and the shopper decides on the spot. Three traits make that decision easier, and none of them depends on how many people search for the category.

Visible proof does most of the work. Products that show a result on camera, such as a skincare effect, a hair tool or a cleaning gadget, convince viewers quickly. Products whose value is hard to see, or that need explanation, struggle in a feed that moves on in seconds.

Price decides whether the decision happens in the app. Shoppers who were not planning to buy will spend modest amounts without comparison shopping. Expensive, considered purchases send shoppers off to research elsewhere, and the sale, if it happens, happens somewhere else.

Repeat purchase pays for the whole thing. Consumables such as beauty products and supplements bring buyers back, which lets brands earn back the cost of creators and advertising over several purchases instead of one.

The formats push in the same direction. The growth of live selling favors products a host can demonstrate and answer questions about in real time. The growth of the Shop tab, where shoppers browse with intent, gives repeat buyers an easy way back to products they already know.

Score the leaders against those traits and the ranking makes sense. Beauty and personal care score well on all three. Apparel scores on visibility and often on price, with returns as its weakness. Sports and outdoors products benefit from showing performance in use, which explains their place among the leaders.

Category size is a poor guide to fit

It is natural to read the ranking as a list of where to be. A brand in a large category may still struggle if its products are expensive or hard to demonstrate, while a brand in a small category can do well if its product shows a striking result at a low price. Fit depends on the product, more than on the category label. The ranking tells a brand where the traits happen to cluster, not whether its own products have them.

Take a home goods brand whose best seller on Amazon is a premium mattress topper. On TikTok Shop it sells poorly, because its benefits are hard to show and its price invites research. The brand’s cheaper cleaning spray, which shows results in seconds, becomes its TikTok Shop best seller and drives searches on Amazon too. Same brand, same category, opposite results, because the two products score differently on the traits.

Category data from third-party trackers is estimated, and categories shift quickly, so it works as a guide rather than an answer. A product that scores well on paper can still fail if the content does not land, which is why small tests come before large creator programs.

Choosing and pricing TikTok Shop products in 2026

The scoring itself is simple. Rate each product on how quickly it shows its value, how close it is to an impulse price and how often shoppers rebuy, and lead with the best scorers. Brands whose range is premium can build smaller sizes or bundles that fit an impulse price and introduce shoppers to the brand. At least one product should sit at a price that invites an impulse purchase and brings new buyers into the range.

Content should follow what the product can show. Demonstrations, before-and-after videos and live selling suit products with visible results, so a product with a clear result is the right candidate for a live session where hosts demonstrate and answer questions as shoppers watch. Consumables deserve a plan for the second order too, through follow-up offers and subscriptions where available.

Apparel needs extra discipline on returns: fit information, garments shown on different body types and profit measured after returns. And because category rankings change as new formats and products catch on, the category data deserves a quarterly review.

The rule is to pick TikTok Shop products by visible proof, impulse price and repeat purchase, and to let category size break ties at most. Matching the right products to the right content on TikTok Shop is how we choose TikTok Shop products for brands.

A0899.title: Regional strategy on Walmart Marketplace: sell by delivery zone
A0899.alt: Pastel-painted wooden pigeonhole shelves holding string-tied brown paper parcels in a sunlit blue room.
A0899.ttag: Regional strategy on Walmart Marketplace: sell by delivery zone | Kwontified
A0899.desc: Walmart competes on local delivery speed, and its tools now let sellers promise delivery by region. Why Marketplace sellers should plan Walmart by region.
A0899.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 9, 2026.
A0899.body:
Search for a patio chair on Walmart.com and two listings can sit side by side with very different promises. One, from Walmart’s own stock, arrives within a day. The other, from a Marketplace seller, arrives next week. The shopper sees two chairs, but the decision is really between two delivery dates.

That gap is the problem regional planning solves. Walmart competes on fast local delivery from its stores, and it has given Marketplace sellers tools to match that speed by region, including next-day Walmart Fulfillment Services delivery in major metros and regional delivery promises for sellers who ship themselves. Sellers do better when they plan Walmart as a set of regions, with inventory near demand and promises set region by region, than as one national storefront.

Regional strategy on Walmart Marketplace starts with Walmart’s speed

Speed defines Walmart’s online business. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, US e-commerce grew 27% and the expedited deliveries Walmart fills from its stores grew more than 50% in sales, according to Walmart’s fourth-quarter results. On the call with analysts, executives put the share of store-fulfilled orders delivered in under three hours at about 35%.

Walmart has extended that speed to sellers. At its seller summit in August 2025, Walmart expanded next-day delivery through Walmart Fulfillment Services in major metros, and it introduced settings that let sellers who ship themselves automate delivery promises by region, the company said in its summit announcement. The next-day expansion covered cities including Los Angeles, New York, Chicago, Houston and Atlanta, RTTNews reported.

The stores bring Marketplace closer still. Walmart also said it would display Marketplace items in stores, and it says around 270 million customers visit its 10,750 stores each week, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Why distance shows up in the delivery date

Walmart’s own inventory often arrives within hours or a day, and shoppers have learned to expect it. When a Marketplace item shows a longer delivery date beside Walmart’s own items, shoppers notice the difference and often choose the faster option.

The cause is mostly geography. Walmart’s own products often sit in nearby stores, while many Marketplace items ship from a seller’s warehouse, which may be hundreds of miles from the shopper. That distance shows up in the delivery date, and the gap widens as Walmart’s own deliveries get faster.

A single national promise cannot describe that geography honestly. A seller shipping from one warehouse can reach nearby shoppers quickly and distant shoppers slowly, so one national delivery promise either overstates speed far from the warehouse or understates it nearby. Regional settings let sellers show the real promise in each area.

Where the inventory sits decides the rest. Sellers using Walmart Fulfillment Services place inventory in Walmart’s network, and next-day coverage in major metros rewards inventory that sits close to those markets. Sellers that ship themselves can add warehouses in other regions to shorten delivery times.

Demand across the country is uneven too. Many products sell better in some regions than others, because of climate, culture or local competition, and a national plan can leave stock in the wrong places and miss demand where it peaks. Seasons move across the country as well, so a product’s best region in March may differ from its best region in July.

Take an outdoor furniture brand that ships all Walmart orders from one Midwest warehouse, with a single delivery promise of five to seven days nationwide. It sets regional promises, moves its best sellers into Walmart Fulfillment Services and adds stock near its strongest southern and western markets. Its delivery promises shorten where most of its shoppers live, and its sales in those regions rise. On the results page, its chair now sits beside Walmart’s with a date the shopper can live with.

Splitting inventory across regions has costs. It raises fulfillment costs and the risk of running out in one place while stock sits idle in another. The sensible start is the best-selling products and the largest markets, rather than every item everywhere, with a check on whether faster promises actually raise sales before regional stock expands further.

Planning Walmart region by region in 2026

The plan begins with a map. Sellers should review where their Walmart orders come from and which products sell best in each region. A few metro areas often account for a large share of orders, which makes them the first places to improve delivery speed.

Promises and placement follow from the map. Sellers who ship themselves should use regional shipping settings to show accurate, faster promises where they can deliver quickly. Products with steady demand are candidates for Walmart Fulfillment Services, especially where next-day coverage reaches a seller’s largest markets. Stock belongs close to the regions that buy most, adjusted for seasons, such as moving warm-weather products south in early spring.

Advertising and shipping charges should match the map as well. Products with fast delivery in a region tend to convert better there, so advertising belongs where a seller can deliver quickly, with a test of whether regional differences show up in results. Shipping costs differ with distance, so shipping charges and free-shipping thresholds deserve a check in distant regions, where costs run highest.

Regional plans fail when one location runs out, so inventory has to be tracked by warehouse and rebalanced before stock runs low. And as Walmart displays Marketplace items in stores, sellers with strong regional sales may benefit first, which is one more reason to keep listings and stock ready.

The question for any Walmart seller is simple: where do your delivery promises lag Walmart’s own, and which of those places hold your customers? Planning fulfillment and advertising around that answer is how we run Walmart Marketplace for sellers.

A0900.crumb: Sustainability on Target Plus: an edge in…
A0900.title: Sustainability on Target Plus: an edge in curation, not a rule
A0900.alt: Amber dropper bottles, a twine-tied kraft envelope and a potted fern on a wooden shelf against a deep red wall.
A0900.ttag: Sustainability on Target Plus: an edge in curation, not a rule | Kwontified
A0900.desc: Target Plus is invite-only, and Target holds itself to public sustainability goals. Why proven sustainability helps sellers get chosen, and why claims need it.
A0900.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 14, 2026.
A0900.body:
Public sources do not list sustainability as a requirement for selling on Target Plus. A seller could read that and conclude the topic does not matter. On an invite-only marketplace, the opposite logic applies: a quality that is not required but that the retailer cares about is exactly where a seller can stand out.

Target Plus is a marketplace where Target chooses its sellers, and Target holds itself to public sustainability goals, including net zero emissions by 2040. Proven sustainability can help a seller fit those priorities and get chosen. The practical consequence is to present sustainability as evidence-backed differentiation and to avoid any claim that cannot be proved.

Sustainability on Target Plus starts with how the marketplace is built

Target Plus is curated by design. The marketplace is invite-only, and Target has aimed to carry one vendor per item, Fortune reported. Its goal is a marketplace with more than $5 billion in sales within five years, up from more than $1 billion, Modern Retail reported.

Target also recruits sellers actively. It partnered with Shopify to bring more merchants onto Target Plus, the Fortune report said, and the marketplace grew more than 30% in the fourth quarter of 2025, Target said in its quarterly results. More applicants competing for a limited number of slots raises the value of anything that sets a seller apart.

Target’s own goals on climate and waste are public:

Target goal or resultFigure
Net zero greenhouse gas emissionsby 2040
Owned-brand products meeting its reusable, recyclable or compostable packaging criteria34%
Reduction in its own operations’ emissions since 201741.3%
Share of electricity from renewable sources76%

The figures come from Target’s 2025 sustainability report, Packaging Journal reported. Target also labels reduced-waste products: its Target Zero program uses an icon in stores and online to identify products designed to reduce waste, according to an explainer from The Mars Agency written when the program was new.

How curation turns a priority into an advantage

On an open marketplace, a seller lists its products and competes for shoppers. On a curated marketplace, the retailer first decides which sellers to admit, and each slot is limited. Curation means selection, and selection means judgment. When Target decides which seller to add, it weighs how well the seller’s products fit its assortment, its standards and its story to shoppers, and sustainability is one of the stories Target tells, through its own goals and the Target Zero label.

Packaging is where a seller’s choices reach Target’s shoppers directly. Marketplace sellers usually ship their own orders, so the box, filler and product packaging they choose are what Target’s shoppers open at home. A seller’s packaging becomes part of how shoppers experience Target, which gives the retailer a reason to care about it. A seller whose products support goals the retailer has made public offers more than a product; it offers a better match with how the retailer wants to be seen.

That is why the missing requirement makes proof more valuable rather than less. A requirement would set a minimum that every seller meets, and a minimum separates no one. An advantage rewards the sellers that can show more than the minimum, and the only way to show more is with evidence. That is also why the seller with the vaguest claims gains the least from the topic, however sincere its intentions: a merchant choosing between applicants cannot weigh what it cannot check.

Take two similar cleaning products brands seeking a place on Target Plus. One describes its products as eco-friendly without detail. The other documents refillable packaging, recycled content percentages and third-party certifications. The second brand gives Target specific reasons to choose it, and its claims can appear on product pages without risk. The two brands may be equally sustainable in practice; only one has given the merchant something to compare.

The edge from sustainability has real limits. Target’s own sustainability goals focus mainly on its owned brands, its operations and its supply chain. Marketplace decisions also depend on price, quality, demand and operations, so sustainability should not be oversold as the deciding factor, and unsupported environmental claims carry legal and reputational risk of their own.

Building a sustainability case Target can use in 2026

The work starts with evidence. Every sustainability claim needs documentation, such as recycled content percentages, certifications and packaging specifications. Specific facts, such as refillable packaging or a certified material, are more credible than general words like green or eco-friendly, and they give Target’s merchants something concrete to compare across sellers. Third-party certifications that shoppers and retailers recognize carry more weight than self-made badges, so the certification should match the claim it supports.

The case should connect to Target’s stated priorities, such as reducing packaging waste, without claiming more than the evidence supports. Shipping packaging deserves its own review: the boxes and fillers a seller ships in, with excess material reduced and recycled or recyclable options used where possible.

What protects the claims over time is consistency. The same claims should appear on Target Plus, Amazon, Walmart and the brand’s own site, backed by the same evidence. Product formulas and packaging change, so claims need updating when products change, removing when they can no longer be supported, and a record of the evidence behind each one.

None of this replaces the basics. Sustainability helps only when price, quality, delivery and service meet Target’s standards, and a strong sustainability case cannot make up for late shipments or poor reviews.

The rule is to treat sustainability as an advantage you can prove, never as a label you add. Preparing that evidence for a curated marketplace is how we help brands earn a place on Target Plus.

A0901.title: Mother’s Day 2026 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards
A0901.alt: A kraft gift box tied with a pink satin ribbon and blank tag beside pale pink tulips on a rustic wooden table.
A0901.ttag: Mother’s Day 2026 on marketplaces: what gifting rewards | Kwontified
A0901.desc: Mother’s Day shoppers buy for someone else, on a deadline, and want gifts that feel unique. What that rewards on marketplaces, and how brands should get ready.
A0901.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 16, 2026.
A0901.body:
Picture the search a week before Mother’s Day. Someone types “gifts for mom” into a marketplace and scrolls past a dozen necklaces and candles. They stop on the listing that answers three questions at once: will it arrive in time, will it look like a gift when it does, and is it something she would not have bought herself? Price matters, but it is rarely the question that closes the sale.

Those three questions are the shape of the holiday. Mother’s Day shoppers buy for someone else, against a fixed date, and say they want gifts that feel unique or create a memory. Marketplaces reward listings that promise delivery before May 10, present products as ready to give and explain what makes them special, so brands should plan Mother’s Day 2026 around those needs rather than around discounts alone.

Mother’s Day 2026 on marketplaces follows a big, online-first holiday

Mother’s Day is a large spending moment. Shoppers expected to spend $34.1 billion on Mother’s Day in 2025, up from $33.5 billion in 2024, according to the National Retail Federation’s survey with Prosper Insights & Analytics. Those celebrating planned to spend $259.04 on average, and the holiday trails only the winter holidays in average spending, the NRF said.

Online led the way in 2025. It was the top shopping destination for the holiday, chosen by 36% of shoppers, ahead of department stores at 32%, specialty stores at 29% and local or small businesses at 25%, according to the same survey.

What shoppers say they want is meaning. Nearly half, 48%, said finding a gift that is unique or different mattered most, and 42% said finding a gift that creates a special memory mattered most, the NRF said. Shoppers expected to spend $6.8 billion on jewelry, $6.3 billion on special outings and $3.5 billion on gift cards.

They buy for different people, too. Most celebrants, 57%, were shopping for a mother or stepmother, followed by a wife at 23% and a daughter at 12%. The most popular gift types were flowers at 74%, greeting cards at 73% and special outings at 61%. Gifts of experience remain popular, with 36% of men planning to give one in 2025, up from 29% in 2019, according to the survey.

Mother’s Day 2026 falls on Sunday, May 10.

A gift buyer reads a listing differently

Gift shoppers buy for someone else, and they often know less about the product than the person receiving it. They lean on reviews, photos and descriptions to judge quality and fit, so listings that answer their questions quickly win their confidence. Size guides, clear return policies and gift receipts reduce the worry of choosing wrong.

The deadline changes the rest of the behavior. A gift that arrives after Mother’s Day loses most of its value. As the date approaches, shoppers favor listings that promise delivery in time, and marketplaces show delivery dates prominently. Products with slow or uncertain delivery lose sales in the final week, even at lower prices.

Presentation matters more than usual, because the shopper wants a gift that looks like a gift. Gift-ready packaging, gift messages and images that show the product as it will be received help shoppers picture the moment of giving. And when shoppers say they want something unique or memorable, a discount alone rarely persuades them. Listings that explain what makes a product special, such as personalization, craftsmanship or a story, give shoppers a reason to choose it.

Search shifts with the season as well. Shoppers search for gifts by recipient and occasion, such as gifts for mom, as well as by product, and brands that include gift-related terms in titles, descriptions and advertising appear in those searches.

Take a jewelry brand that has relied on Mother’s Day discounts and watched its sales drop sharply in the final week. For Mother’s Day 2026 it adds gift-ready images, highlights personalization, uses gift-related search terms, moves inventory into faster fulfillment and sets advertising to peak while delivery before May 10 is still guaranteed. The bet is that sales hold up through the final week without deeper discounts, because the listing now answers the questions the shopper is actually asking.

Not every product suits gifting, and forcing a Mother’s Day angle onto products shoppers would not give as gifts wastes effort that belongs on the products that fit.

Preparing listings, stock and ads for May 10

Delivery dates come before anything else. Brands should confirm which products can arrive before May 10 through each fulfillment option, and stock fast fulfillment early. Stock needs daily attention in the last two weeks, because running out of a popular gift in the final week loses sales that will not return after the holiday, and advertising should pause on products that are running low.

The listing does the persuading. Images should show products as gifts, and descriptions should mention gift packaging, gift messages and who the product suits, along with the personalization, materials, craftsmanship or story that makes it memorable. Titles, descriptions and keywords should carry phrases shoppers use, such as gifts for mom, alongside product terms. Gift sets and bundles make choosing easier and raise order value.

Advertising should follow the calendar. It builds in the weeks before Mother’s Day, peaks while delivery is still assured and then shifts to products with fast delivery or to digital gift cards and experiences. With experience gifts popular, brands can also pair products with experiences, such as a cooking class kit or a spa set, or offer digital gift cards for late shoppers.

The shopper scrolling a week out is asking whether the gift will arrive, whether it will look like a gift and whether it means something; listings that answer all three win the week. Planning that across listings, stock and advertising is how we prepare brands for seasonal moments on marketplaces.

A0903.title: Differentiating beyond price wars: what Temu cannot copy
A0903.alt: A tan leather satchel on a rustic workbench surrounded by leatherworking tools and spools of thread in a warm workshop.
A0903.ttag: Differentiating beyond price wars: what Temu cannot copy | Kwontified
A0903.desc: Temu competes on price, and rising fees make price wars costlier for brands. Why brands should compete on what low-price platforms cannot copy cheaply.
A0903.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 21, 2026.
A0903.body:
From April 17, 2026, Amazon applied a 3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge to fulfillment fees for US and Canadian sellers, until further notice, CP24 reported. A brand facing a cheaper lookalike on Temu now pays more to sell each unit, and the instinct is still to cut the price. That combination is how a brand ends up selling more and earning less.

Price is the one contest a low-price platform is designed to win. Temu has shown it can keep winning it even after the rules change, so cutting prices to match only confirms that price is what matters. The better answer is to compete on what a low-price rival cannot copy cheaply: proven quality, product knowledge, service, delivery speed and exclusive range.

Differentiating beyond price wars starts with how Temu adapted

The duty exemption that helped Temu ship straight from China covered packages under $800. When the US moved to end it, shares of PDD, Temu’s parent, fell, CNBC reported. By then, Marketplace Pulse data cited by Reuters put about 20% of Temu’s US sales with local sellers already.

That shift began well before the rule changed. Temu began bidding to attract sellers that keep inventory in US warehouses in March 2024, nearly a year before the tariff change, the Reuters report said. Local inventory lets low-price sellers deliver faster, which removes one of the advantages brands used to count on.

The transition was expensive for Temu. After the exemption ended on May 2, 2025, Temu’s US daily users fell 58% as the company cut US advertising, and net income at PDD dropped 47% in the first quarter, according to RetailWire’s report. But the model survived the change of rules, which is the part that matters for brands planning against it.

Why a price cut fights on the rival’s strongest ground

A low-price platform is designed around low prices. Its sourcing, its seller base and its marketing all aim at the cheapest offer. A brand that matches those prices is competing where the rival is strongest, with a cost structure built for something else.

Rising costs make the arithmetic worse. When fees and tariffs rise, every price cut takes a larger share of a brand’s margin, and a brand that cuts prices while its costs rise can end up selling more and earning less. The cuts also outlast the promotion: brands that discount often train shoppers to expect lower prices, which weakens full-price sales long after the sale ends.

Nor can brands wait for policy to solve it. Temu’s move toward local sellers shows that the model can survive changes in rules, so tariffs alone will not remove low-price competition.

The way out runs through how shoppers compare. They compare on price only when they see little else to compare. When two products look the same, the cheaper one wins. When one offers clear proof of quality, better information, faster delivery or something the other cannot offer, price becomes one factor among several.

So the effective response to a price war is often to make the product harder to compare on price, rather than cheaper. Bundles, exclusive sizes, detailed product information and strong service change what shoppers weigh; price cuts only confirm that price is the thing to weigh. A shopper who sees a warranty, a test result and a bundle sold nowhere else is no longer comparing two products; she is comparing two offers, and only one of them can be matched at a lower price.

Take a kitchenware brand whose best-selling pan starts appearing as low-priced lookalikes on several marketplaces. Instead of cutting its price, it adds clear evidence of its materials and testing, a lifetime warranty, recipe content and a bundle with a lid sold only on Amazon. Its sales hold and its margin stays intact, while the lookalikes compete with each other on price.

Differentiation is not a universal answer. Some categories truly compete on price, and some shoppers will always choose the cheapest option, so brands in commodity categories may need efficient costs as well as differentiation. Differentiation also costs money, and it has to be worth more to shoppers than it costs to deliver.

What to build instead of a discount in 2026

The starting point is a list: the attributes that set a brand’s products apart, such as materials, testing, warranties, design and service, with the strongest leading the listing. Proof turns that list into a reason to pay more. Certifications, test results and detailed reviews separate genuine products from lookalikes, and reviews that mention durability, fit or results, gathered through approved programs, help shoppers see why a product costs more.

Comparison can be made harder on purpose. Bundles, sizes and variants sold only on certain channels make direct price comparisons difficult, and detailed descriptions, comparison charts and how-to content show differences that photos alone cannot. Fast, reliable delivery and easy returns give shoppers further reasons to pay more, most of all where low-price rivals still ship slowly or handle returns poorly.

Margin needs protecting before prices move. The effect of rising fees should be modeled product by product before deciding where to adjust prices, rather than cutting across the range. A clear pricing plan across channels matters too, since wide gaps between marketplaces and a brand’s own site invite price matching and weaken trust. And marketplaces need watching for products that copy a brand’s listings or designs, with brand protection tools used where they apply.

The test before any price cut is whether a low-price rival could match it tomorrow; if it could, the money is better spent on something the rival cannot copy. Building that defense across marketplaces is how we protect brand margins against low-price competition.

A0905.title: Discovery-driven commerce at Zalando: what brands need now
A0905.alt: A camel coat, cream sweater, dark jeans, brown crossbody bag and ankle boots laid out on a white bed.
A0905.ttag: Discovery-driven commerce at Zalando: what brands need now | Kwontified
A0905.desc: Zalando now wins shoppers in its feed and assistant, before they search. Brands that sell there need content, data and fit details built to be recommended.
A0905.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 23, 2026.
A0905.body:
Watch someone open a fashion app on the train home. They rarely type anything. They scroll, save a jacket, tap through to a pair of boots they did not know they wanted, and leave without searching once. Zalando has built its next phase around that habit, with an AI-powered discovery feed, a shoppable assistant and matching models that pair shoppers with products and sizes.

That changes what a brand needs to bring. On a platform where the feed picks the products, discovery-driven commerce at Zalando rewards brands whose content and product data give the system something to recommend. Accurate size and fit information and a plan for Zalando’s growing retail media now matter more than search rank and price alone.

Discovery-driven commerce at Zalando, in the company’s own numbers

The platform is growing steadily. Group gross merchandise value rose 14.7% to 17.6 billion euros in 2025, and active customers reached a new high of 62 million, helped by the acquisition of ABOUT YOU, Zalando said in its full-year results. It now runs three apps, Zalando, ABOUT YOU and Lounge by Zalando, each aimed at a different shopper.

Discovery sits at the center of the strategy. The AI-powered feed already draws more than nine million weekly users, which the company says is turning the platform from a transactional destination into a daily lifestyle companion. The Zalando Assistant reached six million users, a fourfold increase, according to the same results. Zalando also said its matching models increased items added to bags by 13%, and that its Size and Fit tool, built on real body measurements from more than a million customers, cut size-related returns by more than 8%.

The range is widening beyond fashion. Sports, beauty, kids and family and designer grew 13% in 2025, and Zalando connects 62 million active customers with more than 7,000 brands across 29 markets, the company said. AI also improved the precision of its real-time delivery promises by 22 percentage points.

Most of these figures are Zalando’s own reporting, and a feed rewards some brands more than others, so each brand should read its own results before assuming a feature will help it.

Who holds the shopper when the feed decides

A search box serves the shopper who already knows what they want. A feed serves the one who does not, and fashion is full of those shoppers: people looking for an idea, a trend or an outfit. Every daily visit gives the platform another chance to show them something new, and it is the platform, not the brand, that decides what that something is.

Follow where the value lands. Zalando’s Plus loyalty program reached 16.8 million members and accounted for nearly half of fourth-quarter gross merchandise value, and its retail media business grew 42% in 2025, the company said. The member relationship sits with Zalando, and so does a growing share of brand marketing budgets. Its business services, including ZEOS logistics, SCAYLE software and Tradebyte marketplace integration, serve more than 1,200 merchants and enable around 11 billion euros in gross merchandise value.

The same pattern extends to AI shopping outside the app. Zalando is one of two European launch partners for Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, which lets customers discover and buy products through AI chatbots such as Gemini, the company said, and it describes itself as the top fashion platform referred by conversational AIs.

For brands, influence moves to the inputs. When a feed or an assistant picks products for each shopper, it works from product data, images, engagement and fit information. A product with thin data gives the system less to work with, and it is shown less often.

Fit is where that becomes margin. Fashion returns are expensive and wrong sizes cause many of them, so a tool that helps a shopper choose the right size protects Zalando’s margin and the brand’s at the same time.

Take an outerwear brand whose jackets sell well in Zalando search but rarely surface in the discovery feed. Its fix is in its own hands: lifestyle images that work in a feed, complete attributes for material, fit and occasion, and detailed size information. Each gives the recommendation system a reason to show the jacket to someone who never searched for it, and better size data should send fewer of those jackets back.

What Zalando-ready looks like in 2026

Content comes first. Feeds need lifestyle images and styling content alongside the standard product shots, because a white-background photo answers a searcher’s question but gives a browser little reason to stop.

Product data is the second input. Detailed attributes such as material, fit, occasion and style help the AI match products to shoppers, and missing attributes leave a product less likely to be recommended. Accurate size charts and fit details feed Zalando’s fit tools and reduce returns.

Each app deserves its own plan. Inspiration lives in the main Zalando app, trends in ABOUT YOU and deals in Lounge, so brands should decide where their products belong and tailor content and pricing to each.

Retail media is worth testing, with care. With Zalando’s retail media growing, sponsored placements suit launches and key seasons, and the useful measure is whether they lift sales beyond what discovery would have delivered anyway. Plus members shop often, which makes offers and early access aimed at them a natural home for new collections. Brands in sports, beauty and the other growing categories have room on Zalando beyond fashion.

The data that feeds Zalando’s own feed will also feed the AI chatbots Zalando is connecting to, so the work pays twice. Leadership teams should ask which person in the business owns those attributes and images, since on a platform where the feed chooses, they decide whether the brand is chosen at all. Building that product data and content is how we run Zalando for fashion brands.

A0908.crumb: Handbags on Amazon in 2026: what changed…
A0908.title: Handbags on Amazon in 2026: what changed in accessories
A0908.alt: A tan leather handbag displayed on a stone block with cream tissue paper in a sunlit navy-framed shop window.
A0908.ttag: Handbags on Amazon in 2026: what changed in accessories | Kwontified
A0908.desc: Coach showed that a premium handbag brand can sell on Amazon. The brands that follow treat it as a curated storefront, not a clearance rack or a place to avoid.
A0908.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Apr 30, 2026.
A0908.body:
At a department store handbag counter, the brand controls almost everything a shopper sees: the lighting, the glass, the sales associate who knows which bag holds a laptop. Search for a leather tote on Amazon and most of that disappears. The bag sits in a grid between a reseller’s listing of last season’s style and a lookalike at a third of the price, and the photos have to do the associate’s job.

For years that grid kept premium accessories brands away. What changed is that accessible luxury brands such as Coach began selling there directly, showing that the marketplace can carry a premium name. For the brands that follow, Amazon works best as a curated storefront. That means a chosen set of styles, protected prices and authenticity, and imagery that carries the weight, rather than a place to avoid or a place to list everything.

Handbags on Amazon changed when Coach arrived

Coach began selling on Amazon in 2023, a move that followed flat sales at its parent company, Glossy reported. Amazon gave the launch prominent placement on its homepage under the heading “Coach classics, now at Amazon,” WWD reported. Neil Saunders, an analyst at GlobalData, told Glossy that Amazon has an extensive reach, and that while it may not always be seen as a channel for luxury, many consumers search there.

Coach has since become the engine of its parent. It accounted for nearly 80% of the parent company’s sales, while sales at its sister brand Kate Spade fell 10% in the prior year, Fortune reported. The company also sold its Stuart Weitzman shoe brand, according to the report.

The advertising side points the same way. In a 2023 survey, Amazon was marketers’ most popular retail media partner, with 76% saying they used it to sell their companies’ products, compared with 24% for Walmart Connect and 21% for Target’s Roundel, according to Glossy research. A brand that sells on Amazon can reach shoppers through the retail media network marketers use most.

The cost of being there is climbing, too. US and Canadian sellers have paid a 3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge in addition to Amazon’s fulfillment fees from April 17, 2026, until further notice, CP24 reported. On lower-priced styles with thin margins, every fee shows up in the accessories P&L.

Why staying away stopped working

Many shoppers begin product searches on Amazon, handbags included. A brand that stayed off the marketplace did not keep its bags off it. It found them sold by resellers at whatever price those sellers chose, or it found shoppers picking a brand that was present. Once a recognized accessible luxury name sold directly, the stigma eased for everyone else, and the conversation inside premium brands moved from whether they belong on Amazon to how they should appear there.

How they appear is mostly a question of what they leave out. Premium brands rarely list their full range. Many choose core styles, accessible price points or select collections, and keep their newest and most exclusive pieces for their own stores and sites. The Amazon assortment becomes a deliberate edit of the brand.

The four pressures a premium brand manages there

Authenticity comes first, because handbags attract counterfeits and gray-market sellers more than most categories. A shopper paying a premium wants assurance that the bag is genuine, which an official brand store and a short, documented list of authorized sellers provide. Brand protection programs and prompt reporting of counterfeit listings keep that assurance intact.

Wholesale partners are the second pressure, since many accessories brands still sell through department stores and specialty retailers, and those partners watch Amazon prices closely. When an Amazon price falls below theirs, they notice, and the relationship suffers. Keeping prices consistent with the brand’s own site and its partners, and avoiding deep discounts, protects both the prestige and the wholesale book. Telling partners how Amazon fits the plan, and not undercutting them on exclusive styles, does the rest.

In a grid, imagery carries the sale, because shoppers judge size, material, color and hardware from photos and video. Detailed images, size comparisons and interior views reduce returns and build confidence, and a bag shown worn or carried tells a shopper more about its size than a flat product shot.

Advertising is the last lever, and it works best narrowly: on core styles, and on branded searches where resellers and lookalikes would otherwise take the click. Handbags and small accessories are popular gifts, so stock and advertising for gifting seasons belong in the same plan.

Take a leather accessories brand whose bags already appear on Amazon through resellers at inconsistent prices. The curated route would be an official store with a short range of best-selling styles, detailed imagery and size guides, enrollment in brand protection, and its newest collection kept for its own site. The aim is to win back the reseller traffic at full price without giving wholesale partners a reason to complain.

Amazon is still not the right channel for every premium brand. A brand whose value rests on scarcity or a tightly controlled experience may lose more than it gains, and the decision comes down to reach weighed against the effect on its image and its partners.

Questions to settle before listing the first bag

  1. What is Amazon for: reach, core styles or one price tier? The assortment follows from the answer, starting with core styles that have steady demand, clear sizing and strong reviews.
  2. Which styles stay off Amazon, and does every wholesale partner know the plan?
  3. Who owns authenticity day to day, from the authorized seller list to counterfeit reports?
  4. Do the images answer the questions an associate at the counter would answer?

On Amazon, the listing has to do the work the counter used to do. Building a curated Amazon store that protects price and partners is how we help accessories brands sell on Amazon.

A0910.crumb: Amazon’s Q1 2026 results: what ad revenue…
A0910.title: Amazon’s Q1 2026 results: what ad revenue says about clicks
A0910.alt: A tall stack of coins beside a twine-tied bundle of kraft paper envelopes on a wooden table.
A0910.ttag: Amazon’s Q1 2026 results: what ad revenue says about clicks | Kwontified
A0910.desc: Amazon’s ad revenue grew about twice as fast as its online store sales in Q1 2026. What that says about the price of a click, and why conversion decides margin.
A0910.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 5, 2026.
A0910.body:
Amazon’s online stores sold $64.3 billion in the first quarter of 2026, up 12%. In the same quarter, Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 24% to $17.24 billion, ahead of analysts’ expectations, SiliconANGLE reported. Brands bought advertising about twice as fast as shoppers bought from the stores that advertising sits in.

That gap is the number to read. When ad revenue outgrows the sales it supports, brands as a group are paying more in advertising for each sale, because more budget is chasing roughly the same shoppers. Expect advertising to take a larger share of Amazon costs, measure it against total sales and incremental lift, and compete on conversion rather than on bids.

What Amazon’s Q1 2026 results showed

MetricFirst quarter 2026Growth
Advertising revenue$17.24 billion24%
Online stores sales$64.3 billion12%
Net sales$181.5 billion17%

Amazon’s own framing of the ad number was slightly lower. Chief executive Andy Jassy put advertising growth at 22% on the earnings call and said advertising had passed $70 billion in revenue over the trailing twelve months, MarketBeat reported. The two growth rates likely differ because of currency effects, since foreign exchange added $2.9 billion to the quarter’s net sales, according to the same report. Excluding currency effects, net sales rose 15%.

The business as a whole grew too. Net sales rose 17% to $181.5 billion, and Amazon expects second-quarter net sales of $194 billion to $199 billion, Fortune reported, citing the Associated Press.

The pattern holds across quarters. Advertising revenue rose 23% to $21.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, TheWrap reported. Advertising has now grown by more than 20% in consecutive quarters, and in the first quarter it again outpaced overall net sales growth of 17%.

Some of that growth sits outside the search results page. Jassy cited an expanded relationship with Netflix through Amazon Audiences, a collaboration with Comcast Advertising on local advertising and the expansion of the Creative Agent tool to more countries, the MarketBeat report said.

Why the price of a click rises when ads outgrow sales

A retailer’s advertising revenue is what brands pay to reach its shoppers. Divide it by the sales those shoppers make and you get a rough price of advertising per sale across the whole store. When the top of that fraction grows 24% and the bottom grows 12%, the ratio climbs.

New formats explain part of the gap. Video and partner audiences reach people outside Amazon’s store, and that spend does not raise search costs directly. But much of Amazon’s ad business still sits in search results, where brands bid against each other for the same shoppers. Third-party sellers make up a large share of what Amazon sells, so many brands compete for each search, and when budgets grow faster than searches, the price of each click tends to rise.

Fees squeeze from the other side. From April 17, 2026, Amazon added a 3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge to fulfillment, in force until further notice, CP24 reported. With fees and advertising both rising, the margin on each sale shrinks from two directions.

So why do some brands keep bidding into a market where every click costs more? Because for them, it does not cost more per sale. The auction sets the price per click, but the brand sets the price per sale through its conversion rate. Two brands paying the same for a click pay very different amounts per order if one listing converts and the other does not, and as clicks get more expensive, that difference widens. A rising auction is a tax on weak listings more than on strong ones.

Take a home brand whose cost per click rose through 2025. Its reflex is to raise bids to hold position, which buys the same clicks at a higher price. The alternative is to fix images, reviews and prices on its best sellers so that more of the clicks it already buys turn into orders. If conversion improves faster than click prices rise, its cost per sale falls even as the auction gets more expensive.

Amazon’s results describe its whole advertising business, not any single category or brand, and some categories see far more competition than others. Check your own costs before assuming the average applies.

Reading your own account against the average

Advertising as a share of total sales is the number that shows whether this is happening to you. Tracking ad cost only against ad-attributed sales hides it, because attributed sales can rise with spend while the business does not. A rising share is an early warning that margin is under pressure.

Incrementality is the second check. Some advertised sales would have happened anyway, especially on branded search. Holdout tests, where some regions or periods run without certain campaigns, show what advertising truly adds.

New formats need their own yardstick. Video, partner audiences and off-Amazon reach can find new shoppers, so judge them on new customers and total sales. They often show weaker attributed returns than search, which means they need longer measurement windows.

The calendar matters as well. Amazon confirmed on April 29 that Prime Day will run in June, 9to5Toys reported. With the event earlier than usual, expect click costs to rise around it and set budgets accordingly, deciding in advance which products can carry more advertising alongside rising fees and which cannot.

For a quarter like this one, the working rule is to expect clicks to cost more, fix the weakest listings before adding budget to them, and judge the result by cost per sale, not cost per click. Watching that ratio against total sales each month is how we manage Amazon advertising as costs rise.

A0911.crumb: Which team owns being chosen by an AI…
A0911.title: Which team owns being chosen by an AI shopping agent
A0911.alt: White robotic arm with soft grippers lifting a ceramic vase from a wooden shelf of vases by a sunny window.
A0911.ttag: Which team owns being chosen by an AI shopping agent | Kwontified
A0911.desc: An AI shopping agent weighs product data, reviews, price, stock and ads in one answer. Brands split those inputs across teams, so someone has to own the whole.
A0911.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 7, 2026.
A0911.body:
Put one question to a brand’s leadership team: when Amazon’s Rufus answers a shopper in your category and leaves your products out, whose problem is that? The catalog lead will point to product data, the creative lead to images and copy, operations to stock and delivery, finance to price and the media team to advertising. Every one of those inputs feeds the same recommendation, and at many brands nobody is accountable for the recommendation itself.

That gap is the decision now in front of leadership. An AI shopping agent judges products on data, reviews, content, price, availability and advertising at once, so being chosen by one is a channel that runs through every team. It needs one person or group with clear ownership, and measures that the catalog, content, operations and media teams share.

Why the AI shopping agent question reached the leadership table

Shoppers are using these assistants in volume. Monthly active users of Rufus, Amazon’s AI shopping assistant, rose 115% year over year and engagement rose 400%, chief executive Andy Jassy said on Amazon’s first-quarter call, Modern Retail reported. Amazon had disclosed in February that Rufus was used by 300 million customers in 2025 and helped drive nearly $12 billion in incremental annualized sales, according to the same report. Amazon also says customers who use Rufus are 60% more likely to complete a purchase.

The assistant is turning into an ad surface and a buyer as well. Amazon began rolling out sponsored prompts in November, and nearly 20% of shoppers who interact with a brand prompt continue the conversation about that brand, Jassy said, as Modern Retail noted. Amazon also introduced a feature called Auto Buy that lets customers use Rufus to purchase products automatically when they reach a set price. Jassy added that shoppers will likely start with assistants built by the retailers they already use.

Amazon is not alone in this. Walmart found that purchases completed inside ChatGPT converted at about one-third the rate of shoppers it sent to its own site, and it is moving its own assistant, Sparky, into ChatGPT, MarTech reported. In Europe, Zalando’s own 2025 results name it as one of two launch partners in Europe for the Universal Commerce Protocol, Google’s standard for checking out inside AI chatbots such as Gemini.

The advertising side is changing in parallel. Amazon Ads opened an MCP server in February 2026 that lets AI agents query performance and build campaigns that still need approval, PPC Land reported. Brands may soon have agents on both sides of the shelf: one placing their media, another deciding whether to buy their product.

Each team owns one input, and no one owns the answer

When a shopper asks an assistant for a recommendation, the system draws on product titles and attributes, images, reviews, questions and answers, price, delivery speed and stock, and it may show sponsored prompts alongside. A store shelf at least puts price, packaging and stock in one place where someone can look at them together. The assistant blends them into a few sentences that name some products and leave others out.

Inside the brand, those inputs live on different floors. At many companies a catalog team owns product data, a creative or brand team owns content, operations owns stock and delivery, finance or sales owns price and a media team owns advertising, each with its own goals and its own reports. When an agent leaves a product out, the cause may be a missing attribute, a weak review profile, a stock gap or a slow delivery promise, and each team sees only its own line of that list. So the problem can sit unowned.

Price shows how far the channel reaches. With Auto Buy, a shopper’s price threshold turns a pricing decision into a trigger: when the price meets the threshold the agent completes the sale, and when it does not, the sale never happens. The team that sets price has joined the agent channel, whether or not anyone in the planning meeting has said so.

The reports have not caught up either. Search ranking and ad performance reports were built for shoppers who type keywords and scroll results. Agent recommendations do not fit neatly into those reports, so teams often cannot tell how often their products are suggested, and a gap nobody can measure rarely lands on anyone’s list.

Retailers do not fully explain how their assistants choose products, and the systems change quickly. That argues for treating agent readiness as an ongoing practice with an owner, rather than a formula handed to each team once.

What the owner of being chosen actually does

The decision itself is narrow. Leadership names one person or group accountable for how products appear in AI shopping assistants and gives that owner the authority to pull the other teams into one review. The owner does not take over catalog, pricing or media. The job is to see the answer whole and coordinate the fixes.

That begins with shared measures, such as how often the brand’s products appear in assistant answers to the questions its shoppers ask, reviewed together each month by the teams that feed them. Someone also has to ask the assistants those questions on a regular schedule and record which products come back.

Product data usually comes first, because complete titles, attributes, size and compatibility details and current answers to common questions give agents what they need. Reviews and content come next, since agents draw on them to explain a product, which makes addressing common complaints and keeping content accurate part of the same work. Availability sits on the same list: an out-of-stock product cannot be sold, whatever recommends it, so stock and delivery promises are part of being chosen.

Price rules and paid formats complete the remit. With automatic purchases tied to price thresholds, price changes need deliberate rules and a watch on how they move sales through assistants. Media teams can test conversational formats such as sponsored prompts and bring the results back to the owner, so the paid answer and the unpaid one are read side by side.

Take a household brand whose products rarely appear when shoppers ask Rufus for recommendations in its category. A review across teams could turn up missing attributes, outdated answers to common questions and frequent stockouts on its best seller, three problems held by three different teams. With one manager owning the outcome, those become one project with one set of measures, fixed before any new advertising goes in.

When an assistant leaves a product out, the useful answer in the leadership meeting is a name. Giving one owner the whole answer, across data, content, stock, price and media, is the kind of channel work we run day to day for brands selling through AI assistants.
