A0912.crumb: How to run an incrementality holdout…
A0912.title: How to run an incrementality holdout without pausing everything
A0912.alt: Two wooden raised garden beds with lettuce, herbs and seedlings beside a vine-covered wall at sunset.
A0912.ttag: How to run an incrementality holdout without pausing everything | Kwontified
A0912.desc: Brands skip incrementality tests because they fear switching ads off. A holdout needs only a small, matched group, and it costs far less than never testing.
A0912.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 12, 2026.
A0912.body:
Many brands have never measured what their Amazon advertising adds, and the reason sounds prudent: they assume a test means switching the ads off and giving up sales for a season. An incrementality holdout asks for much less. It needs a small group left unexposed, such as a share of an audience, a few regions or one campaign type for a limited period, and the most it can cost is the sales that small group’s ads would have caused.

That flips which choice is expensive. If the advertising truly drives sales, a narrow holdout on the largest or most doubtful spend gives up only a little. If it does not, the test costs nothing and shows where money can move. The costly habit is never testing, because every campaign then keeps its budget at the level its attributed results suggest.

Where incrementality holdout testing stands

Measurement practice in the TransUnion and EMARKETER surveyShare of marketers
Platform-provided attribution65.8%
Incrementality testing and experiments52%
Marketing mix modeling49.5%
Plan to invest in incrementality testing over the next 12 months36.2%
Expanding incrementality testing is a top priority27.6%

Platform-provided attribution remained the most common method in a 2025 TransUnion and EMARKETER survey of marketers, PPC Land reported, with incrementality testing and experiments close behind. The share planning to invest in incrementality testing comes from the same survey, as EMARKETER reported, and EMARKETER points to data clean rooms such as Amazon Marketing Cloud as a privacy-safe place to run those tests.

The obstacles depend on who is answering. Brands are more likely than agencies to cite a lack of internal expertise as an obstacle to measurement, while agencies more often cite trouble removing double counting across channels, according to the PPC Land report.

The money at stake keeps growing. Amazon booked $17.24 billion in advertising revenue in the first quarter of 2026, up 24%, SiliconANGLE reported. As budgets grow, so does the amount spent on campaigns whose effect nobody has tested. The tools are closer at hand, too. Since September 2025, sponsored ads advertisers have been able to open Amazon Marketing Cloud directly, on a self-service basis, from the advertising console, where getting in previously required partners or account representatives, PPC Land reported.

Why a small holdout group is enough

Incrementality is the share of sales the advertising caused. You find it by comparing people or places that saw the ads with similar ones that did not, and the difference between the two groups is the advertising’s real effect.

Attributed results feel like that answer already. A platform report credits an ad with a sale when the shopper saw or clicked it before buying, and the sequence looks like cause and effect. The flaw is that many of those shoppers would have bought anyway, so attributed results usually overstate what advertising adds. Only a comparison group separates the two.

That comparison group can be small. It has to be similar to the exposed group and left unexposed long enough to compare, which can mean a random share of an audience, a set of matched regions or a single campaign type paused for a few weeks. Nothing about the method requires turning off all advertising.

So the fear is pointed at the wrong cost. The sales a holdout gives up are limited to the incremental sales of the held-out slice. The money a brand gives up by never testing is spread across every campaign funded on its attributed numbers. That includes campaigns that mostly claim sales the brand would have made anyway. Branded search is the usual suspect, since shoppers searching for a brand often buy it whether or not an ad appears.

Take a supplement brand that puts a large share of its budget into branded search and hesitates to test because it fears losing sales. It can pause branded search in a small set of matched regions for four weeks and compare total sales with similar regions where the ads keep running. If the difference is small, branded search was mostly collecting sales that would have happened, and part of that budget can move to campaigns that reach new customers.

Holdouts can mislead when the groups are not comparable, when they run too briefly or during unusual weeks, or when too few sales occur to measure a difference. Each of those produces a number that looks precise and means little. A holdout needs careful design, enough volume and one clear question.

Running a holdout on Amazon without losing a season

Every useful holdout starts with one question. Pick a single campaign type, such as branded search, and ask how many sales it adds. Then choose the method that fits it: audience holdouts in Amazon Marketing Cloud suit display and video, while regional or time-based pauses suit search campaigns that cannot hold out individual shoppers.

Size and matching come next. A small share of an audience or a few regions limits the risk while still showing a difference, as long as enough sales occur in each group to measure. The regions or audiences should be similar in size, sales history and seasonality. The test should run across a full buying cycle and avoid major events such as Prime Day, which distort results.

Reading the result is where most of the value sits. Compare total sales between the groups, not only ad-attributed sales, and keep a log of each test’s setup, dates, results and decisions, so later tests build on earlier ones and the findings survive when teams change. Then act: move budget from campaigns that add little to campaigns that bring new customers, and test again each quarter.

The working rule is to hold out a small, well-matched group, starting with the spend you are least sure about, and judge it on total sales. Designing that first holdout and reading it honestly is how we measure what Amazon advertising adds for brands.

A0914.crumb: Prime Day in June: planning around an…
A0914.title: Prime Day in June: planning around an earlier event
A0914.alt: Windowsill with a kraft-paper parcel, lemonade pitcher, straw hat and pink peonies in a glass vase.
A0914.ttag: Prime Day in June: planning around an earlier event | Kwontified
A0914.desc: Prime Day moves to June in 2026, pulling deadlines into May and budgets into the second quarter. What the four-day 2025 event taught, and how to plan now.
A0914.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 14, 2026.
A0914.body:
Walk into a brand’s planning room in spring 2026 and the Prime Day plan on the wall probably still says July: stock landing at Amazon’s warehouses in June, creative due a few weeks before, the advertising budget parked in the third quarter. Amazon has moved the event, and that plan now runs a month late.

Amazon announced on April 29 that Prime Day 2026 will take place in June across 26 countries, earlier than its usual July timing, without giving exact dates, 9to5Toys reported. A June event pulls deal, inventory and creative deadlines into May, shifts spending into the second quarter and may separate Prime Day from rivals’ July sales. The longer 2025 event adds a second lesson about pacing, and together they argue for rebuilding stock, budgets and daily spend on the June calendar instead of adjusting the July plan.

Prime Day in June changes the quarter, not just the date

Bloomberg had reported in March that the move would shift Prime Day sales into Amazon’s second quarter, according to a Reuters report. For the brands selling on Amazon, the same shift lands in their own books. Spending that sat in the third quarter now falls in the second, which matters at any company that sets and approves budgets by quarter, and the finance team may have planned that money for July.

The competitive calendar may move as well. Walmart Deals and Target Circle Week also ran in early July 2025, Supermarket News reported, clustered around Amazon’s event. If Walmart and Target hold their summer events in July again, a June Prime Day separates them and gives brands two moments rather than one crowded week. If the rivals move too, the calendar crowds again.

What the four-day event in 2025 showed

Amazon ran Prime Day 2025 from July 8 to 11, expanding it to four days from two, Reuters reported. US online spending across retailers during the event reached $24.1 billion, up 30.3% from 2024, according to Adobe data cited by Barron’s. A year earlier the two-day event had driven $14.2 billion in US online spending, according to Adobe data cited by Chain Store Age. Doubling the length added sales, and it also spread them out.

Brands felt that spread in their own numbers. Their total sales rose 34% from the prior year during Prime Day 2025 while total ad spend rose 48%, but average daily sales fell 33% across the longer event, Pacvue reported. Cost per click fell 11% during the 2025 event, after rising 12% in 2024, Tinuiti reported.

That cheaper click may not repeat. Amazon took in $17.24 billion of advertising revenue in the first quarter of 2026, a 24% increase, SiliconANGLE reported, and more advertisers chasing Prime Day shoppers can push click prices up again. Costs on the other side of the margin are higher too: Amazon has applied a 3.5% surcharge for fuel and logistics to its fulfillment fees since April 17, 2026, CP24 reported.

Working back from June

The latest point in the calendar is the event itself, and the work runs backward from it. Deal submissions, stock shipments to Amazon’s warehouses and creative production all happen weeks before Prime Day. For a June event, that work falls in May, a month many brands had set aside for June preparation. Confirming the June deadlines for deal submissions and stock arrival is the first job, and everything else is scheduled back from those dates.

Stock is the hardest part to move. Inventory ordered for a July event may not arrive in time, and a product that runs out during Prime Day loses sales and ranking, with an effect that lasts beyond the event. Brands that import their products face the longest lead times and the least room to adjust. Sending Prime Day stock early, with room for higher demand on top sellers, protects the event days. Margins need the same early look: with the surcharge in place, discounted products deserve a check before deal prices are set.

The budget move belongs in the same weeks. Prime Day spending has to move into the second-quarter budget and get its approvals in time, because a request that arrives after the quarter’s plan is signed is a request for money nobody set aside.

Shoppers often research before the event, so the weeks leading into June are part of it. Building awareness then means shoppers already know a brand’s products when deals go live, and compare them with fewer rivals.

During the event, pacing decides who still has budget at the end. The 2025 results showed that four days raised total sales but lowered sales per day, and brands that spent heavily on the first day risked running out before the last. Setting a budget for each day, protecting spend for the final day and watching daily results replace a single event budget, since daily caps that suited a two-day event can run out early in a longer one.

July then needs its own plan. If other retailers keep their summer events in July, those sales deserve a separate budget and stock plan rather than whatever is left after June.

Take a skincare brand that planned 2025 around July and spent most of its budget in the first two days. On the June calendar, its stock deadline moves into early May, its Prime Day spending moves into the second-quarter budget, each day of the event gets its own budget, and a separate plan covers July sales at other retailers. It enters June with stock in place and budget left for the final day.

Amazon has not yet announced exact dates or the event’s length, so the plan has to hold for a range of dates in June and adjust when Amazon confirms them. Rebuilding stock, budgets and pacing on that calendar now is how we plan Prime Day in June with brands.

A0918.crumb: Trade policy and the de minimis loophole…
A0918.title: Trade policy and the de minimis loophole: what its end changed
A0918.alt: Brown paper parcels with blank tags stacked on a worn metal table beside a brass rubber stamp.
A0918.ttag: Trade policy and the de minimis loophole: what its end changed | Kwontified
A0918.desc: The US ended duty-free entry for low-value parcels in 2025. Low-price platforms moved stock into US warehouses and got faster. What that means for brands.
A0918.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 21, 2026.
A0918.body:
For years the cheapest lookalike on a marketplace carried its own handicap. It shipped as a single parcel from an overseas factory or warehouse, so the price was low and the delivery date was late. A brand selling the original from US stock could point to the calendar as much as to the product.

The de minimis loophole is what made that model pay, and its end in 2025 changed the trade-off. Once every parcel faced duties, the low-price platforms lost their cost edge on single shipments and moved toward US warehouses and local sellers. That made them faster. Brands now face cheaper rivals with stock close to the shopper, and the advantage they have left sits in trust, product information and service rather than delivery speed.

How the de minimis loophole closed

Under the de minimis rule, shipments valued at $800 or less could enter the United States duty-free, law firm White & Case explained in an alert after the July 2025 order. The volume had grown fast: de minimis shipments reached 309 million in fiscal 2025 through June 30, compared with 115 million for all of fiscal 2024, according to a White House fact sheet cited in the alert.

DateWhat changed
May 2, 2025Duty-free treatment ends for low-value packages from China and Hong Kong
July 4, 2025The One Big Beautiful Bill Act is signed, permanently repealing the legal basis for the exemption
July 30, 2025An executive order suspends duty-free de minimis treatment for all countries
August 29, 2025The suspension for all countries takes effect
July 1, 2027The statutory repeal takes effect

China came first. After the exemption ended for packages from China and Hong Kong, Temu’s US daily users fell 58% as it cut US advertising, RetailWire reported. The order for all countries and the dates in the act come from the White & Case alert, which also notes that packages sent through the international postal network are treated differently from other shipments, with duties assessed under separate methods. Which rules apply depends on how a seller ships.

Where the value went when parcels lost duty-free entry

The platforms built on the exemption shipped individual orders straight from overseas factories and warehouses. Each package entered duty-free, which kept prices low even though delivery took longer. Once every package faced duties, that single-parcel model lost much of its price advantage, and the platforms that wanted to stay cheap had to find savings elsewhere. Bulk shipments into US warehouses offered one route.

Temu was already partway there. By early 2025, local sellers accounted for about 20% of its US sales, and it had been courting sellers with US warehouses since March 2024, according to Marketplace Pulse data cited by Reuters. The end of the exemption made that shift more valuable, and the sellers already holding US stock were best placed to collect on it.

Follow the money and the picture cuts both ways for brands. Low-price rivals gave up a cost advantage at the border, but the ones that moved stock into the United States gained delivery speed. A shopper comparing a brand’s product with a cheaper lookalike may now see similar delivery dates, and the old handicap is gone.

Domestic logistics also takes a larger share. On Amazon, fulfillment fees have carried a 3.5% surcharge for fuel and logistics since April 17, 2026, CP24 reported, and an 8% USPS fuel surcharge on select package services took effect on April 26, Shippo reported. Moving stock into the United States avoids duties on each package but brings its own rising costs.

The change also reached brands that never thought of themselves as low-price sellers. Any brand that shipped small orders from abroad, including some direct-to-consumer brands with overseas fulfillment, lost duty-free treatment too and had to rethink how it serves US customers.

What brands compete on once delivery dates match

Speed stops being the tiebreaker, so the reasons to pay more have to be visible on the page. Product information, reviews, warranties and service matter more when delivery is no longer a clear advantage, and shoppers comparing similar products need a reason to choose the one that costs more. In categories where lookalikes are common, it is safer to assume cheaper competitors now hold stock in the United States and can match delivery dates. Local sellers of lookalike products can also list quickly, which makes brand protection tools worth using where they apply.

Take a home accessories brand that counted on slower delivery from low-price rivals as a reason for shoppers to choose its products. Once some of those rivals ship from US warehouses as quickly as it does, that reason disappears. The brand’s case then has to rest on what the listing shows: fuller product information, a warranty and reviews brought forward, rather than an attempt to win on speed alone.

The cost side needs the same discipline. Brands that ship small orders from abroad should price the duties and weigh holding inventory in the United States. A full landed cost for each product, including duties, freight, warehousing and marketplace fees, kept current as rules change, shows what each sale is really worth. Duties may narrow the price gap with some rivals, but tracking competitor prices beats assuming the gap has closed. With the statutory repeal set for July 1, 2027, planning as if the small-parcel exemption will not return is sensible even if the current executive order changes.

Trade policy keeps moving, and tariff rates on the goods themselves still vary by country, so none of the current rules should be treated as permanent. What has already changed is where the low-price competition sits: closer to home, faster and still cheaper, but no longer exempt from duties. Mapping which of those rivals now ship from US warehouses, and giving shoppers reasons to choose your product anyway, is the marketplace work we take on for brands facing low-price competition.

A0919.crumb: The B2B customer on Mercado Libre: why…
A0919.title: The B2B customer on Mercado Libre: why business buyers differ
A0919.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes on wooden pallets beside a yellow pallet jack in a sunlit warehouse corner.
A0919.ttag: The B2B customer on Mercado Libre: why business buyers differ | Kwontified
A0919.desc: Mercado Libre now serves business buyers through Negocios. They order more, return less and value invoices and steady stock over a few cents saved.
A0919.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 26, 2026.
A0919.body:
Mercado Libre says business buyers on its platform can get discounts of up to 50%. That sounds like a race to the lowest unit price, and for a consumer buying one bottle of floor cleaner it can be. A purchasing manager buying for an office behaves differently, because the price of a unit is only part of what a purchase costs the company.

That buyer orders on behalf of a business, reorders the same items in volume and has to account for every purchase with a valid invoice. A missed delivery or an invoice that accounting rejects costs more than a few cents saved per unit. The B2B customer on Mercado Libre rewards the seller that fits its purchasing process, through business pricing, invoices, sensible pack sizes and reliable stock, more than the seller with the lowest price.

Where the B2B customer on Mercado Libre stands

Mercado Libre Negocios is a unit dedicated to business and wholesale transactions, serving small businesses, large companies and government buyers. More than 4 million users across Latin America have been authorized to make wholesale purchases since testing began in late 2024, Digital Commerce 360 reported. Companies open accounts linked to their tax ID to reach volume discounts, approved invoices and financing through Mercado Pago. The service was live in Argentina, Mexico and Chile, with more than 2.6 million products listed in Argentina alone, according to the same report.

Brazil has its own version. Mercado Livre launched its Brazilian business unit with more than 1.3 million products priced for businesses, and the most sought-after items included office supplies, technology, food, cleaning supplies, furnishings and auto parts, Exame reported. Registered business buyers there pay lower shipping costs, which Mercado Livre said would help them cut logistics costs and offer more competitive prices. The company also cited Statista estimates that business-to-business e-commerce is about four times larger than consumer e-commerce worldwide.

The platform underneath is growing fast. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Mercado Libre’s revenue grew 45% to $8.8 billion and its gross merchandise volume grew 37% to $19.9 billion, the company said in its fourth-quarter results.

Why a business buyer weighs process above price

A consumer pays the shelf price and walks away. A business buyer carries the purchase into its own books, and that changes the arithmetic. The relevant cost is the unit price plus everything that can go wrong around it. That includes a delivery that misses the day the office needed it, stock that runs out between orders, an invoice that fails the country’s tax rules and has to be chased. Each of those creates work or risk for the company, and none of them shows up in the listing price.

So the order pattern differs too. Mercado Libre says wholesale customers typically place larger, more frequent orders with lower return rates, according to the Digital Commerce 360 report. A seller that wins one order from a business may win a stream of them, because once a purchasing manager finds a supplier that delivers, invoices correctly and stays in stock, switching carries its own cost.

The way business buyers search follows from the same logic. They usually know what they need and look by item, size and quantity. Listings that show unit counts, case quantities and business prices plainly let them buy in one pass.

The trade-off for a brand is real on both sides. Business pricing narrows the margin on each unit, and the discounts on offer can be steep. Against that, the buyer orders more at a time, comes back more often and sends less back. Which side wins depends on the product: items businesses consume and reorder, such as office, cleaning, food service or auto supplies, have the repeat volume to cover a thinner unit margin, while a product bought once rarely does. The numbers lean toward serving business buyers where the product fits that reorder pattern, and toward leaving it alone where it does not.

Take a cleaning supplies brand that sells single bottles to consumers on Mercado Libre at the lowest price it can manage. Adding case packs, business pricing for tax-ID accounts and invoicing that works every time is the move that could bring repeat orders from offices and small restaurants, buyers who reorder on a schedule and rarely return items. The test is whether that volume and repeat business make up for the lower price per unit.

Selling to business buyers on Mercado Libre

Pricing and paperwork come first. Volume tiers or business prices for tax-ID accounts, set where margins allow, give business buyers a reason to choose a listing. Invoicing has to work for every order in every country served, since tax rules and invoice formats differ across Latin America, and a single rejected invoice can lose an account.

Pack sizes and shipping follow. Case packs and multi-unit listings suit buyers who order in volume and can lower shipping and handling costs per unit. Larger orders weigh more and may ship to offices or stores, so shipping costs and delivery options for business addresses deserve their own check.

Stock and payment terms keep the account. Repeat buyers expect items to be available every time, which argues for forecasting business demand separately from consumer demand. Mercado Pago financing can help business buyers place larger orders, and it is worth understanding how that affects when the brand gets paid.

The measure that matters is the reorder. Track how often business accounts come back, because a business account that orders monthly can be worth far more than its first purchase suggests. The rule for this channel is simple: serve the business buyer’s process, and price will matter less. Setting that up country by country is part of how we run Mercado Libre for brands across Latin America.

A0921.crumb: Health and household on Amazon in 2026…
A0921.title: Health and household on Amazon in 2026: what changed
A0921.alt: Amber glass pump bottles, a kraft refill pouch and a soap bar with cotton pads on a wooden bathroom shelf.
A0921.ttag: Health and household on Amazon in 2026: what changed | Kwontified
A0921.desc: Everyday essentials became one of Amazon’s fastest-growing businesses. What changed in health and household, and why brands now compete on the reorder.
A0921.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published May 28, 2026.
A0921.body:
Nobody browses for paper towels the second time. Once a shopper finds a roll, a dish soap or a vitamin they trust, the next order is usually a reorder, placed with little or no searching. The shelf the brand fought for on the first visit barely matters on the fifth. That habit sits at the center of how health and household on Amazon now works.

The category has become one driven by repeat purchases. In early 2025, everyday essentials were growing faster than everything else Amazon sells in the United States, and health subcategories crowded the list of its fastest growers. For brands, that changes the contest: it is won on what repeat buying rewards, meaning subscriptions, steady stock, compliant claims and trusted reviews, while cheaper alternatives keep pressing on price.

Health and household on Amazon grew on the reorder

In the first quarter of 2025, Amazon’s everyday essentials grew more than twice as fast as all other categories in the United States and represented one out of every three units sold, Amazon said in a 2025 post. Amazon counts groceries and household essentials together in that measure and offers nearly 3 million of them. Its definition reaches into the center of the store: pantry staples, pet care, health and personal care, and household goods like dish soap, paper towels and batteries.

Health stands out within that. Health and household subcategories made up 20% of the 100 fastest-growing subcategories on Amazon in the first half of 2025, measured by raw revenue gain, according to an analysis by Momentum Commerce published by PMG. Over-the-counter medication posted the largest raw dollar gain, up 7%, the analysis said.

Amazon is also building the reorder into its assistants. With its Auto Buy feature, a customer can tell the shopping assistant to buy a product on its own once the price reaches a level the customer sets, Modern Retail reported. On May 13, Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping, combining its Rufus assistant with Alexa+, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

The economics underneath are tight. Since April 17, 2026, Amazon’s fulfillment fees have included a 3.5% surcharge covering fuel and logistics, CP24 reported, and fees weigh most on low-priced essentials, where the margin on each unit is thin.

Why the first order is worth more than it looks

Delivery speed is what made essentials an online habit. Shoppers buy everyday items online when delivery is fast enough to replace a store trip, and Amazon has invested in delivery for these items, its post said. Fast delivery turns an occasional online purchase into a routine one, and a routine purchase is a reorder.

That makes the first sale the expensive one and the later ones cheap. Many essentials sell at low prices, so fees and advertising take a large share of each sale. A brand that pays for advertising on every order can struggle to make the numbers work, while a brand with loyal repeat buyers spreads those costs over many purchases. Subscriptions that schedule repeat deliveries go further, keeping customers on the same brand without sending them back to a search page where a competitor is waiting.

Assistants add to the incumbent’s edge. When a shopper can ask an assistant to reorder a product, or tell it to buy at a set price, the brand already in that shopper’s history starts ahead. Winning the first purchase may keep the customer with little further effort.

Health raises the stakes on trust. Shoppers buying medication, supplements or personal care products care about safety and accuracy, and clear ingredients, honest claims and strong reviews help them decide. Misleading claims can damage a brand quickly. Health products also face rules on claims, labeling and approval that vary by product type, and compliance problems can remove listings altogether.

Price pressure never goes away. Essentials are easy to compare, and shoppers often switch to cheaper options when products look alike, so a brand has to show on the page why its product is worth more.

What a brand built for the reorder looks like

The first purchase deserves the investment, in content, reviews and advertising, because repeat orders follow it. Subscription offers should be clear and attractive for anything bought on a regular schedule. Pack sizes do quieter work: larger multipacks suit repeat buyers and can improve value per unit, while smaller trial sizes let new shoppers try a product at lower risk.

Stock is the part that breaks most easily. Running out interrupts subscriptions and sends shoppers to competitors, so careful demand forecasting and safety stock protect the reorder itself. Consistent product names, sizes and variants matter for the same reason, since assistants and shoppers both need to find the same item again.

Claims need a process, not a copywriter’s judgment. Every health or performance claim should be reviewed for accuracy and compliance before it goes live, with the evidence behind it on file. Clear ingredients, usage instructions and certifications do the rest of the trust work, and they are also how a brand shows what makes it different from the cheaper option beside it, whether that is quality, ingredients or effectiveness.

Take a supplement brand that relies on advertising to win each sale and watches those costs rise. Adding multipacks, encouraging subscriptions, improving ingredient information and keeping stock steady are the moves that shift it toward repeat orders, and advertising cost per customer can fall as those orders build.

The measure that ties it together is lifetime value. Judging advertising on repeat orders and subscriptions, and not only on the first sale, is how a health and household brand sees what its spend is really buying. Building that view of the reorder into an Amazon plan is part of how we run health and household brands on Amazon.

A0917.crumb: The SP-API MCP: what changes for brands…
A0917.title: The SP-API MCP: what changes for brands running their own data
A0917.alt: Small locked white cabinet with a glass door showing glowing server drives, on a sideboard beside dried branches.
A0917.ttag: The SP-API MCP: what changes for brands running their own data | Kwontified
A0917.desc: Amazon dropped its planned SP-API fees and released AI tools for its seller API. Building got cheaper, so the risk moves to what automation may do.
A0917.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 1, 2026.
A0917.body:
From November 2025, a brand weighing a custom Amazon integration faced two costs: developers who knew the Selling Partner API (SP-API), the interface sellers use to pull data and automate tasks, and a planned annual fee for using it. In May 2026 Amazon dropped the fee, and later that month it released tools that let AI coding assistants do much of the developer’s work.

Building automation on a brand’s own Amazon data just got cheaper and easier. That moves the hard part of the job. When almost anyone can build a workflow that touches a live account, what matters is controlling what it is allowed to do: build where a workflow is unique, buy where it is common, and set firm rules for credentials, testing and approvals.

What changed with the SP-API MCP

Amazon’s Selling Partner Developer Services team announced Local MCP for SP-API on May 28, 2026. The package lets AI coding assistants search the Selling Partner API documentation, generate code, review integrations, guide version migrations and build multi-step workflows, according to its announcement. Tools that make live API calls require SP-API credentials, while the rest run locally without them, the post said.

The fee reversal came first. Amazon had announced on November 3, 2025 that third-party developers would pay a $1,400 annual subscription from January 31, 2026 and usage fees from April 30, 2026, PPC Land reported. It postponed the fees indefinitely on March 9, 2026, and on May 12, 2026, it told developers it would not move forward with the usage and annual fees, Nova Data reported. The annual subscription will not be billed for 2026, according to the report.

The advertising side opened earlier. Amazon Ads launched an MCP server for advertising in February 2026, PPC Land reported, so both the selling and the advertising interfaces now accept AI agents.

Why cheaper building moves the risk to control

An integration with Amazon’s seller API used to need specialized developers who knew its endpoints, rate limits and version changes. An AI assistant with the documentation and code generation tools can now handle much of that work, and the cost falls twice. Developers spend less time writing and updating integrations, and the cancelled fees remove a planned charge on tools built for others. Work that once needed a dedicated engineering team may now be within reach of a small operations team with one capable developer.

Software vendors gain from the same changes. Companies and agencies that build on the Selling Partner API also avoid the cancelled fees and can use the same AI tools, so brands that buy software may see faster product updates. It is fair to ask a vendor whether some of the savings will reach its customers.

That shifts the build-versus-buy line. A brand that relied on third-party software for every task can now build specific tools for the workflows that matter to it, such as replenishment rules, custom reports or listing checks.

The catch is what cheap building does to risk. When the cost of writing a workflow approaches the cost of describing it, more workflows get written, and each one that can create shipments or change listings can cause real damage if it runs on the wrong data or without review. The scarce skill moves from writing code to deciding what automation may do.

Take a home goods brand whose team uses AI tools to build a workflow that checks stock and creates replenishment shipments automatically. Suppose a data error in testing would have sent the wrong quantities. An approval requirement for shipments above a set size, plus a first run against a sandbox account, catches the problem before any shipment exists. Without those two rules, the same error ships.

None of this makes building the default. Many brands lack in-house developers, and commercial software still brings support, security reviews and features that would be costly to rebuild. Building pays only where a brand’s workflow is truly different.

Rules for SP-API automation on live accounts

Start with an inventory. List the Amazon tasks the team repeats most, such as reporting, replenishment and listing updates, and mark which are unique to the business and which take the most staff time. Custom automation fits the workflows that commercial tools handle poorly or that give the brand an edge, while standard reporting and common tasks are usually better served by established software.

Credentials and testing come before anything goes live. Limit who and what can use live SP-API credentials, store them securely and rotate them when people or tools change. Run new workflows against test accounts or with limited scope first, and check their output against manual records. Any workflow that creates shipments, changes prices or edits listings should need human approval above a set threshold, and every automation should leave a log of what it did and when, so problems can be traced.

Upkeep is the part teams forget. Amazon updates API versions over time, and an integration that falls behind can stop working without warning, so the migration tools need an owner who keeps integrations current. The new package’s migration guidance gives that owner a head start, but someone still has to schedule the work and check the result. Contracts deserve a look too: with the planned developer fees cancelled, check whether vendors priced those fees into their agreements and ask for an adjustment where they did.

The working rule is to build what is unique, buy what is common and control everything that touches a live account. Drawing that line, and writing the approval rules before the first workflow runs, is part of how we help brands automate safely on their Amazon data.

A0924.crumb: Prime Day 2026 forecast: ranges for a…
A0924.title: Prime Day 2026 forecast: ranges for a four-day June event
A0924.alt: Four kraft-paper gifts tied with twine and sprigs of rosemary, thyme and eucalyptus on a sunny windowsill.
A0924.ttag: Prime Day 2026 forecast: ranges for a four-day June event | Kwontified
A0924.desc: Prime Day 2026 runs June 23 to 26, as long as the 2025 event, so last year’s growth will not repeat. Our ranges for spending, brand sales and click costs.
A0924.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 3, 2026.
A0924.body:
Prime Day 2025 lifted US online spending across retailers 30.3% above the year before, and that number is about to anchor a lot of 2026 plans. It should not. Much of the jump came from a one-time change: Amazon doubled the event from two days to four. Prime Day 2026 is four days again, so the length effect is gone, while the price of a click keeps rising with advertising demand.

Kwontified’s forecast builds in both forces. We expect US online spending across retailers during Prime Day 2026 to rise 5% to 18% from 2025. For brands running deals and advertising into the event, we expect sales to rise 5% to 20% from their own 2025 event, and cost per click to rise 5% to 15%. Planning for the middle of those ranges, and pacing budgets to protect margin, beats planning for another year like 2025.

The Prime Day 2026 forecast by scenario

ScenarioUS online spending vs 2025Implied spendingBrand event sales vs 2025Cost per click vs 2025
Conservative+5%$25.3 billion+5%+5%
Standard+10%$26.5 billion+12%+10%
Reach+18%$28.4 billion+20%+15%

The implied spending applies each growth rate to the 2025 base of $24.1 billion. The standard case is the reference figure; the other two set the range a plan should survive.

The calendar is now confirmed. Amazon announced on June 2 that Prime Day 2026 will run from June 23 through June 26 across more than 35 categories, with early deals already live, iClarified reported, citing Amazon’s announcement.

Why last year’s growth will not repeat

Prime Day 2025 ran four days, July 8 to 11, after Amazon expanded it from two, Reuters reported. Adobe data cited by Barron’s put US online spending across retailers for those four days at $24.1 billion, 30.3% more than in 2024, when the two-day event generated $14.2 billion, according to Adobe figures cited by Chain Store Age.

The pull of that 30.3% is easy to understand. It is the most recent number, it is large, and it describes the same event, so it feels like the natural starting point for this year’s target. But it measures two extra days as much as it measures shopper demand.

The 2025 detail shows how. The two extra days added volume and thinned each day: brands’ total sales grew 34% over the 2025 event, yet average daily sales dropped 33%, Pacvue reported. With the 2026 event the same length, growth has to come from more shoppers, larger baskets or more deals, and none of those doubled. A plan anchored on 30.3% would set stock and budgets for growth the calendar no longer supplies.

Click costs pull in the opposite direction. Cost per click slipped 11% during the 2025 event after climbing 12% in 2024, Tinuiti reported. Amazon’s advertising revenue rose 24% to $17.24 billion in the first quarter of 2026, while its online stores grew 12%, SiliconANGLE reported. Ad revenue growing about twice as fast as store sales means more advertisers bidding for the same shoppers, which tends to push click costs back up after the 2025 dip.

The event’s design changes the rhythm too. Amazon will add limited-time offers through Today’s Big Deals three times a day, at 12 a.m., 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. Pacific time, and shoppers can use Alexa for Shopping to check price history and buy automatically at a target price, the iClarified report said. Traffic may spike around those deal drops, and shoppers can judge discounts more easily. Moving the event from July to June may also shift some back-to-school demand and changes how Prime Day sits beside other retailers’ summer sales.

These are ranges, not results. Prime Day outcomes depend on deals, shopper mood and competition, and a June Prime Day has no recent precedent to check against, which is why the plan should hold across all three cases.

Planning a four-day event on the ranges

Take a kitchen brand that planned 2025 around strong growth from the longer event and spent heavily on day one. For 2026, the forecast suggests a standard-case target of 12% sales growth, a budget that absorbs a 10% rise in click costs, spend split across the four days, and extra stock on its best sellers. Front-loading day one is exactly the habit the 2025 daily numbers punished.

The same logic carries across a portfolio. Stock and budgets belong on the standard case, with fallback plans for the conservative and reach cases, and margins should hold even if click costs land at the high end. Stock on top products should cover the reach case, because running out costs both sales and ranking. Brands with strong conversion and well-stocked best sellers can lean toward the higher end of sales growth; brands in crowded categories should plan for the higher end of click costs.

Pacing is where the 2025 lesson pays. Treat the event as four separate days, each with its own budget, and keep spend in reserve for June 26. Budget caps sized for the old two-day format can run dry early, so reset them before June 23 rather than in the middle of the event. Advertising should go first to products that convert well, since higher click costs hurt them least. Brands with deals in the daily drops should watch results hour by hour and adjust bids around each release.

Afterward, compare the result with your own 2025 event, not with the market headline, and carry the difference into the next plan. Pacing the four days against these ranges, and judging the event on margin rather than last year’s growth rate, is how we plan Prime Day with brands.

A0925.crumb: Instagram Shop versus TikTok Shop: where…
A0925.title: Instagram Shop versus TikTok Shop: where to invest in 2026
A0925.alt: Two smartphones with colorful abstract wallpapers standing in oak stands on a wooden table.
A0925.ttag: Instagram Shop versus TikTok Shop: where to invest in 2026 | Kwontified
A0925.desc: TikTok Shop keeps the sale inside the app, while Instagram now sends shoppers to brand websites. Why that split should decide where a brand puts its money.
A0925.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 4, 2026.
A0925.body:
When Instagram and TikTok sit on one budget line called social commerce, the planning debate becomes a question of how to split that line between them. That framing assumes the two platforms do the same job. Since 2025 they have not. TikTok Shop keeps discovery and checkout inside its app, while Meta moved Instagram and Facebook Shops to checkout on the brand’s own website.

So the decision in front of a marketing leader is less about which platform is bigger and more about which job each one does for the brand. TikTok Shop now works as a store. Instagram works as a source of traffic. The money should follow the role: TikTok Shop behind products that sell through content and creators, and Instagram behind brands whose own websites convert well.

Where Instagram Shop versus TikTok Shop stands

TikTok Shop is a fast-growing store. Its US gross merchandise value rose 68% to $15.1 billion in 2025, led by beauty and personal care, then womenswear and underwear, then sports and outdoors, according to Momentum Works and Tabcut data cited by DealStreetAsia. The growth was broad: every category grew on TikTok Shop in the US in the first half of 2025, with kids’ fashion growing fastest, according to a Momentum Works report.

Shoppers buy in more than one place inside the app. In 2025, live streams’ share of TikTok Shop’s US sales went from 10% to 14%, and the Shop tab’s share went from 32% to 36%, TechNode Global reported. TikTok is also steering advertising toward automation: Shop merchants must run GMV Max, the platform’s automated campaign type, Digiday reported.

Instagram went the other way. Meta began moving Facebook and Instagram Shops from in-app checkout to website checkout in June 2025, Shopifreaks reported. Shops ads now support only the Purchase conversion event, as checkout moves to merchants’ websites, PPC Land reported, and PPC Land wrote in its analysis that the move suggests Meta is prioritizing advertising revenue over fees from transactions. Meta has automated too. For sales objectives, its automated campaign structure is now the default, with manual controls still available, PPC Land reported.

Two platforms, two jobs inside the brand

On TikTok, a shopper can watch a video, see a product, buy it and go back to scrolling without leaving the app. Content, creators and checkout sit in one place, so the platform sees the whole path from video to purchase and handles the order. On Instagram, shoppers still discover products in posts, Reels and ads, but the purchase finishes on the brand’s website. The brand keeps the customer relationship and the order data, and the sale depends on how well its own site converts.

That split lands on different teams. TikTok Shop needs a steady flow of videos, creator partnerships and live streams, plus fulfillment that meets TikTok’s shipping and service standards, which pulls in content, partnerships and operations. Instagram needs strong creative for ads and posts and a website that converts visitors quickly, which pulls in the e-commerce and web teams. A single social commerce line hides the fact that each platform is really a request on a different part of the company.

Measurement splits the same way. TikTok Shop reports sales inside the platform. Instagram’s results depend on tracking visits and purchases on the brand’s site, which can be harder to connect, especially when a shopper sees an ad on one device and buys on another. Judging Instagram by sales inside the app would undercount it, and judging TikTok Shop by website visits would miss most of what it does.

Take a beauty brand that sells well on TikTok Shop through creator videos and live streams, but whose website converts poorly. Its Instagram Reels build awareness and engagement, yet few sales. For that brand, the next Instagram dollar does little until its product pages improve; once they do, Instagram ads have somewhere to send shoppers, and TikTok Shop can stay its main social store.

Both platforms change their commerce features often, and results vary by category, so neither role is permanent. That argues for small, measured tests before large budgets move.

How to split the social commerce budget

Product fit is the opening question for the room. Products that sell through demonstration, creators and impulse suit TikTok Shop, because the video that shows the product and the button that sells it sit on the same screen. Products that need research or carry higher prices may do better as Instagram traffic sent to a strong website, with landing pages that match the product in the ad so shoppers do not have to search again.

Capacity comes next, meaning whether the brand can actually supply what each role demands week after week. Instagram spend is only as good as the site it lands on, so page speed and conversion come before scale. TikTok Shop rewards a steady stream of videos and live streams, so creator and production budgets come before commitment, along with an affiliate program with clear commissions and sample plans that tracks which creators actually drive orders. Fulfillment has to meet TikTok’s standards before launch.

Each platform also needs its own scorecard, or the comparison between them will mislead. TikTok Shop belongs on sales and margin inside the platform, net of its fees and affiliate commissions. Instagram belongs on the traffic and website sales it drives, with its cost sitting mainly in advertising. Comparing the full cost of a sale on each, before either scales, keeps the split honest. Building both roles and measuring them separately is how we run TikTok Shop and Instagram for brands.

A0926.crumb: Grocery and CPG on TikTok Shop: why…
A0926.title: Grocery and CPG on TikTok Shop: why bundles beat single items
A0926.alt: Wooden crate tied with twine holding jars of grains, a burlap coffee sack, dried pasta and olive oil.
A0926.ttag: Grocery and CPG on TikTok Shop: why bundles beat single items | Kwontified
A0926.desc: Low unit prices leave CPG brands little margin on TikTok Shop once fees, commissions and shipping are paid. Why bundles and product tests do better.
A0926.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 9, 2026.
A0926.body:
A bag of chips is close to the ideal TikTok product. It costs a few dollars, it looks good on camera and nobody deliberates before buying one. Those same traits make it hard to sell at a profit on TikTok Shop. Every order carries platform fees, creator commissions and the cost of picking, packing and shipping. Much of that cost stays put whether the box holds one item or several.

That is why CPG brands on TikTok Shop should lead with bundles, multipacks and limited editions rather than single items, and treat the platform as a place to test new products before scaling them in other channels. The bundle is usually the offer that still makes money after the order’s costs are paid.

Grocery and CPG on TikTok Shop now draw the largest brands

Demand is not the constraint. TikTok Shop’s food and beverage category has more than doubled since early 2024, and TikTok Shop as a whole has grown 120% year over year, said Amanda Parker, TikTok Shop’s head of food, as Modern Retail reported. Early success came mainly from smaller entrepreneurs, and major CPG companies such as Mars and Coca-Cola have now joined TikTok Shop, according to the same report.

TikTok is pitching itself to these brands as a test lab. Food and beverage brands can introduce new flavors or products, do research and development, or offer limited-time flavors on TikTok Shop, work they historically did through grocery partners, the report said. TikTok is reaching into fresh food as well, working with select brands and sellers to offer fresh meat products in the US. TikTok Shop also guides food and beverage brands on how to work with creators and whether to buy top-of-funnel ads.

Vitamins and supplements are the largest category on TikTok Shop, according to a NielsenIQ presentation at Expo West in March 2026.

The platform around these categories keeps getting bigger. In 2025, TikTok Shop’s US gross merchandise value grew 68% to $15.1 billion, per Momentum Works and Tabcut figures that DealStreetAsia cited. Live streams took a growing slice of it, with their share of TikTok Shop’s US sales rising from 10% to 14% in 2025, TechNode Global reported. The advertising side runs on automation, since Shop merchants have to run GMV Max, TikTok’s automated campaign type, Digiday reported.

A cheap item carries the same order costs as an expensive one

Grocery and CPG products suit TikTok for reasons any category manager would recognize. They are inexpensive, easy to show in a short video and often bought on impulse, so a snack, drink or cleaning product can go from video to cart in seconds.

The low price is also where the trouble starts. Platform fees, affiliate commissions for creators and the cost of picking, packing and shipping attach to every order. Many of them do not shrink when the product is cheap. On a low-priced single item, they can consume most or all of the margin.

Take a snack brand that sells a single bag for $5, and say picking, packing and shipping cost $4 an order regardless of what is in the box.

Per orderSingle bagFour-bag variety pack
Price$5$20
Pick, pack and ship$4$4
Share of the price spent on fulfillment80%20%

On the single bag, 80% of the price is gone before the platform fee, the creator’s commission or the product itself has been paid for. The variety pack carries the same $4 across a larger sale, so fulfillment takes 20% and the rest of the cost stack has room to fit. That is the whole argument for bundles in one row: the same shipping and handling now supports a bigger basket.

Brands often lead with their cheapest single item because it makes the purchase easy. On TikTok Shop, the better offer for many CPG brands is the larger bundle, because it is the one that can make money after costs.

Novelty pushes in the same direction. Limited editions and new flavors give creators a reason to post and shoppers a reason to buy now, and a brand can learn which products resonate before committing to wider distribution. Back to the snack brand: launching with variety packs and a limited-edition flavor bundle instead of single bags raises the value of each order, and the limited flavor’s sales tell the brand which flavor to produce in larger volumes.

Where the bundle argument runs out

Bundles raise the price of entry, which can reduce first-time purchases. That cost is real, and it argues for testing bundle sizes rather than abandoning them. A smaller trial bundle can lower the barrier to a first order while still covering what the order costs.

Shelf life sets the second limit. Food products need careful stock planning, since short shelf life limits how much a brand can hold. A viral moment can sell out stock quickly, and slow weeks can leave product sitting near its expiry date.

Prices, commissions and ad targets all answer to the order margin

The pricing work comes before launch. Calculate each order’s full cost, including fees, commissions, packaging and shipping, and set prices from that number rather than from the shelf price in a grocery store.

Creators need the same discipline. Creators who show products in use help shoppers decide quickly, which is why the commission matters: set it at a level that still leaves a margin, and favor creators whose audiences match the product, such as home cooks for pantry items.

Advertising is where single items creep back in. Automated campaigns aim for sales, not profit, so set their targets on margin after fees; otherwise the campaign can end up pushing unprofitable single items.

Then take the results elsewhere. The flavors and products that sell through TikTok Shop are evidence for which ones to scale in grocery stores and other marketplaces, which turns the platform’s test-lab pitch into a planning input.

The test for any TikTok Shop offer is whether the order still makes money once fulfillment, fees and commission are paid; if fixed costs take most of the price, change the offer before buying more traffic. Pricing bundles against the full cost of the order is how we run TikTok Shop for CPG brands.

A0928.title: Building a marketplace-ready brand for Target Plus
A0928.alt: Stack of red gift boxes tied with twine beside a spool of red ribbon and a roll of kraft paper on a table.
A0928.ttag: Building a marketplace-ready brand for Target Plus | Kwontified
A0928.desc: Target Plus is invite-only, with one seller per item, so Target judges a brand before it applies. How to look ready for its marketplace before an invitation.
A0928.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 11, 2026.
A0928.body:
Nothing reaches a shelf in a Target store without a buyer deciding it belongs there. Target Plus, the company’s online marketplace, runs on the same instinct. It is invite-only and curated, with one vendor per item, Fortune reported, so a brand cannot simply list its catalog and start competing the way it can on an open marketplace.

That leaves a brand that wants in with an awkward question: what should it do before anyone asks? The answer is to become marketplace-ready in advance. That means meeting Target’s standards for assortment fit, content, reliable operations and guest experience, and planning Roundel advertising and Target’s new creator programs alongside them, so the brand already looks like a good partner when an invitation arrives.

Target Plus is selective, and Target wants it much bigger

Selective does not mean static. Target wants Target Plus, which starts from more than $1 billion of gross merchandise value, to reach more than $5 billion within five years, according to Modern Retail. Target also partnered with Shopify to bring more merchants to Target Plus, according to the Fortune report.

Growth has followed in recent quarters. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Target’s marketplace posted growth of more than 30%, according to the company’s quarterly results. In the first quarter of 2026, non-merchandise sales grew 24.6%, reflecting growth in Roundel advertising, Target Circle 360 membership and the Target+ marketplace, Target said in its first-quarter results. Comparable digital sales rose 8.9% in that quarter, led by more than 27% growth in same-day delivery powered by Target Circle 360.

Creators have become part of the plan as well. In a May 6 announcement, Target launched Club Target for everyday creators and Target Ambassadors, powered by LTK, for established creators.

On a curated marketplace, the brand is judged before it applies

The model is defined by curation. On an open marketplace, many sellers compete on the same listing and the shopper sorts them out. Target Plus lists one seller per item, Target chooses who sells, and it protects the guest experience by being selective. The marketplace has borrowed the logic of the store aisle, and that changes what readiness means: elsewhere a brand can list first and earn its place later, while at Target it has to look like a good partner first. Target is likely to look for products that fit its assortment, content that matches its standards and operations that will not disappoint its guests.

In a store, a buyer can judge whether a product fits the aisle by standing in front of it. Online, the clearest evidence of fit a brand can offer is what it has already done elsewhere: its listings, its reviews and its record on other channels. That record works as the brand’s portfolio, and it is built long before any conversation with Target starts.

Of all of these, reliability matters most. A seller that ships late or runs out of stock reflects on Target. Brands with clean records on other marketplaces, such as fast shipping and few cancellations, are better placed to be trusted.

Content has to fit the house style. Target’s site has a consistent look and tone, so brands with strong images, clear descriptions and accurate details fit more easily, and they may convert better once listed.

Values can help, though they are not a stated rule. Target reported that 34% of its owned-brand products met its criteria for reusable, recyclable or compostable packaging in its 2025 sustainability report, Packaging Journal reported. Brands with credible sustainability or quality credentials may stand out in a curated assortment, but there is no public evidence that such credentials are required.

None of this comes with a guarantee. Target does not publish a full checklist for invitations, and its priorities can change, so readiness improves a brand’s chances rather than securing a place.

A seat on the marketplace comes with an ad plan and a creator plan

Target+ sits beside Roundel advertising and the new creator programs inside the business, and a brand that joins can use both to build demand. A new listing needs visibility, which is why a Roundel budget belongs in the launch plan rather than in a later quarter. Early advertising helps build sales history and reviews, and those support the listing over time. The creator programs offer another way to build demand, so the brand should know before launch how creators will feature its products.

Take a home décor brand that sells well on its own website and on Amazon but has not been invited to Target Plus. Its work is unglamorous: clean up its shipping record, rebuild product content to a higher standard and narrow its range to the products that fit Target’s style. If Target expands the marketplace, a brand in that state can apply through a partner channel and launch with strong content from day one, instead of starting the cleanup after the invitation.

Questions to settle before an invitation arrives

  • Which of our products suit Target’s guests, and which should stay out? A smaller, well-chosen range often makes a stronger first impression than a full catalog.
  • Do our shipping, stock and service records on other channels show we can meet Target’s delivery expectations, including fast shipping, with enough stock to support demand if a product takes off?
  • Do our images, titles and descriptions match the quality Target guests expect, and do we present our sustainability, safety or quality credentials clearly and accurately, without overstating them?
  • Who will track sales, ratings, shipping performance and advertising returns once we are live? Strong results can support a wider assortment over time.

Waiting passively for Target to call is the one approach these questions rule out; routes such as Target’s partnership with Shopify exist for brands that prepare. Building that readiness into the catalog, the operations and the Roundel plan is how we help brands get ready for Target Plus.

A0930.crumb: Can Zalando defend Europe against Shein…
A0930.title: Can Zalando defend Europe against Shein, Temu and Vinted?
A0930.alt: Camel coat displayed in an arched shop window and a rack of bagged coats on a sunny cobblestone street.
A0930.ttag: Can Zalando defend Europe against Shein, Temu and Vinted? | Kwontified
A0930.desc: Shein, Temu and Vinted win on price, a fight Zalando cannot win. Why Zalando can still defend branded fashion in Europe, and how brands should split plans.
A0930.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 16, 2026.
A0930.body:
In 2025, Vinted’s gross merchandise volume rose 47% to 10.8 billion euros, MarketScreener reported. Zalando’s gross merchandise value grew 14.7% that year. Add the parcels: about 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, more than 90% of them from China, SGI Europe reported. On growth rates and parcel counts, the price-led rivals look like the side that is winning Europe.

Shein and Temu compete on very low prices through direct parcels, and Vinted competes on low prices through second-hand goods. Zalando cannot win on price, and the arithmetic of its business says it should not try. What it can defend is the branded middle of European fashion, through membership, service and AI-driven discovery, with some help from a new EU parcel duty from July 2026. For brands, that means using Zalando for full-price, branded sales and planning separately for shoppers who put price first.

Zalando, Shein, Temu and Vinted are selling to different instincts

Zalando is still growing strongly. In 2025 it took gross merchandise value to 17.6 billion euros, up 14.7%, with a record 62 million active customers, the company said in its 2025 results. First-quarter gross merchandise value rose 21.7% to 4.3 billion euros, a figure that includes About You, which Zalando acquired in 2025, RTÉ reported, citing Reuters.

The loyalty base sits underneath those totals. The Zalando Plus membership program counted 16.8 million members, and they produced nearly half of the gross merchandise value in the fourth quarter. Retail media revenue rose 42% in 2025, the company said. Zalando is also strengthening its European logistics network, which it has opened to partners, and images created with AI helped it publish about 85% more content, the RTÉ report said. Its AI-driven discovery feed reached more than 9 million weekly users, according to the 2025 results.

Vinted is growing faster from a different base. Its revenue rose 38% to 1.1 billion euros in 2025, as it expanded into categories such as electronics and homeware and launched in three new countries, RTÉ reported, citing Reuters. Net profit fell to 62 million euros from 77 million euros, which Vinted attributed to investments in cheaper delivery in Germany, new categories and new countries, according to the same report.

2025ZalandoVinted
Merchandise volume17.6 billion euros, up 14.7%10.8 billion euros, up 47%
What the shopper comes forBrands, membership and serviceLow prices on second-hand goods

Brussels has picked a side on the parcels. EU finance ministers agreed on December 12, 2025 to set a 3-euro customs duty on low-value parcels from July 1, 2026, as part of efforts to curb cheap imports from platforms such as Shein and Temu, Reuters reported.

The price floor belongs to the parcel sellers and the resale market

Each player’s lowest possible price is set by what it has to pay for. Shein and Temu ship individual parcels from Chinese factories at very low prices. Vinted lets shoppers buy second-hand items, often cheaper than new. All three appeal to shoppers who put price first.

Zalando sells mostly branded new goods, and it carries the costs of stocking, delivering and handling returns for those brands. It cannot match Shein, Temu or Vinted on price without destroying its own margins.

So Zalando competes on something else. Membership, fast delivery, easy returns and a wide range of trusted brands appeal to shoppers who value convenience and quality, and the Plus numbers show that base already carries the business: members generated nearly half of the fourth quarter’s gross merchandise value. Discovery adds to the case. If shoppers start their fashion search inside Zalando’s feed, the price comparison with Shein matters less.

Policy helps at the margin. The 3-euro duty raises the cost of each cheap parcel, narrowing the gap between direct imports and products sold from European stock. It is not a permanent wall, since Shein and Temu may adapt by holding stock in Europe and avoiding the parcel duty.

Matching the rivals on price, and why the numbers lean against it

For a brand selling on Zalando, the case for cutting prices is real. Vinted’s growth and the parcel volumes show how many European shoppers put price first, and second-hand fashion competes for the same wardrobes. A brand watching lookalikes sell cheaply on Temu will feel the pull.

The case against is in Zalando’s own figures. Its most valuable shoppers are members who come for brands they recognize and service they trust, and retail media gives brands a paid way to reach them. Zalando’s strongest defense is to look less like a discount store. Chasing Shein on price would pull it into a fight it cannot win and weaken the brand partnerships that set it apart. The same logic applies to a brand on its shelves: deep discounts undercut full-price positioning, because shoppers who learn to wait for markdowns stop paying full price.

Take an outerwear brand weighing price cuts on Zalando to compete with lookalikes on Temu. The alternative is to keep full prices on Zalando, invest in Zalando’s retail media and membership promotions, and sell older stock through outlet channels. Under that plan, its Zalando sales grow at full margin while price-driven shoppers are served elsewhere. On the evidence here, that is the better side of the trade.

The risks deserve a place in the plan. Resale keeps growing, the duty may be routed around, and J.P. Morgan analysts noted ongoing concerns about Zalando’s mid-term outlook from the development of agentic commerce, the RTÉ report on Zalando’s first quarter said.

Two plans for one continent

Zalando is the place for brand building: full-price, branded sales and new collections suit its shoppers, and membership promotions and retail media are how a brand reaches the members who drive a large share of sales. Rich, accurate product data belongs in the same plan, because it helps Zalando’s AI tools recommend a brand’s items.

Price-driven shoppers get a separate plan. Outlet channels, off-price partners or entry lines may serve shoppers who would otherwise buy from Shein or Temu, and margin should be compared across Zalando, outlets and other channels so price-driven sales do not erode overall profit. Vinted belongs in the tracking too: strong resale value can reassure shoppers who pay full price for new items.

Zalando can defend the branded middle of the market, but not the price floor, and a brand’s European plan works best built the same way. Keeping full price where the brand is the reason to buy, and a separate channel where price is, is how we plan Zalando and Europe’s other marketplaces for brands.

A0931.title: Visual search and multimodal shopping: how images became queries
A0931.alt: Smartphone on a stand showing a cut-out image of the blue-and-white porcelain vase standing behind it.
A0931.ttag: Visual search and multimodal shopping: how images became queries | Kwontified
A0931.desc: Shoppers now search with cameras and photos as well as words. How visual search reads product images, and what brands should change in their listings.
A0931.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 18, 2026.
A0931.body:
A shopper sees a lamp in a café and wants it. She could try to describe it in a search box (brass, curved arm, some kind of linen shade), or she could take a photo. More and more shoppers take the photo. Visual search tools match what the camera sees against product images, and AI assistants then explain the results, which turns a brand’s own images into search terms.

That shift asks something new of the listing. Brands should build image sets that show products clearly, accurately and in real-life settings, and back them with complete product details, because the photo finds the product and the details close the sale.

Visual search is now a mainstream way to shop

Google Lens already operates at enormous scale. Google introduced Shopping ads in Google Lens in October 2024, reaching nearly 20 billion monthly visual searches, PPC Land reported.

Amazon raised its bet in 2025. It introduced Lens Live, an AI-powered tool that scans products through the phone camera and shows matching items in a swipeable carousel inside the Amazon Shopping app, Retail Dive reported. Rufus, Amazon’s AI shopping assistant, is built into Lens Live and suggests questions and summaries about products while customers use the camera, according to the same report. Lens Live launched for tens of millions of customers in the Amazon Shopping app on iOS, with plans to expand to all US customers over the following months, the PPC Land report said.

Shoppers are picking up the habit. Amazon said Lens usage grew more than 50% over the past year, with tens of millions of monthly users and photo searches more than doubling each year, Benzinga reported. Amazon had already added the ability to include text with an Amazon Lens image search for more precise results, the Retail Dive report noted, and in May 2026 it launched Alexa for Shopping, combining Rufus with Alexa+, Digital Commerce 360 reported.

Whoever owns the camera keeps the shopper

Look at what each platform built and the incentive is plain. Google sells Shopping ads inside Lens, so the photo a shopper takes on the street becomes ad inventory. Amazon put its camera search inside its own app and wired Rufus into it, so the shopper who points a phone at a lamp gets Amazon’s matches and Amazon’s explanation without leaving Amazon. Pinterest made visual search a key part of its strategy in 2025, and its chief executive said the company had effectively become an AI-enabled shopping assistant, the Retail Dive report said.

Each of them is competing to be the place a picture turns into a purchase, and the platform that wins that moment captures the shopper relationship and the data that comes with it. The brand does not own the camera. What it owns is the material the camera is matched against: its images, its titles, its attributes and the accuracy of all three. That material is where a brand can still win visual search, and all of it sits inside the listing.

What a camera photo asks of a product image

Shoppers point instead of typing because many products are hard to describe in words. A lamp in a café or shoes on a stranger can be photographed faster than anyone can find the right keywords.

The tools read images, not just words. Visual search compares the shape, color, pattern and style in a photo with product images in a catalog, and the closer a brand’s images match what the shopper captured, the more likely its product appears. Once a match appears, assistants such as Amazon’s Alexa for Shopping summarize the product and suggest questions, drawing on product details, reviews and descriptions rather than the image alone.

Shoppers also mix their inputs. A shopper may photograph a chair and then add words such as “in green” or “under $200.” The search uses the image to find the shape and style, and the words to narrow the results. That is multimodal shopping in practice: images, words and sometimes voice working together.

This is where the old image set falls short. A single clean photo on a white background helps a shopper compare products in a grid, but a camera photo is taken in the real world, from an angle, in imperfect light. Products shown from several angles and in real settings give visual tools more to match against. Accuracy matters more too. If a product photo shows a color that differs from the real item, the visual match may fail, or the shopper may return the product.

Take a home décor brand whose listings carry one stylized hero image per product. A shopper who photographs a similar vase in a friend’s living room is unlikely to land on it, because nothing in the listing looks like a vase in a living room. Adding images from several angles, photos in real rooms and accurate color details gives the visual tools something to match, and accurate color is also what keeps color-mismatch returns down.

Platforms do not fully explain how their visual matching works, and results vary by category. That argues for testing changes and measuring results rather than assuming a formula.

The listing work that follows

The image set comes first: products from several angles, close up and in use, with lifestyle images that place them in homes, outfits or rooms, since shoppers rarely photograph products against a plain white background. Color should be checked on several screens before publishing, and each color, size and style needs its own accurate images and labels, so a visual match leads the shopper to the exact variant they saw.

The words still matter, because the assistant does the explaining. Titles, attributes and descriptions should be complete, and they should answer the refining questions shoppers add to a photo about color, size, material or price. Brands should also photograph their own products with visual search tools to see which listings appear, and test whether Google’s Shopping ads in Lens reach new shoppers.

One test belongs in the next listing review: if a shopper photographed our best-selling product in someone’s home, would our listing come back first? Building image sets and product details that pass it is part of how we run marketplace listings for brands.
