A0932.title: Walmart Marketplace’s maturity curve: why early position pays
A0932.alt: Rows of young fruit trees in an orchard beside a weathered blue barn at golden sunset.
A0932.ttag: Walmart Marketplace’s maturity curve: why early position pays | Kwontified
A0932.desc: Walmart’s marketplace grew nearly 50% in early 2026 from a small base. Why that early stage favors brands that build position now, before competition matures.
A0932.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 23, 2026.
A0932.body:
Walmart’s US third-party marketplace grew nearly 50% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the quarter ended April 30, 2026. Chief financial officer John David Rainey said third-party marketplace sales growth reached its highest level in two and a half years, Marketplace Pulse reported. And it is growing from a base of roughly a tenth of Walmart’s US e-commerce sales.

Fast growth from a small base puts Walmart early on a marketplace’s maturity curve, where competition per shopper is thinner than on Amazon. Reviews, sales history and fulfillment performance compound, so the brands that build position on Walmart now will pay less for visibility than the ones that arrive after more sellers and more advertising have filled the marketplace.

Walmart Marketplace by the numbers

The marketplace still starts from a small base. Walmart’s marketplace gross merchandise value is estimated at roughly $15 billion, around 10% of its $150 billion US e-commerce business. That compares with an estimated 69% third-party share of Amazon’s roughly $440 billion in US gross merchandise value, according to Marketplace Pulse estimates in the same analysis. Walmart has an estimated 200,000 active sellers, Marketplace Pulse said.

Everything around the marketplace grew in the same quarter:

Walmart US, quarter ended April 30, 2026Growth
Third-party marketplacenearly 50%
E-commerce sales26%
Store-fulfilled deliveryabout 45%
Same-day or next-day units through Walmart Fulfillment Servicesnearly 150%
US advertising36%
Marketplace sellers’ advertising spendingmore than 50%
Walmart Connect, excluding VIZIO44%

The e-commerce figure comes from The Shelby Report, which also reported the Walmart Connect growth. The delivery, fulfillment and advertising figures come from executives on the earnings call, as summarized by Barchart. Walmart can now reach about 60% of the US population in 30 minutes or less, executives said, and it launched its marketplace cross-border into Canada and Mexico, the Barchart summary said.

Why the early seller collects the compound interest

A marketplace early in its growth has fewer sellers competing for each shopper. When shoppers arrive faster than sellers, the brands already selling capture more of the new demand, and that demand leaves a residue: reviews, sales history and a fulfillment record.

That residue is what ranks. On marketplaces, sales history, reviews and fulfillment performance shape where a product appears in search. Adoption of Walmart Fulfillment Services has long shaped where listings appear in search results, Marketplace Pulse noted. A brand that builds reviews and sales now ranks better later, and ranking better later brings more sales, which adds to the history again.

The other side of the curve is cost. As more sellers join and more of them advertise, competition for placement grows. Sellers’ advertising spending on Walmart already rose more than 50% in the quarter. The cost of visibility tends to climb as a marketplace matures, as it did on Amazon.

Put the two curves together and timing becomes the variable a brand actually controls. The ranking benefit of history keeps accruing to whoever started early, while the price of the clicks needed to start that history keeps rising for everyone who has not.

Amazon shows what the later stage looks like. Amazon’s own retail business has taken back unit share from third-party sellers for two straight quarters, while Walmart’s growth is coming from the opposite direction, led by third-party sellers expanding its assortment, Marketplace Pulse noted. A mature marketplace leaves less room for each new seller.

The case for waiting, and where it breaks

Many brands wait to invest in Walmart until it looks as big as Amazon. That instinct is reasonable on its face, given how much smaller the marketplace is. But the advantage Walmart offers comes from its being smaller and earlier. By the time it looks like Amazon, much of the easy position will be taken.

Take a pet supplies brand that treats Walmart as a minor channel and lists only a few products. If it expands its range, joins Walmart Fulfillment Services and supports launches with Walmart Connect, its products can build reviews quickly and rank well while competition is thin. A competitor that arrives later faces higher advertising costs to reach the same placements, because by then the reviews and sales history belong to someone else.

There are real limits to the argument. Walmart’s marketplace is still far smaller than Amazon’s, and not every category sells well there. Testing with the strongest products and measuring returns before shifting large budgets is the sensible order.

Building position on Walmart in 2026

The first lever is range. List the strongest products on Walmart, not just a few, because a narrow range limits how many searches a brand can appear in and how much sales history it can build. Test Walmart Fulfillment Services for top products and compare its costs with your own fulfillment, since fast delivery helps search placement and conversion. Then keep stock steady: running out interrupts sales history and can cost placement, so forecast Walmart demand separately and keep WFS inventory topped up.

Reviews and launch advertising work together. Programs that help new listings earn reviews support ranking and give shoppers confidence in a less familiar seller, and Walmart Connect can give new listings visibility while they build sales history. Launch budgets can come down once products rank well on their own.

Cost per click is the gauge to watch as competition grows. Adjust bids to protect returns, and read rising costs in a category as a sign that the marketplace is maturing there. Cross-border is the last lever: sellers can now reach Canada and Mexico through the same platform, which may extend the value of listings and reviews built in the United States.

On a marketplace where shoppers arrive faster than sellers, reviews and sales history cost less to earn early than late, and they keep paying once earned. Building that position across range, fulfillment and Walmart Connect is how we run Walmart Marketplace for brands.

A0934.crumb: Grocery on Amazon in 2026: what changed…
A0934.title: Grocery on Amazon in 2026: what changed in the category
A0934.alt: Paper grocery bag on a kitchen counter spilling bread, eggs, apples, chard and a bottle of milk.
A0934.ttag: Grocery on Amazon in 2026: what changed in the category | Kwontified
A0934.desc: Amazon moved fresh groceries into its main cart with same-day delivery and closed its Fresh and Go stores. What changed in grocery, and what brands should do.
A0934.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 25, 2026.
A0934.body:
Look at an Amazon order that holds a phone charger, a bag of dog food, a carton of strawberries and a pound of ground beef, all arriving the same day. Not long ago those items would have come from separate Amazon services, each with its own checkout. Now they sit in one cart. Amazon moved fresh groceries into its main shopping cart, added same-day delivery of perishables in thousands of cities and closed its Amazon Fresh and Go stores.

The result is that grocery on Amazon has become a frequent, fast, single-cart habit. For grocery brands, the competition is no longer only for a search result. It is for a place in a basket that gets rebuilt again and again, which means planning for same-day availability, pack sizes that suit frequent orders and visibility in everyday orders.

Grocery on Amazon now runs through the main cart

Amazon started the shift in 2025. It rolled out same-day delivery of fresh food to more than 1,000 cities in August 2025, letting customers check out fresh food and other items from the same cart, CNN reported. Same-day delivery is free for Prime members on orders over $25 in most cities, with a $2.99 fee below that, and costs $12.99 for customers without Prime, the report said. Chief executive Andy Jassy said about 20% of customers in the pilot used the service multiple times within the first month, according to the same report.

The footprint grew quickly. Amazon expanded same-day delivery of perishable groceries to more than 2,300 US cities and towns, and fresh foods became nine of the top 10 bestselling items in areas where the service is available, eWeek reported. The number of perishable items available for same-day delivery grew by more than 30% since August 2025, the eWeek report said.

The scale behind it is large. Customers who add fresh groceries to their same-day orders shop about twice as often as those who do not, Amazon said, and Amazon generated more than $100 billion in grocery-related sales in 2024, according to the same report. Growth continued into 2026: Amazon offers grocery delivery in more than 5,000 US cities and towns, and perishable grocery sales through its same-day service have grown 40 times since January 2025, the company said in a company post.

A basket that refills often rewards the products already in it

For years, grocery on Amazon meant separate services, such as Amazon Fresh and Whole Foods delivery, often with their own checkouts and fees, and physical stores were another experiment. The single cart changed the habit. Once shoppers could add milk, fruit and meat to the same order as household goods and other products, grocery became part of an everyday Amazon visit rather than a separate trip.

Speed is what made it practical. Same-day delivery, and now tests of 30-minute delivery, let shoppers use Amazon for fresh items they need the same day, not just pantry staples bought ahead. And frequency raised the stakes for brands. When shoppers order more often, the products already in their routine get bought again and again, so a brand that wins a place in that routine gains repeat sales. A brand that is missing from the same-day assortment is simply not in the basket being built.

That is where a category’s planning meeting can lag. A pack size built for the stock-up trip fits poorly when the shopper is adding a few items to an order that already holds strawberries. Take a snack brand that sells mainly multipacks through standard delivery and sees slow growth. If it makes sure its products are stocked for same-day delivery and adds smaller packs that suit frequent baskets, its products can start appearing alongside fresh items in everyday orders, which is where repeat purchases come from.

The $25 free-delivery threshold adds its own pull. Prime members who are just short of it may add an item to reach the minimum, and products that round out a basket, such as snacks, sauces or breakfast staples that pair naturally with fresh items, are the ones that benefit.

Amazon’s stores have become the side business

Amazon decided to close its Amazon Go and Amazon Fresh physical stores, converting some locations to Whole Foods Market, and plans to open more than 100 new Whole Foods Market stores over the next few years, the same company post said. Amazon is also testing Amazon Now, which delivers thousands of essential items in about 30 minutes or less.

Closing Fresh and Go while expanding same-day delivery signals that Amazon sees its grocery future mainly online, with Whole Foods as its main physical format. The promotional calendar points the same way. Amazon’s vice president of Prime said groceries and household items would be a real focus of Prime Day 2026 promotions, according to CNBC reporting cited by Shopifreaks.

None of this is settled. Same-day perishable delivery is not available everywhere, and Amazon’s grocery strategy has changed several times, so brands should watch availability in their key markets rather than assume the current model is permanent.

Planning for the routine basket

The planning work starts with availability. Confirm that products are available for same-day delivery in key cities, because a shopper building a same-day order can only add products available for it, and keep stock steady, because running out breaks the routine and sends shoppers to alternatives. Offer both pack sizes where it makes sense: smaller packs for shoppers who order often, larger packs for stock-up trips.

Prime Day 2026 needs a margin check. With groceries a focus of Prime Day 2026 promotions, deal margins deserve a careful look before a brand matches deep discounts. Brands that sell natural or organic products should also think through how the Whole Foods expansion affects their plans, and every grocery brand should measure how often customers reorder, since frequency is what drives grocery value on Amazon now.

The planning meeting that fits this category starts from the strawberries and the ground beef, the order that keeps refilling, rather than from the warehouse pallet. Building that same-day assortment, the pack sizes and the reorder tracking is part of how we run Amazon grocery for brands.

A0936.crumb: Placement multipliers and the clicks you…
A0936.title: Placement multipliers and the clicks you would have won anyway
A0936.alt: Plain white box resting on a carved Corinthian column capital on a wooden shelf against a yellow wall.
A0936.ttag: Placement multipliers and the clicks you would have won anyway | Kwontified
A0936.desc: High top-of-search multipliers can buy clicks a brand would have won organically. Why the best-looking placement may add the least, and how to test it.
A0936.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jun 30, 2026.
A0936.body:
In a Sponsored Products placement report, top of search tends to look like the best money in the account. The clicks convert, the attributed return is strong, and the obvious next step is a bigger multiplier. Amazon allows a lot of room for that step: placement adjustments run up to 900%.

The strong return is real, but part of it is borrowed. Top-of-search placements capture the most motivated shoppers, and where a product already ranks near the top organically, many of those clicks would have happened anyway. Brands should judge placement multipliers by the sales they add, using organic rank and holdout tests, rather than by attributed return alone.

How placement multipliers work on Amazon

Multipliers raise a bid according to where the ad appears. Amazon lets advertisers set placement bid adjustments for Sponsored Products ads at the top of search results and on product pages, ranging from 0% to 900%. The base bid is multiplied by the adjustment, Search Engine Land reported when the feature launched in 2019. A third adjustment came later. Amazon added a bid adjustment for rest of search placements in January 2024, working the same way as the adjustments for top of search and product pages, Helium 10 reported.

The money flowing through those auctions keeps growing. In the first quarter of 2026 Amazon took $17.24 billion in advertising revenue, up 24%, SiliconANGLE reported. As more advertisers compete for the same placements, the cost of top positions tends to rise. Click prices also swing. Cost per click fell 11% during Prime Day 2025, after rising 12% in 2024, Tinuiti reported, so a multiplier set months earlier can quietly change what a brand pays for each top position.

Most of the industry still reads these placements through attribution. Platform-provided attribution remained the most common measurement method, used by 65.8% of marketers in a 2025 TransUnion and EMARKETER survey, PPC Land reported. Attribution credits an ad with a sale when a shopper clicked it before buying.

Why the best-looking placement can add the least

Top-of-search placements sit above everything else on the page. Shoppers who click there often know what they want, so these clicks convert well and attributed returns look strong.

The organic results sit just below. When a product already ranks first or second organically for the same search, the shopper sees both the ad and the organic listing, and many would click the organic listing if the ad were absent. Attribution cannot see that. It credits the ad for the sale because the shopper clicked it.

That is where the mental pull starts. A report that ranks placements by return puts top of search first, and a number that good feels like an instruction. The higher return encourages a higher multiplier, which buys more of the same clicks, which keeps the return high. Nothing in the report is wrong; it simply answers a different question from the one the budget decision needs. The placement with the best attributed return may be the one adding the fewest new sales, because its strong numbers come partly from shoppers who were already on their way to the product.

The bid settings around a multiplier compound the effect. A placement adjustment sits on top of the base bid, and dynamic bidding can raise or lower the result further. A brand that sets a high multiplier and allows bids to rise may pay far more than its base bid suggests for the very clicks it was most likely to win anyway.

Organic rank decides what a multiplier buys

The same multiplier does different work on different searches:

When the product...A top-of-search ad mostly buysWhat to do with the multiplier
already ranks first or second organicallyclicks the organic listing would likely have wontest reductions in a holdout
ranks poorly organicallyshoppers who would never have seen the productthis is where higher multipliers earn their cost

There is a defensive case for keeping the ad, and it is not trivial. Top positions also defend against competitors who might take the slot, and removing an ad can let a rival appear above an organic listing. If rivals take the top slot when a multiplier falls, the ad may be defending sales after all, and a moderate multiplier may be worth keeping. That argues for testing reductions carefully rather than cutting multipliers everywhere at once.

Take a cookware brand that sets a high top-of-search multiplier across all campaigns because top of search shows its best return. Its own brand searches and best-selling generic searches, where it already ranks first organically, absorb most of that spend. The test: cut the multiplier on those searches in a set of regions for four weeks, then set total sales there against the regions left alone. If total sales barely move, the savings belong on the searches where it ranks lower.

Setting multipliers by the sales they add

The work starts with organic rank. Know where each product ranks organically for its key searches before setting multipliers, and track how that rank changes. Then separate searches the product already leads from searches where it ranks low, often in separate campaigns, so each group can carry its own multiplier.

Judge every change by total sales, not just attributed ad sales, using holdouts where possible. Review placement adjustments together with base bids and bidding strategy so the team knows the most it could pay for a top position. Revisit the settings as organic rankings shift, because a multiplier that made sense at one rank stops making sense at another.

A multiplier earns its keep where the shopper would not otherwise have seen the product, and should prove itself in a holdout everywhere else. Running those holdouts across placements is how we test placement multipliers for brands on Amazon.

A0937.crumb: TikTok Shop logistics: what the shipping…
A0937.title: TikTok Shop logistics: what the shipping reversal shows
A0937.alt: White delivery van with rear doors open full of cardboard boxes, parked by a loading dock beside a U-turn arrow.
A0937.ttag: TikTok Shop logistics: what the shipping reversal shows | Kwontified
A0937.desc: TikTok Shop tried to require its own logistics for US sellers, then reversed after backlash. What the episode shows, and how brands should plan now.
A0937.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 2, 2026.
A0937.body:
For a few weeks early in 2026, operations leads at brands selling on TikTok Shop had a real decision on the table. They could keep shipping TikTok orders from their own warehouses, or start moving stock into TikTok’s network because the platform was about to require it. Then TikTok withdrew the requirement, and the decision went back into the drawer.

It should not stay there. TikTok Shop announced in January 2026 that US sellers would have to use its own logistics, then reversed the plan in February after merchants objected to costs and uneven service. The episode shows a platform that wants Amazon-style control of fulfillment but still depends on merchant goodwill. The question for leadership is no longer whether to comply, but how to stay ready: test TikTok’s logistics where they help, keep the brand’s own shipping options and plan for the push to return.

How the TikTok Shop logistics mandate came and went

TikTok Shop told US sellers in emails between January 20 and 22, 2026 that it would phase out seller shipping. Existing sellers would be moved over from February 25 to March 31, and new sellers had to use TikTok’s logistics after February 9, Easyship reported. An earlier step had already arrived: sellers using USPS had to buy labels through TikTok Shipping from January 2026, Viral Nation reported.

The options would have been TikTok’s own. Sellers would have had to use TikTok Shop’s logistics services or approved integrations, and third-party logistics providers would have needed to connect through approved systems, PPC Land reported.

Merchants pushed back quickly. Some brands and consultants said TikTok’s logistics services had historically been uneven, citing operational errors, shipping delays and limited support, and some merchants planned to reduce products, pull back on promotions or leave the marketplace, Digiday reported, citing Modern Retail.

TikTok reversed course in February. In an email to sellers, TikTok Shop said seller shipping remains unchanged and previously shared deadlines would not take effect, Modern Retail reported. It remained unclear whether TikTok would introduce a revised policy later, according to the report.

None of this happened on a small platform. TikTok Shop’s US gross merchandise value reached $15.1 billion in 2025, a rise of 68%, in Momentum Works and Tabcut data that DealStreetAsia cited.

What TikTok wants, and why merchants said no

Read the mandate as a statement of intent. TikTok already controls discovery and checkout. Controlling shipping too would let it set delivery standards, track every order and potentially earn margin on shipping, much like the model Amazon built with its own fulfillment.

The merchants’ side of the table looked different. Brands with their own warehouses or third-party partners had built shipping costs into their margins, and moving to TikTok’s logistics meant new fees, stock held in TikTok’s network and reliance on a service some had found unreliable. Viral demand made the change harder still. TikTok sales can spike suddenly when a video takes off, and holding stock in a platform’s warehouses ahead of unpredictable demand ties up cash and risks running out in the wrong place.

The platform was also under strain. Users had experienced technical issues on TikTok around the same time, the Digiday report said, adding to merchants’ doubts about relying on its systems for every order. And the timing was sensitive: the change came as TikTok’s US business settled under new ownership that includes Oracle and investment firms Silver Lake and MGX, the Digiday report noted. Merchants already uncertain about the platform had less patience for a forced change.

The reversal is a reading of bargaining power. TikTok needs a broad base of merchants to keep its shop full and its videos shoppable, and when enough of them threatened to pull back, the platform backed down. That is a position that can change as the shop grows and as TikTok’s own logistics improve.

The decision to make before the next notice arrives

The brands in the best position for a second attempt are the ones that treat the reversal as time to prepare rather than as the end of the story. TikTok has not said the plan is gone for good, and platform logistics can improve quickly, so the current flexibility is not a safe assumption.

Take an apparel brand that ships TikTok orders from its own warehouse alongside website and Amazon orders. Facing the mandate, it would model the cost of moving stock to TikTok’s network and might find margins shrinking. With the reversal in hand, a sensible path is to keep its own shipping for most products and test Fulfilled by TikTok on two fast-moving items, comparing delivery times and costs before going further.

The rest of the preparation is operational. Keep the brand’s own fulfillment capability for TikTok orders rather than dismantling it to save costs in the short term. Calculate shipping costs under each option, including storage fees, inbound shipping to TikTok’s warehouses and the cost of returns, so a future mandate does not catch the business unprepared. Decide in advance how much stock to hold for TikTok and where, and how quickly more can move if a video takes off. Brands using third-party logistics providers should confirm their systems can connect to TikTok’s approved tools if needed and ask partners how they would handle a future mandate.

Two habits reduce the exposure further. Brands that sell on TikTok Shop, their own sites and other marketplaces are less exposed when one platform changes its rules, and someone on the team should own TikTok’s seller notices, because TikTok may return with a revised plan.

If that notice comes, the meeting that matters is the one where operations can show the margin under each shipping option on the first day rather than weeks later. Building that readiness is part of how we run TikTok Shop programs for brands.

A0939.crumb: Prime Day 2026 results: where the outcome…
A0939.title: Prime Day 2026 results: where the outcome fell against forecast
A0939.alt: Four feathered arrows clustered in the center of a round straw archery target on sunny grass.
A0939.ttag: Prime Day 2026 results: where the outcome fell against forecast | Kwontified
A0939.desc: Prime Day 2026 drove $26.4 billion in US online spending, up 9.3%, just below our standard case. What the daily pattern shows, and what we cannot yet judge.
A0939.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 7, 2026.
A0939.body:
Before Prime Day 2026, our standard case put US online spending during the event at roughly $26.5 billion. The market came in at $26.4 billion. US retailers drove that much in online spending from June 23 to June 26, up 9.3% from a year earlier and above Adobe’s own forecast of $26.3 billion, Adobe said in its Prime Day results.

That is just below the 10% standard case in our forecast and well within its range. The event kept its four-day length, so growth had to come from underlying demand, and the daily pattern again dipped mid-event and recovered on the last day. Brands should keep planning for modest growth and four-day pacing, and judge their own results against their own data rather than market totals.

Prime Day 2026 results against the forecast

We set three ranges before the event: US online spending during Prime Day 2026 up 5%, 10% or 18% from 2025 in conservative, standard and reach scenarios.

ScenarioGrowth from 2025US online spending
Conservative5%roughly $25.3 billion
Standard10%roughly $26.5 billion
Reach18%roughly $28.4 billion
Actual (Adobe)9.3%$26.4 billion

At $26.4 billion and 9.3% growth, the result came in about $0.1 billion below our standard case and well above the conservative case.

The forecast rested on one mechanism. The 2026 event kept the same four-day length as 2025, so the sharp growth that came from doubling the event in 2025 would not repeat, and growth would have to come from underlying demand. That is what happened.

The logic is simple once the length is held still. Doubling the event in 2025 added selling days that had not existed the year before, so growth measured against the shorter event looked large partly for that reason. With the length unchanged, that source of growth disappears, and what remains is how many shoppers show up and how much they buy, which tends to move more slowly.

The daily shape repeated as well. In 2025, brands’ daily sales averaged lower as the longer event went on, Pacvue reported. In 2026, online spending reached $8.3 billion on the first day, $8.1 billion on the second, $4.6 billion on the third and $5.4 billion on the fourth, according to Adobe. Spending fell sharply on the third day and recovered on the last, so brands that kept budget for June 26 had shoppers to reach.

For pacing, that shape matters more than the total: a budget spread evenly across the four days would put as much money behind the third day as the first, when the first drew far more spending.

A forecast that lands near the middle can look unremarkable, and the useful part was never the number. It was the reasoning about event length. Brands that planned for 2025-style growth would have overspent; brands that planned for modest growth and four-day pacing were closer to what happened.

What the spending was made of

Household essentials were among the strongest sellers. Online purchases of household goods such as trash bags, detergents and paper products rose 60% compared with average daily sales in June 2026, and personal hygiene products rose 125%, Adobe said. That fit Amazon’s positioning of the event as a vehicle for grocery and household essentials deals, Quartz reported.

Mobile and flexible payment grew. Mobile drove 54.2% of online sales, or $14.2 billion, and Buy Now, Pay Later orders accounted for $2.1 billion in online spending, up 9.5% from a year earlier, according to Adobe.

Discount depth barely moved from 2025. Electronics discounts peaked at 24% off listed prices, compared with 23% in 2025, and apparel discounts held at 24%, Adobe said. Shoppers traded up in some categories: the share of the most expensive goods rose 19% across categories compared with average levels earlier in the year, while shoppers chose lower-priced products in grocery and home and garden.

Partners and AI changed the traffic mix. Affiliates and partners, including social media influencers, accounted for 21.3% of revenue share, while social media accounted for 4.4% and grew fastest, Adobe reported. Visitors arriving from AI services converted 40% better than visitors from other channels, compared with converting 23% worse during the 2025 event.

What the market total cannot tell a brand

Some parts of our forecast cannot yet be judged. We also forecast sales growth for brands that run deals and advertise, and changes in cost per click. Public market totals do not measure either, and brand-level results vary widely, so those parts should be judged against client data rather than market totals. Adobe also measures spending across US retailers, not Amazon alone, and a single market total hides wide differences between categories and brands.

That makes the post-event review a brand’s own job. Measure sales, advertising costs and margins against the targets you set, not the headline total. Check whether budgets lasted through the third-day dip and the final-day recovery, and whether bids rose or fell with traffic each day. Look at how your category behaved, since shoppers traded up in some categories and down in grocery and home and garden.

Discounts and traffic sources deserve the same scrutiny. With discounts roughly flat from 2025, check whether deeper discounts paid off or whether shallower deals would have delivered similar sales at better margins. AI-referred shoppers converted better than in 2025, so product data should be ready for AI assistants, and with affiliates and partners driving a large share of revenue, it is worth checking which partners delivered sales.

Plan the next event from the mechanism, such as event length and competition, rather than from the prior year’s growth rate, then measure your own results against it. Building those event plans and the post-event measurement is how we plan retail events for brands on Amazon and beyond.

A0941.crumb: What Prime Day 2026 revealed about brands…
A0941.title: What Prime Day 2026 revealed about brands and retailers
A0941.alt: Wooden shopfront with three windows displaying stacks of red, blue and gold wrapped gift boxes.
A0941.ttag: What Prime Day 2026 revealed about brands and retailers | Kwontified
A0941.desc: Prime Day 2026 put Amazon, Target and Walmart sales into one June week while discounts held flat. What that shows brand leaders about planning the next event.
A0941.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 9, 2026.
A0941.body:
A brand’s summer promotions calendar used to have room to breathe: Prime Day in July, a Walmart event nearby, a Target sale somewhere close. In 2026 those boxes landed on top of one another. Prime Day ran June 23 to 26, Target put its own sale on the same four days, and Walmart Deals wrapped around both. The e-commerce lead who used to stagger stock and budget across three events had a single week to cover all of them.

That collision is what Prime Day 2026 revealed. The summer sale now behaves like one shared week across Amazon, Walmart and Target, discounts inside it barely moved, and shoppers behaved very differently from one category to the next. A brand that still plans each retailer’s event on its own is planning for a calendar that has gone.

Prime Day 2026 put three retailers in one week

Target announced that Target Circle Deal Days would run June 23 to 26, matching Prime Day, with one-day offers of 40% off or more on some brands, according to its June announcement. Walmart Deals was set to open on June 22 for Walmart+ members and run through June 28, 9to5Toys reported, attributing the dates to Walmart. The June timing was itself a break with habit, since Amazon had held Prime Day in July for five consecutive years, Quartz reported.

The convergence had been building. Walmart Deals and Target Circle Week already ran in early July 2025 alongside Prime Day, Supermarket News reported. In 2026, Target matched Prime Day’s exact dates and Walmart scheduled its event around them. Each retailer appears to have concluded that shoppers in deal mode compare across stores, so sitting the week out carried more risk than competing head to head.

Amazon, meanwhile, aimed the event at the household basket. Its vice president of Prime singled out groceries and household items as a real focus of the event’s promotions, in CNBC reporting that Shopifreaks cited.

What shoppers did once the week arrived

The total grew at a modest pace. US retailers drove $26.4 billion in online spending during the event, up 9.3% from a year earlier, Adobe said in its Prime Day results.

Discount depth hardly changed. The deepest electronics discounts reached 24% off listed prices, against 23% in 2025, and apparel held at 24%, according to Adobe. Brands appear to have treated the event as a known quantity, taking part while protecting margin instead of racing one another down.

Inside those flat discounts, shoppers behaved like two different people. Adobe measured a 19% rise across categories in the share going to the most expensive goods, as shoppers in categories such as electronics and toys used the deals to trade up. In grocery and in home and garden, they chose lower-priced products. Purchases of household goods rose 60% and personal hygiene products 125% compared with average daily sales in June, according to the same report.

The daily curve carried its own lesson. On the first day online spending came to $8.3 billion; it slipped to $4.6 billion on day three and climbed back to $5.4 billion on day four, Adobe’s figures show. Many shoppers seem to have browsed early, held off and come back before the deals ended, and brands that ran out of budget or stock before the last day missed them. Shoppers also used Buy Now, Pay Later for $2.1 billion of online orders, up 9.5% on the year before.

Two channels outside the retailers’ own pages also mattered. Shoppers who came from AI services converted 40% better than those from other channels, a reversal from 2025, when they converted 23% worse, by Adobe’s count. Affiliates and partners, influencers among them, took 21.3% of revenue share during the event, which means about a fifth of the selling ran through creators and partner sites.

Why the plan has to start from the shared week

When the events fell weeks apart, planning each retailer’s sale on its own made sense. Stock left over from one could serve the next, each account got its own advertising budget, and nobody had to choose between retailers in the same seven days. The overlap removes that slack, and the decision moves from the account level to whoever can see all three retailers at once.

Take a home brand that planned Prime Day on its own and ran a separate Walmart promotion in July, as it had in prior years. In 2026 its Walmart event fell into the same week as Prime Day and Target’s sale, and its budget and stock were suddenly split three ways without anyone having decided the split. For the next event, it builds one calendar across all three retailers, sets deeper discounts only on products where shoppers trade up and keeps essentials at steady prices.

One year does not settle the pattern. Retailers may pull their events apart again, and the June timing may not repeat. The evidence from 2026 leans toward a shared summer week, and that is the safer assumption for the next plan.

Questions for the next event plan

  • Who owns the combined calendar for Amazon, Walmart and Target, and does that person decide how stock and advertising are split before the week begins?
  • Which products deserve a deeper discount because shoppers trade up in their category, and which essentials should hold a steady price?
  • Are creators, affiliates and partner sites lined up in advance, now that they carry about a fifth of event revenue, and are product data, prices and images accurate for shoppers arriving from AI assistants?
  • After the event, can the team compare results by retailer and see where each dollar of discount and advertising worked best?

Answering those questions once, for all three retailers, is how we plan and run marketplace channels across Amazon, Walmart and Target.

A0942.crumb: Agents in the ad console: what to…
A0942.title: Agents in the ad console: what to automate and what to keep human
A0942.alt: Row of brass levers with wooden handles on a mounted panel, most secured with small brass padlocks, two left open.
A0942.ttag: Agents in the ad console: what to automate and what to keep human | Kwontified
A0942.desc: Amazon’s Ads Agent can build campaigns, recommend targeting and write queries. Why agents should run execution while people keep goals and measurement.
A0942.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 14, 2026.
A0942.body:
Give an agent a target return on ad spend and it will chase that number. That is both the appeal and the risk. Amazon’s Ads Agent and tools like it can now build campaigns, recommend targeting, pace budgets and write data queries, and they handle that measurable, repetitive work well. What they cannot do is question the number they were handed, and they pursue it faster and across more campaigns than any person could.

So the split for a brand team is straightforward to state and harder to hold: let agents run execution, and keep goals, budget trade-offs and incrementality checks with people.

What agents in the ad console already do

For the people on a brand’s advertising team, the useful question is which parts of their week an agent can already take, and which parts are still announcements.

Amazon rebuilt its console around agents at its unBoxed event in November 2025. It introduced a unified Campaign Manager that combines Amazon DSP and the Ads Console into one media-buying tool supported by agentic AI, and the agent can generate creative, build campaigns, recommend targeting and write complex Amazon Marketing Cloud queries, MediaPost reported.

Ads Agent automates tasks such as audience identification, campaign pacing and query generation for data analysis. It was available in Amazon Marketing Cloud. Its expansion into Campaign Manager was expected later in 2026, according to Storyboard18. Creative work has its own tool: Amazon Ads announced Creative Agent, an agentic AI tool to help UK advertisers create professional-quality ads, Advanced Television reported. Ads Agent has also launched in Australia, according to B&T.

Outside tools can reach in as well. Amazon opened its advertising APIs to AI agents through an MCP server in February 2026, letting agents query performance and build campaigns that require approval, PPC Land reported. On May 28, 2026, Amazon released local tools for its Selling Partner API that let AI assistants search documentation, generate code and build workflows against seller data, according to its developer announcement.

Put together, the shipped tools already reach bids, pacing, audiences, queries and creative. The announced step, Ads Agent inside Campaign Manager, would bring them into the tool where media buying happens. That is a real change in who does the clicking.

An agent optimizes exactly the target it is given

Agents do well where inputs are clear and feedback is quick. Adjusting a bid, pacing a budget through the day, building an audience and writing a query all produce measurable results within hours or days. An agent can repeat them across thousands of keywords without tiring.

The same literalness is the danger. An agent told to maximize return on ad spend will move spend toward whatever produces the highest attributed return. It does not know whether those sales would have happened anyway, whether the product is about to run out or whether the brand needs new customers in that particular quarter. It also sees only the data someone has connected. Without margin, warehouse stock or next month’s promotion plan, it makes confident decisions on partial information.

Speed turns a small error into a large one. A person working toward the wrong target makes slow mistakes that are easy to spot. An agent working toward the wrong target makes many fast decisions across many campaigns before anyone notices. So the more execution an agent takes over, the more the result depends on the goals, constraints and measurement that people set.

Take a skincare brand that hands its bids to an agent with a target return on ad spend. The agent moves spend toward brand searches and best-selling products, where attributed returns are highest. Reported return improves, but total sales barely move. When the team changes the goal to new-to-brand sales and puts a ceiling on spend for brand searches, the agent’s decisions shift toward growth. Nothing about the agent changed; the target did.

Agents are improving quickly, and they may soon account for more of the business factors people weigh today. The judgment about what the business needs in a given quarter still sits with the people who own the business.

How to split the work between agents and people

WorkOwnerReason
Bid changesAgent, within limits the team setsFaster and more consistent than people across large keyword sets
Budget pacingAgentKeeps budgets on track through the day and across events such as Prime Day
Reporting and queriesAgentWrites data queries and summarizes performance, freeing analysts to interpret results
Goal settingPeopleDecides what the agent optimizes for (new customers, total sales or margin) and revisits it when priorities change
Budget trade-offsPeopleAmazon versus Walmart, or growth versus profit, depends on business context an agent does not have
MeasurementPeopleHoldout tests check whether the agent’s results add sales, since attribution alone can mislead

The table only works with guardrails around it. Cap spend on brand searches, set inventory limits and require approval for large structural changes, such as new campaigns or major budget shifts. Begin by letting agents read data and suggest changes, and allow them to act once their suggestions prove reliable. Then review what the agent changed, and why, every week, because that review is where drift shows up early. An agent should not grade its own work.

A test worth applying before any agent gets write access: if the team cannot say in one sentence what the agent is optimizing for, and which holdout would show that it added sales, the agent is not ready to act alone. Setting that target and the holdout behind it is how we run Amazon advertising with agents in the workflow.

A0943.title: Will ultra-discount ecommerce survive? Yes, in a new shape
A0943.alt: Warehouse shelving of orange bins filled with grey mailer bags, with a heap of mailers piled on the floor in front.
A0943.ttag: Will ultra-discount ecommerce survive? Yes, in a new shape | Kwontified
A0943.desc: The end of duty-free parcels in the US and Europe hit Temu and Shein. Why ultra-discount ecommerce will survive by changing shape, and what brands should do.
A0943.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 16, 2026.
A0943.body:
The ultra-discount model rested on a customs rule few shoppers had heard of. Shipments valued at $800 or less entered the United States duty-free, so a platform could send one item at a time from a Chinese factory to a shopper’s door without paying duty or holding stock nearby. That rule is now gone in the United States, and Europe has begun charging duty on the same kind of parcel.

The platforms are not disappearing. They are moving stock into local warehouses and recruiting local sellers, which keeps them in business and narrows the price gap that defined them. Ultra-discount ecommerce will survive in a new shape, closer to an ordinary marketplace, and brands should compete with it on value and judge it as one more channel.

How the rules behind ultra-discount ecommerce changed

The United States moved first. An executive order signed on July 30, 2025 suspended duty-free treatment for all countries from August 29, 2025, according to a White & Case alert. Separate legislation signed on July 4, 2025 permanently repeals the exemption from July 1, 2027, the same alert noted, so the change is written into law rather than left to an order.

The flow that rule had carried was large and rising quickly. White House figures cited by White & Case put these de minimis shipments at 309 million in the part of fiscal 2025 running through June 30, against 115 million across the whole of fiscal 2024.

Temu had felt the change early. Once the exemption for China and Hong Kong ended on May 2, 2025, the number of Temu’s daily active users in the US fell 58% and the company cut US advertising, RetailWire reported.

Europe faced the same flood of small boxes. In 2024 the EU took in about 4.6 billion low-value parcels, and China was the origin of more than 90% of them, SGI Europe reported. On July 1, 2026, the European Union began charging a €3 customs duty on low-value parcels, replacing the exemption for parcels worth €150 or less from platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, Euronews reported.

The strain shows in the parent company’s results. PDD Holdings, Temu’s parent, reported first-quarter 2026 revenue up 11% to 106.23 billion yuan, while net profit fell 15% to 12.55 billion yuan, XTB reported. Temu was only just returning to stability after the US change, and it was adapting by building local warehouses and recruiting local sales staff, at a cost, according to the same report.

Moving stock closer changes who keeps the margin

Under the parcel model, a platform shipped individual items straight from Chinese factories. Each parcel was small enough to avoid duties, and the platform skipped the cost of holding stock near the shopper, two costs that retailers with domestic inventory carry. Once each parcel carried duties or fees, shipping single items from overseas lost much of that advantage, especially on very cheap products, where a few dollars or euros make a large difference.

The response has been to move stock closer. Local warehouses and local sellers let a platform ship in bulk, pay duty once on a large shipment and deliver faster. Temu started early. Since March 2024 it had been recruiting sellers who stock goods in US warehouses, and Marketplace Pulse estimated that about 20% of its US sales came from those local sellers, Reuters reported.

Follow the money through that change and the advantage moves. Warehouses, local staff and bulk duties cost money, and those costs push the platform’s prices toward those of other marketplaces. Delivery gets faster, but the price gap that defined ultra-discount shopping narrows. A Temu that ships from local warehouses through local sellers still competes on low prices, but it now carries costs closer to those of its rivals. The edge it lost goes partly to whoever already held stock near the shopper: brands with domestic inventory, and in Europe, brands holding stock there rather than shipping parcels from overseas.

Take a kitchenware brand that lost sales to near-identical products on Temu while those items shipped duty-free from overseas. After the duty changes, the price gap on comparable items narrows, and the brand’s faster delivery and better reviews win back some shoppers. It also tests listing its own products through Temu’s local-seller program, treating the platform as another marketplace to measure rather than only a competitor.

None of this means the platforms are finished. They have deep resources and have adapted quickly before, PDD’s revenue is still growing, and policy can change again. The evidence leans toward a price advantage that narrows without disappearing.

What the new shape asks of brands

With the price gap shrinking, delivery speed, quality, reviews and brand trust carry more of the decision, so brands should make those strengths visible in titles, images and reviews. Prices on comparable items are worth tracking as the platforms move stock into local warehouses, since that is where a brand will see the gap change.

The harder shift is in how the team thinks about these platforms. Temu and others now court local sellers, so the question is no longer only how to compete with them but whether selling there fits the brand’s positioning and margins. Brands that do list should set clear pricing rules to avoid undercutting their own prices elsewhere, because marketplaces and shopping assistants compare prices across retailers. Europe needs its own review, since the €3 duty changes the economics there. And because trade rules on small parcels have changed quickly in both the United States and Europe, channel plans deserve a fresh look whenever duties or fees shift.

The question for the next planning meeting is whether the team still treats Temu only as a price to defend against, or has started judging it as a channel. Making that call market by market is how we choose and run marketplaces for brands in the United States and Europe.

A0945.crumb: FBA capacity and fees: inventory planning…
A0945.title: FBA capacity and fees: inventory planning as an ad decision
A0945.alt: Warehouse aisle lined with tall pallet racks of cardboard boxes, lit by sunlight from a high window.
A0945.ttag: FBA capacity and fees: inventory planning as an ad decision | Kwontified
A0945.desc: Amazon’s 2026 holiday cutoffs land weeks before each event and capacity tightens as the season goes on. Why the summer inventory plan is the first ad decision.
A0945.byline: By Jordan Taylor, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 21, 2026.
A0945.body:
Out-of-stock losses rose 185% year over year during Prime Day 2026, CommerceIQ data showed, PPC Land reported. Even before the event, a separate CommerceIQ dataset had found stockout-related revenue losses up 24% year over year, according to the same report. None of that looks like an advertising problem on the surface. All of it shows up in advertising results.

The reason is simple and easy to forget in October. An ad can only sell what is in stock and carries the Prime badge, and Amazon’s FBA capacity and fees calendar fixes that stock weeks before holiday ad budgets are often final. The inventory plan made in summer sets the ceiling on fourth-quarter ad results, so it should be treated as the first ad decision of the season.

The FBA capacity and fees calendar for the 2026 holidays

Amazon posted its holiday readiness announcement on July 7, 2026, with fees unchanged from 2025 and deal submissions open from July 8, EcomCrew reported. Working backward from the events, the dates that matter are these:

DateWhat it decides
September 2Prime Big Deal Days inventory must reach Amazon Warehousing and Distribution
September 9Prime Big Deal Days cutoff for FBA with minimal shipment splits
September 16Prime Big Deal Days cutoff for FBA with Amazon-optimized splits
October 14Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday cutoff for Amazon Warehousing and Distribution
October 15Holiday peak fulfillment fees begin, running through January 14, 2027
October 21Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday cutoff for FBA with minimal splits
October 28Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday cutoff for FBA with Amazon-optimized splits
October 31Last day of the off-peak monthly storage rate for Amazon Warehousing and Distribution with automatic replenishment

Missing a cutoff removes the Prime badge from the product during the event window, EcomCrew noted. Capacity also tightens through the season: fulfillment centers shift from receiving inbound shipments to processing customer orders in November and December, so receiving times lengthen as the season progresses. The peak fees add an average of $0.32 per unit over non-peak rates, with a 3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge on top, according to EcomCrew.

Why stock sets the ceiling on what ads can sell

An ad sends a shopper to a product page. If the product is out of stock, the click is wasted. If the product lacks the Prime badge because its inventory arrived late, the shopper sees a weaker offer and is less likely to buy.

The damage outlasts the stockout. On Amazon, sales history shapes search ranking, so a product that runs out during a peak event loses the sales that would have supported its rank. Winning that rank back later costs more advertising.

Timing is what turns this into an advertising decision. Inbound cutoffs in September and October mean the inventory available for Black Friday is largely decided by late summer. Capacity limits mean a brand cannot simply send everything. It has to choose which products get space.

Holiday advertising budgets, meanwhile, are often set in September or October, after the stock is committed. By then the ad plan has to fit whatever inventory exists, rather than the other way around.

That is why the largest efficiency gain in fourth-quarter advertising may come from the warehouse plan, not from bids. A brand that puts its capacity behind the products its ads will push can spend with confidence. A brand that spreads capacity evenly may find its best ads pointing at empty shelves.

Take a home goods brand that splits its limited capacity evenly across the catalog and then concentrates holiday ads on five best sellers. Two of them run out during Black Friday week, and the ads keep spending on them until someone on the team notices. Reversing the order fixes it: rank products by expected ad investment first, give those products priority in the inventory plan and send backup stock to Amazon Warehousing and Distribution.

Holding more stock is not free. It costs money, especially at peak storage rates, and forecasts can be wrong. The cost of extra inventory has to be weighed against the cost of a stockout, product by product.

Planning inventory and ads as one decision

Start with the ad plan, not the warehouse. Decide early which products will carry holiday advertising, because those need the most reliable stock, and give the products with the most planned ad spend priority in limited FBA capacity.

Bulk storage can serve as the buffer. Sellers who enrolled in Amazon Warehousing and Distribution during the fourth quarter of 2025 saw more than 13% more shipped units and more than 30% fewer out-of-stock days, according to Amazon’s announcement as reported by EcomCrew. Timing matters there too: inventory sent through Amazon Warehousing and Distribution with automatic replenishment keeps the off-peak monthly storage rate through October 31, 2026, even though peak fees start October 15.

Build the calendar backward from September 16 and October 28 to set ordering and shipping dates, and put peak fees and surcharges into margins before setting deal prices and ad targets. Then connect the two systems directly: set rules that reduce or pause ads when a product’s stock falls below a set level, and restart them once new stock arrives. None of these steps needs a new tool. They need the people who own inventory and the people who own advertising in the same planning meeting, before the first September cutoff.

The test for any holiday plan is the order in which its decisions were made. Decide which products your ads will push before you decide where your inventory goes, which is how we plan Amazon advertising and inventory together.

A0947.title: Back-to-school 2026: what an earlier season does to planning
A0947.alt: School notebooks, colored pencils, and a canvas backpack on a wooden table beside a ceramic pitcher and retro fan.
A0947.ttag: Back-to-school 2026: what an earlier season does to planning | Kwontified
A0947.desc: Back-to-school 2026 began with the June sales events, and many families are still waiting for deals. Why brands should plan from June into the fall.
A0947.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 23, 2026.
A0947.body:
Back-to-school used to have a shape anyone in retail could sketch from memory: a quiet early summer, a rush through late July and August, then a drop once the first bell rang. In 2026 the rush began in June. By early July, 62% of consumers had already started their back-to-school shopping, the National Retail Federation said in its survey release, and more than half of those who had shopped used the June sales events to do it.

The season no longer peaks in August so much as slopes from June into the fall, with deal-waiters in the middle and budget-spreaders at the end. Brands still planning around one August spike should spread stock, deals and advertising across that whole stretch.

How back-to-school 2026 got its early start

The early start is not new, but it held. The 62% who had begun by early July compares with 67% at the same point in 2025 and 55% in 2024, according to the NRF. More telling is where they shopped: 54% of those who had started said they used major June sales events such as Prime Day, Walmart Deals and Target Circle Deal Days specifically for school-related purchases.

Adobe’s Prime Day results show the same pull from the retailer side. During Prime Day 2026, online purchases of kids’ apparel rose 140%, backpacks 115% and lunch boxes 105% compared with average daily sales in June.

Moving Prime Day into June brought school buying forward with it. Parents shopping deals on backpacks and kids’ clothes in late June were starting the season weeks earlier than a July event would have prompted. And because Walmart and Target ran their sales in the same week, the June window became a back-to-school moment across retailers rather than an Amazon one. For a merchandising team, that changes the order of work: the back-to-school assortment, the deal calendar and the advertising plan all have to be settled before Prime Day, not after it.

Record spending, spread thinly across each family

The totals are records. Families with students in elementary through high school expect to spend $43.3 billion, up from $39.4 billion in 2025, and college spending is expected to reach $103.5 billion, the NRF said.

Per family, the picture is steadier. Households with K-12 students plan to spend an average of $863.86, up slightly from $858.07 in 2025, including $250.29 on clothing and accessories, $174.01 on shoes and $146.45 on school supplies. Electronics were the top K-12 category, at an average planned spend of $293.11. The record total comes from modest gains spread across categories, not a surge in what each family spends.

College is the larger ticket. College shoppers plan to spend an average of $1,437.79, up from $1,325.85 in 2025 and above the previous record set in 2023. The NRF surveyed 7,677 consumers between July 1 and 8.

Why the season now runs into the fall

Two kinds of shopper stretch the calendar. Among those who had not yet bought at least half of their items, 46% said they were waiting for the best deals to finish, so demand continues through July and August instead of arriving all at once. Another 23% of unfinished shoppers said they were spreading their budgets, and many consumers were delaying purchases until later in the season, according to the NRF. That points to more school buying in late August, September and beyond.

The store aisle is also back in the picture. Only 50% of K-12 shoppers plan to buy items online, down from 55% in 2025, with department stores and discount stores among the leading destinations. A brand that sells through marketplaces and stores alike now has families comparing its price and availability in both places before they buy.

Take a stationery brand that used to concentrate its stock and advertising in late July and early August. In 2026 its backpack and notebook sales jump during the June events, and it runs short of best sellers by mid-July. Its fix is to plan three waves instead of one peak: June event deals, a steady presence through July and August, and replenishment-focused advertising in September.

Survey intentions do not always match behavior, and the share of early starters dipped slightly from 2025. The season may not stretch this far every year. Still, the evidence leans toward a longer season, and a plan built for one can be trimmed if the late weeks turn out quieter.

Planning the season in three waves

The first wave belongs to the June events, which now open back-to-school and need stock and deals ready before they start. The second runs through July and August: keep inventory steady between the June events and the final weeks before school, and plan a second round of offers for late July and August aimed at the shoppers who are waiting for deals. The third comes after school starts, when budget-spreaders are still buying and supplies and advertising should stay active.

Two groups need their own plans inside that frame. College shoppers spend more per student and may shop closer to move-in dates, so brands selling dorm and electronics products should plan a later peak for them. And with electronics the top K-12 category, brands there should plan for the largest demand of the season. Across all three waves, prices and availability need to match online and in stores, since families compare both.

So ask the team one thing before the next season: when does the company’s back-to-school budget start being spent, and does it still stop in August? Spreading that plan across Amazon, Walmart and Target from June into the fall is how we run seasonal marketplace plans for brands.

A0949.crumb: Walmart shopper vs Amazon shopper: one…
A0949.title: Walmart shopper vs Amazon shopper: one person, two habits
A0949.alt: A paper grocery bag of produce and bread beside a cardboard box on a wooden bench against a blue wall.
A0949.ttag: Walmart shopper vs Amazon shopper: one person, two habits | Kwontified
A0949.desc: Most Walmart+ members also pay for Prime, yet they use Walmart for grocery and essentials trips. Why brands should build a Walmart plan, not copy Amazon’s.
A0949.byline: By Elaine Kwon, Co-Founder and Managing Partner. Published Jul 30, 2026.
A0949.body:
The proposal tends to arrive as a shortcut. The Amazon plan works, Walmart is the next channel, and the fastest route is to carry the listings, the pack sizes and the advertising structure straight across. Whether to take that shortcut is a real decision for a leadership team. The case for it looks strong at first, because the two audiences overlap heavily: 83% of Walmart+ members also have an Amazon Prime membership, according to a Numerator study that EcommerceBytes reported.

The overlap is exactly why the shortcut fails. The same person shops Walmart for different trips, centered on grocery, household essentials and local delivery, and behaves like a different shopper on each platform. Walmart assortment, content and advertising should be built around those trips rather than copied from Amazon.

Walmart shopper vs Amazon shopper in the membership data

The profiles differ even where the people overlap. Walmart+ members tend to have lower incomes than Prime members and larger households with children. They live mainly in regions where Walmart has strong physical roots, while Prime members are spread evenly across regions, Chain Store Age reported, citing the same Numerator research.

What they buy at Walmart is the household basket. Walmart+ members spend 38% of their Walmart dollars on categories such as grocery, pet and baby, nearly twice the share of the average Walmart shopper. And 81% used Walmart’s grocery delivery in the past year, compared with 20% of all Walmart shoppers, according to Chain Store Age.

Membership also changes spending far more at Walmart than at Amazon, in Numerator’s figures:

Walmart+ membersPrime members
Spend compared with the retailer’s average shopper76% more (206% more at walmart.com)12% more
Share of their dollars spent at Walmart26%15%
Share of their dollars spent at Amazon12%13%

Walmart+ members also buy online in routine ways. They are more likely than Prime members to make weekly online purchases, buy in bulk online or use subscription and auto-replenishment services.

Grocery is where the split is starkest. In a PYMNTS Intelligence survey, 29.9% of consumers said their most recent grocery purchase was from Walmart, compared with 1.3% from Amazon, Supermarket News reported. Holding both memberships is common among younger adults: 37% of millennials in the survey said they belong to both. For a brand, that means the shopper scrolling its Amazon listing on a Tuesday evening may be the same one adding groceries to a Walmart pickup order on Saturday morning.

How two retailers trained one shopper

Each retailer built a habit. Amazon became the place for a wide range of items delivered to the door. Walmart built its strength on stores, groceries and everyday essentials, then extended that into pickup and delivery. The memberships reinforce the habits: Walmart+ members use theirs mainly for grocery delivery, while Prime members spread their spending across categories, so one household can hold both and give each a different job.

The trip decides what sells. A shopper on Walmart is often building a grocery and household order, and products that fit that basket, such as everyday consumables in practical pack sizes, have a natural place in it. Products bought on a separate, one-off trip may do better on Amazon. Geography adds to the difference, because Walmart’s members cluster where its store network is strong, and local delivery and pickup shape demand in ways Amazon’s national pattern does not.

Two forces are widening the Walmart trip, and both matter for brands deciding what to list there. Marketplace growth is one. Walmart’s US third-party marketplace expanded by nearly 50% in its first quarter as sellers widened the assortment, Marketplace Pulse reported, so shoppers can add items to an essentials order that they once bought only on Amazon.

The customer base is the other. Walmart reported share gains across categories and income groups in its first quarter of fiscal 2027, particularly among upper-income households, according to a results summary. As more affluent households shop Walmart, the gap between the two shoppers narrows in some categories, though the trip stays anchored in essentials.

Building the Walmart plan around the trip

Take a pet food brand that copies its Amazon listings and ad plan to Walmart, leading with large variety packs and premium positioning. Sales lag. When it adds smaller, everyday pack sizes, writes listings around routine feeding and advertises against grocery and household searches, its Walmart sales grow, while its Amazon plan stays as it was.

The leadership question, then, is not whether Walmart deserves its own plan but which trip that plan is built for. Start from the basket a Walmart shopper is building when they meet the product. Brands with repeat-purchase products should make them easy to reorder, given how readily Walmart+ members use auto-replenishment. Everyday pack sizes and practical price points suit grocery and household trips, listings can stress everyday value and reliability rather than discovery, and search ads should target the routine needs that bring shoppers to the platform. Because pickup and delivery shape Walmart demand, stock levels and fulfillment speed belong in the plan alongside the listing.

Two cautions keep the plan honest. Some of the membership research dates from 2024, and Walmart’s shopper base is changing quickly as it gains higher-income households. Brands should check current data in their own categories and test premium products on Walmart rather than assume they will not sell. And Walmart should be judged against its own benchmarks, not Amazon’s, since basket size, repeat rate and category mix differ.

When the Walmart plan next comes up for review, ask the team which trip it was built for. Answering that well is how we build Walmart programs around how its shoppers buy.
